cards.title: Post-Op Bleeding Workup
cards.quickAnswer: New or rising chest tube output + Hgb drop or hemodynamic change in post-op cardiac surgery patient → obtain vitals immediately, trend CT output hourly, send STAT CBC/INR/PTT/fibrinogen/Type & Cross, warm patient, notify APP + CT surgery fellow. Re-exploration trigger thresholds: >200 mL/hr ×1h, >100 mL/hr ×3h, >1500 mL total. CRITICAL: Sudden drop in CT output is NOT reassurance—suspect clotted tube + developing tamponade. Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol if instability develops. Coagulopathy response targets: fibrinogen ≥150 mg/dL, INR <1.5, platelets ≥100k with active bleeding.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, who gets it.

  • Definition: Bleeding after cardiac surgery, occurring across the CPB circuit interface, sternal edges, cannulation sites, and tissue planes. May manifest as chest tube (mediastinal / pleural) drainage, surgical site oozing, or occult pericardial / mediastinal accumulation.
  • Incidence: Clinically significant bleeding occurs in 20–40% of adult cardiac surgery; ~5–15% require re-exploration (Bojar, 2020). Most occurs within first 24 hours post-op.
  • Who this applies to: All post-op cardiac surgery patients (CABG, valve, aortic, complex), high-acuity units and step-down settings during first week.
  • Why it matters: Bleeding is a leading cause of cardiac surgery mortality and morbidity. Early recognition prevents tamponade, shock, and death. Delayed recognition or missed tamponade physiology is a common adverse event.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac-surgery bleeding is near-universal in some quantity and multifactorial, stemming from the unique hemostatic challenge of cardiopulmonary bypass:

Platelet dysfunction from CPB: Contact of blood with the pump circuit activates and depletes platelets within 30 minutes. Remaining platelets have impaired aggregation and adhesion, lasting 24–48 hours post-op (Bojar, 2020).

Residual heparin and heparin rebound: Protamine incompletely reverses heparin at closure; heparin redistributes from tissue stores 2–4 hours post-op, causing "heparin rebound" and renewed anticoagulation (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025).

Fibrinogen consumption: Major CPB runs consume fibrinogen below threshold (< 150 mg/dL) through activation of the coagulation cascade and fibrinolysis. Replacement with cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate is often needed.

Factor dilution and hypothermia: Pump prime and crystalloid boluses dilute clotting factors; every 1 °C below 36 °C slows enzymatic coagulation measurably (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).

Pre-op antiplatelets: Aspirin (5–7 day effect), clopidogrel, ticagrelor (7+ day effect) extend bleeding risk beyond the immediate post-op period. CABG frequently proceeds on dual antiplatelet therapy.

Acquired hemostatic defects: AVR in severe aortic stenosis can trigger acquired von Willebrand disease; VAD patients develop similar patterns. Correction occurs post-valve or VAD exchange.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-op cardiac surgery patient:

  • Chest tube output > 150 mL/h on single hourly check, especially if rising
  • Single-hour CT output exceeding re-exploration thresholds (see §5A, point 6)
  • Visible bleeding at sternotomy, chest tube site, harvest site, or cannulation sites
  • Hemoglobin drop ≥ 2 g/dL from baseline or between serial draws within 2–4 hours
  • New hypotension or tachycardia (HR > 110) in previously stable post-op patient
  • Pallor, anxiety, or "impending doom" — classic sympathetic tell of acute blood loss or late tamponade
  • Sudden drop in CT output to near-zero with NO improvement in clinical stability — paradoxical sign of clotted tube + pericardial fluid accumulation
  • Widening mediastinum on morning chest X-ray
  • Rising central venous pressure (if line present) paired with falling systolic BP

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs: HR, BP (systolic and pulse pressure), SpO₂, RR, mental status, perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature, color)
  • Work of breathing: respiratory effort, air hunger (suggestive of tamponade)
  • CT output trend: review last 4–8 hourly values, not just current hour; note color (bright red = active; dark = older; clots present = higher tamponade risk)
  • CT patency: examine tubing for dependent loops; water seal integrity; observe for air leak bubbles
  • Incision inspection: sternotomy, drain sites, harvest sites — oozing, saturation of dressing, hematoma size
  • Recent labs: baseline hemoglobin, trend over last 2–4 hours; INR, PTT, platelets, fibrinogen if available; iCa²⁺
  • Medication review (MAR): home antiplatelets (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor); any therapeutic anticoagulation; recent protamine dose and timing
  • Lines / IV access: number and gauge of peripheral IVs; central line present; prior transfusion this admission
  • Surgery context: procedure type (CABG, valve, aortic), ECC time, redo sternotomy (higher bleed risk), bilateral internal mammary harvest (more sternal ooze), radial harvest

sections.heading: 5A. Stable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP > 65, no chest pain or dyspnea, HR < 110, mental status baseline, cap refill < 2 sec)

  1. Recheck VS at 5 minutes — confirm trend; avoid isolated data points triggering false alarm
  2. Establish CT patency — inspect for dependent loops, hand-milk (per [Institution policy] if permitted; avoid aggressive stripping due to tissue trauma risk), reposition tubing to gravity
  3. Send STAT labs: CBC, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, Type & Cross (2–4 units), iCa²⁺, VBG or ABG with lactate
  4. Ensure adequate IV access — minimum two large-bore (18G+); if only one present, start second; flag for possible central line if output trend worsens
  5. Aggressive rewarming — room temperature to 75 °F, warm blankets, Bair Hugger if available. Target core ≥ 36.0 °C. Hypothermia worsens coagulopathy exponentially (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).
  6. Check re-exploration thresholds — apply local institutional policy or use evidence-based triggers:
    • >200 mL/hr ×1h → discuss with CT surgery
    • >100 mL/hr ×3h → escalate
    • >1500 mL cumulative → escalate
    • Sudden drop to near-zero + any hemodynamic change → suspect tamponade; do NOT relax vigilance
    • Notify APP + CT surgery fellow directly — bleeding is a CT surgery problem, not a floor provider decision
    • Optimize pain / sedation — uncontrolled pain drives hypertension and bleeding; hold NSAIDs absolutely
    • Address modifiable coagulopathy (under provider orders):
    • Ionized Ca²⁺ ≥ 1.1 (citrate from transfusion drops iCa²⁺; check with each 2 units blood)
    • Fibrinogen ≥ 150 mg/dL → transfuse cryoprecipitate (10-unit pool) or fibrinogen concentrate if available
    • Platelets < 100k + active bleeding → transfuse 1 apheresis unit (single-donor equivalent to 6-pack)
    • Platelets < 50k → transfuse regardless of bleeding (prophylactic threshold post-CPB)
    • INR > 1.5 + active bleeding → FFP 10–15 mL/kg (transient effect; recheck INR)
    • Consider protamine re-dose (25–50 mg slow IV) if heparin rebound suspected (check ACT or aPTT at 2–4h post-op)
    • Document comprehensively: every CT output value (time-stamped), VS trend, lab results, interventions, team communication with exact time and name of provider contacted

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension SBP < 90 or MAP < 65, tachycardia > 110, altered mental status, pallor, air hunger, acute JVD, narrowing pulse pressure, or sudden hemodynamic change)

  1. STAT call CT surgery fellow + APP + charge RN + blood bank — do NOT leave bedside alone
  2. Activate Rapid Response / Code team if not already present
  3. Ensure airway and large-bore IV access — minimum two 18G peripheral lines; place intraosseous if peripheral fails emergently
  4. Position: HOB per tolerance (flat if profoundly hypotensive; upright if air hunger dominates)
  5. Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) per [Institution policy] if any criterion met:
    • Hemoglobin drop with hemodynamic instability
    • CT output > 500 mL in a single hour
    • Anticipated ongoing surgical bleeding
    • 4+ units already transfused with continued instability
    • Send STAT: full coagulation panel + CBC + Type & Cross + iCa²⁺ + ABG + lactate; repeat every 30–60 min during active bleed
    • Aggressive rewarming — warm IV fluids and blood via fluid warmer; active external warming (Bair Hugger); room temperature up
    • If tamponade suspected (narrowing pulse pressure, rising CVP, muffled heart sounds, sudden CT output drop without bleeding improvement, paradoxical hypotension):
    • STAT CT surgery attending notification
      • Prepare for Emergent Bedside Sternotomy (→ Emergent Bedside Sternotomy — Tamponade scenario card)
      • Bedside echocardiography in parallel — confirm fluid around heart, septal bowing, RV collapse
      • Have backup oxygenation ready (prepare for crash intubation if altered mental status worsens)
      • Prepare for OR return — NPO status, final Type & Cross, consent discussion if time permits, notify OR team via CT surgery chief resident
      • Intensive documentation: rhythm strip / cardiac monitor recording at event, CT drainage strip printout, lab values with timestamps, medication administration records, team communication log. These records guide M&M and are critical for both quality improvement and medicolegal protection.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure], with significant chest tube bleeding." B: "CT output has been [current hour value] mL this last hour. Prior 4 hours: [values]. BP [current / trend], HR [value], SpO₂ [value]. Most recent Hgb [value] drawn at [time], prior Hgb [value] at [prior time]. Current INR [value], platelets [value], fibrinogen [value]. I've sent STAT repeat labs." A: "Patient is currently [stable / unstable / deteriorating]. [Describe symptoms: chest pain, dyspnea, anxiety, dizziness.] On [home antiplatelets / heparin / none]. Transfusion history: [X units RBC / platelets / FFP received so far]." R: "Requesting [T&C for 2 units / mass transfusion protocol activation / bedside echo / consideration for OR re-exploration / immediate evaluation]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Rising but sub-threshold CT output, stable VS APP + CT surgery fellow
Meets re-exploration thresholds OR cumulative >1500 mL CT surgery attending + fellow + RRT standby
Hemodynamic instability with ongoing bleeding RRT/code team + CT surgery STAT + blood bank (activate MTP)
Suspected tamponade (sudden CT drop + instability, narrowing pulse pressure, JVD, muffled heart sounds) CT surgery attending STAT + prepare bedside sternotomy
Suspected HIT (platelet drop ≥50% at POD 5–10, new thrombosis) CT surgery + hematology; stop all heparin immediately
Transfusion reaction (fever, chills, hemoglobinuria, hemodynamic change mid-transfusion) Blood bank + APP immediately; stop transfusion

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Coagulopathy after CPB — diagnostic and management approach
sections.bodyHtml:
The five-point workup (adapted from Hardin & Kaplow, 2020):

  1. Platelet count and function — CPB causes platelet depletion and dysfunction lasting 24–48h. Goal ≥ 100k if bleeding, ≥ 50k routine post-CPB.
  2. Fibrinogen level — normal 200–400 mg/dL; < 100 is severe and always needs replacement. 100–150 is marginal (replace if bleeding). Goal ≥ 150 mg/dL.
  3. Prothrombin time (PT/INR) — reflects factors II, V, VII, X (vitamin K–dependent factors diluted by pump prime). Elevated INR (> 1.5) with bleeding requires FFP or PCC.
  4. Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) — reflects factors in the contact pathway and factors V, VIII, IX, X, XII. Elevated aPTT suggests residual heparin or factor deficiency.
  5. Thrombin time (TT) or heparin assay — if aPTT elevated out of proportion, check for circulating heparin (direct test for heparin rebound).

When to escalate to advanced testing: - Thromboelastography (TEG) or rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) — point-of-care test showing platelet function, clot strength, fibrinolysis in real-time. Increasingly standard in cardiac surgery ICUs; available in some step-down units. Guides faster decision-making than waiting for traditional labs.

Heparin rebound — the 2–4 hour phenomenon:

  • Heparin is incompletely reversed by protamine at closure (protamine:heparin ratio varies; excess protamine can paradoxically worsen bleeding).
  • At 2–4 hours post-op, heparin re-equilibrates from tissue stores, raising ACT/aPTT.
  • Classic sign: initially good hemostasis, then CT output rises again at 2–4h; aPTT rises.
  • Re-dose protamine (25–50 mg slow IV, watching for anaphylaxis or pulmonary hypertension) or continue observation if asymptomatic.

Factor replacement targets (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025; always confirm with provider):

  • Fibrinogen < 150 mg/dL → cryoprecipitate 10-unit pool OR fibrinogen concentrate (2–4 g if available)
  • INR > 1.5 + bleeding → FFP 10–15 mL/kg (transient; re-check) OR PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate) if warfarin-related
  • PT > 16 s without response to FFP → suspect factor V deficiency (FFP replacement is the only therapy)
  • Platelet count < 100k + bleeding → transfuse 1 apheresis unit

sections.heading: 7.2 Surgical vs. coagulopathic bleeding differentiation
sections.bodyHtml:
Surgical bleeding (anatomic source, bright red, localized):

  • Identified bleeding source at sternotomy, anastomosis, cannulation site, or tissue plane
  • Brisk, red bleeding; clots present in chest tube
  • High CT output early (POD 0–6 hours)
  • Lab values initially normal (problem is anatomy, not coagulation)
  • Management: CT surgery re-exploration and hemostasis
  • Nursing role: notify surgeon early; prepare for OR

Coagulopathic bleeding (diffuse ooze, dark blood, distributed across multiple sites):

  • No single identifiable anatomic source
  • Slow, continuous dark ooze; small clots or no clots
  • Occurs at any time post-op (can be late, at POD 5+)
  • Lab abnormalities: ↓ fibrinogen, ↑ INR/PTT, ↓ platelets, ↑ lactate
  • Management: lab correction (fibrinogen, factors, platelets, calcium), rewarming, correct rate control
  • Nursing role: STAT labs, product transfusion per protocol, optimize rewarming

Reality: most post-op bleeding is mixed — some surgical ooze + some coagulopathy. Both may need intervention.

sections.heading: 7.3 Protamine and heparin rebound — mechanism and clinical pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
Protamine mechanism:

  • Protamine is a positively charged polypeptide that forms an irreversible complex with negatively charged heparin.
  • Dosed at ~1 mg per 100 units of heparin (adjusted by ACT at end of CPB).
  • Incomplete reversal at closure is common; heparin later re-equilibrates from tissue and fat (heparin rebound).
  • Protamine itself is a platelet inhibitor and can trigger anaphylaxis in NPH insulin users.

Heparin rebound timing and detection:

  • Occurs 2–4 hours post-op, sometimes as late as 6h.
  • Suspect if: ↑ CT output in the late early post-op period (2–4h) after initial hemostasis, elevated aPTT, or ACT > 180 if re-checked.
  • Do NOT routinely re-check ACT post-op (not standard); rely on clinical judgment + aPTT.
  • Re-dosing protamine: 25–50 mg slow IV over 10 minutes, watching for anaphylaxis (risk higher in NPH insulin users, fish allergy, or prior protamine exposure). Risk of protamine-induced pulmonary hypertension (rare but serious).

When to consider protamine re-dose:

  • Confirmed aPTT elevation (> 45–50s) with rising CT output at 2–4h post-op
  • Continued oozing despite fibrinogen/platelet/factor correction

sections.heading: 7.4 Special populations and subgroups
sections.bodyHtml:
Redo sternotomy patients:

  • Adhesion vasculature at the sternum is extremely fragile; increased bleeding by default.
  • Re-exploration threshold may be lower (discuss with surgeon) — a lower CT output may warrant earlier re-exploration.

BIMA (bilateral internal mammary artery) harvest:

  • Increases sternal oozing and mediastinitis risk.
  • Sternal blood supply is compromised; expect higher CT output first 24–48h.
  • Monitor for sternal wound complications (drainage, cellulitis) downstream.

Off-pump CABG (OPCAB):

  • Avoids CPB-related platelet dysfunction and heparin rebound; expect less postop bleeding overall.
  • Heparin reversal is still needed (same protamine dosing); still risk of heparin rebound.

Chronic anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC):

  • Home AC is held 3–5 days pre-op; timing of restart post-op is surgeon-dependent.
  • INR elevation from underlying coagulopathy may persist despite FFP; check INR response.
  • If INR critically elevated post-op (> 3) + bleeding, PCC (not FFP) is preferred for faster reversal.

Renal failure / dialysis patients:

  • Uremia impairs platelet function; transfuse platelets empirically even if count > 50k.
  • Cryoprecipitate may be more rapidly consumed.
  • Bleeding risk extends longer post-op.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate immediately.

  • CT output trending up hour-over-hour — even if each single hour is under threshold, cumulative risk rises; escalate at ~1000–1500 mL total
  • Hemoglobin drop across serial draws — 2 g/dL drop over 6–8 hours without explanation; Hgb is a late marker in acute bleeding
  • Rising lactate — suggests inadequate tissue perfusion even if BP looks "okay"; early sign of decompensation
  • Narrowing pulse pressure (widened diastolic narrowing) — classic sign of tamponade or hypovolemia; stroke volume is falling
  • Patient reports sudden anxiety, dread, or "doom" — pre-hemorrhagic sympathetic surge; subconscious recognition of inadequate perfusion
  • Sudden drop in CT output after steady hourly amount — NOT reassurance; often indicates clotted tube with fluid accumulating elsewhere (pericardium, pleural space)
  • Widening mediastinum on repeat CXR — radiographic sign of mediastinal bleeding or tamponade
  • Tachycardia creeping up within "normal" range — HR 78 → 90 → 102 is a red flag; trajectory matters more than absolute value
  • Increasing work of breathing — early tamponade or hemothorax physiology
  • Rising central venous pressure (if line present) on values that had been stable — preload problem or tamponade
  • Capillary refill lengthening, extremities cool — centralized perfusion compensation for low cardiac output
  • Dressing progressively more saturated with blood — quantify the soak; flag for possible infection risk later
  • Platelet drop ≥ 50% from baseline at POD 5–10 — think HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) even if not grossly bleeding; risk of paradoxical thrombosis
  • Oozing at IV sites, gum bleeding, ecchymoses spreading — systemic coagulopathy signal, not just surgical ooze

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Sudden drop in CT output is NOT reassurance. It signals a clotted tube with fluid trapped elsewhere (pericardium, mediastinum). Always pair CT output changes with a full vital-sign check; don't relax vigilance.

  2. Hemoglobin lags behind real blood loss. In acute hemorrhage, Hgb equilibrates late because intravascular volume hasn't redistributed. Trust vital signs and CT output trend over Hgb; use Hgb as a confirmatory marker, not a primary trigger.

  3. Protamine rebound occurs at 2–4 hours post-op. Many units miss this because they don't re-check ACT or aPTT routinely. If CT output rises at 2–4h after initial hemostasis, re-check aPTT or flag for clinical assessment.

  4. Warm the patient aggressively. Coagulopathy is exponentially temperature-dependent. Room temp to 75 °F, Bair Hugger, warm blankets. A patient at 35.3 °C will bleed; bring them to ≥ 36.0 °C. Recheck labs after rewarming (may improve without transfusion).

  5. Do NOT give NSAIDs in bleeding post-op patients. Ever. NSAIDs impair platelet function and mask pain, leading to continued upregulation of sympathetic tone and bleeding.

  6. Don't dismiss an anxious post-op patient. Pre-hemorrhagic anxiety is a real entity; sympathetic surge precedes hemodynamic collapse. An alert, nervous patient may be your only warning.

  7. Platelets < 100k + recent antiplatelet therapy + active bleeding warrant transfusion even though "routine" trigger is < 50k. Context (surgery type, drugs, bleeding risk) overrides algorithm.

  8. Pre-op clopidogrel and ticagrelor bleed for 5–7 days post-op. ASA-only continues at baseline risk. Newer P2Y12 inhibitors are higher bleeding risk than ASA; document the discharge timeline clearly.

  9. Fibrinogen < 150 mg/dL is a critical result post-CPB. Cryoprecipitate (10-unit pool) or fibrinogen concentrate is the fastest replacement. FFP takes a huge volume. Prioritize cryo or fibrinogen concentrate.

  10. Heparin rebound is real and you can catch it. At 2–4h, if CT output rises and the surgeon says "looks good," check aPTT. Abnormal aPTT + rising CT at 2–4h = protamine re-dose discussion with the team.

  11. CT stripping is controversial. Some units permit gentle hand-milking per protocol; others avoid it due to tissue trauma. Know your unit's policy. Many studies show aggressive stripping worsens outcomes.

  12. Check ionized calcium with every 2 units of blood. Citrate in stored blood drops iCa²⁺; this impairs contractility AND coagulation. Calcium supplementation (usually CaCl₂ or gluconate) is under-ordered but often needed.

  13. Pulse oximetry drops LATE. Don't wait for a saturation signal; look at every other vital sign first. BP, HR, mental status, cap refill, lactate, and urine output all precede SpO₂ in acute bleeding.

  14. The chart is a legal document AND a teaching tool. Time-stamp every CT output, vital sign, intervention, and team communication. M&M, quality reviews, and sometimes depositions depend on your notes. Vague notes hurt the team later.

  15. When in doubt, escalate. There is NO penalty for a stable patient after a call. The penalty for a delayed call is measured in units of blood and potentially in lives. Call early; let the team decide it's not urgent.

cards.title: Pre-Op Optimization Admission
cards.quickAnswer: Cardiac surgery patient admitted 1–3 days pre-op for final work-up completion, cardiac and non-cardiac optimization, and baseline establishment. Risk stratify with STS/EuroSCORE II and assess frailty (Rockwood CFS); optimize HF medications (GDMT for HFrEF, rhythm control), coronary (revascularization decisions), renal function, pulmonary status, nutrition (albumin ≥3.5, target HbA1c <8%), dental clearance, smoking cessation (even 24–48 h improves outcomes); manage anticoagulation transition; confirm medications (continue β-blocker, statin; hold SGLT2i 3–5d, DOAC per renal function, P2Y12i 5–7d); document informed consent and family meeting. Discharge directly to operating room.

Risk stratify with STS/EuroSCORE II and assess frailty (Rockwood CFS); optimize HF medications (GDMT for HFrEF, rhythm control), coronary (revascularization decisions), renal function, pulmonary status, nutrition (albumin ≥3.5, target HbA1c <8%), dental clearance, smoking cessation (even 24–48 h improves outcomes); manage anticoagulation transition; confirm medications (continue β-blocker, statin; hold SGLT2i 3–5d, DOAC per renal function, P2Y12i 5–7d); document informed consent and family meeting. Discharge directly to operating room.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → STS/EuroSCORE Risk Stratification (2018) → 2024 ERAS Cardiac Surgery Guidelines → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Bojar (2020) → AHA/ACC Perioperative Guidelines (2007/2014) → AACN Critical Care Standards

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — who this patient is and why they are admitted.

  • Definition: Elective admission for a patient scheduled to undergo cardiac surgery (CABG, valve replacement, aortic repair, MAZE, combined procedures) within 1–3 days.
  • Trigger for admission: Completion of outstanding pre-operative imaging (CTA, MRI, repeat catheterization); anticoagulation bridging; final medical optimization; functional baseline assessment; informed consent review and family meeting.
  • Who this applies to: Adult patients referred for elective cardiac surgery by outpatient cardiology or primary care, stable on medical regimen, arriving with confirmed surgical date and initial pre-operative workup already underway in clinic.
  • Why it matters: Comprehensive pre-operative optimization (risk stratification, cardiac and non-cardiac optimization, medication management, functional assessment) directly reduces perioperative morbidity, mortality, length of stay, and post-operative complications (Bojar, 2020; ERAS Cardiac, 2024).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why pre-operative optimization matters.

Elective cardiac surgery carries measurable perioperative risk stratified by patient variables, comorbidities, and surgical complexity. Comprehensive pre-operative assessment serves three goals:

  1. Risk stratification: Quantify perioperative risk using validated tools (STS Risk Calculator, EuroSCORE II) to identify high-risk patients who benefit from intensified optimization, discuss realistic expectations with patient/family, and enable shared decision-making.

  2. Modifiable risk reduction: Optimize cardiac function (HF medications, revascularization decisions, rhythm control), correct non-cardiac contributors (glycemia, renal function, nutrition, anemia, pulmonary status), address behavioral factors (smoking cessation, alcohol screening), and ensure anticoagulation bridging—each intervention reduces complications independently.

  3. Baseline and consent: Establish functional baseline (frailty, mobility, strength), document informed consent with realistic discussion of risks/benefits/alternatives, engage family in post-operative expectations, and enable early post-operative rehabilitation planning.

Frailty (assessed by Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale) is not captured by surgical risk calculators but independently predicts ICU delirium, infection, prolonged recovery, and discharge disposition. Nutritional status (albumin, prealbumin) predicts wound healing and infection risk. Glycemic control (HbA1c <8%) and smoking cessation (>4 weeks ideal; even 24–48 h improves outcomes) reduce surgical site infections and pulmonary complications.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
What triggers pre-operative admission and typical patient presentation.

  • Scheduled surgery date confirmed by cardiothoracic surgeon; time assigned by OR scheduler
  • Interim changes since clinic evaluation — new symptoms (chest pain, dyspnea, syncope), medication changes, recent illness, dental work, substance use changes
  • Pre-operative workup partially or fully complete in outpatient clinic; admission finalizes outstanding imaging, confirmatory testing, or anticoagulation planning
  • Social/logistic factors — patient traveling from out of state, family visiting, need for extended pre-operative teaching or substance withdrawal screening
  • Complex comorbidities — advanced age, significant frailty, multiple prior surgeries, renal disease, diabetes, COPD requiring intensive pre-operative optimization

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / Gather Information*
sections.bodyHtml: Pure information-gathering. Competent systematic bedside and chart review. Target: first 2 hours.

sections.heading: Initial evaluation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Vital signs: Baseline BP, HR, temp, SpO₂, respiratory rate; compare to outpatient baseline if available
  • Interim history since clinic: new chest pain, dyspnea, orthopnea, leg edema, syncope/presyncope, fever, recent illness, medication changes, substance use
  • Review pre-operative workup:
  • Current cardiac imaging (echo, CTA, MRI, catheterization); any new findings?
  • Current labs: CBC, CMP, PT/INR, aPTT, HbA1c, albumin, prealbumin; abnormalities flagged
  • EKG: baseline, any new ischemic changes or rhythm?
  • Risk calculator scores: STS score, EuroSCORE II calculated; results in chart
  • Medication reconciliation: Home medications vs. hospital medications; discrepancies resolved
  • Anticoagulation status: If on warfarin, DOAC, or antiplatelet agents, document current regimen and transition plan (heparin bridge, hold timing)
  • Frailty assessment: Ask about falls, exhaustion, weight loss, gait changes; document physical appearance (robust vs. frail); arrange PT/OT functional baseline

sections.heading: Systematic assessment (by system)
sections.bodyHtml:
System Assess
Cardiac Orthopnea, PND, leg edema, chest pain character/timing; auscultate for murmur, crackles, S3; assess JVD; extremity perfusion
Pulmonary Dyspnea at rest vs. exertion; cough, sputum; respiratory rate; crackles on exam
Renal Recent Cr/GFR; urine output baseline; edema; medication dosing per renal function
Metabolic HbA1c, recent fasting glucose; insulin use, hypoglycemia history; diet pattern
Nutritional Recent weight loss, appetite, albumin/prealbumin levels; ability to swallow; dentures/teeth status
Neurologic Baseline mental status, memory, language; focal weakness; prior stroke/TIA
Vascular Carotid bruits (auscultate), peripheral pulses, absence of femoral/pedal pulses (amputation); claudication history
Infectious Fever, recent infections, dental disease, active wounds; immunization status (flu, pneumococcal)
Psychosocial Anxiety level, depression screening, substance use (alcohol, tobacco, drugs), social support, living situation

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: No Stable/Unstable fork for medical-admit cards. Management sections address the four pillars of pre-operative optimization.

sections.heading: 5A. Risk Stratification and Baseline Assessment
sections.bodyHtml:
STS Risk Calculator (Society of Thoracic Surgeons)

Variable What to gather Perioperative risk associated with
Age, sex, BMI Baseline demographics Older age + female sex increases mortality and morbidity risk
EF, prior cardiac surgery, NYHA Cardiac function and history Reduced EF, NYHA IV significantly increase mortality
Renal function (Cr Cl), diabetes, COPD Comorbidities CKD >60% increase mortality; insulin diabetes increases infection risk
CVA/stroke history, carotid disease Neurologic risk Prior stroke/TIA, severe carotid stenosis increase perioperative stroke risk
Hemodynamic stability, inotrope use Acuity Unstable patients need ICU-level prep

EuroSCORE II (European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation)

Similar variables to STS; easier calculation (web calculator); useful for international comparison and shared decision-making with European literature.

Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS)

Essential complement to surgical risk calculators. 1–7 scale:

  • CFS 1–2 (Very fit to well): low frailty risk
  • CFS 3–4 (Managing well to vulnerable): intermediate frailty; consider PT/OT prep
  • CFS 5–7 (Mildly frail to terminally ill): high frailty risk; realistic discussion with patient/family; consider SNF post-op, intensive PT

NYHA Functional Class (baseline, pre-op)

Class Definition Risk
I No symptoms with ordinary activity Low
II Symptoms with ordinary activity; asymptomatic at rest Moderate
III Symptoms with minimal activity; asymptomatic at rest Moderate-high
IV Symptoms at rest High

LVEF and HF phenotype

  • HFrEF (EF ≤40%): requires GDMT optimization pre-op
  • HFmrEF (EF 41–49%): assess for optimization
  • HFpEF (EF ≥50%): focus on rate control, diuretics for volume, pulmonary optimization

Document in chart: STS score + mortality/morbidity percentile, EuroSCORE II, CFS level, NYHA class, current EF, Cr Cl, baseline albumin/prealbumin, HbA1c. Share with patient/family and team.

sections.heading: 5B. Cardiac Optimization
sections.bodyHtml:
Heart Failure Management (GDMT)

Category Agent Goal pre-op Hold/Continue
ACE-I/ARB Lisinopril, valsartan, etc. Continue for cardioprotection Continue OR hold AM surgery per surgeon/anesthesia
Beta-blocker Metoprolol, carvedilol, bisoprolol Continue (perioperative β-blockade reduces MI) CONTINUE through pre-op; give with small sip of water AM surgery
MRA Spironolactone, eplerenone Continue Continue OR hold AM surgery
ARNI Sacubitril/valsartan Continue Continue OR hold AM surgery
SGLT2 inhibitor Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin HOLD 3–5 days pre-op (euglycemic DKA risk) HOLD — reinitiate post-op after glycemia stable
Statin Atorvastatin, simvastatin CONTINUE (perioperative statin reduces MI) CONTINUE; give AM surgery with small sip

Rhythm Control

  • If on amiodarone: continue through pre-op (takes weeks to wash, hold only if QTc prolonged)
  • If on other antiarrhythmics: clarify with surgeon/cardiology (some held pre-op)
  • If new/recent AF: rate control + consider rhythm control strategy with cardiology pre-op

Revascularization Decisions

  • Assess unrevascularized coronaries (if recent cath): is CABG indicated, or is percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) an option? Involve cardiothoracic surgeon + cardiology if debate exists
  • If PCI done recently (<12 mo): dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) timing is critical; coordinate with cardiology and surgeon

sections.heading: 5C. Non-Cardiac Optimization
sections.bodyHtml:
Glycemic Control

Target Evidence Action
HbA1c <8% AACM standard; HbA1c >8.5 correlates with infection, delayed healing Verify HbA1c; if >8.5, consider delaying elective surgery 4–6 weeks for intensive insulin optimization (0.5–1.0 reduction possible in 2–3 weeks)
Fasting glucose 120–180 mg/dL Perioperative target Continue home insulin; adjust regimen pre-op for slightly higher targets (avoid hypoglycemia)
Endocrinology consult if HbA1c >9 or brittle control Complex insulin regimens Secure insulin specialist input pre-op

Dental Assessment and Clearance

Finding Action Timing
Caries, plaque, gingivitis Routine cleaning, possible fillings Complete ≥24–48 h pre-op if possible
Abscess, periapical infection, loose teeth Extraction or root canal per dentistry Complete ≥24–48 h pre-op if possible; less than 24 h = infection risk
Valve surgery planned Prophylactic antibiotics peri-operatively Penicillin V or amoxicillin cover dental work; IV cefazolin ± gentamicin ± vancomycin peri-op if valve surgery
No dental work needed Clearance letter from dentistry File in chart

Nutrition and Albumin Status

Lab Normal Action if low
Albumin ≥3.5 g/dL <3.5 = mild malnutrition; <3.0 = significant risk for infection, delayed healing. Dietitian consult, high-protein diet (1.5 g/kg/day), consider appetite stimulant (dronabinol, megestrol)
Prealbumin 20–40 mg/dL <20 = inadequate visceral protein. Target 1.5 g/kg/day protein, supplemental nutrition if swallowing safe
Weight trend Stable Recent unintentional loss >10 lbs in 3 mo = nutritional risk flag; intensify pre-op nutrition

Smoking Cessation

  • Ideal: quit ≥4 weeks pre-op (ciliary recovery, reduced infection, reduced MI risk)
  • Acceptable: quit ≥24–48 h pre-op (still significant benefit; do NOT delay surgery for cessation)
  • Pharmacotherapy: Nicotine patches (full dose safe pre-op), gum, lozenge, or varenicline (stop 2 weeks pre-op due to nausea risk)
  • Counseling: Involve social work, smoking cessation specialist, or chaplain; discuss post-op benefits (faster healing, easier breathing, less infection)

Anemia Correction

Hemoglobin Pre-op target Action
Hgb <7 g/dL Transfuse to 8–9 (especially elderly, planned large blood loss) IV iron (works faster than PO), rule out bleeding source, screen for hemolysis
Hgb 7–8 g/dL Often transfuse if high-risk surgery Individualize based on age, comorbidities, anticipated blood loss
Hgb >8 g/dL Acceptable No routine transfusion; correct underlying cause if anemia new

Renal Optimization

Creatinine Clearance Implication Action
>60 mL/min Normal Standard pre-op prep
30–60 mL/min Stage 3 CKD Adjust drug dosing (DOAC, aminoglycosides, contrast). Monitor post-op. ACE-I/ARB continue.
<30 mL/min Stage 4 CKD or dialysis Cardiology + nephrology input. DOAC timing adjusted. ACE-I/ARB may hold AM surgery. Diuretics carefully titrated.

Pulmonary Optimization

  • Baseline pulmonary function: dyspnea grade, COPD exacerbations, sleep apnea (OSA)
  • Pulmonary rehab referral if COPD or significant dyspnea; teach incentive spirometry pre-op (reduces post-op pneumonia)
  • Bronchodilators continue pre-op
  • Sleep apnea: inform anesthesia; consider positive airway pressure (PAP) machine at home if applicable

sections.heading: 5D. Anesthesia Planning and Medication Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Informed Consent Review

Element Document
Procedure, alternative approaches "Discussed CABG vs. PCI" or "AVR with native tissue vs. mechanical valve"
Risks: bleeding, infection, stroke, MI, need for re-operation, death Patient verbalizes understanding; family present if possible
Benefits: symptom relief, improved survival, quality of life Realistic expectations set
Patient questions answered Time spent, clarity assessed

Medications to Hold

Drug Hold interval Rationale
SGLT2 inhibitors 3–5 days pre-op Euglycemic DKA risk; metabolic acidosis obscured
DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban) 24–48 h pre-op (renal-adjusted: Cr Cl <30 may need longer) Bleeding risk; renal clearance variable
Clopidogrel (Plavix) 5–7 days pre-op Platelet function recovery; exception: recent stent (<12 mo) = cardiology + surgeon discussion
Ticagrelor (Brilinta) 3–5 days pre-op Faster reversibility than clopidogrel; confirm with cardiology if recent stent
Prasugrel (Effient) 7 days pre-op Longest washout; confirm with cardiology
Diuretics Hold morning of surgery Avoid hypovolemia intra-op
ACE-I/ARB Hold AM surgery OR continue per surgeon/anesthesia Team-dependent; discuss with anesthesia

Medications to Continue

Drug Dose AM of surgery Rationale
Beta-blocker Home dose CONTINUE with small sip of water Perioperative β-blockade reduces cardiac events
Statin Home dose CONTINUE with small sip of water Perioperative statin reduces MI risk
Antiarrhythmic (amiodarone, sotalol) Home dose CONTINUE (takes weeks to wash) Avoid withdrawal arrhythmias
Home antithyroid, endocrine, neurologic meds Confirm with anesthesia Individualized Avoid withdrawal syndromes

Anticoagulation Bridging Plan (if applicable)

Scenario Bridge agent Goal aPTT Timing to stop
Warfarin (mechanical valve, AF) → hold for surgery IV unfractionated heparin 50–70 (non-cardiac); some surgeons: 40–60 4–6 h pre-op per surgeon/anesthesia
DOAC → hold for surgery LMWH or UFH bridge if high thromboembolic risk 50–70 Per bridging protocol
Bridge back post-op UFH SC or restart warfarin/DOAC Post-op per surgeon; heparin often started evening of surgery Surgeon-specific protocol

Pre-operative Workup Checklist

Item Target Interval
Labs CBC, CMP, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, type & screen, HbA1c, albumin, prealbumin, troponin baseline Within 7–24 h of surgery
Imaging CTA, MRI, cath report reviewed and filed Results in chart; communicated to surgeon
EKG Baseline; compare to prior On file
Chest X-ray Baseline; rule out acute pathology On file
Physical exam Airway assessment, cardiac exam, neuro baseline Documented by anesthesia
NPO status Patient and family understand NPO time (usually midnight) Verbal + written instructions
Type & screen ABO/Rh confirmed; alloimmunization flagged Communicated to blood bank
Medication list Hold vs. continue finalized Patient education on changes
Consent Signed by patient, surgeon, anesthesia Both risks and realistic expectations documented
Family meeting Expectations, post-op ICU course, discharge planning Chaplain/social work present if needed

Pre-operative Teaching & Baseline Assessment (PT/OT)

  • Incentive spirometry: Teach pre-op; goal 80% of predicted; practice daily
  • Gait, balance, strength baseline: PT/OT assess; identify fall risk; post-op rehab intensity planned
  • Pain management expectations: "You'll have discomfort, not severe pain. We use multiple medicines."
  • Early mobilization: "Walking in the ICU starting post-op day 1 is critical for recovery; we'll support you."
  • Sternal precautions: (if sternotomy planned) "No lifting >10 lbs for 6–8 weeks; log rolling for position changes."
  • Cough and deep breathing: Teach effective technique; practice q2h.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], admitted [date] for pre-op optimization s/p [procedure planned]." B: "Patient is [stable/unstable]. [Current vital signs, oxygen saturation]. [Notable labs: HbA1c, albumin, Cr, INR]. [Relevant history: prior cardiac events, renal disease, frailty level]." A: "[New symptom or concern: chest pain, dyspnea, fever, infection sign, medication issue, imaging finding]. [Exam findings]. [Timeline]." R: "Requesting [imaging review / medication adjustment / specialist consult / delay surgery discussion / other intervention]."

Who to Call

Situation Contact
Decompensated HF (new dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles) Primary cardiologist → CT surgeon
Unstable angina (chest pain at rest, ST changes) Cardiology STAT → CT surgeon
New arrhythmia (AF, bradycardia, VT) Cardiology; notify CT surgeon
Acute stroke or focal neuro deficit Stroke code team; notify CT surgeon
Fever/infection signs (abscess, cellulitis, UTI, pneumonia) Infectious disease consult; discuss surgery timing with CT surgeon
Severe anemia (Hgb <7 without transfusion) Blood bank + CT surgeon; consider transfusion vs. delay
Acute renal injury (Cr spike, oliguria) Nephrology consult; discuss surgery timing
Medication issue (allergy, interaction, hold discrepancy) Pharmacy → anesthesia → CT surgeon
Anticoagulation complication (over/under-anticoagulation, bleeding, HIT) Anticoagulation team + CT surgeon
Social crisis (housing, transportation, substance withdrawal) Social work → case management; may delay surgery

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Sections are.

Risk Stratification Detail — STS Calculator Inputs & Output Interpretation The Society of Thoracic Surgeons Risk Calculator (2018 update) uses ~50 patient and procedural variables to predict:
  • Mortality (operative death within 30 days)
  • Major morbidity (MI, stroke, infection, renal failure, respiratory failure)
  • Individual patient risk as a percentile vs. national cohort Key inputs:
    • Valve pathology, coronary anatomy (left main disease, triple-vessel, single vessel)
    • Ejection fraction, NYHA class
    • Prior cardiac surgery (reoperation increases risk)
    • Comorbidities: diabetes, renal disease, COPD, cerebrovascular disease, peripheral vascular disease
    • Hemodynamic status (cardiogenic shock = very high risk)
    • Age, female sex, BMI Interpretation:
    • Low risk (mortality <2%, major morbidity <10%): routine pre-op prep; outpatient work-up sufficient
    • Intermediate risk (mortality 2–5%, major morbidity 10–20%): standard admission pre-op optimization; realistic discussion with patient/family
    • High risk (mortality >5%, major morbidity >20%): intensified pre-op optimization; consider ICU-level pre-op monitoring; realistic discussion of alternatives (medical management, staged approach) Limitations of STS:
    • Estimates population risk, not individual risk
    • Does not capture frailty, nutritional status, or psychosocial factors
    • Outcome variance within a risk category is large (some low-risk patients have bad outcomes; some high-risk patients do well)
    • Always pair with CFS frailty assessment, albumin status, and direct patient conversation
Frailty & Pre-habiliation Evidence — Rockwood CFS + PREHAB Trial Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (1–7) predicts post-operative delirium, infection, falls, prolonged recovery independent of surgical risk score. - CFS 1–2 (Very fit to well): Low frailty; routine discharge home - CFS 3 (Managing well): Some vulnerability; low risk but monitor - CFS 4 (Vulnerable): Measurable frailty; PT pre-op + post-op planning; consider intermediate-term rehab - CFS 5 (Mildly frail): Dependence in IADLs; high post-op delirium risk; SNF post-op likely; intensive PT pre-op - CFS 6–7 (Moderately/Severely frail): Dependence in ADLs; palliative care consideration; discuss alternatives to surgery PREHAB Trial (2022) and subsequent literature:
  • Pre-operative rehabilitation (PT 2–3×/week for 4–6 weeks) combined with nutritional optimization + anxiety reduction reduces post-op complications, length of stay, and ICU delirium
  • Even brief intervention (1–2 weeks of PT) shows benefit
  • Most cost-effective for CFS ≥4 Clinical implication: Frail patients admitted for pre-op should have PT/OT involved immediately for baseline, home exercise programming, and post-op planning—not just surgical clearance.
ERAS Cardiac Surgery Pathway — Enhanced Recovery After Cardiac Surgery ERAS Cardiac principles (2024 update) reduce length of stay and complications through:
  1. Pre-operative: smoking cessation, nutritional optimization, anxiolytic pre-med (low-dose oral midazolam), education
  2. Intra-operative: minimal invasive incisions where possible, short bypass times, restrictive fluid strategy, multimodal analgesia (regional blocks, NSAIDs, acetaminophen, opioid-sparing)
  3. Post-operative: early extubation (goal 4–6 h), early mobilization (ICU POD 1), oral intake when alert, multimodal analgesia, DVT/PE prophylaxis, discharge to home by POD 5–6 for uncomplicated CABG/AVR Pre-operative admission tasks aligned with ERAS:
    • Educate on expectations (fast-track extubation, early walking)
    • Optimize nutrition pre-op (albumin ≥3.5)
    • Smoking cessation (24–48 h minimum)
    • Anxiety screening + support (reduce need for pre-med)
    • Physical baseline + home PT if frail (enable early post-op mobilization)
Glycemic Control & DSWI Prevention — HbA1c <8% Target HbA1c >8% pre-operative correlates with:
  • Increased surgical site infections (2–3× higher)
  • Delayed sternal wound healing
  • Increased mortality (HbA1c >9: ~4× higher mortality in cardiac surgery) Mechanism: Hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function, collagen synthesis, and angiogenesis. Evidence-based approach:
  • HbA1c <7% ideal for elective surgery (requires weeks to months of optimization)
  • HbA1c 7–8% acceptable; continue pre-operative insulin
  • HbA1c >8.5%: Consider delaying elective surgery 4–6 weeks for intensive insulin optimization (typical reduction 0.5–1.0 per 2–3 weeks)
  • Perioperative targets: Fasting 120–180 mg/dL; avoid hypoglycemia (<100) and severe hyperglycemia (>250) Medication adjustment pre-op:
  • Increase basal insulin 10–20% day before surgery if HbA1c borderline
  • Reduce meal-time insulin slightly (decreased intake before NPO)
  • Avoid SGLT2i 3–5 days pre-op (euglycemic DKA risk)
  • Resume normal regimen post-op once glycemia stabilizes
Dental Clearance & Endocarditis Prevention — Valve Surgery Special Consideration Dental pathology as endocarditis source:
  • Untreated caries, periapical abscess, gingivitis = bacteremia risk during valve surgery → early post-op prosthetic valve endocarditis
  • Incidence of post-op endocarditis in valve surgery: 0.5–2.0%; significantly higher if pre-existing dental infection Pre-operative dental protocol (especially for valve surgery):
    1. Screening: Evaluate all pre-operative patients for caries, abscess, loose/mobile teeth, bleeding gums
    2. Clearance (if no active infection): Routine cleaning, fillings; complete ≥24–48 h pre-op
    3. Extraction (if necessary): Complete ≥24–48 h pre-op if possible; cover with antibiotics (penicillin V 2 g PO QID × 7d post-procedure)
    4. Active infection pre-op: Urgent extraction + IV antibiotics pre-operatively; delay surgery if possible until infection controlled
    5. Peri-operative prophylaxis (valve surgery): Cefazolin 1–2 g IV at induction (± gentamicin 1.5 mg/kg IV + vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV if PCN-allergic)
    6. Post-operative endocarditis prophylaxis (mechanical or bioprosthetic valve): Patient receives wallet card; all future dental/invasive procedures require antibiotic prophylaxis Exceptions: Mitral valve repair (lower endocarditis risk) may not require aggressive pre-operative dental intervention, but assessment still recommended.
SGLT2 Inhibitor Management — Euglycemic DKA Risk SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, canagliflozin):
  • Increase urinary glucose excretion; reduce blood glucose and HbA1c
  • BUT: increase ketone production even with normal glucose levels (euglycemic DKA)
  • Risk elevated 5–7 days perioperatively, especially if:
  • Post-operative stress, decreased PO intake (fasting state mimics starvation ketosis)
  • Surgical infection or sepsis
  • Dehydration (diuretics, NPO status)
  • Acute illness (MI, pancreatitis, DVT) Pre-operative protocol:
  • HOLD SGLT2i 3–5 days pre-op (conservative approach: 5 days)
  • Educate patient: "We're stopping your SGLT2i before surgery to prevent a rare but serious metabolic complication."
  • Resume post-op once post-operative ileus resolves, oral intake adequate, and glycemia stable (usually POD 2–3)
  • Document in chart: restart date, indication for resumption
  • Educate patient on euglycemic DKA signs (nausea, vomiting, abdominal discomfort, fatigue, dyspnea despite normal glucose)
DOAC Hold Timing — Renal-Adjusted Intervals Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are renally cleared at variable rates. Pre-operative hold timing depends on:
DOACNormal Cr Cl (>60)Cr Cl 30–60Cr Cl <30
Apixaban (Eliquat)Hold 24 h pre-opHold 24–48 hHold 48–72 h; bridging recommended
Rivaroxaban (Xarelto)Hold 24 h pre-opHold 24–48 hHold 48–72 h; bridging recommended
Edoxaban (Savaysa)Hold 24–48 h pre-opHold 24–72 hAvoid if Cr Cl <15; bridging recommended
Dabigatran (Pradaxa)Hold 24 h pre-opHold 24–48 hHold 48–72 h; bridging recommended
High thromboembolic risk (mechanical valve, recent stent, thrombophilia, recent DVT/PE):
  • Consider UFH or LMWH bridge from DOAC hold until post-op
  • Heparin stopped 4–6 h pre-op per surgeon
  • Resume post-op: restart DOAC day 1–2 post-op once bleeding risk minimal; can overlap with heparin × 24 h Post-operative restart:
    • Typically day 1–2 post-op if hemostasis stable, no major bleeding
    • Restart full dose (not loading dose) unless pre-op indication was recent VTE or mechanical valve (then loading dose considered)
Antiplatelet Therapy Timing — ASA, Clopidogrel, Ticagrelor, Prasugrel Aspirin (ASA):
  • CONTINUE perioperatively in most cardiac surgery cases (reduces MI risk; bleeding risk acceptable)
  • Rare exception: surgeon explicitly requests hold (e.g., certain redo operations); discuss
  • Give with small sip of water AM of surgery P2Y12 inhibitors (clopidogrel, ticagrelor, prasugrel):
    DrugHold intervalRationaleException
    Clopidogrel (Plavix)5–7 days pre-opIrreversible platelet inhibition; recovery takes 5–7 daysRecent stent (<12 mo) = cardiology + CT surgeon discussion; may shorten hold or continue at reduced dose
    Ticagrelor (Brilinta)3–5 days pre-opReversible inhibition; faster offset than clopidogrelRecent stent: shorter hold acceptable; coordinate with cardiology
    Prasugrel (Effient)7 days pre-opLongest washoutRecent stent: discuss, rarely shortened
    Key caveat: Recent coronary stent (<12 months) increases risk of stent thrombosis if P2Y12i held. Coordinate with cardiology + CT surgeon together before holding antiplatelet therapy. Options:
  • Proceed with surgery on DAPT (increases bleeding risk but prevents stent thrombosis)
  • Hold P2Y12i for minimum acceptable interval (e.g., 3 days instead of 5 if ticagrelor + recent stent)
  • Bridge with PCI to a different lesion to minimize stent risk
  • Delay surgery if possible (e.g., elective AVR can wait 1 year post-PCI; urgent CABG cannot)
Amiodarone Washout — Weeks, Not Days Amiodarone characteristics:
  • Very long half-life (26–107 days; average ~40 days)
  • Highly lipophilic (accumulates in fatty tissues)
  • Takes weeks to months to eliminate, even after stopping Pre-operative implications:
  • If patient on home amiodarone, CONTINUE pre-op and perioperatively (most surgeons); do NOT hold
  • If amiodarone stopped in clinic pre-operatively, effects persist for weeks; patient remains "covered" for arrhythmia suppression
  • Drug interactions (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin) persist even after discontinuation Toxicity monitoring pre-op:
  • QTc prolongation (amiodarone prolongs QT; check baseline EKG)
  • Bradycardia (combined with beta-blocker, can be severe)
  • Hypotension (especially if IV amiodarone given)
  • Thyroid dysfunction (hypo- or hyperthyroidism; check TSH pre-op if long-term use)
  • Pulmonary toxicity (rare but serious; baseline CXR helpful) Pearl: Amiodarone-loading post-op is often used for POAF; anticipate hypotension and have fluid/vasopressor plan.
Nutrition Biomarkers & Pre-operative Protein Goals Albumin (half-life 20 days):
  • Normal: ≥3.5 g/dL
  • Mild nutritional impairment: 3.0–3.4
  • Moderate-to-severe: <3.0
  • Reflects overall protein nutrition status
  • Predicts infection risk, wound healing Prealbumin (TBPA; half-life 2–3 days):
  • Normal: 20–40 mg/dL
  • More sensitive to recent nutritional changes than albumin
  • Rises quickly with improved nutrition; falls quickly with stress Pre-operative targets:
  • Albumin ≥3.5 g/dL ideal; <3.0 = significant risk
  • Prealbumin ≥20 mg/dL; <17 = marginal Interventions if nutritional risk:
  • Dietitian consult: high-protein diet (1.5 g/kg/day)
  • Supplemental nutrition (Ensure, Boost, amino acid supplements)
  • Appetite stimulant if indicated (dronabinol 2.5–5 mg BID, megestrol 400–800 mg daily)
  • Zinc supplementation (25–30 mg daily) if deficient
  • Minimize NPO window pre-op (avoid extended nothing-by-mouth) Post-operative follow-up:
  • Repeat albumin, prealbumin POD 3–4 if pre-operative risk identified
  • Aggressive post-op nutrition (high-protein, high-calorie, advance diet quickly post-op)
  • Early PT mobilization (muscle protein synthesis enhanced by activity)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any occur, re-escalate immediately.

  • New or worsening angina at rest or with minimal exertion; ST-segment changes on EKG → unstable angina; notify cardiology + CT surgeon
  • New dyspnea or orthopnea → acute HF exacerbation; assess for pulmonary edema (crackles, elevated JVP)
  • Syncope or presyncope paired with palpitations → dangerous arrhythmia; 12-lead EKG, notify cardiology
  • Fever >100.4°F without clear source → workup for infection (cultures, UA, CXR); dental abscess risk; may delay surgery
  • Infection signs (redness, drainage, abscess, cellulitis, pneumonia on CXR) → delay surgery; treat infection first
  • Acute anemia (Hgb drop >1 g/dL) → bleeding source; notify team; may transfuse
  • Thrombocytopenia <100K on heparin bridge → HIT screening (4Ts score, PF4 antibody); consider DTI or LMWH
  • Over-anticoagulation (INR >4 on warfarin, aPTT >90 on heparin) → bleeding risk; hold AC, repeat labs, notify provider
  • Under-anticoagulation (INR <1.8 on warfarin, aPTT <40 on heparin) → clot risk; increase dosing, repeat labs
  • Acute renal injury (Cr spike, oliguria) → assess hydration, medication toxicity, rhabdomyolysis; may delay surgery
  • Hyperglycemia >250 mg/dL unresponsive to insulin; DKA risk if on SGLT2i (should be held) → workup for infection, intensify insulin
  • Hypoglycemia <70 with altered mental status → seizure risk pre-op; give dextrose; review insulin dosing
  • New focal neurologic deficit (weakness, facial droop, speech change, confusion) → stroke code; CT head; notify neurology + CT surgeon
  • Altered mental status, delirium → assess for hypoxia, hypoglycemia, medication toxicity, infection, alcohol withdrawal; review psychosocial stressors

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. STS risk estimates population risk, not individual risk. A patient with "15% mortality risk" does not mean 85% will survive and 15% will die. It means the population of patients similar to this one has a 15% mortality rate; individual outcomes vary widely. Pair STS with CFS frailty, direct conversation, and realistic expectations.

  2. Frailty is not captured by STS, yet independently predicts delirium, infection, and discharge disposition. Always perform Rockwood CFS assessment (1–7 scale). CFS ≥5 = high risk; engage PT/OT, discuss realistic post-operative recovery timeline ("May take 3–4 months to fully recover strength"), plan SNF post-op if CFS ≥6.

  3. HbA1c >8.5% pre-operative is a red flag. Delay elective surgery if possible (4–6 weeks) for intensive insulin optimization. Decrements of 0.5–1.0 HbA1c achievable in 2–3 weeks with intensified regimen. If surgery cannot be delayed, accept higher perioperative risk and plan aggressive post-operative glucose control (target 140–180 mg/dL intra-op, 120–180 post-op).

  4. Dental clearance + prophylactic antibiotics for valve surgery is non-negotiable. Untreated pre-operative dental infection = prosthetic valve endocarditis risk post-op. Complete dental work ≥24–48 h pre-op. Cover extractions with penicillin V 2 g PO QID × 7 days. Valve surgery patient gets endocarditis prophylaxis card for future dental procedures.

  5. Smoking cessation timing is counterintuitive — 4–8 weeks ideal; even 24–48 hours helps. Do NOT delay elective surgery waiting for 4-week quit date. Offer NRT (patches, gum, lozenge) at full dose pre-op; patches are safe pre-op and post-op. Varenicline (Chantix) stopped 2 weeks pre-op (nausea risk intra-op). Frame to patient: "Quitting now, even for a few days, lowers infection risk."

  6. Albumin <3.0 g/dL = significant malnutrition; infection and wound-healing risk. Dietitian consult mandatory. Target 1.5 g/kg/day protein. Appetite stimulant (dronabinol, megestrol) if intake poor. Even 1–2 weeks of high-protein nutrition improves prealbumin and outcomes.

  7. SGLT2 inhibitor hold 3–5 days pre-op is essential. Euglycemic DKA (normal glucose + metabolic acidosis) can occur in the perioperative window even in well-controlled diabetes. Hold pre-op; resume post-op once glycemia stable and oral intake adequate (usually POD 2–3). Educate patient on rare but serious risk.

  8. DOAC hold timing is renal-function dependent. Apixaban/rivaroxaban 24 h if Cr Cl >60; 24–48 h if Cr Cl 30–60; 48–72 h if <30. Consider heparin bridge for high thromboembolic risk (mechanical valve, recent stent). Heparin stopped 4–6 h pre-op per surgeon.

  9. Clopidogrel 5–7 days pre-op, ticagrelor 3–5 days, prasugrel 7 days — but recent stent (<12 mo) changes the game. Stent thrombosis if P2Y12i held. Cardiology + CT surgeon TOGETHER must discuss risk/benefit: proceed on DAPT (increased bleeding), shorten hold interval, or delay surgery. Do not hold P2Y12i for recent stent without team consensus.

  10. ASA continues perioperatively in most cardiac surgery. Reduces MI risk; bleeding risk acceptable. Give with small sip of water AM of surgery unless surgeon explicitly requests hold (rare).

  11. Beta-blocker continuation through pre-op is critical. Perioperative beta-blockade reduces cardiac events, mortality. Give AM surgery with small sip of water. Do NOT hold even if BP borderline; discuss with surgeon/anesthesia if uncertain.

  12. Heparin bridge plan MUST be written and communicated. Document: "Heparin 18 u/kg/hr, target aPTT 50–70, hold if >90, increase if <40. Stop 4–6 h pre-op per surgeon." Miscommunication = bleeding or clot. Verify aPTT trending appropriately q6h.

  13. Informed consent is not a checkbox. Verify patient understands why surgery, what procedure, risks (bleeding, infection, stroke, MI, need for re-op, death), and benefits (symptom relief, improved survival). If patient seems reluctant or confused, notify surgeon before consent is signed. Document time spent, questions asked, family present.

  14. Frailty + nutritional risk + social determinants = post-op disaster without early planning. Housing instability, transportation issues, no family support, substance use, low health literacy = worse outcomes. Involve social work pre-op. Arrange post-operative resources (home health, PT, meal support, case management) before discharge; do not wait until POD 6.

  15. Amiodarone takes weeks to wash out — do NOT hold pre-op. Long half-life (~40 days). If given IV post-op for POAF, anticipate ~25% hypotension; have fluid/vasopressor plan. Monitor QTc; if >500 ms, hold/decrease amiodarone.

cards.title: Pulmonary Hypertension
cards.quickAnswer: PH is defined as mPAP ≥20 mmHg on RHC (2022 ESC/ERS threshold, not 25). Hemodynamic classification: precapillary (PAWP ≤15, PVR ≥2 WU) vs. postcapillary (PAWP >15). WHO groups 1–5 drive everything: Group 1 (PAH) gets PDE-5i/ERAs/prostanoids; Group 2 (LV disease—most common in cardiac surgery) gets standard HF therapy, NOT PAH drugs; Group 3 (lung) = oxygen; Group 4 (CTEPH) = PTE or riociguat; Group 5 = supportive. RHC is gold standard—echo RVSP is estimated only. Perioperative PH raises RV failure risk sharply; post-op RV decompensation (low CO + high CVP) is primary concern. Avoid hypoxemia, hypercarbia, acidosis (all increase PVR).
