sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation—definition, epidemiology, who is affected.

  • Definition: Hemodynamic diagnosis of abnormally elevated pulmonary arterial pressure, defined by mPAP ≥20 mmHg at rest at sea level (2022 ESC/ERS guideline update; prior definition >25 mmHg now obsolete). PH is not a disease itself—the underlying etiology drives all management (WHO Group classification).
  • Precapillary vs. postcapillary: Precapillary PH (PAWP ≤15, PVR ≥2 Wood units) reflects pulmonary vascular pathology; postcapillary PH (PAWP >15) reflects left heart disease backing up into the lungs.
  • Epidemiology:
  • General population prevalence ~1% (autopsy studies); higher in cardiac disease populations (HF, valvular disease).
  • Group 2 (LV disease) is most common, especially in elderly and post-cardiac-surgery populations.
  • PAH (Group 1) is rare (~1–2 per million) but highly morbid.
  • CTEPH (Group 4) occurs in ~2–4% of acute PE survivors.
  • Female predominance in PAH; often diagnosed in young-to-middle-aged women.
  • ICU context: Pre-op cardiac surgery patients with known PH; post-op RV dysfunction assessment; transplant candidacy workup; acute-on-chronic decompensation.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology mechanisms (expandable)

Pulmonary vascular disease (PAH—Group 1): Primary pathology of the small pulmonary arteries—endothelial dysfunction, smooth-muscle proliferation, thrombosis, inflammation → increased PVR (resistance), RV pressure overload, RV hypertrophy → eventual RV dilation + dysfunction.

Left heart disease (Group 2): Elevated left atrial pressure (from LV systolic/diastolic dysfunction or mitral stenosis) transmits backward → passive pulmonary venous hypertension → if chronic, may cause reactive PVR elevation ("out-of-proportion" PH).

Lung disease/hypoxia (Group 3): Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction + loss of capillary bed + chronic alveolar hypoxemia → PVR elevation.

Chronic thromboembolism (Group 4): Fixed mechanical obstruction of pulmonary vascular bed from organized thrombi; increases PVR fixed to distal vasculature.

Multifactorial (Group 5): Combination of mechanisms or unclear etiology.

Clinical presentation (general features):

  • Dyspnea on exertion — most common presenting symptom
  • Fatigue, weakness, chest pain, palpitations
  • Syncope or pre-syncope — RV pressure overload limits cardiac output; exertional trigger common
  • Signs of RV failure: Jugular venous distension (JVD), peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, RV heave on exam
  • Late findings: Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND), ascites (advanced RV failure)

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
When and how PH is encountered in the ICU.

  • Pre-op cardiac surgery patient: Known PH from pre-operative workup; awaiting optimization and surgical planning
  • Incidental finding: High RVSP on routine pre-op echo; may indicate undiagnosed PH requiring RHC confirmation
  • Post-op RV dysfunction: Acute or worsening RV failure in immediate post-op period; may unmask or worsen underlying PH
  • Transplant assessment: PH patient being evaluated for heart or heart-lung transplantation; requires vasoreactivity testing to determine candidacy
  • Acute decompensation: Patient with known PH presenting with acute dyspnea, syncope, hemodynamic instability; requires ICU-level support

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. Target: 5 minutes at bedside or chart review.

Vital signs & perfusion:

  • HR, BP, SpO₂ (maintain >90%), capillary refill, skin temperature, mental status
  • Orthostatic vitals if syncope reported

Physical exam:

  • Heart: RV heave (left sternal border, end-expiration), loud P₂ (pulmonary closure), systolic flow murmur (TR if RV dilated)
  • Lungs: Crackles (if pulmonary edema), diminished bases, wheeze (if lung disease)
  • Abdomen/extremities: JVD (elevated CVP), hepatomegaly (RV failure), peripheral edema, ascites
  • Neurologic: Syncope history, mental status (oligemia risk)

Recent labs & hemodynamics:

  • BNP or NT-proBNP (elevated in RV failure/wall stress)
  • Hemoglobin, creatinine, electrolytes
  • If recent RHC: mPAP, PCWP, PVR, cardiac output, vasoreactivity response
  • If PA catheter in place: PA pressures, CVP, PCWP, CI trends

Echocardiography findings (if available):

  • RVSP estimate (Doppler TR jet + RA pressure)
  • RV size (RV:LV ratio at base), RV function (TAPSE, RVFAC, S' on tissue Doppler)
  • Septal position, D-sign (RV-LV interaction)
  • Pericardial effusion, RA dilation, IVC size + collapsibility
  • Important caveat: Echo RVSP is estimated only; does not measure diastolic or mean PA pressure; cannot calculate PVR without invasive data

MAR / medication history:

  • Home PH-specific medications (sildenafil, bosentan, etc.) and adherence
  • Home beta-blockers, diuretics, oxygen requirement
  • Recent anticoagulation status

Surgery/procedure context:

  • What cardiac surgery (if post-op), POD, intra-op events (long CPB, ischemic time)
  • Pre-op RHC findings if available
  • Transplant workup status

sections.heading: 5A. Group 1 — Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH)
sections.bodyHtml:
PAH-specific therapies targeting pulmonary vascular pathology.

Supportive care (all PAH):

  1. Maintain SpO₂ >90% at rest and with activity; supplemental O₂ as needed
  2. Diuretics judiciously for RV-HF symptoms (edema, ascites); avoid excessive diuresis (drops CO)
  3. Anticoagulation: Evidence mixed; warfarin (INR 1.5–2.5) widely used in idiopathic PAH to prevent in-situ thrombosis; less clear in secondary PAH or CTD-associated PAH
  4. Counsel: Avoid hypoxemia, dehydration, strenuous exertion; pregnancy is very high-risk (maternal/fetal mortality ~30–50%)

PAH-specific pharmacotherapy — typical escalation:

Drug Class Agent Mechanism Route Key Notes
Endothelin Receptor Antagonist (ERA) Bosentan Blocks endothelin-A/B receptors PO BID Hepatotoxicity risk; CYP3A4/2C9 inhibitor; teratogenic
Ambrisentan Selective endothelin-A blocker PO daily Less hepatotoxicity; teratogenic
Macitentan Selective ET-A; tissue-targeting PO daily SERAPHIN trial showed mortality benefit; long half-life
PDE-5 Inhibitor Sildenafil Inhibits PDE-5 → ↑ cGMP PO TID or daily First-line in many centers; avoid with nitrates/riociguat (severe hypotension)
Tadalafil PDE-5 inhibitor, longer half-life PO daily Convenient dosing; similar efficacy to sildenafil
Guanylate Cyclase Stimulator Riociguat Directly activates soluble GC PO TID ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION with PDE-5i or nitrates (profound hypotension)
Prostacyclin Receptor Agonist Selexipag IP receptor agonist PO BID GRIPHON trial showed mortality benefit; well-tolerated
Prostacyclin Analogs Epoprostenol (Flolan) IV potent vasodilator IV infusion via central line Gold standard; short half-life (~6 min); requires strict sterility; bridge therapy during escalation
Treprostinil (Remodulin) Stable prostacyclin analog SC, IV, or inhaled Less potent than epoprostenol; longer half-life; SC/IV pump
Iloprost Stable prostacyclin analog Inhaled QID Multiple daily inhalations; less convenient

Initial strategy:

  • Low-risk: Monotherapy (ERA or PDE-5i), uptitrate over weeks; reassess response at 3–6 months
  • Intermediate-to-high-risk or inadequate monotherapy response: Combination therapy (e.g., ERA + PDE-5i, or PDE-5i + selexipag, or ERA + selexipag)
  • Very high-risk or severe decompensated: Consider IV/SC epoprostenol early (most potent option)

Response monitoring (all PAH):

  • Clinical: NYHA functional class, dyspnea, syncope, RV-HF symptoms
  • Functional: 6-minute walk distance (goal >380 m), exertional desaturation
  • Biomarker: BNP/NT-proBNP trending downward; arbitrary goal <180 pg/mL
  • Echo: RVSP, RV size/function, pericardial effusion, RA area
  • RHC (often repeat at 3–6 months or annually): mPAP, PVR, CO trends

sections.heading: 5B. Group 2 — Left Heart Disease PH
sections.bodyHtml:
DO NOT use PAH-specific drugs. These cause systemic vasodilation → worsening pulmonary edema and hypoxemia in elevated PCWP.

Management: 1. Optimize LV function:

  • Beta-blockers, ACE-I/ARB, aldosterone antagonist (standard HF therapy)
  • Diuretics to euvolemia; titrate carefully
  • Coronary revascularization if CAD present
  • Valve replacement if valvular pathology (mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis)
  • Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) if appropriate

  1. Afterload reduction: Judicious vasodilators (nitrates, hydralazine, nicardipine) only if hypertensive; monitor for systemic hypotension

  2. Pulmonary edema management: Aggressive diuresis, nitrates for congestion

  3. Transplant: If refractory HFrEF, assess candidacy; PH often reverses post-transplant as LV function restored

sections.heading: 5C. Group 3 — Lung Disease / Hypoxia
sections.bodyHtml:
Primary therapy: oxygen. Treat underlying lung disease.

  1. Supplemental oxygen: Target SpO₂ >88–90% at rest, with activity, at night - Home oxygen assessment; portable oxygen for mobility - Continuous or intermittent per pulmonary function

  2. Treat underlying condition:

    • COPD: bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids, smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation
    • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF): antifibrotic agents (pirfenidone, nintedanib)
    • Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA): CPAP/BiPAP therapy

  3. PDE-5i (sildenafil): Considered in advanced Group 3 with significant hypoxemia + RV dysfunction, but oxygen is cornerstone; limited evidence

  4. Avoid infections — worsen hypoxemia + PVR reflexively

sections.heading: 5D. Group 4 — Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH)
sections.bodyHtml:
Potentially surgically curable. Diagnosis requires V/Q scan (gold standard) + CT PA adjunct.

Pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (PTE) — curative if operable:

  • Surgical candidate: mPAP ≥25–30 mmHg with proximal/accessible thrombi; requires expert center (UCSD, UC CTEPH consortium, etc.)
  • Outcomes: ~50–60% of CTEPH patients are surgical candidates; post-PTE mean mPAP typically drops from ~45 to ~20 mmHg; PVR normalizes
  • Preparation: Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC) perioperatively; optimize RV function pre-op

Medical therapy (if inoperable or pre-op bridge): 1.

Riociguat (guanylate cyclase stimulator) — only proven medical benefit in CTEPH - Dose: 0.5–2 mg PO TID - ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION with PDE-5i (profound hypotension) - Monitor BP carefully

  1. Lifelong anticoagulation: Warfarin (INR 2–3) or DOAC; prevents recurrent thromboembolism

  2. Diuretics, oxygen as needed for RV-HF symptoms

  3. Balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA): Emerging catheter-based option for inoperable CTEPH; multiple procedures over time; still investigational

sections.heading: 5E. Post-Cardiac Surgery PH Considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
RV failure is the primary post-operative concern.

Pre-op assessment with known PH:

  1. RHC is essential — echo RVSP underestimates or overestimates; RHC provides mPAP, PCWP, PVR, vasoreactivity
  2. WHO Group classification — changes pre-op strategy (Group 2 vs. Group 1)
  3. Vasoreactivity testing — positive response (PVR drops ≥10% on iNO ± IV vasodilator) suggests surgical candidacy and post-op RV tolerance
  4. Consider PA catheter if mPAP >40 or PVR >3 Wood units

Intra-operative management:

  1. Preload balance: RV is preload-dependent (needs filling) but fixed PVR means excess volume → pulmonary edema
  2. Minimize systemic vasoconstriction — increases RV afterload
  3. Inotropy + inhaled vasodilators: Milrinone (inotrope + mild pulmonary vasodilation) preferred over pure vasoconstrictors
  4. Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO): Selective pulmonary vasodilator; starting 10–20 ppm, titrate to response
  5. Avoid hypoxemia, hypercarbia, acidosis — all increase PVR reflexively; avoid hypothermia

Post-operative RV management:

  1. Monitor for RV failure: Low cardiac output (CI <2.2), elevated CVP (>15), oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h), rising lactate
  2. Continue iNO if needed; aggressive weaning once stabilized (risk of rebound PVR elevation)
  3. Optimize ventilation: Maintain FiO₂, moderate PEEP; avoid hypercarbia
  4. Inotrope selection: Milrinone + dobutamine common; avoid pure vasoconstrictors
  5. PA catheter (if in place) allows ongoing PVR trending

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room]." B: "[Patient context: POD X s/p cardiac surgery / pre-op awaiting optimization / post-PE workup]. Known PH or high RVSP on echo. Most recent mPAP/PCWP/PVR [if available]. Current SpO₂ [value], HR [value], BP [value]." A: "[New acute event: acute dyspnea, syncope, hypotension, oliguria, desaturation]. RV-HF signs: JVD, hepatomegaly, new edema. [Recent labs: BNP, troponin, lactate if available]." R: "Requesting [RHC for diagnosis confirmation / escalation to ICU / mechanical support evaluation / vasoreactivity testing for transplant candidacy]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Incidental high RVSP on pre-op echo; suspected PH diagnosis Cardiology + CT surgery team
Known PH awaiting cardiac surgery — pre-op optimization CT surgeon + cardiologist + perfusionist (plan iNO, PA catheter)
Post-op RV failure (low CO, high CVP) CT surgeon + ICU attending + perfusionists (consider iNO, inotropes, mechanical support)
Acute PH decompensation (dyspnea, syncope, hemodynamic instability) ICU attending + cardiology; consider ECMO / mechanical support team
Pre-transplant vasoreactivity testing or PVR reversal assessment Transplant team + cardiology + RHC lab
CTEPH diagnosis suspected (V/Q abnormality post-PE) Pulmonology + CT surgery (if potentially operable) + refer to expert PTE center
Acute RV failure despite iNO/inotropes Consider ECMO evaluation; notify surgical leadership + ICU attending

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
WHO Classification Deep-Dive — hemodynamic definitions & decision tree (expandable) Group 1 — Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension (PAH):
  • Precapillary: mPAP ≥20, PAWP ≤15, PVR ≥2 WU
  • Primary or secondary pulmonary vascular disease (no LV dysfunction, no lung disease, no thromboembolism)
  • Subtypes: idiopathic PAH, heritable (BMPR2, TLR4 mutations), drug/toxin-induced (anorexigens, cocaine, methamphetamine), connective tissue disease (scleroderma, SLE, mixed CTD), congenital heart disease (Eisenmenger), HIV-associated, portal hypertension, schistosomiasis
  • Management: PAH-specific drugs ONLY (ERA, PDE-5i, prostacyclin analogs, guanylate cyclase stimulators, prostacyclin receptor agonists) Group 2 — PH Due to Left Heart Disease:
  • Postcapillary: mPAP ≥20, PAWP >15 (or elevated LV end-diastolic pressure)
  • Or mixed pre/postcapillary if PVR elevation disproportionate to PCWP elevation
  • Causes: HFrEF, HFpEF, valvular disease (mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis), LV systolic/diastolic dysfunction, cardiomyopathy
  • Most common PH in general population and cardiac surgery population
  • Management: Treat LV disease ONLY (beta-blockers, ACE-I/ARB, diuretics, revascularization, valve replacement). Do NOT give PAH drugs — worsen pulmonary edema Group 3 — PH Due to Lung Disease and/or Hypoxia:
  • Usually mildly elevated PCWP with variable PVR
  • Causes: COPD, ILD (IPF), OSA, hypoventilation, high-altitude exposure
  • Management: Oxygen + treat lung disease. PDE-5i considered in advanced disease with severe hypoxemia; oxygen is cornerstone Group 4 — Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH):
  • Precapillary: mPAP ≥20, PAWP ≤15, PVR ≥2 WU
  • Perfusion defects on V/Q (>ventilation defects); can confirm with CTA showing organized thrombi
  • Occurs in ~2–4% of PE survivors; often delayed presentation (months to years post-PE)
  • Management: Pulmonary thromboendarterectomy (curative) if operable; riociguat + anticoagulation if inoperable Group 5 — PH with Unclear Multifactorial Mechanisms:
  • Heterogeneous, rare; diagnosis of exclusion
  • May include occult malignancy, medications, metabolic disorder, hematologic disease
  • Management: Supportive care; treat identifiable causes; research protocols
Hemodynamic Criteria Table — normal vs. PH values (expandable)
ParameterNormalPH ThresholdWHO Group Context
mPAP (mean PA pressure)<20 mmHg≥20 mmHgDiagnostic threshold (2022 ESC/ERS)
PAWP (pulmonary artery wedge pressure)≤15 mmHg>15 mmHgDistinguishes Group 2 (elevated PAWP) from precapillary (normal PAWP)
PVR (pulmonary vascular resistance)<2 Wood units≥2 WUIndicates vascular remodeling; normal <2.4 mmHg/L/min
Cardiac Output (CO)4–6 L/minVariable; often decreased in PAHAssessed during RHC; impacts prognosis
CVP (central venous pressure)2–8 mmHgOften elevated in RV failure (>12)Reflects RV preload; elevated CVP + low CO = RV failure
RVSP (RV systolic pressure by Doppler)15–30 mmHgVaries; often misestimatedEcho-derived estimate; unreliable without RHC confirmation
REVEAL 2.0 Risk Score — PAH prognosis & management intensity (expandable) Predicts 1-year mortality in PAH. Components:
  • WHO functional class
  • 6-minute walk distance
  • BNP/NT-proBNP level
  • RVSP or pericardial effusion
  • Presence/absence of pericardial effusion on echo
  • Renal insufficiency (creatinine >1.5) Risk stratification:
    • Low risk: REVEAL score ≤6 → monotherapy often sufficient
    • Intermediate risk: Score 7–8 → combination therapy recommended
    • High risk: Score ≥9 → aggressive multi-drug + close monitoring; early transplant discussion Helps guide intensity of initial PAH therapy and transplant timing.
Right Heart Catheterization (RHC) — Diagnostic technique & vasoreactivity testing (expandable) Gold standard for PH diagnosis. Directly measures:
  • PA pressures: systolic, diastolic, mean (mPAP ≥20 diagnostic)
  • PCWP (left atrial pressure proxy): ≤15 precapillary, >15 postcapillary
  • Cardiac output (CO)
  • PVR calculation: (mPAP – PCWP) / CO in Wood units or mmHg/L/min Vasoreactivity testing during RHC:
    • Trial of inhaled nitric oxide (iNO 10–20 ppm) ± IV adenosine, epoprostenol, or milrinone
    • Positive response: ≥10% drop in mPAP + PVR decrease with same or improved CO
    • Predicts response to PAH-specific drugs (especially calcium channel blockers in idiopathic PAH)
    • Important for transplant candidacy: PVR reduction to <2.5 WU on vasodilators → candidate; failure to reduce → high post-transplant RV failure risk Why RHC matters in cardiac surgery:
    • Distinguishes Group 2 from Group 1 (PCWP differentiates)
    • Identifies vasoreactive patients (better surgical risk)
    • Guides pre-op iNO/inotrope planning
    • Determines transplant candidacy in borderline patients
PAH-specific therapies — mechanism & class comparison (expandable) Pathophysiology target: Pulmonary vasoconstriction + smooth-muscle proliferation + thrombosis. Modern PAH drugs target three main pathways: Endothelin Pathway (ERA):
  • Endothelin-1 promotes vasoconstriction + proliferation
  • ERAs block ET-A (vasoconstriction) and/or ET-B (clearance) receptors
  • Examples: bosentan (blocks both), ambrisentan & macitentan (ET-A selective)
  • Hepatotoxicity monitoring required (LFTs); teratogenic; CYP450 interactions Nitric Oxide Pathway (PDE-5i, riociguat):
  • NO → cGMP → vasodilation, anti-proliferation
  • PDE-5i (sildenafil, tadalafil) inhibit phosphodiesterase-5, ↑ cGMP
  • Riociguat directly activates soluble guanylate cyclase (acts independently of NO)
  • Riociguat + PDE-5i = CONTRAINDICATED (severe hypotension) Prostacyclin Pathway (selexipag, prostacyclin analogs):
  • Prostacyclin (PGI₂) promotes vasodilation, anti-platelet, anti-proliferative
  • Selexipag: prostacyclin receptor (IP) agonist; oral, twice-daily
  • Prostacyclin analogs: epoprostenol (IV, short half-life, potent), treprostinil (SC/IV/inhaled, longer half-life), iloprost (inhaled, QID) Combination strategies:
  • Low-risk: Start monotherapy, uptitrate
  • Intermediate/high-risk: Combine agents from different pathways (e.g., ERA + PDE-5i)
  • Severe/refractory: Triple therapy (ERA + PDE-5i + prostacyclin analog)
CTEPH Workup & Diagnosis — V/Q scan mandatory; PTE vs. BPA decision (expandable) Clinical suspicion: Dyspnea persisting >3 months post-PE, RV dilation on echo, elevated RVSP, no other obvious cause. Diagnostic algorithm:
  1. V/Q Scan (ventilation-perfusion) — MANDATORY for CTEPH diagnosis
    • Shows subsegmental or larger perfusion defects in absence of corresponding ventilation defects
    • Sensitivity ~90% for CTEPH; specificity excellent
    • Normal V/Q essentially excludes CTEPH
    • CTA Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) — adjunct to V/Q
    • Detects central/lobar thrombi (surgical anatomy planning)
    • Assesses lung parenchyma for other disease
    • Often done alongside V/Q
    • Right Heart Catheterization — confirm diagnosis + severity
    • mPAP ≥20, PAWP ≤15, PVR ≥2 WU (precapillary)
    • Guides operability assessment Operability assessment (expert CTEPH center):
    • Operable: mPAP ≥25–30, proximal/accessible thrombi, patient fit for surgery
    • Inoperable: Distal small-vessel disease, medical comorbidities, patient refusal Management:
    • Operable → PTE (curative): Refer to expert center (UCSD, UC CTEPH consortium, NIH) for surgical evaluation
    • Inoperable → medical therapy:
    • Riociguat 0.5–2 mg PO TID (only proven medical benefit)
    • Lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin INR 2–3 or DOAC)
    • Consider balloon pulmonary angioplasty (emerging, investigational)
Post-cardiac Surgery RV Failure — triggers & management (expandable) RV failure post-op manifests as: Low cardiac output (CI <2.2) + elevated CVP (>15) + oliguria + rising lactate, often despite "adequate" BP. Triggers in PH patient:
  • Inadequate pre-op preparation (high PVR, negative vasoreactivity test)
  • Long CPB time, ischemic injury, inadequate cardioplegia
  • Hypoxemia, hypercarbia, acidosis intra-op or post-op (all ↑ PVR)
  • Volume overload (RV doesn't tolerate excess volume; impedes systemic venous return)
  • Loss of inotropic support or iNO prematurely Management priorities:
    1. Optimize ventilation: FiO₂ high, moderate PEEP, avoid hypercarbia
    2. Inotropy: Milrinone + dobutamine preferred (inotrope + mild pulmonary vasodilation); avoid pure vasoconstrictors
    3. Inhaled vasodilators: Continue iNO; titrate to response; wean gradually (rebound risk)
    4. Diuretics: Judicious; RV is volume-sensitive; overzealous diuresis worsens CO
    5. Afterload reduction: Minimize systemic vasoconstriction; maintain MAP but don't aim for hypertension
    6. Monitor PA pressures: PA catheter trending mPAP, PVR helpful for escalation decisions
    7. Mechanical support consideration: If declining despite above, ECMO evaluation

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Pattern recognition for proficient/expert clinicians. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • New dyspnea or increased O₂ requirement — can precede hemodynamic decompensation
  • Syncope or new near-syncope — RV pressure generation failing; cardiac output dropping
  • Rising BNP/NT-proBNP — indicates worsening RV wall stress
  • Progressive RV dilation on echo — structural RV remodeling; worse prognosis
  • Desaturation on exertion or at rest — hypoxemia raises PVR reflexively
  • JVD rising, edema worsening, weight gain >2–3 lb/day — RV-HF decompensation
  • Rising CVP with oliguria despite "adequate" BP — early RV failure; CO likely low (not reflected in BP alone)
  • Rising lactate or worsening renal function — tissue hypoperfusion from low CO
  • Altered mental status, anxiety — subtle hypoperfusion warning
  • Atrial arrhythmias (new POAF or SVT) — RV dilation + pressure load predispose
  • Syncope + mechanical prosthesis or LV thrombus — embolic risk high; escalate for imaging/anticoagulation check
  • POAF patient with high RVSP on echo — consider acute RV strain from secondary PH

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. New 2022 ESC/ERS threshold is mPAP ≥20 mmHg, not 25. Many clinicians still use the old cutoff. Know the updated definition or you'll miss mild PH.

  2. PAWP ≤15 = precapillary; PAWP >15 = postcapillary. This distinction (from RHC) separates Group 1/4 from Group 2. Echo alone cannot distinguish.

  3. Group 2 (LV disease) is the most common PH in general population and in cardiac surgery. Many HFrEF or valvular disease patients have PH as a consequence, not primary pathology. Treat the LV disease; sildenafil given to a Group 2 patient with PCWP >20 risks acute pulmonary edema.

  4. Do NOT give PAH-specific drugs to Group 2 patients. Systemic vasodilation worsens pulmonary edema. This is a critical error with high morbidity.

  5. Echo RVSP is estimated (from TR Doppler + RA pressure) and often misleading. Weak TR jet, poor windows, RA pressure guesswork → unreliable.

    RHC is gold standard—order it if PH is in the differential.

  6. RHC gold standard for diagnosis. Some labs report high RVSP on echo as "PH"—it may be, but without mPAP + PVR + PCWP, etiology is unknown and management may be wrong.

  7. V/Q scan is mandatory for suspected CTEPH. Perfusion defects > ventilation defects are the classic finding. Normal V/Q essentially excludes CTEPH. CTA is adjunct, not replacement.

  8. CTEPH is surgically curable with PTE if patient is operable. Missed diagnosis = years of disability when surgery could normalize hemodynamics.

  9. PH limits transplant candidacy. Fixed PVR (unable to drop on vasodilators) predicts RV failure post-transplant.

    Vasoreactivity testing (iNO ± IV vasodilator trial during RHC) is not optional—it determines candidacy.

  10. RV is afterload-sensitive (opposite of LV). RV failure worsens with increased PVR; improves with afterload reduction (iNO). Systemic vasoconstrictors (norepinephrine, phenylephrine) worsen RV afterload; milrinone (inotrope + mild pulmonary vasodilation) preferred.

  11. Acute PH decompensation = ICU. Signs: acutely worsening dyspnea, syncope, hypoxemia, hypotension, oliguria. Needs iNO + IV inotropes + PA monitoring; consider ECMO.

  12. Hypoxemia, hypercarbia, acidosis all raise PVR reflexively. In PH patients (esp. post-op), maintain aggressive oxygenation, avoid hypercarbia, correct acidosis ASAP.

  13. iNO weaning is gradual. Abrupt discontinuation causes "rebound" PVR elevation—stepwise reduction over hours-to-days as tolerated.

  14. Pregnancy + PAH is very high-risk. Maternal/fetal mortality ~30–50% even in idiopathic PAH. Counsel women of childbearing age with PAH on reliable contraception; pregnancy requires specialist team.

  15. Post-op RV failure often manifests as oliguria + rising CVP + rising lactate despite "adequate" BP. Don't reassure yourself by BP alone. Escalate low-CI states early; RV can decompensate suddenly.

cards.title: Prosthetic Valve Endocarditis
cards.quickAnswer: PVE = infection of prosthetic valve (mechanical, tissue, or TAVR); 1–6% lifetime incidence. Fever in any prosthetic valve patient = PVE until proven otherwise. Workup: 3 sets blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics; TEE is mandatory (sensitivity ~90% vs TTE ~50%); FDG-PET/CT now major Duke-ISCVID 2023 criterion (glucose uptake at valve). Empiric ABX: vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampin essential for staph (biofilm penetration). 6-week course. Surgical threshold LOWER than native: any prosthetic dehiscence, persistent bacteremia, abscess, fistula, or large vegetation requires urgent CT surgery consult. Mortality 20–40%.

cards.sourcePrecedence: Duke-ISCVID 2023 (Fowler et al.) → 2015 AHA IE Guideline (Baddour et al.) → ESC/EACTS NVE/PVE consensus → institution policy

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, clinical context.

  • Definition: Microbial infection of a surgically placed prosthetic valve (mechanical, bioprosthetic tissue, or transcatheter aortic valve [TAVR]). Ranges from valve vegetation to paravalvular abscess, ring abscess, dehiscence, and septic emboli.
  • Incidence: 0.3–1.2% per patient-year (varies by valve type and care setting). Lifetime incidence 1–6%.
  • Early PVE (< 12 months post-implant): nosocomial origin; staph epidermidis, staph aureus, gram-negatives, fungal.
  • Late PVE (> 12 months): community-acquired; viridans streptococcus, enterococcus, staph aureus (similar to native endocarditis).
  • Mortality: 20–40% despite appropriate therapy (higher than native valve endocarditis at 15–20%).
  • Clinical significance: Post-operative or hospitalized prosthetic valve patient with fever is a medical emergency. Early diagnosis and treatment reduce mortality; surgical intervention often required.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Why prosthetic valve endocarditis occurs — mechanism and risk factors.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Early PVE (< 12 months post-implant):

  • Perioperative bacteremia from surgical site, indwelling lines, contaminated prosthetic material
  • Seeding at sewing ring (most common for ring abscess), mechanical pivot points, valve surface
  • Early colonization of prosthetic material (biofilm formation)
  • Nosocomial pathogens: staph epidermidis (device-related, most common early), staph aureus (more aggressive), gram-negatives, Candida

Late PVE (> 12 months post-implant):

  • Transient bacteremia from dental work, GI/GU procedures, poor dental hygiene, community infection
  • Community pathogens: viridans streptococcus, enterococcus, staph aureus
  • Pathophysiology similar to native endocarditis

sections.heading: Progression
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Bacteremia → seeding of prosthetic valve surface
  2. Vegetation formation (friable, prone to embolization)
  3. Ring abscess or annular abscess (especially aortic root, threatens conduction system)
  4. Prosthetic dehiscence (sewing ring separation; risk of catastrophic regurgitation)
  5. Paravalvular leaks (new or worsening from active infection)
  6. Septic emboli → stroke (most common embolic sequela), peripheral emboli, splenic/renal infarcts
  7. Aortic root abscess → conduction delay, PR prolongation, high-degree AV block (surgical emergency)

sections.heading: Risk amplification in prosthetic material
sections.bodyHtml:
• Biofilm formation: prosthetic material permits biofilm organization, protecting bacteria from antibiotics (reason for higher antibiotic doses and need for adjunctive rifampin)
  • Sewing ring inflammation: most prosthetic infections localize at the sewing ring interface with native tissue
  • TAVR-specific: stent frame in aortic annulus increases ring abscess risk compared to surgical prosthetics

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Who presents with PVE and what they look like.

sections.heading: Presentation (often subacute, may be indolent)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Constitutional symptoms (common; may be insidious): fever (80–90%; may be low-grade or absent in chronic cases), chills, malaise, fatigue, weight loss, night sweats
  • Cardiac symptoms: new or changing murmur (regurgitation from valve damage/dehiscence, paravalvular leak), dyspnea, orthopnea, palpitations, syncope (if heart block from abscess)
  • Embolic phenomena (20–40% of PVE): ischemic stroke (most common embolic event), TIA, peripheral arterial emboli, splenic/renal infarcts
  • Conduction abnormality: new PR prolongation, bundle branch block, or high-degree AV block (red flag for aortic root abscess)
  • Signs of heart failure: acute or progressive hemodynamic decompensation from large paravalvular leak or valve dysfunction

sections.heading: Physical exam findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Fever (may be absent in chronic or immunocompromised patients)
  • New or changing cardiac murmur: regurgitant murmur from valve damage or paravalvular leak
  • Peripheral stigmata (less common in PVE than native endocarditis): splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, petechiae
  • Splenomegaly (from emboli or chronic infection)
  • New arrhythmia on exam or by report

sections.heading: When to suspect PVE at the bedside
sections.bodyHtml:
• Post-discharge phone call: patient with prosthetic valve reports fever, new dyspnea, or malaise
  • Readmission: patient with prosthetic valve + fever, even if "stable" appearing
  • Incidental finding: new murmur or unexplained sepsis in known prosthetic valve patient
  • Post-operative complication: fever > POD 3 in prosthetic valve surgery patient is high-risk for early PVE

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. Target: 5 minutes at bedside or during phone screen.

  • Vital signs: temperature (core preferred), HR, BP, respiratory rate, SpO₂
  • Cardiac exam: auscultation for murmur (location, timing, radiation), apical-radial pulse deficit, JVD, peripheral edema
  • Neurologic screen: alert and oriented, focal deficits, speech, cranial nerves
  • Signs of sepsis: capillary refill, skin perfusion, lactate if available
  • Recent history: timing of prosthetic valve implant, prior endocarditis, recent procedures (dental, GI, GU)
  • Recent labs (if available): WBC, CRP, ESR, baseline creatinine, baseline blood cultures if already drawn
  • MAR review (if inpatient): current antibiotics, fever curve, recent cultures
  • Valve history: prosthetic type (mechanical vs tissue), location (aortic, mitral, tricuspid), TAVR vs surgical

sections.heading: 5A. Diagnosis Workup — Mandatory immediate steps
sections.bodyHtml:
Do NOT delay diagnosis for imaging. Start workup in parallel.

  1. Blood cultures (STAT) — draw 3 sets from separate venipunctures BEFORE antibiotics - Standard timing: if intermittently febrile, draw during fever spike if possible - If antibiotics already given: wait minimum 48 hours before recultivating - Culture sensitivity 85–95% in PVE (higher than native endocarditis)

  2. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) — urgent, within 24 hours - TTE sensitivity only 50–60% in prosthetic patients (acoustic window obscured by prosthesis)

    • TEE sensitivity 90–95% — detects vegetations, ring abscesses, paravalvular leaks, dehiscence
    • Order: "Evaluate for endocarditis; rule out prosthetic valve pathology"
    • Look for: new vegetation, prosthetic dehiscence (rocking motion), paravalvular leak (new or enlarged), annular/ring abscess (anechoic space at sewing ring), restricted leaflet motion

  3. Electrocardiography (ECG) — STAT - Red flags: new or progressive PR prolongation, bundle branch block, high-degree AV block (suggests aortic root abscess → surgical emergency) - Baseline for comparison during therapy

  4. FDG-PET/CT — emerging major Duke-ISCVID 2023 diagnostic criterion - Detect metabolic activity (glucose uptake) at prosthetic site - Particularly useful if TEE non-diagnostic or clinical suspicion remains high despite negative TEE - Timing: typically after 2 weeks of antibiotics for optimal specificity - Sensitivity 90–95% in recent series

  5. Laboratory studies

    • CBC (anemia, elevated WBC — not specific)
    • CMP (renal function baseline, LFTs)
    • ESR, CRP (baseline; helpful for monitoring response to therapy)
    • Baseline echocardiogram if not already done

sections.heading: 5B. Empiric Antibiotics
sections.bodyHtml: Start ONLY AFTER 3 sets of blood cultures obtained. Empiric regimen covers early and late PVE organisms pending culture results.

sections.heading: Empiric Coverage (Staph epidermidis + CoNS presumption for early PVE)
sections.bodyHtml:
Organism / Scenario Antibiotic Regimen Duration Notes
Early PVE empiric (presumed CoNS/staph) Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h + rifampin 300–600 mg IV q8h + gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV 6 weeks Add rifampin for biofilm penetration. Vancomycin trough goal 15–20 mcg/mL. Monitor renal function closely (gentamicin nephrotoxicity).
Staph aureus (oxacillin-sensitive, if susceptible) Oxacillin/nafcillin 2 g IV q4h + rifampin 300–600 mg IV q8h + gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV 6 weeks More aggressive than native IE due to prosthetic material biofilm. Rifampin essential.
Staph aureus (MRSA confirmed) Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg/dose q8–12h + rifampin 300–600 mg IV q8h + gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV 6 weeks Higher mortality than susceptible staph. Ensure adequate vancomycin levels.
Viridans streptococcus Penicillin G 4 million units IV q4h + gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV (for first 2 weeks) 6 weeks Gentamicin synergy for first 2 weeks, then PCN alone if susceptible.
Enterococcus Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h + gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV 6 weeks Synergy required — do not use monotherapy. Watch gentamicin levels.
Fungal (empirically suspected; culture pending) Amphotericin B IV + surgical consultation IMMEDIATELY Surgery preferred Fungal PVE has very high mortality with medical therapy alone. Early valve replacement is standard. Do not delay surgery for antibiotic trial.

sections.heading: Key adjunctive therapy
sections.bodyHtml:
• Rifampin 300–600 mg IV q8h — strongly recommended as adjunct for ALL staph PVE (enhances biofilm penetration; crucial for prosthetic-associated infection). Do not omit.
  • Gentamicin — 3 mg/kg/day IV (or per institutional gentamicin dosing protocol); monitor renal function, peak/trough levels per protocol
  • Vancomycin — goal trough 15–20 mcg/mL for endocarditis (higher than standard infection threshold); monitor levels q3–5 days
  • Monitoring: ECG every 3–5 days or if new symptoms; increasing PR interval or new block → abscess extension → notify CT surgery urgently

sections.heading: Drug interactions & considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Rifampin CYP3A4 inducer: reduces effectiveness of warfarin, statins, oral contraceptives; coordinate with pharmacist/provider if patient on any of these
  • Gentamicin nephrotoxicity: check BUN/Cr baseline, at 1 week, then q1–2 weeks; report rising creatinine to team
  • Vancomycin infusion reaction: slow infusion rate if patient reports flushing, pain at site

sections.heading: 5C. Distinguishing Early vs. Late PVE — Guides empiric organism coverage
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature Early PVE (< 12 mo post-op) Late PVE (> 12 mo)
Origin Nosocomial; perioperative Community-acquired
Common organisms Staph epidermidis, staph aureus, gram-negatives, fungal Viridans strep, enterococcus, staph aureus
Empiric coverage Vanc + gent + rifampin Can start PCN-based if low-risk, but empiric vanc safer
Mortality Higher (~25–40%) Somewhat lower (~20–30%)
Ring abscess incidence Higher Lower
Surgical urgency Often earlier Often medical initially, surgery if complications

sections.heading: 5D. Surgical Indications — **LOWER threshold than native endocarditis**
sections.bodyHtml:
Class I Indications (strong — consider surgery immediately):

  • Prosthetic valve dehiscence (any degree, even if hemodynamically stable) — high risk of catastrophic regurgitation and cardiogenic shock
  • Ring abscess or annular abscess (especially aortic root) — impinging on conduction system or causing structural instability; medical therapy fails
  • Paravalvular abscess with significant hemodynamic consequence or septic foci not responding to antibiotics
  • Fungal endocarditis (Candida, Aspergillus, Histoplasmosis) — medical therapy nearly always fails; needs early surgery
  • Uncontrolled sepsis despite appropriate antibiotics (recurrent bacteremia, persistent fever > 7–10 days, persistent emboli)
  • Severe prosthetic valve regurgitation causing pulmonary edema or cardiogenic shock
  • Recurrent septic emboli despite appropriate antibiotics (indicates large/friable vegetation)
  • Difficult-to-treat organisms (Coxiella, Brucella, Mycobacterium, fastidious gram-negatives)

Class IIa Indications (moderate — involve CT surgery urgently):

  • Large vegetations (> 10 mm) with high embolic risk
  • Prosthetic aortic valve PVE with paravalvular leak (higher risk of extension to root)
  • Persistently positive blood cultures beyond 48 hours of appropriate therapy

Surgical approach:

  • Timing: ideally within 48 hours of decision to operate; delay only if acute hemorrhagic stroke (discuss with neurosurgery)
  • Procedure: removal of prosthetic valve + all infected tissue, extensive debridement of abscess cavities, valve replacement (may use allograft if extensive aortic root involvement), reconstruction of aortic root/mitral annulus as needed
  • Mortality: in-hospital mortality 5–15% for early surgery vs 50%+ if delayed
  • Contact: notify CT surgery immediately if any Class I indication present; they will advise on timing and operative readiness

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template (to call provider/CT surgery):

S: "Dr. [name], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], [timing relative to prosthetic valve implant]." B: "Patient with [valve type] prosthetic [location] developed fever at [time]. Temperature [value], HR [value], BP [value]. Blood cultures obtained × [number] sets. TEE [status — pending/done, findings]." A: "[Stable / unstable]. [Symptoms: chest pain, dyspnea, neuro change, murmur]. Recent [meds, pertinent labs]." R: "Requesting [rate vs rhythm plan / urgent TEE / CT surgery consult / additional labs / STAT cardioversion]."

Who to call — escalation matrix

Clinical Scenario Immediate Contact Secondary
Suspected PVE with fever (stable) Attending or APP (infectious disease/cardiology preferred) —
Fever + hemodynamic instability STAT: CT surgery + APP + rapid response ICU if not already there
New high-degree AV block + fever STAT: CT surgery (aortic root abscess) Cardiology for pacing bridge
Recurrent/persistent fever despite ABX × 7–10 days CT surgery (consider surgical intervention) Infectious disease for organism review
Fungal cultures returned STAT: CT surgery (plan early surgery) Infectious disease
Post-op prosthetic valve patient, fever POD 1–3 Attending surgeon first, then infectious disease

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Expandable sections for detailed learning.

Expanded pathophysiology — biofilm formation and why rifampin matters

sections.heading: Biofilm and antibiotic resistance
sections.bodyHtml:
Prosthetic material (mechanical, tissue, TAVR stent) permits biofilm formation — a protected, matrix-enclosed bacterial community resistant to single-agent antibiotics and immune clearance.

  • Native valve endocarditis: bacteria adhere loosely to valve leaflets; antibiotics penetrate well
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis: bacteria colonize sewing ring and prosthetic surface, forming biofilm; penetration of standard beta-lactams and glycopeptides is poor

Rifampin's role:

  • Lipophilic (crosses biofilm matrix well)
  • Inhibits bacterial RNA polymerase
  • Achieves high intracellular and biofilm concentrations
  • Essential adjunct for staph (esp. CoNS) and must not be omitted from empiric regimen

Evidence: Rifampin adjunct reduces relapse rates in prosthetic staph endocarditis compared to dual therapy alone.

TTE vs. TEE sensitivity in PVE — why TTE fails

sections.heading: Why TTE is insufficient for PVE diagnosis
sections.bodyHtml:
TTE (transthoracic) sensitivity in prosthetic valves: ~50%

  • Acoustic windows obscured by metallic or large tissue prosthesis
  • Cannot adequately visualize sewing ring or paravalvular region
  • Vegetations on prosthetics are often small and may be echogenic (hard to distinguish from prosthetic material)
  • Posterior structures (mitral annulus, posterior annular abscess) poorly imaged from transthoracic approach

TEE (transesophageal) sensitivity in prosthetic valves: ~90–95%

  • Proximity of esophageal probe to left atrium and posterior heart structures
  • Superior resolution of mitral annulus, paravalvular region, sewing ring
  • Can detect even small vegetations, early abscess cavities
  • Can assess degree of dehiscence (rocking motion) in real time
  • Gold standard for prosthetic valve evaluation

Clinical implication: If TEE is ordered for "rule out endocarditis" in a prosthetic valve patient and the order says "TTE," escalate to provider. Insist on TEE.

FDG-PET/CT as emerging major Duke-ISCVID 2023 criterion

sections.heading: Duke-ISCVID 2023 updates relevant to PVE
sections.bodyHtml:
New major criterion: FDG-PET/CT showing intense glucose uptake at prosthetic site (or cardiac implantable device) now counts as a major diagnostic criterion (previously only echo findings were major).

Mechanism: Inflammation and infection at the prosthetic valve cause increased glucose metabolism; PET detects this signal with high sensitivity (90–95%).

Timing: Perform after 2 weeks of antibiotics (allows for some inflammatory resolution and improves specificity over acute phase).

When to consider:

  • TEE non-diagnostic or inconclusive
  • Clinical suspicion remains very high despite negative TEE
  • Fever persists despite negative blood cultures and TEE
  • Evaluating for mycotic aneurysms or septic emboli to other organs

Duke criteria now include:

  • Major: blood culture positive (2 typical organisms, OR 1 persistent) + echocardiography findings + FDG-PET/CT uptake
  • Diagnosis: ≥ 2 major OR ≥ 1 major + ≥ 3 minor

Early vs. late PVE pathogen profiles and empiric strategy

sections.heading: Early PVE organisms (nosocomial)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Staph epidermidis (30–40%) — coagulase-negative, from skin flora or contaminated lines; relatively less virulent but resistant to many antibiotics
  • Staph aureus (20–30%) — more aggressive; higher mortality, higher embolic rate, higher ring abscess incidence
  • Gram-negatives (E. coli, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella) — nosocomial sources (UTI, respiratory, abdominal seeding)
  • Fungal (Candida, Aspergillus) — indwelling lines, TPN, immunosuppression; very poor prognosis with medical therapy alone

Empiric strategy for early PVE: Assume coagulase-negative staph (most common) and start vanc + gent + rifampin immediately.

sections.heading: Late PVE organisms (community)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Viridans streptococcus (30–40%) — oral flora; most common cause of late PVE
  • Staph aureus (20–25%) — dental/skin sources; more common in late than early
  • Enterococcus (10–15%) — GI or GU source
  • HACEK group — fastidious gram-negatives; require prolonged culture

Empiric strategy for late PVE: Still safer to start vanc + gent; can narrow to penicillin once viridans strep identified.

Prosthetic valve thrombosis vs. endocarditis — differential

sections.heading: Thrombosis mimics PVE
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanical prosthetic valves can develop acute thrombosis without infection, presenting with:

  • New or worsening regurgitation
  • Dyspnea
  • Hemodynamic instability

Red flags for thrombosis (not endocarditis):

  • Recent interruption of anticoagulation
  • Subtherapeutic INR (if on warfarin) or missed DOAC dose
  • No fever or only low-grade fever
  • Blood cultures negative
  • No vegetation on TEE; just leaflet immobility or reduced excursion

Key distinction:

  • Thrombosis: mechanical cause; treat with anticoagulation, consider thrombolysis or surgery if unstable
  • Endocarditis: infectious cause; requires antibiotics and often surgery

Both can occur simultaneously — be vigilant. If TTE/TEE shows mechanical dysfunction + fever + positive cultures, it's endocarditis until proven otherwise.

Annular/ring abscess complications — fistula formation and conduction system involvement

sections.heading: Ring abscess — structure and consequence
sections.bodyHtml:
Aortic root ring abscess (most common location for ring abscess):

  • Anechoic space adjacent to sewing ring, visible on TEE
  • Represents infected cavity extending into aortic root tissue or extending toward left ventricle
  • Risk: extension to conduction system (AV node, bundle of His)

Conduction consequences:

  • Progressive PR prolongation (earliest sign)
  • Bundle branch block
  • High-degree or complete AV block (emergency — risk of asystole)
  • Temporary pacemaker often required as bridge to surgery

Fistula formation (rare but catastrophic):

  • Aortic root abscess ruptures into left ventricle (aorta-to-LV fistula)
  • Or into right atrium (aorta-to-RA fistula)
  • Presents as acute hemodynamic collapse, large "shunt" physiology
  • Diagnosis: color Doppler on TEE shows flow across fistulous tract
  • Requires emergent surgical repair

On TEE, look for: anechoic space at sewing ring, color flow across fistulous tract, septal involvement.

CIED (pacemaker/ICD) leads and valve endocarditis — lead extraction decisions

sections.heading: Prosthetic valve endocarditis + CIED leads
sections.bodyHtml:
If patient has both a prosthetic valve AND a pacemaker or ICD:

  • Lead-associated endocarditis risk: infected device leads can seed the prosthetic valve or vice versa
  • Management complexity: may require both valve replacement AND lead extraction (high-risk procedure)
  • Lead extraction timing: usually concurrent with or shortly after valve surgery
  • Consultation: electrophysiology + CT surgery must coordinate

Red flags:

  • Negative blood cultures but patient has pacing leads + fever → think lead endocarditis seeding valve
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis + prior CIED → high suspicion for lead involvement

Workup: Blood cultures, TEE (assess lead position, vegetations), ECG.

Homograft vs. mechanical vs. tissue replacement options after valve explant

sections.heading: Surgical replacement options in prosthetic valve endocarditis
sections.bodyHtml:
When infected prosthetic valve must be removed, the surgeon chooses a replacement:

  • Mechanical valve: durable; requires lifelong anticoagulation; risk of thrombosis if INR not therapeutic post-op (already high-risk population)
  • Tissue (bioprosthetic): no anticoagulation required; but degenerates; limited lifespan (10–20 years)
  • Allograft (homograft): cadaveric human valve; excellent for endocarditis (low reinfection rate); superior hemodynamics; but limited supply, higher cost, eventual degeneration

Allograft preference in endocarditis, especially:

  • Extensive aortic root involvement requiring root replacement
  • Fungal or fastidious gram-negative endocarditis
  • Recurrent endocarditis (higher reinfection risk with mechanical/tissue)

Consult with surgeon on choice — depends on anatomy, extent of infection, patient factors.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Watch for these signs; if any appear, re-escalate to provider/CT surgery.

  • Progressive PR prolongation on serial ECGs — suggests evolving aortic root abscess extending toward conduction system; may presage complete heart block
  • New bundle branch block or high-degree AV block — aortic root abscess impinging on conduction; cardiac emergency; notify CT surgery immediately
  • Fever persisting > 7–10 days despite appropriate antibiotics — suggests uncontrolled infection; consider surgical intervention
  • Recurrent positive blood cultures after 48 hours of appropriate therapy — resistant organism or infected emboli; CT surgery consult
  • Worsening dyspnea or new pulmonary edema on stable regimen — paravalvular leak enlarging or dehiscence developing; may presage acute decompensation
  • New neurologic deficit (weakness, speech change, facial droop) — septic emboli; stroke code + neurology + CT surgery
  • Hypotension unresponsive to fluids on stable antibiotics — sepsis worsening or acute valve dysfunction; may need ICU escalation
  • New arrhythmia or change in baseline rhythm — infection spreading to myocardium or pericardium; obtain ECG and notify provider
  • Rising inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) despite appropriate therapy — suggests inadequate source control; may need imaging (repeat TEE, FDG-PET) or surgery

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Fever in any prosthetic valve patient = PVE until proven otherwise. Do not assume viral, UTI, or "low-risk" infection. Escalate immediately. This is the #1 bedside pearl.

  2. Blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics — non-negotiable. Positive in 85–95% of PVE. Delaying antibiotics by 1–2 hours to obtain cultures is acceptable and standard of care. Compromising this step is a common error.

  3. TTE is insufficient for prosthetic valve endocarditis. TEE is mandatory. TTE sensitivity is only ~50%; TEE ~90–95%. If attending orders "echo" without specifying TEE, escalate and clarify.

  4. FDG-PET/CT is now a major Duke-ISCVID 2023 criterion for PVE diagnosis. If TEE is non-diagnostic or clinical suspicion remains very high, discuss PET/CT with cardiology/infectious disease.

  5. Rifampin is ESSENTIAL for all staph PVE (CoNS and aureus). Biofilm formation on prosthetic material requires this drug. Do not omit. If your regimen is missing rifampin, escalate to pharmacy/ID.

  6. Early PVE (< 12 months) is often CoNS, resistant, and aggressive. Empiric vanc + gent + rifampin. Late PVE may be viridans strep (PCN-susceptible), but still safer to start vanc empirically until culture results available.

  7. TAVR-PVE is rising in incidence. Do not assume TAVR patients are "lower risk." Management is identical to surgical prosthetics. Same workup, same antibiotics, same surgical thresholds.

  8. Ring abscess or annular abscess = surgical emergency. TEE findings of an anechoic space at the sewing ring, especially aortic, indicate tissue destruction and risk of catastrophic dehiscence. CT surgery must be notified immediately.

  9. New complete heart block + fever in prosthetic valve patient = aortic root abscess until proven otherwise. Temporary pacemaker is a bridge; surgery is definitive. Do not delay. Notify CT surgery STAT.

  10. Prosthetic valve dehiscence (rocking motion on TEE) = urgent surgery needed, even if hemodynamically stable at diagnosis. Risk of sudden massive regurgitation and cardiogenic shock is high. Ideally within 24 hours.

  11. Fungal endocarditis (Candida, Aspergillus) almost always requires surgery. Medical therapy fails. If fungal cultures return, alert CT surgery immediately. Plan surgery, not continued medical management alone.

  12. Mortality is 20–40% in PVE. Higher than native (15–20%). Have conversations with patients/families early about gravity of diagnosis, prognosis, and need for possible surgery.

  13. Paravalvular leak = surgical indicator if new or worsening. A small paravalvular leak may be stable pre-PVE. But new or enlarged paravalvular leak during endocarditis = active infection at sewing ring. Usually requires surgery.

  14. Antibiotic compliance is critical for 6-week course. Missed doses can result in relapse. If patient misses a dose, notify team; do not "double up" next dose. Teach patient the stakes.

  15. Antibiotic prophylaxis is lifelong for prosthetic valve patients. Any dental, GI/GU, or invasive procedure requires prophylaxis. Provide a wallet card at discharge. This is post-discharge prevention that saves lives.

cards.title: Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS)
cards.quickAnswer: A 10-point scale (−5 to +4) measuring sedation level and agitation in a single assessment. Positive scores indicate agitation (+1 to +4); zero is alert and calm; negative scores indicate deepening sedation (−1 to −5). Target for most post-cardiac patients is −1 to 0 (calm, alert). RASS is mandatory *before* CAM-ICU delirium screening (RASS must be ≥ −3 for CAM-ICU validity). Key pitfall: hypoactive delirium often scores −1 to −2 and is mistaken for "sedated"—always pair RASS with CAM-ICU assessment.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: A 10-point scale (−5 to +4) measuring sedation level and agitation in a single assessment. Positive scores indicate agitation (+1 to +4); zero is alert and calm; negative scores indicate deepening sedation (−1 to −5). Target for most post-cardiac patients is −1 to 0 (calm, alert). RASS is mandatory before CAM-ICU delirium screening (RASS must be ≥ −3 for CAM-ICU validity). Key pitfall: hypoactive delirium often scores −1 to −2 and is mistaken for "sedated"—always pair RASS with CAM-ICU assessment.
cards.sourcePrecedence: Sessler et al. (2002) → Ely et al. (2001, 2003) → SCCM PADIS (2013) → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → AACN Delirium Guideline (2016)

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml: The Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) is a 10-point, one-dimensional tool for rapid, objective assessment of consciousness and behavioral state. Originally developed and validated for mechanically ventilated ICU patients (Sessler et al., 2002), it has been extended to stepdown units and non-intubated populations. RASS scores span a spectrum from violent agitation (+4) to unarousable deep sedation (−5), with alert and calm at zero. It is the required first step in the CAM-ICU screening algorithm (Ely et al., 2003): a patient must achieve RASS ≥ −3 before CAM-ICU assessment is valid. RASS is also foundational to the SCCM PADIS (Pain, Agitation, Delirium, Infection, Sleep) bundle (Barr et al., 2013), which guides evidence-based sedation and cognitive support in post-acute care.

sections.heading: 2. The 10-Point RASS Scale
sections.bodyHtml:
Score Label Description Observation
+4 Combative Violent; openly combative with staff, physically aggressive Patient attacks staff; requires restraint or sedation urgently
+3 Very Agitated Pulls or removes tubing; aggressive behavior toward staff Yanks IV lines, ETT, catheters; may strike
+2 Agitated Frequent non-purposeful movement; fights ventilator Restless, thrashing limbs; resists care; agitated speech
+1 Restless Anxious, apprehensive; no aggression Writhes in bed; seeks attention; worried expression
0 Alert and Calm Spontaneously awakens; calm; engaged with environment Follows commands; eye contact; conversant; relaxed
−1 Drowsy Sustained eye opening to verbal stimulation (> 10 s); aware of surroundings Call name: eyes open sluggishly, then drift closed
−2 Light Sedation Briefly opens eyes to verbal stimulation (< 10 s); no sustained awareness Call name: brief eye opening, then closes immediately
−3 Moderate Sedation Movement or eye opening to physical stimulation; no response to voice Shake arm: opens eyes or moves; voice does not arouse
−4 Deep Sedation No response to voice; movement only to vigorous/repeated physical stimulation Vigorous sternal rub or arm shake: minimal or no response
−5 Unarousable No response to voice or physical stimulation Unresponsive; no arousal to any stimulus

sections.heading: 3. Target RASS Ranges by Clinical Scenario
sections.bodyHtml:
Patient Group Target RASS Clinical Intent CAM-ICU Pairing
Most post-cardiac (routine CAD, valve) −1 to 0 Calm, alert; ready for mobility; baseline cognition evident RASS score q shift minimum; if positive → assess delirium presence
High-risk delirium (advanced age, dementia, prior ICU) −1 to 0 Same target; enhanced monitoring; early recognition CAM-ICU q shift if RASS ≥ −3; escalate if CAM-ICU positive
Intentional post-op sedation (pain, anxiety control) −2 to −3 Comfort while maintaining arousability; brief window (POD 0–1) Not assessable for delirium; reassess daily for wean plan
Neuro vigilance (DHCA, stroke, neuro injury) −1 to 0 Alert for early deficit detection; deeper sedation masks focal changes Continuous CAM-ICU vigilance if delirium high-risk
Weaning from sedation / mechanical support −1 to 0 Awake for respiratory effort, cough, mobilization; avoid over-sedation Assess readiness q shift using RASS + CAM-ICU fork

Key principle: Deeper sedation (−3 or below) excludes safe early mobility. Avoid −3 or deeper unless specific indication (refractory agitation, high ventilation demand, seizure risk).

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use — Integration with Delirium Bundle
Assessment Protocol (observe-only)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Observe the patient without interaction. Note spontaneous arousal, purposefulness, agitation.
  2. Call name at normal conversational volume. Watch for eye opening, responsiveness, latency.
  3. Shake gently (if no voice response) at shoulder or sternal region. Note movement or eye opening.
  4. Score and document on flowsheet with time; note any triggers (pain, anxiety, hypoxia, medication change).

sections.heading: Minimum Frequency & CAM-ICU Coupling
sections.bodyHtml:
• Minimum: once per shift on routine patients; q4–6h if score < −2 or > +1 to detect deterioration or emergence.
  • Mandatory CAM-ICU requirement: RASS must be ≥ −3 for CAM-ICU assessment to be valid. If RASS ≤ −4, patient cannot be assessed for delirium; document "Unable to assess CAM-ICU — RASS at [score]."
  • Titration decision fork: RASS +1 or higher → assess cause (pain, anxiety, infection); RASS 0 to −1 → maintain current plan; RASS −2 to −3 → plan wean unless contraindicated; RASS ≤ −4 → exclude from mobility, reassess q4h.

sections.heading: ABCDEF Bundle Mapping
sections.bodyHtml:
Bundle Element RASS Connection
A — Assess pain RASS +1 to +2 may reflect pain agitation; distinguish from other causes
B — Both SAT & SBT RASS −1 to 0 enables safe spontaneous breathing trial and oxygen weaning
C — Choice of sedation Avoid benzodiazepines; they drive RASS negative and increase delirium risk despite "target" sedation
D — Delirium screening CAM-ICU requires RASS ≥ −3; pair RASS score with CAM-ICU result q shift if high-risk
E — Early mobility Exclude from mobility if RASS ≤ −3; target −1 to 0 for safe supervised movement
F — Family & sleep RASS −1 to 0 enables effective family communication and sleep hygiene interventions

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Inter-rater variability and calibration (10 sec rule) Discrepancy between two raters on the same patient can be ±1 to ±2 points without training. The critical discriminator is the 10-second sustained eye-opening threshold at RASS −1 (Drowsy) vs RASS −2 (Light Sedation). Standard definition: "sustained" means > 10 seconds; "brief" means < 10 seconds. Calibrate your team early with case examples and paired scoring on the same patient to minimize drift.
Dementia baseline and individual differences A patient with advanced dementia may score −2 at baseline (drowsy, slow to respond) when fully awake for them. Know the prior baseline from family or chart; don't assume all −2 means "over-sedated." Serial RASS compared to patient baseline is more clinically useful than absolute score alone.
Sensory adaptation — hearing loss, language barriers Shouting does not improve RASS scoring. Use gestures, visual stimuli (eye-to-eye contact, pointing), or substitute tactile stimulation early (gentle shake, sternal touch). Involve interpreter if available for non-English-speaking patients; language barrier can artificially lower apparent responsiveness.
Hypoactive delirium — the hidden trap Hypoactive delirium (disoriented, withdrawn, slow) often scores RASS −1 to −2 and is mistaken for "sedated." The patient is conscious but cognitively abnormal. Pair RASS with CAM-ICU every time. If CAM-ICU is positive but RASS −1 to 0, you have delirium, not sedation. Treat underlying cause (infection, hypoxia, medications, dehydration), not with more sedation.
Benzodiazepine paradox — negative RASS + positive delirium A benzodiazepine given for anxiety may lower RASS to −2 while simultaneously worsening delirium risk. This is the "chemical restraint" trap. Prefer non-pharmacologic strategies (orientation, family presence, mobility, sleep hygiene) or opioids for pain-driven agitation.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Inter-rater drift is silent. Without explicit team calibration on the 10-second eye-opening rule, RASS scores will drift ±1 to ±2 points between staff. Spot-check paired ratings q month.

  2. Dementia changes baseline consciousness. A patient's "normal" RASS may be −2 (drowsy) due to cognitive impairment, not over-sedation. Always ask family: "Is this how they usually are?"

  3. Hypoactive delirium is the missed diagnosis on the floor. Withdrawn, slow, disoriented patients score −1 to −2 and clinicians assume "sedated." Pair RASS with CAM-ICU—if CAM-ICU positive, it's delirium, not sedation.

  4. RASS ≤ −3 means "not assessable for delirium." CAM-ICU requires arousal to command. If RASS −4 or −5, note on chart: "Unable to assess CAM-ICU — RASS [score]." Don't force CAM-ICU; instead, focus on sedation wean.

  5. Benzos + RASS = dilemma. Benzodiazepines lower RASS but increase delirium risk. Use only for refractory agitation or seizure prophylaxis; prefer acetaminophen, NSAIDs, opioids, and non-pharmacologic measures.

  6. Over-sedation causes delirium and deconditioning. Patients held at RASS −2 to −3 for convenience develop ICU-acquired weakness, contractures, and prolonged delirium on emergence. Target −1 to 0 unless contraindicated.

  7. Target RASS must be explicitly documented. Write on daily sign-out: "RASS target −1 to 0; current −1; on track" or "RASS target −1 to 0; current −3; plan wean sedatives POD 2." Prevents team drift and supports accountability.

  8. The −3-or-below mobility rule is a hard stop. Mobilizing a patient at RASS −4 (deep sedation, minimally arousable) is unsafe and futile. Wait for RASS ≥ −2 before supervised ambulation; this is a non-negotiable safety criterion.

  9. Rewarming, low potassium, and pain masquerade as agitation. POD 0 hypothermia, low K⁺, and uncontrolled pain may drive RASS to +1 or +2 (restless, agitated). Don't reflexively sedate; correct temperature, potassium, pain, and hypoxia first.

  10. Hearing loss and language barriers lower apparent RASS. A deaf patient or non-English speaker may score −1 to −2 not from sedation but from inability to process verbal stimuli. Use visual, gestural, or tactile assessment; involve interpreter if needed.
