cards.title: Restrictive Cardiomyopathy and Cardiac Amyloidosis
cards.quickAnswer: RCM is diastolic dysfunction without significant dilation; hallmark is apical sparing on echo ("cherry-on-top"). Infiltrative disease dominates: amyloid (ATTR wild-type/hereditary, AL), sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis. ATTR: 99mTc-PYP detects it; tafamidis/patisiran/vutrisiran/acoramidis are disease-modifying. AL: hematologic emergency; daratumumab-based chemotherapy + autologous stem cell transplant is paradigm-shifting. Critical differential: constrictive pericarditis — differentiate by echo (pericardial thickening), CMR (T1 mapping), cath (septal bounce). Preload-sensitive physiology: cautious diuresis, avoid negative inotropes, preserve atrial kick.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
ATTR: 99mTc-PYP detects it; tafamidis/patisiran/vutrisiran/acoramidis are disease-modifying.

AL: hematologic emergency; daratumumab-based chemotherapy + autologous stem cell transplant is paradigm-shifting.

Critical differential: constrictive pericarditis — differentiate by echo (pericardial thickening), CMR (T1 mapping), cath (septal bounce). Preload-sensitive physiology: cautious diuresis, avoid negative inotropes, preserve atrial kick.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF Guideline (Heidenreich et al., 2022) → Maurer ATTR-ACT trial (Maurer et al., 2018) → Adams patisiran RCT (Adams et al., 2018) → Witteles cardiac amyloid series (Witteles et al., 2019) → Kirklin cardiac surgery (Kirklin & Blackstone, 2026)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is a disorder of diastolic function characterized by stiff, noncompliant ventricles with elevated filling pressures, markedly impaired ventricular relaxation, and normal or mildly reduced ejection fraction. The ventricles cannot relax or fill adequately despite preserved contractility.

  • Epidemiology:

  • Rare compared to dilated or ischemic cardiomyopathy, but increasingly recognized due to amyloid screening advances.
  • Cardiac amyloidosis is now the most common cause of RCM in developed countries (Witteles et al., 2019).
  • ATTR amyloidosis: wild-type (senile, male >70), heritable (hereditary ATTR-v, age 40–60), or acquired — median survival wild-type ~70 years post-symptom onset; hereditary more aggressive.
  • AL (light-chain) amyloidosis: plasma cell dyscrasia; median age 65; median survival without treatment ~4 months if cardiac involvement; with daratumumab-based therapy, 3–4 years or better.

  • Other etiologies: cardiac sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, Loeffler endocarditis (eosinophilic), endomyocardial fibrosis (endemic regions), Fabry disease, radiation cardiomyopathy — collectively less common but each requires distinct workup and management.

  • Typical patient: Elderly male with dyspnea, orthopnea, right-sided heart failure, and red-flag systemic findings (carpal tunnel syndrome bilateral, spinal stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, autonomic dysfunction) initially labeled "HFpEF." Alternatively, younger patient with genetic ATTR variant or individual with known plasma cell disorder now presenting with cardiac decompensation.

  • When it matters: ICU admission for decompensated HF, pre-transplant optimization, amyloid-directed therapy initiation (tafamidis, patisiran, daratumumab), low-cardiac-output support, AF management, diuretic titration in preload-sensitive state, post-transplant immunosuppression monitoring.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner teaching on why this happens.

sections.heading: Core mechanism
sections.bodyHtml: Myocardial infiltration or fibrosis deposits non-contractile material into the interstitium and myocytes, obliterating compliance. Result: stiff ventricles unable to relax or fill, leading to elevated diastolic pressures, high atrial filling pressures, pulmonary and systemic congestion.

sections.heading: Amyloid pathophysiology (most common cause)
sections.bodyHtml:
Amyloid fibrils are misfolded protein polymers that aggregate in tissue. Two main forms in cardiac disease:

  • ATTR (transthyretin amyloidosis):
  • Wild-type (senile ATTR): normal transthyretin gene, but TTR protein misfolds and oligomerizes in aging. Male > female (8:1); age of onset typically 70–85.
  • Hereditary ATTR (ATTR-v): pathogenic TTR gene mutation inherited autosomal-dominant. Earlier onset (40–60), more aggressive systemic features (neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction). Val122Ile is the most common variant in Black Americans (2–4% prevalence); often misdiagnosed as wild-type.
  • Acquired ATTR: rarely, plasma cells produce misfolded TTR (very uncommon).

  • TTR stabilizers (tafamidis) slow amyloid deposition and progression; silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran, antisense) reduce TTR production at hepatic or mRNA level.

  • AL (light-chain amyloidosis):

  • Plasma cell dyscrasia produces monoclonal free light chains (kappa or lambda) that misfold and deposit systemically.
  • High mortality: cardiac involvement is worst prognosticator; untreated AL cardiomyopathy median survival 4 months.
  • Chemotherapy-responsive: daratumumab + bortezomib + dexamethasone is now standard, achieving high response rates and reversing some cardiac dysfunction (Heidenreich et al., 2022).
  • Autologous stem cell transplant (ASCT) considered for eligible patients, further improving outcomes.

sections.heading: Other infiltrative pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
• Sarcoidosis (cardiac): granulomas deposit in myocardium → inflammation, scar, RCM pattern. Steroids + immunosuppression reduce granuloma burden; arrhythmia risk is high.
  • Hemochromatosis (cardiac): excess iron deposits → fibrosis, restrictive physiology. Reversible with iron-lowering therapy (phlebotomy, chelation) if caught early.
  • Loeffler endocarditis (eosinophilic): eosinophil-mediated myocardial and endocardial inflammation → fibrosis, thrombus risk. Associated with hypereosinophilia (FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, lymphoma).
  • Endomyocardial fibrosis: endemic in Africa and parts of Asia; endocardial thickening and fibrosis progress to RCM or dilated cardiomyopathy; surgical stripping rarely beneficial.
  • Fabry disease (X-linked lysosomal storage): globotriaosylceramide accumulates in myocytes → RCM pattern. Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) slows progression if initiated early.

sections.heading: Pathophysiologic consequence: restrictive hemodynamics
sections.bodyHtml:
• ↑ Myocardial stiffness → impaired early diastolic relaxation and reduced mid/late diastolic filling
  • ↑ Diastolic filling pressures → pulmonary capillary wedge pressure rises → orthopnea, pulmonary congestion
  • Biatrial enlargement — compensatory dilation from chronic high filling pressures; dilated LA → AF risk
  • Low stroke volume from restricted filling → low cardiac output, fatigue, syncope on exertion
  • High venous pressure → peripheral edema, hepatic congestion, elevated JVP (hallmark > 10 cm, prominent y-descent)
  • AF propensity: inflamed or fibrotic atria favor ectopic activity; loss of atrial kick → 20–30% acute CO drop, decompensation

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

sections.heading: Cardiac symptoms
sections.bodyHtml:
• Dyspnea on exertion progressing to orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (pulmonary congestion from elevated LA pressure)
  • Right-sided HF symptoms: peripheral edema, hepatic congestion, elevated JVP (often > 10 cm, remarkable for prominent y-descent)
  • Low cardiac output: fatigue, exercise intolerance, exertional syncope (ominous; indicates critically low stroke volume)
  • Atrial fibrillation: new-onset or paroxysmal AF in 15–30% of amyloid patients; can trigger acute decompensation
  • Chest pain: atypical; amyloid infiltration can produce ischemia despite angiographically clean coronaries
  • Palpitations from AF or ectopy

sections.heading: Systemic red flags (amyloidosis-specific)
sections.bodyHtml:
These often precede cardiac diagnosis by years:

  • ATTR-specific (hereditary and wild-type):
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome (often bilateral); can precede cardiac symptoms by 5–10 years
  • Spinal stenosis (lumbar, lumbar radiculopathy)
  • Biceps/triceps tendon rupture (spontaneous or minor trauma)
  • Autonomic dysfunction: orthostatic hypotension, erectile dysfunction, GI dysmotility
  • Polyneuropathy (hereditary ATTR especially; small-fiber > large-fiber sensory predominance)

  • Vitreous amyloid: floaters, cloudy vision, ocular manifestations

  • AL-specific:

  • Fatigue, weight loss, anorexia
  • Neuropathy (length-dependent, distal sensory predominance)
  • Kidney involvement (proteinuria, renal insufficiency)
  • Liver involvement (hepatomegaly, LFT abnormality)
  • "Waxy" or infiltrated skin appearance

  • Macroglossia (classic but rare; massively enlarged tongue from amyloid infiltration)

  • Cardiac sarcoidosis:

  • Respiratory symptoms (dyspnea, cough)
  • Rash (erythema nodosum, lupus pernio)

  • Arthralgia, constitutional symptoms

  • Hemochromatosis:

  • Diabetes mellitus (iron-induced pancreatic beta-cell damage)
  • Arthropathy (especially metacarpophalangeal joints)
  • Sexual dysfunction (hypogonadism from iron overload)
  • Cirrhosis risk (if advanced), skin hyperpigmentation

sections.heading: Physical exam findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Elevated JVP (often > 10 cm, remarkable for prominent y-descent — rapid early diastolic filling followed by abrupt diastolic plateau from restrictive physiology)
  • Hepatomegaly — often pronounced; hepatic pulsatility from restrictive pattern
  • Peripheral edema, ascites if advanced
  • Quiet precordium — no prominent murmur; S3 and S4 may be present but faint (unlike dilated cardiomyopathy with prominent S3 gallop)
  • Pulse alternans possible (alternating beat-to-beat strength)
  • If AF present: irregularly irregular rhythm
  • Amyloid-specific: macroglossia (AL), vitreous haze or pupillary abnormalities (ATTR), signs of neuropathy (foot sensory level, autonomic), carpal tunnel signs

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / Gather Information*
sections.bodyHtml: Competent systematic diagnostic workup (no management actions yet).

sections.heading: Echocardiography — morphologic hallmark
sections.bodyHtml:
• LV structure: concentric, thick-walled LV with small cavity; preserved EF (often 50–65%); biatrial enlargement
  • Diastolic dysfunction pattern: restrictive filling — rapid early filling (E ↑), then plateau; E/A ratio > 1, deceleration time (DT) < 200 ms
  • Amyloid-specific echo sign: Apical sparing — preserved or increased apical longitudinal strain while basal and mid-LV is stiff (the "cherry-on-top" sign). Highly suggestive of amyloid; normal HCM and HFpEF do NOT show this pattern.
  • Doppler: high E/E' ratio (> 14), elevated LA pressure indices (LA volume index > 40), restrictive pattern
  • RV function: may be impaired; RV strain can predict worse outcomes in amyloid

sections.heading: Cardiac MRI (CMR) — tissue characterization
sections.bodyHtml:
Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) pattern:

Etiology LGE pattern Additional features
ATTR amyloidosis Diffuse subendocardial or transmural LGE; "stocking-glove" distribution Elevated native T1; global longitudinal strain impairment. Non-ischemic pattern.
AL amyloidosis Similar diffuse subendocardial/transmural LGE May show less dramatic pattern than ATTR; depends on disease burden.
Cardiac sarcoidosis Patchy, often basal inferior wall or scar-like; can mimic infarct May show wall motion abnormality; granuloma inflammatory activity on FGD-PET.
Hemochromatosis Global dark signal (iron deposition); T2* dramatically shortened Iron appears as signal void; T2* < 20 ms indicates significant iron overload.
Radiation cardiomyopathy Subepicardial or patchy fibrosis History of mediastinal radiation is key clue.
  • Pericardial thickness: helps rule out constrictive pericarditis (CP > 3 mm thickening; RCM pericardium normal or mildly thickened)
  • Tissue characterization: elevated native T1 in amyloidosis; shortened T2* in hemochromatosis
  • Strain imaging: global longitudinal strain impairment in infiltrative disease

sections.heading: ATTR-specific imaging: 99mTc-PYP scintigraphy
sections.bodyHtml:
• Gold standard for noninvasive ATTR detection. Cardiac uptake present in wild-type and hereditary ATTR; absent in AL amyloidosis and other RCM etiologies (Witteles et al., 2019).
  • Highly specific: positive predictive value > 95% for ATTR in a patient with cardiac phenotype.
  • Quantification: semi-quantitative (Perugini score 0–3) or fully quantitative uptake; helps grade disease burden.
  • NOT used in AL screening — PYP negative in AL amyloidosis.
  • Genetic testing: TTR gene sequencing if hereditary ATTR suspected (positive family history, early age, neuropathy). Identifies pathogenic variant and inheritance pattern for family counseling.

sections.heading: Biopsy — tissue diagnosis (when amyloid suspected)
sections.bodyHtml:
Biopsy type Gold standard? Sensitivity Risks Utility
Endomyocardial biopsy Yes, for cardiac amyloid 90–95% for amyloid; immunohistochemistry types (ATTR vs AL) Perforation (~0.5%), arrhythmia, VT Definitive; clarifies ATTR vs AL; allows immunotyping.
Fat pad subcutaneous No, but easy ~60–70% for AL; ~30–40% for ATTR Minimal Lower sensitivity but least invasive; useful screening.
Bone marrow biopsy No, but heme-onc-driven Diagnostic for plasma cell dyscrasia if AL Mild discomfort, infection rare Defines AL clone; guides chemo selection.

Staining and immunohistochemistry: Congo red staining + polarized light microscopy shows apple-green birefringence (pathognomonic for amyloid). Immunohistochemistry (anti-TTR, anti-kappa, anti-lambda) types the amyloid: ATTR vs AL.

sections.heading: Serologic / hematologic workup — screening for AL and plasma cell dyscrasia
sections.bodyHtml:
Test Finding Interpretation
SPEP (serum protein electrophoresis) M-spike; monoclonal band Suggests monoclonal protein; quantifies.
Immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE) Clarifies monoclonal type (IgG, IgA, IgM, etc.) Defines heavy chain type; needed if SPEP abnormal.
Serum free light chains (SFLC) ↑ kappa or lambda; kappa/lambda ratio abnormal (> 1.65 or < 0.26) Sensitive for light-chain disease; >0.4 abnormal on involved/uninvolved ratio. AL typically has high involved FLC.
24-hour urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) Bence Jones proteinuria (light chains in urine) AL patients often shed light chains in urine.
Serum and urine immunofixation Monoclonal light chain (kappa or lambda) Confirms AL if present + biopsy confirmation.
CBC, CMP, LFTs Cytopenias, renal insufficiency, elevated LFTs End-organ involvement; guides treatment.
Cardiac biomarkers: Troponin (hs-cTnI), NT-proBNP, BNP ↑ troponin, very ↑ BNP Prognostic in amyloid; predicts mortality risk (higher = worse). Amyloid cardiomyopathy often has high BNP despite normal/mildly reduced EF.

AL amyloidosis is hematologic emergency: if AL suspected, coordinate immediate hematology-oncology involvement; time to diagnosis and treatment initiation is prognostically critical.

sections.heading: Specialized diagnostics — if differential uncertain
sections.bodyHtml:
• Right heart catheterization: restrictive physiology shows "square root" sign (rapid early diastolic filling, then abrupt diastolic plateau on LV/RV pressure tracing); prominent y-descent in RA pressure; elevated diastolic pressures (LV EDP often 20–30 mmHg). Helps distinguish restrictive cardiomyopathy from constrictive pericarditis (see differential below) and HFpEF (different filling pattern, less restrictive).

  • Stress imaging: assess for inducible ischemia; amyloid myocardium with angiographically clean coronaries can have stress-induced ischemia or reduced coronary flow reserve.

  • Endomyocardial biopsy immunophenotyping: flow cytometry or immunohistochemistry showing monoclonal plasma cell clone (CD38+, CD138+) confirms AL.

  • Thyroid and nutritional markers: FreeT4, TSH, prealbumin, albumin; may be low in advanced ATTR or AL with hepatic/nutritional involvement.

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: ICU-level care focused on preload-sensitive physiology and etiology-specific disease-modifying therapy.

sections.heading: 5A. Medical — Preload-Dependent Physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
RCM is exquisitely preload-dependent. Small volume changes drastically affect cardiac output. General principles apply across all RCM etiologies:

Diuretics — cautious approach

  • Loop diuretics are essential for pulmonary congestion but dose carefully. Rule: small frequent doses better than aggressive diuresis.
  • Lasix 20–40 mg daily or BID (not 80–120 mg push)
  • Spironolactone 12.5 mg daily (for aldosterone blockade; requires K+ monitoring)
  • Monitor aggressively: daily weights (target ≤ 2–3 lb/day loss), urine output, creatinine trend (avoid prerenal azotemia)
  • Escalate if: JVP rising despite diuretics (may signal worsening restriction, new AF, or acute decompensation) or BP dropping below SBP 100 (concerning in amyloid; autonomic dysfunction impairs compensatory vasoconstriction)

Avoid aggressive afterload reduction

  • ACE-I/ARB: limited data in RCM; use cautiously if HTN, avoid as primary therapy; ATTR patients with autonomic neuropathy tolerate poorly
  • Nitrates, hydralazine: drop preload and afterload; can precipitate shock in preload-dependent state
  • Negative inotropes (some beta-blockers, non-DHP CCBs): avoid unless needed for AF rate control

Electrolyte repletion

  • K+: target > 4.0 mEq/L; diuresis pulls K+ down; hypokalemia worsens AF propensity
  • Mg2+: target > 2.0 mg/dL; critical for diastolic stability; refractory AF often reflects Mg deficiency
  • iCa2+: target 1.1–1.3 mmol/L; corrected calcium influences myocardial relaxation

Rhythm management — AF common

  • Rate control: beta-blockers preferred (target HR 60–80 at rest); diltiazem or verapamil if beta-blocker contraindicated
  • Avoid digoxin + CCB in amyloid: digoxin binds amyloid fibrils, reducing efficacy and accumulating cardiotoxically; calcium channel blockers in amyloid can precipitate AV block and hemodynamic collapse
  • Anticoagulation: AF + RCM + low CO = high thromboembolic risk. Anticoagulation is standard unless contraindicated (active bleeding, upcoming biopsy). Balance against GI bleeding risk (AL, ATTR neuropathy with GI involvement).

sections.heading: 5B. Etiology-Specific Therapy — Amyloid and Infiltrative Disease
ATTR Amyloidosis (Wild-Type, Hereditary, or Acquired)
sections.bodyHtml:
Disease-modifying therapy — paradigm-shifting (Maurer et al., 2018; Adams et al., 2018)

Drug Class Indication Mechanism Efficacy Notes
Tafamidis TTR stabilizer ATTR cardiomyopathy (wild-type + hereditary) Binds TTR tetramer; stabilizes native fold; prevents amyloidogenesis ATTR-ACT trial: ↓ NTproBNP rise, improved NYHA, ↓ mortality 29% vs placebo over 30 mo Oral, well-tolerated; takes weeks to reach steady state; monitor renal function; all ATTR cardiac patients should be on this unless contraindicated
Patisiran TTR silencer (RNAi) Hereditary ATTR with polyneuropathy; emerging in cardiac Reduces hepatic TTR mRNA translation; ↓ circulating TTR by ~80% APOLLO trial: ↓ neuropathy progression, improved cardiac biomarkers; IV every 3 weeks Effective for both neurologic and cardiac manifestations; requires liver monitoring
Vutrisiran TTR silencer (RNAi, N-acetylgalactosamine conjugate) Hereditary ATTR (polyneuropathy, cardiomyopathy) Hepatic-targeted RNAi; ~90% TTR reduction Longer dosing intervals (monthly or every 3 mo); in pivotal trials Next-generation silencer; emerging data for cardiac predominant cases
Acoramidis TTR stabilizer ATTR cardiomyopathy (wild-type + hereditary) Novel stabilizer binding TTR at different site than tafamidis Early trials suggest potent stabilization; improved compliance vs tafamidis BID dosing Newer agent; becoming available; once-daily dosing
Inotersen TTR silencer (antisense oligonucleotide) Hereditary ATTR polyneuropathy Hepatic TTR mRNA degradation; IV weekly Can worsen cardiac if advanced at baseline; less preferred for cardiac-predominant Monitor hepatic and renal function closely

Supportive therapy (independent of TTR-directed agent):

  • Diuretics: preload-sensitive dosing (see §5A)
  • Beta-blockers: only if AF rate control needed; otherwise avoid (negative inotrope in already-low-output state)
  • ACE-I/ARB: limited data; use cautiously if HTN; avoid if autonomic neuropathy (orthostatic risk)
  • Avoid: NSAIDs, aggressive vasodilation

Monitoring on TTR-directed therapy:

  • Baseline: renal function, LFTs, BNP/NT-proBNP, troponin, echo
  • On therapy: labs at 4–8 weeks, then 3–6 monthly; track BNP trend (stable or improving is goal); echo annually
  • Counsel patient: tafamidis/patisiran stabilizes TTR and slows progression but does NOT reverse amyloid already deposited; symptom improvement lags biomarker improvement by weeks to months

sections.heading: AL Amyloidosis (Light-Chain) — Hematologic Emergency
sections.bodyHtml:
This demands immediate hematology-oncology collaboration. Untreated median survival is 4 months if cardiac involved.

Modality Role Notes
Chemotherapy (primary treatment) Daratumumab-based regimen standard Daratumumab + bortezomib + dexamethasone (DBd) achieves high response rates (~60–70% hematologic response); reduces free light chains and improves cardiac function. Time to initiation is critical.
Autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) Consolidation in eligible patients Consider if age < 70, ECOG 0–1, no major organ involvement limiting tolerance. Further improves outcomes; median EFS > 7 years with modern protocols.
Response assessment Track during and post-chemo SFLC reduction; BNP/troponin trend; echo; renal function; organ response grading (European Society criteria). Complete hematologic response often precedes cardiac improvement by 3–6 mo.

Cardiac management (supportive during chemo):

  • Diuretics: preload-sensitive dosing; chemo can worsen renal function and fluid overload
  • Anticoagulation: AF high risk; balance against bleeding (AL → GI bleeding risk from infiltration and autonomic neuropathy); DOACs vs warfarin per heme-onc/cardiology team
  • Monitoring during chemo: troponin, BNP, echo baseline and periodically (cardiotoxicity surveillance); electrolytes; renal function
  • Cardiac toxicity risk: some chemo agents (bortezomib) have cardiotoxic potential; baseline EF assessment and serial monitoring needed

Why AL is different from ATTR: AL is a plasma cell disorder; chemotherapy curing the hematologic disease is what saves the heart. Cardiac management is supportive only. Escalate all AL cardiac decisions to hematology-oncology.

sections.heading: Cardiac Sarcoidosis
sections.bodyHtml:
Immune-mediated myocardial granulomatous infiltration → restrictive or dilated physiology, conduction blocks, ventricular arrhythmias.

Modality Agent Dose / Notes
Corticosteroids Prednisone Start 20–40 mg daily (or higher if acute inflammation); taper over months. First-line; reduces granuloma burden and inflammation.
Immunosuppression (steroid-sparing) Azathioprine 1–2 mg/kg/day; alternative to or adjunct for steroid-refractory cases
Immunosuppression (steroid-sparing) Methotrexate 10–25 mg weekly; second-line for inadequate response or steroid toxicity
Immunosuppression (steroid-sparing) Mycophenolate mofetil 1–3 g/day divided; third-line option
Arrhythmia management ICD placement Indicated if sustained VT documented or signs of high arrhythmia risk (scar + reduced EF); sarcoid patients have conduction abnormalities; baseline ECG needed
Conduction block management Pacemaker If high-degree AV block or bradycardia from granuloma infiltration
Imaging to guide therapy Cardiac MRI + FDG-PET CMR shows scar (LGE patchy/basal); FDG-PET identifies active inflammation (guides steroid initiation and response monitoring).

Why sarcoidosis is distinctive: granulomas are inflammatory and often responsive to steroids, unlike amyloid or hemochromatosis. Active inflammation on PET predicts steroid responsiveness. Conduction disease and VT risk are greater than in amyloid.

sections.heading: Hemochromatosis (Cardiac)
sections.bodyHtml:
Iron overload causes oxidative damage, fibrosis, restrictive physiology. REVERSIBLE if caught early.

Modality Agent Mechanism / Notes
Phlebotomy (first-line) Regular blood draws 1 unit (500 mL) every 1–2 weeks until ferritin target reached (~50–100 ng/mL). Most effective and well-tolerated if patient can tolerate volume loss.
Chelation (if phlebotomy inadequate or contraindicated) Deferoxamine IV/SQ; chelates ferric iron; can cause ototoxicity, retinal damage with long-term use.
Chelation (oral alternative) Deferiprone 25–33 mg/kg/day divided; oral; risk of agranulocytosis (needs monitoring).
Chelation (oral alternative) Deferasirox 20–30 mg/kg/day; oral; good efficacy; GI side effects; renal monitoring needed.
Cardiac support ACE-I / ARB, beta-blocker, diuretics For HF as needed; monitor function.
Monitoring Ferritin, transferrin saturation, DEXA Check ferritin trend; goal < 100 ng/mL for cardiac benefit. Assess bone density (cirrhosis risk, osteoporosis).
Arrhythmia AF + ICD risk AF common; anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2; ICD if LV dysfunction + VT risk.

Why early detection matters: cardiac dysfunction from iron overload is often reversible if iron-lowering starts early. Late presentation (advanced cirrhosis, fibrosis) carries worse prognosis.

sections.heading: Loeffler Endocarditis (Eosinophilic)
sections.bodyHtml:
Eosinophil-mediated myocardial and endocardial inflammation → fibrosis, restrictive physiology, thromboembolism risk.

Modality Management
Hypereosinophilia workup Identify underlying cause (FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion [imatinib-responsive], lymphoma, idiopathic). Hematology collaboration.
Corticosteroids High-dose (prednisone 20–40 mg/day or higher); reduce eosinophil burden and inflammation.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitors Imatinib if PDGFRA fusion documented; dramatically reduces eosinophils.
Anticoagulation AF + endocardial thrombus risk; balance against bleeding.
Surgical Endocardial stripping if severe LV obstruction or massive thrombus burden; high surgical mortality; rarely performed in modern practice.

sections.heading: Endomyocardial Fibrosis
sections.bodyHtml:
Endemic in Africa and parts of Asia; restrictive physiology from endocardial fibrosis and thrombus.

  • Medical: diuretics, AF management, anticoagulation if low CO + thrombotic risk
  • Surgical: endocardial stripping if severe and refractory; high mortality (5–25%); rarely done outside endemic regions
  • Transplant: selected severe cases may be transplant candidates

sections.heading: Fabry Disease (X-Linked Lysosomal Storage)
sections.bodyHtml:
Globotriaosylceramide accumulates in myocytes → RCM pattern, progressive LV dysfunction, AFib.

Modality Agent Mechanism Notes
Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) Agalsidase alfa Recombinant human alpha-galactosidase A Given IV every 2 weeks; slows progression of cardiac and renal disease if started early (pediatric patients especially benefit)
Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) Agalsidase beta Recombinant human alpha-galactosidase A Alternative ERT; IV every 2 weeks
Substrate reduction therapy (SRT) Migalastat (chaperone) Oral; stabilizes native enzyme; oral convenience Oral option; may be better tolerated; emerging as first-line in some guidelines
Cardiac support ACE-I/ARB, beta-blocker, diuretics Standard HF therapy
Genetic counseling Family screening essential X-linked inheritance; carrier females may have disease manifestations; siblings at risk

Why early detection matters: Fabry progression is slow but relentless; ERT initiated in childhood can prevent cardiac and renal complications. Adult-onset Fabry may already have significant myocardial involvement.

sections.heading: 5C. Transplantation — Selected Cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Heart transplantation is the only definitive cure for RCM, but candidate selection is critical.

Indications for transplant evaluation:

  • Refractory symptoms despite optimal medical therapy and amyloid-directed therapy (ATTR) or chemotherapy (AL)
  • Recurrent hospitalizations for decompensated HF
  • Hemodynamic instability or low-output requiring inotropic support
  • ATTR: some transplant centers consider earlier listing if advanced disease (very elevated BNP, functional decline) because transplant outcomes improving and amyloid-directed therapies don't reverse already-deposited amyloid
  • AL: historically considered high-risk; now, if hematologic complete response achieved with chemo + ASCT, transplant is considered

Transplant-specific considerations:

Factor Issue Management
ATTR heritable Transplanted heart receives amyloid-free donor organ BUT patient's liver continues producing mutant TTR; cardiac amyloid can recur in the graft Consider combined heart + liver transplant in young hereditary ATTR patients; patisiran/vutrisiran post-HTx can slow systemic ATTR progression
AL amyloidosis If hematologic complete response achieved, transplant outcomes improving Prerequisite: confirmed hematologic CR (SFLC normalized, marrow clone eradicated); cardiac-only transplant usually sufficient
Immunosuppression monitoring Standard post-transplant monitoring (rejection surveillance) Troponin, BNP, echo; biopsy if concern for rejection; baseline LVEF and diastolic parameters establish. Calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) and mycophenolate are standard.
Preop optimization Optimize nutrition, renal function, amyloid-directed therapy If ATTR, maximize tafamidis/patisiran benefit pre-transplant; may delay disease and improve outcomes; optimize diuretic balance

Outcomes:

  • ATTR: heart transplant outcomes now similar to other cardiomyopathy indications (1-year survival ~85–90%); amyloid recurrence in graft takes years
  • AL: if hematologic remission achieved, transplant outcomes comparable; hematologic relapse is primary concern, managed with chemotherapy re-induction
  • Other etiologies (sarcoid, hemochromatosis, Loeffler): transplant outcomes variable; sarcoid may recur in allograft (controversial); transplant generally reserved for refractory cases

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml: ICU-level communication framework for patient deterioration or diagnostic uncertainty.

sections.heading: SBAR Template for RCM/Amyloid Patient Decompensation
sections.bodyHtml:
S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], [brief context: 'POD 2 s/p [procedure]' or 'admitted yesterday with dyspnea on exertion, suspected RCM/amyloid']."

B: "Patient has [diagnosis: RCM suspected amyloid / confirmed ATTR / AL amyloidosis / sarcoidosis, etc.]. Known hemodynamics: [EF, restrictive pattern on echo, elevated filling pressures]. Current status: [diuretic regimen, inotropic support if any]."

A: "Patient now [presentation: new hypotension, worsening dyspnea despite diuretics, new AF with RVR, syncope, etc.]. Current vitals: HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. JVP [level], exam [findings]. Labs: K+ [value], Mg2+ [value], Cr [value], BNP/troponin [trend]. Most recent echo/cath [key findings]."

R: "Requesting [specific action: diuretic adjustment, inotrope initiation, urgent echo, invasive hemodynamics to clarify restrictive vs constrictive, urgent biopsy if amyloid diagnosis still pending, heme-onc consult if AL, transplant consultation if refractory, etc.]."

sections.heading: Who to Call
sections.bodyHtml:
Situation Contact Urgency
Stable RCM patient, routine admission Primary cardiologist / APP Routine
Suspected amyloidosis, diagnostic workup pending Cardiology (advanced imaging, biopsy coordination) Urgent
Confirmed AL amyloidosis, newly diagnosed Hematology-oncology + cardiology (chemotherapy initiation) STAT — median survival 4 mo if untreated with cardiac involvement
ATTR on tafamidis, decompensated HF Cardiology (escalate diuretics, inotropes, transplant eval if refractory) Urgent
New/worsening AF with hemodynamic compromise APP/fellow + charge nurse; activate RRT if unstable (cardioversion standby) Urgent/STAT
Syncope or low-output shock Cardiology fellow/attending + ICU team; consider invasive hemodynamics, inotrope support, VAD/ECMO if cardiogenic shock STAT
Diagnostic dilemma: RCM vs constrictive pericarditis Cardiology (CMR, catheterization, possible pericardial biopsy/drainage) Urgent
Refractory HF, transplant evaluation Transplant cardiologist / transplant surgery Urgent (weeks, not days)
Post-transplant rejection surveillance Transplant team + cardiology Per protocol (days for labs/echo; biopsy if concern)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive on mechanisms, edge cases, and clinical reasoning. All subsections below are expandable in the PowerApp render.

ATTR Genetics: Wild-Type vs Hereditary and Implications Wild-type ATTR (senile systemic amyloidosis):
  • Normal TTR gene; aging-related misfolding and oligomerization of wild-type TTR protein
  • Males >> females (8:1); onset typically age 70–85
  • Cardiac-predominant; neuropathy and autonomic involvement uncommon
  • Progressive but slower than hereditary; median survival ~70 years post-symptom onset
  • Val122Ile variants: NOT truly "wild-type" but acquired de novo TTR variants found in ~2–4% of Black Americans; often called "wild-type" erroneously; earlier onset, more symptomatic (earlier 60s–70s vs 80s+)
  • Clinical pearl: Elderly Black man with "HFpEF" and carpal tunnel → screen for Val122Ile ATTR urgently; prevalence is high and underdiagnosed Hereditary ATTR (ATTR-variant, ATTR-v):
  • Pathogenic TTR gene mutation inherited autosomal-dominant
  • Onset 40–60 (vs 70–85 for wild-type); more aggressive multi-system involvement
  • Classic presentations: cardiac predominant (young, age 50–60, thick LV, restrictive), neurologic predominant (peripheral neuropathy, autonomic dysfunction), ophthalmologic (vitreous amyloid, ocular manifestations)
  • TTR gene variants: >100 known pathogenic variants; Val30Met (Portuguese, Swedish, Japanese families) most common globally; Val122Ile (Ile-122 allele in African ancestry); Leu111Met, Leu58His, and many others
  • Screening: positive family history is key; if multiple family members with carpal tunnel, spinal stenosis, or HFpEF, consider genetic testing
  • Implications for management: patisiran and vutrisiran (TTR silencers) work for hereditary ATTR; tafamidis (stabilizer) also approved; both can slow systemic progression Acquired ATTR (rare):
  • Plasma cells produce misfolded TTR (distinct from AL light-chain amyloidosis); very uncommon
  • Managed like hereditary ATTR; chemotherapy targeting plasma cells may reduce amyloid production
TTR Stabilizers vs TTR Silencers — Mechanism and Clinical Logic TTR Stabilizers (e.g., tafamidis, acoramidis):
  • Mechanism: bind to TTR tetramer and stabilize the native fold, preventing dissociation into monomers that then misfold and oligomerize into amyloid fibrils
  • Result: slows amyloid fibril formation and disease progression; does NOT degrade existing amyloid fibrils already deposited
  • Timeline: effective over months to years; benefit is stabilization/slowing, not reversal
  • Efficacy data: ATTR-ACT trial (Maurer et al., 2018) showed tafamidis reduced NTproBNP progression, improved NYHA functional class, and reduced 30-month mortality by 29% vs placebo
  • Advantages: oral, well-tolerated, minimal monitoring burden, effective for wild-type and hereditary ATTR, can initiate as monotherapy
  • Limitations: does NOT treat systemic disease in hereditary ATTR (liver still produces mutant TTR); does NOT reverse amyloid already deposited TTR Silencers (e.g., patisiran, vutrisiran, inotersen, acoramidis — some agents are hybrid):
  • RNAi silencers (patisiran, vutrisiran): reduce hepatic TTR mRNA translation → dramatic ↓ circulating TTR (80–90% reduction); amyloid fibril formation stops
  • Antisense oligonucleotide (inotersen): triggers hepatic TTR mRNA degradation
  • Result: stops new amyloid deposition; systemic disease progression halted or reversed in some patients
  • Timeline: rapid effect (weeks); biomarkers (BNP, neuropathy scores) improve over months
  • Efficacy data: APOLLO trial (Adams et al., 2018) showed patisiran reduced neuropathy progression and cardiac biomarker worsening; VTURA trial (vutrisiran) similarly effective
  • Advantages: can treat both neurologic and cardiac manifestations; dramatic TTR reduction; reversal of systemic disease possible
  • Limitations: IV infusions (patisiran q3 weeks, inotersen weekly, vutrisiran monthly), higher cost, hepatic/renal monitoring needed, may exacerbate cardiac disease if already advanced at baseline (reduced TTR production doesn't reverse infiltrated myocardium) Clinical decision-making:
  • Mild to moderate cardiac ATTR, no neuropathy: tafamidis monotherapy often sufficient
  • Cardiac + neuropathy, hereditary ATTR: patisiran or vutrisiran preferred (treat systemic disease)
  • Advanced cardiac ATTR at baseline: silencers may worsen cardiac output transiently (less TTR available for native synthesis); consider stabilizer + low-dose silencer or tafamidis monotherapy
  • Sequential therapy: increasingly, tafamidis + patisiran/vutrisiran used together for comprehensive ATTR control
Red-Flag Clinical Clues Suggesting ATTR Before Cardiac Diagnosis ATTR often presents with systemic features years before cardiac symptoms. Recognition of these red flags can accelerate diagnosis: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome:
  • Classic ATTR red flag; can precede cardiac diagnosis by 5–10 years
  • Bilateral distinguishes from mechanical CTS (unilateral often)
  • Carpal tunnel is so common in ATTR that presence of CTS + dyspnea + HFpEF = amyloid screen urgent Lumbar spinal stenosis:
  • ATTR causes amyloid deposition in spinal ligaments and nerve roots → stenosis, radiculopathy, lower-extremity weakness
  • Suspect ATTR if spinal stenosis + carpal tunnel + cardiac symptoms Biceps or triceps tendon rupture (spontaneous or minor trauma):
  • Amyloid weakens tendons; even minor trauma can rupture a tendon infiltrated with amyloid
  • If patient reports spontaneous or minimal-trauma tendon rupture + systemic symptoms → amyloid workup
  • Other soft-tissue involvement (shoulder, Achilles) less specific but possible Autonomic dysfunction:
  • Orthostatic hypotension (ATTR neuropathy damages autonomic fibers)
  • Erectile dysfunction (autonomic dysfunction + vasculopathy)
  • GI dysmotility (constipation, alternating with diarrhea; amyloid infiltration of GI smooth muscle)
  • Urinary retention, orthostatic syncope
  • In context of HFpEF + dyspnea → amyloid-directed autonomic workup Peripheral neuropathy (length-dependent, distal sensory):
  • Hereditary ATTR especially; small-fiber neuropathy common
  • ATTR → stocking-glove sensory distribution, weakness, foot drop in advanced cases
  • If neuropathy + HFpEF + cardiac symptoms → strong ATTR suspicion Low-voltage ECG with thick LV wall (pathognomonic pattern):
  • "Small QRS complexes despite thick wall" is amyloid signature
  • Contrast to HCM: HCM shows high-voltage (thick wall, huge QRS)
  • Amyloid: low-voltage ECG + thick LV on echo = SCREEN FOR AMYLOID URGENTLY Pseudo-infarct pattern on ECG:
  • Q waves in inferior or apical leads (simulates old MI)
  • Troponin often elevated despite angiographically clean coronaries
  • Amyloid infiltration causes segmental necrosis → pseudo-infarct pattern
  • Angiography normal but troponin ↑ + thick LV + low voltage = amyloid "Speckled" myocardium on echo (amyloid texture):
  • Characteristic granular or "speckled" appearance of myocardium from infiltration
  • Distinct from smooth LV hypertrophy (HCM) or dilated cardiomyopathy
  • Sonographer may describe as "bright" or "granular" texture Very elevated BNP/NT-proBNP with normal or mildly reduced EF:
  • Amyloid cardiomyopathy characteristically has disproportionate BNP elevation
  • Normal-EF patients with BNP > 400 → amyloid high on differential
  • Prognostically ominous; elevated BNP despite normal EF predicts worse outcomes
AL Amyloidosis Workup and Hematologic Emergency Recognition AL amyloidosis is plasma cell disorder; early recognition and heme-onc involvement are life-saving. AL workup cascade:
  1. Serologic screening: SPEP, UPEP, SFLC (serum free light chains)
    • Look for M-spike, Bence Jones proteinuria, elevated involved SFLC
    • If SPEP abnormal: immunofixation to clarify heavy chain type (IgG, IgA, IgM, light chain only)
    • Tissue confirmation: endomyocardial biopsy (gold standard for cardiac) or fat pad biopsy
    • Congo red staining + polarized light → apple-green birefringence (amyloid)
    • Immunohistochemistry: anti-lambda, anti-kappa → identifies light-chain type
    • Distinguishes AL from ATTR
    • Plasma cell characterization: bone marrow biopsy + flow cytometry
    • Identifies monoclonal plasma cell clone (CD38+, CD138+)
    • Quantifies clonal burden; guides chemotherapy intensity
    • Prognostic staging: ISS (International Staging System) score predicts chemo response
    • Cardiac biomarkers: baseline troponin (hs-cTnI), BNP/NT-proBNP
    • Elevated troponin is independent adverse prognosticator in AL
    • AL Mayo stage incorporates troponin + BNP to risk-stratify; stage III (both elevated) has median survival ~4 months untreated
    • Track during chemo as response marker; SFLC reduction often precedes cardiac parameter improvement by weeks
    • Organ involvement assessment: renal function, LFTs, cardiac echo/cath, neuro exam
    • AL is multi-organ; establish baseline organ involvement profile
    • Guides treatment selection (renal → adjusted dosing) Hematologic emergency recognition:
      • Cardiac AL with elevated troponin → median survival 4 months without treatment
      • Daratumumab-based chemotherapy (DBd) is now standard-of-care: dramatically improved response and survival (3–4 years or better with optimal response)
      • Time matters: every week delay in diagnosis/treatment initiation worsens outcomes
      • Escalate immediately to hematology-oncology: do NOT delay for further cardiac workup if AL suspected; parallel workup with heme-onc is standard
Cardiac Sarcoidosis: Steroid-Responsive Granulomatous Disease Cardiac sarcoidosis is granulomatous myocardial infiltration; steroids are cornerstone and can reverse active inflammation. Diagnostic recognition:
  • Restrictive or dilated cardiomyopathy in patient with systemic sarcoidosis (or isolated cardiac sarcoidosis, rare)
  • Conduction blocks, ventricular arrhythmias (VT), granulomas on biopsy
  • CMR shows patchy LGE (basal inferior wall often, scar-like); FDG-PET shows active inflammation Management cornerstone: corticosteroids + immunosuppression
  • Prednisone 20–40 mg/day (or higher if acute inflammation); taper over months
  • Response assessment: FDG-PET improves with steroid response; clinical improvement (EF, arrhythmia burden) may lag by weeks
  • Steroid-sparing agents: azathioprine, methotrexate, mycophenolate if inadequate response or toxicity Arrhythmia management:
  • Granulomatous scar → VT substrate; ICD indicated if sustained VT documented or LV dysfunction + high arrhythmia risk
  • Conduction blocks → pacemaker if high-degree AV block Why sarcoidosis is distinctive:
  • Unlike amyloid (irreversible), sarcoidosis is potentially reversible with immunosuppression
  • FDG-PET active inflammation predicts steroid responsiveness
  • VT risk is higher than in amyloid due to focal scarring
Fabry Disease: Lysosomal Storage with Progressive Cardiac Involvement X-linked lysosomal storage disorder; globotriaosylceramide (GL-3) accumulates in myocytes, kidney, nerves, skin. Cardiac manifestations:
  • Restrictive physiology, concentric LV hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction
  • Progressive LV dysfunction; AF common
  • Conduction blocks, arrhythmias
  • Stroke risk (cerebral vasculopathy) Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) is disease-modifying:
  • Agalsidase alfa or beta: IV infusions every 2 weeks; recombinant human alpha-galactosidase A
  • Effect: slows cardiac, renal, and neurologic progression if initiated early (pediatric diagnosis ideal)
  • Evidence: long-term ERT halts or reverses LV hypertrophy and preserves renal function Substrate reduction therapy (SRT) — emerging alternative:
  • Migalastat: chaperone; stabilizes native enzyme; oral dosing (much more convenient than IV)
  • Emerging as first-line in some guidelines for early-stage Fabry Genetic counseling essential:
  • X-linked inheritance; heterozygous females can have disease manifestations (variable lyonization)
  • Siblings and female family members at risk; screening recommended Clinical pearl: Fabry can present as HCM mimic (young patient with LV hypertrophy); if HCM diagnosis unclear, consider Fabry (especially if systemic features: neuropathy, renal disease, stroke history). ERT initiated early can prevent progression.
RCM vs Constrictive Pericarditis — Critical Differential Diagnosis Both present with restrictive hemodynamics (elevated filling pressures, diastolic dysfunction), but etiology and management are opposite.

sections.heading: Differentiation Strategy
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature RCM (Myocardial) Constrictive Pericarditis (Pericardial)
Pathophysiology Stiff myocardium (amyloid, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, fibrosis) Inelastic pericardium (fibrosis, adhesion, thickening) prevents expansion
LV wall thickness Typically thick (especially amyloid) Normal (pericardium is external)
Pericardial thickening on CMR/echo Normal or mild (< 3 mm) Thickened (> 3 mm); often 5–8 mm
LGE pattern on CMR Diffuse subendocardial or transmural (amyloid); patchy (sarcoidosis); dark signal (hemochromatosis) Pericardial thickening; myocardium may show "halo" pattern of enhancement at constriction line
T1 mapping (CMR native T1) Elevated (amyloid) Normal
T2* (CMR, iron assessment) Normal unless hemochromatosis (shortened) Normal
Apical sparing on echo Present in amyloid (cherry-on-top) Absent; normal LV strain pattern
RV pressure tracing at cath Diastolic pressure = LV diastolic pressure (concordant); dip-plateau in both Discordant diastolic pressures (RV diastolic lower than LV); marked dip-plateau; septal bounce (LV pressure rises while RV pressure drops early in diastole due to septal shift)
Interventricular septal motion Normal or mildly reduced Prominent septal bounce (septal motion toward RV in early diastole due to mechanical coupling from stiff pericardium)
PA response to inspiration Minimal (< 3 mmHg drop) Exaggerated (> 3 mmHg drop in PA pressure with inspiration; Kussmaul sign: JVP rises with inspiration)
History clues Amyloid red flags (carpal tunnel, spinal stenosis, prior chest radiation for hemochromatosis) Prior cardiac surgery, pericarditis, tuberculosis, malignancy, post-radiation
Echo — biatrial size Enlarged (from chronic high filling pressures) Variable; may be normal or enlarged depending on chronicity

sections.heading: Diagnostic approach when RCM vs CP unclear:
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Echo: measure pericardial thickness (CP > 3 mm); assess apical sparing (RCM present, CP absent)
  2. CMR: pericardial thickening (CP), LGE pattern (diffuse RCM vs pericardial rim CP), native T1 (elevated RCM amyloid), T2* (hemochromatosis)
  3. Right heart catheterization: septal bounce, discordant diastolic pressures, Kussmaul sign (CP); concordant pressures, dip-plateau in both (RCM)
  4. Tissue diagnosis if amyloid suspected: endomyocardial biopsy (Congo red staining confirms amyloid)

sections.heading: Why this matters:
sections.bodyHtml:
CP is surgically curable (pericardiectomy); delay = progressive right-sided HF and end-organ dysfunction.

RCM is managed medically (diuretics, disease-specific therapy); pericardiectomy is harmful. Misdiagnosis = wrong treatment trajectory.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration in Stable RCM Patients
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appear in stable ICU/stepdown patient; if present, re-escalate and reassess.

  • JVP rising despite diuretics → worsening restriction, new AF with loss of atrial kick, or acute decompensation; notify team
  • New AF, especially with HR > 120 → loss of atrial kick = 20–30% CO drop; patient may decompensate rapidly; escalate
  • Syncope or presyncope → critically low stroke volume from restrictive physiology; risk of cardiogenic shock; STAT assessment
  • Acute hypotension (SBP < 100) → preload-sensitive physiology failing; overdiuresis or AF likely; stop diuretics, bolus if hypovolemic, notify team
  • Increasing creatinine despite stable BP → prerenal azotemia from diuretics; reassess volume and renal perfusion
  • New hypoxia or increased O₂ requirement → can precede hemodynamic decompensation; may signal flash pulmonary edema or low cardiac output state
  • Troponin rising or NT-proBNP spiking → acute myocardial strain or rhythm disturbance; escalate
  • Worsening renal function (Cr > 2.0 or ↑ by 0.5 from baseline) → cardiorenal syndrome; reduces medication options; notify nephrologist and cardiology
  • Altered mental status → can reflect low cardiac output, electrolyte derangement, or sepsis in immunosuppressed (AL chemo patients); STAT labs and neuro exam
  • Recurrent syncope or falls → marker of severe autonomic dysfunction or arrhythmia burden; transplant urgency may increase

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
(10–15 high-yield teaching points for proficient/expert nurses)

  1. HFpEF mimic is underdiagnosed ATTR. Every elderly male with "HFpEF," elevated BNP, and history of carpal tunnel syndrome (especially bilateral), spinal stenosis, or spontaneous tendon rupture should trigger ATTR screening. Get 99mTc-PYP, echo looking for apical sparing, and SPEP/UPEP. ATTR wild-type is buried in the HFpEF cohort; prevalence is ~5–10% of HFpEF in older men. This is not rare; it's under-recognized.

  2. Low-voltage ECG + thick LV wall = amyloid screen URGENT. "Small QRS despite thick wall" is pathognomonic for amyloid. Normal HCM shows high voltage. Contrast this instantly in your head: if patient has low QRS voltage + LV thickness + normal-to-mildly-reduced EF + elevated BNP → order 99mTc-PYP and echo apical sparing NOW, don't wait for cardiology clinic.

  3. Apical sparing on echo is amyloid fingerprint. If report notes "preserved apical longitudinal strain while basal and mid-LV strain is reduced (cherry-on-top)," mention this explicitly to the team. Normal HCM and HFpEF do not show apical sparing. This is an amyloid clue.

  4. Tafamidis (ATTR-ACT trial) revolutionized ATTR cardiomyopathy outcomes. The 2018 trial showed tafamidis reduced NTproBNP progression, improved NYHA functional class, and reduced 30-month mortality by 29% vs placebo.

    All ATTR cardiac patients should be on tafamidis unless contraindicated. If ATTR patient not on tafamidis, escalate and ask why (cost, contraindication, recent diagnosis?). This is standard of care now.

  5. AL amyloidosis is a hematologic emergency — time to chemotherapy initiation is prognostically critical. Median survival without treatment: 4 months if cardiac involved. Daratumumab + bortezomib + dexamethasone is transformative; response rates now 60–70%, and median survival 3–4 years or better.

    Do NOT spend weeks on cardiac workup alone. If AL suspected, escalate to heme-onc STAT for parallel workup and chemo initiation. Chemotherapy curing the hematologic disease is what saves the heart.

  6. Constrictive pericarditis is the critical differential — and it's surgically curable. RCM hemodynamics (elevated filling pressures, restrictive pattern) mimic constrictive pericarditis perfectly. Distinguish by: (a) Echo: apical sparing + thick LV = RCM; pericardial thickening > 3 mm = CP; (b) CMR: pericardial thickness, LGE pattern, native T1 (elevated amyloid); (c) Cath: septal bounce, discordant diastolic pressures, Kussmaul sign = CP.

    Misdiagnosis = wrong treatment: CP is pericardiectomy; RCM is medical. Don't confuse them.

  7. Preload sensitivity is absolute — RCM patients crash from mild dehydration. Small volume changes devastate cardiac output. Use small frequent diuretic doses (lasix 20–40 mg daily, spironolactone 12.5 mg daily), NOT aggressive diuresis. Monitor daily weights (goal ≤ 2–3 lb/day loss), urine output, creatinine. If JVP rising or hypotension develops, STOP diuretics and reassess. "Preload-dependent" means the patient is a "Goldilocks" problem: too dry = shock, too wet = pulmonary edema. The margin is narrow.

  8. Amiodarone hypotension is predictable in ~25% — decrease drip early, don't wait for frank hypotension. Amiodarone is rhythm drug of choice in RCM/amyloid AF, but it drops BP in ~1 in 4 patients. If on amiodarone drip and BP trending down, proactively decrease to 0.5 mg/min BEFORE SBP hits 90. Waiting for hypotension = preventable shock. This is a teaching moment for anticipatory nursing.

  9. AF in RCM is hemodynamically catastrophic — loss of atrial kick = 20–30% CO drop. A patient in normal sinus rhythm may suddenly deteriorate when AF develops. New AF in RCM = escalate immediately; loss of synchronous atrial contraction is not tolerable. Rate control is urgent; rhythm control preferred (amiodarone). If patient becomes hypotensive on new AF, cardioversion may be emergent.

  10. Biopsy is gold standard for amyloid confirmation; fat pad is easy but lower sensitivity. Endomyocardial biopsy = 90–95% sensitive and immunohistochemistry types it (ATTR vs AL). Fat pad = 60–70% for AL, 30–40% for ATTR, but minimally invasive. If fat pad negative but clinical suspicion high, endomyocardial is justified. Congo red + polarized light = apple-green birefringence (pathognomonic for amyloid).

  11. Digoxin + CCB are harmful in amyloid — digoxin binds amyloid, reducing efficacy and accumulating toxically. Avoid digoxin (rate control) in amyloid patients. Prefer beta-blockers. Similarly, non-DHP CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) can precipitate AV block and collapse in amyloid-infiltrated conduction system. Use with caution; beta-blocker preferred.

  12. ACE-I/ARB are poorly tolerated in ATTR with autonomic neuropathy — orthostatic hypotension risk is real. ATTR patients often have autonomic dysfunction; ACE-I/ARB can unmask or worsen orthostatic hypotension. Avoid as primary therapy; use only if HTN is unavoidable, and titrate cautiously. This is different from dilated cardiomyopathy, where ACE-I is standard.

  13. Hemochromatosis is reversible if caught early — phlebotomy can halt and reverse cardiac dysfunction. Early iron-lowering (ferritin target 50–100 ng/mL, transferrin saturation goal < 50%) can reverse restrictive physiology. Late presentation (cirrhosis, advanced fibrosis) is irreversible. Screen young RCM patients (ferritin, transferrin saturation, iron panel). Not all iron overload is hereditary; transfusion-dependent and sideroblastic anemia cause secondary iron cardiomyopathy.

  14. Post-MAZE AF is expected in first 4 weeks — DCCV is usually ineffective until atrial scarring matures. MAZE patients in AF early post-op: don't be aggressive with cardioversion. Atrial scarring takes 4+ weeks to mature; DCCV often recurs. Rate control + amiodarone is default. Scarring maturation is necessary for DCCV efficacy.

  15. Cardiac sarcoidosis is steroid-responsive and potentially reversible — unlike amyloid. If granulomas on biopsy + CMR evidence, high-dose steroids (prednisone 20–40 mg/day, taper over months) can reduce inflammation and improve EF. FDG-PET active inflammation predicts steroid response. VT risk is high; ICD indicated if sustained VT or LV dysfunction + arrhythmia burden. This is different from amyloid (irreversible) and hemochromatosis (iron-mediated).

cards.title: Sepsis / Septic Shock
cards.quickAnswer: Suspected infection + SIRS criteria (fever >38.3 °C or <36 °C, HR >90, RR >20, WBC abnormality) → immediate sepsis workup. Hypotension (MAP <65) OR lactate >4 = septic shock → Hour-1 Bundle: lactate, blood cultures ×2, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h, 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus, vasopressor (norepinephrine) for MAP <65. Identify source — line, wound, lung, GU, GI — and address source control (line removal, drainage, debridement). Post-cardiac surgery: common sources are HAP, sternal wound/mediastinitis, CLABSI, CAUTI, endocarditis.
