sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, who gets it, why it matters.

  • Definition (Sepsis-3): Life-threatening organ dysfunction (SOFA ≥2) caused by dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock = sepsis with refractory hypotension (MAP <65 despite fluids) or lactate >2 mmol/L indicating tissue hypoperfusion (Singer et al., 2016).
  • Incidence: ~5% of post-cardiac surgery patients develop sepsis; varies by procedure and source. HAP most common on ICU admission; sternal/mediastinal infection feared for highest mortality (10–25%).
  • Who this applies to: any patient with actual or suspected infection + SIRS criteria. Especially relevant in post-operative cardiac surgery (POD 0–7), post-central-line placement, post-invasive procedures, or immunocompromised admissions.
  • When it matters: early hour-1 bundle recognition and source control are the strongest predictors of survival. Delay >1 hour correlates with increased mortality (Evans et al., 2021).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Sepsis cascade:

  1. Infectious source — entry through sterile barrier (surgical wound, indwelling line, aspiration, translocation from GI tract)
  2. PAMP recognition — pathogen-associated molecular patterns trigger toll-like receptors on immune cells
  3. Innate immune surge — TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8 release in massive quantities; neutrophil activation
  4. Vasodilation & capillary leak — endothelial dysfunction, fluid shifts to interstitium (edema, oliguria), maldistribution of microcirculation
  5. Microvascular thrombosis — platelet consumption, DIC cascade, tissue microinfarcts
  6. Myocardial depression — direct cytokine effect + mitochondrial dysfunction reduce contractility
  7. End-organ hypoperfusion — anaerobic metabolism, lactate accumulation, organ failure (AKI, hepatic dysfunction, encephalopathy)
  8. Compensatory tachycardia/tachypnea — fail to maintain perfusion; positive-feedback spiral
  9. Multi-organ failure & death — if source not controlled + resuscitation inadequate

Post-cardiac surgery context: sternotomy breach, indwelling lines (central, PICC, Foley, chest tubes, pacer wires), CPB-induced systemic inflammation (complement cascade, leukocyte priming), immobility, aspiration risk all amplify infection susceptibility.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

sections.heading: Temperature abnormalities
sections.bodyHtml:
• New fever >38.3 °C (or two readings >38.0 °C one hour apart)
  • Hypothermia <36 °C (worse prognostic sign; often with shock)

sections.heading: Vital sign or metabolic derangement
sections.bodyHtml:
• Tachycardia >90 bpm unexplained by pain, anxiety, or anemia
  • Tachypnea >22 breaths/min or dyspnea on exertion
  • Altered mental status — drowsiness, confusion, agitation, delayed response (even subtle changes count)
  • Hypotension: MAP <65 or >40 mmHg drop from baseline
  • Oliguria: UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h × 2 h

sections.heading: Lab abnormalities
sections.bodyHtml:
• Lactate >2 mmol/L (concerning); >4 mmol/L (shock criteria)
  • WBC >12,000 or <4,000 with left shift / bandemia
  • Elevated procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL with fever
  • CRP >10 mg/L

sections.heading: Clinical findings suggesting infection source
sections.bodyHtml:
• Sternal: erythema, swelling, purulent drainage, dehiscence, sternal click or motion on palpation
  • Lines: site erythema/induration, purulent drainage (central, PICC, A-line)
  • Lung: productive cough, yellow/green sputum
  • GU: dysuria, cloudy urine, pyuria on UA
  • GI: diarrhea (±C. difficile history), abdominal tenderness/distention
  • Harvest site (leg/radial): swelling, drainage, crepitus, spreading cellulitis

sections.heading: Source epidemiology — what to expect post-cardiac surgery
sections.bodyHtml:
• POD 0–1: Post-pump SIRS (sterile inflammation) most common — fever is normal; cultures often negative but still drawn
  • POD 2–7: HAP (hospital-acquired pneumonia) most frequent sepsis source (~30%), followed by sternal wound/DSWI (~5–10%), CLABSI (~1–3%)
  • Any POD: CAUTI if Foley in place >5 days; C. difficile if prolonged empirics; endocarditis rare but high-mortality if prosthetic valve or IAD

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml: Pure information gathering. No actions yet. Competent systematic bedside exam.

sections.heading: Vital signs and perfusion
sections.bodyHtml:
• Current HR, BP (MAP), RR, SpO₂, temperature (24–48 h trend)
  • Mental status — alert, confused, lethargic; oriented to person/place/time
  • Perfusion — capillary refill (<2 sec), skin temp (warm vs. cool), urine output last 1–2 h

sections.heading: Source survey — physical exam each site
sections.bodyHtml:
• Sternal: erythema, swelling, drainage (clear, serous, purulent), opening/dehiscence, click on palpation
  • Harvest (leg, radial): crepitus, induration, cellulitis, drainage
  • Drain sites: location, character (expected vs. suspicious)
  • Lines: central site erythema/induration, PICC site, A-line, Foley meatus
  • Lungs: auscultation (crackles, consolidation), sputum character (color, volume, odor)
  • GI/GU: abdominal exam (soft, tender, distended), last BM (timing, character), urine color/clarity

sections.heading: Recent labs (chart review)
sections.bodyHtml:
• CBC: WBC, left shift, bands; Hgb/Hct (anemia drives tachycardia)
  • CMP: Cr, BUN (AKI trajectory), glucose (hyperglycemia is stress response)
  • Lactate (if <4 h old; STAT if not available)
  • LFTs, PT/INR, D-dimer if DIC concern
  • Pending culture results from past 24–48 h

sections.heading: Antimicrobial & allergy history
sections.bodyHtml:
• Pre-op prophylaxis timing; current antimicrobials on board (drug names, duration)
  • Recent antibiotic courses in past 30 days (C. difficile risk)
  • Allergy history — beta-lactam severity? (rash vs. anaphylaxis)

sections.heading: Recent procedures/line placements
sections.bodyHtml:
• Central line when inserted? Duration in place?
  • Foley placement timing; any recent catheterization
  • Intubation/extubation timeline; re-intubation
  • Recent cath lab, percutaneous drain, dialysis access

sections.heading: Immunosuppression / comorbidity
sections.bodyHtml:
• Diabetes, renal failure, liver disease, malignancy
  • Chronic steroid use (blunts fever + exam findings)
  • Transplant status (even higher infection risk)

sections.heading: Surgical context
sections.bodyHtml:
• Procedure type, POD
  • Intra-op complications (transfusion, prolonged CPB, IABP, low-output state)

sections.heading: 5A. STABLE path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Fever or SIRS signs present, but MAP >65, lactate <4, alert, perfusing; no shock criteria.)

Timing: All steps 1–10 within 1 hour of identification.

  1. Recheck vitals in 10–15 min — confirm temperature, HR, BP, RR trend; do not anchor on single reading

  2. Focused source survey — systematic physical exam:

    • Sternal: look + palpate (click?); document
    • Harvest: inspect legs/radial; palpate for crepitus
    • Lines: erythema/induration; erythema tracking toward trunk
    • Lungs: auscultate all fields; sputum color, volume
    • Abdomen: soft/tender/distended?

  3. STAT labs — do not delay:

    • CBC w/ differential (WBC, bands)
    • CMP (Cr, BUN, glucose, K, Ca)
    • Lactate STAT (prognostic)
    • Blood cultures ×2 — one peripheral, one central line if present (before antibiotics, same time)
    • Procalcitonin if available (trend better than single value)
    • PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer if DIC concern
    • UA + urine culture if dysuria or oliguria
    • CXR (portable if needed)
    • Sputum culture if productive cough
    • Stool PCR (C. difficile) if diarrhea
    • Wound culture if drainage (swab, anaerobic transport if available)

  4. Establish IV access — two large-bore (18 G) preferred if not in place

  5. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition — do not wait for culture results:

Component Drug Dose
Gram-positive (MRSA) Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h; trough goal 15–20 mcg/mL
Gram-negative & Pseudomonas Cefepime 2 g IV q8h
Alternative gram-negative Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h (covers anaerobes)
Antifungal (if high risk) Fluconazole 400 mg IV/PO q12h

Confirm against current institutional antibiogram and [Institution policy]. Document infusion start time.

  1. Notify provider team — APP, on-call fellow, or hospitalist via SBAR (see §6)

  2. Request ID consult if sepsis suspected — they will refine choice once cultures return

  3. Source control plan — discuss with team:

    • Central line: consider removal if high CLABSI suspicion (site erythema, fever within 48 h of placement); place temporary peripheral during transition
    • Sternal concern: CT surgery notified immediately if sternal click, significant drainage, fever >24 h post-op + worsening clinical picture
    • Leg/radial: vascular surgery if crepitus or spreading cellulitis
    • HAP: aggressive pulmonary toilet, positioning, mobilization; extubation if appropriate

  4. Fever management — acetaminophen 650–1000 mg PO/IV q6h prn for patient comfort + reduced metabolic demand (not for vital-sign cosmetics)

  5. Continuous reassessment — hourly vitals if concerning trajectory; lactate q4–6h until trending down; reassess source q4h; escalate to 5B immediately if shock criteria develop

sections.heading: 5B. UNSTABLE / SEPTIC SHOCK path
sections.bodyHtml:
(MAP <65 despite 500–1000 mL fluid OR lactate >4 mmol/L OR rapid deterioration: altered mental status, poor perfusion, cool extremities.)

Hour-1 Bundle — all steps within 1 hour of shock recognition.

  1. STAT activation:

    • Call APP/fellow + charge RN immediately — do not leave patient alone
    • Activate RRT / Rapid Response (or code team if cardiogenic shock cannot be ruled out)
    • Notify ID, hospitalist, CT surgery (if post-cardiac surgery)
    • Request ICU bed stat

  2. Hour-1 Bundle steps (start clock at shock recognition):

a) Measure lactate STAT - Draw baseline; repeat q2–4h while unstable

b) Blood cultures ×2 BEFORE antibiotics

  • Peripheral and central (if in place); separate sticks preferred
  • Don't delay antibiotics >45 min for culture draws

c) Broad-spectrum antibiotics IV within 1 hour

  • Same empiric as 5A (vanc + cefepime ± fluconazole per antibiogram)
  • Document exact time infusion started

d) IV crystalloid bolus: 30 mL/kg in first 3 hours

  • Preferred: Lactated Ringer or Plasma-Lyte (low-chloride, balanced)
  • Avoid: normal saline (hyperchloremic acidosis)
  • Example: 70 kg patient → 2100 mL bolus; 1000 mL in first 30 min, then reassess
  • Caution in HF/valve disease/RV failure: titrate in 500 mL boluses; some patients tolerate rapid large bolus poorly
  • Goal: MAP >65, UOP 0.5+ mL/kg/h, lactate trending down

e) Vasopressor: Norepinephrine for MAP <65 despite fluid

  • Initiate peripheral IV (16 G) while central access placed
  • Typical: Norepi 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min (0.5–5 mcg/min) titrated to MAP ≥65
  • Goal: MAP ≥65 + lactate clearance
  • Place CVC (central venous catheter) ASAP + arterial line for continuous monitoring

  1. Place central access ASAP — CVC for definitive pressor delivery; a-line for continuous MAP

  2. Source control assessment:

    • Central line: Remove immediately if CLABSI suspected; send line tip culture
    • Sternal: Urgent CT surgery evaluation if any concern for mediastinitis; may require OR exploration/drainage
    • Urinary: Foley removal if CAUTI (pyuria + fever); reculture post-void in 48 h
    • Other sources: drain abscess, debride wound, remove infected hardware

  3. ICU transfer — arrange stat transport; inform ICU team of lactate, vitals, pressor requirement

  4. Stress-dose steroids (if patient on chronic steroids or refractory shock):

    • Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h × 7 days (or 200 mg/day continuous infusion)
    • Rules out adrenal insufficiency in critical illness

  5. Reassess frequently:

    • Lactate recheck q2–4h (goal: >10% clearance per hour)
    • Lactate NOT clearing by 6h → inadequate resuscitation, missed source, or severe illness; escalate
    • Vitals, UOP, perfusion q15–30 min while unstable

  6. Document meticulously:

    • Time shock recognized
    • Time cultures sent, antibiotics started, fluids started (volume), vasopressor started (dose)
    • These timestamps guide intensity and prognosis discussions

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [name], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure] [OR admission diagnosis]."

B: "Patient has fever [temp], [vitals: HR, BP, RR, SpO₂]. [Clinical clue — e.g., 'sternal drainage,' 'productive cough']. Labs: WBC [#], lactate [#], Cr [#]. [Recent significant finding]."

A: "Assessment: Suspected sepsis [with or without shock]. [Key symptoms or deterioration: altered mental status, hypotension, poor perfusion]."

R: "Requesting: [antibiotic orders / source control eval / ICU bed / ID consult / RRT activation]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Rationale
Stable fever + SIRS, cultures sent, perfusing Primary APP / on-call fellow Empiric antibiotic authorization
Septic shock (MAP <65 × 10 min or lactate >4) RRT + APP + hospitalist Emergent; ICU likely needed; Hour-1 Bundle
Sternal drainage/click + fever, POD 0–3 CT surgery STAT Mediastinitis risk; urgent exploration vs. imaging
Suspected CLABSI (central line + fever within 48 h) APP → ID → consult for line removal Source control; new access placement
Fever >48h despite appropriate antibiotics ID + APP Wrong organism, inadequate dosing, missed source (abscess, retained hardware)
Diarrhea + antibiotic exposure APP C. difficile; send stool PCR; hold antimicrobials if possible
New petechiae, purpura, or skin lesions RRT + APP DIC, meningococcemia, endocarditis emboli
Suspected endocarditis (fever + prosthetic valve or IAD) ID + CT surgery + cardiology High mortality; requires TTE/TEE, 3 blood culture sets, possible re-operation

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive on pathophysiology, definitions, source-specific management, and controversies. All subsections below are — collapsed by default.

Sepsis-3 definitions: SIRS vs. qSOFA vs. SOFA (and why Sepsis-3 shifted the paradigm) SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) — 2 or more of:
  • Temperature >38 °C or <36 °C
  • HR >90 bpm
  • RR >20 (or PaCO₂ <32 mmHg)
  • WBC >12,000 or <4,000 or >10% bands SIRS is non-specific — post-pump SIRS, pancreatitis, trauma, major surgery all trigger it without infection. Key shift in Sepsis-3: SIRS alone is no longer the definition of sepsis. qSOFA (quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) — bedside screening for high-risk sepsis:
  • Altered mental status (AMS)
  • Respiratory rate ≥22
  • Systolic BP ≤100 mmHg qSOFA ≥2 = high risk. Requires full SOFA scoring and source investigation. More specific than SIRS for predicting ICU mortality. SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) — severity score (0–24 points):
  • Respiration: PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio
  • Coagulation: platelet count
  • Liver: bilirubin
  • Cardiovascular: MAP or vasopressor requirement
  • CNS: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
  • Renal: creatinine or urine output SOFA ≥2 = sepsis (even without qSOFA criteria). SOFA ≥4 = high mortality risk. Sepsis-3 (2016 consensus): Life-threatening organ dysfunction (SOFA ≥2) caused by dysregulated host response to infection. Lactate >2 mmol/L is a proxy for tissue hypoperfusion even if BP appears adequate. Key principle: early recognition and bundle-driven resuscitation (within 1 hour) matter more than perfect diagnostic certainty.
Post-cardiac surgery SIRS vs. sepsis differentiator — why POD 0–1 fever is usually sterile Post-CPB inflammatory response (sterile SIRS):
  • Peaks POD 0–1 (sometimes extends 24–48h)
  • Caused by: cardiopulmonary bypass circuit activation, complement cascade, leukocyte priming, ischemia-reperfusion injury, endotoxemia from GI translocation
  • Often includes fever >39 °C, leukocytosis (WBC >15k), tachycardia, low-grade coagulopathy
  • Blood cultures almost always negative (sterile)
  • Resolves spontaneously in 24–72h with supportive care Sepsis post-op (true infection):
  • Temperature may be higher, hypothermia is more worrisome
  • Lactate elevated (>2, especially >4)
  • Altered mental status, hypotension (early sign of organ dysfunction)
  • Source localizable (wound, line, lung, urine, etc.)
  • Blood cultures positive (grows organisms)
  • Requires antibiotics + source control Clinical pearl: Send blood cultures on all febrile post-op patients POD 0–1 (they're cheap) but do not over-treat sterile SIRS with prolonged empiric antibiotics. If cultures return negative at 48h and patient clinically improving, consider stopping antimicrobials. Prolonged exposure increases C. difficile and resistance risk.
Common post-cardiac surgery infection sources — diagnosis & management table
SourceIncidenceCluesDiagnosticControl Strategy
HAP (Hospital-acquired pneumonia)~30% of ICU sepsisProductive cough (purulent), fever POD 3–7, hypoxiaCXR (infiltrate), sputum culture, procalcitonin (↑)Extubate early; HOB >30°; oral care; aspiration precautions; pulmonary toilet
Sternal wound infection (SWI) / DSWI~2–5% post-CABG; ~10% post-TAVR; mediastinitis 0.5–2%Fever POD 4–10, sternal swelling/drainage, pain, sternal click/motion on palpationSternal CT (mediastinal lucency, fluid collection), labs show WBC >15kCT surgery urgent evaluation; may need OR for drainage/debridement; vac-assisted closure often needed
CLABSI (central line bloodstream infection)~1–3 per 1000 CVC daysFever within 48 h of line placement, no other localizing sourceBlood cultures from line + peripheral same time; positive culture faster from lineCentral line removal; place new peripheral access during transition; send line tip culture
PICC-related infection~0.5% PICC linesFever, arm swelling/erythema, positive culture from PICCBlood culture (PICC + peripheral simultaneously), PICC tip culturePICC removal; confirm with new peripheral culture; line culture guides de-escalation
CAUTI (catheter-associated UTI)~5% if Foley >7 daysDysuria (if able to communicate), fever, turbid/malodorous urineUA (>10 WBC/hpf, leukocyte esterase+, nitrites), urine cultureFoley removal; reculture post-void in 48h; avoid empiric antibiotics for asymptomatic pyuria
Harvest site (leg / radial artery)~2%Cellulitis, swelling, purulent drainage, crepitus (necrotizing risk)Physical exam (key is crepitus/tracking); CXR if spreading to thoraxVascular surgery eval; debridement if necrotizing fasciitis; avoid delay
C. difficile (pseudomembranous colitis)~1–3% if on prolonged antibioticsDiarrhea (often watery, profuse, foul-smelling), fever, leukocytosis, abdominal pain/crampingStool PCR (most sensitive, culture less so), CXR if toxic megacolon suspectedHold antibiotics if possible; start vancomycin PO 125 mg QID or fidaxomicin 200 mg BID; avoid antimotility agents
Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) / prosthetic device infectionRare but very high mortalityFever any POD, new murmur, embolic phenomena (stroke, splinter nails, Osler nodes), elevated CRP/ESR3 blood culture sets from separate sites (not single collection); TTE/TEE (vegetations; TEE more sensitive)ID + CT surgery early involvement; TEE mandatory; may require re-operation; long-course IV antibiotics (6 wks for PVE)
Acute abdomenRare post-CABG; higher risk post-valve on anticoagulationAbdominal pain, distention, vomiting, diarrheaAbdominal exam, KUB, CT abdomen if peritonitis suspectedSurgical eval; may need exploratory laparotomy; watch for post-op bleeding interaction with source
Key principle: Source control is mandatory — antibiotics alone cannot cure abscess, infected hardware, or necrotic tissue. Must drain, remove, or debride.
Lactate interpretation and prognostic significance — when to worry Lactate = anaerobic metabolism byproduct from tissue hypoperfusion and/or mitochondrial dysfunction.
Lactate (mmol/L)InterpretationClinical Action
<2NormalReassuring; no tissue hypoperfusion
2–4ConcerningMild hypoperfusion; investigate source; recheck lactate q6h
>4Shock criteriaSeptic shock, cardiogenic shock, severe illness; Hour-1 Bundle required immediately
>8Severe shock / poor prognosisMassive tissue hypoperfusion; very high mortality if not rapidly corrected
Lactate clearance = most important prognostic indicator:
  • Goal: >10% decrease per hour (e.g., 4 → 3.6 mmol/L in 1 h)
  • Failure to clear by 6h = inadequate resuscitation, missed source (abscess), or intrinsically severe illness
  • Persistent lactate >4 despite fluids + pressors → aggressive source control needed immediately Pitfalls:
  • After aggressive fluid bolus or beta-2 agonist infusion, lactate can rise transiently from increased hepatic lactate delivery (not more hypoperfusion)
  • Liver failure, cirrhosis, metformin toxicity can cause high lactate without shock ("Type B lactate")
  • Use trend, not single value. Failing to clear is more ominous than absolute value.
Source control principles — why antibiotics alone fail Critical concept: Antibiotics sterilize fluid. They do not drain pus, remove infected hardware, debride necrotic tissue, or remove biofilm-coated lines. Source control maneuvers by source:
SourceTimingStrategy
Central line CLABSIUrgent (within 24 h)Remove line; establish new peripheral or central access; culture line tip
Sternal wound (superficial)Semi-urgent (24–48 h)Bedside drainage, saline flushes, packing; watch for progression
DSWI / mediastinitisEMERGENT (same day, hours)CT surgery evaluation; operative exploration ± drainage; often requires vac-assisted closure
Leg/radial infection with crepitusEMERGENTVascular surgery eval; immediate debridement if necrotizing fasciitis suspected
HAPSupportive (not surgical)Aggressive pulmonary toilet, positioning, mobilization, extubation when appropriate
CAUTIUrgent (24 h)Foley removal; reculture post-void
C. difficile colitisSupportive initiallyHold antibiotics if possible; vanc PO only; avoid antimotility agents; colectomy if toxic megacolon
Intra-abdominal sourceUrgentCT imaging; surgical consultation for possible lap; drainage of loculated collections
Warning sign: Fever persisting >48h despite "appropriate" antibiotics = source not controlled, not antibiotic resistance. Reassess imaging, consider repeat cultures, consider ID consult or surgical re-exploration.
Empiric antibiotic selection — Keck antibiogram guide and de-escalation strategy Antibiotic choice depends on:
  1. Local resistance patterns (institutional antibiogram — updated annually)
  2. Source suspected
  3. Allergy history (ask severity: rash vs. anaphylaxis)
  4. Renal function (renally dose agents)
  5. Timing (prophylaxis vs. empiric sepsis treatment) Typical empiric regimen for post-operative sepsis — confirm with current [Institution policy] and antibiogram:
    ComponentDrugDoseNotes
    Gram-positive (MRSA)Vancomycin15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h; trough 15–20 mcg/mLPreferred for sternal wound, line infection. Check renal function; adjust interval for Cr >2.
    Gram-negative & PseudomonasCefepime2 g IV q8hOR piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h. Covers ESBL. Good lung penetration for HAP.
    Alternative gram-negativePiperacillin-tazobactam4.5 g IV q6hCovers anaerobes; good for intra-abdominal source; higher cost.
    Antifungal (if high risk)Fluconazole400 mg IV/PO q12hConsider if: prolonged ICU stay, prolonged empiric antibiotics, central line, hematologic malignancy, prior azole exposure
    Micafungin100 mg IV q24hIf fluconazole resistance suspected or C. auris concern
    De-escalation strategy:
    • Once culture results available (24–48 h), narrow to target organism
    • Stop unnecessary drugs (e.g., vancomycin if all cultures negative and gram-positive unlikely)
    • Continue empiric until source controlled (line removed, wound drained, etc.) Allergy history guidance:
    • Penicillin allergy (true allergy vs. rash): cross-reactivity with cephalosporins <2% if rash; usually safe if not anaphylaxis. Ask severity. Consider cephalosporin if gram-negative coverage needed.
    • Vancomycin "allergy" (red man syndrome): not true anaphylaxis; pre-medicate with diphenhydramine 25 mg IV before infusion
Steroid use in septic shock — when and why Hydrocortisone for refractory shock:
  • Indication: Septic shock requiring norepinephrine ≥0.05 mcg/kg/min × ≥1 h despite adequate fluid resuscitation, OR chronic steroid user in shock
  • Rationale: Rule out relative adrenal insufficiency; catecholamine-resistant shock may respond to steroid augmentation
  • Dose: Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h × 7 days (or 200 mg/day continuous infusion)
  • Evidence: 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign = weak recommendation; lower threshold for use in septic shock (Evans et al., 2021)
  • Risk: Hyperglycemia, transient immunosuppression; acceptable trade-off if shock refractory Special consideration: Chronic steroid users
  • Higher sepsis risk due to baseline immunosuppression
  • Blunted fever response (may be afebrile despite severe infection)
  • Adrenal insufficiency risk in critical illness
  • Default to giving stress-dose steroids if hypotensive despite fluids + pressors
Vasopressor second-line agents — when norepinephrine alone fails Norepinephrine is first-line. If MAP target not achieved despite adequate fluids and norepi at 0.1+ mcg/kg/min:
DrugMechanismDoseUse caseCaveats
VasopressinV1 receptor agonist; restores vascular tone0.04 u/min (fixed dose, not titrated)Refractory shock; reduces norepi requirementsNo titration; used alongside norepi, not replacement
EpinephrineAlpha + beta agonist; increases contractility & tone0.05–0.3 mcg/kg/minSeptic shock with low cardiac outputHigher arrhythmia risk; use if hypotensive + low CO
PhenylephrinePure alpha; vasoconstriction only0.5–1.4 mcg/kg/minShock with tachycardia as compensationNo inotropic effect; hyporeactivity reported in sepsis
Sequential strategy: Start norepi. If MAP <65 despite norepi 0.1+ mcg/kg/min + adequate fluids, add vasopressin 0.04 u/min. Consider epinephrine if cardiac output thought to be low.
Procalcitonin as a diagnostic and de-escalation tool Procalcitonin (PCT) = precursor of calcitonin; rises in bacterial/fungal sepsis, stays low in viral infection.
PCT LevelInterpretationAction
<0.5 ng/mLBacterial sepsis unlikelySupport discontinuation of empiric antibiotics if clinical improving
0.5–2 ng/mLPossible sepsis; gram-negative or fungal favoredStart or continue empiric; repeat in 24–48h
>2 ng/mLHigh likelihood of bacterial/fungal sepsisContinue empiric antibiotics; source control priority
Trend > single valueFalling PCT = source controlled; rising = inadequate controlGuide de-escalation or escalation decisions
Strengths:
  • More specific for bacterial sepsis than CRP or WBC
  • Trend better than absolute value for monitoring treatment response Limitations:
  • Many non-infectious conditions elevate PCT (major surgery, trauma, necrosis)
  • Can be falsely reassuring in early sepsis (takes 24–48h to rise)
  • Should not delay antibiotics if clinical sepsis suspected
Post-sepsis syndrome — discharge planning for survivors Post-sepsis syndrome (PSS) — occurs in ~50% of sepsis survivors; often underrecognized. - Cognitive impairment: "sepsis brain" (brain fog, memory loss, difficulty concentrating, PTSD-like symptoms)
  • Fatigue: profound weakness for weeks to months; exceeds expected post-op recovery
  • Mood disorders: depression, anxiety, PTSD (recurrent nightmares of ICU)
  • Physical deconditioning: muscle wasting, prolonged weakness; significant rehab needs
  • Immunosuppression window: increased susceptibility to new infections for weeks post-sepsis Discharge counseling should include:
    • Expect 3–6 month recovery; cognitive/physical rehab may be needed
    • Red flags for readmission: fever, chills, new infection signs, severe fatigue interfering with ADLs
    • Follow-up with primary care in 1 week; PT/OT referral if functional limitations
    • Sepsis survivors have increased mortality 1–3 years post-sepsis (mainly from comorbidity, not sepsis recurrence)
    • Anticipatory guidance on cognitive recovery; reassure that "brain fog" typically improves over months

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Watch-fors in stable sepsis that predict shock or treatment failure. If any appear, re-escalate immediately.

  • Lactate NOT clearing despite resuscitation — recheck q4–6h; persistent or rising lactate at 6h = source not controlled, missed abscess, or intrinsically severe illness
  • Altered mental status or worsening sensorium — confusion, lethargy, decreased responsiveness; encephalopathy is marker of severe illness
  • Rising creatinine — AKI from hypoperfusion; oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h); BUN/Cr ratio rising (pre-renal)
  • Fever persisting >24h despite appropriate antibiotics — wrong organism, inadequate dosing, or missed source (abscess, infected line, retained hardware)
  • Tachycardia accelerating — HR rising despite intervention; sign of continued inflammatory drive or pain
  • Blood pressure trending down despite fluid boluses — developing fluid-refractory shock; pressor needed soon
  • New petechiae, purpura, or skin lesions — DIC (early sign); meningococcemia; septic emboli
  • Falling platelet count — DIC trajectory; risk of thrombosis + bleeding simultaneously
  • Escalating pressor requirement — need for higher doses of norepinephrine; may need vasopressin/epinephrine addition
  • New hypoxemia or rising O₂ requirement — can precede ARDS; distinguish fluid overload from sepsis lung (see diastolic dysfunction)
  • Cool extremities + "normal" BP + high lactate — compensated shock (peripheral vasoconstriction masking central failure); very high mortality if not recognized
  • Wound dehiscence + crepitus ± fever — necrotizing fasciitis (rare but surgical emergency)
  • Sternal click + fever >24h post-op + leukocytosis — deep sternal wound infection / mediastinitis; CT surgery STAT
  • Suspected prosthetic valve endocarditis — fever + new murmur + recent cardiac surgery; requires 3 blood culture sets, TTE/TEE, high index for re-operation

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Hour-1 Bundle is the standard of care. Culture, antibiotics, fluids, vasopressor — time matters more than perfect drug selection. Delay >1 hour correlates with increased mortality (Evans et al., 2021). Document exact times of each intervention.

  2. Cultures BEFORE antibiotics — but don't delay antibiotics >45 min. Get two blood culture sets within 15 min if possible; obtain from separate sites/sticks if available. Do NOT wait >45 min for cultures; start empirics if high suspicion.

  3. 30 mL/kg crystalloid is guideline-based but context matters. Post-cardiac surgery patients with HF, severe aortic stenosis, or RV dysfunction tolerate rapid large bolus poorly. Titrate in 500 mL aliquots; reassess after each. Goal is MAP ≥65 + lactate clearance, not a fixed number. Use balanced crystalloid (LR, Plasma-Lyte), not normal saline.

  4. Lactate is the bedside truth-teller. Single temperature or BP can be falsely reassuring. Lactate tracks tissue perfusion; if high, believe it. Trend it every 4–6h in stable sepsis; every 2–4h in shock. Failure to clear >10% per hour by 6h is dire.

  5. Post-pump SIRS POD 0–1 is usually sterile inflammation, not sepsis. Standard post-CPB response peaks 24–48h. But send cultures anyway — they're cheap and occasionally positive. If cultures negative at 48h and patient improving, consider stopping empiric antibiotics to prevent C. difficile.

  6. DSWI / mediastinitis is the feared post-cardiac complication — mortality 10–25%, often requires re-exploration. Sternal click, significant drainage, fever POD 3–7 + leukocytosis = CT surgery STAT, not just APP. Don't try to treat empirically for 48h; urgent surgical evaluation is needed.

  7. C. difficile in antibiotic-exposed patients — prolonged empirics for surgical site infection or vancomycin exposure = high risk. Send stool PCR before attributing diarrhea to laxatives. Hold antibiotics if possible; start vancomycin PO 125 mg QID if positive. Avoid antimotility agents.

  8. Persistent fever >48h on appropriate antibiotics = source not controlled. Not "the infection is resistant." Rather: abscess not drained, infected hardware not removed, wrong diagnosis, or missed source. Reassess imaging, repeat blood cultures, consider ID consult or surgical re-exploration.

  9. Acetaminophen for fever = patient comfort + reduced VO₂ demand, not vital-sign cosmetics. Some clinicians avoid fever meds thinking fever kills bacteria. Benefit is modest; patient comfort is real.

    Avoid NSAIDs (renal risk, post-operative bleeding risk).

  10. Fever is blunted in elderly, chronic steroid users, and immunosuppressed patients. Relative tachycardia, altered mental status, elevated procalcitonin, or hypotension may be the only sign of infection. Lower threshold to work up non-febrile sepsis in these populations.

  11. Endocarditis / prosthetic device infection is a different pathway. Requires 3 blood culture sets from separate sites (NOT same collection tube), TTE/TEE, early ID + CT surgery involvement. Mortality 30–40% even with treatment. Think about it in any post-operative cardiac patient with persistent fever ± embolic phenomena (stroke, splinter nails).

  12. Stress-dose steroids if chronic steroid user in shock. They're at high risk of adrenal insufficiency in critical illness. Hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h × 7 days is appropriate if hypotensive despite fluids + pressors (Evans et al., 2021).

  13. Procalcitonin rises in bacterial/fungal sepsis, stays low in viral. Single value <0.5 ng/mL makes bacterial sepsis less likely. Trend better than single value. Rising PCT = inadequate source control; falling PCT = source controlled. Use to guide de-escalation.

  14. Lactate clearance >10% per hour is reassuring; failure to clear by 6h is dire. This metric guides intensity of resuscitation. If lactate not dropping despite fluids, pressors, antibiotics, and source control, consider: missed abscess (CT imaging), infected hardware not removed, or consider ICU transfer for ECMO/aggressive resuscitation.

  15. Post-discharge sepsis awareness critical. Sternal infections often present 2–6 weeks post-op. Family teaching at discharge: fever, sternal redness, drainage, or sternal "click" = call surgeon immediately or go to ED.

cards.title: Severe Symptomatic Aortic Stenosis Awaiting TAVR / SAVR
cards.quickAnswer: Severe AS patient awaiting TAVR / SAVR: hemodynamic stability via preload-dependent hypertrophic LV. AVOID vasodilators (nitrates, hydralazine, ACE/ARB held), tachycardia, and excessive diuresis. Phenylephrine first-line for hypotension; gentle diuresis only; maintain sinus rhythm. Decompensated or crashing: balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) as bridge stabilizes to reach TAVR. Work-up: CT-TAVR (annulus, access), coronary angio, frailty (CFS), STS risk, Heart Team decision. Expected LOS 3–7 days for workup + same-day/next-day TAVR; SAVR 5–7 days post-op.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Severe aortic stenosis (valve area < 1.0 cm² with mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg OR peak velocity ≥ 4.0 m/s) with symptomatic presentation (angina, syncope, dyspnea, HF) in a candidate for TAVR or SAVR.
  • Critical AS subtype: valve area < 0.6 cm², mean gradient > 50 mmHg, hemodynamic instability at rest.
  • Epidemiology: ~5% of adults > age 75 have moderate-to-severe AS; severe AS affects ~1% and carries high mortality without intervention (Otto et al., 2021).
  • Who this applies to: adult patients admitted for pre-operative work-up, acute decompensation with bridge therapy, or emergent intervention.
  • Why it matters: untreated symptomatic severe AS has 50% 2-year mortality. Even brief delays in TAVR/SAVR for decompensated patients increase ICU stay, stroke risk, and mortality.

sections.heading: Core physiology: "Slow, Full, Squeezed"
sections.bodyHtml:
The hypertrophic aortic stenotic left ventricle operates on a knife's edge:

  • Slow: tachycardia dramatically reduces diastolic filling time → lower stroke volume → syncope, shock. Beta-blockade essential.
  • Full: preload-dependent. The small, thick LV needs maximal filling. Even moderate diuresis → syncope or cardiogenic shock.
  • Squeezed: high afterload keeps the ventricle viable, but vasodilators (nitrates, hydralazine, ACE/ARB) drop systemic vascular resistance without relieving valve obstruction → syncope, hypotension, worsened perfusion.

This is the opposite of heart failure due to volume overload — you cannot simply diurese or vasodilate the patient out of trouble.

sections.heading: Mechanical basis
sections.bodyHtml:
The calcified, stenotic aortic valve restricts outflow. LV pressure spikes to overcome the gradient. Over months to years, the LV becomes concentrically hypertrophied and stiff. Peak systolic pressure can exceed 200 mmHg while aortic pressure remains normal — a huge pressure gradient (typically 40–80+ mmHg mean).

Coronary blood flow is diastolic. In severe AS, systolic pressure is so high that it partially compresses intramyocardial coronary vessels during systole, worsening subendocardial perfusion. Even without CAD, patients have demand ischemia from a hypoperfused, hypertrophied ventricle — hence angina is a cardinal symptom.

Syncope occurs when the LV cannot increase stroke volume on exertion (fixed afterload obstruction) — blood pressure falls, cerebral hypoperfusion → loss of consciousness.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — why the patient was admitted.

sections.heading: Acute decompensation scenarios (admission triggers)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Pulmonary edema or acute decompensated HF: orthopnea, PND, exertional dyspnea, rales, elevated JVD, BNP > 400 pg/mL
  • Syncope or near-syncope with hypotension: especially on exertion or during positional change
  • Refractory angina / demand ischemia: chest pain with stress or minimal activity; troponin elevated or EKG changes
  • Cardiogenic shock: hypotension (SBP < 90), signs of hypoperfusion (altered mental status, oliguria, lactate > 2 mmol/L)
  • Pre-operative work-up for planned TAVR/SAVR: elective admission for cath, CT, frailty assessment, optimization

sections.heading: Physical exam findings (pre-operative baseline)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Cardiac auscultation: harsh, loud systolic ejection murmur (crescendo-decrescendo), best at right upper sternal border, radiates to carotids
  • Carotid pulses: slow-rising (parvus tardus), reduced amplitude, narrow pulse pressure (SBP − DBP often < 40 mmHg)
  • Apical impulse: hyperdynamic but sometimes non-displaced (because LV is small and thick)
  • Paradoxically split S2 or single S2: aortic component reduced due to prolonged LV ejection

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (initial 4 hours)
sections.bodyHtml: Competent systematic data gathering. No interventions yet.

sections.heading: Vital signs & hemodynamics
sections.bodyHtml:
• HR, BP (sitting, standing if safe), SpO₂, RR, temperature
  • Orthostatic BP changes; syncope risk if orthostatic drop > 20 systolic
  • JVD, peripheral edema, weight vs dry weight
  • Perfusion: capillary refill, skin temperature, mental status, urine output

sections.heading: Symptoms & timeline
sections.bodyHtml:
• Onset of chest pain, syncope, dyspnea; triggers (exertion, positional, rest); severity scale
  • Prior episodes of syncope / presyncope
  • Orthopnea, PND, exertional limitation
  • Recent hospitalizations or prior AS diagnosis

sections.heading: Physical exam (complete)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Cardiac auscultation (murmur character, loudness, radiation)
  • Carotid pulse quality bilaterally (parvus tardus indicator)
  • Peripheral pulses (femoral, dorsal pedis quality for access planning)
  • Lung auscultation (crackles, reassess after any diuresis)
  • Abdominal exam (hepatomegaly, ascites from RV failure)

sections.heading: Diagnostic labs (STAT)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Troponin, BNP / NT-proBNP — assess decompensation severity, ischemia
  • CBC, CMP, coagulation studies, creatinine — baseline renal function (contrast risk)
  • Magnesium, calcium, phosphate — electrolyte abnormalities worsen arrhythmia risk
  • EKG (12-lead) — LVH with strain, AF, ischemic changes; baseline for post-TAVR comparison
  • Chest X-ray — pulmonary edema, cardiac silhouette, aortic knob calcification

sections.heading: Imaging (expedited)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) STAT — gold standard for AS diagnosis
  • Aortic valve area (planimetry or continuity equation), mean/peak gradient
  • LV ejection fraction, wall thickness, cavity size (typically normal or small with concentric hypertrophy)
  • Diastolic function assessment (restrictive or pseudonormal patterns common)
  • AR severity (coexisting aortic regurgitation changes management)
  • Estimate PA pressure, RV function
  • TEE — if needed for redo patient assessment or if TTE quality poor
  • Coronary angiography — within 24–48 h if TAVR/SAVR planned (determine need for concurrent CABG)
  • CT-TAVR (cardiac CT with TAVR protocol) if TAVR likely
  • Annulus sizing (perimeter, diameter, eccentricity) — crucial for valve size selection
  • Iliofemoral vessel assessment (diameter, calcification, tortuosity → can transfemoral TAVR be done?)
  • Aortic root-to-coronary ostial distances (LMCA > 10 mm essential to avoid coronary obstruction)
  • Aortic arch morphology, branch vessel take-off

sections.heading: Clinical context
sections.bodyHtml:
• MAR / home medication review — when were beta-blockers, ACE/ARB, diuretics last given?
  • Prior cardiac history — CABG, prior AVR, AF, CAD, renal insufficiency
  • Frailty assessment — gait, cognition; Cardiovascular Frailty Scale (CFS) score ≥ 5 → favors TAVR
  • STS risk calculator — estimate perioperative mortality if SAVR being considered
  • Social factors — living situation, support system, DNR/advance directive preferences

sections.heading: 5. Management — Acute Stabilization & Bridge to TAVR / SAVR
Preface: Stable vs. Unstable fork for medical-admit
sections.bodyHtml:
Stable: awaiting TAVR, hemodynamically tolerated work-up, no acute decompensation
Unstable: syncope with hypotension, decompensated HF, cardiogenic shock, or patient deteriorating despite gentle management → bridge therapy (BAV) or emergent TAVR/SAVR may be needed.

sections.heading: 5A. Acute stabilization (Stable patient)
sections.bodyHtml: Goal: maintain perfusion, prevent decompensation, complete work-up safely.

sections.heading: Hemodynamic support & medications
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Beta-blockade (first priority)

    • Target HR 55–80 bpm. Every beat counts toward diastolic filling.
    • IV options: metoprolol 5 mg IV q6–8h (titrate to HR), or esmolol infusion 50–300 μg/kg/min
    • PO transition: metoprolol 25–50 mg BID or extended-release alternative; target HR < 100
    • Red flag: HR > 100 → escalate; new AF with RVR is ICU-level emergency in AS

  2. Blood pressure management

    • Target SBP 100–120 mmHg — enough perfusion, not so high it increases demand ischemia
    • Phenylephrine FIRST-LINE for hypotension (not nitrates, hydralazine, or ACE/ARB)

    • Mechanism: alpha-1 agonist increases SVR → increases diastolic aortic pressure → improves coronary perfusion without increasing contractility
    • Usual: 40–80 mg in 250 mL D5W or NS, start 0.5–1.4 μg/kg/min, titrate to SBP goal
    • Avoid excessive doses (SVR > 1200, worsens afterload sensitivity)
    • AVOID: nitrates (especially SL nitroglycerin — can precipitate syncope), hydralazine, ACE inhibitors, ARBs
    • Why: drop afterload without relieving valve obstruction; syncope, shock

  3. Diuresis (GENTLE)

    • Crackles or orthopnea present? Low-dose IV furosemide (10–20 mg IV, not 40–80 mg)
    • Recheck lung sounds in 2 hours; only retreat if persistent rales
    • No crackles? Hold diuretics entirely. Preload is precious.
    • Trend daily weight — watch for gains > 2 lbs suggesting fluid overload, but avoid overcorrection
    • Goal: euvolemia (JVD 5–8 cm, no rales, patient comfortable), NOT dryness

  4. Electrolyte repletion

    • Target K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 — critical for sinus rhythm
    • Replace per Electrolyte Replacement protocol; IV repletion if urgent
    • Do NOT hold ACE/ARB purely for K⁺ sparing — the AS physiology forbids ACE/ARB use anyway

sections.heading: Pain control
sections.bodyHtml:
• IV opioids PRN for angina or anxiety (morphine 2–4 mg IV q2–4h or hydromorphone 0.5–1 mg IV q2–4h)
  • Avoid NSAIDs (contrast bleeding risk if proceeding to cath; thrombosis risk post-TAVR)
  • Avoid sublingual nitroglycerin (syncope risk)

sections.heading: Thromboprophylaxis & anticoagulation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Sequential compression devices (SCDs) on legs (AS patient often at risk for DVT from immobility)
  • Aspirin typically held 3–5 days pre-procedure per anesthesia; can resume post-op TAVR immediately
  • Home anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC) — continue if indicated for AF or prior VTE; hold per surgeon if SAVR planned

sections.heading: Monitoring & observation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Continuous telemetry — watch for new AF, bradycardia, ectopy
  • Daily EKG — track LVH, ischemic changes, new arrhythmias
  • Daily labs: CBC, CMP, troponin trend, BNP
  • Vital signs & orthostatics each shift — key indicator of decompensation
  • Auscultation each shift — confirm murmur, assess for new AR, listen to lungs

sections.heading: Workup completion
sections.bodyHtml:
• Coordinate cardiology & CT surgery consults — heart team conference ideally by Day 2
  • TEE if needed — redo valve assessment, better visualization than TTE
  • Coronary angiography — expedite within 24–48 h; identify CAD, LMCA disease
  • CT-TAVR if TAVR likely — annulus sizing, access planning
  • Frailty assessment — CFS score, ADL capability
  • STS calculator — if SAVR in discussion
  • Anesthesia pre-op evaluation — airway, cardiac risk, spinal vs general anesthesia preference for TAVR
  • Type & screen / type & cross — blood available before any procedure

sections.heading: Patient & family communication
sections.bodyHtml:
• Shared decision-making: TAVR vs SAVR risks/benefits, life expectancy, durability
  • Goals of care: if patient very frail or limited life expectancy, clarify whether intervention is desired
  • NPO status & timing — once procedure date set, NPO 6 h food, 2 h clear liquids

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path — acute decompensation & bridge therapy
sections.bodyHtml: Patient declining despite 5A measures, or arriving in shock.

sections.heading: Immediate escalation (STAT)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Call APP/fellow + charge nurse STAT — do NOT manage alone
  2. ICU transfer if not already there — continuous monitoring, invasive lines
  3. Call CT surgery — may need BAV, emergent TAVR, or SAVR
  4. Place central line, arterial line, consider pulmonary artery catheter for hemodynamic assessment

sections.heading: Diagnostic assessment (rapid)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Repeat EKG STAT — R-wave progression, ischemic changes
  • Troponin STAT — significant elevation (> 1 ng/mL) suggests ACS-equivalent or complication
  • Lactate, ABG — assess perfusion adequacy
  • Echo STAT (bedside TTE or TEE) — confirm severe AS, rule out new AR from leaflet rupture, assess EF, pericardial effusion, tamponade
  • Chest X-ray STAT — pulmonary edema, pericardial effusion, PTX (if prior line placement)

sections.heading: Hemodynamic optimization
sections.bodyHtml:
• Reduce phenylephrine or discontinue if patient is in overt pulmonary edema / cardiogenic shock (paradoxically, very high afterload worsens CO)
  • IV diuretics — now slightly more aggressive: furosemide 20–40 mg IV, repeat in 2 h if persistent crackles
  • Consider nitroglycerin drip cautiously (only if pulmonary edema is severe AND SBP > 120; discontinue if SBP drops or syncope develops)
  • Inotrope support — if shock persists (SBP < 90 + oliguria + altered mental status):
    • Dobutamine 2.5–5 μg/kg/min — increases contractility without dropping afterload as much as milrinone
    • Low-dose epinephrine 2–5 μg/min — alpha + beta; maintains SVR while boosting contractility
    • (Avoid milrinone alone; afterload drop worsens AS physiology)

sections.heading: Bridge therapy: Balloon Aortic Valvuloplasty (BAV)
sections.bodyHtml:
Indication: cardiogenic shock, refractory pulmonary edema, syncope with hypotension, TAVR delayed > 24 h

Goal: temporary reduction in gradient, stabilization to bridge to definitive TAVR/SAVR

Procedure:

  • Retrograde femoral arterial approach or antegrade (transseptal) depending on access
  • Serial inflations of balloons (typically 30–50 mm) to rupture calcified leaflet cusps
  • Target: reduce gradient from 60+ mmHg to 30–40 mmHg mean

Hemodynamics post-BAV:

  • CO increases, BP rises, pulmonary pressures decrease, urine output improves
  • Gradient creeps back up over hours to days (leaflets calcify again; NOT a permanent fix)
  • Refractory AR may develop from leaflet damage

Timeline post-BAV: TAVR must occur within 24–72 h (often SAME-DAY if patient stabilizes enough)

sections.heading: Precautions in decompensation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Do NOT routinely give ACE/ARB, ARB, or hydralazine — preload already threatened
  • IABP contraindicated if AR present — diastolic augmentation pushes blood back through leaky aortic valve
  • Watch for flash pulmonary edema after BAV — paradoxically, improved CO can unmask LV dysfunction
  • Anticoagulation: if BAV performed, heparin anticoagulation during procedure; post-procedure anticoagulation per team

sections.heading: Escalate to emergent TAVR / SAVR if
sections.bodyHtml:
• Shock does not respond to BAV within 4–6 h
  • Acute severe AR develops from leaflet rupture
  • Cardiac output remains inadequate despite inotropes + PEEP
  • Renal failure (creatinine > 2.5) or hepatic hypoperfusion (elevated lactate, hyperbilirubinemia)

sections.heading: Last 12 hours pre-op
sections.bodyHtml:
1. NPO status: 6 hours food, 2 hours clear liquids (or per anesthesia protocol)
  2. Baseline imaging & labs:
    • Final chest X-ray (for post-op comparison)
    • Final CBC, CMP, coagulation studies, troponin
    • Type & cross / type & screen (TAVR: usually 2 units; SAVR: 4–6 units available)
    • Pre-anesthesia visit — airway exam, IV access plan, sedation vs general anesthesia choice, spinal vs epidural if TAVR
    • Medications pre-op:
    • Continue: beta-blockers (unless anesthesia holds for hypotension), statin, home respiratory meds
    • Hold: ACE/ARB (spinal-induced hypotension risk), aspirin 3–5 days, clopidogrel hold if possible, diuretics
    • Verify: vancomycin/antibiotic prophylaxis per protocol (2 g IV vanc pre-incision, redose per renal function)

sections.heading: Day of procedure — transport to OR / cath lab
sections.bodyHtml:
• Confirm NPO status, void, remove jewelry / dentures
  • Final vital signs, neuro check
  • Place on monitor during transport
  • Hand-off to anesthesia / cath lab staff

sections.heading: SBAR Template
sections.bodyHtml:
S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [patient name], room [X], admitted with severe aortic stenosis awaiting TAVR / SAVR."

B: "[Patient age, prior cardiac history]. Presenting with [syncope / pulmonary edema / angina]. TTE shows [valve area, gradient, EF]. Labs: K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value], troponin [value], BNP [value]."

A: "Patient is currently [stable / decompensating / shock]. HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. [Symptoms]. On phenylephrine [dose], beta-blocker [dose]."

R: "Requesting [completion of workup / hemodynamic support plan / escalation to BAV / expedited TAVR / ICU transfer]."

sections.heading: Who to Call
sections.bodyHtml:
Situation Contact
Stable, routine workup Primary cardiologist or on-call fellow
New or worsening syncope On-call fellow + CT surgery (same-day or next-day TAVR acceleration)
Pulmonary edema refractory to gentle diuresis On-call fellow + ICU team (consider CPAP, IV diuretics, transfer)
Cardiogenic shock (SBP < 90 + hypoperfusion) STAT: Fellow + CT surgery + ICU (BAV or emergent TAVR)
New AF with RVR (HR > 110) STAT: Fellow + ICU (rate control, electrolyte repletion, possible DCCV)
Chest pain + troponin > 1 ng/mL Fellow + CT surgery (ACS-equivalent; may accelerate TAVR)
New murmur of aortic regurgitation STAT: Fellow + cardiology (TEE; may change management urgency)
Syncope with documented bradycardia or high-degree AV block STAT: Fellow + ICU (consider pacer, cardiology evaluation)
Stroke or TIA symptoms STAT: Stroke code + neurology (MRI, neuro assessment)
Acute limb ischemia (post-catheterization) STAT: Vascular surgery (femoral access thrombosis)
After TAVR: bradycardia with hypotension STAT: Fellow + ICU (new conduction block; transcutaneous pacing ready)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections below are — collapsed by default.

7.1 Pathophysiology: Severe AS hemodynamic trap

sections.heading: Why AS is different from typical heart failure
sections.bodyHtml:
In volume overload (DCM, HF from hypertension), the failing heart is unable to generate pressure — you dilate, you reduce afterload (vasodilators, diuretics), increase contractility (inotropes). This is backwards for AS.

In AS, the heart can generate extreme pressure (systolic LV pressures > 180 mmHg), but the valve won't open. The LV is stiff, not weak. The problem is mechanical obstruction, not contractile failure.

sections.heading: Consequences of the "Slow, Full, Squeezed" physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Slow (HR): Diastole is when the stiff LV fills (slowly, painfully). Tachycardia (from AF, pain, anxiety, or drugs like dobutamine) cuts diastolic time → filling falls sharply → stroke volume crashes → syncope, shock.

  2. Full (preload): The hypertrophied LV operates on the steep ascending limb of the Frank-Starling curve. A small drop in end-diastolic volume → disproportionate fall in stroke volume. Over-diuresis → syncope, cardiogenic shock. This is the opposite of HF where you diurese to relieve congestion.

  3. Squeezed (afterload): The LV generates enormous pressure to force blood through the stenotic valve. This requires high systemic vascular resistance to maintain diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion. Vasodilators drop SVR → diastolic pressure falls → coronary hypoperfusion → worsening angina, potentially syncope. The calcified valve obstruction doesn't improve no matter how much you dilate vessels.

sections.heading: Why syncope happens
sections.bodyHtml:
During exertion, the rigid AS valve cannot increase flow. The LV can't produce enough cardiac output to sustain BP, so BP drops → cerebral hypoperfusion → LOC. It's a mechanical limit, not a weak heart.

Sublingual nitroglycerin in AS patient → drop in afterload (from nitrates) + drop in preload (venous pooling) → double hit → severe syncope or cardiogenic shock.

sections.heading: Coronary perfusion in AS
sections.bodyHtml:
Normal coronary perfusion is diastolic (aortic pressure > LVEDP). In severe AS:

  • Systolic LV pressure spikes to 150–200+ mmHg, compressing intramyocardial vessels
  • Diastolic aortic pressure is often normal or low (afterload obstruction), reducing diastolic perfusion pressure gradient
  • Result: subendocardial ischemia even without CAD (demand ischemia)
  • Angina is common and does NOT mean epicardial CAD; often relieved by TAVR/SAVR

sections.heading: Why certain medications work (or backfire)
sections.bodyHtml:
Phenylephrine (alpha-agonist):

  • Increases SVR → aortic diastolic pressure ↑ → coronary perfusion ↑
  • Does NOT increase contractility (unlike epinephrine)
  • In AS: "perfect" drug because you need afterload support without inotropic drive
  • Slight LVH regression if BP control improves over time

Beta-blockers:

  • Slow HR → more diastolic fill time
  • Reduce contractility demand → reduce myocardial O₂ demand
  • Reduce risk of tachycardia-induced decompensation
  • In AS: essential, near-curative if tolerated

Nitrates:

  • Vasodilate (drop preload and afterload)
  • Relief of angina in CAD (increases coronary flow)
  • In AS: catastrophic — preload drop → hypovolemia → syncope; afterload drop → coronary hypoperfusion
  • Historical teaching: "contraindicated in AS" — still true for acute AS

ACE/ARB:

  • Reduce afterload via angiotensin blockade
  • Beneficial in HF (reduce LV remodeling)
  • In severe AS: afterload drop without valve relief → syncope, shock
  • Hold entirely pre-TAVR/SAVR; restart post-op only if reduced EF

sections.heading: The paradox of low-flow low-gradient AS
sections.bodyHtml:
Some patients have severe AV calcification (restrictive valve), normal EF (> 50%), but low gradient (< 40 mmHg) and low stroke volume (< 35 mL/m²).

Why? Severe LV hypertrophy + stiffness → LV cavity is tiny → absolute stroke volume is low, but EF ratio is maintained because EDV is also tiny.

The valve is severely obstructed, but the LV is protecting itself by generating less output to avoid exceeding the fixed obstruction (Starling mechanism in reverse).

Diagnosis requires stress echo (increase HR with dobutamine) or cardiac catheterization (measure CO, gradient simultaneously) to prove the valve is truly obstructive.

Treatment: TAVR or SAVR is indicated (Mack et al., 2019; PARTNER 3), but these patients are often older, sicker (higher surgical risk), so TAVR often preferred.

7.2 TAVR vs SAVR decision-making framework

sections.heading: The shared decision-making conversation
sections.bodyHtml:
TAVR advantages:

  • Less invasive (no sternotomy)
  • Faster recovery (discharge POD 1–2 vs POD 5–7)
  • Lower peri-operative mortality in high-risk (Mack et al., 2019; PARTNER 3 extended TAVR to low-risk)
  • No lifelong anticoagulation if mechanical (dual antiplatelet only 3–6 mo)

TAVR limitations:

  • Shorter prosthesis durability (10–15 year data limited; concern for structural degeneration, valve-in-valve re-intervention)
  • Paravalvular AR risk (5–10% mild, 1–2% moderate)
  • Post-TAVR conduction blocks (10–20% new RBBB; 1–2% complete AVB requiring pacemaker)
  • Cost (though offset by shorter LOS)

SAVR advantages:

  • Mechanical valve nearly lifetime durable (20–30+ years)
  • Bioprosthetic 10–20 year lifespan (lower anticoagulation burden)
  • Better long-term freedom from reintervention
  • Proven safety in low-risk, younger patients

SAVR limitations:

  • Invasive (full sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass)
  • Longer recovery (ICU 1–3 days, stepdown 3–4 days, home discharge POD 5–7)
  • Higher peri-operative mortality in very high-risk
  • Lifelong warfarin if mechanical (INR monitoring, dietary restrictions, bleeding risk)
  • Redo SAVR (after prior CABG or prior cardiac surgery) has substantially higher mortality

sections.heading: Decision factors
sections.bodyHtml:
Factor TAVR favored SAVR favored
Age > 80 y < 60 y
Frailty (CFS score) ≥ 5 (frail) < 3 (robust)
STS mortality score > 8% < 3%
EF < 30% acceptable > 40% preferred
Prior CABG Yes (avoids graft manipulation) High-risk (redo)
Life expectancy < 10 years (fast relief, less concern for durability) > 15 years (durability matters)
Aortic root Normal size ok Annular calcification, abscess, root pathology → SAVR root replacement often preferred
LMCA ostium > 10 mm from aortic valve (safe for TAVR) Not relevant
Access Transfemoral (< 5 mm vessel) preferred; transapical ok All anatomies feasible
Pregnancy planned N/A (mechanical AC contraindicated in pregnancy) Bioprosthetic preferred (no warfarin)

sections.heading: Timing after decision
sections.bodyHtml:
TAVR:

  • Often same-day admission to same-day discharge, or next-day discharge
  • Procedurally expedited (2–4 h from decision to catheterization)
  • Increasingly common outpatient TAVR (elective cases)

SAVR:

  • 1–3 days pre-operative optimization and work-up
  • Procedure 2–4 hours
  • 5–7 days post-operative hospital stay typical

7.3 Avoiding medications in severe AS

sections.heading: The "avoid" list and why each is dangerous
sections.bodyHtml:
Nitrates (sublingual nitroglycerin, IV NTG, isosorbide dinitrate)

  • Mechanism: vasodilate, increase venous pooling → drop preload + drop afterload
  • In AS: preload already marginal (small LV) → syncope, cardiogenic shock
  • Historical red flag: nitroglycerin syncope is classic presentation
  • Exception: only in rare setting of AS + acute pulmonary edema + SBP > 120, and only briefly while preparing for TAVR/BAV

ACE inhibitors / ARBs (lisinopril, enalapril, losartan, valsartan)

  • Mechanism: block angiotensin II → vasodilation, reduce afterload
  • In AS: afterload drop without obstruction relief → syncope, hypotension
  • Common mistake: continuing patient's home lisinopril because of "hypertension history"
  • Must hold pre-TAVR/SAVR; often restart post-op only if EF < 50%

Hydralazine

  • Mechanism: direct arteriolar vasodilation
  • In AS: same afterload-drop danger as nitrates
  • If high BP in AS patient (and NOT in shock), use phenylephrine instead (SVR support + coronary perfusion)

Nifedipine (dihydropyridine CCB)

  • Mechanism: arteriolar vasodilation, reflex tachycardia possible
  • In AS: tachycardia is enemy #1; plus afterload drop
  • Alternative: non-dihydropyridine (diltiazem, verapamil) if rate control needed (but avoid in reduced EF)

SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin)

  • Mechanism: diuretic + afterload reduction
  • In AS: volume loss + afterload drop → danger (though rare acute crisis)
  • Recommendation: stop SGLT2i 48 hours pre-TAVR/SAVR (restart post-op)

Diuretics (over-aggressive dosing)

  • Mechanism: reduce preload → relieve congestion
  • In AS: preload is precious → over-diuresis → syncope, cardiogenic shock
  • Safe approach: gentle (10–20 mg furosemide IV) only if overt crackles; recheck in 2 h

Positive inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) — use cautiously - Dobutamine: increases contractility + causes reflex vasodilation - Danger: reflex tachycardia (diastolic time ↓, syncope risk) + afterload drop - Use only if shock + CO is failing; keep doses low; pair with vasopressor (phenylephrine)

  • Milrinone: inodilator (increases contractility + vasodilates)
  • Danger: severe afterload drop in AS patient
  • Avoid as single agent; if used, pair with phenylephrine

Amiodarone drip (if AF develops)

  • Amiodarone is excellent for rhythm control but causes hypotension in ~25%
  • In AS: BP drop is catastrophic (see Section 9 Pitfall)
  • Approach: bolus amiodarone slowly (150 mg over 10 min), keep drip at low rate (0.5–1 mg/min)

7.4 Managing special scenarios

sections.heading: Severe AS + concurrent atrial fibrillation (AF)
sections.bodyHtml:
Problem: AF in AS is high-risk. Patient loses atrial kick (20–30% of CO in AS patients) → syncope, cardiogenic shock.

Management:

  1. Rate control URGENT — target HR < 100 even if stable - IV beta-blocker (metoprolol 5 mg IV) first-line - IV diltiazem if beta-blocker contraindicated - Do NOT use IV verapamil if reduced EF
  2. Rhythm control: amiodarone preferred - Bolus 150 mg over 10 min; may repeat - Drip 1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min; watch for hypotension
  3. Electrolytes URGENT — K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0
  4. Anticoagulation decision: if AF > 48 h, stroke risk high (CHA₂DS₂-VASc calculation) - Discuss with team; often heparin bridge post-TAVR, then dual antiplatelet (not warfarin unless other indication)
  5. Cardioversion if unstable: synchronized DCCV (100 → 200 → 300 J biphasic)

sections.heading: Severe AS + low ejection fraction (EF < 30%)
sections.bodyHtml:
Paradox: some severely stenotic valves cause secondary LV dysfunction (afterload mismatch → systolic dysfunction).

Findings: EF 20–30%, dilated LV cavity (unlike typical AS with small cavity), low stroke volume, high gradient may be blunted (low gradient + low EF = high-risk).

Decision: TAVR strongly favored over SAVR (surgical risk higher, but TAVR relieving afterload obstruction can improve EF).

Post-TAVR: often dramatic EF recovery within weeks to months as afterload normalizes.

sections.heading: Severe AS + concurrent significant aortic regurgitation (AR)
sections.bodyHtml:
Problem: AR indicates aortic leaflet damage (endocarditis, rupture, or chronic aortic root dilation).

Management: combined AS-AR is complex - If AR mild: proceed with TAVR/SAVR as planned; AR improves or stays stable post-op - If AR moderate-to-severe:

  • Rule out endocarditis (blood cultures, TEE)
  • TAVR may worsen AR (valve-in-valve sitting on diseased root)
  • SAVR (with or without root replacement) often preferred

sections.heading: Severe AS + Heyde syndrome (AS + gastrointestinal bleeding from angiodysplasia)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology: high shear stress from turbulent flow across stenotic valve damages von Willebrand factor (vWF) → loss of large vWF multimers → bleeding from AVMs.

Clinical: older patients with severe AS present with GI bleed (often intermittent, recurrent).

Management:

  • Do NOT assume GI source is simple peptic ulcer
  • Do NOT transfuse excessively (exacerbates shear stress, worsens bleeding)
  • TAVR / SAVR usually resolves the bleeding (normalizes shear stress, vWF multimers recover)
  • Approach: TAVR if candidate; if SAVR, expedite

sections.heading: Severe AS awaiting TAVR + prior CABG
sections.bodyHtml:
Problem: prior CABG grafts are in the aorta or left main system → complicate TAVR access or imaging.

TAVR still feasible:

  • Transfemoral approach avoids sternotomy / graft manipulation (advantage over redo SAVR)
  • CT-TAVR annulus sizing and access planning still done
  • Coronary ostial distance critical (grafts may alter coronary takeoff geometry)
  • Graft patency review recommended (patent LMCA graft carries low coronary obstruction risk; occluded native LMCA safer for TAVR)

Heart Team discussion: usually TAVR > redo SAVR (which has 2–3× mortality vs primary SAVR).

sections.heading: Severe AS + advanced age (> 85 years) or frailty
sections.bodyHtml:
Frailty Scale (CFS):

  • CFS 1–3: robust to competent → SAVR reasonable if life expectancy > 10 years
  • CFS 4–5: vulnerable to frail → TAVR strongly favored (less invasive, faster recovery)

Considerations:

  • Life expectancy: if < 5 years, symptom relief faster with TAVR is priority
  • Cognitive status: post-TAVR delirium/stroke lower risk than post-SAVR lengthy ICU stay in frail patient
  • TAVR durability less concerning if life expectancy 5–10 years

Shared decision-making: TAVR often optimal in frail; discuss prosthesis lifetime vs patient lifetime.

sections.heading: Valve-in-valve TAVR (redo TAVR or TAVR in degenerated surgical valve)
sections.bodyHtml:
Scenario: patient had prior SAVR with bioprosthetic, now degenerated (structural failure), candidate for TAVR-in-valve.

Challenges:

  • Valve-in-valve leaflet geometry differs from native valve TAVR
  • Coronary obstruction risk may be different (prior surgical valve geometry)
  • Paravalvular leak risk similar or lower
  • CT-TAVR critical for pre-procedure planning (access, valve size, coronary clearance)

Outcome: valve-in-valve TAVR highly successful in experienced centers; durability 5+ years, often longer due to newer TAVR devices.

7.5 Post-TAVR conduction disturbances

sections.heading: Why TAVR causes heart block
sections.bodyHtml:
TAVR valve deployment mechanically distorts the aortic annulus and adjacent right bundle branch (which sits just below the aortic valve, near the AV node in the membranous septum).

Incidence: new RBBB in 10–20% post-TAVR; new complete AVB in 1–3% requiring pacemaker.

sections.heading: Recognition and management
sections.bodyHtml:
In the ICU post-TAVR (POD 0–1):

  • Daily 12-lead ECGs are mandatory
  • Compare to baseline pre-TAVR EKG
  • New RBBB: monitor closely for progression (watch for PR prolongation, QRS widening)
  • New LBBB: less common, lower risk for progression than RBBB

Bradycardia + hypotension post-TAVR: RED FLAG - Immediate EKG: look for high-degree AV block, complete heart block - Transcutaneous pacing pads on - IV atropine 0.5 mg (limited efficacy; don't rely on it) - Transvenous temporary pacemaker insertion often needed (femoral approach preferred; post-TAVR sheath often in femoral artery)

sections.heading: Pacemaker insertion criteria
sections.bodyHtml:
• New complete heart block (symptomatic or asymptomatic)
  • High-degree AV block (3:1, 2:1 block with bradycardia) that doesn't resolve within hours
  • Symptomatic bradycardia with hemodynamic compromise

Timing: some patients improve within 24–48 h (transient edema resolves); others need permanent pacemaker pre-discharge.

sections.heading: Prevention strategies
sections.bodyHtml:
• Avoid oversizing TAVR valve (mild oversizing standard practice, 5–15%, to prevent paravalvular leak; excessive oversizing increases annular stress, heart block risk)
  • Slower deployment (reduced force on annulus, theoretically lower block risk; not proven)
  • Avoid deep seating of valve (too deep compresses more of conduction system)
7.6 Balloon aortic valvuloplasty (BAV) as bridge

sections.heading: When BAV is indicated
sections.bodyHtml:
BAV is a bridge, not definitive therapy. Gradient reduction is temporary (hours to days).

Indications for BAV pre-TAVR:

  • Cardiogenic shock unresponsive to medical optimization
  • Severe pulmonary edema unresponsive to gentle diuretics
  • Syncope with persistent hypotension despite beta-blocker + fluids
  • Waiting for TAVR team / operating room availability (bridges patient to definitive intervention)
  • "Bailout" for patient crashing during pre-TAVR workup

sections.heading: Procedure technique
sections.bodyHtml:
Access: usually retrograde via femoral artery (femoral sheath 14–18F)

Balloons: 30–50 mm balloon catheters, inflated sequentially across the stenotic valve

Method:

  1. Fluoroscopic guidance; position balloon across annulus (use "waist" at annulus as landmark)
  2. Inflate first balloon (e.g., 30 mm) to nominal pressure; deflate
  3. Upsize balloons (e.g., 40, 50 mm) with sequential inflations
  4. Goal: break calcified leaflets apart, increase valve area

sections.heading: Hemodynamic response
sections.bodyHtml:
Immediate (within hours):

  • Gradient drops (from 60–80 mmHg to 30–40 mmHg mean)
  • Cardiac output rises
  • BP normalizes
  • Urine output improves
  • Pulmonary edema improves

Duration: gradient creep back up over 24–72 hours as calcified leaflets re-approximate

Complications:

  • AR (new or worsened) from leaflet disruption: monitor post-BAV echo
  • Aortic regurgitation may be severe (aortic root perforation, leaflet rupture)
  • Vascular injury (femoral artery dissection, perforation)
  • Stroke (emboli from leaflet material)
  • Cardiac perforation (rare)

sections.heading: Post-BAV management
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Repeat echo within 6 hours — assess new AR, LV function
  2. Heparin anticoagulation during procedure; continue post-BAV until TAVR (thrombus risk on disrupted valve)
  3. Close telemetry monitoring — arrhythmia risk from manipulation
  4. Expedite TAVR — usually same-day or within 24–48 h
  5. Do NOT discharge after BAV alone — valve is unstable, gradient will worsen

sections.heading: Prognostication: BAV futility
sections.bodyHtml:
If patient remains hypotensive, anuric, or acidotic despite BAV + inotropes, prognosis is poor. Discuss with family:

  • May indicate end-stage cardiogenic shock not reversible by any intervention
  • Goals of care conversation needed
  • Palliative approach may be appropriate if patient wishes

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Any of these in a patient deemed "stable" on admission → escalate.

  • Acute syncope or new presyncope — suggests worsening gradient or arrhythmia; STAT EKG; escalate TAVR timing
  • New or worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, PND — HF exacerbation; may signal need for gentle IV diuretics or BAV bridge
  • Chest pain refractory to rest — demand ischemia from AS; troponin may not rise; STAT EKG; escalate TAVR
  • HR trending upward — tachycardia worsens diastolic filling; escalate beta-blocker or rate control
  • BP trending downward despite adequate perfusion** — may signal inotropic failure or volume depletion; investigate (lactate, UOP, skin perfusion)
  • Crackles developing or worsening — pulmonary edema; address with gentle diuresis, not aggressive diuretics
  • Oliguria (UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/h) × 2 shifts — cardiogenic shock (low CO) or contrast-induced nephropathy risk; escalate
  • Lactate > 2 mmol/L or rising — tissue hypoperfusion; ICU transfer, BAV/TAVR acceleration
  • New AF with RVR (HR > 110) — loss of atrial kick catastrophic in AS; ICU transfer, urgent rate control
  • QTc prolonging on amiodarone — torsades risk; hold amiodarone, obtain EKG
  • New focal neuro deficit — stroke (embolic from AF, TAVR thrombus); activate stroke code
  • Syncope with documented bradycardia or high-degree AV block — pre-TAVR conduction system disease or post-TAVR block progression; ICU, pacemaker consideration
  • Troponin > 1 ng/mL with hemodynamic instability — acute coronary event or TAVR-related complication; STAT cardiology/CT surgery
  • Pericardial friction rub or new effusion on echo — pericarditis, tamponade risk; STAT echo, cardiology
  • Temperature > 38.5°C with new murmur — endocarditis risk; blood cultures, TEE, ID consult
  • New murmur of aortic regurgitation — leaflet rupture or endocarditis; STAT echo, TEE; changes urgency

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. "Slow, Full, Squeezed" is NOT the time for vasodilators. Reflex: give nitrates or hydralazine for elevated BP. WRONG. The stiff AS LV needs preload + high afterload to perfuse. Vasodilators drop BP without relieving valve obstruction → syncope, shock, TAVR urgency. Use phenylephrine (alpha-agonist) to raise BP and improve coronary perfusion via increased diastolic aortic pressure, not by increasing contractility. TAVR urgency depends on this pearl.

  2. Tachycardia is the enemy. HR > 100 in AS patient is a warning sign. Every beat, the LV races through diastole (its fill time). Tachycardia cuts diastolic duration → less fill time → lower stroke volume → hypotension, syncope. Beta-blockade is near-essential; AF with RVR is ICU-level emergency.

  3. IABP contraindicated if aortic regurgitation coexists. IABP diastolic augmentation (pushing blood back into aorta) is counterproductive if aortic valve leaks — you push blood back through the leaky valve into the LV. Always echo before considering IABP in AS + suspected AR.

  4. Diuretics must be gentle. Over-diuresis (goal "dry" patient) is catastrophic in AS — preload-dependent LV → hypovolemia → syncope, cardiogenic shock, AKI. Only diurese if overt crackles; use 10–20 mg IV furosemide, not 40–80 mg. Recheck volume status in 2 hours. Goal: euvolemia (JVD 5–8 cm, no rales, patient comfortable).

  5. Syncope in AS is RED FLAG for urgent intervention. Syncope = valve so tight heart can't maintain BP during demand. Patient on brink of shock. Don't treat as orthostatic; escalate TAVR/SAVR timing. Syncope + hypotension in AS = emergent TAVR/BAV/SAVR (same-day intervention).

  6. Paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS is a diagnostic trap. Patient has severe AV calcification (on echo), normal EF (> 50%), but low gradient (< 40 mmHg) and low stroke volume (< 35 mL/m²). The valve is severely obstructive; the LV is small because hypertrophy is restrictive. Stress echo or cath needed to confirm. Treat as severe AS; TAVR/SAVR indicated.

  7. Systolic anterior motion (SAM) risk in hypertrophic AS. If LV hypertrophy is extreme (HCM-like), aggressive diuresis or vasodilation can trigger SAM — anterior mitral leaflet bulges into LVOT during systole, doubling obstruction. Avoid diuretics if SAM suspected; beta-blockade only.

  8. Post-TAVR conduction blocks are common. 10–15% develop new RBBB; 1–2% complete AVB requiring pacemaker.

    Daily EKGs post-TAVR are mandatory. New RBBB + PR prolongation = monitor closely for progression to AVB. Bradycardia + hypotension post-TAVR = transcutaneous pacing pads on immediately; transvenous pacer often needed.

  9. Prior CABG patient often does better with TAVR than redo SAVR. Redo SAVR after CABG has 2–3× mortality (graft manipulation, dissection risk, difficult cardioplegia delivery). TAVR avoids sternotomy, so TAVR often triaged first in prior CABG patients.

  10. Frailty (CFS ≥ 5) strongly favors TAVR over SAVR. Frail patients recover poorly from sternotomy. TAVR's less-invasive approach offers lower peri-operative risk and faster recovery, even though valve durability is shorter-term. CFS score is a major shared decision-making factor.

  11. AF concurrent with severe AS = complex anticoagulation. AF carries stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 1). If anticoagulated (warfarin/DOAC), reduces stroke but increases bleeding. If not anticoagulated, increases stroke. Post-TAVR, patient on dual antiplatelet (aspirin + clopidogrel) for 3–6 months, not warfarin. If AF also present, anticoagulation plan is team discussion — don't default to "AC all AF patients" post-TAVR.

  12. Spinal anesthesia vs GA for TAVR is deliberate choice. Spinal anesthesia (epidural) is used in frail TAVR candidates because it preserves hemodynamic stability (no induction drugs, no intubation). But if patient needs emergent conversion to transseptal (antegrade) access, anesthesia must deepen. Discuss with anesthesia pre-op.

  13. Transcatheter aortic valve thrombosis is rare but catastrophic. Post-TAVR valve thrombus can develop (low-flow states, AF, early post-op). Presents as sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, high valve gradient on echo. Dual antiplatelet therapy reduces risk. If suspected, STAT echo/CT/cath; may need anticoagulation, fibrinolysis, or valve-in-valve TAVR.

  14. SGLT2 inhibitors should be held 48 hours pre-TAVR / SAVR. SGLT2i cause diuresis + mild afterload reduction — in AS patient, this is dangerous. Stop 48 h pre-procedure; restart post-op after hemodynamic stability confirmed. Common oversight.

  15. Syncope post-sublingual nitroglycerin in AS patient = emergent TAVR acceleration. Classic presentation: patient given SL NTG for "chest pain" → syncope, cardiogenic shock. Sign of severe, decompensated AS needing same-day TAVR / BAV. Do NOT give nitrates in severe AS (ever).
