cards.title: Spinal Cord Ischemia (SCI) — Anatomy and Rescue Physiology
cards.quickAnswer: Spinal cord ischemia (SCI) is ischemic injury to the anterior spinal cord, classically anterior cord syndrome, caused by compromise of the anterior spinal artery (ASA) and its critical segmental feeders, particularly the artery of Adamkiewicz (typically T9–L2 origin). Rescue physiology: spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) = MAP − CSF pressure; target SCPP ≥70 mmHg → MAP ≥85–90, CSF drain <10 mmHg. Classic bedside finding: bilateral lower-extremity weakness + loss of pain/temperature sensation with preserved vibration/proprioception (dorsal column sparing). Crawford Extent II TAAA repairs carry highest SCI risk (10–15%). C-O-P-S protocol (CSF drain, oxygenation, permissive MAP, steroids) is time-critical rescue initiated within minutes of recognition.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: Spinal cord ischemia (SCI) is ischemic injury to the anterior spinal cord, classically anterior cord syndrome, caused by compromise of the anterior spinal artery (ASA) and its critical segmental feeders, particularly the artery of Adamkiewicz (typically T9–L2 origin). Rescue physiology: spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCPP) = MAP − CSF pressure; target SCPP ≥70 mmHg → MAP ≥85–90, CSF drain <10 mmHg. Classic bedside finding: bilateral lower-extremity weakness + loss of pain/temperature sensation with preserved vibration/proprioception (dorsal column sparing). Crawford Extent II TAAA repairs carry highest SCI risk (10–15%). C-O-P-S protocol (CSF drain, oxygenation, permissive MAP, steroids) is time-critical rescue initiated within minutes of recognition.
cards.sourcePrecedence: Isselbacher et al. (2022) ACC/AHA Aortic Guideline → Safi et al. (CSF drain rescue) → Coselli & Estrera (TAAA outcomes) → Crawford classification + anatomy textbooks (Rexed laminae, ASA/PSA supply)

sections.heading: 1. Definition and Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Spinal cord ischemia (SCI) is ischemic injury to spinal cord tissue resulting in neurologic deficit (motor weakness, sensory loss, sphincter dysfunction). Post-aortic-surgery SCI is mechanistically distinct from:

  • Traumatic SCI — mechanical contusion/laceration from spinal cord injury (different pathophysiology, different prognosis)
  • Spontaneous spinal cord infarction — atherosclerotic ASA occlusion, fibrocartilaginous embolism, or idiopathic (often not emergent)
  • Iatrogenic non-surgical — epidural anesthesia needle/catheter trauma (epidural hematoma), radiation necrosis, aortic catheterization

Post-aortic-surgery SCI specifically: occurs in 3–15% of open thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm (TAAA) repair and 2–5% of thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) due to intercostal artery ligation/thrombosis, compromising blood supply to the anterior spinal cord and Adamkiewicz artery. Immediate-onset (POD 0) or delayed-onset (POD 2–7) presentations both clinically relevant.

sections.heading: 2.1 Anterior Spinal Artery (ASA) and Posterior Spinal Arteries (PSA)
sections.bodyHtml:
Vessel Supply Territory Clinical note
ASA (single midline) Anterior 2/3 of cord: gray matter, anterior/lateral white matter Motor tracts (corticospinal), spinothalamic (pain/temp) Vulnerable to occlusion; supplies ~80% of cord
PSA (paired, left + right) Posterior 1/3 of cord: dorsal columns (vibration, proprioception, position sense) Posterior columns (fasciculus gracilis, cuneatus) More redundant; less affected by aortic surgery

Key clinical point: anterior cord syndrome (motor + pain/temp loss, but preserved vibration/proprioception) indicates ASA compromise with PSA intact — the diagnostic hallmark of post-aortic-surgery SCI.

sections.heading: 2.2 Adamkiewicz Artery (Arteria Radicularis Magna)
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature Detail
Definition Largest segmental medullary artery feeding the ASA in thoracolumbar cord
Typical origin Left-sided T9–L2 intercostal or lumbar artery (variable: range T5–L5)
Supplies T8–L1 spinal cord segment (lumbosacral enlargement); critical for lower-extremity motor control
Significance Often the ONLY dominant source to thoracolumbar cord; loss = catastrophic anterior cord ischemia
Pre-op mapping CTA or MRA may identify Adamkiewicz origin; helps guide surgical intercostal re-implantation strategy

Variability: Adamkiewicz does not always originate at T9–L1. Surgeon may document "Adamkiewicz at T6" or "L1 origin" — this variability means intercostal re-implantation strategies vary by case.

sections.heading: 2.3 Segmental Intercostal and Lumbar Arteries
sections.bodyHtml: Intercostal arteries T5–T12 and lumbar arteries connect the aorta to the ASA via segmental medullary arteries (radicular arteries). Only 2–3 of these ~20 intercostal arteries are "dominant" and contribute significantly to cord perfusion. During TAAA open repair, intercostals T5–T12 are typically ligated during the dissection and repair. Selection and re-implantation of critical intercostal arteries (often T9–L1 based on intra-operative anatomic estimation) may preserve Adamkiewicz.

sections.heading: 2.4 Watershed Zones
sections.bodyHtml: Mid-thoracic spinal cord (T4–T8) and lower thoracic cord (T10–T12) are anatomically vulnerable watershed zones between ASA main trunk (fed by vertebral arteries cervically) and dominant Adamkiewicz supply. Loss of collateral intercostal feeders can render these zones ischemic.

sections.heading: 3.1 Anterior Cord Syndrome (Classic Post-Aortic-Surgery SCI Pattern)
sections.bodyHtml:
Finding Mechanism
Bilateral LE weakness (paraplegia or paraparesis) Corticospinal tracts in anterior cord damaged; typically symmetric but asymmetry common
Loss of pain/temperature sensation (spinothalamic) at/below lesion level Spinothalamic tracts in anterior cord damaged
PRESERVED vibration and proprioception Dorsal columns (PSA territory) intact — KEY DIAGNOSTIC CLUE
Urinary retention ± absent anal tone Sacral parasympathetic and motor nuclei in anterior gray matter damaged
Initially flaccid (spinal shock); hyperreflexia develops later Transient loss of reflex arc integrity in acute phase

sections.heading: 3.2 Posterior Cord Syndrome (Rare Post-Aortic Surgery; Different Pathology)
sections.bodyHtml: Motor relatively preserved; vibration/proprioception lost; sensory ataxia. Not the typical post-aortic-surgery pattern. If a post-TAAA patient has bilateral leg weakness + loss of vibration/proprioception, consider other diagnosis (cauda equina, stroke, Guillain-Barré).

sections.heading: 3.3 Central Cord Syndrome (Traumatic, Not Post-Aortic Surgery)
sections.bodyHtml: Greater upper-extremity weakness than lower-extremity; often cape-like sensory loss. Associated with traumatic hyperextension or hemorrhage into cord central gray matter. Rare post-aortic surgery.

sections.heading: 3.4 Brown-Séquard Syndrome (Hemisection; Rare Post-Surgical)
sections.bodyHtml: Ipsilateral motor weakness + contralateral pain/temperature loss. Indicates half-cord damage, typically from surgical trauma (retraction, instrumentation) rather than ischemia. Uncommon in aortic surgery SCI.

sections.heading: 3.5 Cauda Equina Syndrome (NOT true SCI; Lumbosacral Nerve Roots)
sections.bodyHtml: Bilateral leg pain + asymmetric weakness (nerve-root pattern) + saddle anesthesia + urinary retention. Below the spinal cord proper (L1–2) — different anatomy, different urgency pathway. Can occur with massive lumbosacral epidural hematoma from CSF drain; requires urgent MRI + decompression.

sections.heading: 4. Rescue Physiology — Spinal Cord Perfusion Pressure and C-O-P-S
4.1 Spinal Cord Perfusion Pressure (SCPP)
sections.bodyHtml:
Analogous to cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP − ICP):

SCPP = MAP − CSF pressure (intrathecal pressure)

Clinical targets:

  • SCPP ≥50 mmHg = minimum acceptable
  • SCPP 60–70 mmHg = target in rescue phase
  • Typical post-op patient: MAP ~75–85, CSF ~5–8 mmHg → SCPP ~70 mmHg (borderline in SCI)
  • SCI acute rescue: MAP ≥85–90, CSF <10 mmHg → SCPP ≥75–80+ mmHg

Two-lever approach:

  1. Raise MAP (vasopressors, fluid, inotropes) — increases SCPP directly
  2. Lower CSF pressure (CSF drain to <10 mmHg) — decreases the subtracted term, increases SCPP

Both are essential; neither alone is sufficient.

sections.heading: 4.2 Oxygen Delivery to Spinal Cord
sections.bodyHtml:
Spinal cord oxygen delivery (DO₂) = Cardiac Output × (1.34 × Hgb × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂)

Bedside optimization:

  • Hemoglobin ≥10 g/dL (target higher than routine post-op Hgb 7–8 threshold; each g Hgb carries ~1.34 mL O₂/100 mL blood)
  • SpO₂ >95% (supranormal target >98% in some protocols; avoid any hypoxia)
  • Cardiac output optimization — maintain HR/rhythm, ensure adequate preload, use inotropes if needed

sections.heading: 5. Clinical Use — How Bedside Nurses Interpret This Knowledge
5.1 Recognizing the Pattern (Anterior Cord Syndrome)
sections.bodyHtml:
When assessing a post-TAAA patient with new bilateral lower-extremity weakness:

  1. Check the dorsal columns first. Ask the patient: "Can you feel this?" (vibration, 128 Hz tuning fork at toes). If vibration is preserved, you're likely looking at anterior cord syndrome (ASA compromise). If vibration is lost, think cauda equina, posterior cord, or different diagnosis.

  2. MRC grading. Document bilateral strength systematically: hip flexors, knee extensors/flexors, ankle dorsiflexors/plantarflexors. Use the scale (0–5/5):

    • 0 = no contraction
    • 1 = trace contraction
    • 2 = gravity-eliminated movement
    • 3 = against gravity (key threshold for independence)
    • 4 = against some resistance
    • 5 = normal

Asymmetry is common (one leg MRC 0, other MRC 2); document each side separately.

  1. Sensory level. Pin-prick bilaterally from abdomen downward; note the highest dermatome where sensation is lost. In anterior cord, this level reflects the ischemic cord segment.

  2. Sphincter tone. Gentle digital rectal exam; note tone (normal, diminished, absent). Urinary post-void residual >200 mL is a clue to neurogenic bladder.

sections.heading: 5.2 Understanding Crawford Risk Stratification
sections.bodyHtml:
Know your patient's Crawford Extent (from OR note or surgery card):

Extent Your vigilance level Why
Extent II MAXIMUM — watch closely POD 0–7 Highest SCI risk (10–15%); entire descending aorta involved; all intercostals typically ligated
Extent III HIGH Moderate risk (5–8%); lower thoracic start; some intercostal preservation possible
Extent I or IV MODERATE Lower risk (2–8%); fewer intercostals involved or Adamkiewicz more likely preserved

sections.heading: 5.3 Why C-O-P-S Matters (and Why You Explain It to Patients)
sections.bodyHtml:
When the CSF drain is placed emergently and MAP is being run high:

  • CSF Drain <10 mmHg: "We're draining fluid around your spinal cord to reduce pressure and improve blood flow to the cord."
  • MAP ≥85–90: "We're running your blood pressure higher than usual to push blood to the spinal cord. This is not typical post-op, but it's critical right now."
  • Oxygen/Hemoglobin: "We're keeping your oxygen levels up and your blood cells high to feed the spinal cord tissue."
  • Steroids (if ordered): "We're giving steroids to reduce inflammation and swelling in the cord."

Time-sensitive: Recognition and rescue within minutes-to-hours may reverse deficits. Delayed recognition (POD 2–3) still warrants aggressive intervention, but prognosis worsens. Week-old paraplegia is likely permanent.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. "Dorsal column preservation = anterior cord syndrome" is your bedside diagnostic clue. Preserved vibration/proprioception despite motor/pain-temp loss = SCI post-aortic surgery. Lost vibration/proprioception = cauda equina, posterior cord, or different diagnosis. This exam finding guides urgency and escalation.

  2. Adamkiewicz is NOT always at T9–L1. Surgeon may report origin at T6, T12, or L1. Variability is why protective strategies (CSF drain + permissive MAP) matter — you cannot always re-implant the Adamkiewicz intraoperatively.

  3. Anterior cord syndrome supplies 2/3 of the cord, not 1/2. ASA supplies anterior 2/3 (gray matter + anterior white matter); posterior 1/3 (dorsal columns) is PSA territory. This 2:1 ratio explains why anterior cord syndrome is the dominant SCI pattern.

  4. Crawford Extent II is the HIGHEST SCI risk (10–15%), not "biggest surgery." Extent IV repairs (abdominal aorta) are lower risk (2–5%) because Adamkiewicz is often lower and spared. Know the extent number from the OR note.

  5. SCPP target ≥70 mmHg drives TWO actions simultaneously: MAP UP and CSF DOWN. Do not optimize only one lever. CSF pressure at 15 mmHg with MAP 90 leaves SCPP = 75 — not ideal. MAP 100 with CSF 12 leaves SCPP = 88 — better. Both matter.

  6. Hemoglobin <10 g/dL reduces cord oxygen delivery. This contradicts typical post-op transfusion thresholds (Hgb >7–8). In acute SCI, transfuse to Hgb ≥10 g/dL per CT surgery/neurosurgery explicit orders.

  7. The scenario card is your operational protocol; this glossary is the anatomy reference. The scenario card tells you what to DO (C-O-P-S steps, escalation, SBAR language). This glossary explains the ANATOMY and PHYSIOLOGY underlying those actions.

  8. Cauda equina syndrome is NOT spinal cord ischemia. Below L1–2, you're in nerve roots, not cord. Bilateral leg pain + asymmetric weakness + saddle anesthesia = cauda equina.

    Different urgency, different anatomy, still emergent but different workup.

  9. Watershed zones (T4–T8, T10–T12) are particularly vulnerable. If Adamkiewicz is high (T6) or low (L1), these zones may be underperfused. Mid-thoracic cord ischemia → lower-thoracic/lumbar weakness pattern.

  10. Pre-operative baseline neuro exam is THE comparison point. If no documented pre-op neuro exam, post-op deterioration may go unrecognized. Insist on baseline MRC grading, sensory level, and sphincter tone before transfer to stepdown.

  11. MRC 3/5 vs. MRC 4/5 is clinically crucial. MRC 3 = movement against gravity but not resistance (patient can lift leg off bed, cannot kick against resistance). MRC 4 = movement against some resistance. MRC 3 is the threshold for some basic ADL independence; <3 requires assistive device. This distinction drives rehab planning.

  12. Post-void residual (PVR) >200 mL is an underused diagnostic clue. Straight-cath after spontaneous void; >200 mL PVR + new leg weakness = neurogenic bladder from SCI. Coordinate with urology if long-term catheterization needed.

  13. Epidural anesthesia during early post-op exam can mask sensory findings. Local anesthetic diffusion from an epidural pain catheter may blunt pin-prick sensation even if the cord is intact. Coordinate with anesthesia: reduce epidural concentration temporarily or use non-neuraxial analgesia if sensory level is critical for SCI diagnosis.

  14. SCPP = MAP − CSF pressure is analogous to CPP, but target SCPP ≥70 is HIGHER than some CPP targets. Spinal cord is more vulnerable to hypoperfusion than brain. Remember: SCPP ≥70, not ≥50.

  15. Delayed-onset SCI (POD 2–7) is REAL and UNDERRECOGNIZED. Up to 40–50% of post-TAAA SCI is delayed. Normal neuro exam on POD 0 does NOT rule out SCI. Serial exams on stepdown are non-negotiable.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(expandable — novice and advanced beginner deep-dive)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Spinal cord laminae and tract anatomy (Rexed classification) The spinal cord gray matter is organized into Rexed laminae (I–X), organized dorsal-to-ventral. Anterior horn motor neurons (alpha motor neurons) reside in lamina IX. Spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature) crosses immediately and ascends in the anterior/lateral white matter. Posterior columns (fasciculus gracilis, cuneatus) remain ipsilateral and ascend in the dorsal white matter. SCI implication: anterior cord ischemia damages laminae I–VI (dorsal horn + spinothalamic decussation) + anterior/lateral white matter, sparing posterior columns (laminae VII–X + dorsal columns). This is why anterior cord syndrome shows motor + pain/temp loss but preserved vibration/proprioception.
Adamkiewicz variability and pre-operative imaging (CTA/MRA) Pre-operative CTA or MRA may identify the Adamkiewicz artery origin in candidates for elective TAAA repair. Identification allows the surgeon to plan intercostal re-implantation. However:
  • Not all surgeons routinely image for Adamkiewicz (adds time, cost, radiation/gadolinium)
  • Even with imaging, the artery may be difficult to identify intraoperatively
  • Intraoperative ultrasound or neuromonitoring (spinal cord evoked potentials) may assist identification, but not universally available Bedside nursing point: know whether your patient had pre-op Adamkiewicz imaging. If yes, the surgeon may have documented the origin; if the post-op neuro exam is abnormal, that imaging may become crucial for retrospective understanding of what happened.
SCPP physiology and target ranges The spinal cord, like the brain, requires a minimum perfusion pressure to maintain ischemic penumbra (tissue at risk but not yet infarcted). SCPP = MAP − CSF pressure Normal values in a resting post-op patient:
  • MAP = 75–85 mmHg
  • CSF pressure = 5–10 mmHg
  • SCPP = 65–80 mmHg (acceptable, but low-normal in acute SCI context) In acute SCI rescue:
  • Target MAP ≥85–90 mmHg (permissive hypertension)
  • Target CSF <10 mmHg (often <8 mmHg in aggressive protocols)
  • Target SCPP ≥70–80 mmHg Two-lever mechanism:
    1. Raising MAP: phenylephrine, norepinephrine, fluid, inotropes
    2. Lowering CSF pressure: CSF drain to gravity/collection bag; monitor manometer Why both matter: if CSF pressure is 15 mmHg and MAP is 100, SCPP = 85 — good. But if CSF pressure climbs to 20 mmHg (over-drainage risk, catheter malposition), SCPP drops to 80 — now you need higher MAP. Continuous monitoring of BOTH parameters is essential.
C-O-P-S protocol detail (CSF drain, oxygenation, pressure, steroids)

CSF Drain: Target <10 mmHg. Lumbar catheter or ventriculostomy. Monitor CSF color (clear normal; xanthochromic or bloody suggests infarction or epidural hematoma). Output typically 10–20 mL/h; >30 mL/h may indicate over-drainage. Weaned slowly over 3–5 days once cord perfusion stabilized.

Oxygenation: SpO₂ >95%, preferably >98%. Hemoglobin ≥10 g/dL (transfuse if <8–9; maintain at ≥10 target in acute phase). Intubation if respiratory compromise (high thoracic SCI can impair diaphragm via phrenic involvement). Avoid hypoxia absolutely.

Pressure (MAP): Target ≥85–90 mmHg, ideally 90–100 mmHg. This is NOT typical post-op (usually SBP <120). Use phenylephrine (pure alpha-1, no tachycardia) or norepinephrine (stronger, more inotropic). Fluid bolus if hypovolemic; avoid excessive fluids (worsens cord edema). Arterial line for continuous monitoring.

Steroids (evidence limited): Some protocols use high-dose methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg bolus + 5.4 mg/kg/h × 23 h), adapted from spinal cord trauma guidelines. Evidence is mixed.

Always verify with CT surgery + neurosurgery before starting. Not a universal standard.

Rare variant syndromes and differential diagnosis

Posterior cord syndrome post-aortic surgery (rare): Motor relatively preserved; vibration/proprioception lost; sensory ataxia (loss of position sense). Usually indicates PSA compromise (from lateral aortic dissection) or posterior epidural hematoma. Less common than anterior cord.

Central cord syndrome: Greater UE weakness than LE; cape-like sensory loss; associated with hemorrhage into cord central gray matter.

Uncommon in aortic surgery; more typical in traumatic hyperextension. Cauda equina: Bilateral leg pain + asymmetric weakness + saddle anesthesia + urinary retention. Below L1–2 (nerve roots, not cord). Associated with massive lumbosacral epidural hematoma (from CSF drain complication).

Different anatomy, still emergent; may require decompression. Brown-Séquard (hemisection): Ipsilateral motor + contralateral pain/temp loss. Indicates half-cord damage, usually surgical trauma (retraction, instrumentation).

Rare in aortic surgery SCI.

Recovery patterns and prognostic factors Early phase (POD 0–7): Spinal shock (flaccid paralysis, areflexia, urinary retention) is expected in acute SCI. Serial neuro exams q6–12h track improvement vs. deterioration vs. plateau. Intermediate phase (POD 1–4 weeks): Spinal shock resolves; hyperreflexia and spasticity emerge. Motor recovery trajectory becomes clear:
  • Good prognosis: improving MRC (2→3→4 over days–weeks); may regain some function
  • Guarded: plateauing at MRC 2–3; likely partial paralysis, orthotics needed
  • Poor: no improvement by week 1–2; likely permanent paraplegia Late phase (4+ weeks): Inpatient spinal cord rehabilitation; intensive PT/OT; spasticity management. Prognosis factors:
    • Time to recognition + intervention (golden window = minutes–hours)
    • Severity at nadir (complete paraplegia MRC 0–1 worse than incomplete MRC 3+)
    • MRI extent of T2 hyperintensity (smaller area better prognosis)
    • Motor recovery by POD 7 (any improvement by day 7 predicts better long-term outcome)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, who gets it, why it matters.

  • Definition: Ischemia of the anterior spinal cord (supplied by the anterior spinal artery and segmental medullary arteries, particularly the artery of Adamkiewicz, T8–L1) resulting in motor, sensory, and sphincter dysfunction. Classic pattern: bilateral lower-extremity weakness + loss of pain/temperature sensation (anterior cord syndrome), with preserved vibration and proprioception (posterior columns spared).
  • Incidence:
  • Open TAAA repair: 3–15% overall; highest with Crawford Extent II–III repairs (paravertebral dissection + maximum intercostal artery loss)
  • TEVAR: 2–5% (endografts covering intercostal origins, especially when landing zones T6–T12)
  • Ascending/arch surgery: <1% (less common; usually only if distal repair required)
  • Who this applies to: all adults post-operative from descending aortic surgery (open or endovascular). Recognition needed in ICU and on stepdown/telemetry; delayed-onset can declare POD 2–7 after transfer.
  • Why it matters: SCI is a time-critical emergency. Intervention within minutes-to-hours may reverse motor deficits; delayed recognition → permanent paralysis, loss of continence, long-term disability.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
The anterior spinal artery (ASA) is a single midline vessel supplying two-thirds of the spinal cord (anterior 2/3); the posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns and posterior gray matter.

Vulnerable segment: The thoracolumbar cord (T8–L1) depends critically on the artery of Adamkiewicz (also called the arteria radicularis magna), which typically arises from a left-sided T9–L2 intercostal or lumbar artery. During descending aortic repair:

  • Open TAAA: intercostal arteries T5–T12 are directly ligated or divided during the repair, removing collateral circulation to Adamkiewicz
  • TEVAR: the endograft covers intercostal origins; the stent-graft may also thrombose patent intercostal arteries
  • Result: ASA pressure falls below critical threshold; spinal cord tissue oxygen delivery is interrupted

Presentations:

  • Immediate-onset: neurologic deficit noted within minutes of emergence from anesthesia (POD 0) — patient wakes up paralyzed or with acute weakness
  • Delayed-onset: neurologic deficit appears 24–72 hours post-op, sometimes up to POD 7 — represents either late reperfusion failure, edema progression, or thrombosis of collateral flow

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Immediate-onset (POD 0, on emergence):

  • Nursing staff reports patient unable to move lower extremities on emergence from anesthesia
  • Motor exam: bilateral LE weakness (can be asymmetric), often complete paraplegia (MRC 0–1/5) if severe
  • Sensory exam: loss of pain/temperature sensation at/below mid-thoracic to lower thoracic/lumbar level (sensory level follows the ischemic cord segment)
  • Sphincter: urinary retention (may present as distended bladder, absent voiding); absent/diminished anal sphincter tone

Delayed-onset (POD 2–7):

  • Patient initially had normal neuro exam post-op (documented baseline)
  • Sudden new lower-extremity weakness, often first noticed when:
  • Patient complains of "legs feel heavy" or "can't move my feet"
  • Nursing attempts to stand patient at bedside; unable to bear weight
  • Catheterization needed for inability to void (post-void residual >200 mL)
  • May be preceded by back pain (spinal cord edema) or vague leg discomfort

Physical findings in both presentations:

  • Bilateral LE weakness (asymmetric weakness is common; one leg may be worse)
  • Loss of pain/temperature sensation in a dermatome level (often mid-thoracic → lumbar)
  • Preserved vibration sense and proprioception in lower extremities (posterior columns intact — key differentiator from posterior cord syndrome)
  • Urinary retention ± post-void residual >200 mL
  • Decreased or absent anal sphincter tone on digital rectal exam
  • Preserved upper-extremity strength (unless cervical cord involved — rare)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Establishes baseline; guides urgency and escalation.

Vital signs & perfusion:

  • HR, BP, SpO₂, respiratory rate, temperature, MAP (target: ensure MAP ≥85–90 mmHg to optimize cord perfusion)
  • Capillary refill, skin perfusion, signs of shock

Detailed neurologic exam (do this serially — document at baseline and q30min initially):

  • Motor: MRC strength grading (0–5/5) of bilateral hip flexors, knee extensors, knee flexors, ankle dorsiflexors, ankle plantarflexors
  • MRC 0 = flaccid (no contraction)
  • MRC 1 = trace contraction, no movement
  • MRC 2 = movement with gravity eliminated
  • MRC 3 = movement against gravity (key threshold)
  • MRC 4 = movement against some resistance
  • MRC 5 = normal power
  • Sensory: pain/temperature level (use pin-prick bilaterally, identify the highest dermatome where sensation is lost)
  • Proprioception/vibration: 128 Hz tuning fork at toes/knees — should be preserved in anterior cord syndrome
  • Reflexes: patellar, Achilles (may be diminished early in acute SCI)
  • Rectal exam: anal sphincter tone (normal = squeeze around examiner's finger)
  • Post-void residual (PVR): straight-cath after spontaneous void; >200 mL suggests neurogenic bladder

Recent labs & imaging:

  • Hemoglobin (low Hgb <10 worsens cord oxygen delivery; transfuse if Hgb <8–9)
  • Renal function (creatinine, assess hydration)
  • If CSF drain in place: CSF pressure (manometer reading), CSF appearance (xanthochromic, hemorrhagic?), CSF output last 12 h

Surgery context & timeline:

  • Type of aortic repair (open TAAA vs TEVAR; Crawford extent if TAAA)
  • Time of incision, cross-clamp, reperfusion
  • Any intraoperative complications (hypotension, hemorrhage, prolonged repair time)
  • CSF drain placed intraoperatively? (status, when placed)
  • Medications on board: vasopressors (phenylephrine, norepinephrine dose/rate), inotropes

Lines & access:

  • Arterial line (for continuous MAP monitoring)
  • Adequate IV access for potential emergency medications + fluids
  • Foley catheter patent and draining

sections.heading: 5A. Stable-appearing path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Acute weakness detected but vitals stable, patient alert, responsive. Still EMERGENT.)

  1. STAT call: CT surgery attending + neurosurgery (not consult desk — direct to attending) + ICU fellow/charge nurse. Do not delay while gathering information.
  2. STAT neurologic exam — complete motor/sensory/reflex exam as detailed in Section 4. Document baseline MRC scores bilaterally.
  3. Implement C-O-P-S rescue immediately (do not wait for imaging): - CSF Drain:
    • If no drain in place: neurosurgery will place emergently (lumbar catheter or ventriculostomy). Notify them of urgency.
    • If drain already in place: check CSF pressure (target <10 mmHg; some protocols <8). If pressure >10 mmHg, open drain to gravity/collection bag. Monitor CSF output (expect 10–20 mL/h); excessive drainage (>30 mL/h) may indicate over-drainage — contact neurosurgery.
    • Oxygenation: maintain SpO₂ >95% (consider supplemental O₂ if not already on it; avoid hypoxia absolutely). Goal is to maximize oxygen delivery to ischemic cord.
    • Pressure: maintain MAP ≥85–90 mmHg (target 90–100 mmHg is sometimes used in SCI protocols). This is not the typical post-op goal of SBP <120. Start/increase vasopressor if needed (phenylephrine bolus → drip; norepinephrine if hypotension refractory). Fluid-resuscitate cautiously (goal euvolemia, not excess fluid in setting of spinal cord edema).
    • Steroids: per neurosurgery + CT surgery consensus; some protocols use IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg bolus + 5.4 mg/kg/h × 23 h (evidence limited; not universal standard). Verify before administering.
  4. Maintain hemoglobin ≥10 g/dL — transfuse if Hgb <8–9 (lower threshold) or <10 (goal if available) to optimize oxygen delivery.
  5. STAT imaging:
    • MRI spine (URGENT): defines spinal cord hyperintensity (T2 signal change confirms ischemia) and rules out epidural hematoma (absolute contraindication to CSF drain; surgical emergency if present).
    • If MRI unavailable/contraindicated: CT myelogram as fallback (lower sensitivity for SCI ischemia but can detect hematoma).
    • Optimize positioning: slight reverse Trendelenburg or neutral spine to maximize spinal perfusion; avoid hip/knee flexion (can impair lower-extremity perfusion).
    • Continuous monitoring: cardiac tele, ABP line, SpO₂, repeat neuro exam q30min × 2 h, then q1h × 6 h to track trajectory (improving vs. worsening vs. stable).
    • NPO status: anticipate possible operative intervention (epidural hematoma evacuation, etc.).

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Severe motor deficit with acute respiratory compromise, hemodynamic collapse, progressive neurologic decline, or suspected epidural hematoma on imaging.)

  1. STAT CODE / RAPID RESPONSE: CT surgery + neurosurgery + ICU fellow/attending present at bedside; notify OR that emergency case may be incoming.
  2. Airway management: if respiratory muscles weak (high thoracic SCI → phrenic involvement → diaphragm weakness), prepare for intubation. Do not delay.
  3. Hemodynamic support:
    • MAP target ≥90–100 mmHg; escalate vasopressor (switch to norepinephrine if phenylephrine alone insufficient)
    • Aggressive fluid resuscitation only if hypovolemic (post-op oozing); limit if cord edema is concern
    • CSF drain management: open to gravity immediately; if no drain in place, neurosurgery places emergently while ICU stabilizes.
    • STAT MRI / CT imaging to rule out epidural hematoma (presents as new/worsening back pain + acute motor decline; requires immediate decompression). If hematoma confirmed, neurosurgery coordinates emergency evacuation.
    • Continuous neuro exams (q15min) while stabilizing; document deterioration trajectory.
    • Prepare for possible transfer to OR for epidural hematoma evacuation or other intervention.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "This is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [aortic procedure: open TAAA / TEVAR]." B: "Patient developed [immediate / delayed] bilateral lower-extremity weakness [describe: paraplegia MRC 0/5 vs. MRC 3/5 hip flexors]. Sensory level at [T level]. Urinary retention / post-void residual [value] mL. Last neuro exam [time] showed [baseline]. Current BP [value], MAP [value], SpO₂ [value]%. CSF drain [in place / not in place]; if in place, CSF pressure [mmHg]." A: "This is consistent with acute spinal cord ischemia. Patient is [stable / unstable / deteriorating]. Currently on C-O-P-S protocol: CSF drain [status], SpO₂ >95%, MAP targeting 85–90+, steroids [started / pending order]." R: "Requesting [immediate evaluation by CT surgery + neurosurgery / STAT MRI spine / emergent CSF drain placement / vasopressor escalation]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Immediate-onset LE weakness POD 0 CT surgery attending (STAT, not page desk) + Neurosurgery attending (STAT)
Delayed-onset weakness POD 2–5 CT surgery attending + Neurosurgery (same-day urgent evaluation)
CSF drain placement needed (no pre-operative drain) Neurosurgery for emergent lumbar puncture + catheter placement or ventriculostomy
MRI shows epidural hematoma Neurosurgery (STAT) + CT surgery — OR alert: emergency evacuation
Worsening motor deficit despite C-O-P-S Escalate vasopressor + MAP (CT surgery), recheck MRI, neurosurgery re-evaluation
Post-op SCI + fever / signs of infection Neurosurgery (CSF drain infection concern; may need culture, antibiotics, drain repositioning)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Spinal cord vascular anatomy
sections.bodyHtml:
The anterior spinal artery (ASA) is a single midline vessel running from the foramen magnum to the conus medullaris (L1–2). It supplies roughly 80% of the spinal cord (anterior 2/3) and receives blood from two sources:

  1. Vertebral arteries (cervical cord C1–4 predominant supply)
  2. Segmental medullary arteries — intercostal and lumbar arteries that connect the aorta to the ASA. Only 2–3 major segmental arteries are typically "dominant" and supply the thoracolumbar cord.

The artery of Adamkiewicz (arteria radicularis magna):

  • Largest segmental medullary artery, supplies T8–L1 (lumbosacral enlargement of cord)
  • Arises from left-sided intercostal artery (T9–L2 most common; range T5–L5)
  • Often the only dominant contributor to lower thoracic and lumbar cord
  • Critical for motor control of lower extremities

Posterior spinal arteries: paired vessels (left + right) supplying the posterior 1/3 of cord (dorsal columns = vibration, proprioception, position sense). These are more redundant and less affected by aortic surgery.

Watershed zones: areas between major segmental artery territories are especially vulnerable to hypoperfusion. The mid-thoracic cord (T5–T8) and lower thoracic cord (T10–T12) are high-risk zones if Adamkiewicz is ligated.

Spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCP):

  • SCP = MAP − CSF pressure (or intrathecal pressure)
  • Target: SCP ≥ 50 mmHg; ideally SCP 60–70 mmHg
  • Lowering CSF pressure (via drain) and raising MAP both improve SCP

sections.heading: 7.2 Crawford TAAA classification and SCI risk
sections.bodyHtml:
Crawford classification divides thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm (TAAA) by extent of aortic involvement and determines both surgical approach and SCI risk.

Crawford Extent Aortic segments involved SCI Risk (%) Why higher / lower
Extent I T2–T6 to diaphragm (visceral) 5–8% Upper thoracic; some intercostal preservation possible
Extent II T2 to visceral vessels; includes full descending aorta 10–15% (HIGHEST) Maximum thoracic aorta involvement; all intercostal arteries T5–T12 typically ligated; Adamkiewicz almost always sacrificed
Extent III T6 to visceral 5–8% Lower thoracic start; some intercostal preservation in upper segment
Extent IV Visceral vessels to iliac bifurcation 2–5% Descending aorta mostly spared; Adamkiewicz often preserved or accessible from distal aorta

SCI in open TAAA context: Extent II repairs carry the highest risk because the entire descending aorta (including all intercostals T5–T12) is typically involved in the dissection/resection, leaving no collateral intercostal supply to Adamkiewicz. Modern mitigation strategies (selective re-implantation of critical intercostals, CSF drainage, permissive hypotension limits) have reduced but not eliminated SCI risk.

sections.heading: 7.3 Anterior cord syndrome vs. other presentations
sections.bodyHtml:
Anterior cord syndrome (classic SCI pattern post-aortic surgery):

  • Motor: bilateral LE weakness (paraplegia if severe, paraparesis if partial)
  • Pain/temperature: loss of spinothalamic tract = bilateral loss of pain/temp at/below the level
  • Vibration/proprioception: PRESERVED (dorsal columns intact) — key finding
  • Reflexes: initially flaccid (spinal shock); may become hyperreflexic after weeks

Posterior cord syndrome (rare post-aortic surgery; more common in trauma/flex-distraction injury):

  • Motor: relatively preserved (anterior horn cells spared)
  • Pain/temperature: preserved (spinothalamic tract intact)
  • Vibration/proprioception: LOST (dorsal columns damaged)
  • Gait: sensory ataxia (loss of position sense)

Cauda equina syndrome (lumbosacral nerve root involvement, not true cord ischemia):

  • Bilateral leg pain (often radiating down legs)
  • Asymmetric weakness (nerve root pattern)
  • Bilateral urinary retention + fecal incontinence (saddle anesthesia)
  • Often associated with massive central disc herniation, cauda equina hematoma
  • Requires urgent MRI + neurosurgery; may require operative decompression

Differentiation tip: preserved vibration/proprioception in LE = anterior cord syndrome (spinal cord ischemia). Lost vibration/proprioception = posterior cord or cauda equina, or different diagnosis (stroke, Guillain-Barré).

sections.heading: 7.4 C-O-P-S protocol deep dive
sections.bodyHtml:
C = CSF Drain

Target CSF pressure <10 mmHg (some aggressive protocols <8 mmHg).

  • Lumbar catheter (most common) or ventriculostomy allows controlled drainage to reduce intrathecal pressure
  • Mechanism: CSF pressure is a component of spinal cord perfusion pressure (SCP = MAP − CSF pressure). Lowering CSF pressure increases SCP, improving cord blood flow
  • Placement: performed by neurosurgery (emergent if no pre-operative drain in place). Can be placed at bedside in ICU or in OR
  • Monitoring:
  • Manometer reading on the drain line (target <10 mmHg at level of Foramen of Monro)
  • CSF color/consistency (clear and colorless is normal; xanthochromic or hemorrhagic suggests cord infarction, old bleed, or epidural hematoma)
  • CSF output (expect 10–20 mL/h; >30 mL/h may be excessive and requires neurosurgery consultation)
  • Drain dislodgement or kinking (check tubing, transducer leveling)
  • Complications of CSF drain:
  • Epidural hematoma (most feared; presents as sudden worsening LE weakness + new/severe back pain; STAT MRI; requires urgent evacuation)
  • Infection (meningitis, ventriculitis if EVD; fever, headache, elevated CSF cell count)
  • Overdrainage (negative pressure, cord adhesions, catheter malposition → worsening symptoms)
  • Catheter fracture, obstruction, dislodgement
  • Duration: typically 3–5 days; weaned slowly after cord perfusion stabilized

O = Oxygenation

Target SpO₂ >95%; maintain adequate hemoglobin; liberal PaO₂ goal.

  • Mechanism: spinal cord ischemia is fundamentally a problem of tissue oxygen delivery. Optimizing O₂ content (FiO₂, SpO₂) and cardiac output (via MAP, HR, contractility) maximizes cord oxygen
  • Actions:
  • Supplemental O₂ (target SpO₂ >95%; consider target >98% in some protocols)
  • Intubation if respiratory compromise (high thoracic SCI → phrenic nerve involvement → diaphragm weakness)
  • Maintain hemoglobin ≥10 g/dL (transfuse if Hgb <8–9); each g of Hgb carries ~1.34 mL O₂/100 mL blood
  • Avoid hypoxia at all costs (even brief desaturations compound ischemic injury)

P = Pressure (MAP ≥85–90 mmHg, target 90–100 mmHg)

Maintain elevated mean arterial pressure to maximize spinal cord perfusion pressure.

  • Mechanism: SCP = MAP − CSF pressure. Raising MAP (via vasopressors, fluid, inotropes) increases SCP and cord blood flow
  • Target: MAP ≥85–90 mmHg is minimum; many protocols target MAP 90–100 mmHg acutely. This is not typical post-op cardiac goal (which is SBP <120).
  • Achieving MAP:
  • Vasopressors (first-line):
    • Phenylephrine (pure alpha-1 agonist, increases SVR): 50–200 mcg/min IV drip; titrate to MAP goal. No beta effect → doesn't increase HR reflexively; doesn't worsen rhythm disturbances
    • Norepinephrine (alpha + beta agonist): 2–20 mcg/min; stronger than phenylephrine; increases contractility in addition to SVR (more inotropic effect); consider if low cardiac output + low MAP
  • Fluids: gentle fluid bolus (500 mL crystalloid) if hypovolemic; excessive fluids worsen spinal cord edema
  • Inotropes (second-line): milrinone, dobutamine if low cardiac output + low MAP despite vasopressors
  • Monitoring: arterial line for continuous MAP; goal is consistency at target, not swings

S = Steroids (evidence limited; not universal)

Some protocols use high-dose methylprednisolone; others omit. Verify institutional/team consensus before administering.

  • Rationale: steroids may reduce inflammatory cascade and cord edema, improving microcirculation. Evidence is mixed and controversial
  • Dosing (if ordered): IV methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg bolus over 15 min, then 5.4 mg/kg/h × 23 h (adapted from spinal cord trauma guidelines; less robust evidence for SCI post-aortic surgery)
  • Controversy: NASCIS 2 trial (1990) supported high-dose methylprednisolone in traumatic SCI; subsequent trials questioned benefit. Post-aortic-surgery SCI is mechanistically different (ischemia vs. traumatic contusion) and evidence is sparse
  • Current consensus: use is institutional-dependent. Some centers use it; others reserve for severe deficits. Always verify with CT surgery + neurosurgery before starting.

sections.heading: 7.5 CSF drain complications
sections.bodyHtml:
Complication Presentation Timeline Management
Epidural hematoma Sudden worsening LE weakness or new/severe back pain, sometimes with fever/infection signs Hours to POD 2–3 STAT MRI spine to confirm. Neurosurgery emergency evacuation. Do NOT continue CSF drainage if hematoma confirmed (high risk of massive bleed). Call attending STAT.
Infection / meningitis Fever, headache, CSF turbidity/elevated WBC, mental status change POD 2–5 typically CSF gram stain + culture, blood cultures, ABx (ceftriaxone + vancomycin empirically), consider drain repositioning/removal per neurosurgery.
Overdrainage Worsening motor deficit, new headache (intracranial hypotension), CSF output >30 mL/h During active drainage Decrease drainage rate (raise collection bag higher above foramen of Monro) or clamp drain briefly. Notify neurosurgery. Check for catheter malposition.
Catheter obstruction / kinking CSF output suddenly decreases to near zero Any time Check tubing for kinks, reposition patient, flush per protocol (if safe), contact neurosurgery. May need replacement.
Catheter fracture / dislodgement No CSF output; tubing disconnected or broken During bedside care / transport Do not re-insert (contamination risk). Notify neurosurgery for emergent replacement if still needed.
Pneumocephalus (rare) Headache, altered mental status, air in ventricles on CT POD 1–2 Usually resolves with time; elevate HOB; avoid Valsalva; rarely requires intervention.

sections.heading: 7.6 Imaging findings in SCI
sections.bodyHtml:
MRI spine (GOLD STANDARD for SCI diagnosis and epidural hematoma exclusion):

  • T2-weighted images: hyperintense signal in spinal cord gray matter (reflects cord edema and ischemia). Extent of T2 hyperintensity correlates with severity and prognosis.
  • T1-weighted + gadolinium: may show enhancement of cord (reflects blood-brain barrier disruption, associated with poor prognosis)
  • Epidural hematoma: appears as crescent-shaped T2 dark/T1 bright signal adjacent to cord; compressing cord. Requires emergency decompression.
  • Cord atrophy: delayed finding (weeks–months post-SCI); indicates irreversible injury

CT spine / CT myelogram (fallback if MRI contraindicated):

  • Lower sensitivity for acute ischemia (does not show T2 hyperintensity well)
  • Can demonstrate epidural hematoma (blood density hyperdense relative to CSF)
  • Often used pre-operatively to plan aortic repair; limited utility for post-op SCI diagnosis

Timing: STAT imaging is critical. Any delay in ruling out epidural hematoma increases risk of massive epidural bleed if CSF drain continues.

sections.heading: 7.7 Recovery trajectory and rehabilitation
sections.bodyHtml:
Early phase (POD 0–7):

  • Initial spinal shock period: flaccid paralysis, areflexia, urinary retention (expected in acute SCI)
  • Serial neuro exams q6–12h to detect improvement or deterioration
  • ICU/stepdown level of care; continuous monitoring
  • Foley catheter (straight-cath q4–6h to assess PVR; transition to intermittent cath once stable)
  • Physical therapy (passive ROM, positioning) to prevent contractures

Intermediate phase (POD 1–4 weeks):

  • Spinal shock resolves → hyperreflexia, spasticity emerge (often week 1–2)
  • Motor recovery trajectory becomes clearer:
  • Good prognosis: improving motor strength (MRC 2→3→4 over days–weeks); may regain some function
  • Guarded prognosis: plateauing at MRC 2–3 (partial paralysis); may require orthotics
  • Poor prognosis: no improvement by week 1–2; likely permanent paraplegia
  • Bowel / bladder program: intermittent catheterization (q4–6h) vs. indwelling Foley (if unable to participate in IC program); laxatives + digital stimulation for bowel regimen
  • PT/OT escalation: sit-to-stand, transfers, wheelchair mobility if paraplegia; AFO (ankle-foot orthosis) fitting if partial LE weakness

Late phase (4+ weeks):

  • Inpatient rehabilitation transfer (spinal cord injury center if available)
  • Intensive PT/OT, psychosocial support, vocational rehab planning
  • Independence in mobility, ADLs, continence management
  • Spasticity management (baclofen, botox, orthotic support)

Prognosis factors:

  • Time to recognition + intervention: immediate-onset SCI recognized and treated within hours → better chance of reversal than delayed-onset discovered POD 5
  • Severity at nadir: complete paraplegia (MRC 0–1/5) → poorer prognosis than incomplete (MRC 3+/5)
  • Extent of cord involvement on MRI: smaller area of T2 hyperintensity → better prognosis
  • Motor recovery by POD 7: any motor improvement by day 7 → better long-term outcome

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any develop, escalate immediately.

  • New or worsening lower-extremity weakness despite C-O-P-S protocol in place — recheck CSF pressure (if drain in situ), recheck BP/MAP, notify CT surgery + neurosurgery for escalation (increased vasopressor, repeat imaging)
  • Severe acute back pain (especially midline) or new back tenderness — classic for epidural hematoma; STAT MRI + neurosurgery STAT
  • CSF drain output suddenly decreases to near-zero (or becomes bloody/xanthochromic) — catheter obstruction, kinking, malposition, or hematoma forming; notify neurosurgery emergently
  • Patient becoming increasingly anxious / confused / sleepy — may indicate hypotension, shock, or rising intracranial pressure; check BP/MAP, mental status, pupillary reactivity
  • Progressive respiratory compromise (tachypnea, use of accessory muscles, dropping SpO₂) — high thoracic SCI can impair phrenic nerve (C3–5) and diaphragm; prepare for intubation; do not delay
  • Hemoglobin dropping below 8–9 g/dL — reduces oxygen delivery to ischemic cord; transfuse promptly
  • Hypertension > 180 mmHg systolic — may indicate post-op pain, urinary retention, or rising intracranial pressure; treat pain, empty bladder, consider hydralazine if refractory (but do not drop MAP below 85–90)
  • No improvement or worsening by POD 2 — SCI is typically a one-time insult; no "second window" treatment exists. Lack of improvement suggests extensive cord necrosis; confirm imaging, ensure C-O-P-S optimized, discuss prognosis with patient/family
  • CSF drain left clamped too long — resuming drainage after prolonged clamping (>12 h) may cause sudden cord decompression and worsen edema; communicate with neurosurgery before unclamping
  • Patient "too comfortable" post-op (excessive sedation, missing back pain or weak legs) — bedside sedation assessment and systematic neuro exams are non-negotiable; do not over-sedate in first 24–48h

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Delayed-onset SCI is REAL and UNDERDIAGNOSED. Up to 40–50% of SCI post-TAAA is delayed (POD 2–5+, mean POD 2). Do NOT assume a patient with a normal neuro exam on POD 0 is in the clear. Serial exams on stepdown are essential. A patient reporting "weak legs" or unable to move feet on POD 3 requires the same urgent workup as POD 0 onset.

  2. CSF drain pressure is the KEY parameter, not just the presence of a drain. A drain in place but at 20 mmHg pressure is worse than no drain (false security + high pressure). Target <10 mmHg actively.

  3. MAP ≥85–90 mmHg is non-negotiable in acute SCI; this is NOT the typical post-op goal. Most post-op patients target SBP <120 to avoid bleeding. SCI patients need elevated BP to maintain spinal cord perfusion. Do not allow the ICU/stepdown team to "dial down" BP to their usual goal without explicit CT surgery + neurosurgery approval.

  4. Aggressive diuresis WORSENS SCI risk. Diuretics lower intravascular volume, drop MAP, and reduce spinal cord perfusion. In the acute phase (POD 0–2), use minimal diuresis and maintain euvolemia (not overloaded, but not dry).

  5. Hemoglobin <10 g/dL reduces oxygen delivery to the ischemic cord. Transfuse liberally (target Hgb ≥10) in the acute phase. This contradicts usual post-op transfusion thresholds (Hgb >7–8) and requires explicit orders from CT surgery.

  6. Epidural hematoma is the CSF drain's worst complication — it's a surgical emergency. Sudden worsening of LE weakness + new back pain (especially in the 12–48 h post-drain placement window) = epidural hematoma until proven otherwise. STAT MRI. Do NOT continue CSF drainage while waiting for imaging. Neurosurgery must evacuate emergently.

  7. Preserved posterior column function (vibration, proprioception) indicates ANTERIOR cord syndrome, confirming spinal cord ischemia. If vibration/proprioception are lost AND motor/pain sensation lost, think cauda equina, posterior cord syndrome, or different diagnosis (stroke, Guillain-Barré).

  8. Reversibility is time-dependent — the "golden window" is minutes-to-hours. SCI recognized and treated within the first few hours of symptoms onset may have dramatic recovery. Delayed recognition (POD 2–3) still warrants aggressive intervention, but prognosis is worse. Week-old paraplegia is likely permanent.

  9. Normal neuro exam must be DOCUMENTED in detail on every shift. If the handoff note says "neuro intact," but there's no recorded MRC scores, sensory level, or sphincter tone, and a patient suddenly appears weak, the team may assume the weakness is new-onset when it may have been missed earlier. Use the standardized MRC scale and document dermatome-level sensory testing.

  10. Patients on epidural analgesia (post-op epidural pain catheter) can have MASKED sensory exams. Local anesthetic diffusion can blunt pain/temperature sensation even with an intact spinal cord. Coordinate with anesthesia/pain team: reduce epidural concentration transiently, or use non-neuraxial analgesia during acute SCI assessment if sensory level is critical for diagnosis.

  11. Bilateral symmetric weakness is classic, but ASYMMETRIC weakness is common. One leg may be MRC 0 and the other MRC 2. Document each leg separately. Asymmetry does not rule out SCI.

  12. Urinary retention + post-void residual are underutilized diagnostic clues. Straight-cath post-void residual >200 mL (especially in a patient without pre-existing urinary retention) + new leg weakness = SCI until proven otherwise. Coordinate with urology if catheterization needed long-term.

  13. MRC 3/5 vs MRC 4/5 is a critical distinction. MRC 3 = movement against gravity but not against resistance (patient can lift leg off bed, but cannot kick back against resistance). MRC 4 = movement against some resistance. MRC 3 is the threshold for independence in some basic tasks; MRC <3 requires assistive devices. This distinction drives rehab planning.

  14. Crawford Extent II TAAA repairs are the HIGHEST SCI risk (10–15%). If your patient just underwent a Crawford Extent II open repair, heightened vigilance for SCI is warranted. Extent IV repairs are lower-risk (2–5%).

  15. The CSF drain may be the only intervention that matters in the first golden hours. Imaging, steroids, and optimizing MAP are important, but getting CSF pressure below 10 mmHg ASAP may be the difference between reversible and permanent paralysis. Neurosurgery should be placing a drain within minutes of recognition if none is in place.

cards.title: Stable CAD / Chronic Coronary Syndromes
cards.quickAnswer: Stable CAD (chronic coronary syndromes): fixed coronary stenosis causing exertional ischemia—angina-equivalent symptoms + diagnostic imaging (coronary CT angiography or catheterization). Risk stratification via CAD-RADS (CT severity) or SYNTAX score (angiographic complexity). Medical therapy first-line per ISCHEMIA trial (aspirin, high-intensity statin LDL <70, beta-blocker, ACE-I/ARB, BP <130/80, A1c <7% if diabetic); revascularization (PCI/CABG) for symptom relief, left main disease, proximal LAD, or 3-vessel disease + diabetes (SYNTAX/FREEDOM favor CABG). Post-revascularization: lifelong GDMT, cardiac rehabilitation, secondary prevention (smoking cessation, lipid targets, BP control). ISCHEMIA paradigm: invasive strategy no mortality advantage over medical therapy alone in stable CAD without high-risk anatomy—quality of life and symptom relief drive intervention choice.
