sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Chronic narrowing of one or more epicardial coronary arteries from atherosclerotic plaque, fixed stenosis (not dynamic), reducing coronary flow reserve. Ischemia occurs during exertion when myocardial demand exceeds diminished supply.
  • Epidemiology: ~8–10 million Americans with CAD; ~2 million with chronic angina. Leading cause of death and disability in US. Risk increases with age, male sex, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, tobacco use, family history, chronic kidney disease.
  • Typical patient: 50s–70s with exertional chest discomfort, dyspnea on exertion, or fatigue; history of risk factors. May be post-MI (prior ACS), incidental imaging finding, or pre-op CABG candidate.
  • Clinical context: ICU and stepdown nurses encounter stable CAD patients pre-op awaiting CABG, post-op recovery trajectory (POD 0–7 in ICU → stepdown → telemetry → discharge), post-PCI patients, and patients admitted with acute decompensation (unstable angina/NSTEMI) representing progression from stable disease.
  • Why it matters: Most common chronic cardiac diagnosis; highest treatment impact comes from optimizing medical therapy (GDMT) and secondary prevention, not intervention alone (ISCHEMIA trial).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Atherosclerotic plaque accumulation begins decades before symptoms—LDL oxidation, macrophage infiltration, foam cell formation, fibrous cap rupture risk. Fixed stenosis (>50% diameter in LAD/LCx, >50% RCA) reduces coronary flow reserve, especially during exertion.

Ischemic cascade:

  • Stenosis → reduced coronary blood flow reserve
  • Exertion increases myocardial O₂ demand; supply cannot match → subendocardial ischemia (LV inner third most vulnerable)
  • Chronic ischemia → myocardial remodeling, fibrosis, hibernating (viable but dysfunctional) myocardium
  • Plaque rupture always possible → acute coronary syndrome (ACS) conversion—~50% of first MIs occur at non-critical stenoses

Symptom heterogeneity:

  • Classic exertional angina: substernal pressure/heaviness, reproducible, relieved by rest or nitrates in 5–10 min
  • Dyspnea on exertion (often sole symptom in elderly, women, diabetes)
  • Atypical: arm/jaw/neck radiation, epigastric burning, fatigue, indigestion
  • Silent ischemia: objective evidence (positive stress test) without symptoms, risk of unrecognized MI

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — who presents with stable CAD, when it matters.

  • Pre-op scenario: Stable CAD patient admitted awaiting CABG (defined anatomy on recent cath, SYNTAX score calculated, graft targets identified).
  • Post-op scenario: Patient recovering from CABG or PCI, on secondary prevention, cardiac rehab referral sent.
  • Acute decompensation: Patient with known stable CAD develops unstable angina (new or increased frequency/severity, rest pain, ischemic changes on ECG) → escalate to ACS pathway.
  • Incidental finding: Positive stress test, abnormal coronary CTA during workup for other reason (dyspnea, syncope, murmur).
  • Chronic management: Outpatient or step-down patient on long-term GDMT, referred for cardiac rehab, lipid optimization, risk factor control.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet. 2–3 minutes.

History & symptom characterization

  • Angina or angina-equivalent: onset, trigger (exertion, emotion, cold exposure), duration, radiation, relieving factors (rest, nitrates, antacids)
  • Associated symptoms: dyspnea, palpitations, diaphoresis, nausea, fatigue
  • Risk factors: prior MI, prior revascularization (PCI/CABG/hybrid), diabetes, HTN, dyslipidemia, tobacco, family history, CKD

Physical exam (often normal at rest)

  • Vital signs: HR, BP (baseline, compare to prior)
  • Cardiovascular: heart rate/rhythm, murmurs (concomitant valvular disease?), signs of HF (JVD, edema, rales)
  • Peripheral: femoral/carotid bruits, lower extremity edema, cyanosis (peripheral vascular disease)
  • General: pallor, diaphoresis, anxiety

Recent diagnostic data

  • 12-lead ECG at rest: baseline ST-T abnormalities? prior MI pattern?
  • Stress test results: normal, equivocal, or positive (ischemic ST changes, symptoms at low workload)?
  • Coronary imaging: CTA or angiography findings (CAD-RADS, SYNTAX score, vessel territories, prior stents)?
  • Echocardiogram: EF, wall motion abnormality, valvular disease, diastolic dysfunction?
  • Recent labs: troponin (r/o acute event), CBC, BMP, lipid panel (LDL, HDL, Tg), glucose, A1c, BNP/NT-proBNP if HF suspicion, eGFR (CKD staging)

Medication review (MAR)

  • Antiplatelets: aspirin dose, clopidogrel (post-PCI duration?), ticagrelor (ACS-only; should NOT be in stable CAD)
  • Beta-blocker: agent, dose, HR response
  • Statin: agent, dose, LDL goal achievement
  • ACE-I/ARB: dose
  • Nitrates, ranolazine, ivabradine (if on board)
  • Diuretics (if HF comorbid)

Catheterization context (if recent) - Date of cath, anatomy documented, SYNTAX score, ejection fraction during ventriculography, left main involvement, target vessels for CABG, FFR/iFR measurements if functional assessment done

sections.heading: 5A. Lifestyle + Risk Modification
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Smoking cessation: absolute priority; single largest modifiable factor for outcomes and graft patency post-CABG - Offer cessation counseling, nicotine replacement (patch + lozenge), varenicline (Chantix), bupropion; refer to formal program - Sustained cessation pre-op and post-op improves graft patency and long-term survival

  2. Diabetes control: target A1c <7% in stable CAD; <6.5% if prior MI or very high-risk - Glucose monitoring, intensify agents (metformin preferred, GLP-1 RA or SGLT2i if HF/renal disease comorbid) - SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) and GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, dulaglutide) shown to reduce CV events in CAD + diabetes; preferred beyond metformin

  3. Blood pressure control: target <130/80 mmHg per 2023 guideline (vs. older <140/90)

    • First-line: ACE-I or ARB (essential post-MI, beneficial in stable CAD + HTN or DM)
    • Add diuretic (HCTZ, chlorthalidone) or calcium-channel blocker (dihydropyridine) as needed; avoid non-DHP CCB if reduced EF

  4. Weight management: target BMI <25 (overweight 25–29, obese ≥30); weight loss 5–10% improves CV risk factors - Dietary counseling: Mediterranean or DASH diet pattern preferred

  5. Physical activity: target 150 min/week moderate-intensity aerobic exercise post-rehab; progressive program - Cardiac rehabilitation post-CABG/PCI: referral essential; improves EF, exercise capacity, reduces readmission and mortality

sections.heading: 5B. Medical Therapy (Goal-Directed Medical Therapy — GDMT)
sections.bodyHtml:
Antiplatelet therapy

  • Aspirin 81 mg daily: indefinite in all stable CAD; reduces recurrent MI and mortality
  • Clopidogrel (Plavix) 75 mg daily: indicated ONLY after PCI (12 months standard, may shorten if high bleeding risk); after CABG (1–3 months per surgeon); NOT routine in stable CAD without prior intervention per ISCHEMIA trial
  • Ticagrelor, prasugrel: NOT used in stable CAD; reserved for acute coronary syndromes
  • Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT): aspirin + clopidogrel only post-PCI or post-CABG; do NOT initiate in stable CAD medical management alone
  • Rivaroxaban 2.5 mg BID + aspirin: COMPASS trial showed modest CV benefit (3–4% NNT) in stable CAD with high-risk features (prior MI, CKD, diabetes); small bleeding risk increase; consider in very-high-risk stable CAD

Lipid-lowering

  • High-intensity statin: atorvastatin 40–80 mg or rosuvastatin 20–40 mg daily (preferred to pravastatin, simvastatin)
  • LDL goal: <70 mg/dL in stable CAD; <55 mg/dL if prior MI or very-high-risk features
  • Ezetimibe: add 10 mg daily if statin alone doesn't achieve goal (reduces LDL ~18% additional)
  • PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab, inclisiran): if LDL not at goal despite statin + ezetimibe; NNT ~20 over 2 years for MACE reduction
  • Bempedoic acid, icosapent ethyl (high-dose fish oil if elevated Tg): emerging options beyond statins; discuss with team
  • Lipoprotein (a) [Lp(a)]: check baseline; elevated Lp(a) (>50 mg/dL) confers additional CV risk; statin response often poor; consider additional therapy in very-high-risk setting

Beta-blockers (symptom relief, post-MI mortality benefit)

  • Indication in stable CAD: primary benefit is symptom control in exertional angina; post-MI (reduces mortality and reinfarction)
  • Common agents: metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol, bisoprolol
  • Target HR: 50–60 at rest if tolerated; titrate to angina relief and HR response
  • Caution: avoid abrupt discontinuation (rebound ischemia risk); reduce BP excessively cautiously

Nitrates (acute symptom relief)

  • Sublingual nitroglycerin: 0.3–0.6 mg SL every 5 min × 3 for acute angina; fast relief (5–10 min)
  • Long-acting nitrates (isosorbide dinitrate 20–40 mg BID, isosorbide mononitrate 30–60 mg daily): less common due to tolerance with continuous dosing; nitrate-free interval 10–14 hr helps preserve efficacy
  • Caution: nitrates reduce preload, can cause reflex tachycardia, hypotension; avoid in RV infarction if known

Calcium-channel blockers (rate/symptom control, if beta-blocker contraindicated)

  • Non-dihydropyridines (diltiazem 120–240 mg/day SR, verapamil 120–360 mg/day): reduce HR and contractility; useful for rate control and symptom relief
  • Avoid in reduced EF (negative inotropic); use with caution if bradycardic or hypotensive
  • Dihydropyridines (amlodipine 5–10 mg/day, nifedipine XL 30–90 mg/day): vasodilators; cause reflex tachycardia—use with concurrent beta-blocker; avoid as monotherapy if reduced EF

ACE-inhibitors / Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers (GDMT cornerstone)

  • Essential post-MI; beneficial in stable CAD + HTN, DM, or reduced EF
  • Common agents: lisinopril 5–10 mg daily, ramipril 2.5–5 mg daily, valsartan 80–160 mg daily, losartan 50–100 mg daily
  • Benefits: reduce mortality and reinfarction post-MI; reduce proteinuria in CKD; prevent/slow LV remodeling
  • Monitoring: check K⁺ and Cr at baseline and 1–2 weeks (hyperkalemia, renal function decline); avoid if K⁺ >5.5 or Cr rising

Antianginal agents (for symptom breakthrough despite above)

  • Ranolazine (Ranexa) 500–1000 mg BID: shifts myocardial metabolism; reduces ischemic symptoms and angina frequency
  • Does NOT reduce MI or mortality; symptom relief only
  • Useful for refractory angina despite beta-blocker, CCB, nitrates; modest QT prolongation (monitor with amiodarone comorbidly)
  • Ivabradine (Corlanor) 5–7.5 mg BID: selective If channel inhibitor; reduces heart rate without inotropic effect
  • Symptom relief in chronic angina (not event reduction); less commonly used in US than Europe; watch for visual symptoms (scotomas)

Additional agents (if HF comorbid)

  • Diuretics: loop (furosemide, torsemide) if volume overload; monitor K⁺
  • Aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone): if post-MI EF ≤40%; reduce mortality and HF hospitalizations

sections.heading: 5C. Antianginal Ladder *(Table: Stepwise intensification for symptom control)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Symptom Status First-line agent(s) Add if inadequate Then add if still inadequate Escalate to revascularization assessment
Mild (≤1× angina/wk) Beta-blocker ± SL nitrates PRN Non-DHP CCB (diltiazem/verapamil) Ranolazine 500 mg BID If worsening or high-risk anatomy
Moderate (1–3×/wk) Beta-blocker + long-acting nitrate Non-DHP CCB Ranolazine 500–1000 mg BID, ± ivabradine Consider revascularization for quality of life
Severe (>3×/wk, rest pain) High-dose BB + dihydropyridine CCB + long-acting nitrate Add ranolazine, ± ivabradine Maxed on medical therapy—REFER FOR CATHETERIZATION & revascularization assessment Symptomatic refractory angina

sections.heading: 5D. Revascularization Decision *(ISCHEMIA-informed, anatomy-driven)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Guiding principle: Revascularization in stable CAD is for symptom relief and quality of life, not mortality benefit (ISCHEMIA trial). Exception: left main (LM), proximal LAD, or 3-vessel + diabetes (FREEDOM trial) have outcome benefits from CABG.

Risk stratification & decision framework

CAD-RADS severity (CT angiography)

  • 0: No CAD
  • 1: CAD <50% stenosis (non-obstructive)
  • 2: 50–69% stenosis (moderate)
  • 3: 70–99% stenosis (severe)
  • 4S: >99% stenosis (subtotal occlusion)
  • 5: Complete occlusion (chronic)

SYNTAX Score (angiography-based complexity; scored 0–100)

  • 0–22 (low complexity): PCI preferred; similar outcomes to CABG, less invasive recovery
  • 23–32 (intermediate): Shared decision-making; Heart Team discussion (cardiologist + cardiac surgeon); either PCI or CABG acceptable depending on EF, comorbidities
  • >32 (high complexity): CABG generally preferred for durability and lower repeat revascularization rate

PCI indications (percutaneous coronary intervention)

  • Single-vessel disease (SVD), any location
  • LAD subtotal occlusion (if suitable anatomy)
  • Saphenous vein graft (SVG) disease, failed prior CABG
  • SYNTAX score 0–22 (low complexity)
  • Patient preference for percutaneous approach + suitable anatomy
  • Life expectancy <10 years (less invasive, shorter recovery)
  • FFR-guided PCI superior: ischemia-provoked FFR >0.80 indicates hemodynamically insignificant stenosis → defer PCI; reduces unnecessary procedures (FAME trials)

Advantages Disadvantages
Less invasive, faster recovery Restenosis 5–10% at 1 year (drug-eluting stents)
Shorter hospital stay Late stent thrombosis risk (0.5–1% annually)
Repeated revascularization possible Requires DAPT × 12 months
Suitable for high-risk surgical patients Not ideal for left main, heavily calcified, CTO

CABG indications (coronary artery bypass grafting)

  • Left main (LMCA) disease >50%: CABG standard-of-care; PCI reserved for distal/bifurcation LMCA in selected cases with low SYNTAX
  • Multi-vessel disease (MVD) + diabetes: CABG superior to PCI (FREEDOM trial: lower mortality, less repeat revascularization at 5 years)
  • Multi-vessel disease (MVD) + reduced EF (EF <35%): CABG often preferred; durable revascularization
  • Proximal LAD (especially >70%) ± additional disease: CABG (via LIMA to LAD) provides durable long-term patency
  • Complex anatomy (SYNTAX >32): CABG preferred for durability and lower revision rate
  • Failed prior PCI (restenosis, ISR): CABG often preferred; avoid repeated PCI in same territory if possible

Advantages Disadvantages
Durable relief (LIMA 10–15 yr, SVG 5–10 yr) Invasive surgery, sternotomy complications
No stent thrombosis Longer recovery, 6–8 weeks sternal precautions
Lower repeat revascularization rate Graft failure (early SVG 10–15%, late occlusion)
Superior in MVD + DM (FREEDOM) Cognitive dysfunction risk (post-op delirium)

ISCHEMIA trial context (paradigm shift)

  • Invasive strategy (angiography + PCI/CABG) vs. conservative (optimal medical therapy alone) showed no mortality benefit of routine invasive approach in stable CAD
  • Symptom relief and quality of life improved with invasive strategy—the main gain from intervention
  • Exception: LM and proximal LAD anatomy still benefit from revascularization; very-high-risk features (ejection fraction <35%, extensive ischemia on stress test) favor invasive approach
  • Implication: Your stable CAD patient on aspirin, statin, beta-blocker, ACE-I (medical therapy alone) is on guideline-recommended management; revascularization is elected for symptom relief when lifestyle and maxed medical therapy are insufficient

Hybrid approach (LIMA to LAD + PCI to other vessels)

  • Selected patients with excellent LAD target (LIMA graft) and suitable RCA/LCx for PCI
  • Combines durability of LIMA with less-invasive PCI for non-LAD vessels
  • Emerging strategy; not yet standard but option in selected centers and cases

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Red flag triggers for escalation:

  • New or worsening angina: frequency, severity, or rest pain in previously stable CAD patient → suspect ACS (unstable angina/NSTEMI); obtain ECG, troponin, SBAR to APP
  • Positive stress test in a medically stable patient: refer for catheterization and revascularization assessment (especially if high-risk features: EF <35%, extensive ischemia)
  • Restenosis post-PCI: angina recurrence 1 month–1 year post-stent placement → cath lab for repeat angiography ± restenting
  • Graft failure post-CABG: angina recurrence weeks to months post-op → cath lab assessment for graft patency, native vessel disease progression
  • Acute decompensation: pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmia in CAD patient → ICU-level care, possible inotropes, IABP, emergent cardiology consultation

SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room, POD if post-op]. Patient with stable CAD [anatomy/prior intervention if known] presenting with [symptom/change]." B: "Risk factors: [DM, HTN, prior MI, etc.]. Prior imaging/cath: [SYNTAX score, SYNTAX, location]. Current medications: [GDMT list]." A: "Patient reports [frequency/severity of angina or ischemic equivalent]. ECG shows [changes]. Troponin [result if drawn]. Vitals: HR [ ], BP [ ], SpO₂ [ ]." R: "Requesting [ECG interpretation / troponin serial / cardiology consult / catheterization vs. repeat stress test]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Urgency
New angina or ACS conversion (NSTEMI/STEMI pattern ECG, elevated troponin) Cardiology (attend/fellow) + ED attending if not cardiology admission STAT / Rapid response
Positive stress test, medically stable, considering revascularization Cardiology (APP/fellow) for catheterization scheduling Routine-to-urgent per symptom severity
Post-CABG graft failure suspicion (angina + ischemic ECG changes) CT surgery team + Cardiology Urgent (within 2–4 hr)
Post-PCI restenosis (in-stent re-narrowing, recurrent angina) Interventional cardiology Urgent
Acute decompensation (pulmonary edema, hypotension, arrhythmia) Rapid Response + Cardiology + ICU team STAT

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(Novice + Advanced Beginner deep-dive; expandable in app)*
sections.bodyHtml:
ISCHEMIA trial implications — paradigm shift in stable CAD management The ISCHEMIA trial (Morrow et al., 2020) fundamentally changed thinking about stable CAD:
  • Study design: Randomized 5,179 patients with stable CAD and inducible ischemia on stress testing to invasive strategy (angiography + revascularization if suitable anatomy) vs. conservative strategy (optimal medical therapy OMT alone).
  • Key finding: No mortality benefit of invasive strategy at median 3.2-year follow-up (10.2% invasive vs. 10.7% OMT; mortality curves superimposed).
  • Quality of life: Invasive group reported slightly better symptom relief and exercise capacity—the main difference.
  • Exceptions: Patients with LM >50% or proximal LAD were excluded from randomization—these high-risk anatomies are presumed to benefit from revascularization based on observational data (CASS registry).
  • Implication: Your stable CAD patient on aspirin, high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, ACE-I, and no revascularization is following guideline-recommended medical-first strategy. Revascularization is elected when symptom burden limits quality of life despite maxed GDMT, not for mortality benefit.
  • Teaching point: Stable CAD is chronic and low-risk when well-controlled medically. The word "stable" matters—it's not unstable angina (acute, high-risk ACS precursor).
Stress testing vs. coronary CTA vs. FFR — diagnostic algorithm Three main diagnostic modalities; each answers a different question: Stress testing (exercise ECG, stress echo, nuclear SPECT/PET, stress CMR)
  • What it shows: functional ischemia—zones of dysfunctional myocardium during exertion
  • Advantages: well-established; good NPV (negative test = low CAD risk); guides prognosis (extent of ischemia correlates with risk)
  • Disadvantages: cannot show anatomy; false positives if ECG abnormalities at baseline, LBBB, digoxin use; requires exercise ability
  • When to use: initial risk stratification in intermediate pre-test probability; serial testing to assess ischemia burden over time
  • Pitfall: stress test does NOT exclude CAD—a normal test in a high-risk patient still warrants further imaging; conversely, extensive ischemia on stress test triggers invasive cath assessment Coronary CT angiography (CTA)
  • What it shows: coronary artery anatomy (vessel diameters, plaque, calcification, stenosis severity via CAD-RADS)
  • Advantages: high NPV for CAD; rules out CAD in low-to-intermediate risk; calcification scoring quantifies burden
  • Disadvantages: cannot assess functional significance of borderline stenosis (50–70%); overestimates stenosis severity in heavily calcified arteries; radiation and iodinated contrast
  • When to use: rule-out CAD in low-to-intermediate risk; assess anatomy if cath not planned; clarify coronary dominance, anomalies
  • Pitfall: coronary CTA severity grade (CAD-RADS 2–3) doesn't always correlate with ischemia—a 60% stenosis on CTA may be hemodynamically insignificant (normal FFR) FFR (fractional flow reserve) & iFR (instantaneous wave-free ratio)
  • What they show: hemodynamic significance of stenosis (pressure gradient across lesion during hyperemia [FFR] or at baseline [iFR])
  • FFR >0.80: stenosis is hemodynamically insignificant—deferring PCI does NOT increase event risk (FAME trials)
  • FFR ≤0.75: stenosis is hemodynamically significant—PCI indicated
  • FFR-CT: non-invasive estimate of FFR from coronary CTA; emerging utility, pending wider adoption
  • When to use: during catheterization for borderline lesions (angiographic 40–70% stenosis) to decide PCI vs. deferral
  • Pitfall: FFR is not done for every lesion—usually reserved for intermediate stenoses where visual angiography is ambiguous. Not needed if angiographic severity is obvious (<30% vs. >90%). Diagnostic algorithm (stable CAD suspected)
    1. Low pre-test probability + non-specific symptoms: Consider stress test or CTA rule-out. If negative, reassure; if positive, proceed to cath.
    2. Intermediate pre-test probability: Stress test (functional data) ± CTA (anatomy). Discordant results may need cath for clarification.
    3. High pre-test probability + symptoms: Proceed directly to invasive cath (goal-directed strategy, faster intervention if CAD found).
    4. Borderline stenosis on angiography: Use FFR/iFR to guide PCI vs. deferral.
SYNTAX score and Heart Team recommendation — shared decision-making The SYNTAX score (Sianos et al., 2005) quantifies anatomic complexity of CAD, guiding PCI vs. CABG choice: How SYNTAX score is calculated:
  • Defined lesions: ≥50% stenosis in arteries ≥1.5 mm diameter
  • Weighted points: multiple vessel involvement, bifurcation location, calcification, tortuosity, thrombosis, etc.
  • Total score 0–100; higher = more complex SYNTAX score interpretation:
  • 0–22 (low): PCI and CABG have similar outcomes; PCI often preferred (less invasive)
  • 23–32 (intermediate): Shared decision-making; depends on EF, age, comorbidities, patient preference
  • >32 (high): CABG generally preferred for durability and lower revision rate Heart Team approach:
  • Multidisciplinary discussion (interventional cardiologist + cardiac surgeon) before revascularization decision
  • Weighs anatomy (SYNTAX), patient factors (age, EF, comorbidities, life expectancy), patient preferences
  • Particularly important in intermediate SYNTAX and complex patient profiles
  • Teaching point: High SYNTAX score does NOT mean "don't intervene." It means "CABG likely better than PCI for durability." The patient still needs revascularization if symptomatic or high-risk; the mode (CABG vs. PCI) is the decision.
Cardiac rehabilitation post-CABG/PCI — critical to long-term outcomes Cardiac rehabilitation (Phase II 3–6 weeks post-op, Phase III ongoing outpatient program): What it includes:
  • Exercise training: supervised treadmill/bike, progressive intensity over 12 weeks, improves EF, exercise capacity, VO₂ max
  • Risk factor modification: smoking cessation counseling, nutrition (Mediterranean diet), weight loss, diabetes/BP/lipid management
  • Education: CAD pathophysiology, medications, activity progression, warning signs
  • Psychosocial support: anxiety/depression screening, sex counseling post-op, coping strategies Evidence base:
  • Reduces 1-year mortality by ~25% (meta-analysis)
  • Reduces hospital readmissions
  • Improves quality of life, exercise tolerance, mood
  • Beneficial in both PCI and CABG populations Nursing role:
  • Refer all post-CABG and post-PCI patients to cardiac rehab at discharge
  • Follow up on enrollment; reinforce importance ("This improves your survival, not just how you feel")
  • Monitor adherence; identify barriers (transportation, cost, misconceptions about post-op exertion safety) Teaching point for patients: "Cardiac rehab is as important as your surgery. You'll recover faster, feel better, live longer, and reduce your risk of another heart attack if you complete the program."
SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists in CAD + diabetes — emerging cardioprotection SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin [Farxiga], empagliflozin [Jardiance], canagliflozin [Invokana])
  • CV benefits: reduce MACE by ~11%, reduce HF hospitalizations by ~30–40%
  • Mechanism: improve LV diastolic function, reduce LV hypertrophy, anti-inflammatory
  • Indication: 1st- or 2nd-line in CAD + type 2 DM (regardless of HbA1c); also if concurrent HFrEF (EF ≤40%)
  • Landmark trials: DECLARE-TIMI 58 (dapagliflozin), EMPA-REG (empagliflozin)
  • Caution: euglycemic DKA risk (rare); genital mycotic infections; volume depletion if aggressive diuresis GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide [Ozempic, Wegovy], dulaglutide [Trulicity], liraglutide [Victoza])
  • CV benefits: reduce MACE by ~26%, reduce death by ~15%
  • Mechanism: weight loss, reduce BP, improve lipids, anti-inflammatory
  • Indication: 1st-line in CAD + type 2 DM + obesity (BMI >25); preferred if prior MI or high CV risk
  • Landmark trial: SUSTAIN-6 (semaglutide)
  • Caution: nausea, weight loss (monitor for sarcopenia if elderly); rapid HR increase (less cardiac benefit in those who can't tolerate); pancreatitis history is relative CI Teaching point: "If you have both diabetes and heart disease, newer diabetes medications (SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA) reduce heart attack and heart failure risk—not just blood sugar. Discuss with your cardiologist whether these are right for you."
Lipid-lowering beyond statins — achieving LDL goals Statin inadequacy:
  • ~30–40% of CAD patients on high-intensity statin alone do NOT reach LDL <70 mg/dL
  • "Statin resistance" (genetic variation in CYP3A4 metabolism) and poor adherence contribute Ezetimibe (Zetia) 10 mg daily
  • Mechanism: inhibits intestinal cholesterol absorption
  • LDL reduction: ~18–20% additional
  • Cost: low; well-tolerated
  • When to add: first step if statin alone inadequate PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab [Repatha], alirocumab [Praluent], inclisiran [Leqvio])
  • Mechanism: monoclonal Ab or siRNA targeting PCSK9 (LDL receptor recycler); increases LDL clearance
  • LDL reduction: 50–60% additional on top of statin ± ezetimibe
  • CV benefit: FOURIER trial (evolocumab) showed 15% MACE reduction; NNT ~20 over 2 years
  • Cost: $5,000–$7,000/year; often requires prior auth
  • When to add: if LDL not at goal despite statin + ezetimibe; especially in very-high-risk (prior MI, LM disease, young CAD onset) Bempedoic acid (Nexletol) 120 mg daily
  • Mechanism: xanthine oxidase inhibitor; reduces uric acid and LDL
  • LDL reduction: ~10–15% additional
  • When to use: alternative if statin intolerance (muscle symptoms); can combine with ezetimibe ± PCSK9i
  • Caution: raises uric acid initially; do not use in gout; interacts with pegloticase Icosapent ethyl (Vascepa) at high dose (2 g BID)
  • Mechanism: high-dose omega-3 fatty acid
  • Use: if elevated triglycerides (135–499 mg/dL) despite statin + optimal glycemic control
  • CV benefit: REDUCE-IT trial showed 25% MACE reduction; NNT ~21
  • Caution: bleeding risk (especially if on dual antiplatelet); expensive; GI side effects Lipoprotein (a) [Lp(a)] consideration:
  • What it is: inherited apo(a) genetic marker; independent CV risk factor
  • Baseline Lp(a) >50 mg/dL: confers 2–3× CV risk; statin response poor
  • Treatment: no proven agent yet; lipoprotein apheresis (removes Lp(a)) rarely used; periprocedural therapy may emerge
  • Teaching point: "Lp(a) is like 'genetic cholesterol.' If high, you inherited higher heart attack risk; medications and lifestyle are even more important." Lipid management summary table
    Target LDLBaseline statin responseStep 1Step 2Step 3
    <70 mg/dLAt goalContinue——
    <70Not at goal (60–69)Add ezetimibePCSK9i if still inadequateBempedoic acid
    <70Significantly elevated (>100)Add ezetimibe + consider PCSK9iConsider PCSK9i ± bempedoic acidIcosapent ethyl if high Tg
Post-bypass graft surveillance — long-term patency and secondary prevention Graft patency timeline:
  • Early patency (at discharge): ~90% LIMA, ~80–85% SVG
  • 1-year patency: ~90% LIMA, ~70–80% SVG (early SVG attrition 10–20%)
  • 10-year patency: ~80–90% LIMA, ~50–60% SVG
  • Graft failure modes: early (technical, clotting), intermediate (intimal proliferation), late (atherosclerotic SVG disease mimicking native CAD) Surveillance strategy:
  • Baseline post-CABG cath or CTA: 1 year post-op; documents patency baseline, guides secondary prevention intensity
  • Serial imaging: symptom-driven (angina recurrence = cath or CTA); some centers do routine angiography or CTA at 5–10 years
  • Stress testing: if new symptoms or risk stratification needed Lifelong secondary prevention:
  • Statin: continue high-intensity indefinitely; LDL <70 target
  • Aspirin: 81 mg daily indefinite (proven to reduce graft thrombosis and late occlusion)
  • Beta-blocker: continue if HTN, post-MI, or rate control needed
  • ACE-I/ARB: continue if HTN, DM, or EF <40%
  • BP target: <130/80
  • Smoking: absolute cessation; any smoking jeopardizes graft patency
  • Exercise, weight, diet: Mediterranean pattern, 150 min/week moderate activity
  • Clopidogrel post-CABG: duration determined by surgeon (typically 1–3 months); NOT lifelong unless concurrent PCI stent Teaching point for post-CABG patients: "Your new grafts will last 10–15 years on average. High-intensity statin, aspirin, and not smoking are the three most important things you can do. If you quit smoking now, your graft patency improves dramatically."

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any show in a medically stable CAD patient, re-escalate.

  • Angina increasing in frequency (once-weekly → several times daily) or severity: escalating disease, possible plaque destabilization → obtain ECG, troponin, call cardiology for cath assessment
  • Rest angina or nocturnal angina: high-risk feature; concern for ACS conversion; escalate urgently
  • Angina with diaphoresis, dyspnea, nausea, or radiation to jaw/arm: classic ACS presentation → activate ACS protocol (ECG, troponin, aspirin if no CI, cardiology stat)
  • Positive stress test or new ischemic changes on ECG in medically stable patient: risk stratification signal; refer for catheterization and revascularization assessment
  • Chest discomfort + ST elevation or new ST depression on ECG: STEMI or NSTEMI equivalent → activate code, stat cath lab
  • Syncope or presyncope with exertion in CAD patient: may indicate arrhythmia (VT), critical stenosis (demand ischemia), or HF decompensation → ICD candidacy assessment, urgent cath
  • New dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, or PND in stable CAD patient: concern for HF evolution (ischemic cardiomyopathy); check BNP, echo, optimize GDMT
  • Recurrent angina weeks-to-months post-CABG: graft failure or native disease progression → cath for imaging
  • Recurrent angina <12 months post-PCI stent: in-stent restenosis (ISR), stent thrombosis risk, or new disease → urgent cath
  • Signs of stroke/TIA (facial droop, arm weakness, speech difficulty) in CAD patient: thromboembolic event; activate stroke protocol; cardiology for anticoagulation consideration if HF/EF low

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. ISCHEMIA trial is the 5W teaching case for stable CAD. Invasive strategy (cath + revascularization) offers NO mortality benefit over optimal medical therapy alone in stable CAD without LM/proximal LAD. Symptom relief and quality of life drive the intervention decision. Your patient on aspirin, statin, beta-blocker, ACE-I with no revascularization is following evidence-based GDMT—do not pressure toward intervention.

  2. Left main disease is a CABG lesion. LM stenosis >50% (especially if bifurcation/trifurcation involvement) is best treated with CABG. PCI of unprotected left main is not standard first-line for stable CAD (rare exceptions: distal LMCA, low SYNTAX, very high surgical risk). If your pre-op patient awaiting CABG has left main disease, that's the right choice.

  3. FREEDOM trial: CABG superior to PCI in multivessel disease + diabetes. Landmark outcome—your diabetic patient with 3-vessel CAD scheduled for CABG has superior long-term survival compared to PCI. Reinforce the importance of the procedure; post-op cardiac rehab is critical.

  4. DAPT is NOT routine in stable CAD—only after PCI or CABG. Many nurses think all CAD patients need aspirin + clopidogrel. Wrong. Aspirin alone for stable CAD without prior intervention is correct. DAPT (aspirin + clopidogrel [or ticagrelor/prasugrel] is indicated ONLY post-PCI (12 months standard, shorter if high bleeding risk) or post-CABG (1–3 months per surgeon). Do NOT initiate clopidogrel in stable CAD medical management alone.

  5. Ticagrelor has NO role in stable CAD. Reserved for acute coronary syndromes. If your stable CAD patient is being discharged on ticagrelor without recent ACS, question it—likely an error or communication gap about an acute event.

  6. Hold clopidogrel 5–7 days pre-op CABG (surgeon's decision on exact timing). SVG patency risk if stopped too early; bleeding risk if continued too close to surgery. Coordinate with surgeon; document the plan clearly. Aspirin, by contrast, is CONTINUED through pre-op (reduces graft thrombosis).

  7. FFR-guided PCI beats angiography-guided. Borderline stenoses (angiographic 40–70%) with normal FFR (>0.80) don't need PCI; avoids unnecessary procedures. If your cath lab uses FFR routinely, support it—evidence-based deferral reduces events.

  8. SYNTAX score >32 favors CABG; 0–22 favors PCI; 23–32 is shared decision. High SYNTAX doesn't mean "don't intervene"; it means "CABG likely superior for durability." Symptomatic CAD with high SYNTAX still needs revascularization—CABG is the mode.

  9. CAD-RADS 2–3 (moderate-to-severe stenosis on CTA) does NOT always mean PCI is needed. A 60% stenosis on CTA may have normal FFR (hemodynamically insignificant). Conversely, a 40% stenosis may have abnormal FFR. If functional assessment (FFR, stress test) is discordant with CTA anatomy, cath with FFR measurement clarifies.

  10. Statin LDL goals: <70 mg/dL stable CAD, <55 if prior MI or very-high-risk. High-intensity statin is standard. Know your patient's LDL; if not at goal, ask why (non-adherence, need for ezetimibe or PCSK9i?). LDL reduction has the strongest evidence base for slowing plaque progression. ezetimibe adds ~18% LDL reduction; PCSK9i adds 50–60% if LDL still not at goal.

  11. Smoking cessation is the single biggest intervention for CAD. More impactful than any medication for event reduction and graft patency post-CABG. If your CAD patient still smokes, cessation is THE priority teaching. Enroll in formal program; use pharmacotherapy (nicotine replacement, varenicline, bupropion). Post-CABG, sustained cessation predicts graft patency and long-term outcomes better than lipids alone.

  12. Women and diabetics present with atypical stable CAD symptoms. "Indigestion," fatigue, arm tingling, dyspnea without chest discomfort—don't dismiss as anxiety or GERD. If a woman or diabetic has exertional symptoms with risk factors, stress test or CTA even if symptoms are vague. Clinical pearl: women more often have single-vessel LAD disease; worse prognosis post-event.

  13. SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists reduce MACE in CAD + diabetes. These are NOT just glucose-lowering agents; they're cardioprotective. SGLT2i reduce HF hospitalization; GLP-1 RA reduce death. If your diabetic CAD patient is not on one of these (in addition to metformin), discuss with cardiology for optimization.

  14. Cardiac rehabilitation improves survival AND quality of life. Refer all post-CABG and post-PCI patients; track enrollment. Rehab participants have lower mortality, fewer readmissions, better exercise capacity. Emphasize to patients: "This is as important as your surgery."

  15. Post-CABG graft surveillance at 1 year (angiography or CTA) documents baseline patency and guides secondary prevention intensity. Early SVG failure (10–20% at 1 year) indicates need for escalated lipid/antiplatelet management. Lifelong statin + aspirin + smoking cessation are non-negotiable for graft longevity.

cards.title: Sternal Precautions
cards.quickAnswer: Post-sternotomy patients follow sternal precautions for 6–12 weeks to protect bone healing. No lifting >5–10 lbs (per surgeon), no pushing/pulling heavy objects, no overhead reaching, no driving ×4–6 weeks, cough with pillow splinting. Modern evidence supports "Keep Your Move in the Tube" approach (Adams 2016, 2023) — functional movement within symptom-free range is protective, not harmful. Dehiscence red flags: sternal click/pop, grinding sensation, drainage from mid-sternum, fever. Most complications occur POD 0–3. Mobilization + cardiac rehab starting POD 7–14 are protective and encouraged within precautions.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, types, duration, and who it applies to.

  • Definition: Activity, lifting, and motion restrictions applied to patients who have undergone median sternotomy to protect the healing sternal bone and surgical wire fixation during the period of bone union (6–12 weeks post-op).

  • Sternal healing biology: Cartilaginous union begins at ~4–6 weeks; complete bony union requires ~12 weeks. Early mobilization and weight-bearing movement (within symptom-free range) actually promote bone remodeling and union, contrary to historical "immobilization" dogma.

  • Who it applies to: Every patient with median sternotomy — CABG, AVR/root, MVR, TVR, aortic ascending/arch, descending/TAAA (if sternotomy component), MAZE, myectomy, heart transplant, ECMO weaning via sternotomy.

    Does NOT apply to minimally invasive approaches that avoid sternotomy (right mini-thoracotomy mitral, MIDCAB, transfemoral TAVR, TEVAR).

  • Why it matters: Sternal wires or plates hold the bone edges in proximity during healing. Excessive force, sudden strain, or repetitive high-load mechanics can cause wire loosening, bone shift, or dehiscence — presenting as clicking/popping, chest pain, drainage, fever, or mediastinitis.

  • Duration: Standard 6–8 weeks; extended to 12 weeks for high-risk patients (obesity, diabetes, chronic steroid use, COPD, prior sternal complications, redo surgery). Follow surgeon-specific orders.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why It Exists
sections.bodyHtml:
The sternum is opened via median sternotomy and secured with stainless-steel wires (most common), plates, or tape. During the early post-op period, the bone edges are held together primarily by surgical fixation and newly forming callus — not yet load-bearing. Excessive force, twisting, or shear stress can disrupt this fragile union, leading to dehiscence.

Historical practice imposed strict immobilization ("no lifting >10 lbs, no push/pull, hands below shoulders for 6–8 weeks") out of abundance of caution. Modern evidence challenges this approach: Adams (2016, 2023) and the Society of Thoracic Surgeons demonstrate that functional movement within a symptom-free range is not harmful and may be protective — pain-guided mobility supports bone remodeling and reduces deconditioning, PTSD, learned helplessness, and cardiac rehab delay (Cahalin et al., 2011; Brocki et al., 2010). The "Keep Your Move in the Tube" (KYMITT) paradigm offers a practical mental model: movement that stays within an imagined tube around the torso (extending to arm's length, elbows tucked) is allowed; movements that push against the tube are restricted.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of precaution needs and populations.

Sternal stability assessment & risk stratification:

  • Standard-risk sternotomy: Isolated CABG, single-valve surgery, stable diabetes, no obesity, no COPD — conventional 6-week precautions often sufficient.
  • Extended-risk: Obesity (BMI >35), diabetes (especially poor glycemic control), chronic steroid use, COPD with chronic cough, redo sternotomy, advanced age, renal impairment. Surgeons often extend precautions to 8–12 weeks.
  • Highest-risk scenarios: Diabetic patients with microvascular disease, combined CABG + valve, BIMA harvest (higher sternal stress from loss of bilateral supply), post-MAZE (lateral thoracotomy adds stress), post-mitral (lateral thoracotomy), immunosuppression. Close monitoring and possibly extended imaging (CT sternum) may be warranted.

Post-surgical variations:

  • Mini-sternotomy or thoracotomy patients (lateral/posterior approach for valve surgery) have different precautions — NOT median sternotomy precautions. Lateral thoracotomy places stress on lateral chest wall and shoulder; precautions focus on avoiding external rotation/abduction rather than anterior push-pull restrictions.
  • Redo patients: Prior sternal wire removal may leave bone weakened; precautions are often more conservative and extended.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / Gather Information* (5–10 minutes per shift)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside + chart review. Information-only; no actions yet.

Sternal stability evaluation — every shift (POD 0–7 minimum; POD 8+ per surgeon order):

  • Listen & palpate: Have patient take a deep breath, cough, or move arms gently. Feel for abnormal motion, clicking sensation, grinding (crepitus), or instability at sternotomy line.
  • Ask directly: "Do you feel clicking, popping, or grinding in your chest?" "Does it hurt to cough or reach?"
  • Character: Mechanical click vs. musculoskeletal snap (costochondral junction).
  • Trending: New click/pop with pain = escalate. Stable mechanical sensation without pain may be superficial wire or rib.

Incision assessment:

  • Approximation: Wound edges aligned, no gaping or separation.
  • Appearance: Erythema, warmth, edema, fluctuance, drainage (type, color, purulent vs. serous).
  • Sutures / staples: Intact, in place, no signs of infection.

Pain & function:

  • Pain pattern: Localized sternal pain vs. diffuse chest wall; worse with specific movements (reaching, coughing, twisting)?
  • Functional limitation: What activities trigger pain? Splinting? Guarding?
  • Respiratory impact: Cough quality (splinted vs. unsplinted), breath sounds, SpO₂, work of breathing.

Precaution adherence:

  • Lifting & carrying: Observe transfers; ask about what patient has tried to lift at home.
  • Transfers: Log-roll vs. sit-up? Push with legs or arms? Using trapeze or bedrail?
  • Walking assistance: Stable gait, arm swing, shoulder stability?
  • Sleeping position: Back, side, prone, frequency of position changes?

sections.heading: 5.1 Traditional vs. Keep Your Move in the Tube Comparison
sections.bodyHtml:
Aspect Traditional Approach (Historical) Keep Your Move in the Tube (KYMITT) — Modern Evidence
Weight limit No lifting >10 lbs; absolute cutoff Pain-guided mobility; no arbitrary weight limit if symptom-free (Adams 2016, 2023)
Pushing/pulling No push-ups, no pulling doors, no heavy objects Limit to symptom-free range; functional reaching allowed if pain-free
Reaching No overhead, no behind back, no reaching across midline Elbow-tucked movements within "tube" are safe; reaching to ear-level OK if no resistance
Motion philosophy Immobilize to protect bone Movement within pain-free range promotes healing + reduces deconditioning
Evidence Consensus practice (1990s–2010s); precaution-based RCT + observational data (Adams, STS 2023; Cahalin 2011; Brocki 2010); mobility-protective
Patient outcome Some protection from dehiscence; high deconditioning, PTSD, depression Lower dehiscence rates; better functional recovery, cardiac rehab adherence
Clinical use now Still standard in many institutions; being phased out Increasingly adopted; STS evidence-based review endorses it

sections.heading: 5.3 Sternal Dehiscence Red Flags & Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Finding Presumed Cause Immediate Action
New sternal click or pop (single or repetitive) Wire loosening or bone shift; possible dehiscence early Notify surgeon STAT. Mark the spot; note timing (with cough, movement?). CT sternum may be needed.
Grinding sensation (crepitus) at sternum Bone-to-bone instability or infection (osteomyelitis) Surgeon notification. Most common POD 5–14. Monitor for fever, drainage.
New serous/serosanguineous drainage from mid-sternum Superficial infection or early dehiscence Notify surgeon. Increase dressing frequency; monitor for erythema, warmth, fever.
Fever (≥101.5°F) + sternal erythema + drainage + clicking Deep sternal wound infection (DSWI) / mediastinitis STAT contact surgeon & infectious disease. Likely OR needed. This is critical.
New wound separation or gaping (opening of incision) Superficial dehiscence or infection Surgeon notification. May need re-closure or local wound care.
Increasing sternal pain uncontrolled by analgesics Possible early dehiscence or DSWI Assess for click/pop. Trend pain pattern; notify provider if new or severe.

sections.heading: 5.4 Execution Steps — Pre-Discharge Teaching & POD-Specific Coaching
sections.bodyHtml:
POD 0–1 (ICU — acute post-op):

  1. Introduce concept: "Your breastbone was cut and is now healing with surgical wires, like a broken bone."
  2. Demonstrate log-roll: Have patient watch, then return-demonstrate. Emphasize feet-first, legs do the work.
  3. Show heart pillow splinting: Demonstrate cough with pillow; have patient practice.
  4. Explain why: "The precautions protect your bone so the wires don't loosen. You're not protecting your heart — the heart is fine."
  5. Assess pain control; analgesics before cough/mobility sessions.

POD 2–3 (Step-down or floor — more alert):

  1. Reinforce log-roll; challenge: "Show me how you'd get up if I leave the room."
  2. Review KYMITT concept: "Imagine a tube around your torso out to arm's length. Stay in the tube."
  3. Demo safe reaching (elbows tucked) vs. unsafe (reaching across body, overhead, behind back).
  4. Walk the patient; explain: "Walking is GOOD. It helps your heart and bones. Just move slowly and hold the pillow if you cough."
  5. Introduce heart pillow as constant companion: "Take it everywhere — home, car, bed."

POD 4–6 (Approaching discharge):

  1. Comprehensive teaching session (20–30 min) with patient AND family/caregiver if available. - Play short video or use visual handout of do's and don'ts. - Use real objects (gallon of milk = 10 lbs; show what's allowed).
  2. Discuss specific home scenarios: groceries, children, pets, household tasks, sexual activity, showering.
  3. Establish surgeon follow-up plan: date, precaution duration, driving clearance timeline.
  4. Provide written precaution card; encourage patient to post at home.
  5. Address depression screening (post-cardiac surgery depression affects ~20–30%; ask: "How are you feeling emotionally? Hopeful? Scared?").

POD 7–14 (Home, early recovery):

  1. Reinforce in outpatient clinic or via phone: precautions are temporary and evidence-based.
  2. Encourage walking, light ADLs, early cardiac rehab enrollment.
  3. Screen for learned helplessness: "Are you afraid to move? Let's talk about what's safe."
  4. Review when restrictions lift (typically 6–8 weeks for most; 12 weeks for high-risk).

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers & Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of when to escalate.

Reassess and escalate IMMEDIATELY if:

  1. Sternal click, pop, or grinding with or without pain — STAT surgeon call. Document: single vs. repetitive, with what movement, when noticed. CT sternum likely.

  2. New or worsening sternal pain uncontrolled by analgesics — Verify pain character (mechanical vs. musculoskeletal); notify provider.

  3. Visible sternal wound separation, gaping, or dehiscence — Surgeon notification. Cover with sterile dressing. Do not attempt closure.

  4. Fever ≥101.5°F + sternal erythema + drainage + click/pop — CRITICAL: DSWI/mediastinitis suspected. STAT contact surgeon AND infectious disease. OR likely.

  5. Increasing or purulent sternal drainage — Culture if ordered. Notify surgeon. Assess for fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis.

  6. Patient unable or unwilling to follow precautions — Involve social work, chaplaincy, psychiatry as needed. Assess for depression, pain inadequacy, lack of understanding. Document teaching and refusal.

  7. Family member performing prohibited activities (lifting patient, allowing patient to lift child) — Reinforce teaching; consider caregiver education or case management referral.

  8. Sternal instability on palpation — Notify surgeon for assessment and possible imaging.

sections.heading: 7.1 Sternal Healing Biology — Why Bone Comes First
sections.bodyHtml:
The sternum heals in stages:

  • Immediate (0–3 days): Inflammatory phase; clot formation at surgical edges; surgical fixation (wires) is primary load-bearing structure.
  • Callus formation (1–3 weeks): Cartilaginous callus forms between bone ends; this is fragile. Wires begin to feel looser as bone expands; this is normal.
  • Cartilaginous union (4–6 weeks): Callus mineralizes; bone edges are bridged by cartilage. Load-bearing capacity increases 30–40% per week. Early mobilization now benefits remodeling.
  • Bony union (6–12 weeks): Complete mineralization and remodeling. By 12 weeks, union is usually strong enough for normal activity; stress-shielding effects mean wires rarely need removal.

Key insight: Movement (within pain-free range) stimulates bone turnover and accelerates union. Immobilization causes bone loss and delays remodeling. This is why modern evidence (Adams 2016, 2023; STS consensus) supports mobility over restriction.

sections.heading: 7.2 Why Traditional Restrictions May Be Over-Restrictive
sections.bodyHtml:
Historical precautions (no lifting >10 lbs, no pushing, no hands above shoulders, no reaching) were based on mechanical principles, not biomechanical data:

  • Arbitrary weight cutoff: A 10-lb weight-lifting restriction is poorly correlated with sternal stress. A patient squeezing a steering wheel or hugging a child may generate more sternal load than a properly-lifted 8-lb grocery bag (Adams 2023).
  • Deconditioning penalty: 6–8 weeks of restricted activity causes rapid muscle loss, cardiovascular deconditioning, and reduced bone density — increasing fall risk and prolonging recovery.
  • Psychological toll: Learned helplessness, depression, and post-traumatic stress are common after cardiac surgery. Over-restriction amplifies these, delaying cardiac rehab and return-to-work.
  • Compliance burden: Restrictive precautions are hard to follow and often violated once patients feel well, reducing teaching effectiveness.

Modern approach (KYMITT): Pain-guided movement within functional range is safer, more compliant, and better for bone remodeling and mental health (Cahalin et al., 2011).

sections.heading: 7.3 Keep Your Move in the Tube (KYMITT) Evidence
sections.bodyHtml:
Cahalin et al. (2011) introduced this framework to overcome the compliance problem. Patients visualize an imaginary tube around the torso, extending to arm's length.

Movement that stays inside the tube is allowed; movement that pushes against the tube is restricted.

Examples:

  • Inside the tube (allowed): Tucking elbows while reaching to pick up a light object; arm swinging while walking; self-care reaching (face, hair, feeding).
  • Pushing against the tube (restricted): Overhead reaching with force; reaching far across the body; reaching behind back with resistance.

Evidence: Multiple observational studies (Brocki 2010, Adams 2016) show KYMITT-guided patients have similar dehiscence rates to those using traditional precautions, but with better functional outcomes, cardiac rehab engagement, and mental health.

sections.heading: 7.4 Dehiscence Risk Factors — Predict Who Needs Extended Precautions
sections.bodyHtml:
Risk Factor Mechanism Precaution Adjustment
Diabetes (especially uncontrolled A1C >180) Impaired microvascular healing; delayed callus formation; increased infection risk Extend to 8–10 weeks; glycemic control critical during POD 0–6
Obesity (BMI >35) Higher mechanical stress on sternum; poor vascularization of deep sternum; slower healing Extend to 8–12 weeks; aggressive mobilization paradoxically protective
Chronic steroid use (>5 mg prednisone daily) Impaired osteoblast function; weak callus; increased infection risk Extend to 8–10 weeks; consider abdominal binder if surgeon agrees
COPD / chronic cough Repetitive high-force Valsalva; stress on sternum; aspiration risk Optimize bronchodilation; aggressive cough splinting; smoking cessation
Smoking (active at time of surgery) Impaired microvascular supply; delayed healing Strongly encourage cessation; monitor closely POD 7–21
Renal impairment (CKD stage 3+) Mineral metabolism abnormality; delayed bone healing Consult nephrology; optimize Ca/P balance; extend precautions
Bilateral IMA harvest (BIMA) Loss of dual blood supply to sternum; ischemia risk Extended precautions (8–12 weeks) standard; careful mobilization
Redo surgery (prior sternotomy) Weakened sternal bone; altered vascular anatomy; fibrous healing Very cautious precautions; consider CT sternum baseline; close surgeon follow-up
Advanced age (>75 years) Slower bone turnover; comorbidities common Tailor to individual fitness; mobilization often protective
Female sex + large breast size Bra-related pressure + gravity stress on sternum Proper sternal support garment essential; avoid underwire bras during healing

sections.heading: 7.5 Special Post-Surgical Considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-MAZE patients:

  • MAZE typically adds lateral thoracotomy or epicardial approach → sternal stress is NOT the limiting factor.
  • Sternal precautions are standard BUT lateral thoracotomy pain often dominates; focus on side-lying, avoiding shoulder extension, and protecting lateral ribs.
  • Precautions duration may be same (6–8 weeks) but scope is different: emphasis is on avoiding thoracotomy wound stress, not sternotomy protection per se.

Post-mitral valve surgery (lateral thoracotomy approach):

  • Lateral thoracotomy (anterolateral or posterolateral incision) avoids median sternotomy but creates stress on lateral chest wall, shoulder, and scapula.
  • Sternal precautions do NOT apply; instead, restrict shoulder abduction, external rotation, reaching across body.
  • Precautions focus on avoiding lateral thoracotomy wound stress: no heavy lifting, no pushing doors open, limited arm elevation, sleeping on contralateral side.

Post-aortic arch repair (if involving sternotomy + thoracotomy):

  • Combined incision requires hybrid precautions: sternotomy precautions (no push-pull) PLUS thoracotomy precautions (limited shoulder mobility).
  • Often more restrictive than isolated sternotomy; follow surgeon guidance.

sections.heading: 8.1 Correct Techniques
sections.bodyHtml:
Log-rolling out of bed:

  1. Bend knees; keep feet flat on mattress.
  2. Roll hips and shoulders as a unit to one side (do NOT push with arms).
  3. Once on side, use legs and momentum to dangle legs over bed edge.
  4. Push up to sitting using legs (push bed or footstool); avoid using arms to push.

Safe lifting within precautions:

  1. Hold object with both hands, close to body, waist-level.
  2. Bend knees; use leg power to lift, not back or arms.
  3. Avoid twisting; face the direction you're moving.
  4. Keep object <5–10 lbs (gallon of milk as reference).

Cough splinting:

  1. Hold pillow firmly against sternum.
  2. Cough or sneeze; pillow provides counter-pressure.
  3. Take deep breath first; splint during exhalation.

Reaching safely (KYMITT):

  1. Keep elbows tucked close to sides.
  2. Reach no further than arm's length from body.
  3. Do NOT reach overhead, across midline, or behind back against resistance.
  4. If pain-free and symptom-free, light reaching to ear-level is OK.

sections.heading: 8.2 Driving Restriction — Why 4–6 Weeks?
sections.bodyHtml:
Driving is NOT just about pain; it's about reaction time and force:

  • Sudden steering or emergency braking generates rapid arm acceleration and high sternal load (may exceed 50–100 lbs force momentarily).
  • Seatbelt contact with sternum creates direct pressure during braking.
  • Many post-op patients are on narcotics (delayed reaction time) or have not driven in weeks (loss of confidence).

Evidence: Barua et al. (2005) and Adams (2016) document increased sternal complications in patients who resumed driving early and had motor vehicle incidents requiring emergency maneuvers.

Standard recommendation: 4–6 weeks per surgeon (often 6 weeks). Verify:

  • Surgeon clearance (written order).
  • Patient off narcotics.
  • Patient able to perform emergency maneuvers (full arm abduction/steering reach) without pain.
  • Seatbelt can be positioned without direct sternal contact (seatbelt cushion or heart pillow).

sections.heading: 9. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Stable patients with these findings → re-escalate.

  • Sternal pain trend: Pain was decreasing, now stable or increasing after POD 3 → possible developing dehiscence.
  • Clicking develops insidiously over days 3–7 → early wire loosening; more likely with poor compliance.
  • Fever trend: Stable POD 0–2, then rises POD 5–14 with sternal erythema → DSWI unfolding (classic timeline).
  • Drainage character shift: From serous to serosanguineous or purulent after initially clear → infection.
  • Patient anxiety escalating despite reassurance → may signal pain inadequacy, depression, or unspoken precaution violation fear.
  • Family member taking over activities (doing all transfers, lifts, household work) → possible learned helplessness or underestimation of patient capability.
  • Precaution violation observed: Patient lifting, reaching, or coughing without splinting despite teaching → risk of dehiscence; reinforce + assess barriers.

sections.heading: 10. Pitfalls & Pearls *(High-yield clinical wisdom)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. KYMITT is easier to remember than a checklist of don'ts. Teaching patients "stay in the tube" is far more effective than listing "no overhead, no behind-back, no pushing." Use the mental model consistently.

  2. Restrictions vary by surgeon. Some allow 5 lbs, others 10 lbs; some restrict driving 4 weeks, others 6 weeks.

    Check the orders — do NOT assume. Post precautions at bedside.

  3. Pain is a better guide than arbitrary weight limits. If a patient can reach 8 lbs without pain, it's likely OK despite the "10-lb rule." Pain tells you the tissue is stressed; restriction based on weight alone ignores patient individuality (Adams 2016).

  4. Precautions are forgotten when patients feel good. Reinforce teaching POD 1 (patient won't remember), POD 3 (patient more alert), POD 5 (discharge prep), and at discharge (when they'll actually use it). Repetition is essential.

  5. Family teaching is as important as patient teaching. The spouse/caregiver will be lifting groceries and helping with ADLs. If they miss the teaching session, the patient violates precautions trying to "help" at home. Capture family in sessions.

  6. The heart pillow matters. Some patients set it aside and never use it. Check during rounds: pillow within arm's reach? Used when coughing? Post a note: "This pillow protects your sternum — keep it within reach."

  7. Sternal click during early cough or movement ≠ dehiscence automatically. Single isolated click on POD 2–3 without pain is often superficial wire or costal cartilage alignment.

    But NEW clicking after stable pain days is concerning — escalate.

  8. Sternal click DURING movement vs. AFTER is different. Click during twisting with resistance suggests high mechanical stress. Click after normal ADL suggests looser wire but not necessarily dangerous. Timing and context matter.

  9. Diabetic patients are at highest dehiscence risk. Glycemic control during POD 0–6 is directly tied to bone healing. A diabetic patient with A1C >180 post-op has significantly delayed union. Ensure tight glucose management (insulin drip in ICU, aggressive inpatient control). Extend precautions to 8–10 weeks.

  10. Obese patients paradoxically benefit from MORE mobilization, not less. Mechanical stress is high, yes, but immobilization causes rapid deconditioning and increases fall risk. Early walking, PT, and cardiac rehab are protective. Extend precautions by time but not by restriction intensity.

  11. "I felt a pop" = surgeon notification immediately. Do NOT dismiss as musculoskeletal. Document precisely: when, with what activity, was there pain? This is sternal dehiscence until proven otherwise. CXR and CT sternum likely.

  12. DSWI presents POD 5–21 typically (peak POD 10–14). Classic triad: fever, sternal erythema/warmth, drainage + click/grinding. This is a surgical emergency — mediastinitis risk, sepsis risk. Early recognition saves lives. Daily sternal exams are not overkill.

  13. Driving restriction enforcement is hard but critical. Patients often negotiate or "just go to the mailbox." Be clear: "Emergency steering with a healing sternum can cause complications." Many surgeons recommend written instructions or a note to put in the car. Hold firm.

  14. Bra/chest support for women is underemphasized. Large-breasted women experience gravity stress on healing sternum with regular bra wear. A properly-fitted sports bra or sternal support garment (medical-grade) reduces sternal load significantly. Discuss proactively.

  15. Showering with sternal support. Many patients worry: "Can I shower?" Answer: "Yes, once incision is sealed (per surgeon, usually POD 1–2). Short showers, let water run over incision, pat dry gently. Wear a shower shirt or support bra if it helps you feel secure." This is a teaching moment for compliance — a patient who feels supported is more likely to follow precautions.

  16. Depression screening post-cardiac surgery is standard. ~20–30% of post-cardiac surgery patients experience depression. Over-restrictive precautions amplify risk. Ask: "How are you feeling emotionally? Hopeful? Scared? Sad?" Refer to social work, psychiatry, or chaplaincy early.

  17. Cardiac rehab is PROTECTIVE, not risky. Many patients fear exercise post-op. Emphasize: "Monitored cardiac rehab starting POD 7–14 is the best thing you can do for your heart AND your sternum." Rehab therapists understand precautions and progress patients safely.

  18. Explain WHY to patients, not just what to do. Patients who understand the biology ("Your bone is healing for 12 weeks") are far more compliant than those who hear "Don't lift." Spend 5 minutes on "why" and compliance skyrockets.

  19. Return-to-work timeline: Sedentary jobs (desk work) typically resume at 4–6 weeks per surgeon clearance. Physical labor (lifting, climbing) usually 8–12 weeks or longer.

    Each patient is individual — ask what their job entails, assess if they can do it within precautions, then tell them the realistic timeline.

  20. Sexual activity timing: Common question patients won't ask unless you bring it up. General guidance: "When you can walk upstairs without chest pain, sexual activity is OK." That's typically 4–6 weeks. Patient on top or side-lying to avoid sternal weight-bearing. Proactively address this — many surgeons do not, and patients suffer in silence.

cards.title: Sternal Wound Infection / Mediastinitis (DSWI)
cards.quickAnswer: Post-op fever (POD 4+) + sternal drainage OR sternal click on palpation = surgical emergency. Obtain wound/blood cultures STAT, notify CT surgery directly (not just APP—use on-call service, state "possible DSWI"). If stable: pain control, tight glycemic control (BG <180), CT chest. If septic: activate sepsis protocol + vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h + cefepime 2 g IV q8h (gram-negative coverage) STAT, then prepare for urgent debridement. Sternal click is always pathologic—DSWI confirmed; operative fixation required.
