sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, who it applies to, why it matters.

  • Definition: Deep sternal wound infection (DSWI), also called mediastinitis when involving the mediastinal space. Infection of fascia and deeper structures (muscle, bone, mediastinum) following sternotomy.
  • Incidence: ~0.5–2% of all cardiac surgery patients (Meldrum et al., 2020); up to 3–5% in high-risk subgroups (bilateral IMA + diabetes). Mortality 10–25% if untreated or delayed.
  • Presentation timing: Peak onset post-operative day (POD) 7–30; importantly, ~40% present after discharge (POD 14–30 at home), making family education critical.
  • Who this applies to: Every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient (any sternotomy: CABG, valve, composite, MAZE). Highest risk: diabetes + BIMA, obesity, prolonged CPB, redo surgery, immunocompromised.
  • Why it matters: Leading cause of infection-related mortality in post-operative cardiac patients. Requires urgent operative intervention, extended IV antibiotics (6 weeks), possible flap reconstruction. Delays in recognition increase morbidity and mortality.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Multifactorial infection bridging the skin inoculum to mediastinal space.

Seeding and early infection:

  • Intraoperative inoculation — skin flora (Staphylococcus aureus, Cutibacterium acnes) or environmental contamination (gram-negatives) during sternotomy, despite prophylactic antibiotics.
  • Sternal ischemia — improper internal mammary artery harvest (excessive skeletonization, thermal injury from cautery) impairs blood supply to bone; sternal bone is relatively avascular distally.
  • Biofilm formation on sternal wires or necrotic bone — organisms protected from antibiotics.

Impaired wound healing (the convergence):

  • Hyperglycemia (post-op glucose >180 mg/dL) — impairs neutrophil function, collagen synthesis, angiogenesis; risk increases 2–3× with poor control.
  • Obesity (BMI >30) — increased wound hematoma, impaired perfusion, higher bacterial inoculum in adipose tissue.
  • Bilateral internal mammary artery (BIMA) — double the sternal ischemic risk vs single IMA; highest risk when combined with diabetes.
  • Long CPB time (>180 min) — systemic inflammation, altered immunity, hemodilution.
  • Malnutrition — albumin <3.0 g/dL, prealbumin <20 mg/dL impair collagen synthesis and immune function.

Progression to mediastinitis:

  • Infection tracks along sternum and into mediastinal space → mediastinal cellulitis → tissue necrosis → sternal bone involvement (osteomyelitis) → loss of sternal integrity → sternal instability (click/movement).
  • Sternal instability marks the point of no return for antibiotics alone; operative debridement + reconstruction required.

El Oakley/Wright Classification (timing and microbiology):

  • Type I (early, 0–2 weeks) — aggressive pathogens (often gram-negative), high virulence.
  • Type II (delayed, 2–4 weeks) — mixed flora, moderate virulence, moderate outcomes.
  • Type III (late, >4 weeks) — indolent organisms, chronic course, fungal risk in immunocompromised.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-op cardiac patient (POD 4+, including post-discharge):

  • Fever (>38.3°C / 101°F) on or after POD 4, especially if recurrent after discharge
  • Purulent sternal drainage (gross pus, not serous or serosanguineous)
  • Sternal pain with movement, coughing, or deep breathing — new onset or worsening
  • Sternal click, "give," or instability on palpation or with patient movement — THIS IS DEFINITIVE FOR DSWI
  • Erythema and edema extending significantly beyond immediate incision edges (>1 cm)
  • Sternal dehiscence — visible or palpable edge separation
  • Patient reports sensation — "felt something pop," "chest giving way," "pulling apart"
  • Wound not healing — persistent purulent drainage, failure to close, foul odor after POD 7–10
  • Systemic signs of sepsis — rising WBC (>12), rising CRP, fever refractory to antipyretics, tachycardia, hypotension, altered mental status

Epidemiology — novice needs to know:

  • Superficial surgical site infection (SSI) — skin/subcutaneous involvement only; ~1–2% incidence, POD 3–7 onset, often responds to antibiotics + local care.
  • Deep sternal wound infection (DSWI) — fascial and deeper involvement; ~0.5–2% baseline incidence (up to 5% in high-risk), POD 7–30 peak, 10–25% mortality if untreated.
  • BIMA + diabetes = 3–5× incidence — this triad is the highest-risk combination.
  • Post-discharge presentation is common — families call ED from home POD 15–30; must be triaged urgently.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: bedside systematic exam.

  • Wound appearance: erythema (extent, sharp vs diffuse boundary), edema (localized vs tracking upward/downward), drainage (serous/serosanguineous vs frankly purulent, color, odor), skin integrity (intact vs gaping), edges (well-approximated vs separating)
  • Palpation (GENTLY, gloved): test incision — is there fluctuance (abscess), cellulitis, tenderness out of proportion? CRITICAL: Does the sternum move independently or click with gentle palpation or with patient cough/breathing? (Sternal click = DSWI pathognomonic)
  • Systemic vital signs: temperature trend, HR, RR, BP, mental status, signs of sepsis trajectory
  • Patient history: When did symptoms start? Fever duration? Any chest pain with cough/movement? Any wound issues noted at home if post-discharge?
  • Surgical context: POD from surgery, procedure type (CABG/valve/composite), single vs bilateral IMA harvest, any re-exploration post-op, known wound complications
  • Labs (recent): WBC (baseline vs current), CRP, CBC, lactate, prealbumin/albumin if available
  • MAR review: Current antibiotics? Pain management? Glycemic control (glucose trend)? Home medications (steroids, immunosuppressants)?
  • Chart review: Discharge summary, prior cultures from any out-of-hospital care, intra-op cultures if obtained

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP > 65, no sepsis criteria, patient monitoring feasible, no sternal instability on exam)

  1. Obtain wound culture STAT — swab deep within the wound or expressed fluid (not surface epithelium), place in aerobic/anaerobic transport bottles per lab protocol
  2. Obtain blood cultures × 2 — from separate sites, before any antibiotics (critical for organism identification and sensitivity; cultures drawn after antibiotic start have ~50% lower sensitivity)
  3. Stat labs: CBC (WBC trend), CRP, lactate, basic metabolic panel, prealbumin/albumin if available
  4. Notify CT SURGERY DIRECTLY — use on-call service number, state "possible DSWI post-op day [X]" to trigger priority callback. Do NOT rely on APP to relay — direct call ensures surgical evaluation is prioritized over routine consultation chain
  5. Do NOT start empiric antibiotics yet — unless patient meets sepsis criteria (see 5B). Cultures obtained after antibiotics started have 50% lower sensitivity for organism ID. If truly septic, draw cultures while preparing antibiotic infusion (do not let perfect be the enemy of good)
  6. Order CT chest (if not already done) — assess for substernal collection, mediastinal involvement, fluid tracking along sternum, bone destruction
  7. Document wound appearance — photograph per institutional policy; measure and mark erythema extent with marker if tracking; aid surgical team assessment
  8. Pain control: IV opioid (morphine 2–4 mg, hydromorphone 0.5–1 mg q2–4h) — DSWI pain is severe; do NOT under-treat. Pain → splinting → impaired breathing → worse healing
  9. Tight glycemic control: target glucose <180 mg/dL throughout hospital stay. Post-op glucose >180 increases SSI risk 2–3×; coordinate with provider on insulin dosing (may need insulin gtt initially if running 200+)
  10. NPO status — DSWI almost always requires operative debridement; keep patient NPO in anticipation
  11. Continuous monitoring: telemetry, pulse ox, vital signs q2–4h; prepare for possible emergent OR transfer
  12. Sternal precautions: reinforce — no pushing, pulling, arm raising; walker if ambulating; splint cough with pillow/hands

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension [SBP <90], severe tachycardia, altered mental status, high fever, sepsis criteria, sternal instability on exam, or suspected sepsis)

  1. Activate Sepsis Protocol / Rapid Response — notify APP + charge nurse immediately; do NOT leave patient alone
  2. STAT call CT SURGERY — state clearly "suspected DSWI + sepsis" or "sternal instability + fever"; provide POD and procedure type; they will advise on OR urgency
  3. Obtain wound and blood cultures × 2 IMMEDIATELY — time to culture is critical but does NOT delay antibiotics in sepsis
  4. Stat labs: lactate, CBC, CMP, blood gas, prealbumin
  5. START empiric antibiotics IMMEDIATELY (do not wait for culture results):
    • Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (covers MRSA, CoNS) PLUS cefepime 2 g IV q8h (gram-negative coverage) OR piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h (broader, covers anaerobes)
    • Adjust for renal function; confirm dosing with provider
    • Typical empiric regimen in post-op cardiac patients: vanc + cefepime is standard in most cardiac units (MRSA colonization prevalence high)
    • Fluid resuscitation per sepsis protocol — 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus if hypotensive; reassess after; target MAP >65
    • Prepare for urgent OR — DSWI + sepsis typically requires emergent surgical debridement; anticipate ICU/OR transfer
    • Remove unnecessary lines if safe (extra A-lines, catheters causing continued contamination) per protocol; maintain at least one secure IV for antibiotics
    • Source control assessment: if external collection/abscess palpable, discuss with CT surgery whether bedside drainage is feasible (usually no — defer to OR)
    • Document: vital sign trend, sepsis sign onset time, cultures drawn (time/site), antibiotics administered (drug/dose/time), patient response

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure type: CABG/AVR/etc.], date of surgery [date]."

B: "Patient presenting with [fever/purulent drainage/sternal pain/sternal instability] starting [time/date]. Temperature [value], HR [value], BP [value]. Purulent drainage [yes/no], sternal click on palpation [yes/no]. WBC [current/baseline], CRP if available. Cultures obtained [yes/no, time]. CT chest ordered [yes/no]."

A: "Patient is [stable / unstable with sepsis signs]. [Specific symptoms]. [DSWI or sepsis criteria met: yes/no]. Concern for superficial SSI vs DSWI/mediastinitis based on [click / fever + drainage / systemic signs]."

R: "Requesting urgent surgical evaluation for possible DSWI. Ready to [start empiric antibiotics / prepare for OR]. Patient is NPO. [Any additional info: renal function, antibiotic allergies, etc.]"

Who to call

Situation Contact When
Sternal pain + low-grade fever, stable exam, no click Primary APP or CT surgery APP Routine (same-shift)
Fever + purulent drainage, stable, no systemic signs CT surgery DIRECTLY (on-call service) STAT (do not wait for APP)
Sternal click / instability on exam CT SURGERY DIRECTLY — STAT Do not delay — surgical emergency
Fever + sepsis signs (hypotension, lactate ↑, altered MS) + possible DSWI CT surgery + RRT/code team + activate sepsis protocol STAT — call simultaneously
Post-discharge patient: fever + "chest feels like it's pulling apart" + drainage ED physician → activate CT surgery consult STAT STAT — likely DSWI post-DC
Wound culture positive (S. aureus, Klebsiella, gram-negative) CT surgery + ID consult Within 2 hours of result

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(expandable — novice + advanced beginner deep-dive)*
7.1 CDC SSI Classification & El Oakley staging
sections.bodyHtml:
Classification details CDC Superficial Incisional SSI:
  • Infection in skin or subcutaneous tissue only (above fascia)
  • Onset ≤30 days post-op
  • At least one sign: purulent drainage, positive culture, OR (pain/tenderness + erythema/edema/warmth) on exam, OR physician diagnosis
  • Does NOT predict DSWI progression but can evolve to deep infection if untreated or if infection tracks deeper CDC Deep Incisional SSI (equivalent to DSWI for cardiac surgery):
  • Involves fascia and deeper structures (muscle, organ space, mediastinum)
  • Onset ≤30 days post-op (or ≤1 year if prosthetic implanted)
  • At least one sign: purulent drainage from deep incision, positive culture from deep tissue/fluid, fever + dehiscence OR fever + fluctuance, OR imaging evidence of collection/infection in deep space
  • Mortality 10–25% for cardiac DSWI (Meldrum et al., 2020); median hospital LOS extension 20–30 days El Oakley/Wright Classification (cardiac mediastinitis, staging by timing + microbiology):
  • Type I (early): onset 0–2 weeks post-op, aggressive pathogens (gram-negatives predominate, high virulence)
  • Type II (delayed): onset 2–4 weeks, mixed flora (Staph + gram-negative), moderate virulence
  • Type III (late): onset >4 weeks, indolent organisms (fungal, atypical bacteria in immunocompromised), chronic course
  • Type I carries highest acute mortality risk; Type III may present insidiously

sections.heading: 7.2 Risk factors (modifiable and non-modifiable)
sections.bodyHtml:
Risk factor detail Major Non-Modifiable Risk Factors:
  • Diabetes mellitus — glucose >180 post-op increases SSI 2–3×; tight control (<180) is protective
  • Obesity (BMI >30) — increased wound hematoma, impaired perfusion, higher bacterial inoculum in adipose
  • Advanced age (>75) — slower healing, comorbidities
  • Steroid use (chronic or perioperative) — immunosuppression, impaired wound healing
  • Immunocompromise — HIV, chronic dialysis, transplant recipients Major Procedural / Surgical Risk Factors:
  • BIMA (bilateral internal mammary artery) harvest — double the ischemic risk vs single IMA; highest risk when combined with DM + obesity (triad)
  • Prolonged CPB time (>180 min) — systemic inflammation, altered immunity, hemodilution
  • Reoperation within 30 days — breaks sealed wound, reintroduces contamination
  • Intraoperative transfusion (>2 units) — immunomodulation, worse SSI outcomes Modifiable Risk Factors (Preventive Interventions):
  • Glycemic control: perioperative target <180 fasting, <200 random post-op; insulin infusion in OR through POD 1 reduces DSWI incidence significantly
  • Proper IMA harvest technique: avoid excessive skeletonization, minimize thermal injury, maintain sternal blood supply
  • Prophylactic antibiotics: cefazolin or vancomycin IV within 60 min of incision; redose if long CPB (q2h)
  • Normothermia maintenance — core temp ≥36°C intra-op and early post-op
  • Sternal precautions: rigid adherence reduces mechanical stress and wound breakdown risk
  • Smoking cessation: ≥4 weeks pre-op improves healing
  • Nutritional optimization: adequate protein (1.2–1.5 g/kg), vitamin C (500 mg BID), zinc if deficient

sections.heading: 7.3 Organisms and empiric antibiotic coverage
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathogen table and empiric regimens Common Pathogens in Cardiac SSI/DSWI:
OrganismFrequencyTypical PresentationEmpiric Coverage
Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA vs MRSA)40–50%Acute to subacute; often endogenous floraVancomycin (MRSA) or oxacillin/nafcillin (MSSA)
Coagulase-negative Staph10–15%Often skin contaminant but can cause DSWI; usually methicillin-resistantVancomycin
Gram-negatives (Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, E. coli)30–40%More aggressive, higher mortality; may produce ESBLCefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam or carbapenem
Anaerobes (rare in DSWI)<5%Odorous drainage, deep/necrotizing infectionPiperacillin-tazobactam, carbapenem, or clindamycin
Fungal (late/immunocompromised)<3%Late presentation (Type III), indolent courseFluconazole or echinocandin (if Candida/Aspergillus); escalate ID
Empiric Coverage (post-op cardiac DSWI, standard regimen):
  • First-line: Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (covers MRSA, CoNS) PLUS cefepime 2 g IV q8h (covers gram-negatives including ESBL producers)
  • Alternative gram-negative coverage: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h (broader spectrum, includes anaerobes)
  • Duration: IV antibiotics × 6 weeks from last debridement (for DSWI; superficial SSI may be 10–14 days depending on response)
  • Caveats: adjust dosing for renal function; avoid vancomycin + aminoglycosides (nephrotoxicity risk); check vancomycin trough (15–20 µg/mL) and adjust dose accordingly MRSA colonization prevalence in post-op cardiac populations is high. Most cardiac units default to vancomycin empirically unless local epidemiology strongly favors MSSA-only.

sections.heading: 7.4 Operative management and reconstruction options
sections.bodyHtml:
Surgical approach and post-flap nursing Indications for operative intervention:
  • Sternal instability (click) on exam — DEFINITIVE
  • DSWI confirmed or highly suspected — operative culture, debridement essential
  • Large substernal collection on imaging
  • Failure to improve on IV antibiotics + supportive care after 48–72 hours
  • Sepsis trajectory associated with sternal signs Operative approach:
    1. Full median sternotomy re-exploration — assess extent of sternal involvement (superficial necrosis vs full-thickness bone loss), debride all nonviable tissue
    2. Intraoperative sternal and mediastinal cultures — definitive organism ID and sensitivities
    3. Assess sternal blood supply — if small area of necrosis and bleeding intact, may re-wire; if extensive bone loss or osteomyelitis, wiring will fail
    4. Copious saline irrigation; some centers use antibiotic solutions (vancomycin-saline) as adjunct Reconstruction (when needed):
    5. Pectoralis major myocutaneous flap — most common choice, maintains muscle blood supply, provides bulk and vascularization to sternal defect, superior outcomes in most cases
    6. Omental flap — preferred for extensive defects, excellent blood supply, can fill large cavities, superior perfusion in full-thickness defects; outcomes often better but less commonly done
    7. Latissimus dorsi flap — alternative if pectoralis unavailable or inadequate
    8. VAC (vacuum-assisted closure / negative-pressure wound therapy) — may bridge between serial debridements or before flap reconstruction
    9. Reduces edema, improves perfusion, prepares wound bed
    10. NOT definitive treatment — flap reconstruction still required for sternal stability
    11. Dressing changes q48–72h, portable VAC unit for mobile patients
    12. Patient can ambulate with VAC (battery pack available) but remains on close monitoring Post-operative considerations:
    13. Patient typically returns to ICU or high-acuity monitored bed (not directly to floor)
    14. Prolonged immobility post-flap (5–7 days minimal activity)
    15. Pectoralis flap: strict ROM restrictions (no chest/arm stretching ≥4 weeks), specific PT protocol
    16. Omental flap: similar restrictions, increased awareness of flap location (abdominal incision)
    17. IV antibiotics: typically 6 weeks from last debridement
    18. Infection cure rates: 70–85% with appropriate debridement + flap + prolonged antibiotics; recurrence possible if inadequate source control

sections.heading: 7.5 Sternal wound classification and healing
sections.bodyHtml:
Sternal wound progression and nursing implications Superficial vs. Deep Sternal Wound Infection — Key Differences:
FeatureSuperficial SSIDSWI / Mediastinitis
Tissues involvedSkin, subcutaneous fat (above fascia)Fascia, muscle, bone, mediastinum
Incidence~1–2%~0.5–2% baseline (up to 5% high-risk)
Typical onsetPOD 3–7POD 7–30 (40% post-discharge)
Sternal clickAbsentPresent (pathognomonic)
DrainageSerous or small amount purulent; localizedFrankly purulent, may track deep
Erythema extentLocalized (≤1 cm from incision)Diffuse, tracking upward/downward
Systemic signsMinimal or absentFever, ↑WBC, ↑CRP, sepsis risk
TreatmentAntibiotics + local wound care (often outpatient)Emergent surgical debridement + 6 wk IV ABX
Mortality<1%10–25% if untreated
Why superficial SSI can mask DSWI:
  • Early deep infection may have localized drainage that looks superficial
  • Steri-strips covering incision may hide small opening hiding larger deep collection below
  • Patient education for post-discharge: "purulent drainage + fever = return to ED immediately, not wait to see your surgeon"

sections.heading: 7.6 Special subgroup considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
Obesity + BIMA + diabetes triad; CPB time; smoking; immunocompromise
  • Obesity (BMI >30) + BIMA + Diabetes = highest-risk triad — incidence can reach 5–8%. Some surgeons now counsel against BIMA in patients with all three risk factors. Nursing should identify these patients on admission and implement heightened monitoring (more frequent wound checks, lower threshold for imaging/cultures, aggressive glycemic control).
  • CPB time >180 min: associated with worse DSWI outcomes (more aggressive Type I pathogens, deeper mediastinal involvement). Appreciate the link: long pump run → systemic inflammation → impaired immunity → higher infection risk.
  • Smoking: pre-op smoking cessation ≥4 weeks significantly improves healing. Post-discharge: reinforce smoking cessation as infection prevention.
  • Immunocompromise (HIV, chronic dialysis, post-transplant): higher risk for atypical/fungal organisms (Type III mediastinitis). Consider earlier ID consult. VAC therapy may extend if flap reconstruction delayed.
  • Sternal wires: help hold sternum but cannot prevent DSWI; if sternal bone is devitalized and infected, wires alone will fail → sternal click emerges as wires cut through infected bone.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate immediately.

  • Fever persisting or rising despite appropriate antibiotics after 48 hours — indicates inadequate source control; surgical re-evaluation needed
  • WBC not trending down within 48–72 hours of antibiotics — poor response to empiric coverage or resistant organism emerging
  • Lactate remaining elevated or rising — underlying tissue hypoperfusion, sepsis trajectory worsening
  • Sternal pain intensifying despite adequate opioids — suggests progressive infection or new sternal instability
  • Drainage becoming more purulent or increasing in volume — infection overwhelming antibiotics
  • Erythema and edema tracking upward toward neck or downward toward abdomen — cellulitis spreading beyond incision
  • Patient becoming more anxious, restless, confused, or slowing in mentation — evolving sepsis, altered perfusion
  • BP trending down, HR trending up even if patient reporting feeling "okay" — compensatory response failing; early decompensation
  • Sternal click or new instability emerging on serial exams — DSWI confirmed if not already; operative intervention required
  • New substernal bulge or fluctuance on palpation — abscess formation; surgical drainage/debridement needed
  • Chest wall edema significant enough to limit breathing or phonation — respiratory mechanics compromised
  • Incision dehiscence widening (edges separating further) — sternal support failing, instability imminent
  • Refractory hypoxia — may indicate septic emboli to lungs, impending respiratory failure, or septic shock

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Sternal click is ALWAYS pathologic and DEFINITIVE for DSWI. Do not order one more CT or wait for culture confirmation. A click means loss of sternal continuity and sternal instability; operative debridement + fixation or reconstruction is required. Call CT surgery STAT.

  2. Superficial SSI can mask DSWI underneath. Small opening at skin level can hide a large deep collection. Steri-strips covering the incision may conceal the opening. Educate patients: if they see even small purulent drainage + fever, return to ED immediately; do NOT wait to see surgeon in office.

  3. DSWI peak is POD 14–30, and 40% present AFTER discharge. Families call the ED from home on POD 18 saying "the incision opened and smells bad." These patients must be triaged as surgical emergencies; ED physician must activate your CT surgery team STAT. They will need ICU/OR. Discharge teaching is critical: "If fever, purulent drainage, sternal separation feeling, or severe pain develop, go to ED immediately."

  4. Do NOT start empiric antibiotics before cultures if patient is stable. Cultures drawn after antibiotics are started have ~50% lower sensitivity for organism ID. Wait for cultures (5–10 min draw time) unless patient is in frank sepsis. If septic, draw cultures WHILE setting up antibiotic infusion—do not let perfect be the enemy of good.

  5. Call CT surgery DIRECTLY for suspected DSWI, not just the APP. An APP will escalate appropriately, but direct call to on-call surgeon is faster. State "possible DSWI post-op day [X]" to trigger priority callback. Saves 30–60 min often.

  6. BIMA harvest + diabetes + obesity = highest-risk triad — incidence reaches 5–8%. Some surgeons now counsel against BIMA in this subset. Identify these patients on admission; implement heightened monitoring (more frequent wound checks, lower threshold for imaging, aggressive glycemic control).

  7. Insulin infusion in the OR through POD 1 reduces DSWI incidence significantly. Tight perioperative glycemic control (<180) is infection prevention, not just glucose management. Escalate to provider if diabetic post-op patient's glucose runs 200+.

  8. Superficial cellulitis can progress to DSWI if fever develops. Do not assume "it's just surface infection." If a patient with localized drainage also develops fever and systemic signs by POD 7, escalate. Order CT or call surgery; do not wait for antibiotics to work.

  9. Sternal precautions prevent mechanical exacerbation of DSWI. A patient coughing without splinting, pulling on bed rails, or doing arm raises while already infected increases mechanical stress on an unstable sternum. Vigorous, repeated sternal precaution education—not just mentioning once but reinforcing at every interaction—may prevent acute dehiscence.

  10. Post-debridement VAC patients need high-level nursing oversight. VAC dressing changes are stressful and noisy; patients fear what they will see. Excellent pain control, reassurance, and clear explanation ("this is helping infection drain and healthy tissue grow back") are essential. Monitor seal integrity and output religiously; compromised seal is ineffective and risks further contamination.

  11. Pectoralis flap patients have STRICT ROM restrictions (4–6 weeks). Even after acute infection is cleared, these patients cannot do chest/arm stretches or resistive exercises. PT protocol is specific. Coordinate with PT at discharge; ensure patient and family understand restrictions. Non-compliance impairs functional outcomes.

  12. Delayed presentation (POD 14+) often means more aggressive, deeper infection. El Oakley Type II (2–4 weeks) and Type III (>4 weeks) presentations often require more extensive debridement, larger flap reconstruction, longer recovery. A POD 21 DSWI often has deeper mediastinal involvement than POD 7 presentation.

  13. Coughing without splinting can precipitate acute sternal dehiscence. A patient with early DSWI who has a strong cough and does not splint may acutely lose sternal continuity. Teach splinting proactively; reinforce before a crisis.

  14. The "pop" or "give" sensation in chest = possible acute sternal dehiscence. Patient calls light saying they felt something give—this is urgent. Assess immediately, photograph, notify CT surgery. May need emergent OR.

  15. MRSA coverage should be default in most post-op cardiac units. Colonization prevalence is high. Include vancomycin in empiric regimen unless institutional epidemiology strongly favors MSSA-only (rare in most cardiac centers).

cards.title: STS Risk Score
cards.quickAnswer: The STS Risk Score is a procedure-specific statistical model that predicts a patient's operative mortality (PROM) and major morbidity risk using 40+ patient and procedural variables from the national database. Calculated pre-operatively via dedicated web calculator (riskcalc.sts.org) or EHR integration; outputs PROM (%), stroke %, renal failure %, prolonged ventilation %, mediastinitis %, re-operation %, and short/long LOS probabilities. Used for informed consent, TAVR-versus-SAVR shared decision-making, and post-operative anticipatory planning. Bedside nurses interpret the score from admission notes to set ICU stay expectations, complication vigilance, and discharge complexity.

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
The STS Risk Score is a suite of procedure-specific statistical risk models built from the Society of Thoracic Surgeons National Adult Cardiac Surgery Database. Models are procedure-specific — distinct calculators exist for:

  • Isolated CABG
  • Isolated aortic valve (AVR)
  • Isolated mitral valve (MV)
  • Aortic valve + CABG
  • Mitral valve + CABG
  • Aortic root / ascending aorta procedures
  • Tricuspid valve procedures

Each model outputs:

  • PROM (Predicted Risk of Operative Mortality) — expressed as a percentage (e.g., 2.5%, 8%, 15%)
  • Predicted risk of major morbidity endpoints — stroke, renal failure, prolonged ventilation, mediastinitis, re-operation for bleeding

The calculation requires a dedicated STS risk calculator (web-based or EHR-integrated); it cannot be reliably estimated by clinical judgment alone.

sections.heading: 2. STS Outputs — Key Morbidity and Mortality Endpoints
sections.bodyHtml:
Output Typical Range Interpretation
PROM (%) 0.5–25 Expected operative mortality; drives risk category (see Section 3)
Stroke (%) 1–5 Major neurologic complication risk
Renal failure (%) 3–15 New-onset AKI requiring dialysis or persistent elevation in creatinine
Prolonged ventilation (%) 5–25 Extubation > 24 h post-op (risk increases with age, EF < 25%, COPD)
Mediastinitis (%) 0.5–3 Deep sternal wound infection / surgical site infection
Re-operation for bleeding (%) 2–8 Return to OR for bleeding control POD 0–3
Discharge short LOS (%) 5–50 Probability of discharge by POD 3 without major morbidity
Discharge long LOS (%) 10–80 Probability of LOS > POD 3

sections.heading: 3. Risk Stratification — PROM Categories
sections.bodyHtml:
PROM (%) Risk Stratum Clinical Consideration Typical Post-Op Trajectory
< 1 Very low Routine surgical AVR or CABG; minimal alternative discussion POD 2–3 discharge; minimal complications expected
1–3 Low Straightforward surgical AVR or CABG; TAVR not typically discussed POD 3–4 discharge; standard monitoring
3–8 Intermediate TAVR discussed as alternative for isolated AS; CABG proceeds with moderate risk precautions; shared decision-making emphasized POD 3–5 on unit; anticipate 1–2 minor complications
8–15 High TAVR strongly preferred for aortic stenosis; high-risk CABG pathway (shortened CPB, off-pump candidate); intensive pre-op optimization POD 5–7+ on unit; higher vigilance for AKI, bleeding, delirium, POAF
> 15 Prohibitive / inoperable TAVR or medical management for AS; palliative / comfort-focused pathway for CABG candidates; transplant / VAD evaluation if appropriate ICU-length stay; high morbidity and mortality risk; complex discharge planning

Morbidity composite (M&M) interpretation:

  • Typical expected range across procedures: 10–25%
  • Composite includes all major endpoints (mortality + stroke + renal failure + prolonged ventilation + mediastinitis + re-operation)
  • High-PROM patients usually have elevated risk across multiple domains

sections.heading: 4. Components of the STS Calculator Input
sections.bodyHtml:
The STS models incorporate 40+ patient and procedural variables:

Category Examples
Demographics Age, sex, body surface area (BSA)
Cardiac function Left ventricular ejection fraction (LV EF), posterior wall motion, cardiogenic shock, recent myocardial infarction (timing)
Prior cardiac history Prior cardiac surgery, endocarditis, mechanical circulatory support
Comorbidities Chronic kidney disease (CKD) / creatinine, COPD, peripheral arterial disease (PAD), cerebrovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, hypertension
Coronary / valve anatomy Left main CAD, number of diseased vessels, valve pathology, aortic atherosclerosis
Pre-operative status New York Heart Association (NYHA) class, intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) use, recent cardiac catheterization
Procedure factors Emergent vs elective, concomitant procedures, estimated cross-clamp time, estimated cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) time

Input method: Dedicated STS web calculator (riskcalc.sts.org) or EHR-integrated tool. The calculator applies logistic regression coefficients from the national database to generate predictions.

sections.heading: 5. Clinical Use
sections.bodyHtml:
Pre-operative context:

  • STS score is calculated during pre-op evaluation and documented in the pre-op H&P, surgical consent form, and procedure plan.
  • High-STS patients trigger discussion of alternatives (TAVR for aortic stenosis, off-pump CABG, staged procedures).
  • Score is included in informed consent conversations — patients and families should understand their estimated mortality and morbidity risk (Shahian et al., 2018).

Bedside nurse interpretation:

  • Bedside nurses rarely calculate the score but interpret it from admission notes, hand-off reports, and care plans.
  • Low-STS patient (< 3%) → expect POD 2–3 discharge, standard ICU/stepdown monitoring, routine teaching.
  • Intermediate-STS patient (3–8%) → expect POD 3–5 stay on unit; anticipate monitoring for AKI, arrhythmias, bleeding; extended family teaching.
  • High-STS patient (8–15%) → expect POD 5–7+ on unit; higher vigilance for complications (stroke, renal failure, prolonged ventilation, POAF); frequent interdisciplinary touch-points (PT/OT, case management, social work); extended discharge planning.
  • Prohibitive-STS patient (> 15%) → ICU-level care trajectory; complexity similar to high-risk medical admissions; palliative discussions may be ongoing.

Nursing actions driven by STS:

  • Set ICU stay expectations and family education accordingly.
  • Anticipate higher complication rates and monitoring frequency for high-STS patients.
  • Inform early mobilization timeline — high-STS patient may not be mobilized to chair on POD 1 if hemodynamic, renal, or respiratory concerns are present.
  • Drive discharge planning complexity — high-STS patient likely needs extended LOS, post-acute care (skilled nursing, rehab), or frequent outpatient follow-up.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls *(high-yield for bedside practice)*
sections.bodyHtml:
• STS ≠ EuroSCORE. EuroSCORE II uses different coefficients and produces different percentages. STS is the U.S. standard; EuroSCORE II is used in Europe. A 5% STS is not equivalent to 5% EuroSCORE — know which model your institution uses.

  • High STS does NOT mean "don't operate." It means "consider alternatives AND prepare intensively for high-risk outcomes." Many high-STS patients proceed to surgery successfully with careful planning (Otto et al., 2020).

  • STS is population-level, not individual-deterministic. A patient with STS PROM 8% has an 8% average risk in the database, but individual outcomes vary widely. Use STS as a planning and communication tool, not as a predictor of what will happen to this specific patient.

  • Procedure-specific, not diagnosis-specific. STS PROM for isolated AVR ≠ STS PROM for AVR + CABG. The calculator must match the actual procedure performed.

  • Not validated for all populations. STS models are developed from North American cardiac surgery patient cohorts. Applicability to frail, dialysis-dependent, transplant-candidate, or other high-risk subgroups is limited. Clinical judgment required.

  • TAVR has its own risk model. Do not use surgical STS to compare with TAVR risk estimates. TAVR uses the Society of Thoracic Surgeons/American College of Cardiology (STS/ACC) TAVR risk calculator — different coefficients.

  • Frailty is not captured well in STS. Physical frailty, cognitive status, social support, living situation, and patient goals add critical context beyond the numerical score. A high-STS but robust, cognitively intact, well-supported patient may do better than a low-STS frail patient.

  • Model versions are updated periodically. STS versions released in 2009, 2014, and 2018; newer iterations may be released. Coefficients shift slightly as the database grows. Check which STS version your institution uses; older versions may show different risk estimates.

  • Patient awareness is key. The STS score should be discussed during pre-op consent. Families appreciate understanding risk estimates; it builds trust and sets expectations. Example: "Your STS was 6%, which means statistically 6 out of 100 similar patients don't survive the operation; we're planning extra support."

  • Keck TAVR program risk threshold. Many institutions accept intermediate-to-prohibitive-risk patients (STS ≥ 3% for aortic stenosis) for TAVR. Low-risk TAVR indications have expanded post-2019 (PARTNER 3, Evolut Low Risk trials); some low-STS patients may also be TAVR candidates if anatomy favors it.

  • Morbidity endpoints are separate from mortality. Stroke, renal failure, prolonged ventilation, and mediastinitis each have independent risk percentages. A patient with high stroke risk might have low mortality risk (or vice versa). Review the full morbidity breakdown.

  • STS "Short LOS" (SSL) metric. Increasingly reported; measures proportion of patients discharged by POD 3 without major morbidity. High-STS patients rarely qualify; it's a marker of efficiency for routine cases. Use as a post-op benchmark.

  • "Your patient's STS was X" is actionable hand-off. Ask the resident or APP for the STS score at sign-out. Treat it like a vital sign for the first 48 h post-op.

  • Long CPB time and cross-clamp time modify post-op risk. STS inputs cross-clamp and CPB time estimates, but actual operative times may exceed pre-op predictions. Ask intra-op team for actual times post-op; longer runs increase AKI, stroke, and bleeding risk independent of baseline STS.

  • STS updates are released periodically. Check the STS website (sts.org) for model updates and recalibration publications; do not assume your calculator is the latest version.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
STS Data Sources and Calibration The STS National Adult Cardiac Surgery Database contains records from over 900 participating hospitals in North America, tracking > 3 million patient-procedures. The 2018 models (Shahian et al., 2018) represent the most widely used current versions in the U.S. Each model is derived via logistic regression, with coefficients fitted to the outcome frequency in the national cohort. Key database characteristics:
  • Prospective data collection from participating institutions
  • Standardized definitions for outcomes (mortality, stroke, renal failure, prolonged ventilation, mediastinitis, re-operation)
  • Recalibration every 3–5 years as case volumes grow
  • Outcomes tracked up to 30 days post-op Calibration and discrimination:
  • Calibration (does the predicted risk match observed risk?) is verified by comparing predicted outcomes to national outcome rates. STS models show good calibration across risk strata.
  • Discrimination (can the model separate high-risk from low-risk patients?) is measured by c-statistic; STS models typically show c-statistics of 0.70–0.80, indicating reasonable separation but acknowledging that clinical unpredictability remains. Limitations of the database:
  • Outcomes are institution-reported and may reflect local coding practices or audit frequency
  • Missing data for some variables requires imputation
  • Long-term outcomes (beyond 30 days) are not captured
  • Non-operative outcomes (e.g., readmission, quality of life) are not tracked
Model Updates and Version History 2009 STS Risk Models — original logistic regression models for CABG, isolated valve surgery, and combined procedures. 2014 STS Risk Models — updated with expanded database; refined coefficients for several risk factors (e.g., renal function, frailty indicators). 2018 STS Risk Models (Shahian et al., 2018) — current standard. Published in three parts:
  • Part 1: CABG (Shahian et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2018; 105:1411–1418)
  • Part 2: Isolated Valve Surgery (O'Brien et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2018; 105:1419–1428)
  • Part 3: Valve + Other Procedures (Jacobs et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2018; 105:1429–1439) Why versions matter:
    • Procedural technique evolution (e.g., minimally invasive techniques, shorter CPB runs, improved perfusion strategies) may shift risk profiles over time
    • Institutional outcomes often improve as experience accumulates, even with same patient mix
    • Using an outdated model may over- or under-estimate risk Future models: STS is continuously enrolling new data. The next major release will incorporate more recent cases and expanded variable sets (e.g., cognitive frailty measures, frailty testing scores).
STS vs EuroSCORE vs Other Risk Models Multiple risk models exist for cardiac surgery patients; differences are important. STS Risk Score (U.S.):
  • Database: 900+ North American hospitals, 3 million+ patients
  • Outcome: 30-day mortality + specific morbidity endpoints
  • Procedure-specific models (CABG, AVR, MV, combinations)
  • Calculation: logistic regression with 40+ variables
  • Web access: riskcalc.sts.org EuroSCORE II (Europe):
  • Database: European cohort, developed in 1990s and updated in 2012
  • Outcome: in-hospital mortality (not procedure-specific morbidity breakdown)
  • Single model for all adult cardiac procedures
  • Uses fewer variables (17–19 vs STS 40+)
  • Web access: euroscore.org Key differences:
  • STS and EuroSCORE II both predict mortality but use different coefficients; a given patient may have very different predicted risks from each model
  • STS procedure-specific approach allows tailored prediction; EuroSCORE uses one model for all
  • STS provides morbidity-specific predictions (stroke %, AKI %, etc.); EuroSCORE provides mortality-only
  • STS is the U.S. standard; EuroSCORE is standard in Europe Other models:
  • RACHS-1 (Risk Adjustment for Congenital Heart Surgery) — used for pediatric cases
  • Parsonnet score — older model, less frequently used
  • ACEF score (Age, Creatinine, Ejection Fraction) — simpler bedside approximation, less accurate Clinical pearl: Always confirm which model your institution uses in its EHR/calculator. Mixing models in discussions will cause confusion.

cards.title: Mixed Venous (SvO₂) and Central Venous (ScvO₂) Oxygen Saturation
cards.quickAnswer: SvO₂ (mixed venous saturation from a PA catheter) and ScvO₂ (central venous saturation from SVC tip) both reflect the balance of oxygen delivery (determined by CO, Hgb, and SaO₂) versus tissue consumption (VO₂). Post-operative targets: SvO₂ ≥ 65%, ScvO₂ ≥ 70%. Falling saturation signals either inadequate DO₂ (low cardiac output, anemia, or hypoxemia) or increased VO₂ (fever, agitation, sepsis). Trend matters far more than a single value. ScvO₂ runs 5–10% higher than SvO₂ but tracks identically and is preferred on non-ICU units because PA catheters are rare.

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
SvO₂ (Mixed Venous Oxygen Saturation) is the oxygen saturation of blood withdrawn from the distal port of a pulmonary artery catheter. It represents the weighted average of all venous return — right atrium, coronary sinus, and systemic veins — reflecting global tissue oxygen extraction.

ScvO₂ (Central Venous Oxygen Saturation) is the oxygen saturation of blood drawn from a central venous catheter tip positioned in the superior vena cava. It is a close surrogate for SvO₂ (typically 5–10% higher) and is the practical choice in stepdown and telemetry settings where PA catheters are rarely inserted.

Both are dynamic indicators of perfusion adequacy; a single static value is clinically less informative than direction and slope over hours.

sections.heading: 2. Formula / Fick Equation
sections.bodyHtml:
Physiologic relationship and the Big 4 drivers Fick Equation (relates VO₂, CO, and oxygen content): ``` VO₂ = CO × (CaO₂ − CvO₂) where: CaO₂ = arterial oxygen content CvO₂ = venous oxygen content (determines SvO₂) CO = cardiac output ``` Rearranged: CvO₂ = CaO₂ − (VO₂ / CO) Therefore SvO₂ is determined by four and only four drivers — the "Big 4":
DriverEffect on SvO₂Mechanism
Cardiac Output (CO)↓ CO → ↓ SvO₂Higher CO delivers more O₂ per unit time; lower CO forces tissues to extract more oxygen per RBC, reducing venous saturation
Hemoglobin (Hgb)↓ Hgb → ↓ SvO₂Each RBC carries less oxygen; DO₂ drops proportionally
Arterial Oxygenation (SaO₂)↓ SaO₂ → ↓ SvO₂Fewer oxygen molecules available for delivery; DO₂ falls
Tissue O₂ Consumption (VO₂)↑ VO₂ → ↓ SvO₂Fever, agitation, shivering, sepsis, seizure increase metabolic rate; tissues extract more oxygen from each RBC
Normal arteriovenous saturation gradient: SaO₂ − SvO₂ ≈ 20–25% at rest. When CO falls, this gradient widens as tissues increase oxygen extraction from each RBC to maintain metabolic demand.

sections.heading: 3. Normal Range / Targets
sections.bodyHtml:
SvO₂ / ScvO₂ Range Clinical Interpretation
SvO₂ 65–75% or ScvO₂ 70–80% Normal resting; adequate global perfusion
SvO₂ 60–65% or ScvO₂ 65–70% Mild impairment; assess Big 4 drivers; monitor trending
SvO₂ 50–60% or ScvO₂ 55–65% Significant impairment; lactate likely rising; intervention indicated
SvO₂ < 50% or ScvO₂ < 55% Critical; severe tissue hypoxia; urgent resuscitation needed
SvO₂ > 80% or ScvO₂ > 85% in a sick patient Paradoxically high — may indicate sepsis (cytopathic hypoxia), toxin exposure, AV shunt, or severe sedation masking hypoperfusion

Post-operative targets (ICU → stepdown transition):

  • SvO₂ target ≥ 65% (some protocols target ≥ 60%)
  • ScvO₂ target ≥ 70%

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use
sections.bodyHtml:
When and how each measurement is obtained:

  • PA Catheter (SvO₂): Uncommon outside ICU; obtained via distal port with balloon deflated. Requires attention to technique — wedged catheter yields arterial (falsely high) saturation.
  • Central Venous Catheter (ScvO₂): Preferred when a CVC is already in place for CVP monitoring. Drawn during routine lab work; no additional line placement needed.
  • Continuous fiberoptic monitoring: Vigilance-type catheters provide real-time waveforms but are reserved for ICU; rarely used stepdown.

Hand-off interpretation — most common clinical use:

Scenario Interpretation
"His SvO₂ was 58% in ICU this morning but came up to 68% after a fluid bolus" Improving. Suggests fluid-responsive hypoperfusion; trend favors continued monitoring
"She's been ScvO₂ 72–75%, steady on current support" Stable. Perfusion adequate; no acute intervention indicated
"SvO₂ dropped from 72% to 52% over 2 hours despite vasopressor support" Deteriorating. Red flag for CO decompensation, acute sepsis, or VO₂ surge; urgent reassessment needed

Key principle: Treat the trend and clinical context, not the single number.

sections.heading: 5. The Big 4 Drivers — Differential Diagnosis
sections.bodyHtml:
Systematic approach to falling SvO₂ When SvO₂ or ScvO₂ falls, ask systematically which driver has changed:
DriverBedside AssessmentInitial Interventions
↓ Cardiac OutputHR, BP, MAP, CVP, UOP, capillary refill, lactate, echo if availableIV fluid bolus (if hypovolemic), inotrope, afterload reduction, rhythm check
↓ HemoglobinTrending Hgb from preop/surgery, signs of active bleeding, Hct, chest tube outputStop bleeding, correct coagulopathy, transfuse if Hgb target not met
↓ Arterial Sat (SaO₂)Pulse ox, ABG, lung exam, CXRSupplemental O₂, address pulmonary cause (atelectasis, effusion, aspiration, pneumonia)
↑ Oxygen ConsumptionTemp, agitation, pain, shivering, respiratory rate, sedation scoreTreat fever (acetaminophen, cooling), analgesia, anxiolytic, neuromuscular blockade if needed
Clinical reasoning example:
  • Patient POD 1, SvO₂ drops to 62%, HR 95, BP 110/60 (stable), CVP 6, temp 38.5°C, Hgb 9.5 g/dL (stable from POD 0), SpO₂ 96% on 2L.
  • Most likely driver: fever-driven VO₂ increase. Action: acetaminophen, cooling measures, recheck SvO₂ in 30–60 min.
  • If SvO₂ stays low despite fever control → assess CO next (IV fluid, consider inotrope).

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. The Big 4 is both diagnostic and therapeutic. When SvO₂ drops, ask "which of CO, Hgb, SaO₂, or VO₂?" and fix it. No single intervention works for all causes.

  2. ScvO₂ is 5–10% higher than SvO₂ and trends identically. Do not confuse the two scales; use the same target-driven logic regardless of which you have.

  3. High SvO₂ in a sick patient is NOT reassurance. Paradoxically high saturation may indicate sepsis (cells cannot extract oxygen despite adequate delivery), AV shunt, recent transfusion, or severe sedation suppressing VO₂.

  4. Wedged PA catheter yields arterial blood. If drawing from a PAC, ensure the balloon is deflated (ventricular waveform on monitor). Wedged catheter falsely elevates SvO₂ and misleads the team.

  5. Fever raises VO₂ ~10% per degree Celsius. Treat fever before chasing low SvO₂; recheck saturation 30–60 min after fever control.

  6. Shivering raises VO₂ dramatically — 200–300% in some cases. Post-op shivering with falling SvO₂ warrants sedation or muscle relaxant (ICU setting) before other interventions.

  7. Anemia reduces DO₂ significantly. Hgb drop from 10 → 7 reduces oxygen delivery ~30%, pulling SvO₂ down proportionally. Transfusion (target Hgb > 7–8 post-op) restores saturation.

  8. Lactate and SvO₂ track together as perfusion markers. SvO₂ < 50% + lactate > 2 = tissue hypoxia confirmed. Normal SvO₂ + rising lactate suggests sepsis (cytopathic), liver failure, or mitochondrial dysfunction.

  9. SvO₂ is a trailing indicator, not a dial to titrate directly. It reflects net perfusion; use it as a sanity check: "Is perfusion state consistent with current management?"

  10. In sedated or anesthetized patients, SvO₂ will be falsely high. Anesthesia and sedation suppress VO₂. A "good" SvO₂ in deep sedation may reflect low demand, not good perfusion. Lighten sedation and recheck before reassuring the team.

cards.title: Systemic and Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (SVR / PVR)
cards.quickAnswer: SVR = afterload on the left ventricle; calculated as (MAP − CVP) / CO × 80; normal 800–1200 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵. PVR = afterload on the right ventricle; (mPAP − PCWP) / CO × 80; normal 150–250 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ or < 3 Wood units. Measured via PA catheter (ICU). Low SVR suggests distributive shock or vasoplegia; high SVR with low CO signals cardiogenic shock. PVR > 3 Wood units flags pulmonary hypertension and RV dysfunction risk. Pressors raise SVR; inhaled nitric oxide and milrinone lower PVR.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
• SVR definition: Afterload (resistance) against which the left ventricle pumps. Reflects integrated resistance of systemic arteries and arterioles to blood flow.
  • PVR definition: Afterload against which the right ventricle pumps. Reflects resistance of the pulmonary circulation — a low-resistance, high-capacitance system at baseline.
  • Measurement requirement: Both require simultaneous pulmonary artery catheter data (pressures) and cardiac output (thermodilution, Fick, or non-invasive surrogate).
  • Clinical context: SVR/PVR are derived indices. Rarely placed in non-ICU settings; interpretation occurs during ICU handoff or post-op summary review.

sections.heading: SVR Calculation
sections.bodyHtml:
SVR (dyne·s·cm⁻⁵) = (MAP − CVP) / CO × 80

  • MAP = mean arterial pressure (mmHg)
  • CVP = central venous pressure (mmHg)
  • CO = cardiac output (L/min)
  • Conversion factor = 80

Indexed variant: SVRI = SVR / BSA (dyne·s·cm⁻⁵·m⁻²)

sections.heading: PVR Calculation
sections.bodyHtml:
PVR (dyne·s·cm⁻⁵) = (mPAP − PCWP) / CO × 80

  • mPAP = mean pulmonary artery pressure (mmHg)
  • PCWP = pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (mmHg)
  • CO = cardiac output (L/min)

Indexed variant: PVRI = PVR / BSA (dyne·s·cm⁻⁵·m⁻²)

sections.heading: Unit Conversions
sections.bodyHtml:
From To Factor
dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ Wood units ÷ 80
Wood units dyne·s·cm⁻⁵ × 80

sections.heading: SVR Ranges
sections.bodyHtml:
Category SVR (dyne·s·cm⁻⁵) Clinical Scenario
Low < 800 Sepsis, anaphylaxis, vasoplegia, advanced cirrhosis
Normal 800–1200 Healthy at rest; goal in most acute care
High > 1200 Compensatory (low CO with reflex vasoconstriction), hypertension, catecholamine excess

Type SVR CO Example Bedside Recognition
Cardiogenic High Low MI, acute VSD, severe valve disease Cool extremities, low urine output, high lactate

sections.heading: PVR in ICU Settings
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiotomy (CABG, valve, complex): Mild PVR elevation (200–300) is expected from cardiopulmonary bypass inflammation. Usually resolves over 24–72 h with diuresis, inhaled nitric oxide, and milrinone.

Heart transplant evaluation: PVR > 3 Wood units flags increased RV failure risk with donor heart. Reversibility testing (inhaled NO, diuretics, milrinone) can reduce PVR and improve candidacy. Fixed PVR = contraindication or requires special donor matching.

Post-LVAD implantation: If PVR remains > 5 Wood units after LVAD, RV failure risk is high; inotropes and inhaled pulmonary vasodilators are essential.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Afterload physiology detail Afterload is the force (resistance) the ventricle must overcome to eject blood. Higher afterload = more myocardial work. SVR applies to systemic circulation (LV faces systemic vascular tree); PVR applies to pulmonary circulation (RV faces lungs). The pulmonary circulation is normally a low-pressure, high-capacitance system; the RV is thin-walled and poorly tolerates acute pressure/resistance increases. The LV, thick-walled, tolerates high SVR better.
Drug effects on SVR and PVR
Drug ClassSVR EffectPVR EffectNotes
Norepinephrine↑↑↑ slightlyPure alpha-1 (SVR) + some beta-1; first-line pressos
Phenylephrine↑↑↑↑Pure alpha-1; no cardiac stimulation
Epinephrine↑ at low dose, ↓ at high dose↑Beta-1 dominant low-dose; alpha-1 dominant high-dose
Vasopressin↑↑ minimalNon-catecholamine; useful in vasoplegia resistance
Dobutamine↓↓↓Beta-2 causes systemic vasodilation; inotropic benefit may not justify SVR drop
Milrinone↓↓↓PDE-3 inhibitor; inotrope + lusitrope + vasodilator; valuable RV support
Inhaled NO→↓↓Selective pulmonary vasodilation; no systemic BP drop
Sildenafil / PDE-5i→↓ (chronic)Long-acting; weeks to months; not acute
Reversibility testing for pulmonary hypertension In heart transplant evaluation, PVR is tested before and after pharmacologic challenge. If PVR drops ≥ 20% and remains < 3–4 Wood units, it is "reversible" and transplant candidacy improves. Drugs used: inhaled NO (5–20 ppm), milrinone IV, furosemide IV, or combination. Fixed PVR (no drop) = poor prognostic sign and relative contraindication unless special donor matching is planned.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Low SVR ≠ always sepsis. Vasoplegia post-CPB, warm-phase distributive shock, advanced cirrhosis, or over-vasodilation from milrinone all lower SVR. Integrate BP, perfusion, lactate, and context.

  2. High SVR with low CO = cardiogenic shock until proven otherwise. The heart is failing; the body clamps down. Inotropes + diuretics, not pressors alone.

  3. PVR > 3 Wood units is a major concern at transplant eval. This single number can swing candidacy. Insist on documentation of (a) baseline PVR, (b) PVR after reversibility testing, (c) whether it is fixed or reversible.

  4. Inhaled NO is selective PVR reduction. It dilates the pulmonary vasculature without systemic BP drop. Systemic vasodilators (hydralazine, nitroprusside) lower both SVR and PVR; iNO preferentially targets lungs.

  5. Milrinone + epinephrine combo for RV protection. Milrinone is a positive inotrope + PVR reducer. Low-dose epinephrine adds SVR back. Common post-complex surgery for biventricular failure.

  6. Vasopressin preserves SVR without raising PVR as much. If a patient is on norepinephrine and developing vasoplegia resistance, adding low-dose vasopressin (0.04 U/min) can raise SVR with less afterload penalty.

  7. Dobutamine lowers SVR via beta-2 effects. Potent inotrope (beta-1) but causes systemic vasodilation (beta-2). SVR may drop even as CO rises. Monitor BP; often paired with phenylephrine.

  8. Sildenafil and other PDE-5 inhibitors for chronic pulmonary hypertension. These lower PVR over weeks to months; not acute interventions. Seen in patients with known pHTN from connective tissue disease, COPD, or idiopathic causes.

  9. Post-cardiotomy hypertension is usually temporary and nicardipine-responsive. Rebound SVR/MAP post-op is normal. This is not chronic resistant hypertension. Nicardipine or immediate-release nifedipine works quickly.

  10. PVR is a KEY decision metric for LVAD candidacy. High baseline PVR (> 5 Wood units) + failure to drop with reversibility testing = poor RV reserve. Some centers will not implant; others use strict RV-support protocols. Know your institutional threshold.

cards.title: Late Post-Op Pericardial Tamponade
cards.quickAnswer: Late tamponade (POD 4+) presents subtly—fatigue, falling urine output, rising creatinine, narrowing pulse pressure—easily mislabeled "deconditioning" or slow recovery. Peak incidence POD 7–10 but can appear 2–6 weeks post-op. Key findings: pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg, JVD, tachycardia without obvious cause, new dyspnea. Bedside echo is diagnostic—look for RA/RV diastolic collapse, IVC plethora, respiratory variation. Stable presentation: pericardiocentesis; unstable or recurrent: pericardial window or sternotomy. Critical: do not aggressively diurese—removing preload crashes a tamponading patient. Call CT surgery STAT if suspected, even in the asymptomatic re-admitted patient with vague malaise.
