sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation—definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Post-operative pericardial effusion with hemodynamic compression of the right heart, presenting insidiously during the subacute recovery window (POD 4+). The pericardium stretches over days–weeks, masking very large volumes (often > 1 L) until decompensation occurs.
  • Incidence: 1–3% of post-cardiac-surgery patients develop clinically significant late tamponade (Bojar, 2020). Peaks POD 7–14 but can present out to 4–6 weeks post-discharge.
  • Who this applies to: any post-operative cardiac surgery patient in stepdown, ICU, or telemetry care, and discharged patients presenting with non-specific complaints 1–6 weeks post-op. Highest risk: anticoagulated patients, mitral surgery, prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB > 180 min), post-pericardiotomy syndrome.
  • Why it matters: the classic miss is attributing symptoms to "slow recovery" or deconditioning. Death and readmission occur when the diagnosis is delayed. Early echo recognition prevents hemodynamic collapse.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Acute tamponade (POD 0–3) is brisk surgical bleeding into the pericardium—usually recognized and drained urgently.

Late tamponade (POD 4–14+) is slow accumulation of serous, serosanguinous, or inflammatory fluid. The pericardium accommodates stretched fibers, allowing pressure to rise insidiously. Compensatory tachycardia and catecholamine surge maintain cardiac output until ventricular compliance fails and systemic perfusion collapses.

Key physiologic mechanisms:

  • RV compression first: the thin-walled right ventricle is most vulnerable to external pressure. Diastolic filling is impaired, stroke volume falls, systemic perfusion declines.
  • Pulsus paradoxus: enhanced ventricular interdependence during inspiration causes an exaggerated drop in systolic pressure (> 10 mmHg is abnormal).
  • IVC plethora: elevated intrapericardial pressure is transmitted upstream, causing jugular venous distention and hepatic congestion.

Inflammatory/anticoagulation-driven effusions can develop from post-pericardiotomy syndrome (autoimmune response to pericardial blood, ~15% incidence, < 2% become tamponade) or from anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC, heparin) converting a benign effusion into a hemorrhagic one. POAF initiation on anticoagulation is a specific risk multiplier: new AF triggers AC, AC converts a small effusion to bleeding effusion, resulting in late tamponade.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition—what the patient looks like at bedside.

In-hospital (stepdown/ICU patient, POD 4–14):

  • Unexplained fatigue, anorexia, or reduced exercise tolerance (classic "deconditioning" attribution)
  • New or worsening dyspnea not explained by volume status or cardiac output state
  • Tachycardia (HR > 100) that does not resolve with pain control, reassurance, or sedation
  • Falling urine output (oliguria) or rising creatinine with no obvious volume cause
  • New right-sided pleural effusion on chest X-ray (CXR)—pericardial overflow pathology
  • Jugular venous distention on bedside exam; muffled heart sounds (late sign)
  • Narrowing pulse pressure (e.g., SBP 130/DBP 115 → SBP 125/DBP 115, pulse pressure 20–25 mmHg)
  • Unexplained low-grade fever with fatigue (post-pericardiotomy syndrome pattern, POD 10–21)

Re-admitted patient (1–6 weeks post-discharge):

  • Vague complaint: "I just can't do what I could before"; "I'm more tired than yesterday"
  • Family reports "not themselves"—subjective but often the first sign
  • No fever or focal complaints; vital signs may look "normal"

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs: trend HR, BP, RR, SpO₂; calculate pulse pressure (SBP − DBP); note any narrowing
  • Appearance: diaphoretic? pale? anxious? reclining to breathe? energy level vs. baseline
  • Neck: JVD at 30–45° angle; measure height if visible; hepatojugular reflux
  • Heart sounds: muffled, distant, or clear? pericardial rub (post-pericardiotomy syndrome tell)?
  • Lungs: crackles base bilaterally (pulmonary edema from RV failure), diminished base-right (pleural effusion)
  • Pulse palpation: check apical–radial discrepancy; attempt pulsus paradoxus by cuff (inflate above systolic, slowly deflate, note first Korotkoff sound at inspiration vs. expiration; difference > 10 mmHg is abnormal)
  • Recent labs: creatinine trend (rising suggests falling cardiac output), hemoglobin trend (anemia is risk factor for symptom expression), albumin (nutritional status vs. "deconditioning"), INR/PTT if on anticoagulation
  • Imaging: most recent CXR (cardiac silhouette size, right-sided pleural effusion, mediastinal widening), any recent echo (baseline effusion size and physiology)
  • MAR review: anticoagulation agent + timing (warfarin, DOAC, heparin, POAF-driven start?); diuretics being given?; recent beta-blocker or pain medication changes?
  • Surgery context: procedure type, POD number, any intraoperative complications, prolonged CPB, need for re-exploration, mitral surgery (higher risk)

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP > 65, no air hunger, no hypotension yet; BP has wide pulse pressure or normal-range readings but patient subjectively declining.)

  1. Obtain 12-lead ECG STAT — look for low voltage (all QRS < 5 mm), electrical alternans, nonspecific ST-T changes, sinus tachycardia
  2. Request bedside echocardiogram STAT — this is the diagnostic test; effusion size, RA/RV diastolic collapse, IVC plethora, respiratory variation across mitral/tricuspid inflow
  3. Obtain CXR — cardiac silhouette size, pleural effusion (especially right-sided), mediastinal widening
  4. Send labs: CBC, BMP (creatinine trend, electrolytes, urine output comparison), coagulation panel (INR/PTT if anticoagulated), BNP/NT-proBNP, troponin (if new tachycardia/chest pain)
  5. Initiate continuous telemetry monitoring — watch for HR creeping up, new ectopy, low-voltage QRS progression
  6. Ensure adequate IV access — 2 large-bore IVs preferred for potential drainage procedure
  7. Hold diuretics — if currently prescribed, hold the dose; aggressive diuresis worsens tamponade physiology rapidly
  8. Gentle fluid support if hypovolemic — a 250 mL bolus may transiently improve RV preload and stabilize the patient, but is NOT a replacement for drainage
  9. Avoid high-dose beta-blockers — compensatory tachycardia is maintaining cardiac output; blocking it crashes perfusion
  10. Notify APP + CT surgery team — tamponade, even suspected on clinical grounds, is a CT surgery call; request echo STAT and bedside evaluation
  11. Prepare for pericardiocentesis per [Institution policy] — consent, marking laterality, sterile tray, echo guidance, continuous telemetry, proceduralist availability

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension SBP < 90, narrow pulse pressure < 20 mmHg, tachycardia > 120, altered mental status, dyspnea at rest, diaphoresis.)

  1. STAT activation: call CT surgery + APP + charge nurse + RRT — do NOT leave the room alone
  2. Activate Rapid Response or Code Team
  3. IV fluid bolus 250–500 mL rapidly while preparations continue — transiently supports preload
  4. Set up for emergent drainage:
    • Pericardiocentesis (subxiphoid, echo-guided) if effusion is free and serous/serosanguinous
    • Pericardial window or re-sternotomy if blood clot/loculated effusion suspected or recurrence expected
    • Emergent bedside sternotomy if crashing (cross-link to procedural card)
    • Prepare bedside echo — may guide or precede drainage
    • Pacer pads on chest — ensure backup pacing is ready
    • Consider chronotropic support — epinephrine low-dose (5–10 mcg/min) under team direction may temporize perfusion
    • Avoid intubation if possible — positive-pressure ventilation worsens tamponade by dropping RV preload; if required, bolus fluid + pressors before induction
    • Crossmatch / ensure blood products available — if hemorrhagic effusion anticipated
    • Strict time-stamped documentation — vital signs q5min, rhythm strips, echo findings, drainage timing, output volume/appearance
    • Transfer to ICU or OR per team disposition

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit name]. I'm concerned about late tamponade in [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient has developed [fatigue / dyspnea / tachycardia / oliguria / rising Cr] since [onset time/date]. Vital signs now: HR [value], BP [value], RR [value], SpO₂ [value], pulse pressure [SBP − DBP]. Physical exam shows [JVD / muffled sounds / none]. Creatinine trended [prior value → current value]. CXR shows [findings]. Currently on [AC agent and date started] / [not anticoagulated]." A: "Patient is [stable / borderline / unstable]. I am concerned about pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology." R: "I am requesting STAT bedside echo, CT surgery evaluation, and guidance on fluid orders / diuretic hold. Should I start IV fluids? Should I transfer to ICU?"

Who to call

Situation Contact
Suspected late tamponade, stable presentation CT surgery fellow + APP; echo technician STAT
Confirmed effusion with new hemodynamic findings CT surgery attending; ICU bed request
Acute hemodynamic collapse, altered mental status, hypotension RRT/code team + CT surgery STAT + OR charge nurse; prep for bedside sternotomy
Post-discharge patient with concerning symptoms Surgeon on-call; ED as first-contact option; consider direct CT surgery line per discharge paperwork
Suspected post-pericardiotomy syndrome (low-grade fever, rub, smaller effusion, pleuritic pain, POD 10–21) Primary CT surgery team; colchicine/NSAID regimen discussion

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections below are — collapsed by default in PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Beck's Triad and clinical recognition
sections.bodyHtml:
Beck's triad is taught in medical school but rarely all three are present in late tamponade:

  • Hypotension — may be absent early in compensated late tamponade
  • JVD — specific, but not always visible on casual exam
  • Muffled heart sounds — late finding, easily overlooked in a busy ICU

Better screening for late tamponade:

  • Pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg (most sensitive early finding)
  • Falling urine output + rising creatinine without obvious volume cause
  • Unexplained tachycardia + fatigue in POD 7–14 window
  • Right-sided pleural effusion on CXR
  • Falling hemoglobin trend (even without active bleeding)

sections.heading: 7.2 Late vs. acute tamponade comparison
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature Acute (POD 0–3) Late (POD 4–14+)
Onset Minutes to hours; post-op bleeding event Gradual over days–weeks
Fluid origin Fresh surgical blood Serous, serosanguinous, inflammatory
Pericardial volume Smaller (150–300 mL) before symptoms Large (> 1 L) before decompensation
Presentation Hemodynamic collapse, obvious emergency Insidious; "slow recovery," anorexia, fatigue
Physical findings Beck's triad present; obvious sick patient Subtle; JVD/pulse pressure narrowing only clues
Diagnosis Clinical + STAT echo/imaging Echo required; easily missed on exam alone
Management STAT drainage (pericardiocentesis or sternotomy) Pericardiocentesis or window; plan for recurrence
Outcome if missed Cardiac arrest within 30–60 min Readmission within 1–6 weeks; possible crash

sections.heading: 7.3 Echocardiography findings table
sections.bodyHtml:
The echo is the diagnostic test. These findings confirm tamponade physiology.

Echo Finding Measurement / Observation Meaning
Pericardial effusion size > 10 mm concerning; > 20 mm severe Quantifies fluid volume; larger is more likely tamponade
RA late-diastolic collapse Inversion of RA free wall > 1/3 of RA area for > 1/3 of diastole Most sensitive early sign of elevated pericardial pressure
RV diastolic collapse RV free wall indentation in early diastole Specific for tamponade physiology
IVC plethora IVC diameter > 2.1 cm with < 50% respiratory variation Indicates elevated CVP; poor collapsibility is red flag
Mitral inflow variation Respiratory variation in early-diastolic (E) wave velocity > 25% Pulsus paradoxus equivalent; respiratory filling abnormality
Tricuspid inflow variation Respiratory variation > 40% More sensitive than mitral variation for tamponade
Septal bounce Abnormal leftward septal motion in early diastole Ventricular interdependence indicator
Loculated effusion Clot or thickened fluid in fixed location(s) May not be accessible to pericardiocentesis; window likely needed
Swinging heart Heart oscillates within effusion; visible on M-mode Electrical alternans equivalent; very large effusion

sections.heading: 7.4 Differential diagnosis of post-op hypotension (cross-link to Hypotension Differential scenario)
sections.bodyHtml:
Late tamponade is ONE cause of hypotension POD 4+. Rule out:

Diagnosis Key Features Echo Finding Physiology
Late tamponade Insidious; pulsus paradoxus; falling UOP/Cr RA/RV collapse; IVC plethora ↓ RV filling, ↓ CO
Myocardial dysfunction (stunned LV, new MR) New systolic murmur or echo finding; elevated BNP ↓ EF, wall motion abnormality, MR ↓ LV contractility
Sepsis Fever, tachycardia, lactic acidosis; line-related Normal/hyperdynamic LV; normal pericardium Vasodilation + myocardial depression
Hypovolemia Oliguria responsive to fluids; narrow pulse pressure unrelated to respiration Underfilled LV; normal IVC ↓ Preload
Acute MI Ischemic ECG changes; elevated troponin; chest pain Regional wall motion abnormality Coronary occlusion
Acute right ventricular infarction ST elevation V3R, V4R; RV-dominant ECG; elevated JVD Dilated RV; low EF; normal LV RV ischemia
Valvular acute insufficiency New diastolic or systolic murmur; post-op valve issue Echo shows regurgitation; chamber enlargement Valve malfunction

sections.heading: 7.5 Pulsus paradoxus measurement technique
sections.bodyHtml:
Pulsus paradoxus is the exaggerated drop in systolic BP during inspiration (> 10 mmHg is abnormal).

Technique at bedside (blood pressure cuff method):

  1. Place BP cuff on arm; inflate well above patient's known systolic BP
  2. Slowly deflate the cuff while the patient breathes normally
  3. Note the pressure at which you first hear a Korotkoff sound during expiration (only)
  4. Continue deflating slowly
  5. Note the pressure at which you hear Korotkoff sounds throughout the respiratory cycle (during both inspiration and expiration)
  6. The difference between these two pressures is the pulsus paradoxus
  7. Normal: ≤ 10 mmHg; abnormal (tamponade): > 10 mmHg (often 15–25 mmHg in late tamponade)

sections.heading: 7.6 Anticoagulation reversal and urgency
sections.bodyHtml:
Late tamponade in an anticoagulated patient is a critical priority:

  • Warfarin: INR goal is typically 2–3 post-op; in hemorrhagic effusion, urgent reversal (FFP, PCC, vitamin K per team) is considered before drainage
  • DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran): no rapid reversal agent except dabigatran (idarucizumab); most focus shifts to drainage ASAP
  • Heparin: easily reversible with protamine; most urgent situation if actively bleeding into pericardium
  • Bridging decision: do NOT start or hold AC without CT surgery team input. POAF + AC initiation is a setup—new AF triggers AC, AC converts benign effusion to hemorrhagic effusion, hemorrhagic effusion becomes late tamponade.

sections.heading: 7.7 Post-pericardiotomy syndrome as a mimic
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-pericardiotomy syndrome (PPS) is an autoimmune inflammatory response to pericardial blood, occurring 2–8 weeks post-op in ~15% of cardiac surgery patients. < 2% develop tamponade.

Feature PPS (usually stable) Late tamponade (hemodynamic risk)
Presentation Fever, pleuritic chest pain, pericardial rub Insidious fatigue, oliguria, tachycardia
Effusion size Smaller (usually < 2 cm) Larger (often > 2 cm)
Echo signs No RA/RV collapse RA/RV diastolic collapse present
JVD Absent or mild Prominent, elevated
Management NSAID (ibuprofen 600 mg TID with PPI) + colchicine (0.6 mg daily–BID) Drainage (pericardiocentesis or window)
Prognosis Self-limited; 3-month course on meds Excellent post-drainage if drained promptly

Key: PPS with effusion but NO tamponade physiology = medical management; effusion WITH tamponade physiology = procedural.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate immediately.

  • HR rising over hours — 85 → 100 → 115 without clear trigger (pain, fever, anxiety)
  • Pulse pressure narrowing — SBP/DBP gap of 35–40 → 20–25 mmHg over hours (calculate at every assessment)
  • Creatinine trending up — 1.0 → 1.3 → 1.6 over 24–48 h without explanation
  • Urine output falling — < 0.5 mL/kg/h not responding to fluid challenge; oliguria is late but highly sensitive
  • Increasing dyspnea or work of breathing — at rest or with minimal exertion
  • New or worsening right-sided pleural effusion on serial CXR
  • Transient or positional hypotension — BP drops with position changes; patient reports lightheadedness
  • New altered mental status — subtle: increased drowsiness, decreased concentration, confusion
  • Loss of appetite + increasing fatigue — subjective but trust it; family will often report "something's off"
  • New arrhythmia (AF/flutter) — tamponade can precipitate POAF or unmask previously compensated rhythm issues
  • Low-grade fever + pericardial rub + pleuritic pain (POD 10–21) — think post-pericardiotomy syndrome; may precede large effusion
  • Pericardial drain output drops abruptly after window — may indicate drain clot, not resolution; re-imaging indicated if clinical picture worsens

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. The classic miss is calling it "deconditioning." If a POD 5–10 patient is declining in PT, losing appetite, getting more tired by the day, think tamponade before you think rehab. Echo is cheap insurance.

  2. Pulse pressure narrows BEFORE systolic BP drops. Teach new grads to calculate pulse pressure at every shift assessment. A 20–25 mmHg pulse pressure in a post-op patient is a red flag; < 20 is alarming.

  3. Falling UOP + rising Cr in a patient without obvious volume cause is the most reliable lab pattern for subclinical late tamponade. Watch the 24–48 h trend, not a single creatinine value.

  4. Do NOT diurese. Removing preload worsens tamponade physiology acutely. Hold the furosemide order and call the team. Many clinicians reflexively want to diurese "slow recovery"; this crashes a tamponading patient in minutes.

  5. Do NOT intubate without a team plan. Positive-pressure ventilation drops venous return; a tamponading patient can arrest on induction. If intubation is unavoidable, bolus IV fluid + have pressors ready + anticipate higher sedation/paralytic needs.

  6. Compensatory tachycardia is maintaining cardiac output. Do NOT reflexively beta-block a tachycardic late-tamponade patient. You will crash them. Tachycardia is appropriate; address the cause (tamponade), not the symptom.

  7. Gentle fluid bolus buys time. A 250–500 mL bolus increases RV preload transiently, stabilizing perfusion for 30–60 min while drainage is prepared. Not a replacement for drainage but a bridge.

  8. The 2-week return visit is a classic presentation. Discharged patient calling in: "I just can't do what I could yesterday; I'm more tired" → tamponade until ruled out. Low threshold for echo. Family will often call first: "He's not himself."

  9. POAF + new anticoagulation is a setup for late tamponade. New AF triggers AC discussion; AC (warfarin, DOAC, heparin) converts a benign serous effusion into a hemorrhagic one. POD 4–14 window with AC initiation = close monitoring for 10–14 days. Consider baseline echo after AC starts if patient has any risk factors.

  10. Mitral valve patients are higher-risk. Longer CPB time, more pericardial manipulation, more AF requiring AC, more post-pericardiotomy syndrome. Keep the threshold for echo low.

  11. Right-sided pleural effusion on serial CXR is a classic tell for pericardial-overflow pathology. Don't dismiss. The pericardium drains via phrenic and mediastinal lymphatics toward the right lung base; a new right pleural effusion in POD 7–14 is pericardial origin until proven otherwise.

  12. BNP elevated without overt HF symptoms can reflect RV stretch from tamponade. Don't default to "diastolic HF" thinking; get an echo.

  13. Bedside echo is the fastest diagnostic answer and often the cheapest intervention. The threshold to get one should be very low. Cheaper than 8 h of RN time spent worried and documenting instability.

  14. Anticoagulation + POAF + dilated RV from RV strain = embolic risk multiplier. A patient with new AF in late tamponade is at risk for both mechanical complications (RV dysfunction, shock) and thromboembolism. Low threshold for team involvement.

  15. Family teaching at discharge is underrated. Families see the patient more and recognize "not themselves" first. At discharge, explicitly tell families: "Call us if you have shortness of breath and fatigue together. Ask to be checked for fluid around your heart." This simple teaching prevents re-admissions and crashes.

cards.title: TAVR (Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement)
cards.quickAnswer: TAVR is transcatheter aortic valve replacement via transfemoral (most common) or alternative access (transcarotid, transaxillary, transapical). No CPB, rapid recovery, POD 1 discharge common. Key vigilance: new conduction abnormality (LBBB, CHB requiring PPM 10–20%) with continuous telemetry POD 0–2; vascular access bleeding (watch retroperitoneal hemorrhage: tachycardia + flank/back pain + Hgb drop → CT stat); paravalvular leak (PVL) if new HF symptoms; contrast-induced AKI in CKD. DAPT 1 month (ASA 81 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg daily) then ASA lifelong; no warfarin unless AF develops.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Percutaneous aortic valve replacement via femoral artery (transfemoral, TF-TAVR, ~85% of cases) or alternative access (transcarotid, transaxillary, transapical). Balloon-expandable (SAPIEN, Edwards) or self-expanding (Evolut, Medtronic) valves.
  • Typical patient: Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis in intermediate-, high-, or prohibitive-surgical-risk cohort; indications expanding to low-risk patients (PARTNER 3 / Evolut Low Risk trials).
  • Procedure: Most commonly transfemoral with monitored anesthesia care (MAC) or conscious sedation; minimal-access protocols increasingly standard (no general anesthesia, no central line, rapid recovery).
  • CPB status: No cardiopulmonary bypass. Rapid ventricular pacing (transient, seconds to minutes) used during valve deployment only.
  • Standard length of stay: POD 1 discharge (50%+ of TF-TAVR at many centers); 2–3 days for alternative access or complications.
  • Context: TAVR recovery is rapid and complication profile differs fundamentally from surgical AVR (access site >> sternal; DAPT >> warfarin; no sternal precautions; no cardiac rehab Phase 1 in hospital). This card focuses on TAVR-specific deviations; refer to AVR / Aortic Root Replacement card for shared post-cardiac surgery content.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why TAVR works; how it differs from surgical AVR.

Device deployment and anatomy:

  • Aortic valve disease (stenosis, regurgitation, or degenerated bioprosthesis) restricts blood flow from left ventricle to aorta, increasing LV afterload, LV hypertrophy, and eventually ejection-fraction decline.
  • TAVR uses rapid ventricular pacing (180–200 bpm, seconds to minutes) to reduce annular motion, allowing precise catheter-guided valve positioning. Sheath sizes 14–16 Fr depending on valve type.
  • No surgical cardiopulmonary bypass required; procedure duration typically 1–2 hours. Transfemoral access via percutaneous closure device (AngioSeal, Perclose, VenaSeal) or manual compression allows bedrest for 4–6 hours, then rapid mobilization.

Conduction risk — key TAVR physiology:

  • Aortic annulus lies in direct proximity to the left main coronary and the atrioventricular (AV) conduction bundle (His bundle, left bundle branch).
  • Rigid prosthetic valve frame can mechanically compress the His bundle at the point of deployment, or annular edema can delay conduction over the first 48–72 hours post-procedure.
  • Self-expanding valves (Evolut, Medtronic) have higher reported conduction risk (10–15% new LBBB, 5–15% PPM placement) compared to balloon-expandable (SAPIEN, Edwards: ~5–10% new LBBB, ~5–10% PPM).
  • Peak detection window is POD 0–2 (24–72 h post-procedure); delayed third-degree block can occur up to 2 weeks post-discharge, necessitating event monitor outpatient.

Vascular access injury risk:

  • Femoral artery puncture can perforate the iliac vessel, leading to bleeding into the retroperitoneum — a clinical space where hemorrhage is insidious and symptoms delayed.
  • Pseudoaneurysm (pulsatile mass at groin) and arteriovenous fistula (continuous bruit, expanding hematoma) are iatrogenic complications requiring vascular surgery or IR intervention.

Paravalvular leak (PVL) and hemolysis:

  • Mild PVL (trivial-to-mild regurgitation) is common and well-tolerated; moderate-to-severe PVL (≥ moderate on echo) drives readmission and poor long-term outcomes.
  • Severe PVL can cause mechanical hemolysis — RBC fragmentation across the regurgitant jet — manifesting as jaundice, dark urine, elevated LDH (>500), low haptoglobin (<30), elevated indirect bilirubin, and AKI.

Contrast-induced acute kidney injury (CI-AKI):

  • TAVR procedures use significant iodinated contrast (typically 100–200 mL). In pre-existing CKD, hyperglycemia, or volume depletion, contrast is nephrotoxic, causing acute tubular necrosis.
  • Peak Cr rise occurs 48–72 hours post-procedure; most cases are mild and reversible with supportive hydration.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context — TAVR-Specific Admission Profile
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — typical post-TAVR presentation on ICU/stepdown arrival.

Typical arrival (POD 0 evening or POD 1 morning from cath lab):

  • Hemodynamically stable, chest pain-free, alert & oriented
  • Access site: groin dressing (transparent or gauge + transparent) with possible small hematoma (common, usually benign)
  • Monitoring lines: peripheral IV × 2, access site dressing, rarely temporary transvenous pacer if new heart block in cath lab, rarely Foley catheter if urinary retention
  • On DAPT (ASA 81 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg daily, initiated in cath lab or on arrival)
  • Vitals stable; minimal supplemental O₂ (if needed) for residual sedation recovery

Alternative-access TAVR (transapical, transaxillary, transcarotid):

  • Generally sicker, longer procedures, higher bleeding/stroke risk
  • Often ICU-level care POD 0–3, delayed discharge
  • Do NOT apply minimalist playbook; treat closer to post-open-surgical-AVR standard

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / Gather Information* (POD 0 arrival, ~15 min checklist)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet. Target: 2–5 minutes.

  • Vital signs and hemodynamics: HR, BP (both arms), RR, SpO₂, temperature, MAP, perfusion (capillary refill, skin warmth)
  • Neurologic screening: Alert & Oriented × 3, pupils equal/round/reactive, motor/sensory symmetry, facial symmetry, speech clear, no focal deficit
  • Cardiac exam: rate and regularity (telemetry vs palpation), murmurs, peripheral pulses (bilateral femoral, popliteal, dorsalis pedis)
  • Access site: dressing clean and intact, hematoma present (measure dimensions: length × width in cm), color (blue-black vs pink), blanching, no active oozing or pulsatile mass
  • Chest and lungs: breath sounds clear bilaterally, no crackles/wheezes, chest wall pain-free on palpation
  • Abdomen: soft, no tenderness, no distention, no pulsatile mass, no flank/back pain
  • Extremities: no edema, warmth/color symmetric, no calf tenderness
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr (baseline and post-procedure), Hgb, PT/INR, troponin (if elevated pre-op)
  • Medications: review MAR — DAPT initiated? Home beta-blockers restarted? Anticoag status?
  • Lines and wires: temporary pacer if placed in cath lab (confirm threshold, capture, sensing, planned removal timing)
  • Procedure context: which valve (SAPIEN vs Evolut), which access (TF vs alternative), any complications noted in cath lab report, any protamine given?

sections.heading: 5. Management by POD Arc
sections.bodyHtml: (Shorter arc than surgical AVR — TAVR is minimally invasive with rapid discharge. POD 0 recovery → POD 1 discharge planning.)

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 Post-Procedure Recovery (CCU or Stepdown)
sections.bodyHtml:
Bedrest and mobilization:

  1. Bedrest 4–6 h per sheath size and closure method (manual hold 6 h, percutaneous closure device 4 h per protocol)
  2. Access site monitoring q30–60 min initially — measure hematoma dimensions (length × width), mark border with pen, note time. Examine for active oozing, warmth, pulsatile mass
  3. Telemetry continuously — obtain rhythm strip at baseline, monitor for new LBBB, PR prolongation, Mobitz II, or third-degree block (peak detection POD 0–2)
  4. Bedside sitting after 4–6 h bedrest, then bathroom privileges per protocol (typically after sheath pull, or per closure method)
  5. Vital signs q1h × 4 h, then q4h — watch for tachycardia + hypotension (retroperitoneal bleed until proven otherwise)
  6. Groin dressing — keep clean and dry; typical protocol is pressure dressing × 4–6 h post-closure, then transparent or open to air for observation
  7. Pain and symptom control — if chest discomfort, obtain 12-lead ECG; treat pain to facilitate mobility
  8. Electrolyte repletion — K⁺ goal ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 per Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement protocol
  9. Hydration — ensure adequate PO intake or IV fluids (IVF) for contrast clearance; encourage PO if tolerating
  10. Labs POD 0: baseline Cr post-procedure (for CI-AKI trending), CBC, basic metabolic panel, troponin per institution policy

Temporary pacing wire management (if placed in cath lab):

  • Verify pacer function: pacing rate, capture threshold, sensing, sensing mode
  • Secure catheter to prevent dislodgement; assess threshold and sensing q8h
  • Know removal plan (typically POD 1–2 if no ongoing bradycardia)

sections.heading: 5B. POD 1 Discharge Planning (or Transfer to Telemetry / Ward)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Telemetry review — any new conduction abnormality, arrhythmia, or ST changes overnight? If new LBBB or second/third-degree block, notify provider; may need repeat EKG, echo, or extended monitoring
  2. Access site final check — measure hematoma (if still present), assess for expansion or new bleeding, confirm no pulsatile mass or bruit
  3. Vitals stable × 8 h minimum — HR 60–100, MAP > 65, SpO₂ > 94% on room air
  4. Ambulation — patient should stand and walk (short distances) to assess tolerance, dizziness, chest pain
  5. Oral intake — tolerating regular diet without nausea
  6. Bowel / bladder — voiding spontaneously, no retention, bowel function expected (monitor if opioid-dependent)
  7. Labs POD 1 morning: Cr (for CI-AKI trending), Hgb (rule out access-site bleed), K⁺, Mg²⁺
  8. Discharge readiness assessment per Discharge Specifics (§5B discharge checklist below)
  9. Discharge if no complications — most TF-TAVR patients eligible for POD 1 home discharge; alternative-access or PPM-placement patients may stay POD 2–3

POD 1 Discharge Checklist (before home):

  • DAPT prescription written and verified with patient (both patient and PCP copies; clarify that clopidogrel is NOT warfarin)
  • Endocarditis prophylaxis wallet card and teaching — lifelong for new valve; amoxicillin 2 g PO 1 h before dental/GI procedures, or cephalexin if penicillin allergy
  • Groin care instruction — no heavy lifting × 5–7 days, no tub baths × 48 h (showers OK), watch for expanding hematoma or active bleeding, keep dressing clean/dry
  • When to call surgeon / go to ED: expanding groin hematoma or persistent oozing, bright red bleeding at access site, sudden weakness/numbness, chest pain or shortness of breath, syncope or severe dizziness, fever > 100.4°F, severe back/flank pain
  • 30-day echocardiogram scheduled (assess PVL, valve gradient, LV function)
  • Event monitor × 2–4 weeks (arrhythmia surveillance, especially if new LBBB)
  • 1–2 week TAVR team visit (interventional cardiology or cardiothoracic surgery per procedure)
  • Cardiac rehab phase 2 outpatient referral (many TAVR patients defer until after 30-day echo)
  • Labs trending outpatient: Cr at 5–7 days (confirm CI-AKI recovery if pre-op CKD)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation — SBAR + Who to Call
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for conduction abnormality, access-site concern, or hemodynamic change:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p TAVR." B: "Patient received [valve type] TAVR via [access] on [date]. Currently [hemodynamics, rhythm on tele, access site status]." A: "[Symptom or finding]. 12-lead shows [ECG changes if applicable]. Recent labs: K⁺ [value], Cr [value], Hgb [value]." R: "Requesting [EKG, echo, extended monitoring / vascular imaging / repeat labs]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Urgency
New LBBB or PR prolongation Primary APP / fellow STAT
Mobitz II or third-degree block APP/fellow + cardiology + consider temporary pacer STAT
Expanding hematoma (> 5 cm or rapid growth) Vascular surgery consult STAT
Retroperitoneal bleed suspected (tachycardia + flank pain + Hgb drop) Vascular surgery + CT abdomen/pelvis STAT EMERGENT
Pseudoaneurysm (pulsatile mass at groin, bruit) Vascular surgery consult URGENT
New acute chest pain or ST changes Cardiology / APP + ECG + troponin STAT
New focal neurologic deficit Stroke code + neurology + CT surgery EMERGENT
New HF symptoms + hemolysis labs suggesting severe PVL CT surgery / interventional cardiology URGENT
Access site bleeding not controlled with direct pressure × 5 min Vascular surgery or IR standby URGENT

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(Expandable in app — novice + advanced beginner deep-dive)*
sections.bodyHtml:
TAVR valve types, access sites, and device selection Balloon-expandable (SAPIEN 3/3Ultra, Edwards):
  • Mechanism: inflatable balloon inside valve; allows precise, repositionable deployment; deflated after positioning
  • PPM risk: ~5–10% new LBBB, ~5% PPM placement
  • Sheath size: 14 Fr standard
  • Niche: calcified annuli, small aortic roots (>20 mm), need for repositionability
  • Key advantage: repositionable if initial position suboptimal; lower self-expanding radial force (may reduce coronary obstruction risk in some anatomies) Self-expanding (Evolut R/PRO/X, Medtronic):
  • Mechanism: nitinol frame self-expands at deployment; height adjustable before full release; recapturable
  • PPM risk: ~10–15% new LBBB, ~10–15% PPM placement
  • Sheath size: 14–16 Fr depending on size
  • Niche: heavily calcified aortic roots, smaller annuli, patients with low ejection fraction
  • Key advantage: radial force (useful for heavily calcified or irregular anatomy); recapturability if deployment trajectory is off Access selection (transfemoral vs. alternative):
  • Transfemoral eligibility: iliofemoral vessel diameter ≥ 5.5 mm on CT angiography, no severe tortuosity or atherosclerotic disease
  • Transcarotid (via carotid artery): for patients with severe iliofemoral disease, ascending aorta access unsuitable; requires groin cutdown, involves carotid manipulation (stroke risk); longer recovery than TF
  • Transaxillary (via axillary artery): alternative for small or diseased iliofemoral vessels; surgical cutdown in axilla; higher bleeding risk at access site
  • Transapical (via left ventricular apex): most invasive; thoracotomy, ICU stay typical POD 0–3, delayed discharge; reserved for prohibitive peripherals or anatomy unsuitable for other routes
  • Transaortic (via ascending aorta via mini-sternotomy): rare, mainly in prohibitive-peripheral high-risk cohort; mini-sternotomy allows rapid healing vs full sternotomy Contrast volume and renal risk:
  • Typical TAVR contrast load: 100–200 mL iodinated contrast
  • Contrast-to-creatinine ratio (CCR): divide mL of contrast by serum Cr (mg/dL). CCR > 3–4 increases CI-AKI risk
  • Renal protection strategy: ensure euvolemia before procedure, use iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast, avoid concurrent nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE-I if borderline Cr), encourage PO hydration POD 0–1
Conduction disturbance mechanism and monitoring strategy Anatomic basis for new LBBB / heart block:
  • Aortic valve annulus is a fibrous ring at the junction of left ventricle, aorta, and right atrium
  • The AV conduction bundle (His bundle) runs along the left side of the ventricular septum, in close proximity to the left-main coronary artery
  • At the point where the left main exits from the aorta (aortic root), the His bundle is only 5–10 mm away from the valve seat
  • Rigid prosthetic frame (especially self-expanding valves with high radial force) can compress or mechanically irritate the bundle during or immediately after deployment
  • Annular edema and inflammation can develop over POD 0–2, further delaying conduction across the bundle
  • Result: new left bundle-branch block (LBBB) in 10–15% of self-expanding TAVR, ~5–10% of balloon-expandable TAVR; complete heart block (CHB) in 5–15% requiring temporary or permanent pacemaker Monitoring strategy:
    1. Baseline 12-lead ECG immediately post-procedure (before transfer to ICU/stepdown) to document pre-admission rhythm
    2. Continuous telemetry POD 0–2 (24–72 h minimum) — do NOT wean off monitor just because LOS is short
    3. Repeat 12-lead EKG stat if new LBBB or rhythm change detected on tele
    4. Notify provider immediately if Mobitz II, third-degree block, or hemodynamically significant bradycardia (HR < 50 or SBP drop)
    5. If temporary pacing wire placed in cath lab: verify capture and sensing q8h, know removal plan (typically POD 1–2 if conduction recovers)
    6. Discharge planning:
    7. If new LBBB developed POD 0–2, prescribe event monitor × 2–4 weeks for outpatient arrhythmia surveillance (delayed heart block possible)
    8. If PPM placed during hospitalization: full post-op PPM care applies (Keck PPM protocol)
    9. If conduction normalized by POD 2, standard discharge clearance; event monitor still reasonable given delayed block risk
Paravalvular leak (PVL) assessment and severity grading Pathophysiology:
  • After valve deployment, if the prosthetic frame does not fully conform to the aortic annulus, blood can regurgitate backward (aortic regurgitation) around the valve edges — this is paravalvular leak
  • Mild PVL (trivial or mild on echocardiography) is very common (20–30% of TAVR patients) and is well-tolerated long-term
  • Moderate-to-severe PVL (≥ moderate on echo: ERO ≥ 20 mm² or vena contracta ≥ 4 mm) is associated with worse outcomes and may require repeat intervention Echocardiographic grading (transthoracic echo typically POD 0–1 or POD 1–2):
  • Trivial: tiny color jet, not graded as significant AR
  • Mild: small color jet (< 10% of annulus width), AR velocity mildly elevated
  • Moderate: color jet 10–30% of annulus, diastolic velocity ≥ 2.5 m/s, vena contracta 4–6 mm
  • Severe: large color jet (> 30% annulus), holodiastolic flow reversal in descending aorta, vena contracta > 6 mm, ERO ≥ 30 mm² PVL-related hemolysis:
  • When severe PVL causes high-velocity regurgitant jet, RBCs can fragment across the turbulent jet → mechanical hemolysis
  • Laboratory findings: LDH > 500 U/L (hemolysis marker), haptoglobin < 30 mg/dL (consumed by free Hgb), elevated indirect (unconjugated) bilirubin > 2 mg/dL, low Hgb, elevated reticulocyte count
  • Clinical features: jaundice, dark urine (hemoglobinuria), dyspnea (anemia + HF), abdominal or flank discomfort (hemolysis pain)
  • Management: obtain echo to quantify PVL severity; if severe PVL + hemolysis, discuss with CT surgery / interventional cardiology regarding percutaneous PVL closure device or redo TAVR (valve-in-valve) When to get echo for PVL assessment:
  • Routine: POD 1 transthoracic echo (baseline for 30-day follow-up comparison)
  • Urgent: if new dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, new diastolic murmur, jaundice, dark urine, or signs of hemolysis POD 0–2
DAPT regimens and anticoagulation rationale post-TAVR Standard DAPT for TF-TAVR without pre-existing AF:
MedicationDoseDurationRationale
Aspirin (ASA)81 mg PO dailyLifelongPrevents platelet adhesion to valve surface and endothelial damage
Clopidogrel (Plavix)75 mg PO daily1 month, then stopPrevents stent-like thrombosis on new valve; recent POPular TAVI trial (NEJM 2020) supports ASA monotherapy after 1 mo over lifelong DAPT
Total DAPT duration:
  • 1 month standard: ASA 81 mg + clopidogrel 75 mg daily × 30 days, then ASA 81 mg alone lifelong
  • Some centers extend to 3–6 months based on valve type, annular calcification, or procedural complexity; cardiology-directed If pre-existing or new post-op AF:
    ScenarioRegimenDurationNotes
    Pre-op AF (known before TAVR)OAC (warfarin INR 2–3 OR DOAC) + ASA 81 mgOAC lifelong; ASA × 3 mo, then reassessAvoid triple therapy (OAC + dual antiplatelet). Most centers do OAC + ASA for 3 mo, then OAC alone after 3 mo if AF persistent.
    New POAF (develops POD 0–2)Start OAC (heparin bridge or loading DOAC) + ASA; clopidogrel may continue or hold per teamOAC lifelong if AF persistent; ASA/clopi individualizedComplex decision — do NOT start AC without CT surgery team input (balance stroke vs surgical bleeding risk)
    TAVR + recent PCI (stent < 12 mo)ASA + clopi ± short OAC (depends on AF + stent type)Individualized, often 6–12 moRare scenario — avoid triple therapy; attend-directed
    Key misconceptions to address:
  • DAPT ≠ warfarin. ASA + clopidogrel are antiplatelet agents (prevent clotting), NOT anticoagulants. Patients often confuse "blood clot preventer" with warfarin (anticoagulant). Teach clearly: "You are taking two blood clot preventers (aspirin and Plavix). This is NOT the same as warfarin. Continue both unless told otherwise."
  • Warfarin is NOT first-line post-TAVR (POPular TAVI, NEJM 2020, showed no advantage and higher bleeding risk)
  • DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) is increasingly used post-TAVR if AF develops (preferred over warfarin for convenience)
Stroke risk and cerebral protection devices Incidence and timing:
  • Ischemic stroke occurs in ~3–5% of TAVR patients post-procedure
  • Most strokes happen within 72 hours post-procedure
  • Mechanism: atheroembolic debris from catheter/guidewire manipulation, thrombus formation on foreign material, plaque dislodgement from aorta Cerebral embolic protection device (Sentinel, Abbott):
  • Mesh device placed in left main coronary artery ostium before aortic valve crossing; captures atherosclerotic debris
  • Deployed before valve exchange, retrieved after valve deployment
  • Reduces stroke incidence to ~2–3% vs ~3–5% without (modest benefit, not definitive stroke prevention)
  • Adds ~5–10 min to procedure; requires patent, non-ostial-stenotic left main
  • Increasingly standard at many centers; controversial whether benefit justifies cost/complexity Post-TAVR stroke surveillance:
  • Neurologic exam q shift minimum: Alert & Oriented, motor/sensory symmetry, facial droop, speech, gait if ambulating
  • New focal neurologic deficit → stat stroke code and neurology alert
  • Time-dependent thrombolysis or thrombectomy eligibility applies (3-hour window for IV tPA, up to 24 h for select thrombectomy candidates per current guidelines)
Valve thrombosis — subclinical detection and management Subclinical valve thrombosis (SVT):
  • Silent thrombus formation on TAVR valve leaflets; detected on 4D CT or multi-slice CT with cine imaging
  • No clear clinical evidence that anticoagulation for SVT improves outcomes — management is evolving and controversial
  • Appears more common with self-expanding valves; unclear if clinically significant long-term Clinical (symptomatic) valve thrombosis:
  • Presents as rising mean aortic gradient on echo (≥ 10 mmHg rise from baseline)
  • Reduced valve opening area, dyspnea, decreased ejection fraction
  • Management: OAC (warfarin or DOAC) to prevent progression; repeat echo 4–6 weeks to confirm resolution Monitoring strategy:
  • Baseline post-TAVR echo establishes valve gradient
  • 30-day echo confirms stable gradient and minimal PVL
  • If gradient rises on follow-up echo (> 10 mmHg rise or absolute gradient > 30 mmHg), consider 4D CT to rule out thrombosis
  • If confirmed, discuss anticoagulation with cardiology (warfarin or DOAC × 3–6 months)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear, re-escalate.

  • New LBBB on telemetry or repeat EKG — may presage progression to second/third-degree block; extended monitoring and repeat EKG warranted
  • Tachycardia without obvious trigger (HR 100–120 s/o stable baseline) — often first sign of retroperitoneal bleed, sepsis, or hemolysis; investigate source before reassuring
  • Tachycardia + lower back pain or flank pain (even mild) — retroperitoneal hemorrhage until proven otherwise; CT abdomen/pelvis stat
  • Unexplained Hgb drop (≥ 2 g/dL) — occult bleeding (retroperitoneal, GI) or hemolysis; check hematocrit trend, request heme labs if hemolysis suspected
  • Hematoma expanding from baseline measurement (e.g., 3 cm × 4 cm → 4 cm × 5 cm on same shift) — increased bleeding risk; escalate
  • Pulsatile mass or continuous bruit at groin — pseudoaneurysm; vascular ultrasound and vascular surgery consult
  • New back or flank tenderness on palpation — raise suspicion for retroperitoneal bleed; do not wait for hemodynamic instability
  • New jaundice, dark urine, elevated indirect bilirubin + LDH > 500 — hemolysis; likely from severe PVL; echo and escalate
  • New dyspnea or orthopnea — HF from severe PVL or other cardiac complication; echo and escalate
  • New focal neurologic change (weakness, facial droop, speech change) — stroke; activate code immediately
  • Fever ≥ 101°F on POD 1–2 — sepsis or early infection; blood cultures and WBC trending
  • Creatinine rising disproportionately (> 25% from baseline or absolute Cr > 2.0) on POD 2–3 — CI-AKI or rhabdomyolysis; ensure hydration, avoid nephrotoxins, monitor urine output and color

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. TAVR is NOT post-cardiotomy. Do not force the post-surgical-AVR mental model. No sternal precautions, no sternal care, no prolonged bedrest, no cardiac rehab Phase 1 in hospital. Often home POD 1.

  2. Next-day discharge means 12–18 hours to catch a conduction problem, access-site bleed, or early PVL. High vigilance required in a compressed window.

    Keep telemetry running continuously; do NOT plan to wean off monitor early.

  3. New LBBB POD 0–2 requires continuous telemetry and repeat EKG. Peak detection is 24–72 h. If new second- or third-degree block develops, notify provider immediately. If temporary pacer placed in cath lab, verify thresholds and removal plan.

  4. Self-expanding valves (Evolut) carry higher PPM risk (~10–15%) than balloon-expandable (SAPIEN ~5–10%). Know which valve your patient received. If Evolut, heighten suspicion for conduction abnormality; lower threshold for repeat EKG.

  5. Retroperitoneal bleed is the miss. Unexplained tachycardia + lower back/flank pain + Hgb drop (≥ 2 g/dL) + hypotension without visible bleeding = CT abdomen/pelvis STAT. Do NOT assume "patient feels fine" — get imaging. Vascular surgery standby if confirmed.

  6. Mark hematoma borders with pen and measure dimensions (length × width) at each check. Quantify, do not eyeball. If hematoma expands from baseline (e.g., 3 cm × 4 cm → 4 cm × 5 cm), escalate to provider and possibly vascular imaging.

  7. DAPT ≠ warfarin. Patients and families confuse dual antiplatelet therapy (ASA + clopidogrel) with warfarin. Teach clearly: "You are taking two blood clot preventers (aspirin and Plavix), NOT a blood thinner like warfarin. Keep taking both unless told otherwise. Do NOT stop them early."

  8. Endocarditis prophylaxis is LIFELONG for the new TAVR valve. Critical teaching at discharge: new prosthetic valve requires lifetime antibiotics (amoxicillin 2 g PO 1 h before dental/GI procedures) before any dental work, instrumentation, or GI procedures. Wallet card and PCP notification essential.

  9. New back or flank pain on POD 1 is NOT 'muscle ache' until retroperitoneal bleed is excluded. Tachycardia + flank pain + Hgb drop → imaging, not reassurance. This is the most commonly missed TAVR complication.

  10. Paravalvular leak-related hemolysis shows up as jaundice, dark urine, dyspnea, elevated LDH (> 500), low haptoglobin (< 30), elevated indirect bilirubin. If suspected, obtain echo + heme labs. Severe PVL may require percutaneous closure or repeat TAVR; support RBC transfusion if Hgb < 7 and symptomatic.

  11. A new fever ≥ 3 months post-TAVR = rule out prosthetic valve endocarditis, NOT sinusitis or URI. Blood cultures, echocardiogram, cardiology consultation. Empiric antibiotics per endocarditis protocol pending culture results.

  12. TAVR patients are often frail, elderly, or deconditioned preoperatively. Do not assume "next-day discharge" means they can sit in bed. Early PT/OT, standing at bedside POD 1, gait training — prevent deconditioning and fall risk. Delirium risk is real in frail patients; early mobilization is preventive.

  13. Contrast-induced AKI trends at 24–72 hours. Trend Cr daily; do not base decisions on single value. Most CI-AKI is mild and reversible. Preventive hydration and avoiding further nephrotoxins are mainstay.

  14. If patient had temporary transvenous pacer placed in cath lab and transferred to ICU/unit, know the pacing rate, capture threshold, sensing, and planned removal time. Wire dislodgement or pacer failure during transport is preventable with secure fixation. Pacemaker check q8h while in situ.

  15. Alternative-access TAVR (transapical, transaxillary, transcarotid) recovery looks MORE like open surgical AVR than minimalist TF-TAVR. Do NOT reflexively apply the next-day-discharge / low-monitoring playbook. These patients often have longer ICU stays, delayed extubation, and higher bleeding/stroke risk. Treat closer to post-surgical standard.

cards.title: Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (TAA)
cards.quickAnswer: Thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) = progressive aortic dilation; ascending > descending in frequency; most asymptomatic (incidental finding). Ascending threshold: ≥5.5 cm general, ≥5.0 cm bicuspid with risk factors, ≥4.5 cm Marfan/Loeys-Dietz, ≥4.0 cm vEDS. Descending/arch ≥5.5–6.0 cm. Growth > 0.5 cm/year = urgent surgery regardless of size. Surveillance: serial CT or cardiac MR q6–12 months (imaging protocol); beta-blocker + ACE-I/ARB target SBP ≤130, HR ≤60. Genetic syndromes require family screening. Red flags: sudden severe chest/back pain, pulse differential, hemodynamic instability = dissection until proven otherwise; contact surgery emergently. Avoid fluoroquinolones (black box warning).

Genetic syndromes require family screening. Red flags: sudden severe chest/back pain, pulse differential, hemodynamic instability = dissection until proven otherwise; contact surgery emergently. Avoid fluoroquinolones (black box warning).
