sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who gets it.

  • Definition: Chronic progressive dilation of the thoracic aorta to >3 cm diameter (normal ≤4 cm at sinuses of Valsalva). Classified by location: ascending (root to innominate), arch (innominate to left subclavian), descending (left subclavian to diaphragm), thoracoabdominal (TAAA) (crosses diaphragm).
  • Epidemiology:
  • Prevalence 1–2 per 10,000 in general population; rising with age, hypertension screening, widespread imaging
  • Degenerative/atherosclerotic — most common (50–80%); typically elderly, HTN, smoking history
  • Bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) aortopathy — congenital; ascending root dilation in 50–80% of BAV patients; can present in 20s–60s
  • Genetic aortopathies — Marfan (~1 in 5,000; 80% develop aortic disease), Loeys-Dietz (TGFBR1/2), vEDS (COL3A1), familial TAAD (TAAD panel); often younger presentation
  • Prior aortic dissection — Type A survivors 10–15% risk of late aneurysm; Type B → descending TAA
  • Inflammatory — giant cell (temporal) arteritis, Takayasu arteritis; systemic symptoms + elevated inflammatory markers
  • Infectious/mycotic — secondary to bacteremia or endocarditis; rarer; urgent intervention
  • Trauma — post-traumatic pseudoaneurysm of descending aorta; may present acutely or delayed
  • Typical patient presentation: pre-op awaiting ascending/arch TAA surgery (post-dissection or elective for size); pre-op awaiting descending/TAAA repair; incidental TAA on cardiac imaging; post-dissection surveillance; genetic aortopathy family screening.
  • Clinical settings: ICU (acute dissection concern, urgent pre-op); stepdown (stable pre-op, post-op recovery); outpatient cardiology (surveillance, family screening).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Novice + advanced beginner teaching — why TAA develops.

sections.heading: Degenerative / atherosclerotic TAA
sections.bodyHtml: Chronic hypertension → medial smooth muscle degeneration, elastic fiber loss, metalloproteinase activation → progressive wall thinning → dilation. Rupture risk increases exponentially with aortic size.

sections.heading: Bicuspid aortopathy
sections.bodyHtml: Turbulent jet flow → endothelial dysfunction → accelerated medial degeneration. Often asymmetric root dilation (right-coronary sinus predominant). Associated with NOTCH1 mutations in some families.

sections.heading: Genetic aortopathies
sections.bodyHtml:
• Marfan (FBN1): fibrillin-1 defect → impaired microfibril assembly → exaggerated TGF-β signaling → medial smooth muscle dysfunction + weakened elastic fibers
  • Loeys-Dietz (TGFBR1/2, SMAD3): TGF-β dysregulation → severe, early aortic disease; arterial tortuosity, aneurysms at multiple sites
  • vEDS (COL3A1): Type III collagen defect → fragile vessel wall → rupture risk at smaller sizes; spontaneous arterial dissection
  • Familial TAAD (TAAD panel): ACTA2, MYH11, MYLK, PRKG1 mutations → familial clustering without syndromic features

sections.heading: Inflammatory aortitis
sections.bodyHtml: Giant cell arteritis → transmural inflammation, giant cells, elastic laminae disruption (medial sclerosis); Takayasu → inflammation of aortic branches + root.

sections.heading: Post-dissection
sections.bodyHtml: Intimal tear → blood enters media → wall weakening → chronic false lumen dilation or distal aorta aneurysm formation over weeks to months.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology of rupture
sections.bodyHtml: Progressive wall weakness → loss of elastic fibers and smooth muscle → aneurysm growth follows Laplace law (wall stress ∝ pressure × radius). Once rupture occurs, >50% mortality even with emergency surgery. Saccular (localized) aneurysms rupture at smaller sizes than fusiform (circumferential).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like.

sections.heading: Asymptomatic (most common)
sections.bodyHtml: Incidental finding on CTA, cardiac MR, or transthoracic echo ordered for other indication (MI work-up, pneumonia, aortic regurgitation evaluation, family screening).

sections.heading: Symptomatic TAA
sections.bodyHtml:
• Chest or back pain — anterior chest (ascending), inter-scapular back pain (arch/descending); may mimic acute coronary syndrome
  • Dyspnea — mass effect on lungs, heart, esophagus, tracheobronchial tree; can present as "dyspnea on exertion"
  • Dysphagia — arch TAA compressing esophagus
  • Hoarseness — recurrent laryngeal nerve compression (arch TAA)
  • Upper extremity hypertension, pulse differential — branch vessel compromise (innominate, left carotid)
  • Lower extremity claudication, malperfusion — descending/TAAA with visceral branch involvement

sections.heading: Acute dissection (red flag, see Escalation §6)
sections.bodyHtml: Sudden, severe, tearing chest or back pain; pulse deficit (upper vs. lower extremity or between arms >20 mmHg); focal neurologic deficit (stroke, paraplegia); hemodynamic instability. Hypertensive urgency common; can progress to cardiovascular collapse in minutes.

sections.heading: Physical exam
sections.bodyHtml:
Often unremarkable in uncomplicated TAA:

  • HTN if underlying disease present
  • Aortic regurgitation murmur (diastolic, high-pitched) if root dilation with aortic valve incompetence
  • Pulse differential if branch vessel compromise or dissection
  • BP differential >20 mmHg between arms suggests innominate/carotid involvement or dissection
  • Signs of genetic syndrome: Marfan (tall habitus, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, skin striae, pectus deformity), vEDS (hyperelasticity, thin fragile skin, easy bruising), LDS (hypertelorism, bifid uvula, arterial tortuosity)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic evaluation. Pure information-gathering, no actions yet.

Vital signs & hemodynamics

  • Heart rate, blood pressure (both arms), SpO₂, mental status, skin perfusion (capillary refill, temperature)
  • Active chest or back pain? Severity and character?

Symptoms

  • Chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, syncope or near-syncope, focal weakness/numbness?
  • Hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, lower extremity pain/numbness?

Physical findings

  • Pulse differential (radial vs. radial, upper vs. lower extremity)
  • Auscultation: aortic regurgitation murmur? Heart failure sounds?
  • Neurologic exam: focal deficits, symmetric strength, cranial nerves

Recent imaging & labs

  • Most recent CTA/cardiac MR: aortic diameters (specify level: sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, mid-ascending, arch, descending, TAAA); location; branch involvement
  • Baseline prior imaging for growth rate calculation
  • Recent labs: troponin, creatinine, electrolytes, hemoglobin, lactate, coagulation studies

History & context

  • Known aortic disease? Prior dissection? Genetic syndrome (Marfan, LDS, vEDS, FTAA)?
  • Prior aortic surgery? Surveillance plan in place?
  • Home medications: beta-blocker, ACE-I, ARB, others on board?
  • Recent imaging at outside institution? Comparison available?
  • Pregnancy status (if female of childbearing age)

Relevant procedures & lines

  • Current arterial line? Large-bore IV access in place?
  • Pre-op workup completed (echo, CTA, labs, EKG)?

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: No Stable/Unstable fork for diagnosis cards. Management subdivided by clinical approach.

sections.heading: 5A. Medical management — hypertension & medical optimization
sections.bodyHtml:
Tight blood pressure control

  • Target SBP ≤130 mmHg, HR 50–60 (if tolerated). Reduces wall stress (Laplace law), slows growth, decreases dissection risk (Isselbacher et al., 2022)
  • First-line agents: beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol) ± ACE-I/ARB (lisinopril, losartan)
  • Additional agents: non-DHP calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) if additional control needed; avoid reflex-tachycardia vasodilators (hydralazine without beta-block; short-acting agents)
  • Labetalol or esmolol for rapid control if needed
  • Home BP monitoring essential. Adjust meds if home BP >140 systolic consistently

Beta-blockade

  • Standard of care. Beta-blockers slow aortic root growth, especially in Marfan syndrome (propranolol, metoprolol data); reduces wall stress (decreased dP/dt)
  • Target resting HR 50–60; hold if HR <45 or SBP <90 without team approval
  • Do NOT wean post-op or discontinue for mild bradycardia (HR 48–50) without cardiology consult

ARB use in Marfan syndrome

  • Losartan offered as adjunct to beta-blockade (LOAT, COMPARE trials showed mixed results; losartan-as-monotherapy not proven superior to beta-block + ACE-I)
  • Current practice: losartan often combined with beta-blockade in Marfan; not universally proven but emerging evidence supports addition (Isselbacher et al., 2022)
  • Routine losartan NOT recommended for non-Marfan TAA (Isselbacher et al., 2022)

Fluoroquinolone contraindication — absolute

  • Fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin) are FDA black-box contraindicated — associated with aortic aneurysm, dissection, and rupture (FDA 2018 warning)
  • All TAA patients: substitute alternative antibiotic (beta-lactam, macrolide, others per infectious disease)
  • If patient on fluoroquinolone + TAA discovered: escalate immediately for antibiotic switch
  • Nursing education: if TAA patient is prescribed fluoroquinolone, flag it

Risk factor modification

  • Smoking cessation: contributes to TAA progression; refer to tobacco cessation
  • Strenuous exertion, heavy lifting, contact sports, isometric exercise: avoid; promote low-intensity aerobic activity
  • Cocaine, amphetamines, sympathomimetics: acute hypertensive surges, dissection risk; counsel avoidance
  • NSAIDs: can elevate BP; prefer acetaminophen for analgesia
  • Avoid Valsalva maneuvers (straining, hard stools): bowel regimen, stool softeners

Pregnancy counseling (female, childbearing age)

  • TAA + pregnancy = high dissection risk (hemodynamic changes: ↑ cardiac output, ↓ SVR, ↑ plasma volume; hormonal elastin degradation)
  • Requires maternal-fetal medicine + cardiology co-management
  • Contraception counseling essential
  • Lower surgical thresholds may apply if pregnancy planned

Genetic counseling & family screening

  • Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vEDS, familial TAAD: refer for genetic testing if young TAA or family history
  • First-degree relatives of confirmed genetic syndrome: aortic imaging screening (echocardiography ± CTA/cardiac MR) + genetic testing
  • Ensure family screening referrals arranged before discharge

sections.heading: 5B. Surveillance imaging
sections.bodyHtml:
Frequency based on size and growth

TAA Size Stable Growth Imaging Schedule
<5.0 cm <0.3 cm/year CTA or cardiac MR every 12 months
5.0–5.5 cm <0.3 cm/year CTA or cardiac MR every 6–12 months
>5.5 cm (ascending) <0.3 cm/year CTA or cardiac MR every 3–6 months
Any size >0.5 cm/year SURGICAL INDICATION — notify team urgently
Post-dissection Initial CTA within 1 week; then weekly-to-monthly until stable; q3–6 months longterm

Imaging selection

  • Cardiac MR preferred for young patients, genetic aortopathies, lifelong surveillance (no radiation; excellent soft-tissue contrast; same-scanner same-sequence allows longitudinal comparison)
  • CTA excellent for acute settings (speed, calcification detection, branch involvement); radiation dose a consideration for serial surveillance in young patients
  • Transthoracic echo: first-line for ascending aorta/root at routine follow-up (non-invasive, no radiation); limited for descending/TAAA
  • TEE: high sensitivity for ascending/arch + dissection; bedside utility if dissection suspected and CTA unavailable; used intra-operatively

Measurement technique critical

  • Measure at same anatomic level on each scan (sinuses of Valsalva for root, sinotubular junction, mid-ascending, etc.)
  • Same imaging phase (systole or diastole) for longitudinal comparison — cardiac MR and CTA protocols must specify
  • Size indexing: aortic size index (aortic size / body surface area) matters for small patients; aortic height index also used in some centers
  • Document imaging measurements in a longitudinal tracking table (date, location, size, growth rate)

sections.heading: 5C. Surgical referral thresholds — elective repair
sections.bodyHtml:
Ascending aorta

Etiology Threshold Notes
Degenerative/HTN ≥5.5 cm Fusiform TAA; saccular = lower threshold
Bicuspid AV ≥5.0 cm (with risk factors*) Risk factors: male, family hx dissection, AR, SBP >150, syncope
Bicuspid AV ≥5.25–5.5 cm (without RF) Debate ongoing; some centers use 5.5 cm strict
Marfan syndrome ≥4.5–5.0 cm FBN1 mutation confirmed; TGF-β dysfunction
Loeys-Dietz syndrome ≥4.5 cm TGFBR1/2 mutations; severe aortopathy
vEDS ≥4.0–4.5 cm COL3A1; fragile vessel wall; rupture risk at smaller sizes
Post-dissection Type A ≥5.0 cm Distal aorta residual aneurysm

*Risk factors: male, family history of dissection, aortic regurgitation, SBP >150, syncope history

Arch

Etiology Threshold Notes
Degenerative/HTN ≥5.5 cm Arch slightly higher than ascending (dissection mechanics)
Marfan / LDS ≥5.0–5.2 cm Syndromic aortopathy
vEDS ≥4.5 cm Lower threshold due to rupture risk
Post-dissection ≥5.0 cm Type B dissection with arch involvement

Descending thoracic / TAAA

Etiology Threshold Notes
Degenerative/HTN ≥6.0 cm Lower initial rupture risk than ascending; spinal cord ischemia risk with repair
Marfan / LDS ≥6.0 cm Syndromic descending usually treated like degenerative (higher thresholds)
vEDS ≥5.5 cm Fragile vessel; lower threshold
TAAA (crosses diaphragm) ≥6.5 cm Highest thresholds due to operative morbidity (visceral ischemia, paraplegia risk)
Post-dissection ≥6.0 cm Type B false lumen aneurysm

Growth rate as independent indication

  • Growth >0.5 cm/year = urgent surgical consideration regardless of absolute size (Isselbacher et al., 2022)
  • Example: 5.0 cm TAA growing at 0.7 cm/year requires surgery sooner than 5.4 cm stable TAA
  • Serial imaging critical; document growth velocity at each interval

Saccular (localized) vs. fusiform (circumferential)

  • Saccular = higher rupture risk per cm than fusiform; often seen with infection, trauma
  • May lower surgical threshold; escalate to team if identified

sections.heading: 5D. TEVAR vs. open repair decision (descending / arch)
sections.bodyHtml:
Decision point TEVAR eligible Open repair preferred
Anatomy Adequate proximal/distal landing zones; favorable neck Unfavorable anatomy; zone 0–2 involvement; small aorta <20 mm
Age No absolute cutoff Consider in younger patients (durability)
Comorbidities High operative risk; suitable for less-invasive approach Stable; able to tolerate surgery
Urgent dissection Type B, hemodynamically stable, distal → TEVAR reasonable Type A or hemodynamically unstable → open repair emergent
Prior abdominal surgery Consider TEVAR to avoid re-entry bleeding —
Aortic branches Can cover branch arteries; visceral perfusion? Open allows branch reconstruction

TEVAR increasingly first-line for descending/arch TAA in appropriate anatomy; open repair preferred in younger patients and certain anatomic scenarios.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room]. Patient is [POD X / admission Y] with thoracic aortic aneurysm [location, size]." B: "Recent aortic imaging shows [size, growth rate]. Patient is currently [hemodynamic status]. Medications: [beta-blocker, ACE-I/ARB doses, others on board]." A: "[Stable on current management / new symptom: chest/back pain / rapid growth on repeat imaging / hemodynamic change: hypotension / new pulse deficit]." R: "Requesting [surgical consultation / urgent imaging / optimization plan / other]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Urgency
Suspected acute dissection (sudden severe chest/back pain, pulse deficit, focal neuro deficit) Cardiothoracic surgeon + code team + neuroradiology (stat CTA) EMERGENT
Aortic rupture (shock, sudden back/flank pain, hemodynamic collapse) Cardiothoracic surgeon + code team + operating room EMERGENT
Asymptomatic TAA at surgical threshold (pre-op planning) Cardiothoracic surgeon + cardiology Routine (same day if possible)
Rapid growth on imaging (>0.5 cm/year or acute increase) Cardiothoracic surgeon + cardiology Urgent (same day)
Symptomatic TAA (chest/back pain, dyspnea, not dissection) Cardiothoracic surgeon + cardiology Urgent (same day)
Mycotic aneurysm (fever + aortic aneurysm on imaging + positive blood cultures) Cardiothoracic surgeon + infectious disease EMERGENT (surgery + antibiotics)
Anticoagulation question (AF, post-dissection, post-op) Cardiothoracic surgeon — do NOT start/stop AC without team input Urgent (phone consult)
Genetic syndrome confirmation (young TAA, family hx) Genetics + cardiology Routine (within days)
Family screening referral (Marfan, LDS, vEDS identified) Genetics + cardiology Routine (arrange before discharge)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner deep-dive. Sections marked expandable.

Anatomy & surgical implications — ascending vs. arch vs. descending Ascending aorta (root to innominate)
  • Arises from left ventricle, within pericardium
  • Contains coronary ostia (left main, right coronary) — must identify pre-operatively for safe repair planning
  • Root dilation often involves aortic valve (aortic insufficiency) — may require simultaneous valve replacement (Bentall procedure)
  • Ascending repair: Graft tube with or without valve (Bentall for root), VSARR (valve-sparing root replacement), hemi-arch (more limited)
  • Spinal cord risk: low (ascending artery off brachiocephalic, not critical to cord) Arch (innominate to left subclavian)
  • Contains branch vessels: innominate, left carotid, left subclavian
  • Repair requires branch vessel re-implantation or debranching (hybrid approach with TEVAR)
  • ATRIAL FIBRILLATION risk post-arch repair: high (inflammation, cross-clamping); anticipate POAF
  • Arch involvement complicates dissection (malperfusion to head, upper extremities)
  • Open arch repair: requires circulatory arrest, selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP) Descending thoracic (left subclavian to diaphragm)
  • Below pericardium, extrapleural
  • Critical blood supply to spinal cord: artery of Adamkiewicz (usually T9–L2, left-sided 80%); cross-clamping → spinal cord ischemia risk
  • TEVAR increasingly used; less invasive than open thoracotomy
  • Post-op neuro checks essential (paraplegia risk, delayed onset possible) Thoracoabdominal (TAAA, crosses diaphragm)
  • Extends into abdominal aorta; may involve visceral branches (celiac, SMA, renal)
  • Highest operative risk (visceral ischemia, paraplegia, renal failure)
  • Crawford classification (Type I–V) predicts complexity and morbidity
  • Open repair gold standard; some centers adopting hybrid/fenestrated TEVAR
Imaging modality comparison — CT vs. cardiac MR for surveillance CT Angiography (CTA)
  • Speed: minutes; good for acute settings
  • Radiation: significant dose; concern for cumulative exposure over decades
  • Advantages: detects calcification, branch involvement, dissection flap, pseudoaneurysm; 3D reconstruction; multiplanar assessment
  • Limitations: contrast (creatinine clearance needed); radiation for young patients with lifelong surveillance
  • Reproducibility: phase matters (systole vs. diastole); protocol must be standardized Cardiac MR
  • No radiation: major advantage for serial surveillance in young/genetic patients
  • Soft-tissue contrast: excellent for wall assessment, branch flow
  • Limitations: longer acquisition time; MR not suitable with ferromagnetic implants (pacemakers, older metallic devices); cannot assess calcification well; contrast (gadolinium) requires renal function
  • Reproducibility: same-scanner same-sequence preferred for decades of follow-up; allows precise longitudinal comparison
  • Timing: systole vs. diastole critical; must be identical between scans Transthoracic echo
  • No radiation, bedside, real-time: ideal for routine follow-up of ascending aorta/root
  • Limited field: cannot assess descending aorta adequately
  • Operator-dependent: quality varies
  • Use: first-line for ascending root measurement; limited as sole surveillance tool for full thoracic aorta Recommendation for longitudinal surveillance: For young patients with genetic aortopathies (Marfan, LDS, vEDS, FTAA), cardiac MR is preferred to avoid cumulative CT radiation. If MR unavailable or contraindicated, CTA with minimized dose protocols acceptable. Measurement must be at identical anatomic level, same imaging phase each time.
Size indexing — aortic size index & aortic height index Aortic size index (ASI)
  • Formula: aortic diameter (cm) / body surface area (m²)
  • Clinical use: important in small patients; a 4.5 cm aorta in a 1.4 m² BSA patient (ASI 3.2) may have similar risk to 5.5 cm in a 1.9 m² BSA patient (ASI 2.9)
  • Marfan thresholds often expressed as ASI: ≥3.0–3.1 cm/m² may trigger surgery in Marfan (equivalent to ~4.5 cm in 1.5 m² patient)
  • vEDS thresholds: often lower ASI (2.4–2.7 cm/m²) due to fragile tissue Aortic height index (AHI)
  • Formula: aortic diameter / height (cm/cm, unitless ratio)
  • Used in some centers (especially Marfan protocols) to normalize for patient stature
  • Less common than BSA-based ASI in current practice Nursing pearl: if patient is notably small or large, ask whether size thresholds have been adjusted for BSA or height by the surgical team. Don't assume all patients with 5.5 cm ascending aorta are at identical surgical threshold.
Genetic syndromes — inheritance, surveillance, surgical thresholds Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation)
  • Inheritance: autosomal dominant; ~25% de novo mutations
  • Cardiac manifestations: aortic root dilation (80%), aortic regurgitation, mitral valve prolapse
  • Surgical threshold: ascending aorta ≥4.5–5.0 cm (lower than degenerative)
  • Medical management: beta-blockers (propranolol, atenolol) standard; losartan adjunct
  • Family screening: first-degree relatives (siblings, children, parents) need genetic testing + aortic imaging
  • Pregnancy risk: significant; requires maternal-fetal medicine + cardiology
  • Aortic event risk: ~50% if untreated; ~10% with beta-blockade + surgery at threshold Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1/2 mutations)
  • Inheritance: autosomal dominant
  • Vascular manifestations: early, severe aortic disease; arterial aneurysms at multiple sites; aortic dissection can occur spontaneously
  • Surgical threshold: ascending ≥4.5 cm (aggressive); even smaller if symptomatic or rapidly growing
  • Systemic features: hypertelorism, bifid uvula, high-arched palate, skin hyperextensibility, joint hypermobility
  • Family screening: essential; ~50% of relatives affected
  • Prognosis: worse than Marfan; aortic events can occur despite surgery (need lifelong post-op surveillance) Vascular Ehlers-Danlos (vEDS, COL3A1 mutations)
  • Inheritance: autosomal recessive (rare) or autosomal dominant (more common)
  • Vascular manifestations: fragile vessel wall, spontaneous arterial dissection, aortic rupture, bowel/uterine perforation
  • Surgical threshold: ascending aorta ≥4.0–4.5 cm (lowest threshold due to rupture risk at smaller sizes)
  • Systemic features: thin translucent skin, easy bruising, small stature, joint hypermobility
  • Surgical challenge: tissue friability makes repair technically difficult; high operative mortality
  • Prognosis: median lifespan ~48 years if vascular involvement present
  • Family screening: imperative; genetic counseling recommended before pregnancy Familial thoracic aortic disease (TAAD panel — ACTA2, MYH11, MYLK, PRKG1)
  • Inheritance: autosomal dominant
  • Phenotype: aortic root + descending involvement; young patients without syndromic features
  • Surgical threshold: variable; typically ≥5.5 cm but context-dependent
  • Family screening: genetic testing of relatives with aortic imaging surveillance Syndromic vs. non-syndromic aortopathy distinction important for counseling:
  • Marfan, LDS, vEDS = systemic disease; affects eyes, skeletal system, connective tissue systemically
  • FTAA = aortic-limited inheritance (no systemic features), but still genetic; family screening critical
Bicuspid aortic valve & aortopathy — valve function, aortic disease risk Bicuspid AV epidemiology
  • 1–2% of general population
  • 50–80% develop aortic root/ascending TAA
  • Age of aortic disease onset: wide range (20s–60s+) Aortic regurgitation + bicuspid AV
  • Root dilation often causes aortic insufficiency
  • Some bicuspid patients need AVR (aortic valve replacement) before aortic size reaches surgical threshold
  • Post-AVR, aortic root continues to dilate in many patients → lifelong surveillance even after valve replacement Surgical thresholds for bicuspid + TAA
  • Without risk factors: ≥5.5 cm (some centers 5.25 cm)
  • With risk factors (male, family hx dissection, AR, SBP >150, syncope): ≥5.0 cm
  • Risk stratification helps individualize threshold Post-AVR surveillance
  • AVR does NOT halt aortic root dilation; surveillance continues
  • Some centers recommend post-AVR imaging q1–2 years if root was dilated pre-op
  • Prosthetic valve complication monitoring (paravalvular regurgitation, endocarditis risk) separate from aortic surveillance Family screening
  • Bicuspid AV has familial clustering; first-degree relatives should be screened with echo
  • Not all relatives inherit bicuspid, but those who do should be monitored for TAA
Beta-blockers vs. ARBs in Marfan — evidence summary Beta-blockade in Marfan
  • Evidence: propranolol slows aortic root growth in Marfan patients (landmark studies late 1990s–2000s)
  • Mechanism: reduces dP/dt (rate of pressure change), decreases wall stress
  • Current guideline: beta-blockers (propranolol, atenolol, other) standard of care in Marfan with aortic involvement
  • Target HR: resting 50–60 bpm
  • Efficacy: ~50% reduction in growth rate with beta-block vs. untreated ARBs (losartan) in Marfan — ongoing debate
  • LOAT trial (2013, small): losartan + atenolol vs. atenolol alone → losartan arm showed lower growth rate
  • COMPARE trial (2018, larger): losartan + beta-blockers vs. beta-blockers alone → no significant difference in primary outcome (aortic diameter growth), but secondary outcomes favored combination
  • Current interpretation: losartan shows modest additional benefit in some studies; not proven definitively superior to beta-block + ACE-I
  • Practice variation: many centers use losartan as adjunct; not universally mandated Isselbacher 2022 guideline:
  • Beta-blockers: Class I (standard of care) in Marfan with aortic disease
  • ARBs: acceptable as adjunct; more evidence needed for firm recommendation Key teaching point: Beta-blockers essential; losartan adjunct is reasonable but not mandatory. Do NOT stop beta-blockers based on losartan availability.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear, re-escalate.

  • Sudden, severe chest or back pain (inter-scapular especially) → dissection until proven otherwise; STAT CTA, code team
  • New pulse differential (upper vs. upper, or upper vs. lower extremity) → branch malperfusion from dissection or aneurysm growth
  • Focal neurologic deficit (weakness, facial droop, speech change, paraplegia) → stroke or spinal cord ischemia; activate stroke code
  • Acute hypertensive crisis (SBP >180, reflex tachycardia) on current regimen → medication non-adherence or inadequate dosing; escalate for optimization
  • Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, tachycardia, cool extremities) → dissection, rupture, or cardiogenic shock; immediate team notification
  • New or worsening dyspnea — heart failure from AR, pulmonary edema, or pericardial effusion
  • Rapid aortic growth on serial imaging — any increase >0.5 cm over 1 year is alarming; contact team even if absolute size below threshold
  • Aortic regurgitation murmur developing de novo — root dilation worsening, consider earlier surgery
  • Fever + aortic aneurysm finding → mycotic aortitis (endocarditis sequela); blood cultures, antibiotics, urgent surgery
  • Pre-op patient with worsening anxiety, restlessness — may herald anesthetic or dissection concern; notify team
  • Post-dissection patient with sustained hypertension — residual aortic disease; ensure close follow-up imaging

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Ascending aorta surgical threshold DIFFERS markedly by etiology — don't apply one universal cutoff. Marfan/LDS ≥4.5 cm; vEDS ≥4.0 cm; bicuspid ≥5.0 cm with risk factors; degenerative ≥5.5 cm. Asking "what's the threshold?" without knowing the patient's etiology is the #1 error. Check operative note, consult summary, or genetic testing results. When in doubt, ask the surgical team explicitly: "What's our threshold for THIS patient?"

  2. Growth >0.5 cm/year is a surgical indication regardless of absolute size. A 5.0 cm TAA growing at 0.7 cm/year takes priority over a 5.4 cm stable TAA. Serial imaging is critical — don't lose track of baseline measurements. Document growth velocity at each interval; flag for surgical team if accelerating.

  3. Genetic syndrome family screening is essential, not optional. Marfan/LDS/vEDS first-degree relatives have 50% inheritance risk. Not screened = future surprise aneurysm or dissection in a relative. Ensure genetics referral + family imaging screening arranged before discharge. This is a discharge planning requirement, not a "nice-to-have."

  4. Fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) are contraindicated in ALL TAA patients — FDA black box warning (2018). If TAA patient is prescribed fluoroquinolone, escalate immediately for antibiotic switch. Educational opportunity for nursing staff to flag this with prescribers.

  5. Pregnancy + aortopathy = catastrophic dissection risk. Hemodynamic changes (↑ CO, ↓ SVR, ↑ plasma volume) + hormonal elastin degradation increase dissection risk 100-fold. Any female of childbearing age with TAA needs contraception counseling and pregnancy risk discussion (maternal-fetal medicine + cardiology consult if pregnancy planned). Lower surgical thresholds often apply.

  6. BP target SBP ≤130 mmHg, HR 50–60 is stricter than standard HTN management. Error: accepting SBP 140–150 because "that's the patient's baseline." In TAA, lower is better (slows growth, reduces dissection). Adjust meds upward if not at goal; don't default to "patient's baseline."

  7. Beta-blockers slow aortic root growth in Marfan; assume they're essential. Don't wean post-op, don't stop for mild bradycardia (HR 48–50) without cardiology approval. Hold only if HR <45 or SBP <90; call team before discontinuing. Beta-blockers are often the most important medication in Marfan TAA.

  8. Losartan in Marfan is adjunctive, not proven definitive. LOAT and COMPARE trials showed modest benefit at best. Beta-blockers are the anchor; losartan is optional. Document whether patient's regimen includes losartan and the rationale; practice variation is common.

  9. CT radiation cumulative burden matters for young patients. Genetic aortopathies (Marfan, LDS, vEDS, FTAA) need lifelong surveillance. Young patient getting CTA q6 months for 60 years = significant cumulative radiation. Cardiac MR is no-radiation alternative; excellent for same-scanner longitudinal comparison. Discuss with patient + team; advocate for MR when available.

  10. Measure aortic size at identical anatomic level + imaging phase each time. Root growth can be asymmetric; measuring sinuses of Valsalva on one scan, sinotubular junction on the next = false positive growth.

    Same-scanner, same-sequence imaging preferred for decades of surveillance. Document the exact measurement site in the chart.

  11. Aortic size index (aortic diameter / BSA) matters for small or large patients. A 5.5 cm aorta in a 1.4 m² patient has different stress than 5.5 cm in a 2.1 m² patient. Ask if thresholds have been adjusted for BSA; don't assume all 5.5 cm thresholds are identical.

  12. Saccular (localized) aneurysms rupture at smaller sizes than fusiform (circumferential). If imaging describes saccular component, escalate to surgical team; may lower surgical threshold. More common with infection, trauma, or pseudoaneurysm.

  13. Mycotic aneurysm is a surgical EMERGENCY. Aortic aneurysm secondary to bacteremia (endocarditis, UTI, pneumonia, other) has extremely high rupture risk. Presentation: fever, sepsis, aortic aneurysm on imaging. Requires emergent surgery + antibiotics. If blood cultures positive + aortic aneurysm found, this is a level-1 emergency.

  14. Bicuspid AV aortopathy continues post-AVR. AVR does NOT halt aortic root dilation. Many post-AVR patients need continued surveillance and may require redo aortic root surgery 10–20 years later. This is a common teaching point for patients who think "the valve surgery fixed it all."

  15. Incidental TAA finding must not be lost to follow-up. Patient discovered with 4.5 cm TAA on CTA for pneumonia must have: cardiology referral, genetic work-up if young, baseline imaging for future comparison, written surveillance plan. Error: radiologist notes aneurysm, but no follow-up arranged; patient lost to clinic. Ensure discharge summary includes imaging follow-up schedule and cardiology referral.

cards.title: Tricuspid Regurgitation
cards.quickAnswer: Tricuspid regurgitation (TR) = backflow of blood across the tricuspid valve during RV systole. Secondary (functional) TR (~80–90%: RV dilation from LV failure, pulmonary HTN, or AF) dominates; primary TR (~10–20%: endocarditis, carcinoid, Ebstein, CIED lead) is less common. Severe TR presents as right-sided HF: peripheral edema, ascites, congestive hepatopathy, elevated JVD. Treatment: diuretics (loop + MRA) for fluid management; treat underlying cause (LV disease, pulmonary HTN); surgical repair (annuloplasty or replacement, often concurrent with LV/mitral surgery); transcatheter options (TriClip, PASCAL, Evoque FDA-approved 2023–2024 per TRILUMINATE/TRISCEND data). Isolated TV surgery carries 10–15% mortality; prefer concurrent LHS repair. Post-op: RV recovery takes weeks; monitor for arrhythmias and mechanical complications.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who it applies to, why it matters.

  • Definition: Blood regurgitates backward across the tricuspid valve during RV systole, decreasing forward flow to the pulmonary circulation and causing systemic venous congestion.
  • Epidemiology:
  • Most common valvular lesion overall (present in ~90% of autopsy series); usually asymptomatic/mild
  • Functional (secondary) TR: ~80–90% of cases; caused by RV and tricuspid annulus dilation from LV disease, pulmonary hypertension, RV cardiomyopathy, or chronic AF
  • Primary (organic) TR: ~10–20% of cases; intrinsic valve pathology (endocarditis, carcinoid, Ebstein anomaly, CIED lead-related, blunt trauma, rheumatic disease)
  • Who this applies to: Preoperative patients awaiting TV repair/replacement or transcatheter TR intervention; postoperative TV surgery patients; patients with RV failure related to severe TR; ICU/stepdown patients with decompensated venous congestion
  • Why it matters: Often underdiagnosed ("forgotten valve") until hepatic decompensation appears. Severe TR increases morbidity and mortality if untreated. Emerging transcatheter options (TriClip, PASCAL, Evoque) now offer alternatives to surgery for high-risk patients.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Why this happens. Mechanism explanation for novice and advanced beginner.

sections.heading: Primary vs. Secondary TR
sections.bodyHtml:
Primary (Organic) Valve Disease

The valve itself is damaged or structurally abnormal:

  • Endocarditis — most common primary cause; especially in IVDU (S. aureus); septic vegetations cause leaflet perforation or destruction; septic pulmonary emboli
  • Carcinoid heart disease — serotonin-mediated fibrosis causes valve thickening and retraction; bilateral involvement (tricuspid + pulmonic, not isolated TR)
  • Ebstein anomaly — congenital; apical displacement of posterior and septal leaflets creates atrial chamber; TR + arrhythmia (WPW, SVT) + cyanosis
  • CIED lead-related — iatrogenic leaflet injury from pacemaker or ICD lead; risk increases with duration and lead manipulation; often underrecognized
  • Rheumatic heart disease — rare, usually combined with mitral or aortic disease
  • Blunt trauma — papillary muscle rupture or leaflet tear (uncommon)

Secondary (Functional) Valve Disease — The Dominant Form

The valve leaflets are intrinsically normal, but the annulus and RV dilate, preventing leaflet coaptation:

  • RV dilation from any cause (LV systolic dysfunction, pulmonary HTN, RV cardiomyopathy) → annulus stretches → leaflets fail to coapt → regurgitation
  • LV dysfunction (dilated cardiomyopathy, CAD, post-MI) → pulmonary HTN + RV dilation → functional TR
  • Pulmonary hypertension (any etiology: chronic lung disease, interstitial lung disease, PE history, connective tissue disease, idiopathic) → RV strain → dilation
  • RV cardiomyopathy (primary or secondary to chronic load)
  • Atrial fibrillation → RA dilation → annular stretch → functional TR

The annular dilation (>40 mm) is the primary driver of functional TR; RV dilation follows.

sections.heading: Hemodynamic Consequences
sections.bodyHtml:
RIGHT-sided heart failure phenotype:

  • Volume overload: RA pressure rises → systemic venous hypertension → transmitted to hepatic veins, portal system, and subcutaneous tissues
  • Peripheral edema — gravity-dependent; worse end of day; RA pressure > 10–12 mmHg exceeds plasma oncotic pressure
  • Ascites — elevated RA/hepatic venous pressure → sinusoidal pressure increase → portal hypertension physiology
  • Congestive hepatopathy — hepatic capsule stretch, hypoxia from venous stasis → hepatomegaly, RUQ pain; can progress to hepatic cirrhosis
  • Anorexia, early satiety — hepatic congestion, ascites compress stomach
  • Weakness, fatigue — low cardiac output (regurgitation volume competes with forward flow)
  • Pulsatile hepatomegaly — hepatic vein distension transmitted to liver; pathognomonic sign
  • Arrhythmias — RA strain from chronic hypertension predisposes to AF, which worsens TR further

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: What the patient looks like at bedside — observable signs and demographic patterns.

sections.heading: Typical Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Secondary TR from LV disease:

  • Patient with known dilated cardiomyopathy, CAD, or hypertensive heart disease develops peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly
  • May be asymptomatic for years (mild TR tolerated well), then decompensates with LV disease progression
  • RV often dilated and hypokinetic pre-operatively if awaiting cardiac surgery

Primary TR — Endocarditis:

  • IVDU patient with fever, new murmur, SOB, RUQ pain (lung emboli + hepatic infarcts)
  • Sepsis + positive blood cultures
  • May present with septic shock, need for early surgery

Primary TR — Carcinoid:

  • Patient with known carcinoid tumor or new constellation of flushing, diarrhea, wheezing, GI symptoms
  • Bilateral valvular involvement (tricuspid + pulmonic)
  • More guarded surgical prognosis

Primary TR — CIED Lead-Related:

  • Patient with pacemaker or ICD; new or worsening TR on echo; no other valve pathology
  • Risk increases with years of pacing; lead manipulation increases risk
  • Often discovered incidentally; may contribute to RV dysfunction

sections.heading: Physical Examination Findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Holosystolic murmur at left lower sternal border (4th–5th intercostal space), increases with inspiration (Carvallo sign)
  • Pulsatile hepatomegaly — hepatic systolic pulsation synchronous with carotid pulse; hallmark of significant TR
  • Elevated JVD with prominent systolic CV waves (systolic regurgitant wave); visible neck pulsations
  • Peripheral edema (bilateral, dependent)
  • Ascites (may be massive)
  • RV heave (RV enlargement and hypertrophy)
  • S3 or S4 gallop (RV dysfunction)
  • Atrial fibrillation on ECG (common in chronic RA pressure elevation)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml: Systematic information gathering. No actions yet. Target: 5 minutes of bedside and chart review.

sections.heading: Physical Exam & Vital Signs
sections.bodyHtml:
• Hemodynamics: Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, SpO₂, perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature, mental status)
  • Venous pressure: JVD height at 45° angle; prominent CV waves; hepatojugular reflux
  • Cardiac exam: Apical impulse (displaced/diffuse if RV enlarged), RV heave, murmur character (holosystolic at LSB + inspiration)
  • Abdominal: Liver size, tenderness, pulsatility, ascites, edema, skin integrity
  • Extremities: Bilateral lower extremity edema grade; capillary refill; skin color/temperature

sections.heading: Labs & Prior Imaging
sections.bodyHtml:
• Recent ECG: Rate, rhythm (AF?), QTc (if considering antiarrhythmic), signs of RV strain
  • Echocardiography (TTE/TEE): Assess TR severity (jet area, vena contracta, RA/RV size, vena contracta width), RV systolic function (TAPSE, FAC, RV strain), TV leaflet morphology, annulus diameter, estimate RA/RV pressures
  • Liver function tests: AST, ALT, bilirubin, albumin (congestive hepatopathy may depress all; INR may be elevated)
  • Renal function: Creatinine, BUN (diuretic effect; prerenal azotemia from low CO)
  • Electrolytes: K⁺, Mg²⁺ (diuretic losses; important if considering antiarrhythmic)
  • Hemoglobin: Baseline before surgery (blood loss risk in cirrhotic hepatopathy)
  • BNP/NT-proBNP: Elevated; correlates with RV strain
  • Coagulation: PT/INR, platelets (congestive hepatopathy reduces synthesis; portal HTN may cause thrombocytopenia)
  • Chest X-ray: RA/RV enlargement, pulmonary vascular pattern (rule out pulmonary disease as source of pulmonary HTN)
  • Cardiac catheterization (if planned surgery): RA pressure tracing (prominent S wave); measure PVR; assess for CAD; inform surgical planning

sections.heading: RV Function Assessment
sections.bodyHtml:
• TAPSE (Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion) — normal ≥17 mm; <17 mm suggests RV dysfunction; load-dependent (see pitfalls)
  • FAC (RV Fractional Area Change) — normal >35%; <35% indicates RV systolic impairment
  • RV strain (RV S' on tissue Doppler) — normal >10 cm/s; <10 cm/s indicates systolic impairment
  • RV free-wall longitudinal strain — increasingly used; more load-independent than TAPSE

sections.heading: Medications & Comorbidities
sections.bodyHtml:
• Current diuretics: Loop dose, thiazide use, K-sparing agent (spironolactone?); response to diuretics
  • ACE-I/ARB, beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists — baseline for LV disease management
  • Antiarrhythmics: On amiodarone, sotalol, dofetilide? Baseline QTc?
  • Anticoagulation: Home warfarin/DOAC? Mechanical prosthetic TV if prior repair/replacement?
  • Comorbidities: COPD, OSA, pulmonary HTN, liver disease, renal disease, diabetes, prior cardiac surgery (device, valve prosthesis?)

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Focused on the three pillars: medical, transcatheter, and surgical. Diagnostic TR (primary) vs. functional TR requires different escalation paths.

sections.heading: 5A. Medical Management (Bridging to Intervention or Symptom Control)
sections.bodyHtml:
Diuretic Strategy — Cornerstone of Symptom Relief

Unlike aortic stenosis, TR patients tolerate aggressive diuresis well because RV dysfunction is often overcongestion-driven.

  • Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide) — first-line; target euvolemia (reduce ascites, edema, pulmonary congestion)
  • Initial: furosemide 40–80 mg IV BID–TID or torsemide 20 mg IV BID (torsemide has better bioavailability if transitioning to PO)
  • Escalate if resistance developing (higher doses or more frequent dosing)
  • Thiazides — add for loop-resistant edema
  • Potassium-sparing agents / MRA (spironolactone) — especially beneficial for RV-related congestion
  • Typical: spironolactone 12.5–25 mg daily, titrate to max 50 mg daily; recheck K⁺ and Cr within 1 week
  • Improves RV function; addresses hepatic cirrhosis pathophysiology; prevents hypokalemia from loop use
  • Monitor K⁺ closely (hyperkalemia risk if renal dysfunction); acceptable range 4.0–5.0 mEq/L in this population

Treat Underlying Cause

  • LV dysfunction: ACE-I/ARB, beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists (standard HF therapy); many patients with moderate functional TR improve significantly with LV optimization alone — recheck echo in 3–6 months before committing to TV surgery
  • Pulmonary hypertension: Follow institutional PH protocol (inhaled nitric oxide, phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, endothelin antagonists per echo guidance)
  • Atrial fibrillation: Rate-control (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCBs); consider anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2

Medications to Avoid or Use Cautiously

  • Negative inotropes at high doses — RV already struggling; avoid aggressive beta-blockade in hemodynamically tenuous patients
  • Excessive diuresis — reduces RV preload; worsens CO and systemic perfusion; diuretics are needed but balanced against adequate filling

Endocarditis Prophylaxis

  • Not routinely indicated for native TR per guidelines
  • Post-valve repair/replacement (prosthetic) — antibiotic prophylaxis IS indicated for dental/invasive procedures
  • High suspicion for IVDU endocarditis — obtain blood cultures before antibiotics; TEE often diagnostic (vegetations); notify surgery team early (many require early intervention)

sections.heading: 5B. Transcatheter Therapies
sections.bodyHtml:
Emerging Game-Changer Options — FDA approved 2023–2024; rapidly expanding access for high-risk patients

Device Mechanism Indication Key Data Niche
TriClip (MitraClip adapted for TV) Catheter-based edge-to-edge clip; reduces TR jet Functional TR; moderate-to-severe; good leaflet anatomy; high surgical risk TRILUMINATE (Sorajja et al., 2023) — 80% ≥1-grade improvement; 50% ≥2-grade improvement High-risk surgical candidates; elderly; multiple comorbidities; can be same-day discharge
PASCAL (Cardiovalve) Similar edge-to-edge concept; broader leaflet coverage Functional TR; anatomically favorable; high-risk patients TRISCEND (Sorajja et al., 2020) — >80% success rate; lower thrombosis risk vs TriClip Alternative to TriClip; broader landing zone
Evoque (Cardiac) Intracardiac spacer; fills regurgitant orifice without crossing annulus Functional TR; RV-dilated phenotype; severe symptoms FDA approved 2024; early data: significant symptom improvement Purely intracardiac approach; avoids annular device
Annuloplasty bands (Cardioband, others) Transcatheter band reduces annular diameter Functional TR; annular dilation >40 mm Approved in Europe, emerging US experience Durable; addresses root cause (annular dilation)

Inclusion Criteria for Transcatheter Intervention:

  • High or prohibitive surgical risk (elderly, frailty, multiple comorbidities, LVEF <35%, RVEF <30%, severe pulmonary HTN)
  • Anatomy favorable (3D TEE needed)
  • Symptomatic (NYHA II–IV or significant volume overload)
  • Failure of medical optimization
  • Multidisciplinary team consensus (CT surgery, Interventional Cardiology, Echocardiography, Anesthesia)

Advantages vs. Surgery:

  • Minimal invasiveness; same-day discharge feasible for TriClip
  • No cardiopulmonary bypass
  • Lower perioperative morbidity
  • Reduced recovery time

Limitations:

  • Requires specialized expertise (interventional cardiology, advanced echocardiography)
  • Long-term durability data still emerging (especially for devices approved 2023–2024)
  • Not suitable for primary valve disease (endocarditis, carcinoid) — structural pathology requires surgical replacement
  • Anatomy may be unfavorable (severely deformed leaflets, massive RV dilation, severe annular dilation)

sections.heading: 5C. Surgical Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Surgical Indications — When to Escalate to the OR

Severe TR is a surgical disease. Consider surgical intervention (repair or replacement) in these scenarios:

Class Indications
Class I (Strong) Symptomatic severe TR (NYHA III–IV or significant volume overload refractory to medical therapy)
Severe TR + undergoing other cardiac surgery (MV repair/replacement, AVR, CABG) — repair at time of LHS
Primary TR (endocarditis, carcinoid, Ebstein, CIED lead) + significant symptoms
Severe functional TR + progressive RV dilation + signs of RV failure (TAPSE <17 mm, FAC <35%)
Class IIa (Reasonable) Asymptomatic severe TR + progressive RV dilation on serial echo (Stage C1)
Moderate functional TR + RV dilation + planned LV surgery (repair concurrent with LHS)
Recurrent severe functional TR post-op from prior cardiac surgery

Surgical Approaches

Approach Indication Technique Notes
TV Annuloplasty Functional TR; good leaflet mobility; isolated or concurrent with LHS De Vega suture; ring annuloplasty (Carpentier, Duran, Edwards); edge-to-edge (Alfieri) Preferred approach for functional TR; ~10% recurrence if isolated
TV Replacement Primary TR (endocarditis, carcinoid, Ebstein); failed annuloplasty; poor leaflet tissue quality Mechanical (St. Jude, CarboMedics); bioprosthetic (porcine, bovine, decellularized) Higher morbidity than repair; requires anticoagulation if mechanical
Annular Size-Specific Prostheses TV annulus >40 mm; need to downsize; standard bands fail Specialized rings (Contegra, SynerGraft) Emerging data showing better outcomes than undersizing

Postoperative Considerations

  • RV dysfunction is the dominant post-op concern — RV is often enlarged and dysokinetic pre-operatively; recovery takes weeks (see Related Cards: Tricuspid Valve Repair / Tricuspid Valve Replacement)
  • Arrhythmias — common post-TV surgery; AF, heart block, ectopy from surgical trauma/atriotomy
  • Mechanical complications — prosthetic regurgitation (replacement), dehiscence (rare), thrombosis (mechanical prosthesis requires anticoagulation)
  • Hepatic recovery — congestive hepatopathy often improves dramatically post-TV repair as RA pressures normalize; hepatic synthetic function may recover over weeks to months

sections.heading: 5D. Post-LHS Concomitant TV Surgery Indications
sections.bodyHtml:
Key Principle: Repair at time of LV/MV surgery if any significant TR present

When a patient is already in the OR for mitral or LV surgery, even moderate functional TR should be addressed surgically because:

  1. Additional operative time/risk is minimal (TV is easily accessible)
  2. Secondary TR improves with LV/MV correction but repair concurrent with LHS is more durable than watchful waiting
  3. Reoperation for late worsening TV regurgitation is high-risk

Indications for concurrent TV surgery during LHS:

  • Any degree of moderate or greater functional TR
  • Mild TR + markedly dilated annulus (>40 mm) + RV dilation
  • Mild TR + severe RV dysfunction (TAPSE <17 mm, FAC <35%)
  • Mild TR + planned complex LV surgery (extensive resection, replacement, LVAD insertion)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for notifying the provider:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room, preop/postop status]."

B: "Patient with [primary vs. secondary] tricuspid regurgitation, [brief cause: e.g., dilated cardiomyopathy, endocarditis]. Current NYHA class [II–IV] / on diuretics [loop, spironolactone doses]. Recent echo [date]: [TR severity, annulus size, RV size, TAPSE]."

A: "Patient is [stable on current regimen / decompensating despite diuretics / presenting with acute symptoms]. [Specific symptoms: edema, ascites, new palpitations, SOB]. Labs: K⁺ [value], Cr [value], liver function [trending]. Current diuretic response: [improvement, plateau, worsening]."

R: "Requesting [optimization of diuretics / escalation to transcatheter assessment / surgical consultation / echocardiography / catheterization]. Would you like me to [specific action: transfer to ICU, hold diuretics pending labs, prepare for procedure]?"

Who to call

Situation Contact
Mild–moderate TR, stable on medical therapy Primary cardiologist / hospitalist; can defer to next clinic visit
Moderate-to-severe TR, symptoms refractory to optimized diuretics Interventional cardiologist (transcatheter assessment) + CT surgery (surgical option)
Severe primary TR (endocarditis, carcinoid) CT surgery STAT; infectious disease if endocarditis
Severe TR + acute decompensation (pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock) CT surgery + ICU team; consider ECMO if cardiogenic shock
CIED-related TR (pacemaker/ICD lead) EP (device) + CT surgery (TV repair/lead revision)
Post-op TV repair/replacement + hemodynamic instability CT surgery (return to ICU; possible return to OR for mechanical complication)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections — collapsed by default on PowerApp.

7.1 The 5-Grade TR Severity Scale (ASE 2023) American Society of Echocardiography recommends a 5-grade severity scale for functional TR, moving beyond the traditional mild/moderate/severe categorization:
GradeJet Area (cm²)Jet/RA RatioVena Contracta (cm)RV SizeRA SizeClinical Correlate
I (Mild)<3.5<20%<0.3NormalNormalIncidental; rarely symptomatic
II (Moderate)3.5–6.020–40%0.3–0.6Normal–dilatedDilatedMay become symptomatic with RV dilation
III (Moderately Severe)6.0–8.540–60%0.6–0.8DilatedMarkedly dilatedOften symptomatic; increased mortality risk untreated
IV (Severe)8.5–10.560–80%0.8–1.0Markedly dilatedMarkedly dilatedSymptomatic; high mortality untreated; surgical/transcatheter candidate
V (Torrential)>10.5>80%>1.0Massive dilationMassive dilationHemodynamically critical; urgent intervention required; RV may be dysmotile
Clinical Pearl: Echo severity must correlate with clinical findings. A patient with "moderate TR on echo" but orthopnea, massive ascites, and pulsatile hepatomegaly is functionally severe and needs intervention. Treat the patient, not the number.
7.2 Annular Dilation as Primary Driver of Functional TR The tricuspid annulus normally measures 32–35 mm. When it dilates beyond 40 mm, leaflet coaptation fails even if the leaflets are intrinsically normal. Mechanisms of annular dilation:
  • RV dilation — most common; RV stretches the annulus
  • RA dilation — increases annular diameter directly
  • Atrial fibrillation — RA remodeling from chronic atrial pressures and loss of atrial kick
  • Chronic pulmonary hypertension — RV hypertrophy + dilation → annular stretch
  • LV disease — LV dilation raises RA pressure → RA dilation → annular stretch Surgical implication: Annuli >40 mm should trigger consideration of annuloplasty or downsizing because simple "watchful waiting" often fails — the annulus continues to dilate as RV disease progresses. Transcatheter implication: Annuloplasty bands (Cardioband) are increasingly used to reduce annular diameter in functional TR, addressing the root cause rather than just treating the jet.
7.3 CIED Lead-Induced TR (Increasing Problem with Leadless Pacers) Mechanism:
  • Transvenous pacemaker or ICD leads cross the tricuspid valve
  • Chronic lead-valve interaction → leaflet perforation, thickening, or immobility
  • Risk increases with:
  • Duration of pacing (risk substantial after 5+ years)
  • Lead manipulation during device replacements
  • Multiple leads (dual-chamber > single-chamber)
  • Lead repositioning Clinical significance:
  • Often asymptomatic until RV dilation develops
  • Discovered incidentally on routine echo in pacemaker patients
  • Can contribute to RV dysfunction and TR progression
  • Leadless pacers emerging as alternative to reduce lead-valve interaction, but long-term data still accumulating Evaluation:
  • Device interrogation (sensing, capture thresholds)
  • TEE assessment of lead position and valve interaction
  • Serial echocardiography to track TR progression Management:
  • If mild TR and no symptoms: observe; serial echo annually
  • If moderate-to-severe TR or progressive: consider lead extraction + leadless pacer insertion OR TV repair at time of device replacement
  • EP + CT surgery collaboration needed
7.4 Ebstein's Anomaly Congenital malformation: apical displacement of the posterior and septal leaflets of the tricuspid valve. Pathophysiology:
  • Abnormal leaflet development results in "atrialized" RV (part of RV acts as extension of RA)
  • Reduced functional RV volume
  • Predisposition to arrhythmias (Wolff-Parkinson-White, orthodromic SVT common) Spectrum:
  • Mild: asymptomatic, discovered incidentally
  • Severe: cyanosis (right-to-left shunt if ASD present), severe TR, arrhythmias, RV dysfunction Presentation:
  • May be asymptomatic in childhood, symptoms manifest in adulthood with RV dilation/dysfunction
  • Dyspnea, palpitations, syncope (arrhythmia)
  • Cyanosis (if ASD component) Management:
  • Surgical timing depends on: severity of TR, degree of cyanosis, RV function, arrhythmia burden
  • Surgical options: TV repair (leaflet plication, annuloplasty), TV replacement (if repair not feasible)
  • Arrhythmia management: may require MAZE or catheter ablation concurrently Special considerations: Pregnancy in Ebstein's patients requires careful planning (increased RV load, arrhythmia risk).
7.5 Carcinoid Heart Disease Mechanism: Serotonin (and other vasoactive amines) secreted by neuroendocrine tumors causes fibrosis and retraction of right-sided valves. Pathophysiology:
  • NOT isolated TR — typically bilateral involvement (tricuspid + pulmonic)
  • Leaflet thickening, retraction, shortened (shortened), immobile
  • Severe regurgitation + stenosis possible
  • RV dysfunction from chronic afterload Epidemiology:
  • Associated with GI carcinoid (midgut), bronchial carcinoid (less common)
  • Occurs in ~50% of carcinoid patients; higher with hepatic metastases (portal venous involvement) Clinical presentation:
  • GI symptoms: diarrhea, abdominal pain
  • Cutaneous flushing, wheezing
  • Right-heart failure (ascites, edema, hepatomegaly) Diagnosis:
  • 5-HIAA (24-hour urine)
  • Octreoscan imaging
  • Echocardiography (bilateral valve thickening, regurgitation, stenosis) Management:
  • Medical: somatostatin analogs (octreotide) slow tumor growth; diuretics/afterload reduction for RV failure
  • Surgical: both tricuspid + pulmonic valve replacement often needed; outcomes more guarded than isolated valve surgery (higher mortality, increased need for re-operation)
  • Cardio-oncology collaboration — coordinate with primary tumor management
7.6 RV Assessment — TAPSE, FAC, RV Strain (Load-Dependence Caveat) TAPSE (Tricuspid Annular Plane Systolic Excursion)
  • Normal: ≥17 mm (by 2D echocardiography)
  • Mild impairment: 12–17 mm
  • Moderate impairment: 8–12 mm
  • Severe impairment: <8 mm
  • Limitation: load-dependent — RV preload and afterload affect TAPSE; low preload (hypovolemia, aggressive diuresis) falsely lowers TAPSE even if RV systolic function intact
  • Clinical application: Serial measurement in same patient (relative change) more reliable than absolute values; pair with FAC and RV strain for comprehensive assessment FAC (RV Fractional Area Change)
  • Normal: >35%
  • Mild impairment: 25–35%
  • Moderate impairment: 15–25%
  • Severe impairment: <15%
  • Advantage: Integrates RV systolic and diastolic function; more robust to preload changes than TAPSE
  • Limitation: Requires good RV endocardial definition on echo RV Systolic Strain (Tissue Doppler S' or Speckle-Tracking)
  • Normal RV free-wall S': >10 cm/s (tissue Doppler) or global RV strain >−20% (2D speckle-tracking)
  • More load-independent than TAPSE
  • Increasingly used: better prognostic value; emerging standard in guidelines (Otto et al., 2023) Clinical Integration:
  • Use all three (TAPSE, FAC, strain) together for holistic RV assessment
  • Serial measurement in same patient more reliable than absolute values
  • Pair echo findings with clinical status; a patient with borderline TAPSE but clinical signs of RV failure (elevated JVD, hepatomegaly, ascites) needs intervention
7.7 Hepatic Congestion as RV Failure Marker — ALT, AST, Bilirubin, Albumin, MELD-XI Congestive hepatopathy = cardiac cirrhosis Chronic venous hepatic congestion causes:
  • Sinusoidal hypertension from elevated RA pressure transmitted to hepatic veins
  • Hepatic ischemia from reduced cardiac output
  • Zone III (central) necrosis with chronic inflammation and fibrosis
  • Progressive cirrhosis if untreated Laboratory markers:
    • ALT, AST — elevated (hepatocyte necrosis); AST > ALT pattern common
    • Bilirubin — may rise (cholestasis component)
    • Albumin — falls with advanced cirrhosis (reduced synthetic function)
    • INR/PT — elevated (reduced factor synthesis)
    • Platelets — low (portal HTN + bone marrow suppression) MELD-XI Score for Pre-TV Surgical Risk Assessment MELD-XI (Model for End-Stage Liver Disease-XI) incorporates INR and bilirubin: MELD-XI = 10 × {0.643 × ln(INR) + 0.957 × ln(bilirubin)} + 21.3
    • <15: low surgical risk from hepatic standpoint
    • 15–20: moderate risk; increased transfusion requirement
    • >20: high risk; consider delaying surgery to optimize cardiac function + allow liver recovery if possible Clinical Pearl: Post-TV repair/replacement, hepatic function often recovers dramatically as RA pressures normalize and cardiac output improves. INR, albumin, platelet count can normalize over weeks to months even if cirrhotic picture pre-operatively. This "hepatic recovery" is one of the strongest arguments for surgical intervention in severe symptomatic TR with hepatic congestion.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in currently stable patients; if any develop, re-escalate urgently.

  • Worsening peripheral edema or new ascites despite diuretics — diuretic-resistant congestion; may herald decompensation; check diuretic dosing and compliance; escalate to interventional team if not improving
  • Elevated creatinine or rising BUN/Cr ratio — diuretic-induced prerenal azotemia from low CO; may need reduced diuretics despite ongoing congestion (delicate balance)
  • Falling albumin or rising INR despite diuresis — hepatic synthetic dysfunction worsening; may indicate progression of hepatic cirrhosis; escalate for surgical candidacy assessment
  • New or worsening palpitations / irregular rhythm — AF is common; verify rhythm, check K⁺/Mg²⁺, notify team for rate vs. rhythm plan
  • RV dilation on serial echo — progressive RV remodeling; indicates worsening functional TR; triggers escalation for intervention consideration
  • Declining TAPSE (<17 mm) or FAC (<35%) — RV systolic dysfunction evolving; high-risk trajectory if untreated
  • Marked hepatomegaly with RUQ pain and fever — consider hepatic infarction from acute TR decompensation or acute endocarditis; escalate urgently
  • Unexplained fever + new murmur — think endocarditis until proven otherwise; blood cultures, TEE, CT surgery notification

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
10–15 high-yield teaching points for proficient and expert clinicians.

  1. "The forgotten valve" — clinical correlation trumps echo severity. TR is the most underdiagnosed valve lesion. Echo report may say "trivial/mild TR" but patient has massive hepatomegaly, ascites, pulsatile hepatic pulse.

    Treat the patient, not the echo grade. Severe symptomatic TR is a surgical disease.

  2. IVDU + sepsis + new murmur = tricuspid endocarditis until proven otherwise. Classic triad: fever, SOB, RUQ pain (lung emboli + hepatic infarcts). Blood cultures before antibiotics. TEE often diagnostic (vegetations). High mortality untreated; early surgery often needed.

    Notify CT surgery STAT; do not delay.

  3. Secondary functional TR from LV disease often improves with LV optimization alone. Don't assume all TR needs surgery. Many patients with moderate functional TR improve significantly with ACE-I/ARB, beta-blockers, spironolactone, diuretics targeting the LV problem.

    Recheck echo in 3–6 months before committing to TV surgery. This is the exception to "treat early"; watch-and-wait with serial echo is reasonable for asymptomatic moderate secondary TR.

  4. Isolated TV surgery carries 10–15% mortality; prefer concurrent repair at time of LHS. If a patient is already in the OR for mitral or LV surgery, repair even mild-to-moderate TR then rather than risk reoperation later.

    Concurrent repair is more durable than waiting for late decompensation.

  5. Congestive hepatopathy IS NOT primary liver disease — it's cardiac cirrhosis. Elevated bilirubin, low albumin, thrombocytopenia, even varices.

    Critical distinction: improve cardiac function = improve liver. Do NOT treat as primary cirrhosis; don't escalate to hepatology unless liver shows no recovery post-TV repair.

    Post-TV repair, liver function often normalizes or improves dramatically as RA pressures normalize.

  6. Tricuspid annulus >40 mm should trigger surgical consideration. Simple ring annuloplasty or newer transcatheter annuloplasty bands (Cardioband) address the root cause. Downsizing alone (no ring) often fails; annulus continues to dilate.

  7. Pacer wire-related TR is under-recognized and increasing. Chronic pacing → lead impingement → leaflet damage → regurgitation.

    If pacemaker/ICD + new or worsening TR, consider pacer lead as culprit. Device interrogation + TEE needed. May require lead extraction + leadless pacer or TV repair.

  8. Carcinoid heart disease = bilateral tricuspid + pulmonic, not isolated TR. Serotonin-mediated fibrosis affects right-sided valves. Wheezing, flushing, GI symptoms from primary carcinoid.

    TV + PV replacement often needed; outcomes more guarded. Consult carcinoid specialist + CT surgery for complex planning.

  9. Ebstein anomaly — congenital apical displacement, not acquired disease. May manifest in adulthood with RV dilation. TR + arrhythmias (WPW, SVT) hallmark.

    Surgical timing depends on RV function, cyanosis severity, arrhythmia burden. TV repair vs. replacement decision made with congenital specialist.

  10. TAPSE is load-dependent; don't over-interpret single value. RV preload and afterload affect TAPSE. Aggressive diuresis can artificially lower TAPSE even if RV systolic function intact.

    Use TAPSE in combination with FAC and RV strain; serial measurements (relative change) more reliable than absolute. Pair with clinical findings (JVD, hepatomegaly, ascites).

  11. Functional TR may improve with LV/MV surgery alone; watch first vs. concurrent repair is a team decision. Some patients with mild-to-moderate secondary TR + severe MV/LV disease are best managed with watchful waiting (no concurrent TV repair), rechecking echo 3–6 months post-op. Others with moderate TR + RV dilation warrant concurrent repair.

    Depends on annular size, RV function, and surgeon judgment. This is where multidisciplinary conference shines.

  12. Transcatheter TR options (TriClip, PASCAL, Evoque, Cardioband) are game-changers for high-risk/elderly/frail patients, with FDA approvals 2023–2024. Different postoperative trajectory than surgical repair — earlier mobilization, same-day discharge feasible for TriClip.

    Requires specialized interventional expertise (catheterization lab, advanced echo guidance); not all centers have this yet.

  13. MRA (spironolactone) is especially beneficial in TR. Not just for K-sparing strategy — improves RV function and reduces fibrosis.

    Check baseline K⁺ and Cr; recheck in 1 week, then periodically. Hyperkalemia risk is real but manageable; therapeutic benefit justifies the monitoring.

  14. Hepatic congestion creates a late consequence of chronic TR that's often missed. Cirrhotic-appearing labs (low albumin, elevated INR, low platelets) develop slowly.

    Pre-operative MELD-XI >20 signals high surgical risk. But here's the pearl: post-TV repair, many of these "cirrhotic" lab abnormalities improve or normalize as RA pressures fall. This hepatic recovery potential argues strongly for intervention even in patients with congestive hepatopathy.

  15. Post-TV repair/replacement, RV dysfunction dominates the postop picture. RV is often enlarged and hypokinetic pre-op; recovery slow (weeks). Inotropic support common.

    Realistic expectations with patient/family about recovery timeline prevent demoralizing the team and family with "slow" progress that is actually typical. See Tricuspid Valve Repair and Tricuspid Valve Replacement cards for full postop trajectory.

cards.title: Tricuspid Valve Surgery (Repair and Replacement)
cards.quickAnswer: TV surgery (repair > replacement; isolated TV = 10–15% mortality; usually concurrent with MV/AVR) → POD 0 ICU: Accept CVP 12–15 cmH₂O if cardiac output adequate—RV is preload-sensitive, not volume-tolerant; avoid aggressive diuresis. POD 1–3: Watch for POAF (~30–40%, same as mitral), heart block (5–10%, AV node at TV annulus), hepatic congestion resolution (bilirubin weeks). POD 4+: Stepdown mobilization, long RV remodeling trajectory (weeks–months). Discharge: ASA for repair; warfarin (bioprosthetic 3 mo, then ASA; mechanical lifelong INR 2.5–3.5); if IVDU endocarditis, addiction medicine consult + behavioral contract mandatory—recurrence >50% without MAT engagement. Transcatheter options (TriClip, PASCAL, Evoque) emerging but repair/replacement still standard. RV dysfunction recovery slow; serial TTE at 30 days, 3 months.
