sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, population.

  • Definition: Tricuspid valve repair (annuloplasty ring, De Vega, edge-to-edge) or replacement (bioprosthetic/mechanical) via median sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB). Repair strongly preferred; replacement rare. Most TV cases are concomitant with mitral or aortic surgery; isolated TV surgery carries high mortality (Kirklin & Blackstone, 2013).

  • Epidemiology: Isolated TV repair ~3% of cardiac surgeries; replacement <1%. Indications: severe functional TR (secondary to RV dilation from MV disease, RV infarction, pulmonary hypertension); primary valve pathology (carcinoid heart disease, Ebstein anomaly); endocarditis (IVDU, prosthetic); post-LVAD TR. Mean age 65–70 years; male predominance for IVDU endocarditis.

  • Transcatheter alternatives emerging: TriClip (edge-to-edge), PASCAL, Evoque (replacement). Suitable for high-risk or anatomically challenging patients; still investigational or early adoption at many centers.

  • Standard LOS: ICU 1–2 days uncomplicated repair; 10–14 days if replacement, RV failure, IVDU endocarditis. RV remodels slowly—weeks to months post-op.

  • Lines/devices on ICU arrival: Peripheral IV or midline; pacer wires (atrial + ventricular common for heart block risk); chest tubes (CTs) may still be draining; Foley usually out POD 1–2.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why RV dysfunction dominates TV surgery

Pre-operative state: Severe tricuspid regurgitation (functional or primary) causes chronic right ventricular dilation and remodeling. The RV becomes thick-walled, hypertrophied, and stiff in an attempt to eject against increased afterload. Simultaneously, elevated right atrial (RA) and CVP chronically perfuse the liver backward—hepatic congestion develops, impairing hepatic synthetic function and renal perfusion (cardiorenal syndrome).

At surgery: Sternotomy, CPB exposure, and right atriotomy traumatize the atrium and annulus. Annuloplasty immediately reduces TR burden, but the RV—now stiff and hypertrophic—cannot acutely improve compliance. The ventricle has lost the "relief" from chronic regurgitation and must now eject against new impedance from annuloplasty or prosthesis.

POD 0–3 hemodynamic challenge: RV filling pressures remain elevated (CVP 12–18 expected). If this elevation accompanies adequate cardiac output and normal lactate, it reflects the RV's slow remodeling—preload-dependence, not failure. However, if CVP rises AND cardiac output falls, the RV is decompensating and escalation is required.

Long-term remodeling: Unlike LV (recovers in days), RV remodeling takes 3–6 months. Gradual reduction in chamber size, improvement in function on serial echocardiography. Serial TTE at POD 30 and 3 months documents this trajectory.

Hepatic congestion: Pre-operative elevated CVP has already congested the liver. Post-operative RV dysfunction perpetuates it. Liver enzyme recovery (ALT/AST) occurs in days; bilirubin normalization takes weeks. True synthetic dysfunction (INR elevation, albumin drop) from ischemia is rare but possible if severe low-output state occurs.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context — TV Surgery Population
sections.bodyHtml:
Who undergoes TV surgery:

  • Functional TR (secondary): RV dilation from chronic MV disease, RV infarction, atrial fibrillation with RV dilation, pulmonary hypertension, cardiomyopathy
  • Primary valve disease: Carcinoid syndrome (endocardial fibrosis), Ebstein anomaly (displaced RV leaflet), rheumatic disease
  • Infection: Native valve endocarditis (IVDU), prosthetic valve endocarditis
  • Post-transplant/LVAD: RV-to-LV mismatch after heart transplant; progressive TR after LVAD placement
  • Congenital: Glenn procedure-associated TR (single-ventricle physiology)

Timing and presentation: Elective TV repair: planned, often concurrent with LV surgery. Urgent: endocarditis with hemodynamic compromise, large vegetation, septic emboli. Emergency: acute RV failure, cardiogenic shock from severe acute TR.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: 2 minutes at bedside.

ICU/Stepdown admission:

  • Vital signs: HR, BP (MAP target >60), SpO₂, CVP if line present, RR, temperature
  • Perfusion: Capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output (mL/h)
  • Physical exam: Lung fields (bilateral effusions common post-TV), JVD assessment (baseline expectation CVP 12–15), hepatomegaly (pre-existing from chronic TR), peripheral edema
  • Cardiac: Auscultation (new murmur if prosthesis? mechanical "click"?), heart rate and rhythm on monitor, pacer wire capture if present
  • Abdomen: Hepatomegaly, ascites (if chronic pre-op), distension, bowel sounds
  • Labs (obtained POD 0): CBC (hemoglobin trend post-op), PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, BMP (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr), LFTs (AST, ALT, bilirubin, albumin), lactate
  • Lines/devices: Pacer wires (A + V, intact and captured), CTs (output character, volume), Foley output, arterial line (if still present), IV access
  • Medications on board: Inotropes (milrinone, epinephrine), vasodilators (inhaled NO), beta-blocker status, diuretics, sedation (if ventilated)
  • Recent echo or other imaging: Any intraoperative TEE report findings (residual TR, RV function assessment, prosthesis position)

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 (ICU) — RV Support, Volume Cautious
sections.bodyHtml:
Hemodynamic goal: CVP 12–15 cmH₂O, MAP >60, CI ≥2.2, lactate <2, urine output >0.5 mL/kg/h

  1. Accept elevated CVP as expected. If CVP 14 + CO adequate + perfusion good + normal lactate → this is NOT fluid overload, this is preload-dependence. Do NOT pull fluids reflexively.

  2. Maintain preload: Infuse PRN to maintain CVP target. RV is thin-walled and needs filling pressure. Discontinue diuretics; hold even timed doses.

  3. Optimize oxygenation: SpO₂ ≥92%, target Hemoglobin >8 (avoid over-transfusion which increases viscosity and RV afterload). Mechanical ventilation (if intubated) with permissive hypercapnia acceptable if pH >7.25.

  4. Start or continue inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) if available: 10–20 ppm (gold standard for RV afterload reduction). If not available, IV milrinone 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min (inotrope + vasodilation, spares systemic vascular resistance for RV perfusion).

  5. Beta-blocker: Start IV metoprolol 12.5 mg q6h (if hemodynamics permit) or oral atenolol 25 mg daily POD 0–1. Reduces HR (decreases RV work), reduces afterload.

    Not harmful post-TV despite negative inotropic effect.

  6. Pacer wires: Verify capture and sensing thresholds. Both A + V wires typically in place; monitor AV conduction; do NOT pull early (heart block risk 5–10%, higher than CABG).

  7. Chest tubes: Monitor for brisk output. Right atrium ooze is common; expect high output POD 0 (>200 mL/h first 6 h acceptable). Ensure adequate hemostasis; if bleeding persists, notify surgeon.

  8. Labs and imaging: Serial labs q6–8 h POD 0 (CBC, BMP, LFTs, lactate). Repeat labs q12 h if stable. CXR (lung fields, mediastinal widening, CTs position). Avoid repeat echo unless clinical change or persistent hypotension.

sections.heading: 5B. POD 1–3 (ICU or Early Stepdown) — Hepatic Congestion Resolution, Diuresis Guided by RV Response
sections.bodyHtml:
Hemodynamic transition: CVP may remain 12–15, but CO should be improving (CI trending >2.4). If lactate normalizing and urine output adequate, begin gentle diuresis.

  1. Extubation: Target extubation POD 1 if uncomplicated (no active bleeding, adequate oxygenation, hemodynamically stable). Slow daily spontaneous breathing trial; avoid over-sedation.

  2. Diuresis strategy (CRITICAL for TV): Start low, go slow.

    Goal net diuresis −500 mL/day maximum, not −1,000 to −1,500 (standard post-op goal). RV remodeling is slow; over-diuresis precipitates acute RV failure and shock. - Furosemide 20–40 mg IV q6–8 h (adjust based on UOP and CVP response). - Watch CVP trend: if falling >2 cmH₂O over 12 h, consider holding next diuretic dose. - Do NOT chase CVP below 12 in first week.

  3. Electrolyte replacement: K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0 (critical for arrhythmia prevention). Check q12 h; replace aggressively. POAF risk peaks POD 2–3.

  4. POAF monitoring: ~30–40% incidence. Obtain 12-lead ECG at first irregular rhythm; have POAF protocol ready (see Scenario: POAF). Have beta-blocker + amiodarone on hand.

  5. Heart block surveillance: Continue pacer wire monitoring. If AV block develops (HR 30–50, loss of capture), activate pacing immediately (A+V at 80–90 bpm). If high-grade block persists >6 h despite pacing, consult Cardiology/EP for PPM evaluation.

  6. Hepatic congestion: LFTs may show marked elevation (AST/ALT >500, bilirubin >2). This is ischemic hepatitis from pre-existing chronic CVP elevation + post-op low CO, not acute liver failure. It improves as RV remodels. Monitor albumin, PT/INR, bilirubin daily. Do NOT hold warfarin solely for elevated INR from liver dysfunction; distinguish from over-anticoagulation.

  7. Bowel regimen (CRITICAL): Start immediately—hepatic congestion + opioids = severe constipation. Docusate 100 mg PO BID + senna 1–2 tabs BID + miralax 17 g daily. Do not skip.

  8. Continue iNO/milrinone: Wean only if RV function improving, CVP trending down, CI maintained. Abrupt withdrawal can trigger RV decompensation.

sections.heading: 5C. POD 4+ (Stepdown, Telemetry) — Stepdown Mobilization, Long Trajectory
sections.bodyHtml:
Clinical milestone: Extubated, off pressors, tolerate PO, stable hemodynamics.

  1. Progressive mobility: PT/OT cleared for out-of-bed, ambulation. Start light activity POD 4–5; progress as tolerated.

    Expect reduced exercise tolerance for months—RV recovers slowly. Counsel patient on realistic timeline (3–6 months to normal exertion).

  2. Pacer wire management: Thresholds checked daily. If AV conduction has normalized and no episodes of high-grade block, wires may be pulled POD 4–5 (typically by surgeon or EP).

    Do NOT pull early if any history of block. Retain wires POD 7–10 if block occurred.

  3. Diuresis continuation: Continue gentle diuresis (goal net −500 mL/day). Monitor CVP + CI q shift. If CVP rising and CO falling, escalate to iNO/milrinone infusion; may require ICU readmission.

  4. Medications:

    • Beta-blocker: Continue (PO if not already). Essential for RV recovery.
    • ACE-I/ARB: Initiate if EF <45% or LV dysfunction present (common if concomitant MV repair).
    • Statin: Continue (standard post-cardiac surgery).
    • iNO/milrinone: Wean as RV function improves; target off by POD 7.

  5. Hepatic recovery: LFTs should be trending downward. Bilirubin recovery lags (weeks). Monitor INR closely for anticoagulation dosing (may need adjustment as hepatic synthetic function recovers).

  6. Discharge planning: Target POD 6–8 uncomplicated repair; POD 10–14+ if replacement, RV failure, or IVDU endocarditis.

sections.heading: 5D. Discharge — Hepatic Function Normalization, Anticoagulation by Valve Type
sections.bodyHtml:
Pre-discharge:

  1. Anticoagulation:
Procedure Discharge–3 Mo After 3 Mo INR Target
Repair (no AF) Warfarin × 3 mo (optional at some centers; reduces thromboembolic risk) ASA 81 mg daily lifelong (or warfarin if AF develops) INR 2.0–3.0 if warfarin; ASA monotherapy if no AF
Repair + POAF Warfarin INR 2.5–3.0 (mandatory) Warfarin LIFELONG INR 2.5–3.0
Bioprosthetic TVR Warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 × 3 mo ASA 81 daily lifelong (DC warfarin if no AF) INR 2.0–3.0 × 3 mo, then ASA monotherapy
Mechanical TVR Warfarin INR 2.5–3.5 + heparin bridge until therapeutic Warfarin INR 2.5–3.5 LIFELONG (DOACs not recommended) INR 2.5–3.5 LIFELONG

  1. Medications at discharge:

    • Beta-blocker (indefinite)
    • ACE-I/ARB if EF <45% (indefinite)
    • Statin (indefinite)
    • Warfarin or ASA per table above
    • Stool softener + senna (hepatic congestion may persist; prevent constipation)
    • Pain management (avoid excessive opioids; they worsen constipation)

  2. Hepatic function recovery: Expect LFTs to normalize over weeks. Bilirubin may remain mildly elevated (1–2) at discharge; resolves over 2–4 weeks at home as RV remodels.

    Do NOT hold discharge for mildly elevated LFTs if synthetic function (INR, albumin) is adequate.

  3. Follow-up:

    • 1 week: incision check
    • 4–6 weeks: surgeon + cardiology office visit
    • POD 30: transthoracic echocardiogram (assess RV function, residual TR, prosthesis function)
    • POD 3 months: repeat TTE (document RV improvement)
    • If IVDU endocarditis: 30-day Infectious Disease follow-up + addiction medicine + behavioral contract + syringe services program referral

  4. Special situation — IVDU Endocarditis:

    • Addiction medicine consult BEFORE discharge (if not done pre-op)
    • Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) candidacy assessment: buprenorphine or methadone
    • Behavioral contract: urine drug screens, compliance monitoring, strict follow-up adherence
    • Social work: stable housing, insurance, transportation
    • Documentation: flag chart for high-risk follow-up; ensure PCP aware of endocarditis + addiction medicine involvement
    • Discharge counseling: "Surgery alone will NOT prevent recurrence. You must engage with addiction medicine and treatment. Recurrence risk >50% without behavioral change."

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [TV repair/replacement]." B: "[Surgical indication—functional TR, endocarditis, etc.]. Currently on [iNO/milrinone/beta-blocker]. CVP [value], CI [value], lactate [value]." A: "[Hemodynamic status: stable/declining]. HR [rate], BP [value], UOP [mL/h]. Labs: K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value]." R: "Requesting [escalation action—ICU admission, iNO initiation, DCCV for POAF, etc.]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Action
Stable POD 0–1 questions Primary APP / on-call cardiothoracic surgery fellow Order review, medication adjustment
CVP >15 + CI <2.0 + rising lactate CT surgery + cardiology ICU readmission, iNO/milrinone, escalation imaging (echo, labs)
Heart block (HR 30–50, loss of capture) CT surgery + cardiology/EP Activate pacing, ECG, assess need for PPM consult
POAF (hemodynamically stable) Primary APP Rate vs rhythm plan, electrolyte replacement
POAF (unstable—hypotension, altered MS) RRT/Rapid Response + CT surgery DCCV preparation, ICU activation
Fever + new murmur/suspicious blood cultures CT surgery + Infectious Disease Endocarditis workup (TEE, blood cx × 3), broad-spectrum antibiotics
Brisk bleeding (>300 mL/h × 2 h) CT surgery STAT Return to OR for hemostasis, massive transfusion protocol
Acute hepatic decompensation (INR >4, encephalopathy) Hepatology + CT surgery Vitamin K, FFP, consider ICU, imaging (CT abdomen r/o ischemia)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 TV Annuloplasty Ring vs De Vega Suture Repair
sections.bodyHtml:
Annuloplasty ring (DeVries, Carpentier-McCarthy, other brands):

  • Prosthetic ring sewn to annulus; reduces RA-RV opening, coapts TV leaflets
  • Advantage: durable, predictable, lower recurrent TR
  • Disadvantage: foreign body, small risk thrombosis or infection; requires lifelong anticoag if mechanical TVR done
  • Most surgeons' preference for isolated TV repair

De Vega suture annuloplasty:

  • Pledgeted suture plicates annulus along posterior leaflet insertion
  • Advantage: no foreign body, simpler if redo surgery needed later
  • Disadvantage: higher recurrence of TR (20–30% at 5 years vs 5–10% with ring)
  • Less common now but still used for specific anatomy

Bottom line: Ring repair is the standard. Ask your surgeon's preference if patient info available.

sections.heading: 7.2 TV Replacement: Bioprosthetic vs Mechanical
sections.bodyHtml:
Bioprosthetic TVR (typically porcine or bovine pericardium):

  • Advantage: lower thromboembolism risk; less anticoag burden; preferred for most TV patients
  • Disadvantage: durability (10–15 years before re-op stenosis/regurgitation); smaller size options; failure accelerated in young patients, pregnancy
  • Why bioprosthetic preferred for TV: TV position higher thrombosis risk with mechanical (highest among all prostheses); patient acceptance of biopro durability trade-off usually good for TV given lower flow demands

Mechanical TVR (bileaflet, tilting-disk):

  • Advantage: durability (30+ years); valve hemodynamics excellent
  • Disadvantage: thrombosis risk very high—mechanical TV is the highest-risk prosthesis position. INR target 2.5–3.5 (higher than all other positions). Non-compliance = catastrophic
  • Nearly obsolete for TV replacement; reserved for young patients with excellent compliance likelihood or specific anatomy

Transcatheter alternatives (emerging):

  • TriClip (Abbott): Edge-to-edge repair for secondary TR; approved FDA 2024; less durable than surgical repair but option for high-risk
  • PASCAL: Similar mechanism; investigational
  • Evoque (Boston Scientific): Replacement valve, investigational

sections.heading: 7.3 RV Function Assessment Post-Op
sections.bodyHtml:
Clinical indicators:

  • CVP trend (should decline gradually over days–weeks)
  • Cardiac index (CI ≥2.2 acceptable)
  • Lactate (should normalize by POD 1–2)
  • Urine output (>0.5 mL/kg/h)

Echo indicators (on POD 30 TTE):

  • TAPSE (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion): >16 mm = preserved RV function; <16 mm suggests RV dysfunction
  • FAC (fractional area change): normal >35%; <35% suggests RV dysfunction
  • RV free wall strain: should be <−20%; more negative is better (less negative = worse function)
  • RV size: should show gradual reduction over 3 months as remodeling occurs
  • Residual TR: mild-to-moderate common; usually improves with RV remodeling

PAPi (pulmonary artery pulsatility index): (sPAP − dPAP) / CVP = if <1.0, associates with poor RV outcomes; if >2.0, generally favorable

sections.heading: 7.4 Hepatic Recovery Post-TV
sections.bodyHtml:
Pre-operative hepatic congestion: Chronic elevated CVP from severe TR causes hepatic sinusoidal pressure buildup, centrilobular ischemia, fibrosis. Patients may present with cirrhosis or near-cirrhosis.

Post-operative recovery timeline:

  • POD 0–2: ALT/AST spike (surgical injury, CPB), then gradual downtrend
  • POD 3–7: ALT/AST normalizing; bilirubin still elevated
  • Weeks 2–6: Bilirubin normalization; albumin slowly recovering
  • Weeks 6+: Full hepatic synthetic recovery (INR, albumin normal)

Monitoring:

  • Daily LFTs POD 0–3, then q2–3 days until trending normal
  • PT/INR critical—reflects synthetic function AND anticoagulation effect. If INR rises despite warfarin hold, likely represents hepatic dysfunction, not over-anticoagulation. May need Vitamin K to distinguish.
  • Albumin: slow to recover; if <2.5 at discharge, consider albumin replacement (each 1 g/kg pulls 4 L fluid into intravascular space—useful for ascites mobilization).

If severe hepatic decompensation (INR >3.5, encephalopathy, ascites refractory to diuretics):

  • Hepatology consult
  • Consider liver biopsy (ischemic necrosis vs cirrhosis vs pure congestion)
  • ICU-level monitoring
  • Lactulose, rifaxomicin for hyperammonemia
  • Careful fluid/electrolyte management

sections.heading: 7.5 Nutrition and Ascites Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Malnutrition risk: Pre-op hepatic congestion + post-op low cardiac output + opioid use = poor oral intake.

Nutritional support:

  • Early PO encouragement (POD 1–2 if tolerating)
  • Dietitian referral if intake <50% goal
  • Albumin supplementation if serum <2.5 (each 25 g IV = 100 mL albumin push, temporarily increases serum albumin by ~0.5 g/dL and pulls fluid)
  • Avoid over-feeding (increases CO₂ production, RV work)

Ascites management:

  • Usually resolves with RV remodeling + diuresis over weeks–months
  • Large ascites (>2 L, cause respiratory compromise, pain) → therapeutic tap + albumin replacement (1 g per L removed, infused IV)
  • Spironolactone 25 mg daily (if refractory, escalate to 50 mg BID) for longer-term management
  • Sodium restriction (2 g/day)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear, re-escalate.

  • CVP trending up over 12–24 h despite diuretics → worsening RV function or volume overload; escalate if CVP >18
  • CI trending down → myocardial depression or afterload crisis; requires iNO/milrinone consideration
  • Lactate rising or stalled >2 despite adequate CVP/CO → inadequate tissue perfusion; escalate
  • Urine output declining → renal hypoperfusion from low CO or hepatic congestion; risk AKI
  • New or persistent tachycardia → pain, afib, sepsis, or RV decompensation; always investigate
  • Oxygen requirement increasing → pulmonary edema (elevated LA or pulmonary venous congestion), pleural effusion, or atelectasis; CXR
  • Fever → endocarditis (especially IVDU pre-op), surgical site infection, or other post-op infection; blood cultures, TEE if valve patient
  • Bleeding from CTs persisting >24 h or sudden increase in output → re-exploration risk
  • New irregular rhythm → POAF; obtain ECG immediately
  • Loss of pacer capture → wire malposition, lead fracture, or threshold rise; check threshold, reposition, or pull and replace
  • Encephalopathy, asterixis, or confusion → hepatic decompensation, electrolyte derangement, or sedation accumulation; check ammonia, K⁺, Mg²⁺, drug levels
  • New focal neurologic deficit → embolic stroke (especially if endocarditis, AF, or mechanical prosthesis); activate stroke protocol
  • Severe constipation despite bowel regimen → opioid accumulation, ileus, or abdominal distension; reduce opioids, escalate laxatives, abdominal imaging if severe

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. CVP ≤15 is NOT fluid overload post-TV. If CVP 14 + CI 2.4 + lactate normal + perfusion good, patient is fine. Do not diurese. This error causes RV failure and shock.

  2. RV recovery is SLOW. Unlike LV (days), RV remodels over weeks–months. Serial TTE at POD 30 and 3 months shows gradual improvement. Counsel patient: expect exertional dyspnea for months.

  3. Heart block post-TV is MORE common than post-CABG (5–10% vs 1–2%). AV node is at posterolateral TV annulus. Keep pacer wires longer; monitor AV conduction daily. Fixed block → PPM pre-discharge.

  4. POAF post-TV is ~30–40% incidence (same as mitral). Have POAF protocol ready. Electrolyte repletion (K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0) is critical. AF post-repair mandates lifelong warfarin due to stroke risk.

  5. IVDU endocarditis demands addiction medicine. Do NOT discharge without confirmed MAT enrollment (buprenorphine or methadone), behavioral contract, and 30-day ID + addiction medicine follow-up. Recurrence rate >50% without this.

  6. Mechanical TV is a thrombotic landmine. INR target 2.5–3.5 (higher than all other prostheses). Non-compliance = acute thrombosis = cardiogenic shock + death.

    Bioprosthetic TV almost always preferred.

  7. Isolated TV surgery = 10–15% mortality. Far higher than concurrent MV/AVR. Late-stage disease, MELD-XI high, advanced hepatic congestion. Transcatheter options now offer alternatives for high-risk.

  8. Hepatic congestion takes weeks to resolve. LFTs marked elevation (AST >500) is common and expected from ischemic hepatitis (pre-existing + post-op low CO). Do NOT panic. Improves as RV remodels. Monitor albumin, INR, bilirubin.

  9. Bowel regimen is NOT optional. Hepatic congestion + opioids = constipation that is severe. Docusate + senna + miralax from POD 1. No exceptions.

  10. iNO or milrinone are valuable post-TV. iNO 10–20 ppm (gold standard) or milrinone 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min. Do NOT withhold if CVP elevation + low CO. Wean slowly as RV improves.

  11. Beta-blockade is protective, not harmful post-TV. Reduces HR (RV work), reduces afterload. Start POD 0–1 if hemodynamics permit. Negative inotropic effect is desired.

  12. Residual TR post-repair is common. Echo often shows mild-to-moderate regurgitation despite repair. Usually improves as RV remodels. Give it 3 months before considering redo.

  13. Over-diuresis in first week is a frequent error. RV needs preload. Net diuresis goal −500 mL/day max, NOT −1,000 to −1,500. Aggressive diuresis → RV failure → shock.

  14. Transcatheter TV (TriClip, PASCAL, Evoque) are emerging options. Less durable than surgical repair but suitable for high-risk anatomy or prohibitive surgical risk. Ask your interventional cardiology colleagues.

  15. CIED lead extraction with TV surgery if lead-mediated TR. If patient has pacemaker/ICD with lead-related tricuspid regurgitation, lead extraction may be concurrent with TV repair. Plan for this; discuss with EP pre-op.

cards.title: Unwitnessed Fall (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: Patient found on floor → do NOT move until c-spine cleared (if unwitnessed/unexplained); stat vitals + glucose; assess level of consciousness; head-to-toe exam including skull/clavicles/sternum; neuro exam (GCS, NIHSS if focal); telemetry review for syncope-suggesting rhythms (bradycardia, pause, runs of SVT). CT head STAT if anticoagulated, head strike, or altered mental status (low threshold). Sternal integrity check if sternotomy/thoracotomy. Common causes: orthostatic hypotension (POD 1–3, beta-blocker + diuretic + deconditioning), syncope from arrhythmia, acute stroke, hypoglycemia, hyperactive delirium, medication effect. Post-fall: incident report, family notification, enhanced precautions (bed alarm, 1:1 sitter if delirium), PT/OT consult.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Patient discovered on the floor or ground during an unwitnessed or unexplained fall episode. May or may not have sustained injury; head/c-spine trauma a concern.
  • Incidence: Post-cardiac surgery fall rates are 3–5 times higher than medical floor baseline, peaking POD 1–3 during recovery phase. Falls with injury occur in ~20–30% of post-op falls.
  • Who this applies to: All post-op cardiac surgery patients on continuous monitoring. Highest risk: age > 65, POD 1–3, Morse Fall Scale ≥45, hyperactive delirium, beta-blocker + diuretic use.
  • Why it matters: Head injury and c-spine trauma are real concerns. Falls increase length of stay, mortality, and quality-of-life impact. Prevention is team-based.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-op cardiac patients fall from convergent physiologic pressures:

  • Orthostatic hypotension — beta-blockers + diuretics + post-op dehydration create a "triple threat" for orthostatic intolerance. Fluid shifts post-CPB; diuresis POD 1–3 pulls intravascular volume down faster than sympathetic compensation can raise peripheral resistance. Sitting/standing BP drop >20 mmHg systolic or >10 mmHg diastolic is common, especially POD 1–3.

  • Syncope from cardiac arrhythmia — POAF with rapid ventricular response (HR > 130), bradyarrhythmia/heart block, or VT can cause syncope with no prodrome; patient has no memory of fall.

  • Acute stroke — AF + hypercoagulable post-op state = embolic risk. Perioperative emboli from aortic manipulation or new wall-motion abnormality. Presents with sudden weakness, facial droop, speech change; patient may fall before recognizing deficit.

  • Hypoglycemia — insulin requirement fluctuates post-op; hypoglycemia mimics stroke (focal neuro), syncope (sudden LOC), and delirium (confusion, aggression). Bedside glucose is a must-first check—immediately reversible.

  • Delirium (hyperactive > hypoactive) — 15–50% of cardiac post-op patients experience delirium; peak POD 1–3. Hyperactive: combative, agitated, unsafe mobility, pulling at lines. Hypoactive: quiet, withdrawn, appearing "fine" but with poor judgment about mobility limits. Delirious patients won't call for help or remember precautions.

  • Medication-related falls — over-sedation from opioids/benzos; beta-blocker blunting tachycardic compensation; diuretics causing electrolyte loss (K, Mg → arrhythmia risk).

  • Sternal precaution violation — patient taught not to pull self up by arms, but habit is strong. Pulling destabilizes sternal healing and can cause loss of balance. Often happens early morning when patient tries to get OOB to use commode without assistance.

  • Deconditioning + slipping — post-op patient strength is 30–50% baseline. Simple mechanical slip (wet floor, dropped item) compounds peripheral neuropathy from positioning or epidural. Hospital socks without non-slip soles increase risk.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following:

  • Patient found on floor; fall not witnessed by nursing staff
  • Witnessed fall or patient reports fall even if not directly observed by staff
  • Patient discovered with acute change in mental status + evidence of fall (altered location, disheveled, blood on skin)
  • Telemetry reading missed during fall window due to monitor disconnect or movement artifact
  • Patient with documented high fall risk (Morse ≥45 or Hendrich II ≥5) found in unsafe location (chair, bedside, standing) without supervision
  • Ambulation attempt during shift change or with minimal staffing that resulted in loss of balance

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Competent systematic bedside exam.

Immediate surroundings:

  • Where was patient found? Chair, bed, floor? Evidence of trauma (blood, vomit, incontinence, positioning)?
  • Patient position & movement — can they move all extremities? Obvious limb deformity? Neck pain or guarding?

Vital signs:

  • HR, BP (compare to baseline; orthostatic component if feasible post-fall), SpO₂, RR, temperature
  • Glucose fingerstick STAT

Mental status:

  • Awake? Alert? Oriented? Responsive to commands?
  • Any head-turning deficit, facial asymmetry, slurred speech?
  • Delirium screening result (CAM, CAMICUI) if available?

Neuro exam:

  • Pupils, extraocular movements, facial symmetry, speech, grip strength, leg strength
  • Gait if safe to attempt standing
  • GCS; NIHSS if focal deficits present

Physical findings for injury:

  • Visible abrasions, swelling, bruising on face, skull, extremities, chest (avoid deep palpation until cleared)
  • Palpate skull for deformity, step-off, Battle sign (mastoid ecchymosis), raccoon eyes
  • Clavicles, ribs, sternal wound integrity (sternal wound separation or drainage change?)
  • Neck stiffness? Midline tenderness?

Telemetry & cardiac:

  • Rhythm strip at time of fall (or reconstruction from tele if available)
  • HR trend? Any syncope-suggesting rhythm? (sudden bradycardia, pause, runs of SVT)
  • Tele disconnect during event?

Recent history:

  • Review MAR — sedating meds on board? Beta-blocker dose/timing? Diuretic given past 24h? Pain meds? Anticoagulation status?
  • Was BP stable pre-fall? Trending down? Orthostatic check documented?
  • Last orthostatic vitals — was SBP drop >20/10 documented?
  • Mobility status — on bed rest, limited precautions, or cleared for ambulation?
  • Sternal precaution documented as being taught?
  • Morse Fall Scale or Hendrich II score if documented

Recent labs: - Glucose (when last checked), electrolytes, hemoglobin, creatinine from recent labs

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Witnessed fall, simple slip/trip, no LOC change, normal neuro exam, normal vitals.)

  1. Ensure patient is in safe position on floor or chair — do NOT pull up by arms (sternal precaution violation); use lift sheet or 2–3 staff to roll onto back and assess
  2. STAT vitals — HR, BP (compare to baseline), SpO₂, RR, temperature
  3. STAT glucose fingerstick — hypoglycemia mimics everything and is immediately reversible
  4. Head-to-toe exam — palpate skull, clavicles, ribs, sternal wound (integrity?), abdomen, pelvis, all extremities; assess motor + sensory
  5. Neuro exam: pupils, extraocular movements, facial symmetry, speech, grip strength, leg strength, safe gait if attempted
  6. Review telemetry — any syncope-suggesting rhythm change? Tele disconnect during event?
  7. Get patient off floor safely — mechanical lift or 2–3 staff assist; do NOT allow self-assisted arm pull; splint any suspected fracture before moving
  8. Notify provider of fall — SBAR report (time, mechanism, vitals, neuro exam, injuries); request assessment and imaging orders as indicated
  9. Place on continuous tele if not already
  10. Incident report initiation — document fall, injuries, circumstances; family notification per [Institution policy]

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Unwitnessed/unexplained fall, head strike, LOC change, neck/spine pain, neuro deficit, altered mental status, anticoagulated.)

  1. DO NOT MOVE the patient until c-spine clearance if fall was unwitnessed or unexplained
  2. Stat call to provider + RRT/charge RN — do NOT leave room alone
  3. STAT vitals + glucose — draw labs at same time (glucose, CBC, BMP, troponin, ABG/lactate)
  4. ECG STAT — syncope workup must include 12-lead to rule out arrhythmia, ischemia, prolonged QT
  5. Detailed neuro exam — LOC (GCS), pupils, extraocular movements, facial symmetry, speech, motor + sensory bilaterally, gait assessment only if c-spine cleared
  6. Head/neck exam — any skull deformity, Battle sign, raccoon eyes, CSF rhinorrhea/otorrhea? Neck stiffness? Midline tenderness?
  7. Activate c-spine precautions if fall unexplained or high-energy mechanism — collar per [Institution protocol]
  8. Stat labs — glucose, CBC, BMP (K, Mg, Ca, Cr), troponin, ABG/lactate, coagulation studies if anticoagulated
  9. Stat imaging orders likely — CT head non-contrast STAT if: anticoagulated, head strike, any LOC, altered mental status, or any concern for intracranial injury.
  10. Sternal imaging if sternotomy/thoracotomy + falls with sternal trauma — CXR for sternal wire integrity, CT chest if sternal pop/click on cough or concern for dehiscence
  11. Document rhythm strip at time of event (or reconstruction from tele); save for review
  12. Prepare for imaging transport — maintain c-spine precautions en route if indicated

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for fall call:

S: "[RN name] on the ICU calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient found on floor [or witnessed fall] at [time]. [Mechanism: slipped while ambulating / unwitnessed / syncope-like onset]. Current vitals: HR [X], BP [X/X], SpO₂ [X]. Glucose [X]. Anticoagulation status: [on/off heparin/DOAC/warfarin]." A: "Neuro: alert and oriented [Y/N], moving all extremities [Y/N], focal deficits [Y/N]. Visible injuries: [describe]. Tele rhythm: [normal sinus / irregular / syncope-suggesting pattern]." R: "Requesting [physical exam / CT head / imaging / ECG / neuro consult / ortho eval]. Enhanced fall precautions and prevention huddle pending."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Mechanical fall, no injury, normal exam Primary APP / on-call provider
Fall with any head strike or LOC Charge RN + APP STAT; prepare for CT head; neuro consult if focal deficits
Fall + anticoagulated Charge RN + APP STAT; low threshold for CT head
Fall with suspected syncope Primary APP + ECG STAT; cardiology if arrhythmia suspected
Fall with neck/spine pain or unexplained mechanism Charge RN + APP, c-spine precautions, imaging per protocol
Fall with sternal trauma or pop/click on cough CT surgery notification; CXR STAT, CT chest if concern for sternal dehiscence
Severe delirium contributing to fall Primary APP + Psychiatry / Geriatrics consult
Orthopedic injury suspected Orthopedic surgery consultation
Imaging + anticoag + head strike Pharmacy for reversal review (if warfarin → vitamin K + FFP; if DOAC → idarucizumab per DOAC type); CT surgery if sternal concern

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Subsections.

sections.heading: 7.1 Fall prevention bundle — evidence-based components
sections.bodyHtml:
Environmental:

  • Bed alarm + chair alarm for all patients with Morse ≥45 or Hendrich ≥5; test alarm daily
  • Non-slip footwear — hospital socks with grips; inspect for adequacy each shift
  • Room tidy — no clutter, cords secured, IV pole positioned to not trip, commode by bed (not bathroom trip when possible)
  • Lighting adequate — night light on; call bell in reach at all times
  • Bathroom access — commode by bed preferred over long bathroom walk for delirium/retention-prone; toilet seat height check (may need raised seat)

Care delivery:

  • 2-person assist for first ambulations (POD 0–3) — sternal precautions mean patient cannot stabilize self by pulling on arms; always contact guard + assist
  • Orthostatic checking BEFORE ambulation — seated → supine → slow sit-up, wait 1 min → stand with support, measure BP/HR after 1 min standing. If SBP drop >20 or dizziness → hold ambulation, notify provider, recheck in 4h
  • Sternal precaution education — reinforce no pulling up by arms at every bedside interaction; teach correct method (push with legs, use trapeze, ask for help); ask patient to "show me" how they'll get up
  • Scheduled toileting — every 2h for delirium/retention-prone; offer bedpan or commode; avoid bladder overdistension (worsens delirium)
  • 1:1 sitter for hyperactive delirium — if patient is pulling at lines, attempting unsafe mobility, or Hendrich ≥5; sitter provides constant supervision
  • Call-bell in reach — test that patient can reach and knows how to use; check function

Medication & monitoring:

  • PT/OT consult on POD 0–1 — mobility plan, assistive device prescription, home safety planning
  • Medication review — any non-essential sedating meds? Can opioids or benzos be reduced? Is beta-blocker dose appropriate for symptomatic orthostasis?
  • Continuous telemetry — watch for syncope-suggesting rhythms; educate patient on call-bell if palpitations
  • Glucose monitoring — check before high-risk times (early morning, post-ambulation); treat hypoglycemia immediately
  • Blood pressure monitoring — orthostatic checks; trend over time; notify provider if persistent SBP <100 or orthostatic drops >20/10
  • Delirium screening daily — CAM, CAMICUI, or bedside mental check; escalate to psychiatry/geriatrics if not improving

Education at discharge:

  • Home fall prevention — remove throw rugs, secure electrical cords, adequate lighting, grab bars in bathroom, step stool use with supervision, pet trip hazards
  • Sternal precautions at home — no pulling with arms, log-roll technique, activity limits, when to call surgeon
  • Orthostatic awareness — slow position changes, sit 1–2 min before standing, dangle legs, move to edge of bed slowly
  • Activity pacing — increase activity gradually; don't overestimate capacity; supervised first walks at home

sections.heading: 7.2 Morse Fall Scale & Hendrich II risk stratification
sections.bodyHtml:
Morse Fall Scale (0–125 points; ≥45 = high risk):

  • History of falls: 0 / 25
  • Secondary diagnosis (≥2 comorbidities): 0 / 15
  • Ambulatory aid (bed rest/assist vs cane/walker vs none): 0 / 0 / 0
  • IV/heparin lock: 0 / 20
  • Gait (normal vs weak/impaired vs bed rest): 0 / 10 / 20
  • Mental status (oriented vs forgetful/disoriented): 0 / 15

Post-op cardiac patient typical score: history of falls (if any) 25, secondary DX 15, gait impaired 10–20, mental status +/- 15, IV access 20 = easily 60–80 points in immediate post-op. This is expected. The fall prevention plan should be active and multi-modal, not just "document the risk."

Hendrich II Fall Risk Model (8 variables; ≥5 = high risk):

  • Confusion/disorientation/delirium: +4
  • Symptomatic depression: +2
  • Antiepileptic (phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital): +2
  • Benzodiazepine use: +1
  • IV therapy: +1
  • Orthostatic hypotension (≥20 mmHg systolic drop): +1
  • Toileting need assistance: +1
  • Age ≥75 years: +1

Post-op cardiac patient typical score: delirium (if present) +4, IV therapy +1, orthostatic risk (high) +1, toileting assist +1, age >75 (if applicable) +1 = 5–8 points = high risk.

sections.heading: 7.3 Anticoagulation + head trauma considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Any anticoagulated patient with head strike = CT head STAT, even minor mechanism. Bleeding risk is real.
  • Delayed intracranial bleeds can present hours after injury. Don't default to "patient is alert now, so no CT."
  • Warfarin reversal — Vitamin K 10 mg IV slowly (risk of phlebitis) + FFP 10–15 mL/kg or prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) if stat reversal needed; recheck INR in 4–6 h.
  • DOAC reversal — if apixaban/edoxaban: apixaban 5 mg IV (Aripizo) per weight; if dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV (2.5 g boluses); consult pharmacy on agent type.
  • Heparin — hold and monitor aPTT; reversal rare but protamine 1 mg per 100 units heparin if bleeding concerns.

sections.heading: 7.4 Delirium as a fall risk factor — cross-link
sections.bodyHtml:
• Hyperactive delirium — combative, agitated, unsafe mobility, pulling at lines, attempting to climb out of bed. Patient cannot accurately report symptoms and will not call for help.
  • Hypoactive delirium — quiet, withdrawn, appearing "fine" but with impaired cognition, poor judgment about mobility limits, unsafe decision-making.
  • Delirium screening: CAM (Confusion Assessment Method) or CAMICUI (Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU) daily. If delirium present, escalate: consider 1:1 sitter, psychiatry/geriatrics consult, medication review (minimize benzos/opioids), optimize sleep/light/noise.
  • Delirium + fall = high-risk combination. Delirious patient won't remember precautions and won't call for help. 1:1 sitter cost is far less than a hip fracture.

sections.heading: 7.5 Medications that increase fall risk
sections.bodyHtml:
Class Examples Mechanism Mitigation
SSRIs sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine hyponatremia, SIADH, psychomotor effect check Na⁺, consider SNRI alternative
Beta-blockers metoprolol, atenolol, carvedilol blunt orthostatic compensation; orthostatic hypotension verify dose; orthostatic checks before ambulation; may need to reduce dose if symptomatic
Diuretics furosemide, torsemide, bumetanide volume depletion, electrolyte loss (K, Mg) trend orthostatic vitals; replace electrolytes per protocol; adjust dose if orthostatic
Opioids morphine, hydromorphone, fentanyl patch sedation, impaired cognition, fall risk minimize doses; assess for nonpain alternatives; monitor for over-sedation
Benzodiazepines lorazepam, midazolam sedation, impaired cognition, delirium risk (paradoxical in elderly) minimize doses; taper if possible; 1:1 sitter if on high doses
Anticholinergics diphenhydramine, atropine, glycopyrrolate delirium, urinary retention, impaired cognition avoid if possible; switch to non-anticholinergic alternative
Antihypertensives amlodipine (new-started), hydralazine orthostatic hypotension verify need; orthostatic checks; adjust dose if symptomatic

sections.heading: 7.6 Sternal precautions — fall risk dimension
sections.bodyHtml:
• Patient taught: no pulling self up by arms; limits self-stabilization during transfers or ambulation.
  • Habit is strong: especially early morning when patient tries to get OOB without assistance.
  • Pulling destabilizes chest: can cause loss of balance and increase fall velocity.
  • Correct technique: push with legs, use trapeze if available, ask for help. Verify understanding by asking patient to "show me" how they'll get up.
  • Education reinforcement: at every bedside interaction, especially if catching patient attempting unsafe transfer.
  • Sternal wound exam: after any fall with sternal trauma, assess for wound separation, drainage change, or wires palpable under skin (sign of dehiscence).

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear or worsen post-fall, re-escalate.

  • LOC worsening or GCS dropping — head injury can be delayed; serial neuro checks essential
  • New onset focal neuro deficit — sudden weakness, facial asymmetry, speech change → stroke code immediately
  • Severe headache developing or neck pain worsening — c-spine injury or intracranial bleed progression
  • Vomiting post-fall — red flag for intracranial pressure rise
  • Tachycardia or bradycardia post-fall with syncope-like presentation — arrhythmia as fall cause; ECG interpretation critical
  • Blood glucose <70 on repeat check — hypoglycemia as fall etiology; treat and recheck q15min until stable >100
  • Persistent orthostatic BP drop >20/10 mmHg despite IV fluids — ongoing orthostasis increases refall risk
  • Delirium deepening — hyperactive to very combative, or hypoactive patient becoming more withdrawn/unresponsive
  • Signs of internal injury — abdominal tenderness, rib pain on palpation, bruising over flank or abdomen → imaging consideration
  • Sternal wound separation or drainage change — fall with sternal trauma can injure healing site
  • Increasing pain at fall site — deferred fracture (esp. ribs, hip) can develop over hours
  • Anticoagulated patient with any head strike — low threshold for CT head; even minor mechanism warrants imaging
  • Patient expressing fear of falling again — good sign for engagement in prevention; conversely, patient dismissing fall risk → re-education needed

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Do NOT move patient if fall unexplained or unwitnessed. Assume c-spine injury and head trauma until cleared. Even a "gentle" assisted movement can cause quadriplegia if cervical fracture present. Immobilize, get imaging, clear first — then move.

  2. Glucose fingerstick FIRST — before any workup. Hypoglycemia <70 presents as syncope, stroke, delirium, and altered mental status. Takes 30 seconds; restores consciousness if glucose is culprit. If low, treat with D50 IV or fast carbs PO, recheck q15min, then re-assess neuro.

  3. CT head if anticoagulated OR head strike OR altered mental status — LOW THRESHOLD. Post-cardiac patients are on heparin or DOAC; bleeding risk is real. Even a "soft" landing with LOC change warrants CT non-contrast. Don't default to "patient is alert now, so no CT." Delayed intracranial bleeds present hours later.

  4. Syncope workup requires ECG + telemetry review + echo later if indicated. Don't assume orthostatic hypotension as diagnosis if patient has POAF, bradycardia history, or no prodromal symptoms. Syncope onset suggests cardiac. Get 12-lead ECG immediately; review tele strip for rhythms during fall window; later echo if concerned about new wall-motion or cardiomyopathy.

  5. Incident report per [Institution policy] EVEN IF NO INJURY. Many nurses file reports only if visible injury or "serious" fall. Policy says all falls get reported. Incident report is a patient safety tracking tool, not a quality mark against you. Complete accurately and promptly.

  6. Family and power of attorney notification per [Institution policy] — MANDATORY. Families expect transparency. Call (don't just document) — explain fall, injuries (if any), workup done, precautions being implemented. Document notification: date, time, who called, who spoke to, what was discussed. Lack of notification is a liability.

  7. Orthostatic check BEFORE ambulation — make it routine. Don't skip it because patient "looks fine" or is eager to walk. Sitting BP 110/70 can drop to 90/50 on standing — patient won't know until upright and too late. Technique: seated 1 min, supine 1 min, stand with support 1 min, measure. Document all three. If drop >20 systolic or symptoms, hold ambulation and notify provider.

  8. 2-person assist for first ambulations POD 1–3 is the DEFAULT. Sternal precautions mean patient cannot pull self up by arms, stabilize via armrests, or self-correct balance. One person is not enough; second person acts as contact guard. Not optional for high-risk patients.

  9. Sternal precautions — patient cannot pull self up by arms (this is a FALL RISK). Educate at every bedside interaction. Many patients revert to habit (pulling up by arms while sitting in chair, getting OOB without help). Pulling destabilizes chest, causes loss of balance, increases fall velocity. Teach: push with legs, use trapeze, ASK for help. Check understanding; ask patient to "show me" how they'll get up.

  10. Medication review ESSENTIAL post-fall. Is beta-blocker dose contributing to orthostasis? Can opioids be reduced? Is patient on new benzodiazepine that's over-sedating? Is diuretic timing too aggressive? Verify home medications that were restarted (missed beta-blocker is a common trigger). Notify provider of suspected medication contribution; work with pharmacy for adjustment. Falls are often multifactorial.

  11. Delirium is the HIGHEST RISK FACTOR for falls. Hyperactive or hypoactive, delirium impairs judgment, awareness, motor control. Delirious patient won't call for help, won't remember precautions, won't acknowledge falls. Consider 1:1 sitter for high-delirium risk (age >65, ICU stay, baseline cognitive impairment, polypharmacy). Sitter cost is far less than hip fracture or head injury. Daily CAM or CAMICUI screening essential; escalate to Psychiatry or Geriatrics if delirium not improving.

  12. Commode by bed > bathroom trip. Post-op cardiac patient who must walk 30 feet to bathroom at 3am with impaired proprioception and orthostasis is a fall waiting to happen. Keep commode at bedside for POD 0–3. Toilet schedule: every 2h for delirium-prone or retention-prone. Saves falls and urinary complications.

  13. Bed alarm + chair alarm for high-risk patients (Morse ≥45 or Hendrich ≥5) — TEST daily. Don't assume it works. Alarms fail silently; batteries die; sensor gets dirty. Test each shift: trigger alarm, verify it sounds, check volume is audible. Alarm is not substitute for sitter or observation but adds layer of awareness for unwitnessed events.

  14. "Patient says they didn't hit their head" is not reliable evidence. Patient may not remember fall, may be in denial, may have impaired cognition from delirium/hypoglycemia. If ANY found-on-floor + anticoag, CT head is low-threshold. Assume head strike unless clearly not possible (e.g., patient fell forward from sitting in chair onto padded armrest).

  15. Prevention is TEAM effort — involve PT/OT, pharmacy, family, AND patient. Nurses can't prevent all falls alone. PT/OT does mobility assessment, prescribes devices, identifies environmental hazards. Pharmacy reviews meds. Family can supervise and reinforce precautions. Patient engagement is critical — explain the "why" (sternal healing, deconditioning, arrhythmia risk) so they buy into precautions. Post-fall huddle for prevention planning is ideal; document consensus plan.

cards.title: Vasoplegia (Vasoplegic Syndrome) Post-CPB
cards.quickAnswer: Post-CPB vasoplegia = distributive shock with preserved or high cardiac output, low SVR, persistent MAP <65 despite adequate volume, requiring norepi >0.25 mcg/kg/min. Incidence 5–25%; peak POD 0–1. Pathophysiology: CPB-induced NO-mediated vasodilation overriding catecholamine response. Management: restore electrolytes (K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0), escalate pressors (norepi → vasopressin → methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 20–30 min, or hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV), consider stress-dose hydrocortisone 50 mg q6h if chronic steroids, and ICU-level monitoring. Methylene blue earlier is far more effective than late.
