sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, and who this applies to.

  • Definition: Post-CPB vasoplegia is persistent hypotension (MAP <65 mmHg) after cardiopulmonary bypass despite adequate intravascular volume and preserved (or high) cardiac output. Characterized by warm extremities, wide pulse pressure (>40 mmHg), low systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and pressor requirement (typically norepi >0.25 mcg/kg/min) refractory to fluid resuscitation.

  • Incidence: 5–25% of post-CPB patients; peaks at 6–24 hours post-CPB. Highest risk in cardiac transplantation (40–50%), valve surgery, and prolonged CPB time.

  • Who this applies to: Adult ICU or high-acuity step-down patients within the first 48 hours after cardiac surgery. Hemodynamic monitoring (arterial line) and frequent lab assessment required.

  • Why it matters: Delayed recognition and treatment associated with worse mortality, increased length of stay, and greater end-organ dysfunction (Levin et al., 2009).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: nitric oxide, SIRS, and catecholamine resistance Cardiopulmonary bypass triggers a systemic inflammatory response (SIRS) through blood contact with non-endothelial surfaces, endotoxin translocation from gut ischemia, complement activation, and massive cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10). These inflammatory mediators stimulate inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) throughout the vascular endothelium and macrophages, leading to sustained, excessive production of nitric oxide (NO). Excess NO causes:
  • Persistent direct vasodilation (overwhelms sympathetic vasoconstriction)
  • Inhibition of myocardial contractility
  • Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation (impairs mitochondrial ATP production)
  • Relative vasopressin deficiency — NO suppresses V1 receptor-mediated vasoconstriction Result: Distributive shock characterized by low SVR, warm peripheries, wide pulse pressure, high (or adequate) cardiac output, but inadequate MAP for end-organ perfusion. Why catecholamines alone fail: In the presence of chronic NO elevation and metabolic acidosis, alpha-adrenergic receptors become desensitized. Standard-dose norepinephrine reaches a functional ceiling; escalation beyond 20 mcg/min yields minimal MAP rise despite further dose increases. Vasopressin advantage: Acts via V1 receptors (distinct pathway from catecholamines), with response preserved even in acidotic, catecholamine-resistant states. Synergistic with norepi when combined. Methylene blue mechanism: Inhibits guanylate cyclase, directly blocking the NO → cGMP → vasodilation cascade. This targets the pathophysiology rather than reflexively escalating pressors, accounting for often-dramatic MAP response if given early (Levin et al., 2009). Hydroxocobalamin mechanism: Directly scavenges (binds) NO, reducing bioavailable NO. Less studied in cardiac surgery than methylene blue but effective when methylene blue is contraindicated.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in the first 48 hours post-CPB:

  • Persistent MAP <65 mmHg despite adequate intravascular volume (CVP normal or elevated) and good cardiac output (CI >2.5 or assessed high on echo/POCUS)
  • Warm extremities + wide pulse pressure (difference between systolic and diastolic >40 mmHg)
  • Recently weaned from vasopressors in ICU and now rebounding hypotensive, requiring reinitiation or escalation
  • On low-dose vasopressor at handoff from ICU to step-down — presence of ongoing pressor requirement at a higher acuity level may signal inappropriate placement
  • Patient "feels warm" but BP low and urine output marginal (differs from cool, oliguric cardiogenic shock)
  • Lactate stable or trending down despite hypotension (distinguishes from progressive cardiogenic or hemorrhagic shock)

Risk factor context:

  • Prolonged CPB time >180 minutes
  • Pre-op ACE inhibitor or ARB use within 24 h pre-op (highest modifiable risk)
  • Cardiac transplant, valve surgery, aortic root surgery
  • Pre-op low EF (<30%), age >70, pre-existing sepsis, beta-blocker continuation

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No treatment actions in this section.

  • Vital signs: MAP, pulse pressure (systolic − diastolic), heart rate, SpO₂, core temperature trend
  • Physical exam: skin temperature (central vs peripheral), capillary refill, mottling, JVP if visible, CVP if line present
  • Mental status: alert and oriented, lethargy, confusion, agitation
  • Urine output: recent hourly rate, color, concentration; compare to prior 2–4 h
  • Perfusion markers:
  • Lactate (if drawn in last 2 h) and trajectory
  • Recent hemoglobin, electrolytes, ABG (pH, base deficit)
  • Recent CBC (WBC, bands — rule out sepsis)
  • Lines & access: Arterial line in place? Central line? Peripheral IV integrity?
  • Medication review (MAR):
  • Current pressor drips: agent, dose, duration, time of last adjustment
  • Recent boluses (fluid or vasopressor)
  • Recent antihypertensive agents (ACE-I, ARB, beta-blocker, CCB) — held or continued?
  • Chronic corticosteroid use (risk for adrenal insufficiency if not stress-dosed)
  • Intra-operative context:
  • CPB time (minutes); >180 min raises risk substantially
  • Pre-op EF and baseline cardiac function
  • Procedure type (CABG, valve, transplant, root — transplants highest risk)
  • Estimated blood loss, fluid prime volume, transfusion count
  • Pre-op ACE-I / ARB held or given?
  • Recent labs: most recent cortisol level (if chronic steroids); lactate trajectory over last 4 h
  • Sepsis screen: fever, WBC trend, cultures sent, recent antibiotics, exam for infection source (wound, line, lung)

sections.heading: 5A. Stable pathway
sections.bodyHtml:
(MAP 60–65, alert and oriented, good perfusion, lactate stable/down, adequate UOP)

  1. Recheck vital signs in 5 minutes — confirm reading and establish trend
  2. Crystalloid bolus 250–500 mL IV (assess CVP if line present; don't over-bolus if CVP already elevated 12–15 cm H₂O)
    • Rationale: even in distributive shock, intravascular volume is often partially depleted; modest bolus may raise MAP without requiring escalation
    • Hold any recent antihypertensive dose — verify ACE-I, ARB, beta-blocker, CCB not given in last 2–4 h
    • Send STAT labs: lactate, ABG, BMP (K, Mg, Ca, glucose), CBC, cortisol level (if on chronic steroids, rule out adrenal insufficiency)
    • Assess for sepsis: fever, WBC/bands, cultures pending, exam for infection source; if sepsis cannot be excluded, notify APP early
    • Initiate peripheral norepinephrine bridge (2–10 mcg/min) if MAP remains <65 after bolus
    • Note: peripheral norepi acceptable short-term at low dose with close bedside monitoring; do not delay central line if escalation anticipated
    • Vasopressin 0.04 units/minute if norepi alone insufficient to maintain MAP >65
    • Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (see Section 6); do NOT attempt prolonged pressor management without ICU-level setup
    • Document: time of onset, VS trend, fluid/pressor given, patient response, who was notified, escalation plan

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable pathway
sections.bodyHtml:
(MAP <55, altered mental status, oliguria/anuria, lactate rising, pressor escalating, or progressive deterioration)

  1. STAT call: APP/fellow + ICU team + RRT; do NOT manage alone
  2. Request ICU bed immediately — patient requires continuous hemodynamic monitoring, frequent labs, multi-agent pressor support
  3. Norepinephrine titration: start 5–10 mcg/min, titrate to MAP >65 (usual range 5–20 mcg/min per provider order)
  4. Add vasopressin 0.04 units/minute to norepi (synergistic effect, especially in acidotic states)
  5. Stress-dose hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h (for 24 h minimum) if:
    • Patient on chronic corticosteroids (prednisone ≥5 mg/day, dexamethasone, or equivalent at home), OR
    • Suspected septic shock pattern (fever, WBC, hypotension unresponsive to volume/single pressor)
    • Methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV over 20–30 minutes (per [Institution policy]; escalate for order immediately, do NOT delay)
    • Typical dose: 50–100 mg for 70 kg patient
    • Timing critical: earlier administration (within 3–4 h of hypotension onset) associated with improved outcomes
    • Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV (alternative if methylene blue contraindicated — see Teaching Layers, Section 7.2)
    • STAT cultures (blood × 2) if sepsis cannot be excluded; initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics per [Institution sepsis protocol]
    • Transthoracic or TEE echo (if immediately available) to assess CO, rule out tamponade, RV failure, LV thrombus
    • Continuous A-line monitoring + frequent labs (lactate q2–4h, BMP, CBC); consider ABG q1h if worsening
    • ICU transfer with active resuscitation — do NOT delay transport for "one more bolus"
    • Document: exact time of onset, VS/lactate trajectory, each pressor dose + time, methylene blue administration time, who called and when, transport time

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed hypotension starting at [time]. Current MAP [value], HR [rate], BP [reading], SpO₂ [value]. Exam shows [warm/cool extremities, pulse pressure ___]. Recent labs: K [value], Mg [value], lactate [value] at [time]. Currently on [pressor, dose, duration]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable / deteriorating]. [Symptoms: mental status, UOP trend, perfusion]. Pre-op risk factors: [ACE-I use, CPB time, EF, procedure type]. Intra-op fluid balance [+/– mL]." R: "Requesting [pressor adjustment / methylene blue / ICU bed / transfer]."

Who to call — scenario hierarchy

Situation Primary Contact Secondary Notes
Stable MAP 60–65, norepi restarted, trending stable APP / on-call fellow — Confirm: escalation plan, antihypertensive hold, ICU criteria
MAP 55–60, on norepi, trending down despite bolus APP + RRT call CT surgery notify Likely ICU transfer; prep now
MAP <55, AMS, oliguric, lactate rising, escalating pressor APP + RRT STAT CT surgery STAT Activate ICU bed immediately; prepare for multi-agent support
On norepi/vasopressin >6 h post-op without improvement APP + CT surgery + ICU attending — Methylene blue / hydroxocobalamin likely indicated; escalate early
Fever + hypotension + hyperlactatemia APP + ID consult CT surgery Sepsis differential; STAT cultures, broad-spectrum antibiotics
Recent cortisol <10 on chronic home steroids + refractory hypotension APP Endocrine consult (consider) Stress-dose hydrocortisone empirically; cortisol stim test later

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Pathophysiology detail — comprehensive mechanism review

sections.heading: NO-cGMP pathway and the basis for methylene blue
sections.bodyHtml:
The nitric oxide → soluble guanylate cyclase → cyclic GMP → smooth muscle relaxation cascade is the final common pathway for vasodilation in distributive shock. In CPB-induced vasoplegia, iNOS-generated NO continuously activates this pathway, leading to unopposed vasodilation.

Methylene blue intervention: Methylene blue is an inhibitor of soluble guanylate cyclase, blocking the cGMP production step. This directly interrupts the NO-mediated vasodilation, explaining the often-dramatic MAP response if given early. By contrast, catecholamine escalation alone tries to overcome the NO effect with stronger vasoconstriction signals — a brute-force approach that eventually fails due to receptor desensitization.

Vasopressin's role: Vasopressin's V1 receptors activate a distinct intracellular pathway (phospholipase C → IP₃ → calcium mobilization) that is partially independent of the cGMP cascade, allowing vasoconstriction even when NO levels are high. This explains why vasopressin + norepi is superior to norepi alone.

Hydroxocobalamin: Directly binds NO (forming cyanocobalamin), reducing free NO concentration. This is a scavenging strategy rather than a pathway inhibitor, less targeted than methylene blue but effective.

Adrenal insufficiency differential: Chronic corticosteroid users (prednisone ≥5 mg/day for >2 weeks) experience atrophy of the zona fasciculata. Under acute surgical stress, endogenous cortisol production cannot meet demand. The presentation is identical to vasoplegia — hypotension, warm shock, low SVR — but cortisol levels will be low (<10 mcg/dL) and electrolytes may show hyponatremia + hyperkalemia. Stress-dose hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q6h) is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

Risk factor taxonomy — pre-operative, intra-operative, and post-operative identifiers Pre-operative modifiable risk factors:
FactorMechanismAction
ACE-I/ARB within 24 h pre-opACE-I/ARB inhibit angiotensin II, which synergizes with catecholamines for vasoconstriction. Holding 24 h allows baseline catecholamine responsiveness to return.Verify held 24 h pre-op. If not held, escalate for future protocol refinement.
Beta-blocker continuationParadoxical: beta-blockers reduce POAF and arrhythmias, but may worsen initial vasoplegia response. Risk-benefit context-dependent.Confirm with provider; may hold 1–2 post-op doses if refractory hypotension. Restart when stable.
Chronic corticosteroid useIncreases baseline inflammatory burden; also risk for adrenal insufficiency in stress if not stress-dosed.Send cortisol level; give stress-dose hydrocortisone empirically if chronic use + refractory hypotension.
Pre-op EF <30%Lower baseline cardiac reserve makes vasoplegia more consequential for perfusion pressure.Expected worse initial tolerance; expect earlier escalation to methylene blue.
Intra-operative fixed risk factors:
FactorIncidence / Context
Prolonged CPB time >180 minLinear relationship: longer CPB → more SIRS exposure → higher vasoplegia risk.
Cardiac transplantationIncidence 40–50% (vs 5–25% general post-CPB). Highest-risk subgroup.
Valve surgery (aortic or mitral)Higher incidence than CABG alone; ~30–40% depending on complexity.
Large fluid primeDilutional effect + greater SIRS exposure.
Aortic crossclamp time >60 minExtended ischemia prolongs SIRS activation post-reperfusion.
Pre-existing sepsis or sepsis-adjacent baselinePatient already pro-inflammatory pre-operatively; additive effect.
Post-operative identifiers (bedside assessment):
  • Warm extremities at handoff from ICU
  • Recent weaning from vasopressor (rebounds into hypotension 1–6 h later)
  • High urine output earlier post-op (diuretic phase masking hypovolemia), now low
  • Lactate normal or only mildly elevated (distinguishes from cardiogenic/hemorrhagic shock)
  • Normal or high mixed venous O₂ saturation (SvO₂ >80%) — poor oxygen extraction from peripheral vasoplegia
Pressor pharmacology — why the escalation sequence matters

sections.heading: Norepinephrine (Levophed, Adrenaline)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Receptor activity: Alpha-1 > beta-1 adrenergic
  • Clinical effect: vasoconstriction (alpha) + modest inotropic support (beta-1)
  • Onset: 1–2 minutes; titrate every 2–5 minutes to effect
  • Dosing: 2–20 mcg/min; "peripheral norepi" acceptable <15 mcg/min short-term with close monitoring
  • Ceiling: 20 mcg/min. Beyond this, catecholamine resistance dominates; further escalation yields minimal MAP gain. This is the critical threshold for shifting strategy (add vasopressin or consider methylene blue).
  • Advantages: rapid onset, titrable, moderate inotropic benefit, familiar to nursing staff
  • Why first-line: starts working immediately while methylene blue (15–30 min onset) is being prepared

sections.heading: Vasopressin (Pitressin)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Receptor activity: V1 receptor agonist (distinct pathway from catecholamines)
  • Non-titrable: fixed dose 0.04 units/min in SIRS/shock contexts
  • Onset: 5–15 minutes; peak effect 30–60 min
  • Advantage: response preserved in acidosis and catecholamine-resistant states. Different pathway = synergistic with norepi.
  • Disadvantage: can cause splanchnic and coronary vasoconstriction at higher doses; stay at 0.04 units/min in acute post-CPB
  • Special note: norepi + vasopressin separate drips is standard; some protocols use pre-mixed combination drips — confirm local approach
  • Typical use: added once norepi >10 mcg/min or MAP plateau evident despite escalation

sections.heading: Methylene blue (1–2 mg/kg)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Mechanism: guanylate cyclase inhibitor; blocks NO → cGMP → vasodilation at source
  • Dosing: 1–2 mg/kg IV over 20–30 minutes (typical 50–100 mg)
  • Onset: 15–30 minutes; MAP response often dramatic if given early, gradual if delayed
  • Effect: directly addresses pathophysiology (NO excess), not reflex pressor escalation. MAP rise 10–20 mmHg common.
  • Timing crucial: Levin et al. (2009) demonstrated improved mortality with initiation within 3–4 h of hypotension onset vs late. Do NOT wait for "full pressor optimization" — recognize vasoplegia pattern and escalate early.
  • Contraindications: G6PD deficiency (hemolysis risk), concurrent MAOI, high-dose SSRI + other serotonergic agents (serotonin syndrome), linezolid
  • Side effects: urine bright blue-green (harmless, warn patient/family), photosensitivity, IV line and tubing stain blue
  • Pulse oximetry artifact: methylene blue can cause false low SpO₂ readings on some monitors (transient); check against clinical perfusion

sections.heading: Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit, 5 g)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Mechanism: direct NO scavenger (binds and inactivates NO)
  • Dosing: 5 g IV infusion over 15 minutes; may repeat × 1 if needed
  • Onset: 15–30 minutes; similar to methylene blue
  • Advantages: no serotonin syndrome risk, no G6PD contraindication, less drug-drug interaction burden
  • Disadvantages: more expensive, less data in cardiac surgery (more established in cyanide toxicity), less familiar to ICU teams, less commonly stocked
  • Side effects: urine bright red (alarming if not warned), transient elevated creatinine (from pigment), no major drug interactions
  • Availability: verify [Institution] stock before crisis; consider pre-ordering if methylene blue contraindicated patients anticipated

sections.heading: Rescue agents (empirical data limited in cardiac surgery)
sections.bodyHtml:
Agent Mechanism Context Reference
Hydrocortisone, stress-dose (50 mg q6h) Restores endogenous catecholamine responsiveness; addresses adrenal insufficiency if present Chronic steroids at home OR septic shock pattern Standard sepsis bundle; [Institution policy]
Fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily Mineralocorticoid; may improve catecholamine sensitivity Consider if prolonged vasopressor dependence beyond 24 h Controversial; limited data in cardiac post-op
Methylene blue — contraindications, interactions, and practical details

sections.heading: Absolute contraindications
sections.bodyHtml:
Condition Reason Alternative
G6PD deficiency Methylene blue oxidizes RBCs → hemolysis, acute anemia, renal failure Hydroxocobalamin 5 g IV
Concurrent MAOI (phenelzine, tranylcypromine, linezolid) Serotonin syndrome risk (agitation, tremor, hyperthermia, rigidity, seizure) Hydroxocobalamin
Concurrent high-dose SSRI + other serotonergic agents Serotonin syndrome — rare at standard methylene blue dose but reportable Hold SSRI briefly if possible; or use hydroxocobalamin

sections.heading: Relative cautions
sections.bodyHtml:
• Severe renal failure (Cr >3 or eGFR <15): methylene blue may accumulate. Still used, but ICU-level monitoring + consider dose reduction (0.5–1 mg/kg vs 1–2 mg/kg)
  • Cardiac arrhythmia history: methylene blue can prolong QT; verify EKG pre-dose if time permits
  • Photosensitivity history: advise light avoidance post-infusion for 24 h

sections.heading: Practical nursing points
sections.bodyHtml:
• Urine color: bright blue-green, sometimes appearing dark blue-black. Warn patient, family, and night shift. Reassure that color is harmless and resolves in 24–48 h.
  • IV line staining: tubing and connections turn blue. Cosmetic only, not harmful.
  • Do NOT mix in same IV line with other drugs. Use separate IV or flush well between infusions. Some incompatibilities reported.
  • Serotonin syndrome symptoms: agitation, confusion, tremor, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, tachycardia, hypertension (paradoxical), hyper-reflexia. RARE with standard dose but reportable to provider immediately.
  • Pulse oximetry artifact: SpO₂ may read falsely low (transient) during/immediately post-infusion on some monitors. Check against clinical perfusion (skin color, capillary refill). Artifact resolves as drug clears.

sections.heading: Contraindication check workflow
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Review MAR for SSRIs, linezolid, MAOIs before ordering
  2. Confirm G6PD status if unknown (send test if post-op status unclear)
  3. Document allergy/contraindication status before order placed
  4. If conflict exists, notify APP immediately; discuss hydroxocobalamin alternative
Differential diagnosis — sepsis vs vasoplegia vs adrenal insufficiency

sections.heading: Sepsis and vasoplegia overlap — both SIRS + NO excess + distributive shock
sections.bodyHtml:
A post-CPB patient with vasoplegia can simultaneously be developing sepsis (e.g., wound infection, line sepsis, aspiration pneumonia). The presentations overlap substantially.

Distinguishing features (not always clear-cut):

Feature Vasoplegia alone Sepsis ± vasoplegia
Fever Absent or low-grade (CPB-induced) Fever >38.5°C or hypothermia
WBC Normal or mildly elevated (CPB effect) WBC >12 or <4; left shift (bands)
Lactate Normal/slightly elevated; trends DOWN with pressor/MB Persistently elevated; worsens despite therapy
Cultures Negative (or contaminant) Positive blood or source culture
Source None identifiable Wound, line, pneumonia, other source on exam
Procalcitonin <0.5 (low) or normal >2 (elevated)
Timeline Immediately post-CPB (hours 0–24) POD 2+ (unless pre-existing)
Response to methylene blue Dramatic MAP rise within 20 min Minimal response; requires ongoing pressors + antibiotics

Clinical approach:

  • If sepsis cannot be excluded: do NOT wait for culture results. Send STAT cultures (blood × 2, others if source apparent) + initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics per [Institution sepsis protocol]
  • Co-management: even if you suspect "pure vasoplegia," cover for sepsis if fever/WBC/lactate pattern suggests infection
  • Stress-dose hydrocortisone: indicated for suspected septic shock regardless of adrenal insufficiency status
  • Key principle: antibiotics do not harm in pure vasoplegia; delayed antibiotics in true sepsis worsen mortality substantially

sections.heading: Adrenal insufficiency — identical presentation, different pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Chronic corticosteroid users (prednisone ≥5 mg/day for >2 weeks) have adrenal atrophy. In acute stress (surgery, sepsis), endogenous cortisol cannot rise to meet demand → relative or absolute adrenal insufficiency.

Distinguishing from pure vasoplegia:

Feature Vasoplegia Adrenal insufficiency
Peripheral perfusion Warm, well-perfused May be warm or cool depending on shock severity
Hypotension trigger Immediately post-CPB Can develop gradually post-op if stress prolonged
Electrolytes Usually normal Hyponatremia + hyperkalemia common
Glucose Hyperglycemia (post-op stress) Hypoglycemia possible (if not fed)
Cortisol level Normal or high (stress-response) <10 mcg/dL (inadequate stress response)

Assessment and management:

  1. Cortisol level: send early if chronic steroid use + refractory hypotension
  2. Do NOT delay: start stress-dose hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h empirically if chronic steroid use + shock pattern. Do not wait for cortisol result.
  3. Restart home corticosteroid at baseline dose once acute stress resolves (POD 1–2 if transfer back to ICU resolves quickly)
  4. ACTH level (optional): confirms primary adrenal failure; not needed for initial management
Special subgroups — transplant, LVAD, post-transplant chronic vasoplegic syndrome

sections.heading: Cardiac transplant recipients
sections.bodyHtml:
• Incidence: 40–50% (vs 5–25% general post-CPB population)
  • Mechanism: donor heart has been subjected to extended ischemia + reperfusion injury; immunosuppression + increased NO production
  • Timing: often delayed (POD 1–3 vs immediate post-CPB in other patients)
  • Management: same pressor escalation; early methylene blue often needed
  • Risk modifier: pre-transplant ACE-I/ARB use (common in heart failure patients) — higher vasoplegia risk

sections.heading: LVAD patients (post-implant vasoplegia)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Incidence: 5–10% in primary LVAD, higher in LVAD-to-transplant bridge scenarios
  • Mechanism: long CPB time, advanced heart failure baseline, potential SIRS from LVAD itself
  • Special consideration: MAP targets may differ with LVAD (LVAD function is afterload-sensitive); work closely with LVAD coordinator for pressor strategy
  • Methylene blue timing: particularly important; avoid prolonged low MAP that reduces LVAD forward flow

sections.heading: Post-transplant chronic vasoplegic syndrome (rare but documented)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Timeline: develops weeks to months post-transplant, not acute post-op
  • Mechanism: chronic rejection + allosensitization + NO dysregulation
  • Associated factors: chronic ACE-I/ARB use pre-transplant (ongoing), amiodarone for post-transplant arrhythmias, recurrent acute rejection
  • Management: different from acute post-CPB; may require long-term low-dose vasopressors + phosphodiesterase inhibitors; escalate to transplant team

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear in a stable patient, re-escalate immediately.

  • MAP slowly drifting down despite escalating pressor (norepi 15+ mcg/min, vasopressin running, lactate stable) — suggests vasopressor resistance; needs methylene blue or ICU escalation NOW
  • Lactate trending UP despite fluid/pressor optimization — signals deepening shock, worsening tissue perfusion; re-escalate
  • Urine output falling — from hourly to scant/oliguric; sign of renal hypoperfusion; critical threshold for ICU transfer
  • New fever or WBC rising — sepsis complicating vasoplegia; early culture + antibiotic initiation per [Institution] protocol
  • Cool extremities developing — transitioning from warm/distributive to mixed shock or profound cardiogenic component; echo needed
  • Altered mental status — from baseline alert to drowsy, confused, restless; hypoperfusion of brain; urgent escalation
  • Requiring second pressor (vasopressin added because norepi alone insufficient) — beyond simple floor management; activate ICU bed NOW
  • Recurrent need for boluses (>2 boluses in 2 h) — underlying hypovolemia + vasoplegia; ICU-level hemodynamic monitoring indicated
  • Methylene blue not delivering expected MAP rise — expect 10–20 mmHg within 20 min if given early; minimal response suggests refractory vasoplegia; consider hydroxocobalamin, escalate urgently
  • Pulse pressure narrowing (systolic dropping faster than diastolic, PP <30 mmHg) — shift toward cardiogenic component; echo for CO/tamponade/RV failure
  • New arrhythmia (AFib, SVT, ectopy) with hypotension — may worsen perfusion; notify provider
  • Worsening oxygenation — SpO₂ drop, new O₂ requirement; pulmonary edema from aggressive fluid bolusing or cardiogenic component

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Vasoplegia-level pressor support is ICU, not floor. The infrastructure for multiple vasopressors, continuous A-line, frequent labs q1–2h, and methylene blue is ICU-based. If escalating pressor beyond simple norepi, activate ICU bed immediately; do not try to manage complex pressor titration on a lower-acuity unit.

  2. Warm peripheries + wide pulse pressure + low MAP = distributive shock; never default to hypovolemia assumption. Reflex bolusing a euvolemic vasoplegic patient (already on pressor, high UOP earlier post-op, CVP adequate) worsens pulmonary edema without raising MAP. Assess CVP / JVP first; fluid responsiveness is limited.

  3. Pre-op ACE-I/ARB is the single most modifiable risk factor. Many surgeons hold ACE-I/ARB 24 h pre-op specifically to reduce vasoplegia risk. If a patient on lisinopril or losartan pre-op was NOT held, escalate for future protocol refinement with CT team; this is a quality improvement opportunity.

  4. Vasopressin works when catecholamines fail, especially in acidotic or catecholamine-resistant states. Do NOT skip vasopressin waiting for "one more norepi bolus." If norepi >10 mcg/min and MAP still plateauing, add vasopressin immediately. The V1 pathway is independent and synergistic.

  5. Methylene blue earlier is FAR more effective than late. Levin et al. (2009) demonstrated improved mortality with initiation within 3–4 h of hypotension onset. Waiting until profound shock (MAP <50, lactate >4, organ failure) significantly worsens outcomes. If vasoplegia suspected at MAP 60 and trending down, advocate for early methylene blue — do not accept "let's optimize fluids and pressors first for another hour."

  6. Methylene blue + any serotonergic drug = serotonin syndrome risk. Review the MAR carefully for SSRIs (sertraline, fluoxetine, etc.), linezolid, MAOIs, atypical antipsychotics. [Institution] order set should flag, but always double-check. If conflict exists, notify APP immediately and consider hydroxocobalamin alternative.

  7. Methylene blue turns urine bright blue-green. Warn the patient, family, and night shift BEFORE infusion. Patients and unfamiliar nurses often panic thinking they are bleeding into urine or being stained. One sentence prevents unnecessary callbacks and anxiety.

  8. Hydroxocobalamin is an effective alternative when methylene blue contraindicated, but availability may be limited. Verify [Institution] supply and stock status before crisis. Cost is higher; not all ICUs routinely stock.

  9. Adrenal insufficiency from chronic home steroids causes refractory hypotension indistinguishable from vasoplegia. Always ask: "On prednisone or dexamethasone at home?" If yes + hypotension, send cortisol level AND start stress-dose hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h empirically without waiting for result. Do not delay empiric treatment for assay return.

  10. SvO₂ in vasoplegia is often HIGH (>80%). Vascular dilatation means poor peripheral oxygen extraction, distinguishing it from cardiogenic shock (low SvO₂ <60%). If a monitor is available, check this; it teaches the pathophysiology and confirms distributive mechanism.

  11. Cardiogenic shock (RV failure, tamponade, LV thrombus) can co-exist with or mimic vasoplegia. Echo always when diagnostic uncertainty exists. "Warm shock" can be pure vasoplegia, cardiogenic with adequate CO, or mixed; only echo / hemodynamic monitoring clarify. Don't assume warm = vasoplegia.

  12. Sepsis drives an identical picture to vasoplegia: hypotension, warm peripheries, high CO, low SVR. Culture + broad-spectrum antibiotics if differential includes infection. Do not delay antibiotics for culture growth; mortality worsens dramatically with delays.

  13. Lactate trends are a better metric than MAP trend alone. A patient with MAP 62 and lactate 1.2 trending down is doing better than MAP 68 with lactate 3.5 trending up. Lactate reflects tissue perfusion adequacy; use it to guide escalation decisions.

  14. Titration speed matters. Increase norepi in mcg increments (1–2 mcg/min every 2–5 min), not double-doses or halving. Slow titration prevents overshoot, maintains hemodynamic stability, and allows time to assess pressor response before next dose adjustment.

  15. Peripheral norepi IV site risk. Peripheral IV acceptable for norepi <15 mcg/min short-term with close bedside monitoring. But if pressor escalation anticipated, place central line within first 24 h to avoid extravasation tissue necrosis. Do not wait until norepi is already at 20 mcg/min; anticipate central line need early.

cards.title: Ventricular Tachycardia / Ventricular Fibrillation (VT/VF)
cards.quickAnswer: Pulseless VT/VF = STAT defibrillate 200 J biphasic immediately + CPR + epinephrine 1 mg q3–5 min + amiodarone 300 mg after 2nd shock. Pulse + stable: amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min, replace K⁺ ≥ 4.5, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.5; identify ischemia, electrolytes, QT-prolonging drugs. Pulse + unstable (hypotension, shock, syncope): synchronized cardioversion 100 J → 200 → 300 → 360 J + sedation. Always check 12-lead ECG, ischemia (troponin, ST changes), post-CABG graft risk, ICD status.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
Pulseless VT/VF = STAT defibrillate 200 J biphasic immediately + CPR + epinephrine 1 mg q3–5 min + amiodarone 300 mg after 2nd shock. Pulse + stable: amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min, replace K⁺ ≥ 4.5, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.5; identify ischemia, electrolytes, QT-prolonging drugs.

Pulse + unstable (hypotension, shock, syncope): synchronized cardioversion 100 J → 200 → 300 → 360 J + sedation. Always check 12-lead ECG, ischemia (troponin, ST changes), post-CABG graft risk, ICD status.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Ventricular Tachycardia (VT): organized, wide-complex tachycardia (QRS >120 ms) originating below the AV node. May perfuse the brain and organs (pulsed VT) or cause immediate loss of perfusion (pulseless VT).
  • Ventricular Fibrillation (VF): chaotic, disorganized ventricular electrical activity with no organized QRS; no cardiac output; immediate loss of consciousness and death without defibrillation.
  • Incidence post-cardiac surgery: 1–3% overall; higher (5–10%) in CABG patients with ejection fraction < 35%, ischemic cardiomyopathy, or perioperative myocardial infarction (Topjian et al., 2020).
  • Why it matters: VT/VF is a cardiac arrest rhythm; survival depends on immediate recognition, defibrillation within 1–3 minutes, and continuous CPR. Delay of even 1 minute reduces survival by 7–10%.
  • Who this applies to: adult post-operative cardiac surgery patients on telemetry; ICU-level and stepdown-level monitoring populations.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative VT/VF arises from the collision of multiple destabilizing forces: ischemic injury from incomplete revascularization or graft thrombosis, electrolyte depletion from diuresis and cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) prime dilution, sympathetic surge from pain and inflammation, and drug-induced QT prolongation. The mechanism determines the rhythm pattern and, therefore, the treatment pathway.

Monomorphic VT reflects a single, stable re-entry circuit—typically scar-related, arising from prior myocardial infarction or surgical scar. Regular rate and consistent QRS morphology allow the ventricles to maintain some coordinated contraction, preserving perfusion in many patients. In post-CABG patients, monomorphic VT within the first 72 hours strongly suggests ischemia from graft occlusion or incomplete revascularization.

Polymorphic VT signals multiple, disorganized electrical foci or rapidly changing re-entry circuits—most commonly triggered by acute ischemia or drugs that prolong the QT interval. The chaotic morphology reflects the myocardium's loss of electrical synchrony. Torsades de pointes, a specific polymorphic pattern with the characteristic "twisting of the points" appearance, indicates prolonged QT interval complicated by early afterdepolarizations (Topjian et al., 2020).

Ventricular Fibrillation represents complete electrical chaos, devoid of organized depolarization. The ventricle quivers ineffectively; no cardiac output occurs. Patient loses consciousness immediately and will die within minutes without defibrillation.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following warrants immediate assessment:

  • Telemetry alarm: wide-complex tachycardia (QRS >120 ms, HR >120 bpm) sustained >30 seconds
  • Sudden loss of pulse in a previously hemodynamically stable patient
  • Witnessed sudden collapse with loss of consciousness
  • Patient reports syncope or near-syncope during palpitations (or palpitations followed by loss of awareness)
  • Repeated non-sustained VT (NSVT) runs increasing in frequency, duration, or complexity
  • Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD) delivering shock(s); asymptomatic shocks still require escalation
  • Electrical storm pattern: ≥3 VT/VF episodes in 24 hours, each requiring therapy

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Check pulse immediately (carotid or femoral) — pulse presence determines the ACLS pathway
  • Vital signs if pulse present: HR, BP, SpO₂, capillary refill, skin temperature/perfusion
  • Rhythm strip: obtain immediately and save; note monomorphic vs polymorphic morphology, HR
  • 12-lead ECG: STAT if pulse present; assess for ischemic changes (ST elevation, dynamic T waves), QTc duration, AV dissociation
  • Patient symptoms (if responsive): chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, presyncope, lightheadedness, altered mental status
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, troponin (rising troponin signals MI), serum creatinine for drug clearance
  • MAR review: QT-prolonging drugs on board? (methadone, haloperidol, ondansetron, fluoroquinolones, azoles, amiodarone); recent dosing of digoxin, diuretics
  • Surgery context: POD, procedure type (CABG/valve/hybrid), pre-op ejection fraction, prior VT/ICD, prior myocardial infarction, ischemic cardiomyopathy
  • ICD/pacer status: Is an ICD in place? Has it fired? Are epicardial pacing wires still in place (allows ATP attempt)?
  • Airway / breathing: patient breathing? Oxygen saturation acceptable? Lung sounds clear?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Pulse present, MAP > 65 mmHg, no hypotension, patient awake or near-awake, no chest pain or respiratory distress, no altered mental status.)

  1. STAT call APP / on-call fellow + charge RN — stay at bedside
  2. Obtain 12-lead ECG STAT — confirm diagnosis (wide QRS, AV dissociation, ischemic changes, QTc)
  3. Save rhythm strip at onset and document timestamp in chart
  4. Defibrillator pads on chest — be ready for decompensation into pulseless rhythm
  5. Ensure large-bore IV access (two lines preferred) — verify patency
  6. Replace electrolytes aggressively per post-op protocol:
    • K⁺ target ≥ 4.5 mEq/L (higher threshold for VT context than standard post-op 4.0)
    • Mg²⁺ target ≥ 2.5 mg/dL
    • iCa²⁺ target ≥ 1.1 mmol/L (maintain normal range)
    • Initiate rate/rhythm control:
    • Monomorphic VT with stable hemodynamics: amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min (may repeat to max 2.2 g/24 h); OR lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg loading dose if amiodarone contraindicated
    • Polymorphic VT or suspected torsades: magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 10 min; remove QT-prolonging drugs from MAR STAT
    • Identify and treat reversibles:
    • Ischemia: ECG changes? Troponin rising? → cath lab pathway per team (post-CABG graft occlusion is high-risk)
    • Electrolytes: aggressive replacement to goals above
    • Hypoxia: SpO₂ target > 94%; supplemental oxygen if needed
    • Fever: treat to normothermia (36.5–37.5 °C)
    • Medications: hold QT-prolongers immediately; check digoxin level if on digoxin
    • Cardiology consultation early — escalate per Section 6
    • Consider transient overdrive pacing for torsades (if epicardial pacing wires in place) — requires provider/EP approval
    • Continuous telemetry with trending — prepare for escalation to unstable pathway
    • Document with precise timestamps: onset, rhythm at onset, ECG obtained, interventions, drugs/doses, rhythm response

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(No pulse, OR pulse with hypotension/shock, chest pain, altered mental status, respiratory distress, pulmonary edema.)

  1. CALL CODE BLUE STAT — notify charge nurse; activate rapid response team
  2. Begin CPR immediately — push hard and fast on lower half sternum at least 2 inches; allow complete recoil; minimize interruptions; rotate compressions every 2 min
  3. Defibrillate if VF or pulseless VT — 200 J biphasic (per device specifications); resume CPR immediately without pulse check
  4. Assess pulse and rhythm every 2 minutes — only at end of each 2-min CPR cycle
  5. Epinephrine 1 mg IV push — first dose after initial shock; repeat q3–5 min during CPR (draw and push during chest compressions)
  6. After 2nd defibrillation attempt: amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus (preferred); OR lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg IV if amiodarone unavailable/contraindicated
  7. Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 1–2 min — for torsades de pointes or suspected long QT
  8. Treat reversibles (Hs and Ts) — (see Teaching Layers section)
  9. ROSC achieved? Post-ROSC: ICU transfer; targeted temperature management (TTM) per institutional protocol; neuroprognostication pathway at 48–72 h
  10. Document everything — strict time stamps: collapse time, CPR start time, shock times/joules, drug doses/routes/times, ROSC time, post-ROSC interventions. Code reviews depend on accurate charting.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed [pulseless VF/pulseless VT/sustained wide-complex VT with pulse] at [time]. Rhythm: [monomorphic / polymorphic / VF]. HR [if pulse] [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value]. [Symptoms or code status / CPR ongoing]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable / in code]." R: "Requesting [ACLS team activation / amiodarone protocol / electrolyte replacement / cath evaluation / ICD check / EP consult]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable monomorphic VT, first episode Primary APP / on-call fellow + cardiology
Stable polymorphic VT / torsades de pointes APP/fellow + cardiology + EP consultation
Pulseless VT/VF, any episode CODE TEAM STAT + cardiology + CT surgery
Recurrent VT/VF despite antiarrhythmics Cardiology + EP consultation; ICU transfer if not already
ICD patient with multiple shocks (electrical storm) Code team + EP consultation; may need sedation + esmolol
VT post-CABG with ST elevation / rising troponin Cardiology + cath lab evaluation (graft occlusion?) + CT surgery
Polymorphic VT + QTc > 500 ms Cardiology + EP + remove QT-prolonging drugs STAT

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections collapsible for expert skim.

sections.heading: 7.1 Monomorphic vs polymorphic VT
sections.bodyHtml:
Monomorphic VT:

  • Single, organized re-entry circuit; usually scar-related (prior MI, surgical scar, post-CABG graft occlusion)
  • Regular rate/rhythm; consistent QRS morphology beat-to-beat
  • If perfusing, some patients maintain conscious perfusion (BP stable, alert)
  • Less immediately life-threatening than VF if hemodynamically tolerated; allows time for drug/pacing therapy
  • Post-op context: monomorphic VT in first 72 hours post-CABG suggests acute ischemia (graft issue); requires ECG + troponin + cath evaluation

Polymorphic VT:

  • Multiple, disorganized foci or rapidly varying re-entry circuit
  • Irregular rate/morphology; appears "chaotic"; varying QRS axis beat-to-beat
  • Torsades de pointes: specific polymorphic VT in setting of prolonged QT interval; EKG shows QRS amplitude/axis "twisting" with each beat
  • Highest risk of degeneration to VF; requires emergent reevaluation and treatment
  • Mechanism: early afterdepolarizations (EAD) triggered by prolonged QT; often drug-induced (amiodarone paradox, methadone, haloperidol, ondansetron, fluoroquinolones, azoles) or from severe electrolyte depletion

Ventricular Fibrillation:

  • Chaotic, disorganized electrical activity; no organized QRS complex
  • No perfusing rhythm; immediate loss of consciousness; certain death within minutes without defibrillation
  • Only effective treatment: immediate defibrillation + CPR
  • Mechanism: complete loss of organized ventricular depolarization; may evolve from untreated VT

sections.heading: 7.2 ACLS algorithm
sections.bodyHtml:
Pulseless VT/VF pathway (Code Blue Algorithm):

Step Action Timing
1. Check pulse + rhythm If no pulse + VF/VT → defibrillate Within 1 min of collapse
2. Defibrillate 200 J biphasic Immediately; resume CPR without pause
3. CPR cycle Push hard/fast, allow complete recoil, rotate q2 min Continuous until ROSC or termination
4. Pulse/rhythm check Only at 2-min intervals Every 2 min of CPR
5. Epi 1 mg IV After initial shock; then q3–5 min 1st dose after shock 1; continue throughout resuscitation
6. Shock 2 200 J biphasic After 2 min CPR
7. After shock 2 Amiodarone 300 mg IV bolus (or lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg) May repeat amiodarone at 3–5 min
8. Shock 3 200 J biphasic After 2 min CPR
9. Epi repeat 1 mg IV q3–5 min Continue throughout
10. Treat reversibles Hs and Ts (see section 7.3) Ongoing during resuscitation

Perfusing VT — Stable pathway:

  • Obtain 12-lead ECG and SBAR escalation
  • Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min (preferred) OR lidocaine load
  • Replace K⁺/Mg²⁺ to post-op goals
  • Identify ischemia, electrolytes, QT-prolonging drugs
  • Prepare for decompensation → sync cardioversion

Perfusing VT — Unstable pathway:

  • Synchronized cardioversion per ACLS: 100 J → 200 → 300 → 360 J biphasic
  • Sedation + airway support required
  • Post-conversion: amiodarone load, electrolyte replacement, identify trigger

sections.heading: 7.3 Reversibles (Hs and Ts)
sections.bodyHtml:
Hypoxia

Recognition Immediate Treatment
SpO₂ < 94%, cyanosis, RR increased Ensure airway patent; supplemental O₂ 100%; bag-mask ventilation; intubation if needed; target SpO₂ ≥ 94%

Hypovolemia

Recognition Immediate Treatment
Flat neck veins, poor capillary refill, recent bleeding Bolus IV fluids (LR 250 mL q10min); assess for ongoing bleeding (surgical? GI?); transfusion if indicated

Hyperkalemia / Hypokalemia

Recognition Immediate Treatment
Peaked T waves, prolonged PR, widened QRS (high K⁺); flattened T waves, prominent U waves (low K⁺) Draw STAT K⁺. If K⁺ > 6.5: calcium gluconate 1 g IV (protective of myocardium), insulin 10 U IV + dextrose 25 g IV (D50 1 amp), albuterol 10–20 mg nebulized. If K⁺ < 3.5: aggressive KCl replacement IV (20–40 mEq per liter, max 10 mEq/h peripheral, 20 mEq/h central). In VT context, target K⁺ ≥ 4.5.

Hypothermia

Recognition Immediate Treatment
Core temperature < 32 °C, bradycardia, decreased perfusion, shivering ceases Rewarming protocol (passive external, active external, ECMO if severe); withhold IV drugs until core temp > 30 °C; space IV drugs q10 min during rewarming

Acidosis (Hydrogen ion)

Recognition Immediate Treatment
pH < 7.2, elevated lactate, respiratory acidosis Hyperventilation during CPR; sodium bicarbonate 1 mEq/kg IV if severe metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.1)

Tension PTX (Pneumothorax)

Recognition Immediate Treatment
JVD, hypotension, decreased breath sounds unilateral, tracheal deviation, POCUS shows absent lung sliding Needle decompression 2nd ICS midclavicular line; follow with chest tube

Tamponade

Recognition Immediate Treatment
Beck triad: hypotension, JVD, muffled heart sounds; POCUS shows RA/RV collapse Pericardiocentesis STAT or surgical drainage; notify CT surgery immediately; continue CPR during procedure

Toxins

Recognition Immediate Treatment
History of drug ingestion, OD; specific EKG patterns (TCA — widened QRS/peaked T; methadone — prolonged QTc; antipsychotics — prolonged QT) Activated charcoal if ingestion within 1–2 h; antidote-specific (naloxone for opioid, fomepizole for methanol, etc.); contact poison control

Thrombosis — Coronary

Recognition Immediate Treatment
STEMI on ECG, reciprocal changes, rising troponin, post-CABG status STAT ECG; STAT troponin; cath lab activation (primary PCI or assessment of graft patency); continue CPR; CT surgery aware if post-CABG

Thrombosis — Pulmonary

Recognition Immediate Treatment
Chest pain, hypoxia, hypotension, elevated D-dimer, recent surgery/immobility STAT CT angiography if stable enough; consider empiric anticoagulation if high clinical suspicion (post-op); notify CT surgery before starting anticoagulation

sections.heading: 7.4 Antiarrhythmic drug dosing — ACLS 2020
sections.bodyHtml:
Amiodarone (Class III — preferred first-line antiarrhythmic):

Scenario Dose Notes
Pulseless VT/VF — 1st dose 300 mg IV bolus After 2nd defibrillation
Pulseless VT/VF — repeat 150 mg IV bolus q3–5 min Max 2.2 g per 24 h
Stable VT — loading 150 mg IV over 10 min May repeat; total first 24 h = 1 g
Stable VT — maintenance drip 1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min × 18 h Hypotension in ~25%; decrease drip early (to 0.5 mg/min) when BP drops
Stable VT — PO transition 400 mg PO TID × 7–10 days Then 200–400 mg daily maintenance
Side effects Hypotension, bradycardia, phlebitis Use central line for drip when possible; anticipate BP drop

Lidocaine (Class IB — alternative if amiodarone unavailable/contraindicated):

Scenario Dose Notes
Pulseless VT/VF 1–1.5 mg/kg IV (typical 75–100 mg) Repeat 0.5–0.75 mg/kg q5–10 min; max 3 mg/kg in first hour
Stable VT 1–1.5 mg/kg load + 1–4 mg/min infusion Titrate to effect; avoid levels > 5 mcg/mL (toxicity)
Advantages Better for ischemic VT; lower hypotension risk than amiodarone Less effective for polymorphic VT than amio

Magnesium sulfate:

Scenario Dose Notes
Torsades de pointes (pulseless) 2 g IV over 1–2 min Even if serum Mg²⁺ is "normal"; empiric dosing for suspected long QT
Torsades de pointes (perfusing) 2 g IV over 10 min Can repeat 1 g q5–10 min × 1–2 doses
Post-ROSC continuation 1 mg/min × 6 h (some protocols) Continue if torsades suspected

Procainamide (Class IA — rarely stocked on floors; effective for monomorphic VT):

Scenario Dose Notes
Stable monomorphic VT Loading: 20–50 mg/min IV until arrhythmia suppressed, hypotension, QRS > 50% wider, or 17 mg/kg given Maintenance: 1–4 mg/min
Use case When amiodarone/lidocaine fail; requires EP/cardiology request Less commonly stocked post-op; order STAT from pharmacy

sections.heading: 7.5 Torsades de pointes — specific management
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition: polymorphic VT in setting of prolonged QT interval. EKG shows "twisting of the points" — QRS axis and amplitude shift beat-to-beat.

Causes in post-operative setting:

  • QT-prolonging drug stack: amiodarone (paradoxical — used to treat VT but prolongs QT), methadone, haloperidol, ondansetron, fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin), azole antifungals (fluconazole, itraconazole), cisapride
  • Electrolyte depletion: K⁺ < 3.5, Mg²⁺ < 1.8, Ca²⁺ < 7.5
  • Bradycardia: long pause preceding ectopic activity creates substrate for early afterdepolarization (EAD)
  • Inherited channelopathy: long QT syndrome (rare; may be undiagnosed pre-operatively)

Management priorities:

  1. Magnesium 2 g IV over 10 min immediately — first-line, even if serum Mg²⁺ is "normal" (serum may not reflect intracellular depletion)
  2. Remove offending QT-prolonging drugs STAT — discontinue methadone, haloperidol, ondansetron, fluoroquinolone, azole antifungal
  3. Replace K⁺ to ≥ 4.5 mEq/L and Mg²⁺ to ≥ 2.5 mg/dL — aggressive IV replacement
  4. Correct bradycardia — if HR < 60, use atropine 0.5–1 mg IV or transcutaneous pacing to raise rate > 100 (increases diastolic interval, suppresses EAD)
  5. Consider transient overdrive pacing (via epicardial wires if available) at rate 100–120 to suppress EAD
  6. Avoid Class IA antiarrhythmics (procainamide, disopyramide) — further prolong QT
  7. If degenerates to VF: defibrillate per ACLS algorithm
  8. Post-event: continuous telemetry; avoid QT-prolonging drugs; EP consultation; consider cardiology/EP investigation for inherited long QT if no obvious drug cause

sections.heading: 7.6 ICD and post-cardiac surgery context
sections.bodyHtml:
ICD patient with VT/VF:

  • ICD will attempt antitachycardia pacing (ATP) first (painless, low-energy termination of monomorphic VT)
  • If ATP fails, ICD delivers internal shock (patient may feel "thud" or chest pain)
  • Do NOT place external defibrillator pads directly over ICD device — magnet interference; offset pads 2–3 inches if possible
  • If pulseless or ICD shocks not terminating rhythm, proceed with external defibrillation per standard ACLS
  • Asymptomatic ICD shock ("I felt nothing") still requires evaluation — escalate to cardiology/EP for device interrogation
  • Electrical storm (≥ 3 VT episodes in 24 h requiring therapy): sedation (propofol, dexmedetomidine) + IV beta-blocker (esmolol drip) + antiarrhythmic + EP evaluation

Post-CABG monomorphic VT:

  • High suspicion for acute ischemia (graft thrombosis, incomplete revascularization) if sustained monomorphic VT occurs POD 0–3
  • STAT 12-lead ECG: look for ST elevation in CABG territory
  • STAT troponin: rising troponin confirms MI
  • Cath lab activation — may need angiography ± intervention (graft thrombus removal, balloon angioplasty, stent)
  • CT surgery notification is mandatory — may need re-exploration or urgent intervention

Reperfusion arrhythmia post-CABG:

  • Polymorphic VT in first 24–48 hours post-CABG is common; often self-resolves with electrolyte optimization + amiodarone + watchful waiting
  • Usually reflects transient reperfusion injury, not acute graft failure
  • Treat with magnesium 2 g IV, K⁺/Mg²⁺ replacement, and monitoring; cath/troponin not always necessary if rhythm terminates

Post-MAZE arrhythmias:

  • Sustained arrhythmias in first 4 weeks post-MAZE are common due to incomplete atrial scarring
  • Direct-current cardioversion often ineffective until scarring matures
  • Rate control + amiodarone preferred; escalate to EP per protocol

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear in a stable VT patient, re-escalate immediately.

  • Monomorphic VT increasing in rate or frequency — may herald imminent loss of perfusion
  • Morphology shifting from monomorphic to polymorphic — suggests evolving ischemia or drug-induced QT prolongation; higher degeneration risk
  • QTc > 500 ms on QT-prolonging drug — torsades de pointes risk rising; hold/decrease offending drug STAT
  • K⁺ trending down despite aggressive replacement — ongoing diuresis, hemodialysis loss, or malabsorption; recheck q2–4h during VT event
  • Mg²⁺ < 2.0 mg/dL — severe deficiency; high arrhythmia risk; IV replacement 2–4 g/day may be needed
  • New or evolving ST elevation / dynamic T wave changes — acute ischemia; cath evaluation needed (post-CABG graft occlusion is high-risk)
  • Troponin rising on POD 0–3 — perioperative MI or graft thrombosis; call cardiology + CT surgery STAT
  • BP trending down on amiodarone drip — expected in ~25% of patients; decrease drip preemptively to 0.5 mg/min rather than chasing hypotension
  • SpO₂ declining, RR increasing, signs of pulmonary edema — VT reducing cardiac output; patient may not tolerate rate despite BP appearing stable
  • New mental status change, confusion, anxiety — reduced cerebral perfusion from VT; re-escalate immediately
  • Recurrent NSVT runs despite antiarrhythmic — substrate unstable; high risk for sustained VT/VF
  • ICD receiving multiple shocks in rapid succession — electrical storm pattern; EP consult + sedation pathway STAT
  • New QT-prolonging medication added (azole, fluoroquinolone, methadone, ondansetron) to existing amiodarone — torsades risk escalating
  • Worsening renal function (creatinine rising, UOP falling) — reduced drug clearance; amiodarone/lidocaine dosing adjustment needed
  • No recent electrolyte labs available — unblinded therapy; always draw STAT K⁺/Mg²⁺/Ca²⁺ in VT patient; do not treat blind

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Sustained VT ≥ 30 seconds is treated as sustained VT regardless of hemodynamics. Don't wait for a 12-lead or cardiology confirmation in the unstable patient; escalate and prepare for defibrillation/cardioversion immediately.

  2. Pulse check is the THE decision point. No pulse + VF/VT = CODE BLUE + defibrillate immediately. Pulse + stable = amiodarone/electrolytes. Pulse + unstable = synchronized cardioversion. Get this fork right and the algorithm cascades.

  3. Defibrillation timing kills or cures. Each minute delay in defibrillation = 7–10% survival drop (Topjian et al., 2020). Call code, get defibrillator, shock within 1 minute. CPR and drugs come after.

  4. Synchronized cardioversion for stable monomorphic VT with pulse; unsynchronized defibrillation for VF or pulseless VT. The sync button is CRITICAL — never sync on VF (rhythm too chaotic). For pulseless or VF, no sync; for unstable monomorphic with pulse, sync.

  5. Magnesium for torsades de pointes — give it even if serum Mg²⁺ is "normal." Serum levels may not reflect intracellular depletion; empiric 2 g IV for any suspected torsades (prolonged QT on ECG).

  6. Identify and REMOVE QT-prolonging drugs immediately. Methadone, haloperidol, ondansetron (especially in combination), fluoroquinolones, azoles, amiodarone (paradoxical). Don't just treat the arrhythmia; discontinue the offending agent(s) STAT and notify pharmacy.

  7. Hyperkalemia can masquerade as wide-complex "VT." Peaked T waves, widened QRS, bradycardia. Check K⁺ STAT; if > 6.5, treat with calcium gluconate, insulin, albuterol. Do NOT defibrillate for pseudo-VT from hyperkalemia.

  8. Post-CABG sustained monomorphic VT = think graft occlusion. VT POD 0–3 + ST elevation in CABG territory + rising troponin = cath lab pathway STAT. Don't just load amiodarone; call CT surgery + cardiology for possible urgent intervention.

  9. Reperfusion arrhythmia is often self-limited. Polymorphic VT in first 24–48 h post-CABG often resolves with electrolyte optimization + watchful waiting. Amiodarone + K⁺/Mg²⁺ repletion is usually sufficient; may not need emergency cath.

  10. Polymorphic VT WITHOUT prolonged QT = think acute ischemia. Different mechanism from torsades de pointes. Obtain ECG + troponin + cath evaluation for graft/coronary issue.

  11. Antitachycardia pacing (ATP) via epicardial pacer wires can convert some monomorphic VT. If temp wires in place and VT hemodynamically tolerated, notify provider — EP may try ATP before drugs/shock.

  12. Beta-blockers are UNDERUSED in electrical storm. Esmolol IV drip is high-yield; reduces sympathetic trigger and can suppress recurrent VT. Don't forget this alongside antiarrhythmics + sedation.

  13. Amiodarone hypotension is PREDICTABLE — ~25% of patients drop BP. Anticipate with fluid bolus plan; preemptive decrease of drip to 0.5 mg/min when BP starts dropping is better than chasing severe hypotension.

  14. Procainamide is gold for monomorphic VT but rarely stocked on floors. If available via pharmacy STAT, it's effective where amio/lido fail. Requires EP/cardiology request and urgent pharmacy coordination.

  15. Document EVERYTHING — code reviews live or die by the chart. Time stamps: onset, pulse check, shock times/joules, drug doses/routes/times, ROSC time, post-ROSC interventions. Incomplete documentation raises sentinel event flags.

cards.title: VTE Prophylaxis Post-Cardiac Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: Post-cardiac surgery = high VTE risk (3–10% DVT without prophylaxis; ~1–2% PE). Standard: combined mechanical (sequential compression devices [SCDs] bilaterally, continuous in bed) + pharmacologic (heparin 5000 u SC q8h OR enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily — adjust for CrCl < 30) started POD 1–2 when bleeding risk acceptable. Early ambulation is the best prevention. HIT history → argatroban or bivalirudin for prophylaxis. Continue through length of stay; extended prophylaxis for high-risk patients at discharge (enoxaparin 10–14 days post-op if prior VTE, active cancer, obesity, age > 75, or anticipated immobility).
