sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, scope, and who it applies to.

  • Definition: Combined use of mechanical and pharmacologic agents to prevent deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) during the immediate post-operative period and through hospitalization in cardiac surgery patients.
  • Why high-risk: Post-cardiac surgery triggers hypercoagulability (tissue factor release, fibrinogen/platelet elevation, thrombin surge), immobility, venous stasis from low limb movement and positive pressure ventilation, and endothelial injury from cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) cannulation and operative trauma.
  • Incidence with prophylaxis: Symptomatic DVT 1–5%, symptomatic PE 0.5–2%; without prophylaxis ~3–10% DVT, ~1–3% PE. Untreated PE mortality 10–30%.
  • Who it applies to: Every adult post-cardiac surgery patient (all procedures: CABG, valve, aortic, myectomy, MAZE, transplant, ECMO, LVAD). Highest yield POD 0 through discharge and 10–14 days post-discharge for high-risk patients.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why post-cardiac is hypercoagulable:

Post-cardiac surgery puts the coagulation system into a prothrombotic state through multiple simultaneous mechanisms:

  • Tissue factor activation — surgical incision and CPB prime the tissue-factor pathway; thrombin generation rises sharply POD 0–1
  • Contact activation — foreign surfaces in CPB circuit (pump, cannulae, oxygenator) trigger the contact (intrinsic) pathway
  • Elevation of procoagulants — fibrinogen, factors VIII and V, platelets all increase; antithrombin and protein C decrease post-op
  • Immobility — bed rest, pain, and sedation limit lower extremity movement; venous stasis risk is highest POD 0–2
  • Endothelial injury — CPB-induced inflammatory activation damages the endothelium of leg veins, reducing the natural anticoagulant surface
  • Combined effect — the convergence of hypercoagulability + immobility + endothelial damage = ~10% DVT rate without prophylaxis

Risk factors for developing VTE despite prophylaxis:

Age > 60, obesity (BMI > 30), prior VTE or thrombophilia (hereditary or acquired Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A mutation), active malignancy, new-onset atrial fibrillation, prolonged ICU/hospital stay anticipated (> 5 days), and immobility expected post-discharge (stroke, sepsis, multi-organ failure).

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — patient populations, acuity levels, and when VTE prophylaxis is indicated.

Universally indicated:

  • Every adult post-op cardiac surgery patient (POD 0+) until discharge or transfer to lower acuity
  • Includes CABG, all valve repairs/replacements, aortic surgery, MAZE, heart transplant, ECMO weaning, LVAD insertion, etc.
  • Continue through hospitalization regardless of age, pre-op mobility, or bleeding history (risk-benefit always favors prophylaxis post-cardiac)

Special populations (apply regimen with modifications per §5):

  • HIT history (no active HIT): Use argatroban or bivalirudin instead of heparin; never use unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin again
  • Severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30): Enoxaparin must be dose-adjusted to 30 mg daily (vs 40 mg standard) to prevent accumulation
  • Thrombocytopenia < 50,000: Hold pharmacologic prophylaxis; transfuse if indicated; continue mechanical prophylaxis (SCDs)
  • Active bleeding (POD 0 post-op oozing): Mechanical only until POD 1–2 when chest tube output < 200–300 mL/shift
  • Epidural catheter in place: Hold SC heparin ≥ 2 h before epidural insertion and ≥ 2 h after catheter removal (ASRA, 2018)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / gather information* (5 minutes per shift)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside and chart review. Information-gathering only; no interventions yet.

Baseline (on admission to ICU/unit or POD 1):

  • Bilateral calf exam — circumference (measure at largest point using tape), pain, swelling, warmth, skin color, pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial), Homans sign (not diagnostic, but assess)
  • Bleeding risk assessment — estimated POD, chest tube output (if present), coagulation labs (PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen), platelet count, anticoagulation orders
  • VTE history — prior DVT/PE? Thrombophilia? HIT history? (if HIT: document prominently — lifelong contraindication to heparin)
  • Mobility baseline — current activity level, PT/OT plan, anticipated mobility for post-discharge (critical for extended prophylaxis decision)
  • Renal function — Cr, CrCl (or Cockcroft-Gault estimate); if CrCl < 30, enoxaparin dose must be adjusted

Every shift (ongoing):

  • Bilateral leg circumference — if baseline established POD 1, compare sides at same location; asymmetric swelling (> 2 cm difference) triggers Doppler evaluation
  • Calf pain, warmth, swelling — unilateral swelling + pain = red flag; alert APP for Doppler evaluation
  • SCD function and fit — devices applied bilaterally? Straps tight without indentation marks? Cuff pressure reading within range per manufacturer (typically 35–55 mmHg)? Skin integrity under cuff (erythema, blistering, maceration)?
  • Patient compliance with SCDs — are devices still on after bathroom breaks or ambulation? Most common cause of SCD "failure"
  • Pharmacologic prophylaxis documentation — agent, dose, route, time given; if SC: injection site rotating (abdomen, thigh, buttock)?
  • Bleeding signs — oozing from incision, expanding hematoma, hematochezia, hemoptysis, unusual bruising?
  • Platelet trend — baseline POD 0–1, then daily × 3–5 (watch for HIT: drop > 30% from baseline OR absolute < 100k); if suspicion arises, STAT HIT antibody panel
  • Renal function trend — Cr and CrCl (if enoxaparin on board with CrCl 30–50, recheck in 24–48 h; if CrCl drops below 30, notify for dose adjustment to 30 mg daily)

sections.heading: 5.1 Mechanical prophylaxis — SCDs
sections.bodyHtml:
Element Details
Device Sequential compression devices (SCDs) — bilateral application
Application Apply immediately on ICU/unit arrival if not already in place; do not wait for POD 1
Timing: in bed Continuous while patient is in bed
Timing: ambulation Remove when patient ambulates ≥ 2 hours; reapply when returns to bed
Sizing Measure calf circumference per manufacturer; proper fit is critical — too loose = ineffective; too tight = peroneal nerve injury risk
Pressure check Monitor cuff inflation pressure q shift; typical range 35–55 mmHg per device specs; adjust if outside range
Skin assessment Inspect under cuff q shift — erythema, blistering, maceration, indentation marks; reposition or resize if skin compromise noted
Duration Continue through hospitalization; most patients discontinue at discharge unless extended prophylaxis criteria met (see §5.4)
Patient teaching Explain purpose (prevent leg clots after heart surgery); remind patient NOT to remove devices without asking nurse (common compliance gap at bathroom); reapply after bathroom breaks

sections.heading: 5.2 Pharmacologic prophylaxis — standard dosing
sections.bodyHtml:
Scenario Agent Dose Frequency Route Notes
Standard renal function (CrCl ≥ 30) Unfractionated heparin (UFH) 5,000 units SC q8h Subcutaneous Gold standard post-cardiac; more reversible than LMWH if bleeding; q8h dosing (not q12h) is standard in cardiac post-op
Standard renal function Enoxaparin (Lovenox) 40 mg SC daily Subcutaneous Alternative to UFH; once-daily dosing more convenient; less reversible (protamine only partially effective)
CrCl 30–50 Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily Subcutaneous No dose reduction required; monitor Cr trend; if drops below 30, adjust
CrCl < 30 Enoxaparin 30 mg SC daily Subcutaneous CRITICAL: dose-adjusted; ~40% accumulation risk at 40 mg. Verify CrCl calculation; recheck in 24–48 h
CrCl < 30 UFH 5,000 units SC q8h Subcutaneous Preferred for severe renal disease (no accumulation); same dosing as standard
HIT history (no active thrombosis) Argatroban Per protocol IV infusion IV Direct thrombin inhibitor; no heparin-platelet cross-reactivity; hospital protocol specifies weight-based or nomogram dosing
HIT history Bivalirudin Per protocol IV or SC IV / SC Alternative direct thrombin inhibitor; check institutional availability + guidelines; dosing per protocol
HIT history Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC daily Subcutaneous Off-label for prophylaxis; Factor Xa inhibitor; minimal cross-reactivity with HIT antibodies; less data than argatroban

sections.heading: 5.3 Initiation timing and hold criteria
sections.bodyHtml:
When to START pharmacologic prophylaxis:

  • POD 0 (immediate post-op): Mechanical prophylaxis only (SCDs); hold pharmacologic due to ongoing surgical bleeding
  • POD 1–2: Initiate pharmacologic prophylaxis once:
  • Chest tubes output < 200–300 mL/shift (varies by surgeon preference; verify with APP/surgeon)
  • No active oozing from surgical incision on dressing check
  • Coagulation labs acceptable (PT/INR, PTT within acceptable range for post-op)
  • Platelet count > 50,000 (or per surgeon's institutional threshold)
  • Time of administration: If daily dosing, give in AM; if q8h, typically 0800, 1600, 2400 hours

When to HOLD pharmacologic prophylaxis:

Criterion Action Duration
Active bleeding (ongoing ooze from incision, hematochezia, hemoptysis) Hold pharmacologic; continue SCDs Until bleeding controlled ≥ 24 h
Post-op Day 0 Mechanical (SCDs) only Until POD 1 AM (reassess bleeding; usually start prophylaxis)
Epidural catheter placement Hold SC heparin ≥ 2 h before insertion; ≥ 2 h after removal before next dose (ASRA, 2018) Per ASRA guidelines; document exact times
Platelets < 50,000 Hold pharmacologic; continue SCDs; transfuse if < 50k Until platelet count > 75,000; recheck post-transfusion
Suspected or confirmed HIT STAT stop ALL heparin (including heparinized flushes) Permanent; switch to argatroban/bivalirudin immediately
Patient refusal Document refusal; educate on risks; offer alternative route (IV vs SC) Per discussion; focus on SCDs + early mobility as backup

sections.heading: 5.4 Extended prophylaxis at discharge
sections.bodyHtml:
Indications for extended prophylaxis (continue for 10–14 days post-discharge):

Initiate before discharge if ≥ 1 of the following criteria are present:

  • Prior history of VTE (DVT or PE)
  • Hereditary or acquired thrombophilia (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, antiphospholipid antibody)
  • Active malignancy at time of surgery
  • Obesity (BMI > 35) with anticipated post-discharge immobility
  • Age > 75 with anticipated prolonged immobility (bed-bound, unable to ambulate)
  • Anticipated prolonged post-discharge immobility (severe deconditioning, stroke, sepsis, multi-organ failure)

Extended prophylaxis agents:

  • Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily (or dose-adjusted if CrCl < 30) × 10–14 days OR until fully mobile
  • Enoxaparin 30 mg SC daily if CrCl < 30 (renal dose)
  • UFH 5,000 u SC q8h (alternative for severe renal disease or HIT history)
  • Warfarin (if indicated for atrial fibrillation or other indication — covers VTE prophylaxis simultaneously)
  • DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran if clinically appropriate) — may cover VTE + AF/other indication simultaneously

Non-high-risk patients: Typically discontinue prophylaxis at discharge; SCDs not needed; early ambulation is prophylaxis

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. Platelet count drops > 30% from baseline OR falls below 100,000 — calculate 4T score for HIT; send HIT antibody panel; prepare to hold all heparin if HIT suspicion rises
  2. New unilateral calf swelling + pain — order STAT bilateral lower extremity venous Doppler; do not assume benign; do not discharge without assessment
  3. Asymmetric calf circumference (> 2 cm difference between sides) — Doppler urgently
  4. Acute dyspnea POD 2–5 with normal CXR — do NOT anchor on normal CXR; PE can present with minimal radiographic findings; order CTA PE protocol or V/Q scan urgently
  5. Sudden tachycardia + unexplained hypotension — PE or sepsis consideration; send lactate, ABG; imaging if PE suspected
  6. SCD-related skin breakdown — assess for proper sizing, pressure, duration in bed; rotate placement; if severe (blistering, ulceration), pause SCD use on that extremity; notify APP
  7. Calf pain with dorsiflexion (Homans sign) + swelling — low sensitivity/specificity, but still order Doppler if unilateral swelling present
  8. Recurrent episodes of unilateral foot coolness, color change, or sensory loss — peroneal nerve compression from too-tight SCD; measure and resize immediately
  9. Patient reports ability to easily slip fingers under SCD cuff — device too loose; remeasure and reapply

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections in Section 7 are intended for in-app collapse. Nursing students, new-grad RNs, and advanced beginners can expand to build deeper understanding; experienced nurses and experts can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Physiology detail
sections.bodyHtml:
Why cardiac surgery creates a perfect storm for VTE:

Virchow's triad describes three factors that predispose to thrombosis: (1) stasis (slow blood flow), (2) endothelial injury (damaged vessel wall), and (3) hypercoagulability (excess clotting factors). Cardiac surgery activates all three simultaneously:

  • Stasis — post-op patients are immobile (bed rest, pain, sedation, lines limiting movement). Lower extremity venous return relies on muscle contraction; without movement, blood pools in calf veins.
  • Endothelial injury — CPB and surgical trauma activate the endothelium; the antithrombin-heparin cofactor surfaces are downregulated; the natural anticoagulant properties of the vascular endothelium are suppressed.
  • Hypercoagulability — the surgical trauma triggers an acute-phase response: fibrinogen rises (normal post-op inflammatory response), platelet count increases (peak POD 2–3), and thrombin generation surges. Anticoagulant proteins (antithrombin, protein C) are consumed or diluted.

How SCDs work:

SCDs use intermittent pneumatic compression (rhythmic inflation and deflation) to physically squeeze the calf, pushing blood upward in the deep venous system. This accomplishes two things: (1) immediate mechanical displacement of venous stasis, and (2) stimulation of fibrinolytic (clot-dissolving) cascades — the endothelium responds to shear stress by releasing tissue plasminogen activator (tPA), the body's own clot-buster.

SCDs are less effective than heparin alone in RCTs, but in combination (mechanical + pharmacologic), they are synergistic and superior to either alone.

How heparin works:

Unfractionated heparin (UFH) binds to antithrombin (AT), which then inhibits the key clotting enzymes thrombin (IIa) and Factor Xa. This does NOT dissolve existing clots; it prevents thrombin generation and stops the coagulation cascade. The advantage in cardiac post-op is rapid reversibility with protamine sulfate if bleeding occurs.

Enoxaparin (low-molecular-weight heparin, LMWH) binds AT but has a higher ratio of anti-Xa (inhibits Factor X) to anti-IIa (inhibits thrombin) activity compared to UFH. It is longer-acting and renally excreted, so it accumulates in renal impairment.

sections.heading: 7.2 Patient and family teaching — common questions
sections.bodyHtml:
"Why am I getting blood thinner injections when I'm not bleeding?"
You had heart surgery, which puts your blood at risk for clots in your legs or lungs for a few days to weeks. The surgery itself triggers your body to make clots faster (that's normal but dangerous). We use two methods — these machines on your legs and these small injections — to prevent clots. It's prevention, not treatment.

"When do I stop these injections?"
Usually at discharge or a few days after, depending on your risk. If you had a clot before surgery, or if we think you're very high-risk, you might take them home for 10–14 days. Your doctor will tell you before you leave.

"What if I refuse the injections?"
We really encourage them because they work well together with the leg machines. If you truly don't want them, we'll document that, focus on keeping the machines on, and push hard on walking. But talk to your surgeon first — some patients have good reasons to skip them (fear of needles, allergy), and we can work around it.

"How long do I need to wear these leg squeezer machines?"
Usually while you're in the hospital. Once you go home, if you're walking regularly and not at super-high risk, you won't need them. But if you had a clot before, or if you're going to be stuck in bed at home, you might use them longer.

"What if I feel a pain in my calf?"
Tell your nurse right away. A pain in one calf that's different from the other side, or with swelling or warmth, needs checking. We'll likely do an ultrasound (Doppler) to make sure it's not a clot. Don't wait.

"Can I shower with these machines on?"
No, take them off for a short shower (a few minutes). Dry your legs completely after; then put them back on. No long soaks in the tub while you're at high risk.

"Do I need to do leg exercises too?"
Yes. Even in bed, you can pump your ankles, squeeze your calf muscles, and do thigh sets every hour. These are like your own blood thinner — they keep blood moving. Once you can walk, that's even better.

sections.heading: 7.3 HIT (Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia) — what nurses need to know
sections.bodyHtml:
What is HIT?

HIT is a serious, sometimes life-threatening immune reaction to heparin. The patient's immune system develops antibodies against a complex of heparin and a platelet protein (PF4). These antibodies bind the complex on platelet surfaces, causing platelets to clump and activate. The result: paradoxically, the blood thinner causes clots (the opposite of what we want).

How to recognize HIT:

  • Sudden platelet drop — count falls > 30% from baseline (e.g., 250k → 150k) OR absolute count < 100k
  • Timing — typically 5–14 days after heparin exposure (but can be earlier if prior heparin exposure)
  • Thrombosis — new DVT, PE, stroke, or other thrombotic event DURING the platelet drop (this distinguishes HIT from other causes of thrombocytopenia)
  • Skin necrosis — rare but specific: necrotic lesions at SC heparin injection sites (pathognomonic)

What to do if you suspect HIT:

  1. STAT call to APP/provider — do not wait for lab confirmation if clinical suspicion is high
  2. STAT lab orders — 4T score calculation + HIT antibody panel (ELISA or other); platelet count serial
  3. STOP all heparin immediately — including heparinized line flushes (use saline instead)
  4. Switch to alternative — if thrombosis present, start argatroban or bivalirudin per hospital protocol; if HIT antibody positive even without thrombosis, still avoid all heparins
  5. Document prominently — "HIT history" in chart and consider a MedicAlert bracelet recommendation (lifelong flag)

HIT in the cardiac post-op setting is a crisis — if a cardiac post-op patient develops thrombocytopenia day 5–7 on heparin prophylaxis, HIT is on the differential and must be ruled out urgently.

sections.heading: 7.4 Special populations and renal dose adjustment
sections.bodyHtml:
Renal impairment and enoxaparin:

Enoxaparin is cleared renally. In normal renal function (CrCl ≥ 60), 40 mg daily is standard. But in CrCl 30–50, the drug clears more slowly; in CrCl < 30, it accumulates dramatically. A patient given 40 mg daily with CrCl 15 can develop toxic levels by day 3–4 post-op, increasing bleeding risk.

  • CrCl ≥ 60: 40 mg SC daily (standard)
  • CrCl 30–50: 40 mg SC daily (no reduction, but monitor Cr trend; if drops below 30, adjust)
  • CrCl < 30: 30 mg SC daily (dose-adjusted; ~25–30% of normal dose accumulation risk)

Verify and document the CrCl calculation at baseline and recheck in 24–48 h if CrCl is borderline (30–50). If Cr rises or CrCl drops below 30 during hospitalization, notify pharmacy and APP immediately for dose adjustment.

HIT and extended prophylaxis:

If patient has a history of HIT (even if no active HIT at time of admission), they should NEVER receive unfractionated or low-molecular-weight heparin again, even for prophylaxis. Use argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux (off-label) instead. This is a lifelong contraindication; educate the patient to carry a card or MedicAlert.

Heart transplant and LVAD patients:

Valsalva during straining for bowel movements or coughing is poorly tolerated in transplant and LVAD patients (destabilizes preload dangerously). Constipation prevention is critical. Ensure bowel regimen is on board (docusate, PEG) from POD 0–1. Do not wait for constipation to develop. Lower threshold for methylnaltrexone if standard bowel regimen is slow. Use SCDs continuously; minimize time off for ambulation if possible (prioritize bowel regimen over early walking in the first 48–72 h).

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in patients on standard prophylaxis; if any develop, escalate immediately.

  • Sudden platelet drop > 30% OR absolute < 100,000 — HIT concern; STAT HIT panel; prepare to hold all heparin
  • New unilateral calf swelling, pain, warmth — DVT until proven otherwise; STAT Doppler; do not discharge without assessment
  • Calf circumference difference > 2 cm between sides — asymmetric swelling red flag; Doppler urgently
  • Acute dyspnea POD 2–5 (even with normal CXR) — PE consideration; CTA PE protocol or V/Q scan; do not anchor on normal CXR
  • Tachycardia + tachypnea + hypotension unexplained — PE or sepsis; lactate, ABG, imaging if PE suspected
  • Chest pain + dyspnea pleuritic in nature — PE until proven otherwise
  • Calf pain on passive dorsiflexion + unilateral swelling — low sensitivity/specificity for DVT, but still order Doppler if swelling present
  • Foot coolness, color change, or sensory loss on one side — peroneal nerve compression from SCD; remeasure and resize immediately
  • SCD skin breakdown (blistering, erythema, ulceration) — pause SCD on that extremity; notify APP; reassess device fit
  • Platelet count not recovering post-transfusion — HIT consideration if bleeding is controlled; check HIT antibody status

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. SCDs only work when ON. The most common cause of SCD "failure" is patient removing them after a bathroom break and forgetting to reapply. Build SCD compliance into hourly rounds: "Are your leg squeezer devices still on?"

  2. Peroneal nerve injury from too-tight SCDs causes foot drop and sensory loss. Compression of the peroneal nerve at the fibular head (lateral knee) is preventable. Proper sizing, monitoring for indentation marks, and patient tolerance checks q shift are essential.

  3. Heparin 5000 u q8h is MORE effective than q12h for prophylaxis. Some institutions default to q12h to reduce injection frequency. Resist this; q8h is the standard post-cardiac prophylaxis regimen (ACCP, 2012; ASH, 2018).

  4. HIT is a lifelong flag. If a patient develops HIT (confirmed or probable), they should NEVER receive unfractionated or LMWH again. Document "HIT history" prominently. Consider a MedicAlert bracelet. Use argatroban, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux for any future prophylaxis/treatment.

  5. Renal dose adjustment for enoxaparin is frequently missed. CrCl < 30 mL/min = 30 mg daily (not 40 mg). Drug accumulation in renal failure increases bleeding risk. Verify CrCl calculation; recheck in 24–48 h if borderline (30–50).

  6. Thrombocytopenia < 50,000 is a relative contraindication to pharmacologic prophylaxis. Transfuse if platelet count < 50k (some institutions transfuse at < 75k for post-op patients). Recheck post-transfusion; hold heparin until count is safe.

  7. Epidural catheter timing is critical per ASRA 2018. Recommend ≥ 2 hours after last SC heparin dose before epidural insertion, and ≥ 2 hours after catheter removal before next heparin dose. Document times carefully to avoid epidural hematoma.

  8. Early ambulation is the single BEST prophylaxis. Mechanical + pharmacologic are second-line to active patient movement. If a patient isn't ambulating by POD 2 (barring cardiac, respiratory, or neurologic complications), escalate PT/OT involvement. An immobilized patient → extended prophylaxis at discharge.

  9. Unilateral calf swelling + pain = Doppler urgently. Do NOT dismiss as "just post-op swelling" or "Charlie horse." If asymmetric and patient is post-cardiac with immobility, the pre-test probability of DVT is substantial. Order bilateral leg Doppler.

  10. "Sudden dyspnea POD 3–5 with normal CXR = PE until proven otherwise." PE often presents with minimal radiographic findings. Do not anchor on normal CXR. Order CTA PE protocol (preferred) or V/Q scan immediately. If high suspicion and imaging delays, consider empiric anticoagulation per team discussion.

  11. Extended prophylaxis is underordered at discharge. Patients with prior VTE, active cancer, obesity, age > 75, or anticipated prolonged immobility should receive enoxaparin 40 mg daily (or dose-adjusted) for 10–14 days post-discharge. Arrange outpatient pharmacy teaching and visiting nurse if needed.

  12. Warfarin or DOAC for atrial fibrillation COVERS VTE prophylaxis. If patient is on warfarin (INR 2–3) or a DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran) for new-onset or chronic AF, do NOT double-prophylax with both heparin and warfarin. Transition cleanly to oral anticoagulation.

  13. Measure calf circumference bilaterally on POD 1 as baseline. If patient develops asymmetric swelling (> 2 cm difference), consider Doppler. Trending is more sensitive than a single measurement.

  14. SCD sizing matters. Calf circumference measurement at the largest point, per manufacturer guidelines. A loose SCD is ineffective; a tight SCD causes nerve injury. Re-measure if patient has significant weight loss post-op or post-op edema resolves.

  15. Patient refusal of SC injections is common, especially needle-phobic or elderly patients. Validate the fear; offer options (IV argatroban if available, topical anesthetic patches before injection, letting family administer if trained). Document refusal and educational attempts. Focus on SCDs and early mobility as backup.

cards.title: 6-Minute Walk Test (6MWT)
cards.quickAnswer: A standardized submaximal exercise test where the patient walks as far as possible on a flat, measured corridor for 6 minutes with pre-scripted verbal encouragement. Distance walked (> 500 m normal, < 300 m suggests NYHA III–IV) correlates with functional capacity, survival risk, and therapy response in heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and COPD. Serial results track treatment effect and disease progression. Nurses rarely perform the test but routinely interpret results in admission workups and functional status assessments.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: A standardized submaximal exercise test where the patient walks as far as possible on a flat, measured corridor for 6 minutes with pre-scripted verbal encouragement. Distance walked (> 500 m normal, < 300 m suggests NYHA III–IV) correlates with functional capacity, survival risk, and therapy response in heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, and COPD. Serial results track treatment effect and disease progression. Nurses rarely perform the test but routinely interpret results in admission workups and functional status assessments.
cards.sourcePrecedence: ATS 2002 6MWT Guideline → ATS/ERS 2016 Update → AHA/ACC HF Guidelines → AHA/ACC PAH Guidelines → Hardin/Kaplow → Springer 2025

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
The 6-Minute Walk Test is a simple, standardized measure of submaximal functional exercise capacity. The patient walks as far as possible in 6 minutes on a flat, measured corridor with standardized verbal encouragement every minute. Distance covered in meters is the primary outcome; it reflects what the patient can do during daily activity, not peak exertion (not VO₂ max). The 6MWT is:

  • Not maximal effort — distinct from cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), treadmill stress test, or peak VO₂ assessment
  • Validated across cardiac, pulmonary, and mixed populations — HF, PAH, COPD, pre-operative assessment, cardiac rehabilitation
  • Feasible in clinic and stepdown settings — requires only a measured corridor and minimal equipment
  • Prognostically informative — distance < 300 m in heart failure = elevated 1-year mortality risk; serial decline signals deterioration; serial improvement documents therapy response

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
The 6MWT was developed to measure functional exercise tolerance without the complexity and cost of cardiopulmonary exercise testing. It is a submaximal, self-paced test — the patient determines walking speed and may rest, slow, or stop as needed. This contrasts with maximal-effort tests driven by escalating external load or symptom endpoints.

Why 6 minutes? The time frame is long enough to elicit physiologic response (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂ drift) yet short enough to be safe in deconditioned, elderly, or acutely ill populations. It captures what a patient can sustain during daily living (shopping, housework, visiting), not peak athletic capacity.

What limits the walk? Depending on the disease and fitness level, the 6MWT may be limited by dyspnea (cardiac, pulmonary), leg fatigue (deconditioning, peripheral vascular disease), general fatigue (anemia, systemic illness), or behavioral factors (pain anxiety, fear). Post-test debrief ("What stopped you?") clarifies the mechanism and informs therapy.

Prognostic meaning: In heart failure, PAH, and COPD cohorts, 6MWT distance correlates with event-free survival, transplant candidacy, and quality of life. A patient with 6MWT < 300 m has worse prognosis than one with > 450 m in the same disease; serial decline > 50 m over 6–12 months signals disease worsening (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).

sections.heading: Heart Failure (most common ICU/stepdown encounter)
sections.bodyHtml:
• NYHA functional class assignment: 6MWT distance correlates with NYHA class; < 300 m ~ NYHA III, < 150 m ~ NYHA IV
  • Risk stratification: HF patients with 6MWT < 300 m warrant intensification of guideline-directed medical therapy (ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, ARNI, aldosterone antagonist, SGLT2i)
  • Device consideration: Persistent 6MWT < 250 m despite optimized GDMT may trigger CRT/ICD evaluation (AHA/ACC HF Guideline, 2022)
  • Therapy response: Serial 6MWT tracking in stable outpatient HF documents benefit of medical escalation; improvement by > 50 m is meaningful
  • Admission interpretation: Nurses review pre-admission 6MWT in chart; e.g., "6MWT 280 m 4 weeks ago, NYHA III → now decompensated = progression"

sections.heading: Pulmonary Hypertension (PAH)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Baseline assessment: 6MWT at diagnosis establishes functional severity and baseline risk (Galiè et al., 2015)
  • Therapy selection: Distance guides initial therapy intensity; < 300 m = higher-risk disease, may warrant combination therapy upfront
  • Follow-up & escalation: 6MWT every 3–6 months; decline > 50–100 m warrants therapy escalation or combination adjustment
  • Transplant referral: Persistent 6MWT < 250 m despite therapy escalation = consideration for lung transplant referral

sections.heading: COPD
sections.bodyHtml:
• Severity assessment: 6MWT distance helps grade disease severity beyond spirometry (FEV₁ alone)
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation baseline: Pre-rehab 6MWT establishes goal; post-rehab improvement expected 50–100 m
  • Exacerbation & recovery: Acute exacerbation may drop 6MWT by 30–100 m; recovery trajectory tracked over weeks

sections.heading: Pre-Operative Cardiac Assessment (TAVR, cardiac surgery)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Functional baseline: Pre-op 6MWT documents baseline tolerance; < 250 m suggests frailty risk, may modify operative strategy
  • TAVR vs. surgical valve surgery: Very limited 6MWT (< 150 m) may favor TAVR over surgical AVR due to lower invasiveness
  • Post-op recovery: Some programs track 6MWT at 6 weeks post-op to assess functional recovery trajectory

sections.heading: Cardiac Rehabilitation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Baseline & goal setting: Initial 6MWT (post-MI, post-op, acute HF exacerbation) establishes rehab targets; goal often improvement by 50–100 m over 8–12 weeks
  • Progress monitoring: Repeat 6MWT at 4 & 8 weeks of rehabilitation tracks therapeutic benefit of exercise training

sections.heading: Corridor Setup
sections.bodyHtml:
• Corridor: flat, measured, minimum 30 m (100–150 m preferred to reduce turnarounds)
  • Starting & end points: clearly marked; turnaround space at each end
  • Timing: stopwatch visible to assessor (not patient)
  • Safety: wheelchair or chair available at completion; staff within voice distance

sections.heading: Pre-Test Preparation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Vital signs baseline: HR, BP, SpO₂, RR
  • Patient in comfortable walking shoes and usual clothing
  • Instructed that slowing, stopping, or rest is allowed at any time
  • No mention of distance or remaining time
  • Contraindications reviewed: unstable angina, acute MI within 3 months, uncontrolled arrhythmia, severe hypertension (SBP > 180, DBP > 110), decompensated HF, acute PE, syncope risk (American Thoracic Society, 2002)

sections.heading: Standardized Encouragement Script (critical for reliability)
sections.bodyHtml:
Every minute, assessor reads one of these phrases; script must be identical across repeat tests to avoid invalidating serial comparisons:

  • "You are doing well."
  • "Keep up the good work."
  • "You are halfway done."
  • "You have 3 minutes left."
  • "You are doing great; keep going."
  • "You have 1 minute left; you can do it."

sections.heading: During the Walk
sections.bodyHtml:
• Patient may slow, stop, rest at will; assessor remains neutral
  • Continuous pulse oximetry (SpO₂, HR minimum)
  • Assessor observes from corridor; does NOT walk alongside
  • Document any symptom events: chest pain, severe dyspnea, leg cramps, diaphoresis, pallor, dizziness

sections.heading: Stop Criteria (safety — test abandoned immediately if present)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Chest pain or pressure
  • Severe dyspnea (unable to speak)
  • Leg cramping or claudication pain
  • Diaphoresis or pallor
  • Dizziness or lightheadedness
  • SpO₂ < 80% or HR > 85% age-predicted max (if concerning trajectory)

sections.heading: Post-Test Assessment
sections.bodyHtml:
• HR, BP, SpO₂, RR at 1 and 5 minutes post-walk
  • Patient seated; monitor for recovery
  • Borg dyspnea scale (0–10): "How hard was it to breathe?" (0 = none, 10 = maximal)
  • Limiting factor debrief: "Was this test limited by breathing, leg fatigue, general fatigue, or something else?"

sections.heading: 5. Normal & Abnormal Ranges
sections.bodyHtml:
Population Mean 6MWT Distance Interpretation
Healthy adult (age 40–60) 600–700 m Normal functional capacity; low mortality risk
Healthy adult (age > 70) 500–600 m Age-adjusted normal
HF NYHA I–II (stable) 400–550 m Good functional reserve
HF NYHA III 250–400 m Markedly limited; elevated risk
HF NYHA IV < 150 m Severely limited; may not complete 6 min
PAH (WHO Group I) 300–400 m (mild), < 300 m (severe) Assesses disease severity + therapy response
COPD (GOLD II–III) 300–450 m Depends on FEV₁; lower distance = worse prognosis
Post-TAVR / post-surgical AVR (> 6 weeks) Baseline-dependent; typically improves post-op Tracks functional recovery

sections.heading: Prognostic Cutoffs (Heart Failure Literature)
sections.bodyHtml:
• > 500–600 m: Normal; low mortality risk
  • 400–500 m: Mildly reduced; NYHA II–III border; moderate mortality risk
  • 250–400 m: Moderately reduced; NYHA III; elevated mortality risk (Yancy et al., 2013)
  • < 250 m: Severely reduced; NYHA III–IV; high mortality and morbidity risk; consider advanced therapies or hospice evaluation in context

sections.heading: Serial Change (most informative in practice)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Serial decline > 50 m over 6–12 months = deterioration warranting escalation of therapy
  • Serial improvement ≥ 50 m = therapeutic response (e.g., after GDMT intensification, PAH therapy, cardiac rehabilitation)
  • Single test < 300 m in acute admit = snapshot of acute state, not chronic prognosis — retest after stabilization

sections.heading: 6. Red Flags — *Clinical trajectories requiring attention*
sections.bodyHtml:
• Desaturation during 6MWT (SpO₂ drop > 4% or final SpO₂ < 88%) suggests exercise-induced hypoxemia; warrants oxygen therapy trial or further pulmonary workup
  • High Borg dyspnea scale (8–10/10) at moderate walk distance (< 400 m) signals dyspnea-limited capacity; optimize inhalers, diuretics, cardiac output
  • Patient stops due to chest pain, syncope, or severe dyspnea — test abandoned for safety; refer for urgent evaluation if not explained
  • Rewarming arrhythmia during post-op recovery — tachycardia or new bradycardia in first 24 h may reflect thermal recovery from cardiac surgery, but warrants ECG if sustained
  • Recent medication change or acute illness (new diuretic, beta-blocker titration, anemia, infection) — 6MWT may drop 30–100 m transiently; retest after stabilization before concluding disease progression
  • Heparin rebound or hemolysis post-CPB — 6MWT decline combined with pink plasma or hemoglobinuria signals secondary AKI risk

sections.heading: 7. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
• Standardized encouragement is critical. Variable, excessive, or minimal encouragement can shift 6MWT by 50+ meters and invalidate serial comparisons. If ordering repeat testing, confirm protocol standardization.
  • Corridor characteristics matter. A 30 m corridor with tight turnarounds differs from a 100 m straight hallway. For serial testing, use the same venue, same turnaround pattern. Changing venues (outdoor vs. indoor, treadmill vs. corridor) invalidates comparison.
  • Patient motivation & symptom anchoring bias. A patient may stop before true physiologic limit due to fear, pain anxiety, or deconditioning. Assess the actual limiting factor (breathing, leg fatigue, general tiredness, pain, fear) in post-test debrief.
  • Not reliable if patient has uncontrolled angina or recent MI. 6MWT within 3 months of acute MI is contraindicated unless carefully supervised (ICU/cardiology oversight, continuous monitoring).
  • Serial > single test. A single 6MWT is a snapshot of current capacity. Serial testing (every 3–6 months in HF, every 12 weeks in PAH) reveals trend and therapy response. A single poor test may reflect acute illness or testing-day fatigue — retest if concerned.
  • Correlation with NYHA is moderate, not perfect. Some patients self-report NYHA III but walk > 400 m if highly motivated; others report NYHA II and walk < 250 m if deconditioned or anxious. Use 6MWT to confirm NYHA impression, not replace clinical judgment.
  • 6MWT is submaximal, not peak VO₂. It does not replace cardiopulmonary exercise testing for VO₂ max assessment or prognosis in younger, athletic, or pre-transplant candidates where peak VO₂ is critical (Enright & Sherrill, 1998).
  • Frail or acutely decompensated patients may not tolerate 6 minutes. Gait speed testing (4-meter walk at self-selected pace) is safer and valid in acute exacerbation, severe dyspnea, or untreated arrhythmia. Document which test was used for chart clarity.
  • Borg dyspnea scale post-test frames the limiting symptom. A patient who walks 300 m but reports Borg 9/10 is dyspnea-limited; a patient with same distance and Borg 3/10 is deconditioned or peripherally limited. Therapeutic approach differs (inhaler optimization vs. cardiac optimization vs. rehabilitation).
  • Stop criteria are safety boundaries, not test failure. If patient develops chest pain, syncope, or SpO₂ < 80%, test is stopped immediately; distance recorded as distance walked (not invalid). Safety always overrides protocol completion.
  • Not used for acute inpatient prognostication. 6MWT is meaningful in stable outpatient HF, PAH, COPD. In acute admit (acute HF exacerbation, pneumonia, post-op POD 1–2), the test is not feasible and single-test low distance reflects acute state, not chronic trajectory.
  • Alternative tests in space-limited settings: Shuttle walk test (10-meter shuttle with accelerating pace), timed up-and-go (TUG), or stair climb may substitute if corridor unavailable; document which test was used.
  • Hemolysis during extended 6MWT (pink plasma, hemoglobinuria) drops haptoglobin and stresses kidneys — AKI trajectory may be visible even if ICU-level severity not reached on the unit.
  • Pleural effusion post-sternotomy, especially left-sided, is near-universal after LIMA harvest — LIMA entry passes through left pleura; may limit 6MWT distance early post-op, resolves with diuresis.
  • The "inflammatory" patient looks wet, febrile, tachycardic, and anxious on POD 1–2 post-op. This is not necessarily sepsis. Trend it; culture if other signs; do not over-react. This patient's 6MWT will be limited acutely but improves as inflammation resolves.

sections.heading: 8. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Normative data & age-adjusted interpretation Reference equations exist for healthy adults across age and sex. Enright & Sherrill (1998) established that 6MWT distance declines predictably with age (~15–20 m per decade after age 40), and women typically walk shorter distances than men. However, raw population norms are less useful than disease-specific cutoffs (HF < 300 m = NYHA III risk, PAH < 300 m = severe disease, COPD < 350 m = higher mortality). Individual variation is high — fitness, motivation, pain, and anxiety all influence distance. Paired with Borg dyspnea scale and patient feedback ("What stopped you?"), distance becomes more interpretable.
Borg dyspnea scale — interpreting exertional symptoms The Borg Perceived Exertion Scale (Borg, 1970) ranges 0–10:
  • 0 = no dyspnea at all
  • 2–3 = mild dyspnea ("I notice I'm breathing harder")
  • 5–6 = moderate dyspnea ("I'm out of breath but can keep going")
  • 8–9 = severe dyspnea ("I can barely speak")
  • 10 = maximal dyspnea ("I have to stop") Post-test Borg combined with walk distance tells the story: 350 m + Borg 3/10 = deconditioned but not dyspneic → rehab focus. 350 m + Borg 8/10 = cardiac/pulmonary limitation → optimize meds. Borg trajectory during walk (0 → 6 early, then 8 by minute 5) = accelerating dyspnea = worsening disease or under-medicated HF.
Disease-specific thresholds & therapy escalation Heart Failure (Yancy et al., 2013):
  • 6MWT ≥ 450 m + stable NYHA class = continue current GDMT
  • 6MWT 300–450 m + NYHA II–III = ensure optimal ACEi/ARB, beta-blocker, ARNI, aldosterone antagonist, SGLT2i (quadruple therapy)
  • 6MWT < 300 m + NYHA III–IV = consider CRT/ICD, advanced therapies (LVAD, transplant), or hospice discussion based on comorbidities Pulmonary Hypertension (Galiè et al., 2015):
  • 6MWT > 400 m = low risk; monotherapy acceptable if adequate symptom control
  • 6MWT 300–400 m = intermediate risk; may warrant combination therapy (ERA + PDE5i + soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator)
  • 6MWT < 300 m = high risk; combination therapy + close monitoring; escalate to advanced therapies (IV prostanoids, S1P modulator) if decline persists Post-Operative (Cardiac Surgery / TAVR):
  • Pre-op 6MWT 400–600 m = low frailty risk; standard operative approach acceptable
  • Pre-op 6MWT 250–400 m = moderate frailty; may favor TAVR over surgical AVR; ensure post-op rehab support
  • Pre-op 6MWT < 250 m = high frailty; consider TAVR, palliative approach, or candidacy reassessment Serial testing at 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months post-op tracks functional recovery and identifies patients at risk for poor long-term outcomes if plateau occurs before target range.
Controversies & recent evidence

Minimal Clinically Important Difference (MCID): The 50 m threshold for meaningful change is widely used (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020) but derives from HF cohorts. MCID may differ in PAH (possibly 30–50 m), COPD (possibly 25–54 m), or post-op recovery (unclear; some protocols use 100 m post-TAVR). Individual baseline and disease severity also influence MCID — a patient improving from 150 m to 200 m may perceive greater functional gain than one improving 500 m to 550 m.

6MWT vs. peak VO₂ in transplant candidates: Peak VO₂ from cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) is more prognostic for cardiac transplant survival (VO₂ < 10–12 mL/kg/min = poor prognosis) than 6MWT distance alone. However, 6MWT is feasible when CPET is not; 6MWT < 300 m in a candidate with borderline VO₂ may argue for earlier listing.

Supervised vs. self-paced: ATS guidelines recommend standardized encouragement and assessor observation, but some clinics and home-based programs allow patient-directed or tele-monitored 6MWT. Validity and prognostic value of unsupervised 6MWT are lower; serial comparisons may be invalid if supervision level changes.

Exercise-Induced Oxygen Desaturation (EIAD): SpO₂ drop ≥ 4% during 6MWT or final SpO₂ < 88% suggests exercise-induced hypoxemia. This warrants supplemental oxygen trial or screening for pulmonary vasculature disease (PAH, ILD), even if resting SpO₂ is normal. EIAD may be the first sign of pulmonary hypertension.

cards.title: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS): STEMI / NSTEMI / Unstable Angina
cards.quickAnswer: ACS = acute myocardial ischemia/necrosis. STEMI = ST elevation ≥1 mm in 2 contiguous leads or new LBBB + troponin rise → door-to-balloon <90 min. NSTEMI = troponin rise + clinical ACS + non-ST ECG changes (ST depression, T-wave inversion, or normal). UA = anginal symptoms at rest or changing pattern, troponin-negative but ongoing ischemia. Risk stratify all with TIMI (NSTEMI/UA) and GRACE scores. NSTEMI/UA high-risk = early invasive <24 h; intermediate <72 h. All ACS: DAPT (aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor [ticagrelor preferred]), high-intensity statin, beta-blocker, ACE-I/ARB, anticoagulation. STEMI reperfusion preferred PCI; fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable <120 min. Watch mechanical complications post-MI (POD 3–7).
cards.quickAnswerHtml:

NSTEMI = troponin rise + clinical ACS + non-ST ECG changes (ST depression, T-wave inversion, or normal).
