STEMI reperfusion preferred PCI; fibrinolysis if PCI unavailable <120 min. Watch mechanical complications post-MI (POD 3–7).
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASE/ASNC/HFSA/SCMR ACS Guideline (Virani et al.) → 2023 ESC ACS Guideline (Byrne et al.) → 2013 STEMI Guideline (O'Gara et al.) → 2014 NSTE-ACS Guideline (Amsterdam et al.) → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Brown Manual of Cardiac Intensive Care (2023)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, classification, epidemiology.

  • Definition: ACS is acute myocardial ischemia and/or necrosis triggered by rupture or erosion of a coronary atherosclerotic plaque, leading to thrombotic occlusion and insufficient coronary perfusion. Classified into three clinical subtypes by ECG and biomarker pattern.

  • Classification by presentation:

  • STEMI (ST Elevation MI): ST elevation ≥1 mm in 2+ contiguous leads OR new LBBB + positive troponin. Indicates complete coronary occlusion with transmural ischemia. Most time-sensitive; requires emergent reperfusion.
  • NSTEMI (Non-ST Elevation MI): Positive high-sensitivity troponin + clinical ACS symptoms + non-ST ECG findings (ST depression, T-wave inversion, dynamic changes, or normal ECG). Indicates subendocardial or patchy transmural ischemia.

  • Unstable Angina (UA): Anginal symptoms at rest or changing pattern (new-onset, increasing frequency/severity) with no troponin elevation. Represents high-risk plaque with critical stenosis but preserved microvascular flow.

  • Epidemiology: ~650,000 ACS cases annually in US. STEMI ~30%, NSTEMI ~65%, UA ~5% of ACS presentations. In-hospital mortality: STEMI 3–5%, NSTEMI 2–3%, UA <1% with modern reperfusion and dual antiplatelet therapy.

  • Who this applies to: All ICU patients with acute chest pain/anginal equivalent, post-operative cardiac surgery patients with recurrent ischemia or rising troponin, and patients at risk for demand ischemia (sepsis, high-output states, anemia post-op).

sections.heading: Plaque rupture cascade
sections.bodyHtml: Erosion or rupture of lipid-rich atherosclerotic plaque exposes thrombogenic core material (tissue factor, phosphatidylserine) to circulating blood. Extrinsic coagulation cascade activation → platelet aggregation via P-selectin and GPIIb/IIIa receptors → thrombin generation → fibrin cross-linking. Net result: intraluminal thrombus occludes the coronary lumen partially (NSTEMI/UA) or completely (STEMI).

sections.heading: Ischemia-to-necrosis timeline
sections.bodyHtml:
• 0–20 min: Loss of contractility, metabolic derangement (lactate accumulation, pH drop), diastolic dysfunction
  • 20–40 min: Irreversible myonecrosis begins at subendocardium (highest metabolic demand, lowest perfusion pressure)
  • 3–6 h: Transmural necrosis in STEMI if untreated; wavefront of cell death spreads centrifugally
  • 6–12 h: Necrosis extends to epicardium; salvage window largely closed but some benefit from reperfusion still exists

Troponin leak detects as early as 2–4 h post-MI onset (conventional troponin) or within 1–3 h (high-sensitivity troponin). Peak at 24–48 h; remains elevated for 7–14 days.

sections.heading: Systemic inflammatory response
sections.bodyHtml: Cardiomyocyte necrosis → cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) → systemic inflammation → remote myocardial involvement, endothelial dysfunction, arrhythmia substrate formation. Post-MI remodeling (LV dilation, aneurysm, fibrosis) unfolds over days to weeks and increases arrhythmia risk.

sections.heading: Type 1 vs Type 2 MI
sections.bodyHtml:
• Type 1 MI — atherosclerotic plaque rupture/erosion with coronary thrombosis (classic ACS; ~85% of MIs)
  • Type 2 MI — demand ischemia (supply-demand mismatch without epicardial thrombosis): sepsis, hypoxia, anemia, tachycardia, hypertension/hypotension, post-operative stress. Common in post-op patients and ICU admissions.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner and competent recognition — signs and symptoms at bedside.

sections.heading: Classic ACS presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Chest discomfort — pressure, squeezing, heaviness, burning, often substernal, may radiate to arm, jaw, epigastrium, or back
  • Onset at rest or minimal exertion — UA often at rest; STEMI often sudden and severe
  • Associated symptoms: diaphoresis, nausea, shortness of breath, autonomic activation
  • Duration: UA/NSTEMI symptoms intermittent or waxing/waning; STEMI pain typically continuous and severe (>30 min)

sections.heading: Atypical presentations *(higher prevalence in women, elderly, diabetics, post-op patients)*
sections.bodyHtml:
• Dyspnea without chest pain ("anginal equivalent")
  • Fatigue, weakness, malaise
  • Epigastric discomfort or indigestion-like pain
  • Jaw, throat, left arm, or shoulder pain without chest component
  • Syncope or near-syncope from arrhythmia or cardiogenic shock
  • Acute delirium, confusion, or agitation (elderly, diabetic with autonomic neuropathy)
  • Post-operative context: pain may be attributed to surgical wound; high index of suspicion for ACS if troponin rises

sections.heading: Physical examination findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Often unremarkable early in ACS
  • Vital sign clues: tachycardia (pain, heart failure), bradycardia (inferior MI, vagal tone), hypertension (pain/stress response), hypotension (cardiogenic shock, RV infarct, arrhythmia)
  • Diaphoresis, anxiety, skin pallor
  • Pulmonary findings if HF: crackles/rales, elevated JVP, S3 gallop, pulmonary edema
  • Cardiac auscultation: new murmur (mechanical complication), pericardial friction rub (post-MI pericarditis), irregular rhythm (arrhythmia)
  • Inferior MI-specific: bradycardia, 1st/2nd/3rd degree AV block, RV infarct (elevated JVP despite clear lungs)
  • Anterior STEMI-specific: larger infarct territory, greater EF reduction risk, cardiogenic shock more likely

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* *(2–5 minutes)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside evaluation. Pure information-gathering; no actions yet.

  • Vital signs: HR, BP (both arms), RR, SpO₂, temperature; assess perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature, mental status)
  • Symptoms: onset time, character of chest pain, radiation, associated symptoms (dyspnea, nausea, diaphoresis), severity (1–10 scale)
  • History context: prior MI, prior PCI/stent, CAD risk factors (HTN, DM, hyperlipidemia, smoking, family history), medications (antiplatelet, statin, beta-blocker)
  • Recent labs: troponin (serial draws if first is negative), K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr, CBC (hemoglobin), lactate; recent chest X-ray (pulmonary congestion)
  • Medication reconciliation: home antiplatelet agents, statin, beta-blocker, ACE-I/ARB status; any recent holds or changes
  • 12-lead ECG: ST elevation/depression, T-wave changes, new LBBB, QT prolongation, prior Q waves. Compare to prior ECGs if available. Obtain serial ECGs q15–30 min if initial is normal but suspicion high.
  • Posterior leads (V7–V9): if inferior STEMI suspected and standard 12-lead shows only subtle changes
  • Right-sided leads (V4R): if inferior STEMI to rule out RV involvement (guides fluid management)

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Section 5 structure for DIAGNOSIS cards: organized by ACS type and risk stratification, NOT Stable/Unstable fork.

sections.heading: 5A. Medical Management — initiation and titration
sections.bodyHtml:
Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT)

Agent Loading Dose Maintenance Key Characteristics
Aspirin 325–600 mg PO/PR or 150–300 mg IV 81 mg daily long-term Irreversible COX-1 inhibitor; give immediately in all ACS. Blocks thromboxane A₂.
Ticagrelor 180 mg PO 60 mg BID P2Y12 inhibitor; faster, more potent than clopidogrel (PLATO trial 2009 — mortality benefit). Reversible. BID dosing is compliance challenge. Avoid if HR <40 or high-degree AV block.
Clopidogrel 600 mg PO (300 mg if elderly/low body weight) 75 mg daily P2Y12 inhibitor; slower onset, less potent than ticagrelor. Preferred if ticagrelor contraindicated (severe bradycardia, advanced AV block). Prodrug (CYP450).
Prasugrel 60 mg PO (5 mg if <60 kg or >75 yo) 5–10 mg daily P2Y12 inhibitor; most potent; TRITON-TIMI 38 showed superior outcomes vs clopidogrel but more bleeding. Avoid if prior stroke/TIA, >75 yo, <60 kg.

DAPT principles:

  • Minimum 12 months of dual therapy after stent placement (all ACS types per 2023 guidelines)
  • High bleeding risk (HAS-BLED ≥3): shorten per MASTER DAPT trial — 1 month DAPT + aspirin monotherapy thereafter acceptable in some cases; shared decision-making required
  • Do NOT interrupt DAPT without cardiology sign-off. Stent thrombosis (2–5% risk if DAPT stopped early) is life-threatening
  • Non-cardiac procedures: maintain DAPT if possible; if surgery required, notify cardiology ≥24 h prior for bridging strategy

High-Intensity Statin

Agent Dose LDL Goal Notes
Atorvastatin 80 mg daily (can escalate by 4–12 weeks if LDL not at goal) <55 mg/dL or >50% reduction from baseline Preferred; rapid onset; good CNS penetration; efficacy in ACS trials. Give immediately in acute MI (PO or IV if available).
Rosuvastatin 40 mg daily <55 mg/dL Similar efficacy; alternative if atorvastatin intolerance. Start immediately.
  • Loading: Give immediately in acute ACS (high-intensity statin now, before or concurrent with angiography)
  • Statin intolerance (myalgia, CK elevation, hepatic injury): switch to ezetimibe (10 mg daily) + PCSK9 inhibitor (evolocumab 140 mg SC q2 weeks, or alirocumab 75–150 mg SC q2 weeks)
  • Monitor: LDL at 4–12 weeks; adjust if <55 mg/dL target not met

Beta-blocker

  • Start within 24 h of STEMI if no contraindications
  • Target: HR 50–70 bpm at rest; allow bradycardia (therapeutic)
  • Hold if: HR <60, SBP <100 mmHg, signs of cardiogenic shock/decompensated HF, 2nd/3rd degree AV block, severe reactive airway disease
  • Common agents: metoprolol 25–100 mg BID, carvedilol 3.125–25 mg BID, atenolol 50–100 mg daily
  • RV infarct-specific caution: avoid excessive beta-blockade; RV is preload-dependent; maintain volume, avoid diuretics

ACE Inhibitor or ARB

  • Start within 24 h post-MI if EF reduced (<40%) or anterior/large infarction
  • Target: ramipril 2.5–5 mg BID, lisinopril 10–20 mg daily, enalapril 5–10 mg BID, or losartan 50–100 mg daily
  • Benefit: reduces ventricular remodeling, improves survival (SAVE, AIRE, TRACE trials)
  • Hold if: SBP <90 mmHg, acute K⁺ >5.5 mEq/L, Cr rise >30%

Anticoagulation (acute phase, through hospitalization or invasive strategy)

Agent Use case Dosing Notes
UFH STEMI + PCI (preferred for primary PCI) 60 U/kg bolus (max 5,000 U), then 12 U/kg/hr infusion Shorter half-life; reversible with protamine; target aPTT 50–70 sec. Allows reversal if complications.
Enoxaparin NSTEMI if delayed PCI or conservative strategy 30 mg IV bolus + 1 mg/kg SC q12h Longer acting; renally cleared (caution if CrCl <30). Continue through intervention or 48–72 h if medical management.
Bivalirudin PCI strategy (HIT or high bleeding risk) 0.75 mg/kg IV bolus, 1.75 mg/kg/hr infusion during procedure Direct thrombin inhibitor. Non-heparin alternative. Monitor for rebound thrombosis post-PCI.
Fondaparinux NSTEMI/UA if conservative medical management 2.5 mg SC daily NOT for primary PCI (thrombotic risk); safe for medical management. Factor Xa inhibitor.
  • STEMI: UFH preferred (allows reversal, shorter acting); continue through PCI
  • NSTEMI: UFH, LMWH, or fondaparinux × 48–72 h or until invasive strategy completed
  • Post-discharge: transition to oral anticoagulation only if LV thrombus, atrial fibrillation, or cardiogenic shock (warfarin INR 2–3 or DOAC if EF recovering)

Adjunctive agents

Agent Indication Notes
Oxygen SpO₂ <90% ONLY DETO2X-AMI trial: hyperoxia worsens outcomes (oxidative stress). Target SpO₂ 94–98%. Do NOT give blanket supplemental O₂ to normoxic patients.
Nitroglycerin (SL/IV) Chest pain, pulmonary edema Caution: hypotension, reflex tachycardia. AVOID in RV infarct, inferior STEMI with hypotension.
Morphine Severe pain, pulmonary edema Use with CAUTION. CHAMPION PHOENIX trial: morphine delays P2Y12 inhibitor absorption, associated with worse outcomes. Prefer fentanyl (IV), dilaudid, or other opioids for pain. Reserve morphine for severe pulmonary edema if no better option.
Diuretics HF/pulmonary edema Gentle diuresis. Avoid over-diuresis; ischemic LV is stiff and preload-dependent. Over-diuresis worsens CO and end-organ perfusion.

sections.heading: 5B. Revascularization
sections.bodyHtml:
STEMI Reperfusion Strategy

  • Primary PCI (preferred): door-to-balloon time <90 min from first medical contact (FMC)
  • Emergent coronary angiography + percutaneous coronary intervention (stent, typically drug-eluting stent [DES])
  • Aspiration thrombectomy if large clot burden
  • Mechanical support (intra-aortic balloon pump, Impella) if cardiogenic shock develops

  • ECMO or temporary LV assist if massive anterior STEMI with cardiogenic shock

  • Fibrinolytic therapy (alternative if PCI unavailable):

  • If PCI not available within 120 min of FMC and no contraindications
  • Agents: alteplase (tPA), reteplase (rPA), tenecteplase (TNK) — dosing per protocol
  • Contraindications to lytics: prior ICH, active bleeding, recent major surgery, severe uncontrolled HTN (SBP >180, HR >110), suspected aortic dissection
  • Reperfusion window: symptom onset to lytic <12 h (best <3 h)
  • Rescue PCI: if lytic fails (no ST resolution at 60–90 min) → immediate angiography and PCI

NSTEMI Risk Stratification and Invasive Timing

Use TIMI risk score (NSTEMI/UA) and GRACE score (in-hospital/6-month mortality) to guide timing:

TIMI Risk Score (7-point scale; predicts 14-day MACE)

  • 1 point each: age ≥65, ≥3 CAD risk factors, prior CAD (≥50% stenosis), aspirin use in prior 7 d, >2 anginal episodes in 24 h, ECG ST changes, elevated troponin
  • Score 0–2: low risk; Score ≥5: high risk

GRACE Score (predicts mortality)

  • Components: age, systolic BP, heart rate, Killip class, cardiac biomarker, ST deviation, creatinine
  • Calculated via online calculator; guides intensity of intervention

Invasive timing by risk:

  • High-risk NSTEMI or UA (TIMI ≥5, elevated troponin, ST depression, hemodynamic instability, mechanical complication): early invasive <24 h
  • Intermediate-risk: early invasive <72 h
  • Low-risk UA/troponin-negative: selective invasive (ischemia-guided); may manage medically if stable, troponin serially negative

sections.heading: 5C. Post-ACS Discharge and Secondary Prevention
sections.bodyHtml:
Medications (discharge summary)

  • Aspirin 81 mg daily indefinitely
  • P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 60 mg BID, clopidogrel 75 mg daily, or prasugrel 5–10 mg daily) × 12 months post-PCI
  • High-intensity statin (atorvastatin 80 mg or rosuvastatin 40 mg daily); target LDL <55 mg/dL
  • Beta-blocker (metoprolol, carvedilol, or atenolol) titrated to HR 50–70 at rest
  • ACE-I/ARB if EF <40% or anterior MI (continue indefinitely)
  • Consider: SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin 10 mg daily) post-MI regardless of EF (DAPA-HF, SGLT2i trials show benefit); emerging evidence for post-MI mortality reduction
  • Consider: PCSK9 inhibitor if LDL not at goal on statin + ezetimibe or statin intolerance

Lifestyle and rehab

  • Cardiac rehabilitation: class IIa recommendation; 12 weeks supervised exercise + education improves outcomes, reduces readmission
  • Diet: heart-healthy, low sodium (<2 g/day), low saturated fat, Mediterranean or DASH diet pattern
  • Activity progression: gradual return to activities; sexual activity typically safe POD 7–14 if stable and no angina on exertion testing
  • Smoking cessation: critical; refer to tobacco treatment program
  • Stress management, sleep, weight loss if overweight
  • Diabetes control: tight glycemic control (target HbA1c <7%) reduces recurrence

Follow-up

  • Cardiology clinic within 2–4 weeks post-discharge
  • Repeat echocardiography at 6 weeks if anterior STEMI or if EF concerns (assess for LV thrombus, aneurysm, mechanical complication)
  • Consider cardiac MRI or stress testing if viability assessment or ischemia evaluation needed
  • ICD evaluation if EF <40% persists at 40 days post-MI (consider class I indication if EF ≤35% at 40 d)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] or presenting with [ACS symptoms]." B: "Patient has chest pain/dyspnea × [duration] with troponin [value] at [time]. ECG shows [ST elevation / ST depression / T-wave inversion / normal]. HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]." A: "Patient is [stable / hemodynamically unstable]. [Symptoms]. [Pending labs/imaging]." R: "Requesting [immediate ECG / stat troponin / cardiology consult / emergent cath lab activation / DCCV prep / ICU transfer]."

When to escalate (indications for cardiology/cath lab/ICU)

Situation Contact Urgency
Chest pain + STEMI on ECG Interventional cardiology, cath lab STAT — door-to-balloon <90 min
Positive troponin + NSTEMI ECG changes, hemodynamically stable Cardiology — high-risk NSTEMI Urgent <24 h invasive
Recurrent chest pain despite therapy or rising troponin despite medications Cardiology, cath lab Urgent <24 h for re-angiography or escalation
New HF/cardiogenic shock post-MI Cardiology + ICU STAT — mechanical support may be needed
New murmur, hemodynamic instability POD 2–7 post-MI CT surgery, echo stat STAT — mechanical complication until proven otherwise
Electrical instability (VT, VF, high-degree block) Code team + cardiology STAT ACLS
Acute stroke signs in post-MI patient on anticoagulation Neurology + cardiology STAT stroke code

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Marked — collapsed by default.

Type 1 vs Type 2 MI: pathophysiology and implications

Type 1 MI — atherosclerotic plaque rupture/erosion with coronary thrombosis. Classic ACS. Accounts for ~85% of acute MIs. ECG often shows localized territorial ST elevation; angiography reveals occlusive thrombosis.

Type 2 MI — demand ischemia (supply-demand mismatch WITHOUT coronary thrombosis). Occurs when oxygen supply inadequate relative to myocardial demand: sepsis, hypoxia, anemia (Hgb <7), tachycardia/tachyarrhythmia (AF with RVR), severe hypertension or hypotension, post-operative stress (inflammation, bleeding, fluid shifts). Troponin rises (indicating necrosis) but angiography shows no culprit lesion or non-occlusive disease. Often diffuse ECG changes or normal ECG. Prognosis worse than Type 1 (higher mortality if untreated underlying cause). Management: treat the inciting cause (infection, hypoxia, anemia, HTN) + medical therapy (antiplatelet, statin, beta-blocker, ACE-I). Does NOT require urgent PCI unless there is concurrent Type 1 (plaque rupture superimposed).

Clinical implication: Post-operative rise in troponin may be Type 2 (demand from surgery itself, inflammation, hemorrhage) rather than Type 1 (new graft occlusion, progression of native disease). Always assess troponin trend (rise + fall = necrosis) and angiography findings. Rising troponin after cardiac surgery is expected (graft manipulation, cardioplegia injury, hypothermia); steady rise or very high troponin raises suspicion for Type 1 or major perioperative MI.

Troponin kinetics and high-sensitivity assay algorithms High-sensitivity troponin (hs-troponin) detects myocardial injury earlier and more sensitively than conventional troponin:
  • Detectable within 1–3 hours of MI onset (vs 3–6 h for conventional)
  • 0/1/3-h algorithm: Baseline troponin, 1 h, then 3 h. If 0-h and 1-h both <99th percentile + clinical probability low → MI ruled out with >99% sensitivity/NPV. If rise ≥5 ng/L or fall ≥20% in 1–3 h → MI ruled in.
  • Peak at 24–48 h post-MI; remains elevated 7–14 days
  • Specificity caveat: hs-troponin elevated in sepsis, heart failure, PE, renal disease, Type 2 MI (demand ischemia), cardiac trauma, post-cardiac surgery (expected). Troponin is a biomarker of myocardial injury, NOT specific for ischemia. Serial troponins are standard: admission, 3 h (hs-troponin), then q6–12 h depending on clinical course. Peak troponin correlates with infarct size and prognosis. Clinical pearl: Troponin-negative at presentation does NOT exclude MI. Serial troponins mandatory. If clinical suspicion high (chest pain + ECG changes + risk factors) but troponin negative, repeat at 3 h (hs-troponin) or 6 h (conventional).
ECG territorial localization and culprit vessel prediction 12-lead ECG localization (identifies territory; helps predict culprit vessel):
  • Anterior (V1–V4, I, aVL): LAD occlusion → high risk for cardiogenic shock, conduction block (LAD supplies His bundle and AV node in some patients)
  • Inferior (II, III, aVF): RCA (~85% of people) or LCx (~15%) → often bradycardia/AV block (RCA supplies AV node); RV infarct likely
  • Lateral (V5–V6, I, aVL): LCx or diagonal branch of LAD
  • Posterior (reciprocal): ST depression in V1–V2 + tall R wave in V1 (mirror image). RCA occlusion. Risk: posterior descending artery to posterior papillary muscle.
  • Right ventricular (RV): inferior STEMI + ST elevation in V4R. Critical: RV is preload-dependent; avoid diuretics, maintain volume, use inotropes if needed. Serial ECGs: obtain at 15–30 min intervals if initial ECG normal but suspicion high. Dynamic ST/T changes on serial tracings are concerning for ongoing ischemia. Posterior leads (V7–V9): if inferior STEMI and initial 12-lead subtle — V7–V9 may show ST elevation not visible on standard 12-lead; isolated posterior MI can be missed.
Echocardiography findings: wall motion abnormalities, mechanical complications Echocardiography post-MI (typically transthoracic; TEE if endocarditis suspected or valve involvement):
  • Wall motion abnormality (WMA): localized hypokinesia (reduced motion) or akinesia (no motion) in territory supplied by occluded vessel. E.g., anterior STEMI → anterobasal, anteroapical WMA.
  • EF: global systolic dysfunction if large infarct or multiple territories; serial echo at discharge, 6 weeks (assesses for LV thrombus, aneurysm, remodeling)
  • Diastolic dysfunction: common post-MI; restrictive pattern (elevated E/e' ratio) indicates worse prognosis
  • Mechanical complications (POD 2–7):
  • VSD: holosystolic murmur, sudden HF, large V-wave on PA catheter; echo shows defect
  • Papillary muscle rupture: apical/posterolateral murmur, acute mitral regurgitation, shock; echo shows prolapsing leaflet(s)
  • Free wall rupture: hemopericardium, tamponade physiology, electrical-mechanical dissociation; echo shows pericardial effusion, RA/RV collapse
  • LV thrombus: risk if akinetic wall, anterior STEMI, low EF. Screening echo POD 1–5; if detected, anticoagulate × 3 months (warfarin INR 2–3 or DOAC) to prevent systemic embolism
  • Pericardial effusion: common post-MI (inflammation); usually small and asymptomatic; large effusion or signs of tamponade require drainage
Post-MI mechanical complications: timing, presentation, management Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD)
  • Timing: POD 2–5 (peak 3–5 d)
  • Incidence: 1–2% of MI (now rare with timely reperfusion); higher in anterior STEMI
  • Presentation: sudden new holosystolic murmur (loudest at left lower sternal border), left-to-right shunt, acute HF, cardiogenic shock, large V-wave on PA line
  • Diagnosis: echo shows defect; Qp/Qs ratio elevated (left-to-right shunt fraction)
  • Management: surgical repair urgently (mortality ~25–50% if untreated); supportive care (inotropes, vasodilators, intra-aortic balloon pump if shock); delay surgery only if unstable acutely (stabilize first) Papillary Muscle Rupture (PMR)
  • Timing: POD 2–7 (peak ~4 d)
  • Incidence: 0.5–1% of MI; higher in inferior STEMI (posteromedial papillary muscle)
  • Presentation: acute mitral regurgitation, apical or posterolateral systolic murmur, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, large V-wave on PA line
  • Severity: partial rupture (chordae) vs complete (muscle head) — complete is catastrophic
  • Diagnosis: echo shows prolapsing leaflet, severe MR, ruptured papillary muscle head
  • Management: urgent cardiac surgery (MVR ± VSD repair if coexistent); stabilize with inotropes, vasodilators, IABP; mortality ~25% even with surgery, ~90% without Free Wall Rupture (FWR)
  • Timing: POD 3–7 (peak ~4 d)
  • Incidence: 1–3% of MI (now rare with reperfusion)
  • Presentation: sudden catastrophic decompensation — hypotension, JVP elevation, muffled heart sounds (Beck's triad), pericardial tamponade, electrical-mechanical dissociation, cardiac arrest
  • Diagnosis: echo shows hemopericardium, RA/RV collapse, tamponade physiology; CXR may show widened mediastinum
  • Management: emergency pericardiocentesis if tamponade, then emergent surgical repair. Mortality ~90% without surgery; even with surgery survival <50%. Nursing vigilance: New murmur + hemodynamic instability post-MI = STAT echo + cardiology + surgical team. These are surgical emergencies.
Cardiac rehabilitation and SGLT2 inhibitors post-MI Cardiac Rehabilitation
  • Class IIa recommendation (guideline-supported) for post-MI patients
  • Benefits: improves exercise capacity, reduces symptoms, psychological support, educates on secondary prevention, reduces readmission (20–30%), likely reduces mortality
  • Timing: start in-hospital (phase I, bedside exercises) → phase II (supervised outpatient, 12 weeks, 2–3 sessions/week) → phase III (community-based, maintenance)
  • Components: aerobic exercise (target 150 min/week moderate intensity), resistance training, education (medications, diet, stress, sexual activity), psychosocial support
  • Outcomes: post-MI patients in rehab have 20–30% lower 2-year readmission, improved EF recovery, reduced AF incidence SGLT2 Inhibitors Post-MI
  • Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or empagliflozin 10 mg daily — emerging evidence supports use post-MI regardless of EF or diabetes
  • Mechanism: improves myocardial energetics, reduces fibrosis, anti-inflammatory, promotes natriuresis (mild diuretic effect)
  • Evidence: DAPA-HF, SGLT2i trials show benefit in HF post-MI (reduced HF hospitalization, mortality)
  • Consider: all post-MI patients, especially if reduced EF or HF develops; contraindicated if eGFR <20 or acute kidney injury
  • Counseling: rare risk of euglycemic DKA in type 1 diabetics; advise to hold if acute illness/dehydration/fasting Novel therapies under investigation: finerenone (non-steroidal MRA), colchicine, levosimendan in some countries
Special considerations: Wellens' syndrome, LBBB + MI criteria, isolated posterior MI Wellens' Syndrome
  • Pattern: deeply inverted T waves in V2–V3 (sometimes V1–V4), chest pain, troponin may be negative or minimally elevated
  • Represents: critical LAD stenosis (not yet occlusion); impending anterior STEMI
  • Pitfall: subtle; can be missed by novice. Specific T-wave pattern in V2–V3 with LAD territory ischemia
  • Action: urgent angiography + PCI even if troponin negative (prevent STEMI) New LBBB + MI
  • Criterion for STEMI equivalent: new LBBB + clinical ACS symptoms = STEMI equivalent, activate cath lab
  • ECG criteria for MI in LBBB (Sgarbossa criteria, modified by Smith): ST elevation concordant with QRS, ST depression in V1–V3, or exaggerated ST elevation discordance in left-sided leads
  • Pitfall: LBBB obscures traditional ST elevation; many clinicians miss it. If new LBBB in ACS context, treat as STEMI Isolated Posterior MI
  • Presentation: inferior pain, but ST elevation only in posterior leads (V7–V9), not standard 12-lead
  • Pitfall: may be missed if posterior leads not obtained; patient may arrive with normal 12-lead and be discharged
  • Action: obtain V7–V9 if inferior STEMI suspected but standard 12-lead subtle; repeat ECG with posterior leads in high-suspicion patients

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in currently stable post-MI patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These indicate worsening or imminent decompensation.

  • Rising troponin despite therapy — stent thrombosis, re-MI, new coronary occlusion; escalate for repeat angiography
  • New or worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, PND — developing heart failure; increased crackles, elevated JVP, S3 gallop
  • Hypotension or shock — cardiogenic shock, mechanical complication, arrhythmia; STAT assessment
  • New murmur (holosystolic, late systolic, diastolic) — VSD (holosystolic), papillary rupture (holosystolic MR), aortic insufficiency; STAT echo
  • Electrical instability: recurrent VT/VF, high-degree AV block, rapid SVT — risk of sudden cardiac death; prepare for DCCV, pacing, ECMO
  • Recurrent chest pain post-PCI — stent thrombosis, re-MI, angiography needed; escalate immediately
  • Stroke symptoms (focal neuro deficit) — LV thrombus embolism, AF-related; activate stroke code
  • Unexplained tachycardia (HR persistently >100) — may herald HF, arrhythmia, sepsis, or ongoing ischemia
  • Metabolic derangement: worsening lactate, severe hyperkalemia or hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis — end-organ hypoperfusion or renal failure
  • Altered mental status, confusion, agitation — cardiogenic shock, sepsis, hypoxia, or post-ischemic encephalopathy
  • Pericardial friction rub + chest pain — post-MI pericarditis (Dressler syndrome) or acute pericarditis; monitor for tamponade
  • Fever, leukocytosis POD 3–7 — expected inflammatory response but rule out post-MI infection/endocarditis if new murmur or sepsis features

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. STEMI door-to-balloon <90 minutes is non-negotiable. Delay beyond 90 min increases mortality by 7.5% per hour. Notify charge nurse, cath lab, and attending immediately upon STEMI recognition. Expedite all steps (EKG within 10 min, IV access, aspirin/loading dose antiplatelet).

  2. New LBBB = STEMI equivalent until proven otherwise. Don't wait for confirmation or troponin; activate cath lab. LBBB obscures ST elevation but represents complete LAD occlusion in acute MI context.

  3. Normal ECG does NOT exclude ACS. 10–15% of NSTEMI and UA patients have normal initial ECG. Serial ECGs (q15–30 min) and serial troponins mandatory. Troponin-negative does not mean "safe" — repeat at 3 h (hs-troponin) or 6 h (conventional). Rise + fall pattern confirms MI.

  4. High-sensitivity troponin 0/1/3-h algorithm: If baseline <99th percentile AND 1-h unchanged AND 3-h unchanged or minimal rise, MI ruled out at 99% sensitivity. If rise ≥5 ng/L or delta ≥20% in 1–3 h, MI ruled in. This algorithm shortens diagnostic time to 3 h.

  5. DAPT minimum 12 months post-PCI. Even if high bleeding risk, cutting DAPT short increases stent thrombosis (2–5% risk). MASTER DAPT trial allows 1-month DAPT in carefully selected high-bleed-risk patients; otherwise 12 months is standard.

    Never stop DAPT abruptly without cardiology input.

  6. Ticagrelor > clopidogrel in most ACS (PLATO trial). Faster onset, more potent, mortality benefit.

    Exception: ticagrelor avoided if baseline HR <40, 2nd/3rd degree AV block, or if develops severe symptomatic bradycardia. Clopidogrel is acceptable alternative but inferior outcomes.

  7. Post-CABG ACS = graft occlusion until proven otherwise. Native disease progression + early graft failure (saphenous vein grafts within 1–5 years) are common. Angiography must assess graft patency; urgent re-grafting may be needed.

    High-risk anatomy for repeat CABG.

  8. Morphine may worsen outcomes in ACS (CHAMPION PHOENIX trial). Delays P2Y12 inhibitor absorption, possible hemodynamic depression. Use fentanyl (IV), hydromorphone, or other opioids instead. Reserve morphine for severe pulmonary edema if no better option.

  9. Oxygen only if SpO₂ <90% (DETO2X-AMI trial). Hyperoxia increases oxidative stress, worsens outcomes. Target SpO₂ 94–98%; do NOT give blanket supplemental O₂ to normoxic patients.

  10. Mechanical complications (VSD, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture) POD 2–7 = surgical emergencies. Any new holosystolic murmur post-MI + hemodynamic instability → STAT echo + cardiology + surgical team. FWR is nearly universally fatal without emergent repair; VSD and PMR mortality ~25–50% even with surgery.

  11. Post-infarct LV thrombus requires anticoagulation × 3 months minimum. Risk of systemic embolism (stroke, mesenteric ischemia, limb ischemia) is real. Screening echo POD 1–5; if detected, warfarin (INR 2–3) or DOAC. Repeat echo at 3 months before stopping anticoagulation.

  12. Dressler pericarditis timing: POD 2 weeks to 2 months post-MI. Pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, fever, elevated ESR/CRP, ECG with PR depression or diffuse ST elevation. Manage with NSAIDs (indomethacin, colchicine); avoid high-dose steroids (impair scar formation). Distinguish from acute pericarditis (viral, autoimmune).

  13. NSTEMI early invasive <24 h for high-risk patients (TIMI ≥5). Use TIMI and GRACE scores to risk-stratify. NSTEMI + elevated troponin + ST changes + hemodynamic instability or mechanical complication = high-risk → angiography within 24 h. Delay increases mortality.

  14. Unstable angina (troponin-negative) with ongoing ischemia = high-risk ACS. Don't be falsely reassured by negative troponin. If clinical symptoms ongoing (rest angina, crescendo pattern, ECG changes), treat as high-risk NSTEMI; early invasive strategy warranted.

  15. Avoid aggressive diuresis in cardiogenic shock post-MI. Ischemic LV is stiff and preload-dependent. Over-diuresis worsens CO, worsens organ perfusion, increases mortality. Gentle diuretics + inotropes/vasopressors (milrinone, dobutamine, low-dose epinephrine) preferred. RV infarct especially requires volume repletion, NOT diuretics.

cards.title: Activated Clotting Time (ACT)
cards.quickAnswer: Point-of-care test measuring time to fibrin clot formation in whole blood. Baseline 80–120 s (varies by device/activator). Targets vary dramatically: CPB > 400–480 s, ECMO 160–220 s, cath lab 250–300 s, dialysis 200–250 s. On the ICU, ACT is a historical data point from the OR or ECMO record; bedside coagulopathy assessment uses PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, and viscoelastic tests instead.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: Point-of-care test measuring time to fibrin clot formation in whole blood. Baseline 80–120 s (varies by device/activator). Targets vary dramatically: CPB > 400–480 s, ECMO 160–220 s, cath lab 250–300 s, dialysis 200–250 s. On the ICU, ACT is a historical data point from the OR or ECMO record; bedside coagulopathy assessment uses PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, and viscoelastic tests instead.
cards.sourcePrecedence: Gravlee et al. (2024) → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Stanford CVICU Handbook (2024) → ELSO Guidelines (2023)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Activated Clotting Time is a rapid, point-of-care test of whole-blood coagulation that measures the time from blood collection to visible fibrin clot formation in the presence of a surface activator (celite or kaolin).

Key distinctions:

  • ACT (whole blood) vs. PTT (plasma): ACT is bedside-available and directly measures heparin effect; PTT requires centrifugation and is sensitive to fibrinogen, platelet count, and other factors.
  • ACT vs. Anti-Xa: ACT is functional clot time; anti-Xa is heparin concentration. They correlate imperfectly.
  • ACT vs. TEG/ROTEM: These measure clot dynamics and strength over time; ACT measures only time to clot initiation.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
The contact-phase coagulation cascade is initiated by the activator, bypassing in vivo tissue-factor and phospholipid variables. ACT reflects the functional anticoagulant effect in the whole-blood compartment, integrating heparin concentration, fibrinogen level, platelet count, and temperature.

Pre-analytical factors affecting result:

  • Temperature: Device warmed to 37 °C; patient hypothermia → falsely prolonged ACT
  • Hematocrit: Anemia → prolonged; polycythemia → shortened
  • Fibrinogen: Low fibrinogen → prolonged
  • Platelet count: Thrombocytopenia → prolongation
  • Hemodilution: CPB prime dilutes platelets and fibrinogen

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Common point-of-care devices:

  • Hemochron (ITC) — most common intraoperative + ECMO; celite-based; whole blood
  • CoaguChek — portable but less common in OR
  • iSTAT — multiparameter analyzer with ACT module

Where ACT is used (and where it isn't):

  • Used: CPB anticoagulation titration, ECMO anticoagulation monitoring, catheterization lab heparin dosing, hemodialysis circuit patency
  • Not used on ICU: Bedside post-operative coagulopathy assessment defaults to PT/INR, PTT, CBC, fibrinogen, D-dimer, and viscoelastic tests

sections.heading: 4. Normal Baseline & Target Ranges by Procedure
sections.bodyHtml:
Setting Baseline Target ACT Notes
Screening (no anticoagulation) 80–120 s — Varies with activator type and device brand.
CPB (on-pump, full heparinization) 80–120 s > 400–480 s Heparin ~300–400 IU/kg bolus IV; additional 50 IU/kg q30–60 min. Hypothermia prolongs.
ECMO (VV or VA) 80–120 s 160–220 s Center-specific targets; ELSO flexible. Lower than CPB due to continuous circuit + thrombus/bleed trade-off.
Catheterization lab (PCI + heparin) 80–120 s 250–300 s Goal 2–3× baseline; initial heparin ~100 IU/kg.
Catheterization lab (PCI + bivalirudin) 80–120 s 250–350 s ACT less reliable; PT/anti-IIa preferred.
Hemodialysis circuit 80–120 s 200–250 s Maintains circuit patency.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: <details><summary>Device-to-device variability</summary> Hemochron ACT 400 ≠ iSTAT ACT 400 necessarily. Intra-operative consistency (same device throughout) is critical. If device changes mid-case, serial ACT values are not directly comparable. </details> <details><summary>Protamine reversal physiology</summary> Heparin is reversed at ~1 mg per 100 IU given IV (typical dose 30–50 mg post-CPB). ACT should fall to baseline within minutes. "ACT rebound" (late-rising ACT 1–2 h post-reversal) can occur if reversal is incomplete or heparin continues to leak from tissues — watch for re-bleeding in the ICU. </details> <details><summary>HIT and alternative anticoagulants</summary> HIT patients cannot use heparin. Switch to argatroban or bivalirudin. ACT is less validated for these drugs; PT/PTT and platelet count are preferred. Do NOT use heparin to normalize ACT if HIT is a possibility. </details> <hr />

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. ACT is NOT heparin level. Prolonged ACT indicates heparin effect but does not reveal actual drug concentration. Fibrinogen, platelets, and hypothermia affect ACT independent of heparin dose.
  2. Hypothermia in CPB prolongs ACT. Patient at 34 °C with ACT 500+ is not over-heparinized; rewarming will shorten it. Not an indication to give protamine.
  3. Platelet dysfunction in CPB is real. Even with ACT 450, post-pump bleeding occurs if platelets are severely low or dysfunctional. ACT does not measure platelet quality.
  4. Fibrinogen drop in long pump times. Extended CPB consumes fibrinogen; an "adequate" ACT may coexist with critical hypofibrinogenemia. Check fibrinogen level separately.
  5. On the unit, order PT/INR, PTT, CBC, fibrinogen, and D-dimer—not ACT. ACT is an OR/critical-care tool; ICU bleeding assessment uses laboratory coagulation studies.

cards.quickAnswer: Acute aortic dissection (AAD) = intimal tear with blood dissecting into aortic wall; sudden tearing chest or back pain + pulse/BP differential between arms or mediastinal widening on imaging. sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, and clinical context.

Definition: Acute aortic dissection (AAD) is a tear in the aortic intima through which blood tracks along the aortic media, creating a true lumen and a false lumen. The false lumen may thrombose, partially perfuse, or remain widely patent. Hemodynamic shear forces (dP/dt = rate of change of pressure) propagate the tear.

Classification:

  • Stanford Type A: Involves ascending aorta (proximal to brachiocephalic artery), regardless of origin or extent. Includes DeBakey I and II. Surgical emergency.
  • Stanford Type B: Does NOT involve ascending aorta; typically distal to left subclavian artery. Includes DeBakey III. Medical ± TEVAR per complication status.

Epidemiology:

  • Incidence: 3–5 per 100,000/year
  • Peak age: 60–80 years (earlier in genetic syndromes)
  • Sex: Male > Female (2:1)
  • Risk factors: chronic hypertension (70%), cystic medial degeneration, Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve with aortopathy, cocaine use, pregnancy, trauma, rapid deceleration
  • Mortality: Type A untreated ~1% per hour; Type A surgically repaired 8–10%; Type B medically managed 1–2%

Who this applies to: Critically ill patients presenting with acute chest/back/flank pain and hemodynamic stress; post-operative recovery from Type A repair or Type B TEVAR; patients admitted with suspected dissection awaiting operative/interventional repair.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Novice + advanced beginner teaching — why dissections happen and propagate.

sections.heading: Mechanism
sections.bodyHtml: An intimal tear (usually at the sinotubular junction in Type A, or just distal to the left subclavian in Type B) allows blood to dissect along the media, creating two lumens separated by the intimal flap. The false lumen's fate depends on its patency: thrombosed false lumens are stable; patent lumens propagate due to hemodynamic shear (dP/dt). The false lumen may rupture externally (tamponade, hemorrhage), into adjacent structures (aortic regurgitation, pericardium), or compress branch vessels (malperfusion).

sections.heading: Pathophysiologic Consequences
sections.bodyHtml:
Consequence Mechanism Clinical Impact
Propagation Shear stress (dP/dt) extends the tear proximally and distally Progressive malperfusion; increased surgical complexity
External rupture False lumen ruptures through aortic wall Tamponade (Type A), hemorrhagic shock, death within minutes
Aortic regurgitation Intimal flap prolapses into aortic valve or annulus distorts Acute AI; volume overload; cardiogenic shock (Type A)
Branch vessel occlusion Flap obstructs ostium or dissection extends into branch Malperfusion syndromes (stroke, renal, mesenteric, spinal, limb)
Coronary involvement Dissection extends into RCA or LCA ostium (Type A) Inferior or anterior STEMI physiology

sections.heading: Risk Factors
sections.bodyHtml:
Non-modifiable: Age >60, male sex, Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos (type IV), bicuspid aortic valve with aortopathy, familial thoracic aortic aneurysm, Turner syndrome.

Modifiable: Chronic hypertension (most common, >70%), cocaine use, heavy lifting/strenuous exertion, rapid deceleration trauma, pregnancy (10× risk in Marfan/LDS).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — how dissections present at the bedside.

sections.heading: Classic Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Sudden maximal-intensity tearing or ripping chest, back, or flank pain — often the "worst pain of life"
  • Pain character: sharp, tearing, ripping; may migrate distally as dissection propagates
  • Associated symptoms: diaphoresis, nausea, sense of dread, anxiety
  • Physical exam findings:
  • Pulse or BP differential >20 mmHg between arms (present in ~30% Type A)
  • Early diastolic murmur (aortic insufficiency)
  • Neurologic deficit (stroke, paraplegia, altered mental status)
  • Syncope or presyncope
  • Malperfusion signs: cold limb, absent femoral pulse, oliguria, mesenteric ischemia

sections.heading: Atypical (Dangerous) Presentations
sections.bodyHtml:
• 15% Type A present with NO chest pain — only stroke, syncope, or acute neuro deficit. High clinical suspicion essential.
  • "STEMI mimic" — inferior ST elevation from right coronary artery (RCA) dissection → patient sent to cath lab rather than CT and aortic repair (catastrophic error).
  • "Stroke mimic" — arch involvement causes acute neurologic deficit; tPA is contraindicated and causes rupture.
  • Isolated back pain — confused with back strain or abdominal aortic aneurysm.
  • Painless dissection — rare; seen in Marfan syndrome, sedated/intubated patients, or spinal cord ischemia masking the pain.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure information-gathering; no actions yet. Target: 2 minutes at bedside.

  • Vital signs: HR, BP (check BOTH arms, flag differential >20 mmHg), SpO₂, mental status, perfusion
  • Pain: character, location, radiation, migration pattern
  • Symptoms: diaphoresis, nausea, dread, focal neuro symptoms (weakness, speech change, vision change)
  • Physical exam:
  • Auscultate for early diastolic murmur (AI)
  • Palpate bilateral radial, femoral, pedal pulses (asymmetry = branch involvement)
  • Neuro: bilateral arm strength, facial symmetry, speech, lower extremity strength/sensation (spinal cord ischemia)
  • Skin: perfusion, temperature differential between extremities
  • Abdomen: tenderness, distension (mesenteric ischemia)
  • Recent labs: troponin, lactate, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr (baseline organ function); CBC (hemoglobin drop if rupture/pericardial bleed)
  • Imaging: CXR on hand? Widened mediastinum, pleural effusion, tracheal deviation?
  • ECG: look for ST elevation pattern; don't fixate on "STEMI" without aortic imaging
  • Access & monitoring: arterial line? Central line? Epicardial pacing wires?

sections.heading: 5A. Type A Acute Aortic Dissection — Immediate Actions (Surgical Emergency)
Pre-operative Phase
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Notify cardiothoracic surgery STAT — Type A mortality is ~1% per hour without surgery. Time is critical.

  2. Activate massive transfusion protocol — alert blood bank: crossmatch 6–8 units pRBCs, 4 FFP, 2–4 units platelets.

  3. Establish vascular access:

    • Two large-bore IVs (18 G or better)
    • Arterial line (right radial preferred for continuous monitoring; left may be involved)
    • Central venous line (right internal jugular typical)

  4. Obtain imaging STAT:

    • CT angiography chest/abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (1st choice if hemodynamically stable) — shows intimal flap, false lumen, malperfusion extent, pericardial effusion/tamponade, coronary involvement
    • Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) if hemodynamically unstable and cannot tolerate CT — can be done in OR or ICU
    • Plain CXR (screening, not diagnostic — don't delay for CXR)

  5. Obtain 12-lead ECG STAT — look for ST elevation pattern; don't confuse with MI. CTA is the diagnosis.

  6. Initiate pharmacologic impulse control IMMEDIATELY (before imaging if high clinical suspicion):

Step 1: Beta-blockade FIRST (non-negotiable)

  • Goal: HR ≤ 60 bpm, reduce dP/dt
  • Labetalol IV: 10–20 mg bolus over 1–2 min, repeat q10 min up to 50–80 mg cumulative; OR continuous infusion 0.5–2 mg/min titrated to HR ≤ 60
  • Esmolol IV: Loading 500 mcg/kg over 1 min, then maintenance 50–300 mcg/kg/min to HR ≤ 60
  • NEVER skip this step or give vasodilator first — reflex tachycardia from vasodilators WIDENS dissection

Step 2: Vasodilation (AFTER beta-blockade achieved)

  • Goal: SBP ≤ 120 mmHg
  • Nicardipine IV: 5–15 mg/h (balanced arterial/venous dilator; no reflex tachy if beta-blocked)
  • Nitroprusside IV: 0.5–10 mcg/kg/min (if immediate BP reduction needed; monitor for cyanide toxicity if >4 hours continuous)
  • AVOID: nitrates alone, hydralazine monotherapy

  1. Analgesia (opioids):

    • Morphine 4–8 mg IV or fentanyl 50–100 mcg IV q1–2h
    • Pain control reduces sympathetic surge; do NOT withhold for fear of hypotension (dissection patients tolerate opioids well under controlled BP)

  2. Anticoagulation: HOLD unless surgeon directs otherwise. Heparin increases rupture risk preoperatively.

  3. NPO status — patient will go to OR imminently.

  4. Labs & monitoring:

    • Send: CBC, CMP, PT/INR/PTT, fibrinogen, troponin, lactate, type & screen, blood cultures if fever
    • Continuous cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, BP q5 min
    • Foley catheter — monitor UOP and color (myoglobinuria?)
    • Watch for rupture: acute hypotension, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus, JVD (tamponade); new focal neuro deficit (stroke/spinal ischemia)

  5. Family communication:

    • Brief, clear: "Your loved one has a tear in the aorta that requires emergency surgery. The team is preparing now."
    • Obtain informed consent (patient or health care proxy)
    • Discuss risks (operative mortality 8–10%), alternatives (none — surgery is only option)

sections.heading: Operative Repair (Surgical Team)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Median sternotomy; cardiopulmonary bypass
  • Ascending aorta and/or arch replacement with Dacron graft
  • Aortic root replacement (Bentall, valve-sparing root procedure) if root/valve involved
  • Coronary ostia reimplanted if dissection involves coronaries
  • Arch branch vessel (brachiocephalic, left carotid, left subclavian) reimplanted or separate grafts
  • Descending aorta repair: may be acute (Type I) or staged (hemodynamically fragile)
  • Spinal cord protection: mild hypothermia, CSF drainage (drain placed in ICU post-op if needed)

sections.heading: 5B. Type B Uncomplicated — Medical Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Criteria for "uncomplicated": No malperfusion, no rupture, pain controlled, BP controlled.

  1. Impulse control identical to Type A preop:

    • Beta-blocker FIRST: labetalol/esmolol, HR ≤ 60
    • Then vasodilator: nicardipine/nitroprusside, SBP ≤ 120

  2. Pain control: opioids (morphine/fentanyl). Do NOT withhold; pain drives hypertension.

  3. Bowel regimen: stool softener (docusate) + osmotic laxative (MiraLAX); avoid enemas/suppositories to prevent straining.

  4. Transition to PO antihypertensives (POD 1–3):

    • Labetalol or metoprolol + amlodipine; goal SBP 120–130, HR 60–80
    • Add lisinopril if needed (ACE inhibitor reduces aortic remodeling in chronic phase)

  5. Serial imaging surveillance: - CTA or MRA at 6 weeks, 6 months, 1 year, then annually × 2 years, then q2–3 years for life

  6. Discharge planning:

    • Strict lifetime BP control (SBP ≤ 120, HR ≤ 60)
    • Avoid heavy lifting (>20 lbs), strenuous exercise, cocaine, sympathomimetics, NSAIDs, straining
    • Genetic counseling if Marfan/Loeys-Dietz/BAV with aortopathy/family Hx
    • Follow-up: cardiothoracic clinic 1–2 weeks; primary care for hypertension management
    • Home BP monitoring; log readings

sections.heading: 5C. Type B Complicated — TEVAR (Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair)
sections.bodyHtml: Indications for TEVAR: Malperfusion (limb, renal, mesenteric, spinal cord ischemia), aortic rupture, rapid expansion (>5 mm/week), refractory pain or hypertension despite maximal medical management.

sections.heading: Pre-TEVAR
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Notify vascular/interventional radiology STAT — urgent imaging and team coordination

  2. Impulse control: maintain HR ≤ 60, SBP ≤ 120 (same as Type A/Type B uncomplicated)

  3. Address malperfusion components:

    • Renal: monitor Cr, UOP; initiate dialysis if AKI severe
    • Mesenteric: monitor lactate trends, abdominal exam; consider CT angiography abdomen to grade ischemia
    • Spinal: neuro checks q2h; watch for paraplegia

  4. Prepare for interventional procedure: CTA/CTP (aortic angiography) to guide stent-graft sizing and positioning

sections.heading: Post-TEVAR (ICU/Stepdown)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Maintain MAP ≥ 85 mmHg for spinal cord perfusion (distinct from general BP targets; prevent over-aggressive control → paraplegia)

  2. CSF drain management (if placed):

    • Target output 10–20 mL/h
    • Overdrain (>30 mL/h) → raise drain, call team (subdural hematoma risk)
    • Underdrain (<5 mL/h) → lower drain, check for kinks, call team
    • Discontinue POD 2–3 if no cord ischemia signs and MAP ≥ 85

  3. Neuro checks every 2–4 hours:

    • Lower extremity: new weakness, foot drop, paraplegia = spinal cord ischemia → STAT call
    • Upper extremity: unilateral weakness = stroke
    • Pupils, mentation: mydriasis or confusion → call team

  4. Pain & impulse control: continue HR ≤ 60, SBP ≤ 130 (slightly higher to protect spinal cord); pain control essential

  5. Anticoagulation: aspirin 81 mg daily (lifelong); clopidogrel 75 mg daily × 3–6 months per interventional team protocol

  6. Serial imaging: CTA at 1 month, 6 months, annually thereafter to monitor endoleak, stent migration, distal aortic remodeling

  7. Activity: bed-to-chair POD 0–1, ambulation POD 1–2; prevent straining; bowel regimen essential

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "[Patient name, room #], POD [X] s/p [procedure / presenting with suspected dissection]." B: "Sudden [chest/back/flank] pain. VS: HR [rate], BP [arm 1] / [arm 2] (differential [X] mmHg), SpO₂ [value]. Recent labs: troponin [value], lactate [value]. CXR [findings]. ECG [findings]." A: "Highly suspicious for acute aortic dissection. [Stable / unstable]. [Focal neuro findings / malperfusion signs, if any]." R: "Requesting STAT CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis and immediate CT surgery evaluation. [Requesting cardiothoracic team to bedside if suspected Type A]. [Requesting interventional team if Type B with malperfusion]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Type A suspected Cardiothoracic surgery STAT + ED/hospitalist if in ED
Type B uncomplicated, stable Cardiothoracic team + ED (if in ED); admit to ICU
Type B complicated (malperfusion, rupture, refractory HTN) Vascular/interventional radiology STAT + CT surgery + ICU
Hemodynamically unstable / ruptured Code team + CT surgery + activate massive transfusion
New stroke symptoms mid-dissection Stroke code + CT surgery + neurology (do NOT give tPA)
Post-repair paraplegia Neurosurgery (CSF drain) + CT surgery + spinal cord ischemia protocol

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Stanford vs. DeBakey Classification
sections.bodyHtml:
Classification comparison table
ClassificationOriginAnatomyIncidenceSurgical Urgency
Stanford Type AProximal (ascending aorta)Involves ascending aorta, regardless of extentDeBakey I + II = 50%Surgical emergency
Stanford Type BDistal (descending)Beyond left subclavian arteryDeBakey III = 50%Medical ± TEVAR per complications
DeBakey Type IAscending aortaExtends from ascending through arch to descending~40% of all dissectionsSurgical emergency
DeBakey Type IIAscending aorta onlyConfined to ascending aorta; does not extend beyond innominate~10% of dissectionsSurgical emergency
DeBakey Type IIIDistal (descending)Descending aorta, usually distal to left subclavian origin~50% of dissectionsMedical ± TEVAR
Clinical pearls: Stanford is simpler (2 types) and guides management (Type A = surgery, Type B = medical ± TEVAR). DeBakey is more anatomically detailed but doesn't change immediate management algorithm. Use Stanford at bedside.

sections.heading: 7.2 AAD-ADD Score + D-dimer Rule-Out Strategy
sections.bodyHtml:
Risk stratification AAD-ADD Score (predicts Type A in acute aortic syndrome):
VariablePoints
Age ≥ 60 years1
Hypertension or on antihypertensives1
Aortic atherosclerosis on imaging1
D-dimer > 0.5 mcg/mL3
Diabetes1
Interpretation: Score ≥ 2 = increased risk for Type A. Highest yield when combined with troponin (TnI/T normal) and CXR (normal does NOT rule out). D-dimer as rule-out tool:
  • D-dimer >99% sensitive for acute aortic syndrome (Type A and Type B combined)
  • Normal D-dimer (<0.5 mcg/mL) is excellent rule-out for dissection if clinical suspicion is low
  • Elevated D-dimer is NOT diagnostic — confirms suspicion but requires CTA to differentiate dissection from other acute aortic conditions (aneurysm, intramural hematoma, penetrating aortic ulcer)
  • Use in low-risk populations: young, no risk factors, normal CXR → normal D-dimer = safe to defer imaging (rare scenario) Key point: D-dimer is only a rule-out test. Never use an elevated D-dimer alone to diagnose dissection — always get CTA.

sections.heading: 7.3 Diagnostic Workup
sections.bodyHtml:
Gold-standard imaging and supplemental tests
TestSensitivity / SpecificityUse Case
CT angiography (CTA) chest/abdomen/pelvis95–98% sens / 98% specGOLD STANDARD for all suspected Type A/B; shows intimal flap, false lumen, malperfusion, rupture, pericardial effusion, coronary involvement
Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)~95% sens for ascending involvementHemodynamically unstable; can be done in OR/ICU without transport
MR angiography (MRA)High sens/specChronic follow-up; contraindicated in acute hemodynamic instability
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)Poor for dissection diagnosisScreening only; shows pericardial effusion, AR, root dilation
CXR60% sensitiveWidened mediastinum, pleural effusion, tracheal deviation; normal CXR does NOT exclude dissection
ECGNonspecificMay show STEMI pattern if RCA involved (don't fixate); get CTA
D-dimer>99% sensitiveHigh NPV for rule-out in low-risk patients; not diagnostic alone
Clinical decision: If suspicion is high (sudden tearing pain + pulse differential or hypertension crisis), get CTA immediately. Don't wait for CXR or ECG results.

sections.heading: 7.4 Malperfusion Syndromes — Recognition & Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Branch vessel complications
VesselSigns / SymptomsMechanismBedside Clues
Carotid / cerebralAcute ischemic stroke, TIA, altered mental status, blindness (amaurosis fugax)Carotid ostial obstruction or intimal flap at archUnilateral weakness, speech change, vision loss
VertebralPosterior circulation stroke, vertigo, bilateral symptomsVertebral origin involvement at archDizziness, diplopia, ataxia
Spinal cord (Artery of Adamkiewicz, usually T9–L2 left-sided)Acute paraplegia, paresthesias, loss of sensation/motor below levelDissection extending into descending thoracic, compromising segmental supplyLower extremity weakness, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention
Renal arteryAcute rise in creatinine, oliguria, flank painDissection flap into renal artery ostium or branchUOP drops, Cr spikes, hyperkalemia
Mesenteric (SMA/IMA)Acute abdominal pain (out of proportion), bloody diarrhea, metabolic acidosisMalperfusion of bowel; high mortality if not recognizedElevated lactate, falling platelet count, peritoneal signs
Iliac / femoralAcute limb ischemia, cold limb, absent femoral pulse, pain, paresthesiasFalse lumen compression or direct occlusion at iliac originUnilateral cool extremity, mottled skin, ischemic pain
Coronary (RCA > LCA)Inferior STEMI physiology, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmiaRCA ostium involvement (Type A); true coronary dissection rareInferior ST elevation, elevated troponin, hemodynamic collapse
Malperfusion management:
  • Spinal cord ischemia → maintain MAP ≥ 85, place CSF drain, neuro checks q2h
  • Renal → monitor Cr/UOP, initiate dialysis if needed
  • Mesenteric → monitor lactate, check abdomen, consider exploratory laparotomy if peritonitis
  • Limb → ensure adequate distal perfusion; angiography may be needed to guide revascularization

sections.heading: 7.5 Impulse Control Medication Ladder
sections.bodyHtml:
Why β-blocker FIRST, then vasodilator The physiology: Vasodilators (nitroprusside, nicardipine) drop aortic pressure acutely. In the absence of β-blockade, the baroreceptor reflex triggers sympathetic surge → increased heart rate and contractility (dP/dt) → shear stress WIDENS the dissection. The algorithm:
  1. β-Blocker FIRST: Reduce HR to ≤60 and dP/dt (rate of pressure change). This alone may control BP in ~30% of patients. Achieves goal before vasodilator added.
  2. Vasodilator AFTER β-blockade: Now the reflex tachycardia is blocked, and vasodilation safely lowers pressure to SBP ≤120 without worsening shear. Agents:
    DrugRoleMechanismDose
    Labetalol IVβ-blocker + vasodilatorα + β blockade10–20 mg bolus q10min up to 80 mg, then 0.5–2 mg/min infusion
    Esmolol IVβ-blockerUltra-short-acting β1-selective500 mcg/kg load, then 50–300 mcg/kg/min
    Nicardipine IVVasodilatorDHP CCB; balanced arterial/venous dilator5–15 mg/h, titrate to SBP ≤120
    Nitroprusside IVVasodilatorNitric oxide donor; immediate effect0.5–10 mcg/kg/min; monitor thiocyanate if >4 h
    Morphine IVAnalgesia + anxiolyticμ-opioid; reduces sympathetic surge4–8 mg q1–2h
    Transition to PO (Type B uncomplicated, POD 1–3):
    • Labetalol PO (200–400 mg TID) or metoprolol (25–50 mg BID) + amlodipine (5–10 mg daily) ± lisinopril (10–20 mg daily)
    • Goal: SBP 120–130, HR 60–80 NEVER:
    • Vasodilator monotherapy (reflex tachycardia widens dissection)
    • Hydralazine first (potent reflex tachy)
    • Nitrates alone (reflex tachy)

sections.heading: 7.6 IRAD Registry Findings — Type A Mortality Predictors
sections.bodyHtml:
In-hospital mortality risk stratification The IRAD (International Registry of Acute Aortic Dissection) identified 5 independent Type A mortality predictors:
Risk FactorPoints
Age > 70 years1
Renal failure (Cr > 2.0 mg/dL)1
Preop shock or hemodynamic instability1
Tamponade (echo-proven pericardial effusion + hemodynamic evidence)1
Neurologic deficit (stroke, paraplegia)1
Mortality by score:
  • Score 0–1: ~5%
  • Score 2–3: ~12%
  • Score 4–5: ~25–50% Clinical use: Identify high-risk patients early; communicate with family about operative mortality (8–10% overall for Type A repair). These scores predict operative risk but don't change the decision to operate (Type A is always surgical).

sections.heading: 7.7 Endovascular Repair (TEVAR) Evolution & Outcomes
sections.bodyHtml:
When TEVAR is indicated for Type B TEVAR (thoracic endovascular aortic repair) = stent-graft placement to cover the dissection origin and eliminate false-lumen flow. Indications:
  • Malperfusion (organ, limb, spinal cord ischemia)
  • Aortic rupture (actual or threatened)
  • Rapid aortic expansion (>5 mm/week)
  • Refractory pain or hypertension despite maximal medical management
  • Intramural hematoma with expansion Evidence (INSTEAD-XL trial):
  • Compared TEVAR vs medical management in Type B uncomplicated dissection
  • Medical management has equivalent outcomes at 1 year if uncomplicated; TEVAR reserved for complications
  • TEVAR has ~2–5% procedural stroke/paraplegia risk; long-term requires surveillance for endoleaks and stent migration Post-TEVAR trajectory:
  • Immediate: maintain MAP ≥85 for spinal cord, monitor neuro q2–4h
  • POD 2–7: serial imaging (CTA), CSF drain management if placed, continue impulse control
  • Discharge: lifelong surveillance imaging (CTA at 1 mo, 6 mo, annually), aspirin + clopidogrel per protocol
  • Long-term: monitor for endoleaks, stent migration, distal aortic aneurysm formation, need for re-intervention Complications: endoleak (persistent false-lumen flow), stent migration, occlusion of visceral branches, late rupture, need for re-intervention in ~20% at 5 years.

sections.heading: 7.8 Genetic Syndromes & Pregnancy
sections.bodyHtml:
Heritable aortopathy and peripartum risk Marfan Syndrome:
  • Fibrillin-1 defect → cystic medial necrosis → aortic root dilation, dissection risk
  • Aortic root diameter typically >5 cm at presentation; 10× dissection risk vs general population
  • Management: β-blocker or ARB (losartan) to slow aortic remodeling; serial echo/CTA monitoring; elective root replacement if diameter >5.5 cm
  • Pregnancy counseling: 10× dissection risk in pregnancy; often managed with cesarean delivery before labor Loeys-Dietz Syndrome (LDS):
  • TGF-β pathway defect (TGFBR1/TGFBR2) → rapid aortic dilation, aortic aneurysm, dissection
  • Earlier onset and more aggressive than Marfan; root diameter >5 cm not uncommon in young adults
  • Management: ARB preferred (losartan) over β-blocker per emerging evidence; very close monitoring (CTA q6–12 mo)
  • Pregnancy: extremely high risk; planned cesarean in early term advised Bicuspid Aortic Valve (BAV) with aortopathy:
  • Bicuspid valve + ascending aorta dilation (disproportionate to aortic stenosis/regurgitation severity)
  • Dissection risk higher in men; dilation can progress rapidly
  • Management: β-blocker, serial echo/CTA; aortic root replacement if diameter >5.0–5.5 cm depending on risk factors
  • Pregnancy: borderline aortic root diameter (4.5–5.0 cm) requires close monitoring Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (Type IV / vascular type):
  • COL3A1 defect → fragile vessels, spontaneous arterial rupture, dissection
  • Can present at any age; often with minimal warning
  • Management: ARB or β-blocker; avoid strenuous activity and high-intensity exercise; surgical repair challenging due to tissue fragility Pregnancy + dissection:
  • Peak risk: third trimester and peripartum (aortic remodeling, volume shifts, hemodynamic stress)
  • Management: planned cesarean delivery (avoids labor-related hypertension); continue IV impulse control during labor/delivery; neonatal considerations (medication exposure)
  • Pre-conception counseling: essential for Marfan/LDS/vascular EDS patients; discuss 10× risk, management strategy, fetal implications

sections.heading: 7.9 Post-Repair Surveillance & Re-Intervention
sections.bodyHtml:
Chronic phase management Post-Type A repair:
  • Surveillance CTA: 1 month, 6 months, 1 year, then annually × 2 years, then q2–3 years
  • Watch for: false aneurysm at graft site, pseudointimal flap (healed dissection), descending aorta aneurysm formation, progressive distal aortic dilation
  • Remaining aortic segments: residual dissection may be thrombosed or patent; patent false lumens can cause late aneurysm
  • Re-operation rates: ~10–20% at 5–10 years for distal aorta complications Post-Type B repair (medical or TEVAR):
  • Medical: same surveillance as Type A (CTA q6–12 mo initially, then per findings)
  • Post-TEVAR: CTA at 1 month, 6 months, annually; watch for endoleaks, stent migration, need for extension grafts
  • Endoleak management: Type Ia (proximal seal failure) or Type Ib (distal seal failure) may require intervention; Type II (back-bleeding from branches) often observed if stable Aortic root surveillance in chronic dissection:
  • Root diameter should stabilize after acute phase; serial echo/CTA recommended to detect late dilation
  • Bicuspid AV + dissection: ascending aorta may be at risk for late aneurysm; lower threshold for root replacement if diameter trends >5.0 cm
  • Root replacement electively (before rupture) is safer than emergency repair Activity restrictions (lifelong):
  • No heavy lifting (>20 lbs), no strenuous/competitive sports, no Valsalva maneuver (straining, coughing hard)
  • Controlled aerobic exercise (walking, swimming) with HR ≤100 bpm is safe
  • Avoid cocaine, pseudoephedrine, NSAIDs, uncontrolled hypertension Medication compliance:
  • Lifetime BP control (SBP ≤120 mmHg target) is non-negotiable
  • β-blocker or ACE inhibitor/ARB essential; amlodipine or other add-ons as needed
  • Patient education: "Your aorta depends on your BP medication — never miss a dose"

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, escalate immediately.

  • New or recurrent tearing pain after initial control → rupture, re-dissection, or contained leak → STAT imaging (CTA/TEE), call surgery
  • Acute change in pulse differential between arms/legs (new >20 mmHg spread) → progressive dissection into arch branches → escalate
  • New focal neurologic deficit (weakness, speech change, vision loss, altered mental status) → stroke or spinal cord ischemia → call team immediately
  • Sudden onset paralysis or sensory loss in lower extremities → spinal cord ischemia (can be delayed to POD 3–5) → STAT call, raise MAP ≥85, check CSF drain
  • New or worsening oliguria with rising creatinine → renal malperfusion → monitor lactate, consider dialysis, notify team
  • Bloody diarrhea, abdominal pain, rising lactate → mesenteric malperfusion → STAT abdomen imaging, assess for peritonitis
  • Acute limb ischemia (cold extremity, absent pulse, ischemic pain) → limb malperfusion → notify vascular surgery
  • Unexpected hypotension on stable antihypertensive regimen → rule out rupture, tamponade, sepsis → STAT call, imaging
  • New early diastolic murmur (if not present initially) → aortic regurgitation progression → may signal aortic root instability or valve compromise → notify team
  • Type A patient NOT in OR within hours of diagnosis → explain delay; verify imaging done, surgical scheduling confirmed
  • Type B patient not improving with medical management by 24–48 hours (persistent severe pain or hypertension, expanding aorta on serial imaging) → consider TEVAR → discuss with interventional team

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. NEVER vasodilator BEFORE β-blocker. Reflex tachycardia from nitroprusside/nicardipine first widens the dissection. Always HR ≤60, then SBP ≤120. Non-negotiable.

  2. 15% Type A present with NO chest pain — only stroke, syncope, or neuro deficit. High clinical suspicion required; dissection until proven otherwise.

  3. "Dissection as stroke" is deadly. When dissection involves the arch and causes acute stroke, tPA is contraindicated and causes rupture. Get CTA chest/arch BEFORE thrombolytics.

  4. Inferior ST elevation may be RCA dissection, not MI. Don't send straight to cath lab without aortic imaging. Cardiac cath in dissection = catastrophe.

  5. Normal CXR does NOT rule out dissection. CXR is 60% sensitive; ~40% of dissections have normal mediastinal silhouette. High suspicion = get CTA immediately.

  6. D-dimer is only a rule-out tool. Normal D-dimer (<0.5 mcg/mL) is helpful in low-risk populations; elevated D-dimer is NOT diagnostic and must be followed by CTA.

  7. Strict BP/HR targets are evidence-based, not arbitrary. SBP ≤120 and HR ≤60 reduce aortic shear (dP/dt). Permissive hypertension is dissection-unfriendly.

  8. MAP ≥85 is the SPINAL CORD target (distinct from general BP control). Over-aggressive vasodilator titration → paraplegia. Ask before dropping MAP below 85.

  9. New lower extremity weakness = SPINAL CORD ISCHEMIA. Can occur immediately or delayed (POD 3–5) after TEVAR. STAT call; maintain MAP ≥85; check CSF drain.

  10. Type A mortality is ~1% per hour untreated. Preoperative delays of >6 hours without surgical planning are unacceptable. Push for OR expeditiously.

  11. Type B can crossover to "complicated" mid-hospitalization. A patient initially uncomplicated can develop malperfusion or rupture within hours. Stay vigilant; re-image if clinical deterioration.

  12. Pregnant dissection is highest-risk in Marfan/Loeys-Dietz. OB should be contacted emergently; aortic repair often concurrent with peripartum management. Pre-conception counseling: 10× risk.

  13. Check BP in BOTH arms EVERY shift. Pulse differential >20 mmHg between arms is a classic finding in arch dissection; trend the differential to detect progressive involvement.

  14. Post-repair false aneurysm risk is real. Residual false lumens or graft sites can dilate over months/years. Lifetime imaging surveillance is mandatory; some patients need re-operation at 5–10 years.

  15. Bicuspid AV + ascending aorta surveillance. Bicuspid valve patients with dissection have higher risk of progressive aortic root dilation; lower threshold for elective root replacement (target <5.0 cm) to prevent late rupture.

cards.title: Acute Stroke Recognition and Response
cards.quickAnswer: New focal neuro deficit → activate stroke code STAT, determine last-known-well time, fingerstick glucose, STAT CT head ± CTA, labs (CBC, coagulation panel, BMP), 12-lead ECG, NPO. Recent cardiac surgery is a relative contraindication to systemic tPA due to bleeding risk; mechanical thrombectomy is preferred when large-vessel occlusion (LVO) is found on CTA. Blood pressure targets differ from routine post-op: permit systolic HTN up to 220 mmHg (or MAP ≤ 130 mmHg) if NOT a tPA candidate to preserve penumbral perfusion. Preserve the clock—document LKW rigorously; it determines all treatment windows. Thrombectomy is feasible up to 6 hours from LKW (standard) or up to 24 hours with favorable perfusion imaging.
