sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, who gets it, why it matters.

  • Definition: New-onset focal neurologic deficit occurring in the post-cardiac surgery patient, consistent with acute ischemic stroke (embolic, thrombotic, or hypoperfusive mechanism) or less commonly acute intracranial hemorrhage.
  • Incidence: Post-operative cardiac surgery stroke occurs in 1–3% of patients (higher with preoperative carotid stenosis, new-onset atrial fibrillation (POAF), atheromatous aorta, or prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)). Peak timing is POD 0–3 but can occur throughout admission.
  • Who this applies to: every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient on telemetry or continuous monitoring from admission through at least POD 7. Highest-yield period is POD 0–5.
  • Why it matters: Stroke is a time-critical emergency; every minute of ischemia costs functional brain tissue. Recent surgery complicates treatment decisions but does not eliminate intervention options. Early recognition, LKW documentation, and rapid imaging are the keys to salvaging ischemic brain.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative stroke is multifactorial, driven by surgical trauma, anticoagulation reversal, and inherent cardiac disease. Three broad mechanisms:

Embolic (most common, ~70%):

  • Aortic atheroma dislodged during cannulation, cross-clamping, or manipulation (epiaortic ultrasound screening reduces this risk)
  • Atrial fibrillation (POAF in ~30% of CABG, ~40% of valve surgery) with thrombus in the atrial appendage or left ventricle
  • Air emboli trapped in coronary or cerebral circulation during CPB
  • Mechanical valve thrombosis (in patients with prosthetic valves)
  • Native or prosthetic valve debris (endocarditis, thrombus)

Thrombotic:

  • Preoperative carotid stenosis with perioperative hypotension or low cardiac output state
  • In-situ thrombosis on instrumented carotid artery (post-carotid endarterectomy)
  • Prothrombotic state post-operatively (elevated fibrinogen, platelet activation, hemoconcentration)

Hypoperfusive:

  • Systemic hypotension during or after CPB (inadequate pump flow, hemodilution, vasodilation)
  • Low cardiac output in immediate post-op period (bleeding, sepsis, cardiogenic shock)
  • Cerebral autoregulation disrupted by anesthesia, CPB, or acute cardiac dysfunction

Hemorrhagic (less common, ~5%):

  • Intracranial hemorrhage in anticoagulated patients or post-thrombectomy
  • Reperfusion injury or bleeding into established ischemic infarct

Risk factors for post-operative stroke include female sex, age > 75 years, preoperative carotid disease, new POAF, low cardiac output, aortic manipulation without epiaortic ultrasound guidance, mechanical valve, prior stroke, and prolonged CPB time > 180 minutes (Powers et al., 2019).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

BEFAST screening — any one positive domain warrants stroke code activation:

Acronym Assessment Example Finding
B Balance Ataxia, loss of balance, abnormal gait, inability to walk straight
E Eyes Vision loss in one or both eyes, diplopia, gaze deviation, nystagmus
F Face Facial asymmetry, droop, inability to smile symmetrically
A Arm Unilateral weakness, drift, inability to hold arm elevated against gravity
S Speech Slurred speech, aphasia (expressive or receptive), dysarthria, word-finding difficulty
T Time This is the clock. Any acute-onset focal neurologic finding, regardless of other signs

Associated presentation:

  • Patient reports palpitations, chest discomfort, fatigue, dyspnea, or lightheadedness at time of stroke onset
  • Altered mental status, confusion, somnolence (may obscure motor findings in sedated patients)
  • Seizure activity (post-op seizures mimic stroke; EEG required to distinguish)
  • Anesthesia emergence delayed or patient difficult to arouse

Timing patterns by post-operative day:

  • POD 0–1: Intraoperative emboli (aortic manipulation, air), hypoperfusion (CPB duration, low output), detected immediately upon neuro check or emergence
  • POD 2–5: New-onset POAF with cardioembolic stroke, inflammatory thrombotic cascade, inflammatory cascade post-CPB
  • POD 5+: POAF-related (embolic), aspiration pneumonia with hypercoagulability, less commonly late graft occlusion

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (target 2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Competent systematic exam. Do not delay stroke code activation to complete assessment.

Time-sensitive assessment:

  • Last known well (LKW): This is the clock that governs all treatment windows. Ask family or review chart: when was the patient definitely neurologically normal? Not "when we noticed the deficit" but the last moment the patient was confirmed awake, alert, and without focal findings. If patient was asleep: when last known awake and normal?
  • Symptom onset time: when did the patient / observer first notice the abnormality?
  • BEFAST screening: systematically check each domain per table above
  • NIHSS mental run-through: level of consciousness (alert/drowsy/stuporous), attention, language (receptive/expressive), motor (arm/leg), sensory, visual fields, ataxia. Full formal NIHSS will be performed by stroke team; your role is rapid identification of focal deficit.

Laboratory and monitoring:

  • Fingerstick glucose: hypoglycemia (< 70 mg/dL) is a treatable stroke mimic and must be corrected immediately
  • Vital signs: baseline BP, HR, RR, SpO₂, temperature, perfusion assessment (capillary refill, skin temperature)
  • Anticoagulation status: review chart for any AC drugs given in OR or PACU, bridging therapy status (relevant for tPA/thrombectomy decision and bleeding risk)
  • Airway assessment: can patient protect airway? Any aspiration risk? Swallow status? Evidence of tongue biting, post-ictal state?
  • 12-lead ECG STAT: look for atrial fibrillation (POAF is common post-CABG and represents cardioembolic mechanism), acute ST changes (may indicate concurrent MI or graft occlusion), QT prolongation

Context:

  • Surgery context: what procedure and when (POD clock starts from time of surgery)
  • Recent labs: most recent K⁺, glucose, hemoglobin, creatinine (obtained routinely post-op)
  • MAR review: medications that were held pre-op or post-op; antiplatelet/anticoagulation restart status
  • Lines and wires: arterial line, adequate IV access for contrast or pressors? Epicardial pacing wires in place?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Suspected stroke, hemodynamically stable — "stable" means no imminent airway/perfusion crisis. This is still a STAT workflow; activation is mandatory.)

  1. Stroke code activation STAT — institutional overhead page, emergency department notification, or code team alert per [Institution policy]. Notify stroke neurology, cardiac surgery, critical care, and cardiothoracic attending simultaneously. Document the exact time of activation.

  2. Last known well (LKW) documentation — write the LKW time clearly and prominently in the chart. This drives all downstream treatment windows (tPA window 0–4.5 h, thrombectomy window 0–6 h standard, 6–24 h extended).

  3. Fingerstick glucose STAT — if < 70 mg/dL, administer dextrose IV (50 mL of 50% dextrose, or 25 mL of 100% dextrose diluted to 50% concentration) immediately and recheck after 1–2 minutes. Hypoglycemia resolves in seconds to minutes; true stroke does not.

  4. Vital signs + baseline neuro exam — document BP, HR, RR, SpO₂, temperature. Perform or document quick NIHSS (or at minimum GCS, pupil size/reactivity, motor strength bilaterally, speech clarity). Record findings with timestamp.

  5. IV access and STAT labs — two large-bore IVs if not already present. Stat labs: complete blood count (CBC), comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP; especially glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, renal function), coagulation panel (PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer per stroke protocol), troponin (rule out concurrent MI), arterial blood gas (ABG) if available to assess oxygenation/ventilation and acid-base status.

  6. 12-lead ECG STAT — look for new atrial fibrillation (common trigger post-CABG), ST elevation or depression (concurrent MI or graft occlusion), QT prolongation.

  7. STAT CT head non-contrast — to rule out hemorrhage (blood in ventricles, subarachnoid, epidural, subdural, or intracerebral). Do NOT delay for other tests. Head CT is essential to differentiate ischemic vs. hemorrhagic stroke. Follow immediately with CTA head/neck to assess for large-vessel occlusion (LVO) if stroke protocol permits; some institutions perform this before CT perfusion.

  8. Keep patient NPO — pending dysphagia screening; no oral meds, no food/drink (aspiration risk is high post-stroke).

  9. Serial neuro exams every 15 minutes — until CT results available and stroke team arrives on-site; then per stroke team protocol. Document time, GCS, focal findings (motor strength, speech, visual fields, pupils) with each exam. Flag any deterioration (worsening GCS by ≥ 2 points, new anisocoria, signs of herniation) for immediate escalation to 5B path.

  10. Blood pressure management (non-tPA candidate pathway):

    • If NOT a tPA or thrombectomy candidate: permit systolic HTN up to 220 mmHg (or MAP up to 130 mmHg) for the first 24 hours to maximize penumbral (at-risk tissue) perfusion. Cerebral autoregulation is disrupted in acute stroke; aggressive BP lowering reduces collateral flow and expands the infarct. After 24 hours, gradually lower BP to usual post-op targets (SBP 130–140).
    • If hypotensive (SBP < 90, MAP < 70): This is a stroke emergency. Cerebral perfusion pressure is already threatened by infarction. Low MAP worsens ischemia and expands the infarct core. Administer IV fluid bolus (500 mL–1 L normal saline over 15 minutes); if MAP remains < 70 after fluid, initiate vasopressor support (norepinephrine 0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min IV infusion, titrate to target MAP 80–90). Notify cardiac surgery, critical care, and stroke team immediately.

  11. CT surgery + stroke neurology discussion re: tPA eligibility: Recent major surgery (sternotomy, CPB) is a relative contraindication to systemic thrombolysis due to bleeding risk. This is NOT an absolute contraindication. The stroke team and cardiac surgery must jointly assess: What is the stroke severity (NIHSS)? What is the infarct core size on imaging? Is the estimated bleeding risk from recent surgery acceptable? Document this discussion and the decision reached (proceed with tPA vs. pursue thrombectomy vs. observe). tPA may still be considered in very high-NIHSS, large-LVO strokes if thrombectomy is not immediately available AND cardiac surgery judges bleeding risk acceptable.

  12. Mechanical thrombectomy: If CTA head/neck shows LVO (internal carotid artery, M1 segment of middle cerebral artery, M2 distal MCA, or vertebrobasilar occlusion), activate endovascular / interventional radiology team STAT. Thrombectomy is the preferred intervention in post-operative patients with LVO because it avoids systemic fibrinolysis and has higher recanalization rates. Thrombectomy is feasible 0–6 hours from LKW (standard window, Class I evidence) or up to 24 hours if perfusion imaging shows favorable mismatch (ischemic penumbra present, minimal infarct core) per DAWN and DEFUSE-3 trial criteria (Nogueira et al., 2018; Albers et al., 2018).

  13. Family notification — inform next of kin of stroke recognition and ongoing evaluation as soon as feasible. Verify code status and goals of care if not previously documented.

  14. Dysphagia screen — BEFORE ANY ORAL INTAKE, including medications or water. Aspiration pneumonia is the #1 post-stroke infection and leading cause of post-stroke morbidity. Use institutional bedside screening protocol (alert patient, palpate larynx during dry swallow, observe for cough or wet voice, trial small sip of water) or request speech pathology evaluation if high-risk features present.

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Airway compromise, GCS ≤ 8, signs of herniation, intractable hypertension > 220/120 unresponsive to single agents, hypotension refractory to fluids, active seizure, rapid neurologic deterioration, imminent transtentorial herniation.)

  1. STAT stroke code + Rapid Response Team (RRT) + code team + cardiac surgery + critical care — notify all teams simultaneously. Do NOT delay for imaging.

  2. Airway priority:

    • Positioning: head midline, head-of-bed (HOB) elevated 30° (unless specific hypoperfusion crisis with refractory hypotension, in which case HOB may be lowered transiently to 0°; note: HeadPoST trial [2017] showed no mortality difference between HOB 0° and 30°, so default to 30° per current evidence)
    • Oxygenation: supplemental O₂ to target SpO₂ > 95%; gentle oral airway suctioning
    • Anticipate rapid sequence intubation (RSI): prepare medications — induction agent (propofol or etomidate preferred; avoid thiopental in low-output states), paralytic (rocuronium preferred; avoid succinylcholine which transiently raises intracranial pressure)
    • Post-intubation: place nasogastric tube if prolonged NPO anticipated; verify placement with chest X-ray; secure with tube holder and document depth

  3. Blood pressure control per acute stroke pathway:

    • If SBP > 220 or MAP > 130 and NOT a tPA/thrombectomy candidate: administer labetalol 10–20 mg IV push, may repeat every 10–20 minutes (maximum 80 mg total), OR initiate nicardipine infusion starting 5 mg/hour, titrate by 2.5 mg/hour every 5–15 minutes to goal SBP < 220
    • If hypotensive (SBP < 90, MAP < 70): administer normal saline bolus 500 mL–1 L over 15 minutes; if MAP remains < 70, initiate vasopressor (norepinephrine 0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min IV infusion, titrate to target MAP 80–90). Notify critical care and cardiac surgery.

  4. Seizure management (if actively seizing):

    • First-line: lorazepam 2–4 mg IV push, repeat once at 10-minute interval if seizure continues
    • Load antiepileptic: levetiracetam 20–30 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes (typical dose 1500–2000 mg for adult) OR fosphenytoin 15–20 PE/kg IV at rate ≤ 150 mg PE/minute
    • Monitoring: order continuous EEG monitoring for all sedated or intubated patients (to detect non-convulsive seizures)

  5. ICU-level transfer and monitoring — critical care bed with continuous cardiac telemetry, SpO₂ monitoring, end-tidal CO₂ (ETCO₂) capnography if intubated, invasive blood pressure monitoring via arterial line (enables tight BP control and frequent labs without repeated needle sticks)

  6. NPO + NG tube — place nasogastric tube if intubated; secure with tube holder, mark depth at nares, verify placement on chest X-ray

  7. Strict time documentation — timestamps drive treatment decisions:

    • Time of stroke code activation
    • Time of LKW
    • Time of CT door arrival and CT completion
    • Time of CTA completion
    • Time of door-to-needle if tPA administered
    • Time of groin puncture if thrombectomy performed
    • Time of each serial neuro exam (every 15 min initially)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for stroke code communication:

S (Situation): "This is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room number], post-op day [#] s/p [procedure name]. Patient has acute onset [specific deficit — example: right arm weakness, expressive aphasia, left facial droop]. BEFAST positive for [specific domain]. Last known well was [time]. Stroke code activated at [time]."

B (Background): "Patient is [age] with risk factors [list: carotid disease, new AF, HTN, DM, prior stroke, mechanical valve]. Current medications include [AC status, antiplatelet status, cardiac meds]. Most recent neuro exam [time and findings]. Relevant past medical history [CPB time, cannulation sites, atheromatous aorta noted intraoperatively]."

A (Assessment): "Suspected acute ischemic stroke. Time from LKW [#] minutes — [within/outside] standard tPA window. Possible LVO pending CTA. Patient is currently [hemodynamically stable / unstable with BP X/Y]. NIHSS [estimated score]. CT imaging [pending / in progress / completed — describe findings if available]."

R (Recommendation): "Stroke team evaluation and CTA interpretation needed. Specific questions: [Is patient a tPA candidate given recent cardiac surgery? Should we activate endovascular team for thrombectomy? What are BP targets?]"

Who to call (priority order):

Contact Indication Communication Point
Stroke neurology (or RRT → neurology) Any suspected acute stroke Lead diagnostic and management team
Cardiac surgery / cardiothoracic attending Post-op patient Assess bleeding risk, tPA vs. thrombectomy decision, coordinate with neurology
Critical care / ICU Unstable patient, anticipated admission Bed availability, monitoring setup
Interventional radiology / endovascular team LVO on CTA STAT activation for thrombectomy if indicated
Anesthesia Intubation needed, airway compromise Rapid sequence intubation, medication selection (avoid succinylcholine)
Chaplain / palliative care Goals-of-care conversation indicated Family meeting if poor prognosis anticipated

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections below are — collapsed by default.

Post-operative stroke timing and type patterns POD 0–1 (intraoperative / emergence):
  • Embolic mechanism (aortic manipulation, valve manipulation, air emboli trapped in circulation)
  • Hypoperfusive mechanism (prolonged CPB, low cardiac output, systemic hypotension during bypass)
  • Often detected immediately upon neuro check post-extubation or during anesthesia emergence
  • Highest mortality if large middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory; consider urgent thrombectomy
  • Outcome often poor if large infarct core; still pursue thrombectomy per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 criteria POD 2–5:
  • New-onset post-operative atrial fibrillation (POAF) is the leading trigger; occurs in ~30% of CABG and ~40% of valve surgery patients
  • Cardioembolic mechanism (thrombus in atrial appendage, left ventricle if ejection fraction severely reduced, prosthetic valve)
  • Inflammatory thrombotic cascade post-CPB contributes
  • Earlier intervention window still feasible (within 6 h or extended window with perfusion imaging)
  • May still be tPA candidates if CT surgery approves bleeding risk POD 5+ (late strokes):
  • Primarily POAF-related (cardioembolic)
  • Aspiration pneumonia with hypercoagulability may contribute
  • Longer time from LKW, but still potentially within thrombectomy window if LVO and perfusion-imaging favorable
  • May have transitioned out of ICU setting; high-yield to screen all post-op cardiac patients through discharge for stroke symptoms
tPA eligibility in post-operative cardiac surgery patients — the bleeding dilemma Recent major surgery (within 3 months, especially cardiac surgery with sternotomy and CPB) is classified as a relative contraindication to systemic thrombolysis. This is NOT an absolute bar. The decision framework:
  • Stroke team + cardiac surgery joint discussion: What is the stroke severity (NIHSS score)? What is the estimated infarct core size on CT perfusion? What is the estimated bleeding risk from sternotomy and CPB?
  • Favorable scenario for tPA: high NIHSS (suggesting large territory at risk), large ischemic penumbra (salvageable tissue) on perfusion imaging, small infarct core, low bleeding risk (minimal serous drainage, low coagulation parameters at baseline, clean surgical field)
  • Unfavorable scenario for tPA: low NIHSS (small territory), large infarct core (tissue already dead), ongoing oozing or hemodynamic instability, active anticoagulation reversal in progress
  • Preferred alternative: mechanical thrombectomy avoids systemic fibrinolysis, has higher recanalization rates (80–90% vs. 40–50% for tPA alone), and is safe in post-op patients. Thrombectomy window is longer (0–6 h standard, 0–24 h extended with favorable imaging).
  • Documentation: Chart the discussion, who was called, what risk/benefit reasoning was applied, and who made the final decision (proceed with tPA, pursue thrombectomy, or observe). Reference: Powers et al. (2019) guideline; Nogueira et al. (2018) DAWN trial.
Large-vessel occlusion (LVO) and mechanical thrombectomy LVO definition: Occlusion of the internal carotid artery (ICA), M1 segment of middle cerebral artery (MCA), M2 (distal MCA branches), or vertebrobasilar system that prevents distal blood flow. Detection: CT angiography (CTA) of head and neck shows abrupt cutoff of arterial enhancement, hypodensity at the occlusion site, and absence of distal vessel filling. Thrombectomy time windows:
  • Standard window: 0–6 hours from LKW (Class I recommendation, highest evidence; DAWN trial, DEFUSE-3 trial)
  • Extended window: 6–24 hours from LKW if perfusion imaging (CT perfusion or MR perfusion) shows favorable mismatch — i.e., significant ischemic penumbra (tissue at risk) on perfusion maps with relatively small infarct core on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) or CT perfusion core map. DAWN and DEFUSE-3 trials established this extended window.
  • Activation: call endovascular / interventional radiology STAT if LVO identified on CTA. Outcomes in post-operative patients: Thrombectomy outcomes are superior to systemic tPA in post-op patients because recanalization rates are higher (80–90% vs. 40–50%) and bleeding risk is minimized. References: Nogueira et al. (2018) DAWN; Albers et al. (2018) DEFUSE-3.
Blood pressure targets — non-standard rules for acute stroke This section diverges sharply from routine post-operative HTN management:
Clinical ScenarioSBP TargetRationale
Acute ischemic stroke, NOT tPA/thrombectomy candidatePermissive HTN up to 220 mmHg (or MAP ≤ 130) for first 24 hThe penumbra (tissue at risk of infarction) requires adequate cerebral perfusion pressure to maintain collateral flow. Aggressive lowering of BP reduces collateral perfusion, paradoxically expanding the infarct. After 24 h, gradually lower to standard post-op SBP 130–140 to protect anastomoses and minimize bleeding.
Acute ischemic stroke, tPA or thrombectomy candidate< 185/110 pre-treatment; < 180/105 for 24 h post-treatmenttPA increases risk of intracranial hemorrhage (ICH); strict BP control reduces ICH rate. Thrombectomy also raises reperfusion-injury risk; maintained BP control is protective.
Acute intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) post-stroke< 160/90 (or permissive if hematoma stable and small)Limit hematoma expansion; balance perfusion needs. Avoid aggressive lowering that compromises penumbral perfusion.
Routine post-operative cardiac (no stroke)SBP ≤ 140, typically 110–130Protects fresh anastomoses, reduces bleeding risk at surgical sites.
Hypotension (SBP < 90, MAP < 70) in acute stroke = EMERGENCY:
  • Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP − intracranial pressure) is already threatened by infarction
  • Low MAP worsens ischemia and expands the infarct core
  • Common causes: hypovolemia, sepsis, cardiogenic shock, over-sedation, medication effect
  • Immediate treatment: IV fluid bolus 500 mL–1 L normal saline over 15 minutes; if MAP remains < 70, initiate vasopressor (norepinephrine 0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min, titrate to MAP 80–90). Notify cardiac surgery, cardiology, and critical care.
Dysphagia screening and aspiration prevention post-stroke Aspiration pneumonia is the most common post-stroke infection and a leading cause of post-stroke morbidity and mortality. Pre-oral-intake screening (mandatory):
  • Timing: before ANY oral intake — water, medications, food, even ice chips
  • Bedside screening protocol: (1) confirm patient is alert and able to follow commands; (2) assess for wet voice quality or drooling; (3) have patient perform a dry swallow and listen for quality; (4) palpate larynx to feel for swallow movement; (5) if screen passes, offer small trial sip (5 mL) of water and observe for cough, dysphonia, or aspiration signs
  • If screen fails or high-risk features: NPO, request formal speech pathology swallow evaluation; nasogastric tube for nutrition if prolonged NPO
  • Medications: crush tablets and dissolve in water ONLY after swallow confirmed safe; hold PO antiplatelets and anticoagulants until cleared by speech path or stroke team
  • Return to oral diet: only after written clearance by speech pathology or stroke neurology team
Head-of-bed (HOB) positioning: 0° vs. 30° — evidence review

Historical practice: flat (HOB 0°) was recommended to maximize cerebral perfusion pressure by gravity.

Current evidence (HeadPoST trial, 2017): Randomized controlled trial of early mobilization and HOB positioning in acute ischemic stroke found NO significant difference in functional outcomes at 90 days between HOB 0° and HOB 30°. Pressure ulcer risk was actually higher with flat positioning (Anderson et al., 2017).

Current practice: HOB 30° is standard unless specific hypoperfusion crisis (refractory hypotension, very low cardiac output). In those cases, HOB may be lowered transiently to 0°, but evidence does not support prolonged flat positioning.

Clinical action: Follow [Institution policy]. If institutional protocol specifies HOB position, adhere to it and communicate clearly with stroke neurology team.

NIHSS (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale) — bedside overview and application The NIHSS is a validated 15-item scale (score 0–42) that quantifies stroke severity and predicts outcomes. A score > 10 suggests large-territory stroke and increases thrombectomy candidacy. NIHSS domains assessed:
  1. Level of consciousness (0–3)
  2. Gaze / eye movement (0–2)
  3. Visual fields (0–3)
  4. Facial droop (0–3)
  5. Motor arm (0–4, tested separately for left and right)
  6. Motor leg (0–4, tested separately for left and right)
  7. Limb ataxia (0–2)
  8. Speech (0–3)
  9. Aphasia / language (0–3)
  10. Dysarthria (0–2)
  11. Extinction / inattention (0–2) At bedside (your role): Perform rapid screening for focal motor weakness, speech abnormality, visual asymmetry, and gaze deviation. Document findings with timestamps. Full formal NIHSS will be performed by stroke neurology or trained stroke team member. Clinical use: NIHSS ≥ 6 or NIHSS ≥ 10 is strongly associated with LVO on CTA; higher scores support earlier thrombectomy activation. Caveat in intubated/sedated patients: NIHSS cannot be reliably calculated in sedated or paralyzed patients. Document pre-intubation NIHSS if possible. Cross-link: See glossary card NIHSS Scoring for full scoring rules.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these signs in stable patients; if any appear, re-escalate to unstable pathway immediately.

  • Decreasing level of consciousness: GCS declining by ≥ 2 points, increasing somnolence, difficulty arousing → indicates cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation, or brainstem involvement
  • Anisocoria (unequal pupils): suggests ipsilateral mass effect or uncal herniation (uncal sign); STAT neurology + CT
  • Cushing response (triad of HTN + bradycardia + irregular respiration): classic sign of elevated intracranial pressure and impending herniation; requires STAT intervention
  • Expanding neuro deficit: progressive weakness, new speech difficulty, new vision loss, new ataxia → suggests infarct growth or hemorrhagic transformation
  • Deteriorating airway: stridor, change in voice quality, increased aspiration, difficulty handling secretions → plan intubation
  • New seizure activity: focal or generalized seizure; treat with lorazepam 2–4 mg IV; load antiepileptic; obtain EEG
  • Hemorrhagic transformation on repeat CT: blood within the infarction (common ~40% of patients, usually asymptomatic; symptomatic form is rare but catastrophic)
  • Uncontrolled hypertension: SBP > 220 mmHg despite labetalol/nicardipine; may indicate cerebral edema or herniation; escalate management and imaging
  • Fever: elevates intracranial pressure and worsens stroke outcomes; check for infection source (aspiration PNA, UTI, line infection); manage aggressively with antipyretics and source control
  • Hemodynamic instability: hypotension, tachycardia, low cardiac output; may be cardiogenic shock from underlying cardiac pathology (graft occlusion, mechanical complication); notify cardiac surgery + cardiology
  • Arrhythmia (new): new atrial fibrillation, sustained ventricular tachycardia; may trigger or worsen stroke; treat per ACLS + cardiology consult
  • Myocardial infarction signs: chest pain, ST changes on serial ECG; post-CABG graft may be occluded; notify cardiac surgery + cardiology

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Last-known-well (LKW) is the clock, NOT the time of deficit discovery. If a patient had breakfast at 6 a.m. (confirmed awake, normal mental status), then 2 hours later is found with hemiparesis, the LKW is 6 a.m., NOT the discovery time. This single data point can move the patient from outside into the tPA window or extend the thrombectomy window. Drill this into new staff: ask family, review chart, and ask yourself "when was patient last definitely normal?"

  2. Fingerstick glucose first — hypoglycemia is a stroke mimic. A glucose < 70 mg/dL must be corrected immediately with dextrose IV. Hypoglycemia resolves in seconds to minutes; true stroke does not. Always check glucose before attributing deficits to stroke.

  3. Do not reflexively lower blood pressure in acute ischemic stroke. The post-operative habit of strict HTN control must be consciously broken. Permissive HTN (up to 220/120) in non-tPA patients preserves penumbral perfusion. Aggressive BP lowering paradoxically expands the infarct by reducing collateral flow. Only lower BP if tPA/thrombectomy planned or if SBP persistently > 220 refractory to single agents.

  4. Recent sternotomy + systemic tPA = team decision, not reflexive. The stroke and cardiac surgery teams must jointly assess whether tPA bleeding risk is acceptable. Document this discussion. Mechanical thrombectomy is usually the preferred pathway in post-operative patients with LVO.

  5. Mechanical thrombectomy is the preferred pathway in post-operative large-vessel occlusion. It avoids systemic fibrinolysis, achieves 80–90% recanalization rates (vs. 40–50% for tPA alone), and is feasible up to 24 hours with favorable perfusion imaging. Do not assume tPA is the default; activate endovascular team STAT if LVO on CTA.

  6. Dysphagia screen before ANYTHING oral — including medications and water. This is non-negotiable. Aspiration is the #1 post-stroke infection and leading cause of post-stroke morbidity. Even one sip of water without clearance can seed aspiration pneumonia. Hold oral medications until screen is passed.

  7. New atrial fibrillation (POAF) in post-op patient + anticoagulation for 5 days does NOT rule out stroke. POAF is common (30% post-CABG); AC therapy is incomplete initially. Stroke can still occur despite AC therapy (inadequate intensity, valve thrombus, atrial appendage clot). Do not be falsely reassured by AC status. High index of suspicion for embolic mechanism.

  8. A "confused" patient without focal motor or speech findings is delirium until proven otherwise. Confusion alone is not stroke. Look for BEFAST deficits: focal weakness, speech slurring, visual asymmetry, gaze deviation, or balance loss. If neuro exam is entirely normal, the problem is likely delirium (sepsis, medication, hypoxia, anesthesia residual), not acute stroke. NIHSS in a purely confused patient may be very low.

  9. Type A aortic dissection can present as acute stroke. Patient may have arm weakness, aphasia, but the real problem is dissection. Red flags: are both arm BPs equal? Are radial pulses intact or asymmetric? Is there back pain? Mediastinal widening on chest X-ray? If dissection is suspected, tPA + thrombectomy = catastrophic bleeding into false lumen. Obtain CT angiography of the aorta if dissection is even remotely suspected.

  10. Mechanical valve thrombosis is a surgical emergency, not a stroke. A prosthetic-valve patient presenting with acute stroke may have a clotted valve, not a cerebral embolus. Imaging will show both. Valve thrombosis requires emergency surgery (valve replacement or thrombus removal), not tPA. Notify cardiac surgery immediately.

  11. Post-carotid endarterectomy (CEA) patients have a different stroke pathway. Recent CEA is a special case. Reperfusion injury is a real risk; blood pressure targets may differ from standard ischemic stroke. Ensure stroke team and vascular surgery communicate. Thrombectomy may be contraindicated if dissection risk is high.

  12. Intubation worsens the neuro exam — complete NIHSS before RSI if possible. If possible, perform the full NIHSS assessment and detailed neuro exam BEFORE rapid sequence intubation (RSI). Once intubated and sedated, you cannot assess language, motor cooperation, or certain cranial nerves. Sedation depth and paralysis will confound all future neuro exams for 24+ hours.

  13. Hypotension is a disaster in acute stroke — treat aggressively. Do not accept SBP < 90. Low MAP worsens ischemia and expands infarct core. Bolus IV fluids (500 mL–1 L) and initiate vasopressor support (norepinephrine); target MAP 80–90. Notify critical care and cardiac surgery. Document the cause (hypovolemia, sepsis, cardiogenic shock, medication) and address it.

  14. Document time with every single neuro exam. Stroke teams reconstruct the timeline of neurologic events from your serial exams. Write: "10:30 a.m. — alert, NIHSS ~8, right arm strength 3/5, speech fluent, eyes conjugate." Then "10:45 a.m. — drowsy, NIHSS ~10, right arm strength 2/5, expressive deficit noted, right pupil 4 mm vs. left 3 mm, brisk." Precise timestamps and serial comparisons guide stroke team decisions about intervention.

  15. Stroke mimics in post-op setting: hypoglycemia, post-ictal state, toxic/metabolic encephalopathy, ICU delirium, medication effect. Always obtain glucose, basic labs (electrolytes, renal function, liver function, toxicology screen if indicated), and EEG if seizure suspected. Post-operative anesthesia residual, opioid effect, benzodiazepine accumulation, or sepsis can all present as altered mental status or apparent focal deficit.

  16. Establishing LKW in sedated or intubated patient — documentation is critical. If the patient was sedated pre-operatively or post-intubation, review the chart meticulously for the last documented time patient was awake, alert, and neurologically intact (e.g., pre-op baseline assessment, last neuro check before extubation). If LKW is truly unknown, document "time unknown" and note why (sedated throughout, family unavailable). This uncertainty may exclude tPA eligibility but does not exclude thrombectomy with perfusion imaging.

  17. Neck vessel injury from prior cannulation — rare but catastrophic. Post-operative neck dissection or significant cannulation-site hematoma can injure the carotid or vertebral artery, leading to thrombosis or dissection-related stroke. Check for unilateral neck swelling, asymmetric carotid pulses, or Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis). If suspected, obtain CTA or neck ultrasound. Vascular surgery may be needed.

cards.title: Acute Type B Aortic Dissection — Medical Management
cards.quickAnswer: Acute Type B dissection (tear distal to left subclavian artery) = uncomplicated if no malperfusion, rupture, or refractory pain. Medical management first: strict impulse control (HR ≤60, SBP 100–120, IV β-blocker → vasodilator), IV access ×2, arterial line, serial neuro + peripheral pulses q shift, serial imaging at 48–72h. Complicated Type B (malperfusion/expansion/refractory pain/HTN) → TEVAR (endovascular). Uncomplicated bridge to chronic with imaging surveillance; consider pre-emptive TEVAR per INSTEAD-XL for durability. 90-day mortality 10–20% uncomplicated, higher for complicated. Length of stay 5–10 days initially; SBAR who-to-call: vascular surgery for TEVAR, ICU for acute complications, IR for branch interventions.

Uncomplicated bridge to chronic with imaging surveillance; consider pre-emptive TEVAR per INSTEAD-XL for durability.

90-day mortality 10–20% uncomplicated, higher for complicated. Length of stay 5–10 days initially; SBAR who-to-call: vascular surgery for TEVAR, ICU for acute complications, IR for branch interventions.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → 2022 AHA/ACC Aortic Disease Guideline (Isselbacher et al.) → Nienaber et al. INSTEAD-XL trial → IRAD Registry → Hardin & Kaplow → Bojar 6e → Springer 2025

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition and epidemiology.

  • Definition: Tear in the intimal layer of the descending thoracic aorta (distal to left subclavian artery origin); false lumen may be patent or partially thrombosed.
  • Classification: Stanford Type B (distal to left subclavian) vs Type A (ascending aorta involvement — see related Acute Aortic Dissection diagnosis card). DeBakey Type III.
  • Incidence: ~3–5 per 100,000 per year; Type B represents 35–40% of acute aortic dissection cases. Peak age 60–75 years (hypertension) or 30–50 years (genetic aortopathy: Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid aortic valve).
  • Uncomplicated vs Complicated: uncomplicated = no organ malperfusion, no rupture, pain/BP controlled on medical therapy. Complicated = malperfusion (spinal, renal, mesenteric, limb), expanding diameter, rapid progression, refractory symptoms → surgical/endovascular intervention candidate.
  • Who this applies to: all post-acute Type B admissions expected for ≥5 days of hemodynamic stabilization and imaging surveillance. Transition to discharge planning by POD 5–7.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Type B dissection occurs when blood enters the medial layer of the aorta through an intimal tear, creating a false channel alongside the true lumen. The initial tear is typically longitudinal in the descending thoracic aorta. Hemodynamic forces (dP/dt — rate of pressure change) and elevated blood pressure propagate the dissection; conversely, reducing dP/dt through beta-blockade slows or halts progression and allows the intimal tear to scar (Isselbacher et al., 2022).

Why impulse control matters:

  • Beta-blockers first reduce contractility (dP/dt) and heart rate, slowing aortic wall stress
  • Vasodilators second maintain organ perfusion while further reducing pressure
  • Never vasodilator-first — unopposed alpha antagonism causes reflex tachycardia, which accelerates aortic wall stress and dissection propagation
  • MAP ≥85 required for spinal cord perfusion; inadvertent hypotension risks paraplegia

False lumen perfusion states:

  • Patent false lumen — continues perfusing (high risk for expansion and rupture if large; some advocate pre-emptive TEVAR)
  • Partially thrombosed — mixed risks (thrombus may embolize; re-entry tears create hemodynamic instability)
  • Thrombosed — lower rupture risk, but aortic diameter and false lumen extent still guide long-term surveillance

Risk factors for progression to complicated disease:

  • Aortic diameter >50 mm (rupture risk)
  • Distal ulcer-like projection (intimal tear in false lumen wall)
  • Rapid expansion (>5 mm/week)
  • Branch vessel involvement (celiac, SMA, renal, iliac arteries)
  • Partial false lumen thrombosis with hemodynamic re-entry (causes pressure swings)
  • Refractory pain or hypertension despite maximum medical therapy

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at admission.

Presentation:

  • Acute onset tearing or ripping chest, back, or abdominal pain (classic but not universal)
  • Hypertensive urgency/emergency: SBP often 140–180+ mmHg initially
  • Hemodynamically variable: some patients appear stable; others show signs of malperfusion or hemorrhage (hypotension, altered mental status, lower extremity weakness, oliguria, mesenteric ischemia)
  • Imaging confirmation: CTA or MRA chest showing intimal flap, true vs false lumen, extent of dissection, branch vessel involvement, aortic diameter
  • Admission from: ED after CTA/TEE workup; transferred from outside hospital post-diagnosis; occasionally direct admission if pre-hospital diagnosis made

At-risk populations: longstanding uncontrolled hypertension (most common); genetic aortopathy syndromes (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular EDS, bicuspid AV); cocaine use (sympathomimetic surge); pregnancy (Marfan at highest risk); iatrogenic (arterial catheterization complication — catheter-induced dissection).

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: 2 minutes at bedside. Competent systematic exam.

Vital signs & hemodynamics:

  • BP both arms (differential >20 mmHg = branch vessel involvement)
  • HR, MAP, respiratory rate, SpO₂, mental status
  • Trend since arrival; ongoing escalation or stabilization?

Neurologic exam (critical — paraplegia / stroke risk):

  • Lower extremities: bilateral leg strength (proximal hip flexion/extension, knee extension/flexion, ankle dorsi/plantarflexion), sensation to light touch and pinprick, patellar and Achilles reflexes
  • Upper extremities: grip strength, shoulder abduction, arm movement; unilateral weakness suggests stroke
  • Cranial nerves: pupils size/reactivity, visual fields, facial symmetry
  • Baseline mental status: orientation, attention, ability to follow commands

Pulse exam (asymmetry suggests branch involvement):

  • Bilateral radial, femoral, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial pulses; grade 0–4
  • Any new pulse deficit since baseline → escalate for possible limb malperfusion

Cardiac auscultation:

  • Regular vs irregular rhythm; new murmur (aortic regurgitation if arch involvement)
  • S1/S2 present; pericardial rub (pericarditis if dissection extends near pericardium)

Abdominal exam:

  • Baseline tenderness, rebound/guarding (mesenteric ischemia if pain out of proportion)
  • Bowel sounds present
  • Palpable aorta (rarely; do not aggressively palpate in acute dissection)

Peripheral perfusion & pain:

  • Bilateral extremity warmth, color, capillary refill
  • Presence/absence of pain; location and character (tearing vs dull)
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr, lactate (trending up = malperfusion), troponin (cardiac involvement?), CBC (Hgb baseline if bleeding concern)

Lines & access:

  • Current IV access adequate (two large-bore 18G+ lines needed; central line preferred for ICU phase)
  • Arterial line placement planned or present?
  • Foley for urine output monitoring (oliguria = renal malperfusion)

sections.heading: 5A. Medical-First Approach (Uncomplicated Type B)
sections.bodyHtml:
Immediate actions (POD 0–1: ICU or high-acuity monitored bed):

  1. Establish IV access:

    • Two large-bore peripheral IVs (18G+) or one central line (right internal jugular preferred)
    • Arterial line (radial preferred) for continuous BP monitoring and blood draws
    • Foley catheter for strict urine output tracking (goal ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; oliguria = renal malperfusion)

  2. Monitoring setup:

    • Continuous cardiac monitor, pulse oximetry, BP q5–15 min initially (goal HR ≤60, SBP 100–120)
    • Neuro checks q2h (lower extremity strength baseline critical)
    • Pulse exam baseline (bilateral radial, femoral)

  3. Impulse Control Protocol — Beta-blocker FIRST:

Step Target Agent Dose
Step 1: HR ≤60 Reduce dP/dt Labetalol IV 10–20 mg bolus q10 min; or esmolol loading 500 mcg/kg/min × 1 min, then infusion 50–300 mcg/kg/min titrated to HR
Step 2: Reassess BP If SBP >120 Nicardipine IV 5–15 mg/h, titrate q5–15 min by 2.5 mg/h increments
Step 2b: If SBP 100–120 Monitor only None Hold vasodilator; titrate beta-blocker only
Step 2c: If SBP <100 or MAP <85 HOLD vasodilator IV fluids or low-dose pressors Call team; maintain MAP ≥85 for spinal cord perfusion

CRITICAL: Never give vasodilator before beta-blocker achieved — reflex tachycardia widens dissection.

  1. Pain management:

    • Morphine 4–8 mg IV or fentanyl 50–100 mcg IV q1–2h PRN
    • Opioids well-tolerated if BP controlled; pain → sympathetic surge → dissection propagation
    • Goal pain 0–3/10

  2. Initial labs (stat):

    • CBC, CMP, lactate, troponin, PT/INR/PTT, type & screen
    • Baseline troponin important (cardiac involvement → consider Type A re-evaluation)

  3. NPO initial (advance to clear liquids POD 1 if stable)

Days 2–3 (Acute stabilization):

  1. Continue IV impulse control:

    • Titrate labetalol/esmolol + nicardipine to targets: HR 55–60, SBP 100–120, MAP ≥85
    • Check BP q2h; document HR, SBP, MAP, dP/dt estimate
    • Daily labs: CBC, CMP, lactate (trending up = malperfusion indicator)

  2. Surveillance imaging (48–72 hours):

    • CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (or MRA if renal insufficiency)
    • Assess: dissection morphology, aortic diameter at dissection level and mid-descending, false lumen perfusion state, branch vessel patency, pericardial effusion, any new malperfusion
    • Key measurements for TEVAR decision: aortic diameter, length of dissection, celiac/SMA/renal involvement
    • If adverse features identified (see Section 5B criteria) → early discussion with vascular surgery re: TEVAR timing

  3. Transition to PO antihypertensives (if hemodynamically stable):

    • Labetalol PO 200–400 mg BID/TID, titrate q2–3 days
    • Amlodipine 5–10 mg daily (vasodilation)
    • Lisinopril (or equivalent ACE-I) 5–20 mg daily (renal protection, afterload reduction)
    • Discontinue IV agents once PO regimen established and goals sustained ≥4–6 hours

  4. Bowel regimen:

    • Docusate 100 mg BID + MiraLAX 17 g daily (prevent straining/Valsalva)
    • Goal: soft stool q1–2 days without straining; avoid enemas/suppositories

  5. Activity:

    • Bed rest Days 1–2; strict bedside commode only
    • POD 2–3: bed-to-chair with assistance if stable
    • No lifting, bending, strenuous activity

Days 4–10 (Convalescence on telemetry/stepdown):

  1. Continue PO impulse control:

    • Daily BP log (morning and evening SBP/DBP/HR with calibrated cuff)
    • Target: SBP 100–130, HR 60–80
    • Adjust labetalol, amlodipine, lisinopril; some patients need hydralazine 25–50 mg BID–TID if SBP remains 130–140s (always with beta-blocker + vasodilator to prevent reflex tachycardia)
    • Avoid NSAIDs (dissection risk), pseudoephedrine (sympathomimetic), excessive caffeine/salt

  2. Repeat imaging before discharge (Day 5–7):

    • Follow-up CTA/MRA to confirm stable dissection, no interval expansion, no new malperfusion
    • Some centers obtain discharge baseline for future surveillance (1 mo, 6 mo, 1 yr, annually)

  3. Discharge preparation:

    • Finalize PO regimen; patient teaches back medications by name, dose, frequency
    • Home BP monitoring: patient demonstrates home cuff use; logs readings daily ×1 week pre-discharge, then per cardiothoracic clinic
    • Diet: DASH diet, sodium <2 g/day, fluid restriction if hypertensive
    • Activity: gradual ambulation, no lifting >20 lbs ×6 weeks, no strenuous exercise ×8 weeks
    • Red flag symptoms: severe tearing chest/back/abdominal pain (rupture/re-dissection), new lower extremity weakness (spinal ischemia), syncope, diplopia/visual loss (stroke), focal neuro deficit → call 911
    • Arrange: CT surgery follow-up 1–2 weeks (imaging review, TEVAR discussion if indicated), primary care within 1 week

sections.heading: 5B. Complicated Type B Dissection — TEVAR Indication
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition of complicated:

Feature Indication Level
Malperfusion syndromes TEVAR emergent
Spinal cord (paraplegia, sensory level deficit) TEVAR + CSF drain
Renal artery (acute oliguria, rising Cr, elevated lactate, rhabdo) TEVAR or medical bridge per anatomy
Mesenteric (pain out of proportion, acidosis, lactate, elevated WBC) TEVAR + possible bowel resection
Limb (acute leg pain, pallor, weak/absent pulse, cool extremity) TEVAR or thrombectomy
Aortic rupture Hemodynamics: hypotension, acute pericardial effusion with tamponade physiology (JVD, muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxus), acute mental status change
Rapid expansion >5 mm aortic diameter growth per week on imaging
Aortic diameter >50 mm Rupture risk (especially with patent false lumen)
Distal ulcer-like projection Intimal tear in false lumen wall; risk of rupture, re-dissection
Partial false lumen thrombosis with hemodynamic instability Re-entry tears; BP swings; rhythm instability
Refractory pain or hypertension Maximum IV agents (labetalol + nicardipine) inadequate; persistent pain despite opioids

Immediate actions if complicated features identified:

  1. STAT escalation:

    • Call vascular surgery and ICU team immediately (not routine consult)
    • Notify cardiothoracic surgery fellow/attending

  2. Imaging & diagnostics:

    • STAT CTA or TEE if not already done; assess for malperfusion, rupture, impending rupture (pericardial effusion enlargement)
    • Labs: lactate (malperfusion marker), troponin (myocardial involvement), CBC, CMP, urinalysis (myoglobin if dark urine = rhabdo)
    • If malperfusion syndrome suspected: ECG + troponin serial (cardiac involvement), ABG (acidosis), renal function (Cr, BUN), mesenteric ultrasound or CT if bowel ischemia concern

  3. Maximize medical therapy while arranging TEVAR:

    • Push IV beta-blocker + vasodilator to absolute targets (some patients tolerate HR 50–55, SBP 90–110 if no organ ischemia)
    • Aggressive pain control (don't let pain → sympathetic surge worsen dissection)
    • If hypotensive: consider pressors (maintain MAP ≥85 for organ perfusion) rather than vasodilators

  4. TEVAR logistics:

    • Vascular surgery determines TEVAR vs open repair candidacy
    • Spinal cord malperfusion: TEVAR + CSF drain + neuromonitoring (see §7 Teaching Layers — CSF drain protocol)
    • Branch vessel involvement (renal, celiac, SMA): fenestrated or branched grafts may be needed; refer to specialized TEVAR team
    • Limb malperfusion: TEVAR proximal control + possible thrombectomy, embolectomy, or limb revascularization
    • Mesenteric ischemia: TEVAR + possible bowel resection if necrotic

  5. ICU transfer if not already:

    • Continuous hemodynamic monitoring, neuro checks, urine output, lactate trends
    • Prepare for intubation if deteriorating or going to OR

sections.heading: 5C. Uncomplicated Type B Bridge to Chronic Phase
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition of uncomplicated: No malperfusion, no rupture, pain/BP controlled, aortic diameter <50 mm or stable, false lumen thrombosing.

Medical management strategy (14+ days post-admission into chronic phase):

  1. Transition to long-term PO antihypertensives:

    • Labetalol 200–400 mg BID–TID (first-line; titrate to HR 60–80, SBP 100–130)
    • Amlodipine 5–10 mg daily (dihydropyridine; safe in HF, renal disease)
    • Lisinopril 10–20 mg daily (ACE-I; renal protection, particularly if diabetes or kidney disease; check K⁺ and Cr)
    • Add hydralazine 25–50 mg BID–TID if SBP remains 130–140s (never monotherapy; prevents reflex tachycardia)
    • Goal: SBP 100–130, HR 60–80 (some experts advocate SBP ≤120 as ideal long-term, but 100–130 is practical for most)

  2. Imaging surveillance schedule (per Isselbacher guideline):

    • Month 1: CTA/MRA (assess false lumen thrombosis, aortic diameter trend, branch patency)
    • Month 6: CTA/MRA
    • Month 12: CTA/MRA
    • Year 2+: CTA/MRA yearly or q18 months depending on stability (if stable diameter and false lumen thrombosed, may extend to q2–3 years)
    • At each imaging: measure aortic diameter at dissection level and mid-descending; assess false lumen perfusion/thrombosis; check branch vessel patency; look for enlargement of pericardial effusion

  3. TEVAR decision at chronic phase:

    • INSTEAD-XL trial (Nienaber et al., 2013) showed that even in initially "uncomplicated" Type B, pre-emptive TEVAR improved aortic outcomes (reduced false lumen expansion and aortic diameter growth at 2 years) compared to medical therapy alone
    • Shared decision-making: discuss with patient and surgeon:

    • Pros of TEVAR: prevents false lumen expansion, reduces late rupture risk, shortens aortic remodeling time, may improve long-term durability
    • Cons of TEVAR: procedural risk (spinal cord ischemia ~2%, paraplegia 0.3–1% depending on graft length), need for CSF drain, branch vessel coverage considerations, need for long-term endoleak surveillance
    • Consider age: younger patients with long life expectancy may benefit more from early TEVAR (prevents aortic diameter growth over decades); elderly patients with comorbidities may prefer conservative medical management if truly stable
    • Thresholds for offering TEVAR: aortic diameter approaching 50 mm, rapid expansion trend, distal ulcer-like projection, persistent patent false lumen, patient preference for intervention

  4. Lifestyle & prevention:

    • Medication adherence lifesaving — every missed dose risks re-dissection
    • Avoid: heavy lifting >20 lbs, Valsalva/straining, strenuous isometric exercise, heated yoga, saunas (heat → vasodilation)
    • Avoid substances: cocaine, pseudoephedrine, NSAIDs, anabolic steroids
    • Stress management: meditation, relaxation techniques
    • DASH diet, sodium <2 g/day, adequate protein for vascular healing
    • Sleep apnea screening (HTN contributor); treat if present

  5. Genetic counseling if aortopathy suspected:

    • Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz, vascular EDS, bicuspid AV with aortopathy → genetic counseling, family screening
    • First-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) need imaging to screen for aneurysm/dissection
    • Aortic diameter >50 mm in family: imaging surveillance, possible prophylactic surgery

  6. Pregnancy counseling (if applicable):

    • Do NOT get pregnant with untreated dissection; pregnancy 10× increases dissection risk
    • If Type B stable on medical management and aortic diameter <50 mm: pregnancy may be considered with close cardiothoracic monitoring (expert opinion)
    • Ideally repair (TEVAR) or stabilize before pregnancy planning

sections.heading: 5D. Chronic Phase Transition (≥14 days)
sections.bodyHtml:
Surveillance & transition to outpatient care:

  • ICU or telemetry transfer criteria: HR stable 60–80, SBP stable 100–130 on PO agents, pain well-controlled, neuro exam stable, no ongoing malperfusion concerns
  • Stepdown/floor criteria: no acute complications, hemodynamics stable ≥24 hours, tolerating PO intake, self-care capable
  • Discharge planning: completed by POD 7–10; patient educated on medications, home BP monitoring, red flag symptoms, follow-up imaging
  • Outpatient vascular surgery follow-up: 1–2 weeks (imaging review, TEVAR discussion if features warrant)
  • Primary care follow-up: within 1 week (HTN management, medication refills, lifestyle counseling)
  • Long-term surveillance: CTA/MRA imaging per protocol (1 mo, 6 mo, 1 yr, annually); vascular surgery clinic annually or per surgeon preference
  • Patient education: understand aortic dissection as chronic disease requiring lifelong medication adherence, imaging surveillance, activity modification

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p acute Type B aortic dissection admission for medical management." B: "Patient has been on IV impulse control (labetalol + nicardipine) targeting HR ≤60, SBP 100–120. Current vital signs: HR [rate], BP [SBP/DBP], MAP [value], SpO₂ [value]." A: "Patient [is stable / is deteriorating]. [Describe acute change: new pain, new weakness, oliguria, lactate elevation, imaging findings, etc.]. Current K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value], Cr [value], lactate [value]." R: "Requesting [escalation to ICU / TEVAR evaluation / increased antihypertensive management / urgent imaging / neurology consult]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable uncomplicated Type B, routine management Primary team (APP/resident)
New malperfusion signs (spinal weakness, oliguria, mesenteric pain) Vascular surgery (emergent); ICU team if not already
Uncontrolled hypertension despite IV agents Vascular surgery + cardiology (IR may assist); possible transfer to ICU
Rupture signs (acute pain, hemodynamic instability, pericardial effusion with tamponade) STAT vascular surgery + ICU code team; prepare for operating room
Imaging findings suggesting TEVAR (adverse features, expansion, large diameter) Vascular surgery (non-emergent consult for chronic phase discussion; urgent if complicated)
Renal failure or dark urine (myoglobinuria) Vascular surgery (consider TEVAR for renal protection); nephrology if AKI
New focal neurologic deficit (stroke, spinal cord ischemia) Stroke code (neurology) + vascular surgery; CT surgery notified

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(expandable in app — novice/advanced beginner deep-dive)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology: False lumen hemodynamics and thrombosis The false lumen is the newly created space between the separated intimal and medial layers. Its perfusion state determines prognosis:
  1. Patent false lumen (blood actively flowing in and out through re-entry tears) → continues to expand; highest rupture risk; INSTEAD-XL trial rationale for early TEVAR (exclude proximal entry tear, induce false lumen thrombosis)
  2. Partially thrombosed (some areas clotted, some still perfused) → unstable; re-entry tears can cause pressure swings and hemodynamic instability; risk of thrombus embolization to branch vessels
  3. Thrombosed (fully clotted over time) → remodeling phase; aortic diameter may still expand (Windkessel effect from residual false lumen size), or may shrink if false lumen obliterates; surveillance imaging tracks this trajectory Goal of medical management + potential TEVAR: induce false lumen thrombosis by lowering aortic wall stress (impulse control) and/or by excluding the proximal entry tear (TEVAR). Once false lumen is thrombosed, rupture risk drops dramatically, but aortic diameter still requires monitoring (can re-enlarge decades later → chronic TAAA).
INSTEAD-XL trial: rationale for pre-emptive TEVAR in uncomplicated Type B The Investigation of STEnt grafts in Aortic Dissection with long-term follow-up (INSTEAD-XL) trial randomized 476 uncomplicated acute Type B patients to:
  • Medical group: optimal medical therapy (beta-blockers, vasodilators, antihypertensives)
  • TEVAR group: TEVAR + identical medical therapy Primary endpoint at 2 years: aortic remodeling (false lumen expansion, aortic diameter growth, re-entry tears, branch compromise). Results:
    • TEVAR group had significantly less aortic diameter growth at 2 years (mean +2.4 mm vs +6.2 mm medical-only)
    • TEVAR group had improved false lumen thrombosis and aortic remodeling
    • Mortality and morbidity similar between groups at 2–5 years (TEVAR has ~2% spinal cord ischemia risk, paraplegia ~0.3–1%)
    • TEVAR group had fewer aortic-related deaths at long-term follow-up (>5 years)
    • Conclusion: TEVAR in uncomplicated Type B prevents aortic expansion, reduces long-term rupture risk, and should be considered even in initially stable patients, especially younger patients with long life expectancy Clinical implication for v2.3 card: shared decision-making at chronic phase (2–4 weeks post-admission) should include INSTEAD-XL discussion. Factors favoring TEVAR: age <70, large aortic diameter (>48 mm), patient preference for intervention. Factors favoring continued medical management: age >75, multiple comorbidities, patient choice for conservative approach, true stability with thrombosed false lumen.
Spinal cord protection during TEVAR: CSF drain protocol cross-link Spinal cord ischemia (SCI) is the most feared TEVAR complication. Incidence ~2% of TEVAR in aortic dissection, with paraplegia (complete or near-complete lower extremity paralysis) in ~0.3–1%. Mechanism: TEVAR grafts that cover the thoracic aorta reduce blood flow to the artery of Adamkiewicz (typically T9–L2 level), which supplies the anterior spinal cord. Additionally, dissection itself may compromise spinal arteries if the false lumen expands into segmental artery ostia. SCI prevention strategies (see related CSF Drain protocol card):
  1. CSF drainage — catheter placed in lumbar spine pre-op or intra-op; CSF can be withdrawn to increase spinal perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP – CSF pressure). Goal: maintain MAP ≥85 mmHg post-op and consider draining 10–15 mL CSF q4–6h if MAP <85.
  2. Intercostal artery reimplantation — surgical graft branches to cover and revascularize segmental arteries at T9–L2
  3. Staged TEVAR — if extended coverage needed (>20 cm), split procedure into 2 stages (days to weeks apart) to allow collateral circulation to develop
  4. High MAP targets post-op — maintain MAP ≥90 mmHg (versus standard post-op MAP 65–80) for 24–72 hours post-TEVAR to maximize spinal cord perfusion while CSF drain in place
  5. Monitoring: continuous lower extremity neuro checks (strength, sensation, reflexes) for 5–7 days post-op; spinal cord ischemia can declare 12–72 hours post-op or even later For uncomplicated Type B with spinal cord compromise: TEVAR becomes emergent, CSF drain is standard of care, and patient should be transferred to center with TEVAR + neuro-monitoring capability.
TEVAR delivery systems and device selection TEVAR grafts used for Type B dissection:
  1. Standard thoracic stent-grafts (e.g., Medtronic Thoracic, Cook TX2, Gore C-TAG)
    • Entry tear coverage: proximal landing zone covers primary intimal tear
    • Branch preservation: device designed to land above celiac artery (preserves aortic branch vessels)
    • False lumen exclusion: excludes proximal false lumen from systemic circulation; induces thrombosis
    • Fenestrated stent-grafts (e.g., custom-made fenestrated TX, Fenestrated Relay, Gore Thoracic + Aortic)
    • Indications: dissection extends into celiac, superior mesenteric, or renal artery origins; standard device would occlude these vessels
    • Design: small holes (fenestrations) cut into the graft to allow branch vessel cannulation with bridging stents
    • Risk: complex; requires expert TEVAR team and specialized imaging
    • Branched grafts (thoracoabdominal application)
    • Indications: dissection involves both descending thoracic AND abdominal aorta (thoracoabdominal aortic dissection — see related card)
    • Design: graft body + integral branches for visceral vessels (celiac, SMA) and renal arteries
    • Deployment: requires specialized technique; referral to centers with TAAA expertise
    • Endovascular aortic repair (EVAR) principles in Type B:
      • Proximal landing zone: ideally 2 cm above primary entry tear; if tear is very proximal (near left subclavian), coverage of left subclavian may be needed with carotid-subclavian bypass (see pitfall §9)
      • Distal landing zone: 2 cm into true lumen below re-entry tear(s)
      • Access: typically femoral artery (percutaneous or open); occasional iliac access if femoral stenotic Device-specific considerations: Always verify with vascular surgery and interventional radiology that selected graft landing zones avoid visceral/renal branches unless fenestrated/branched option indicated.
Genetic syndromes presenting as acute Type B dissection Marfan syndrome (FBN1 mutation):
  • Connective tissue dysplasia → medial degeneration → aortic root/ascending dilation; Type B dissection less common than Type A but occurs (especially if untreated)
  • Diagnosis: family history, lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), high arched palate, arachnodactyly, skin striae; genetic testing
  • Management: beta-blockers (or ARBs) from diagnosis; prophylactic aortic root surgery if root diameter >55 mm (or >50 mm if family history of dissection); Type B → medical management + imaging surveillance; consider TEVAR if diameter risk factors present
  • Pregnancy: 10× dissection risk; advise against pregnancy until Type B stabilized/repaired Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1/TGFBR2 mutations):
  • More aggressive aortic disease than Marfan; aneurysm rupture can occur at smaller aortic diameters (45–50 mm)
  • Presentation: can present as dissection (Type A more common, but Type B occurs)
  • Diagnosis: hypertelorism, bifid uvula, small mouth, skin striae, vascular tortuosity, family history
  • Management: prophylactic root surgery if diameter >50 mm (lower threshold than Marfan); Type B dissection warrants aggressive TEVAR consideration Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1 mutations):
  • Rare but severe: spontaneous arterial rupture, aortic dissection at young age, poor surgical outcomes
  • Diagnosis: family history of sudden death, thin translucent skin, easy bruising, poor wound healing
  • Management: Type B dissection in vEDS is high-risk; medical management alone often unsatisfactory; TEVAR feasibility limited (fragile tissue); multidisciplinary team essential; discuss prognosis carefully Bicuspid aortic valve + aortopathy:
  • Incidence: ~2% of general population; ~50% develop aortic root/ascending dilation
  • Presentation: can present with Type A dissection (more common); Type B dissection less typical but occurs if dissection propagates distally
  • Management: imaging surveillance of aortic root; prophylactic root surgery if root diameter >55 mm; Type B managed per standard protocol Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1):
  • Vascular dysplasia → early-onset dissection (often <40 years)
  • Diagnosis: neurofibromas, café-au-lait spots, optic nerve gliomas
  • Management: Type B → standard medical approach + early TEVAR consideration Screening recommendation: All acute Type B patients <50 years, or with family history of dissection/sudden cardiac death, or with clinical stigmata (tall stature, lens dislocation, skin striae, hypertelorism) should undergo genetic counseling and testing (Marfan/Loeys-Dietz/EDS panel) and family imaging screening (first-degree relatives need aortic imaging).
Aorto-esophageal fistula: late dissection complication Definition: Erosion of the aortic wall through the esophageal wall, creating a pathologic communication between the two structures. Incidence: ~0.04% of aortic dissections; usually occurs weeks to months after dissection (not acute), but can occur with chronic untreated dissection or post-TEVAR from graft migration/erosion. Mechanism: expanding dissection or false lumen erodes through aortic wall into adjacent esophagus; can also occur post-TEVAR if graft erodes through aortic wall (rare but catastrophic). Presentation (classic triad, but variably present):
  1. Sudden massive hematemesis (vomiting blood)
  2. Chest pain (thoracic dissection or graft erosion)
  3. Sepsis/fever (bacterial translocation from esophagus) Diagnosis:
    • CT angiography with oral contrast may show air track between aorta and esophagus, or abnormal enhancement
    • Esophagoscopy (if patient stable and suspected) — may see blood, esophageal defect, aortic pulsation visible through defect
    • Often diagnosed at autopsy or after rapid exsanguination if untreated Management:
    • STAT general surgery + vascular surgery — usually requires both esophageal and aortic repair
    • Antibiotics (cover oral flora)
    • NPO + NG tube (reduce oral flora transit to esophagus)
    • Surgical approach: esophageal repair + aortic reconstruction or TEVAR; some cases unsalvageable if massive bleeding
    • Mortality high (50–100% historically; improved with rapid diagnosis and treatment) Prevention: long-term imaging surveillance of Type B dissection (especially those not receiving TEVAR); if dissection expands toward esophagus on imaging, discuss TEVAR to stabilize aortic wall and reduce erosion risk. Clinical note for v2.3 card: aorto-esophageal fistula is a rare but catastrophic late complication. Educate patients on red flag symptoms (sudden vomiting blood, severe chest pain, fever) and recommend they seek immediate care. Long-term follow-up imaging helps detect aortic wall erosion trends.
Chronic Type B → degenerative thoracoabdominal aneurysm (TAAA) Natural history of Type B dissection (20–30 year follow-up): Some patients with initially "stable" uncomplicated Type B dissection develop progressive aortic dilation over years/decades, eventually forming a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm (TAAA) involving descending thoracic, thoracoabdominal, and/or abdominal aorta. Mechanism:
  • False lumen thrombosis but size persistence: even if false lumen thromboses, the aortic diameter may not shrink back to normal; "scar" tissue and residual false lumen space maintain enlarged diameter
  • Windkessel effect: aortic wall stiffness + residual false lumen compliance cause paradoxical dilation over time (years/decades)
  • Medial degeneration: the initial dissection event causes irreversible medial disruption; subsequent dilation continues even after acute phase
  • Inadequate medical management: suboptimal blood pressure control, medication non-adherence, or underlying genetic aortopathy (undiagnosed Marfan, Loeys-Dietz) accelerates progression Imaging findings over time:
  • Year 1–2: aortic diameter may stabilize or even decrease slightly (false lumen thrombosis)
  • Year 5–10: gradual diameter growth resumes (median 0.3–0.5 mm/year, highly variable)
  • Year 15–30: some patients develop TAAA with aortic diameter >55 mm, especially if untreated or suboptimally treated Clinical impact:
  • Reinforces importance of lifelong imaging surveillance (yearly or every other year, not just first 1–2 years)
  • Supports INSTEAD-XL rationale: TEVAR early (prevents immediate expansion, thromboses false lumen) may reduce late TAAA development
  • Supports strict lifelong BP control (slows late expansion)
  • Explains why genetic counseling and screening is essential (underlying syndrome increases TAAA risk) Management if chronic TAAA develops:
  • TAAA surgery or endovascular approach (see related Aortic Descending/TAAA card)
  • If prior TEVAR performed: may need extended endovascular graft or branched graft to cover expanded aorta
  • Spinal cord ischemia risk high if TAAA extends into thoracoabdominal zone; CSF drain + intercostal reimplantation standard for open TAAA Patient education: Type B dissection is a chronic disease with lifelong imaging needs; short-term (1–2 year) imaging stability is reassuring but does not eliminate long-term rupture risk. Compliance with medications, follow-up, and imaging is lifesaving.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these in stable Type B patients; if any occur, re-escalate.

  • HR creeping upward despite IV/PO beta-blocker — rebound tachycardia, pain not controlled, infection, hypovolemia, or medication inadequate; escalate beta-blocker dose or call team
  • BP trending upward toward 140–150 mmHg despite escalating antihypertensives — vasodilator failure, medication non-adherence, inadequate diuresis, pain; call team for possible ICU transfer or TEVAR discussion
  • New onset lower extremity weakness, foot drop, or loss of sensation → spinal cord ischemia (major red flag); call CT surgery immediately; may need CSF drain, ICU transfer, or TEVAR
  • Rising creatinine (Cr trend baseline → +0.3–0.5 → AKI) — renal artery malperfusion; call team; may need TEVAR for renal protection; avoid nephrotoxic agents
  • Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h × 2h) despite adequate circulating volume — renal malperfusion or acute kidney injury; labs (lactate, Cr), call team
  • Dark or cola-colored urine — myoglobinuria (rhabdomyolysis); stat urinalysis + myoglobin quantitation, increase fluids, alert CT surgery
  • Rising lactate, falling UOP, worsening capillary refill — perfusion failing even if BP looks adequate; mesenteric ischemia risk; call team
  • Severe abdominal pain out of proportion to exam, with elevated lactate and acidosis → mesenteric ischemia (surgical emergency); STAT CTA + CT surgery consult
  • New acute leg pain, pallor, cold extremity, weak/absent pulse — limb malperfusion; vascular surgery consult; may need TEVAR or thrombectomy
  • New tearing chest/back/abdominal pain after initial control → re-dissection or rupture; STAT CTA/TEE, call team, prepare for ICU/OR
  • Sudden hypotension (SBP <95) not responsive to fluids — rupture, tamponade, or severe hemorrhage; STAT call, ICU, prepare for OR
  • Patient becoming increasingly anxious, confused, restless, or sleepy — subtle mental status changes often precede hemodynamic collapse; escalate monitoring
  • Recurrent POAF (post-operative atrial fibrillation) despite rate control — adds stroke risk; notify team; may need anticoagulation discussion
  • New focal neurologic deficit (unilateral weakness, vision loss, speech slur, facial droop) → acute stroke; activate stroke code; notify vascular surgery (dissection complicating stroke management)
  • Persistent fever without obvious source despite antibiotics — line infection, abscess, or occult infection; blood cultures, infectious disease consult

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Impulse control is non-negotiable — both HR ≤60 AND SBP 100–120 are evidence-based. (Isselbacher et al., 2022) Permissive hypertension (SBP >130) → propagation and rupture. If patient drifts to SBP 140+, escalate: increase labetalol or amlodipine BEFORE it becomes urgent.

  2. Beta-blocker FIRST, vasodilator SECOND — never reverse the order. Reflex tachycardia from unopposed vasodilation widens aortic wall stress (increases dP/dt) and dissection propagation. Establish HR ≤60 first with beta-blocker, THEN add vasodilator for BP. This principle is non-negotiable.

  3. New lower extremity weakness = spinal cord malperfusion → STAT escalation. Spinal cord ischemia can be delayed (POD 3–5); don't assume baseline weakness because patient is stable now means nothing changes Day 4. Serial bilateral leg strength testing every shift is essential. Any new weakness: call CT surgery immediately; may need CSF drain, ICU, TEVAR, or MAP escalation.

  4. Rising creatinine + oliguria = renal artery malperfusion. Dissection may occlude renal artery ostium. Monitor Cr daily (baseline → +0.3–0.5 → AKI pattern). If rising, call team; may need TEVAR for renal protection. Avoid NSAIDs and minimize IV contrast exposure.

  5. Mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion + lactate up + acidosis) is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Dissection extending into SMA/IMA causes ischemic bowel. Early presentation: severe abdominal pain with benign exam (ischemia precedes peritonitis). If suspected: STAT CT angiography + CT surgery consult; likely TEVAR + possible bowel resection needed. Don't minimize "pain out of proportion."

  6. New tearing pain after initial control = re-dissection or rupture, not breakthrough pain. Get STAT CTA/TEE immediately; patient may need return to ICU/OR. Separate pain control from impulse control: never withhold opioids to control BP — instead escalate antihypertensive regimen and pain medication.

  7. Limb malperfusion is often subtle in Type B because false lumen may provide some perfusion. Watch for gradually increasing leg pain, progressive coolness, weakening pulses on serial exams. Acute limb ischemia with cool, pale, pulseless leg is obvious; gradual onset is easily missed. Serial lower extremity exams every shift are essential.

  8. Limb ischemia from dissection may require TEVAR + thrombectomy/embolectomy or limb revascularization. Do NOT assume that if femoral pulse is present, the limb is well-perfused. Compare bilateral legs; check capillary refill, foot temperature, calf tenderness (compartment syndrome risk post-revascularization).

  9. TEVAR is increasingly favored even in initially "uncomplicated" Type B per INSTEAD-XL trial and contemporary practice. Adverse imaging features (aortic diameter >50 mm, rapid expansion, distal ulcer-like projection, refractory pain) warrant early TEVAR discussion. If surgeon recommends TEVAR, discuss with patient: INSTEAD-XL showed improved 2-year aortic outcomes with TEVAR; mortality from rupture if untreated is ~30% in complicated disease; TEVAR prevents progression and is especially valuable in younger patients with long life expectancy.

  10. Complicated Type B is a surgical/endovascular emergency, not a medical disease. Once malperfusion, rupture, or rapid expansion confirmed, medical management is a holding pattern while TEVAR logistics arranged. Don't delay imaging or team escalation hoping medical therapy will resolve complications — it won't.

  11. Discharge planning must include TEVAR discussion. Some uncomplicated patients will need TEVAR during hospitalization or within weeks if imaging shows progression. Set expectation from Day 1: "We may recommend a stent procedure (TEVAR) to protect your aorta long-term. We'll discuss options with the surgeon."

  12. Surveillance imaging schedule is strict: 48–72h, pre-discharge, 1 mo, 6 mo, 1 yr, then annually. Don't skip or delay. Imaging trends tell the story: stable/decreasing diameter + false lumen thrombosing = good prognosis; expanding, re-entry, or ulcer-like projection = TEVAR threshold lowered. Patient and surgeon must review images together at each interval.

  13. Fluoroquinolone avoidance: cipro, levofloxacin increase aortic dissection/rupture risk. Avoid or use only if no alternatives; prefer beta-lactams, azithromycin if infection suspected.

  14. Anticoagulation is typically HELD in acute Type B dissection. No routine anticoagulation unless surgeon directs (rare). Risk of bleeding into false lumen >> benefit of thromboembolism prevention. If patient on warfarin pre-admission (AFib, mechanical valve), discuss with CT surgeon: hold vs bridge to heparin per bleeding risk/thromboembolic risk.

  15. Pain-free by POD 3–4 doesn't mean "cured." Patient may feel better, want to leave. Educate: dissection remodeling takes weeks to months; compliance with BP control, medications, and imaging surveillance is lifesaving. Inadequate follow-up → sudden rupture at home. Reinforce that lifelong medication adherence and yearly imaging are non-negotiable.

cards.title: Adrenal Insufficiency / Adrenal Crisis (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: Refractory hypotension + hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + hypoglycemia in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient with any history of chronic steroid use (≥5 mg prednisone × 3 weeks within the past year) → STAT hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus, then 50 mg IV q6h (or 200 mg/24h infusion). Do not delay for cortisol testing. Replace K⁺, Na⁺, and glucose in parallel. Identify the precipitant (sepsis, hypovolemia, etomidate on induction). If stable and high-risk (known chronic steroid dependence), ensure perioperative stress dosing was given; if missed, discuss repletion strategy with the team immediately.

Do not delay for cortisol testing. Replace K⁺, Na⁺, and glucose in parallel. Identify the precipitant (sepsis, hypovolemia, etomidate on induction).
