sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, and clinical context.

  • Definition: Adrenal insufficiency is the inability of the adrenal cortex to produce adequate cortisol and/or aldosterone in response to physiologic stress. In cardiac surgery, this manifests acutely as adrenal crisis — a life-threatening state of hemodynamic and metabolic collapse.
  • Epidemiology: Affects up to 10–15% of critically ill patients with sepsis or severe critical illness (Endocrine Society, 2016). In post-operative cardiac surgery, the at-risk population is smaller but highly vulnerable: patients on chronic exogenous corticosteroids (≥5 mg prednisone daily × ≥3 weeks in the preceding 12 months) undergoing major surgery without perioperative stress dosing.
  • Who it applies to: All adult post-operative cardiac surgery patients, especially those with known rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune disease, COPD, asthma, polymyalgia rheumatica, temporal arteritis, organ transplant, or pituitary disease. Peak risk is POD 0–3; CIRCI can unmask itself later.
  • Why it matters: Mortality in untreated adrenal crisis approaches 100%. Early recognition and empiric treatment prevent full decompensation; survival improves dramatically with timely hydrocortisone replacement.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
The hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis normally mounts a robust cortisol response to physiologic stress (surgery, sepsis, critical illness). Cortisol mobilizes glucose, maintains vascular tone, suppresses inflammation, and supports cardiac output.

Secondary adrenal insufficiency (most common in post-operative patients):

  • Chronic exogenous corticosteroid use (≥5 mg prednisone × ≥3 weeks) suppresses ACTH secretion via negative feedback at the pituitary level.
  • When steroids are abruptly stopped or dosed inadequately at the time of major stress (surgery, sepsis, critical illness), the pituitary cannot acutely resume ACTH production.
  • Result: cortisol deficiency when physiologic demands are at their peak.
  • Does NOT cause hyperkalemia (aldosterone production is preserved).

Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease — less common post-operatively but higher mortality if unrecognized):

  • Destruction or dysfunction of the adrenal cortex itself (autoimmune, infection, hemorrhage, malignancy).
  • Elevated ACTH (attempt to stimulate failing gland) but low cortisol.
  • Loss of mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) production → hyperkalemia, severe hyponatremia, hypovolemia.
  • Can be unmasked or exacerbated by surgery.

Critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency (CIRCI):

  • In septic shock or severe critical illness, some patients develop relative insufficiency despite reported "normal" baseline cortisol levels.
  • Defined as insufficient increase in cortisol from baseline (Δ cortisol < 9 mcg/dL on cosyntropin stimulation) despite elevated baseline cortisol.
  • Reflects adrenal exhaustion, inadequate response to stimulus, or target-organ resistance to cortisol.

Post-operative triggers in cardiac surgery:

  • Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) is an intense inflammatory stressor, triggering massive catecholamine and cortisol demand.
  • Etomidate (if used for induction) causes transient single-dose adrenal suppression lasting ~24 hours.
  • Sepsis (sternal wound infection, endocarditis, mediastinitis).
  • Hypovolemia or ongoing blood loss.
  • Medication interactions (mitotane, ketoconazole) — rare but important.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient, especially POD 0–3:

  • Refractory hypotension unresponsive to fluid boluses and escalating vasopressor support (noradrenaline, vasopressin) despite seemingly adequate preload
  • Hypoglycemia (glucose < 70 mg/dL) despite dextrose-containing fluids
  • Hyponatremia (Na < 130 mEq/L) developing or worsening in the post-operative period
  • Hyperkalemia (K > 5.5 mEq/L; more common in primary insufficiency; less in secondary)
  • Altered mental status — nausea, vomiting, lethargy, obtundation, or confusion in a previously alert patient
  • Unexplained fever (pseudofever in some cases; true fever if concurrent infection)
  • Eosinophilia (> 4% on CBC) — uncommon but specific finding
  • Combination presentation: hypotension + hyponatremia + hyperkalemia + hypoglycemia in the absence of sepsis, pump failure, or hypovolemia

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (3–5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic information-gathering. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs: BP, HR, capillary refill, skin turgor, perfusion status (mottling, coldness of extremities)
  • Mental status: alertness, orientation, agitation vs lethargy; baseline assessment
  • GI symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal distension
  • Recent labs: Na⁺, K⁺, glucose, cortisol (if drawn), ACTH (if drawn), hemoglobin, WBC with differential (eosinophilia?), albumin, lactate, ABG if perfusion questionable
  • Intake–output trends: urine output trajectory, IV fluid input vs. urine output ratio, signs of polyuria
  • Surgical context: procedure type, timing (POD #), any intraoperative events (prolonged CPB, hypotension requiring pressors, massive bleeding)
  • Home medication list (CRITICAL): chronic corticosteroid therapy? Prednisone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone for RA, asthma, COPD, lung disease, transplant, polymyalgia rheumatica, temporal arteritis, autoimmune disease? Dose, frequency, duration, date of last dose?
  • Perioperative steroid orders: Did the patient receive pre-operative stress dose? (Hydrocortisone 50–100 mg IV at induction, then q 8 h × 24–48 h?) Was it documented and actually given? Check anesthesia record.
  • Anesthetic agents used: Was etomidate used for induction? Single dose suppresses adrenal function transiently; red flag in at-risk patients.
  • Vascular access: patent IV, preferably central line in place post-operatively? Adequate for rapid bolus administration?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hemodynamically stable, alert, no signs of shock; high-risk patient with known chronic steroid dependence; or suspected chronic AI in a stable patient.)

  1. Alert provider immediately if no perioperative stress dose documented (POD 0–1 setting)

    • Pre-op stress dose should be: hydrocortisone 50–100 mg IV at induction, then 50 mg IV q 8 h × 24–48 h post-op
    • If missed, discuss repletion strategy with the team (some will cover retroactively for the first 24–48 h)

  2. Verify hydrocortisone continuation or conversion (if patient is on home steroid)

    • Home dose must be converted to perioperative equivalent and continued or stress-dosed
    • Holding chronic prednisone on the day of surgery = crisis risk

  3. If already on hydrocortisone, taper gradually

    • POD 0–1: 50–100 mg q 6–8 h
    • POD 2: 50 mg q 12 h
    • POD 3+: resume home dose
    • Do NOT abruptly discontinue; rebound insufficiency can occur

  4. Patient/family education (pre-discharge planning)

    • Chronic steroid replacement: physiologic replacement hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in divided doses (e.g., 10 mg on waking, 5 mg at noon, 5 mg at 4 PM)
    • Stress dosing for illness: double usual dose during colds/flu; triple dose for gastroenteritis; 100 mg IV for severe acute illness or surgery
    • Discharge prescriptions: steroid replacement + written schedule
    • Steroid wallet card (download from Endocrine Society website)
    • Medical alert bracelet
    • Endocrinology follow-up within 1–2 weeks post-discharge

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Adrenal crisis — refractory hypotension + clinical suspicion of adrenal insufficiency ± risk factor. Do NOT delay; empiric treatment is indicated.)

  1. STAT call to APP / on-call provider — notify of suspected adrenal crisis immediately; anticipate order for hydrocortisone stat

  2. Obtain IV access — ensure patent IV (preferably central line already in place post-operatively)

  3. Send STAT labs while preparing hydrocortisone administration:

    • Cortisol (random) — < 10 mcg/dL is suggestive; 10–20 indeterminate; > 20 less likely (but does NOT exclude insufficiency in CIRCI). Do NOT delay treatment.
    • ACTH level — helps distinguish primary (elevated ACTH) vs. secondary (low ACTH)
    • Basic metabolic panel — Na⁺, K⁺, glucose, Cr, BUN
    • CBC with differential — Hgb, WBC, eosinophil count
    • Lactate, ABG — perfusion status; consider early sepsis workup (cultures, procalcitonin)

  4. DO NOT WAIT for cortisol result — initiate hydrocortisone empirically immediately:

    • Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus (push undiluted or diluted in 10–20 mL normal saline over 1–2 min)
    • Immediately follow with hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q 6 h (or continuous infusion 200 mg/24 h if profoundly hypotensive and expected prolonged crisis)

  5. Address electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities in parallel:

    • Hypoglycemia: Start dextrose-containing IV fluid (D5LR or D5NS) at 100–150 mL/hr, or 50 mL 50% dextrose bolus if critical (glucose < 40)
    • Hyponatremia: Fluid restrict to 800–1000 mL/day (do NOT rapidly correct — risk of osmotic demyelination); hydrocortisone will help via improved kidney perfusion and reduced SIADH
    • Hyperkalemia: Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% IV over 2–5 min (cardiac membrane stabilization), then insulin 10 units IV push + 25 g dextrose (drives K⁺ intracellularly); kayexalate 15 g PO/PR if tolerated

  6. Identify and treat the precipitant:

    • Is there a source of sepsis? Blood cultures, urine culture, lactate; start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics if infection suspected
    • Is the patient hypovolemic? Give fluid bolus, vasopressor titration
    • Any medication triggers? Etomidate on induction day (residual 24 h suppression)? Mitotane? Ketoconazole?
    • Review recent events: prolonged CPB, massive transfusion, ongoing bleeding?

  7. Continuous hemodynamic monitoring:

    • Reassess BP q 15 min initially
    • If still hypotensive after hydrocortisone bolus + fluids, titrate vasopressors (noradrenaline, vasopressin)
    • Hydrocortisone effect takes ~10–15 min; full benefit may take several hours
    • Re-check electrolytes q 4–6 h initially, then per protocol as patient stabilizes

  8. Prepare for ACTH stimulation test if diagnostic clarity is needed:

    • Cosyntropin 250 mcg IV; cortisol measured at baseline, 30 min, 60 min
    • Normal: cortisol rise ≥ 9 mcg/dL from baseline (or absolute cortisol > 18 mcg/dL at 60 min)
    • Abnormal: rise < 9 mcg/dL → suggests adrenal insufficiency
    • Note: Can perform while empirically treating — does NOT preclude treatment or invalidate the test
    • If performing, use dexamethasone instead of hydrocortisone for ongoing dosing (hydrocortisone cross-reacts with cortisol assay)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "[Physician name], this is [RN name] on [unit name], calling about [patient name, room], post-operative day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient is presenting with refractory hypotension despite fluids and vasopressor support (BP [value], on [vasopressor] at [mcg/kg/min]). Labs show Na⁺ [value], K⁺ [value], glucose [value]. Critically, patient has a significant history of chronic steroid use: [dose, frequency, duration, date of last dose]. Perioperative stress dose [was/was not] documented or given." A: "Clinical picture is highly concerning for adrenal insufficiency / adrenal crisis. STAT cortisol [result or pending]. No clear septic source yet, but patient is critically ill." R: "Requesting immediate hydrocortisone order (100 mg IV bolus, then 50 mg q 6 h) ± ACTH stimulation testing. Can we start empirically now?"

Who to call

Situation Contact
Suspected adrenal crisis (refractory hypotension + risk factor) Primary APP / on-call fellow + Endocrinology consult (stat or ASAP)
Confirmed adrenal insufficiency with chronic steroid history Endocrinology for long-term management plan + home steroid taper strategy
ACTH stimulation test abnormal (rise < 9 mcg/dL) Endocrinology for diagnosis confirmation + imaging (CT adrenal if primary suspected)
Primary adrenal insufficiency (elevated ACTH + low cortisol) Endocrinology + consider CT abdomen to rule out adrenal bleed, lymphoma, TB, malignancy
Pituitary apoplexy suspected (adrenal crisis + severe headache + vision changes + neck stiffness) Neurosurgery + Endocrinology (MRI brain emergent)
Etomidate-related suppression suspected (induction hypotension, ongoing instability) Primary APP / intensivist; hydrocortisone coverage; consider Endocrinology input

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive on pathophysiology, diagnosis, medications, and edge cases. All subsections are — collapsed by default in PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 HPA axis suppression and the ≥5 mg prednisone × 3 weeks threshold
sections.bodyHtml:
• The critical threshold: Exogenous corticosteroid use at ≥5 mg prednisone daily (or equivalent) for ≥3 weeks is known to suppress endogenous ACTH and cortisol production (Endocrine Society, 2016).
  • Duration of suppression: After stopping chronic steroids, HPA axis recovery takes weeks to months. A patient who stopped prednisone 3 months ago may still have blunted ACTH response.
  • Timing in perioperative period: The first 24–48 hours post-operatively are the highest-risk window. Cortisol demand is maximal due to CPB-induced inflammation, and endogenous production is suppressed.
  • Why ask every patient: Many patients do not volunteer steroid use or underestimate the dose/duration. Rheumatoid arthritis, COPD, asthma, temporal arteritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, transplant patients — all high-yield for chronic steroid use.

sections.heading: 7.2 Stress-dosing strategies for perioperative periods
sections.bodyHtml:
Stress-dose hydrocortisone depends on the magnitude of physiologic stress:

Stress Level Surgery Example Hydrocortisone Stress Dose
Minor stress Minor outpatient procedure, dental work, biopsy 25–50 mg IV/IM at induction; may give single dose only
Moderate stress Hernia repair, cholecystectomy, appendectomy 50–75 mg IV at induction, then 25 mg IV q 6–8 h × 24–48 h
Major stress CABG, valve surgery, thoracic surgery, CPB 100 mg IV at induction, then 50–100 mg IV q 6–8 h × 24–48 h
Post-operative crisis Developing adrenal crisis on POD 0–3 100 mg IV bolus, then 50 mg q 6 h (or 200 mg/24 h infusion)

Key principle: Taper gradually post-operatively. Abrupt withdrawal or insufficient dosing = crisis risk. POD 3+ approach the patient's home dose if clinically stable.

sections.heading: 7.3 Cosyntropin stimulation test interpretation
sections.bodyHtml:
Test protocol:

  • Obtain baseline cortisol (0 min)
  • Administer cosyntropin 250 mcg IV push
  • Repeat cortisol at 30 min and 60 min
  • Abnormal (insufficient response): cortisol rise < 9 mcg/dL from baseline
  • Normal (adequate response): cortisol rise ≥ 9 mcg/dL, or absolute cortisol > 18 mcg/dL at 60 min

Interpretation in critically ill:

  • Test can be performed while empirically treating — hydrocortisone treatment does NOT invalidate the result
  • If using hydrocortisone for treatment, switch to dexamethasone for the ACTH stimulation test (dexamethasone does not cross-react with cortisol assay, whereas hydrocortisone does)
  • Baseline cortisol interpretation:
  • < 10 mcg/dL: suggestive of insufficiency
  • 10–20 mcg/dL: indeterminate; depends on ACTH level and clinical context
  • > 20 mcg/dL: makes insufficiency less likely, BUT does NOT exclude it (especially in CIRCI)

sections.heading: 7.4 CIRCI concept and relative adrenal insufficiency in sepsis
sections.bodyHtml:
• Definition: Critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency occurs when the adrenal gland fails to mount an adequate cortisol response to a provocative stimulus (cosyntropin), despite elevated baseline cortisol.
  • Etiology: In septic shock, the adrenal may be inflamed, infiltrated, or necrotic; or there may be target-organ resistance to cortisol's effects.
  • Diagnostic cut-off: Δ cortisol (cortisol at 60 min minus baseline cortisol) < 9 mcg/dL on cosyntropin stimulation defines CIRCI (Marik, 2019).
  • Clinical significance: CIRCI is associated with prolonged vasopressor dependence, multi-organ failure, and higher mortality if untreated.
  • Treatment: Stress-dose hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q 6 h) can be considered in septic shock meeting CIRCI criteria, though evidence is evolving.

sections.heading: 7.5 Etomidate induction and single-dose adrenal suppression
sections.bodyHtml:
• Mechanism: Etomidate inhibits 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1), the enzyme required for the final step of cortisol synthesis. A single induction dose causes transient adrenal suppression lasting approximately 24 hours.
  • Clinical relevance: Single-dose etomidate does NOT cause crisis in a patient receiving appropriate perioperative stress dosing. However, in an at-risk patient (chronic steroid use, sepsis), it is an additional hit.
  • Best practice: If etomidate is used for induction in a chronically steroid-dependent patient, ensure stress-dose hydrocortisone is given at or immediately after induction.
  • Red flag: If a patient develops unexplained hypotension on POD 0–1, and etomidate was used for induction, and the patient is also on chronic steroids, consider etomidate-related suppression as a contributing factor.

sections.heading: 7.6 CRH vs. ACTH stimulation and differential diagnosis
sections.bodyHtml:
• Cosyntropin (synthetic ACTH) test: Tests the adrenal gland's ability to respond to ACTH. Abnormal result (Δ cortisol < 9) indicates adrenal dysfunction (primary AI).
  • CRH (corticotropin-releasing hormone) test: Rarely used in acute settings; primarily a research/specialist tool. Tests pituitary ACTH response to hypothalamic CRH. Less useful acutely.
  • ACTH level (baseline):
  • ACTH > 100 pg/mL + low cortisol → primary insufficiency (adrenal gland failure; Addison disease)
  • ACTH < 50 pg/mL + low cortisol → secondary insufficiency (pituitary/hypothalamic failure; chronic steroid suppression)
  • ACTH elevated but cortisol also high (insufficient rise on stimulation) → CIRCI (relative insufficiency in critical illness)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable post-operative patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. In a patient initially recovering well, these may signal developing adrenal insufficiency.

  • Hypotension in the recovery phase — initially responsive to fluid, then becoming refractory despite vasopressors; or hypotension developing after pressors are being weaned
  • Hyponatremia worsening — trending down despite normal osmolality and euvolemia (suggests SIADH or adrenal insufficiency)
  • Glucose trending down — hypoglycemia developing or worsening despite dextrose-containing fluids and IV dextrose boluses
  • Hyperkalemia emerging — especially if patient is not oliguric and on a normal diet (suggests mineralocorticoid loss; red flag for primary insufficiency)
  • Unexplained nausea, vomiting — GI symptoms in a post-operative patient without clear surgical explanation (bowel obstruction, pancreatitis ruled out)
  • Fever without source — temperature > 38.5°C despite no positive cultures or obvious infection; may be an early sign of adrenal crisis
  • Eosinophilia on CBC — absolute eosinophil count > 400/μL; uncommon but specific finding in adrenal insufficiency
  • Mental status deterioration — lethargy, confusion, agitation progressing; not explained by opioids or lingering anesthesia
  • Hypothermia — core temperature < 36.5°C unrelated to anesthesia; reflects severely impaired metabolism (late, ominous sign)
  • Patient cannot be weaned from vasopressors — despite improving lactate, normal urine output, adequate preload; suggests underlying adrenal insufficiency, not primary pump problem
  • Recurrent episodes of hypotension — after initial recovery, patient has episodic crashes; suggests inadequate steroid cover for ongoing stressors

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield insights)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Chronic steroid history is THE critical risk factor. Ask every patient on admission: "Have you been on any steroid tablets long-term — prednisone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone — for any reason?" RA, COPD, asthma, polymyalgia rheumatica, temporal arteritis, organ transplant, autoimmune disease. If YES and dose ≥ 5 mg daily × 3 weeks in past year, flag immediately. Pre-operative notes MUST document this. OR must give stress dose.

  2. Perioperative stress dosing for chronic steroid users is ESSENTIAL and prevents crisis. Hydrocortisone 50–100 mg IV at induction, then q 8 h × 24–48 h. Verify doses were actually given — check anesthesia record. If missed, notify the team immediately; some surgeons will backdate coverage.

  3. Refractory hypotension + low sodium + high potassium + low glucose = adrenal crisis until proven otherwise. Do NOT assume sepsis, cardiogenic shock, or hypovolemia alone. Cortisol acts in ~10 min; empiric hydrocortisone will NOT hurt a patient in shock.

  4. Random cortisol > 20 mcg/dL in critically ill has high negative predictive value. If cortisol > 20, insufficiency is less likely. But < 20 is NOT specific; still need clinical context.

    Do NOT wait for results if the clinical picture screams crisis.

  5. Empiric hydrocortisone does NOT preclude testing. Give the 100 mg bolus immediately, then use dexamethasone for the ACTH stimulation test instead of hydrocortisone (dexamethasone does not cross-react with cortisol assay). Cosyntropin test can be done same shift; does NOT delay life-saving treatment.

  6. Etomidate for induction in an at-risk patient is a red flag. Single-dose etomidate suppresses adrenal function transiently (~24 h). If etomidate was used AND patient is on chronic steroids, ensure stress-dose hydrocortisone was given. If patient develops hypotension later, consider etomidate-related suppression as a contributing factor.

  7. Holding chronic prednisone the day of surgery = crisis risk. Home steroid dose must be converted to perioperative equivalent and continued or stress-dosed. NEVER hold it assuming "NPO" rules.

  8. Hydrocortisone has mineralocorticoid effect; dexamethasone does not. In acute adrenal crisis, use hydrocortisone (not dexamethasone) because you need both glucocorticoid AND mineralocorticoid activity. Dexamethasone is reserved for ACTH stimulation testing or when prolonged steroid loading is needed (e.g., cerebral edema — but not in AI crisis).

  9. Cosyntropin test + delayed cortisol labs = steroid response delays. Cortisol assays may have turnaround of 2–4 hours. Do NOT wait. Empiric treatment is faster and safer than diagnosis-first thinking.

  10. Refractory hypotension + no clear cause on bedside ultrasound or clinical exam = think adrenal insufficiency. Ask the team: "Is there a steroid history we're missing?"

  11. Hyperkalemia + hyponatremia + hypotension = Addison disease classic triad. Consider primary AI (not just secondary). Check ACTH level. If ACTH > 100 + cortisol low, order CT abdomen to rule out adrenal bleed, lymphoma, TB.

  12. Etomidate induction → 24 hours of adrenal suppression. If a patient receives etomidate and then declines, do not assume the issue is fixed at 24 h. Stress dose should cover the first post-op day.

  13. Withdrawal from steroid taper needs slow reduction. If a patient was on hydrocortisone stress dose for > 48 h, do NOT stop abruptly. Taper: 50 mg q 8 h → 50 mg q 12 h → 25 mg q 12 h → home dose. Abrupt cessation = rebound insufficiency.

  14. Cortisol random level < 10 mcg/dL in the stress state = adrenal insufficiency. This is suggestive, not diagnostic. But in a hemodynamically unstable patient, act on it empirically.

  15. Discharge teaching is critical. Chronic-steroid patients must: (1) know their daily replacement dose + schedule, (2) carry steroid wallet card, (3) wear medical alert bracelet, (4) understand stress-dosing rules (double for illness, triple for GI illness, 100 mg IV for surgery/severe illness), (5) have Endocrinology follow-up scheduled within 1–2 weeks, (6) have extra steroid supply at home.

cards.title: Atrial Flutter and SVT
cards.quickAnswer: Narrow-complex tachycardia on 12-lead — identify rhythm (flutter waves vs P waves vs buried atrial activity). Stable (MAP > 65, no chest pain, awake) → vagal maneuvers → adenosine 6–12–12 mg IV rapid push + 20 mL saline flush (diagnostic for aflutter, terminates AVNRT/AVRT ~90%); rate control with beta-blocker or diltiazem if refractory; consider overdrive pacing via epicardial wires. Unstable (hypotension, chest pain, altered mental status, pulmonary edema) → STAT synchronized cardioversion 50–100 J (aflutter) or 100–200 J (SVT) biphasic. Anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc (aflutter carries same stroke risk as AF).
cards.quickAnswerHtml:

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — what this is and who gets it.

  • Typical atrial flutter (most common): macroreentrant circuit around tricuspid annulus, atrial rate 250–350 bpm (classic 300), ventricular rate depends on AV node conduction (usually 2:1 = 150 bpm). ECG hallmark: sawtooth flutter waves in leads II, III, aVF. Second most common post-op arrhythmia after POAF.
  • Paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT, AVRT, focal AT): sudden-onset tachycardia, ventricular rate 150–250 bpm. AVNRT (60% of SVT) reentrant circuit within AV node; AVRT (30%) involves accessory pathway (e.g., WPW); focal atrial tachycardia (10%) harder to ablate. No sawtooth; P wave location guides diagnosis.
  • Incidence: aflutter peaks post-cardiac surgery and post-AF ablation; SVT episodic in young/middle-aged, often pre-existing accessory pathway.
  • Who this applies to: any cardiac ICU/post-op patient on telemetry with sudden-onset regular or regularly-regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
  • Why it matters: both carry stroke risk and hemodynamic consequence if untreated; aflutter requires anticoagulation (CHA₂DS₂-VASc); SVT rarely causes stroke unless concurrent AF.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Typical Atrial Flutter

Organized macroreentrant circuit dependent on cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) — the tissue bridge between the inferior vena cava and tricuspid annulus. The circuit perpetuates because tissue conduction properties create a one-way (unidirectional) block, allowing reentry.

  • Atrial rate: 250–350 bpm; ventricular rate determined by AV node blocking properties (2:1 conduction → HR ~150; 3:1 or 4:1 → HR ~100–125; variable → irregular ventricular response)
  • ECG: "sawtooth" pattern (especially leads II, III, aVF) where flutter waves create a continuous undulating baseline
  • Stroke risk: YES — same as AF per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; >48 hr or CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 requires anticoagulation
  • Common contexts: post-cardiac surgery (especially post-AF ablation or MAZE), sometimes post-cardiac catheterization, can emerge weeks to months post-op as scar tissue matures

Paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT/AVRT)

  • AVNRT (atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia, ~60% of SVT): reentrant loop within or immediately adjacent to the AV node. Typically involves a "fast" pathway and "slow" pathway with conduction block in one direction. Sudden initiation, sudden termination (classic on patient history: "palpitations that start and stop suddenly").
  • AVRT (atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia, ~30% of SVT): reentrant pathway involving an accessory pathway — an extra muscular connection between atrium and ventricle that bypasses the AV node. Most common accessory pathway in SVT is in WPW syndrome.
  • Focal atrial tachycardia (AT, ~10%): automatic focus in the atrial tissue, usually near the pulmonary veins, crista terminalis, or coronary sinus. Less responsive to adenosine than AVNRT/AVRT; requires RF ablation for cure.
  • ECG: narrow QRS (unless aberrant conduction); P wave location is diagnostic (AVNRT: buried in QRS or pseudo-R' in V1; AVRT: after QRS in ST segment; AT: before QRS but abnormal axis)
  • Stroke risk: NO (unless concurrent AF or structural heart disease)

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a cardiac post-op patient or patient with known SVT history:

  • Telemetry alarm: rapid regular rhythm, HR typically 140–200+ bpm
  • Patient symptoms: sudden palpitations, chest discomfort, dyspnea, lightheadedness, syncope, or presyncope
  • Exam findings: hemodynamically variable; some patients very symptomatic with stable vital signs; others relatively asymptomatic despite rapid rate
  • 12-lead ECG: narrow QRS complex; atrial rate 250–350 (aflutter) or 150–250 (SVT); visible flutter waves (aflutter) or difficult-to-see P waves (SVT)
  • Onset context: sudden (SVT classic; aflutter can be sudden or gradual over hours); post-cardiac surgery; post-AF ablation at higher risk for atypical aflutter; known WPW or prior SVT history
  • Post-MAZE patient: transition rhythms (aflutter → AF → sinus) over weeks post-op expected; not a sign of surgical failure

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure observation; no interventions yet.

  • Vital signs: HR, BP, SpO₂, mental status, perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output if monitored)
  • Symptoms: chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, syncope/near-syncope, anxiety, diaphoresis
  • Rhythm character: regular or irregular? (aflutter typically regular; AVNRT/AVRT regular; irregular suggests variable conduction or concurrent AF)
  • Physical exam: apical–radial pulse deficit? (common in aflutter with regular rhythm)
  • 12-lead ECG immediately: obtain STAT; document rate, QRS width, flutter waves (sawtooth), P wave location/timing, PR interval on conducted beats
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, iCa²⁺, Hgb, Cr, troponin (if any chest pain)
  • MAR review: home antiarrhythmic meds held? Beta-blocker restarted? Adenosine given recently (half-life <10 sec; unlikely to recur)? On dipyridamole or carbamazepine (potentiates adenosine)? Anticoagulation status?
  • Lines/wires: epicardial atrial pacing wires in place? A-line? Active IV access for adenosine? Size and location of IV (big vein preferred for adenosine; peripheral hand/foot IV less reliable)?
  • Surgery context: post-op day? Prior AF ablation? MAZE patient? Known WPW or accessory pathway? Valve surgery (higher POAF incidence)?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP > 65, no chest pain, perfusing, patient tolerating.)

  1. Obtain 12-lead ECG STAT — confirm narrow-complex rhythm; identify flutter waves (sawtooth) vs P wave timing vs buried atrial activity; measure rate
  2. Save rhythm strip at onset and document in chart (time, HR, patient description of symptom onset)
  3. Establish IV access (if not present) — ensure large-bore IV in central line or upper extremity (preferred for adenosine administration and rapid flush)
  4. Perform vagal maneuvers (in sequence):
    • Modified Valsalva (REVERT trial superior): blow into 10-mL syringe against 40 mmHg for 15 seconds, then immediately lie patient supine and elevate legs 90 degrees for 45 seconds. Do NOT strain first; blow against resistance creates effective pressure.
    • Standard Valsalva (if modified not feasible): strain for 15 seconds, then cough
    • Carotid massage (only if no carotid bruit, not in elderly with cerebrovascular disease): gentle, unilateral, 5–10 seconds
    • If rhythm persists after vagal maneuvers (allow 1–2 minutes):
      • Adenosine 6 mg IV rapid push + immediate 20 mL saline flush (speed of push is critical — inject over < 2 sec, flush immediately; delay reduces efficacy)
      • Warn patient: "You may feel your heart skip, chest pressure, or shortness of breath for a moment — this is expected and will pass quickly"
      • If no response in 1–2 minutes: adenosine 12 mg IV rapid push + flush
      • If still no response: adenosine 12 mg IV × 1 more time (max 36 mg cumulative)
      • Note: adenosine is diagnostic (unmasks flutter waves in aflutter) and therapeutic (terminates AVNRT/AVRT ~90%)
      • If adenosine unsuccessful or contraindicated:
      • IV metoprolol 5 mg slow push over 2 minutes, may repeat q5min × 3 (max 15 mg) — first-line for rate control if no contraindication
      • OR IV diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg (typically ~20 mg) over 2 minutes — preferred if COPD, asthma, or bronchospasm concern; watch for hypotension, bradycardia
      • Target HR < 110 while arranging provider contact
      • If stable but refractory to adenosine + rate control:
      • Consider IV amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes (confirm with provider; requires acceptable LV function)
      • Notify APP/on-call provider STAT with SBAR (see §6) — request rhythm vs rate plan and anticipate need for DCCV if recurrent
      • Continuous telemetry monitoring — watch trajectory; anticipate escalation if destabilization appears (see §8 Red Flags)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension < 90 systolic, altered mental status, chest pain, pulmonary edema, loss of consciousness, severe dyspnea.)

  1. STAT call APP/fellow + charge RN — do NOT leave the room alone; activate Rapid Response if not already present
  2. Pads on chest STAT, ensure patent IV access, elevate head-of-bed for perfusion and work of breathing
  3. Prepare for synchronized DCCV:
    • Atrial flutter: 50–100 J biphasic (lower energy than AF; organized reentry responds to modest energy; start 50 J, escalate if needed)
    • SVT: 100–200 J biphasic (similar range to AF; start at 100 J)
    • Set monitor to synchronized mode; confirm sync indicator active on each discharge
    • Procedural sedation per institution policy — obtain procedural sedation consent if patient alert; anesthesia presence may be required outside ICU
    • If epicardial atrial pacing wires in place AND provider at bedside:
    • Overdrive pacing (provider-initiated) may be considered as alternative to DCCV — especially elegant for aflutter; paces at rate ~20 bpm above native, then abruptly stops (often converts to sinus)
    • Requires provider at bedside; not a first-line/independent nursing action
    • Send STAT labs: ABG, lactate, electrolytes, troponin, CBC if active bleeding concern
    • Document: rhythm strip at onset, strip entering cardioversion, strip post-conversion
    • Post-cardioversion: anticipate recurrence; prepare for repeat DCCV or escalation to IV amiodarone drip + esmolol/diltiazem for rate control

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed sudden rapid regular rhythm at [time], confirmed narrow-complex tachycardia on 12-lead. Flutter waves visible? [Yes/No]. HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. Current symptoms: [chest pain / palpitations / dyspnea / syncope / none]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. Vagal maneuvers [attempted / not attempted]. Adenosine [given / not given — reason]. Current rhythm status." R: "Requesting [further adenosine / rate control agent / DCCV prep / rhythm vs rate plan / ICU transfer]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable aflutter/SVT, first episode Primary APP / on-call fellow
Unstable aflutter/SVT (hemodynamically compromised) APP/fellow + RRT/code team; CT surgery if post-op
Recurrent aflutter/SVT despite adenosine + rate control APP + EP consult consideration
Aflutter/SVT + new focal neuro deficit (weakness, facial droop, speech change) Stroke code + neurology + primary team
Aflutter/SVT + chest pain / troponin elevation Cardiology; rule out MI; consider ACS protocol
WPW + AFib with rapid ventricular response DO NOT give adenosine — call provider STAT; prepare DCCV immediately

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Adenosine: diagnostic + therapeutic mechanism
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: competitive blocker of adenosine A1 receptors → slows/blocks conduction through the AV node → breaks reentrant circuits in AVNRT/AVRT; transiently unmasks atrial activity in aflutter (reveals flutter waves without QRS obscuring them)

Dosing: 6 mg → 12 mg → 12 mg IV rapid push + immediate saline flush

Effect timeline:

  • Adenosine half-life < 10 seconds
  • Transient AV block occurs → may see brief asystole on monitor (2–5 seconds; normal and expected)
  • Patient may feel chest pressure, dyspnea, flushing, palpitations during the asystole (warn them: "This is brief and expected")
  • If AVNRT/AVRT → abrupt termination to normal sinus rhythm; patient typically feels relief
  • If aflutter → no termination, but flutter waves now clearly visible without QRS overlay; atrial rate unchanged → diagnostic win

Diagnostic clues after adenosine:

  • AVNRT: abrupt conversion to NSR; may reinitiate within seconds if retrograde conduction re-engages (see recurrence in 5A red flag)
  • AVRT: abrupt conversion to NSR; if WPW, look for delta wave on sinus rhythm ECG (pre-excitation)
  • Aflutter: no conversion; flutter waves crystallize; atrial rate unchanged; may see 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 conduction transiently as AV block appears

Why adenosine unmasks aflutter but does NOT cardiovert it: aflutter's reentrant loop is entirely in the atrium (CTI-dependent); AV block does not disrupt that loop. In contrast, AVNRT/AVRT depend on AV node or accessory pathway conduction; AV block terminates them.

Adenosine contraindications/cautions:

  • Severe asthma/COPD: adenosine triggers bronchospasm; use diltiazem or esmolol instead
  • Sinus node disease: risk of prolonged asystole; caution advised
  • On dipyridamole or carbamazepine: potentiates adenosine — dose reduction may be needed
  • Heart transplant (denervated): severe adverse effects (profound asystole, bradycardia); use alternative
  • WPW + AFib with rapid VR: DO NOT use adenosine — paradoxically accelerates conduction down accessory pathway → can precipitate VF

sections.heading: 7.2 Adenosine vs rate control vs rhythm control logic
sections.bodyHtml:
For Aflutter:

  • Rhythm control first (adenosine): attempt 6–12–12 adenosine to terminate; if successful and patient stable, follow-up EPS consult for elective ablation
  • Rate control fallback: if adenosine fails, IV beta-blocker (metoprolol) or diltiazem; target HR < 110
  • Overdrive pacing: if epicardial wires in place, elegant alternative — provider-directed trial often successful, no sedation needed
  • DCCV: highly effective (50–100 J); lower energy than AF due to organized reentry
  • Definitive cure: RF ablation of CTI; >90% cure rate; elective procedure once stable

For SVT (AVNRT/AVRT):

  • Rhythm control first (adenosine): 6–12–12 adenosine is first-line; ~90% effective in AVNRT/AVRT
  • If adenosine fails: IV beta-blocker or diltiazem for rate control while awaiting EP consultation
  • Amiodarone: if refractory and patient stable; effective but slower onset
  • DCCV: usually reserved for unstable/syncope; highly effective but overkill if adenosine works
  • Definitive cure: RF ablation of accessory pathway (AVRT) or AV nodal modification (AVNRT); >95% cure rate

Post-op context:

  • Atypical aflutter (non-CTI-dependent) may emerge after AF ablation; RF ablation often needed for definitive cure
  • MAZE patient with aflutter: expected in first 4 weeks as scar tissue matures; rate control + amiodarone; DCCV usually ineffective until scarring stabilizes

sections.heading: 7.3 Modified Valsalva vs standard Valsalva
sections.bodyHtml:
Modified Valsalva (REVERT trial — superior):

  1. Patient sits upright (or semi-upright)
  2. Blow into 10-mL syringe against 40 mmHg resistance for 15 seconds (this creates sustained elevated intrathoracic pressure)
  3. Immediately lie patient flat and elevate legs 90 degrees (knees bent, feet up) for 45 seconds (augments venous return)
  4. Roughly 2× more effective than traditional Valsalva; success rate ~43% vs 20% in REVERT trial

Standard Valsalva:

  1. Strain (bear down) for 15 seconds
  2. Then cough
  3. Less effective than modified but simpler to teach

Why it works: both maneuvers exploit the baroreceptor reflex. Elevated intrathoracic pressure triggers carotid/aortic arch mechanoreceptors → parasympathetic surge → AV node slowing. Leg elevation augments venous return, which magnifies the reflex. Modified Valsalva optimizes both components.

sections.heading: 7.4 AVNRT vs AVRT mechanism — clinical pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
AVNRT (dual AV nodal pathway disease):

  • Two AV nodal conduction pathways: "fast" (shorter refractory period, slower conduction) and "slow" (longer refractory period, faster conduction)
  • Typical AVNRT: antegrade conduction via "slow" pathway, retrograde via "fast" pathway
  • P wave buried in QRS or pseudo-R' in V1 on tachycardia ECG (retrograde P buried in early part of QRS)
  • Antecedent PR prolongation on sinus rhythm may hint at dual pathway
  • Adenosine works: blocks AV node → terminates reentrant loop
  • Ablation targets "fast" or "slow" pathway to prevent reentry; ~95% cure

AVRT (accessory pathway reentry):

  • Two conduction pathways: AV node (antegrade) + accessory pathway (retrograde)
  • Typical AVRT: antegrade via AV node, retrograde via accessory pathway (Kent bundle in WPW)
  • P wave after QRS, in ST segment (retrograde conduction via accessory pathway)
  • Baseline ECG in sinus rhythm: look for delta wave (slurred PR interval start, thick QRS) = WPW = pre-excitation
  • Adenosine works: blocks AV node → terminates reentrant loop
  • Ablation targets accessory pathway; >95% cure
  • Caveat: if patient has WPW + AFib with rapid VR, adenosine is contraindicated (see 7.1)

Why the distinction matters:

  • ECG diagnosis: P wave location (buried vs after QRS) guides mechanism
  • Ablation planning: different targets (dual AV pathways vs accessory pathway)
  • Drug choices: AVRT + WPW demands care — avoid AV nodal blockers if pre-excited AFib present

sections.heading: 7.5 Anticoagulation in aflutter
sections.bodyHtml:
• Aflutter = same stroke risk as AF per CHA₂DS₂-VASc; do NOT default to "aflutter is benign"
  • CHA₂DS₂-VASc scoring:
  • CHF (1), HTN (1), age ≥ 75 (2), DM (1), stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), vascular disease (1), age 65–74 (1), female sex (1)
  • Score ≥ 2 → anticoagulation indicated if rhythm lasts > 48 hr
  • Post-op timing: balancing stroke risk vs surgical bleeding is team-dependent; never start/hold AC without CT surgery team input
  • Home anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC): typically held 3–4 days pre-op, restarted 24–72 hr post-op per surgeon preference
  • Bridging with LMWH/UFH: if prolonged pre-op hold and no AC on board, may bridge while awaiting DOAC restart
  • Persistent aflutter: same anticoag strategy as persistent AF

sections.heading: 7.6 WPW caveat and drug avoidance
sections.bodyHtml:
The Danger: If a patient has WPW + AFib with rapid ventricular response (bypass accessory pathway conducting faster than AV node), AV nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem) can paradoxically accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway → extreme tachycardia and potential VF.

How to spot it:

  • Baseline ECG: delta wave (short PR interval, slurred QRS start) = pre-excitation = WPW = accessory pathway
  • In AFib: if the ventricular response is > 200 bpm and very irregular with some wide-complex beats → suggest accessory pathway conduction
  • Classic teaching: "pre-excited AFib" or "AF with WPW"

What to do:

  • DO NOT give adenosine, beta-blockers, or calcium channel blockers
  • Call provider STAT
  • Prepare for synchronized DCCV
  • Amiodarone or procainamide (prolongs accessory pathway refractoriness) may be options per team

sections.heading: 7.7 Overdrive pacing via epicardial wires for aflutter
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: provider sets pacemaker to pace atrium at rate ~20 bpm faster than native aflutter rate (e.g., if aflutter at 300, pace at 360 bpm). After 10–30 seconds of overdrive, provider abruptly stops pacing. Often converts to normal sinus rhythm.

Why it works: overdrives the reentrant circuit → resets the tissue excitability → allows organized sinus rhythm to re-emerge

Advantages:

  • No sedation needed (elegant, no hemodynamic depression from anesthesia)
  • Low energy (no electrical discharge)
  • Can be attempted at bedside if wires functioning
  • ~70–80% success for typical aflutter

Requirements:

  • Epicardial atrial pacing wires in place (routine post-cardiac surgery)
  • Pacemaker system capable of demand pacing (check system type)
  • Provider at bedside to initiate (not a nursing independent action)
  • Baseline capture + sensing thresholds documented

Pitfall: confirm wires are functional (test daily: sensing, capture, impedance). If nonfunctional, overdrive not an option.

sections.heading: 7.8 TEE-guided cardioversion for flutter lasting > 48 hours without anticoagulation
sections.bodyHtml:
The question: if a patient has been in aflutter for > 48 hours without anticoagulation, can we safely cardiovert without a 3-week anticoagulation window?

TEE-guided approach:

  • Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) performed by cardiology/anesthesia
  • Visualizes left atrial appendage (LAA)
  • If no thrombus seen on TEE, synchronized DCCV is considered safe even without prior anticoagulation
  • Allows urgent rhythm restoration without waiting for anticoag level to rise

Post-cardioversion anticoagulation: patient then requires anticoagulation per CHA₂DS₂-VASc score to prevent stroke during the "stunning" period (transient mechanical dysfunction of atrium after cardioversion)

Pragmatic note: most ICU-level patients with < 48 hr of symptoms proceed directly to DCCV without TEE. TEE is reserved for patients with uncertain symptom onset or borderline anticoag status.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear or worsen, re-escalate immediately.

  • HR rising despite rate-control agents — inadequate dosing, drug failure, or ongoing triggering focus (e.g., fever, pain, hypovolemia); escalate dose or add second agent; notify provider
  • BP trending down — especially on diltiazem or amiodarone drip; consider weaning/discontinuing or adding vasopressor support; amiodarone hypotension (~25%) is predictable — anticipate early
  • Altered mental status, confusion, restlessness — subtle perfusion failure or anxiety; reassess hemodynamics, labs (lactate, CO₂), mental baseline
  • Chest pain or dyspnea worsening — may signal cardiogenic shock, demand ischemia, or PE; send troponin, lactate, ABG
  • Lactate rising, UOP falling, capillary refill slowing — perfusion failing; prepare for escalation to ICU/DCCV
  • Patient becoming diaphoretic, pale, anxious — sympathetic activation; often precedes frank decompensation
  • Rhythm converting to/from AFib — transition rhythms (especially MAZE patient); notify provider; may indicate evolving instability
  • QTc prolonging on amiodarone — approaching 500 ms → torsades risk; hold/decrease per provider
  • Recurrence after successful adenosine termination — especially within minutes; suggests triggering focus (atrial tachycardia) or re-engagement of accessory pathway; notify provider; anticipate repeat adenosine vs amiodarone load
  • WPW patient developing AFib with rapid VR — call code team STAT; prepare for DCCV; avoid AV nodal blockers

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. "Sawtooth" flutter pattern on 12-lead is pathognomonic for typical aflutter — leads II, III, aVF show the classic undulating baseline. If you see it, you've diagnosed it. Document immediately and show the provider.

  2. Adenosine's brief asystole scares everyone on first use — warn the patient before pushing: "You may feel your heart skip and chest pressure for a moment — this is expected and safe." Brief AV block is the mechanism; resolves in < 5 seconds.

  3. Adenosine is diagnostic in aflutter — if rhythm doesn't convert but flutter waves become crystal clear, you've confirmed aflutter and guided the next step (rate control vs DCCV vs ablation).

  4. Overdrive pacing via atrial epicardial wires is elegant for aflutter/SVT — know the wires are there and functional (document sensing/capture thresholds daily). A provider-directed trial can convert aflutter without sedation and without DCCV energy.

  5. Aflutter carries the same stroke risk as AF — CHA₂DS₂-VASc applies. Do not default to "aflutter is benign." If > 48 hr or CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2, the anticoag conversation must happen.

  6. DCCV energy is LOWER for aflutter (50–100 J) than for AF (100–200 J) — aflutter's organized reentry responds to lower energy. Start at 50 J; escalate if needed.

  7. Modified Valsalva (REVERT trial) is syringe blow + legs up — superior to regular Valsalva — blow against 40 mmHg for 15 seconds, then immediately lie flat + elevate legs 90 degrees for 45 seconds. Roughly 2× more effective.

  8. DO NOT give adenosine to WPW + AFib with rapid VR — adenosine can paradoxically accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway, precipitating VF. This is a code situation; call team STAT, prepare DCCV.

  9. Diltiazem drops BP more than metoprolol — use metoprolol first if borderline hypotensive. Watch for rebound tachycardia on diltiazem drip wean.

  10. Amiodarone hypotension is common (~25%) — anticipate with a fluid plan; decrease drip to 0.5 mg/min early when BP trends down rather than chasing a falling BP.

  11. Distinguish AVNRT from AVRT by retrograde P wave timing — AVNRT = P buried in QRS or pseudo-R' in V1; AVRT = P in ST segment. This distinction guides ablation planning post-op.

  12. Lewis lead (modified lead III, right sternal border) can reveal buried atrial activity — if flutter waves are subtle on standard 12-lead, ask for Lewis lead.

  13. RF ablation is highly effective for atypical aflutter — post-ablation/MAZE patients with flutter should be evaluated for ablation once stable; cure rates > 90%.

  14. AFL with 2:1 conduction at HR ~150 exactly is a red flag — 2:1 AV conduction is classic; HR of exactly 150 should trigger suspicion. Obtain 12-lead immediately; look for flutter waves.

  15. Avoid adenosine with severe asthma/COPD — use diltiazem or esmolol instead. Adenosine-induced bronchospasm can be severe and refractory.

  16. Check for WPW on baseline (sinus) ECG — delta wave = pre-excitation = potential for AVRT + accessory pathway. Knowing this pre-op guides drug choices and alerts you to avoid adenosine in AFib context.

  17. Atrial tachycardia (focal) is harder to terminate and ablate — doesn't convert to adenosine like AVNRT/AVRT; requires EP study + mapping for localization. If you see this, notify provider early.

  18. MAZE patients transitioning through aflutter weeks post-op is EXPECTED — this is not failure; scar tissue is maturing. Rate control + amiodarone; don't panic over rhythm changes.

  19. Post-AF ablation patients are at risk for atypical aflutter — CTI ablation for typical aflutter is standard; atypical circuits can emerge in weeks/months. Consider EP follow-up if recurrent post-discharge.

cards.title: AKI / Oliguria
cards.quickAnswer: UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/hr sustained ≥ 6 h OR serum Cr rise ≥ 0.3 mg/dL in 48 h = KDIGO Stage 1 AKI (Nadim et al., 2018). Assess volume status (legs, JVP, CVP). Hold nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE-I/ARB if dehydrated, contrast). Maintain MAP ≥ 65. Hyperkalemia is the urgent complication—obtain ECG and treat K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes or K ≥ 6.5 without ECG changes immediately with calcium gluconate, insulin + dextrose, and albuterol. CSA-AKI occurs in 20–40% of cardiac surgery patients.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — what this is and who gets it.

  • Definition: Acute kidney injury (AKI) post-cardiac surgery is characterized by oliguria (UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/hr) or rising serum creatinine in the first 2–7 days after cardiac surgery, confirmed by KDIGO staging.
  • Epidemiology: CSA-AKI occurs in 20–40% of cardiac surgery patients (Nadim et al., 2018). Increases length of stay 2–3× and mortality 3× at KDIGO Stage 3 (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).
  • Who this applies to: Every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient. Highest yield POD 0–3, but can occur later as a late complication (sepsis, delayed contrast reaction).
  • Why it matters: Most common renal complication post-op cardiac surgery. Uncontrolled hyperkalemia is life-threatening; oliguria with fluid overload requires CRRT planning. Early recognition improves outcomes.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardiac surgery triggers multiple simultaneous renal injury mechanisms. CSA-AKI is almost always multifactorial:

  • Ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury on CPB: Non-pulsatile flow, hypothermia, and hemodilution during bypass cause tubular epithelial injury and inflammatory cascade activation (Nadim et al., 2018).
  • Hemolysis and myoglobinuria: Free hemoglobin and myoglobin precipitate in renal tubules, causing acute tubular necrosis (ATN). Look for cola-colored urine and elevated indirect bilirubin, LDH.
  • Intra-operative hypotension: Renal perfusion pressure drop, especially if MAP < 55 mmHg × prolonged interval during surgery.
  • Systemic inflammation: Bypass triggers complement activation, cytokine release, and endothelial injury, worsening tubular damage.
  • Contrast nephropathy: Delayed onset (peak Cr at 48–72 h) if intra-op or pre-op CTA, coronary catheterization, or aortography performed.
  • Medication nephrotoxicity: NSAIDs, ACE-I/ARB in volume-depleted state, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B.

Risk factors: Age > 70, prior AKI, pre-op Cr ≥ 1.5, left ventricular ejection fraction < 35%, CPB time > 180 min, emergency surgery (Nadim et al., 2018).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following:

  • Oliguria: UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/hr sustained > 6–12 h post-op
  • Creatinine rise: ≥ 0.3 mg/dL from baseline in first 48 h, OR ≥ 1.5× baseline Cr
  • Anuria: No urine output × ≥ 2 h post-op (always abnormal; rule out Foley obstruction immediately)
  • Dark or cola-colored urine (hemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria)
  • Rising potassium with or without UOP change (hyperkalemia risk in AKI)
  • Metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.35) developing post-op with oliguria
  • Weight gain > 2 kg in 24 h with UOP drop (fluid overload, pulmonary edema risk)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs & perfusion: HR, BP, MAP, SpO₂, capillary refill, skin temperature, mental status
  • Symptoms: fatigue, dyspnea, chest discomfort, palpitations, lightheadedness
  • Volume status exam:
  • Jugular venous pressure (elevated = overloaded; flat = depleted)
  • Bilateral leg edema (pitting, warmth, perfusion)
  • CVP line if available (goal 5–8 mmHg post-op cardiac patient)
  • Lung auscultation (crackles = pulmonary edema)
  • Urine output and quality: Color (clear, straw, dark, cola-colored), volume, trend hourly
  • Foley catheter: Patent, kinked, clamped, clotted? Position?
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Cr, BUN, Cl, CO₂, Mg²⁺, iCa²⁺, Hgb, lactate; baseline pre-op Cr if available
  • MAR review: NSAIDs given? ACE-I/ARB restarted? Vancomycin or aminoglycoside on board? Last doses?
  • Surgery context: Type of procedure, CPB time, intra-op complications, blood loss, transfusions, contrast exposure

sections.heading: 5A. Stable Oliguria path
sections.bodyHtml:
(UOP low, K < 6.0, no respiratory distress, MAP > 65, no ECG changes.)

  1. Verify oliguria is real — do not act on a single low hour

    • Bladder scan immediately (if > 300 mL, retention is culprit)
    • Flush Foley per protocol or replace if obstructed; inspect for kinks or clots
    • Recheck UOP over next 2–4 h; re-assess before escalating

  2. Assess and document volume status

    • Palpate JVP (elevated vs flat)
    • Examine legs for edema, warmth, perfusion
    • Check CVP line if available
    • Trend I/O hourly; daily weights
    • Auscultate lungs for crackles (pulmonary edema)

  3. Order STAT labs

    • BMP: K⁺, Cr, BUN, Cl, CO₂, bicarb (baseline for comparison)
    • CBC: Hgb, Hct (drop suggests bleeding or hemolysis)
    • Urinalysis: RBCs, WBCs, casts, eosinophils, color, specific gravity
    • Urine electrolytes: Calculate fractional excretion of sodium (FeNa), FeUrea to distinguish prerenal from ATN
    • Lactate, troponin

  4. Hold nephrotoxins — notify provider before restarting

    • NSAIDs: hold immediately (contraindicated post-op AKI)
    • ACE-I/ARB: verify volume status; hold if dehydrated + Cr rising
    • Aminoglycosides: check trough level; extend interval if CrCl < 50
    • Vancomycin: target trough 15–20 µg/mL; adjust dosing per renal function

  5. Optimize perfusion — maintain MAP ≥ 65

    • Check current BP and vasopressor support
    • If euvolemic and oliguric: cautious fluid trial → 250–500 mL crystalloid bolus over 1 h; recheck UOP and JVP
    • Do NOT bolus if: lung crackles, elevated JVP, pulmonary edema evident

  6. Notify APP/MD with volume assessment, K level, Cr trend, meds held, and your recommendation

    • Request nephrology consult if: Stage 2–3 AKI, K rising trend, metabolic acidosis, or hemoglobinuria
    • Monitor continuously; re-assess q1–2h if Stage 1 AKI

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable Oliguria path
sections.bodyHtml:
(K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes, OR K ≥ 6.5 without ECG changes; anuria; respiratory distress from overload; altered mental status.)

STAT actions in parallel (not sequential):

  1. Hyperkalemia emergency protocol — call STAT MD + charge nurse

    • STAT 12-lead ECG (peaked T waves, widened QRS, prolonged PR, sine wave pattern?)
    • If K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes OR K ≥ 6.5 without ECG changes — treat immediately:

    • Calcium gluconate: 1 g (10 mL of 10% solution) IV push over 2–5 min; stabilizes cardiac membrane (does NOT lower K); may repeat q5–10 min × 2 if ECG worsening
    • Insulin + Dextrose: 10 units regular insulin IV, then 25 g dextrose (D50); shifts K intracellularly (onset 10–20 min, duration 4–6 h)
    • Albuterol: 10–20 mg nebulized; additional K shift (onset 30 min, duration 2–4 h)
    • Kayexalate or Lokelma: 15–30 g kayexalate PO/PR OR Lokelma 10 g PO (removes K; newer agent, faster/more reliable than kayexalate)

  2. Volume overload + respiratory distress

    • Position upright if tolerated
    • Oxygen to SpO₂ ≥ 92%
    • Diuretic trial (furosemide) only if UOP present AND MAP ≥ 65 (do NOT force if anuric)
    • Prepare for ICU transfer if worsening

  3. STAT labs while stabilizing - BMP, ABG, CBC, lactate, troponin, urine microscopy

  4. Rule out urinary retention

    • If anuric: bedside bladder scan or catheterize Foley
    • Send urine for urinalysis + culture

  5. Activate Rapid Response / ICU team

    • AKI Stage 3 + hemodynamic instability = ICU level of care
    • Nephrology STAT consult for CRRT evaluation
    • CRRT indications mnemonic (AEIOU): Acidosis (pH < 7.20), Electrolytes (K > 6.5 uncontrolled), Ingestion (certain toxins), Overload (pulmonary edema + oliguria), Uremia (confusion, pericarditis, bleeding)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed oliguria/AKI at [time]. UOP [value] mL/hr, baseline Cr [value], current Cr [value]. K [value], pH [value]. [Volume status: flat JVP vs elevated; edema; lung sounds]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Symptoms]. [Meds held: NSAIDs / ACE-I / etc.]." R: "Requesting [nephrology consult / CRRT evaluation / additional labs / ICU transfer]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Oliguria + stable, Stage 1 AKI Primary APP / on-call fellow
Oliguria + Cr rising, suspected ATN APP + nephrology consult (non-urgent)
K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes, OR K ≥ 6.5 STAT APP/fellow + ICU team + nephrology STAT
Anuria × ≥ 2 h + hemodynamic instability STAT ICU + rapid response + nephrology
Stage 3 AKI (Cr ≥ 3× baseline or anuria ≥ 24 h) STAT ICU + nephrology for CRRT
Pulmonary edema + respiratory distress STAT APP + ICU + respiratory therapy
Metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.20) worsening STAT APP + ICU + labs
Dark urine + hemolysis labs STAT APP + nephrology for hemoglobin-induced ATN management

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections in Section 7 are — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Prerenal vs. Intrinsic vs. Postrenal AKI
sections.bodyHtml:
Understanding the bucket is the key to targeted management.

Prerenal AKI (most common post-op, usually reversible)

  • Cause: Volume depletion, bleeding, low cardiac output (cardiogenic shock), sepsis with vasodilation, abdominal compartment syndrome
  • Urine findings: FeNa < 1% (or FeUrea < 35%), BUN:Cr ratio > 20:1, U/Osm > 500 mOsm/kg, U Na < 20 mEq/L
  • Tubular cells: Intact; no casts or minimal granular casts
  • Management: Fluid resuscitation, address bleeding/shock, optimize perfusion pressure
  • Prognosis: Usually reverses within hours to days of correction

Intrinsic Renal (ATN from I/R, hemolysis, nephrotoxins)

  • Ischemic ATN: Tubular epithelial cell necrosis from hypoperfusion + reperfusion on CPB
  • Toxic ATN: Myoglobin/hemoglobin precipitation, drug metabolites (aminoglycosides, contrast, amphotericin)
  • Urine findings: FeNa > 2% (or FeUrea > 50%), BUN:Cr < 20:1, U/Osm < 350 mOsm/kg, U Na > 40 mEq/L
  • Tubular cells: Epithelial cell casts, "muddy brown" granular casts on microscopy (hallmark)
  • Course: Takes 1–3 weeks to recover; diuretic-resistant
  • Management: Supportive care; address underlying toxin; volume management careful; RRT if needed

Postrenal (obstructive)

  • Cause: Foley obstruction (clot, kink, malposition), ureteral stricture, bilateral obstruction
  • Assessment: Bladder scan > 300 mL, anuria in post-op immediately after Foley placement
  • Immediate action: Flush or replace Foley catheter; if persistent anuria → renal ultrasound or CT for bilateral obstruction

sections.heading: 7.2 KDIGO Staging for Acute Kidney Injury
sections.bodyHtml:
Table-first reference for staging and escalation triggers.

Stage Creatinine Criteria Urine Output Criteria Clinical Significance
1 (mild) 1.5–1.9× baseline OR Cr rise ≥ 0.3 mg/dL in 48 h < 0.5 mL/kg/h × 6–12 h Stable intervention: fluid optimization, nephrotoxin review, close monitoring
2 (moderate) 2.0–2.9× baseline < 0.5 mL/kg/h × ≥ 12 h Escalation: nephrology consult, labs q6–12h, prep for CRRT discussion
3 (severe) ≥ 3× baseline OR Cr ≥ 4.0 mg/dL OR RRT initiated < 0.3 mL/kg/h × ≥ 24 h OR anuria ≥ 12 h Urgent: CRRT likely indicated; ICU level of care; frequent reassessment

Use baseline pre-op Cr. If unavailable, estimate from pre-op eGFR or use population norm (alert nephrology to clarify baseline).

sections.heading: 7.3 Cardiac Surgery-Associated AKI (CSA-AKI) Mechanism
sections.bodyHtml:
Why cardiac surgery causes AKI — four simultaneous insults:

  1. Ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) on CPB

    • Non-pulsatile flow, hypothermia, hemodilution
    • Tubular epithelial cell injury; inflammatory cytokine release
    • Peak injury at 24–48 h; recovery 1–3 weeks

  2. Hemolysis and myoglobinuria

    • CPB causes mechanical hemolysis of RBCs
    • Free hemoglobin + myoglobin from muscle injury precipitate in renal tubules
    • Myoglobin-induced ATN requires aggressive hydration + alkaline urine (sodium bicarbonate, target urine pH > 6.5)
    • Look for: cola-colored urine, elevated LDH, elevated indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin

  3. Intra-operative hypotension

    • Renal perfusion pressure (mean arterial pressure − renal venous pressure) must be adequate
    • CPB nadir often drops MAP < 55 mmHg; sustained hypotension increases AKI risk
    • Combined with non-pulsatile flow = severe renal vasoconstriction

  4. Systemic inflammation

    • Bypass triggers complement cascade, inflammatory cytokine surge (IL-6, TNF-α)
    • Endothelial injury increases vascular permeability; fluid shifts into third space
    • Contributes to oliguria even with adequate perfusion pressure

sections.heading: 7.4 Nephrotoxic Medications — post-op cardiac surgery context
sections.bodyHtml:
Drug Class Agent Mechanism Post-Op Caution Management
NSAIDs Ibuprofen, ketorolac, indomethacin Inhibit prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriole dilation; reduce GFR in volume-depleted state NEVER in post-op AKI trajectory — even one dose can convert Stage 1 → Stage 2 Hold absolutely; document hold; flag on medication reconciliation
ACE-I/ARB Lisinopril, losartan, enalapril, valsartan Reduce efferent arteriole tone; dangerous if dehydrated Hold if Cr rising + JVP flat / legs dry; dangerous combo: ACE-I on POD 1 + dehydration Restart only after volume stabilized; verify with team; dosed per CrCl
Aminoglycosides Gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin Cumulative tubular toxicity; renally cleared; nephrotoxic accumulation if doses not extended Check trough level before second dose; extend dosing interval if CrCl < 50 Extended interval dosing (e.g., once daily instead of q8h); monitor levels q24h
Glycopeptides Vancomycin Nephrotoxic, especially if trough > 20 µg/mL; worsens with concurrent aminoglycosides Target trough 15–20 µg/mL; q12h dosing if CrCl 30–60, q24h if < 30 Therapeutic drug monitoring required; adjust interval, not dose
Amphotericin B Liposomal formulation preferred Direct tubular toxicity; osmotic stress on renal tubules Minimize use; prefer liposomal over conventional Hydrate before/after infusion; monitor Cr daily if used
Contrast agents Iopamidol, iohexol, iosomide (low-osmolar or iso-osmolar) Osmotic stress + direct tubular injury; delayed peak Cr at 48–72 h Delay elective contrast studies if Cr already rising post-op Hydrate pre-/post-procedure; avoid repeat contrast within 48–72 h

sections.heading: 7.5 Hyperkalemia Emergency Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Potassium > 6.0 mEq/L in the oliguric post-op patient is immediately life-threatening (Nadim et al., 2018).

Mechanism of hyperkalemia in AKI:

  • Oliguria prevents renal excretion of daily K load (~40–60 mEq/day from diet + catabolism)
  • Tissue catabolism + hemolysis release intracellular K into serum
  • Acidosis (low pH) drives K out of cells into serum (1 K rises ~0.6 mEq/L for each 0.1 pH drop)

ECG progression (do NOT delay treatment for ECG):

  • Peaked T waves (earliest sign; T base narrowing)
  • PR interval prolongation
  • QRS complex widening
  • P wave loss or flattening
  • Sine wave pattern (pre-arrest rhythm)
  • Asystole or ventricular fibrillation

Treatment priorities (all happen in parallel):

  1. Membrane stabilization — protects heart; does NOT lower K - Calcium gluconate: 1 g (10 mL 10% solution) IV push over 2–5 min - Onset 1–3 min; duration 30–60 min - May repeat q5–10 min × 2 if ECG worsening or recurrent peaked T's - Explain to team: "Calcium stabilizes the heart membrane while we work on removing potassium."

  2. K shift into cells — lasts 4–6 h; buys time, not definitive removal - Insulin 10 units regular IV + D50 25 g IV (or 500 mL D10 if concern about volume)

    • Onset 10–20 min, peaks 30–60 min; last 4–6 h
    • Monitor fingerstick glucose q30 min × 4–6 h (hypoglycemia risk)
    • Have dextrose at bedside; repeat serum K in 30–60 min to assess response
    • Albuterol 10–20 mg nebulized (additional shift mechanism)
    • Onset 30 min, duration 2–4 h

  3. K removal from body — definitive, but slower - Kayexalate (sodium polystyrene sulfonate): 15–30 g PO q6h or 50 g PR once - Slow onset (6–24 h); ineffective if ileus present; volume load with sorbitol - Lokelma (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) 10 g PO q6h (newer agent; faster onset than kayexalate, less volume)

    • CRRT / Dialysis: Only truly definitive removal mechanism
    • Coordinate with nephrology STAT; dialysis can remove 50–100 mEq K in a single session

Monitoring after insulin + D50:

  • Fingerstick glucose q30 min × 4–6 h minimum (hypoglycemia can be as dangerous as hyperkalemia)
  • Serum K recheck in 30–60 min to assess response
  • ECG 30 min after treatment to assess T wave changes
  • If anuric + K persists > 6.0 despite medical management: dialysis is inevitable; plan early

sections.heading: 7.6 Special subgroups & edge cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-IABP or mechanical support patients

  • IABP malposition can cause renal artery occlusion and ischemic AKI
  • Confirm placement on imaging if AKI develops acutely after IABP insertion
  • Vascular surgery may need to evaluate for aortic atherosclerotic disease causing shearing

Post-TAAA (thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm) surgery

  • Triple insult: renal artery coverage during repair, spinal cord ischemia, mesenteric ischemia
  • Expect severe AKI; coordinate with vascular surgery on ischemic time and perfusion strategy
  • High rate of CRRT requirement; nephrology involvement mandatory

Abdominal compartment syndrome (post-op ileus + gross distention)

  • Intra-abdominal pressure compression reduces renal perfusion pressure acutely
  • Measure intra-abdominal pressure via Foley manometry (bladder pressure > 20 cm H₂O is abnormal)
  • Decompress abdomen or escalate for surgical evaluation

Contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN)

  • Delayed Cr rise at 24–72 h post-contrast exposure (CTA, coronary cath, aortography)
  • Expect peak Cr rise around POD 2–3, then downward trend if mild injury
  • Prevention: hydration pre-/post-procedure, minimize contrast volume, avoid repeat contrast within 48–72 h
  • Metformin: hold if eGFR < 30 or acute AKI risk (restart after Cr stabilizes)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear in stable patients, re-escalate.

  • K trending upward: 5.2 → 5.6 → 6.0 (exponential rise suggests urgent K removal, not just intracellular shift)
  • Rising lactate despite fluid resuscitation: Tissue hypoperfusion or sepsis superimposed on AKI (ominous combination)
  • Widening anion-gap metabolic acidosis: pH < 7.30 + gap > 12; indicates metabolic derangement beyond simple oliguria; risk of cardiac dysrhythmia
  • Worsening volume overload + hypoxia: Pulmonary edema + rising Cr + inability to diurese = ICU/CRRT decision point
  • New altered mental status: Confusion, restlessness, decreased responsiveness (etiology: uremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia, sepsis); escalate immediately
  • Pericardial rub on auscultation: Uremic pericarditis (friction rub); indicates severe uremia; ICU-level urgency
  • Bleeding signs: Oozing from wounds, hematochezia, melena (uremia impairs platelet function; watch chest tubes and drains closely)
  • Hemoglobinuria (dark/cola-colored urine): Hemolysis on pump; obtain Hgb, hematocrit, indirect bilirubin, LDH, reticulocyte count; prepare for aggressive hydration + urine alkalinization
  • Progressive anuria despite fluid resuscitation: Suggests intrinsic AKI, not prerenal; likely needs CRRT
  • Hypotension unresponsive to fluids: May indicate septic shock superimposed on AKI; obtain blood cultures, start broad-spectrum antibiotics per protocol

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. UOP drop is the early canary; Cr rise is the late marker. Monitor UOP and Cr trends hourly starting POD 0. A 0.3 mg/dL Cr rise in 48 h = KDIGO Stage 1 AKI even if UOP appears okay. Early recognition unlocks better outcomes.

  2. Always bladder scan before calling it oliguria — clamped, kinked, or clotted Foley is the most common mimic. 20% of apparent "oliguria" in the first 6 h post-op is urinary retention from Foley obstruction. Scan, flush, or replace the catheter immediately.

  3. Dark cola-colored urine = hemoglobinuria from hemolysis on pump. Obtain plasma-free hemoglobin, haptoglobin, LDH, indirect bilirubin, reticulocyte count. Hemoglobin-induced ATN requires aggressive hydration + alkaline urine target (sodium bicarbonate, urine pH > 6.5); coordinate with nephrology.

  4. Volume-depleted patients look and feel dry: flat JVP, cool periphery, dry mucous membranes, tachycardia. A cautious 250 mL bolus is both a therapeutic trial and diagnostic test. If UOP improves within 1–2 h and JVP rises slightly, the kidney was prerenal.

  5. NSAIDs are never okay in post-op cardiac patients with AKI trajectory. Even one dose of ketorolac in a dehydrated post-CABG patient can convert Stage 1 → Stage 2 AKI. Flag on medication reconciliation; document hold.

  6. ACE-I/ARB on POD 1 in a dehydrated patient is a dangerous combination. Verify with team before restarting in setting of Cr rise + low UOP. Common prescribing error.

  7. Vancomycin trough and aminoglycoside levels matter — check BEFORE dosing, not after. Empiric q8h vancomycin dosing in renal failure leads to toxic troughs (> 25 µg/mL) and worsening kidney injury. Extend intervals based on CrCl.

  8. Contrast-induced AKI is delayed — expect peak Cr at POD 2–3 post-CTA. Prevent volume overload with careful I/O tracking and judicious diuresis. If Cr is already rising, delay elective contrast studies.

  9. Abdominal compartment syndrome compresses the renal vasculature. Measure intra-abdominal pressure via Foley manometry if post-op ileus with gross distention suspected (bladder pressure > 20 cm H₂O abnormal). Decompress or escalate.

  10. Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) can cause renal ischemia from malposition or aortic atherosclerotic disease. If AKI develops acutely after IABP insertion, confirm placement on imaging; vascular surgery may need to evaluate for aortic shearing.

  11. Hyperkalemia ECG is life-or-death interpretation: peaked T's → PR prolongation → QRS widening → sine wave → asystole. Treat K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes or K ≥ 6.5 without ECG changes immediately. Do NOT wait for ECG to treat.

  12. Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac membrane but does NOT lower K. It buys 30–60 min while insulin/albuterol and dialysis work. Explain to patient and team: "Protecting the heart right now; removing the potassium next."

  13. Insulin + D50 + albuterol shift K intracellularly for a few hours — they BUY TIME, not fix the problem. Kayexalate, Lokelma, and dialysis are the actual removal mechanisms. If anuric and K rising, dialysis is inevitable; plan it early.

  14. Monitor fingerstick glucose q30 min after insulin + D50 for at least 4–6 h — hypoglycemia can be as dangerous as hyperkalemia. Have dextrose at bedside; recheck serum glucose 1–2 h after bolus.

  15. Nephrology sees post-op nursing notes more closely than the APP sometimes. Document volume status clearly: JVP height, leg edema, CVP if available, I/O trend, daily weights, MAP, sedation level, exact medication times, and urine color/quality. Good documentation guides better decisions.

cards.title: Anaphylaxis
cards.quickAnswer: EPINEPHRINE IM 0.3–0.5 mg (1:1000), lateral thigh, IMMEDIATELY — nothing else matters. Repeat every 5–15 minutes if needed. Establish IV access; give normal saline 1–2 L bolus if hypotensive; secure airway if angioedema threatens. Adjuncts after epi (NOT instead): H1 blocker (diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV), H2 blocker (famotidine 20 mg IV), steroids (methylprednisolone 125 mg IV), albuterol for bronchospasm. If on beta-blockers and refractory: glucagon 1–5 mg IV. Observe 4–6 hours post-resolution for biphasic recurrence (5–20% of cases).
