sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, and clinical context.

  • Definition: Rapid, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction mediated by IgE-mast cell degranulation (classical) or direct mast cell activation (non-IgE). Involves two or more organ systems within minutes to 1 hour of trigger exposure.
  • Incidence: 1–2 per 10,000 persons per year in the general population; higher in perioperative settings (estimated 1 per 10,000 procedures for anesthesia).
  • Who this applies to: any ICU or perioperative patient with acute onset cutaneous, respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal symptoms after medication infusion, blood product transfusion, contrast exposure, or perioperative manipulation.
  • Why it matters: anaphylaxis is one of the most time-critical diagnoses in medicine. Delay in epinephrine administration is the #1 preventable death cause. Mortality without treatment approaches 30%; with immediate epi, < 1%.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Anaphylaxis represents a convergence of mast cell and basophil mediator release. Classical IgE-mediated anaphylaxis occurs when an allergen cross-links IgE bound to high-affinity receptors on mast cell surfaces, triggering immediate cascading release of:

  • Histamine — causes urticaria, pruritis, vascular permeability, bronchospasm, hypotension
  • Tryptase — serine protease; same effects as histamine; measurable in serum post-event
  • Leukotrienes (C4, D4, E4) — potent bronchoconstrictor and vasodilator; drives airway edema and shock
  • Prostaglandins and platelet-activating factor (PAF) — amplify hypotension, bronchoconstriction, thrombosis

Timeline: onset typically minutes to 1 hour from allergen exposure; peak symptoms within 5–30 minutes.

Non-IgE-mediated mechanisms (e.g., vancomycin "red man syndrome," some contrast reactions) involve direct mast cell activation or complement cascade activation without IgE involvement; often reversible with slower infusion rates.

Biphasic anaphylaxis: 5–20% of cases experience recurrence of symptoms 1–72 hours after initial resolution and treatment. Second wave may be more severe than the first. Mechanism remains unclear; hypotheses include delayed mediator release, recruitment of eosinophils/neutrophils, or reformation of IgE–antigen complexes. Mandatory observation post-resolution.

Why epinephrine is the single most critical intervention:

  • Alpha-1 effects: vasoconstriction reverses hypotension and shock, restores coronary/cerebral perfusion
  • Beta-2 effects: bronchodilation, suppression of further mast cell degranulation
  • Direct mast cell stabilization, preventing further mediator release
  • Antihistamines, steroids, fluids are adjuncts and DO NOT replace epi

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — observable signs and timing.

Triggers in the ICU and perioperative setting:

Category Examples Notes
Antibiotics Vancomycin, penicillins, cephalosporins, sulfonamides Vancomycin "red man" is often infusion-rate histamine release (NOT IgE anaphylaxis); slow infusion and premedicate. True IgE anaphylaxis rare.
Latex Gloves, catheters (Foley, central lines), tourniquet, ECG pads Ubiquitous in OR, ICU. Sensitized patients can react within minutes of exposure.
Iodinated contrast Radiographic contrast media Incidence up to 3% of exposed patients; premedication (steroids + antihistamine) reduces recurrence to < 1%.
Protamine Heparin reversal post-CPB Rare but highly lethal. Known cross-reactivity with fish allergy.
Blood products Packed RBC, FFP, platelets, IVIG Risk higher in multiply transfused or IgA-deficient patients.
Chlorhexidine Central line dressing, skin prep, oral rinse Rising incidence of IgE sensitization. Cross-reactivity with other biguanides.

Clinical presentation (any combination):

  • Cutaneous: urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema of lips/face/throat
  • Respiratory: wheezing, stridor, dyspnea, laryngeal edema, hypoxia
  • Cardiovascular: hypotension, syncope, altered mental status, shock, cardiac arrhythmia
  • Gastrointestinal: cramping, vomiting, diarrhea, involuntary defecation

Diagnostic criteria (World Allergy Organization): Anaphylaxis is highly likely when any of the following occur:

  1. Acute onset (minutes to 1 hour) of skin/mucosal findings (urticaria, pruritus, flushing) OR respiratory compromise OR hypotension, in a patient with likely allergen exposure
  2. Two or more of: skin/mucosal, respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal involvement after likely allergen exposure
  3. Hypotension alone after known allergen exposure in a susceptible patient

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (1–2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs: heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, respiratory rate, temperature, perfusion (capillary refill, skin color and temperature)
  • Observe symptoms: wheeze, stridor, dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, syncope, confusion, anxiety
  • Examine skin: urticaria distribution, flushing, angioedema location (lips, tongue, face, throat, airway threat?)
  • Assess airway: phonation quality, drooling, ability to swallow saliva, neck stiffness, voice change, stridor
  • Review trigger timeline: what infusion was running? When did symptoms start relative to medication/blood product administration? Recent latex exposure? Contrast procedure timing?
  • Check allergy history: documented allergies in chart? What was the reaction type (rash, respiratory, shock, anaphylaxis)?
  • Note atopy history: eczema, asthma, seasonal allergies, food allergies? Higher baseline mast cell load.
  • Assess medication list: patient on beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol, other)? Beta-blockade makes anaphylaxis more severe and refractory.
  • Assess trajectory: is this worsening in real-time? Progressive wheeze? Dropping BP? Spreading urticaria?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Mild systemic symptoms — localized urticaria, mild wheeze, NO hypotension, NO airway compromise, normal mental status.)

  1. GIVE EPINEPHRINE IM 0.3–0.5 mg (1:1000) in lateral thigh immediately — do NOT delay even if mild - Draw from multi-dose vial or use auto-injector (EpiPen 0.3 mg if available; if re-dosing needed q 5–15 min, use multi-dose vial of 1:1000)
    • Inject into vastus lateralis muscle (mid-outer thigh), NOT subcutaneous, NOT IV
    • Document time, dose, site
    • Establish IV access — two large-bore IVs if possible
    • Place on continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitor
    • Assess airway closely — if ANY angioedema developing, escalate to 5B immediately
    • Give normal saline 1–2 L bolus IV if systolic BP trending downward or is < 90 mmHg
    • Administer adjuncts AFTER epi given:
      • H1 blocker: diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV
      • H2 blocker: famotidine 20 mg IV
      • Steroid: methylprednisolone 125 mg IV or hydrocortisone 200 mg IV (does not treat acute reaction but may reduce biphasic recurrence)
      • Albuterol nebulized 2.5–5 mg if bronchospasm present
      • Identify and STOP the trigger immediately — discontinue infusion, remove latex gloves, cover chlorhexidine exposure, etc.
      • Document trigger in chart and update allergy armband for future reference
      • NOTIFY APP/on-call provider and Rapid Response Team STAT — even mild presentations can progress to biphasic anaphylaxis
      • Observe minimum 4–6 hours post-symptom resolution in ICU-level setting with continuous monitoring; longer for severe or refractory cases

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension, airway compromise, severe respiratory distress, altered mental status, shock.)

  1. STAT call APP/fellow + activate Rapid Response Code — do NOT leave room unattended
  2. GIVE EPINEPHRINE IM 0.3–0.5 mg (1:1000) lateral thigh IMMEDIATELY
    • This is the single most critical action. Delay kills.
    • Can repeat every 5–15 minutes based on response; consider IV transition after 1–2 IM doses if refractory
    • Place on continuous monitoring: cardiac, SpO₂, blood pressure (preferably arterial line if available)
    • Establish two large-bore IV lines immediately — expect difficult access in shock state
    • Fluid resuscitation: start normal saline wide-open, prepare 2–4 L aggressive bolus if hypotensive
    • Prepare for IV epinephrine: if refractory to IM doses (still hypotensive after 1–2 doses) or rapidly deteriorating:
    • Mix epi drip: 1 mg epinephrine (1:1000) in 250 mL normal saline = 4 mcg/mL concentration
    • Start at 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min IV, titrate upward to 0.5 mcg/kg/min as needed for MAP/HR response
    • Requires continuous hemodynamic monitoring (ideal: ICU transfer for central line, arterial line)
    • Airway assessment and preparation:
    • If angioedema present, assume rapid progression
    • Do NOT delay intubation waiting for worsening — laryngeal edema progresses exponentially fast
    • Pre-oxygenate with 100% O₂, prepare suction, have difficult airway cart ready
    • Consider early fiberoptic or surgical airway if pharyngeal/laryngeal edema is severe
    • Administer adjuncts AFTER epi given:
    • Diphenhydramine 25–50 mg IV (can give concurrent with epi)
    • Famotidine 20 mg IV
    • Methylprednisolone 125 mg or hydrocortisone 200 mg IV
    • If patient on beta-blocker and anaphylaxis refractory to epi: give glucagon 1–5 mg IV bolus (can repeat q 5 min, or start drip 1–4 mg/hr); glucagon bypasses beta-blockade by increasing cAMP via non-adrenergic pathway
    • Send STAT labs: CBC, CMP, troponin, lactate, ABG, tryptase (if available — mast cell marker, elevated in anaphylaxis confirms diagnosis post-hoc)
    • Stop the trigger immediately — discontinue infusion, remove IV, change gloves, cover chlorhexidine
    • Document aggressively: time of onset, trigger identified, epi dose(s) and time(s), vital sign trajectory, response to treatment, labs, ICU transfer details
    • Prepare for ICU transfer if not already there — arrange for refractory anaphylaxis, airway intervention, continuous epi infusion, hemodynamic monitoring

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room]." B: "Patient developed acute onset [skin/respiratory/CV symptoms] at [time], approximately [time interval] after [trigger: antibiotic/contrast/latex/protamine/blood product/other]. Currently HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. Has received epi [dose/time]." A: "Patient is [stable/unstable]. [Current status: wheeze, BP trending, angioedema severity?]. On home beta-blockers? [Yes/No]." R: "Requesting [continued management / transfer to ICU / additional epi doses / airway backup / additional labs]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Any anaphylaxis suspected, even mild APP/on-call provider + Rapid Response Team (all patients)
Unstable (hypotension, airway, severe respiratory) STAT Code + APP/fellow + RRT immediately
Airway angioedema progressing Anesthesia + ENT (airway backup) + prepare for intubation
Refractory to IM epi (still hypotensive after 1–2 doses) ICU attending + prepare ICU transfer + plan IV epi drip
Contrast-induced reaction Radiology notified + add premed protocol for future
Protamine reaction (known fish allergy history) Cardiac surgery team (cross-reactivity known) + ensure slow infusion protocol

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections in Section 7 are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Mast cell mediators and pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
The clinical manifestations of anaphylaxis stem from four principal mediators:

  • Histamine (stored in mast cell granules; released within seconds to minutes)
  • Binds H1 receptors → urticaria, pruritis, vascular permeability (shock), bronchospasm
  • Binds H2 receptors → gastric acid inhibition, but also some cardiac effects

  • Antihistamines (H1/H2 blockers) provide symptom relief but do NOT replace epi

  • Tryptase and other serine proteases (released along with histamine)

  • Serum tryptase level is measurable 15 minutes to 3 hours post-symptom onset and confirms mast cell degranulation
  • Elevated tryptase (> 11.4 ng/mL) is consistent with anaphylaxis; normal tryptase does not rule it out

  • Useful for post-hoc diagnosis and documentation, NOT for acute treatment decisions

  • Leukotrienes (C4, D4, E4) (newly synthesized after IgE cross-linking; released over 5–10 minutes)

  • Potent bronchoconstrictor; drives lower airway obstruction and laryngeal edema
  • Not directly blocked by antihistamines; mainly affected by corticosteroids and leukotriene antagonists (long-term prevention)

  • Leukotriene effects explain why some anaphylaxis cases have predominantly respiratory rather than cardiovascular features

  • Platelet-activating factor (PAF) (newly synthesized)

  • Amplifies hypotension, bronchoconstriction, and thrombotic cascades
  • Contributes to shock and late-phase biphasic recurrence

Why epinephrine works:

  • Epi's alpha-1 effects cause immediate vasoconstriction, reverses vascular leak, restores perfusion pressure, prevents shock
  • Beta-2 effects cause bronchodilation and suppress further mediator release from mast cells
  • Acts within 1–5 minutes of IM injection; systemic epi effect seen in all tissues simultaneously

sections.heading: 7.2 Biphasic anaphylaxis and observation protocol
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition: Recurrence of anaphylactic symptoms 1–72 hours after initial onset and treatment, even after apparent complete resolution.

Incidence: 5–20% of all anaphylaxis cases; higher in severe presentations.

Clinical presentation of biphasic phase:

  • Often identical to first wave (cutaneous, respiratory, CV, GI)
  • May be more severe than first wave
  • May involve different organ systems (e.g., first wave: urticaria only; second wave: airway obstruction)

Proposed mechanisms:

  • Newly synthesized mediators (leukotrienes, PAF) released hours after initial event
  • Recruitment of eosinophils, neutrophils, and other inflammatory cells from circulation
  • Reformation of IgE–antigen complexes if allergen persists
  • Unclear why some patients biphasic and others not; severity of first wave and protamine reactions are risk factors

Observation protocol:

  • Minimum 4–6 hours of continuous monitoring post-symptom resolution in ICU or monitored bed
  • For severe anaphylaxis (cardiovascular instability, airway intervention required), extend to 8–12 hours or longer per provider judgment
  • If biphasic symptoms appear, repeat full anaphylaxis protocol (epi IM, supportive care, adjuncts)
  • Have epi readily accessible at bedside during entire observation period

sections.heading: 7.3 Beta-blocker modifier and glucagon rescue
sections.bodyHtml:
Problem: Patients on beta-blockers (metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol, labetalol, others) experience MORE SEVERE and MORE REFRACTORY anaphylaxis.

Mechanism:

  • Beta-blocker antagonism of epi's beta-2 effects: blunts bronchodilation and mast cell suppression
  • Leaves unopposed alpha-1 effects: paradoxical worsening of hypertension followed by refractoriness to further epi
  • Makes standard-dose epi IM appear less effective

Clinical clues:

  • Patient on home beta-blocker; anaphylaxis occurs
  • First-line epi dose given; minimal improvement
  • Continued respiratory distress, persistent hypotension despite epi and fluids

Management:

  • Escalate epi more aggressively (larger IM doses, shorter repeat intervals, earlier IV transition)
  • Primary treatment: Glucagon 1–5 mg IV bolus
  • Glucagon activates adenylyl cyclase via non-adrenergic (G-protein) pathway, increasing cAMP
  • Bypasses beta-blockade entirely
  • Can repeat IV bolus q 5 minutes, or start continuous drip 1–4 mg/hour for sustained effect
  • May cause hyperglycemia and nausea
  • Combine epi IV infusion + glucagon for optimal effect

sections.heading: 7.4 Protamine reaction subtypes and cross-reactivity
sections.bodyHtml:
Background: Protamine is used to reverse heparin after cardiopulmonary bypass. Anaphylaxis to protamine is rare (< 1% of exposed patients) but can be highly lethal.

Three types of protamine-heparin reactions (Levy classification):

Type Mechanism Clinical presentation Timeline Management
I IgE-mediated histamine release Transient hypotension, flushing, wheezing Minutes during infusion Slow infusion, give antihistamine pre-infusion next time
II Complement-mediated, thromboxane release Pulmonary hypertension, RV afterload crisis Delayed ~30 min post-infusion Inhaled nitric oxide, IV vasodilators, may resolve spontaneously
III True IgE anaphylaxis Full anaphylaxis: urticaria, airway, shock Minutes; can be severe and refractory Full epi protocol; highest mortality rate

Risk factors for protamine anaphylaxis:

  • Prior protamine exposure (sensitization)
  • Fish allergy (IMPORTANT: cross-reactivity with protamine is known; ~10–20% of fish-allergic patients will react to protamine)
  • Insulin history (neutral protamine Hagedorn [NPH] insulin exposure; contains protamine)
  • Male gender (higher incidence)

Prevention and management:

  • Always ask fish allergy history pre-operatively before protamine-requiring procedures
  • If fish allergy known and protamine needed:
  • Slow protamine infusion (over 10 minutes instead of rapid infusion)
  • Have epi at bedside, patient on monitoring
  • Premedicate with antihistamine + steroid (controversial; discuss with anesthesia)
  • If anaphylaxis occurs despite precautions: standard full epi protocol; have second peripheral IV ready; may need ICU transfer

sections.heading: 7.5 Vancomycin red-man syndrome vs. true IgE anaphylaxis
sections.bodyHtml:
"Red man syndrome" (histamine release from vancomycin infusion rate):

Feature Red man syndrome True IgE anaphylaxis to vancomycin
Timing During or immediately after infusion Minutes to 1 hour
Mechanism Direct mast cell histamine release (infusion rate dependent) IgE-mediated
Presentation Flushing, erythema, pruritus (CONFINED to face/neck/torso) Systemic: urticaria, respiratory, CV, GI
Resolved with Premedication (diphenhydramine 25 mg PO 30 min before), slow infusion (< 1 g/hour) Full epi protocol; rechallenge unlikely; switch ABX
Airway involvement No Yes; stridor, angioedema
Hypotension Rare Common
Management Slow infusion, give H1 blocker pre-dose; monitor closely Stop infusion; epi IM 0.3–0.5 mg; full protocol

Pearl: Not all vancomycin flushing is red-man syndrome. Ask: "Does the rash have urticaria? Any dyspnea? Any GI symptoms?" Systemic findings = true anaphylaxis until proven otherwise.

sections.heading: 7.6 Contrast-induced vs. IgE-mediated reactions
sections.bodyHtml:
Context: Approximately 0.7–3% of patients exposed to iodinated contrast develop hypersensitivity reactions.

Contrast reaction classification:

Feature Contrast-induced (osmotic/chemotoxic) IgE-mediated anaphylaxis
Prevalence ~70% of contrast reactions ~10–15% of contrast reactions
Mechanism Direct osmotic toxicity, chemotoxic effect on endothelium IgE cross-linking on mast cells
Risk factors Prior contrast reaction, renal impairment, dehydration, diabetes Shellfish allergy (historical link; now debated)
Presentation Delayed (may take hours); flushing, nausea, headache, mild dyspnea Immediate (minutes): urticaria, airway, hypotension
Management Hydration, observation Full epi protocol
Premed efficacy Limited High (steroids + antihistamine reduce recurrence < 1%)

Premed protocol for known contrast allergy:

  • Methylprednisolone 50 mg PO at 12 hours, 12 hours, and 1 hour before procedure (OR hydrocortisone 200 mg IV 1 hour before)
  • Diphenhydramine 50 mg PO or IV 1 hour before
  • Some institutions add famotidine 150 mg PO 1 hour before
  • Use non-ionic, low-osmolar contrast preferred
  • If reaction occurs despite premed: epi IM immediately (same protocol as any anaphylaxis)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear in a stable or mild patient, re-escalate to unstable pathway immediately.

  • Angioedema developing or progressing — lips, tongue, throat swelling; ANY voice change, stridor, dysphagia. Airway compromise is imminent. Escalate to airway prep immediately; do not delay intubation.
  • Wheeze increasing, stridor appearing, SpO₂ dropping — progressive lower airway obstruction or laryngeal edema
  • BP trending down despite IV fluids — epi response is waning; prepare for repeat IM dose or IV drip
  • HR rising > 120 but BP still dropping — compensatory tachycardia in shock; not therapeutic epi effect, true decompensation
  • Altered mental status appearing (confusion, anxiety, restlessness, lethargy) — cerebral hypoperfusion; shock developing
  • Urticaria spreading rapidly — systemic mediator release ongoing; indicates systemic rather than localized reaction
  • Abdominal cramping/vomiting/diarrhea worsening — GI involvement indicates severe systemic reaction
  • Cyanosis, mottled skin, poor capillary refill — peripheral vasoconstriction and developing shock
  • Symptoms worsening after initial improvement — early biphasic reaction (can occur even after successful epi treatment)
  • No response to 1–2 IM epi doses — refractory anaphylaxis; transition to IV epi, escalate to ICU immediately

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. EPINEPHRINE DELAY = DEATH. This is the #1 preventable death cause in anaphylaxis. Give IM immediately, even if you are not 100% sure of the diagnosis. False-positive epi administration (treating mild allergic reaction as anaphylaxis) causes no harm; false-negative (failing to give epi) kills. Err on the side of giving epi.

  2. Lateral thigh IM, not IV, not subcutaneous. Vastus lateralis muscle, mid-outer thigh. If no IV on board at onset, IM epi is FASTER and SAFER than attempting IV line while in shock. IV epi requires careful titration and carries dysrhythmia/stroke/MI risk; only appropriate in ICU with continuous hemodynamic monitoring.

  3. Red man syndrome from vancomycin is NOT true anaphylaxis. Histamine release from infusion rate. Slow the infusion, give diphenhydramine pre-infusion next time, premedicate. If truly anaphylactic (urticaria + respiratory + CV), will have systemic symptoms beyond flushing. True vancomycin anaphylaxis is rare.

  4. Protamine reaction post-CPB: always ask about fish allergy history. Cross-reactivity is known and real. If patient has fish allergy + protamine needed, use slow infusion (over 10 minutes), have epi at bedside, monitor closely. If anaphylaxis occurs, standard full epi protocol.

  5. Beta-blocker on board = glucagon rescue. Metoprolol, atenolol, propranolol, labetalol all blunt epi effect. Ask medication list. If patient refractory to epi IM × 2, give glucagon 1–5 mg IV bolus (can repeat q 5 min or start drip 1–4 mg/hr). Glucagon bypasses beta-blockade; overcomes epi refractoriness.

  6. Biphasic anaphylaxis is real and dangerous; observe 4–6 hours minimum. Symptoms resolve, epi given, patient looks great. Then 30 min to 3 hours later, another wave. Can be more severe than first. Mandatory observation post-resolution for all cases.

  7. IV epi drip only with hemodynamic monitoring in ICU. Do NOT infuse epi IV on the floor without ICU-level monitoring. Risk of dysrhythmias, MI, stroke. If refractory IM anaphylaxis, transfer to ICU immediately, establish drip there.

  8. Antihistamines and steroids are NOT first-line and DO NOT prevent death. Give them AFTER epi. Ordering diphenhydramine first while waiting for epi is a killer mistake. Epi first, adjuncts second. H1/H2 blockers reduce symptoms but do not reverse hypotension or airway edema.

  9. EpiPen 0.3 mg only has 0.3 mg in one injection. If re-dosing needed q 5–15 min, draw from multi-dose vial of 1:1000 epinephrine (0.3–0.5 mg per dose). Do NOT use multiple EpiPens unless no vial available.

  10. Contrast allergy = premed protocol. Document clearly. If patient with contrast allergy needs imaging, order steroids + antihistamine 12 hours before (or minimally 1 hour before if urgent). Reduces recurrence to < 1%.

  11. Chlorhexidine is a rising trigger in the ICU. Antiseptic in central line dressing, skin prep, oral rinse. IgE sensitization increasing. If no obvious trigger identified and patient has central line or recent skin prep, suspect chlorhexidine.

  12. Pediatric dosing follows body weight. IM epi: 0.15 mg for < 30 kg, 0.3 mg for 30–50 kg, 0.5 mg for > 50 kg. IM every 5–15 min as for adults. IV drip: 0.1 mcg/kg/min, titrate to 1 mcg/kg/min as needed. Protocol is the same; only the dose scales.

  13. Pregnancy = epi is safe and indicated. Maternal shock harms placental perfusion far more than epi. No dose reduction needed. Epinephrine crosses placenta minimally and does not cause fetal harm at anaphylaxis doses.

  14. Document trigger on allergy armband AND in chart lifelong. Ensure allergy is clearly documented so future providers know the full reaction type (urticaria only vs. cardiovascular collapse) and can implement premed protocols or avoidance.

  15. Tryptase level can confirm anaphylaxis post-hoc (if available). Elevated tryptase (> 11.4 ng/mL) is consistent with mast cell degranulation. Normal tryptase does not rule out anaphylaxis. Draw between 15 minutes to 3 hours post-symptom onset. Use for documentation and confirming diagnosis retrospectively, not for acute treatment decisions.

cards.title: Peri-Operative Anticoagulation Bridging
cards.quickAnswer: Pre-op: Hold warfarin 5 days until INR <1.5; hold DOAC 48–72 hours per renal function. Risk-stratify first: high-thromboembolic-risk patients (mechanical mitral valve any indication, mechanical aortic + additional risk, recent stroke/VTE <3 months, CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥7) MUST BRIDGE with IV heparin (UFH preferred post-op, titrated PTT 60–80); low-risk per BRIDGE trial do NOT bridge — increased bleeding 2-fold. Post-op: Restart heparin 12–24h if hemostasis stable; continue until INR therapeutic ×24h then stop. DOAC restart 24–48h, no heparin overlap. HIT history: argatroban or bivalirudin ONLY (never heparin). INR targets by valve: aortic 2.0–3.0 (On-X 1.5–2.5 if ≥3 mo); mitral 2.5–3.5.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition and scope.

  • Definition: Coordinated management of anticoagulation around cardiac surgery: hold anticoagulant preoperatively, assess thromboembolic risk, provide bridging anticoagulation to high-risk patients perioperatively, and resume therapeutic anticoagulation post-operatively. Goal: balance thromboembolism risk (stroke, valve thrombosis, arterial embolism) against surgical bleeding risk.
  • Who it applies to: All adult patients on chronic anticoagulation (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) or with mechanical heart valves undergoing elective or urgent cardiac surgery (CABG, valve replacement/repair, aortic, transplant, MAZE, device implantation).
  • When it applies: Preoperative planning through POD 7–10 discharge planning. Peak complexity: POD 1–3 when bridging decisions are finalized.
  • Why it matters: (Douketis et al., 2012) landmark work and BRIDGE trial (2015) showed that indiscriminate bridging increases major bleeding 2-fold in low-risk patients without reducing stroke risk. Conversely, high-risk patients (mechanical mitral valve, CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥7) absolutely require bridging. The critical skill is risk stratification first, then tailored bridging.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative anticoagulation management balances two competing physiologic pressures:

Thromboembolic risk drivers:

  • Mechanical valve thrombosis — intrinsic valve surface thrombogenicity. Mitral ≥ aortic. Untreated: ~2–3%/year risk for mitral, 1–2% for aortic.
  • Atrial fibrillation emboli — AF + CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 substantially raises stroke risk; even transiently after surgery, sustained AF >48h requires anticoagulation consideration.
  • Recent VTE — DVT/PE <3 months on anticoagulation is high-risk if AC is interrupted.
  • Surgical atrial inflammation — post-CPB and pericardial manipulation can trigger POAF and transient thrombotic microenvironment.

Bleeding risk drivers:

  • Surgical hemostasis window — POD 0–2 is peak surgical bleeding phase. Heparin (half-life ~60–90 min) is held 4–6h pre-op to allow dissipation.
  • Coagulopathy from CPB — cardiopulmonary bypass consumes platelets and factors, hemodilutes, and requires time (24–72h) to normalize.
  • Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — rare but catastrophic if not recognized. Mandatory hard stop on heparin/LMWH if HIT suspected or confirmed.

The clinical synthesis: High-risk patients accept the bleeding risk of bridging because untreated thromboembolism (e.g., mechanical valve thrombosis) has mortality >50% in acute setting. Low-risk patients tolerate brief therapeutic gaps because the stroke/embolism risk is already low and bridging adds unnecessary bleeding.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — patient populations and decision triggers.

Universally indicated for:

  • Every patient with a mechanical heart valve, regardless of indication
  • Patients with mechanical valve + additional risk (AF, EF <35%, recent stroke/TIA, hypercoagulable state)
  • Recent VTE (<3 months) on anticoagulation
  • Rheumatic mitral stenosis + AF
  • CHA₂DS₂-VASc score ≥7 in AF on anticoagulation

Risk-stratified for:

  • Mechanical aortic valve, isolated, no additional risk factors → consider bridge (moderate risk)
  • AF + CHA₂DS₂-VASc 5–6 → consider bridge
  • Bioprosthetic valve in AF → consider bridge
  • VTE >3 months ago, good adherence → consider bridge

Explicitly NO bridge needed per BRIDGE trial (2015, N=1884):

  • AF alone, CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4–6, no recent stroke
  • Isolated mechanical aortic valve, CHA₂DS₂-VASc <5
  • Bioprosthetic valve, no AF, CHA₂DS₂-VASc <5
  • DVT/PE >3 months ago, fully anticoagulated

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Gather baseline perioperative anticoagulation status* (5–10 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic review. Information-only; no interventions yet.

Pre-operative baseline (admission or pre-op visit):

  • Current anticoagulant — agent, dose, frequency, last dose date/time
  • Compliance history — any missed doses, INR/PT variability
  • INR status (warfarin only) — check within 24h of surgery; goal <1.5 at time of incision
  • Renal function — baseline CrCl or eGFR; critical for DOAC hold duration and LMWH dosing
  • HIT history — prior HIT diagnosis or HIT antibody test (positive/negative). This is a deal-breaker for heparin/LMWH. Document clearly.
  • Bleeding risk factors — recent antiplatelet use, NSAIDs, herbal anticoagulants, thrombocytopenia, coagulopathy
  • Thromboembolic risk factors — see §3 above; calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc, note valve type, prior VTE, stroke history
  • Bridging plan in chart — verify preop orders specify AC hold duration and bridging agent/plan

Post-operative POD 0–1:

  • Bleeding assessment every shift — chest tube output (expect 100–300 mL first 24h; >500–1000 mL is concerning), incision ooze, Hgb trend
  • Hemostasis trajectory — stable, improving, or ongoing bleeding? This guides when bridging can safely start (usually 12–24h post-op).
  • Heparin initiation status — if ordered, confirm timing, dose, PTT draws scheduled per protocol
  • Warfarin/DOAC initiation status — POD 1 or POD 2 per surgeon preference
  • Electrolyte repletion — K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0 essential for heparin response and atrial stability

sections.heading: 5.3 Bridging Agents — Dosing & Monitoring
sections.bodyHtml:
Agent Initiation Dosing Monitoring Hold Pre-op Restart Post-op Notes
IV UFH (Unfractionated Heparin) POD 1–2 if high-risk; sometimes POD 0 evening Loading: 80 U/kg IV bolus. Drip: 18 U/kg/h; titrate to PTT 60–80 sec per institutional protocol. PTT q6h until therapeutic ×2, then q12–24h. Alternative: anti-Xa assay 0.3–0.7 IU/mL if PTT unreliable. 4–6h before incision 12–24h post-op if chest tube output stable (<100–150 mL/shift) Preferred post-cardiac surgery. Rapid on/off (t½ 60–90 min). Reversible with protamine. No renal dosing.
LMWH (Enoxaparin) POD 1–2 if high-risk; also for pre-op bridge Weight-based: 1 mg/kg IV or SC q12h (therapeutic). Reduce to 1 mg/kg q24h if CrCl <30. Anti-Xa level drawn 3–4h post-injection, target 0.5–1.0 IU/mL. Do NOT use PTT. 24h if last dose ≤12h; 12h if >12h 24h post-op if bleeding minimal. Overlap with warfarin until INR therapeutic ×24h. SC preferred in ward/outpatient. IV option for acute post-op. Less ideal than UFH post-cardiac surgery (harder titration, slower kinetics). Used if UFH unavailable.

Once INR therapeutic ×24h, stop argatroban. Mandatory if HIT confirmed or HIT antibody positive. Do NOT use heparin or LMWH. Reversible partially (t½ ~45 min). Idarucizumab NOT effective.
Bivalirudin (DTI) POD 1–2 if HIT and bridging needed; less common than argatroban 0.15–0.20 mg/kg/h IV; titrate by aPTT 1.5–2.5 × baseline aPTT q4–6h then per protocol N/A Per argatroban pathway. Start warfarin overlap; plan 72–96h bridge. Alternative to argatroban for HIT. Shorter t½ (~25 min). Idarucizumab NOT available.

sections.heading: 5.4 Post-operative Anticoagulation Resumption Timeline
sections.bodyHtml:
Timeline Warfarin Heparin (UFH or LMWH) DOAC Clinical Pearls
POD 0 (day of surgery) Do NOT restart. Warfarin takes 3–5 days to work. Hold. Restart 12–24h post-op if hemostasis acceptable. Do NOT restart. Bleeding risk peaks POD 0. Observe for tamponade, ongoing ooze.
POD 1 Can start if bleeding stable. INR baseline ordered. Warfarin 5 mg PO (or patient's home dose) if PO diet tolerated. Restart per above if not done POD 0. Titrate per PTT/anti-Xa q6–12h. Do NOT start. Heparin bridge begins POD 1; allows 3–5 day warfarin ramp-up.
POD 2–3 INR check. Usually 1.0–1.5 (sub-therapeutic expected). Continue heparin + warfarin overlap. Continue. Check PTT/anti-Xa q12–24h. Overlap warfarin + heparin until INR ≥2.0 ×24h. Start 24–48h post-op if bleeding minimal. No loading required; begin maintenance dose. Overlap period allows warfarin to work. Do NOT stop heparin until INR therapeutic AND stable ×24h.
POD 4–7 INR should reach 2.0–3.0 by POD 4–5. Once INR ≥2.0 ×24h, STOP heparin bridge. STOP heparin when INR ≥2.0 ×24h. Do not over-extend (increases bleeding risk). Continue DOAC monotherapy. No overlap needed; DOAC acts immediately. Brief warfarin + heparin overlap is normal. Extended overlap (>7–10 days) increases bleeding. Arrange follow-up INR in 2–3 days post-discharge.
POD 8+ Discharge with warfarin. Confirm PCP or anticoagulation clinic follow-up in 2–3 days. INR check weekly until stable. Bridge complete. Continue DOAC per home regimen. Reinforce adherence. For warfarin: emphasize INR monitoring, dietary vitamin K consistency, drug interactions.

sections.bodyHtml:
Prosthesis / Indication INR Target Duration Clinical Notes
Mechanical mitral valve (any) 2.5–3.5 Lifelong Highest stroke risk (~2–3%/year untreated). Some centers add ASA 75–100 mg if recurrent embolism.
Mechanical aortic valve (standard) 2.0–3.0 Lifelong Standard target. Lower risk than mitral but still significant (~1–2%/year untreated). Add ASA if additional risk or embolism history.
Mechanical aortic valve (On-X brand, ≥3 mo post-op) 1.5–2.5 Lifelong Off-label per PROACT trial (2009). Requires documented surgeon/hematology agreement, excellent INR adherence, informed consent. NOT first-line.
Bioprosthetic valve (AC indicated) 2.0–3.0 3 months post-op (if AF present); then ASA If no AF + no other indication, switch to ASA monotherapy after 3 months.
Atrial fibrillation (warfarin-treated) 2.0–3.0 Indefinite per CHA₂DS₂-VASc AFFIRM trial standard. CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥1 male, ≥2 female warrants AC. DOACs now preferred if suitable.

sections.bodyHtml:
DOAC Agent Pre-op Hold Post-op Restart Timing Bridging? Monitoring Special Notes
Apixaban (Eliquat) 48h (CrCl ≥50); 72h (CrCl <50) 24–48h post-op No. DOAC replaces bridge; no overlap. No routine INR. Renal annually. Assess adherence. Preferred DOAC post-op AF/VTE. Fast on/off (~3h).
Rivaroxaban (Xarelto) 24–48h per bleed risk + renal function 24–48h post-op No. No routine monitoring. Annual renal check. Once-daily dosing. High protein binding; longer effective t½.
Dabigatran (Pradaxa) 48–96h per CrCl + bleed risk 24–48h post-op No. No routine monitoring. Annual renal check. Verify idarucizumab availability pre-op. Idarucizumab reversal available for emergencies.
Edoxaban (Savaysa) 48h (CrCl >50); 72h (<50) 24–48h post-op No. No routine monitoring. Annual renal check. Less trial data than apixaban/rivaroxaban. Safe restart per trials.

Important: DOACs are NOT bridged with heparin post-operatively. They have rapid onset (peak effect 2–3h). Simply restart maintenance dose; no loading required. Exception: Only if extremely high bleeding risk POD 0–1, can delay DOAC restart 24–48h or briefly use heparin, but standard is direct restart.

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. INR >2.0 the day before elective surgery — contact surgeon; may need delay or FFP/phytonadione (takes 12–24h).
  2. No heparin bridge initiated by POD 1 despite high-risk indication — verify chart; may be inadvertent omission. Escalate.
  3. Heparin PTT persistently out of goal despite dose adjustments — consider baseline prolonged aPTT (lupus anticoagulant); switch to anti-Xa assay.
  4. Patient develops HIT-like thrombocytopenia on heparin bridge — STOP heparin immediately. Verify HIT serology. Switch to argatroban or bivalirudin. Do NOT re-challenge heparin.
  5. Warfarin INR remains <1.5 by POD 5 despite appropriate dosing — check adherence, drug interactions, liver function. Escalate.
  6. Bleeding worsens despite heparin hold — verify PTT/anti-Xa is actually zero, not just off-goal. If truly bleeding, may need imaging or surgical re-exploration.
  7. Prolonged heparin bridge >10 days — increases bleeding risk without additional benefit; escalate for INR goal confirmation and heparin discontinuation.
  8. Patient on DOAC is prescribed heparin bridge incorrectly — DOACs do not require heparin bridge; escalate for removal of redundant therapy.
  9. Patient with mechanical valve has been prescribed DOAC by outside provider — escalate immediately. DOACs contraindicated in mech valves. Requires hematology/CT surgery review and likely switch to warfarin.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections are intended for in-app collapse. Nursing students, new-grads, and advanced beginners can expand; experienced nurses and experts can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Physiology detail
sections.bodyHtml:
Why warfarin takes 3–5 days:

Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, and X. Factor VII has the shortest half-life (~4–6h); factors II, IX, X last 24–72h. Prothrombin time (PT, measured as INR) reflects primarily factor VII, so PT/INR can look therapeutic within 24–48h. But the clinically important factors (II, IX, X) are still present, and a patient is NOT truly anticoagulated until ALL vitamin K factors are depleted, which takes 3–5 days. This is why overlap with heparin is essential — the heparin provides immediate anticoagulation while warfarin works.

Why DOACs don't need heparin bridge:

DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) inhibit Factor Xa or IIa directly and have peak plasma levels within 2–3 hours. Restarting the maintenance dose post-operatively immediately re-establishes anticoagulation. No ramp-up time needed. Thus, no heparin bridge.

Why heparin is rapid:

Unfractionated heparin binds antithrombin III, which directly inhibits thrombin (IIa) and Factor Xa. Effect is immediate. Half-life is 60–90 minutes, so it's reversible quickly if bleeding develops (protamine reversal).

Mechanical valve thrombosis risk:

Mechanical valves have an exposed cloth sewing ring and ball or leaflet surface that are inherently thrombogenic. Even brief periods without anticoagulation (24–48h) can lead to valve thrombosis, which manifests acutely as stroke, acute pulmonary edema (if mitral), or sudden hemodynamic collapse. Untreated mechanical valve thrombosis has mortality >50%, justifying the bleeding risk of perioperative bridging.

sections.heading: 7.3 CHA₂DS₂-VASc scoring for perioperative context
sections.bodyHtml:
The CHA₂DS₂-VASc score predicts stroke risk in AF and guides AC indication. Components:

  • Congestive heart failure (1 point)
  • Hypertension on meds (1)
  • Age ≥75 (2)
  • Diabetes (1)
  • Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2)
  • Vascular disease (prior MI, PAD, aortic plaque) (1)
  • Age 65–74 (1)
  • Sex category female (1)

Scoring threshold for perioperative bridging: ≥7 generally warrants bridging; ≥5–6 is "consider bridging" (moderate risk). <4 is typically low-risk and does not require bridge per BRIDGE trial.

sections.heading: 7.4 Special populations and edge cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Patients on warfarin with INR >2.0 day before surgery:

  • Delay elective surgery if feasible.
  • If urgent, give FFP 10–15 mL/kg or 4-factor PCC (more efficient; preferred if available).
  • Phytonadione (vitamin K) 10 mg IV takes 12–24h to work; useful if surgery can be delayed.

Patients with HIT (confirmed or suspected):

  • Absolute contraindication to heparin or LMWH — risk of thrombotic complication.
  • Use argatroban or bivalirudin instead.
  • Verify institutional DTI protocol pre-op.
  • If patient on DOAC with HIT history, can continue DOAC (NOT heparin-dependent).

Patients on DOAC with severe renal impairment (CrCl <30):

  • Some DOACs contraindicated or require reduced dosing.
  • Dabigatran: CrCl 15–30 = 75 mg BID; CrCl <15 = avoid.
  • Apixaban: CrCl <15 = avoid.
  • Rivaroxaban: CrCl 15–50 = 15 mg daily.
  • Edoxaban: CrCl 15–50 = 30 mg daily.
  • On-X aortic valve: lower INR target (1.5–2.5) requires surgeon agreement + excellent INR adherence; off-label.

Post-MAZE patients:

  • Early post-op AF is expected in the first 4 weeks.
  • Do NOT assume AF requires acute DCCV — rate control + amiodarone is default.
  • Anticoagulation decision is team-dependent (post-op bleeding risk vs AF stroke risk).

Heart transplant or LVAD patients:

  • Valsalva during straining is poorly tolerated (hemodynamically destabilizing).
  • Prioritize stool softeners + early mobility to avoid constipation-related straining.
  • Heparin bridge tolerance may be limited by hemodynamic fragility.
  • Escalate early if concern for thromboembolism.

sections.heading: 7.5 Anticoagulation teaching for patients
sections.bodyHtml:
"Why We Stop and Restart Your Blood Thinner"

Your heart valve (or AF, blood clot history) requires blood thinner year-round. Before surgery, we stop it to reduce bleeding during the operation. After surgery, we restart it carefully — sometimes with a temporary IV drip bridge while your warfarin starts working.

Pre-operative hold (patient must understand):

  • Warfarin: Stop 5 days before surgery. We check your INR the day before to make sure you're ready for surgery (thin enough but not too thin).
  • DOAC (Eliquat, Xarelto, Pradaxa, Savaysa): Stop 2–3 days before surgery.
  • Aspirin: Usually continue through surgery (ask your surgeon).
  • Do NOT restart AC early. Even if you feel fine, your body needs time to clear the old dose and you could bleed unnecessarily.

The bridge (if needed):

  • You'll get an IV blood thinner (heparin) after surgery if your surgeon says you need it.
  • This is temporary (usually 3–7 days) while your warfarin restarts.
  • We check blood tests (PTT) frequently to get the dose right.
  • The bridge stops once your warfarin INR is therapeutic.

Post-operative restart:

  • Warfarin: Starts POD 1–2. We check INR every day or every other day until the level is right. Takes 3–5 days to work fully.
  • DOAC: Restarts POD 1–2 at your normal dose. No special blood tests, but we monitor you for bleeding signs.
  • Both: We overlap IV blood thinner (heparin) with warfarin for 3–5 days until warfarin INR is at goal.

At home:

  • Warfarin: Take same time every day (evening typical). Keep INR follow-up appointment (2–3 days post-discharge; then weekly until stable). Eat consistent leafy greens (vitamin K affects INR). Avoid overuse of aspirin/ibuprofen. Report nose bleeds, blood in urine, black stools immediately.
  • DOAC: Take prescribed times every day — do NOT skip doses. No routine INR checks. Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs unless approved. Report bleeding immediately.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in patients who were "stable" on the regimen.

  • Bleeding worsens despite heparin hold — may need imaging, surgical re-exploration, or reversal consideration
  • INR trending down on warfarin despite dose increases — drug interaction, malabsorption, or non-adherence; escalate
  • INR >4.0 on warfarin — bleeding risk increases significantly; reduce dose; check for drug interactions; escalate if INR >5.0
  • Heparin PTT persistently high (>100 sec) despite dose reduction — possible HIT (check platelet count, 4T score); escalate to switch agents
  • Platelet count dropping on heparin bridge (from 250 to <100 in 24–48h) — HIT until proven otherwise; STOP heparin immediately
  • Patient becomes tachycardic, hypotensive, or dyspneic despite stable bleeding assessment → possible valve thrombosis, embolism, or decompensation; STAT escalation
  • Patient with mechanical valve absent or skips doses at home → immediate admission risk for thrombosis; urgent evaluation needed
  • New focal neuro deficit (weakness, aphasia, facial droop) → stroke code activation
  • New chest pain or severe dyspnea with mechanical mitral valve on reduced AC → possible valve thrombosis; STAT escalation
  • Swelling, warmth, erythema at groin or upper extremity with femoral/subclavian access on heparin → DVT consideration; escalate

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. BRIDGE trial (2015) changed practice — low-risk patients do NOT benefit from bridging. N=1884 randomized to bridge vs no bridge. Result: NO difference in stroke/embolism, but 2× more major bleeding with bridging. Pearl: Risk-stratify FIRST. Do NOT bridge every mechanical valve patient automatically.

  2. Mechanical mitral valve = ALWAYS bridge. No exceptions without explicit team documentation. Mitral thromboembolism risk is highest (~2–3%/year untreated). If team deviate from bridging, confirm hematology/surgeon are aware and have discussed bleeding risk.

  3. HIT history = NEVER heparin or LMWH. Hard rule. If HIT antibody is positive or HIT diagnosed, heparin is forbidden. Use argatroban or bivalirudin. Check idarucizumab and andexanet alfa availability pre-op if patient on DOAC + HIT history.

  4. Warfarin's 3–5 day onset means heparin overlap is ESSENTIAL. Stopping heparin too early (before INR ≥2.0 ×24h) risks clot. Stopping too late (>10 days) risks bleeding. Pearl: "INR ≥2.0 ×24h" is the trigger to stop heparin, NOT a fixed calendar day.

  5. INR checks are frequent early post-warfarin-restart. POD 2 or 3 (usually <2.0), then per protocol. Don't space >48h while ramping. Some surgeons want daily INR ×3, then every other day until stable. Verify local protocol.

  6. PTT monitoring for UFH is institutional. Some hospitals use aPTT goal 60–80 sec; others use anti-Xa assay 0.3–0.7 IU/mL. Verify your institution's protocol. If PTT is hard to interpret (baseline prolonged aPTT, lupus anticoagulant), use anti-Xa. Nursing should escalate if PTT/anti-Xa discrepancies.

  7. On-X mechanical aortic valve = special case. If patient's chart documents On-X valve ≥3 months post-implant on LMWH + ASA, INR target may be lower (1.5–2.5) per PROACT trial. This is off-label. Verify surgeon/hematology agreement pre-discharge.

  8. DOAC in mechanical valve patient = NO. DOACs NOT prospectively studied in mech valve patients; contraindicated. Patient with mech valve on DOAC = escalate immediately. Requires hematology/CT surgery review; likely switch to warfarin.

  9. Bleeding trajectory post-cardiac surgery is POD 0–2 peak. Most surgical bleeding happens first 48h. Heparin bridge typically does NOT start until 12–24h post-op for this reason. If patient has ongoing bleeding (chest tubes >500–1000 mL/day), delay heparin further. Pearl: Talk to surgeon before starting heparin if concerned about bleeding. Don't just wait for standing orders.

  10. Post-op resumption timing is a CT surgery decision, not automatic protocol. Post-cardiac surgery bleeding varies widely. Some patients safe for heparin at 12h; others need 48–72h. Surgeon makes final call based on bleeding trajectory. Do NOT start heparin without checking with team if patient still actively bleeding.

  11. Combining AC + antiplatelet + heparin bridge (triple therapy) = high bleeding risk. Usually reserved for high-thromboembolic + high-CAD risk (e.g., mech MV + recent STEMI). Surgeon directs. If orders show triple therapy, confirm intentional, not med rec error.

  12. DOAC reversal agents have limitations. Idarucizumab (dabigatran) works well. Andexanet alfa (Xa inhibitor reversal) expensive, requires 2-hour infusion, availability varies. Check pre-op if high-bleeding-risk DOAC patient. If reversal unavailable, consider bridging strategy or case delay.

  13. Epidural catheter + LMWH = ASRA timing. If patient on LMWH bridge and epidural removal planned, ASRA guidelines require 12h after last LMWH dose before removal. Coordinate with anesthesia.

  14. Discharge warfarin teaching is intensive. Patient must understand INR follow-up importance, dietary vitamin K consistency, drug interactions. Many post-discharge complications result from poor adherence or gaps in monitoring. Provide written instructions; confirm PCP/anticoagulation clinic follow-up booked; have patient repeat back schedule. Consider point-of-care INR machine if available.

  15. Patients with mechanical valves who stop AC face emergent admission risk. If patient calls saying stopped warfarin or missed doses, risk of valve thrombosis is ~1% per day. They need urgent evaluation (possibly imaging, labs, bridging). "Call the surgeon" scenario, not routine.

cards.title: Aortic Ascending / Arch Surgery (Open Repair)
cards.quickAnswer: Major sternotomy with CPB; most arch cases use DHCA (deep hypothermic circulatory arrest, 18–22°C) ± antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP) for neuroprotection. Ascending aorta + arch surgery carries stroke risk (3–5% with modern protection), heart block (AV node proximity), recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarseness, weak cough), and expected coagulopathy. SBP target < 120 mmHg strictly post-op (fragile anastomoses). Yearly imaging lifelong; genetic testing if syndromic or family history. POD 0 → ICU recovery with extended neuro vigilance (hourly × 24h, then q4h × 48–72h); POD 2–3 → stepdown transfer when stable; discharge POD 7–10 elective, POD 10–14+ for Type A dissection.
