sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition

Surgical replacement of the ascending aorta ± aortic arch using a Dacron graft. Often combined with aortic valve repair (Bentall procedure — composite graft + valve + coronary button reimplantation) or valve-sparing root replacement (VSARR). Arch reconstruction requires neuroprotection via deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA, cooled to 18–22°C) with selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP) via axillary or innominate artery cannulation. Extended arch or descending involvement may employ "frozen elephant trunk" (FET) technique — prosthetic graft partially deployed into descending aorta for staged second operation.

Typical Patient

  • Thoracic aortic aneurysm > 5.5 cm ascending (> 5 cm with bicuspid AV, Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome)
  • Type A acute aortic dissection (urgent/emergent — ~1% mortality per hour untreated)
  • Intramural hematoma (penetrating aortic ulcer, PAU)
  • Post-dissection pseudoaneurysm or recurrent aneurysmal dilation

Surgical Approach

  • Incision: median sternotomy standard
  • CPB access: femoral or axillary cannulation preferred for arch work (avoids manipulating atheromatous or dissected proximal aorta)
  • Cardioplegia: antegrade via coronary ostia (Bentall) or retrograde via coronary sinus
  • Cerebral protection: DHCA cooled 18–22°C; circulatory arrest time 20–45 min with continuous monitoring of core/brain temperature; ACP via axillary (SACP) maintains selective antegrade perfusion to brachiocephalic/carotid at ~10–15°C brain core
  • Graft: Dacron tube, branched graft for brachiocephalic/left carotid/left subclavian reimplantation

Standard LOS

  • Elective ascending/hemiarch: ICU 2–4 days, total 7–10 days
  • Type A dissection: ICU 4–6+ days, total 10–14+ days (higher complication burden, delayed extubation)

Lines / Devices on ICU Arrival

  • Pacer wires (epicardial, in place POD 4–7; do NOT remove on floor)
  • Chest tubes (1–2); CSF drain if descending extension (output goal 10–20 mL/h, position at foramen magnum level)
  • Foley, arterial line, 1–2 central lines
  • Labs on arrival: CBC, CMP, coagulation panel, troponin, LDH/haptoglobin (if mechanical valve component)

Why This Matters on Stepdown / Telemetry

Aortic arch patients are among the sickest post-operative cardiac patients: prolonged CPB + DHCA + multiple transfusions + high stroke/heart block/spinal cord ischemia risk create intensive inflammatory cascade and extended hemodynamic fragility. Stepdown care manages critical BP transitions, extended neuro vigilance (stroke windows extend beyond POD 3), pacing support weaning, electrolyte repletion, bleeding surveillance, and discharge teaching on lifelong aortic surveillance imaging + activity restriction.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why DHCA Is Necessary

Aortic arch reconstruction requires interruption of cerebral blood flow to access the distal arch vessels. DHCA—cooling the patient to 18–22°C core temperature—markedly reduces cerebral metabolic rate by ~50%, permitting up to 40–45 minutes of safe circulatory arrest without permanent neurologic injury. At normal temperature (37°C), irreversible brain damage begins at ~4–5 minutes; at DHCA, the window extends to ~40 minutes (Kirklin & Blackstone, 2026).

Antegrade Cerebral Perfusion (ACP / SACP)

Selective ACP via axillary artery cannula maintains moderate perfusion (20–25 mL/kg/min) to the brachiocephalic and left carotid arteries while the patient is in DHCA. This hybrid approach (DHCA + ACP) offers superior neuroprotection compared to DHCA alone, reducing stroke incidence to 3–5% (vs. 8–10% with DHCA alone) (Isselbacher et al., 2022).

Stroke Risk Factors

  • Aortic atheroma manipulation → embolic stroke (most common mechanism)
  • DHCA hypoperfusion injury → watershed strokes (high border zones)
  • Retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP) residual emboli → focal deficits
  • Intimal flap occlusion of brachiocephalic/carotid → flow-limiting stenosis

Stroke deficits can declare acutely (POD 0–1) or evolve over 48–72 hours as rewarming completes and reperfusion injury develops.

Coagulopathy Mechanism

CPB-induced consumption of platelets + fibrinogen + coagulation factors, dilutional coagulopathy from massive transfusion, and prolonged heparin exposure create expected post-operative bleeding POD 0–1. DHCA exacerbates this via hypothermia-induced platelet dysfunction (reversed by rewarming to > 34°C). Multiple anastomoses (ascending + arch) elevate baseline chest tube output vs. CABG alone.

Heart Block / AV Node Proximity

Proximal aortic surgery (root replacement, composite graft root) places sutures in close proximity to the AV node and His bundle. Post-operative edema, ischemia from surgical manipulation, or delayed nodal ischemia can trigger complete heart block or high-degree AV block, often manifesting POD 1–4 (later than CABG).

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
POD 0 (ICU) — Immediate Post-Op

Patient arrives intubated, sedated, paralyzed (sometimes), with core temperature 22–28°C (actively rewarming). DHCA-related pulmonary edema, diaphragm dysfunction, and depressed mental status are expected. Bleeding is monitored closely (q15–30 min CT output assessment). Neuro exam is heavily depressed by sedation; baseline will be established POD 1 AM once sedation weans.

POD 1–3 (ICU → Stepdown transition)

Extubation target is POD 1–2 if no major complications. DHCA deficits can still declare over 48–72 hours (late emboli, reperfusion injury), making neuro vigilance a core requirement. Heart block may first manifest. Coagulopathy typically resolves by POD 2–3 as rewarming completes and fibrinogen normalizes. Bleeding should trend downward; any persistent rise (> 200 mL/h) triggers re-exploration discussion.

POD 4–7 (Stepdown / Telemetry)

Pacer wires remain in place (longer than CABG). Incision healing, PT/OT mobilization, oral diet advancement. Discharge teaching on BP control, activity restriction, and surveillance imaging schedule. CSF drain (if placed) typically removed POD 3–5 once output < 10 mL/8h and neuro exam stable.

Discharge (POD 7–10 elective; POD 10–14+ Type A dissection)

Patient on stable oral BP regimen (SBP ≤ 120 target), tolerating diet and mobility. Pacer wires removed day before discharge or POD 5–7 per surgeon preference. Cardiac rehab referral in place. Home going regimen: strict BP control, anticoagulation (if mechanical valve component), activity restrictions, and lifelong yearly imaging schedule emphasized.

sections.heading: 4A. POD 0 (ICU — Not Stepdown)
sections.bodyHtml:
Neurologic Vigilance — Prime Responsibility

  • Neuro exam q1h × 4 hours, then q4h: focal deficits (facial droop, unilateral weakness, speech slurring), lower extremity strength/sensation (spinal cord ischemia risk if descending extension), mental status / agitation / delirium
  • Baseline typically profoundly depressed by sedation; clear baseline will be POD 1 AM
  • Stroke windows extend 48–72h beyond POD 0 — deficits can declare late as rewarming completes
  • Any new focal finding → STAT stroke code alert + CT surgery + neurology

Hemodynamic Management

  • SBP target ≤ 120 mmHg STRICTLY via IV labetalol (10–20 mg q10 min) or nicardipine (5 mg/h titrated)
  • Rationale: Anastomoses are fragile; SBP overshoot → suture line rupture, pseudoaneurysm, re-exploration
  • Rewarming caution: avoid rapid BP drops in first hour (watershed stroke risk); taper gradually
  • Target MAP ≥ 65 for renal perfusion, but SBP ≤ 120 takes priority

Bleeding Surveillance

  • Chest tube output q15–30 min initially, trend for decrease
  • Target Hgb ≥ 9 for ongoing bleeding; <8 if age > 70 or prior CAD
  • Re-exploration thresholds (higher baseline expected post-arch): > 400 mL/h × 1 hr, > 300 mL/h × 2–3 hrs, > 200 mL/h × 4 hrs
  • Monitor for tamponade: sudden drop in CT output + rising CVP/JVD + hypotension → STAT echo + CT surgery notification

Temperature & Rewarming

  • Core temp goal 36–37°C by end of POD 0
  • Gradual rewarming (avoid overshoot → overcorrection → watershed stroke)
  • Hypothermic coagulopathy reverses as rewarmed above 34°C; platelet function improves > 34°C

Pacer Wire Threshold

  • Check capture + sensing thresholds; document
  • AV conduction baseline important for later comparison (delayed heart block common POD 1–4)

CSF Drain (If Descending Extension)

  • Position at level of foramen magnum (external auditory canal reference)
  • Output goal 10–20 mL/h; monitor hourly
  • MAP goal ≥ 85 to ensure spinal cord perfusion
  • Character: clear/serosanguineous expected initially

sections.heading: 4B. POD 1–3 (ICU, Transfer to Stepdown when Stable)
sections.bodyHtml:
Extubation Preparation

  • Goal extubation POD 1–2 if hemodynamically stable, neuro baseline clear, adequate respiratory effort
  • Common delays: post-DHCA pulmonary edema, diaphragm dysfunction, RLN injury (weak cough)
  • RLN injury red flag: hoarseness, weak cough, dysphagia — do NOT start PO diet without swallow eval
  • Aggressive pulmonary toilet, incentive spirometry

Neuro Vigilance Continuation

  • DHCA deficits declaring over 48–72h — do not lower vigilance after extubation
  • Screen every shift minimum; q4h preferred through POD 3
  • Delirium very common (hyperactive form easy to miss); support sleep protocol, reorientation, family at bedside
  • If new focal deficit emerges → stroke code immediately

Coagulopathy Trends

  • CBC, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen daily; transfuse if Hgb < 8 (< 9 if age > 70 / CAD)
  • Coagulopathy typically normalizes POD 2–3 as fibrinogen recovers and platelets rebound
  • If persistent → thromboelastography (TEG), hematology consult
  • FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets per lab results + clinical bleeding

Heart Block / Arrhythmia Monitoring

  • Continuous telemetry; any new bradycardia, block, or POAF → 12-lead ECG
  • Complete heart block can manifest POD 1–4; loss of capture on pacer wire → transvenous pacing or PPM may be needed (~7–10% require permanent pacing after aortic root surgery)
  • POAF (30–40% incidence, peak POD 2–3): replace K⁺ ≥ 4, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2; notify APP for rate vs rhythm plan

BP Control Transition

  • Remain strict SBP ≤ 120; transition from IV to oral agents as diet advanced
  • Initiate beta-blocker PO (metoprolol 25–50 mg BID) when tolerating po; continue IV labetalol ± nicardipine bridge

CSF Drain Management (If Present)

  • Continue hourly output monitoring; MAP goal ≥ 85
  • New lower extremity weakness while drain in place → STAT call + raise MAP goal immediately (spinal cord ischemia concern)
  • Removal criteria: output < 10 mL/8h × 8h, neuro exam stable, no new deficits

Transfer to Stepdown Criteria

  • Off vasopressors/inotropes, stable hemodynamics
  • Extubated or on minimal support
  • Neuro exam baseline stable
  • CTs either removed or minimal output
  • Pacer wires in place (remain until POD 5–7)

sections.heading: 4C. POD 4–Discharge (Stepdown / Telemetry)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pacer Wire Management

  • Remain in place POD 4–7 (longer than CABG due to AV node proximity in proximal aortic surgery)
  • Do NOT remove on floor without physician order
  • Threshold check each shift; document capture + sensing
  • Removal POD 5–7 or day before discharge (surgeon-specific preference); notify surgeon before discontinuing

Continuing Neuro Vigilance

  • Stroke windows extend beyond POD 3; q shift neuro exam minimum
  • Late manifestations of DHCA ischemia or emboli can appear
  • Red flag: new focal deficit, altered mental status progression → notify APP stat

Chest Tube Removal

  • CTs removed when drainage < 150 mL/8h × 8h (no air leak)
  • Notify surgeon before removal per protocol
  • Pneumothorax risk post-removal — watch for acute dyspnea, desat, unilateral decreased breath sounds

Electrolyte Repletion

  • Daily K⁺, Mg²⁺, PO₄²⁻; target K⁺ ≥ 4, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2, PO₄ ≥ 2.5
  • Critical for rhythm stability and to prevent arrhythmia

BP Control — Transition to Oral Regimen

  • Goal SBP ≤ 120 mmHg strictly lifelong
  • Typical discharge regimen: labetalol 200–400 mg PO BID/TID + nicardipine ER 30–60 mg daily + ACE inhibitor (lisinopril 10–20 mg daily, enalapril 10 mg BID, ramipril 5 mg daily)
  • Educate patient on the criticality of BP control (suture line rupture risk, aneurysm progression prevention)

Anticoagulation (By Prosthesis Type)

Component Anticoagulation Regimen Duration
Dacron graft alone (no valve) Aspirin 81 mg daily Lifelong
Tissue valve component (rare in arch) Aspirin 81 mg; warfarin × 3 months optional Tissue: 3 mo then ASA
Mechanical valve component (Bentall) Warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 + aspirin 81 Lifelong
Type A dissection (graft alone) Warfarin × 3 months (surgeon-dependent) to prevent false lumen thrombosis Varies
  • Bridges: if mechanical valve, heparin (PTT 50–70) until warfarin INR > 2.0 × 24 hours, typically started POD 1–2

Discharge Teaching — Non-Negotiable Components

  1. Lifelong aortic surveillance imaging schedule:

    • CTA 1 month post-discharge (baseline post-repair)
    • CTA 6 months
    • CTA 12 months
    • CTA annually thereafter (lifetime)
    • Rationale: ascending aorta re-dilation, false lumen re-expansion (dissection), native distal aortic disease declaration

  2. Activity Restrictions Lifelong:

    • No heavy lifting > 10 lbs × 6 weeks (sternal precautions)
    • No contact sports lifelong
    • Avoid Valsalva (straining) — mandatory bowel regimen (docusate 200 mg BID, senna, PEG)
    • Avoid isometric lifting (weight-bearing exercises)
    • Pregnancy with residual aorta = high-risk

  3. Blood Pressure & Heart Rate Control:

    • SBP ≤ 120, HR ≤ 80 (beta-blocker essential for remaining aorta protection)
    • Non-negotiable; correlates with long-term aortic stability
    • Follow-up with PCP for titration; cardiac rehab for monitoring

  4. Genetic Counseling (If Syndromic):

    • Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos (vascular type), familial thoracic aortic aneurysm (FTAAD)
    • First-degree relatives screening mandatory — aortic imaging, genetic testing
    • Reproductive counseling if FTAAD

  5. Endocarditis Prophylaxis (If Mechanical Valve Component):

    • Lifetime prophylaxis if high-risk procedures (dental, urologic, GI)
    • Provide AHA wallet card; educate on signs/symptoms
    • (2021 AHA update: all prostheses now require lifetime prophylaxis)

  6. Pacer Wire Removal Follow-up:

    • Confirm wire removal with surgeon before discharge or POD 5–7
    • Watch for new AV block in first few weeks post-removal

  7. Elephant Trunk Patients (Staged Procedure):

    • Discharge teaching includes timing of second operation (TEVAR or open total aortic replacement, typically 6–12 weeks post-index)
    • CTA before second stage to plan approach
    • Strict BP control between stages
    • Close surgeon follow-up for surgical planning

sections.heading: 5. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR Template

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room, POD X] s/p [aortic ascending/arch repair procedure]." B: "[New event — stroke code, heart block, rapid bleeding, BP crisis, etc.]. [Vital signs]. [Relevant labs — Hgb, electrolytes, coags if bleeding]." A: "[Patient is stable / unstable / deteriorating]. [Neuro status / hemodynamics / bleeding rate]. [Last exam at [time], new finding at [time].]" R: "[Request — stroke team notification, re-op discussion, DCCV prep, STAT labs, etc.]"

Who to Call

Situation Contact Rationale
New focal neuro deficit (any time) STAT Stroke code + CT surgery + neurology Stroke is 3–5% risk; time-critical thrombolysis window
New hoarseness + weak cough APP + ENT + speech-language pathology RLN injury; aspiration risk; swallow eval before PO diet
Complete heart block / loss of pacer capture APP/fellow STAT May need transvenous pacing or PPM (~7–10% incidence)
POAF unstable STAT call + RRT, pads on; pacing support ready Prepare for synchronized cardioversion per ACLS
Chest tube output > 300 mL/h × 2–3 h CT surgery + APP Discuss re-exploration vs. medical optimization
SBP > 150 repeatedly APP for regimen adjustment Watershed stroke risk if overshoot; reduce gradually
New lower extremity weakness (CSF drain in place) APP STAT + raise MAP goal Spinal cord ischemia; optimize CSF drain + perfusion
Pneumothorax post-CT removal APP STAT, assess for tension May need emergent pigtail/chest tube
Fever + elevated WBC + sternal instability CT surgery STAT + culture DSWI / mediastinitis — surgical emergency
Suspected graft infection CT surgery + ID STAT + blood cultures Aortitis / graft infection — catastrophic; OR consultation

sections.heading: 6. Teaching Layers *(expandable — novice + advanced beginner deep-dive)*
sections.bodyHtml:
DHCA Physiology & Safety Parameters Temperature Targets & Times
  • 18–22°C core temperature: brain metabolic rate suppressed to ~50% of normal, permitting circulatory arrest to ~40–45 minutes safely
  • Monitoring during DHCA: esophageal or bladder temperature; pulmonary artery catheter temperature; brain temperature probe (research settings)
  • Rewarming rate: ~1–2°C every 5–10 minutes (avoid rapid overshoot causing reperfusion injury / watershed stroke)
  • Safe arrest time: 40–45 minutes at 18–22°C; beyond 45 minutes, neurologic risk escalates Reperfusion Injury Window
  • POD 0–3: rewarming phase carries highest risk for embolic and hypoperfusion stroke
  • Watershed zones at risk: between ACA/MCA territories, between MCA/PCA territories (high border zones)
  • Red flags: new deficits appearing POD 1–2 as rewarming completes and reperfusion-mediated edema/microvascular dysfunction develops Monitoring Post-DHCA
  • Hourly neuro exam × 24 hours, then q4h × 48–72h (per Isselbacher 2022, AHA/ACC Aortic Disease Guidelines)
  • Baseline exam POD 1 AM once sedation wears off is critical reference point
  • Document motor/sensory, mental status, language, vision, cranial nerves
Cerebral Protection Strategies & Comparison DHCA Alone
  • Circulatory arrest at 18–22°C without additional perfusion
  • Older technique; stroke rate ~8–10%
  • Advantage: simpler setup, shorter cannulation time
  • Disadvantage: relies solely on metabolic suppression; no active perfusion to ischemic-prone areas DHCA + Antegrade Cerebral Perfusion (ACP / SACP)
  • Axillary artery cannula delivers selective perfusion to brachiocephalic + left carotid at ~20–25 mL/kg/min while patient in DHCA
  • Brain core cooled to 10–15°C; moderate systemic hypothermia 25–28°C
  • Stroke rate ~3–5% (Isselbacher et al. 2022)
  • Widely adopted; reduces embolic + hypoperfusion stroke risk
  • Technique: cannulate distal axillary artery (or innominate) via side graft; infuse cooled blood at measured rate DHCA + Retrograde Cerebral Perfusion (RCP)
  • Cannula in superior vena cava infuses blood retrograde into cerebral venous system
  • Lower stroke reduction than ACP; rarely used as sole technique now
  • May be used as adjunct with ACP (bidirectional perfusion)
  • Concern: retrograde flow can carry atheroma embolus from aortic arch Modern Standard: DHCA + SACP for most arch repairs (Isselbacher et al., 2022; Springer 2025)
Aortic Surgery Scope: Ascending vs. Arch vs. Descending Surgical Anatomy: Aortic Zones
  • Zone 0: ascending aorta (from aortic root to innominate origin)
  • Zone 1: proximal arch (innominate to left common carotid)
  • Zone 2: distal arch (left common carotid to left subclavian)
  • Zone 3: proximal descending (left subclavian to 2 cm below)
  • Zone 4: mid-to-distal descending aorta Ascending Aorta Repair (CABG-like incision, femoral cannulation common)
  • No arch involvement = no DHCA needed
  • Simple tube graft; often combined with AVR or VSARR if root involved
  • Shorter pump time, lower morbidity vs. arch repair Hemiarch (Partial Arch) Repair
  • Involves zone 0–1, stops at or before left carotid
  • Requires DHCA + ACP for arch portion
  • ~30–45 min circulatory arrest typical
  • Brachiocephalic + left carotid reimplanted; left subclavian left in situ or reimplanted depending on approach Total Arch Repair
  • Zones 0–2 (ascending through distal arch)
  • All three arch vessels (innominate, left carotid, left subclavian) reimplanted
  • Longest circulatory arrest times (40–45 min); highest DHCA-related morbidity
  • Reserve for dissection or extensive aneurysm Frozen Elephant Trunk (FET) / Elephant Trunk Technique
  • Hemiarch or total arch repair with prosthetic graft partially deployed into descending aorta
  • "Trunk" left in descending aorta provides landing zone for second operation
  • Staged approach: index procedure (hemiarch/total arch + FET) → wait 6–12 weeks → second operation (open TAAA or TEVAR) to replace distal aorta
  • Reduces spinal cord ischemia risk in staged approach vs. one-stage open TAAA (Borst et al., 1990 seminal paper) Descending Aorta / TAAA Repair (Not This Card)
  • Descending thoracic or thoracoabdominal
  • CSF drain often indicated (higher paraplegia risk than arch)
  • No DHCA needed
  • See related Aortic Descending / TAAA / TEVAR Surgery card
Stroke Differential Post-DHCA: Embolic vs. Hypoperfusion vs. Focal Embolic Stroke (Most Common, ~50%)
  • Mechanism: atheroma dislodged during aortic manipulation, DHCA setup/takedown, RCP residual embolism
  • Presentation: acute focal deficit at time of graft placement (intra-op) or within hours post-op (POD 0)
  • Territories: MCA (most common — contralateral arm weakness, facial droop, speech); ACA (ACA territory weakness); vertebrobasilar (rare, but ataxia, vertigo)
  • Thrombolysis consideration: tPA high bleeding risk post-op; balance against benefit; CT surgery team input essential Hypoperfusion Stroke (Watershed, ~30%)
  • Mechanism: DHCA ischemic time, inadequate ACP perfusion pressure, post-reperfusion edema reducing collateral flow
  • Presentation: delayed, can appear POD 1–2 as rewarming completes; "border zone" territories (ACA/MCA junction, MCA/PCA)
  • Territories: bilateral high MCA/anterior cerebral junction (both arms), parasagittal parietal lobe
  • Prevention: adequate ACP rate, gradual rewarming, avoid excessive post-reperfusion hyperemia Focal Intimal Flap Ischemia (~10%)
  • Mechanism: Type A dissection where intimal flap prolapses into brachiocephalic or carotid ostium, occludes flow
  • Presentation: focal deficit correlating to vessel territory (carotid → MCA; brachiocephalic → vertebrobasilar)
  • Imaging clue: dissection extending into arch vessels; look for flow compromise on CTA post-op Hemorrhagic Stroke (<5%)
  • Mechanism: post-DHCA coagulopathy, anticoagulation reversal incomplete, hypertensive crisis post-op
  • Presentation: acute neurologic deterioration with headache, seizure, reduced consciousness; CT shows blood
  • Prevention: meticulous BP control (SBP < 120), careful protamine dosing, coagulopathy correction POD 0–1 Seizure (Rare, ~1–2%)
  • Post-DHCA neurotoxicity, embolic stroke trigger, metabolic derangement
  • First Actions: safety (airway, padding); labs (glucose, K, Ca, Mg, Phos); head CT; seizure precautions
  • Medications: lorazepam 2–4 mg IV (or propofol/midazolam per ICU protocol); phenytoin or levetiracetam loading
Genetic Syndromes & Aortic Disease Screening Marfan Syndrome (Fibrillin-1 Mutation, FBN1)
  • Aortic phenotype: root dilation + ascending aneurysm (most common cardiac manifestation); dissection risk if untreated
  • Diagnostic threshold for surgery: > 5.0 cm if bicuspid AV or family history of dissection; > 5.5 cm otherwise
  • Management post-op: lifelong β-blocker + ARB (losartan); annual imaging
  • Family screening: first-degree relatives need echocardiography, genetic testing; reproductive counseling Loeys-Dietz Syndrome (TGFBR1/TGFBR2, TGF-β receptor mutations)
  • Aortic phenotype: root dilation, ascending aneurysm, increased dissection risk at smaller aortic diameters (may present at < 5.0 cm)
  • Presentations: vascular EDS phenotype (hypermobility, velvety skin, easy bruising), cleft palate, ocular hypertelorism
  • Surgery threshold: > 5.0 cm or with family history of early dissection
  • Post-op management: aggressive β-blocker + ARB; frequent imaging (q6–12 months)
  • Family screening + genetic counseling mandatory Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome, Vascular Type (COL3A1, type III collagen)
  • High spontaneous dissection risk; surgery often elective at smaller diameters or for acute dissection
  • Major concern: poor tissue quality, anastomotic integrity, healing complications
  • Post-op: close follow-up; yearly imaging; pregnancy counseling (very high dissection risk)
  • Family screening + genetic counseling mandatory Familial Thoracic Aortic Aneurysm (FTAAD, MYH11, ACTA2, MYLK)
  • Inheritance pattern variable (autosomal dominant most common)
  • Aortic phenotype: ascending/arch aneurysm ± dissection; often younger presentation (< 50 years)
  • Family screening: identify at-risk relatives; genotype if possible
  • Post-op: lifelong imaging; genetic counseling for relatives and reproductive planning Bicuspid Aortic Valve (BAV) with Aortopathy
  • ~10% of population have BAV; ~50% develop aortic root/ascending aneurysm
  • Surgery threshold: > 5.0 cm (vs. > 5.5 cm in tricuspid valve)
  • Post-op: annual imaging; β-blocker standard; genetic testing if syndromic features or strong family history
  • Counsel patient on family screening (bicuspid + aortopathy clusters in families) Post-Op Counseling Framework All aortic surgery patients should receive:
  • Genetic risk assessment (pre-op history of dissection, family history, Marfan/Loeys-Dietz features)
  • If syndromic or familial pattern: genetic counseling referral (pre-op or post-op)
  • First-degree relative screening: encourage echocardiography, genetic testing per guidelines
  • Reproductive counseling if FTAAD or connective tissue syndrome (pregnancy carries dissection risk)
Concomitant Bentall (Composite Valve Graft) vs. VSARR (Valve-Sparing Root) Bentall Procedure (Composite Graft: Dacron Tube + Mechanical Valve + Coronary Buttons)
  • Indications: aortic root replacement needed + acceptance of lifelong anticoagulation (mechanical valve)
  • Graft types: St. Jude, Carpentier-Edwards Perimount (tissue), others
  • Surgical steps: root excised, Dacron composite graft anastomosed to LV outflow tract, coronary arteries reimplanted as osial buttons into graft
  • Complications specific to Bentall: coronary button ischemia (ostial stenosis, kinking, compression), pseudoaneurysm at button sites, LV outflow tract stenosis if graft too small
  • Post-op management: warfarin lifelong (INR 2.0–3.0); endocarditis prophylaxis lifelong; yearly imaging for button patency + graft stability
  • Anticoagulation: warfarin bridge starting POD 1–2, heparin cover until INR > 2.0 × 24h
  • Surveillance: annual echo (button flow, LV function, graft stability) + CTA for aortic integrity Valve-Sparing Aortic Root Replacement (VSARR)
  • Indications: aortic root replacement needed WITH native aortic valve preservation (if valve leaflets are structurally normal)
  • Techniques: David procedure (reimplantation of aortic root + valve within Dacron tube), Yacoub procedure (remodeling), others
  • Advantages: NO lifelong anticoagulation (only aspirin); better long-term hemodynamics; avoids prosthesis-related morbidity
  • Disadvantages: more complex surgery, longer operative time; requires normal aortic valve (no moderate-severe AR or stenosis)
  • Post-op management: aspirin lifelong; NO warfarin; echo at 1 month, 6 months, 12 months, then annually (assess for aortic regurgitation development)
  • Surveillance: yearly echo + CTA; if AR develops (from valve remodeling/structural changes), may need later AVR conversion (rare, ~5–10% at 10 years) Hybrid Frozen Elephant Trunk in Aortic Root Repair
  • FET technique can be combined with Bentall or VSARR for extensive arch involvement
  • Increases operative complexity + DHCA time but enables single-stage repair of root + arch + proximal descending (with FET trunk left for later TEVAR/second operation)
  • Post-op teaching includes both root anticoagulation (if Bentall) + elephant trunk staging plan
CSF Drain Management — Spinal Cord Ischemia Prevention Indications for CSF Drain
  • Descending aorta or TAAA extension (this card covers ascending/arch; CSF drain more often indicated for descending)
  • Extended arch (total arch) with risk of segmental artery occlusion
  • Decision per surgeon — not always placed even in descending cases; depends on approach and risk assessment Physiology
  • Segmental arteries (artery of Adamkiewicz at T9–L2, usually left-sided) supply spinal cord
  • Aortic cross-clamping or surgical manipulation can occlude these arteries → ischemia → paraplegia
  • CSF drainage lowers intrathecal pressure, improving spinal cord perfusion pressure (MAP − CSF pressure)
  • CSF drain goal: maintain MAP ≥ 85 mmHg + drain output 10–20 mL/h Placement
  • Lumbar (L3–L4) catheter placed by anesthesia/neurosurgery at time of aortic surgery
  • Tunneled subcutaneously to allow post-op monitoring
  • Secured to skin; connected to sterile drainage bag Management Protocol
    AspectTarget / Action
    Output goal10–20 mL/h; monitor q1h
    PositioningAt level of foramen magnum (external auditory canal landmark)
    MAP target≥ 85 mmHg (some surgeons prefer ≥ 90)
    CharacterClear/serosanguineous expected initially; RBC count declining over POD 0–1
    Removal criteriaOutput < 10 mL/8h × 8h; neuro exam stable × 24h; no new deficits
    Typical removal PODPOD 3–5 depending on output trend
    Red Flags — Spinal Cord Ischemia
  • New lower extremity weakness (paraplegia or paraparesis) while drain in place
  • New sensory level (loss of sensation below a dermatomal level)
  • Loss of sphincter control (urinary/fecal incontinence despite Foley)
  • Timing: often delayed POD 1–3; can emerge over hours Immediate Actions if Spinal Cord Ischemia Suspected
    1. STAT call to APP + CT surgery + neurology
    2. Verify drain patency + position (ensure not kinked, properly positioned)
    3. Raise MAP goal (e.g., 85 → 90–95 mmHg) via vasopressor/fluid bolus if hemodynamically safe
    4. Check neuro level + lower extremity strength/sensation bilaterally
    5. Consider spinal imaging (MRI if stable) to rule out epidural hematoma or graft-related thrombosis
    6. May need return to OR if mechanical complication (clot) suspected Drain Removal
    7. Surgeon notification before removal per protocol
    8. Confirm output < 10 mL/8h + neuro exam stable
    9. Remove under sterile technique; observe removal site for CSF leak
    10. Continue neuro checks q4h × 24h post-removal (delayed paraplegia can occur even after drain removal if ischemia window was prolonged)
Post-DHCA Pulmonary Dysfunction & Extubation Challenges Why DHCA Causes Respiratory Issues
  • Phrenic nerve injury: retraction during surgical exposure; ~10–15% transient dysfunction post-arch
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury: ~15–20% temporary, rare permanent; denervates left vocal cord + intrinsic laryngeal muscles
  • Pulmonary edema: CPB-related capillary leak exacerbated by DHCA hypothermia/rewarming reperfusion
  • Diaphragm dysfunction: transient paralysis from phrenicinjury; typically recovers 6–12 weeks
  • Atelectasis: shallow breathing from sternotomy pain, immobility, CPB effects Extubation Considerations
  • Delayed extubation common: POD 1–2 vs. POD 0 for CABG
  • RLN injury assessment: before extubation, document voice quality when patient wakes; hoarseness post-op = RLN injury until proven otherwise
  • Weak cough post-RLN injury → high aspiration risk → mandatory swallow eval before PO diet
  • Phrenic injury: check fluoroscopy (diaphragm paradoxical motion) if persistent hypoxemia/dyspnea unexplained Aggressive Pulmonary Toilet
  • Incentive spirometry q2h while awake
  • Early mobilization (OOB to chair POD 1 if stable)
  • Adequate analgesia (splinting from pain reduces cough effectiveness)
  • Position upright (gravity aids diaphragmatic excursion) Respiratory Compromise Red Flags
  • Persistent hypoxemia despite weaning support (may indicate phrenic injury, pleural effusion, pneumonia)
  • Stridor post-extubation (bilateral RLN injury, rare but airway emergency)
  • Elevated hemidiaphragm on CXR (phrenic injury confirmed) Swallow Protocol Post-RLN Injury
  • NPO until speech-language pathology swallow eval completed
  • Avoid aspiration (weak cough = poor airway protection)
  • May progress to thin liquids → regular diet per SLP assessment
  • NG tube if NPO prolonged (TPN rarely needed; most recover in 4–8 weeks)
Anticoagulation Strategy: Bridging for Mechanical Valve Component Warfarin Bridge Timing (Bentall Procedure)
  • Start: POD 1–2 (acceptable bleeding risk has passed; suture lines sealed)
  • Loading: 5–10 mg PO daily × 2–3 days, adjust based on INR response
  • Target INR: 2.0–3.0 (standard for aortic mechanical valve)
  • Heparin bridge: start simultaneously (UFH bolus 80 U/kg, then 18 U/kg/h; PTT goal 50–70 sec)
  • Bridge duration: continue both until INR ≥ 2.0 × 24 hours, then discontinue heparin; warfarin lifelong Perioperative Heparin Management
  • Intraoperative: full heparinization (300 U/kg typical pre-CPB); protamine reversal post-op (calculated dose based on heparin given)
  • Residual heparin POD 0: protamine incompletely reverses heparin; expect minor ongoing anticoagulation effect
  • Heparin flushes: if on warfarin bridge, clarify with team (some protocols include heparin flushes for line maintenance even on warfarin) Aspirin Role
  • Mechanical valve: aspirin 81 mg daily ADDED to warfarin (dual anticoagulation) lifelong
  • Graft alone (no valve): aspirin 81 mg daily as sole anticoagulation Type A Dissection Special Consideration
  • Graft alone: some surgeons advocate warfarin × 3 months to prevent false lumen thrombosis (reduces stroke risk from thromboembolism); others use aspirin only
  • Discuss with team — no universal consensus; surgeon preference guides Monitoring
  • INR daily initially (POD 1–4), then every 2–3 days until stable, then weekly
  • Warfarin dietary interactions (vitamin K in green vegetables, alcohol)
  • Drug interactions (macrolides, NSAIDs, etc., can potentiate warfarin effect)
  • Bleeding precautions; review all new medications with pharmacist

sections.heading: 7. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • New focal neuro deficit, ANY TIME: immediately activate stroke code; do not assume resolved; last normal time critical for thrombolysis decision
  • Hoarseness developing or worsening — RLN injury progressing; ensure swallow eval done before PO diet advancement
  • Weak cough paired with dyspnea — aspiration risk rising; re-assess swallow study; consider NG feeds if declining PO intake
  • Elevated hemidiaphragm on serial CXR — phrenic nerve injury likely; expect 6–12 week recovery; plication option if severe
  • SBP trending ≥ 130 despite regimen escalation — increases anastomotic rupture/pseudoaneurysm risk; do NOT accept "close enough"; add agent or titrate upward
  • SBP dropping acutely (e.g., 120 → 90) — overshoot in first few hours post-op can trigger watershed stroke; avoid aggressive reduction; taper gradually
  • Pacer wire threshold rising (capture threshold > 5 mV or sensing threshold declining) — early warning of loss of capture; notify APP
  • New bradycardia (HR < 55) with symptoms (dizziness, syncope, hypotension) — delayed complete heart block; prepare for transcutaneous pacing; check pacer wire function
  • Chest tube output not trending down after POD 1; rising again POD 2+ — tamponade risk; STAT echo; notify CT surgery
  • Sudden drop in chest tube output paired with rising CVP/JVD/hypotension — tamponade physiology; STAT echo + call
  • Atrial fibrillation onset (peak POD 2–3) — replace electrolytes; notify APP for rate vs rhythm; amiodarone hypotension risk at ~25%
  • Persistent elevated temperature POD 2+ (> 38.3°C, uptrending) — fever workup (5 Ws: wind/water/walking/wound/wonder); culture; CXR; UA; rule out DSWI/graft infection/HAP
  • New weakness or paresthesias in lower extremities while CSF drain in place — spinal cord ischemia; STAT call + raise MAP; assess drain patency
  • Rising lactate, falling urine output, cool extremities despite adequate BP — perfusion failure; consider vasopressor escalation or ICU re-transfer
  • Patient becoming increasingly anxious, restless, or unexpectedly drowsy — subtle mental status changes often precede hemodynamic decompensation; do not dismiss as "delirium alone"
  • Oxygen requirement trending up post-extubation — pneumonia, pulmonary edema, atelectasis, phrenic injury; CXR, cultures, RT consult
  • Recurrent arrhythmia after cardioversion — inadequate load; check electrolytes (K, Mg, Ca); escalate to amiodarone drip or rhythm-control regimen; notify APP
  • QTc prolonging on amiodarone (approaching 500 ms) — torsades risk; hold/decrease amiodarone; obtain ECG
  • Sternal instability with fever — DSWI / mediastinitis red flag; cultures before antibiotics; CT surgery STAT
  • Graft-related fever (fever without other clear source, may be low-grade persistent) — consider graft infection / aortitis; blood cultures × 2; CTA; ID + CT surgery STAT
  • Anticoagulation reversal concern: INR < 1.5 in Bentall patient despite warfarin — check adherence, drug interactions; notify provider
  • Elephant trunk patient not scheduled for second operation by POD 5–7 — discharge teaching includes timing; if not confirmed, contact CT surgery for staging plan

sections.heading: 8. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Stroke is the headline complication — 3–5% with modern DHCA + ACP, but 8–10% with older DHCA-only techniques. Vigilance must be extended (q shift minimum through POD 4+). Deficits declaring over 48–72 hours as rewarming completes are common; do not lower your guard after POD 1. Know the last normal time for thrombolysis window.

  2. DHCA neuro deficits DECLARE over 48–72 hours; it's not just POD 0. Baseline neuro exam is unreliable POD 0 (sedation, anesthesia residual). Establish clear baseline POD 1 AM; this is your reference point. Late-emerging deficits (POD 1–3) represent reperfusion injury, emboli declaring, or watershed ischemia from hypoperfusion.

  3. "Hoarseness post-op = recurrent laryngeal nerve injury until proven otherwise." Do NOT start PO diet without swallow evaluation. ENT + speech-language pathology consult. Weak cough = high aspiration risk; patient may need NG feeds until RLN recovers (6–12 weeks typical for neuropraxia).

  4. Phrenic nerve injury → elevated hemidiaphragm on CXR + persistent unexplained dyspnea / hypoxemia. May recover in 6–12 weeks (neuropraxia). If severe + persistent, plication (surgical procedure anchoring diaphragm) is a surgical option. Document on imaging for future reference.

  5. SBP ≤ 120 STRICTLY for first 4–6 weeks post-op. These patients WILL pop suture lines if BP runs. Not optional; a hard requirement. Overshoot in first hour → watershed stroke risk. Reduce BP gradually (avoid aggressive titration down); goal drift to SBP 100–120 over 1–2 hours, not 20–30 min crash.

  6. Pacer wires stay POD 4–7, LONGER than CABG. AV node proximity in proximal aortic repairs (root replacement especially) = delayed complete heart block risk. Do NOT remove on floor without surgeon/APP order. Heart block can manifest POD 2–4; loss of capture on pacer wire = transcutaneous pacing + possible PPM need (7–10% of root repair patients).

  7. CSF drain if descending extension — manage output 10–20 mL/h, MAP ≥ 85 goal. Any new lower extremity weakness = STAT call + raise MAP goal immediately. Drain is neuromonitoring as much as CSF management. Removal criteria: < 10 mL/8h × 8h; neuro exam stable.

  8. Bleeding is expected POD 0–1 but monitor re-op thresholds closely. Multiple suture lines (ascending + hemiarch/arch anastomoses) → higher baseline CT output vs. CABG. If trending > 400/h → trending toward re-exploration territory. Monitor coags; expect higher transfusion burden post-arch vs. CABG.

  9. Vasoplegia can persist on stepdown/telemetry transfer after prolonged pump + DHCA. If vasopressor requirement escalating POD 2–3 → may need ICU re-transfer. Discuss early with APP; avoid reflexive diuresis.

  10. Type A dissection patients are hemodynamically fragile. RV may be impaired from proximal involvement or ischemia. Treat preload carefully; avoid aggressive diuresis early. Expect longer ICU stay (POD 4–6+) vs. elective ascending repair (POD 2–3).

  11. "Elephant trunk" is a STAGED procedure — patient will need second operation in 6–12 weeks. This is not a subtle point. Discharge teaching must emphasize timing of second operation (TEVAR or open TAAA repair), imaging schedule (CTA before second op), and strict BP control between stages. If second operation delayed > 3 months, false lumen may re-expand.

  12. Marfan / Loeys-Dietz / Ehlers-Danlos / BAV aortopathy patients — first-degree relatives need screening. Genetic counseling + family teaching are part of discharge. Not optional. Reproductive counseling if FTAAD (pregnancy carries dissection risk).

  13. Acute Type A dissection = surgical EMERGENCY, ~1% mortality per hour untreated. ER → OR pathway, not ICU → floor pathway. These patients arrive sicker, stay sicker, have higher complication rates. Expect longer ICU stay, higher transfusion burden, more frequent re-exploration.

  14. Anticoagulation after arch repair WITHOUT mechanical valve = aspirin only, NOT routine warfarin. Common misconception: people assume all cardiac surgery requires lifelong warfarin. Graft thrombosis is rare; anticoagulation risk outweighs benefit unless prosthetic valve component present.

  15. Lifelong surveillance imaging is non-negotiable — CTA at 1 month, 6 months, 12 months, then annually. Ascending aorta can re-dilate despite successful repair (especially in Marfan / connective tissue disease). False lumen in dissection can re-expand if patent. Native distal aortic disease can declare. Patients MUST understand this at discharge. Many miss follow-up imaging — proactive phone calls, PCP coordination essential.

  16. Avoid heavy lifting > 10 lbs × 6 weeks, contact sports lifelong, Valsalva. Bowel regimen is MANDATORY (straining = Valsalva = aortic stress on fresh anastomoses). ACE inhibitor + beta-blocker are not optional — blood pressure control IS aortic survival. Family should understand this severity.

  17. Elephant trunk false lumen thrombosis monitoring. Some patients develop distal aortic expansion despite "successful" hemiarch repair if false lumen remains patent. Surveillance imaging essential; second operation may be needed sooner than planned if false lumen expands rapidly.

  18. Acute coronary button ischemia in Bentall patients manifests as ST elevation + cardiogenic shock. Suspect button compression, kinking, or ostial stenosis. Requires urgent catheterization vs. re-op. Low threshold for ECG + troponin in any post-Bentall patient with chest pain or hemodynamic change.

cards.title: Aortic Descending / TAAA / TEVAR Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: Open repair vs TEVAR vs hybrid. Open descending/TAAA via left thoracotomy carries highest paraplegia risk (5–20% by Crawford type); TEVAR percutaneous, lower risk (2–5%). Spinal cord ischemia is preventable. Headline protective measures: CSF drain (target <10 mmHg pressure × 48–72h, 10–20 mL/h output; drain positioned below heart); MAP ≥85 mmHg mandatory for spinal perfusion pressure; hourly lower-extremity motor and sensory checks × 24–48h. Post-op stroke, renal failure from visceral cross-clamp, respiratory compromise (pleural effusion), and coagulopathy all high-risk. Post-discharge: lifelong BP control (SBP <120), surveillance CTA q6 months × 12 months then annually, activity restrictions (no heavy lifting >10 lbs × 6 weeks).

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Surgical repair of descending thoracic aorta and/or thoracoabdominal aorta via open repair (left thoracotomy with aortic cross-clamp, visceral/renal re-implantation) or endovascular repair (TEVAR — percutaneous stent graft deployment). Open TAAA involves sequential re-implantation of visceral (celiac, superior mesenteric, renal) arteries onto synthetic graft.

  • Three surgical variants:

  • Open TAAA (Crawford I–IV): Left thoracotomy ± laparotomy; aortic cross-clamp; 4–7 days ICU; paraplegia 5–20%
  • TEVAR: Percutaneous bilateral femoral access; <1 day ICU; paraplegia 2–5%; endoleak surveillance needed

  • Hybrid / Branched: Combined open visceral + endovascular descending; 3–6 days ICU; intermediate risk

  • Incidence & indications:

  • Descending thoracic aneurysm ≥6 cm or rapid expansion (rupture risk)
  • Type B aortic dissection (acute complicated or chronic expanding)
  • Intramural hematoma (PAU) with descending involvement

  • Traumatic aortic injury

  • Why it matters: Highest mortality cardiac surgery (open TAAA ~5–10% in-hospital). Spinal cord ischemia is the single-most-feared complication — paraplegia rates 5–20% open, potentially reversible if caught early. Patients require intensive neuro monitoring (q1–2h lower extremity strength × 48–72h), strict hemodynamic targets (MAP ≥85, SBP ≤120 simultaneously), CSF drain management, and lifelong surveillance imaging.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why this happens. Mechanism and risk factors.

Spinal Cord Perfusion Physiology

  • Spinal cord perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF pressure. The artery of Adamkiewicz (critical segmental supply, T9–L2, left-sided ~80%) is vulnerable during aortic cross-clamp.
  • Open TAAA cross-clamping occludes segmental arteries proximal to graft. Visceral/renal ischemia time (goal <60 min) must balance organ preservation against spinal cord ischemia risk.
  • CSF drain placement (lumbar puncture, catheter at thoracic level) allows controlled CSF withdrawal to lower intrathecal pressure and increase cord perfusion pressure (spinal perfusion = MAP − CSF pressure).

Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury

  • Aortic cross-clamp → distal ischemia (lower body, viscera, spinal cord). Reperfusion after clamp release triggers inflammatory cascade: rhabdomyolysis, myoglobin release, hyperkalemia, AKI, lactic acidosis.
  • Visceral ischemia time >60 min increases mesenteric ischemia risk; renal ischemia during suprarenal clamping increases AKI risk (20–40% incidence).

Crawford Classification — Anatomic extent predicts operative complexity and paraplegia risk

Type Proximal Distal Ischemia Time Paraplegia Risk Surgeon Challenge
I Left subclavian Suprarenal aorta 40–60 min 15–20% (highest) All visceral arteries involved; longest clamp time; most organ ischemia
II Left subclavian Infrarenal aorta 40–60 min 15–20% (highest) Both renal arteries in ischemia interval; highest morbidity
III Below left subclavian (mid-descending thoracic) Infrarenal aorta 30–45 min 5–10% Visceral sparing; shorter ischemia time
IV Diaphragm Infrarenal aorta 15–30 min 5–10% (lowest) Mostly abdominal; minimal thoracic; lowest paraplegia risk

Why Paraplegia Occurs

  • Segmental artery occlusion during cross-clamp (Adamkiewicz artery if involved = catastrophic)
  • Epidural hematoma compressing cord post-op
  • CSF pressure elevation or inadequate drainage (cord swelling + high CSF pressure = ischemia)
  • Inadequate MAP post-op (spinal perfusion pressure drops below critical threshold)

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation — Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
When this patient appears on your unit.

POD 0 (ICU arrival)

  • Patient arriving from OR post-open TAAA or TEVAR: intubated or extubated depending on procedure type, bleeding trend, hemodynamics
  • Lines/devices expected: arterial line, central line, CSF drain (open TAAA), chest tubes (open TAAA, 1–2), Foley, possibly epidural catheter
  • Vital signs: post-op hypertension common (SBP 130–160s despite IV agents); HR variable; MAP goal already established by surgical team
  • Neurologic status: baseline neuro exam performed POD 0 (establishing baseline lower extremity motor, sensation, rectal tone for comparison)

POD 1–3 (Unit care, transition phase)

  • Patient may transfer from ICU to step-down unit once off vasopressors/inotropes, neuro stable, pain controlled on PO regimen
  • CSF drain still in place (open TAAA); hourly output monitoring continues
  • Neuro vigilance window still acute (q1–2h lower extremity exams continuing)
  • Bleeding trend stabilizing; if hemodynamically stable, walking to chair is goal

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / Gather Information* (first 2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information gathering. No actions yet.

Vital Signs & Hemodynamics

  • HR, BP, MAP, SpO2, core temperature
  • Peripheral perfusion: capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output
  • Recent labs: Hgb trend, platelets, PT/INR/PTT, fibrinogen, electrolytes (K+, Mg2+, Ca2+, Phos), creatinine, BUN, lactate, troponin, LDH (hemolysis), lipase (mesenteric ischemia marker)

Neurologic Exam (most critical for post-TAAA vigilance)

  • Mental status: alert, oriented, pain level, anxiety
  • Cranial nerves: if any concern for stroke
  • Motor (bilateral lower extremities): hip flexion (iliopsoas, L2–L3), knee extension (quadriceps, L3–L4), ankle dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior, L4–L5), plantarflexion (gastrocnemius, S1–S2); grade 0–5 each side
  • Sensation: light touch, pinprick in both legs; establish sensory level if any loss
  • Reflexes: patellar, ankle (brisk, normal, diminished, absent)
  • Rectal tone (if paraplegia suspected; loss of tone = spinal shock)
  • Comparison to prior exam: document any new weakness or sensory loss (STAT escalation criterion)

Chest, Respiratory

  • Breath sounds (expect decreased on left post-thoracotomy; pleural effusion common)
  • O2 requirement; SpO2 on current support
  • Chest tube output: character (serous, serosanguineous, bloody), volume (should be trending down POD 0–1)
  • Pain with breathing; cough strength

Cardiovascular

  • Peripheral pulses bilaterally (especially post-TEVAR: assess groin access sites for pulse, hematoma, false aneurysm)
  • JVD; capillary refill
  • Arrhythmia (POAF common POD 2–3)

CSF Drain Assessment (open TAAA only)

  • Output volume (goal 10–20 mL/h); character (clear, serosanguineous, bloody)
  • Drain position: level of foramen magnum (external auditory canal level approximately)
  • CSF pressure reading (if available from drain gauge): goal <10 mmHg
  • Dressing intact, no leakage at puncture site

Abdomen

  • Soft, tender, bowel sounds
  • Assess for signs of mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion, distention, bloody stool (catastrophic if present)

Incision(s)

  • Thoracotomy incision: clean, dry, no dehiscence or drainage
  • Groin sites (post-TEVAR): pulses present, no expanding hematoma, no drainage

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 (ICU — Spinal Cord Protection Acute Phase)
sections.bodyHtml:
CSF Drain Target: <10 mmHg pressure; 10–20 mL/h output; position at foramen magnum level Neuro Checks: q1h lower extremity motor + sensory × 4h, then q2h × 20h MAP Target: ≥85 mmHg (spinal perfusion priority) SBP Target: 100–120 mmHg (prevent graft bleeding) Coagulopathy Management: Platelet dysfunction from CPB (partial TAAA); monitor PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen; transfuse FFP/platelets/cryo per labs and bleeding trend

  1. Continuous CSF drain monitoring:

    • Measure output q1h; position at foramen magnum level; inspect character
    • If output >20 mL/h: over-drain risk (subdural hematoma); reduce drain height slightly or notify APP
    • If output drops to 0: check for kink/obstruction; reposition; notify APP

  2. Establish neurologic baseline & maintain vigilance:

    • Perform detailed lower extremity motor/sensory exam q1h × 4h, then q2h × 20h
    • Compare to baseline established immediately post-op
    • NEW weakness or sensory loss = STAT call APP + spinal cord ischemia protocol (see escalation below)

  3. Maintain MAP ≥85 mmHg & SBP 100–120 mmHg simultaneously:

    • Obtain IV vasopressor (phenylephrine preferred: pure alpha-agonist maintains diastolic pressure for spinal perfusion without excessive SBP)
    • Add IV vasodilator if SBP overshooting (nicardipine 5–10 mg/h titrate)
    • Combination therapy often needed (phenylephrine + nicardipine)

  4. Bleeding management:

    • Chest tube (thoracic + abdominal) output q30 min → q1h
    • Hgb trend; transfuse goal Hgb ≥8 (≥9 if age >70, CAD, or ischemia risk)
    • PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen; transfuse FFP/cryo if coagulopathy
    • If output >500 mL/h × 1h OR >400 mL/h × 2h → notify surgeon for possible re-exploration

  5. Pain control (thoracotomy is severe):

    • Epidural analgesia (if placed intraop) excellent pain control
    • IV opioids titrated to effect (thoracotomy requires higher doses than CABG)
    • Acetaminophen scheduled; NSAIDs held initially (bleeding risk)

  6. Pulmonary (extubation goal if tolerating): - Spontaneous breathing trial if stable; aim for extubation early morning POD 1

sections.heading: 5B. POD 1–3 (Unit Step-Down — Spinal Cord Vigilance Continues)
sections.bodyHtml:
CSF Drain: Output goal still 10–20 mL/h; continue hourly checks; removal criteria assessment starting POD 2 Neuro Checks: Continue q2h lower extremity exams (window extends beyond POD 3 for late paraplegia) MAP Target: ≥85 mmHg × 48h minimum (some surgeons extend to 72h) SBP Target: ≤120 PO agents starting

  1. CSF drain management — assess removal readiness:

    • Measure output q2h; if <10–15 mL/8h × 2 consecutive 8h periods + neuro stable → removal may be appropriate
    • Some surgeons prefer 24h clamping trial (drain capped, left in place) prior to removal; assess tolerance
    • If still draining >20 mL/8h: continue management; do NOT remove prematurely

  2. Neuro vigilance — maintain q2–4h lower extremity exams:

    • Window for late paraplegia extends POD 1–7 (though most common POD 0–2)
    • NEW weakness = STAT call; do NOT wait
    • If new deficit appears: raise MAP to >90 mmHg; reduce CSF drain output if over-draining; notify neuro/spine team STAT

  3. Labs & monitoring:

    • CBC, BMP, coags, lactate, troponin, LDH, lipase
    • Urine output (oliguria indicates AKI); monitor Cr trend

  4. Pain management — transition to PO agents:

    • Epidural rate reduction or removal POD 1–2 (if comfortable)
    • Transition to PO multimodal: opioids (titrate down), NSAIDs (once bleeding controlled POD 1–2), acetaminophen, gabapentin for neuropathic pain
    • Aggressive analgesia non-negotiable (pain impairs mobility and breathing)

  5. Pulmonary toilet — pleural effusion management:

    • Expect left pleural effusion post-thoracotomy (nearly universal)
    • Incentive spirometry q1–2h; early mobility; sit upright
    • Assess breath sounds, O2 requirement; if large symptomatic effusion → notify APP (may need thoracentesis POD 2–3)

  6. Bowel regimen:

    • Avoid Valsalva (straining stresses graft); constipation = major issue with opioids
    • Docusate 200 mg BID, senna, MOM, bisacodyl PRN per protocol

sections.heading: 5C. POD 4–Discharge (Step-Down Unit → Home)
sections.bodyHtml:
Neuro Checks: q4–8h lower extremity exams (window still open through POD 7 for late paraplegia) BP Control: PO agents; SBP target ≤120 Activity: Gradual mobilization; discharge after tolerating PO diet, pain controlled, ambulating safely

  1. CSF drain removal (if not already removed POD 2–3):

    • Remove per surgeon order once drainage criteria met
    • Monitor for post-removal headache (common 24–48h; usually benign; conservative care)
    • Continue neuro exam q4h × 48h post-removal

  2. Pain management — opioid weaning:

    • Continue multimodal analgesia; wean opioids as tolerated
    • Thoracotomy pain can persist weeks; neuropathic component may develop (gabapentin helpful)

  3. Discharge teaching — CRITICAL:

    • Lifelong BP control: SBP <120 non-negotiable; medications compliance essential
    • Activity restrictions × 6 weeks: No heavy lifting >10 lbs, no contact sports, no driving while on opioids, avoid Valsalva
    • Lifelong surveillance imaging: CTA abdomen/pelvis at 1 month, 6 months, 12 months, then annually (assess graft patency, native aorta expansion, false lumen re-expansion if dissection)
    • FEV-1/DLCO testing if thoracotomy: baseline for long-term pulmonary function tracking
    • NEW neurologic symptoms post-discharge: If weakness/numbness develops in legs after going home, go to ER immediately (reversibility window may still exist)
    • Medication regimen: Continue ASA 81 mg daily indefinitely; beta-blocker; ACE inhibitor; statin

sections.heading: 5D. TEVAR-Specific Path (POD 0–2 Uncomplicated)
sections.bodyHtml:
POD 0–1 (Usually Discharged)

  • Minimal bleeding (percutaneous approach)
  • Groin site checks q1h × 4h, then q2h: assess for hematoma expansion, pulse, color
  • Neuro check q4h (baseline established; endoleak-related ischemia unlikely but possible)
  • CTA abdomen/pelvis ordered POD 1–2 (assess graft position, type of endoleak if present)
  • Oral pain control (usually minimal; acetaminophen + NSAIDs typical)

Discharge (POD 1–2)

  • Groin site care: keep dry; watch for delayed hematoma, pseudoaneurysm, infection
  • Follow-up imaging review discussion (Type I endoleak = high urgency; Type II = observation often sufficient)
  • ASA 81 daily indefinitely; ±DAPT per vascular team
  • Vascular surgery follow-up @ 2–4 weeks
  • Activity: no heavy lifting × 4–6 weeks; rapid return to normal (faster than open)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Spinal Cord Ischemia (NEW PARAPLEGIA)

SBAR:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [open TAAA / TEVAR]." B: "Patient developed NEW lower extremity weakness / sensory loss at [time]. Motor exam: [describe specific deficit — e.g., 'bilateral hip flexion now 2/5, was 5/5 POD 0']. CSF drain output [volume], position [level], MAP [current value], SBP [current value]." A: "This is a spinal cord ischemia emergency. Need immediate intervention: MAP escalation, CSF drain assessment, possible re-op if hematoma suspected." R: "STAT spinal cord ischemia protocol: (1) Increase MAP to >90 mmHg; (2) review CSF drain (reduce output if over-draining); (3) possible MRI / CT spine for epidural hematoma; (4) spinal surgery notified."

Who to call
ScenarioContact
NEW lower extremity weakness or sensory loss POD 0–3APP/fellow + Neurosurgery + Spine surgery STAT (do NOT wait)
Paraplegia confirmed; ischemic pattern on examNeurosurgery + CT surgery + MRI/CT for hematoma r/o
Reversible paraplegia within 24–48h of aggressive interventionSpinal cord ischemia center referral for ongoing neuro rehab

Mesenteric Ischemia (CATASTROPHIC)

SBAR:

S: "Dr. [X], POD [X] s/p [TAAA], patient with acute abdominal pain, rising lactate." B: "Pain out of proportion to abdominal exam. Lactate [value], metabolic acidosis, [WBC], [HR], [BP]. Bowel sounds [present/absent]. No diarrhea/melena yet." A: "Concern for acute mesenteric ischemia — surgical emergency." R: "STAT CTA abdomen/pelvis if hemodynamically stable. If unstable, go to OR without imaging. Immediate CT surgery + general surgery consult."

Other High-Risk Escalations

Scenario Contact
CSF drain output >20 mL/h × 2 consecutive checks APP (over-drain risk; adjust drain height or notify for management)
Chest tube output >500 mL/h × 1h or >400 mL/h × 2h CT surgery (re-exploration criteria)
Acute stroke (facial droop, weakness, speech change) Stroke code STAT + CT surgery + Neurology
Hemodynamic instability, acute hypotension APP; assess volume, vasopressor need, rule out tamponade
POAF (irregular rhythm, HR >110) APP for rate vs rhythm plan; stable path = electrolyte replacement + rate control; unstable = STAT call for DCCV
Acute limb ischemia post-TEVAR (cold leg, absent pulse) Vascular surgery STAT (thrombectomy may be indicated)
Groin hematoma expansion post-TEVAR Vascular surgery consult; assess for pseudoaneurysm or arteriovenous fistula

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Crawford TAAA Classification & Risk Stratification Crawford Type I–IV predicts surgical complexity, ischemia time, and paraplegia risk.
TypeProximal ExtentDistal ExtentIschemia TimeParaplegia %Nursing Implications
Type ILeft subclavian arterySuprarenal aorta (above renals)40–60 min15–20% (highest)All visceral branches require re-implantation. Longest aortic cross-clamp time. Highest AKI risk from renal ischemia. Most aggressive neuro monitoring required. Expect ICU × 4–7 days.
Type IILeft subclavian arteryInfrarenal aorta (below renals)40–60 min15–20% (highest)Both renal arteries IN ischemia interval. Highest morbidity/mortality. Same vigilance as Type I.
Type IIIBelow left subclavian (mid-descending thoracic)Infrarenal aorta30–45 min5–10%Visceral artery sparing (shorter clamp time). Lower paraplegia risk than Types I–II but still vigilant. AKI risk moderate.
Type IVDiaphragmInfrarenal aorta15–30 min5–10%Mostly abdominal; minimal thoracic involvement. Shortest ischemia time; lowest paraplegia risk. May not require CSF drain (surgeon-dependent).
Nursing takeaway: Know the Crawford type POD 0. Types I–II patients need the most aggressive neuro exam frequency (q1h). Types III–IV lower risk but vigilance still essential (window extends POD 1–7).
Spinal Cord Vascular Anatomy & Ischemia Prevention Artery of Adamkiewicz — Critical Spinal Supply
  • Largest segmental artery to thoracolumbar spinal cord
  • Location: T9–L2 (variable), left-sided ~80%
  • If involved in aortic cross-clamp without adequate collateral → acute paraplegia risk Thoracic vs Lumbar Cord Supply
  • Thoracic cord: Limited collateral supply; highly vulnerable to segmental artery occlusion
  • Lumbar cord: Better collateral supply from lumbar arteries; less ischemia-prone Intercostal Artery Reimplantation — Surgeon preservation strategy
  • Renal arteries: ALWAYS re-implanted (essential for renal perfusion)
  • Visceral arteries (celiac, SMA): ALWAYS re-implanted
  • Intercostal arteries T8–L1: reimplanted if surgeon can do safely; balances cord perfusion against ischemia time trade-off CSF Drain Physiology — How It Protects Cord
  • Spinal perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF pressure
  • Normal CSF pressure: 10–20 cm H2O (7.5–15 mmHg)
  • Drain removal of CSF → drops CSF pressure → increases spinal perfusion pressure without changing MAP
  • Optimal CSF pressure goal: <10 mmHg
  • Over-drain (subdural hematoma risk) vs under-drain (cord ischemia risk): 10–20 mL/h output is the sweet spot MAP ≥85 mmHg Rationale
  • At MAP 85 and CSF pressure 10 mmHg: spinal perfusion pressure = 85 − 10 = 75 mmHg (adequate)
  • If MAP drops to 75 AND CSF pressure 10: perfusion pressure drops to 65 mmHg (marginal; high ischemia risk)
  • Phenylephrine (pure alpha) preferred over norepinephrine (mixed alpha/beta) because it maintains diastolic pressure (component of perfusion pressure) without excessive SBP increase Motor-Evoked Potential (MEP) Monitoring Intraop
  • Surgeon uses MEP during cross-clamp to detect real-time cord ischemia
  • Drop in MEP amplitude = signal to surgeon to reduce clamp time or implement distal perfusion
  • If MEP drops, surgeon adjusts: reduce ischemia time, increase distal aortic perfusion rate, consider naloxone
CSF Drain Management Protocol in Detail Placement & Position
  • Placement: intraoperative lumbar puncture (usually L3–L4 or L4–L5), catheter threaded cephalad to mid-thoracic region
  • Position height: level of foramen magnum (external auditory canal landmark approximately)
  • DO NOT position drain too high (over-drain) or too low (under-drain) Hourly Assessment Checklist
  • Measure output (mL) in collection chamber
  • Assess character: clear (normal), serosanguineous (some blood OK immediately post-op), persistently bloody (may indicate epidural bleed)
  • Check drain position: ensure at foramen magnum level; patient movement may lower it
  • Inspect dressing for CSF leakage at puncture site
  • If available, read CSF pressure from drain gauge (goal <10 mmHg) Output Interpretation
  • Goal 10–20 mL/h
  • >20 mL/h: Over-drain; risk of subdural hematoma. Action: lower drain height 1–2 cm (increases CSF pressure back to goal), or notify APP for adjustment. Do NOT abruptly clamp (risk of sudden CSF pressure spike → cord swelling)
  • <5 mL/h: Under-drain; risk of cord ischemia. Action: ensure patency (check for kink in tubing), reposition patient to help flow, notify APP if output remains low Complications During Drain Management
  • Headache: Common if CSF pressure kept too low; manage conservatively (pain meds, fluids, supine positioning)
  • Epidural hematoma: Persistent bloody CSF + new neuro deficit = STAT imaging + possible surgical evacuation
  • CSF leak at puncture site: Rare; notify APP if oozing continues >POD 2
  • Infection (meningitis): Fever + headache + neuro change = cultures STAT + antibiotics Removal Protocol
  • Removal criteria: output <10–15 mL/8h × 2 consecutive 8h periods + neuro exam stable + patient alert/cooperative
  • Clamping trial (optional): some surgeons order 24h clamping trial (drain capped, left in place) before removal; assess tolerance
  • Post-removal: apply pressure dressing; monitor puncture site q30 min × 2h, then q4h
  • Monitor for post-removal headache (common, usually benign; conservative care)
  • Continue neuro exam q4h × 48h post-removal (late paraplegia window still open)
Open vs TEVAR vs Hybrid Comparison
AspectOpen TAAATEVARHybrid
AccessLeft thoracotomy ± laparotomyBilateral femoral (percutaneous)Laparotomy + endovascular
Aortic cross-clampYes (40–60 min)NoPartial
CPB / PerfusionPartial LV bypass ± distal perfusionNone (local anesthesia common)Partial
CSF drainYes (mandatory)NoOften used
ICU LOS4–7 days0–1 day3–6 days
Total LOS7–10 days2–4 days (uncomplicated)6–10 days
Paraplegia risk5–20% (Crawford-dependent)2–5%3–8%
RecoverySlow; pain severe; pleural effusion commonFast; minimal pain; endoleak surveillanceIntermediate
Endoleak riskN/A (open)10–30% (mostly Type II, low-risk)Similar to TEVAR
Retrograde dissectionVery rareRare but catastrophicRare
DischargePOD 7–10POD 1–2POD 6–10
BP control post-dischargeStrict: SBP <120Moderate: SBP <130 (surgeon-dependent)Strict
Surveillance imagingCTA at 1mo, 6mo, 12mo, then annualCTA baseline if endoleak; else 6mo, annualSimilar to open
Nursing Pearl: TEVAR patients deceive — they look "recovered" POD 1, but endoleak vigilance is lifelong. Open TAAA patients are systemically sicker but have defined recovery arc (paraplegia window POD 0–7, neuro vigilance weeks).
TEVAR Endoleak Types & Management Implications Endoleak = blood flow outside graft, inside aneurysm sac; detected on CTA; predicts need for surveillance or intervention.
TypeDefinitionCauseRiskCTA AppearanceManagement
Type IAttachment site leak (proximal or distal)Inadequate overlap; proximal/distal neck oversizingHigh (sac expansion, rupture)Contrast at graft edgeOften requires intervention (proximal cuff, distal extension, or redo)
Type IIRetrograde branch vessel leakSegmental, lumbar, IMA backflowLow (sac may thrombose)Contrast in sac remote from graft; no graft edge leakObservation + serial CTA; intervention only if sac expanding
Type IIIGraft defect (fabric tear, modular separation)Material failure; graft fractureHigh (rupture risk)Continuous contrast through graft defectUsually requires urgent intervention (stent extension)
Type IVGraft material porosity (rare)Microscopic graft fabric leakageLow (usually transient)Blush around graft POD 0–1Observation; resolves within days usually
Type VEndotension (no visible leak)Pressure in sac WITHOUT endoleakVariableSac expansion WITHOUT visible leak on CTAComplex diagnosis; observation + aggressive imaging; may require redo
Nursing implication: Understand endoleak type from imaging discussion with vascular team. Type I = urgent concern (follow-up imaging sooner). Type II = reassure patient (often observation-only). Affects outpatient surveillance cadence.
FEV-1/DLCO Testing & Pulmonary Function Post-Thoracotomy Background
  • Left thoracotomy causes acute pleural effusion (nearly universal) and may cause left lower lobe atelectasis
  • Long-term lung function after thoracotomy: most patients recover baseline by 12 weeks, but small percent have persistent restrictive defect Baseline Ordering (Discharge)
  • Order pulmonary function tests (FEV-1, FVC, DLCO) at discharge or 4–6 weeks post-op (allows pleural effusion reabsorption, acute inflammation to resolve)
  • FEV-1 <50% pre-operatively is relative contraindication to open surgery (higher respiratory failure risk)
  • Post-op FEV-1 decline typically 10–20% from baseline (expected; usually recovers) Teaching Point for Discharge
  • "You will feel short of breath for 2–4 weeks post-discharge. This is normal from the thoracotomy and effusion. If shortness of breath worsens or doesn't improve by 6 weeks, call your surgeon."
  • "Pulmonary function tests will be done at your 4–6 week visit to establish baseline; your lungs will continue improving over 3–6 months."
Renal Protection Intraoperative Strategies AKI Risk Factors Post-TAAA
  • Suprarenal aortic cross-clamping: direct renal artery ischemia (ischemia time goal <60 min)
  • CPB-related ischemia-reperfusion
  • Post-op hypotension
  • Hemolysis (rhabdomyolysis from lower body reperfusion)
  • Radiocontrast exposure (if TEVAR with CTA) Intraoperative Adjuncts (Surgeon-Dependent)
  • Cold crystalloid renal perfusion: some surgeons infuse cold saline into renal arteries during ischemia interval (reduces metabolic demand)
  • Ischemic preconditioning: brief periods of clamp/release before prolonged clamp (may condition kidney to ischemia)
  • Minimize cross-clamp time (target <60 min for suprarenal clamping) Post-op Monitoring
  • Target MAP ≥65 mmHg (renal perfusion)
  • Avoid aggressive diuresis (volume-depleted kidney at high AKI risk)
  • Monitor Cr trend (baseline → POD 1 → POD 2); rise ≥0.3 mg/dL in 48h = AKI by KDIGO
  • Encourage PO hydration if tolerating (avoid contrast nephropathy post-TEVAR)
  • Hold nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, ACE-I temporarily if Cr rising acutely) High-Risk Patients
  • Pre-existing CKD (eGFR <30): closer monitoring; nephrology consult if rising Cr
  • Diabetes: higher AKI risk; aggressive glycemic control + hydration

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these in currently stable patients.

  • NEW lower extremity weakness or sensory loss (any POD) — automatic STAT escalation; do NOT assume will improve
  • CSF drain output suddenly 0 — check for kink/obstruction; reposition; notify APP (under-drain = cord ischemia risk)
  • CSF drain output >20 mL/h × 2 checks — over-drain; reduce height or notify APP
  • Persistent blood in CSF after POD 1 — may indicate epidural hematoma; notify APP
  • Chest tube output >500 mL/h — bleeding escalation
  • Acute hypotension despite fluids — assess for cardiac tamponade, sepsis; notify APP
  • MAP drifting <85 despite vasopressor escalation — spinal cord perfusion at risk; escalate conversation with APP
  • SBP >140 refractory to IV antihypertensives — graft bleeding / anastomotic rupture risk; escalate vasodilator therapy
  • Abdominal pain out of proportion to exam + rising lactate — MESENTERIC ISCHEMIA; STAT call
  • Irregular rhythm (POAF) — q1h vitals; electrolyte replacement; notify APP for rate vs rhythm plan
  • Oxygen requirement increasing — may indicate pleural effusion worsening or atelectasis; pulmonary toilet, sit upright
  • Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr — oliguria; assess volume, MAP, Cr trend; notify APP (AKI risk)
  • Dark urine + elevated CPK — rhabdomyolysis; aggressive hydration (goal UOP >200 mL/h); notify APP
  • New focal neurologic deficit (facial droop, speech change) — STROKE CODE; CT head STAT
  • Anxiety / restlessness despite adequate pain control — may precede hemodynamic decompensation; assess perfusion
  • Groin hematoma expansion post-TEVAR — pseudoaneurysm risk; vascular surgery consult
  • Cold leg + absent pulse post-TEVAR — acute limb ischemia; vascular surgery STAT
  • Fever without source POD 2+ — r/o infection (cultures, CXR, UA); notify APP (post-op fever workup)

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Spinal cord ischemia is preventable and sometimes reversible if caught early. This is NOT a passive complication. q1–2h lower extremity neuro exams, CSF drain at 10–20 mL/h, MAP ≥85, and RAPID escalation of MAP if new weakness develops can mean the difference between ambulation and permanent paraplegia. Assume worst; escalate immediately.

  2. CSF drain is NOT set-and-forget. Hourly assessment non-negotiable. Over-drain (>20 mL/h) → subdural hematoma (catastrophic). Under-drain (<5 mL/h) → cord ischemia. Target 10–20 mL/h. If output suddenly drops to 0, check for kink/obstruction; do NOT clamp abruptly.

  3. The SBP ≤120 AND MAP ≥85 window is TIGHT. These patients often need combination therapy: phenylephrine (pure alpha-agonist; raises MAP + diastolic pressure for cord perfusion) + nicardipine (pure vasodilator; lowers SBP). Discuss early with APP; this is not simple.

  4. MAP ≥85 is non-negotiable for 48–72 hours. Not a suggestion — a hard target. Spinal perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF pressure; if MAP drops and CSF pressure stays high, cord ischemia declares rapidly.

  5. Paraplegia can declare acutely (POD 0–2) or over days (POD 3–7). Vigilance window extends beyond POD 3. Late paraplegia from epidural hematoma or delayed spinal cord edema is real. Discharge patient education: "If you develop leg weakness or numbness after going home, go to ER immediately."

  6. Thoracotomy pain is SEVERE and different from sternotomy pain. It's muscle-tearing, not bone-splitting. Epidural analgesia highly effective; intercostal nerve blocks excellent adjunct. Do NOT undertreat — pain limits breathing, mobility, recovery. Aggressive multimodal analgesia non-negotiable.

  7. Left pleural effusion is nearly universal post-thoracotomy. Anticipate dyspnea, decreased breath sounds on left, hypoxemia POD 1–2. Pulmonary toilet, early mobility, sit upright. Small effusions reabsorb; large effusions (>2/3 hemithorax) may need thoracentesis. Do NOT dismiss as "expected."

  8. Mesenteric ischemia post-TAAA is CATASTROPHIC and often MISSED early. "Pain out of proportion to exam" + rising lactate + metabolic acidosis = STAT surgical consultation. Do NOT wait for diagnostic imaging if hemodynamically unstable; go to OR. >50% mortality if delayed.

  9. Rhabdomyolysis after TAAA cross-clamp is REAL. Reperfusion of ischemic lower body + viscera → myoglobin release → dark urine, CPK elevation, AKI risk. Aggressive hydration (goal UOP >200 mL/h) is preventive. Check urine color + CPK POD 0–1. Dark urine = red flag.

  10. Renal failure is common — 20–40% AKI incidence post-TAAA from suprarenal clamping. Monitor Cr trend POD 0–2. Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) + rising Cr ≥0.3 mg/dL = KDIGO AKI; notify APP. Nephrology consult if Stage 3 or RRT indication.

  11. TEVAR paraplegia risk lower (2–5%) than open TAAA (5–20%), but endoleak-related malperfusion is still a threat. Delayed paraplegia from endoleak with visceral ischemia can occur. Surveillance CTA at 1 month (if endoleak) is important; patient must comply with follow-up.

  12. TEVAR access site complications are common (pseudoaneurysm ~3%, hematoma, thrombosis). Assess distal pulses bilaterally POD 0–1. Expanding groin hematoma → vascular surgery consult. Cold leg + absent pulse = limb-threatening ischemia; urgent vascular assessment.

  13. Endoleak types differ in urgency. Type I (attachment site) = high urgency (rupture risk; may need early intervention). Type II (branch vessel) = observation often sufficient (low risk; may thrombose spontaneously). Know which type from vascular team imaging discussion; affects follow-up intensity.

  14. Intercostal artery reimplantation balances cord perfusion against ischemia time. Surgeon may or may not reimplant T8–L1 intercostals depending on anatomy and cross-clamp time. If surgeon notes intercostal NOT reimplanted, be aware paraplegia risk may be higher; vigilance more aggressive.

  15. Lifelong surveillance imaging and BP control are NON-NEGOTIABLE at discharge. CTA abdomen/pelvis at 1 month, 6 months, 12 months, then annually. Native distal aorta expansion, graft re-dilation, false lumen re-expansion can declare years later. Patient must understand this is lifelong, not a one-time surgery.

cards.title: Aortic Regurgitation
cards.quickAnswer: Aortic regurgitation is incompetence of the aortic valve allowing diastolic backflow into the left ventricle. Acute severe AR (endocarditis, dissection) = surgical emergency with pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, high mortality without immediate intervention. Chronic AR is often asymptomatic for years until LV dilates and systolic function declines. Severity graded by vena contracta (>6 mm severe), pressure half-time (<200 ms severe), regurgitant fraction (≥50% severe), and regurgitant volume (≥60 mL severe). 2020 AHA/ACC valve guideline indications for surgery: symptomatic severe AR or asymptomatic severe AR with LV dysfunction (LVEF <50%) or dilation (LVESD >50 mm). Bicuspid aortic valve is the most common congenital abnormality; ~50% of bicuspid patients develop aortopathy requiring lifelong surveillance. IABP is contraindicated in severe AR.
