sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Failure of the aortic valve leaflets to coapt during diastole, permitting retrograde blood flow from the aorta into the left ventricle. Creates volume overload, progressive LV dilation, and eccentric hypertrophy.
  • Incidence and epidemiology:
  • Primary valve disease — degenerative (most common in older adults), bicuspid aortic valve (~1–2% population, higher aortic surgery risk), rheumatic, endocarditis, connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz)
  • Secondary (aortic root disease) — aortopathy (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, familial), hypertension, aortic dissection, syphilis (rare)
  • Bicuspid aortic valve: ~20% have family history; ~50% develop progressive aortic root dilation requiring lifelong surveillance
  • Who this applies to: younger to middle-aged patients with bicuspid or degenerative valve presenting with exertional dyspnea or found incidentally on echocardiography; acute presentations with endocarditis or dissection; older patients with hypertensive aortopathy; ICU patients after cardiac surgery; preoperative candidates for AVR or aortic root replacement.
  • Clinical context: ICU nurses care for preoperative AR patients awaiting AVR or valve-sparing aortic root replacement, acute severe AR from endocarditis or dissection requiring emergency surgery, and post-operative AVR or root replacement patients.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Why AR develops and how the heart responds.

sections.heading: Acute vs. Chronic AR: Fundamentally Different Pathophysiology
Acute Severe AR
sections.bodyHtml:
• Acute dyspnea at rest, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  • Pulmonary edema on auscultation (rales, crackles); bat-wing pattern on chest X-ray
  • Hemodynamic instability: hypotension (SBP <90), tachycardia (>120), cool extremities, altered mental status, decreased urine output
  • Shock physiology: weak pulses, pale skin, delayed capillary refill
  • May have pre-closure of mitral valve on echocardiography (diastolic MV closure from elevated LVEDP)
  • Underlying causes visible in history: fever + positive blood cultures (endocarditis), acute chest/back pain + BP differential between arms (Type A dissection), blunt trauma

sections.heading: Chronic AR
sections.bodyHtml:
• Often asymptomatic — discovered on routine echocardiography or during pre-operative evaluation
  • When symptomatic: exertional dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance early
  • Anginal chest pain (rare, from coronary steal physiology)
  • Late findings: orthopnea, PND (indicates decompensation phase)
  • Palpitations, awareness of heartbeat
  • Classic physical exam signs (see Assessment section below)

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — what acute and chronic AR patients look like at bedside.

sections.heading: Acute Severe AR
sections.bodyHtml:
• Acute dyspnea at rest, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  • Pulmonary edema on auscultation (rales, crackles); bat-wing pattern on chest X-ray
  • Hemodynamic instability: hypotension (SBP <90), tachycardia (>120), cool extremities, altered mental status, decreased urine output
  • Shock physiology: weak pulses, pale skin, delayed capillary refill
  • May have pre-closure of mitral valve on echocardiography (diastolic MV closure from elevated LVEDP)
  • Underlying causes visible in history: fever + positive blood cultures (endocarditis), acute chest/back pain + BP differential between arms (Type A dissection), blunt trauma

sections.heading: Chronic AR
sections.bodyHtml:
• Often asymptomatic — discovered on routine echocardiography or during pre-operative evaluation
  • When symptomatic: exertional dyspnea, fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance early
  • Anginal chest pain (rare, from coronary steal physiology)
  • Late findings: orthopnea, PND (indicates decompensation phase)
  • Palpitations, awareness of heartbeat
  • Classic physical exam signs (see Assessment section below)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml: Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: 2 minutes at bedside (acute) or systematic pre-op evaluation (chronic).

sections.heading: Vital Signs & Hemodynamics
sections.bodyHtml:
• HR, BP (both arms if dissection suspected), RR, SpO₂, temperature
  • Wide pulse pressure in chronic AR (high systolic, low diastolic) — classic finding
  • Orthostatic vital signs if patient able to stand

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.bodyHtml:
• Dyspnea (acute onset or exertional), chest pain, syncope, palpitations
  • Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (late finding — decompensation)
  • Fever or chills (endocarditis context)

sections.heading: Physical Exam — Cardiac
sections.bodyHtml:
• Apical impulse: displaced laterally (LV dilation in chronic AR); hyperdynamic (vigorous)
  • Auscultation: high-pitched, blowing, diastolic decrescendo murmur at left sternal border (early diastole), best heard leaning forward in full expiration
  • Austin Flint murmur — mid-diastolic rumble at apex from AR jet impacting anterior mitral leaflet (NOT mitral valve pathology)
  • Pulse quality: check for water-hammer pulse (Corrigan's pulse — rapid rise and collapse of carotid pulse)
  • Carotid pulse: bounding in chronic AR

sections.heading: Physical Exam — Special Signs of Chronic AR
sections.bodyHtml:
• Hill's sign: systolic leg BP >20 mmHg higher than arm BP (LV stroke volume hyperdynamic)
  • Quincke's pulse: systolic pulsation of nail bed (visible blanching with pressure on nail bed)
  • Duroziez's sign: systolic and diastolic murmur heard over femoral artery on auscultation with stethoscope diaphragm (Korotkoff-like sounds)
  • Musset's sign: head nodding with systole (hyperdynamic LV stroke volume)
  • Bounding pulses in extremities; wide pulse pressure on palpation

sections.heading: Pulmonary Exam
sections.bodyHtml:
• Rales, crackles (pulmonary edema, especially acute AR)
  • Tachypnea, work of breathing

sections.heading: Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP)
sections.bodyHtml: • May be elevated in decompensated chronic AR or acute AR with shock

sections.heading: Perfusion
sections.bodyHtml:
• Capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output
  • Altered mental status in shock states (acute AR)

sections.heading: Lines & Access (if ICU/post-op)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Arterial line waveform (bounding dicrotic notch in AR)
  • Central venous access adequacy
  • Epicardial pacing wires (post-op)

sections.heading: Key Labs & Imaging
sections.bodyHtml:
• Recent echocardiography: AR severity (vena contracta, PHT, ERO, RV, RF), LV dimensions (LVESD, LVEDD), LVEF
  • ECG: conduction abnormalities (aortic root abscess from endocarditis → AV block), LV hypertrophy pattern
  • Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema pattern, widened mediastinum (dissection concern)
  • Recent hemoglobin, creatinine, electrolytes: baseline renal function, anemia (affects surgical risk)
  • Troponin, lactate (if acute AR with shock)
  • Blood cultures (if endocarditis suspected — draw before antibiotics)

sections.heading: Surgery Context (Pre-op)
sections.bodyHtml:
• What procedure is planned and why? (AVR, VSARR, Bentall, SAVR + root replacement)
  • Prior cardiac surgery? (affects aortic anatomy, graft considerations)
  • Baseline LVEF, LVESD/LVEDD from most recent pre-op echo
  • Aortic root size from CTA (diameter at sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, ascending aorta)
  • Coronary anatomy (from recent angiography or risk assessment)
  • Bicuspid AV? Marfan? Family history of aortic disease?

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Diagnosis card: Management subsections replace the Stable/Unstable fork.

sections.heading: 5A. Medical Management (Bridge Therapy, Not Definitive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pharmacologic approach:

Agent Mechanism Indication Dose/Monitoring Limitations
ACE inhibitor (lisinopril, enalapril) Reduces afterload, may slow LV dilation Asymptomatic severe AR; HTN with AR; chronic AR bridge to surgery Lisinopril 10–40 mg daily; monitor K⁺, Cr Benefit in asymptomatic AR debated; no RCT proof of surgery prevention
ARB (losartan, valsartan) Afterload reduction, aortic remodeling benefit (especially aortopathy) Chronic AR with aortic root dilation; Marfan or Loeys-Dietz AR Losartan 50–100 mg daily; monitor K⁺, Cr Similar evidence gap to ACE-I; may stabilize root growth rate
Dihydropyridine CCB (amlodipine) Afterload reduction without negative inotropy Chronic AR if ACE-I/ARB not tolerated; HTN + AR Amlodipine 5–10 mg daily Less negative inotropic effect than non-DHP CCBs; reflex tachycardia possible
Beta-blocker (metoprolol, atenolol) HR control (slower diastole = less regurgitant time) Asymptomatic severe AR; HTN + AR; aortopathy bridge (Marfan/LDS) Metoprolol 50–200 mg daily; target HR 60–80 Use cautiously in reduced-EF AR (negative inotropic effect); bradycardia risks forward CO
Diuretics (furosemide) Symptom relief in HF Chronic AR with volume overload symptoms; acute AR with pulmonary edema Titrate to euvolemia; avoid over-diuresis Preload-sensitive; over-diuresis may worsen forward CO

Hemodynamic goals (chronic AR, pre-op):

  • BP target: 100–140 mmHg systolic (higher end acceptable in AR, unlike AS)
  • HR target: 70–90 bpm (mild tachycardia 90–110 acceptable; faster HR shortens diastole → reduces regurgitant fraction per beat)
  • Avoid: hypotension (SBP <90), bradycardia (<60), tachycardia >110 (except acute AR where it reflects shock)
  • Preload: maintain adequate filling (CVP 5–8 cm H₂O); AR patients are preload-dependent

Important caveats:

  • No medication stops progression of AR. Definitive treatment is surgery.
  • Afterload reduction benefit in asymptomatic severe AR is controversial; use to manage symptoms and HTN, not proven to defer surgery
  • Endocarditis prophylaxis: NOT routinely recommended for native valve AR per ACC/AHA 2020 guideline; IS required after prosthetic valve placement

sections.heading: 5B. Chronic AR Surveillance — Serial Echocardiography & Surgical Timing
sections.bodyHtml:
Assessment intervals (ACC/AHA 2021):

AR Severity LVEF & Dimensions Echo Interval
Mild-moderate AR Normal LVEF, normal dimensions Every 3–5 years
Severe AR, asymptomatic Normal LVEF, normal dimensions Every 6–12 months
Severe AR, asymptomatic Normal LVEF, dilated LV (LVESD 50–55 mm or LVEDD 65–70 mm) Every 3–6 months
Severe AR, any dysfunction EF <50% OR LVESD >55 mm OR LVEDD >70 mm Escalate to surgery discussion

Surgical indications (Class I, Class IIa — 2020 AHA/ACC Valvular Guideline):

Class Indication Rationale
Class I Symptomatic severe AR (any symptom: dyspnea, angina, syncope) Symptoms indicate LV decompensation; mortality untreated >10% annually
Class I Asymptomatic severe AR + LV dysfunction (LVEF ≤50%) EF decline is irreversible; surgery halts progression in most
Class I Asymptomatic severe AR + LV dilation (LVESD >50 mm or LVEDD >65 mm) Progressive dilation predicts sudden decompensation; early surgery prevents systolic dysfunction
Class IIa Asymptomatic severe AR + very severe regurgitation burden (RV >90 mL, RF >80%, ERO >40 mm²) Extreme severity warrants consideration even with preserved dimensions
Class IIa Severe AR requiring other cardiac surgery (CABG, valve replacement) Single operative intervention preferred to staged approach

Monitoring for decompensation (red flags for escalation):

  • Any new cardiac symptom (dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, palpitations)
  • LVEF decline (EF drops >10% or falls below 50%)
  • Rapid LV dilation (LVESD or LVEDD increase >5 mm on consecutive echo)
  • New atrial fibrillation (loss of atrial kick triggers decompensation in AR; see Section 6)
  • Uncontrolled hypertension despite medical therapy

sections.heading: 5C. Surgical AR Repair vs. Replacement Timing
sections.bodyHtml:
Approach selection (based on aortic root size, patient age, valve pathology):

Procedure Root Size / Indication Prosthesis Advantages Disadvantages Considerations
SAVR (Standard AVR) Root <50 mm; severe symptomatic or asymptomatic dilated AR Tissue (bioprosthesis) No anticoagulation; acceptable hemodynamics; simpler technique Limited durability 10–15 years; structural degeneration in younger patients; redo risk Good for older patients (>70); acceptable if life expectancy <15 years
Mechanical Excellent durability 20+ years; predictable longevity Lifelong warfarin INR 2–3; thromboembolic risk; pregnancy precautions Preferred for younger patients (<60) if compliant with anticoagulation
VSARR (Valve-sparing AR root replacement) Severe AR + root <55–60 mm; younger patients; desire no anticoagulation; structurally normal leaflets Native valve preserved (Tirone David, Yacoub reimplantation technique) Preserves native leaflets; no prosthetic complications; no anticoagulation; excellent hemodynamics; avoids future redo Steep learning curve; specialized surgeons only; intraoperative TEE-dependent; risk residual AR if poorly performed; valve durability ~80–90% at 10 years; root remodeling possible Consider in younger patients; requires dedicated center expertise
Bentall procedure Severe AR + moderate-severe root dilation (>55–60 mm), root aneurysm, acute Type A dissection, Marfan, Loeys-Dietz Mechanical valve composite graft (valve + graft as single unit) Single operation addresses valve + root pathology; prevents proximal aortic rupture; definitive for aortopathy Lifelong warfarin required; coronary reimplantation necessary; longest operative time; highest perioperative bleeding risk; proximal aorta may dilate beyond graft Standard for aortopathy (Marfan, LDS, familial aneurysm); necessary in Type A dissection with root involvement
SAVR + separate root graft Moderate root dilation (50–60 mm) without severe aortic disease Tissue or mechanical AVR + tube graft Flexibility in valve selection; avoids full composite graft; avoids coronary reimplantation Two suture lines; proximal aorta remains at risk if rapidly enlarging; longer operative time Intermediate approach; requires root measurement and surgeon judgment

Special populations:

  • Bicuspid AR: VSARR often preferred if root <60 mm and leaflets structurally intact; lifelong aortic imaging surveillance mandatory post-op (root may dilate, especially if family history of dissection)
  • Marfan + LDS: Bentall procedure standard; prophylactic surgery at smaller root diameters (Marfan >50 mm, LDS >45 mm with family history of dissection) prevents rupture/dissection
  • Post-dissection AR: If Type A dissection with root involvement → urgent Bentall; if distal dissection (root uninvolved) → may do AVR alone, but aortic imaging follow-up critical

sections.heading: 5D. Acute Severe AR — Emergency Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Recognition & immediate hemodynamic support:

  • Acute dyspnea at rest + hemodynamic instability + AR on echo = surgical emergency
  • Preload-dependent; maintain CVP 8–10 cm H₂O (higher than typical)
  • Diuretics cautiously for pulmonary edema (furosemide bolus 40–80 mg IV); avoid over-diuresis
  • Inotropic/vasopressor support: dobutamine (2–20 mcg/kg/min), low-dose epinephrine (0.02–0.1 mcg/kg/min), or milrinone (0.25–0.75 mcg/kg/min) if shock
  • Avoid excessive tachycardia (increases regurgitant volume); balance CO support against HR acceleration
  • Goal: improve perfusion pressure without worsening AR

IABP is CONTRAINDICATED in acute severe AR:

  • IABP inflates during diastole — precisely wrong for AR
  • Inflation increases aortic pressure during diastole → increases retrograde flow → worsens LVEDP → worsens pulmonary edema and shock
  • If IABP placed pre-op, notify OR team immediately; may need removal
  • Mechanical support alternative: venoarterial ECMO if cardiogenic shock refractory to inotropes, pending emergency surgery

Emergent surgical workup (stat, in parallel):

  • Stat CTA chest with IV contrast — delineate aortic root, rule out dissection, plan surgical approach
  • Transthoracic + transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) — assess AR severity, leaflet damage, vegetations, MV involvement, LV function, presence of pericardial effusion
  • Labs: CBC, BMP, coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT), blood cultures (BEFORE antibiotics if endocarditis suspected), lactate (tissue hypoperfusion marker), ABG
  • 12-lead ECG: conduction abnormalities (aortic root abscess may erode into AV node → high-degree AV block)
  • Chest X-ray: pulmonary edema, widened mediastinum (dissection concern)
  • Coronary angiography: rarely needed pre-op (time-sensitive); skip unless anatomy unknown and time permits

Antibiotics (if endocarditis suspected):

  • Do NOT delay surgery waiting for culture results. Mortality without urgent surgery >70% in acute endocarditis AR
  • Draw blood cultures immediately (before antibiotics)
  • Start empiric broad-spectrum coverage after cultures: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h + ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h + gentamicin 7.5 mg/kg/day IV (adjust for renal function)
  • Adjust based on culture results and susceptibilities
  • Continue antibiotics for full course post-op (typically 4–6 weeks post-aortic root surgery, depending on organism and valve type)

Procedural consideration (acute endocarditis):

  • Large vegetation (>10 mm), leaflet perforation, perivalvular abscess, valve destruction → likely requires composite graft (Bentall) or aortic root reconstruction
  • Smaller vegetation with severe AR but intact root anatomy → may be amenable to SAVR alone, but aggressive post-op monitoring for recurrent endocarditis

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
When to call and what to communicate.

SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room]." [Add operative day if post-op: "POD [X] s/p [procedure]"] B: "[Patient context — pre-op awaiting AR surgery / post-op Day X / on telemetry with new findings]. Known severe AR [or acute AR]. Recent echo: LVEF [%], LVESD [mm], LVEDD [mm], aortic root [mm]." A: "[Current status — vitals, symptoms, physical findings, labs if abnormal]. [Acute changes if present: new murmur, new instability, new AF, new chest pain]." R: "[What you need — e.g., increased diuresis, medication adjustment, urgent surgical evaluation, transfer to ICU]."

Who to call — by clinical scenario:

Situation Contact
Pre-op AR patient, stable, routine pre-op visit Primary attending / surgical team at pre-op clinic
Pre-op AR patient with worsening dyspnea or new orthopnea Cardiologist + surgical team (may accelerate surgery)
Pre-op AR patient with new syncope or chest pain Cardiology STAT + surgical team; consider ICU admission
Acute severe AR (endocarditis, dissection, traumatic) with hemodynamic instability CT surgery STAT + ER/ICU team + anesthesia (operating room imminent)
Post-op Day 0–1 AR patient with excessive bleeding (>300 mL/h × 2 h) CT surgery + blood bank; prepare for re-exploration
Post-op AR patient with new cardiac murmur (possible paravalvular leak or prosthetic dysfunction) CT surgery (may need echo + possible re-exploration)
Post-op AR patient with new fever + elevated WBC + possible prosthetic valve endocarditis ID + CT surgery + cardiology; blood cultures, TEE
Pre-op or post-op AR patient with new irregular rhythm (POAF, SVT) Cardiology / APP; consider EP evaluation if recurrent
Any AR patient with new focal neurologic deficit (post-op stroke risk) Neurology STAT + CT surgery (stroke code considerations)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive — expandable in clinical application)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology detail: LV remodeling in chronic AR Eccentric hypertrophy and compensation:
  • The volume-overloaded LV responds to chronic AR by dilating (eccentric hypertrophy — increased cavity size and length with normal or reduced wall thickness).
  • Eccentric hypertrophy preserves systolic function initially through mechanisms of preload and LaPlace's law: larger cavity maintains stroke volume despite reduced ejection fraction.
  • This is fundamentally different from concentric hypertrophy (aortic stenosis), where increased wall thickness maintains function against high afterload.
  • The compensated phase lasts years to decades in mild-moderate AR; patient is asymptomatic, very active, LVEF normal.
  • The transition to decompensation is abrupt once critical LV dimensions are exceeded (LVESD >55 mm, LVEDD >70 mm): forward stroke volume drops, EF falls, pulmonary pressures rise, patient becomes symptomatic.
  • This is why serial echocardiography is the standard of care: the goal is to catch LV dilation before EF declines (irreversible phase). Diastolic dysfunction in acute AR:
  • Acute AR loads a non-dilated LV with a massive volume of regurgitant blood during diastole.
  • Because the LV is still stiff (not remodeled), pressure rises sharply → LVEDP rises to >25 mmHg within minutes.
  • High LVEDP pushes the mitral valve open prematurely (diastolic mitral regurgitation); if severe enough, mitral valve may precose (close before the next systole).
  • Preclosure of the mitral valve reduces forward stroke volume → cardiogenic shock.
  • Pulmonary venous pressure rises → pulmonary edema, often in the form of acute pulmonary edema with orthopnea within hours.
Echocardiographic AR severity criteria (ASE/EACVI 2017) Vena contracta width (VCW) — narrowest diameter of the AR jet as it enters the LV:
  • Mild: <3 mm
  • Moderate: 3–6 mm
  • Severe: >6 mm
  • Most reliable single measure of AR severity (less affected by eccentric jets and hemodynamics) Pressure half-time (PHT) — time for AR regurgitant pressure to decay to half its peak (measured on continuous-wave Doppler):
  • Mild: >500 ms
  • Moderate: 200–500 ms
  • Severe: <200 ms
  • Short PHT indicates rapid equalization of aortic and LV pressures (large regurgitant orifice, high LVEDP) Effective regurgitant orifice (ERO) — area of the regurgitant jet:
  • Mild: <10 mm²
  • Moderate: 10–30 mm²
  • Severe: >30 mm² Regurgitant volume (RV) — volume of blood flowing backward per beat:
  • Mild: <30 mL
  • Moderate: 30–59 mL
  • Severe: ≥60 mL Regurgitant fraction (RF) — percentage of LV stroke volume that regurgitates:
  • Mild: <30%
  • Moderate: 30–49%
  • Severe: ≥50% LV dimensions:
    • LVESD (LV end-systolic dimension): progressive dilation sign; >50 mm warrants surgery consideration
    • LVEDD (LV end-diastolic dimension): >65 mm warrants surgery consideration
    • LVEF: declines late in the course; EF <50% is a Class I surgery indication Key point: Mild jet width alone does NOT define severity; must integrate multiple measures. Eccentric jets (off-axis) may appear smaller on one view but be severe on another; VCW is most reliable.
Bicuspid aortic valve: features, aortopathy risk, surveillance Bicuspid AV anatomy:
  • Congenital; ~1–2% of population (most common congenital heart lesion)
  • Two leaflets instead of three (usually anterior-posterior orientation, sometimes right-left)
  • Leaflets often have fibrous raphe (echogenic line mimicking commissure)
  • Structurally abnormal leaflets; higher risk of both stenosis and regurgitation over lifetime Aortopathy in bicuspid AV:
  • ~50% of bicuspid AV patients develop aortic root or ascending aorta dilation
  • Root dilation may be present at diagnosis (detected on initial echo or CTA) or develop progressively
  • Risk of aortic dissection is real but lower than Marfan/LDS (still 5–10× general population)
  • First-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) have 20% inheritance risk and should be screened with echo Surveillance recommendations (post-op and ongoing):
  • Pre-op CTA mandatory — document aortic root diameter at level of sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, ascending aorta, aortic arch
  • Post-op echo at 4–6 weeks, then annually to track root size
  • CTA or cardiac MRI every 1–3 years depending on baseline root size:
  • Root <45 mm: every 3–5 years
  • Root 45–50 mm: every 1–2 years
  • Root >50 mm: consider prophylactic surgery (>50 mm in bicuspid vs. >55 mm in degenerative valves)
  • Family screening: first-degree relatives should have echocardiography to determine if bicuspid, aortic size, need for future surveillance Surgical approach in bicuspid AR:
  • If root <50 mm and leaflets structurally intact: VSARR (Tirone David or Yacoub) preferred if valve-sparing feasible
  • If root >50 mm or rapid growth: consider prophylactic root replacement even if AR asymptomatic
  • If root >55 mm: strong consideration for aortic root surgery concurrent with any aortic valve procedure
  • Post-op: lifelong aortic imaging surveillance is non-negotiable
Aortic root measurements and surgical thresholds Measurement locations (from CTA or cardiac MRI, preferred over TTE for precise root sizing):
  • Sinuses of Valsalva (SOV) — widest diameter of the aortic root, at the level of the coronary ostia
  • Sinotubular junction (STJ) — transition zone between root and ascending aorta
  • Ascending aorta (AA) — proximal ascending aorta above the STJ Surgical thresholds for aortic root replacement (to prevent rupture/dissection):
    PopulationThreshold (SOV diameter)Context
    Marfan syndrome>50 mm (absolute)Higher dissection risk due to fibrillin-1 defect
    Marfan + family history of dissection>45 mmMore aggressive threshold
    Loeys-Dietz syndrome>45–50 mmVery high dissection risk; consider prophylactic at 45 mm
    Loeys-Dietz + family dissection history>40–45 mmMost conservative threshold
    Bicuspid AV alone (no family history)>50–55 mmLower dissection risk than genetic syndromes; threshold debated
    Bicuspid AV + family history of dissection/rupture>45 mmCascade screening identifies at-risk relatives
    Familial aortic aneurysm syndrome>50 mm (varies by family)Genetic testing may refine threshold
    Degenerative aortopathy (HTN, age)55–60 mmLowest dissection risk; threshold higher
    Acute Type A dissectionAny size; emergent surgerySurvival depends on speed to OR
    Rapid growth triggers prophylactic surgery regardless of absolute size:
  • Growth >5 mm per year warrants discussion of surgery
  • Growth >10 mm per year is indication for urgent surgery discussion
Post-surgical AR: repair vs. replacement outcomes VSARR outcomes (valve-sparing aortic root replacement — Tirone David or Yacoub):
  • Advantages: native leaflets preserved; no prosthetic valve complications; no anticoagulation required; excellent hemodynamics
  • Valve durability: ~80–90% freedom from aortic regurgitation at 10 years; some patients develop mild-to-moderate AR over time (valve tissue stretches)
  • Reoperation risk: 5–10% at 10 years (lower than tissue bioprosthesis, higher than mechanical prosthesis)
  • Root remodeling: reticulation can occur; proximal aorta may dilate beyond graft (lifelong imaging surveillance needed)
  • Best outcomes: younger patients (<65), bicuspid AV with structurally intact leaflets, root <55 mm, experienced valve-sparing center Mechanical AVR (St. Jude, CarboMedics, OnX):
  • Durability: excellent; 20+ years or lifetime in most patients; no structural degeneration
  • Anticoagulation: lifelong warfarin INR 2–3; requires INR monitoring every 2–4 weeks
  • Thromboembolism risk: ~0.5–1.5% per year (varies by model, position)
  • Hemodynamic performance: good; mechanical valves have predictable gradients
  • Reoperation rate: low (~1% per year for structural reasons); higher for pannus formation or endocarditis
  • Best for: younger patients (<60) if reliable with anticoagulation compliance; patients with long life expectancy (20+ years) Tissue bioprosthesis (ATAVIS, Mosaic, Trifecta, Carpentier Edwards, Inspiris):
  • Durability: limited; structural degeneration typical at 10–15 years (younger patients fail sooner)
  • No anticoagulation: only aspirin required; appeals to patients with contraindications to warfarin
  • Hemodynamic performance: good; gradients low (especially newer designs like Inspiris)
  • Reoperation rate: 10–15% at 10 years (redo aortic valve replacement, typically AVR again)
  • Best for: older patients (>70), life expectancy <15 years, patient preference against anticoagulation
  • Note: tissue valves in AR position may degenerate faster than in mitral position due to higher pressure gradient Bentall procedure (composite graft — mechanical valve + Dacron tube):
  • Durability: excellent; both valve and graft very durable (20+ years)
  • Anticoagulation: lifelong warfarin required (mechanical valve component)
  • Aortic pathology addressed: single operation fixes valve + root + proximal ascending aorta
  • Complexity: coronary reimplantation necessary (adds operative time, bleeding risk)
  • Proximal aorta risk: aorta beyond graft can still dilate; lifelong imaging surveillance mandatory
  • Reoperation risk: ~5–10% at 10 years (mostly for pannus, endocarditis, or proximal aorta dilation)
  • Best for: Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, acute Type A dissection, aortopathy with root dilation
TAVR in aortic regurgitation: role and limitations Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) is approved for aortic stenosis and increasingly used in some AR patients, but not first-line in native valve AR:
  • Indication: TAVR in AR is limited; most guidelines consider it high-risk or contraindicated in pure AR (regurgitation)
  • Problem with native valve AR: aortic valve regurgitation is often due to the annulus being too large for the valve leaflets (root dilation, functional AR). A prosthetic TAVR valve in a large, regurgitant annulus is likely to develop paravalvular leak (backflow around the valve).
  • TAVR in aortic stenosis with mild-moderate AR: reasonable option in high-risk surgical candidates
  • TAVR in pure severe native AR: contraindicated in most current systems due to high paravalvular leak risk and poor outcomes
  • Special case — prosthetic AR: TAVR-in-TAVR (valve-in-valve TAVR) for failed prosthetic aortic valve can be considered in AR if the prosthesis is calcified and stenotic; but native AR remains problematic
  • Annulus-stabilizing devices: newer TAVR systems (e.g., ACURATE, Allegra) offer more stability in larger annuli, but native pure AR remains off-label Clinical bottom line: Native valve AR → surgical AVR or root replacement. TAVR plays a niche role in TAVI-associated AR or failing prosthetic AVR; not primary therapy for native AR.
Acute AR pathophysiology and non-dilated LV decompensation Why acute AR is a surgical emergency (and chronic AR is not): The key difference is LV volume tolerance:
  • Chronic AR: non-dilated LV gradually becomes dilated LV over months-years; myocardium remodels and adapts; patient tolerates massive RV (60–90+ mL) while remaining asymptomatic
  • Acute AR: non-dilated, stiff LV is suddenly loaded with massive regurgitant volume → LVEDP skyrockets → pulmonary edema and shock within hours Mechanistic cascade in acute AR:
    1. Sudden valve incompetence (vegetation perforation, dissection flap, leaflet endothelial damage)
    2. Large regurgitant volume (RV often 40–60 mL) into a non-dilated LV
    3. LVEDP rises to 25–40+ mmHg within minutes (compare: normal LVEDP ~5–12 mmHg, chronic severe AR LVEDP may be only slightly elevated because of compensatory dilation)
    4. Mitral valve opens prematurely in diastole due to high LVEDP forcing the leaflet open
    5. Preclosure of mitral valve: if LVEDP becomes very high very fast, the MV may actually close before systole begins (diastolic mitral closure), eliminating forward stroke volume
    6. Pulmonary edema: high LVEDP transmitted backward to pulmonary veins → transudation into alveoli (often orthopnea, PND within hours)
    7. Cardiogenic shock: reduced forward stroke volume (from preclosed MV) → hypotension, tachycardia, altered mental status, renal hypoperfusion, lactate elevation
    8. Death without surgery: mortality rises sharply; median survival without urgent surgery in acute endocarditis AR is <1 week Why IABP worsens acute AR:
    9. IABP inflates during diastole, increasing aortic diastolic pressure
    10. In acute AR, LVEDP is already dangerously high; increasing diastolic aortic pressure worsens the pressure gradient driving regurgitation
    11. More regurgitant volume → even higher LVEDP → worsens pulmonary edema and shock
    12. IABP is contraindicated and can precipitate sudden deterioration in acute AR Contrast with aortic stenosis:
    13. In AS, IABP inflates during diastole → increases aortic pressure → increases the gradient pushing blood forward through the stenotic valve (helpful)
    14. In AR, the same diastolic inflation worsens regurgitation (harmful)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in stable AR patients; if any show, re-escalate.

Pre-op AR patient:

  • New or worsening dyspnea (may indicate LV decompensation; escalate for earlier surgery)
  • New syncope or near-syncope (suggests decompensated LV or arrhythmia; urgent cardiology evaluation)
  • New orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (late sign of decompensation; consider ICU admission)
  • New irregular pulse or palpitations (new AF risk in AR; loss of atrial kick can precipitate cardiogenic shock)
  • New chest pain or anginal symptoms (AR can cause coronary steal; rule out ACS, discuss urgent surgery)
  • New S₃ gallop (indicates LV dysfunction; may signal transition from compensated to decompensated phase)
  • Rapid increase in JVP or new peripheral edema (volume overload; escalate diuretic therapy or surgery timing)

Post-op AR patient (SAVR, VSARR, root replacement):

  • Sudden new diastolic murmur (possible paravalvular leak from prosthetic valve; obtain echo, notify surgeon)
  • Hemodynamic instability out of proportion to the operation (possible prosthetic malfunction, tamponade, endocarditis)
  • Fever + elevated WBC + malaise in first 2 years post-op (prosthetic valve endocarditis risk; blood cultures, TEE, ID consult)
  • Acute AR recurrence post-VSARR (rare but possible; valve tissue may regress or structural valve failure; re-operation likely needed)
  • Widening mediastinum or increasing chest drainage (possible aortic graft leak; notify CT surgery)

Acute AR patient (ICU):

  • Dropping systolic BP despite inotropes (cardiogenic shock worsening; prepare for immediate OR, consider ECMO)
  • Increasing pulmonary edema on CXR or worsening hypoxia despite diuretics (LVEDP rising; surgical emergency)
  • Rising lactate (tissue hypoperfusion marker; indicates inadequate perfusion; emergent OR)
  • Altered mental status or decreasing urine output (end-organ hypoperfusion; emergent OR)
  • Arrhythmia (VT, rapid SVT in context of acute AR = poor prognostic sign; surgical emergency)

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Acute severe AR is a surgical emergency; chronic AR is a surveillance condition. Chronic AR asymptomatic patient may be very well-appearing and stable for years. Acute AR (endocarditis, dissection) is hemodynamically unstable and dying within days. Don't confuse them. Acute AR = ICU, urgent imaging, emergent OR. Chronic AR = serial echo every 6–12 months, escalate only if symptoms, LVEF decline, or LVESD >50 mm develop.

  2. IABP is CONTRAINDICATED in severe AR. Balloon inflation occurs during diastole, worsening diastolic aortic pressure and increasing regurgitant flow. Do NOT place IABP in severe AR without full team awareness and explicit plan. If IABP already placed before AR diagnosis, notify OR team immediately. Consider venoarterial ECMO instead for mechanical support.

  3. Bicuspid aortic valve: screen the ascending aorta and organize family screening. 50% of bicuspid patients develop aortic root dilation; risk of dissection is real. Pre-op CTA is mandatory to document root diameter. Post-op surveillance should continue indefinitely (root can dilate even after valve surgery). First-degree relatives should be screened for bicuspid valve (20% inheritance); if present, they need aortic imaging too.

  4. Marfan and Loeys-Dietz aortopathy require prophylactic surgery at smaller root diameters and lifelong family screening. Aortic root can dilate rapidly and dissect unpredictably. Standard surgical thresholds: Marfan >50 mm, LDS >45 mm (even more aggressive if family history of dissection). Genetic counseling is essential; first-degree relatives need cascade screening.

  5. Endocarditis with severe AR is an urgent surgical indication — do NOT delay waiting for culture results. Large vegetations (>10 mm), leaflet perforation, perivalvular abscess, or any severe AR from endocarditis warrants emergent OR evaluation. Mortality without surgery >70% in acute presentations. Draw cultures, start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, escalate to CT surgery.

  6. Chronic AR tolerates exertion beautifully until LV decompensates — then sudden downhill. Patients compensate for years because LV dilates and maintains EF through eccentric hypertrophy. Once EF declines, LVESd >55 mm, LVEDD >70 mm reached, they can decompensate acutely (new dyspnea, syncope, shock). This is why serial echo every 6–12 months is non-negotiable in severe AR.

  7. Afterload reduction (ACE-I/ARB) benefit in asymptomatic severe AR is debated. Some cardiologists use for symptom management and HTN control; no randomized trial proves they prevent surgery. Key management: serial echo every 6–12 months, escalate if symptoms develop, LV dilates, or EF declines. BP target: SBP <140 (normal-to-slightly-elevated is OK in AR, unlike AS).

  8. Pregnancy with severe AR is high-risk. Pregnancy increases preload, heart rate, and cardiac output 40–50% → worsens AR hemodynamically. Severe symptomatic AR should be corrected pre-conception. If pregnant with severe AR, close cardiology monitoring + possible hospitalization 3rd trimester; plan for delivery at high-risk obstetric center with cardiothoracic surgery available.

  9. Watchful waiting with serial echocardiography is the standard for asymptomatic severe AR. ACC/AHA 2020/2021 guideline: escalate to surgery only when symptoms develop, EF declines below 50%, LVESD >50 mm (or >25 mm/m² BSA), or LVEDD >65 mm (or >32 mm/m² BSA). Earlier surgery for very severe regurgitation burden (RV >90 mL, RF >80%).

  10. Austin Flint murmur is pathognomonic for hemodynamically significant AR. Mid-diastolic rumble at apex caused by AR jet impinging on anterior mitral leaflet. Does NOT indicate mitral valve pathology; leaflets are structurally normal. Echo will show no primary MV disease. Presence of Austin Flint murmur suggests at least moderate-to-severe AR.

  11. Wide pulse pressure and water-hammer pulse are classic physical signs but don't quantify severity. Corrigan's pulse (carotid bounding + collapse), Hill's sign (leg BP >20 mmHg higher than arm), Quincke's pulse (nail bed pulsation), Duroziez's sign (femoral murmur) all indicate hemodynamically significant AR. But physical exam alone doesn't grade severity; echocardiography (vena contracta, PHT, ERO, RV, RF) is required.

  12. Post-SAVR/VSARR hemodynamic targets are exacting. Different prostheses require different SBP targets: mechanical AVR post-AR surgery prefer higher SBP (110–140) to avoid valve stress; tissue valve lower (100–130) to reduce degeneration risk; VSARR aim 100–130 (native leaflets sensitive to high afterload). Off-protocol BP management stresses new valve and suture lines. Know the target for each prosthesis type.

  13. Lifelong aortic root surveillance is mandatory in bicuspid, Marfan, and LDS patients after any aortic valve or root surgery. Root replacement prevents rupture but doesn't prevent proximal aorta dilation. Imaging (CTA or cardiac MRI) every 1–3 years depending on family history and rate of growth. A root that was 50 mm at surgery can reach 60 mm by year 5; prophylactic reoperation may be needed.

  14. New diastolic murmur in post-AVR patient is aortic regurgitation — likely paravalvular leak. Notify surgeon immediately; may need echocardiography (assess leak severity) and possible re-exploration if hemodynamically significant. Paravalvular AR is the most common complication of post-SAVR; can develop early (days) or years later.

  15. Hemodynamic instability in acute severe AR often precedes pulmonary edema on CXR — watch for it early. Preclosure of mitral valve or rapid LVEDP rise can cause cardiogenic shock even without florid pulmonary edema visible yet. Hypotension + dyspnea + tachycardia in acute AR = call OR immediately. Don't wait for rales or bat-wing CXR pattern; escalate on hemodynamic signs alone.

  16. Aortic root size matters for surgical planning; document carefully and communicate. Root <50 mm + severe AR → candidate for VSARR (valve-sparing). Root 50–60 mm → shared decision (Tirone David vs. SAVR + graft). Root >60 mm → usually Bentall composite graft. Pre-op CTA with root measurements at SOV, STJ, and ascending aorta is mandatory; communicate dimensions and growth rate to surgical team so approach is planned.

  17. Tachycardia can be therapeutic in chronic AR but harmful in acute AR. In chronic AR, mild tachycardia (90–110 bpm) shortens diastole → reduces regurgitant stroke volume per beat → may improve symptoms and exercise tolerance. In acute AR, tachycardia reflects inadequate forward cardiac output and cardiogenic shock; it's a red flag for deterioration, not a therapeutic goal.

  18. LV dilation in chronic AR is adaptive early, then suddenly decompensates. Progressive LVEDD dilation (65 → 70 → 75 mm) is tolerated, then critical dimension exceeded (~75 mm) and systolic dysfunction accelerates rapidly, sometimes over weeks. This is why serial echocardiography is essential — the goal is catching dilation before EF declines, because EF decline is often irreversible.

  19. New onset atrial fibrillation in AR patient is an emergency, not routine post-op arrhythmia. Loss of atrial kick can drop cardiac output 20–30% in AR patient (annulus is large, LV is volume-loaded, AF eliminates the coordinated atrial contraction). AF + rapid ventricular response worsens AR (shorter diastolic filling time per beat). Escalate immediately; aggressive rate control and rhythm control consideration required.

cards.title: Aortic Stenosis
cards.quickAnswer: Aortic stenosis is left ventricular outflow obstruction from aortic valve narrowing (calcific, rheumatic, bicuspid) causing concentric hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction. Severity graded by echocardiography: jet velocity ≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, aortic valve area ≤1 cm² = severe. Symptomatic severe AS (angina, syncope, dyspnea) has 50% untreated 2-year mortality; symptomatic = surgical indication. TAVR is increasingly first-line in low-to-intermediate risk patients (PARTNER 3, Evolut Low Risk trials extend to younger age groups). Avoid vasodilators, nitrates, and excessive diuresis — can cause syncope and hemodynamic collapse. Phenylephrine is first-line vasopressor. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty serves as bridge to definitive surgery only.
