sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Obstruction to left ventricular outflow due to narrowing at the aortic valve level. Creates pressure overload, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, diastolic dysfunction, and eventually symptoms (angina, syncope, heart failure).
  • Epidemiology and valve types:
  • Calcific (degenerative) AS — most common; elderly patients >70 years; progressive leaflet calcification and fibrosis
  • Bicuspic aortic valve — congenital; ~1–2% of population; earlier onset (50s–60s); higher surgery risk due to associated aortopathy
  • Rheumatic AS — rare in developed countries; more common globally; usually accompanied by mitral stenosis
  • Who this applies to: elderly patients presenting with exertional dyspnea, angina, or syncope; younger patients with bicuspid AV and aortic root dilation; ICU patients pre-op awaiting SAVR or TAVR; post-op AVR/TAVR patients; patients admitted with decompensated heart failure related to undiagnosed severe AS.
  • Clinical context: ICU nurses care for pre-operative AS patients awaiting surgical (SAVR) or transcatheter (TAVR) aortic valve replacement, patients with symptomatic severe AS requiring emergent intervention, post-operative AVR/TAVR patients, and high-risk patients being evaluated for TAVR candidacy.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Why AS develops and how the left ventricle responds over time.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology: Pressure Overload & LV Adaptation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Progressive valve narrowing (leaflet calcification, fibrosis, commissural fusion) → LV pressure rises to maintain cardiac output across the stenotic valve
  • Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy develops: wall thickens, cavity size remains small (differs from eccentric hypertrophy of volume overload)
  • Diastolic dysfunction from LVH: stiff, hypertrophied LV requires high filling pressures and depends critically on atrial kick to maintain diastolic filling
  • Compensated phase lasts years: patient may remain asymptomatic despite severe AS, especially if sedentary (activity adaptation disguises symptom onset)
  • Subendocardial ischemia risk increases: hypertrophied myocardium compresses microvasculature; oxygen demand ↑↑ while coronary blood flow ↓
  • End-stage decompensation: LV systolic function declines → pulmonary congestion, HF, death without intervention

sections.heading: The Classical Symptom Triad (Once Any Symptom Develops = Surgical Urgency)
sections.bodyHtml:
Symptom Pathophysiology Untreated Median Survival
Angina Subendocardial ischemia from hypertrophied myocardium with reduced coronary perfusion 5 years
Syncope Paradoxical vasodilation + loss of atrial kick → sudden CO drop; also increased LV pressure → baroreceptor malfunction 3 years
Heart failure (dyspnea, orthopnea, PND) LV decompensation → systolic dysfunction, pulmonary congestion 2 years

Critical principle: Once ANY symptom develops, the patient requires urgent surgical intervention. Median survival drops precipitously. Delaying surgery beyond symptom onset carries >10% annual mortality risk untreated.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — what AS patients look like at bedside.

sections.heading: Asymptomatic Severe AS
sections.bodyHtml:
• Often discovered incidentally on echocardiography during pre-operative evaluation or routine cardiac screening
  • Patient reports no dyspnea, chest pain, or presyncope
  • May have adapted activity (sedentary lifestyle masks exertional limitation); explicitly ask: "What's the most strenuous activity you do? How far can you walk?"

sections.heading: Symptomatic Severe AS (The Classic Triad)
sections.bodyHtml:
Exertional angina:

  • Substernal chest pressure or heaviness during exertion; relieved by rest
  • May not respond fully to nitrates; in severe AS, nitrates can precipitate syncope (see Pitfalls)
  • Often represents true coronary ischemia from LVH + demand mismatch, though CAD also common

Exertional syncope (or presyncope/dizziness):

  • Loss of consciousness or near-syncope during exertion or immediately after
  • Mechanism: exertional vasodilation in peripheral muscles → CO cannot increase to match → cerebral perfusion drops acutely
  • Also: loss of atrial kick (if arrhythmia triggers syncope) in stiff LV is catastrophic
  • Syncope in known AS = OMINOUS finding and surgical emergency; median survival ~3 years untreated

Dyspnea (exertional progressing to orthopnea, PND):

  • Initially exertional; gradually worsens with decompensation to orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  • Indicates LV failure with pulmonary congestion; advanced AS pathophysiology

sections.heading: Physical Exam Findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at right upper sternal border (aortic area), radiating to neck/carotids and apex (Gallavardin phenomenon); holosystolic at apex
  • Ejection click (early systolic) if bicuspid AV (bicuspid leaflets open less smoothly)
  • Paradoxically split S₂ (delayed A₂ closure) in severe AS due to prolonged LV ejection
  • Parvus et tardus carotid pulse: slow-rising, low-amplitude pulse (delayed upstroke from LV outflow obstruction)
  • Sustained apical impulse (not laterally displaced unless LV is decompensated)
  • S₄ gallop (atrial kick into stiff LV)
  • Signs of heart failure if decompensated (elevated JVP, peripheral edema, rales, hepatomegaly)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml: Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: 2 minutes at bedside (acute) or systematic pre-op evaluation (chronic).

sections.heading: Vital Signs & Hemodynamics
sections.bodyHtml:
• Heart rate, blood pressure (both arms), respiratory rate, SpO₂, temperature
  • Orthostatic vital signs if patient able to stand (syncope risk)
  • In post-op setting: arterial line (trace — slow-rising with small pulse pressure in severe AS)

sections.heading: Symptoms
sections.bodyHtml:
• Dyspnea (exertional vs. at rest), chest pain/angina, syncope, presyncope, palpitations
  • Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (decompensation signs)
  • Exercise tolerance: "How far can you walk? Do you climb stairs? Do stairs cause dyspnea or chest pain?"

sections.heading: Physical Exam — Cardiac & Pulses
sections.bodyHtml:
• Auscultation: crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at RUSB; check for ejection click (bicuspid)
  • Palpate carotid pulse: slow-rising (parvus et tardus) in severe AS
  • Apical impulse: location (not displaced unless decompensated), character (sustained)
  • S₁, S₂ (split A₂ in severe AS), S₃, S₄ presence
  • JVP assessment
  • Palpate for thrills (palpable murmur indicates severe stenosis)

sections.heading: Pulmonary Exam
sections.bodyHtml:
• Rales, crackles (pulmonary edema — indicates decompensation)
  • Work of breathing, orthopnea positioning

sections.heading: Key Labs & Imaging
sections.bodyHtml:
• Recent echocardiography: aortic jet velocity (Vmax), mean gradient, aortic valve area (AVA), LV wall thickness, LVEF, LV dimensions (cavity size — should be small in compensated AS), indexed measures
  • Special maneuvers: Valsalva (murmur gets LOUDER in AS unlike MR) or leg-raise (confirms AS murmur increases with preload)
  • ECG: left ventricular hypertrophy pattern (deep S waves V1-V2, tall R waves V5-V6); left axis deviation; conduction abnormalities
  • Chest X-ray: cardiomegaly (if decompensated), aortic valve calcification (visible in some), pulmonary edema pattern (late sign)
  • Recent hemoglobin, BMP, renal function: baseline for surgery risk
  • Troponin, lactate (if acute decompensation)
  • Baseline EF, LV dimensions: track for decompensation

sections.heading: Pre-op Surgery Context
sections.bodyHtml:
• Procedure planned (SAVR vs. TAVR; type of prosthesis if known)
  • Coronary anatomy: CAD present? Will need CABG concurrent with AVR?
  • Aortic root dimensions (from CTA if available — bicuspid AV risk for aortopathy)
  • LVEF, LV cavity size, wall thickness from pre-op echo
  • Bicuspid AV? Rheumatic features? Family history of aortic disease?
  • STS score (Society of Thoracic Surgeons predicted mortality — used to risk-stratify for SAVR vs. TAVR decision)

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Diagnosis card: Management subsections replace the Stable/Unstable fork. Aortic stenosis is primarily a surgical disease; medical therapy is bridge only.

sections.heading: 5A. Medical Management (Bridge Therapy, NOT Definitive Treatment)
sections.bodyHtml:
Critical principle: No medication slows AS progression. Statins have no proven benefit in AS.

The only definitive treatment is aortic valve replacement (surgical or transcatheter).

What works (symptom management while awaiting surgery):

Agent Role Indication Dose / Monitoring
Rate-control beta-blocker (metoprolol, atenolol) Slows HR → lengthens diastole → improves ventricular filling in stiff LV Pre-op AS; HTN + AS Metoprolol 25–100 mg BID; target HR 60–80; caution if EF <40%
ACE inhibitor (lisinopril, enalapril) Afterload reduction; may reduce LVH gradually Asymptomatic AS + HTN; AS + CAD Lisinopril 10–40 mg daily; monitor K⁺, Cr; use cautiously if hypotensive
Calcium channel blocker — DHP (amlodipine) Afterload reduction; BP control AS + HTN if ACE-I not tolerated Amlodipine 5–10 mg daily; avoid non-DHP (negative inotropy)
Diuretics (furosemide) Symptom relief only; reduces pulmonary congestion Symptomatic AS with volume overload or HF Titrate carefully to avoid over-diuresis; AS preload-dependent
Aspirin (if CAD coexists) Antiplatelet AS + CAD 81–325 mg daily; reduce bleeding risk perioperatively

Hemodynamic goals (pre-op AS patient):

  • BP target: 100–140 mmHg systolic (SBP <100 is dangerous; triggers syncope/shock in severe AS)
  • HR target: 60–80 bpm (tachycardia shortens diastolic filling; bradycardia drops CO)
  • Preload: maintain adequate volume on board (hypovolemia → syncope/shock; hypervolemia → pulmonary edema) — tight I/O, daily weights
  • Sinus rhythm critical: new AF → loss of atrial kick → can drop CO by 20–30% in patient with stiff LV; escalate promptly

AVOID in severe AS (absolutely critical):

  • Nitrates — reduce preload → precipitate syncope and hemodynamic collapse in severe AS; can cause sudden death in ambulatory AS patients
  • Vasodilators (ACE-I/ARB at high doses, hydralazine, direct-acting vasodilators) — can cause profound hypotension
  • Negative inotropes (non-selective beta-blockers in decompensated AS, some calcium channel blockers) — reduce forward CO
  • Aggressive diuresis — reduces preload → worsens LV filling in stiff ventricle → syncope, shock
  • Valsalva maneuvers (straining, heavy lifting, aggressive bowel movements) — transient preload drop → syncope risk

sections.heading: 5B. Surveillance — Asymptomatic Severe AS & Serial Echocardiography
sections.bodyHtml:
Surveillance approach (asymptomatic, preserved LV function):

AS Severity Jet Velocity Mean Gradient AVA Echo Interval Special Considerations
Mild <3.0 m/s <25 mmHg >1.5 cm² Every 3–5 years Low surgery risk; routine follow-up
Moderate 3.0–4.0 m/s 25–40 mmHg 1.0–1.5 cm² Every 1–2 years Accelerate echo if symptoms develop
Severe >4.0 m/s >40 mmHg ≤1.0 cm² Every 6–12 months Escalate to surgery if symptoms or LV dysfunction
Very severe >5.0 m/s >60 mmHg — Every 3–6 months Aggressive surveillance; consider surgery even asymptomatic

Red flags for escalation (asymptomatic severe AS):

  • Development of ANY symptom (angina, syncope, dyspnea) → surgical referral immediately
  • LVEF declines <50% → Class IIa surgical indication
  • LV cavity dilates or wall thickens abnormally (rapid change) → closer follow-up
  • Jet velocity increases >5 m/s or rapidly progressive gradient → urgent re-evaluation
  • New atrial fibrillation → loss of atrial kick → may precipitate decompensation; escalate

sections.heading: 5C. Surgical & Interventional Decision: TAVR vs. SAVR
sections.bodyHtml:
Indications for intervention (ACC/AHA 2021):

Class Indication Context
Class I (Strong) Symptomatic severe AS (any symptom: angina, syncope, dyspnea) Median survival 2–5 years untreated; surgery transforms prognosis
Class I Asymptomatic severe AS + LV dysfunction (LVEF ≤50%) EF decline is often irreversible; early surgery halts progression
Class I Severe AS + very high gradient (mean >60 mmHg or Vmax >5.0 m/s) Even asymptomatic; extreme severity warrants surgery
Class IIa Asymptomatic severe AS + AVA <0.6 cm²/m² BSA Extreme anatomic severity; borderline indication for asymptomatic
Class IIa Severe AS undergoing other cardiac surgery (CABG, mitral valve, ascending aorta) Single operative intervention preferred

TAVR vs. SAVR Decision Matrix (Post-PARTNER 3, Evolut Low Risk Era):

Factor TAVR Favored SAVR Favored Shared Decision
Age ≥75 years or <75 with high surgical risk <65 years, low surgical risk 65–75 years, intermediate risk
Surgical risk (STS score) ≥4% (high risk, frailty, comorbidities) <2% (low risk) 2–4% (intermediate)
Valve type Trileaflet native valve Congenital bicuspid AV (limited TAVR data), small annulus Native trileaflet, moderate size annulus
Aortic annulus size 20–27 mm (platform-dependent) <20 or >27 mm (annulus too small/large for current TAVR) Mid-range (21–26 mm)
Bicuspid AV Increasingly used (newer data supports feasibility) Better long-term data if structurally amenable Institutional expertise drives choice
Porcelain aorta (heavily calcified ascending aorta) Favored (avoids aortic cross-clamp) Extremely high risk (may be contraindication) —
ILiofemoral access Patent, adequate caliber (>5.5 mm) Poor access; consider SAVR alternative access —
Durability expectation Reasonable for age >80 or life expectancy <10 years Longer life expectancy (>15 years) especially if <60 —
Anticoagulation tolerance Acceptable if cannot manage warfarin Mechanical valve requires lifelong anticoagulation —
Prosthesis type Self-expanding (CoreValve, Evolut) or balloon-expanding (SAPIEN) Tissue (bioprosthesis) or mechanical —

Landmark trials extending TAVR to lower-risk patients:

  • PARTNER 3 (2019): TAVR non-inferior to surgery in low surgical risk patients (STS <3%)
  • Evolut Low Risk (2019): Self-expanding TAVR (Evolut) non-inferior to surgery in low-risk AS
  • PARTNER III Extended: Recent data support TAVR even in select younger, low-risk patients (discussion with Heart Team)

Heart Team process (essential for shared decision-making):

  • Cardiologist, cardiothoracic surgeon, interventional cardiologist, nursing, sometimes geriatrics/frailty specialist
  • Discussion of TAVR vs. SAVR options, alternative pathways (medical management if truly asymptomatic with preserved EF)
  • Patient education re: anticoagulation (mechanical valve), bioprosthesis durability, TAVR durability data, reoperation risks
  • Document patient preference and reasoning

sections.heading: 5D. Symptomatic Severe AS = Emergent Intervention
sections.bodyHtml:
Recognition:

  • Symptomatic severe AS (any of: angina, syncope, dyspnea at rest or minimal exertion) + echo-confirmed severe AS = surgical/interventional emergency
  • Do NOT delay for elective scheduling; escalate urgently to cardiothoracic surgery or interventional cardiology

Immediate management (while arranging urgent intervention):

  • Avoid hypotension — SBP <90 is critical; phenylephrine IV infusion 0.5–1.4 mcg/kg/min first-line vasopressor (pure alpha; maintains coronary perfusion)
  • Avoid tachycardia (>100) — shortens diastolic filling time; beta-blocker titration or sedation if needed
  • Avoid aggressive diuresis — AS patients are preload-dependent; euvolemia only
  • Avoid nitrates, vasodilators, negative inotropes — same as above
  • Maintain sinus rhythm — new AF is a catastrophe in severe AS; consider IV rate control (diltiazem, metoprolol) or amiodarone if hemodynamically stable
  • Consider ICU-level monitoring — continuous telemetry, arterial line, frequent assessment
  • Expedite surgical/interventional workup: CTA (aortic root sizing for TAVR planning, rule out porcelain aorta), echocardiography (confirm severity, assess CAD need, LV function), coronary angiography if needed pre-op
  • Prepare for rapid transfer to OR/cath lab — time is myocardium

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
When to call and what to communicate.

SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room]. [Add operative context if post-op: POD [X] s/p [procedure]]" B: "[Patient context — pre-op awaiting SAVR/TAVR / post-op recovery / on telemetry]. Known severe AS [or critical AS]. Most recent echo: AVA [cm²], Vmax [m/s], mean gradient [mmHg], LVEF [%]." A: "[Current status — vitals, symptoms, physical findings, labs if abnormal]. [Acute changes: new syncope, new angina, new dyspnea, new murmur, new arrhythmia, new hemodynamic instability]." R: "[What you need — e.g., urgent surgical evaluation, cardiology assessment, transfer to ICU, medication adjustment, expedited intervention]."

Who to call — by clinical scenario:

Situation Contact
Pre-op AS patient, stable, routine pre-op visit Primary cardiologist / surgical team at pre-op clinic
Pre-op AS patient with worsening exertional dyspnea Cardiologist + CT surgery (may accelerate surgery)
Pre-op AS patient with new angina or chest pain Cardiology STAT; rule out ACS + discuss urgent surgery; ECG
Pre-op AS patient with SYNCOPE or PRESYNCOPE CT surgery STAT + cardiology; this is emergent; ICU admission likely
Symptomatic severe AS awaiting intervention with hemodynamic instability CT surgery (SAVR) or interventional cardiology (TAVR) STAT; prepare OR/cath lab
Post-op AS patient (POD 0–1) with excessive bleeding (>300 mL/h × 2 h) CT surgery + blood bank; prepare for re-exploration
Post-op AS patient with new cardiac murmur (paravalvular leak) CT surgery + echocardiography; assess severity
Post-op AS patient with new heart block or conduction abnormality Cardiology + CT surgery (may need pacing; TAVR carries higher AV block risk)
Pre-op or post-op AS patient with new irregular rhythm (POAF, SVT) Cardiology; consider anticoagulation, rate control, EP evaluation
Any AS patient with syncope in hospital setting STAT cardiologist + CT surgery; do not treat as simple fall

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive — expandable in clinical application)*
sections.bodyHtml:
AS pathophysiology: Concentric hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction The pressure overload cascade: Stenotic aortic valve obstructs LV outflow → LV pressure rises above normal to maintain cardiac output across the narrow orifice. This pressure overload triggers a remodeling response: the LV wall thickens concentrically (increased wall thickness, normal or reduced cavity size) to normalize wall stress (Laplace's law). Concentric hypertrophy (different from eccentric in AR):
  • Wall thickens in response to pressure load (unlike eccentric hypertrophy in volume-overload states where the cavity dilates)
  • Cavity size stays small — the thickened wall maintains forward stroke volume despite pressure elevation
  • Fibrosis accompanies hypertrophy — the hypertrophied myocardium develops microscopic scarring
  • Diastolic dysfunction emerges: the stiff, thickened LV resists filling → requires high filling pressures and atrial kick for adequate diastolic filling
  • Loss of atrial kick is catastrophic: new AF in severe AS can drop cardiac output 20–30% because the stiff LV depends on atrial contraction The compensated phase:
  • Can last years to decades in mild-moderate AS
  • Asymptomatic patient despite severe stenosis — just sedentary and unaware
  • LVEF remains normal (usually 50–70%); cavity size stays small Decompensation (when symptoms develop):
  • LV systolic function declines (LVEF drops below 50%)
  • LV cavity dilates (as the hypertrophied wall fails)
  • Pulmonary pressures rise → dyspnea, orthopnea, PND
  • Once symptoms develop, median survival 2–5 years without surgery Subendocardial ischemia mechanism:
  • Hypertrophied myocardium has increased oxygen demand (more mass)
  • Coronary blood flow is diastolic and compressed by the contracted myocardium
  • Net result: oxygen demand outstrips supply → ischemic chest pain (angina) even without coronary artery disease
Low-flow, low-gradient aortic stenosis: A critical diagnostic challenge Classic low-flow low-gradient (LFLG) AS:
  • Severe anatomic AS (small aortic valve area ≤1.0 cm²) but low mean gradient (<40 mmHg)
  • Occurs in patients with reduced LVEF (<50%) and low stroke volume (cardiac output severely impaired)
  • Why? Stenotic valve + poor LV function → reduced flow across valve → gradient underestimated
  • The valve IS truly severe (anatomy), but poor flow makes the gradient look deceptively mild
  • Risk: clinician may think "low gradient = mild AS" and delay surgery → catastrophic error Paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS (a.k.a. pseudo-severe or hypertensive hypertrophic AS):
  • Preserved LVEF (>50%) but small LV cavity (hypertrophic, non-dilated)
  • AVA typically ≤1.0 cm² BUT gradient low (<40 mmHg) because stroke volume is LOW (small cavity, even though EF is high)
  • Occurs in older, hypertensive patients with severe LVH and small cavity
  • Also called "paradoxical" because EF is preserved but stroke volume is reduced
  • Risk: misclassification as mild-moderate AS How to distinguish truly severe from pseudo-severe:
  • Dobutamine stress echocardiography — gold standard
  • Dobutamine increases contractility → increases stroke volume (if myocardium is viable)
  • In true severe AS: AVA stays <1.0 cm², gradient increases ≥40 mmHg → confirms severity
  • In pseudo-severe AS: AVA increases to >1.5 cm² with dobutamine, gradient drops → suggests mild-moderate stenosis
  • Low-dose dobutamine (5–10 mcg/kg/min) is preferred for safety (reduces hypotension risk vs. high-dose) Surgical decision in LFLG AS:
  • True severe LFLG AS: surgery/TAVR indicated because mortality without intervention is high (same as high-gradient severe AS)
  • Pseudo-severe AS: medical therapy (BP control, LVH regression with antihypertensives) may be trial; surgery not emergent
  • If unclear after dobutamine: many surgeons recommend proceeding with intervention in clinical context of severe LVH + small AVA, as risk of missing true severe AS is greater than risk of unnecessary intervention
Bicuspid aortic valve: Genetics, aortopathy, surveillance, and family screening Bicuspid AV anatomy:
  • Congenital; ~1–2% of population (most common congenital heart lesion)
  • Two leaflets instead of normal three (usually right-left orientation; anterior-posterior less common)
  • Leaflets often have echogenic fibrous raphe (raphe = fibrous ridge mimicking a commissure)
  • Structurally abnormal leaflets → higher lifelong risk of both stenosis AND regurgitation Aortopathy associated with bicuspid AV:
  • ~50% of bicuspid AV patients develop aortic root or ascending aorta dilation over lifetime
  • Root dilation may be present at diagnosis (detected on pre-op CTA) or develop progressively
  • Aortic dissection risk is real but lower than Marfan/Loeys-Dietz (~5–10× general population, vs. 100× in Marfan)
  • Familial clustering: ~20% of first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) also have bicuspid AV Pre-operative evaluation in bicuspid AS:
  • Transthoracic echocardiography: confirm bicuspic morphology; assess for associated AR
  • CTA chest/aorta (mandatory): document aortic root diameter at sinuses of Valsalva, sinotubular junction, ascending aorta; rule out significant dilation
  • Family screening: first-degree relatives should have echocardiography if age >15 years (bicuspid prevalence 20%) Post-operative surveillance (mandatory):
  • Echocardiography: 4–6 weeks post-op, then annually
  • CTA or cardiac MRI: every 1–3 years depending on baseline root size
  • Root <45 mm: imaging every 3–5 years
  • Root 45–50 mm: every 1–2 years
  • Root >50 mm: consider prophylactic replacement even if valve itself is asymptomatic
  • Goal: catch root dilation before rupture/dissection risk becomes unacceptable Surgical approach in bicuspid AS:
  • If root <45 mm: standard AVR (SAVR or TAVR per risk profile)
  • If root 45–55 mm: consider concomitant root replacement (or at least planning for future root surgery if rapid growth)
  • If root >55 mm: strong consideration for composite graft (Bentall) or separate root replacement + AVR at time of AS surgery
  • Lifelong follow-up is non-negotiable: root can dilate even after successful AVR Family screening (10–20% inheritance):
  • First-degree relatives should be offered echocardiography
  • If bicuspid found: they need aortic root imaging (CTA) and long-term surveillance
  • Cascade screening can identify at-risk relatives before complications
Heyde syndrome: AS + acquired vWD → GI bleeds What is Heyde syndrome?
  • Aortic stenosis + acquired von Willebrand disease (vWD) → recurrent GI bleeding
  • Occurs in ~5% of severe AS patients
  • High-shear forces across stenotic valve → mechanical destruction of von Willebrand factor (vWF) molecules
  • Loss of large vWF multimers → bleeding disorder (acquired vWD Type II)
  • Leads to bleeding from acquired angiomas (AVMs) in the GI tract, especially right colon Clinical presentation:
  • Recurrent GI bleeding (melena, hematochezia, iron-deficiency anemia)
  • Multiple negative colonoscopies initially (angiomas are small, multiple, evanescent — can be hard to find)
  • May require multiple transfusions
  • Bleeding typically resolves after TAVR or SAVR (shear forces gone → vWF recovers) Diagnosis:
  • History of severe AS + recurrent GI bleeding
  • Bleeding workup (EGD, colonoscopy) may or may not find source
  • vWF assay: low vWF activity, especially low large multimers (Type II vWD pattern) Management:
  • Definitive treatment: TAVR or SAVR (relieves shear forces → vWF recovers within weeks)
  • Temporary: IV desmopressin (DDAVP) may transiently improve vWF levels (not reliable)
  • Manage anemia aggressively (transfusions, iron)
  • Consider GI surveillance (repeat endoscopy) after valve replacement to document healing Pearl: Unexplained GI bleeding in a patient with AS is Heyde syndrome until proven otherwise. Don't attribute bleeding to diverticulosis or AVMs and miss the AS. After TAVR/SAVR, GI bleeding typically resolves, confirming diagnosis retrospectively.
Cardiac amyloid overlap: ATTR with AS-like physiology ATTR amyloidosis and aortic valve disease:
  • Transthyretin (ATTR) amyloid accumulation can affect aortic valve and myocardium simultaneously
  • Can present as "aortic stenosis" on echo but actually amyloid infiltration of myocardium + valve thickening
  • Seen in older patients, especially if wild-type (wt-ATTR, formerly senile systemic amyloidosis)
  • Also hereditary ATTR (hATTR) if positive family history of polyneuropathy or cardiomyopathy Red flags for amyloid overlap:
  • Severe AS + disproportionately severe LVH (wall thickness very thick relative to AS severity)
  • AS + reduced LVEF without clear ischemic pattern on coronary angiography
  • AS + restrictive physiology on echocardiography (markedly elevated filling pressures, septal bounce, abnormal strain pattern)
  • AS + granular myocardial texture on echo (sparkling appearance)
  • AS + concomitant symptoms suggesting polyneuropathy (neuropathic pain, autonomic dysfunction) Diagnostic approach:
  • Cardiac MRI: late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) pattern can suggest amyloid (diffuse subendocardial LGE, thinning of mid-myocardium)
  • Technetium-99m PYP scan: highly sensitive for ATTR amyloid (cardiac uptake = ATTR likely; renal/thyroid also uptake in wt-ATTR)
  • Genetic testing: if family history or young age suggests hATTR
  • Kidney/liver biopsy: if diagnostic uncertainty (Congo red stain for amyloid) Surgical implications:
  • If ATTR confirmed: AVR alone may not address the progressive cardiomyopathy
  • Medical options (tafamidis for hATTR) available; discuss with amyloid specialists
  • Prognosis in ATTR typically worse than isolated AS; median survival without treatment ~2 years in restrictive phenotype
Pregnancy and severe aortic stenosis: High-risk obstetric scenario Pathophysiology: Why pregnancy + severe AS is dangerous:
  • Pregnancy increases cardiac output 40–50%, heart rate, and preload (blood volume ↑)
  • Severe AS cannot accommodate increased CO → maternal hemodynamics decompensate
  • Placental demands + AS hemodynamic stress = recipe for cardiogenic shock
  • Maternal mortality 10–20% if severe symptomatic AS not corrected pre-conception Risk stratification (for counseling):
  • Low risk: Asymptomatic mild-moderate AS (Vmax <3 m/s, gradient <40 mmHg)
  • Intermediate risk: Asymptomatic severe AS (Vmax >4 m/s) with preserved LV function and small cavity
  • High risk: Symptomatic AS of any severity; asymptomatic severe AS + LV dysfunction or dilation
  • Contraindicated: Symptomatic severe AS; should defer pregnancy until post-AVR/TAVR Pre-conception counseling:
  • Symptomatic severe AS: correct before attempting conception (maternal mortality risk 10–20%, fetal loss risk significant)
  • Asymptomatic severe AS: intervention recommended; shared decision with patient; if defer pregnancy, requires close monitoring In-pregnancy management (if pregnant with AS):
  • Frequent cardiology monitoring: monthly initially, then every 2 weeks 3rd trimester
  • Echocardiography: assess for any change in gradient, LV function, LVEF
  • Activity restriction: avoid strenuous exercise; bed rest in 3rd trimester
  • Diuretics cautiously: avoid excessive diuresis (preload-dependent)
  • Avoid labor/vaginal delivery if possible: consider planned cesarean section (~36 weeks or earlier if decompensation)
  • Planned delivery at tertiary care center with cardiothoracic surgery, obstetrics, neonatology immediately available
  • Regional anesthesia preferred (epidural) over general if delivery; avoid systemic vasodilators Postpartum period: highest risk time for hemodynamic decompensation as fluid shifts resolve; close monitoring continues
Rheumatic aortic stenosis: Global perspective and surgical approach Epidemiology:
  • Rare in developed countries (declining since antibiotics advent)
  • Common globally: parts of Africa, Asia, South America where acute rheumatic fever (ARF) incidence remains high
  • Caused by post-streptococcal immune-mediated valve inflammation → commissural fusion, leaflet thickening, calcification over years Characteristics:
  • Usually mitral valve involved FIRST (mitral stenosis ± regurgitation); aortic stenosis develops later or concurrently
  • Mixed lesions common: AS + AR, MS + MR, or all four valves involved
  • Onset typically younger (30s–50s) compared to calcific AS (>70s)
  • Often more rapidly progressive than degenerative AS Surgical considerations in rheumatic AS:
  • Need for MVR simultaneous with AVR: most rheumatic AS patients have mitral pathology requiring intervention
  • Anticoagulation demands: mechanical valve needed for high-risk young patients (endocarditis recurrence risk, pregnancy considerations)
  • Tissue valve selection: some centers prefer mechanical for rheumatic disease given high recurrent endocarditis risk
  • TAVR role: limited in pure rheumatic AS due to mitral involvement requiring surgical access; increasingly used in "off-pump" world for isolated rheumatic AS in select cases Global epidemiology note: rheumatic heart disease remains leading cause of acquired heart disease worldwide; prevalence underappreciated in developed countries where patients may immigrate with undiagnosed disease
Medications to AVOID in severe aortic stenosis: Mechanisms of harm Nitrates (SL, IV, topical):
  • Mechanism: Reduce preload (venous dilation) → LV filling pressure drops → cardiac output falls acutely
  • Why dangerous in AS: Stiff, non-compliant LV DEPENDS on high filling pressures to maintain CO. Preload reduction triggers sudden CO collapse → syncope, shock, death
  • Risk: Used for angina (which IS present in severe AS) but can be lethal — syncopal collapse or even sudden death reported with SL nitrates in severe AS
  • Pearl: Chest pain in severe AS may be true ischemic angina OR may be pain from LVH; nitrates can help neither and harm both
  • Alternative: Phenylephrine (pure alpha vasopressor) maintains afterload + coronary perfusion without preload reduction ACE inhibitors & ARBs (at high doses):
  • Mechanism: Afterload reduction → systemic vascular resistance drops → BP falls → LV pressure drops → forward CO may not compensate
  • Why dangerous: AS LV is afterload-dependent; removing afterload without increasing contractility → shock
  • Safe approach: Use cautiously, low-medium doses for HTN control; avoid aggressive titration; monitor BP Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (dihydropyridines like amlodipine, nifedipine):
  • At high doses: reflex tachycardia + vasodilation can drop preload → same risk as nitrates
  • Safe approach: moderate doses, monitor HR (target <80–90), ensure BP adequate Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem):
  • Mechanism: Negative inotropic effect (reduce LV contractility) + AV nodal blockade
  • Why dangerous in AS: reduced contractility drops forward CO in patient who already has reduced CO from obstruction
  • Risk: AV block in setting of AS can cause syncope
  • AVOID in decompensated AS; use beta-blockers instead for rate control Diuretics (excessive):
  • Mechanism: Over-diuresis → preload reduction (same as nitrates)
  • Why dangerous: AS LV is preload-dependent; excessive diuresis → syncope, shock
  • Safe approach: diuretics for symptomatic pulmonary edema only; titrate to euvolemia (not "dry"); monitor I/O closely
  • Tight I/O and daily weights mandatory in pre-op AS patients Negative inotropes (non-selective beta-blockers, some antiarrhythmics):
  • High-dose beta-blockers can reduce contractility excessively
  • Some antiarrhythmics (flecainide, propafenone) have negative inotropic effects
  • Why dangerous: already reduced forward CO gets worse → shock
  • Safe approach: Use selective beta-blockers (e.g., metoprolol) at moderate doses for rate control; target HR 60–80

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in stable AS patients; if any show, re-escalate.

Pre-op AS patient:

  • Any new cardiac symptom (first angina, first syncope, first dyspnea) = escalate to CT surgery immediately; this changes from asymptomatic to symptomatic = surgical urgency
  • Worsening exertional dyspnea or exercise tolerance declining = LV decompensation signal; may accelerate surgery
  • New orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea = LV failure developing; ICU admission consideration
  • Syncope or presyncope = OMINOUS in AS; surgical emergency; median survival ~3 years untreated
  • New irregular pulse or palpitations = new AF risk; loss of atrial kick in stiff LV can cause sudden cardiogenic shock; escalate promptly
  • New S₃ gallop = LV systolic dysfunction developing; transition from compensated to decompensated
  • Rapid rise in JVP or new peripheral edema = volume overload; escalate diuretic therapy or surgery timing

Post-op AS patient (SAVR or TAVR):

  • Sudden new diastolic murmur = paravalvular leak (most common post-SAVR complication); notify surgeon, obtain echo
  • Hemodynamic instability out of proportion to operation = prosthetic malfunction, paravalvular leak, tamponade; escalate
  • Fever + elevated WBC + malaise in early post-op (first 2 years) = prosthetic valve endocarditis; blood cultures, TEE, ID consult
  • New or worsening systolic murmur = structural issue (stuck valve, pannus, endocarditis); notify surgeon
  • Conduction block or heart block development (especially post-TAVR) = implanted valve impinging conduction tissue; may require pacing
  • Widening mediastinum or high chest tube output = possible aortic graft leak or bleeding; notify CT surgery

Acute decompensated AS (ICU):

  • Dropping BP despite vasopressors = cardiogenic shock worsening; prepare for emergent OR/ECMO
  • Increasing pulmonary edema on CXR despite diuretics = LVEDP rising; surgical emergency
  • Rising lactate = tissue hypoperfusion; emergent intervention needed
  • Altered mental status or decreasing urine output = end-organ hypoperfusion; emergent OR
  • New arrhythmias (VT, rapid SVT, new AF) = poor prognostic sign in acute AS; surgical urgency

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Symptomatic severe AS = surgical emergency, not chronic disease. Once angina, syncope, or dyspnea develops, median survival 2–5 years untreated. Do NOT delay surgery for "more testing" or "elective scheduling." Escalate to cardiac surgery immediately. Asymptomatic severe AS is different — watchful waiting with echo every 6–12 months is OK.

  2. Syncope in severe AS is OMINOUS, not vasovagal. Exertional syncope or syncope at rest in patient with known AS is red flag for imminent decompensation or sudden catastrophic CO drop. Median survival ~3 years untreated. Do NOT work it up as routine fall; escalate to CT surgery STAT.

  3. AVOID nitrates and vasodilators in severe AS — they can cause syncope and sudden death. Stiff, non-compliant LV depends on high filling pressures. Nitrates reduce preload → CO collapses → syncope/shock/death. Even SL nitroglycerin can be lethal in severe AS. Use phenylephrine (pure alpha) as first-line vasopressor instead.

  4. AVA is load-dependent; low flow underestimates severity. In patients with low cardiac output (poor LV function, shock states), a truly severe AS valve may show a lower gradient and larger AVA than it truly is. Dobutamine stress echocardiography clarifies true vs. pseudo-severe; do NOT reassure based on single echo in low-flow state.

  5. Low-flow low-gradient (LFLG) AS is STILL severe and requires intervention. Many clinicians wrongly think "low gradient = mild AS" and delay surgery. LFLG occurs in severe AS + poor LV function; valve IS truly severe. Dobutamine stress echo confirms (AVA stays <1 cm², gradient increases). Surgery/TAVR indicated.

  6. Heyde syndrome = severe AS + acquired vWD + recurrent GI bleeds. Shear forces from stenotic valve destroy von Willebrand factor molecules → acquired vWD → bleeding from GI angiomas. Bleeding typically resolves after TAVR/SAVR. Don't attribute GI bleeding to diverticulosis and miss the AS; think Heyde.

  7. Bicuspid aortic valve: screen the aortic root and organize family screening. ~50% develop aortic root dilation over lifetime; dissection risk is real. Pre-op CTA mandatory; post-op surveillance lifelong. First-degree relatives have 20% inheritance — screen with echo and consider imaging if bicuspid found.

  8. Cardiac amyloid (ATTR) can phenocopy aortic stenosis. Severe LVH + severe AS + preserved EF + granular myocardium on echo + restrictive physiology = amyloid until proven otherwise. Check PYP scan; if positive, medical therapy may be preferred over surgery alone (tafamidis for hATTR). MRI with LGE pattern suggestive of diffuse subendocardial enhancement.

  9. Pregnancy + severe symptomatic AS = contraindication to pregnancy; 10–20% maternal mortality. Correction (TAVR/SAVR) MUST occur pre-conception. If already pregnant with severe AS, close cardiology monitoring + possible hospitalization 3rd trimester + planned early delivery at high-risk center. Counsel accordingly.

  10. The "silent" severe AS patient. Some deny symptoms because they've voluntarily restricted activity. "I'm fine, I just don't walk far anymore" = symptomatic AS. Ask explicitly: "What's the most strenuous thing you do? Can you climb stairs? Any chest pain or dyspnea with exertion?" Functional decline = symptom, even if they don't call it that.

  11. Rapid worsening of gradient on serial echos is a red flag. Jet velocity increasing >5 m/s or mean gradient rising >10 mmHg year-over-year = acceleration in progression; escalate surveillance and discuss surgery sooner rather than later.

  12. Phenylephrine is first-line vasopressor in severe AS. Pure alpha activity maintains BP + coronary perfusion without reflex tachycardia (tachycardia is bad in AS; shortens diastolic filling). Avoid epinephrine (beta effects → reflex tachycardia) and norepinephrine (beta activity at high doses). Have phenylephrine readily available in pre-op setting.

  13. New atrial fibrillation in severe AS patient is a hemodynamic emergency, not just an arrhythmia. Loss of atrial kick in stiff, stenotic LV can drop CO by 20–30%, causing shock. Don't treat it as routine POAF; aggressive rate control and rhythm control consideration needed. Call cardiology immediately.

  14. TAVR increasingly first-line in low-to-intermediate risk patients (PARTNER 3, Evolut Low Risk). Paradigm shift away from "older patients only get TAVR." Data now support TAVR in select younger, low-risk patients. Heart Team discussion essential; individual anatomy (annulus size, aortic calcification) drives choice.

  15. Balloon aortic valvuloplasty is a BRIDGE only, not definitive. Used as temporary measure (a few days to weeks) to stabilize hemodynamics while arranging urgent TAVR/SAVR in cardiogenic shock. Restenosis is rapid (days to weeks); always plan definitive surgery/intervention within days of BAV.

cards.title: Aspiration / Aspiration Pneumonitis and Pneumonia
cards.quickAnswer: Witnessed aspiration event OR silent aspiration suspected (acute desaturation, cough, fever 24–48h post-op) → NPO immediately, raise HOB to 30–45°, gentle oropharyngeal suction, supplemental O₂ if SpO₂ <94%, STAT portable CXR, notify APP with SBAR. Dysphagia screen by SLP BEFORE any PO attempt (food, fluids, medications). Stable: monitor closely; Unstable (stridor, SpO₂ <92% despite O₂, RR >30, respiratory distress) → STAT call RRT, prepare for intubation. Distinguish aspiration pneumonitis (acute, chemical, supportive care) from aspiration pneumonia (fever + infiltrate 24–48h later, antibiotics if indicated per IDSA guidelines).

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who gets it.

  • Definition: Aspiration is the entry of oropharyngeal or gastric contents into the lower airway below the vocal cords. Can trigger chemical pneumonitis (acute inflammatory injury from acid + pepsin), bacterial aspiration pneumonia (delayed infection), or silent aspiration with no immediate symptoms (Donzelli et al., 2019).
  • Incidence in post-op cardiac patients: Silent aspiration occurs in 50–70% of post-extubation patients; clinically overt aspiration occurs in 5–15% (Tolep et al., 1996). Post-extubation dysphagia (PESD) affects ~50% of post-cardiac surgery extubated patients.
  • Peak risk: POD 0–3 immediately post-extubation through early swallow resumption. Critical window: within hours post-extubation and at first PO meal attempt.
  • Who this applies to: every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient at risk for altered mental status, weakened swallow, vocal cord dysfunction, or prolonged intubation. Highest yield from extubation through POD 5–7.
  • Why it matters: one full aspiration with pneumonia adds 10–14 days to ICU/floor stay, >$50K cost, and increases mortality. Silent aspiration is undetectable by observation alone; requires formal dysphagia screening.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome):

  • Acute sterile chemical inflammatory response to aspirated gastric acid (HCl, pepsin) and food particles entering the lungs
  • Timing: minutes to hours post-aspiration event; severity depends on acid pH and volume
  • Pathology: direct chemical burn to airway epithelium, alveolar epithelial damage, increased vascular permeability, pulmonary edema, potential ARDS progression
  • Clinical presentation: sudden cough, wheezing, tachypnea, hypoxemia; may be transient (self-limited in 24–48h) or severe
  • CXR findings: diffuse bilateral infiltrates in dependent zones (lower lobes, posterior); mimics ARDS
  • Course: variable — may resolve with supportive care alone (O₂, HOB elevation, monitoring) or progress to respiratory failure requiring intubation
  • Antibiotics: withhold unless secondary bacterial infection suspected (fever + purulent sputum >48h, rising WBC, bacterial sputum culture)

Aspiration pneumonia:

  • Bacterial infection from aspirated oropharyngeal flora (predominantly anaerobes, streptococci, Gram-negatives) colonizing dependent lung zones
  • Timing: delayed onset, typically 24–48h or longer after aspiration event; fever appears as sign of bacterial growth
  • Pathology: anaerobic and microaerophilic bacteria from dental caries, gingivitis, periodontal disease; localized necrotizing inflammation; often lower lobes, basilar, posterior
  • Clinical presentation: fever, productive cough, dyspnea, tachycardia, tachypnea; malaise
  • CXR findings: localized infiltrate in dependent zones; air bronchograms; may progress to abscess or empyema
  • Course: requires antibiotics per IDSA guidelines; typically community-acquired oral anaerobes (peptostreptococcus, prevotella, fusobacterium, gram-negatives)
  • Antibiotics: IDSA 2016 recommends amoxicillin-clavulanate or fluoroquinolone as first-line (moved away from routine anaerobic coverage unless specific features present: putrid sputum, dental disease, lung abscess)

Key distinction for clinical decision-making:

Feature Pneumonitis Pneumonia
Cause Chemical (acid, pepsin, food) Bacterial
Onset Minutes to hours 24–48h or later
Fever Absent initially Present (>38.5°C)
WBC May be normal or mildly elevated Elevated (>12K typical)
Sputum Clear, foamy, or blood-tinged Purulent, yellowish-green
CXR Diffuse bilateral infiltrates Localized, dependent zones
Antibiotics Hold; supportive care only Indicated; IDSA-guided selection
Prognosis Often self-resolves 24–48h Requires treatment

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Witnessed aspiration event:

  • Coughing, choking, gagging, or sputtering during oral intake (food, fluids, medications)
  • Visible food or fluid regurgitation with inhalation

Silent aspiration suspected:

  • Sudden oxygen desaturation (SpO₂ drop ≥3–5%) during or shortly after meals, without obvious trigger
  • New or worsening cough, wheezing, stridor
  • Wet voice quality, drooling, oropharyngeal pooling
  • Fever appearing 24–48h post-op without other clear source (urinary, line, wound)

Post-extubation risk signs:

  • Hoarse voice, weak cry, weak cough, weak voice quality (suggests RLN injury or vocal cord dysfunction)
  • Difficulty handling secretions or frequent suctioning required
  • Oropharyngeal pooling requiring frequent suctioning

Associated patient factors in cardiac surgery:

  • Altered mental status during/after meals: delirium patient with meal-related desaturation; unable to protect airway adequately
  • Recent aortic arch surgery or procedures with RLN injury risk: first meal attempt = high-risk window
  • Persistent aspiration risk 24–48h post-op with new infiltrate on CXR: now pneumonia suspect

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Competent systematic bedside exam.

  • Immediate post-event vital signs: HR, BP, RR, SpO₂, temperature; color, work of breathing, stridor or wheezing on auscultation
  • Mental status: alert, oriented, cooperative? Delirious? Drowsy? Able to protect airway?
  • Swallow assessment: ask patient to swallow saliva — pain, difficulty, wet voice quality, drooling? Can patient handle secretions?
  • Voice/cry quality: hoarse (RLN injury), breathy, weak? Cough strength and coordination.
  • Risk context — chart review:
  • Extubation timing: POD 0 vs later (higher risk 24–48h post-extubation)
  • Procedure type: aortic arch, ascending, root, CABG → RLN injury risk
  • NG tube: still in place? If yes, aspiration risk is high during PO attempts
  • Medications: opioids, sedatives, anticholinergics (all slow swallow and reduce protective reflexes)
  • OSA documented? If yes, baseline aspiration + PESD risk increased
  • Diet order: when was PO cleared? By whom? Was swallow screen completed?
  • Temperature and WBC trend, lactate if available

  • Baseline CXR post-op (POD 0 or POD 1) for comparison to current if concern for infiltrate

  • Lung exam: baseline sounds vs new crackles, consolidation, wheezing; auscultate both bases carefully

  • Recent imaging: baseline CXR (post-op POD 0–1) available for comparison?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Small-volume coughing/choking event; SpO₂ recovered or stable ≥94%; no respiratory distress; alert, able to protect airway; secretions handled)

  1. Call NPO immediately — no food, fluids, or medications PO until formal swallow evaluation complete
  2. Raise HOB to 30–45° — maintain this position for 30+ minutes after any aspiration concern; gravity assists swallowing, reduces reflux
  3. Gentle oropharyngeal suction — remove pooled secretions; avoid aggressive suctioning or gag triggering (may worsen aspiration)
  4. Place on continuous pulse oximetry — monitor for delayed desaturation (can develop hours later); set alarms at SpO₂ <94%
  5. Supplemental O₂ if SpO₂ <94% — aspiration pneumonitis may develop acutely; have bag-mask available at bedside
  6. Obtain STAT portable CXR — establishes baseline for future comparison; may show infiltrate, air bronchogram in dependent zones, or aspiration evidence
  7. Notify APP/physician with SBAR — communicate event timing, current VS, O₂ requirement, any risk factors (RLN hoarseness, NG tube, delirium)
  8. Request SLP (speech-language pathology) referral STAT — dysphagia/swallow evaluation MUST occur before resuming any PO (food, fluids, medications, ice chips)
  9. Contact dietary — place hold on pending diet order until SLP clearance obtained and documented
  10. Document: exact event time, what was aspirated (if visible), witness account, SpO₂ trend before/after, interventions, response; do NOT re-attempt oral intake without SLP evaluation and provider order

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Severe coughing, stridor, wheezing, hypoxemia SpO₂ <92% despite supplemental O₂, RR >30, visible respiratory distress, altered mental status, inability to protect airway)

  1. STAT call APP/fellow + RRT — activate Rapid Response; do NOT leave patient alone; prepare for possible intubation
  2. Raise HOB to high Fowler's (vertical if tolerated) — maximize ventilation efficiency
  3. Gentle oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal suction — if large food particle visible, remove carefully with yankauer; do NOT dislodge particle deeper into trachea
  4. Apply high-flow O₂ immediately — target SpO₂ ≥94%; have bag-mask + intubation equipment at bedside
  5. Establish/verify patent IV access — prepare for medications, fluid resuscitation, emergency intubation drugs
  6. STAT portable CXR — rule out aspiration vs other causes (pneumothorax, pulmonary edema, PE, cardiac cause)
  7. Send STAT labs: ABG (oxygenation, ventilation, pH), lactate (perfusion assessment), CBC with differential (WBC baseline), BMP (electrolytes for repletion if needed)
  8. Cardiac monitor continuous — aspiration can trigger vagal response → bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmia
  9. Prepare for bronchoscopy if large food particle suspected and patient not responding to conservative measures; discussion with provider and pulmonology
  10. Document: exact event time, what was aspirated (if known), SpO₂ trend (pre-event baseline → nadir → current), interventions, response, time of provider/RRT notification
  11. Anticipate intubation if respiratory status worsens → alert anesthesia per code protocol; pre-oxygenate, prepare difficult airway equipment

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient had aspiration event at [time] — [witnessed coughing / silent desaturation]. Current SpO₂ [value] on [O₂ delivery method]. RR [value], HR [value], BP [value]. NG tube [present/absent]. Baseline CXR [timing, findings if known]." A: "Patient is [stable with resolved symptoms / unstable with persistent hypoxemia/respiratory distress]. [Any hoarseness, recent arch surgery, altered mental status, fever?]." R: "Requesting [SLP evaluation STAT / orders for aspiration precautions / antibiotics if fever/infiltrate 24–48h / intubation readiness]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable aspiration event, fully recovered, no ongoing desaturation Primary APP / on-call fellow (arrange SLP same-day)
Stable aspiration event, SpO₂ dropped 3–5% but recovered Primary APP + SLP STAT
Hypoxemia or respiratory distress post-aspiration APP + RRT; consider pulmonology consult if persistent
Aspiration + fever or new infiltrate 24–48h post-op APP + consider infectious disease for antibiotic selection
Aspiration + hemoptysis or evidence of ongoing bleeding APP + CT surgery (source control concern)
Hoarse voice post-op + aspiration event APP + ENT (RLN injury evaluation) + SLP co-management

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Subsections are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Risk factors specific to post-cardiac surgery — cardiac-specific mechanisms
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-extubation swallow dysfunction (PESD):

  • Occurs in ~50% of post-cardiac surgery extubated patients (Tolep et al., 1996)
  • Mechanism: mucosal and laryngeal edema, vocal cord paralysis (RLN), generalized muscle weakness from ICU deconditioning, residual sedation effects, pain/fear with first swallow
  • Timing: resolution usually 48–72h; RLN injury may persist weeks or indefinitely
  • Aspiration risk highest POD 0–1 immediately post-extubation

Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) injury from cardiac surgery:

  • Aortic arch repair: RLN injury rate 5–30% (nerve runs under aortic arch on left side)
  • CABG: RLN injury rate 1–2% (from dissection, retraction, internal mammary artery harvest)
  • Ascending aorta/root procedures: RLN injury risk if near left RLN path
  • Clinical signs: hoarse voice, weak cry, weak cough, weak voice quality, inability to clear secretions, aspiration risk
  • Swallow impact: reduced laryngeal elevation, incomplete glottic closure during swallow, aspiration risk persists until recovery or neurologic compensation achieved
  • Recovery timeline: variable — some recover in weeks, permanent recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis possible if nerve transection occurs

Delirium in post-operative cardiac patients:

  • Postoperative delirium (hyperactive > hypoactive) occurs in 30–80% of cardiac surgery patients
  • Mechanism: cardiopulmonary bypass-induced systemic inflammation, sleep disruption, medications (opioids, anticholinergics, benzodiazepines), ICU stressors, pain
  • Aspiration mechanism: delirious patient may not cooperate with swallow precautions, may eat rapidly without pacing, not sense food going wrong, forget medication administration instructions
  • High-risk moment: delirium + mealtimes = mandatory close monitoring

NG tube placement:

  • Impairs pharyngeal sensation via tube irritation
  • Interferes with laryngeal closure reflexes
  • Increases aspiration risk if PO attempted while NG still in place
  • Best practice: coordinate with provider to remove NG tube BEFORE formal swallow evaluation to restore pharyngeal reflexes

Medications slowing swallow and reducing airway protection:

  • Opioids: delay swallow initiation, reduce laryngeal closure intensity, reduce cough reflex
  • Benzodiazepines and sedative residual effects: muscle weakness, reduced airway protective reflexes, drowsiness
  • Anticholinergics: dry mouth, reduced pharyngeal peristalsis, impaired secretion clearance
  • Timing strategy: coordinate medication administration with mealtimes; avoid tight clustering of opioids immediately before meals

Sleep apnea (OSA) and aspiration:

  • Baseline reduced pharyngeal muscle tone and upper airway collapse tendency
  • Aspiration risk is higher in OSA patients; PESD recovery often slower
  • Critical error to avoid: CPAP during meals increases risk by forcing air into esophagus (esophageal insufflation). Remove CPAP for meals, patient sitting upright, resume CPAP at night.

Cardiac surgery-specific factors:

  • Esophageal edema from sternal retraction and internal mammary artery dissection
  • Reduced post-extubation cough reflex (airway inflammation, residual sedation)
  • Generalized ICU deconditioning: muscles, swallow strength, endurance
  • Aspiration can trigger vagal response → bradycardia, hypotension, arrhythmia (cardiac significance)

sections.heading: 7.2 Dysphagia screening and SLP evaluation pathway
sections.bodyHtml:
Why swallow screen is non-negotiable:

  • One full aspiration with pneumonia adds 10–14 days ICU/floor stay, >$50K cost, mortality risk increase
  • Silent aspiration occurs in 50–70% of cases — cannot be detected by observation or patient report alone
  • Formal SLP evaluation (bedside swallow exam ± FEES/MBSS) is gold standard (Logemann, 1998)
  • One missed screen on an aspirator = patient safety event

Timing of screen:

  • BEFORE first PO attempt — this is the rule with zero exceptions
  • Before first medication PO — medications go down quickly; high aspiration risk if no screen done
  • Even if patient feels ready, hungry, or asking for water — screen first, eat after clearance
  • Extubation evening → screen completed next morning before breakfast

Bedside swallow screen includes:

  • Alert, cooperative, able to follow commands?
  • Cranial nerves II, V, VII, IX, X, XII intact? (assess gag, cough reflex, voice quality, swallow trials with saliva)
  • Cough strength and coordination; wet voice quality?
  • Swallow trials (ice chips, water, pudding per SLP protocol)
  • Observation for: cough during/after swallow, wet voice, drooling, residue in pharynx, delayed swallow initiation
  • Screen failure → recommendation for modified barium swallow (MBSS) or fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallow (FEES) per SLP and provider

FEES vs MBSS:

  • FEES (Flexible Endoscopic Evaluation of Swallow): bedside or outpatient; real-time visualization of larynx, pharynx, aspiration; no radiation; can assess secretion clearance
  • MBSS (Modified Barium Swallow Study): fluoroscopy in radiology; visualizes bolus transit mouth → pharynx → esophagus; no secretion assessment; better for identifying specific swallow phase delays
  • Choice: SLP and provider decide based on clinical scenario; often FEES first (faster, bedside, repeatable)

Dietary modifications after SLP clearance:

  • NPO if severe dysphagia with high aspiration risk
  • Thickened liquids (nectar, honey, pudding consistency) if thin-liquid aspiration risk; modality and thickness decided by SLP based on MBSS/FEES findings
  • Soft, minced, or pureed diet depending on chewing/swallowing strength
  • Small, frequent meals; patient takes time — rushing increases aspiration risk
  • 1:1 supervision during meals if high-risk; pulse oximetry monitoring recommended in first 48h post-event

Post-thickened-liquid controversy:

  • Thickened liquids increase viscosity → slower swallow passage → more time for laryngeal closure. However, some studies suggest thickened liquids may not always improve outcomes and can reduce hydration (patient drinks less).
  • Current standard: SLP determines thickness per individual patient's swallow physiology on MBSS/FEES; patient/family education critical

sections.heading: 7.3 Antibiotic approach: IDSA HAP 2016 on aspiration pneumonia
sections.bodyHtml:
Outdated teaching vs. current IDSA 2016:

  • Old: aspiration pneumonia = anaerobes → clindamycin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, piperacillin-tazobactam with routine anaerobic coverage
  • Current (IDSA 2016): routine anaerobic coverage is NOT recommended unless specific features present (Mandell et al., 2007)

IDSA 2016 recommendations for community-acquired aspiration pneumonia (applies to post-op setting):

Indications to START antibiotics:

  • Fever (>38.5°C) + infiltrate on CXR appearing 24–48h or more after aspiration event
  • Productive purulent sputum, rising WBC (>12K), elevated lactate
  • DO NOT give antibiotics acutely after witnessed aspiration if no fever/infiltrate — aspiration pneumonitis is chemical and self-limited

First-line empiric (if no severe immunosuppression):

  • Amoxicillin-clavulanate (amox-clav) 875/125 mg PO TID, OR
  • Fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg daily) if GI intolerance or unable to take PO, OR
  • Cephalosporin (cephalexin 500 mg QID) for step-down after IV

IV for hospitalized patients (initial):

  • Piperacillin-tazobactam (pip-tazo) 4.5 g IV Q6H (covers most aerobes + anaerobes), OR
  • Cefepime 2 g IV Q12H + Metronidazole 500 mg IV Q8H (separate agents for anaerobic specificity), OR
  • Ampicillin-sulbactam 3 g IV Q6H

When to ADD anaerobic coverage (metronidazole, clindamycin):

  • Putrid sputum (foul smell = gas-producing anaerobes like peptostreptococcus, prevotella)
  • Severe periodontal disease, gingivitis, recent dental work
  • Lung abscess on imaging
  • Empyema
  • Otherwise, omit routine anaerobic coverage → reduces drug exposure, Clostridioides difficile risk, cost

Post-transplant / severely immunosuppressed (broader coverage):

  • Add gram-negative coverage (fluoroquinolone or antipseudomonal cephalosporin)
  • Consider fungal coverage (Candida, Aspergillus) per ID consult
  • IV preferred initially

Duration: typically 5–7 days; longer if septic, clinical deterioration, or not improving

When NOT to start antibiotics immediately: - Aspiration pneumonitis (chemical, no fever, no purulent sputum) → supportive care only (O₂, HOB up, monitor). Antibiotics only if fever or bacterial signs develop at 24–48h

sections.heading: 7.4 Differential dysphagia after cardiac surgery
sections.bodyHtml:
Cause Mechanism Timeline SLP Findings Management
Post-extubation edema Laryngeal/mucosal edema from intubation tube 24–72h post-extubation Reduced laryngeal clearance; improved with time Conservative; FEES/MBSS if not improving POD 3
RLN injury Vocal cord paralysis left or right from aortic/CABG surgery Immediate to days post-op Weak/absent vocal cord movement; unilateral or bilateral paralysis; incomplete glottic closure ENT evaluation; SLP compensation therapy; may recover weeks–months or persist
TEE probe trauma Direct mucosal abrasion from intraoperative transesophageal echocardiography probe 24–48h post-op Mild pharyngeal/laryngeal irritation; usually transient Conservative; resolves spontaneously in 24–48h
Intubation trauma Vocal cord abrasion, arytenoid injury from tube position 24–72h post-extubation Bruising on FEES; reduced mobility transiently Conservative; usually resolves as edema recedes
Medication effects (opioids, benzos) CNS depression, reduced swallow initiation While medications on board Delayed swallow reflex; may improve with time or medication reduction Optimize medication timing; coordinate with meals
Delirium Altered mental status, uncooperativeness Variable May appear to have dysphagia; actually inability to concentrate/cooperate Treat underlying delirium; reassess swallow as mental status clears
Aspiration Oropharyngeal contents entering lower airway Acute event Cough, desaturation during swallow trials; positive aspiration on MBSS/FEES NPO; thickened liquids if appropriate; SLP management

Clinical pearl: most post-extubation dysphagia is transient (24–72h) and related to edema/intubation trauma, NOT permanent RLN injury. RLN injury risk is much lower unless arch surgery or large dissection performed.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable post-aspiration patients; if any show, re-escalate immediately.

  • Progressive hypoxemia despite O₂ increase — suggests pneumonitis worsening or bacterial pneumonia developing; prepare for higher acuity care, possible intubation
  • RR trending up >25 persistently — work of breathing increasing; may signal ARDS progression or sepsis; prepare for intubation readiness
  • Fever developing 24–48h post-aspiration — now in pneumonia risk zone; repeat CXR, labs (WBC, lactate, blood cultures if febrile); consider antibiotics per IDSA criteria
  • Sputum becoming purulent (yellowish, greenish) — bacterial colonization likely; WBC will likely rise
  • New crackles on lung exam or infiltrate expanding on CXR — pulmonary edema, pneumonitis worsening, or pneumonia progression
  • Lactate rising or elevated above baseline — perfusion/cellular metabolism worsening; sepsis trajectory
  • Mental status declining, drowsiness, reduced alertness — hypoxemia affecting cognition; prepare for intubation if trend continues
  • Tachycardia persistent (HR >120) — compensatory; suggests infection, shock, or severe hypoxemia
  • Recurrent aspiration event — new choking, wet voice returning, SpO₂ drop during next meal → NPO immediately, re-escalate, repeat SLP evaluation
  • Hemoptysis — rare but serious; suggests tissue necrosis, bleeding source, or lung abscess; notify team immediately
  • Stridor or difficulty breathing at rest — laryngeal edema or upper airway obstruction; prepare for emergency intubation

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Silent aspiration is most common — you will NOT see coughing or choking 50–70% of the time. Delirious or sedated patient eating quietly does NOT mean safe swallowing. Watch pulse oximetry during meals; unexpected desaturation SpO₂ drop is the clue. Document any drop, report immediately.

  2. Dysphagia screen BEFORE any PO (food, fluids, medications, ice chips) is non-negotiable. One missed screen on an aspirator = patient safety event + regulatory scrutiny. Even if patient hungry/asking for water, screen first. Document the screen was completed and who performed it.

  3. Hoarse voice post-aortic arch surgery = RLN injury until proven otherwise. Immediately notify APP, request ENT involvement, order SLP evaluation. Hoarse voice + first meal attempt = setup for aspiration. Do not discharge or liberalize diet without ENT/SLP clearance.

  4. IDSA 2016 moved away from routine anaerobic coverage. Many clinicians still default to clindamycin or amox-clav. Current standard: amox-clav or pip-tazo; add metronidazole ONLY if putrid sputum, severe periodontitis, or lung abscess. Check institutional policy before prescribing.

  5. Do NOT give antibiotics for aspiration pneumonitis reflexively. Chemical pneumonitis from acid is NOT bacterial initially. No fever, no purulent sputum = observation only. Fever + infiltrate at 24–48h = consider antibiotics. Acutely, supportive care (O₂, HOB up, monitor for ARDS) is the correct play.

  6. Tracheal suction aspirate is NOT a valid diagnostic specimen. Do not send for culture after aspiration event. Will grow normal oropharyngeal flora; does NOT guide antibiotic choice. Send sputum only if spontaneously expectorated and purulent, or endotracheal aspirate if re-intubated.

  7. HOB 30° during meal AND 30+ minutes after meal. Lowering HOB immediately after patient finishes eating defeats gravity's benefit for swallowing and promotes reflux aspiration risk. Keep it up during the window when reflux is highest risk.

  8. Thickened liquids are SLP's choice, not the nurse's choice. Cannot substitute regular water for "thickened" because patient prefers it or family requests. Thin-liquid aspiration is the reason thickening was ordered. If patient refuses ordered consistency, document refusal and notify SLP/provider.

  9. NG tubes impair swallowing. If NG still in place, coordinate with provider to remove it BEFORE bedside swallow screen. Screen with NG in place will overestimate aspiration risk and may unnecessarily keep patient NPO. Once removed, reassess.

  10. Sleep apnea (OSA) patient with meals = high aspiration risk. Do NOT put CPAP on during meals (increases esophageal air insufflation, worsens aspiration risk). Remove CPAP, patient eats upright, wait 30+ min, resume CPAP at night. OSA patients also have higher PESD risk — plan for longer swallow recovery.

  11. Delirium + meal = close monitoring mandatory. Hyperactive delirious patient may eat too fast, not signal when choking, forget swallowing precautions. Consider 1:1 observation during meals or frequent checks (q5–10 min). Reassess swallow as delirium resolves.

  12. Medication aspiration is real and preventable. Crush tablets + mix with thickened liquids per SLP; do NOT re-constitute crushed meds with thin liquids. Opioid dose right before meal = aspiration setup. Coordinate medication administration; avoid high-risk timing.

  13. Pneumonitis vs pneumonia is a timing issue. Acute aspiration with hypoxemia = pneumonitis (chemical, supportive). Fever + infiltrate 24–48h later = pneumonia (bacterial, antibiotics). Document the timeline carefully. Early antibiotics do NOT prevent pneumonitis and may delay recognition of pneumonia.

  14. Family often pushes for diet advancement. "My spouse wants regular food, not puree." Education: aspiration pneumonia adds weeks to hospitalization, increases mortality, prolongs recovery. Reinforce dietary restrictions with family; dietitian should reinforce at visit; engage family in prevention.

  15. CPAP is NOT a substitute for HOB positioning. Patient on CPAP during meals does NOT mean aspiration precautions are in place. Remove CPAP, sit upright, eat, wait 30+ min, resume CPAP. Communicate this clearly to patient, family, and team; update the care plan visibly.

cards.title: Atelectasis / Mucus Plugging (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: Post-operative hypoxemia + decreased breath sounds (often left lower lobe after LIMA harvest) + CXR consolidation → atelectasis until proven otherwise. Start pulmonary toilet NOW: incentive spirometry q1h awake (goal 10 breaths, ~750 mL baseline), cough + deep breathing with sternal splint, ambulation TID–QID, pain control first (opioid 15–20 min before IS). Worsening hypoxia (SpO₂ <88% on 4L) → CPAP 5 cm H₂O or BiPAP 10–12 insp/5 exp. Fever + purulent sputum → rule out HAP. Massive mucus plug unresponsive to toilet × 4–6 hours → bronchoscopy consideration.
