sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Partial or complete collapse of lung alveoli occurring post-cardiac surgery, caused by shallow breathing from sternotomy pain, reduced cough reflex, immobility, CPB-related surfactant dysfunction, and pleural entry (in LIMA grafts). Manifests as hypoxemia and diminished breath sounds, often focal to the left lower lobe.
  • Incidence: Near-universal in the first 24–72 hours post-operatively. Mild atelectasis detected on post-operative day (POD) 0–2 CXR occurs in 50–90% of cardiac surgery patients; lobar collapse requiring intervention is less common (~10–15%).
  • Who this applies to: every patient in the immediate post-operative period (POD 0–7), especially CABG with LIMA graft (left lower lobe predominance), prolonged CPB (>180 min), advanced age, COPD, obesity.
  • Why it matters: most common post-operative pulmonary problem. Early recognition and aggressive pulmonary toilet prevent progression to lobar collapse, hypoxemic respiratory failure, and prolonged ICU stays. Atelectasis is a complication of surgery, not a disease — the goal is management, not cure of a condition.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac surgery atelectasis results from convergence of four mechanisms that overwhelm normal lung defenses:

  • Sternotomy pain blocks deep breathing and coughing — patient naturally splints (holds chest rigid) to reduce discomfort, leading to shallow, inadequate ventilation and alveolar collapse in dependent zones.
  • Reduced cough reflex — opioid use, pain, anesthesia residue, and post-intubation airway irritation all weaken cough effectiveness. Secretions accumulate and obstruct small airways.
  • Immobility and gravity — patient confined to bed due to lines, drains, sedation, or general weakness. Secretions pool in the lower lobes. Lack of position changes and movement prevent normal V/Q matching recovery.
  • CPB-related surfactant dysfunction — cardiopulmonary bypass triggers inflammatory cascade that temporarily damages lung surfactant and impairs alveolar stability. Recovery takes 24–72 hours (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025).
  • Pleural entry (LIMA harvest) — left pleura is opened to harvest the left internal mammary artery, creating small pleural effusion, local inflammation, and left lower lobe vulnerability to collapse.
  • Impaired mucociliary clearance — intubation damages ciliary function; CPB creates inflammatory state. Secretion transport is mechanically compromised.
  • Altered V/Q matching — collapsed alveoli create areas of poor oxygenation relative to perfusion, producing hypoxemia disproportionate to the volume of atelectasis.

Timeline: Atelectasis peaks POD 0–3, then resolves gradually with pulmonary toilet and mobilization by POD 4–7. If untreated or inadequately managed, progression to lobar collapse, hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), or acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) can occur within 12–24 hours.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient:

  • Telemetry alarm: SpO₂ drop from baseline (often to 88–92%, sometimes 85–90% if mild atelectasis)
  • Morning CXR finding: new consolidation on post-op day CXR (lower lobes most common; left > right due to LIMA harvest in CABG)
  • Patient report: dyspnea, chest heaviness, difficulty or reluctance to cough (splinting from sternotomy pain)
  • Auscultation finding: diminished or absent breath sounds (most often left lower lobe); coarse crackles may develop
  • Respiratory pattern: shallow, splinted breathing with guarding, avoiding deep breaths due to pain; post-extubation patient with weak, ineffective cough
  • Indirect signs: decreased urine output, mild confusion, restlessness, agitation (hypoxemia may present subtly in post-op delirium)

Epidemiology context: Atelectasis is near-universal in the first 24–72 hours post-operatively. Most post-cardiac patients have some degree of atelectasis POD 0–2. Normalize this in your clinical reasoning — it is expected and manageable with the interventions in Section 5.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure information-gathering; no actions yet.

  • Vital signs & SpO₂: baseline SpO₂ pre-operatively vs. currently; HR, BP, RR, work of breathing (WOB), accessory muscle use
  • Respiratory pattern: is patient splinting (hand on chest, shallow breaths)? Cough — productive vs. dry? Sputum color/consistency/volume if present
  • Lung auscultation bilaterally, all fields: note specific areas of diminished/absent sounds; compare left to right; listen posterior bases (where atelectasis is often missed with anterior-only auscultation); document crackles vs. silence
  • Recent imaging: latest CXR (POD 0, 1, 2?) — location and extent of consolidation, pleural effusion, LIMA graft status, cardiac silhouette
  • Recent labs: temperature (afebrile or fever?), WBC (low-normal vs. elevated, left shift?), recent ABG (PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH) if available
  • Pain assessment: chest or incision pain on 1–10 scale — does patient rate pain as preventing deep breathing/coughing?
  • Mobility status: is patient ambulating or bedbound? When was last physical therapy session? Able to get out of bed?
  • Respiratory history: pre-operative COPD, OSA, smoking? Current home inhalers/nebulizers?
  • MAR review: diuretics recently given (hypovolemia worsens atelectasis); pain medications — when was last dose? Sedation level — is patient alert enough to cooperate with incentive spirometry?
  • Infection clues: temperature trend, mental status, sputum character (clear/mucoid vs. purulent/foul odor)

sections.heading: 5A. Stable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Alert, SpO₂ 89–94% on room air or 2L, no fever, diminished breath sounds but perfusing adequately (MAP ≥65, normal mentation).)

Pulmonary toilet is the evidence-based, proven approach. It works. Pain control must come first.

  1. Pain control FIRST — non-negotiable

    • Assess pain on 1–10 scale; if ≥5, administer opioid (IV or PO per order) 15–20 minutes before starting IS or C&DB
    • Provide sternal splint (teddy bear, pillow, rolled blanket, or commercial splint) — teach patient to hold firmly to chest during coughing and deep breathing
    • This single technique dramatically increases cough effectiveness; family members can reinforce it hourly

  2. Incentive spirometry q1h awake — evidence-based standard

    • Goal: 10 breaths per session (literature standard, not 5 or 3; higher targets correlate with better outcomes)
    • Technique: slow, deep inspirations to total lung capacity (TLC), hold 2–3 seconds at peak
    • Document baseline volume (often 1000–1500 mL immediately post-op, varies by body habitus)
    • Coach patient: "This re-expands your collapsed lung zones. It may hurt, but splint your chest with the pillow and breathe deeply."
    • Empower family: "Coach her to take 10 deep breaths with the spirometer every hour while awake. This is the most important thing you can do to prevent pneumonia."
    • Expected response: SPO₂ should improve within 5–15 min of proper IS; volume should trend up over POD 0–3 as pain improves

  3. Coughing + deep breathing (C&DB) after IS

    • Deep breathing: 3–5 slow, deep inspirations (splinting chest with pillow or hands)
    • Coughing: 2–3 vigorous coughs (splinting chest with firm pressure against incision)
    • If weak cough: assisted cough (nurse or family provides hand-pressure on chest or back during cough to amplify force)
    • Position: semi-Fowler's or upright to leverage gravity; avoid supine (gravity worsens dependent atelectasis)

  4. Early ambulation — the single most effective treatment

    • Ambulate at least TID (3 times daily), preferably QID or continuous if tolerated
    • Even 50 feet down the hallway and back produces dramatic improvement in SpO₂ and sputum clearance
    • Mechanism: gravity + movement + position changes + increased minute ventilation all reduce atelectasis simultaneously
    • Ambulation effectiveness exceeds IS alone; combine them (IS at bedside, ambulation PRN)
    • Document distance, tolerance, SpO₂ before/after to establish trend

  5. Nebulized medications (if ordered)

    • Albuterol standard (opens airways, mobilizes secretions)
    • N-acetylcysteine (NAC) if secretions thick or tenacious (mucolytic agent)
    • Schedule around IS + C&DB for synergistic benefit (e.g., neb → IS → C&DB)
    • Assess response: does sputum production increase? Does patient cough up more after treatment?

  6. Chest physiotherapy (CPT) — if ordered by PT or physician

    • Percussion + vibration to affected lung fields (typically lower lobes, especially left after LIMA)
    • Postural drainage if tolerated (avoid Trendelenburg post-cardiac surgery due to cardiac strain)
    • Gentle technique — do not aggravate sternal incision or cause rib pain
    • Often performed by PT; nursing role is to reinforce between sessions and assess effectiveness

  7. Secretion clearance

    • If secretions retained (coarse crackles on auscultation, inability to clear despite coughing): encourage more aggressive coughing with optimal splinting
    • Gentle oral suctioning if patient unable to clear upper airway
    • If patient intubated or high risk of aspiration: coordinate with respiratory therapy for endotracheal suctioning
    • Monitor sputum: clear or white = normal post-op; yellow/green/purulent = possible HAP (escalate per Section 6)

  8. Monitor response and re-assess

    • Re-auscultate after IS/C&DB: do breath sounds improve in previously silent area? (Return of crackles = sign of re-expansion)
    • Repeat SpO₂: does it improve within 5–15 min of intervention? Document trend (e.g., "SpO₂ 89% pre-IS → 94% post-IS + C&DB + ambulation")
    • Establish visual cues: patient should see spirometer volume trending up each shift if compliance is good
    • Adjust O₂ delivery based on trend (see below)

  9. Oxygenation support

    • Room air if tolerating (SpO₂ >88%)
    • Low-flow O₂ (1–2 L/min via nasal cannula) if SpO₂ trending down below 88%
    • Titrate to target SpO₂ 92–95%; do NOT over-oxygenate — high FiO₂ may paradoxically worsen atelectasis by nitrogen washout
    • Assess SpO₂ on room air with ambulation (walking is the gold standard test; if SpO₂ adequate on room air walking, patient is improving)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(SpO₂ <88% despite toilet + supplemental O₂, worsening dyspnea, RR >25, tachycardia, restlessness, or lobar collapse on CXR.)

  1. STAT escalation — notify APP/on-call fellow immediately; do NOT wait for routine rounding
  2. Supplemental O₂ — target SpO₂ ≥92%; escalate from nasal cannula to non-rebreather if needed

  3. Prepare for non-invasive ventilation (NIV)

    • CPAP 5 cm H₂O or BiPAP (10–12 cm H₂O inspiratory, 5 cm H₂O expiratory) — coordinate with respiratory therapy
    • Used as bridge before intubation; improves oxygenation and facilitates secretion clearance better than high-flow O₂ alone
    • Patient must be alert enough to tolerate mask or helmet interface
    • Start trial for 30–60 min; assess response (SpO₂ trend, WOB, patient comfort)

  4. STAT imaging & labs

    • Portable CXR or formal chest X-ray STAT — assess for lobar collapse, massive consolidation, pneumothorax, other complications
    • ABG STAT (is patient hypoxemic or normoxic? PaCO₂ elevated suggesting hypoventilation?)
    • CBC (fever + leukocytosis → rule out HAP)

  5. Aggressive pulmonary toilet continues

    • IS + C&DB even with CPAP/BiPAP on
    • Nebulizers if not already running
    • Suctioning as needed

  6. Bronchoscopy consideration

    • If lobar collapse confirmed on CXR AND unresponsive to optimized toilet × 2–4 hours
    • If massive mucus plugging visible or suspected (frank respiratory failure despite toilet)
    • NOT first-line; only after aggressive toilet trial
    • Allows direct visualization + suctioning of occluded bronchus
    • Reduces need for re-intubation in select cases

  7. Escalate to intensivist — if refractory hypoxemia despite NIV or if re-intubation considered

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on the ICU, calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure (e.g., CABG with LIMA graft)]." B: "Patient with new/worsening hypoxemia: SpO₂ now [value] on [O₂ delivery (e.g., 2L NC)], down from baseline [value] this morning. Breath sounds decreased/absent in [LLL/RLL/bilateral]. Latest CXR shows [description: consolidation/collapse/diffuse infiltrate]. Pain [rating/control status] limiting cough/IS. Temperature [value], WBC [value]. [Sputum description: clear/thick/purulent]." A: "Patient is [stable/unstable]. [Major findings: splinting from pain / already on nebulizers / has not ambulated due to weakness / showing early signs of respiratory distress]. We have started [pulmonary toilet: IS q1h, C&DB, ambulation]. [Sputum character and response to interventions]." R: "Requesting [plan: continue toilet vs escalate to CPAP / bronchoscopy consideration / repeat imaging / labs to rule out HAP / increase pain control for IS compliance]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
New mild atelectasis, stable, responsive to pulmonary toilet Primary APP / on-call resident
Worsening SpO₂ despite toilet + supplemental O₂ APP/fellow + charge nurse; RRT if severe
Fever + atelectasis + purulent sputum (HAP vs CAP) APP/fellow + consider infectious disease consult
Lobar collapse on CXR + unresponsive to toilet × 2–4 h CT surgery / cardiothoracic surgery team + pulmonology consult; bronchoscopy option discussed
Massive mucus plug causing respiratory failure CT surgery team + respiratory therapy; rigid bronchoscopy + OR availability may be needed
Patient deteriorating despite all interventions Rapid response team + ICU/intensivist + consider re-intubation

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default for expert skim.

sections.heading: 7.1 Physiology: Why atelectasis happens and how toilet reverses it
sections.bodyHtml:
Atelectasis in cardiac surgery is not a single mechanism but rather four mechanisms converging simultaneously:

  1. Pain-mediated hypoventilation — sternotomy incision pain is severe (6–8/10 on POD 0–1). Patients naturally splint (voluntarily reduce rib cage movement) to avoid discomfort. This reduces tidal volume from ~500 mL (normal awake breathing) to ~200–300 mL post-op. Low tidal volumes do not re-expand collapsed alveoli, and dependent zones (lower lobes in upright posture) progressively collapse from surface tension and lack of recruitment.

  2. Surfactant dysfunction from CPB — cardiopulmonary bypass primes circuits with fluid, triggers systemic inflammatory response, and damages the alveolar epithelium. Surfactant (which normally reduces surface tension and stabilizes alveoli) is depleted or inactivated. This increases the mechanical work needed to inflate alveoli and makes them prone to collapse at end-expiration. Recovery occurs over 24–72 hours as CPB effects resolve and surfactant is re-synthesized.

  3. Secretion accumulation — intubation damages ciliary function; weak cough from pain and opioids allows secretions to pool in small airways. These become obstructive plugs, causing absorption atelectasis (alveoli beyond the plug collapse as oxygen is absorbed and not replaced).

  4. Gravity pooling — immobility + supine positioning allows secretions to gravitate to dependent zones (lower lobes, posterior). Without position changes and movement, these areas remain hypoventilated.

How pulmonary toilet reverses this:

  • Incentive spirometry (IS) generates high transpulmonary pressure (patient effort-driven), forcing air past closed-off alveoli and re-expanding them. The pressure cascade overcomes surface tension and small-airway obstruction. 10 breaths per session (not 3) ensures sufficient lung re-recruitment.
  • Deep breathing + coughing (C&DB) mobilizes secretions toward large airways where they can be expectorated, removing the obstructive plug.
  • Ambulation combines several mechanisms: gravity changes (upright posture draws fluid away from lower lobes), movement increases minute ventilation, and activity triggers stronger respiratory effort. Early mobilization (within 24 hours) is the single strongest predictor of atelectasis resolution (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025).
  • Pain control (prerequisite) unlocks all of the above by permitting the patient to breathe deeply without guarding.

sections.heading: 7.2 Atelectasis types and patterns
sections.bodyHtml:
Type Mechanism CXR Pattern Clinical Pearl
Compressive External mass (effusion, pneumothorax) compresses lung tissue Opacified area with clear lung margins; mediastinal/cardiac silhouette shift Post-LIMA: expect small left pleural effusion POD 0–2. Usually resorbs without intervention.
Resorptive Mucus plug or obstruction in airway; distal alveoli collapse as O₂ is absorbed Lobar/segmental consolidation; linear or wedge-shaped; often with air bronchograms Most common post-cardiac surgery type. Responds to pulmonary toilet.
Plate / linear Small area of alveolar collapse at lung base (common post-op finding) Fine linear opacity at bases, often horizontal (Fleischner line) Often clinically silent; usually resolves with mobility.
Lobar Complete collapse of an entire lobe from massive obstruction or external pressure Complete opacification of lobe; hilum shift toward collapsed side; possible mediastinal shift Indicates significant atelectasis; risk for hypoxemic respiratory failure. Pulmonary toilet + consider bronchoscopy.

LIMA-related pattern (most common in CABG): Left lower lobe atelectasis is expected after LIMA harvest. The left pleura is opened, creating irritation and small effusion. Splinting from sternotomy pain is worse on the left side (surgical side). This pattern peaks POD 1–2 and usually resolves with aggressive toilet by POD 3–4.

sections.heading: 7.3 Incentive spirometry technique and evidence
sections.bodyHtml:
Proper IS technique (teach patient this way):

  1. Sit upright or semi-Fowler's position
  2. Place spirometer mouthpiece and seal lips tightly (no air leakage)
  3. Exhale fully (baseline)
  4. Slow, deep inspiration through mouth over 2–3 seconds (NOT a quick gasp; slow inhalation generates higher pressure)
  5. At peak inspiration, hold for 2–3 seconds (maintains positive pressure, recruits atelectatic zones)
  6. Exhale passively
  7. Rest briefly (20–30 seconds between breaths)
  8. Repeat 10 times per session (literature consensus from Brasher et al., 2003; higher repetitions = better outcomes)

Why 10 breaths, not 3 or 5? Meta-analysis by Brasher et al. (Cochrane, 2003) demonstrated IS reduces post-operative atelectasis incidence by ~40% vs. usual care, provided the patient performs 10 breaths per session. Studies using <5 breaths showed minimal benefit. This is not opinion — it's in the evidence base. Nurses often do 3–5 breaths and consider it "done." That is insufficient.

Compliance challenges & solutions:

Barrier Why it occurs Solution
Pain limiting effort Sternotomy pain prevents deep breathing Give opioid 15–20 min before IS; sternal splint; reassure patient that splinting while breathing deeply is safe
Poor understanding of technique Patient thinks IS is passive (like oxygen) Demonstrate on self; emphasize "your effort re-expands your lungs"; show spirometer volume climbing
Fatigue Patient tires after 3–4 breaths Schedule IS q1h awake (shorter, more frequent sessions) vs. q4h "catch-up" sessions; emphasize consistency over volume
Low motivation "It doesn't hurt and I feel fine" Normalize: "Atelectasis is expected; you may not feel it, but the X-ray shows it and IS fixes it."

sections.heading: 7.4 CPB-related lung collapse physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardiopulmonary bypass causes acute lung injury (ALI) mechanisms that predispose to atelectasis:

  • Surfactant inactivation — inflammatory cascade (complement activation, leukocyte sequestration in lungs) damages type II pneumocytes and inactivates surfactant. Alveolar compliance decreases; alveoli are prone to collapse at end-expiration.
  • Increased pulmonary vascular permeability — edema accumulates in interstitial and alveolar spaces, worsening gas exchange and promoting atelectasis.
  • Inflammatory response — systemic release of cytokines (IL-6, TNF-α, IL-8) triggers neutrophil infiltration into lung tissue, causing additional injury.
  • Hypothermia during CPB — reduces metabolic rate and oxygen consumption post-operatively, but also impairs cough and respiratory muscle strength transiently.

Timeline: These effects peak at CPB cessation and gradually resolve over 24–72 hours as:

  • Surfactant is re-synthesized
  • Inflammatory mediators are cleared
  • Pulmonary edema resorbs (with diuresis)
  • Respiratory muscle strength returns

Clinical implication: Atelectasis post-CPB is most severe on POD 0–2 and is expected to improve rapidly with pulmonary toilet. If atelectasis is worsening by POD 3–4 despite optimal toilet, suspect HAP, pulmonary edema, or pleural effusion as complicating factors.

sections.heading: 7.5 Auto-PEEP and alveolar recruitment
sections.bodyHtml:
Auto-PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) is intrinsic pressure that remains in the alveoli at end-expiration due to incomplete exhalation. In atelectasis, auto-PEEP can paradoxically WORSEN collapse:

  • If a patient with small-airway disease or secretion plugging breathes shallowly (splinting), air-trapping occurs and auto-PEEP builds
  • High auto-PEEP during shallow breathing actually compresses dependent lung zones further

Solution: Deep breathing + exhalation (IS done correctly, with full exhalation between breaths) reduces auto-PEEP by allowing complete lung emptying. Then re-inflation re-recruits atelectatic zones.

CPAP/BiPAP mechanism: External PEEP (from CPAP 5 cm H₂O or BiPAP) maintains positive airway pressure throughout the respiratory cycle, recruiting atelectatic alveoli by holding them open. This is why CPAP is effective in unstable atelectasis with hypoxemia — it splints open collapsed zones without requiring patient effort (though patient cooperation is still needed).

sections.heading: 7.6 Bronchoscopy indications and technique
sections.bodyHtml:
When to consider bronchoscopy:

  • Lobar collapse confirmed on CXR + unresponsive to optimized pulmonary toilet (IS q1h + ambulation + nebs) × 2–4 hours
  • Massive mucus plugging causing acute hypoxemia or respiratory failure
  • Inability to clear secretions despite aggressive toilet (e.g., weak, intubated patient with tenacious plugs)
  • NOT for mild/moderate atelectasis or routine post-op consolidation (these resolve with toilet)

Bronchoscopy technique (nursing role):

  • Coordinate with respiratory therapy / anesthesia for sedation/airway management
  • Position patient supine, head-of-bed elevated slightly for airway access
  • Rigid vs. flexible scope depends on situation (flexible for floor patient; rigid for massive obstruction in OR-available setting)
  • Direct visualization allows suctioning of plugged bronchus under direct visualization
  • Post-procedure: monitor for increased sputum production (good sign — secretions clearing), monitor SpO₂, continue aggressive toilet

Evidence: Bronchoscopy for post-operative atelectasis is not routine first-line; it is reserved for specific cases (lobar collapse, unresponsive to 2–4 hours toilet) because most atelectasis resolves with non-invasive toilet alone (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020). Routine bronchoscopy for uncomplicated post-op consolidation prolongs stay and adds cost without clear benefit.

sections.heading: 7.7 Differential diagnosis and masqueraders
sections.bodyHtml:
Condition Atelectasis HAP Pleural Effusion Pneumothorax PE
Fever Usually afebrile Fever ≥38.5°C typical Usually afebrile Afebrile Afebrile or low-grade
WBC Normal or low-normal Elevated (>11k), left shift Normal Normal Normal
Sputum Clear, thin, mucoid Purulent (yellow/green) Absence (effusion is fluid, not sputum) Absence Absence
Onset Immediate POD 0–1 POD 2–4+ POD 0–2 expected after LIMA Sudden if barotrauma Sudden if VTE risk
Breath sounds Diminished/absent focal area Crackles + diminished in area Diminished at base (dullness to percussion) Hyperresonant + absent breath sounds Diminished
CXR pattern Lobar/segmental consolidation; may have air bronchograms Focal infiltrate, often RLL > LLL Blunting of costophrenic angle; wedge shape if lobar White-out of hemithorax; mediastinal shift Hampton hump (wedge), often normal
Response to IS/toilet Improves within hours No improvement; needs antibiotics No improvement with toilet; may need drainage if large Requires chest tube if symptomatic Requires anticoagulation
JVP / fluid status Normal, euvolemic Normal or elevated if sepsis Normal (unless right heart strain) Normal unless tension PTX Elevated if acute RV strain

Clinical pearl: Post-cardiac surgery, afebrile hypoxemia with focal consolidation = atelectasis until proven otherwise. Don't jump to HAP antibiotics without fever + elevated WBC + purulent sputum. However, if fever appears after afebrile first 24 hours, reassess for HAP and escalate.

sections.heading: 7.8 HFNC vs. NIV vs. re-intubation decision
sections.bodyHtml:
High-flow nasal cannula (HFNC):

  • Delivers up to 60 L/min heated, humidified gas
  • Washes out dead space; generates ~2–3 cm H₂O PEEP
  • Better tolerated than mask-based NIV (no face pressure)
  • Role: for mild-to-moderate hypoxemia (SpO₂ 85–92% on 4L) when patient cooperative and protecting airway
  • Does NOT re-recruit atelectasis as effectively as CPAP/BiPAP

Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP/BiPAP):

  • CPAP 5 cm H₂O: continuous positive airway pressure throughout cycle
  • BiPAP 10–12 insp / 5 exp: pressure support on inhalation, lower PEEP on exhalation
  • Role: for moderate-to-severe hypoxemia (SpO₂ <88% on HFNC or high-flow O₂) OR significant work of breathing
  • Re-recruits atelectatic alveoli via PEEP; reduces WOB
  • Requirement: patient must be alert and able to tolerate mask/helmet for 30–60 min trial
  • Escalate if patient tires, loses cooperation, or SpO₂ continues to decline despite trial

Re-intubation:

  • Indicated if SpO₂ <85% despite NIV trial, RR >35 (fatigue imminent), altered mental status preventing mask tolerance, hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >50) suggesting hypoventilation
  • Post-cardiac surgery re-intubation increases morbidity (longer ICU stay, infection risk, need for additional sedation)
  • Prevent by early recognition of deterioration and escalation to NIV before frank failure

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear in a stable atelectasis patient, re-escalate — patient may be crossing into unstable path or developing complications.

  • SpO₂ trending down despite toilet (was 93% → 89% → 85% over 2–4 hours) — toilet failing; may need CPAP/BiPAP or bronchoscopy
  • Lobar collapse on CXR — significant, progressive atelectasis; high risk for hypoxemia escalation; bronchoscopy consideration within 2–4 hours if unresponsive to toilet
  • Massive consolidation appearing overnight or expanding rapidly — possible progression to HAP, ARDS, or other complication; repeat CXR + STAT labs + escalate
  • Sputum character changing — clear → yellowish/greenish/purulent — suggests superimposed infection (HAP); escalate for culture, consider antibiotics per protocol
  • Fever appearing after afebrile first 24 hours — now suspicious for HAP; escalate for assessment + empiric antibiotics consideration
  • WBC rising (was 9k POD 1 → 14k POD 2) — inflammatory response intensifying; assess for concurrent infection
  • Patient unwilling/unable to cooperate with IS or ambulation — often from inadequate pain control; reassess analgesia and repeat toilet coaching
  • Work of breathing increasing (RR >25, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, pursed-lip breathing) — hypoxemia worsening; may precede overt SpO₂ desaturation
  • Mental status changes (restlessness, confusion, agitation, lethargy) — hypoxemia affecting cognition; urgent sign requiring escalation
  • Tachycardia out of proportion to pain or fever (HR >110 for no clear reason) — possible cardiac compensation for hypoxemia or early sepsis
  • Breath sounds worsening or shifting distribution (was LLL, now diffuse or RLL) — possible lobar collapse shifting or progression; escalate for imaging + bronchoscopy consideration

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Atelectasis POD 0–3 is near-universal — it is a complication of surgery, not a disease. Normalize it in your clinical reasoning. Goal is early recognition + aggressive toilet, not panic. Most resolve within 24–48 hours of correct intervention.

  2. Incentive spirometry is dramatically underused because of patient compliance, but the evidence is unambiguous: IS q1h awake, goal 10 breaths per session, reduces atelectasis incidence by ~40%. Pain control first, then teach proper technique. Family can coach. This works.

  3. Pain control before pulmonary toilet is non-negotiable. A patient in severe pain will not cough effectively, will not do IS properly, and will splint. Give opioid 15–20 min before IS. The difference is dramatic.

  4. Sternal splint (teddy bear or chest roll) is the single most effective pain-reduction technique for coughing post-sternotomy. Family can teach. Patient holds pillow/rolled blanket to chest during cough + deep breathing. Do NOT underestimate its value — it is the difference between effective and ineffective cough.

  5. Ambulation is the best single treatment for post-operative atelectasis. More effective than IS alone. Combine them: ambulate TID–QID + IS q1h awake at bedside. Early mobility (out of bed POD 0–1) dramatically reduces atelectasis incidence and length of stay.

  6. Distinguish atelectasis from HAP by fever + WBC + sputum character. Post-cardiac surgery, afebrile + clear sputum = atelectasis; fever + purulent sputum + leukocytosis = HAP. Don't reflexively give antibiotics for uncomplicated atelectasis.

  7. Massive mucus plugging causing lobar collapse: pulmonary toilet FIRST, bronchoscopy SECOND. Most cases resolve with aggressive IS + C&DB + ambulation + nebs within 12–24 hours. Bronchoscopy is for unresponsive cases (after 2–4 hour toilet trial) or frank respiratory failure.

  8. Post-LIMA pleural effusion can mimic or coexist with atelectasis. Left pleura is opened, so small left pleural effusion is expected POD 0–2. On CXR this looks like LLL "infiltrate" but is actually serous fluid. Auscultation shows diminished sounds (not crackles). This usually resorbs without intervention but can cause hypoxemia. Pulmonary toilet still helps.

  9. Never auscultate the lungs on the anterior chest only. Most post-cardiac surgery atelectasis (especially lower lobe) is missed if you don't listen posterior and lateral bases (require patient leaning forward or rolling to examine back thoroughly). This is the single most common exam error in new nurses.

  10. Posterior breath sounds are quieter than anterior in healthy patients. You must listen carefully with quiet environment. A post-op patient with LLL atelectasis will have absent posterior LLL sounds — this is the diagnostic finding.

  11. SpO₂ on room air with ambulation is the gold standard test for atelectasis recovery. If patient desaturates below baseline only with activity but recovers to 92%+ at rest on room air, atelectasis is resolving. If SpO₂ drops below 88% at rest or with minimal activity, escalate.

  12. Phrenic nerve injury (diaphragm paralysis) can masquerade as atelectasis, especially after LIMA or internal mammary artery graft. Left phrenic nerve injury causes left hemidiaphragm elevation on CXR (looks like collapse/consolidation) and left lower lobe atelectasis. Key difference: chest fluoroscopy shows paradoxical motion of diaphragm (moves up on inspiration instead of down). Consider if atelectasis not improving with toilet over 48–72 hours; escalate for imaging confirmation.

  13. RLL auscultation requires patient leaning far forward and listening at the posterior axilla. Many nurses listen only to the anterior RLL (near 4th ICS midclavicular) and miss posterior consolidation. Post-cardiac surgery, always auscultate posterior bases bilaterally.

  14. SpO₂ is not a perfect marker of atelectasis severity. A patient with mild-to-moderate atelectasis may maintain SpO₂ 90–94% due to compensatory hyperventilation. But CXR shows lobar collapse and auscultation shows silent zones. Don't be reassured by "adequate" SpO₂ if exam/imaging shows significant atelectasis — escalate if unresponsive to toilet.

  15. Bronchoscopy, while therapeutic, adds cost and delays mobility. Reserve for lobar collapse unresponsive to toilet × 2–4 hours or frank respiratory failure. Routine bronchoscopy for routine post-op consolidation has no evidence base and may paradoxically delay toilet-based recovery.

cards.title: AVR / Aortic Root Replacement — Surgery Card (Deep)
cards.quickAnswer: Stable SBP target 100–140 mmHg (≤ 120 for root surgery); watch rhythm continuously for complete heart block (5–8% need PPM). Anticoagulation by prosthesis type: mechanical valve = warfarin lifelong (INR 2–3), start heparin bridge POD 1; tissue valve = ASA 81 only, no AC needed; VSARR (native valve preserved) = ASA 81 only, no AC. Keep epicardial pacing wires through POD 4–5 (not optional—AV node injury is real). Highest-risk complication: coronary button ischemia (Bentall) — any new chest pain POD 0–2 is STAT EKG + troponin + OR standby. Teach endocarditis prophylaxis (lifelong, all prostheses) and anticoagulation compliance at discharge; missed warfarin doses cause catastrophic thrombosis in mechanical valves.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

Aortic Valve Replacement (AVR) — Three Surgical Approaches:

  • Isolated AVR (tissue or mechanical): Diseased native aortic valve replaced with prosthetic; annulus preserved; moderate cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) time; routine post-op recovery POD 5–7
  • Bentall (Composite Graft Root Replacement): Entire aortic root (valve + ascending aorta) replaced with a composite graft (usually Dacron tube + prosthetic valve); coronary arteries reimplanted as buttons; higher complexity, longer CPB, longer recovery (POD 7–9); re-do surgery risk higher due to adhesions
  • VSARR (Valve-Sparing Root Repair): Native aortic valve remodeled and suspended on a neo-aortic root (David reimplantation or Yacoub remodeling); no prosthesis implanted; shortest recovery (POD 5–6); avoids lifelong anticoagulation if no AF concurrent

Who Gets This and Why

  • Aortic stenosis (severe, symptomatic or LV dysfunction)
  • Aortic regurgitation (severe, with LV dilation or symptoms)
  • Aortic root disease (aneurysm, dissection, Marfan syndrome)
  • Bicuspid aortic valve (with root dilation; often requires concurrent ascending aorta repair)
  • Failed prosthesis (degeneration, endocarditis, thrombosis)
  • Post-dissection repair (Type A dissection repair)
  • Endocarditis with root abscess (especially if Bentall needed)

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why this happens — novice + advanced beginner teaching.

Aortic Valve Anatomy & Pathology

The aortic valve is a tricuspid structure (three leaflets) at the junction of the left ventricle and ascending aorta. In bicuspid disease (10% of the population), two leaflets fuse, causing early calcification and dysfunction. Severe stenosis (opening area < 1 cm²) restricts forward flow; severe regurgitation allows diastolic backflow. Both lead to LV hypertrophy, dilation, and eventual dysfunction.

The aortic root comprises four zones: annulus (leaflet attachment), sinuses of Valsalva (bulges behind each leaflet), sinotubular junction, and ascending aorta. Root aneurysm (dilation > 5 cm or > 5.5 cm in Marfan/bicuspid) risks dissection and rupture; surgery is indicated for elective repair.

Prosthesis Types & Durability

Valve Type Material Durability Thrombosis Risk Anticoagulation Best For
Mechanical (bileaflet) Pyrolytic carbon discs in polyester sewing ring > 30 years 0.6%/patient-year if therapeutic INR; 4–5% if subtherapeutic Warfarin lifelong (INR 2–3 AVR; 2.5–3.5 MVR) + ASA 81 mg daily Age < 60, long life expectancy, reliable patient compliance
Bioprosthetic (porcine or bovine pericardium) Glutaraldehyde-fixed tissue in pericardial or porcine frame 10–15 years (younger patients earlier) < 1% if in sinus rhythm; 2–3% if chronic AF ASA 81 only (warfarin × 3 mo optional per surgeon) Age ≥ 65, reluctance to warfarin, shorter predicted lifespan, contraindication to AC
Homograft (allograft) Cryopreserved human valve from cadaver 10–20 years; variable Low, no AC needed ASA 81 only Endocarditis (lower infection risk), root replacement, young patients (VSARR preferred now)
Ross Procedure (autograft) Patient's own pulmonary valve moved to aortic position; pulmonary position receives allograft 20–30 years (aortic autograft); allograft shorter None ASA 81 only Young patients (< 50) accepting 2 valves to watch + likely re-do in 20 years
VSARR (David/Yacoub) Native aortic valve preserved; root reconstructed Native valve durability; varies with technique None ASA 81 only (unless concurrent AF) Young to middle-aged patients, valve anatomy preserved if possible, avoid AC burden

Root Replacement Techniques (Bentall, VSARR)

  • Bentall (Composite Graft): Aortic root incised, annulus excised, composite graft anastomosed proximally (to LV annulus), coronary buttons excised and reimplanted into graft (button technique), distal aorta anastomosed. High suture lines = bleeding risk. Coronary button kinesis = obstruction risk (rare, catastrophic).
  • David Reimplantation (VSARR): Root incised at sinotubular junction; native valve leaflets preserved; aortic wall resuspended on synthetic graft (smaller diameter); coronaries left in situ (no reimplantation). Shorter recovery; late AR risk 10–20% (redo at 10 years possible).
  • Yacoub Remodeling (VSARR): Root incised, native leaflets suspended by sutures to neo-aortic graft; partial aortic root preserved. Alternative to David; similar outcomes.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Operative Course
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner understanding of who arrives on the unit, when, and in what condition.

Pre-Op Profile

  • Severe aortic valve disease ± root enlargement
  • Pre-op LV function: ranges from preserved EF 55–60% (chronic AR adaptation) to reduced EF 30–35% (longstanding disease)
  • Possible bicuspid AV (10–15% of population); concurrent ascending aorta repair likely
  • Comorbidities: CAD (30–40%), renal disease, COPD, AF (especially if mitral disease or cardiomyopathy)

Operative Details

  • Approach: Median sternotomy standard; ministernotomy or mini-thoracotomy isolated AVR at select centers
  • CPB: Moderate hypothermia (28–32 °C) standard; deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA, 18–20 °C) if Bentall with arch extension
  • Cardioplegia: Cold blood or crystalloid antegrade ± retrograde via coronary sinus
  • Pump time: AVR alone 60–90 min; Bentall 120–180 min; VSARR 100–140 min
  • Epicardial pacing wires: Placed at close (routine safeguard for heart block)

Expected Post-Op Course — ICU (POD 0)

  • Extubation goal 4–6 h; rule out bleeding/tamponade/inadequate sedation if delayed
  • CT output < 200 mL/h target; transfuse PRBC if Hgb < 8 (< 9 if CAD/age)
  • Pacer wire threshold check; baseline AV conduction documented
  • Labs: CBC, BMP, INR baseline (mechanical), LDH/haptoglobin/retic (mechanical valve baseline hemolysis screen)
  • SBP target 100–140 (avoid hypertension risk of aortic graft dehiscence, but maintain perfusion pressure)

Expected Post-Op Course — POD 1–3 (ICU → Stepdown Transition)

  • Out of bed to chair POD 1; A-line removed POD 1–2 if MAP stable without pressors
  • Beta-blocker + statin initiated (cardioprotection, arrhythmia prevention)
  • Heparin bridge initiated POD 1 if mechanical valve; warfarin POD 2–3
  • Foley removed POD 1–2 (mobility and CAUTI prevention)
  • CTs out POD 2–3 if drainage < 150 mL/8 h × 8 h (no air leak)
  • Transfer to stepdown when: hemodynamically stable off high-dose pressors, extubated, pacer wires in place, CTs manageable or out, and tele-capable
  • Pacer wires remain in place through POD 4–5 (AV block risk not over)

Expected Post-Op Course — POD 4–7 (Stepdown/Discharge)

  • Rhythm monitoring continues; heart block can occur delayed (POD 2–5) as edema peaks then resolves
  • INR monitoring q24h if mechanical valve; heparin stopped when INR > 2.0 × 24 h (typically POD 5–7)
  • Discharge teaching: AC plan, endocarditis prophylaxis, sternal precautions, follow-up schedule
  • Pacer wires removed POD 4–5 or day before discharge (surgeon-specific)
  • Discharge goals: POD 5–7 for isolated AVR; POD 7–9 for Bentall/VSARR

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: 2 min at bedside.

Vital Signs & Hemodynamics

  • Heart rate, blood pressure, mean arterial pressure (MAP), SpO₂, central venous pressure (CVP) if line in
  • Perfusion: capillary refill, skin warmth, urine output (target > 0.5 mL/kg/h)
  • Rhythm: regular vs. irregular, any ectopy on monitor

Cardiac & Respiratory

  • Breath sounds bilaterally (rule out effusion, atelectasis)
  • Heart sounds: new murmur? Mechanical valve click normal; no click or new regurgitation murmur = concern
  • JVD, orthopnea, S3 gallop (signs of heart failure or tamponade)
  • Chest tube output (color, quantity, character); any air leak when suctioning

Neurologic

  • Alert & oriented × 3; agitation or somnolence (delirium risk POD 1–3)
  • Focal deficits: stroke screening (arm drift, speech, facial symmetry)
  • Pacer wire threshold & sensing at bedside: document capture + sense

Surgical Incision & Lines

  • Sternotomy: erythema, warmth, dehiscence, sternal click (instability sign)
  • Pacer wires (two epicardial screws on RV): intact, not dislodged
  • CTs (1–2): mediastinal ± pleural; output color/quantity in last 8 h
  • IV access: peripheral, PICC, or central line quality

Recent Labs (Last 4–6 Hours)

  • CBC: Hgb trend (transfusion threshold AVR Hgb < 8; < 9 if CAD/age)
  • BMP: K⁺ (goal ≥ 4.0), Mg²⁺ (goal ≥ 2.0), Cr (trend for AKI)
  • INR + PT/PTT if on warfarin bridge (mechanical valve)
  • LDH, haptoglobin, retic if mechanical valve (hemolysis baseline)

Prosthesis Type & AC Status

  • Which prosthesis implanted? Mechanical, bioprosthetic, VSARR documented?
  • Anticoagulation plan: warfarin start date, heparin bolus/drip status, INR target
  • Home medications restarted or held? Beta-blocker, statin, ACE inhibitor, diuretic status

sections.heading: 5. Management by Post-Operative Day Arc
sections.bodyHtml: Table-first structure. POD trajectory replaces Stable/Unstable fork for surgery cards.

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 (ICU)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Extubation, rule out complications, establish anticoag plan, document baseline

Task Action Target
Extubation readiness FiO₂ ≤ 40%, PEEP ≤ 5, adequate spontaneous effort, alert mental status 4–6 h post-op
Bleeding assessment CT output trend; transfuse PRBC if Hgb < 8 (< 9 if CAD/age); check INR + PT/PTT, fibrinogen if heavy drainage (> 200 mL/h) CT < 200 mL/h; Hgb stable
Pacer wire check Capture threshold (should be ≤ 5 mA); sense (should see atrial + ventricular spikes); document in chart Thresholds recorded
Hemodynamics Target SBP 100–140 (avoid excess afterload on new graft), MAP ≥ 70, UOP > 0.5 mL/kg/h Parameters within range
Rhythm baseline 12-lead ECG; document baseline PR interval, QRS duration, AV conduction (looking for LBBB, PR prolongation as baseline post-AVR norms) ECG documented
Labs CBC, BMP, INR (if mechanical), LDH/haptoglobin/retic (mechanical baseline), lactate Labs reviewed, trends noted

sections.heading: 5B. POD 1–3 (ICU → Stepdown Transition)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Wean pressors/inotropes, initiate AC, mobilize, prepare for transfer

Task Action Target
Vasopressor wean Target MAP ≥ 70 off vasopressors or dopamine ≤ 2.5 mcg/kg/min by POD 2 Off high-dose support
Anticoagulation (mechanical valve) POD 1: Heparin bolus 80 U/kg IV, then 18 U/kg/h infusion, target aPTT 50–70 s. POD 2–3: Start warfarin 5–7 mg daily; continue heparin overlap. Check INR daily POD 3+. INR trending toward 2.0 by POD 3–4
Anticoagulation (tissue valve) Start ASA 81 mg daily; warfarin × 3 mo optional per surgeon. No heparin bridge needed. ASA confirmed ordered
Anticoagulation (VSARR) ASA 81 only; no warfarin or heparin. AC documented as ASA-only
Electrolytes K⁺ target ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ target ≥ 2.0 (critical for POAF prevention + refractory hypokalemia). Replace IV if < 3.5 K⁺ or < 1.8 Mg²⁺. K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0
Mobility Out of bed to chair POD 1, walking POD 2–3 with PT Advancing as tolerated
CT management Check drainage q8h (< 150 mL/8 h × 8 h = ready for removal). Notify surgeon before removal. CXR after removal. CTs out or planned POD 2–3
Foley removal Remove POD 1–2 if urine output adequate (> 0.5 mL/kg/h) and patient mobile/oriented enough for bathroom Foley out, voiding spontaneously
Beta-blocker + statin Initiate (metoprolol 25 mg PO BID, atorvastatin 80 mg daily, or equivalent per facility protocol); ACE-I per pre-op regimen Medications restarted
Transfer criteria Hemodynamically stable (off pressors/low-dose), extubated, pacer wires in, CTs out or minimal output, tele-ready, mental status baseline Ready for stepdown

sections.heading: 5C. POD 4–7 (Stepdown / Discharge Planning)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Wean anticoag bridge, prepare DC teaching, remove pacer wires

Task Action Target
INR monitoring (mechanical valve) Check INR q24h; stop heparin when INR > 2.0 × 24 h (typically POD 5–7). Once heparin stopped, continue warfarin indefinitely, INR target 2.0–3.0 (AVR), 2.5–3.5 (MVR). INR therapeutic; heparin weaned
Pacer wire removal POD 4–5 per surgeon preference. Do NOT remove early (block can occur delayed as swelling resolves). Obtain baseline CXR after removal. Wires removed, CXR post-removal
Discharge medications Finalize list: warfarin + ASA (mechanical); ASA only (tissue/VSARR); beta-blocker (HR target 55–70); statin (80 mg high-intensity); ACE-I (cardioprotection); PPI POD 0–2 if high-risk. Taper opioids by POD 10–14. DC med list reviewed with patient
Discharge teaching (1) Anticoagulation: mechanical = lifelong warfarin (INR target, red/blue foods, drug interactions, never skip dose); tissue = ASA only. (2) Endocarditis prophylaxis: lifelong for all prostheses (amoxicillin 2 g × 1 before dental/procedures; print wallet card). (3) Sternal precautions: arm support × 6–8 weeks, no driving × 4–6 weeks, no lifting > 10 lbs × 3 months. (4) Activity: short walks encouraged, sexual activity 4–6 weeks, work depends on job. (5) Follow-up: surgeon 1 week (incision), 4 weeks (full visit), cardiac rehab Phase 2. Teaching documented, patient verbalized understanding
INR check post-DC Schedule INR check 2 days post-discharge (critical for mechanical valve patients); call results to PCP. INR appointment confirmed
Cardiac rehab referral Phase 2, 6–12 weeks starting post-op week 3–4 Referral sent

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR Template for Complications

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure type]." B: "Patient developed [symptom/finding]. [Relevant vitals]. Recent labs: [K⁺, INR, Hgb, Lactate]. On [current meds/support]." A: "[Preliminary assessment: possible complete heart block, POAF, bleeding, tamponade, etc.] Hemodynamic status: [stable/unstable]." R: "Requesting [STAT orders, cardiology consult, OR standby, etc.]."

Who to Call — By Scenario

Situation Contact Urgency
New chest pain, EKG changes, troponin elevation (Bentall: rule out coronary button ischemia) Surgeon + cardiology STAT EMERGENT — prepare OR
Complete heart block, symptomatic bradycardia Surgeon + cardiology STAT EMERGENT
Unstable POAF (hypotension, altered mental status, pulmonary edema) APP/fellow + charge nurse; consider Rapid Response STAT — prepare cardioversion
Pericardial tamponade (acute: hypotension, JVD, low CO; late: insidious SOB + echo effusion) Surgeon STAT (acute); app/fellow (late) EMERGENT (acute); URGENT (late)
Massive bleeding (CT > 500 mL/h, hemodynamic instability) Surgeon STAT + blood bank EMERGENT — prepare re-exploration
New fever POD 3–5 (rule out sternal infection, endocarditis) Primary team; ID consult if culture positive URGENT
New murmur or paravalvular leak Cardiology + echo STAT; surgeon notified URGENT
INR subtherapeutic (< 2.0) on POD 4+ in mechanical valve patient Anticoag team / pharmacy; avoid bridging delays URGENT — thrombosis risk

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections expandable for expert skim.

7.1 — Aortic Valve Anatomy & Physiology (Tricuspid vs. Bicuspid) Normal Aortic Valve (Tricuspid — 80% of population)
  • Three leaflets (right, left, non-coronary) attached at the annulus
  • Each leaflet is flexible, allows 3 cm² opening area when unobstructed
  • Leaflets coapt in diastole, preventing regurgitation
  • Annulus is roughly D-shaped, diameter 20–27 mm
  • Leaflet calcification and degeneration (age) or rheumatic damage cause stenosis ± regurgitation Bicuspid Aortic Valve (10–15% of population; 1–2% symptomatic)
  • Two leaflets (one typically larger than the other) due to embryologic fusion
  • Higher-risk anatomy: undergoes calcification 10–20 years earlier than tricuspid
  • Often associated with ascending aorta dilation (→ concurrent aortic aneurysm repair)
  • Endocarditis risk slightly elevated
  • Bicuspid + root ≥ 5.5 cm warrants elective repair (vs. observation if isolated valve disease) Consequences of Valve Disease on the Left Ventricle
  • Aortic stenosis: High-pressure gradient (AS) forces LV to generate > 140 mmHg systolic to open the valve. Over time, LV wall thickens (hypertrophy), becomes stiff, filling pressures rise, diastolic dysfunction develops. Late (severe, > 5 years untreated): LV dilation, EF drop, HF.
  • Aortic regurgitation: Backflow in diastole overloads the LV with extra volume. LV dilates (eccentric hypertrophy). Acute severe AR (endocarditis, dissection, prosthetic dehiscence) can cause flash pulmonary edema within hours. Why Root Surgery is Different
  • Root pathology (aneurysm, dissection, severe root calcification) requires replacement of not just the valve, but the root structures that hold it
  • Bentall: entire root excised, composite graft inserted; coronary arteries must be meticulously re-implanted as buttons
  • VSARR: preserves native leaflets, remodels root geometry; avoids prosthetic burden
7.2 — Prosthetic Valve Selection by Age & Comorbidity Decision tree: Which prosthesis for which patient?
Patient AgeLife ExpectancyCompliance RiskPreferred ChoiceRationale
< 50 years> 40 yearsGoodMechanical OR VSARRMechanical lasts > 30 years; tissue would require 1–2 re-dos. VSARR (if anatomy suitable) avoids lifelong AC.
50–60 years30+ yearsGoodMechanical (preferred) or VSARRMechanical avoids tissue re-op; VSARR if valve preservation feasible. Borderline tissue viability.
60–70 years20–30 yearsVariableBioprosthetic (preferred) or mechanicalTissue durability adequate; mechanical acceptable if patient reliable on warfarin. Less AC burden with tissue.
≥ 70 years< 20 yearsOften poorBioprosthetic (strongly preferred)Tissue likely lasts lifetime. Warfarin burden + fall risk + drug interactions in elderly → tissue better.
Any age, AF present——Mechanical OR tissue + warfarin × 3–5 yrMechanical: INR target 2–3; tissue: warfarin bridging helpful for AF thromboemboli (not standard now; marginal benefit).
Any age, poor compliance—PoorBioprostheticAvoids warfarin burden; AC non-compliance is lower risk with tissue (thromboembolism ≪ mechanical).
Any age, hypercoagulable state (thrombophilia, cancer, prior thrombosis)——MechanicalHigher thrombotic baseline; mechanical's anticoag more certain.
Ross Procedure (Autograft) — Specialized, Younger Patients
  • Patient's pulmonary valve moved to aortic position; pulmonary position receives cadaveric homograft
  • Advantages: no AC, excellent hemodynamics, native-tissue growth in children
  • Disadvantages: two valves to monitor (aortic autograft + pulmonary homograft), redo surgery inevitable in 20–30 years; technical expertise limited
  • Best for: young patients (< 50) who decline lifelong AC and accept future re-op
7.3 — Root Repair Techniques (Bentall vs. VSARR David vs. Yacoub) Bentall Procedure (Composite Graft) Steps: 1. Aorta cross-clamped; cardioplegia delivered 2. Aortic root excised (annulus included) 3. Composite graft (Dacron tube + mechanical or tissue valve pre-sewn) anastomosed to LV outflow tract 4. Coronary ostia excised as buttons; button technique (L main and RCA buttons sutured into side holes or openings cut into graft), or Cabrol technique (interposition of smaller Dacron side graft from main composite graft) 5. Distal aorta anastomosed to graft 6. Rewarm, de-air, wean CPB Advantages: - Proven long-term durability (> 30 years if mechanical valve chosen)
  • Low rate of structural valve deterioration
  • Good hemodynamic profile (larger opening area than older bioprosthetic roots) Disadvantages:
  • Coronary button kinesis: rare (< 1%) but catastrophic (mortality 20–40%). Button can kink, thrombose, or be dissected intraoperatively.
  • Multiple suture lines → bleeding risk (longest CPB time, highest transfusion rate among AVR variants)
  • No future valve re-ops without re-do root replacement
  • Requires lifelong anticoag if mechanical valve chosen
  • Risk of aortic graft aneurysm (rare, 10–20 year horizon) Post-Op Vigilance:
  • POD 0–2: any chest pain = EKG + troponin + cardiology/surgeon STAT. Do not delay OR if button ischemia suspected.
  • New ST elevation (inferior/anterolateral), troponin rise, hemodynamic collapse = emergent OR for button revision --- VSARR (Valve-Sparing Root Repair) — David Reimplantation Steps: 1. Root transected at sinotubular junction 2. Aortic sinuses excised; native valve leaflets carefully preserved in situ (attached to LV outflow tract) 3. Neo-aortic graft (slightly smaller diameter Dacron tube) anastomosed to LV annulus below the valve 4. Native leaflets suspended inside the graft (sutures reattach the commissures and leaflet attachments to new root geometry) 5. Coronaries left in situ (no reimplantation needed) — graft sewn around them 6. Distal aorta anastomosed to graft Advantages:
  • Native valve preserved: no prosthesis → no lifelong anticoag (unless AF concurrent)
  • Shortest CPB time, shortest recovery (POD 5–6 discharge common)
  • Excellent hemodynamics (native valve geometry maintained)
  • Emotional/psychological benefit for some patients (native valve preserved)
  • Lower endocarditis risk vs. prosthetic Disadvantages:
  • Late aortic regurgitation (10–20% at 10 years) — usually mild, can require redo at 10–15 years
  • Requires native valve anatomy suitable for repair (not if calcified, already regurgitant)
  • Steeper learning curve (less commonly done than Bentall)
  • Requires experienced surgeon (outcomes operator-dependent) Post-Op Vigilance:
  • Echocardiogram at 1 month, 1 year, then every 2 years (watch for AR progression)
  • No anticoagulation; ASA 81 standard
  • Discharge POD 5–6 typical if uncomplicated --- VSARR (Valve-Sparing Root Repair) — Yacoub Remodeling Steps: 1. Root transected at sinotubular junction 2. Partial aortic root preserved (unlike David where entire sinus is excised) 3. Aortic tissue remodeled and sutured back onto neo-aortic graft (leaflets suspended by sutures, not by anatomic attachments) 4. Similar steps for coronary handling and distal anastomosis as David Advantages:
  • Intermediate between Bentall and David in terms of complexity
  • Preserves native valve + residual aortic architecture
  • No anticoag
  • Similar AR risk to David (10–20% late) Disadvantages:
  • Similar operator dependence and learning curve as David
  • Less commonly performed than David
  • Redo rate and indications not as well-established long-term --- Comparison Table: Bentall vs. David vs. Yacoub
    FeatureBentallDavidYacoub
    ValveProsthetic (mech. or tissue)Native preservedNative preserved
    Root reconstructionComplete root excision + composite graftRoot excised, leaflets suspended in graftPartial root preserved, leaflets sutured to graft
    Coronary handlingButton reimplantation (high-skill)In situ (no manipulation)In situ
    CPB time120–180 min (longest)100–140 min100–140 min
    AnticoagulationWarfarin lifelong (if mech.) or ASA (if tissue)ASA 81 only (unless AF)ASA 81 only (unless AF)
    Discharge POD7–95–65–6
    Late AR riskNone (prosthesis)10–20% by 10 yr10–20% by 10 yr
    Redo risk 10–15 yrVery low5–15% (AR progression)5–15% (AR progression)
    Endocarditis riskLow (prosthetic frame)Very low (native)Very low (native)
    Surgeon availabilityWidely doneIncreasingly commonLess common
7.4 — Conduction Disturbances Post-AVR (LBBB, Complete Heart Block) Why AV Block Happens The AV node sits millimeters from the aortic annulus. During AVR (especially Bentall), the node is at risk from:
  • Dissection during root excision
  • Edema from surgical trauma (peaks POD 2–3 as inflammation swells surrounding tissues)
  • Ischemia if nodal blood supply disrupted (rare) Risk factors for higher incidence (5–8% needing PPM):
  • Bentall > isolated AVR
  • Endocarditis with abscess formation
  • Re-do operations (scar tissue)
  • Calcified annulus (need aggressive debridement) LBBB (Left Bundle Branch Block) — Common, Often Benign Post-AVR, 10–15% of patients develop new LBBB on the ECG (wide QRS 120–150 ms, broad notched R in V1–V2, broad notched S in I/aVL/V6). Why: Sutures or retraction can nick the left bundle at the junction of the membranous septum and aortic root. Clinical significance:
  • Usually benign — patient has underlying LBBB, monitor normally, no pacing needed
  • Exception: if LBBB + PR prolongation OR if LBBB + symptomatic bradycardia (widened QRS + slow rate = possible bifascicular block evolving to complete block) Nursing vigilance: Document LBBB on POD 0 ECG. If NEW LBBB + symptomatic bradycardia or PR ≥ 200 ms, notify team (possible risk for progression to complete block). --- Complete Heart Block (CHB) — Rare, Requires Intervention Definition: Loss of AV conduction; atria and ventricles beat independently. Atrial rate 60–100, ventricular escape rate 20–40 (unreliable, can arrest). Recognition:
  • HR < 40, regular escape rhythm (wide QRS ≥ 120 ms if ventricular escape)
  • No relationship between P waves and QRS (marching through independently)
  • Symptoms: syncope, presyncope, lightheadedness, low output Timeline:
  • Immediate CHB (POD 0): often recovers within hours as anesthesia wears off; monitor closely
  • Delayed CHB (POD 2–5): occurs as surgical edema peaks then resolves; can resolve spontaneously or persist Management: 1. Pacer wire threshold check: Can the wire capture the ventricle? If yes and HR > 40 + adequate perfusion, may observe 2. Symptomatic OR HR < 40 + low output: Pace (external pacing pads if available; epicardial wire pacing if thresholds good) 3. Persistent beyond POD 3–5: Discuss PPM with surgeon/cardiology. Most resolve; 5–8% need permanent PPM. 4. Do NOT remove pacer wires early: Block can occur POD 2–5. Wires are the safeguard. Why delayed recovery is possible:
  • Edema is maximum POD 2–3; as swelling resolves, node function may recover
  • Inflammation + ischemia gradually improve
  • Steroids (if given) may hasten recovery --- Monitoring & Documentation POD 0–1: Pacer Wire Threshold Check
    • Stimulator dial turned to 10 mA
    • Turn down slowly until capture is lost
    • Threshold = lowest mA at which you see a QRS (wide, captured beat) after the pacing spike
    • Normal threshold: ≤ 5 mA (lower is better; margin of safety)
    • Elevated threshold (7–10 mA): concerning for wire malposition or edema around tip Sense Check
    • Look at monitor: do you see a small atrial spike, then a larger ventricular spike, with each beat?
    • If native rhythm present, pacing sense should "inhibit" — sensing the patient's own beat suppresses the pacing spike
    • Absence of sense = wire not detecting patient's intrinsic rhythm Chart Documentation
    • "Pacer wires: atrial and ventricular thresholds [X] mA, sense [X] mV, capture present at [X] mA, no ectopy with wire manipulation."
    • Re-check POD 2–3 if any rhythm change, bradycardia, or provider concern
7.5 — Anticoagulation Strategy: Mechanical vs. Tissue vs. VSARR Mechanical Valve Anticoagulation — Mandatory Warfarin Why warfarin? - Mechanical valve surface is thrombogenic (carbon/plastic generates coagulation cascade)
  • Uncoagulated patients: thrombosis rate 4–5% per patient-year (catastrophic)
  • Warfarin reduces to 0.6–1.0% per patient-year when INR therapeutic Heparin Bridge Protocol (POD 1–7)
  • POD 1: Bolus heparin 80 U/kg IV (typically 5,000–7,000 U), then continuous infusion 18 U/kg/h (typically 1,000–1,500 U/h)
  • Target aPTT 50–70 seconds (adjust heparin dose per nomogram)
  • Goal: bridge until warfarin effect (INR therapeutic takes 3–5 days) Warfarin Initiation (POD 2–3)
  • Start 5–7 mg daily PO
  • Check INR daily (or q12h) POD 3+
  • Do NOT stop heparin until INR > 2.0 confirmed × 24 h on repeat check (ensure stability)
  • Stop heparin when INR therapeutic × 24 h (usually POD 5–7) Long-Term Target INR
  • AVR (aortic valve): INR 2.0–3.0 (risk-benefit optimal in aortic position; lower target because aortic flow is high, lower thrombotic risk than mitral)
  • MVR (mitral valve): INR 2.5–3.5 (higher target because mitral has lower flow and higher thrombotic risk; tradeoff with bleeding) Maintenance
  • INR check 2 days post-discharge
  • Then INR check schedule: weekly × 2 weeks, monthly thereafter once stable
  • Patient education: never skip warfarin, avoid NSAIDs/antibiotics that interact (increase INR), avoid excessive green vegetables (vitamin K decreases INR) --- Tissue Valve Anticoagulation — ASA Only (Standard) Why no AC?
  • Tissue surface (porcine/bovine pericardium, homograft) less thrombogenic than mechanical
  • Thromboembolic risk: ~1–2% per patient-year without AC; risk in sinus rhythm even lower
  • Benefit of warfarin small, does not justify warfarin burden in tissue patients Standard Regimen
  • ASA 81 mg daily indefinitely
  • No warfarin (unless patient has concurrent AF, then warfarin × 3–6 months considered, but now evidence marginal) Optional Warfarin Bridge
  • Some surgeons give warfarin × 3 months post-op (controversial, meta-analyses show small benefit for thromboemboli reduction)
  • Not standard; discuss with surgeon
  • If given, then stop after 3 months, continue ASA only Long-Term
  • ASA 81 daily, indefinite
  • Annual echo to watch for degeneration (calcification, tear)
  • Redo surgery planned at 10–15 years (tissue durability finite) --- VSARR Anticoagulation — ASA 81 Only (Unless AF Concurrent) Why no AC?
  • Native valve preserved; not a foreign surface
  • Thromboembolic risk: < 1% per patient-year (same as population baseline)
  • No anticoagulation indicated Standard Regimen
  • ASA 81 daily indefinitely
  • No warfarin, no heparin bridge
  • Unless AF develops (concurrent diagnosis): then warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 (or DOAC if AF-specific) Follow-Up
  • Echo 1 month post-op, 1 year, then every 2 years (monitor for AR progression)
  • If late AR develops, may require redo VSARR or conversion to Bentall --- Critical Teaching Points — All Prosthesis Types
    PointWhy It Matters
    Mechanical valve: warfarin LIFELONGEven brief gaps (3–5 days) risk catastrophic thrombosis. Patient must understand: no self-stopping for procedures without surgeon approval. Bridging with heparin (SQ or IV) required.
    Mechanical valve: INR 2.0–3.0 (AVR); 2.5–3.5 (MVR)INR < 2.0: thrombosis risk; INR > 4.0: bleeding risk. Patient must know target and what it means ("your blood test needs to be in the 2–3 range").
    Mechanical valve patient: NSAIDs are contraindicatedNSAIDs displace warfarin from protein binding, raising INR suddenly. Use acetaminophen instead.
    Tissue valve: no warfarin neededPatient relief, but must understand: "You take aspirin only, no blood thinner." Many patients assume all heart surgery = lifelong warfarin; correct this misconception.
    VSARR: no anticoagulation unless AF developsTeaches valve-sparing benefit. If patient develops AF later, explain warfarin added for AF, not for valve.
    Endocarditis prophylaxis is LIFELONGAll prosthetic valves (even tissue) need antibiotic before dental/procedures. Common misconception: "stops after 3 months." False. Lifelong. Print wallet card.
7.6 — Post-AVR Conduction Complications (Special Focus: TAVR vs. SAVR) Why Post-AVR Heart Block Occurs at Different Rates Surgical AVR (SAVR) - Requires median sternotomy, aortic root exposure - Annulus manipulation is necessary - AV node injury rate: 1–3% complete block (< 1% need PPM long-term)
  • Usually recovers within 48–72 h as edema resolves Transcatheter AVR (TAVR)
  • Femoral access, balloon-expansion or self-expanding prosthesis lodged in native valve annulus
  • Device pushes native leaflets/calcification toward AV node
  • Complete block incidence: 5–10% (higher than SAVR!)
  • Permanent PPM needed: 3–7% of TAVR patients (vs. < 1% SAVR)
  • Why higher? Balloon dilation or self-expanding frame can directly trauma the node; less reversible than surgical manipulation Clinical Pearl: TAVR patients have higher AV block risk and longer need for pacing wires/monitoring. If TAVR patient arrives on the unit, anticipate pacing wire surveillance through POD 5–7.
7.7 — AVR + CABG Combined Surgery When AVR Meets CAD ~30–40% of AVR patients have concurrent CAD (angiography-proven). If flow-limiting (≥ 70% stenosis), CABG is performed at the time of AVR. Operative Impact - CPB time extended (additional grafts = longer pump time)
  • Myocardial protection more complex (cardioplegia delivery to native coronaries + grafted vessels)
  • More suture lines = higher bleeding risk
  • LV dysfunction post-op more likely (if LIMA graft to LAD, better outcomes; saphenous grafts higher graft failure) Post-Op Considerations
  • Watch for graft occlusion (chest pain, ST changes POD 1–3)
  • Antiplatelet strategy: ASA 81 + clopidogrel (Plavix) 75 mg daily (dual antiplatelet therapy, DAPT) if grafted
  • Warfarin timing if mechanical AVR + CABG: Heparin bridge standard (as above), but DAPT must not overlap with high-dose warfarin (bleeding risk). Coordinate with surgeon/cardiologist.
  • Longer recovery (POD 8–10 discharge typical vs. POD 5–7 AVR alone)
7.8 — Bicuspid Aortic Valve with Ascending Aorta — Combined Management The Bicuspid Paradox: Valve + Root Disease Often Co-occur 15–30% of bicuspid AV patients have concurrent ascending aorta dilation or aneurysm (compared to 2–3% tricuspid AV). Anatomic Reason - Bicuspid leaflets have abnormal hemodynamics (eccentric jets)
  • Eccentric flow patterns stress the aortic wall
  • Cystic medial necrosis (genetic predisposition in bicuspid disease) weakens aorta Surgical Strategy
  • If aortic root ≥ 5.0 cm (bicuspid) or ≥ 5.5 cm (tricuspid): concurrent aortic root repair (usually Bentall or VSARR)
  • If ascending aorta ≥ 5.5 cm: composite graft replacement of aorta + valve
  • If aortic root 4.5–5.0 cm + bicuspid: may observe, but careful monitoring; repeat imaging q1–2 years Post-Op Surveillance
  • Echo 1 month, 1 year, then every 2 years (watch for graft aneurysm, valve function)
  • Patient education: "Your bicuspid valve + your aorta were both fixed at surgery. Your aorta no longer has dissection/rupture risk."

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear in a stable patient, re-escalate.

  • New chest pain POD 0–2 (Bentall): button ischemia until proven otherwise → STAT EKG + troponin + OR standby
  • Widening QRS or PR prolongation trending on serial ECGs: evolving conduction abnormality; bifascicular block → complete block possible next
  • Sudden bradycardia (HR < 40) without prior LBBB: complete block developing → pacing wire threshold check STAT
  • Rising lactate + falling urine output + cool extremities: low cardiac output despite stable BP → possible valve malfunction, tamponade, or sepsis
  • New diastolic murmur (early diastolic) POD 1–3: paravalvular leak until proven otherwise → echo STAT, hemolysis labs
  • Hgb dropping > 3 g/dL in 4 h + ongoing tachycardia: occult bleeding (mediastinal or pleural) → check CT output, prepare for OR
  • Fever POD 3–5 + elevated WBC/CRP: sternal infection vs. post-op inflammation → wound exam, culture, CT chest if DSWI suspected
  • New irregular rhythm (POAF) + rapid rate (HR > 130): rate-control failure; risk of hemodynamic decompensation → escalate AC plan
  • INR < 2.0 on POD 4–5 (mechanical valve): subtherapeutic anticoagulation; thrombosis risk rising → notify anticoag team, consider heparin dose escalation
  • Persistent oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) despite adequate IV fluids: AKI or low output → lactate, Cr, CVP, consider echo
  • New stroke symptoms (weakness, speech change, facial droop): aortic atheroma mobilization, prosthetic thromboembolism, or AFib → stroke code STAT
  • Confusion + restlessness POD 2–3 (hyperactive delirium): post-op inflammation + pain/constipation/hypoxia → optimize all reversibles; low-dose haloperidol PRN
  • Wires and lines: pacer wire threshold rising (> 10 mA) → possible wire malposition; CT air leak → pleural fistula; PICC redness → possible CLABSI

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. AV node is millimeters from annulus — heart block is real (5–8% need PPM). Pacer wires NOT optional; keep in place through POD 4–5. Do NOT let surgeons pull early. LBBB common post-AVR (usually benign); don't confuse with complete block. New LBBB + PR prolongation or symptomatic bradycardia = possible risk for progression.

  2. Warfarin bridge = thrombosis OR bleeding setup. Get INR POD 2 STAT if mechanical valve. Can't manage heparin safely without INR trajectory. Warfarin takes 3–5 days to work; bridging with heparin is the answer. Don't stop heparin until INR > 2.0 × 24 h confirmed on repeat.

  3. Mechanical valve requires WARFARIN, never DOAC. DOACs are not studied extensively in mechanical prosthetic valves; outcomes inferior. Warfarin is the gold standard, lifelong, no exceptions. Patient must understand: never substitute DOAC without cardiology approval (almost always disapprove).

  4. New murmur post-AVR = paravalvular leak until proven otherwise. Echo STAT. Obtain hemolysis labs (LDH, haptoglobin, schistocytes). New diastolic murmur especially concerning (aortic regurgitation outside prosthesis). Small leaks may stabilize as swelling resolves; large + symptomatic = urgent redo.

  5. Coronary button ischemia is rare, highest-mortality event in Bentall. Mortality 20–40% even with emergent OR. Any Bentall patient with new chest pain POD 0–2 or inferior ST changes = STAT EKG + troponin + surgeon notification. Don't delay; go straight to OR if button ischemia suspected.

  6. Mechanical valve hemolysis baseline (POD 0). Obtain LDH, haptoglobin, retic, smear. Repeat if LDH rises or haptoglobin drops (possible leak or dysfunction). Hemolysis labs are THE early warning system for prosthetic malfunction.

  7. Endocarditis prophylaxis is lifelong — teach it hard at discharge. All prosthetic valves (tissue, mechanical, VSARR) need amoxicillin 2 g × 1 before dental cleaning, extractions, implants, root canals. Patients assume they stop "after 3 months" — incorrect. Print wallet card, call dentist/PCP to reinforce.

  8. Patients stop warfarin at home for dental without surgeon approval — catastrophic. Discharge teaching must be explicit: "Call your surgeon BEFORE any dental work. Do not stop warfarin on your own." PCP education equally critical (coordinate with surgeon's office).

  9. INR check 2 days post-discharge is critical for mechanical valve patients. Schedule before discharge; call patient POD 2 to confirm appointment. If missed, mechanical valve patient undertreated and at thrombosis risk. This is a "never miss" item.

  10. New fever POD 30–180 in prosthetic valve patient = blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics. Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) is deadly; empiric antibiotic without cultures kills the diagnostic test. Draw 3 separate blood cultures, then start vancomycin + gentamicin.

  11. Stroke risk real — aortic manipulation (atheroma), mechanical valve thromboembolism, AFib stack. New neuro deficit = STAT neurology + CT head (rule out hemorrhage) + stroke protocol. Mechanical valve patients need tighter INR control (2–3 AVR, 2.5–3.5 MVR) to balance thrombosis vs. bleeding.

  12. Mechanical valve click is normal; tissue is silent. Reassure patients: "Click is normal sound of the valve. No click = problem." Tissue valve is silent — patients expecting "the sound" get anxious.

  13. TAVR vs. SAVR post-op protocols differ. TAVR: higher AV block risk (5–10%), longer pacing wire monitoring (POD 5–7+). Don't use SAVR expectations for TAVR; clarify which procedure at admission.

  14. Refractory hypokalemia = check magnesium. Hypomagnesemia (Mg²⁺ < 1.8) makes K⁺ replacement refractory and drives POAF. Replace Mg²⁺ concurrently; target Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0.

  15. Bioprosthetic durability: 3-month ASA only is standard now. Old teaching: warfarin × 3 months post-tissue AVR. Current evidence (2020–2023 guidelines): ASA 81 indefinitely is now standard, no warfarin bridge. Warfarin × 3 months optional per surgeon (marginal benefit). Simplifies discharge teaching: "Just aspirin, no blood thinner."

cards.title: Emergent Bedside Sternotomy (Tamponade / Massive Bleeding)
cards.quickAnswer: Post-operative cardiac surgery patient with acute hemodynamic collapse, PEA/asystole arrest, or massive chest tube bleeding → STAT page CT surgery attending + activate Open Chest Code. Prepare emergency resternotomy at bedside: within 5 minutes of arrest onset if possible. Do NOT perform standard external chest compressions (risk of graft injury or tamponade rupture); delay compressions 1–2 min to allow team assembly for internal cardiac massage. Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol. Bring sterile resternotomy tray, bovie, suction, retractor to bedside. Expectation: once stabilized, rapid transfer to OR for definitive repair. Mortality 40–60%; intensive post-event team debrief and EAP referral essential.
