sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition and who this applies to.

  • Definition: Emergency re-opening of the sternum at the bedside (rather than in the operating room) in response to acute cardiac arrest, tamponade, or exsanguinating hemorrhage immediately post-cardiac surgery.
  • Timing: Can occur any time post-op but highest risk POD 0–3. Rare but highly morbid in step-down units.
  • Indications: (1) Post-cardiac-surgery cardiac arrest (PEA/asystole) with suspected tamponade or bleeding; (2) acute tamponade with incipient or frank arrest; (3) exsanguinating hemorrhage not controlled by ongoing resuscitation.
  • Who this applies to: all nurses caring for post-cardiac-surgery patients (ICU, step-down, telemetry). Although rare in step-down, trajectory awareness is essential — a POD 2–5 patient may transfer to step-down and then decompensate.
  • Why it matters: Bedside resternotomy is the definitive resuscitation for post-cardiotomy arrest; delays in decision-making or team assembly sharply increase mortality. Estimated incidence: 0.5–2% of cardiac surgery patients (varies by surgical complexity, anticoagulation, re-do status).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Post-cardiac surgery, the sternum is wired closed but the pericardium is partially left open to allow bleeding and fluid drainage. Two distinct emergencies converge here:

sections.heading: Tamponade physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Blood (or clot) accumulates in the pericardial space, raising intrapericardial pressure. When intrapericardial pressure exceeds the diastolic filling pressure of the right atrium or right ventricle, venous return is impaired → cardiac output falls → shock → PEA (Bojar, 2020). Classic trigger: chest tubes clot off (appearance of drainage stops, blood accumulates under tension). This is different from "bleeding has slowed" — the distinction determines outcomes.

Post-op tamponade risk factors:

  • Active surgical bleeding not controlled intra-op
  • Anticoagulation resumption (warfarin, DOAC, heparin bridge) early post-op
  • Redo sternotomy with adhesions
  • Chest tube occlusion (patient roll, heparin-coated tube interaction, clot)

sections.heading: Exsanguinating hemorrhage physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Massive bleeding from an anastomosis, suture line, or vessel injury. Blood loss exceeds resuscitation capacity. Typical triggers: CABG graft disruption, valve prosthesis dehiscence, aortic suture line bleed, ITA-to-vessel injury. The volume of bleeding is the problem; external ACLS cannot provide adequate cardiac output when ~50% of blood volume is lost into the mediastinum (Bojar, 2020).

Post-op bleeding thresholds that drive return to OR (Bojar, 2020):

  • > 400 mL/hr sustained × 1 hour
  • > 300 mL/hr × 2–3 hours
  • > 200 mL/hr × 4 hours
  • Acute surge (e.g., 500 mL in 15 minutes)

sections.heading: Why external CPR is contraindicated early (and why 5 minutes matters)
sections.bodyHtml:
External chest compressions over a fresh sternotomy:

  • Disrupt sternal closure → wound dehiscence, infection
  • Damage internal mammary artery to LAD graft (present in ~85% of CABG)
  • Lacerate prosthetic valves or valve repairs
  • Cause cardiac laceration if sternal wires are displaced inward

Most post-cardiotomy arrest protocols delay external compressions for 1–2 minutes while the team assembles for emergency resternotomy. If the sternum can be opened within 5 minutes, internal cardiac massage is used instead. If resternotomy will take > 5 minutes, external compressions are started — tissue injury is preferable to prolonged cardiac arrest (Dunning et al., 2009).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — clinical picture at bedside.

sections.heading: Trigger A — Tamponade with incipient cardiac arrest
sections.bodyHtml:
• Sudden drop in BP with narrowing pulse pressure over minutes
  • Rising CVP (if available), tachycardia, oliguric urine output in the preceding 5–15 minutes
  • Sudden drop or cessation of chest tube output — this is the red flag. Clot occlusion means blood is accumulating in the pericardium, not draining.
  • Muffled heart sounds, JVD, pulsus paradoxus on physical exam
  • Mental status change or syncope
  • Echocardiogram (if time allows): pericardial fluid with RA/RV diastolic collapse
  • Progression to PEA if untreated within 2–5 minutes

sections.heading: Trigger B — Exsanguinating hemorrhage
sections.bodyHtml:
• Acute surge in chest tube output (> 400 mL/hr sustained, or sudden gush of 500+ mL)
  • Dropping hemoglobin (sometimes visible as darkening of tube drainage)
  • Hypotension, tachycardia, pale diaphoretic appearance
  • Anxiety, air hunger, mental status change from hypoperfusion
  • Mediastinal widening on CXR if imaging obtained in time (rarely done — team moves faster than imaging)

sections.heading: Context clue
sections.bodyHtml: The timing from surgery matters. Tamponade is more common POD 1–5 (delayed anticoagulation effect), whereas massive bleeding can occur POD 0 immediately. A patient at POD 5 on step-down with "fever and not feeling right" for 2 days, now acutely hypotensive — think delayed tamponade.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* *(2 minutes, concurrent with team call)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside information-gathering. While others are calling.

  • Vital signs trend: last BP, HR, SpO₂, CVP (if line present); trajectory over last 15 minutes
  • Chest tube character and output: current total, last 1–2 hour volumes, appearance (bright red, clots, none)
  • Mental status and perfusion: eyes open, responsive to command? Skin temperature, capillary refill, color
  • Recent labs on chart: hemoglobin, platelet count, INR/PTT, fibrinogen, lactate, pH, base deficit
  • Anticoagulation status: heparin running? Recent ASA/Plavix dose? Warfarin or DOAC restarted? Last dose and timing
  • Lines: patent IV access (minimum 2 × 18g), arterial line in place? Central line? Pacer wires present?
  • Blood product availability: uncrossmatched O-negative available? Recent T&S current? Blood bank aware?
  • Surgery context: POD (hours or days), which procedure (CABG, valve, aortic, combo), any intra-op complications?
  • Resuscitation readiness: crash cart in room? Defibrillator paddles at bedside? Code medications drawn?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Suspected surgical cause — rising CVP, declining output, borderline BP, but patient still conscious and perfusing.)

  1. STAT page CT surgery attending — use direct pager + operator backup; do NOT rely on single message
  2. Notify charge RN and request rapid response team to standby
  3. Prepare for potential OR transfer: call OR charge, alert anesthesia, bring patient to center of bed, position for access
  4. Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol per [Institution policy] — blood bank begins pooling products
  5. Obtain STAT labs: CBC, coagulation panel, fibrinogen, ABG, lactate, type & crossmatch (6-unit minimum)
  6. Replace electrolytes: K⁺ target ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 (required before any defibrillation)
  7. Support hemodynamics: fluid bolus if hypovolemic (but cautious if tamponade suspected — fluids buy time only), consider low-dose pressors (norepinephrine 0.02–0.05 mcg/kg/min) to bridge to OR
  8. Continuous monitoring: tele, A-line if available
  9. STAT CT exam or bedside echo if available without delaying OR prep — pericardial fluid confirms tamponade; do NOT delay surgery for imaging
  10. Prepare for transport: at least 2 nurses, anesthesia, CT surgeon, full resuscitation supplies; keep patient on monitor during transfer

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path — acute collapse or cardiac arrest
sections.bodyHtml:
(PEA/asystole, acute shock, loss of consciousness.)

Immediate (first 30 seconds):

  1. STAT page CT surgery attending + activate Open Chest Code per [Institution policy] — use overhead + direct pager; do NOT leave patient alone to call
  2. Activate Rapid Response Team / Code Blue — this triggers anesthesia, additional nursing, emergency resternotomy cart delivery
  3. Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol — verbally to blood bank; no delay for orders
  4. Position patient: supine, flat, head of bed down. Move to center of bed if possible — surgeon needs access from both sides
  5. Pads on chest in ACLS position — do NOT begin external compressions yet (see CPR caveat below)
  6. Ensure patent large-bore IV × 2 (minimum 18g). If only central line, alert team to peripheral access
  7. Clear the room of non-essential personnel; designate roles (procedural RN, circulating RN, charge RN, anesthesia, respiratory)

Next 2–3 minutes (while team assembles):

  1. Anesthesia to bedside for airway management (intubate if needed) and sedation/paralysis during procedure
  2. Draw STAT labs if not already done: CBC, coags, fibrinogen, ABG, lactate, type & crossmatch
  3. Prepare emergency resternotomy cart at bedside: sterile supplies organized, wire cutter accessible, bovie tested, suction set up
  4. Document time of decompensation, time of each call, and anticipated time of surgeon arrival — time is prognostic

CPR caveat (critical): Do NOT perform standard external chest compressions in the first 1–2 minutes post-cardiac-arrest in a post-cardiotomy patient. External compressions risk graft disruption, valve injury, and cardiac laceration.

Delay external compressions for 1–2 minutes to allow resternotomy preparation. If the surgeon will clearly not arrive within 5 minutes, external compressions begin — inadequate circulation is worse than graft injury. Internal cardiac massage is the goal; external compressions are backup.

If cardiac arrest occurs and resternotomy will not be possible (e.g., surgeon unavailable, patient outside ICU and no resternotomy protocol): external ACLS begins at 2 minutes with recognition that graft injury is a risk.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template (make this call STAT with high acuity tone):

S: "Dr. [CT surgeon name], this is [RN name] on the ICU / unit. I have a STAT situation. [Patient name], [room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]. Patient is [in arrest / acutely unstable]." B: "Patient developed [sudden hypotension / cessation of CT output / massive CT bleeding / altered mental status] at [time]. BP [current], HR [current], SpO₂ [current]. CT output [amount and character]. [Key recent lab value]. Anticoagulation status: [heparin / warfarin / DOAC / none]." A: "Patient is [PEA / asystole / shocked / tamponade physiology]. I am activating Open Chest Code and Massive Transfusion Protocol now." R: "Need you and the emergency resternotomy cart to [location] STAT. Anesthesia and RRT are en route."

Who to call — simultaneous, NOT sequential

Resource Mechanism Contact Person / Info
CT surgery attending + fellow Direct pager STAT + operator backup Primary surgical team — do NOT wait for callback
Rapid Response Team / Code Blue Hospital emergency code line Activates anesthesia, additional RN, respiratory
Anesthesia STAT page / bedside if in hospital Airway + sedation + hemodynamic support
Blood bank Direct call — MTP activation verbal Massive Transfusion Protocol setup; release O-neg products
OR charge RN [Institution OR line] Notify of incoming urgent transfer; hold room if possible
Charge RN (your unit) In-unit or overhead Coordinate logistics, family notification, additional staffing
Chaplaincy / Social Work Non-emergent page (after stabilization if needed) Family support and presence
Unit manager / supervisor Non-emergent (post-event) Critical incident coordination

sections.heading: 7. Procedural Detail — Bedside Resternotomy Steps
sections.bodyHtml: Detailed walkthrough for nurses participating in the procedure. All personnel should know what to expect.

sections.heading: 7.1 Emergency resternotomy cart contents
sections.bodyHtml:
Mandatory (must be checked per shift per [Institution policy]):

  • Sterile gowns, gloves, masks, protective eyewear (goggles or face shield) for surgeon, assistant, scrub nurse
  • Large prep solution (chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine in sterile container)
  • Full thoracic sterile drape (or 4 large sterile towels + surgical drape)
  • Wire cutter — cannot open sternum without this; verify before code
  • Heavy needle holder (alternative if wire cutter unavailable)
  • Scalpel with #10 blade
  • Sternal retractor (one-piece, self-retaining if available)
  • Suction setup × 2 (wall suction + Yankauer with sterile tubing)
  • Sterile normal saline (several liters, warm preferred)
  • Sterile gauze, lap sponges, packing material
  • Vascular clamps (small and large)
  • Electrocautery (bovie) with sterile paddles, tested pre-shift
  • Sutures (large: 0 or 1 silk or prolene for bleeding control)
  • Internal defibrillator paddles (if available; check battery)
  • Irrigation solution with antibiotic (per surgeon preference)

Space and staffing prep:

  • Bed positioned in center of room; all 4 sides accessible
  • Overhead lighting maximized; portable OR light if available
  • Clear path to door for rapid transport to OR
  • Personnel roles assigned before surgeon gowns:
  • Surgeon (scrub): opening sternum, identifying bleeding source, internal massage if needed
  • Nurse 1 (scrub nurse): opening supplies in sequence, passing instruments, managing sterile field
  • Nurse 2 (circulating): running the code — time stamps, medication administration, blood product coordination, family updates
  • Charge RN: logistics, staffing, OR readiness, family coordination
  • Anesthesia: airway, sedation (etomidate + rocuronium if RSI needed), hemodynamics
  • Respiratory: ventilator management, supplemental O₂ titration

sections.heading: 7.2 Procedure walkthrough
sections.bodyHtml:
The surgeon performs:

  1. Skin prep with chlorhexidine or iodine (wide field from neck to lower abdomen)
  2. Incision over the sternal wires using scalpel
  3. Wire cutting with dedicated cutter (or suture scissors if sutures used) — must clear all wires
  4. Sternal separation using one-piece retractor — chest opens
  5. Pericardium inspection — if tamponade, may see clot or blood under tension
  6. Pericardiotomy if needed for decompression
  7. Clot evacuation with suction (careful not to dislodge a thrombus that's tamponading)
  8. Bleeding source identified — manual pressure with finger or 4×4 sponge first
  9. Volume resuscitation via existing IV lines (should be running wide open)
  10. Internal cardiac massage if asystole/PEA: two-handed technique, hand behind the heart, gentle compression between palms (not aggressive squeezing like external CPR)
  11. If VF/pulseless VT: internal defibrillator paddles applied directly to heart, low energy (5–10 J biphasic internal, much lower than external)
  12. Once bleeding controlled or source identified, patient moves to OR for definitive repair

Scrub nurse role:

  • Opens supplies in sequence as requested: drapes first → retractor → wire cutter → instruments → suction → gauze
  • Pour prep solution into sterile basin
  • Pass instruments as surgeon calls for them
  • Maintain sterile field integrity (challenging in emergent setting — expect some non-sterile touches and move on)
  • Suction management: clear field of blood for visibility
  • Retraction assistance if asked (hold organ retractor or chest retractor)

Circulating nurse role:

  • Time-stamp every event: decompensation onset, call placed, surgeon arrived, chest opened, perfusion restored, meds given, transport initiated
  • Push medications as ordered by surgeon/anesthesia
  • Coordinate blood product delivery (should be arriving continuously during MTP)
  • Update OR on status and estimated transport time
  • Family communication: if family is present or nearby, brief updates via charge RN or social work (bedside nurse stays with patient)
  • Monitor patient response: return of pulse, BP trend, pupil reactivity, color

sections.heading: 7.3 Post-procedure (if stabilized)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Do NOT close the chest at the bedside. Sternum remains open.
  • Cover the open wound with sterile drape or Ioban (plastic barrier) for transport
  • Anesthesia, CT surgeon, and at least 1 nurse accompany to OR
  • Continue resuscitation during transport: running IV lines, blood products, medications, monitor attached
  • Notify OR, anesthesia, perfusion, and blood bank of imminent arrival

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable post-op patient
sections.bodyHtml: Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch-fors that predict the crash is coming; distinct from Section 5B unstable criteria.

sections.heading: Pre-tamponade warning signs
sections.bodyHtml:
• Trending drop in chest tube output (not zero, but progressively less over 2–4 hours) paired with rising CVP or rising cardiac chamber pressures on echo
  • Clots visible in chest tube tubing with concurrent HR trend up, CVP creeping up, urine output falling — the constellation matters
  • Patient becoming increasingly anxious, dyspneic, diaphoretic without other explanation (pain, fever, hypoxia ruled out)
  • New pulsus paradoxus on arterial line (BP systolic variation > 10 mmHg with respiration)
  • "Subtle" delayed tamponade on POD 3–7: patient reports "I don't feel right," creatinine trending up, HR up 10–15 bpm, UOP falling, patient quiet and withdrawn (not talkative) — this is the classic delayed tamponade presentation that gets missed. Escalate.

sections.heading: Pre-massive-bleeding warning signs
sections.bodyHtml:
• Chest tube output trending upward over several hours, not yet at threshold but on a clear trajectory
  • Uncontrolled hypertension without explanation (more bleeding under pressure)
  • Patient on anticoagulation bridge or recent heparin + platelet count dropping
  • New oozing from multiple sites: central line, incision, IV sites, foley — suggests coagulopathy rather than single surgical bleeder
  • Hemoglobin dropping faster than expected with no clear cause (no recent draws, no fluid resuscitation explanation)

sections.heading: Unit-level context (step-down specific)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Patient recently transferred from ICU with stable-seeming hemodynamics
  • Pacer wires recently removed with heparin on board
  • Anticoagulation resumption (warfarin or DOAC restarted) within last 24 hours
  • Known difficult re-do sternotomy with adhesions mentioned in operative note
  • Prior re-exploration for bleeding this admission — higher recurrence risk

If any of these appear or worsen: escalate early to CT surgery + APP. Obtain stat CBC and coagulation panel. Ensure T&C is current. Confirm emergency resternotomy equipment is operational on your unit. Do NOT wait for a code to activate thinking.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. The decision window is 5 minutes. From arrest to sternum open. Bojar and EACTS/STS guidelines emphasize that if resternotomy will take > 5 minutes, outcome is substantially worse. The first call you make (to CT surgery) is the most time-critical.
  2. Clotted chest tubes are the cardinal trap. "Output has slowed" can mean (a) bleeding has genuinely stopped, or (b) tubes are clotted and blood is pooling in the pericardium under tension. If output stops ABRUPTLY and the patient deteriorates, assume clotted tubes until proven otherwise. Do NOT gently strip tubes hoping to fix it; escalate.
  3. Don't aggressively milk or strip chest tubes. This practice has been associated with parenchymal lung injury and is not standard post-cardiac surgery. Gentle milking once per shift toward the collection chamber only. Major output changes = escalation, not tube manipulation.
  4. "Open chest code" is a defined institutional code, not a free-form activation. Know EXACTLY what it triggers at your institution — differs from generic code blue. It should summon CT surgery, anesthesia, and the resternotomy cart automatically.
  5. CT surgery attending is the most important phone call. RRT handles logistics; only CT surgery can authorize and perform resternotomy. Calls happen in parallel, but if you had to prioritize, it's the surgeon.
  6. Massive Transfusion Protocol activation is a NURSING call. You do NOT need a physician order to activate MTP if you meet criteria (major ongoing hemorrhage, shock, suspected tamponade). Know the criteria and activation number at your institution. Call blood bank directly; do NOT wait for orders.
  7. External CPR may be harmful in the first minutes post-cardiotomy. This is opposite of standard ACLS teaching. A post-op cardiac arrest is NOT a medical arrest — graft injury and valve damage are real risks. Most protocols delay external compressions 1–2 minutes to allow resternotomy prep. This is hard to teach to new staff accustomed to "start CPR immediately" — discuss it in advance, clarify your institutional protocol, and role-play.
  8. Family notification during the event is the charge RN's job, NOT the bedside nurse. Don't add it to your cognitive load mid-crisis. But advocate for it to happen — "Come to hospital immediately" messaging sets expectations.
  9. Transport to OR before stabilization is a common error. Bojar emphasizes: resuscitate first, transport second. A patient who arrests in the elevator does worse than one who is stabilized first. Wait for return of perfusion or at least organized electrical activity before moving.
  10. Anesthesia may need to intubate at the bedside if the patient is already extubated. Have airway equipment staged before anesthesia arrives — difficult airway cart if known difficult airway, RSI supplies otherwise.
  11. Internal defibrillator paddles use much lower energy than external. 5–10 J biphasic internal vs. 200+ J external. If the surgeon calls for internal defibrillation, the defibrillator energy setting MUST be adjusted downward, or paddles will not work correctly.
  12. The mediastinum is irrigated before closure in the OR. Have warm saline (usually with antibiotic per surgeon request) available on the sterile field at bedside to irrigate any clots.
  13. "Resternotomy tray location" must be known in advance. Every unit should have a designated location for the emergency resternotomy cart. It should be checked at shift change. If you work per-diem, ask where it is on day 1.
  14. Perfusion standby is critical. If the patient is not responding to internal massage and medications, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or cardiopulmonary bypass may be needed. Perfusionist should be paged EARLY in the code, not as an afterthought.
  15. After the event, the unit is NOT okay — even if the patient survives. Bedside resternotomy is one of the most traumatic codes for ICU and step-down nurses. Advocate for a formal team debrief within 24 hours. Mention EAP (Employee Assistance Program) and psychiatric support explicitly to involved staff — do NOT assume they know how to access it.
  16. Documentation is both medical AND legal. Every minute is critical in the chart. If possible, have the circulating nurse maintain a running log in real time (time of call, time of arrival, time of chest opening, time of perfusion restoration, meds given, blood products transfused) rather than reconstructing from memory. This protects the team and the patient's care record.

sections.heading: 10. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections in Section 10 are — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 10.1 Cardiac Advanced Life Support (CALS) vs. standard ACLS
sections.bodyHtml:
Standard ACLS (Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support) assumes a medical cardiac arrest (MI, arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism). The mantra is "push hard and fast" external compressions.

Cardiac Advanced Life Support (CALS) in post-cardiotomy arrest modifies ACLS because the sternum is fresh and the mediastinal contents are vulnerable:

  • Delay external compressions 1–2 minutes to allow resternotomy prep
  • Internal cardiac massage is preferred if sternum is open — two-handed, hand behind heart, gentle compression between palms
  • External compressions as backup if resternotomy will take > 5 minutes
  • Internal defibrillation if VF/pulseless VT (5–10 J biphasic internal, not 200 J external)
  • Specific reversible causes to consider (the 5 Hs and 5 Ts are modified):
  • Hypovolemia (massive bleeding)
  • Hypothermia (less common post-op)
  • Hypoxia (ventilator problem)
  • Hydrogen ion (severe acidosis from poor perfusion)
  • Hyperkalemia (rare post-op)
  • Tamponade (most common in post-cardiotomy arrest)
  • Tension pneumothorax (from surgical injury)
  • Thrombosis (coronary graft occlusion or thromboembolism)
  • Toxins (drug reaction)
  • Thromboembolism (rare post-op)

Reference: Dunning et al. (2009) EACTS guideline on resuscitation in cardiac arrest after cardiac surgery.

sections.heading: 10.2 Indications for bedside vs. operating room resternotomy
sections.bodyHtml:
Bedside resternotomy is indicated if:

  • Post-cardiac-surgery cardiac arrest (PEA, asystole, or pulseless VT) within POD 10
  • Suspected tamponade with hemodynamic collapse (BP unmeasurable, loss of consciousness)
  • Exsanguinating hemorrhage with shock refractory to resuscitation
  • Failed external resuscitation — 2 minutes of ACLS with no ROSC
  • CT surgery team can be at bedside within 5 minutes

Operating room resternotomy is used for:

  • Stable or near-stable patients with suspected bleeding who can tolerate transport
  • Elective re-exploration in the OR for prolonged postop bleeding (POD 1–3 with output > 200 mL/hr)
  • Any resternotomy not meeting emergent bedside criteria

The distinction is acuity + hemodynamic tolerance. If the patient is crashing NOW, bedside. If stable enough to ride the elevator, OR.

sections.heading: 10.3 Who performs bedside resternotomy
sections.bodyHtml:
• CT surgery attending or senior fellow — must be a surgeon comfortable with emergency thoracotomy and internal cardiac massage
  • Attending cannot be present immediately? Most protocols allow the senior available cardiac surgery resident to START the resternotomy (opening the sternum, identifying the bleeding source) while the attending is en route. The attending may then take over for definitive repair.
  • Not a interventional radiologist, emergency medicine physician, or trauma surgeon. Cardiac surgery training is required because of the complexity of reopening a sternotomy and managing cardiac injuries.

sections.heading: 10.4 Post-event care trajectory
sections.bodyHtml:
Immediate post-resternotomy (if stabilized):

  • Patient goes to OR for definitive repair and sternal re-closure (do NOT close the chest at the bedside)
  • Chest is covered with sterile drape or Ioban for transport
  • Full resuscitation team accompanies (surgeon, anesthesia, 1+ nurses)
  • Continuous monitoring and support during transport

If the patient does not survive:

  • Time of death documented by attending
  • Chaplaincy and social work engaged for family
  • Body care per [Institution policy] — open chest requires special handling notification to morgue staff
  • Team debrief scheduled within 24 hours

If stabilized in OR and returns to ICU:

  • Usually requires vasopressor support (norepinephrine, epinephrine) due to post-arrest myocardial stunning
  • Vasoplegia is common post-resternotomy (vasoplegic shock — low SVR despite high catecholamine requirements). Expect vasopressin, steroids (hydrocortisone), or phenylephrine
  • Mechanical circulatory support (ECMO, IABP) often needed — mortality is high; goal is bridge to recovery or transplant decision
  • Hypothermia protocol may be initiated (34–36 °C) to reduce post-arrest neurologic injury
  • Multiple organ dysfunction likely — renal failure, hepatic dysfunction, DIC common
  • Length of ICU stay: weeks if survival; mortality 40–60% in published series (Dunning et al., 2009; varies by era and selection)
  • Long-term follow-up: neuropsychologic recovery, cardiac function recovery, rehabilitation needs

sections.heading: 10.5 Tray contents detail and rationale
sections.bodyHtml:
Why each item matters:

  • Wire cutter: Sternal wires are typically 1–2 mm diameter stainless steel. A scalpel cannot cut them. If the wire cutter is not immediately available, the resternotomy is delayed. Check it every shift.
  • Bovie (electrocautery): For hemostasis of small bleeding sources. Must be tested for function before the code.
  • Retractor: One-piece self-retaining retractors (e.g., Farabeuf) are faster than handheld. The chest must open wide for visibility and access.
  • Suction × 2: One for surgery, one as backup. Blood obscures the surgical field immediately; clearing it is critical for identification of the bleeding source.
  • Sutures (0 or 1): For ligation of bleeding vessels. A needle holder is needed.
  • Internal defibrillator paddles: If VF/pulseless VT is the arrest rhythm. Standard external paddles will not work on the surface of the heart; specialized internal paddles are required.
  • Sterile gloves in multiple sizes: Varies by surgeon hand size; have small, medium, large available.

sections.heading: 11. Red Flags — Advanced Early Warning System
sections.bodyHtml:
Additional watch-fors beyond Section 8 that predict imminent collapse.

Hemodynamic cascade you may see in the hour before arrest:

  • Mild tachycardia (HR 95–105) → moderate tachycardia (HR 110–130) → marked tachycardia (HR 130+) with falling BP = shock progression
  • CVP rising steadily (5 → 8 → 12 mmHg) over 1–2 hours = venous congestion (tamponade picture)
  • Urine output falling (usually first sign): 100 mL/hr → 50 mL/hr → near-oliguria in < 2 hours
  • Lactate > 4 mmHg = tissue hypoperfusion beginning; > 8 = severe shock

Physical findings:

  • Altered mental status (patient drowsy, not tracking, confused) = hypoperfusion of brain; this is a red flag for imminent arrest
  • Skin changes: pale, mottled, cool peripheries despite warm core
  • Breath sounds: crackles if pulmonary edema (can precede cardiogenic shock)

Tube and output changes:

  • Chest tube output suddenly stops entirely after hours of drainage = clotted tube (assume tamponade until proven otherwise)
  • Chest tube suddenly starts draining frank bright blood after period of serous drainage = bleeding source opening
  • Pacing wires dislodged or loose (pacing capture lost) = risk of arrhythmia

sections.heading: 12. Pitfalls & Pearls (Summary)
sections.bodyHtml:
(This section condenses high-yield errors and teaching moments — see Section 9 for full expansion.)

  1. Clotted tubes = accumulation; don't strip aggressively
  2. 5-minute decision window is critical — early CT surgery call saves lives
  3. Standard ACLS (external CPR) may be HARMFUL post-cardiotomy; CALS protocol differs
  4. Massive Transfusion Protocol activation is a NURSING call
  5. Open Chest Code is a defined institutional code — know what it triggers
  6. Bedside resternotomy is rare but lethal; trajectory awareness is key for step-down nurses
  7. Post-event debrief and EAP support are MANDATORY
  8. Documentation during the code is legal protection and quality learning
  9. Post-resternotomy survivors often need ECMO, vasoplegia management, hypothermia protocol
  10. Vasoplegia is common after resternotomy (expect vasopressor escalation)

cards.title: Post-Cardiotomy Bowel Regimen
cards.quickAnswer: Start the bowel regimen POD 1 as scheduled — do not wait for constipation to develop. Standard stack: docusate 200 mg PO BID + PEG 17 g PO daily (scheduled); escalate with senna 2 tabs qHS, bisacodyl 10 mg PR, MOM 30 mL PO q8h (all PRN tiers). Always correct K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0, Phos ≥ 2.5 before assuming regimen failure. Opioid-induced constipation refractory to standard stack → methylnaltrexone 8–12 mg SC per team order. Red flag: distention + vomiting + no flatus + rising lactate = acute abdomen, not ileus; NPO and team call.

Always correct K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0, Phos ≥ 2.5 before assuming regimen failure. Opioid-induced constipation refractory to standard stack → methylnaltrexone 8–12 mg SC per team order. Red flag: distention + vomiting + no flatus + rising lactate = acute abdomen, not ileus; NPO and team call.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, scope, and when it applies.

  • Definition: A scheduled plus PRN oral/rectal regimen designed to prevent and treat constipation and functional ileus after cardiac surgery. Not for mechanical obstruction — that is a surgical emergency.
  • Why it matters: Post-cardiac-surgery patients face stacked insults to GI motility (opioids, immobility, CPB inflammation, electrolyte depletion). Without a proactive regimen, 60–80% develop significant constipation or ileus by POD 3–4 (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025). Uncorrected, this delays mobility, prolongs length of stay, masks acute abdomen, and increases discomfort.
  • Who it applies to: Every adult post-cardiac-surgery patient (all procedures: CABG, valve, aortic, transplant, ECMO, etc.) receiving PO intake, unless explicitly contraindicated (see §6).
  • When to start: POD 1 — the moment the patient is tolerating PO and hemodynamically stable. Do not wait for a missed bowel movement (BM).
  • When to stop: Typically at discharge. Most patients continue scheduled docusate at home through the first 6–8 weeks (sternal precautions window) while on opioids; cessation is individual.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why It Exists
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac-surgery constipation and ileus result from the convergence of multiple physiologic pressures on an already-stressed intestinal tract:

Stacking of risk factors:

  • Opioids — the single most modifiable driver. Every dose slows colonic transit time; cumulative burden by POD 2–3 is substantial.
  • Immobility and bedrest — reduced physical activity suppresses the gastrocolic reflex, the strongest mechanical driver of colonic evacuation.
  • CPB-induced splanchnic inflammation — mesenteric vasoconstriction during cardiopulmonary bypass → transient gut ischemia → mucosal edema and dysmotility for 24–72 hours post-op.
  • Electrolyte depletion — acute diuresis (common post-op) pulls K⁺ and Mg²⁺ below the thresholds needed for smooth muscle contraction.
  • Reduced oral intake — NPO status, anorexia, diet progression, inadequate fluid intake.
  • Sympathetic surge — post-op catecholamine release and pain inhibit parasympathetic (enteric nervous system) motor activity.
  • Anticholinergic medication burden — scopolamine patches, diphenhydramine, certain antiemetics further blunt enteric neurotransmission.

The POD 2–3 peak in bowel dysfunction reflects the combined timing of maximum inflammatory burden, maximum fluid mobilization, opioid nadir, and beta-blocker withdrawal (if held for hypotension).

Clinical implication: Standing prevention is far more effective than reactive rescue. A patient who has already missed two BMs and is distended requires days to recover motility; one started on scheduled softeners on POD 1 rarely becomes symptomatic.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — patient populations and clinical triggers for initiation.

Universally indicated:

  • Every post-op cardiac surgery patient (POD 1+) on PO intake and with intact GI tract
  • Includes CABG, all valve repairs/replacements, aortic surgery, MAZE, heart transplant, ECMO weaning, etc.
  • Regardless of age, pre-op bowel function, or opioid allergy (non-opioid analgesia plans still require bowel support)

Special populations (apply regimen with modifications per §6):

  • Renal impairment (CKD stage 3+): Avoid MOM (hypermagnesemia risk); prefer PEG or senna. Monitor Mg levels.
  • Acute kidney injury: Hold MOM entirely if Mg > 2.5 or K⁺ < 3.0; use PEG + docusate only until electrolytes replete.
  • Recent bowel surgery or anastomosis: Avoid rectal suppositories for 2+ weeks post-op (perforation risk).
  • Neutropenia: Avoid rectal suppositories and tap water enemas (infection risk).
  • Active GI bleed: Hold PEG/MOM during active bleeding; restart after hemostasis.
  • Mechanical obstruction or acute abdomen workup: NPO, hold all laxatives, surgical consult.
  • Heart transplant or VAD patients: Prioritize from POD 0 — Valsalva during straining destabilizes preload dangerously.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Gather baseline and ongoing status* (5 minutes per shift)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside and chart review. Information-only; no interventions yet.

Baseline (on POD 1 or transfer to unit):

  • Pre-op bowel function — frequency, consistency, any chronic constipation history?
  • Current symptom review — abdominal pain, distention, nausea, feeling of fullness
  • Abdominal exam — soft vs distended, tender, bowel sounds in all quadrants (present, absent, hypoactive, hyperactive), tympanic?
  • Medications on board — opioids (dose, frequency), anticholinergics, any pre-op laxatives or fiber supplements?
  • Pre-op statin use — statin continuation is associated with lower post-op ileus; note if held or restarted

Every shift (ongoing):

  • Last BM — date, time, character (hard, soft, diarrhea, bloody?). Chart even if unchanged.
  • Flatus — passing? First flatus is a major POD milestone.
  • Current bowel sounds — auscultate four quadrants; document presence/absence and quality.
  • Abdominal girth — if distention concern, measure at umbilicus and track (example: girth 32" → 33.5" signals progression).
  • Symptoms — new nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, bloating, inability to pass gas?
  • MAR compliance — did patient take scheduled docusate/PEG? Any refusals and reason?
  • Feeding tolerance — nausea with PO? Able to finish meals?
  • Labs (if not routine) — K⁺, Mg²⁺, Phos, creatinine (to guide laxative selection)

sections.heading: 5.1 The standard stack — scheduled + PRN tiers
sections.bodyHtml:
Tier Agent Dose Route Schedule Onset Notes
Scheduled Docusate sodium 200 mg PO BID × 6–8 weeks 24–72 h Stool softener; core of the regimen. Most patients continue at home post-discharge.
Scheduled Polyethylene glycol (PEG) 3350 17 g packet PO in 8 oz liquid Daily × 1–4 days 12–72 h Osmotic laxative. Mix in juice, chilled water, or weak tea for palatability.
PRN tier 1 Senna (sennosides) 2 tabs (17.2 mg) PO qHS for no BM × 24 h 6–12 h Stimulant. Causes cramping (set expectations). Hold if diarrhea develops.
PRN tier 2 Bisacodyl 10 mg PR suppository PRN for no BM × 48 h on tier 1 15–60 min Fast-acting; useful when patient is "close." Avoid in neutropenic patients.
PRN tier 3 Milk of magnesia (MOM) 30 mL PO q8h PRN 30 min – 6 h Osmotic + saline laxative. Hold if Mg > 2.5 or CKD stage 4–5. Risk of hypermagnesemia.
Rescue Methylnaltrexone (Relistor) 8–12 mg (weight-based) SC Once PRN for refractory opioid-induced constipation 30 min – 4 h Peripheral mu antagonist; preserves opioid analgesia. Dramatically effective. Within 30–60 min BM in ~80% of patients.

Escalation protocol:

  • POD 1 or on initiation: Start scheduled docusate + PEG both on day 1 if PO tolerated. Do not wait.
  • No BM by POD 2 (48 h post-op): Both scheduled agents on board? Yes → activate senna (tier 1) qHS PRN.
  • No BM by POD 3 (72 h post-op): Add bisacodyl suppository (tier 2) PRN. Consider KUB if distention is worsening.
  • No BM by POD 4 (96 h post-op): Notify APP/provider. Verify electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Phos). If electrolytes OK, consider methylnaltrexone. If electrolytes low, replicate first, then reassess in 12–24 h.
  • Distention + no flatus + vomiting + feculent emesis + rising lactate: STOP all laxatives immediately. This is acute abdomen until proven otherwise — see Red Flags (§8) and team escalation.

sections.heading: 5.2 Route selection and substitutions
sections.bodyHtml:
• PO preferred — most cost-effective, physiologic, and reliable when the patient has intact GI tract and no dysphagia.
  • PR (rectal) for faster action or PO intolerance — bisacodyl suppository acts in 15–60 min and is especially useful on POD 3 when the patient is distended and anxious. Avoid in neutropenia or recent colorectal surgery.
  • SC methylnaltrexone — peripheral-selective mu antagonist. Does NOT cross blood–brain barrier, so analgesia is preserved. Reserved for opioid-induced constipation confirmed after standard stack failure. Weight-based dosing: 8 mg if 38–62 kg, 12 mg if > 62 kg.
  • NG tube for decompression — Not routine. Used for documented ileus with distention, emesis, and imaging confirmation; team decision only.
  • Enemas (avoid) — Fleet (sodium phosphate) enemas are largely out of favor in cardiac surgery due to phosphate shifts and potential cardiotoxicity. Tap water enema is an option but rarely needed if the above tiers are used.

sections.heading: 5.3 Reversible factors to correct *before* escalating laxatives
sections.bodyHtml:
Always check and address these first — they look like "ileus failure" but are eminently fixable:

Factor Target Action
Hypokalemia K⁺ ≥ 4.0 mmol/L Replicate per Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement protocol.
Hypomagnesemia Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 mg/dL Replicate per electrolyte protocol.
Hypophosphatemia Phos ≥ 2.5 mg/dL Replicate per protocol.
Dehydration UOP ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h Review I/O balance; consider IV fluid bolus per team if appropriate.
Opioid overload Lowest effective analgesic dose Switch to opioid-sparing multimodal pain plan (see Opioid-Sparing / Multimodal Pain Management protocol).
Immobility OOB to chair ≥ TID, ambulation per PT plan Push mobility relentlessly — the gastrocolic reflex is the most potent interventionthe patient controls.
Anticholinergic meds Minimize burden Audit MAR for scopolamine patches, diphenhydramine, tricyclic antidepressants; discuss D/C or alternatives with provider.

sections.heading: 5.4 Diet and lifestyle support
sections.bodyHtml:
• POD 0–1: NPO → clear liquids → soft foods as tolerated
  • POD 1–2: Full cardiac diet (low sodium, heart-healthy); introduce solid food gradually. Avoid large fiber bulk early (can worsen distention without adequate motility).
  • POD 2+: Encourage fluids (≥1.5 L/day if not fluid-restricted). Regular meals on schedule. Warm liquids (warm water, broth, warm prune juice) first thing in the morning have mild laxative effect.
  • Ambulation — single most effective patient-controlled intervention. Encourage OOB to chair TID minimum and walking per PT plan.
  • Privacy and dignity — patients won't attempt toileting if the curtain is half-open or nursing staff are hovering. Provide privacy, adequate time on the commode, and positive reinforcement.

sections.heading: 5.5 Contraindications / hold criteria
sections.bodyHtml:
Situation Action
Suspected bowel obstruction (distention + vomiting + obstipation + abnormal imaging) Hold all oral laxatives immediately. NPO. STAT surgical consultation.
Acute abdomen workup pending Hold laxatives until team clears.
Active GI bleed (hemodynamic or transfusion-requiring) Hold PEG and MOM. Docusate + ambulation only until bleeding controlled.
Severe AKI with hypermagnesemia (Mg > 2.5) Hold MOM. Use PEG + docusate preferentially.
Neutropenia (ANC < 500) Avoid PR suppositories and enemas (infection risk). PO only.
Hyponatremia (Na < 130) Use PEG cautiously (osmotic fluid load); avoid large free-water intake. Favor docusate + ambulation.

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. No BM × 3+ days on full scheduled regimen — verify compliance (patient actually took meds), check electrolytes, consider methylnaltrexone or imaging (KUB/CT).
  2. Increasing abdominal girth (e.g., 32 → 34 inches) despite scheduled regimen — possible worsening ileus; inform team.
  3. Inability to pass flatus for > 48 h post-op — concerning for partial obstruction or significant dysmotility; imaging consideration.
  4. Severe cramping pain out of proportion to minimal distention — may suggest early/partial obstruction or ischemia (see Red Flags).
  5. Vomiting with feeding attempts — stop advancing diet; notify team; NPO standby.
  6. Feculent (brown, foul-smelling) emesis — suggests high bowel obstruction; NPO + imaging + team call.
  7. Sudden voluminous diarrhea replacing prior constipation (especially post-antibiotics) — rule out Clostridioides difficile; send PCR. Do not assume regimen "finally worked."
  8. Rising lactate or metabolic acidosis concurrent with abdominal distention + pain — NOT simple ileus; possible bowel ischemia. STAT surgical evaluation.
  9. Patient becomes hypotensive or tachycardic with worsening abdominal signs — sepsis concern; STAT team call.
  10. Documented hypermagnesemia (Mg > 2.5) after MOM use — D/C MOM; use PEG only; monitor renal function and Mg.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections in Section 7 are intended for in-app collapse. Nursing students, new-grad RNs, and advanced beginners can expand to build deeper understanding; experienced nurses and experts can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Physiology detail
sections.bodyHtml:
The three-line defense against post-op constipation:

  1. Stool softener (docusate) — reduces surface tension → allows water penetration into stool → softer stool easier to pass → reduces straining and Valsalva risk (critical in cardiac post-op patients who cannot strain without destabilizing hemodynamics/pacer rhythm).

  2. Osmotic laxator (PEG) — draws water into the bowel lumen osmotically → increased stool volume → stimulates stretch receptors in the rectal wall → triggers defecation reflex. Effective in 12–72 h.

  3. Stimulant or mechanical triggers (senna, bisacodyl, MOM) — senna activates enteric smooth muscle; bisacodyl irritates the colonic mucosa to provoke peristalsis; MOM provides both osmotic action and saline catharsis. All work faster (6 min to 6 h) but are meant as tier-1 PRN only, not standing.

Why electrolytes matter:

  • K⁺ deficiency — hypokalemia directly impairs smooth muscle membrane potential and contractility. A patient on scheduled docusate will not achieve BM if K⁺ is 3.2.
  • Mg²⁺ deficiency — hypomagnesemia is a cofactor in muscle contraction (Mg-ATP); low Mg literally stalls the enteric muscle machinery.
  • Phos deficiency — less direct, but hypophosphatemia can worsen muscle weakness and fatigue globally, including GI smooth muscle.

Correcting electrolytes first, then re-assessing the regimen, avoids needless escalation to methylnaltrexone or imaging.

sections.heading: 7.2 Common laxative agents — mechanism and practical tips
sections.bodyHtml:
Agent Class Onset Notes for nurses
Docusate 200 mg BID Stool softener (anionic surfactant) 24–72 h Safest, most tolerable. Core of every regimen. Patients often can continue at home indefinitely. No cramping.
PEG 17 g daily Osmotic 12–72 h Dissolves completely; no taste if mixed in juice. Some patients find it chalky in water. Chill it. Takes 12–72 h, so be patient.
Senna 2 tabs qHS Stimulant (anthraquinone) 6–12 h Cause mild-to-moderate cramping (normal). Patient may wake with urgency between 6 am and 10 am. Set expectations. Long-term use (weeks) can cause melanosis coli (benign skin darkening); not a concern post-op.
Bisacodyl 10 mg PR Stimulant (diphenylmethane) 15–60 min Most underused agent on post-op floors. Rectal suppository acts fast. Patients dislike rectal administration (shame/privacy), so introduce matter-of-factly: "This will get your bowel moving in 20–30 minutes." Invaluable on POD 3 for distended, anxious patient.
MOM 30 mL q8h Saline + osmotic 30 min – 6 h Contains Mg; contraindicated in renal impairment or if already on Mg repletion. Watch Mg levels (> 2.5 = hold). Tastes bitter; chill it. Metallic aftertaste is common.
Methylnaltrexone 8–12 mg SC Peripheral mu antagonist 30 min – 4 h Gold standard for opioid-induced constipation. BM in 30–60 min in ~80% of patients on opioids. Weight-based: 8 mg (38–62 kg), 12 mg (> 62 kg). Does NOT reverse analgesia. Expect BM within 1 h — have bedpan or commode ready. Side effect: brief cramping before BM. Patient love it (fast relief) and nurses love it (works).

sections.heading: 7.3 Patient and family teaching — common questions
sections.bodyHtml:
"Why am I getting a laxative when I'm not even constipated?"
Because the surgery + pain meds + lying in bed make almost every post-op patient constipated by POD 3 if we don't get ahead of it. The easiest, cheapest fix is to prevent it from day 1. By the time you feel constipated, you're already distended and frustrated. We'd rather you never get there.

"How long will I take these?"
Usually through your first 6–8 weeks at home while you're on pain meds and not moving normally. Docusate is the one most patients keep on hand longest. Once you're off opioids and walking daily, your own rhythm comes back.

"Will I need these forever?"
No. Most patients are off all laxatives by the 4–6 week follow-up, when opioid weaning is done and normal activity resumes.

"What if I still don't go despite all this?"
Tell us. We have more options — suppositories, stronger laxatives, or a special medicine (methylnaltrexone) that works fast for opioid-related constipation.

"Can I take my home fiber supplement?"
Usually okay, but not a substitute for the scheduled regimen. Fiber without adequate fluid intake and motility can actually worsen distention. Tell us if you bring one.

"Will prune juice work instead?"
It can help add to the regimen, but not alone. Use it as an extra drink, not a replacement for the scheduled medicines.

"Why do I feel bloated even though I went yesterday?"
Partial ileus can produce gas and bloating without blocking stool. It gets better with walking and time. Keep moving.

"Is it normal to have diarrhea now?"
Often yes, especially after a big dose of senna or MOM. If it lasts more than 24 h, or if there's blood, tell us. If it's right after antibiotics, we may need to check for infection.

"Should I worry if I go less often than before surgery?"
Your bowel rhythm takes a few weeks to reset after surgery. If you're going every 2–3 days without straining and without pain, you're fine. Return to your personal baseline by 4–6 weeks.

sections.heading: 7.4 Special populations and edge cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Heart transplant and LVAD patients:

  • Valsalva during straining is poorly tolerated (destabilizes preload).
  • Prioritize the regimen from POD 0–1. Do not wait for constipation to develop.
  • Aggressive early mobility + stool softener + PEG.
  • Consider earlier methylnaltrexone if standard stack is slow.

Pacer-wire-dependent patients (atrial pacing):

  • Straining and Valsalva can trigger atrial ectopy and temporary loss of capture.
  • Keep stool very soft (docusate + PEG + ambulation).
  • Avoid senna on these patients if possible (cramping-induced straining).
  • Bisacodyl (fast, less cramping) is preferable if PRN needed.

Post-MAZE patients:

  • Post-MAZE atrial fibrillation is common and early DCCV is ineffective.
  • No special bowel consideration, but note: some of the antiarrhythmic drugs (amiodarone, sotalol) have anticholinergic effects and worsen constipation.
  • Standard regimen applies.

Renal impairment (CKD stage 3–5):

  • Avoid MOM entirely if CKD stage 4–5 (Mg accumulation).
  • Use PEG + docusate + senna or bisacodyl if needed.
  • Monitor Mg level after any MOM dose even in stage 3; hold if trending up.
  • If AKI + hyperkalemia, hold docusate doses until K < 5.5 (docusate does not directly shift K, but the act of defecation does not help K excretion either).

Post-bariatric patients (prior gastric bypass or sleeve):

  • Rare post-cardiac surgery, but if present: intact short gut and rapid transit. Risk is diarrhea, not constipation.
  • Use docusate only; skip PEG and stimulants unless truly obstructed.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in patients who were "stable on the regimen"; if any develop, re-escalate immediately.

  • Increasing abdominal girth over 24 h (e.g., 32 → 33.5 → 35 inches) — progressive distention; imaging (KUB) and team notification.
  • Absence of flatus for > 48 h post-op — suggests significant dysmotility or partial obstruction; do not escalate laxatives further without imaging.
  • Nausea with feeding despite tolerated diet earlier — can herald early obstruction or ileus worsening.
  • Vomiting, especially feculent (brown, foul) emesis — high suspicion for bowel obstruction; NPO + imaging + surgical consult.
  • Abdominal pain out of proportion to physical findings — classic red flag for ischemia or impending perforation; this is NOT simple ileus.
  • Rising lactate or worsening metabolic acidosis paired with GI distention — bowel ischemia concern; STAT evaluation.
  • Hypotension or tachycardia developing with worsening abdominal exam — possible sepsis from translocation; STAT team call.
  • Sudden voluminous diarrhea replacing prior constipation (especially post-antibiotics) — Clostridioides difficile or infectious colitis until proven otherwise.
  • Fever + abdominal tenderness + rising lactate — sepsis from GI source; cultures, imaging, broad-spectrum antibiotics per team.
  • Documented hypermagnesemia (Mg > 2.5) after MOM doses — d/c MOM; risk of hypermagnesemia complications (cardiac, neurologic); monitor.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
(10–15 high-yield bullets for experienced nurses and experts)

  1. The regimen is preventive, not reactive. By the time a post-op patient complains of constipation, they are already distended and emotionally frustrated. Starting docusate + PEG on POD 1 (before the patient feels bad) is the standard of care. Waiting for a missed BM is a miss.

  2. Scheduled stack gets under-ordered on unit admission from the ICU. Always verify on shift sign-off that both docusate AND PEG are on the MAR. A common miss is docusate alone without PEG.

  3. Patients refuse the softener because they "don't feel constipated." Reframe the conversation: "We're not treating constipation; we're preventing it." This simple framing cuts refusals in half. Document refusals.

  4. Check K⁺, Mg²⁺, and Phos before calling it 'ileus.' Low electrolytes look exactly like early ileus and the fix is different. A patient with K⁺ 3.2 and Mg²⁺ 1.8 will not have a BM until you replicate. Do not escalate laxatives; replicate electrolytes first.

  5. Senna causes cramping that patients fear. Set expectations at bedtime: "You may wake with crampy urgency between 6 and 10 am; that means it's working. It's not dangerous — it's what we want." Most patients accept it once primed.

  6. Bisacodyl PR (rectal suppository) is dramatically underused. Many nurses default to escalating PO agents when a 10 mg bisacodyl suppository acts in 15–60 minutes. Especially useful on POD 3 for a distended, anxious patient. Matter-of-fact introduction: "This is a rectal suppository. It will help you have a BM in 20–30 minutes." Patients are usually relieved (fast action).

  7. Methylnaltrexone is dramatically effective for opioid-induced constipation. BM in 30–60 min in ~80% of patients. Nurses should advocate for it when refractory to standard stack. Weight-based dosing: verify the order. Patient gratitude is high.

  8. MOM can cause hypermagnesemia in renal impairment. A patient with eGFR 45 on MOM 30 mL q8h can accumulate Mg over 24–48 h. Monitor the level; d/c if Mg > 2.5.

  9. Fleet (sodium phosphate) enemas are out of favor. Avoid due to phosphate shifts and potential cardiotoxicity in cardiac post-op patients. If needed, tap water enema is safer.

  10. Distention + no flatus + vomiting + feculent emesis + rising lactate is NOT ileus. This is acute abdomen (obstruction, ischemia, perforation) until proven otherwise. NPO, team call, imaging, surgical evaluation. Do NOT push more laxatives; stop everything oral.

  11. Heart transplant and LVAD patients tolerate constipation poorly. Valsalva is hemodynamically destabilizing. Prioritize regimen from POD 0–1; do not wait for symptoms. Lower threshold for methylnaltrexone.

  12. Early flatus is a better progress marker than early BM. Chart "first flatus" on POD 2–3; it indicates return of peristalsis even if BM hasn't happened yet.

  13. C. difficile mimics resolved constipation. If sudden voluminous diarrhea replaces obstinate constipation after antibiotics, do not assume the regimen "finally worked." Send Clostridioides difficile PCR before escalating.

  14. Document BM or absence thereof on every shift. Omitting it from the documentation ("no change") creates gaps in the picture. A patient who had no BM on POD 2, nothing charted on POD 3 (shift coverage gap), then distended on POD 4 looks like a sudden change. Continuous charting prevents this.

  15. Pacer-dependent patients should avoid senna. Cramping-induced straining and Valsalva can trigger ectopy. Docusate + PEG + bisacodyl (if needed) is safer.
