sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, and who this applies to.

  • Definition: Symptomatic bradycardia (HR <60 bpm) or conduction system disturbance (1°, 2°, or 3° AV block) occurring in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient, causing hemodynamic or neurologic symptoms.
  • Incidence: Varies by procedure. Post-aortic valve replacement (AVR): 5–8% progress to permanent pacemaker. Post-mitral/tricuspid valve surgery: 2–4%. CABG alone: <1% unless extensive dissection. Peak onset: post-operative day (POD) 0–3, but can occur any time during hospitalization.
  • Who this applies to: all post-operative cardiac surgery patients on telemetry, particularly those with AVR, mitral valve, tricuspid valve, or MAZE procedures.
  • Why it matters: bradycardia can cause syncope, falls, acute mental status change, and hypoperfusion. Early recognition and intervention prevent progression to asystole and end-organ injury. Pacemaker dependency requires meticulous wire management.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced-beginner teaching — why this happens.

Surgical mechanisms:

Post-operative bradycardia arises from injury or edema to the conduction system — particularly the AV node, which lies in the "danger zone" near the aortic and mitral annuli. (Kusumoto et al., 2019)

  • AV node edema (most common): surgical retraction, cannulation, and pericardial inflammation swell tissues around the AV node.
  • Direct trauma: suture placement during valve annulotomy, especially in AVR and mitral repair.
  • Ischemia: prolonged aortic cross-clamp, deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA), or inadequate cardioplegia distribution deprives the nodal blood supply.
  • Inflammatory surge: cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) triggers cytokine release, transiently depressing nodal function.
  • Hypothermia and electrolyte shifts: post-CPB rewarming and diuresis raise conduction block risk.

Procedure-specific risks:

  • Aortic valve replacement (AVR): highest risk (~5–8%). The AV node lies directly below the non-coronary cusp.
  • Mitral valve repair/replacement (MVR): moderate-high risk (~2–4%). Mitral annulus proximity to AV node.
  • Tricuspid valve repair/replacement: variable; higher if septal approach.
  • MAZE procedure: common early junctional rhythms (POD 0–2) from atrial ablation; most self-resolve by POD 5–7.
  • CABG alone: <1% risk unless extensive left anterior descending dissection.

Medical exacerbating factors:

  • Beta-blockers, diltiazem, verapamil, amiodarone, digoxin — reduce nodal conduction
  • Hypokalemia (K⁺ <4.0) — raises pacemaker capture thresholds dramatically
  • Hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia — prolong AV conduction
  • Hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypothermia — reflex bradycardia + impaired conduction
  • Vagal triggers (suctioning, bowel distention, urinary retention) — cause reflex bradycardia
  • Inferior wall ischemia (RCA territory) — common in acute MI; usually self-resolves over 3–5 days
  • Hypothyroidism — chronic cause, rare acutely post-op

Transplant special case:

Heart transplant patients have a denervated (parasympathetically insensitive) graft. Atropine is ineffective. New bradycardia signals acute rejection or infection — contact transplant team immediately. (Kusumoto et al., 2019)

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following should trigger assessment:

  • Telemetry alarm: HR <60 bpm or new wide-complex bradycardia
  • Unexplained syncope or near-syncope in immediate post-op period
  • Hypotension (SBP <90) + bradycardia (HR <50) without obvious other cause
  • Symptomatic dizziness, fatigue, chest discomfort, dyspnea paired with slow HR
  • Altered mental status (confusion, lethargy, agitation) with bradycardia — cerebral hypoperfusion
  • Loss of pacer capture on a paced patient (visible P or QRS not followed by mechanical pulse)
  • New AV block pattern on telemetry (Wenckebach, Mobitz II, or complete heart block)
  • Pacer-dependent patient with abrupt loss of pacing artifact

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure observation — no interventions yet.

  • Vital signs: HR (trend over last 4–12 h), BP (systolic, diastolic, MAP), SpO₂, mental status, skin perfusion (capillary refill, temperature)
  • Symptoms: lightheadedness, syncope, palpitations, chest pain, dyspnea, confusion
  • Physical findings: pulse quality and regularity; focal neurologic deficit (consider hypoperfusion vs. stroke)
  • Telemetry: rhythm strip at onset showing HR trend (gradual vs. sudden), AV block pattern, QRS width, PR interval
  • 12-lead ECG: review for AV block classification, QRS width (>120 ms = infranodal block), ST changes, ischemic pattern
  • Pacer wire status (if in place):
  • Atrial, ventricular, or both wires present?
  • Generator on and connected?
  • Current mode (DDD, VVI, VDD, AAI)? Rate setting? Output (mA)? Sensitivity (mV)?
  • Most recent capture/sensing thresholds (this shift or last shift)?
  • Any recent setting changes?
  • Recent medications: beta-blocker dose and timing, diltiazem, amiodarone, digoxin, opioids (cause reflex bradycardia)
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, digoxin level (if on digoxin), troponin, TSH (hypothyroidism)
  • Surgery context: procedure type, POD, prior conduction history (pre-op 1° AV block?), intraoperative events (prolonged ischemia, DHCA), bypass time, cannulation sites
  • IV access: adequate lines for medication? Second line available if needed?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(HR 40–60, no hypotension, asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic, MAP >65, alert, preserved perfusion.)

  1. Obtain 12-lead ECG STAT if not already done — classify AV block type (1°, Mobitz I/II, 3°)
  2. Save rhythm strip at onset and document HR trend, QRS width, PR interval in chart
  3. Correct electrolytes immediately per institutional Electrolyte Replacement protocol:
    • K⁺ ≥ 4.0 mEq/L (some services target 4.5) — hypokalemia is a hidden threshold killer and dramatically raises pacer capture requirements
    • Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 mEq/L (some services target 2.5)
    • Ca²⁺ ≥ 8.0 mg/dL
    • Do not chase pacer thresholds before correcting electrolytes.
    • Address reversible triggers:
    • Nodal blockers: hold or reduce beta-blocker, diltiazem, amiodarone dose per team; verify intent if held for low BP earlier
    • Digoxin: check level; digitalis toxicity causes bradycardia + ectopy
    • Pain, hypoxia, fever: treat underlying causes aggressively
    • Vagal triggers: address suctioning needs, bowel distention, urinary retention
    • If epicardial pacing wires are in place:
    • Verify capture and sensing thresholds:
      • Atrial: usual capture threshold 1–2 mA, sensitivity 2–4 mV
      • Ventricular: usual capture threshold 1–3 mA, sensitivity 2–4 mV
      • Rising thresholds shift-to-shift (>1 mA rise) suggest wire displacement or insulation failure
    • If thresholds acceptable, increase output incrementally (e.g., 5 mA → 8 mA) to achieve 2× capture threshold safety margin
    • Switch polarity if available (unipolar → bipolar) to improve capture
    • Change pacing mode based on functional wires:
      • DDD (dual-chamber): best hemodynamics if both atrial and ventricular wires working
      • VVI (ventricular demand): acceptable single-chamber fallback; ~20% CO loss from loss of atrial kick
      • DOO or VOO (asynchronous): emergency mode if sensing failure suspected; paces regardless of intrinsic rhythm (avoid competitive pacing in normal rhythm)
    • Rate setting: verify 60–80 bpm typical for post-op
    • Refer to institutional Pacer Wire Routine Management protocol for detailed threshold testing
    • If no epicardial wires present:
    • Place transcutaneous pacer pads on standby (do NOT activate yet)
    • Verify defibrillator and crash cart nearby
    • Ensure adequate IV access for medication
    • Continuous telemetry while notifying provider
    • Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (see Section 6) — request rate plan and rhythm classification
    • Frequent reassessment — watch for trajectory change (worsening bradycardia, rising thresholds, mental status decline)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(HR <50 with hypotension [SBP <90], altered mental status, chest pain, signs of pulmonary edema, or loss of pacer capture in pacer-dependent patient.)

  1. STAT call APP/fellow + charge RN + activate Rapid Response — do NOT leave room alone
  2. Ensure patent IV access — establish second line immediately for medication drips
  3. Apply transcutaneous pacer pads (anterior-lateral or anterior-posterior per ACLS):
    • Dry skin, clip hair (do not shave), apply pads firmly with adhesive down
    • Set rate: 60–80 bpm
    • Start at 0 mA output, increase in 5–10 mA increments until electrical capture achieved (wide QRS following each spike)
    • Verify mechanical capture: palpate femoral or carotid pulse synchronous with pacer spike — electrical capture alone is insufficient
    • Increase output 5–10 mA higher for safety margin (overcapture)
    • Provide analgesia IMMEDIATELY: transcutaneous pacing is painful. Order IV fentanyl 25–50 mcg boluses or morphine 2–4 mg; sedate patient per institutional policy
    • If pacer wires present and patient pacer-dependent:
    • Increase atrial output to maximum and assess for capture (watch for P wave on monitor)
    • If atrial capture fails → switch to ventricular pacing mode (VVI), increase output until capture achieved
    • If sensing failure suspected → switch to asynchronous mode (VOO or DOO) to pace without regard to intrinsic rhythm
    • Notify pacer technician (if available) for bedside emergency troubleshooting
    • Medication administration per provider order / ACLS algorithm:
      • Atropine 0.5 mg IV push, repeat every 3–5 minutes, max 3 mg total
        • Note: atropine is ineffective in AV nodal block (Mobitz I, 2°) and transplant denervation; most effective in sinus bradycardia and type II infranodal block
        • If atropine fails and patient remains unstable → start chronotropic infusion:
        • Epinephrine 2–10 mcg/min IV infusion (preferred if hypotensive; alpha + beta agonist increases HR, contractility, BP)
        • OR Isoproterenol 2–10 mcg/min IV (pure beta agonist; increases HR + contractility; use caution in CAD — risk of coronary steal)
        • DO NOT combine multiple chronotropic agents without provider oversight
      • Send STAT labs: ABG, lactate, electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺), troponin, digoxin level (if applicable)
      • Notify cardiothoracic surgery, EP, and anesthesia:
      • CT surgery: if within 48–72 hours of surgery (may need re-exploration for wire issues)
      • EP: may place transvenous pacing wire if epicardial wires non-functional
      • Anesthesia: for sedation if transvenous wire placement anticipated
      • Document meticulously:
      • Rhythm strips at onset, during interventions, after stabilization
      • Pacer capture/sensing thresholds before/after adjustments
      • Medications, doses, times, patient response
      • All provider communications and interventions

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed bradycardia (HR [rate] bpm) at [time]. Rhythm: [sinus bradycardia / AV block pattern]. BP [value], SpO₂ [value], mental status [alert / altered]. Current K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Symptoms if any]. [Hemodynamics]. Pacer wires [present/absent]; if present: [capture status, recent thresholds]." R: "Requesting [rate/rhythm plan / orders for pacing / medication orders / labs / bedside evaluation]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Urgency
Stable bradycardia (HR 40–60), asymptomatic Primary APP / on-call fellow STAT (within 15 min)
Unstable bradycardia (hypotension / altered / chest pain) APP/fellow + Rapid Response + CT surgery STAT (now)
Loss of pacer capture in pacer-dependent patient APP/fellow + pacer technician (if available) STAT (now)
Bradycardia persisting >24 h despite intervention EP consult + CT surgery STAT
New complete heart block (3°) on telemetry CT surgery + EP + anesthesia STAT (now)
Bradycardia + new neurologic deficit Rapid Response + neurology (rule out stroke) Code / STAT

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced-beginner deep-dive. Sections below are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 AV Block Classification and Prognosis
sections.bodyHtml:
Quick reference table:

Block Type ECG Finding Mechanism Risk Post-Op Management Prognosis
1° AV block PR interval >200 ms; all atria conduct Prolonged AV node conduction; benign Low Monitor; avoid nodal blockers Usually resolves; observe for progression
Mobitz I (Wenckebach) Progressive PR lengthening, then dropped beat; usually atrial rate > ventricular Incremental AV node fatigue; benign Low–moderate Monitor; IV atropine if symptomatic Often self-resolves; rarely needs PPM
Mobitz II Sudden dropped P without prior PR change; often 2:1 block Infranodal block; high risk High Transcutaneous pacing on standby; atropine; prepare for TVP/PPM Frequently progresses to 3°; ~50% need PPM
3° (Complete Heart Block) P waves and QRS completely dissociated; junctional escape 30–60 bpm or ventricular escape <30 bpm Complete nodal or infranodal failure High Transcutaneous pacing; prepare for TVP; assume PPM likely Recovery ~10% by POD 7; majority need PPM

PPM timing post-op:

  • Typically wait 5–7 days post-op to allow resolution of surgical edema and inflammation
  • If AV block persists >5–7 days → PPM evaluation per 2019 ACC/AHA/HRS guidelines (Kusumoto et al., 2019)
  • Some services use POD 8 as the decision boundary
  • Symptomatic bradycardia earlier may warrant earlier evaluation per team discretion and ejection fraction

sections.heading: 7.2 Conduction System Anatomy and Post-AVR Risk
sections.bodyHtml:
The AV node blood supply and location place it at risk during valve surgery:

  • AV node location: lies in the triangle of Koch, bounded by the coronary sinus (posteriorly), the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve (anteriorly), and the membranous septum (superiorly)
  • Proximity to aortic valve: the AV node is directly beneath the non-coronary cusp. During AVR, retraction and suture placement near the annulus threaten the node.
  • Proximity to mitral valve: the mitral annulus runs near the posterior AV node pathway. MVR carries similar risk.
  • Bundle of His location: descends from the AV node toward the ventricular septum. Proximal nodal block typically manifests as PR prolongation; distal (infranodal) block shows QRS widening.

Key point: Understanding the anatomy explains why AVR and MV surgery carry the highest PPM rates and why bradycardia may develop unexpectedly on POD 2–3 (edema peaks after initial inflammatory response).

sections.heading: 7.3 Epicardial Wire Troubleshooting
sections.bodyHtml:
Common issues and fixes:

Problem Diagnostic Steps Fix
No capture Check connection first (80% of "failures" are loose connectors); measure capture threshold (should be 1–3 mA) Increase output 2–5 mA above threshold; switch polarity; check for wire fracture or dislodgement on CXR
Rising thresholds Compare shift-to-shift; if rise >1 mA, suspect displacement or insulation break Increase output incrementally; obtain CXR; notify CT surgery for possible re-exploration
Rising thresholds + normal K⁺/Mg²⁺ Rising despite electrolyte correction Likely wire problem, not medication effect; urgent CT surgery notification
Loss of sensing No inhibition of pacing despite intrinsic rhythm visible; pacing spikes override intrinsic beats Switch to asynchronous mode (VOO or DOO) as bridge; check wire connection; increase sensitivity if available
Intermittent capture Capture works sometimes but not reliably Increase output substantially above threshold (aim for 2× threshold); check for loose lead or myocardial perforation (pericardial effusion on echo?)

Emergency wire management:

  1. Connections first — loose sterile connectors are the most common culprit; physically inspect and reseat
  2. Increase output 2–5 mA above threshold for safety margin
  3. Switch polarity (unipolar ↔ bipolar) to probe for better contact
  4. Switch mode to asynchronous (DOO or VOO) if sensing is failing
  5. Verify generator battery — ensure on and running
  6. If still no capture → suspect wire fracture, lead dislodgement, or myocardial perforation; STAT notify CT surgery

sections.heading: 7.4 Pacing Modes and Physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Mode Chambers When Used Hemodynamic Benefit
DDD Dual-chamber (atrial and ventricular) Both atrial and ventricular wires functional Best; maintains AV synchrony; ~20% CO advantage vs VVI
VDD Ventricular sensing, atrial pacing Atrial wire works; ventricular sensing intact Intermediate; atrial pacing without AV sync
VVI Ventricular demand Ventricular wire only; atrial wire failed Acceptable fallback; some CO loss but stable rate
AAI Atrial only Rare post-op; ventricular wire failed but patient has intact AV conduction Unusual; assumes functioning AV node
DOO / VOO Asynchronous (dual or ventricular) Emergency; sensing failure or noise immunity needed No physiologic benefit; paces regardless of intrinsic rhythm — use only as bridge

Recommendation: always aim for DDD if possible; fall back to VVI if necessary. Asynchronous modes are temporary bridges, not long-term solutions.

sections.heading: 7.5 Medication Table for Bradycardia Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Confirm all doses with provider and institutional order set.

Drug Dose Onset Mechanism Pitfalls Notes
Atropine 0.5 mg IV push q3–5 min; max 3 mg total 1–2 min Parasympatholytic (blocks vagal input to AV node) Ineffective in AV nodal block; useless in transplant (denervated heart); paradoxical worsening if dose <0.5 mg (unopposed vagal effect) Use in sinus bradycardia + vagal triggers; expect HR rise to 100–130
Epinephrine 2–10 mcg/min IV infusion 2–5 min Alpha + beta agonist; increases HR, contractility, BP Tachycardia, arrhythmias, increased myocardial O₂ demand; may cause hypertension Preferred if hypotensive; safe in CAD
Isoproterenol 2–10 mcg/min IV infusion 2–5 min Pure beta agonist; increases HR + contractility Coronary steal in CAD; hypotension; arrhythmias Use caution with ischemia; less preferred than epi
Dopamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min IV infusion 3–5 min Dose-dependent: low (2–5) dopamine; mid (5–10) beta; high (>10) alpha Unpredictable effects; arrhythmias Rarely used as bradycardia-only agent; consider other infusions first

Medication principles:

  • Atropine is the initial agent for symptomatic sinus bradycardia, particularly with vagal triggers (suctioning, bowel distention)
  • Chronotropic infusions (epi/dopamine/isoproterenol) are preferred for unstable AV block and pacer-dependent loss of capture
  • Hold beta-blockers and diltiazem during unstable bradycardia; restart cautiously once stable
  • Avoid atropine in heart transplant (denervated graft will not respond)

sections.heading: 7.6 Transcutaneous Pacing Technique
sections.bodyHtml:
Step-by-step:

  1. Preparation:

    • Dry the skin completely; clip (do not shave) excess hair to reduce artifact
    • Apply pads: anterior-lateral preferred (right pad mid-axillary line at 5th space; left pad anterior axillary at 4th–5th space) OR anterior-posterior for large breasts/hairy chest

  2. Initiation:

    • Set rate: typically 60–80 bpm for post-op cardiac
    • Mode: demand mode (not asynchronous) unless sensing failure suspected
    • Start output at 0 mA

  3. Titration:

    • Increase output in 5–10 mA increments watching for electrical capture (wide QRS after each spike)
    • Continue increasing until electrical capture achieved (usually 50–100 mA)

  4. Verify mechanical capture:

    • Palpate femoral or carotid pulse — must be synchronous with pacer spike
    • Watch BP waveform — should show synchronous pulse pressure
    • Electrical capture ≠ mechanical capture; BOTH required

  5. Safety margin: - Once mechanical capture confirmed, increase output 5–10 mA higher for overcapture buffer

  6. Analgesia:

    • Transcutaneous pacing is PAINFUL. Order fentanyl 25–50 mcg IV bolus or morphine 2–4 mg NOW.
    • Consider IV sedation per institutional policy (propofol, midazolam)
    • Do not delay pacing for analgesia if patient is hemodynamically critical

  7. Duration:

    • Do NOT use transcutaneous pacing long-term (max 2 hours)
    • Transition to transvenous wire or permanent pacemaker as soon as possible (Kusumoto et al., 2019)

sections.heading: 7.7 Special Subgroups and Edge Cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Heart transplant:

  • Denervated graft does not respond to atropine or standard reflex-mediated mechanisms
  • New bradycardia = acute rejection until proven otherwise
  • Rely on chronotropic infusions (epinephrine, isoproterenol)
  • Contact transplant team immediately; biopsy/echo often needed

MAZE procedure:

  • Early junctional rhythms (POD 0–2) common and expected from atrial ablation
  • Do NOT default to pacing — most self-resolve by POD 5–7 as edema resolves
  • If symptomatic, rate control + atropine or chronotropic support sufficient
  • DCCV usually ineffective until atrial scarring matures (~4 weeks)

Low ejection fraction (EF <35%):

  • Intolerant of rapid rates (demands increase, ischemia worsens)
  • Even junctional rhythm at HR 40 may decompensate
  • Lower threshold for transcutaneous pacing + chronotropic support

Patients with mechanical mitral or aortic valve:

  • Thromboembolism risk high with bradycardia (stasis in LA/LV)
  • More aggressive rate support + anticoagulation strategy

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in Currently Stable Patients
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear in a currently stable patient, re-escalate.

  • HR trending further down despite intervention — progressive nodal depression or block progression
  • Pacer capture/sensing thresholds rising shift-to-shift (>1 mA) — suggests lead displacement or insulation break
  • Thresholds rising despite normal K⁺/Mg²⁺ — indicates wire problem, not medication effect
  • New QRS widening (>120 ms) — block progression from AV node to infranodal level
  • New ectopy or PVCs on atropine or catecholamine drips — toxicity or underlying irritability
  • Worsening mental status (confusion, drowsiness, combativeness) — cerebral hypoperfusion
  • New chest pain or pressure — ischemia, pericarditis, or wire-related perforation
  • Ischemic ECG changes on serial 12-leads — inferior or anterior wall MI
  • BP trending down despite fluid/pressor support — cardiogenic shock
  • Pulse pressure narrowing (SBP − DBP <30) — low cardiac output
  • Urine output dropping (<0.5 mL/kg/h) — end-organ hypoperfusion
  • QTc prolonging on amiodarone (approaching 500 ms) — torsades risk
  • Loss of capture on pacer-dependent patient — even if still perfusing, high risk of rapid decompensation

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Hypokalemia is a hidden threshold killer that mimics wire failure. A patient with K⁺ 3.2 and rising thresholds is not losing the wire — correct K⁺ ≥ 4.0 and recheck thresholds post-replacement. Most capture threshold rises are electrolyte-related, not hardware.

  2. Know your pacer-dependent patients. A patient with minimal spontaneous rhythm and rising thresholds is a slowly unfolding emergency. Distinguish from stable sinus bradycardia with intact backup.

  3. Connections first — 80% of "pacer failure" is a loose sterile connector, not lead displacement or fracture. Inspect and reseat before escalating.

  4. Atropine is ineffective in AV nodal block. Mobitz I and 2° block with dropped beats will not improve with atropine. Use transcutaneous pacing + epinephrine/isoproterenol instead. Save atropine for sinus bradycardia.

  5. Transplant heart is denervated — atropine is useless. New bradycardia in transplant = rejection until proven otherwise. Use chronotropic infusion and notify transplant team immediately.

  6. Atropine dose matters. Doses <0.5 mg may paradoxically worsen bradycardia (unopposed vagal effect). Always give ≥0.5 mg.

  7. Wenckebach (Mobitz I) is usually benign and self-resolves; Mobitz II and complete heart block (3°) often progress and require pacing. Watch the trend; don't assume all AV blocks are created equal.

  8. Persistent AV block >5–8 days post-op warrants PPM evaluation. Don't delay the decision; waiting beyond this window increases morbidity/mortality risk.

  9. Avoid high-dose beta-blockers in 1° or 2° AV block. Beta-blockers can convert benign block to higher-degree block. Hold or reduce dose once bradycardia develops.

  10. Carotid sinus massage and Valsalva maneuver exacerbate bradycardia. Avoid in unstable patients; only trained EP clinicians should attempt in stable, monitored settings.

  11. Atrial wires can be diagnostic. Atrial electrogram clarifies junctional rhythm vs ectopic vs paced rhythm. Ask pacer technician if available.

  12. Transcutaneous pacing is very painful — sedate BEFORE pacing, not after. Have fentanyl/morphine drawn up and ready.

  13. Document the underlying intrinsic rhythm by briefly reducing pacer rate to 30–40 bpm (if stable BP-wise) to see what rhythm the heart maintains. Informs PPM programming and prognosis.

  14. Dig toxicity mimics AV block. Check digoxin level; bradycardia + PVCs + AV block = classic dig tox triad. Verify no recent digoxin overdose before attributing block to surgery.

  15. Post-AVR patients awaiting PPM often need patience and support. Wait the 5–7 day window; many recover. Premature PPM implantation exposes patient to device complications and long-term pacemaker dependency.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) — Three Surgical Approaches

  • On-pump CABG (traditional): Median sternotomy; full cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB); moderate hypothermia; aortic cross-clamp with cardioplegia; typically 2–4 grafts in 60–120 min of CPB. Most common approach; ~80% of CABG volume. Routine recovery POD 5–7 home.
  • Off-pump CABG (OPCAB): Median sternotomy; CPB on standby (not used); beating-heart revascularization on stabilizer device; no aortic clamp; shorter CPB exposure, lower systemic inflammation, reduced stroke risk (1–2% vs. 2–3% on-pump), but technically demanding and incomplete revascularization risk. Selected for high-risk patients (age >70, CKD, carotid disease) or surgeon preference.
  • MIDCAB: Minimally invasive; small anterior thoracotomy; LIMA-to-LAD only; off-pump; often hybrid with percutaneous intervention to remaining vessels. Niche indication; expert centers only.

Who Gets CABG and Why

  • Left main coronary artery disease (≥ 50% stenosis) — superior survival vs. PCI
  • Three-vessel disease with reduced EF (< 40%) — superior survival vs. PCI (FREEDOM trial)
  • Two-vessel disease including proximal LAD — especially if EF reduced
  • Failed PCI (restenosis, diffuse disease, poor targets)
  • Concurrent valve disease requiring surgical repair/replacement
  • Post-MI mechanical complication (VSD, papillary muscle rupture) — CABG often concurrent

Graft Conduit Selection by Target

Graft Target Vessel Patency at 1 yr Patency at 5 yr Patency at 10 yr Ideal Use Special Considerations
LIMA (Left Internal Mammary) LAD (best outcome) > 95% > 90% > 80% Standard to LAD — single most determinant of long-term survival Low mediastinitis risk; pleural entry near-universal (LLL effusion expected); left-side weakness/climbing stairs 3–6 mo common; no endarterectomy needed
RIMA / BIMA Circumflex, RCA (sequential if multiple targets) 85–90% 75–85% 60–70% BIMA = two arteries → superior long-term outcomes; avoid BIMA if DM + obesity (DSWI risk ↑) Bilateral harvest → longer pump time, higher bleeding; skeletal necrosis risk if sternal devascularization; requires careful sternal flow assessment
SVG (Saphenous Vein) RCA, OM, diagonal (non-LAD targets) 80–85% 60–70% 40–50% Standard venous conduit; durable in high-flow targets Requires DAPT × 1 year; atherosclerosis process accelerated in SVG; harvest site edema/infection risk; EVH reduces morbidity vs. open harvest
Radial Artery Circumflex, OM, diagonal (non-LAD targets) 85–90% 80–85% 75–80% Superior to SVG for non-LAD (better patency) Spasm risk (intraop + POD); requires calcium-channel blocker ± nitrates; Allen's test pre-op mandatory; cold hand postop = emergency check; forearm incision healing slow

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why this happens — novice + advanced beginner teaching.

Coronary Artery Disease & Indications for CABG

Coronary artery disease (CAD) occurs when atherosclerotic plaque narrows one or more epicardial coronary arteries, limiting myocardial blood flow and causing ischemia. The left anterior descending (LAD) supplies the anterior wall and septum; the left circumflex (LCx) supplies the lateral wall and obtuse marginals (OM); the right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the inferior wall and right ventricle.

Severe CAD (≥ 70% stenosis for single/dual vessel, ≥ 50% for left main) carries high risk of myocardial infarction and death. Surgical revascularization (CABG) is superior to percutaneous intervention (PCI) in specific high-risk subsets:

  • Left main disease (30–40% of CABG population)
  • Three-vessel disease with reduced ejection fraction (EF < 40%) — the FREEDOM trial (2012) and ISCHEMIA trial (2019) affirmed CABG superiority in multivessel CAD with substantial ischemia
  • Incomplete revascularization achievable only via surgery

On-Pump vs. Off-Pump Physiology

On-pump CABG uses a cardiopulmonary bypass machine (heart-lung machine) that assumes gas exchange and circulation while the heart is arrested (cardioplegia) and surgeon operates in a bloodless field. Advantages: clear operative field, complete revascularization, ability to perform multiple grafts. Disadvantages: systemic inflammatory response (CPB-induced SIRS), hemodilution, hemolysis, platelet dysfunction, bleeding risk, higher stroke rate (2–3%) from aortic manipulation and emboli.

Off-pump CABG (OPCAB) avoids CPB entirely; the heart beats while the surgeon uses a stabilizer device to immobilize the target vessel region. Advantages: no CPB inflammation, lower transfusion need, lower stroke rate (1–2%), faster recovery. Disadvantages: technically demanding (steep learning curve), smaller operative field, incomplete revascularization more common, hemodynamic instability possible during graft placement, longer operative time.

The SYNTAX trial (2008) and ART trial (2016) examined on-pump vs. off-pump outcomes: stroke and mortality similar at 1 year; long-term graft patency favors on-pump (complete revascularization), but individual patient selection matters (elderly, high-risk patients may benefit from OPCAB).

Graft Biology & Patency Mechanisms

LIMA (Internal Mammary Artery) is the gold standard. A muscular artery, the LIMA has unique endothelial properties (low thrombogenicity, high resistance to atherosclerosis) and superior long-term patency (> 90% at 5 years, > 80% at 10 years). The LIMA to LAD is the single most important determinant of long-term and event-free survival post-CABG (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020). Even in OPCAB (where incomplete revascularization is a risk), LIMA-to-LAD is almost always performed.

Radial Artery grafts offer superior patency to SVG for non-LAD targets (80–85% at 5 years) because radial is muscular/arterial and resistant to atherosclerosis, unlike SVG. However, radial artery has high propensity for vasospasm — both intraoperatively (during harvest/manipulation) and postoperatively. Prophylactic calcium-channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) and nitrates are standard in radial graft patients. If radial graft spasm occurs intraoperatively, nicardipine or nitroprusside is used to relax the vessel.

Saphenous Vein (SVG) grafts are readily available, carry low morbidity if harvested endoscopically (EVH), and have acceptable short-term patency (80–85% at 1 year). However, SVG undergoes medial smooth-muscle proliferation and atherosclerosis at accelerated rates compared to native coronary arteries. Patency drops to 60–70% at 5 years and 40–50% at 10 years.

Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) — ASA + clopidogrel (Plavix) — × 1 year is mandatory to reduce early SVG thrombosis and slow atherosclerotic degeneration. Lifelong ASA continues.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Operative Course
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner understanding of who arrives on the unit and operative flow.

Pre-Op Profile

  • Symptomatic or ischemia-induced CAD (angina, ACS, ischemia on stress test)
  • Angiography-proven: left main ≥ 50%, three-vessel ≥ 70%, or high-risk subset
  • Variable EF: preserved (55–60%) to reduced (30–35% or less)
  • High-risk comorbidities common: age > 70, diabetes (25–30%), CKD, COPD, carotid disease, prior stroke
  • Pre-op medications: ASA (not held day-of-surgery), beta-blocker, statin, ACE-I, diuretics

Operative Details

  • Approach: Median sternotomy standard (can be ministernotomy or mini-thoracotomy in MIDCAB)
  • CPB (on-pump): Moderate hypothermia (28–32 °C); aortic cross-clamp; antegrade ± retrograde cardioplegia (cold blood or crystalloid)
  • CPB standby (off-pump): Beating heart; stabilizer device; NO aortic clamp or cardioplegia
  • Pump time: On-pump CABG 60–120 min; OPCAB 90–150 min (longer due to technical difficulty of beating-heart grafting)
  • Grafts: Typically LIMA-to-LAD (standard) + 1–3 additional grafts (SVG or radial) to RCA, OM, diagonal
  • Epicardial pacing wires: Placed at close (standard safeguard for rhythm disturbances)
  • Chest tubes: 1–2 mediastinal; sometimes 1 pleural (if left pleura entered during LIMA harvest)

Expected Post-Op Course — ICU (POD 0)

  • Arrival intubated, sedated, mild active warming; continuous CT output monitoring q15 min → q1h
  • Low-dose NTG running × 24 h for graft protection (prevents radial/SVG spasm, protects grafts)
  • Extubation readiness 4–6 h post-op: assess FiO₂ requirement, PEEP, sedation, mental status
  • Bleeding assessment: CT output trend; transfuse PRBC if Hgb < 8 (< 9 if age/CAD); check INR + PT/PTT, fibrinogen if high output (> 200 mL/h)
  • Pacer wire threshold check; baseline rhythm ECG
  • Labs: CBC, BMP, lactate; baseline LDH/haptoglobin if mechanical issue suspected
  • Vasopressor wean by POD 1 goal

Expected Post-Op Course — POD 1–3 (ICU → Stepdown Transition)

  • Out of bed to chair POD 1; walking POD 2–3 with PT/OT support
  • A-line removed POD 1–2 if MAP stable without pressors
  • CTs out POD 2–3 if mediastinal drainage < 150 mL/8 h × 2 consecutive 8-hour periods (no air leak). Pleural tube out when output minimal or reexpands.
  • Pacer wires remain through POD 3–4 (POAF risk peaks POD 2–3; arrhythmia pacing may be needed)
  • Beta-blocker + statin initiated (cardioprotection, arrhythmia prevention)
  • Foley removed POD 1–2 (mobility and CAUTI prevention)
  • Transfer to stepdown when: hemodynamically stable off pressors or low-dose dopamine, extubated, rhythm stable or pacer wires functional, CTs out or manageable, tele-capable
  • Amiodarone 200 mg PO daily started for AF prophylaxis (varies by surgeon)

Expected Post-Op Course — POD 4–7 (Stepdown/Discharge)

  • Rhythm monitoring continues; heart block or delayed POAF possible POD 4–5
  • Pacer wires removed POD 4–5 or per surgeon (baseline CXR post-removal if wires had been capturing)
  • Labs: trend CBC, BMP, electrolytes; early labs can be discontinued if stable
  • Wound checks; incision care teaching (sternal precautions × 6–8 weeks)
  • Discharge medications finalized: ASA 81 daily indefinitely + Plavix 75 daily × 1 year (DAPT standard for SVG/radial); beta-blocker + statin indefinite; bowel regimen completion
  • Discharge goal: POD 5–7 for routine uncomplicated CABG
  • Cardiac rehab referral (Class I recommendation; improves outcomes, mortality reduction)
  • Follow-up: surgeon 1–2 weeks (incision check), 4–6 weeks (full assessment)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: 2 min at bedside.

Vital Signs & Hemodynamics

  • Heart rate, blood pressure, MAP, SpO₂, CVP if central line in place
  • Perfusion: capillary refill, skin warmth/color, extremity temperature
  • Urine output (target > 0.5 mL/kg/h); estimate from Foley or incontinent episodes

Cardiac & Respiratory

  • Breath sounds bilaterally (rule out atelectasis, effusion, pneumothorax post-CT removal)
  • Heart sounds: regular vs. irregular; mechanical valve click (if concurrent valve surgery); new murmur
  • JVD, orthopnea, rales (signs of heart failure or tamponade)
  • Chest tube output: color (serosanguinous expected), quantity per 8h; any air leak

Neurologic

  • Alert & oriented × 3; any acute mental status change (delirium risk POD 1–3)
  • Focal deficits: arm drift, speech clarity, facial symmetry (stroke screening every shift POD 0–3)

Surgical Incision & Lines

  • Sternotomy: erythema, warmth, purulent drainage, sternal click/instability (sign of infection/dehiscence)
  • Pacer wires (two epicardial screws RV): intact, position stable
  • Chest tubes (1–2): mediastinal ± pleural; output color/quantity; any air leak
  • Harvest sites: LIMA (left anterior chest), SVG (lower extremity), radial (forearm)
  • Assess for erythema, swelling, hematoma, drainage
  • ACE wrap on SVG harvest leg — should be at 24 h post-op mark; if present and overdue, note for removal

Recent Labs (Last 4–6 Hours)

  • CBC: Hgb trend (transfusion threshold Hgb < 8; < 9 if age >70, CAD, comorbidity)
  • BMP: K⁺ (goal ≥ 4.0), Mg²⁺ (goal ≥ 2.0 to prevent POAF), Cr (trend for AKI)
  • Coagulation: PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen if heavy bleeding
  • Lactate: trend for low output or ischemia

Rhythm & Pacer Status

  • ECG rhythm: rate, regularity, ectopy
  • Pacer wire setting: mode, rate, threshold, sensed activity (if applicable)
  • Any pacing spikes captured; loss of capture = urgent attention

sections.heading: 5. Management by Post-Operative Day Arc
sections.bodyHtml: Table-first structure. POD trajectory replaces Stable/Unstable fork for surgery cards.

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 (ICU)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Extubation, rule out life-threatening complications, establish baseline, graft protection

Task Action Target
Extubation readiness FiO₂ ≤ 40%, PEEP ≤ 5, adequate spontaneous respiratory effort, alert mental status; no ongoing hemodynamic collapse 4–6 h post-op extubation goal
Bleeding assessment CT output q15min → q1h; trend visual appearance (serosanguinous expected); transfuse PRBC if Hgb < 8 (< 9 if age >70/CAD); check INR + PT/PTT, fibrinogen if drainage > 200 mL/h CT < 200 mL/h; Hgb stable; coags normalized
NTG for graft protection Low-dose NTG (0.5–1 mcg/kg/min) running × 24 h to prevent radial/SVG spasm 24 h post-op (taper/discontinue POD 1)
Pacer wire check Capture threshold (≤ 5 mA is normal; > 7 mA concerning); sense (should see atrial + ventricular spikes); document baseline; ECG for LBBB/widened QRS Thresholds/sense recorded; ECG baseline in chart
Hemodynamics Target MAP ≥ 70 (perfusion pressure), SBP 100–140 (avoid graft tension/dehiscence), HR 60–90 (avoid tachycardia-induced demand ischemia), UOP > 0.5 mL/kg/h Parameters within range; wean vasopressors if possible
Electrolytes baseline K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 (POAF prevention); check Ca²⁺, Ph; replace if low K⁺, Mg²⁺ in target range
Labs CBC, BMP, lactate, PT/PTT/INR, fibrinogen; LDH/haptoglobin baseline (hemolysis screening); blood glucose (non-diabetics often elevated post-CPB) Labs reviewed, trends noted
Glycemic control Glucose target 140–180 mg/dL post-op (tighter control reduces POAF, infection, LOS); correctional insulin per protocol if > 180; monitor q4h or per unit protocol Glucose 140–180; insulin ordered

Electrolytes K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 (critical for POAF prevention); recheck after replacement; Mg²⁺ < 1.8 causes refractory hypokalemia K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0; rechecked

sections.heading: 5C. POD 4–7 (Stepdown / Discharge Planning)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Prepare discharge medications, remove lines/wires, finalize teaching, confirm follow-up

Task Action Target
Pacer wire removal POD 4–5 per surgeon preference. Do NOT remove early — delayed AV block or bradyarrhythmia possible POD 4–5. Obtain baseline CXR after removal. Wires removed; CXR post-removal
Discharge medications — Final List Mandatory indefinite: ASA 81 mg daily; beta-blocker (HR goal 55–70); statin 80 mg high-intensity; ACE-I cardioprotection. × 1 year: Plavix 75 mg daily (if SVG/radial grafts). Bowel regimen: Docusate 200 mg BID, senna 2 tabs qHS PRN, MOM PRN; taper opioids by POD 10–14. Optional: Amiodarone 200 mg daily (AF prophylaxis, surgeon-dependent); PPI if high-risk for stress ulcer. Discharge med list reviewed with patient + family; verified against home list
Discharge teaching (1) ASA + Plavix: "ASA forever, Plavix for 1 year — both protect your new grafts. Never stop ASA. Never stop Plavix without surgeon OK." (2) Medications: Explain each drug and why (statin = cholesterol, beta-blocker = heart rate, ACE = heart protection). Take list home. (3) Activity: Walking encouraged daily; sexual activity 4–6 weeks; no lifting > 10 lbs × 3 months; no driving × 4–6 weeks. (4) Sternal precautions: Arm support × 6–8 weeks; no arm crossing; pillow hug when cough. (5) Wound care: Keep sternum clean/dry; watch for redness, drainage, warmth (call surgeon if present). (6) Harvest site leg/forearm: Elevate leg 3–4 weeks; watch for swelling, redness, drainage. Radial graft forearm: watch for cold hand or numbness (call surgeon). (7) Cardiac rehab: Start phase 2 in 3–4 weeks; provides supervised exercise + education. (8) Follow-up: Surgeon 1 week (incision), 4–6 weeks (full); PCP for chronic management. (9) Symptoms to report: Chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, fever, leg swelling, new weakness. Teaching documented; patient/family verbalized understanding; written discharge sheet given
Cardiac rehab referral Class I recommendation — mortality reduction, improved outcomes. Contact rehab program; confirm enrollment POD 3–4. Referral sent; patient has contact info + start date
Labs — Early D/C possible If CBC, BMP stable and no ongoing bleeding/electrolyte issues, can D/C labs early (POD 3–4). Recheck only if new issue. Labs discontinued if stable; plan documented
Wound check Inspect sternum and harvest sites; assess for erythema, drainage, dehiscence. Obtain cultures if purulent drainage. Photograph per [Institution policy] if any concern for infection. Wound documented; culture sent if indicated; infection ruled out

Who to Call — By Scenario

Situation Contact Urgency

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections expandable for expert skim.

7.1 — Coronary Artery Anatomy & Graft Selection by Target The Three Coronary Systems
  • Left Anterior Descending (LAD): Supplies anterior wall, septum, and diagonal branches. Most critical vessel — LAD occlusion often results in large MI and low EF. Best served by LIMA.
  • Left Circumflex (LCx): Supplies lateral wall and obtuse marginals (OM1, OM2). Often overlooked clinically (often occluded late in disease progression). Radial or SVG acceptable.
  • Right Coronary Artery (RCA): Supplies inferior wall, RV, and AV nodal branches. RCA occlusion can cause RV infarction ± bradyarrhythmia. SVG standard; radial acceptable. LIMA-to-LAD: The Gold Standard Graft The left internal mammary artery (LIMA) to LAD is the single most important determinant of long-term and event-free survival post-CABG. Reasons:
  • Superior patency: > 95% at 1 year, > 90% at 5 years, > 80% at 10 years (vs. SVG 60–70% at 5 years)
  • Low atherosclerosis rate: LIMA has unique endothelial biology; resists atherosclerotic changes
  • Better outcomes: Patients with LIMA-to-LAD have longer survival and fewer reoperations compared to LIMA-to-non-LAD or SVG-to-LAD Routine strategy: LIMA to LAD (always attempted unless contraindicated by anatomy or prior LIMA use). If LAD is a poor target (small, diffusely diseased), LIMA may go to diagonal or LCx, and another graft (SVG or radial) goes to LAD. --- Graft Selection by Non-LAD Targets
    Target1st Choice2nd ChoiceAvoid
    Circumflex / OMRadial artery (superior patency: 80–85% @ 5yr)SVG (acceptable, 60–70% @ 5yr)RIMA in young patient (better reserved for RCA)
    RCASVG (high-flow, durable)Radial (acceptable; may have spasm risk in RCA due to flow mismatch)RIMA if available for circumflex instead (OM graft with RIMA acceptable but not preferred)
    DiagonalSVG or radial (both acceptable)RIMA (if LIMA-to-LAD done)—
    --- Special Case: Sequential Grafting (BIMA or RIMA for Multiple Targets)
  • BIMA (Bilateral Internal Mammary): Uses both LIMA and right internal mammary (RIMA); RIMA typically serves RCA or sequential to OM+RCA. Superior long-term outcomes (lower reop rates) compared to LIMA + SVG. However: DSWI risk significantly higher if DM + obesity. Many surgeons avoid BIMA in diabetics to mitigate sternal infection.
  • RIMA alone: Grafts RCA or OM; LIMA to LAD standard. RIMA provides improved durability vs. SVG for RCA. ---
7.2 — On-Pump vs. Off-Pump Physiology & Trade-offs On-Pump CABG (Cardiopulmonary Bypass) Mechanism: Heart arrested with cardioplegia (cold potassium-containing solution); external pump provides circulation and gas exchange; aorta cross-clamped. Advantages:
  • Clear operative field (bloodless, easier for surgeon)
  • Ability to perform multiple grafts efficiently
  • Lower operative time
  • Easier coronary endarterectomy if needed
  • Can do concurrent valve surgery without additional complexity Disadvantages:
  • Systemic inflammatory response (SIRS): CPB triggers complement cascade, cytokine release, endothelial activation
  • Hemodilution (dilute hemoglobin, coagulation factors)
  • Platelet dysfunction (thrombocytopenia + dysfunction)
  • Higher transfusion requirement
  • Higher stroke rate (2–3%) from aortic atheroma mobilization, emboli, hypoperfusion
  • Postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) more common (~35–40%)
  • Renal injury risk (ischemia-reperfusion, low flow states) Post-op manifestations: More bleeding, more need for blood products, higher POAF risk, slower cognitive recovery. --- Off-Pump CABG (OPCAB) Mechanism: Heart beating; surgeon uses a stabilizer device to immobilize target vessel; CPB on standby (can be activated emergently if patient becomes hemodynamically unstable). Advantages:
  • No CPB inflammation (no complement activation, lower cytokine surge)
  • Lower transfusion requirement (avoids hemodilution, platelet dysfunction)
  • Lower stroke rate (1–2%) — no aortic clamp, less aortic manipulation
  • Faster recovery (less inflammation)
  • Potentially good for high-risk patients (elderly, CKD, carotid disease) Disadvantages:
  • Technically demanding (steep learning curve for surgeon + team)
  • Smaller operative field (stabilizer limits access)
  • Hemodynamic instability during graft placement (moving the heart for vessel exposure can reduce LV filling temporarily)
  • Higher incomplete revascularization rate (10–20% of target vessels not grafted due to technical difficulty or surgeon discretion)
  • Longer operative time
  • Not suitable for all anatomy (e.g., RCA graft very difficult off-pump if not accessible) Post-op manifestations: Less bleeding, fewer transfusions, lower POAF risk, but risk of graft failure if revascularization incomplete. --- SYNTAX and ART Trials — Evidence Summary
    • SYNTAX trial (2008): Compared CABG vs. PCI for complex CAD. Showed CABG superior for 3-vessel disease; outcomes similar (stroke, MI, mortality) at 1 year, but long-term graft patency issues in both groups.
    • ART trial (2016): On-pump vs. off-pump CABG. No difference in 1-year mortality or stroke. Off-pump had slightly lower transfusion; on-pump had better graft patency (more complete revascularization). Long-term outcomes (5 year) showed benefit of on-pump for graft patency, but mortality similar. Bottom line: Surgeon expertise matters most; on-pump better for complete revascularization; off-pump reasonable for high-risk, selected patients. ---
7.3 — Graft-Specific Physiology: LIMA, Radial, SVG LIMA Physiology & Harvest Considerations The left internal mammary artery arises from the left subclavian artery and runs down the left anterior chest wall in the mediastinum, just lateral to the sternum. It supplies intercostal branches (anterior left ribs) and perforating branches to the chest wall. Harvest: Surgeon opens left pleura (near-universal); dissects LIMA from mediastinal tissue; ligates intercostal branches. The left lower lobe atelectasis and pleural effusion are expected, near-universal findings post-LIMA harvest — not pathologic unless large/compressive. Consequences of LIMA harvest:
  • Left-sided pleural effusion (common, usually small, self-limited)
  • Left lower lobe atelectasis (shallow breathing, pain-related; encourage incentive spirometry)
  • Left chest wall numbness (intercostal nerve irritation; resolves in weeks)
  • Occasional chylothorax (rare, lymphatic duct injury; presents as milky drainage)
  • Weakness in left arm/shoulder (LIMA dissection denervates some pectoral muscles; improves over 3–6 months) Postoperative pearls:
  • Persistent LLL atelectasis is expected; aggressive pulmonary toilet (IS, ambulation, pain control) standard
  • Pleural effusion < 1 L usually observed; larger effusions may require thoracentesis
  • Climbing stairs or heavy lifting causes transient left anterior chest wall pain (costochondral/muscular) for weeks; distinguish from angina --- Radial Artery Graft Physiology The radial artery is a muscular artery in the forearm. It is an excellent conduit due to:
  • Muscular medial layer (resistant to atherosclerosis)
  • Small size (similar caliber to LAD)
  • Superior patency vs. SVG (80–85% at 5 years vs. 60–70%) Harvest: Forearm incision (wrist to elbow); radial artery isolated and ligated distally (ulnar artery provides collateral blood flow via palmar arch). Allen's test pre-op confirms ulnar adequacy. Critical post-op issue: Radial Artery Spasm:
  • Intraoperative spasm during harvest/manipulation is common; can be reversed with nicardipine (5–10 mcg IV) or nitroprusside
  • Postoperative vasospasm can occur POD 0–3; patient reports cold hand, cyanosis, numbness. Treated with:
  • Keep arm warm (blanket, avoid ice packs)
  • Calcium-channel blocker (diltiazem 60 mg PO TID or long-acting equivalent)
  • Avoid vasoconstrictors (norepinephrine preferred over phenylephrine if pressors needed)
  • Nitroglycerin patch or oral nitrates Postoperative complications:
  • Cold hand, pulseless radial: Call surgeon immediately; assess Allen's test, initiate vasodilation protocol
  • Forearm incision slow to heal: Delayed wound healing (weeks); elevate arm for 3–4 weeks
  • Numbness in thumb/index (lateral forearm): Radial sensory nerve irritation; resolves in weeks Patient teaching:
  • "You have a small incision on your forearm. Keep it clean and dry. Elevate arm for 3–4 weeks."
  • "If your hand becomes cold or numb, call your surgeon immediately."
  • "Don't lift heavy things with that arm for 3 months." --- Saphenous Vein Graft (SVG) Physiology The saphenous vein (long saphenous, not short saphenous) is harvested from the inner thigh, from groin to knee. It is:
  • Easily accessible, ample length/diameter
  • Compatible with arterial pressures (with adaptation)
  • But subject to accelerated atherosclerotic degeneration Why SVG fails over time:
  • Endothelial injury during harvest
  • Smooth muscle layer proliferation (intimal hyperplasia) — SVG undergoes medial smooth-muscle migration and proliferation, a process exacerbated by high-flow arterial pressures
  • Atherosclerotic plaque forms rapidly (years vs. decades in native coronary)
  • Antiplatelet therapy (ASA + Plavix) slows but doesn't prevent this process Patency decline:
  • 1 year: 80–85% (relatively good)
  • 5 years: 60–70% (significant drop)
  • 10 years: 40–50% (majority have some disease) Mitigation strategies:
  • DAPT (Dual Antiplatelet Therapy): ASA 81 mg + clopidogrel (Plavix) 75 mg daily × 1 year — reduces early SVG thrombosis and slows atherosclerosis. Lifelong ASA after year 1.
  • Statin high-intensity: Slows atherosclerotic process in SVG; indefinite
  • ACE inhibitor: Cardioprotection; reduces remodeling Harvest considerations:
  • Open harvest (traditional): Long incision; higher wound complications (hematoma, seroma, infection)
  • Endoscopic vein harvest (EVH): Smaller incisions, less leg wound morbidity, acceptable patency (similar to open). Standard at many centers now.
  • ACE wrap × 24 hours: Compression dressing on harvest leg; reduces swelling and hematoma Postoperative leg management:
  • Elevation × 3–4 weeks (reduces edema, seroma risk)
  • Compression stocking optional
  • Watch for cellulitis (warmth, redness, drainage)
  • Some swelling expected; persistent swelling after month = notify surgeon ---
7.4 — POAF (Post-Operative Atrial Fibrillation) — Mechanism & Prevention Why POAF Occurs POAF is the most common complication post-CABG (~30–40% incidence, peaks POD 2–3). Multiple mechanisms:
  • Atrial inflammation from CPB, surgical manipulation, pericardial irritation
  • Sympathetic surge from surgical stress, pain, catecholamines
  • Electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia)
  • Hypoxia, fever, sepsis — nonspecific triggers
  • Withdrawal of beta-blockers (if discontinued pre-op)
  • Ischemia (less common; usually if graft failure) Risk factors for POAF:
  • Age > 70 (highest risk)
  • Pre-existing AF or paroxysmal AF
  • Reduced EF
  • Diabetes
  • Chronic kidney disease
  • Prolonged CPB time --- Prevention Strategies — POD 0–3
    StrategyMechanismEvidence
    Beta-blockersRate control + antiarrhythmic (continued from pre-op or restarted POD 1)Standard; Class I recommendation
    Magnesium repletionMg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 prevents electrolyte-induced arrhythmiasStrong evidence; often used prophylactically
    Potassium repletionK⁺ ≥ 4.0 prevents hypokalemia-induced arrhythmiasStandard practice; critical for POAF prevention
    Amiodarone 200 mg PO dailyIa + III antiarrhythmic; prophylaxis POD 1–3 or longerSurgeon-dependent; variable adoption
    StatinsPleiotropic anti-inflammatory effectSome evidence; standard post-CABG anyway
    PacingAtrial or AV pacing at rate > 90 to suppress ectopyNot standard prophylaxis
    --- Recognition & Management of POAF — See Scenario Card Irregularly irregular rhythm, HR often > 110, symptoms (palpitations, dyspnea, chest discomfort, syncope). Management: replace electrolytes (K⁺ ≥ 4, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2), confirm with 12-lead ECG, escalate to team for rate control (beta-blocker, diltiazem, verapamil, digoxin) or rhythm control (amiodarone IV, sotalol) depending on hemodynamics and presentation. ---
7.5 — LIMA Pleural Involvement & Left Lower Lobe Atelectasis Pleural Entry During LIMA Harvest LIMA dissection from the mediastinum requires entry into the left pleura to mobilize the artery safely and ligate intercostal branches. This is routine and expected. Consequence: Pleural Effusion (Small, Self-Limited)
  • Incidence: Present in 50–80% of LIMA patients by CXR POD 1–2
  • Character: Usually serosanguinous (blood-tinged from harvest), left-sided
  • Volume: Most are small (< 500 mL); some modest (500–1000 mL); large (> 1000 mL) rare
  • Clinical significance: Small effusions are NOT pathologic — simply the result of pleural irritation. Do NOT drain unless symptomatic (dyspnea, large volume, hemoptysis). Management:
  • Observe small effusions; resolve over weeks
  • Large effusions (if causing dyspnea/hypoxemia): consider therapeutic thoracentesis or pigtail placement
  • Only drain if patient has symptoms; culture if purulent (infection) --- Left Lower Lobe Atelectasis
  • Incidence: Near-universal finding POD 1–2
  • Mechanism: Shallow breathing (sternal pain), reduced pulmonary toilet, pleural irritation
  • CXR appearance: Consolidation ± atelectasis in left base
  • Clinical significance: Expected finding; does NOT indicate pneumonia unless fever + productive cough + infiltrate
  • Management: Aggressive pulmonary toilet
  • Incentive spirometry q1h awake
  • Ambulation POD 1–3
  • Adequate pain control (opioids + multimodal)
  • Chest physiotherapy if available
  • Nebulizers optional ---
7.6 — Bleeding Post-CABG: Coagulopathic vs. Surgical Hemostasis Expected Bleeding POD 0–1 Mild serosanguinous drainage (50–150 mL/h POD 0 → declining to 50–100 mL/h POD 1) is normal. Patient on full heparin during CPB; residual heparin + platelet dysfunction from CPB explains early bleeding. --- Differentiation: Coagulopathic Bleeding vs. Inadequate Surgical Hemostasis
FeatureCoagulopathicSurgical
TimingUsually POD 1–3 (persists after initial control)POD 0–1 (immediate or early)
CT output characterOozing, slow; brisk but persistentBrisk, then rapid filling if inadequate hemostasis
LabsLow platelets (<75K) or high INR (>1.5) or low fibrinogen (<100) or low factorsLabs normal or mildly low
Response to transfusionImproves with FFP/platelets/cryoprecipitateNo improvement; keeps bleeding
Exam findingsSometimes oozing from multiple sites; coagulopathy signs (bruising, petechiae)Bleeding localized to incision/CT sites
ManagementGive blood products (FFP, platelets, cryo); warm patient; target INR < 1.5, Plt > 50K, fibrinogen > 100Notify surgeon for return to OR if meets criteria
--- Re-op Bleeding Thresholds (when to return to OR for re-exploration) - > 400 mL/h × 1 consecutive hour
  • > 300 mL/h × 2–3 consecutive hours
  • > 200 mL/h × 4 consecutive hours
  • Always consider tamponade if CT output suddenly decreases (clotted tube, pericardial tamponade) — contact surgeon immediately --- Antifibrinolytic Use Some surgeons use tranexamic acid (TXA) intraoperatively to reduce bleeding. If used, takes effect over first 4–6 hours; reduces bleeding by ~30–50%. Still expect some oozing POD 0. ---
7.7 — Sternal Wound Infection (DSWI) & Risk Factors DSWI (Deep Sternal Wound Infection) Incidence & Consequence
  • Incidence: 0.5–2% of CABG patients; higher in high-risk groups
  • Mortality: ~10–20% even with aggressive treatment (surgical debridement, IV antibiotics, flap reconstruction)
  • Morbidity: Prolonged hospitalization, osteomyelitis, mediastinitis, sepsis --- Risk Factors for DSWI
    ModifiableNon-Modifiable
    Diabetes (especially if poorly controlled)Age > 70
    Obesity (BMI > 30)Female sex
    Bilateral internal mammary graft (BIMA) + DMCOPD
    Prolonged surgery (CPB time > 120 min)Immunosuppression
    Excessive bleeding / multiple transfusionsRe-do CABG
    Poor glycemic control post-op—
    High-Risk Profile: Diabetic + obese + BIMA = DSWI risk can reach 5–10%. Many surgeons avoid BIMA in diabetics to mitigate this risk. --- Recognition — Classic Triad
    1. Fever POD 3–10
    2. Sternal wound: erythema, warmth, purulent drainage, or sternal click (instability sign indicating bone involvement)
    3. Leukocytosis --- Management — Early Escalation Critical
    4. Cultures before antibiotics — swab or fluid for aerobic/anaerobic/fungal; blood cultures
    5. Notify CT surgery directly (not just resident or APP) — may need emergent debridement
    6. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam or equivalent per facility) initiated after cultures
    7. OR debridement — surgeon assesses extent, debrides necrotic bone/tissue, irrigates, obtains intraoperative cultures
    8. Flap reconstruction (pectoralis major or latissimus dorsi) common
    9. Continued IV antibiotics × 4–6 weeks depending on organism + extent ---
7.8 — Perioperative MI / Graft Occlusion Post-CABG Incidence & Timing
  • Early graft failure (< 30 days): 5–10% of grafts; usually technical (inadequate anastomosis, competitive flow, distal vessel too small)
  • Early perioperative MI: 2–4% of CABG patients; presents POD 0–3
  • Late graft failure (> 1 year): SVG atherosclerosis process --- Recognition — POD 0–3
  • Chest pain (may be masked by sedation/anesthesia POD 0)
  • New ST changes (inferior, anterior, or lateral depending on graft territory)
  • Troponin elevation beyond expected post-op rise
  • Hemodynamic change (hypotension, low output, arrhythmia)
  • New regional wall motion abnormality on bedside echo --- Differential Diagnosis
    CauseTimelineManagement
    LIMA-to-LAD thrombosisPOD 0–3EMERGENT: ECG + troponin + prep OR or cath (decision per surgeon/cardiology)
    SVG or radial graft thrombosisPOD 0–3EMERGENT: similar workup
    Native vessel progression / distal embolizationPOD 0–3STAT cardiology; may not be graft; assess LAD/LCx/RCA
    Radial graft vasospasmPOD 0–3Vasodilators (nitrates, calcium-channel blocker); usually not MI pattern
    Myocardial stunning (expected post-CPB)POD 0–1Supportive; serial troponins; usually resolves
    --- Post-op Troponin Interpretation Post-CABG troponin rise is expected from surgical manipulation, cross-clamp ischemia, reperfusion. Expected patterns:
  • POD 0: Troponin may be mildly elevated (< 1–2 ng/mL baseline in many labs)
  • POD 1: Troponin often peaks (can be 5–10 ng/mL or higher even without MI)
  • POD 2–3: Troponin should trend down If troponin is rising POD 2–3 (instead of falling) or accompanied by EKG changes: Think MI / graft failure. ---
7.9 — Discharge Antiplatelet Regimen: ASA + Plavix × 1 Year Standard Post-CABG Antiplatelet Therapy ASA 81 mg daily — LIFELONG. Do NOT hold pre-op; continue day-of-surgery and indefinitely. ASA prevents atherosclerotic events and graft thrombosis. Plavix 75 mg daily × 1 year — if SVG or radial grafts used. Rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) reduces early SVG graft thrombosis (within first month) and slows atherosclerotic degeneration in SVG. After 1 year, continue ASA alone (Plavix stopped). Special case — LIMA-only CABG: Some sources suggest Plavix not strictly necessary if only LIMA-to-LAD (LIMA has excellent patency). However, many institutions + guidelines (including many cardiothoracic surgeons) recommend ASA + Plavix × 1 year universally post-CABG for SVG/radial protection and to simplify discharge teaching (single regimen rather than surgeon-dependent variation). --- Discharge Teaching Essentials
  • "Take ASA forever. Never stop ASA without calling your surgeon."
  • "Take Plavix for exactly 1 year (not 6 months, not 2 years — 1 year). After 1 year, stop Plavix but keep taking ASA forever."
  • "Never miss a dose of either medication. Missing even 3–5 days can cause graft clotting."
  • "Don't take NSAIDs with ASA + Plavix (increases bleeding risk)."
  • "Tell any doctor or dentist you're on these medications before procedures." --- Drug Interactions & Cautions
  • NSAIDs + ASA + Plavix: Increased GI bleeding risk; use acetaminophen instead
  • Proton-pump inhibitor (PPI): Omeprazole reduces Plavix effectiveness; if PPI needed, use pantoprazole or ranitidine instead
  • Stopping Plavix for procedures: Coordinate with surgeon/cardiologist; bridging heparin sometimes needed for high-risk patients ---
7.10 — Cardiac Rehabilitation Referral & Outcomes Cardiac Rehab — Class I Recommendation Post-CABG cardiac rehabilitation is a Class I, Level of Evidence A recommendation (AHA/ACC). Mortality reduction ~20–30% compared to no rehab. Phases of Cardiac Rehab
  • Phase 1 (Inpatient, POD 0–5): Supervised mobilization, risk stratification
  • Phase 2 (Early outpatient, 3–6 weeks to ~12 weeks post-op): Supervised exercise, education, psychosocial support
  • Phase 3 (Late outpatient, 3–6+ months): Continued exercise, independence --- Benefits
  • Improved functional capacity
  • Reduced mortality
  • Reduced depression + anxiety
  • Better compliance with medications
  • Patient education on CAD risk factors
  • Smoking cessation support
  • Psychosocial assessment + support --- Discharge Planning
  • Referral made POD 2–3; contact rehab program to confirm enrollment
  • Start Phase 2 in weeks 3–4 post-op (allow initial healing, wound closure)
  • Provide patient with contact information + expected start date
  • Discharge teach: "You'll meet an exercise therapist 3 days/week for 6–12 weeks. This program significantly improves your outcomes." ---

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear in a stable patient, re-escalate.

  • New chest pain POD 0–3 (no previous CP) + ST changes or troponin rise: perioperative MI or graft failure until proven otherwise → STAT ECG + troponin + surgeon notification
  • Sudden drop in CT output (was 150 mL/h, now 20 mL/h): tamponade (clotted tube or pericardial fluid accumulation) → check tube patency immediately; if patent, STAT echo + surgeon
  • Progressive rising lactate (1.5 → 2.5 → 3.5 over 4 hours) + cool extremities: low cardiac output or sepsis → assess hemodynamics, lactate clearance; escalate if persists
  • Fever POD 3–5 + sternal erythema/drainage: deep sternal infection until proven otherwise → cultures, notify surgeon directly
  • Cold radial graft hand (pulseless, cyanotic): radial spasm or thrombosis → warm hand, notify surgeon, initiate vasodilation
  • Suddenly confused POD 2–3 (was baseline alert): delirium vs. POAF vs. hypoxia → assess reversibles (SpO₂, glucose, K⁺, Mg²⁺, urine output, pain)
  • New irregular rhythm + HR > 130 (unstable POAF): hemodynamic decompensation risk → prepare for rate control or cardioversion
  • Worsening dyspnea + new crackles: pulmonary edema vs. effusion vs. pneumonia → CXR, assess JVD, diuresis, echo if tamponade suspected
  • Weak pulses + cool extremities despite MAP ≥ 70: low output state → echo, lactate; possible sepsis, graft failure, or pump failure
  • New focal neuro deficit (weakness, speech change): stroke → stroke code STAT, CT head, notify neurology + surgeon
  • Refractory hypokalemia (K⁺ 3.2 despite repeated repletion): check Mg²⁺ (if Mg²⁺ < 1.8, K⁺ won't correct); correct magnesium first
  • Wires and lines: pacer wire threshold rising toward 10 mA (was 3 mA) = edema around tip, possible malposition; check again; if persistent, notify surgeon

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. LIMA-to-LAD is the single most important graft — never compromise on this target. If LAD is small or diffusely diseased, discussion with surgeon is warranted. LIMA to LAD determines long-term survival more than any other factor. Patients with LIMA-to-LAD have superior outcomes vs. LIMA-to-diagonal or LIMA-to-OM.

  2. Plavix × 1 year is standard now — don't let someone discontinue early without surgeon approval. Post-CABG graft thrombosis can occur weeks later if antiplatelet therapy stopped prematurely. Some new APPs or rotating teams may not know the Plavix standard; verify with surgeon if questioned.

  3. Do NOT hold pre-op ASA. Ubiquitous question from anesthesia or surgery teams: "Should we hold the ASA?" Answer: No, continue ASA through surgery day. ASA is not held for CABG (unlike some other surgeries). Only hold if surgeon explicitly directs otherwise.

  4. POAF is expected (~30–40%), not a failure. Nurses sometimes panic when patient converts to AFIB POD 2. Educate: "Atrial fibrillation is common after bypass surgery and usually manageable. Prevention is key — keep K⁺ ≥ 4 and Mg²⁺ ≥ 2." Early treatment (rate control + electrolyte repletion) resolves POAF in many.

  5. Refractory hypokalemia? Check magnesium first. Hypomagnesemia (Mg²⁺ < 1.8) drives refractory hypokalemia. Repleting Mg²⁺ allows K⁺ correction. Target both: K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0.

  6. Left-sided pleural effusion post-LIMA is near-universal — not pathologic. Many nurses chart "pleural effusion" as an abnormality. Educate: "This is expected from LIMA dissection. Small effusions resolve on their own over weeks. Observe unless symptomatic." Only drain if causing dyspnea or large volume.

  7. Atelectasis LLL post-LIMA is expected — encourage pulmonary toilet aggressively. CXR POD 1–2 often shows LLL consolidation. This is not pneumonia unless accompanied by fever, cough, and productive sputum. Incentive spirometry, ambulation, and pain control resolve it.

  8. Radial artery graft spasm = EMERGENT call to surgeon. Cold hand or pulseless radial post-op is vasospasm or thrombosis; both require surgeon notification. Don't assume it will resolve; keep arm warm, avoid vasoconstrictors, have surgeon assess.

  9. BIMA (bilateral internal mammary) carries higher DSWI risk in diabetics. If patient is DM + obese + BIMA, DSWI risk can be 5–10%. Sternal infection prevention (glycemic control, skin prep, prophylactic antibiotics) is critical.

  10. Bleeding vs. coagulopathy distinction matters. If CT output is 400 mL/h and labs are normal, it's surgical bleeding (inadequate hemostasis) — surgeon may need to return to OR. If labs show low platelets/fibrinogen/high INR and output is oozing, give blood products and warm patient. Know the difference.

  11. Glucose control is not optional post-CABG. Van den Berghe data shows tight glucose control (140–180 post-op) reduces POAF, infection, and LOS. Hyperglycemia > 180 should trigger insulin; don't tolerate it. Non-diabetics often have elevated glucose POD 0–1 (stress response); this improves with insulin + time.

  12. Chest pain POD 0–3 is an MI until proven otherwise. Common bias: "It's just sternal incision pain." Any chest pain POD 0–3 warrants STAT ECG + troponin + surgeon notification. Don't assume costochondral pain; take the chest pain seriously in the immediate post-op period.

  13. ACE wrap on harvest leg is often forgotten at transfer to stepdown. The wrapper should come off at 24 hours post-op. Day-shift nurses on stepdown often inherit an overdue ACE wrap; remember to remove it and assess limb perfusion.

  14. Post-op PFTs worse than pre-op for weeks — this is normal. Patient (and sometimes teams) worry their "lungs got worse." Actually, CPB + atelectasis + pain reduce pulmonary function temporarily. By 4–6 weeks, PFTs typically recover to baseline or better. Reassure: "Your lungs will recover; this is expected post-surgery."

  15. On-pump vs. off-pump post-op expectations differ. OPCAB patients typically have less bleeding, fewer transfusions, earlier extubation. On-pump patients may have more CT output, more POAF. Know which procedure was done; tailor expectations accordingly.

cards.title: CAM-ICU
cards.quickAnswer: A bedside 4-feature delirium screening tool — Feature 1 (acute onset/fluctuation) + Feature 2 (inattention) + [Feature 3 (RASS ≠ 0) OR Feature 4 (disorganized thinking)] = positive. Screen every shift on all high-risk ICU patients (age > 65, low EF, prolonged CPB, prior delirium). Hypoactive delirium is silent and easily missed. RASS ≤ −3 prevents valid assessment. Positive screen triggers Delirium Workup scenario.
