sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
The CAM-ICU is a validated bedside diagnostic algorithm for identifying delirium in ICU and step-down patients (Ely et al., 2001). Delirium is acute-onset, fluctuating altered mental status from a reversible medical or surgical cause. The CAM-ICU combines four observable clinical features:

  1. Acute onset and/or fluctuating course — change from baseline within hours to days, or fluctuation within a single shift
  2. Inattention — inability to focus, sustain, or shift attention
  3. Altered level of consciousness (RASS ≠ 0) — any deviation from baseline alertness
  4. Disorganized thinking — incoherent responses, illogical speech, or inability to follow commands

Scoring rule: CAM-ICU is POSITIVE if Features 1 + 2 + (Feature 3 OR Feature 4) are all present. It is a screening tool, not a diagnostic test; a positive screen prompts delirium workup to identify reversible causes.

sections.heading: 2. Four Features: Detailed Breakdown
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature How to Assess Positive Finding
Feature 1: Acute Onset + Fluctuation Ask family/check prior notes about baseline cognition. Compare mental status now vs. earlier this shift. Change from baseline (hours–days) AND/OR fluctuating alertness or cognition within a shift.
Feature 2: Inattention Intubated/non-verbal: Picture Inattention Test — point to 10 line-drawn objects; count correct. Verbal: Letters Attention Test — spell "CAFEF" backward or recite months backward. < 8/10 pictures correct OR > 2 errors on letters test.
Feature 3: Altered LOC Assess RASS (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale) first. RASS ≠ 0 (any value from −4 to +4) indicates abnormal consciousness. Cannot assess if RASS ≤ −3. RASS −2, −1, +1, +2, +3, or +4 (anything other than 0).
Feature 4: Disorganized Thinking Four yes/no questions: (1) "Will a stone float on water?" (2) "Are there fish in the sea?" (3) "Does 1 lb weigh more than 2 lbs?" (4) "Can you use a hammer to pound a nail?" Plus simple command: "Hold up 2 fingers" or "Close your eyes." ≥ 1 incorrect response to yes/no questions OR inability to follow the 1-step command.

sections.heading: 3. Scoring & Interpretation
sections.bodyHtml:
Result Criteria Action
CAM-ICU POSITIVE Feature 1 AND Feature 2 AND (Feature 3 OR Feature 4) present Proceed to Delirium Workup scenario — assess oxygenation, labs (CBC, CMP, glucose, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺), cultures if fever, medication review, pain assessment. Document findings + positive screen. Repeat per protocol (minimum q shift).
CAM-ICU NEGATIVE Does not meet above criteria Low delirium risk at this moment. Repeat per institutional protocol on high-risk patients.
CANNOT ASSESS RASS ≤ −3, language barrier, unconsciousness, non-verbal without assessment tool Document reason (e.g., "RASS −4 from propofol drip"). Reassess when sedation is lightened.

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use — Timing & Triggers
sections.bodyHtml:
Screen at minimum every shift (day, evening, night) on all patients with any of these risk factors:

  • Age > 65 years
  • Ejection fraction < 35%
  • Prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB > 180 min pump time or > 90 min cross-clamp)
  • Prior delirium or dementia
  • Multiple sedative medications (benzodiazepines, opioids)
  • Known anticholinergic exposure
  • Acute metabolic derangement (hypoxia, hypoglycemia, electrolyte imbalance)

High-yield patient populations: post-operative cardiac surgery (POD 0–7), ICU patients on mechanical ventilation, sepsis, advanced age, chronic kidney disease.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Delirium pathophysiology & risk stratification

Why delirium happens: Delirium reflects acute brain dysfunction from reversible medical or surgical insult. Common ICU triggers include hypoxia, sepsis, medications (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, opioids), metabolic derangement, sleep deprivation, and pain. Post-operative patients are at especially high risk due to inflammatory response, fluid shifts, and beta-blocker nadir at POD 2–3.

Hypoactive vs. hyperactive delirium: Hyperactive delirium is obvious (agitation, combativeness) but accounts for only 30–40% of cases. Hypoactive delirium — quiet, withdrawn, slow-to-respond — is more common and more easily missed. The "calm" or "sleeping" patient may be profoundly delirious and at risk for complications.

Inattention assessment by patient population
  • Mechanically ventilated, non-verbal: Picture Inattention Test is the only valid assessment. Requires functioning vision and ability to nod/blink. If patient blind or unable to respond, document "Unable to assess Feature 2 — non-verbal, no adequate response modality."
  • Extubated, verbal: Either Pictures or Letters test; Letters is faster. If patient non-English speaking, use Pictures or culturally-familiar concrete questions (not "spell backward").
  • Deaf or hearing-impaired: Use Pictures or written questions (if literate); provide hearing aids.
  • Low-literacy patients: Pictures preferred; or use simple yes/no questions ("Can you fly?" "Is fire cold?").
RASS assessment workflow RASS scoring:
  • −4 = Unarousable
  • −3 = Responsive only to tactile stimulation
  • −2 = Responsive only to verbal stimulation
  • −1 = Not fully alert but arousable
  • 0 = Alert and calm
  • +1 = Restless
  • +2 = Agitated
  • +3 = Pulling at lines or fighting
  • +4 = Combative, dangerous Critical rule: If RASS ≤ −3, do NOT attempt CAM-ICU. Instead document: "Unable to assess CAM-ICU — RASS [−4/−3], too deeply sedated" and plan reassessment when sedation is lighter.
Medication & non-pharm interventions for positive screen Medications to review / consider reducing:
  • Benzodiazepines (propofol, midazolam) — hold/taper if possible
  • Opioids (fentanyl, morphine, hydromorphone) — optimize dose; consider rotation if tolerance
  • Anticholinergics (atropine, glycopyrrolate, diphenhydramine) — hold
  • H2-blockers (ranitidine, famotidine) — can accumulate
  • Corticosteroids (in high doses) — delirium risk Non-pharmacologic interventions (first-line):
  • Reorient frequently (use name, date, location, explain procedures)
  • Ensure glasses/hearing aids present and functional
  • Normalize sleep-wake cycle (lights, windows, minimize nighttime disruptions)
  • Early mobilization (sit in chair, ambulate if safe)
  • Avoid restraints (restraints often escalate agitation in delirium; address reversible causes instead)
  • Pain control optimization
  • Family presence and reassurance
  • Single-occupancy room if possible (reduces sensory overload)

sections.heading: 6. Red Flags & Pitfalls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. RASS assessment must come FIRST. RASS ≤ −3 prevents valid CAM-ICU; document reason and reassess when sedation is lighter.
  2. Hypoactive delirium is the silent killer. Quiet, withdrawn, slow-to-respond patients are OFTEN MORE delirious than agitated ones. Always test — do not assume calmness = clarity.
  3. Sensory deprivation creates false positives. Patient without glasses fails Picture Test; deaf patient cannot hear yes/no questions. Rule out missing hearing aids, glasses, or language barrier BEFORE calling positive.
  4. Language and education barriers complicate Features 2 & 4. Non-English or low-literacy patients may fail question test despite intact cognition. Use Pictures; document language limitation.
  5. Dementia baseline requires differentiation. Demented patient has cognitive baseline impairment before surgery. Delirium is the ACUTE CHANGE from that baseline. Always ask: "Compared to home before surgery, is this worse?" Acute worsening = delirium risk, regardless of baseline dementia.
  6. Screen BOTH shifts to catch fluctuation. Delirium fluctuates hour-to-hour. Morning-only screening misses afternoon/evening confusion. Feature 1 depends on detecting change across time.
  7. Training and inter-rater reliability matter. Inconsistent application of Picture Test or yes/no questions reduces sensitivity. Ensure all clinicians complete annual CAM-ICU training; periodic competency validation recommended.
  8. Non-verbal patients: Use Picture Test for Feature 2. For Feature 4 (disorganized thinking), use simple commands (nod, blink, squeeze hand) rather than yes/no questions.
  9. "Unable to assess" is valid and useful documentation. Do NOT force a score if criteria cannot be met. Instead document: "Unable to assess Feature 2 (inattention) — patient non-verbal, no hearing aids available; suggest cochlear implant assessment or use picture test with device in place."
  10. Positive screen ≠ diagnosis of delirium. CAM-ICU screens for delirium RISK. The cause may be hypoxia, infection, medication, pain, sleep deprivation, or metabolic. Do NOT reflexively start antipsychotics; find and treat the reversible cause first.

cards.title: Cardiac Output (CO) and Cardiac Index (CI)
cards.quickAnswer: CO = HR × stroke volume; CI = CO indexed to body surface area. Normal CO 4–8 L/min; normal CI 2.5–4.0 L/min/m². Post-operative target CI > 2.2 L/min/m²; CI < 2.0 = low-output state—assume cardiogenic shock until proven otherwise. Increase CO/CI by (1) optimizing preload (fluid bolus, position); (2) reducing afterload (vasodilator); (3) enhancing contractility (dobutamine or milrinone); (4) restoring heart rate and rhythm (pace, cardioverse, antiarrhythmic).

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardiac Output (CO) is the volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle per minute (L/min). It reflects the heart's ability to meet whole-body metabolic demand.

Cardiac Index (CI) is CO normalized to body surface area (BSA), expressed in L/min/m². CI is the preferred hemodynamic parameter in critical care because it accounts for patient size.

Both are derived parameters—calculated from direct measurements (HR, stroke volume) or inferred from indirect clinical signs (urine output, lactate, SvO₂, extremity perfusion). Rarely measured at bedside on units outside ICU.

sections.heading: Basic Equations
sections.bodyHtml:
CO = HR × SV

  • HR = heart rate (beats/min)
  • SV = stroke volume (mL/beat), typically 60–100 mL

CI = CO / BSA

  • BSA in m² (Mosteller: √[height cm × weight kg / 3600])
  • Typical adult BSA ≈ 1.7–2.0 m²

Example: HR 70 bpm, SV 70 mL → CO = 4.9 L/min; BSA 1.8 m² → CI = 2.7 L/min/m²

sections.heading: Determinants of Stroke Volume — Four-Factor Framework
sections.bodyHtml:
Factor Definition Clinical lever
Preload End-diastolic ventricular volume; Frank-Starling mechanism Fluid bolus, diuretics, position, CVP/PCWP
Afterload Resistance ventricle overcomes to eject (SVR) Vasodilators (nitroprusside, hydralazine), pressors
Contractility Intrinsic force-generating capacity independent of pre/afterload Inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone, epinephrine)
HR & rhythm Frequency + AV synchrony; dyssynchrony (AF, heart block) drops SV 15–25% Pacing, antiarrhythmic, cardioversion

sections.heading: 3. Normal Range / Targets
sections.bodyHtml:
Parameter Normal range Post-op cardiac target Low-output (cardiogenic shock) Hyperdynamic / septic
CO (L/min) 4.0–8.0 > 4.5 < 3.5 > 8.0
CI (L/min/m²) 2.5–4.0 > 2.2 < 2.0 > 4.5
SVR (mmHg·min/L) 800–1200 800–1200 > 1200 (cold, pale) < 600 (warm, flushed)
MAP (mmHg) 70–100 > 65 (procedure-dependent) < 60 ± oliguria > 100 ± restless

Key post-op thresholds:

  • CI > 2.2 = goal (CABG, AVR, MVR, cardiac transplant)
  • CI 2.0–2.2 = marginal; intervention based on context (symptoms, lactate, urine output)
  • CI < 2.0 + hypotension + oliguria + elevated lactate = cardiogenic shock; emergency support
  • CI > 4.5 + warm extremities + low SVR = consider sepsis, thyroid storm, anemia

sections.heading: Transferred Patient with PA Catheter
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Trend CI q4–6h; CI drop in real-time signals deterioration
  2. CI < 2.2: assess preload (fluid bolus if CVP < 8), reduce afterload (vasodilator if SVR elevated), add inotrope if low SV + high SVR
  3. CI drop > 15–20% from baseline even if absolute is "normal" → investigate arrhythmia, tamponade, sepsis, cardiac dysfunction

sections.heading: Most Patients (No PAC)
sections.bodyHtml:
Use indirect hemodynamic assessment in order of reliability:

Sign Interpretation Action threshold
MAP Perfusion pressure surrogate MAP < 65 = act; > 80 in post-CABG reassuring
Urine output Renal perfusion UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/h despite adequate fluid = concerning
Lactate Tissue hypoperfusion Lactate > 2 or rising = low-output state
SvO₂ or ScvO₂ Oxygen extraction SvO₂ < 60% = low CO or sepsis
Extremity warmth Peripheral perfusion Cold, mottled + hypotension = poor CO
Mentation Cerebral perfusion New confusion / lethargy = red flag

sections.heading: Decision Framework (No CO/CI Available)
sections.bodyHtml:
IF low MAP + cold extremities + oliguria + high lactate: → Assume low CO (cardiogenic) → optimize preload (fluids), reduce afterload (vasodilator), add inotrope

IF low MAP + warm extremities + low lactate + low SVR: → Assume high CO, low SVR (distributive/septic) → antibiotic, source control, vasopressor

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Measurement methods — which technique when
MethodMechanismProsConsAvailability
PA catheter thermodilutionCold bolus RA → PA thermal sensorClinical gold standard~10% error, skill-dependentICU only
Pulse-contour (FloTrac, LiDCO)Arterial waveform analysisContinuous trendingFails in arrhythmia, severe AR, IABPOccasional ICU transfer
NICOM / bioreactanceThoracic impedance changeNon-invasiveLess accurate absolute valuesResearch only
Echocardiography (LVOT VTI)LVOT area × velocity-time integral × HRReal-time structure + functionOperator-dependent, image qualityEcho lab / ICU
Fick principleCO = VO₂ / (CaO₂ − CvO₂)Conceptually cleanImpractical bedside (mixed venous sample)Rarely used post-op
Clinical reality on unit: PAC-derived CO/CI uncommon outside ICU. Bedside relies on indirect markers (MAP, UOP, lactate, SvO₂, skin warmth, mentation).
Inotrope decision framework — cardiogenic vs distributive vs preload Cardiogenic low-output (cold, pale, oliguria, high lactate, high SVR):
  • First-line inotrope: Dobutamine (5–15 µg/kg/min; β₁ agonist, lowers SVR)
  • Alternative: Milrinone (0.25–0.75 µg/kg/min; PDE-3 inhibitor, inodilator, improves diastolic function)
  • Combine with low-dose phenylephrine (0.5–1.4 µg/kg/min) if BP drops → maintain MAP while reducing afterload Distributive / septic (warm, flushed, low lactate initially, low SVR):
  • Norepinephrine (0.05–0.5 µg/kg/min; α > β, maintains SVR + CO)
  • Avoid pure vasodilators (milrinone) until fluid-resuscitated and antibiotics on board Preload-limited (low CVP, low PCWP, flat JVD):
  • Fluid bolus 250–500 mL over 5–10 min; measure CI or surrogate at 15 min
  • CI rise > 15% = volume responsive → continue fluids
  • Flat response = preload-independent → reduce afterload, add inotrope
Measurement methods in practice — SV response testing Volume responsiveness testing:
  1. Baseline CI or surrogate (MAP, UOP)
  2. Fluid challenge: 250–500 mL IV bolus over 5–10 min
  3. Recheck at 15 min
  4. CI rise > 15% or UOP sustained ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h = volume responsive
  5. Flat response + oliguria = preload-independent problem (reduce afterload or add inotrope) Do NOT use static CVP alone to guide fluids. Dynamic indices (pulse pressure variation, CVP trend during challenge, SV response) are more reliable.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls (5–10, High-Yield)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Trend + context > absolute number. A single CI of 3.8 L/min/m² that was 5.2 just 2 h ago is a 27% drop—act, even if 3.8 is "technically" low-normal.

  2. Heart rate is a lever, not just a number. SV 60 mL, HR 100 → CO 3.5 L/min; drop HR to 60 (rate control or heart block) → CO 2.1 L/min. Fix the rhythm (pacing, cardioversion, antiarrhythmic)—not fluids.

  3. AV dyssynchrony drops SV 15–25%. New atrial fibrillation or loss of AV sync (VVI pacing) → CI drop. Restoring sinus rhythm or upgrading pacing (DDD) is the primary intervention.

  4. PA catheter has ~10% inherent error. Do not react to a 2.3 vs 2.1 L/min/m² reading; trend for 15–20% swings before intervening.

  5. Pulse-contour unreliable in: severe arrhythmia, acute aortic regurgitation, IABP support, RV failure. If patient develops AF or severe AR on pulse-contour, question the reading.

  6. Tamponade declares early in CO. CI drops before MAP falls—narrow pulse pressure (SBP − DBP < 30) + falling CI + rising CVP = high suspicion. Do not wait for hypotension.

  7. Static CVP poorly predicts volume responsiveness. Dynamic tests (pulse pressure variation, CVP trend during bolus, SV response) are more reliable than single CVP number.

  8. High CO ≠ tissue perfusion. Septic patient with CO 7.0 L/min can still have microvascular dysfunction and elevated lactate. Treat underlying sepsis, not just the CO number.

  9. Post-operative troponin rises without infarction. Transient myocardial stunning from ischemia-reperfusion may suppress CO transiently; usually recovers in 24–72 h. Serial troponin + echo distinguish cardiogenic shock (EF < 30%, kinetic segment) from stunning.

  10. Procedure-dependent CI interpretation. Post-CABG or isolated AVR patient with CI 2.2 + normal MAP = reassuring. Post-myectomy HCM patient with CI 2.0 + normal MAP + normal lactate may be physiologically normal (LVOT obstruction relieved)—do not give inotropes reflexively.

cards.title: Cardiac Rehabilitation Referral
cards.quickAnswer: Class I, Level A evidence (mandatory for eligible patients): All patients post-CABG, valve surgery, MI, stable angina, heart failure, and transplant should be referred to comprehensive outpatient cardiac rehabilitation — supervised exercise, risk factor counseling, psychosocial support, medication education. 25% mortality reduction and 18% hospitalization reduction (Thomas, 2019), yet national referral rate remains <40%. Start 2–6 weeks post-op with surgeon clearance. Medicare covers 36 sessions; most insurance covers with minimal copay. Nursing role: ensure discharge referral order, verify insurance, identify local program, address barriers, close equity gaps. Home-based and telehealth options available.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: Class I, Level A evidence (mandatory for eligible patients): All patients post-CABG, valve surgery, MI, stable angina, heart failure, and transplant should be referred to comprehensive outpatient cardiac rehabilitation — supervised exercise, risk factor counseling, psychosocial support, medication education. 25% mortality reduction and 18% hospitalization reduction (Thomas, 2019), yet national referral rate remains <40%. Start 2–6 weeks post-op with surgeon clearance. Medicare covers 36 sessions; most insurance covers with minimal copay. Nursing role: ensure discharge referral order, verify insurance, identify local program, address barriers, close equity gaps. Home-based and telehealth options available.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → Thomas et al. (AHA 2019) → AACVPR (2021) → 2022 AHA/ACC Heart Failure Guidelines

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, scope, candidacy.

  • Definition: Comprehensive, evidence-based outpatient program consisting of supervised exercise training, risk factor modification counseling (smoking, diet, stress), medication education, psychosocial support, and return-to-activity guidance for secondary prevention post-cardiac event or surgery.
  • Indication: Class I, Level A — all eligible post-CABG, valve repair/replacement, post-MI, stable angina, heart failure, and transplant patients.
  • Timing: Start 2–6 weeks post-op (CABG/valve) or 3–14 days post-acute MI. Phase II duration typically 4–12 weeks, 2–3 sessions/week.
  • Outcomes: 25% mortality reduction, 18% hospitalization reduction, improved functional capacity, reduced symptoms, better medication adherence (Thomas, 2019; AACVPR, 2021).
  • Who gets this: Every eligible post-cardiac patient; highest priority for post-CABG, post-valve, post-transplant.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why It Exists
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardiac rehabilitation addresses the integrated physiologic and psychological recovery needed after cardiac surgery or acute MI. The combination of supervised exercise, education, and psychosocial support addresses multiple simultaneous recovery challenges:

  • Deconditioning and lost functional capacity — ICU/bed rest → limited mobility → 1–2 MET loss per week. Supervised, progressive exercise restores aerobic capacity and confidence.
  • Sympathetic overdrive and arrhythmia risk — post-event catecholamine surge, anxiety, and beta-blocker changes create dysrhythmia risk. Monitored exercise, stress reduction, and medication optimization reduce recurrent events.
  • Modifiable risk factor burden — smoking, hypertension, dyslipidemia, diabetes, obesity, sedentary lifestyle. Rehab provides structured counseling, medication adherence support, and behavioral coaching.
  • Depression and psychosocial distress — common post-MI and post-CABG; associated with worse outcomes and reduced rehab adherence. Screening and supportive referral critical.
  • Return-to-life uncertainty — patients fear exercise, driving, work, sexual activity. Rehab provides clear, phased return-to-activity guidance with monitored progression.

The gap between evidence (25% mortality benefit) and practice (<40% national referral rate) reflects barriers: knowledge gaps, insurance confusion, transportation, cost, competing priorities, and systemic inequities affecting women, minorities, elderly, and low-income populations. Nursing role is to actively close this gap.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Class I Indications
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — who is eligible.

Universally indicated (Class I, Level A):

  • Post-CABG (any complexity)
  • Post-valve repair or replacement (aortic, mitral, tricuspid)
  • Post-acute myocardial infarction (STEMI or NSTEMI)
  • Stable angina pectoris
  • Heart failure (systolic and diastolic)
  • Status post heart transplant
  • Other cardiac procedures: PCI with stent, cardiomyopathy, select congenital heart disease

Does NOT apply to:

  • Unstable angina or acute decompensated heart failure (contraindicated until stabilized)
  • Uncontrolled arrhythmias, uncontrolled hypertension, acute illness

Special populations (modify per institutional protocol):

  • Elderly (>75): age alone is NOT a contraindication; modified programs available and often highest benefit
  • Renal impairment: cardiac rehab safe; coordinate electrolyte monitoring
  • Heart transplant and LVAD: cardiac rehab essential (specialized programs preferred)
  • Rural or isolated patients: home-based or telehealth options available

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Discharge Planning Phase* (15 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic assessment to identify candidates, barriers, and plan.

Baseline screening (POD 1 or transfer):

  • Procedure type and date — eligible procedure per §3?
  • Current functional status — mobility level, any orthopedic/pulmonary limits to exercise?
  • Baseline exercise tolerance — stair climb, 6-minute walk if available
  • Psychosocial screen — depression (PHQ-9), anxiety, support system, substance use, health literacy
  • Insurance status — primary insurance, coverage for CR, copay, coverage limits

Barrier identification (per discharge assessment):

  • Transportation: does patient have access to car or public transit?
  • Cost: concern about copay or fees?
  • Time: work schedule, childcare, competing medical appointments?
  • Knowledge/fear: understands benefits? Anxious about exercise? Cultural health beliefs?
  • Social support: spouse/family willing to participate or provide transport?

Insurance pre-authorization (call before discharge):

  • Verify coverage (Medicare always covers; private insurance usually covers with copay)
  • Confirm session limits (Medicare 36 standard, some private 24–48)
  • Identify copay per session and total out-of-pocket cost
  • Confirm baseline stress test requirement (program-dependent)

Local program identification:

  • Keck outpatient cardiac rehab (if available at institution)
  • Community center-based programs (Cedars-Sinai, other centers nearby)
  • Home-based vendors (Cardiac Training International, AHA telehealth, others)
  • Hybrid telehealth options for access barriers

sections.heading: 5.1 Phase II program components
sections.bodyHtml:
Supervised exercise training (2–3 sessions/week for 4–12 weeks):

  • Aerobic: treadmill, stationary bike, elliptical, rowing; 10–15 min initial, progressing to 30–40 min; intensity 50–85% max HR reserve, RPE 11–15/20
  • Resistance (start week 6–8 post-op after sternal precautions lift): upper/lower body; light resistance, 1–2 sets, 10–15 reps for functional endurance
  • Flexibility/cool-down: stretching, relaxation techniques
  • Monitoring: continuous telemetry, vital signs, symptoms; nurse/therapist present

Risk factor counseling + education:

  • Smoking cessation: pharmacotherapy + counseling (rehab staff trained)
  • Nutrition: heart-healthy diet (Mediterranean or DASH emphasis); lipid management; salt restriction if HF
  • Blood pressure, diabetes, lipid management: medication adherence, home monitoring, lifestyle modifications
  • Stress management: relaxation techniques, coping strategies
  • Medication education: mechanism, side effects, adherence for ACE-I, beta-blockers, statins, antiplatelet agents

Psychosocial support:

  • Depression screening (PHQ-9); referral for counseling if indicated
  • Anxiety assessment; reassurance about exercise safety
  • Support group participation; peer connection for adherence and motivation

Return-to-activity guidance: - Driving (typically 4–6 weeks post-op per surgeon); return-to-work timing (desk 4–6 weeks, physical labor 8–12 weeks); return-to-sexual-activity (when stairs without symptoms, typically 4–6 weeks); household/hobbies — individualized; sternal precautions integrated

sections.heading: 5.2 Program format options
sections.bodyHtml:
Format Setting Supervision Barriers Addressed Notes
Center-based Cardiac rehab facility High (nurse + therapist each session) Social engagement, direct monitoring Most effective; traditional; requires transportation
Home-based Patient's home Low (phone/video counseling, video exercise) Transportation, time, isolation, childcare, cost Effective for access barriers; requires adherence/self-direction
Telehealth hybrid Home + periodic center visits Medium (remote + in-person) Transportation, time, flexibility Emerging; growing evidence base
Community-based YMCA, senior centers with CR endorsement Variable Cost (often lower copay), community, transportation Available; quality varies

sections.heading: 5.3 Nursing coordination tasks
sections.bodyHtml:
Discharge order and referral:

  • Ensure discharge order explicitly says "Referral to Phase II cardiac rehabilitation" (not a suggestion)
  • Provide referral form to local CR program before discharge if possible
  • Schedule first appointment before hospital discharge when feasible

Patient and family education:

  • Explain benefits: "Cardiac rehab reduces your risk of another event by 25%, improves your strength, and helps you feel better sooner."
  • Address fears: "Exercise under supervision is safe. We've helped thousands of people. Your heart is stronger after this program."
  • Discuss program format options and patient preference (center-based vs. home-based)
  • Set expectations: duration (4–12 weeks), frequency (2–3/week), components (exercise + education + support)

Insurance verification and barrier solutions:

  • Call insurance + CR program; confirm coverage, copay, session limits
  • If cost is barrier: discuss copay, explore community programs (lower cost), social work referral
  • If transportation is barrier: ask about public transit, family availability, telehealth option
  • If time is barrier: flexible scheduling, telehealth, home-based option
  • If fear is barrier: provide reassurance, patient education materials, consider home program start with periodic center visits

Equity considerations (active, documented effort):

  • Women: proactive outreach (historically under-referred); identify women's programs if available; address childcare/caregiver role barriers
  • Minorities: language-appropriate materials and programs; identify culturally concordant programs if available
  • Elderly (>75): counter age bias; explain modified programs available; high benefit in this group
  • Low-income: prioritize home-based or telehealth; explore subsidized programs; social work
  • Rural: distance barrier mitigated by home-based or telehealth options

Documentation:

  • Referral order placed (date/time)
  • Patient education performed: benefits, expectations, local options, insurance verification
  • Barriers identified and plan documented
  • First appointment scheduled or next steps communicated
  • Patient understanding documented

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Referral Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. Patient declines referral — document barriers, offer alternatives (home-based, telehealth), re-educate, involve social work/case management
  2. Insurance denies coverage — verify policy, appeal if appropriate, explore community programs, discuss out-of-pocket cost vs. benefit
  3. No program availability within reasonable distance — activate home-based or telehealth option; connect to national programs (AHA telehealth, CTI, etc.)
  4. Patient no-shows to first appointment — outreach call, reassess barriers, adjust format (telehealth?), reschedule
  5. Baseline stress test not completed pre-rehab — verify program requirement; schedule ETT if needed before starting
  6. Medical contraindication develops — uncontrolled arrhythmia, unstable angina, acute illness — defer rehab, restart when cleared

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections intended to collapse in PowerApp. Nursing students and advanced beginners can expand for deeper understanding; experts can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Why Phase II is critical
sections.bodyHtml:
• Early intervention (POD 7–14) accelerates recovery — supervised exercise removes fear, restores confidence, prevents deconditioning spiral
  • Medication optimization — rehab staff monitor response to beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, diuretics; can flag side effects (beta-blocker fatigue, cough, myalgia) to prescriber
  • Risk stratification — baseline stress test (if required) identifies patients needing closer monitoring or advanced intervention
  • Psychosocial screening — depression/anxiety identified early; referral for counseling prevents worse outcomes
  • 3-month window is high-leverage — most patients complete phase II in 12 weeks; adherence to full program predicts long-term secondary prevention success

sections.heading: 7.2 Evidence summary
sections.bodyHtml:
Outcome Data Source
All-cause mortality reduction 25% Thomas et al., 2019 AHA Statement
Hospitalization reduction 18% Thomas et al., 2019
Functional capacity gain 4–5 METs average Multiple RCTs; Hardin & Kaplow, 2020
National referral rate <40% Quality metric gap; CMS incentive
Home-based CR effectiveness Non-inferior to center-based for adherence and outcomes Anderson et al. (Cochrane) 2017
Telehealth CR growth Emerging evidence; meta-analyses show non-inferiority 2020–2025 literature

sections.heading: 7.3 Medication considerations in CR
sections.bodyHtml:
Drug Class Rehab Consideration Coaching Point
Beta-blockers Blunt HR response (normal); may report fatigue "Your HR won't climb as high during exercise — this is normal and protective."
ACE inhibitors Dry cough is common (~10%); can impair exercise "If you develop a cough, tell your doctor — we can adjust."
Statins Rare myalgia; contact prescriber if exercise-limiting pain "Muscle aches that worsen with activity warrant discussion with your cardiologist."
Diuretics May need electrolyte monitoring during rehab phase "We'll check your K⁺ and Mg regularly; dehydration during exercise is monitored."
Antiplatelet / anticoagulation Bleeding risk with trauma (falls); normal with supervised exercise "Your blood thinner is protective. Exercise under supervision is safe."

sections.heading: 7.4 Special populations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Heart transplant: cardiac rehab essential (immunosuppression, deconditioning, denervation physiology). Specialized transplant programs available. Start POD 3–5 when stable.
  • LVAD: rehab essential for device complication prevention and functional recovery. Durable device programs available. Coordinate with device center.
  • Elderly (>75): modified programs with lower initial intensity, shorter session duration, frequent reassessment. Benefit often greatest in this group (improved mobility, confidence, independence).
  • Renal impairment: safe; coordinate K⁺/Mg monitoring if stage 3+ CKD. Dialysis scheduling considerations if end-stage.
  • Decompensated HF pre-op: refer to heart-failure-specific program post-optimization if possible.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration or Disengagement in Referred Patients
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in patients enrolled in CR; if any develop, escalate.

  • Patient disengages after 2–3 sessions — common; barrier re-assessment needed (cost? fear? transportation?); offer alternative format
  • Functional decline despite enrollment — may indicate medical complication (infection, arrhythmia, HF exacerbation); notify primary team
  • Depression or anxiety emerging or worsening — screening should have caught this; reinforce mental health referral
  • New cardiac symptoms during exercise (chest pain, syncope, palpitations) — stop exercise, notify team; re-risk-stratify
  • Non-adherence to medications identified by rehab staff — address barriers to adherence; social work referral if needed
  • Social/environmental crisis during phase II (job loss, divorce, housing instability) — increase support; consider extending phase II timeline if barriers are temporary

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Cardiac rehab is Class I Level A, not optional. Not a suggestion; every eligible post-cardiac patient should be referred. National <40% referral rate is a quality gap.

  2. Women are under-referred despite equal benefit. Proactive outreach, women's-specific programs, and home-based options help close this gap.

  3. Elderly patients often assumed "too old." Age alone is not a contraindication. Modified programs available; mobility and psychological benefit often greatest in this group.

  4. Racial/ethnic minorities under-referred. Language barriers, cultural health beliefs, health literacy → provide materials in preferred language; identify culturally concordant programs.

  5. Insurance verification BEFORE discharge prevents no-shows. Call insurance + program; confirm coverage, copay, session limits. Surprises (high copay, limited sessions) deter engagement.

  6. Baseline stress test requirement varies by program. Verify during pre-authorization; schedule ETT if required before first rehab session.

  7. Fear of exercise is nearly universal post-cardiac event. Validate fear; explain monitored environment; encourage gradual progression; peer support powerful for confidence.

  8. Depression post-CABG and post-MI is common and under-screened. PHQ-9 at baseline; refer for counseling. Depression worsens outcomes and reduces rehab adherence.

  9. Smoking cessation integral to CR. Many programs offer pharmacotherapy + counseling. Post-cardiac event is high-leverage intervention point.

  10. Mediterranean diet emphasis in rehab counseling. Standard DASH good; Mediterranean superior for secondary prevention post-MI (Thomas, 2019).

  11. Heart failure-specific programs exist. If patient has HF, identify specialized HF-CR program if available; outcomes superior to generic cardiac rehab.

  12. Home-based CR solves access barriers. Effective for transportation, cost, time, isolation constraints. Some patients thrive with center-based (social, supervised); others prefer home (flexible, private). Offer both.

  13. Telehealth cardiac rehab increasingly validated. Remote exercise + phone counseling + wearable HR monitoring; non-inferior to center-based for adherence and outcomes.

  14. The 36-session Medicare benefit should be fully used. Some patients stop early or miss sessions. Encourage completion; 36 sessions optimal for long-term secondary prevention benefit.

  15. Return-to-work timing varies by occupation. Desk 4–6 weeks post-CABG; physical labor 8–12 weeks; specialized work longer. Rehab team guides; work conditioning programs available for gradual return.

cards.title: Cardiogenic Shock
cards.quickAnswer: Cardiogenic shock (CS) = inadequate cardiac output with end-organ hypoperfusion despite adequate preload; hemodynamic hallmark is cardiac index (CI) <2.2 L/min/m² plus pulmonary wedge pressure (PCWP) >15 mmHg or CVP >10, with SBP <90 mmHg and/or lactate ≥2 mmol/L and/or end-organ dysfunction (oliguria, altered mental status). SCAI staging A–E (At risk → Extremis) drives escalation. Most common cause: acute MI (~75–80%), followed by post-cardiotomy shock and acute HF decompensation. Management is SCAI stage-based: SCAI B–C: optimize preload/afterload, inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) ± pressors (norepinephrine); SCAI C–D: escalate to temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) — IABP, Impella, VA-ECMO; SCAI D–E: bridge to recovery, LVAD, or transplant. Team-based Shock Team approach (cardiology, cardiac surgery, critical care, advanced HF) improves outcomes. 30-day mortality 40–50% for acute MI-CS, lower with early intervention + tMCS. Early revasc in ischemic CS and post-MI mechanical complication repair are non-negotiable.

cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF Guideline (Heidenreich et al.) → SCAI Classification (Baran et al., 2019, 2022 update) → SHOCK trial (Hochman et al.) → CULPRIT-SHOCK (Thiele et al., 2017) → ALTSHOCK-2 Trial → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Bojar (2020)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to, and why it matters.

  • Definition: Cardiogenic shock is a clinical and hemodynamic state of inadequate cardiac output producing insufficient systemic perfusion despite adequate (or elevated) preload. Hemodynamic criteria: cardiac index (CI) <2.2 L/min/m² with pulmonary wedge pressure (PCWP) >15 mmHg (LV failure phenotype) OR CVP >10 mmHg + CI <2.2 (RV failure phenotype); plus clinical markers: SBP <90 mmHg for ≥30 minutes (vasopressor-dependent or not), plus end-organ hypoperfusion: lactate ≥2 mmol/L, oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/hr, altered mental status, or cool extremities.

  • Epidemiology:

  • Acute cardiogenic shock incidence: 2–4% of acute MI; up to 10% of post-cardiotomy cases
  • Acute myocardial infarction accounts for ~75–80% of acute CS
  • Post-cardiotomy shock: 1–2% of cardiac operations; carries higher early mortality than AMI-CS without advanced support
  • Acute HF decompensation + CS: 5–10% of acute HF admissions

  • In-hospital mortality: 30–50% for AMI-CS (improved with early revascularization + tMCS); 40–60% post-cardiotomy (varies by etiology); 35–45% HF-CS

  • Risk factors: Age > 70, anterior MI, multivessel CAD, prior HF or cardiomyopathy, diabetes, chronic kidney disease, RV involvement (inferior MI), perioperative complications (graft failure, anastomotic issues, cardiac arrest, prolonged bypass time), myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, severe valvular disease, takotsubo, mechanical complications of MI (VSD, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture, acute MR, tamponade).

  • Why ICU/ICU-adjacent units see this: Cardiogenic shock is an ICU-level condition, and recovery typically occurs in ICU with tMCS devices. Units caring for post-operative cardiac patients may encounter: (1) early recognition of CS developing on the surgical floor → urgent ICU transfer; (2) post-tMCS weaning and recovery monitoring on stepdown/intermediate care after hemodynamics stabilize (rare, but represents bridge-to-recovery cohort); (3) post-LVAD or post-transplant transition. This card frames CS as an emergent ICU diagnosis with potential for unit-neutral post-recovery stepdown. All active CS belongs in ICU.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced-beginner teaching — why CS develops.

sections.heading: Mechanism of cardiogenic shock
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardiogenic shock represents a cascade of inadequate cardiac output (CO = heart rate × stroke volume) leading to systemic hypoperfusion. The primary cardiac defect can be:

  1. Left ventricular systolic dysfunction (~70% of acute CS)

    • Acute MI with extensive infarction (anterior wall >40% LV territory, extensive inferior MI, multivessel involvement)
    • Acute myocarditis or peripartum cardiomyopathy
    • Decompensated chronic HFrEF (HF exacerbation, arrhythmia, infection, medication non-adherence)
    • Post-cardiotomy myocardial stunning (usually transient, recovers in hours to days)
    • Takotsubo (stress cardiomyopathy) — transient apical ballooning; most resolve within 1–2 weeks

  2. Right ventricular dysfunction (20–30% of acute CS or co-factor in LV-CS)

    • RV infarction (typically inferior MI extending into RV territory)
    • Massive pulmonary embolism (obstructive RV failure; technically not cardiogenic but hemodynamically similar)
    • Acute RV afterload crisis (acute respiratory failure, ARDS, severe pneumonia)
    • Post-cardiotomy RV failure (particularly after RV outflow tract surgery or RVAD)
    • Chronic RV dysfunction decompensating (pulmonary hypertension, COPD, interstitial lung disease)

  3. Mechanical complications of acute MI (5–10% of AMI, surgical emergency)

    • Ventricular septal defect (VSD) — left-to-right shunt, acute volume overload, ↑ PAWP
    • Acute mitral regurgitation (papillary muscle rupture, head rupture, chordae rupture)
    • Free wall rupture → tamponade or exsanguination (immediately fatal without surgical repair)
    • Acute aortic dissection with involvement of LMCA or RCA

  4. Valvular emergencies

    • Prosthetic valve thrombosis (mechanical valve)
    • Native valve endocarditis with large vegetation
    • Acute aortic regurgitation (dissection, endocarditis, prosthetic dehiscence)

  5. Arrhythmia-driven shock (co-factor, not primary CS)

    • Sustained ventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter with RVR, severe bradycardia, complete heart block
    • Usually accompanies other cardiac pathology; arrhythmia plus underlying pump dysfunction = CS

sections.heading: Pathophysiology cascade
sections.bodyHtml:
• Initial insult → reduced stroke volume (LV/RV dysfunction, mechanical barrier, arrhythmia)
  • Compensatory response → tachycardia + sympathetic surge + venoconstriction (to maintain BP) + fluid retention (aldosterone, ADH)
  • Decompensation → progressive end-organ hypoperfusion despite vasoconstriction
  • Lactic acidosis from anaerobic metabolism (lactate ↑)
  • Oliguria from renal hypoperfusion (AKI)
  • Altered mental status from cerebral hypoperfusion
  • Cool extremities from peripheral vasoconstriction
  • Vicious cycle → as shock deepens, catecholamine requirement increases, afterload rises, cardiac output worsens, end-organ dysfunction accelerates
  • SCAI stage progression → A → B → C → D → E tracks this cascade in clinical time

The SCAI framework (Baran et al., 2019; updated 2022) has replaced older "Stable/Unstable" binary thinking. All phases of cardiogenic shock carry risk; SCAI staging allows precise documentation of trajectory and guides escalation timing.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced-beginner recognition — what CS looks like at bedside and which populations are at highest risk.

sections.heading: Typical presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Acute onset (AMI, acute myocarditis, post-cardiotomy) or gradual decompensation (acute HF exacerbation over hours)
  • Symptoms: chest pain or discomfort, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, or progressive fatigue
  • Signs of hypoperfusion:
  • Altered mental status (confusion, restlessness, obtundation — not explained by sedation or anesthesia residual)
  • Cool, clammy, mottled extremities (vasoconstriction, poor peripheral perfusion)
  • Oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr, often <0.3 mL/kg/hr in severe CS)
  • Lactic acidosis (lactate ≥2–4 mmol/L correlates with shock severity)
  • Signs of pulmonary congestion (if LV-dominant CS):
  • Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, severe dyspnea at rest
  • Pulmonary crackles/rales on auscultation, elevated JVP
  • Hypoxia, orthopnea despite supplemental O₂

sections.heading: Physical examination
sections.bodyHtml:
• Vital signs:
  • Hypotension: SBP <90 mmHg (may be lower in severe shock; some patients maintain SBP 90–100 initially then decompensate)
  • Tachycardia: compensatory (HR >100, often >120), except in bradyarrhythmia-driven shock
  • Tachypnea: RR >20, reflecting pulmonary edema and metabolic acidosis

  • Hypoxia: SpO₂ <92% on room air

  • Perfusion assessment:

  • Skin: pale, clammy, cyanotic, possibly mottled or marbled pattern (ominous sign)
  • Capillary refill: delayed (>2 seconds indicates poor peripheral perfusion)
  • Central–peripheral temperature gradient: >4°C suggests severe vasoconstriction

  • Apical pulse difficult to palpate (low output); radial pulse may be weak, thready

  • Cardiac auscultation:

  • S1 (often diminished if low output)
  • S3 gallop (common in acute systolic HF shock)
  • New or changing murmur: mechanical complication (VSD — holosystolic, apical; acute MR — holosystolic at apex; acute AR — early diastolic at left sternal border)
  • Pericardial friction rub (post-operative, post-MI rupture, pericarditis)

  • Muffled/distant heart sounds (tamponade, emphysema)

  • Lung examination:

  • Bilateral crackles/rales consistent with pulmonary edema (LV-dominant CS)
  • Unilateral crackles (aspiration, pneumonia complicating CS)

  • Diminished air entry (pleural effusion, pneumothorax)

  • JVP and peripheral edema:

  • Elevated JVP (>8 cm H₂O) if RV failure or biventricular congestion
  • Flat JVP if hypovolemic component
  • Peripheral edema if chronic component or prolonged high CVP

sections.heading: High-risk patient populations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Post-MI (first 24–72 hours): anterior wall (>40% territory), inferior + RV involvement, multivessel disease
  • Post-cardiac surgery (POD 0–3, can occur up to POD 10+): inadequate graft/anastomosis, tamponade, excessive bleeding, dissection, arrhythmia, sepsis
  • Acute HF exacerbation: HFrEF with trigger (infection, medication non-adherence, HTN crisis, arrhythmia)
  • Myocarditis, peripartum cardiomyopathy, takotsubo: typically younger, more acute presentation
  • Mechanical complication of MI: new holosystolic murmur = surgical emergency

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml: Competent systematic assessment. Information-gathering only; no interventions yet. Target: 2–5 minutes at bedside.

sections.heading: Vital signs and perfusion (continuous monitoring)
sections.bodyHtml:
• HR (trend, regularity, and response to activity), BP (both arms, trend), RR, SpO₂, temperature
  • Capillary refill, peripheral temperature, color of extremities
  • Urine output (mL/hr and mL/kg/hr for baseline trends)
  • Mental status (alert, confused, obtunded, responsive only to pain)

sections.heading: Cardiac and pulmonary history
sections.bodyHtml:
• Relevant past medical history: prior MI, HF, cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, arrhythmia, HTN, DM, CKD
  • Current presentation: when symptoms started, character of chest pain (if present), dyspnea timeline
  • Recent surgery or procedure: cardiac surgery date/type, interventional procedure, CVC placement
  • Medication adherence: beta-blockers, ACE-I, diuretics held or continued?

sections.heading: Diagnostic data (obtain STAT or review existing)
sections.bodyHtml:
• 12-lead ECG: ischemic changes (ST elevation, ST depression, T-wave inversion), arrhythmia, conduction abnormality
  • Chest X-ray: pulmonary edema (bilateral infiltrates, Kerley B lines), cardiac silhouette size, pleural effusion, pneumonia, pneumothorax, mediastinal widening (post-op)
  • Troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP: confirms acute cardiac injury; BNP >400 supports cardiogenic etiology
  • Basic labs: CBC, CMP (K, Cl, Cr, glucose), lactate (baseline and trend), arterial blood gas (pH, BE, base deficit)
  • Echocardiography (STAT bedside TTE, ideally before intervention):
  • Global LV and RV systolic function (EF, S' velocities)
  • Wall motion abnormalities (infarction pattern suggests STEMI or myocarditis)
  • RV/LV size and strain pattern
  • Mechanical complications: VSD (see shunt jet), acute MR (flail leaflet or rupture), free wall rupture (pseudoaneurysm, pericardial effusion)
  • Tamponade physiology (pericardial effusion with RV/RA diastolic collapse)
  • Estimate PA pressure (TR jet gradient)
  • LV and RV filling pressures (E/A ratio, E/E', S' velocity)
  • PA catheter (Swan-Ganz) or non-invasive hemodynamic monitoring (PAPi, NICOM, bioreactance):
  • Cardiac output (CO), cardiac index (CI), pulmonary wedge pressure (PAWP), CVP, SVR, PVR, SvO₂
  • Hemodynamic profile guides inotrope/pressor selection
  • Lactate clearance guides escalation decision
  • Lactate and lactate trend: single value less informative than trajectory; rising lactate = deterioration, escalate
  • Coronary angiography (if AMI suspected): confirms STEMI/NSTEMI, identifies culprit lesion, guides PCI strategy

sections.heading: SCAI stage assessment (document stage at recognition and with any transition)
sections.bodyHtml: Use hemodynamic criteria + clinical markers to assign SCAI stage (see table in §2). This drives all downstream decisions.

sections.heading: Lines and vascular access
sections.bodyHtml:
• Central line status and placement date (infection risk if >5 days)
  • Arterial line for continuous BP monitoring
  • Adequate IV access for vasopressors and inotropes (ideally central line preferred)
  • Femoral vascular access (if Impella or IABP anticipated)

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: This entire section applies to all cardiogenic shock — no Stable/Unstable fork. All CS is emergent and requires escalation. Management is SCAI stage-based.

sections.heading: 5A. SCAI Stage B–C: Immediate stabilization with inotropes and vasopressor support
sections.bodyHtml:
Situation: Beginning shock (SCAI B) with early hemodynamic compromise or classical shock (SCAI C) with overt hypoperfusion.

  1. Immediately identify and treat the underlying cause - Acute MI (STEMI or NSTEMI): Emergency coronary angiography + percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) is non-negotiable

    • SHOCK trial (Hochman et al., 2003): early revascularization (PCI or CABG) within 3 hours superior to medical management alone; goal door-to-balloon <90 min
    • CULPRIT-SHOCK trial (Thiele et al., 2017): culprit-vessel-only PCI superior to multivessel PCI in AMI-CS → revascularize infarct-related artery (IRA) first; defer staged PCI to later
    • Mechanical complication (VSD, acute MR, free wall rupture, tamponade): Stabilize with medical therapy (inotropes + pressors + nitroprusside to reduce afterload); surgical repair is definitive; if free wall rupture suspected, immediate cardiothoracic surgery consultation and OR preparation (discuss salvageability with team; mortality extremely high)
    • Decompensated HF (non-ischemic): Treat exacerbation trigger (diuretics cautiously if not profoundly hypotensive, treat infection, optimize rhythm, initiate advanced HF/VAD workup); do NOT hold standard HF meds (beta-blockers, ACE-I) unless acutely decompensated
    • Myocarditis: Supportive care; MCS bridge if refractory; avoid NSAIDs; consider immunosuppression if biopsy-proven giant-cell or specific serology; transplant/LVAD evaluation if EF does not recover
    • Post-cardiotomy shock: Echocardiography for tamponade/effusion (may require emergent resternotomy and pericardial drainage); assess for graft failure/dissection (may require reopen); manage sepsis if present
    • Acute valvular disease (prosthetic thrombosis, endocarditis, dissection): Urgent cardiothoracic surgery consultation; may require emergent valve repair/replacement

  2. Optimize preload

    • Assess volume status via bedside echo (IVC diameter + collapsibility), PA catheter (CVP, PAWP), or clinical exam
    • LV-dominant (cold-wet) CS: PAWP >18 mmHg with elevated JVP → gentle fluid restriction; cautious diuresis with loop diuretic only if RR >25 or hypoxia present; target euvolemia (PAWP 12–18) not "dry"
    • RV-dominant (cold-dry) CS: CVP >10 mmHg with low CI and low PAWP → avoid aggressive diuresis; cautious fluid bolus (250 mL crystalloid) if IVC <2 cm; target CVP 10–15 for RV preload
    • Mixed phenotype: balance with PA catheter; PAWP >20 + high CVP may require modest diuresis + inotropes; do NOT over-diurese into hypotension
    • DO NOT initiate routine diuretics; Hypotension + oliguria from low CO is NOT responsive to diuretics

  3. Initiate inotrope + vasopressor combination (per institutional protocol; verify doses with provider)

First-line combination: Norepinephrine + Dobutamine or Milrinone

Drug Dose Mechanism Indications Cautions
Norepinephrine (norepi) 2–20 mcg/min IV (titrate to MAP ≥65) α-adrenergic > β1; increases SVR + modest inotropy First-line vasopressor in CS; maintains coronary perfusion; decreases lactate Avoid excessive doses (>0.2 mcg/kg/min); peripheral vasoconstriction can worsen tissue perfusion if MAP target exceeded; use with inotrope in CS (not monotherapy)
Dobutamine 2.5–20 mcg/kg/min IV β1 (inotropy + mild chronotropy), β2 (vasodilation), α minimal ↑ CO, mild ↓ SVR; good for LV dysfunction with decent baseline BP Caution in acute MI: tachycardia + demand ischemia risk; avoid without concomitant revascularization or norepi support. Arrhythmia risk. Hypotension if given alone (require pressor). Not recommended in RV failure (use milrinone for RV).
Milrinone 0.125–0.75 mcg/kg/min IV PDE3 inhibitor; ↑ cAMP → inotropic effect + lusitropy + vasodilation ↑ CO, ↓ PAWP, improves diastolic function; useful in HFrEF component; less tachycardia than dobutamine Hypotension risk: ~50% of patients require concurrent vasopressor (norepi standard). Tachycardia, thrombocytopenia, hyperglycemia. Avoid as monotherapy. ALTSHOCK-2 trial: milrinone + dobutamine similar efficacy in SCAI C-D, but milrinone preferred if hypotension anticipated.
Epinephrine 0.02–0.2 mcg/kg/min IV Low dose (0.02–0.1): β1/β2 dominant; high dose (>0.1): α dominant Can be substituted for norepi if refractory hypotension or as bridge while awaiting tMCS Excessive vasoconstriction at high doses, tachycardia, demand ischemia, lactate elevation (may misinterpret as worsening shock). Use lowest effective dose; transition to norepi once BP stable.

Practical approach:

  • Start: Norepinephrine 5–15 mcg/min + Dobutamine 5–10 mcg/kg/min
  • If BP drops on dobutamine: Reduce dobutamine, increase norepi; or substitute dobutamine with milrinone 0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min (requires pressor already on board)
  • If RV failure (CVP elevated, PAWP low): Use milrinone + norepi (avoids beta-1 driving RV afterload); avoid dobutamine
  • Escalation: If lactate rising, urine output worsening, altered MS progressive on dual-agent maximal doses → escalate to mechanical circulatory support (tMCS) — do NOT chase pressors alone

  1. Optimize afterload

    • Goal MAP ≥65 mmHg (minimum for organ perfusion); some recommend 70–80 in CS for better renal/cerebral perfusion
    • Avoid excessive afterload reduction (target SVR 900–1200 dyne·s·cm⁻⁵) — reduce SVR only if >1400 and causing worsening CO
    • Nitroprusside (0.25–5 mcg/kg/min): if mechanical complication (VSD, acute MR) to reduce afterload; combined with inotropes; requires close BP monitoring; light-sensitive, limits use to <4 hours
    • Nitroglycerin: modest afterload reduction; may be used adjunctively if hypertensive component or ongoing ischemia (avoid in RV infarction)
    • Hydralazine: rarely used in acute CS (slower onset); avoided unless hypertensive + HF component and nitroglycerin insufficient

  2. Ensure adequate oxygenation and ventilation

    • Non-rebreather mask or high-flow nasal cannula targeting SpO₂ >90%
    • Intubation considerations: if pulmonary edema refractory to inotropes + diuretics (rare), or if mental status declining → airway protection (but delay intubation if possible to avoid positive pressure worsening RV preload)
    • CPAP/BIPAP: first-line if respiratory distress + no need for intubation

sections.heading: 5B. SCAI Stage C–D: Escalation to temporary mechanical circulatory support (tMCS)
sections.bodyHtml:
Situation: Persistent SCAI C or progression to SCAI D (rising lactate, worsening organ function, increasing pressor requirement) despite adequate inotrope/vasopressor combination.

  1. Activate "Shock Team" (cardiology, cardiac surgery, critical care, advanced HF) immediately if not already involved
  2. Determine anatomy suitability for tMCS (size of femoral arteries, vascular disease)
  3. Choose tMCS modality based on etiology and hemodynamics:
Device Mechanism Flow Indications Pros Cons / Contraindications
IABP (Intraaortic balloon pump) Diastolic inflation (↑ coronary perfusion) + systolic deflation (↓ afterload) ~0.5 L/min augmentation Historical bridge in AMI-CS while awaiting PCI; post-MI mechanical complication stabilization (VSD, acute MR); bradycardia standby Improves diastolic pressure, ↓ afterload, lower cost, simple insertion via femoral approach, allows leg movement IABP-SHOCK II (2012): No mortality benefit vs medical therapy alone in AMI-CS; not preferred tMCS now. Contraindicated in severe aortic insufficiency. Inadequate for severe LV dysfunction alone (need Impella or ECMO).
Impella (axial-flow LV pump) Catheter-based; draws blood from LV apex or LV body, ejects to aorta Impella 2.5: 2.5 L/min; CP: 3.5–4 L/min; 5.0: 5 L/min; 5.5 RP: 5.5 L/min SCAI C-D bridge-to-recovery (myocarditis, early post-MI, post-cardiotomy) or bridge-to-decision (waiting for PCI results, LVAD/transplant eval). Primary choice for isolated LV dysfunction. Direct LV unloading, ↓ PAWP, improves renal/peripheral perfusion, allows mobilization, lower infection risk vs ECMO, allows weaning trials Requires larger femoral artery access (15–17 F for 5.0); limb ischemia risk (distal perfusion cannula helps); hemolysis if malpositioned; cost; complex insertion; requires imaging (TTE/TEE) for positioning; weaning requires gradual support reduction + close monitoring
VA-ECMO (venoarterial ECMO) Drains deoxygenated blood from venous system (IJ or femoral vein), returns oxygenated to arterial system (femoral artery or aorta) 4–6 L/min (supports entire CO + full oxygenation) SCAI D-E refractory shock, biventricular failure (LV + RV), cardiogenic + respiratory failure (ARDS), bridge-to-transplant, post-cardiotomy fulminant shock, survival from cardiac arrest Supports both heart and lungs, rescues from cardiac arrest, high flow allows rapid stabilization Increases LV afterload (returning oxygenated blood to aorta increases LVEDP + pulmonary edema risk) → often requires Impella or IABP ("ECMELLA") for LV decompression. Limb ischemia risk (use distal perfusion cannula), thromboembolic complications, bleeding (systemic heparinization required), driveline infection, sedation required, ICU-only support, high cost, complex weaning. Post-cardiotomy VA-ECMO mortality remains high (~40–50%) but represents survival population without ECMO.
LVAD (durable continuous-flow pump) Surgical implant; LV apex to aorta; continuous or pulsatile 5–10 L/min (full hemodynamic support) Bridge-to-transplant (if transplant candidate + long waitlist), destination therapy (non-transplant, EF <35%, failed recovery attempt). Not acute tMCS — requires stable enough for surgery. Durable, allows home discharge in some centers, 5-yr survival improved vs medical management, improves QOL in destination therapy Requires surgery, high perioperative mortality, pump thrombosis risk, RV failure post-implant (~25%), bleeding, stroke, driveline infection, lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin INR 2.5–3.5), expensive, commitment required. Destination therapy considered after 2–3 months of tMCS if EF not recovering.

  1. SCAI guideline recommendations (2022 update):

    • SCAI B: Close monitoring, optimize medical therapy
    • SCAI C: Consider Impella or IABP if refractory to inotropes; refer to advanced HF team (discuss bridge strategy, recovery timeline)
    • SCAI D: Escalate to Impella (if LV-dominant) or VA-ECMO (if biventricular); consider ECMELLA (Impella + ECMO) if severe LV dysfunction on ECMO
    • SCAI E: VA-ECMO with emergent escalation intent (transplant or recovery); consider extracorporeal CPR (eCPR) if cardiac arrest occurs

  2. Post-tMCS management:

    • Monitoring: continuous hemodynamic monitoring, lactate trend, urine output, perfusion markers
    • Anticoagulation: systemic heparin (aPTT goal 40–60 sec for IABP; activated clotting time goal 200–250 for ECMO per protocol)
    • Assess for complications: limb ischemia (Impella/VA-ECMO), device thrombosis, bleeding, infection, hemolysis (Impella), arrhythmia

sections.heading: 5C. SCAI Stage D–E: Bridge-to-recovery, LVAD, or transplant decision
sections.bodyHtml:
Situation: Patient deteriorating to SCAI E (refractory shock, cardiac arrest risk) or failure to wean from tMCS after 5–14 days (bridge-to-recovery not occurring).

  1. Reassess the primary pathology:

    • Is the underlying cause being treated? (PCI done if MI? Valve repaired if mechanical? Infection controlled if sepsis-triggered?)
    • Is recovery possible? (Ejection fraction trajectory, biomarker trends, end-organ recovery, lactate clearing?)

  2. Bridge-to-recovery strategy (short-term tMCS, anticipate myocardial recovery)

    • Typical timeline: 5–14 days on Impella/IABP; 3–7 days on VA-ECMO (longer implies recovery unlikely)
    • Weaning criteria before tMCS removal:

    • MAP ≥65 mmHg on minimal inotrope (dobutamine ≤5 mcg/kg/min or milrinone ≤0.125 mcg/kg/min)
    • CI ≥2.2 (or CO >4 L/min) on echo or hemodynamic monitor
    • PAWP normalized (12–18 mmHg) or CVP <10 if RV-dominant
    • Lactate normalized or trending down over 24–48 hours
    • End-organ function improving: urine output >0.5–1 mL/kg/hr, mental status normalizing, creatinine plateauing or declining
    • EF recovery evident on echo (LV EF >35–40%) or myocardial contractility improving
    • Trial of support reduction: Gradually ↓ device flow over hours, monitor BP/CO/perfusion; if hemodynamics stable, proceed to decannulation
    • Post-decannulation: intensive monitoring for recurrence, wean inotropes slowly, cardiac rehab, risk factor modification

  3. Bridge-to-LVAD strategy (escalation if recovery not occurring after 2–3 weeks on tMCS)

    • Candidate criteria: age <70 (relative), no contraindication to anticoagulation, social support for lifelong device care, goal either transplant or destination therapy
    • Timing: if EF not recovering by day 14–21 on tMCS, move toward LVAD evaluation (if transplant candidate) or discuss destination therapy (if not transplant-eligible)
    • Destination therapy LVAD: for patients ≥70 or non-transplant candidates with persistently low EF (<25–30%) after adequate recovery attempt; improves 1-yr and 5-yr survival vs continued medical management

  4. Bridge-to-transplant strategy (if EF <25% and unlikely to recover despite tMCS + optimal medical therapy)

    • Heart transplant evaluation: age, creatinine, ability to comply with immunosuppression, psychosocial support, frailty assessment
    • LVAD as bridge: if transplant waitlist expected to be long (>6 months) and patient stable enough for LVAD surgery, LVAD may be preferred over extended ECMO
    • Palliative care involvement: if transplant/LVAD not feasible, discuss goals and end-of-life planning early

  5. Escalation to extracorporeal CPR (eCPR) if cardiogenic shock progresses to cardiac arrest - eCPR consideration: cardiac arrest complicating refractory CS (may facilitate rapid cannulation for ECMO) - Institutional protocols vary — discuss with cardiothoracic surgery and critical care teams in real time

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml: SBAR framework and who to call for various shock scenarios.

sections.heading: SBAR template
sections.bodyHtml: S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] [if post-op] / admitted [date] [if not post-op] with [admission diagnosis]." B: "Patient developed signs of shock at [time]: SBP [value], HR [rate], urine output [mL/hr], mental status [alert/confused/obtunded]. Lactate [value] [and trend if available]. Currently on [current meds: inotropes, vasopressors]. Recent echo shows EF [%], [any mechanical complications]." A: "Patient is trending toward/in SCAI [stage], with [rising lactate / oliguria / altered MS / peripheral vasoconstriction]. No response to [current regimen]." R: "Requesting [urgent evaluation / PCI activation / tMCS consultation / code team standby]. Patient may require escalation to [ICU / ECMO center] if not already there."

sections.heading: Who to call — by scenario
sections.bodyHtml:
Scenario Immediate Contact Secondary Notes
New shock on post-op floor Cardiac surgery team + hospitalist Code team standby Do NOT wait; escalate STAT. ICU transfer likely.
Acute MI with shock (STEMI/NSTEMI) Interventional cardiology + cardiothoracic surgery Critical care if ICU not primary Cath lab activation for emergent PCI.
Shock + mechanical complication (new murmur) Interventional cardiology + cardiac surgery Echocardiography (stat) VSD/acute MR/tamponade = surgical emergency.
Refractory SCAI C → D Advanced HF / cardiomyopathy team + cardiac surgery ECMO center consult (if not available locally) tMCS evaluation + transplant/LVAD discussion.
Shock + RV dysfunction (CVP >10, PAWP low) Cardiology + critical care PAC placement if not present RV-specific inotropes (milrinone preferred).
Shock + acute kidney injury Nephrology + critical care Dialysis standby Early renal replacement therapy if anuria or severe acidosis.
Shock + altered mental status / stroke concern Neurology + cardiology Stat CT/CTA head Rule out embolic stroke (AFib, LV thrombus, dissection)
Shock + new arrhythmia Electrophysiology + cardiac surgery + critical care Pacing / defibrillation standby Rhythm control + tMCS may be needed.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced-beginner deep-dive on pathophysiology, shock phenotypes, medication rationale, and edge cases. All subsections are collapsible in the app render.

7.1 — Cardiogenic shock phenotypes: LV-dominant vs RV-dominant vs biventricular

sections.heading: LV-dominant cardiogenic shock (most common, ~70%)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Hemodynamic profile: PAWP >18 mmHg (elevated), CI <2.2, SVR elevated, CVP normal
  • Clinical picture: pulmonary edema (crackles, orthopnea, hypoxia), cool extremities (peripheral vasoconstriction)
  • Etiology: anterior MI, extensive LV infarction, acute myocarditis, decompensated HFrEF, post-cardiotomy stunning
  • Management: inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) + vasopressor (norepi); gentle diuresis if pulmonary edema; Impella if refractory (direct LV unloading)

sections.heading: RV-dominant cardiogenic shock (~20–30%, often overlooked)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Hemodynamic profile: CVP >10 mmHg (elevated), PAWP low or normal (<15), CI <2.2, SVR elevated
  • Clinical picture: elevated JVP, peripheral edema, oliguria but no pulmonary edema (RV failure = low LV preload); subtle presentation
  • Etiology: RV infarction (inferior MI extending into RV), massive PE, post-cardiotomy RV failure, severe RV afterload crisis (ARDS, acute respiratory failure)
  • Management: Avoid aggressive diuresis (reduces already-low LV preload); cautious fluid (250–500 mL boluses); RV-specific inotropes (milrinone preferred over dobutamine, which increases RV afterload); pressors for MAP; Impella rarely used (low PAWP limits unload strategy)

sections.heading: Biventricular cardiogenic shock (~10–15%)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Hemodynamic profile: Both CVP and PAWP elevated, CI <2.2, SvO₂ low
  • Clinical picture: signs of both RV and LV failure (pulmonary edema + elevated JVP + oliguria)
  • Etiology: post-cardiotomy shock, acute myocarditis with RV involvement, advanced HF, VA-ECMO cannulation (if using venoarterial, increases afterload)
  • Management: ECMELLA strategy (Impella + VA-ECMO) — Impella reduces LV afterload + PAWP while ECMO provides systemic support; or VA-ECMO alone with careful fluid management

sections.heading: Mixed phenotypes and Forrester quadrants
sections.bodyHtml:
Classic Forrester classification (warm-cold / wet-dry) less useful in acute CS, but helpful for conceptualizing:

LV failure (cold-wet) Cold Wet High High Anterior MI with pulmonary edema ← most common CS
RV/hypovolemic (cold-dry) Cold Dry Low High RV infarct, hypovolemia, PE

7.2 — PA catheter interpretation in cardiogenic shock: key parameters and thresholds Why Swan-Ganz in CS: Guides inotrope/vasopressor selection, quantifies shock severity, monitors response to therapy.

Hemodynamic goals during shock management:
  • CI: >2.2 L/min/m² (ideal >2.5 if possible on inotropes)
  • MAP: ≥65 mmHg (some advocate ≥70 for better organ perfusion)
  • CVP: 8–12 mmHg (balance RV preload; <5 = hypovolemic, >15 = RV failure or overload)
  • PAWP: 12–18 mmHg (balance LV preload; <8 = hypovolemic, >20 = pulmonary edema)
  • SvO₂: ≥60% (reflects tissue oxygen extraction)
  • Lactate: trending downward (clearance indicates improving perfusion)
7.3 — Inotrope + vasopressor matrix and selection rationale Concept: Inotropes ↑ contractility (±afterload effect); vasopressors ↑ SVR/MAP without inotropy. In CS, combine for synergy. Inotropes in CS (all require concurrent vasopressor in CS to prevent hypotension):
