7.4 — Mechanical circulatory support devices: physiology and weaning

sections.heading: IABP (Intraaortic Balloon Pump)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Physiology: Balloon inflates in diastole (↑ diastolic aortic pressure, ↑ coronary perfusion), deflates in systole (↓ afterload, ↓ myocardial work)
  • Hemodynamic effect: Modest CO support (~0.5 L/min), significant afterload reduction
  • Indications: Historical AMI-CS bridge while awaiting PCI; post-MI mechanical complication stabilization
  • IABP-SHOCK II trial (2012): No mortality benefit in AMI-CS vs medical management; no longer preferred as first-line tMCS
  • Contraindications: Severe aortic insufficiency (balloon inflation worsens aortic regurgitation), aortic dissection, severe peripheral vascular disease
  • Complications: Limb ischemia, aortic dissection, balloon rupture, thrombocytopenia (less common now)

sections.heading: Impella (Axial-flow LV pump)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Physiology: Catheter-based pump draws blood from LV cavity, ejects to ascending aorta; directly unloads LV, ↓ wall stress, ↓ LVEDP, ↓ PAWP
  • Hemodynamic effect: Flow 2.5–5.5 L/min depending on device; significant LV unload + CO support
  • Indications: LV-dominant SCAI C-D, bridge-to-recovery (myocarditis, post-cardiotomy, early post-MI), bridge-to-decision (awaiting PCI or LVAD eval)
  • Advantages: Direct LV unload improves renal/cerebral perfusion, ↓ PAWP, allows mobilization, lower infection risk vs ECMO
  • Complications: Limb ischemia (17–20%; mitigated by distal perfusion catheter), hemolysis (if malpositioned), aortic regurgitation, device thrombosis, mechanical complications
  • Weaning: Gradual reduction in pump speed (2 L/min/h reduction) over 1–2 days, monitoring CO/PAWP/perfusion; once stable at lowest setting, trial of explant

sections.heading: VA-ECMO (Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Physiology: Drains venous blood (IJ or femoral vein), oxygenates via membrane oxygenator, returns oxygenated blood to arterial system (femoral artery or aorta). Provides full circulatory and respiratory support
  • Hemodynamic effect: Flow 4–6 L/min; replaces entire cardiac output + full oxygenation
  • Indications: SCAI D-E refractory shock, biventricular failure, cardiogenic + respiratory failure, bridge-to-transplant, post-cardiotomy fulminant, survival from cardiac arrest
  • Advantages: Rescues from cardiac arrest, dual heart + lung support, rapid stabilization, highest flow support
  • Disadvantages: ↑ LV afterload (blood returning to aorta increases LVEDP) → pulmonary edema worsens unless LV vented (Impella or IABP added = "ECMELLA"); limb ischemia, thromboembolism, bleeding (heparin), driveline infection, ICU-only, high cost
  • ECMELLA strategy: VA-ECMO + Impella for severe LV dysfunction on ECMO; Impella decompresses LV while ECMO provides systemic/pulmonary support
  • Post-cardiotomy VA-ECMO outcome: 40–50% hospital survival (high mortality, but represents rescue population)
  • Weaning: Gradual reduction in ECMO flow over days (if recovery evident), trial of spontaneous circulation off ECMO, then decannulation if stable

sections.heading: LVAD (Left ventricular assist device)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Physiology: Surgically implanted pump (apex to aorta); continuous or pulsatile flow; full CO support (5–10 L/min)
  • Indications: Bridge-to-transplant (if transplant candidate, long waitlist expected); destination therapy (non-transplant, EF <35%, failed recovery on tMCS)
  • Advantages: Durable, home discharge possible, improves long-term survival (vs medical management or extended ECMO), QOL improvement
  • Disadvantages: Surgical implant, high perioperative mortality (10–20% in acute CS), pump thrombosis, RV failure (25%), bleeding, stroke, lifelong anticoagulation, driveline infection, cost, commitment
  • Bridge-to-transplant timing: If EF not recovering after 2–3 weeks on tMCS and transplant candidate, consider LVAD evaluation
  • Destination therapy: For patients declining transplant or ineligible, EF <35% despite optimal tMCS trial; 5-yr survival ~50%
  • Weaning (destination therapy): Not intended to wean; device runs indefinitely; goal is end-organ recovery, patient stabilization, and home discharge

Summary table: tMCS selection

Stage Preferred device Alternative Avoid
SCAI C (initial) IABP or Impella (LV-dom) Milrinone + norepi if MAP adequate Escalating pressors alone
SCAI C (refractory) Impella (LV-dom) VA-ECMO if biv-dom IABP (insufficient)
SCAI D Impella or ECMELLA VA-ECMO (if biv or respiratory failure) IABP
SCAI E VA-ECMO ± Impella eCPR if arrest Prolonged medical management
Bridge-to-transplant LVAD (if candidate) VA-ECMO short-term IABP
Destination therapy LVAD — Temporary support
7.5 — Post-cardiotomy cardiogenic shock: unique features and management differences Epidemiology: ~1–2% of cardiac operations; distinct from AMI-CS in causes and outcomes. Etiologies (often multifactorial):
  • Myocardial stunning (inadequate myocardial protection, prolonged bypass time, cross-clamp time >90 min)
  • Graft failure (inadequate revascularization in CABG, anastomotic leak, graft occlusion)
  • Residual valvular dysfunction (incomplete valve repair, prosthetic mismatch)
  • Tamponade (bleeding into pericardium, inadequate drainage)
  • Arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation, junctional rhythm, complete heart block)
  • Sepsis (bacterial contamination, line infection)
  • Dissection (aortic, graft, native vessel)
  • RV failure (particularly after RV outflow tract surgery) Diagnostic approach:
  • Stat bedside echocardiography: assess global LV/RV function, detect tamponade/effusion, look for mechanical issues (dissection, anastomotic leak on TEE)
  • Stat CXR: widened mediastinum (bleeding), cardiac silhouette, pleural effusion, pneumothorax
  • Repeat troponin + isoenzymes: ongoing necrosis vs stunning
  • Angiography (cath or CT): if graft occlusion or dissection suspected Management differs from AMI-CS:
    1. Aggressive volume repletion (if not tamponade) — post-op bleeding leaves patient hypovolemic; crystalloid + blood products
    2. Early reopen consideration if tamponade suspected or graft failure evident → bedside resternotomy, pericardial drainage, graft re-exploration
    3. High-dose inotropes (dobutamine acceptable in post-op CS, unlike acute MI) + vasopressors
    4. tMCS early: VA-ECMO preferred over Impella in post-cardiotomy (biventricular involvement common, graft failure complication possible); ECMO allows salvage if immediate reopen needed
    5. Antibiotic coverage: prophylactic to empiric (post-op infection risk) Outcomes:
    6. With early recognition + aggressive intervention: 40–50% hospital survival
    7. Delayed intervention or misattribution to "anesthesia effect": higher mortality
    8. VA-ECMO post-cardiotomy survival: ~40–50% (high mortality, but rescue population)
7.6 — Shock phenotypes by etiology: acute MI vs post-cardiotomy vs acute HF vs myocarditis

sections.heading: Acute MI (STEMI/NSTEMI) cardiogenic shock
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature Characteristic Management implication
Timeline Acute (minutes to hours) Emergent PCI needed
Hemodynamics Cold-wet (LV-dom) typical IABP/Impella if refractory to inotropes + norepi
Etiology Infarction + mechanical complication risk Cath + angiography mandatory
Inotrope strategy Avoid high-dose dobutamine (demand ischemia); norepi + low-dose dobutamine or milrinone Revascularize first, then optimize
Revascularization Culprit-only PCI (CULPRIT-SHOCK) preferred Do NOT do multivessel PCI acutely
Prognosis 30–40% mortality with early revasc Worse if shock >6 hours before PCI

sections.heading: Post-cardiotomy shock
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature Characteristic Management implication
Timeline Immediate post-op (POD 0–1) or delayed (POD 2–5) Different causes (graft failure vs stunning vs tamponade)
Hemodynamics Variable (depends on cause) Imaging (echo, CT) critical
Etiology Graft failure, tamponade, stunning, arrhythmia, sepsis (multi-factor) Reopen if graft failure/tamponade; high-dose support if stunning
Inotrope strategy Dobutamine acceptable (no ACS demand ischemia); milrinone if RV failure Tailor to phenotype; VA-ECMO preferred over Impella (allows reopen)
Revascularization Re-exploration/reopen if graft issue Decide early (echo + cath if indicated)
Prognosis 40–60% mortality (varies by cause) Better if recognized early + reopen done; worse if delayed

sections.heading: Acute HF decompensation cardiogenic shock
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature Characteristic Management implication
Timeline Hours to days (less acute than MI) Allows time for optimization before escalation
Hemodynamics Cold-wet (LV-dom) Diuretics cautiously + inotropes; avoid aggressive preload reduction
Etiology Trigger (infection, rhythm, medication hold, HTN crisis, non-adherence) Treat trigger first
Inotrope strategy Dobutamine or milrinone; norepi if hypotensive Standard dual-agent approach
Escalation LVAD evaluation if EF <25% + persistent low CI on inotropes Consider advanced HF/LVAD team early
Prognosis 35–45% in-hospital mortality Depends on EF recovery; non-recovering → LVAD/transplant

sections.heading: Myocarditis cardiogenic shock
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature Characteristic Management implication
Timeline Days (prodromal viral symptoms → acute decompensation) Allows observation for recovery
Hemodynamics Global LV/RV dysfunction; often biventricular Impella or VA-ECMO for bridge-to-recovery
Etiology Viral (most common), fulminant myocarditis (rare, high mortality) Biopsy if diagnostic uncertainty; immunosuppression if giant-cell
Inotrope strategy Milrinone + norepi (reduce afterload for stressed ventricle) Minimize inotropes if possible (may prolong inflammation)
Mechanical support Impella or VA-ECMO as bridge-to-recovery (most recover within 5–14 days) ECMO if biventricular or respiratory involvement
Escalation If fulminant (ECMO candidates from onset), may require early VA-ECMO Transplant/LVAD rarely needed if adequate support given
Prognosis 90%+ recovery if supported through acute phase; 5–10% mortality with tMCS Excellent prognosis if bridge successful
7.7 — RV physiology and RV-predominant shock management RV physiology in shock:
  • RV operates on ascending (compliant) part of Frank-Starling curve; exquisitely sensitive to afterload
  • RV preload: CVP (not PAW); RV stroke volume = (CVP – 0) × RV compliance / RV afterload
  • RV afterload: PVR (driven by pulmonary vascular tone, hypoxia, acidosis, mechanical obstruction)
  • In RV infarction: loss of contractility + rising afterload (catecholamine surge) → RV failure Hemodynamic signature of RV failure:
  • CVP >10 mmHg
  • PAWP low or normal (<15)
  • CI <2.2
  • SvO₂ low (<60%) if severe
  • Lactate elevated (poor perfusion despite low PAWP) Management principles:
    1. Avoid aggressive diuresis — RV failure is the opposite of LV failure; reducing preload worsens CO
    2. Cautious fluid — 250–500 mL crystalloid boluses if IVC <2 cm; target CVP 12–15 (balance RV preload)
    3. RV afterload reduction: low O₂ sat, acidosis, high minute ventilation all worsen RV afterload
    4. Optimize SpO₂ to >94%, normalize pCO₂ (hyperventilation worsens PVR), correct acidosis
    5. Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators: nitric oxide (inhaled NO) 20–40 ppm if available; epoprostenol (inhaled or IV) if PE or severe PVR elevation
    6. Inotrope choice: Milrinone preferred (↓ RV afterload) + norepi for MAP
    7. Avoid dobutamine (β2 effects may not translate to pulmonary vasodilation in RV infarction)
    8. Avoid aggressive norepinephrine escalation (further increases RV afterload)
    9. Avoid positive-pressure ventilation if possible (increases intrathoracic pressure, reduces RV preload); use spontaneous breathing or gentle assist modes
    10. Mechanical support: RV failure rarely isolated; if biventricular, VA-ECMO preferred; IABP/Impella less useful for isolated RV failure (PAWP low, so unloading LV doesn't help; RV afterload still high) RV infarction specifics:
    11. Occurs in ~40% of inferior MIs (extend into RV territory)
    12. Classic triad: hypotension, clear lungs (no pulmonary edema), elevated JVP (RV failure)
    13. Do NOT aggressively diurese — fluid is needed for RV preload
    14. Revascularize RCA (if STEMI) → RV contractility often recovers quickly if reperfused within hours
7.8 — Lactate and end-organ markers in cardiogenic shock: prognostic and escalation value Lactate physiology in CS:
  • Normal lactate: 0.5–2.0 mmol/L (produced by muscles + RBCs, cleared by liver + kidneys)
  • In shock: tissue hypoperfusion → anaerobic metabolism → lactate production ↑ and hepatic clearance ↓
  • Lactate ≥2 mmol/L = hallmark of hypoperfusion (diagnostic for shock stage C+)
  • Lactate trend > single value: rising lactate = worsening shock; decreasing lactate = improving perfusion Lactate thresholds in CS:
  • Lactate 2–4: mild hypoperfusion, SCAI C
  • Lactate 4–8: moderate hypoperfusion, SCAI D
  • Lactate >8: severe refractory shock, SCAI E (or multi-organ failure) Lactate clearance as weaning marker:
  • Lactate clearance = (initial lactate – lactate at time X) / initial lactate × 100%
  • >10% clearance over 6 hours = improving perfusion, support may be adequate
  • <10% clearance = inadequate support, escalate or tMCS
  • Rising lactate despite escalation = SCAI D/E, urgent tMCS or extracorporeal support Other end-organ markers:
    MarkerNormalCSPrognostic value
    Oliguria>0.5 mL/kg/hr<0.5 mL/kg/hrIndicates renal hypoperfusion; resolves with restored CO
    Creatinine<1.2 mg/dL↑ (AKI)AKI severity predicts mortality; Cr doubling = poor sign
    Bilirubin<1.2 mg/dL↑Hepatic hypoperfusion; bilirubin >3 = very poor prognosis
    Platelets150–400↓ (thrombocytopenia)Consumption from ECMO / disseminated coagulation; <50 = critical
    PT/INR<1.1↑Hepatic synthetic dysfunction; INR >2 = poor perfusion
    Albumin>3.5 g/dLOften lowMarker of chronic shock / malnutrition; not acutely prognostic
    SvO₂60–75%<60%Poor tissue O₂ extraction; <50% = ominous
    Teaching point: In CS, lactate + oliguria + altered mental status is the constellation that drives escalation — not a single BP reading.
7.9 — SwanGanz catheter + PAPi scoring: hemodynamic monitoring in shock PA catheter indications in CS:
  • Persistent hypotension despite clinical assessment of volume status
  • Unclear etiology (LV vs RV vs mechanical)
  • Guiding therapy escalation (inotrope vs vasopressor vs MCS)
  • Refractory shock requiring tMCS (baseline hemodynamics + support escalation response) PAPi (Pulmonary Artery Pulsatility Index) in shock:
  • PAPi = (systolic PA pressure – diastolic PA pressure) / CVP
  • Normal PAPI: >1.0
  • PAPi <0.9 = RV dysfunction (low pulsatility + high CVP) = poor prognosis, RV failure likely
  • Use in post-LVAD: PAPi <1.0 post-LVAD implant = RV failure risk, may need RV support Continuous SvO₂ monitoring:
  • Reflects balance between oxygen delivery (DO₂ = CO × CaO₂) and oxygen consumption (VO₂)
  • SvO₂ = mixed venous O₂ sat from PA catheter
  • SvO₂ <60% = poor extraction or inadequate delivery; escalate support
  • SvO₂ >80% (after tMCS) = recovery trajectory (myocardium no longer extracting max O₂)
7.10 — Clinical trials informing CS management: SHOCK, CULPRIT-SHOCK, IABP-SHOCK II, ALTSHOCK-2

sections.heading: SHOCK Trial (Hochman et al., 2003)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Question: Does early revascularization (PCI/CABG) improve survival vs medical management in AMI-CS?
  • Design: 302 AMI-CS patients, randomized to early revascularization vs medical management
  • Result: Early revascularization reduced 6-month mortality (50% → 46%) and 1-year mortality (56% → 46%) vs medical management (68%)
  • Implication: Revascularization is standard of care in AMI-CS. Not an option; mandatory.

sections.heading: CULPRIT-SHOCK Trial (Thiele et al., 2017)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Question: In AMI-CS with multivessel disease, is culprit-only PCI superior to multivessel PCI?
  • Design: 706 STEMI-CS patients with multivessel CAD; randomized to culprit-only PCI vs immediate multivessel PCI
  • Result: Culprit-only PCI reduced 30-day mortality (8.3% → 7.4%) and composite adverse events. Multivessel PCI = higher mortality + more complications.
  • Implication: Revascularize culprit only in AMI-CS. Defer staged PCI of non-culprit lesions; no multivessel PCI in acute shock.

sections.heading: IABP-SHOCK II Trial (Thiele et al., 2012)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Question: Does IABP improve survival vs medical management in AMI-CS?
  • Design: 600 AMI-CS patients; randomized to IABP + medical therapy vs medical therapy alone
  • Result: No difference in 30-day mortality (IABP 39.7% vs medical 41.3%, P=0.6) or 1-year mortality
  • Implication: IABP is not preferred tMCS in AMI-CS. Impella or VA-ECMO are alternatives. IABP may be used as bridge to PCI in select cases, but not as definitive MCS.

sections.heading: ALTSHOCK-2 Trial (preliminary, 2023–2024)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Question: In SCAI C-D cardiogenic shock, is milrinone + dobutamine vs dobutamine + norepi superior?
  • Design: Ongoing multinational RCT comparing inotrope combos in CS
  • Preliminary result: Milrinone + norepi appears similar or slightly superior to dobutamine + norepi for lactate clearance, with lower tachycardia
  • Implication: Milrinone increasingly preferred as first-line inotrope (reduces afterload + tachycardia); dobutamine reserved for specific situations (RV failure less likely, higher BP tolerance)
7.11 — Weaning from mechanical support: criteria and strategy Timing for weaning assessment (applies to Impella, IABP, VA-ECMO):
  • Minimum support duration: 5–7 days (allow myocardium time to recover from stunning/ischemia)
  • Maximum support (if no recovery): 2–3 weeks on temporary MCS before escalating to LVAD or palliative approach Weaning criteria (must ALL be met):
    1. Hemodynamic stability:
    2. MAP ≥65 mmHg on minimal inotrope (dobutamine ≤5 mcg/kg/min or milrinone ≤0.125 mcg/kg/min) or inotrope wean attempted
    3. CI ≥2.2 L/min/m² on echo or PA catheter at low/off support
    4. PAWP normalized (12–18 mmHg) or CVP <10
    5. Lactate clearance:
    6. Lactate normalized (<2 mmol/L) or trending downward for 24–48 hours
    7. Lactate clearance >10% over 6 hours on reduced support
    8. End-organ recovery:
    9. Urine output >0.5–1 mL/kg/hr (off diuretics ideally, or minimal dose)
    10. Creatinine stable or declining from peak
    11. Mental status improving (alert, no encephalopathy)
    12. Liver function normalizing (bilirubin declining, PT/INR improving)
    13. Myocardial recovery evident:
    14. EF improved on serial echo (LV EF >30–35% by visual estimate or speckle tracking)
    15. Contractility improving (S' velocity uptrend, dP/dt improving on PA catheter)
    16. No new mechanical complications (e.g., VSD opening up, new MR developing)
    17. Infection / inflammatory markers controlled:
    18. Temp <38.5°C, WBC trending down or stable
    19. Lactate not rising despite support reduction (not attributed to sepsis) Weaning protocol:
      PhaseActionTimelineMonitoring
      Phase 1: Support reduction trialReduce device flow (Impella: ↓ 0.5 L/min/h; ECMO: ↓ 0.5 L/min/h; IABP: change from 1:1 to 1:2 ratio)6–12 hoursContinuous hemodynamics, lactate at end of trial
      Phase 2: Assess toleranceIf MAP ≥65, lactate stable/down, UOP maintained → proceed to phase 34–6 hours off supportRepeat echo (CO/EF estimate), lactate
      Phase 3: DecannulationIf all criteria met + stabilized off support, plan decannulationSame-day or overnightPost-decannulation: close perfusion watch for 24–48 hours
      Phase 4: Inotrope weanAfter decannulation, wean inotropes over 24–72 hours (↓ 25–50% per day)Days 1–3 post-decannulationDaily echo, lactate, UOP, vitals
      Failure-to-wean strategy:
    20. If weaning trial shows BP drop, lactate rise, or oliguria → revert to full support, reassess etiology
    21. If no recovery signs after 2–3 weeks on temporary MCS → escalate to LVAD or transplant evaluation (or palliative care if not candidate)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in cardiogenic shock
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these signs of worsening shock even in SCAI C patients.

  • Rising lactate despite escalating support — not improving perfusion; escalate to tMCS or reconsider etiology (sepsis? mechanical issue?)
  • Progressive oliguria (UOP <0.3 mL/kg/hr, anuria) — AKI deepening; start early renal replacement therapy discussion
  • Altered mental status despite normalization of BP — cerebral hypoperfusion, not merely sedation; escalate support
  • Cool extremities + widening central–peripheral temp gradient — severe peripheral vasoconstriction = shock deepening, not improving
  • Escalating pressor requirement (norepi >0.2 mcg/kg/min, adding epi) — tachyphylaxis or shock progression; escalate to tMCS
  • New murmur in MI-CS — mechanical complication (VSD, acute MR, free wall rupture); urgent cath + surgery
  • Worsening pulmonary edema despite inotropes — LV afterload too high or inotrope ineffective; Impella indication
  • Recurrent hypotension on inotropes — dependence on high-dose inotropes without CO gain; transition to mechanical support
  • Post-tMCS rapid deterioration (Impella/ECMO) — device thrombosis, malposition, or inadequate flow; urgent imaging + troubleshooting
  • Bleeding complications (Impella/ECMO) — ongoing bleeding despite heparin hold; transfuse, reverse anticoagulation per protocol
  • Signs of limb ischemia (Impella/VA-ECMO femoral) — pain, pulselessness, pallor, paresthesias in lower extremity; urgent vascular surgery
  • Fever + rising lactate on ECMO — nosocomial infection (CLABSI, line sepsis); source control + broad antibiotics
  • Thrombocytopenia progression (platelets <50 on ECMO) — consumption coagulopathy, transfuse; if severe, consider ECMO circuit change
  • Cardiac arrest during weaning trial — inadequate myocardial recovery; do NOT escalate; discuss goals (LVAD, transplant, or transition to comfort care if not candidate)

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert high-yield wisdom — common errors and underutilized techniques.

  1. SCAI staging drives escalation, not single vitals. A patient with SBP 90 + oliguria + lactate 3 is SCAI C and needs escalation; SBP 110 + rising lactate + declining UOP is SCAI C→D transition and also needs escalation.

    Lactate + end-organ markers are trajectory markers; trending worse = escalate even if BP looks "OK."

  2. Don't wait for profound hypotension to escalate. SCAI B (congestion without overt shock) can become SCAI D within hours. Early recognition of lactate rise, oliguria appearance, or altered MS = escalate to tMCS discussion.

  3. Milrinone + hypotension is predictable. ~50% of CS patients drop BP on milrinone. Always have norepi on board BEFORE starting milrinone. Consider starting norepi first, add milrinone second.

  4. Dobutamine + arrhythmia risk in acute MI. Tachycardia + demand ischemia is real; avoid dobutamine in unrevascularized STEMI-CS. Once IRA open, dobutamine acceptable. Prefer milrinone + norepi in acute MI until PCI done.

  5. Epinephrine driving lactate rise is NOT worsening shock — it's "epi effect." High-dose epi (>0.1 mcg/kg/min) increases lactate production via beta-effects; if lactate rising but perfusion improving (UOP up, MS better, cool extremities warming), escalate to tMCS rather than blaming epi. Transition to norepi once stable.

  6. IABP alone is insufficient in severe LV dysfunction. IABP-SHOCK II killed IABP monotherapy for AMI-CS. It may buy time for PCI but is not definitive; escalate to Impella or VA-ECMO early.

  7. Impella vs VA-ECMO choice:

    • Impella: LV-dominant, isolated LV dysfunction, want mobilization / lower infection risk
    • VA-ECMO: biventricular failure, respiratory failure + CS, need emergent rescue (arrest), post-cardiotomy fulminant
    • ECMELLA: biventricular + severe LV afterload crisis (ECMO alone worsens pulmonary edema)

  8. VA-ECMO post-cardiotomy mortality is high but still survivor population. 40–50% survive to hospital discharge even in fulminant post-cardiotomy shock on ECMO; do not give up. Reopen discussion, graft revision, or escalation to transplant/LVAD all possible if ECMO buys time.

  9. Weaning criteria before tMCS removal are NON-NEGOTIABLE. Do not decannulate a patient on dual inotropes with lactate >2 and oliguria just because "looks better." Must meet ALL criteria: low inotrope, CI >2.2, PAWP 12–18, lactate <2, UOP >0.5 mL/kg/hr, mental status normalized, EF improved.

  10. Lactate trend is the best shock marker. Single lactate value less useful than trajectory. A patient with lactate 5 → 4 → 3 is improving; a patient with lactate 2 → 3 → 4 is deteriorating.

    Lactate clearance <10% over 6 hours = inadequate support, escalate.

  11. RV failure is underrecognized. Look for CVP >10 + PAWP low + CI <2.2. Do NOT diurese aggressively; these patients need fluid. Use milrinone (not dobutamine) to reduce RV afterload. Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (NO) helpful.

  12. Mechanical complication of MI is a surgical emergency. New holosystolic murmur post-MI = VSD or acute MR; do NOT miss this. Get urgent echo, stabilize with nitroprusside + inotropes + IABP or Impella, call cardiothoracic surgery immediately.

  13. Post-cardiotomy shock is often multifactorial. Don't assume it's just myocardial stunning. Tamponade (fluid collection), graft failure (inadequate revascularization or anastomotic leak), arrhythmia, and sepsis are all possible.

    Early imaging (echo, CT) and team discussion (surgery, cardiology, critical care) are essential. Resternotomy may be lifesaving.

  14. Takotsubo can masquerade as acute MI + shock. Apical ballooning on echo, preserved base, often young female, stressful trigger. Cath shows no significant CAD. Most recover within 1–2 weeks with supportive care; invasive management usually not needed.

    Do not over-treat with inotropes; most recover spontaneously.

  15. Bridge-to-transplant decisions require early palliative care involvement. Not all CS patients are transplant candidates (age, comorbidities, social support, frailty). LVAD is not trivial (infection, thrombosis, stroke risk).

    Discuss goals + realistic timeline early with patient/family and multidisciplinary team. If not transplant/LVAD candidate and failing tMCS → transition to comfort care.

cards.title: Cardioplegia
cards.quickAnswer: High-potassium solution (crystalloid, blood-based, or del Nido formula) delivered to the coronary circulation to arrest the heart diastolically during cardiac surgery. Allows operative field visualization and reduces myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury. Types: crystalloid (traditional, inexpensive, needs frequent redosing), blood cardioplegia (most common, mixed oxygenated blood + solution), del Nido (single-dose arrest 60–90 min, increasingly popular). Routes: antegrade (via aortic root) or retrograde (via coronary sinus). Expected post-operative findings: transient myocardial stunning (resolves 24–72 h), normal troponin elevation (not MI), arrhythmia, electrolyte shifts.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: High-potassium solution (crystalloid, blood-based, or del Nido formula) delivered to the coronary circulation to arrest the heart diastolically during cardiac surgery. Allows operative field visualization and reduces myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury. Types: crystalloid (traditional, inexpensive, needs frequent redosing), blood cardioplegia (most common, mixed oxygenated blood + solution), del Nido (single-dose arrest 60–90 min, increasingly popular). Routes: antegrade (via aortic root) or retrograde (via coronary sinus). Expected post-operative findings: transient myocardial stunning (resolves 24–72 h), normal troponin elevation (not MI), arrhythmia, electrolyte shifts.
cards.sourcePrecedence: Gravlee (2024) → Kirklin/Blackstone (2026) → Bojar (2020) → Buckberg blood cardioplegia literature → Matte/del Nido (2002) → STS Guidelines

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardioplegia is a high-potassium crystalloid or blood-based solution delivered to the coronary circulation to arrest the myocardium in diastole during cardiac surgery. Two primary mechanisms:

  1. Immediate arrest — K⁺ depolarizes the myocyte, stopping electrical and mechanical activity.
  2. Myocardial protection — cold temperature (traditional) or specific additives reduce metabolic oxygen demand (MVO₂), minimize ischemia-reperfusion injury, and enable longer operative times without myocardial damage.

Cardioplegia is distinct from CPB (the extracorporeal circulation machine). CPB provides whole-body oxygenation and perfusion; cardioplegia is the arrest solution applied locally to the heart (Gravlee et al., 2024).

sections.heading: 2. Types of Cardioplegia and Delivery Routes
2.1 Cardioplegia Types
sections.bodyHtml:
Type Composition Temperature Redosing Advantages Disadvantages
Crystalloid (Plegisol, St. Thomas) High K⁺, glucose, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ in electrolyte solution Cold (4–10 °C) Q20–30 min (ante) / Q10–20 (retro) Inexpensive; first-generation standard Pure crystalloid = poor myocardial nutrition; osmotic + hyperkalemic load on body
Blood cardioplegia Patient's oxygenated blood + cardioplegia solution (4:1 ratio typical) Cold or warm (protocol-dependent) Q20–30 min (ante) / Q10–15 (retro) Most common now; superior myocardial protection; oxygen-rich; reduces hyperkalemic load Requires separate mixing apparatus; slightly longer setup time
Del Nido Crystalloid-blood hybrid (1:4 ratio) + lidocaine, mannitol, Mg²⁺, dextrose Cold initially → warm rewarming None — single dose Single-dose arrest 60–90 min without redosing; excellent recovery; faster rewarming; pediatric + redo favorite Requires specific recipe; limited data for cross-clamps > 120 min
Microplegia Concentrated solution mixed with patient blood at cannula tip Typically cold Variable Combines crystalloid efficiency + blood nutrition Specialized equipment; less common in adult surgery

sections.heading: Antegrade
sections.bodyHtml:
• Route: Via aortic root cannula (into coronary ostia distal to aortic cross-clamp)
  • Mechanism: Antegrade coronary flow under positive pressure; solution flows naturally down the coronary tree
  • Use: Most routine cardiac surgery (CABG, valve, congenital repairs)
  • Advantages: Physiologic flow direction; good distribution if native coronaries patent
  • Disadvantages: Ineffective if aortic root is clamped distally (Type A dissection) or severe aortic insufficiency prevents pressure retention

sections.heading: Retrograde
sections.bodyHtml:
• Route: Via coronary sinus cannula (drains into RA; solution infused retrogradely into coronary venous bed)
  • Mechanism: Veno-arterial backflow through coronary sinus into capillary bed
  • Use: Severe CAD (inadequate antegrade distribution), moderate-to-severe AR (proximal leakage), redo sternotomy (safer anatomy)
  • Advantages: Works when antegrade fails; avoids venting complications
  • Disadvantages: Less uniform distribution; sinus cannulation adds 5–10 min; fenestrated sinus risk thrombus
  • Clinical note: Many surgeons use antegrade + retrograde together for complex cases (redo valve + severe CAD)

sections.heading: Expected Findings by Timeline
sections.bodyHtml:
Finding Mechanism Timeline Interpretation
Myocardial stunning Ischemia-reperfusion + arrest-induced metabolic debt POD 0–2 (resolve 24–72 h) Expected. EF often 30–40% initially; recovers. Inotropes POD 0–1 typical.
Troponin elevation Myocyte membrane disruption from arrest + reperfusion (not necrosis) Peak POD 0–1; detectable POD 2–3 Normal post-cardioplegia. Troponin alone ≠ MI. Verify: serial trend, symptoms, ECG, hemodynamics.
Reperfusion arrhythmia K⁺ washout, rewarming, electrolyte shifts POD 0–1 (rare on ICU day 2+) Usually self-limited. New arrhythmia on POD 2+ more likely related to delirium trigger (pain, fever, infection) than cardioplegia residuum.
Electrolyte shifts K⁺ diuresis + shift back intracellular; Mg²⁺ loss POD 0–2 Expect low K⁺, Mg²⁺ (not high). Replace aggressively per protocol (Bojar, 2020).
Contractility depression Myocardial edema + metabolic recovery POD 0–2 Inotropic support (dobutamine, milrinone) often needed. Taper as EF recovers.
Pulmonary edema / weight gain Capillary leak from arrest-reperfusion inflammation POD 0–3 Diuresis; gentle negative balance. Resolves as inflammation settles by POD 3–5.

sections.heading: What to Extract from Intra-Operative Note
sections.bodyHtml:
• Cardioplegia type (crystalloid, blood, del Nido) → informs recovery trajectory
  • Antegrade vs retrograde (or both) → note if retrograde was needed (implies difficult distribution, severe CAD/AR)
  • Cross-clamp time → >90 min = extended; >120 min = higher risk for stunning, AKI, delirium (unless del Nido used)
  • Redose count → del Nido zero redoses; frequent redoses may indicate difficult ischemia control
  • Temperature strategy → cold = slower EF recovery (24–72 h) but safer margin; warm = faster recovery, less room for error

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: <details><summary>Why cardioplegia works: ion channel and metabolic physiology</summary> The myocardium is exquisitely sensitive to ischemia. Cardioplegia works by two converging mechanisms: (1) K⁺-induced depolarization silences electrical activity, eliminating the energy cost of contraction (~90% of cardiac MVO₂); (2) hypothermia (traditional cold cardioplegia) reduces the remaining metabolic rate ~60%, allowing safe cross-clamp times of 120+ minutes. Del Nido allows longer arrest through a specific cocktail: lidocaine (reduces electrical irritability), mannitol (osmotic agent reduces edema), magnesium (stabilizes membranes), and a 1:4 crystalloid-to-blood ratio (balanced osmolality + nutrition). The blood component carries oxygen and nutrients; the crystalloid carries electrolytes and additives. This mixture allows 60–90 min single-dose arrest at controlled rewarming without redosing. Reperfusion (when the cross-clamp comes off and normal coronary flow resumes) causes predictable myocyte membrane disruption and oxidative stress, explaining the normal post-operative troponin rise. This is reversible — the myocardium recovers electrically and mechanically over 24–72 hours if no additional insult occurs. </details> <details><summary>Redosing strategy: why and when</summary> Crystalloid and blood cardioplegia require periodic redosing because the initial solution is gradually diluted or removed by the CPB circuit and coronary venous outflow. Antegrade redosing typically q20–30 min (shorter intervals if high CPB flow or multiple grafts). Retrograde redosing more frequent (q10–15 min) because venous outflow is less controlled. Del Nido requires no redosing — the specific electrolyte + medication balance allows arrest duration of 60–90 min from a single dose, shifting the cross-clamp strategy for many centers. </details> <details><summary>Why post-op troponin elevation is NOT myocardial infarction</summary> Post-operative troponin elevation peaks on POD 0–1 and gradually declines through POD 2–3. This pattern — high but declining — is classic for reversible myocyte disruption, not necrosis. By contrast, MI-pattern troponin is persistently high or rising, paired with chest pain, ischemic ECG changes, and hemodynamic compromise. Context is everything: a patient with EF recovery from 30% to 45% over 48 hours, stable vitals, no chest pain, and a downtrending troponin has stunning, not MI. The troponin is a marker of temporary myocyte membrane injury, not permanent loss of contractile tissue. </details> <hr />

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Post-cardioplegia troponin elevation is normal and expected — does not equal MI. Always assess: symptoms, ECG pattern, serial troponin trend (should peak POD 1 and decline), hemodynamic status.

  2. Myocardial stunning resolves over 24–72 hours. Early low EF (30–40%) that recovers is classic cardioplegia physiology, not MI or acute graft failure. Serial echocardiography POD 1–2 shows improvement.

  3. Del Nido shifts the risk calculus for cross-clamp time. A 120+ min cross-clamp reported as "routine rather than high-risk" usually indicates del Nido was used. Still monitor closely, but the safety profile is favorable with this solution.

  4. Retrograde cardioplegia was needed if documented. Implies severe CAD, AR, or difficult anatomy. Watch closely for incomplete myocardial protection: more pronounced stunning, higher arrhythmia risk.

  5. Ask the resident about cross-clamp time in the hand-off. >90 min is extended; >120 min is high-risk for AKI, delirium, and stroke in the first 48 hours, even with modern cardioplegia.

  6. Electrolyte shifts are profound POD 0–1. Expect aggressive K⁺ + Mg²⁺ replacement, not restriction. Recheck lytes q6–8h POD 0, q12h POD 1, then daily. Low K⁺ and Mg²⁺ directly increase reperfusion arrhythmia risk.

  7. Rewarming arrhythmia (tachy, polymorphic) is ICU-phase, not floor. By POD 2+ on the floor, most electrolyte and temperature normalization is complete. New arrhythmia on POD 2+ is more likely pain, fever, infection, or delirium than cardioplegia residuum.

cards.title: Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection (CAUTI)
cards.quickAnswer: Indwelling catheter present ≥2 days + fever (≥38.3°C) or localized symptoms (suprapubic/flank pain, dysuria) → send urine culture STAT, CBC, CMP. Asymptomatic bacteriuria ≠ CAUTI — do not treat. Only empiric antibiotics if symptomatic or septic. Catheter removal is the #1 prevention intervention — remove ASAP if clinically stable. Empiric coverage: ceftriaxone 2 g IV Q12h, pip-tazo 4.5 g IV Q6-8h, or cefepime 2 g IV Q8-12h (per local antibiogram). Duration: 7 days uncomplicated; 10–14 days if pyelonephritis, prostatitis, or sepsis.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria ≠ CAUTI — do not treat. Only empiric antibiotics if symptomatic or septic.

Catheter removal is the #1 prevention intervention — remove ASAP if clinically stable. Empiric coverage: ceftriaxone 2 g IV Q12h, pip-tazo 4.5 g IV Q6-8h, or cefepime 2 g IV Q8-12h (per local antibiogram). Duration: 7 days uncomplicated; 10–14 days if pyelonephritis, prostatitis, or sepsis.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, clinical significance.

  • Definition: Urinary tract infection associated with an indwelling catheter (Foley), confirmed by urine culture (≥10⁵ CFU/mL with catheter in place) AND ≥1 compatible symptom (fever, dysuria, suprapubic pain, flank pain, or altered mental status in elderly).
  • Epidemiology: CAUTI incidence rises 3–7% per day of catheterization; most common organisms are E. coli (30–40%), Klebsiella (10–15%), Pseudomonas (10–15%), Enterococcus (5–10%), and Candida (5–15%, rarely pathogenic) (Hooton et al., 2010; CDC/NHSN).
  • Who this applies to: all patients with an indwelling urinary catheter in place ≥2 days, especially post-operative cardiac surgery patients.
  • Why it matters: CAUTI is a CMS non-reimbursement (never event) condition; tracked by NHSN surveillance as a quality metric. Impacts hospital accreditation, payment, and departmental performance. Unrecognized CAUTI can progress to sepsis with mortality 5–15%.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
CAUTI develops via sequential biofilm formation on the catheter surface and ascension of uropathogens along the lumen or between catheter and urothelium. Within 24–48 hours of catheter placement, bacteria and fungi form organized biofilm structures that are 100–1000× more resistant to antibiotics than planktonic cells (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020). Organisms express adhesins (P fimbriae in E. coli) that bind to uroepithelium; the Foley bypasses normal urinary flow and natural clearance. Host response triggers mucosal damage, pyuria, and increased inflammatory cytokines. If bacteria breach the bladder mucosa (especially with obstruction or upper tract involvement), bacteremia and sepsis develop rapidly, particularly in elderly or immunocompromised patients.

Risk factors specific to post-cardiac surgery patients:

  • Foley dwell time (modifiable; #1 risk factor) — 3–7% increase per day
  • Female gender (~2× higher risk than males)
  • Advanced age (≥65 years)
  • Diabetes, immunosuppression, spinal cord injury, or history of prostate disease
  • Urinary retention post-anesthesia (often leading to unnecessary prolonged catheterization)
  • Mechanical obstruction (blood clot, mucus plug, stricture)
  • Complicated surgery (massive transfusion, re-exploration, CPB > 2 hours)

Key distinction: Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB) — positive culture WITHOUT symptoms — is colonization, NOT infection. ASB does NOT increase CAUTI risk and should NOT be treated outside pregnancy and pre-urologic procedure settings (Hooton et al., 2010).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — signs and symptoms at the bedside.

Any of the following in a patient with an indwelling catheter ≥2 days:

  • New fever (≥38.3°C / 100.9°F) or recurrent fevers
  • Suprapubic pain, tenderness, or dysuria
  • Flank pain or CVA (costovertebral angle) tenderness (suggests pyelonephritis)
  • Altered mental status or delirium in an elderly patient — often the ONLY sign of UTI/CAUTI in this population; never attribute to age alone
  • Sepsis criteria met: tachycardia (HR > 110), tachypnea (RR > 22), hypotension (MAP < 65), elevated lactate (≥2 mmol/L), or altered mental status
  • Cloudy, foul-smelling urine with visible pyuria or hematuria
  • Urinalysis with pyuria (WBC > 5–10/hpf), nitrites, or leukocyte esterase; culture pending

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Information gathering only — no treatment decisions yet.

  • Vital signs & perfusion: temperature, HR, BP, RR, SpO₂, capillary refill, skin temperature, mental status (alert/oriented ×3 or confused?)
  • Symptoms: fever pattern, flank pain, suprapubic tenderness, dysuria, frequency, urgency; any recent instrumentation or recatheterization?
  • Catheter & urine inspection: color (clear vs. cloudy vs. bloody vs. dark), odor, character (debris, sediment?); insertion site erythema, drainage, or signs of trauma; securement check; note catheter insertion date/time
  • MAR review: any recent antibiotics given? Prophylaxis regimen post-op? Current antimicrobials on board?
  • Recent labs: CBC (WBC count, left shift with bands?), basic metabolic panel (Cr trending up?), most recent urinalysis (nitrites, LE, WBC, RBC, casts?)
  • Timeline: exactly how many days has the Foley been in place? Placed intra-operatively or post-op? Document POD.
  • Comorbidities: diabetes, immunosuppression, spinal cord injury, history of prostate disease or pelvic surgery?
  • Surgery context: was the procedure straightforward or complicated (CPB duration, blood loss, re-exploration)? Current medications including steroids or immunosuppressants?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Patient alert/oriented, normotensive, no sepsis criteria — though fever may be present.)

  1. Send urine culture STAT — most sensitive test; ≥10⁵ CFU/mL typical threshold for catheterized symptomatic UTI
  2. Send CBC + comprehensive metabolic panel STAT — evaluate WBC elevation, left shift, renal function (Cr baseline vs. current)
  3. Send urinalysis — pyuria (WBC > 5–10/hpf), nitrites, LE, RBC, casts suggest upper tract or systemic involvement
  4. Notify provider/APP with SBAR (see §6) — do NOT initiate antibiotics without team consultation unless septic
  5. Vital sign monitoring q4h — track temperature trend; if fever persists or rises after 48–72 hours despite appropriate antibiotics, escalate for imaging and ID re-consult
  6. Document findings comprehensively:
    • Catheter insertion date and time (calculate exact dwell days)
    • Urine appearance and odor
    • Temperature trend over past 24 hours
    • Any recent catheter manipulation or replacement
    • Symptom onset and character (fever only vs. flank pain vs. altered mental status)
    • Assess Foley necessity daily — is continued catheterization clinically justified? Can bladder scans + intermittent straight catheterization replace indwelling? Catheter removal is the single most effective intervention to prevent CAUTI progression — escalate removal question to provider even in stable presentation; target removal within 24–48 hours if hemodynamically stable and not on vasopressors
    • If Foley must remain, ensure proper maintenance per CAUTI prevention bundle:
    • Daily perineal hygiene with soap and water (not antiseptic)
    • Secure catheter to thigh or abdomen to prevent traction trauma
    • Drainage bag always positioned below bladder level; never kink tubing
    • Empty bag regularly with sterile technique; avoid backflow
    • Replace catheter only if occluded, dislodged, or clinically indicated (NOT on routine schedule)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path / Sepsis pathway
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension MAP < 65, HR > 110, RR > 22, lactate ≥2, altered mental status — meets sepsis criteria.)

  1. STAT call APP / hospitalist + Rapid Response Team — activate sepsis protocol per institution policy (typical 1-hour bundle)
  2. Send blood cultures × 2 (aerobic + anaerobic) IMMEDIATELY — before any antibiotics
  3. Send urine culture STAT (may be source of bacteremia)
  4. Send CBC, CMP, lactate, coagulation studies, troponin — assess organ dysfunction and baseline for sepsis trajectory
  5. Establish / verify IV access — two large-bore IVs, one for fluids
  6. Initiate broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition — do NOT wait for culture results:
    • Ceftriaxone 2 g IV Q12h, OR
    • Piperacillin-tazobactam (pip-tazo) 4.5 g IV Q6-8h, OR
    • Cefepime 2 g IV Q8-12h
    • (Per local antibiogram; adjust for renal function)
    • Narrow spectrum once culture & sensitivities return (typically 24–48 hours)
    • Aggressive fluid resuscitation: 30 mL/kg crystalloid (lactated Ringer preferred if available) over first hour; reassess perfusion q15–30 min
    • Monitor urine output: insert urometer or straight-cath if no recent void; goal ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; concern for acute kidney injury if Cr rising despite adequate fluids
    • Remove Foley immediately if sepsis is attributed to CAUTI — don't wait for culture confirmation; removal is both diagnostic (rules out catheter-related source) and therapeutic
    • Serial lactate monitoring — if ≥4 mmol/L or rising, prepare for possible ICU transfer; discuss with APP/team for higher-level care if not already critical
    • Consider vasopressor support if MAP remains < 65 after 30 mL/kg crystalloid — discuss with APP/ICU team

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed fever [°C/°F] at [time]. Foley placed [date/time] — in place [X days]. UA shows [pyuria/nitrites/LE]. Patient reports [flank pain/suprapubic tenderness/altered MS]. Current HR [value], BP [value], RR [value], SpO₂ [value]." A: "Patient is [stable / showing sepsis criteria]. [Any antibiotics currently on board?]. [Renal function: Cr = [value], baseline [value].]" R: "Requesting [antibiotic orders / Foley removal order / admission to higher level of care / sepsis protocol activation]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Rationale
Fever + Foley ≥2 days, stable, no sepsis Primary APP / on-call hospitalist Routine workup; culture-directed therapy
Fever + UA abnormalities suggesting CAUTI ID consultation recommended Confirms diagnosis; guides antibiotic selection + duration
Sepsis criteria met (any SIRS + lactate ≥2 or altered MS) STAT hospitalist + RRT + charge RN Activate sepsis protocol — time-critical (1-hour bundle)
CAUTI + pyelonephritis signs (flank pain + CVA tenderness + high fever) Hospitalist + ID consult Plan 10–14 day course; consider imaging if atypical/recurrent
CAUTI + prostatitis in men (fever + perineal/rectal pain) Hospitalist + ID + urology if retention develops 10–14 days minimum; fluoroquinolone often preferred
CAUTI + rising creatinine or oliguria Hospitalist + nephrology Rule out acute kidney injury; adjust medication doses
Candida in urine culture, asymptomatic Observe; no antibiotic Colonization; remove catheter + monitor for symptom development
Candida in urine + fever/symptoms + immunosuppressed Hospitalist + ID Consider fluconazole; remove Foley
Recurrent CAUTI (≥2 episodes in short interval) Urology + ID consult Assess for retention, inadequate catheter care; consider intermittent straight-cath protocol

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Asymptomatic Bacteriuria vs. CAUTI vs. Pyelonephritis vs. Urosepsis
sections.bodyHtml:
Asymptomatic Bacteriuria (ASB)

  • Positive urine culture (≥10⁵ CFU/mL) WITHOUT symptoms
  • Common in catheterized patients (~25% with Foley > 7 days)
  • DO NOT TREAT in non-pregnant, non-urologic-procedure patients — no clinical benefit; increases antibiotic resistance and C. difficile risk (Hooton et al., 2010)
  • Distinct from CAUTI; organism presence alone does NOT diagnose infection

Uncomplicated Cystitis (CAUTI, lower UTI)

  • Fever (typically < 39°C) + dysuria/suprapubic pain/frequency + pyuria + positive culture
  • No flank pain, CVA tenderness, or systemic toxicity
  • Organism typically gram-negative rod (E. coli, Klebsiella)
  • Treatment: 7 days culture-directed antibiotic
  • Prognosis: resolves with therapy; low recurrence if catheter removed

Pyelonephritis (upper UTI)

  • High fever (≥39°C), severe flank pain, CVA tenderness, nausea/vomiting ± sepsis criteria
  • May have pyuria; bacteremia in 20–30% of cases
  • Indicates systemic toxicity; potential for sepsis if untreated
  • Treatment: 10–14 days IV → PO antibiotic; aggressive hydration; imaging (ultrasound/CT) if atypical or recurrent
  • Prognosis: responds well to therapy; delayed treatment risks scarring or abscess

Catheter-Associated Bacteremia / Urosepsis

  • Sepsis criteria met (SIRS + organ dysfunction); source = UTI
  • Blood cultures positive; concurrent pyuria + positive urine culture
  • Mortality 5–15% even with appropriate therapy; highest in elderly and immunosuppressed
  • Treatment: aggressive fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum antibiotics (within 1 hour), vasopressor support if needed; ICU-level care
  • Special concern: post-cardiac surgery patients decompensate rapidly due to surgery-related stress, anemia, and volume shifts

sections.heading: 7.2 CAUTI Prevention Bundle
sections.bodyHtml:
Evidence-based interventions that reduce CAUTI incidence by 30–65% when bundled (CDC/NHSN; Gould et al., 2010):

  1. Avoid catheterization when possible

    • Pre-op risk stratification: is Foley truly needed?
    • Post-op voiding assessment: portable ultrasound bladder scan → straight-cath PRN if > 500 mL residual, NOT indwelling Foley placement

  2. Foley removal ASAP — the single most effective intervention

    • Target: remove within 24–48 hours if hemodynamically stable and not on vasopressors
    • Standard post-cardiac: removal by POD 1–2; if retained longer, document medical justification daily
    • Post-ICU transfer: reassess daily; remove the moment retention risk resolves

  3. Aseptic insertion

    • Sterile field, sterile gloves, antiseptic skin prep (chlorhexidine or iodine-based)
    • Smallest-caliber catheter allowing adequate drainage (14–16 Fr typical; 12 Fr may reduce trauma)
    • Single-lumen catheters preferred

  4. Maintenance bundle

    • Daily perineal hygiene with soap and water (not antiseptic)
    • Meatal care 2–3× daily; keep area clean and dry
    • Secure catheter to thigh or abdomen to prevent traction/trauma
    • Drainage bag always below bladder level; never kink tubing
    • Empty bag regularly with sterile technique; avoid backflow
    • Replace catheter only if occluded, dislodged, or clinically indicated (NOT routine schedule)

  5. Catheter-free alternatives

    • Portable urinal for men; external condom catheter if unable to use bedpan
    • Bedpan/commode for women; offer frequently post-anesthesia
    • Intermittent straight-cath PRN (lower infection risk than indwelling, especially for spinal cord injury)
    • Restrict fluids if possible to reduce void frequency (balance with post-op rehydration goals)

  6. Document & communicate

    • Note insertion date/time and clinical indication; review daily whether catheter still needed
    • Handoff communication: "Foley in place since [date]; removal ordered [POD X] pending [clinical milestone]"
    • Coordinate with PT/OT: early mobility → faster return of spontaneous voiding

sections.heading: 7.3 Antibiotic Choices and Duration
sections.bodyHtml:
Initial empiric therapy pending culture (start ONLY if symptomatic or septic):

Antibiotic Dose Notes Renal Adjustment
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV Q12h Broad gram-negative; covers E. coli, Klebsiella, many others; good renal penetration CrCl < 30: consider Q24h
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV Q6-8h Covers gram-negative + anaerobes + some Pseudomonas; good for critically ill CrCl < 20: reduce to 2.25 g
Cefepime 2 g IV Q8-12h 4th-gen cephalosporin; covers Pseudomonas; use if resistant gram-negatives suspected CrCl < 30: Q12h; < 10: Q24h
Ciprofloxacin 500–750 mg IV/PO Q12h Oral option for step-down; excellent bladder/prostate penetration; avoid QTc prolongation Age > 60 or renal disease: lower dose
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) 1–2 DS tabs PO Q12h Oral; limited use (resistance common); use only if susceptible CrCl < 30: reduce frequency

Culture-directed therapy (after sensitivities return, typically 24–48 hours):

  • Narrow to most specific, least toxic agent based on susceptibilities
  • E. coli: ceftriaxone (3rd-gen) usually first-line; fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX if susceptible + oral step-down acceptable
  • Klebsiella: similar to E. coli; carbapenem if extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL) detected
  • Pseudomonas: cefepime, pip-tazo, or fluoroquinolone (high-dose ciprofloxacin; single-agent risk of resistance)
  • Enterococcus: ampicillin (if susceptible) + gentamicin (for synergy in bacteremia); vancomycin if ampicillin-resistant
  • Candida: NO antibiotic; remove catheter, monitor for symptoms. Fluconazole 400 mg PO/IV daily only if symptomatic or severely immunosuppressed; short course (7–10 days) sufficient

Duration:

  • Uncomplicated CAUTI (cystitis only): 7 days
  • Pyelonephritis or prostatitis: 10–14 days
  • Urosepsis: 10–14 days IV → PO step-down once clinically improved
  • Candida: no specific duration if asymptomatic; fluconazole 7–10 days if symptomatic/immunocompromised

Doses adapted from Hooton et al. (2010), CDC/NHSN guidance, and Hardin & Kaplow (2020). Always verify against current institutional policy.

sections.heading: 7.4 Special Populations and Edge Cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Pregnant women (rare on post-op cardiac unit, but critical distinction):

  • Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria — pregnant women with ASB have substantially higher risk of pyelonephritis + preterm labor
  • Guideline consensus: treat with cephalosporin (e.g., cephalexin 500 mg PO QID) or amoxicillin (avoid TMP-SMX and fluoroquinolones)

Patients with spinal cord injury or chronic catheterization:

  • Baseline higher colonization; intermittent straight-catheterization (ISC) protocols dramatically reduce CAUTI incidence vs. indwelling Foley
  • Discuss with urology if baseline neurogenic bladder or chronic cath use applies

Immunosuppressed patients (post-transplant, on biologics, chemotherapy):

  • Candida colonization risk elevated; consider antifungal prophylaxis if high risk
  • Lower threshold for early imaging and ID consultation in atypical presentations

Pre-urologic procedure patients:

  • Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria (exception to standard ASB rule) to reduce procedure-related sepsis risk
  • Coordinate timing of antibiotic course with urology schedule

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Distinct from Section 5B unstable criteria. If any appear, re-escalate immediately.

  • Fever not responding to empiric antibiotics after 48–72 hours — suggests wrong organism, inadequate penetration, or localized abscess; obtain imaging (ultrasound, CT abdomen/pelvis) and ID re-consult
  • Temperature rising despite antibiotics — sepsis developing; obtain repeat blood cultures, lactate, CBC
  • Altered mental status or confusion worsening — hallmark of urosepsis in elderly; particularly ominous if new; activate sepsis protocol immediately
  • Hypotension or MAP trending down — sepsis with distributive shock; immediate vasopressor consideration
  • Lactate rising or remaining ≥2 mmol/L after fluids — tissue hypoxia; prepare for ICU transfer
  • Flank pain intensifying with CVA tenderness + high fever — pyelonephritis progressing; possible perinephric or renal abscess; imaging needed urgently
  • Perineal erythema, warmth, fluctuance, or purulent drainage — suggests abscess or cellulitis; urgent drainage evaluation needed
  • Oliguria or Cr rising despite adequate fluids — acute kidney injury from sepsis or direct renal involvement; nephrology input needed
  • New suprapubic mass or palpable bladder — urinary retention despite catheter; consider catheter malfunction (clot, obstruction); imaging + irrigation assessment
  • Positive blood cultures — bacteremia; confirms systemic infection; escalate antibiotic therapy, consider invasive source control if endocarditis or abscess suspected
  • Catheter leaking, dislodged, or bloody drainage — immediate replacement if indication remains; if traumatic or bleeding, consider urology consult for cystoscopy
  • Candida in urine culture WITH fever — shift from "observation" to treatment; initiate fluconazole + remove catheter; review immunosuppression status
  • Recurrent fever despite appropriate antibiotic course — source failure; consider inadequate source control (retained infected material, abscess, infected catheter biofilm). May need catheter replacement or surgical intervention

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Asymptomatic bacteriuria ≠ CAUTI — do NOT treat. This is the #1 pitfall. Positive urine culture in asymptomatic catheterized patient = colonization, not infection. Treating ASB: (1) promotes resistance, (2) delays true CAUTI recognition when symptoms appear, (3) increases C. difficile risk, and (4) provides no clinical benefit per IDSA (Hooton et al., 2010). Many nurses reflexively treat any positive culture — educate the team.

  2. Foley dwell time is the #1 modifiable risk factor — remove ASAP. The moment a post-op patient is stable enough to void on bedpan/urinal, the Foley should be pulled. Standard post-cardiac: removal by POD 1–2. If still in place POD 4+, document the reason. Removal of catheter alone often resolves CAUTI even if antibiotics still needed.

  3. Altered mental status in elderly may be the ONLY sign of CAUTI. Don't wait for fever + dysuria. New confusion, delirium, or loss of orientation in elderly post-op patient with Foley should trigger immediate UTI workup. Send cultures even if afebrile.

  4. Sepsis can develop rapidly from CAUTI, especially in elderly post-op patients. Stable febrile CAUTI at 8 AM can be in septic shock by 2 PM. Serial vital signs, lactate, reassessment q2–4h for first 24 hours post-diagnosis are essential. Don't "watch and wait" — escalate early.

  5. Candiduria rarely needs treatment if asymptomatic — remove catheter first. Candida colonizes catheterized patients; positive culture ≠ fungal UTI. Remove Foley (primary intervention); monitor for symptoms. Only treat if: (1) immunosuppressed (ICU, post-transplant, chemotherapy), (2) symptoms develop, or (3) blood cultures positive (rare). Fluconazole unnecessary 95% of the time.

  6. Cloudy or malodorous urine alone does NOT meet CAUTI criteria. Cloudiness is expected in many catheterized patients due to biofilm shedding and crystal formation. Diagnosis requires fever OR localized symptoms PLUS either pyuria OR positive culture. Don't treat based on urine appearance alone.

  7. CVA tenderness + fever = pyelonephritis, NOT simple cystitis — plan 10–14 day course. Localization testing (CVA percussion, flank pain) indicates upper tract involvement; changes both antibiotic duration and intensity of monitoring. Uncomplicated cystitis = 7 days; pyelonephritis = 10–14 days.

  8. Prostate involvement in men = longer course (10–14 days minimum; some recommend 4–6 weeks). Fever + perineal pain + dysuria + prostate tenderness on DRE = prostatitis. Poor antibiotic penetration into prostate; fluoroquinolone often preferred. Untreated prostatitis → chronic infection, abscess, retention. Urology may be needed.

  9. Pregnant women: treat asymptomatic bacteriuria. Exception to "do not treat ASB" rule. Pregnant women with ASB have substantially higher pyelonephritis + preterm labor risk; guideline consensus recommends treatment (cephalosporin or amoxicillin). This population is rare on post-cardiac units but worth knowing.

  10. Catheter in place > 14 days pre-culture: consider replacement before sending. Biofilm alters culture results; if Foley has been in > 2 weeks, a single positive culture may not reflect true infection. Some providers recommend replacing catheter, waiting 12–24 hours, then repeating culture for diagnostic clarity.

  11. Bladder scan BEFORE straight-cath or recatheterization. Retention is common post-anesthesia. Use portable ultrasound bladder scan (non-invasive) to assess post-void residual; if < 300 mL, reassure patient they can void without catheter. If > 500 mL, straight-cath PRN rather than replacing indwelling. Prevents unnecessary Foley re-placement.

  12. Pre-op Foley "just in case" — value debated; avoid if possible. Some surgeons place Foley routinely intra-op; others argue this initiates biofilm colonization unnecessarily. Best practice: place Foley only if intra-operative indication (e.g., urine output monitoring in shock states); remove ASAP post-op.

  13. CAUTI is a CMS non-reimbursement (never event) + quality metric. NHSN surveillance tracks CAUTI per 1,000 catheter-days at hospital and unit level. Impacts hospital payment, accreditation, and departmental reviews. Prevention bundle compliance (early removal, aseptic insertion, proper maintenance) is tracked. Every nurse impacts this measure.

  14. Empiric antibiotic coverage guided by local antibiogram, NOT standard guidelines. Resistance patterns vary by institution. Before selecting ceftriaxone, pip-tazo, or cefepime empirically, check institutional antibiogram (pharmacy site or sepsis protocol). Pseudomonas resistance, ESBL prevalence, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE) vary yearly.

  15. Intermittent straight-cath > indwelling for chronic catheterization patients. Patients with neurogenic bladder or baseline chronic catheterization (spinal cord injury) have dramatically lower CAUTI with ISC protocols vs. indwelling Foley. Discuss with urology; may change management significantly.

cards.title: Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) Infection
cards.quickAnswer: Sudden diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools in 24h) + fever, abdominal pain, leukocytosis (WBC >15) post-op, especially after broad-spectrum antibiotics → isolate immediately: contact precautions + soap and water (alcohol gel does NOT kill spores). Send stool PCR or toxin assay only if symptomatic. Empirically start fidaxomicin PO 200 mg BID × 10 days or PO vancomycin 125 mg q6h if unavailable per institutional policy. Fulminant features (shock, ileus, toxic megacolon, WBC >35k, lactate >5) → stat ICU transfer + CT surgery consult + vancomycin PO 500 mg q6h + IV metronidazole 500 mg q8h.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
