sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Toxin-mediated colitis caused by Clostridioides difficile (Gram-positive anaerobic spore-forming bacterium). Presents as diarrhea (≥3 unformed stools in 24h) with or without systemic symptoms.
  • Epidemiology: develops in 1–3% of hospitalized patients overall, but up to 10–15% of patients on broad-spectrum antibiotics. Peak onset post-operative day 3–7, though may occur during hospitalization or weeks after discharge.
  • Who this applies to: any hospitalized patient (acute care, stepdown, ICU) with new-onset diarrhea and recent antibiotic exposure. Post-operative cardiac or general surgery patients are exceptionally high-risk due to prolonged perioperative antibiotics, PPI use, and extended hospital stay.
  • Why it matters: CDI increases mortality, length of stay, and healthcare costs. Fulminant disease (toxic megacolon, shock) carries 10–20% mortality even with treatment (McDonald et al., 2021).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism of infection:

C. difficile is found ubiquitously in hospital and healthcare environments. Infection requires three conditions: (1) spore ingestion, (2) disruption of normal colonic flora by antibiotics, and (3) germination of spores to toxin-producing vegetative cells.

  • Spore germination occurs when broad-spectrum antibiotics (fluoroquinolones, cephalosporins, clindamycin, penicillins) suppress competing flora. C. difficile is resistant to these agents and overgrows.
  • pH shift from PPI use elevates gastric pH, allowing more spores to survive passage through the stomach and reach the colon.
  • Toxin production: vegetative cells produce toxins A (enterotoxin) and B (cytotoxin), which inactivate Rho GTPases → loss of epithelial tight junctions → fluid secretion, mucosal necrosis, and inflammatory response.
  • Systemic toxin absorption in severe disease leads to multi-organ dysfunction, septic shock, and death if untreated.

Fulminant disease pathophysiology:

  • Toxic megacolon: massive colonic inflammation causes transverse colon dilation >6 cm (visible on abdominal X-ray); perforation risk.
  • Ileus: paralysis of coordinated bowel contractions; fluid and bacteria pool; septic shock may develop from bacterial translocation.
  • Post-operative patients are exceptionally high-risk because perioperative antibiotics (cefazolin extended POD 1–2, vancomycin + cefepime for HAP, piperacillin-tazobactam for SSI) are prolonged, broad-spectrum, and suppress flora maximally. Add PPI stress ulcer prophylaxis, advanced age, and immunosuppression from CPB, and the setup is complete.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a hospitalized or recently discharged patient:

  • Diarrhea alert: ≥3 unformed stools within 24 hours, OR abrupt change from baseline constipation to significant diarrhea
  • Systemic symptoms: fever (≥38.5°C / 101.3°F), abdominal pain or cramping, abdominal distention
  • Lab abnormality: WBC elevation (often >15 with left shift; leukemoid reaction common with WBC 20–40 in severe cases); serum creatinine trending upward
  • Patient complaint: "I'm having loose stools," "my abdomen feels bloated," "I don't feel right"
  • Nursing observation: new skin breakdown in perineal area from frequent stools; stool sample sent for culture grows no pathogen but symptoms persist

Clinical context that raises suspicion: patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics (cefazolin, fluoroquinolone, cephalosporin, clindamycin), PPI use, recent endoscopy or colonoscopy, advanced age (>65), immunosuppression, or prior CDI history.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (3–5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions here; actions come in Section 5. Competent systematic exam.

  • Observe stool characteristics: appearance (watery, mucoid, blood-tinged, visible blood), frequency in past 12 and 24 hours, odor (foul in severe disease)
  • Assess vital signs: temperature, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation — looking for shock, tachycardia, fever
  • Assess perfusion and mental status: capillary refill, skin temperature, alertness, orientation (sepsis manifests as altered mental status)
  • Abdominal exam: distention (measure girth if possible and compare to baseline), tenderness (focal vs diffuse), rebound/guarding (suggests peritonitis), bowel sounds (high-pitched in early ileus, hypoactive or absent in advanced ileus or toxic megacolon)
  • Review history: recent or current antibiotics (type, duration)? PPI use? Recent endoscopy or colonoscopy? Immunosuppression (steroids, dialysis, transplant)? Prior CDI? Prior severe infection?
  • Review recent labs: WBC trend (rising is ominous); creatinine (baseline vs today); albumin/protein (hypoalbuminemia predicts worse severity); lactate if available
  • Skin assessment: check perineum and buttocks for erythema, maceration, breakdown from frequent diarrhea
  • Fluid status: input/output balance, dry mucous membranes, skin turgor, urine color (dehydration common; compensatory tachycardia may mask true severity)
  • Lines and access: adequate IV access for fluids or medications? Nasogastric tube in place (affects oral medication absorption)?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake and alert, MAP >65, no signs of shock, no severe pain, minimal abdominal distention, no toxic megacolon features.)

  1. Isolate immediately: contact precautions + hand hygiene with SOAP AND WATER, not alcohol gel. (Spores are alcohol-resistant; soap physically removes them.)

    • Post isolation sign on door (visible to all staff and visitors)
    • Ensure all visitors, clinical staff, PT/OT understand soap-and-water requirement
    • Reinforce at every shift change
    • Dedicated stethoscope, BP cuff, pulse ox in room if possible; if shared, wash with soap and water between uses

  2. Send stool sample for testing — test ONLY if patient has ≥3 unformed stools in 24h (avoid false positives from colonization). - Preferred: PCR for C. difficile toxin genes (highest sensitivity ~95–99%, specific; now preferred per IDSA 2021)

    • Alternative: Toxin EIA (enzyme immunoassay) if PCR unavailable (sensitivity ~75–90%)
    • AVOID: Stool culture (not standard; slow) or repeat testing same day
    • Label with time of last stool and frequency count; send promptly
    • Do NOT test for "test of cure" once improving (see Pitfalls)

  3. Obtain baseline labs:

    • CBC (WBC, differential, hemoglobin); comprehensive metabolic panel (creatinine, albumin, electrolytes, phosphate)
    • Lactate if available (predicts severity)
    • Repeat as indicated by clinical trajectory

  4. Empirically start fidaxomicin PO 200 mg BID × 10 days if high pre-test probability per institutional policy and drug available. - If unavailable or patient cannot tolerate PO: vancomycin PO 125 mg q6h × 10 days - Do NOT use metronidazole as monotherapy (IDSA 2021: metronidazole now reserved for non-severe CDI only if fidaxomicin/vancomycin unavailable; evidence is weak)

    • Hold antimotility agents (diphenoxylate, loperamide, atropine); they increase risk of toxic megacolon
    • If patient has nasogastric tube or high NG output, discuss with pharmacy whether oral drug will reach colon

  5. Maintain hydration and replace losses:

    • IV fluids (lactated Ringer or normal saline) if PO intake inadequate or stool output >500 mL/day
    • Monitor urine output, intake/output ratio, daily weights
    • Encourage PO fluids if tolerated (water, clear broths, Gatorade; avoid high-fiber, lactose, high-fat foods initially)
    • Monitor and replace sodium, potassium, phosphate (diarrhea causes significant losses)

  6. Monitor for dehydration complications:

    • Daily weight and trend
    • Capillary refill, skin turgor, mucous membrane hydration
    • Urine color and specific gravity
    • CVP if line in place; otherwise clinical assessment

  7. Skin and perineal care:

    • Gentle cleansing with each loose stool (use warm water initially; avoid harsh soap that further irritates skin)
    • Pat dry gently (don't rub); apply thick protective cream (zinc oxide, dimethicone, or lanolin) with each change
    • Use incontinence pads; change every 2–4 hours
    • Educate patient and visitors on hand hygiene after toileting (patient performs own hygiene when possible)
    • Monitor for secondary candidiasis or bacterial superinfection

  8. Notify APP / provider with SBAR (see §6 for template):

    • Stool sample sent; results pending or positive
    • Empiric fidaxomicin or vancomycin started and time given
    • Baseline labs obtained
    • Request discussion of escalation triggers and follow-up plan

  9. Continuous monitoring trajectory:

    • Stool frequency (q2–4h initially; trend direction)
    • Vital signs q4–6h minimum (more if concerning)
    • Abdominal exam q8–12h or if symptoms change
    • Watch for red flags (see Section 8)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable / Fulminant path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension despite fluids, severe abdominal pain, signs of shock: altered mental status, rising lactate, WBC >20–35, Cr >1.5× baseline, signs of ileus or toxic megacolon—absent/minimal bowel sounds, rigid abdomen, severe distention.)

  1. STAT call: provider/APP, charge RN, ICU team. Do NOT leave patient alone. Activate Rapid Response if appropriate.

  2. Notify CT surgery team immediately — fulminant CDI may require colectomy; early awareness is critical.

  3. Transfer to ICU — fulminant CDI is a medical emergency requiring ICU-level monitoring for organ dysfunction and organ support decision-making.

  4. Establish IV access: two large-bore IVs if not in place; consider central line per ICU team (aggressive fluid resuscitation often required).

  5. Start maximal antimicrobial therapy per IDSA fulminant protocol:

    • Vancomycin PO 500 mg q6h × 10 days (higher dose than non-severe; maximizes colonic concentration. Fidaxomicin not studied in fulminant; vanco preferred.)
    • Metronidazole IV 500 mg q8h (penetrates systemic circulation; used adjunctively for presumed invasive toxin delivery)
    • Do NOT delay antibiotics waiting for test results if fulminant presentation

  6. Aggressive fluid resuscitation:

    • Bolus 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension; repeat as needed to MAP >65 and improve lactate clearance
    • Monitor lactate trending; if not improving with fluids, consider vasopressor support (norepinephrine first-line per sepsis guidelines)
    • Place urinary catheter if not in place; target UOP 0.5–1 mL/kg/min
    • Monitor for fluid overload (auscultate lung sounds, assess JVD, watch for tissue edema) — balance is critical in fulminant disease

  7. Surgical consult for possible colectomy:

    • Indicated for uncontrolled sepsis despite medical therapy ≥24–48h, toxic megacolon unresponsive to conservative care, or perforation
    • Subtotal colectomy + ileostomy is procedure of choice (lower anastomotic leak risk in fulminant disease)

  8. Continuous ICU monitoring:

    • Hemodynamics (MAP, CVP, lactate, serial troponin if cardiac involvement suspected)
    • Organ function (creatinine, INR, bilirubin, platelet count; DIC risk in sepsis)
    • Lactate q2–4h until trending down; persistent elevation predicts poor outcome

  9. Contact precautions + isolation enforcement — same as stable path but more critical in ICU with multiple team members

  10. Consider infectious disease consult for FMT decision if recurrent CDI develops after this episode clears

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for provider notification:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit/ICU], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient with [duration] diarrhea (last count: [number] unformed stools in past 24h). Fever [temperature], abdominal [pain/distention/pain severity]. WBC [current value] (was [prior value]), Cr [current] (baseline [baseline]), lactate [if available]. Stool sample sent for C. difficile PCR at [time]. [Vitals: BP, HR, RR, SpO₂]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable / fulminant]. Symptoms: [fever, pain grade, distention, shock signs]. Empiric [fidaxomicin or vanco] started at [time]. Contact precautions + soap/water confirmed." R: "Requesting [clinical guidance on empiric vs test-result-driven therapy / discussion of escalation triggers / ICU transfer / surgical consult / additional labs]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Suspected CDI (stable) Primary APP or on-call provider
Fulminant CDI (shock, toxic megacolon, ileus) APP + ICU team + CT surgery consult
CDI + rectal perforation or peritonitis Stat CT surgery + ICU + anesthesia
CDI + sepsis unresponsive to 24–48h medical therapy Infectious disease consult + CT surgery
Post-treatment recurrence (diarrhea + positive test after therapy completed) Infectious disease consult (FMT candidate)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are collapsible — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Testing strategy: PCR vs. toxin EIA — clinical logic
sections.bodyHtml:
• PCR (nucleic acid amplification test): detects C. difficile toxin genes; gold standard per IDSA 2021 (McDonald et al., 2021). Superior sensitivity (~95–99%). Can differentiate toxigenic from non-toxigenic strains. However, detects colonization as well as infection — positive test does NOT always mean infection.
  • Toxin EIA (enzyme immunoassay): detects toxins A/B in stool. Older standard; still widely available. Moderate sensitivity (~75–90% depending on disease severity). More specific than PCR (fewer colonization positives).
  • Colonoscopy: visualizes pseudomembranes (yellow-white plaques) in severe/fulminant disease. NOT for diagnosis (invasive, not needed for treatment decisions); reserved for suspected CDI with persistent severe colitis when diagnosis unclear.
  • CT abdomen/pelvis: for suspected toxic megacolon, perforation, or severe disease unresponsive to therapy. Shows colonic dilation >6 cm, wall thickening, free air if perforation present.

Testing errors to avoid:

  • Do NOT test formed stool (false negatives likely)
  • Do NOT test asymptomatic colonized patient for "burden verification"
  • Do NOT repeat testing same day (toxin shedding is intermittent)
  • Do NOT do "test of cure" after symptom resolution (IDSA 2021 explicitly advises against; positive PCR may persist for weeks)

When to test:

  • YES: ≥3 unformed stools in 24h + symptoms (fever, pain, leukocytosis, elevated Cr) suggestive of CDI
  • NO: asymptomatic patient or formed stool (colonization, not infection)
  • NO: after therapy completion if clinically improving
  • MAYBE: persistent diarrhea despite appropriate therapy + fulminant features → rule out alternate diagnosis (ischemic colitis, infectious enteritis)

sections.heading: 7.2 CDI severity classification
sections.bodyHtml:
Severity Criteria Treatment Escalation
Non-severe WBC ≤15 k/µL; Cr ≤1.5× baseline; no severe colitis signs Fidaxomicin PO 200 mg BID × 10d (preferred) OR vanco PO 125 mg q6h × 10d Provider notification; ongoing monitoring
Severe WBC >15 k/µL OR Cr >1.5× baseline; severe colitis signs present but NO fulminant features (no shock, ileus, megacolon) Fidaxomicin PO 200 mg BID × 10d (preferred) OR vanco PO 125 mg q6h × 10d Provider notification; q8–12h reassessment
Fulminant Shock (hypotension, lactate >2–5), ileus, toxic megacolon (colon >6 cm on imaging), WBC >35 k/µL, acute kidney injury, altered mental status, or peritonitis signs Vanco PO 500 mg q6h × 10d PLUS metronidazole IV 500 mg q8h STAT ICU transfer + CT surgery consult + surgical standby

Source: McDonald et al. (2021) IDSA/SHEA 2021 Guideline.

sections.heading: 7.3 Drug table — CDI pharmacotherapy
sections.bodyHtml:
Drug Dose (non-severe) Dose (fulminant) Route Notes
Fidaxomicin 200 mg BID × 10d Not studied in fulminant; avoid PO (tablets swallowed) Preferred first-line per IDSA 2021; minimal absorption; recurrence ~15%; expensive (~$3,000–4,000/course)
Vancomycin 125 mg q6h × 10d 500 mg q6h × 10d PO (capsules/tablets swallowed; if NG tube, consult pharmacy on powder absorption) Second-line non-severe; first-line fulminant (higher dose for colonic penetration); recurrence ~25%; not absorbed systemically (safe in renal failure)
Metronidazole 500 mg q8h × 10d (only if fidaxomicin/vanco unavailable) 500 mg IV q8h (adjunctive with vanco PO) PO or IV Third-line per IDSA 2021 (weak evidence); systemic absorption (can reach severe colitis if vanco/fidaxomicin unavailable)

Avoid:

  • Antimotility agents (diphenoxylate, loperamide, atropine) — increase toxic megacolon risk
  • Metronidazole monotherapy for severe/fulminant disease
  • Antacids/PPIs if possible (reduce gastric acid barrier); continue only if absolutely necessary for other indication, and document rationale
  • Fidaxomicin in patients with ileus or high NG output (drug must reach colon to work)

Duration: Standard is 10 days (POD 1–10 of therapy); longer courses not routinely indicated; shorter courses (<7 days) increase recurrence.

sections.heading: 7.4 Recurrence management and FMT
sections.bodyHtml:
• Recurrence incidence: 15–25% after first episode; risk increases with age >65, immunosuppression, fulminant initial infection.
  • First recurrence: repeat course of original agent (fidaxomicin or vanco) OR switch to fidaxomicin if vanco used initially.
  • Second or subsequent recurrence (multiply recurrent CDI): Fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) strongly recommended per IDSA 2021 (McDonald et al., 2021).
  • FMT restores normal colonic flora diversity; recurrence after FMT ~10–15% (vs >50% with repeated antibiotics).
  • Procedure: stool from healthy donor (screened for pathogens) delivered to colon via colonoscopy, enema, or capsule.
  • Success rate: 85–95% for cure of multiply recurrent CDI.
  • Discuss with infectious disease; not yet standard for initial non-severe CDI but emerging evidence promising.
  • Probiotics: NOT recommended for treatment or prevention per IDSA 2021. Emerging research on specific strains; not yet standard of care.

sections.heading: 7.5 High-risk subgroups
sections.bodyHtml:
• Post-operative cardiac surgery patients: exceptionally high-risk due to prolonged perioperative broad-spectrum antibiotics (cefazolin extended POD 1–2, vancomycin + cefepime for HAP, piperacillin-tazobactam for SSI), PPI stress ulcer prophylaxis, advanced age (60–75), CPB-induced immunosuppression, and extended hospital stay.
  • Patients on chronic corticosteroids or other immunosuppression: reduced clearance of toxins; worse prognosis.
  • Patients with prior CDI: recurrence risk 15–25%; previous sensitization may increase severity.
  • Renal failure or dialysis patients: hypervolemia from IV fluids challenging; monitor volume status carefully.
  • Mechanical ventilation or ICU-level care: aspiration of contaminated secretions; isolation compliance critical.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear or worsen in a stable CDI patient, re-escalate immediately.

  • Fever worsening or spiking higher — may indicate systemic toxin absorption or bacterial translocation; trend matters more than single temperature
  • Stool frequency NOT decreasing by POD 2–3 of therapy — suggests inadequate drug effect, alternate diagnosis, or ongoing trigger (laxative continuation?)
  • Abdominal distention increasing — risk of ileus developing; measure girth and compare to baseline; increase >3–4 cm is concerning
  • Abdominal pain worsening or becoming severe — may indicate wall necrosis, perforation, or toxic megacolon developing
  • WBC climbing (not falling) despite therapy — suggests ongoing inflammation; WBC >20 moves patient toward fulminant classification
  • Serum creatinine rising above 1.5× baseline — indicates systemic toxin effect on kidneys; IDSA criterion for severe disease
  • Serum albumin falling below 2.5 g/dL — predicts worse outcomes; nutritional decline ongoing
  • Altered mental status, confusion, or delirium — subtle sign of sepsis; may appear before frank hypotension
  • Hypotension despite fluids — suggests septic shock developing; urgent escalation
  • Lactate rising or >2 mmol/L — indicates tissue hypoperfusion; trending lactate more important than single value
  • Absent bowel sounds or inability to pass stool despite diarrhea onset — ileus may be developing; if combined with distention = toxic megacolon risk
  • Diarrhea stopping suddenly with worsening pain — paradoxical sign; may indicate ileus or megacolon onset (stopped passage, not cure)

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Alcohol gel DOES NOT kill C. difficile spores. This is the most critical pitfall. Nurses may resist the "extra step" of soap and water. Reinforce: "Soap and water removes spores; alcohol cannot. Spores are the infectious stage and persist in the environment. We MUST use soap or risk transmission to other patients." Model correct hand hygiene at shift change.

  2. Do NOT test asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic patients. Many hospitals over-test loose stool post-op. Rule: test ONLY if ≥3 unformed stools in 24h + symptoms (fever, pain, leukocytosis, elevated Cr). Testing 1–2 loose stools after laxative use = false positive → unnecessary isolation and treatment.

  3. PPI + broad-spectrum antibiotics = CDI setup. Post-op cardiac patients are on dual risk: prolonged perioperative antibiotics + PPI prophylaxis. If possible, discuss PPI discontinuation with provider once past POD 3–4 (GI bleeding risk declines after stress-ulcer window closes).

  4. Sudden diarrhea after post-op constipation can seem like "success"— but might be CDI, NOT the laxative working. Common error: "Patient had lactulose yesterday, now loose stools today — probably the laxative working." If there's fever, pain, or leukocytosis, test for CDI. Don't assume laxatives; assume CDI and test.

  5. "Just diarrhea" patient with severe abdominal pain + distention = possible toxic megacolon NOW. Abdominal pain in CDI can be deceptively severe. If patient reports "my belly hurts a lot" and exam shows distention, high bowel sounds (early ileus) or absent (advanced ileus), escalate immediately — ICU consult, surgical standby. Do not assume pain from cramping alone.

  6. Metronidazole is no longer first-line. IDSA 2018 and 2021 evidence show weak efficacy vs fidaxomicin/vanco. Expect prescribers to order fidaxomicin or vanco. If metronidazole ordered for "non-severe" CDI, it's not contraindicated but suboptimal; ask provider if fidaxomicin available.

  7. Fidaxomicin is expensive and REQUIRES PO route to work. If patient has ileus, cannot tolerate PO, high NG output, or vomiting → fidaxomicin may not reach colon and work; switch to vanco PO. Communicate swallowing issues to provider early.

  8. "Test of cure" is WRONG per IDSA 2021. Patient finishes 10-day vanco, feels better, no diarrhea for 2 days. Nurse or provider says "let's send one more stool to confirm cure." DO NOT TEST asymptomatic patient. PCR may remain positive for weeks; testing cured patient is not indicated. Document: "CDI therapy completed; clinical improvement documented; per IDSA 2021, test of cure not recommended."

  9. Loperamide in fulminant CDI is catastrophic. Antimotility agents increase toxic megacolon risk and septic shock. Hold all diphenoxylate, loperamide, and atropine-containing products. Educate patient and team on the danger.

  10. Recurrence is common (15–25%) and FMT is a real option. If patient had CDI, recovered, discharged, then returned 2–4 weeks later with diarrhea + positive CDI test = recurrent CDI. First recurrence: repeat antibiotic course.

    Second or later recurrence = FMT indicated; call infectious disease consult. Nurses should know this option exists and advocate for it.

  11. Skin breakdown from high-volume diarrhea happens FAST. Perineal skin is delicate. By POD 3 of untreated diarrhea, breakdown and candidiasis can develop. Meticulous skin care (frequent gentle cleansing, barrier cream q2–4h) is nursing-owned and critical to prevent secondary infection.

  12. Hypoalbuminemia predicts worse outcomes. If pre-operative albumin was low (cardiac surgery often includes malnutrition) and CDI develops, that patient is at higher risk of fulminant disease and poor prognosis. Flag low albumin to provider; consider nutrition consult for supplementation.

  13. Isolation continues 48 hours AFTER diarrhea resolves, NOT from day 1 of therapy. Common mistake: "Patient started antibiotics today, so isolation today through POD 11." CORRECT: "Patient started therapy POD 5, diarrhea resolved POD 8 (patient passing formed stool), so isolation continues until POD 10 at earliest (48h after last loose stool)."

  14. Don't confuse bladder perforation signs with toxic megacolon. Both present with severe abdominal pain + distention. Toxic megacolon: high fever, diarrhea, high WBC, rising lactate, absent bowel sounds. Bladder perforation: history of instrumentation, painful urination, suprapubic pain, abdominal distention but often WITHOUT diarrhea or fever. Imaging differentiates.

  15. Retest within 7 days after therapy is NOT indicated. Nucleic acid from dead C. difficile cells persists in stool for weeks after clinical cure. If patient still has symptoms, the question is "why?" not "is there residual PCR DNA?" Retesting risks false positives and confusion. Focus on symptoms and clinical trajectory.

cards.title: CHA₂DS₂-VASc Score
cards.quickAnswer: Stroke risk calculator for patients with atrial fibrillation that assigns points for age, hypertension, heart failure, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease, and female sex. Score ≥2 indicates anticoagulation is indicated; score 1 warrants shared decision-making with HAS-BLED consideration; score 0 typically requires no anticoagulation (males only). Valvular AF (moderate-severe mitral stenosis, mechanical valve) mandates warfarin regardless of score. Recalculate annually or with new comorbidity; post-cardiac surgery timing is surgeon-driven despite high scores to balance thromboembolism and bleeding risk.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: Stroke risk calculator for patients with atrial fibrillation that assigns points for age, hypertension, heart failure, diabetes, prior stroke/TIA, vascular disease, and female sex. Score ≥2 indicates anticoagulation is indicated; score 1 warrants shared decision-making with HAS-BLED consideration; score 0 typically requires no anticoagulation (males only). Valvular AF (moderate-severe mitral stenosis, mechanical valve) mandates warfarin regardless of score. Recalculate annually or with new comorbidity; post-cardiac surgery timing is surgeon-driven despite high scores to balance thromboembolism and bleeding risk.

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml: The CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is the contemporary standard stroke risk stratification tool for non-valvular atrial fibrillation endorsed by the 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/HRS guideline (Joglar et al., 2023). It quantifies annual cardioembolic stroke risk by integrating comorbidity burden and demographic factors, and drives anticoagulation initiation, agent selection (warfarin vs. DOAC), and reassessment intervals. The score appears in handoff summaries, discharge planning conversations, anticoagulation bridging protocols, and post-discharge follow-up documentation across ICU, stepdown, and outpatient settings.

sections.heading: 2. Scoring Components & Table
sections.bodyHtml:
Component Points Definition
C — Congestive heart failure / LV dysfunction 1 Clinical signs of HF or objective LV systolic dysfunction (EF ≤40%); includes acute decompensation POD 0–2
H — Hypertension 1 On antihypertensive therapy OR SBP > 140 mmHg documented
A₂ — Age ≥75 years 2 Chronological age ≥75 (double-weight because stroke risk steepens sharply)
D — Diabetes mellitus 1 On oral agent or insulin; or FG ≥126 mg/dL fasting or HbA1c ≥6.5%
S₂ — Prior stroke / TIA / thromboembolism 2 Any ischemic stroke, TIA, or systemic embolic event (double-weight; highest single-item risk)
V — Vascular disease 1 MI, PAD, or aortic plaque on imaging (does NOT include CAD alone without prior MI/revascularization)
A — Age 65–74 years 1 Chronological age 65–74 (note: overlaps with A₂; score once per age band)
Sc — Sex category female 1 Biological female; guideline debate exists on inclusion if it alone raises score to 1

Maximum score: 9 points

sections.heading: 3. Annual Stroke Risk & Anticoagulation Recommendations
sections.bodyHtml:
Score Annual Stroke Risk AC Recommendation (Non-Valvular AF)
0 0.2% No AC (males only; female score 0 debate)
1 0.6–0.9% Consider AC; discuss risk vs. benefit; or apply HAS-BLED for net-benefit assessment
2 2.2% AC indicated
≥5 > 6% AC strongly indicated; DOACs typically preferred over warfarin

Special note — Valvular AF:

  • Moderate-severe mitral stenosis = warfarin indicated regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc score
  • Mechanical prosthetic valve = warfarin indicated regardless of score
  • Bioprosthetic valve or native valve disease without MS = score-guided AC

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use
sections.bodyHtml:
Every patient admitted with a history of AF or developing new-onset AF (including postoperative AF) receives CHA₂DS₂-VASc assessment:

  • Calculated on every new POAF — before discharge planning or AC initiation; communicate to surgical and medical teams immediately
  • Recalculated on every admission with AF history — comorbidities may have changed since last score
  • Part of discharge anticoagulation decision — score drives the "warfarin vs. DOAC vs. no AC" conversation with team and patient
  • Post-cardiac surgery timing nuance — in ICU, AC is typically held POD 0 for bleeding precaution; restarted or initiated POD 1–5 depending on procedure type, hemostasis, and surgeon discretion. CHA₂DS₂-VASc score determines whether to restart/initiate, but not when — timing is surgeon-driven to balance thromboembolism risk against surgical-site bleeding

sections.heading: 5. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
• Do NOT use CHA₂DS₂-VASc for valvular AF. Mechanical valves and moderate-severe mitral stenosis mandate warfarin regardless of score. Using the score alone to avoid AC in these populations is dangerous.

  • Female sex is 1 point, but guideline controversy exists on whether to include it if score would otherwise be 0. Current standards include it; however, individualize risk assessment. A 64-year-old healthy woman with no comorbidities except female sex (score = 1) may not mandate AC per shared decision-making and HAS-BLED context.

  • Score does NOT include CAD alone. Prior MI or peripheral revascularization = 1 vascular disease point. Stable CAD without MI history does not earn points; distinguish from post-MI status.

  • PAF vs. persistent vs. permanent AF = same score. The CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is independent of AF type; all warrant stratification if AC is being considered.

  • Score does not account for immediate post-cardiac surgery transient bleeding risk. A high CHA₂DS₂-VASc score does not override the surgeon's hold on AC in the immediate post-operative window. Honor team consensus on AC timing.

  • Pair with HAS-BLED for net-benefit assessment. CHA₂DS₂-VASc quantifies stroke risk; HAS-BLED quantifies bleeding risk. A score ≥3 on both suggests higher bleeding risk that may argue for closer monitoring or proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) prophylaxis rather than avoiding AC entirely.

  • Annual recalculation is standard. Update the score yearly or whenever a new comorbidity is documented (new HF diagnosis, new MI, age turning 65 or 75, new stroke/TIA).

  • DOAC is preferred over warfarin for most non-valvular AF. Apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, and dabigatran are first-line per 2023 guideline (Joglar et al., 2023); warfarin reserved for valvular AF, renal contraindications, or patient preference. Know which agent was prescribed at discharge.

  • Score of 1 in a low-risk population may warrant additional clinical context. Not all score-1 patients need AC; shared decision-making is standard practice. Refer to HAS-BLED, age, frailty, and patient goals.

  • Do not confuse CHA₂DS₂-VASc with risk of POAF itself. The score identifies stroke risk once AF is established. Postoperative AF prophylaxis (beta-blockers, amiodarone) is separate; use prophylaxis guidelines, not stroke risk stratification.

  • If valvular status is unclear on admission (e.g., no recent echo), assume non-valvular and calculate the score pending clarification. A new mechanical valve or moderate MS on echo changes the anticoagulation strategy entirely, overriding the calculated score.

  • "Stroke risk" does not equal "all bleeding risk." The score measures cardioembolic stroke specifically, not hemorrhagic complications from AC. HAS-BLED addresses the latter and should inform the AC vs. no-AC conversation.

  • Age overlaps (A vs. A₂) mean a 75-year-old patient scores 2 for age alone, not 3. Do not double-count; follow the scoring rules strictly.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Age scoring detail Why double-counting matters: The CHA₂DS₂-VASc scoring system uses age 75+ as a double-weight point (A₂ = 2) because epidemiologic evidence shows a steep inflection in stroke risk at this age threshold. A patient aged 75 scores 2 points for age alone; a patient aged 74 scores 1 point. There is no scenario where a patient receives both A and A₂ points — use whichever applies:
  • Age < 65: no age points
  • Age 65–74: 1 point (A)
  • Age ≥75: 2 points (A₂) This design prevents double-counting and ensures the maximum score remains 9. Clinically, it means a 75-year-old with no other comorbidities already meets threshold for AC discussion.
Vascular disease clarification What counts as "vascular disease" (V = 1 point):
  • Prior MI (any, not just acute coronary syndrome)
  • PAD (claudication, prior intervention, imaging confirmation)
  • Aortic plaque on imaging (CT, ultrasound, or autopsy finding) What does NOT count:
  • CAD documented on angiography but WITHOUT prior MI
  • Stable angina without MI history
  • Positive stress test or abnormal EKG alone
  • Family history of CAD This distinction is clinically important: many patients have documented CAD without prior MI and do not earn the V point. Ask specifically about MI or revascularization history to avoid over-scoring.
Valvular AF nuances

Mechanical prosthetic valve: Always warfarin. No exception. DOACs have not been studied in mechanical valve patients and are contraindicated.

Bioprosthetic valve: Use CHA₂DS₂-VASc to guide AC as if native valve (score-based decision).

Moderate to severe mitral stenosis (native): Always warfarin, regardless of score. This is a hemodynamic emergency waiting to happen if not anticoagulated — thromboembolism risk is high enough to mandate warfarin despite any low score.

Mild mitral stenosis, aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, tricuspid disease: Use score-based decision-making.

TEA (thromboendarterectomy) patients with AF post-op: These are high-risk for both thromboembolism and bleeding. Discuss timing with surgery; score still applies but post-op AC hold is longer.

DOAC vs. warfarin selection First-line agents (non-valvular AF):
  • Apixaban 5 mg BID (or 2.5 mg BID if age ≥60 and weight ≤60 kg)
  • Rivaroxaban 20 mg daily with food
  • Edoxaban 60 mg daily (or 30 mg if CrCl 15–30, weight ≤60 kg)
  • Dabigatran 150 mg BID (or 110 mg BID if age ≥75 or high bleeding risk) Warfarin indication:
  • Mechanical prosthetic valve (only option)
  • Moderate-severe mitral stenosis
  • CrCl < 15 (DOAC contraindicated)
  • Patient preference after discussion
  • Pregnancy (DOACs contraindicated) Renal considerations:
  • CrCl 15–30: all DOACs require dosing adjustment; apixaban preferred
  • CrCl < 15: warfarin only
  • CrCl > 30: standard doses
POAF and acute AF in post-cardiac surgery context

New-onset AF in ICU post-op (POAF): Common on POD 1–3. Calculate CHA₂DS₂-VASc immediately to guide anticoagulation strategy, but do not initiate AC before surgeon discussion. Timing of AC initiation depends on hemostasis, chest tube output, and surgeon comfort — it is NOT score-driven.

Known AF on admission for cardiac surgery: Calculate score pre-op; patient likely already on AC. Perioperative protocol dictates bridging strategy. Score does not change intra-op.

Atrial fibrillation prophylaxis (separate from stroke risk assessment): Beta-blockers, amiodarone, or colchicine used perioperatively to prevent POAF. These are not stroke prevention and do not replace CHA₂DS₂-VASc assessment for anticoagulation decisions once AF occurs.

cards.title: Chest Tube Routine Management
cards.quickAnswer: Chest tubes drain blood and air from the mediastinal (post-cardiac surgery) or pleural space. Monitor drainage volume and character hourly (POD 0–1), q2h if stable. Maintain system below chest level at all times. Assess for tidaling (normal ± breathing) and air leaks (continuous bubbling = system or lung leak). Removal criteria: drainage < 150 mL/8 h, no air leak × 24 h, serous fluid, hemodynamically stable. Sudden output cessation with hemodynamic change = STAT call (suspect tamponade). Gentle milking only if visible clot in tubing; aggressive stripping is contraindicated.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
Monitor drainage volume and character hourly (POD 0–1), q2h if stable. Maintain system below chest level at all times. Assess for tidaling (normal ± breathing) and air leaks (continuous bubbling = system or lung leak).

Sudden output cessation with hemodynamic change = STAT call (suspect tamponade). Gentle milking only if visible clot in tubing; aggressive stripping is contraindicated.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, types, and clinical context.

  • Definition: Plastic catheters placed intraoperatively to evacuate air and fluid from the pericardial space (post-open-heart surgery: CABG, valve, aortic) or pleural space (lung).
  • Typical types: Mediastinal tubes (anterior retrosternal, drains serous + blood); pleural tubes (apical for air, basilar for fluid); pigtail catheters (10–14 Fr, increasingly used for post-discharge effusion).
  • Drainage system: Three-chamber collection unit (Pleur-evac or Atrium). Collection chamber quantifies output; water seal chamber acts as one-way valve; suction control regulates negative pressure.
  • Why it matters: Prevents tamponade, pneumothorax, and allows lung re-expansion. Early removal reduces infection risk and pain; delayed removal signals clinical concern (air leak, continued bleeding, or obstruction).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why It Exists
sections.bodyHtml: Post-operative chest tubes manage two complementary goals: evacuation of serous fluid and blood that would otherwise compress the heart or lungs, and prevention of negative-pressure collapse (pneumothorax). The three-chamber system allows passive gravity drainage (via water seal) or active suction, with the water seal acting as a one-way valve — fluid/air escape but no back-flow. Most cardiac post-op tubes can transition to water seal by POD 1–2 and be removed by POD 2–4 if drainage criteria are met.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — populations and initiation context.

Universally indicated:

  • Every post-op cardiac surgery patient with intraoperative chest tube placement (CABG, valve, aortic, MAZE, transplant, ECMO weaning, etc.)
  • Routine presence until drainage criteria met; no special contraindication except mechanical valve or severe coagulopathy (team-driven decision)

Special populations:

  • Recent bowel surgery: Avoid aggressive milking that could perforate adjacent structures
  • Anticoagulated or coagulopathic: Monitor for persistent bleeding; higher threshold for intervention
  • Patients post-MAZE or aortic arch repair: Longer expected drainage; extended time to removal expected

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Gather information* (5 minutes per shift)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside + chart review. Information-only; no interventions yet.

Every shift — quantify and trend:

  • Drainage volume & character: mL, color (serous/serosanguineous/bright red), clarity, debris
  • Water seal chamber: Tidaling present (yes/no); bubbling (none/forced-exhale/continuous); quality (small/medium/large)
  • Suction control: Correct level (wet system at -20 cm H₂O or dry system set per order); gentle bubbling intact
  • Tubing integrity: No kinks, dependent loops, tension on insertion site; connections taped and secure
  • Dressing: Dry, intact, non-purulent; anchoring suture in place; signs of infection (erythema, warmth, drainage)
  • Subcutaneous emphysema: Palpate around site and upper chest/neck; crepitus? Mark borders if present; track progression
  • Patient respiratory status: Bilateral breath sounds, SpO₂, work of breathing, pain, mobility tolerance

sections.heading: 5.1 Drainage output guidelines and escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Timing Expected Volume Consistency Escalation
POD 0 (immediate) 100–300 mL/h initially; slowing Serosanguineous to serous q 15–30 min monitoring; expect decrease over 4–6 h
POD 1–2 < 150 mL/8 h (some surgeons accept < 200 mL/24 h) Serous (clear to light pink) May be ready for removal if other criteria met
POD 3+ < 50 mL/8 h Serous Removal anticipated within 24–48 h
Sudden cessation + hemodynamic change Rapid drop to zero — STAT call — suspect clot/tamponade
Bright red, increasing (> 150 mL/h) Rising output, crimson color — Notify provider — active bleeding; monitor coagulation

sections.heading: 5.2 Water seal and suction assessment
sections.bodyHtml:
Tidaling (normal post-op):

  • Expected ± 2 cm oscillation with patient breathing (up on inspiration, down on expiration)
  • Absence suggests: lung fully expanded, tube kinked, internal clot, or patient holding breath
  • Response: have patient deep-breathe and cough; reposition; check connections

Air leak classification:

  • Small: Bubbling only with forced exhalation (normal early post-op, resolves POD 1–2)
  • Medium: Bubbling with normal breathing (may require extended water seal trial)
  • Large: Continuous bubbling (warrants investigation; lung leak or system leak — see troubleshooting)

Suction control:

  • Wet system: maintain water level at -20 cm H₂O (or per surgeon order); check daily
  • Dry system: set per order; check for malfunction indicator

sections.heading: 5.3 Troubleshooting and immediate actions
sections.bodyHtml:
Problem Suspected Cause Immediate Action
No tidaling Lung expanded, kinked tubing, internal clot Deep breath/cough; check for kinks; if persistent, notify provider
Continuous bubbling in water seal Air leak (lung or system) Clamp near patient's chest briefly — if stops = lung leak; if continues = system leak
Sudden drop in output + hypotension/tachycardia Clot/tamponade STAT provider call; check for kinks; prepare for emergency
Bright red, increasing drainage Active bleeding Notify provider; assess coagulation; prepare for possible OR return
Subcutaneous emphysema new/worsening Air tracking from lung or around tube site Mark borders; notify provider; serial exams q4h; most self-limited 24–72 h
Dependent loops in tubing Tubing coiled below drainage chamber Reposition to bed surface, coil above chamber; improves output
Tube pulled out partially/fully Accidental dislodgement Cover site immediately with sterile petrolatum gauze; notify provider STAT
Accidental disconnection from system Tubing separated from drainage unit Submerge distal end in sterile water/saline immediately; call provider; maintain sterile field

sections.heading: 5.4 Milking and stripping
sections.bodyHtml:
• Gentle milking: Hand-to-hand squeeze with lotion on visible clots in tubing is acceptable per unit protocol; preserves hemostasis
  • Aggressive stripping (hand-over-hand): Out of favor — creates negative pressure exceeding -400 cm H₂O, risks tissue trauma and clot dislodgement
  • Never routinely clamp for transport. Brief clamping only during system exchange or troubleshooting. Prolonged clamping with air leak risks tension pneumothorax.

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When to Escalate
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate immediately if:

  1. Sudden cessation of drainage with hemodynamic instability — STAT call; suspect cardiac tamponade
  2. Bright red drainage exceeding 150 mL/h — active bleeding; notify provider; assess coagulation
  3. Continuous air leak unresolved by troubleshooting — may require extended water seal or imaging
  4. Subcutaneous emphysema progressing to neck/face — airway concern; team call
  5. Persistent high output (> 200 mL/8 h) beyond POD 2 — may delay removal; verify electrolytes and coagulation
  6. Infection signs: fever, purulent drainage, erythema, warmth around insertion site
  7. Tubing disconnection or tube dislodgement — immediate sterile intervention; provider notification

sections.heading: 7.1 Drainage system physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
The three-chamber design parallels the patient's physiology:

  • Collection chamber: Quantifies output; gravitational drain allows passive flow
  • Water seal chamber: Contains 2 cm water; acts as a one-way valve. Fluid/air can escape (pressure gradient during expiration/straining), but positive atmospheric pressure cannot re-enter. Tidaling reflects intrathoracic pressure swings with breathing.
  • Suction control: Regulates applied negative pressure; wet system uses water-column height (-20 cm H₂O is standard); dry system uses spring mechanism

sections.heading: 7.2 Common bedside questions
sections.bodyHtml:
"Why is the tube still here?"
"It drains fluid and air that would otherwise compress your heart and lungs. We remove it once drainage drops and there's no air leaking—usually 2–4 days."

"Will it hurt when it comes out?"
"You'll feel pressure and a pulling sensation. It's quick—your surgeon does it in under a minute. We give you pain medicine first."

"Can I move around?"
"Yes, walking is important. We keep the drain below chest level and taped so it won't pull. Movement actually helps drainage."

"Why is there bubbling?"
"Some bubbling early is normal—air is draining out. We watch it. If it doesn't stop, we investigate to make sure the tube or lungs aren't leaking."

sections.heading: 7.3 Special populations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Heart transplant or LVAD: Valsalva during straining is poorly tolerated; minimize coughing strain; optimize analgesia
  • Post-MAZE: Expect longer drainage duration; early air leaks are common and usually resolve with extended water seal
  • Aortic arch repair: Often dual tubes; monitor each separately for drainage character and air leak

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Stable patients with these findings → re-escalate.

  • Output trending up despite stable vital signs — may herald bleeding unfolding; follow coagulation studies
  • Sudden hypotension, tachycardia, or muffled heart sounds with "dry" tube — classic tamponade triad; STAT evaluation
  • Air leak persistent beyond POD 2 — suggests ongoing parenchymal leak; may need extended trial or imaging
  • New dyspnea after transfer or shift change — check for tube clamping, kinking, or disconnection (most common iatrogenic cause)
  • Fever + purulent drainage + erythema around insertion site — infection; monitor WBC, consider culture and antibiotic coverage
  • Subcutaneous emphysema spreading to neck/face or jaw — rare but airway risk; team escalation
  • Patient becoming anxious or uncomfortable despite adequate analgesia — may signal pending tube pull or instability
  • Drainage character shifting from serous to serosanguineous — possible new bleeding; trend and alert provider if worsening

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Sudden drop in output is NOT reassurance. Suspect internal clot and developing tamponade. A "dry" tube with hemodynamic instability is an emergency.

  2. Never routinely clamp for transport. Old practice risks tension pneumothorax. Keep system upright, below chest; brief clamping only during exchange.

  3. Ambulate the patient with tube in place. Upright positioning and walking promote gravity drainage and lung re-expansion; supine/dependent positioning impedes output.

  4. Check for dependent loops hourly. Coiled tubing below the Pleur-evac acts as siphon and creates resistance. Reposition to bed surface; improves output.

  5. Bubbling with a cough is NORMAL post-op. Continuous bubbling during quiet breathing suggests air leak. Clamp near chest to distinguish lung leak (stops) from system leak (continues).

  6. "No drainage" on POD 0–1 is suspicious, not reassuring. Suspect internal clot, misplacement, or occlusion. Reposition, cough, check for kinks; call provider if tube remains dry.

  7. Stripping is out of favor. Aggressive hand-over-hand stripping exceeds -400 cm H₂O and risks tissue trauma. Use gentle milking only if visible clot in tubing per protocol.

  8. Chest tube pain is often worse than sternal pain. Optimize analgesia before mobility and deep breathing; poor pain control limits coughing and risks atelectasis.

  9. Subcutaneous emphysema post-removal is often self-limited. Mark borders, note date/time, perform serial exams. Most resorb within 24–72 h without intervention.

  10. Always clamp the tube NEAR THE PATIENT'S CHEST during system changes. Never leave prolonged clamps; risk of tension pneumothorax with active air leak.

  11. Keep the water seal chamber BELOW chest level at all times. If lifted above chest, gravity siphoning can back-flow fluid/air into pleural space.

  12. Post-removal CXR is essential even if patient feels fine. Asymptomatic pneumothorax is present in ~5% of cases; can become symptomatic with exertion.

  13. Drainage trend > single volume. A patient with 120 mL/8h → 20 mL/8h differs from steady 120 mL. Trend and character (serous vs. serosanguineous) guide clinical decisions.

  14. Air leak classification matters. Distinguish small (forced exhale only), medium (normal breathing), large (continuous) for surgeon communication.

  15. Accidental disconnection = immediate sterile water submersion. Do NOT clamp prolonged; call provider and maintain sterile technique for reconnection.

cards.title: Central Line-Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI)
cards.quickAnswer: Fever (>38.3°C) with central line in place >48 hours and no other apparent source → STAT blood cultures (peripheral AND through line, simultaneously); CBC, lactate. Notify APP and infection control. Stable (alert, MAP >65, no shock) → empiric antibiotics if high pre-test probability; daily line necessity reassessment. Unstable (septic shock, lactate >4, altered mental status) → STAT call + Hour-1 Sepsis Bundle + urgent line removal if Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas, or Candida. Key diagnosis: differential time to positivity (DTP) ≥2 hours (line positive before peripheral) strongly suggests line-source infection.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
Stable (alert, MAP >65, no shock) → empiric antibiotics if high pre-test probability; daily line necessity reassessment.

Unstable (septic shock, lactate >4, altered mental status) → STAT call + Hour-1 Sepsis Bundle + urgent line removal if Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas, or Candida. Key diagnosis: differential time to positivity (DTP) ≥2 hours (line positive before peripheral) strongly suggests line-source infection.
