sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, applicability.

  • Definition: Bacterial or fungal bloodstream infection with the central venous catheter (CVC) as the likely or confirmed source, occurring ≥48 hours after line insertion (CDC NHSN definition). Includes PICs, tunneled cuffed CVCs, and non-tunneled percutaneous central lines.
  • Incidence: 0.8–1.5 CLABSI per 1000 CVC-days in ICU populations. Varies by line type (PICC dwell-time >14 days carries higher risk); anatomy (femoral >IJ >subclavian); insertion conditions (emergency placement outside OR increases risk).
  • Who this applies to: every adult patient with a CVC in the ICU, stepdown, or acute care settings on telemetry. Highest acuity period: POD 0–7 post-op; dwell-time >7 days for any population.
  • Why it matters: increases mortality (~35% attributable mortality if Candida), prolongs ICU stay, drives antibiotic resistance, and is a sentinel quality indicator for infection control programs.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
CLABSI develops through three convergent steps: microbial colonization of the catheter (intraluminal biofilm, hub contamination, insertion site, or external surface), translocation into the bloodstream, and failure of the host immune response to sterilize the blood before symptomatic bacteremia occurs.

Pathophysiology drivers:

  • Biofilm formation: Bacteria adhere to the catheter surface within hours of insertion. Biofilms are metabolically slower (lower antibiotic penetration) but mechanically resistant to antibiotics; this is why removal, not antibiotics alone, often becomes necessary for Candida, Pseudomonas, or persistent Staphylococcus aureus infections.
  • Hub contamination: The most modifiable risk — contaminated stopcocks, three-way connectors, or IV tubing hubs introduce skin flora with each access. Proper "scrub the hub" technique (15+ seconds with friction, allow to dry) kills biofilm at this entry point.
  • Insertion-site colonization: Breaks in sterile technique or prolonged dressing integrity loss allow skin microbes to migrate along the tunnel toward the bloodstream.
  • Host factors: Immunosuppression (renal failure, steroids, malignancy), electrolyte depletion (reduces immune function), and systemic inflammation (post-op state, CPB) impair bacterial clearance.

Risk factors on the ICU:

  • Dwell time: each additional day >2 increases risk ~1.4×. PICCs dwell 14–28 days (higher cumulative risk) vs short-term lines 7–10 days.
  • Site of insertion: Femoral >IJ >subclavian (~3× higher infection risk for femoral vs subclavian; femoral also associated with thrombosis and mobility restrictions).
  • Emergency placement: Lines placed outside OR without maximal sterile precautions (full-body drape, sterile gown/gloves, cap, mask) carry ~2× higher CLABSI risk.
  • Post-operative status: Immunosuppression from CPB, pain-driven catecholamine surge, electrolyte wasting from diuresis.
  • TPN dependency: High-glucose solutions promote biofilm growth; candidemia risk substantially elevated.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — observable bedside signs.

Any of the following in a patient with a CVC:

  • New fever (>38.3°C / 101°F or ≥100.9°F × 2+ hours apart) without obvious source (negative for UTI on UA, pneumonia on imaging, surgical site infection)
  • Patient reports chills, myalgia, or feeling "septic" even with modest fever
  • New hypotension, tachycardia (HR >110), tachypnea (RR >20), altered mental status, or metabolic acidosis in the presence of a CVC
  • Visible erythema, induration, warmth, purulent drainage, or fluctuance at the line insertion site
  • Line tip culture positive after removal (even if patient asymptomatic at the time of removal) — evidence of catheter colonization

Epidemiology context: CLABSI peak incidence occurs POD 2–5 post-operative; can present as late as POD 7–10 or beyond if dwell time extended.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside and chart review. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs: Core temperature (preferred), HR, BP, RR, SpO₂, mental status, perfusion markers (capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output trend)
  • Symptoms: Onset of fever (time), chills, myalgia, confusion, nausea/vomiting, dysuria, chest discomfort, dyspnea
  • Line history: Insertion site anatomic location (femoral/IJ/subclavian?), exact insertion date (calculate dwell time), indication, any dressing changes, visible erythema/drainage
  • Recent labs: WBC (left shift? bands?), lactate (baseline perfusion), procalcitonin (if ordered), renal function (Cr, BUN), liver function, most recent blood glucose
  • Line site exam: erythema, warmth, induration, purulent drainage, fluctuance, intact dressing, transparency of any occlusive dressing
  • MAR review: what prophylactic or therapeutic antibiotics on board? Last dose timing? Antifungals? Anticoagulation status?
  • Clinical context: post-operative day and procedure type; immunosuppression (steroids, renal failure, malignancy, chemotherapy); TPN dependency; recent antibiotic exposure (↑ Candida risk); prior CLABSI history; line necessity today (still needed for pressors, vasopressors, specialized medications, TPN, or frequent labs?)
  • Culture history: any prior blood cultures this admission? Any positive results? Sources (peripheral, line, other)?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, alert, MAP >65, no shock signs, adequate perfusion.)

  1. Blood cultures ×2 sets, drawn simultaneously — one from peripheral vein, one through the central line at the same moment. This is the gold standard for CLABSI diagnosis; DTP (differential time to positivity) interpretation requires both. Label with site, exact time, and patient identifier.
  2. CBC with differential — assess WBC elevation, left shift (bands), and hemoglobin (baseline for later trending)
  3. Serum lactate — baseline perfusion marker; >2 mmol/L is concerning and warrants escalation even if patient looks stable
  4. Notify APP / on-call provider immediately via SBAR (see Section 6) — emphasize: fever + line >48 h + no other source identified
  5. Notify infection control — they manage surveillance, decolonization protocols, and isolation precautions per institutional policy
  6. Reassess line necessity — daily line necessity review is a prevention bundle cornerstone. Is the patient on vasopressors (line essential)? Antibiotics requiring central access? Labs q4h or more? TPN? If none of these, flag early for removal discussion.
  7. Empiric antibiotic initiation discussion with provider — typical coverage: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (renally dosed) + gram-negative coverage (cefepime 2 g q8h OR piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g q6h) ± antifungal (echinocandin if TPN, immunocompromised, or recurrent Candida). Do NOT delay while awaiting cultures if patient is septic or high pre-test probability (SHEA/IDSA, 2022).
  8. Continuous monitoring — telemetry, vital signs q4h minimum; watch for hemodynamic deterioration or fever spike
  9. Document DTP communication plan — ensure microbiology knows to report line vs peripheral culture positivity timing; ensure this is communicated to the team within 24 h of receipt

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Septic shock: hypotension requiring vasopressors, altered mental status, lactate >4, severe sepsis criteria.)

  1. STAT call: APP/fellow + charge nurse + activate Rapid Response or code team if not already present — do NOT leave room alone
  2. Implement Hour-1 Sepsis Bundle (coordinate with institutional sepsis protocol):
    • Lactate measurement STAT + repeat q1h × 3, then per protocol
    • Blood cultures STAT (peripheral + through line) before antibiotics if possible, but do NOT delay antibiotics >60 minutes for culture draw
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics STAT per sepsis protocol (e.g., meropenem 1 g q8h + vancomycin + antifungal OR piperacillin-tazobactam if pseudomonal coverage adequate for that patient's risk factors)
    • Fluid resuscitation: 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus for hypotension/lactate >4; use balanced fluids (lactated Ringer, Plasma-Lyte) preferred
    • Vasopressor initiation (norepinephrine) if hypotension persists after fluid bolus; target MAP ≥65 mmHg
    • Central line removal urgent — S. aureus, Pseudomonas, or Candida CLABSI mandate line removal. Even for coagulase-negative staph, removal is strongly recommended if hemodynamically unstable or persistent bacteremia >72 hours. Line removal is a source-control measure equivalent to abscess drainage.
    • Prepare for line removal:
      • Obtain line tip culture immediately upon removal — aseptically clip ~2 cm of distal catheter into sterile tube (BHI broth or similar); >1000 CFU by standard culture (or >100 CFU by quantitative culture) confirms device-related bacteremia
      • Plan for new line placement if urgent access still needed; place at different anatomic site (if femoral → IJ or subclavian on opposite side preferred)
      • Timing: new line can be inserted immediately upon removal if urgent access needed; line tip culture does NOT delay this
      • Send STAT labs: blood glucose, PT/INR, troponin (myocardial stress marker), additional blood cultures from other anatomic sites if multifocal infection suspected
      • Continuous reassessment: Q15min vital signs, lactate trending, urine output, mental status; escalate to ICU if not already present

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure, if applicable]." B: "Patient developed fever [temp, time] with central line in place [site — femoral/IJ/subclavian, X days]. HR [rate], BP [value], lactate [value]. No obvious source on exam (UA negative, CXR/imaging negative). Obtained blood cultures peripheral + through line at [time]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable / septic with shock]. [Symptoms]. On [current antibiotics/medications]. WBC [value], left shift [yes/no]. Line site [erythema/purulent drainage/intact]." R: "Requesting orders for [empiric antibiotics / lactate recheck / line removal / line tip culture / new line placement / additional labs]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable fever + line, no sepsis signs Primary APP / on-call fellow
Unstable with sepsis / septic shock APP/fellow + RRT/code team; cardiothoracic surgery (if post-cardiac-op) notified
Recurrent bacteremia despite antibiotics ×2 sets Infectious disease consult; reassess line necessity + source control
Positive Staphylococcus aureus from line Infectious disease + transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) for endocarditis screening; cardiothoracic surgery if post-op
Positive Candida blood culture Infectious disease; ophthalmology for retinal exam (screen for Candida retinitis); consider echinocandin vs fluconazole per azole susceptibility
PICC removal — need continued IV access Interventional radiology or cardiothoracic surgery for percutaneous central line; evaluate PICC vs new CVC based on dwell-time risk/benefit

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Organisms you'll encounter and their management implications
sections.bodyHtml:
Coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (CoNS) — most common isolate, often contaminant Frequency: ~30–40% of CLABSI cases. Key clinical dilemma: CoNS is normal skin flora AND a pathogenic CLABSI organism. Single positive culture from one draw site is likely a contaminant (especially if patient asymptomatic). But multiple positive sets from the same patient, especially from line, are real infection. Decision algorithm:
  • Single positive CoNS from peripheral vein in asymptomatic patient on line → likely contaminant; repeat cultures immediately; observe clinically; do NOT start vancomycin yet
  • CoNS positive from line draw + fever or clinical signs → real infection; treat
  • Multiple positive sets (≥2 from same patient, different times or same time from line + peripheral) → treat as real infection Antibiotic choice: Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (renally dosed) for 5–7 days AFTER line removal (not counting days with line in place). If PCN allergy confirmed, vancomycin is standard. De-escalate if cephalosporin-susceptible and patient has low allergy risk. Line removal: Consider removal if multiple positive sets, hemodynamic instability, or metastatic signs. Can retain line if clinical response documented (defervescence, hemodynamic stability, lactate normalizing within 48 h) AND patient has no alternative access (dialysis patients, long-term TPN).
Staphylococcus aureus — serious pathogen, line always removed Frequency: ~20–30% of CLABSI cases. Critical rule: One positive S. aureus blood culture from a patient with a CVC = line removal. No exceptions. S. aureus bacteremia left untreated or with line in place risks endocarditis (~25% of SAB patients), abscess formation, and septic thrombophlebitis. Endocarditis screening (mandatory): All S. aureus bacteremia require transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) to rule out endocarditis. Transthoracic echo (TTE) is inadequate in post-operative patients (poor acoustic windows). Notify infectious disease and cardiothoracic surgery STAT. Antibiotic choice:
  • MSSA (methicillin-susceptible): cefazolin 2 g IV q8h, OR ceftriaxone 2 g q12h (preferred if renal disease); covers both CAD and device (O'Grady et al., 2017)
  • MRSA: vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (renally dosed) OR daptomycin 6 mg/kg IV q24h if available Duration: 14 days of IV antibiotics AFTER line removal + first negative blood culture (= ~21 days total if line remained in place for 7 days during initial therapy). Repeat cultures: Blood cultures at 48–72 h to document clearance. Persistent bacteremia >72 h despite antibiotics + line removal → endocarditis, abscess, or metastatic foci; escalate to ID + TEE + source re-evaluation.
Gram-negative rods (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter) — 20–30% of CLABSI Pseudomonas aeruginosa — special note: Line removal is mandatory. Pseudomonas forms biofilms resistant to antibiotics; mechanical removal is non-negotiable. Other gram-negatives: Often originate from GI translocation or environmental contamination. Antibiotic choice:
  • First-line empiric (pending susceptibilities): Cefepime 2 g q8h OR piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g q6h (covers Pseudomonas)
  • For resistant organisms: Carbapenem (meropenem 1 g q8h) or fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin 750 mg PO q12h) if susceptible
  • Cephalosporins (ceftriaxone, cefazolin) do NOT cover Pseudomonas; if Pseudomonas identified on culture, de-escalate to agents above Duration: 7–14 days IV antibiotics after line removal + first negative culture. Source control: Assess for secondary foci (urinary, abdominal); manage obstruction or perforation if identified.
Candida albicans / non-albicans — 5–15%, opportunistic, line always removed Risk factors: TPN dependency (high-glucose fuels biofilm), prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics (dysbiosis), immunosuppression, renal failure, recent steroids, indwelling urinary catheters (portal of entry). Critical rule: Candida CLABSI requires line removal. Echinocandins and azoles penetrate poorly into biofilm; antifungals fail without mechanical removal. Screening for disseminated disease:
  • Ophthalmology urgent exam: Candida can seed the retina; 50% of candidemia patients have Candida retinitis. Unfamiliar with fundus findings = ask optho to look.
  • Echocardiography: Screen for marantic endocarditis or valve vegetations (rarer but serious)
  • Source identification: Any urinary catheter? Recent abdominal surgery? Perforated viscus? GI translocation risk? Antifungal choice:
  • First-line: Echinocandin (anidulafungin 200 mg load, then 100 mg daily; OR caspofungin 70 mg load, then 50 mg daily) — preferred for initial therapy and biofilm penetration
  • Alternative: Fluconazole 400–600 mg PO/IV daily IF organism susceptible AND line already removed; inferior to echinocandin for biofilm
  • Azole resistance: Non-albicans Candida may be fluconazole-resistant; always await susceptibilities before stepping down Duration: 14 days IV antifungal after first negative blood culture; dwell on azole susceptibilities before PO transition.

sections.heading: 7.2 Differential time to positivity (DTP) — the diagnostic clincher
sections.bodyHtml:
How DTP works and when to use it Definition: The time interval between positivity of the line-drawn blood culture bottle vs the peripherally-drawn culture bottle from the same patient, drawn at the same time. Interpretation:
  • Line culture positive ≥2 hours BEFORE peripheral culture → strong evidence of line-associated bacteremia (sensitivity ~85%, specificity ~95%). This indicates higher bacterial burden in the catheter lumen vs systemic circulation, pointing to the line as the source.
  • Both cultures positive at similar times (within 30 min) → suggests either secondary hematogenous seeding of the line or contamination; less specific for line-source infection.
  • Peripheral positive before line → suggests line is NOT the source; consider alternative sources. Requirements for valid DTP interpretation:
  • Blood cultures drawn SIMULTANEOUSLY (not sequential)
  • Time of positivity accurately recorded on culture bottles (many labs auto-log this; confirm)
  • Both sets truly incubated in automated blood culture systems with real-time monitoring
  • Microbiology lab's written procedure for DTP reporting should be reviewed with the clinical team Common errors:
  • Drawing cultures sequentially instead of simultaneously (invalidates DTP)
  • Mislabeling time of draw (later redrawn cultures labeled as original time)
  • Not communicating DTP results to clinician team within 24 h of culture positivity Teaching point: Teach new nurses to hold both bottles side-by-side while drawing (one hand peripheral, one hand through line), label in real time with the clock moment. This is a high-yield, high-impact prevention step.

sections.heading: 7.3 Line removal decision tree and antibiotic lock therapy
sections.bodyHtml:
When to remove the line and when you might retain it ALWAYS remove the line if:
  • Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia (any source from CVC)
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa CLABSI
  • Candida species (any Candida in blood on a line) — exception: rare case of transient candidemia from other source without line involvement
  • Persistent bacteremia >72 hours despite appropriate antibiotics + line in place
  • Septic thrombophlebitis (imaging confirmed: clot + infection of the central vein)
  • Fungemia on any organism Consider removal if:
  • Coagulase-negative staph CLABSI with hemodynamic instability, septic shock, or signs of metastatic spread
  • Gram-negative CLABSI with persistent fever >48–72 h despite appropriate antibiotics
  • Tunnel infection (erythema/fluctuance tracking along the subcutaneous line tract from entry to insertion site) Can retain the line if:
  • Coagulase-negative staph CLABSI, patient hemodynamically stable, responds to antibiotics, patient has no alternative vascular access (dialysis-dependent, long-term TPN, no suitable peripheral sites)
  • Single positive from one set of cultures in asymptomatic patient (likely contaminant); repeat cultures; close observation
  • Documented clinical improvement within 48 h: defervescence (temp <38°C), hemodynamic stability off vasopressors, lactate normalized, WBC trending down Antibiotic lock therapy (ALT) — not standard but may bridge critical gaps:
  • ALT instills antibiotic solution (e.g., vancomycin + heparin) into the line lumen, leaves it locked between uses
  • Not recommended for routine CLABSI (Mermel et al., 2009) — mechanical removal is the standard
  • Rare exception: Dialysis catheter CLABSI in patient with no other vascular access; then ALT might bridge 7–10 days until temporary access established
  • Never use ALT alone — always pair with systemic IV antibiotics; confirm with ID before considering New line placement:
  • If removal is necessary, place new line at different anatomic site. Avoid same location to minimize re-infection risk.
  • Timing: New line can be inserted immediately at bedside upon removal of infected line if urgent access needed (no need to wait for line tip culture results)
  • Alternative: Temporary peripheral IV (if medications tolerate) + PICC placement once acute infection stabilized (lower CLABSI risk than CVC, but slower infusion for pressors)

sections.heading: 7.4 CVC placement and maintenance bundle — prevention is highest yield
sections.bodyHtml:
Bundle elements and evidence base At insertion (maximal sterile precautions — non-negotiable):
  • Hand hygiene: alcohol-based handrub for 30+ seconds before gloving
  • Maximal sterile barrier: sterile gown, double sterile gloves, cap, mask, full-body sterile drape (extends beyond line insertion site) — all present in the field
  • Skin antisepsis: Chlorhexidine 0.5% in 70% alcohol, applied in concentric circles from insertion site outward, allowed to dry completely (drying is critical — it maximizes bacterial kill). If chlorhexidine allergy, second-line: iodine-based prep (povidone-iodine or iodine tincture); allow dry time same.
  • Site selection: Subclavian >IJ >femoral for infection risk. Avoid femoral if possible in post-operative and mobile patients (3× infection risk vs subclavian; also thrombosis and mobility issues).
  • Antibiotic ointment: Mupirocin at insertion site post-insertion. (Exception: avoid in dialysis catheters — increased infection risk. Exception: MRSA colonization — ointment benefit reduced, but still applied per institutional policy.) Daily maintenance (every shift):
  • Line necessity assessment: Single most important prevention step after insertion. Is this line still essential? Pressors? Vasoactive meds? Specialized antibiotics? TPN? Labs q4h+? Daily necessity review + removal within 24 h of lost indication reduces CLABSI incidence by ~30% (Mermel et al., 2009).
  • Chlorhexidine gluconate 4% bathing (once daily, all-body): Reduces CLABSI incidence by ~25–30%. Applied to entire body surface (except face/eyes); allowed to dry. Some patients develop contact dermatitis (~2–3% incidence); if present, switch to chlorhexidine-impregnated cloths or temporary alcohol-based cleanser; do not discontinue — continue bathing.
  • Dressing changes: Non-transparent dressings if drainage present (change immediately). Transparent dressings changed per institutional schedule (typically q5–7 days or if soiled/loose/non-adherent). Inspect dressing edge daily.
  • Hub scrubbing — the HIGHEST YIELD maintenance element: Scrub the line hub (where IV tubing connects) with alcohol swab (70% isopropyl) or chlorhexidine swab for minimum 15 seconds with friction. Let dry before accessing. Do this every time you access the hub (medications, flushes, labs, monitoring device setup). Hub contamination drives ~30% of late CLABSI. This is the step most commonly rushed or skipped by new nurses; teaching and modeling are essential.
  • Flushing protocols: Heparin (if per institutional standard) or saline flushes after medication, before labs, per institutional protocol. Use sterile technique; minimize number of accesses per day.
  • In-line filters: If used per institutional protocol, they reduce bacterial contamination but add cost; confirm compatibility with tubing. At removal (sterile technique):
  • Sterile technique: Mask, gloves, clean field during removal
  • Line tip culture: Aseptically clip ~2 cm of distal catheter into sterile tube (BHI broth or similar sterile transport medium). Label with patient ID, date, time, line type.
  • Culture interpretation: Significant growth = >1000 CFU by standard culture (or >100 CFU by quantitative/semi-quantitative culture) suggests device-related bacteremia. Correlate with blood culture results (matching organism?). Evidence base (per SHEA/IDSA, 2022):
  • Maximal sterile precautions reduce CLABSI vs standard precautions (RCT, moderate evidence)
  • Chlorhexidine-based prep superior to iodine (RCT data)
  • Chlorhexidine bathing reduces CLABSI by ~25–30% (multiple RCTs)
  • Daily line necessity assessment + removal within 24 h of lost indication reduces CLABSI (strong evidence)
  • Scrub-the-hub compliance (15+ sec with friction) reduces hub colonization and late CLABSI

sections.heading: 7.5 Stable vs unstable — clinical recognition
sections.bodyHtml:
Defining the fork in immediate actions Stable CLABSI presentation:
  • Alert, oriented
  • MAP >65 mmHg without vasopressors
  • No chest pain, dyspnea at rest, or altered mental status
  • Lactate <2 mmol/L or baseline
  • Perfusion intact (capillary refill <2 sec, warm extremities, urine output normal)
  • Example: Low-grade fever 38.5°C, tachycardia 105, stable BP 110/70, clear lungs, patient interactive Unstable CLABSI / septic shock:
  • Hypotension (SBP <90, MAP <65 mmHg) requiring vasopressors OR responding to aggressive fluid resuscitation
  • Altered mental status (confusion, obtundation, or decreased GCS <15)
  • Lactate >4 mmol/L, or >2 mmol/L with poor lactate clearance after resuscitation
  • Signs of end-organ dysfunction: oliguria, rising creatinine, metabolic acidosis
  • Severe sepsis: ≥2 SIRS + suspected/confirmed infection Trajectory matters: A patient who is currently stable but trending toward unstable (rising lactate hour-to-hour, declining BP even on fluids, new confusion) should be escalated and treated as unstable pending team arrival.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in stable patients and predict decompensation. If any appear, re-escalate immediately.

  • Fever not responding to antipyretics after 24 h OR rising fever despite antibiotics after 48 h — suggests inadequate source control (line not removed when indicated) or unidentified secondary focus (endocarditis, abscess)
  • Lactate rising or staying elevated (>2 mmol/L) despite antibiotics + resuscitation — perfusion failure; consider line source not yet controlled or metastatic foci (liver, spleen, joints)
  • Hypotension emerging or worsening even with fluid bolus (30 mL/kg crystalloid) — transition to septic shock pathway; prepare vasopressors + potential ICU transfer
  • Confusion, restlessness, or new altered mental status — sepsis-induced encephalopathy; high risk for cardiovascular collapse imminent
  • Petechial or purpuric rash appearing — suggests invasive organism (meningococcemia, gonococcemia, Gram-negative rod endocarditis); isolate immediately, notify infection control, culture rash site
  • Embolic phenomena: new focal neurologic deficit (stroke from septic emboli), acute dyspnea (pulmonary embolus from septic thrombophlebitis or endocarditis vegetations)
  • Positive blood cultures at 48–72 h post-treatment initiation — persistent bacteremia; verify line removed, confirm organism susceptibility, assess for endocarditis (especially S. aureus), consider metastatic foci
  • S. aureus bacteremia confirmed — TEE mandatory immediately if not already ordered; endocarditis changes management dramatically and increases mortality
  • Candida bacteremia confirmed — ophthalmology consult urgent (examine for retinal infiltrates — 50% incidence); assess vision status and treat accordingly
  • CRP or procalcitonin worsening or plateauing after 48–72 h post-antibiotic start — trend should be downward; lack of downtrend suggests inadequate control
  • Thrombocytopenia developing (platelet drop >50K in 24 h) — may signal DIC, TTP, or metastatic sepsis; order CBC diff, PT/INR, D-dimer, fibrinogen
  • Myalgias intensifying, joint pain/swelling appearing — consider osteomyelitis, septic arthritis (especially from S. aureus) — order imaging (XR, MRI, U/S per site)
  • Unilateral arm swelling, collateral veins on chest wall appearing — septic thrombophlebitis of central vein; order imaging (venous U/S or CT); may need anticoagulation + extended antibiotics

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Simultaneous blood cultures (peripheral + line) are non-negotiable for CLABSI diagnosis. DTP interpretation is impossible without both. If only peripheral cultures were drawn, notify team and request a repeat set immediately. Explain this to new nurses.

  2. Single positive coagulase-negative staph from one draw is likely contamination, not infection. Don't reflexively start vancomycin. Repeat cultures, observe clinically, and treat only if multiple positive sets or patient is septic. This prevents unnecessary antibiotic exposure and resistance.

  3. Multiple positive coagulase-negative staph sets (≥2 from same patient) = treat as real infection. The dilemma is distinguishing single contamination from true bacteremia; multiple positives resolve the question.

  4. Candida on a line: never attempt to salvage. Line removal is mandatory. Echinocandins and azoles do not penetrate biofilm adequately. Retention → treatment failure and dissemination.

  5. Differential time to positivity ≥2 hours (line positive before peripheral) is the diagnostic clincher for line-source infection. Make sure times are accurately labeled on culture bottles and communicated to the clinical team within 24 h. This guides whether to remove the line or look for secondary sources.

  6. Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics must cover MRSA + gram-negative + Candida in the right patient. Vancomycin + cefepime/piperacillin-tazobactam ± echinocandin. Adjust when culture/susceptibilities available. Do NOT wait for cultures to treat if patient is septic or high pre-test probability.

  7. Scrub the hub 15+ seconds minimum with friction. Ask a new nurse to demonstrate; many rush through it in 3 seconds. Friction + contact time kills biofilm. This is one of the highest-yield prevention steps a bedside nurse controls directly. Model it every time.

  8. Daily line necessity review prevents CLABSI. If the patient can survive without the line, remove it. Every day in place is cumulative risk. Use a checklist: On pressors? Vasoactive meds requiring central delivery? Antibiotics needing central access? TPN? Labs q4h+? If none, flag it.

  9. Chlorhexidine bathing daily reduces CLABSI by ~25–30%. It's simple and powerful. ~2–3% of patients develop contact dermatitis; if so, switch to chlorhexidine-impregnated cloths or temporary alternative; do not skip the bath entirely.

  10. Femoral lines are higher-risk in ICU patients. ~3× infection vs subclavian, plus thrombosis and mobility issues. If a femoral line is in place >5–7 days, advocate for removal + conversion to IJ or subclavian if indication persists.

  11. TPN + central line = substantially elevated Candida risk. High-glucose solutions feed biofilm. Lower threshold for antifungal empirics if fever develops in TPN patients. If Candida confirmed, line removal is non-negotiable.

  12. Immunosuppressed patients (steroids, renal failure, malignancy) present atypically. They may not mount fever or WBC elevation even with significant bacteremia. Don't wait for fever + leukocytosis; if at-risk patient has even mild tachycardia, lactate >2, or chills, consider CLABSI in differential.

  13. Line tip culture guides post-removal antibiotic duration and confidence in diagnosis. Positive tip (>1000 CFU) + matching organism in blood = definitive CLABSI. Negative tip makes CLABSI less likely; may shorten antibiotic duration pending team discussion.

  14. Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia ALWAYS requires TEE for endocarditis screening. Transesophageal echo (TEE) is mandatory; transthoracic (TTE) is inadequate in post-operative patients (poor acoustic windows). 25% of SAB patients have IE. Notify ID + cardiothoracic surgery STAT.

  15. Persistent bacteremia >72 hours despite appropriate antibiotics + line removal = escalate hard. You're now worried about endocarditis, abscess, or retained material. Re-escalate to ID, arrange repeat imaging, repeat blood cultures, consider TEE if not done.

cards.title: Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS)
cards.quickAnswer: The CFS is a 9-point clinician-assigned scale (1 = very fit, 9 = terminally ill) that assesses pre-morbid fitness and frailty independent of acute illness. Assessed 1–2 weeks before surgery, not at bedside post-op. CFS ≥ 5 (pre-frail/frail) predicts longer ICU/unit length of stay (+3–5 days mean), acute kidney injury (≥ 30%), post-op delirium (60–80%), 30-day readmission (10–20%), and 1-year mortality. CFS 7+ bumps surgical risk profile for TAVR discussion and triggers geriatric consultation; CFS 8–9 is relative contraindication to most surgical intervention.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
The Clinical Frailty Scale is a validated, rapid global measure of fitness and frailty in older adults, developed by Rockwood and colleagues within the Canadian Study of Health and Aging (Rockwood et al., 2005). It captures pre-morbid baseline function—how the patient was functioning in the 1–2 weeks before the index illness or admission—independent of acute decompensation. The scale integrates observed physical function, cognition, and social independence into a single ordinal score (1–9).

Key distinction: CFS is clinician-assigned, not self-reported. It requires observation, chart review, caregiver/family collateral, and clinical judgment. It is not a laboratory test or objective physical measure, though it can be paired with gait speed (< 0.8 m/s) or handgrip strength for validation.

Population: Applied across cardiac surgery (open surgical, TAVR, high-risk medical admits), but increasingly standard in older adults undergoing any major intervention.

sections.heading: 2. The 9-Point Scale (Mandatory Table)
sections.bodyHtml:
Score Category Description
1 Very fit Active, energetic; regular exercise; no active disease
2 Well No active disease; less active than category 1
3 Managing well Medical problems controlled; not regularly active beyond routine ADLs
4 Vulnerable Not dependent but noticeably slowed down; symptoms limit activity; mild cognitive or physical decline
5 Mildly frail Needs help with some instrumental ADLs (finances, transportation, heavy housework, medications); slow gait; reduced independence
6 Moderately frail Needs help with some IADLs and bathing; difficulty with stairs or dressing; variable dependence on support
7 Severely frail Completely dependent for personal care but stable; usually in facility or with live-in support; may be bed-bound
8 Very severely frail Completely dependent; near end of life; high mortality risk in next 6 months
9 Terminally ill Actively dying; life expectancy < 6 months; may not otherwise be evidently frail (e.g., advanced metastatic cancer)

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Why CFS matters in cardiac surgery:

Frailty—independent of age—is a stronger predictor of post-operative complications, mortality, and discharge disposition than chronologic age alone (Afilalo et al., 2012). An 85-year-old at CFS 2 typically tolerates surgery better than a 65-year-old at CFS 6. The CFS captures vulnerability that chronologic thresholds miss, enabling nuanced risk conversations with patients and families.

When is CFS assessed?

  • Pre-op: Ideally 2–4 weeks before planned cardiac surgery. Obtained from patient, caregiver, family, and chart review of ADL/IADL dependence, living situation, mobility, and cognition prior to acute illness.
  • Not at bedside post-op. A patient admitted with sepsis and delirium may appear CFS 7–8, but the true pre-morbid frailty may be CFS 3–4. Document delirium and acute illness separately.
  • Late arrival: If CFS is missing on admission, assess by POD 1 from ICU summary, family interview, and chart review of baseline function.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Information Gathering (2 minutes at admission)*
sections.bodyHtml:
• Observe current mobility, cognition, functional independence during initial exam; compare to collateral history
  • Ask the patient (if clear): "How far can you walk? Do you need help at home with finances, medications, heavy chores? Can you dress and bathe yourself?"
  • Ask caregiver/family: Living situation, ADL/IADL dependence, baseline cognition, activity level 1–2 weeks before illness
  • Review chart: Prior admission notes, functional status from prior visits, social work assessment, case manager notes, PT/OT reports
  • Physical clues supporting CFS ≥ 5: slow gait (< 0.8 m/s), handgrip weakness, clear ADL/IADL dependence, cognitive changes, living in facility or with 24/7 caregiver
  • Assign a score that reflects pre-morbid baseline, not current acute state

sections.heading: 5. Clinical Use
sections.bodyHtml:
Screening & documentation:

  • Document CFS on admission for any cardiac surgery patient, particularly those ≥ 65–70 years (per institutional protocol).
  • Use structured caregiver interview, family input, and pre-admission chart review.

Risk conversations & escalation:

  • CFS ≤ 3: Low frailty; standard surgical risk counseling.
  • CFS 4–5 (intermediate frailty): Candidate for prehabilitation (4–8 weeks nutrition, PT/OT, supervised exercise); higher operative risk; TAVR often preferred over SAVR to avoid sternotomy morbidity; geriatric consultation recommended (Afilalo et al., 2012).
  • CFS 6–7 (severely frail): Relative contraindication to most cardiac surgery; discuss medical management, palliative intent, realistic recovery timeline (6–12 weeks minimum), and goals of care. ICU-level care highly likely post-op.
  • CFS 8–9: Palliative focus; discuss symptom relief vs. cure; catheter-based or medical options preferred over surgical; realistic life expectancy < 6–12 months.

Discharge & care planning:

  • CFS ≤ 3: Likely safe for home discharge or outpatient prehab.
  • CFS 4–5: Candidate for home health nursing, outpatient PT/OT, close follow-up, intensive family teaching. Consider skilled nursing facility (SNF) if no caregiver support.
  • CFS ≥ 6: Strong candidate for SNF (temporary or longer-term). Home discharge requires robust home health package, 24/7 caregiver availability, and explicit family education on wound care, activity restrictions, medication management.

Prehabilitation eligibility:

  • CFS 4–5 patients are ideal candidates for 4–8 week pre-op prehabilitation (nutrition optimization, PT/OT 2–3×/week, supervised home exercise). Evidence shows 1-point CFS reduction possible pre-op (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020), which lowers post-op complications.
  • CFS ≥ 6 may benefit from nutrition optimization but surgical prehab is less likely to substantially improve frailty; focus on discharge planning.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
• Assess pre-morbid baseline, not admission state. A previously fit 80-year-old admitted with sepsis and confusion is not CFS 7; assess how they functioned 1–2 weeks before acute illness. Document admission delirium separately from frailty.

  • CFS assessed 1–2 weeks pre-op, not at bedside post-op. The scale captures steady-state frailty, not acute post-operative decline. Do not reassign CFS during acute post-op period; instead track recovery trajectory.

  • CFS 5+ triggers geriatric consultation (per institutional protocol). These patients have measurable post-op morbidity: longer ICU/unit stay (+3–5 days mean), higher AKI (≥ 30%), higher post-op delirium (60–80%), more 30-day readmission (10–20%), and higher 1-year mortality.

  • Frailty is independent of age. An 85-year-old at CFS 2 typically tolerates surgery better than a 65-year-old at CFS 6. Age is only one input; frailty is the stronger predictor of post-op outcomes.

  • CFS 7+ bumps surgical risk profile for TAVR/SAVR discussion. TAVR is often preferred in CFS 4–7 (intermediate to severely frail) to avoid sternotomy morbidity, longer cross-clamp time, and higher delirium risk. CFS 8–9 is relative contraindication to most surgical intervention.

  • Inter-rater variability is real. Different clinicians (surgeon, cardiologist, RN, social work) may assign slightly different scores. Use caregiver reports, chart review, and consensus; don't rely solely on patient self-report if acutely ill or cognitive impairment is present.

  • Pair CFS with objective measures for validation. Gait speed < 0.8 m/s, handgrip strength < 11 kg (women) or < 27 kg (men), or exhaustion on simple activities support CFS ≥ 5 assignment.

  • Post-op CFS often worsens transiently by 1–2 points (POD 0–7) due to acute illness, delirium, pain, and medication side effects. Document recovery trajectory; most frail patients recover 1–2 points by 8–12 weeks post-op.

  • CFS worsening post-op (> 2-point drop from baseline) is a red flag for delirium, depression, infection, or acute medical complication. Evaluate for UTI, wound infection, electrolyte abnormality, hypoxia, medication toxicity, or undermanaged pain.

  • Prehabilitation is evidence-based for CFS 4–5. Nutrition support (prealbumin, albumin, high-protein diet), supervised PT/OT 2–3×/week, and home exercise over 4–6 weeks can reduce CFS by 1 point pre-op and lower post-op complications.

  • Discharge planning at CFS ≥ 5 must be explicit and early. SNF placement, home health orders, family education on wound care, activity restrictions, and medication management should be arranged by POD 2–3 to avoid unnecessary delays.

  • CFS informs the nutrition conversation. Prealbumin < 17 mg/dL or significant weight loss (> 5% in past 6 months) at CFS ≥ 5 = high surgical-site infection and delirium risk; consider oral supplementation, tube feeds, or short-term parenteral support.

  • Post-op CFS often worsens by 1–2 points in ICU level immediately post-op (POD 0–7). This is expected acute illness response. Most frail patients recover 1–2 points by 8–12 weeks.

  • CFS 8–9 is a relative contraindication to most surgical intervention. These patients have high perioperative mortality and prolonged ICU/facility-level care. Frame discussions around goals (symptom relief vs. cure), palliative options (catheter-based therapies, medical optimization), and realistic life expectancy (Bojar, 2020).

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers (expandable — novice + advanced beginner deep-dive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Frailty phenotype comparison: CFS vs. Fried vs. FRAIL vs. eFI The CFS is one of several validated frailty measures. Nurses may encounter these in different settings:
InstrumentFormatTimeValidation in cardiacWhen used
CFS (Rockwood)Clinician-assigned, global, 1–9 ordinal2–5 minCardiac surgery, TAVR, HFMost cardiac surgery centers
Fried phenotype5 criteria: slowness, weakness, low activity, exhaustion, unintentional weight loss10–15 minOlder adults, some cardiacResearch, some geriatric units
FRAIL scale5 yes/no items (Fatigue, Resistance, Ambulation, Illness, Loss of weight)3–5 minSome cardiac populationsSimplified screening; less validated in cardiac
eFI (electronic Frailty Index)Automated from EHR data (36 deficits)AutomatedLimited cardiac validationPrimary care, UK NHS
CFS advantage: Single clinician judgment integrates multiple domains (physical, cognitive, social) into one ordinal score; well-validated in cardiac; fast; captures pre-morbid baseline. CFS limitation: Subjective; inter-rater variability; requires clinical skill and collateral history. Most ICU-level cardiac care uses CFS (Rockwood, 2005) as the standard frailty metric (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).
CFS validation in cardiac surgery populations Afilalo et al. (2012) demonstrated that addition of frailty and disability to standard cardiac surgery risk scores (STS, EuroSCORE) identified elderly patients at highest risk of post-op mortality or major morbidity. Subsequent studies (Stortecky et al., 2012; Sundermann et al., 2011) confirmed CFS ≥ 5 predicts:
  • Longer ICU/unit length of stay
  • Higher incidence of delirium, AKI, bleeding
  • Prolonged discharge to facility vs. home
  • 1-year mortality increase CFS is now standard in preoperative risk assessment for TAVR (ESC 2021 HF Guidelines, 2021) and surgical AVR/CABG populations (Bojar, 2020).
Prehabilitation strategy for CFS 4–5 Patients at CFS 4–5 can improve frailty pre-op. A typical 4–8 week prehabilitation protocol:
  1. Nutrition: Prealbumin supplementation, high-protein diet (1.0–1.2 g/kg), vitamin D, B12, iron repletion
  2. Exercise: PT/OT 2–3×/week, supervised ambulation, leg strengthening, balance work
  3. Cognition: Sleep hygiene, cognitive engagement, fall prevention education
  4. Goals: Reduce CFS by 1 point, improve gait speed, improve ADL independence Evidence shows 1-point CFS reduction achievable over 4–6 weeks, associated with lower post-op complications (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020). CFS ≥ 6 patients may improve nutrition but surgical prehab is less likely to substantially shift frailty category; focus on discharge planning and family education instead.
Goals of care conversation template (CFS 7–8) For severely frail (CFS 7) or very severely frail (CFS 8), before surgery is scheduled:
  • Establish baseline: "Before we talk about surgery, help me understand what a good day looks like for you right now. What's important to you?"
  • Outline the stakes: "Major cardiac surgery for someone at your current level of function carries significant risk — a 20–40% chance of prolonged ICU stay, 10–15% chance of needing permanent nursing facility care, and a real risk of post-surgical complications or death."
  • Explore options: "We can pursue surgery and accept those risks. Or we can focus on medical management, palliative care, or catheter-based options. What matters most to you — trying to live longer, or being comfortable and at home?"
  • Document: Record patient/family values, goals, and shared decision-making in chart. Involve palliative care, social work, and institutional ethics if trajectory is unclear.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *Deterioration trajectory in currently stable post-op frail patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
• Worsening confusion, lethargy, or unresponsiveness beyond POD 2–3. Delirium in frail patients can persist or worsen into POD 4–5; evaluate for infection (UTI, aspiration pneumonia, wound), electrolyte abnormality, hypoxia, undermanaged pain, or medication toxicity.

  • Acute functional decline beyond expected post-op trajectory. Sudden inability to ambulate, feed self, or void spontaneously on POD 4–5 signals decompensation, not normal recovery.

  • Persistent high-output chest tubes (> 200 mL/h) beyond POD 2. In frail patients, prolonged bleeding can trigger cascade of complications; escalate for possible surgical re-exploration.

  • Oliguria or rising creatinine with fluid overload. AKI is common (≥ 30% of CFS ≥ 5); monitor UOP, creatinine trend, and fluid balance closely. Consult nephrology if Cr rises > 50% from baseline or UOP < 0.3 mL/kg/h.

  • Persistent vasodilation, tachy, or hypotension on POD 1–2. Post-pump inflammatory activation in frail patients can trigger vasoplegia requiring norepinephrine; if persistent or worsening, escalate for hemodynamic assessment.

cards.title: Constrictive Pericarditis
cards.quickAnswer: Constrictive pericarditis is a rigid, thickened pericardium mechanically limiting diastolic filling, presenting as right-sided heart failure (JVD, hepatic congestion, ascites, edema) with preserved ejection fraction. Key etiologies: post-cardiac surgery (0.2–0.3%), tuberculosis (global), radiation (5–20 years post-mediastinal RT), idiopathic. Diagnosis: cMR showing pericardial thickening >3 mm, septal bounce on TTE, RHC equalization of diastolic pressures + square-root sign. Critical differential: constrictive vs. restrictive cardiomyopathy (cMR + tissue Doppler e' distinguishes). Management: Medical (diuretics for volume, cautious with preload), anti-inflammatory (colchicine + NSAIDs for transient post-op constriction, may resolve), pericardiectomy (definitive; 5–10% operative mortality; best outcomes when done early at high-volume center). Kussmaul sign (paradoxical JVP rise with inspiration) is pathognomonic.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who gets it, why it matters.

  • Definition: A rigid, non-compliant pericardium mechanically restricts ventricular diastolic filling and equalizes ventricular diastolic pressures. Impaired cardiac output despite preserved systolic function.
  • Epidemiology:
  • Post-cardiac surgery (most common in developed world) — 0.2–0.3% of post-cardiac-surgery patients; typically develops months to years post-op
  • Radiation-induced — occurs 5–20 years after mediastinal radiation; increasing in cancer survivors
  • Tuberculosis — historically most common globally; endemic in high TB-burden regions; rare in developed countries
  • Idiopathic/viral — post-viral pericarditis can progress to chronic constriction
  • Connective tissue disease — SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma
  • Uremia — inadequately treated uremic pericarditis
  • Malignancy — direct pericardial involvement or post-chemotherapy/radiation
  • Typical presentation: Post-CABG or post-valve-surgery patient with progressive dyspnea, edema, and ascites months to years post-op; OR cancer survivor with prior mediastinal radiation presenting with right-sided heart failure; OR patient with unrecognized TB with right heart failure syndrome.
  • Why this matters: Constrictive pericarditis is surgically curable (unlike restrictive cardiomyopathy) but requires accurate diagnosis and timely pericardiectomy. Medical management alone is palliative; transient post-op constriction can respond to anti-inflammatory therapy and avoid surgery if caught early.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Pathophysiology detail

sections.heading: Mechanism
sections.bodyHtml:
• Pericardial fibrosis, thickening (>3 mm), and sometimes calcification → loss of distensibility
  • Normal pericardium stretches passively during diastole; constricted pericardium is inelastic and prevents ventricular expansion beyond a fixed limit
  • Diastolic filling becomes biphasic: early rapid fill (ventricular interdependence allows initial filling) followed by abrupt cessation (pericardial limit reached = plateau)
  • Elevated and equalized diastolic pressures — right atrial (RA), right ventricular (RV), pulmonary artery diastolic (PAd), left ventricular end-diastolic (LVEDP) all within 5 mmHg of each other
  • Ventricular interdependence — the two ventricles compete for space within the rigid pericardium; LV filling impairs RV filling and vice versa
  • Impaired cardiac output results from reduced stroke volume, not systolic dysfunction — LV systolic function is typically normal or near-normal in pure constriction
  • Increased venous congestion → hepatic congestion, ascites, edema, elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP)

sections.heading: Pathophysiologic hallmarks
sections.bodyHtml:
• Kussmaul sign — JVP paradoxically rises with inspiration (instead of normal fall). Reflects inability of RV to expand into the pericardium despite negative intrathoracic pressure. Nearly pathognomonic for constriction.
  • Pericardial knock — early diastolic sound (S2 + ~60 ms), earlier than S3 gallop. Reflects abrupt cessation of ventricular filling as pericardial limit is reached.
  • Pulsus paradoxus — exaggerated drop in systolic BP with inspiration (>10 mmHg). Reflects ventricular interdependence and reduced LV stroke volume during RV filling.
  • Ventricular septal bounce — during early diastole, the septum bows into the LV due to RV filling pressure spikes, then reverses as RV pressure equilibrates. Seen on echo.

sections.heading: Post-cardiac surgery continuum
sections.bodyHtml:
• Acute post-op pericarditis (weeks 1–4) — typical inflammatory response; may present as effusive pericarditis
  • Transient constrictive pericarditis (weeks 2–12) — effusive-constrictive pattern; constriction component may be temporary, responsive to anti-inflammatory therapy (colchicine, NSAIDs)
  • Permanent constrictive pericarditis (months to years) — fibrosis progresses; becomes refractory to medical management; requires pericardiectomy

sections.heading: Clinical summary
sections.bodyHtml: Constrictive pericarditis is a state of mechanical constraint on the ventricles. The physiology resembles restrictive cardiomyopathy superficially but the underlying cause is different: rigid pericardium (curable) vs. stiff myocardium (incurable). This distinction is critical for management, as only constrictive physiology responds to pericardiectomy.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: What the patient looks like at bedside. Observable signs and history.

sections.heading: Symptomatology
sections.bodyHtml:
• Progressive dyspnea evolving to orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  • Peripheral edema — ankle and leg swelling, often symmetric
  • Abdominal distension from ascites
  • Hepatic congestion — right upper quadrant discomfort, hepatomegaly
  • Fatigue and exertional intolerance out of proportion to LV dysfunction
  • Syncope or near-syncope — rare but possible with severe restriction + volume loss
  • Palpitations if atrial fibrillation develops

sections.heading: Physical examination findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Elevated JVP (often >8 cm H₂O, sometimes severe 12–15 cm H₂O)
  • Kussmaul sign — JVP paradoxically rises (not falls) with inspiration. Highly specific for constriction or severe RV failure.
  • Pericardial knock — early diastolic sound (earlier than S3), reflects abrupt cessation of ventricular filling. Distinguishes from S4 (presystolic) and S3 (mid-diastolic).
  • Diminished or muffled heart sounds if pericardial effusion present
  • Hepatomegaly — smooth, tender, non-pulsatile edge (unless severe TR present)
  • Ascites — often prominent; can mimic cirrhosis or portal hypertension; usually transudative
  • Peripheral edema — ankle/leg swelling, sometimes anasarca in advanced cases
  • Reduced pulse pressure if cardiac output severely impaired
  • Normal carotid pulse (unlike aortic stenosis) and unremarkable precordial impulse
  • Atrial fibrillation — common; assess for irregular rate and pulse deficit

sections.heading: Key distinction
sections.bodyHtml: Right-sided heart failure signs out of proportion to LV dysfunction. Patient may have normal or mildly reduced LV ejection fraction yet have marked JVD, ascites, hepatomegaly, and peripheral edema. This mismatch is a red flag for constriction.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml: Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: 2 minutes at bedside.

sections.heading: Vital signs and bedside exam
sections.bodyHtml:
• Vital signs: HR, BP, SpO₂, respiratory rate, temperature
  • JVP assessment: height, waveform (look for prominent y descent, absent or blunted x descent)
  • Pulsus paradoxus: measure systolic BP change with inspiration (normal <10 mmHg; constrictive often >10 mmHg)
  • Kussmaul maneuver: observe JVP during inspiration (paradoxical rise is pathognomonic)
  • Heart sounds: listen for S3, S4, pericardial knock
  • Lung exam: clear vs. crackles (pulmonary edema suggests acute decompensation)
  • Abdominal exam: ascites, hepatomegaly, liver edge tenderness, splenomegaly
  • Extremity exam: edema grade (0–4), skin turgor, capillary refill

sections.heading: History and context
sections.bodyHtml:
• Cardiac surgery timeline: when was prior CABG, valve surgery, or other cardiac procedure? Post-op course (any complications, prolonged intubation)?
  • Radiation history: prior mediastinal radiation for breast cancer, lymphoma, or other malignancy? How many years ago?
  • TB exposure or history: travel to endemic area, household TB contact, prior TB diagnosis or treatment?
  • Connective tissue disease: SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma?
  • Renal function: baseline creatinine; on dialysis?
  • Medications: diuretics, beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, NSAIDs, colchicine?
  • Recent clinical trajectory: progressive vs. acute onset? Weight gain/loss? Change in edema or ascites?

sections.heading: Recent labs and imaging
sections.bodyHtml:
• Electrolytes: K⁺, Na⁺, Mg²⁺ (diuretic-induced depletion common)
  • Renal function: creatinine, BUN, eGFR
  • Hepatic function: AST, ALT, albumin, bilirubin, INR (cardiac cirrhosis can develop)
  • Hemoglobin: anemia can worsen symptoms
  • Troponin: not typically elevated; if elevated, consider acute decompensation or concurrent ACS
  • BNP/NT-proBNP: usually elevated (right atrial stretch); not specific for constriction
  • Most recent CXR: pericardial calcification? Pulmonary congestion?
  • Most recent echo (TTE or TEE): pericardial thickness visible? RV/LV dilation? Septal bounce? E/A ratio? Tissue Doppler e'? IVC diameter and collapse?

sections.heading: 5A. Medical Management (palliative; not curative for permanent constriction)
Diuretics — volume management with caution
sections.bodyHtml:
• Goal: relieve congestion (ascites, edema, pulmonary edema) while maintaining adequate preload for filling
  • Unique challenge in constriction: paradoxically depends on adequate venous filling to work against rigid pericardium. Over-diuresis drops venous pressures → reduced filling → worsening cardiac output → syncope, fatigue, AKI
  • Starting regimen (typical): loop diuretic (e.g., furosemide 20–40 mg PO daily or BID) with aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone 12.5–25 mg daily) and possibly thiazide (HCTZ 12.5 mg daily) for refractory cases
  • Titration: target gradual weight loss (0.5–1 lb/day) with goal resolution of ascites and edema over weeks-to-months
  • Monitoring: daily weights at same time, I/O logs, electrolytes q1–2 weeks, creatinine trend, signs of over-diuresis (fatigue, dizziness, rising Cr, hypotension)
  • Caution: if patient develops worsening fatigue, syncope, rising creatinine, or hypotension → hold or decrease diuretics immediately; alert team

sections.heading: Anti-inflammatory therapy (for transient post-op constriction ONLY)
sections.bodyHtml:
• NSAIDs — ibuprofen 600–800 mg three times daily for 6–8 weeks (or equivalent naproxen, indomethacin); goal is to reduce periosteal inflammation and prevent fibrosis progression
  • Indication: early post-op (weeks 2–12 post-op) pericardial effusion with mild constriction; transient pericarditis component
  • Contraindication: renal insufficiency (creatinine >2.5 mg/dL), active GI bleeding, prior GI ulcer, advanced liver disease
  • Monitoring: assess for GI symptoms; check creatinine after 2 weeks NSAID use
  • Colchicine — 0.6 mg once or twice daily × 3 months; decreases periosteal inflammation, prevents fibrosis progression in transient disease
  • Indication: same as NSAIDs; particularly effective for post-op pericarditis
  • Contraindication: severe renal disease (CrCl <30 mL/min; adjust dose), severe hepatic disease
  • Monitoring: GI side effects common (diarrhea); reduce dose if intolerant
  • Corticosteroids — prednisone taper (start 0.5 mg/kg/day × 2–4 weeks, then taper by 10 mg every 1–2 weeks) if severe inflammation or NSAIDs contraindicated; rare indication but used for severe idiopathic/viral pericarditis with early constriction
  • Caution: long-term steroids impair healing; reserve for exceptional cases
  • Serial echocardiography: obtain echo at baseline and every 4–6 weeks during anti-inflammatory therapy to track effusion resolution and constriction improvement

sections.heading: What does NOT work
sections.bodyHtml:
• ACE inhibitors / ARBs — minimal role; LV function is usually normal in constriction
  • Beta-blockers — no benefit for pericardial pathology; not contraindicated but not curative
  • Statins — no role in constriction
  • Inotropes — risk worsening BP without improving filling; not indicated
  • No medication slows or reverses established pericardial fibrosis. Once fibrosis is mature (typical >3–6 months post-op), medical therapy is palliative only

sections.heading: Anticoagulation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Atrial fibrillation: if new or chronic AF develops, anticoagulate per standard AF guidelines (CHA₂DS₂-VASc assessment)
  • No routine anticoagulation for constrictive pericarditis alone in sinus rhythm

sections.heading: 5B. Anti-inflammatory Medications — Transient Constriction Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Medication Dose Duration Indication Key Cautions
Ibuprofen 600–800 mg TID 6–8 weeks Early post-op (<12 wks) effusive-constrictive with mild constriction Renal insufficiency, GI ulcer history, NSAIDs allergy
Indomethacin 25–50 mg TID 6–8 weeks Alternative if ibuprofen not tolerated Greater GI risk; use only if ibuprofen fails
Colchicine 0.6 mg once or BID 3 months Early post-op pericarditis; synergistic with NSAIDs CrCl <30 mL/min (requires dose adjustment); GI side effects
Prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day, taper over 4–6 weeks Variable Severe inflammation, NSAID contraindication; rare Risk of reactivation of latent TB if on anti-TB drugs; impairs healing

sections.heading: Indications for pericardiectomy
sections.bodyHtml:
• Symptomatic constrictive pericarditis refractory to medical therapy for ≥2–3 months (or evident permanence earlier)
  • Hemodynamically significant constriction with functional limitation (dyspnea on exertion, inability to perform ADLs, orthostatic hypotension)
  • Progressive worsening despite optimized diuretics and anti-inflammatory therapy
  • Permanent post-op constriction (not responsive to NSAIDs + colchicine within 3 months)
  • Radiation or TB constriction where permanence is already established

sections.heading: Contraindications to pericardiectomy
sections.bodyHtml:
• Severe renal failure (creatinine >2.5 mg/dL, not on dialysis or transplant list) — high post-op mortality
  • End-stage liver disease (cirrhosis from cardiac cause) — coagulopathy, ascites control, post-op complications
  • Very low ejection fraction (<25%) with severe RV dysfunction — poor reserve; consider mechanical support bridge first
  • Active untreated infection (including TB) — must be treated first

sections.heading: Pericardiectomy procedure and outcomes
sections.bodyHtml:
• Partial pericardiectomy — most common approach; removes visceral pericardium and parietal pericardium from pulmonary artery distally to diaphragm
  • Right-side-first approach — preferred technique to minimize LV ischemic injury; RV free wall pericardiectomy first, then gradual extension to septum and LV
  • Intraoperative TEE — critical to assess pericardial separation, RV/LV function response, and filling improvements real-time
  • Post-op considerations: watch for acute RV failure if strip too aggressive; may need temporary mechanical support (IABP, VA-ECMO)

sections.heading: Pericardiectomy outcomes by etiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Etiology Operative Mortality Improvement in Symptoms Long-term Survival (5-year) Comments
Post-cardiac surgery (idiopathic) 4–7% 80–85% excellent/good 75–80% Best outcomes if performed early (within 1–2 years of symptom onset); skilled center mandatory
Radiation-induced 8–10% 70–75% 65–70% Higher risk due to adherent, calcific pericardium and mediastinal fibrosis; longer operative time
TB-related 10–15% 60–70% 60–65% Requires anti-TB therapy pre- and post-op; adhesions often dense
Idiopathic/viral 6–8% 80–85% 75–80% Similar to post-surgical outcomes if constriction pure; worse if restrictive component present

sections.heading: Post-op timeline and recovery
sections.bodyHtml:
• POD 0–1: Usually extubated same day or POD 1; ICU-level monitoring for hemodynamics, output, arrhythmia
  • POD 2–3: Transfer to stepdown/telemetry unit if stable
  • POD 3–7: Diuretics typically decreased (RV now compliant, can fill better); monitor for over-diuresis
  • Discharge readiness: Resolution of ascites/edema, diuretic optimization, pain controlled, tolerating PO, return toward baseline activity, follow-up cardiology/CT surgery scheduled
  • Post-op complications: Atrial fibrillation (20–30%), low-output syndrome (2–5%), pericardial re-effusion (5–10%), re-constriction from re-thickening (rare acutely; can occur years later)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml: When to notify the clinical team and communication framework.

sections.heading: SBAR template for escalation

S: "Dr./APP [name], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room number]." B: "[Patient context]: POD [X] s/p [procedure if post-op], admitted with [chief complaint]. Comorbidities: [relevant history — TB history, prior radiation, prior cardiac surgery].

sections.heading: Who to call — constrictive pericarditis scenarios
sections.bodyHtml:
