sections.heading: Escalation triggers (when to call without waiting)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Acute hemodynamic deterioration: SBP <90 mmHg, HR >120 or <50, SpO₂ <90%, altered mental status, oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr × 2 hrs)
  2. New or worsening respiratory distress: RR >28, accessory muscle use, orthopnea despite positioning and diuretics
  3. Rapid increase in ascites or peripheral edema — within hours despite diuretics
  4. Signs of cardiogenic shock: cool extremities, delayed capillary refill, altered mental status, rising lactate
  5. Suspected pericardial effusion with tamponade: acute hypotension, muffled heart sounds, elevated JVP, pulsus paradoxus >20 mmHg
  6. New arrhythmia (AF with RVR or malignant arrhythmia) — in setting of constrictive physiology, AF can rapidly decompensate

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced-beginner deep-dive on pathophysiology, diagnostics, management nuances, and edge cases. All subsections below are marked — collapsed by default.

7.1 Pathophysiology deep-dive: Dip-and-plateau, ventricular interdependence, Kussmaul sign

sections.heading: The dip-and-plateau RV pressure tracing (square root sign)
sections.bodyHtml:
During right heart catheterization in constriction, the RV pressure tracing is pathognomonic:

  • Early diastole (the "dip"): RV pressure drops sharply and rapidly as ventricle begins filling — this is a rapid early-diastolic filling phase
  • Mid-to-late diastole (the "plateau"): RV pressure abruptly plateaus and remains elevated and flat as it hits the pericardial constraint limit
  • The shape resembles a square root symbol (√): sharp drop, then flat horizontal line

This is nearly diagnostic of constriction. In contrast, restrictive cardiomyopathy has a more gradual, prolonged diastolic filling phase without the sharp plateau.

sections.heading: Ventricular interdependence
sections.bodyHtml:
In constrictive pericarditis, the RV and LV are mechanically coupled within a rigid container:

  • During inspiration: negative intrathoracic pressure increases venous return to the right heart; RV diastolic pressure rises; the RV expands slightly but is constrained by the rigid pericardium; increased RV pressure compresses the LV across the septum → LV filling worsens, LV stroke volume decreases, LV systolic pressure drops
  • During expiration: venous return to the right heart decreases; RV relaxes; LV filling improves; LV stroke volume increases

On echocardiography, this appears as septal bounce: the septum bows into the LV during RV filling (early diastole, inspiration), then reverses as RV pressure equilibrates (late diastole, expiration).

On Doppler: mitral inflow E-wave velocity increases >25% with expiration; tricuspid inflow E-wave increases >25% with inspiration — ventricular concordance (RV and LV pressures move together due to pericardial constraint).

sections.heading: Kussmaul sign explained
sections.bodyHtml:
Normally, when a person breathes in (inspiration):

  1. Intrathoracic pressure becomes more negative
  2. This "sucks" blood into the chest, increasing venous return to the right side of the heart
  3. But increased venous return increases RV diastolic filling, which stretches the RA
  4. So the JVP should drop during inspiration (more negative intrathoracic pressure "pulls" the RA downward)

In constriction, this normal physiology is reversed:

  • During inspiration, the RV tries to expand to accommodate increased venous return
  • But the rigid pericardium prevents RV expansion
  • The RV pressure rises sharply instead of accommodating the new blood volume
  • Increased RV diastolic pressure is transmitted back through the RA to the jugular veins
  • Result: JVP paradoxically rises during inspiration (opposite of normal)

This is Kussmaul sign — nearly pathognomonic for constriction (or other conditions with severe RV failure like RV infarction or severe RV dysfunction from other causes).

sections.heading: Pulsus paradoxus
sections.bodyHtml:
Normal: systolic BP varies <10 mmHg between inspiration and expiration. With inspiration, systolic BP may drop slightly (due to increased RV filling and septal shift), but not noticeably.

In constriction: the exaggerated ventricular interdependence and septal shift cause systolic BP to drop >10 mmHg with inspiration. This is called pulsus paradoxus.

Mechanism:

  • Inspiration → increased RV filling and diastolic pressure
  • Septal bulge into LV → LV cavity reduced → LV stroke volume decreases
  • LV systolic pressure (and hence aortic systolic BP) drops noticeably

Clinical detection: palpate the radial pulse during slow inspiration. If the pulse disappears briefly with inspiration, pulsus paradoxus is present. Alternatively, inflate a BP cuff above systolic, then slowly deflate while patient breathes quietly; note the systolic level where the first Korotkoff sound is heard only during expiration (disappears with inspiration) vs. where it's heard throughout the breathing cycle.

7.2 Diagnostic imaging deep-dive: TTE Doppler, cMR, CT, RHC findings (expandable)

sections.heading: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)
sections.bodyHtml:
Morphologic findings:

  • Pericardial thickening: may be visible as echogenic layer around the heart; normal pericardium is thin and often not visualized; thickened pericardium >3 mm is suggestive (but not diagnostic in isolation)
  • RV/LV cavity size: RV often dilated from chronic pressure elevation; LV normal or small
  • RV function: may be reduced (D-shaped septum, reduced RV FAC)
  • Atrial enlargement: RA often enlarged due to elevated RA pressure; LA may be enlarged if chronic AF present

Hemodynamic findings (Doppler):

  • Mitral inflow E-wave: early mitral filling velocity; respiratory variation >25% is highly suggestive (E-wave increases >25% during expiration when LV filling improves)
  • Tricuspid inflow E-wave: increases >25% during inspiration (RV filling improves as RV pressure drops slightly with RV volume accommodation from negative intrathoracic pressure, but is still constrained)
  • Tissue Doppler e' velocity: PRESERVED (>8 cm/s) — KEY FINDING TO DISTINGUISH FROM RESTRICTIVE CARDIOMYOPATHY
  • In constriction, the longitudinal myocardial relaxation is normal; the constraint is mechanical (pericardial), not myocardial
  • In restriction, the myocardium is stiff; e' is reduced (<8 cm/s)
  • Annulus paradoxus (TDI): reduced annular velocity during diastole, with relative "bounce-back" during systole
  • Septal bounce: prominent bowing of the septum into the LV during early diastole (RV filling dominates), then reverses during late diastole
  • IVC diameter: usually dilated (>2 cm) with minimal collapsibility, reflecting elevated RA pressure
  • RA/RV pressure assessment: elevated E/A ratio; RA area enlarged
  • Pericardial effusion: may or may not be present; small effusion is common; large effusion suggests effusive-constrictive disease or early progression

Limitations of TTE:

  • Cannot reliably measure pericardial thickness >3 mm; must be confirmed by cMR or CT
  • Doppler findings are suggestive but not diagnostic (can also be seen in restrictive cardiomyopathy, severe RV failure, or tamponade)
  • Requires good acoustic windows; technically limited in some patients

sections.heading: Cardiac magnetic resonance (cMR) — gold standard for pericardial pathology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why cMR is superior:

  • Direct visualization of pericardium: T1/T2-weighted sequences show pericardial thickening, fibrosis, inflammation, calcification
  • Pericardial thickness measurement: cMR can measure pericardial thickness accurately; >3 mm is consistent with constriction; >4 mm is more specific
  • Cine sequences: show ventricular septal bounce and ventricular interdependence
  • T1/T2 mapping: shows edema or inflammation (useful in acute pericarditis phase)
  • Tissue tagging: quantifies ventricular strain and confirms regional wall motion abnormalities (typically normal in constriction)
  • No radiation exposure

cMR findings in constriction:

  • Pericardial thickening >3 mm (often 4–8 mm)
  • Septal bounce during early diastole
  • Preserved LV and RV systolic function (global strain normal)
  • Ventricular interdependence (confirmed by flow studies or tagging)

Limitations:

  • Contraindicated in some patients (non-MR-compatible devices, claustrophobia)
  • Takes time (30–45 minutes); may not be available urgently
  • Calcification is poorly visualized (CT is better for calcification)

sections.heading: Computed tomography (CT) chest
sections.bodyHtml:
Strengths:

  • Excellent for pericardial calcification — seen as rim of high-density material around the heart; highly specific for advanced constriction (though calcification can also be seen in TB, radiation, and post-surgical constriction)
  • Pericardial thickening: measurable; >4 mm is consistent with constriction
  • Pericardial anatomy: useful if pericardiectomy is planned, to assess adhesions and RA/RV relationship
  • Fast; widely available

Limitations:

  • Radiation exposure
  • Cannot assess tissue properties (fibrosis vs. inflammation) as well as cMR
  • Less sensitive for septal bounce

sections.heading: Right heart catheterization (RHC) — hemodynamic confirmation
sections.bodyHtml:
RHC is performed when echo + cMR findings are consistent with constriction and diagnosis needs hemodynamic confirmation, or when there is diagnostic uncertainty between constriction and restriction.

Classic findings in constriction:

  • RA pressure: elevated (often 10–20 mmHg); prominent y descent (steep descent as blood is ejected from the atrium at the beginning of ventricular filling)
  • RV pressure: dip-and-plateau pattern (square root sign); rapid early diastolic dip, then flat plateau; RVDP elevated (often 15–25 mmHg)
  • PA diastolic pressure: elevated (often 15–25 mmHg)
  • LVEDP: elevated and equal to RVDP within 5 mmHg — this equalization is nearly diagnostic of constriction
  • Cardiac output: normal or low-normal at baseline; does not increase appropriately with exercise
  • Ventricular interdependence: RV and LV pressures show concordance (rise and fall together in phase due to ventricular coupling in the rigid pericardium)

RHC limitations and pitfalls:

  • Requires invasive catheterization (small risk of arrhythmia, perforation, infection)
  • May not always distinguish constriction from restriction (both can show similar pressures); septal bounce on simultaneous LV/RV pressures + pericardial imaging is usually needed
  • Pericardial tamponade can mimic constriction (equalized pressures); clinical context and pericardial imaging distinguish them

7.3 Post-cardiac surgery pericarditis continuum: Acute → transient → permanent (expandable)

sections.heading: Timeline and progression
sections.bodyHtml:
Most patients who develop constriction after cardiac surgery do so in the context of a post-op pericardial effusion. The course typically follows one of these patterns:

Pattern 1: Acute pericarditis (weeks 1–4 post-op) → spontaneous resolution

  • Very common (30–50% of post-op patients have some pericardial effusion early)
  • Usually asymptomatic or mild symptoms (chest pain, low-grade fever)
  • Effusion resolves on its own within 2–4 weeks
  • No constriction develops

Pattern 2: Acute pericarditis → transient constrictive pericarditis (weeks 2–12) → resolution with anti-inflammatory therapy

  • Less common (5–10% of post-op patients)
  • Effusive-constrictive physiology develops; hemodynamics show elevated diastolic pressures + effusion
  • Responsive to NSAIDs + colchicine — constriction component may be reversible, related to inflammation rather than fibrosis
  • Serial echos show gradual effusion resolution and normalization of diastolic filling over 2–6 months
  • Avoid pericardiectomy if this pattern is recognized — allow medical therapy time to work (2–3 months)
  • If medical therapy fails over 3 months, constriction has likely become permanent → consider pericardiectomy

Pattern 3: Acute pericarditis → transient → permanent constrictive pericarditis (months to years)

  • Chronic pericardial effusion with gradual fibrosis; constriction worsens over time
  • Becomes refractory to anti-inflammatory therapy after initial response
  • Eventually requires pericardiectomy

Pattern 4: Acute pericarditis → early permanent constrictive pericarditis (weeks to months)

  • Rare but can occur; fibrosis develops rapidly
  • Limited response to anti-inflammatory therapy from the start
  • May require earlier pericardiectomy

sections.heading: Clinical decision-making: transient vs. permanent
sections.bodyHtml:
How to distinguish transient from permanent constriction early:

  1. Timing: transient constriction typically develops weeks 2–12 post-op; permanent constriction often develops later (months to years)
  2. Pericardial imaging: transient constriction may have large pericardial effusion visible on cMR/CT; permanent constriction has fibrotic, thickened pericardium with variable effusion
  3. Response to NSAIDs + colchicine: transient disease shows improvement (effusion shrinks, RV/LV diastolic pressures drop, functional capacity improves) within 4–8 weeks; permanent disease shows minimal response
  4. Serial echocardiography: repeat echo at 4–6 weeks on NSAIDs; if constriction component is improving (respiratory variation of mitral E decreasing, diastolic pressures normalizing, effusion shrinking), transient disease is likely; if worsening, permanent disease is likely

Management algorithm:

  • Early post-op (POD 2–12) symptomatic pericardial effusion + signs of constriction → trial of NSAIDs 6–8 weeks + colchicine 3 months + serial echos
  • If improving on anti-inflammatory therapy → continue; expect resolution over 2–6 months; pericardiectomy avoided
  • If no improvement after 8 weeks, or worsening → constriction is likely permanent; discuss pericardiectomy with CT surgery
  • If permanent constriction diagnosed earlier (functional decline, worsening hemodynamics despite anti-inflammatory therapy) → consider earlier pericardiectomy referral (after optimization of diuretics, electrolytes, renal function)

7.4 Special subgroups and edge cases (expandable)

sections.heading: Constrictive pericarditis in the setting of prior cardiac surgery
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-CABG: most common post-op scenario; incidence 0.2–0.3%; typically develops months to years post-op; can be effusive-constrictive early or permanent fibrotic disease

Post-valve surgery: slightly higher incidence than CABG (~0.4–0.5%); similar timeline; valve type (mechanical vs. bioprosthetic) does not significantly alter constriction risk

Post-complex surgery (Fontan, arterial switch, etc.): rare but can occur; diagnosis may be delayed if symptoms attributed to baseline cardiac anatomy

sections.heading: TB-related constriction
sections.bodyHtml:
• Presentation: often insidious; TB pericarditis can smolder for months before constriction becomes apparent
  • TB status: must be confirmed or ruled out (TB culture from pericardial fluid or biopsy if pericardial sampling done; also test CSF and sputum if TB is in differential)
  • Imaging findings: pericardial thickening often prominent (>4 mm); may have calcification visible on CT; caseating granulomas may be visible on cMR T2 images
  • Management approach:
  • If TB confirmed: begin anti-TB therapy immediately (4-drug regimen: INH, RIF, PZA, EMB for 2 months, then INH + RIF for 4 months = standard 6-month course)
  • Role of pericardiectomy: if constriction persists despite adequate anti-TB therapy (6 months), pericardiectomy is indicated; if TB diagnosis is early and constriction mild, anti-TB therapy alone may prevent progression
  • Prognosis: TB patients have higher pericardiectomy operative mortality (10–15%) due to dense adhesions and mediastinal inflammation; survival after pericardiectomy is good if TB is controlled

sections.heading: Radiation-induced constriction
sections.bodyHtml:
• Latency: typically develops 5–20 years after mediastinal radiation (breast cancer, lymphoma, esophageal cancer)
  • Imaging: pericardial thickening and calcification are common; may also see extensive mediastinal fibrosis and adherent pericardium
  • Operative findings: pericardium is often very thickened, fibrotic, and densely adherent to the epicardium and mediastinal structures; extended operative time; higher risk of RV/LV injury
  • Operative mortality: 8–10% (higher than post-surgical or idiopathic constriction due to technical difficulty)
  • Outcomes: still good (75–80% improvement in symptoms) but recovery can be slower; requires high-volume center with experience in radiation-induced disease

sections.heading: Malignancy-related constriction
sections.bodyHtml:
• Mechanisms: direct pericardial infiltration by metastatic cancer, or constrictive physiology from post-chemotherapy/radiation pericardial fibrosis
  • Prognosis: depends on cancer stage and prognosis; if constriction is from chemotherapy/radiation in a cured cancer patient, pericardiectomy can be beneficial; if constriction is from active metastatic disease, prognosis is poor and pericardiectomy may not be appropriate
  • Management: case-by-case assessment with oncology team regarding life expectancy and appropriateness of pericardiectomy

sections.heading: Connective tissue disease-related constriction
sections.bodyHtml:
• SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma can all cause constrictive pericarditis
  • Presentation: may be indolent, developing over months to years
  • Imaging: pericardial thickening and inflammation (T2 hyperintense on cMR); may have pericardial effusion
  • Management: optimize disease-modifying therapy (methotrexate, biologics, etc.); may respond partially to NSAIDs + colchicine; pericardiectomy if medical therapy fails

sections.heading: Constrictive pericarditis in uremia
sections.bodyHtml:
• Setting: patient on hemodialysis with inadequate ultrafiltration or intermittent dialysis
  • Mechanism: uremic pericarditis inadequately treated or chronic uremic inflammation
  • Management: optimize dialysis (increase frequency or duration); if pericarditis persists or constriction develops, NSAIDs are limited (renal insufficiency); pericardiectomy if necessary (high surgical risk due to renal disease and potential coagulopathy)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Signs that a seemingly stable constrictive-pericarditis patient is deteriorating.

  • Worsening ascites despite maximized diuretics — suggests progressive fibrosis or inadequate pericardiectomy candidacy assessment
  • New or worsening orthostatic hypotension / syncope — sign of over-diuresis or volume-dependent failure
  • Rising creatinine despite stable hydration — suggests worsening cardiorenal syndrome from low cardiac output
  • Rapid weight gain (>2–3 lbs/day) despite diuretics — fluid reaccumulation from constriction progression
  • New hepatic dysfunction (elevated transaminases, bilirubin, INR) — hepatic congestion progressing to cardiac cirrhosis
  • New atrial fibrillation — common complication; rapidly reduces cardiac output in constriction (loss of atrial contribution); rate must be controlled aggressively
  • Increased dyspnea at rest or with minimal activity — suggests decompensation; may precede acute hemodynamic crisis
  • Resting tachycardia (HR >100) without fever/pain — compensatory response to low cardiac output
  • Falling urine output (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) despite adequate BP — suggests declining renal perfusion
  • Increasing JVP despite diuretics — persistent venous congestion; may indicate need for pericardiectomy escalation
  • Acute pericardial effusion development (seen on repeat echo) — suggests effusive-constrictive disease; may be transient (medically manageable) or herald permanent disease progression
  • Mental status changes — subtle confusion, lethargy, or agitation; sign of hypoperfusion or hepatic encephalopathy from worsening cardiac cirrhosis
  • Syncope or near-syncope episodes — red flag for acute decompensation; high risk for arrhythmia or cardiogenic shock

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Post-cardiac surgery is the #1 cause in developed world (0.2–0.3%). Any post-op cardiac-surgery patient with progressive RV failure, ascites, and JVD months to years post-op should raise suspicion for constrictive pericarditis. Don't default to "post-op remodeling" or "cardiomyopathy"; send echo + cMR if suspicion is high.

  2. Constrictive vs. restrictive is crucial for management — constrictive is surgically curable; restrictive is not. Physiology is similar but treatment is completely different. cMR showing pericardial thickening >3 mm + tissue Doppler e' preserved is the key differentiator. If unsure, get both cMR and RHC; don't guess.

  3. Right-sided heart failure out of proportion to LV dysfunction = red flag. Patient with normal EF but marked JVD, ascites, hepatomegaly, and edema screams constriction. Work up aggressively with echo + cMR.

  4. Kussmaul sign (JVP rising with inspiration) is nearly pathognomonic for constriction or severe RV failure. Teach this to new nurses: "JVP should drop when the patient breathes in, but in constriction it rises because the RV can't expand into the pericardium." Identify it; it confirms you're on the right track.

  5. Pericardial calcification on CXR/CT is striking but not diagnostic. Calcification is more common in TB and post-radiation constriction; post-surgical constriction may have minimal calcification early.

    Absence of calcification does NOT rule out constriction.

  6. Transient post-op constriction can resolve with colchicine + NSAIDs — don't rush to pericardiectomy. Post-cardiac-surgery effusive-constrictive pattern responding to colchicine 0.6 mg daily + ibuprofen 600 mg TID over 6–8 weeks can resolve completely. Give medical therapy 2–3 months to work; monitor with serial echos. If improving, avoid surgery.

  7. Doppler pattern ≠ hemodynamic catheterization pattern always. RV diastolic pressures can look elevated on echo (E/A >1) but RHC may show lower pressures than expected, or vice versa. Don't rely solely on echo Doppler; if diagnosis is uncertain, proceed to RHC for hemodynamic confirmation.

  8. cMR tagging is excellent for confirming constriction. Tagging sequences show normal LV/RV strain despite restrictive hemodynamics — this excludes restrictive myocardium and supports mechanical (pericardial) constraint. Tagging is underutilized; ask for it if cMR shows thickened pericardium but diagnosis remains uncertain.

  9. Pericardiectomy should be performed at a high-volume center with cardiac surgery expertise. Operative mortality is 5–10%; outcomes vary widely. Referral to quaternary center (especially for radiation or TB constriction) is strongly recommended.

  10. Post-cardiac surgery constrictive pericarditis may be early transient (responsive to anti-inflammatory within weeks) or permanent (fibrotic, refractory to medical therapy). The distinction requires clinical judgment: timing (early vs. late post-op), pericardial imaging (large effusion vs. thickened, fibrotic pericardium), and response to NSAIDs + colchicine (improving vs. worsening over 4–8 weeks).

  11. Calcific pericardium on CT is a specific sign for advanced constriction. If seen, constriction is likely present and pericardiectomy will be more challenging (dense, adherent tissue). Operative time will be longer; risk of RV/LV injury is higher.

  12. Pericardial thickness >4 mm on cMR or CT strongly suggests constriction. While >3 mm is the formal threshold, >4 mm is more specific. Thickness <2 mm makes constriction unlikely (unless effusive-constrictive with minimal fibrosis yet).

  13. Annulus paradoxus (annular velocity on tissue Doppler) is an underrecognized sign. The mitral annulus moves less during diastole (constraint) but "bounces" back during systole. This finding, combined with preserved e', helps distinguish constriction from restriction. Not all echo labs report it routinely; ask the sonographer to measure it.

  14. Hepatic "cirrhosis" from chronic constriction is reversible with pericardiectomy, unlike true cirrhosis. Patients with long-standing constriction can develop hepatomegaly, ascites, elevated transaminases, low albumin, and coagulopathy ("cardiac cirrhosis" from centrilobular necrosis). Histology shows congestion, not true cirrhosis.

    The key is that pericardiectomy can reverse it. Don't label as cirrhosis without biopsy; include echo/cMR to diagnose constriction first.

  15. Often misdiagnosed as cirrhosis or idiopathic ascites. Constrictive pericarditis can present with isolated ascites (few symptoms if LV compensation is good). Workup for cirrhosis (liver biopsy, imaging) returns normal hepatic parenchyma; then echo is obtained and constriction is found.

    Include echo early in any new-onset ascites workup, especially if liver imaging is normal.

cards.title: Cardiopulmonary Bypass (CPB)
cards.quickAnswer: A technique that takes over heart and lung function during cardiac surgery — blood is diverted from the venae cavae, oxygenated and CO₂-stripped by a membrane oxygenator, warmed or cooled by a heat exchanger, and returned to the ascending aorta by a pump. Most post-cardiotomy complications that nurses encounter trace back to CPB effects: coagulopathy, inflammation, AKI, delirium, fluid shifts.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: A technique that takes over heart and lung function during cardiac surgery — blood is diverted from the venae cavae, oxygenated and CO₂-stripped by a membrane oxygenator, warmed or cooled by a heat exchanger, and returned to the ascending aorta by a pump. Most post-cardiotomy complications that nurses encounter trace back to CPB effects: coagulopathy, inflammation, AKI, delirium, fluid shifts.
cards.sourcePrecedence: Hardin/Kaplow → Kirklin 5e → Bojar 6e → Brown 2023 → Springer 2025 → Gravlee CPB textbook

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardiopulmonary bypass is extracorporeal circulation and gas exchange that allows surgeons to operate on a still, bloodless heart. During CPB the patient's own heart and lungs are effectively offline; the machine maintains systemic perfusion and oxygenation. CPB is distinct from:

  • Off-pump CABG (OPCAB) — sternotomy + beating-heart surgery with stabilization devices; CPB is on standby but not used.
  • MECC (minimized extracorporeal circulation) — a smaller, closed-circuit variant with less prime volume and less inflammatory activation.
  • ECMO — conceptually similar extracorporeal circulation run for hours to days as support, not for a discrete operative window.

sections.heading: 2. Components (what's on the circuit)
sections.bodyHtml:
Component Purpose
Venous cannula(e) Drain blood from RA / SVC + IVC (bicaval for MV, TV, and most valve cases)
Reservoir Holds circulating volume
Oxygenator (membrane) Adds O₂, removes CO₂
Heat exchanger Warms / cools (mild 32–34 °C to deep 18–22 °C for DHCA)
Pump (roller or centrifugal) Returns blood to arterial cannula
Arterial cannula Ascending aorta typically (or femoral / axillary in select cases)
Cardioplegia delivery Antegrade / retrograde high-K⁺ solution to arrest the heart
Cell saver Recovers blood from field; processes + returns
In-line filters Removes air + microemboli

sections.heading: 3. Typical intra-op parameters (for reference — bedside nurses do not titrate)
sections.bodyHtml:
Parameter Target
MAP on pump 50–70 mmHg (higher in chronic HTN, cerebrovascular disease, elderly)
Pump flow 2.2–2.4 L/min/m²
ACT (activated clotting time) > 400–480 s on pump
Hematocrit > 22–25% (higher in cyanotic, peds)
Nasopharyngeal temp Per surgical target (normothermic, mild hypothermia, deep hypothermia)
Cross-clamp time < 90 min routine; 90–180 extended; > 180 high risk
Total pump time ~ 60–240 min typical; redo / complex > 240

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use — what bedside nurses encounter
sections.bodyHtml:
Nurses do not see the pump. They see the downstream effects. Nearly every post-cardiotomy complication traces back to a CPB mechanism:

Bedside finding CPB mechanism
POD 0–1 bleeding / coagulopathy Platelet dysfunction + heparin + fibrinogen consumption + protamine variability
Low K⁺, Mg²⁺ POD 1–2 Dilutional + diuresis + insulin-glucose shifts
AKI (CSA-AKI) 20–40% Ischemia-reperfusion + low-flow + hemolysis pigmentation
Post-pump SIRS / fever POD 0–1 Systemic inflammatory response to circuit contact
Post-op delirium POD 2–4 Neuroinflammation + microemboli + hypoperfusion
Pulmonary — atelectasis, effusion Lung collapse during CPB + capillary leak
Ileus POD 1–3 Splanchnic hypoperfusion
Hyperglycemia Insulin resistance + dextrose prime + stress response
Vasoplegia (ICU level, occasional carry-over to stepdown) NO-mediated vasodilation from inflammatory activation
Elevated troponin without infarction Myocardial stunning from arrest / reperfusion
Peripheral edema / weight gain Capillary leak — resolves over 3–5 days with diuresis

Known risk-stratifiers from CPB:

  • Long cross-clamp time (> 180 min) → higher AKI, stroke, bleeding
  • Long pump time (> 240 min) → same + higher delirium, POAF
  • DHCA used (for aortic arch cases) → neuro vigilance 48–72 h; transient coagulopathy; hypothermia-induced arrhythmia risk
  • Redo sternotomy → more bleeding from adhesion vasculature + longer pump to complete

On-pump vs off-pump CABG: OPCAB avoids pump-associated coagulopathy, inflammation, and stroke risk in selected patients (often older, frail, renal, or heavily atheromatous aortas) (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020). OPCAB trade-off: incomplete revascularization is more common, and technical demand is higher. Know which your patient had.

sections.heading: 5. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
• Most POD 0–1 bleeding is coagulopathy from the pump, not surgical. It resolves over 24–48 h as platelets recover and fibrinogen is replaced. Surgical bleeding is a different trajectory — see Scenario: Post-Op Bleeding Workup.
  • Fever POD 0–1 is usually post-pump SIRS, not infection. If cultures are negative and WBC/CRP trend is falling by POD 2, inflammatory pattern fits. Don't start antibiotics reflexively.
  • "Long pump time" in hand-off is a real concern, not trivia. > 180 min cross-clamp or > 240 min pump time = watch closely for AKI, stroke, delirium, POAF.
  • DHCA patients need neuro checks at 1, 4, 12, 24, 48, and 72 h. Focal deficits may evolve over days as hypothermic damage declares itself.
  • Rewarming arrhythmia is common during emergence. Any new tachy/brady in the first 24 h may be thermal recovery.
  • Heparin rebound at 2–4 h post-pump can re-bleed a stable patient — mostly an ICU event but occasionally seen on early transfer.
  • Hemolysis (pink plasma, hemoglobinuria) during a long run drops haptoglobin and stresses kidneys — AKI trajectory may be visible on the unit even if never ICU-severe.
  • Pleural effusion, especially left-sided, is near-universal after LIMA harvest — LIMA entry passes through the left pleura.
  • The "inflammatory" patient looks wet, febrile, tachy, and anxious on POD 1–2. This is not necessarily sepsis. Trend it; culture if other signs; do not over-react.
  • Vasoplegia that persists into POD 1 signals a more severe inflammatory activation; usually handled in ICU but occasionally transfers on low-dose pressors.
  • Ask the resident / APP on hand-off for pump time and cross-clamp time. It's a line in the intra-op note; treat it like a vital sign for the first 48 h.

cards.title: CSF Drain Management for TAAA / TEVAR
cards.quickAnswer: CSF lumbar drains reduce paraplegia risk from 25–30% to <5% in open TAAA, TEVAR, and elephant trunk procedures by lowering CSF pressure and improving spinal cord perfusion. Placement pre-op at L3–L4 or L4–L5 by anesthesia. Nursing role: strict asepsis, hourly output tracking (target 10–20 mL/h), neuro checks q1–2h (LE strength, sensation, pain), maintain MAP ≥85 mmHg + CSF pressure ≤10 mmHg concurrently. Cord perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF pressure. Over-drain (CSF <0 mmHg) causes subdural hematoma (worse outcome than typical SDH); under-drain causes cord ischemia. Typical removal POD 2–3; post-removal: flat bedrest 2–4 h + leak surveillance. [INFOGRAPHIC: Cord Perfusion Pressure (CoPP) equation visual with MAP and CSF pressure relationship]
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
CSF lumbar drains reduce paraplegia risk from 25–30% to <5% in open TAAA, TEVAR, and elephant trunk procedures by lowering CSF pressure and improving spinal cord perfusion. Nursing role: strict asepsis, hourly output tracking (target 10–20 mL/h), neuro checks q1–2h (LE strength, sensation, pain), maintain MAP ≥85 mmHg + CSF pressure ≤10 mmHg concurrently.

Cord perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF pressure. Over-drain (CSF <0 mmHg) causes subdural hematoma (worse outcome than typical SDH); under-drain causes cord ischemia. Typical removal POD 2–3; post-removal: flat bedrest 2–4 h + leak surveillance.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → 2022 AHA/ACC Aortic Disease Guidelines → Safi et al. (CSF drain safety/efficacy) → Estrera et al. (spinal cord protection TAAA) → STS Database literature → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → AACN perioperative neurovascular protocols

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, scope, when it applies.

  • Definition: A percutaneous lumbar catheter placed pre-operatively into the subarachnoid space at L3–L4 or L4–L5. Connected to a closed drainage and monitoring system, it lowers cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure during and after thoracic aortic surgery (TAAA, TEVAR, elephant trunk) to improve spinal cord perfusion during aortic cross-clamping and in the immediate post-operative period.

  • Indications: Open thoracic aortic aneurysm repair (TAAA) extent II–III, thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) for zone I–II coverage, elephant trunk procedures, selected ascending aortic arch repairs with extensive circulatory arrest.

    Not indicated: uncomplicated ascending aorta alone, TAVR, minimally invasive endovascular cases with short clamp time.

  • Duration: Pre-op placement → typically removed POD 2–3 (range POD 1–5 per surgeon and clinical presentation); post-removal vigilance for CSF leak and late cord deterioration for 4–7 days.

  • Why it matters: Paraplegia is a catastrophic complication of aortic surgery. CSF drainage is one of the most evidence-supported neuroprotection strategies alongside hypothermia and distal perfusion (Hiratzka et al., 2022).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Spinal cord ischemia mechanism during aortic cross-clamp:

Aortic cross-clamping occludes major feeding arteries (artery of Adamkiewicz, typically T9–L2); spinal cord blood flow drops precipitously. Ischemia begins within minutes without augmentation. The cord is perfused by a tenuous single longitudinal vessel in many patients, making it exquisitely sensitive to pressure gradients.

CSF pressure lowering increases cord perfusion:

Spinal cord perfusion pressure (CoPP) = MAP − CSF pressure. When CSF pressure is elevated, CoPP drops even if MAP is maintained normally. Lowering CSF pressure increases the pressure gradient across the spinal cord microvasculature, improving blood flow during the critical period of aortic cross-clamping and in the first 24–72 hours post-op.

Target parameters:

  • CSF pressure ≤10 mmHg (target 5–10 mmHg; some protocols allow ≤15 mmHg)
  • MAP ≥85 mmHg (many maintain 85–90 mmHg; some target ≥90)
  • CoPP = MAP − CSF → target ≥75 mmHg typical

Risk factors for paraplegia: Aortic clamp >40 minutes, extent II–III TAAA, low ejection fraction, previous aortic surgery, diabetes, older age (Safi et al., 1998; Estrera et al., 2005).

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — patient populations and timing.

Every patient undergoing open TAAA or high-risk TEVAR receives a CSF drain unless contraindicated. Placement typically occurs 30–60 minutes pre-operatively at bedside or in the OR under sterile technique by anesthesia or neurosurgery. The ICU nursing role begins intra-operatively during aortic cross-clamp management and extends through post-op POD 2–3 (removal) and beyond (leak surveillance, late cord deterioration monitoring).

Coagulation prerequisite: INR <1.5, platelets >100k typical. Anticoagulation held pre-procedure per ASRA guidelines (12 h for low-molecular-weight heparin typical).

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Gather baseline and ongoing status*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside examination. Information-gathering only; no interventions yet.

At placement (intra-op):

  • Baseline CSF character — color (clear, xanthochromic, bloody), clarity, RBC/WBC if sent
  • Baseline pressure (normally 8–15 cmH₂O at rest, supine)
  • Transducer leveling established and marked (critical for accurate pressure)
  • Expected initial output 0–5 mL in first 30 min
  • Bloody TAP on placement? Document; delayed AC resumption likely (discuss with surgeon; bleed usually clears 24–48 h)

Every shift post-op (ongoing — HOD 0 through removal):

  • CSF output volume hourly: Document on graduated reservoir; mark time, date, volume (mL)
  • CSF character: Clear (normal), straw-colored (okay), pink-tinged (resolving hematoma), frank blood (ongoing ooze), turbid/purulent (infection alert)
  • CSF pressure reading q1–2h: Check transducer level before each read; must be at the agreed anatomic reference point
  • Neurologic checks q1–2h: Lower extremity motor strength (hip flexion, knee extension, ankle dorsi/plantarflexion; grade 0–5 bilateral); sensation (light touch, pin-prick, lower extremities and sacrum); pain (spinal, leg, radicular); bowel/bladder function (continent, sensation to fullness)
  • Drain site inspection every shift: Erythema, purulence, CSF leak at skin, dressing integrity
  • Tubing integrity: Kinks, disconnects, blood in tubing, secure catheter position
  • Fever ≥101°F: Potential meningitis; CSF drain infection incidence 3–5%; higher if drain >5 days
  • Headache assessment: Distinguish post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) from over-drain headache

sections.heading: 5.1 Placement technique (anesthesia role — summary)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Location: L3–L4 or L4–L5 interspace (landmark: iliac crest = L4)
  • Technique: Sterile prep + local anesthesia → 18–20G Tuohy needle midline → slow advance → "pop" or loss of resistance at dura → catheter threaded into subarachnoid space (typically 10–15 cm from skin) → stylet removed → CSF flows freely → secured with sutures → connected to closed system

sections.heading: 5.2 Intra-operative management (anesthesia + ICU coordination during clamp)
sections.bodyHtml:
Parameter Target Action
MAP ≥85 mmHg Maintain with vasopressors, IV fluids, optimize anesthetic depth; may increase during clamp
CSF pressure 5–10 mmHg Monitor continuously or q5–10min during clamp; anesthesia may ask ICU nurse to open drain or adjust stopcock
CoPP ≥75 mmHg Calculate as MAP − CSF; communicate both parameters to team
Drain output during clamp 5–15 mL over 30–60 min clamp time Titrate gently to pressure target; stop if CSF <0 mmHg (over-drain risk)
Core temperature 32–34°C if hypothermia protocol Moderate hypothermia provides independent cord protection
Hematocrit >25% Improves oxygen delivery to cord

If MEP / SSEP decline during clamp:

  1. Increase MAP immediately (bolus, vasopressor, fluid)
  2. Lower CSF pressure (open drain further)
  3. Increase core temperature (warm fluids, reduce cooling)
  4. Check technical issues (loose lead, transducer error)

sections.heading: 5.3 Post-operative monitoring (POD 0–3, nursing role)
sections.bodyHtml:
Output and character (track hourly):

  • Normal range: 10–20 mL/h typical
  • Alert if <5 mL/h: Under-drain risk; increase drain patency or lower drain bag
  • Alert if >30 mL/h: Over-drain risk; contact surgeon; may need to clamp drain or reduce bag height
  • Cumulative daily output: Communicated to team during rounds

Pressure management:

  • Alert if >15–20 mmHg: Contact surgeon (under-drain; increase drain patency or lower drain bag)
  • Alert if <0 mmHg or negative: Contact surgeon (over-drain risk; may clamp drain, reduce bag height)

Neuro checks q1–2h (critical):

  • New or worsening LE weakness, sensory loss, or pain = STAT notification to surgeon + neuro assessment
  • Do NOT assume pain or residual anesthesia
  • Ischemia evolves in hours
  • Raise MAP immediately (call anesthesia), lower CSF pressure, prepare for MRI

Positioning & precautions:

  • Supine or flat per surgeon order (some protocols allow HOB 0–15°)
  • Avoid clamping without order — clamping without clinical indication risks cord ischemia
  • Log-roll if repositioning needed (minimize spinal stress)
  • Bed rest while drain in place

Aseptic technique mandatory:

  • Sterile dressing changes with sterile gloves, chlorhexidine or per protocol
  • Never disconnect tubing except per protocol during controlled dressing change
  • Drainage bag below patient level (gravity flow; prevent backflow)
  • Label all CSF samples (date, time, patient ID, "CSF") if sent for culture/cell count

sections.heading: 5.4 Drain removal protocol (typically POD 2–3)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pre-removal:

  1. Clamp drain for 4–24 h (per protocol) to observe for CSF reaccumulation or pressure spike
  2. Neuro checks during clamp period
  3. Surgeon decision based on: clinical stability, no cord dysfunction, adequate time post-op (≥24–48 h), CSF character normalization

Removal procedure:

  1. Sterile technique
  2. Withdraw catheter slowly; inspect for intact tip
  3. Sterile occlusive dressing over puncture site
  4. Send catheter tip for culture if febrile or clinical concern

Post-removal (critical):

  • Flat bedrest 2–4 hours (per protocol) — allows CSF pressure to normalize, reduces post-dural puncture headache
  • Hourly neuro checks × 4 h, then q4h for 24 h
  • Monitor for CSF leak at puncture site (clear fluid soaking dressing) → reinforce dressing, report; may need secondary closure or epidural blood patch
  • Monitor for PDPH (positional headache, neck stiffness, tinnitus) → conservative (bed rest, fluids, NSAIDs) vs. epidural blood patch per protocol
  • Monitor for late cord deterioration (can evolve 2–7 days post-op, especially if cord edema) → new weakness = MRI + neurosurgery consult

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

  1. New or worsening LE weakness during or after drain placement — ischemia until proven otherwise; STAT neuro checks, raise MAP, lower CSF pressure, prepare for MRI
  2. CSF output <5 mL/h despite normal pressure reading — catheter may be kinked, occluded, or migrated; check tubing, flush gently if ordered, contact surgeon
  3. CSF pressure >15–20 mmHg unresponsive to position/drain adjustment — under-drain; contact surgeon; may need catheter repositioning or imaging
  4. CSF pressure trending negative or <0 mmHg — over-drain risk; clamp drain, contact surgeon immediately; over-drain causes subdural hematoma (worse outcome than typical)
  5. Fever ≥101°F + headache + neck stiffness — meningitis until proven otherwise; culture CSF and blood, start empiric antibiotics per protocol, contact ID
  6. Bloody CSF persisting >48 h or frank ongoing bleeding — monitor trend; delayed AC resumption typical; document; discuss with surgeon re: imaging or intervention
  7. Catheter migration or visible movement at skin — do NOT attempt to reposition; check sutures, notify surgeon; may need replacement
  8. CSF leak at puncture site persisting after removal — reinforce dressing; may need epidural blood patch, fibrin glue, or secondary suture closure
  9. Severe headache worse when supine after drain removal — over-drain headache; contact surgeon; may need emergency drain reinsertion or epidural intervention
  10. Any worsening neurologic exam in the first 7 days post-op — can represent late cord deterioration from edema; contact neurosurgery; consider MRI

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections are intended for in-app collapse. Novice and advanced beginner RNs can expand; experienced nurses and experts can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Cord perfusion pressure (CoPP) physiology detail
sections.bodyHtml:
The critical equation: Cord Perfusion Pressure = MAP − CSF pressure

This is the single most important concept for understanding CSF drain management. It is NOT sufficient to target MAP alone or CSF pressure alone; both must be optimized concurrently.

Example 1 (inadequate CoPP despite "normal" MAP):

  • Patient A: MAP 90 mmHg, CSF pressure 20 mmHg → CoPP = 70 mmHg (marginal, at risk)
  • Patient B: MAP 80 mmHg, CSF pressure 5 mmHg → CoPP = 75 mmHg (better perfusion despite lower MAP)

Example 2 (why over-drain is dangerous): - Over-drain (CSF <0 mmHg) causes traction on bridging subdural veins → venous sinus bleeding → subdural hematoma. This is a WORSE outcome than typical traumatic SDH because the patient is anticoagulated post-op. Literature supports this (Safi et al., 1998).

Normal cord blood flow: ~40 mL/100 g/min; ischemia threshold ~10 mL/100 g/min. Cross-clamp drops this to near-zero in seconds. CSF pressure reduction is the most immediate intervention available.

sections.heading: 7.2 Complications and troubleshooting
sections.bodyHtml:
Complication Recognition Nursing Action Prevention
Over-drain (CSF <0) Headache worse supine, confusion, new focal deficit, seepage from site, output >30 mL/h Lower drain bag, clamp drain, check transducer level, contact surgeon; may need CT head Monitor pressure hourly; target 5–10 mmHg; avoid aggressive draining
Under-drain (CSF >15–20) New/worsening LE weakness, sensory loss, minimal output despite high pressure Increase drain patency (flush gently if ordered), lower bag further, check for kinks/clots, ensure proper leveling; contact surgeon Monitor pressure q1–2h; responsive adjustment; ensure MAP ≥85 concurrent
Subdural hematoma Severe headache worse supine, decreased mental status, focal deficit, seizure STAT neuro checks, CT head, notify surgeon emergently; prepare for drain removal or ICU monitoring Avoid CSF <0; titrate gradually; check pressure frequently
Meningitis / ventriculitis Fever ≥101°F, headache, neck stiffness, confusion, elevated WBC, CSF turbidity Culture CSF/blood; Gram stain; start empiric antibiotics (vancomycin + 3rd-gen cephalosporin per protocol); notify ID; may require drain removal Strict asepsis; sterile dressing changes; limit duration (remove by POD 3–5); chlorhexidine prep
Bloody CSF on placement Blood in first aliquot; usually clears 24–48 h Document color, trend (clears or persists), note in chart; delay AC resumption if ordered (consult surgeon); repeat specimen if persistent Use ultrasound guidance if available; experienced operator; inform anesthesia
Catheter migration Loss of CSF flow despite normal pressure, high readings, visible catheter movement Check sutures (gentle tug test), consider ultrasound, notify surgeon; maintain sterile precautions Secure with 2–3 sutures; reinforce dressing; educate patient; limit mobility
Catheter occlusion No flow despite patent system, high pressure, little output Gently flush with sterile saline (0.5–1 mL) if protocol allows; do NOT force; notify surgeon if unsuccessful Maintain adequate flow; avoid compression; monitor trends
CSF leak post-removal Clear fluid soaking dressing; positive glucose on dip; persistent drainage Reinforce sterile dressing; notify surgeon; may require epidural blood patch, fibrin glue, or secondary closure Flat bedrest 2–4 h post-removal; avoid straining
PDPH Positional headache (worse upright), neck stiffness, tinnitus; typically POD 1–3 Conservative: bed rest, hydration, analgesics, NSAIDs; reassure (self-limited in most); if severe >48 h, epidural blood patch Optimize hydration; avoid straining; know blood patch protocol
Transducer leveling error Inconsistent pressure readings, sudden jump/drop without clinical change Re-zero to agreed reference point; mark reference line on patient/bed; educate staff Establish reference point at insertion; mark with marker; reinforce each shift

sections.heading: 7.3 Special populations and edge cases
sections.bodyHtml:
• Elephant trunk / staged procedures: CSF drain in first stage; removed if patient returns to ICU between stages; reinserted at second stage if needed. Discuss timing with CT surgery team.
  • Type A aortic dissection with aortic root involvement: CSF drain is rarely needed alone (focus is root replacement + DCP); discuss with surgical team.
  • Patients with prior spinal instrumentation or pathology: May affect landmark identification and catheter placement; alert anesthesia pre-op.
  • Anticoagulation timing post-op: ASRA guidelines: 12 h hold for LMWH post-placement; warfarin variable (often 4–5 days); bloody CSF extends hold. Coordinate with hematology/surgery. Document clearly in orders.

sections.heading: 7.4 Patient and family teaching
sections.bodyHtml:
"Why do I have this drain?"
It actively protects your spinal cord from being damaged when the aorta is clamped during surgery. Without it, the paraplegia risk is 25–30%. With it, we reduce that to less than 5%.

"How long will I have it?"
Usually 2–3 days after surgery. Once your spinal cord has recovered and you are doing well neurologically, the surgeon will remove it.

"Why do I need to stay flat in bed?"
The drain works better when you are lying flat. It helps the fluid drain and maintain the pressure we want. We'll help you move carefully and gradually.

"What happens when it's removed?"
The surgeon will take out the catheter under sterile conditions. We'll watch your spine carefully for a few more days for any leakage and check your legs regularly.

"Can I move around?"
While the drain is in place, you need to stay in bed. We'll help you with bed rest activities and gentle movement. Once it's removed, you can gradually start walking with our help.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in patients who were initially stable; if any develop, re-escalate immediately.

  • New or worsening LE weakness at any time — cord ischemia until proven otherwise; STAT neuro assessment, raise MAP, lower CSF pressure
  • CSF pressure trending upward despite drain opening — possible catheter occlusion or migration; check tubing, flush if ordered, contact surgeon
  • CSF pressure consistently negative (<0 mmHg) — over-drain in progress; risk of subdural hematoma; clamp drain, contact surgeon immediately
  • Headache worsening and becoming positional (worse supine) — over-drain headache vs. PDPH; if accompanied by motor change, contact surgeon emergently
  • Fever developing + headache + neck stiffness — meningitis; culture CSF/blood immediately, start antibiotics per protocol, contact ID
  • New sensory level or asymmetry — cord ischemia evolution; STAT neuro exam, imaging, neurosurgery consult
  • Bowel/bladder dysfunction (new incontinence, inability to void, no sensation to fullness) — cord dysfunction; STAT evaluation
  • Bloody CSF persisting >72 h or increasing in volume — contact surgeon; may need imaging or intervention
  • CSF output suddenly ceasing despite normal pressure — catheter occlusion, migration, or kinking; check tubing, flush if ordered, notify surgeon
  • Patient becoming more anxious or confused — may herald deterioration; obtain neuro checks, contact team
  • Vital sign instability (hypotension, tachycardia) with worsening neuro findings — possible cord shock; STAT team call

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
(10–15 high-yield bullets for proficient/expert nurses)

  1. MAP ≥85 + CSF ≤10 TOGETHER — not independently. Cord perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF. Communicate BOTH parameters. A patient with MAP 90 and CSF 20 has CoPP 70 (marginal); one with MAP 80 and CSF 5 has CoPP 75 (better). Don't fixate on one alone.

  2. New LE weakness during/after placement = STAT call to surgeon + neuro assessment. Do not assume pain or anesthesia residual. Ischemia evolves in hours. Raise MAP immediately, lower CSF pressure, prepare for MRI. Time is spinal cord.

  3. Over-drain causes subdural hematoma with WORSE outcomes than typical SDH (literature supports this; Safi et al., 1998). Target CSF 5–10 mmHg. Never chase negative pressure. If CSF <0, clamp drain and notify surgeon immediately.

  4. Headache + neuro change = over-drain until proven otherwise. Distinguish from PDPH (positional, self-limited, no motor deficit). Over-drain headache often worse supine + motor/sensory change. Get CT head; contact surgeon.

  5. Infection risk 3–5%; increases after POD 3–4. Strict asepsis with every dressing change. Fever is meningitis until proven otherwise. Drain duration extension beyond POD 3–4 increases risk; removal timing is critical.

  6. Drain placement requires coagulation optimization. INR <1.5, platelets >100k pre-procedure. Check labs before anesthesia. Bloody tap on placement delays AC resumption (consult surgeon; bleed clears 24–48 h).

  7. ASRA anticoagulation + drain timing: 12 h hold for LMWH post-placement; warfarin variable. Bloody CSF extends hold. Coordinate with hematology/surgery. Document clearly in orders.

  8. Bloody CSF on placement does NOT mean drain failed. Expect clotting to resolve 24–48 h. Trend the output (decreasing pink = resolving). Only escalate if persistent frank blood, high volume, or neuro change.

  9. Tubing-dependent loops and transducer leveling alter pressure readings profoundly. A loop 5 cm below transducer adds ~4 mmHg error. Route tubing without loops. Re-zero before each read. Mark reference point; educate all staff.

  10. Patient transport with drain is high-risk for disconnection/contamination. Establish SOP: Is drain clamped? Is transducer held at same height? Are connections capped? Brief patient: do not pull tubing. Recheck connections after arrival.

  11. Removal timing (POD 2–3) balances benefits vs. infection risk. Clamp 4–24 h pre-removal to observe for reaccumulation or pressure spike. Post-removal: flat bedrest 2–4 h and leak surveillance 2–7 days. Late cord deterioration can occur; new weakness = MRI + neurosurgery.

  12. Direct communication with CT surgery if ANY concerns. Paraplegia is devastating. No communication gap is acceptable. Drain status, neuro changes, infection risk, removal timing — all warrant direct surgeon discussion.

  13. Monitor for cord ischemia signs beyond weakness. Sensory level, bowel/bladder change, pain (neuropathic burning in legs). Loss of vibration/proprioception may precede motor loss. Document baseline pre-op; compare daily.

  14. Patient education on drain purpose and duration. Many assume it is temporary monitoring; educate that it actively protects cord. Explain why flat bedrest, why frequent neuro checks. Informed patients are safer (fewer self-removals, better compliance).

  15. First flatus is a major post-op milestone (indicates return of some spinal cord function and generalized recovery). Chart it. Different from bowel regimen; spinal cord is working.

cards.title: Central Venous Pressure (CVP)
cards.quickAnswer: Pressure in the superior vena cava and right atrium, measured directly via central venous catheter with transducer at phlebostatic axis. Post-operative target 8–12 mmHg (higher than awake baseline due to post-pump fluid shifts and stiff post-ischemic LV). Critical: CVP is a poor stand-alone indicator of volume responsiveness — trending over hours plus clinical signs (perfusion, urine output, lactate) matters far more than a single numeric value. Transducer leveling errors of 5–6 mmHg are common; re-level after every position change.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: Pressure in the superior vena cava and right atrium, measured directly via central venous catheter with transducer at phlebostatic axis. cards.sourcePrecedence: CVICU Handbook → Hardin/Kaplow → Brown 2023 → Bojar 6e → AACN → Marik 2008 review

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
Central venous pressure (CVP) is the blood pressure in the superior vena cava near the junction with the right atrium. It reflects right atrial pressure and, under normal filling conditions, right ventricular end-diastolic pressure — a component of RV preload.

Measured directly via indwelling central venous catheter (IJ, subclavian, or femoral) connected to a fluid-filled transducer system that converts hydrostatic column pressure into a numeric display in mmHg.

Critical distinction: CVP is a pressure (what the RA "sees"), not a volume. This explains why CVP alone is a poor predictor of whether additional fluid will improve cardiac output — the landmark Marik 2008 meta-analysis showed minimal correlation between baseline CVP and fluid responsiveness.

sections.heading: Transducer Positioning
sections.bodyHtml:
• Phlebostatic axis: intersection of 4th intercostal space (sternal border) and midaxillary line — anatomic level of RA in supine patient
  • Leveling error: Every 5 cm mismatch between transducer height and phlebostatic axis = ~4 mmHg artifact
  • Routine practice: Re-zero and re-level after patient position changes (HOB elevation, recline, ambulation)

sections.heading: CVP Waveform (normal sinus rhythm)
sections.bodyHtml:
Component Timing Meaning
a wave Atrial contraction RA contracts against closed tricuspid valve
c wave Tricuspid valve closure TV cusp bulges into RA
x descent Atrial relaxation RA pressure falls as it relaxes
v wave Atrial filling Passive RA filling while TV closed
y descent Tricuspid valve opening TV opens; blood drains into RV

Abnormal waveforms signal valve pathology or rhythm disturbance (see §6 Pitfalls).

sections.heading: 3. Normal Range / Post-Op Targets
sections.bodyHtml:
Population CVP target Notes
Healthy awake adult 2–8 mmHg Baseline
Post-cardiac surgery 8–12 mmHg Expected due to fluid shifts + stiff LV
RV failure or tricuspid surgery 12–15 mmHg Transiently tolerated; escalate if > 15 with hypotension
Concerning (hypotensive + high CVP) > 15 mmHg Red flag for tamponade, RV failure, or heart strain

Why higher post-op: Fluid shifts from cardiopulmonary bypass prime, crystalloid resuscitation, and capillary leak expand intravascular volume. Post-ischemic myocardium (especially LV) is stiff and requires higher filling pressure for adequate stroke volume. RV may be transiently depressed from bypass or intraoperative manipulation.

Trend matters more than the number. A patient with CVP 8 → 14 in 2 hours with falling BP or rising lactate is concerning despite 14 being "normal" post-op range.

sections.heading: Direct Measurement & Trending
sections.bodyHtml:
Central lines placed intraoperatively (IJ or subclavian) remain in place through POD 1–2; then removed. CVP is displayed on bedside monitor and documented per protocol in chart.

Trend the CVP, not the value. Stable CVP 10 is reassuring; CVP 8 → 15 with hemodynamic change is a red flag.

sections.heading: Volume Assessment
sections.bodyHtml:
Distinguish hypovolemia from cardiogenic shock using CVP + clinical picture:

Finding CVP Other signs Likely cause
Tachycardia, hypotension, low UOP Low (< 5) Cool periphery, low JVP Hypovolemia → cautious fluid bolus
Tachycardia, hypotension, low UOP High (> 12) Elevated JVP, edema, cool extremities Cardiogenic shock → inotropes, afterload reduction
Stable BP, low UOP, rising CVP High (> 12) Edema, hepatomegaly, rising LFTs RV failure → decrease PEEP, inhaled NO, avoid diuresis

sections.heading: Tamponade Recognition
sections.bodyHtml: Rising CVP in a previously stable patient + falling BP + narrowing pulse pressure = tamponade until proven otherwise. However, tamponade can present with "normal" CVP in chronically hypovolemic patients — absence of "high CVP" does not rule it out. If clinical suspicion is high, call the surgical team; echo or re-exploration may be needed.

sections.heading: RV Failure
sections.bodyHtml: Persistently elevated CVP (12–15 mmHg or higher) despite adequate cardiac output suggests RV systolic or diastolic dysfunction. Associated findings: peripheral edema, hepatic congestion (rising bilirubin, LFTs climbing), oliguria despite "adequate" filling pressure. Management: reduce PEEP, consider inhaled nitric oxide, optimize preload without over-filling, support RV with inotropes if hypotensive.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Why CVP is not a volume measure CVP reflects pressure in a distensible chamber (the RA). The relationship between pressure and actual blood volume is nonlinear and varies with:
  • Ventricular compliance — a stiff post-ischemic ventricle requires higher filling pressure to achieve the same stroke volume as a compliant ventricle
  • Intrathoracic pressure — positive-pressure ventilation falsely elevates CVP by 2–5 mmHg; a patient on PEEP 12 may have true CVP 6 that reads as 10
  • Pericardial constraint — thickened pericardium or pericardial fluid shifts the pressure-volume curve upward This is why Marik (2008) found that baseline CVP is a poor predictor of fluid responsiveness. A CVP of 10 does not reliably distinguish a patient who needs more fluid from one who does not.
Waveform abnormalities — clinical patterns
  • Giant v wave: tall v wave obliterating the x descent signals tricuspid regurgitation — common post-op from RV dilatation or TV surgery. Not an emergency; reflects RV afterload mismatch and usually improves with recovery
  • Giant a wave: prominent a wave without prominent v wave suggests forceful RA contraction against a stiff RV — RV diastolic dysfunction
  • Cannon a wave (giant irregular a): occurs when RA contracts against a closed tricuspid valve; seen in junctional rhythms or atrial contractions against ventricular contraction
  • Blunted y descent: loss of the normal diastolic dip suggests RV failure or restrictive physiology — RV cannot relax normally to accept filling
PEEP and mechanical ventilation artifact Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) and positive-pressure ventilation increase intrathoracic pressure and falsely elevate CVP by 2–5 mmHg (sometimes more). Clinical pearls:
  • Always document ventilator settings when recording CVP
  • A patient on PEEP 12 may have true CVP 6 that reads as 10
  • If CVP seems inconsistent with clinical picture (patient looks hypovolemic but CVP is 10), check ventilator settings first
  • When a patient extubates, watch for a sudden drop in CVP that may reflect true hemodynamics for the first time — this is expected and not necessarily a sign of hypovolemia

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls *(5–10 high-yield)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. CVP is a poor stand-alone measure of volume responsiveness. Marik 2008 meta-analysis (Chest) showed minimal correlation between baseline CVP and fluid responsiveness in critical care. Patients with CVP 8 may be hypovolemic; patients with CVP 15 may have preload-responsive physiology if the problem is RV failure. Trend + clinical picture > single number.

  2. Transducer leveling is everything. A transducer left at shoulder level instead of phlebostatic axis can read 5–6 mmHg too high; one below the level reads falsely low. Re-level after every position change. If CVP seems off, level the transducer first.

  3. PEEP and positive-pressure ventilation falsely elevate CVP. Document ventilator settings when recording CVP. A patient on PEEP 12 may have true CVP 6 that reads as 10. If the patient extubates, watch for a sudden drop in CVP that reflects real hemodynamics for the first time.

  4. Position changes change CVP. Raising the head-of-bed from flat to 45° can increase CVP 2–4 mmHg without changing actual preload. When the patient ambulates, recline them to the reference position before drawing a CVP comparison.

  5. Tricuspid regurgitation produces giant v waves. Tall v waves obliterating the x descent signal TR — common post-op from RV dilatation or TV surgery. TR is not an emergency; it reflects RV afterload mismatch and usually improves with recovery.

  6. RV failure produces giant a waves. Prominent a waves without prominent v waves suggest forceful RA contraction against a stiff RV — RV diastolic dysfunction.

  7. High CVP + low urine output + good MAP ≠ "give more fluid." This triad suggests tamponade, RV failure, or right heart strain — adding fluid worsens it. Call the surgical team; do not give empiric fluids.

  8. Low CVP + high heart rate + cool periphery + low UOP = hypovolemia. Cautious fluid bolus (250–500 mL LR or NS over 15–30 min) is reasonable while investigating the source. Recheck CVP, BP, and HR. If unresponsive, escalate.

cards.title: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM)
cards.quickAnswer: DCM = dilated left ventricle (LVEDD >60 mm) with reduced systolic function (LVEF ≤40%) not explained by coronary artery disease, pressure overload, or volume overload. Etiologies: ~30–40% genetic (TTN titin, LMNA lamin, others); inflammatory/myocarditis; toxic (alcohol, cocaine); peripartum; chemotherapy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab, checkpoint inhibitors); tachycardia-induced (reversible with rate control); thyroid, hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis. Management: HFrEF four-pillar GDMT (ACE-I/ARNI, beta-blocker, aldosterone antagonist, SGLT2i) + etiology-specific therapy + genetic testing and family cascade screening if familial. LMNA carriers have higher arrhythmia risk (earlier ICD consideration). Peripartum may partially recover; alcoholic and tachycardia-induced are potentially reversible. Cross-link to HFrEF diagnosis, VAD, heart transplant.
