sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — who gets this and why it matters.

  • Definition: Primary dysfunction of the heart muscle characterized by dilation of the left ventricle (LVEDD >60 mm or >2.7 m/m² indexed) or biventricular dilation, reduced contractility (LVEF ≤40%), and absence of significant coronary artery disease, hypertension, or valvular disease to explain the phenotype.
  • Epidemiology: Most common form of cardiomyopathy in developed countries. Accounts for ~40% of all heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) etiologies. Annual incidence ~0.5 per 100,000 in developed populations. Genetic variants identified in ~30–50% of idiopathic cases. TTN (titin) mutations account for ~25% of familial DCM; LMNA (lamin A/C) ~10%; hundreds of other genes increasingly recognized.
  • Who this applies to: Newly presenting HF symptoms (dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue); incidental LV dysfunction on imaging for other reason; family screening after genetic variant identified in a relative; ICU admission for acute decompensation or cardiogenic shock; preoperative workup for VAD or heart transplant; arrhythmia monitoring for ventricular tachycardia (VT) or sudden cardiac death risk stratification.
  • Why bedside care matters: DCM patients admitted for acute HF decompensation, preoperative device evaluation, arrhythmia monitoring, GDMT optimization, or postoperative recovery after device implantation require vigilant volume management, medication adherence monitoring, early recognition of arrhythmia, and family-centered genetic counseling.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner teaching. Mechanism explanation.

Primary mechanism:

  • Myocardial contractile dysfunction → loss of force-generating capacity
  • LV dilation (Laplace's law) — chamber enlarges to maintain stroke volume via Frank-Starling mechanism, but increased wall stress worsens dysfunction (maladaptive remodeling spiral)
  • Systolic dysfunction (EF ≤40%) → reduced cardiac output, inadequate organ perfusion
  • Diastolic dysfunction → restrictive filling pattern, elevated left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), pulmonary congestion (orthopnea, dyspnea)

Compensatory activation (initially helpful, eventually harmful): - Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), sympathetic nervous system (SNS), and cytokine cascade initially preserve cardiac output but promote progressive fibrosis, remodeling, and further EF decline

Arrhythmia substrate:

  • Abnormal LV geometry + regional wall motion abnormality + myocardial scarring (in genetic and inflammatory forms) → electrical heterogeneity → increased ventricular tachycardia (VT) and ventricular fibrillation (VF) risk
  • LMNA mutations carry particularly high arrhythmia risk and sudden cardiac death (SCD) risk

Thromboembolic risk:

  • Dilated LV chamber with reduced contractile function + regional wall motion abnormality → prothrombotic state
  • Risk of left ventricular thrombus (LVT) formation, especially if LVEF <20%
  • Atrial fibrillation common (develops in ~20–30% of DCM patients), further increasing stroke risk

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Acute decompensated HF presentation:

  • Dyspnea (exertional, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea), peripheral edema, fatigue, rapid weight gain
  • Elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), hepatomegaly, pulmonary crackles
  • S3 gallop (sign of elevated LVEDP), laterally displaced point of maximal impulse (PMI; dilated LV)
  • Hypotension or borderline blood pressure in cardiogenic shock; decreased urine output, altered mental status, cold extremities
  • Arrhythmias: new-onset atrial fibrillation (common; high stroke risk), sustained VT, symptomatic ventricular ectopy

Chronic compensated DCM:

  • Dyspnea on exertion, reduced activity tolerance, fatigue
  • Mild to moderate peripheral edema, elevated JVP at rest
  • Laterally displaced PMI
  • S3 gallop; often preserved resting systolic blood pressure

Arrhythmia-predominant presentation:

  • Palpitations, syncope, unwitnessed sudden cardiac death
  • Sustained VT on electrocardiogram (ECG) or monitor; frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs), non-sustained VT (NSVT) on ambulatory monitoring
  • Rapid atrial fibrillation (RVR)

Peripartum DCM: - Third trimester or first postpartum month; may partially recover with aggressive GDMT

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Information-gathering only (2–3 minutes).

  • Vital signs: Heart rate, blood pressure (look for hypotension or borderline perfusion), SpO₂, respiratory rate, temperature
  • Perfusion markers: Capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output, mental status
  • Cardiac exam: JVP height, PMI location (displaced laterally if dilated), S3/S4 presence, murmurs, apical–radial pulse deficit on palpation (suggests arrhythmia)
  • Pulmonary: Lung sounds for crackles (pulmonary edema), work of breathing, dyspnea severity
  • Systemic: Peripheral edema grade, hepatomegaly, weight trend
  • Recent labs: Serum potassium (K⁺), magnesium (Mg²⁺), creatinine, hemoglobin, troponin, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP); echocardiography results (LVEF, LVEDD, wall motion)
  • Medication review: Current GDMT medications on board? Home doses held? Recent antiarrhythmic or beta-blocker changes?
  • Monitor review: Telemetry rhythm; arrhythmia burden if on continuous monitoring
  • Surgery context (if applicable): Procedure type and date; any epicardial pacing wires; recent device interrogation if ICD/CRT in place

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Diagnosis-specific management subsections (no Stable/Unstable fork for diagnosis cards).

sections.heading: 5A. GDMT — Four-Pillar HFrEF Standard
sections.bodyHtml:
All DCM patients with reduced ejection fraction should be on all four pillars, if tolerated:

  1. ACE inhibitor OR Angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) OR Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI)

    • ACE-I (lisinopril, enalapril) or ARB (losartan, valsartan) first-line
    • ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) superior in some trials; target dose sacubitril/valsartan 97/103 mg BID
    • Titrate to maximum tolerated dose; monitor K⁺ and creatinine (contraindicated if Cr >3 or K⁺ >5.5)

  2. Beta-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol)

    • Titrate to target: carvedilol 25 mg BID; metoprolol succinate 190 mg daily; bisoprolol 10 mg daily
    • Reduces mortality and HF hospitalizations; critical for all HFrEF
    • Monitor for hypotension, bradycardia, worsening fatigue

  3. Aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone or eplerenone)

    • Spironolactone 12.5–50 mg daily (monitor K⁺; hold if K⁺ >5.5 or Cr >3)
    • Eplerenone 25–50 mg daily (more selective; fewer gynecomastia/sexual dysfunction side effects)
    • Initiate after ACE-I/ARB established; reduces mortality beyond ACE-I/beta-blocker alone

  4. SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin or empagliflozin)

    • Dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or empagliflozin 10 mg daily
    • Reduces HF hospitalizations and mortality independent of diabetes status
    • Recent guideline addition (2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA); well-tolerated

Additional agents per recent guidelines:

  • Vericiguat — if recent decompensation (hospitalization or IV diuretics in past year); 2.5 mg BID, titrate to 5 mg BID
  • Finerenone — newer non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist; emerging evidence for HFrEF role
  • Ivabradine — if resting heart rate >70 and EF ≤35% despite beta-blocker, or beta-blocker contraindication; 5 mg BID

Diuretics:

  • Symptom relief only, not mortality-reducing
  • Titrate to euvolemia; loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide) if significant volume overload
  • Monitor electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺); replace if depleted

sections.heading: 5B. Etiology-Specific Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Tailored interventions depend on identified or suspected etiology:

Idiopathic DCM (no identified cause):

  • Standard GDMT; genetic testing offered if LVEDD >60 mm, age <50, or family history of HF/sudden death
  • Comprehensive workup to exclude reversible causes (see Teaching Layers, §7.1)

Genetic DCM (TTN, LMNA, MYBPC3, MYH7, others):

  • Standard GDMT
  • First-degree family screening: baseline echo + ECG; cascade genetic testing if pathogenic variant identified in proband
  • Genetic counseling offered to patient and family
  • LMNA mutation carriers: Particularly high arrhythmia risk; consider ICD at LVEF <30% (lower threshold than standard ≤35%); early EP consultation recommended

Viral myocarditis (acute or recovering phase):

  • Standard GDMT
  • Anti-inflammatory therapy (corticosteroids, immunosuppressive agents) remains controversial; most patients recover ejection fraction over 3–6 months with supportive care alone
  • Endomyocardial biopsy may confirm diagnosis if clinical suspicion high but etiology unclear; informs prognosis
  • Serial echocardiography every 3–6 months to document EF recovery

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM; onset third trimester to 1 month postpartum):

  • Standard GDMT + diuretics
  • Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist, prolactin antagonist) has shown promise in small trials; dose 2.5 mg daily × 2 weeks then 2.5 mg BID × 6 months; mechanism: reduces prolactin-mediated myocardial damage
  • Expectation of partial to substantial EF recovery in many patients; most recover within 6–12 months with treatment
  • Critical: Future pregnancies carry 40–50% maternal mortality risk; strict contraception counseling mandatory unless specialized high-risk obstetric + cardiology management available at referral center
  • Consider anticoagulation if LVEF <20% or LVT documented; balance with postpartum hemorrhage risk

Alcoholic cardiomyopathy:

  • Standard GDMT + strict alcohol abstinence (essential therapy, not lifestyle advice)
  • EF may partially or completely recover with weeks to months of sobriety; recovery potential distinguishes this from genetic/idiopathic DCM
  • Addiction medicine consult; social work; support groups (AA)
  • Counsel on modest alcohol consumption = further decline; complete abstinence optimal

Cocaine-induced cardiomyopathy:

  • Standard GDMT + cessation of cocaine use
  • EF recovery possible with sustained abstinence + GDMT
  • Addiction medicine, social work, behavioral health consults

Chemotherapy-induced cardiomyopathy (anthracyclines, trastuzumab, checkpoint inhibitors, tyrosine kinase inhibitors):

  • Standard GDMT
  • Cardio-oncology consult essential — assess feasibility of stopping/modifying causative agent
  • Anthracycline cardiotoxicity is dose-dependent; if EF drop >10% detected early and anthracycline discontinued, EF may stabilize or recover with GDMT
  • Trastuzumab (HER2-directed) cardiotoxicity often reversible if caught early; hold trastuzumab during HF treatment; can often resume once EF recovers
  • Checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4) cause fulminant myocarditis in rare cases; if suspected, high-dose corticosteroids + immunosuppression; consider temporary holding
  • Baseline troponin, BNP, and LVEF mandatory before initiating cardiotoxic chemotherapy; serial monitoring during and after treatment

Thyroid dysfunction-related cardiomyopathy:

  • Treat underlying thyroid disease (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism)
  • HF often improves markedly or completely once euthyroid achieved
  • TSH, free T4 at baseline and during follow-up

Hemochromatosis-related cardiomyopathy:

  • Iron chelation (deferasirox, deferoxamine) + phlebotomy
  • Standard GDMT
  • Ferritin, transferrin saturation monitoring; cardiac iron quantification on CMR to guide chelation intensity

Sarcoidosis-related cardiomyopathy:

  • Immunosuppression: corticosteroids ± immunosuppressive agents (mycophenolate, azathioprine)
  • Standard GDMT
  • ICD consideration for sustained VT or LVEF <35% (arrhythmia risk high in sarcoid)
  • Rheumatology/pulmonology consult

Amyloidosis-related cardiomyopathy (infiltrative phenotype):

  • Etiology-specific agents: tafamidis (ATTR stabilizer) if ATTR amyloidosis; newer therapies emerging
  • Modified HFrEF GDMT (often restrictive physiology; caution with aggressive diuresis)
  • Amyloid serology, genetic testing for TTR mutations, biopsy if diagnostic uncertainty
  • Hematology/oncology consult for light-chain or secondary amyloidosis
  • High mortality; early specialty consultation critical

Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (TIC):

  • Rate control or rhythm control of primary arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, incessant supraventricular tachycardia [SVT], frequent PVCs)
  • Key feature: EF may substantially recover (often normalization) once heart rate controlled — this is one of the few truly reversible DCM forms
  • If atrial fibrillation: beta-blocker, non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker, or rhythm control (amiodarone) to target HR <100 at rest
  • If frequent PVCs or incessant SVT: catheter ablation often definitive and curative
  • EP consultation recommended
  • Prognosis excellent if rate/rhythm controlled early

sections.heading: 5C. Device Therapy
sections.bodyHtml:
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) — primary prevention:

  • Indicated if LVEF ≤35% on optimal GDMT for ≥40 days (Class IIa recommendation)
  • Exception — LMNA mutations: Lower threshold; consider ICD at LVEF <30% or if recurrent arrhythmias, given high SCD risk
  • Mandatory if prior sustained VT/VF (secondary prevention)
  • EP consultation; baseline electrolyte panel, renal function

Cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT):

  • Indicated if LBBB (left bundle branch block) with QRS duration ≥120 milliseconds AND LVEF ≤35%
  • Improves symptoms, exercise tolerance, and mortality in selected patients
  • Requires ECG confirmation of LBBB pattern; echo assessment of mechanical delay

sections.heading: 5D. Advanced Therapies
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanical circulatory support — left ventricular assist device (LVAD):

  • Destination therapy or bridge to transplant for patients with LVEF <25%, persistent HF symptoms despite optimal GDMT, or cardiogenic shock
  • Good candidate: no absolute contraindications (severe renal insufficiency, advanced liver disease, uncontrolled infection, severe COPD, active malignancy)
  • Improves survival and quality of life vs. inotrope-dependent palliation
  • Refer to VAD specialty team; see VAD-specific cards for management

Heart transplantation:

  • DCM is the second most common indication for heart transplant (after ischemic cardiomyopathy)
  • Candidate criteria: LVEF <25%, New York Heart Association (NYHA) Class III–IV symptoms despite optimal GDMT, expected post-transplant survival >5 years, no absolute contraindications
  • Critical: Reversible causes (myocarditis, alcoholic, peripartum, tachycardia-induced, chemotherapy-related) should be given time to recover before listing; genetic and truly idiopathic DCM rarely improve and are appropriate for transplant
  • Refer to transplant team; extensive workup (cardiopulmonary exercise testing, right heart catheterization, psychosocial evaluation, infectious serology, malignancy screening)
  • Survival: ~95% at 1 year, ~75% at 5 years (organ-dependent)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR framework for calling the care team.

SBAR template:

S: "Dr./APP [name], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room/location], admitted for [indication — e.g., acute HF decompensation, preop VAD workup]." B: "Patient has diagnosed [DCM etiology if known, e.g., 'idiopathic DCM'] with EF [%], presented with [initial symptoms/events]. Current volume status: [JVP, lung sounds, edema]; latest K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value]. On GDMT: [list ACE-I/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i status]." A: "I'm concerned about [specific change — worsening dyspnea, hypotension, new arrhythmia, weight gain >2 lbs/day, altered mental status, syncope]. Vital signs: HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [%]. Telemetry shows [rhythm if applicable]." R: "I need [orders for diuretics, medication adjustment, urgent labs, ECG, echocardiography, EP consultation, or escalation to on-call fellow/attending]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable outpatient or elective admission for workup Cardiologist or HF specialist (daytime)
Acute HF decompensation with hypotension, pulmonary edema On-call cardiology fellow or attending; may need ICU consideration
Sustained VT or syncope (arrhythmia-predominant) On-call EP fellow/attending; consider ACLS protocols for unstable VT (see emergency pathway)
Peripartum cardiomyopathy presentation OB/GYN + cardiology co-management; consider ICU/high-risk obstetric unit
Suspected myocarditis (fever, fulminant presentation) Cardiology + Infectious Disease ± rheumatology
Chemotherapy-induced cardiomyopathy Cardio-oncology specialist; primary oncology team
Genetic DCM with family screening needed Genetic counseling service; cardiology for family echo/ECG
Preop VAD/transplant workup complications VAD or transplant surgery team
Cardiogenic shock or need for inotropic support Cardiology fellow/attending; consider ICU transfer; evaluate LVAD/transplant urgency

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Sections marked are collapsible by default.

7.1 Diagnostic workup: How do we confirm DCM and determine etiology? Echocardiography (first-line):
  • Confirms LV dilation (LVEDD >60 mm or >2.7 m/m² indexed), systolic dysfunction (LVEF ≤40%)
  • Assesses wall motion pattern (global vs. regional; regional pattern may suggest ischemic etiology)
  • Rules out significant valvular disease, pericardial disease, HCM, restrictive CMP
  • Evaluates right ventricle, atrial size, intracardiac thrombus 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG):
  • Screens for arrhythmia (AF, VT, frequent PVCs)
  • Left bundle branch block (LBBB) present in ~30% of HFrEF; indicates worse prognosis and suggests CRT candidacy
  • LMNA mutations may show PR prolongation, AV block, conduction abnormalities
  • TTN mutations may show no specific pattern
  • Low voltage may suggest infiltrative disease (amyloid) Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE):
  • Critical for etiology determination; should be obtained in all new DCM unless contraindicated
  • Midwall LGE pattern: Suggests genetic (LMNA, TTN, MYBPC3) or inflammatory (myocarditis, sarcoid) etiology
  • Subendocardial or transmural LGE: Suggests ischemic cardiomyopathy pattern (even if coronary angiography shows no significant stenosis, raises concern for microvascular ischemia)
  • Patchy inflammatory enhancement: Acute or recovering myocarditis (viral or autoimmune)
  • Infiltrative pattern: Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis, hemochromatosis, fabry disease
  • Normal LGE: Idiopathic DCM (but may still harbor genetic variant; does not rule out genetic etiology)
  • Iron quantification: If hemochromatosis suspected Biomarkers:
  • BNP or NT-proBNP: Elevated in proportion to LV dysfunction; prognostic marker; serial trending guides GDMT escalation
  • Troponin: May be elevated in myocarditis, cardiomyopathy with ongoing myocardial injury; indicates worse prognosis
  • CBC: Anemia contributes to decreased oxygen delivery; optimize Hgb if chronic anemia
  • Renal function (Cr, eGFR): Baseline; guides GDMT dose and renal congestion assessment
  • Electrolytes: K⁺, Mg²⁺ critical for arrhythmia risk and GDMT tolerance Coronary angiography:
  • Mandatory in most patients to rule out coronary artery disease (CAD) as etiology
  • Indicated if: CAD risk factors (age >40, smoking, diabetes, hypertension, family hx of premature CAD), ischemic-appearing wall motion on echo, abnormal stress test, clinical suspicion
  • ≥70% stenosis in major epicardial vessel → reclassify to ischemic cardiomyopathy
  • Consider if CMR shows subendocardial LGE pattern (raises suspicion for ischemia even with angiographically silent CAD) Genetic testing (DCM gene panel):
  • Increasingly standard of care; offered if any of the following:
  • Familial DCM (first-degree relative with DCM, HF, or unexplained SCD)
  • Age <50 years at presentation
  • LVEDD >60 mm
  • Strong personal or family hx of sudden cardiac death
  • Idiopathic DCM (even without family hx; ~30–40% yield)
  • Common genes: TTN (largest cohort), LMNA, MYBPC3, MYH7, TNNT2, TNNC1, DSP, ACTC1, VCL, LAMA4, and ~50–100 others
  • Panel size and gene selection varies by lab and institutional protocol
  • Yield: ~20–35% in idiopathic DCM; ~40–50% in familial DCM
  • Results guide family screening, prognostic counseling (LMNA = high arrhythmia risk), and device planning Family history and cascade screening:
  • Obtain detailed pedigree: first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) with HF, arrhythmia, unexplained SCD, syncope
  • If genetic variant identified in proband: first-degree relatives offered baseline echo + ECG
  • Periodic follow-up echo/ECG (every 1–2 years or sooner if genetic variant identified) to detect early LV dysfunction
  • Early GDMT in asymptomatic carriers with LV dilation can prevent progression Infectious serology and biomarkers (if myocarditis suspected):
  • Viral panel: Enterovirus, adenovirus, parvovirus B19, influenza, HIV, others per clinical suspicion
  • Autoimmune serology: Anti-cardiac myosin, anti-troponin (rarely ordered; low specificity)
  • Inflammatory markers: CRP, ESR (elevated in acute myocarditis)
  • Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB): Gold standard for myocarditis diagnosis; rarely performed but may be pursued if fulminant presentation, arrhythmias out of proportion to EF, or atypical disease course. EMB findings (viral genome, inflammatory infiltrate, giant cells) guide prognosis and immunosuppression decisions. Toxin and medication history:
  • Alcohol consumption: Quantify drinks/day, duration; assess for withdrawal risk if hospitalized
  • Cocaine, amphetamines, other stimulants: Timing of last use; assess risk of recurrence
  • Chemotherapy exposure: Agent, cumulative dose, timing relative to HF presentation
  • Medications: NSAIDs (worsen HF), some antiarrhythmics, corticosteroids (long-term)
  • Environmental toxins: Lead, cobalt (rare) Additional testing by suspected etiology:
  • Hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism: TSH, free T4 (thyroid-related CMP is reversible with treatment)
  • Hemochromatosis: Serum iron, ferritin, transferrin saturation, HFE genetic testing
  • Sarcoidosis: ACE level, calcium, chest CXR, PET scan, serum angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level
  • Amyloidosis: Serum and urine free light chains, biopsy (cardiac, abdominal fat pad, or bone marrow), genetic testing for TTR mutations, SAP nuclear scintigraphy ---
7.2 LMNA (lamin A/C) mutations: Why are they so important? Genetics and prevalence:
  • Autosomal dominant inheritance (can be de novo)
  • Accounts for ~8–10% of familial DCM; rare in sporadic idiopathic DCM unless age <50 or strong arrhythmia hx
  • Gene encodes nuclear lamins (structural proteins of nuclear envelope)
  • Loss of function → abnormal nuclear mechanics → cardiomyocyte death Clinical phenotype — aggressive course:
  • Earlier onset (mean age ~40–50 years, often younger than TTN)
  • Rapid EF decline; often reaches LVEF <30% within 5–10 years of diagnosis
  • High arrhythmia risk: ~50% of carriers develop sustained VT or VF by age 50
  • Conduction system disease common: PR prolongation, AV block, bradycardia requiring pacemaker
  • Atrial fibrillation early and persistent (difficult to rhythm-control)
  • Sudden cardiac death risk high even with mild EF reduction Management implications:
  • Lower ICD threshold: Standard recommendation LVEF ≤35% does NOT apply; consider ICD at LVEF <30% or even <35% given high VT/VF risk and conduction disease
  • Early EP consultation: Baseline EP study, Holter monitoring, frequent follow-up
  • Frequent monitoring: Echo every 6–12 months or more frequently if EF declining
  • Beta-blocker essential: May slow progression; bradycardia from conduction disease often requires pacemaker
  • Lifestyle restrictions: Avoid strenuous activity, competitive sports; increased SCD risk during exertion
  • Genetic counseling: Inheritance autosomal dominant; 50% of first-degree relatives carry mutation Family screening in LMNA:
  • Very high penetrance; most carriers develop phenotype by adulthood
  • First-degree relatives: genetic testing offered; if positive, baseline echo + ECG + EP studies
  • Children of affected carriers: Consider earlier baseline ECG/echo (may have early conduction abnormalities or subtle EF reduction) ---
7.3 Peripartum cardiomyopathy: Unique presentation and variable recovery Definition and timing:
  • New-onset cardiomyopathy in third trimester or first 1–5 months postpartum
  • Thought to involve: pregnancy-related hemodynamic stress, prolactin overexpression (promotes 16 kDa prolactin fragment with anti-angiogenic/pro-apoptotic effects), autoimmune activation, viral myocarditis Epidemiology:
  • Incidence: ~1 in 1,500–4,000 live births (higher in some populations: African descent, multiparity, older maternal age, preeclampsia)
  • May be misdiagnosed as postpartum cardiomyopathy vs. hypertensive emergency vs. sepsis Presentation:
  • Dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, fatigue, palpitations in late pregnancy or early postpartum period
  • May present as fulminant cardiogenic shock or gradual decompensation
  • Often preceded by preeclampsia or gestational hypertension (risk factor) Diagnostic workup:
  • Echocardiography: Confirm LV dilation, global hypokinesis, LVEF usually 20–40%
  • CMR: May show myocarditis pattern (inflammatory enhancement) or midwall LGE
  • Rule out acute coronary syndrome (troponin, ECG, angiography if indicated)
  • Biomarkers: BNP/NT-proBNP usually markedly elevated Management — PEACE protocol + GDMT:
  • PEACE trial findings: Bromocriptine + standard GDMT improved EF recovery and reduced adverse outcomes vs. GDMT alone in PPCM
  • Bromocriptine (dopamine agonist, prolactin inhibitor): Dose 2.5 mg daily × 2 weeks, then 2.5 mg BID × ~6 months
  • Mechanism: Blocks 16 kDa prolactin fragment; reduces myocardial apoptosis, inflammation
  • Standard GDMT: ACE-I/ARB, beta-blocker, diuretics; aldosterone antagonist and SGLT2i as tolerated
  • Breastfeeding: Bromocriptine contraindicated; if nursing desired, may need to delay bromocriptine; discuss with OB/cardiology
  • Anticoagulation: If LVEF <20% or LVT documented; balance with postpartum hemorrhage risk (shared decision-making with OB)
  • Immunosuppression: Not routinely recommended; reserved for biopsy-proven myocarditis with fulminant course Recovery trajectory:
  • Variable: Some recover LVEF to normal or near-normal within 6–12 months; others have persistent dysfunction
  • Prognostic factors: Worse outcome if older age, multiparity, delayed presentation, LVEF <25%, BMI >30, hypertension
  • Serial echo every 3–6 months to document recovery
  • Majority have substantial improvement; ~50% achieve LVEF >50% by 1 year Critical counseling: Future pregnancies.
  • Maternal mortality in repeat pregnancy: 40–50% if EF remains <50%
  • If EF recovered to >50%: Still high-risk; close cardiology + OB co-management essential; serial echo during pregnancy; many advise against further pregnancy regardless of EF recovery
  • Strict contraception counseling unless pregnancy is attempted with specialist co-management at high-risk pregnancy center
  • Long-acting reversible contraception (IUD, implant) preferred ---
7.4 Chemotherapy-induced cardiomyopathy: Cardio-oncology considerations Agents and mechanisms:
  • Anthracyclines (doxorubicin, daunorubicin, idarubicin): Most cardiotoxic; dose-dependent; mechanism = oxidative stress, free radical generation, topoisomerase 2 inhibition; can cause acute myocarditis or chronic dose-dependent cardiomyopathy
  • Trastuzumab (HER2 inhibitor): Off-target HER2 inhibition of cardiac myocytes; usually reversible; dose-dependent
  • Checkpoint inhibitors (anti-PD-1/PD-L1, anti-CTLA-4): Immune-mediated myocarditis; rare but fulminant; high mortality if not recognized/treated
  • Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (sunitinib, sorafenib): VEGFR inhibition; hypertension + LV dysfunction; chronic cardiomyopathy risk
  • 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU): Coronary vasospasm, myocarditis, HF possible Risk stratification:
  • Cumulative dose (anthracyclines: >300 mg/m² = high risk)
  • Baseline LVEF, prior cardiac disease, age >60, female sex, concurrent hypertension, diabetes
  • Mediastinal radiation history (compounds cardiotoxicity) Monitoring strategy:
  • Baseline: LVEF (echo or MUGA), troponin, BNP before initiating cardiotoxic agent
  • During chemotherapy: Serial LVEF every 1–3 cycles or at ~50% of cumulative dose; troponin/BNP monitoring (rising troponin predicts EF drop)
  • Post-chemotherapy: Continue monitoring for 5–10 years; late cardiotoxicity can occur months to years after treatment Early detection and cardioprotection:
  • EF drop >10% or absolute LVEF <50% warrants hold/dose reduction of chemotherapy ± GDMT initiation
  • Cardioprotection with beta-blockers ± ACE-I: May prevent or mitigate cardiotoxicity in high-risk patients; consider starting ACE-I + beta-blocker before or early during chemotherapy
  • Dexrazoxane (iron chelator): May reduce anthracycline cardiotoxicity but not widely used due to secondary malignancy risk
  • Newer agents (tafamidis, finerenone) being studied Management of established cardio-oncology cardiomyopathy:
  • Standard GDMT: ACE-I/ARNI, beta-blocker, aldosterone antagonist, SGLT2i
  • Decision to hold/modify/restart chemotherapy:
  • Anthracyclines: Hold if EF drops >10%; may restart at lower dose if EF improves; assess cumulative dose
  • Trastuzumab: Hold for HF management; can often resume once EF recovers to >50% (trastuzumab cardiotoxicity often reversible)
  • Checkpoint inhibitors: High-risk for fulminant myocarditis; if suspected, urgent cardiology consult; may require high-dose corticosteroids ± immunosuppression; consider temporary hold pending evaluation
  • Coordinate with primary oncology team: cancer control vs. cardiac risk balance Prognosis:
  • Anthracycline: Variable; dose-dependent; may stabilize or recover EF with GDMT; late dysfunction possible
  • Trastuzumab: Often reversible; good prognosis if caught early
  • Checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis: High mortality if fulminant; improve with immunosuppression
  • Overall: Survivors of cancer with therapy-induced cardiomyopathy have increased long-term mortality vs. cancer-free HF population ---
7.5 Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (TIC): The reversible form Definition:
  • LV dilation + systolic dysfunction caused by incessant or frequent tachycardia
  • Distinct feature: EF substantially improves or normalizes with rate/rhythm control
  • Mechanism: Chronic rapid rate → shortened diastolic filling time → inadequate ventricular recovery → progressive LV dilation and dysfunction Common culprits:
  • Atrial fibrillation (uncontrolled rapid ventricular response)
  • Atrial flutter with rapid AV conduction
  • Incessant supraventricular tachycardia (SVT; AVNRT, AVRT)
  • Frequent premature ventricular contractions (PVCs; rare; usually if >20% of beats)
  • Sinus tachycardia from chronic illness (hyperthyroidism, anemia, sepsis, etc.) Clinical presentation:
  • May present acutely or insidiously; often misdiagnosed as idiopathic DCM initially
  • Dyspnea, fatigue, palpitations, syncope
  • Echocardiogram shows dilated LV with reduced EF; may have regional wall motion abnormality (apical ballooning if frequent PVCs) Diagnostic clues:
  • Tachycardia present during workup (HR often >100 at rest, sometimes much higher)
  • History of palpitations, arrhythmia events
  • Troponin may be mildly elevated (from incessant tachycardia)
  • CMR: Usually normal (no LGE); rules out scar-based causes
  • Holter/event monitor: Captures arrhythmia burden Management — rate or rhythm control:
  • Rate control approach: Beta-blocker or non-DHP calcium channel blocker to target HR <80–90 at rest (goal: lower rate = better EF recovery potential)
  • IV diltiazem or verapamil if acute; transition to PO maintenance
  • Beta-blockers (metoprolol, carvedilol) preferred for long-term
  • Monitor: BP, HR, AV conduction
  • Rhythm control approach: Preferred for SVT; may use antiarrhythmic (amiodarone) or catheter ablation (definitive for SVT, AVNRT, AVRT with accessory pathway)
  • Ablation particularly effective and curative for accessory pathway-mediated tachycardia
  • High success rate; low recurrence if performed by experienced operator
  • If atrial fibrillation: Rate control first-line (goal HR <100 at rest); may escalate to rhythm control if rate control inadequate
  • GDMT: May initiate if severe dysfunction, but priority is arrhythmia control; beta-blocker serves dual purpose Recovery trajectory:
  • Excellent prognosis if arrhythmia controlled
  • EF often improves within weeks to months of effective rate/rhythm control
  • Many achieve normal or near-normal EF once HR normalized
  • Serial echo every 3–6 months to document recovery
  • Some patients may not need long-term GDMT if EF fully recovers; reevaluate after 6–12 months Key teaching point:
  • TIC is one of the few DCM phenotypes that are truly reversible
  • Early recognition (history of tachycardia, arrhythmia on monitor, high resting HR) and aggressive rate/rhythm control = excellent outcomes
  • Do not assume idiopathic DCM without exploring TIC etiology ---

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear, re-escalate to care team.

  • Worsening dyspnea at rest or increasing orthopnea — pulmonary edema progression; may need diuretic escalation or ICU transfer for inotropic support
  • Acute hypotension (drop >20 mmHg systolic from baseline) — cardiogenic shock, medication side effect, arrhythmia; assess perfusion (mental status, urine output, lactate); may need ICU, inotropes, or mechanical support consideration
  • New or worsening arrhythmia: New-onset atrial fibrillation with RVR, sustained VT, frequent PVCs — escalate to EP if VT; AF may need rate control or rhythm control adjustment
  • Syncope or presyncope — may indicate VT, profound bradycardia, or hemodynamic decompensation; obtain ECG, troponin; consider telemetry escalation
  • Altered mental status — hypoxia, hypotension, hypercarbia, medication effect (check ammonia if liver disease); obtain ABG if not recent
  • Acute kidney injury (rising creatinine, falling urine output) — cardiorenal syndrome; may reflect inadequate perfusion; reassess diuretics, fluids, medications; monitor K⁺ closely
  • Hyperkalemia (K⁺ >5.5) — ACE-I/ARB, aldosterone antagonist toxicity; may need medication hold, glucose + insulin, loop diuretics; high arrhythmia risk
  • Hypotension + hypoxia + rising JVP (backward + forward failure) — cardiogenic shock; escalate to attending/fellow; may need ICU, inotropes, mechanical support (LVAD, ECMO)
  • New systolic murmur or friction rub — suggests acute papillary muscle rupture or pericarditis (rare in DCM); urgent echo, cardiology consult
  • Rapid weight gain (>2–3 lbs/day) — decompensation; diuretic escalation, sodium/fluid restriction reinforcement
  • Acute neurologic deficit (stroke symptoms) — may indicate LV thrombus embolism or secondary stroke in AF; stroke code; urgent imaging (CT/MRI); anticoagulation discussion
  • Chest pain — may indicate ischemia, myocarditis, pericarditis, or PE; obtain ECG, troponin, CXR; if unstable, ICU evaluation
  • Fever + new murmur + elevated WBC — concern for infective endocarditis (if recent line placement, drug use, or bacteremia); blood cultures, echo (TEE if transthoracic inconclusive)
  • Hematuria, pulmonary edema, acute pulmonary embolism signs — if on anticoagulation, bleeding complication; if not anticoagulated, thromboembolism (LVT, AF emboli); imaging, labs, coagulation studies
  • Patient reports rapid weight gain, new orthopnea, or increased fatigue — symptom burden escalation; patient self-report is high-yield early warning

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. 30–40% of "idiopathic" DCM is genetic. TTN (titin) and LMNA (lamin A/C) are the most common genetic causes; ~20–35% of idiopathic DCM cases will have an identifiable pathogenic variant on genetic panel. Never assume idiopathic = non-genetic. Offer genetic testing to all idiopathic DCM patients, especially if LVEDD >60 mm, age <50, or family hx of HF/sudden death.

  2. Cascade family screening is non-negotiable. If genetic variant identified in proband, first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) should be offered baseline echo + ECG, then periodic follow-up (every 1–2 years). Early GDMT in asymptomatic mutation carriers with LV dilation can prevent progression and sudden death. Document cascade screening plan in chart.

  3. LMNA mutations = aggressive course, high arrhythmia risk, lower ICD threshold. ~50% of LMNA carriers develop VT/VF by age 50. Do not wait for LVEF ≤35%; consider ICD at LVEF <30% or even <35% with LMNA. Conduction disease common; pacemaker may be needed. Early EP involvement critical.

  4. Alcoholic cardiomyopathy may partially or fully recover with strict abstinence. This is one of the few reversible DCM forms. Emphasize abstinence as therapy, not lifestyle suggestion. Recovery can take weeks to months. Addiction medicine, social work, and behavioral health support essential; do not discharge without these resources.

  5. Peripartum cardiomyopathy: Bromocriptine + GDMT improves outcomes; future pregnancy counseling is critical. PEACE trial showed bromocriptine (prolactin antagonist) improves EF recovery vs. GDMT alone. EF recovery is variable and may be substantial.

    BUT: Future pregnancies carry 40–50% maternal mortality risk if EF remains depressed. Strict contraception counseling mandatory; genetic counseling important if LMNA or familial form identified.

  6. CMR with LGE pattern tells the etiology. Midwall LGE = genetic/inflammatory; subendocardial = ischemic (even if coronary angiography negative, raises concern for microvascular disease); patchy inflammatory = myocarditis; infiltrative = amyloid/sarcoid/hemochromatosis; normal = idiopathic but may still be genetic. Never skip CMR in new DCM workup.

  7. Chemotherapy-induced cardiomyopathy: Early detection + GDMT + dose reduction/modification can prevent irreversible damage. Anthracyclines are dose-dependent; EF drop >10% or absolute LVEF <50% warrants hold/modification. Trastuzumab cardiotoxicity is often reversible; can resume after EF recovery. Checkpoint inhibitor myocarditis is rare but fulminant; requires high-dose steroids. Cardio-oncology consult essential; close oncology–cardiology partnership needed.

  8. Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (TIC) is reversible. Do not label as "idiopathic DCM" without exploring arrhythmia etiology (AF, SVT, frequent PVCs). EF often normalizes with rate or rhythm control. Catheter ablation for SVT is curative. Excellent prognosis if arrhythmia controlled early.

  9. Myocarditis: Expect EF recovery over 3–6 months with supportive care + GDMT. Anti-inflammatory therapy (steroids, immunosuppression) remains controversial and not routine unless fulminant presentation or biopsy-confirmed giant cell myocarditis. Serial echo every 3–6 months; most recover substantially. Endomyocardial biopsy may guide prognosis and inform immunosuppression decisions.

  10. Genetic counseling is not optional. If genetic variant identified or familial DCM suspected, offer genetics consultation. Helps with inheritance pattern education, risk stratification, family screening logistics, reproduction planning (especially peripartum/female carriers).

  11. DCM is not automatically irreversible transplant candidacy. Viral myocarditis, alcoholic CMP, peripartum CMP, tachycardia-induced, and chemotherapy-related forms may recover. Give these time to improve with targeted treatment before listing for transplant. Genetic and truly idiopathic forms rarely improve and are appropriate for transplant.

  12. Pregnancy in DCM is high-risk; peripartum CMP is a known entity. Women with prior DCM have 40–50% mortality in future pregnancies if EF remains depressed. Strict contraception counseling mandatory. If pregnancy attempted despite risk, close cardiology + obstetrics co-management at a specialized high-risk pregnancy center is essential. Preconception discussion should include genetics, medication safety (ACE-I teratogenic; avoid), and risk stratification.

  13. LV thrombus risk high in severe DCM (LVEF <20%). Dilated cavity + reduced flow + regional wall motion abnormality = prothrombotic state. Echocardiography and/or CMR should assess for thrombus. If present, anticoagulation mandatory. If LVEF <20% without visible thrombus, anticoagulation discussion ongoing (some advocate universal AC; others risk-stratify based on additional factors like AF, prior VTE).

  14. Do not miss reversible or partially reversible etiologies. Myocarditis (viral, autoimmune), tachycardia-induced CMP, thyroid dysfunction, hemochromatosis, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis — all can present as DCM. Comprehensive workup (CMR, TSH, iron studies, serology, EP assessment) essential before assuming "idiopathic." Some reversible etiologies have specific, curative treatments (e.g., ablation for TIC, iron chelation for hemochromatosis, immunosuppression for giant cell myocarditis).

  15. Early ICD discussion warranted in LMNA, peripartum (if very low EF), and other high-arrhythmia-risk forms. Standard threshold LVEF ≤35% may miss high-risk patients. LMNA carriers, myocarditis with giant cells, cardiac sarcoidosis, and others benefit from lower ICD threshold or closer arrhythmia surveillance (Holter, event monitor, EP studies).

cards.title: Decompensated Heart Failure — Pre-Op Optimization (Medical Admit)
cards.quickAnswer: Admitted with acute decompensated heart failure (pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, or refractory congestion) requiring pre-operative medical optimization. Euvolemia first: IV loop diuretics (furosemide 2× home dose or 10 mg/h drip) ± metolazone 2.5 mg daily (target 1–2 L/day negative balance); daily weights, strict I/O, monitor urine sodium and diuretic response. Once euvolemic (rales cleared, JVP ≤ 4 cm, orthopnea resolved): initiate all four GDMT pillars in parallel (ARNi/ACE-I, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i); escalate every 2 weeks toward target doses. Parallel workup: echo, coronary angiography + RHC for hemodynamics and pulmonary HTN reversibility assessment, CPET if candidate for LVAD/transplant. Surgical fork: viable CAD → CABG; severe AS → AVR/TAVR; severe functional MR → repair/replacement; refractory decompensation + pulmonary HTN → LVAD bridge/transplant eval. Delay elective surgery until euvolemic + stable renal function. High-risk: IABP/Impella bridge if cardiogenic shock. LOS: 5–14+ days depending on diuresis response and surgical urgency. Nursing focus: daily weights, I/O strictness, K+/Mg/Cr trending, telemetry for new AF, multidisciplinary rounds.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

Definition:

  • Acute heart failure decompensation (systemic or pulmonary congestion, cardiogenic shock, or both) occurring in a patient who requires pre-operative medical optimization before planned cardiac surgery.
  • The clinical trajectory spans admission through medical stabilization, diagnostic workup, GDMT escalation, surgical decision-making, and discharge or operative intervention.

Epidemiology & who this applies to:

  • HFrEF (EF typically ≤ 35%) or HFpEF with new or worsening symptoms (dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary edema, hypotension, altered mental status, elevated lactate)
  • May present with new-onset cardiogenic shock (hypotension + poor perfusion + pulmonary congestion) or chronic HF exacerbation
  • Underlying etiology often ischemic cardiomyopathy (CAD candidate for CABG), valvular disease (AS, MR, AI), idiopathic DCM, or acute coronary syndrome
  • Expected LOS: 5–7 days uncomplicated; 10–14+ days if refractory diuresis, shock, or major workup delays
  • Disposition: discharge home with close follow-up (if surgery deferred), direct to OR (if surgical candidacy confirmed), or bridge facility (if inotrope support, LVAD, or transplant workup ongoing)

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Expand for pathophysiology detail Why acute decompensation occurs: The transition from compensated to acute decompensated HF reflects loss of equilibrium between cardiac output and systemic/pulmonary demand, usually triggered by:
  • Afterload increase (HTN crisis, new-onset AF with RVR)
  • Preload increase (fluid/salt overload, renal dysfunction)
  • Myocardial ischemia (ACS, demand mismatch from tachycardia)
  • Arrhythmia (AF, VT, bradycardia from high-degree AV block)
  • Infection (pneumonia, UTI, sepsis raising cardiac demand)
  • Anemia (demand for higher CO to maintain oxygen delivery)
  • Iatrogenic (NSAID use, beta-blocker withdrawal, positive inotrope cessation, excessive IV fluids) Hemodynamic profiles (Forrester/Stevenson):
    • Warm & dry: normal CO, normal filling pressures → stable; optimize GDMT
    • Warm & wet: normal CO, elevated PCWP/JVP → congestion primary; diuresis + vasodilation
    • Cold & wet: low CO + elevated PCWP → cardiogenic shock; inotrope ± mechanical support
    • Cold & dry: low CO, normal PCWP → inadequate preload or severe shock; fluid challenge, inotrope, mechanical support Why euvolemia must precede GDMT escalation: Beta-blockers worsen hemodynamics in fluid-overloaded patients (negative inotropic effect); ACE-I/ARB/MRA reduce renal perfusion if intravascular volume depleted. Diuresis first restores optimal LV operating point on the Frank-Starling curve, allowing GDMT to lower SVR and improve EF without triggering prerenal azotemia or hypotension.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation (Clinical Context)
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — observable signs and timing.

Admission presentation:

  • Pulmonary edema: orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, rales on lung exam, elevated JVP, S3 gallop, elevated BNP (> 400 pg/mL)
  • Cardiogenic shock: hypotension (SBP < 90 mmHg), altered mental status, oliguria (UOP < 200 mL/8 h), elevated lactate (> 2 mmol/L), cool extremities, poor capillary refill
  • Systemic congestion: peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, elevated JVP, ascites, weight gain (acute swelling 3–5 lbs in days)
  • New or worsening dyspnea on exertion, often preceded by upper respiratory infection, MI, hypertensive crisis, or medication non-adherence

Timing to surgical decision:

  • Days 1–3: stabilization, diagnosis, initiate diuresis
  • Days 4–7: diuresis progression, parallel workup (cath, echo, RHC)
  • Days 8–14: GDMT optimization, surgical decision point (CABG, valve, LVAD, transplant, or medical management)
  • Urgent cases (cardiogenic shock, acute severe MR, ischemic VSD): surgical decision may come POD 1–2

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. Target: 2–5 minutes at bedside.

Vital signs & hemodynamics:

  • Heart rate (goal 60–100 euvolemic; tachycardia = inadequate preload reduction or ischemia)
  • Blood pressure (SBP goal ≥ 90 for perfusion; accept lower if euvolemic + asymptomatic)
  • Respiratory rate (tachypnea = pulmonary congestion or metabolic acidosis)
  • Oxygen saturation (goal > 92% on RA; hypoxemia may indicate pulmonary edema or comorbid lung disease)
  • Temperature (fever = infection driver of decompensation)

Volume status:

  • Daily weight (loss 1–2 lb/day indicates successful diuresis; +2 lb = escalate)
  • Intake & output (target 1–2 L/day negative balance; document all IV fluids, oral intake, urine, NG, drains)
  • Lung exam (auscultate bases; rales = congestion; clearing = euvolemia)
  • JVP (normal ≤ 4 cm H₂O; elevation suggests inadequate diuresis or RV dysfunction)
  • Peripheral edema (grade location, severity; should resolve with euvolemia)
  • Orthopnea, PND (should resolve as pulmonary edema improves)

Cardiac exam:

  • Apical impulse (displaced suggests dilated LV)
  • S3 gallop (present in HF; may persist despite euvolemia if low EF)
  • Murmur (new holosystolic = MR; crescendo-decrescendo = AS; high-pitched blowing = AR)
  • Thrill (palpable vibration = significant stenosis or regurgitation)

Renal & perfusion status:

  • Urine color, volume, frequency (adequate output = renal perfusion; dark/scanty = dehydration concern or worsening renal failure)
  • Capillary refill (< 2 sec normal; > 2 sec = inadequate perfusion)
  • Skin temperature, color (cool extremities = low CO; flushed = sepsis or fever)
  • Altered mental status (can indicate hypoxemia, hyperammonemia from hepatic congestion, or end-stage HF)

Recent labs & trends:

  • K+ (goal 4.0–5.5 on GDMT; hypokalemia worsens arrhythmia risk; hyperkalemia risks conduction block)
  • Creatinine (expect modest rise 5–10% during diuresis from prerenal component; > 30% rise or > 2.5 absolute = AKI concern)
  • BUN (elevated BUN/Cr ratio > 20:1 suggests prerenal; < 10:1 suggests renal parenchymal disease)
  • Magnesium (goal > 1.7 mg/dL; low Mg worsens hypokalemia refractory to supplementation)
  • BNP/NT-proBNP (baseline; should decline with diuresis; persistently elevated despite euvolemia = ongoing ischemia or complication)
  • Lactate (elevated > 2 mmol/L indicates inadequate tissue perfusion; should normalize with improved CO)
  • Troponin, CBC, liver function tests, TSH (assess for ACS, anemia, hepatic congestion, hypothyroidism)
  • Hemoglobin (anemia worsens dyspnea + increases CO demand)

Medication adherence & MAR review:

  • Home diuretic dose + compliance
  • Prior GDMT (was patient on all four pillars? At what doses?)
  • Beta-blocker timing (when last dose, why held if applicable)
  • ACE-I/ARB/MRA (when last dose, renal function at initiation)
  • Recent medication changes or discontinuations

Diagnostic imaging & testing status:

  • Echo performed (EF, chamber sizes, wall motion, RV function, valvular disease, pericardial effusion)?
  • Coronary angiography (scheduled, pending, completed)?
  • Right heart catheterization (assess hemodynamics + pulmonary HTN reversibility)?
  • CPET status (if transplant/LVAD candidate)?
  • Chest X-ray impression (pulmonary edema, cardiomegaly, other pathology)
  • 12-lead ECG (ischemia, arrhythmia, prior MI pattern)

sections.heading: 5A. Euvolemia — IV Diuretics & Daily Monitoring
sections.bodyHtml:
Immediate diuresis (Days 1–3):

  1. IV furosemide bolus or infusion:

    • Typical starting dose: 2× home oral dose as IV bolus, or continuous infusion 10 mg/h
    • Example: if home dose 80 mg daily PO → start 160 mg IV q4–6h or 10 mg/h infusion
    • Titrate based on urine output; goal 1–2 L/day negative balance

  2. Diuretic resistance protocol (if minimal response after 24 h):

    • Add metolazone 2.5 mg PO daily or 30 minutes before next IV loop dose
    • Metolazone blocks proximal + distal tubules (synergistic with loop diuretics)
    • Escalate IV furosemide frequency (q2–4h instead of q6h) if still inadequate
    • Avoid NSAIDs (reduce renal perfusion, promote fluid retention)
    • Optimize GDMT in parallel (improve CO, reduce RAAS activation)
    • Consider RV dysfunction, occult ischemia, or inotrope need if no response

  3. Daily monitoring during diuresis:

    • Daily weights (same time, same scale, before breakfast): loss 1–2 lb/day = success; +2 lb = flag escalation
    • Strict I/O tallying: record all IV fluids (boluses, drips, oral fluids, tube feeds), all outputs (urine, NG, drains); calculate net balance daily
    • K+ & Mg trending: loop + thiazide diuretics deplete; check labs q3 days during active diuresis; supplement if K+ < 4.0 or Mg < 1.7
    • Creatinine monitoring: expect modest rise (5–10%) from prerenal component; accept if BUN/Cr > 20:1; if Cr rises > 30% or absolute > 2.5, hold diuretics, assess for AKI
    • Orthostatic vitals: avoid overshoot hypotension (SBP < 90); measure BP supine and sitting
    • Lung exam each shift: auscultate bases bilaterally; rales = ongoing congestion; clearing = euvolemia progressing
    • JVP trending: goal normal (≤ 4 cm H₂O) when euvolemic; persistent elevation = inadequate diuresis or RV dysfunction

  4. Euvolemia endpoint (typically Days 3–5):

    • Orthopnea resolved
    • Rales cleared from lung bases
    • JVP normal (≤ 4 cm)
    • Peripheral edema resolved or marked improvement
    • Daily weights stable (no daily > 1 lb swing)
    • BNP declining trend (not necessarily normal, but downward trajectory)

sections.heading: 5B. GDMT Optimization — Initiate All Four Pillars Parallel (Once Euvolemic)
sections.bodyHtml:
Timing: Do NOT start beta-blockers or escalate GDMT during acute decompensation. Wait until euvolemic + stable HR + adequate BP.

Table: GDMT Pillars During Titration

Pillar Drug Example Starting Dose Target Dose Titration Interval Monitoring Caution
ARNi / ACE-I Sacubitril/valsartan (Entresto) 49/51 mg BID 97/103 mg BID q2 weeks BP (goal SBP ≥ 90), K+, Cr Hypotension may limit; ACE-I cough common
Lisinopril 2.5 mg daily 10 mg daily q2 weeks K+, Cr, BP Hyperkalemia risk with renal dysfunction
Beta-blocker Carvedilol 3.125 mg BID 25 mg BID q2 weeks HR (goal 60–100), BP, fatigue NO escalation during acute decompensation; continue existing dose
Metoprolol succinate (Toprol-XL) 25 mg daily 190 mg daily q2 weeks HR, BP, fatigue Reduce if hypotension or bradycardia
MRA Spironolactone 12.5–25 mg daily 50 mg daily q2 weeks K+ closely (hold if > 5.5) Hyperkalemia risk; monitor K+ post-initiation + post-titration
Eplerenone 25 mg daily 50 mg daily q2 weeks K+, Cr (monitor Cr-eplerenone interaction) Renal function dependent
SGLT2i Dapagliflozin (Farxiga) 10 mg daily 10 mg daily no titration Urine glucose/ketones, volume status, DKA risk Hold 3–5 days pre-op (euglycemic DKA risk); no dose adjustment needed
Empagliflozin (Jardiance) 10 mg daily 10 mg daily no titration Urine glucose/ketones, volume status, DKA risk Hold 3–5 days pre-op; benefit independent of diabetes

Initiation protocol (all four in parallel):

  1. ARNi or ACE-I:

    • Start low (Entresto 49/51 mg BID or lisinopril 2.5 mg daily)
    • Monitor BP 1–2 h post-first dose (expect transient drop; measure again supine if symptomatic)
    • Escalate every 2 weeks toward target if SBP ≥ 90 and K+ < 5.5
    • Watch for persistent cough (ACE-I side effect; switch to ARNi or ARB if intolerable)

  2. Beta-blocker (only if euvolemic):

    • Start low (carvedilol 3.125 mg BID or metoprolol 25 mg daily)
    • DO NOT escalate during acute decompensation — negative inotropic effect worsens hemodynamics when fluid-overloaded
    • Once euvolemic + stable, escalate every 2 weeks
    • Goal resting HR 60–100; accept HR 50–60 if asymptomatic
    • Hold if SBP < 85 persistently or HR < 50

  3. MRA (spironolactone or eplerenone):

    • Start spironolactone 12.5–25 mg daily
    • Monitor K+ closely: check baseline, 3–7 days post-initiation, post-titration
    • Hold if K+ > 5.5; recheck in 5 days before restarting
    • Escalate by 12.5–25 mg every 2 weeks toward 50 mg daily if K+ tolerates

  4. SGLT2 inhibitor:

    • Start dapagliflozin 10 mg daily or empagliflozin 10 mg daily immediately
    • No dose titration needed; benefit independent of diabetes
    • Monitor for euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (rare but serious): hold 3–5 days pre-op in diabetic patients
    • Continue in non-diabetic HF patients (SGLT2i reduces hospitalizations regardless of glucose control)

BP and symptom monitoring during GDMT:

  • Measure BP daily during first 2 weeks, then weekly
  • Accept SBP 85–90 mmHg if euvolemic + asymptomatic + perfusing (e.g., normal lactate, urine output)
  • Do NOT reduce GDMT for mild hypotension; reduce diuretics instead
  • Watch for dizziness, syncope (orthostasis); resolve with diuretic reduction, not GDMT cessation

sections.heading: 5C. Rhythm Management — AF with RVR & Anticoagulation
sections.bodyHtml:
Atrial fibrillation post-admission (common, especially post-op or when recovering):

  1. New AF recognition:

    • Telemetry alarm: irregular rhythm, HR often > 110
    • Palpitations, chest discomfort, dyspnea, lightheadedness
    • Apical–radial pulse deficit on exam

  2. Immediate actions if AF with RVR (HR > 120):

    • Obtain 12-lead ECG to confirm AF (irregularly irregular, absent P waves)
    • Replace electrolytes: K+ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 (prerequisite for rate control)
    • Address reversible triggers: pain control, oxygen if hypoxic, fluid repletion if dehydrated, treat fever
    • Notify provider for rate vs rhythm plan
    • Continuous telemetry monitoring

  3. Rate control medications (if stable):

    • IV metoprolol 5 mg over 2 min, may repeat q5 min × 3 (avoid if bronchospasm or decompensated HF)
    • IV diltiazem 0.25 mg/kg over 2 min (preferred for COPD; watch for hypotension + bradycardia)
    • Diltiazem infusion 5–15 mg/h (non-DHP CCB; avoid in reduced-EF HF due to negative inotropic effect)
    • Goal HR 60–110 (or 80–110 for acute decompensation)

  4. Rhythm control (amiodarone preferred in HF):

    • IV amiodarone bolus 150 mg over 10 min, may repeat up to 6–8 boluses in 24 h
    • IV amiodarone drip: 1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min × 18 h (total 1 g load in first 24 h)
    • Watch for hypotension (~25% experience drop): anticipate, decrease drip early to 0.5 mg/min rather than chasing hypotension
    • Transition to PO: 400 mg TID until 10 g total load, then 200–400 mg daily maintenance
    • Monitor QTc on amiodarone (hold if > 500 ms; risk of torsades)

  5. Anticoagulation strategy (AF lasting > 48 h):

    • CHA₂DS₂-VASc assessment: score ≥ 2 generally indicates anticoagulation benefit (CHF 1 pt, HTN 1 pt, age ≥ 75 2 pts, DM 1 pt, stroke/TIA 2 pts, vascular disease 1 pt, age 65–74 1 pt, female 1 pt)
    • Post-op timing is complex: balance stroke risk against surgical bleeding risk; coordinate with CT surgery team
    • Home anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC): usually held 3–4 days pre-op, restarted 24–72 h post-op per surgeon preference
    • Bridge heparin: consider if high stroke risk + prolonged AF
    • Do NOT start or hold anticoagulation without CT surgery team input

sections.heading: 5D. Heart Team Decision — High-Risk Stratification & Mechanical Support Consideration
sections.bodyHtml:
Surgical candidacy fork (assessed during Days 8–14 or when cath/RHC results available):

Decision tree:

Finding Likely Intervention
Viable coronary disease (≥ 70% LAD/LCx, ≥ 50% RCA or left main) CABG (off pressors, euvolemic, HR < 100, stable Cr)
Severe AS (AVA < 1 cm², mean gradient > 40 mmHg, symptomatic) AVR or TAVR (depends on surgical risk assessment)
Severe functional MR (reg vol > 45 mL, vena contracta > 6 mm, LV dilation) Mitral valve repair (preferred) or replacement; reassess after GDMT (may improve)
Refractory HF despite max GDMT + pulmonary HTN (PAPsys > 50–60 mmHg with reversibility on RHC iNO/milrinone trial) LVAD bridge to transplant or destination therapy
Cardiogenic shock unresponsive to IV diuretics + mild inotropes Emergent ECMO ± LVAD if transplant/destination candidate; else comfort measures

LVAD eligibility assessment:

  • SCAI Class C–D: recurrent HF hospitalizations despite GDMT, inotrope dependence, cardiogenic shock, bridge-to-transplant intent
  • No irreversible organ dysfunction (severe liver cirrhosis, advanced CKD, stroke, active malignancy, active infection)
  • Age-appropriate, psychosocial stability, compliance capacity (LVAD requires lifelong anticoagulation, driveline care, device monitoring)
  • Frailty assessment (Clinical Frailty Scale): CFS 1–5 acceptable; CFS 6–9 higher perioperative risk

Heart transplant workup (if not LVAD candidate or concurrent):

  • Psychiatry clearance, social work support, financial stability (insurance), immunologic testing
  • May occur in parallel with GDMT optimization (not sequential)

Stable vs Unstable fork in pre-op decompensation:

Stable Decompensation Unstable Decompensation (Cardiogenic Shock)
Signs: euvolemic or mild congestion; SBP ≥ 90; normal mental status; normal lactate; UOP adequate Signs: hypotension (SBP < 90); altered mental status; oliguria (< 200 mL/8 h); elevated lactate (> 2); cool extremities
Management: IV diuretics + GDMT titration; parallel workup; elective surgery timing flexible Management: ICU-level care; inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone) if not improving; IABP ± Impella bridge; emergent ECMO ± LVAD if transplant/destination candidate
Timeline: 1–2 weeks to optimization Timeline: days to hours; surgical decision urgent

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room, POD]." B: "[Patient context: HFrEF EF%, admitted for decompensation, on day X of diuresis]. Current weight [X] lb (trend), vitals [HR, BP, SpO₂]. Daily urine output [X] mL, net balance [X] L negative/positive. Current K+ [X], Cr [X], BNP [X], lactate [X]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Clinical trajectory: e.g., rales clearing, JVP normalizing; or worsening dyspnea, persistent tachycardia, oliguria]. [Recent events: e.g., new AF, hypotension on GDMT, escalation to metolazone]. Current plan: [diuresis ongoing / GDMT initiated / workup scheduled]." R: "[Request: e.g., escalate IV furosemide, initiate metolazone, order labs, notify CT surgery, prepare for DCCV / escalate to ICU / initiate ECMO evaluation]. Recommendation: [e.g., delay surgery until euvolemic, bridge IABP while awaiting workup, consult palliative care]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable diuresis + routine GDMT escalation Cardiology APP / on-call fellow
Worsening dyspnea despite IV diuretics Cardiology + charge nurse; prepare ICU transfer
New AF with RVR Cardiology; prepare DCCV if unstable
Hypotension (SBP < 90) + altered mental status STAT call Cardiology + RRT; prepare ICU / inotropes / IABP
Oliguria despite IV diuretics + rising Cr Cardiology + nephrology; assess for AKI vs cardiorenal syndrome
Unstable cardiogenic shock Code team + ECMO consult if transplant/destination candidate; palliative care if not
High-risk pre-op candidate (pulmonary HTN, low EF) LVAD / transplant center, cardiac surgery team
Recurrent or intractable arrhythmia EP consult; prepare for cardioversion ± device therapy
New neurologic deficit Stroke code + neurology + cardiology

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Subsections below are collapsible in PowerApp.

sections.heading: 7.1 Pre-Op Euvolemia Verification Checklist
sections.bodyHtml:
Before surgical clearance, confirm:

  • Daily weights: stable (no daily > 1 lb swing) for 3 consecutive days; compare to "euvolemic weight" (usually baseline pre-decompensation)
  • JVP: ≤ 4 cm H₂O; no hepatomegaly, ascites, or pedal edema
  • Lung exam: rales cleared bilaterally; no orthopnea, PND, or dyspnea on exertion
  • BNP trend: declining from admission (absolute value matters less than trajectory)
  • Lactate: normal (< 2 mmol/L) indicating adequate tissue perfusion
  • Creatinine: stable or improving; BUN/Cr ratio < 20:1
  • K+, Mg: within goal range (K+ 4.0–5.5, Mg > 1.7)
  • Patient perception: "feels better"; able to lie flat without dyspnea; sleeping through night without orthopnea

sections.heading: 7.2 Beta-Blocker Hold/Reduce During Acute Decompensation vs Continue in Chronic HFrEF
sections.bodyHtml:
The paradox resolved:

  • Acute decompensation + fluid overload: beta-blockers worsen cardiac output (negative inotropic effect) when patient is on wrong side of Frank-Starling curve. Hold or reduce beta-blocker dose until euvolemic.
  • Chronic HFrEF at euvolemic baseline: beta-blockers reduce mortality + hospitalizations. Continue home beta-blocker (do not hold) unless hypotensive or bradycardic.
  • Key distinction: the timing of GDMT escalation depends on volume status, not time spent in ICU.
  • Euvolemic + stable → escalate beta-blocker every 2 weeks
  • Still congested + hypotensive → hold beta-blocker, continue diuresis, then escalate once euvolemic

sections.heading: 7.3 SGLT2 Inhibitor Hold 3–5 Days Pre-Op (Euglycemic DKA Risk)
sections.bodyHtml:
Why hold SGLT2i perioperatively:

  • SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) can trigger euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis (euDKA) in perioperative stress (surgery, illness, medication changes).
  • Euglycemic DKA: metabolic acidosis + elevated lactate + normal glucose (insidious; blood glucose < 250 mg/dL); can be fatal if unrecognized.
  • Protocol: Hold SGLT2i 3–5 days pre-op; restart 3–5 days post-op once patient euvolemic + eating + stable renal function.
  • Non-diabetic HF patients: still get SGLT2i benefit (hospitalizations, mortality reduction); hold perioperatively only.
  • Monitoring: watch for new dyspnea, fruity breath, altered mental status (signs of DKA) in immediate post-op period.

sections.heading: 7.4 AF Rhythm vs Rate Control — TEE-Guided Cardioversion if Indicated
sections.bodyHtml:
Rhythm vs rate control decision logic:

  • Rhythm control preferred for new-onset POAF: most patients convert to sinus rhythm with amiodarone within 24–48 hours, shortening LOS + reducing thrombotic risk.
  • Rate control fallback: if rhythm control fails or contraindicated, target HR 60–110 with IV beta-blocker or non-DHP calcium channel blocker.
  • Direct-current cardioversion (DCCV): first-line for hemodynamically unstable AF. For stable AF, reserved for pharmacologic conversion failure.
  • TEE-guided cardioversion: if AF > 48 h duration or unknown duration, obtain TEE to rule out left atrial thrombus before DCCV (reduces stroke risk).
  • If thrombus present → anticoagulate 3 weeks (warfarin goal INR 2–3) before elective DCCV, or use intracardiac thrombus aspiration if urgent.
  • If no thrombus → can proceed with DCCV.
  • MAZE patients: AF in first 4 weeks post-op expected; DCCV usually ineffective until atrial scarring matures (~4 weeks). Rate control + amiodarone is default.

sections.heading: 7.5 IABP as Bridge to Higher-Level Support or Surgery
sections.bodyHtml:
Intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) utility in decompensated HF:

  • Mechanism: augments diastolic pressure (improves coronary perfusion) while reducing afterload (aortic unloading in systole), improving cardiac output without inotrope dependency.
  • Indications:
  • Cardiogenic shock unresponsive to IV diuretics + mild inotropes
  • Mechanical complications post-MI (VSD, papillary muscle rupture, free wall rupture)
  • Bridge to LVAD/transplant if awaiting OR/workup
  • High-risk pre-op patients (low EF + pulmonary HTN + borderline hemodynamics)
  • Cautions:
  • Requires ICU-level monitoring + anticoagulation (heparin)
  • Limb complications (ischemia, thrombosis) in 5–10%; assess distal pulses q4h
  • Not intended as long-term support (bridge only; max 7–10 days typical)
  • Contraindicated if severe aortic regurgitation (balloon inflation worsens AR)
  • Impella (alternative microaxial pump): similar bridge concept; percutaneous; may reduce limb ischemia vs IABP; more operator-dependent

sections.heading: 7.6 Delay Non-Urgent Surgery for Optimization (3–6 Months Often Tolerated)
sections.bodyHtml:
When surgery can be deferred safely:

  • Patient medically stable on diuretics + GDMT, euvolemic, no shock, normal lactate
  • Condition is not immediately life-threatening (e.g., chronic severe AS vs acute aortic dissection)
  • GDMT has not yet reached target doses (escalation typically continues weeks to months)
  • Benefits of delay:
  • EF may improve (reverse remodeling) with GDMT escalation, reducing periop risk
  • Patient strengthens physically, improving post-op recovery
  • Frailty may improve with optimization + rehabilitation
  • Nutritional status improves (albumin < 3.0 = wound healing concern; delay allows time to supplement)
  • Examples of deferrable cases: chronic severe functional MR (improves with GDMT), stable severe AS (works up for TAVR vs AVR), HFrEF with stable CAD (CABG can wait 3–6 months if medically optimized)
  • Non-deferrable cases: acute aortic dissection, acute MR from papillary muscle rupture, ischemic VSD, free wall rupture, cardiogenic shock refractory to medical therapy → urgent OR

sections.heading: 7.7 Acute Reversible Causes Take Priority
sections.bodyHtml:
When HF decompensation is secondary to acute trigger:

  1. Sepsis (pneumonia, UTI, endocarditis): antibiotics, source control → HF may reverse dramatically
  2. New-onset AF with RVR: rate control or rhythm control → systemic congestion often improves
  3. Acute coronary syndrome: revascularization (PCI or CABG) may restore EF
  4. Medication non-adherence or withdrawal: restart home meds → symptom resolution
  5. Hypertensive crisis: blood pressure control → diuresis becomes effective
  6. Pulmonary embolism: anticoagulation, thrombolytics if massive → RV unloads

Key principle: address the trigger aggressively; HF is often the consequence, not the primary problem.

sections.heading: 7.8 Palliative Discussion if Not Surgery Candidate
sections.bodyHtml:
When LVAD/transplant not appropriate:

  • Advanced HF, recurrent hospitalizations, low EF (< 20%), multiorgan dysfunction, limited functional status
  • Palliative care referral is parallel, not replacement of medical therapy
  • Goals:
  • Symptom management (morphine for dyspnea, high-dose diuretics for comfort, NOT just euvolemia)
  • Advance directives (code status, DNR, DNI clarity)
  • Family support + honest prognosis conversation
  • Transition of care coordination (may move from ICU to step-down or palliative unit)
  • Many HF patients live years with comfort-focused care; others decompensate rapidly. Palliative team helps navigate.
  • Concurrent medical therapy encouraged: patients on optimal GDMT + diuretics may have extended survival even with palliative frame

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear in stable patient, re-escalate.

  • Worsening dyspnea despite IV diuretics — suggests inadequate response, new pulmonary issue (infection, PE, pneumothorax), RV decompensation, or escalation to ICU-level care needed
  • New or worsening orthopnea — pulmonary edema worsening; may need higher diuretic dose, ICU transition, or BiPAP
  • Persistent crackles after 2–3 days diuresis — diuretic resistance, worsening LV function, new valvular lesion, or pulmonary edema unresponsive to current strategy
  • New AF with RVR (> 120 bpm) — common; rate control needed ± anticoagulation; assess if triggered by hypokalemia, hypoxemia, or ischemia
  • Hypotension (SBP < 90) on diuretics or GDMT — over-diuresis, cardiomyopathy progression, sepsis, RV dysfunction, or pericardial effusion; reassess volume status
  • Persistent tachycardia (HR > 100 at rest) despite beta-blocker — inadequate preload reduction, ischemia, infection, arrhythmia, anemia, or thyroidism
  • Oliguria (UOP < 200 mL/8 h) despite IV diuretics — diuretic resistance; assess RV dysfunction, renal artery stenosis, cardiorenal syndrome
  • Rising lactate (> 2 mmol/L) or persistent elevation — inadequate tissue perfusion; may herald cardiogenic shock; escalate
  • Rising BUN/Cr ratio (> 20:1) despite euvolemia — suggests prerenal + renal parenchymal disease; may need nephrology consult
  • Altered mental status — assess hypoxemia, hyperammonemia (liver congestion), hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, sepsis, end-stage HF
  • Recurrent VT or new bradycardia (HR < 40) — may indicate myocardial ischemia, medication toxicity, or arrhythmia progression
  • Patient appearing anxious, restless, or sleepy — subtle mental status changes often precede frank decompensation

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield teaching moments)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Diuresis too fast causes AKI + prerenal azotemia; too slow delays surgery. Target 1–2 L/day negative balance as the sweet spot. Rapid diuresis (> 3 L/day) risks acute kidney injury; slow diuresis (< 0.5 L/day) prolongs stay. Monitor Cr, BUN/Cr ratio, and urine electrolytes. If Cr rises > 30% from baseline, hold diuretics, reassess volume status, consider intrinsic renal disease.

  2. Beta-blocker in acute decompensation may worsen shock. Do NOT escalate beta-blocker until euvolemic + stable. This is the most common GDMT timing mistake. Wait for orthopnea resolution, rales clearance, and JVP normalization before increasing beta-blocker dose.

  3. SGLT2i hold 3–5 days pre-op for euglycemic DKA risk. Perioperative stress (surgery, illness, medication changes) can trigger euglycemic DKA (metabolic acidosis + normal glucose; insidious). Hold SGLT2i 3–5 days pre-op; restart 3–5 days post-op once euvolemic + eating.

  4. Amiodarone for AF has hepatotoxicity, pulmonary toxicity, thyroid toxicity. Monitor LFTs (q3–6 months), check chest X-ray for pulmonary infiltrates, and check TSH (hypothyroidism common). If QTc > 500 ms, hold/decrease amiodarone (torsades risk). Hypotension in ~25% of loading; anticipate, decrease drip early.

  5. Anesthesia in high-risk patients (low EF, decompensated) without optimization is dangerous. Never proceed to surgery if patient is still congested, hypotensive, in shock, or on high-dose inotropes. Delay surgery; optimize first. Anesthesia will exacerbate hemodynamics if baseline is unstable.

  6. Diabetic patients: HbA1c goal < 8% for perioperative outcomes. Poorly controlled diabetes increases infection + cardiovascular complications. Screen HbA1c on admission; if > 8%, optimize glucose control pre-op (days to weeks). SGLT2i hold perioperatively only (good glucose control agent during hospitalization).

  7. Nutritional status critical for post-op recovery. Albumin < 3.0 = delayed wound healing concern. Screen on admission; supplement with PO/tube feeding PRN. Dietitian consult early if malnourished. HF patients are often catabolic; caloric support reduces complications.

  8. Frailty assessment (Clinical Frailty Scale) determines LVAD/transplant candidacy as much as EF. Strong EF recovery potential means nothing if patient is CFS 7–9 (severely frail), homeless, active substance use, or cognitively impaired. Comprehensive assessment: psychiatry clearance, social work stability, living situation. LVAD/transplant success requires lifelong compliance.

  9. Functional MR improves with diuresis + GDMT. Severe functional MR (from LV dilation + annular dilation) often resolves or improves significantly once EF improves and LV unloads. Don't rush to MV surgery if MR acute; wait 2–4 weeks post-GDMT initiation to reassess severity. Repair preferred over replacement if persistent severe MR.

  10. BNP/NT-proBNP trends matter more than absolute values. Patient may have chronically elevated BNP even when euvolemic + on GDMT. Trending BNP downward = appropriate response to therapy. Persistently elevated BNP despite euvolemia + stable weight = concern for ongoing ischemia, arrhythmia, or progression.

  11. BB hold/reduce during acute decompensation, but continue in chronic HFrEF. The paradox: beta-blockers worsen shock when fluid-overloaded (negative inotropic), but reduce mortality long-term. Resume/escalate once euvolemic.

  12. Renal dysfunction + HF = cardiorenal syndrome. Rising Cr during aggressive diuresis = prerenal azotemia (OK, transient). If Cr plateaus or rises on repeated labs despite euvolemia, consider intrinsic renal disease (CKD from HTN, DM) or need for mechanical support (renal perfusion improves with LVAD). Dialysis is NOT contraindication to LVAD; can run concurrently.

  13. Right heart catheterization (RHC) is essential pre-transplant/LVAD, optional pre-CABG/valve. If pulmonary HTN suspected (echo PA pressure > 45 mmHg) and considering LVAD/transplant, get RHC for true PA pressures, CO, SVR, and reversibility testing (iNO or milrinone trial). Fixed pulmonary HTN (no drop in PAP with inhaled vasodilators) = LVAD tolerance lower; RV failure risk higher post-implant.

  14. Post-op AF (POAF) is highly common post-HF surgery (~40–50% after CABG or valve). Beta-blocker is first-line rate control. Magnesium supplementation + low-chloride balanced fluids may reduce POAF incidence. Statin continuation pre-op associated with lower POAF.

  15. Cardiogenic shock is emergent, not medical admission. If patient arrives with SBP < 90 + altered mental status + elevated lactate + oliguria = ICU transfer, not step-down. Consider ECMO bridge if transplant/LVAD candidate awaiting workup. Do NOT delay inotropes or mechanical support for "medical optimization" in shock.

cards.title: Post-Op Delirium (Hyperactive, Hypoactive, Mixed)
cards.quickAnswer: Acute mental status change from baseline → CAM-ICU screen immediately (peaked POD 2–4, ~30% post-cardiac surgery incidence). Address reversibles first: hypoxia, electrolytes, infection, pain, retention, anticholinergics, sleep debt. Nonpharmacologic bundle (ABCDEF): reorient, dark nights, family, mobility, manage pain. Avoid benzodiazepines (worsen delirium). Haloperidol 0.5–2 mg IV q4–6h PRN if unstable (QTc < 500 ms baseline). Critical: Hypoactive delirium is most common subtype, most missed, and has worst prognosis—monitor quiet patients closely.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
Avoid benzodiazepines (worsen delirium). Haloperidol 0.5–2 mg IV q4–6h PRN if unstable (QTc < 500 ms baseline).

Critical: Hypoactive delirium is most common subtype, most missed, and has worst prognosis—monitor quiet patients closely.
