sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — what this is, epidemiology, who gets it.

  • Definition: Acute, fluctuating disturbance in attention and awareness, with disorganized thinking or altered level of consciousness, occurring post-operatively (hours to 1–2 days after cardiac surgery).
  • Subtypes: Hyperactive (agitation, hallucinations, combativeness; ~30%), hypoactive (withdrawn, slow, flat affect, shallow breathing; ~50%), mixed (fluctuating; ~20%).
  • Incidence: ~25–50% of cardiac surgery patients. Peak incidence post-operative day (POD) 2–4. Hypoactive subtype is more common than hyperactive but severely underrecognized.
  • Risk factors: Age > 70, pre-operative cognitive impairment, prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), severity of illness, substance use history (alcohol, benzodiazepines).
  • Why it matters: Hypoactive delirium is associated with longer length of stay, higher mortality, worse long-term cognitive recovery, and aspiration risk. Most cases are reversible with identification and treatment of underlying triggers.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative delirium is multifactorial, driven by convergence of neuroinflammation, drug effects, metabolic derangements, and environmental stressors:

  • Neuroinflammation: CPB triggers systemic inflammatory cascade (IL-6, TNF-α elevation, microglial activation); blood–brain barrier disruption → altered neurotransmission and impaired attention networks
  • Anticholinergic burden: Diphenhydramine, scopolamine, benztropine, atropine block acetylcholine → confusion, hallucinations, urinary retention, decreased mobility
  • Sleep deprivation: ICU environment (noise, continuous cares, fluorescent lights, absence of dark period) → REM and deep sleep loss → cognitive dysfunction alone
  • Metabolic derangement: Hyponatremia (SIADH), hypocalcemia (from transfusion), hyperglycemia, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia — each reversible
  • Drug stacking: Combination of opioids + benzodiazepines + anticholinergics + insufficient pain control → synergistic delirium
  • Infection & hypoxia: UTI, aspiration, atelectasis, pulmonary edema reduce cerebral oxygen delivery
  • Pre-existing vulnerability: Advanced age, dementia, depression, sensory impairment, chronic alcoholism, Parkinsonism increase susceptibility

The POD 2–4 peak reflects maximum inflammatory response, fluid mobilization from diuresis, and cumulative medication effects (Devlin et al., 2018).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Hyperactive presentation:

  • Agitation, combativeness, pulling lines, refusal of care
  • Hallucinations, paranoia, confusion
  • Rapid speech, insomnia, psychomotor restlessness
  • Family: "This is not like him/her"

Hypoactive presentation (MORE COMMON, MOST MISSED):

  • Withdrawn, slow mentation, flat affect, sparse speech
  • Poor nutritional intake, shallow breathing
  • Slow responses to commands; may appear cooperative and "pleasant"
  • Often mistaken for depression, fatigue, or appropriate post-operative sedation
  • Family may not notice change if they have not seen patient's baseline

Mixed presentation:

  • Fluctuates between hyperactive and hypoactive phases across shifts or within hours
  • Often labeled "sundowning" (worsening in evening/night, but this is NOT a diagnosis—it is delirium with temporal pattern)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic exam. Gather data for 2 minutes; no actions yet.

Mental status exam:

  • CAM-ICU screen: Acute onset + inattention + (disorganized thinking OR altered level of consciousness) = positive delirium. Document score and date/time.
  • Months-backward test, vigilance (squeeze-hands) test, or visual tracking — inability or errors suggest inattention
  • Baseline cognition: Ask family if patient was independent, had dementia, or other cognitive history pre-op

Vital signs & oxygenation:

  • HR, BP, RR, SpO₂, temperature, mental status, perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature)
  • Recent trend of vital sign changes

Reversibles checklist:

  • Hypoxia: SpO₂ goal ≥ 94% on current FiO₂; ABG if low SpO₂ or high RR
  • Electrolytes: Most recent Na, K, Ca, Mg, glucose, phosphate
  • Infection: Temperature, WBC trend, UA dipstick/culture (UTI is most common culprit), CXR if respiratory change, wound exam, line site inspection
  • Pain: Verbal or CPOT scale each shift; assess multimodal pain control adequacy
  • Retention: Bladder scan (post-void residual), foley patency, stool frequency (constipation impairs cognition)
  • Drugs: MAR review — any new anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, scopolamine, benztropine)? Benzodiazepines? High-dose or stacked opioids? Recent steroids? Substance use history (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids)?
  • Sleep debt: Nights of poor sleep, insufficient dark period, overnight vitals/cares disrupting sleep
  • Intracranial: Focal neurologic signs (weakness, facial droop, gaze deviation, speech changes)? → stroke protocol, not delirium

Surgery context:

  • Days since surgery, CPB time, transfusion volume
  • Recent extubation? Recent line removal?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, maintains airway, safety intact, vitals reassuring.)

  1. STAT CAM-ICU screen and document score + time; establish baseline
  2. Obtain STAT labs: BMP (Na, K, Ca, Mg, glucose), CBC, ABG if SpO₂ < 94% or RR > 25
  3. Infection workup (STAT): UA + urine culture (UTI = most common reversible cause), blood cultures if febrile, CXR if respiratory change, wound/line inspection
  4. STAT CT head only if focal neuro signs (new weakness, gaze deviation, speech slurring) — do not assume delirium; rule out stroke/intracerebral hemorrhage
  5. Eliminate anticholinergics immediately: STOP diphenhydramine, scopolamine, benztropine, atropine. Check MAR for redundancy (e.g., diphenhydramine + Foley-related anticholinergic burden).
  6. Pain assessment & multimodal control: Verbal or CPOT q shift. Use acetaminophen + NSAIDs ± low-dose opioid (not standing benzodiazepine). Reassess q1–2h post-op.
  7. Bladder & bowel management: Bladder scan (goal post-void residual < 400 mL). Foley if retention. Bowel regimen if constipated (docusate + senna; see related card Bowel Regimen Protocol).
  8. Sleep & reorientation protocol:
    • Dark room 10 p.m.–6 a.m. (strict—nightlight only if safety concern)
    • Cluster cares: consolidate vitals, meds, assessments into one visit
    • Minimize or defer overnight vitals if stable (q8h sufficient overnight)
    • Reorient every shift: name, date, location, reason for hospitalization, post-operative day
    • Provide sensory aids: glasses, hearing aids, dentures, familiar objects
    • Early mobility if safe: POD 1–2 if stable/extubated—chair sitting or hallway ambulation for 10–15 minutes improves cognition and prevents delirium perpetuation
    • Engage family: Contact POD 1–2 to describe baseline cognition, delirium signs, and invite bedside presence (especially critical for hypoactive delirium). Family provides reorientation and comfort.
    • Continuous assessment: CAM-ICU q shift minimum; trend to detect response to interventions
    • Notify APP: Report CAM-ICU score, reversibles workup status, safety level. If focal neuro deficits: neurology consult STAT. If safety escalating: proceed to 5B path.

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Safety risk: combative/line-pulling, refusal of essential care, respiratory compromise, hemodynamic instability from agitation, or severe hypoactive delirium with aspiration risk.)

  1. STAT call: Activate rapid response / code team. APP to bedside immediately. Charge RN + security standby present.
  2. Safety measures: 1:1 sitter at bedside continuously. Remove unnecessary equipment/lines that could be pulled. Do NOT leave patient alone. ICU transfer if not already there.
  3. Vitals STAT: If SpO₂ < 92%: increase FiO₂, call respiratory therapy, get ABG. If HR > 120 or SBP > 180: assess pain, hypoxia, bladder fullness, fever first—before pharmacologic sedation.
  4. Do STAT labs if not yet done: BMP, CBC, ABG, UA, blood cultures if febrile, troponin/BNP if cardiac concern
  5. Pharmacologic management per APP (confirm QTc < 500 ms baseline before antipsychotic):
    • Haloperidol (first-line antipsychotic): 0.5–2 mg IV/IM/PO q4–6h PRN. Start 0.5 mg, titrate cautiously. Faster onset IV (15–30 min). Baseline ECG + q24h monitoring for QTc; hold if QTc > 500 ms.
    • Quetiapine (alternative if Parkinsonism / Lewy body / QTc borderline): 12.5–50 mg PO qHS ± BID PRN. Slower onset, fewer extrapyramidal effects, more sedating.
    • Melatonin (adjunct for sleep): 3 mg PO qHS—low toxicity, supports circadian rhythm
    • AVOID benzodiazepines → paradoxical agitation, respiratory depression, dependency. Exception: alcohol/benzo withdrawal only (CIWA > 10 or seizure risk); then lorazepam or chlordiazepoxide taper per CIWA protocol
    • Continuous cardiac monitor & pulse oximetry. Reassess mental status q1h; document CAM-ICU score each assessment.
    • Restraints LAST, not first: Use only if imminent danger + all nonpharmacologic/pharmacologic options exhausted + 1:1 sitter + APP order. Document entry/exit times; reassess every 15 min if restrained.
    • ICU transfer criteria: High-dose antipsychotics, continuous sedation/monitoring, airway concern, or hemodynamic instability

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "This is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]. Acute mental status change since [time], now [hyperactive/hypoactive/mixed]. CAM-ICU [score]." B: "Baseline cognition [intact / mild dementia / other]. CPB time [X] min. Current meds: [list new sedatives, anticholinergics, opioids]. ETOH/benzo use history? [yes/no]. Vitals: HR [X], BP [X], SpO₂ [X], temp [X]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Describe immediate concern: combative vs. withdrawn, respiratory status, safety risk]. Reversibles workup [in progress / pending results]." R: "Requesting [APP bedside eval / pharmacist med review / neurology consult if focal signs / ICU evaluation / antipsychotic order]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Acute agitation, line-pulling, combative behavior APP, charge nurse, rapid response
New focal neuro deficit (weakness, gaze deviation, speech change) Neurology + stroke protocol STAT
Fever + elevated WBC + clinical sepsis signs APP, infectious disease
Refractory agitation despite haloperidol dose escalation APP, psychiatry, pharmacist review
Suspected alcohol/benzo withdrawal (tremor, CIWA rising) APP, ICU evaluation (STAT if CIWA > 10)
QTc > 500 ms on antipsychotic Cardiology, APP — hold antipsychotic
Suspected aspiration (cough during PO, fever, infiltrate on CXR) APP, speech-language pathology

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(expandable in app; all subsections collapsed by default)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology in depth — inflammation, drugs, and reversibles cascade Post-operative delirium reflects acute brain dysfunction under physiologic stress. The four major mechanisms:
  1. Neuroinflammation from CPB: Cardiopulmonary bypass activates monocytes and macrophages, triggering release of IL-6, TNF-α, and other pro-inflammatory cytokines. These cross the disrupted blood–brain barrier and impair the neurotransmitter balance that supports attention and executive function. Microglial activation perpetuates the cycle.
  2. Anticholinergic toxidrome: Anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, scopolamine, benztropine, atropine) block acetylcholine—the neurotransmitter essential for attention, memory formation, and arousal. Even a single postoperative dose can tip a patient into delirium, especially in older adults with reduced acetylcholinesterase activity.
  3. Sleep deprivation: ICU environment (noise, overnight cares, absent dark period, continuous light) disrupts REM and slow-wave sleep. Sleep loss alone is sufficient to cause delirium in vulnerable patients; combined with CPB inflammation and medications, it becomes nearly inevitable without intervention.
  4. Metabolic derangement: Post-operative diuresis pulls electrolytes below thresholds for neurologic stability. Hyponatremia (from SIADH), hypocalcemia (from transfusion calcium binding), hypomagnesemia, hyperglycemia, and hypophosphatemia each impair neurotransmitter synthesis and synaptic function. The POD 2–4 peak reflects convergence timing: maximum inflammatory response at 48–72 hours, diuresis-induced electrolyte nadir, cumulative medication effects, and sleep debt accumulation. Pre-existing vulnerability (age > 70, dementia, depression, alcoholism, Parkinsonism) lowers the threshold—these patients delirous with smaller insults.
Subtypes table — hyperactive vs. hypoactive vs. mixed recognition and prognosis
SubtypeFrequencyPresentationFamily/Staff RecognitionPrognosisManagement Pearl
Hyperactive~30%Agitation, hallucinations, combativeness, line-pulling, refusal, insomnia, rapid speech, paranoiaEASILY RECOGNIZED — family alerts, staff pages, alarms triggerDisruptive but escalation visible; addresses fasterSafety-first: 1:1 sitter, haloperidol, reversibles
Hypoactive~50%Withdrawn, slow mentation, flat affect, sparse speech, poor intake, shallow breathing, "pleasant but confused," sleepinessMOST MISSED — attributed to depression, fatigue, appropriate sedation. Quiet patient = "well" patient (false). Family may not notice without baseline.WORST: Longer LOS, higher mortality, worse long-term cognition, aspiration/DVT risk. Missed delirium → decline unaddressed.CAM-ICU q shift mandatory. Target reversibles aggressively. Mobility + family engagement. Monitor breathing.
Mixed~20%Fluctuates hyperactive ↔ hypoactive across hours or across shifts; often mislabeled "sundowning"Recognized if caregiver witnesses both phases; unclear if dominant subtypeDepends on dominant type + adequacy of reversibles treatmentTreat as reversible delirium, not inevitable evening phenomenon. Sleep protocol + reorientation + reversibles.
Critical insight: Hypoactive delirium is the most common post-cardiac surgery subtype and the most underrecognized. Many cases are still in hospital charts labeled "appropriate sedation," "depression," or "fatigue." Screening q shift is mandatory. A quiet, slowly-responding patient with acute onset is delirium until proven otherwise.

Appropriate Abx per culture.UTI does not always present with dysuria in post-op setting; may present only as delirium. Low threshold for culture.

Reorientation cues every shift (name, date, location, reason). Family at bedside.Sensory deprivation alone causes delirium. Post-op patients often cannot locate or use aids; nursing must facilitate.

See related card Acute Stroke Recognition and Response.Do NOT anchor on "patient is delirious" and dismiss focal findings. UUrinary/fecalBladder scan (goal post-void residual < 400 mL). Foley if retention. Bowel regimen if constipated (docusate + senna; see related card Bowel Regimen Protocol).Retention and constipation impair cognition directly and reduce mobility. Inotropic support if cardiogenic shock.Hypoxia and low cardiac output reduce cerebral perfusion. Delirium may be the first sign of MI, HF decompensation, or sepsis. Assume physiologic cause until proven otherwise.
Nonpharmacologic ABCDEF bundle (SCCM PADIS) with detailed implementation The ABCDEF bundle (Devlin et al., 2018) is first-line. Pharmaceutical interventions are adjuncts, not replacements.
ComponentImplementationTimingEvidence
A: Assess painVerbal pain scale q shift (or CPOT if unable to report). Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen 650 mg q6h + NSAID (ibuprofen 400–600 mg q6h if no contraindication) + low-dose opioid PRN (morphine 2–4 mg IV q2–4h PRN). Reassess q1–2h post-op. Consider neuropathic pain (gabapentin 300 mg TID, pregabalin 75–150 mg BID) if present.Every shift; escalate frequency post-opInadequate pain control perpetuates delirium and prevents sleep. Multimodal reduces opioid dose + adverse effects.
B: Breathing (respiratory)Monitor RR, work of breathing, SpO₂. Encourage spirometry q2–4h. Coughing, turning, early mobilization. Avoid oversedation (target = awake + interactive). No standing benzodiazepine orders.Every shiftHypoxia → delirium. Oversedation → respiratory depression → hypoxia. Mobilization → improved oxygenation.
C: Choice (minimize sedation)Nonpharmacologic interventions first (reorientation, dark night, family, pain control). If PRN sedation needed (for painful procedure, high anxiety): ketamine 0.5–1 mg/kg IV or dexmedetomidine 0.5–1 mcg/kg/h infusion preferred over benzodiazepines. No standing benzodiazepine orders.PRN basis, not standingBenzodiazepines are associated with prolonged delirium, respiratory depression, dependence. Ketamine and dexmedetomidine preserve cognition better.
D: Delirium assessmentCAM-ICU q shift minimum (more often if unstable). Document score + date/time in note. Trend over time to measure response to interventions.Every shiftScores allow team tracking and adjustment. Untreated delirium trajectories worsen over 24–48h. Serial assessment detects deterioration.
E: Early mobilityPOD 1–2 if stable + extubated: chair sitting 10–15 min or hallway ambulation with supervision. PT/OT consult if needed. Even brief mobilization improves cognition, prevents DVT/PE, speeds recovery.POD 1–2 onward, dailyEarly mobilization is associated with shorter delirium duration, shorter LOS, better functional recovery. Immobility perpetuates delirium.
F: Family engagementContact family POD 1–2 to describe baseline cognition and delirium signs. Invite 24/7 bedside presence (especially critical for hypoactive delirium—family is primary intervention). Family provides reorientation, comfort, emotional support, and behavioral monitoring.POD 1 onwardFamily presence reduces delirium severity and duration. Family describes delirium changes better than staff in brief shifts. Therapeutic effect is strong.
Sleep protocol (critical for delirium prevention):
  • Dark room 10 p.m.–6 a.m. (strict—use nightlight only if safety concern)
  • Cluster cares: one visit for vitals, medications, assessments; avoid multiple interruptions
  • Minimize overnight vitals if stable: q8h sufficient (not q4h)
  • No diphenhydramine or trazodone sleep aids (anticholinergic). Prefer melatonin 3 mg PO qHS or dexmedetomidine drip if sedation required
  • Cool, quiet room; door closed if possible
  • Remove unnecessary alarms (limit non-essential monitoring) Sleep recovery alone resolves many delirium cases in 24–48 hours.
Pharmacologic management table — antipsychotics, alternatives, what to AVOID *Confirm all doses with APP and institutional order set. Start low, titrate slowly. QTc baseline ECG required before any antipsychotic.* First-line antipsychotic
DrugDoseRouteOnsetNotes
Haloperidol0.5–2 mgIV preferred; IM or PO if no IV15–30 min IVGold standard. Rapid onset. ECG baseline + q24h (QTc target < 500 ms). Monitor for neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare, < 1%). Extrapyramidal effects possible.
Alternative antipsychotics
DrugDoseRouteOnsetNotes
Quetiapine12.5–50 mgPO (no IV form)30–60 minUse if Parkinsonism, Lewy body, or QTc borderline (460–500 ms). Fewer extrapyramidal effects. Sedating (advantage for sleep). May cause hypotension—monitor.
Melatonin3 mgPO30–60 minSleep + circadian rhythm support. Low toxicity, safe in renal/hepatic impairment. Adjunct to haloperidol for sleep.
Medications to AVOID
Drug ClassReasonException
Benzodiazepines (lorazepam, diazepam, midazolam)Paradoxical agitation, respiratory depression, dependence, prolonged cognitive recoveryONLY for alcohol/benzo withdrawal (CIWA > 10) or seizure risk; then taper over 5–7 days per CIWA
Anticholinergics (diphenhydramine, scopolamine, benztropine, atropine)Directly cause delirium; worsen inattentionSTOP immediately; no exceptions post-op
Opioid stacking (high-dose opioid + benzo + anticholinergic)Synergistic delirium + respiratory depressionUse multimodal analgesia instead; opioids at lowest effective dose
Special pharmacologic situations:
  • Alcohol withdrawal: CIWA protocol; lorazepam 2–4 mg IV q15–30min if CIWA > 10 (seizure risk). Taper lorazepam or switch to chlordiazepoxide PO taper over 5–7 days. Thiamine 100 mg IV/PO daily (depleted in heavy ETOH users). ICU monitoring if high CIWA or seizure history.
  • Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia: AVOID haloperidol (neuroleptic hypersensitivity). Use quetiapine 12.5–50 mg PO qHS, melatonin, and aggressive reversibles.
  • QTc prolongation (460–500 ms baseline or on amiodarone/sotalol): Use quetiapine or melatonin; haloperidol only if urgently needed and QTc carefully monitored q4–6h.
  • QTc > 500 ms: HOLD all antipsychotics. Focus on reversibles + nonpharmacologic. Consult cardiology + psychiatry.
  • Severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30): Haloperidol clearance impaired; use lower doses or longer intervals. Quetiapine requires dose adjustment. Doses adapted from SCCM PADIS Guidelines (Devlin et al., 2018), Elmistekawy & Shallik (2025), and Bojar (2020). Always verify against current institutional policy.
Emergence delirium (intra-operative to immediate post-op) vs. post-operative delirium (POD 1+) Two distinct syndromes, sometimes confused: Emergence delirium (in OR recovery, 0–2 hours post-op):
  • Agitation + disorientation while waking from anesthesia
  • Expected in small degree in most patients; resolves with reorientation + environmental calm
  • Caused by anesthetic residual (inhaled agents, propofol, opioid hangover) + pain + hypoxia
  • Management: reassure, reorient, check O₂/pain, dim lights, minimize stimulation
  • Analgesics (morphine, fentanyl) + low-dose sedatives (propofol 10–20 mg IV push) if persistent
  • Usually resolves within minutes to 1–2 hours of full wakefulness Post-operative delirium (POD 1+ onward):
  • Develops 12+ hours post-op; caused by inflammation, infection, metabolic, drugs, sleep loss
  • Hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed subtypes
  • Reversible with identification of triggers (infection, electrolytes, pain, etc.)
  • Management: CAM-ICU screening, reversibles workup, nonpharmacologic bundle, antipsychotics PRN The clinical distinction matters: emergence delirium is a normal anesthetic response and resolves with simple reassurance; post-operative delirium is pathologic and requires investigation + intervention. Chronic cognitive trajectory post-delirium:
  • Patients who experience post-operative delirium have higher long-term cognitive decline (1–5 years) even after delirium resolves acutely
  • This "post-operative cognitive dysfunction" (POCD) is associated with increased mortality and worse functional outcomes at 1 year
  • Mechanism not fully understood; may involve persistent neuroinflammation, cumulative sleep loss, or CPB-related injury
  • Early aggressive treatment of delirium + post-op cognitive rehabilitation (PT/OT, cognitive games, community engagement) may reduce long-term cognitive decline, but evidence is still evolving

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear, re-escalate care immediately.

  • Worsening agitation/combativeness despite haloperidol: Line-pulling escalating, refusal of essential care, striking staff → consider haloperidol dose increase, pharmacist med review, or new trigger (infection, hypoxia, pain).
  • Transition from hyperactive → hypoactive: Still delirium, but masked as "settling down" or "calming with haloperidol." Danger: aspiration, poor mobility, missed decline in mental status. Monitor breathing, intake, mobility closely.
  • Worsening hypoxemia or respiratory distress: Agitation + hypoxia feedback loop. Check SpO₂, ABG. Rule out pulmonary edema, pneumonia, aspiration, atelectasis.
  • New focal neurologic deficit (weakness, facial droop, gaze deviation, speech slurring): STAT neurology + stroke protocol. Never assume delirium without neuroimaging. Time-sensitive.
  • Persistent fever ± escalating WBC despite antibiotics: Sepsis trajectory. Notify APP/infectious disease; review culture results + adjust antibiotics; ICU evaluation if hemodynamically unstable.
  • QTc prolonging on haloperidol toward 500 ms: Torsades de pointes risk. Hold haloperidol, call cardiology. Consider quetiapine instead.
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (rare but life-threatening): High fever (> 39°C), severe muscle rigidity, autonomic instability (tachycardia, labile BP). STAT—STOP haloperidol immediately, ICU, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV over 5 min, cooling measures, check CK.
  • Acute fall or head trauma: CT head to rule out intracranial injury, even with delirium history.
  • Aspiration suspected: Cough during PO intake, new fever, infiltrate on CXR, decreased O₂. Hold PO, notify APP, consider NG tube or speech-swallow evaluation.
  • Declining level of consciousness (GCS dropping): Possible sepsis, stroke, ICU-level event. STAT labs (lactate, blood cultures), CT head, ICU evaluation.
  • Hypoactive delirium with shallow breathing (RR < 12): Risk of hypoventilation + hypoxia. Monitor closely. Increase RR monitoring to q1h. Consider ICU transfer.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Hypoactive delirium is the most common and most missed subtype. CAM-ICU q shift is mandatory, especially in older patients. "Quiet" or "pleasant but confused" patient is delirium until proven otherwise. Missed hypoactive delirium = worse length of stay, mortality, and long-term cognition.

  2. Benzodiazepines paradoxically worsen delirium. Avoid reflexively. Benzos suppress breathing, increase falls, build dependence. Use only for alcohol/benzo withdrawal (CIWA > 10), seizure risk, or prior benzo dependence (taper only). First-line is haloperidol or quetiapine + reversibles workup.

  3. Anticholinergic stack is a major cause. Diphenhydramine + Foley (inherent anticholinergic) + opioids + scopolamine patch = convergent delirium. STOP all anticholinergics immediately. Work with pharmacist to eliminate redundancy.

  4. New focal neuro sign = stroke until proven otherwise. Do not anchor on "patient is delirious." CT/CTA STAT. Stroke window is time-sensitive (thrombolytics < 4.5 h, thrombectomy < 24 h).

  5. "Sundowning" is not a diagnosis—it is delirium with temporal pattern. Evening confusion = reversible causes (pain, fatigue, darkness, sleep debt). Treat reversibles + enforce sleep protocol; never just accept sundowning as inevitable.

  6. Sleep protection is potent and underused. Dark 10 p.m.–6 a.m., cluster cares, minimal overnight vitals, melatonin 3 mg qHS. Many delirium cases resolve with sleep recovery alone in 24–48 hours.

  7. Glasses and hearing aids matter. Sensory deprivation IS delirium. Post-op patients cannot locate aids. Nursing must provide and ensure use. Orient frequently if sensory-impaired.

  8. Steroid psychosis is real. Chronic or high-dose perioperative steroids (> 20 mg dexamethasone equivalent) → hallucinations, paranoia, agitation. Steroid taper resolves symptoms as dose decreases.

  9. Restraints worsen delirium. Use 1:1 sitter first. Optimize reorientation, family, sleep, pain, mobility. Pharmacotherapy second. Restraints only if imminent danger + all else failed + APP order. Monitor q15min if restrained.

  10. Document with a screening score, not "pleasant but confused." CAM-ICU or 4AT score in the note. Scores allow trend tracking and team adjustment of care. Narrative alone misses hypoactive cases.

  11. Family is a therapeutic intervention, not a visitor. Family presence reduces delirium duration and severity. Family describes baseline + alerts staff to changes. Especially critical for hypoactive delirium. Invite 24/7 if possible.

  12. Alcohol withdrawal is dangerous and delayed. Onset 24–72h post-op. Any positive ETOH history: CIWA protocol POD 1–2 if autonomic signs present. CIWA ≥ 10 = ICU + intensive benzo taper. Missed withdrawal → seizure, arrhythmia, death.

  13. Acute pain is a reversible trigger, often overlooked in rush to sedate. Treat pain multimodal (acetaminophen + NSAID + low-dose opioid). Pain control often dramatically improves delirium + sleep. Insufficient pain management perpetuates the cycle.

  14. Hypoactive delirium with low respiratory rate is high-risk. RR < 12 + shallow breath + hypoactivity = aspiration + hypoxia risk. Monitor q1h. Low threshold for ICU transfer.

  15. UTI is the most common reversible trigger in older post-op patients. UA dipstick + culture STAT. Do not wait for dysuria or urgency symptoms (often absent post-op). Delirium + fever + pyuria = treat UTI even if asymptomatic.

cards.title: Deep Hypothermic Circulatory Arrest (DHCA)
cards.quickAnswer: Deep hypothermia (18–22 °C) + complete circulatory arrest + antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP) protects the brain during aortic arch surgery. Post-operative stroke risk is 3–15% — deficits may declare late (48–72 h). Mandatory vigilance: NIHSS or focal neuro checks q shift for first 72 h, replace electrolytes (K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0), monitor for delirium (peak POD 2–4) and coagulopathy. Late deficits warrant immediate neuro consult and imaging.

cards.sourcePrecedence: Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Kirklin & Blackstone (2026) → Bojar (2020) → Svensson et al. (2005) → Estrera & Safi (2009) → Mariani et al. (2018) → [Institution PolicyStat]

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest combines three protective elements:

  1. Profound hypothermia — core cooled to 18–22 °C (or moderate 22–28 °C with ACP adjuncts)
  2. Complete circulatory arrest — all systemic perfusion stopped during operative window
  3. Selective cerebral perfusion adjuncts — antegrade (ACP) or retrograde (RCP) blood flow to brain at low rates during arrest

DHCA enables safe open repair of thoracic aortic arch dissections, aneurysms, and root-arch composites on a dry operative field. Hypothermia extends safe arrest time by slowing cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO₂) ~7% per °C drop in core temperature. At 18 °C, the brain tolerates 30–40 min of complete arrest if re-warming is gradual and brain perfusion is maintained (Kirklin & Blackstone, 2026).

sections.heading: 2. Mechanism / CMRO₂ Physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Core principle: cerebral metabolic demand decreases as temperature drops, allowing longer arrest tolerance.

Temperature CMRO₂ (% baseline) Safe arrest time Clinical context
37 °C (normotherm) 100% < 5 min Standard brain metabolism; arrest catastrophic
28–34 °C (mild) ~50–55% 15–20 min With ACP, safe for moderate procedures
22–28 °C (moderate) ~50% 15–30 min Sweet spot for ACP; most arch repairs
18–22 °C (deep) ~25% 30–40 min Profound protection; allows RCP alone
< 18 °C (profound) < 25% up to 45 min Rare; marginal benefit, extreme coagulopathy risk

At deep hypothermia, low CMRO₂ means neurons do not demand oxygen, do not accumulate ischemic lactate and intracellular Ca²⁺, and tolerate arrest durations that would cause catastrophic injury at higher temperatures (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).

sections.heading: 3. Variants — DHCA vs Moderate Hypothermia + ACP
sections.bodyHtml:
Surgeons select approach by expected cross-clamp time, arch extent, and institutional preference.

Approach Core temp Arrest time Cerebral method Clinical scenario
Profound DHCA 14–18 °C 40–45 min RCP for air flushing; minimal perfusion Extensive arch, intracranial involvement, elephant trunk
Deep DHCA 18–22 °C 30–40 min ACP common; RCP acceptable Type A dissection, aortic root + arch, standard repair
Moderate hyp + ACP 22–28 °C up to 60 min with ACP ACP via R subclavian or innominate Moderate arch, good collaterals, brief arrest preference
Mild hyp + ACP 28–34 °C "as needed" with ACP ACP mandatory; RCP supplemental Proximal arch only, high-risk (frail, prior stroke)

Antegrade Cerebral Perfusion (ACP): arterial cannula placed in right subclavian or innominate artery delivers oxygenated, nutrient-rich blood to carotids and circle of Willis while aortic arch is open. Allows longer operations (up to 60 min) at moderate temperatures. Standard for most arch repairs > 30 min (Estrera & Safi, 2009).

Retrograde Cerebral Perfusion (RCP): blood perfused backward through superior vena cava cannula at low pressure (25–30 mmHg). Flushes air and debris, but limited nutritive value; provides washout only. Falling from favor vs. ACP as primary strategy; still used as adjunct during final arch manipulation.

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use — Post-Op Neuro Vigilance
sections.bodyHtml:
ICU inherits post-DHCA arch patients — ascending aortic replacement with arch, Bentall operations, acute Type A dissection repair, descending aorta/TAAA repair with arch component, elephant trunk procedures. These are among the highest-acuity post-operative patients. Operative insult is severe: long cardiopulmonary bypass, deep hypothermia, circulatory arrest, open aortic arch, profound coagulopathy. Nurses must anticipate aggressive bleeding, delirium, stroke, spinal cord ischemia, renal injury, and seizure.

Hand-off essentials:

  • Total DHCA time (minutes of complete circulatory arrest)
  • Lowest core temperature achieved
  • ACP or RCP used, and for how long
  • Total cross-clamp time and total pump time
  • Cell saver volume, estimated blood loss
  • Baseline neuro exam (any intra-op deficits)
  • Coagulation labs at ICU discharge (PT/PTT, platelets, fibrinogen)

Immediate vigilance (POD 0–3):

  • NIHSS or focal neuro checks q 4–6 h POD 0, then q shift POD 1–3 minimum: alert/orient × 3, visual fields, facial symmetry, arm drift, speech, gait. Any new focal deficit → immediate MD/NP notification + likely neuro consult.
  • Deficits may evolve late — normal exam at 4 h does not exclude stroke at 24–48 h.
  • Coagulopathy: expect baseline thrombocytopenia (80–120k), prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen. Most recover 48–72 h. Surgical ooze common POD 0–1; should taper. Persistent bleeding after POD 1 suggests re-exploration.
  • Delirium: DHCA triggers neuroinflammation and microemboli. Peak POD 2–4. Use CAM-ICU q shift; rule out reversibles (hypoxia, hypocarbia, infection, electrolyte disorder). Haloperidol or dexmedetomidine may be used; benzodiazepines worsen delirium post-cardiac surgery.
  • Electrolytes: replace K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 per Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement protocol.
  • Renal: AKI is common after long pump + DHCA. Monitor Cr, BUN, urine output. Hemoglobinuria from massive hemolysis stresses kidneys; early fluid optimization and avoiding nephrotoxins are critical.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Why late stroke happens Stroke post-DHCA can declare late (POD 1–3) because:
  • Microemboli generated during arch manipulation lodge in distal cerebral vessels and occlude gradually over hours to days
  • Cerebral edema from ischemia-reperfusion injury worsens the first 24–48 h post-op
  • Re-warming arrhythmia and transient hypotension may worsen distal perfusion
  • Hyperglycemia and inflammatory state promote thrombosis and vasospasm Continuous vigilance for 72 h is the standard because the neurologic window is long. Small neurologic changes (1-point NIHSS drift, mild arm weakness, subtle speech delay) can signal evolving stroke and warrant immediate notification and imaging.
Coagulopathy after DHCA + CPB Post-DHCA coagulopathy is dual-hit: CPB causes platelet dysfunction and consumptive coagulopathy; hypothermia causes additional platelet dysfunction and fibrinolysis inhibition (paradoxically). Result: baseline thrombocytopenia (80–120k), prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, dysfibrinogenemia. Most recover by POD 3–5 as normothermia is restored and CPB effects wear off. Transfusion thresholds and reversal agents follow standard cardiac surgery guidelines (Bojar, 2020).
Spinal cord ischemia risk If DHCA repair extends to descending aorta or includes elephant trunk, spinal cord ischemia risk is real. Paraplegia can occur acutely or evolve over hours post-op. If CSF drainage is in place, maintain CSF pressure < 10 mmHg per protocol. Assess lower-extremity strength and pain q shift. Any new weakness or sensory change → immediate notification and imaging.
Arrhythmia during re-warming Re-warming arrhythmia (Osborn waves, atrial fibrillation, bradycardia) is common during ICU emergence but rare by post-op ward transfer. If it persists into the ICU step-down phase, it is usually self-limited and responds to gentle core re-warming, vasodilation, and electrolyte correction. Avoid aggressive rate control unless hemodynamically unstable.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Neuro deficits from DHCA declare LATE. A normal exam at 4 h post-op does not exclude stroke. Vigilance window is 48–72 h; do not abbreviate neuro checks POD 1–2.

  2. NIHSS or formal neuro exam q shift for first 72 h is the minimum standard. Know baseline from operative note. Small changes (1-point NIHSS drift) signal evolving stroke.

  3. Hoarseness post-arch surgery indicates recurrent laryngeal nerve injury — operative approach sequela, not DHCA per se. Swallow eval indicated; most recover over weeks to months.

  4. Phrenic nerve injury (especially left, from LIMA dissection) causes elevated hemidiaphragm on CXR and may worsen oxygenation. ENT or phrenic consultation warranted if suspected.

  5. Delirium peak is POD 2–4, not POD 0. Many post-op patients are sedated POD 0. As sedation wears off, delirium may worsen before improving. CAM-ICU q shift essential. Rule out reversibles before starting antipsychotics.

  6. DHCA + long pump = extended bleeding risk. Coagulopathy is dual-hit. Thresholds for transfusion and re-exploration are standard cardiac surgery; bleeding may persist longer (48–72 h taper).

  7. DHCA does NOT directly cause lasting neurologic damage if performed correctly with adequate brain protection. Most morbidity traces to underlying disease (dissection, aneurysm), arch manipulation (emboli), or inadequate brain perfusion during arrest. Know the difference.

  8. Long DHCA time (> 40 min) is a harbinger of higher morbidity. Morbidity increases with DHCA duration, pump time, and cross-clamp time. Heighten vigilance for AKI, stroke, delirium, and bleeding.

  9. Thrombocytopenia post-DHCA is common — platelet count often 80–120k POD 0, recovers by POD 3–5. If persistently low (< 50k) or paradoxically drops after initial recovery, HIT differential warranted. Protamine reaction and autoimmune platelet destruction also possible.

  10. Hyperkalemia can occur intra-operatively; by the ICU, hypokalemia is more common. Routine K⁺ monitoring is essential. As myocytes rewarm, K⁺ shifts back intracellularly; dilution and diuresis drop K⁺ post-op.

cards.title: Discharge Readiness Criteria Post-Cardiac Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: Safe discharge requires stability across 12 domains: hemodynamic stability off drips ×24 h, stable rhythm, room air or home O₂ plan, tolerating diet, independent voiding, clean incision, ambulating ≥200 ft, pain on oral meds, baseline cognition, reconciled medications with teach-back, comprehensive discharge teaching, and arranged disposition with home services. Interdisciplinary team engaged; readmission risk stratified; 48–72 h post-D/C phone call mandatory. Do NOT discharge if any domain is unmet — hold and escalate per Deviation Triggers (§6).

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, scope, and when it applies.

  • Definition: A structured, multidisciplinary assessment confirming that a patient has met physiologic, functional, cognitive, and social readiness benchmarks for safe discharge home, SNF, or acute rehab following cardiac surgery.
  • Scope: All adult cardiac surgery patients (POD 2–7) regardless of procedure (CABG, valve, aortic, transplant, TAVR, MAZE, myectomy — all sternotomy-based or percutaneous discharge).
  • Why it matters: 30-day readmission is a CMS quality metric; structured discharge criteria reduce readmissions 8–15% vs ad-hoc decisions (Rockwell et al., 2016). Premature discharge = falls, medication errors, sepsis, heart failure exacerbation, hemorrhage, VTE. Delayed discharge = deconditioning, depression, cost inflation.
  • When to apply: Assessment begins POD 1 (discharge planning huddle); daily readiness checklist POD 3–6; final assessment and teaching day-of-discharge.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardiac surgery creates a physiologic debt across multiple organ systems. Discharge readiness is the moment when the patient regains autonomy across 12 discrete domains:

Hemodynamic recovery — weaning from vasoactive support; managing fluid shifts; rhythm stability.

Respiratory function — weaning from supplemental O₂; independent secretion clearance; incentive spirometry.

Gastrointestinal recovery — tolerating PO diet; bowel function resuming; no ileus.

Renal function — adequate urine output; electrolytes repleted; voiding spontaneously.

Wound healing — incisions clean/dry/intact; infection ruled out; cellulitis absent.

Mobility and function — ambulation distance improving; pain controlled on oral meds; sternal precautions understood.

Cognition — baseline mental status; delirium resolved; understanding of discharge plan.

Medication reconciliation — all home + new meds listed; teach-back performed; prescriptions filled.

Discharge teaching — sternal precautions, activity, red flags, diet, follow-up appointments, rehab enrollment.

Disposition and support — home environment safe; family/support confirmed; home health / SNF arranged if needed.

Risk stratification — readmission risk assessed; intensified follow-up planned for high-risk patients.

Communication plan — receiving provider notified; follow-up appointments scheduled; 48–72 h post-D/C phone call arranged.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — patient populations and clinical triggers.

Universally indicated:

  • Every adult post-op cardiac surgery patient (POD 1+), regardless of age, pre-op status, or comorbidities
  • All discharge destinations: home, SNF, acute rehab, skilled nursing facility
  • All procedures: CABG, valve repair/replacement, aortic surgery, MAZE, heart transplant, TAVR, etc.

Does NOT apply to:

  • Patients remaining hospitalized long-term (VAD, awaiting transplant, mechanical support weaning)
  • Pediatric patients (use age-adjusted criteria)

Special populations (apply full criteria with modifications per Deviation Triggers):

  • Age >75: higher frailty; lower discharge threshold for home health or SNF
  • CKD stage 4–5: electrolyte repletion more critical; medication renally-adjusted
  • Recent reintubation: extend monitoring; lower threshold for acute rehab vs home
  • Heart transplant / LVAD: prioritize early mobility; aggressive bowel regimen
  • Post-MAZE in early AF: DCCV ineffective until atrial maturity; anticoagulation priority

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Gather baseline and ongoing status* (5 minutes per shift)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside and chart review. Information-only; no interventions yet.

Baseline (POD 1 or unit transfer):

  • Cardiovascular: baseline BP, HR, rhythm; any home rate/rhythm meds held? Recent transfusions? Drips still running?
  • Respiratory: home O₂ requirement? SpO₂ on room air? Incentive spirometry independence? Last extubation? Reintubation history?
  • GI/GU: pre-op bowel function? Current diet tolerance? Last BM? Foley still in or removed? Post-void residual?
  • Wound: incision appearance (sternal, harvest sites)? Any erythema, drainage, dehiscence? Sutures/staples status?
  • Mobility: pre-op functional baseline? Current ambulation distance? Pain level? Transfer independence?
  • Cognition: alert & oriented? Delirium screening (CAM-ICU)? Understanding teaching?
  • Meds: all pre-op meds reconciled? New post-op agents listed? OTC + supplements included?
  • Social: home environment safe? Family/support available? Living situation? Financial barriers?

Daily shift assessment (POD 3–6):

  • Check 12 domains against readiness tables (§5)
  • Flag any NOT met: do NOT discharge; escalate to provider/case manager
  • Re-check q24 h until domain is met or alternative plan is in place

sections.heading: 5. Standard Practice — Readiness Criteria by Domain
5.1 Hemodynamic & Cardiac Stability Checklist
sections.bodyHtml:
Domain Criteria Action
BP/MAP Stable ×24 h; no escalating vasopressor need; MAP ≥65 mmHg VS trend q6h × 24 h; no uptrending pressors
Drips All infusions OFF ≥24 h (rare exception: weaning order documented) D/C summary lists any pending tapers or home continuation
HR/Rhythm HR 50–120 or baseline; stable sinus OR chronic arrhythmia with rate control achieved EKG within 24 h of D/C; rhythm stable on tele
Post-op AF Anticoagulation plan written; INR appointment scheduled (if warfarin); follow-up echo/EKG arranged Pharmacy consult documented; appointments in D/C summary
Chest tubes All tubes out ≥24 h; last drain output <30 mL/8 h; post-removal CXR acceptable CXR read; drain log reviewed; no air leak
Pacer wires Wires out OR clear removal plan with timeframe documented D/C summary: "removed POD ___" or "removal scheduled POD ___ at clinic"

sections.heading: 5.2 Respiratory Readiness
sections.bodyHtml:
Domain Criteria Action
Oxygenation SpO₂ ≥90% on room air OR stable home O₂ prescription written with patient/family trained O₂ order with liter flow; pulse oximeter prescribed for home
Dyspnea No acute dyspnea at rest or with ADL; RR <25; no accessory muscle use Nursing assessment; if dyspnea, workup for PE, HF, pneumonia
Secretion clearance Independent; incentive spirometry ≥1000 mL if goal-dependent; no reintubation risk Last IS volume documented; ability to use device confirmed

sections.heading: 5.3 Gastrointestinal & Elimination Readiness
sections.bodyHtml:
Domain Criteria Action
Feeding Tolerating diet without N/V, distention, or diarrhea; goal diet (cardiac, diabetic, renal) understood Diet order; RN/dietitian assessment; teach-back if special diet
Bowel BM documented POD 1+ OR reasonable plan; bowel regimen written for home (colace, senna, PEG, etc.) Last BM date; home meds ordered; prevents post-discharge impaction
Foley Catheter removed; voiding spontaneously; UOP normal (≥0.5 mL/kg/h); post-void residual ≤100 mL if checked Last void >300 mL; no dysuria; no hematuria

sections.heading: 5.4 Wound & Infection Status
sections.bodyHtml:
Domain Criteria Action
Incision Sternal + harvest incisions (if present) clean, dry, intact; no open edges or purulent drainage RN wound assessment; photo if high-risk; no cellulitis
Infection markers Temp <101°F × 48 h; WBC trending down or stable; culture results if obtained Last temp, last WBC; any fever workup completed
Cellulitis No erythema/induration ≥2 cm beyond incision line; no spreading redness Visual exam; inflammatory markers obtained if concern
Wound care Patient/family trained on incision care (keep dry, pat dry after shower); understand infection red flags Wound care handout given; teach-back confirmed

sections.heading: 5.5 Mobility & Functional Status
sections.bodyHtml:
Domain Criteria Action
Ambulation Walking ≥200 feet (or baseline if frail) with supervision or contact guard; no acute fall risk Functional score documented (FAC, MIF, or bedside distance)
Stairs If home has stairs, able to negotiate with supervision (if not achieved, discharge plan adjusted) Stair negotiation attempted ± OT observation
Pain control Pain ≤4/10 at rest, ≤6/10 with activity, on oral analgesics only Pain trend; opioid taper plan in place
Opioid taper Clear taper plan written (e.g., "reduce by 1 dose q3-5 days") D/C opioid Rx + taper instructions provided to patient

sections.heading: 5.6 Cognitive & Behavioral Readiness
sections.bodyHtml:
Domain Criteria Action
Cognition Alert & oriented ×3; no active delirium; CAM-ICU negative if done Mental status exam documented; delirium screening completed
Understanding Patient verbalizes understanding of discharge instructions (teach-back method) "Patient taught [topic] and returned demonstration" × each topic
Mood No active suicidality or severe depression (screen with PHQ-9 post-CABG if indicated) Mood assessment; SW consult if PHQ-9 >10 or concern for safety

sections.heading: 5.7 Medication Reconciliation & Education
sections.bodyHtml:
Domain Criteria Action
Complete list All home + new post-op meds listed (including OTC + supplements); no duplicates or interactions Reconciled med list verified by pharmacy
Teach-back For each new medication: indication, dose, timing, side effects, when to call MD Teach-back note per medication documented
Warfarin/INR If on warfarin: INR appointment within 3–5 days; goal range written; patient has appointment card Lab order in EHR; appointment scheduled BEFORE D/C
Prescriptions D/C Rx sent to pharmacy; patient/family confirms pickup location/time; electronic delivery options offered Pharmacy verification note; confirmation with patient
Allergies Allergy list reviewed and flagged in D/C summary; no contraindicated agents prescribed Allergy list reconciled

sections.heading: 5.8 Discharge Teaching Topics — Standardized Curriculum
sections.bodyHtml:
Topic Key Content Verification
Sternal precautions No lifting >10 lbs; no driving ×4–6 weeks; cough splinting; log-roll to sit Return-demo of log-roll + heart pillow use
Activity progression Walking, stairs, return-to-work timeline, sexual activity at 4–6 weeks Patient voices timeline; family present
Red flag symptoms Chest pain, dyspnea, fever >101°F, drainage, palpitations, syncope, severe swelling Laminated wallet card reviewed; patient names ≥3 warning signs
Medications Why, how much, when, side effects, interactions (see §5.7) Teach-back per medication documented
Weight monitoring Daily weigh, call if gain >2–3 lbs in 1 week (HF sign) Digital scale provided or confirmed at home
Incision care Keep dry, shower OK after 1 week, pat dry, watch for infection signs Teach-back; infection red flags named
Cardiac rehab Program location, dates, importance (↓ mortality, readmission) Rehab enrollment confirmed BEFORE D/C or within 1 week
Diet & fluids Cardiac diet <2 g Na/day; fluid restriction if EF <35%; meal planning reviewed Dietary handout; understanding of "salty foods" verified
Follow-up appointments Surgeon 4 weeks, cardiologist 2–4 weeks, PCP 1–2 weeks, INR if warfarin Calendar given; each appointment in D/C summary

sections.heading: 5.9 Disposition Decision Tree
sections.bodyHtml: Patient meets ALL 12 readiness domains? ├─ YES: Safe home environment + strong support + young/independent │ └─ DISCH to HOME (no home health) — standard follow-up │ ├─ YES: Safe home environment BUT age >75 OR lives alone OR moderate frailty (CFS ≥5) OR high complexity │ └─ DISCH to HOME + HOME HEALTH (RN ± PT/OT) ×2–3 weeks │ └─ Criteria: Age >75 OR CFS ≥5 OR CKD stage 4+ OR poor mobility OR lives >1 h from surgeon │ ├─ YES: Home unsafe (stairs, lives alone, advanced dementia, no support) │ └─ DISCH to SNF ×7–14 days │ └─ Pre-auth obtained; bed confirmed POD 1; PT/OT at SNF; transition home after │ ├─ YES: High complexity (frailty, polypharmacy, CKD stage 4+, recent reintubation, post-VAD) │ └─ DISCH to ACUTE REHAB ×7–14 days │ └─ Intensive PT/OT; med optimization; re-eval and transition to SNF or home │ └─ NO: Does NOT meet criteria └─ HOLD DISCHARGE └─ Identify barrier (pending tube removal? pain control? teaching incomplete?) └─ Interdisciplinary team huddle └─ Reassess q24 h └─ Escalate if barriers unresolved >48 h

sections.heading: 5.10 Readmission Risk Stratification
sections.bodyHtml:
Risk Level Characteristics Discharge Plan Modifications
Low risk Age <65; LVEF ≥40%; no CKD; no diabetes; independent; strong support Home without home health; standard follow-up q2-4 weeks
Moderate risk Age 65–75; LVEF 30–40%; CKD stage 3; diabetes; lives alone; adequate support Home + home health RN ×2–3 visits; close PCP follow-up
High risk Age >75 OR LVEF <30% OR CKD stage 4+ OR recent reintubation OR post-VAD; weak support SNF ×10–14 days OR Acute Rehab; home health RN + PT ×3–4 weeks; intensified follow-up
Very high risk Palliative candidate (NYHA IV + multiple comorbidities); expected survival <1 year Palliative care consult BEFORE D/C; hospice discussion; comfort focus; simplified med list

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. No BM × 3+ days on bowel regimen — verify compliance; check electrolytes; consider imaging (KUB) or methylnaltrexone (see Bowel Regimen protocol)
  2. Persistent dyspnea despite room air trial — exclude PE, pneumonia, HF exacerbation; extend O₂ trial; may delay D/C
  3. Pain not controlled on oral meds — reassess need for extended opioid prescription or multimodal alternatives; do NOT discharge in severe pain
  4. Delirium persists or worsens — hold discharge; workup for UTI, hypoxia, metabolic derangement; psychiatry consult if indicated
  5. Incision showing signs of deep infection — erythema spreading, fluctuance, feculent drainage, fever + elevated WBC + rising lactate = DSWI until proven otherwise; surgical consult; do NOT discharge
  6. Ambulation distance declining or patient deconditioned — aggressive PT; re-assess POD 5–6; may warrant SNF or acute rehab
  7. Home environment unsafe and NO family support identified — mandatory SNF or acute rehab placement; delay D/C if beds unavailable
  8. Medication list incomplete or teach-back failed — do NOT discharge until all meds reconciled and patient can repeat back indication + dose for each new agent
  9. Readmission risk HIGH or VERY HIGH but disposition not arranged — do NOT discharge home without home health or to facility; escalate to case manager
  10. Post-D/C phone call plan NOT documented — assign responsibility to RN or home health; note in D/C summary

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
— novice + advanced beginner deep-dive)

Readiness domain details and common barriers

Hemodynamic: Most common miss = beta-blocker restarted late. AFib + off beta-blockers for >48 h is a setup for POAF. Verify home meds restarted POD 2–3.

Respiratory: Home O₂ weaning should be conservative post-discharge. Better to over-prescribe 2 LNC than send patient home desaturating. Incentive spirometry independence is less critical than room air SpO₂ goal.

GI/GU: Foley catheter still in = do NOT discharge (UTI/CAUTI risk). Post-void residual >150 mL is abnormal and warrants urology consult or pelvic floor PT. Bowel regimen non-negotiable: 60–80% of post-op patients experience constipation; starting docusate + PEG POD 1 prevents distention.

Wound: A "clean" incision = pink, slightly swollen, no drainage. "Clean-contaminated" = minimal serosanguineous drainage, no cellulitis. "Contaminated" = purulent drainage, erythema >2 cm, fever, elevated WBC = call surgeon STAT. DSWI can present late (POD 7–10), so discharge summaries must flag infection red flags clearly.

Mobility: >200 feet is a rough benchmark for independent home ambulation. Frail elderly may discharge at 100–150 feet if home health arranged. If patient cannot negotiate stairs and home has stairs, PT must visit before D/C or discharge to facility.

Cognition: Delirium on POD 3–5 is common but must RESOLVE before discharge. Discharging a delirious patient = medication errors, falls at home, readmission within 48 h. If delirium persists, psychiatry consult + metabolic workup (UTI, hypoxia, electrolytes, infection). Do NOT blame it on "normal post-op." Meds: Teach-back is THE most powerful intervention. Patients asked to explain back their meds show 50%+ better compliance. Written list + pillow organizer + family present + clear red flag card = discharge success.

Addressing common patient fears and family questions "I'm not ready; I feel weak." → "Weakness is normal. The goal is safe discharge to a place where you can keep recovering. We may send you to rehab for a few days of PT. Recovery takes 6–8 weeks at home." "What if something goes wrong at home?" → "You'll have a phone number for your surgeon and cardiologist. We're setting you up with a home health nurse who will visit within 24 hours. We'll also call you within 48 hours to check in." "I don't want to go to a nursing home." → "Home health at your house is an option. We're here to make the safest plan for YOU." "Who's going to help me at home?" → "We've talked to [family member/support person]. They're on the plan. If you live alone, we'll arrange home health visits." "My incision still looks red." → "Pink and slightly swollen is normal. We want you to watch for spreading redness, pus, or opening up. Here's a photo card of what to worry about." "I don't understand all these medications." → "We're going to go through each one step by step. You tell me back what it does and when you take it. We'll write it down and give you a card for your wallet."
High-yield timing and milestones

POD 1: Discharge planning huddle (case manager, SW, PT/OT, pharmacy, RN). Identify barriers early. Frailty screening.

POD 2–3: Risk stratification. Home environment check. Disposition decision (home vs SNF vs acute rehab). Pre-auth bed if facility discharge.

POD 3–4: Begin comprehensive discharge teaching (inform → verify → confirm model).

POD 4–5: Teach-back method for medications + sternal precautions + red flags.

POD 5–6: Final functional assessment. Finalize disposition. Verify all appointments scheduled.

POD day: Final D/C summary review. Red flag card in hand. Post-D/C phone call RN assigned. Patient leaves with: med list, appointment calendar, contact numbers, red flag card, dietary handout.

POD 1–2 post-D/C: RN phone call home. Assess pain, meds, incision, any red flag symptoms.

POD 3–7 post-D/C: Home health RN visit (if arranged). Wound check, vitals, med verification.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These indicate re-escalation or intervention needed.

  • Fever ≥101°F + incision erythema/drainage — possible early DSWI; culture wound; do NOT discharge until cleared
  • Incision opening or dehiscence — call surgeon immediately; assess if superficial or deep sternal involvement
  • Increasing dyspnea despite room air trial — rule out PE, pneumonia, acute HF; may warrant extended O₂ or hospitalization
  • Persistent or worsening delirium — metabolic workup mandatory; UTI/sepsis screen; psychiatry consult
  • Declining ambulation distance or acute weakness — possible unrecognized complication (sepsis, AKI, MI); reassess; do NOT discharge if trending down
  • Severe uncontrolled pain despite opioid escalation — consider alternative diagnoses (PE, pericarditis, MI); extended admission may be needed
  • Hypotension refractory to fluid or developing shock — hold discharge; escalate to ICU if needed
  • Inability to void post-Foley removal + abdominal distention — urinary retention; may need straight catheterization; pelvic floor PT consult
  • Bowel obstruction signs (distention + vomiting + obstipation + rising lactate) — NPO + imaging + surgical consult; do NOT attempt discharge
  • Patient or family refusal of discharge teaching or plan — document refusal; involve social work; consider capacity evaluation if safety at risk

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
(10–15 high-yield bullets for experienced nurses and experts)

  1. Teach-back is NOT information-giving; it's verification of understanding. Many nurses dump information and assume retention. Instead: "I've explained your blood pressure med. Can you tell me what it does and when you take it?" Listen carefully. Correct misunderstandings on the spot.

  2. Written instructions MUST go home with every patient. Verbal teaching alone = 50% retention. Provide handout, laminated wallet card with red flags, med list printout. Confirm patient physically has it.

  3. Family/caregiver presence at discharge teaching is NON-NEGOTIABLE. If partner isn't available, delay teaching or use video call. Many post-D/C errors are due to family not understanding the plan (lifting restrictions, medication timing, red flags).

  4. Medication reconciliation must include OTC + supplements. Patients underreport ASA, ibuprofen, multivitamins, herbal teas, fish oil — all of which interact with cardiac meds. Ask directly: "What pills, vitamins, or supplements do you take at home?"

  5. INR follow-up cannot be "call them tomorrow." Schedule the lab appointment BEFORE discharge. Patient leaves with appointment card. Put it in the D/C summary. Pharmacist verifies patient knows where to go.

  6. Cardiac rehab referral is universal, but underutilized. 30–40% of eligible patients don't start rehab. Say: "Cardiac rehab is as important as your meds. It reduces your risk of dying and coming back to the hospital. I'm enrolling you now; here's where you go."

  7. Home health services for frail or high-risk patients prevent readmission. Use Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS ≥5 = moderate frailty). If CFS ≥5 OR lives alone AND no family support OR poor mobility, order home health. Intensive follow-up (3–4 visits ×2 weeks) cuts readmissions.

  8. Disposition decision MUST happen POD 1–2, not on D/C day. Late decisions delay discharge, create bottlenecks, increase patient anxiety. Case manager + SW + RN huddle on POD 1: Is home safe? If not, which facility? Pre-auth bed today.

  9. Readmission rates are a quality + cost metric. 30-day readmission = lower CMS star rating, penalties, reputation damage. Every nurse contributes. Safe discharge planning is core nursing work.

  10. Post-discharge phone calls (RN, within 48–72 h) reduce 30-day readmissions by 5–8% (Rockwell et al., 2016). Five minutes: "How's your pain? Are you taking your meds? Is your incision healing? Any fevers or shortness of breath?" Catches problems early.

  11. Palliative care consult should happen early for NYHA IV + multiple comorbidities. Don't wait until D/C day. Palliative care helps with goals-of-care conversations, symptom management, family support. Simplifies med list; improves quality of life.

  12. Cognitive impairment requires simplified plans. If patient has dementia or delirium at D/C, simplify: fewer meds, written + visual instructions, caregiver heavily involved, increase follow-up frequency. A complex med list for a confused patient is a recipe for error.

  13. Social determinants matter as much as medical readiness. Ask: "Can you afford your meds? Do you have reliable transportation to follow-up visits? Do you have food at home?" If barriers exist, involve social work early. Financial hardship + unmet food/transport needs = readmission.

  14. Patient portal activation at discharge improves adherence. Many patients don't access their portal. Walk them through it: show how to message surgeon, view test results, refill Rx. Patients who use the portal have better outcomes.

  15. Pill organizer use significantly improves compliance in patients on ≥5 meds. Ask: "Do you take your meds from bottles, or do you use an organizer?" Many elderly benefit from pre-filled organizers. Small tool, big impact.

cards.title: Discharge Disposition Decisions
cards.quickAnswer: Start disposition planning POD 1–2, not discharge day. Decision depends on functional status (CFS, ambulation), cognitive status, social support, home environment, and medical complexity (IV antibiotics, wound care). Involve interdisciplinary team (MD, case manager, PT/OT, SW, pharmacy) in daily rounds. Home (no services) requires independence + adequate informal support. Home with home health = PT/OT at home, nursing for wound/IV care, 7–21 days typical. SNF = skilled nursing ongoing (IV antibiotics, complex wounds, PT multiple days/week), 14–30 days. IRF = intensive rehab 3+ hours/day post-stroke/amputation, requires PT/OT clearance. LTACH = medically complex, vent-dependent, multi-organ support. Hospice = comfort care, terminal. Early planning + appropriate placement prevents readmission and reduces length of stay.
