sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, scope.

  • Definition: A structured, interdisciplinary decision process that matches a patient's medical, functional, cognitive, and social needs to the appropriate post-acute care setting at discharge.
  • Why it matters: Appropriate disposition reduces unplanned 30-day readmissions (CMS quality metric), optimizes hospital length of stay, enables recovery, and prevents cost overruns. Housing-insecure and language-limited patients need intensive planning early.
  • Who it applies to: Every patient discharged from acute care except those transferred to another inpatient facility or who expired.
  • When to start: POD 1–2, not discharge day. Early planning prevents bottlenecks, enables SNF/IRF coordination, and prevents inappropriate placements that delay discharge.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Key Drivers
sections.bodyHtml:
Appropriate disposition depends on convergence of four decision drivers:

Functional status — Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS 1–3 = home reasonable; 4–5 = home with services or SNF; 6–7 = SNF, LTACH, or hospice); ambulation (independent vs assistive device vs wheelchair); ADL independence (Katz scale).

Cognitive status — Delirium may reverse; baseline dementia affects discharge safety.

Lives alone + cognitive impairment = HIGH RISK for medication errors, falls, wandering → SNF required.

Social support — 24/7 caregiver available and willing? Not just "yes" — verify employment status, burnout, ability. Living alone nearly impossible to discharge home without services.

Home environment and medical complexity — Stairs to bathroom (mobility barrier), grab bars, accessible shower. IV antibiotics (home if short course, reliable caregiver, RN access; otherwise SNF). Complex wounds (professional assessment daily = SNF). Ventilator (home vent care requires specialized training, backup power; otherwise LTACH).

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — patient populations and timing.

Universally indicated:

  • Every cardiac surgery patient on POD 1–2 regardless of expected acuity level
  • Includes CABG, valve repair/replacement, aortic surgery, transplant, ECMO weaning

Timing triggers:

  • Admission day for complex or expected-long-stay cases (preoperative optimization, transplant workup)
  • POD 1 for routine post-operative patients once hemodynamically stable

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Gather baseline information* (10 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic review. Information-only; no recommendations yet.

Functional baseline (pre-hospitalization):

  • Lived independently? Required assistance? Institutionalized?
  • Ambulation: independent, walker, wheelchair, bedbound?
  • ADL independence: feeding, dressing, toileting, bathing, continence?

Current function (ongoing POD 1+):

  • CFS score (reassess every 2–3 days)
  • 6-minute walk test if mobility safe
  • Cognition: alert, oriented, CAM delirium screen
  • Mood: depression screen if indicated

Social structure:

  • Lives alone vs with partner/family?
  • Caregiver available 24/7? Willing? Employment status?
  • Housing stable? Homeless/housing-insecure?
  • Insurance: Medicare, Medicaid, private, uninsured?

Home environment:

  • Stairs to entrance or bathroom?
  • Grab bars, accessible shower/toilet?
  • Single-level vs multi-level?

Medical complexity:

  • IV antibiotics ongoing? Duration?
  • Wound care needs (daily dressing changes, complex wounds)?
  • Monitoring needs (INR, glucose, output, labs)?
  • Cognitive impairment + lives alone = high risk for discharge failure

sections.heading: 5.1 Disposition options — criteria, services, and duration
sections.bodyHtml:
Option Setting Functional Level Medical Complexity Typical Duration Skilled Services Key Criteria
Home (no services) Own home/apt Independent (CFS ≤3) Stable, no wound/IV/monitoring Indefinite None; informal support Meets all readiness criteria; adequate informal support; patient/family independent ADL
Home with home health Own home/apt Mostly independent to modified independence (CFS 2–5) Moderate: IV antibiotics, wound dressing, INR monitoring, PT/OT 7–21 days (extends to 60 days) RN 2–3×/week; PT/OT 1–3×/week Skilled nursing + PT/OT feasible; home setting preferred; limited duration; family can support
SNF Licensed facility Dependent to modified independence (CFS 4–6) Ongoing skilled nursing (IV antibiotics, complex wounds, daily assessment); PT/OT multiple days/week 14–30 days (4–6 weeks) RN 24/7; PT/OT daily or >2×/week 24/7 supervision needed; complex or slow-healing wounds; medically complex; cognitive impairment + isolation
Inpatient Rehab (IRF) Rehabilitation hospital Dependent to modified independence (CFS 3–6) Moderate: recovering from CVA, amputation, severe deconditioning; stable medically 14–21 days (extends to 60 days) PT/OT/SLP >3 h/day; RN 24/7; team rounds Can tolerate 3+ h/day therapy; stroke/amputation/deconditioning rehab potential; PT/OT clearance required
LTACH LTACH facility Dependent (CFS 5–7) High: tracheostomy/vent weaning, organ support, complex wounds, sepsis/prolonged illness 21–60+ days RN 24/7; respiratory therapy; specialized wound care Medically complex; vent-dependent or vent-weaning; organ support; specialized wound care; ICU-level monitoring
Hospice Home or inpatient facility Dependent to totally dependent (CFS 6–7) Terminal; comfort-focused; palliative care Days to weeks RN/aide for comfort; symptom management; spiritual support Terminal prognosis; comfort-focus goals; <6 months life expectancy

sections.heading: 5.2 Decision process — POD-by-POD timeline
sections.bodyHtml:
POD 1–2: Screen for discharge risk factors

  1. Document functional baseline (pre-op and current), cognitive status, social support, home environment, medical complexity
  2. Identify discharge risk factors early (cognitive impairment, isolation, housing insecurity, complex medical needs)

POD 2–3: Involve interdisciplinary team

  • PT/OT: assess functional prognosis and rehab potential
  • Case manager: verify insurance coverage, SNF/IRF bed availability, prior authorization needs (DO NOT WAIT until POD 6)
  • Social worker: assess living situation, caregiver, barriers (family meeting early if needed)
  • Pharmacy: evaluate medication complexity, compliance risk

POD 4–5: Propose disposition + obtain consent

  • By POD 4, disposition documented and family meeting held if preference conflicts with clinical recommendation
  • Use shared decision-making; document if patient choice differs from clinical recommendation

POD 5–6: Coordinate placement + finalize teaching

  • SNF: referral submitted, facility accepts/declines within 24 h, transportation arranged
  • IRF: PT/OT clears; prior auth submitted; admission scheduled
  • Home health: orders written; referral submitted; first visit within 24–48 h
  • Discharge teaching reinforces disposition rationale, follow-up, red flags

sections.heading: 5.3 Clinical decision scenarios
sections.bodyHtml:
Clinical Picture Recommended Disposition Rationale
CFS 1–2, ambulating, no wound/IV, lives with partner, stable Home no services Independent; adequate support; meets all readiness criteria
CFS 3–4, walker, 1–2 weeks IV antibiotics, lives with partner, PT/OT needed Home with home health Skilled nursing + PT/OT feasible; limited duration (14–21 days); family support adequate
CFS 4–5, minimal ambulation, cognition impaired, lives alone; no caregiver SNF Cannot be home-safe; cognitive impairment + isolation = high risk; SNF provides 24/7 supervision
CFS 3–4, post-stroke, mild deficit, strong rehab potential, motivated, medically stable Inpatient Rehab (IRF) Can tolerate 3+ h/day therapy; stroke recovery trajectory supports intensive rehab; requires PT/OT clearance
CFS 4–5, post-major amputation, on multiple pressors, complex wounds, vent risk LTACH Medically complex, organ support, specialized wound care, vent weaning; IRF not appropriate
CFS 6–7, advanced HF/cancer, comfort goals, declining trajectory Hospice Can be home if caregiver 24/7, or inpatient if alone; palliative consult POD 1–2

sections.heading: 5.4 Reversible barriers and escalation triggers
sections.bodyHtml:
Always address these factors before assuming disposition failure:

Factor Target Action
Housing insecurity Stable housing identified or plan in place Intensive SW coordination; may need extended facility stay until housing secured; work with community partners
Language / literacy barriers Interpreter services confirmed; discharge materials in patient language Order interpreter for initial home health visit; use teach-back method + pictures/symbols
Caregiver burnout Realistic support plan + respite options Validate family exhaustion; SNF transition is appropriate support, not failure; plan ongoing family involvement
Insurance barriers Coverage verified; prior auth submitted early Case manager must verify Medicare Part A days, Medicaid coverage, private plan copays by POD 2–3
Medical complexity not matching placement Skilled services aligned with medical needs Communicate complexity clearly to receiving facility; escalate if services insufficient

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Needs Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. Proposed disposition conflicts with clinical picture — e.g., patient insists home, CFS 6, cognitive impairment, lives alone → MD/social worker discussion; document shared decision-making
  2. Insurance barriers block placement — Medicare Part A days exhausted, Medicaid doesn't cover SNF in this state, private insurance denies prior auth → case manager to explore alternatives (extended facility stay pending auth, Medicaid application, community resources)
  3. No 24/7 caregiver available but patient/family insist on home → home health can supplement, but cannot replace 24/7 supervision for dependent patient; renegotiate expectations or escalate to SNF
  4. Cognitive impairment appears to improve by POD 4 (delirium reversing) — reassess disposition if original plan was SNF based solely on acute confusion
  5. Family meeting uncovers significant social barriers (substance use, domestic violence, homelessness, language isolation) → escalate to social worker for intensive planning; may delay discharge
  6. PT/OT assessment reveals lower rehab potential than expected — if patient cannot tolerate 3+ h/day therapy, IRF not appropriate; SNF + PT/OT is better choice
  7. Medical complexity increases unexpectedly (new infection, vent dependence, organ support) → escalate from home/SNF to LTACH; coordinate transfer early

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections intended for in-app collapse. New-grad and advanced-beginner staff expand for deeper understanding; experienced nurses can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Medicare and insurance requirements
sections.bodyHtml:
SNF eligibility:

  • Requires 3-day qualifying hospital admission (document; some patients don't meet this)
  • Medicare Part A covers up to 100 days
  • First 20 days: fully covered
  • Days 21–100: patient pays daily copay (~$200/day in 2026)
  • Medicaid coverage varies by state; some states limit SNF days or require SNF trial before IRF

IRF eligibility:

  • Medicare requires qualifying diagnosis (stroke, amputation, spinal cord injury, major joint replacement, cardiac surgery with major deficit, polytrauma, neurological disease)
  • Patient must be able to tolerate 3+ h/day of therapy (PT/OT/SLP combined)
  • Prior authorization required; process 24–48 h
  • Medicare covers 60 days; private insurance copay variable

LTACH eligibility:

  • Requires 3-day qualifying hospital admission
  • Medicare Part A covers; limited bed availability (coordinate early)
  • Not appropriate for patients who can recover at SNF/IRF

Home health coverage:

  • Medicare covers if homebound, skilled nursing or PT/OT indicated, MD orders written
  • No copay (100% covered)
  • Medicaid coverage varies by state
  • Private insurance variable; some require prior auth

sections.heading: 7.2 Common discharge decision conflicts — shared decision-making language
sections.bodyHtml:
Patient/family says: "I want to go home." Clinically appropriate for SNF.

Response: "I understand you want to be home — most people do. Based on your medical needs right now (complex wound care, IV medications, needing help with bathing), home with family as your only support would put you at risk for complications. SNF provides the skilled nursing care you need short-term, and we expect a 3–4 week stay while you recover. We can arrange daily family visits, and you'll be working with therapy to strengthen your independence. Does that help?"

Patient/family says: "Why does PT say I need 3+ hours of therapy? That sounds exhausting."

Response: "The therapy intensive is designed to help you recover faster and more completely. IRF patients typically go home sooner and with better function than SNF-only patients. We won't start at 3 hours on day 1 — we'll build up gradually. If you can't tolerate it, we can adjust. But the research shows this intensity works."

Patient says: "My daughter can take care of me at home." Daughter works full-time.

Response: "Your daughter is clearly committed to helping. Home health nursing and PT can supplement during the day, but she can't provide 24/7 care and work too. SNF doesn't mean she's not involved — she can visit daily, help with decisions, practice the care techniques we teach. Many families do this transition for 2–3 weeks while the patient recovers. After that, home might be more realistic with her part-time help. What does your daughter think?"

sections.heading: 7.3 Special populations and edge cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Heart transplant and LVAD patients:

  • Valsalva during straining is poorly tolerated; prioritize bowel regimen from POD 0
  • Mobility and rehab are critical; IRF often preferred over SNF for intensive PT/OT
  • Consider earlier disposition planning (POD 0) due to complexity

Pacer-wire-dependent patients:

  • Early mobility essential; SNF PT/OT must understand pacing-wire limitations
  • Higher fall risk early; facilities should be notified

Post-MAZE patients:

  • Early AF common; rate control + amiodarone, not cardioversion, until scarring matures
  • Otherwise standard disposition criteria apply

Homeless or housing-insecure patients:

  • Cannot safely discharge to shelter + home health
  • May need extended facility stay until housing secured (work with community partners, housing voucher programs)
  • SW consult POD 1–2 essential

Language-dependent or illiterate patients:

  • Home health success depends on interpreter access and teach-back method
  • Visual/pictorial discharge materials essential
  • Consider SNF if language/literacy barriers substantial; facility staff can provide translated care

sections.heading: 7.4 Advanced strategies — high-yield tactics
sections.bodyHtml:
Early family meeting (POD 2–3) prevents discharge delays. Rather than waiting until POD 5 for a family meeting, involve family early if disposition is not straightforward. This builds alignment and prevents surprises.

"SNF as a bridge" — shared decision-making for uncertain cases. For borderline cases (e.g., CFS 4, limited informal support), a realistic approach is: "Let's try SNF for 2–3 weeks while you recover and build strength. We can reassess discharge-to-home feasibility after that." This reduces readmissions and builds family trust.

Communicate medical complexity clearly to receiving facility. Write discharge summary that explicitly lists IV antibiotics, wound care complexity, monitoring needs, cognitive status. SNF nurses and IRF therapists perform better when they know what they're walking into.

Home health does not replace 24/7 caregiver. If patient is dependent (CFS ≥5) and lives alone, home health RN 2–3×/week is NOT enough. Be explicit in family discussion: "Home health supplements but cannot provide 24/7 supervision."

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration in a Currently "Stable" Disposition Plan
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any develop, re-escalate disposition decision.

  • Sudden cognitive decline (delirium not improving, baseline dementia worsening) — home-safe status changes; SNF may be required
  • Unplanned readmission from previously "appropriate" disposition — retrospectively indicates misplacement; examine barriers (inadequate home health, caregiver collapse, medical complexity underestimated)
  • Family requesting SNF pivot after deciding on home — caregiver burnout or medical complexity emerging; listen and escalate
  • Pacer dysfunction or new arrhythmia post-op — mobility and early discharge plans may need modification
  • Wound complication emerging (infection, dehiscence) — "simple dressing" becomes "complex care"; SNF consideration increases
  • Transportation barriers identified late — no family to drive to IR PT, no wheelchair-accessible transport to home; escalate before discharge
  • Substance use or untreated mental illness emerging during admission — affects home-safety and caregiver capacity; SW consult
  • Significant pain or depression evident POD 4–5 — pain control in home setting may be inadequate; home health assessment needed
  • Insurance denial of placement at last moment — have backup plan ready (extended facility stay, alternative facility, Medicaid application)

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Disposition planning starts POD 1–2, not discharge day. Waiting until POD 6 creates bottlenecks and forces inappropriate placements. Early team huddle prevents crises.

  2. CFS ≥5 often needs SNF or home with 24/7 caregiver. Don't assume high-CFS patients can go home. Assess social support first.

  3. Social support is as important as medical complexity. A patient with IV antibiotics but loving spouse at home can manage home health. Same patient alone? SNF.

  4. Insurance verification is critical—do it early (POD 2–3). Prior authorization takes 24–48 h. Case manager must verify Medicare Part A days, Medicaid coverage, private copays.

  5. SNF can manage IV antibiotics for 4–6 weeks (e.g., endocarditis). No need to delay discharge for ongoing antibiotics; SNF has IV infrastructure.

  6. IRF requires 3+ h/day therapy tolerance + realistic rehab potential. Not every stroke patient is IRF candidate. If patient plateaus or cannot tolerate >2 h/day, SNF is better choice.

  7. "Home without services" is rare. Verify 24/7 caregiver is truly available (not working full-time, not burned out). Most "independent" discharges still benefit from home health RN visit × 1 for safety assessment.

  8. Patient/family preference matters, but not the sole determinant. If patient insists home but CFS ≥6, lives alone, cognitively impaired → MD discussion required. Document shared decision-making; ensure informed consent.

  9. Readmission is a quality metric. Patients discharged to wrong level of care readmit within 30 days, increasing cost and worse outcomes. Early, appropriate placement prevents this.

  10. Interdisciplinary rounds reduce LOS. Daily huddle (MD, RN, case manager, PT/OT, SW) discussing disposition shortens hospital stay and prevents bottlenecks.

  11. Palliative care consult POD 1–2 for advanced disease. Early honest goals conversation prevents futile escalation and supports smooth hospice transition.

  12. Homeless/housing-insecure patients need SW intensive planning. Cannot discharge to shelter + home health. May need extended facility stay until housing secured.

  13. Cognitive impairment + lives alone = NOT home-safe. Even if delirium reverses, if baseline cognition impaired and no caregiver, SNF is indicated.

  14. Language barriers affect home teaching success. Order interpreter for initial RN visit. Use teach-back method + pictures/symbols. Consider SNF if barriers substantial.

  15. Document disposition rationale and patient/family consent clearly. If disposition preference differs from clinical recommendation, document the discussion, patient understanding, and final decision.

cards.title: Early Mobility Post-Cardiac Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: Start mobility POD 0–1 post-extubation if hemodynamically stable (MAP ≥ 65, HR 40–120, no active bleeding, pain ≤ 5/10). Progression: dangle legs → sit in chair → stand at bedside → walk with gait belt + 2-person assist. Anticipate orthostatic hypotension universal POD 1–2 — use sit-1-min, stand-1-min, march-1-min protocol. Pain medications 15–30 min before mobility, not after. Sternal precautions (elbows tucked, no pushing with arms) integrate with walking — do not restrict ambulation. Document every mobility attempt: distance, vital signs, symptoms, assist level. Nursing-led BID ambulation (morning + evening walks) is the real driver; PT is supplement, not sole provider.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, scope, when it applies.

  • Definition: Systematic, progressive physical activity initiated immediately post-extubation in post-cardiac surgery patients to prevent complications (HAP, VTE, ileus, delirium), optimize oxygenation, reduce length of stay, and improve functional recovery.
  • Why it matters: Early mobility (first steps POD 0–1) reduces hospital-acquired pneumonia by 28%, VTE by 20%, and length of stay by 1–2 days; improves preservation of muscle mass and psychological recovery (Morris et al., 2008; Bailey et al., 2007).
  • Who it applies to: Every extubated post-cardiac surgery patient (CABG, valve, aortic, myectomy, MAZE, heart transplant, etc.) unless hemodynamically unstable (see §4).
  • Timeline: POD 0 (post-extubation) → POD 1–3 (progressive ambulation) → POD 4+ (independent walking) → discharge with home walking plan.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why Early Mobility
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative immobility creates a cascade of pathophysiologic stress on an already-compromised patient:

  • Splinting (pain + fear + sternal precaution misconception) — patients often refuse movement, believing "sternotomy = absolute bed rest"
  • Deconditioning cascade — 24 hours of bed rest causes measurable muscle atrophy; by POD 3, immobilized patients are deconditioning faster than they can recover
  • Venous stasis — recumbency → reduced lower-extremity muscle pump → DVT/PE risk
  • Pulmonary atelectasis — shallow breathing, reduced mobility → secretion pooling → HAP risk
  • Delayed GI motility — opioids + immobility + electrolyte shifts compound constipation; early ambulation activates the gastrocolic reflex
  • Delirium risk — bed rest paradoxically worsens delirium; early mobility + activity corrects it
  • Cardiovascular decoupling — lying supine for 48+ hours reduces autonomic tone; standing/walking retrains cardiovascular reflexes (orthostatic tolerance)

The evidence: AACN Practice Alert (2024) recommends early ICU mobility as a core component of the ABCDEF bundle. RCTs (Morris 2008, Bailey 2007) show feasibility and safety; meta-analyses support outcome benefit.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — inclusion and exclusion.

Universally indicated:

  • Every extubated post-op cardiac surgery patient able to follow commands and cooperate with transfers
  • Applies to CABG, all valve procedures, aortic surgery, MAZE, heart transplant, ECMO weaning, etc.
  • Regardless of age, pre-op functional status, or comorbidities — adapts per individual tolerance

Modified or delayed progression:

  • Redo surgery: slower progression; extended sternal precaution monitoring (altered sternal architecture)
  • Obesity or frailty: earlier 2-person assist; shorter walks; more frequent rest periods
  • Advanced age (> 75) + multiple comorbidities: conservative progression; earlier PT formalization
  • LVAD or heart transplant: prioritize from POD 0 (Valsalva during straining destabilizes preload); lower threshold for mobility escalation
  • Atrial fibrillation or pacing-dependent: monitor rhythm during exertion; stop if VT, loss of capture, or severe symptoms

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — Safety Criteria
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic evaluation. Do NOT mobilize if ANY criterion not met.

Safety Criterion Threshold Rationale
Hemodynamic stability MAP ≥ 65 mmHg; SBP 90–180 mmHg per [Institution policy]; HR 40–120 bpm, no new arrhythmia Hypotension = syncope/stroke/MI risk; hypertension = bleeding risk; arrhythmia = ischemia/cardiac decompensation
Bleeding Chest tube output stable (typically < 100 mL/hr recent, < 200 mL/4 hr); incision dry, no active oozing Surging output = contraindication; notify surgeon before mobilizing
Vasopressor support NOT on high-dose pressors — define per unit threshold (typically low-dose neosynephrine or epinephrine ≤ 2 mcg/kg/min only) High-dose = unstable; mobility will worsen hypotension
Pain control Numeric rating ≤ 5/10 at rest, ≤ 6/10 with movement Inadequate pain = splinting, poor breathing, refusal to move
Respiratory FiO₂ < 60%; SpO₂ ≥ 90% on current support; RR 10–30; no severe dyspnea at rest Hypoxia = mobility burden exceeds O₂ delivery
Cardiac rhythm Sinus rhythm or controlled rate rhythm; NO new VT, SVT, 3rd-degree heart block, loss of pacing capture Arrhythmia in motion = ischemia/syncope risk
Lines/tubes secure Chest tubes taped; central line stable; Foley secured; all patent and functioning Unsecured lines = dislodgement during transfers
Mental status Oriented or baseline mental status; NOT in severe acute delirium with violence/extreme agitation Severe agitation = fall risk (mild confusion OK with supervision)
No explicit restrictions Review surgeon/APP orders; no documented mobility restriction Surgeon may restrict post-exploration or after massive transfusion

Every-shift re-assessment: Do not assume yesterday's stable = today's stable. Re-check vital signs, chest tube output, pain, mental status, new orders.

sections.heading: 5. Standard Practice — Progression by POD
sections.bodyHtml:
POD Milestone Prerequisites Nursing Action Vital Sign Response PT/OT Role
0 (post-extubation) Sit on edge bed; dangle legs 5–15 min Extubated; stable vitals; pain controlled; alert Assist dangling ×1–2; monitor HR/BP/SpO₂; document tolerance; rest if dizzy HR may rise 10–20 bpm; acceptable SpO₂ dip to 88–90% if recovers Bedside eval if available; educate family
POD 1 Transfer to chair ×2–4 hrs; stand at bedside; walk 10–25 ft with gait belt + 2-person assist Tolerates POD 0; pain ≤ 5/10; no orthostatic symptoms Sit-1min, stand-1min, march-1min protocol; continuous SpO₂ monitor if on supplemental O₂; reduce assist as tolerated; gait belt required HR 20–30 bpm rise during walk acceptable; SpO₂ should not drop > 5% or below 85% Formal PT consult; gait training; reinforce sternal precautions
POD 2–3 Walk 25–50 ft BID; reduce to 1-person + gait belt; address barriers (pain, delirium, fatigue) Tolerates POD 1 well; orthostatic symptoms resolved; no new complications Nurse-led BID walks (AM + PM minimum); increase distance per tolerance; optimize pain meds pre-walk; engage family HR plateau by POD 3; SpO₂ stable without drop; orthostatic symptoms rare by end POD 2 PT daily or per frequency; focus on barriers; teach home progression
POD 4+ Walk 50–100 ft; independent with gait belt; stairs if appropriate; prepare discharge home plan Consistent tolerance POD 2–3; pain controlled; no new complications; cleared by surgeon Continue BID walks; reduce assist to belt-only; begin discharge teaching: daily home walking, gradual increase, warning signs; cardiac rehab referral HR/BP response predictable; minimal SpO₂ variation Final functional assessment; home exercise prescription; rehab letter

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. Safety criteria no longer met during walk (systolic BP drops < 90, HR > 120, new arrhythmia, SpO₂ < 85% not recovering, chest pain, severe dyspnea) — stop walk immediately, sit/lie flat, notify APP
  2. Chest tube output surges during or after walk (e.g., 50 mL/hr → 200 mL/hr) — assess for bleeding source; may need to halt mobility pending evaluation
  3. Orthostatic symptoms worsen despite sit-1-min/stand-1-min protocol (e.g., patient syncope or near-syncope) — notify APP; assess for dehydration, anemia, or cardiac etiologies; may need IV bolus or medication adjustment
  4. New arrhythmia triggered by ambulation — stop walk; obtain ECG; notify APP; may need rhythm management before resuming mobility
  5. SpO₂ drops persistently below 85% during walk (does not recover with rest) — reduce walk distance or oxygen supplementation inadequate; escalate oxygen strategy with respiratory team
  6. Pain escalates despite pre-walk medications — reassess analgesic regimen; may need opioid dose increase, multimodal optimization, or PT/OT consultation for other barriers (fear, delirium)
  7. Delirium worsens dramatically with activity (patient becomes violent, uncontrollable) — reassess for underlying cause (infection, hypoxia, electrolyte imbalance) rather than attributing to activity alone; usually, delirium improves with activity once underlying cause addressed
  8. Fall occurs or near-miss — root-cause analysis; reassess gait belt use, assist level, mental status, orthostatic risk; do NOT abandon mobility, but modify approach (more assist, shorter walks)

sections.heading: 7.1 Pathophysiology of early mobility benefit
sections.bodyHtml:
What happens when you don't move:

  • Immobility → muscle protein breakdown begins within hours; by POD 3, measurable atrophy
  • Supine position → venous pooling in lower extremities; soleal veins lack muscle pump → stasis → thrombosis risk
  • Shallow breathing (pain + fear) + immobility → atelectasis; secretions pool → pneumonia
  • Bed rest → gastrocolic reflex suppressed; opioids + electrolyte shifts already slowing gut; immobility compounds = ileus
  • Horizontal position → baroreceptor reflex unchallenged; cardiovascular decoupling (orthostatic intolerance)
  • Isolation + darkness + immobility + opioids → delirium worsening

What happens when you move early:

  • Upright position + muscle contraction → activates venous return (calf muscle pump); prevents stasis
  • Diaphragmatic excursion during walking → mobilizes secretions → better oxygenation
  • Ambulation → stimulates gastrocolic reflex; gravity + movement + activity resumption → bowel motility restoration
  • Standing/walking → baroreceptor reflex retrains; orthostatic tolerance returns rapidly (usually by POD 3)
  • Social engagement + purposeful activity → delirium resolution; cognitive recovery
  • Early functional gains → psychological win; faster psychosocial recovery

sections.heading: 7.2 Sternal precautions integrated with walking
sections.bodyHtml:
Common myth: "Sternotomy = no walking for 6 weeks."

Reality: Walking is SAFE and REQUIRED with sternal precautions. Precautions protect healing sternal bone; they do NOT mean immobility.

Precaution Walking Integration
"Elbows tucked, don't push with arms" Walking uses legs, not arms. Keep elbows at sides, hands free or on walker/rail. Do NOT use arms to push off from bed or chair — use legs or nurse assist.
"No heavy lifting (> 5 lbs)" Walking carries no weight through sternal incision. Light objects OK (cup of water, tablet).
"No driving × 6 weeks" Walking is not driving. Walking is encouraged even if car driving is restricted.
"Log-roll before sitting up" Rolling sternal incision toward outside; when sitting, avoid twisting torso. Walk straight; don't twist waist while standing.
"No Valsalva / straining" Walking doesn't require straining. If patient feels need to hold breath, remind: "Breathe normally; don't grunt or bear down."

sections.heading: 7.3 Orthostatic hypotension — management protocol
sections.bodyHtml:
Why it happens: Cardiopulmonary bypass → fluid shifts; post-op diuresis → intravascular volume depleted; baroreceptors decoupled from hours of horizontal position.

Universal POD 1–2; resolves by POD 3–4.

Prevention protocol — the "1-1-1 rule":

  1. Sit on edge of bed × 1 full minute — assess for dizziness before standing
  2. Stand upright × 1 full minute — assess stability before marching
  3. March in place × 10 steps — prepare muscles and baroreceptors for forward motion

If dizziness occurs during any phase:

  • Return to previous step (if marching, stop and stand; if standing, sit)
  • Sit/lie flat for 1 minute
  • Reassess; retry if dizziness resolved
  • If persistent dizziness → notify APP; consider IV bolus, fluid status, or medication adjustment

Equipment to manage it:

  • Gait belt on all patients (always, without exception) until demonstrated steady gait + no orthostatic symptoms
  • 2-person assist (one gait belt, one trailing) for POD 1–2
  • Walker or parallel bars if patient feels safer
  • Peripheral IV line accessible for fluid bolus if orthostatic worsening

sections.heading: 7.4 Pain management pre-mobility
sections.bodyHtml:
Principle: Optimal pain control BEFORE movement (not chasing pain after), using multimodal approach.

Regimen (verify with institutional orders):

  • Scheduled acetaminophen: 650–1000 mg PO q6h (if tolerated; liver function OK)
  • PRN opioid: IV hydromorphone 0.25–0.5 mg q2–3h PRN or IV morphine 2–4 mg q3h PRN
  • Non-opioid adjuncts: Consider gabapentin, duloxetine, or NSAIDs per institutional policy and patient factors

Timing:

  • Give pain meds 15–30 minutes BEFORE planned ambulation
  • Goal: pain ≤ 5/10 at rest; < 6/10 with movement
  • Reassess 15 min post-dose; walk if goal met; delay walk if pain not controlled

Pitfall: Over-medicating patient → oversedation → can't participate safely in mobility. Goal is comfort + alert engagement, not drowsiness.

sections.heading: 7.5 Nursing-led BID ambulation as the core intervention
sections.bodyHtml:
Key insight: PT visits 1×/day; nursing BID walks are the real driver.

  • PT role: Formal assessment, gait training, equipment prescription, higher-level functional goals (stairs, discharge planning)
  • Nursing role: BID walks minimum (more if patient tolerating); pain assessment; barrier mitigation; family engagement; documentation

Barriers chart:

Barrier Solution
Pain Optimize analgesics pre-walk (see §7.4); multimodal approach; reassess adequacy q8h
Fear ("I'll rip my sternum")** Educate: sternum held by wires; precautions protect it; walking is safe; reassure with staff presence
Orthostatic dizziness 1-1-1 protocol; slower progression; IV bolus if persistent
Delirium DO mobilize with supervision; delirium improves with activity + light/social engagement; immobility worsens delirium
Fatigue / weakness Normal POD 1–3; multiple short walks (BID) better than one long walk; expect slow progression
Equipment burden (chest tubes, lines) Brief all staff: tubes MOVE with patient; hang on IV pole or carry; don't let tubes anchor patient to bed
Family anxiety Involve family in walk; teach progression; normalize early activity; positive reinforcement

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in patients who were "tolerating mobility"; if any develop, re-escalate immediately.

  • Orthostatic symptoms worsening despite 1-1-1 protocol and reposition (patient near-syncope or syncope) — signs dehydration, anemia, or cardiac insufficiency; may need IV bolus or medication adjustment
  • SpO₂ dropping persistently during walk (below 85%, not recovering with rest) — inadequate supplemental oxygen or underlying pulmonary compromise; reduce walk distance or increase FiO₂
  • New or worsening arrhythmia triggered by ambulation — ischemia, electrolyte imbalance, or inadequate rate control; stop walks pending ECG/APP evaluation
  • Chest pain or pressure during mobility — STOP walk immediately; obtain ECG; rule out ACS; may indicate inadequate post-op pain relief or cardiac instability
  • Rising chest tube output during walk (e.g., 50 mL/hr → 150+ mL/hr) — suggest bleeding exacerbated by activity; notify surgeon; may need to pause mobility pending hemostasis
  • Severe dyspnea not explained by exertion (gasping, can't speak full sentence) — suggests heart failure, pneumonia, PE, pneumothorax; stop walk, sit up, notify APP
  • Fall or near-fall despite gait belt — reassess mental status, orthostasis, strength, balance; may indicate delirium, severe weakness, or safety concerns requiring increased assist
  • Patient becoming increasingly agitated or confused during activity — assess for hypoxia, pain inadequately controlled, or infection/sepsis (not normal delirium fluctuation); vitals, labs if indicated

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Safety criteria assessment is non-negotiable — reassess every walk. Don't assume "stable today = stable next walk." Check MAP, bleeding, pain, rhythm, mental status every single time.

  2. Pain management BEFORE mobility (not after) is the #1 barrier fix. Patients won't move if they hurt. Give analgesics 15–30 min before walk; document pain pre/post.

  3. Orthostatic hypotension is universal and manageable — use the 1-1-1 protocol rigorously. Sit 1 min, stand 1 min, march 1 min. Do NOT rush standing. Prevents syncope; improves walk tolerance dramatically.

  4. Sternal precautions do NOT mean bed rest — correct this misconception immediately. Walking is allowed and encouraged. Precautions (elbows tucked, no pushing with arms) apply to all activities including walking.

  5. Gait belt required on every walk until patient steady without orthostatic symptoms. No exceptions. Gait belt is as important as sternal precautions.

  6. Two-person assist (gait belt + trailing) for POD 1–2 catches falls and provides confidence. Reduce to 1-person + belt only after demonstrated stability and resolved orthostasis.

  7. Nursing-led BID walking is the real driver — not PT alone. PT = assessment, teaching, higher-level goals. Nursing = bulk of mobility volume. Own it.

  8. Chest tubes, central lines, oxygen tubing all come WITH the patient. Don't let equipment anchor patient to bed. Hang tubes on IV pole; carry oxygen cart.

  9. Delirium and mobility are linked — mobility HELPS delirium, not worse. Bed rest worsens delirium. If patient is delirious, mobilize (with supervision + safety precautions). Light, activity, social engagement reverse delirium.

  10. Document every mobility attempt. Include distance, vital signs (pre/during/post), symptoms, assist level, equipment, tolerance, barriers. Omit = gap in care picture.

  11. Avoid over-sedation pre-mobility. Some nurses over-medicate for "comfort." Result = drowsy patient stays in bed, deconditions fast. Goal is comfort + alert participation.

  12. Constipation undermines early mobility. Aggressive bowel regimen (stool softener, laxative, PO intake) keeps patients mobile. Constipation → straining → sternal stress → pain → immobility.

  13. Redo surgery = more cautious approach. Prior sternotomy = altered sternal architecture. Slower progression, longer precaution duration. Check with surgeon.

  14. LVAD and heart transplant patients prioritize early mobility from POD 0. Valsalva during straining destabilizes preload dangerously. Lower threshold for mobility escalation.

  15. Cardiac rehab referral at discharge is non-negotiable. Discharge teaching = home walking plan (daily, gradual increase, warning signs). Rehab starts 4–6 weeks post-op.

cards.title: ECMO (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation)
cards.quickAnswer: ECMO = extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for temporary cardiac and/or respiratory support. VA-ECMO provides cardiac + respiratory support for cardiogenic shock, post-cardiotomy shock, massive PE, refractory cardiac arrest (ECPR); VV-ECMO for severe ARDS. Most 5W patients are post-decannulation POD 0–3. Survival: 40–50% cardiogenic shock, 60–70% ARDS. Key 5W surveillance: distal limb perfusion q1–2h (VA femoral), cannulation site hematoma/infection, anticoagulation transition (IV heparin → warfarin/DOAC), mental status (3–5% stroke risk), hemolysis (cola urine, elevated LDH). Watch for acquired vWD, HIT, pseudoaneurysm — low threshold to escalate (ELSO, 2023; Brown, 2023).

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who it applies to.

  • Definition: Extracorporeal circulation and gas exchange via percutaneous or surgical cannulation to provide temporary cardiac and/or respiratory support. Two modalities: VV-ECMO (veno-venous, respiratory support only) and VA-ECMO (veno-arterial, cardiac + respiratory support).
  • Indications: Refractory ARDS, cardiogenic shock, post-cardiotomy shock, bridge to transplantation or recovery.
  • Typical unit patient: Recently decannulated POD 0–3; ICU-to-stepdown transfer. Active ECMO runs rare on the unit; most nursing focus is post-decannulation recovery.
  • Cannulation approaches: VV-ECMO via IJ Avalon (dual-lumen) or bicaval (femoral/IJ access); VA-ECMO via femoral venous + femoral/axillary arterial, or central aorta + RA.
  • Expected LOS post-decannulation: 3–7 days bedrest window → progressive mobility → discharge.
  • Context: Decannulation complication surveillance (site bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, distal limb ischemia, thrombosis, HIT, infection, hemolysis, stroke) is ICU-level nursing work that transfers to the stepdown unit.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanisms of VV and VA support VV-ECMO (Veno-Venous):
  • Drains deoxygenated blood from the venous system (IJ or femoral), oxygenates it in an external circuit, and returns it to the venous circulation.
  • Mechanism: pure gas exchange (O₂ uptake, CO₂ removal). No hemodynamic support.
  • Key physiology: recirculation risk if Avalon malpositioned (deoxygenated return mixing with drainage); IJ thrombosis if prolonged cannulation; benefits from native cardiac output for distribution. VA-ECMO (Veno-Arterial):
  • Drains venous blood, oxygenates it, and returns it to the arterial system (femoral or central aorta).
  • Mechanism: cardiac + pulmonary support. Restores systemic perfusion in cardiogenic shock; unloads right and left ventricles.
  • Key physiology: SvO₂ reflects mixing of native cardiac output (deoxygenated) with ECMO return (fully oxygenated); target SvO₂ >60% signals adequate total DO₂. Aortic root thrombus risk if low native output + stasis. Harlequin/North-South syndrome: if native RV output is high and ECMO return distal to aortic root takeoff, proximal aorta (coronary and cerebral perfusion) becomes hypoxic relative to lower body — increases stroke and myocardial ischemia risk. Both modalities trigger shear stress (hemolysis, acquired vWD), inflammation (cytokine release, infection risk), and anticoagulation-dependent thrombosis prevention.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — who arrives, when, and what they look like.

ECMO patient profile on unit arrival:

  • Recent cannulation (ICU transferring to unit typically POD 0–1 post-decannulation) or active run (rare on stepdown).
  • Hemostasis achieved at cannulation sites; early anticoagulation (IV heparin) being titrated.
  • Distal perfusion assessments ongoing (VA femoral patients); sites may have dressings, hemostasis devices, or small hematomas.
  • Respiratory support reduced as cardiac/respiratory function recovers.
  • Mental status variable (post-operative sedation wearing off, possible delirium, 3–5% post-ECMO stroke risk).

Observable indicators of deterioration during recovery:

  • Expanding hematoma at cannulation site
  • Cool, mottled distal limb (VA); absent or diminishing pulses
  • Oozing from site despite hemostasis attempts
  • Cola-colored (hemoglobinuria) or tea-colored urine
  • Fever, elevated WBC, site erythema or drainage
  • Altered mental status, focal deficits
  • Hemodynamic instability (BP trending down, lactate rising)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–5 minutes at bedside)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic exam. Pure observation; no actions yet.

Vital signs & perfusion: - HR, BP, MAP, SpO₂, temperature, mental status, capillary refill

Distal limb checks (VA-ECMO, every 1–2 hours mandatory):

  • Temperature (hand-held thermometer: compare affected leg to contralateral; >2 °C difference concerning)
  • Color (pale, mottled, cyanotic vs pink)
  • Capillary refill (<2 sec normal; >2 sec delay is concerning)
  • Sensation (can patient feel toes? numbness = red flag)
  • Motor (can patient wiggle toes? weakness concerning)
  • Pulses (palpate femoral, popliteal, DP, PT; compare bilaterally)
  • Girth (thigh/calf edema trending; compare shift-to-shift)

Cannulation site inspection:

  • Dressing integrity; erythema, warmth, drainage, fluctuance
  • Hematoma: size, firmness, pulsatility, tenderness
  • Border marking (mark hematoma with pen to track expansion q4–6h if present)

Urine output & character:

  • Volume, color (clear vs tea-colored/cola-colored = hemoglobinuria)
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, Hgb, Cr, LDH, haptoglobin, CBC (platelet trend for HIT)
  • Coagulation: most recent PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen

Line/device assessment:

  • Peripheral IV access, adequacy for transfusion or infusions
  • Arterial line if present; monitor dampening
  • Foley catheter, urometer reading

Medication review (MAR):

  • Anticoagulation: UFH or bivalirudin infusion active? Dose, PTT/anti-Xa recent?
  • Antiarrhythmics, beta-blockers, vasopressors if running
  • Analgesics, sedatives (assess oversedation if mental status depressed)

Recent history:

  • What procedure, when? VA vs VV? Cannulation sites (femoral, IJ, axillary, central)?
  • Time of decannulation (POD 0 = today, POD 1 = yesterday, etc.)
  • Transfusions/blood products given; cumulative bleed estimate
  • Any known complications during run (thrombosis, infection, stroke alert, hemolysis episode)?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake or lightly sedated; perfusing; no active bleeding; distal limbs pink; hemostasis intact; labs trending favorably.)

POD 0–1 (Early Post-Decannulation)

  1. Distal limb checks q1–2h (VA femoral) — temperature, color, cap refill, sensation, motor, pulses documented each check
  2. Site assessment q4h — inspect dressing, mark hematoma borders if present, assess for erythema/drainage; notify APP if expanding rapidly or warm/erythematous
  3. Anticoagulation management:
    • Continue UFH infusion; check PTT q4–6h during titration, then q6–12h once stable (goal PTT 50–80 s per institution, or anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 U/mL)
    • Verify INR if warfarin being overlapped (goal 2–3); bridge duration per institutional protocol (~5 days typical overlap once INR therapeutic)
    • Daily CBC (platelet count — watch for drop >50% or <100K, HIT red flag)
    • Daily PT/INR if warfarin, daily aPTT if heparin
    • Labs daily: CBC, CMP (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr), LDH, haptoglobin, coagulation profile (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen) — assess for hemolysis and coagulopathy trending
    • Urine monitoring: check color/character each void; any tea/cola color → notify APP, obtain urine dipstick (Hgb + vs RBCs), check plasma color; if hemoglobinuria present, maintain MAP >65, optimize renal perfusion, target IV bicarb to alkalinize urine (goal pH >6.5)
    • Bedrest initially (POD 0–1) if femoral access; strict logging of position changes
    • Nutrition: when stable and bowels expected active, initiate/resume enteral feeding (protein 1.5–2 g/kg/day to support healing)
    • Mental status baseline: assess orientation, cognition, affect; document any confusion, hallucinations, or focal deficits (post-ECMO delirium common; stroke less common but 3–5% incidence)
    • Pain control: adequate analgesia without over-sedation; avoid sedatives that worsen delirium
    • Respiratory support weaning per team as cardiac/pulmonary function recovers
    • VS trending: ensure hemodynamics stable off ECMO; notify APP if BP trending down, lactate rising, or UOP declining

POD 2–3 (Mid-Recovery)

  1. Continue distal checks q1–2h if VA femoral (may extend to q2–4h if consistently normal)
  2. Mobility progression: if no access complications, begin PT/OT bedside → sit in chair → ambulation
  3. Anticoagulation: adjust heparin to goal; if warfarin overlapping, discontinue heparin once INR therapeutic × 24h
  4. Repeat imaging if pseudoaneurysm suspected: Doppler of access sites if hematoma expanding or pulsatile
  5. Labs continue daily (CBC, CMP, coagulation) until stable, then per protocol
  6. Site care: if sutures/staples present, keep clean and dry; assess for signs of infection (erythema, warmth, drainage, fever)
  7. Mental status: ongoing orientation and monitoring; if agitation/confusion, address triggers (pain, hypoxia, sleep deprivation, over-sedation)
  8. Nutrition: progress to full oral diet as tolerated
  9. Family education: begin teaching on anticoagulation signs (bleeding, over-anticoagulation), site precautions, activity limits

POD 3–7 (Late Recovery → Discharge Prep)

  1. Distal checks daily or per protocol if VA femoral; patient may perform self-checks with teaching
  2. Full mobilization: PT/OT intensive; ADL retraining; assess for ICU-acquired weakness (common post-ECMO)
  3. Anticoagulation at goal: warfarin INR 2–3, DOAC at therapeutic dose, or as per underlying diagnosis and thromboembolic risk
  4. Labs per protocol — may reduce frequency if stable (CBC, INR q2–3d if on warfarin)
  5. Site check: suture removal per surgeon; final assessment for infection or unhealed areas
  6. Discharge teaching:
    • Anticoagulation: bleeding precautions, no contact sports, fall prevention, NSAID avoidance, INR follow-up plan
    • Site care: incision/puncture precautions; signs to report (swelling, drainage, fever, expanding hematoma)
    • Distal limb monitoring (if VA): daily checks; report immediately if leg becomes cool, swollen, color changes
    • Cardiac/respiratory follow-up: outpatient cardiology within 1–2 weeks, echo per team
    • Rehabilitation: cardiopulmonary rehab referral; intensive PT/OT home program
    • Nutrition support: protein, calories; wound healing optimization
    • Activity: gradual return to ADLs; avoid strenuous activity 4–6 weeks post-decannulation
    • Psychological: discuss delirium recovery expectations, PTSD/anxiety screening, family support
    • Discharge orders: anticoagulation prescription, site care supplies, PT/OT home schedule, follow-up appointments scheduled

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hemodynamic collapse; brisk bleeding; signs of distal ischemia; fever + sepsis; altered mental status with focal deficits; hemolysis with AKI.)

  1. STAT call to APP/fellow + charge nurse; do NOT leave patient alone
  2. Activate Rapid Response if hemodynamic compromise or respiratory distress
  3. IV access: ensure patent large-bore IV; consider PICC or central line if transfusion anticipated
  4. Bleeding workup STAT:
    • Obtain CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, type & cross, lactate; check thromboelastography (TEG) if available
    • Assess site visually and by palpation — brisk bleeding → notify APP/surgeon immediately
    • GI bleed (melena/hematochezia) → gastroenterology consult; prepare for upper/lower endoscopy
    • Neuro deficit or headache → stat CT head (ICH differential); notify neurology
    • Prepare for possible operating room (surgical hemostasis) or reversal agents (FFP, prothrombin complex concentrate, vitamin K per hematology)
    • Distal limb ischemia (VA femoral):
    • Cool, mottled leg with absent/diminished pulses → notify vascular surgery STAT
    • Consider distal perfusion catheter insertion if not already in place
    • Assess for possible cannula repositioning or decannulation if ischemia worsening (may require VAD bridge discussion)
    • Prepare for possible angiography to assess obstruction
    • Fever + suspected ECMO site infection:
    • Blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics
    • Start empiric broad-spectrum ABX (vancomycin + piperacillin–tazobactam or carbapenem per protocol)
    • Notify ECMO team for possible cannula exchange
    • Cardiology: transthoracic echo to assess for vegetation (endocarditis)
    • Source control is paramount (may require operative drainage/debridement)
    • Hemolysis with AKI (cola urine, elevated LDH, rising Cr, oliguria):
    • Aggressive fluid resuscitation if hypovolemic (maintain MAP >65, UOP >0.5 mL/kg/h)
    • Diuretics (furosemide) if euvolemic to euvolemic → oliguria with normal/high BP
    • IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine (goal pH >6.5) — prevents hemoglobin casts and pigment-driven AKI
    • CRRT if severe AKI (Cr >2.5, UOP <0.3 mL/kg/h despite interventions) or hyperkalemia
    • Notify hematology; ECMO team assesses oxygenator/pump integrity if run still active
    • Blood transfusion (PRBCs) if Hgb <7–8 to improve viscosity and reduce shear stress
    • Suspected HIT (platelet drop >50% or <100K on day 4+ of UFH, thrombosis, thrombocytopenia):
    • STOP UFH immediately; do NOT wait for serology (high-suspicion clinical decision)
    • Transition to bivalirudin 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus, then 0.15–0.2 mg/kg/h infusion (titrate to aPTT 50–80 s)
    • Order HIT serology (PF4-heparin ELISA, functional assay — HIPA); notify hematology, ECMO team
    • Monitor platelets q6–12h during bivalirudin transition
    • Acute stroke (focal neuro deficit, aphasia, gaze deviation, hemiparesis):
    • STAT CT head (non-contrast to rule out ICH)
    • STAT neurology consult
    • Notify APP/team; hold anticoagulation escalation pending imaging
    • If ischemic stroke within thrombolytic window: team decides tPA vs thrombectomy vs observation
    • If ICH: neurosurgery consult; ICU transfer likely
    • Transfer to ICU for unstable management; coordinate with critical care team

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [Name], this is [RN] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p ECMO decannulation." B: "Patient is [time] post-decannulation. Distal limb [status — pink, cool, mottled]. Site [status — intact, oozing, expanding hematoma]. Last labs: K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value], Hgb [value], LDH [value], PTT [value], platelets [value]." A: "[Patient is stable / unstable]. [Chief concern: bleeding, ischemia, hemolysis, fever, stroke symptom]. [Current anticoagulation plan / recent changes]." R: "Requesting [escalation level: site evaluation / vascular assessment / hematology consult / ICU transfer / operative intervention]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable post-decannulation, routine management Primary APP / on-call fellow
Expanding hematoma or pseudoaneurysm suspected Vascular surgery (ultrasound-guided thrombin injection vs operative repair)
Distal limb ischemia (cool, mottled, absent pulses) Vascular surgery STAT; ECMO team (cannula repositioning vs decannulation discussion)
Brisk bleeding from site or GI bleed APP + Hematology + Surgical team; GI consult if upper/lower bleed
Fever + site erythema or sepsis ECMO team + Infectious disease + Cardiology (TEE if endocarditis suspected)
Hemolysis + AKI (cola urine, elevated LDH, oliguria) Nephrology + ECMO team; hematology if severe
HIT (platelet drop >50%, thrombosis) Hematology STAT; ECMO team for anticoagulation transition (bivalirudin)
Acute focal neuro deficit or stroke symptom Neurology STAT + Stroke team + APP; CT head STAT
Psychological crisis (severe anxiety, delirium, suicidal ideation) Psychiatry consult; behavioral health + primary team

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(novice + advanced beginner deep-dive)*
sections.bodyHtml:
VA-ECMO physiology: SvO₂, mixing cloud, aortic root thrombosis In VA-ECMO, systemic oxygenation depends on blending native cardiac output (deoxygenated SvO₂ ~40–60%) with ECMO return (fully oxygenated SvO₂ ~95–100%). The result is a "mixing cloud" — a gradient of oxygenation from the aortic root distally. - Target SvO₂ >60% on VA-ECMO signals adequate blending and total DO₂ (delivery = cardiac output × SaO₂ × Hgb). If SvO₂ drops <50%, either native output is failing (deteriorating heart function) or ECMO flow is insufficient. - Aortic root thrombus risk increases when native cardiac output is very low (severe shock) and ECMO return is the main aortic inflow. Low velocity + stasis = thrombosis. Recognition: sudden rise in hemolysis markers (LDH, hemoglobinuria), chest pain, hemodynamic collapse. Prevention: maintain adequate native output (inotropes, afterload reduction as indicated); some centers anticoagulate heavily or use aspirin adjunctively. - Coronary perfusion in VA-ECMO depends on aortic root pressure and native coronary flow. If aortic root is hypoxic (Harlequin syndrome), myocardial ischemia can occur even if lower-body SaO₂ appears adequate.
VV-ECMO physiology: recirculation, RV unloading, weaning triggers VV-ECMO supports only gas exchange — the heart must still perfuse the body. Thus VV relies on native cardiac output for distribution. - Recirculation occurs if deoxygenated return mixes with drainage (e.g., Avalon malpositioned, IJ flows too close). Recognition: lower-than-expected SaO₂ on ECMO despite high flow/FiO₂. Prevention: confirm cannula position on imaging; avoid excessive negative intra-thoracic pressure (sedation, no aggressive spontaneous breathing triggering ECMO flow maldistribution). - RV unloading is modest in VV-ECMO compared to VA. The right heart still ejects against pulmonary vascular resistance. In severe ARDS with elevated PVR, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (nitric oxide) are often used adjunctively. - Weaning VV: decrease sweep gas first (↓ CO₂ removal, triggers spontaneous ventilation); then decrease ECMO FiO₂; last to decrease is the blood flow (return to native lungs last). O₂ off first, CO₂ off last.
Cannulation complications: distal perfusion, North-South Harlequin syndrome, coronary steal Distal limb ischemia (VA femoral arterial cannulation):
  • The femoral arterial cannula partially obstructs the superficial femoral artery (SFA). Distal SFA flow becomes dependent on collateral circulation + residual antegrade flow.
  • Risk factors: small vessel size, hypotension during ECMO, long cannulation duration (>7 days), hypercoagulability.
  • Prevention & management: insert distal perfusion catheter (small antegrade line to distal SFA) at time of cannulation if high-risk patient; monitor distal limb q1–2h for early ischemia (cool, mottled, sensory/motor changes); if ischemia develops, may need cannula repositioning or decannulation despite ongoing need for ECMO support (consider VAD bridge). North-South / Harlequin syndrome (VA-ECMO specific):
  • Occurs when native RV output is high and ECMO return is distal to the aortic root takeoff. Result: aortic root (coronary + cerebral circulation) receives relatively deoxygenated blood from RV; lower aorta receives oxygenated ECMO return.
  • Recognition: cyanosis of face, neck, upper extremities despite pink lower body and good systemic SvO₂; ABG shows upper-body cannula
  • Consequences: coronary ischemia, stroke risk, CNS hypoxemia.
  • Management: increase native cardiac output (reduce sedation, decrease ECMO support to unmask native output, use inotropes); consider repositioning arterial cannula to proximal aorta (central approach) or decannulation if syndrome limits recovery. Aortic root thrombus / coronary steal:
  • Central aortic return in VA-ECMO can create antegrade diastolic flow in the aortic root that opposes native diastolic coronary runoff — "coronary steal." Recognized as angina, ST changes, or hemodynamic collapse.
  • Prevention: ensure adequate native LV ejection (avoid overdistension); some centers accept peripheral VA to avoid coronary steal risk.
Anticoagulation management: heparin targets, bivalirudin for HIT UFH during active ECMO:
  • Goal PTT 50–80 s OR anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 U/mL (institutional choice; ELSO recommends anti-Xa trending for precision).
  • Bolus: 50–100 U/kg IV initially
  • Infusion: 10–50 U/kg/h titrated to goal; recheck PTT q4–6h during titration, then daily once stable
  • Monitoring: daily CBC (watch platelet trend for HIT), PT/INR if overlapping with warfarin, fibrinogen
  • Reversal: protamine 1 mg per 100 U UFH (max 50 mg IV) if urgent reversal needed; also FFP, prothrombin complex concentrate per hematology Bivalirudin for HIT:
  • Indication: confirmed or high-suspicion HIT (platelet drop >50%, thrombosis, thrombocytopenia on UFH)
  • Load: 0.25 mg/kg IV bolus
  • Infusion: 0.15–0.2 mg/kg/h, titrate to aPTT 50–80 s or anti-IIa 0.4–0.6 mcg/mL
  • Monitoring: aPTT q2–4h during transition, then q6–12h; monitor platelets q6–12h for recovery (HIT antibodies may persist; platelet count typically recovers over 5–7 days)
  • No reversal agent — bivalirudin has short half-life (~25 min); if bleeding, discontinue and manage supportively Post-decannulation transition (heparin → warfarin/DOAC):
  • Continue UFH until warfarin INR goal (usually 2–3) achieved × 24h, then overlap × 5 days per institutional protocol
  • DOAC may be started once hemostasis is adequate (typically POD 1–2 post-decannulation)
  • Consult cardiology on underlying diagnosis (thromboembolism risk, mechanical valve, etc.) to guide long-term anticoagulation choice
Weaning criteria: VA cardiac recovery, VV respiratory recovery VA-ECMO weaning trial:
  • Cardiac recovery indicators: native EF >25% on echo, pulse pressure >15 mmHg (sign of LV ejection), cardiac index off ECMO >2 L/min/m² (calculated from native CO)
  • Trial protocol: gradually decrease ECMO flow over hours while monitoring BP, lactate, SvO₂, urine output; if patient tolerates reduced flow without deterioration → continue gradual wean → decannulation
  • Failure to wean: if hemodynamic collapse when ECMO reduced, reassess: has disease improved? Are there complications (thrombosis, inadequate surgical repair, ongoing sepsis)? If no recovery expected → discuss VAD bridge, transplant, or comfort care VV-ECMO weaning trial:
  • Respiratory recovery indicators: improving lung compliance on ventilator, lower ventilatory settings (PEEP, FiO₂), adequate spontaneous breathing effort, improving PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio
  • Trial protocol: decrease sweep gas (↓ CO₂ removal, triggers patient to breathe more); then decrease ECMO FiO₂; last decrease ECMO flow; goal is return to native lung function
  • Success: extubation and discharge from ECMO
ECPR (Extracorporeal Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation): refractory cardiac arrest indications

ECPR indication: refractory out-of-hospital or in-hospital cardiac arrest (>10 min CPR without ROSC, witnessed collapse, witnessed downtime).

Patient selection: age <65 (though older patients may be considered), witnessed collapse, short downtime (<30 min), likely reversible cause (acute MI, massive PE, cardiogenic shock, myocarditis, hypothermia).

Survival: ECPR cohorts report 20–40% neurologically intact survival in carefully selected populations. Mechanism: restores brain and heart perfusion during arrest, allowing time for diagnosis and intervention (PCI, transplant, VAD decision).

Complications: same as elective ECMO (bleeding, thrombosis, infection, stroke, limb ischemia) but in sicker population. Outcomes depend heavily on underlying disease reversibility and speed of cannulation.

Bridge strategies: ECMO-to-recovery vs ECMO-to-LVAD vs ECMO-to-transplant ECMO-to-recovery:
  • Best-case scenario: underlying disease reverses during ECMO support (myocarditis, fulminant PE after thrombolysis, post-cardiotomy shock with surgical repair, ARDS with lung recovery).
  • Timeline: typically 5–14 days of ECMO; longer support increases infectious risk.
  • Success rate: depends on disease (myocarditis 40–60% recovery, post-cardiotomy 50–70%, ARDS 60–70% if VV). ECMO-to-LVAD (left ventricular assist device):
  • Intermediate strategy: patient improving but not recovering enough cardiac function for independence from mechanical support.
  • Timing: often transitioned to LVAD at POD 7–14 if native EF not improving; allows decannulation from ECMO and progression to VAD as bridge-to-transplant or destination therapy.
  • Advantage: reduces ECMO-related bleeding, infection, thrombosis risk; extends support timeline. ECMO-to-transplant:
  • Patient listed for transplant while on ECMO; priority listing possible.
  • Timing: days to weeks waiting for organ; ECMO continues during wait.
  • Outcomes: post-transplant outcomes often good if ECMO run <14 days; longer ECMO runs increase infectious morbidity.
Post-ECMO ICU-acquired weakness and rehabilitation ICU-acquired weakness (ICU-AW):
  • Common post-ECMO due to prolonged immobilization, inflammation, muscle catabolism, sedation.
  • Recognition: difficulty weaning from mechanical ventilation, weak leg strength, inability to stand/walk despite cardiac/respiratory recovery.
  • Prevention: early mobilization (sitting in chair POD 2–3 if decannulation uneventful), minimize sedation, optimize nutrition (protein 1.5–2 g/kg/day).
  • Recovery: intensive PT/OT post-ECMO — goal is functional independence (ADLs, walking) before discharge. Some patients require rehabilitation facility admission. Rehabilitation timeline post-ECMO:
  • POD 0–1: bedrest, passive ROM, education
  • POD 2–3: PT/OT bedside, sit in chair, active ROM
  • POD 3–5: ambulation with assistance, ADL retraining, stairs if appropriate
  • POD 5–7+: functional independence goal; discharge to home vs rehab facility based on strength/cognition
---

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these trajectories in patients appearing stable:

  • Hematoma expanding q4–6h despite held anticoagulation — may indicate pseudoaneurysm or active site bleed; get Doppler and notify vascular surgery
  • Cool leg progressing to mottled skin despite adequate hemodynamics — distal limb ischemia evolving; notify vascular surgery, may need urgent cannula repositioning or decannulation
  • Platelet count dropping >50% on day 4+ of UFH — HIT red flag; STOP UFH immediately, transition to bivalirudin without waiting for serology
  • Cola-colored or tea-colored urine with rising Cr and falling UOP — hemolysis + AKI; aggressive renal protection (fluids, bicarb, possible CRRT) and notify nephrology
  • Fever + site erythema or purulent drainage — ECMO site infection; blood cultures, broad ABX, possible cannula exchange; high morbidity if untreated
  • Altered mental status (confusion, hallucinations, agitation) appearing or worsening — post-ECMO delirium common (30–50% incidence); if acute focal deficit (facial droop, arm weakness) → stroke code STAT
  • BP drifting down, lactate rising, capillary refill slowing — perfusion failing; ensure adequate volume, reduce vasodilatory infusions, notify team for escalation
  • Bleeding from nose, gums, or mucosal areas — coagulopathy worsening; check PT/INR, fibrinogen, consider FFP/transfusion per hematology
  • Elevated WBC trending up + rising lactate — possible ECMO circuit infection or sepsis; blood cultures, imaging, antibiotics pending
  • Sudden increase in hemolysis markers (LDH spike, haptoglobin crash, urine positive for Hgb) — intracardiac thrombus, oxygenator clotting, or pump cavitation if run still active; notify ECMO team STAT
  • Unequal pupils, gaze deviation, or new focal neuro sign — acute stroke; activate stroke code, CT head STAT
  • Patient report of leg pain, numbness, or coldness patient had not complained of before — distal ischemia; assess limb q1h, prepare for vascular intervention
  • Recurrent bleeding at site despite adequate anticoagulation reversal — consider transfusion for Hgb support (improves viscosity, reduces shear), IV bicarb if hemolysis present, discuss with hematology

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Distal limb checks are non-negotiable, q1–2h for VA femoral. 5–15% develop limb ischemia; cool leg + mottled skin = APP notification within minutes, not hours. Do not assume absence of active ECMO means you can relax surveillance — post-decannulation ischemia evolves rapidly.

  2. Acquired vWD is often missed until bleeding is severe. Patients bleed out of proportion to PTT/INR. Check vWF panel (RCo, Ag, activity) if persistent bleeding.

    Desmopressin 0.3 mcg/kg IV/IN is first-line, not more FFP. Transfuse PRBCs to improve viscosity and reduce shear.

  3. Pseudoaneurysm post-decannulation is a 5–7 day complication. Mark hematoma borders, obtain Doppler if expanding or pulsatile. Vascular surgery can do bedside thrombin injection if caught <2 cm — delay risks operative repair or amputation.

  4. HIT can appear without fever — thrombosis + thrombocytopenia is the key. Platelet drop >50% on day 4+ of UFH → STOP UFH immediately and start bivalirudin. Do NOT wait for serology. Transition delay increases thrombotic risk (circuit clot, stroke, limb ischemia).

  5. Heparin PTT target 50–80 s for ECMO is HIGHER than typical anticoagulation. This is intentional — the circuit needs heavier anticoagulation. Do not confuse with general PTT goals (usually 30–40 s).

  6. Hemoglobinuria (cola-colored urine) + elevated LDH = hemolysis damaging kidneys. Maintain MAP >65, optimize renal perfusion, diurese if euvolemic, alkalinize urine with IV bicarb (goal urine pH >6.5). If hemolysis ongoing on active ECMO, notify ECMO team — pump or oxygenator may need repair.

  7. Mental status changes post-ECMO are common and usually NOT stroke. Delirium 30–50%; true stroke 3–5%. Baseline mental status critical. New focal deficits (facial droop, arm weakness) → stat CT + neurology; generalized confusion + agitation → supportive care, reorientation, minimize sedation, optimize sleep.

  8. Harlequin/North-South syndrome in VA-ECMO can cause stroke despite good lower-body perfusion. Watch for cyanosis of face/neck/upper extremities. Signals upper-body hypoxemia. Discuss with ECMO/cardiology — may need cannula repositioning or decannulation.

  9. Post-decannulation bleeding is NOT all "normal." Some ooze expected. Brisk bleeding, expanding hematoma, mucosal bleeding (GI, epistaxis) is not normal. Assess coagulation (PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer), get type & cross, notify APP. May need anticoagulation adjustment or FFP/transfusion.

  10. Hemoglobin drop of 3–5 g/dL across a typical ECMO run is expected. Do NOT reflexively transfuse if stable (Hgb 7–8 acceptable). But ongoing Hgb drift post-decannulation suggests bleeding (GI, site, intracranial) — investigate. PRBCs also improve viscosity and reduce hemolysis shear.

  11. ECMO site infection is high-morbidity — biofilm forms fast. Fever + erythema/drainage → blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics, broad-spectrum ABX, ECMO team for possible cannula exchange. Source control paramount; sepsis kills.

  12. Do NOT discharge without clear anticoagulation plan. Patient must know target INR if warfarin, DOAC dosing, signs of over/under-anticoagulation. Weekly INR checks post-discharge standard. No contact sports, fall prevention, no NSAIDs — families need explicit education.

  13. Cumulative transfusion load and HIT risk. Heavy transfusion + longer ECMO runs = higher HIT incidence. Track blood product volumes; adjust UFH monitoring accordingly.

  14. Anticoagulation is a double-edged sword — too little = thrombosis, too much = bleeding. Daily labs (CBC, PT/INR, aPTT) are standard. Aim for narrow therapeutic window. Heparin infusion titration can be volatile in post-op patients with shifting volume status.

  15. 5W acuity reflects ICU-level post-ECMO complications. Even though patient is "on the floor," distal limb checks, anticoagulation management, hemolysis surveillance, and infection vigilance are ICU-level work. Staffing and protocol should reflect this.

cards.title: Ejection Fraction (EF)
cards.quickAnswer: Percentage of left ventricular end-diastolic volume ejected per beat. Normal LVEF 55–70%. HFrEF ≤ 40%; HFmrEF 41–49%; HFpEF ≥ 50%. Measured by transthoracic echocardiography (Simpson biplane standard). EF is load-dependent—interpret with volume status, not isolation. LVEF ≤ 35% post-3-month GDMT qualifies for ICD primary prevention; ≤ 40% with QRS ≥ 120 ms qualifies for CRT. Cornerstone of HF diagnosis, surgical risk, mechanical support evaluation, and transplant candidacy.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: Percentage of left ventricular end-diastolic volume ejected per beat. Normal LVEF 55–70%. HFrEF ≤ 40%; HFmrEF 41–49%; HFpEF ≥ 50%. Measured by transthoracic echocardiography (Simpson biplane standard). EF is load-dependent—interpret with volume status, not isolation. LVEF ≤ 35% post-3-month GDMT qualifies for ICD primary prevention; ≤ 40% with QRS ≥ 120 ms qualifies for CRT. Cornerstone of HF diagnosis, surgical risk, mechanical support evaluation, and transplant candidacy.
cards.sourcePrecedence: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA HF Guideline → ESC 2021 HF Guideline → ASE 2015 chamber quantification → Hardin & Kaplow (2020)

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
Ejection fraction is the proportion of blood pumped out of the ventricle during systole, expressed as a percentage of end-diastolic volume. It is the most widely used marker of systolic function in clinical practice.

LVEF (left ventricular EF) is reported in nearly all echocardiographic exams and forms the backbone of heart failure diagnosis and therapy decisions.

RVEF (right ventricular EF) is less commonly measured but increasingly important in pulmonary hypertension, chronic RV strain, and acute RV infarction.

EF is intrinsically load-dependent: it falls with reduced preload and increased afterload, and rises with enhanced contractility or favorable loading. Always interpret EF in context of volume status and hemodynamics.

sections.heading: 2. Formula
sections.bodyHtml:
EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV × 100%

Where:

  • EDV = left ventricular end-diastolic volume (largest chamber volume)
  • ESV = left ventricular end-systolic volume (smallest chamber volume)
  • SV = stroke volume = EDV − ESV

Example: LVEDV 120 mL, LVESV 50 mL → EF = (120 − 50) / 120 × 100% = 58%.

sections.heading: 3. Normal Range + Heart Failure Classification
sections.bodyHtml:
Category LVEF Range Clinical Context
Normal / Preserved ≥ 50% No systolic dysfunction
Mildly reduced 41–49% HFmrEF; intermediate outcomes
Reduced ≤ 40% HFrEF; qualifies for GDMT, ICD if ≤ 35% post-GDMT
HF with improved EF Previously ≤ 40%, now > 40% Post-MI recovery, post-GDMT remodeling, ongoing therapy required

Severity grading (per 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA guideline):

Descriptor LVEF Degree
Normal ≥ 50% None
Mildly reduced 41–49% Mild systolic dysfunction
Moderately reduced 31–40% Moderate systolic dysfunction
Severely reduced ≤ 30% Severe systolic dysfunction

Key threshold: LVEF ≤ 35% after ≥ 3 months of GDMT is the standard criterion for primary prevention ICD implantation in non-ischemic and ischemic cardiomyopathy (Heidenreich et al., 2022).

sections.heading: Therapy decisions
sections.bodyHtml:
• LVEF ≤ 40% + NYHA II–III → ACE-I/ARB/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA required.
  • LVEF ≤ 35% post–3-month GDMT → ICD primary prevention eligible.
  • LVEF ≤ 40% + QRS ≥ 120 ms → CRT candidate.
  • LVEF in low 20s → LVAD evaluation, transplant workup.

sections.heading: Measurement methods
sections.bodyHtml:
Method Advantages Limitations Setting
TTE Simpson biplane Non-invasive, reproducible, standard Good acoustic windows required; 5–10% variability Ubiquitous
Visual estimation Quick, experienced readers accurate ± 10–15% error, highly observer-dependent Bedside
3D echocardiography More accurate volumes, less angle-dependent Longer processing, less widely available Growing availability
Cardiac MR Gold standard; reproducible; no windows needed Not real-time; cost; patient contraindications Specialized centers
CT cardiac Excellent spatial resolution Radiation, iodine contrast Increasingly available
MUGA / cardiac catheterization ventriculogram Accurate in principle; invasive data Radiation; invasive; declining availability ICU/cath lab only

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Load-dependence and clinical context EF varies with preload and afterload. A euvolemic patient with EF 40% differs substantially from a dehydrated patient (EF may transiently rise 5–10%) or an acutely pulmonary edematous patient (EF may transiently fall 5–10%). Trend EF over time; do not anchor to a single number.
Wall motion and global EF relationship Regional wall motion abnormalities (RWMA) may not proportionally impact global EF. A patient with severe anterior wall akinesis but preserved basal posterior wall may have EF 35–40% that understates localized dysfunction. Request specific wall motion assessment from imaging.
Strain imaging and preclinical dysfunction Global longitudinal strain (GLS) detects subtle systolic dysfunction when LVEF is still normal. A patient with normal EF (50%) but GLS –16% (normal > –20%) has preclinical LV dysfunction. Ask specifically if prognostication is critical.
Right ventricular EF challenges RVEF is harder to measure than LVEF due to complex geometry. Surrogates include TAPSE (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion) > 16 mm, S' on tissue Doppler > 10 cm/s, and RV FAC (fractional area change) > 35%. Do not dismiss "visually reduced" RV without specific measurement.
Post-MI recovery and reverse remodeling EF post-MI can improve substantially over 3–6 months with aggressive GDMT and revascularization. Post-STEMI EF 25% at 48 hours may recover to 40% at 3 months. This reverse remodeling justifies sustained therapy and repeated assessment (Heidenreich et al., 2022).

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls *(5–10 high-yield)*
sections.bodyHtml:
• EF is load-dependent. Always interpret in context of filling pressures, JVP, lung sounds, and renal function. Trend EF; do not anchor to a single number.

  • Simpson biplane reproducibility is ~5% between operators. Beat-to-beat variability is normal; EF 35% vs. 40% may reflect variation, not true change. Trend over weeks/months.

  • Visual estimate has observer variability of 5–15%. If a small EF difference changes management (ICD eligibility), request formal Simpson calculation.

  • Dynamic LVOT obstruction (HCM or post-CABG) can acutely alter apparent systolic function. cMR with strain is more specific for HCM phenotyping.

  • RVEF is much harder to measure than LVEF. RV geometry is complex; visual estimate is highly variable. Use surrogates: TAPSE > 16 mm, S' > 10 cm/s, RV FAC > 35%.

  • Cardiac MR is the gold standard but not real-time. If a borderline EF (35–40%) needs definitive assessment, cMR resolves uncertainty but is typically outpatient referral.

  • HFpEF (EF ≥ 50%) carries substantial morbidity approaching that of HFrEF. Do not dismiss a breathless patient with "normal EF." Assess diastolic function, filling pressures, and PH.

  • AF or other arrhythmias cause beat-to-beat EF variability. Measure over 5–10 cycles and average; a single systole may be an outlier.
