cards.title: Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement
cards.quickAnswer: Post-op cardiac surgery goals: K⁺ ≥ 4.0 mEq/L, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 mg/dL, Phos ≥ 2.5 mg/dL, iCa²⁺ ≥ 1.1 mmol/L (total Ca ≥ 8.4 mg/dL). Replace K⁺ and Mg²⁺ together — they're Na/K-ATPase cofactors. Central line preferred for IV doses ≥ 10 mEq/h; peripheral max 10 mEq/h over 1 h (dilute in 100 mL). Recheck 1 h after IV, 4 h after PO. Hold K⁺ replacement in AKI or if already ≥ 5.0 mEq/L; always verify Cr and UOP before dosing.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition and who this applies to.

  • Definition: A standing order set and PRN protocol to maintain serum K⁺, Mg²⁺, iCa²⁺, and Phos within a tighter-than-standard range post-cardiac surgery, because the freshly operated heart has lower tolerance for electrolyte swings that would be acceptable in general medical patients.
  • Why post-op goals are higher than standard: Arrhythmia thresholds are depressed in the early post-op period. A K⁺ of 3.6 mEq/L acceptable on a medical ward becomes a setup for POAF or ectopy here. The standard lower limits (K⁺ 3.5, Mg²⁺ 1.7) are floor baselines, not cardiac-surgery baselines.
  • Who this applies to: Every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient from ICU admission through hospital discharge.
  • When to start: On admission to the step-down unit or ICU. Labs typically BID (twice daily) for POD 1–3, then daily until discharge.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why It Exists
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac surgery patients deplete electrolytes faster than medical patients because of convergent physiologic stressors:

  • Aggressive diuresis (POD 1–3) — Fluid mobilization and Loop diuretics shift K⁺, Mg²⁺, and Phos into urine.
  • Insulin + glucose drives on CPB and post-op — Hyperglycemia management and stress response push K⁺ and Phos intracellularly.
  • Refeeding phenomenon in malnourished pre-op patients — Intracellular shifts of Phos, K⁺, Mg²⁺ upon re-feeding.
  • CPB pump prime dilution — Cardiopulmonary bypass prime dilutes iCa²⁺ and Mg²⁺ acutely.
  • Surgical drainage losses — Mediastinal and pleural chest tube drainage carries electrolytes.
  • Beta-agonist and catecholamine drips (epinephrine, dobutamine, albuterol nebs) — Intracellular K⁺ shift via beta-2 stimulation.
  • Alkalosis (contraction alkalosis, respiratory hyperventilation) — Acid-base shifts drive K⁺ intracellularly.
  • Citrate from blood products — Massive transfusion citrate binds and chelates iCa²⁺.

The POD 2–3 nadir: Peak depletion often coincides with maximal inflammatory response, fluid mobilization, and beta-blocker nadir — hence the need for more-frequent electrolyte checks early.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
• Applies: All post-operative adult cardiac surgery patients (age ≥ 18).
  • Does NOT apply: Pediatric patients (different physiology and goals), chronic dialysis patients (modified targets per renal team), patients with severe hypermagnesemia or hypercalcemia (different management).
  • Trajectory: This protocol spans ICU → step-down → telemetry → home. Recheck frequency decreases as the patient stabilizes.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *pre-replacement check* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Information-gathering before deciding route and dose.

  • Current labs: Review BMP / CMP for K⁺, Mg²⁺, iCa²⁺, Phos, Na⁺. Note most recent Cr and eGFR.
  • Renal function context: Is Cr rising? UOP trending down? Oliguria (< 20 mL/h × 4 h)? → impacts K⁺ dosing.
  • Trend, not single value: Plot the electrolyte over POD. Is it dropping despite recent dose? Signals ongoing losses.
  • Cardiac rhythm: Scan tele for U waves (hypokalemia), peaked T waves (hyperkalemia), QTc prolongation (hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia).
  • Oral tolerance: Can the patient take PO? Is NGT patent? Aspiration risk? → impacts route choice.
  • IV access: Central line available for doses ≥ 10 mEq K⁺? Or peripheral access only?
  • Active drips: What's on board? Beta-agonists, insulin infusion, loop diuretics, K⁺-sparing agents? Each impacts replacement decisions.
  • Recent transfusion or massive fluid shifts? → anticipate iCa²⁺ drop from citrate.

Hold criteria checklist before giving K⁺ replacement:

  • AKI with rising Cr (new or worsening) — consult team; consider half-dose or hold
  • Oliguria (UOP < 20 mL/h × 4 h) — hold pending team discussion
  • K⁺ already ≥ 5.0 mEq/L — do NOT give; notify team
  • K⁺ ≥ 6.0 mEq/L — urgent hyperkalemia protocol, not routine replacement
  • On K⁺-sparing diuretic (spironolactone, eplerenone) — reduce replacement dose or hold
  • ACE-I / ARB on board — caution; often fine but watch trend

sections.heading: 5.1 Post-op goals table — narrow cardiac-surgery-specific range
sections.bodyHtml:
Electrolyte Replace if ≤ Critical (urgent call) if ≤ Target range Critical high
K⁺ (mEq/L) 4.0 3.0 4.0–5.0 ≥ 5.5 (hold); ≥ 6.0 (treat)
Mg²⁺ (mg/dL) 2.0 1.5 2.0–2.5 (target 3.0–3.5 in high arrhythmia-risk populations — e.g., POAF-prone, recurrent VT/VF, QTc-prolonged, torsades risk) > 3.5 with signs of toxicity (hyporeflexia, respiratory depression, hypotension) — rare, usually iatrogenic in AKI/CKD
iCa²⁺ (mmol/L) 1.1 0.9 1.1–1.3 ≥ 1.4
Total Ca²⁺ (mg/dL) 8.4 7.5 8.4–10.5 ≥ 11.0
Phos (mg/dL) 2.5 1.5 2.5–4.5 ≥ 5.5
Na⁺ (mEq/L) 134 125 135–145 ≥ 150

Goals adapted from CVICU Handbook (2017) and Elmistekawy & Shallik (2025). Confirm against current institutional policy; institutional policy supersedes if different.

sections.heading: 5.2 Potassium (K⁺) replacement
sections.bodyHtml:
K⁺ level (mEq/L) Replacement dose Route Recheck timing
3.5–3.9 KCl 40 mEq PO ×1 (or 20 mEq IV × 2) PO preferred if tolerating 4 h after PO / 1 h after IV
3.0–3.4 KCl 60 mEq (split PO/IV per access) IV preferred if central available 1 h after IV
< 3.0 KCl 20 mEq IV × 3–4 doses, each over 1 h Central line preferred; peripheral max 10 mEq/h 1 h after each dose
≥ 5.0 HOLD K⁺. Notify team. Recheck STAT. — Repeat if on K⁺-sparing agent
≥ 6.0 Hyperkalemia protocol (IV Ca gluconate, insulin + D50, albuterol, kayexalate/lokelma) — Telemetry + serial ECG

Route pearls for K⁺:

  • Central line preferred for doses ≥ 10 mEq/h. Periphery maximum is 10 mEq/h; dilute in 100 mL normal saline and infuse over 1 hour.
  • Peripheral infusion burns. Warn the patient; offer warm compress. If pain severe, slow the rate or switch to central line.
  • PO KCl is underused. 40 mEq liquid or powder works fine when tolerating; cheaper, doesn't tie up IV access. Tastes bad — mix with juice.
  • Never give KCl IV push. Fatal arrhythmias reported. Always infuse over ≥ 1 hour.

sections.heading: 5.3 Magnesium (Mg²⁺) replacement
sections.bodyHtml:
Mg²⁺ level (mg/dL) Replacement dose Route Recheck timing
1.7–1.9 MgSO₄ 2 g IV over 1 h IV 4 h
1.4–1.6 MgSO₄ 4 g IV over 2 h IV 2 h
< 1.4 MgSO₄ 4 g IV over 1 h + telemetry monitoring IV 1 h, then 4 h

Critical: Replace K⁺ and Mg²⁺ together. Mg²⁺ is an obligate cofactor for Na/K-ATPase. You cannot correct refractory hypokalemia without correcting Mg²⁺ first.

If K⁺ keeps dropping despite adequate replacement, check Mg²⁺ next — not dose escalation.

Hold criteria for Mg²⁺:

  • AKI with Mg²⁺ already ≥ 2.5 mg/dL — notify team before dosing
  • Myasthenia gravis (rare) — caution; Mg²⁺ can worsen weakness
  • Complete heart block without pacemaker — Mg²⁺ slows conduction further

PO Mg²⁺ (magnesium oxide, magnesium gluconate) is poorly absorbed and causes diarrhea. Stick to IV on the unit unless the patient is at baseline on PO for chronic constipation.

sections.heading: 5.4 Phosphorus (Phos) replacement
sections.bodyHtml:
Phos level (mg/dL) Replacement dose Route Recheck timing
2.0–2.4 K-Phos 15 mmol PO (or 15 mmol IV over 4 h if NPO) PO preferred 4 h
1.5–1.9 K-Phos 30 mmol IV over 6 h IV 6 h
< 1.5 K-Phos 30 mmol IV over 4 h + telemetry + team notification IV 4 h

K-Phos adds potassium. Each 30 mmol dose of K-Phos also delivers ~44 mEq K⁺. Factor it into the K⁺ plan or the patient becomes hyperkalemic. If K⁺ is already elevated (> 4.5 mEq/L), use Na-Phos instead to replace Phos without the K⁺ load.

Hold criteria for Phos:

  • iCa²⁺ < 1.0 mmol/L — Phos binds Ca²⁺; replacement causes symptomatic hypocalcemia. Correct iCa²⁺ first.
  • Severe AKI — team decision.

sections.heading: 5.5 Calcium (Ca²⁺) replacement
sections.bodyHtml:
iCa²⁺ level (mmol/L) Replacement dose Route Notes
1.0–1.1 Ca gluconate 1 g IV over 30 min IV peripheral OK Monitor for warmth / flushing
0.85–1.0 Ca gluconate 2 g IV over 30 min IV peripheral Monitor BP + heart rate
< 0.85 Ca gluconate 2 g IV over 30 min × 2 doses; notify team IV peripheral Telemetry
Critical (QTc prolongation, tetany, Chvostek/Trousseau sign) Ca chloride 1 g IV via central line only Central line required High elemental Ca²⁺; extravasation causes necrosis

Why iCa²⁺, not total Ca²⁺: Total calcium is albumin-bound and not physiologically active. Post-op patients often have low albumin, making total Ca²⁺ artifactually low.

iCa²⁺ is the clinical truth. Always order and target ionized calcium.

Ca chloride vs Ca gluconate:

  • Ca chloride: 3× more elemental calcium; preferred in code/arrest. Must go central because extravasation burns tissue.
  • Ca gluconate: Peripheral-safe; lower elemental Ca²⁺ but acceptable for routine post-op replacement.

sections.heading: 5.6 Sodium (Na⁺) — overview only
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-op Na⁺ derangements reflect volume status or SIADH, not simple electrolyte depletion. Protocol on the unit is recognize + notify team, not replace:

Na⁺ level (mEq/L) Action
130–134 Document; notify APP; review fluid I/O and ongoing fluid plan
125–129 Team call — likely fluid restriction (SIADH) vs hypertonic saline depending on volume status
< 125 Urgent — neuro assessment, team call, possible ICU transfer
≥ 150 Team call — dehydration vs diabetes insipidus

Never correct Na⁺ faster than 8–10 mEq/L per 24 hours. Risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome. This is an attending-level decision, not a nursing-protocol one.

sections.heading: 5.7 Recheck timing
sections.bodyHtml:
Route / Scenario Recheck window Rationale
IV (any electrolyte) 1 h after dose completes Fast equilibration; sooner wastes a blood draw
PO K⁺ 4 h after dose GI absorption slower than IV
PO Phos 4 h after dose Variable absorption
PO Mg²⁺ 4–6 h (rarely used post-op) Slow and unreliable absorption
After multi-dose series (e.g., K⁺ 3.2 → three 20-mEq doses) 4 h after final dose Lets equilibrium settle before interpreting

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / Refractory cases
sections.bodyHtml:
When standard replacement isn't working.

  • Refractory hypokalemia: K⁺ dropping despite adequate IV replacement → check Mg²⁺ immediately. You cannot correct K⁺ without Mg²⁺. Also assess for ongoing losses: NGT drainage, diarrhea, aggressive diuresis. If Mg²⁺ is normal and losses minimal, consider:
  • Beta-agonist drip (epinephrine, dobutamine) driving intracellular shift — ask if drip can be weaned
  • Respiratory alkalosis — re-assess ventilator settings

  • Inadequate replacement dose — escalate to higher IV K⁺ doses per provider

  • Rising Cr with hypokalemia: Do NOT continue routine K⁺ dosing if renal function is worsening. Halve the dose or hold; notify team. This is a setup for iatrogenic hyperkalemia.

  • Hyperkalemia (K⁺ ≥ 6.0): Activates hyperkalemia protocol — IV calcium (cardiac membrane stabilization), insulin + dextrose, albuterol, potassium-binding resin (kayexalate or newer lokelma). Notify team immediately.

  • Refractory hypomagnesemia: Mg²⁺ not rising despite repeated IV doses (rare) → consider ongoing losses (TPN, GI drainage) or malabsorption if attempting PO supplementation. Escalate dosing per team.

  • Hypophosphatemia not correcting: Confirm you're using the right salt (K-Phos vs Na-Phos) given the K⁺ level. If K⁺ is high, Na-Phos is the choice. Also check iCa²⁺ — if < 1.0, Phos won't correct until Ca²⁺ is repleted (binds Phos).

sections.heading: 7.1 Why post-op cardiac patients deplete fast
sections.bodyHtml:
The post-op cardiac patient faces a convergence of physiologic stressors that don't affect general medical patients:

Diuretic stress (POD 1–3):

  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) accelerate K⁺, Mg²⁺, and Phos wasting.
  • Fluid mobilization from CPB prime and third-spacing is brisk; diuresis timing coincides with peak inflammatory response (POD 2–3).

Metabolic stress:

  • Stress hyperglycemia and insulin administration drive K⁺ and Phos intracellularly via Na/K-ATPase stimulation.
  • Refeeding phenomenon (in chronically malnourished pre-op patients) causes massive intracellular shift of Phos, K⁺, and Mg²⁺ within hours of first large meal.

CPB dilution:

  • The pump prime (typically 1–2 liters of non-blood prime) acutely hemodilutes all ions, especially ionized Ca²⁺.
  • This dilution is compounded by aggressive post-pump fluid administration (volume resuscitation).

Surgical drainage: - Mediastinal chest tube output (serous, bloody) contains electrolytes. High drainage (> 200 mL/h early post-op) accelerates loss.

Catecholamine & medications:

  • Beta-agonists (epinephrine, dobutamine, albuterol nebulizers) activate beta-2 receptors on skeletal muscle, driving K⁺ intracellularly via Na/K-ATPase.
  • This is a shift, not a loss — the total body K⁺ doesn't decrease, but serum K⁺ drops, creating arrhythmia risk.

Acid-base dynamics:

  • Respiratory alkalosis (over-ventilation) and contraction alkalosis (diuresis) both drive K⁺ intracellularly.
  • Correcting the pH first may partly correct K⁺ without additional replacement, but electrolyte replacement should not wait.

Transfusion & citrate:

  • Massive transfusion (> 4 units FFP, > 6 units PRBC in 6 hours) introduces citrate-based anticoagulation.
  • Citrate chelates iCa²⁺; some ICU protocols prophylactically replace ionized Ca²⁺ every 2–4 units transfused.

sections.heading: 7.2 Route decisions detail
sections.bodyHtml:
When to choose IV vs PO:

Route Best for Avoid if
IV K⁺ < 3.5 mEq/L, NPO status, nausea/vomiting, urgent replacement Peripheral access only (K⁺ ≥ 20 mEq/dose) — causes pain
PO K⁺ 3.5–3.9 mEq/L, tolerating oral, stable GI, avoids IV access burden Nausea, dysphagia, aspiration risk, active NGT drainage, malabsorption

IV peripheral safety:

  • Maximum concentration: 10 mEq K⁺ per 100 mL over 1 hour.
  • Faster infusion or higher concentration → phlebitis, burning vein, extravasation risk.
  • Warm compress during infusion alleviates burning.
  • If patient reports severe pain, STOP, flush with normal saline, and consider switch to central line or PO.

Central line advantage:

  • Allows 20 mEq K⁺ per 100 mL at faster rates (up to 20 mEq/h if necessary, though usually 10 mEq/h preferred).
  • Used for refractory hypokalemia (K⁺ < 3.0 mEq/L) where you need rapid correction.

PO pearls:

  • KCl 20 mEq packets or liquid are cost-effective and work fine if the patient tolerates oral.
  • Mix with juice to mask bad taste.
  • Take with food to reduce GI upset.
  • Warn about potential diarrhea or nausea.

sections.heading: 7.3 Hold criteria rationale
sections.bodyHtml:
Acute kidney injury (AKI) + K⁺ replacement = disaster.

  • If Cr is rising or new oliguria is present, the kidney cannot clear K⁺.
  • Routine replacement dose → hyperkalemia.
  • Solution: halve the dose, extend recheck interval, or hold pending team.

Oliguria (< 20 mL/h × 4 h): - Urine output is the indicator that the kidney is still clearing; if it stops, stop K⁺ until output resumes.

K⁺ ≥ 5.0 mEq/L:

  • This is the threshold where hyperkalemia risk rises and ectopy/bradycardia begins.
  • Check ECG for peaked T waves.
  • Notify team and hold replacement.

K⁺-sparing agents (spironolactone, eplerenone) on board:

  • These drugs block aldosterone, which normally promotes K⁺ excretion.
  • On such drugs, routine K⁺ dosing can cause iatrogenic hyperkalemia.
  • Reduce the replacement dose or hold; check K⁺ more frequently.

ACE-I / ARB on board:

  • These reduce aldosterone indirectly, promoting K⁺ retention.
  • Often fine in post-op; monitor trend. Not an absolute hold, but grounds for caution.

Recent massive transfusion:

  • Transfused RBCs contain potassium; even though they're refrigerated (mitigates release), large volumes can transiently raise serum K⁺.
  • Hold routine replacement if K⁺ just checked; recheck in 2–4 hours after transfusion ends.

sections.heading: 7.4 Electrolyte-specific physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Potassium (K⁺) and the cardiac action potential:

  • K⁺ determines the resting membrane potential of cardiomyocytes (typically −90 mV at K⁺ 4.0 mEq/L).
  • Low K⁺ hyperpolarizes the membrane, slowing repolarization (prolonged QT, U waves) and predisposing to early afterdepolarizations (EAD) → premature beats, POAF.
  • High K⁺ depolarizes the resting potential, shortening APD and promoting phase-0 abnormalities (peaked T waves) → bradycardia, asystole at K⁺ > 7.

Magnesium (Mg²⁺) and Na/K-ATPase:

  • Mg²⁺ is an obligate cofactor for the Na/K-ATPase pump.
  • Without sufficient Mg²⁺, K⁺ replacement cannot be retained intracellularly.
  • This is why refractory hypokalemia is the classic sign of hypomagnesemia — the cell can't keep K⁺ inside.

Ionized calcium (iCa²⁺) and the QT interval:

  • iCa²⁺ regulates phase 0 (depolarization) and phase 2 (plateau) of the action potential.
  • Low iCa²⁺ prolongs phase 2 → QT prolongation → torsades de pointes risk (especially if Mg²⁺ also low).
  • High iCa²⁺ shortens repolarization (short QT).

Phosphorus (Phos) and ATP:

  • Phos is essential for ATP synthesis and cellular energy metabolism.
  • Severe hypophosphatemia (< 1 mg/dL) → respiratory muscle weakness, rhabdomyolysis, hemolytic anemia, impaired cardiac contractility.
  • Often overlooked post-op because K⁺ and Mg²⁺ grab attention, but Phos depletion is real.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory
sections.bodyHtml:
Pattern recognition for proficient/expert staff. These appear in currently stable patients; if any manifest, re-escalate.

  • K⁺ trending down despite adequate IV replacement — check Mg²⁺ immediately; also assess for ongoing losses (diarrhea, NGT, diuretics) and beta-agonist drip.
  • Cr trending up while replacing K⁺ — kidney function worsening; reduce dose or hold K⁺; notify team.
  • UOP dropping (< 20 mL/h sustained) — oliguric; hold K⁺ replacement until urine resumes.
  • New peaked T waves on tele with K⁺ 4.5+ — early hyperkalemia; notify team, prepare for kayexalate/insulin.
  • QTc prolonging on Mg²⁺ replacement or staying long after Ca²⁺ + Mg²⁺ doses — risk of torsades; obtain ECG, notify team, hold Mg²⁺ if QTc > 500 ms.
  • New ectopy (PACs, PVCs) despite electrolyte goals — consider other triggers (hypoxia, pain, anxiety, fever); do not over-interpret as electrolyte failure.
  • Muscle weakness, cramping, or paresthesias — could indicate severe K⁺ or Mg²⁺ depletion; obtain labs STAT.
  • Tremor, hyperreflexia, or Chvostek/Trousseau sign — hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia; obtain iCa²⁺, Mg²⁺ STAT.
  • Respiratory muscle weakness (weak cough, rapid RR) — could be hypophosphatemia; obtain Phos STAT.
  • Seizure or confusion in hyponatremic patient — symptomatic hyponatremia; neuro assessment, team call, possible ICU transfer.
  • New arrhythmia cluster after diuresis or line removal — assume electrolyte trigger until proven otherwise; obtain BMP STAT.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Always replace K⁺ and Mg²⁺ together. You cannot correct K⁺ without Mg²⁺. If K⁺ is refractory, check Mg²⁺ first—not dose escalation.

  2. Peripheral KCl burns. Max 10 mEq/100 mL over 1 hour. Warn the patient; offer warm compress. If pain severe, switch routes or central access.

  3. Never give KCl IV push. Fatal arrhythmias reported. Always infuse IV over ≥ 1 hour.

  4. K-Phos delivers both K⁺ and Phos. 30 mmol K-Phos = 44 mEq K⁺. If K⁺ is already high (> 4.5), use Na-Phos instead to avoid stacking.

  5. iCa²⁺, not total Ca²⁺. Low albumin makes total Ca²⁺ artifactually low. iCa²⁺ is the clinical truth; always order ionized.

  6. Ca chloride extravasation causes tissue necrosis. Central line only. Ca gluconate is peripheral-safe and is the floor default.

  7. Check Cr before any K⁺ dose. AKI + routine K⁺ = iatrogenic hyperkalemia. Easy to miss on a busy shift; set a checklist.

  8. Refeeding depletes all three (Phos, K⁺, Mg²⁺) within hours of the first large meal after extended NPO. Anticipate and pre-check labs if NPO > 24 hours.

  9. Beta-agonist drips cause hypokalemia by intracellular shift, not loss. Replacement floats serum K⁺ briefly, but the drip keeps pulling it in. Track trend; don't chase with bigger doses.

  10. Alkalosis (contraction or respiratory) drops K⁺ intracellularly. Replacing without addressing the alkalosis is chasing. Ask if over-ventilation can be reduced.

  11. MOM (magnesium oxide) in CKD causes hypermagnesemia over 48–72 hours. If the patient has received PRN MOM for constipation, watch Mg²⁺ trend; switch to stool softener.

  12. Citrate from massive transfusion binds iCa²⁺. If the patient is transfusing briskly (> 4 units in 6 hours), expect iCa²⁺ drop. Some protocols replace prophylactically per unit.

  13. QTc prolongation is an early sign of low Mg²⁺ / iCa²⁺. Scan strips for QTc, not just rate and rhythm. A QTc approaching 500 ms warrants Mg²⁺ / Ca²⁺ check before it triggers torsades.

  14. Check tele before and after replacement. Before-after comparison of flat T's (hypokalemia) or U waves is teaching gold for new grads.

  15. Document the recheck. Replacement without a recheck is an incomplete task. Set a timer on your phone or in the EHR.
