cards.title: Infective Endocarditis Admission
cards.quickAnswer: IE patient on ICU admission: 3 blood culture sets BEFORE antibiotics (if not septic), TTE→TEE (mandatory for diagnosis), Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria. Empiric vancomycin (15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h, goal trough 15–20 μg/mL) + ceftriaxone (2 g IV q12h) ±gentamicin (target peak 3–5 μg/mL) pending culture results; switch to organism-specific regimen at 48–72 h. Surgical indications (lower threshold for prosthetic vs native): cardiogenic shock, large (>10 mm) mobile vegetation, perivalvular abscess, new heart block, persistent bacteremia, recurrent emboli. Addiction medicine consult critical for IVDU patients (medication-assisted treatment, harm reduction integral to cure). PICC line (lifesaving access, infection-risk monitoring essential). OPAT planning for 4–6 week IV antibiotic course — case management, home infusion setup. Heart team (cardiology, CT surgery, ID, addiction medicine) engaged Day 1–2.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
IE patient on ICU admission: 3 blood culture sets BEFORE antibiotics (if not septic), TTE→TEE (mandatory for diagnosis), Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria. Empiric vancomycin (15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h, goal trough 15–20 μg/mL) + ceftriaxone (2 g IV q12h) ±gentamicin (target peak 3–5 μg/mL) pending culture results; switch to organism-specific regimen at 48–72 h.

Surgical indications (lower threshold for prosthetic vs native): cardiogenic shock, large (>10 mm) mobile vegetation, perivalvular abscess, new heart block, persistent bacteremia, recurrent emboli. Addiction medicine consult critical for IVDU patients (medication-assisted treatment, harm reduction integral to cure). PICC line (lifesaving access, infection-risk monitoring essential). OPAT planning for 4–6 week IV antibiotic course — case management, home infusion setup. Heart team (cardiology, CT surgery, ID, addiction medicine) engaged Day 1–2.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → Fowler et al. (2023) Duke-ISCVID criteria → Baddour et al. (2015) AHA Infective Endocarditis Guidelines → Habib et al. (2015) ESC VHD Guidelines → IDSA Clinical Practice → CVICU Handbook 2017 → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Bojar (2020)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Infection of native or prosthetic heart valve (or endocardial surface) by bacteria, fungi, or HACEK organisms, confirmed by blood culture + clinical criteria (Duke-ISCVID 2023) or TEE findings.
  • Native valve endocarditis (NVE): commonly Streptococcus viridans (low virulence, slower progression), Staphylococcus aureus (high virulence, rapid deterioration, higher emboli rate), or coagulase-negative staph. Tricuspid endocarditis almost always IVDU-related (S. aureus).
  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE): 0.5–1% per patient-year risk; early PVE (< 2 months post-op) often nosocomial (coagulase-negative staph, Gram-negatives); late PVE (> 2 months) similar to NVE pathogens.
  • Right-sided (tricuspid) IE: most commonly IVDU (S. aureus), often medically treatable, repair preferred over replacement if possible. Septic pulmonary emboli common.
  • Epidemiology: ~15–30 cases per million per year in developed countries; increasing incidence with IVDU (now largest risk factor). 30-day mortality ~20%; 1-year mortality ~40% if surgery needed.
  • Why it matters: untreated IE is rapidly fatal. Even with optimal therapy, mortality remains high if surgical indications arise. Early heart team involvement, aggressive diagnostic evaluation, and rapid diagnostic confirmation critical.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: for novice + advanced beginner deep-dive.

sections.heading: Core mechanism: bacteremia → seeding → vegetation growth
sections.bodyHtml:
IE develops when circulating bacteria (or fungi) seed the heart endocardium, particularly abnormal or traumatized valves. Formation of vegetation — colony of bacteria embedded in a biofilm surrounded by platelets, fibrin, and inflammatory cells — makes treatment difficult (antibiotics penetrate poorly into biofilm; high bacterial density).

Three-stage progression:

  1. Bacteremia (transient or persistent): bacteria enter bloodstream (from skin, GI, GU, respiratory, or dental source). In healthy endocardium, bacteria usually cleared. In damaged valve, abnormal flow turbulence, or prosthetic material → bacteria lodge, multiply.

  2. Vegetation growth (days to weeks): biofilm-embedded bacteria replicate in microaerophilic environment. Platelets and fibrin accumulate. Vegetation grows, eroding into valve tissue, perforating leaflets, or extending into annulus (abscess formation, conduction system involvement).

  3. Complications: vegetation detachment → septic emboli (lungs, brain, spleen, kidneys); valve regurgitation from leaflet destruction → acute HF; annular abscess → aortic root rupture, pericarditis, new heart block; septic shock from persistent bacteremia.

sections.heading: Why Strep viridans vs S. aureus matters (clinical trajectory)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Strep viridans — alpha-hemolytic strep, often from dental source, low virulence. Slower progression (weeks to months). Smaller vegetations, lower emboli rate. Often medically treatable.
  • S. aureus — high virulence. Rapid, aggressive progression (days to weeks). Large vegetations, high emboli rate (20–25%), early valve destruction, higher mortality. Surgical threshold lower. IVDU + S. aureus tricuspid IE may progress to septic shock.

sections.heading: Addiction medicine context (for IVDU endocarditis)
sections.bodyHtml: IVDU endocarditis is a chronic infection superimposed on opioid use disorder (OUD). Recidivism without addiction medicine intervention is high (relapse rates 60–80% if MAT not offered). Medication-assisted treatment (buprenorphine, methadone) + harm reduction (sterile needles, syringe services) are evidence-based medical interventions, not "enablement." Patients perceiving non-judgmental care + addiction medicine integration are more likely to complete the prolonged antibiotic course.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — why the patient was admitted.

sections.heading: Acute presentation scenarios (admission triggers)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Sepsis + new cardiac murmur: fever, elevated lactate, tachycardia, new or changing murmur
  • Acute decompensated heart failure: new regurgitant lesion from vegetation, valve perforation, or root abscess
  • Septic emboli: acute stroke, limb ischemia, abdominal pain (splenic infarction), pulmonary emboli (right-sided IE)
  • New arrhythmia or conduction abnormality: fever + new PR prolongation, AV block suggests root abscess
  • Persistent fever + positive blood cultures despite appropriate antibiotics for > 7–10 days
  • Immunocompromised patient with fever + new cardiac finding on any imaging
  • Positive blood cultures from non-invasive source (e.g., skin flora grown from multiple sets) in patient with cardiac risk
  • IVDU history + fever + any new cardiac findings (murmur, embolic event, shortness of breath)

sections.heading: Physical exam findings (may be subtle; absent in modern IE)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Cardiac auscultation: new or changing murmur (regurgitant lesion from vegetation or perforation)
  • Embolic stigmata (rarely seen): Janeway lesions (painless, flat erythematous macules on palms/soles), Osler nodes (tender nodules on fingertips — actually immune complex vasculitis), splinter hemorrhages (nail beds — may be traumatic), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages with white centers — rare, specific)
  • Petechiae: non-blanching, scattered, not pathognomonic (bacterial vs embolic origin unclear)
  • Splenomegaly: immune complex vasculitis
  • New or worsening heart failure signs: rales, elevated JVD, new S3, signs of shock

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (initial 4–8 hours)
sections.bodyHtml: Competent systematic data gathering. No interventions yet.

sections.heading: Blood cultures (STAT, BEFORE antibiotics if possible)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Draw 3 separate sets × 3 sites (not 3 bottles from same site — different means different organisms, not contamination)
  • 10 mL blood per bottle (aerobic + anaerobic per set)
  • Before antibiotics if patient not immediately septic (if septic, start antibiotics immediately after cultures drawn)
  • Document exact time, site (peripheral vs line), culture set number
  • HOLD ANTIBIOTICS pending culture results only if patient hemodynamically stable; if shock/sepsis → start empiric ABX immediately after cultures

sections.heading: Vital signs & hemodynamics
sections.bodyHtml:
• HR, BP (sitting, orthostatic if safe), SpO₂, RR, temperature (trending)
  • Perfusion: capillary refill, skin temperature, mental status, urine output
  • Evidence of heart failure: JVD, peripheral edema, weight vs dry weight
  • Evidence of septic shock: hypotension, tachycardia, lactate

sections.heading: Symptoms & timeline
sections.bodyHtml:
• Fever pattern (intermittent vs continuous), chills, night sweats
  • Fatigue, malaise, weight loss (subacute IE)
  • New or worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, chest pain
  • Recent dental procedures, skin infections, IVDU, cardiac surgery, invasive procedures
  • Embolic symptoms: focal neurologic deficit, focal pain (limb, abdomen), visual changes
  • Prior IE, prosthetic valve, intra-cardiac device

sections.heading: Physical exam (complete cardiac + embolic + skin assessment)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Cardiac: auscultation (new murmur?), signs of HF (rales, edema, JVD)
  • Neurologic: baseline mental status, focal deficits (stroke), cranial nerves (CN palsy from mycotic aneurysm if left-sided IE)
  • Skin: petechiae location, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway/Osler lesions, injection sites (IVDU)
  • Abdominal: splenomegaly, LUQ/RUQ tenderness (splenic infarct), signs of peritonitis
  • Extremity pulses: assess for embolic limb ischemia
  • Eyes: Roth spots (fundoscopy)

sections.heading: Diagnostic labs (STAT)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Troponin, BNP — assess myocardial involvement, HF severity
  • CBC: baseline WBC, Hgb, platelets (thrombocytopenia can develop)
  • CMP, creatinine: baseline renal function (aminoglycosides, contrast risk)
  • Coagulation studies (PT/INR, PTT): baseline (emboli, anticoagulation if needed)
  • Magnesium, calcium, phosphate: electrolytes matter for dysrhythmia risk
  • Lactate, ABG — assess perfusion, sepsis severity
  • EKG (12-lead) STAT — baseline PR interval, AV block, ischemic changes (embolic)

sections.heading: Imaging (expedited)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) STAT (same day, next morning if stable)
  • Vegetation presence, size, location, mobility
  • Aortic regurgitation, mitral regurgitation, tricuspid regurgitation (from vegetation or perforation)
  • Prosthetic valve assessment (if PVE)
  • Abscess or pseudoaneurysm
  • LVEF, wall motion abnormalities (embolic or myocarditis)
  • Estimated PA pressure, RV function
  • Sensitivity ~60–70% for vegetation; 90%+ if vegetation > 3 mm

  • TEE mandatory for prosthetic valve, inconclusive TTE, or high clinical suspicion

  • Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) — essential (pursue same day or next AM)

  • Gold standard for vegetation detection (sensitivity > 95%), abscess assessment
  • Better visualization of posterior structures, prosthetic valves, left atrial appendage
  • Assess for perforation, regurgitation severity

  • Guide surgical planning if needed

  • CT chest ± PE protocol or chest X-ray: rule out pneumonia, pulmonary emboli (right-sided IE)

  • Look for septic pulmonary emboli (wedge-shaped infiltrates in right-sided IE)

  • Brain MRI (if neurologic signs, no contraindications): assess for septic stroke, mycotic aneurysm

  • Even asymptomatic emboli (20–25% of IE) — some centers screen MRI routinely
  • Mycotic aneurysm (infected cerebral artery) — complication of left-sided IE

sections.heading: Microbiologic workup
sections.bodyHtml:
• Gram stain, culture media selection: standard media (blood agar, chocolate agar) for typical bacteria; hold cultures 2–3 weeks if HACEK suspected; special media for Bartonella, Brucella, fastidious organisms
  • Serologic studies if cultures negative (culture-negative IE ~5–10%): Bartonella serology, Brucella, Coxiella, Q fever, fungi (if immunocompromised)
  • PCR / 16S rRNA (some labs): if cultures negative and IE still likely

sections.heading: Clinical context & risk assessment
sections.bodyHtml:
• Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria: collect data for major criteria (typical echo findings, blood cultures, HACEK, emboli, vascular/immunologic phenomena) and minor criteria (predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunologic phenomena)
  • Addiction medicine history (for IVDU IE): current OUD treatment status (MAT yes/no?), injection frequency, last use, substance type, prior rehab attempts, support system
  • Prior cardiac history: rheumatic disease, prior endocarditis, congenital disease, prosthetic valve, intra-cardiac device (ICD, pacer), cardiac surgery
  • Prophylaxis history: were dental procedures covered with antibiotics? (inadequate prophylaxis common in IE)
  • Social factors: housing, health literacy, ability to comply with 4–6 week outpatient IV therapy

sections.heading: 5. Management — Diagnostic Confirmation & Antibiotic Therapy Initiation
Preface: Stable vs. Unstable fork for medical-admit
sections.bodyHtml:
Stable: fever, new murmur, positive cultures, but hemodynamically compensated, no signs of shock, no acute HF decompensation — pursue 4–6 week IV antibiotic course with careful monitoring.

Unstable: cardiogenic shock, acute pulmonary edema, septic shock, recurrent emboli despite antibiotics, large vegetation with risk of embolization, new heart block — surgical consultation URGENT; may need early (empiric) valve replacement regardless of antibiotic duration.

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path — diagnostic confirmation & empiric antibiotic initiation
sections.bodyHtml: Goal: confirm diagnosis, start organism-specific therapy, complete diagnostic workup, assess for surgical indications.

sections.heading: Blood cultures & diagnostic confirmation
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Draw 3 blood culture sets BEFORE antibiotics (if not immediately septic)

    • Different sites (arm, hand, groin — not from lines if possible)
    • Each set: 10 mL aerobic + 10 mL anaerobic bottle
    • Document timing, source
    • Notify lab of IE suspicion (special handling, extended incubation)

  2. Review Duke-ISCVID 2023 criteria as cultures return (Fowler et al., 2023)

    • Major criteria: (1) typical blood cultures from IE organisms, (2) echocardiogram: vegetation, abscess, new prosthetic dehiscence, new regurgitation, (3) HACEK serology
    • Minor criteria: predisposition (valve disease, IVDU), fever ≥ 38°C, vascular phenomena (septic emboli, Janeway, splinter), immunologic (Osler, Roth, glomerulonephritis)
    • Definite IE: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor
    • Possible IE: 1 major + 1 minor, or 3 minor

sections.heading: Imaging (TTE → TEE)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. TTE STAT (same day or next AM)

    • If positive vegetation (esp. > 3 mm) + positive blood cultures → supports definite IE diagnosis
    • If negative but high clinical suspicion → proceed to TEE

  2. TEE (within 24 h, sooner if unstable)

    • Higher sensitivity; essential for prosthetic valves, posterior structures, abscess assessment
    • Guides surgical planning if needed

sections.heading: Empiric antibiotic regimen (pending culture results)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Vancomycin (first-line coverage, especially for prosthetic valve or MRSA risk)

    • 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (goal trough 15–20 μg/mL, NOT the older 15 μg/mL goal — modern guideline raises target)
    • Measure trough just before dose 4–5
    • Renal dosing: adjust if Cr > 2.0 or eGFR < 30
    • Obtain vanc level at steady state (after dose 4–5); therapeutic drug monitoring standard

  2. Ceftriaxone (broad Gram-positive/negative coverage)

    • 2 g IV q12h (total 4 g/day)
    • If renal impairment: adjust dose proportionally
    • Pair with vanc for synergy (dual therapy standard for empiric IE)

  3. Gentamicin (aminoglycoside; synergy with beta-lactams/vancomycin)

    • Dosing: 3 mg/kg IV q8h (renal dosing, goal peak 3–5 μg/mL)
    • Hold if: SCr > 2.0, oliguria, pre-existing ototoxicity
    • Measure peak + trough: peak at 30 min post-infusion, trough just before next dose
    • Duration: often 2 weeks empiric, switch to 2-agent regimen after; full duration (4–6 wk) for highly resistant organisms
    • Monitor: serial Cr, BUN, baseline + periodic audiogram if extended course

  4. Adjust to organism-specific regimen at 48–72 h once culture identification + susceptibilities return - Strep viridans (penicillin-sensitive): penicillin G 4 million U IV q4h + ceftriaxone, ± gentamicin short course - Strep bovis / gallolyticus: as viridans - S. aureus (MSSA): nafcillin/oxacillin 2 g IV q4h (preferred) OR cefazolin + gentamicin (reduces septic emboli risk)

    • S. aureus (MRSA): vancomycin ± gentamicin (extended course)
    • Enterococcus: ampicillin (if susceptible) + gentamicin; if VRE → linezolid or daptomycin
    • HACEK organisms: ceftriaxone ± gentamicin short course (excellent prognosis, rarely need surgery)
    • Fungal IE: remove valve; antifungal therapy inadequate monotherapy
    • Culture-negative IE (5–10%): continue empiric therapy (vanc + cephalosporin) after negative repeat cultures; consider serology if HACEK/Bartonella/Q fever suspected

  5. Serial blood cultures to document clearance - Repeat cultures q48h until negative (should clear within 48–96 h if appropriate therapy) - Persistent positive cultures after 1 week → treatment failure, surgical indication, or inadequate source control

sections.heading: Monitoring & observation (daily)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Vital signs + hemodynamics each shift

    • HR trending up (tachycardia worsens prognosis)
    • BP stability (signs of decompensation)
    • Fever curve (should trend down by day 3–5)

  2. Cardiac exam daily

    • New murmur? Change in existing murmur? (new regurgitation)
    • Crackles? JVD? (signs of HF)

  3. Neurologic exam daily (embolic stroke risk 20–25%)

    • Baseline mental status, language, gait, pupils
    • New focal deficit → STAT head CT ± MRI, stroke code activation

  4. Embolic event assessment (daily)

    • Extremity pulses (limb ischemia)
    • Abdominal exam (splenic infarction — LUQ pain, splenic rub)
    • Visual changes (retinal infarction)
    • Chest symptoms (pulmonary emboli in right-sided IE)

  5. EKG (daily × 3 days, then daily if concerning)

    • New PR prolongation → warning of root abscess
    • New AV block → urgency sign (abscess involving conduction system)
    • New ischemic changes (embolic coronary event, demand ischemia from HF)

  6. Labs (daily × 3–5 days, then weekly)

    • CBC (trend WBC, Hgb, platelets)
    • CMP (renal function — vanc + gent nephrotoxic; electrolytes)
    • Vanc + gent drug levels (adjust therapy for trough goals)
    • CRP, ESR (should trend down on effective therapy)
    • LDH, bilirubin, INR (if liver congestion from HF)

sections.heading: PICC line placement & access management
sections.bodyHtml:
1. PICC line insertion (POD 3–5 typical)
    • Essential for 4–6 week IV antibiotic course (peripheral lines = high failure rate, thrombophlebitis)
    • Daily PICC exit site assessment: erythema, drainage, swelling → culture + notify APP
    • Dressing changes: per protocol, aseptic technique mandatory
    • Line flushing: per protocol (heparin or saline lock)
    • Risk of line infection: in IE patient, line bacteremia seeds new infection; high index of suspicion for line-related infection if fever persists or recurs

sections.heading: Addiction medicine consult (IVDU endocarditis)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Immediate referral (Day 1–2) for IVDU patients
    • Assessment for opioid use disorder (OUD) severity
    • Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) options: buprenorphine (Suboxone) preferred if no liver disease, or methadone
    • Harm reduction: sterile needle access, syringe services, naloxone
    • Social work: housing, insurance, follow-up arrangements
    • Goal: initiate MAT DURING hospitalization (not delayed to discharge)
    • Communication: non-judgmental, addiction medicine as essential clinical service (not punishment or moralism)

sections.heading: Cardiac team engagement & surgical decision-making
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Cardiology consult Day 1 (if not already following)

    • Ongoing echocardiographic surveillance
    • Antibiotic regimen coordination
    • Surgical consultation if indications arise

  2. CT surgery consult Day 1–2

    • Risk stratification: does patient have early surgical indication?
    • Surgical planning if needed (valve replacement vs repair, root reconstruction if abscess)
    • Team discussion: optimal timing (complete antibiotic course pre-op vs earlier intervention)

  3. ID consult Day 1 (if not already)

    • Antibiotic selection, duration, drug levels
    • Culture interpretation
    • Microbiologic ID of fastidious organisms
    • PK/PD monitoring

sections.heading: Patient & family education
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Explain the 4–6 week course

    • "The bacteria live in a biofilm on the valve. It takes this long to fully clear."
    • PICC line care, flushing technique, dressing changes
    • Fever calling criteria (fever after 5 days of appropriate therapy is concerning)
    • Future endocarditis prophylaxis for dental/invasive procedures
    • For IVDU: integration of addiction medicine into the treatment plan (not shame-based, evidence-based)

  2. Discuss AMA risk early

    • Patients often "feel fine" by day 7–10 and want to leave
    • Early education + social work + addiction medicine engagement reduce AMA discharge

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path — acute decompensation & surgical urgency
sections.bodyHtml: Patient declining despite 5A measures, or arriving in shock/overt HF.

sections.heading: Immediate escalation (STAT)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Call APP/fellow + charge nurse STAT — do NOT manage alone
  2. ICU transfer if not already there — continuous monitoring, invasive hemodynamic support
  3. Call CT surgery STAT — early surgical consultation for possible urgent/emergent intervention
  4. Place invasive monitoring: central line, arterial line, consider PA catheter for hemodynamic assessment

sections.heading: Diagnostic assessment (rapid)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Repeat EKG STAT — new AV block? Ischemic changes?
  • Troponin STAT — significant elevation suggests embolic coronary event or septic myocarditis
  • Lactate, ABG — assess perfusion adequacy
  • Echo STAT (bedside TTE or TEE): confirm vegetation status, reassess for new abscess, assess EF, pericardial effusion (tamponade?), valve regurgitation severity
  • Chest X-ray STAT — pulmonary edema, pneumonia, septic emboli
  • Blood cultures STAT — if not already done; persistent bacteremia on antibiotics is surgical indication
  • CT angiography (if PE concern) — septic PE in right-sided IE

sections.heading: Hemodynamic optimization
sections.bodyHtml:
1. For cardiogenic shock (SBP < 90, oliguria, altered mental status, lactate > 2):

    • IV vasopressor: norepinephrine 2–10 μg/min (alpha + beta; SVR + HR support) OR phenylephrine 0.5–1.4 μg/kg/min if hypertensive shock
    • IV inotrope: low-dose dobutamine 2.5–5 μg/kg/min (increases contractility) or milrinone 0.25–0.75 μg/kg/min (if systolic HF with elevated afterload)
    • IV diuretics: furosemide 20–40 mg IV, repeat q2–4h based on crackles (gentle approach, avoid hypovolemia)
    • Mechanical support (if shock refractory): consider ECMO or IABP (though IABP risky if severe AR)

  2. For acute pulmonary edema (crackles, SpO₂ < 90%, RR > 20):

    • CPAP / BiPAP if available (reduces intubation risk)
    • IV diuretics: furosemide 20–40 mg IV bolus, repeat q1–2h; titrate to decrement in crackles
    • Vasodilators cautiously: if hypertensive (nitroprusside or nitroglycerin brief course while preparing for surgery)
    • Mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure develops

  3. For septic shock (fever + hypotension + lactic acidosis despite fluids):

    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics (if not already started): vanc + cephalosporin + gentamicin standard
    • Vasopressor: norepinephrine first-line (Surviving Sepsis guidelines)
    • Fluid bolus: 30 mL/kg crystalloid ONCE (sepsis protocol); reassess after
    • Lactate clearance goal: < 2 mmol/L; if persistent elevation → prognostication discussion needed

sections.heading: Surgical decision-making (urgent/emergent indications)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Emergent (same-day) surgery for:

    • Cardiogenic shock unresponsive to hemodynamic support (inotropes + vasopressors failing)
    • Acute severe aortic regurgitation from vegetation/rupture + shock (perioperative mortality high but medical failure otherwise certain)
    • Large (> 15 mm) vegetation with recurrent emboli despite antibiotics (septic shower continuing)
    • Aortic root perforation / rupture (chest pain, pericarditis, tamponade)

  2. Urgent (within 24–48 h) surgery for:

    • Perivalvular abscess (fistula, conduction disturbance, extension risk)
    • New complete heart block (abscess infiltrating AV node)
    • Prosthetic valve endocarditis (higher mortality if medical only)
    • Fungal endocarditis (antibiotics alone insufficient; removal only curative option)
    • Persistent bacteremia > 7–10 days despite optimal antibiotics
    • Large mobile vegetation (10–15 mm) even if hemodynamically stable (emboli risk)

sections.heading: Special scenario: tricuspid (right-sided) IE in IVDU
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Generally managed medically (tricuspid repair/replacement higher mortality than left-sided surgery)
    • Empiric therapy (vanc + cephalosporin ± gent) standard
    • Extended echocardiographic surveillance for progression, septic PE risk
    • Pulmonary imaging routine: CXR + CT chest to assess for septic emboli
    • Surgical indications for tricuspid: massive vegetation (> 20 mm) with recurrent PE despite emboli-trapping IVC filter, or right heart failure from severe TR
    • Addiction medicine integration critical: relapse during 4–6 week hospitalization common; MAT + harm reduction essential

sections.heading: 5C. Day-of-admission through end of antibiotic course — ongoing monitoring & OPAT transition
Week 1 (first 7 days): stabilization & diagnostic completion
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Complete imaging suite

    • TEE by POD 2–3 (if not done)
    • MRI brain (if neurologic symptoms OR routine screening in some centers — 20–25% have emboli)
    • CT abdomen if abdominal symptoms (splenic infarction, abscess)

  2. Antibiotic optimization

    • Culture results back at 48–72 h; narrow therapy to organism-specific regimen
    • Vanc/gent drug levels at steady state (after dose 4–5); adjust dosing
    • Repeat blood cultures q48h × 3 sets until negative documented

  3. Team meetings

    • Cardiology + CT surgery + ID + addiction medicine (if applicable) alignment on prognosis, surgical threshold, timeline
    • Family conference: explain diagnosis, treatment plan, duration (4–6 weeks), risks

sections.heading: Weeks 2–6: maintenance antibiotic course with OPAT transition planning
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Weekly labs

    • CBC, CMP (renal function, vanc/gent nephrotoxicity watch)
    • Vanc + gent levels (q1–2 weeks if stable, more frequently if dose adjustments needed)
    • CRP/ESR trend (should be declining; plateau or rise suggests treatment failure)

  2. Weekly/biweekly echocardiography

    • Track vegetation size (shrinkage good sign; growth suggests failure)
    • Reassess regurgitation severity (new AR from progression)
    • Monitor LVEF (myocarditis can cause systolic dysfunction)

  3. Ongoing embolic event surveillance

    • Neurologic exam daily
    • Consider repeat head MRI at end of week 2–3 if prior emboli detected (assess evolution)
    • Physical exam for splenic/limb ischemia signs

  4. PICC line management

    • Daily exit site checks
    • Aseptic technique with all accesses
    • If fever persists, line infection suspected → line removal + new PICC placement (line cultures)

  5. OPAT planning (by week 2–3)

    • Case management involvement: insurance, home infusion company coordination
    • Home infusion service: IV pump setup, nursing visits 2–3× weekly for labs, assessments
    • Patient education: self-administration of antibiotics, line flushing, dressing changes, when to call
    • Discharge criteria: afebrile × 48–72 h, hemodynamically stable, compliant, reliable access, understanding of plan
    • Typical discharge: week 3–4 if progress good; complete 4–6 week course at home with ID follow-up

sections.heading: Surgical decision point (can occur any phase)
sections.bodyHtml: 1. If indications arise (see 5B #7), escalate urgently** - Example: week 2, repeat echo shows new large vegetation + recurrent bacteremia → call CT surgery same day - Timing: complete pre-operative antibiotics ideally (24–48 hours post-last positive culture) to reduce prosthetic valve endocarditis risk, BUT do not delay if patient deteriorating

sections.heading: Discharge preparation
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Before discharge to home/OPAT:
    • Final labs (CBC, CMP, vanc/gent level if applicable)
    • Final echo (document valve status, EF, regression of vegetations if visible)
    • Scheduling of post-discharge appointments: ID (within 1 week), cardiology (2 weeks), CT surgery (if surgical candidate/pending)
    • Endocarditis prophylaxis card: patient carries written documentation of diagnosis, antibiotic regimen, and future prophylaxis needs for dental/invasive procedures
    • For IVDU: ongoing addiction medicine enrollment (outpatient MAT continuation, harm reduction resources, syringe services, naloxone distribution)
    • Patient hotline / emergency contact: who to call if fever, chills, worsening SOB, syncope, severe headache, focal neuro symptoms

sections.heading: SBAR Template
sections.bodyHtml:
S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [patient name], room [X], admitted with endocarditis secondary to [organism if known / IVDU if applicable]."

B: "[Patient age, prior cardiac history, IVDU status]. Presenting with [fever, new murmur, embolic event]. TEE shows [vegetation size/location, AR/MR severity, abscess if present]. Blood cultures: [culture results, number of sets positive, organism if available]."

A: "Patient is currently [stable/decompensating/shock]. HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value], T [temp]. On [antibiotic regimen]. Labs: WBC [value], Cr [value], vanc trough [if available], CRP [trend]. [New finding if applicable: new murmur / new AV block / persistent fever despite ABX / recurrent bacteremia]."

R: "Requesting [continuation of current regimen / antibiotic adjustment / surgical consultation / urgent imaging / escalation to ICU]."

sections.heading: Who to Call
sections.bodyHtml:
Situation Contact
Stable admission, confirmation of IE, routine antibiotic course Primary ID or on-call fellow
New or worsening cardiac murmur Cardiology ± CT surgery (assess for progression)
New PR prolongation or AV block on EKG STAT: Cardiology + CT surgery (root abscess; surgical indication)
Cardiogenic shock (SBP < 90 + hypoperfusion) STAT: Fellow + CT surgery + ICU (emergent valve surgery)
Acute pulmonary edema refractory to IV diuretics STAT: Fellow + ICU (CPAP/intubation, urgent echo)
Persistent fever > 5 days on appropriate antibiotics ID + Cardiology (treatment failure? Line infection? Inadequate source control?)
Persistent positive blood cultures > 48–72 h STAT: ID + CT surgery (repeat cultures to confirm; surgical indication if persists)
New embolic event (stroke, limb ischemia, abdominal pain) STAT: Appropriate specialist (stroke code, vascular, surgery) + Cardiology
Large vegetation (> 10 mm) on repeat echo CT surgery (surgical risk/benefit assessment)
Fungal endocarditis identified STAT: CT surgery (surgical removal only curative)
PICC-related infection (fever + new bacteremia on same organism from PICC) URGENT: ID + Vascular (line removal + new access)
New focal neuro deficit STAT: Stroke code + Neurology (MRI for mycotic aneurysm)
Case management for OPAT Social work / discharge planning (home infusion setup, addiction medicine coordination)
IVDU patient with relapse risk Addiction medicine (MAT intensification, behavioral health, social determinants)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections below are — collapsed by default.

7.1 Modified Duke-ISCVID criteria v2023 update

sections.heading: The diagnostic framework (Fowler et al., 2023)
sections.bodyHtml:
Duke-ISCVID criteria are the gold standard for infective endocarditis diagnosis in clinical practice (95% sensitivity, specificity when applied).

Major Criteria (1 point each):

  1. Typical blood culture organism in 2+ separate sets OR 1+ positive persistent culture (organism typical of IE)

    • Streptococcus species (viridans, bovis, gallolyticus)
    • Staphylococcus aureus
    • Enterococcus species
    • Gram-negative aerobic bacteria (HACEK group)
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae (rare in IE, usually bacteremia from other source)
    • Candida species (fungal IE — uncommon but high-mortality)

  2. Echocardiographic findings:

    • Oscillating intracardiac mass on valve, supporting structures, or implanted device
    • Vegetation OR prosthetic valve/device dehiscence OR paravalvular regurgitation
    • New regurgitation (worsening of pre-existing) — suggest vegetative pathology
    • NB: echo finding + positive BC = definite IE even without fever or other criteria

  3. HACEK serology (IgG antibodies to HACEK organisms)

    • HACEK = slow-growing Gram-negative bacteria (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella)
    • Often culture-negative or take 2+ weeks to grow
    • Serology helpful in delayed presentations or prior abx exposure

Minor Criteria (1 point each; max 5 points from clinical findings):

  1. Predisposition (structural valve disease, IVDU, prosthetic valve, prior IE, intracardiac device)
  2. Fever ≥ 38.0°C (100.4°F)
  3. Vascular phenomena: septic emboli (lung, brain, spleen, kidney), Janeway lesions, septic arteritis, mycotic aneurysm
  4. Immunologic phenomena: glomerulonephritis, Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor
  5. Microbiologic findings (not meeting major criteria): single positive culture of organism consistent with IE, or serologic evidence (Coxiella, Bartonella, Brucella if multiple antibodies positive)

Diagnostic Classification:

  • Definite IE: 2 major criteria OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor criteria
  • Possible IE: 1 major + 1 minor OR 3 minor criteria
  • Rejected IE: < 1 major + < 3 minor (alternative diagnosis more likely)

sections.heading: New in v2023 update: PET/CT as major criterion
sections.bodyHtml:
Previously: echocardiography (TTE/TEE) was the only imaging major criterion.

Now: PET/CT (positron emission tomography) with fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) is recognized as equivalent to TEE for detecting vegetation/inflammation in prosthetic valve IE, aortic root infection, and culture-negative IE.

Implication: PET can be ordered if TEE non-diagnostic or contraindicated (per team discussion).

sections.heading: Application to clinical practice
sections.bodyHtml:
• Empiric diagnosis: patient with fever + new murmur + 2 positive blood culture sets = Definite IE on Duke criteria alone (even before echo)
  • Delayed diagnosis: patient with subacute fever + normal echo (TTE) + negative initial cultures → pursue TEE + repeat cultures + serology before declaring "culture-negative IE"
  • Fungal concern: Candida in blood culture = automatic major criterion + escalate to surgery (antifungal monotherapy inadequate)
7.2 TTE vs TEE: when each is needed (expandable)

sections.heading: TTE (Transthoracic Echocardiography)
sections.bodyHtml:
Advantages:

  • Non-invasive, portable, rapid
  • First-line for most IE evaluations
  • Good for large vegetations (> 3 mm), AR, MR assessment

Limitations:

  • Sensitivity ~60–70% (misses small vegetations, posterior structures, leaflet perforations)
  • Poor acoustic window in obese, COPD, post-op patients
  • Prosthetic valves: acoustic shadowing limits visualization

Indications:

  • Initial IE screening — all suspected IE patients get TTE
  • Follow-up documentation — if TEE already diagnostic

sections.heading: TEE (Transesophageal Echocardiography)
sections.bodyHtml:
Advantages:

  • Sensitivity > 95% (high-resolution near endocardium)
  • Excellent for abscess, fistula, leaflet perforation, prosthetic valves
  • Defines surgical anatomy (extent of disease, which valve involved)

Indications:

  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis — MANDATORY (TTE inadequate)
  • TTE inconclusive (negative/unclear but high clinical suspicion)
  • Native valve IE if TTE positive — consider for surgical planning (abscess? Fistula?)
  • Culture-negative IE — optimize imaging for emboli, abscess
  • Complications assessment — root abscess, fistula, perforation

Contraindications / precautions:

  • Esophageal stricture, recent esophageal surgery, severe esophageal pathology (relative)
  • Thrombocytopenia (platelet < 20K: relative; transfuse 1 unit → 1 unit for unit proc)
  • Coagulopathy (INR > 1.5; correct before procedure if possible)

Sedation: mild sedation (midazolam ± opioid) or local anesthesia; consider general anesthesia if intubated

sections.heading: Decision tree: TTE → TEE?
sections.bodyHtml:
TTE positive (vegetation ± regurgitation) + positive cultures = Definite IE → may not need TEE unless

  • Surgical planning needed (extent of abscess?)
  • Prosthetic valve (always TEE)
  • Complications suspected (perforation, fistula, abscess)

TTE negative / inconclusive + high clinical suspicion (fever + positive BC + emboli) → TEE indicated

TTE technically limited (obesity, COPD, post-op) → TEE for imaging quality

7.3 Embolic events in IE: left-sided vs right-sided (expandable)

sections.heading: Incidence and risk
sections.bodyHtml: Frequency: septic emboli occur in 20–25% of IE cases overall - Higher in left-sided IE (mitral, aortic vegetation) - Lower in right-sided IE (tricuspid) because emboli are typically to lungs (may not be clinically apparent)

sections.heading: Left-sided IE embolic destinations
sections.bodyHtml:
Stroke (10–20% of left-sided IE):

  • Septic emboli lodge in cerebral arteries
  • Mycotic aneurysm (infected vessel wall) — rupture risk
  • Imaging: head CT (initial, rapid), MRI (better detail; assess microemboli)
  • Clinical pearl: asymptomatic emboli detected on MRI in ~25% — some centers screen routinely

Limb ischemia (5–10%):

  • Femoral, popliteal, radial arteries occluded by septic thrombi
  • Acute pain, pallor, pulselessness → vascular surgery urgency
  • Emboli trapped in thrombus; may be culturable (diagnostic)

Splenic infarction (10–20%):

  • Often asymptomatic (discovered on CT)
  • Symptomatic: LUQ pain, splenic rub on exam
  • Risk: splenic rupture (rare but catastrophic)
  • Management: typically conservative (no splenectomy unless rupture)

Renal infarction: asymptomatic, detected on imaging; no specific treatment

Mesenteric emboli (rare): abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea; acute surgical abdomen risk

sections.heading: Right-sided IE embolic destinations
sections.bodyHtml:
Pulmonary emboli (common, often asymptomatic):

  • Vegetation on tricuspid → septic PE to lungs
  • CXR may show wedge-shaped infiltrates (septic emboli, not bland PE)
  • Diagnosis: CT chest ± PE protocol
  • Clinical pearl: recurrent PE despite IVC filter is surgical indication for tricuspid valve replacement (rare but occurs)

Systemic septic emboli (uncommon in right-sided): septal defect or right-to-left shunt required

sections.heading: Management of embolic events
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Acute stroke:

    • Activate stroke code
    • Head CT (exclude hemorrhage)
    • MRI with MRA (define infarct size, mycotic aneurysm)
    • Neurology consult
    • Anticoagulation: controversial; heparin sometimes considered to prevent recurrent emboli, but bleeding risk from mycotic aneurysm is real
    • Team discussion: cardiology + neurology + ID on AC vs observation

  2. Limb ischemia:

    • Vascular surgery consult STAT
    • Angiography + embolectomy if recent (< 24 h)
    • Thrombus sent for culture (may grow IE organism, diagnostic + therapeutic)

  3. Splenic infarction:

    • Usually observed (antibiotics + anticoagulation controversial)
    • Surgical intervention only if rupture/hemorrhage

  4. Pulmonary emboli (right-sided IE):

    • Treat underlying IE (cure bacteremia → stop septic showers)
    • IVC filter if recurrent PE despite antibiotics
    • Surgical consideration (tricuspid valve replacement) if embolization recurrent despite filter

sections.heading: Timing of embolic events
sections.bodyHtml:
• Early IE: emboli occur before antibiotics clearance (especially S. aureus — high vegetative burden)
  • Embolization can continue for weeks despite adequate therapy — septic material lodged in vegetation continues to fragment
  • Routine imaging (MRI brain, CT abdomen) recommended even if asymptomatic (guides prognosis, neurosurgical planning if aneurysm)
7.4 Culture-negative IE and fastidious organisms (expandable)

sections.heading: Why cultures negative (5–10% of IE)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Prior antibiotics — patient received oral penicillin, cephalosporin, or macrolide before culture (kills organisms, reduces yield)
  2. Slow-growing organisms — HACEK, Bartonella, Coxiella, Brucella (require prolonged incubation, special media)
  3. Fastidious bacteria — require enriched media; standard media suboptimal
  4. Fungi — Candida, Aspergillus (slow growth; require special fungal media)
  5. Abscesses / sequestration — organism walled off, not circulating
  6. Serologic diagnosis only — no culture growth but serology diagnostic (Q fever, Brucella, Bartonella)

sections.heading: Key pathogens in culture-negative IE
sections.bodyHtml:
HACEK group (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella):

  • Gram-negative, slow-growing, require enriched media
  • Often require 2–3 week incubation (standard incubation is 5 days)
  • Serology useful (IgG antibodies to HACEK)
  • Good prognosis — rarely need surgery; respond to antibiotics (cephalosporin + gentamicin typical)

Bartonella species (B. henselae, B. quintana):

  • Cat scratch disease (B. henselae), louse-borne (B. quintana)
  • Rarely grows on standard culture (requires special media, PCR or serology for diagnosis)
  • Lyme disease-like serology confusion; IgG antibodies diagnostic
  • Treatment: doxycycline + gentamicin (or ceftriaxone)

Coxiella burnetii (Q fever endocarditis):

  • Fastidious, intracellular organism
  • Serology only reliable (phase 1 + II antibodies; chronic Q fever = phase 1 antibody > phase II)
  • Associated with prosthetic valve, prior cardiac surgery
  • Treatment: doxycycline + quinolone (long-term, months)

Brucella species:

  • Zoonotic (exposed to infected animals, unpasteurized dairy)
  • Slow growth, requires special handling
  • Serology diagnostic (IgM + IgG)
  • Treatment: doxycycline + gentamicin ± rifampin (prolonged course)

Fungi (Candida, Aspergillus):

  • Rare but devastating
  • Risk factors: IVDU (non-sterile injection), prosthetic valve, immunocompromised
  • Often large, friable vegetations
  • Surgery almost always required (antifungal monotherapy failure rate ~90%)

sections.heading: Diagnostic workup for culture-negative IE
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Repeat blood cultures (hold 2–3 weeks if HACEK suspected)
  2. Molecular testing (PCR, 16S rRNA) — if available
  3. Serology panel:
    • HACEK serology (if organisms typical of IE)
    • Bartonella serology (IgG)
    • Brucella serology (IgM + IgG)
    • Coxiella phase 1/II antibodies (Q fever)
    • Fungal serology if immunocompromised
    • Culture on special media — fastidious organism media, fungal media, BioMérieux systems
    • Echocardiography — TTE + TEE (define vegetation size, location)
    • Consider PET-CT (new v2023 major criterion alternative; detects inflammation in prosthetic IE)

sections.heading: Management approach
sections.bodyHtml:
• Empiric therapy continued until culture results, serology, or PCR clarifies diagnosis
  • Vancomycin + cephalosporin ± gentamicin covers most fastidious organisms
  • Switch to organism-specific regimen once ID'd (HACEK: cephalosporin + gent; Bartonella: doxycycline + gent; Coxiella: doxycycline + quinolone)
  • Surgical consultation if fungal (removal is curative; antifungals alone inadequate)
7.5 IVDU endocarditis and addiction medicine integration (expandable)

sections.heading: The epidemiology shift
sections.bodyHtml:
IVDU is now the #1 risk factor for IE in developed countries (overtaking valve disease, prosthetic valves in many centers).

S. aureus tricuspid endocarditis is the classic IVDU IE presentation. Tricuspid valve (right side) seeded by Staph from injection site bacteremia.

sections.heading: Why IVDU patients are high-risk for recidivism
sections.bodyHtml:
The challenge: endocarditis treatment requires 4–6 weeks of IV antibiotics. IVDU patients face:

  • Ongoing craving (opioid use disorder is a chronic disease, not a moral failing)
  • Lack of addiction treatment access (MAT unavailable at many hospitals)
  • Trauma, housing instability, social determinants
  • Stigma from medical teams (negative attitudes correlate with worse outcomes)

Recidivism rates without MAT:

  • 60–80% of IVDU IE patients relapse during or shortly after treatment
  • Relapse = new bacteremia, new endocarditis, death in many cases

Recidivism rates WITH MAT:

  • Rates drop to 20–30% (still high, but vastly improved)
  • Patients who stay in treatment complete antibiotic course at higher rates
  • Social stability improves with MAT + case management

sections.heading: Medication-assisted treatment (MAT) options
sections.bodyHtml:
Buprenorphine (Suboxone):

  • Partial mu opioid agonist
  • Safer ceiling for respiratory depression (lower OD risk)
  • Better cardiac safety profile (no QT prolongation)
  • Preferred for hospitalized IE patients
  • Induction: 2–8 mg sublingual, titrate based on withdrawal sx
  • Maintenance: 8–24 mg daily (single dose often adequate)

Methadone:

  • Full mu agonist (stronger analgesic effect)
  • QT prolongation risk (especially > 100 mg/day) — EKG baseline + periodic
  • Cardiac concerns in IE patients (potential for torsades)
  • Still option if buprenorphine contra-indicated

Naltrexone (opioid antagonist):

  • Not preferred during acute hospitalization (patient may leave to use)
  • Useful post-discharge for opioid use prevention

sections.heading: Harm reduction principles
sections.bodyHtml:
Not "enablement" — evidence-based:

  • Sterile needle/syringe programs (SSPs) reduce injection-related infections 50%
  • Naloxone (Narcan) distribution saves lives (opioid reversal)
  • Supervised consumption sites improve connection to care
  • Housing, employment support reduce relapse

Integration into IE care plan:

  • Refer patient to SSP on discharge
  • Supply naloxone kit at discharge
  • Case management for housing, food, childcare support
  • Trauma screening (PTSD, domestic violence, child loss)

sections.heading: Communication approach (non-judgmental)
sections.bodyHtml:
Harmful language:

  • "Addict" (stigmatizing; use "person with opioid use disorder")
  • "Dirty" (referring to positive UDS)
  • "Non-compliant" (if patient refuses MAT, ask why; barriers often external)
  • Moralizing ("you did this to yourself")

Evidence-based language:

  • "Opioid use disorder is a medical condition. We treat it."
  • "Medication-assisted treatment is part of your endocarditis cure."
  • "Relapse is common; it's part of the disease process, not failure."
  • "We're here to help you stay healthy, not judge."

sections.heading: Team composition (ideal)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Addiction medicine physician — MAT prescribing, OUD assessment, behavioral therapy coordination
  • Social worker — case management, housing, insurance, post-discharge resources
  • Infectious disease — antibiotic therapy, monitoring
  • Cardiology — valve status, surgical planning
  • Peer recovery specialist — IVDU patient who recovered; credibility, role modeling
  • Nursing — compassionate, non-judgmental care (floor nurses set culture tone)

sections.heading: Addiction medicine consult timing
sections.bodyHtml:
• Within 24 h of admission (not wait until discharge)
  • Initiate MAT during hospitalization (if patient agrees)
  • Transition plan documented before discharge (outpatient MAT provider identified, appointment scheduled)

sections.heading: High-risk discharge (AMA risk)
sections.bodyHtml:
Red flags:

  • Patient refusing MAT
  • No housing identified
  • Active substance use during hospitalization
  • Poor medication compliance
  • Early "feeling better" despite incomplete course

Interventions:

  • Daily team rounding on patient (show consistent engagement)
  • Peer recovery specialist bedside visits (role modeling, hope)
  • Family/support person involvement
  • Do NOT discharge before 4–6 week antibiotic course is outlined and understood
  • Consider court-ordered treatment (if jurisdiction permits) for severe AMA risk

7.6 Long-term IV access: PICC line, midline, tunneled catheter logistics (expandable)

sections.heading: PICC line (Peripherally Inserted Central Catheter)
sections.bodyHtml:
Advantages:

  • No surgical procedure (bedside insertion, can place in inpatient unit)
  • Single, durable central access (vs multiple PIVs)
  • Suitable for 4–6 week antibiotic therapy
  • Cost-effective

Placement:

  • Bedside or ultrasound-guided (basilic vein preferred; cephalic vein alternative)
  • Inserted via arm vein; tip positioned in SVC

Complications:

  • Line infection (1–3 per 1000 catheter-days): fever + positive blood culture from PICC — remove line, new PICC placed
  • DVT (5–10%): arm swelling, difficulty flushing; Doppler confirmation; anticoagulation consideration
  • Malposition: CXR check post-insertion; may migrate; reposition or replace
  • Mechanical phlebitis: inflammation around insertion site; aseptic technique essential

Dressing/flushing protocol:

  • Transparent dressing changed q7 days (sooner if soiled/wet/loose)
  • Chlorhexidine cleansing q dressing change
  • Flush q8–12h (heparin lock typical; institution protocol varies)
  • Aseptic technique for all access

Duration:

  • Can stay in situ 4–6 weeks (some centers limit to 28–30 days per protocol)
  • Remove at end of IV therapy (residual line infection risk)

sections.heading: Midline catheter
sections.bodyHtml:
Advantages:

  • Non-tunneled central option (less infection risk than PICC in some studies)
  • Easier insertion than PICC
  • Acceptable for moderate-duration therapy (2–4 weeks)

Limitations:

  • Shorter lifespan than PICC (typically 14 days)
  • Not suitable for the full 4–6 week IE course without replacement
  • May require replacement mid-course

sections.heading: Tunneled central catheter (Hickman, Groshong)
sections.bodyHtml:
Advantages:

  • Surgical placement (small incision, catheter tunneled subcutaneously)
  • Most stable, lowest infection risk per day
  • Can remain in situ indefinitely with proper care
  • Preferred for long-term OPAT

Limitations:

  • Requires operating room (not bedside)
  • Surgical risks (infection at insertion site, pneumothorax)
  • Cost higher than PICC

Indications:

  • OPAT going > 4 weeks or requiring multiple antibiotic course
  • IVDU patients (PICC pulls easier at risk of vascular injury; tunneled catheter more secure)
  • Prior PICC complications (recurrent infection or thrombosis)

sections.heading: Infection prevention in IE patients
sections.bodyHtml:
Special concern: PICC-line bacteremia can seed the newly-treated valve (prosthetic valve endocarditis risk).

Strategies:

  1. Aseptic technique EVERY access (not casual about it)
  2. Daily visual inspection (erythema, drainage, swelling)
  3. Dressing changes per protocol (do not "extend" dressing change intervals)
  4. Minimize line manipulation (consolidate lab draws, medication administration)
  5. Remove line ASAP at end of therapy (do not leave in "just in case")
  6. Patient education on line care (dressing integrity, no water immersion, what to watch for)

sections.heading: Transition to OPAT
sections.bodyHtml:
• PICC acceptable for home therapy if patient reliable, nursing support available
  • Home infusion company manages: pump, IV supplies, nursing visits
  • Caregiver training: dressing changes, flushing, troubleshooting
  • ID follow-up: weekly or biweekly visits (assess line, take labs, clinically reassess)
7.7 Surgical decision-making: timing and indications in IE (expandable)

sections.heading: The paradox: antibiotics alone fail in ~30% of IE cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Early surgery needed for:

  • Large, mobile vegetations (embolization risk)
  • Prosthetic valve infection (high mortality if medical only)
  • Perivalvular abscess / root involvement
  • Fungal IE (antibiotics never curative)
  • Persistent bacteremia despite optimal therapy (≥ 7–10 days)
  • HF from acute severe regurgitation (valve destroyed)

vs. Complete antibiotic course first (if possible):

  • Reduces prosthetic valve endocarditis risk post-op
  • Sterilizes vegetation, reducing operative infection seeding

sections.heading: Timing framework (ESC/AHA consensus)
sections.bodyHtml:
Emergent (same-day):

  • Cardiogenic shock unresponsive to medical support
  • Acute severe aortic regurgitation with hypotension
  • Large vegetation with recurrent septic emboli
  • Aortic root rupture / tamponade

Urgent (24–48 h):

  • Prosthetic valve endocarditis
  • Perivalvular abscess
  • New complete heart block
  • Fungal endocarditis
  • Persistent bacteremia > 7–10 days
  • Large mobile vegetation (10–15 mm) risk of embolization

Delayed (after 7–10 days antibiotic course if stable):

  • Native valve, stable hemodynamics, no emboli
  • Complete antibiotic course pre-op ideal (reduces PVE risk)
  • Caveat: if deterioration occurs, escalate urgently

sections.heading: Valve repair vs replacement
sections.bodyHtml:
Tricuspid (right-sided IE, IVDU):

  • Repair strongly preferred (lower mortality than replacement)
  • Commissurotomy, valvuloplasty with annuloplasty
  • Replacement only if repair not feasible (massive vegetations, diffuse valve destruction)

Mitral:

  • Repair possible if leaflet perforation localized
  • Most IE requires replacement (vegetation usually large, destructive)
  • Bioprosthetic preferred in many cases (avoids lifelong anticoagulation)

Aortic:

  • Replacement almost always needed (repair rarely adequate for IE)
  • Root involvement (abscess) → complete root replacement (Bentall, valve-conduit) required
  • Mechanical vs bioprosthetic: discuss with patient (durability vs anticoagulation burden)

sections.heading: Antibiotic coverage perioperatively
sections.bodyHtml:
• Continue IV antibiotics through surgery and into post-op (first few days at least)
  • Typical post-op duration: 2–4 additional weeks after surgery (total 4–6 week course uncommon if surgery done early)
  • Adjust post-op regimen based on organism susceptibilities

sections.heading: Prognosis post-op
sections.bodyHtml:
• In-hospital mortality: 5–10% for native valve surgery, 10–20% for PVE
  • Morbidity: stroke (5–10%), renal failure, new conduction blocks, reoperation (2–3%)
  • Long-term: if prosthetic valve placed, antibiotic prophylaxis for life (for any bacteremia-risk procedure — dental, GU, GI)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Any of these → escalate.

  • New murmur or change in existing murmur — new regurgitation from leaflet perforation or progressive vegetation damage; cardiology + CT surgery consult
  • New PR prolongation on EKG or new AV block — RED FLAG for aortic root abscess (extension into conduction system); STAT cardiology/CT surgery
  • Persistent fever > 5 days on appropriate antibiotics — treatment failure signal; repeat cultures, repeat TEE, reassess for abscess/source control problem, consider line infection
  • Persistent positive blood cultures > 48–72 h into appropriate therapy — organism still circulating; suggests inadequate source control (septic valve, abscess, inadequate antibiotic penetration); escalate team
  • New heart failure signs — dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles, weight gain, elevated JVD — vegetation growing, valve regurgitation worsening; gentle diuretics, escalate TAVR/surgery timing
  • New focal neurologic deficit — septic stroke, mycotic aneurysm rupture, brain abscess; activate stroke code, STAT head CT/MRI, neurology + ID consult
  • Septic emboli to limb — acute pain, pallor, pulselessness in extremity; vascular surgery consult, embolectomy risk, thrombus culture diagnostic
  • Abdominal pain (LUQ suspected splenic infarction) — can rupture; CT abdomen confirms; observe typically, surgery only if rupture
  • Large (> 10 mm) vegetation on repeat echo — embolization risk; surgical threshold met even if hemodynamically stable
  • Tachycardia unresponsive to fever control — HR trending up is bad prognostic sign (suggests hemodynamic deterioration); escalate
  • Hypotension despite volume/pressors — cardiogenic shock from HF or sepsis; ICU transfer, urgent valve surgery
  • Oliguria (UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/h) — cardiogenic shock, sepsis, or aminoglycoside nephrotoxicity; escalate, consider holding gent
  • Lactate > 2 mmol/L or rising — tissue hypoperfusion; ICU level; surgical urgency
  • New positive blood culture on antibiotics — organism escaped therapy; verify organism is same (contamination vs true persistent); escalate
  • Temperature > 38.5°C after 5 days of antibiotics — inadequate source control, abscess walling off, or line infection; imaging + repeat cultures
  • PICC site erythema, drainage, or swelling — line infection risk; culture site, remove line if confirmed; new PICC placement
  • New embolic event (stroke, splenic, renal) — septic emboli continuing despite antibiotics; vegetation not sterilizing; surgical urgency

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Blood culture SETS, not bottles. Three separate SETS (different sites, different bottles) = proper sampling. Three bottles from one site = increased contamination risk, doesn't prove bacteremia. Advocate for 3 sets pre-antibiotic if not septic. If antibiotics unavoidable before cultures, still go ahead (sensitivity drops but not zero).

  2. TEE is mandatory for native valve if TTE positive, ALWAYS for prosthetic valve. TTE sensitivity ~60%; TEE > 95%. Don't "skip" TEE because TTE is positive and patient already on antibiotics — TEE guides surgical anatomy (abscess location, perforation extent, fistula). Worth the extra endoscopy.

  3. New PR prolongation = aortic root abscess until proven otherwise. It's the early warning of conduction system involvement. Not a "monitoring item" — STAT cardiology/CT surgery call. This is a surgical indication. Escalate immediately.

  4. Repeat blood cultures q48h until clearance documented. Persistent positive cultures > 48–72 h into appropriate therapy = treatment failure red flag. Don't assume "got it"; verify sterilization. Persistent bacteremia = surgical indication in many cases.

  5. PICC line is lifesaving access and a potential source of deadly infection. In an IE patient on a PICC, a new line infection = new endocarditis (prosthetic valve seeding), high mortality. Daily visual inspection, aseptic technique ALWAYS, not casual. Remove ASAP at end of therapy.

  6. Tricuspid endocarditis from IVDU often managed medically; don't rush to surgery. Tricuspid valve repair/replacement has high mortality (~10–20% in-hospital). Medical cure possible in many IVDU IE cases. Surgical indication: massive vegetations (> 20 mm) with recurrent septic PE despite IVC filter, or right heart failure from massive TR. Otherwise, optimize antibiotics, ensure harm reduction + addiction medicine engaged.

  7. Addiction medicine is not optional — it's essential treatment. Without MAT + harm reduction, IVDU IE relapse rate is 60–80%. With MAT, drops to 20–30%. Initiate MAT during hospitalization (buprenorphine preferred). If team defers addiction medicine to discharge planning, patient likely defaults and relapses into new IE. This is as critical as antibiotic selection.

  8. Strep viridans IE (slower, often streptococci from dental source) may be medically curable. Short antibiotic course (2 weeks or less for some low-risk viridans IE) possible. S. aureus IE requires full 6 weeks; lower surgical threshold due to virulence. Know which organism you're treating.

  9. Embolic events continue despite antibiotics. 20–25% of IE patients have septic emboli. Emboli can occur anytime during the course, even "late" (weeks 3–4 if vegetation fragments). Routine imaging (MRI brain, CT abdomen if symptoms) recommended. Asymptomatic emboli ~25% on screening.

  10. Fungal endocarditis = surgery essential. Candida in blood culture is a red flag, not a "treat with fluconazole and monitor" item. Antifungal monotherapy fails ~90% of cases. Valve removal + antifungal therapy is gold standard. Escalate to CT surgery same-day.

  11. Culture-negative IE is not "bad data" — it's HACEK or serologic diagnosis. Before declaring "endocarditis of unknown origin," check: (1) were cultures held 2–3 weeks? (2) was special media used? (3) serology done (HACEK, Bartonella, Q fever)? HACEK IE has excellent prognosis (rare surgery needed). Bartonella + other fastidious organisms respond to doxycycline + gent.

  12. Surgical threshold lower for prosthetic valve than native valve. A small vegetation (5 mm) on a prosthetic valve at 10 days = surgical consideration. Same vegetation on native valve = observe with antibiotics. PVE has higher mortality if medical-only; lower tolerance for infection.

  13. "Feeling fine, can I leave?" is common. Explain relapse/death risk early. Endocarditis patients often feel well by day 7–10 and don't understand they need 4–6 weeks. Emphasize: treatment is for bacteria in biofilm on valve, not for symptoms. Leaving early = relapse, surgery, death. Engage social work + behavioral health early if AMA risk.

  14. Don't signal-boost moralism with IVDU patients. Using language like "dirty," "addict," "non-compliant" correlates with worse outcomes. Team negativity drives patients away. Evidence-based harm reduction + addiction medicine + compassionate care = better adherence + better outcomes. This is not "enabling"; it's medicine.

  15. Rifampin + warfarin interaction. If patient on warfarin (mechanical valve prosthetic) + on rifampin for resistant organism — warfarin metabolism increases, INR drops, thrombosis risk. Close INR monitoring essential. May need warfarin dose increase 30–50%.

cards.title: Infective Endocarditis — Native Valve — Diagnosis
phase: Preop` *(Or Medical Only If No Surgical Indication)*
cards.quickAnswer: Infection of native heart valve from bacteremia presenting acutely (Staph aureus) or subacutely (viridans streptococcus, enterococcus, HACEK). Diagnosis: 3 sets blood cultures from separate sites BEFORE antibiotics (30-min minimum intervals); TTE first, TEE if high suspicion or prosthetic; Modified Duke criteria (≥2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 3 minor = definite IE). Empiric vancomycin + ceftriaxone pending organism identification. Management: 4–6 weeks targeted antibiotics based on organism and susceptibilities. Surgical indications: severe valve dysfunction with heart failure, perivalvular abscess, persistent bacteremia despite antibiotics, large/mobile vegetation (≥10 mm) with embolic events, recurrent emboli. Involve cardiothoracic surgery + infectious disease early.
