sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation.

  • Definition: Microbial (bacterial, fungal, rarely viral) infection of native endocardium, typically at a valve. Leads to vegetation formation, valve destruction, septic emboli, systemic complications, and potentially cardiogenic shock or sepsis.
  • Epidemiology: Annual incidence 3–10 per 100,000 population (varies by region and risk factors). Mortality untreated ~100%; with antibiotics and surgery 5–30% depending on organism and complications (Fowler et al., 2023).
  • Microbiology (native valve): Staph aureus (most common, especially IVDU and healthcare-associated; acute presentation), viridans streptococcus (older/community-acquired; subacute), enterococcus (~5–15%), HACEK group (fastidious gram-negatives; subacute, 4-week cephalosporin course), fungal rare (usually Candida/Aspergillus). Blood culture-negative IE 5–10% (prior antibiotics, fastidious organism, viral).
  • Risk factors: IVDU, prosthetic valve, prior IE, congenital cyanotic disease, rheumatic heart disease, hemodialysis, poor dentition, recent bacteremia-generating procedures.
  • Why it matters for nurses: Pre-op evaluation for valve surgery, acute admission with sepsis + new murmur, medical management during 4–6 week antibiotic course.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology: Bacteremia from a source (dental, skin, GI, GU) seeds abnormal or normal valve endocardium. Bacteria, fibrin, immune cells accumulate on valve leaflet creating friable mass. Enzymes and inflammation erode leaflet, causing regurgitation or perforation. Vegetations break off and lodge in coronary, pulmonary, mesenteric, splenic, renal, cerebral, or limb arteries. Infection spreads beyond leaflet into annulus/septum, causing abscess formation and conduction abnormalities. Systemic inflammation triggers fever, elevated CRP/ESR, immune complex deposition (Osler nodes, Roth spots) (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).

Acute vs. subacute:

  • Acute (Staph aureus, Strep pyogenes): Rapid onset (days to 1–2 weeks), high fever (>39°C), sepsis appearance, rapid progression to shock, new murmur, embolic phenomena early. ICU admission likely; high risk of cardiogenic shock.
  • Subacute (viridans Strep, Enterococcus, HACEK): Insidious onset (weeks to months), low-grade fever, fatigue, weight loss, murmur may be missed. Embolic phenomena may precede cardiac diagnosis. Often diagnosed after 2–4 weeks of symptoms.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context & Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition.

Observable presentations:

  • New or changing heart murmur — most sensitive clinical finding. Aortic valve IE → early diastolic murmur (aortic regurgitation). Mitral valve IE → pansystolic murmur. Tricuspid IE → pulsatile hepatomegaly, prominent JVP (right-sided).
  • Fever — present ~90% but may be absent in elderly, immunosuppressed, renal failure.
  • Embolic phenomena: focal neurologic deficit (stroke), limb pain/pallor, left upper quadrant pain (splenic infarct), abdominal pain (mesenteric emboli).
  • Splenomegaly — 25–50% (splenic infarction risk).
  • Exam findings (increasingly rare in modern era): Janeway lesions (painless, flat erythematous macules on palms/soles, from emboli), Osler nodes (tender nodules on fingertips, from immune complexes), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages on fundoscopy), splinter hemorrhages, petechiae.
  • Sepsis appearance — tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension if advanced. In IVDU patients, may see track marks or vascular injury.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / Gather Information* (2–5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs & perfusion: HR, BP, SpO₂, respiratory rate, temperature, capillary refill, skin color/temperature
  • Cardiac exam: auscultate for new or changing murmur (apex, right sternal border); palpate apical-radial pulse deficit on irregular rhythm
  • Embolic signs: focal neuro deficit, limb pallor, recent stroke symptoms
  • Splenic infarction signs: left upper quadrant tenderness, recent left shoulder/left-sided pain
  • Skin findings: petechiae, splinter hemorrhages under nails, Janeway lesions (palms/soles), IV drug use sites
  • Funduscopy: if Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages) suspected
  • Recent labs: most recent CBC, CMP (renal function — antibiotics are nephrotoxic), CRP/ESR, lactate, troponin if available
  • ECG findings: assess PR interval and AV conduction (new PR prolongation or AV block = aortic root abscess)
  • Recent imaging: prior TTE/TEE, cardiac imaging
  • Source assessment: dental work, invasive procedure, skin infection, IV line, indwelling catheter, IVDU history
  • Antibiotic history: when were cultures drawn? Any antibiotics given yet?

sections.heading: 5A.1 Blood Cultures (Most Critical)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Timing: BEFORE antibiotics if possible. If septic/unstable, draw and start ABX simultaneously. If not septic, delay antibiotics 1–2 hours to secure cultures.
  • Technique:
  • 3 sets from separate peripheral sites (NOT from central lines if possible; if central-line draw, document)
  • Each set = 1 aerobic bottle + 1 anaerobic bottle (20 mL total blood per set)
  • 30-minute minimum intervals between draws (unless septic, then draw simultaneously)
  • Clean skin with chlorhexidine or iodine; allow to dry; insert fresh needle
  • Clearly label with exact time and site
  • Transport to lab immediately
  • Processing: Incubate 5–10 days; organism identification and susceptibilities
  • Interpretation: 2 separate draws with same typical organism = major criterion; 1 draw = minor criterion; 3+ sets increases confidence

sections.heading: 5A.2 Echocardiography
sections.bodyHtml:
Transthoracic echo (TTE) — initial test:

  • Sensitivity ~60% for vegetation. Assess valve anatomy, vegetation presence/size, regurgitation degree, ventricular function
  • Can identify abscess or perforation (though TEE more sensitive)
  • Proceed with TTE first — faster, non-invasive, rules in ~60% of cases

Transesophageal echo (TEE) — indicated if:

  • TTE negative but high clinical suspicion persists (new murmur + positive cultures, or new PR prolongation)
  • Known prosthetic valve (TTE poor acoustic window) — TEE mandatory even if TTE positive
  • Assessment of surgical features: vegetation size, mobility, abscess location/extent, perivalvular leak, perforation
  • Sensitivity ~90% for vegetation; gold standard for detecting abscess, perforation, dehiscence
  • Must be done pre-operatively if surgery anticipated (helps surgeon plan repair vs replacement)

Key echo findings to communicate to team:

  • Vegetation size (≥10 mm = higher embolic risk, surgical indication)
  • Regurgitation degree (correlates with hemodynamic impact)
  • Abscess presence/location (suggests surgical debridement needed)
  • Perforation or dehiscence (advanced infection)
  • Ventricular dysfunction (acute regurgitation or septic myocarditis)

sections.heading: 5A.3 ECG
sections.bodyHtml:
• Assess PR interval and AV conduction immediately
  • New PR prolongation or AV block = aortic root abscess until proven otherwise — escalate STAT
  • Serial ECGs may show progressive conduction disease

sections.heading: 5A.4 Laboratory Workup
sections.bodyHtml:
• CBC: WBC elevation (typically 10–15K), anemia (chronic infection), thrombocytopenia possible
  • CMP: baseline renal function (antibiotics nephrotoxic), electrolytes
  • CRP/ESR: elevated; useful for tracking response to therapy (should decline on adequate antibiotics)
  • Lactate: elevated if shock present
  • Liver function tests: baseline
  • Repeat blood cultures: if initially negative but high suspicion, repeat at 48h (consider HACEK media, fungal cultures, or 16S rRNA PCR if available)

sections.heading: 5A.5 Imaging (as indicated)
sections.bodyHtml:
• CT chest/abdomen: mycotic aneurysm screening (especially if neurologic symptoms), septic pulmonary embolism (right-sided IE), splenic/mesenteric infarction
  • MRI brain: if embolic stroke suspected or neurologic deficit present
  • PET/CT: if blood culture-negative IE suspected (major criterion in 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria) (Fowler et al., 2023)

sections.heading: 5B. Duke Criteria for Diagnosis
sections.bodyHtml: Modified Duke criteria (Fowler et al., 2023 update). Definite IE, Possible IE, or Rejected based on major + minor points.

sections.heading: Major Criteria (1 point each)
sections.bodyHtml:
Criterion Definition
Blood cultures typical organism ≥2 positive cultures from separate sites, separate draws (ideally 30+ min apart). Typical for IE: viridans Strep, Strep bovis, HACEK, Strep pneumoniae, enterococcus, Staph aureus (MSSA/MRSA). Alternative: 1 culture of Coxiella burnetii or anti-phase I IgG >1:800 (Q fever).
Echocardiographic evidence Vegetation, perivalvular abscess, new partial dehiscence of prosthetic valve, or new regurgitation (NOT just valve insufficiency — must be new).
PET/CT major criterion (2023 Duke-ISCVID update) PET/CT showing abnormal uptake consistent with IE (Fowler et al., 2023).

sections.heading: Minor Criteria (1 point each)
sections.bodyHtml:
Criterion Definition
Fever Temperature >38°C (100.4°F)
Predisposition IVDU, prosthetic valve, prior IE, congenital cyanotic disease, cardiac surgery
Vascular phenomena Septic emboli (pulmonary, limb), mycotic aneurysm, Janeway lesions, septic pulmonary infarcts
Immunologic phenomena Osler nodes, Roth spots, rheumatoid factor positive, glomerulonephritis
Microbiologic evidence Positive culture not meeting major criterion (e.g., staph from only 1 draw, or fastidious organism), or positive serologic for culture-negative organisms

sections.heading: Diagnostic Algorithm
sections.bodyHtml:
Criteria Diagnosis
2 major criteria Definite IE
1 major + 3 minor Definite IE
3 minor Definite IE
1 major + 1 minor Possible IE
3 minor alone Possible IE
0 major + ≤2 minor Rejected (alternative diagnosis more likely)

sections.heading: Empiric Coverage (Before Cultures)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Standard empiric: Vancomycin + Ceftriaxone (covers staph, strep, HACEK, enterococcus partially)
  • Alternative if high MRSA suspicion: Vancomycin + Gentamicin
  • Start ASAP if septic; delay if stable to ensure good cultures

Empiric Regimens

Drug Dose Notes
Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV Q8–12H (trough goal 15–20 mcg/mL) Check trough day 3–5. Nephrotoxic; monitor renal function.
Ceftriaxone 2 g IV Q12H Broad-spectrum; covers HACEK, streptococci. Adjust for renal function.
Gentamicin (if added) Calculated dose IV Q8–24H (goal peak 3–4, trough <1 mcg/mL) Only first 3–5 days typically (ototoxicity/nephrotoxicity long-term).

sections.heading: Organism-Directed Therapy (After Sensitivities)
sections.bodyHtml:
Organism Typical Regimen Duration
Strep viridans, non-penicillin-resistant Penicillin IV (4M units Q4H) OR ceftriaxone 2g IV Q12H 4 weeks (6 weeks if prosthetic)
Strep viridans, penicillin-resistant Vancomycin (trough 15–20 mcg/mL) 4–6 weeks
Enterococcus (penicillin-susceptible) Ampicillin 2g IV Q4H + gentamicin (peak 3–4, trough <1) 6 weeks
Staph aureus (MSSA, no prosthetic) Nafcillin/oxacillin 2g IV Q4H ± gentamicin 4 weeks
Staph aureus (MRSA) Vancomycin (trough 15–20) ± gentamicin OR daptomycin 6 mg/kg IV Q24H 4–6 weeks
HACEK Ceftriaxone 2g IV Q12H 4 weeks
Fungal (Candida, Aspergillus) Surgery + amphotericin B OR fluconazole (if stable) Surgery essential; 6+ weeks antifungal
Culture-negative Empiric regimen, modify if organism identified or TEE definitive 6 weeks

sections.heading: Drug Levels & Monitoring
sections.bodyHtml:
• Vancomycin trough: target 15–20 mcg/mL; check day 3–5, at steady state
  • Gentamicin: peak 3–4 mcg/mL if used; monitor renal function closely
  • Aminoglycosides: typically only first 3–5 days (toxicity risk long-term)
  • Repeat blood cultures q48h until documented clearance (should sterilize within 24–48h on appropriate antibiotics)

sections.heading: When to Escalate to Cardiothoracic Surgery
sections.bodyHtml:
Emergent surgery (hours to POD 0):

  • Cardiogenic shock from acute severe aortic or mitral regurgitation (pulmonary edema, hypotension despite vasopressors)
  • Large perivalvular abscess with hemodynamic compromise
  • Free rupture into another chamber

Urgent surgery (24–72 hours):

  • Perivalvular abscess on TEE (especially aortic root) — prevents conduction system destruction; risk of rupture
  • Large vegetation (≥10 mm) with prior embolic event — indicates unstable, friable vegetation at high recurrence risk
  • Fungal endocarditis — antibiotics alone insufficient; surgery almost always needed
  • Resistant organism (e.g., VRE with high gentamicin MIC, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus) if unresponsive to antibiotics
  • Recurrent systemic emboli despite appropriate antibiotics — suggests large/mobile vegetation
  • Heart failure from acute valve insufficiency not controllable medically
  • Persistent bacteremia (positive cultures >5–7 days on appropriate antibiotics) — suggests inadequate source control

Elective surgery (once stabilized, no rush if good response):

  • Non-complicated IE responding well to antibiotics
  • Completion of 4–6 week antibiotic course pre-op preferred (decreases prosthetic valve infection risk)

Non-surgical medical management (appropriate if):

  • Small vegetation (<5–10 mm)
  • Good antibiotic response (fever gone by day 3–5, CRP declining)
  • No embolic events
  • Adequate ventricular function
  • Susceptible organism with reliable antibiotics available
  • Patient and team concordant

sections.heading: Valve-Specific Presentations
sections.bodyHtml:
Valve Typical Organisms Murmur Surgical Risk Features Notes
Aortic (AV) Staph, viridans Early diastolic (AI); may have systolic if perforation Root abscess (conduction block), perforation, acute HF High risk for heart block; ECG mandatory
Mitral (MV) Viridans, Staph, enterococcus Pansystolic (MR) Perforations, large vegetations, HF Most common site overall
Tricuspid (TV) Staph aureus (IVDU) Systolic (TR); pulsatile hepatomegaly, prominent JVP Septic pulmonary emboli; emboli to lungs (not brain) Right-sided; lower embolic mortality but high morbidity (septic pulmonary infarction)
Pulmonary (PV) Very rare Rare Rare Unusual site; almost never surgical intervention

sections.heading: Team Involvement
sections.bodyHtml:
• Infectious disease: organism identification, susceptibilities, antibiotic regimen, duration of therapy, follow-up cultures
  • Cardiothoracic surgery: operative planning if indications met; timing; repair vs replacement decision
  • Cardiology: echo interpretation, hemodynamic assessment, anticoagulation management
  • Critical care: hemodynamic support, sepsis management, ICU-level monitoring
  • Addiction medicine (if IVDU-related): MAT (medication-assisted treatment) involvement, non-judgmental care, discharge planning to reduce AMA risk
  • Social work: housing, financial assistance, follow-up care coordination

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for handoff:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], admitted [date] with [relevant history]." B: "[Patient presentation.] Blood cultures drawn [dates/times]; [number] sets positive for [organism]. TEE/TTE findings: [key findings — vegetation size, abscess, regurgitation]. Current on [antibiotic regimen]." A: "IE suspected per Duke criteria [major/minor breakdown].

[Hemodynamic status — stable/unstable]. [Any acute changes — increased fever, new murmur, embolic event, heart block, worsening renal function]." R: "[Request: surgical evaluation, additional imaging, antibiotic adjustment, escalation level, specific labs/cultures]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Rationale
Stable NVE, first presentation Infectious disease + cardiology (non-urgent) Outpatient diagnostic plan, antibiotic selection
Unstable NVE (septic shock, cardiogenic shock) STAT: CT surgery + ID + critical care Operative planning, hemodynamic support
New heart block or AV conduction delay STAT CT surgery + cardiology + EP Aortic root abscess — surgical emergency
Recurrent/persistent bacteremia CT surgery + ID consult Source control failure; possible need for repeat surgery or imaging
Embolic stroke during IE treatment STAT neurology + CT surgery + neuroradiology Hemorrhagic conversion risk before surgery; timing considerations
Fungal organism on culture STAT CT surgery + ID + infectious diseases Surgery nearly always needed; expedited planning
Prosthetic valve involvement on TEE STAT CT surgery (prosthetic valve IE — different epidemiology) Escalate to PVE pathway

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections expandable.

7.1 Duke Criteria 2023 Update (ISCVID) — What Changed The 2023 Duke-ISCVID criteria (Fowler et al., 2023) updated the 2000 Modified Duke criteria: New major criterion: PET/CT imaging
  • PET/CT (usually ¹⁸F-FDG) showing abnormal uptake in the area of a prosthetic valve or a perivalvular lesion suggestive of abscess is now a major criterion — equivalent to positive blood culture or vegetation on echo
  • Particularly helpful in blood culture-negative IE, where traditional major criteria may be hard to meet
  • Standard TTE/TEE still first-line, but PET/CT can provide definitive diagnosis in cases where cultures fail and echo is equivocal Emphasis on 16S rRNA and PCR for fastidious organisms
  • Culture-negative IE often caused by fastidious organisms (HACEK, Bartonella, Brucella, Coxiella, Legionella, fungi)
  • If available, blood PCR/16S rRNA increases diagnostic yield and can be used as microbiologic evidence (minor criterion) Strep bovis reclassification
  • Now recognized as Strep gallolyticus subspecies gallolyticus
  • Still indicates GI source workup (colonoscopy) for occult malignancy or GI polyps
7.2 TTE vs. TEE — When Each Is Needed TTE (Transthoracic Echo)
  • First test always — non-invasive, readily available, good for assessing vegetation, regurgitation, ventricular function
  • Limitations: poor acoustic windows (obesity, COPD, mechanical ventilation), limited views of posterior mitral, aortic root detail, abscess assessment
  • Proceed with TTE first unless urgent TEE is clinically indicated (unstable, high surgical suspicion) TEE (Transesophageal Echo)
  • Mandatory indications:
  • Prosthetic valve IE — TTE acoustic window poor; TEE required even if TTE appears normal
  • High suspicion + TTE negative — e.g., new murmur + positive cultures, or new heart block
  • Pre-operative planning for any suspected surgery — TEE defines vegetation size, abscess extent, perforation, perivalvular leak
  • Complications assessment — abscess, perforation, leaflet mobility
  • Sensitivity: ~90% for vegetation; gold standard for abscess, perforation, dehiscence
  • Risks: esophageal intubation discomfort, transient esophageal injury, aspiration if sedated — requires proper consent and monitoring Clinical practice point: If IE is being considered for surgery, TEE is mandatory pre-operatively. Do NOT delay TEE if surgery is anticipated — TEE findings directly affect surgical planning (repair vs replacement, approach, extent of debridement).
7.3 Embolic Events — Recognition & Screening Emboli occur in ~30–50% of IE cases and may be the presenting sign. Pulmonary emboli (right-sided IE — IVDU tricuspid):
  • Often multiple septic infarcts, not typical DVT/PE
  • CXR may show wedge-shaped infiltrates or small "septic foci"
  • Clinically: hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea
  • CTPA (CT pulmonary angiogram) may show peripheral wedge infarcts Systemic/cerebral emboli (left-sided IE — aortic, mitral):
  • Ischemic stroke: most common embolic complication; occurs in 10–20% of IE
  • Splenic infarction: left upper quadrant pain, left shoulder pain, elevated LDH
  • Mesenteric emboli: abdominal pain, diarrhea, GI bleeding
  • Renal infarction: hematuria, flank pain, elevated creatinine
  • Limb arterial occlusion: cold limb, pallor, pain
  • Mycotic aneurysm: rupture can cause subarachnoid hemorrhage, meningitis-like symptoms, or sudden death Screening for emboli:
  • Clinical history: any recent stroke, TIA, unexplained abdominal pain, splenic infarction, limb ischemia?
  • Neuroimaging: MRI brain if any neuro symptoms → detect ischemic infarcts, mycotic aneurysm
  • Splenic imaging: abdominal CT if left upper quadrant pain
  • Consider: renal function trending, hematuria, mesenteric CT if abdominal symptoms Key teaching point: Embolic phenomena can precede cardiac diagnosis. A patient presenting with unexplained stroke or splenic infarction should raise suspicion for IE, especially if febrile or if risk factors (IVDU, poor dentition, recent procedure) present.
7.4 Right-Sided IE (IVDU Tricuspid) — Special Features Epidemiology: IVDU is the dominant risk factor for native valve IE in the US. ~60% of IVDU IE is tricuspid. Pathophysiology: Dirty needle → tricuspid valve seeding via right heart. Vegetations are often large and friable. Emboli go to the lungs (not brain). Clinical presentation:
  • Fever + respiratory symptoms (hemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea)
  • New systolic murmur at left sternal border (tricuspid regurgitation)
  • Pulsatile hepatomegaly, elevated JVP (signs of severe TR)
  • CXR may show septic pulmonary infiltrates or "shotgun" pattern Echo findings:
  • TTE may be sufficient — tricuspid is anterior, better visualized on TTE than posterior (mitral, aortic)
  • Large oscillating vegetation on tricuspid leaflet
  • Tricuspid regurgitation (can be severe, causing RV failure)
  • TEE still indicated if surgery planned or if TTE non-diagnostic Treatment:
  • Antibiotics: same organism-directed regimen as left-sided IE; 4–6 weeks
  • Surgery: indicated for vegetation >10 mm with septic pulmonary emboli, large abscess, or endocarditis failing medical therapy
  • Tricuspid repair preferred over replacement (avoids prosthetic and lifelong anticoagulation; preserves native valve)
  • Many IVDU patients refuse surgery — long-term addiction medicine/MAT involvement critical for compliance
  • IVDU management: addiction medicine consult for MAT, counseling, non-judgmental care, discharge planning to sterile environment High-yield nursing point: Tricuspid IE can be medically managed if vegetation is small (<10 mm) and no septic pulmonary emboli. Repeat echo at 2–4 weeks to document improvement. But if septic pulmonary infarcts develop, surgery becomes likely.
7.5 Culture-Negative IE & Fastidious Organisms Incidence: 5–10% of suspected IE cases remain culture-negative despite incubation for 5–10 days. Causes:
  • Prior antibiotics (most common) — even 1–2 doses can sterilize blood cultures
  • Fastidious organisms — slow-growing or require special media
  • Viral or unusual pathogens — PCR/16S rRNA may identify
  • Inoculum too small — occasional Fastidious pathogens to consider:
    OrganismMediaCulture TimeNotes
    HACEK group (Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter, Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella)Special media (fastidious gram-negative)7–10 daysRequires special lab communication; often missed if standard media only
    Bartonella (cat-scratch disease)Chocolate agar, special enrichment; lysis-centrifugation preferred1–3 weeksAssociated with homelessness, cat exposure; can cause chronic IE
    BrucellaSpecialized media2+ weeksAssociated with animal/agricultural exposure
    Coxiella burnetii (Q fever)Cell culture or serology—Diagnosis via serology (phase I IgG >1:800 is major criterion) — cultures often not helpful
    LegionellaSpecial media; buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE)1–2 weeksRespiratory involvement; associated with environmental water sources
    Candida, Aspergillus (fungal)Standard + fungal mediaVariableAlways communicate suspected fungal IE to lab
    Diagnosis of culture-negative IE:
  • Meeting Duke criteria with ≥1 minor criterion + high clinical suspicion
  • PET/CT major criterion (2023) — if available, can establish definite IE diagnosis
  • Serology: Q fever (phase I IgG), Bartonella, Brucella serology if epidemiologic clues
  • PCR/16S rRNA: if available; increasingly offered in tertiary centers
  • Repeat cultures at 48h and 72h if initial cultures negative but clinical suspicion high Management: Empiric antibiotics (usually vanc + ceftriaxone + gentamicin if culture-negative at 48h) for 6 weeks. If organism identified later, switch to targeted regimen.
7.6 Drug-Resistant Organisms & Special Regimens Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus (VRE):
  • Inherent ampicillin resistance + vancomycin resistance = limited options
  • Treatment options: daptomycin (6 mg/kg IV Q24H), linezolid, ceftaroline, or combination therapy per ID
  • Prognosis worse; surgery may be needed for source control Methicillin-resistant Staph aureus (MRSA):
  • Staph aureus bacteremia is highly virulent — usually needs surgery (abscess, large vegetation)
  • Vancomycin standard, but daptomycin is alternative (6 mg/kg IV Q24H)
  • Combination therapy (vanc + rifampin, or vanc + gentamicin for first 3–5 days) considered for persistent bacteremia
  • High embolic risk — low threshold for imaging (CT/MRI) and early surgical evaluation Strep bovis (Strep gallolyticus) IE:
  • Associated with GI malignancy or polyps — colonoscopy mandatory post-IE treatment
  • Standard penicillin/cephalosporin therapy
7.7 Pathophysiology Deep-Dive — From Bacteremia to Vegetation Seeding the valve:
  • Transient bacteremia from dental procedure, skin/soft tissue infection, GI source, GU instrumentation
  • Turbulent blood flow (especially pre-existing valve lesion) promotes bacterial adhesion
  • Staph aureus is highly adhesive; can seed normal valves
  • Viridans Strep and enterococcus preferentially seed abnormal/stenotic valves Vegetation formation (biofilm):
  • Bacteria secrete exopolysaccharide (biofilm matrix)
  • Fibrin and platelets accumulate, creating friable mass
  • Encapsulation protects bacteria from antibiotics and immune cells
  • Biofilm bacteria have reduced metabolic activity — sometimes harder to kill with antibiotics (higher MICs needed) Valve destruction:
  • Bacterial enzymes and lipases damage valve architecture
  • Inflammatory response (cytokines, neutrophils) causes tissue damage
  • Regurgitation develops from leaflet erosion or perforation Septic emboli:
  • Vegetations are friable and prone to fragmentation
  • Septic particles lodge in small arteries, causing infarction or microabscess
  • Right-sided vegetation → pulmonary emboli (septic infarcts)
  • Left-sided → cerebral, splenic, renal, mesenteric, limb emboli Perivalvular extension (abscess formation):
  • Infection spreads beyond leaflet into annulus, myocardium, or septum
  • Creates localized abscess collection
  • Can erode into conduction pathways (heart block, PR prolongation)
  • May rupture into adjacent chamber or perforate pericardium (tamponade) Systemic inflammation:
  • Circulating immune complexes form (antigen-antibody-complement)
  • Deposit in small vessels → vasculitis
  • Classic immune complex phenomena: Osler nodes, Roth spots, RF positivity, glomerulonephritis
  • Fever from IL-1, TNF-alpha, other cytokines

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Distinct from unstable criteria. If any appear, re-escalate.

  • Persistent fever >72h on appropriate antibiotics — may indicate inadequate source control, abscess, or wrong organism identification; repeat imaging (TEE, CT), repeat cultures
  • New heart block or PR prolongation on serial ECGs — aortic root abscess growing; urgent surgical evaluation
  • Declining renal function despite adequate hydration — acute glomerulonephritis from immune complexes, or aminoglycoside toxicity; check vanc/gentamicin levels
  • Rising lactate or falling urine output — perfusion failing; may herald septic shock or cardiogenic shock
  • New or worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, or pulmonary edema — acute valve regurgitation or septic pulmonary emboli; urgent echo + chest imaging
  • New focal neurologic deficit (stroke, TIA, weakness, speech change) — activate stroke code immediately
  • Recurrent fever after initial response — may indicate inadequate antibiotic penetration, relapsing infection, or embolic seeding to another site
  • Vegetating on antibiotics (vegetation size increasing on repeat echo) — treatment failure; may require surgery sooner
  • Worsening thrombocytopenia — immune consumption or sepsis progression
  • Elevated troponin + new ECG changes — septic myocarditis or coronary embolus (rare); heightens surgical urgency

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. 3 sets blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics — non-negotiable. If septic, draw and start simultaneously. If not septic, delay 1–2 hours. A single set is diagnostic inadequacy; 2 sets from same draw are not separate draws. Staggered timing (30-min intervals) catches bacteremia better.

  2. Central-line cultures are admissible but mark as such — more contamination risk; ID team weights them accordingly. Prefer peripheral sites when possible.

  3. TEE mandatory if prosthetic valve on TTE, even if TTE appears normal. Prosthetic valves have poor acoustic windows on TTE; sensitivity <50%. TEE is gold standard and should be done pre-operatively for any suspected surgery.

  4. New PR prolongation or AV block on ECG = aortic root abscess until proven otherwise. Escalate STAT. Abscess is a surgical emergency — high risk of rupture, free-wall perforation, tamponade, or conduction system destruction.

  5. Large vegetation (≥10 mm) + embolic event = surgical indication. Indicates unstable vegetation at high recurrence risk. Do not manage medically.

  6. Fungal endocarditis requires surgery. Antifungals alone do NOT sterilize infected valves. If Candida or Aspergillus on culture, expect expedited OR planning. Mortality without surgery approaches 100%.

  7. IVDU endocarditis — addiction medicine consult is essential. Patient at high risk for leaving AMA. Non-judgmental care, MAT involvement, and discharge planning to clean environment improve outcomes. Tricuspid repair (not replacement) preferred to avoid lifelong anticoagulation.

  8. Staph aureus bacteremia is virulent. If persistent bacteremia (positive cultures >5–7 days on appropriate antibiotics), suggests relapsing infection, occult abscess, or inadequate source control. Imaging (CT, repeat TEE) or surgery often needed.

  9. Repeat blood cultures q48h until clearance. Cultures should sterilize within 24–48h on appropriate antibiotics. Persistent positive cultures indicate treatment failure or inadequate source control.

  10. HACEK pathogens need special media. Fastidious gram-negatives often missed if only standard culture media used. Communicate "fastidious organism suspected" or "HACEK possible" to lab at admission.

  11. Culture-negative IE — think prior antibiotics first. Even 1–2 preemptive doses can sterilize blood cultures. Consider 16S rRNA PCR, PET/CT, serology for fastidious organisms if available.

  12. Mycotic aneurysm screening in IVDU or persistent bacteremia. Can rupture → subarachnoid hemorrhage, sudden stroke, or shock. If embolic phenomena or prolonged bacteremia, consider MRI brain + angiography.

  13. Septic pulmonary emboli (right-sided IE) vs. systemic emboli (left-sided). Right-sided emboli go to lungs (hemoptysis, septic infarcts on CXR); left-sided go to brain, spleen, kidneys, limbs. Clinical presentation differs; imaging strategies differ.

  14. Janeway lesions vs. Osler nodes — distinguish for teaching. Janeway = painless, flat, erythematous on palms/soles (embolic). Osler nodes = tender nodules on fingertips (immune complex). Roth spots require fundoscopy; if suspected, involve ophthalmology.

  15. Valve repair preferred over replacement when feasible (especially tricuspid IE). Native valve repair avoids prosthetic complications, lifelong anticoagulation, and prosthetic valve IE risk. Surgeon decides feasibility at OR.

cards.title: Infective Endocarditis Prophylaxis
cards.quickAnswer: Only 4 high-risk cardiac conditions warrant lifelong IE prophylaxis: prosthetic heart valve (surgical or TAVR), prior infective endocarditis, unrepaired/residual congenital cyanotic heart disease, and heart transplant with cardiac valvulopathy. Give amoxicillin 2 g PO 30–60 minutes before dental manipulation, respiratory incision, or oral surgery. No routine GI/GU prophylaxis. Counsel on oral hygiene, wallet card, and avoid piercings/tattoos. Clindamycin removed from 2021 guideline (C. difficile risk exceeds benefit). All doses are one-time; no post-procedure redosing.

Give amoxicillin 2 g PO 30–60 minutes before dental manipulation, respiratory incision, or oral surgery. No routine GI/GU prophylaxis. Counsel on oral hygiene, wallet card, and avoid piercings/tattoos. Clindamycin removed from 2021 guideline (C. difficile risk exceeds benefit). All doses are one-time; no post-procedure redosing.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → 2021 AHA Prevention of Viridans Group Streptococcal Infective Endocarditis (Wilson et al.) → 2007 AHA Prophylaxis of Infective Endocarditis → 2017 AHA/ACC Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines → 2003 ADA/AHA Joint Guidelines → IDSA Endocarditis Guidelines

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, scope, and who this applies to.

  • Definition: Antimicrobial prophylaxis given to patients with specific high-risk cardiac lesions before procedures known to cause bacteremia, preventing colonization and septic emboli that lead to infective endocarditis (IE).
  • 2021 AHA simplification: Prophylaxis now restricted to 4 cardiac conditions only (Wilson et al., 2021), down from prior broader indications.
  • Incidence and impact: IE remains a rare but serious infection in the general population; risk is substantially elevated in the four defined conditions. Untreated, IE carries high morbidity and mortality.
  • Who this applies to: All patients with prosthetic valves, prior IE, cyanotic congenital heart disease (unrepaired/residual), or heart transplant recipients with valvular dysfunction. Applies to pediatric and adult populations.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Infective endocarditis arises when bacteremia colonizes abnormal endocardium or a foreign object (prosthetic valve, pacemaker lead, hemodialysis catheter). The four high-risk cardiac conditions share a common feature: turbulent blood flow or a foreign surface creates endothelial injury and platelet-fibrin deposits that are highly susceptible to bacterial adhesion.

Pathophysiology in the four conditions:

  • Prosthetic valve (surgical or TAVR): Foreign material in the high-pressure left heart creates a nidus for platelet-fibrin deposition. Mechanical valves are slightly higher risk than bioprosthetic initially; TAVR frames are prosthetic devices.
  • Prior endocarditis: Even after successful antibiotic treatment, the healed valve is scarred and fibrotic, predisposing to recurrent IE.
  • Unrepaired/residual cyanotic CHD: Right-to-left shunt bypasses the lungs' bacterial filtration; direct bacteremia seeds the right heart and paradoxical emboli reach systemic circulation.
  • Heart transplant with valvulopathy: Allograft vasculopathy and any degree of post-transplant valvular regurgitation or stenosis creates turbulent flow.

Why NOT other cardiac lesions? Native valve disease (even severe aortic stenosis or mitral regurgitation), isolated ASD/PFO, repaired simple defects > 6 months post-op, and CABG alone carry low enough IE risk that prophylaxis is not justified (risk of antibiotic adverse events exceeds IE prevention benefit).

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Cardiac Conditions Requiring Lifelong Prophylaxis
sections.bodyHtml: Novice + advanced beginner recognition of who is at risk.

sections.heading: Table 1: High-Risk Cardiac Conditions
sections.bodyHtml:
Condition Mechanism Duration Notes
Prosthetic heart valve (surgical or TAVR) Foreign material; turbulent flow; platelet-fibrin nidus Lifelong Includes aortic, mitral, pulmonary, tricuspid. All prosthetic types (mechanical, bioprosthetic, TAVR frame) equally warrant lifelong prophylaxis.
Prior infective endocarditis Scarred, fibrotic endocardium; high recurrence risk Lifelong Even if valve infection cleared and no structural defect remains. Highest-risk group for recurrence.
Unrepaired or residual congenital cyanotic CHD Right-to-left shunt; bacterial bypass of lung filtration; endothelial damage Lifelong Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition, truncus arteriosus, HLHS with palliative shunt, PDA (unclosed). Includes palliative procedures and conduits.
Heart transplant recipient with cardiac valvulopathy Allograft vasculopathy; abnormal hemodynamics; valvular dysfunction Lifelong NEW in 2021 guidelines. Any degree of new aortic or mitral regurgitation/stenosis or tricuspid regurgitation post-transplant.

sections.heading: Does NOT require prophylaxis
sections.bodyHtml:
• Isolated atrial septal defect, patent foramen ovale, secundum ASD
  • Prior surgically repaired simple lesions (ASD, VSD, PDA) > 6 months post-op with no residual defect
  • Native valve disease (even severe AS, MR, AR)
  • Bioprosthetic valve > 5–10 years (individual surgeon decision; conservative approach: treat as prosthetic if < 10 years post-implant)
  • CABG without valve involvement
  • Post-TAVR in patients without a prosthetic valve frame (rare)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Identify Candidates*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic chart and interview. Information-gathering only.

Pre-procedure identification (preop, dental, endoscopy, etc.):

  • Chart history: Prosthetic valve? Prior IE? Congenital heart disease? Transplant status?
  • Patient interview: "Have you ever had a replaced heart valve or heart infection?" "Do you have any birth defect of the heart?"
  • Physical exam: New cardiac murmur? Signs of prior cardiac surgery (sternotomy scar)?
  • Penicillin/cephalosporin allergy assessment: Type of reaction (rash vs. anaphylaxis) guides antibiotic selection.
  • Recent labs/ECG: Baseline if available; not required for prophylaxis decision.
  • Procedure type: Determine if it's on the "requires prophylaxis" list (Table 2).

sections.heading: Table 2: Procedures — Prophylaxis Required vs. Not Required
sections.bodyHtml:
Procedure Type Prophylaxis Rationale
DENTAL
Extraction, periodontal scaling/root planing YES Gingival manipulation; bacteremia with viridans streptococci
Periodontal surgery, dental implant placement YES Bone/periosteal disruption
Endodontic (root canal) beyond coronal third YES Apical manipulation
Endodontic (coronal third only) NO Minimal apical bacteremia
Routine cleaning, exam, x-ray, fluoride application NO No mucosal disruption
Restorations without gingival extension NO Minimal bacteremia
RESPIRATORY TRACT
Rigid bronchoscopy, bronchoscopy with biopsy YES Respiratory mucosa incision/biopsy
Flexible bronchoscopy (diagnostic) NO Minimal mucosal trauma (Wilson et al., 2021)
Intubation (routine, elective) NO Short-term; bacteremia minimal/transient
Intubation (emergency/traumatic) Consider Mucosal trauma; individualize per risk/benefit
Chest tube placement YES Pleural membrane incision
GASTROINTESTINAL
Esophageal endoscopy (no biopsy) NO Minimal bacteremia (2007 AHA revision)
Colonoscopy NO Prophylaxis NOT recommended (2007 AHA)
Biliary/pancreatic procedures NO Unless immunocompromised (separate guidelines)
Variceal bleeding treatment Consider Higher bacteremia risk; team decision
GENITOURINARY
Urinary catheterization (uncomplicated) NO No longer recommended (2007 AHA)
Cystoscopy NO Routine prophylaxis NOT indicated
Urologic surgery / prostate biopsy NO NOT routine; individualize if immunocompromised
Vaginal delivery NO Vaginal flora bacteremia low risk
INTEGUMENTARY / REPRODUCTIVE
Body piercing (ear, navel, tongue, genital) NO BUT counsel high-risk patients: risk of infected piercing leading to IE; avoid if possible
Tattooing NO BUT counsel: infected tattoo ink can cause IE; use sterile, licensed professionals only
Transesophageal echocardiography NO Minimal risk; monitor post-procedure

sections.heading: 5.2 Antibiotic Regimen — Timing and Dosing
sections.bodyHtml: Fundamental rule: One-time dose, 30–60 minutes before procedure. Maximum benefit if given within 2 hours before. No post-procedure redosing recommended (Wilson et al., 2021).

sections.heading: Table 3: Prophylaxis Regimens
sections.bodyHtml:
Patient Status First-Line Prophylaxis Alternative (PCN allergy, non-anaphylaxis) Alternative (Anaphylaxis) Unable to Take PO
No PCN/cephalosporin allergy Amoxicillin 2 g PO — — Ampicillin 2 g IV/IM
PCN allergy, non-anaphylaxis (rash) — Cephalexin 2 g PO — Cefazolin 1 g IV/IM OR Ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM
PCN anaphylaxis — Azithromycin 500 mg PO OR Doxycycline 100 mg PO Azithromycin 500 mg IV OR Doxycycline 100 mg IV Clindamycin 600 mg IV (if no CDAD history; avoid if possible)
Unable to take PO, no allergy — — — Ampicillin 2 g IV/IM OR Cefazolin 1 g IV/IM

Pediatric dosing (adjust for weight/age):

  • Amoxicillin: 50 mg/kg PO (max 2 g)
  • Cephalexin: 50 mg/kg PO (max 2 g)
  • Azithromycin: 15 mg/kg PO (max 500 mg)
  • Doxycycline: age > 8 years and > 45 kg (max 100 mg)
  • Ampicillin: 50 mg/kg IV/IM (max 2 g)

Verify all doses with provider and institutional order sets before administration.

sections.heading: 5.3 Implementation Across Care Settings
sections.bodyHtml:
Pre-operative dental clearance (valve surgery, TAVR patients):

  • Coordinate pre-op dental evaluation 2–4 weeks before cardiac surgery
  • Extract or treat infected/questionable teeth before surgery (prophylaxis not needed; treatment)
  • Clear emergency dental issues; post-op IE from untreated dental infection is preventable
  • Document dental clearance in pre-op workup

Discharge teaching for at-risk patients:

  • Provide IE prophylaxis wallet card (see Section 7)
  • Instruct patient to carry card and inform ALL providers (dentists, urologists, gastroenterologists, surgeons) before any invasive procedure
  • Teach patient which procedures require prophylaxis (dental work, respiratory procedures) and which do not (most GI/GU)
  • Reinforce: "Oral hygiene (brush, floss, regular cleanings) prevents more IE than prophylaxis"
  • Schedule baseline dental exam post-discharge if not completed pre-op

Ongoing reinforcement (every clinic visit):

  • Ask: "Have you had your wallet card and does it still make sense to you?"
  • Gauge understanding: "Can you tell me which procedures need the antibiotic?"
  • For prosthetic valve or post-IE patients: "Remember, this is lifelong protection"

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Needs Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of edge cases and atypical presentations.

  1. Allergy history unclear. If patient says "penicillin allergy" but cannot describe the reaction, ask: "Did you get a rash? Trouble breathing? Swelling?" Rash = likely safe to give cephalosporin. Anaphylaxis or throat swelling = use azithromycin/doxycycline.

  2. Patient forgot antibiotic before procedure. If procedure is ongoing (e.g., dental extraction halfway through), still administer prophylaxis if within 2 hours of procedure start. Post-procedure dosing is not recommended; do not re-dose.

  3. Procedure delayed past the 30–60 min window. Reschedule antibiotic or discuss with provider. If the delay is > 2 hours, contact the provider/dentist about whether to still give it or defer.

  4. Patient on home anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC) or antiplatelet therapy. Prophylactic antibiotics do not require AC adjustments. Continue home AC per usual. Inform provider if there is a concern about bleeding with invasive procedure (surgeon's decision).

  5. Patient with chronic kidney disease or dialysis-dependent. Most prophylaxis doses do not require adjustment for mild-moderate renal impairment. High-dose regimens (e.g., vancomycin) may need dosing adjustment — consult pharmacy if CKD stage 4–5.

  6. Immunocompromised patient (post-transplant on CNI/MMF, HIV, chemotherapy). Standard prophylaxis regimens apply. Do not add extra doses. Coordinate with ID specialist if complex immunosuppression.

  7. Pregnant patient. Amoxicillin and cephalexin are safe in pregnancy (Category B). Azithromycin is generally safe. Avoid doxycycline (pregnancy Category D; teratogenic). If anaphylaxis risk, use azithromycin.

  8. Patient with penicillin allergy AND cephalosporin allergy. Use azithromycin 500 mg PO or doxycycline 100 mg PO (if age > 8 and weight > 45 kg). Clindamycin is a last resort due to C. difficile risk; avoid unless absolutely necessary.

  9. Procedure is emergency/cannot wait for 30–60 min pre-op window. Administer prophylaxis ASAP after procedure start; still protective if given within 2 hours. Communicate with surgical/procedural team.

  10. Patient refuses oral medication and cannot take IV. Discuss with provider. IM administration (ampicillin 2 g IM) is an option. If patient absolutely refuses all options, document the discussion and escalate.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections in Section 7 are intended to collapse in PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Patient Education — Key Teaching Points
sections.bodyHtml:
"You have a heart condition that needs antibiotic protection before certain procedures."

  • Your heart valve [or prior infection / birth defect] makes you at higher risk if bacteria get into your bloodstream.
  • Certain procedures (dental cleaning, some lung exams) can release bacteria into your blood.
  • A single dose of antibiotic 30–60 minutes before the procedure prevents infection.
  • This protection is needed for life (or for the duration your condition persists).

Oral hygiene is more powerful than prophylaxis:

  • Daily brushing, flossing, and water rinses prevent cavities and gum disease.
  • Regular professional cleaning every 6 months prevents the need for emergency dental work.
  • Prevention is better than waiting for a cavity to form and needing antibiotics.
  • Infected gums are a common source of bacteremia.

When YOU need the antibiotic:

  • Dental work: extraction, deep cleaning, root canal, implant, gum surgery
  • Lung procedure: bronchoscopy with biopsy, chest tube
  • Most GI and urinary procedures do NOT require prophylaxis — but always check with your doctor

What to do BEFORE any procedure:

  1. Call your dentist / specialist 2 weeks ahead if possible
  2. Show them your IE prophylaxis wallet card (keep it with you at all times)
  3. Ask: "Do I need an antibiotic before this procedure?"
  4. If yes: Take amoxicillin 2 grams by mouth 30–60 minutes before the procedure
  5. If allergic to penicillin, ask your doctor which alternative (cephalexin, azithromycin, or doxycycline)
  6. Tell the dentist/doctor that you took the antibiotic when you arrive

Avoid these risks:

  • Body piercings (ears, navel, tongue, genital): Infected piercings can seed bacteremia → IE. Discuss with your cardiologist. Some limit to ear piercing only.
  • Tattoos: Use only licensed, sterile facilities. Infected tattoo ink is a documented cause of IE (can present weeks/months later).
  • Untreated cavities and gum disease: Home for bacteria that can seed bloodstream with minimal trauma.

Call your doctor / go to ED if you develop:

  • Fever, chills, night sweats × 3+ days
  • New heart murmur or shortness of breath
  • Splinter hemorrhages (red lines under fingernails)
  • Osler nodes (painful bumps on finger/toe pads) or Janeway lesions (painless red spots on palms/soles)
  • New joint or muscle pain with fever
  • These are possible signs of endocarditis — seek urgent care.

sections.heading: 7.2 Wallet Card Template
sections.bodyHtml:
Provide to every at-risk patient at discharge and at every cardiac clinic visit. Instruct patient to keep in wallet or purse.

``` ===== INFECTIVE ENDOCARDITIS PROPHYLAXIS ===== NAME: _____ DATE OF BIRTH: __ CARDIAC CONDITION: [ ] Prosthetic valve [ ] Prior IE [ ] Cyanotic CHD [ ] Transplant valvulopathy

CARDIOLOGIST: ____ PHONE: __

ANTIBIOTIC PROPHYLAXIS REQUIRED:

  • AMOXICILLIN 2 grams by mouth
  • 30–60 minutes BEFORE dental work, respiratory procedures
  • Show this card to dentist/doctor BEFORE any procedure

IF ALLERGIC TO PENICILLIN: - CEPHALEXIN 2 g OR AZITHROMYCIN 500 mg OR DOXYCYCLINE 100 mg (Check with your doctor which is safe for you)

PROCEDURES REQUIRING PROPHYLAXIS:

  • Dental: extraction, deep cleaning, root canal, implant, gum surgery
  • Respiratory: bronchoscopy, chest tube
  • Ask your provider before any invasive procedure

PROCEDURES NOT REQUIRING PROPHYLAXIS:

  • Routine dental exam, cleaning, fluoride
  • Most GI and urinary procedures (Always confirm with your provider)

LAST UPDATED: ___ CARDIOLOGIST SIGNATURE: _______ ```

sections.heading: 7.3 Mechanism of Prophylaxis
sections.bodyHtml:
Why amoxicillin works:

Amoxicillin is a beta-lactam antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis. Viridans group streptococci (the most common cause of IE from dental procedures) are exquisitely susceptible to amoxicillin at therapeutic levels. A single 2 g dose achieves bactericidal serum levels for 6–12 hours, covering the window of bacteremia from dental manipulation.

Why the 2 g dose?

2 g achieves peak serum concentration of 4–8 mcg/mL in ~1 hour. Viridans strep MIC (minimum inhibitory concentration) is 0.06–0.5 mcg/mL; the 2 g dose provides a 10- to 100-fold safety margin. Smaller doses (500 mg) are for treatment of infection, not prophylaxis.

Why no post-procedure redosing?

The bacteremia from dental work is transient (minutes to hours). A single pre-procedure dose provides sustained coverage throughout the procedural window. Post-procedure re-dosing does not improve outcomes and only increases antibiotic exposure and risk of adverse effects.

Cross-reactivity of cephalosporins in PCN allergy:

True IgE-mediated cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is < 2% for first-generation cephalosporins (cephalexin). Cephalosporins can be safely used in most PCN-allergic patients unless prior anaphylaxis. Always clarify: "When you had the penicillin reaction, did you have trouble breathing or throat swelling?" Anaphylaxis = use azithromycin/doxycycline. Rash = safe to use cephalosporin.

Why clindamycin was removed (2021):

Older guidelines (2007) listed clindamycin 600 mg as an alternative. Evidence has accumulated showing that clindamycin substantially increases risk of Clostridioides difficile infection, especially in older adults and those with multiple prior antibiotic exposures (Wilson et al., 2021). The benefit of IE prevention does not outweigh the harm. Do not use clindamycin for routine IE prophylaxis.

sections.heading: 7.4 Risk Assessment — CHA₂DS₂-VASc–like thinking
sections.bodyHtml:
IE risk is not uniform across the four conditions. While all four warrant prophylaxis, relative risk informs counseling intensity:

Condition Relative Risk Counseling Emphasis
Prior IE Highest (~5% annual recurrence) Most intensive teaching. Lifelong prophylaxis non-negotiable. Excellent oral hygiene. Wallet card essential.
Prosthetic valve (early, < 5 yrs) High (0.5–1% annually) Intensive teaching. Lifelong prophylaxis.
Cyanotic CHD (complex, unrepaired) High (1–5% per procedure if untreated) Age-dependent teaching. Family involvement critical. Adolescent risk-taking counseling needed.
Transplant + valvulopathy Moderate (lower than others, but still significant) Tailored to post-transplant medication burden. Coordinate with transplant team.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Signs of IE in Patients at Risk
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in patients with high-risk conditions even if prophylaxis was given.

  • Fever + heart murmur — classic IE presentation. New murmur or change in pre-existing murmur = Duke criteria major.
  • Fever + positive blood culture — even a "contaminant" (e.g., coagulase-negative Staph) can be IE in prosthetic valve patients.
  • Fever + no obvious source × 3+ days — especially in prosthetic valve or prior IE patient.
  • Fever + embolic events (splinter hemorrhages, Osler nodes, Janeway lesions, septic emboli to lungs/spleen/brain).
  • Fever + new focal neuro deficit — septic emboli to brain; high mortality if not diagnosed early.
  • Prosthetic valve dehiscence on imaging — mechanical complication of valve IE.
  • Vegetation on echocardiography — confirms IE; TEE more sensitive than TTE.
  • Prior IE patient presenting with non-specific malaise, weight loss, low-grade fever — IE can have insidious onset.
  • Failure to improve on standard antibiotics — immune compromise or unusual organism driving IE.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. 2021 AHA simplified to 4 conditions only. Nurses and providers must resist over-prophylaxis. Patients with isolated native valve disease, post-repair ASD/VSD > 6 months, or prior CABG without prosthetic valve do NOT need prophylaxis. Verify appropriateness before giving antibiotic.

  2. Tissue vs. mechanical valve — both lifelong. Old teaching said tissue valves need prophylaxis only 6 months. Current guideline: lifelong for ALL prosthetic valves (mechanical + bioprosthetic + TAVR frame), indefinitely (Wilson et al., 2021).

  3. TAVR is a prosthetic valve frame. Transcatheter aortic valve replacement involves implanting a prosthetic valve on a catheter-delivered frame. Patient needs IE prophylaxis lifelong. This is NOT the same as a transfemoral access catheterization without valve implant.

  4. Prior IE = lifelong prophylaxis EVEN IF valve looks normal on echo. This is the highest-risk group. Some patients had IE that resolved with antibiotics only (no surgery). The scarred, fibrous endocardium remains a nidus. Lifetime risk is substantial.

  5. Cyanotic CHD: unrepaired or residual defects only. Secundum ASD, isolated PFO, and post-op ASD repairs with zero residual DO NOT need prophylaxis. Complex cyanotic disease (Tetralogy of Fallot, transposition, truncus, HLHS with palliative shunt) does. When in doubt, clarify with cardiology.

  6. Routine cleaning, exam, x-ray do NOT need prophylaxis. Only deep scaling (subgingival), extraction, implant placement, periodontal surgery, endodontic work beyond coronal third DO. Educate patients and dentists so they don't reflexively order prophylaxis for routine cleaning.

  7. GI/GU prophylaxis is NOT recommended. Routine endoscopy, colonoscopy, cystoscopy, urinary catheter, vaginal delivery do NOT warrant prophylaxis in high-risk patients. This was a major 2007 AHA change. Exception: immunocompromised patients may warrant individualized approach (consult ID).

  8. Body piercings + tattoos: counsel, don't prophylax. Prophylaxis doesn't prevent piercing or tattoo infection. Counsel high-risk patients to avoid body piercings (except ears, if acceptable to patient) and to use licensed, sterile tattoo artists only. Infected tattoo ink is a known cause of IE weeks to months later.

  9. Clindamycin REMOVED from 2021 guideline. Older guidelines listed clindamycin 600 mg as alternative. Evidence shows C. difficile risk outweighs IE prevention benefit.

    Do not use clindamycin for routine IE prophylaxis. Use cephalexin, azithromycin, or doxycycline instead.

  10. Cephalosporin cross-reactivity is low. < 2% true IgE-mediated cross-reactivity with penicillins. If patient had rash (delayed reaction), cephalexin is safe. If anaphylaxis, avoid and use azithromycin/doxycycline.

  11. Oral hygiene prevents more IE than prophylaxis. Patients who brush/floss daily, see dentist every 6 months, and avoid smoking have lower bacteremia risk overall. Prevention is the goal; prophylaxis is secondary insurance.

  12. Dental clearance before cardiac surgery is prophylaxis. Coordinate pre-op dental evaluation for all valve/TAVR patients: extract/treat infected/questionable teeth before surgery to prevent post-op IE from untreated dental source.

  13. Amoxicillin 2 g is the ONLY prophylaxis dose. Do NOT give 500 mg (that is for infection treatment). Single 2 g dose 30–60 min before procedure is standard. No post-procedure re-dosing.

  14. Wallet card = compliance tool. Many patients forget lifelong prophylaxis need or think it is temporary ("just after surgery"). Wallet card in purse/wallet reminds them to notify providers. Reinforce at each visit: "Do you still have your card? Can you show me?"

  15. Post-CABG WITHOUT prosthetic valve = NO prophylaxis. Native coronary disease, even if treated with CABG, does NOT warrant IE prophylaxis. Patient must have actual valve replacement OR meet one of the 4 defined conditions.

cards.title: Fluid Overload / Pulmonary Edema (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: Post-operative fluid retention is expected POD 0–3 (capillary leak 3–5 kg); becomes problematic when crackles, SpO₂ drop, orthopnea, or weight gain >2 lb/day appears. Stable: IV furosemide 20–40 mg (or 2× home dose), fluid/sodium restriction, daily weights, K⁺ ≥4.0 / Mg²⁺ ≥2.0 replacement. Unstable (respiratory distress, hypoxemia, pink frothy sputum): HOB up, high-flow O₂/BiPAP, IV furosemide 40–80 mg or infusion 5–10 mg/hr, nitroglycerin if SBP >100, STAT APP/cardiology/CVICU notification.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
Stable: IV furosemide 20–40 mg (or 2× home dose), fluid/sodium restriction, daily weights, K⁺ ≥4.0 / Mg²⁺ ≥2.0 replacement.

Unstable (respiratory distress, hypoxemia, pink frothy sputum): HOB up, high-flow O₂/BiPAP, IV furosemide 40–80 mg or infusion 5–10 mg/hr, nitroglycerin if SBP >100, STAT APP/cardiology/CVICU notification.
