sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who it applies to.

  • Definition: Abnormal fluid retention and pulmonary edema occurring after cardiac surgery, arising from cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB)–induced capillary leak, inflammation, pump dysfunction, or perioperative over-resuscitation.
  • Incidence: Fluid overload is the most common problem in the first 72 hours post-cardiac surgery. Expected fluid sequestration 5–10 L over POD 0–3; becomes symptomatic in ~30–40% of patients.
  • Who this applies to: Every post-operative cardiac surgery patient on ICU or stepdown units, peak presentation POD 1–3. Higher yield from CABG, valve surgery, complex procedures.
  • When it matters: Distinguishing expected asymptomatic edema from symptomatic pulmonary congestion drives escalation decisions.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
The post-operative cardiac patient enters a unique state of fluid pathology resulting from the convergence of three mechanisms:

CPB-induced capillary leak (POD 0–3):

  • Cardiopulmonary bypass triggers systemic inflammatory response (SIRS) → complement activation, cytokine release, endothelial dysfunction (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020)
  • Capillary endothelial tight junctions become permeable; water and small proteins leak into interstitial space
  • Expected fluid sequestration is 3–5 kg over the first 72 hours — this is normal, expected, and self-resolving
  • Resolves naturally as inflammation wanes (POD 2–5) and endothelial function restores (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025)

Why fluid retention becomes pathologic:

  • Symptomatic presentation (crackles, orthopnea, SpO₂ drop) signals pulmonary edema with impaired gas exchange
  • Weight gain >2 lb in 24 hours indicates sodium/water retention beyond expected capillary leak
  • Hypoxemia indicates alveolar filling and reduced oxygen diffusion capacity

Contributing mechanisms in the post-cardiac patient:

  • Transient RV dysfunction from myocardial stunning (improved by POD 2–3) raises right-sided pressures → pulmonary edema
  • LV dysfunction from inadequate cardioplegia, myocardial ischemia, or pre-existing cardiomyopathy → pulmonary congestion + hypotension
  • Acute kidney injury (AKI) from CPB ischemia, hypotension, or rhabdomyolysis → oliguria → inability to excrete fluid
  • Over-aggressive early resuscitation — well-meaning boluses to maintain BP in POD 0–6 can overdistend the failing pump
  • Heart failure decompensation — pre-op EF <35% or residual valve pathology (e.g., MV regurgitation) → fluid intolerance
  • Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) — rapid blood product infusion in anemic post-op patients → acute circulatory overload
  • Anemia — low Hgb (5–7) reduces oxygen-carrying capacity; compensatory fluid retention and increased cardiac output

The diuresis window (POD 2–5):

  • By POD 2–3, capillary leak resolves as endothelial function normalizes
  • Fluid shifts out of interstitium back into intravascular space
  • Patients naturally lose 1–2 lb/day — this is expected recovery, not over-diuresis
  • If diuresis does not occur by POD 3, suspect RV failure, persistent LV dysfunction, or AKI (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025)

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following while caring for a post-operative cardiac surgery patient:

  • Acute increase in work of breathing: RR >24, labored breathing, grunting, accessory muscle use
  • New or increasing crackles on lung exam, especially bilateral and dependent lobes
  • SpO₂ dropping to <92–94% on room air or requiring supplemental O₂ escalation
  • Patient reports orthopnea (unable to sleep flat) or wakes gasping at night
  • Neck vein distention or new hepatojugular reflex
  • Rapid weight gain: 1–2 lb overnight or >2 lb in 24 hours
  • Frothy or pink-tinged sputum — pathognomonic for acute pulmonary edema
  • Chest X-ray findings: new cephalization, Kerley B lines, pleural effusions, pulmonary edema pattern
  • Decreased urine output despite adequate intake
  • Patient reports chest tightness, fatigue, or inability to complete activities

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (3–5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Respiratory status: RR, work of breathing, accessory muscle use, stridor, gurgling sounds, oxygen requirement trend
  • Oxygen saturation: current SpO₂, trend over past 4–6 hours, desaturation with activity?
  • Lung auscultation: location and quality of crackles (lower lobes bilateral vs focal), wheeze, air movement, egophony
  • Position tolerance: can patient lie flat on one pillow? Orthopnea present? Orthostatic symptoms?
  • Vital signs & perfusion: HR, BP, MAP, capillary refill, skin temperature/color, signs of peripheral vasoconstriction
  • JVD assessment: at 45 degrees, is JVD visible? Pulsatile hepatomegaly present?
  • Dependent edema: hands, feet, presacral (if bedbound), ascites
  • Weight trend: compare today to post-op day 1, 2, baseline. Flag >1 lb overnight or >2 lb in 24h
  • Intake & output: cumulative I/O since OR; urine color, character, and amount; is patient keeping up with intake?
  • Recent labs: creatinine trend (AKI?), potassium, magnesium, albumin, hemoglobin
  • Imaging: baseline CXR (from OR) vs current CXR; cephalization, Kerley B lines, effusions, cardiac silhouette
  • Comorbidities: prior HF history, pre-op EF, valvular disease, renal disease, diabetes
  • Medication review: on diuretics? Last dose and UOP response? Anticoagulation status?
  • Surgery context: CABG vs valve (valve = higher fluid sensitivity), CPB time, any pump run complications, TEE contractility findings

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Mild crackles, SpO₂ 94–97% on O₂, no orthopnea, no respiratory distress, MAP ≥65)

  1. Elevate head of bed (HOB) to 45 degrees minimum — improves V/Q matching and reduces work of breathing
  2. Oxygen to target SpO₂ 94–98% — nasal cannula or face mask; titrate down as status improves
  3. IV diuretic:
    • Furosemide IV (first-line): If diuretic-naive → 20–40 mg IV once; if on home oral furosemide → 2× home daily dose IV once (e.g., home 20 mg daily → 40 mg IV)
    • Alternative — Torsemide IV (higher potency, better absorption): 10–20 mg IV once if preferred
    • Expect urine output within 15–30 min; monitor for electrolyte losses
    • Fluid restriction: 1–1.5 L/day; eliminate free water; assess current IV rates and encourage pacing of PO fluids
    • Sodium restriction: <2 g/day; review all meds for hidden sodium content
    • Daily weights: same time each morning (post-void, after diuretic, before meals); alert provider if gain >2 lb in 24 hours
    • Strict I/O charting every shift, including estimated insensible losses; note urine color and character
    • Electrolyte replacement — loop diuretics waste K⁺ and Mg²⁺; check labs q6–12h initially (AHA/ACC, 2022):
    • K⁺ goal ≥4.0 (some services ≥4.5 post-op); replace if <4.0
    • Mg²⁺ goal ≥2.0 (some services ≥2.5); replace if low
    • Hypokalemia causes arrhythmias; hypomagnesemia impairs diuretic efficacy and promotes arrhythmias
    • Monitor urine output: expect 150–300 mL/hr after IV diuretic in responsive patients; <50 mL/hr = concern for diuretic resistance or AKI
    • Continuous pulse oximetry & telemetry — monitor for arrhythmias as electrolytes shift
    • Reassess in 2–4 hours — has SpO₂ improved? Crackles improving? Weight stable? If worsening → escalate to 5B
    • Notify APP / on-call fellow with SBAR (see §6) — request diuretic plan, electrolyte targets, fluid restriction specifics

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Respiratory distress, RR >30, SpO₂ <92% despite O₂, pink frothy sputum, extreme orthopnea, altered mental status from hypoxemia)

  1. STAT call APP/fellow + charge RN + prepare for ICU transfer — do NOT leave patient unmonitored
  2. Position patient upright (Fowler's, high side-lying if cannot sit); legs dependent if possible (venous pooling reduces preload)
  3. High-flow oxygen immediately: start non-rebreather mask (15 L/min) to target SpO₂ >94%; prepare for BiPAP if available & tolerated
    • BiPAP parameters: start IPAP 10–12 cm H₂O, EPAP 5 cm H₂O; titrate IPAP upward if work of breathing remains high
    • Consider ICU transfer if BiPAP needed — coordinate with cardiology/CVICU
    • IV diuretic bolus:
    • Furosemide 40–80 mg IV push (higher if chronic diuretic user); if severe, consider continuous infusion: 5–10 mg/hr titrated to urine output 200–400 mL/hr
    • Torsemide 20–40 mg IV as alternative
    • Place Foley catheter if needed for accurate UOP monitoring
    • Nitroglycerin if systolic BP >100 mm Hg — venodilator effect reduces preload acutely:
    • SL nitroglycerin 0.3–0.6 mg now; repeat q5 min × 2 if BP tolerates
    • IV nitroglycerin infusion 5–10 mcg/min; titrate up q5–10 min to effect or until SBP <90
    • Avoid if hypotensive or RV-dependent (inferior MI, RVOT obstruction, mechanical RV support)
    • Obtain STAT labs: ABG (pH, lactate, oxygenation), electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cl⁻), creatinine, BNP, troponin
    • STAT CXR — document degree of pulmonary edema, pleural effusions, cardiac silhouette, mediastinal fluid
    • Prepare for ICU-level care: continuous diuretic infusions, non-invasive ventilation, possible vasodilator therapy, intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) if cardiogenic shock
    • Notify CT surgery + cardiology + CVICU attending — brief them on surgery type, CPB time, pre-op EF, current meds, urine output response to diuretics
    • Document everything: time of symptom onset, interventions, medication doses, urine output response, vital signs every 5–15 min while unstable
    • Re-assess after each intervention (every 5–10 min while unstable) — is SpO₂ improving? RR dropping? Patient more comfortable?

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for notifying provider:

S: "Dr./APP [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient has developed [pulmonary edema/fluid overload/hypoxemia] with [crackles/SpO₂ drop/orthopnea]. Current SpO₂ [value]% on [device], RR [value], HR [value], BP [value]. Weight today [X] kg; gained [X] lb overnight. Last I/O: intake [X] mL, output [X] mL in past 12 hours. K⁺ [value], Cr [value], last diuretic dose [time and drug]." A: "Patient is [stable/unstable]. [Current respiratory status/symptoms]. Currently on [HOB elevation, O₂ device, oral/IV diuretic status, fluid restriction]." R: "Requesting [IV diuretic order/electrolyte replacement protocol/fluid restriction parameters/ICU consideration]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Urgency
Stable fluid overload (mild crackles, SpO₂ 94–97% on O₂) Primary APP or on-call fellow Within 30–60 min
Worsening crackles despite diuretic, SpO₂ trending down APP/fellow STAT STAT call
Acute pulmonary edema (respiratory distress, frothy sputum) APP + cardiology fellow + CVICU attending STAT call
Diuretic-resistant fluid overload (minimal UOP despite IV diuretic × 2) CT surgery + cardiology (consider ultrafiltration) STAT
Acute decompensation with hemodynamic instability (cardiogenic shock) Rapid Response + CT surgery + cardiology + CVICU CODE team

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections in Section 7 are — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Post-operative fluid physiology and risk stratification
sections.bodyHtml:
Who is at highest risk for symptomatic fluid overload?

  • Pre-existing reduced EF (<35%) or clinical heart failure (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020)
  • Renal dysfunction (pre-op Cr >2.0, eGFR <30) — prolonged AKI post-op
  • Valve surgery (especially mitral repair) — higher sensitivity to volume
  • COPD or severe pulmonary disease — limited pulmonary reserve; even mild edema causes symptoms
  • Obesity — increased fluid requirements, greater capillary leak
  • Diabetes — diastolic dysfunction, higher AKI risk
  • Age >75 — impaired renal compensation, lower cardiac reserve
  • Prolonged CPB time (>180 min) — greater inflammatory response, larger capillary leak
  • Complex surgery (redo, multiple valve, arch) — longer cross-clamp time, deeper hypothermia

Post-op factors predicting fluid intolerance:

  • Low cardiac output post-op (systolic BP <100, lactate >2, low UOP) — triggers over-aggressive resuscitation
  • Inotrope requirement post-op — suggests poor contractility; fluid-sensitive
  • TEE findings of RV or LV dysfunction immediately post-CPB
  • Persistent metabolic acidosis on POD 1 — microvascular dysfunction, tissue hypoperfusion
  • Slow recovery of sinus rhythm — prolonged post-op AF increases atrial filling pressures

sections.heading: 7.2 Diuretic mechanism and selection
sections.bodyHtml:
Loop diuretics (first-line for post-operative pulmonary edema):

Drug Mechanism Dosing (IV) Key Notes
Furosemide Blocks Na/K/2Cl reuptake in thick ascending limb; powerful natriuretic 20–40 mg bolus; 5–20 mg/hr drip if continuous Standard choice; high-ceiling; ototoxicity risk at high doses
Torsemide More potent than furosemide; longer half-life; better oral bioavailability 10–20 mg bolus; 5–10 mg/hr drip Preferred by some for chronic HF; more predictable PO absorption
Bumetanide Similar to furosemide; 40× more potent on a mg basis 0.5–1 mg bolus Alternative if allergy; rarely used IV post-op

Aldosterone antagonists (adjunctive, slower onset):

Drug Mechanism Dosing (PO) Key Notes
Spironolactone Blocks aldosterone → reduces distal Na reabsorption; K-sparing 12.5–25 mg daily Delays K excretion; monitor K⁺ closely; takes 2–3 days for effect; reserve for POD 3–5+
Eplerenone Aldosterone antagonist; fewer endocrine side effects 25–50 mg daily Newer; less post-op data

IV → PO diuretic conversion: Furosemide 1 mg IV ≈ 2 mg PO (approximately 50% oral bioavailability). When transitioning stable patient: IV 40 mg → PO 80 mg furosemide once daily (or BID based on response).

Diuretic ladder for escalating fluid overload:

sections.heading: 7.3 Expected vs. pathologic post-operative fluid gain
sections.bodyHtml:
Expected fluid gain (days 0–3):

Finding Expected? Action
Weight gain 3–5 kg over POD 0–3 Yes — normal CPB capillary leak Monitor; reassess daily; no action if asymptomatic
Mild peripheral edema (hands, feet, presacral) Yes — interstitial fluid shift Monitor; elevate extremities; no diuretic needed if asymptomatic
Mild crackles (lower lobes only, improve with position change) Yes — dependent atelectasis + edema Monitor; position changes; gentle diuresis if weight gain >2 lb/day
SpO₂ 94–97% on room air or low O₂ Yes — normal post-op reduced FRC Monitor; supplemental O₂ PRN; no diuretic unless trending down

Pathologic findings (warrant intervention):

Finding Severity Action
Bilateral crackles mid-lung or higher Moderate IV diuretic; fluid/Na restriction; reassess q2–4h
SpO₂ <92% on room air or requiring escalation Moderate IV diuretic; O₂ support; notify APP
Orthopnea (unable to sleep flat) Moderate → severe IV diuretic; HOB elevation; urgent APP notification
Weight gain >2 lb in 24 hours Moderate IV diuretic; fluid/Na restriction; electrolyte panel
Respiratory distress, RR >28, pink frothy sputum Severe STAT escalation; high-flow O₂/BiPAP; IV furosemide 40–80 mg; ICU consideration
Hypoxemia (SpO₂ <88%) despite O₂ + BiPAP Severe STAT CVICU transfer; continuous diuretic infusion; possible mechanical ventilation

sections.heading: 7.4 Diuretic response and resistance
sections.bodyHtml:
Normal diuretic response:

  • Urine output 150–300 mL/hr within 15–30 min of IV furosemide bolus
  • Weight loss 0.5–1.5 kg/day during active diuresis phase (POD 2–5)
  • Improving crackles, SpO₂ trending upward, patient more comfortable

Diuretic resistance (minimal UOP despite adequate dose):

Mechanisms and workup:

  • Acute kidney injury (AKI): Cr rising, oliguria despite adequate CPP. Check fractional excretion of sodium (FENa), urinary osmolality. If FENa <1% = prerenal (optimize perfusion); if >2% = intrinsic renal damage (minimize nephrotoxins, consider CRRT).
  • Hypoalbuminemia: Low albumin (<2.5 g/dL) reduces oncotic pressure and diuretic delivery to proximal tubule. Check serum albumin; consider albumin 25% bolus if severely low.
  • Hypokalemia: K⁺ <3.5 impairs the Na/K/2Cl pump in the loop; cannot reabsorb sodium to excrete. Replace K⁺ first; then retry diuretic.
  • Hypomagnesemia: Mg²⁺ <1.5 impairs loop diuretic efficacy. Replace Mg²⁺ to goal ≥2.0; then retry loop diuretic.
  • Ongoing vasoplegic state (POD 0–1): Early post-CPB vasodilation + fluid shifts may reduce effective circulating volume despite total volume excess. Optimize perfusion (fluid bolus if hypotensive), then escalate diuretic as hemodynamics stabilize.
  • IABP or mechanical support: Check if patient is on inotropes or pressors; these may limit renal perfusion pressure despite adequate MAP.

Escalation for diuretic resistance:

  • Increase furosemide dose (40 mg → 80 mg IV bolus) or switch to continuous infusion (5–10 mg/hr titrated to UOP)
  • Add synergistic agent: thiazide 30 min before loop diuretic (hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg PO blocks proximal Na reabsorption; loop blocks distal — dual blockade)
  • Add metolazone (powerful; doses 2.5–5 mg PO daily, but monitor K⁺ and Mg²⁺ closely — severe hypokalemia risk)
  • Correct electrolytes first: restore K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0, and albumin if <2.0
  • Consider CVVHF ultrafiltration if diuretic-resistant with AKI (creatinine >2.0, rising); mechanical fluid removal bypasses diuretic response requirement (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020)

sections.heading: 7.5 Sodium restriction, dietary teaching, and discharge planning
sections.bodyHtml:
Why sodium restriction matters:

  • Sodium is the primary driver of fluid retention (osmotic gradient pulls water). Fluid restriction alone is incomplete without sodium control.
  • Post-operative sodium reabsorption is enhanced by aldosterone activation from volume depletion triggers; patients are "Na-avid" post-op.
  • Long-term sodium restriction is the 50% of management that happens at home; sets up patient for success.

Sodium restriction targets:

  • Acute phase (POD 0–3): <2 g/day (strict); all meals unsalted, avoid processed foods
  • Transition phase (POD 4–7): <2.5 g/day; begin teaching about label reading, low-sodium substitutes
  • Discharge phase (POD 7+): <3 g/day for post-discharge, with written dietary counseling

Common hidden sodium sources:

  • Bread (1 slice = 150–300 mg Na)
  • Deli meats, bacon, sausage (1 oz = 300–500 mg)
  • Canned soups, broths (1 cup = 800–1200 mg)
  • Soy sauce, hot sauce (1 tsp = 300–1000 mg)
  • Cheese, processed cheese (1 oz = 150–300 mg)
  • Oral medications in sodium-containing formulations (some ACE inhibitors, other suspensions)

Patient/family teaching (discharge):

  • "Weigh yourself each morning after urinating, before breakfast. If you gain 2–3 lb in 2 days, or more than 5 lb in a week, call your cardiologist before you get short of breath. Early detection prevents ER visits."
  • "Read all food labels. 'No salt added' is not the same as 'low sodium.' Aim for <140 mg Na per serving."
  • "Choose fresh fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins. Avoid canned, processed, and fast foods."

sections.heading: 7.6 ACE/ARB and beta-blocker timing in post-operative fluid management
sections.bodyHtml:
ACE inhibitors and ARBs (renal-protective, aldosterone-reducing):

  • Start post-op if tolerated (BP ≥90 systolic, Cr stable or improving)
  • Beneficial in reduced-EF patients post-op (reduce aldosterone, improve diastolic function)
  • Do NOT withhold for mild diuresis; renal perfusion pressure is maintained by systemic BP, not by avoiding ACE-I

Beta-blockers (reduce sympathetic drive, improve diastolic function):

  • Often held pre-op for hemodynamic stability; resume once BP >90 systolic and stable
  • Beta-blockade improves fluid tolerance and reduces POAF incidence (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025)
  • Timing: resume by POD 1–2 if hemodynamically tolerated

Key principle: Do NOT hold ACE-I/ARB or beta-blockers during active diuresis. These agents improve long-term fluid tolerance and cardiac remodeling. Diuretics + afterload reduction + beta-blockade together optimize outcomes.

sections.heading: 7.7 Ultrafiltration and CRRT for refractory fluid overload
sections.bodyHtml:
Indications for ultrafiltration / CRRT:

  • Diuretic-resistant fluid overload (minimal UOP despite ≥2 IV diuretic boluses, or Cr >2.0 rising)
  • AKI with severe volume overload (acute respiratory failure from pulmonary edema + rising creatinine)
  • Cardiogenic pulmonary edema not responding to medical management after 6–12 hours
  • Need for continued feeding and medication delivery while managing severe congestion

Mechanism:

  • Continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVHF): passive ultrafiltration removes plasma water directly; net fluid removal 500–1000 mL/hr
  • Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT): CVVHF + dialysate allows simultaneous dialysis (solute removal) if AKI present
  • Advantage: removes intravascular fluid without relying on diuretic response or renal function

Requirements and logistics:

  • Central line (femoral or internal jugular)
  • CVICU-level monitoring and 24/7 technician availability
  • Anticoagulation (regional citrate preferred to avoid systemic heparin if post-op bleeding risk)
  • Nursing familiarity with CRRT circuit management

Initiation: Discuss with CT surgery + cardiology + CVICU. CRRT can be initiated emergently for acute respiratory failure from pulmonary edema.

sections.heading: 7.8 Special considerations: HFrEF vs HFpEF diuretic response patterns
sections.bodyHtml:
HFrEF (ejection fraction <40%) post-op:

  • Fluid-sensitive; aggressive diuresis is generally safe if BP maintained
  • Respond well to loop diuretics + ACE-I/ARB + beta-blockers
  • Often benefit from afterload reduction (vasodilators, ACE-I) simultaneously with diuresis
  • Target: euvolemia; avoid over-diuresis (Cr rising, prerenal azotemia)

HFpEF (ejection fraction ≥50%) post-op:

  • Diastolic dysfunction; filling pressures are high even with normal EF
  • More dependent on rate control and diastolic relaxation than on diuresis alone
  • Often require gentler diuresis (risk: hypovolemia → reduced diastolic filling → worsening diastolic function)
  • Target: light euvolemia; avoid aggressive diuresis

Key principle: Check pre-operative EF. HFrEF patients tolerate more diuresis; HFpEF patients need gentler approach with emphasis on rate control, beta-blockers, and aldosterone antagonists.

sections.heading: 7.9 Complications of aggressive diuresis
sections.bodyHtml:
Acute kidney injury (prerenal azotemia from over-diuresis):

  • Over-diuresis → hypovolemia → reduced glomerular filtration pressure → Cr rises, UOP drops despite loop diuretic
  • Prevention: monitor BP, UOP, and Cr trends; hold diuretics if SBP <90 or UOP <50 mL/hr
  • Management: NS bolus 250–500 mL, reassess Cr in 6–12 hours

Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia:

  • Loop diuretics waste K⁺ and Mg²⁺; hypokalemia (K⁺ <3.0) and hypomagnesemia (Mg²⁺ <1.5) cause arrhythmias
  • Prevention: check electrolytes q6–12h during active diuresis; replace proactively
  • Management: KCl 20–40 mEq IV or PO q6h if K⁺ 3.0–4.0; aggressive replacement if <3.0

Hypotension and cardiogenic shock:

  • Over-diuresis in the setting of poor contractility → underfilling → hypotension, reduced cardiac output, shock
  • Prevention: monitor BP continuously; hold or reduce diuretic if SBP trending <90
  • Management: stop diuretic, NS bolus, add inotrope (dobutamine, milrinone) if needed; notify team

Metabolic alkalosis:

  • Loop diuretics waste Cl⁻ (chloride); hypochloremia → metabolic alkalosis (paradoxical alkalemia despite volume depletion)
  • Alkalosis paradoxically impairs diuresis (kidney reabsorbs Na with HCO₃⁻ to maintain electroneutrality)
  • Prevention: use balanced crystalloids (LR, Plasma-Lyte) for boluses; monitor Cl⁻ and pH
  • Management: if pH >7.45 and Cl⁻ <100, give normal saline 250–500 mL

Digoxin and arrhythmia risk during diuresis:

  • Hypokalemia + digoxin → increased arrhythmia risk (digoxin toxicity threshold lowers as K⁺ drops)
  • Do NOT load digoxin during active diuresis unless K⁺ ≥4.0 and Mg²⁺ ≥2.0

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients on diuretics; if any show, re-escalate.

  • SpO₂ trending down despite O₂ escalation — may be progressing from mild pulmonary edema to acute respiratory failure
  • RR trending up to >28 — work of breathing increasing; hypoxemia driving tachypnea
  • Crackles progressing from lower-lobe dependent to mid-lung bilateral — edema worsening; pulmonary compromise increasing
  • New or increasing orthopnea — cannot lie flat; sleep interrupted; severe dyspnea developing
  • Frothy or pink-tinged sputum appearing — classic sign of acute pulmonary edema; medical emergency
  • Patient becoming restless, anxious, or confused — hypoxemia-induced altered mental status; decompensation
  • BP trending down while on diuretics — over-diuresis or cardiogenic shock; reduce diuretic rate or add inotrope
  • Urine output dropping to <50 mL/hr despite IV diuretic — diuretic resistance or acute worsening of renal function
  • New arrhythmia or rapid ventricular response — hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia from diuresis; check labs STAT
  • Lactate rising or remaining elevated — tissue perfusion failing; may need ICU-level support
  • Peripheral cyanosis, cool extremities — end-organ hypoperfusion; cardiogenic shock
  • JVD worsening or new hepatojugular reflex — right-sided congestion increasing
  • Rapid weight gain continuing despite diuretics — inadequate diuretic response or ongoing over-resuscitation
  • New focal wheezing or asymmetric breath sounds — consider aspiration, pneumothorax, or superimposed pneumonia

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Post-CPB edema is expected — don't treat routine asymptomatic POD 1–2 edema. The first 48–72 hours of mild edema, weight gain 1–2 lb, and even minimal crackles are normal recovery. Symptomatic crackles, SpO₂ drop, or orthopnea are the triggers to diurese. Know the difference between "the patient is wet" and "the patient is symptomatic from being wet."

  2. Weight is a more sensitive early warning than crackles. Crackles are a late finding. A patient with 2-lb overnight weight gain may have minimal crackles yet be at high risk for pulmonary edema development. Weigh daily at the same time and scale (post-void). Trend is everything.

  3. Orthopnea means "sleep with head up." Ask directly: "Can you lie flat on one pillow, or do you need 2–3 pillows or a chair?" Orthopnea is an urgent sign of pulmonary edema; do not accept vague patient reports of "sleeping OK."

  4. POD 3–5 is the usual "diuresis window" — expect natural weight loss 1–2 lb/day. As capillary leak resolves and fluid shifts back to intravascular space, patients naturally diurese. This is expected recovery, not over-diuresis. Don't hold diuretics in fear; continue them through this window.

  5. Diuresing a patient who is still vasoplegic (POD 0–1) = hypotension. If BP is borderline and fluid status is borderline, optimize perfusion pressure first (cautious NS bolus, start inotrope if indicated) before aggressive diuresis. Read the hemodynamic picture before diuretics.

  6. Chasing creatinine during diuresis may misread "dry-AKI" as true renal failure. In the post-op phase, a rising Cr during active diuresis may reflect prerenal azotemia (hypovolemia) not intrinsic AKI. Check Cr trend, UOP, and BP together. If Cr rises while diuresing, hold the diuretic and reassess volume status.

  7. Too-rapid diuresis → AKI + prerenal azotemia. If a patient loses >2 kg in 24 hours (or >4 kg in 48 hours), you've pulled too much volume. Result: Cr rises, UOP drops, hypotension. Slow the diuretic rate, give NS bolus, reassess.

  8. Thiazide dosing for synergy: give 30 minutes BEFORE the loop diuretic. Thiazide blocks proximal Na reabsorption; loop blocks distal. The sequential blockade is more effective than either alone. Timing matters.

  9. IV-to-PO diuretic conversion done too fast may rebound. Furosemide PO has ~50% bioavailability; when converting from IV, the PO dose must be doubled. Convert too early or with insufficient dose → diuresis stops → fluid reaccumulation. Verify conversion orders.

  10. "Tea-and-toast" sodium restriction is the teaching cliché — and it's inadequate. "Tea and toast" implies unsalted diet, but many breads and even some "unsalted" items contain Na. Teach label-reading: anything >140 mg Na per serving is moderate-sodium. Patient education before discharge prevents post-discharge readmission for HF.

  11. Digoxin loading during active diuresis with low K⁺ = torsades risk. If K⁺ <4.0, do NOT load digoxin. Correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺ first, then load if indicated. Hypokalemia lowers the digoxin toxicity threshold dramatically.

  12. Metolazone is powerful and requires K⁺/Mg²⁺ monitoring. Metolazone (2.5–5 mg PO daily) synergizes with loop diuretics for refractory edema, but causes severe hypokalemia. Check electrolytes q6h when on metolazone; replacement is mandatory.

  13. Tamponade mimics volume overload — diuretics make it WORSE. JVD + muffled heart sounds + narrow pulse pressure + hypotension + crackles = think tamponade.

    Do NOT diurese. Confirm with echo (pericardial effusion with diastolic collapse) and notify CT surgery immediately for possible bedside drainage.

  14. RV failure: peripheral > pulmonary edema (opposite of LV failure). If a patient has marked peripheral edema and ascites but clear lungs, think RV failure. RV is "upstream" of lungs; fluid backs up into systemic venous system → liver, belly, legs. Diuretics alone don't help much; inotropes + pulmonary vasodilators are needed more than diuretics.

  15. TACO during transfusion — slow the transfusion + diuretics, not more fluids. If acute respiratory distress develops during rapid PRBC transfusion (especially POD 1–2 when anemic), consider TACO. Stop or slow the transfusion, give IV furosemide, sit patient up. Resolves in 1–2 hours if caught. Failure to recognize = continued transfusion + worsening respiratory failure.

cards.title: Frank-Starling Mechanism
cards.quickAnswer: The Frank-Starling curve describes how ventricular stroke volume changes with end-diastolic volume (preload): on the ascending limb, more filling increases cardiac output; on a flat or descending limb, additional volume doesn't help or worsens output. The curve shifts down with contractility loss (HFrEF) or diastolic stiffness (HFpEF), and shifts up with inotropes. Core bedside question: does the patient lie on an ascending limb (give volume) or flat/descending limb (give inotrope, not volume)?
cards.quickAnswerHtml: The Frank-Starling curve describes how ventricular stroke volume changes with end-diastolic volume (preload): on the ascending limb, more filling increases cardiac output; on a flat or descending limb, additional volume doesn't help or worsens output. The curve shifts down with contractility loss (HFrEF) or diastolic stiffness (HFpEF), and shifts up with inotropes. Core bedside question: does the patient lie on an ascending limb (give volume) or flat/descending limb (give inotrope, not volume)?
cards.sourcePrecedence: Guyton → Hardin/Kaplow (2020) → Brown (2023) → Monnet et al. (2016) → Bojar (2020) → Michard et al. (2000)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
The Frank-Starling mechanism states that stroke volume increases with increased ventricular filling (preload), up to a physiologic limit. Mechanistically, increased sarcomere length (stretched myocardial fibers) optimizes overlap of actin and myosin filaments, increasing contractile force per beat. This principle underpins every fluid-responsiveness decision in cardiac critical care:

  • Ascending limb: patient is volume-responsive; additional preload increases cardiac output
  • Plateau / flat limb: patient is preload-insensitive; further filling produces little change
  • Descending limb: patient is over-filled; additional volume worsens output
  • Curve shifts: inotropes, contractility loss, diastolic stiffness, and chamber compliance all move the curve up, down, left, or right

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
The Frank-Starling relationship emerges from myocardial fiber mechanics. At the sarcomere level, myosin heads interact with actin filaments; optimal spacing (achieved by moderate stretch) maximizes cross-bridge formation and force generation. Beyond this optimum, sarcomeres over-stretch, myofilament overlap declines, and contractile force drops. Clinically, this translates to a curve with three regions: ascending (steep rise in stroke volume), plateau (shallow), and descending (actual decline in output).

The curve is not static—it shifts with changes in contractility (the load-independent ability to generate force). Catecholamines and inotropes shift the curve upward: the same preload now produces higher cardiac output. Conversely, myocardial dysfunction (HFrEF, stunning, beta-blockade, acidosis, hypothermia) shifts it downward: the same preload produces lower output. Diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF, restrictive cardiomyopathy, tamponade) shifts the curve rightward: higher end-diastolic volumes are needed to achieve the same stroke volume, and filling pressures rise steeply.

Mechanistic detail — sarcomere physiology At optimal sarcomere length (~2.2 micrometers), actin and myosin filaments overlap maximally, creating the most cross-bridges. The overlap zone is defined by:
  • Myosin thick filament length: ~1.6 micrometers
  • Actin thin filament length: ~1.0 micrometer per side When the ventricle stretches (increased EDV), sarcomeres lengthen, and filament overlap is maintained near-optimal up to ~2.4 micrometers. Beyond that, overlap declines and force drops (descending limb). Pathologic scenarios:
  • Acute HFrEF: The ventricle dilates acutely; sarcomeres are already over-stretched on admission, so the patient sits on the descending limb from day one. Additional volume worsens output.
  • Septal myectomy, post-op acute: Fresh surgical trauma and edema reduce compliance; the ventricle becomes stiff, requiring higher pressures to achieve filling (rightward shift). Preload is critical, but filling pressures are elevated.
  • Constrictive pericarditis / tamponade: Pericardial restriction prevents ventricular filling; the curve is severely right-shifted. Output is low even at high pressures; pericardiocentesis is definitive.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context — Preload, Afterload, and Contractility
sections.bodyHtml:
Three independent determinants govern cardiac output:

Determinant Definition Role in Frank-Starling Clinical Handle
Preload End-diastolic volume (ventricular filling) Defines position on the x-axis of the curve IV volume, diuretics, vasodilators (afterload-reducing)
Contractility Intrinsic force-generating ability (load-independent) Shifts the curve up or down Inotropes, beta-blockers, myocardial dysfunction
Afterload Resistance the ventricle pumps against (MAP, SVR) Indirectly affects stroke volume via myocardial fiber length Vasopressors, vasodilators, mechanical support

On the ascending limb, stroke volume is preload-sensitive: volume in yields cardiac output out. On a flat or descending limb, the ventricle is preload-insensitive: volume in does not improve (and may worsen) cardiac output. The key distinction:

  • Fluid challenge: 250–500 mL IV bolus over 5–10 min
  • Cardiac output rises > 10% → ascending limb; patient is volume-responsive

  • Cardiac output unchanged or falls → flat/descending limb; patient is volume-unresponsive

  • Passive leg raise (PLR): Reverse-Trendelenburg or manual thigh compression to acutely preload 300–400 mL, non-invasively and reversibly

  • CO rise > 10% suggests volume responsiveness without committing to IV fluid
  • No rise suggests volume-unresponsive; omit volume challenge
  • Preferred in mechanically ventilated patients; predicts response to bolus better than static CVP

sections.heading: 4. Preload-Dependent States
sections.bodyHtml:
Certain cardiac conditions sit on steep, preload-sensitive curves. In these states, even modest volume loss worsens cardiac output, and aggressive diuresis risks hemodynamic collapse.

State Physiology Curve Position Management Implication
HCM (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) Hypertrophied LV, septal obstruction, afterload-sensitive Steep ascending limb; extremely preload-dependent Maintain preload (CVP 12–14); avoid diuretics, vasodilators, negative inotropes; small volume loss worsens LVOT obstruction
Septal myectomy (post-op acute, POD 0–2) Fresh surgical injury, edema, altered geometry Severely preload-dependent; rightward-shifted Full preload mandatory; fluid bolus BEFORE any inotrope; CI may recover over days as swelling resolves
Severe aortic stenosis (AS) Fixed orifice, high afterload, LV demand for preload Steep ascending limb; preload crucial for CO Full preload before diuresis; careful diuresis (risk of cliff drop in CO); low threshold for inotrope + diuretic strategy
Cardiac tamponade Pericardial fluid restricts filling Severely right-shifted; minimal CO at high pressures Preload-dependent but filling pressures high; pericardiocentesis definitive; fluid bolus temporizes
Acute RV infarction RV ischemia, poor contractility; RV is preload-sensitive in both directions Steep ascending AND descending limbs; narrow window Avoid diuretics (crash CO); maintain high RA pressure; nitrates/vasodilators contraindicated; inotrope + fluids
Acute HFrEF decompensation Dilated, failing LV, often on descending limb from admission Shifted down and rightward; descending limb dominant Diuresis is treatment (moves back up curve); inotrope + diuretic strategy; avoid pure volume

sections.heading: 5. Assessment — Common Fluid Responsiveness Scenarios
sections.bodyHtml: Recognize where the patient sits on the curve; gather information before acting.

sections.heading: Scenario 1: Post-Op Hypotension or Low Cardiac Index (CI)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Assess: JVD, CVP trend, lung exam (crackles vs clear), lactate, urine output
  • Hypovolemic picture (flat JVD, clear lungs, low CVP, high lactate) → ascending limb likely; try fluid challenge
  • Euvolemic/hypervolemic picture (elevated JVD, crackles, high CVP) → flat/descending limb likely; skip volume

sections.heading: Scenario 2: Preload-Dependent State Identified (HCM, AS, Myectomy)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Goal: maintain full preload at all times
  • CVP target 12–14 mmHg; avoid diuretics unless frank pulmonary edema
  • If hypotensive: fluid bolus FIRST; only if that fails, add inotrope

sections.heading: Scenario 3: Acute HFrEF with Pulmonary Edema and Low CO
sections.bodyHtml:
• Presentation: crackles, orthopnea, high CVP, SBP 90–100, CI low
  • Curve position: descending limb (over-filled)
  • Do NOT give volume bolus; start diuretic (furosemide) + low-dose inotrope (milrinone)

sections.heading: Scenario 4: Mechanically Ventilated Patient — Passive Leg Raise Test
sections.bodyHtml:
• Elevate legs to 45° (supine); measure CO/CI before and after 30–60 s
  • CO rise > 10% → volume-responsive; plan IV bolus
  • No rise → volume-unresponsive; omit volume, use inotrope

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Fluid responsiveness assessment informs escalation triggers.

SBAR template:

S: Patient is hypotensive (MAP < 65) or has low cardiac index (CI < 2.0) post-operatively or in the ICU setting.

B: [Detail preload-assessment findings: CVP, JVD, lung crackles, lactate, urine output; curve position estimate.] A: Fluid challenge attempted / passive leg raise test performed; patient is [volume-responsive / volume-unresponsive]; on [ascending / flat / descending] limb.

R: [If volume-responsive] Continue fluid resuscitation; [if volume-unresponsive] Initiate inotrope support (milrinone / dobutamine); consider vasopressor if MAP remains inadequate.

Who to call

Situation Contact
Hypotension with unclear fluid status; requires hemodynamic assessment Bedside intensivist / attending; cardiothoracic surgeon (if post-op)
Patient on descending limb with pulmonary edema + low CO; needs diuretic + inotrope strategy ICU team (if floor patient has deteriorated)
Suspected cardiac tamponade (severely right-shifted curve, elevated pressures, low CO despite fluids) Cardiac surgeon; cardiology; prepare for pericardiocentesis or OR

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers (expandable — novice + advanced beginner deep-dive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology detail — the full curve from stretch to dysfunction The Frank-Starling curve is best understood as a map of myocardial fiber mechanics across a range of sarcomere lengths:
  1. Ascending limb (ascending stretch): Sarcomeres lengthen from baseline to optimal (~2.2 micrometers). Filament overlap increases; cross-bridge density rises. Stroke volume climbs steeply.
  2. Plateau (optimal stretch): Sarcomeres sit at optimal overlap. Actin and myosin zones align; further modest stretch doesn't improve overlap. Stroke volume plateaus.
  3. Descending limb (over-stretch): Sarcomeres over-stretch beyond ~2.4 micrometers. Filament overlap declines; cross-bridges are lost. Stroke volume falls. Below-baseline shifts occur when contractility is reduced wholesale (HFrEF, stunning, beta-blockade, acidosis, hypothermia, sepsis). The same preload now produces less force. Right-shifted curves indicate reduced compliance (HFpEF, restrictive patterns, constrictive pericarditis, tamponade, acute RV infarction).
Drug class effects on the curve
Drug ClassMechanismCurve EffectClinical Use
Inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone)Beta-adrenergic (dobutamine) or phosphodiesterase inhibition (milrinone); increase intracellular calcium and myosin cross-bridge cyclingUpward shift; lusitropic (improved relaxation)HFrEF, cardiogenic shock, low CO states; milrinone preferred if hypertensive baseline
Beta-blockers (metoprolol, esmolol)Reduce sympathomimetic drive; decrease myocardial oxygen demandDownward shift; blunt CO reserveChronic HF, AFib rate control; caution in acute decompensation
Vasodilators (nitroprusside, nicardipine)Reduce afterload (SVR, MAP); ventricle pumps against less resistanceUpward effective CO by reducing impedance; also leftward shift if reduce preloadHypertensive crisis, afterload-dependent states (HCM, severe AS); caution in hypotensive HFrEF
Diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide)Reduce circulating volume; leftward shift along same curveMove patient leftward on curve toward lower preload; if on descending limb, moving left may move UP the curve, improving COPulmonary edema, volume overload; counterintuitive in HFrEF on descending limb
Fluid bolus (crystalloid, albumin)Increase EDV acutelyRightward shift along curve; if ascending limb → higher SV; if descending limb or plateau → no SV gain, worsened pulmonary edemaHypovolemia, volume-responsive states
Subgroup / edge cases — HFrEF, HFpEF, restrictive cardiomyopathy HFrEF (heart failure with reduced ejection fraction):
  • Dilated LV with poor contractility; curve is shifted down and to the right
  • Patient often sits on descending limb from admission (over-filled state)
  • Treatment: diuretic (move left on curve) + inotrope (upward shift) to improve both CO and pulmonary congestion
  • Counter-intuitive: low CO + pulmonary edema = diuresis is NOT the problem; it's part of the solution HFpEF (heart failure with preserved ejection fraction):
  • Stiff, hypertrophied LV with normal contractility; curve is severely right-shifted
  • Patient requires HIGH filling pressures to maintain adequate output
  • Problem: high pressures → pulmonary edema even without excessive volume
  • Treatment: inotropes are ineffective (contractility already preserved); focus on diuretics (accepting higher filling pressures) + rate control (longer diastolic fill time) + afterload reduction (better relaxation) Restrictive cardiomyopathy, amyloid, constrictive pericarditis:
  • Ventricle cannot relax normally; curve is extremely right-shifted
  • Filling pressures are elevated (CVP, PAWP); CO is low
  • Diuretics may worsen CO further; preload is critical but already at high pressures
  • Mechanical intervention (pericardiocentesis in tamponade; heart transplant in end-stage restrictive) is often needed
Controversies / recent evidence — SVV, PPV, and the limits of fluid responsiveness prediction Stroke volume variation (SVV) and pulse pressure variation (PPV):
  • SVV > 12% or PPV > 13% in mechanically ventilated patients correlates with positive fluid response (ascending limb)
  • SVV < 10% suggests plateau or descending limb (fluid-unresponsive)
  • Caveat: Only reliable in controlled ventilation; off with spontaneous breathing, arrhythmias, or low tidal volumes (< 8 mL/kg) Passive leg raise (PLR) utility:
  • Meta-analyses (Monnet et al., 2016; Cavallaro et al., 2010) show PLR sensitivity 66–81% and specificity 72–88% for predicting fluid responsiveness
  • Advantage: Non-invasive, reversible, bed-side; no need for arterial line or CI monitoring
  • Caveat: Requires reliable CO/CI measurement; less useful if patient cannot tolerate leg elevation or if baseline CO is already measured at head-up angle Fluid challenge protocol debates:
  • Traditional: 500 mL bolus over 5–10 min; reassess
  • Conservative: 250 mL bolus (smaller risk if descending limb) + reassess; repeat if needed
  • Lactate trend: Some advocate serial lactate measurement over CO/CI (more bed-side-friendly in non-invasive settings)
  • Bottom line: All methods correlate moderately; individual patient response matters more than the method

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
• Rising CVP with falling urine output and rising lactate. May signal transition from ascending to descending limb; worsening compliance. Stop fluids; add inotrope or diuretic.
  • Acute rise in respiratory rate, hypoxemia, or orthopnea despite adequate MAP. Sign of pulmonary edema from over-filling or worsening diastolic dysfunction. Patient may be descending limb; reassess curve position.
  • Hypotension unresponsive to fluid bolus (CI unchanged or fell). Confirms volume-unresponsiveness; curve is flat or descending. Immediate need for inotrope, not more fluids.
  • Acute fall in urine output to < 0.5 mL/kg/h despite fluid challenge. Suggests either (a) pre-renal azotemia from persistent hypoperfusion (inadequate inotrope), or (b) descending-limb state (over-filled kidneys). Reassess MAP, lactate, CVP trends.
  • New or worsening arrhythmia (SVT, AFib, PVCs) on inotropes. May signal catecholamine-induced irritability or electrolyte depletion (low K, low Mg from diuresis). Check EC; consider pulling back inotrope dose.
  • Sudden hypotension after inotrope weaning. Curve was being held up by drug; as inotrope dose falls, curve slides down. May need to re-hydrate preemptively or wean more slowly.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
• Frank-Starling reserves are NOT limitless. Post-operative and acutely inflamed patients can lose 500 mL to third-space in 2–4 h. That doesn't mean they're on an infinite ascending limb—reassess frequently.

  • CVP alone is NOT a fluid responsiveness test. A CVP of 8 does not guarantee ascending limb; CVP of 15 does not guarantee descending limb. Always pair CVP with cardiac output assessment (CI, blood pressure, lactate, urine output).

  • Preload-dependent states demand full preload at all times. HCM, myectomy, severe aortic stenosis: maintain CVP 12–14. "Normal" CVP of 8 may represent under-filling. Do not diurese aggressively.

  • Post-op acute HFrEF is often on descending limb. Stunned myocardium after long pump runs, high-dose inotropes, fluid resuscitation = pulmonary edema + low CO. Diuretic + inotrope is the right strategy, not more volume.

  • Passive leg raise is reversible; fluid challenge is not. Always perform PLR first in sedated, mechanically ventilated patients to predict response without committing 500 mL to a volume-unresponsive state.

  • SVV and PPV predict fluid responsiveness in mechanically ventilated patients. SVV > 12% or PPV > 13% suggests ascending limb; SVV < 10% suggests plateau or descending. Better predictors than CVP alone.

  • Fluid challenge 250–500 mL is the standard. More than that in a single bolus risks pushing a borderline patient from ascending to descending; less than 250 mL may not produce detectable CO change.

  • Inotropes shift the curve upward wholesale. A patient on milrinone or dobutamine tolerates lower preload (lower CVP) and still maintains CO. When weaning inotrope, watch for hypotension; may need to re-hydrate.

  • Decompensated HFrEF on descending limb: diuresis IS the treatment. Counter-intuitive: low CO + pulmonary edema = start diuretic + inotrope together. This moves the patient back up the curve (lower afterload, lower preload, improved contractility).

  • HFpEF is a right-shifted curve; filling pressures are high but contractility is preserved. These patients are stiff, not weak. Inotropes won't help (contractility is normal)—focus on diuretics, rate control, and afterload reduction. Accept higher CVP.

  • Contractility and preload both matter—one does not substitute for the other. A hypotensive patient with low CO needs BOTH adequate preload AND adequate inotropy. Do not assume inotrope alone will fix low CO from hypovolemia; you will crash their pressure further.

  • "Fluid refractory" pulmonary edema signals curve is flat or descending. Patient does not improve with diuresis alone; inotrope or vasopressor support is needed to shift curve upward and restore CO.

cards.title: GI Bleed (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: Hematemesis/melena/hematochezia/Hgb drop in post-cardiac patient → stat vitals (tachycardia, hypotension), 2 large-bore IVs, NPO, type & cross 2–4 units, IV PPI stat, STAT labs (CBC, coags, BMP, lactate), hold AC/antiplatelet pending team, GI consult for endoscopy within 24h. Unstable (SBP <90, shock, altered MS, massive bleed) → STAT call team, activate massive transfusion protocol, reverse anticoag: warfarin → PCC 25–50 u/kg + vitamin K; dabigatran → idarucizumab 5 g; Xa inhibitor → andexanet alfa 400 mg bolus + 4 mg/min infusion; ASA/clopidogrel → platelet transfusion. Critical post-cardiac pearl: mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion + rising lactate) is rare but >50% fatal if missed. Heyde syndrome (aortic stenosis + angiodysplasia): consider in older AS patients with lower GI bleed.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
