sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — what this is and who gets it.

  • Definition: Gastrointestinal hemorrhage (upper or lower) occurring in the post-operative period after cardiac surgery. Presentations range from occult blood loss (falling Hgb) to massive hemorrhage (hemodynamic shock).
  • Incidence: Post-cardiac GI bleeding occurs in ~2–4% of cardiac surgery patients (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020). Upper GI bleed (esophageal, gastric, duodenal) is ~3× more common than lower GI bleed (colonic, small bowel) in this population.
  • Peak timing: Post-operative day (POD) 1–3 due to stress ulcer formation and anticoagulation restart; can occur throughout hospital stay and post-discharge.
  • Who this applies to: every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient on anticoagulation, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), or prophylactic acid suppression. Highest yield: patients with recent CABG, valve replacement, or POAF requiring anticoagulation.
  • Why it matters: increases length of stay, requires urgent source control, and complicates anticoagulation decisions. Mesenteric ischemia as a subset is catastrophic if not recognized (>50% mortality).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Upper GI Bleed Mechanism (Esophageal, Gastric, Duodenal):

Stress ulceration and erosive gastritis are the most common post-operative upper bleeding sources. During cardiac surgery, cardiopulmonary bypass triggers splanchnic hypoperfusion, exacerbating gastric mucosal ischemia. Post-operative stress (surgical pain, inflammation, catecholamine surge, vasopressor use) increases gastric acid secretion and overwhelms mucosal healing. Restarting aspirin, clopidogrel (DAPT), or warfarin for mechanical valve or POAF compounds bleeding risk. Gastric acid suppression (proton pump inhibitor, PPI) is the cornerstone of prevention and acute treatment (American College of Gastroenterology, 2021).

Lower GI Bleed Mechanism (Small Bowel, Colonic):

Post-operative low cardiac output states (cardiogenic shock, sepsis, prolonged CPB) cause mesenteric hypoperfusion, leading to ischemic colitis (right colon most vulnerable). Diverticulosis, angiodysplasia (vascular malformations), and Heyde syndrome (aortic stenosis–associated angiodysplasia) are additional risk factors in post-cardiac patients, especially elderly. Mucosal ischemia → sloughing → bleeding; bacterial translocation → sepsis; full-thickness necrosis → perforation (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025).

Risk Factor Summary:

  • Stress ulcer: post-operative stress, aspiration risk, mechanical ventilation, renal failure, corticosteroids, NSAIDs, prior peptic ulcer disease
  • Post-cardiac bleeding: dual antiplatelet therapy (ASA + clopidogrel post-ACS), warfarin (mechanical valve, POAF with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2), newer anticoagulants (dabigatran, apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban)
  • Mesenteric ischemia: prolonged CPB, aortic cross-clamp, low cardiac output states, pre-existing vascular disease
  • Angiodysplasia risk (Heyde): age >65, aortic stenosis, borderline renal function

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Upper GI Bleeding presentations:

  • Hematemesis (bright red or coffee-ground emesis)
  • Melena (black, tarry stool from gastric acid conversion of hemoglobin to hematin)
  • Positive NG aspirate (blood or coffee-ground material)
  • Falling Hgb without obvious source

Lower GI Bleeding presentations:

  • Bright red per rectum (BRBPR) — suggests right colon or rectal source
  • Dark melena from right colon (blood oxidized by colonic bacteria)
  • Hgb drop with positive fecal occult blood
  • Diarrhea or loose stool (ischemic colitis pattern)

Hemodynamic warning signs (any of these → escalate):

  • Tachycardia (HR >110) out of proportion to pain or activity
  • Hypotension (SBP <90) or MAP <65
  • Orthostatic changes (lying → sitting/standing BP drop >20 mmHg systolic)
  • Altered mental status, confusion, lethargy
  • Pallor, diaphoresis, cool extremities (poor perfusion)
  • Persistent tachypnea (RR >25)

Lab signals:

  • Hgb drop ≥2 g/dL since baseline or last check
  • INR >5 on warfarin (elevated bleeding risk)
  • Platelets <50 K + active bleeding (transfusion trigger)
  • Rising lactate (marker of tissue hypoperfusion; mesenteric ischemia red flag)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic exam. Pure information-gathering; no actions yet.

  • Vital signs: HR, BP (sitting and standing if safe), RR, SpO₂, core temperature; repeat q15min in unstable patient
  • Perfusion markers: capillary refill, skin temperature (warm vs cool), mucous membrane moisture, urine output (trend over last 2–4h)
  • Bleeding source clues:
  • Inspect vomitus (bright red vs coffee-ground vs none) → upper bleed likelihood
  • Inspect stool (melena vs BRBPR vs normal) → upper vs lower
  • Rectal exam (if stable): hemorrhoids, fissures, masses, stool color/consistency
  • Any visible blood in urine catheter? (bleeding from urethra or bladder, rare but possible)
  • Abdominal exam: distension, tenderness (location, severity), rebound, rigidity, bowel sounds; pain out of proportion to exam is red flag for mesenteric ischemia
  • Symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain (severity, location, whether worsening), lightheadedness, chest or back pain
  • Recent labs: baseline Hgb pre-bleed, INR/PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, platelet count, BUN/Cr, lactate (if available; rising lactate = ischemia concern)
  • MAR & anticoag status: which AC or antiplatelet agents are on board? Warfarin + ASA + clopidogrel (DAPT)? DOAC? When were they restarted post-op?
  • Lines & access: A-line (continuous BP monitoring), central line, functional IV access (how many, size)
  • Surgery context: procedure type and date; time since surgery (hours vs days—POD affects bleed risk)
  • Comorbidities: prior ulcer disease, H. pylori status, NSAID use, cirrhosis/portal HTN, liver disease, renal failure, aortic stenosis (Heyde risk)

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP >65, HR 80–120, no shock, good perfusion)

  1. Call for assistance — do not manage alone; second RN for monitoring while you act
  2. Establish 2 large-bore IVs (18 G or larger) — obtain labs at insertion if possible
  3. Stat labs: CBC, CMP (BUN, Cr, electrolytes, glucose), coagulation panel (INR/PT, aPTT, fibrinogen), lactate, type & screen (T&C 2–4 units), troponin (rule out demand ischemia from anemia)
  4. Place NG tube (if upper bleed suspected) — gentle insertion, aspirate, irrigate with normal saline until return is clear; leave on low intermittent suction to decompress stomach (improves endoscopy access)
  5. NPO status immediately — prepare for possible endoscopy or IR intervention
  6. Initiate PPI therapy:
    • Pantoprazole 40 mg IV push stat, then q12h (standard post-op dosing), OR
    • Omeprazole 20–40 mg PO daily if tolerating PO (less common in acute bleed)
    • Rationale: high-dose PPI raises gastric pH, stabilizes clots, decreases rebleeding risk in peptic ulcer (American College of Gastroenterology, 2021)
    • Verify anticoag/antiplatelet status: document which agents on board, restart dates, current doses
    • Hold AC/antiplatelet agents pending provider discussion — do NOT restart without team input (balancing bleed vs thrombotic risk)
    • Perform full rectal exam (if not already done) — assess for hemorrhoids, fissures, masses, stool characteristics
    • Continuous monitoring: vitals q15min, strict I&Os (input + output), trend perfusion (capillary refill, skin temp, UOP)
    • Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (see §6) — request GI consult for endoscopy within 24h (sooner if any unstable features emerge)
    • Document carefully: time of onset, description of bleeding, VS at discovery, lab results, NG aspirate findings, interventions, patient tolerance

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Shock: SBP <90 or MAP <65, HR >110, altered mental status, active hemorrhage, transfusion requirement)

  1. STAT call APP + charge nurse + GI + IR + CT surgery + Blood Bank — do NOT delay for labs
  2. Activate Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP) if not already activated — criteria vary by institution; typically 2+ units PRBCs requested acutely
  3. Airway prep:
    • Elevate head-of-bed for upper bleed patient (assists work of breathing, may slow aspiration risk)
    • Position for airway access; have suction, airway equipment at bedside
    • Intubation considerations: massive hematemesis, unable to protect airway, RR >30 or SpO₂ <90% despite O₂, altered mental status, worsening consciousness
    • Do not delay resuscitation for intubation; coordinate with anesthesia/ICU per protocol
    • Large-bore IV access × 2 (18 G minimum), plus central line if not present (central access facilitates mass transfusion)
    • Aggressive resuscitation — target SBP ≥90, MAP ≥65:
    • PRBCs: type-O uncross-matched if type & screen not back; hang 2 units, reassess Hgb after each 2-unit increment
    • FFP (fresh frozen plasma): 10–15 mL/kg bolus if INR >1.5 or aPTT significantly prolonged; recheck coags q4h during active transfusion
    • Platelets: if count <50 K and active bleeding, transfuse to 50–100 K (higher if ongoing massive transfusion)
    • Ionized calcium (iCa⁺⁺): drops during massive transfusion (citrate anticoagulant binds Ca⁺⁺); check iCa⁺⁺ q2h, replace to goal >8.5 mg/dL with CaCl₂ (central line preferred) or calcium gluconate (peripheral)
    • Permissive hypotension (if no head/spinal trauma): maintain SBP 80–90 to minimize ongoing bleed, pending source control
    • Send stat labs: CBC, coags, BMP, lactate, fibrinogen, blood bank repeat crossmatch
    • GI + IR consultation immediately:
    • Upper bleed → endoscopy STAT: thermal coagulation, clips, epinephrine injection, band ligation (variceal)
    • Lower bleed → colonoscopy STAT (if hemodynamically permits) or IR angiography (if unstable; allows embolization)
    • Reverse anticoagulation per agent (see §7.2 detailed table):
    • Warfarin: PCC (Kcentra) 25–50 u/kg IV bolus + vitamin K 5–10 mg IV slow; check INR q4h
    • Dabigatran: idarucizumab 5 g IV (one dose, can repeat once if needed)
    • Apixaban/Edoxaban/Rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa 400 mg bolus, then 4 mg/min infusion (up to 2h)
    • Aspirin/Clopidogrel: platelet transfusion (1 unit raises count ~5–7 K); irreversible at enzyme level
    • Avoid aggressive crystalloid resuscitation until bleeding source identified — risks volume overload, dilution of clotting factors, worsening bleeding
    • Monitor for massive transfusion complications:
      • Hyperkalemia: cell lysis from transfused RBCs releases K⁺; watch for peaked T waves on EKG, arrhythmias
      • Hypothermia: massive transfusion cools patient; use blood warmer, active rewarming (blankets), target core temp ≥35.5°C
      • Coagulopathy worsening: dilutional or consumptive; request repeat coags + fibrinogen; consider DIC criteria
    • NG tube management in unstable upper bleed: place gently if not already in place (lavage may briefly activate clot, but decompression aids endoscopy access)
    • ICU transfer coordination — prepare for ICU admission after initial stabilization
    • Document: time of all calls, units transfused (pRBC, FFP, platelets, calcium), reversal agents given, hemodynamic response, ongoing output, labs before/after

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure, e.g., CABG]." B: "Patient has [hematemesis / melena / BRBPR / Hgb drop] starting at [time]. VS: HR [value], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. Baseline Hgb [value] → current [value]. On [list AC/antiplatelet agents + doses]. NG aspirate [positive/negative/clear]; stool [description]. Lactate [value], INR [value]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [List symptoms: pain, dizziness, mental status change]. Second RN present, IVs placed, labs pending, NPO status, continuous monitoring in place." R: "Requesting [GI consult + endoscopy within 24h / STAT GI + IR / orders for AC reversal / blood bank coordination / ICU bed and time frame]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Timing
Stable upper or lower GI bleed, first episode Primary APP / on-call fellow + GI Within 30 min
Unstable / active hemorrhage, shock APP/fellow + GI + IR + CT surgery + charge RN + Blood Bank + ICU STAT
Rebleeding after endoscopic hemostasis GI + IR (angiographic embolization) STAT
Mesenteric ischemia suspected (pain out of proportion + rising lactate) CT surgery + IR + general surgery STAT
AC reversal guidance needed (agent selection, dosing) APP/fellow + pharmacy STAT if unstable; routine if stable
Post-discharge GI bleed on DAPT/AC Emergency Department (may not return to original facility) Patient/family advised to call 911

sections.heading: 7.1 Upper vs Lower GI Bleed Differentiation
sections.bodyHtml:
Feature Upper GI Bleed Lower GI Bleed
Anatomic location Proximal to ligament of Treitz: esophagus, stomach, duodenum Distal to ligament of Treitz: jejunum, ileum, colon, rectum
Presentation Hematemesis (bright red or coffee-ground), melena (black tarry stool), positive NG aspirate BRBPR (often right colon), dark melena (slow right colon bleed), diarrhea (ischemic colitis)
Most common post-cardiac cause Stress ulcer / stress gastropathy (from CPB, post-op stress, restarted DAPT/AC) Ischemic colitis (mesenteric hypoperfusion), diverticulosis, angiodysplasia
Incidence ratio post-cardiac ~3× more common than lower ~1×
Diagnostic priority NG tube aspiration (diagnostic gold); endoscopy (definitive hemostasis) Colonoscopy (if stable) or IR angiography (if unstable); CTA abdomen if mesenteric ischemia suspected
Initial treatment IV PPI (high-dose), NPO, transfusion if Hgb <7, endoscopy within 24h (sooner if unstable) Supportive care, NPO, potential IR embolization; surgical consult if perforation/peritonitis
Red flag Ongoing hematemesis, rebleeding after initial hemostasis Pain out of proportion to exam findings (mesenteric ischemia), rising lactate

Why upper is more common post-cardiac: stress ulcer prophylaxis is selective but common; post-op acid suppression is routine. DAPT/AC restart increases risk.

Why lower can be more catastrophic: ischemic colitis and mesenteric ischemia carry >50% mortality if not recognized early; surgical resection may be needed.

sections.heading: 7.2 Stress Ulcer & Prophylaxis Strategy
sections.bodyHtml:
Stress Ulcer / Stress Gastropathy:

  • Definition: acute mucosal erosions in the proximal stomach triggered by severe physiologic stress (CPB, post-op pain, shock, mechanical ventilation)
  • Pathophysiology: ischemia + gastric acid + mucosal injury → superficial breaks; bacterial colonization + inflammation worsen bleeding risk
  • Incidence: historically 5–15% of untreated post-op patients; PPI prophylaxis has reduced symptomatic GI bleeding to ~1–2% (American College of Gastroenterology, 2021)

Stress Ulcer Prophylaxis — Current Practice:

  • Traditional: universal PPI for all post-op cardiac patients
  • Current evidence (2021–2025): selective PPI use based on risk factors is increasingly favored; universal PPI increases Clostridioides difficile risk and magnesium/calcium malabsorption
  • Selective use criteria: risk factors include age >65, anticoagulation on board, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, renal failure, prior ulcer disease
  • Recommended agents:
  • Pantoprazole 40 mg IV q12h (standard post-op; faster onset than PO)
  • Omeprazole 20–40 mg PO daily (if tolerating PO; less common acute phase)
  • Duration: typically 4–8 weeks post-op; taper if risk factors resolve
  • Note: [Institution policy] may specify local prophylaxis thresholds

sections.heading: 7.3 Assessment Tools: Glasgow-Blatchford & Rockall Scores
sections.bodyHtml:
Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS) — Pre-Endoscopy Risk Stratification (Upper GI Bleed):

  • Components: age, systolic BP, pulse, melena, syncope, hepatic disease, cardiac failure (each scored 0–4)
  • Score 0 → low risk (<5% mortality); candidate for outpatient endoscopy
  • Score >0 → higher risk; requires admission, transfusion if needed, urgent endoscopy
  • Limitation: designed for elective population; less reliable in acutely unstable or post-surgical patients (most post-cardiac bleeds warrant admission regardless)

Rockall Score (RS) — Post-Endoscopy Risk (Rebleeding & Mortality):

  • Calculated after endoscopy to guide admission/discharge and follow-up timing
  • Components: age, comorbidity, shock status, endoscopic findings (ulcer site, visible vessel, clot), therapy given (scored 0–3 each)
  • Score <3 → low risk (rebleed ~5%, mortality ~0%)
  • Score 3–8 → intermediate risk (rebleed ~10–20%, mortality ~5–10%)
  • Score >8 → high risk (rebleed >30%, mortality >10%)
  • Utility in post-cardiac setting: most post-cardiac bleeds warrant hospital admission; Rockall guides level of monitoring post-endoscopy and need for repeat procedure

sections.heading: 7.4 Post-Cardiac Bleed Risk Factors Table
sections.bodyHtml:
Risk Factor Relevance Mitigation
Dual antiplatelet therapy (ASA + clopidogrel) Very high bleeding risk; irreversible platelet inhibition Platelet transfusion if active bleed; do not restart without CT surgery + cardiology input
Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOAC) High risk; risk-benefit depends on indication (mechanical valve vs POAF) Selective reversal based on bleeding severity + indication; timing of restart individualized
Corticosteroids Increase stress ulcer risk Taper if possible post-op; continue PPI coverage if ongoing steroids
NSAIDs Direct gastric irritant; increase ulcer risk Avoid post-op; use acetaminophen or opioids for pain
Age >65 Physiologic stress response diminished; slower healing Assume higher bleed risk; lower threshold for transfusion
Prior peptic ulcer disease High recurrence risk post-op stress Continue PPI indefinitely; consider H. pylori eradication if positive
Renal failure Impairs platelet function; prolongs coagulopathy Closer coagulation monitoring; consider dialysis-related bleeding management

sections.heading: 7.5 Anticoagulation & Antiplatelet Reversal — Agent-Specific Approach
sections.bodyHtml:
Warfarin Reversal (Vitamin K1, PCC):

  • Time-sensitive: every hour delay increases both thrombotic and hemorrhagic risk
  • Agents:
    1. Vitamin K 5–10 mg IV slow infusion — corrects INR over 12–24h; give while awaiting PCC
    2. PCC (Prothrombin Complex Concentrate, e.g., Kcentra): 25–50 u/kg IV bolus
    3. INR 2–4: 25 u/kg
    4. INR 4–6: 35 u/kg
    5. INR >6: 50 u/kg
    6. Onset: minutes to hours; recheck INR 2–4h after; may repeat once if still elevated
    7. FFP 10–15 mL/kg — older method, less preferred (slow, large volume, further dilutes factors); reserve for PCC unavailability
    8. Goal INR: 1.5–2.0 (adequate for hemostasis without complete reversal)
    9. Thrombotic risk post-reversal: mechanical valve patients and recent stent patients must restart warfarin urgently; POAF with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥4 also high-risk for stroke if AC held >5 days

DOAC Reversal:

  • Dabigatran (direct thrombin inhibitor):
  • Idarucizumab (Praxbind) 5 g IV bolus — rapid, complete reversal within minutes; can repeat once
  • Preferred agent for life-threatening dabigatran bleed
  • Apixaban, Edoxaban, Rivaroxaban (Xa inhibitors):
  • Andexanet alfa (Ondexxya): 400 mg bolus over 15–30 min, then 4 mg/min continuous infusion (up to 2h or until hemostasis)
  • Note: high cost (~$10,000–20,000 per dose); verify availability with pharmacy
  • Alternative if andexanet unavailable: FFP + activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC, e.g., FEIBA)—less effective but option
  • Rationale: DOACs have shorter half-lives (12–24h) than warfarin; many stable bleeds manage with transfusion + source control without reversal. Reserve reversal for life-threatening bleed or urgent surgery.

Aspirin & Clopidogrel (DAPT — Irreversible Antiplatelet Agents):

  • Mechanism: ASA irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase; clopidogrel irreversibly blocks ADP P2Y12 receptor
  • Pharmaceutical reversal is NOT possible — effects last life of platelet (7–10 days)
  • Management:
  • Platelet transfusion: 1 unit per 5–10 K platelet deficit; transfuse to 50–100 K if actively bleeding
  • Goal: restore functional platelets to bypass antiplatelet effect
  • Timing: adjunctive to source control (endoscopy, IR); transfusion alone will not achieve hemostasis without source control
  • Caution: post-transfusion platelet increments may disappoint in septic or massively transfused patients (immune/non-immune platelet consumption)

Combined Anticoag + Antiplatelet (e.g., Warfarin + Aspirin + Clopidogrel for Mechanical Valve + Recent ACS):

  • Highest bleeding risk combination post-op; requires careful team coordination
  • Reversal priority: address most life-threatening agent first (typically warfarin with PCC); follow with platelet transfusion if DAPT component
  • Restart timing: never restart full DAPT without CT surgery + cardiology team input; risk of valve thrombosis vs ongoing bleeding must be weighed explicitly

sections.heading: 7.6 Transfusion Triggers & Coagulation Management
sections.bodyHtml:
Scenario Transfusion Trigger Target Notes
Stable GI bleed, no cardiac ischemia risk Hgb 7 g/dL 8–9 g/dL Restrictive strategy preferred to minimize volume overload
Active bleeding, ongoing transfusion requirement Hgb 8 g/dL 9–10 g/dL More aggressive; aim for better oxygen-carrying capacity
Massive transfusion (>10 units pRBC in 24h) Transfuse fresh frozen plasma 1:1–1.5 ratio with pRBC INR <1.5, aPTT <1.5× control Prevent dilutional coagulopathy; check coags q4h
Thrombocytopenia + active bleed Platelet <50 K 50–100 K (higher if massive bleed) Avoid over-transfusion (immune refractoriness); use HPA-matched if immune-alloimmunized
Ionized hypocalcemia during massive transfusion iCa⁺⁺ <8.5 mg/dL >8.5 mg/dL Citrate anticoagulant in pRBC/FFP binds Ca⁺⁺; recheck q2h
Fibrinogen depletion Fibrinogen <1.5 g/L during active transfusion 1.5–2.5 g/L Request fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate (10 units raises fibrinogen ~50 mg/dL)

sections.heading: 7.7 Mesenteric Ischemia — The Silent Killer
sections.bodyHtml:
Why it matters: Mesenteric ischemia is rare (~1% of post-cardiac patients) but catastrophic (mortality >50% if not recognized within 24–48 hours). It can masquerade as routine GI bleeding when the patient presents with hemodynamic instability and melena.

Mechanism post-cardiac: Prolonged CPB, aortic cross-clamp, or severe post-operative low-output state (cardiogenic shock, sepsis) compromise mesenteric perfusion. Small bowel and right colon are most vulnerable. Ischemia → mucosal sloughing (bleeding) → bacterial translocation (sepsis) → full-thickness necrosis (perforation, peritonitis, death).

Red flag: Pain out of proportion to exam findings.

  • Patient has mild abdominal tenderness on exam but reports severe, escalating cramping pain
  • Classic phrase: "the pain is terrible, but the belly is benign"—until mesenteric ischemia is proven otherwise

Other concerning signs:

  • Rising lactate (serial measurements more sensitive than single draw) — indicates tissue hypoperfusion
  • Diarrhea or loose stool (not constipation)
  • Persistent tachycardia despite resuscitation
  • Abdominal distension, ileus
  • Rectal exam: hemorrhagic mucosa, frank blood

Diagnosis:

  • Lactate trending: check serially q2–4h; rising lactate + pain = strong suspicion for ischemia
  • CT angiography (CTA) abdomen: imaging of choice if hemodynamically stable (shows arterial cut-off, bowel wall thickening, free fluid)
  • Endoscopy: upper scope may be done for "GI bleed" but reveals no source—suspect lower/mesenteric ischemia
  • Colonoscopy: visualizes ischemic colitis (pale mucosa, patchy ulceration, "thumbprint" edema); does not rule out small bowel ischemia

Management:

  • NPO immediately — rest gut
  • Notify CT surgery + IR immediately — time is critical
  • IR angiography ± intervention: if arteries patent but hypoperfused, consider vasodilators (papaverine) or thrombectomy
  • Surgical exploration: if imaging shows segmental necrosis or perforation, bowel resection is necessary
  • Supportive care: aggressive resuscitation (pressors if needed to maintain MAP >80), broad-spectrum antibiotics (translocation coverage), ICU monitoring
  • Timing is critical: delay >6–12 hours from recognition substantially worsens outcome

Post-cardiac pearl: If patient post-CABG or valve surgery presents with Hgb drop + melena but endoscopy shows no upper source, mesenteric ischemia is high on the differential. Check lactate. Image abdomen. Do not assume lower GI bleed and discharge casually.

sections.heading: 7.8 Heyde Syndrome (Aortic Stenosis + Angiodysplasia)
sections.bodyHtml:
What it is: Heyde syndrome is the association between aortic stenosis (especially moderate-to-severe) and bleeding from intestinal angiodysplasia (vascular malformations). Post-operatively, after AVR, the condition typically resolves as stenosis is relieved (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).

Mechanism: Severe AS increases shear stress on blood vessels and alters von Willebrand factor (vWF) activity, promoting angiodysplasia formation and bleeding risk. Post-AVR (aortic valve replacement), hemodynamics normalize and vWF improves, usually resolving bleeding tendency.

Clinical recognition:

  • Older patient (age >65) with known moderate-to-severe AS presenting with lower GI bleed, often chronic or recurrent
  • May have been labeled as "unexplained GI bleed" pre-operatively
  • Post-op GI bleed in Heyde patient is unusual but can occur if valve replacement is recent (vWF recovery takes weeks) or if patient has other post-op GI triggers (stress ulcer, mesenteric ischemia)

Management:

  • If encountered pre-op (before valve surgery): supportive care, PPI, iron supplementation; address AS urgently
  • If encountered post-op (after AVR): often resolves spontaneously; manage conservatively (PPI, transfusion if needed); low threshold for endoscopy to rule out stress ulcer
  • Rebleeding post-op is uncommon if valve repair is successful; if recurrent, query compliance with acid suppression or consider other post-op bleed sources

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these in stable GI bleed patients; if any appear or worsen, re-escalate.

  • HR trending up despite stable BP — early compensation for ongoing blood loss; recheck Hgb urgently
  • BP trending down, especially orthostatic changes — active or ongoing bleeding; move toward unstable pathway
  • Hgb drop >1–2 g/dL since last check (interval 2–4h) — ongoing bleed; accelerate workup, consider transfusion
  • Change in output: increase in melena volume, new BRBPR, or coffee-ground emesis after period of "clearing" → rebleeding
  • Abdominal pain increasing or pain out of proportion to exam — RED FLAG for mesenteric ischemia; check lactate immediately
  • Lactate rising or persistently >2 mmol/L — tissue hypoperfusion; high concern for mesenteric ischemia or inadequate resuscitation
  • NG tube output increasing — ongoing gastric bleed; verify tube position, may need repeat imaging
  • Mental status changes: anxiety, confusion, somnolence — altered perfusion from blood loss or shock
  • Tachypnea (RR >25) — compensatory (blood loss) or pulmonary edema (over-transfusion)
  • Recurrent vomiting — aspiration risk; airway compromise risk
  • Fever — suggests translocation, ischemic bowel, or sepsis
  • Rebleeding after initial endoscopic hemostasis (within 48–72h) — high-risk scenario; urgent repeat endoscopy or IR intervention
  • Coagulopathy worsening despite transfusion — dilutional or consumptive coagulopathy; check coags + fibrinogen; consider DIC

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Hemoglobin is a LATE indicator of bleeding. A compensating patient can lose 15–20% of blood volume before Hgb drops 1 g. Trust vital signs and lactate first; trend Hgb serially, not as point-in-time.

  2. Upper vs lower GI bleed determines your entire workup. Hematemesis or coffee-ground emesis → upper bleed → NG tube + endoscopy. No hematemesis but melena/BRBPR → NG aspirate diagnostic; if positive → upper; if negative/bilious → likely lower.

  3. NG tube aspiration is diagnostic gold for upper bleed. Place gently (fragile post-op mucosa), aspirate, interpret: clear/bilious → lower; coffee-ground/blood → upper. Document return volume; coiled tube in esophagus gives falsely negative aspirate.

  4. Post-cardiac ischemic colitis is often missed. Patient had borderline cardiac output post-op, now diarrhea + Hgb drop.

    Assume ischemic colitis until proven otherwise. Colonoscopy shows pale, friable mucosa. Management is NPO, antibiotics, NG tube, serial lactate; surgery if perforation.

  5. Mesenteric ischemia mortality >50% if missed. Pain out of proportion to exam is the key phrase. Every post-cardiac Hgb drop + GI bleed + severe abdominal pain needs lactate measured q2–4h and CTA abdomen if stable enough. Rising lactate = surgical emergency.

  6. Anticoag reversal differs radically by agent. Do NOT use one strategy for all. Warfarin → PCC + vitamin K. Dabigatran → idarucizumab. Apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban → andexanet. ASA/clopidogrel → platelets (no pharmaceutical reversal). Know the agent before calling pharmacy.

  7. Platelet transfusion for DAPT-on-board bleeder. Patient on ASA + clopidogrel for recent ACS, now GI bleed. You cannot "un-inhibit" platelets pharmacologically. Transfuse to 50–100 K and rely on fresh donor platelet function.

  8. Ionized calcium (iCa⁺⁺) drops during massive transfusion. Citrate in PRBCs and FFP binds Ca⁺⁺. Watch for prolonged QT, peaked T waves, worse bleeding.

    Check iCa⁺⁺ q2h during active transfusion; replace to >8.5 mg/dL with CaCl₂ (central line) or calcium gluconate (peripheral).

  9. Warm the patient during massive transfusion. Cold blood + massive fluids → hypothermia → worsened coagulopathy. Use fluid warmer, active rewarming blankets. Target core temp ≥35.5°C.

  10. Avoid NG tube trauma. Post-cardiac patients have fragile mucosa. Insert gently, confirm placement (X-ray if uncertain), avoid aggressive suctioning. A perforation converts manageable bleed into surgical emergency.

  11. High-dose IV PPI in active bleed. Pantoprazole 40 mg IV q12h is standard; some use bolus + drip (80 mg bolus, 8 mg/h) to maintain pH >6. IV is superior to PO for acute hemostasis.

  12. Endoscopy timing: within 24h for stable, sooner for unstable. Current guidelines (American College of Gastroenterology, 2021) recommend 12–24h for stable, STAT for unstable. On the unit, GI consult will triage; escalate acuity in your communication if hemodynamically unstable.

  13. H. pylori testing during/after endoscopy. If stress ulcer diagnosed, test for H. pylori (urea breath test, serology, stool Ag, biopsy). If positive, eradicate post-discharge with triple/quadruple therapy to prevent recurrence.

  14. Ischemic hepatitis mimics acute liver injury. Post-cardiac shock + transient AST/ALT elevation >1000 + INR rise = ischemic hepatitis, not acute hepatitis. Bilirubin rises later. Reassess in 24–48h; ischemic pattern improves with resuscitation; true hepatitis worsens.

  15. Post-discharge GI bleed on DAPT/AC is common. Patient goes home on ASA + clopidogrel or warfarin, stops PPI prematurely, then bleeds 2–4 weeks post-discharge.

    Educate before discharge: "Coffee-ground vomit, black tarry stool, bright red blood → call 911, go to ED. Do NOT stop aspirin or blood thinner without talking to cardiologist." Document this teaching in discharge paperwork.

cards.title: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP)
cards.quickAnswer: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) = pneumonia ≥48 hours after admission. Ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) = HAP occurring ≥48 hours after intubation. Clinical diagnosis: new or worsening infiltrate on chest imaging + ≥2 of (fever >38°C, leukocytosis or left shift, purulent sputum, worsening hypoxia). Risk factors post-cardiac surgery: aspiration, atelectasis, prolonged intubation, reduced cough from sternotomy pain. Send sputum + blood cultures STAT, obtain CXR/CT, labs (CBC, CMP, lactate, procalcitonin). Empiric antibiotics within 1 hour: vancomycin (or linezolid) for MRSA + antipseudomonal beta-lactam (piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, or meropenem) per institutional antibiogram — escalate immediately if hypoxic (SpO₂ <90%), hypotensive, or in septic shock. De-escalate with culture results; typical duration 7 days (longer for MRSA/Pseudomonas or structural lung disease).

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, and relevance.

  • Definition: HAP = bacterial pneumonia developing ≥48 hours after hospital admission; VAP = HAP in a mechanically ventilated patient. Diagnosis requires new or progressive infiltrate on imaging + clinical evidence of infection (fever, purulent sputum, leukocytosis, hypoxemia).
  • Incidence: ~10–15% of post-cardiac surgery patients; peak incidence post-operative day (POD) 3–7. VAP risk depends on duration of mechanical ventilation.
  • Who this applies to: all post-operative adult cardiac surgery patients; highest-yield monitoring POD 0–10. Critically important for recently extubated and re-intubated patients.
  • Why it matters: mortality 20–30% even with appropriate antibiotics; increases length of stay and healthcare costs. Early recognition and source control (mobility, pulmonary toilet, pain management) substantially improve outcomes.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac surgery patients converge multiple pathophysiologic pressures that promote HAP:

  • Prolonged intubation — endotracheal tube bypasses upper airway defenses; microaspiration of contaminated secretions; biofilm formation on tube surface
  • Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) immunosuppression — complement activation, leukocyte sequestration, impaired cytokine response in first 3–7 days post-pump; reduced bacterial clearance
  • Atelectasis — reduced functional residual capacity from pain, sedation, immobility; hypoxemic lung regions are susceptible to bacterial colonization
  • Aspiration risk — delayed consciousness, dysphagia, supine positioning, impaired cough reflex from sternotomy pain and surgical nerve injury
  • Reduced cough effectiveness — sternotomy pain severely limits deep inspiration and cough strength; general deconditioning; weakened respiratory muscles
  • Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) — pre-existing or post-operative sleep fragmentation worsens airway patency and clearance

Cascade: aspiration/inhalation of contaminated secretions → bacterial proliferation (impaired mucociliary clearance) → inflammatory PMN infiltration → alveolar consolidation and V/Q mismatch → hypoxemia → sepsis and multi-organ failure if untreated.

Key insight: Many post-cardiac patients have transient atelectasis (collapsed lung segments from anesthesia, pain, immobility) that radiographically mimics HAP. Critical differentiator: atelectasis improves with mobilization + pain control + incentive spirometry over 24–48 hours WITHOUT antibiotics. HAP consolidates or worsens. Avoid reflexive antibiotic escalation in stable patients; attempt aggressive pulmonary toilet first.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following ≥48 hours post-admission, with special attention to POD 3–7 post-cardiac surgery:

Respiratory findings:

  • New or worsening infiltrate on CXR (lobar, segmental, or diffuse), not present 24 hours prior
  • Fever ≥38°C (or two readings ≥38.0°C within 1 hour apart) appearing ≥48 hours after admission
  • Change in sputum character: purulent (yellow, green, or blood-tinged) vs. prior clear or minimal secretions
  • Worsening SpO₂ or increasing O₂ requirement (FiO₂ or nasal cannula flow increase)
  • Tachypnea >22 breaths/min or dyspnea on exertion with reduced mobilization tolerance
  • Hemoptysis (rare; raises concern for aspiration with anaerobes or necrotizing infection)

Laboratory findings:

  • Leukocytosis >12,000 (or leukopenia <4,000) with left shift (bands); WBC change from prior
  • Elevated procalcitonin (if available; >0.5 ng/mL more specific for bacterial infection than CRP)

Post-cardiac surgery context (risk stratification):

  • Recent extubation (VAP risk if intubated; HAP risk if recently extubated but intubation history within 48h)
  • Prolonged intubation (>24 hours pre-op or immediate post-op)
  • Atelectasis on imaging or focal diminished breath sounds on exam
  • Aspiration risk: known dysphagia history, impaired swallow, delayed consciousness, supine positioning
  • OSA history: upper airway collapse predisposes to impaired clearance post-op
  • CPB duration ≥120 minutes (stronger immunosuppression signal)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic exam. Pure information gathering; no actions yet.

Vital signs and oxygenation:

  • Current HR, BP, RR, SpO₂, temperature with trend over past 12–24 hours
  • FiO₂ requirement (nasal cannula L/min, face mask %, non-rebreather %)
  • Work of breathing — accessory muscle use, ability to speak in full sentences, dyspnea on exertion
  • Mental status — alert, drowsy, confused, agitated, appropriate?

Respiratory exam:

  • Auscultation bilateral: crackles, consolidated breath sounds, diminished sounds (atelectasis?), wheeze
  • Sputum quality — color, thickness, volume produced per cough
  • Cough strength — strong productive vs. weak dry vs. splinted by pain
  • Chest wall stability — any sternotomy restrictions or pain limiting breathing/mobilization?

Recent imaging and oxygenation trajectory:

  • Most recent CXR date and findings: location of infiltrate (lobar? segmental? diffuse?), associated atelectasis, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion
  • Trend in SpO₂ and FiO₂ over 24–48 hours: stable, improving, worsening?
  • Prior intubation/extubation: when extubated? Any re-intubation attempts?

Recent labs (within 24 hours):

  • CBC: WBC count, differential (bands, segs), hemoglobin (anemia impairs immune response)
  • CMP: creatinine (renal clearance for drug dosing), glucose (hyperglycemia impairs immune response), electrolytes
  • Lactate if available; procalcitonin if drawn
  • Any prior sputum/blood culture results (pending or results already back?)

Antibiotic and respiratory support history:

  • Current O₂ mode and duration on current level
  • Chest tubes: location, output character (serosanguineous normal; turbid/foul-smelling concerning)
  • Recent antibiotics: names, start dates, duration (prior empiric coverage for this admission?)
  • Allergy history: penicillin, cephalosporin, vancomycin, fluoroquinolone hypersensitivity

Aspiration and swallow risk:

  • Formal swallow evaluation done? Any documented aspiration or dysphagia?
  • NPO status or diet restrictions
  • NG tube present? Placement verified recently?
  • Recent GI procedures or interventions

Immunocompromise and comorbidity:

  • Diabetes (pre-existing or stress hyperglycemia?)
  • COPD or prior lung disease
  • Chronic corticosteroid use (blunts fever; higher infection risk)
  • Renal failure (impaired drug clearance; impaired immune response)
  • Chemotherapy or transplant history

Surgery context:

  • Procedure type and POD: CABG, valve, aortic, combined; when performed?
  • Intra-op complications: prolonged CPB, massive transfusion, low cardiac output state, difficult intubation?
  • Acute decompensation concern: cardiogenic pulmonary edema vs. infectious pneumonia?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Patient alert, MAP ≥65, SpO₂ >90% on ≤2 L nasal cannula, no acute distress, perfusing adequately.)

Timing: All steps within 2–4 hours. Do not delay cultures and imaging.

  1. Recheck vital signs in 10–15 minutes — document fever, SpO₂, respiratory rate; establish baseline trajectory.

  2. Focused respiratory exam — bilateral auscultation, sputum character, work of breathing, cough strength; compare to prior shifts.

  3. STAT labs — do NOT delay:

    • Sputum gram stain + culture — send expectorated sputum, endotracheal aspirate (if intubated), or induced sputum. Quality criteria: ≥25 PMNs and <10 squamous epithelial cells/lpf indicate lower respiratory tract specimen (not saliva).
    • Blood cultures ×2 (one peripheral, one from central line if present) — draw before antibiotics; same timing.
    • CBC with differential — WBC count, bands, hemoglobin
    • CMP — creatinine, glucose, potassium, calcium
    • Lactate — if concerned for sepsis or worsening oxygenation
    • Procalcitonin — if available; helps guide duration decisions; trend more useful than single value
    • Arterial or venous blood gas — if SpO₂ borderline or RR >25; assess PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH

  4. Imaging STAT:

    • Portable CXR — compare to most recent prior exam; document new infiltrate location (RLL? LLL? bilateral?), air-bronchograms, associated pleural effusion, pulmonary edema pattern, atelectasis.
    • CT chest (if CXR unclear, high suspicion for HAP but infiltrate not obvious, or concern for abscess/empyema).

  5. Optimize oxygenation and position:

    • Head of bed ≥30° (higher if tolerated) — promotes secretion drainage, improves ventilation/perfusion matching
    • Oxygen support: nasal cannula or face mask as needed to target SpO₂ ≥92%; escalate to non-rebreather if SpO₂ <90% despite 2+ L
    • If atelectasis evident and patient stable: initiate aggressive pulmonary toilet (see step 7 below) before jumping to antibiotics; may resolve mobilization alone over 24–48h

  6. Empiric antibiotic initiation (per institutional antibiogram) — timing critical:

    • MRSA coverage: Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (target trough 15–20 mcg/mL) OR Linezolid 600 mg IV q12h
    • PLUS Pseudomonas/gram-negative coverage (choose one):

    • Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6h (broadest; covers ESBL, anaerobes), OR
    • Cefepime 2 g IV q8h (Pseudomonas + gram-negative; no anaerobic coverage), OR
    • Meropenem 1 g IV q8h (carbapenem; broadest; use if ESBL or high-resistance suspected)
    • Adjunctive consideration: add aminoglycoside (gentamicin or tobramycin, renally dosed) or fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg IV q24h) if:
    • High MDR risk (recent prior antibiotics within 90 days, ICU stay ≥5 days, hemodynamic instability)
    • Gram stain shows gram-negative rods suspicious for Pseudomonas mono-microbial infection
    • Document: exact time infusion started (crucial for infection timeline and duration calculation)

  7. Aggressive pulmonary toilet (if stable and atelectasis suspected):

    • Incentive spirometry: goal 10 breaths q2h while awake; target volume ≥1500 mL (post-cardiac baseline is lower but attainable)
    • Splinted coughing: teach patient to hug pillow over sternum to reduce sternotomy pain during cough
    • Assisted cough or chest percussion if weak or unable to generate pressure
    • Mobilization: chair transfer, ambulation if able (best "incentive spirometer" is walking); escalate gradually per tolerance
    • If intubated or recently extubated with weak cough: deep suctioning, consider manual hyperinflation (if RN certified)

  8. Notify provider team — use SBAR format (see Section 6):

    • APP, on-call fellow, or hospitalist
    • Emphasize: new infiltrate + fever + cultures sent
    • Request empiric antibiotic authorization

  9. Address reversible triggers:

    • Pain control: adequate IV acetaminophen + opioid PRN (not oversedation); improves cough and mobilization
    • Reduce sedation: minimize unnecessary sedating medications if patient alert; monitor for delirium (impairs cough, swallow)
    • Nutrition: ensure adequate protein intake; monitor for dysphagia
    • Glycemic control: target 140–180 mg/dL post-op; tight glucose improves immune clearance

  10. Monitoring and reassessment (q4–6h initially):

    • Recheck CXR in 48–72h if clinically improving (confirm infiltrate resolution); sooner if worsening
    • Reassess sputum, SpO₂, temperature, mental status q4h
    • Recheck lactate q4–6h if elevated; trend is more informative than single value
    • Sputum gram stain results usually within 1–2h; culture results 24–48h
    • If worsening at 48–72h → re-escalate to 5B path

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(SpO₂ <90% on 2+ L O₂, altered mental status, hemodynamic instability [MAP <65, lactate >4], or rapid deterioration.)

Timing: Urgent escalation. All steps within 1 hour.

  1. STAT activation — do NOT leave the room:

    • Call APP/fellow + charge RN immediately
    • Activate Rapid Response Team (RRT) — concern for respiratory failure or sepsis
    • Notify surgery team (if recent post-op; rule out surgical complications)
    • Notify ICU — likely admission needed

  2. Oxygen support escalation:

    • Target SpO₂ ≥94%
    • If SpO₂ not improving on 4–6 L nasal cannula or simple face mask → non-rebreather mask (up to 15 L FiO₂)
    • If SpO₂ still <90% or rising RR/work of breathing → consider non-invasive ventilation (CPAP 5–10 cm H₂O, BiPAP) or prepare for re-intubation
    • If re-intubation needed: notify anesthesia; request subglottic suction endotracheal tube for post-intubation VAP prevention

  3. STAT labs and blood gas:

    • Sputum + blood cultures ×2 STAT (if not already sent)
    • Arterial blood gas STAT — assess PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH; hypercarbia indicates tiring/impending failure
    • CBC, CMP, lactate STAT
    • Procalcitonin, CRP
    • Cardiac biomarkers (troponin, BNP) if concern for cardiogenic pulmonary edema vs. HAP

  4. Imaging STAT:

    • Portable CXR STAT — bilateral infiltrates, ARDS pattern, pulmonary edema, pneumothorax (post-op risk)
    • CT chest with contrast (if rapid deterioration and CXR unclear; assess for abscess, empyema, pneumothorax, PE)

  5. Broad-spectrum antibiotic initiation (escalate empirically if high MDR suspicion): - Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV + Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV (or Meropenem 1 g IV) + consider aminoglycoside/fluoroquinolone

    • If fungal concern (prolonged ICU, prior azole exposure, immunocompromised): add Fluconazole 400 mg IV q12h or Micafungin 100 mg IV q24h
    • Document time antibiotics started

  6. Hemodynamic support (if septic shock: MAP <65 or lactate >4):

    • Rapid assessment for sepsis criteria
    • IV access: two large-bore IVs if not already present
    • Crystalloid bolus: 30 mL/kg in first 3 hours; titrate in 500 mL aliquots (e.g., 70 kg → 2100 mL normal saline or Plasma-Lyte)
    • Vasopressor if MAP <65 despite fluid: initiate norepinephrine 0.05–0.1 mcg/kg/min, titrated to MAP ≥65
    • Repeat lactate in 2–4h — assess clearance (goal >10% per hour)

  7. Source control assessment:

    • Reassess sputum character and exam — any signs of aspiration (foul-smelling sputum, food particles)?
    • Consider complicating factors: abscess, parapneumonic effusion/empyema, airway obstruction (mucus plug, clot, secretion impaction)

  8. ICU transfer — arrange STAT transport:

    • Notify ICU of current lactate, oxygenation status, ventilatory support needed, antibiotic start time
    • Ensure continuity of cultures and antibiotic dosing during transport

  9. Reassess frequently:

    • SpO₂, RR, oxygenation q15–30 min while unstable
    • Recheck lactate in 2–4h (trend is critical)
    • If not improving by 6h → consider ICU-level bronchoscopy with lavage/biopsy for diagnostic workup

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for calling:

S: "Dr. [name], this is [RN name], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]."

B: "Patient developed fever [temperature] at [time], now with new infiltrate on CXR [location]. Productive cough with [color] sputum. SpO₂ [value] on [O₂ mode]. RR [value]. WBC [value]."

A: "Assessment: Suspected HAP/VAP. Patient is [stable/unstable]. [Perfusing? Hypoxemic?]. Lactate [value if available]. Sputum + blood cultures sent STAT."

R: "Requesting: Empiric antibiotic authorization (vancomycin + antipseudomonal beta-lactam per antibiogram). [ID consult if septic?]. [CT chest if imaging unclear?]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Rationale
New infiltrate + fever, hemodynamically stable Primary APP or on-call fellow Empiric antibiotic authorization; cultures pending
SpO₂ <90% on 2+ L O₂ or RR >25 APP/fellow + charge RN Respiratory failure risk; escalate to non-invasive or invasive ventilation
Septic shock (MAP <65, lactate >4) RRT + APP + ICU Emergent; sepsis hour-1 bundle activation
Aspiration suspected (foul sputum, food particles) APP Adjust antibiotic empiricism; consider different coverage
HAP not improving by 48–72h on appropriate antibiotics ID consult + APP Wrong organism, missed source, abscess, resistance; consider bronchoscopy
Bilateral infiltrates + pulmonary edema pattern APP + cardiology consult Rule out cardiogenic vs. infectious; BNP and echo helpful
Hemoptysis or necrotizing features APP + ICU Highest mortality; likely Pseudomonas or anaerobic necrotizing infection

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are collapsed by default in PowerApp.

HAP vs. VAP definitions and epidemiology

Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP): Pneumonia occurring ≥48 hours after hospital admission, not present at time of admission. Diagnosis requires imaging evidence (infiltrate) + clinical evidence (fever/leukocytosis/purulent sputum/hypoxia).

Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP): HAP occurring in a mechanically ventilated patient ≥48 hours after intubation. VAP is a subset of HAP with higher mortality and more resistant organisms.

Key distinction: Post-cardiac surgery patients may have HAP (recently extubated) or VAP (currently or recently intubated). Both require identical approach. Prevention bundle emphasis differs (subglottic suction more relevant for VAP).

Incidence and epidemiology: HAP affects ~10–15% of post-CABG patients; higher in valve/aortic surgery (~15–20%). VAP incidence is duration-dependent (rises with each day of mechanical ventilation). Peak HAP onset POD 3–7 reflects combined CPB immunosuppression nadir + fluid mobilization + bacterial proliferation timeline.

Mortality: 20–30% even with appropriate antibiotics; higher in elderly, immunocompromised, or septic-at-presentation cohorts.

Post-cardiac surgery risk factors and pathophysiology cascade Why cardiac surgery patients are high-risk:
  1. Cardiopulmonary bypass immunosuppression — complement cascade activation, leukocyte sequestration in lungs, impaired IL-6/TNF-α response. Maximal at POD 1–3, gradually recovering by POD 7.
  2. Aspiration risk — delayed consciousness from anesthesia, dysphagia from intubation/nerve injury, supine positioning, sedation
  3. Atelectasis — massive reduction in functional residual capacity from pain, sedation, immobility; hypoxemic lung regions are bacterial seeding grounds
  4. Reduced cough effectiveness — sternotomy incision limits deep inspiration (splinting from pain); reduced respiratory muscle strength post-op
  5. Prolonged intubation — especially if intra-op difficulties or post-op respiratory compromise; ETT bypasses upper airway defenses
  6. Recurrent intubation — extubated and re-intubated patients have compounded HAP/VAP risk Cascade to infection: aspiration of gastric/oropharyngeal flora → bacterial inoculation of lower airways → impaired mucociliary clearance (CPB, intubation, smoking history) → bacterial proliferation + biofilm formation on ETT (if intubated) → PMN-mediated inflammation → alveolar consolidation + V/Q mismatch → hypoxemia → sepsis cascade if untreated. Critical clinical pearl: Distinguish transient atelectasis (improves with mobilization) from HAP (consolidates or worsens). Both have infiltrates; HAP has fever + purulent sputum + worsening trajectory. Aggressive pulmonary toilet + mobilization for 24–48h may resolve atelectasis without antibiotics, avoiding unnecessary resistance emergence.
HAP microbiology and resistance patterns post-cardiac surgery Most common organisms (post-cardiac surgery, per Keck antibiogram — verify current local patterns):
OrganismFrequencyCoverageNotes
MSSA~20–30%Beta-lactams, cephalosporinsEarly HAP (POD 1–3); aspiration-associated. Sensible to empiric coverage.
MRSA~20–30%Vancomycin, linezolid, dalbavancinLater HAP (POD 4+); post-antibiotic exposure. Cephalosporins poor lung penetration.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa~15–25%Antipseudomonal beta-lactam, fluoroquinoloneMDR organism; ICU stay >5 days; prolonged intubation. Resistant to fluoroquinolones in 30–40%.
Klebsiella pneumoniae (often ESBL)~10–15%Carbapenem if ESBL; pip-tazoGram-negative; can be highly resistant.
E. coli~10–15%Cephalosporins, fluoroquinoloneEarly HAP; gram-negative enteric; usually sensible.
Enterobacter (ESBL+)~5–10%Carbapenem preferredMDR risk; ICU-associated.
Acinetobacter baumannii~5%Colistin, aminoglycosideRare on step-down (more ICU); highly resistant.
Stenotrophomonas maltophilia~3–5%TMP-SMX, fluoroquinoloneEmerging; carbapenem-resistant; prolonged antibiotics exposure.
Anaerobes~10–20% (if aspiration)Piperacillin-tazobactam, beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitorsAspiration pneumonia feature. IDSA 2016 de-emphasized routine anaerobic coverage — now only if strong aspiration clinical features (dysphagia, witnessed aspiration, foul-smelling sputum).
IDSA 2016 landmark change: Empiric anaerobic coverage (clindamycin, pip-tazo for anaerobes) is NO LONGER routinely recommended. Standard empiric (vancomycin + antipseudomonal beta-lactam) has equivalent outcomes without anaerobic coverage. Add anaerobic agents only if clinical suspicion of aspiration is strong. Post-cardiac surgery context: Most patients received pre-operative prophylactic cephalosporins (±vancomycin), satisfying "prior 90-day antibiotic exposure" MDR risk criterion. This pushes nearly all post-CABG/valve patients into the HIGH-risk category for empiric MRSA + Pseudomonas coverage.
Diagnostic approach — sputum quality, cultures, imaging, severity scoring Sputum gram stain and culture — most practical diagnostic tool:
  • Quality criteria: ≥25 polymorphonuclear leukocytes (PMNs) and <10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field (LPF) indicate lower respiratory specimen (not saliva contamination).
  • Poor-quality specimen: >10 epithelial cells/lpf or <25 PMNs — indicates saliva; do not report culture results; request new specimen.
  • Gram stain turn-around: 1–2 hours; guides initial therapy (gram-positive cocci → MSSA/MRSA coverage; gram-negative rods → Pseudomonas coverage).
  • Culture results: 24–48 hours; allows de-escalation once organism identified and sensibilities available. Blood cultures:
  • Positive in ~20–30% of HAP cases
  • NOT required for HAP diagnosis; positive culture = bacteremia = sepsis concern
  • If positive, identifies causative organism and guides de-escalation Chest imaging:
  • CXR: New or worsening infiltrate = part of HAP case definition. Location (lobar, segmental, diffuse), air-bronchograms, associated effusion, pulmonary edema all inform differential.
  • Atelectasis on CXR: linear opacities, volume loss, basilar distribution. Differentiator: improves with mobilization; HAP consolidates.
  • CT chest: Consider if CXR unclear, high suspicion but infiltrate not obvious, or concern for complications (abscess, empyema, pneumothorax). Supporting labs:
  • Procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL: higher specificity for bacterial infection than CRP alone; trend useful for duration decisions
  • Lactate >2–4: suggests tissue hypoperfusion (sepsis concern); recheck q4–6h; trend matters more than absolute value
  • CBC: WBC >12k with left shift more specific than elevated count alone (post-op elevation common); leukopenia <4k concerning CPIS score (Pugin; controversial but sometimes used for VAP prediction):
  • Temperature, leukocytes, sputum purulence, oxygenation, CXR infiltrate, culture data
  • CPIS >6 suggests VAP; <6 suggests non-infectious cause
  • Limitation: CPIS is subjective and inconsistently predictive; clinical judgment + culture results more reliable than score alone
  • Modern trend: move away from CPIS toward sputum culture interpretation + clinical response
Empiric antibiotic selection, dosing, and renal adjustment Core principle: Empiric therapy must cover MRSA + gram-negative (especially Pseudomonas) in nearly all post-cardiac surgery HAP cases (high MDR risk category per IDSA 2016). Standard empiric regimen (IDSA 2016 HAP/VAP guideline):
ComponentDrugDoseLung PenetrationNiche
MRSAVancomycin15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h (trough 15–20 mcg/mL)ModerateGold standard; requires TDM (therapeutic drug monitoring)
Linezolid600 mg IV q12hExcellentAlternative if vanc-intolerant; excellent lung penetration; may cause thrombocytopenia with prolonged use
Gram-negative/PseudomonasPiperacillin-tazobactam4.5 g IV q6hGoodBroadest spectrum; covers ESBL, anaerobes; good for complex/aspiration HAP
Cefepime2 g IV q8hGoodPseudomonas + gram-negative; no anaerobic coverage; less broad than pip-tazo
Meropenem1 g IV q8hExcellentCarbapenem; reserved for ESBL or high-resistance suspicion; broadest β-lactam coverage
Adjunctive (high-risk)Gentamicin7 mg/kg IV q24h (renally dosed)ModerateSynergy with β-lactam for Pseudomonas; monitor renal function; requires TDM
Levofloxacin750 mg IV q24hExcellentAlternative gram-negative/Pseudomonas if β-lactam allergy; fluoroquinolone resistance emerging in Pseudomonas
Typical combinations per IDSA 2016:
  • Standard empiric (most common): Vancomycin + Piperacillin-tazobactam
  • Alternative (β-lactam allergy): Linezolid + Cefepime
  • Severe/septic/MDR concern: Vancomycin + Meropenem (±aminoglycoside) When to add aminoglycoside or fluoroquinolone:
  • Septic shock (lactate >4, MAP <65)
  • Gram stain shows gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas concern)
  • Recent fluoroquinolone exposure (increased resistance risk)
  • High mortality risk (elderly, immunocompromised, high SOFA) Renal dosing (post-cardiac AKI common):
  • Adjust all above drugs if eGFR <60
  • Monitor creatinine daily
  • Vancomycin + aminoglycosides require TDM; coordinate with pharmacy Institutional antibiogram: Confirm current resistance patterns at your institution; tailor empiric if local epidemiology differs from national averages.
De-escalation strategy and duration of therapy De-escalation principle: Narrow antibiotics once culture + sensibilities available (24–48h). Goal is shortest effective course to reduce resistance emergence and adverse effects. Typical de-escalation scenarios:
Culture ResultDe-escalationRationale
MSSA onlyStop vanc; continue cephalosporin or β-lactam aloneUncomplicated MSSA HAP; narrower = less toxicity
MRSA, Pseudomonas sensible to cefepimeVanc + Cefepime; stop piperacillin-tazobactamNarrower than pip-tazo; adequate coverage
Pseudomonas, fluoroquinolone sensibleConsider levofloxacin monotherapyHigh lung penetration; oral step-down option; watch for resistance emergence
Multiple organisms, aspiration patternDe-escalate only if source controlled + sensibilities concordantLikely aspiration; cover each organism sensibly
No organism isolated, clinically improvingContinue empiric 7–10 days; reassess at day 5Empiric coverage sufficient; cultures may be contaminant or culture not yet positive
Duration of therapy:
ScenarioDurationRationale
Simple HAP (MSSA, rapid defervescence, infiltrate resolving)~7 daysIDSA 2016 standard; uncomplicated HAP responds quickly
MRSA or Pseudomonas~10–14 daysSlower response; higher relapse risk if shortened
Structural lung disease (cavitation, abscess, empyema)~14–21 days or longerRequires source control (drainage if needed); longer courses standard
Septic shock at presentation~10–14 daysSevere infection; immune response slower
Immunocompromised patient14–21 daysHigher relapse risk; longer courses standard
Procalcitonin-guided duration (if available):
  • Falling procalcitonin (>25–50% drop from peak) = source controlled; safe to stop at ~7 days even for MRSA/Pseudomonas
  • Persistently elevated = reassess source, repeat imaging, consider longer course Clinical response criteria for antibiotic cessation:
  • Defervescence (fever resolved >24 hours)
  • Improving sputum (less purulent, lower volume)
  • Stable or improving SpO₂ on same FiO₂
  • CXR infiltrate stable or resolving
  • Normal hemodynamics (WBC normalizing, lactate cleared, no sepsis signs)
VAP/HAP prevention bundle and aspiration precautions Post-cardiac surgery VAP/HAP prevention (applies to intubated + recently extubated patients):
InterventionEvidenceHow on the Unit
Elevate HOB ≥30°AACN, CDC; reduces aspiration microaspirationEnforce after all position changes; reinforce with patient/family
Oral care with chlorhexidineCDC, VAP bundle; reduces pathogenic colonization2–4× daily; teach splinting-friendly technique (gentle, avoid aspiration)
Spontaneous breathing trials (SBT)ERS/ESICM; shortens ventilator daysFor intubated patients; ICU-level; assess readiness daily
Minimize sedation/daily sedation interruptionImproves cough, swallow, mobilityOn step-down already mostly non-sedated; avoid unnecessary sedatives
Early mobilization — chair, ambulationMultiple RCTs; improves clearance + V/Q matchingKey intervention; encourage despite sternotomy pain; pain control is prerequisite
Subglottic suction drain (in ETT)AACN, CDC; drains pooled secretions above cuffICU standard; if re-intubated, request ETT with subglottic port
Avoid gastric overdistentionReduces aspirationPromote regular diet, small meals if PO tolerating
Avoid supine positioningReduces aspiration; improves oxygenationEnforce HOB ≥30° or semi-recumbent; side-lying if bedbound
Aseptic suctioning techniqueReduces bacterial translocationClosed suctioning if on vent; limit depth + frequency
DVT/PPI prophylaxisPrevents immobility-related clot + stress ulcerStandard post-op; contributes to VAP prevention indirectly
Aspiration precautions (if dysphagia risk identified):
  • NPO until formal swallow evaluation
  • HOB ≥30° at all times
  • Supervise PO intake; slow meals, small bites, seated upright
  • Monitor for coughing/choking with swallows
  • NG feeding tube only if recurrent aspiration despite precautions (rare post-CABG; more common post-stroke or with severe dysphagia) Teaching bundle compliance:
  • HOB elevation is most under-performed bundle element; reinforce with every shift handoff
  • Oral care technique often poor; show new staff how to avoid aspiration risk during chlorhexidine rinse
  • Mobilization is highest-yield; prioritize pain control to enable early chair and ambulation
Differentiating HAP from atelectasis, cardiogenic pulmonary edema, and aspiration pneumonia Clinical dilemma: Post-cardiac surgery patient has new CXR infiltrate + fever. Is it HAP, atelectasis, cardiogenic edema, or aspiration?
FeatureHAPAtelectasisCardiogenic EdemaAspiration Pneumonia
OnsetPOD 3–7 (gradual)POD 0–2 (acute post-op)Anytime if CHF/fluid overloadWith aspiration event or dysphagia
FeverYes (>38°C)No (unless concurrent infection)NoYes (if bacterial superinfection)
SputumPurulent (yellow/green)Clear, scantFrothy, pink-tingedFood particles; foul smell if anaerobes
Infiltrate patternLobar, segmental; air-bronchogramsLinear, subsegmental; volume lossBilateral, perihilar; butterfly patternOften lower lobes (gravity-dependent)
CXR trendStable or worsens over daysImproves with mobilization within 24–48hImproves with diuresisProgresses if untreated
WBC responseElevated (>12k) with left shiftUsually normalUsually normalElevated (if infection established)
LactateMay be elevated (sepsis)NormalNormalElevated if aspiration + sepsis
BNPNormal or lowNormalElevated (if CHF)Normal
ProcalcitoninElevated (>0.5 ng/mL)NormalNormalElevated (if infection)
Response to antibioticsImproves 3–5 daysDoes NOT improve with ABX; improves with mobilizationDoes NOT improve; improves with diureticsImproves 3–5 days
Clinical approach if new infiltrate + fever:
  1. Obtain sputum culture + gram stain ASAP — quality specimen is critical
  2. Assess aspiration risk — dysphagia history? Witnessed aspiration? Foul sputum? If yes → aspiration precautions + empiric ABX (anaerobic coverage only if strong clinical suspicion)
  3. Check BNP, I/O, fluid status — if volume overloaded + elevated BNP + pulmonary edema pattern → diuretics first
  4. Try aggressive pulmonary toilet (mobilization, splinted coughing, incentive spirometry) — if improving over 24–48h WITHOUT antibiotics → likely atelectasis; hold ABX pending cultures
  5. If worsening despite mobilization or cultures positive → start/continue antibiotics Key pearl: Don't reflexively start antibiotics for atelectasis in a stable patient. Mobilization + pain control + incentive spirometry can resolve in 24–48h, avoiding unnecessary resistance emergence.
Special populations — immunocompromised, transplant, VAD, ECMO Transplant patients (heart, lung, or combined):
  • Higher infection risk (baseline immunosuppression)
  • Different pathogen spectrum: consider fungal (Candida, Aspergillus) and viral (CMV, RSV)
  • Empiric antifungal coverage may be warranted (fluconazole or micafungin)
  • Longer antibiotic courses often needed (14–21 days)
  • ID + transplant team involvement early Chronic steroid users (pre-existing or post-op stress):
  • Blunted fever response; may be afebrile with severe infection
  • Higher HAP mortality
  • Monitor procalcitonin, lactate as surrogate for infection severity
  • Ensure stress-dose steroids if septic shock develops VAD patients (LVAD, RVAD, BiVAD):
  • Driveline infection risk overlaps with HAP risk
  • HAP outcomes often worse (limited cardiac reserve)
  • Early aggressive management critical
  • Coordinate with VAD/transplant team ECMO or prolonged mechanical support:
  • Highest infection risk (anticoagulation, ischemia-reperfusion injury, prolonged intubation)
  • Fungal infections more common
  • HAP treatment intensity higher; longer courses standard
  • ICU-level management always required
When HAP fails to improve — persistent fever despite appropriate antibiotics Red flag: Persistent fever >48–72h on appropriate antibiotics = diagnostic and management challenge. Differential diagnosis (mnemonic: "WINDMILLS"):
  • Wrong organism — culture data conflicts with empiric choice; repeat cultures, consider fungal/AFB if immunocompromised
  • Inadequate drug levels — verify dosing for renal function; ensure adequate absorption if PO step-down; check vancomycin trough
  • No response to therapy — resistant organism; repeat sensibilities; Pseudomonas may be fluoroquinolone-resistant despite gram stain
  • Drug toxicity — vancomycin nephrotoxicity, aminoglycoside ototoxicity; can mimic worsening infection
  • Missed source control — abscess not drained, infected hardware, empyema, bronchial obstruction
  • Immunocompromise — slower response expected; may need longer course or adjunctive immune support
  • Lined up problems — concurrent infection (C. difficile, CLABSI, sternal infection); get cultures of each site
  • Lungs not the problem — PE, acute MI, heart failure exacerbation, pericardial effusion/tamponade
  • Superinfection — fungal HAP (rare; usually airway colonization, not pathogenic) Management of persistent fever:
  • Repeat sputum + blood cultures — assess for new organism, fungal, AFB
  • Review prior culture sensibilities — de-escalate if organism more sensible; escalate if resistant
  • CT chest — assess for abscess, empyema, pneumothorax, other complication
  • Bronchoscopy with lavage/biopsy (ICU-level) — if diagnosis unclear; obtain specimen for fungal, AFB
  • ID consult — expert guidance on resistant organism management, duration decisions
  • Reassess diagnosis — expect defervescence by day 3–5 for MSSA; day 5–7 for MRSA/Pseudomonas; if not → reconsider

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear in a stable HAP patient, re-escalate to 5B path.

  • SpO₂ trending down despite optimized FiO₂ — may indicate worsening pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary edema; recheck blood gas, repeat CXR
  • RR >25–30 or increased work of breathing — early respiratory fatigue; consider non-invasive ventilation trial or re-intubation prep
  • Fever persisting >48–72h on appropriate antibiotics — wrong bug, inadequate source control, or wrong diagnosis; repeat imaging and cultures
  • New or worsening infiltrates on repeat CXR — HAP progressing; escalate therapy, reassess diagnosis
  • Altered mental status, confusion, or decreased sensorium — encephalopathy from hypoxemia, hypercarbia, sepsis, or metabolic derangement
  • Lactate rising or not clearing despite fluid/vasopressor — tissue hypoperfusion; risk of septic shock; escalate to 5B
  • Hemoptysis — suggests necrotizing infection (Pseudomonas, anaerobes, aspergillus); high mortality; urgent escalation
  • Unilateral decreased breath sounds + hypoxia — concern for pneumothorax (post-op risk), large effusion, or lobar consolidation; CXR STAT
  • Acute hypotension or tachycardia accelerating — may signal septic shock or cardiac decompensation; escalate immediately
  • Sputum becoming grossly bloody or foul-smelling — necrotizing pneumonia or aspiration with sepsis; high mortality
  • Unable to expectorate/mobilize secretions despite pulmonary toilet — inadequate airway clearance; consider re-intubation if worsening
  • Triad: confusion + tachycardia + fever + low BP — septic shock from HAP; urgent 5B escalation
  • Rising procalcitonin after initial fall — new bacterial challenge or inadequate source control; reassess imaging and cultures
  • Patient anxiety/agitation without clear cause — subtle sign of hypoxemia or metabolic stress; objective vital sign reassessment warranted

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. New infiltrate alone is NOT diagnostic of HAP. Post-operative atelectasis, pulmonary edema (cardiogenic), pleural effusion, and aspiration are common mimics.

    Infiltrate + fever + purulent sputum + positive culture = HAP. Avoid unnecessary antibiotics if atelectasis likely.

  2. Sputum quality matters enormously. Gram stain with >10 squamous epithelial cells/lpf = saliva contamination; results misleading. Reject poor-quality specimens; request new.

    ≥25 PMNs + <10 epithelial cells/lpf = good specimen.

  3. IDSA 2016 landmark change: Routine anaerobic coverage is NO LONGER recommended for empiric HAP. Standard vanc + antipseudomonal β-lactam is sufficient. Only add anaerobic agents if strong aspiration features (dysphagia, witnessed aspiration, foul sputum).

  4. Atelectasis vs. HAP is the most common diagnostic dilemma post-cardiac. Both have infiltrates; both may have low-grade fever. Atelectasis improves with mobilization + pain control + incentive spirometry over 24–48h without antibiotics. HAP consolidates or worsens. Try aggressive pulmonary toilet first in stable patients.

  5. Post-cardiac surgery = automatic HIGH-risk category for MRSA/Pseudomonas empirically. Nearly all patients got pre-op prophylactic antibiotics. Broad empiric (vancomycin + antipseudomonal β-lactam) is justified; don't start with cephalosporin monotherapy.

  6. Procalcitonin-guided duration can shorten courses safely without increasing relapse. If procalcitonin trending down >25–50% by day 3–5 despite MRSA/Pseudomonas, safe to stop at ~7 days rather than 10–14. Reduces resistance emergence.

  7. Post-cardiac surgery pulmonary function is worse than pre-op for weeks. Patients feel more short of breath, cough less effectively, desaturate more easily than baseline. Don't misattribute normal post-op decline to new HAP.

    Clue: infiltrate on imaging + fever + purulent sputum + worsening trajectory.

  8. Incentive spirometry is chronically under-ordered. Most post-CABG patients don't reach realistic goals (often 500–1000 mL post-op; target 1500+ mL).

    Teach splinting over sternum. Emphasize: walking is the best incentive spirometer.

  9. Aspiration risk heightens with delirium, OSA, post-stroke status, dysphagia. Identify at admission; reinforce HOB ≥30°, oral care, supervised diet. Post-operative delirium (hypoactive subtype especially) increases aspiration silently.

  10. Immunocompromised patients (transplant, chronic steroids, chemotherapy) have different pathogen spectrum — consider Candida, Aspergillus, Nocardia, PCP. Default to antifungal + standard antibiotics if severely immunosuppressed.

  11. Persistent fever despite appropriate antibiotics ≠ antibiotic resistance in most cases. Think source not controlled (abscess, empyema), wrong bug, or wrong diagnosis. Reassess imaging, repeat cultures, consider bronchoscopy or CT for abscess.

  12. Fungal HAP (Candida sputum colonization) is rare and usually reflects airway colonization, not pathogenic infection. Routine antifungal coverage is NOT recommended by IDSA unless high-risk patient (prolonged ICU, prior azole exposure, neutropenia).

  13. Stenotrophomonas and Acinetobacter emerging in prolonged ICU stay. Stenotrophomonas is carbapenem-resistant; treat with TMP-SMX or fluoroquinolone. Rare on step-down but common if patient bounces back to ICU.

  14. HAP mortality 20–30% even with appropriate therapy. Not a trivial infection. Reinforce to patients/families that early recognition and source control (mobility, suctioning, extubation) improve prognosis.

  15. Pain control is critical to pneumonia prevention AND recovery. Under-medicated post-CABG patients can't cough, breathe deeply, or mobilize. Adequate analgesia (IV acetaminophen + opioid PRN) + regional techniques optimize both comfort and pneumonia prevention/resolution. Over-sedation worsens outcomes (impairs clearance, increases aspiration).

cards.title: Harvest Site Infection
cards.quickAnswer: Erythema, warmth, or drainage at harvest site (leg or arm) → wound culture if purulent; gentle debridement if superficial. No systemic signs: oral cephalexin 500 mg QID × 7–10 days, elevate limb, compression stocking per surgeon. Systemic signs (fever ≥38.5°C, HR >110, WBC >13k, purulent drainage) → STAT IV antibiotics (cefazolin 1–2 g IV Q8H or vancomycin per MRSA risk), blood cultures, surgical washout likely needed. EVH infections may hide — fever without visible wound site = suspect tunnel infection. Radial harvest: no BP cuff/IV on harvest arm; verify pre- and post-op Allen test. Elevating limb and compression stockings are prevention cornerstone.
