sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — what this condition is and who it affects.

  • Definition: Surgical site infection (SSI) at the conduit harvest incision(s), occurring after saphenous vein graft (SVG), radial artery, or other arterial conduit removal for CABG. Presents with local erythema, warmth, drainage, swelling, or systemic signs (fever, tachycardia, elevated WBC).
  • Incidence: Endoscopic vein harvest (EVH) 2–5%; open vein harvest 5–15%; radial artery harvest 1–3% (Bojar, 2020; STS National Database). EVH lower infection but tunnel infections are concealed. Diabetics and obese patients have 2–3× higher risk.
  • Who it applies to: All post-CABG patients, especially those with diabetes, peripheral arterial disease (PAD), obesity (BMI >35), immunosuppression, or advanced age. Peak detection POD 4+, but can present post-discharge.
  • Why it matters: SSI increases length of stay, mortality, costs, and complications (abscess, necrotizing fasciitis, osteomyelitis, sepsis). Early recognition and appropriate management reduce morbidity.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology & epidemiology of conduit harvest SSI Conduit harvest site infection results from the convergence of surgical trauma, microvascular ischemia, and bacterial contamination in a host with immune and perfusion compromise: Mechanism:
  • Ischemia at wound edges: Surgical disruption of microvascular perfusion creates hypoxic tissue susceptible to bacterial colonization
  • Seroma / hematoma formation: Fluid collections provide favorable anaerobic environment for secondary infection and bacterial proliferation
  • Bacterial inoculation: Skin flora (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, gram-negatives) enter at time of surgery; difficult to fully irrigate tunnel spaces Host risk factors:
  • Diabetes mellitus: Hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil function, angiogenesis, and wound healing; 2–3× higher SSI risk
  • Obesity (BMI >35): Poor perfusion in adipose tissue; higher skin bacterial burden
  • Peripheral arterial disease: Compromised baseline circulation in harvested limb; reduced ability to fight infection or manage edema
  • Chronic renal disease: Uremic impairment of immune function; delayed healing
  • Advanced age (>75): Slower immune response, slower angiogenesis
  • Immunosuppression: Steroids, biologics, post-transplant status Surgical technique factors:
  • EVH (endoscopic harvest): Creates blind tunnel 30–40 cm long; harder to inspect, irrigate, thoroughly drain. Smaller incisions = better cosmesis, better tissue-plane preservation, but more tunnel dead-space. SSI 2–5%; tunnel infection is the hidden threat.
  • Open vein harvest: Larger incisions, easier to manage but greater tissue trauma and longer healing window. SSI 5–15%; infection is visible at bedside but progression can be rapid.
  • Radial artery harvest: Requires careful periosteal stripping; hematoma common (15–20%); infection rare (1–3%) but can damage brachial plexus or compromise hand perfusion via ulnar artery dominance if extensive
Risk stratification for harvest SSI Highest-risk patient profile:
  • Type 2 diabetes with HbA1c >7% OR on insulin
  • BMI >35
  • Chronic renal disease (eGFR <60 or Cr >1.5)
  • Documented PAD (claudication, prior revascularization, ABI <0.9)
  • Immunosuppression (chronic steroids, biologics, post-transplant)
  • Age >75 with multiple comorbidities
  • Female sex (minor independent risk factor per STS) High-risk surgical combinations:
  • EVH in obese patient (technical difficulty, increased dead-space)
  • Open harvest in patient with prior groin/leg surgery or lymph node dissection (lymphedema risk)
  • Bilateral leg harvest (rare; very high morbidity) OR preventive measures (already accomplished):
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis at induction (cefazolin or vancomycin per MRSA risk)
  • Skin antisepsis (chlorhexidine or iodine-based prep)
  • Careful hemostasis, thorough irrigation
  • ACE wrap × 24 h post-EVH to reduce hematoma
  • Consideration of subcuticular closure ± skin adhesive for smaller incisions (vs staples)
EVH tunnel infection — the hidden threat Why it's different from open harvest infection: Endoscopic tunnel runs 30–40 cm from a small groin or thigh incision. Infection in this tunnel is not visible on examination until it tracks to the skin or produces systemic signs (fever, elevated WBC). This leads to delayed diagnosis. Presentation of EVH tunnel infection:
  • Fever (≥38.5°C) + tachycardia on POD 2–5 without an obvious wound finding
  • Elevated WBC (>13k) with no clear source
  • Lower extremity swelling or pain out of proportion to the small incision
  • Vague thigh/lower leg discomfort, warmth to palpation in tunnel path Why it's missed:
  • Surgeon closes the small incision meticulously; clinician assumes "perfect" closure = no problem
  • Bedside nurse sees tiny, well-approximated incision and does not suspect deep infection
  • By the time purulent drainage appears at skin surface (if ever), patient may be discharged home
  • Tunnel imaging (ultrasound, CT) is often not obtained until late in the course Management of EVH tunnel infection:
  • Often requires surgical re-exploration, tunnel irrigation, and drainage
  • Antibiotics alone rarely succeed if there is significant collection or necrotic tissue
  • Imaging (ultrasound or CT) can confirm fluid in tunnel but may not be obtained until clinical deterioration
  • Consider imaging early in any EVH patient with fever and no other clear source
Allen test — pre- and post-operative significance for radial harvest Pre-operative Allen test:
  • Both radial and ulnar arteries compressed at wrist; patient makes fist → hand blanches
  • Release ulnar artery; observe color return to hand within 5 seconds (normal) or >15 seconds (abnormal)
  • Abnormal Allen test (slow return / incomplete perfusion) is a contraindication to radial harvest — substantial risk of hand ischemia post-op
  • If patient has abnormal pre-op Allen test, surgery should not proceed with radial harvest (request is often made to pre-op clinic, not always honored) Post-operative Allen test significance:
  • Must be repeated before discharge to confirm restoration of hand perfusion via ulnar artery alone post-radial-harvest
  • Some surgeons perform this POD 1 or in post-op recovery room; others check pre-discharge
  • Abnormal post-op Allen → inadequate ulnar perfusion to hand → urgent surgical involvement required
  • If radial harvest + infection at arm site → additional risk of vascular compromise from swelling/abscess → emergent surgical involvement indicated

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following while caring for a post-CABG patient, typically POD 4+, but can occur post-discharge:

  • Visual inspection of leg or arm harvest site shows erythema, warmth, induration, edema
  • Purulent or serous-to-purulent drainage from harvest site or small incisions
  • Patient reports leg or arm pain, warmth, swelling in the harvested region
  • Fever ≥38.5°C (101.3°F) in a post-CABG patient with any wound finding
  • Tachycardia (HR >110), tachypnea (RR >20), or elevated WBC (>12k) post-op without obvious source — suspect EVH tunnel infection
  • Unilateral leg swelling + warmth + calf tenderness — DVT differential but infection is on the differential list
  • Examination findings: tense edema, fluctuance, severe cellulitis extending beyond local site, crepitus (gas-forming organisms), red streaking (lymphangitis)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs: Fever, HR, BP, RR, SpO₂; mental status; perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature)
  • Observe the wound site visually:
  • Color: erythema extent (cm), dusky or normal skin?
  • Drainage: purulent, serous, sanguinous, foul odor?
  • Swelling: tense edema, soft, localized or diffuse throughout limb?
  • Skin integrity: intact incision, gaping, tunneling, opening?
  • Palpate carefully: warmth, fluctuance, induration, crepitus (emergent sign), cord-like lymphangitis
  • Assess limb perfusion: cap refill <2 sec, color, warmth, sensory deficits
  • Radial harvest specifics: hand cap refill, nail bed color, sensation in radial nerve distribution (lateral forearm, thumb-index web)
  • Review the MAR: antibiotics on board? What was the harvest type (open vs EVH vs radial)?
  • Review operative report: harvest method, closure technique, any intraop complications, drain placement
  • Check recent labs: WBC trend, Cr (baseline for antibiotic dosing), prior cultures if patient was sent home and returning
  • Assess contralateral limb: is harvest site normal? (baseline comparison)
  • Note drain placement: any drains present? Output character?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Localized erythema and warmth, serous drainage only; HR <110, no fever, WBC normal or mild elevation; no systemic signs; alert and oriented; adequate perfusion.)

  1. Obtain wound culture if any drainage present — swab for serous, culture bottle for purulent drainage
  2. Gentle wound inspection and debridement — remove loose eschar, necrotic tissue, dried debris WITHOUT aggressive manipulation
  3. Cleanse the site with normal saline per [Institution policy]; consider gentle wet-to-dry dressing
  4. Start empiric oral antibiotic — select based on allergy history and coverage:
    • Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID × 7–10 days (if no beta-lactam allergy) — covers gram-positive skin flora
    • OR Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg PO BID × 7–10 days — broader coverage including anaerobes
    • Adjust based on culture/sensitivity results
    • Elevate the harvested limb — pillow under calf or foot; educate patient to keep leg elevated while sitting or lying (reduces swelling, improves perfusion)
    • Compression stocking on leg per surgeon preference — reduces swelling, may improve venous return (not contraindicated in mild cellulitis)
    • Analgesia as needed — acetaminophen, ibuprofen, or PRN opioid per orders; pain impairs compliance and healing
    • Patient education — watch for spreading erythema (>5 cm/day), increasing purulent drainage, fever, red streaking (lymphangitis sign), systemic symptoms; return or call immediately if worsen
    • Re-assess daily — check site daily, document findings, trend; if no improvement in 3–5 days on oral antibiotic, escalate to provider for possible IV antibiotics
    • Notify APP / surgeon with findings and plan; document in EHR

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Purulent or foul-smelling drainage; fever ≥38.5°C; HR >110 not explained by pain/anxiety; RR >20; WBC >13k; systemic signs; cellulitis rapidly spreading; crepitus; fluctuance; hemodynamic instability; altered mental status; signs of necrotizing process.)

  1. STAT call APP / on-call surgeon — do NOT delay; code-level escalation if signs of sepsis
  2. Activate Rapid Response if not already present — sepsis workup
  3. Obtain blood cultures × 2 (before antibiotics) if febrile
  4. Deep wound culture — if purulent drainage, culture from deep wound edge or fluid (not just surface swab); send in appropriate media (aerobic, anaerobic, culture bottle)
  5. STAT labs: CBC with differential (WBC, left shift), CMP (creatinine for dosing, glucose), lactate (if septic picture), consider troponin if concerned for cardiac involvement
  6. Start empiric IV antibiotic STAT — pending culture results:
    • Cefazolin 1–2 g IV Q8H (if penicillin non-allergic; excellent gram-positive skin coverage) ± gram-negative coverage per surgeon, OR
    • Vancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV Q8–12H (if MRSA risk, beta-lactam allergy, or renal function requires extended dosing) — dosing per [Institution protocol]
    • Consider adding clindamycin 600–900 mg IV Q6–8H for anaerobic coverage if crepitus present
    • Gentle debridement if superficial involvement only — do NOT probe or force open tunneled areas at bedside (risk of deeper dissemination)
    • Elevate and keep site clean; apply sterile dressing — may need frequent changes if heavy drainage
    • NPO status pending surgical evaluation — may require operative washout / debridement
    • Adequate IV access — ensure patent, adequate lines for fluid resuscitation if signs of early sepsis (lactate ↑, UOP ↓, MAP trending down)
    • Continuous monitoring — reassess perfusion, spread of erythema, progression every 1–2 hours until surgeon evaluates
    • Prepare for operating room transfer — have chart, imaging (ultrasound of tunnel if indicated), cultures ready; notify surgical team

sections.heading: 5C. Radial harvest site specifics
sections.bodyHtml:
If infection involves radial artery harvest arm:

  1. CRITICAL: DO NOT place BP cuff, tourniquet, or IV line on the harvest arm — absolute contraindication. Risk of additional vascular compromise or vein (radial graft conduit) puncture
  2. Check Allen test pre-op documentation — confirm ulnar artery supplied hand perfusion baseline and whether test was normal or abnormal
  3. Assess post-op hand perfusion RIGHT NOW: cap refill <2 sec on all fingers, pink nail beds, no cyanosis, intact sensation in radial nerve distribution (lateral forearm, thumb-index web), normal hand temperature
  4. If perfusion is already compromised + infection: immediate surgeon notification — may need urgent washout ± vascular intervention to restore perfusion
  5. Hematoma vs infection differential: Radial hematoma is common and usually stable. Distinguish between:
    • Tense but stable hematoma (common; often resolves without intervention)
    • Rapidly expanding hematoma (risk of compartment syndrome, nerve compression)
    • Hematoma + fever/warmth/purulent drainage (infected, requires antibiotics and surgical drainage)
    • Monitor hand / forearm carefully — pain, new numbness, coolness, color change, diminished cap refill are urgent signs; notify surgeon immediately
    • All IV access must be placed in other arm or central line — enforce throughout hospitalization

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for surgeon/provider:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p CABG with [vein/radial] harvest." B: "Patient developed wound findings at [leg/arm harvest site] at [time]. [Describe: erythema extent in cm, drainage character, warmth, swelling]. Temperature [value], HR [value], RR [value], WBC [value]. [Pre-op harvest type and any documented pre-op issues]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Describe: systemic signs present/absent, symptoms, mental status, perfusion status]. Cultures obtained [specify what sent and when]." R: "Requesting [site evaluation / operative washout / IV antibiotic orders / imaging such as ultrasound of tunnel]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Urgency
Superficial cellulitis, no systemic signs, first notification Primary surgeon or on-call fellow Same-day evaluation
Purulent drainage, fever, elevated WBC On-call surgeon + Infectious Disease consult if not resolving STAT
Spreading cellulitis, crepitus, systemic instability, hemodynamic changes On-call surgeon + charge RN + rapid response EMERGENT
Radial harvest + hand ischemia signs, perfusion compromise On-call surgeon + Vascular surgery EMERGENT
Septic picture (lactate ↑, ↓UOP, mental status change, hypotension) Sepsis response protocol: surgeon + ICU + Infectious Disease CODE-LEVEL

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 EVH vs open harvest infection: incidence and clinical implications
sections.bodyHtml:
Why endoscopic harvest has lower infection but higher index of suspicion Endoscopic harvest (EVH): 2–5% SSI rate; lower infection incidence than open harvest, but:
  • Creates blind tunnel 30–40 cm long, difficult to irrigate thoroughly
  • Small incision ≤ 3–4 cm → appears "perfect" to novice bedside assessment
  • Infection tracks along tunnel → fever/elevated WBC appear without visible wound finding
  • Often diagnosed late when patient has systemic signs or returns post-discharge
  • When diagnosed, often requires re-exploration and tunnel drainage (antibiotics alone insufficient if abscess present) Open harvest: 5–15% SSI rate; higher infection incidence but:
  • Larger incisions (groin-to-knee, sometimes longer) → visible at bedside
  • Superficial infection easier to spot early, but progression can be rapid
  • More tissue trauma, larger wound surface, longer healing window
  • More suitable for very obese patients where EVH is technically challenging Clinical pearl: EVH patient with fever POD 2–3 and "perfect" incision = assume tunnel infection until proven otherwise. Image early (ultrasound of thigh tunnel); do not wait for surface drainage.

sections.heading: 7.2 Harvest site infection risk stratification and prevention
sections.bodyHtml:
Risk groups and outpatient vs inpatient management implications Highest-risk profile → inpatient IV antibiotics:
  • Diabetes + BMI >35 + any warmth/erythema → start IV (cefazolin or vanc) upfront; do NOT try outpatient PO
  • PAD + leg harvest site infection → poor baseline perfusion makes infection harder to control; IV antibiotics justified
  • Immunosuppressed (steroids, biologics) + any infection sign → IV
  • EVH with fever but no visible wound → IV until tunnel infection ruled out Lower-risk profile → outpatient PO antibiotics acceptable:
  • No systemic signs
  • Superficial erythema and serous drainage only
  • Non-diabetic or well-controlled DM (HbA1c <7%)
  • Normal renal function
  • Reliable patient, able to elevate limb, return if worsens Prevention cornerstones (post-op ICU/telemetry/stepdown):
  • ACE wrap × 24 h post-EVH to reduce hematoma (CRITICAL: remove on POD 1 AM per standing orders; do not leave in place longer)
  • Leg elevation + compression stockings (reduces swelling, improves perfusion, decreases infection)
  • Early mobilization (ambulation reduces DVT + prevents prolonged edema)
  • Optimize glycemic control (target glucose 140–180 mg/dL post-op per [Institution protocol])
  • Adequate pain control so patient will move / ambulate
  • Bowel regimen (stool softeners + osmotic laxative so patient isn't straining, worsening abdominal/venous pressure in leg)

sections.heading: 7.3 Radial artery harvest: Allen test, hand numbness, compartment syndrome
sections.bodyHtml:
Radial-specific post-operative considerations and safety precautions Allen test pre- and post-operative:
  • Pre-op: Abnormal Allen test (slow hand color return >5 sec) is contraindication to radial harvest; if patient had abnormal pre-op Allen and surgery proceeded anyway, this is a risk factor for post-op hand ischemia
  • Post-op: Allen test must be repeated before discharge to confirm adequate ulnar perfusion to hand post-graft removal
  • If post-op Allen abnormal: urgent notification to surgeon; may require urgent vascular assessment or intervention Hand numbness post-radial-harvest:
  • Transient numbness in lateral forearm and thumb-index web space is common (radial sensory nerve involvement from dissection)
  • Usually resolves within 3–6 months as nerve inflammation settles
  • Red flag: progressive or severe numbness (vs expected transient) → possible nerve injury or ongoing compression; notify surgeon
  • Teach patient: numbness expected, will resolve; report if worsens or hand gets cool/pale Radial compartment syndrome (rare but surgical emergency):
  • Risk factors: extensive swelling, hematoma, infection with rapid expansion, tourniquets, tight dressings
  • Presentation: forearm pain out of proportion, pain with passive hand/finger extension, coolness, numbness, weakness
  • If suspected: immediate surgical evaluation; may require fasciotomy
  • Prevention: do NOT apply tight dressings; remove ACE wrap promptly if placed; monitor perfusion daily; encourage elevation + active hand exercises Arm restrictions post-radial harvest:
  • NO BP cuffs on harvest arm — absolute rule throughout hospitalization and outpatient care
  • NO IV lines on harvest arm (vein puncture risk for remaining radial/ulnar branches, risk of thrombosis)
  • NO tourniquets, tight blood pressure cuffs, or restrictive clothing on arm
  • Patient education: arm care sheets should be provided; many patients don't know these restrictions unless explicitly told

sections.heading: 7.4 Antibiotic selection and dosing
sections.bodyHtml:
Empiric antibiotic options for outpatient and inpatient harvest SSI
ScenarioFirst-lineAlternativeNotes
Superficial cellulitis, outpatient (oral)Cephalexin 500 mg PO QID × 7–10 daysAmoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg PO BID × 7–10 daysCovers Staph, Strep, some gram-negatives. Adjust if resistance documented.
Purulent/systemic signs, inpatient (IV)Cefazolin 1–2 g IV Q8HVancomycin 15–20 mg/kg IV Q8–12HCefazolin preferred if no MRSA risk / PCN allergy. Vanc if MRSA risk, allergy, or renal dosing needed.
MRSA suspected or documentedVancomycin (dosing as above)Linezolid 600 mg IV Q12HVanc first-line. Linezolid for intolerance. Monitor drug levels (goal trough 15–20 mcg/mL for serious infection).
Beta-lactam allergyClindamycin 600–900 mg IV Q6–8HFluoroquinolone (levofloxacin 750 mg IV Q24H)Clindamycin covers gram-pos, anaerobes; less gram-negative coverage. FQ covers gram-neg better. Confirm allergy type (IgE-mediated vs rash).
Crepitus / gas-formers suspectedClindamycin 600–900 mg IV Q6–8H + broad gram-negative coverage (ceftazidime or meropenem)See unstable pathwaySuspect necrotizing fasciitis; urgent surgical involvement.
EVH tunnel infectionSame as systemic infection above; likely requires IV + possible tunnel irrigationAdd imaging (ultrasound) earlyAntibiotics alone often insufficient if abscess present.
Dosing adjustments:
  • Renal impairment (Cr >1.5 or eGFR <60): adjust per [Institution dosing protocol] — common in post-op cardiac patients
  • Obesity (BMI >35): may require weight-based dosing for antibiotics; confirm with pharmacy
  • Allergy verification: distinguish true beta-lactam allergy (IgE-mediated: anaphylaxis, rash, angioedema) from intolerance (GI upset, photosensitivity). Many patients tolerate cephalosporins despite penicillin allergy if reaction was non-IgE.

sections.heading: 7.5 Wound care and compression therapy for harvest site swelling
sections.bodyHtml:
Leg elevation, compression stockings, and VAC therapy indications Leg elevation:
  • Standard: pillow under calf/foot, elevate above heart level while lying or seated
  • Purpose: reduces interstitial pressure, improves capillary perfusion, decreases swelling, facilitates lymphatic drainage
  • Is non-negotiable even for mild cellulitis — edema worsens infection, impairs antibiotic delivery
  • Compliance challenge: post-op patients often in pain, anxious, want to ambulate. Educate that elevation ≠ immobility; patient can walk to bathroom, then return to elevated position. Compression stockings:
  • Indication: post-harvest leg swelling, especially post-EVH (common 15–20% hematoma incidence)
  • Goal: graduated compression (not contraindicated in mild cellulitis; escalate decision if deep abscess suspected)
  • Sizing: measure calf / ankle per [Institution protocol]; proper fit is essential (too loose = ineffective; too tight = tourniquet effect / compartment risk)
  • Duration: typically started POD 0–1, may continue 2–6 weeks depending on swelling trajectory Negative-pressure wound therapy (VAC):
  • Indication: extensive necrotic tissue, large open area after debridement, recurrent infection despite antibiotics and dressing changes
  • NOT routine — reserved for wounds that fail standard wet-to-dry or other dressing strategies
  • Requires surgeon decision and monitoring — not bedside nurse decision Wet-to-dry dressing:
  • Standard for superficial cellulitis: gauze moistened with normal saline, allowed to dry, then removed (derides necrotic tissue)
  • Change frequency: TID to QID depending on drainage volume
  • Alternative: silver-impregnated or antimicrobial gauze if drainage is heavy or infection refractory

sections.heading: 7.6 Lymphedema post-SVG harvest
sections.bodyHtml:
Long-term swelling, compression, and patient education Lymphedema post-saphenous vein harvest:
  • Occurs when saphenous vein or its tributaries are removed along with lymph nodes/vessels in the harvest zone
  • Incidence: 5–15% post-open harvest (especially groin-to-knee), <2% post-EVH (smaller incision, less disruption)
  • Timeline: swelling can appear weeks to months post-op; some patients develop persistent limb swelling even 1–2 years out
  • Presentation: unilateral leg heaviness, tightness, swelling, inability to fit into shoes/clothing, recurrent skin infections more common Management of post-SVG lymphedema:
  • Prevention: leg elevation, early mobilization, compression stockings (indefinite duration in some patients)
  • If develops: outpatient lymphedema specialist referral; may require compression sleeves, lymphatic drainage massage, skin care education
  • Red flag: swelling + fever + cellulitis in lymphedemic leg = very high infection risk; treat aggressively with IV antibiotics Patient teaching: "Saphenous vein removal can cause long-term leg swelling. Wear compression stockings daily, keep leg elevated when sitting/lying, avoid prolonged standing or sitting without elevation. Watch for skin breakdown, redness, warmth — these need immediate attention as lymphedemic legs are prone to infection."

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear in a patient initially deemed stable, re-escalate.

  • Erythema spreading >5 cm per day — rapid progression suggests aggressive organism or inadequate source control; escalate immediately
  • Red streaking up the leg or arm (lymphangitis) — ascending infection along lymphatic vessels; risk of bacteremia; emergent call to surgeon
  • Purulent drainage appearing after initially serous — conversion from sterile hematoma to infected collection; re-escalate antibiotic strategy
  • Fever developing in previously afebrile patient — transitioning to systemic involvement; send blood cultures, escalate to IV antibiotics
  • WBC rising despite oral antibiotic × 48–72 hours — inadequate source control; likely requires surgical intervention, imaging, or IV therapy
  • Spreading edema, tense induration, skin blanching over area — suggests deep abscess or cellulitis; risk of necrotizing fasciitis; urgent imaging + surgery consult
  • Crepitus on palpation — gas-forming organisms (Clostridium, Escherichia coli); emergent surgical evaluation for necrotizing process
  • Signs of systemic toxicity: fever >39°C, HR >120, BP trending down, lactate ↑, UOP falling, confusion or altered mental status — activate sepsis protocol
  • Radial harvest + hand getting cooler, pale, or showing new/progressive numbness — vascular compromise from infection or hematoma expansion; emergent evaluation
  • Patient becoming poorly compliant, not elevating limb, unable to care for site — high risk for progression; consider escalating to IV antibiotics, wound clinic, or inpatient observation
  • No improvement in cellulitis after 5–7 days of appropriate oral antibiotic — source control failure; imaging (ultrasound of wound/tunnel) and possible surgical intervention indicated

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. EVH tunnel infection is the most commonly missed post-CABG SSI. Fever or elevated WBC in an otherwise "perfect" EVH site = infection until proven otherwise. Do not discount systemic signs because the incision looks great. If EVH + fever + no other source, call surgeon and request imaging (ultrasound of thigh tunnel).

  2. EVH has lower infection rate (2–5%) than open harvest (5–15%), but requires different clinical vigilance. You cannot see the tunnel. A patient with EVH who spikes fever on POD 2–3 needs early consideration of deep wound culture, imaging, and escalation.

  3. ACE wrap removal on POD 1 is mandatory. Placed to reduce hematoma, but if left on >24 hours, it creates risk of compartment syndrome in the calf or skin necrosis. Check standing orders — should explicitly say "remove on POD 1 AM." Verify removal before signing off.

  4. Diabetes + obesity + open leg harvest = your highest-risk patient for SSI. A diabetic with BMI >35, HbA1c >8%, and a large leg incision who develops any warmth/erythema should receive IV antibiotics, not oral. Be proactive; escalate early.

  5. Leg elevation + compression stockings are the prevention cornerstone. Edema impairs perfusion, worsens infection, slows healing. Educate patients: elevation is not immobility; they can walk to the bathroom, then return to elevated position. Compression stockings should fit properly (measure per protocol).

  6. Peripheral arterial disease is a major independent risk factor for harvest SSI. If patient had documented PAD pre-op, pay extra attention to the harvest leg. Poor baseline perfusion + surgical ischemia = slow wound healing, higher infection, and slower response to antibiotics.

  7. Superficial cellulitis without systemic signs can be treated with oral antibiotics, but draw the line carefully. If patient has ANY fever (>38.5°C), tachycardia (HR >110 not explained by pain), or elevated WBC (>13k), start IV. Do not spend 48–72 hours on oral antibiotics waiting to see if they work — risk of progression.

  8. No BP cuff, no IV lines on the radial harvest arm. This is non-negotiable. If patient needs a line, use the other arm or a central line. Tourniquet use, cuff inflation, or needle puncture risks vein perforation (if the radial graft is still in the arm pre-discharge) and vascular compromise to the hand via loss of radial perfusion.

  9. Allen test is pre-operative AND post-operative. Many bedside nurses have never heard of it. If radial harvest: (1) confirm abnormal pre-op Allen did not occur (if yes, why did they harvest?); (2) ensure post-op Allen is documented before discharge. Abnormal post-op Allen = hand perfusion via ulnar alone is inadequate = urgent surgeon notification.

  10. Radial hematoma is common (15–20%) but infection is rare (1–3%). Distinguish between a tense, stable hematoma (common, often resolves) vs a rapidly expanding hematoma (risk of compartment syndrome, nerve compression) vs hematoma with fever/warmth/drainage (infected). Tense stable hematomas do NOT automatically need antibiotics; expanding or infected hematomas do. Palpate and assess daily.

  11. Bowel regimen is post-op standard because straining worsens leg swelling. Patients on opioids often become constipated and avoid walking/moving the leg to the bathroom. Straining increases abdominal and venous pressure in the leg, worsening edema. Prophylactic stool softener + osmotic laxative (per [Institution protocol]) and educate on benefits of early mobility.

  12. Don't forget to remove the ACE wrap on POD 1 if applied post-EVH. Standing orders should specify "remove on POD 1 AM," but mistakes happen. If left on >24 hours, compartment syndrome risk ↑, skin necrosis risk ↑. Verify removal, document, and reassess leg.

  13. Osteomyelitis is rare but possible if harvest site infection goes untreated. If patient develops persistent warmth, drainage, or pain over the tibia (anterior shin) or other bone after weeks of antibiotics without source control, imaging (bone scan, CT) and Infectious Disease involvement is warranted.

  14. DVT is a differential diagnosis for unilateral leg swelling + warmth post-CABG. Harvest site infection, hematoma, lymphedema, and DVT can all present similarly. If unilateral calf swelling + warmth + pain, consider venous duplex imaging. A patient with EVH may also have a DVT in the same leg (discuss imaging with surgeon).

  15. Swelling ≠ infection early post-op. Expected hematoma and edema are normal in the first week; swelling alone does not indicate infection. The combination of swelling + erythema + warmth + drainage + or systemic signs is the infection picture. Educate patients: "Some swelling is normal after surgery. Watch for spreading redness, warmth, drainage, fever, or red lines up the leg — those are signs of infection that need immediate attention."

cards.title: HAS-BLED Score
cards.quickAnswer: A 7-factor bleeding risk score for atrial fibrillation patients on or considering anticoagulation. Scored from hypertension control (SBP > 160), renal/liver dysfunction, stroke history, prior bleeding, INR lability (warfarin), age > 65, and concurrent antiplatelet/NSAID/alcohol use. Scores ≥ 3 flag modifiable bleeding risks — not a contraindication to anticoagulation. High HAS-BLED still favors anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2; focus on optimizing blood pressure, INR stability, and reducing unnecessary antiplatelet agents.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: A 7-factor bleeding risk score for atrial fibrillation patients on or considering anticoagulation. Scored from hypertension control (SBP > 160), renal/liver dysfunction, stroke history, prior bleeding, INR lability (warfarin), age > 65, and concurrent antiplatelet/NSAID/alcohol use. Scores ≥ 3 flag modifiable bleeding risks — not a contraindication to anticoagulation. High HAS-BLED still favors anticoagulation if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2; focus on optimizing blood pressure, INR stability, and reducing unnecessary antiplatelet agents.
cards.sourcePrecedence: Pisters R et al. *Chest* 2010 → Lane DA, Lip GYH review → Joglar JA et al. 2023 AHA/ACC AF guideline → Hindricks G ESC 2020 → Apostolakis S validation → Hardin/Kaplow → Bojar

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml: HAS-BLED is a clinical prediction rule that estimates major bleeding risk in atrial fibrillation patients who are candidates for or already on anticoagulation (Pisters et al., 2010). It was developed on the European Heart Survey cohort and refined through international validation (Apostolakis et al., 2011). The score identifies modifiable bleeding risk factors — particularly blood pressure control, INR lability on warfarin, concurrent antiplatelet agents, NSAIDs, and alcohol use — not to serve as a contraindication to anticoagulant therapy. Current guidelines (Joglar et al., 2024; Hindricks et al., 2021) emphasize that high HAS-BLED does not automatically mean withhold anticoagulation; instead it signals the need to optimize modifiable risks and confirm net clinical benefit via CHA₂DS₂-VASc.

sections.heading: 2. Scoring Table
sections.bodyHtml:
HAS-BLED is calculated as the sum of points below. Maximum score is 9.

Factor Criterion Points
H — Hypertension Uncontrolled; SBP > 160 mmHg or on antihypertensive therapy 1
A — Abnormal renal function Serum Cr > 200 µmol/L, dialysis, or kidney transplant 1
Abnormal liver function Cirrhosis, bilirubin > 2× ULN, or AST/ALT/alkaline phosphatase > 3× ULN
(Abnormal renal OR liver can contribute up to 2 points total)
S — Stroke history Prior stroke, TIA, or thromboembolism 1
B — Bleeding history Prior major bleeding or bleeding predisposition (e.g., known coagulopathy, anemia requiring transfusion) 1
L — Labile INR Time in therapeutic range (TTR) < 60% on warfarin 1
E — Elderly Age > 65 years 1
D — Drugs or alcohol Antiplatelet agent (aspirin, clopidogrel) concurrent with anticoagulation, or NSAID use 1
Alcohol abuse (≥ 8 drinks per week) 1
(Drugs/alcohol can contribute up to 2 points total)

Total possible: 9 points

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Use
sections.bodyHtml:
Score Risk Category Clinical Implication
0 Low risk Consider anticoagulation per stroke risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 1)
1–2 Moderate risk Anticoagulation benefit typically outweighs risk; optimize any modifiable factors
≥ 3 High risk Flag for modifiable factors (uncontrolled BP, labile INR, concurrent antiplatelet/NSAID, alcohol); do NOT automatically withhold anticoagulation; confirm net benefit via CHA₂DS₂-VASc (usually still favors anticoagulation unless CHA₂DS₂-VASc 0–1)

Critical principle: A high HAS-BLED score identifies opportunities to reduce bleeding risk — it does not mean anticoagulation is contraindicated. The balance of stroke prevention vs bleeding prevention is determined by comparing both HAS-BLED and CHA₂DS₂-VASc together with clinical judgment.

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Applications at Bedside
sections.bodyHtml:
• Admission assessment: Calculate HAS-BLED on all AF patients, especially those newly admitted or with history of AF and anticoagulation consideration.
  • Discharge planning: Recalculate or review at discharge for AF and post-operative AF (POAF) patients going on or continuing anticoagulation.
  • Modifiable factor tracking: Use HAS-BLED as a teaching tool during hospitalization. Example: "Your HAS-BLED is 4 today because of uncontrolled blood pressure (160), age 72, and your NSAID — let's control BP this admission, and we'll stop the NSAID at discharge."
  • Trending: Reassess if a modifiable factor changes (e.g., BP control improves, patient stops NSAID, warfarin INR stability improves). Score may drop as risks are addressed.
  • Team conversations: Present alongside CHA₂DS₂-VASc when discussing anticoagulation initiation or continuation with patients and families. Emphasize that high HAS-BLED does not mean "no blood thinner" — it means "optimize and monitor carefully."

sections.heading: 5. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
• HAS-BLED is a flag, not a veto. High score signals modifiable risks and need for vigilant monitoring, not automatic cessation of anticoagulation. Most patients with HAS-BLED ≥ 3 still derive net benefit from anticoagulation for stroke prevention.

  • Only one factor (labile INR) is specific to warfarin. DOAC-treated patients do not accrue points for INR lability, making DOACs attractive in unstable INR scenarios. Recalculate HAS-BLED if switching from warfarin to DOAC and vice versa.

  • Three to four factors are broadly modifiable: uncontrolled hypertension (lowest-hanging fruit), concurrent antiplatelet/NSAID use (often unnecessary in AF), alcohol abuse (commonly overlooked), and INR optimization on warfarin. Renal/liver/bleeding history are less modifiable; age is fixed.

  • Post-cardiac surgery context: Temporary elevation of HAS-BLED may occur due to transient anemia, renal dysfunction, or recent bleeding. Do not necessarily withhold anticoagulation; reassess in 1–2 weeks as these factors normalize.

  • Net-benefit comparison is key. A patient with CHA₂DS₂-VASc 4–5 and HAS-BLED 3–4 nearly always has stroke risk that outweighs bleeding risk on anticoagulation (Lane & Lip, 2016). Guidelines support anticoagulation continuation. Conversely, if CHA₂DS₂-VASc is 0–1, even moderate HAS-BLED may tilt the decision toward deferring anticoagulation.

  • Alcohol is the most overlooked modifiable factor. Direct screening: "How many drinks per week?" — many patients underestimate. ≥ 8 drinks/week is the threshold; counsel all heavy drinkers.

  • Uncontrolled hypertension (SBP > 160) is the easiest target to fix. Aggressive BP control (goal SBP < 140–150 in most AF patients) directly reduces intracerebral hemorrhage and other bleeding complications.

  • Concurrent antiplatelet use without clear indication is common. Many AF patients have aspirin prescribed for unclear reasons; removing it (if coronary artery disease is stable or not present) drops HAS-BLED and simplifies anticoagulation.

  • In frail, elderly, or high-fall-risk patients, pair HAS-BLED with functional/cognitive assessment. HAS-BLED ≥ 3 combined with high fall risk, severe frailty, or cognitive impairment may prompt discussion of alternative strategies (e.g., left atrial appendage occlusion if truly too high-risk for anticoagulation).

  • DOAC is often preferred over warfarin in high HAS-BLED patients because labile INR is eliminated from the equation and DOACs have more predictable pharmacology. If the patient is on warfarin with TTR < 60%, consider conversion.

  • Do not confuse HAS-BLED with CHA₂DS₂-VASc. HAS-BLED predicts bleeding risk; CHA₂DS₂-VASc predicts stroke risk. Both scores drive the anticoagulation decision together, not independently.

  • Reassess HAS-BLED after BP optimization or NSAID withdrawal — the score may drop, validating the intervention to the patient and strengthening the case for continuing anticoagulation.

  • In the ICU or early post-op, transient anemia and renal injury can spike HAS-BLED temporarily — use this as a prompt to optimize, not defer anticoagulation once the patient is stable.

  • LAA occlusion device (Watchman) is a team-based alternative for AF patients deemed truly unsuitable for long-term anticoagulation despite HAS-BLED optimization. This is not a routine bedside decision, but awareness that it exists supports shared decision-making conversations.

cards.title: Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM)
cards.quickAnswer: HCM is a genetic cardiomyopathy (usually sarcomere mutation) with septal wall thickness ≥15 mm or ≥13 mm with family history. LVOT obstruction (gradient ≥30 mmHg resting or provoked) creates dynamic obstruction worsened by dehydration, diuretics, and vasodilators. Beta-blockers are first-line for symptomatic obstructive disease; mavacamten (EXPLORER-HCM 2020) is a new sarcomere myosin inhibitor for refractory cases. Septal myectomy (surgical gold standard) or alcohol ablation for gradient ≥50 mmHg refractory to medical therapy. SCD risk stratification per 2020 AHA/ACC guideline informs ICD decisions (family hx of SCD, LV thickness ≥30 mm, syncope, NSVT, abnormal BP response, LGE on cMR). Family cascade screening with ECG, echo, and genetic testing essential for all first-degree relatives.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Genetic cardiomyopathy caused by mutations in sarcomeric proteins (most commonly cardiac beta-myosin heavy chain, myosin-binding protein C, regulatory/essential light chains, troponins) leading to myocyte disarray, asymmetric septal hypertrophy, and dynamic left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction. Spectrum: obstructive (HOCM) vs. nonobstructive.

  • Epidemiology: Most common inherited cardiovascular disorder, ~1:500 general population. Autosomal dominant inheritance; 40–60% have positive family history. Genetic mutation identified in 40–60% of probands (predominantly sarcomeric genes).

  • Typical presentation: Young to middle-aged (teens to 60s), though can present at any age. May be asymptomatic on screening or symptomatic (exertional dyspnea, angina, syncope, palpitations). Spectrum ranges from athletes with massive LV thickness to mild septal hypertrophy with severe dynamic obstruction.

  • Why the ICU sees this: Pre-op myectomy or alcohol septal ablation for symptomatic obstructive HCM with refractory LVOT gradient ≥50 mmHg; admission for arrhythmia (new AF, sustained VT) or decompensation (syncope, HF); post-op recovery monitoring; ICD placement for primary SCD prevention.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Why this happens. Mechanism explanation.

sections.heading: Sarcomeric mutations and myocyte disarray
sections.bodyHtml: Mutations in sarcomeric proteins → abnormal force generation by myosin and regulatory proteins → myocyte disarray (chaotic arrangement; hallmark on histology). Disarray creates electrical substrate for arrhythmias and mechanical substrate for dynamic obstruction.

sections.heading: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy and LVOT obstruction
sections.bodyHtml:
LV septum thickens disproportionately (basal, midventricular, or apical). During systole, systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve leaflet is drawn toward the hypertrophied septum, dynamically narrowing the LVOT.

The "SLOW, FULL, SQUEEZED" mnemonic defines physiology:

  • SLOW (bradycardia) — increases diastolic filling time → increased preload → SAM resolves, obstruction decreases
  • FULL (adequate volume) — maintains preload; hypovolemia narrows LVOT
  • SQUEEZED (high afterload) — increased resistance resists SAM, decreases obstruction

LVOT gradient worsens with:

  • ↓ preload (hypovolemia, Valsalva, aggressive diuresis)
  • ↑ contractility (exercise, inotropes, catecholamine surge)
  • ↓ afterload (vasodilators, nitrates)

LVOT gradient improves with:

  • ↑ preload (volume, squatting, leg-press maneuvers)
  • ↑ afterload (handgrip, phenylephrine)
  • ↓ contractility (beta-blockers, non-DHP CCB)

sections.heading: Secondary consequences
sections.bodyHtml:
• Mitral regurgitation: secondary to SAM; occurs in ~50% of obstructive HCM
  • Diastolic dysfunction: thick, stiff LV requires high filling pressures; impaired relaxation; risk of atrial fibrillation from chronic LA pressure elevation
  • Microvascular ischemia: small-vessel coronary dysfunction (epicardial coronaries normal); contributes to angina, fibrosis, and SCD substrate
  • Myocardial fibrosis: visible on cardiac MRI as late gadolinium enhancement (LGE); strong SCD risk marker

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context & Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: What the patient looks like at bedside. Observable signs and epidemiology.

sections.heading: Asymptomatic presentation (30–40%)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Diagnosed incidentally on echo for other reasons or via family screening
  • May carry substantial SCD risk if high-risk features present (family hx of SCD, massive LVH, LGE)

sections.heading: Symptomatic presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Dyspnea — exertional (most common) or at rest; due to diastolic dysfunction, SAM-induced MR, or dynamic obstruction
  • Exertional syncope or presyncope — ominous sign; suggests LVOT obstruction, arrhythmia, or inadequate BP response to exercise
  • Angina — exertional chest discomfort mimicking coronary artery disease; due to LVOT obstruction, subendocardial ischemia, or concurrent CAD
  • Palpitations — from frequent ectopy, paroxysmal AF, or SVT
  • Sudden cardiac death — feared outcome, may be first manifestation in young athletes or family members
  • Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea — from pulmonary congestion; can be provoked by dynamic obstruction changing with body position
  • Atrial fibrillation — occurs in 20–25% of HCM patients; poorly tolerated (loss of atrial kick + LA pressure elevation = pulmonary edema, syncope)

sections.heading: Physical examination findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Systolic murmur at left lower sternal border — crescendo-decrescendo pattern (distinct from aortic stenosis, which is right upper sternal border)
  • Increases with Valsalva, standing, leg raise (↓ preload → ↑ obstruction)
  • Decreases with squatting, leg press, handgrip (↑ preload → ↓ obstruction) — pathognomonic finding
  • Bifid carotid pulse (bisferiens) — two systolic peaks; classic finding in obstructive HCM
  • Hyperdynamic, displaced PMI — sustained, forceful apex beat
  • S4 gallop — prominent atrial kick into stiff LV
  • Pulsatile hepatomegaly — if RV dysfunction or elevated RA pressure from pulmonary hypertension

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / Gather Information*
sections.bodyHtml: Systematic information-gathering; no actions yet.

sections.heading: History and symptom review
sections.bodyHtml:
• Exertional dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, palpitations, arrhythmia symptoms
  • Family history of HCM or sudden cardiac death (age and number of affected relatives)
  • Prior diagnostic testing (echo, ECG, cardiac MRI, stress testing)
  • Current medications (beta-blockers, CCBs, antiarrhythmics, diuretics, ACE-I/ARB)
  • Medication adherence and side effects
  • Activity level, competitive sports history, exercise limitations
  • Recent dehydration, illness, medication changes

sections.heading: Physical examination
sections.bodyHtml:
• Vital signs with orthostatic BP if appropriate
  • Heart rate and rhythm (regular vs. irregular)
  • Blood pressure in both arms
  • Cardiac auscultation — murmur character, response to Valsalva and position changes
  • Carotid pulse character (bifid)
  • Apical impulse — location, character (hyperdynamic)
  • Hepatic pulsatility
  • Lung sounds (crackles from pulmonary edema)
  • Peripheral edema, jugular venous pressure

sections.heading: Diagnostic review
sections.bodyHtml:
• Recent 12-lead ECG — LVH, Q waves (anterior or inferior), T-wave inversions (particularly "giant negative T waves" in apical HCM), QTc, LA enlargement
  • Transthoracic echocardiogram — septal thickness, LVOT gradient (rest, Valsalva, post-ectopic), SAM, mitral leaflet elongation, MR severity, LA enlargement, LV function
  • Cardiac MRI with LGE — fibrosis pattern, wall thickness accuracy, detection of apical HCM, assessment of SCD risk
  • Stress echo or exercise treadmill — LVOT gradient provocation, BP response, exercise tolerance
  • Holter monitor or rhythm monitor — NSVT runs, ectopy burden, paroxysmal AF
  • Genetic testing status — identified mutation and implications for family screening
  • Coronary angiography if CAD suspected (pre-op workup, age >50, risk factors)

sections.heading: Current clinical status
sections.bodyHtml:
• Hemodynamic stability (MAP, UOP, perfusion)
  • Arrhythmia status — regular rhythm vs. AF, heart rate control
  • Volume status — JVP, orthopnea, edema, weight trend
  • Recent interventions (myectomy, ASA, ICD placement, cardioversion)
  • Days post-op and trajectory if post-operative
  • ICU level of care and monitoring capability

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: For HCM diagnosis cards, management is organized by intervention category rather than Stable/Unstable fork.

sections.heading: 5A. Medical Management (First-line for nonobstructive HCM and initial therapy for obstructive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals:

  • Relieve symptoms
  • Reduce LVOT obstruction (if obstructive)
  • Prevent arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death
  • Optimize filling and hemodynamics
  • Facilitate family screening and genetic counseling

First-line medications:

Drug Mechanism Indication Dose/Notes
Beta-blockers (metoprolol, carvedilol, atenolol, propranolol) ↓ HR (↑ fill time); ↓ contractility; ↓ gradient Standard first choice for symptomatic HCM ± obstruction Start moderate dose; titrate to symptom relief or HR 60–80 target; continue indefinitely
Non-DHP CCB: Verapamil ↓ HR; ↓ contractility; ↑ LV filling Added if beta-blocker insufficient or inadequate symptom control Negative inotrope + chronotrope; avoid in reduced LVEF or significant obstruction with decompensation
Disopyramide (Class IA antiarrhythmic) ↓ dP/dT (contractility); negative inotrope; ↓ SAM Refractory LVOT obstruction despite beta-blocker + verapamil Often effective for gradient reduction; anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention); use cautiously in elderly

Avoid — worsen LVOT obstruction or contraindicated:

  • Diuretics — aggressive diuresis drops preload → worsens obstruction; use only for frank pulmonary edema
  • Vasodilators (nitrates, high-dose ACE-I/ARB, hydralazine) — drop afterload → worsen dynamic obstruction
  • DHP calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nifedipine) — pure vasodilation; contraindicated in obstructive HCM
  • Positive inotropes (digoxin, dobutamine, milrinone) — increase contractility → worsen gradient and obstruction
  • Digoxin — specifically contraindicated in obstructive HCM (positive inotropy worsens gradient)

Symptomatic HF (nonobstructive HCM or decompensated obstructive HCM):

  • Consider cautious ACE-I/ARB + beta-blocker for HFrEF trajectory
  • Diuretics for pulmonary congestion, but avoid hypovolemia
  • Aldosterone antagonist may be considered

sections.heading: 5B. Mavacamten (New pharmacologic option)
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: First-in-class cardiac myosin inhibitor — directly reduces cardiac myosin function; ↓ contractility and LVOT gradient

FDA approval: 2022 for symptomatic obstructive HCM

Indication: LVOT obstruction (gradient ≥50 mmHg at rest or ≥30 mmHg provoked) remaining symptomatic despite optimized beta-blocker and/or CCB therapy

Key evidence: EXPLORER-HCM trial (Olivotto et al., 2020) demonstrated mavacamten improves exercise capacity and substantially reduces LVOT gradient; sustained benefit at 1-year follow-up.

Dosing and monitoring:

  • Starts low (~2.5 mg daily); titrate carefully based on symptom response and echo findings
  • Requires baseline echocardiogram and serial echo monitoring (3 months, 6 months, then annually) for LV function and gradient assessment
  • Risk: potential for LV dysfunction at higher doses; careful dose titration essential
  • Cost: expensive; insurance barriers common
  • Drug interactions: moderate CYP3A4 inhibitor; verify with patient's other medications
  • Excellent option for young, symptomatic obstructive HCM patients as bridge to or alternative to invasive therapy

sections.heading: 5C. Septal Reduction Therapy (Myectomy vs. Alcohol Septal Ablation)
sections.bodyHtml:
Indications for invasive therapy:

  • Symptomatic obstructive HCM (NYHA II–IV dyspnea, exertional syncope, limiting angina)
  • LVOT gradient ≥50 mmHg at rest or ≥80 mmHg provoked (some centers use different cutoffs)
  • Refractory to optimal medical therapy (beta-blocker + verapamil ± disopyramide) with inadequate symptom relief or unacceptable side effects

A. Surgical Septal Myectomy (Gold Standard)

Feature Detail
Definition Surgical resection of basal interventricular septum via transaortic approach under direct visualization to relieve LVOT obstruction
Approach Median sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass, transaortic (through aortic valve) or transventricular
Success rate ~95% eliminate or significantly reduce LVOT obstruction; symptom relief in >85%
Operative mortality <1–2% at specialized centers; higher at lower-volume centers
Complications Iatrogenic VSD (rare, <1% with modern extended myectomy); heart block requiring PPM (~5–10%); residual/recurrent SAM (~5%); bleeding; VT/AF
Concurrent MV repair ~5–10% require; most do not if septal resection adequate
Advantage Durable symptom relief; direct visualization; can assess and address MV pathology; lower re-intervention rate than ASA
Disadvantage Surgical risk; median sternotomy; longer recovery; PPM risk (~10%); requires experienced cardiac surgeon at high-volume center
Referral consideration Preferred in younger patients, first-time intervention, or if MV pathology suspected

B. Alcohol Septal Ablation (Percutaneous)

Feature Detail
Definition Catheter-based delivery of ethanol into septal perforator artery → controlled myocardial infarction of basal septum; septal thinning and LVOT relief over weeks/months
Approach Right heart catheterization; locate first or second septal perforator; temporary occlusion balloon to ensure blood supply to target only; ethanol infusion; gradual septal necrosis
Success rate ~80–90% reduce gradient significantly; symptom relief in 70–80%
Procedure mortality <1% in experienced centers; rare but possible complications (complete heart block, tamponade, septal rupture)
Complications Permanent pacemaker requirement: 15–30% (much higher than myectomy); heart block common from septal necrosis; VT/VF risk from scar; residual/recurrent obstruction (~5–10% re-intervention); MI of non-target territory if ethanol leaks
Advantage Percutaneous; no surgery; shorter hospitalization; lower initial mortality; suitable for high-surgical-risk patients, elderly
Disadvantage High PPM rate (15–30%); ventricular scar substrate for VT; cannot address MV pathology; less durable (higher re-intervention); arrhythmia risk from necrotic scar
Referral consideration Preferred in elderly (>70), high surgical risk, or recurrent obstruction after prior myectomy

Choice between myectomy vs. ASA:

  • Myectomy preferred: Young patient, first intervention, potential MV involvement, lower PPM tolerance
  • ASA considered: Elderly >70, high surgical risk, patient preference for percutaneous approach
  • Referral: high-volume HCM center (Center of Excellence) with expertise in both procedures

sections.heading: 5D. Sudden Cardiac Death Prevention (ICD Risk Stratification)
sections.bodyHtml:
SCD risk stratification per 2020 AHA/ACC HCM Guideline:

Major risk factors (any one = consider ICD):

  • Prior cardiac arrest (VF, VT)
  • Sustained VT
  • Family history of HCM with SCD (especially ≤50 years or multiple family members)
  • LV wall thickness ≥30 mm
  • Unexplained syncope (exertional or nocturnal)
  • NSVT on Holter monitor (≥3 consecutive beats at HR >120)

Minor risk factors (cumulative; inform discussion):

  • LGE on cardiac MRI (any extent)
  • Abnormal BP response to exercise (failure of SBP to increase ≥20 mmHg or paradoxical drop)
  • LV apical aneurysm
  • High-risk LVOT obstruction pattern
  • Atrial fibrillation

ICD decision: Primary prevention ICD typically offered to patients with HCM + ≥2 major risk factors, or 1 major + ≥2 minor factors, or individualized assessment. Class IIa recommendation in high-risk subset per ACC/AHA 2020 (Ommen et al.).

Additional risk calculator: European HCM Risk-SCD calculator (web-based) incorporates US major/minor factors plus family history of SCD, LGE extent, LV apical aneurysm, abnormal BP response → 5-year SCD risk estimate. Different approach than US guideline; useful for informed discussion.

Family screening and genetic counseling:

  • All first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) should undergo screening:
  • 12-lead ECG
  • Transthoracic echocardiogram
  • Consider stress echocardiography if baseline echo normal
  • Annual screening from ~age 15 until age 50 (penetrance rare after 50)
  • Genetic testing: Proband should undergo molecular testing (if not already done); identified mutation enables targeted cascade screening of relatives
  • Genetic counseling essential — autosomal dominant inheritance means 50% of first-degree relatives carry mutation
  • Discussion of athletic participation restrictions, activity counseling, symptom recognition

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Trigger-to-escalation criteria:

Situation Action Contact
Syncope or presyncope in known HCM STAT call; evaluate for arrhythmia, gradient worsening, or hemodynamic collapse APP/attending + charge nurse; consider ED evaluation if no recent assessment
New-onset AF with rapid ventricular response (HR >120) or symptoms STAT escalation; pads on; prepare for rate/rhythm control or cardioversion APP/fellow + RRT if unstable
New NSVT detected on monitoring Notify APP; obtain 12-lead ECG and troponin On-call cardiology; EP consult if sustained or hemodynamically significant
Acute decompensation (dyspnea, pulmonary edema, hypotension) STAT escalation; call team immediately APP + RRT; prepare for possible transfer to higher level of care
Recurrent syncope or presyncope Emergency assessment; rule out malignant arrhythmia ED / cardiology urgent evaluation

SBAR template for escalation:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room]. This is a [age]-year-old with HCM s/p [procedure or medical management]." B: "[Duration of care]; known LVOT gradient [value]; on [current meds]. Last echo [date]; genetic status [mutation known or not]." A: "Patient has developed [symptom/finding]. HR [value], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. [Exam findings — murmur, orthostasis, etc.]. [Recent labs if relevant]." R: "Requesting [specific action — rate control orders, cardioversion prep, higher level of care, additional testing]."

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are.

Pathophysiology detail — Sarcomeric mutations and myocyte disarray The ~1:500 prevalence of HCM reflects the diversity of sarcomeric mutations:
  • Beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7) — ~35% of genotyped patients; often associated with early-onset and severe phenotype
  • Myosin-binding protein C (MYBPC3) — ~25%; slightly later presentation, more benign course in some
  • Regulatory and essential light chains (MYL2, MYL3) — ~10%; often associated with apical HCM or unusual presentations
  • Troponins (TNNI3, TNNT2, TPM1) — ~5–10%; heterogeneous phenotypes
  • Other genes (titin, α-actin, etc.) — rare; newly discovered mutations emerging Myocyte disarray: the hallmark histologic finding — myocytes arranged chaotically rather than in organized parallel bundles. Creates:
    1. Mechanical dysfunction — asymmetric contraction, SAM generation
    2. Electrical substrate — disorganized conduction pathways, substrate for re-entry arrhythmias (NSVT, VT, AF)
    3. Fibrosis accumulation — visible on cMR as LGE; strong SCD risk marker; associated with reduced strain imaging Phenotypic variability: same mutation can present with ranges of wall thickness, gradient, and SCD risk. Environmental factors (exercise, dehydration, infection, pregnancy, surgical stress) can precipitate decompensation or arrhythmia in mutation carriers.
Diagnostic criteria and severity tables HCM diagnostic criteria (2020 AHA/ACC):
CriterionDefinition
LV wall thickness ≥15 mm on echo (or ≥13 mm with family hx of HCM)Major diagnostic criterion
LVOT obstruction (resting gradient ≥30 mmHg or provoked ≥50 mmHg)Defines obstructive phenotype; not required for diagnosis
Genetic mutation in sarcomeric geneSupports diagnosis; found in 40–60%
Family history of HCM or SCDEnhances likelihood
LV wall thickness classification:
ThicknessRisk assessment
<15 mmNot diagnostic for HCM (does not meet major criterion)
15–29 mmTypical range; SCD risk present if other features (family hx, syncope, NSVT, LGE)
≥30 mmMassive LVH — independent SCD risk factor; warrants aggressive risk assessment and ICD evaluation
LVOT gradient severity:
GradientClassificationClinical significance
<30 mmHgNonobstructive HCMNot clinically significant; medical therapy not indicated for obstruction
30–50 mmHgBorderline / labile obstructionMay worsen with exertion; symptom-dependent; consider beta-blocker/CCB
≥50 mmHgClinically significant obstructionWarrants medical optimization; if symptomatic despite meds, consider myectomy/ASA
>100 mmHg (stress-provoked or rest)Severe obstructionOften symptomatic; high syncope risk; interventional referral indicated
Diagnostic testing and SCD risk assessment Key diagnostic tests:
TestRoleKey HCM findings
ECGFirst-line screeningLVH; deep Q waves (anterior > inferior, can mimic MI); T-wave inversions (deep, often in II–V1; "giant negative T waves" in apical HCM); prolonged QTc; left axis deviation; P-wave broadening (LA enlargement)
Echocardiogram (TTE)Primary diagnostic testSeptal thickness ≥15 mm (can exceed 30 mm); asymmetric pattern; LVOT gradient at rest, Valsalva, or post-ectopic; SAM; mitral leaflet elongation; MR severity; LA enlargement; LV function
Stress echocardiographyProvokes latent LVOT obstruction~30% of asymptomatic/mildly symptomatic patients have no resting gradient but develop significant obstruction (≥50 mmHg) with exercise or Valsalva; critical for risk stratification
Cardiac MRI (cMR) with LGEGold standard for tissue characterization and SCD riskLGE pattern (fibrosis location and extent) predicts arrhythmia risk and SCD; LGE correlates with NSVT and syncope; excellent for apical HCM detection; accurate wall thickness assessment; emerging prognostic tool
24–48 h Holter or rhythm monitorAnnual arrhythmia surveillanceNSVT runs (≥3 consecutive beats at HR >120) = SCD risk factor; ectopy burden; paroxysmal AF detection
Treadmill exercise test with BP responseRisk stratification; exercise toleranceAbnormal BP response (failure of SBP to increase ≥20 mmHg or paradoxical drop) = SCD risk factor; helps identify high-risk patients; assess functional capacity
Genetic testingIdentifies pathogenic variant; enables family screeningSarcomeric genes (see Teaching Layer 7.1 for breakdown); mutation allows targeted cascade screening of first-degree relatives
Coronary angiographyPre-op workup if CAD suspected or age >50Epicardial coronaries typically normal in primary HCM (excludes secondary causes); invasive gradient measurement possible
SCD risk calculation approaches: US guideline approach (Ommen et al., 2020): count major and minor risk factors → binary decision (ICD yes/no). European HCM Risk-SCD calculator: web-based tool incorporating US factors + family SCD history + LGE extent + apical aneurysm + abnormal BP response → 5-year SCD risk percentage. Useful for prognostication and shared decision-making.
Valsalva maneuver and SAM pathophysiology — bedside teaching

HCM murmur: increases with Valsalva (↓ preload → ↑ SAM → ↑ LVOT obstruction → louder murmur). Increases with standing (blood pools in legs, ↓ preload).

Decreases with squatting or leg press (↑ preload → ↓ SAM → quieter murmur). This opposite response is pathognomonic.

Why? In AS, more force = louder murmur. In HCM, less preload = more SAM = more obstruction = louder. The dynamic nature makes the murmur change with loading conditions.

Teaching moment at bedside: "Watch what happens to the murmur as the patient stands up slowly, then squats down. In HCM, the murmur gets LOUDER when they stand (less blood in the heart), and QUIETER when they squat (more blood in the heart). That's the opposite of aortic stenosis."

Athlete's heart vs. HCM differentiation Young athletes with elite endurance training can develop LV wall thickness similar to HCM (~12–15 mm). Key differentiators:
FeatureAthlete's HeartHCM
LV diastolic dysfunctionAbsent or mildPronounced; abnormal strain patterns
LA sizeNormalOften enlarged
Septum patternSymmetric hypertrophyAsymmetric
LVOT gradientNonePresent (≥30 mmHg)
Genetic mutationNone40–60% identified
Family history of HCM/SCDAbsentMay be present
LGE on cMRAbsentMay be present (strong SCD marker)
Regression with detrainingYes — hypertrophy regresses with 3–6 mo off trainingNo — permanent
Exercise toleranceExcellent; athlete continues high-level trainingVariable; many symptomatic with exertion
Cardiac MRI is key differentiator — athlete's heart shows no LGE; HCM typically shows LGE (fibrosis burden). Also assesses diastolic parameters more accurately than echo. Implications: Athletes with HCM are restricted from competitive and intense recreational athletics due to SCD risk with extreme exertion. Requires cardiology assessment, genetic counseling, family screening, and activity restriction counseling.
Apical HCM (Yamaguchi syndrome) — rare, important variant

Definition: HCM with hypertrophy concentrated at the LV apex; can be isolated apical or coexist with basal septal hypertrophy.

Prevalence: ~2–10% of HCM patients; more common in Asian populations.

Presentation: Often atypical chest pain or asymptomatic; syncope less common than basal HCM.

ECG: Giant negative T-waves in the precordial leads (V1–V6); can mimic STEMI → common source of misdiagnosis.

Echo findings: Apical wall thickness ≥15 mm; "spade-shaped" appearance of apical chamber on apical 4-chamber view; often no LVOT gradient.

cMR: Gold standard for diagnosis; clearly shows apical-predominant hypertrophy; can detect LGE (apical fibrosis).

Risk: Can develop LV apical aneurysm (rare but associated with VT, SCD); LVOT obstruction less common but possible.

Prognosis: Generally more benign than basal HCM with LVOT obstruction, but SCD risk still present if high-risk features.

Teaching moment: "Patient with chest pain and giant negative T-waves on ECG — looks like STEMI, but echocardiogram shows apical hypertrophy, not coronary occlusion. Apical HCM can masquerade as an MI."

Amyloid phenocopy — distinguishing HCM from cardiac amyloidosis Cardiac amyloidosis (particularly wild-type transthyretin amyloidosis, ATTR-wt) can mimic HCM:
FeatureHCMCardiac Amyloidosis (ATTR-wt)
Age at presentationTeens to 60sUsually >60 (wt); can be younger if hereditary
GenderAutosomal dominant; equal M/FATTR-wt predominantly male (male predominance ~10:1)
Septum patternOften asymmetricUsually concentric (symmetric wall thickening)
ECGLVH, deep Q waves, T-wave inversionsVoltage-concordant LVH (low voltage in limb leads despite thick septum on echo)
Troponin/BNPOften normal in early diseaseOften markedly elevated
LGE pattern on cMRSeptal fibrosis; variableSubendocardial LGE (characteristic); often diffuse
Genetic mutationSarcomericTTR mutations (hereditary amyloid) or wild-type TTR (acquired)
Biopsy/AL testingNot needed for HCM diagnosisEndomyocardial biopsy showing amyloid + Congo red staining; genetic testing for TTR
Family historyHCM phenotype in relativesATTR-wt typically sporadic; ATTR-hereditary shows autosomal dominant inheritance of TTR mutation
PrognosisVariable; long-term survival possible with medical/interventional managementWorse prognosis historically; new treatments (transthyretin stabilizers, gene silencers) improving outcomes
Key teaching point: Older patient (>60) presenting with concentric LVH, low voltage on ECG despite thick walls, and elevated troponin/BNP → think amyloidosis before HCM. Cardiac MRI is essential for differentiation.
Mavacamten mechanism and EXPLORER-HCM trial Mavacamten (Camzyos®): First-in-class cardiac myosin inhibitor. Mechanism: Binds to the myosin head and reduces the rate of myosin-actin cross-bridge formation → ↓ cardiac contractility and ↓ LVOT gradient. Does NOT inhibit myosin ATPase activity (preserves basal cardiac function). EXPLORER-HCM trial (Olivotto et al., 2020):
  • Phase 3 randomized controlled trial in symptomatic obstructive HCM patients
  • Mavacamten vs. placebo over 16 weeks
  • Primary endpoint: reduction in LVOT gradient + improvement in NYHA functional class
  • Results: mavacamten reduced LVOT gradient by median ~50% (from ~68 to ~32 mmHg); improved exercise capacity; NYHA class improvement in responders
  • Safety: well-tolerated; serial echo monitoring required to detect LV dysfunction (rare but possible at higher doses); requires careful dose titration
  • 1-year data: benefits sustained; no unexpected safety signals Clinical implications:
  • Bridges gap between medical therapy and invasive intervention
  • Alternative to or bridge toward septal myectomy/ASA
  • Particularly valuable for young, symptomatic patients
  • Requires robust echo surveillance
  • Cost and insurance access remain barriers Dosing: typically starts 2.5 mg daily; titrate based on symptom response and echo findings. Doses up to 10 mg daily used in trials.
Disopyramide role in LVOT obstruction management Disopyramide: Class IA antiarrhythmic with strong negative inotropic effect (↓ dP/dT) and anticholinergic properties. Why it works in obstructive HCM:
  • The negative inotropic effect (↓ contractility) reduces SAM force
  • Anticholinergic effects (↑ HR slightly) may increase diastolic filling time
  • Often reduces LVOT gradient by 10–30 mmHg, sometimes more Indication: Refractory LVOT obstruction despite optimized beta-blocker + verapamil Dosing: typically 400–600 mg daily in divided doses (check current labeling; varies by formulation) Side effects and monitoring:
  • Anticholinergic: dry mouth, urinary retention, urinary hesitancy (problematic in elderly, BPH patients)
  • Can prolong QT interval → arrhythmia risk; requires baseline ECG and periodic monitoring
  • Negative inotropic → avoid if reduced EF or hemodynamic instability
  • Drug interactions: avoid with other QT-prolonging agents
  • Useful in HCM but less commonly used now due to side effect profile; mavacamten gaining preference Teaching point: "Disopyramide is not an antiarrhythmic we use in HCM because it's an antiarrhythmic — we use it because it has a powerful negative inotropic effect that reduces the heart's ability to squeeze hard, thereby reducing the LVOT obstruction. The anticholinergic side effects are the tradeoff."
LVOT obstruction handling in the ICU — avoiding the pitfalls The fundamental principle: obstructive HCM is the inverse of most cardiac post-op patients. Typical post-op cardiac patient: Keep them FULL, FAST, and pushing hard.
  • Full preload (maintain volume)
  • Fast heart rate (tachycardia okay)
  • Inotropes to increase contractility HCM patient: SLOW, FULL, SQUEEZED.
  • Slow heart rate (bradycardia beneficial)
  • Full preload (maintain volume)
  • Squeezed (high afterload; preserve systemic vascular resistance) What NOT to do in obstructive HCM:
    1. Aggressive diuresis — ↓ preload → ↑ LVOT obstruction → syncope risk. Even "standard" ICU diuresis protocols are dangerous. Only diurese for frank pulmonary edema, and monitor carefully.
    2. Vasodilators (NTG, nitroprusside, nicardipine, hydralazine, high-dose ACE-I/ARB) — ↓ afterload → ↑ SAM → ↑ LVOT obstruction. Do NOT reflexively use for hypertension in HCM. Use beta-blockers and increase afterload instead (phenylephrine preferred).
    3. Positive inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone, dopamine) — ↑ contractility → ↑ SAM → ↑ obstruction. Last choice. If hypotension needs support, phenylephrine (pure alpha) is preferred because it ↑ afterload without inotropic effect.
    4. Tachycardia from pain, anxiety, infection, or inadequate beta-blockade — every beat is wasted opportunity for diastolic filling. Aggressive pain control and anxiety management. Beta-blocker adherence non-negotiable.
    5. Dehydration or high-dose diuretics for "volume overload" — worsens obstruction. If patient has pulmonary edema and LVOT obstruction, the obstruction → reduced CO → pulmonary edema (secondary), not primary volume overload. Cautious diuresis + improve contractility reduction is the answer. Preferred pressors and agents:
    6. Phenylephrine — pure alpha-adrenergic; ↑ afterload without inotropic effect or reflex tachycardia. Vasopressor of choice in HCM.
    7. Beta-blockers — essential; titrate to HR 60–80 and symptom control
    8. Non-DHP CCB (verapamil) — negative inotrope; adds to beta-blocker effect What TO do:
    9. Maintain preload (adequate IV volume; monitor I/Os, CVP, daily weights)
    10. Optimize beta-blocker dose and timing
    11. Use phenylephrine for hypotension (not NTG or other vasodilators)
    12. Pain and anxiety control (reduces sympathetic surge)
    13. Monitor for syncope, dyspnea, hypotension as red flags for obstruction worsening

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these in stable patients; if any appear, re-escalate.

  • Syncope or presyncope — represents either dynamic LVOT obstruction with inadequate CO or arrhythmia; not a "fall" or routine syncope. Escalate urgently.
  • Sudden dyspnea or orthopnea — can indicate pulmonary edema from dynamic obstruction + MR, AF with loss of atrial kick, or developing arrhythmia.
  • New-onset irregular rhythm or palpitations — AF risk high in HCM; can precipitate hemodynamic collapse.
  • Persistent tachycardia despite pain/anxiety control — indicates inadequate beta-blockade, ongoing sympathetic surge, or arrhythmia. Verify medication compliance and escalate.
  • Hypotension trending down — may indicate inadequate preload, vasodilator over-use, inotrope failure, or cardiogenic shock from increased obstruction.
  • Declining urine output despite adequate intake — suggests decreased cardiac output from obstruction worsening or arrhythmia.
  • Increasing respiratory distress or O₂ requirement — pulmonary edema from dynamic obstruction, MR, or AF with RVR.
  • Chest pain not consistent with ischemia — can represent angina from LVOT obstruction or microvascular ischemia.
  • New murmur louder than baseline or new S3 — may indicate worsening SAM, MR, or developing HF.
  • Anxiety, restlessness, or altered mental status — subtle sign of perfusion failure; do not dismiss as "just anxiety."
  • Recurrent syncope after myectomy or ASA — recurrent/residual obstruction, block heart, arrhythmia; escalate for EP evaluation.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. "SLOW, FULL, SQUEEZED" is not intuitive. Make it a team mantra. A myectomy or ASA patient diuresed aggressively or given inotropes will crash from dynamic obstruction worsening. Opposite of typical post-op cardiac surgery thinking.

  2. Vasodilators are contraindicated in symptomatic obstructive HCM. Reflex reach for NTG or nicardipine for hypertension is dangerous. Use beta-blockers, increase afterload with phenylephrine instead.

  3. Diuretics are dangerous in obstructive HCM. Volume depletion → ↓ preload → ↑ LVOT obstruction → syncope or hemodynamic collapse. Use only for frank pulmonary edema, and monitor closely.

  4. Digoxin is contraindicated in obstructive HCM (positive inotropy worsens gradient). But low-dose digoxin for AF rate control is acceptable if other agents insufficient — nuance matters. Always clarify intent with team.

  5. Phenylephrine is the vasopressor of choice in HCM — pure alpha, no inotropic effect, no reflex tachycardia. Avoid epinephrine (inotropic + chronotropic) and dopamine (dose-dependent effects).

  6. DHP-CCBs (amlodipine, nifedipine) are contraindicated in obstructive HCM. Non-DHP CCBs (verapamil) are safe. Confusion is common; verify drug class before administering.

  7. Syncope in HCM is an emergency. Represents either LVOT obstruction with inadequate CO or malignant arrhythmia. Do NOT treat as routine "fall." Escalate to team urgently; consider ED evaluation if no recent assessment.

  8. The "silent" severe HCM patient adapts by restricting activity. Ask specifically: "How far can you walk? Do you get short of breath on stairs?" Don't accept "no symptoms" at face value if they've quietly limited their life.

  9. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac MRI is a major SCD risk marker. Not just a research tool — increasingly part of risk stratification for ICD decision-making. If cMR has been done, ask about LGE extent and discuss with team.

  10. Apical HCM (Yamaguchi syndrome) presents with giant negative T-waves and can mimic STEMI. Don't reflexively activate cath lab for "anterior MI" without echocardiographic correlation and checking for prior HCM diagnosis.

  11. Amyloid phenocopy of HCM — especially ATTR-wt in elderly males. Look for concentric hypertrophy + low voltage on ECG + elevated troponin/BNP. Cardiac MRI shows subendocardial LGE pattern (different from HCM). Genetic testing and TTR stabilizers may be indicated.

  12. AF + HCM: anticoagulation threshold is LOWER than traditional CHA₂DS₂-VASc. Even CHA₂DS₂-VASc score "low-risk" — HCM patients with AF almost always get anticoagulation. Stroke risk is higher due to LA substrate and diastolic dysfunction. Don't delay AC based on traditional scoring.

  13. Mavacamten is new and expanding non-invasive options for symptomatic obstructive HCM. If patient on it, monitor serial echo for LV dysfunction trends. Insurance barriers common; cost prohibitive. EXPLORER-HCM trial showed sustained benefit at 1 year.

  14. Alcohol septal ablation has ~15–30% permanent pacemaker rate — different risk profile than myectomy. If patient has undergone ASA and later develops bradycardia/blocks, this is expected complication, not procedure failure. Plan PPM accordingly.

  15. First-degree relatives MUST be screened. Autosomal dominant inheritance = 50% of siblings, children, parents at risk. Annual screening age ~15 to 50 is standard. If proband has identified mutation, targeted genetic screening of relatives is transformative for early detection.
