cards.title: Orthotopic Heart Transplantation (OHT)
cards.quickAnswer: Heart transplant = definitive therapy for end-stage heart failure refractory to maximal medical management. Post-op priorities: RV failure most common early complication — target iNO + milrinone; denervated heart HR 90–110 is normal, atropine ineffective — use isoproterenol for bradycardia. Lifelong triple immunosuppression (tacrolimus trough 8–15 ng/mL POD 0–3, then individualize + mycophenolate + prednisone taper) + mandatory endomyocardial biopsy surveillance (weekly × 1 month, then tapering). Rejection often asymptomatic — biopsy is diagnostic gold standard. Infection risk highest POD 0–30 bacterial, POD 30–180 opportunistic CMV/PJP. 1-year survival > 85%; 10-year ~55%.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, patient population.

  • Definition: Surgical removal of failed native heart and orthotopic replacement with donor allograft using bicaval (preferred, lower arrhythmia risk) or biatrial anastomotic technique. Irreversible commitment to lifelong immunosuppression and surveillance.
  • Typical patient: End-stage heart failure refractory to maximal guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), inotrope-dependent (SCAI Stage C–D), or bridged via mechanical circulatory support (VAD); biventricular or RV-predominant failure; elevated or reversible pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR); listed per UNOS criteria.
  • Operative details: CPB mandatory; cold ischemic time typically 4–6 hours (shorter better for outcomes). Standard LOS: ICU 1–2 weeks (often > 7 days due to RV failure, inotrope dependency, induction immune therapy); total hospital 2–4 weeks.
  • Expected lines on ICU arrival: central venous access, PA catheter (often POD 0–3 for RV assessment), Foley, pacing wires if bicaval technique, telemetry, likely dual iNO + milrinone for RV support, triple immunosuppression on board.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Denervated graft and allogeneic mismatch create unique post-operative challenges:

Denervated heart physiology

  • No vagal innervation — resting HR 90–110 is normal. Tachycardia alone does not indicate pain, infection, or hypovolemia.
  • Atropine completely ineffective — denervated heart has no parasympathetic response. Use pacing wires or low-dose isoproterenol for bradycardia instead.
  • No ischemic angina — denervated graft may not produce anginal chest pain even during coronary ischemia. Silent graft vasculopathy develops over years.
  • Blunted heart rate response to exercise — compensation via circulating catecholamines occurs over minutes, not seconds. Early mobilization requires hemodynamic monitoring.
  • Exaggerated BP response to catecholamines — avoid excessive epinephrine; titrate low-dose carefully.

RV failure vulnerability

  • Donor RV is "unconditioned" to the recipient's chronic PVR burden. Elevated recipient PVR exceeds donor RV capacity within hours of reperfusion.
  • Elevated CVP (> 12 mmHg), low CO, rising lactate, oliguria, hepatic congestion signal RV afterload mismatch.
  • Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (iNO, epoprostenol), milrinone (inotrope + vasodilator), low-dose epinephrine are cornerstones.

Allogeneic immunity + infection balance

  • Triple immunosuppression (CNI + antimetabolite + steroid) prevents rejection but increases infection risk across timeline: POD 0–30 bacterial; POD 30–180 opportunistic (CMV, PJP, fungal); POD > 180 EBV-driven PTLD, CMV reactivation.
  • Rejection can be completely asymptomatic — biopsy surveillance is non-negotiable, not PRN.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Recovery Arc
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner situational awareness — level-of-care transitions and timeline.

POD 0 (ICU): Arrival intubated; active rewarming; bleeding checks q15 min → q1h; assess RV function by hemodynamics (RAP, PCWP, CO); target extubation 6–12 h if RV stable, but many remain intubated through POD 1. Induction immunosuppression (ATG or basiliximab) + triple maintenance therapy (tacrolimus IV, mycophenolate, methylprednisolone pulse) initiated. iNO + milrinone routine for RV support. CMV and PCP prophylaxis started.

POD 1–7 (ICU → stepdown): Extubation if RV stable; inotrope weaning per hemodynamics and RV response; first endomyocardial biopsy (timing varies by program: POD 2–3 or per clinical indication). PA catheter removed when RV off pressors. Pacing wires available for rate control (denervation-related bradycardia). Foley out when stable and voiding. Transition to oral immunosuppression. Biopsy schedule initiated (q 1–2 wk × 3 months per protocol).

POD 7–discharge (stepdown/telemetry → floor): Full oral diet; oral immunosuppression established (tacrolimus target trough per team); continue triple therapy; advance mobility and cardiac rehab. Endomyocardial biopsies performed per schedule (non-negotiable). Intense discharge teaching on medication adherence, infection prevention, rejection symptoms, biopsy schedule, activity/driving/activity restrictions. Enrollment in post-transplant surveillance program — outpatient cardiology (biweekly/monthly for biopsies × 3 months), ID (lifelong), baseline CAV angiography screening.

Discharge (goal POD 21–28, varies widely): Lifelong triple immunosuppression + prophylaxis; established biopsy schedule; confirmed outpatient follow-up (cardiology, ID, cardiac rehab); medication list with no generic substitutions; written rejection/infection red flags; dietary/pet/travel restrictions; activity/driving permissions per local law.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering phase. No actions yet. Target: 10–15 min initial assessment.

Vital signs + perfusion - HR, BP, SpO₂, RR, mental status; capillary refill, skin temperature; urine output trend

Hemodynamics (if PA catheter in place) - RAP, PCWP, cardiac output, PVR; lactate, ABG

Physical exam - Lung auscultation (pleural effusions common), heart sounds, abdomen (hepatic congestion), edema, JVD

Surgical wounds + drainage - Sternal incision; CT output (should decline over POD 0–1); CTs still in place?

Recent labs - Tacrolimus trough, K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr, CBC, LFTs, coagulation studies, troponin, BNP

Medications - Immunosuppression (tacro, mycophenolate, steroid), prophylaxis (valganciclovir, TMP-SMX, antifungal), inotropes on board

Lines + devices - IV access (central lines), PA catheter presence/function, Foley, pacing wires (capture and sensing thresholds documented), telemetry

Biopsy schedule - Is patient due for endomyocardial biopsy today or this week? Confirm appointment in system.

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 (ICU — immediate post-operative)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goal: Stabilize graft, assess RV function, initiate immunosuppression and prophylaxis, control bleeding, prepare for extubation.

Bleeding management

  1. Check chest tube output q15 min × 2 h, then q30 min × 2 h, then q1h. Typical POD 0: 50–150 mL/h declining.
  2. Reexploration criteria: > 400 mL/h × 1 hr, or > 300 mL/h × 2–3 hrs, or > 200 mL/h × 4 hrs.
  3. Coagulation labs (PT, PTT, fibrinogen, platelets); T&C available; blood products per protocol.

RV function assessment

  1. Assess hemodynamics (RAP, PCWP, CO if PA catheter in place); target CVP 10–14 mmHg, PCWP 12–18 mmHg.
  2. If RAP > 14 or PVR > 3 Wood units: optimize preload, increase iNO (start 20–40 ppm, titrate to SpO₂ > 90% and PCWP goal), add milrinone (0.25–0.75 mcg/kg/min).
  3. Low-dose epinephrine (0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min) for inotropic support if CO still low despite iNO + milrinone.
  4. Rewarming complete; target core temp > 36.5°C.

Immunosuppression induction

  1. Induction antibody: Basiliximab 20 mg IV on POD 0 and POD 4 (or ATG 1.5 mg/kg IV daily × 3–5 days per protocol).
  2. Tacrolimus IV: 0.05–0.1 mg/kg/day divided BID/TID (target trough 8–15 ng/mL POD 0–3); level drawn at 12 h post-dose.
  3. Mycophenolate IV: 1000 mg IV BID (or 1500 mg PO BID if tolerating PO). GI side effects common; monitor for diarrhea.
  4. Methylprednisolone pulse: 500 mg IV daily × 3 days, then taper to 20 mg prednisone PO daily by discharge.

Infection prophylaxis — initiate day 0

  1. CMV prophylaxis: Valganciclovir IV (or PO if tolerating) — standard is 900 mg IV daily × 3–6 months (longer if D+/R− mismatch).
  2. PCP prophylaxis: TMP-SMX DS 1 tablet daily or 1 tablet 3×/week × 6–12 months.
  3. Antifungal: Fluconazole 400 mg daily or voriconazole per risk and protocol; typical duration 3 months.
  4. Bacterial: Perioperative antibiotics per protocol; discontinue post-operative cephalosporin/vancomycin by POD 1–2.

Extubation readiness (if RV stable)

  • Target extubation 6–12 h post-op if: RV off pressors, FiO₂ < 0.4, SpO₂ > 90%, SaO₂/FiO₂ > 200, alert/following commands, adequate pain control.
  • Many patients remain intubated through POD 1 due to RV dysfunction or bleeding risk.

sections.heading: 5B. POD 1–7 (ICU → Stepdown)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goal: Wean inotropes, transition to oral immunosuppression, initiate biopsy surveillance, prepare for stepdown level of care.

Inotrope weaning (POD 1–3 if RV stable)

  1. Assess RV response: HR, BP, SVR, lactate, UOP trend.
  2. iNO wean: decrease from 40 ppm → 20 ppm → 10 ppm over 24–48 h if RV tolerating (CVP stable, CO maintained, UOP ≥ 0.5 mL/kg/h).
  3. Milrinone wean: decrease from 0.75 → 0.5 → 0.25 mcg/kg/min over 24–48 h. Watch for rebound hypertension; may need beta-blocker.
  4. Epinephrine wean: discontinue once milrinone at maintenance.
  5. Do not wean too fast — RV failure can take 48–72 h to improve fully. Lactate and urine output are the best guides.

Transition to oral immunosuppression (POD 2–3 if tolerating PO)

  1. Tacrolimus PO: start 0.05–0.1 mg/kg/day divided q8h or q12h (check institutional protocol). Hold IV when PO level is therapeutic.
  2. Mycophenolate PO (switch from IV): 1000 mg BID.
  3. Prednisone PO: continue taper per protocol (typically 20 mg → 15 mg → 10 mg daily by POD 5–7).

Endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) — first biopsy POD 2–3 (timing varies by program; some centers do baseline or at clinical suspicion)

  1. Coordinate with interventional cardiology/cath lab.
  2. Sample 4–6 myocardial fragments from right ventricular septum and free wall.
  3. ISHLT grade result: 0R (none), 1R (mild), 2R (moderate), 3R (severe).
  4. Discuss result with transplant team same day — any ≥ 1R grade requires treatment discussion.

Pacing wire management

  1. Document atrial + ventricular capture and sensing thresholds each shift.
  2. Denervation may cause sinus rates 90–110 or episodic bradycardia (< 60 not uncommon and may be benign if asymptomatic).
  3. Pacing wire available for rate control if symptomatic bradycardia; do NOT use atropine.

PA catheter removal - Remove when RV off pressors and hemodynamically stable (CVP, CO, lactate normalized). Typical POD 2–3.

Foley removal - Remove when patient alert, hemodynamically stable, voiding on schedule. Typical POD 2–3.

Infection monitoring

  1. Daily temperature and cultures if febrile.
  2. CMV PCR q 1–2 wk (standard surveillance).
  3. CXR daily × 2, then per clinical indication (pleural effusions and atelectasis are common).

sections.heading: 5C. POD 7–Discharge (Stepdown/Telemetry/Floor)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goal: Full oral diet + medication, advance mobility, establish biopsy schedule, finalize discharge teaching and outpatient follow-up.

Oral medication optimization

  1. Tacrolimus trough target (long-term): 5–12 ng/mL per team protocol. Check level at least biweekly until stable.
  2. Mycophenolate: 1000 mg BID (switch to EC form if GI intolerance).
  3. Prednisone: taper toward 5–10 mg daily by discharge (specific taper schedule per protocol).
  4. Prophylaxis: valganciclovir, TMP-SMX, antifungal per protocol; continue indefinitely or per duration guidance.

Endomyocardial biopsy schedule (non-negotiable)

  • Weeks 1–12 POD: q 1–2 wk (4–6 biopsies typically).
  • Months 3–6: q 1 month.
  • Month 6+: q 3 months, tapering to annual after 1 year in stable patients.
  • Patient education: biopsies are mandatory for rejection surveillance, not scheduled PRN for symptoms. Rejection is often asymptomatic.

Rejection monitoring at bedside

  • Watch for subtle signs: new fatigue, mild fever (even 99–100.5°F), mild dyspnea, mild transaminitis (AST/ALT up).
  • Nurses often first to spot rejection through serial vital signs, mood, energy trends.
  • Escalate any concern to transplant team STAT — do not wait for biopsy result to treat if hemodynamically significant.

Cardiac rehab referral

  • Phase II cardiac rehab (supervised exercise progression); essential for post-transplant recovery.
  • Early mobilization improves outcomes and reduces delirium.

Dietary / infection prevention education

  1. Food: no raw/undercooked meat, eggs, unpasteurized dairy, raw shellfish. Cryptosporidium risk in immunocompromised — filter water or boil. Wash all produce.
  2. Pets: avoid stray animals, cats (Toxoplasma litter risk), reptiles/amphibians (Salmonella). Limit pet exposure.
  3. Travel: avoid endemic fungal zones (Histoplasmosis, Coccidioidomycosis) if possible; discuss with ID if necessary.
  4. Handwashing: frequent, especially before eating and after gardening/bathroom.

Activity + driving restrictions

  • Sternal precautions × 6–8 weeks: no lifting > 10 lbs, no bracing with arms during transfers, no driving if chest pain with braking.
  • Return to work: light duty 6 weeks, full duty by 3 months depending on job.
  • Driving: usually safe at 2–4 weeks post-op if not on high-dose opioids; check local law.

Medication education (CRITICAL)

  1. Take exactly as prescribed, every day, forever. This is #1 long-term determinant of graft survival.
  2. No generic substitution without permission — bioavailability may differ; tacrolimus brand consistency is critical.
  3. Tacrolimus levels are monitored; any brand change affects level.
  4. Refill prescriptions before running out.
  5. Written list of all medications (drug name, dose, frequency, refill source) provided to patient + copy to outpatient providers.

Drug interaction education

  • Avoid grapefruit, NSAIDs (nephrotoxic).
  • Statins: use pravastatin or rosuvastatin (less interaction with tacro than simvastatin/lovastatin).
  • Azoles (fluconazole, voriconazole) increase tacro levels significantly — monitor trough if started.
  • Notify ID/transplant team before adding any new medication.

sections.heading: 5D. Discharge (Long-term)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goal: Empower patient for lifelong adherence and surveillance; prevent rejection, infection, and CAV.

Lifelong immunosuppression

  • Triple therapy indefinitely: tacrolimus (trough per protocol, usually 5–12 ng/mL), mycophenolate (1000 mg BID), prednisone (5–10 mg or lower daily).
  • Dose adjustments based on trough levels, rejection episodes, infection rate, renal function.

Lifelong infection prophylaxis

  • CMV prophylaxis: valganciclovir 900 mg daily or per protocol; typical duration 3–6 months or longer if high-risk (D+/R−).
  • PCP prophylaxis: TMP-SMX DS daily or 3×/week; typical duration 6–12 months or lifelong if CD4-equivalent remains low.
  • Antifungal: azole (fluconazole or voriconazole) × 3 months typical, longer if endemic fungal zone or heavy immunosuppression.

Outpatient surveillance schedule

  • Transplant cardiology: weekly × 1 month, biweekly × 2 months, monthly × 3 months, q 3 months stable patients. Routine with scheduled EMB visits.
  • ID: per protocol, typically biweekly × 3 months, then q 3 months; lifelong monitoring for medication interactions, vaccine counseling, opportunistic infection risk.
  • Cardiac rehab: 2–3 times per week × 8–12 weeks minimum; progressive exercise with hemodynamic monitoring.
  • Baseline coronary angiography: within first month to establish CAV screening baseline.
  • Echocardiography: baseline post-transplant, then at intervals (1 month, 3 months, 1 year).
  • Endomyocardial biopsy: established schedule per protocol (q 1–2 wk × 3 mo → q mo × 3 mo → q 3 mo); patient education on adherence is critical.

Red flags — CALL IMMEDIATELY if:

  • New or worsening fatigue
  • New or worsening dyspnea
  • New or worsening palpitations or irregular heartbeat
  • Fever (even low-grade 99–100.5°F)
  • New or worsening edema (legs, abdomen)
  • Weight gain > 2–3 lbs per day
  • Decreased urine output
  • New abdominal pain
  • New chest pain
  • Do NOT wait for biopsy results — call if symptoms develop. Biopsy is scheduled, not PRN.

Outpatient medication reconciliation

  • Confirm no generic substitution of tacrolimus.
  • Verify all prophylaxis medications filled and understood.
  • Review drug interactions at each visit (especially statins, azoles, trimethoprim).

Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) screening

  • Baseline coronary angiography (often POD 0–14).
  • Repeat angiography at 1 year, then per protocol or clinical indication.
  • Risk factors: prior rejection, CMV, smoking, dyslipidemia, hypertension — aggressive risk factor modification.
  • CAV is accelerated atherosclerosis; denervated graft means silent ischemia — angiography is the diagnostic standard, not stress testing.

Lifestyle + long-term adherence

  • Smoking, alcohol: must quit. Accelerate CAV and infection risk.
  • Medication adherence: most important long-term factor. Non-adherence is #1 reason for late graft failure. Consider pill organizers, alarms, automated pharmacy refills.
  • Sternal precautions: continue × 6–8 weeks; avoid contact sports lifelong (cardiac trauma risk).
  • Pregnancy counseling (if applicable): high-risk; requires ID/OB/transplant co-management; avoid pregnancy in first year; discuss with team before conception.
  • Annual screenings: dermatology (full-body skin exam — melanoma risk 20–50×), eye (CMV retinitis), GYN if female (cervical cancer risk), colonoscopy age ≥ 50.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for transplant team notification:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [#] s/p heart transplant." B: "Patient is on day [#] post-transplant with triple immunosuppression and current tacro level [value]. [Recent relevant labs/hemodynamics]." A: "Patient [is stable/is unstable with the following signs]. [Specific clinical concern — bleeding, RV failure, rejection concern, infection, arrhythmia, etc.]." R: "Requesting [specific intervention — EMB, medication adjustment, escalation to ICU, etc.]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
RV failure refractory to iNO + milrinone CT surgery + Transplant cardiology STAT
Chest tube output > 400 mL/h or rising CT surgery STAT — possible reexploration
Rejection concern (fatigue, fever, LFT rise) Transplant cardiology STAT (do NOT wait for biopsy)
Fever + immunocompromised (POD > 7) ID consult + transplant team (CMV, PCP, fungal workup)
AF/arrhythmia unstable (hypotension, chest pain) CT surgery/fellow STAT + RRT; DCCV ready
Acute neurologic change Neurology STAT + transplant team (PRES, stroke, other)
Suspected bleeding complication CT surgery STAT
Acute abdomen or hemodynamic collapse CT surgery + general surgery STAT

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Cardiac denervation: what the transplant nurse must understand The donor heart loses all vagal and sympathetic innervation during harvest. Reinnervation occurs incompletely over years. Physiology:
  • Resting HR 90–110 is NORMAL. Do not interpret as tachycardia, pain, or infection.
  • Atropine DOES NOT WORK. The denervated heart has zero parasympathetic response. No vagal tone to block.
  • Bradycardia < 60: use pacing wires or low-dose isoproterenol (0.5–2 mcg/min IV drip), NOT atropine.
  • HR response to exercise is blunted. Compensation is via circulating catecholamines, which takes minutes. Early mobilization requires hemodynamic monitoring.
  • Exaggerated response to exogenous catecholamines. Avoid high-dose epinephrine; titrate low-dose (0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min) with blood pressure monitoring.
  • No angina with ischemia. Denervated graft does not perceive ischemic pain. Silent graft vasculopathy can develop undetected over years — coronary angiography surveillance is critical. Clinical pearl: The "HR 90" heart is doing fine. The "HR 50" heart needs pacing, not atropine. The asymptomatic transplant patient needs their biopsy anyway.
Right ventricular failure post-HT: pathophysiology and management RV failure is the most common early post-operative complication in heart transplant. It results from mismatch between an unconditioned donor RV and the recipient's chronic PVR burden. Mechanism:
  • The donor heart (typically from a young, brain-dead donor) has a normal RV adapted to normal PVR (< 2 Wood units).
  • The recipient with end-stage HF has chronically elevated PVR (often 3–8 Wood units or higher) from pulmonary vascular disease.
  • Upon reperfusion, the donor RV is suddenly exposed to the recipient's high afterload. If PVR is not acutely reduced, RV dilates, septum bows left, LV filling worsens → cardiogenic shock. Recognition:
  • Hemodynamic: CVP > 12 mmHg, PCWP 12–15, CO < 4, lactate rising, RAP-PCWP ratio > 1.5.
  • Bedside: oliguria, hepatic congestion, cool extremities, rising lactate, JVD.
  • Echo: dilated RV, hypokinetic RV, septal deviation toward LV. Management — first-line:
    1. Optimize preload: CVP target 10–14 mmHg (lower than traditional post-op; avoid RV overdistension).
    2. Reduce PVR aggressively:
    3. iNO (nitric oxide, inhaled): start 20–40 ppm, titrate to SpO₂ goal (> 90%) and PCWP goal (12–15). Selective pulmonary vasodilator; reduces PVR without systemic hypotension.
    4. Milrinone (IV): 0.25–0.75 mcg/kg/min. Positive inotrope + vasodilator; improves RV contractility + systemic vascular tone balance.
    5. Low-dose epinephrine: 0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min for additional inotropy if CO still low.
    6. Avoid excessive fluid: RV dysfunction is worsened by fluid overload. Gentle diuresis once pressors on board and CO stable.
    7. Mechanical support if refractory: ECMO rarely needed if proper pharmacologic management; decision within first 24–48 h. Weaning:
    8. Do NOT wean iNO/milrinone quickly. RV improvement takes 48–72 h. Lactate and UOP are best guides; tolerate higher CVP temporarily.
    9. Wean iNO first (40 → 20 → 10 ppm over 24–48 h), then milrinone (0.75 → 0.5 → 0.25 over 24–48 h).
Immunosuppression protocols: induction and maintenance Induction therapy (POD 0)
  • Basiliximab (anti-CD25 monoclonal AB): 20 mg IV on POD 0, then POD 4. Reduces early acute rejection. Lower cytokine release risk vs ATG.
  • OR ATG (anti-thymocyte globulin): 1.5 mg/kg IV daily × 3–5 days. More potent but higher fever/rash/cytokine release risk. Requires premedication (acetaminophen, diphenhydramine, sometimes steroids). Maintenance triple therapy — lifelong
    AgentTypical doseTargetMonitoringKey caveats
    Tacrolimus0.05–0.1 mg/kg/day (IV or PO)Trough 8–15 ng/mL POD 0–3; long-term 5–12 ng/mLLevel q 12 h initially, then per protocol (weekly × 1 mo, then q 2–4 wk). Renal function, K⁺.Nephrotoxic. Major drug interactions: statins (avoid simvastatin/lovastatin), azoles, diltiazem, grapefruit. Hyperkalemia risk.
    Mycophenolate1000 mg PO BID (mofetil) or 1500 mg BID (EC sodium)N/A; monitor CBCCBC q 1–2 wk × 1 mo, then per protocol. Watch for myelosuppression.GI side effects (diarrhea, nausea). EC form less likely to cause diarrhea. Trimethoprim increases level.
    PrednisoneStart 1 mg/kg, taper to 5–10 mg dailyN/ATaper schedule per protocol. Monitor glucose, BP, mood.Hyperglycemia, hypertension, insomnia, mood changes. Avoid abrupt discontinuation (rejection risk).
    Rejection treatment (if biopsy ≥ 1R)
  • Mild (1R): observation sometimes, or pulse methylprednisolone 500 mg IV daily × 3 days.
  • Moderate–severe (2R–3R): methylprednisolone 500–1000 mg IV daily × 3–5 days, then adjust chronic immunosuppression (↑ tacro target, ↑ MMF, ↑ prednisone) or add antibody therapy (OKT3, rabbit ATG).
  • AMR (antibody-mediated rejection): plasmapheresis, IVIG, rituximab (anti-B cell), eculizumab (C5 complement inhibitor); consider temporary escalation of CNI. Anticoagulation (post-HT standard, not transplant-specific but relevant)
  • Most programs do NOT start routine anticoagulation post-transplant unless mechanical prosthesis or prior clot risk.
  • If new AF developing, CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2 → anticoagulation discussion with team (balancing AF thromboembolic risk vs post-op bleeding risk).
Rejection classification: ISHLT grading system Acute cellular rejection (ACR)
  • 0R (Grade 0): No rejection; normal myocardium.
  • 1R (Grade 1, mild): Focal infiltrate, no damage. Often observed or treated.
  • 2R (Grade 2, moderate): Multifocal infiltrates, myocyte necrosis. Treat with pulse steroid + adjust chronic IS.
  • 3R (Grade 3, severe): Diffuse infiltrates, widespread myocyte necrosis, hemorrhage. Treat aggressively; consider antibody therapy. Antibody-mediated rejection (AMR)
  • Hallmark: C4d deposition on capillary endothelium, microvascular inflammation, endothelial injury.
  • May occur with or without concurrent ACR.
  • More aggressive than ACR; requires aggressive treatment (plasmapheresis, IVIG, rituximab). Chronic rejection (cardiac allograft vasculopathy, CAV)
  • Accelerated atherosclerosis of donor coronary arteries.
  • ISHLT grading: mild (1a), moderate (1b), severe (2–3).
  • Appears years post-transplant; denervation means silent ischemia — angiography surveillance is gold standard.
Endomyocardial biopsy: schedule, indications, result communication Schedule (ISHLT standard, variable by center)
  • Weeks 1–12 POD: every 1–2 weeks (4–6 biopsies typical).
  • Months 3–6: every 1 month.
  • Month 6+: every 3 months, extending to 6 months or annual in stable patients.
  • Additional: PRN if clinical concern (fever, fatigue, LFT rise). Procedure:
  • Performed in cath lab under light sedation. RV septal approach. 4–6 myocardial fragments.
  • Staining: H&E (morphology), immunohistochemistry (C4d for AMR), electron microscopy if indicated. Result interpretation by bedside nurse:
  • Grade 0R, 1R: often no intervention needed (though mild rejection may be treated).
  • Grade 2R, 3R: STAT notify team — medication adjustment and possibly hospitalization for IV therapy.
  • AMR: STAT notify team — unique treatment protocol. Patient education:
  • Biopsies are MANDATORY, not PRN. Rejection is often asymptomatic; biopsy is the only way to diagnose.
  • Schedule appointments well in advance; missing biopsy = missing early rejection → late-stage rejection/graft failure.
  • Biopsy itself is low-risk; complication rate < 1%.
Infection risk timeline and prophylaxis strategy

POD 30–180 (Intermediate): Opportunistic pathogens emerge. Triple therapy + rejection episodes at maximum intensity. - CMV: reactivation in D+/R− mismatch (donor-seropositive, recipient-seronegative = highest risk). Prophylaxis valganciclovir 900 mg daily × 3–6 months is standard. - PCP (Pneumocystis jirovecii): CD4 equivalent < 200; prophylaxis TMP-SMX DS daily or 3×/week × 6–12 months. - Fungal (Aspergillus, Candida, Cryptococcus, endemic mycoses): azole prophylaxis (fluconazole 400 mg daily or voriconazole) × 3 months typical.

POD > 180 (Late): Return toward baseline infection risk, but PTLD risk (EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disorder) emerging; CMV reactivation still possible; chronic immunosuppression maintains ongoing infection risk.

Prophylaxis duration varies by protocol and risk — always verify with ID/transplant team before stopping prophylaxis.

Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV): mechanisms and surveillance CAV is accelerated atherosclerosis of the donor coronary arteries, unique to transplant. Mechanism:
  • Alloimmune injury: rejection episodes trigger endothelial activation, smooth muscle proliferation.
  • CMV infection: associated with CAV progression.
  • Traditional risk factors: smoking, dyslipidemia, hypertension, metabolic syndrome.
  • Donor factors: donor age, ischemic time, donor cause of death. Natural history:
  • Appears over years (not months). Silent because denervated graft produces no angina.
  • Incidence ~50% by 5-year follow-up; major cause of late graft failure and death.
  • Presents as sudden death, MI, or graft failure — no warning. Screening:
  • Baseline coronary angiography: POD 0–14, establishes CAV-free baseline.
  • Repeat angiography: 1-year standard; then per protocol or clinical suspicion.
  • IVUS (intravascular ultrasound): used at some centers for early detection of intimal thickening.
  • Stress testing: limited value in denervated graft (blunted HR response). Angiography is gold standard. Prevention / risk factor modification:
  • ACE inhibitors / ARBs: reduce CAV progression.
  • Statins: pravastatin or rosuvastatin preferred (less interaction with tacro).
  • Smoking cessation: critical.
  • BP control: aggressive (target < 130/80).
  • Dyslipidemia management: statin + ezetimibe if needed. Treatment (limited options):
  • Retransplantation is the only definitive treatment, but rarely offered due to limited organ availability.
  • Some centers offer intravascular brachytherapy or drug-eluting stents in early focal lesions, but evidence limited.
Drug interaction reference for transplant maintenance Critical interactions to avoid: Tacrolimus + statins
  • Simvastatin, lovastatin: major ↑ in tacro level. AVOID.
  • Atorvastatin: moderate interaction; use lower dose, monitor trough.
  • Pravastatin, rosuvastatin: minimal interaction. PREFERRED. Tacrolimus + azoles (antifungal)
  • Fluconazole, voriconazole: major ↑ in tacro level. If azole needed, reduce tacro dose by 25–50%; check level in 3–5 days.
  • Posaconazole: even stronger interaction. Tacrolimus + diltiazem (rate control)
  • Can ↑ tacro level. Avoid if possible. Alternative: beta-blocker or verapamil (weaker interaction). Mycophenolate + trimethoprim (part of TMP-SMX)
  • Trimethoprim ↑ mycophenolate level. Watch for myelosuppression; check CBC. Tacrolimus + grapefruit
  • Grapefruit juice ↑ tacro level unpredictably. AVOID entirely. ACE-I / ARB + tacrolimus
  • Both affect renal function and K⁺ handling. Monitor Cr, K⁺ closely. OK to use together, but requires monitoring. General rules
  • Always verify new medications with transplant team or clinical pharmacist.
  • Avoid NSAIDs (nephrotoxic, interact with CNI).
  • Avoid live vaccines (contraindicated indefinitely).

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear, escalate to transplant team.

  • HR trending up despite rate control or iNO adjustment — possible rejection, infection, pain, hypovolemia; escalate.
  • Lactate rising, even mildly (> 2) — perfusion failure; RV may be decompensating. Review iNO/milrinone.
  • Urine output declining (< 0.5 mL/kg/h despite adequate MAP) — cardiogenic shock or rejection; escalate STAT.
  • Tacrolimus level jumping unexpectedly — drug interaction (azole started?), absorption change, medication adherence issue; verify.
  • New fever (even 99–100.5°F) + fatigue + mild LFT elevation — subtle rejection presentation; escalate.
  • Mild dyspnea or fatigue, patient "just doesn't look right" — reject early presentations are subtle; escalate.
  • Weight gain > 2–3 lbs in 24 h despite diuretics — possible acute rejection + fluid retention; escalate.
  • K⁺ rising despite no supplementation — tacro-induced hyperkalemia; hold K⁺ supplement, check renal function.
  • Cr rising (even 0.2–0.3 above baseline) — tacro nephrotoxicity or rejection-related cardiogenic shock; escalate.
  • Pacing wire loss of capture — may progress to bradycardia; verify threshold, notify team.
  • AF recurrence after successful cardioversion or amiodarone load — inadequate rhythm control; escalate.
  • New peripheral edema or JVD — volume overload or RV failure recurrence.
  • Chest tube output not declining as expected (still > 100 mL/h on POD 3) — persistent bleeding or possible infection; escalate.
  • Patient becoming withdrawn, anxious, confused — delirium often precedes hemodynamic collapse; escalate.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Atropine is completely ineffective in denervated heart. DO NOT ORDER IT. This is a critical safety point. Denervated heart has zero vagal tone. Use pacing wires or low-dose isoproterenol for bradycardia; never atropine.

  2. HR 90–110 at rest is NORMAL post-transplant. Do not confuse with tachycardia. Lack of vagal tone means baseline is higher. Only escalate if HR > 120 or trending up unprovoked.

  3. Rejection is often asymptomatic — biopsy schedule is non-negotiable, not PRN. Nurses spot rejection first through subtle signs (fatigue, mild fever, modest LFT rise). Do not skip biopsy because patient "feels fine."

  4. RV failure is the dominant early post-op problem, not LV failure. Elevated recipient PVR exhausts donor RV within hours. iNO + milrinone are foundational; do not wean too fast. RV improvement takes 48–72 h or longer.

  5. Tacrolimus drug interactions are rampant and critical. Statins: use pravastatin/rosuvastatin only. Azoles: reduce tacro dose if started. Diltiazem: avoid or use with extreme caution. Grapefruit: contraindicated. Always verify new medications with transplant team or pharmacist.

  6. CMV prophylaxis is universal early; do not stop prophylaxis early. Default is valganciclovir × 3–6 months (longer if D+/R−). Check program protocol; do not shorten course without explicit team order.

  7. PVR reversibility determines candidacy. Pre-transplant fixed PVR > 3 Wood units is contraindication. If borderline reversible, RV failure is common post-op. Pharmacologic reduction is standard.

  8. Tacrolimus levels are critical and volatile. POD 0–3 target 8–15 ng/mL; long-term 5–12 ng/mL (varies by protocol). Check level at least biweekly until stable. Renal dysfunction, infections, medication changes all shift levels. Do not assume level is stable.

  9. Patient adherence is #1 long-term determinant of graft survival. Missed doses = rejection risk. Non-adherence is #1 reason for late graft failure. Educate heavily on lifelong commitment; consider pill boxes, alarms, automated refills.

  10. Infection risk is lifelong, not just early. CMV can reactivate at any point. Opportunistic infections (PCP, fungal, EBV-driven PTLD) are lifelong risk. Vaccination responses wane. Lifelong ID vigilance required.

  11. PTLD can present as mononucleosis-like illness early (polymorph) or lymphoma late. EBV PCR elevation or node adenopathy + fever warrants urgent workup (node biopsy). Reduction of immunosuppression is key early treatment.

  12. Denervated heart = no angina with ischemia. Silent graft vasculopathy develops over years. CAV surveillance (coronary angiography baseline and 1-year) is mandatory because patient will not report chest pain.

  13. Sternal precautions are same as CABG: 6–8 weeks. No lifting > 10 lbs, no driving if chest pain with braking, no contact sports.

  14. Pregnancy is possible but high-risk. Counsel all women of childbearing age. Pregnancy possible but rare. Carries risks to mother (rejection, graft dysfunction, preeclampsia) and fetus (prematurity, IUGR, teratogenic IS agents). Requires ID/OB/transplant co-management. Avoid pregnancy in first year; discuss family planning before transplant.

  15. Discharge teaching is intensive — 3-hour sessions are not excessive. Medications (no generic substitution, exact timing), infection prevention (food/pet/travel), rejection symptoms (call immediately), follow-up adherence (biopsy non-negotiable), lifestyle (smoking cessation, cardiac rehab, activity restrictions) — all must be reinforced, written, understood before discharge.

cards.title: Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Hemodynamic Goals by Procedure
cards.quickAnswer: Post-op hemodynamic goals are procedure-specific and sometimes opposite. CABG / AVR / MV: MAP 65–90, SBP ≤ 140 to protect grafts and suture lines, CVP 8–12, CI > 2.2. Aortic Ascending / Arch Surgery (Open Repair), Bentall, Type A repair: SBP strictly ≤ 120, MAP 65–85. Myectomy / HCM: slow, full, squeezed — avoid tachycardia (< 80), avoid hypovolemia, avoid vasodilators. Transplant: HR 90–110 (denervated), MAP > 70. Always verify patient-specific orders against the generic table.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
• Definition: Consolidated reference of hemodynamic targets by procedure and post-operative phase, intended to answer "is this BP / HR / CVP appropriate for this patient?" in one bedside lookup.
  • Why post-op goals differ by procedure: the surgeon protects different anatomic structures. CABG prioritizes perfusion through fresh grafts but prevents over-pressurization of suture lines. Aortic surgery demands strict SBP control to protect the aorta. Myectomy / HCM requires a counterintuitive approach (slow, full, squeezed) to reduce dynamic LVOT obstruction. One size does not fit all.
  • Who it applies to: every adult cardiac surgery patient from admission through transfer/discharge.
  • Use at bedside: rapid lookup during rounds — "what MAP range am I defending today?" — not a stand-alone policy. Specific attending orders supersede this table.
  • Relationship to SharePoint: this card explains the why per procedure; the Pattern A lookup list is the canonical reference by Procedure × Phase.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why Goals Differ by Procedure
sections.bodyHtml:
Three competing physiologic demands drive the spread of hemodynamic targets:

  • Perfuse the repair or graft — sufficient MAP to fill coronaries, sustain cardiac output, and maintain end-organ perfusion.
  • Protect the repair or graft — excessive pressure risks burst suture lines (aortic anastomoses, fresh vein graft anastomoses, prosthetic seams) or cannulation site bleeding.
  • Respect the underlying physiology — HCM patients decompensate with tachycardia and vasodilation; denervated transplanted hearts depend on intrinsic rate (no vagal tone); RV-failing or pacing-dependent patients tolerate specific filling pressures.

These demands create a spectrum from CABG (moderate MAP, moderate SBP) to Aortic Ascending / Arch (strict SBP ≤ 120) to Myectomy (vasoconstriction-first, vasodilators forbidden).

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
This card applies to:

  • All adult cardiac surgery patients on post-operative days 0 through discharge / transfer.
  • Bedside nurses, advanced practice providers, residents, and intensivists titrating hemodynamic support.
  • Phase-dependent: POD 0 (ICU-level care), POD 1–3 (early post-op period, may still be ICU or stepdown), POD 4+ (late post-op, stepdown or floor).
  • NOT applicable to: pediatric patients (different targets), pre-operative patients (different physiology), non-cardiac surgery patients.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *at-bedside hemodynamic evaluation*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure observation and data gathering. No therapeutic actions yet.

Vital signs and output (q1h POD 0–1, q2h POD 2+):

  • Heart rate, rhythm (sinus, paced, irregular)
  • Systolic / diastolic / mean arterial pressure (arterial line or cuff)
  • Urine output (mL/h and mL/kg/h over 4–8 h)
  • Oxygen saturation (target ≥ 92% or baseline if COPD)
  • Core temperature (normothermia improves perfusion assessment)

Physical perfusion markers:

  • Mental status (alert, appropriate, responsive to command)
  • Capillary refill (< 2 s = adequate)
  • Skin temperature and color (warm, pink = adequate perfusion)
  • Extremity edema (new or worsening)

Lines and hemodynamic data (if present):

  • Central venous pressure (CVP) — if central line in place
  • Arterial line waveform (quality, dampening)
  • PA catheter data if present: SvO₂, PCWP, CO/CI
  • Chest tube output volume and character (sanguineous, serous, air leak)

Medication review:

  • Current drips: nitroglycerin, nicardipine, labetalol, esmolol, phenylephrine, norepinephrine, milrinone (drug + rate)
  • Recent titrations and patient response
  • Last dose / time of bolus medications (IV beta-blockers, vasodilators)

Procedure-specific context:

  • What procedure? CABG, valve, aortic, myectomy, transplant, VAD, ECMO? (Changes goals.)
  • When? POD 0–1, POD 2–3, POD 4–7? (Time-sensitive goals.)
  • Any intraoperative events? Prolonged CPB, excessive bleeding, dysrhythmia, difficult weaning? (Affects early post-op trajectory.)
  • Pacemaker status: epicardial wires in place? Pacing dependent or intrinsic rhythm?

sections.heading: 5.1 Default post-cardiotomy targets (most CABG / valve patients)
sections.bodyHtml:
Parameter POD 0 (ICU) POD 1–3 (early post-op) POD 4+ (late post-op)
MAP 65–90 mmHg 65–90 mmHg 70–90 mmHg
SBP 90–140 mmHg ≤ 140 mmHg ≤ 140 mmHg
HR 80–100 (paced or intrinsic) 60–100 60–100
CVP (if line present) 8–12 mmHg 8–12 mmHg n/a (usually removed)
SvO₂ (if PA catheter) > 65% n/a n/a
Cardiac index > 2.2 L/min/m² clinical proxy only clinical proxy only
UOP > 0.5 mL/kg/h > 0.5 mL/kg/h > 0.5 mL/kg/h
SpO₂ ≥ 92% (or baseline if COPD) ≥ 92% ≥ 92%

sections.heading: 5.2 Procedure-specific targets — *THE core reference*
sections.bodyHtml:
Every row below shows a deviation from §5.1 defaults. Absence of a procedure row means the default applies.

Procedure Key goal deltas Why
CABG (on-pump) SBP ≤ 140. NTG 5–20 μg/min × 24 h for graft protection. Prevent graft spasm; protect distal anastomoses. Monitor MAP to ensure grafts remain perfused.
CABG (off-pump, MIDCAB) SBP ≤ 140 (same as on-pump). Watch trend closely for ischemia; partial revascularization may be intentional (staged PCI plan). Incomplete revascularization is common; graft protection still applies.
AVR (tissue) SBP ≤ 140. HR 70–90. Protect aortic suture line; avoid diastolic underfilling of coronary beds.
AVR (mechanical) SBP ≤ 140. HR 70–90. Anticoagulation per surgeon day-by-day. Same as tissue plus mechanical valve thromboembolism risk.
Bentall / aortic root replacement SBP ≤ 120. MAP 65–85. Fresh aortic root + coronary reimplants carry higher blowout risk than standalone valve.
Aortic Ascending / Arch Surgery (Open Repair) SBP ≤ 120 (strictly). MAP 65–85. Beta-blockade first-line. Anastomoses + residual diseased aorta do not tolerate BP swings; dP/dt control essential.
Aortic Descending / TAAA / TEVAR Surgery SBP 100–120. MAP ≥ 85 to protect spinal cord. CSF drain may be in place; monitor CSF pressure if device present. Spinal cord perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF pressure; below 70 mmHg risks paraplegia.
Acute Type A dissection repair SBP ≤ 120 (strict). HR ≤ 80 to reduce dP/dt. dP/dt control prevents propagation of residual dissection.
Mitral valve repair SBP ≤ 140. Sinus rhythm preferred. Watch LV function (new systolic anterior motion risk post-repair). Preload-dependent; afterload mismatch common early post-op.
Mitral valve replacement (mechanical) SBP ≤ 140. Anticoagulation critical. HR 70–90. Thromboembolic risk is high; rate control reduces thrombosis risk.
Tricuspid valve surgery Watch CVP trend, not absolute value. RV recovery is slow. Allow CVP up to 15 mmHg short-term if patient perfusing. RV dysfunction is expected post-op; goal is forward flow, not perfect numbers.
MAZE (alone or concomitant) HR 70–90 (sinus rhythm preferred, but early AF is expected). New-onset AF in first 4 weeks post-MAZE is common and often self-resolves. DCCV usually ineffective until atrial scarring matures.
Septal Myectomy (HCM) MAP 70–90 with vasoconstriction if needed (phenylephrine preferred). HR 60–80, avoid tachycardia. Full preload — CVP 10–14 mmHg. Avoid vasodilators (NTG, nicardipine, milrinone — contraindicated). Dynamic LVOT obstruction improves with slow heart rate, full preload, and vasoconstriction ("slow, full, squeezed"). Vasodilation and tachycardia re-provoke obstruction and shock.
VAD (LVAD) MAP 70–85 (non-pulsatile — use Doppler cuff). Flow/RPM per device protocol. Avoid over-unloading (suction alarms). No pulse; MAP is the perfusion metric. Over-speed causes septal shift, RV failure, and suction events.
Heart transplant HR 90–110 (denervated — no vagal tone). MAP > 70. Watch for rejection signs (EF drop, new arrhythmia). Denervated heart depends on intrinsic rate + atrial kick for cardiac output. "Slow rate reflex" on hypotension will NOT occur.
Lung transplant MAP > 65. Avoid fluid overload — aggressive diuresis is standard post-op. PAP low-normal. Denervated lungs intolerant of pulmonary edema; RV-sparing strategy essential.
ECMO decannulation recovery MAP > 65. Watch cannulation sites for hematoma / bleeding. Full anticoagulation history complicates assessment. Transition from ECMO support to intrinsic cardiac output; bleeding risk high.

sections.heading: 5.3 Pacing targets
sections.bodyHtml:
Rhythm / wire state Rate goal Notes
Sinus rhythm, stable — (intrinsic) Wires on standby; check sensing and capture thresholds q shift.
Paced dependent (AV block, SSS) 80–90 bpm post-op Avoid excessively fast pacing; check output mA + sensitivity mV.
AF with slow ventricular response 80–100 bpm (if atrial wires) Consider atrial pacing over ventricular-only if wires available.
AV block, complete Pace at 70–90 bpm DDD if atrial + ventricular wires; VVI if only ventricular wire.
Loss of capture — Check wire connections, increase output, notify APP; transcutaneous pacing if symptomatic.
Atrial flutter / SVT Overdrive pace if atrial wires available Consult pacer wire routine protocol.

sections.heading: 5.4 Common agents used to hit targets
sections.bodyHtml:
Agent Effect Typical use Cautions
Nitroglycerin (NTG) 5–40 μg/min Venodilation > arterial; graft-protective Post-CABG routine × 24 h; selective hypertension control Monitor for headache, tolerance; discontinue per order (often over-continued into POD 2)
Nicardipine 2.5–15 mg/h Smooth arterial vasodilation Aortic surgery SBP control; HTN on POD 1+ Rebound HTN if weaned too fast; monitor BP closely
Labetalol 20–80 mg IV q10 min PRN α + β blockade Aortic/root/dissection dP/dt control Watch for bradycardia + hypotension combo; reflex tachycardia in some patients
Esmolol 50–200 μg/kg/min Very short-acting β blockade dP/dt control on aortic dissection; brief rate control Ultra-short half-life; weaning immediately stops effect
Hydralazine 10–20 mg IV q4–6h Arterial vasodilation Second-line HTN; avoid in myectomy Reflex tachycardia is a problem in HCM; can re-provoke LVOT obstruction
Metoprolol PO/IV β blockade Rate control, POAF, routine post-op Hold if SBP < 90; restart once stable
Phenylephrine 20–200 μg/min Pure α vasoconstriction Myectomy / HCM hypotension; LVAD MAP support Pure α only — no reflex tachycardia like other pressors
Norepinephrine 2–20 μg/min α + weak β Vasoplegia (ICU-level — signals need for ICU transfer) Indicates unstable hemodynamics; escalation likely
Amlodipine PO Chronic CCB HTN maintenance on discharge home Not for acute titration

Transition from drip to PO is attending-directed; nursing continues titration per orders.

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers — *when to call the team*
sections.bodyHtml:
Signal First bedside step Escalate if
MAP < 65 × 15 min despite position/leg raise Assess preload: JVP, CVP, UOP, chest tube output. Check for pain, anxiety, fever. Not improving or trending down; patient symptomatic (confused, cold, oliguria)
SBP > goal × 15 min IV antihypertensive per order set; notify APP. Refractory despite medication; rising trend
Sudden SBP drop + rising CVP + narrowing pulse pressure Tamponade until proven otherwise — call STAT. Hemodynamic collapse → activate emergent sternotomy protocol
New tachycardia on myectomy patient Rule out pain, hypovolemia, arrhythmia. IV beta-blocker per order; may need phenylephrine. SBP falling → escalate, do NOT treat tachycardia with vasodilators
UOP < 0.5 mL/kg/h × 4 h Preload / MAP / Cr assessment; notify APP. AKI trajectory (see AKI / Oliguria card)
SvO₂ < 60% (if PA catheter present) Assess CO, Hgb, SpO₂, VO₂ drivers (pain, fever, shivering). Cardiogenic shock criteria
CVP rising without volume given Think RV failure, tamponade, tension PTX. Respiratory compromise → STAT CXR

sections.heading: 7.1 Why "normal BP" is procedure-specific
sections.bodyHtml:
Concept: A BP of 140/85 is "hypertensive" for an aortic dissection patient but "normotensive" or even "hypotensive" for a HCM patient on the myectomy table. The post-operative goal is not a universal number — it's a procedure-tailored target that the whole team must agree on.

Three competing demands:

  1. Perfusion: The repaired heart and grafts need adequate pressure to fill and sustain end-organ function. MAP < 65 for prolonged periods risks stroke, renal injury, mesenteric ischemia.
  2. Protection: Fresh suture lines, anastomoses, and prosthetic seams will rupture if over-pressurized. Aortic surgery patients tolerate SBP 120 because the risk of suture blowout outweighs the perfusion risk at slightly lower pressure.
  3. Physiology: Some hearts respond paradoxically to standard pressure targets. HCM hearts collapse with "normal" pressure + "normal" rate + vasodilation (the triad that causes LVOT obstruction). Transplanted denervated hearts cannot reflex-slow their rate on hypotension.

Why this matters at bedside: a nurse asking "is this BP okay?" must know the procedure-specific answer, not the generic "MAP 65–90" answer. This is why the procedure-specific table (§5.2) is the critical content of this card.

sections.heading: 7.2 Procedure-specific rationale
sections.bodyHtml:
CABG: The new vein graft is vulnerable to spasm in the first 24 h post-op. NTG infusion (5–20 μg/min) is graft-protective and given routinely. SBP ≤ 140 prevents over-pressurization of the fresh anastomosis. Paradoxically, MAP should NOT be aggressively lowered below 65 — grafts need perfusion pressure.

Aortic Ascending / Arch and Type A dissection repair: These patients have the strictest SBP targets (≤ 120) because the anastomoses and residual dissected aorta are at high risk for blow-out or propagation.

dP/dt control is as important as absolute BP. Labetalol and esmolol are preferred because they lower dP/dt directly (rate + contractility), not just pressure. Nicardipine, while effective for SBP, can cause reflex tachycardia and is second-line.

TAAA / TEVAR and spinal cord protection: The complication of paraplegia drives the MAP ≥ 85 rule. The spinal cord is perfused by segmental arteries that were often sacrificed or clamped during repair. Spinal cord perfusion pressure = MAP − CSF pressure (if monitored). Below 70 mmHg, paraplegia risk is real. This is a hard floor, not a guideline.

Myectomy / HCM: The dynamic LVOT obstruction improves with slow, full, squeezed — a counterintuitive strategy. Tachycardia (even HR 95) and vasodilation both worsen obstruction. Phenylephrine (pure α) is preferred because it does NOT cause reflex tachycardia (beta-2 agonism). NTG and nicardipine are avoided because vasodilation can precipitate cardiogenic shock in this population.

Transplant denervated heart: The transplanted heart has no vagal innervation, so it cannot reflex-slow on hypotension. A transplant patient with MAP 55 will NOT develop a protective bradycardia. The HR must be high enough intrinsically (90–110 target) to maintain CO. This is why beta-blockade is limited early post-op.

sections.heading: 7.3 Subgroup / edge cases
sections.bodyHtml:
HCM with LVOT obstruction recurrence:

  • Post-op myectomy with re-obstruction (dynamic or residual) requires aggressive phenylephrine and volume; standard vasodilators contraindicated.
  • If in cardiogenic shock and standard myectomy targets fail, escalation to IABP or ECMO may be needed — call CT surgery + cardiology.

VAD patient over-sped into RV failure:

  • LVAD patients who are over-sped (too-high RPM for their size) develop septal shift, RV failure, and suction alarms.
  • MAP may paradoxically be low despite high pump flow. Suction alarms signal over-unloading, not hypotension.
  • Call VAD team for speed adjustment; do NOT treat with fluid boluses.

Transplant rejection appearing as hemodynamic instability:

  • Acute rejection can present as new arrhythmia, EF drop, or shock-like state in the first weeks post-op.
  • Watch for new AF, PVCs, or decline in perfusion markers even with "adequate" BP.
  • Low threshold for echocardiogram and biopsy if hemodynamics change unexpectedly.

Spinal cord ischemia in TAAA patient:

  • Any sign of paraplegia (lower-extremity weakness, sensory level, bowel/bladder loss) during or after TAAA repair is a neurologic emergency.
  • Elevate MAP immediately toward 90–100 mmHg (with team approval) to maximize spinal cord perfusion pressure.
  • Neurosurgery + CT surgery urgent consultation.

sections.heading: 7.4 Agent pharmacology detail
sections.bodyHtml:
Nitroglycerin (NTG): venodilator > arterial dilator. IV doses 5–40 μg/min produce predominantly preload reduction and graft-protective effect via reducing graft spasm and afterload. Headaches common. Tachyphylaxis (tolerance) develops after 24–48 h continuous infusion, which is why NTG post-CABG is time-limited (typically 24 h). Monitor for excessive preload reduction (MAP drop) and headache.

Nicardipine: non-dihydropyridine CCB agonist produces smooth, titratable arterial vasodilation. Quick onset (5–10 min), quick weaning offset. Rebound hypertension is common if weaned too rapidly; recommend tapering. Preferred for aortic surgery because it's predictable. Can cause reflex tachycardia in some patients, so not ideal for HCM.

Labetalol: combined α + β antagonist. Lowers both MAP and dP/dt (rate + contractility effect), making it ideal for aortic dissection and Type A repair where dP/dt control is essential. Slower onset than nicardipine (~5–10 min). Hypotension + bradycardia can occur; pair with fluid bolus if needed.

Esmolol: ultra-short-acting β blocker (half-life 9 min). Rapid onset and offset make it ideal for precise dP/dt control in dissection. If stopped, effect vanishes in minutes. Useful as a bridge to oral beta-blocker transition.

Hydralazine: direct arterial vasodilator. Second-line for HTN. Reflex tachycardia common (~10–15 bpm increase), so avoid in HCM and aortic dissection. Good for stable CABG / valve patients with isolated HTN.

Phenylephrine: pure α1 agonist. Causes vasoconstriction without beta-2 effects (no reflex tachycardia). Ideal for HCM (maintains MAP while avoiding the tachycardia that would worsen obstruction) and LVAD (supports MAP without over-loading RV). Requires close monitoring because increasing afterload can worsen decompensated HF.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
These are watch-for patterns that may signal a worsening trajectory even if vital signs are currently near goal.

  • Trend of declining MAP despite escalating vasopressor dose → suggests worsening cardiogenic shock, sepsis, or tamponade; escalate STAT.
  • BP dropping on amiodarone drip → predictable in ~25%; expected but needs early drip reduction to 0.5 mg/min before frank hypotension.
  • Tachycardia persisting despite rate-control meds → may signal inadequate load, pain, fever, sepsis, or arrhythmia failure; reassess triggers.
  • New tachycardia developing suddenly in a myectomy patient → high risk for LVOT re-obstruction; treat with beta-blocker + phenylephrine immediately.
  • CVP rising without volume input → RV failure, tamponade, tension PTX, or pulmonary disease; STAT CXR.
  • Narrowing pulse pressure (SBP − DBP narrowing) + rising CVP + falling UOP → classic tamponade triad; call STAT.
  • New hypoxia or rising O₂ requirement → can precede hemodynamic collapse; assess pulmonary edema, pneumothorax, bleeding.
  • Rising lactate, falling UOP despite "adequate" MAP → tissue perfusion failing; escalate to cardiogenic shock protocol.
  • New focal neuro deficit (weakness, speech change, facial droop) → activate stroke code immediately.
  • Mechanical mitral prosthesis patient in new AF → very high embolic risk; escalate for rhythm vs rate decision.
  • Recurrent episodes of goal deviation → suggests inadequate sedation, pain, anxiety, or underlying instability; team discussion on escalation.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Myectomy / HCM flips the rules. The phrase "slow, full, squeezed" summarizes the entire post-op strategy for this population. Tachycardia is the enemy; vasodilation is contraindicated. If treating a myectomy patient in apparent shock, the first move is phenylephrine + volume, NOT vasodilators.

  2. Aortic dissection and root surgery demand strict SBP ≤ 120. Use labetalol or esmolol (both lower dP/dt) before reaching for nicardipine. The goal is not just number control — it's rate and contractility control to prevent propagation.

  3. TAAA / TEVAR patients have a MAP floor of ≥ 85 for spinal cord protection. Under-treating hypotension in this population risks paraplegia. This is an emergent bedside call, not a "watch and see."

  4. Transplant heart is denervated — it will not reflex-bradycardia on hypotension. A transplant patient in shock may remain tachycardic or normal-rate. Judge by perfusion (mental status, UOP, lactate), not heart rate.

  5. LVAD patients have no pulse — MAP is by Doppler cuff. A MAP of 85 with suction alarms means the device is over-sped, not "hypertensive." Call the VAD team for speed adjustment.

  6. RV failure patients tolerate volume poorly. CVP of 16 is a warning sign in a TV surgery or transplant patient; it's a target in a CABG patient with a volume problem. Context is everything.

  7. Narrowing pulse pressure + rising CVP + falling BP = tamponade. This trio should be taught to every new graduate by rote. If seen, call STAT.

  8. MAP > 65 is a floor, not a ceiling. Over-treating hypotension in a fresh aortic arch patient by escalating pressors may blow a suture line. Always check the procedure-specific ceiling.

  9. NTG × 24 h post-CABG is under-discontinued. Chart the order; most stop at 24 h. NTG running on POD 2 is usually leftover by mistake.

  10. Watch the first movement out of bed on POD 1–2. Orthostatic hypotension is common; a MAP drop from 75 to 55 on transfer signals volume depletion or over-diuresis.

  11. Acute pain drives hypertension. Always check pain before escalating antihypertensives. Often the fix is analgesia, not another drip.

  12. Bladder distention causes HTN + tachycardia that mimics anxiety. Always scan the bladder if there's no obvious trigger.

  13. Fluid boluses before pressors on CABG patients (unless CVP is high or tamponade is suspected). Reverse this calculus in myectomy: give both, but phenylephrine first.

  14. Pressor off a peripheral line is not appropriate long-term. If a patient needs continuous norepinephrine, they need a central line and likely an ICU transfer. Short-term peripheral phenylephrine while awaiting central access is acceptable.

  15. Don't confuse cuff artifact with true hypotension. When the automatic cuff inflates, the pulse oximeter pleth goes down temporarily. The "low BP" reading during cuff cycling is artifact, not real.

cards.title: Hepatic Dysfunction Post-Cardiac Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: Elevated LFTs post-op → categorize pattern (hepatocellular vs. cholestatic vs. mixed). Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver): AST/ALT often >1000, peak POD 1–3, normalize POD 7–14 if perfusion restored; Congestive hepatopathy (RV failure): cholestatic pattern with bilirubin > transaminases, elevated CVP, ascites; Drug-induced: review amiodarone, acetaminophen (<3 g/day), statins. Workup: CVP/echo, LFT pattern, INR (synthetic function), rule out sepsis. Stable: optimize RV, restore perfusion, stop hepatotoxins, vitamin K if INR >1.8. Unstable: STAT call, IV access, labs (INR/fibrinogen), prepare for massive transfusion or ECMO.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
