sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, scope.

  • Definition: Acute elevation of liver enzymes (AST, ALT, ALP, bilirubin) or synthetic dysfunction (INR, albumin) occurring POD 0–7 after cardiac surgery.
  • Incidence: Mild transaminitis (AST/ALT 50–300 U/L) in ~40% of post-CPB patients POD 1–2 (benign, self-limited). Clinically significant hepatic dysfunction requiring intervention in ~2–8% depending on acuity and definition.
  • Who it applies to: All adults post-cardiac surgery. Highest risk: pre-existing liver disease, prolonged CPB (>180 min), massive transfusion, intraoperative hypotension or arrest.
  • When it matters: Most critical POD 1–7. Ischemic hepatitis peaks POD 1–3; congestive patterns emerge POD 3–7; drug-induced injury can occur at any time.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Four primary mechanisms in post-cardiac hepatic dysfunction:

sections.heading: 2.1 Ischemic hepatitis ("shock liver")
sections.bodyHtml:
Hepatic blood flow is exquisitely cardiac-output dependent. Any sudden perfusion drop (intraoperative hypotension, cardiogenic shock, massive hemorrhage, arrest) triggers centrilobular hepatocyte necrosis.

  • Peak transaminitis: AST/ALT often 1,000–10,000 U/L, occurring 1–3 days post-event
  • LDH: often exceeds AST/ALT, may be markedly elevated
  • Recovery: rapid if perfusion restored — normalization over 7–14 days
  • Bilirubin / INR: initially normal or mildly elevated; marked elevation suggests added synthetic failure
  • Risk factors: pre-existing liver disease, prolonged CPB, massive transfusion, intraoperative arrest

sections.heading: 2.2 Congestive hepatopathy
sections.bodyHtml:
RV failure or severe tricuspic regurgitation → elevated CVP → hepatic venous congestion and progressive portal fibrosis.

  • LFT pattern: cholestatic > hepatocellular (bilirubin rises out of proportion to AST/ALT; ALP/GGT mildly elevated)
  • Transaminitis level: typically <300 U/L, often normal despite clinical hepatopathy
  • Ascites: develops over days to weeks; accompanied by JVD, peripheral edema, elevated CVP (>8 mmHg)
  • Chronic progression: can evolve to cardiac cirrhosis (irreversible fibrosis) with ascites, splenomegaly, coagulopathy
  • Prevention: early RV optimization, afterload reduction, adequate preload

sections.heading: 2.3 Drug-induced liver injury (DILI)
sections.bodyHtml:
Amiodarone: lipophilic; baseline LFTs + q6mo monitoring recommended; modest AST/ALT elevation common; cirrhosis risk with prolonged high-dose use (>2 years).

Statins: rare hepatotoxicity; mild LFT elevation common; benefit usually outweighs risk; often safely continued.

Acetaminophen: stacking across standing + PRN + compound medications can exceed safe threshold (>3–4 g/day) in hours post-op; toxic metabolite accumulation → hepatocyte necrosis. Often overlooked.

Broad-spectrum antibiotics: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones, macrolides can elevate LFTs; usually reversible.

sections.heading: 2.4 CPB-related mild transaminitis
sections.bodyHtml: ~40% of post-CPB patients develop AST/ALT 50–300 U/L POD 1–2 without shock liver mechanism. Likely multifactorial: hemodilution, endotoxemia, inflammatory response. Benign, self-resolves; does not indicate hepatic insufficiency.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following while caring for a post-operative cardiac surgery patient:

  • Notified of abnormal LFTs on lab review (AST, ALT, bilirubin, ALP, INR >1.5 without anticoagulation)
  • Jaundice (scleral icterus, skin yellowing, dark urine)
  • New ascites or fluid accumulation on abdominal exam after stable earlier assessment
  • INR elevated (>1.5) without expected anticoagulation
  • Acute mental status change (confusion, lethargy, disorientation) — possible hepatic encephalopathy
  • RUQ tenderness, fever, elevated WBC — possible acalculous cholecystitis (0.5–2% of critically ill)
  • Low urine output + rising creatinine + elevated LFTs — hepatorenal syndrome
  • Melena, hematochezia, hematemesis with elevated transaminases — variceal bleed or coagulopathy

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml: Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

sections.heading: Perfusion & hemodynamics
sections.bodyHtml: • HR, BP, MAP, SpO₂, cap refill, skin temperature, urine output (last 2–4 h)

sections.heading: Abdominal exam
sections.bodyHtml:
• RUQ tenderness, hepatomegaly, ascites (fluid wave, shifting dullness), distention, bowel sounds
  • Jaundice: scleral icterus, skin color, palms, urine color (dark → hyperbilirubinuria), stool (clay-colored → cholestasis)

sections.heading: Mental status & bleeding signs
sections.bodyHtml:
• Alert/oriented? Changes from baseline? Confusion, lethargy, asterixis?
  • Melena, hematochezia, hematemesis, gum bleeding, petechiae, unusual ooze from lines/wounds

sections.heading: Peripheral findings
sections.bodyHtml: • JVD, peripheral edema, dependent ascites → suggest elevated CVP from RV failure

sections.heading: Recent labs (already in chart)
sections.bodyHtml: • AST, ALT, bilirubin, ALP, GGT, INR, PT/PTT, albumin, creatinine, electrolytes, lactate

sections.heading: MAR review & surgical context
sections.bodyHtml:
• Amiodarone on board? Acetaminophen total daily dose? Statins? Broad antibiotics?
  • Intraoperative hypotensive episodes? Massive transfusion? CPB time? RV dysfunction pre-op?
  • Echo findings if available: RV size/function, TR grade, estimated CVP from IVC diameter

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP >65, no active bleeding, INR <1.8, no encephalopathy.)

  1. Order comprehensive metabolic panel + INR/PT/PTT STAT (if not done in last 12 h) - Add: AST, ALT, ALP, GGT, total/direct bilirubin, albumin, lactate, LDH
  2. RUQ ultrasound STAT if RUQ pain, fever, or concern for acalculous cholecystitis
  3. Review MAR — document all hepatotoxic agents: amiodarone dose/duration, acetaminophen total daily, statin type/dose
  4. Assess fluid status — weigh patient, measure abdominal girth, note JVD, assess for ascites
  5. Optimize cardiac function:
    • Confirm RV function with echo if available
    • Ensure adequate preload
    • Consider vasodilation (inhaled nitric oxide, milrinone per team) if RV dysfunction
    • Reduce afterload: optimize ventilation, permissive hypercapnia per protocol
    • Adjust hepatotoxic drugs per provider:
    • Amiodarone: usually continued; flag for LFT check at baseline + q6mo
    • Acetaminophen: ensure total dose <3–4 g/day; coordinate across all sources (standing + PRN + compound meds)
    • Statins: often continued despite modest elevation (benefit > risk); confirm with provider
    • Vitamin K 5–10 mg IV slow push if INR >1.8 without active anticoagulation intent (post-op coagulopathy); reassess 24 h
    • Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (see §6):
    • Request liver-specific assessment (shock liver vs. congestive vs. DILI vs. other)
    • Request repeat LFTs timeline (24–48 h depending on trajectory)
    • Consider GI/Hepatology consult if AST/ALT >500, bilirubin >3, or INR >2

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension, active bleeding, INR >2, mental status change, RUQ peritoneal signs.)

  1. STAT call APP / fellow + charge RN — establish roles; do NOT leave the room alone
  2. Activate Rapid Response if not already present; consider MICU transfer pending assessment
  3. IV access: ensure large-bore IV ×2, type & cross if active bleeding
  4. Labs STAT: CBC, CMP, INR/PTT, AST/ALT/bilirubin, lactate, fibrinogen, LDH, blood cultures if fever
  5. If active bleeding:
    • Hold anticoagulation pending team decision
    • Activate [Institution policy] massive transfusion protocol if ongoing hemorrhage
    • Prepare for possible IR/endoscopy if variceal bleed suspected
    • If RUQ pain + fever + elevated WBC:
    • RUQ ultrasound STAT to rule out acalculous cholecystitis
    • Notify surgery team; patient may need urgent percutaneous cholecystostomy if acutely ill
    • If mental status change:
    • STAT labs: ammonia (if available), glucose, sodium, hepatic panel, ABG
    • Treat reversible causes (hypoglycemia, hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypokalemia)
    • Monitor for hepatic encephalopathy; lactulose/rifaxomicin per GI consult
    • Fluid management:
    • If hypotensive: crystalloid bolus 500 mL over 15 min, reassess; prepare vasopressor (norepinephrine)
    • If ascites: restrict free water; furosemide once BP stable
    • Continuous monitoring: cardiac, SpO₂, urine output, ascites trajectory
    • Document: baseline LFTs, timeline of rise, hypotensive episodes, total hepatotoxin exposure

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on the ICU, calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient with elevated LFTs: AST [value], ALT [value], bilirubin [value], INR [value]. LFT pattern is [hepatocellular / cholestatic / mixed]. Recent perfusion: BP [value], MAP [value], lactate [value]. RV function: [known dysfunction / unknown / normal on recent echo]. CVP [elevated / normal]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Symptoms if any: RUQ pain, jaundice, ascites, mental status change]. [Drugs on MAR: amiodarone, statin, acetaminophen total daily]. [Bleeding status: no active / active bleeding present]." R: "Requesting [hepatology consult / categorization of LFT pattern / repeat labs / imaging / medication adjustment]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Mild transaminitis (AST/ALT <300), stable Primary APP / on-call provider
AST/ALT >300 or rising bilirubin APP + consider early hepatology phone consult
Active bleeding + coagulopathy (INR >2) CT surgery + Hepatology + Transfusion Medicine
RUQ pain + fever + elevated WBC + LFTs CT surgery + General surgery (cholecystitis rule-out)
Mental status change / possible encephalopathy APP + Neurology; Hepatology if encephalopathy concern
Shock liver (AST/ALT >1000) post-hypotensive episode MICU consideration + Hepatology
Suspected variceal bleed (hematemesis + LFTs) CT surgery + Hepatology + GI endoscopy team

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive on pathophysiology, drug metabolism, and edge cases. Sections below are collapsible in the app.

Hepatic anatomy & dual blood supply — why cardiac surgery threatens perfusion The liver receives blood from two sources: **hepatic artery** (25% of blood flow, 50% of oxygen) and **portal vein** (75% of flow, 50% of oxygen). During states of low cardiac output, the hepatic artery perfusion pressure drops catastrophically — portal venous flow can also fall if splanchnic vasoconstriction occurs. The result is profound centrilobular ischemia, triggering rapid hepatocyte necrosis. **Key teaching point:** Shock liver is predictable and recovers quickly if perfusion is restored. The dramatic AST/ALT elevation (often >1000) can alarm nurses, but it signals a temporary ischemic insult, not permanent liver failure. Document the timeline of hypotension and reassure the team that recovery is expected.
LFT pattern interpretation — hepatocellular vs. cholestatic vs. mixed **Hepatocellular pattern** (ALT > ALP or AST > ALP):
  • Prominent: AST, ALT (often >500, sometimes >1000)
  • ALP and bilirubin relatively less elevated
  • Characteristic of: ischemic hepatitis (shock liver), viral hepatitis, DILI, cirrhosis with active necrosis
  • Teaching point: AST > ALT suggests ischemic or alcoholic injury; ALT > AST suggests viral or DILI **Cholestatic pattern** (ALP > ALT or ALP/AST ratio >2):
  • Prominent: ALP, GGT, bilirubin
  • AST/ALT minimally elevated or normal
  • Characteristic of: congestive hepatopathy, biliary obstruction, sepsis, some drug reactions (amoxicillin-clavulanate)
  • Teaching point: In post-cardiac surgery, cholestasis with preserved transaminases = think RV failure + CVP elevation first **Mixed pattern:**
  • AST/ALT moderate + ALP/bilirubin also elevated
  • Seen in cirrhosis, advanced DILI, sepsis, multifactorial disease **Clinical decision rule:** Massive AST/ALT >1000 + normal ALP + normal bilirubin = shock liver (look for hypotensive episode). Bilirubin out of proportion + normal/low transaminases + elevated CVP = congestive hepatopathy (optimize RV).
INR and synthetic liver function — vitamin K vs. acute hepatic failure The **INR reflects hepatic synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X).** It is exquisitely sensitive to both acute hepatic dysfunction and vitamin K deficiency. - **Post-op INR >1.8 without anticoagulation** → suspect vitamin K deficiency (NPO, antibiotics killing gut flora) or acute hepatic synthetic failure - **Vitamin K 5–10 mg IV slow push** if INR elevated without planned anticoagulation; reassess in 24 h. If INR does not improve, suspect acute synthetic liver disease - **INR >2.5 + active bleeding** → fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate per [Institution policy] transfusion protocol - **Chronic INR elevation (>1.5 for >2 weeks)** suggests cirrhosis or advanced chronic liver disease; consult Hepatology **Key distinction:** Acute ischemic hepatitis typically shows coagulopathy late (day 3–5, if at all). If INR rises early post-op, think DILI or sepsis. If INR is chronically elevated + ascites + bilirubin, think cirrhosis (unlikely to fully recover).
Right-sided heart failure driving cardiac cirrhosis — why RV dysfunction matters Chronic elevated CVP (from RV failure, severe TR, restrictive cardiomyopathy) causes **passive hepatic congestion** → hepatic venous outflow obstruction → sinusoidal fibrosis → irreversible cirrhosis. - **Hepatocyte injury mechanism:** RV failure + elevated CVP >12 mmHg for weeks → hepatic venous pressure rises → centrolobular congestion and atrophy - **LFT pattern:** cholestatic (bilirubin rises out of proportion); ascites prominent; synthetic function preserved until late - **Irreversibility:** if CVP remains elevated for >4–6 weeks, portal fibrosis becomes permanent even if RV function eventually improves - **Prevention:** early RV optimization (inhaled nitric oxide, milrinone, low-SVR afterload reduction), aggressive diuresis once BP stable, consider RIGHT heart catheterization to quantify CVP + PA pressures if echo is unclear **Teaching point:** A post-cardiac surgery patient with elevated CVP for >2 weeks is already developing cardiac cirrhosis. Early aggressive RV afterload reduction is the only way to prevent irreversible fibrosis.
Drug hepatotoxicity profiles — amiodarone, statins, acetaminophen, TPN **Amiodarone** (antiarrhythmic, lipophilic):
  • Deposits in liver; baseline LFTs + q6mo monitoring recommended
  • AST/ALT elevation: usually modest (1–3 × ULN) but can be higher with cirrhosis risk on prolonged high-dose use (>2 years)
  • Teaching point: Post-cardiac surgery amiodarone loads are common for rhythm control. Flag for baseline LFT check POD 1; then schedule q6mo monitoring outpatient **Statins** (HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors):
  • Rare hepatotoxicity; mild LFT elevation common (1–2 × ULN)
  • Benefit (post-MI secondary prevention, LDL lowering) usually outweighs risk
  • Teaching point: Do NOT reflexively hold statins for mild transaminitis. Team often wants to hold; evidence supports continuing. Confirm with provider, but default assumption is continue. **Acetaminophen** (analgesic; max 2–4 g/day):
  • Metabolized by liver via glucuronidation (saturates) and oxidation (produces toxic NAPQI intermediate)
  • Stacking across standing acetaminophen 650 mg Q6H (2,600 mg/day) + PRN dosing (500–650 mg Q4–6H) + Tylenol in compound meds (e.g., oxycodone/acetaminophen) can exceed safe dose in hours post-op
  • Risk higher in fasting state, alcohol use, chronic liver disease
  • Teaching point: Coordinate with pharmacy. Standing dose should be **lowered to 325–500 mg Q6H** for post-op patients. PRN should be avoided or dosed at 325 mg only. Acetaminophen in compound pain meds must be counted. **TPN (total parenteral nutrition) cholestasis:**
  • Prolonged NPO + TPN infusion can trigger cholestasis (elevated ALP, bilirubin, normal transaminases)
  • Teaching point: If patient is >5 days post-op, NPO, on TPN, with rising ALP + bilirubin, suspect TPN cholestasis. Advance to enteral nutrition as soon as safe.
Acalculous cholecystitis in critically ill — recognition and urgency Occurs in 0.5–2% of critically ill patients; mechanism is bile stasis + ischemia + inflammation during low-flow states. - **Classic presentation:** low-grade fever, leukocytosis, RUQ tenderness + normal abdominal exam otherwise (no peritonitis)
  • **Ultrasound findings:** thickened GB wall (>3–4 mm), pericholecystic fluid, sometimes sludge
  • **Risk:** perforation and sepsis; high mortality if untreated
  • **Management:** urgent percutaneous cholecystostomy in many cases (not cholecystectomy in unstable ICU patients)
  • Teaching point: A stable post-cardiac patient with new RUQ pain + fever needs RUQ ultrasound STAT. Do not assume it is hepatitis.
Hepatorenal syndrome — when liver + kidney fail together Occurs when hepatic dysfunction is severe + splanchnic vasodilation causes renal vasoconstriction → oliguria + rising creatinine despite normal kidney histology. - **Trigger:** often acute decompensation (bleeding, infection, new renal insult)
  • **Labs:** low UOP + rising Cr despite normal urinary sodium (indicative of prerenal azotemia)
  • **Prognosis:** poor without aggressive intervention (ECMO, RRT, liver transplant consideration)
  • Teaching point: If a patient has shock liver + low urine output + rising Cr, notify team immediately. This is hepatorenal syndrome and carries high mortality.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear or worsen in a stable patient, re-escalate.

  • AST/ALT rising rapidly (doubling in 24 h) — ongoing liver injury; may herald shock liver or advancing DILI
  • Bilirubin rising faster than transaminases — cholestasis worsening; concern for congestive hepatopathy progression or biliary obstruction
  • INR rising or PT prolonging despite vitamin K — hepatic synthetic failure; increased bleeding risk
  • New ascites or ascites increasing despite diuretics — cardiac cirrhosis development or decompensation; warrants right heart catheterization to assess RV function and CVP
  • Encephalopathy signs emerging (confusion, lethargy, asterixis) — hepatic encephalopathy; lactulose, rifaxomicin per Hepatology
  • RUQ pain, fever, elevated WBC with LFT rise — acalculous cholecystitis; needs urgent imaging and possible percutaneous drainage
  • Urine output dropping while bilirubin rises — hepatorenal syndrome; poor prognosis; notify team for ECMO/RRT consideration
  • Spontaneous bleeding (ooze from lines, gum bleeding, petechiae) — coagulopathy; check fibrinogen, platelets; consider transfusion
  • CVP elevated (>8 mmHg) + rising transaminases + hyperbilirubinemia — RV failure driving congestive hepatopathy; assess for tricuspid regurgitation, possible right heart catheterization
  • Amiodarone on board + LFTs rising — amiodarone hepatotoxicity; verify loading dose was not excessive; plan q6mo monitoring
  • Acetaminophen total daily dose >4 g — overdose risk; coordinate with pharmacy to lower standing dose immediately
  • Post-hypotensive episode + massive transaminitis 24 h later — classic shock liver; reassure team that recovery is expected if perfusion is restored

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Shock liver (AST/ALT >1000) is predictable after hypotension and recovers rapidly. Peak occurs 1–3 days post-event. Many nurses panic; experienced teams know this is benign if the underlying hypotension is addressed. Document the timeline of the hypotensive episode and the subsequent AST/ALT rise — the pattern is diagnostic.

  2. Congestive hepatopathy pattern is cholestatic (bilirubin > transaminases) more than hepatocellular. AST/ALT are often normal or <200. Missing this pattern is common — team attributes "liver disease" to ischemia when it's really RV failure + elevated CVP.

  3. RV failure + elevated CVP → cardiac cirrhosis (irreversible if chronic). If a patient has had elevated CVP for >4 weeks post-op, the portal fibrosis may be permanent. Early RV optimization is critical to prevent this.

  4. Amiodarone LFT monitoring — baseline + every 6 months. Many post-cardiac patients start amiodarone for rhythm control. Obtain baseline LFTs before load; then q6mo. Cirrhosis risk with prolonged high-dose use. Document in nursing note: "Amiodarone LFT baseline obtained POD [X]."

  5. Acetaminophen total <3–4 g/day; coordinate across all sources. Standing acetaminophen 650 mg Q6H = 2,600 mg/day. Add PRN dosing + Tylenol-containing compounds → exceed safe dose in hours. Pharmacy consult if uncertain. Post-op pain control is important, but not with hepatotoxins.

  6. Post-CPB mild transaminitis (50–300 U/L) POD 1–2 is benign. This is common, reversible, and part of normal post-op inflammation. Do not escalate unless AST/ALT >500 or rapidly rising.

  7. INR reflects hepatic synthesis (factors II, VII, IX, X); also vitamin K deficiency post-op. Give vitamin K if INR >1.8 without anticoagulation intent. If INR does not improve in 24 h, suspect liver synthetic failure. PT is less specific (includes factors V, fibrinogen).

  8. Ascites out of proportion to clinical edema = think cardiac cirrhosis. Some patients have modest peripheral edema but large ascites + elevated bilirubin + normal/low transaminases. This is chronic RV failure → cirrhosis, not acute ischemic hepatitis.

  9. Right heart catheterization if hepatic cirrhosis + cardiac dysfunction unclear. Echo may not fully quantify CVP, PA pressures, RV dysfunction. Right heart cath shows hemodynamics and guides RV afterload reduction strategy.

  10. Acalculous cholecystitis in critically ill with ileus + RUQ pain. Classic presentation is low-grade fever, leukocytosis, RUQ tenderness + normal abdominal exam otherwise. Ultrasound shows thickened GB wall, pericholecystic fluid. Risk: perforation and sepsis. Needs urgent percutaneous drainage in many cases.

  11. Low-flow splanchnic ischemia can affect bowel and liver together. If a patient has shock liver + feeding intolerance + diarrhea, consider that the GI tract is also ischemic. Gut rest, TPN, optimize perfusion.

  12. Statins often continued through modest LFT rise (benefit > risk). Team often wants to hold; evidence suggests continuing is safe and beneficial post-operatively. Confirm with provider, but reflex holding is not warranted.

  13. Coagulopathy is a late sign in acute hepatitis, but early sign in cirrhosis. If INR is rising rapidly early post-op, think ischemic hepatitis (expected recovery) or DILI (stop the drug). If INR is chronically elevated + ascites + bilirubin, think cirrhosis (may not recover).

  14. Contrast-induced AKI often coexists with acute liver injury. If a patient had intraoperative imaging + hypotension + post-op elevated creatinine + elevated LFTs, consider that both organs were ischemic. Maintain euvolemia and avoid further contrast.

  15. Medications requiring hepatic dose adjustment post-dysfunction: midazolam, fentanyl, propofol, certain anticoagulants. Notify pharmacy and providers if INR rises or synthetic function worsens; adjust sedation/analgesia carefully.

cards.title: Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF)
cards.quickAnswer: HFpEF = ejection fraction ≥50% with dyspnea + evidence of diastolic dysfunction or elevated filling pressures (E/e', BNP, PCWP). Diagnose via H2FPEF or HFA-PEFF score (table below) or stress testing if resting echo normal. SGLT2 inhibitors are first-line — empagliflozin (EMPEROR-Preserved) and dapagliflozin (DELIVER) independently reduce hospitalizations in HFpEF, independent of diabetes. Start empagliflozin 10 mg daily or dapagliflozin 10 mg daily immediately. Diuretics for volume control (symptom relief, not outcome). Aggressively manage comorbidities: hypertension (target SBP 120–130), atrial fibrillation (rate control ≤80 bpm), diabetes (SGLT2i + GLP-1), obesity (5–10% weight loss), CKD. Rule out amyloid (ATTR-wt, ATTR-v, AL) with PYP scan + SPEP if wall thickness ≥12 mm or red flags. Emerging: finerenone, semaglutide showing promise in obese HFpEF.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, clinical context.

  • Definition: Heart failure syndrome characterized by ejection fraction ≥50% with dyspnea or HF symptoms plus objective evidence of elevated filling pressures (diastolic dysfunction on echo, elevated natriuretic peptides, or documented elevation of PCWP on right heart catheterization). Primary pathology is diastolic impairment (LV stiffness, impaired relaxation, reduced compliance) rather than systolic contractile failure.

  • Epidemiology:

  • ~50% of heart failure patients now have HFpEF (was 20–30% two decades ago; prevalence rising with aging population)
  • Median age 65–75 years; ~60% female
  • Major risk factors: hypertension (75–80%), atrial fibrillation (50–60%), diabetes (40–50%), obesity (BMI ≥30), older age, chronic kidney disease

  • Heterogeneous syndrome: no single unifying pathophysiology; multiple phenotypes (HTN-related hypertrophy, post-capillary pulmonary hypertension, amyloid, HCM phenocopy, AF-related, obesity-related)

  • Typical presentation: Older patient (female predominance) with hypertension, dyspnea on exertion, normal or near-normal EF on echo but abnormal diastolic parameters. May progress to HFmrEF (EF 41–49%) and rarely to HFrEF. Can decompensate acutely with trigger (AF, infection, HTN crisis, anemia, AKI, diuretic non-adherence).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner teaching. Collapsible for expert skim.

Diastolic dysfunction and ventricular-arterial coupling Core mechanism: diastolic impairment. The LV cannot fill easily at normal filling pressures. Myocardial relaxation is delayed or incomplete; ventricular wall stiffness is increased. Compensatory mechanisms (↑ left atrial [LA] pressure, longer diastasis, enhanced atrial kick) temporarily maintain stroke volume until they fail, leading to pulmonary and systemic congestion. Key physiologic drivers:
  • Impaired relaxation — prolonged isovolumetric relaxation time (IVRT), delayed mitral valve opening, reduced early diastolic mitral annular velocity (e')
  • Increased ventricular stiffness — myocardial fibrosis, infiltration (amyloid, sarcoid, hypertrophy), inflammatory remodeling, endothelial dysfunction
  • Atrial dysfunction — LA remodeling, reduced LA strain, loss of efficient atrial contraction; loss of atrial kick (as in AF) is particularly poorly tolerated in stiff LV
  • Endothelial and microvascular dysfunction — coronary microvascular disease, reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, impaired vasodilation, blunted response to vasodilators
  • Neurohormonal activation — renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS), sympathetic nervous system (SNS), inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6) drive progressive remodeling
  • Ventricular-arterial coupling dysregulation — increased arterial stiffness (from HTN, aging) combines with increased ventricular stiffness to worsen filling dynamics Hemodynamic consequence: Abnormally elevated filling pressures (LA pressure, PCWP) needed to maintain stroke volume at rest. Any acute increase in filling demands (exertion, tachycardia, AF, fluid overload, anemia, hypoxia) → rapid rise in PCWP → pulmonary congestion, orthopnea, dyspnea.
HFmrEF as intermediate category

HFmrEF (mildly reduced EF 41–49%) is an increasingly recognized intermediate phenotype between HFpEF and HFrEF. Patients with EF 41–49% have mixed diastolic + mild systolic dysfunction.

DELIVER trial (Solomon et al., 2022) enrolled both HFmrEF (majority) and HFpEF; dapagliflozin benefit extended across both groups. Similarly, EMPEROR-Preserved enrollment included some HFmrEF. Treat HFmrEF similarly to HFpEF for SGLT2i, comorbidity management, and diuretics; consider cautious use of ACE-I/ARB/ARNi as in HFrEF.

Amyloid phenocopy: ATTR-wt, ATTR-v, AL Cardiac amyloidosis mimics HFpEF perfectly — stiff, thickened LV with diastolic dysfunction, preserved EF, elevated filling pressures. Must be distinguished because treatment is fundamentally different (amyloid-specific therapies outperform standard HFpEF drugs). - ATTR-wt (ATTRwt; senile cardiac amyloid): most common form in elderly men; occurs in ~5–10% of males >80 years; poor prognosis if unrecognized - ATTR-v (hereditary ATTRv): autosomal dominant transthyretin mutations; younger age at onset; heterogeneous progression - AL (light-chain amyloid): clonal plasma cell disorder; worst prognosis; requires hematology-oncology management (proteasome inhibitors, immunosuppression) Red flags for amyloid over isolated HTN-HFpEF:
  • LV wall thickness ≥12–14 mm (unusual in pure hypertensive HFpEF)
  • Reduced global longitudinal strain (GLS) with apical sparing on speckle-tracking echo
  • Low-voltage ECG (QRS < 0.12 s) despite thick-walled LV — pathognomonic mismatch
  • Carpal tunnel syndrome (often bilateral; amyloid infiltration)
  • History of bilateral hip or knee arthroplasty (amyloid infiltration of large joints)
  • Pseudo-infarct pattern on ECG (e.g., Q waves in anterolateral leads with thick walls and preserved EF) Diagnostic workup:
  • Cardiac MRI (CMR): late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) — "apple core" or subendocardial pattern typical of amyloid (vs. midwall fibrosis in HFpEF from HTN)
  • Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) + immunofixation electrophoresis (IFE): screens for monoclonal protein (AL) and transthyretin mutations
  • Technetium-99m pyrophosphate (Tc-99m PYP) scan: highly sensitive and specific for ATTR (cardiac uptake > blood); lower sensitivity for AL
  • Genetic testing: TTR gene sequencing if ATTR-v suspected
  • Biopsy (endomyocardial or extracardiac): definitive diagnosis; Congo red staining under polarized light shows apple-green birefringence Management differs:
  • ATTR-wt or ATTR-v: tafamidis (Vyndaqel®, Vyndamax®) stabilizes transthyretin tetramer, slows progression
  • AL amyloid: chemotherapy (bortezomib-based regimens), immunosuppression; cardiology + hematology-oncology coordination
  • Standard HFpEF drugs (SGLT2i, ACE-I/ARB) have limited benefit in amyloid

sections.heading: Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Classic HFpEF symptoms (insidious onset):

  • Dyspnea on exertion (most common; often gradually progressive, attributed to "deconditioning" or aging)
  • Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND)
  • Fatigue, exercise intolerance, reduced functional capacity
  • Peripheral edema, ascites (less common than in HFrEF)

Acute decompensation triggers:

  • Rapid atrial fibrillation (most common trigger in HFpEF; loss of atrial kick raises filling pressures acutely)
  • Infection / sepsis (catecholamine surge, fluid shifts)
  • Uncontrolled hypertension / hypertensive crisis
  • Acute kidney injury (fluid retention, electrolyte loss)
  • Anemia (↓ oxygen carrying capacity)
  • Non-adherence to diuretics or antihypertensives
  • Post-operative stress or fluid overload (perioperative HFpEF exacerbation is common)

Physical exam findings at presentation:

  • S4 gallop (atrial sound; reflects stiff LV; very common in HFpEF, absent in normal diastolic function)
  • Elevated jugular venous pressure (JVP), hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema (signs of venous congestion)
  • Rales/crackles at lung bases
  • Apical impulse normal location (not displaced laterally as in HFrEF with dilated LV)
  • Signs of AF if present (irregular pulse, prominent JVD with cannon waves if complete AV block)
  • No prominent murmur unless concurrent valvular disease

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
When and where this applies in the ICU.

  • Admission for decompensated HFpEF: acute dyspnea, orthopnea, pulmonary congestion, acute AF with rapid ventricular response
  • Pre-operative optimization: patients with known or suspected HFpEF before non-cardiac surgery (elevated perioperative HF risk if uncontrolled)
  • Post-operative setting: cardiac surgery patients developing acute HFpEF exacerbation (fluid overload post-CPB, tachycardia, new AF)
  • AF patients on ICU admission: AF is extremely common in HFpEF and may unmask or significantly worsen decompensation
  • Phenotyping role: distinguishing HFpEF from other causes of dyspnea in older, hypertensive patient with normal EF (COPD, PE, obesity, anemia, deconditioning)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Novice-to-competent systematic exam targeting key diagnostic and safety data.

Vital signs and hemodynamics:

  • Heart rate (new AF? tachycardia? elevated resting HR correlates with worse outcomes)
  • Blood pressure (baseline vs. current; HTN control is foundational)
  • Respiratory rate, SpO₂, oxygen requirement
  • Temperature (infection as trigger?)
  • Orthostatic vital signs if patient able to safely stand

Symptoms:

  • Onset of dyspnea (acute vs. gradual), triggered by what? (exertion, lying flat, at rest?)
  • Orthopnea, PND, number of pillows needed
  • Chest pain, palpitations, syncope, presyncope
  • Leg swelling, weight gain recently

Physical exam:

  • Lung bases: crackles, diminished sounds, evidence of pulmonary edema
  • Cardiac: rate, regularity (AF vs. regular), murmurs, S3/S4 gallop
  • JVP elevation, hepatojugular reflux, liver size, ascites
  • Peripheral edema (ankle, sacral), calf pain/swelling (DVT screen)
  • Skin perfusion, capillary refill, extremity temperature
  • Mental status (hypoxia, poor perfusion, medication side effect?)
  • Apical–radial pulse deficit if suspected AF

Labs and diagnostics:

  • 12-lead ECG: LV hypertrophy (Sokolow-Lyon, Cornell criteria), AF, prior MI pattern, LBBB, low voltage with thick walls (amyloid clue?)
  • BNP or NT-proBNP: elevated at presentation; trend downward with diuresis; normal BNP makes HFpEF less likely but does not exclude
  • Troponin I or T: rule out acute coronary syndrome
  • Complete metabolic panel: electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺ critical if planning drugs), creatinine, BUN (renal function for SGLT2i safety), glucose
  • Complete blood count: hemoglobin (anemia as trigger?), WBC (infection?)
  • Recent transthoracic echocardiogram: EF, diastolic parameters (E/e', LA volume, RVSP), wall thickness, LA size, wall motion
  • Chest X-ray: pulmonary congestion pattern, cardiac silhouette, rule out pneumonia/PE

Risk assessment:

  • H2FPEF score (calculated from HTN, obesity, AF, E/e', RVSP, age, functional capacity) — see diagnostic tables below
  • HFA-PEFF score (if echo available) — diagnostic confidence
  • Prior HFpEF diagnosis and baseline functional class (NYHA)
  • Comorbidities: HTN, diabetes, obesity, AF, CKD, OSA, anemia

Medication review:

  • Current HF medications (SGLT2i, ACE-I/ARB, diuretics, beta-blockers, MRA)
  • Home BP, rate-control, anti-arrhythmic drugs
  • Recent medication changes (e.g., diuretic reduced by primary care, SGLT2i not filled)
  • Adherence issues? Cost barriers?

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Diagnosis-card context: this section covers medical therapy approach and comorbidity targets. For acute decompensation scenarios, see related Scenario cards.

sections.heading: 5A. SGLT2 Inhibitors — First-line, RCT-proven mortality benefit
sections.bodyHtml:
CRITICAL PARADIGM SHIFT: SGLT2 inhibitors are now guideline-recommended Class 2a for all HFpEF, independent of diabetes status. This represents the largest breakthrough in HFpEF pharmacotherapy in the past decade.

Key trials:

  • EMPEROR-Preserved (Anker et al., 2021): empagliflozin 10 mg daily → 25% reduction in HF hospitalization + cardiovascular death in HFpEF (EF >40%)
  • DELIVER (Solomon et al., 2022): dapagliflozin 10 mg daily → significant benefit in HFmrEF (EF 41–49%) and HFpEF for HF hospitalizations + CV death, independent of diabetes

Agent Dose Mechanism Notes
Empagliflozin 10 mg once daily PO SGLT2 inhibitor; promotes glucosuria/natriuresis EMPEROR-Preserved trial; no dose adjustment for renal function in typical use
Dapagliflozin 10 mg once daily PO SGLT2 inhibitor; promotes glucosuria/natriuresis DELIVER trial; efficacy across HFmrEF and HFpEF; eGFR >20 mL/min/1.73m² generally safe

Mechanism in HFpEF: not fully elucidated but includes natriuresis (improved congestion), improved endothelial function, reduced inflammation, metabolic reprogramming, cardiac energetics.

Initiation:

  • Start immediately upon HFpEF diagnosis (do not wait for optimization of other agents)
  • Check renal function (eGFR) and urine dipstick before starting
  • Counsel on mycotic genital infections (slightly increased risk, especially in women; teach hygiene)
  • Monitor for euglycemic DKA (rare but serious; counsel on unusual symptoms: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, breathlessness)
  • Do not hold for "decompensation." SGLT2i are continued during acute HF hospitalization; diuretics are titrated independently

Special populations:

  • eGFR <20 mL/min/1.73m²: empagliflozin preferred; dapagliflozin contraindicated. Nephrology input recommended.
  • Type 1 diabetes: increased euglycemic DKA risk; use with caution or avoid; coordinate with endocrinology
  • Recent urinary tract infection or sepsis from UTI: screen and treat before starting; no absolute contraindication after clearance
  • Female genital infections: prior candida vaginitis → educate on preventive hygiene; consider alternative in recurrent infections

sections.heading: 5B. Comorbidity Management — Often more impactful than HF-specific drugs
sections.bodyHtml:
Comorbidity Target Management HFpEF benefit Evidence
Hypertension SBP 120–130 mmHg ACE-I, ARB, thiazide-like diuretic (HCTZ), calcium channel blocker (CCB); tight control is foundational ↓ LVH, ↓ diastolic dysfunction progression, ↓ HF events 2022 AHA/ACC HF Guideline; post-hoc analyses
Type 2 Diabetes A1C <7% (individualize ≥65 yr to <8%) SGLT2i (first-line; see 5A), GLP-1 receptor agonist (STEP-HFpEF shows benefit in obese HFpEF), metformin if eGFR adequate SGLT2i definitive mortality benefit; GLP-1 RA benefits weight loss, CV risk reduction EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER, STEP-HFpEF (2023)
Obesity Weight loss 5–10% Structured aerobic + resistance training, dietitian referral, bariatric surgery if BMI >40 + major comorbidities + failed conservative therapy Weight loss ↑ EF, ↓ LA volume, ↓ filling pressures; improves functional capacity and quality of life Multiple RCTs; often underutilized
Atrial Fibrillation HR ≤80 bpm at rest; ≥1 anticoagulation agent if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥1 Rate control primary: beta-blocker (cautious titration in HFpEF; avoid excessive bradycardia), non-DHP CCB (diltiazem, verapamil); rhythm control if AF <1 yr or hemodynamically limiting (amiodarone, cardioversion, ablation); anticoagulation (DOAC preferred over warfarin unless mechanical valve or specific contraindication) Loss of atrial kick worsens filling pressures by 20–30% in stiff LV; new AF in HFpEF = urgent Joglar et al. (2023 AF guideline)
Chronic Kidney Disease Target eGFR ≥30 mL/min/1.73m²; minimize nephrotoxins ACE-I/ARB as BP control agent; SGLT2i provides renal and cardiac protection; limit NSAIDs SGLT2i provides dual benefit (cardiac + renal); closely monitor K⁺ on ACE-I/ARB + SGLT2i KDIGO 2021 guidelines; EMPEROR-Preserved, DELIVER subgroup
Sleep Apnea AHI <5 or well-treated on CPAP CPAP or dental device if OSA present ↓ sympathetic tone, ↓ pulmonary HTN, ↑ exercise tolerance Sleep apnea common in HFpEF; screening underutilized
Anemia Hgb goal ~10–12 g/dL (individualize) Treat underlying cause; iron repletion if Fe-deficient; ESAs only if ESRD + target Hgb Anemia ↓ oxygen carrying capacity, ↓ exercise tolerance; correction ↑ peak VO₂ Common contributor to dyspnea and reduced QOL

Key principle: Pre-SGLT2i era, HFpEF outcomes were driven by aggressive BP control, diabetes management, weight loss, AF rate control. SGLT2i are now the pharmacologic centerpiece, but comorbidity optimization remains essential.

sections.heading: 5C. Diuretics — Symptom control, NOT outcome-reducing
sections.bodyHtml:
Role: Diuretics are the main tool for symptom relief in HFpEF but do not reduce mortality and differ in approach from HFrEF.

Class Agent Dose Notes
Loop diuretic Furosemide 20–40 mg PO daily; titrate to euvolemia goal; IV 20–40 mg for acute decompensation Main agent for congestion relief. Titrate to comfort, not "dry." HFpEF patients tolerate fluid removal less well than HFrEF (lower CO reserve); over-diuresis risks AKI and hypotension.
Torsemide 10–20 mg PO daily Alternative; slightly longer half-life, better absorption than furosemide in some patients
Thiazide-like Chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mg daily Used for mild congestion + HTN control; can be combined with loop agent
Hydrochlorothiazide 12.5–25 mg daily Mild congestion; less potent than chlorthalidone

Targets:

  • Euvolemia goal: no orthopnea, no crackles, no significant edema, weight stable (baseline ±2 lb)
  • Do NOT aggressively diurese past euvolemia. Unlike HFrEF where aggressive diuresis + GDMT is standard, HFpEF preload-dependent; over-diuresis → hypotension, AKI, reduced cardiac output
  • Daily weights: same time, same scale; notify provider of +2 lb in one day or +5 lb in one week

Monitoring:

  • Electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺ — especially if on SGLT2i + ACE-I/ARB together)
  • Creatinine (trend for AKI)
  • Orthostatic vital signs (over-diuresis → syncope risk)
  • Symptom resolution (dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue improving?)

Caution:

  • NSAIDs worsen HFpEF: fluid retention, AKI, HTN worsening; avoid high-dose; acetaminophen preferred
  • Rapid diuresis in setting of AF with RVR: stiff LV depends on atrial kick + filling pressure; rapid rate + aggressive diuresis → hemodynamic collapse

sections.heading: 5D. Emerging and Investigational Agents
sections.bodyHtml:
Agent Class Mechanism Trial / Status Notes
Finerenone Non-steroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (MRA) RAAS antagonism; less hyperkalemia risk than spironolactone FINEARTS-HF (2023, HFpEF subgroup analysis pending) Newer MRA with improved renal profile; potential benefit in HFpEF + CKD; monitor K⁺ and eGFR
Semaglutide (GLP-1 RA) GLP-1 receptor agonist Weight loss, glucose control, CV risk reduction STEP-HFpEF (2023): 21% reduction in HF hospitalizations + CV death in obese HFpEF (BMI ≥27) on top of SGLT2i Emerging first-line for obese HFpEF (BMI ≥27–30); semaglutide (Ozempic®, Wegovy®) or tirzepatide (GLP-1/GIP; Mounjaro®); weight loss 15–20% → improvements in EF and filling pressures
Sacubitril/Valsartan (ARNi) Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor Natriuresis, vasodilation, neurohormonal suppression PARAGON-HF (2019): missed primary endpoint overall; post-hoc: benefit in men, elevated NT-proBNP, preserved renal function Not routine; consider in select patients intolerant to ACE-I/ARB or as escalation after SGLT2i + comorbidity management; not Class I recommendation
Vericiguat Soluble guanylate cyclase stimulator Reduces cardiorenal fibrosis, improves endothelial function VICTORIA trial primarily HFrEF; HFpEF data limited Under investigation in HFpEF; not yet standard of care
Omecamtiv mecarbil Cardiac myosin activator Increases cardiac contractility Not studied in HFpEF Designed for HFrEF; unlikely benefit in HFpEF where contractility is preserved

Clinical approach:

  • First-line: SGLT2i + aggressive comorbidity management (BP, diabetes, weight, AF rate control) + diuretics PRN
  • Second-line (after SGLT2i optimization): consider ACE-I/ARB for HTN control; finerenone if CKD (eGFR 25–90); GLP-1 RA if obese (BMI ≥27) + diabetes (STEP-HFpEF emerging evidence)
  • Third-line: ARNi if intolerant to ACE-I/ARB or select phenotypes

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml: Decompensation, refractory dyspnea, advanced HF phenotyping.

sections.heading: Deterioration triggers
sections.bodyHtml:
• New or worsening dyspnea at rest or with minimal exertion — rising PCWP
  • Orthopnea, PND increasing — pulmonary congestion
  • Weight gain >5 lb in one week or >2 lb in one day — fluid accumulation
  • Persistent hypoxia despite diuretics — consider PE, pneumonia, ARDS, or severe pulmonary edema
  • Syncope or presyncope — hemodynamic compromise (over-diuresis, AKI, new arrhythmia)
  • New or worsening renal dysfunction (Cr rise >30% or eGFR drop >10 mL/min/1.73m²) — cardiorenal syndrome
  • Hyperkalemia (K⁺ >5.5 mEq/L) if on SGLT2i + ACE-I/ARB combo — monitor closely, may need potassium binder
  • Worsening AF with inadequate rate control despite rate-control agents — hemodynamically limiting

sections.heading: **SBAR escalation template**
sections.bodyHtml: S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name]. I'm calling about [patient name, room], admitted [X] days ago with HFpEF." B: "[Age, comorbidities]. EF [%] on prior echo. Baseline NYHA [class]. Current meds: SGLT2i, [others]." A: "Patient is decompensating: dyspnea [acuity], orthopnea [yes/no], weight [+X lb since admission], JVP [elevated/normal], crackles [location], BNP [trend]. O₂ sat [%], HR [rate], BP [value]. Cr [trend], K⁺ [value]." R: "[Increase diuretics / consider IV loop / assess for PE / RHC referral / ICU transfer / palliative care discussion]."

sections.heading: Who to call
sections.bodyHtml:
Situation Contact
Stable HFpEF, new diagnosis, medication initiation Primary cardiologist or hospitalist
Acute decompensation (dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles despite diuretics) Cardiologist (STAT if hypoxic)
Refractory dyspnea despite optimal diuretics + SGLT2i + comorbidity mgmt Cardiologist + advanced HF team (consider RHC, cardiac MRI for phenotyping, transplant/LVAD evaluation if appropriate)
Suspected amyloid (red flags: thick walls, low voltage, GLS reduction, apical sparing) Cardiologist + cardio-oncology (if AL suspected) or hematology (for ATTR workup)
New stroke or TIA Stroke team + neurology
Acute coronary syndrome Cardiology (STEMI protocol)
Life expectancy <6 months, goals-of-care discussion needed Primary team + palliative care / supportive care

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections expandable.

Diagnostic approach: H2FPEF and HFA-PEFF scores H2FPEF Score (Reddy et al., 2018) — clinic-friendly, simple point system:
ComponentPointsDefinition
H: Hypertension on meds1Current antihypertensive therapy
2: Obesity1BMI ≥30 kg/m²
2: Atrial fibrillation1Any prior or current AF
F: Filling pressure elevation1E/e' ≥9 on echo (or ≥14 highly specific)
P: Pulmonary HTN1TR jet velocity → RVSP ≥35 mmHg
E: Elder age1Age ≥60 years
F: Functional capacity reduced1Cannot climb one flight of stairs
Interpretation:
  • 0–1 points: low probability HFpEF; consider alternative diagnoses
  • 2–3 points: intermediate probability; clinician judgment; stress testing or RHC if diagnostic uncertainty
  • ≥4 points: high probability HFpEF in symptomatic patient; reasonable to diagnose and initiate therapy
  • ≥5 points: very high probability; strong diagnostic confidence without RHC Strengths: simple, clinic-practicable, no imaging required. Weakness: lower specificity in borderline cases; normal diastolic parameters on echo lower probability significantly. --- HFA-PEFF Score (Pieske et al., 2019) — more detailed European Heart Association endorsed:
    CategoryMajor (2 points each)Minor (1 point each)
    EchocardiographyE/e' ≥14E/e' 9–13
    LA volume index ≥34 mL/m²LA volume index 26–33 mL/m²
    TR velocity ≥2.8 m/sTR velocity 2.4–2.7 m/s
    BiomarkersNT-proBNP >125 pg/mL (or BNP >35 pg/mL) if sinus, >365 pg/mL if AF[Minor criteria less specific]
    Functional / exercise dataE/e' ≥14 with exercise (stress echo)—
    Scoring:
  • ≥5 points (5 major OR 4 major + 2–3 minor) = diagnostic for HFpEF in symptomatic patient
  • <5 points: HFpEF unlikely unless additional clinical evidence (e.g., elevated PCWP on RHC) Strengths: more specific than H2FPEF; incorporates biomarkers and stress response. Weakness: requires imaging (echo) and biomarker data; less practical in resource-limited settings. --- Clinical decision-making:
  • H2FPEF ≥4 in symptomatic patient + abnormal echo diastolic parameters (E/e' ≥9, LA vol ≥34) + elevated BNP = high confidence in HFpEF diagnosis; start SGLT2i + comorbidity management
  • H2FPEF ≥4 but normal resting echo diastolic parameters: stress echo (dobutamine or exercise) or RHC to assess filling pressures with demand
  • Normal BNP + normal echo + normal stress testing = HFpEF unlikely; reconsider non-cardiac dyspnea (COPD, PE, obesity, anemia, deconditioning)
  • Borderline scoring or conflicting data: RHC for definitive PCWP measurement (elevated at rest ≥18 mmHg or with exercise ≥25 mmHg confirms HFpEF)
Echocardiographic diastolic parameters and diagnostic thresholds
ParameterNormalAbnormal (HFpEF range)Definition
E/e' ratio<8≥9 (moderately abnormal); ≥14 (highly specific)Peak mitral inflow E velocity / early diastolic mitral annular velocity (e'). Reflects filling pressure; noninvasive surrogate for PCWP.
LA volume index<34 mL/m²≥34 mL/m²Left atrial volume / body surface area. Integrates burden of elevated filling pressures over time.
TR velocity / RVSP<35 mmHg (RV)≥35 mmHg; ≥50 suggests severe pulmonary HTNTricuspid regurgitation jet velocity estimate of right ventricular systolic pressure. Post-capillary HTN common in HFpEF.
Isovolumetric relaxation time (IVRT)<105 ms>105 msDuration of isovolumetric relaxation phase. Prolongation indicates impaired relaxation.
Deceleration time (DT)160–240 ms<140 ms (restrictive pattern); >280 ms (relaxation pattern)Time for mitral E velocity to decelerate to zero. Extreme values (very short or very long) indicate abnormal diastolic mechanics.
Tissue Doppler e' (lateral, septal)Lateral e' >10 cm/s; septal e' >8 cm/sLateral e' <10; septal e' <8Early diastolic mitral annular velocity. Reduced e' is marker of impaired relaxation.
Global longitudinal strain (GLS)>−18% (negative indicates contraction)>−15% (reduced GLS)Apical sparing (reduced GLS at base + apex, preserved at midwall) is clue to amyloid rather than isolated HTN-HFpEF.
Pattern recognition:
  • Impaired relaxation: ↑ E/e' (9–14 range), prolonged IVRT, prolonged DT, ↓ e'
  • Pseudonormal pattern: E/e' ≥9 with relatively normal DT (160–240 ms) but abnormal strain; indicates transition to restrictive pattern
  • Restrictive pattern: ↑ E/e' (often ≥14), short DT (<140 ms), markedly ↑ LA volume; indicates severe diastolic dysfunction + elevated PCWP
  • Apical sparing GLS pattern: ↓ GLS at base/midwall but preserved at apex → amyloid phenocopy suspected
Post-cardiac surgery HFpEF and perioperative phenotyping HFpEF in the post-operative context: Many cardiac surgery patients have pre-operative HFpEF (especially valve patients, post-CABG HTN patients). Additional considerations:
  • Fluid accumulation post-CPB: stiff LV + anesthesia + transfused blood volume → rapid fluid accumulation post-op. Diuretics are main tool; tolerance for fluid removal less than HFrEF.
  • Perioperative atrial fibrillation (POAF): ~30% CABG, ~40% valve surgery. Loss of atrial kick worsens HFpEF acutely. Rate control (≤80 bpm) is primary strategy.
  • Temporary RV dysfunction post-op: CPB → transient RV edema, reduced RV contractility. Pulmonary HTN may worsen transiently post-op; usually resolves by POD 3–5.
  • Amyloid and HCM phenocopy: pre-operative echo + CMR or genetic testing (if suspected) guides post-operative expectations (e.g., amyloid requires tafamidis, not standard HFpEF management) Post-operative HFpEF management:
    • SGLT2i: continue home dose immediately post-op (no washout period needed); cardioprotective + mild natriuretic
    • Diuretics: titrate to euvolemia (no crackles, euvolemic weight baseline ±2 lb); do not over-diurese
    • Beta-blockers: reinitiate home dose POD 0–1 if hemodynamically stable; crucial for AF prevention + HR control
    • ACE-I/ARB: hold POD 0–1 if hypotensive; reinitiate when SBP >100 mmHg and labs stable
    • AF management: if POAF develops, rate control primary (HR ≤80); amiodarone for rhythm control if appropriate Discharge planning:
    • Ensure SGLT2i filled and patient educated on adherence
    • Cardiology follow-up within 7 days post-discharge (verify BP control, assess for new AF, weight stability)
    • Cardiac rehab referral (150 min/week aerobic + 2x/week resistance training)
    • Home BP monitoring if HTN; patient keeps log for follow-up
Atrial fibrillation in HFpEF: rate vs. rhythm control AF is present in ~50% of HFpEF at diagnosis and significantly worsens outcomes. Loss of atrial kick → rise in filling pressure by 20–30% in stiff LV; hemodynamically poorly tolerated. Rate control (primary strategy):
  • Target HR ≤80 bpm at rest (some recent data suggest ≤110 acceptable in select patients; LENIENT trial; individualize based on symptoms)
  • Agents: beta-blocker (metoprolol, carvedilol succinate, bisoprolol — titrate cautiously to avoid excessive bradycardia); non-DHP CCB (diltiazem, verapamil) if beta-blocker contraindicated or insufficient
  • Caution in HFpEF: avoid negative inotropic effect; titrate cautiously; excessive bradycardia (HR <50) reduces cardiac output in stiff LV with reduced reserve Rhythm control (consider if AF recent-onset <1 year or hemodynamically limiting):
  • Amiodarone: first-line for rhythm control post-operative or in-hospital AF; IV loading then PO transition
  • Cardioversion: synchronized direct-current cardioversion (DCCV) if unstable or after amiodarone failure
  • Ablation: referral to electrophysiology if frequent recurrent AF despite medical therapy; may be beneficial if AF relatively recent Anticoagulation:
  • CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥1 (most HFpEF patients score ≥2) → anticoagulation indicated
  • DOAC preferred (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) over warfarin for most (easier dosing, fewer interactions, no INR monitoring)
  • Warfarin if mechanical valve, severe renal failure (eGFR <15), or DOAC contraindication
  • Duration: if AF paroxysmal or newly diagnosed, anticoagulation typically lifelong given recurrence/structural substrate (HFpEF)
Chronotropic incompetence and exercise prescription Chronotropic incompetence (CI): inability to increase heart rate appropriately with exercise. Common in HFpEF (especially if on beta-blockers or with intrinsic SA node dysfunction) and correlates with worse prognosis and reduced peak VO₂. Recognition: on stress testing, patient achieves <85% predicted maximum HR despite adequate exertion; blunted blood pressure response; reduced functional capacity. Mechanism: autonomic dysfunction, beta-blocker effect, SA node disease, diastolic dysfunction limiting atrial contribution to CO increase. Clinical implications:
  • Do NOT excessively slow heart rate in HFpEF on beta-blockers; stiff LV depends on rate to maintain CO
  • Exercise prescription: aerobic training (walking, cycling) at moderate intensity (50–70% max HR) + resistance training (2x/week) improves peak VO₂ despite CI
  • Cardiac rehab: supervised program superior to home-based exercise; allows HR/BP monitoring and progression guidance
Coronary microvascular dysfunction in HFpEF Endothelial dysfunction and coronary microvascular disease (CMD): increasingly recognized as important mechanism in HFpEF, especially in diabetics and women. Pathophysiology: reduced nitric oxide bioavailability, impaired flow-mediated vasodilation, capillary rarefaction → inadequate coronary blood flow during exercise despite normal epicardial coronaries. Clinical manifestations:
  • Angina with normal coronary angiography (microvascular angina)
  • Blunted peak VO₂ despite normal LV systolic function and absence of significant diastolic parameters
  • Dyspnea with exertion disproportionate to HFpEF severity Diagnostic workup:
  • Coronary angiography: normal epicardial coronaries (rule out obstructive CAD)
  • Stress testing (exercise or adenosine stress echo): reproduces symptoms, shows ischemic ECG changes or wall motion abnormalities, rises in filling pressures
  • Invasive coronary reactivity testing / acetylcholine provocation (research setting): demonstrates impaired microvascular vasodilation Management:
  • Symptom-targeted: nitrates (caution in HFpEF; may reduce preload excessively); calcium channel blockers (diltiazem, verapamil) for vasodilation
  • Comorbidity targeting: aggressive diabetes control (SGLT2i, GLP-1 RA), hypertension management (ACE-I/ARB + CCB), smoking cessation
  • Exercise: paradoxically, aerobic training improves endothelial function and microvascular vasodilatory capacity over time

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration trajectory in currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Deterioration signals warrant escalation.

  • Worsening dyspnea despite optimized diuretics — rising PCWP, possible pneumonia/PE, worsening renal function (cardiorenal syndrome)
  • New or worsening orthopnea, PND — pulmonary congestion; may need IV diuretics
  • Rapid weight gain (>5 lb/week) — fluid accumulation outpacing diuresis; escalate diuretics or investigate trigger
  • New AF with inadequate rate control — hemodynamically limiting; loss of atrial kick critical in stiff LV
  • Syncope or presyncope — hemodynamic decompensation, arrhythmia, AKI, over-diuresis
  • Renal function worsening (Cr rise >30%, eGFR drop >10 mL/min/1.73m²) — cardiorenal syndrome; assess volume status and perfusion; cautious about SGLT2i continuation (generally safe if eGFR >20)
  • Hyperkalemia (K⁺ >5.5 mEq/L) on SGLT2i + ACE-I/ARB combo — monitor K⁺ closely; may need potassium binder or de-escalation
  • Persistent hypoxia despite diuretics — consider PE (immobility, AF + HFpEF = thromboembolism risk), pneumonia, ARDS
  • Rising troponin, new EKG changes — acute coronary syndrome; myocardial infarction may precipitate HFpEF exacerbation
  • Severe hypertension (SBP >180 mmHg) — HTN emergency; escalate BP medications; may need IV agents
  • Altered mental status, confusion — hypoxia, hypercapnia, medication effect (diuretic-induced hyponatremia), infection/sepsis
  • Cool extremities, low urine output (<0.5 mL/kg/h) — hypoperfusion; possible cardiogenic shock or AKI

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. HFpEF is NOT homogeneous. It is a heterogeneous syndrome with multiple phenotypes: hypertensive remodeling, post-capillary pulmonary HTN, amyloid infiltration, HCM phenocopy, AF-related, obesity-related, post-viral inflammatory. One-size-fits-all management fails. Phenotyping (echo pattern, biomarkers, CMR, genetic testing) guides therapy selection.

  2. Rule out amyloid early if red flags present. Cardiac amyloid mimics HFpEF perfectly — stiff LV, diastolic dysfunction, preserved EF. Red flags: LV wall thickness ≥12–14 mm, reduced GLS with apical sparing, low-voltage ECG despite thick walls, carpal tunnel (bilateral), hip/knee arthropathy history, pseudo-infarct pattern on ECG.

    Screen with PYP scan (ATTR) + SPEP/IFE. If confirmed, tafamidis (ATTR) or chemo (AL) replaces standard HFpEF drugs.

  3. HCM phenocopy (restrictive/non-obstructive HCM presenting as "HFpEF"). Thick-walled LV, small cavity, diastolic dysfunction, elevated filling pressures, but primary pathology is abnormal myofilament dynamics (sarcomeric mutation), not amyloid or HTN remodeling. Genetic testing (HCM gene panel) distinguishes; mavacamtén (first-in-class cardiac myosin inhibitor) now approved for symptomatic HCM but not HFpEF per se.

  4. SGLT2 inhibitors are FIRST-LINE now. EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER trials changed paradigm. All HFpEF patients should be on dapagliflozin 10 mg or empagliflozin 10 mg daily, regardless of diabetes status. This is standard of care, not optional. No washout period; start immediately, continue during acute decompensation.

  5. H2FPEF and HFA-PEFF scores matter. Diagnosis of HFpEF requires objective evidence. Scoring systems provide diagnostic confidence without invasive RHC.

    H2FPEF ≥4 in symptomatic patient with abnormal echo diastolic parameters = reasonable to diagnose and treat HFpEF. Normal resting diastolic parameters → stress echo or RHC; normal BNP makes HFpEF less likely but does not exclude.

  6. Stress testing is underutilized. Many HFpEF patients have normal diastolic parameters at rest but develop abnormal E/e', RVSP, or symptoms with exercise or dobutamine stress. If dyspnea + normal resting echo + high clinical suspicion → stress echo or exercise test. Unmasking HFpEF on stress testing guides therapy and prognostication.

  7. Right heart catheterization is gold standard, not routine. RHC confirms elevated filling pressures (PCWP ≥18 mmHg at rest or ≥25 mmHg with exercise) and distinguishes HFpEF from non-cardiac dyspnea.

    Normal PCWP essentially rules out HFpEF. Reserve for borderline echo / clinical pictures, research trials, or advanced HF phenotyping (LVAD/transplant candidacy assessment).

  8. AF in HFpEF is THE trigger. Present in ~50% at diagnosis; new AF onset is urgent. Loss of atrial kick drops CO by 20–30% in stiff LV.

    Rate control (HR ≤80) is PRIMARY strategy. Rhythm control (amiodarone, cardioversion, ablation) consider if AF new (<1 year) or hemodynamically limiting. Do NOT default to rhythm-control-first thinking; rate control usually sufficient and safer.

  9. Weight loss + exercise are REAL therapies, not adjuncts. Multiple RCTs show 5–10% weight loss ↓ LV filling pressures, ↑ exercise capacity, improves KCCQ (quality of life). Structured aerobic + resistance training ↑ peak VO₂, ↓ exertional dyspnea. Often overlooked for "just take a pill." Dietitian + cardiac rehab referral are critical; data stronger in HFpEF than HFrEF.

  10. HFpEF is preload-sensitive; avoid aggressive over-diuresis. Unlike HFrEF where "wet is bad," in HFpEF the stiff LV depends on adequate preload. Over-diuresis → hypotension, AKI, cardiorenal syndrome, reduced cardiac output.

    Diuretic target is euvolemia (no crackles, no orthopnea), not dryness. Monitor daily weights, orthostatic vitals; escalate if symptomatic hypotension or Cr rise.

  11. Beta-blockers: benefit unclear in HFpEF. Unlike HFrEF where beta-blockers are foundational (reduce mortality), no dedicated HFpEF mortality trials. Benefit for AF rate control, HTN, post-MI. Titrate cautiously (excessive bradycardia ↓ CO in stiff LV). Not contraindicated; useful for AF + HTN; just don't assume essential for HFpEF per se.

  12. ACE-I/ARB/ARNi data are modest in HFpEF. I-PRESERVE trial (irbesartan): negative for primary endpoint (CV death + HF hosp).

    PARAGON-HF (sacubitril/valsartan): missed primary but post-hoc benefit in men, elevated NT-proBNP, preserved renal function. Use for HTN control and comorbidities, not as primary HFpEF therapy. ARNi not routine unless ACE-I/ARB intolerant.

  13. Spironolactone (MRA) in HFpEF: regional variation. TOPCAT trial (2014): spironolactone in HFpEF overall negative for primary endpoint; Americas subgroup post-hoc analysis showed HF hospitalization reduction. Hyperkalemia risk (K⁺ >5.5 mEq/L, especially on combo with SGLT2i + ACE-I/ARB). Consider if secondary hyperaldosteronism suspected (low K⁺, refractory HTN) or AF present; monitor K⁺ closely. Finerenone (newer non-steroidal MRA) may have improved safety profile.

  14. GLP-1 RAs (semaglutide, tirzepatide) emerging in obese HFpEF. STEP-HFpEF (2023): semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly in obese HFpEF (BMI ≥27) showed 21% reduction in HF hospitalizations + CV death on top of SGLT2i. Weight loss 15–20% → EF improvements, LA volume reduction, filling pressure improvements.

    Now consider first-line for obese (BMI ≥27–30) HFpEF with diabetes or metabolic syndrome. Tirzepatide (GLP-1/GIP dual agonist; Mounjaro®) also under investigation.

  15. Post-operative HFpEF: fluid management is key. HFpEF post-op accumulates fluid easily (stiff LV, CPB → transfused volume, anesthesia effects).

    Less likely to develop cardiogenic shock than HFrEF, but fluid shifts are MORE symptomatic (dyspnea, crackles, orthopnea out of proportion).

    Diuretics are backbone; do NOT over-diurese. Goal euvolemia (baseline weight ±2 lb, no crackles, no orthopnea). Continue SGLT2i + reinitiate home beta-blockers POD 0–1. Cardiac rehab referral on discharge.

cards.title: Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)
cards.quickAnswer: HFrEF = EF ≤ 40% (formally ≤ 35% for device therapy) with systolic dysfunction. The four pillars of GDMT—ARNi/ACEI + beta-blocker + MRA + SGLT2i initiated simultaneously and titrated to maximum tolerated doses—reduce mortality by ~73% (Heidenreich et al., 2022). All four are initiated early (even during euvolemia on admission), once decompensation is controlled. Device therapy: ICD at EF ≤ 35% + NYHA II–III on GDMT for ≥ 3 months; CRT for EF ≤ 35% + LBBB QRS ≥ 150 ms. Advanced: LVAD for Stage D (inotrope-dependent, recurrent decompensation, cardiogenic shock); transplant for refractory HF. Nursing pearl: daily weights (+2 lb = escalate diuretic/notify MD), sodium ≤ 2–3 g/day, fluid restrict only if Na < 130, continuous telemetry if EF ≤ 35%.
