sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who it applies to.

  • Definition: Heart failure syndrome with ejection fraction ≤ 40% characterized by systolic dysfunction—the left ventricle fails to contract effectively, reducing cardiac output. Formally, HFrEF is EF ≤ 40% (diagnostic); device eligibility threshold is EF ≤ 35%.

  • Epidemiology:

  • Approximately 6 million symptomatic HF patients in the US; HFrEF accounts for ~50–60% (Heidenreich et al., 2022)
  • Ischemic cardiomyopathy (post-MI): 50–60% of HFrEF; mortality higher than non-ischemic
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM): idiopathic, viral, toxic (chemotherapy, alcohol, cocaine), peripartum, genetic, infiltrative (amyloid, sarcoidosis)

  • Prevalence peaks > 65 years but can occur at any age (myocarditis, peripartum, arrhythmia-mediated)

  • Who this applies to: Patients with prior MI, hypertension, valvular disease, or viral prodrome presenting with progressive dyspnea; patients with known HFrEF admitted for decompensation or non-cardiac surgery; post-cardiac surgery patients; patients requiring device placement or advanced therapies.

  • Why it matters: Most common and most morbid form of heart failure. Mortality without GDMT is high (~50% at 5 years); with optimal GDMT, five-year survival improves to ~60–70%. Uncontrolled rate/volume increases stroke risk, ICU length of stay, and readmission.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner teaching on the mechanism and consequence.

Systolic dysfunction — impaired contractility from myocardial damage, myocyte loss, fibrosis, inflammation, or infiltration.

Neurohormonal activation and adverse remodeling:

  • RAAS activation: low cardiac output triggers renin → angiotensin II → vasoconstriction, fluid retention, inflammation, fibrosis
  • Sympathetic nervous system (SNS) activation: catecholamine surge → increased HR, inotropy (initially compensatory, then harmful), peripheral vasoconstriction
  • Inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, others): drive progressive myocyte apoptosis and remodeling
  • LV remodeling: eccentric hypertrophy (LV dilates, wall thins) → ↑ wall stress → ↓ contractility (vicious cycle) → functional mitral regurgitation → atrial dilation → atrial fibrillation

Hemodynamic consequences:

  • Forward failure: reduced cardiac output → fatigue, exercise intolerance, hypotension, altered mental status, poor organ perfusion
  • Backward failure: elevated LV end-diastolic pressure → pulmonary congestion (dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, crackles, pulmonary edema) and systemic congestion (edema, ascites, hepatomegaly)

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Presentation and recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Chronic compensated HFrEF presentation:

  • Progressive dyspnea (exertional → orthopnea → paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea)
  • Fatigue and exercise intolerance (often earliest symptom)
  • Peripheral edema, ascites, hepatic congestion (RUQ discomfort, hepatomegaly)
  • Nocturia (recumbency improves renal perfusion)
  • Cardiac cachexia in advanced HF (involuntary weight loss) — strong mortality predictor

Acute decompensation presentation:

  • Acute dyspnea at rest, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
  • Pulmonary congestion: bilateral crackles, wheezes ("cardiac asthma"), tachypnea
  • Elevated jugular venous pressure, hepatojugular reflux, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema
  • Oliguria, cool extremities, altered mental status
  • Cardiogenic shock: hypotension, poor perfusion, AKI, elevated liver enzymes

Physical exam findings — classic HFrEF:

  • Tachycardia, tachypnea (compensatory)
  • Bilateral lung crackles (basilar, increasing with supine positioning)
  • S3 gallop (ventricular, pathognomonic in systolic HF); may have S4 if concurrent diastolic dysfunction
  • Displaced point of maximal impulse (lateral, diffuse)
  • Functional mitral regurgitation (holosystolic murmur at apex, radiates to axilla)
  • Elevated JVP, hepatomegaly, hepatojugular reflux, ascites (signs of elevated central venous pressure)
  • Cool extremities, weak pulses, poor capillary refill (if cardiogenic shock)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic exam. Pure assessment; no actions yet.

  • Vital signs: HR, BP (orthostatic if hypotensive), SpO₂, RR, temperature
  • Respiratory: lung auscultation (crackles, wheezes, effusions), accessory muscle use, work of breathing
  • Cardiovascular: JVP height, hepatojugular reflux, apical impulse character (location, size, thrills), heart sounds (S3, S4, murmurs), peripheral pulses, capillary refill
  • Peripheral: edema (location, pitting, brawny), ascites, weight (baseline + acute change), skin temperature, perfusion
  • Neuro: mental status, syncope/presyncope history, signs of stroke
  • Labs — recent and pertinent:
  • BNP or NT-proBNP (baseline on admission; trends during diuresis)
  • Echocardiography (EF, LV dimensions, RV function, valvular disease, thrombus, diastolic function)
  • Creatinine, eGFR (baseline + trends post-GDMT initiation)
  • Electrolytes (K⁺, Na⁺, Mg²⁺) — especially post-MRA/ACEI/SGLT2i start
  • CBC (Hgb, ferritin, TSAT if anemic — iron deficiency worsens symptoms)
  • LFTs, TSH (rule out secondary etiologies)
  • ECG (LBBB for CRT, ischemic pattern, arrhythmia)
  • Troponin if chest pain or acute presentation
  • Medication and surgical history:
  • Home GDMT doses (verify against target doses; identify any at suboptimal therapy)
  • Prior episodes of decompensation; response to diuretics
  • Cardiac surgery history (post-MI, post-CABG, post-valve repair/replacement)
  • Allergies or intolerances to GDMT agents (angioedema on ACEi → switch to ARB or ARNi)
  • Hemodynamic profile (mental model):
  • Warm & dry (euvolemic, good perfusion) — safe for beta-blocker and ACE/ARB uptitration
  • Warm & wet (euvolemic perfusion + volume overload) — diuresis priority, hold uptitration
  • Cold & wet (poor perfusion + volume overload) — inotrope + diuretic, hold uptitration
  • Cold & dry (poor perfusion, euvolemic) — rare; may need IV fluids or inotropes

sections.heading: 5A. GDMT Pillars — Foundation of HFrEF Care
sections.bodyHtml:
"Simultaneous quadruple therapy" is now standard. All four pillars are initiated early (even in-hospital during decompensation once euvolemic) and titrated in parallel over 4–6 weeks to maximum tolerated doses. This approach reduces mortality ~73% compared to standard care (Heidenreich et al., 2022).

Pillar 1: ARNi or ACE-I/ARB

Agent Starting Dose Target Dose Key Considerations
Sacubitril/valsartan (ARNi) [PREFERRED] 49/51 mg BID 97/103 mg BID Superior to ACE-I/ARB (PARADIGM-HF trial, Solomon et al., 2014). Hypotension common during titration. Hold 36 hours after ACE-I for washout (risk of angioedema if overlap). Requires K⁺ monitoring.
Lisinopril (ACE-I) 2.5–5 mg daily 20–40 mg daily Cough in 10–20% → switch to ARB or ARNi. Hyperkalemia risk; monitor K⁺ + Cr. First-line if ARNi not available or patient arrhythmia-intolerant.
Losartan or valsartan (ARB) 25–50 mg daily 50–100 mg daily Better tolerability than ACE-I (no cough). Transition bridge from ACE-I to ARNi acceptable. Monitor K⁺.

Pillar 2: Beta-blocker

Agent Starting Dose Target Dose Key Considerations
Carvedilol 3.125 mg BID 25 mg BID Alpha + beta blockade; non-selective. Initiate only after euvolemia (avoid in hypotension/acute decompensation). Titrate q2 weeks.
Metoprolol succinate (Toprol XL) 12.5–25 mg daily 190–200 mg daily Beta-1 selective. Slower titration than carvedilol. Note: metoprolol tartrate lacks evidence; use succinate formulation.
Bisoprolol 1.25 mg daily 10 mg daily Beta-1 selective; once-daily dosing. Strong European trial evidence. Less US utilization.

Critical: Beta-blockers worsen acute decompensation if patient euvolemic status unclear.

Initiate only after euvolemia achieved. Titrate slowly (every 2 weeks); stop if SBP < 90, HR < 50, or acute decompensation worsens.

Pillar 3: Mineralocorticoid Receptor Antagonist (MRA)

Agent Starting Dose Target Dose Key Considerations
Spironolactone 12.5–25 mg daily 25–50 mg daily Monitor K⁺ and Cr closely (hyperkalemia risk ~5–10%). Combines risk with ACE/ARB + SGLT2i. Gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction (spiro-specific).
Eplerenone (selective MRA) 25 mg daily 50 mg daily Fewer hormonal side effects; similar efficacy. More expensive. Same K⁺/Cr monitoring required.

Rule: Do NOT withhold MRA for mild CKD (eGFR 30–60). Monitor K⁺: check baseline, 3–5 days post-initiation, and after each dose increase.

If K⁺ > 5.5 mEq/L, reduce or hold MRA; recheck in 5–7 days. If Cr rises > 30% from baseline, assess volume status and GDMT tolerance.

Pillar 4: SGLT2 Inhibitor

Agent Starting Dose Target Dose Key Considerations
Dapagliflozin (Farxiga) 10 mg daily 10 mg daily Benefit independent of diabetes status (DAPA-HF trial). Reduces HF hospitalizations + mortality. Mycotic infections risk; rare DKA if type 1 DM (contraindication). Female genital infections.
Empagliflozin (Jardiance) 10 mg daily 10 mg daily Similar efficacy (EMPEROR-Reduced trial). Also works in HFpEF. Use if dapagliflozin not tolerated.

Key: Start immediately; no need to wait for hyperglycemia. SGLT2i are renal-protective and gentler on K⁺ balance than ACE/ARB + MRA.

GDMT Titration Strategy:

  1. Initiate all four pillars in sequence, 2–4 weeks apart, starting with ACEI/ARB (or ARNi if euvolemic), then beta-blocker (if euvolemic + HR > 55), then MRA, then SGLT2i.
  2. Only when euvolemic — aggressive diuresis first; hold uptitration if hypotensive, AKI, or decompensating.
  3. Target: maximum tolerated dose of each. Accept lower doses rather than omit entirely if orthostatic, syncope, or Cr rise.
  4. Monitor K⁺, Cr, and BP at each step. Hyperkalemia and AKI are the main dose-limiting toxicities.
  5. Patient education: drugs work best when all four are optimized; expect titration to take 1–2 months.

Diuretics (Symptom relief, not mortality-reducing)

Agent Starting PO Usual Range IV (Acute) Notes
Furosemide 20–40 mg daily 20–200+ mg daily 40 mg IV; repeat q2–4h First-line loop diuretic; short half-life. Dose escalation if no diuresis in 1–2 h.
Torsemide 10–20 mg daily 10–40 mg daily 10–20 mg IV Longer half-life; potentially lower ototoxicity. Better bioavailability than furosemide.
Bumetanide 0.5–1 mg daily 0.5–2 mg daily 0.5–1 mg IV 40× potency of furosemide. Use if loop-resistant or intolerant.
Metolazone (thiazide-like) — 2.5–5 mg daily — Used 30 min before IV loop for refractory congestion. Synergistic (blocks proximal + distal tubule). Hyperglycemia, hypokalemia risk.

Diuretic principles:

  • Goal: euvolemia — relief of congestion (orthopnea, crackles, edema gone) without hypotension/AKI
  • Daily weights: gold standard for volume status. +2 lb in 24 h or +5 lb in 1 week = escalate diuretic or notify provider
  • I/O tracking: especially post-dose to assess response
  • Diuretic resistance (high-dose loop ineffective) → optimize GDMT (improve CO), add metolazone, switch to IV dosing, restrict NSAIDs

Adjunctive agents (guideline-supported, context-dependent):

Agent Indication Dose Evidence
Hydralazine + isosorbide dinitrate ACE-I/ARB intolerant (cough, angioedema) Hydral 25–75 mg TID; ISDN 20–40 mg TID Mortality benefit in A-HeFT (African American cohort); less robust than ARNi.
Ivabradine HR > 70 at rest on beta-blocker; sinus rhythm 5 mg BID Reduces HR without negative inotropy. Use if beta-blocker inadequate.
Vericiguat Recent HF decompensation/hospitalization; EF ≤ 40%; SBP ≥ 100 2.5–5 mg daily Reduces readmission ~10–15%. Newer agent (2021 approval).

sections.heading: 5B. Device Therapy
sections.bodyHtml:
Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator (ICD) — Primary Prevention

Criterion Detail
EF ≤ 35%
NYHA class II, III
GDMT duration ≥ 3 months at optimized doses
Mechanism Detects and terminates ventricular fibrillation / pulseless VT; prevents sudden cardiac death
Longevity 5–7 years (battery dependent on pacing burden)
Efficacy ~25–30% reduction in sudden cardiac death mortality

Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy (CRT) — Biventricular Pacing

Criterion Detail
EF ≤ 35%
LBBB + QRS ≥ 150 ms (strongest evidence); ≥ 130 ms with additional criteria acceptable per 2022 guidelines (Heidenreich et al., 2022)
GDMT Optimal dosing preferred (not required if contraindicated)
Mechanism Synchronizes RV + LV contraction, improving mechanical efficiency and EF
Responder rate ~70% show EF improvement ≥ 5 points or symptom improvement; ~30% non-responders
Variants CRT-D (defibrillator + CRT if also ICD-eligible); CRT-P (pacemaker + CRT if bradycardic or high AV block, no SCD risk)
Longevity 5–6 years (CRT-D); 4–5 years (CRT-P)

Special considerations:

  • RV function assessment critical: preserved RV-EF improves CRT outcomes
  • Post-cardiac surgery patient: if CRT needed post-op, implantation may be delayed until scar maturation (~6–12 weeks) unless urgently symptomatic
  • ICD secondary prevention: if prior sustained VT/VF or cardiac arrest, ICD indicated regardless of EF (after reversible cause ruled out)

sections.heading: 5C. Advanced Therapies
sections.bodyHtml:
Left Ventricular Assist Device (LVAD)

Aspect Detail
Indication SCAI Class C–D: inotrope-dependent, recurrent hospitalizations, cardiogenic shock despite GDMT
Type Continuous-flow pump (axial or centrifugal); unloads LV, improves systemic perfusion
Purpose Bridge to transplant or destination therapy (permanent support if transplant ineligible)
Major complications Infection (driveline), thromboembolism, bleeding, RV failure, device malfunction
Durability 5–10 years depending on device type
Outcomes Improves functional status and survival vs. inotropes alone

Heart Transplantation

Aspect Detail
Indication Refractory HFrEF (SCAI D), age-appropriate, good compliance/psychosocial stability, no absolute contraindications
Absolute contraindications Uncontrolled infection, active malignancy, irreversible organ dysfunction (liver, lung, kidney), severe PAH
Relative contraindications Age > 70–75 (variable per institution), advanced cachexia, diabetes with complications
Median survival post-transplant 10–15 years
Limitations Organ scarcity, immunosuppression burden, acute/chronic rejection risk (vasculopathy), malignancy risk from immunosuppression

Palliative & Comfort Care

Advanced HFrEF (SCAI C–D, recurrent hospitalizations, GDMT-refractory) warrants early palliative care referral in parallel with medical therapy. Goals-of-care conversation, advance directives, symptom management (morphine for dyspnea is appropriate), hospice. Many patients live years with comfort-focused care alongside GDMT optimization.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for provider communication:

S: "Dr. [Name], this is [RN name] about [patient name, room]." B: "Patient with HFrEF (EF [%], on GDMT since [date]) presenting with [acute change: dyspnea, orthopnea, weight gain +[X] lb, chest pain, syncope, reduced UOP]." A: "Vitals: BP [X], HR [X], RR [X], SpO₂ [X]. Exam: [crackles? JVP? edema? perfusion?]. Recent labs: K [X], Cr [baseline to current], BNP [X]. Current GDMT: [list doses]. Diuretic: [current dose/frequency, response]." R: "Requesting [GDMT escalation / diuretic adjustment / ICU transfer / cardiology consult / advanced therapy evaluation]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Urgency
Stable, GDMT uptitration tolerance assessment PCP or cardiology clinic Routine (24–48 h)
Worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, +2 lb daily weight On-call APP or cardiology fellow Urgent (2–4 h)
Acute pulmonary edema, hypoxia (SpO₂ < 90%), crackles RRT/Rapid Response + cardiology STAT
Cardiogenic shock (hypotension, altered mental status, oliguria) Code team + cardiology fellow/attending + ICU STAT
Syncope, sustained VT, ICD firing Activate code + cardiology + EP STAT
Hyperkalemia (K > 6.0) on GDMT Nephrology + cardiology Urgent (hold MRA/ACEI/SGLT2i, labs)
Acute kidney injury (Cr > 2.5 or > 30% rise) on GDMT Nephrology + cardiology Urgent
Discharge readiness; GDMT optimization Cardiology (7-day post-discharge appointment essential) Routine

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology & neurohormonal cascade — detailed The RAAS–SNS–cytokine feedback loop: In HFrEF, reduced cardiac output triggers low-pressure baroreceptor activation:
  1. Juxtaglomerular apparatus senses ↓ renal perfusion → renin release
  2. Renin → angiotensinogen → angiotensin I → (ACE) → angiotensin II
  3. Angiotensin II effects: vasoconstriction (↑ afterload, worsens CO further), aldosterone release (Na/H₂O retention, ↑ preload, ↑ fluid volume), SNS activation (↑ HR, ↑ contractility acutely, then becomes harmful)
  4. SNS activation: catecholamine surge → ↑ HR (ischemic workload), ↑ contractility (initially helpful, then myocyte damage), peripheral vasoconstriction
  5. Inflammatory cascade: TNF-α, IL-6, IL-1 → myocyte apoptosis, fibrosis, further remodeling
  6. LV remodeling: eccentric hypertrophy (LV dilates, wall thins, radius ↑) → ↑ myocardial stress (Laplace law: Stress = PR/2h) → ↓ contractility → further CO reduction → vicious cycle Why GDMT works:
    • ACE-I/ARB: blocks angiotensin II formation/receptor → ↓ vasoconstriction, ↓ aldosterone, ↓ fibrosis, ↓ myocyte apoptosis
    • ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan): additionally inhibits neprilysin → ↑ natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP) → vasodilation, natriuresis, anti-fibrotic, anti-remodeling
    • Beta-blocker: blocks SNS → ↓ HR (energetically favorable), ↓ myocyte apoptosis, ↓ arrhythmia substrate
    • MRA: blocks aldosterone → ↓ Na retention, ↓ K wasting, anti-fibrotic in LV/vasculature
    • SGLT2i: mechanisms unclear but include improved myocardial energetics, anti-inflammatory, natriuretic, anti-hypertrophic effects
Major HFrEF trials & paradigm shifts PARADIGM-HF (Solomon et al., 2014)
  • Design: ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan) vs. ACE-I (enalapril) in HFrEF
  • Outcome: ARNi superior: ↓ CV death/HF hospitalization by 20%, ↓ CV mortality 16%
  • Impact: ARNi now preferred over ACE-I/ARB as first-line RAAS inhibitor DAPA-HF (Dapagliflozin Trial)
  • Design: SGLT2i (dapagliflozin) vs. placebo in HFrEF (± diabetes)
  • Outcome: ↓ HF hospitalization + CV death by 26%; benefit independent of diabetes status
  • Impact: SGLT2i now 4th pillar, initiated regardless of glucose control EMPEROR-Reduced (Empagliflozin Trial)
  • Design: SGLT2i (empagliflozin) vs. placebo in HFrEF
  • Outcome: Similar benefit to dapagliflozin; also improves HFpEF
  • Impact: Either SGLT2i acceptable; empagliflozin has broader phenotype benefit Quadruple therapy paradigm shift:
  • Old model (pre-2020): sequential add-one-drug-at-a-time to tolerance; delays GDMT benefits
  • Current model (2022 guidelines, Heidenreich et al.): simultaneous quadruple initiation within 2–4 weeks, titrate in parallel; improves adherence + early outcome benefits
Special HFrEF subgroups & etiology-specific management Post-MI HFrEF (ischemic cardiomyopathy):
  • Peak EF recovery occurs over 3–6 months post-MI if revascularized
  • Do NOT place ICD immediately post-MI (unless sustained VT/VF); delay 40–90 days to allow recovery window
  • Aggressive GDMT + revascularization → ~30% of post-MI HFrEF patients recover EF above threshold (no longer ICD-eligible)
  • Cardiac rehab essential; beta-blocker critical for secondary prevention Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (TIC):
  • Chronic high-burden AF, frequent SVT, or high PVC burden causing HFrEF
  • EF recovery is possible with aggressive rate control or ablation; recovery occurs over weeks–months
  • Look for clues: recent arrhythmia onset, persistent tachycardia, high PVC burden on Holter Infiltrative HFrEF (Amyloid, Sarcoid, Hemochromatosis):
  • Standard GDMT is foundation but etiology-specific therapy is critical
  • Amyloid: TTR-lowering agents (tafamidis), immunotherapy for AL amyloid
  • Hemochromatosis: iron chelation (deferoxamine, deferiprone, deferasirox)
  • Sarcoidosis: immunosuppression or immunotherapy; monitor for conduction disease
  • Genetic/familial cardiomyopathy: genetic counseling, family screening, possible genetic therapy in future Peripartum cardiomyopathy:
  • HFrEF onset in last trimester or first 5 months postpartum
  • Often reversible if caught early + aggressive GDMT
  • ARNi/ACE-I/ARB contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic); switch at postpartum
  • ~25% remain persistently reduced EF; ~75% recover to normal/near-normal EF Viral myocarditis with HFrEF:
  • Recent viral prodrome, fever, troponin elevation, CMR shows edema/inflammation
  • May be fulminant → require ECMO/LVAD bridge or transplant
  • Standard GDMT + supportive care; some recover EF over weeks–months
  • Biopsy-proven myocarditis: consider inotropes, mechanical support early Iron-deficient HFrEF:
  • IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) improves exercise capacity + symptoms if ferritin < 100 ng/mL or TSAT < 20%, even with normal hemoglobin
  • Screen all HFrEF; treat if iron-deficient
  • Separate from anemia correction; iron supplementation benefits even non-anemic patients Low-EF + mechanical valve or LV thrombus:
  • Thromboembolism risk high even if hemodynamically stable
  • Early anticoagulation, low threshold for advanced imaging (TEE if thrombus suspected)
  • Device placement may need to be delayed if thrombus present; consider LVAD if transplant contraindicated
ACC/AHA Heart Failure Stages (A–D) and NYHA Functional Classes ACC/AHA Stages (Heidenreich et al., 2022)
StageDefinitionGDMT Focus
AAt risk for HF (HTN, DM, CAD, obesity) but no structural disease, no symptomsRisk factor management: BP control, glucose control, smoking cessation
BStructural heart disease but no HF symptoms (reduced EF on echo, prior MI, LVH)ACE-I/ARB ± beta-blocker for specific etiologies (post-MI, low EF); slow HF progression
C1HF with prior/current symptoms (NYHA I–II)All four pillars: ARNi/ACE/ARB + BB + MRA + SGLT2i, diuretics PRN, device if EF ≤ 35% + LBBB
C2HF with prior/current symptoms (NYHA III–IV)Aggressive GDMT ± inotropes, ICU/step-down; evaluate advanced therapies if refractory
DAdvanced/refractory HF (recurrent hospitalizations despite GDMT, cardiogenic shock, inotrope-dependent, SCAI C–D)LVAD, transplant, mechanical support, palliative care
NYHA Functional Classes
ClassDefinition
INo symptoms with ordinary activity
IISymptoms with moderate exertion (e.g., 2 flights of stairs); asymptomatic at rest
IIISymptoms with minimal exertion (e.g., 1 flight of stairs); limited daily activity
IVSymptoms at rest; unable to perform any physical activity without discomfort
Mapping: NYHA I–II typically = ACC/AHA Stage C1; NYHA III–IV = Stage C2 or D (if refractory).
Hemodynamic profiles (Stevenson/Forrester classification) & clinical correlates Four quadrants of hemodynamic status:
ProfilePerfusion (CO)Congestion (PCWP)Clinical LookManagement
Warm & DryGoodNormalEuvolemic; good perfusion; normal JVP, no cracklesSafe for GDMT titration ← GOAL
Warm & WetGoodElevatedEuvolemic perfusion but volume overload (crackles, edema, ↑ JVP)Diuresis priority; hold BB/ACE uptitration until euvolemic
Cold & WetPoorElevatedPoor perfusion (cool, oliguria, AMS) + volume overloadHigh-risk: may need inotrope ± diuretic; ICU-level care
Cold & DryPoorNormalPoor perfusion + euvolemia (rare)May need IV fluids or inotrope; urgent workup for cardiogenic shock
Clinical application: Nursing assessment → categorize hemodynamic profile → informs whether GDMT uptitration is safe or needs delay.
Post-cardiac surgery HFrEF — unique considerations Recovery & remodeling timeline:
  • Post-MI (acute anterior STEMI): EF often drops to 20–30% acutely; can recover significantly over 3–6 months with revascularization + GDMT
  • Post-CABG or post-valve repair/replacement: may unmask pre-existing HFrEF or new HFrEF emerges if large infarct / poor reperfusion
  • Post-op LV remodeling can continue for weeks–months; avoid early ICD/CRT if reversibility possible (40–90 day window) GDMT timing in post-op period:
  • Often held perioperatively (bleeding risk, renal hypoperfusion with hypotension)
  • Restart as soon as euvolemic and hemodynamically stable (typically POD 2–5)
  • Beta-blocker especially important post-cardiac surgery (protects post-op myocardium, reduces arrhythmia) Device considerations:
  • ICD placement usually deferred until 40–90 days post-MI to allow EF recovery window
  • CRT may be delayed if post-op cardiomegaly expected to improve
  • Urgent ICD if prior cardiac arrest or sustained VT Pericardial effusion post-surgery:
  • Common post-cardiac surgery; usually asymptomatic, self-limited
  • Serial echo to track; tamponade physiology rare but emergent if develops
  • Diuretics may worsen if effusion is large (reduces diastolic filling) Post-op arrhythmia (especially POAF):
  • New AF post-cardiac surgery in HFrEF patient is common; rate control + amiodarone preferred over early DCCV (Joglar et al., 2023)
  • Ensure beta-blocker adequate (often held periop; restart ASAP)
  • Anticoagulation team approach (surgical bleeding vs. stroke risk balance)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *Deterioration in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these in stable HFrEF patients; they signal need for escalation.

  • HR trending upward despite beta-blocker and diuresis → rate-control failure; may need uptitration or rhythm control (if AF)
  • BP trending down on GDMT (especially ACE/ARB initiation) → orthostatic; may need fluid bolus, hold uptitration, reassess volume status
  • Oliguria or rising Cr post-GDMT initiation (especially post-MRA/ACEI) → early AKI; recheck labs in 5–7 days, may need GDMT reduction
  • Hyperkalemia (K > 5.5) on MRA/ACEI/SGLT2i → hold/reduce MRA, recheck in 5–7 days, may need sodium polystyrene sulfonate
  • Weight gain 2–5 lb over 1–2 days → fluid creep; escalate diuretic; rule out medication non-adherence
  • Orthopnea or new crackles despite diuretics → diuretic resistance or inadequate dosing; may need IV loop + metolazone
  • Rising BNP or NT-proBNP (especially if prior downtrend) → decompensation signal; assess compliance, diet, GDMT adherence
  • Mental status change (confusion, somnolence, agitation) → hypoxia, hypotension, or metabolic derangement (electrolytes, renal failure); check vitals, labs urgently
  • Cool extremities, weak pulses, capillary refill > 2 sec → cardiogenic shock trajectory; may need inotropes, ICU transfer
  • New chest pain or troponin rise → ACS superimposed; urgently check ECG, troponin; cardiology consult
  • Syncope or presyncope → arrhythmia (especially if EF ≤ 35%), hypotension from GDMT, or ICD malfunction (if device patient); urgent EP/cardiology evaluation
  • Persistent cough despite diuretics → pulmonary edema still present or alternative etiology (ACE-I cough, infection); check CXR
  • Severe nausea/vomiting → may be sign of cardiogenic shock, medication side effect (SGLT2i genital infections, etc.), or GI ischemia; hold GDMT temporarily
  • New or worsening fatigue out of proportion to exertion → low cardiac output worsening; assess for signs of cardiogenic shock
  • Palpitations or ICD alarm (if device patient) → arrhythmia; urgent cardiology evaluation, check device interrogation

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Quadruple therapy initiation is now SIMULTANEOUS, not sequential. The old paradigm of adding one drug at a time over months delays mortality benefit. Current evidence supports parallel initiation (ARNi, BB, MRA, SGLT2i all started within 2–4 weeks once euvolemic). Educate patients: "All four medicines work together; they're safer and more effective together."

  2. ARNi (sacubitril/valsartan) is superior to ACE-I/ARB (PARADIGM-HF). When euvolemic, transition from ACE-I/ARB to ARNi. Hold ACE-I for 36 hours before starting ARNi to avoid angioedema. If ARNi not tolerated, ACE-I/ARB is acceptable but less robust mortality evidence.

  3. Don't initiate beta-blocker during acute decompensation. Beta-blockers worsen hemodynamics in the "cold & wet" state. Achieve euvolemia first (diuretics + ACE/ARB), then start BB. Once euvolemic + HR > 55, initiate; titrate q2 weeks when patient stable.

  4. Metoprolol tartrate is NOT the same as metoprolol succinate. Tartrate formulation (immediate-release) lacks robust HFrEF evidence. Use metoprolol succinate (Toprol XL, extended-release) for mortality benefit. This is a high-yield teaching point for new staff.

  5. Do NOT withhold MRA for mild CKD. Eplerenone/spironolactone should be started even if eGFR 30–60 (mild CKD). Monitor K⁺ closely (baseline, 3–5 days post-start, after each uptitration).

    If K⁺ > 5.5, reduce/hold; recheck in 5–7 days. SGLT2i are gentler on renal function; initiate SGLT2i for renal protection.

  6. Hyperkalemia is the main dose-limiting toxicity of triple RAAS blockade (ACE/ARB + MRA + SGLT2i). Check K⁺ baseline, 3–5 days post-start, and after each dose increase. Rules: K⁺ > 5.5 → reduce/hold MRA; K⁺ > 6.0 → hold all three; Cr > 2.5 or > 30% rise → reassess GDMT; consider nephrology consult if refractory hyperkalemia.

  7. SGLT2i works in HFrEF regardless of diabetes status. Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin reduce hospitalizations + mortality in HFrEF even in euglycemic patients. Start immediately; don't wait for hyperglycemia. Rare DKA risk if type 1 DM (absolute contraindication); monitor mycotic infections in diabetics.

  8. Daily weights are the nursing gold standard. Weight gain +2 lb in 24 h or +5 lb in 1 week signals impending decompensation.

    Patient reports +2 lb → escalate diuretic or notify provider. Most HFrEF readmissions are preventable with proactive weight monitoring + diuretic self-adjustment (patient in control, within provider parameters).

  9. Diuretic resistance management: optimize GDMT + metolazone synergy. High-dose loop diuretics alone often fail. Add metolazone 2.5–5 mg PO 30 min before IV loop diuretic (synergistic proximal + distal tubule blockade). Monitor K⁺ + glucose (both can drop with metolazone). NSAIDs worsen renal function; avoid.

  10. Orthostatic hypotension on ACE/ARB uptitration is expected. Educate patient: "Stand slowly, sit if lightheaded." Mild orthostasis often resolves with continued dosing; don't reflexively lower dose for single BP reading. Check volume status before lowering GDMT; mild intravascular depletion may need IV bolus (paradoxical in HFrEF but sometimes needed).

  11. Cardiac cachexia (involuntary weight loss) is a mortality bomb. Distinguish from fluid loss: cachexia is protein/muscle wasting, driven by TNF-α, poor appetite, malabsorption.

    Don't be fooled by "patient is underweight" into thinking they're healthy. Manage with high-calorie/high-protein diet, nutritionist referral, appetite stimulants if severe. Associated with poor prognosis.

  12. Post-MI HFrEF has a 3–6 month EF recovery window. Anterior STEMI frequently causes systolic dysfunction. Aggressive GDMT + revascularization = potential significant EF recovery.

    Don't rush ICD/CRT placement; delay 40–90 days unless EF ≤ 20% or hemodynamically unstable. Many patients recover above ICD threshold.

  13. Tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy (TIC) is reversible. Chronic high-burden AF or frequent PVCs/SVT can cause HFrEF. Aggressive rate control or ablation → EF recovery over weeks–months.

    Look for clues: recent arrhythmia onset, persistent tachycardia, high PVC burden on Holter. Address the arrhythmia first.

  14. ARNi + ACEI overlap is dangerous. Angioedema risk if ACE-I not fully washout before ARNi.

    Hold ACE-I for 36 hours minimum before starting ARNi. Educate patients on this timing; don't let overlap happen.

  15. Diuretics are PRN, not pillars. Diuretics manage congestion (symptom relief) but don't improve mortality. GDMT pillars (ARNi, BB, MRA, SGLT2i) improve mortality.

    Goal: euvolemia on minimum diuretic dose. Aggressive diuresis isn't the goal; euvolemia with GDMT is. Over-diuresis causes AKI + GDMT intolerance.

  16. CRT responder rate is ~70%; non-responders exist. If CRT implanted but QRS doesn't narrow post-op or symptoms don't improve, reprogram (AV delay, VV delay), recheck thresholds, assess RV function (RV-EF important predictor). Some patients never improve—consider deprogramming if recurrent device alarms.

  17. RV-EF is underappreciated in HFrEF. Low RV-EF predicts worse outcomes, reduced CRT benefit, higher LVAD/transplant morbidity. Standard echo should report RV-EF; if not, request it. Pulmonary hypertension worsens RV function → assess TR gradient, estimate RVSP; may indicate need for advanced therapies.

  18. Vericiguat (newer agent, 2021 approval) reduces HF readmission by ~10–15%. If recent decompensation/hospitalization, EF ≤ 40%, SBP ≥ 100, consider adding vericiguat after GDMT optimization. Mechanism similar to SGLT2i (mycotic infections, DKA rare).

  19. Goal BP in HFrEF: SBP 90–110 mmHg. This range balances organ perfusion (avoid < 90) vs. GDMT tolerance (avoid over-treatment with very low BP). Some GDMT-related hypotension is expected; don't rush to reduce if SBP 90–100 and patient euvolemic.

  20. Sodium restriction is 2–3 g/day, not 1 g. Teaching patients ≤1 g/day is unrealistic + worsens quality of life without proven benefit.

    2–3 g/day is achievable: avoid processed foods, canned soups (often 800–1200 mg Na per can), read labels. Herbs + spices instead of salt. Realistic targets improve compliance.

cards.title: Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT)
phase: Pod 1 3` (Early Re Exposure), `Pod 4 Plus` (Typical De Novo)
cards.quickAnswer: Platelet drop ≥50% from baseline at POD 5–10 post-heparin (or <24 hours if prior exposure within 100 days) with or without new thrombosis = suspect HIT. STOP ALL HEPARIN immediately (IV drips, flushes, LMWH, heparin-coated catheters; switch lines to saline). Calculate 4T score. Send HIT Ab (ELISA) + SRA (gold standard, confirmatory). Start non-heparin anticoagulant per provider order: argatroban 2 mcg/kg/min IV titrate to aPTT 1.5–3× baseline, or bivalirudin 0.15 mg/kg/hr IV. Notify hematology urgently. Never start warfarin alone—risk of skin necrosis and paradoxical thrombosis.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (platelet count drop ≥50% or nadir 20–150k) triggered by heparin exposure. Characterized by HIT antibody (IgG against heparin-PF4 complex) and paradoxical thrombosis risk despite low platelet count.
  • Incidence: 0.5–1% of general post-operative population; 1–2% in cardiac surgery patients (highest-risk group). ~20–50% of heparin-exposed patients seroconvert (HIT Ab positive) without clinical syndrome.
  • Who this applies to: all ICU patients with heparin exposure in the prior 14 days + new thrombocytopenia, especially post-cardiac surgery, post-vascular surgery, and post-PCI/stent cohorts.
  • When it appears: typical onset POD 5–14 during ongoing heparin exposure; rapid-onset (<24 hours) if prior heparin within 100 days; delayed-onset (days–weeks post-heparin discontinuation) is rare but high-risk.
  • Why it matters: missed or delayed HIT diagnosis leads to catastrophic thrombosis (DVT, PE, limb ischemia, stroke, MI, graft occlusion) with mortality 20–40% in HITT cases. Cardiac surgery patients have worst outcomes if thrombosis occurs.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Immune Complex Formation:

Heparin binds platelet factor 4 (PF4), a protein released from activated platelet alpha-granules. Patient's immune system generates IgG antibodies against the heparin-PF4 complex. IgG antibodies cross-link platelet FcγRIIa surface receptors, causing:

  • Platelet activation and consumption
  • Procoagulant microparticle release
  • Massive thrombogenic cascade — paradoxically causing thrombosis despite low platelets ("white clot syndrome")

Pathophysiology in Cardiac Surgery Context:

Post-operative cardiac patients have maximum heparin exposure (IV bolus, CPB circuit prime, heparin-coated grafts/lines, post-op drips, heparin-bonded PA lines, SQ prophylaxis) + CPB-induced platelet activation + mechanical valve mandate for prolonged heparin bridging. This convergence creates the highest-risk cohort for both sensitization and clinical HIT.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Laboratory Trigger (Primary):

  • Platelet count drop ≥50% from baseline, typically POD 5–10 post-heparin exposure
  • Absolute count <150,000 (even if drop <50%) with known heparin exposure in last 14 days
  • Earlier if prior heparin exposure within 100 days (rapid-onset recall response)

Clinical Triggers (Manifestations):

  • New thrombosis despite or shortly after start of heparin: DVT, PE, stroke, MI, limb ischemia, graft occlusion, SVC syndrome, arterial line thrombus
  • Skin lesions or necrosis at heparin injection sites (pathognomonic)
  • Heparin-induced anaphylactoid reaction: acute flushing, hypotension, dyspnea, chest tightness during heparin bolus (IgE-mediated; contraindication to all heparin formulations)
  • Unexplained fever + thrombocytopenia post-operatively
  • Worsening thrombocytopenia despite stopping heparin initially (ongoing immune activation)

Critical Distinction: Post-CPB platelet drop of 20–30% (normal) vs HIT (≥50% drop OR thrombosis). Timing POD 5–10 is classic HIT; POD 1–3 suggests CPB effect or dilution.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure information-gathering; no actions yet.

Vital Signs & General: - BP, HR, RR, temperature, SpO₂; perfusion (pale vs flushed); capillary refill; diaphoresis; distress level

Hematologic Baseline & Trend:

  • Platelet count baseline (immediate post-op or admission) vs current value
  • Trend direction (falling, stable, recovering)
  • Magnitude of drop: calculate % drop = (baseline − current) / baseline × 100%

Heparin Exposure History:

  • Type(s): IV drip, heparin-bonded catheters, LMWH, subcutaneous prophylaxis, heparin flushes, heparin-coated grafts
  • Start date(s), dose, duration
  • Prior heparin exposure within 100 days? (redo surgery? prior admission? prior LMWH?)

Physical Exam—Skin & IV Sites:

  • Inspect all heparin injection sites, central line entry sites, IV sites for erythema, induration, necrosis, skin sloughing
  • Extremity exam (both legs if DVT suspected): color, warmth, edema, capillary refill, femoral/dorsal pedis/posterior tibial pulses bilaterally
  • Skin for mottling, cyanosis (sign of microthrombi)

Cardiovascular:

  • New arrhythmia? Chest pain? Troponin available?
  • Graft patency exam (if vein graft leg, check for edema, temperature gradient)

Neuro:

  • Level of consciousness, orientation, focal deficits, cranial nerves, motor/sensory (assess for acute stroke)
  • If abnormal: stroke alert

Respiratory: - Lung bases clear or crackles? Unilateral absent breath sounds (PE)? SpO₂ trend?

Recent Labs (Review in EMR):

  • CBC trend (WBC, Hgb, Plt)
  • Coagulation: PT, PTT, INR, fibrinogen, D-dimer
  • Troponin, lactate (perfusion markers if thrombosis suspected)

Medication Review:

  • Current heparin products on MAR (drips, flushes, prophylaxis)
  • Any warfarin, DOAC, aspirin, other antithrombotics
  • Heparin exposure via heparin-bonded catheters, heparin-coated lines

sections.heading: 5A. Stable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP ≥ 65, no active thrombosis, no severe bleeding, platelets falling but patient perfusing well.)

Immediate (Next 15 Minutes):

  1. HOLD ALL HEPARIN products — this means:

    • IV heparin drips (UFH, LMWH)
    • Heparin line flushes (switch to 0.9% normal saline flushes immediately; document prominently)
    • Subcutaneous heparin prophylaxis
    • LMWH doses
    • Heparin-bonded or heparin-coated catheters (request removal if non-essential; if essential, note cannot use heparin flush)

  2. Send STAT labs (flag "HIT suspected"):

    • CBC with differential (platelet count, WBC)
    • HIT Ab (ELISA by immunoassay) — sensitive, ~98%
    • Serotonin Release Assay (SRA) — gold standard, confirmatory, send with HIT Ab (3–5 business days turnaround typically)
    • PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer
    • Peripheral blood smear (schistocytes? giant platelets? evidence of microthrombi?)
    • Troponin (if any chest pain history)

  3. Calculate 4T Score — see Table 1 (Section 5A, subsection below)

  4. Obtain 12-lead ECG if any chest pain, palpitations, or EKG changes

  5. Notify:

    • Attending/APP immediately
    • CT Surgery team (if cardiac surgery patient)
    • Hematology consult (URGENT)

  6. Document prominently in chart:

    • "STOP ALL HEPARIN" order placed and confirmed by provider
    • Alert: "HEPARIN ALLERGY — HIT (SUSPECTED)" — bright-flag all care providers

  7. Start Non-Heparin Anticoagulant (per attending/hematology order) — do NOT wait for confirmatory labs:

Option A: Argatroban (preferred if hepatic function preserved)

  • Loading: 2 mcg/kg/min IV infusion
  • Titrate aPTT to 1.5–3× baseline (target ~50–70 sec) or per institutional protocol
  • Monitor aPTT q2–4 hours initially, then per protocol
  • Avoid if severe hepatic disease (Child-Pugh C); use with caution if elevated transaminases
  • Note: elevates INR artifactually; will discuss transition below

Option B: Bivalirudin (preferred in renal failure, CrCl <30)

  • 0.15 mg/kg/hr IV infusion
  • Bolus 0.25 mg/kg if urgent/PCI context (per provider order)
  • Monitor aPTT, ECT (ecarin clotting time) if available
  • Longer half-life (~25 min) than argatroban; slower onset

Option C: Fondaparinux (emerging, off-label; use with expert consultation)

  • 5–10 mg SQ daily (weight-adjusted)
  • Monitor anti-Xa level (optional); no aPTT monitoring needed
  • Longer half-life (18 h); once-daily dosing
  • Growing evidence supports efficacy in HIT; increasingly used post-acute phase

Do NOT start warfarin alone — risk of warfarin-induced skin necrosis and paradoxical thrombosis (see Pitfalls & Pearls #8).

  1. Platelet Transfusion Policy:

    • Do NOT transfuse prophylactically (plt transfusions are immediately activated and consumed in HIT; paradoxically worsens thrombosis)
    • Transfuse ONLY for active life-threatening bleeding

  2. Monitoring:

    • Continuous cardiac telemetry
    • Daily CBC (track platelet count trajectory; expect recovery 3–4 days after stopping heparin with proper anticoagulation)
    • Repeat aPTT 2–4 hours after anticoagulant initiation, then per protocol
    • Serial troponin if chest pain or EKG changes
    • Serial D-dimer if concerned for occult thrombosis

4T Score Table (for stable patient assessment)

Component 0 points 1 point 2 points
Thrombocytopenia Timing Plt fall <4 days post-heparin Plt fall 4–10 days post-heparin OR <1 day if prior heparin ≤100 days Plt fall ≥11 days OR <24 h with prior heparin
Magnitude of Drop <30% drop 30–50% drop ≥50% drop or nadir 20–150k
Thrombosis or Other Sequelae None Progressive or recurrent thrombosis; skin necrosis; or acute systemic reaction Confirmed thrombosis (imaging) or skin necrosis or acute reaction
Other Cause of Thrombocytopenia Definite other cause Possible No other likely cause
Score Interpretation: 0–3: Low risk (≤2% HIT probability) — HIT unlikely; pursue other cause 4–5: Intermediate risk (15–40% HIT probability) — send HIT Ab + SRA; consider non-heparin AC if high clinical suspicion 6–8: High risk (60–95% HIT probability) — initiate non-heparin AC immediately; send HIT Ab + SRA

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension, active chest pain, altered mental status, pulmonary edema, signs of acute thrombosis — DVT, PE, stroke, limb ischemia.)

STAT Concurrent Actions:

  1. STAT Escalation Calls (do NOT leave patient alone):

    • APP/on-call resident
    • CT Surgery attending
    • Hematology (STAT)
      • Stroke team (if neuro deficit present)
      • Vascular Surgery (if limb ischemia)
      • Interventional Radiology (if arterial thrombus, e.g., graft, mesenteric)
      • Rapid Response Team if not already present

  2. STOP ALL HEPARIN immediately (same as 5A)

  3. STAT Labs: - CBC, HIT Ab, SRA, PT/PTT/INR, fibrinogen, D-dimer, troponin, lactate, ABG

  4. Hemodynamic Support:

    • Establish large-bore IV access (2–3 large-bore lines)
    • Fluid resuscitation if hypotensive (caution: may worsen pulmonary edema)
    • Vasopressor consideration (norepinephrine preferred) per team direction
    • Prepare for possible transfer to ICU or higher level of care

  5. Imaging per Clinical Presentation (STAT):

    • Stroke: CT head (rule out ICH), then MRI/CTA neck and head per stroke protocol
    • PE: CT pulmonary angiography
    • DVT: bilateral LE ultrasound or CT angiography lower extremity
    • Limb ischemia: arterial Doppler, consider CTA lower extremity
    • Graft thrombosis: graft ultrasound, consider CTA
    • MI: ECG, serial troponin, cardiology consult

  6. Start Non-Heparin Anticoagulation URGENTLY:

    • Argatroban or bivalirudin (bolus if urgent, then drip)
    • Goal aPTT 1.5–3× baseline
    • Do NOT wait for lab confirmation of HIT antibody; clinical context is sufficient for initiation

  7. Manage Acute Thrombotic Complication:

    • Acute ischemic stroke: per stroke protocol (thrombolytics vs thrombectomy per neurology; high bleeding risk with HIT + anticoagulation, so team discussion essential)
    • Acute PE: anticoagulation per protocol; IVC filter if contraindication to AC; consider pulmonology input
    • Acute limb ischemia: vascular surgery evaluation for emergent thrombectomy vs amputation decision
    • Acute arterial graft occlusion: surgical exploration ± thrombectomy; OR standby

  8. Continuous Monitoring:

    • Telemetry, frequent vitals (q15 min initially)
    • Neuro checks q1h if stroke present
    • Perfusion exams if limb ischemia (cap refill, temperature gradient, pulses)
    • Urine output, lactate trend

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR Template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "[Patient] has heparin exposure since [date]. Baseline platelet [count]; current count [count] — drop of [%]%. 4T score [score]. [Heparin exposure type: IV, LMWH, lines, etc.]. [Prior heparin within 100 days: Y/N]." A: "Suspected HIT. [Stable/Unstable]. [Symptoms if present: chest pain, dyspnea, focal neuro deficit, limb pain, fever]. HIT Ab and SRA sent STAT." R: "Requesting [start non-heparin AC / hematology consult / imaging orders / escalation per protocol]."

Who to Call

Scenario Primary Contact Secondary Notes
Suspected HIT, platelet drop, stable, 4T ≥4 Hematology (urgent) CT Surgery APP, attending Non-heparin AC per hematology order; confirm with provider before initiation if possible
Suspected HIT, high 4T (6–8), no thrombosis yet Hematology + Attending CT Surgery team Initiate AC immediately; escalation to emergent if thrombosis develops
Acute DVT/PE with HIT Hematology + Pulmonary/Vascular CT Surgery, IR Imaging STAT; anticoagulation urgent; IVC filter discussion if AC contraindicated
Acute ischemic stroke with HIT Hematology + Stroke team CT Surgery, Neuro ICU CT head first; thrombolytics/thrombectomy decision complex due to high bleeding risk
Acute limb ischemia / vascular graft occlusion Hematology + Vascular Surgery CT Surgery, OR Threat to limb/graft; surgical intervention likely emergent
HITT with multiple organ ischemia Hematology + CT Surgery + ICU Anesthesia, perfusion Consider ECMO if cardiogenic shock; cardiothoracic ICU admission mandatory
Anaphylactoid reaction to heparin Allergy/Immunology + Hematology ED, ICU Lifelong contraindication to ALL heparin formulations; document in permanent alert; prescribe medical alert bracelet

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default.

7.1 Pathophysiology Detail: PF4 Immune Complex and Microparticle Thrombogenicity The Immune Activation Loop:
  1. Heparin (UFH or LMWH) binds platelet factor 4 (PF4) — a positively charged protein released from platelet alpha granules
  2. Heparin-PF4 complexes are presented to immune system
  3. IgG antibodies form against the complex (Type II HIT; IgE in Type I, which is non-immune)
  4. IgG antibodies bind FcγRIIa receptors on platelet surface
  5. Platelet cross-linking → platelet activation → P-selectin exposure, microparticle release
  6. Microparticles generate thrombin in a tissue-factor-dependent manner
  7. Paradox: despite thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), excessive thrombin generation drives thrombosis — the hallmark of HIT Why Warfarin Alone Is Dangerous: Warfarin depletes vitamin K-dependent factors in this order:
    1. Protein C (shortest half-life, ~8 h)
    2. Protein S
    3. Factor II, VII, IX, X (longer half-lives, 24–60 h) When protein C depletes first without adequate anticoagulation from a direct thrombin inhibitor, the remaining factors (II, VII, IX, X) create a hypercoagulable state. Result: skin necrosis (microthrombi in skin vasculature, typically POD 3–5), limb gangrene, paradoxical thrombosis. This is why argatroban or bivalirudin must overlap warfarin initiation until platelets recover and INR is stable.
7.2 HIT Type I vs Type II and Clinical Differences
FeatureType IType II
Immune mechanismNon-immune (direct heparin effect on platelets)Immune (IgG + IgA against heparin-PF4)
TimingImmediate (1–2 days of heparin)Delayed (5–14 days typical; <24 h if prior exposure)
Platelet nadirMild (usually >100k, 20–30% drop)Moderate to severe (often <100k, ≥50% drop)
Thrombosis riskNo~30–50% in HITT
HIT Ab testNegativePositive (ELISA and/or SRA)
ManagementContinue heparin if possible; resolve spontaneouslySTOP heparin; start non-heparin AC; often longer anticoagulation course
Clinical noteBenign; reassure patient and providersMedical emergency; lifelong contraindication to heparin
Practically: If a patient develops mild thrombocytopenia (nadir >100k) on day 1–2 post-heparin without antibodies and without thrombosis, that's likely Type I. If ≥50% drop or nadir <100k on POD 5–10, or any new thrombosis + heparin exposure, suspect Type II and initiate workup.
7.3 HIT Antibody Testing: ELISA, SRA, and Interpretation HIT ELISA (Immunoassay):
  • Sensitivity: ~98% (catches most true HIT antibodies)
  • Specificity: ~85–90% (many false-positives — seroconversion without clinical HIT)
  • Turnaround: 1–2 hours to overnight depending on lab
  • What it measures: IgG, IgA, IgM antibodies against heparin-PF4 complex
  • Interpretation: Positive ELISA is sensitive but NOT confirmatory. Many post-operative cardiac surgery patients seroconvert (especially high PF4 stimulus from CPB, surgical manipulation) but never develop thrombosis or thrombocytopenia
  • OD (optical density) value: some labs report OD; higher OD may correlate with higher HIT probability, but clinical 4T score is more predictive than OD alone Serotonin Release Assay (SRA) — Gold Standard:
  • Specificity: ~95–98% (most specific test for functional HIT antibody)
  • Mechanism: patient's serum is incubated with donor platelets containing serotonin; if HIT antibodies present, they activate the donor platelets, releasing serotonin; measured by scintillation counting
  • Turnaround: 3–5 business days typically (slower than ELISA but necessary for confirmation)
  • Interpretation: Positive SRA = functional HIT antibody confirmed; virtually diagnostic of HIT
  • Caveat: SRA is not available at all institutions; some use C-serotonin release assay (CSRA) or platelet aggregometry as alternatives Best Practice:
  • Send BOTH HIT ELISA and SRA together on clinical suspicion (POD 5–10 + ≥50% drop OR 4T ≥4)
  • Use 4T score as your pre-test assessment (guides probability)
  • Start non-heparin AC if 4T ≥4 or high clinical suspicion; do NOT wait for SRA
  • If ELISA positive but SRA negative, HIT is unlikely; consider unmasking another cause (sepsis, DIC, dilution)
7.4 Post-CPB Thrombocytopenia Differential — How to Distinguish HIT from Normal Post-Op Drop
CauseTimingNadirMechanismKey DiscriminatorsManagement
Normal post-CPB dropPOD 1–3~40–50% of baselineCPB-induced platelet consumption, hemodilution, hypothermia recoveryNo thrombosis, no heparin antibody, 4T ≤3, recovery by POD 5–7Supportive; transfuse if bleeding
HITPOD 5–14 (or <24 h if prior exposure)Often <100k or ≥50% dropHeparin-PF4 immune complex + platelet activationThrombosis, 4T ≥4–6, positive HIT Ab + SRA, worsens despite heparin cessationSTOP heparin; start non-heparin AC
Sepsis / DICAny PODVariableCytokine-driven platelet consumption + coagulopathyFever, elevated PT/PTT/D-dimer, low fibrinogen, bleeding, multi-organ dysfunctionAntibiotics, supportive, treat DIC
Drug-induced thrombocytopeniaAny POD (coincident with drug start)VariableDrug-antibody immune complexHistory of vancomycin, linezolid, valproic acid, other culprits; resolves when drug stoppedDiscontinue offending drug
Transfusion-related dilutionPOD 1–3Proportional to units transfusedDilution with massive transfusionRecent massive transfusion, no other explanation, platelets stable once transfusions stopMonitor; transfuse if needed for bleeding
Splenomegaly / DDA (drug-dependent antibodies)VariableVariableSequestration or drug-dependent antibodyClinical context, peripheral blood smear if DDA suspectedManage underlying cause
Bedside Pearl: If platelet drop starts POD 5–10 (later peak) and patient is already off heparin from POD 0, suspect HIT over normal CPB effect. Timing is your first clue.
7.5 Alternative Anticoagulants: Argatroban vs Bivalirudin vs Fondaparinux — Dose, Monitoring, Niche
AgentClassMechanismIV DosingMonitoringAdvantagesDisadvantagesNiche / Preferred In
ArgatrobanDTI (direct thrombin inhibitor)Reversible inhibition of thrombinLoad: 2 mcg/kg/min; titrate aPTT 1.5–3× (typical 50–70 sec)aPTT q2–4 h initial, then per protocolRapid onset (~minutes); no renal clearance; reproducible kinetics; widely availableHepatic metabolism (avoid if Child-Pugh C); elevates INR artifactually; short half-life (~45 min); warfarin transition complexRenal failure (CrCl <30); preferred first-line for acute HIT in most centers
BivalirudinDTIDual-site thrombin binding (both extrinsic and intrinsic sites)Drip: 0.15 mg/kg/hr; bolus 0.25 mg/kg if PCI/urgentaPTT, ECT (ecarin clotting time) preferredBoth arms bound = high specificity; renal clearance (safe if CrCl >30); used in cath lab/OR; less INR interferenceSlower onset (~30 min); renal clearance (caution CrCl <30); expensive; fewer institutions stockCardiac catheterization lab, OR, hepatic failure; preferred in renal failure
FondaparinuxXa inhibitorSelective Factor Xa inhibitionSQ: 5–10 mg daily (weight-adjusted: <50 kg = 5 mg, 50–100 kg = 7.5 mg, >100 kg = 10 mg)Anti-Xa level (optional); no aPTT; no routine monitoring if steady-stateLong half-life (18 h); once-daily SQ; renal clearance OK (CrCl >20); no direct reversal needed; lower bleeding risk vs DTIOff-label in HIT (growing evidence); slower onset; no immediate reversal; some institutions avoid due to off-label statusEmerging preferred post-acute phase; long-term bridging; off-label use requires expert consultation
DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban)Xa inhibitorsDirect Factor Xa inhibitionStandard dosing per indication (e.g., apixaban 5 mg BID)PT/INR; anti-Xa optionalLong-term outpatient; once–twice daily PO; good efficacy post-HIT in late phasesAvoid acute phase; poor bioavailability if GI malabsorption; emerging data; not for initial HIT managementPost-acute phase (after platelet recovery >150k, argatroban overlap, bridge completed); outpatient continuation
Practical Notes:
  • First-line: Argatroban or bivalirudin in acute phase (0–7 days post-HIT diagnosis)
  • Transition: After platelets recover >150k and clinical stability established, consider fondaparinux SQ or DOAC (apixaban preferred) for longer-term anticoagulation
  • Warfarin bridge: Must overlap with DTI or Xa inhibitor until INR therapeutic; argatroban artificially elevates INR, so transition is nuanced (see Pitfalls & Pearls #9)
7.6 Warfarin Bridge Rules in HIT: The "Protein C Paradox" and Safe Transition The Problem in Simple Terms: Warfarin blocks production of all vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X, C, S). Protein C has the shortest half-life (~8 hours). If you start warfarin without a direct anticoagulant, protein C depletes first, leaving the other factors (II, VII, IX, X) temporarily unopposed. This creates a hypercoagulable window and can cause:
  • Skin necrosis (microthrombi in skin and subcutaneous vasculature, typically POD 3–5)
  • Limb gangrene
  • Paradoxical thrombosis despite INR being elevated The Safe Transition in HIT:
    1. Start argatroban or bivalirudin first (see dosing in 7.5 above)
    2. Maintain non-heparin AC during warfarin initiation
    3. When to start warfarin: once clinical stability is established and provider orders initiate warfarin; goal is INR 2–3
    4. Overlap duration: continue argatroban (or bivalirudin) AND warfarin until:
    5. Platelets recover to >150,000 (HIT resolving)
    6. INR 2–3 on warfarin monotherapy (or INR >4 if still on argatroban, per institutional protocol)
    7. Special note on argatroban: Argatroban itself increases INR ~1.5 even without warfarin; when transitioning, you must achieve INR >4 on argatroban monotherapy before starting warfarin, OR use chromogenic Factor X assay for accurate INR (less affected by argatroban). Ask your lab about available methods. Duration of Anticoagulation Post-HIT:
      • If HITT (thrombosis occurred): warfarin or DOAC × 3 months minimum; longer if recurrent thrombosis or catastrophic event (6–12 months)
      • If HIT antibody only, no thrombosis: warfarin × 4 weeks, then stop (short-duration anticoagulation sufficient)
7.7 Reintroducing Heparin in Remote HIT: CPB Re-Exposure and Risk Mitigation The Scenario: A patient with remote HIT history (HIT antibody + thrombosis 2 years ago, now off anticoagulation) needs cardiac surgery. CPB requires heparin exposure. What's the risk? Risk Assessment:
  • If prior HIT was confirmed (ELISA + SRA positive, clinical thrombosis), HIT Abs typically persist for 2–3+ years
  • Re-exposure to heparin carries ~30–50% risk of rapid-onset HIT recurrence (within 24 hours)
  • Some patients have had uneventful repeat heparin exposure (especially if time >3 years); others have had catastrophic recurrence Risk Mitigation Strategies:
    1. Avoid heparin if possible: use bivalirudin for CPB circuit (no cross-reactivity; does not trigger HIT Abs)
    2. If heparin unavoidable: discuss with hematology + CT surgery
    3. Consider prophylactic non-heparin AC (e.g., argatroban drip started pre-induction)
    4. Use minimum heparin exposure on CPB circuit
    5. Have rapid-response HIT protocol in place (watch for platelet drop within 1–24 h post-op)
    6. Post-op anticoagulation: initiate non-heparin AC immediately; expect rapid-onset thrombocytopenia if recurrence occurs Practical Note: Document "REMOTE HIT HISTORY" prominently in chart pre-operatively. Discuss with anesthesia and perfusion before CPB planning.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable HIT Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Any of these in a stable HIT patient → re-escalate immediately.

  • Platelet count falling further despite stopping heparin → ongoing immune activation; may need increased AC, consider plasmapheresis consult
  • New extremity pain, coolness, pallor, diminishing pulses → limb ischemia evolving; vascular emergency
  • New focal neuro deficit, vision change, aphasia, weakness, facial droop → new stroke or TIA; activate stroke code
  • New chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia → PE or cardiac ischemia; imaging STAT
  • New skin erythema, blistering, or necrosis at heparin injection sites → pathognomonic for HIT; risk of skin sloughing; photograph and escalate
  • Acute limb ischemia with cyanotic toes, mottled skin, severe pain → vascular emergency; thrombectomy likely indicated
  • Unexpected graft or vascular access thrombosis post-operatively → assume HIT until proven otherwise
  • Anaphylactoid reaction to heparin bolus: acute severe flushing, hypotension, chest tightness, dyspnea, urticaria → stop heparin immediately, NEVER re-challenge; document lifelong contraindication
  • Rising D-dimer with normal imaging → microparticle-driven thrombosis; consider increasing AC dosing
  • Falling Hgb without obvious bleeding + worsening thrombocytopenia → microparticle-driven DIC; send fibrinogen, PT, PTT; consider plasmapheresis consult
  • Patient anxiety or "just doesn't look right" → early decompensation; vital sign re-check, lactate, troponin, ABG; provider notification

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Post-CPB platelet drop ≠ HIT — timing is your clue. 20–30% drop POD 1–3 is normal CPB effect. HIT shows ≥50% drop OR thrombosis, typically POD 5–10. Early drop without thrombosis? Probably not HIT. Late drop (POD 5+)? HIT is on the differential until proven otherwise.

  2. Timing is everything in HIT diagnosis. Thrombocytopenia starting POD 1–3 is usually CPB-induced or dilutional. Thrombocytopenia starting POD 5–10 is classic HIT. Rapid-onset (<24 h) is HIT recurrence in prior-exposed patients (redo sternotomy within 100 days).

  3. Rapid-onset HIT in redo cardiac surgery is common and often missed. Redo CABG within months of index surgery? Redo valve surgery within 100 days? Watch for platelet drop within 24 hours of heparin re-exposure. This is a high-yield pattern for trainees to recognize.

  4. 4T score ≤3 has ~99% negative predictive value. Low 4T score + clinical doubt? HIT is very unlikely. Reassure the team; pursue other causes. This is a screening tool; it excludes more than it includes.

  5. HIT ELISA is sensitive (~98%) but not specific (~85–90%). Many post-op cardiac patients seroconvert without clinical HIT. SRA (gold standard) takes 3–5 days and is more specific (~95–98%). Send both. Start AC if 4T ≥4 or high clinical suspicion; do NOT wait for SRA. If ELISA positive + SRA negative later, HIT was unlikely; consider unmasking sepsis, DIC, or dilution.

  6. "STOP ALL HEPARIN" means FLUSHES too. Heparin line flushes (1–2 units/mL in saline) are a frequent hidden source of ongoing heparin exposure, often missed by nursing. Prominently document "SALINE FLUSHES ONLY" on every line. This is a common cause of failed HIT diagnosis and ongoing immune activation.

  7. Do NOT transfuse platelets unless actively bleeding. Transfused platelets are immediately activated and consumed in HIT, paradoxically worsening thrombosis and D-dimer elevation. Save transfusions for life-threatening bleeding only. If ≥50% drop but no bleeding, observe with supportive care + anticoagulation.

  8. Warfarin alone in acute HIT = disaster. Warfarin-induced skin necrosis and limb gangrene are devastating complications.

    Always bridge with argatroban or bivalirudin first until platelets recover and INR is stable. Teach this to every provider on the team — this is a high-stakes pearl.

  9. Argatroban artificially elevates INR. On argatroban monotherapy, INR reads ≥1.5 even without warfarin. Transition protocol varies by institution: some require INR >4 on argatroban alone before starting warfarin; others use chromogenic Factor X assay for more accurate INR. Clarify your institutional approach with pharmacy + hematology to avoid delaying warfarin initiation or starting prematurely.

  10. DVT is the most common HIT thrombosis (~50% of HITT cases). But arterial thrombosis (stroke, limb ischemia, MI, graft occlusion) is also frequent and often catastrophic in cardiac surgery patients.

    Don't anchor on DVT as the only thrombotic manifestation.

  11. Acute stroke or limb ischemia in a post-cardiac surgery patient with falling platelets = HIT until proven otherwise. Providers often anchor on "sepsis" or "post-op inflammation." Get 4T score, HIT Ab, SRA, and imaging immediately. This pattern-recognition shift saves lives.

  12. Post-discharge DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban) is increasingly used for HIT outpatient management. After acute phase (argatroban/bivalirudin bridging), transition to DOAC for 3-month anticoagulation (or longer if thrombosis). Growing evidence supports efficacy; cost is lower than prolonged warfarin + INR monitoring. Avoid acutely; use post-platelet recovery + bridge.

  13. Mark chart and armband "HEPARIN ALLERGY — HIT" in BOLD. This is a lifelong contraindication to all heparin formulations (UFH, LMWH, heparin-bonded devices, heparin flushes). HIT + re-heparinization = rapid catastrophic thrombosis and likely death. Fondaparinux technically OK but often avoided out of abundance of caution.

  14. Teach patient and family: medical alert bracelet and provider counseling. HIT survivors must wear a bracelet stating "HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia)" and inform all future providers, surgeons, dentists, anesthesiologists. This is a permanent part of their medical identity.

  15. Microparticle thrombosis can occur without macroscopic thrombus. Elevated D-dimer in a HIT patient with normal ultrasounds and CT imaging is a red flag. Microthrombi in capillary beds drive DIC, multi-organ failure, and death. Don't be falsely reassured by negative imaging. Escalate anticoagulation and escalate to hematology and ICU if not already there. Consider plasmapheresis consultation in severe, refractory HIT.

cards.title: Hyperglycemia / Insulin Management (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: Glucose >180 persistent in the ICU → initiate IV insulin drip (0.05–0.1 units/kg/hr, titrate q1–2h). Target 140–180 mg/dL per STS guidelines — avoid hypoglycemia (<110 mg/dL) which worsens outcomes. POD 1–4 tolerating PO → transition to basal-bolus-correctional subcutaneous insulin, overlap drip for 2–4 hours. Avoid sliding scale alone. Glucose >250 with ketones, acidosis, or altered mental status → STAT ABG + labs, STAT IV insulin drip (0.2 units/kg/hr), aggressive electrolyte replacement (K⁺, Mg²⁺). Anticipate steroid-induced afternoon spikes; add NPH or mealtime bolus coverage. Transition home insulin before discharge — do NOT restart pre-op regimen same-day if poor baseline control (A1c ≥10).
