sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — what this is and who gets it.

  • Definition: Elevation of blood glucose above 180 mg/dL occurring after cardiac surgical procedures. Ranges from mild stress hyperglycemia (responsive to modest insulin dosing) to severe hyperglycemic crisis (DKA or hyperglycemic hyperosmolar state, HHS).
  • Incidence: >75% of post-cardiac surgery patients develop hyperglycemia in the first 48 hours, including non-diabetics (Van den Berghe et al., 2001).
  • Who this applies to: every adult post-operative cardiac patient (CABG, valve, TAA, transplant, VAD, TAVR, pericardial surgery). Highest yield POD 0–3 and again with steroid administration.
  • Why it matters: Sustained hyperglycemia (especially >250 mg/dL) correlates with increased deep sternal wound infection (DSWI), sepsis, length of stay, and mortality. Tight control (target 140–180) improves outcomes; too-tight (<110) causes hypoglycemia and paradoxical worse outcomes (Van den Berghe, 2001; STS 2023).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative hyperglycemia is nearly universal and is driven by multiple physiologic stressors:

  • Surgical stress and catecholamine surge — blood glucose rises from increased epinephrine and cortisol (stress hormones that antagonize insulin and promote hepatic glucose production)
  • Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) inflammation — systemic inflammatory response increases insulin resistance; longer CPB (>180 min) = more severe resistance
  • Exogenous steroids — dexamethasone, methylprednisolone given for pericardial inflammation or ARDS peak in effect 2–6 hours post-dose, causing afternoon glucose spikes
  • IV dextrose fluids — D5-LR or D5-0.9 NS (50 g dextrose/L) may worsen hyperglycemia; prefer non-dextrose fluids (LR, 0.9 NS)
  • Catecholamine drips — epinephrine, phenylephrine, dobutamine all promote hyperglycemia and insulin resistance
  • Pre-existing diabetes with poor baseline control — A1c ≥10 signals poor glycemic reserve; post-op insulin resistance will unmask worsening control
  • Autonomic hyperactivity — sympathetic activation reduces pancreatic beta-cell insulin secretion and increases hepatic gluconeogenesis

The POD 1–2 hyperglycemia peak reflects maximum inflammatory burden and stress hormone surge; glucose typically improves by POD 3–4 in non-diabetic stress hyperglycemia. Pre-existing diabetics require planned long-term insulin regimens.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient:

  • Fingerstick glucose >180 mg/dL on initial post-op checks or trending upward despite oral intake
  • Persistent hyperglycemia (>180 for >2 hours) in the ICU or early post-operative period, even in non-diabetic patients
  • Known diabetes (Type 1 or Type 2) with glucose >250 mg/dL post-op, or A1c unknown at admission
  • On IV dextrose fluids with glucose >200 and rising
  • On corticosteroids (dexamethasone, methylprednisolone) with afternoon-evening glucose acceleration
  • Signs of hyperglycemic crisis: fruity breath, polyuria, polydipsia, lethargy, confusion, Kussmaul respirations (rapid shallow breathing)
  • Urine ketones positive or visual appearance suggests ketonuria

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Fingerstick glucose STAT — use consistent meter, document site and time
  • Pre-op diabetes history: known Type 1, Type 2, gestational? Home insulin regimen (basal, bolus, correction), oral agents, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors? A1c if documented?
  • Glucose trend past 24 hours: admission fingerstick, overnight checks, pre-breakfast, post-meal, any peak values already trended?
  • Current oral intake status: NPO or tolerating oral? Diet type (clear liquids, soft, full)? Tube feeding?
  • Current IV fluids: dextrose concentration? D5-LR, D5-0.9 NS, or non-dextrose (LR, 0.9 NS)?
  • Medications on board: basal insulin (glargine, detemir, degludec)? Bolus insulin (aspart, lispro, glulisine)? Beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors (may mask hypoglycemia symptoms)? Steroids? Catecholamine drips?
  • Physical exam: mental status (hyperglycemia → lethargy; hypoglycemia → agitation), skin turgor (osmotic diuresis → dehydration), fruity breath (ketosis), urine output and appearance
  • Recent labs: baseline renal function (creatinine, BUN), electrolytes (K⁺, HCO3−, Cl−), A1c if available, ABG if DKA suspected (pH, bicarb, anion gap)
  • Vital signs and perfusion: HR, BP, RR, SpO₂, capillary refill, urine output
  • Procedural context: which cardiac procedure? CPB time (>180 min = higher insulin resistance)? Vasopressor support ongoing?
  • Assess for infection triggers: fever, WBC trend, wound erythema, respiratory symptoms (any infection will worsen hyperglycemia)

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, normotensive, no respiratory distress, no ketones, glucose 180–250.)

  1. Confirm fingerstick with lab glucose if value >200 or trending rapidly upward
  2. Discontinue dextrose-containing IV fluids if not contraindicated; switch to LR or 0.9 NS
  3. Nutrition plan coordination:
    • If NPO: hold oral intake pending surgeon clearance; maintain non-dextrose fluids
    • If tolerating PO: progress diet per protocol (clear liquids → soft → full diet); notify dietary of diabetes status
    • Initiate insulin regimen (coordinate with provider order):
    • In ICU or early post-op (glucose persistent >180): start IV insulin drip per titration table (Section 7.2)
      • Initial rate: 0.05 units/kg/hr for glucose 180–250; 0.1 units/kg/hr for glucose 250–350
      • Titrate q1–2h; increase 1–4 units/hr depending on glycemic trend and initial rate
      • Floor patient tolerating PO, glucose stable in target 140–180: transition directly to basal-bolus-correctional subcutaneous insulin (preferred over sliding scale alone)
    • Fingerstick check frequency:
    • On IV insulin drip: q1h until glucose stable in target 140–180 mg/dL; then q2–4h
    • On subcutaneous insulin: q4–6h fasting and pre-meals; increase to q1–2h if recently transitioned from drip or if hypoglycemia unawareness
    • Document:
    • Home diabetes regimen and A1c if available
    • Current glucose, trend, time of last insulin dose (if applicable)
    • Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (see Section 6)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Glucose >250 with ketones, altered mental status, respiratory distress, concern for DKA/HHS.)

  1. STAT fingerstick + venous or arterial blood gas (assess pH, HCO3−, anion gap)
  2. STAT lab: glucose, electrolytes (K⁺, Cl−, HCO3−), creatinine, venous/arterial blood gas, serum beta-hydroxybutyrate or urine ketones, serum osmolarity
  3. STAT call to APP/fellow + charge RN + RRT if needed — do NOT delay if DKA/HHS suspected
  4. Initiate IV insulin drip STAT (per protocol):
    • Glucose >250 with acidosis (pH <7.35) or ketones (DKA): 0.2 units/kg/hr initial; increase 4–6 units/hr q30min until anion gap closes and pH improves
    • Glucose >400 or HHS suspected (osmolarity >320, pH >7.30): 0.1–0.15 units/kg/hr initial; more aggressive fluid replacement than insulin titration
    • Establish large-bore IV access if not already present; continuous cardiac monitoring, pulse oximetry, capnography if respiratory symptoms present
    • Aggressive electrolyte and fluid replacement (K⁺ deficit in DKA/HHS is large even if serum K⁺ normal on admission):
    • Do NOT give potassium until urine output confirmed >200 mL/hr (risk of life-threatening hyperkalemia)
    • K⁺ repletion: typically 20–40 mEq/L IV fluid once UOP established
    • Fluid: 0.9 NS or LR at 500 mL/hr initially; titrate to HR, BP, UOP, and serum osmolarity trending downward
    • Use non-dextrose IV fluids only until blood glucose <250; avoid dextrose-containing fluids in DKA/HHS setting
    • Monitor continuously for complications:
      • Hypoglycemia from drip + intracellular K⁺ shift
      • Hypokalemia (paradoxical risk as insulin drives K⁺ intracellularly even as total-body K⁺ is depleted)
      • Cerebral edema (risk in HHS with rapid glucose correction; correct osmolarity slowly over 48 h)
      • Consider transfer to ICU if not already present — DKA/HHS is a critical event
      • Document: glucose at crisis onset, ABG results, electrolytes, initial insulin dose and drip rate, urine output, mental status on arrival, time to first insulin bolus

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient with [known DM / stress hyperglycemia] has fingerstick glucose [value] at [time]. Most recent trend is [stable / rising / volatile]. Patient is [NPO / tolerating PO]. Current IV fluids are [type]. Last insulin dose [time, if applicable]. A1c [value] if known." A: "Patient is [stable / altered — fruity breath, lethargy, polyuria, Kussmaul respirations]. [Relevant symptoms]. [Other meds: steroids, pressors, etc.]." R: "Requesting [IV insulin drip order / basal-bolus-correctional regimen / A1c order / endocrine consult / STAT labs for DKA/HHS workup / transfer to ICU]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Glucose 180–250, stable, tolerating PO Primary APP / on-call provider
Glucose 250–350, trending up, no symptoms Primary APP / on-call provider (urgent)
Glucose >350 with symptoms (lethargy, polyuria, fruity breath) APP/fellow + RRT (STAT)
Glucose >250 with concern for DKA (fruity breath, rapid breathing, confusion) APP/fellow + RRT + charge RN (CODE — STAT ABG + labs)
Refractory hyperglycemia (>300 despite increasing insulin, POD >2) Endocrinology consult
Hypoglycemia <70 with symptoms (tremor, confusion, diaphoresis) APP/provider + RRT standby + nutrition
Patient on corticosteroids with afternoon hyperglycemia spikes Primary APP (may need afternoon NPH or extra boluses)
A1c ≥10 on admission Endocrinology consult for discharge planning

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Subsections below are — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Insulin Drip Titration & Basal-Bolus-Correctional Transition
sections.bodyHtml:
IV Insulin Drip (ICU or early post-op, glucose persistent >180):

Scenario Initial Rate Titration Strategy Goal Glucose
Glucose 180–250, stable, no diabetes 0.05 units/kg/hr Increase 1–2 units/hr q1–2h if glucose not falling 140–180 mg/dL
Glucose 250–350 0.1 units/kg/hr Increase 2–4 units/hr q1h until glucose <250 140–180 mg/dL
Glucose >350 or DKA 0.2 units/kg/hr Increase 4–6 units/hr q30min; more aggressive electrolyte replacement Close anion gap, pH >7.30

Key monitoring on IV drip:

  • Fingerstick q1h while on drip; once stable in target 140–180, q2–4h
  • Electrolytes (K⁺, Cl−, HCO3−) q4–6h initially; K⁺ falls as insulin drives glucose + K⁺ intracellularly
  • Hypoglycemia unawareness risk: older patients on beta-blockers may not show tremor or tachycardia if glucose drops — lower threshold for q1h checks in this population

Transition from IV insulin drip to subcutaneous basal-bolus-correctional (when tolerating PO):

  1. Initiate subcutaneous basal insulin (long-acting: glargine, detemir, or degludec) 6–12 hours BEFORE stopping drip — provides background coverage
  2. Overlap IV drip with subcutaneous basal for 2–4 hours — ensures seamless transition without hyperglycemia rebound
  3. Calculate basal dose: roughly 40–50% of total daily insulin need (TDI)
    • Non-diabetic stress hyperglycemia: start 10–15 units basal
    • Known Type 2 DM: 0.3–0.5 units/kg basal (conservative initial dose)
    • Type 1 DM: verify basal dose matches pre-op regimen adjusted for post-op insulin resistance
    • Add mealtime (prandial) bolus insulin (rapid-acting: aspart, lispro, glulisine) at breakfast, lunch, dinner
    • Standard ratio: 1 unit per 10–15 g carbohydrate (1:10–1:15)
    • Adjust based on meal composition and glucose response
    • Add correctional (supplemental) insulin scale — for glucose >140 mg/dL at checks:
    • Standard: 1–2 units per 40–50 mg/dL above target (e.g., if glucose 240, give 2–4 units correction)
    • Adjust based on response (some patients need 1 unit per 30 mg/dL; others 1 per 50)
    • Avoid sliding scale alone — sliding scale (correction-only) perpetuates reactive hyperglycemia and increases insulin need. Basal-bolus-correctional is superior (Van den Berghe et al., 2001; ADA 2023).
    • Hold rapid-acting insulin if NPO:
      • Hold breakfast bolus if patient still NPO for diet
      • ALWAYS give basal (long-acting) insulin even if NPO — basal covers baseline glucose production
      • Monitoring on subcutaneous regimen:
      • q4–6h fingersticks on stable floor patient
      • q1–2h if recently transitioned from drip or if hypoglycemia unawareness present
      • Always check before meals and at bedtime initially to establish pattern

Steroid-induced hyperglycemia (dexamethasone, methylprednisolone):

  • Peak effect 2–6 hours post-dose if dosed morning → afternoon/evening hyperglycemia spike
  • Strategy 1: Add intermediate-acting NPH (peaks 4–8h) 6–10 units at breakfast
  • Strategy 2: Increase mealtime bolus insulin 4–6 units at lunch/dinner
  • Strategy 3: Use correctional scale more aggressively (1 unit per 30 mg/dL instead of 1 per 50)
  • Taper steroid-induced insulin coverage proportionally as steroid dose tapers

sections.heading: 7.2 Glucose Targets: Why 140–180, Not 80–110
sections.bodyHtml:
Van den Berghe landmark data (NEJM 2001, "tight control" ICU study):

  • Intensive control target 80–110 mg/dL reduced bloodstream infection, acute kidney injury, transfusions, and mortality in surgical ICU patients
  • Critical caveat: hypoglycemia during the trial was associated with paradoxical increase in mortality. The tight-control benefit vanished when hypoglycemic episodes occurred.

STS 2023 Glycemic Control Guidelines post-cardiac surgery:

  • Recommended target: 140–180 mg/dL post-cardiac surgery
  • Rationale: balance benefit of hyperglycemia reduction (lowers DSWI, infection) against hypoglycemia risk (sudden glucose drop increases arrhythmia, cardiac event risk, mortality)
  • Avoid: target <110 mg/dL in post-op setting (hypoglycemia is harmful)

Clinical pearl: The glucose "sweet spot" for post-cardiac surgery is higher than critical-illness tight control because hypoglycemia risk is especially high in this population (stress hyperglycemia rapidly reverses; insulin doses must be reduced proactively).

sections.heading: 7.3 DKA vs HHS in Post-Cardiac Surgery: Pathophysiology & Recognition
sections.bodyHtml:
Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA):

Feature Details
Mechanism Absolute insulin deficiency (Type 1, or basal insulin accidentally held) + stress hyperglycemia = unchecked hepatic glucose production + uncontrolled lipolysis → ketone overflow
Blood glucose Usually 250–600 mg/dL (can be lower in euglycemic DKA if SGLT2i on board)
pH <7.35 (metabolic acidosis)
Anion gap >12 (elevated from ketones)
Serum/urine ketones Positive beta-hydroxybutyrate or urine ketones
HCO3− <18 mEq/L
Presentation Fruity breath, rapid shallow breathing (Kussmaul), confusion, polyuria, abdominal pain, nausea
Risk post-op Type 1 DM if basal insulin held; post-op stress amplifies ketone production
Mortality 1–5% in hospital if promptly diagnosed; higher if delayed

Hyperglycemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS):

Feature Details
Mechanism Relative insulin deficiency (Type 2, elderly, dehydration) + severe hyperglycemia = extreme hyperosmolarity, profound dehydration, CNS dysfunction
Blood glucose Usually >600 mg/dL
pH >7.30 (NOT acidotic, or mild acidosis only)
Serum osmolarity >320 mOsm/kg
Anion gap Normal or mildly elevated (<12)
Serum/urine ketones Negative or trace (NOT prominent)
Presentation Profound lethargy, confusion, seizure, focal neurologic deficits (may mimic stroke), severe dehydration
Risk post-op Type 2 DM with dehydration from high-output drains, diuretics; elderly patients
Mortality 5–15%, often from complications (stroke, MI, thrombosis)

Key clinical distinction:

  • DKA = acidosis (low pH, high anion gap, positive ketones)
  • HHS = hyperosmolarity WITHOUT severe acidosis (normal or mildly elevated pH, normal anion gap)

Action if DKA or HHS suspected: STAT ABG, glucose, electrolytes, serum beta-hydroxybutyrate or urine ketones, serum osmolarity; STAT IV insulin drip (0.1–0.2 units/kg/hr) + aggressive fluid + electrolyte replacement; STAT ICU + endocrinology consult.

sections.heading: 7.4 Hypoglycemia Recognition & Management in Post-op Cardiac Patients
sections.bodyHtml:
Why hypoglycemia is dangerous in post-op cardiac patients:

  • Sudden glucose drop triggers catecholamine surge (sympathetic activation)
  • Increased cardiac workload, arrhythmia risk, MI risk in patients with coronary disease
  • In older patients on beta-blockers, autonomic symptoms (tremor, tachycardia) are masked → hypoglycemia unawareness

Signs and symptoms (often subtle in older/medicated patients):

  • Autonomic: tremor, palpitations, diaphoresis, anxiety, hunger (often ABSENT on beta-blockers)
  • Neuroglycopenic: difficulty concentrating, confusion, irritability, headache, behavioral change, seizure (if severe)
  • In hypoglycemia-unaware patients: lethargy, only sign may be a sudden seizure or unexplained bradycardia

Fingerstick <70 mg/dL with symptoms = TREAT IMMEDIATELY:

  1. If conscious and able to swallow: 15 g fast carbs (4 oz juice, 3–4 glucose tablets, 1 tbsp honey)
  2. If altered or unable to swallow: D50 IV bolus 12.5 mL (= 500 mg dextrose IV push); may repeat q15min until glucose >100
  3. Recheck fingerstick in 15 minutes; if still <70, repeat carbs or D50
  4. Notify provider — hypoglycemia in post-op patient is a safety event; insulin doses must be reduced

Prevention:

  • Avoid target <110 mg/dL — STS guideline; hypoglycemia is more harmful than mild hyperglycemia
  • q1h fingerstick checks on IV drip, especially in older patients on beta-blockers (unawareness risk)
  • Reduce insulin doses proactively as stress resolves (POD 2–3 stress hyperglycemia often improves; drip rates must decrease)
  • Patient education if going home on insulin: signs of hypoglycemia, carry fast carbs, wear ID bracelet

sections.heading: 7.5 Newer Agents and Perioperative Considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
SGLT2 Inhibitors (SGLT2i) — e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin:

  • Euglycemic DKA risk: SGLT2i can cause DKA even with glucose <250 mg/dL (insulin activity is just enough to suppress ketone production)
  • Perioperative plan: Hold SGLT2i for 24–48 hours before cardiac surgery; restart after glucose control established post-op
  • Red flag: if patient is on SGLT2i pre-op and develops fruity breath + normal-range glucose post-op → check beta-hydroxybutyrate (euglycemic DKA) even if glucose <250

GLP-1 Receptor Agonists (GLP-1 RA) — e.g., semaglutide, liraglutide:

  • Generally safe perioperatively
  • Hold morning dose if significant preoperative fasting
  • May delay gastric emptying → slower oral intake post-op

ACEI/ARB continuance:

  • Continue perioperatively unless contraindicated (hypotension)
  • Help with blood pressure and may reduce post-op AF/POAF risk

Home metformin:

  • Usually held immediately pre-op (renal clearance concern in case of acute kidney injury)
  • May restart once renal function stable and oral intake tolerated (POD 1–2 typically)

sections.heading: 7.6 Pre-Operative A1c Optimization & Discharge Planning
sections.bodyHtml:
A1c ≥10 on admission = red flag:

  • Signals poor baseline glucose control
  • Post-op insulin resistance will unmask worsening glycemic control; expect refractory hyperglycemia
  • Early endocrinology consult for discharge planning and long-term regimen establishment
  • Patient education needed before discharge — home regimen will differ from post-op drip management

Discharge insulin transition (do NOT use pre-op regimen as default):

  1. Establish stable post-op basal-bolus-correctional regimen by POD 3–5 (at least 24–48h of stable doses)
  2. Do NOT transition to pre-op home doses same-day as discharge — regimen usually changes due to:
    • Higher post-op insulin resistance (may take 1–4 weeks to normalize)
    • Surgical inflammation and pain (ongoing insulin need)
    • Dietary intake may differ from home baseline
    • Co-manage with endocrinology if available for discharge regimen; ensure patient/caregiver education on:
    • Basal-bolus-correctional rationale (not sliding scale alone)
    • Hypoglycemia symptoms and treatment
    • When to call for dose adjustments (if persistently >250 or <100)
    • Follow-up plan with primary care or endocrinology within 1–2 weeks post-discharge

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • Glucose trending up despite increasing insulin doses (POD 2+) — suggests infection (pneumonia, UTI, sternal wound infection), inadequate insulin regimen, new steroid dose, or evolving DKA/HHS
  • A1c ≥10 documented at admission — baseline poor control; expect refractory hyperglycemia and higher complication risk
  • New onset polyuria, polydipsia, or fruity breath — early DKA/HHS warning sign
  • Mental status declining: lethargy, confusion, disorientation — could be hypoglycemia (obtain q1h fingersticks immediately) or hyperglycemic hyperosmolarity (glucose >400, osmolarity rising)
  • Rapid respirations (RR >20) with otherwise stable vital signs — Kussmaul breathing (DKA warning); get ABG
  • Urine ketones positive, serum HCO3− <21 mEq/L — metabolic acidosis developing; DKA risk
  • Electrolyte derangement: K⁺ <3.5 (insulin drip driving K⁺ intracellularly; cardiac arrhythmia risk) or rising K⁺ (renal failure, DKA)
  • New infection signs (fever, WBC spike, wound erythema) — infection-driven hyperglycemia; requires more aggressive insulin coverage
  • Glucose persistently >250 by POD 4 without known pre-op DM — suggests undiagnosed DM; check A1c immediately
  • Hypoglycemia episode (glucose <70 with symptoms) — insulin regimen is too aggressive; reduce doses, shorten check intervals, increase frequency
  • Steroid doses increasing (for ARDS, pericarditis) — anticipate afternoon hyperglycemia spike; proactive insulin adjustment needed (add NPH, increase boluses)
  • Patient on dextrose-containing IV fluids — unnecessary in most post-op cardiac patients; switch to LR or 0.9 NS unless strict contraindication

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Stress hyperglycemia is the norm, not the exception. Even non-diabetics spike to 180–250 post-op. Treat it with insulin drip or basal-bolus. Van den Berghe data shows improved outcomes with target 140–180.

  2. Too-tight control (<110 mg/dL) causes hypoglycemia and worse outcomes. The pendulum swung from Van den Berghe's 80–110 target to STS's 140–180 because hypoglycemia is harmful. Avoid aggressive targeting.

  3. Basal-bolus-correctional is the gold standard; sliding scale alone perpetuates reactive hyperglycemia. Basal (long-acting background) + bolus (mealtime) + correctional (supplement for above-target) allows proactive control. New-grad education point.

  4. Hold rapid-acting insulin if patient is NPO. If breakfast bolus is due and patient still NPO, hold it. Rapid-acting without carbs = hypoglycemia risk. Always give basal (long-acting) even NPO.

  5. Long-acting (basal) insulin continues even if NPO. Do NOT hold glargine, detemir, or degludec because patient is NPO. Basal is baseline glucose coverage. Bolus is for meals.

  6. Steroid-induced hyperglycemia is real, predictable, and manageable. Dexamethasone or methylprednisolone given morning → afternoon/evening glucose spike. Anticipate with afternoon NPH or extra mealtime boluses. Taper coverage as steroid tapers.

  7. Post-op dextrose-containing fluids (D5-LR, D5-0.9 NS) are often unnecessary and worsen hyperglycemia. Switch to LR or 0.9 NS. Exception: if patient hypoglycemic and cannot take PO, D50 bolus or D5 drip may be ordered — follow provider direction.

  8. Hypoglycemia unawareness in older diabetics on beta-blockers is common. Tremor and tachycardia are masked; patient may only report "feeling weird" or show behavioral change. Lower threshold for q1h checks in this population.

  9. Type 1 DM requires basal insulin at all times. If basal insulin (NPH, glargine) is accidentally held post-op, DKA risk is extremely high (stress + zero endogenous insulin). Check orders carefully. If basal was held, restart ASAP and get ABG + endocrinology consult.

  10. Euglycemic DKA can occur on SGLT2 inhibitors even with normal glucose. Positive urine ketones + fruity breath but glucose <250 = red flag. Check beta-hydroxybutyrate. Hold SGLT2i pre-op; restart after glucose control established.

  11. Fingerstick q1h on IV drip; q4–6h on subcutaneous insulin. Frequent checks on drip allow rapid titration and prevent hypoglycemia. Less frequent on subcutaneous (q4–6h is standard floor level). Increase to q1–2h if transitioning from drip or if unawareness.

  12. Transition from IV drip to subcutaneous: overlap 2–4 hours with basal initiated 6–12 hours before drip stops. Prevents hyperglycemia rebound. Do NOT stop drip, start subcutaneous, and hope. Overlap is essential.

  13. Home regimen transition before discharge — avoid same-day restart of pre-op doses. If patient goes home on insulin, regimen must be established, titrated, and patient/caregiver educated BEFORE discharge. Do NOT send home with "same as before surgery" if pre-op control was poor (A1c ≥10) or if patient did not tolerate home regimen post-op. Coordinate with endocrinology or case management.

  14. Endocrinology consult if refractory hyperglycemia (glucose >300 despite optimized insulin, POD >2). May uncover undiagnosed DM, thyroid issues, Cushing syndrome from stress, or other endocrine pathology. High-yield consult.

  15. A1c ≥10 on admission is a red flag. Poor baseline control; post-op insulin resistance unmasks this. Expect refractory hyperglycemia, higher DSWI risk, longer length of stay. Early endocrinology involvement and careful discharge planning essential.

cards.title: Hyperkalemia
cards.quickAnswer: K ≥ 5.5 = mild, 6.0–6.4 = moderate, ≥ 6.5 = severe. Obtain STAT 12-lead ECG. Peaked T waves or widened QRS = treat immediately regardless of K level. No ECG changes: treat if K ≥ 6.5, redraw if pseudohyperkalemia suspected (hemolyzed sample, thrombocytosis). Stabilize membrane with calcium gluconate 1 g IV push, shift K intracellularly with insulin 10 units + D50 25 g IV, then albuterol nebulized 10–20 mg. Remove K via lokelma 10 g q6h, patiromer, or dialysis. Post-op AKI is the top driver; cardioplegia-related hyperK possible in first hours post-op.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — what this is and who gets it.

  • Definition: Serum potassium > 5.5 mEq/L with or without ECG changes. Severe when K ≥ 6.5 or any ECG changes (peaked T, widened QRS, sine wave) present.
  • Incidence: 5–15% of post-cardiac surgery patients, peaking POD 1–3. Higher in patients developing acute kidney injury.
  • Who this applies to: post-cardiac surgery patients, especially those with oliguria, AKI, or on potassium-sparing medications.
  • Why it matters: hyperkalemia can cause sudden cardiac arrest with minimal warning. A stable patient can decompensate from peaked T waves to sine wave in minutes once ECG changes appear.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Hyperkalemia post-cardiac surgery results from multiple converging mechanisms:

Primary cause — Acute Kidney Injury (AKI):

  • Cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) induces ischemia-reperfusion injury in renal tubules
  • Non-pulsatile CPB flow, hypothermia, and hemodilution cause acute tubular necrosis (ATN)
  • Oliguria develops POD 1–3; kidneys cannot excrete K normally
  • Hyperkalemia often appears within 12–72 hours post-op alongside rising creatinine and falling urine output (KDIGO, 2012)

Secondary causes:

  • Hemolysis on pump: Intracellular K concentration ~150 mEq/L vs. serum ~5 mEq/L. Even 1–2% hemolysis of total blood volume can raise serum K by 1–2 mEq/L.
  • Acidosis: Hydrogen ion shift into cells drives K out. Every 0.1 unit drop in pH raises serum K by ~0.5 mEq/L.
  • Tissue catabolism & rhabdomyolysis: Post-op pain, inflammation, and muscle injury release intracellular K. Myoglobinuria signals ongoing release.
  • K-sparing diuretics: Spironolactone and eplerenone become dangerous when AKI develops post-op. Many hyperkalemia events are iatrogenic.
  • ACE-I/ARB/ARNI: These agents reduce efferent arteriolar tone and promote K reabsorption. Restarting without K or Cr check in oliguric patients is a common cause of severe hyperkalemia.
  • Blood transfusion: Each PRBC unit contains 50–100 mEq K from storage hemolysis. Massive transfusion (> 6 units) delivers > 500 mEq K.
  • Pseudohyperkalemia (artifact, not true elevation): Hemolyzed sample (tourniquet, prolonged draw), thrombocytosis (platelets > 600), or leukocytosis (WBC > 100) from in-vitro rupture during clotting.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following:

  • Serum potassium ≥ 5.5 mEq/L on routine or STAT labs
  • ECG changes consistent with hyperkalemia: peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval, widened QRS, loss of P wave, sine wave pattern
  • Bradyarrhythmia on telemetry in setting of elevated K
  • Cardiac arrest or unstable rhythm in a post-op patient (always check K immediately)
  • Oliguria or AKI developing POD 0–1 (hyperkalemia is the dominant complication of post-cardiac surgery oliguria)
  • Patient on K-sparing agents (spironolactone, eplerenone, ACE-I/ARB, ARNI) with rising Cr or AKI
  • Recent massive blood transfusion (old blood, K ~50 mEq/L per unit)
  • Rhabdomyolysis suspected: dark urine, very elevated CK

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Obtain STAT 12-lead ECG immediately — parallel to all other actions
  • Vital signs: HR, BP, SpO₂, perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature)
  • Observe symptoms: chest discomfort, palpitations, weakness, paresthesias (perioral, fingertips)
  • Note telemetry rhythm: irregular, bradycardic, peaked appearance on monitor
  • Review the labs:
  • Current serum K and recent K trend (is K rising or stable?)
  • Creatinine and urine output — assess for AKI
  • pH, HCO₃, lactate (acidosis worsens hyperkalemia)
  • CBC: platelet count, WBC (pseudohyperkalemia screening)
  • Hemoglobin (hemolysis screen)
  • Review the MAR: Is patient on ACE-I/ARB, spironolactone, eplerenone, ARNI, NSAIDs? When dosed?
  • Medication/transfusion timeline: When was most recent blood transfusion? Any K-containing IV fluids running?
  • Urine color: Dark/cola-colored (hemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria)?
  • Physical exam: Strength testing (hyperkalemia causes weakness); assess for ascending paralysis pattern

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(K 5.5–6.0 mEq/L, asymptomatic, normal ECG, alert)

  1. Confirm the K result is real — rule out pseudohyperkalemia FIRST:

    • Redraw STAT from peripheral vein with meticulous technique (no tourniquet, or release before collection)
    • If CBC shows thrombocytosis (platelets > 600) or marked leukocytosis (WBC > 100), pseudohyperkalemia is likely
    • If suspected: redraw immediately, hold emergency treatment pending new result, document heavily

  2. Obtain 12-lead ECG if not already done — verify normal intervals (PR, QRS, QTc)

  3. Hold all K-raising medications immediately:

    • ACE-I/ARB (lisinopril, enalapril, losartan, valsartan, etc.)
    • ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan)
    • Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, eplerenone)
    • NSAIDs (ketorolac, ibuprofen, indomethacin)
    • Document exact time of hold in chart

  4. Review and switch IV fluids:

    • Ensure IV fluids are K-free (D5W, normal saline acceptable)
    • Lactated Ringer's has 4 mEq K/L — acceptable but why add K while treating hyperkalemia? Consider switch to normal saline.

  5. Assess renal function and urine output:

    • Document current UOP and 4-hour trend
    • If oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h), notify team immediately — hyperkalemia + AKI = emergent; jump to 5B pathway

  6. Address reversible causes:

    • If acidotic (pH < 7.35), address underlying cause (perfusion, ventilation, metabolic)
    • Treat pain, fever, hypoxia, fluid overload
    • Correct hypomagnesemia if present (Mg < 2.0)

  7. Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (see §6): - "K 5.5–6.0, ECG normal, asymptomatic. Holding [list meds]. Requesting confirmation of holds and recheck labs in 2–4 hours."

  8. Recheck labs in 2–4 hours — trending is critical. If K continues to rise (5.5 → 5.8 → 6.0) despite holding meds, escalate to 5B pathway.

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes [peaked T, widened QRS, prolonged PR, sine wave], OR K ≥ 6.5 regardless of ECG, OR symptomatic [weakness, palpitations])

STAT Treatment Bundle — Execute in parallel (do NOT wait for sequential completion):

  1. STAT 12-lead ECG (if not already done) and continuous telemetry monitoring

    • Document rhythm and ECG changes at onset
    • Place patient on continuous cardiac monitoring; do not leave bedside alone

  2. STAT call APP/fellow + Charge RN

    • Activate Rapid Response team immediately
    • Notify nephrology immediately if not involved (AKI + hyperK = CRRT candidate)

  3. Membrane stabilization — START IMMEDIATELY (protects heart):

    • Calcium gluconate: 1 g (10 mL of 10% solution) IV push over 5–10 minutes
    • OR Calcium chloride 500 mg (5 mL of 10% solution) via central line only (more irritating peripherally)
    • Effect: onset 1–3 minutes; duration 30–60 minutes. Does NOT lower K, only protects cardiac membrane.
    • May repeat calcium q5–10 min × 2 if ECG worsening or recurrent dysrhythmia
    • Monitor for hypercalcemia signs; have furosemide ready if Ca > 10 mg/dL

  4. Intracellular shift — START IN PARALLEL (removes K from serum by pushing it into cells): - Insulin 10 units regular IV push followed immediately by D50 25 g IV push (or concurrent)

    • Onset 10–20 minutes; duration 4–6 hours
    • CRITICAL: Do NOT give insulin without dextrose (risk of severe hypoglycemia)
    • Fingerstick glucose STAT; establish baseline
    • PLUS Albuterol nebulized 10–20 mg (can combine with other nebulized medications)
    • Onset 30 minutes; duration 2–4 hours
    • Side effects: tremor, tachycardia (expect HR increase 10–20 bpm)

  5. K removal (slower onset, but actual elimination): - Lokelma (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) 10 g PO/NG q6h × 3 days

    • Newer agent; preferred over kayexalate
    • Onset 2–6 hours; removes ~1–2 mEq K per dose
    • Can administer via NG tube if unable to swallow
    • OR Patiromer (Veltassa) 25.2 g PO daily (takes 6–24 hours)
    • OR Kayexalate (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) 15–30 g PO q6h or 50 g PR (older, less reliable, falling out of favor due to volume-loading with sorbitol)
    • Loop diuretic (furosemide) 40–80 mg IV if euvolemic or volume-overloaded AND renal function adequate (useless if anuric)

  6. STAT labs (send stat to lab; do not batch):

    • BMP (K, Cr, BUN, Cl, CO₃, pH); troponin; ABG; CBC; lactate
    • Urine electrolytes if AKI workup not completed
    • CK if rhabdomyolysis suspected

  7. Prepare for dialysis:

    • Notify nephrology immediately of K ≥ 6.5 or K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes
    • Alert ICU for possible CRRT (continuous renal replacement therapy) — dialysis is the ONLY definitive K removal in severe/refractory cases
    • If K continues to rise despite membrane stabilization + shift maneuvers within 30–60 min, dialysis is indicated

  8. Glucose monitoring protocol after insulin:

    • Fingerstick glucose immediately after insulin + D50, then q30 min × 4–6 hours
    • Target glucose 150–250 mg/dL (hyperglycemia acceptable; hypoglycemia dangerous)
    • Have D50 at bedside for rapid treatment if glucose < 70 mg/dL
    • Recheck serum glucose 1–2 hours after insulin bolus

  9. Recheck serum K in 30–60 minutes after treatment initiation:

    • If K dropped ≥ 0.5–1.0 mEq/L, treatment is working; continue monitoring
    • If K unchanged or rising, escalate to dialysis immediately; reassess for ongoing K release (hemolysis, rhabdo, tumor lysis)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient's K is [value], Cr [value], UOP [value] last 4 h. ECG shows [describe findings]. We gave calcium gluconate at [time], insulin + D50 + albuterol at [time]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable / critically ill]. [Symptoms]. Most recent K check was [time], current trend. Meds held: [list]." R: "Requesting [urgent recheck of K / nephrology consult / ICU transfer / CRRT evaluation / dialysis]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
K 5.5–6.0, no ECG changes, first event Primary APP / on-call fellow
K 6.0–6.4 with ECG changes APP/fellow + Rapid Response; notify nephrology
K ≥ 6.5 OR K ≥ 6.0 with sine wave STAT CODE TEAM + Rapid Response + Nephrology; prepare for ICU transfer
Rising K trend despite treatment Nephrology STAT + ICU transfer; dialysis evaluation
Cardiac arrest or unstable dysrhythmia Code Blue; treat per ACLS; calcium first, then full bundle
Hemolyzed sample suspected Redraw immediately; hold treatment pending result

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections in Section 7 are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 ECG progression and what each finding means
sections.bodyHtml:
Hyperkalemia causes a predictable ECG progression reflecting increasing cardiac membrane irritability. Each stage represents increasing danger:

K (mEq/L) ECG Finding Clinical Significance Action
5.5–6.0 Peaked T waves (tall, narrow, symmetrical in precordial leads) Early warning; repolarization shortening Hold K-raising meds; plan to recheck
6.0–6.5 PR prolongation (PR interval > 0.20 sec) Atrial and AV nodal conduction slowing Consider treatment; definitely treat if symptomatic
6.5–7.5 QRS widening (> 0.10 sec) + loss of P wave Ventricular conduction delay; atrial standstill TREAT IMMEDIATELY — risk of VT/VF
7.5+ Sine wave pattern (wavy baseline, no distinct PQRST) IMMINENT CARDIAC ARREST EMERGENCY — Full treatment bundle NOW
— Bradycardia (HR < 40) with narrow QRS Hyperkalemia-induced escape rhythm Treat hyperkalemia; consider atropine if symptomatic

Clinical pearl: Do NOT rely on K level alone. A patient with K = 6.2 and peaked T waves is in more danger than a patient with K = 7.0 and normal ECG.

Always treat based on ECG + level combined (AHA, 2020).

sections.heading: 7.2 Treatment mechanism — what each drug does
sections.bodyHtml:
Hyperkalemia treatment works in three tiers:

Tier 1 — Membrane stabilization (calcium):

  • Calcium gluconate stabilizes the cardiac action potential; it does NOT lower serum K
  • Think of it as "buying time" — protects the heart for 30–60 minutes while other treatments work
  • Effect is rapid (1–3 minutes) but short-lived; may need to repeat

Tier 2 — Intracellular shift (insulin + dextrose + albuterol):

  • Insulin drives glucose and potassium into cells
  • Dextrose prevents hypoglycemia (insulin always paired with glucose post-op)
  • Albuterol (β2-agonist) activates Na/K-ATPase in skeletal muscle, shifting K inside
  • These agents SHIFT K into cells but do NOT remove it from the body. Duration 4–6 hours; K will rebound if not also being removed
  • Useful for buying time while dialysis is arranged; not definitive

Tier 3 — K removal (lokelma, patiromer, loop diuretic, dialysis):

  • Lokelma and patiromer are cation exchange resins; bind K in the GI tract and promote fecal excretion
  • Loop diuretic works only if kidneys functioning (> 0.5 mL/kg/h UOP); useless in anuric patients
  • Dialysis is the ONLY definitive K removal in severe/refractory hyperkalemia. CRRT can remove 1–2 mEq K per hour
  • In post-op AKI, if K ≥ 6.5 or K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes, dialysis should be arranged immediately; it is inevitable

The complete bundle: stabilize (calcium) + shift (insulin/D50/albuterol) + remove (lokelma/dialysis). Stabilization buys time; shifting buys more time; removal actually fixes the problem.

sections.heading: 7.3 Pseudohyperkalemia — when K is fake
sections.bodyHtml:
Pseudohyperkalemia is a critical pitfall. The K level is not truly elevated; rather, the sample was damaged during collection or processing:

  • Hemolyzed sample during collection: tourniquet left on too long, prolonged draw time, small-gauge needle, repeated fist clenching
  • Thrombocytosis (platelets > 600): platelets rupture during clotting; release massive K into serum
  • Leukocytosis (WBC > 100): lymphocytes rupture during clotting
  • Diagnosis: Check CBC. If thrombocytosis or leukocytosis present, redraw from different site with meticulous technique.
  • Why it matters: Many patients have received unnecessary calcium, insulin, and dialysis because pseudohyperkalemia was treated as real.

sections.heading: 7.4 Drug class table
sections.bodyHtml:
Confirm all doses with provider and institutional policy.

Membrane stabilization

Drug Dose Notes
Calcium gluconate 1 g (10 mL of 10% solution) IV over 5–10 min Peripheral line acceptable; monitor site for infiltration (irritant)
Calcium gluconate repeat May repeat q5–10 min × 2 if ECG worsening Monitor for hypercalcemia (Ca > 10 mg/dL causes arrhythmia)
Calcium chloride 500 mg (5 mL of 10% solution) via central line only More irritating than gluconate; faster onset; central line only

Intracellular shift

Drug Dose Notes
Regular insulin IV 10 units IV push ALWAYS pair with dextrose; onset 10–20 min; duration 4–6 h
Dextrose 50% 25 g (50 mL of 50% solution) IV push Same syringe as insulin, or immediately after; prevents hypoglycemia
Albuterol nebulized 10–20 mg nebulized Can combine with other nebulized meds; tremor/tachycardia expected

K removal

Drug Dose Notes
Lokelma (sodium zirconium) 10 g PO/NG q6h × 3 days Newer, preferred over kayexalate; slower onset but reliable
Patiromer (Veltassa) 25.2 g PO daily Once-daily dosing; can mix in water; takes 6–24 h
Kayexalate 15–30 g PO q6h, or 50 g PR Older agent; falling out of favor (volume-loading with sorbitol, slower)
Furosemide (if euvolemic or volume-up) 40–80 mg IV Only effective if kidneys functioning; useless if anuric
Dialysis / CRRT Goal K removal 1–2 mEq/h Definitive; coordinate with nephrology immediately if K ≥ 6.5 or refractory

Doses adapted from AHA (2020) and institutional policy. Always verify against current prescribing recommendations.

sections.heading: 7.5 Special subgroup considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Patients with acidosis: Bicarb only helps if truly acidotic (pH < 7.35). Correcting the underlying cause (perfusion, ventilation) is more important.
  • Redistribution vs. total body excess: Shift therapy (insulin, albuterol) temporarily moves K into cells but doesn't remove it. Use for symptomatic or severe K while arranging removal (dialysis, lokelma).
  • Patiromer + sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC) role: Patiromer is preferred for chronic K management (takes 6–24 hours, once daily). Lokelma works faster (2–6 hours) and can be dosed q6h, making it preferred in acute hyperkalemia.
  • Dialysis access considerations: Stroke volume on intermittent HD (IHD) may drop sharply; CRRT (continuous) is more hemodynamically stable in unstable patients or those with reduced EF.
  • ACE/ARB hold and resumption timing: These agents are held pre-op frequently and resumed post-op without K or Cr check. If hyperkalemia develops, hold again; discuss resumption timing with team (typically when K normalizes and Cr stable).

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch-fors in stable or early-moderate hyperkalemia that predict progression to cardiac emergency.

  • K trending upward despite holding K-raising meds: 5.5 → 5.9 → 6.3 (may indicate ongoing K release from hemolysis, rhabdo, or AKI acceleration)
  • New peaked T waves on repeat ECG (even if K < 6.5): sign of ECG progression; treat immediately
  • Bradycardia developing (HR < 50) with narrow QRS: hyperkalemia-induced escape rhythm; ominous sign
  • QRS widening trending: 0.08 → 0.10 → 0.12 sec (ECG progression without rhythm change; may herald sine wave)
  • New weakness or paralysis: ascending paralysis (legs → respiratory muscles) is a hyperkalemia symptom; progresses rapidly to respiratory failure
  • Oliguric output + rising K + rising Cr simultaneously: "Triple threat" — AKI is driving all three; CRRT is inevitable
  • Urine darkening or CK elevation suggesting rhabdomyolysis: ongoing K release; K will continue to rise unless dialyzed
  • Hypotension developing during insulin + D50 treatment: watch for glucose complications or superimposed sepsis
  • Rebound hyperkalemia within 2–4 hours of shift therapy (K rose back up): shift therapy failing; dialysis needed urgently
  • Pulmonary edema or respiratory distress superimposed: volume overload + hyperkalemia + AKI = ICU-level emergency
  • Signs of hemolysis worsening: continued hemoglobinuria, rising indirect bili, falling hematocrit despite transfusion (ongoing intravascular hemolysis)

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Pseudohyperkalemia is the #1 false positive. Hemolyzed sample, thrombocytosis, or leukocytosis can all cause falsely elevated K.

    Before emergency treatment, REDRAW from a different site with meticulous technique. Many patients have received unnecessary calcium and insulin because of this.

  2. Calcium gluconate stabilizes membrane but does NOT lower K. Explain to the team: "The calcium is protecting the heart for now. The insulin and potassium-binding medicines are working to lower it." Calcium buys 30–60 minutes; it is not a complete treatment.

  3. Insulin + D50 + albuterol SHIFT K intracellularly; they do NOT remove it. They buy 4–6 hours. If the patient is oliguric and K is truly elevated, dialysis is inevitable. Plan it early; do not delay referral waiting for shift therapy to "work."

  4. Kayexalate (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) is falling out of favor. Lokelma and patiromer are newer, more reliable, and do not volume-load with sorbitol (which causes severe diarrhea and dehydration in post-op patients). If kayexalate is all available, monitor bowel function closely; avoid PR kayexalate in recent abdominal surgery or ileus (perforation risk).

  5. Glucose rebound hypoglycemia after insulin + D50 is real and dangerous. Fingerstick glucose q30 min for 4–6 hours after insulin. Hypoglycemia (< 70) causes seizures or dysrhythmia just like hyperkalemia. Have D50 at bedside; treat if glucose < 70.

  6. ECG changes precede cardiac dysrhythmia. Do not wait for symptoms or arrest to treat. Peaked T waves alone are indication to treat if K ≥ 6.0. Sine wave is a pre-arrest rhythm; you are now in a race against time.

  7. Hold ACE-I/ARB and K-sparing diuretics (MRA) with K ≥ 5.5 until K normalizes and Cr stabilizes. This is the most preventable cause of post-op hyperkalemia. Many events occur 12–24 hours after home ACE-I/ARB or spironolactone was restarted without a K check. Verify on medication reconciliation that these were held at admission.

  8. Avoid IV fluids with potassium. Post-op ICU patients should run normal saline or D5W. Lactated Ringer's has 4 mEq K/L; acceptable, but why add K while treating hyperkalemia? Switch to K-free fluids while K is elevated.

  9. Blood transfusion delivers a K load. Each PRBC unit has 50–100 mEq K from storage hemolysis. Massive transfusion (> 6 units) delivers > 500 mEq K into a post-op patient already struggling with AKI.

    Monitor K trend closely after large transfusions; check K 1–2 hours post-transfusion. Old blood (> 14 days storage) has higher hemolysis and K content.

  10. Rhabdomyolysis is both a cause and a complication of hyperkalemia. Dark (cola-colored) urine, very high CK (> 5,000), and low urine output are red flags. Hyperkalemia causes muscle weakness, which leads to rhabdo from immobility or crush. Rhabdo releases massive intracellular K, perpetuating hyperkalemia. If suspected, aggressive hydration and alkaline urine (sodium bicarbonate) are needed alongside standard hyperkalemia treatment; dialysis is often required.

  11. Hemolysis on pump is visible in blood bank report and urine. Cola-colored urine, elevated indirect bilirubin, elevated LDH, and low haptoglobin are markers. Hemolysis-induced ATN requires aggressive hydration and consideration of urinary alkalinization (sodium bicarbonate to pH > 6.5). Kidney is at risk of ATN from hemoglobin precipitation. Coordinate with nephrology; this is a CRRT-candidate diagnosis.

  12. Dialysis is definitive but requires coordination. Do NOT assume the on-call nephrologist will call you back immediately. If K ≥ 6.5 or K ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes, notify nephrology and ICU simultaneously. CRRT can be initiated in the ICU while waiting for hemodialysis. Do not wait passively.

  13. The oliguric post-op patient is in a unique danger zone. AKI develops rapidly (POD 0–1), K rises quickly (5.2 → 6.8 in 4 hours with ongoing hemolysis or tissue breakdown), and there is nowhere for K to go (kidneys not filtering). These patients need hourly UOP assessment, q2h K checks (or continuous monitoring if possible), and a low threshold for ICU transfer. Do not wait for the patient to "stabilize" if oliguria and hyperkalemia are both developing.

  14. LR (Ringer's lactate) has 4 mEq K/L. Not a problem in healthy kidney, but post-op AKI patients should avoid it. The lactate is metabolized to bicarbonate (protective in acidosis), but in hyperkalemia context, stick to normal saline.

  15. Peaked T waves can appear and disappear quickly. Do not reflexively get a 12-lead ECG every 5 minutes. Get one STAT at presentation, one after calcium/insulin (10 min), then q15–30 min if unstable or ECG continues to change. Document exact findings (which leads, PR/QRS/QTc measurements) in the chart, not just "peaked T waves."

cards.title: Post-Op Hypertension (non-dissection / non-stroke)
cards.quickAnswer: New SBP >140 on post-cardiac surgery patient → rule out pain, anxiety, bladder distention, hypoxia, medication timing first — these account for 60-70% of POD 0-3 spikes. Targets: SBP ≤140 routine; ≤120 for aortic/root/dissection repair. IV nicardipine 2.5–15 mg/h or labetalol 10–20 mg IV q10 min are first-line. Unstable (SBP >180 with chest pain, ST changes, HF, active bleeding, or neuro deficit) → STAT call, work up the underlying cause (ischemia, dissection, stroke, bleeding) simultaneously with BP control. Never drop SBP >25% in first 60 min; chronic hypertensives are at risk for watershed stroke and graft steal.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: New or worsening hypertension (SBP >140 mm Hg, sustained >15 minutes) within the first 3–7 days after cardiac surgery in a patient without pre-operative dissection, acute stroke, or other contraindication to standard BP targets.
  • Incidence: 30–80% of cardiac surgery patients develop post-op HTN on POD 0–1 (Aronow et al., 2010). Most is transient, catecholamine-driven or pain-driven. Approximately 10% require sustained IV antihypertensive management beyond 24 hours. Peak onset is within 6 hours post-op (recovery room) and again when sedation wears off (POD 1).
  • Who this applies to: Adult post-operative cardiac surgery patients on ICU or stepdown units. Highest yield POD 0–3; still relevant through POD 7.
  • Why it matters: Uncontrolled post-op HTN increases risk of graft failure, suture-line bleeding, myocardial ischemia, acute renal injury, and neurologic events. Rapid, aggressive treatment without addressing reversibles wastes time and medication.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-op hypertension results from multiple overlapping mechanisms:

  • Catecholamine surge from pain, anxiety, hypoxia, inadequate anesthesia during emergence, or sympathetic activation during cardiopulmonary bypass
  • Pain — the single most common modifiable trigger in POD 0–3; splinting, inadequate analgesia, and coughing spike BP acutely
  • Bladder distention — reflex sympathetic activation; often overlooked despite simple catheterization solution
  • Shivering post-op — dramatically increases oxygen consumption and systemic vascular resistance; warming resolves both
  • Missed home antihypertensive medication — beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, and diuretics held pre-op are not restarted immediately post-op; this is the most common modifiable cause in POD 1–3
  • Rebound hypertension — acute withdrawal of short-acting IV agents (esmolol, nicardipine) without overlap to PO agents; occurs 6–12 hours after discontinuation
  • Fluid over-resuscitation from crystalloid boluses in the OR without concurrent diuresis; hypervolemia raises BP and fills the right atrium excessively
  • Cross-clamp rebound — surge in catecholamines and afterload when aortic cross-clamp is released during surgery; present in immediate return from OR, typically resolves within 2–4 hours with adequate sedation and analgesia
  • Stimulant exposure — caffeine, nicotine in the first post-op hours if patient unaware of restrictions
  • Medication cascades — diuretics pull intravascular volume despite "high" BP; IV fluids given for "hypotension" when actually hypertensive, worsening volume status

Most post-op HTN spikes (POD 0–1) resolve within 24–48 hours once pain is controlled, home medications restarted, and reversibles addressed. Persistent HTN beyond POD 2 suggests underlying renal dysfunction, primary hypertension control issues, or secondary causes (rare: pheochromocytoma, renal artery stenosis).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following while caring for a post-op cardiac surgery patient:

  • SBP >140 mm Hg sustained >15 minutes (post-op default target)
  • SBP >120 mm Hg in aortic/root/dissection patient (tighter target for suture-line protection)
  • New SBP spike with pain, anxiety, bladder fullness, or awakening from sedation
  • HTN + chest pain, shortness of breath, or neuro deficit (concern for ischemia, HF, or stroke)
  • HTN + chest tube output rising or oozing at incisions (bleeding risk)
  • Refusal to notify provider of persistently elevated BP trend
  • Return from OR with SBP 160–200+ (expected cross-clamp rebound; address with sedation, analgesia, IV agents if sustained >2–4 h)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (3–5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information gathering. No actions yet. Competent systematic exam.

  • Vital signs: HR, SpO₂, RR, mental status, perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output)
  • Recheck BP: both arms if dissection surveillance relevant; use same arm and position each time
  • Symptom review: chest pain, headache, dyspnea, palpitations, visual changes, anxiety level, new weakness
  • Pain score: location, quality, recent analgesic administration (when, drug, response)
  • Bladder assessment: Foley patent and draining? Last void time and volume? Foley just placed? Bladder scan if retained volume suspected (>300 mL)
  • Recent medications:
  • Missed home BP meds at home? Are they restarted post-op? Check MAR.
  • Recent IV fluid bolus? Recent vasopressor infusion? Nicardipine drip running?
  • When was last beta-blocker dose? ACE inhibitor? Any held for "low BP" earlier?
  • Surgical status: Chest tube output (color, amount, mL/h trend), dressing saturation, incision appearance, any active oozing or new bleeding
  • Neuro check: Baseline mental status comparison; any new weakness, facial asymmetry, speech slurring, vision changes?
  • Cardiac: ECG rhythm on tele, any ST changes or ectopy; troponin if suspicious
  • Review of systems: fever (shivering post-op), anxiety, agitation, recent stimulant use (caffeine, nicotine)
  • Current sedation: propofol infusion running? Opioid dose? Emerging from anesthesia right now?
  • History of home HTN: "What was your BP at home last week?" Knowing baseline vs. acute spike changes escalation strategy.

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(SBP 140–180, asymptomatic, no active bleeding / HF / ischemia / neuro change.)

  1. Recheck BP in 5 minutes — confirm trend, not single reading; use same arm and position each time
  2. Treat reversibles first — these fix 60–70% of post-op HTN spikes:
    • Pain → notify for analgesic (MOST COMMON CAUSE); do NOT skip this; even a small increase in analgesia often drops BP by 20–40 mm Hg
    • Bladder → catheterize or empty Foley; check patency; bladder scan if retained volume >300 mL suspected
    • Anxiety → brief reassurance, lower lights, quiet conversation, family presence if appropriate
    • Hypoxia → increase O₂ or non-rebreather to target SpO₂ >94%; check for secretions, stridor
    • Shivering → warming blanket, check core temp; shivering increases SVR acutely
    • Verify home BP meds restarted post-op — check MAR; this is the most commonly missed escalation factor
    • Assess medication timing: Is a scheduled beta-blocker or antihypertensive due? Was one recently held for low BP?
    • If SBP remains >140 after 15 min of reversible treatment, initiate IV antihypertensive per provider order:
    • Nicardipine drip (preferred on ICU): 2.5 mg/h, titrate by 1.25 mg/h q15 min up to 15 mg/h target (smooth, predictable, least reflex tachycardia)
    • Labetalol 10–20 mg IV push over 1–2 min; may repeat q10 min up to 80 mg per dose or 300 mg per 24 h (dual alpha-beta block; rate control too)
    • Esmolol bolus or drip 50–200 mcg/kg/min IV if HR control also needed (ultra-short half-life; 10 min onset/offset)
    • Continuous telemetry monitoring while provider is paged
    • Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (Section 6) if HTN persists >30 min despite initial measures
    • Prepare for oral transition — anticipate PO agent order (amlodipine, metoprolol XL) on POD 1–2 to bridge off IV
    • Monitor for goal achievement and rebound hypotension as IV drug wears off; do not abruptly discontinue IV without PO on board
    • Document trend: initial BP, time, interventions (especially pain management and reversible triggers), BP response, final status

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(SBP >180 with symptoms: chest pain, ST changes, HF, active bleeding, neuro deficit, aortic surgery patient.)

  1. STAT call APP / on-call fellow + charge nurse + CT surgery (if aortic-related) - Do NOT leave the patient alone; activate Rapid Response if hypotension or altered mental status develops
  2. Treat the CAUSE simultaneously with BP control:
    • Active ischemia (ST changes, troponin rise, chest pain) → 12-lead ECG STAT, troponin STAT, cardiology consult; may need catheterization
    • Active bleeding (rising chest tube output mL/h, dressing saturation, oozing at suture line) → CT surgery notified immediately; may need return to OR; do NOT aggressively lower BP if actively bleeding
    • HF / pulmonary edema (dyspnea, new crackles, elevated JVD) → semi-recumbent position, diuretic consideration, echo if no recent one; nicardipine may be better than labetalol here
    • Aortic concern (sudden HTN + back/chest pain, BP differential between arms, widened pulse pressure) → aortic dissection protocol; call CT surgery + cardiothoracic fellow STAT
    • Neuro deficit (weakness, speech change, facial droop, altered mental status) → stroke code immediately, not just BP control; neuroimaging; do NOT chase BP alone
    • Initiate IV antihypertensive — nicardipine drip typically most titratable:
    • Start nicardipine 2.5 mg/h, titrate by 1.25 mg/h q10 min up to effect (goal 120–140 depending on context)
    • Alternative: labetalol bolus 20–30 mg IV if aortic/dissection and HR control also needed; then drip if sustained
    • Avoid hydralazine in this scenario (unpredictable action, reflex tachycardia undesirable if ischemic)
    • Nitroprusside reserved for ICU-level care only (cyanide toxicity risk, requires continuous A-line)
    • 12-lead ECG and STAT labs: troponin, ABG, lactate, electrolytes, CBC, coagulation panel (PT/INR) if bleeding risk
    • Reduce SBP by 25% in first 60 minutes, then gradually further — rapid aggressive drops cause watershed ischemia and stroke in chronically hypertensive or autoregulatory-impaired patients
    • Transesophageal echo or CT angio if aortic dissection suspected
    • Prepare for ICU transfer if sustained IV drip >4 h or if underlying cause requires ICU-level monitoring (renal crisis, pheo, uncontrolled ischemia)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed new SBP elevation to [value] at [time]. Current HR [rate], SpO₂ [value], no acute chest pain [or note if present]. Medications on board: [list recent antihypertensives/inotropes]. Home BP meds: [list, note if restarted]." A: "I've ruled out pain [pain score], anxiety, bladder distention [Foley/scan result], hypoxia. [Describe any concerning features: ischemic changes, bleeding, neuro change]. Patient is currently [stable / symptomatic with X findings]." R: "Requesting [initiation of IV antihypertensive / additional labs / consultation] and target BP goal."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable HTN, SBP 140–180, reversibles addressed Primary APP / on-call cardiologist
HTN + chest pain or ST changes APP + cardiology STAT; ECG and troponin STAT
HTN + active bleeding or rising chest tube output CT surgery STAT — possible return to OR
HTN + neuro deficit (weakness, speech change, facial droop) Stroke code (neurology + CT surgery); do NOT chase BP alone
HTN + aortic concern (back pain, BP differential, widened pulse pressure) CT surgery STAT — aortic dissection protocol
HTN + pulmonary edema / HF APP + consider echo; diuretic / afterload management
HTN refractory to IV agents or unclear etiology CT surgery + consider cardiology / nephrology consult
Suspected pheochromocytoma crisis (episodic severe HTN >200 with flushing, diaphoresis, headache, palpitations) CT surgery + endocrinology; alpha-block FIRST, then beta-block

sections.heading: 7.1 Procedure-specific HTN targets and autoregulation logic
sections.bodyHtml:
Why targets vary: Autoregulation is impaired post-op and in chronic hypertension. Rapid drops below the "permissive ceiling" cause watershed stroke and low-flow renal injury. Aortic surgery requires tighter control to prevent suture-line rupture. Acute stroke (non-candidate for thrombolytics) requires opposite approach.

Target table — procedure-specific SBP goals:

Procedure Target SBP Rationale Duration
CABG / AVR / MVR (routine) ≤140 mm Hg Prevent graft steal; most common post-op patient POD 0–3
Bentall / Aortic Ascending Repair (open) ≤120 mm Hg Prevent suture-line blowout at aortic root; tightest control required POD 0–7
Acute Type A Dissection Repair ≤120 mm Hg, HR ≤60 Minimize aortic wall stress (dP/dt reduction); beta-blocker essential POD 0–3 (ongoing)
TAAA / TEVAR 100–120 mm Hg with MAP ≥85 Cord perfusion pressure; not hypotensive (prevent paraplegia) POD 0–3
Acute ischemic stroke (non-tPA candidate) ≤220/120 permissive Opposite of cardiac logic: high HTN protects penumbra in acute ischemia First 24 h
Acute ischemic stroke (tPA given) <185/110 before tPA; <180/105 after Prevent hemorrhagic conversion; tight control required Per stroke protocol
Post-CABG POD 1–2 on NTG drip 100–140 mm Hg NTG provides afterload reduction + graft protection; synergistic drop likely While on NTG

The 25% rule: Reduce SBP by no more than 25% in the first 60 minutes, then gradually further over hours. This prevents watershed stroke, acute coronary ischemia (graft steal), and acute renal injury.

Example: Patient with SBP 200 pre-op (baseline HTN) → target 150 at 1 hour (25% drop), then 140–120 by 4 hours.

sections.heading: 7.2 Cross-clamp rebound and emergence-phase HTN
sections.bodyHtml:
Cross-clamp rebound: When the aortic cross-clamp is released during surgery, catecholamine surge and afterload increase acutely. SBP 160–200+ is common in the immediate return from OR.

  • Management in recovery: maintain sedation (propofol), opioid-based analgesia, controlled ventilation. Most cases resolve within 2–4 hours with deep sedation alone.
  • If SBP persists >180 at 2 h post-op: IV nicardipine or labetalol per protocol; do NOT panic or escalate to nitroprusside reflexively.
  • Watch for: if rebound HTN is accompanied by rising chest tube output, this signals possible bleeding from new graft anastomosis or suture line — notify CT surgery immediately.

Propofol weaning phase (POD 1–2): As sedation is lightened for extubation, HTN often spikes. This is pain, anxiety, and sympathetic activation converging. Anticipate with:

  • Pre-planned weaning (slow taper over hours, not abrupt stop)
  • Analgesic optimization (opioid or regional technique) before weaning
  • IV antihypertensive standing order ready if needed

sections.heading: 7.3 Rebound hypertension mechanism and prevention
sections.bodyHtml:
Rebound HTN — the 12–48 hour trap:

  • Abrupt discontinuation of IV nicardipine or labetalol without overlapping PO antihypertensive → rebound HTN 6–12 hours later, often HIGHER than baseline
  • Mechanism: sympathetic nervous system rebound when short-acting IV agent clears; without PO agent on board, BP spikes
  • Prevention (CRITICAL): Always overlap IV and PO agents. Start PO agent 4–6 hours BEFORE stopping IV; verify both are on order before weaning drip
  • Suggested PO bridge: Amlodipine 5–10 mg PO daily (long-acting CCB, forgiving dosing) + Metoprolol XL 25–100 mg PO daily (restart home dose if available)
  • If rebound HTN develops after IV weaning, restart IV nicardipine or labetalol while PO agent is being absorbed (24–48 h later)

Tachyphylaxis: Nitroprusside and nitrates can develop tolerance with continuous use >4 hours without break; nicardipine and labetalol do not.

sections.heading: 7.4 Medication selection by clinical context
sections.bodyHtml:
Rate & dose table:

Agent Dose Mechanism When to use Avoid when Notes
Labetalol (IV) 10–20 mg push over 1–2 min; repeat q10 min max 80 mg/dose or 300 mg/24h; drip 0.5–2 mg/min α + β dual blockade; dP/dt reduction Aortic/dissection (rate control + afterload); bridging from IV to PO; hypertensive urgency Asthma/COPD, decompensated HF, bradycardia <50 Excellent rate control; reflex HR usually minimal
Nicardipine (drip) 2.5–15 mg/h IV, titrate by 1.25 mg/h q15 min Dihydropyridine CCB; smooth arterial vasodilation; minimal reflex HR ICU workhorse — best sustained control; lowest reflex tachycardia; predictable; easily titratable Acute decompensated HF (negative inotrope), hypotension Preferred on stepdown; smooth weaning
Esmolol (drip) 50–200 mcg/kg/min IV titrated Ultra-short beta-1 selective; no alpha; HR control Rate + BP in dissection; very titratable; 10 min half-life; rapid onset/offset Asthma, AV block, bradycardia, acute HF For intra-operative or ICU-level titration; expensive
Clevidipine (drip) 1–8 mg/h IV Dihydropyridine CCB; ultra-short half-life; precise control Intraoperative HTN; ICU-level; rarely on stepdown Lipid emulsion restrictions, hypotension Intraoperative only; not standard post-op
Hydralazine (IV bolus) 10–20 mg IV q4–6 h Direct arterial vasodilator; no beta block Second-line; less predictable onset/offset; eclampsia Reflex tachycardia (contraindicated in dissection, myectomy, HCM, acute ischemia) Unpredictable peak time; avoid in post-op aortic
Nitroprusside (drip) 0.25–10 mcg/kg/min IV Nitric oxide donor; potent; rapid onset/offset ICU-level hypertensive emergency; aortic emergency Cyanide toxicity risk (>4 mcg/kg/min >4 h); requires ICU A-line; wrong for sustained stepdown use NOT for stepdown floor; ICU only
Nitroglycerin (drip) 5–100 mcg/min IV titrated Venodilation > arterial; anti-ischemic Post-CABG protection of grafts; concurrent use on POD 0–1; nitrate stack Do not double-load nitrate; monitor for tachyphylaxis Often running already; check before adding second agent
Metoprolol (IV) 5 mg over 2 min; repeat q5–10 min PRN × 3 Beta-1 selective; rate + BP control Companion to IV antihypertensive when HR control needed; home med restart Asthma, bradycardia, low EF on edge For acute rate control; bridge to PO
Amlodipine (PO transition) 5–10 mg PO daily Long-acting CCB; smooth Transition from IV on POD 1–2; goal bridge before discharge —— Forgiving dosing; baseline effect at 7–10 days
Metoprolol XL (PO transition) 25–100 mg PO daily Extended-release; bid dosing option Restart of home med typically POD 1 if tolerated BP-wise —— Match pre-op home dose when possible
Lisinopril (PO transition) 5–20 mg PO daily ACE inhibitor; renal protective Restart if home med post-op, BUT caution if acute renal bump (Cr >1.5× baseline) Hold if acute renal dysfunction; hyperkalemia Often held intra-op; restart when stable

Dosing adapted from AHA/ACC (2017), CVICU Handbook (2017), Elmistekawy & Shallik (2025), and Bojar (2020). Always verify with current institutional policy and prescribing provider.

sections.heading: 7.5 Nicardipine vs. Nitro vs. Esmolol for aortic patients
sections.bodyHtml:
Aortic surgery special considerations:

  • Nicardipine + esmolol combination — often used together for aortic dissection or root repair: nicardipine handles vasodilation (target SBP ≤120), esmolol handles rate control (target HR ≤60) and dP/dt reduction
  • Avoid nitroprusside unless ICU — cyanide toxicity risk; nicardipine is safer for sustained control
  • Avoid hydralazine — reflex tachycardia worsens dP/dt; bad for aortic wall stress
  • NTG is supplementary — already running for graft protection; do NOT stack another agent without discussing synergistic drop risk with provider
  • Labetalol excellent alternative — dual alpha-beta block achieves both rate and afterload reduction in one agent; good second-line for aortic if nicardipine alone insufficient

sections.heading: 7.6 Beta-blocker reinstitution and cardiac protection
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-op beta-blocker strategy:

  • Why restart? Post-op beta-blockers reduce myocardial oxygen demand, prevent POAF (Post-Op Atrial Fibrillation), and reduce mortality in CAD patients
  • Timing: POD 0–1 if hemodynamically stable; SBP ≥100, HR ≥50, not in cardiogenic shock
  • Dosing: restart at home pre-op dose if available; taper up over POD 1–2 if needed for BP tolerance
  • POAF prevention: beta-blockers are protective against atrial fibrillation; reinitiation reduces POAF incidence by ~30% (Joglar et al., 2023)
  • Missed beta-blocker = highest preventable cause of HTN on POD 1–3 — check MAR immediately; this is a teaching point for new graduates
  • Caution: Do not restart if HR <50, SBP <90, or in acute decompensated HF; escalate to provider

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • BP continuing to climb despite initial IV antihypertensive — medication failure or escalating cause; consider escalating dose, switching agents, or working up secondary cause (renal artery stenosis, pheochromocytoma, intracranial event)
  • New chest pain or ischemic ST changes — acute coronary ischemia; may be caused by aggressive BP lowering (graft steal in CABG) or primary ischemia; notify cardiology STAT
  • New dyspnea, crackles on exam, elevated JVD — acute HF or flash pulmonary edema; may be volume-related or demand ischemia; consider diuretic or downward BP titration
  • Rising chest tube output (mL/h increasing) or dressing saturation with blood — active bleeding; notify CT surgery immediately; do NOT aggressively lower BP if actively bleeding
  • New neuro deficit (weakness, facial asymmetry, speech slurring, vision change, altered mental status) — stroke code immediately; this is NOT hypertensive urgency, this is hypertensive emergency with CNS involvement; do NOT chase BP, work up stroke
  • Widened pulse pressure or new aortic diastolic murmur — aortic dissection concern; check BP in both arms; follow aortic dissection protocol
  • Nicardipine drip escalating past 15 mg/h without achieving goal — refractory HTN suggests secondary cause or inadequate agent choice; consider labetalol, second agent, or ICU consult
  • Acute drop in BP (>20 mm Hg drop in <30 min) — overshoot from IV agent; reduce/hold drip; monitor for renal hypoperfusion and stroke risk (especially if chronic HTN baseline)
  • Reflex tachycardia developing during hydralazine use (HR rising past 110) — dangerous in dissection, myectomy, or ischemic patient; switch to labetalol or esmolol immediately
  • Oozing at suture line or incision despite elevated BP — suggests coagulopathy or surgical bleeding, not simple HTN; notify CT surgery; consider labs (PT/INR, CBC, fibrinogen)
  • Patient becoming more anxious, distractible, or confused — early sign of cerebral hypoperfusion or encephalopathy; do NOT over-treat BP; check mental status baseline

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Pain is the #1 cause of post-op HTN in first 24 hours, NOT primary hypertension. Treat the pain, the BP follows. Do NOT escalate to IV drugs if pain score is ≥6; analgesia is the cure, not nicardipine.

  2. Bladder distention is the #2 reversible cause and is shockingly overlooked. Ask: Is Foley patent? Last void volume? A scan >300 mL often drops BP 30–40 mm Hg when catheterized. Often solves the problem in 5 minutes.

  3. Missed home antihypertensive is the most common preventable cause of POD 1–3 HTN spike. Check the MAR immediately. If patient was on metoprolol, lisinopril, or HCTZ at home, these should be restarted POD 0–1 unless contraindicated. Verify with APP.

  4. ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and thiazide diuretics held intra-op → rebound HTN when forgotten. These are not restarted reflexively post-op; escalate to APP if held >24 h post-op.

  5. Clonidine rebound HTN occurs 12–48 hours after abrupt discontinuation. If patient was on clonidine at home and it was held pre-op, anticipate rebound spike POD 1–2; restart proactively.

  6. Never give sublingual (SL) nifedipine. It causes precipitous, unpredictable drops in BP; no longer recommended. Use IV nicardipine or labetalol instead for fast effect.

  7. Check for pseudo-hypertension (cuff too small). Standard cuff bladder is 12 cm wide. Obese patients may need large adult cuff (15 cm); using a small cuff overestimates BP by 20–30 mm Hg. Recheck with correct cuff size.

  8. Shivering post-op increases SVR acutely and spikes BP. Warming blanket, check core temp. Often forgotten because provider is focused on "low BP" earlier in the shift; post-op metabolic state causes shivering despite normothermia.

  9. Do NOT aggressively lower BP in chronic hypertensive patients. Their autoregulation is shifted rightward; dropping 25% in <1 hour causes watershed stroke and graft steal. Use the 25% rule.

  10. Aortic / root / dissection patients have DIFFERENT targets from routine CABG. Do NOT autopilot the ≤140 default. Know the procedure and the target (≤120 for aortic, dissection, Bentall). Communicate target with provider and team at signout.

  11. Nitroprusside is ICU-level, NOT stepdown. Cyanide toxicity with prolonged use, requires continuous A-line, unpredictable half-life. Wrong choice for floor sustained control. Say no; use nicardipine.

  12. Rebound HTN 12–48 hours after IV drug abrupt stop. Especially labetalol and nicardipine. Always transition to PO 4–6 hours before weaning IV. Verify both on order before starting wean. If rebound spike occurs, restart IV while PO is absorbing.

  13. Propofol weaning = HTN spike anticipated. As sedation lightens POD 1–2, sympathetic tone increases. Pre-plan: optimize analgesia, have IV antihypertensive ready, slow wean over hours not minutes.

  14. Beta-blocker reinitiation prevents POAF and mortality. POD 0–1, if hemodynamically stable, restart home beta-blocker dose. This is a high-yield prevention strategy; missed restart is a common teaching point for new grads.

  15. Pheochromocytoma crisis is rare but exists in post-op setting. Look for episodes of severe HTN (>200) with flushing, profuse sweating, headache, palpitations, and chest/abdominal pain. Suspect if resistant HTN pattern + episodic surges. Notify team; do NOT give labetalol or nicardipine alone (alpha-blockade FIRST per pheo protocol).

cards.title: Hypoglycemia (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: Glucose <70 mg/dL → Level 1 alert. <54 mg/dL with symptoms → Level 2 clinically important. Altered mental status, seizure, or unconscious → Level 3 emergent. If awake and swallowing: 15–20 g oral glucose (4 oz juice, 4 glucose tabs, 1 tbsp honey), recheck 15 min, repeat if still <70. If unable to swallow or unconscious: D50 (25 g IV push) OR glucagon 1 mg IM. Recheck q15min until >100 and asymptomatic. Always identify the cause — insulin drip over-titration, sulfonylurea, β-blocker masking, AKI (insulin clearance), sepsis. Hold insulin; reduce home regimen by 20% if recurrent unpredictable lows.
