If unable to swallow or unconscious: D50 (25 g IV push) OR glucagon 1 mg IM. Recheck q15min until >100 and asymptomatic. Always identify the cause — insulin drip over-titration, sulfonylurea, β-blocker masking, AKI (insulin clearance), sepsis. Hold insulin; reduce home regimen by 20% if recurrent unpredictable lows.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → American Diabetes Association (2023) → Society of Thoracic Surgeons (2023) → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Endocrine Society (2012)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, who this applies to, why it matters.

  • Definition: Glucose <70 mg/dL in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient (post-op day 0 → discharge). Classified by ADA (2023) as Level 1 (54–70, mild symptoms), Level 2 (<54, clinically important), or Level 3 (altered mental status, seizure, unconscious, severe).
  • Incidence: 5–15% of cardiac surgery patients; higher in elderly (>70), those with pre-operative diabetes, prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass, and acute kidney injury.
  • Peak timing: most common POD 1–3 as stress hyperglycemia resolves and insulin sensitivity normalizes post-CPB; can occur any POD if insulin drip is running or medications change.
  • Who this applies to: all post-operative cardiac surgery patients on insulin (drip, scheduled, or home); highest risk in ICU-level care through first 48–72 hours, but risk persists through discharge.
  • Why it matters: post-operative hypoglycemia worsens cardiac outcomes — increased mortality, arrhythmia risk, myocardial ischemia, longer LOS. Elderly and those with prior diabetes often have hypoglycemia unawareness (no warning symptoms until glucose critically low); nocturnal lows go undetected, causing recurrent cumulative damage.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative hypoglycemia arises from an imbalance between glucose delivery (oral intake, dextrose infusions) and glucose disposal (insulin action, increased metabolism from stress/pain/sepsis).

Multifactorial causes (insulin-related ~70%, non-insulin ~30%):

Insulin-related:

  • Insulin drip over-titration — overzealous dosing to treat post-op hyperglycemia; rebound hypoglycemia in 4–8 hours
  • Drip running + PO intake resuming — patient eating full meals while insulin drip still infusing at high rate
  • Transition errors — insulin drip not reduced before switching to scheduled insulin; overlap of long-acting insulin + drip causes stacking

Non-insulin medication:

  • Sulfonylurea toxicity — glipizide, glyburide continue working post-op; glyburide has longer duration (~24 h) and higher recurrence risk (12–72 h lows); consider octreotide 50 mcg SC q6h for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia
  • Beta-blocker masking — mask tachycardia and diaphoresis (early hypoglycemia warning signs); patient may be profoundly hypoglycemic but feel "normal"
  • Corticosteroid weaning — rapid taper post-op can unmask underlying gluconeogenesis deficit; in patients on perioperative dexamethasone, check morning cortisol if refractory lows

Physiologic non-insulin causes:

  • Reduced oral intake — nil-by-mouth status, dysphagia, nausea/vomiting, diarrhea
  • Increased insulin sensitivity post-op — resolution of stress hyperglycemia by POD 1–3; CPB causes inflammatory cascade increasing insulin sensitivity for 48–72 h
  • Acute kidney injury (AKI) — worsening Cr or eGFR → insulin accumulation → prolonged hypoglycemic effect (elderly at highest risk); elderly post-op often develop AKI from volume depletion or contrast-induced injury
  • Hepatic dysfunction — impaired gluconeogenesis; rare but possible after cardiac surgery with ischemic injury
  • Sepsis — early phase may cause hypoglycemia (altered metabolism, increased insulin sensitivity); later phases cause hyperglycemia; check for fever, WBC, lactate
  • Adrenal insufficiency — rare but consider if refractory hypoglycemia + hypotension + hyponatremia in patient on perioperative steroids; cortisol <18 during stress is diagnostic
  • Critical illness — hypoxia, severe heart failure, cardiogenic shock reduce hepatic glucose output
  • Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) learning curve — if patient transitioned to home CGM, inadequate finger-stick verification can cause false-low alarms

Why post-operative cardiac surgery is especially vulnerable:

  • Cardiopulmonary bypass induces inflammatory cascade and increases insulin sensitivity for 48–72 hours
  • Initial hyperglycemia from pain and catecholamine surge followed by rapid sensitivity normalization as pain is controlled
  • Elderly patients (>70) have impaired gluconeogenesis and reduced hypoglycemia awareness; ~50% of those with >20 years diabetes develop impaired awareness of hypoglycemia
  • Beta-blockers (ubiquitous in cardiac population) mask early warning signs
  • Renal function commonly worsens post-operatively (volume depletion, CPB, contrast-induced), increasing insulin accumulation risk
  • Nocturnal hypoglycemia in inpatient setting goes undetected when bedside checks are q4h or less frequent; 02:00–06:00 window is particularly high-risk

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following:

  • Bedside point-of-care glucose (POC) <70 mg/dL — most common trigger; always verify with lab sample if POC shows <54
  • Lab glucose <70 mg/dL from standing orders (typically q4–6h or q1h if on insulin drip)
  • Patient symptoms while POC not yet drawn: shakiness, diaphoresis, palpitations, anxiety, confusion, slurred speech, difficulty concentrating, extreme fatigue, visual changes, headache
  • Altered mental status or personality change in an already confused or sedated patient (compare to baseline)
  • Seizure activity, loss of consciousness, or inability to protect airway — Level 3 emergent
  • Continuous insulin infusion with downward glucose trend — even if not yet <70, anticipate rebound
  • Transition from ICU to stepdown: glucose may rebound or plummet as dextrose-containing fluids are weaned and insulin drip is being discontinued

Epidemiology: Nocturnal hypoglycemia is markedly under-detected — many episodes occur 02:00–06:00 when bedside checks are q4h or longer. Staff report lack of awareness until patient becomes symptomatic (altered MS, seizure).

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information gathering. No actions yet. Competent systematic bedside exam.

  • Level of consciousness & ability to swallow: awake and alert? able to follow commands? protect airway? any drooling, aspiration risk?
  • Vital signs & perfusion: HR, BP, SpO₂, capillary refill, skin temperature/color. Signs of shock?
  • Symptoms (if awake & communicative): shakiness, sweating, palpitations, anxiety, weakness, confusion, visual changes, headache?
  • Glucose value & trend: POC <70 or <54? Lab glucose? Is glucose dropping rapidly (85 → 75 → 65 over 30 min)?
  • Current medications on MAR: insulin drip running (rate, start time)? last bolus insulin dose (time, amount)? when was last meal/tube feed? any recent insulin adjustment?
  • IV access & lines: peripheral IV patent? central line? PICC? saline lock or active fluids running?
  • Recent labs: Cr, BUN, eGFR (renal function — insulin accumulation risk in AKI). Recent Hgb (anemia can worsen symptoms). Cortisol if on steroids or hypotensive.
  • Recent events: sepsis workup started? fever? reduced PO intake? vomiting? diarrhea? recent medication change (corticosteroids, beta-blockers, sulfonylurea)?
  • Post-op context: POD? what surgery? pre-operative diabetes history? home insulin regimen?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, able to swallow safely, oriented, no aspiration risk.)

  1. Treat immediately with 15–20 g oral glucose:
Form Amount Notes
Fruit juice (orange, apple, grape) 4 fluid oz Fast-absorbing; standard first-line
Glucose tablets (4 g each) 4 tablets Portable; standard in home glucose kits
Honey 1 tablespoon ~15 g carb; use if available at bedside
Dextrose paste 15 g tube Squeeze into mouth; if available
Crackers + nut butter Small snack Only if faster options unavailable; slower absorption
  1. Document time of treatment, glucose value, and form of glucose given
  2. Recheck POC glucose at exactly 15 minutes — this is mandatory; do NOT skip
  3. If glucose still <70 at 15 min: repeat 15–20 g oral glucose once more; recheck at 30 min
  4. Once glucose >100 mg/dL AND patient asymptomatic: offer a small meal or snack (6–15 g carb + protein: cheese, peanut butter, yogurt, crackers) to prevent rebound hypoglycemia within 1 hour
  5. Notify APP/provider of the event with SBAR (see Section 6) — cause must be identified even if corrected easily
  6. Continue bedside glucose checks: q1h if on insulin drip; q2–4h if on scheduled insulin; q4h minimum overnight if at home on insulin
  7. Hold insulin dose until provider reviews (reduce next dose by 10–20% if correctable cause, or continue as written if one-time event)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Unconscious, unable to swallow, altered mental status, seizure, or loss of consciousness.)

  1. STAT call for help — do NOT leave patient alone; activate Rapid Response if altered MS or seizing
  2. Position patient on side (aspiration precaution); ensure airway patent
  3. Establish or verify IV access immediately:
    • If IV available (peripheral, central, or PICC): Push D50 (dextrose 50%, 25 g in 50 mL vial) IV push over 1–2 minutes into running line (use largest bore available to minimize phlebitis risk; flush with normal saline before and after)
    • If no IV available or IV placement delayed: Give glucagon 1 mg IM into deltoid or anterolateral thigh (requires reconstitution with 1 mL sterile water from kit); may repeat q15min × 2 more (max 3 mg / 30 min) if no response
    • If PICC or central line available: OK to use (confirm patency & no incompatibilities with concurrent infusions)
    • Draw STAT labs: glucose + Chem-7, CBC, lactate, VBG/ABG if altered MS — verify POC reading with lab result
    • Recheck POC glucose q15 minutes until >100 mg/dL and patient alert/responsive
    • If patient remains unresponsive or seizing after one dose:
    • Repeat D50 (if IV): 25 g q15min (max 75–100 g in first 30 min per ICU protocols) OR
    • Repeat glucagon 1 mg IM once more (total 2 mg over 30 min typical max dose)
    • Notify provider immediately — may need ICU transfer, endocrine consult, investigation for underlying seizure disorder
    • Once glucose >100 and alert: transition to oral carb + protein (small snack) to prevent rebound
    • Set bedside orders: D50 ampule at bedside; q1h fingersticks × 24–48h minimum (or per protocol if ongoing insulin drip)

sections.heading: 5C. Insulin drip running — low glucose path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Most common scenario on stepdown for post-op hyperglycemia management.)

  1. IMMEDIATELY STOP the insulin infusion — disconnect pump or turn rate to 0
  2. Treat glucose <70 with D50 25 g IV push (see 5B steps 3–5)
  3. DO NOT restart insulin drip immediately — wait for glucose rebound (target >150) and provider review of insulin titration
  4. Recheck glucose q15min — dextrose infusion (D5W or higher) may already be running; verify rate
  5. Review recent insulin rate & glucose trend:
    • Was the drip rate increased too aggressively in prior shift?
    • Was patient eating (resuming PO intake) while drip still running at high rate? (double insulin source)
    • Has renal function worsened (Cr, eGFR) since drip was started?
    • Notify provider STAT with glucose value, recent drip rate, and rebound trend — restart drip at lower rate (usually 0.5–1 U/hr less) or switch to monitoring + scheduled insulin
    • Once provider restarts insulin drip (if appropriate): resume q1h fingersticks with glucose goal 140–180 mg/dL post-op (evidence-based target to avoid tight control that causes hypoglycemia-related mortality)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for hypoglycemia event:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit/ICU], calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient's glucose dropped to [value] mg/dL at [time]. [Symptoms: shakiness, confusion, etc. / or asymptomatic]. Currently [awake and alert / unconscious / altered]. Treated with [15-20 g oral glucose / D50 IV / glucagon IM] at [time]." A: "Glucose now [value] at [time]. Patient is [responsive / still altered / seizing]. Recent insulin dose: [X units] at [time]. Is on [insulin drip at Y U/hr / scheduled insulin TID / home insulin on hold]. Renal function: Cr [value]. [Relevant meds: beta-blocker, sulfonylurea, steroid, etc.]" R: "Requesting [assessment for cause / insulin rate change / endocrine consult / ICU-level monitoring / tighter glucose checks]. Is patient safe for floor monitoring or needs ICU transfer?"

Who to call (escalation algorithm)

Scenario Contact Urgency
Glucose <70, awake, alert, corrected easily with 15-20g PO Primary APP / on-call provider Same shift
Glucose <54 even if asymptomatic APP / fellow STAT
Glucose <70, unconscious, altered MS at presentation Rapid Response + APP + charge RN STAT emergent
Seizure or loss of consciousness from hypoglycemia Code team + ICU bed notification EMERGENT
Recurrent hypoglycemia (≥2 episodes in 24h) APP + consider endocrine consult STAT
Hypoglycemia + sepsis concern (fever, lactate up) APP + infectious disease STAT
Hypoglycemia on insulin drip (ongoing) APP (likely ICU transfer) STAT
Sulfonylurea-induced hypo not responding to D50 APP + consider glucagon 1 mg SC q2h + octreotide 50 mcg SC q6h STAT
Suspected adrenal insufficiency (refractory + hypotensive) APP + endocrine; consider hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h STAT

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections — collapsed by default.

7.1 Rule of 15 — evidence-based oral glucose strategy The Rule of 15 (or 15-20 rule) is the evidence-based, bedside approach to conscious, swallowing hypoglycemia management:
  1. Treat: Give 15–20 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (oral only if swallowing safe)
  2. Wait 15 minutes: Let glucose rise; do NOT re-treat immediately
  3. Check: Recheck POC glucose at exactly 15 min
  4. Repeat if needed: If still <70, give another 15–20 g and wait another 15 min
  5. Once >100: Offer a small snack with protein/fat (6–15 g carb + cheese, nut butter, etc.) to prevent rebound Why 15–20 g? Studies show this amount raises glucose by ~40–50 mg/dL in most adults over 15 min, without overshooting into hyperglycemia (which worsens post-op outcomes). Common mistakes to avoid:
    • Giving 20+ g (results in overshoot, hyperglycemia for hours)
    • Repeating every 5 min instead of waiting 15 min (delays rise, causes "stacking")
    • Using complex carbs (crackers, bread) which take 30+ min to absorb — not helpful in acute lows
    • Skipping the follow-up snack and rechecks, leading to rebound hypoglycemia within 1 hour
    • Juice alone without protein/fat (15 g PO juice + crackers is better than juice alone; combination sugar + complex carb prevents rapid rebound)
7.2 Medication specifics — D50, glucagon, insulin reduction D50 (Dextrose 50%) — IV push for unconscious or unable to swallow
PropertyDetail
Concentration50% dextrose in water
Standard vial size50 mL ampule = 25 g dextrose
Dose25 g (50 mL) = 1 full ampule IV push over 1–2 minutes (NOT diluted)
RouteIV only (peripheral, central, or PICC) — never IM or subcu
OnsetRapid: glucose rises within 2–3 minutes
CautionVery hypertonic (irritates veins); flush before/after with NS; use largest-bore IV if possible (minimize phlebitis risk)
Repeat dosingIf glucose remains <70 at 15 min, may repeat once more (total 50 g / 100 mL); further doses require provider order
Glucagon 1 mg IM — if no IV access or IV placement delayed
PropertyDetail
Concentration1 mg vial (requires reconstitution with 1 mL sterile water from kit)
Dose1 mg IM into deltoid or anterolateral thigh
OnsetSlower than D50: glucose rises over 5–15 minutes; peak effect 20–30 min
DurationShort (~1–2 hours); may require repeat or transition to IV dextrose
MechanismWorks via glycogenolysis (breaking down hepatic glycogen); does NOT work if liver severely compromised — avoid if starving (depleted glycogen), end-stage cirrhosis, or alcoholic hepatopathy
Repeat dosingMay repeat 1 mg IM q15min × 2 more (max 3 mg / 30 min) if glucose not rising
Home usePrescribe glucagon kit (Baqsimi nasal spray, or traditional IM emergency kit) at discharge for all insulin-dependent patients; teach family how to use
Teaching pearlsGlucagon for home hypoglycemia only if hepatic glycogen intact — alcohol use, sepsis, prolonged fasting deplete stores. For these patients, family member should call 911 instead.
Insulin reduction strategies after hypoglycemia
ScenarioAction
On insulin dripReduce rate by 0.5–1 U/hr; consider transition to scheduled insulin instead
On scheduled insulin (TID/QID)Reduce total daily dose by 10–20% for next dose; reassess after 1–2 days
At home on long-acting insulin (e.g., Lantus)Reduce by 10–20% (e.g., from 20 U Lantus to 16 U); recheck fasting glucose × 3 days; communicate plan at discharge
Always reassess after episode: Is cause correctable (missed meal, reduced PO)? Is renal function worsening? Can insulin timing, dose, or formulation be changed to prevent recurrence?
7.3 Insulin drip protocols — rationale & transition Post-operative insulin drip target: most protocols use glucose goal 140–180 mg/dL in the immediate post-op period (first 48–72h). Tighter control (target <110) has been abandoned in cardiac surgery because aggressive insulin-induced hypoglycemia caused increased MI, mortality, and longer LOS (evidence from major RCTs, 2009 onwards). Drip titration rules of thumb:
  • Start at 0.5–1 U/hr based on pre-op insulin requirement
  • Increase by 0.5–1 U/hr q1h if glucose rising; decrease if falling
  • When glucose reaches 180, reduce rate by 0.5–1 U/hr and reassess q1h
  • Do NOT allow drip to run without q1h bedside glucose checks (or q30min if rapidly changing glucose) Transition from drip to scheduled insulin:
  • Do NOT switch abruptly — run drip at 0.5 U/hr while giving first dose of scheduled insulin (e.g., NPH or Lantus)
  • Wean drip over 1–2 hours as scheduled insulin begins to work
  • Abrupt cessation of drip → hyperglycemia rebound in 2–4h
  • Typical scheduled regimen post-op: basal (e.g., NPH or Lantus) + meal-time rapidacting (e.g., Humalog), or TID fixed-dose if NPO When to suspect drip over-titration causing hypo:
  • Glucose trend: 180 → 140 → 100 → 60 in <4 hours
  • Patient eating PO while drip still running (double insulin source)
  • Recent drip rate increase without corresponding glucose decrease yet (lag effect, then sudden drop)
  • Renal function worsening (Cr rising, eGFR falling) — insulin accumulation risk increases
7.4 Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia — special management Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glyburide, chlorpropamide) — long duration of action post-op
DrugHalf-lifeDurationPost-Op RiskManagement
Glipizide2–4 h10–16 hLower risk; lows typically resolve in 4–6 hD50 IV or 15-20g PO; standard monitoring
Glyburide10–12 h24 hHigher risk; lows can last 12–72 h; recurrence commonD50 IV; octreotide 50 mcg SC q6h to suppress further insulin secretion; frequent glucose checks
Chlorpropamide30–40 h24–72 hHighest risk; very prolonged effectD50 IV; octreotide 50 mcg SC q6h + q1h glucose checks; prolonged observation
Why sulfonylureas are risky post-op:
  • Mechanism: stimulate beta cells to release insulin directly; effect NOT glucose-dependent, so insulin keeps flowing even as glucose drops
  • Post-op stress, pain, inflammation activate beta cells further
  • Patient may not eat as planned (NPO, nausea, dysphagia) but insulin is still being secreted
  • Elderly on glyburide have multiple episodes over 24–72h if not held Management for recurrent sulfonylurea-induced hypo:
    1. Hold the sulfonylurea immediately — do NOT give next dose
    2. D50 25 g IV push for the acute hypo
    3. Octreotide 50 mcg SC q6h (somatostatin analog; suppresses beta cell insulin secretion)
    4. Q1h fingersticks × 24–72h until glucose stable and sulfonylurea wears off
    5. Notify APP — may need to switch to basal-bolus insulin or hold sulfonylurea for entire post-op period
7.5 Beta-blocker masking — pitfall for cardiac patients The problem: Beta-blockers prevent the autonomic nervous system response to hypoglycemia.
Normal hypoglycemia response (unblocked)Beta-blocked response
Tachycardia (HR > 100)No tachycardia (HR stable at 60–80 despite glucose 35)
Diaphoresis, flushingNo sweating
Tremor, anxietyCalm, unaware
Patient feels the low and alerts staffPatient may have NO warning until seizure or collapse
Why this matters post-op:
  • Cardiac patients are almost always on beta-blockers (atenolol, metoprolol, carvedilol)
  • A 78-year-old with 20 years of diabetes on glyburide + beta-blocker may drop from glucose 80 to 35 with zero awareness
  • Elderly often have impaired hypoglycemia awareness already (chronic diabetes causes this); beta-blocker makes it worse
  • Nocturnal hypoglycemia (02:00–06:00) goes completely undetected Detection strategy for beta-blocked patients:
  • Do NOT rely on patient reporting symptoms ("I feel shaky" → check glucose)
  • Check glucose on schedule, not by symptoms
  • Increase bedside check frequency: q1h × first 48h if on insulin, q2–4h if on scheduled insulin, q4h overnight at minimum if at home on insulin
  • Look for subtle signs: altered mental status, confusion, personality change, unusual irritability, difficulty concentrating
  • Use continuous glucose monitor (CGM) if available — low glucose alert catches nocturnal episodes
7.6 Post-operative glucose targets — evidence-based ranges Current guideline targets (ADA 2023, STS 2023):
SettingTarget GlucoseRationale
ICU post-op (first 48–72h)140–180 mg/dLAllows glucose some room above critical threshold; tight control abandoned due to hypoglycemia-related mortality
Stepdown / telemetry (POD 3–5)140–180 mg/dL until stable, then 100–140 if patient stable and tolerating PO
Floor / pre-discharge (POD 5+) | 100–180 mg/dL | More relaxed as patient mobilizing, eating regular diet, closer to baseline | | Home on insulin | Allow 80–200 mg/dL to reduce nocturnal hypo risk; use CGM if available | Why NOT tight glucose control in post-op cardiac:
  • 2009 Kosiborod study (JAMA): spontaneous hypoglycemia and iatrogenic hypoglycemia (from tight glucose control) both associated with increased mortality in post-MI patients
  • Hypoglycemia causes catecholamine surge, arrhythmia, myocardial ischemia
  • Risk exceeds benefit of preventing hyperglycemia in first 48–72h post-op
  • Once patient is eating, stable, and non-insulin-dependent, tighter targets OK Adrenal insufficiency workup (if glucose persistently low despite stopping insulin):
  • Check morning cortisol <18 during physiologic stress (sepsis, hypotension, critical illness) → diagnostic of adrenal insufficiency
  • Consider in patients on perioperative dexamethasone (suppresses endogenous cortisol)
  • If suspected: hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h while workup proceeds; notify endocrine
7.7 Acute kidney injury (AKI) — insulin accumulation risk The mechanism: Insulin is cleared renally. If GFR drops (AKI), insulin levels accumulate, causing prolonged and severe hypoglycemia. Post-op AKI is common:
  • Volume depletion from diuresis
  • Contrast-induced nephropathy (if cardiac catheterization pre-op)
  • Cardiorenal syndrome (low cardiac output reduces renal perfusion)
  • Elderly (>70) at highest risk Detection:
  • Cr rising (e.g., 1.0 → 1.5 → 2.0 over 24–48h)
  • eGFR falling
  • Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h (oliguria) Management:
  • Reduce insulin dose by 30–50% if Cr >1.5 and trending up
  • Recheck glucose q1h (more frequent than usual)
  • Risk: hypoglycemia may be profound and rebound more slowly than in patients with normal kidney function
  • Alert provider: AKI + insulin = high recurrence risk
7.8 Glucagon at home — prescription & family teaching Why prescribe at discharge:
  • All insulin-dependent post-op patients going home need emergency glucagon access
  • Family member (spouse, adult child) should know how to use it
  • Home hypoglycemia can progress to seizure/unconsciousness before EMS arrives Glucagon formulations:
  • Baqsimi nasal powder: 3 mg, dry powder, inhaled into nostril (no reconstitution, easier for untrained users)
  • Traditional IM kit: 1 mg vial + syringe + reconstitution vial of sterile water (requires assembly; works if hepatic glycogen present) Home use criteria:
  • Effective ONLY if patient has hepatic glycogen stores intact
  • NOT effective in: severe liver disease, alcoholic hepatopathy, starvation, end-stage sepsis
  • Ideal for: incident hypoglycemia in otherwise-healthy post-op patient at home Family teaching checklist at discharge:
  • When to use: patient unconscious, unable to swallow, or seizing
  • How to use (demo on dummy vial or video walkthrough)
  • What to expect: patient may vomit after glucagon; position on side
  • Call 911 immediately after giving glucagon — patient needs hospital evaluation even if glucose rises
  • Always pair with follow-up glucose check and food once patient is alert (prevent rebound hypo)
  • Prescribe: explicit written order + patient/family education form + phone number for nurse hotline

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any appear, re-escalate.

  • Recurrent hypoglycemia (≥2 episodes in 24h) → suggests inadequate insulin adjustment or ongoing uncorrected trigger; STAT provider review
  • Glucose remains persistently low (does not rebound to >100 within 15–30 min of oral or IV treatment) → consider liver disease, sepsis, severe renal failure, adrenal insufficiency
  • Altered mental status persisting after glucose correction → may indicate concurrent stroke, encephalitis, sepsis, or other cause; do NOT assume it will resolve with glucose alone
  • Patient cannot articulate symptoms (sedated, intubated, dementia, elderly) → nocturnal hypoglycemia is being missed; increase bedside check frequency to q1h immediately
  • Seizure activity or loss of consciousness from hypoglycemia → Level 3 emergent; ICU transfer indicated; EEG may be needed to rule out ongoing seizure activity
  • Glucose trend showing step-wise decline despite food intake (POC: 85 → 75 → 65 → 55 over 30 min) → insulin is being absorbed or drip is running; insulin action continues
  • Renal function worsening (Cr rising day-by-day, eGFR falling) → insulin accumulation risk increases exponentially; anticipate more frequent/severe lows; reduce insulin 30–50%
  • Patient becomes hypoglycemia unaware (used to feel shakiness at <70, now has no warning at <50) → risk factor for severe, undetected lows; increase check frequency immediately
  • Sepsis workup or fever present → metabolic picture is unstable; glucose can swing high/low rapidly; close monitoring mandatory
  • Nocturnal hypoglycemia cluster (multiple episodes 02:00–06:00) → bedside checks too infrequent; increase to q1–2h overnight
  • Patient reports anxiety, irritability, tremor at normal glucose → may indicate hypoglycemia unawareness or stress response; consider EEG if tremor persistent
  • Sulfonylurea patient with recurrence >3 hours after treatment → lows lasting longer (glyburide effect); start octreotide, extend monitoring window to 72h

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. "15–20 g oral glucose + recheck at exactly 15 minutes" — this is the bedrock rule. Many nurses skip the 15-min recheck or re-treat every 5 min. Glucose takes time to rise; repeating prematurely delays proper treatment and "stacks" glucose.

  2. "D50 is 25 g in 50 mL — give the FULL ampule IV push, not diluted." Do NOT give half-dose or dilute with saline (common error). One ampule = one 1–2 minute push; if repeat needed, new provider order required.

  3. "Glucagon 1 mg IM if no IV available." Many nurses don't know this or forget to reconstitute the kit. Keep a kit at bedside for unstable patients; prescribe at discharge for all insulin-dependent patients; teach family how to use.

  4. "Recheck glucose q15 minutes until >100 AND asymptomatic." Do NOT stop monitoring after one recheck. Glucose can rebound, then drop again. Aim for stable >100 × 2 checks before resuming routine monitoring schedule.

  5. "Hypoglycemia unawareness in elderly + chronic diabetes." This population CANNOT FEEL lows until glucose is critically low (<40). A 78-year-old with 20 years diabetes often has zero warning signs. Assume none can feel hypoglycemia; increase checks to q1h × first 48h post-op, then q2–4h based on risk.

  6. "Nocturnal hypoglycemia is often missed." Bedside checks at 22:00, 06:00 schedule misses 02:00–05:00 lows. If patient is on insulin, do q1h checks overnight minimum for first 48h post-op, or use CGM if available.

  7. "Insulin drip running + low glucose = STOP drip + bolus D50." Do NOT titrate down slowly. Insulin is actively being infused; patient at risk for severe, recurrent lows. Stop it immediately. Treat. Reassess with provider before restart.

  8. "Renal function worsening + continued insulin = accumulation." Elderly post-op patients often develop AKI (Cr 1.2 → 1.8). Insulin dosed for normal clearance now accumulates. Reduce insulin dose by 30–50% if Cr >1.5 and trending up; recheck glucose q1h.

  9. "Transition from insulin drip to subcu insulin needs overlap, not abrupt switch." Run drip at 0.5 U/hr while giving first scheduled insulin dose; wean drip over 1–2 hours. Abrupt cessation → hyperglycemia rebound.

  10. "Beta-blocker can mask hypoglycemia symptoms." No tachycardia, no sweating even at glucose 40. Patient may be profoundly hypoglycemic and feel "normal." Cardiac patients are on beta-blockers; they cannot feel lows. Check glucose frequently per schedule; do NOT rely on patient report of symptoms.

  11. "Beta-blocker masking means look for altered mental status, not tachycardia." Confusion, difficulty concentrating, irritability, personality change in a normally alert patient = hypoglycemia until proven otherwise in someone on beta-blocker.

  12. "Glyburide is higher risk than glipizide post-op." Glyburide has longer duration (~24h); lows can recur 12–72h after first treatment. If glyburide-induced hypo: use octreotide 50 mcg SC q6h to suppress beta cell secretion; extend glucose checks to q1h × 72h.

  13. "Adrenal insufficiency is rare but possible." Post-MI patient on high-dose dexamethasone (ICU), or patient with known adrenal disease. Refractory hypoglycemia + hypotension + hyponatremia → check morning cortisol if not done. Consider hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h if suspected.

  14. "PO juice + crackers (sugar + complex carb) better than juice alone." Pure juice causes rapid glucose spike, then rebound drop within 1–2 hours. Pairing with protein/fat (cheese, nut butter, crackers) provides sustained rise and prevents rebound.

  15. "Post-op glucose target is 140–180, NOT <110." Tight glucose control was abandoned in cardiac surgery because aggressive insulin-induced hypoglycemia caused more MI and death. Avoid the temptation to "normalize" glucose to <110 in first 48–72h post-op. Leave it slightly high.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — who gets this and why it matters.

  • Definition: Serum potassium < 4.0 mEq/L occurring in the post-operative period after cardiac surgery. Normal extracellular K⁺ is 3.5–5.0 mEq/L, but post-op cardiac patients require tighter targets due to heightened arrhythmia susceptibility.
  • Incidence: Occurs in > 50% of post-op cardiac patients POD 1–3, peaking with aggressive diuresis and intracellular shifts. Most common electrolyte derangement on post-op telemetry units.
  • Why it matters: Left untreated, hypokalemia triggers POAF (post-op atrial fibrillation), ventricular ectopy, life-threatening arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac events. Early recognition and replacement are major modifiable risk factors.
  • Who this applies to: Every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient (CABG, valve, combined, MAZE, aortic, transplant, VAD, ECMO decannulation).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-op cardiac patients lose potassium and magnesium rapidly through multiple, often concurrent mechanisms. The operated heart has depressed arrhythmia thresholds — a K⁺ of 3.5 that would be acceptable on a medical ward becomes arrhythmogenic in fresh post-op cardiac patients.

Renal loss (most common):

  • Aggressive diuresis POD 1–3 — loop diuretics block Na-K-Cl co-transporter in the thick ascending limb, forcing K⁺ excretion alongside sodium. High urine output (> 5 mL/kg/h) correlates with high K⁺ loss.
  • Dilutional effect of cardiopulmonary bypass prime — serum K⁺ starts lower on bypass; further dilution with fluids + diuresis worsens hypokalemia.

Intracellular shift (serum K⁺ drops without total body loss):

  • Insulin + glucose: Post-op stress hyperglycemia is treated with insulin; insulin drives K⁺ intracellularly via Na-K-ATPase activation. Serum K⁺ drops acutely, though total body K⁺ may be unchanged.
  • Beta-agonists (epinephrine, dobutamine, albuterol): Activate Na-K-ATPase; same intracellular shift. Replacement transiently raises serum K⁺, but the drip perpetuates the shift — a "chasing" scenario.
  • Alkalosis (respiratory or metabolic): Over-ventilation or diuretic-induced contraction alkalosis shifts K⁺ intracellularly in exchange for H⁺ leaving the cell. Major contributor early post-op.

GI and drainage loss:

  • Nasogastric (NG) tube losses (if NPO or feeding delayed)
  • Mediastinal and pleural drain output (electrolyte-rich, up to 500 mL/day early post-op)
  • Diarrhea (antibiotics, tube feeds, magnesium-containing laxatives)

Refeeding phenomenon: - When feeding begins after extended NPO, K⁺, phosphorus, and Mg²⁺ all shift intracellularly as cells take up glucose and begin anabolism. All three drop within hours of the first substantial meal.

K-wasting drugs:

  • Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide)
  • Thiazide diuretics
  • Beta-agonists (noted above)
  • Corticosteroids (if on board)
  • Aminophylline (rare post-op, but a trigger if present)

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-op cardiac surgery patient:

  • Lab alert: K⁺ ≤ 4.0 on BMP/CMP (typically POD 1–3 routine draws, but can occur any time)
  • Tele findings: U waves (hallmark hypokalemia marker), flattened T waves, ST depression, QTc prolongation, new ectopy (PVCs, atrial premature contractions)
  • Physical symptoms: Muscle weakness, cramping, paresthesias, fatigue disproportionate to expected post-op recovery
  • Clinical context clues: Heavy diuresis output, NG or drain losses, beta-agonist drips on board (epinephrine, dobutamine), insulin infusion running, witnessed diarrhea, over-ventilation (respiratory alkalosis)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Competent systematic bedside exam.

  • Review the lab: K⁺ value, trend (is it falling?), date/time drawn. Compare to prior draw if available (POD 0 vs POD 1).
  • Assess acuity: Symptomatic (weakness, palpitations) vs asymptomatic discovery on routine labs.
  • Tele observation: Rhythm strip — any U waves, flat T waves, QTc length, ectopy? Compare to recent baseline if available.
  • Physical exam: Ask about muscle weakness, cramping, palpitations; assess for gross weakness (can they lift legs against gravity?); check for Chvostek/Trousseau signs to rule out concurrent hypocalcemia.
  • Review MAR for K-wasting drugs:
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide)
  • Thiazide diuretics
  • Beta-agonists (epinephrine, dobutamine, albuterol nebulizers)
  • Insulin infusions
  • Corticosteroids (if on board)
  • Review I/O and context:
  • Urine output trend — is the patient diuresing hard (> 5 mL/kg/h suggests K⁺ loss)?
  • NG losses if NG tube in place
  • Drain output (mediastinal, pleural)
  • Diarrhea or loose stools
  • Assess renal function: Recent creatinine, trend. AKI would change replacement strategy.
  • Check Mg²⁺ immediately — CRITICAL: Review most recent Mg²⁺ level. Hypomagnesemia is nearly always concurrent and blocks K⁺ correction. If Mg²⁺ < 2.0, you cannot fix K⁺ refractory. This is the #1 reason K⁺ replacement "fails."
  • Note acid-base status: Alkalosis (pH > 7.45) drives K⁺ intracellularly and worsens serum hypokalemia; note if over-ventilated or on diuretic loop.
  • Lines and access: Does the patient have central access? Peripheral only? Matters for dose route per protocol.
  • Surgery context: What operation and what post-op day? Recovery trajectory normal or complicated?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Alert, MAP > 65, no active symptoms, no ectopy on tele, normal ECG)

  1. Confirm K⁺ value — order STAT BMP/CMP if suspicious (e.g., new symptoms but old lab, or if draw was > 4 h ago and patient is actively diuresing). One lab is not enough if trend is unclear.

  2. Replace potassium per Protocol: Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement — do not duplicate dosing tables here; reference the protocol card for exact routes, rates, and recheck timing by K⁺ level (3.5–3.9, 3.0–3.4, < 3.0).

    Key rule: PO first if tolerating (cheaper, no IV pump); IV if K⁺ < 3.5 or patient cannot take PO.

  3. Check and correct Mg²⁺ — NON-NEGOTIABLE:

    • If Mg²⁺ < 2.0, replace per protocol (MgSO₄ IV) before or concurrent with K⁺ replacement. Cannot correct K⁺ refractory without Mg²⁺ normalized.
    • If Mg²⁺ already ≥ 2.0, document and proceed.
    • In high arrhythmia-risk populations (POAF-prone, recurrent VT/VF, QTc prolonged, torsades risk), target Mg²⁺ of 2.0–2.5 baseline, pushable to 3.0–3.5. Note: 3.0 mg/dL is not a critical high.

  4. Identify and address the root cause:

    • Heavy diuresis? Review diuretic orders; discuss holding loop diuretic with APP if patient is already euvolemic or trending negative.
    • Beta-agonist drip? K⁺ drops from intracellular shift, not loss. Replacement will transiently raise serum K⁺, but the drip keeps pulling. Plan for frequent rechecks (q1–2h) while on agonist. Discuss weaning plan with provider.
    • Insulin infusion? Same mechanism — intracellular shift. Recheck 1 h after K⁺ given and 1 h after any insulin dose change.
    • Alkalosis? If pH > 7.45, respiratory or metabolic, discuss with APP. Over-ventilation is common; gentle ventilation adjustment may help K⁺ trend. Avoid sodium bicarbonate unless absolutely necessary (worsens alkalosis).
    • NG/drain losses? Consider holding NG if feasible, or discuss with provider. Mediastinal/pleural drains are expected early — not usually held, but volume is documented for context.
    • Diarrhea? Address underlying cause (antibiotics, magnesium-containing laxatives, other). Antidiarrheal per protocol if safe post-op.

  5. Monitor tele and symptoms — if U waves present on baseline strip, watch for clearing as K⁺ normalizes (teaching moment for new nurses). If ectopy present, should abate with K⁺ correction and Mg²⁺ normalization.

  6. Schedule recheck per protocol:

    • IV replacement → recheck 1 h after dose completes
    • PO replacement → recheck 4 h after dose
    • Set a timer or alarm. Replacement without recheck is an incomplete task.

  7. Document thoroughly on the same note line if possible:

    • K⁺ value and time drawn
    • Replacement order (dose, route, time started)
    • Recheck time and result (link to same documentation)
    • Any holds and reasons (AKI, already ≥ 5.0, etc.)
    • Cause identified and plan to address

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(K⁺ < 2.5, OR symptomatic with tele changes, OR new arrhythmia/ectopy/muscle paralysis)

  1. STAT call to APP/fellow + charge RN — do not manage alone; provide SBAR (see §6 below).

  2. Activate Rapid Response if arrhythmia, hypotension, or altered mental status present.

  3. Continuous cardiac tele monitoring — stay at bedside if K⁺ < 2.5 (risk of VT/VF and sudden collapse). Document baseline rhythm strip.

  4. Aggressive IV replacement per APP orders:

    • Central line strongly preferred for doses ≥ 10 mEq/h or for K⁺ < 2.5 (faster infusion, less vein irritation).
    • Max peripheral rate 10 mEq/h — higher rates burn and damage the vein. If peripheral only, dilute well (10 mEq in 100 mL, run over 1 h minimum) and offer warm compress. Document plan to obtain central access if larger doses needed.
    • Never push KCl IV. Always infuse over ≥ 1 hour.
    • Follow APP orders on frequency; typically recheck q1h if K⁺ < 2.5.

  5. Correct Mg²⁺ immediately — if Mg²⁺ < 2.0, give MgSO₄ IV per protocol concurrent with K⁺. Both are needed. In arrhythmia-prone populations, target Mg²⁺ 2.0–2.5 baseline, pushable to 3.0–3.5.

  6. Send STAT labs while replacement running:

    • BMP (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, phosphorus, acid-base status)
    • Troponin (rule out ischemia if new ectopy)
    • Lactate, ABG if concerned about perfusion

  7. Address triggers aggressively:

    • Hold beta-agonist drips if possible (discuss with APP; may need slow wean due to hemodynamic dependence). Agonists drive K⁺ shift and perpetuate hypokalemia despite replacement.
    • Hold loop diuretics pending APP.
    • Assess airway/ventilation — if over-ventilated, gentle rate reduction helps K⁺ trend.
    • Hold any other K-wasting drugs pending team review.

  8. Prepare for ECG — the APP may want a 12-lead to assess QTc, peaked T waves (hyperkalemia), or flat T/U waves (hypokalemia). Save strips before and after major K⁺ boluses.

  9. Reassess q15–30 min while in unstable range — vitals, tele, symptoms, perfusion until K⁺ ≥ 3.0 and stable. Document each reassessment.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient's K⁺ came back [value] at [time], down from [prior value] on [prior date]. Mg²⁺ is [value]. Patient is [alert/altered], [symptomatic/asymptomatic]. On tele: [U waves/flat T waves/QTc long/ectopy/normal]. Currently on [beta-agonist/insulin/diuretic/other K-wasting drugs]." A: "Patient is [stable/unstable/deteriorating]. Recent outputs: [urine, diarrhea, NG losses]. [Symptoms: weakness/cramping/palpitations/none]. Last K⁺ replacement was [time, dose, route]." R: "Requesting replacement orders [K⁺ / Mg²⁺ by protocol], guidance on [holding diuretics/stopping agonist drip/addressing alkalosis], and plan for recheck timing."

Who to call

Situation Contact
K⁺ 3.5–3.9, asymptomatic, first episode Primary APP / on-call fellow
K⁺ 3.0–3.5, asymptomatic APP / fellow — clarify route and recheck plan
K⁺ < 3.0 or symptomatic (weak, cramping, palpitations) APP/fellow + RRT if arrhythmia present
K⁺ < 2.5 or new ectopy / POAF triggered STAT call APP/fellow — may need ICU transfer, telemetry, central line
K⁺ falling despite replacement, no Mg²⁺ correction APP — investigate ongoing losses, renal failure, medication compliance
Refractory after 2 doses (K⁺ not moving) + low Mg²⁺ Consider Mg²⁺ as the block — replace Mg²⁺ aggressively first, then K⁺

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

Magnesium–potassium relationship (why you cannot fix K⁺ without Mg²⁺) Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia are nearly always concurrent in post-op cardiac patients. They're also mutually dependent in a way that trips up providers:
  • Na-K-ATPase pump requires Mg²⁺ as a cofactor. This pump extrudes 3 Na⁺ and takes in 2 K⁺ per cycle, maintaining the K⁺ gradient. Mg²⁺ enables each cycle.
  • If Mg²⁺ is low, the pump cannot work efficiently, and K⁺ replacement cannot be fully retained. Serum K⁺ will rise transiently (from the dose), then fall again because you're not fixing the underlying Mg²⁺ deficit.
  • Refractory hypokalemia (K⁺ keeps dropping despite replacement) is hypomagnesemia until proven otherwise. Check Mg²⁺ first; if < 2.0, replace it before or concurrent with more K⁺.
  • Typical scenario: K⁺ 2.8, Mg²⁺ 1.6. You give 60 mEq KCl IV. K⁺ rises to 3.4 by the recheck. But 4 h later, K⁺ is back to 2.9. The diuretics continued, yes, but mostly you didn't fix the Mg²⁺ deficit. Now replace Mg²⁺ (MgSO₄ 4 g IV), recheck Mg²⁺, and then give K⁺ again. This time it sticks. Clinical pearl: Always order K⁺ and Mg²⁺ together on post-op labs. If one is low, assume the other is too, and plan replacement for both.
K⁺ replacement dose table (cross-reference protocol) Do not duplicate the full dose table here. Reference Protocol: Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement (Section 5.2, Potassium replacement) for the authoritative dosing by K⁺ level:
K⁺ level (mEq/L)Replacement doseRouteRecheck timing
3.5–3.9KCl 40 mEq PO ×1 (or 20 mEq IV × 2)PO preferred if tolerating4 h after PO / 1 h after IV
3.0–3.4KCl 60 mEq (split PO/IV per access)IV preferred if central available1 h after IV
< 3.0KCl 20 mEq IV × 3–4 doses, each over 1 hCentral line preferred; peripheral max 10 mEq/h1 h after each dose
Key pearls:
  • Central line preferred for doses ≥ 10 mEq/h. Peripheral max is 10 mEq/h; dilute in 100 mL normal saline and run over 1 hour.
  • PO KCl is underused. 40 mEq liquid or powder works fine when tolerating; cheaper, no IV pump needed. Tastes terrible — mix with juice.
  • Never give KCl IV push. Fatal arrhythmias. Always infuse.
ECG and telemetry changes (recognition) Hypokalemia causes distinctive tele and ECG changes that are underrecognized by new nurses:
FindingHypokalemia signature
U wavesHallmark of hypokalemia. Low-amplitude positive waves after the T wave, best seen in V2–V3. Not present in all cases but highly suggestive when present. Normal is no U wave or tiny one. Disappears as K⁺ corrects.
Flat or low T wavesT amplitude decreases as K⁺ drops. Compare to baseline.
ST segment depressionMay see subtle ST sagging.
QTc prolongationK⁺ is not classically a QTc driver, but hypokalemia + hypomagnesemia + hypocalcemia = long QTc. Watch for combined electrolyte deficit.
PR prolongationModest PR lengthening can occur.
Ectopy (PVCs, PACs)Due to altered repolarization and irritability. New ectopy in context of low K⁺ is a red flag.
Atrial fibrillation (POAF)Hypokalemia is a major POAF trigger. New A-fib in the context of K⁺ ≤ 3.5 should prompt immediate K⁺ replacement.
Why it matters for the bedside nurse:
  • Do a before-and-after comparison. Many patients have a baseline strip from admission. When K⁺ is corrected, U waves flatten, T waves normalize, and ectopy resolves. This is powerful teaching for nursing students.
  • Ectopy + low K⁺ = escalate. Do not assume the ectopy is benign. POAF and VT risk are real with K⁺ < 3.5 and active symptoms.
Diagnostic workup for refractory hypokalemia If K⁺ does not rise after one or two replacement doses, or keeps falling despite ongoing replacement, think through:
  1. Hypomagnesemia (most common block):
    • Check Mg²⁺; if < 2.0, replace and recheck before giving more K⁺.
    • If Mg²⁺ is normal-ish but on the low side (1.8–2.0), still replace it for good measure.
    • Ongoing losses:
    • Check UOP — is the patient still diuresing heavily? Discuss holding diuretic.
    • Check NG output, diarrhea, drain outputs. Are losses ongoing?
    • If diuresis is necessary (fluid overload, pulmonary edema), loop diuretic + potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone) is preferable, or more frequent K⁺ dosing is accepted.
    • Metabolic alkalosis (driving K⁺ intracellularly):
    • Check pH and HCO₃⁻. If pH > 7.45, K⁺ will stay low until alkalosis is corrected.
    • Avoid extra sodium bicarbonate; consider gentle ventilation changes if over-ventilated.
    • Saline-responsive alkalosis improves with normal saline bolus (not hypotonic fluids).
    • Ongoing beta-agonist or insulin:
    • If on epinephrine or dobutamine, K⁺ will perpetually shift intracellularly. Plan for frequent rechecks (q1–2h) and accept that K⁺ may stay in the 3.5–4.0 range until the drip is weaned.
    • Similarly, high-dose insulin infusions cause persistent shift. Recheck 1 h after any insulin dose change.
    • AKI or medication non-compliance:
    • If creatinine is rising and UOP falling, don't keep pushing K⁺ — risk of hyperkalemia if renal function worsens. Team discussion.
    • If patient not taking PO, verify it's actually being given. Adherence matters.
    • Rare causes (consider if the above are ruled out):
    • Hypokalemic periodic paralysis (genetic, muscle weakness, recurrent episodes) — rare but can present in the post-op setting.
    • RTA (renal tubular acidosis) — urine electrolytes show high urinary K⁺ despite low serum K⁺ and normal acid-base. Rare post-op but important not to miss.
    • Thyrotoxicosis — rare post-op but beta-blockers held for surgery can unmask it; K⁺ shift + high HR. Workup labs if refractory:
    • Urine electrolytes (urine K⁺, Cl⁻, Na⁺) — high urine K⁺ despite low serum K⁺ suggests renal wasting vs GI loss.
    • ABG or VBG — confirm pH, HCO₃⁻, assess acid-base.
    • Renal function (Cr, BUN, UOP trend).
    • TSH if thyrotoxicosis suspected (rare).
Refeeding phenomenon When a malnourished post-op patient begins eating after extended NPO, K⁺, phosphorus, and Mg²⁺ all shift intracellularly within hours as cells take up glucose and begin anabolism. All three drop acutely. - When to anticipate: First substantial meal or initiation of tube feeds after NPO > 72 h. - Pre-feeding labs essential: Check K⁺, Phos, Mg²⁺ before feeding begins. If any are low, give prophylactic doses. - Timing: Drops occur 2–4 h after the first big meal or start of feeds. - Management: Split K⁺ doses over the first 24 h of feeding; recheck q4h × 2, then q8h. Anticipate need for Phos + Mg²⁺ replacement as well.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • K⁺ trending DOWN despite replacement — investigate Mg²⁺ immediately; consider ongoing losses (heavy diuresis, NG, diarrhea, agonist drip perpetuating shift). Do not just dose bigger K⁺; find the block.
  • New or worsening ectopy on tele (PVCs increasing, PACs, runs of bigeminy) — K⁺ deficit is irritating the myocardium. POAF risk. Escalate even if K⁺ is "only" 3.2; consider concurrent Mg²⁺ low.
  • QTc lengthening (especially if combined electrolyte deficit: low K⁺, low Mg²⁺, low Ca²⁺) — torsades risk. Notify APP. ECG comparison helpful.
  • New hypotension or signs of poor perfusion while correcting K⁺ — if on IV Mg²⁺ or aggressive replacement, can temporarily worsen BP (Mg²⁺ is a vasodilator). Slow rate, discuss with APP.
  • Patient on digoxin + hypokalemia — hypokalemia increases digoxin toxicity risk (hypokalemia increases digoxin binding to Na-K-ATPase). Even moderate hypokalemia + digoxin is concerning; replace aggressively.
  • Paralysis or severe weakness — K⁺ < 2.5 with severe muscle weakness suggests imminent cardiac or respiratory muscle failure. STAT escalation, ICU consideration.
  • Signs of hyperkalemia appearing after replacement (peaked T waves, widened QRS) — especially in AKI patient; over-replacement or unmasked renal failure. Check Cr, reconsider replacement strategy.
  • Concurrent low Mg²⁺ and low Ca²⁺ — all three electrolytes low = high arrhythmia risk. Replace all three per protocol; tele monitoring.
  • Patient becoming more anxious, distractible, fatigued — subtle mental status changes can precede cardiac decompensation.
  • Recurrent hypokalemia after successful correction — suggests ongoing trigger (diuretics, agonist, diarrhea, refeeding). Address the cause or plan for more frequent dosing and rechecks.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Always check Mg²⁺ with K⁺. If you're replacing K⁺ without confirming Mg²⁺, you're chasing ghosts. Refractory K⁺ = Mg²⁺ deficit until proven otherwise. It's the #1 reason K⁺ replacement "doesn't work." You can't fix K⁺ if Mg²⁺ is low.

  2. Never give KCl IV push. Fatal arrhythmias reported. Always infuse over time per protocol — even "urgent" doses are 1 h minimum.

  3. Peripheral KCl burns the vein. Warn the patient before starting the infusion. Dilute well (10 mEq in 100 mL, not undiluted), run over 1 h minimum, offer warm compress. If possible, use central access.

  4. Max peripheral KCl rate is 10 mEq/h. Faster burns and is pharmacy-flagged as unsafe. If bigger doses needed, get central access or split into multiple 10 mEq doses over time.

  5. K-phos adds K⁺. A 30-mmol K-phos bolus also delivers ~44 mEq K⁺. If phosphorus is low and K⁺ is already 3.8, you'll overshoot K⁺ if you're not careful. Consider Na-phos as the counter-ion, or account for it in your K⁺ plan.

  6. Beta-agonist drips perpetuate hypokalemia via shift, not loss. Epinephrine, dobutamine, albuterol inhalers all drive K⁺ intracellularly. You can replace and watch K⁺ rise, but 30 min later it's back down because the drip is still on. Plan for frequent rechecks (q1–2h) while on agonist, and discuss weaning with the APP. Chasing K⁺ on a patient on epi drip is futile.

  7. Insulin does the same thing. High-dose insulin infusions shift K⁺ in. Expect K⁺ to drop 0.3–0.5 after an insulin bolus. Recheck 1 h after dose changes.

  8. Alkalosis drives K⁺ down. pH > 7.45 is the enemy. If over-ventilated, gentle ventilation adjustment helps K⁺ trend without extra K⁺ doses. Don't give sodium bicarb unless absolutely needed; it worsens alkalosis.

  9. Diarrhea is K-wasting. Address the cause. If on antibiotics, reassess necessity. If on magnesium-based laxatives (milk of magnesia, MOM), switch to osmotic (lactulose, MiraLAX) or stool softener; MOM also causes hypermagnesemia over 48–72 h if used frequently.

  10. Diuresis + insulin + alkalosis = triple hit. This is the perfect storm for hypokalemia. All three drive K⁺ down. Early post-op, all three are often present. Be aggressive with K⁺ replacement in this scenario.

  11. NG losses matter. If on NG suction, K⁺ exits. If feasible, discontinue NG early. If it must stay, replace K⁺ at higher baseline and recheck frequently.

  12. Refeeding drops K⁺, phosphorus, and Mg²⁺ within hours. If patient was NPO and now eating (or on tube feeds after long NPO), pre-check labs and give prophylactic doses. Many post-op patients become profoundly hypokalemic 4 h after the first big meal.

  13. Peripheral vs central route matters for big doses. Doses ≥ 10 mEq/h require central line. Not optional for safety. If patient has peripheral only and K⁺ < 3.0, call for PICC or central line placement before aggressive IV dosing.

  14. Recheck timing is non-negotiable. IV → 1 h recheck; PO → 4 h recheck. Set a timer. A dose with no recheck is an incomplete task and you won't know if it worked.

  15. PO is underused and underappreciated. If the patient tolerates PO, 40 mEq KCl liquid or packets work fine, taste bad (juice chaser!), cost way less, and don't require IV resources. Assume PO first unless K⁺ < 3.5 or NPO status.

cards.title: Hypomagnesemia
cards.quickAnswer: Mg²⁺ < 2.0 post-cardiac surgery = replace per Protocol: Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement. Mg is an obligate cofactor for Na/K-ATPase — you cannot correct refractory K⁺ without normalized Mg²⁺ first. Tele changes (QTc prolongation, PR lengthening) with low Mg = concerning. Mg²⁺ < 1.4 symptomatic or torsades confirmed = STAT call + aggressive IV MgSO₄ + continuous tele. Give 2 g MgSO₄ IV bolus over 1–2 min if torsades seen, even if lab Mg appears normal. Critical note: Mg 3.0 is NOT a critical high. In arrhythmia-prone populations (POAF history, recurrent VT/VF, QTc prolongation, torsades risk), targets 3.0–3.5 are appropriate and protective.
