sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition and who this applies to.

  • Definition: Serum magnesium (Mg²⁺) < 2.0 mg/dL occurring after cardiac surgery. Magnesium is a critical cofactor for the Na/K-ATPase pump and the cardiac action potential. Depletion occurs through renal losses (diuresis), intracellular shifts (insulin, catecholamines), and GI/surgical drainage losses.
  • Incidence: > 60% of post-cardiac surgery patients develop hypomagnesemia POD 1–3. Frequently missed because (1) Mg is not on routine labs, (2) the standard "normal" lower limit (1.7 mg/dL) is dangerously low for a cardiac patient, and (3) Mg depletion silently blocks K⁺ correction.
  • Who this applies to: Every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient, especially those on diuretics, insulin infusions, or beta-agonist drips.
  • Why it matters: Hypomagnesemia is the #1 cause of refractory hypokalemia and a major trigger for post-operative arrhythmias (POAF, torsades, ectopy). Low Mg also increases arrhythmia threshold in the freshly operated heart.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac surgery patients deplete magnesium rapidly through multiple, often concurrent mechanisms. Understanding this is essential to recognizing and correcting hypomagnesemia.

Renal loss (most common):

  • Aggressive diuresis POD 1–3 — Loop diuretics (furosemide) block Na-K-Cl co-transporter in the thick ascending limb, where Mg is also reabsorbed. High urine output (> 5 mL/kg/h) = high Mg loss.
  • CPB dilution — Cardiopulmonary bypass prime (1–2 liters of non-blood) acutely dilutes serum Mg²⁺. Magnesium deficit can be profound.

Intracellular shift (serum Mg drops, but total-body effect is complex):

  • Insulin + glucose — Post-op stress hyperglycemia treated with insulin drives Mg intracellularly via Na-K-ATPase activation. Serum Mg drops acutely.
  • Beta-agonists (epinephrine, dobutamine) — Same mechanism. Activate Na-K-ATPase, pulling Mg in. Serum Mg drops.
  • Refeeding phenomenon — When feeding begins after NPO, Mg shifts intracellularly as cells take up glucose and anabolism begins. Mg drops within hours of the first large meal.

GI and drainage loss:

  • NG tube losses (if NPO or delayed feeding)
  • Mediastinal and pleural drain output (up to 500 mL/day early post-op)
  • Diarrhea (antibiotics, tube feeds, magnesium-containing laxatives)

Post-op cardiac sensitivity:

  • Mg²⁺ is a critical cofactor for the Na/K-ATPase pump — extrudes 3 Na⁺ and takes in 2 K⁺ per cycle, maintaining the K⁺ gradient for repolarization.
  • Without Mg²⁺, the pump cannot function. K⁺ replacement alone is futile if Mg is deficient.
  • Low Mg prolongs repolarization (QTc lengthening, PR prolongation), setting up torsades, POAF, and ectopy.
  • The operated heart has lower arrhythmia thresholds due to surgical trauma and inflammation. A Mg of 1.7 mg/dL on a medical patient is acceptable; on a fresh post-op cardiac patient, it is a setup for disaster.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following should trigger Mg assessment:

  • Lab alert: Mg²⁺ ≤ 2.0 on BMP/CMP (routine POD 1–3 draws; can occur any post-op phase)
  • Tele findings: QTc prolongation (> 500 ms), PR lengthening (> 0.2 s), peaked T waves (early phase), flattened T waves, ectopy (PVCs, PACs, runs), new POAF unresponsive to K⁺ correction alone
  • Clinical trigger: Refractory hypokalemia — K⁺ keeps dropping despite adequate replacement. Always suspect Mg²⁺ deficit.
  • Physical symptoms: Muscle weakness, tremor, personality change, vertigo, palpitations, paresthesias, tetany (rare)
  • Arrhythmia trigger: Torsades de pointes on tele (even with "normal" Mg on labs — IV Mg 2 g is diagnostic/therapeutic)
  • Context clues: Heavy diuresis, CPB time > 120 min, insulin infusion, beta-agonists, diarrhea, aggressive refeeding, NG drainage

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Review the lab: Mg²⁺ value, trend (is it falling?), date/time drawn. Compare to prior draw if available.
  • Assess acuity: Symptomatic (weakness, palpitations, altered mental status) vs asymptomatic discovery on routine labs.
  • Tele observation: Rhythm strip — QTc length, PR duration, ectopy, torsades? Compare to recent baseline if available. Torsades seen? Prepare for STAT Mg IV regardless of lab level.
  • Physical exam: Ask about muscle weakness, tremor, personality change, lightheadedness, palpitations. Check for Chvostek sign (tap anterior to ear) and Trousseau sign (inflate BP cuff above systolic for 3 min; wrist flexion = positive). Concurrent hypocalcemia may be present.
  • Review MAR for Mg-wasting triggers:
  • Loop and thiazide diuretics
  • Proton pump inhibitors (chronic; note if on board)
  • Diarrhea (antibiotics, osmotic laxatives, magnesium-based laxatives)
  • Beta-agonists (epinephrine, dobutamine, albuterol nebs)
  • Insulin infusions
  • Review I/O and context:
  • Urine output trend (diuresis > 5 mL/kg/h = Mg loss)
  • NG losses if NG tube in place
  • Mediastinal and pleural drain output
  • Diarrhea or loose stools
  • CRITICAL: Check K⁺ level and trend. If K⁺ < 4.0 or falling despite K⁺ replacement, Mg²⁺ is almost certainly low. Refractory K⁺ = Mg²⁺ deficit until proven otherwise.
  • Assess renal function: Recent Cr, trend, eGFR. CKD or AKI changes Mg clearance and replacement strategy.
  • Check Ca²⁺ and Phos: Concurrent electrolyte deficits (low K, low Mg, low Ca, low Phos) create exponential arrhythmia risk. Plan bundle replacement.
  • Lines and access: Central vs peripheral? Matters for infusion rate and IV safety.
  • Surgery context: What operation, what day post-op? CPB time? Dilution is a major Mg driver. Is the patient on inotropes (epinephrine, dobutamine)? Post-MAZE status?
  • Medication notes: Digoxin on board? (Mg is used to treat digoxin toxicity; low Mg increases toxicity risk.)

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Alert, MAP > 65, no active arrhythmia, no acute symptoms)

  1. Confirm Mg²⁺ value — order STAT BMP/CMP if suspicious (e.g., new symptoms but old lab) or if the draw was > 4 h ago and patient is diuresing. One lab is not enough if trend is unclear.

  2. Replace magnesium per Protocol: Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement — reference the protocol card for exact routes, rates, and recheck timing by Mg²⁺ level. Do NOT duplicate dosing tables here.

    Key rule: IV MgSO₄ is the only route post-op; do not give PO Mg (causes diarrhea, defeats the purpose, unsafe post-op).

  3. Check and replace K⁺ concurrent with or AFTER Mg²⁺:

    • If K⁺ < 4.0, do not give K⁺ replacement first. Replace Mg²⁺ first (or concurrently), then K⁺.
    • If K⁺ is refractory (dropped despite adequate replacement), stop escalating K doses. Correct Mg²⁺ aggressively; then retry K⁺ after Mg recheck.
    • Mg²⁺ is the cofactor for the Na/K-ATPase pump. Without it, K⁺ cannot be held intracellularly, and K⁺ doses will be futile.

  4. Identify and address the cause:

    • Heavy diuresis? Review diuretic orders; discuss holding loop diuretic with APP if patient is euvolemic or trending negative. Mag wasting correlates directly with urine output.
    • CPB dilution? If recently off bypass, Mg²⁺ dropped during the pump prime. Expected; replace proactively.
    • Insulin infusion? Insulin drives Mg intracellularly. High-dose insulin = Mg loss. Plan for frequent rechecks (q1–2h).
    • Beta-agonist drip (epinephrine, dobutamine)? Shifts Mg intracellularly, not loss, but serum drops. Recheck frequently while drip is on.
    • NG/drain losses? Mediastinal/pleural drains carry Mg. Mag-based laxatives if used — switch to osmotic or stool softener; they cause rebound Mg loss.
    • Diarrhea? Investigate cause. If antibiotic-related, reassess necessity. If on Mg-based laxatives, stop — they deplete acutely then cause hypermagnesemia over 48–72 h.

  5. Monitor tele and symptoms — QTc should shorten as Mg normalizes. PR should normalize. Ectopy should abate. Watch the trajectory while provider is notified.

  6. Schedule recheck per protocol:

    • IV replacement → recheck per protocol timing (varies by dose: 1–4 h depending on Mg level)
    • Set a timer or alarm on your phone. Replacement without recheck is an incomplete task.

  7. Document thoroughly:

    • Mg²⁺ value and time drawn
    • K⁺ value and concurrent status
    • Replacement order (dose, route, time started, expected completion)
    • Any concurrent K⁺, Ca²⁺, or Phos replacement
    • Recheck time and result on same note line (ideal)
    • Cause identified and plan to address
    • Tele baseline and any changes (QTc, PR, ectopy resolution)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Mg²⁺ < 1.4 symptomatic, OR confirmed torsades on tele, OR new arrhythmia unresponsive to K⁺ alone)

  1. STAT call to APP/fellow + charge RN — do not manage alone; provide SBAR (see Section 6).

  2. Activate Rapid Response if torsades, VT, hypotension, or altered mental status present.

  3. Continuous cardiac tele monitoring — stay at bedside if Mg²⁺ < 1.4 (torsades risk and sudden dysrhythmia). Document baseline strip.

  4. Aggressive IV Mg replacement per APP orders:

    • If torsades confirmed: Give 2 g MgSO₄ IV bolus over 1–2 min (even if lab Mg appears "normal" — intracellular Mg is depleted). This is the only time Mg is given fast. Mg is both diagnostic and therapeutic for torsades.
    • If Mg²⁺ < 1.4 symptomatic: MgSO₄ 4 g IV over 1 h per protocol + continuous tele.
    • Central line preferred for aggressive dosing (faster, safer, less extravasation risk). Peripheral is acceptable if dilute (4 g in 100 mL) and monitored closely.
    • Assess for adequate IV access before starting.

  5. Correct K⁺ AFTER Mg²⁺ replacement:

    • Do not give large K⁺ boluses before Mg²⁺ is normalized. Recheck Mg²⁺ after first Mg dose; if now ≥ 1.7, then give K⁺ replacement if K⁺ is still low.
    • Concurrent K⁺ + Mg²⁺ replacement is acceptable, but Mg first priority if severely low.

  6. Send STAT labs while replacement running:

    • BMP (Mg²⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Phos, acid-base)
    • Troponin (rule out ischemia if new arrhythmia)
    • Lactate, ABG if concerned about perfusion
    • ECG — assess QTc, peaked T waves, widened QRS

  7. Address triggers aggressively:

    • Hold beta-agonist drips if possible (discuss with APP; may need to reduce slowly due to hemodynamic dependence).
    • Hold loop diuretics pending APP.
    • Stop any Mg-wasting drugs.
    • If diarrhea present, address underlying cause; stop Mg-based laxatives immediately.

  8. Prepare for advanced interventions:

    • If torsades confirmed, continuous IV Mg infusion may be initiated (discuss with APP). Standard is 2 g bolus followed by 1–2 g/h drip until stable, then taper.
    • If Mg replacement does not stop torsades and no other cause found, may need overdrive pacing (if pacer wires in place) or other interventions per APP.

  9. Reassess q15–30 min while in unstable range — vitals, tele, symptoms, perfusion until Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 and arrhythmia resolved.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient's Mg²⁺ came back [value] at [time], down from [prior value] on [prior date]. K⁺ is [value]. Patient is [alert/altered], [asymptomatic/symptomatic with weakness/palpitations/arrhythmia]. On tele: [QTc [duration]/PR [duration]/ectopy/torsades or normal rhythm]. Currently on [diuretics / agonist / insulin / other Mg-wasting drugs]." A: "Patient is [stable/unstable/with active arrhythmia]. [Recent urine output, NG losses, diarrhea, drain output]. [K⁺ refractory to replacement? Previous K replacement attempts?]." R: "Requesting Mg²⁺ replacement orders per protocol, guidance on [holding diuretics / stopping agonist / addressing diarrhea], and plan for recheck timing. [If torsades: STAT Mg 2 g IV bolus approval.]"

Who to call

Situation Contact
Mg²⁺ 1.7–1.9, asymptomatic, first episode Primary APP / on-call fellow
Mg²⁺ 1.4–1.6, asymptomatic APP / fellow — clarify route and recheck plan
Mg²⁺ < 1.4 or symptomatic (weak, tremor, palpitations) APP/fellow — may need aggressive IV dosing
Confirmed torsades on tele STAT call APP/fellow — prepare for 2 g Mg bolus + continuous tele
Mg²⁺ < 1.4 + new arrhythmia unresponsive to K⁺ STAT call + consider Rapid Response — Mg is the answer
Mg²⁺ falling despite replacement + ongoing diuresis APP — discuss diuretic hold or increased Mg dosing frequency
Refractory K⁺ after 2 doses, Mg²⁺ still low Escalate to APP immediately — K⁺ correction blocked by low Mg

sections.heading: 7.1 The Mg-K relationship: why K+ correction fails without Mg
sections.bodyHtml:
This is the most critical clinical relationship for nurses to internalize.

The mechanism:

  • Na-K-ATPase pump requires Mg²⁺ as a cofactor for every single cycle.
  • The pump extrudes 3 Na⁺ out and brings 2 K⁺ in, maintaining the K⁺ gradient across the cell membrane.
  • If Mg²⁺ is low, the pump cannot work, and K⁺ cannot be held intracellularly.

The clinical tragedy:

  • K⁺ 2.8, Mg²⁺ 1.6. Nurse gives 60 mEq KCl IV. K⁺ rises to 3.4 by the 1-hour recheck — "success!"
  • But 4 hours later, K⁺ is back to 2.9. Diuretics continued, yes, but the real reason is that the pump still cannot work because Mg²⁺ is still 1.6.
  • Nurse escalates to 80 mEq KCl IV. K⁺ rises to 3.5. Drops back to 2.8 by next recheck.
  • Provider sees "refractory hypokalemia" and considers ICU transfer, thinking the patient has AKI or digoxin toxicity.
  • But the answer is Mg²⁺. Once Mg is normalized (MgSO₄ 4 g IV), the pump works, and K⁺ finally sticks.

Red flag for refractory K⁺:

  • If K⁺ drops despite adequate replacement, or bounces around without stabilizing, check Mg²⁺ immediately. Often it's sitting at 1.6–1.9, "low-normal" on the lab, but dangerously low for a cardiac patient.
  • If Mg²⁺ < 2.0 and K⁺ is refractory, treat Mg first, then retry K. This is the #1 reason K⁺ replacement "fails."

Clinical pearl: Always order K⁺ and Mg²⁺ together. Assume concurrent deficit. Plan replacement for both. One does not correct without the other.

sections.heading: 7.2 Mg depletion mechanisms and differential diagnosis
sections.bodyHtml:
Renal vs GI loss differentiation:

In refractory hypomagnesemia, the first clinical question is: Is the kidney wasting Mg (renal leak), or is there ongoing GI loss?

  • Renal wasting (most common post-op) — indicated by high urine Mg despite low serum Mg. Caused by loop diuretics, post-CPB diuresis, and osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia.

  • Management: reduce diuretic dosing if euvolemic; increase Mg replacement frequency.

  • GI loss — indicated by low urine Mg despite low serum Mg. Caused by diarrhea, NG tube output, malabsorption.

  • Management: address diarrhea cause; stop Mg-based laxatives; increase replacement frequency if GI loss ongoing.

Fractional excretion of magnesium (FE-Mg) can be calculated (urine Mg × serum Cr / serum Mg × urine Cr) if renal leak is suspected:

  • FE-Mg < 2% = kidney is retaining Mg (suggests GI loss or refeeding)
  • FE-Mg > 2% = kidney is wasting Mg (suggests renal Mg leak from diuretics/CPB)

sections.heading: 7.3 Recognition on telemetry and ECG
sections.bodyHtml:
Hypomagnesemia causes distinctive tele and ECG changes that should alert the bedside nurse immediately, especially in combination with low K⁺ and low Ca²⁺:

Finding Hypomagnesemia signature
QTc prolongation Hallmark of low Mg. QTc > 500 ms is a red flag, especially if K⁺ and Ca²⁺ are also low. Torsades risk rises exponentially.
PR prolongation Mg²⁺ deficiency lengthens PR interval. PR > 0.2 s in a post-op patient + low Mg = escalate.
Widened QRS May see subtle QRS widening.
Peaked T waves (early phase) Can see transiently before progressing to flat T waves (compare to baseline).
Ectopy (PVCs, PACs, runs) Altered repolarization and irritability. New ectopy + low Mg + low K = torsades risk.
Torsades de pointes Characteristic and dangerous. Polymorphic VT with twisting appearance. Can degenerate to VF. Even one episode of torsades on a post-op patient = STAT Mg 2 g IV regardless of Mg level (it's diagnostic and therapeutic).
Atrial fibrillation (POAF) Low Mg is a major POAF trigger, especially concurrent with low K. New A-fib + low Mg + low K = triple trigger.

Why it matters for the bedside nurse:

  • Do a before-and-after comparison. Save the baseline rhythm strip. When Mg is corrected, QTc shortens, PR normalizes, ectopy resolves. This is powerful proof of correction.
  • Torsades on a post-op patient = Mg until proven otherwise. Give 2 g Mg IV bolus immediately (diagnostic), even if "recent" lab was not critically low. Serum Mg can be falsely reassuring; intracellular Mg is depleted.
  • Combined electrolyte deficit = exponential arrhythmia risk. Low K + low Mg + low Ca = call for all three replacements concurrently.

sections.heading: 7.4 Mg in special populations
sections.bodyHtml:
Pregnancy and preeclampsia:

  • Magnesium sulfate (MgSO₄) is the standard therapy for preeclampsia and eclampsia seizure prophylaxis.
  • Toxicity occurs at serum Mg 4–6 mg/dL and presents as areflexia, respiratory depression, hypotension, bradycardia, and altered mental status.
  • Post-partum cardiac surgery patients who received magnesium for preeclampsia may have Mg accumulation if renal function is impaired.

Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and acute kidney injury (AKI):

  • CKD stage 3–4: Mg accumulates; be cautious not to overshoot. Still replace if < 2.0, but slower with more frequent rechecks.
  • AKI (rising Cr, oliguria): Mg accumulation risk is high. Reduce replacement frequency or dose. Check Mg more often (q2–4h vs routine q4h).

Neuromuscular disease (myasthenia gravis, Lambert-Eaton): - Magnesium can worsen muscle weakness. Use caution if patient has known MG or LEMS; coordinate with team before aggressive Mg replacement.

Complete heart block without pacemaker: - Magnesium slows AV conduction. If complete AV block present without pacemaker backup, use caution. Coordinate with team.

sections.heading: 7.5 IV administration safety: rate, concentration, and monitoring
sections.bodyHtml:
MgSO₄ infusion rates and concentrations:

  • Peripheral line: Max 2–4 g Mg in 100 mL normal saline, infused over 1–2 hours. Do NOT exceed 10 mEq/h equivalent.
  • Central line: Can tolerate more concentrated solutions; up to 4 g in 50 mL over 1 hour is acceptable for aggressive dosing.
  • Torsades exception: 2 g bolus over 1–2 minutes (rapid, central or peripheral OK if dilute).

Flushing and reassurance:

  • Patients often report warmth, facial flushing, and a sensation of "something is wrong" during MgSO₄ infusion.
  • This is NOT anaphylaxis. It's a normal vasodilatory effect.
  • Slow the infusion rate and reassure: "This is a normal flushing from the medication. It means the Mg is working. We'll slow it down to make it more comfortable."
  • Document that patient is aware and reassured.

Respiratory depression warning:

  • Rapid IV Mg infusion can cause respiratory depression and apnea.
  • Always use IV pump (not gravity infusion) and monitor respiratory rate closely.
  • If RR falls below 12, slow the infusion and notify APP.

sections.heading: 7.6 Mg as first-line for torsades
sections.bodyHtml:
• Torsades de pointes on a post-op patient is a Mg emergency. Even if the most recent Mg level was "normal" (e.g., 1.9 mg/dL), intracellular Mg depletion is the problem.
  • Give 2 g MgSO₄ IV bolus over 1–2 min immediately. This is both diagnostic (if torsades stops, Mg was the cause) and therapeutic (Mg stabilizes the action potential).
  • Do NOT wait for provider order if torsades is happening. Activate RRT, prepare the mag, and inform the APP by phone — the mag bolus is justified emergently.
  • After the bolus, follow with a drip per APP orders (typically 1–2 g/h) until stable.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in stable patients; if any manifest, re-escalate.

  • QTc lengthening (> 500 ms or widening from baseline) — torsades risk. Notify APP. Mg replacement should be made urgent.
  • New or worsening ectopy on tele (PVCs increasing, PACs, runs) — Mg deficit is irritating the myocardium. Escalate even if Mg is "only" 1.8.
  • PR prolongation new or worsening (> 0.2 s) — Mg effect on AV node. May progress to heart block if not corrected.
  • New POAF or POAF unresponsive to K⁺ correction alone — Mg deficit often the hidden cause. Treat Mg first.
  • Mg trending DOWN despite replacement — investigate ongoing diuresis, diarrhea, NG losses, agonist drip. Do not just escalate Mg dose; find the leak.
  • K⁺ refractory to replacement (keeps dropping despite adequate dosing) — STOP escalating K; check Mg immediately. Refractory K = Mg deficit until proven otherwise.
  • Torsades on tele even with "normal" Mg level — intracellular Mg is depleted. STAT Mg 2 g IV regardless of lab. This is diagnostic and therapeutic.
  • Patient becoming more anxious, tremulous, personality change — subtle signs of Mg depletion. Escalate.
  • Muscle weakness or frank paralysis — Mg < 1.4 with neuro symptoms. STAT escalation.
  • Concurrent low K + low Mg + low Ca — exponential arrhythmia risk. Call for bundle replacement.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Refractory K⁺ correction blocks without Mg²⁺ — this is the #1 pitfall. If K⁺ is not rising or keeps dropping despite adequate replacement, check Mg²⁺ first. Do NOT escalate K doses blindly. Most "refractory" cases are low Mg, not physiology failure.

  2. Hypomagnesemia is underdiagnosed because Mg is not in routine BMP and the standard lower limit (1.7) is too low for a cardiac patient. Add Mg to your mental checklist on every post-op patient's labs, especially if diuresing heavily.

  3. Refractory hypokalemia = check Mg immediately. When you call the provider saying "K is still 2.9 despite 60 mEq KCl, what next?", provider will ask "what's the Mg?" If you say "I didn't check," the conversation ends. Always have Mg level before escalating K.

  4. QTc prolongation is an early warning sign of low Mg. Do not wait for arrhythmia. If QTc is lengthening and Mg is not on recent labs, order it STAT. Many cases of torsades are preventable with earlier Mg recognition.

  5. Torsades treatment IS magnesium 2 g IV bolus, even if "normal" level. If you see torsades on tele in a post-op patient, give Mg 2 g IV immediately (over 1–2 min). The serum Mg level can be falsely reassuring; intracellular depletion is the problem. Mg 2 g is diagnostic and therapeutic. Do not wait for a provider order if torsades is happening; activate RRT and give Mg.

  6. PO Mg causes diarrhea — avoid entirely on the unit. Post-op patients cannot tolerate PO Mg. It worsens diarrhea, defeats the purpose, and is unsafe. Use only IV MgSO₄. If patient asks for "milk of magnesia" or Mg supplement PO, educate: "No — we use IV magnesium because PO causes loose stools and we cannot absorb it well. IV is safer and works better."

  7. Mg IV flushing is normal, NOT a reaction. Patients often report warmth, facial flushing, a sensation of "something is wrong" during MgSO₄ infusion. It is not anaphylaxis. Slow the infusion rate and reassure: "This is a normal flushing from the medication. It means the Mg is working. We'll slow it down to make it more comfortable." Document that patient is aware.

  8. Milk of Magnesia (MOM) + CKD = hypermagnesemia concern. If patient has CKD stage 4–5 and MOM is used chronically, serum Mg will rise over 48–72 h and become dangerously high. Avoid MOM entirely in CKD patients post-op. Use osmotic laxatives (lactulose, MiraLAX) or stool softeners.

  9. Alcohol-use patients are Mg-depleted on admission. Chronic alcohol impairs Mg absorption and increases renal losses. Post-op alcohol-use patients may need more-aggressive early Mg dosing and more-frequent rechecks (q2h).

  10. PPI chronic use = hypomag. If patient is on chronic PPI for reflux (especially if long-term pre-op), they are likely Mg-depleted at baseline. Anticipate need for higher initial replacement.

  11. Mg in AKI/CKD requires caution — accumulation risk. Do not hold Mg if < 2.0, but reduce frequency and watch closely. Recheck more often (q2–4h vs q4h). If Cr is rising or UOP falling, discuss with team before dosing.

  12. Central line required for rates > 2 g/h. Standard post-op Mg dosing (2–4 g IV over 1–2 h) can be given via peripheral, but if aggressive dosing (e.g., 4 g over 30 min or continuous drip at high rate) is needed, central line is preferred. Peripheral infusion of high-dose Mg over short time → extravasation and necrosis risk.

  13. Document recheck timing and result on the same line as the dose. "Mg 2.0 [drawn 0800] → MgSO₄ 4 g IV ordered 0815, hung 0830, completed 1030 → Recheck drawn 1030: Mg 2.3" — all on one note line. You can see the story and the response. If recheck is never documented, the dose is incomplete.

  14. Alkalosis worsens Mg depletion (indirectly). Alkalosis drives K and Mg intracellularly. If patient is over-ventilated or on loop diuretics (causing contraction alkalosis), Mg replacement will be less effective until acid-base is addressed. Gentle ventilation changes or saline bolus to correct alkalosis helps Mg trend.

  15. CRITICAL CLINICAL NOTE: Mg 3.0 is NOT a critical high. In arrhythmia-prone populations (POAF history, recurrent VT/VF, QTc prolongation, torsades risk), targets 3.0–3.5 are appropriate and protective. This is a common misread on alert systems. Do NOT reflexively treat a Mg of 3.0 as too high if the patient is arrhythmia-prone. Check with the provider. Critical high with toxicity signs (areflexia, respiratory depression, hypotension) is > 3.5. A Mg of 3.2 in a post-MAZE patient or a recurrent-VT patient is therapeutic, not an error.

cards.title: Hyponatremia (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: Na⁺ <135 mEq/L is hyponatremia; <120 with neuro symptoms (seizures, coma, lethargy) is emergent. Correction rate is the key safety rule: max 8–10 mEq/L per 24 hours — faster correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (permanent brain damage). Assess volume status and order serum + urine osmolality, urine sodium, TSH, and cortisol. SIADH is most common post-CPB. Symptomatic severe → 3% saline 150 mL IV bolus over 10 minutes; asymptomatic mild (130–134) → fluid restrict 800–1000 mL/day, monitor trend, treat cause.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Serum sodium <135 mEq/L (normal 136–145). Acutely symptomatic at <120 with neurologic signs; chronically asymptomatic until severe.
  • Incidence: ~10–15% of post-operative cardiac surgery patients, typically manifesting POD 1–3 when SIADH from CPB inflammation peaks.
  • Who this applies to: adult post-operative cardiac surgery patients in the acute POD 0–4 window; highest yield after CPB-involving procedures (CABG, valve surgery, complex repairs).
  • Why it matters: usually mild and self-limited but can be life-threatening if severe (<125) and symptomatic. Overcorrection is iatrogenic and causes permanent neurologic damage.
  • Epidemiology POD trajectory: most common POD 2–3; majority self-resolve within 3–4 days as inflammatory SIADH wanes. Persistence beyond POD 4 suggests alternative etiology (adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, medication, hypovolemia).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Hyponatremia post-CPB arises from one of two primary mechanisms:

  • Free water excess (euvolemic or hypervolemic) — most common; reflects SIADH or over-hydration with hypotonic fluids
  • Sodium loss (hypovolemic) — less common; reflects diuretic excess, GI losses, or renal wasting

Post-CPB context: hyponatremia is primarily SIADH-driven and reflects the convergence of:

  • CPB-induced inflammation triggers ADH release: surgical trauma, CPB prime composition, cytokine cascade, endothelial activation, pericardial irritation
  • Pain, stress, opioids, positive-pressure ventilation — all potentiate ADH secretion in the immediate post-op period
  • Excess hypotonic fluid administration — naive bolusing with D₅W, 0.45% NaCl, or LR (becomes hypotonic upon dextrose metabolism) in a high-ADH state causes free-water accumulation
  • Poor free-water clearance — kidneys concentrate urine (high osmolality >400) despite low serum osmolality, perpetuating sodium dilution

Severity classification:

Severity Na⁺ level Symptom pattern Acuity implication
Mild 130–134 Asymptomatic or subtle (mild nausea, headache) Low risk; fluid restriction + monitor
Moderate 125–129 Borderline: may have mild headache, confusion, or be asymptomatic Intermediate risk; provider-directed; close monitoring for progression
Severe <125 Symptomatic: lethargy, confusion, tremor, seizures, coma High risk; emergent; requires 3% saline + ICU monitoring

Acuity matters: acute hyponatremia (hours to POD 1) is more symptomatic at a given Na⁺ level than chronic (days of duration) because the brain has not had time to equilibrate osmotically via idiogenic osmoles (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient:

  • Lab trigger: serum sodium <135 mEq/L on routine labs (most common; often asymptomatic)
  • Symptoms: patient reports confusion, nausea, headache, irritability, behavioral change, dizziness
  • Neuro exam findings: altered mental status, headache unresponsive to analgesics, tremor, muscle weakness
  • Severe presentation: seizure activity or loss of consciousness (rare but life-threatening)
  • Trend: routine morning labs show dropping Na⁺ on consecutive days POD 1–4

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure information-gathering; no actions yet.

  • Vital signs and neuro status: BP, HR, mental clarity, orientation, headache, tremor, focal deficits, seizure activity
  • Volume status assessment:
  • Hypovolemic: tachycardia, orthostasis, poor capillary refill, dry mucous membranes, oliguria
  • Euvolemic: normal perfusion, no edema, euhydration on exam
  • Hypervolemic: peripheral or pulmonary edema, elevated JVP, crackles/pulmonary edema, ascites
  • Recent intake & output: net fluid balance over past 24–48 h, diuretic timing and doses (loop, thiazide), IV boluses, oral intake, urine output volume
  • Medication review (MAR): IV fluids hung (hypotonic vs isotonic), diuretics, opioids, SSRI, antiepileptics (carbamazepine), vasopressin or desmopressin, steroids on board
  • Surgical context: procedure type (CABG, valve repair/replacement, complex), CPB time if documented, time from reperfusion to now
  • Recent lab trend: prior Na⁺ if available; K⁺, Cl⁻, serum osmolality, Cr, BUN, glucose, hemoglobin
  • Vital sign pattern: fever or hypothermia (both trigger SIADH)

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Asymptomatic or mild symptoms; Na+ 130–134; oriented, no headache, no neuro signs, adequate perfusion.)

  1. Stat labs if not already drawn: serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium, TSH, AM cortisol (if available), creatinine, glucose
  2. Hold all hypotonic fluids — switch all IV running fluids to isotonic (0.9% NaCl) or dextrose-free; avoid D₅W and 0.45% NaCl
  3. Implement fluid restriction: typically 800–1000 mL/day total (including IV, PO, tube feeds); more permissive if hypovolemic (allow cautious rehydration with isotonic only)
  4. Hold loop diuretics if you suspect diuretic-induced hyponatremia; verify hold with provider before stopping
  5. Address reversible triggers: normalize temperature (treat fever), optimize analgesia (reduce opioids if possible without compromising comfort), address pain-driven ADH
  6. Verify home medications restarted: if patient on chronic medications that were held, flag resumption time with APP
  7. Notify APP/provider with labs and context — document SIADH assessment or hypovolemic picture — escalation may be observation only if mild and trending stable
  8. Monitor Na⁺ trend: repeat labs in 4–6 hours or per provider; goal: stable to slow rise, <8 mEq/L per 24 h
  9. Neuro checks q4h: track mental status, headache, any new symptoms — establish baseline
  10. Patient education: explain fluid restriction to patient if able (no free water, limit PO intake to help correct Na⁺)

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Symptomatic severe: Na+ <125 with confusion, headache, tremor, altered mental status, or impending seizure.)

  1. STAT page APP/fellow + RRT + charge RN — do NOT leave the room alone
  2. Place on continuous pulse ox and cardiac monitor — prepare for potential seizure
  3. Prepare 3% saline bolus protocol:
    • Secure IV access (central line preferred; peripheral acceptable short-term with frequent assessment for infiltration)
    • Draw up 3% saline 150 mL IV push over 10 minutes
    • Goal: raise Na⁺ 4–6 mEq/L in first 6 hours to stop acute CNS symptoms (seizure risk); then slow correction
    • Provider calculates infusion rate using formula: mEq Na⁺ = [Na⁺ of infusate (513 mEq/L for 3%) − serum Na⁺] × volume (L) × 0.6 × weight (kg)
    • Continuous vital signs q15–30 min during bolus; continuous cardiac monitoring
    • Frequent neuro checks q1h × 6 h, then q2h — document mental status, headache, any seizure activity, improvement in lethargy
    • Stat labs: serum osmolality, Na⁺, K⁺, Mg²⁺, TSH, cortisol, glucose, ABG (assess acid-base status), lactate
    • Do NOT over-correct: recheck Na⁺ q2h strictly during first 6–8 hours post-bolus
    • If Na⁺ rising >10 mEq/L in 24 h → STOP all hypertonic saline immediately and notify provider
    • Over-correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) — permanent motor, cognitive, behavioral impairment
    • Prepare for ICU transfer: symptomatic severe hyponatremia requires ICU-level monitoring for ongoing 3% saline protocol; do not continue management on a floor unit
    • Ensure continuity: document baseline neuro exam, labs in transit, IV access type and location, rhythm status; brief ICU team on rate of Na⁺ rise to-date

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient with Na⁺ [current value] (prior Na⁺ [value] on [date/time]). Volume status: [euvolemic / hypovolemic / hypervolemic]. Symptom status: [asymptomatic / headache / confusion / tremor / impending seizure]." A: "[Recent I&O balance], fluid type hung [hypotonic/isotonic], diuretics [yes/no], recent medications including opioids/SSRIs. Physical exam: [neuro status, perfusion, edema findings]." R: "Requesting [labs / fluid change / 3% saline protocol / ICU consult / endocrine consult / additional monitoring]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Urgency
Asymptomatic mild (130–134), first discovery Primary APP / on-call fellow Routine, within next few hours
Moderate (125–129), borderline symptoms Primary APP / on-call fellow Same-shift decision
Symptomatic severe (Na⁺ <125 with neuro signs) APP/fellow + RRT + charge RN STAT
Recurrent hyponatremia despite fluid restriction Endocrinology consult (SIADH workup) or nephrology Same-day
Suspected adrenal insufficiency Endocrinology Same-day; consider stress-dose steroids empirically
Over-correction (Na⁺ >10 in 24 h) with neurologic changes APP/fellow + ICU team STAT

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are expandable in the PowerApp render — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Classification by volume status — diagnostic framework
sections.bodyHtml:
Volume status assessment is THE diagnostic key — it tells you why the hyponatremia happened and how to correct it:

Volume Status Clinical Signs Urine Osmolality Urine Na⁺ Usual Cause(s) on 5W Rx Approach
Hypovolemic Tachycardia, orthostasis, poor perfusion, oliguria, low JVP High (>400) Low (<20) Diuretic excess, GI losses, renal wasting Isotonic saline; hold diuretics; cautious rehydration
Euvolemic Normal perfusion, no edema, euhydration exam, normal JVP High (>400) High (>40) SIADH (most common post-CPB), medications (SSRI, desmopressin), hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency Fluid restriction 800–1000 mL/day; tolvaptan if resistant
Hypervolemic Edema, elevated JVP, pulmonary edema, ascites, elevated BP Low (<300) Variable Decompensated heart failure, cirrhosis, renal failure (rare post-op) Fluid restrict; loop diuretics; address underlying disease

Clinical Pearl: Most post-CPB hyponatremia is euvolemic SIADH. Hypervolemia is uncommon on the acute post-op floor; more typical in CVICU if patient has low ejection fraction or pre-existing CHF.

sections.heading: 7.2 Post-cardiac surgery causes of hyponatremia — detailed
sections.bodyHtml:
1. SIADH (most common, ~70% of post-op hyponatremia)

  • CPB-induced inflammation and ADH release from posterior pituitary
  • Pain, stress, mechanical ventilation, positive-pressure ventilation, and opioids potentiate ADH
  • Typically lasts 2–4 days post-op, self-limited as inflammation resolves
  • Urine osmolality >400, urine Na⁺ >40, euvolemic on exam
  • First-line: fluid restriction; tolvaptan only if resistant

2. Diuretic-induced hyponatremia

  • Loop (furosemide) or thiazide diuretics cause renal sodium loss + compensatory ADH response
  • Usually mild; often self-corrects when diuretic is held
  • Can occur in aggressive post-op diuresis for pulmonary edema
  • Urine osmolality >400, urine Na⁺ <20 (sodium avidity), hypovolemic picture
  • First-line: hold diuretic; cautious isotonic saline

3. Over-hydration with hypotonic fluids

  • Naive bolusing with D₅W, 0.45% NaCl, or LR (becomes hypotonic after dextrose metabolism)
  • In high-ADH post-op state, free water accumulates instead of being excreted
  • Euvolemic or hypervolemic depending on total fluid load
  • Common cause of iatrogenic severe hyponatremia — often preventable
  • First-line: hold hypotonic fluids; switch to isotonic

4. Adrenal insufficiency

  • Rare but life-threatening; often unmasked by post-op stress
  • Patients on chronic steroids pre-op are at highest risk
  • Mimics euvolemic SIADH (high urine osmolality, high urine Na⁺) but presents with hypotension unresponsive to fluids, hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis
  • Requires immediate cortisol testing (AM cortisol, ACTH stimulation) and stress-dose hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h empirically while awaiting results
  • May have obscured presentation if concurrent fluid restriction is ongoing

5. Hypothyroidism (baseline, undiagnosed or undertreated)

  • Impairs free-water clearance at the kidney
  • Usually causes mild hyponatremia; TSH elevated, free T₄ low
  • Rare as acute post-op precipitant; usually a chronic pre-op condition surfacing
  • Often coexists with adrenal insufficiency in autoimmune contexts

6. Medications

  • SSRIs (paroxetine, fluoxetine, sertraline): SIADH via enhanced ADH action
  • Carbamazepine: ADH release
  • Desmopressin (DDAVP): intentional ADH replacement, but overdose causes SIADH-like picture
  • Opioids (morphine, fentanyl): trigger ADH
  • NSAIDs: reduce renal perfusion + increase ADH
  • Thiazide diuretics: paradoxical hyponatremia via volume depletion + ADH
  • Check MAR; hold or adjust if suspected

7. Decompensated heart failure with dilutional hyponatremia

  • Low cardiac output → ADH release → hyponatremia
  • Usually hypervolemic picture (edema, elevated JVP, pulmonary edema, elevated BNP)
  • Less common on acute post-op floor; more typical in CVICU with low-EF or pre-existing CHF
  • First-line: fluid restriction + loop diuretics + address underlying cardiac function

sections.heading: 7.3 The correction rate rule — WHY it matters
sections.bodyHtml:
THE MOST CRITICAL SAFETY PRINCIPLE IN HYPONATREMIA MANAGEMENT:

Correct serum sodium no faster than 8–10 mEq/L per 24 hours.

Why? Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS; formerly called central pontine myelinolysis or CPM):

  • If serum osmolality rises too fast, brain water shifts OUT of neurons osmotically
  • Neurons shrink; myelin sheath breaks down → permanent motor, cognitive, behavioral dysfunction
  • Symptoms typically appear 24–72 hours after over-correction: quadriparesis, pseudobulbar signs (dysarthria, dysphagia), coma, death in severe cases
  • THE DAMAGE IS IRREVERSIBLE — prevention by careful rate monitoring is your primary job

Safe correction rates by clinical scenario:

Scenario Na⁺ rise target, first 6–24 h Then Total max 24 h
Symptomatic severe (seizure/coma) 4–6 mEq/L in first 6 h (bolus) Slow to 8–10 mEq/L per 24 h thereafter 8–10 mEq/L per 24 h (after acute phase)
Symptomatic moderate (headache, confusion) 6–8 mEq/L in first 24 h Then 4–6 mEq/L per 24 h 8–10 mEq/L per 24 h
Asymptomatic/mild 4–8 mEq/L per 24 h Continue monitoring 8–10 mEq/L per 24 h
Chronic hyponatremia (days of duration) Slower still; max 8–10 mEq/L per 24 h regardless of symptoms Monitor carefully 8–10 mEq/L per 24 h

In practice at the bedside:

  • Check Na⁺ q2–4h during active treatment (3% saline infusion or rapid correction)
  • Use the formula to calculate expected rise: [Na⁺ infused − serum Na⁺] / TBW (total body water = 0.6 × weight in kg)
  • Provider calculates the 3% saline infusion rate to hit target rise; your job is to verify and recheck
  • If you see Na⁺ rising >10 mEq/L in 24 h: STOP hypertonic saline immediately, notify provider stat
  • Hypotonic fluid (D₅W, 0.45% NaCl) may be briefly given to slow correction if Na⁺ rising too fast (rarely done on floor; ICU intervention)

sections.heading: 7.4 SIADH detailed workup
sections.bodyHtml:
Diagnostic labs for suspected SIADH:

Lab Why Interpretation
Serum osmolality Rule out pseudohyponatremia from hyperglycemia or lipemia Low = true hyponatremia; normal/high in pseudohyponatremia
Urine osmolality Assess ADH effect on kidney >400 = ADH-driven concentration (SIADH, diuretic loss); <200 = dilute (primary polydipsia, rare)
Urine sodium Assess renal sodium handling >40 = renal wasting (SIADH, adrenal insuff); <20 = sodium avidity (hypovolemic)
TSH Rule out hypothyroidism Elevated = hypothyroid-induced free-water retention
AM cortisol or ACTH stimulation Rule out adrenal insufficiency Low = adrenal insuff (requires steroids); high = rules out adrenal cause
K⁺, Cl⁻, Cr, BUN Assess electrolyte and renal status K⁺ <3.5 suggests diuretic loss or adrenal insuff; elevated Cr = renal dysfunction

SIADH criteria (all must be met):

  • Hyponatremia (Na⁺ <135)
  • Euvolemia (normal perfusion, no edema, no signs of hypovolemia or hypervolemia)
  • Urine osmolality inappropriately high (>400) relative to low serum osmolality
  • Urine Na⁺ >40 (kidney is not trying to conserve sodium)
  • Normal thyroid function (TSH normal)
  • Normal adrenal function (cortisol normal or high)

sections.heading: 7.5 Medication table: hyponatremia treatment
sections.bodyHtml:
Confirm all doses and institutional protocols with provider before administration.

Fluid restriction (SIADH, euvolemic) — first-line treatment:

Intervention Details
Target intake 800–1000 mL/day total (IV fluids + PO + tube feeds if applicable)
Hypotonic fluid restriction Avoid D₅W, 0.45% NaCl, free water; switch running fluids to isotonic (0.9% NaCl) or LR
Oral fluid restriction Limit PO intake; patient may complain of thirst (driven by low osmolality, not true volume depletion)
Duration Typically 2–4 days post-op as SIADH self-resolves
Monitoring Recheck Na⁺ q4–6h initially; expect slow rise 4–8 mEq/L per 24 h

3% saline (symptomatic severe only — Na⁺ <125 with neuro signs):

Dose / Route Strength Notes
150 mL IV push 3% NaCl (513 mEq/L Na⁺) Over 10 minutes; may repeat q10–15 min × up to 3 doses if seizure persists
Goal: first 6 h Raise Na⁺ 4–6 mEq/L Stops acute CNS symptoms (seizure, coma)
Then slow to 8–10 mEq/L per 24 h Remainder of correction over next 18–24 h
IV access Central line preferred Peripheral acceptable short-term (≤12 h); high infiltration risk — 3% is vesicant
Calculation [desired Na⁺ − current Na⁺] × 0.6 × wt(kg) = mEq deficit Provider calculates infusion rate to hit target

Example: 70 kg patient with Na⁺ = 120, target raise 5 mEq/L in 6 h - Deficit = (125 − 120) × 0.6 × 70 = 210 mEq - At 3% (513 mEq/L): volume = 210 / 513 = ~0.41 L (410 mL) over 6 h = ~68 mL/h infusion rate (or 150 mL bolus q10 min × 3 if acute)

Tolvaptan (vaptans — selective V₂-receptor antagonist):

Parameter Details
Indication Euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia resistant to fluid restriction × 24–48 h
Dose 7.5 mg PO daily; titrate to 15 mg daily if needed
Mechanism Blocks V₂ ADH receptor on collecting duct → free-water excretion without sodium loss
Monitoring LFTs at baseline and q1–2 weeks (hepatotoxicity risk); Na⁺ q4–6h initially
Caution Can cause rapid over-correction if not monitored; risk of ODS if correction >8–10 mEq/L per 24 h
Cost Expensive; specialty pharmacy required; insurance authorization often needed
5W note Rarely initiated on post-op acute floor; typically CVICU or endocrinology decision; not standard first-line

Hold / avoid in post-op hyponatremia:

  • Hypotonic fluids (D₅W, 0.45% NaCl, free water) during high-ADH phase
  • NSAIDs (reduce renal perfusion, increase ADH)
  • Excess opioids if possible (trigger ADH)
  • Thiazide diuretics (increase hyponatremia risk)
  • Loop diuretics if diuretic-induced hyponatremia suspected

sections.heading: 7.6 Pseudohyponatremia and other mimics
sections.bodyHtml:
Pseudohyponatremia (lab artifact; patient is NOT actually hyponatremic):

  • Hyperglycemia: each 100 mg/dL glucose >100 causes ~1.6 mEq/L Na⁺ decrease on flame-photometry analyzers (osmotic effect of glucose draws water into plasma)
  • Clue: high measured glucose, "low" Na⁺, but normal serum osmolality
  • Workup: calculate corrected Na⁺ = measured Na⁺ + (0.016 × [glucose − 100]); if corrected Na⁺ normal, glucose correction is the issue, not primary hyponatremia

  • Rx: treat hyperglycemia; recheck Na⁺ after glucose controlled

  • Lipemia (hyperlipidemia, lipemic pancreatitis): excess lipid in plasma displaces the aqueous phase, reducing measured Na⁺ (older analyzers; modern direct-ISE analyzers correct for this)

  • Clue: visibly lipemic specimen, "low" Na⁺, normal serum osmolality, high triglycerides
  • Workup: request direct-ISE sodium measurement (ion-selective electrode); ask lab if unsure
  • Rx: treat underlying lipemia; recheck with correct method

Other hyponatremia-mimicking situations:

  • Hyperproteinemia (multiple myeloma, advanced cirrhosis): causes pseudohyponatremia on some analyzers (corrected by modern direct ISE)
  • Post-transurethral resection of prostate (TURP) syndrome (not relevant post-cardiac surgery; mentioned for differential completeness): acute hyponatremia from fluid absorption during endoscopic procedure

sections.heading: 7.7 Overcorrection rescue and osmotic demyelination management
sections.bodyHtml:
If Na⁺ has risen >10 mEq/L in 24 hours:

  1. STOP all hypertonic saline immediately — notify provider stat
  2. Check for ODS symptoms: new weakness, facial droop, speech changes, pseudobulbar signs (dysarthria), quadriparesis, behavioral changes, coma
  3. Provider may order:
    • D₅W ± desmopressin (DDAVP) — lower serum osmolality to slow further rise and allow brain water re-entry
    • Re-lower Na⁺ slowly toward target: ~1–2 mEq/L per hour over next 24–48 h
    • ICU transfer — requires continuous monitoring and osm lab checks
    • Note: ODS damage is permanent if full-blown, but early recognition and osmolality reduction can prevent progression
    • Prevention is key — your job is vigilant recheck scheduling and early escalation if drift is too fast

sections.heading: 7.8 Tolvaptan vs desmopressin in context
sections.bodyHtml:
Tolvaptan (V₂ antagonist — "aquaretic"):

  • Mechanism: blocks ADH effect → free-water excretion
  • Use: euvolemic/hypervolemic SIADH resistant to fluid restriction
  • Caution: rapid over-correction if not monitored
  • Post-op context: specialty territory; not first-line on floor

Desmopressin (DDAVP — synthetic ADH):

  • Mechanism: adds ADH → increases aqueous permeability, concentrates urine
  • Use: hypovolemic hyponatremia (replaces "missing" ADH), central diabetes insipidus, overcorrection rescue
  • Post-op context: used in rescue (post-over-correction) to re-lower Na⁺; not first-line for treatment
  • Note: can precipitate SIADH-like picture if overdosed; used judiciously

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear in a stable patient, re-escalate.

  • Worsening headache despite Na⁺ stable or rising slowly — may herald osmotic demyelination if Na⁺ corrected too fast; verify rate of rise
  • New confusion, disorientation, personality change, or drowsiness — hyponatremia effect if Na⁺ <120; early ODS if Na⁺ rising too fast
  • Seizure activity — emergent; symptomatic severe hyponatremia or acute over-correction with ODS
  • Tremor, weakness, facial droop, or pseudobulbar signs — osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS); check Na⁺ rise rate immediately
  • Na⁺ rising >10 mEq/L in 24 h — over-correction; STOP hypertonic saline and notify provider stat
  • Oliguria despite normal BP — suggests worsening SIADH or adrenal insufficiency (hypovolemia); check cortisol and urine sodium
  • Signs of adrenal crisis: hypotension unresponsive to IV fluids, relative bradycardia, hyperkalemia, hyponatremia with elevated urine sodium → obtain cortisol, ACTH; empiric hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h if suspected, do not delay for labs
  • Persistent hyponatremia >4 days post-op — SIADH usually self-resolves by POD 3–4; if persisting, suspect new trigger (infection, medication change, adrenal insuff, hypothyroidism); escalate to endocrinology
  • Hyperglycemia concurrent with hyponatremia — pseudohyponatremia from osmotic glucose effect; correct glucose first, recheck Na⁺
  • Visibly lipemic blood sample with hyponatremia — pseudohyponatremia; request direct-ISE sodium if available, do not treat as true hyponatremia
  • Hypotension + hyponatremia + hypokalemia + metabolic acidosis — adrenal insufficiency until proven otherwise; escalate and consider empiric steroids
  • Na⁺ <120 with new focal neuro deficit — concurrent ischemic stroke from AF or other cause; activate stroke code immediately

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Correction rate is NON-NEGOTIABLE. The single most common iatrogenic complication in hyponatremia management is over-correction. If Na⁺ is rising faster than 8–10 mEq/L per 24 hours, STOP hypertonic saline immediately and page the team. Osmotic demyelination is permanent and entirely preventable by vigilance alone.

  2. 3% saline is ONLY for symptomatic severe (<125 with seizure/altered mental status). Do NOT give 3% saline to asymptomatic mild or moderate hyponatremia. You will over-correct and cause permanent brain damage. Many nurses err on the side of aggressive correction; resist.

  3. Asymptomatic mild hyponatremia (130–134) often resolves with fluid restriction alone. SIADH post-CPB is self-limited. Fluid restrict 800–1000 mL/day, recheck Na⁺ in 4–6 hours. Do not panic; do not escalate prematurely. Patience and monitoring are your best tools.

  4. Urine osmolality and urine sodium are THE diagnostic labs. They tell you if it's SIADH (high osm >400 + high urine Na⁺ >40) vs diuretic-induced hypovolemia (high osm + low urine Na⁺ <20). Do not skip these — they guide whether you fluid-restrict (SIADH) or replace volume (hypovolemic). They are foundational.

  5. SIADH post-CPB is usually self-limited. It typically resolves within 2–4 days as CPB inflammation settles. Fluid restriction is your main therapeutic tool. Tolvaptan is specialty/CVICU territory, not a post-op floor default. Avoid escalating every case.

  6. Adrenal insufficiency mimics SIADH clinically and on labs. Both present euvolemic with high urine osmolality and high urine sodium. The difference: adrenal insuff has low cortisol, hypotension unresponsive to fluids, and hyperkalemia. If patient is on chronic steroids pre-op and now hyponatremic post-op, get a cortisol level. Have a low threshold for empiric stress-dose hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h while awaiting lab confirmation. Missed adrenal insufficiency = potential death.

  7. Pseudohyponatremia from hyperglycemia or lipemia is real and common. Serum osmolality will be normal or high if pseudohyponatremia. If you see Na⁺ 120 but serum osmolality 280–290, the patient may not have true hyponatremia — confirm with blood glucose check and lipid assessment first. Calculate corrected Na⁺ if glucose elevated. Treat glucose, not sodium.

  8. Fluid restriction is the intervention even if the patient is complaining of thirst. SIADH mechanism is broken; free-water craving is driven by the low serum osmolality, not true volume depletion. Thirst will improve as Na⁺ normalizes and ADH wanes. Reassure the patient; do not give free water.

  9. Avoid hypotonic fluids in the immediate post-op period. D₅W becomes hypotonic as glucose is metabolized; if you must give it, do so slowly and only when ADH is expected to be low (late post-op, off pain meds, afebrile). LR is isotonic at the bedside but becomes hypotonic upon dextrose metabolism; ask for 0.9% NaCl or "isotonic fluid" if uncertain. Default to isotonic.

  10. Neuro exam is your bedside marker of hyponatremia severity. Asymptomatic = low risk; proceed with fluid restriction. Headache = intermediate risk; close monitoring and frequent Na⁺ checks. Confusion, tremor, altered mental status = high risk and warrants 3% saline + ICU transfer. Seizure = emergent 3% bolus. Your neuro checks guide escalation and tell you when to push back on conservative plans.

  11. Tolvaptan is expensive and requires LFT monitoring during use (hepatotoxicity risk). It is not routine post-op floor management. A specialist decision (endocrinology or CVICU). Know it exists for resistant SIADH in the chronic outpatient setting, but do not reach for it on the acute floor.

  12. Over-correction happens most often when providers are chasing a "normal" Na⁺ number. Goal is SLOW correction. If provider orders "replicate sodium to 140," push back respectfully: "Target is 8–10 mEq/L per 24 hours. At that rate, we'll reach 140 safely by [time]." You are the safety net. Speak up.

  13. Patients on chronic steroids pre-operatively are at risk for post-op adrenal insufficiency. If a patient with rheumatoid arthritis, temporal arteritis, or other steroid-requiring condition is hyponatremic, hypotensive, hypokalemic post-op, think adrenal insufficiency first. Get cortisol; do not wait. Give stress-dose hydrocortisone 50 mg IV q6h empirically while awaiting results if clinical suspicion is high.

  14. 3% saline infiltration risk is HIGH on peripheral lines. 3% NaCl is a vesicant. If you use a peripheral line (acceptable only as temporary measure until central line placed), reassess the site q5 min for signs of infiltration: pain, swelling, blanching, coolness. Central line is preferred. Do NOT run 3% saline as a continuous drip on the floor without ICU-level monitoring.

  15. The goal of correction in symptomatic severe is 4–6 mEq/L in the first 6 hours, then SLOW down. After the 3% bolus(es) stop seizure/coma risk, your job is to slow the rise to 8–10 mEq/L per 24 h for the remainder. Check Na⁺ q2h × first 6–8 hours, then q4h. Do NOT repeat 3% bolus every 30 minutes chasing a number; you will over-correct. Work with the provider to titrate the infusion rate, not the bolus frequency.

cards.title: Hypotension Differential on the Floor
cards.quickAnswer: New hypotension post-cardiac surgery: MAP < 65 mmHg or SBP drop > 20 mmHg from baseline. Obtain 12-lead ECG immediately (rule out rhythm), assess preload (neck veins, passive leg raise response), check for active bleeding (chest-tube output, Hgb trend), and exclude tamponade (pulse pressure, CVP waveform, bedside echo). If fever, rigors, or lactate elevation: initiate sepsis protocol. Hold recent antihypertensives. If alert and perfusing (Stable): administer 250–500 mL IV bolus over 5–10 min; reassess q5 min. If altered mental status, cool extremities, or lactate rising (Unstable): activate RRT, initiate norepinephrine, notify CT surgery and anesthesia STAT. Call early.
