sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, who this applies to.

  • Definition: New-onset systolic BP < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg in the post-operative period, or a drop > 20 mmHg from the patient's baseline. Occurs in post-cardiac surgery patients across all procedure types and acuity levels on the ward, stepdown, or ICU.
  • Incidence: 15–40% of post-cardiac surgery patients experience hypotension in the first 24–72 hours; most are self-limited with fluid or medication adjustment. Severe or refractory hypotension requiring vasopressor support occurs in ~5–10% (Bojar, 2020).
  • Who this applies to: every post-operative cardiac surgery patient (CABG, valve repair/replacement, aortic surgery, transplant, VAD, complex repairs). Vigilance is highest POD 0–3; can occur later in the hospital course.
  • Why it matters: hypotension is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Missed etiology leads to misdirected therapy (e.g., bolusing a patient in cardiogenic shock, delaying CT surgery return in tamponade, oversedating a septic patient). Identifying the underlying bucket directs appropriate management and prevents deterioration.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative hypotension reflects a mismatch between circulating volume, cardiac output, and systemic vascular resistance. The post-operative state creates a perfect storm: anesthesia-induced vasodilation is wearing off (sympathetic rebound), the inflammatory response to cardiopulmonary bypass is peaking, fluid has mobilized from third spaces, medications are accumulating, and tissue perfusion is marginal—any additional insult tips the balance.

The key insight is the 6-bucket framework: hypotension stems from one or more of six physiologic mechanisms. Identifying the bucket(s) accelerates diagnosis and therapy.

The post-op milieu: Cardiac surgery + CPB create a unique metabolic state—systemic inflammatory response, endothelial dysfunction, exaggerated fluid shifts, and adrenergic sensitivity all peak POD 1–3 (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025). Medications (opioids, anesthetics, antihypertensives) compound vasodilation. Simultaneous triggers are common: a patient with bleeding (bucket 1) + early sepsis (bucket 3) + loss of beta-blocker effect (bucket 6) requires simultaneous salvage of all three.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-op cardiac surgery patient:

  • BP alarm or bedside observation: systolic < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg (or > 20 mmHg decline from documented baseline)
  • Patient symptoms: dizziness, lightheadedness, chest discomfort, dyspnea, palpitations, syncope, confusion
  • Physical findings: cool or mottled extremities, delayed capillary refill, weak peripheral pulses, altered mental status
  • Intraoperative context: just extubated, on day of surgery, or POD 1–7 when most dynamic changes occur
  • Recent medication: antihypertensive dose given 10–30 min prior, or opioid bolus just administered
  • Recent event: position change (upright → supine), large fluid bolus, blood transfusion, or acute surgical complication

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet; information-gathering only.

  • Vital signs: Confirm BP manually (avoid cuff cycle artifact). Core temperature. HR and rhythm on monitor. SpO₂. Respiratory rate.
  • Mentation: Alert vs drowsy vs confused vs unresponsive. Orientation × 3.
  • Skin perfusion: Temperature, color, capillary refill (normal < 2 sec). Mottling present?
  • Neck veins: Observe JVD at 45° supine. Flat, normal, or distended to angle of jaw?
  • Lungs: Breath sounds bilateral and clear vs crackles at bases vs dullness (effusion).
  • Heart: Rate, regularity, murmurs, rubs. S3 or S4 present?
  • Extremities: Pulses (radial, femoral). Color, temperature. Any swelling or asymmetry.
  • Abdomen: Soft, distended, tender? Shifting dullness (ascites)? Rigidity (peritonitis)?
  • Surgical wounds: Inspect dressings for excess bleeding. Chest-tube integrity.
  • Rhythm & pacing: 12-lead ECG (irregular? fast? bradycardic? loss of pacer capture?).
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, glucose, Hgb (baseline + most recent), lactate, creatinine.
  • CVP / hemodynamic data: If central line present, CVP trend and waveform. Passive leg raise test if possible (lift legs 45°; does SBP rise ≥ 5 mmHg?).
  • Medication review (MAR): Recent antihypertensive, opioid, sedative, or diuretic administration. Beta-blocker, statin, ACE-I dose timing.
  • Chest-tube output: Rate (mL/h), color (serous vs serosanguineous vs frank blood), acute increase?
  • Urine output: Recent void? Foley output if present (mL/h). Adequate hydration sign if UOP > 0.5 mL/kg/h.

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, alert, MAP > 60, perfusing well, no altered mental status, cap refill < 3 sec, lactate normal.)

  1. Obtain 12-lead ECG STAT — rule out rhythm-driven hypotension (POAF with RVR, bradycardia, VT, loss of capture)
  2. Save rhythm strip at time of presentation
  3. Call APP/on-call provider — notify of new hypotension; remain at bedside or arrange continuous monitoring
  4. Check recent medication timing — review MAR for antihypertensive, opioid, or sedative given in past 30 min. If temporally related, hold offending agent and recheck BP in 5 min.
  5. Passive leg raise test — lay patient supine, elevate legs 45° for 1 minute - If SBP rises ≥ 5 mmHg: volume-responsive → administer 250–500 mL IV bolus (crystalloid, LR preferred) over 5–10 min - If SBP unchanged: volume not the problem → assess bucket 2–6
  6. Assess chest-tube output — color, rate, any acute change? Exsanguination pattern (sudden increase) warrants escalation
  7. Calculate pulse pressure — SBP − DBP - Narrow (< 25 mmHg): suspect bleeding or tamponade → escalate - Wide (> 40 mmHg) with warm extremities: suspect vasoplegia or sepsis
  8. Obtain core temperature — fever > 38.3°C or hypothermia? If fever: blood cultures, WBC, lactate (sepsis screen)
  9. Bedside ultrasound (if available) — assess LV contractility, RV function, pericardial fluid, IVC diameter. Look for tamponade signs (RV diastolic collapse, RA collapse).
  10. Reassess vital signs and perfusion every 5 minutes. If stable after intervention, continue q15-min trending. If deteriorates → escalate to 5B.

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Altered mental status, cool extremities, decreased UOP, rising lactate, SBP < 80, cannot auscultate MAP, or any acute decompensation.)

  1. Activate Rapid Response Team (RRT) — do not manage alone. Notify ICU, CT surgery, anesthesia standby immediately.
  2. Position for perfusion: Lay flat (remove pillow), legs elevated to augment venous return.
  3. Establish large-bore IV access: Two 18-gauge or larger lines if not already present.
  4. 500 mL crystalloid (LR preferred) bolus — push over 2–3 min while simultaneously working-up.
  5. Start vasopressor bridge — peripheral norepinephrine is bridge to central line:
    • Norepinephrine: 1 mcg/kg/min (e.g., 70 kg = 70 mcg/min) via peripheral IV as temporary measure; arrange central line placement concurrently
    • Phenylephrine alternative: 40–180 mcg/min peripheral, or 50–200 mcg IV push q10–15 min as bridge
    • STAT labs (stat-draw order):
      • Type & cross, CBC (Hgb + plt), comprehensive metabolic panel (K⁺, creatinine, glucose), lactate, ABG, troponin, PT/INR, aPTT
      • Blood cultures if fever
      • STAT imaging:
      • Portable chest X-ray (evaluate for mediastinal widening, effusion, pneumothorax)
      • Bedside echocardiography (rule out tamponade, assess RV function, evaluate for mechanical complication)
      • Risk stratification—identify the bucket(s):
      • Bleeding pattern? (narrow pulse pressure, rising Hgb drop, high chest-tube output) → activate massive transfusion protocol (MTP); notify surgeon + perfusion
      • Tamponade pattern? (distended neck veins + narrow pulse pressure + echo findings) → CT surgery STAT; prepare pericardiocentesis kit at bedside
      • Sepsis pattern? (fever > 38.3°C, rigors, WBC shift left, lactate > 2) → initiate broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam per protocol)
      • Cardiogenic pattern? (JVD + crackles + cool periphery + troponin elevation + low EF on echo) → add inotrope (dobutamine 5 mcg/kg/min or milrinone 0.5 mcg/kg/min); escalate to ICU
      • Rhythm pattern? (irregular rhythm or very fast/slow rate on monitor) → 12-lead ECG; treat rhythm (cardioversion, pacing, antiarrhythmic per rhythm type)
      • Continuous monitoring — telemetry, frequent vital signs (q1–2 min during crisis), trending lactate, UOP, BP response.
      • Prepare for ICU transfer — arrange bed, staff for continuous monitoring, vasopressor titration, and advanced diagnostics.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [Name], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed new hypotension at [time]. Current BP [value], MAP [value], HR [rate], SpO₂ [value]. Baseline BP was [value]. Core temp [value]. Most recent labs: K⁺ [value], lactate [value], Hgb [value]." A: "Patient is [alert / confused / unresponsive]. Skin is [warm / cool / mottled]. Cap refill [normal / delayed]. Extremities [well-perfused / cold]. Chest tube [color, mL/h]. [Any rhythm finding from ECG]. [Passive leg raise result if done]." R: "Requesting [assessment for bleeding / evaluation for tamponade / escalation to ICU / return to OR / sepsis protocol / rhythm control]."

Who to call

Situation Contact Action
Stable, volume-responsive, improving on fluid Primary APP / on-call resident Trend closely q15 min; recheck BP post-bolus
Hypotension persisting or worsening after fluid; MAP < 65 ICU / critical care attending Arrange transfer; initiate vasopressor
Altered mentation, cool extremities, lactate > 2 RRT + ICU + anesthesia STAT assessment; prepare for intensive monitoring
Bleeding phenotype (narrow PP, Hgb drop, high CT output) Surgeon + perfusion Activate MTP; prepare return to OR
Tamponade picture (distended JVD, narrow PP, echo confirmation) CT surgery (STAT) Pericardiocentesis kit at bedside; prepare for sternotomy
Fever > 38.3°C + rigors + lactate + BP drop Infectious disease + primary team Blood cultures; broad-spectrum antibiotics; fluid + pressor
Rhythm abnormality (POAF + RVR, VT, bradycardia) Cardiology / APP + nursing 12-lead confirmed; prepare for cardioversion or pacing

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 The 6-Bucket Framework
sections.bodyHtml: Hypotension post-operatively stems from one or more of six mechanisms. Identifying the bucket(s) directs therapy.

sections.heading: Bucket 1: Preload (Volume Depletion)
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: Circulating volume is contracted; venous return insufficient.

Causes:

  • Chest-tube bleeding (normal < 100 mL/h POD 1; concerning ≥ 200 mL/h)
  • Diuresis (loop diuretics perioperatively)
  • Insensible losses (open wounds, high ventilator tidal volumes)
  • GI losses (vomiting, NG output)
  • Third-spacing into soft tissue

Bedside clues:

  • Flat neck veins when upright or at 45°
  • Low CVP (< 2 mmHg if measured)
  • Urine output low (< 0.5 mL/kg/h)
  • Positive passive leg raise: SBP rises ≥ 5 mmHg → fluid responsive
  • Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor
  • Tachycardia (unless on beta-blocker)

First move: 250–500 mL IV bolus (LR preferred) over 5–10 min. Recheck BP. If recovers, diagnosis confirmed. If no improvement, hypovolemia is not the primary problem.

sections.heading: Bucket 2: Pump (Cardiogenic Shock)
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: Forward cardiac output inadequate; heart fails to perfuse tissues.

Causes:

  • LV dysfunction (acute MI, post-CPB stunning, septic cardiomyopathy)
  • RV failure (post-LVAD implant, post-transplant, RV infarction, massive PE)
  • Valve thrombosis or mechanical malfunction
  • Ventricular septal defect or papillary muscle rupture (surgical complication)
  • Myocarditis (post-viral, hyperacute rejection post-transplant)

Bedside clues:

  • JVD present (CVP elevated)
  • Crackles at lung bases (pulmonary edema)
  • S3 gallop (if audible)
  • Cool or mottled extremities
  • Rising lactate (tissue hypoperfusion)
  • Negative passive leg raise: SBP does not rise; more fluid worsens pulmonary edema
  • Troponin elevated, BNP elevated
  • Echo: low EF, regional wall motion abnormality, large cavity, slow flow (low VTI)

First move: Do NOT bolus fluids; will worsen pulmonary edema. Start inotrope (dobutamine 5 mcg/kg/min or milrinone 0.5 mcg/kg/min) ± pressor (norepinephrine). Obtain echo urgently. Consider IABP, Impella, or ECMO if refractory. Escalate to ICU immediately.

sections.heading: Bucket 3: Afterload (Distributive Shock)
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: Systemic vascular resistance drops; vasodilation exceeds compensation.

Causes:

  • Vasoplegia post-CPB (usually resolves in OR or early ICU; persistence on ward is unusual)
  • Sepsis (fever, rigors, lactate ↑, WBC left shift, new infection source)
  • Anaphylaxis (drug reaction, blood product, contrast agent)
  • Medication side-effect (over-titrated vasodilators: nifedipine, nicardipine, NTG, hydralazine, propofol)
  • Neurogenic (autonomic dysfunction, rarely relevant post-cardiac surgery)

Bedside clues:

  • Warm extremities, normal or brisk cap refill (hallmark)
  • Wide pulse pressure (SBP − DBP > 40 mmHg)
  • Tachycardia (unless paced or on beta-blocker)
  • Fever > 38.3°C or hypothermia
  • History of recent antigen exposure, new rash, or bronchospasm (anaphylaxis hint)
  • Lactate elevated (from maldistribution, not tissue hypoxia)
  • Recent medication administration (vasodilator or opioid)

First move: Pressor is first-line. Phenylephrine 40–180 mcg/min peripheral, or norepinephrine 0.5–1.4 mcg/kg/min. If sepsis suspected: broad-spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam per institutional protocol) + fluid bolus + pressor. Identify and remove offending medication if anaphylaxis or drug side-effect. Recheck in 5 min.

sections.heading: Bucket 4: Obstructive (Mechanical Impedance)
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: Blood cannot exit the heart despite adequate volume and contractility; intrathoracic pressure obstruction.

Causes:

  • Tamponade (pericardial effusion, hemopericardium, clot causing RV diastolic collapse)
  • Tension pneumothorax (rare; redo sternotomy or surgical injury complication)
  • Massive pulmonary embolism (immediate post-op anticoagulation resumption risk)

Bedside clues:

  • Markedly elevated JVD (distended to or above angle of jaw)
  • Narrow pulse pressure (< 25 mmHg)
  • Pulsus paradoxus (SBP drop > 10 mmHg on inspiration; subtle at low BP but classic if present)
  • Muffled or distant heart sounds
  • Acute change in chest-tube output (sudden drop or change in character)
  • Bedside echo: swinging heart, RV diastolic collapse, RA collapse, large pericardial effusion
  • CXR: widened mediastinum, silhouette change, or new opacification

First move: STAT notify CT surgery. Do NOT delay. Obtain bedside echo immediately. Do NOT give fluids (will worsen tamponade). Prepare pericardiocentesis kit at bedside. If in extremis and echo unavailable: blind pericardiocentesis at 5th intercostal space, left of sternum, 1–2 cm into the pericardial sac with needle-over-catheter technique, or arrange immediate sternotomy if available.

sections.heading: Bucket 5: Rhythm (Electrical Dysfunction)
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: Loss of synchronous AV conduction or adequate ventricular filling time; cardiac output collapses.

Causes:

  • POAF with rapid ventricular response (RVR 120–160+ bpm; shortened diastolic filling time)
  • Ventricular tachycardia (pacing artifact, ischemia, electrolyte derangement)
  • Severe bradycardia (complete heart block, loss of pacer capture, beta-blocker + amiodarone stacking)
  • Junctional rhythm with loss of atrial contribution

Bedside clues:

  • Irregular rhythm or very fast/slow rate on monitor
  • 12-lead ECG: narrow irregular (POAF), wide (VT), or slow with AV dissociation (heart block)
  • In POAF + RVR: irregularly irregular, narrow QRS, HR 140–180 bpm
  • In bradycardia: HR < 50 bpm; cool extremities; altered mental status
  • Pacer spikes visible on monitor but not capturing (loss of mechanical contraction)

First move: Treat the rhythm FIRST, not the BP.

  • POAF + RVR (stable): Amiodarone 150 mg IV over 10 min; start rate-control agent (beta-blocker or diltiazem per protocol)
  • POAF + RVR (unstable): Synchronized cardioversion (start 100 J biphasic, escalate per ACLS)
  • Bradycardia: Transvenous pacing (pacer pads as bridge); atropine or epinephrine if symptomatic
  • Loss of capture: Check pacer settings, increase mA, verify lead contact, reposition if loose

BP improves once rhythm normalized.

sections.heading: Bucket 6: Iatrogenic (Medication or Positioning)
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism: Unintended consequence of treatment; "own goal" from care team.

Causes:

  • Recent antihypertensive dose too aggressive or given at wrong interval (metoprolol 25–50 mg, lisinopril, amlodipine, hydralazine, nicardipine, NTG)
  • Beta-blocker stacking (on amiodarone for POAF, then given metoprolol; synergistic bradycardia)
  • Opioid bolus (morphine 5–10 mg, hydromorphone 1–2 mg) → vasodilation + sedation
  • Sedation bolus (propofol, etomidate IV push) → hypotension
  • Excessive diuresis (furosemide 20–40 mg given, hypotension 20 min later)
  • Positioning (upright with small circulating volume → orthostatic drop)

Bedside clue: Timeline correlation—hypotension onset 10–30 min after medication administration.

First move: Check MAR. Hold offending agent immediately. Lay patient flat if upright. Support with small fluids or pressor if ongoing. Reassess in 5 min. Usually self-limited once agent metabolized. If persists > 30 min, re-evaluate as another bucket.

sections.heading: 7.2 Decision Logic: Findings → Bucket
sections.bodyHtml:
Finding Pattern Likely Bucket Diagnostic Move First Therapy
Flat neck veins + low UOP + PLR positive (SBP ↑ 5+ mmHg) Preload Passive leg raise test 250–500 mL IV bolus
JVD + crackles + S3 + cool extremities + lactate ↑ Pump Bedside echo; troponin, BNP Inotrope + pressor; NO fluids
Warm extremities + wide PP (> 40) + fever OR recent vasodilator Afterload Fever workup; medication review Pressor (phenylephrine or norepi); AB if sepsis
Markedly elevated JVD + narrow PP (< 25) + muffled sounds + echo shows RV collapse Obstructive Bedside echo STAT CT surgery STAT; pericardiocentesis prep
Irregular/fast/slow rhythm on monitor; 12-lead confirms dysrhythmia Rhythm 12-lead ECG; rhythm identification Treat rhythm (cardioversion, pacing, antiarrhythmic)
Hypotension onset 10–30 min post-medication; MAR shows recent dose Iatrogenic Timeline + medication review Hold offending agent; observe; recheck

sections.heading: 7.3 Shock State Recognition
sections.bodyHtml:
Stable hypotension (no shock yet):

  • Awake, alert, oriented
  • MAP ≥ 60 mmHg
  • Warm extremities, normal cap refill (< 2 sec)
  • Urine output adequate (> 0.5 mL/kg/h if on catheter)
  • Lactate normal or low
  • No altered mental status

Compensated shock (early):

  • Anxiety, mild confusion, or restlessness
  • MAP 55–65 mmHg
  • Skin cool, cap refill 2–3 sec
  • Decreased urine output (0.25–0.5 mL/kg/h)
  • Lactate mildly elevated (1.5–2.5 mmol/L)
  • Tachycardia present (if not paced/on beta-blocker)

Decompensated shock (escalate immediately):

  • Altered mental status (drowsy, confused, unresponsive)
  • MAP < 55 mmHg, unable to auscultate
  • Mottled, cyanotic extremities; cap refill > 3 sec
  • Minimal or absent urine output
  • Lactate > 3 mmol/L or rising rapidly
  • Cool, clammy skin
  • Bradycardia (late finding; poor prognostic sign)

sections.heading: 7.4 Medication Dosing Reference
sections.bodyHtml:
Verify all doses against institutional policy before administration.

Vasopressors (distributive, cardiogenic, obstructive patterns)

Drug Typical Dose Onset Notes
Norepinephrine 0.5–1.4 mcg/kg/min IV (titrate to MAP > 65) 1–3 min First-line for most shock states. Mix: 4 mcg/mL or 16 mcg/mL (check institutional concentration). Requires central line for prolonged use.
Phenylephrine Peripheral: 40–180 mcg/min; IV push: 50–200 mcg q10–15 min 5–20 min Pure alpha; preserves flow in some contexts. Less reliable in acute shock.
Dopamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min (low dose → renal; high dose → vasoconstriction) 5–10 min Less preferred post-op (arrhythmia risk); used if norepi unavailable.

Inotropes (cardiogenic shock pattern)

Drug Typical Dose Onset Notes
Dobutamine 5–20 mcg/kg/min IV infusion 1–2 min Beta-agonist; increases contractility + causes vasodilation. Risk: arrhythmia, tachycardia, hypotension. Combine with pressor if BP inadequate.
Milrinone 0.5–0.75 mcg/kg/min IV infusion 1–3 min Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor; inotropy + lusitropia + vasodilation. Risk: systemic hypotension if not paired with pressor. Useful in HF + cardiogenic shock.

Antibiotics (sepsis pattern) — empiric broad-spectrum

Regimen Typical Dose Notes
Vancomycin + Piperacillin-tazobactam Vanc 15–20 mg/kg IV q8–12h; Pip-tazo 4.5 g IV q6h Standard empiric post-cardiac surgery sepsis. Covers gram-positive cocci, gram-negative rods, anaerobes. Adjust for renal function.
Vancomycin + Ceftazidime + Metronidazole Vanc 15–20 mg/kg; Ceftaz 2 g IV q8h; Metro 500 mg IV q8h Alternative if PCN allergy or institutional preference.

Doses adapted from Bojar (2020) and Rhodes et al. (2021). Always verify against current institutional protocol and patient renal function.

sections.heading: 7.5 Anticoagulation Considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Post-op timing is complex. Balancing stroke risk (especially post-tamponade or with AF) against bleeding risk is team-dependent.
  • Do NOT hold or restart anticoagulation without the surgical team's input. Many clinicians reflexively hold AC post-op; the plan is often nuanced.
  • Home AC (warfarin, DOAC) is typically held 3–4 days pre-op and restarted 24–72 h post-op per surgeon preference based on bleeding risk.
  • Heparin for AF — if POAF develops and lasts > 48 h, anticoagulation is indicated unless ongoing bleeding precludes it.
  • HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia) can present as acute hypotension + limb ischemia or stroke. Always check CBC with PLT count; HIT antibody if plt drops > 50% or HIT 4Ts score ≥ 6.

sections.heading: 7.6 Special Populations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Transplant recipients: Denervated heart won't mount compensatory tachycardia. Judge shock by BP and lactate, not HR. A HR 80 with SBP 70 is shock in a transplant patient; don't be falsely reassured.
  • VAD / LVAD patients: Pulsatile flow is absent. Assess perfusion by mentation, urine output, lactate, and mixed venous O₂ sat; traditional BP cutoffs are less reliable.
  • Chronic renal disease: Volume status is harder to discern (chronically elevated Cr + JVD). Rely on passive leg raise and echo more than biomarkers.
  • Morbid obesity: Noninvasive BP cuff is unreliable. Use arterial line if available; palpate for pulse.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear, re-escalate immediately.

  • Worsening mental status — even subtle confusion or anxiety is a sentinel sign of deteriorating perfusion
  • Lactate rising despite intervention — suggests inadequate tissue perfusion or resurgent infection
  • Urine output dropping — oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) despite fluids or pressors indicates shock progression
  • Cool extremities spreading — initially distal; if advancing proximally, shock is deepening
  • BP trending down despite vasopressor — inadequate pressor dose or rapidly evolving pathology (e.g., ongoing bleeding)
  • Chest-tube output increasing suddenly — suggests active hemorrhage or pericardial collection
  • New irregular rhythm or rate change — may indicate electrolyte derangement, ischemia, or progression
  • Tachycardia despite pressor + fluids — compensatory; indicates inadequate treatment of underlying bucket
  • Respiratory distress with hypoxia — pulmonary edema from over-aggressive fluids (cardiogenic shock misdiagnosed as hypovolemia)
  • New focal neurologic deficit — stroke from hypoperfusion or embolic source; activate stroke code
  • Fever rising despite antibiotics — uncontrolled sepsis; source control needed (consider echo for vegetations, imaging for source)
  • Falling platelet count — HIT, DIC, or other coagulopathy; check labs and notify team

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Cuff artifact is real. Non-invasive BP cuff cycles; transducer lag occurs. If sudden drop seems inconsistent with exam, recheck manually and verify with capillary refill + mentation.

  2. Passive leg raise is free and diagnostic. A negative PLR (SBP does not rise ≥ 5 mmHg) definitively excludes volume responsiveness; fluids will only worsen pulmonary edema and harm the patient.

  3. Chasing a number misses the patient. A patient with SBP 88 but alert, warm, normal cap refill, and normal lactate is less sick than one with SBP 92 but confused, cool, delayed cap refill, and lactate 3. Treat the clinical picture.

  4. Pulse pressure is a bedside superpower. Narrow PP (< 25 mmHg) post-op = bleeding or tamponade until proven otherwise. Wide PP (> 40) with warm extremities = distributive shock. Calculate it every time.

  5. Reflexive fluid bolus in LVH or HFpEF kills. Diastolic dysfunction (stiff ventricle) cannot tolerate extra volume. Check echo pre-op diagnosis. If reduced EF, inotrope first; if normal/preserved EF, very cautious fluids or inotrope-only.

  6. Vasoplegia post-op is ICU disease. If distributive picture (warm + wide PP) redevelops on POD 2–3 after an initially stable course, assume not safe for floor; escalate.

  7. Check the MAR for medication timing. Hypotensive 30 min after metoprolol, lisinopril, or nicardipine increase is predictable, not surprising. Hold the agent; BP recovers; diagnosis is made by timeline.

  8. Amiodarone or beta-blocker bradycardia mimics cardiogenic shock. HR of 38 post-amiodarone looks like cardiomyopathy on first glance. Check MAR. Atropine or pacing is the answer, not inotropes.

  9. Silent bleeding into pleural or retroperitoneal space is the miss. Normal chest-tube output does NOT rule out bleeding. Check serial CXR (layering effusion?), examine abdomen (shifting dullness, rigidity), and trend Hgb. Pleural and peritoneal bleeding can be "quiet."

  10. Sepsis in post-op is not always fever-centric. Fever may be blunted or absent. Rigors, WBC left shift, lactate, and new hypotension trump temperature. HR 110, T 37.8°C, WBC 16 left shift, lactate 2.2, POD 2 = septic until proven otherwise; start antibiotics.

  11. Don't miss tamponade. Narrow pulse pressure + elevated JVD + echo showing RV diastolic collapse or RA collapse = tamponade until proven. Don't wait for hypotension to be severe; call CT surgery early.

  12. Orthostatic hypotension is universal POD 1–2. First ambulation is an event. Sit on side of bed 1 min, stand 1 min, walk 10 feet. If presyncope or SBP drop > 20 mmHg, lie back down; try later. Document orthostatics.

  13. Bladder distention + sedation mimics hypovolemia. Overfilled bladder → Bezold-Jarisch reflex (vagal) → transient hypotension. Bladder scan; straight cath if distended. BP corrects instantly.

  14. Documentation of timing, findings, interventions, and response is critical. Post-event review will ask: "When did it start? What was done? Did the patient respond? When was the team notified?" Document every 5 min during crisis.

  15. The 6-bucket framework is a teaching tool, not a strait jacket. Most acute post-op hypotension involves 2–3 buckets simultaneously (bleeding + early sepsis + iatrogenic medication). Identify all contributors; salvage all of them.

cards.title: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump (IABP)
cards.quickAnswer: Mechanical circulatory support catheter — a 30–50 mL balloon in the descending thoracic aorta that inflates in diastole (augments coronary perfusion) and deflates in systole (reduces afterload). Used in cardiogenic shock, refractory myocardial ischemia, post-cardiotomy LV failure, and high-risk PCI as a bridge to recovery or escalation. Weaning typically progresses 1:1 → 1:2 → 1:3 → passive over 24–48 h. Unit staff primarily manage post-removal monitoring: continuous limb checks (distal pulses, color, temperature, sensation), bedrest protocol (4–6 h femoral access), and watch for late bleeding or pseudoaneurysm.

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml: The Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump is a 30–50 mL polyurethane catheter inserted percutaneously (femoral artery most common; axillary for early ambulation) into the descending thoracic aorta just distal to the left subclavian artery. An external console drives helium gas inflations and deflations synchronized to the cardiac cycle via ECG R-wave or arterial pressure waveform trigger. The device operates in augmentation ratios (1:1 every beat, 1:2 alternating, 1:3 every third beat) and weaning progresses toward removal as the patient recovers.

sections.heading: 2. Hemodynamic Effects / Augmentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Effect Mechanism Clinical Consequence
Diastolic inflation Balloon expands in early diastole Raises diastolic aortic pressure; increases coronary perfusion (coronary filling occurs in diastole); improves myocardial O₂ supply
Pre-systolic deflation Balloon collapses just before ventricular systole Reduces LV afterload; improves cardiac output; reduces myocardial O₂ demand (MVO₂)
Net hemodynamic effect Supply + demand dual benefit ~10–20% increase in CO; reduced PCWP; reduced LV wall stress; improved diastolic pressure
Augmentation ratios 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, or passive (0:1) More frequent inflation = more support. Weaning typically 1:1 → 1:2 (4–6 h) → 1:3 (4–6 h) → passive trial (2–4 h)

Important limitation: IABP support is LV-focused; does not directly support the RV. RV-dominant failure or ARDS may require escalation to VA-ECMO.

sections.heading: Indications
sections.bodyHtml:
Indication Clinical Context Notes
Cardiogenic shock (post-MI) EF < 30%, hypotension, elevated lactate, end-organ hypoperfusion IABP-SHOCK II (2012) showed no mortality benefit; device used as bridge to recovery or escalation to VAD/ECMO
Refractory myocardial ischemia Ongoing chest pain despite dual antiplatelet + max medical therapy Bridge to revascularization (PCI or CABG)
High-risk PCI bridge Severe CAD, low EF, or hemodynamic instability Reduces intra-procedural hypotension + arrhythmia
Post-cardiotomy LV failure After CABG/AVR/MVR with EF < 25% and low output Bridge to recovery (days–weeks) or escalation
Acute mechanical MI complication VSD or acute MR post-MI with hemodynamic compromise Temporary stabilization; surgical repair is definitive

sections.heading: Contraindications
sections.bodyHtml:
Contraindication Reason Risk
Moderate-to-severe aortic regurgitation Balloon diastolic deflation exacerbates regurgitant flow Paradoxically worsens LV dilation; increases MVO₂
Aortic dissection / severe atherosclerosis Balloon insertion can dissect or perforate diseased aorta Aortic rupture; hemodynamic collapse; acute MI
Aortic aneurysm > 4–5 cm Mechanical stress from balloon expansion Risk of rupture; fatal hemorrhage
Severe peripheral arterial disease Femoral catheter cannot traverse stenosed iliac/femoral vessels Limb ischemia; thrombosis; tissue loss
Recent aortic graft Mechanical trauma on suture line Graft rupture; anastomotic bleed

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use: Post-Removal Monitoring
sections.bodyHtml:
IABP management stays in the ICU. Unit staff commonly see post-removal patients requiring:

  1. Vital signs: Every 15 min × 1 h, then every 30 min × 4 h post-removal
  2. Distal limb assessment every 1–2 h: dorsalis pedis + posterior tibial pulses, color, temperature, sensation, motor
  3. Bedrest protocol: 4–6 h strict bedrest (femoral site); axillary access allows earlier ambulation
  4. Site surveillance: Observe for oozing, pulsatile mass (pseudoaneurysm), continuous bruit (AV fistula), or acute limb ischemia
  5. Anticoagulation monitoring: Heparin continuation 24–48 h post-removal; watch for bleeding escalation

Early signs of limb ischemia: cool extremity, pallor, pain. Late signs: tissue loss, gangrene. Requires emergent vascular evaluation.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Weaning trajectory and readiness

Weaning prerequisites: EF recovery (typically > 30–35%), off vasopressors × 2–4 h, lactate normalized, HR < 100, MAP > 70 mmHg, no new ischemia.

Typical progression: ICU team initiates 1:1 → 1:2 (4–6 h observation) → 1:3 (4–6 h) → Passive/off trial (2–4 h with no augmentation) → If stable during off trial, removal. Timeline: 24–48 h or longer depending on recovery trajectory.

Failure to wean: Indicates persistent LV dysfunction or inadequate recovery trigger; escalation to VAD/ECMO evaluation.

Triggering and waveform interpretation

R-wave trigger (standard): Synchronizes inflation to ventricular depolarization; reliable in normal sinus rhythm.

Pressure trigger (alternative): Synched to dicrotic notch of arterial waveform; required in atrial fibrillation or paced rhythm; operator-dependent and less reliable.

Proper timing on waveform: Inflation begins at dicrotic notch; deflation ends just before next R-wave.

Premature inflation: wastes gas, reduces augmentation.

Late inflation: misses augmentation window.

Waveform drift indicates timing drift, trigger sensor issue, or helium leak — requires console troubleshooting.

Complications and catastrophic events

Balloon rupture: Red blood in helium tubing → STOP IABP immediately, clamp line, call STAT cardiac surgery. Helium embolism (air lock) can cause stroke, MI, or organ infarction.

Limb ischemia: 5–15% incidence with femoral access. Early detection critical — check distal pulses every 1–2 h.

Balloon malposition: Too high (above left subclavian) → absent left radial pulse, possible stroke. Too low (below renal arteries) → acute kidney injury. Confirmed by chest X-ray or fluoroscopy.

Anticoagulation complications: Heparin thrombosis risk; if platelet drop > 50% or HIT antibodies positive, switch to argatroban. Thrombus at catheter tip is rare but catastrophic.

Post-removal bleeding/pseudoaneurysm: Can occur hours to days after removal. Manual compression rarely needed beyond initial hemostasis; Doppler ultrasound if pulsatile swelling or bruit.

AV fistula: Arterial-venous communication at puncture site; presents as continuous machinery bruit + warm dilated vein. Most close spontaneously if small; some require surgical repair.

Helium leak: Sudden loss of augmentation waveform + system pressure drop. Requires balloon replacement or device removal.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. IABP-SHOCK II changed the conversation. 2012 landmark trial showed no mortality benefit in acute MI cardiogenic shock vs optimal medical therapy. Device remains in use mechanistically but mortality advantage not established — affects prognostic discussion with families.

  2. Distal pulse checks are non-negotiable. Limb ischemia is the most feared complication (5–15% incidence). Check dorsalis pedis + posterior tibial every 1–2 h in place; post-removal check every 1–2 h × 4 h minimum.

  3. Console waveform tells the story. Proper timing shows inflation at dicrotic notch + deflation before next R-wave. Drift = timing issue, sensor problem, or helium leak. Escalate to perfusion/ICU team.

  4. Weaning readiness is team-directed, not nursing-initiated. Wait for cardiac surgery or ICU attending to call the weaning plan. Inherited post-removal patients should be stabilizing on minimal support.

  5. Helium leak is catastrophic and fast. Red blood in the gas tubing = STOP, clamp, call STAT surgery. This is an ICU emergency.

  6. Heparin anticoagulation during IABP is standard. Monitor PTT, platelet count, and watch for HIT (> 50% drop). Switch to argatroban if suspected.

  7. Pressure trigger is operator-dependent and less reliable. Most commonly used in atrial fibrillation. Waveform interpretation requires experience.

  8. Post-removal pseudoaneurysm can develop 24–72 h later. Pulsatile mass at puncture site or new bruit warrants Doppler ultrasound and vascular consult.

  9. Axillary IABP allows earlier ambulation. Femoral access requires 4–6 h strict bedrest; axillary still requires monitoring but permits walking sooner.

  10. Hand-off communication matters. Knowing "EF was 25% on IABP 1:1 POD 1, weaned to 1:2 POD 2, off device POD 3" helps interpret clinical trajectory and predict stability.

cards.title: Inotropes vs. Pressors vs. Inodilators
cards.quickAnswer: Pressors raise blood pressure via vasoconstriction (increasing SVR); inotropes boost cardiac contractility; inodilators combine inotropy with vasodilation. Pressors (norepinephrine, phenylephrine, vasopressin) are first-line in distributive shock. Inotropes (dobutamine, epinephrine) treat cardiogenic shock but often cause reflex hypotension. Inodilators (milrinone) lower pulmonary and systemic afterload while improving contractility but require frequent pressor co-infusion. Selection depends on hemodynamic phenotype: distributive shock → pressor-first; cardiogenic shock → inotrope-first; RV failure or mixed shock → combination tailored to physiology.

sections.heading: 1. Definition & Class Framework
sections.bodyHtml:
Three distinct pharmacological approaches to hemodynamic support exist, often used in combination:

Pressors — agents that increase systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and mean arterial pressure (MAP) primarily through α-adrenergic vasoconstriction or non-catecholamine mechanisms. Used when SVR is low (cold periphery, wide pulses) but cardiac output is normal or elevated.

Inotropes — agents that enhance myocardial contractility via β₁-adrenergic stimulation or alternative molecular pathways. Used when cardiac output is low and the heart cannot generate adequate forward flow. Side effect: often cause reflex peripheral vasodilation → hypotension → frequent co-infusion of pressor required.

Inodilators — agents that both increase contractility AND reduce peripheral and pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR/SVR). Used in decompensated heart failure, RV failure, or mixed shock where both low output and high afterload coexist. Hypotension is common → pressor support often required for MAP goal.

Note: Pure vasodilators (nitroglycerin, nicardipine, nitroprusside, hydralazine) lower afterload without inotropy and are not discussed in detail here.

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use — Bedside Monitoring and Titration
sections.bodyHtml:
Nurses caring for patients on vasoactive infusions do not manage the pump circuits. They assess perfusion and titrate within parameters ordered by the team, then recognize decompensation.

Core nursing actions:

  • Assess perfusion — capillary refill, urine output, mental status, extremity warmth, lactate trend (if available).
  • Monitor vital signs and MAP goal — target MAP typically 65 mmHg minimum; higher (75–80) if history of hypertension or cerebrovascular disease. Recheck 5–15 min after each dose change.
  • Titrate doses within pre-set parameters — written order must specify dose range, increment size, and titration endpoint (e.g., "titrate norepinephrine to MAP 65–75 mmHg by 0.1 mcg/kg/min q5min").
  • Recognize hypotension, tachycardia, arrhythmia — escalate; do not ignore new arrhythmia on inotropes.
  • Wean carefully — reduce one agent at a time; recheck hemodynamics 15–30 min post-reduction; if patient decompensates, resume prior dose and notify team immediately.
  • Document each drip reason — e.g., "Norepinephrine for MAP goal in sepsis; dobutamine for CO augmentation post-extubation; milrinone for RV afterload reduction."
  • Cross-check with ICU or team — institution-dependent: many units will not accept patients on > 1–2 simultaneous agents on stepdown; confirm transfer criteria before acceptance.

Typical weaning sequence:

  1. Consolidate if possible — e.g., discontinue dopamine if already on norepinephrine (norepinephrine does dopamine's job better).
  2. Wean inotropes first — reduce dobutamine or milrinone before weaning pressors; rely on norepinephrine or vasopressin for BP.
  3. Last to go — norepinephrine (MAP support) often the final agent; vasopressin can stop abruptly if response good.
  4. Monitor each step — watch lactate, urine output, mental status; if patient "stalls" (unchanged dose > 48 h), escalate to team.

sections.heading: 5. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
• Dobutamine hypotension via β₂. Dobutamine drops SVR; if systolic falls > 10 mmHg at initiation, add or escalate norepinephrine in parallel. Do not increase dobutamine dose hoping for BP recovery — it will not come; add pressor instead.
  • Milrinone accumulates in acute kidney injury (AKI). If creatinine > 2.0 or eGFR < 30, milrinone half-life extends significantly; hypotension may worsen over 12–24 h post-initiation. Coordinate with renal team; may need dose reduction or switch to dobutamine.
  • HCM + dobutamine = disaster. Dobutamine increases contractility → worsens LVOT gradient → syncope, cardiogenic shock, sudden death risk. Use phenylephrine + fluid only. Check patient history on hand-off.
  • Epinephrine lactic acidosis not always ominous. Epinephrine causes mild lactate rise via peripheral vasoconstriction and β₂-mediated metabolism. If lactate < 3 mmol/L and patient otherwise stable, trend it; do not reflexively switch agents. If lactate > 4 + clinical deterioration, reassess.
  • Dopamine falling out of favor. Renal-dose dopamine (< 3 mcg/kg/min) has NO renal benefit (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020); mid-range (3–10) is less selective for β₁ than dobutamine; α effect (> 10) is unpredictable. Norepinephrine or dobutamine + pressor is cleaner. Still used at some centers; confirm your institution's protocol.
  • Peripheral norepinephrine acceptable short-term in emergency. If central line unavailable, norepinephrine via large-bore peripheral IV (18 G or better) at doses up to ~0.5 mcg/kg/min is acceptable for 2–4 h. Titrate carefully; watch for extravasation (phentolamine antidote available). Central line placement remains priority.
  • Vasopressin preserves SVR in acidosis. When acidotic (pH < 7.2), catecholamine effect blunts; vasopressin maintains SVR independent of pH status. Consider early if septic + acidotic.
  • Methylene blue + SSRI/MAOI = serotonin syndrome risk. If patient is on sertraline, paroxetine, fluoxetine, citalopram, or MAOI, methylene blue risks serotonin syndrome (agitation, rigidity, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis). Check med list before bolus; use vasopressin as alternative if contraindicated.
  • Norepinephrine > 1 mcg/kg/min = very high dose. Most septic shock patients respond to 0.1–0.5 mcg/kg/min. If escalating beyond 1 mcg/kg/min, reassess diagnosis: is this truly distributive? Is sepsis worsening? Is source control adequate? Consult ICU or infectious disease if plateau or worsening.
  • Recheck hemodynamics after each titration. Many units do q5min checks during initiation, then q15–30 min during stable periods and weaning. These are not set-and-forget infusions. Document response at each step.
  • Patients on multiple drips — document EACH reason clearly. Chart must read: "Norepinephrine for MAP goal 70 mmHg; dobutamine for cardiac output augmentation; milrinone for RV afterload reduction." Why each? Required for weaning decisions and handoff clarity.
  • Know your institution's transfer criteria. Many ICUs do NOT transfer patients actively on > 1–2 agents to stepdown. Confirm on hand-off: "Patient stable to stepdown on norepinephrine + dobutamine?" vs. "Keep in ICU until off inotropes, then transfer." Policies vary significantly.
  • Recognize tachycardia as a red flag on inotropes. Tachycardia on dobutamine or epinephrine can mask hypoxia, hypotension, sepsis, or septic cardiomyopathy. Do not attribute all tachy to the drug; assess etiology (fever, pain, anxiety, inadequate depth of sedation, or true decompensation).
  • Wean pressors cautiously in distributive shock. Some septic patients remain vasodilatory for 7–10 days. Rapid pressor weaning → sudden MAP drop → tissue hypoperfusion → organ failure. Slow, stepwise weaning with 15–30 min reassessment between steps reduces rebound shock.
  • PDE-3 inhibitors + diuretics can worsen hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia. Milrinone promotes cAMP-driven diuresis; combined with loop diuretics, electrolyte wasting is aggressive. Monitor K⁺ and Mg²⁺ closely; supplement proactively.

sections.heading: 6. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Receptor physiology and dose-response curves

Alpha (α) receptors — smooth muscle vasoconstriction. Increase SVR and MAP. Primary site: arteriolar smooth muscle (peripheral vascular bed). High-dose catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine at > 0.1 mcg/kg/min) activate these. Pure α agents (phenylephrine) have no cardiac effect.

Beta-1 (β₁) receptors — myocardial contractility and chronotropic effect. Increase heart rate and force of contraction. Dose-dependent: dobutamine and epinephrine at low-mid doses activate β₁ preferentially.

Beta-2 (β₂) receptors — vascular smooth muscle vasodilation. At higher doses, dobutamine and epinephrine activate β₂ → peripheral vasodilation → SVR drop and often hypotension as a side effect.

Dopamine receptors (D1) — renal and splanchnic vasodilation at very low doses (< 3 mcg/kg/min). Concept of "renal-dose dopamine" for oliguria protection is disproven (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020); no benefit for AKI prevention.

V1 receptors — vasopressin-specific; non-catecholamine mechanism. Vasoconstriction independent of catecholamine receptor status; useful when adrenergic tone is exhausted or pH is low.

PDE-3 inhibition (milrinone) — phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor increases intracellular cAMP without activating adrenergic receptors. Inotropic effect + vasodilation; useful in catecholamine-resistant states.

Drug mechanism table — detailed pathophysiology
AgentMechanismOnsetDurationMetabolismKey Feature
Norepinephrineα >> β₁ adrenergic agonist1–2 min5–10 min post-infusionHepatic COMT / MAOBalanced pressor + mild inotropy
PhenylephrinePure α₁ agonist5–20 min15–20 minHepatic COMT / MAOStrongest vasoconstrictor; no inotropy
VasopressinV1 (AVP) receptor agonist10–30 min10–20 minHepatic / renalNon-catecholamine; works in acidosis
Methylene BlueGuanylate cyclase + NO inhibitionMinutes4–6 hHepatic reductionSingle-dose intervention; long effect duration
Dobutamineβ₁ > β₂ agonist1–2 min5–10 minHepatic COMTInotrope with β₂ vasodilation side effect
Epinephrineβ₁ = β₂ (low) → α (high dose)1–2 min5–10 minHepatic COMT / MAOUnpredictable mid-range effect; dose-dependent
DopamineD1 < 3; β₁ 3–10; α > 10 mcg/kg/min1–2 min5–10 minHepatic COMT / MAONon-selective; falling out of favor
MilrinonePDE-3 inhibition (cAMP ↑)2–5 min30–60 min (renal clearance)Renal (80%) + hepaticAccumulates in AKI; requires fluid co-therapy
LevosimendanCalcium sensitizer; troponin C binding10–15 min60–90 minHepatic metabolismLong-acting; European use; not FDA-approved
Renal and systemic effects — clinical consequences beyond hemodynamics

Norepinephrine — excellent renal perfusion pressure at moderate doses; sustained high-dose (> 1 mcg/kg/min) can reduce renal blood flow via intense vasoconstriction.

Phenylephrine — pure vasoconstriction includes renal vessels; prolonged use increases AKI risk if volume depletion coexists.

Dobutamine — direct renal vasodilation; used to augment urine output, but diuresis depends on adequate perfusion pressure and cardiac output, not the drug alone.

Epinephrine — at high doses, splanchnic vasoconstriction and gut ischemia risk increase; lactic acidosis often reflects tissue hypoperfusion.

Milrinone — promotes cAMP-driven diuresis; aggressive fluid and electrolyte wasting; accumulates in renal failure (half-life up to 10+ h if GFR < 10).

Dopamine — splanchnic and renal vasodilation at low doses, but no protective effect on AKI proven; tachycardia-mediated increased metabolic demand can worsen lactic acidosis.

Controversies and recent guideline shifts

Dopamine in septic shock — 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign Guidelines recommend against dopamine as first-line; norepinephrine is preferred (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020). Dopamine carries higher arrhythmia risk and less predictable vasoconstriction. Still used at some centers; confirm your institution's protocol.

Epinephrine timing in septic shock — not first-line; reserved for refractory hypotension despite norepinephrine escalation. Risk of lactic acidosis and arrhythmia increases with duration and dose. 2022 AHA/ACC HF Guideline de-emphasizes epinephrine monotherapy for acute HF.

Hydrocortisone in refractory shock — low-dose steroid (50 mg IV q6h) sometimes added if pressor escalation plateaus in septic shock. Evidence is mixed; practice varies by institution.

Methylene blue for vasoplegia — emerging evidence supports single-dose use in post-op and post-transfusion vasoplegia, but limited large RCT data; used as a bridge to steroids rather than monotherapy.

Levosimendan in cardiogenic shock — shows promise in European trials but unavailable in USA. Concept of calcium sensitization without catecholamine effect is attractive for catecholamine-resistant states; future USA trials planned.

sections.heading: 7. Red Flags — Deterioration in Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
• New or worsening tachycardia on inotropes (not just from the drug) — consider fever, pain, inadequate sedation, hypovolemia, sepsis, or cardiac decompensation.
  • MAP decline despite escalating doses — tachyphylaxis, sepsis progression, hemorrhage, or need for combination therapy; reassess diagnosis and physiology.
  • New arrhythmia (atrial fibrillation, ectopy, SVT) — inotropes lower threshold; obtain ECG; assess electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺); may require agent change or rate control.
  • Urine output drop while on inotropes — inotrope-induced tachycardia + splanchnic vasoconstriction (esp. dopamine, high-dose epi) can reduce renal perfusion; reassess MAP goal, consider fluid challenge or agent change.
  • Rising creatinine or BUN despite adequate MAP — may signal AKI from drug-induced renal vasoconstriction (phenylephrine, dopamine) or milrinone accumulation; adjust therapy.
  • Extremity pallor or mottling while on pressor — intense peripheral vasoconstriction may impair tissue perfusion; consider reducing dose, adding inotrope for inotropy, or reassessing shock phenotype.
  • Lactate rising while on therapy — may reflect inadequate tissue perfusion (too much vasoconstriction, not enough inotropy) or epinephrine toxicity; reassess combination + MAP goal.
  • New or worsening mental status changes on inotropes — delirium, agitation, focal deficit; consider hypoglycemia, hypoxia, sepsis, or CNS effect from drug + underlying illness.
  • Rapid weight gain or new pulmonary edema on milrinone — inodilator-induced diuresis failure or fluid overload from IV therapy; reassess fluid balance and diuretics.

cards.title: Periprocedural Anticoagulation Bridging
phase: Preop` *(2–3 Days Pre Procedure)* / `Pod 0` Through `Pod 7` / `Discharge Prep
cards.quickAnswer: Periprocedural AC bridge: evaluate thromboembolic risk (CHA2DS2-VASc for AF, HAS-BLED for bleeding, mechanical valve always requires bridge). BRIDGE trial (Douketis, 2015) supports no bridge for most AF without high-risk features (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5, recent stroke/TIA, mechanical valve, or VTE <3 mo). Hold warfarin 5 days pre-op, target INR <1.5; start UFH (80 units/kg bolus, 18 units/kg/h infusion, goal PTT 60–80 sec) or LMWH bridge if high-risk. Last UFH dose 6h pre-op, LMWH last dose 24h pre-op. Restart AC 24–72h post-op per hemostasis; overlap UFH/LMWH + warfarin 3–7 days to therapeutic INR. DOACs need only 24–48h hold (renal function–dependent), no bridging; restart when hemostasis achieved.
