sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Inpatient management of patients whose ongoing anticoagulation must be interrupted for surgery. Interruption creates a thromboembolic risk gap. Bridging strategy depends on underlying indication (AF, mechanical valve, VTE history) and baseline thrombotic risk.
  • Incidence & prevalence: 5–10% of elective surgeries involve anticoagulated patients (Douketis et al., 2015). Mechanical valve patients = nearly 100% bridge indication. High-risk AF (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5, recent stroke/TIA) ≈ 40% bridge indication. Non-valvular AF alone ≈ <5% bridge indication (BRIDGE trial changed practice).
  • Who this applies to: Patients on chronic warfarin, LMWH, or DOAC requiring a surgical, endoscopic, or ablation procedure lasting >30 min or involving significant bleeding risk.
  • When this applies: Pre-operative period (typically 2–5 days), intra-operative, and post-operative period until oral anticoagulation is restarted and therapeutic (3–7 days typical).
  • Why admission: High-risk patients (mechanical valve, recent VTE, CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5 or prior stroke/TIA) benefit from controlled IV anticoagulation during the AC gap rather than outpatient LMWH, due to reliability of monitoring, dosing, and emergency reversal capability.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Thromboembolic vs bleeding risk balance in perioperative period (expandable) The perioperative anticoagulation dilemma is a collision of two competing physiologies: Thromboembolic risk (increases without AC):
  • Stasis during immobility and surgery
  • Endothelial injury from vascular manipulation
  • Activation of tissue factor and coagulation cascade
  • Risk highest in mechanical valves (left atrial flow stasis), recent VTE (residual thrombus burden), AF with structural heart disease (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5 = stroke risk ~5% per year), and recent stroke/TIA (acute infarct with embolic substrate). Surgical bleeding risk (increases with AC):
  • Anticoagulation prolongs bleeding times, impairs platelet function (via factor inhibition), and reduces fibrin deposition.
  • Risk highest immediately post-op (first 24–72h), especially in cardiac surgery (open heart, pericardial cavity, mediastinal tubes).
  • AC gap for 3–5 days pre-op is necessary to allow INR to fall (<2.0) and permit hemostasis. BRIDGE trial (2015) insight (Douketis et al., 2015): Most patients with AF alone (no mechanical valve, no recent VTE, no prior stroke/TIA) have low absolute thromboembolism risk during a brief AC gap. Perioperative bridging with LMWH/UFH adds bleeding risk without benefit. Strategy shifted to "no bridge for AF unless high-risk features." Mechanical valve exception: Mechanical valves have thrombosis risk 5–10× higher than bioprosthetic valves and remain at constant risk regardless of procedural gap. Bridge is always indicated for mechanical valves.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Who presents with this admission and when.

  • Pre-op bridging admission: Patient scheduled for elective surgery, currently on warfarin or DOAC, assessed as high thromboembolic risk, presents 2–5 days pre-procedure for therapeutic AC via IV heparin while awaiting surgery.
  • Post-op bridging admission: Patient admitted post-op major surgery (especially cardiac surgery or high-bleeding-risk noncardiac), requiring resumption of anticoagulation but not yet able to tolerate or absorb oral anticoagulants reliably. IV heparin restarted 24–72h post-op per hemostasis, then overlapped with warfarin until INR therapeutic.
  • Failed outpatient bridging: Patient initially managed outpatient with LMWH bridge, developed bleeding, subtherapeutic INR, or other complications requiring inpatient transition to IV UFH for more precise control.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Systematic information gathering at admission (pre-op) and daily (intra- and post-op).

Pre-operative admission assessment:

  • Anticoagulation indication: Mechanical valve type (aortic vs mitral) and age; AF duration and CHA2DS2-VASc score; VTE history and timing; prior stroke/TIA; HIT history.
  • Baseline labs: PT/INR, PTT, CBC (baseline platelets for HIT surveillance), CMP (renal function for LMWH dosing), fibrinogen, type & screen.
  • Procedure details: Type, planned duration, expected bleeding risk, surgeon and anesthesia contact/preferences for AC hold timing.
  • Medication reconciliation: Current anticoagulant, dose, last dose taken; home beta-blockers, NSAIDs, antibiotics, herbals (many interact with warfarin).
  • Bleeding history: GI bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, epistaxis, easy bruising, falls, medication adherence, alcohol use.
  • Renal function: CrCl for LMWH dosing and DOAC hold duration.
  • Vital signs & hemodynamics: Baseline BP, HR, perfusion status.

Daily (intra- and post-op) assessment:

  • INR & PTT trends: Daily INR pre-op; INR daily post-op until therapeutic; PTT q6h on heparin drip until stable, then q12h.
  • CBC daily: Platelet count (HIT surveillance), hemoglobin (post-op bleeding).
  • CMP every 12–24h: Renal function, electrolytes (K+, Mg2+ affect arrhythmia and coagulation).
  • Fibrinogen, D-dimer: If concerned about DIC or excessive bleeding post-op.
  • Drain output: Post-op mediastinal/chest tubes q2–4h; quantify volume, character (serous vs sanguineous).
  • Bleeding signs: Incision (erythema, warmth, sanguineous drainage), hematomas, ecchymoses, mucous membrane bleeding, hematuria.
  • Vital signs & perfusion: HR, BP, capillary refill, mental status (indicators of bleeding or thrombosis).
  • Line integrity: IV infiltration, heparin drip running, patent access.
  • Medication adherence & timing: Warfarin given same time daily; UFH/LMWH infusion rates per protocol; any holds or delays documented.

sections.heading: 5A. Pre-operative Bridging (Hold Warfarin → Therapeutic Heparin → Hold Heparin pre-op)
sections.bodyHtml:
Day 1 (admission day):

  1. Verify procedure type, timing, & surgeon preferences for heparin hold (typically 4–6h pre-op for UFH; 24h for LMWH).
  2. Draw baseline labs: PT/INR, PTT, CBC, CMP, fibrinogen, type & screen.
  3. Hold warfarin or DOAC on admission (or confirmed already held).
  4. Do NOT start heparin immediately. Wait for INR to drop below 2.0 (takes 2–4 days post-hold). Starting heparin while INR still elevated = over-anticoagulation and bleeding risk.
  5. Document INR target range for patient's indication: AF or aortic valve = 2.0–3.0; mitral valve = 2.5–3.5.
  6. Begin patient/family education: Explain AC gap risk, why bridging, timeline, why warfarin takes time to work, vitamin K consistency, bleeding precautions.
  7. Assess bleeding risk modifiers: GI bleed history, ICH history, recent trauma → may adjust PTT target or bridge intensity.
  8. Daily INR draw until INR < 2.0.

Day 2–4 (waiting for INR to drop, then heparin infusion):

  1. INR daily. Most patients: INR falls to <2.0 by day 3.
  2. When INR reaches <2.0: Start UFH or LMWH per high-risk determination (see §5A-Risk Stratification table below). - UFH IV bolus + infusion: 80 units/kg bolus, then 18 units/kg/h infusion. - LMWH SC injection: Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h (renal dosing: CrCl <30 = 1 mg/kg/day); dalteparin 200 units/kg/day SC.
  3. UFH monitoring: PTT at baseline, then 6h after start. Goal PTT 60–80 sec (equivalent anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 IU/mL). Adjust infusion q6h per PTT (increase/decrease by 2–4 units/kg/h per protocol).
  4. LMWH monitoring: Baseline PTT; anti-Xa level 3–5 days into infusion if high-risk or renal dysfunction (goal 0.5–1.2 IU/mL for q12h dosing).
  5. Daily CBC: Platelet count >100K is baseline; drop >50% or <100K = HIT suspect; stop heparin, draw HIT serology (ELISA + 4T score), switch to argatroban (2 mcg/kg/min IV, no bolus) or bivalirudin (0.15 mg/kg/h IV).
  6. Daily INR: Remains low (<1.5) while on heparin and off warfarin.
  7. Continue until procedure day.

Pre-operative day (procedure day):

  1. Final PTT 2–4h pre-op: Confirm 60–80 sec range.
  2. Hold UFH 4–6h pre-op (per surgeon direction).
  3. LMWH patients: Last dose given 24h pre-op.
  4. Final INR AM: Should be <2.0 (subtherapeutic is desired for surgery).
  5. NPO status: Per anesthesia.
  6. Confirm surgical team aware of anticoagulation status and plan for resumption post-op.

sections.heading: 5B. Post-operative Bridging (Hold → Assess Hemostasis → Restart UFH + Warfarin → Overlap until INR therapeutic)
sections.bodyHtml:
POD 0 (day of surgery):

  1. Do NOT restart heparin immediately. Wait 12–24h for hemostasis confirmation.
  2. Assess bleeding: Chest tube output, drain character, foley hematuria, dressing saturation, incision ooze.
  3. Baseline labs: PT/INR, PTT, CBC, CMP.
  4. Hold warfarin and any bridging agent pending bleeding assessment.

POD 1:

  1. Verify hemostasis stable: Chest tubes <50–100 mL/h, drains slowing, no active incision ooze.
  2. If bleeding stable: Restart UFH drip—bolus 80 units/kg IV, infusion 18 units/kg/h. Restart warfarin 5 mg PO daily (do NOT wait to start warfarin; it takes 3–7 days to become therapeutic; delay = prolonged admission).
  3. Check PTT 6h after heparin restart. Goal PTT 60–80 sec. Adjust q6h per protocol.
  4. Check INR on POD 1. Usually 1.0–1.2 (not therapeutic yet, expected).
  5. Daily CBC: Platelet count, hemoglobin trend.
  6. Continue anticoagulation assessment: Drain monitoring q4h, vitals q4h first 24h post-op.

POD 2–3 (overlap phase):

  1. Maintain UFH + warfarin overlap. Both running simultaneously until INR ≥2.0 × 24h.
  2. INR daily. Trend toward goal.
  3. PTT q6–12h (adjust UFH per goal).
  4. Warfarin dose adjustment per pharmacist/attending: If INR <1.5 on POD 3, may increase warfarin to 7.5–10 mg (depends on patient, diet, interactions).
  5. CBC daily. Platelet, hemoglobin.
  6. Assess bleeding: Continue drain monitoring.

POD 4–7 (bridging completion, discharge prep):

  1. INR daily until INR ≥2.0 × 24h.
  2. Once INR ≥2.0 × 24h: Discontinue UFH drip.
  3. Continue warfarin at maintenance dose (typically 5–10 mg daily; varies by patient).
  4. Before discharge:
    • INR therapeutic (≥2.0 for AF/aortic valve; ≥2.5 for mitral valve)
    • Warfarin prescription verified and filled
    • INR recheck appointment scheduled (2–3 days post-discharge, then weekly × 4 weeks, then monthly per INR stability)
    • Patient education packet: warfarin timing, vitamin K consistency, bleeding signs, outpatient follow-up contact info
    • PCP summary: bridging indication, warfarin dose, target INR, follow-up INR schedule

sections.heading: 5A. Thromboembolic Risk Stratification & Bridge Decision
sections.bodyHtml:
Decision table — when to bridge:

Risk Category Indication Thromboembolic Risk per Year Bridge Strategy
Very High Mechanical mitral valve ~5–10% (untreated) Always bridge — UFH or LMWH for entire AC gap. No exceptions.
Very High Recent VTE (<3 mo) ~10–15% (untreated) Always bridge — UFH or LMWH; residual thrombus burden high.
Very High Recent stroke/TIA (<3 mo) ~10–15% untreated Always bridge — UFH or LMWH; acute infarct with embolic substrate.
High Mechanical aortic valve ~2–3% (untreated) Bridge — UFH or LMWH strongly recommended; lower risk than mitral but still significant.
High AF + CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5 or CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5 + prior stroke/TIA ~5% yearly Bridge — UFH or LMWH; BRIDGE trial subgroup analysis supports bridge for this group.
Moderate–High AF + CHA2DS2-VASc 3–4 (no prior stroke/TIA) ~2–4% yearly No bridge recommended (BRIDGE trial); UFH/LMWH gap risk similar to perioperative risk. Outpatient LMWH acceptable. Consider bridging if multiple other risk factors (COPD, CHF, advanced age >75).
Moderate AF alone, CHA2DS2-VASc <3 or non-valvular AF no prior VTE/stroke <1–2% yearly No bridge (BRIDGE trial, Douketis 2015) — perioperative gap risk <1% thromboembolism; bridge adds bleeding without benefit.
Low Bioprosthetic valve ~0.5–1% (untreated) No bridge — low thrombosis risk. Standard perioperative AC management (hold 5 days pre-op).
HIT history Any above + prior HIT Variable Use argatroban or bivalirudin — never UFH/LMWH. See §5C HIT-Specific Bridging.

CHA2DS2-VASc score components: C=CHF (1 point), H=HTN (1), A2=age ≥75 (2), D=DM (1), S2=stroke/TIA (2), V=vascular disease (1), A=age 65–74 (1), Sc=female sex (1). Score ≥2 = stroke risk warrants AC. Score ≥5 = high-risk subgroup per BRIDGE analysis.

HAS-BLED score (bleeding risk): H=HTN (1), A=age >60 (1), S=stroke history (1), B=bleeding history (1), L=labile INR (1), E=elderly >65 (1), D=drugs/NSAID (1). HAS-BLED ≥3 = moderate–high bleeding risk; consider bleeding-focused bridging strategy.

sections.heading: 5B. Bridge Agent Selection & Dosing
sections.bodyHtml:
UFH (unfractionated heparin) IV:

Parameter Value Notes
Bolus 80 units/kg IV Once-only at initiation; no repeat bolus.
Infusion 18 units/kg/h IV Started after bolus; titrated q6h per PTT.
PTT goal 60–80 sec Equivalent to anti-Xa 0.3–0.7 IU/mL (some labs use anti-Xa directly).
Monitoring PTT baseline, 6h post-start, then q6h until stable, then q12h More frequent than LMWH; allows rapid adjustment.
Adjustment PTT <60: +2–4 units/kg/h; PTT >80: -2–4 units/kg/h Sliding scale per institutional protocol.
Last dose pre-op Hold 4–6h pre-op (UFH clears rapidly; ~90 min half-life) Confirm PTT 2–4h pre-op in goal range.
Restart post-op POD 1 if hemostasis stable; same bolus + infusion regimen Full dose; do not reduce post-op.
HIT concern Baseline CBC, then daily. Platelet drop >50% or <100K = HIT suspect; stop immediately. Incidence 0.5–1% of UFH exposure.

LMWH (enoxaparin or dalteparin) SC:

Parameter Value Notes
Enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h CrCl >30; renal adjust <30 = 1 mg/kg SC once daily.
Dalteparin 200 units/kg SC daily or 100 units/kg q12h Weight-based; renal adjust <30 per product labeling.
Anti-Xa monitoring Baseline and day 3–5 if high-risk or renal dysfunction Goal anti-Xa 0.5–1.2 IU/mL for prophylactic dosing; may be higher for therapeutic (1.0–2.0 depending on indication).
Last dose pre-op Last dose 24h pre-op 48h if high bleeding risk or CrCl <30.
Restart post-op POD 1 if hemostasis stable; same dose/frequency as pre-op Full dose.
HIT concern CBC baseline and daily for 5 days. Cross-reactivity with UFH ~80–100%; if HIT history, avoid LMWH; use argatroban/bivalirudin. HIT antibodies may be slower to develop on LMWH than UFH.
Advantage over UFH Once or twice daily SC; no drip monitoring; predictable pharmacokinetics; outpatient bridging possible. Disadvantage: cannot reverse rapidly (protamine partial reversal); less flexible for rapid dose changes.

DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) — NO BRIDGING:

DOAC Hold Pre-op Restart Post-op Renal Dosing Notes
Apixaban (Eliquat) 24h before procedure (both low and high risk) 24h post-op if hemostasis achieved; no UFH bridge needed Normal renal function: 5 mg PO q12h. No dose adjustment unless age ≥60, weight ≤60 kg, or Cr ≥1.5.
Rivaroxaban (Xarelto) 24h before procedure 24h post-op if hemostasis achieved; no bridge needed CrCl >50: 20 mg PO daily (AF). CrCl 15–50: 15 mg daily. CrCl <15: not recommended.
Edoxaban (Savaysa) 24–48h depending on CrCl (CrCl <15 = 48h) 24h post-op if hemostasis achieved CrCl >50: 60 mg PO daily. CrCl 15–50: 30 mg daily. CrCl <15: not recommended.
Dabigatran (Pradaxa) 24–48h depending on CrCl and renal function 24h post-op if hemostasis achieved CrCl >50: 110 or 150 mg PO q12h. CrCl <50: use lower dose (110 mg) or avoid.

Key point: DOACs do NOT require bridging. Direct-acting mechanism means the drug is active immediately upon restart. Shorter pre-op hold (24–48h vs warfarin 5 days) reduces AC gap time.

sections.heading: 5C. HIT-Specific Bridging (Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia)
sections.bodyHtml:
If HIT suspected or confirmed (platelet drop >50% or <100K on heparin):

  1. Stop UFH/LMWH immediately. Even if PTT subtherapeutic, do not continue.
  2. Draw HIT serology: ELISA for HIT antibodies + 4T score (Thrombosis, Timing, Thrombocytopenia, no other cause); arrange confirmatory assay if positive (HIPA, washed platelet activation test).
  3. Switch to alternative agent per institution protocol.

Argatroban (alternative anticoagulant for HIT):

Parameter Value Notes
Bolus None required Can give 0.1–0.2 mg/kg if emergent, but not standard.
Infusion Start 2 mcg/kg/min IV No bolus.
Monitoring PTT baseline, 6h post-start, then per sliding scale Goal PTT 1.5–3.0 × baseline (or per lab's anti-Xa equivalent).
Adjustment Typical range 0.5–5 mcg/kg/min Titrate up by 0.5 mcg/kg/min per 30 min if PTT subgoal; max 10 mcg/kg/min.
Renal dosing No renal adjustment — hepatic metabolism Safe in renal failure.
Warfarin overlap Start warfarin POD 1 (same timeline as UFH). Overlap argatroban + warfarin until INR ≥2.0 × 24h. INR may be falsely elevated while on argatroban; recheck INR 4–5 days after argatroban discontinuation.
INR interpretation Argatroban increases INR by ~10–20% independently; true warfarin effect unknown while on argatroban Wait 4–5 days post-argatroban to assess true warfarin INR.
Off-label use Off-label for bridging; check institutional approvals More common for HIT + thrombosis or HIT + cardiac surgery bridging.

Bivalirudin (alternative anticoagulant for HIT):

Parameter Value Notes
Bolus None standard (can give 0.1–0.2 mg/kg if emergent) Direct thrombin inhibitor; rapid onset.
Infusion 0.15 mg/kg/h IV Started without bolus.
Monitoring PTT baseline, 6h post-start, then per protocol Goal PTT 1.5–2.5 × baseline or per lab anti-Xa equivalent.
Adjustment Typical range 0.05–0.20 mg/kg/h Titrate per PTT; slower titration than argatroban.
Renal dosing CrCl <30: reduce by 25%; dialysis: reduce by 50% Renally cleared; requires adjustment in renal failure.
Warfarin overlap Start POD 1; overlap until INR ≥2.0 × 24h. PT/INR prolongs more with bivalirudin than argatroban; verify INR 4–5 days post-discontinuation.
INR interpretation Bivalirudin prolongs PT/INR more than argatroban; prefer PTT or anti-Xa while on bivalirudin. True warfarin INR unknown until 4–5 days post-bivalirudin.
FDA approval Approved for HIT (PCI indication); off-label for perioperative bridging Check institutional HIT protocol.

Fondaparinux (alternative, controversial in HIT):

  • Not first-line for perioperative HIT bridging. Higher rates of HIT thrombosis reported with fondaparinux in cross-reactive settings. Argatroban or bivalirudin preferred.
  • Can be considered for HIT patients requiring longer-term anticoagulation (e.g., post-discharge) under hematology guidance, but avoid perioperative bridging with fondaparinux.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN] calling about [patient, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]. Patient on bridging [UFH/LMWH/argatroban]." B: "Admitted [date] for AC bridge [indication: mechanical valve / high-risk AF / recent VTE / HIT]. Current INR [value], PTT [value] on [agent]. [Relevant recent labs]." A: "Patient is [stable / experiencing bleeding / subtherapeutic anticoagulation / suspected HIT]. [Specific findings]." R: "Requesting [INR check / STAT bleeding assessment / PTT adjustment order / HIT workup / hematology consult / bridging plan clarification]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable pre-op: INR approaching target, heparin therapeutic Attending or primary APP (routine daily check-in)
INR >4.0 pre-op Attending — do NOT proceed to OR; vitamin K adjustment may be needed
Suspected HIT (platelet drop >50%) STAT hematology + attending — stop heparin immediately
Bleeding — minor (nosebleed, hematuria) Attending / APP; hold heparin, draw INR/PTT/CBC
Bleeding — moderate (hematemesis, melena, soaked dressing, chest tube >200 mL/h) STAT Code for bleeding + surgeon — prepare for OR evacuation or reversal (FFP, transfusion)
Bleeding — major (ICH, hemodynamic instability, uncontrolled ooze) ICU transfer + Code blue — heparin reversal, massive transfusion protocol
Suspected DVT/PE post-op STAT imaging (duplex/CTA) + attending; continue heparin
Suspected stroke post-op Stroke code + neurology; STAT head CT; continue heparin pending CT result
Recurrent POAF with bridging CT surgery + EP consult — bridge may complicate arrhythmia management
Pre-discharge: INR subtherapeutic on warfarin despite POD 4–5 Pharmacist + attending; check warfarin timing, diet, interactions, malabsorption; may increase dose or extend admission

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Subsections marked expandable.

sections.heading: 7.1 BRIDGE Trial & the paradigm shift
sections.bodyHtml:
BRIDGE trial — why no bridge for most AF (expandable) The trial (Douketis et al., 2015): Randomized, double-blind trial in 1,884 patients with non-valvular AF undergoing planned surgery, comparing perioperative bridging with LMWH to placebo (no bridging). Key findings:
  • Thromboembolism rate (LMWH bridge): 0.3% (3/1,042 patients during perioperative period)
  • Thromboembolism rate (no bridge): 0.4% (4/842 patients)
  • Major bleeding rate (LMWH bridge): 3.2% (33/1,042)
  • Major bleeding rate (no bridge): 1.3% (11/842)
  • Conclusion: Perioperative bridging with LMWH does NOT reduce thromboembolism in non-valvular AF and increases bleeding significantly (p<0.001). Implication: Most AF patients do NOT need bridging. BRIDGE changed practice from "bridge everyone" to "bridge only if high-risk features." High-risk subgroup per BRIDGE: Patients with CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5 or prior stroke/TIA had more events in the no-bridge arm and may benefit from bridging, but this subgroup analysis was post-hoc. Prospective trials have not confirmed bridging benefit in this group; bridging remains reasonable based on expert consensus (Spyropoulos et al., 2022). Takeaway: No bridge for AF alone, CHA2DS2-VASc <5, no prior stroke/TIA, no mechanical valve, no recent VTE. Bridge always for mechanical valve. Bridge consider for CHA2DS2-VASc ≥5, prior stroke/TIA, or recent VTE.

sections.heading: 7.2 DOAC perioperative management — shorter hold, no bridging
sections.bodyHtml:
DOACs (direct-acting oral anticoagulants) perioperative strategy (expandable) Why no bridge for DOACs:
  • DOACs have direct, rapid mechanism (thrombin inhibitors or Xa inhibitors).
  • Upon restart, therapeutic effect is immediate (plasma levels peak in 1–3 hours depending on agent).
  • No need for overlap with UFH/LMWH to achieve anticoagulation (unlike warfarin, which takes 3–7 days).
  • BRIDGE trial was warfarin-only; DOAC trials (e.g., RE-ALIGN for dabigatran) actually showed WORSE outcomes with bridging (thrombosis, bleeding). Perioperative DOAC timeline:
  • Hold: 24h pre-op for most DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban). Dabigatran and edoxaban: 24–48h depending on CrCl.
  • Last dose: Take last dose 24h (or per agent guideline) before procedure.
  • AC gap: 24–48h gap (much shorter than warfarin's 5–7 day gap).
  • Restart: 24h post-op if hemostasis achieved. Full dose; no bridging with UFH/LMWH.
  • Pharmacokinetics: Peak effect 1–3h; steady-state 3–5 days. Resuming at full dose acceptable post-op (no loading period needed). Renal function is critical:
  • Apixaban: minimal renal clearance; minimal adjustment.
  • Rivaroxaban, edoxaban: renal clearance 50%; moderate adjustment if CrCl <30.
  • Dabigatran: heavily renally cleared; significant adjustment or avoid if CrCl <30. Post-op timing flexibility:
  • DOAC restart is NOT surgeon-dependent (unlike bridging, where surgeon dictates heparin timing).
  • Once hemostasis achieved (no active drain output, incision stable), restart DOAC.
  • Typical: POD 1–2 for most patients. Transition from warfarin to DOAC post-op:
  • If patient was pre-op on warfarin but suitable for DOAC post-op (non-valvular AF, normal renal function), can transition once INR drops below therapeutic.
  • Stop warfarin and UFH once DOAC restarted; no overlap needed (direct effect).
  • Simplifies post-op anticoagulation and shortens admission.

sections.heading: 7.3 Mechanical valve bridging — always bridge
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanical valve perioperative strategy (expandable) Mechanical valve thrombosis risk:
  • Mechanical valves have thrombosis risk 5–10× higher than bioprosthetic valves.
  • Risk is constant (unlike AF, where risk is dynamic based on CHA2DS2-VASc).
  • Left atrial stasis (mitral position) = higher risk than aortic.
  • Even a brief AC gap (<24h) carries unacceptable risk of valve thrombosis and stroke. Bridging is ALWAYS indicated for mechanical valves:
  • No exceptions based on CHA2DS2-VASc or other modifiers.
  • Mechanical mitral >> mechanical aortic in risk; both require bridge. Perioperative mechanical valve timeline:
  • Pre-op: Hold warfarin 5 days pre-op, target INR <2.0. Start UFH (preferred) or LMWH bridge once INR <2.0.
  • UFH preferred over LMWH for mechanical valves — easier to reverse if bleeding; more rapid titration if needed.
  • Last UFH dose: 6h pre-op (to allow reversal if emergency reversal needed).
  • Post-op POD 1: Restart UFH (bolus 80 units/kg, infusion 18 units/kg/h) + warfarin immediately if hemostasis stable.
  • Overlap duration: Mechanical mitral typically requires 3–7 days overlap (longer than AF) to ensure INR ≥2.5 × 24h and valve hemostasis verified.
  • No transition to DOAC: Mechanical valves are a contraindication to DOAC therapy (insufficient stroke prevention data; warfarin remains standard). Special consideration — mechanical valve + recent procedure:
  • Some surgeons recommend brief IV heparin even within the first 24h post-op (12–24h post-op resumption) for mechanical valves given thrombosis risk.
  • Discuss timing with surgeon pre-op; do not assume "wait 24h" for all mechanical valve patients.

sections.heading: 7.4 INR therapeutic timeline and overlap strategy
sections.bodyHtml:
Why warfarin takes 3–7 days and overlap is necessary (expandable) Warfarin pharmacology:
  • Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X) with half-lives 6–60 hours.
  • Factor VII (shortest half-life) is inhibited within 24h → PT/INR rises initially.
  • But factor II (longest half-life, ~60 hours) takes 3–7 days to become significantly depleted.
  • True anticoagulant effect requires all four factors depleted → 3–7 days minimum. Why overlap with UFH/LMWH:
  • Warfarin's rapid INR rise (due to factor VII depletion) is misleading. Early INR elevation does NOT mean therapeutic anticoagulation.
  • During the warfarin "lag phase" (days 1–3), patient is actually at thrombosis risk despite elevated INR.
  • UFH/LMWH bridge provides therapeutic anticoagulation during this lag phase.
  • Once INR ≥2.0 × 24h (meaning factor II is sufficiently depleted), UFH/LMWH can be discontinued. Typical post-op timeline:
  • POD 1: Warfarin started 5 mg PO daily; INR ~1.0–1.2 (not therapeutic; expected)
  • POD 2: Warfarin 5 mg PO daily; INR ~1.5 (approaching but not therapeutic)
  • POD 3: INR ~2.0 (may achieve therapeutic INR; check daily)
  • POD 4–5: INR ≥2.0 × 24h confirmed; discontinue UFH; continue warfarin Patient-specific factors that prolong INR rise:
  • Warfarin-naive patients (slower saturation of vitamin K-dependent factors)
  • Malabsorption (short gut, severe diarrhea)
  • Medication interactions (antibiotics, NSAIDs, supplements reducing warfarin absorption)
  • Vitamin K intake (dietary consistency matters; sudden increase = INR drop)
  • Liver dysfunction (warfarin metabolism via CYP2C9)
  • Genetics (CYP2C9 polymorphisms; VKORC1 variants affect warfarin sensitivity) Do not rush warfarin dose escalation:
  • Common error: INR <2.0 on POD 2 → increase warfarin to 7.5–10 mg to speed INR rise.
  • Often counterproductive: warfarin accumulates; INR overshoots to >4.0 by POD 4.
  • Warfarin dosing is better left to pharmacists/attending unless INR plateau evident by POD 4–5.

sections.heading: 7.5 Post-op bleeding vs thrombosis balance in the AC patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Dual risk management — when to hold, when to continue (expandable) Post-op bleeding risk dominates first 24–72h:
  • Surgical hemostasis is fragile; fresh surgical wounds bleed.
  • Anticoagulation increases bleeding risk by 30–50% in first 24–48h post-op.
  • Strategy: withhold anticoagulation until hemostasis confirmed (stable drain output, no ooze). Thrombosis risk emerges by POD 3–5:
  • Surgical immobility, tissue factor release, and inflammatory state peak POD 2–3.
  • AC gap too long (>5–7 days) increases thrombosis risk, especially mechanical valve or recent VTE.
  • Strategy: resume anticoagulation as soon as hemostasis permits (typically POD 1–2). The balance (POD 0–1):
  • POD 0: No anticoagulation. Hemostasis priority.
  • Late POD 1 or POD 2: If drain output <50 mL/h, incision dry, no clinical bleeding → restart anticoagulation.
  • POD 1 restart is standard for mechanical valve, recent VTE, or high-risk AF.
  • POD 2–3 restart acceptable for low-risk AF if surgeon prefers extra hemostasis window. Scenario: prolonged bleeding (chest tube >200 mL/h POD 1):
  • Do NOT start anticoagulation.
  • Reassess POD 2–3; restart once bleeding stabilizes.
  • Risk: AC gap extends beyond optimal period. Coordinate with surgeon and hematology if delay >3–4 days. Scenario: mechanical valve patient with excessive post-op bleeding:
  • Mechanical valves cannot tolerate prolonged AC gap (thrombosis risk unacceptably high).
  • Many surgeons will restart IV heparin despite active bleeding (using lower-dose target PTT, closer monitoring).
  • This is a high-wire scenario; close team coordination essential. Do not leave hematology/CT surgery out of this decision.

sections.heading: 7.6 HIT-specific perioperative considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
Managing HIT + bridging perioperatively (expandable) HIT incidence and timing:
  • Incidence ~0.5–1% of UFH exposure.
  • Typical onset: 5–10 days of UFH exposure (median day 5); can occur day 1 in re-exposed patients.
  • Definition: platelet drop >50% from baseline OR drop to <100K on heparin. Perioperative HIT recognition:
  • Patient on pre-op UFH bridge develops platelet drop → HIT suspect.
  • Stop heparin immediately; draw HIT ELISA + 4T score.
  • Switch to argatroban or bivalirudin while awaiting HIT confirmatory testing. Argatroban vs bivalirudin choice:
  • Argatroban: No renal dosing; good for renal failure. Increases INR by ~10–15% (complicates warfarin transition). Titration to PTT 1.5–3.0 × baseline.
  • Bivalirudin: Requires renal dosing; better tolerated by some. Prolongs PT/INR more (complicates warfarin transition). Titration to PTT 1.5–2.5 × baseline.
  • Choice: Institutional preference and renal function. Both acceptable. INR interpretation on DTI (direct thrombin inhibitor):
  • Both argatroban and bivalirudin prolong PT/INR independently of warfarin effect.
  • Do NOT rely on INR to assess warfarin effect while on DTI.
  • Measure PTT or anti-Xa preferentially while on DTI.
  • Plan to recheck INR 4–5 days after discontinuing DTI to assess true warfarin INR. Post-HIT bridge transition:
  • Warfarin started POD 1 on argatroban/bivalirudin (same as UFH).
  • Overlap argatroban/bivalirudin + warfarin until INR ≥2.0 × 24h (per standard DTI nomograms; slightly longer overlap may be needed due to INR unreliability).
  • Discontinue argatroban/bivalirudin once INR therapeutic.
  • Recheck INR 4–5 days post-DTI to confirm true warfarin INR. HIT flagging:
  • Document HIT prominently in chart.
  • Flag chart/allergy list for future AC decisions — never re-challenge with UFH/LMWH in same admission; if patient needs bridging again, use argatroban/bivalirudin.
  • Patient education: provide written list of HIT-safe agents (argatroban, bivalirudin, fondaparinux [controversial], warfarin, DOAC).

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • INR plateau at <1.5 on POD 4–5 despite warfarin 5–10 mg daily — malabsorption, drug interaction, or non-adherence; verify warfarin timing/dose, check CMP for renal dysfunction, consult pharmacy.
  • INR overshoot to >4.0 by POD 4–5 — warfarin dose escalated too aggressively; risk of bleeding; reduce warfarin dose per attending/pharmacist; recheck INR in 2–3 days.
  • PTT unstable on UFH drip (bouncing 40–100 sec) — heparin dosing off protocol, IV infiltration, or underlying coagulopathy; verify IV patency, restart if infiltrated, recheck baseline PTT, consult anticoagulation pharmacist.
  • Platelet count trending down (200K → 150K → 100K) — HIT suspect; stop heparin immediately, draw HIT serology and 4T score, switch to argatroban/bivalirudin.
  • Drain output increasing (50 → 100 → 150 mL/h) — bleeding escalation; notify surgeon, hold heparin, draw INR/PTT/CBC/fibrinogen, prepare for possible OR evacuation or reversal.
  • New hypotension or tachycardia unprovoked by pain/anesthesia — occult bleeding or thrombosis; assess perfusion, check drain output, send STAT labs (CBC, lactate, ABG), notify attending.
  • New neurologic deficit (weakness, slurred speech, facial droop) — activate stroke code immediately; STAT head CT (rule out ICH before continuing AC); continue anticoagulation pending CT result if ischemic suspected.
  • New leg swelling or calf pain despite anticoagulation — DVT despite "therapeutic" AC; verify PTT goal achieved, duplex ultrasound, consider inadequate dosing or heparin resistance, adjust dose up, consult hematology if recurrent.
  • Warfarin not given (missed dose documented) — restart immediately; do not double-dose next day; verify reason for miss (patient refusal, pharmacy delay, etc.); extend admission if necessary to ensure compliance.
  • Pre-op: INR remains >3.0 despite 2–3 days warfarin hold — slow INR metabolism; vitamin K 1–2 mg IV may be needed; discuss with attending before proceeding to OR; bleeding risk elevated at OR.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. BRIDGE trial changed practice: no bridge for most AF. Don't bridge non-valvular AF, CHA2DS2-VASc <5, no prior stroke/TIA, no recent VTE. BRIDGE showed equivalent thromboembolism and less bleeding without bridge. Many clinicians still reflexively bridge; know the evidence.

  2. Mechanical valve: ALWAYS bridge, no exceptions. Mitral >>aortic in thrombosis risk. If patient/family refuses bridge, escalate for capacity discussion. Do not proceed to OR without bridge confirmed.

  3. INR check post-warfarin hold is critical. Don't assume INR drops by day 3; some patients take 4–5 days. Wait for INR <2.0 before starting heparin; starting on elevated INR = over-anticoagulation and bleeding.

  4. Heparin dosing is a science, not an art. 80 units/kg bolus, 18 units/kg/h infusion. Adjust by 2–4 units/kg/h per 6h PTT check, not by whim. Undershooting PTT = thrombosis risk; overshooting = bleeding. Follow the sliding scale.

  5. PTT q6h on drip, not once-daily. Heparin is sensitive to infusion fluctuations. Once-daily PTT = missing significant bounces. If PTT unstable (swinging >20 sec), increase to q4h checks.

  6. Warfarin takes 3–7 days to become therapeutic, not 24h. INR elevation on days 1–2 is factor VII (short half-life). True anticoagulation (factor II depletion) takes 3–7 days. Don't discharge or stop heparin until INR ≥2.0 × 24h confirmed.

  7. Platelet drop on heparin = HIT until proven otherwise. Thrombocytopenia on heparin (any drop >50% or level <100K) = HIT suspect. Draw ELISA + 4T score; stop heparin immediately; switch to argatroban/bivalirudin. HIT = thrombosis risk 10–20× baseline; do not delay.

  8. Argatroban and bivalirudin increase INR, masking true warfarin INR. When transitioning from DTI to warfarin-only, recheck INR 4–5 days after DTI discontinuation. Do not rely on INR while on DTI; measure PTT or anti-Xa instead.

  9. Last heparin dose 6h pre-op (UFH); last LMWH dose 24h pre-op. UFH has ~90 min half-life; check PTT 2–4h pre-op to verify it's at goal still. LMWH has longer half-life; last dose 24h before allows near-complete clearance.

  10. Pre-op: INR >4.0 = DO NOT PROCEED to OR. Bleeding risk unacceptably high. Give vitamin K 1–2 mg IV (takes 12–24h to work); postpone surgery or discuss bleeding risk with surgeon/anesthesia. Low-dose vitamin K (1–2 mg, not 10 mg) avoids warfarin resistance post-correction.

  11. Post-op heparin resumption is surgeon's call, not automatic. Some surgeons resume POD 1 if bleeding minimal; others wait POD 2–3. Chest tube output, drain appearance, hemostasis — these drive timing. Do not assume and restart without explicit order; verify with surgeon.

  12. Mechanical valve post-op: some surgeons resume IV heparin 12–24h post-op despite active bleeding. This is high-wire medicine (dual bleeding + thrombosis risk). Discuss expected resumption timing pre-op; close intra-operative and post-op coordination essential.

  13. DOACs don't need bridging and need shorter pre-op hold (24–48h, not 5 days). If suitable for DOAC post-op (non-valvular AF, normal renal function), restart DOAC POD 1 at full dose; no UFH overlap needed. Simplifies and shortens admission.

  14. DOAC renal function is critical — adjustment or avoidance needed if CrCl <30. Dabigatran is renally cleared 80% (significant adjustment needed). Rivaroxaban and edoxaban ~50% renal clearance. Apixaban least renally dependent. Check renal function before post-op DOAC restart.

  15. Overlap 3–7 days bringing warfarin back. Standard is 3–5 days for AF/aortic valve (INR 2.0–3.0). Mechanical mitral may require 5–7 days (target INR 2.5–3.5 and hemostasis assurance). Do not discharge on warfarin without INR therapeutic × 24h and planned follow-up INR.

cards.title: Ischemic Cardiomyopathy
cards.quickAnswer: Ischemic cardiomyopathy: left ventricular dysfunction (EF ≤40%) from coronary artery disease, accounting for 60% of HFrEF cases. Viability assessment (dobutamine echo, CMR LGE, or PET) guides revascularization: STICH trial showed CABG reduces mortality at 5+ years in eligible patients (EF ≤35% + CAD amenable + viable myocardium); PCI has no benefit over GDMT alone (REVIVED-BCIS2). Integrated approach: optimize GDMT (ACE-I/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i), assess viability, consider CABG if viable, ICD for primary prevention (EF ≤35%, NYHA II–III, wait 40+ days post-MI or 90+ days post-revasc), CRT for wide QRS ≥120 ms, LVAD/transplant for end-stage.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: Ischemic cardiomyopathy: left ventricular dysfunction (EF ≤40%) from coronary artery disease, accounting for 60% of HFrEF cases. Viability assessment (dobutamine echo, CMR LGE, or PET) guides revascularization: STICH trial showed CABG reduces mortality at 5+ years in eligible patients (EF ≤35% + CAD amenable + viable myocardium); PCI has no benefit over GDMT alone (REVIVED-BCIS2). Integrated approach: optimize GDMT (ACE-I/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i), assess viability, consider CABG if viable, ICD for primary prevention (EF ≤35%, NYHA II–III, wait 40+ days post-MI or 90+ days post-revasc), CRT for wide QRS ≥120 ms, LVAD/transplant for end-stage.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → 2022 AHA/ACC HF Guideline → STICH Trial (Velazquez et al., 2016) → STICHES 10-year follow-up → REVIVED-BCIS2 (Perera et al., 2022) → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes (2026)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Left ventricular systolic dysfunction (EF ≤40%) caused by significant coronary artery disease (CAD), most commonly from prior myocardial infarction (MI). The LV remodels into a dilated, weakened chamber with inadequate contractility.
  • Epidemiology: Most common cause of HFrEF in developed nations (~60% of all HFrEF). Prevalence increases with age and male predominance. Approximately 30–50% of post-MI patients develop LV dysfunction; 10–20% progress to overt cardiomyopathy.
  • Who this applies to: Patients with significant CAD and LV dysfunction admitted pre-op for CABG (with or without viability assessment), admitted with decompensated HF awaiting revascularization, post-MI patients being evaluated for ICD, or patients progressing to end-stage disease requiring mechanical support or transplant.
  • Why it matters: Leading cause of HFrEF mortality and morbidity. Viability assessment directly drives revascularization decisions. Long-term outcomes depend on integrated medical, revascularization, and device therapy.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
.

Pathophysiology detail

Acute phase (post-MI): Transmural necrosis of myocardium in the distribution of the occluded coronary artery. Loss of contractility in the infarcted zone is partially compensated by hyperkinesis of remote ("normal") myocardium, which initially preserves overall ejection fraction.

Hibernating myocardium: Chronically underperfused but viable tissue with reduced contractility at rest. The key clinical feature is recovery of contractility after successful revascularization — this differentiates hibernation from irreversible scar. Hibernating myocardium is the target for CABG.

Stunning: Reversible contractile dysfunction from transient ischemia (e.g., hours to days post-reperfusion). Distinguishes from hibernation: stunning recovers without requiring revascularization.

Progressive remodeling: Mechanical unloading of the infarcted segment causes wall thinning and chamber enlargement. Eccentric hypertrophy develops. Elevated wall stress worsens dysfunction and triggers secondary mitral regurgitation (papillary muscle displacement). This cycle of remodeling, if unchecked, leads to severe systolic dysfunction (EF 20–30%), high filling pressures, congestion, cardiogenic shock risk, and arrhythmia substrate.

End-stage: EF ≤25%, NYHA IV symptoms, cardiogenic shock, uncontrolled arrhythmias — requires mechanical support (LVAD) or transplant.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner and competent recognition — presentation and workup landscape.

sections.heading: Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Acute phase: Chest pain, dyspnea, hemodynamic distress (if large anterior MI territory); cardiogenic shock if Killip III–IV
  • Chronic phase: Progressive dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, exercise intolerance, fatigue, peripheral edema, ascites (advanced)
  • Arrhythmias: Ventricular ectopy, non-sustained VT (common post-MI), sustained VT (sudden cardiac death risk); atrial fibrillation from elevated filling pressures
  • Syncope: From sustained VT, hypotension, or bradycardia (high-degree AV block if inferior MI)

sections.heading: Physical exam
sections.bodyHtml:
• Displaced, hyperdynamic point of maximal impulse (significant LV dilation)
  • Soft systolic murmur at apex (secondary mitral regurgitation)
  • S3 gallop (hallmark of dilated, failing ventricle)
  • Rales, elevated jugular venous pressure, peripheral edema (volume overload)
  • Cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure (hypoperfusion if cardiogenic shock)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml: Competent systematic workup. Target: establish diagnosis, assess severity, guide revascularization decision.

sections.heading: Diagnostic tests
sections.bodyHtml:
• Electrocardiogram: Q waves in prior MI distribution (anterior, inferior, lateral); ST-segment changes; arrhythmias; QRS duration (LBBB important for CRT eligibility)
  • Echocardiogram: Primary tool for EF assessment and regional wall motion abnormalities (RWMAs) in coronary territories; estimates cavity dimensions; assesses mitral regurgitation severity; screens for LV thrombus
  • Cardiac catheterization: Coronary angiography identifies CAD anatomy; hemodynamic assessment (LA pressure, cardiac output); essential pre-op evaluation for CABG candidacy
  • Viability assessment (CRITICAL decision point):
  • Dobutamine stress echo: Low-dose infusion (5–10 mcg/kg/min) reveals contractile improvement in hibernating segments; segments with no response are likely scar. Sensitivity ~85%, specificity ~70%
  • Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE): Gold standard for scar quantification. <75% transmural scar suggests viability. Also assesses for LV thrombus
  • PET viability imaging: F-18 FDG shows preserved glucose metabolism in hibernating tissue (mismatch with perfusion deficit). High specificity; less widely available
  • Biomarkers: BNP/NT-proBNP (elevated in HF; prognostic); troponin (elevated acutely in MI)
  • Pulmonary function tests: Part of pre-op risk assessment for CABG
  • Recent labs: Baseline creatinine, BUN, electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺), CBC, coagulation studies

sections.heading: Severity classification
sections.bodyHtml:
Measure Mild Moderate Severe
EF (%) 41–49 31–40 ≤30
NYHA class II II–III III–IV
LV cavity dilation Mild Moderate Marked (LVEDV >250 mL/m²)
Regional wall motion Segmental/regional Multi-territorial Global hypokinesis
Cardiogenic shock — — SBP <90, CI <2.2, PCWP >18 mmHg

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Comprehensive integrated approach: GDMT + revascularization decision + device therapy + advanced support.

sections.heading: 5A. GDMT (Four Pillars + adjunctive therapies)
sections.bodyHtml:
This is the foundation for all ischemic CM:

Pillar Agent Mechanism Note
ACE-I / ARB / ARNI Lisinopril, enalapril, valsartan, sacubitril/valsartan Blocks maladaptive neurohumoral activation; reduces remodeling; improves survival ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan) preferred per 2022 AHA/ACC guideline if tolerated. Target dose-dependent.
Beta-blockers Carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol Reduce mortality; improve EF; reduce arrhythmia burden Evidence-based agents only — not all beta-blockers equivalent (carvedilol > metoprolol tartrate). Titrate to goal even if mildly hypotensive.
Aldosterone antagonist Spironolactone, eplerenone Additional mortality benefit in HFrEF Monitor K⁺ closely, especially with ACE-I/ARB/ARNI. Contraindicated if K⁺ >5.0 or Cr >2.5.
SGLT2 inhibitor Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin Reduce HF hospitalization and mortality; cardio-renal benefit Works independent of diabetic status. One of the newer, highest-impact therapies.

Adjunctive:

  • Diuretics: For congestion; not mortality-improving but essential for symptom control and euvolemia
  • Ivabradine: If resting HR >70 in sinus rhythm without beta-blocker contraindication; reduces hospitalization
  • Hydralazine/nitrate combination: Alternative for ACE-I/ARB-intolerant patients (e.g., documented Black patients with benefit)
  • Aspirin + statin: Standard post-MI; secondary prevention

Critical: GDMT optimization precedes ICD placement. Ensure target doses are achieved before finalizing ICD timing.

sections.heading: 5B. Revascularization decision (CABG vs. Medical therapy)
sections.bodyHtml:
STICH vs. REVIVED-BCIS2 comparison table
FactorSTICH (CABG, 2011)REVIVED-BCIS2 (PCI, 2022)
PopulationEF ≤35%, CAD, viable myocardiumEF ≤35%, CTO, viable myocardium
InterventionCABG + GDMTPCI (stent) + GDMT
ControlGDMT aloneGDMT alone
Primary outcome (2 yr)No mortality differenceNo mortality/LVEF benefit
5-year follow-upCABG reduced mortality + HF hosp.N/A
ImplicationCABG beneficial for viable myocardium in eligible patientsPCI NOT beneficial; CABG remains standard

Revascularization indication algorithm:

Clinical finding Recommendation
Viable myocardium (dobutamine echo, CMR LGE, PET) CABG indicated; long-term mortality + HF hospitalization benefit (Velazquez et al., 2016)
Extensive scar burden (>75% transmural LGE) Medical therapy preferred; CABG unlikely to improve outcome
EF <35%, NYHA III–IV, viable myocardium, operable CABG + GDMT recommended (Class IIa evidence); long-term benefit demonstrated
High surgical risk (age >75, renal failure, severe lung disease, prior stroke) Heart team discussion essential; PCI not superior to GDMT alone per REVIVED-BCIS2; consider LVAD bridge, transplant evaluation, or OMT

Key trial insights:

  • STICH (Velazquez et al., 2016): CABG showed NO mortality benefit at 2 years, but at 5+ years (Spertus et al., 2016) demonstrated improved survival and fewer HF hospitalizations in eligible patients with viable myocardium. This delayed benefit is the landmark finding.
  • REVIVED-BCIS2 (Perera et al., 2022): PCI (percutaneous coronary intervention / stenting) to chronically occluded coronaries in ischemic CM with viability did NOT improve mortality, LVEF, or exercise capacity vs. optimal medical therapy. CABG remains the revascularization standard.

sections.heading: 5C. Viability assessment detail
sections.bodyHtml:
Viability imaging modality comparison
ModalityMethodPrincipleSensitivity / SpecificityAvailabilityNotes
Dobutamine echoInfuse low-dose dobutamine (5–10 mcg/kg/min); observe wall motionHibernating myocardium shows contractile reserve; scar does not85% / 70%Widely availableOperator-dependent; contraindicated in uncontrolled HTN or active angina
Cardiac MRI + LGEGadolinium contrast; late imaging (10–20 min post-contrast)Scar uptake (infarct transmurality); <75% transmural = viable88% / 85%Major centersGold standard; also detects LV thrombus; contraindicated if GFR <30 or ferromagnetic implants
PET imagingF-18 FDG metabolism; compare to perfusion (Tc-99m or N-13 ammonia)Metabolically active but hypoperfused = hibernation92% / 84%Specialized centersHighest specificity; limited availability; fewer institutions
Stress-induced EF changeSerial echo or nuclear study at 6–12 wk post-CABG/PCIFunctional improvement = viability—Standard follow-upRetrospective; useful if pre-op imaging unavailable

sections.heading: 5D. ICD placement for primary prevention (post-MI / ischemic CM)
sections.bodyHtml:
Criteria (ACC/AHA 2022):

Criterion Detail
EF ≤35% despite optimal GDMT (verify on repeat echo)
NYHA class II or III (or ambulatory NYHA IV)
Timing post-MI Minimum 40 days post-MI OR minimum 90 days post-revascularization (CABG/PCI)
Guideline class IIb (reasonable) if 40–90 days post-MI; IIa (Class IIa) if >90 days

Rationale: EF often recovers 6–12 months with GDMT + revascularization (Cleland et al., CIBIS-III). Premature ICD placement wastes resources. DINAMIT and IRIS trials showed no benefit to early ICD (days 6–40 post-MI); COPERNICUS data support 90-day wait post-revasc.

Exception: Sustained VT or VF in acute post-MI period → temporary pacing/defibrillation, assess for reversible causes (ongoing ischemia, electrolyte derangement). If sustained arrhythmia recurs, proceed to ICD earlier.

Post-revasc EF recovery: If CABG performed with viable hibernating myocardium present, EF may improve substantially over 6–12 months. Consider repeat echo at 3–6 months; if EF improves to >35%, ICD may be deferred. Removal of an already-implanted ICD is rarely performed.

sections.heading: 5E. CRT (Cardiac Resynchronization Therapy)
sections.bodyHtml:
Indication:

Criterion Detail
QRS morphology LBBB or wide QRS ≥120 ms (preferably ≥150 ms for greatest benefit)
EF ≤35%
NYHA class II–IV

Mechanism: Ischemic CM from LAD infarction often produces LBBB. Asynchronous activation (RV contracts before LV) worsens mechanical efficiency. Biventricular pacing resynchronizes contraction, improves cardiac output, reduces mitral regurgitation, and improves EF and symptoms. Response rates: ~70% in LBBB, ~40% in non-LBBB (e.g., RBBB).

Timing: Can be placed concurrently with ICD (CRT-D device) if both criteria met, or sequentially.

sections.heading: 5F. LV aneurysm workup
sections.bodyHtml:
LV aneurysm vs. thrombus differentiation
FeatureLV AneurysmLV Thrombus
DefinitionDyskinetic (paradoxically outward) segment with thin wall; permanent structural deformityBlood clot adherent to LV endocardium, usually apical
CauseLarge transmural MI; remodeling over weeks–monthsLarge anterior MI; low-flow state; atrial fibrillation
Echo findingsPersistent dyskinesia during systole + diastole; thin wall on ultrasoundMobile or sessile mass; apical location; may move with systole
MRIThin-walled scar; no thrombus signalLV thrombus shows gadolinium uptake or T2 signal (distinguishes from scar)
AnticoagulationNot routinely; if VT occurs, may need AC + ICDYES — warfarin 3–6 months minimum; reassess with repeat imaging
Surgical repairSAVER (Surgical Anterior Ventricular Endoventricular Restoration) rarely performed in modern era; reserved for recurrent VT uncontrolled by ICDNot surgically treated; medical + AC

Screening: All post-MI patients with anterior wall involvement should be screened for thrombus by echocardiography. If present → anticoagulation 3–6 months (warfarin or DOAC), then repeat echo to assess resolution.

sections.heading: 5G. Advanced therapies (LVAD, transplant)
sections.bodyHtml:
LVAD candidacy:

  • EF ≤25% refractory to GDMT, revascularization if viable, and device therapy (ICD/CRT)
  • NYHA IV or recurrent hospitalizations despite optimization
  • Inadequate perfusion: cardiac index <2.0, SBP <80 mmHg, lactate elevation, end-organ dysfunction
  • Indication: bridge to transplant (if transplant candidate) or destination therapy (if not transplant-eligible or declines)
  • Timing: escalate when medical therapy exhausted and patient at risk of cardiogenic shock or imminent death

Transplant candidacy:

  • Age ≤65 years (relative; older patients considered case-by-case)
  • EF ≤25%, NYHA IV refractory to all therapies (including LVAD if bridged)
  • No contraindications: active malignancy (except non-melanoma skin cancer), active infection, severe lung disease (PVR >3–4 Wood units), fixed pulmonary hypertension, uncorrectable hepatic/renal dysfunction
  • Psychiatric evaluation and substance abuse history reviewed
  • Post-transplant survival: median 10–12 years graft survival in current era
  • Waiting list timeline: 6–12 months on average (geographic variation); waiting-list mortality ≤10% per year if hemodynamically stable

sections.heading: 6. ICU Trajectory & Nursing Considerations
sections.bodyHtml: ICU-level framing, unit-neutral.

sections.heading: Pre-op ischemic CM patient awaiting CABG
sections.bodyHtml:
• Stability monitoring: Watch for decompensation (worsening dyspnea, orthopnea, oliguria, cool extremities, altered mental status). Escalate immediately if any develop.
  • GDMT verification: Confirm patient on target doses of ACE-I/ARNI, beta-blocker, MRA, SGLT2i. Coordinate with cardiology team on any recent changes.
  • Arrhythmia surveillance: Continuous telemetry. Non-sustained VT is common; document runs (onset, rate, duration, patient symptoms, recovery). New sustained VT → STAT EKG and team notification (cardiogenic shock risk).
  • Volume status: May be on diuretics; tight intake/output, daily weights, goal euvolemia (not overloaded, not underfilled). Oliguria + rising creatinine = cardiorenal syndrome; notify team.
  • Renal function: Baseline creatinine, BUN; monitor trends. ACE-I/ARNI + MRA + diuretics increase hyperkalemia risk — monitor K⁺ closely.
  • Bleeding risk: Many on antiplatelet therapy (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor if prior PCI); clarify pre-op management with cardiac team.
  • Pain management: These patients are fragile; use caution with opioids (risk of respiratory depression, hypotension). Avoid excessive sedation.
  • Decompensation: If acute HF symptoms develop pre-op → escalate urgently. May need aggressive diuresis, inotropic support, or urgent LVAD/transplant discussion if severe cardiogenic shock.

sections.heading: Post-CABG ischemic CM patient
sections.bodyHtml:
• Refer to CABG surgery card for detailed post-op management.
  • EF recovery: Substantial recovery may take 6–12 months if hibernating myocardium present. Manage expectations with patient/family.
  • Arrhythmia surveillance: Post-op AF is common (POAF); continuous telemetry. VT/VF also possible. See POAF scenario card for management.
  • Inadequate inotropic response: If patient requires sustained vasopressor/inotrope support past POD 2–3 without improvement → consider LVAD evaluation or escalated imaging/catheterization.
  • Renal perfusion: Oliguria + rising creatinine = cardiorenal syndrome; may need diuretics vs. inotropic support or ultrafiltration.
  • Bleeding: Antiplatelet effect wanes; rebleeding risk if restarted. Coordinate timing with CT surgery team.

sections.heading: ICD patient (pre- or post-implant)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Device knowledge: Understand model, shock threshold, HR cutoff, programming parameters. Ensure last interrogation date/results documented.
  • Arrhythmia management: If patient experiences ICD shock → STAT EKG, assess hemodynamics, notify team. Multiple shocks in succession = VT storm (potential incessant VT refractory to device); may need sedation, IV antiarrhythmic (amiodarone), TEE, ablation discussion.
  • Activity restrictions: Post-implant, typically no heavy lifting/contact sports for 6 weeks; clarify team restrictions with patient/family.
  • MRI safety: Confirm device is MRI-conditional. Standard dual-chamber ICDs contraindicate MRI (risk of device malfunction); if urgent MRI needed, may reprogram to VVI mode temporarily.
  • Infection surveillance: Fever, device site erythema/discharge, line cultures positive → infectious endocarditis workup; coordinate with EP team.

sections.heading: Patient / family teaching
sections.bodyHtml:
• Explain ischemic CM: "Your heart muscle has been damaged by heart attacks. The pumping strength is weakened, and we're working to improve it with medication and possibly surgery."
  • Viability and CABG: "If our imaging shows that parts of your heart muscle can recover with improved blood flow, surgery (bypass) may help long-term. The benefit may not be immediate — recovery takes several months."
  • ICD purpose: "The ICD monitors your heart rhythm and delivers a shock if a dangerous rhythm develops. It prevents sudden cardiac death but doesn't cure the underlying heart problem."
  • GDMT importance: "These medications (ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, aldosterone blocker, SGLT2 inhibitor) work together to strengthen your heart and prevent hospitalizations. Taking them exactly as prescribed is as important as any surgery."
  • Transplant/LVAD discussion: "If your heart fails to improve despite all treatments, a mechanical pump (LVAD) can help while you wait for a transplant, or as a long-term solution. This is a complex decision we'll discuss with the whole team."

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections marked — collapsed by default.

Hibernation vs. stunning vs. scar — the viability concept Hibernating myocardium:
  • Chronically underperfused, dysfunctional at rest
  • Retains contractile reserve (responds to dobutamine, positive LGE <75% transmural)
  • Recovers contractility after revascularization ← This is why CABG works
  • Viable tissue that CABG can "wake up" Stunning:
  • Reversible dysfunction from transient ischemia (minutes to hours)
  • Recovers function over hours–days without intervention
  • Example: transient hypotension during anesthesia → transient wall motion abnormality → recovers as BP normalizes
  • Does NOT require revascularization Scar (irreversible infarction):
  • Transmural necrosis; dead tissue
  • No contractile reserve; does NOT improve with dobutamine
  • LGE >75% transmural thickness = scar, not viable
  • CABG will NOT improve function in pure scar Clinical distinction: Viability testing (dobutamine stress, CMR, PET) differentiates hibernation (viable, recoverable) from scar (irreversible). This distinction is THE decision point for CABG.
CMR LGE transmurality interpretation Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) on cardiac MRI is the gold standard for scar vs. viable tissue. Scoring:
  • <25% transmural LGE: Predominantly viable; high likelihood of contractile recovery post-revascularization. CABG beneficial.
  • 25–75% transmural LGE: Mixed scar and viable; intermediate recovery likelihood. CABG may help, but variable.
  • >75% transmural LGE: Predominantly scar; minimal contractile recovery expected. CABG unlikely to improve EF. Transmurality: Measure from epicardium inward. Subendocardial sparing (LGE only at subepicardium, not touching the endocardium) is favorable for recovery. Threshold for viability: Consensus is that viability is present if LGE <75% transmural in a given segment. This is the dividing line for CABG indication. Other MRI findings:
  • Thrombus: Low-signal intensity or T2 hyperintensity, typically apical. If present → anticoagulation 3–6 months.
  • LV size / sphericity index: Assesses degree of remodeling; prognostic.
  • Mitral regurgitation jet area: Secondary MR from remodeling; quantifies severity.
Dobutamine stress echocardiography — what to look for Protocol:
  • Baseline echo obtained at rest
  • Dobutamine infused at increasing doses: 5, 10, 20, 40 mcg/kg/min
  • Wall motion observed at each stage Interpretation:
  • Improving or normalizing wall motion = contractile reserve = viable myocardium (hibernation)
  • Persistent hypokinesia/akinesia = scar (no viability)
  • Biphasic response (improves at low dose, worsens at higher dose with ischemia): suggests viable but precarious; ischemia at higher afterload Sensitivity/Specificity: ~85% / ~70% respectively. Operator-dependent; high sensitivity for hibernation. Limitations:
  • Contraindicated in uncontrolled hypertension, active angina, recent MI with mechanical complication
  • Cannot be done in patients unable to tolerate catecholamines
PET/SPECT viability imaging — perfusion-metabolism mismatch PET viability imaging:
  • Perfusion tracer: Rubidium-82 or N-13 ammonia (shows perfusion deficit in CAD territories)
  • Metabolism tracer: F-18 FDG (fluorodeoxyglucose; shows glucose uptake)
  • Mismatch pattern: Reduced perfusion BUT preserved metabolism = hibernation (viable)
  • Match pattern: Both reduced = scar (not viable) Specificity: Highest of all modalities (~92%), but less widely available than echo or MRI. SPECT:
  • Uses Tc-99m sestamibi for perfusion
  • Less specific for viability than PET
  • Widely available
STICH trial — landmark evidence for CABG in EF ≤35% STICH I (Velazquez et al., 2016):
  • Population: EF ≤35%, significant CAD (EF ≤35%, CAD with viable myocardium on dobutamine echo or imaging)
  • Groups: CABG + GDMT vs. GDMT alone (medical therapy alone)
  • Primary outcome (2 years): No difference in all-cause mortality (36% CABG vs. 41% medical therapy, p=0.12)
  • 5-year follow-up (Spertus et al., 2016): CABG showed mortality benefit AND reduced HF hospitalizations
  • Implication: CABG has delayed long-term benefit in ischemic CM with viable myocardium; no short-term (2-year) advantage
  • Key insight: Viability is the predictive marker; patients with viability benefit from CABG over years 3–5; patients without viability (extensive scar) do NOT benefit STICHES 10-year follow-up:
  • Even longer-term data confirm sustained mortality reduction in CABG group
  • Benefit persists in patients with viable myocardium
REVIVED-BCIS2 trial — PCI does NOT work for ischemic CM REVIVED-BCIS2 (Perera et al., 2022):
  • Population: EF ≤35%, chronic total occlusion (CTO) in LAD/RCA, viable myocardium on imaging (dobutamine echo or CMR), optimal GDMT
  • Intervention: PCI (stent) to the CTO + GDMT
  • Control: GDMT alone (no revascularization)
  • Primary outcome: No difference in all-cause mortality or LVEF recovery at 2 years between PCI + GDMT and GDMT alone
  • Secondary outcomes: No difference in exercise capacity, HF symptoms, or hospitalization rates
  • Implication: PCI does NOT reduce mortality in chronic ischemic CM with viability, unlike CABG
  • Mechanism: PCI via stenting may not adequately restore perfusion in chronic ischemic territory; CABG (surgical bypass) may be more effective at sustained revascularization Clinical takeaway: If a patient with ischemic CM + viable myocardium is referred for revascularization, CABG (not PCI) is the evidence-based approach.
LV aneurysm surgical repair (SAVER) — when and why LV aneurysm:
  • Post-MI remodeling → thin-walled, dyskinetic (paradoxical outward) segment
  • Increases LV cavity volume; worsens efficiency; increases wall stress → promotes further remodeling and arrhythmias Surgical Anterior Ventricular Endoventricular Restoration (SAVER):
  • Excision of dyskinetic scar + closure of cavity (restores normal LV geometry)
  • Rationale: reduce arrhythmia substrate, improve EF, reduce wall stress Modern practice:
  • Rarely performed now; most patients benefit from GDMT + ICD (for VT) without aneurysm resection
  • Reserved for recurrent VT uncontrolled by ICD + antiarrhythmics, or for severe LV dysfunction requiring aggressive remodeling surgery (very rare)
  • If SAVER considered, done in combination with CABG if viable myocardium present LV thrombus post-MI:
  • Common complication of large anterior MI with low ejection fraction
  • Risk stratification: size, mobility, LV function
  • Anticoagulation 3–6 months (warfarin or DOAC) with follow-up echo to confirm resolution
  • If thrombus persists >6 months or enlarges despite AC, consider surgery (rarely done)
ICD timing — DINAMIT, IRIS, COPERNICUS trials DINAMIT trial (2009):
  • Tested early ICD (median 6 days post-MI) vs. standard care in EF ≤35%
  • Result: No mortality benefit with early ICD; trend toward harm
  • Conclusion: Avoid ICD in days 6–40 post-MI IRIS trial (2009):
  • Tested early ICD (mean 11 days post-MI) vs. standard
  • Result: No mortality benefit with early ICD
  • Supports the 40-day minimum waiting period COPERNICUS trial (2003):
  • Tested standard ICD therapy (>40 days post-MI) in EF ≤35%
  • Result: ICD reduced mortality ~25% compared to medical therapy alone
  • Supports ICD placement ≥40 days post-MI Implication: Wait until 40+ days post-MI or 90+ days post-revascularization before ICD placement. Early placement doesn't help and wastes resources. Exception: If sustained VT/VF occurs acutely and recurs despite treatment, proceed to ICD earlier.
CRT response and non-response predictors High response (>60% achieve CRT benefit):
  • LBBB morphology (vs. RBBB or non-specific IVCD)
  • QRS ≥150 ms (wider = better response)
  • Young age (vs. elderly)
  • Non-ischemic cause (vs. ischemic CM) — though ischemic CM still responds ~50% of the time
  • Apical or apical-lateral scar burden <50% Low response (< 40%):
  • RBBB or non-specific wide QRS
  • QRS 120–149 ms (narrower = lower response)
  • Basal/basal-lateral scar >50%
  • EF >25% (less room for improvement) Non-responders (25–30% of implanted patients):
  • May not show EF improvement despite device placement
  • Still eligible for ICD function
  • Consider EKG changes, Cx disease pattern, older age Timing: CRT can be placed as standalone (CRT-P) or combined with ICD (CRT-D) if both criteria met.
SGLT2 inhibitor cardio-renal benefit Mechanism:
  • SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2) inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) enhance urinary glucose excretion
  • Independent of blood glucose or insulin; work even in non-diabetics
  • Reduce cardiac preload, improve cardiac efficiency
  • Enhance renal perfusion and reduce proteinuria (renal protection)
  • Mitigate progression of cardiorenal syndrome Evidence in HFrEF:
  • DAPA-HF trial: dapagliflozin reduced HF hospitalization and cardiovascular death in HFrEF (EF ≤40%) by ~26%, independent of diabetes
  • EMPEROR-Reduced: empagliflozin showed similar benefit in HFrEF
  • Rapid onset of benefit (weeks, not months like ACE-I) Use in ischemic CM:
  • Standard of care now; should be on all HFrEF patients unless contraindicated (eGFR <20, risk of diabetic ketoacidosis)
  • One of the highest-impact modern therapies
Beta-blocker class effects — carvedilol vs. metoprolol succinate vs. bisoprolol
AgentMechanismAdvantageCaveat
CarvedilolBeta-1 + alpha blocker (vasodilation); antioxidantPotent remodeling reduction; mortality reduction in HFrEFCan cause fatigue; hypotension more common
Metoprolol succinate (extended-release)Selective beta-1 blockerGood mortality data in HFrEF; standard agentMUST use succinate salt, not tartrate (immediate-release lacks benefit)
BisoprololSelective beta-1 blockerFavored in Europe; good HFrEF dataLess commonly used in US
Key point: NOT all beta-blockers are equivalent. Evidence supports only carvedilol, metoprolol succinate (ER), and bisoprolol for HFrEF. Metoprolol tartrate (immediate-release) does NOT have mortality benefit in HFrEF — do NOT substitute.
ACEI vs. ARNI — when to prefer sacubitril/valsartan ACE-I / ARB:
  • Reduce angiotensin II, a key maladaptive neurohumoral mediator
  • Reduce remodeling, improve survival
  • Standard therapy ARNI (sacubitril/valsartan):
  • Sacubitril (neprilysin inhibitor) + valsartan (ARB)
  • Neprilysin breaks down natriuretic peptides (BNP, ANP); inhibiting it increases their bioavailability
  • More potent remodeling reduction than ACE-I alone (PARADIGM-HF trial)
  • 2022 guideline: ARNI preferred over ACE-I if tolerated Transition:
  • Cannot give ACE-I + sacubitril together (risk of angioedema)
  • Washout: 36 hours off ACE-I before starting ARNI
  • Start low dose sacubitril/valsartan (26/24 mg PO BID), titrate to 97/103 mg BID target Contraindication: Prior angioedema on ACE-I → use ARB (e.g., valsartan monotherapy) instead of ARNI
Spironolactone MRA — hyperkalemia management Mechanism:
  • Aldosterone antagonist; blocks aldosterone at the collecting duct
  • Reduces potassium secretion (tends to INCREASE K⁺)
  • Additional mortality benefit in HFrEF; independent of ACE-I/ARB/ARNI effect Hyperkalemia risk:
  • Especially if concurrent ACE-I/ARB/ARNI + diuretic use
  • Risk ↑ with renal dysfunction (Cr >2.5 or eGFR <30) Monitoring:
  • Baseline K⁺ and creatinine before starting
  • Recheck K⁺ + Cr at 3–7 days, then at 2–4 weeks
  • Target K⁺ <5.0 mEq/L; do NOT start if K⁺ ≥5.5 or hold if K⁺ >6.0
  • If K⁺ > 5.0: hold spironolactone, recheck in 1 week Dosing:
  • Start 12.5–25 mg daily
  • Titrate to 25–50 mg daily target (rarely need >50)
  • Lower dose if renal function declining Alternative: Eplerenone (non-selective MRA) if spironolactone intolerant (gynecomastia, erectile dysfunction)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any develop, re-escalate.

  • Worsening dyspnea despite diuretics → may indicate inadequate GDMT optimization or acute decompensation from new ischemia/arrhythmia; escalate for imaging/cath
  • Oliguria + rising creatinine → cardiorenal syndrome; inotropic support vs. ultrafiltration consideration; team discussion
  • Recurrent VT despite ICD + antiarrhythmics → VT storm; may need ablation discussion or LVAD evaluation
  • Syncope or presyncope → arrhythmia vs. hemodynamic collapse; STAT EKG and telemetry review
  • Progressive LV dilation on serial echoes despite GDMT → maladaptive remodeling continuing; escalate GDMT or revascularization discussion
  • Atrial fibrillation new-onset → anticoagulation needed; rate/rhythm control plan; thromboembolic risk high in EF ≤35%
  • Fever + device site erythema → infectious endocarditis; blood cultures, echocardiography, EP team notification
  • New or worsening mitral regurgitation on echo → secondary to remodeling; escalate if severe (EROA >40 mm²) as may require surgical intervention
  • Profound hypotension unresponsive to fluids → cardiogenic shock; inotropic support, mechanical support (IABP, ECMO, LVAD), urgent cath/transplant discussion
  • New focal neurologic deficit → stroke from cardioemboli (AF, LV thrombus); activate stroke code; anticoagulation review

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Viability assessment is THE decision point for CABG. Don't assume all ischemic CM patients need CABG; confirm viability (dobutamine echo, CMR LGE, or PET) first. Patients with extensive scar (>75% transmural) are not CABG candidates.

  2. STICH showed CABG benefit at 5+ years, NOT at 2 years. Short-term outcomes favor medical therapy; long-term follow-up (5+ years) favors CABG in viable myocardium. Manage expectations: "This is long-term therapy; you may not feel better immediately."

  3. REVIVED-BCIS2 definitively shows PCI does NOT work in chronic ischemic CM. PCI to chronically occluded coronaries in EF ≤35% + viable myocardium did NOT improve outcomes vs. GDMT alone. CABG (surgical bypass) remains the revascularization standard.

  4. ICD timing: 40+ days post-MI, 90+ days post-revascularization. DINAMIT and IRIS showed no benefit to early ICD (days 6–40 post-MI). Premature placement wastes resources. EF recovery is common in first 90 days. Ensure team honors the waiting period.

  5. Hibernating myocardium recovers with revascularization; stunning recovers without. Understand the distinction: hibernating tissue is chronically dysfunctional but viable (needs CABG to "wake up"), while stunning is transient dysfunction that resolves on its own. Viability testing differentiates them.

  6. GDMT optimization PRECEDES ICD decision. Ensure patient is on target doses of ACE-I/ARNI (titrate to goal), beta-blocker (evidence-based agent only), MRA, SGLT2i before finalizing ICD timing. Better GDMT may improve EF and delay or avoid ICD altogether.

  7. LBBB + wide QRS ≥120 ms = CRT candidate. If ischemic CM patient has LBBB morphology and EF ≤35%, NYHA II–IV, they are CRT candidates. Response rates ~70% in LBBB. Ensure cardiology team considers this; don't overlook.

  8. LV thrombus is common post-large anterior MI. Screen every anterior STEMI patient with echo. If present → anticoagulation for 3 months minimum (warfarin or DOAC), then repeat echo to confirm resolution. Missed thrombus = stroke risk.

  9. Post-MI ventricular aneurysm surgical repair (SAVER) is rare now. Most patients benefit from GDMT + ICD for arrhythmia control. Resection considered only if recurrent VT uncontrolled by ICD + antiarrhythmic, or if severe dysfunction requires aggressive remodeling (very rare in modern era).

  10. Atrial fibrillation + ischemic CM = anticoagulation mandatory. AF in HFrEF requires systemic anticoagulation due to high stroke risk and hypercoagulability from low cardiac output. Do NOT hold AC reflexively; call the team to clarify the plan.

  11. Pre-op high surgical risk CABG requires heart team discussion. If patient age >75, severe renal disease (Cr >2.5), prior CVA, severe PVD, or EF <20%, CABG carries elevated mortality. Multi-disciplinary team (cardiac surgery, cardiology, anesthesia, palliative care if appropriate) should discuss candidacy, timing, and alternatives (LVAD as bridge, transplant evaluation, OMT alone).

  12. Transplant candidacy assessment: age ≤65, refractory EF ≤25%, no contraindications. Contraindications include active cancer (except skin), active infection, severe lung disease (PVR >3–4 Wood), fixed pulmonary hypertension, uncorrectable organ dysfunction. Psychiatric eval and substance abuse history reviewed. Realistic timeline: 6–12 months on list (variable by geography). Waiting-list mortality ≤10% per year if stable.

  13. LVAD decision: bridge vs. destination. Bridge to transplant if candidate (age <65, transplant eligible); destination therapy if >65 or not transplant candidate. Discuss stroke/bleeding/infection risks. LVAD patients require lifelong anticoagulation and regular device follow-up; coordinate care between VAD center + local hospital.

  14. EF recovery post-CABG takes 6–12 months. If patient discharged with EF still 25–35% and ICD implanted, emphasize GDMT adherence and follow-up echo in 3–6 months. EF may improve enough to reconsider ICD necessity (though removal rarely done once implanted). Serial assessment is key.

  15. Cardiogenic shock in ischemic CM is a critical juncture. If patient presents with SBP <90, CI <2.2, pulmonary congestion, acute decompensation requires aggressive intervention: inotropes (dobutamine, milrinone), mechanical support (IABP, ECMO, LVAD), urgent revascularization, transplant/LVAD evaluation. Coordinate with ICU/VAD center immediately. Not a floor-level diagnosis — ICU care mandated.

cards.title: Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ)
cards.quickAnswer: A 23-item self-report questionnaire measuring how heart failure affects the patient's symptom burden, physical limitation, emotional burden, and quality of life. Scored 0–100 (higher = better control). KCCQ ≥ 75 indicates excellent quality of life; < 25 signals severe impairment and high readmission risk. Takes 5–7 minutes to complete. Rarely administered during acute hospitalization, but baseline KCCQ scores from clinic visits inform discharge planning acuity, rehab intensity, and readmission risk stratification.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: A 23-item self-report questionnaire measuring how heart failure affects the patient's symptom burden, physical limitation, emotional burden, and quality of life.
