sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
The Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) is a disease-specific, patient-completed instrument that measures the impact of heart failure on functional capacity, symptom stability, social and emotional well-being, and overall quality of life. Unlike objective measures (ejection fraction, BNP, 6-minute walk distance), KCCQ captures what the patient actually feels and experiences — the patient-centered perspective on symptom burden (Green et al., 2000).

Key features:

  • 23 items (full version); 12 items (KCCQ-12 abbreviated form)
  • Self-report — patient perception; not clinician-assigned
  • Time to complete: 5–7 minutes
  • Score range: 0–100 (higher = better HF control and quality of life)
  • Validated in: HFrEF, HFmrEF, HFpEF, and valve disease populations
  • Clinically meaningful change: 5–10 point shift signals real improvement or deterioration

sections.heading: 2. Domains and scoring structure
sections.bodyHtml:
Domain Description Weight
Physical Limitation (PL) Ability to perform daily activities (walking, climbing stairs, sexual activity) without dyspnea or fatigue 20%
Symptom Frequency (SF) How often patient experiences dyspnea, fatigue, palpitations, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) in past 2 weeks 20%
Symptom Burden (SB) Severity of dyspnea and fatigue when present (mild vs. severe) 20%
Symptom Stability (SS) Whether symptoms are worsening, stable, or improving over recent weeks 10%
Quality of Life (QL) Overall satisfaction and impact on emotional well-being, social engagement, self-care confidence 20%
Social Limitation (SocL) Restriction in work, leisure, or family roles due to HF 10%

Overall KCCQ Score = weighted average of above domains, reported as single 0–100 number.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Use — Interpretation and bedside application
sections.bodyHtml:
Nurses in the ICU and stepdown do not administer KCCQ on the unit. Instead, they receive and interpret KCCQ scores from prior clinic visits or recent hospital records, and use them to contextualize recovery, discharge planning, and rehab intensity:

Clinical Context How KCCQ Informs Care
Admission for decompensation Low baseline KCCQ (< 35) signals expect longer recovery; higher readmission risk; intensive outpatient HF program and rehab are critical post-discharge
Post-MI or acute HF diagnosis Baseline KCCQ (if available) helps set expectations for functional recovery; tracks improvement over weeks of GDMT optimization
Cardiac rehab referral decision KCCQ < 50 → patient likely to benefit from Phase II/III rehab; KCCQ ≥ 75 → patient may be ready for discharge with self-management education alone
TAVR or valve surgery pre-op Pre-op KCCQ baseline documents how much valve disease limits QoL; post-op KCCQ improvement (often 10–20 points) justifies the intervention (Spertus, 2013)
SGLT2i HFpEF trial endpoint KCCQ is primary outcome in trials (DELIVER, EMPEROR); discharge summary may cite "KCCQ improved by 8 points" as evidence of trial-driven benefit
Transplant or VAD candidacy KCCQ < 25 + severe functional impairment may trigger discussion of advanced therapies; re-assessed post-listing or post-implant to measure quality of life gain
Medication adherence teaching Explaining that GDMT escalation (e.g., SGLT2i, ARNI, finerenone) aims to improve KCCQ score gives patient concrete, QoL-centered goal, not just "lower BNP"

Relationship to NYHA Functional Class:

  • NYHA is clinician-assigned at bedside (rapid, functional assessment).
  • KCCQ is patient-reported and more granular. Same patient may be NYHA II but KCCQ 40 (dyspnea on mild exertion) or NYHA II with KCCQ 70 (minimal dyspnea, well-controlled).
  • A rise in NYHA class (II → III) should prompt KCCQ check; if KCCQ also drops, HF decompensation is likely. If KCCQ stable, reassess NYHA assignment (Heidenreich et al., 2022).

sections.heading: 4. Interpretation table — score ranges and clinical action
sections.bodyHtml:
Score Range Category Clinical Meaning Typical Care Action
≥ 75 Excellent HF well-controlled; minimal symptoms; preserved function and QoL Maintain current GDMT; encourage activity and rehab participation
50–74 Good Mild–moderate symptoms; some functional limitation but acceptable QoL Assess GDMT escalation; monitor for decompensation; refer to outpatient HF program for optimization
25–49 Fair Moderate–severe symptoms; notable functional limitation and emotional burden Consider HF therapy intensification (diuretic, ACE-i / ARB / ARNI uptitration, beta-blocker); urgent referral to outpatient HF program or cardiac rehab
< 25 Poor Severe dyspnea, fatigue, functional impairment; high QoL burden; high readmission risk Urgent cardiology / HF clinic review; consider hospitalization if decompensating; intensive outpatient HF program; evaluate candidacy for advanced therapies (CRT, VAD, transplant)

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: <details><summary>KCCQ-12 vs. KCCQ-23 — abbreviated form equivalence</summary> The KCCQ-12 short form (developed by Spertus and colleagues in 2015) contains 12 items vs. 23 in the full version. KCCQ-12 correlates highly with full KCCQ (r > 0.95) and is often used in busy clinical settings to save administration time. Both versions are validated and acceptable for clinical and research use. If a patient has completed KCCQ-12 in clinic, do not re-administer the full 23-item form; the 12-item result is reliable for discharge planning decisions. </details> <details><summary>Serial KCCQ — why change matters more than single baseline</summary> A single low KCCQ score is concerning; a drop in KCCQ over time is a stronger clinical signal. If KCCQ drops ≥ 5–10 points over 3–6 months (clinically meaningful deterioration), intervention or escalation is warranted. Conversely, if KCCQ rises by 5–10 points after starting a new GDMT agent (e.g., SGLT2i, ARNI), the patient is likely experiencing real symptomatic benefit. Use serial KCCQ as a tracking metric for treatment response, not one-time scores. </details> <details><summary>Depression and HF co-morbidity — KCCQ + PHQ-9</summary> Depression and heart failure co-occur in 20–30% of HF populations and independently predict poor outcomes. Low KCCQ combined with poor affect or anhedonia may signal depression, not just HF decompensation. Consider concurrent administration of PHQ-9 (depression screening) alongside KCCQ. A patient with low KCCQ and PHQ-9 ≥ 10 should be referred for psychiatric evaluation and possible antidepressant therapy in addition to HF optimization. </details> <details><summary>Language-validated versions and patient barriers</summary> KCCQ has been translated and validated into Spanish, French, German, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, and other languages. If a patient prefers a non-English questionnaire, check with the outpatient HF clinic for availability. On acute units, if the patient is acutely dyspneic or too ill to complete a questionnaire, defer KCCQ administration to 2–3 weeks post-discharge when they are more stable — the instrument is best completed when the patient is alert and able to reflect on recent symptoms. </details> <hr />

sections.heading: 6. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory
sections.bodyHtml:
• KCCQ drop of ≥ 10 points over 4–12 weeks signals significant deterioration; warrants urgent HF clinic review and possible GDMT escalation.
  • New low KCCQ (< 35) in patient previously > 50 may indicate disease progression or non-adherence; investigate symptom trajectory and medication compliance.
  • KCCQ < 25 + acute decompensation may indicate need for hospitalization, IV diuretics, or advanced therapy evaluation (CRT, VAD, transplant).
  • KCCQ mismatch with bedside assessment (patient reports excellent QoL but looks volume-overloaded and dyspneic) suggests either patient denial, unreliable self-report, or examiner error — trend both metrics and revisit NYHA assignment.

sections.heading: 7. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
• Patient-reported symptom burden is gold standard, not clinician judgment. A nurse who says "patient looks well" but KCCQ is 30 signals a real discrepancy — patient perception of symptoms matters; do not dismiss low KCCQ as "anxiety" without exploring actual symptom burden and HF status.
  • Clinically meaningful change is 5–10 points, not 1–2. Do not over-interpret a 2-point rise as "treatment success." Changes < 5 are often noise or measurement variation; ≥ 5–10 = real signal.
  • Serial KCCQ is more powerful than a single baseline. One low KCCQ score is a snapshot; a drop of ≥ 5 points over 3–6 months is a clinical signal requiring action.
  • KCCQ-12 short form is reliable and equivalent. Do not over-demand the full 23-item form if the patient has completed KCCQ-12 in clinic; the abbreviated version correlates well with full KCCQ and saves patient burden.
  • SGLT2i and ARNI trials (DELIVER, EMPEROR, PARADIGM-HF) used KCCQ as primary outcome. If discharge summary notes "KCCQ improved by 8 points," that is a trial-documented symptomatic benefit; set realistic expectations that the patient may continue to improve as GDMT takes effect.
  • Post-intervention change is a key success metric. After TAVR, AVR, CRT implant, or VAD, KCCQ should improve by ≥ 5 points within 3 months if the intervention was successful. If KCCQ does not rise, investigate: residual valve disease, poor CRT response, depression, medication non-adherence, or other limiting conditions.
  • Depression and low KCCQ co-occur; always screen PHQ-9. Patient with KCCQ < 35 and flat affect or anhedonia should be screened for depression (PHQ-9 ≥ 10) and referred for psychiatry evaluation.
  • Ask the resident or advanced practice provider for prior KCCQ at handoff. KCCQ scores are documented in outpatient HF clinic notes or prior hospitalization summaries; treat baseline KCCQ like a vital sign for prognosis and discharge planning intensity.
  • Do not push KCCQ administration if patient is acutely dyspneic. On ICU or acute units, defer questionnaire completion to outpatient HF clinic 2–3 weeks post-discharge when patient is clinically stable and able to reflect on recent symptom trends.
  • Patient burden can be high if already symptomatic. KCCQ takes 5–7 minutes, but severely ill patients may fatigue or refuse; prioritize clinical stability and readiness before administering.
  • KCCQ baseline predicts readmission risk. Patients discharged with KCCQ < 35 have significantly higher 30-day and 90-day hospital readmission rates. These patients warrant more intensive outpatient follow-up, HF clinic appointment within 7–10 days, and possibly home health referral (Spertus et al., 2007).
  • Translation and cultural validation matters. If offering KCCQ to non-English speakers, use validated language versions; generic translation may not preserve clinical meaning and can introduce bias.
  • KCCQ is NOT a depression screener alone. While low KCCQ correlates with depression, it is not a substitute for PHQ-9 or psychiatric assessment; use both tools for comprehensive patient assessment.
  • Post-op KCCQ improvement validates surgical decision-making. Pre-operative KCCQ documents how valve disease or other cardiac condition limits QoL; post-operative improvement (typically 10–20 points over 3–6 months) provides evidence that the surgery improved the patient's functional status and quality of life, supporting shared decision-making for future similar cases.

cards.title: Lung Transplantation (SLT / BLT)
cards.quickAnswer: Lung transplant for end-stage pulmonary disease; bilateral preferred for most indications (IPF, CF, pHTN) vs single for COPD. Primary graft dysfunction (PGD) — 10–30% at 72h — is biggest early risk (grade 0–3 by ISHLT criteria). Lung-protective strategy: fluid restriction + diuresis, low tidal volumes (4–6 mL/kg IBW), PEEP optimization, avoid hyperoxia, mild permissive hypercapnia if stable. Induction immunosuppression (basiliximab low-risk, ATG higher-risk) + maintenance triple therapy (tacrolimus trough 10–15 ng/mL POD 0–3, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone). Rejection surveillance mandatory: bronchoscopy + transbronchial biopsy POD 1, 3, 5, then q 2 weeks × 1 month, monthly × 3 months (ISHLT A-grade ACR, B-grade AMR grading). Infection prophylaxis critical: CMV (valganciclovir 6 months if D+/R−), aspergillus (voriconazole 3–6 months, monitor tacro interaction), PCP (TMP-SMX). One-year survival ~90% bilateral. 1–2 week ICU, 2–4 week total hospital stay.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to, why it matters.

  • Definition: Surgical removal of native lung(s) — single (SLT) or bilateral (BLT) — with allograft replacement from deceased or living-related donor. Irreversible commitment to lifelong immunosuppression, surveillance, and infection prevention.
  • Indications (who gets it): End-stage pulmonary disease unresponsive to maximal medical therapy. COPD (prefer SLT, older recipients), IPF (prefer BLT, better long-term outcomes), cystic fibrosis (BLT mandatory), pulmonary hypertension (SLT or BLT), sarcoidosis with advanced fibrosis, bronchiectasis (infection-prone, prefer BLT). Lung Allocation Score (LAS) ≥32 (varies by region). High-yield: bilateral preferred for most indications; SLT survival advantage only for COPD.
  • Operative approach: Sternotomy (BLT standard, faster sequential approach), bilateral anterior-lateral thoracotomy/"clamshell" (avoids sternotomy, more muscle trauma), thoracotomy (SLT, limited access). CPB/ECMO used for hemodynamic instability or BLT cross-clamp support.
  • Timeline: ICU 2–5 days (longer if PGD). Total hospital 2–4 weeks. Depends on PGD grade, infection, rejection, chest tube duration.
  • Survival: 1-year ~90% bilateral, ~85% SLT. 5-year ~55–60%. CLAD/BOS is long-term limiter.

sections.heading: 2.1 What makes a post-LTx lung unique: denervated lung physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
• No cough reflex — surgical denervation; reinnervation incomplete/slow. Patient cannot voluntarily cough; secretions accumulate unless aggressively suctioned. Aspiration, atelectasis, infection risk HIGH if pulmonary toilet neglected.
  • Impaired mucociliary clearance — denervation affects ciliary function + cough; gravity-dependent. Upright positioning, mobility critical.
  • Reduced sensation to airway irritation — patient unaware of need to cough; aspiration silent.
  • Pulmonary edema easily triggered — denervated lung endothelium sensitive to capillary hydrostatic pressure. Over-resuscitation (CVP >12) causes rapid non-cardiogenic edema. "Dry lung is protected lung" — core principle.

sections.heading: 2.2 Primary Graft Dysfunction (PGD) — ischemic reperfusion injury
sections.bodyHtml:
PGD is convergence of ischemic injury (cold preservation, ischemic time >8h increases risk), reperfusion injury (oxidative stress, inflammatory cytokines), and alloimmunity triggers.

  • Donor factors: Age >55, marginal oxygenation pre-harvest, infection history, smoking, aspiration
  • Recipient factors: Elevated pre-transplant PVR, female gender, mechanical ventilation pre-LTx, retransplantation
  • Surgical factors: Prolonged CPB/ECMO time, intra-operative ischemia

ISHLT 2016 grading (at 24h, 48h, 72h): Grade 0 (none) → 1R (mild, A/a <225 POD 0) → 2R (moderate, A/a 225–299) → 3R (severe, A/a ≥300 OR need mechanical support OR hemodynamic instability).

Grade 3 PGD = poor prognosis without ECMO support; mortality if untreated high.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Trigger
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at POD 0 arrival or when PGD suspected.

sections.heading: POD 0 (ICU arrival after transplant)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Expected state: Intubated on mechanical ventilation; bilateral chest tubes in place (apical, basal, mediastinal × 1–2 per side common); central line; Foley; multiple peripheral IVs. If ECMO-supported during surgery, may arrive on venoarterial ECMO (being weaned).
  • Immediate post-op focus: Rewarming (if ECMO), aggressive pulmonary toilet, PGD assessment by oxygenation + infiltrates + hemodynamics.

sections.heading: PGD Recognition (POD 0–3, typically peak 24–72h)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Bilateral infiltrates on CXR or CT (new, not pre-existing)
  • Hypoxemia: Low PaO2, elevated A/a gradient, rising FiO2 requirement, increasing PEEP need
  • Hemodynamic stress: Low cardiac output, elevated CVP (if monitored), elevated PA pressures (if swan in place)
  • Degree of urgency: Grade 0–1R = watchful; Grade 2R = escalate immunosuppression optimization + diuresis; Grade 3R = ICU + ECMO consideration if available
  • Special context: Denervated lungs are "silent" — patient won't cough or complain; RT/nursing must actively monitor infiltrates, oxygenation trends, chest tube character.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (POD 0–3 focus)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure observation. No actions yet. Target: systematic 2–5 minute bedside exam each shift POD 0–3 (intensive phase).

Respiratory status

  • SpO2, FiO2 requirement, PEEP level, mechanical ventilation parameters (VT in mL/kg IBW — goal 4–6)
  • Breath sounds (bilateral equal, unilateral consolidation?)
  • Chest tube output × 3–4 tubes: color (serous → sanguineous → serous trend), volume/8h, air leak (presence/absence in water seal)
  • Chest wall: incision integrity, swelling, ecchymosis

Hemodynamics & perfusion

  • HR, BP, MAP (goal ≥65), CVP if available (target 8–12, NOT higher)
  • Skin: warm/cool, cap refill, color
  • Urine output trend, color
  • Lactate, SvO2 if available

Labs (daily POD 0–3)

  • ABG: PaO2, A/a gradient, pH, pCO2 (guide to PGD grade + vent optimization)
  • CBC, CMP, LFTs
  • Tacrolimus level (POD 1–2 first draw; target 10–15 ng/mL)
  • PT/INR, lactate, prothrombin time (if bleeding concern)

Lines & devices

  • Central line placement; function; no signs of CLABSI (erythema, purulent discharge)
  • Foley patent, color of urine
  • Chest tubes × 3–4: all draining; none kinked or occluded

Pain, sedation, delirium

  • CAM-ICU if not on paralytics
  • Pain scale (patient may not perceive airway irritation from denervation)
  • Sedation appropriate for mechanical ventilation

Recent history: pre-transplant & intra-operative context

  • Ischemic time (SLT ~4–6h, BLT ~6–8h typical; >8h = higher PGD risk)
  • Donor age, oxygenation history, infection status
  • CPB/ECMO time during surgery
  • Single vs bilateral; SLT side (right larger, preferred unless contraindication)
  • Recipient PVR pre-transplant (elevated = PGD risk)
  • Intra-operative events (hypotension, arrhythmia, transfusion volume)

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 (ICU) — Graft arrival, PGD assessment begins
sections.bodyHtml:
Immediate arrival priorities (first 2–4h)

  1. Position & stabilize: Head of bed 30–45°; assess bilateral breath sounds; bilateral pulse ox if available.
  2. Pulmonary toilet NON-NEGOTIABLE: Aggressive suctioning (q1–2h, PRN); bronchoscopy STAT for airway clearance (inspect anastomoses, evacuate clots/secretions). RT consult STAT for aggressive coughing assistance + chest PT + postural drainage setup.
  3. Rewarming (if ECMO): Gradual core rewarming; avoid overshoot (hyperthermia increases O2 demand, worsens PGD). Target 36–37°C.
  4. PGD assessment starts: Serial ABGs (POD 0 4h, 8h, 24h at minimum); CXR baseline + repeat q4–6h if deteriorating. Grade by A/a gradient + infiltrates by ISHLT criteria.
  5. Fluid restriction CRITICAL: Target CVP 8–12 (NOT higher). Avoid bolus IVs. Use vasopressors (phenylephrine 0.5–1.4 mcg/kg/min, norepinephrine 0.01–0.05 mcg/kg/min) for MAP ≥65 instead of fluids. Denervated lung vulnerable to non-cardiogenic edema with fluid overload — "dry lung is protected lung."
  6. Ventilation strategy — lung-protective: Tidal volume 4–6 mL/kg IBW; PEEP 8–10 cm H2O (adjust for recruitment without barotrauma); RR ≤25; target plateau pressure <30 cm H2O. Avoid FiO2 >60% if possible (high O2 worsens PGD reperfusion injury); permissive hypercapnia acceptable if pH >7.25 and hemodynamically stable.
  7. Induction immunosuppression: ATG (anti-thymocyte globulin) 1–1.5 mg/kg IV OR basiliximab 20 mg IV (lower-risk, preferred if donor/recipient low immunologic risk). Start POD 0.
  8. Maintenance triple immunosuppression (POD 0):
    • Tacrolimus IV: Initial 0.01–0.03 mg/kg/day divided q12h (or continuous drip 0.03–0.05 mg/kg/day). Draw level POD 1–2 (target 10–15 ng/mL POD 0–3, higher than some cardiac programs due to PGD risk).
    • Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) IV: 1 g q12h (transition to PO when tolerating diet).
    • Methylprednisolone pulse: 500 mg IV once POD 0 OR 500 mg IV × 1–3 doses POD 0–2 depending on program. Then prednisone 1 mg/kg/day (taper to ~10 mg by discharge).
    • CMV prophylaxis: Valganciclovir 900 mg IV q12h (or ganciclovir 5 mg/kg IV q12h if not absorbing PO). Continue 3–6 months (longer if D+/R− mismatch — donor CMV+, recipient CMV− = highest risk).
    • Aspergillus prophylaxis: Voriconazole IV 6 mg/kg q12h × 2 doses, then 4 mg/kg q12h (target trough 1–5.5 mcg/mL; monitor level). Transition to PO when tolerating. CRITICAL: Voriconazole ↑ tacro levels significantly — expect to ↓ tacro dose 30–50%. Check tacro level closely q 2–3 days.
    • PCP prophylaxis: TMP-SMX DS daily (or 3×/week alternatives: dapsone + pyrimethamine, or atovaquone if sulfa allergy). Start POD 0.
    • Chest tube management: Monitor output q1h (expect serous, sanguineous early; should begin clearing by POD 2–3). Apply gentle suction (−10 to −20 cm H2O) to aid lung re-expansion; air leak common and expected first 24–48h. Assess for pneumothorax on CXR; keep chest tubes in longer than cardiac (may need suction ×2–3 weeks if air leak persistent).
    • Labs POD 0: CBC, CMP, LFTs, PT/INR, ABG, lactate, blood cultures (if fever). Tacro level POD 1–2.
    • Monitoring: Continuous pulse ox, tele (POAF risk ~20–25%), UAC if available (avoid if possible — invasive monitoring not routine). Hourly vitals, I/O, chest tube output.

If PGD Grade 1R–2R identified (POD 0–24h)

  • Continue aggressive pulmonary toilet, lung-protective vent strategy
  • Optimize immunosuppression (ensure tacro target reached, mycophenolate adequate)
  • Cautious diuresis (furosemide 0.5–1 mg/kg/dose q12h if fluid overloaded); target euvolemia (not hypovolemic, not edematous). Monitor creatinine closely (tacro + furosemide = AKI risk).
  • Consider prone positioning if available (improves oxygenation, off-loads dependent lung)
  • Nitric oxide not first-line for PGD alone (reserved for pulmonary HTN), but may be considered if coexisting PHT elevated

If PGD Grade 3R identified (POD 0–24h, A/a ≥300 OR hemodynamic instability)

  • ICU-level support: Consider ECMO discussion with transplant surgery (veno-venous ECMO provides oxygenation, allows lung rest, may bridge to recovery; veno-arterial if hemodynamically compromised). ECMO improves outcomes in severe PGD if available within 24–48h.
  • If ECMO unavailable or declined: maximal medical support (optimized vent, inotropes, prone if available), palliative care discussion if deteriorating.
  • Do NOT give up on Grade 3 PGD early — some recover with intensive support over days–weeks.

sections.heading: 5B. POD 1–7 (ICU/step-down transition) — Stabilization, rejection surveillance, infection prevention
sections.bodyHtml:
Daily bedside priorities POD 1–7

  1. Bronchoscopy schedule (mandatory): POD 1, 3, 5 at minimum; then q 1–2 weeks × 4–8 weeks depending on findings.

    Biopsies at EACH bronchoscopy — rejection often asymptomatic; diagnosis is biopsy alone. Also obtains BAL for infection surveillance (viral, fungal, bacterial, CMV, PCP stain/culture). - Anastomotic assessment: Inspect bronchial anastomoses × 1–2 (right and left); assess for stenosis (narrowing), dehiscence (separation, surgical emergency — notify surgery STAT if suspected), inflammation, granulation tissue. - Transbronchial biopsies (ISHLT 2016 grading):

    • A-grade (Acute Cellular Rejection, lymphocytic infiltration): A0 (none) → A1 (minimal) → A2 (mild) → A3 (moderate) → A4 (severe). Presence of perivascular or interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate.
    • B-grade (Lymphoid follicles/aggregates, AMR features): B0 (none) → B1–B4 (increasing follicle prominence).
    • C-grade (Chronic airway rejection): C0 (none) → C1–C2 (airway epithelial damage, fibrosis).
    • BAL interpretation: Cell counts, differential; culture bacterial/fungal/viral; CMV stain/culture; PCP stain; galactomannan (Aspergillus antigen).

  2. Ventilator weaning strategy POD 1–3:

    • Extubation target: FiO2 ≤50%, PEEP ≤8, RR <30, adequate cough reflex (even if weak — patient may fake due to discomfort). Consider extubation by POD 2–3 if PGD minimal (Grade 0–1R) and oxygenation permits.
    • Post-extubation: Aggressive pulmonary toilet continues (suctioning, incentive spirometry, chest PT, positioning). Supplemental O2 titrated to SpO2 ≥90%.

  3. Immunosuppression adjustment POD 1–7:

    • Tacrolimus: IV → PO transition as tolerating (typically PO by POD 2–3). Continue targeting 10–15 ng/mL POD 0–7. Draw trough level q 2–3 days POD 1–7.
    • Mycophenolate: IV → PO transition (1 g PO q12h).
    • Prednisone: Continue taper (1 mg/kg POD 0, taper toward 0.5–0.75 mg/kg by POD 7, target ~0.3 mg/kg or 10 mg by discharge). Some programs maintain 0.5 mg/kg longer.
    • Induction: Complete induction course (typically single ATG or basiliximab dose POD 0; some programs repeat basiliximab q 5 days × 2 total).

  4. Rejection management — if biopsy shows A1 or higher:

    • A0 (no rejection): Continue baseline immunosuppression.
    • A1 (minimal): May observe; OR consider pulse methylprednisolone 500 mg IV × 3 days + ↑ tacro target (to 12–15 ng/mL if not already there) depending on program practice. Repeat biopsy at next bronchoscopy.
    • A2–A4 (mild–severe): Pulse methylprednisolone 500 mg IV × 3 days; ↑ tacro target; ↑ mycophenolate (if on 1 g q12h, some increase to 1.5 g q12h or add thymoglobulin). Consider repeat induction therapy (ATG 1–1.5 mg/kg) if moderate–severe. Repeat biopsy at next bronchoscopy.
    • B-grade (lymphoid follicles): Context-dependent; mild B1 may observe; moderate–severe may warrant pulse steroids + enhanced IS. Indicates higher risk of future rejection.

  5. Infection surveillance POD 1–7:

    • Fever: Mandatory workup — CXR, CBC, BUN/Cr, blood cultures × 2; bronchoscopy STAT for BAL (cultures, PCP stain, fungal stain, CMV, galactomannan). Empiric antibiotics per hospital antibiogram (gram-positive, gram-negative, atypical coverage) until cultures reviewed. Optimize voriconazole (Aspergillus), valganciclovir (CMV).
    • CMV PCR: q 1–2 weeks × 3 months on prophylaxis (monitor for breakthrough viremia even on valganciclovir).
    • Aspergillus galactomannan: If fever + cough, obtain BAL galactomannan; if elevated, escalate voriconazole (ensure trough adequate), consider adding liposomal amphotericin B.
    • PCP: Prophylaxis on board (TMP-SMX); if SOB + hypoxemia + risk factors, consider PCP empirically (induce sputum or BAL for stain; adjunctive steroids if empiric).

  6. Chest tube management POD 1–7:

    • Monitor output trend; air leak should be declining by POD 2–3.
    • Removal criteria per surgeon: typically <150 mL/8h serous output, minimal air leak, well-expanded on CXR. Often remove one tube at a time to assess for re-accumulation.
    • Timeline: most chest tubes out by POD 7–10 if healing progressing well.

  7. Mobility & pulmonary rehab POD 1–7:

    • CRITICAL for denervated lung: Gravity-dependent clearance; upright positioning (seated, standing), walking as tolerated. RT aggressive (suctioning, incentive spirometry, chest PT, postural drainage).
    • Initiate PT/OT POD 1–2; goal sitting edge of bed POD 1–2, standing POD 2–3, ambulating POD 3–5 (timeline varies by PGD grade).

  8. Nutrition POD 1–7: - NPO until extubated; once extubated, diet as tolerated (high-protein, high-calorie to support graft healing + infection prevention). Calorie requirements often elevated post-op.

  9. Labs POD 1–7: Tacro level q 2–3 days; CBC, CMP, LFTs q 3–5 days. Renal function careful monitoring (tacro nephrotoxic, AKI common).

  10. POAF surveillance: Telemetry monitoring; ~20–25% lung tx recipients develop POAF POD 2–7. If new irregular rhythm → 12-lead ECG, replace K ≥4 and Mg ≥2, notify APP for rate vs rhythm plan (see Escalation/POAF section).

sections.heading: 5C. POD 7–14 (Step-down/5W transition) — Rejection/infection surveillance, discharge planning
sections.bodyHtml:
Daily bedside priorities POD 7–14

  1. Bronchoscopy continuation: Usually q 1 week until POD 28, then less frequent (q 2–4 weeks depending on program). Biopsies + BAL at each visit. Track biopsy grades (A/B/C) and any rejection trends.

  2. Immunosuppression stabilization POD 7–14:

    • Tacrolimus: Maintain 10–15 ng/mL; trough level q 5–7 days as stabilizing.
    • Mycophenolate: 1 g PO q12h (some programs use 1.5 g q12h).
    • Prednisone: Taper toward 0.3–0.5 mg/kg or fixed 10 mg daily by POD 14.
    • Antimicrobial prophylaxis: Valganciclovir + voriconazole continuing; TMP-SMX ongoing.

  3. Rejection management if A2+ on biopsy:

    • Pulse methylprednisolone 500 mg IV × 3 days completed.
    • Ensure tacro level adequate (12–15 ng/mL if moderate–severe rejection).
    • Some programs add mycophenolate increase or consider antibody therapy (thymoglobulin, alemtuzumab) if recurrent or high-grade rejection.

  4. Discharge planning (begin POD 7–10, complete by discharge):

    • Oxygen requirement: Assess on room air vs supplemental O2; home pulse ox if needed; home O2 setup if required.
    • Activity restrictions: No lifting >10 lbs × 4–6 weeks; no strenuous exercise × 3 months. Progressive activity per PT/OT.
    • Incision care: Shower allowed once incision closed; keep clean and dry. No tub baths × 2–3 weeks (avoid immersion).
    • Medications at discharge: Tacrolimus (exact dose per protocol, trough level monitored biweekly × 4 weeks then monthly), mycophenolate (1 g PO q12h), prednisone (taper schedule, typically 10 mg daily at discharge), valganciclovir (900 mg PO daily × 3–6 months), voriconazole (transition to PO, maintain for 3–6 months; monitor interaction with tacro), TMP-SMX (daily or 3×/week), PPI (omeprazole 20 mg daily if tolerating — GI protection), beta-blocker if cardiac comorbidity, statin, bowel regimen PRN (mycophenolate often causes diarrhea).
    • Outpatient follow-up: Schedule pulmonary bronchoscopy (q 2 weeks × 1 month, then q 1 month × 3 months, then q 3 months × 1 year, then per protocol). ID follow-up (initial biweekly, then monthly). Transplant surgery 2–4 weeks. Cardiology if pre-transplant cardiac disease. Nephrology baseline + q 1 month POD 0–3 months (tacro monitoring).
    • Spirometry: Baseline FEV1 at discharge; q 3 months indefinitely for BOS surveillance (↓FEV1 ≥10% triggers workup).
    • Patient/family education: Infection prevention (filtered water, avoid stray animals, reptiles, cats; no raw/undercooked meat), rejection symptoms (cough, dyspnea, fever, fatigue — call immediately), medication adherence (no generic substitution of tacro, exact timing), bronchoscopy schedule non-negotiable, infection prevention, activity progression.

  5. Discharge readiness criteria (POD 10–21 typical, highly variable):

    • Off mechanical ventilation × 48–72h stable
    • Tolerating oral diet and medications
    • Ambulating independently or with minimal assist
    • All chest tubes out
    • No active infection (afebrile × 24–48h if had recent fever)
    • Stable renal function (creatinine plateau or improving)
    • Tacro level stable, on target
    • No active rejection on last biopsy (A0 or minimal A1)
    • Home O2 requirement assessed; supplemental O2 stable or not required
    • Incision healing
    • Patient/family demonstrates understanding of medications, rejection symptoms, infection prevention, follow-up schedule

sections.heading: 5D. Discharge & Post-Discharge (Goal POD 21–35, highly variable)
sections.bodyHtml:
At discharge

  • Medications: Tacrolimus (exact dose per protocol; biweekly trough level × 4 weeks, then monthly), mycophenolate (1 g PO q12h), prednisone (taper, typically 10 mg daily at discharge), valganciclovir (900 mg PO daily × 3–6 months, longer if D+/R−), voriconazole (PO, 3–6 months; monitor tacro levels — major interaction), TMP-SMX (daily or 3×/week), PPI, beta-blocker if indicated, statin, bowel regimen PRN.
  • Prophylaxis schedule: CMV (valganciclovir × 3–6 months standard; longer if high-risk D+/R−), aspergillus (voriconazole or inhaled amphotericin × 3–6 months, longer if high-risk), PCP (TMP-SMX ongoing indefinitely).
  • Surveillance schedule: Bronchoscopy q 2–4 weeks × 3 months, q 1–2 months × 6 months, q 3 months × 1 year, then per protocol (q 6 months or annually). Spirometry q 3 months indefinitely. Outpatient pulmonology coordination with bronchoscopy schedule.
  • Monitoring: Tacro level biweekly × 4 weeks, then monthly. CMV PCR q 2 weeks × 3 months (on prophylaxis, monitor for breakthrough). FEV1 baseline at discharge, trend for BOS (≥10% decline triggers workup).
  • Activity: Progressive per PT/OT; cardiac rehab if concurrent cardiac disease; avoid extreme exertion early but mobility essential for airway clearance.
  • Infection prevention: Filtered water (Cryptosporidium), avoid stray animals/reptiles/cats, no raw/undercooked meat, no unpasteurized dairy, hand hygiene, avoid crowded places during respiratory season, avoid sick contacts, annual flu vaccine, pneumococcal per protocol (non-live vaccines only).
  • Smoking/alcohol: MANDATORY cessation (accelerate BOS, infection).
  • Food/nutrition: High-protein, balanced diet. Avoid grapefruit (tacro interaction).
  • Skin care: SPF 50+ daily, avoid midday sun, cover-up clothing; annual dermatology screening (skin cancer risk 20–50-fold elevated on lifelong immunosuppression).
  • Rejection symptoms: Cough, dyspnea, fever, fatigue, malaise — call transplant team immediately (bronchoscopy often warranted even without obvious infiltrate).
  • Adherence: Patient education intensive — missed bronchoscopies = missed rejection diagnosis. Missed medications = rejection/infection. Non-adherence is #1 reason for late graft failure. Written summaries and teach-backs essential before discharge; family involvement critical.

Post-discharge surveillance (3 months – 1 year)

  • Monthly ID visits: CMV prophylaxis monitoring (PCR if symptomatic), aspergillus prophylaxis (trough level if voriconazole), PCP prophylaxis, vaccine counseling (live vaccines contraindicated), medication interactions (voriconazole ↔ tacro critical).
  • Pulmonology coordinate bronchoscopy: q 2–4 weeks × 3 months, then less frequent. Biopsies + BAL protocol. Screen for infection, rejection, anastomotic complications.
  • Spirometry surveillance: q 3 months indefinitely. Baseline FEV1 established at discharge; monitor for ≥10% decline (BOS trigger). If decline detected, repeat spirometry (rule out technique error), bronchoscopy (rule out infection, obstruction, assess airways), imaging (HRCT for BOS/RAS features).
  • BOS (Bronchiolitis Obliterans Syndrome) early management: If FEV1 declining, optimize immunosuppression (ensure tacro adequate), consider adding azithromycin (immunomodulator, some programs use empirically in CLAD), smoking cessation, pulmonary rehab, infection prevention (CMV, aspergillus).

Long-term (1+ years)

  • Lifelong immunosuppression & prophylaxis: Triple therapy (tacro + MMF + prednisone) indefinitely. Prophylaxis (CMV valganciclovir often indefinite or per risk; aspergillus voriconazole 3–6 months then reassess; PCP TMP-SMX indefinite).
  • CLAD/BOS surveillance: Spirometry q 3 months indefinitely. BOS = chronic rejection; defined as FEV1 decline ≥10% from baseline. Develops months to years post-LTx. Two phenotypes: BOS (obstructive, FEV1/FVC <70%) and RAS (restrictive, FVC decline, normal FEV1/FVC). Early intervention (optimize IS, azithromycin, smoking cessation) may slow progression. Late-stage BOS (FEV1 <1 L, rapid decline) → re-transplantation consideration (rare, limited organs) or palliative care.
  • PTLD (Post-Transplant Lymphoproliferative Disorder): Lifetime risk ~1–5%. EBV-seronegative recipients (D+/R− mismatch) at highest risk early (months–1 year). Presents with fever, lymphadenopathy, elevated LDH. EBV PCR screening (some programs) or biopsy if suspicion high. Management: reduce IS (especially MMF, lower tacro target), consider rituximab or chemotherapy depending on grade/staging.
  • Skin cancer screening: Baseline full-body skin exam; annual dermatology. Risk 20–50-fold higher than general population on lifelong IS. Early detection and excision essential.
  • Osteoporosis screening: DEXA scan baseline; prednisone + tacro increase osteoporosis risk. Consider calcium/vitamin D supplementation + bisphosphonate if indicated.
  • Metabolic syndrome: Monitor lipids, glucose (prednisone + MMF increase hyperglycemia risk); statin + ACE inhibitor commonly used. Nephrology follow-up (tacro chronic toxicity).
  • Cardiovascular risk: Accelerated atherosclerosis on transplant; consider stress test if new dyspnea/chest discomfort.

sections.heading: SBAR Communication Template
sections.bodyHtml:
When escalating clinical deterioration, use structured handoff:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p bilateral/single lung transplant on [date]." B: "Patient presenting with [symptom — fever/hypoxemia/hemoptysis/infiltrate on CXR]. Currently [SpO2%, FiO2%, PEEP, VT, RR]. [Recent labs — tacro level, CBC, Cr]. [Last bronchoscopy findings — date, biopsies, BAL results]." A: "Assessment: Concerning for [PGD grade if applicable / rejection / infection — specify]. On current immunosuppression [doses], prophylaxis [what + when started]. [Hemodynamic stability assessment — stable vs unstable.]" R: "Requesting [STAT bronchoscopy / additional labs / medication adjustment / ICU transfer / ECMO consideration]."

sections.heading: Who to Call by Scenario
sections.bodyHtml:
Scenario Primary Contact Secondary Notes
Fever + infiltrate (POD 1–7) Transplant pulmonology + ID Surgeon on-call Fever warrants bronchoscopy + BAL (cultures, stain, antigen) even without obvious infiltrate. Do not wait for imaging.
PGD Grade 3R suspected Surgeon + ICU team ECMO coordinator Consider ECMO if available + early within 24–48h. Do not delay.
Anastomotic dehiscence suspected STAT SURGEON ICU Surgical emergency. Notify OR. Do NOT delay for labs/imaging.
Rejection suspected (A2+ biopsy) Transplant pulmonology Immunology Escalate immunosuppression; pulse steroids; consider induction.
CMV viremia detected (PCR+) ID + transplant — Intensify valganciclovir; may add IV ganciclovir.
Aspergillus suspected ID + pulmonology Respiratory Optimize voriconazole; monitor tacro closely; consider adding amphotericin B.
Pneumothorax expansion Surgeon STAT RT May require intervention. Do NOT delay.
Hemoptysis Surgeon + pulmonology — Bronchoscopy for source; may need embolization.
Post-op bleeding Surgeon + OR Anesthesia Notify OR for potential return.
POAF (new irregular rhythm) APP/fellow RRT if unstable Stable: 12-lead, replace K/Mg. Unstable: STAT call, prepare DCCV.
Acute kidney injury Nephrology + transplant — Hold or ↓ tacro; assess volume; may need RRT.
PRES/seizure Neurology + transplant ICU Likely tacro toxicity. CT/MRI; ↓ tacro target.
Acute stroke Stroke code + transplant Neurology Time last known well. Consider thrombolytics (team decision).
Sepsis Sepsis pathway + ICU + ID Surgeon Blood cultures; broad antibiotics.

sections.heading: 7.1 PGD Pathophysiology — ischemic reperfusion injury
sections.bodyHtml: Ischemia during harvest + cold preservation (4–8h) → hypoxic injury, endothelial damage. Reperfusion → ROS surge, complement cascade, microvascular thrombosis. Result: protein leak, bilateral infiltrates, hypoxemia, edema. Grade 3 PGD = profound injury; organ may not recover without rest (ECMO). Prevention (limited): minimize ischemic time, optimize donor oxygenation, lung-protective ventilation intra-op. Management: protect lung (low VT, PEEP, avoid hyperoxia), restrict fluid, diuresis, ECMO if severe.

sections.heading: 7.2 Lung-protective ventilation strategy
sections.bodyHtml:
Goal: Minimize ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) while maintaining adequate oxygenation.

Parameter Target Rationale
Tidal Volume (VT) 4–6 mL/kg IBW Minimize barotrauma, volutrauma.
PEEP 8–10 cm H2O initially Balance recruitment vs overdistension.
Plateau pressure <30 cm H2O Limit overdistension.
FiO2 Titrate to SpO2 ≥90%, target <50–60% High O2 worsens PGD.
pCO2 target 40–50; permissive hypercapnia (pH >7.25) OK Avoid aggressive hyperventilation.

sections.heading: 7.3 Surveillance bronchoscopy & ISHLT 2016 biopsy grading
sections.bodyHtml:
Why mandatory: Rejection often asymptomatic. Only diagnostic = transbronchial biopsy + ISHLT grading. Do NOT skip biopsies because "patient feels well."

ISHLT A-grade (Acute Cellular Rejection): A0 (none) → A1 (minimal) → A2 (mild) → A3 (moderate) → A4 (severe). Perivascular/interstitial lymphocytic infiltrate.

ISHLT B-grade (Lymphoid follicles/AMR): B0 (none) → B1–B4 (increasing prominence). Indicates activated B cells, possible antibody-mediated immunity.

ISHLT C-grade (Chronic airway rejection): C0 (none) → C1–C2 (airway epithelial damage, fibrosis). Long-term risk of BOS.

sections.heading: 7.4 Induction immunosuppression: basiliximab vs ATG
sections.bodyHtml:
Agent Mechanism Dose Best For
Basiliximab IL-2 receptor antagonist. Non-depleting. 20 mg IV × 2 (POD 0, POD 4) Low-risk pairs; first transplant.
ATG Polyclonal T-cell depletion. Robust. 1–1.5 mg/kg IV × 3–5 days High-risk pairs; HLA mismatch; retransplant.

sections.heading: 7.5 Maintenance immunosuppression: tacrolimus, MMF, prednisone
sections.bodyHtml:
Tacrolimus: Calcineurin inhibitor; IL-2 inhibition. IV 0.01–0.03 mg/kg/day → PO as tolerating.

Target trough 10–15 ng/mL POD 0–3 (narrow window). Monitor level q 2–3 days.

CRITICAL: Voriconazole ↑ tacro 20–50% (need ↓ dose 30–50%), antifungals/macrolides/diltiazem also interact. Grapefruit contraindicated.

Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF): Antiproliferative. IV 1 g q12h → PO 1 g q12h. No trough level needed. Common side effect: GI (diarrhea ~40–50%). Monitor CBC (rare bone marrow suppression).

Prednisone: Anti-inflammatory. POD 0 1 mg/kg → taper to ~10 mg daily by discharge. Long-term most recipients ~5–10 mg indefinitely. Monitor hyperglycemia, insomnia, osteoporosis.

sections.heading: 7.6 CMV prophylaxis & monitoring
sections.bodyHtml:
Valganciclovir: 900 mg PO daily × 3–6 months (adjust for renal function).

Trough monitoring not needed; CMV PCR q 1–2 weeks × 3 months (monitor for breakthrough). D+/R− = highest risk; extend prophylaxis 6–12 months. Side effects: GI, tremor, cytopenias (rare).

sections.heading: 7.7 Aspergillus prophylaxis (voriconazole)
sections.bodyHtml:
Voriconazole: IV 6 mg/kg q12h → PO 200 mg q12h.

Target trough 1–5.5 mcg/mL. Duration: 3–6 months.

CRITICAL INTERACTION: ↑ tacro 20–50% (expect to ↓ tacro dose 30–50%, monitor level q 2–3 days). Hepatotoxicity (monitor AST/ALT); visual disturbances (photopsia in ~30%); photosensitivity. If toxicity → switch posaconazole or isavuconazole.

sections.heading: 7.8 PCP prophylaxis
sections.bodyHtml: TMP-SMX DS daily (or 3×/week). Indefinite on IS. Also covers S. aureus, Toxoplasma. Sulfa allergy alternatives: dapsone + pyrimethamine + leucovorin, or atovaquone (less effective).

sections.heading: 7.9 CLAD / BOS — chronic lung allograft dysfunction
sections.bodyHtml:
BOS = chronic rejection; defined as FEV1 decline ≥10% from baseline. Develops months–years post-LTx. Pathophysiology: recurrent acute rejection + infection + ischemia → airway epithelial damage → fibrosis → obstruction.

Two phenotypes: BOS (obstructive ~70%) and RAS (restrictive ~20%). Management: optimize IS, azithromycin 250 mg 3×/week, smoking cessation, pulmonary rehab. Median BOS-free survival ~5–6 years. Severe (FEV1 <1 L) → re-transplantation rare option or palliative care.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert deterioration trajectory — if any appear in previously stable patient, re-escalate.

  • Infiltrates trending larger/more bilateral despite management → escalate, consider bronchoscopy if not done.
  • FiO2 trending up despite lung-protective ventilation → worsening PGD/infection; ECMO consideration.
  • CVP trending >12 with pulmonary edema worsening → over-resuscitation; tighten fluid.
  • Chest tube output increasing or character changing (hemoptysis, purulent) → bronchoscopy STAT.
  • Tacro level not rising as expected or oral absorption poor → drug interaction? Malabsorption? Check pharmacy.
  • Fever ×2+ days on antibiotics + infiltrate not improving → wrong coverage? Rejection? Bronchoscopy STAT.
  • Creatinine rising (>0.3/48h or >50% baseline) → tacro + voriconazole + hypotension. Check tacro level; assess CVP; hold NSAIDs.
  • K+ trending >5.5 refractory → hyperkalemia from tacro + renal dysfunction. May need dialysis; consider dose reduction.
  • WBC trending down on valganciclovir (<2.5) → ganciclovir bone marrow suppression. Reduce dose; monitor ANC.
  • AST/ALT trending up on voriconazole → hepatotoxicity. Consider dose reduction or switch.
  • Visual disturbances reported (photopsia, blurred vision) → voriconazole toxicity; consider switch.
  • Cough persisting/worsening → concerning for rejection or infection. Do not dismiss.
  • Dyspnea out of proportion to vitals → early rejection/infection/cardiac event. EKG, troponin per suspicion.
  • Desaturation with minimal activity → early PGD/rejection/cardiac. Trend; may need home O2.
  • Patient report of vague symptoms (malaise, fatigue) dismissed by team → trust patient. Escalate for bronchoscopy.
  • Adherence concerns flagged → #1 predictor of graft failure. Intensify education; social work, pharmacy support.
  • Repeat rejection (≥2 A2+ biopsies) → poor match or compliance. Escalate: consider antibody therapy, switch IS regimen.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Denervated lung has NO cough reflex — aggressive pulmonary toilet is non-negotiable, not optional. Scheduled suctioning (q 2–4h), bronchoscopy for clearance, chest PT, positioning, IS mandatory. Neglect → rapid atelectasis, aspiration, infection.

  2. Avoid fluid over-resuscitation — DRY LUNG IS PROTECTED LUNG. Target CVP 8–12 (NOT higher). Use vasopressors (phenyephrine, norepinephrine) for MAP ≥65 instead of IV fluids. Common, preventable mistake → prolonged ventilation, PGD progression.

  3. PGD is most common early post-op problem, graded 0–3 at 24h, 48h, 72h. Grade 0–1R = watchful. Grade 2R = escalate optimization. Grade 3R = poor prognosis without ECMO. Baseline tacro 10–15 ng/mL POD 0–3.

  4. Surveillance bronchoscopy with biopsies is MANDATORY, not PRN. Rejection often asymptomatic. Only diagnostic = biopsy + ISHLT grading. Do NOT skip because "patient feels good." POD 1, 3, 5 minimum; then q 1–2 weeks × 4–8 weeks.

  5. Aspergillus is #1 infectious killer in lung tx — prophylaxis + early detection critical. Voriconazole prophylaxis standard (target trough 1–5.5 mcg/mL × 3–6 months).

    CRITICAL: Monitor tacro closely — voriconazole ↑ tacro 20–50%. Fever + cough → bronchoscopy + BAL.

  6. CMV prophylaxis is universal 3–6 months (longer if D+/R−). Valganciclovir 900 mg daily.

    Do NOT stop early. CMV PCR q 1–2 weeks × 3 months. D+/R− = highest risk; extend 6–12 months.

  7. Tacrolimus-drug interactions pervasive — voriconazole, antifungals, macrolides, diltiazem. GRAPEFRUIT CONTRAINDICATED. New drug → check interaction; consider tacro level q 2–3 days. Narrow therapeutic window.

  8. BOS (Bronchiolitis Obliterans Syndrome) = chronic rejection; FEV1 decline ≥10% from baseline. Baseline FEV1 at discharge; spirometry q 3 months indefinitely. Early intervention critical: optimize IS, azithromycin, smoking cessation. Median BOS-free survival ~5–6 years.

  9. Air leak is common and expected POD 0–2. Gentle suction (−10 to −20 cm H2O), time, lung re-expansion. Most resolve by POD 7–10. Persistent → bronchoscopy; may need fibrin glue or stent.

  10. Anastomotic complications (stenosis, dehiscence, malacia) are unique to lung tx. Surveillance bronchoscopy catches early stenosis.

    Dehiscence is SURGICAL EMERGENCY — notify surgery STAT.

  11. POAF occurs in ~20–25%, peak POD 2–3. Rate control: beta-blockers (metoprolol), diltiazem. Replace K ≥4, Mg ≥2 critical. Anticoagulation decision per team (bleeding risk post-op).

  12. Infection is #1 cause of 1-year mortality. Aspergillus, CMV, PCP, HAP all common. Fever → aggressive workup: CXR, CBC, blood cultures, bronchoscopy STAT (BAL). Do not treat blindly.

  13. Patient adherence is #1 long-term determinant of graft survival. Missed bronchoscopies = missed rejection. Missed meds = rejection/infection. Non-adherence = #1 reason for late graft failure. Educate heavily on lifelong commitment. Written summaries + teach-backs + family involvement.

  14. Nurse often first to spot rejection or infection. Cough, dyspnea, fever, malaise, subtle desaturation — escalate to team. Do NOT dismiss as postop irritation.

  15. Post-discharge: surveillance failure = graft failure. Missed bronchoscopies, skipped meds, delayed ID/pulmonology = undetected rejection/CLAD/PTLD until symptomatic (often too late). Robust outpatient program + patient adherence essential.

cards.title: Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP)
cards.quickAnswer: MAP is the time-weighted average pressure in the arterial tree during one heartbeat — the perfusion pressure sustaining end-organ blood flow. Normal is 65–110 mmHg. Default cardiac surgery target ≥ 65 mmHg; TAAA ≥ 85, LVAD 70–85, acute stroke permissive HTN (MAP ~160). Arterial line (a-line) gold standard; cuff approximation drifts in shock. Re-level transducer at phlebostatic axis q4h to prevent silent position artifact.
cards.quickAnswerHtml: MAP is the time-weighted average pressure in the arterial tree during one heartbeat — the perfusion pressure sustaining end-organ blood flow. Normal is 65–110 mmHg. Default cardiac surgery target ≥ 65 mmHg; TAAA ≥ 85, LVAD 70–85, acute stroke permissive HTN (MAP ~160). Arterial line (a-line) gold standard; cuff approximation drifts in shock. Re-level transducer at phlebostatic axis q4h to prevent silent position artifact.
cards.sourcePrecedence: Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Brown (2023) → CVICU Handbook (2017) → Bojar (2020) → AACN Practice Alerts (2016)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition and clinical scope — novice orientation.

  • Definition: Mean arterial pressure is the pressure-time integral of arterial pressure over one complete cardiac cycle — the perfusion pressure driving blood into end organs (brain, heart, kidneys, mesentery, extremities).
  • Why it matters: MAP, not systolic alone, determines whether tissues perfuse. A patient with SBP 140 but MAP 55 (wide pulse pressure, low diastolic) may be perfusion-compromised.
  • Who this applies to: all post-op cardiac surgery patients receiving hemodynamic monitoring; any patient on vasopressor, inotrope, or aggressive antihypertensive therapy.
  • Gold standard measurement: arterial line waveform integration (true integrated mean). Cuff oscillometric approximation, useful clinically, drifts in shock and extremes.

sections.heading: 2. Formula / Calculation
sections.bodyHtml:
Method Formula Notes
Cuff (oscillometric) MAP ≈ (SBP + 2×DBP) / 3 Approximation; inherent to cuff mechanics. Works well in normotension.
Arterial line (true) Integrated mean over one beat Direct pressure waveform integration. Truth in shock, post-op, high-precision titration.
Pulse Pressure (PP) PP = SBP − DBP Normal 40–60 mmHg. Narrow PP → volume loss or ↓ CO.

Key insight: The cuff formula weights diastole twice (2×DBP) because the cardiac cycle spends ~2/3 time in diastole. An a-line gives the true integrated mean; cuff gives an approximation that drifts in extremes (hypotension, severe HTN, arrhythmia). Calcified arteries (elderly, ESRD, DM chronic) falsely elevate cuff pressure.

sections.heading: 3. Normal Range / Targets
sections.bodyHtml:
Context MAP Target Rationale
Healthy adult (normotensive) 65–110 mmHg Autoregulation preserved across this range.
Cardiac surgery default (most procedures) ≥ 65 mmHg Lowest threshold for adequate end-organ perfusion (Bojar, 2020).
TAAA / TEVAR repair ≥ 85 mmHg Protects artery of Adamkiewicz; under-treating carries paraplegia risk.
Acute ischemic stroke (no tPA) ≈ 160 mmHg (SBP ≤ 220) Permissive HTN accepted; avoids aggressive lowering, which reduces collateral flow.
LVAD patient 70–85 mmHg (by Doppler) Over-MAP → suction events; under-MAP → inadequate pump flow. Requires Doppler or a-line (no pulse).
Septic shock (early resuscitation) ≥ 65 first, individualize Initial MAP target per sepsis protocol; escalate if organ injury evident.

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use
sections.bodyHtml:
How MAP guides bedside intervention and hemodynamic management.

Nurses titrate MAP continuously via goal-directed hemodynamic management:

Intervention Impact on MAP Clinical context
Fluid bolus (250–500 mL NS/LR) ↑ Preload → ↑ CO → ↑ MAP (if not at Starling plateau) Volume-responsive state; verify adequacy before repeat boluses (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).
Vasopressor (phenylephrine, norepinephrine) Direct ↑ MAP via vasoconstriction ± inotropic effect First-line when fluid alone insufficient; phenylephrine pure vasoconstriction, norepinephrine has β effect.
Inotrope (milrinone, low-dose epi) ↑ CO (and ↓ SVR if milrinone) — net MAP effect depends on CO vs SVR balance Milrinone lusitropic + inotropy but ↓ SVR; epi combines both effects at low dose.
Antihypertensive (hydralazine, labetalol, esmolol) ↓ SVR → ↓ MAP; titrate to prevent under-perfusion Watch for overshoot; maintain target MAP.
Diuretic (furosemide) ↓ Preload → ↓ CO → potential ↓ MAP if aggressive Risk if already hypotensive; use cautiously post-op when perfusion margin narrow.

Hemodynamic handoff protocol:

  • Receive MAP target from surgeon / ICU team at transfer; document in orders.
  • Default: maintain ≥ 65 unless procedure-specific target stated (TAAA ≥ 85, LVAD 70–85, stroke 160 if no tPA).
  • A-line is gold standard; cuff adequate for routine floor care if correlation confirmed early in course.
  • Re-level transducer at phlebostatic axis (4th ICS, mid-axillary) q4h or whenever HOB changed; position artifact can shift reading ~0.75 mmHg per inch of elevation.

sections.heading: 5. Pitfalls & Pearls *(high-yield bedside wisdom)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Cuff vs a-line discrepancy is real in shock. In hypotension, sepsis, or cardiogenic shock, a-line MAP is truth. Cuff over-estimates in hypotensive states due to oscillometric artifact. Always trust a-line; verify early discrepancy with resident.

  2. The MAP formula is a cuff-derived approximation. It works well in normotension but fails when BP is extreme (HTN crisis, MAP < 50, severe arrhythmia). A-line integrates the actual waveform; most accurate in extremes.

  3. Atrial fibrillation makes cuff readings noisy. Successive beats vary widely. Average 2–3 cuff cycles or switch to a-line if available. Single-beat cuff = noise; always trend multiple readings.

  4. Calcified arteries (elderly, ESRD, longstanding DM) falsely elevate cuff pressure. The cuff "feels" a stiff vessel and reads high. A-line pressure may be much lower. Correlate cuff and a-line early; a-line becomes your reference.

  5. Position artifact is silent and deadly. Phlebostatic axis = 4th ICS, mid-axillary. If HOB is raised without re-leveling transducer, MAP drifts down ~0.75 mmHg per inch of elevation. Check level q4h; re-level if bed position changed.

  6. MAP defends end-organ perfusion; high SBP does not guarantee adequate perfusion. A patient with SBP 140 but MAP 55 (wide pulse pressure, low diastolic) is perfusion-compromised. Watch MAP, not SBP alone.

  7. In cardiac tamponade, MAP can hold while pulse pressure narrows. Pulsus paradoxus is the sign; SBP may stay 110 while DBP drops to 85 → PP narrows, MAP holds briefly. Don't be fooled; watch the trend and clinical signs (JVD, muffled heart sounds, pulsus > 10 mmHg).

  8. Permissive hypertension in acute stroke without tPA is opposite of cardiac surgery. Goal is MAP ≈ 160 (SBP ≤ 220) to maintain collateral perfusion. Counter-intuitive; confirm target in hand-off.

  9. LVAD patients have no pulse — MAP only by Doppler. A disappearing pulse with rising pump power does not mean MAP is rising; you are seeing suction. Doppler or a-line is mandatory for safety (Bojar, 2020). Over-MAP (pump speed too high) causes suction events; under-MAP causes cardiogenic shock.

  10. TAAA / TEVAR goal MAP ≥ 85 protects the spinal cord. The artery of Adamkiewicz is vulnerable in thoracic aortic surgery. Permissive hypotension (MAP 50–60) is acceptable in routine AAA repair; in TAAA it is paraplegia risk. Know which your patient had.

cards.title: MAZE / Cox-MAZE IV (Surgical Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation)
cards.quickAnswer: MAZE = surgical AF ablation using radiofrequency or cryoablation to create scar lesions in the atria, interrupting re-entrant circuits. Cox-MAZE IV (current standard) adds 15–30 min to concomitant cardiac surgery; LAA ligation integral. Early post-op AF (POD 0–90) is EXPECTED, not failure — 90-day blanking period reflects scar maturation. Success rate 70–85% AF-free at 1 year (paroxysmal AF); lower in persistent/long-standing persistent. Management: rate control + amiodarone (not DCCV) during blanking; anticoagulation ≥6 months minimum; amiodarone bridge 3–6 months typical. CHA₂DS₂-VASc determines post-6-month AC continuation.
