cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution PolicyStat] → Gillinov et al. (2015) → Cox (2004) → Joglar et al. (2023) → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → STS (2023)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
• Definition: Surgical ablation of atrial fibrillation using linear lesions (scars) created by bipolar radiofrequency or cryoablation to interrupt re-entrant circuits in both atria. Cox-MAZE IV (current gold standard) replaces the original cut-and-sew technique with energy-based lesion creation. Concurrent left atrial appendage (LAA) ligation is integral to stroke prevention.
  • Typical patient: Chronic AF (paroxysmal or persistent) refractory to medical therapy, undergoing concomitant cardiac surgery (mitral valve repair/replacement, CABG, aortic valve replacement). Rarely performed in isolation.
  • Procedure approach:
  • Concomitant: added to planned MV, CABG, AVR, or other procedure; uses same sternotomy
  • Lesion pattern: bilateral atrial ablation (LA + RA) + pulmonary vein isolation (PVI) + LAA exclusion/ligation
  • Ablation modality: bipolar RF or cryoablation (no cut-and-sew)
  • CPB: Yes; adds ~15–30 minutes to concomitant procedure
  • Standard LOS: similar to concomitant procedure (CABG/MV 4–6 days); MAZE adds minimal length of stay if concomitant
  • Expected lines/devices on ICU arrival: peripheral IVs; A + V pacer wires (retained longer than routine); chest tubes; Foley

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism of MAZE scarring (expandable) Atrial fibrillation perpetuates through re-entrant circuits — abnormal electrical pathways that form in enlarged or scarred atria. The Cox-MAZE IV procedure creates linear scars (lesions) that block these circuits while preserving conduction pathways for normal sinus rhythm. The classic lesion set includes:
  • Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI): circumferential ablation around the four pulmonary veins (where most ectopic triggers originate)
  • Left atrial lesions: lines connecting the PVI to the mitral annulus and left atrial roof
  • Right atrial lesions: connection to the tricuspid annulus and cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) Lesions are created via bipolar radiofrequency (RF) (heat-based, ~65°C) or cryoablation (freezing, -40 to -60°C). Both achieve transmural lesions; choice depends on surgeon preference and anatomy. RF is faster; cryo may preserve adjacent structures (phrenic nerve, esophagus) better in specific locations. Key physiologic principle: The scars take 6–12 weeks to mature. During this 90-day "blanking period," atrial inflammation, edema, and incomplete fibrosis allow re-entry despite ablation being technically successful. Early post-op AF during blanking is EXPECTED and does NOT indicate surgical failure.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context & Management by POD Arc
3A. POD 0 (ICU) — Immediate Post-Op
sections.bodyHtml:
• Presentation: Arrival intubated; A + V pacer wires in place; standard post-cardiac surgery monitoring
  • MAZE-specific notes: Early AF in first 6–12 hours can occur; if hemodynamically stable, monitor with rate control + amiodarone per provider plan (DCCV ineffective this early). Expected early post-op complications: bleeding (standard thresholds apply), atrial ischemia, temporary AV block
  • Pacer wires: Retain both; check thresholds q4h
  • Extubation: usually 6–12 hours (no MAZE-specific delay)

sections.heading: 3B. POD 1–3 (ICU/Step-Down Transition)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Presentation: Extubated, out of bed; peak window for POAF onset (incidence 40–60%)
  • MAZE-specific management:
  • Restart or initiate beta-blocker early; continue amiodarone for AF prophylaxis
  • If AF develops: confirm with 12-lead, replace K⁺ ≥ 4.0 and Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0, start/escalate rate control (metoprolol or diltiazem IV per provider)
  • Do NOT cardiovert in the first 4 weeks if hemodynamically stable — DCCV usually ineffective until scar maturation; scar is only 72–96 hours old at POD 1–3
  • Amiodarone drip common; anticipate hypotension in ~25%; preemptively decrease drip to 0.5 mg/min rather than chasing BP
  • Pacer wire assessment: Check sensing and capture thresholds; note any paced beats. SA node injury from ablation can manifest as bradycardia or loss of capture.
  • Teaching point: "Early AF is normal. The scars in your heart are just starting to heal. We'll manage the rate with medicine while the scars mature."
  • Transfer readiness: Off drips, stable electrolytes, HR controlled, no active bleeding
  • Anticipated labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, hemoglobin daily; troponin if symptomatic; EBV/CMV (post-cardiac surgery surveillance)

sections.heading: 3C. POD 4+ (Step-Down/Telemetry)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Presentation: Continued amiodarone, anticoagulation, beta-blocker; pacer wires still in place
  • MAZE-specific management:
  • Pacer wires retained until POD 5–7 (vs POD 3–4 in routine CABG/MV) due to 5–10% AV block rate
  • Removal criteria: AV conduction stable over 2–3 days (normal intervals on tele, no pacer dependence)
  • If persistent bradycardia or AV block: EP evaluation for potential PPM pre-discharge
  • Amiodarone continued; typical maintenance 200–400 mg daily after loading phase
  • Anticoagulation continued per protocol (see Section 5)
  • Patient education: Holter monitoring schedule (3, 6, 12 months post-op) explained; realistic 1-year success rates (70–85% paroxysmal; 50–70% persistent)
  • Red flag teaching: "Chest pain + confusion + vomiting blood = call 911" (atreoesophageal fistula awareness, though rare)

sections.heading: 3D. Discharge (Goal POD 5–7)
sections.bodyHtml:
Medications:

  • Amiodarone: 400 mg PO TID × 1 week (loading), then 400 mg BID × 1 week, then 200–400 mg daily × 3–6 months (reassess at EP follow-up)
  • Anticoagulation: continued × 6 months minimum (even if sinus rhythm, per ACC/AHA 2023); then CHA₂DS₂-VASc-guided beyond 6 months
  • Beta-blocker: indefinitely (unless contraindicated)
  • Aspirin 81 mg daily: indefinitely
  • Plavix 75 mg daily × 1 year (if concomitant CABG)

Monitoring & Follow-Up:

  • Holter monitor at 3, 6, 12 months (assess AF recurrence/freedom)
  • Electrophysiology follow-up (timing varies; 6–12 weeks post-op common)
  • Cardiology follow-up for concomitant procedure + MAZE assessment
  • Cardiac rehab referral (standard post-cardiac surgery)

Patient Teaching — Discharge Checklist:

  • Red flags: chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, hematemesis, acute neuro change
  • Medication adherence: amiodarone tapering schedule in writing; explain photosensitivity and need for LFT/TSH monitoring
  • Anticoagulation plan (warfarin vs DOAC); do NOT stop AC in the blanking period without team input
  • Palpitations are common in the first month; Holter monitors catch what the patient doesn't feel
  • Realistic expectations: "Success is 70–85% in the first year for paroxysmal AF. Some patients have early recurrence, which is treated with medicine or repeat catheter ablation later."

sections.heading: 4A. MAZE Types & Success Rates
sections.bodyHtml:
Procedure Type Lesion Set Ablation Modality Blanking Period 1-Yr Success (Paroxysmal) 1-Yr Success (Persistent) CPB Add Time Notes
Cox-MAZE IV (Standard) Bilateral PVI + LA + RA lesions + LAA ligation Bipolar RF or cryo 90 days 70–85% 50–70% 15–30 min Current gold standard; concomitant usual
Cox-MAZE III (Historical) Cut-and-sew lesion pattern Surgical incisions 90 days 65–80% 45–65% 30–45 min Rarely performed; high morbidity vs MAZE IV
Minimally Invasive MAZE Limited lesion set via catheter or mini-thoracotomy RF or cryo 90 days 55–75% 40–60% Variable Not concomitant; separate procedure; less common

sections.heading: 4B. Anticoagulation Post-MAZE
sections.bodyHtml:
Timeline Indication Drug Choice Notes
POD 0–3 Standard post-cardiac surgery (bleeding risk high) Mechanical DVT prophylaxis; hold AC pending surgeon approval Restart AC typically 24–72 h post-op per surgeon preference
POD 4–90 (6 mo) Scar maturation window (AF expected, LAA excluded) Warfarin (INR 2–3) or DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban per dosing) AC × 6 mo minimum even if sinus rhythm; blanking-period AF common. If AF recurs, AC indefinite.
Post-6 mo CHA₂DS₂-VASc-guided Discontinue if CHA₂DS₂-VASc = 0–1 AND sinus rhythm; continue if ≥2 or AF recurrence LAA ligation reduces stroke risk; still assess stroke risk. Document LAA status in chart.

sections.heading: 4C. Amiodarone Bridge Protocol Post-MAZE
sections.bodyHtml:
Phase Dosing Duration Monitoring Notes
IV Load (ICU/Early POD 1–2) 150 mg bolus, may repeat; then 1 mg/min × 6 h, 0.5 mg/min × 18 h (total ~1 g/24 h) 24–48 h QTc baseline + q12h; BP monitoring (↓ in ~25%); telemetry Hypotension predictable; decrease drip early to 0.5 mg/min rather than chasing BP. Transition to PO when stable.
PO Load (POD 2–7) 400 mg PO TID (rapidly loading) 7–14 days until 10 g total QTc, BP, HR; ask re: photosensitivity precautions 400 mg TID loads faster than IV drip; often with less hypotension. Typical total load ~10 g over 1–2 weeks.
PO Maintenance (POD 7–Discharge & Beyond) 200–400 mg daily 3–6 months post-op QTc monthly; TSH + LFTs q3mo while on amio; telemetry as indicated Reassess at EP visit (6–12 weeks). May discontinue if AF-free, or continue longer if recurrent episodes. Document in discharge meds.

sections.heading: 5. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for MAZE-specific concerns:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p MAZE + [concomitant procedure]." B: "New [irregular rhythm / bradycardia / palpitations / chest pain] at [time]. HR [rate], BP [value], K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value]. On [amiodarone dose/modality], [beta-blocker]." A: "[Rhythm strip finding: AF vs flutter vs sinus]. Patient is [stable / unstable — hemodynamics, mental status, perfusion]." R: "Requesting [rate-control plan / electrolyte repletion / DCCV if unstable / EP consult / pacer wire management]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable POAF POD 1–4 Primary APP / on-call fellow
Persistent or recurrent POAF CT surgery team + EP consult
Bradycardia or loss of pacer capture CT surgery + APP; EP evaluation for PPM pre-discharge
Hemodynamic instability (hypotension, altered MS, chest pain) STAT APP/fellow + RRT; prepare for DCCV per ACLS
New neuro deficit Stroke code; CT surgery, neurology
Active bleeding CT surgery — do NOT start/escalate AC without team input
Suspected atreoesophageal fistula (chest pain + neuro + hemoptysis/hematemesis weeks post-op) Surgical emergency: STAT CT imaging + CT surgery + GI

sections.heading: 6. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
6.1 MAZE Lesion Set & Ablation Modalities (expandable) Lesion pattern detail: The Cox-MAZE IV lesion set is designed to isolate the pulmonary veins (where ectopic triggers originate) and create a compartmentalized conduction pattern in the atria:
  1. Pulmonary vein isolation (PVI): circumferential ablation around all four pulmonary veins, isolating them from the left atrium
  2. Left atrial lesions:
    • Anterior wall lesion from PVI to aorta
    • Posterior wall lesion connecting PVI to mitral annulus
    • Roof lesion across the top of the left atrium
    • Right atrial lesions:
    • Cavotricuspid isthmus (CTI) ablation from tricuspid annulus to IVC (blocks atrial flutter circuits)
    • Connection to LA lesions as needed
    • Scar maturation: linear lesions create conduction block immediately, but mature (fibrotic) lesions take 6–12 weeks. During this window, partial conduction recovery is possible, explaining early POAF in the blanking period. Ablation modalities:
    • Bipolar radiofrequency (RF): heats tissue to ~65°C, creating coagulation necrosis. Fast (~2–3 min per lesion); creates discrete lesions. Risk: thermal injury to adjacent structures (phrenic nerve, esophagus) if used near posterior LA.
    • Cryoablation: freezes tissue to -40 to -60°C, creating ice-ball lesion. Slower (~5–10 min per lesion); may preserve adjacent structure function better due to slower cooling. Higher post-ablation pain risk. Similar efficacy to RF. Surgeon choice depends on anatomy, location of lesion, and institutional preference. No clear superiority of one over the other in published trials.
6.2 LAA Ligation Methods & Stroke Prevention (expandable) Why LAA ligation is integral: The left atrial appendage is the site of thrombus formation in ~90% of AF-related strokes. Even if the MAZE procedure restores sinus rhythm long-term, excluding the LAA at the time of surgery provides durable stroke prevention without lifelong anticoagulation (if AF doesn't recur). This is a major advantage over medical AF management. Methods:
  1. Surgical ligation (suture or scissors): Most common. The LAA is identified, ligated at the base with sutures, and divided. Confirmed by direct visualization and, increasingly, by intraoperative TEE.
  2. AtriClip device: Titanium clip applied to the LAA base; less common. Allows future catheter access if needed (e.g., for electrophysiology studies). More expensive; requires specific anatomy.
  3. Staple line exclusion: Less reliable; falling out of favor. Documentation requirement: Confirm LAA exclusion method in the operative report. If LAA was NOT excluded (rare but possible), flag immediately to cardiology/EP — it alters post-op AC decisions and long-term stroke risk. Watchman device vs surgical ligation: Watchman (percutaneous LAA closure device) is an alternative for patients with contraindications to AC. Usually placed via catheter after cardiac surgery if LAA surgical exclusion was not performed. In the MAZE setting, surgical ligation at time of MAZE is standard.
6.3 The 90-Day "Blanking Period" — Why Early AF Is Expected (expandable) What is blanking? The 90-day (or sometimes 6–12 week) blanking period is the interval during which early post-op AF is EXPECTED and does NOT indicate surgical failure. It reflects the time required for surgical/ablation-induced atrial injury to resolve and for scar fibrosis to mature. Timeline of atrial healing post-MAZE:
  • POD 0–7: Acute inflammatory response; atrial edema; partial conduction block from ablation lesions; susceptible to re-entry
  • Week 1–4: Peak inflammation; gradual fibrosis beginning; scar still soft/edematous
  • Week 4–12: Progressive fibrosis; scar hardens and matures; conduction block becomes more durable
  • Week 12+: Mature fibrotic scars; maximum conduction block achieved Why AF is common during blanking: The immature scar allows partial conduction recovery, creating substrate for re-entry. Additionally, post-op atrial inflammation, electrolyte shifts, sympathetic surge, and pain all destabilize the atrium. The combination of immature scarring + post-op physiology = 40–60% early POAF rate — entirely expected. Clinical implication — DCCV is often ineffective during blanking: Direct-current cardioversion can acutely restore sinus rhythm, but because the scars are not yet mature, AF often recurs within minutes to hours. This is frustrating for patients and clinicians; the correct approach is rate control + amiodarone, NOT DCCV, during blanking. Exceptions: hemodynamic instability (hypotension, pulmonary edema, altered mental status) requires DCCV per ACLS regardless of blanking status. Teaching for patients and families: > "Your procedure created scars in your heart to stop irregular rhythms. But scars take time to heal — like any cut on your skin. For the next 90 days, while the scars are healing, you might feel your heart skip or race. That's normal and expected. We'll manage it with medicine, not electricity. By 3 months, most patients feel much better as the scars mature."
6.4 Heart Block & SA Node Injury Post-MAZE (expandable) Frequency: ~5–10% of MAZE patients develop transient or persistent AV block or sinus node dysfunction (higher than routine CABG/MV alone). Why it happens: The right atrial ablation lesions can damage the sinus node or AV nodal region due to proximity. Most resolves in 3–7 days; some persist and require PPM. Clinical recognition:
  • Symptomatic bradycardia (HR < 50, fatigue, presyncope, hypotension)
  • High-degree AV block on tele (junctional rhythm, wide escape, no capture on pacer wires)
  • Loss of atrial paced beats on epicardial wires; loss of sensing Management:
  • Check pacer wire thresholds; adjust sensivity/pacing settings per team
  • Hold beta-blockers, verapamil, amiodarone if bradycardic
  • 12-lead ECG to assess conduction intervals
  • Notify APP; if persistent high-grade block (POD 3–5), EP consult for PPM evaluation pre-discharge Pacer wire retention key: This is why pacer wires are kept until POD 5–7 post-MAZE (vs POD 3–4 post-routine CABG). Extra monitoring window allows distinction between transient and persistent block.
6.5 Repeat Catheter Ablation if MAZE Fails (expandable)

Recurrence rates: ~15–30% of MAZE patients have AF recurrence at 1 year, depending on pre-op AF type (paroxysmal better; persistent worse).

Catheter ablation as salvage: If MAZE fails and AF persists beyond 3–6 months, patients are candidates for repeat catheter-based ablation to re-isolate gaps in the surgical lesion set or treat new arrhythmogenic sites. This is often more straightforward than catheter ablation in medical AF because the surgical scars provide fixed anatomic landmarks.

Typical timeline for re-ablation consideration: 3–6 months post-MAZE. Discussed at EP follow-up visit if early recurrence is evident on Holter monitor.

sections.heading: 7. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
• Persistent AF beyond POD 4 despite adequate rate control and amiodarone — reassess electrolytes, beta-blocker dosing, and trigger reversibility
  • Hemodynamic deterioration (BP trending down, UOP declining, lactate rising) despite rate control — may signal pump failure or evolving pericardial effusion; get echo
  • Loss of pacer capture or sensing with bradycardia — atrial pacing wire malfunction or SA node injury; check thresholds, notify APP
  • New hypoxia or pulmonary edema — can precede AF hemodynamic decompensation; assess lung sounds, get CXR, notify team
  • Amiodarone hypotension worsening (BP < 90 mmHg despite fluids) — preemptively decrease drip to 0.5 mg/min; transition to PO sooner if possible
  • QTc approaching 500 ms on amiodarone — risk of torsades; hold/decrease amiodarone per provider; check electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺)
  • New focal neurologic deficit (weakness, facial droop, speech change) — activate stroke code immediately
  • Recurrent AF after successful conversion (especially within hours) — inadequate load or persistent trigger; escalate to APP for rhythm control reassessment
  • Fever + acute dyspnea + chest pain weeks post-op — concerning for atreoesophageal fistula or post-op infection; CT imaging + CT surgery consult urgently

sections.heading: 8. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Early POAF is EXPECTED, not a surgical failure. 40–60% of MAZE patients develop AF in the first 4 weeks. Scar maturation takes 6–12 weeks. Teach nurses and families upfront to prevent panic and inappropriate escalations.

  2. Do NOT cardiovert a stable MAZE patient in the first 4 weeks post-op. DCCV is often ineffective and may cause harm because atrial scars are immature. Rate control + amiodarone is the default.

    Exception: hemodynamic instability (hypotension, chest pain, altered mental status, pulmonary edema) mandates DCCV per ACLS, but expect failure or rapid recurrence.

  3. Pacer wires stay longer post-MAZE than routine CABG/MV. Retain until POD 5–7 due to ~5–10% AV block rate (vs <2% in routine cases). Don't reflexively pull wires at POD 3 just because "that's when we usually pull them." Verify AV conduction is stable before removal.

  4. Amiodarone hypotension is predictable (~25% of patients). Anticipate with fluid planning.

    Decrease the drip to 0.5 mg/min early when BP starts dropping, rather than chasing hypotension with more drip. Consider earlier transition to PO (400 mg TID) if IV hypotension is problematic.

  5. Confirm LAA exclusion method in the operative report. Matters for long-term stroke risk and AC decision-making. If LAA was NOT excluded (rare), flag immediately to cardiology/EP.

  6. Atreoesophageal fistula is rare (~0.05–0.1% of cases) but lethal if missed. Usually presents weeks post-op with sudden chest pain + neuro deficit (stroke-like) + hemoptysis/hematemesis. Teach patients at discharge: "If you develop chest pain with confusion or vomiting blood, call 911 immediately." This is a surgical emergency.

  7. Post-op AF timeline drives anticoagulation decisions. AF lasting > 48 hours (especially CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2) increases stroke risk substantially. But post-MAZE with LAA excluded + blanking-period AF = AC for 6 months anyway. At 6 months, if sinus and LAA excluded, AC can be discontinued if CHA₂DS₂-VASc < 2; otherwise continue. Cardiology/EP makes the final call.

  8. Holter monitoring is the truth-teller. Patients may feel fine (no palpitations) but Holter reveals paroxysmal AF, or vice versa. Complete the 3-, 6-, 12-month Holter series to assess true AF burden and guide long-term therapy.

  9. Success rates vary by pre-op AF type. Paroxysmal AF → 70–85% AF-free at 1 year. Persistent AF → 50–70% AF-free at 1 year. Long-standing persistent AF (>1 year) → 30–50% AF-free at 1 year. Counsel patients realistically upfront; avoid over-promising "cure."

  10. Concomitant procedure adds complexity. MAZE + CABG means managing post-op bleeding, graft patency, AND AF simultaneously. Don't get tunnel vision on MAZE — standard CABG precautions (NTG ×24 h for graft protection, Plavix regimen, ASA hold status) still apply.

  11. Amiodarone drug interactions and monitoring are serious. Clarify with pharmacy if patient is on verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin, beta-blockers — potential for bradycardia/hypotension. QTc baseline + q3 months while on amio; TSH and LFTs annually. Photosensitivity counseling at discharge.

  12. Don't assume "irregular = AF." Confirm with 12-lead ECG. Could be atrial flutter (rate may be more regular), SVT with aberrancy, frequent PACs, or pacer malfunction. 12-lead is fast and definitive.

  13. Electrolyte replacement is non-negotiable for any post-op AF. K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 before assuming amiodarone or rate-control failure. Low electrolytes = AF substrate. This applies to MAZE just as to routine post-op cardiac AF.

  14. "MAZE" terminology is historic; "Cox-MAZE IV" is current. You'll hear both; they're synonymous in modern practice (RF or cryo lesion pattern, not cut-and-sew). Older literature uses "MAZE I, II, III" — know that Cox-MAZE IV is the current standard.

  15. Teach differentiation: AF symptoms vs anxiety. Palpitations can be AF, but also anxiety about "is my surgery working?" Reassure patients that early palpitations are normal, but always confirm with telemetry/12-lead.

cards.title: Medication Reconciliation Post-Cardiac Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: Three mandatory reconciliation points — admission (pill bottles + pharmacy records beat patient recall), transfer (document intra-op holds + rationale), discharge (final list with explicit rationale for every change + teach-back + pharmacy counseling). Pill bottles are the gold standard source. At admission: RN documents all home meds (prescription, OTC, supplements, herbals) and confirms with patient; pharmacist flags discrepancies vs. admission orders. At transfer (POD 0–1): verify which home meds are back on, which held, why; document rationale. At discharge (24 h pre-release): write final med list with reason for every add/remove/dose change; perform teach-back; provide written copy; ensure pharmacy counseling for complex regimens. All three points are Joint Commission requirement and prevent 25–30% of medication-related adverse events.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, scope, and when it applies.

  • Definition: Medication reconciliation is a systematic process comparing a patient's current medication orders to all known prior medication use (home prescriptions, OTC, supplements, herbals) to identify and resolve discrepancies. In cardiac surgery, this occurs at three vulnerable transitions: admission, intra-operative transfer of care, and discharge.
  • Why it matters: Cardiac surgery patients face significant medication changes (deliberate holds for bleeding risk, new post-op agents, dose adjustments). Discrepancies between what patients think they're taking and what's actually ordered account for 25–30% of all medication-related adverse events. Joint Commission NPSG 03.06.01 mandates med rec at all care transitions.
  • High-risk medications in cardiac surgery: Antiplatelets (ASA, clopidogrel, ticagrelor), anticoagulants (warfarin, DOAC), beta-blockers, ACE-I/ARB, statins, insulin, metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors, chronic opioids, benzodiazepines.
  • Who it applies to: Every adult admitted for cardiac surgery (CABG, valve, aortic, TAVR, transplant, MAZE, myectomy, etc.), from pre-op admission through discharge and follow-up.
  • Key outcomes: Quality med rec + patient education reduce 30-day readmission rates by 5–12%, decrease medication errors, and improve patient satisfaction.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why It Matters
sections.bodyHtml:
Peri-operative medication management is uniquely complex because:

  • Deliberate holds (aspirin vs. clopidogrel; ACE-I; metformin; SGLT2i; insulin) change patient regimens significantly — patients often unaware whether discontinuation is temporary or permanent
  • New post-op agents (antiarrhythmics, anticoagulants, inotropes, vasopressors) are added without clear discontinuation plan — patients assume these are lifelong
  • Patient memory is unreliable, especially in the perioperative period (fasting, anxiety, medication, post-operative haze)
  • Pill bottles are the gold standard source (actual visual confirmation) but are often unavailable, dismissed, or replaced with fallible patient/family recall
  • Drug interactions compound errors — warfarin + new NSAID; DOAC + new interacting agent; acetaminophen stacking (>3 g/day)
  • Missing doses (metformin, SGLT2i) with delayed restart create hyperglycemia or euglycemic DKA risk
  • Missed documentation of hold rationale means PCP and patient are unaware why a medication was discontinued — often restart independently, recreating the risk

The three-point framework (admission, transfer, discharge) addresses each transition systematically and is proven to reduce readmission rates and adverse events.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — patient populations and timing.

Universally indicated (every admission):

  • All adult cardiac surgery patients, all procedure types (CABG, valve repair/replacement, aortic, TAVR, transplant, MAZE, myectomy, ECMO, etc.)
  • Especially high-risk: age >75, polypharmacy (≥10 home meds), diabetes, renal disease, prior cardiac events, prior anticoagulation/antiplatelet use

Timing of each point:

  • Admission reconciliation: Within 24 hours of admission (same day for day-of-surgery admits)
  • Ongoing review: Each shift during hospitalization; document on rounds
  • Transfer reconciliation: POD 0–1 hand-off (document intra-op holds + restart rationale)
  • Discharge reconciliation: 24 hours before planned discharge

Shared responsibility:

  • RN: Documents initial med list, verifies discrepancies, performs teach-back, provides written materials
  • Pharmacist: Reviews home list vs. admission/post-op orders, flags drug interactions, verifies hold/restart rationale, counsels on new agents
  • Provider (attending/APP): Documents clinical rationale for all holds, additions, dose changes in discharge summary; writes PCP letter
  • Patient/Family: Brings pill bottles, participates in teach-back, confirms understanding

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — Three Reconciliation Points
sections.bodyHtml: Competent systematic process for each transition. Information-gathering phase (no interventions yet).

sections.heading: 4.1 Point 1: Admission Reconciliation (Pre-Op)
sections.bodyHtml:
Sources of truth (rank-ordered by reliability):

  1. Pill bottles (patient brings from home) — BEST — visual confirmation of drug, dose, frequency
  2. Home pharmacy records (call pharmacy) — verifiable, current, authoritative
  3. Outpatient EMR (PCP records, if accessible) — good if current and verified
  4. Patient self-report — prone to error (forgets dose, doesn't know generics, confuses meds)
  5. Family report — useful cross-check but still secondary to documentation

What to document:

  • Prescription medications — drug name (generic + brand), dose, route, frequency, indication
  • Over-the-counter (OTC) — acetaminophen, NSAIDs, antacids, laxatives, cold meds, sleep aids
  • Supplements — multivitamins, fish oil, magnesium, CoQ10, vitamin D, probiotics
  • Herbals — ginkgo, garlic, St. John's Wort, ginger (critical for bleeding + drug interactions)
  • Inhalers, patches, drops, creams — often forgotten; ask explicitly

Process:

  1. Request pill bottles on admission (ask family to retrieve if not present)
  2. RN documents on med rec worksheet: drug (generic + brand), dose, route, frequency, reason
  3. RN includes OTC and supplements explicitly
  4. If pill bottles unavailable: call patient's home pharmacy directly; verify current fills
  5. Pharmacist reviews home list vs. admission orders; flags all discrepancies
  6. Resolve discrepancies with provider:
    • Is home med intentionally omitted from admission orders? (e.g., metformin held for contrast)
    • Is new admission order not on home list? (prophylactic antibiotic, etc.)
    • Is there a dose change (intentional vs. error)?
    • Document resolution on med rec form; verify with patient: "I see you take metoprolol 50 mg twice a day at home — is that right?"
    • File med rec worksheet in medical record

sections.heading: 4.2 Point 2: Transfer Reconciliation (Intra-Op & POD 0–1)
sections.bodyHtml:
Timing: Document during intra-op hand-off (anesthesia/CT surgery to ICU) and review again on first post-op shift.

What changes from home list:

  • Intentional holds (with documented reason: bleeding risk, renal safety, contrast risk, vasoplegia risk, hypoglycemia risk, etc.)
  • Intra-operative medications (heparin, inhaled vasodilators, antibiotics, protamine)
  • New post-op orders (nitroglycerin, milrinone, heparin infusion, beta-blocker restart, statin, antiarrhythmic)

Process:

  1. RN reviews intra-op record for documented holds + reasons
  2. Verify with anesthesia/CT surgery at hand-off: which home meds held, why?
  3. Create POD 0 med list: document what's running, what's held, why
  4. Pharmacist reviews post-op orders for continuation/restart of home meds vs. new regimen
  5. Clarify with attending/APP: "We're holding metformin until POD 2 per protocol (renal safety + contrast); beta-blocker restarted POD 1 at half-dose for hemodynamic monitoring."
  6. Document on transfer form with explicit rationale for each hold
  7. Communicate to nursing: "These meds held for these reasons; will resume on this date per provider order."

sections.heading: 4.3 Point 3: Discharge Reconciliation
sections.bodyHtml:
Timing: 24 hours before planned discharge; involves RN, pharmacist, and attending/APP.

Process: 1.

Create final discharge med list — compare: admission home list + intra-op holds + current inpatient regimen - Home meds: continue vs. discontinue? - New additions: new DAPT, new anticoagulant, new antiarrhythmic, new diuretic? - Dose changes: reduced beta-blocker, new statin dose? - Timing changes: once-daily to twice-daily?

  1. Document rationale for every change (Joint Commission required; critical for continuity): - Example: "ASA 81 mg daily — continue, ongoing CAD protection"

    • Example: "NEW: Clopidogrel 75 mg daily × 1 month — DES placed intra-op, DAPT required; stop [DATE] per cardiologist instructions"
    • Example: "NEW: Amiodarone 400 mg daily × 1 week, then 200 mg daily — post-op AFib prophylaxis; d/c per cardiology after 3–6 months if no recurrent AFib"
    • Example: "DISCONTINUED: Metformin — hold × 48 h post-op due to contrast; labs POD 3; resume if CrCl >45"

  2. Write prescriptions for all discharge medications:

    • Correct drug, dose, route, frequency, quantity (e.g., "#30 tablets" = 30-day supply)
    • Include refill count
    • Legible or electronic

  3. Write letter to PCP — include:

    • Surgery performed, date
    • All discharge medications with rationale for changes
    • Temporary holds with restart criteria
    • Follow-up appointments, labs needed, specialty referrals
    • Teaching summary

  4. Perform teach-back with patient AND family/caregiver (if possible):

    • Ask patient to state purpose and timing of each medication
    • Correct misinformation; repeat if needed
    • Document: "Patient correctly described ASA for heart protection, clopidogrel for stent, amiodarone for rhythm. Family present. No language barriers."
      • For language barriers: use interpreter; provide written materials in patient's language
      • For complex regimens: provide written calendar or pre-filled pill organizer

  5. Pharmacy counseling for complex new regimens:

    • Indication + expected duration
    • How to take (with/without food, time of day, missed dose instructions)
    • Common side effects + warning signs (e.g., "Amiodarone can cause blue-gray skin; call if shortness of breath, cough, yellow eyes")
    • Drug interactions (e.g., "Warfarin + vitamin K — keep vitamin K consistent; no new supplements without asking")
    • When to stop (if temporary) or refill (if ongoing)
    • When to call PCP vs. cardiologist vs. ED

  6. Provide written materials:

    • Discharge med list (copies for patient, PCP, medical record)
    • Patient-specific teaching handout (not generic)
    • Contact info: pharmacy, PCP, cardiologist, ED
    • Red flag symptoms: "Call 911 if chest pain, severe dyspnea, signs of bleeding. Call cardiologist for irregular heartbeat, syncope, medication questions."

sections.heading: 5.1 Peri-Operative Medication Holds and Restarts — by Drug Class
sections.bodyHtml:
Confirm all decisions with provider and institutional policy. This table is a reference baseline; individual cases may vary.

Medication Hold Duration Rationale Restart Criteria
Aspirin 81 mg Rarely held Low-dose bleeding risk minimal; ongoing IHD protection critical Continue post-op immediately
Clopidogrel (Plavix) 5–7 days pre-op Elective CABG — allows platelet recovery; thrombosis risk < bleeding benefit POD 1–2 if no major bleed; per surgeon
Ticagrelor (Brilinta) 5–7 days pre-op Shorter half-life (8–10 h) but standard hold for elective CABG POD 1–2; per surgeon
Warfarin 5 days pre-op INR fall to <1.5 (safer for surgery); bridge with LMWH if high thromboembolic risk POD 1–2; bridge if indicated; target INR per indication
DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) 48–72 h pre-op (varies by CrCl) Renal clearance determines hold; dabigatran longest POD 1–2; confirm CrCl unchanged
ACE-I / ARB 24 h pre-op (institution-dependent) Vasoplegia + hypotension post-op (some surgeons); check preference POD 2–3 if BP stable (MAP >65)
Beta-blocker CONTINUE through surgery Abrupt hold = tachycardia, HTN, MI risk, POAF risk POD 1 at same or reduced dose; titrate up as tolerated
Statin CONTINUE through surgery Pleiotropic benefits (anti-inflammatory, antirhythmic, POAF prevention) Continue immediately post-op
Metformin 24 h pre-op Contrast + lactic acidosis risk; hold allows safe contrast use; reassess renal function POD 2–3 if CrCl ≥45 on labs; resume home dose
SGLT2 inhibitor 3 days pre-op Euglycemic DKA risk perioperatively POD 3–4 after stable glucose control confirmed
Long-acting insulin Reduce or hold Fasting + surgery = hypoglycemia risk; basal requirement drops post-op POD 1–2 at reduced dose; adjust per glucose trend
Chronic opioid CONTINUE basal dose Abrupt cessation = withdrawal + pain surge + readmission Maintain baseline equivalent; stack with multimodal analgesia
Chronic benzodiazepine DO NOT HOLD abruptly Abrupt cessation = seizure + withdrawal symptoms Continue minimized home dose or slow taper; no abrupt stop

sections.heading: 5.2 New Medications Added Post-Op (Common Discharge Additions)
sections.bodyHtml:
Medication Class Indication Duration Key Teaching Point
Dual Antiplatelet (DAPT): Clopidogrel 75 mg daily DES placed during CABG or TAVR 1–12 months (depends on stent type) "Take aspirin and clopidogrel together for [X] months to keep the stent open. DO NOT stop early without cardiologist approval — stopping early can cause a heart attack. Call on [DATE] for instructions to stop."
Anticoagulant (new): Warfarin or DOAC New post-op AFib Duration per team; often 3–6 months for POAF Warfarin: "Keep vitamin K steady. Same time daily. Regular INR checks required." DOAC: "Take same time daily. Don't skip doses. If you miss a dose, take as soon as you remember but don't double up."
Antiarrhythmic: Amiodarone 400 mg daily × 1 week, then 200 mg daily POAF prophylaxis Often 3–6 months, then discontinue "Amiodarone can turn your skin slightly blue-gray (not dangerous). Avoid grapefruit juice. Watch for shortness of breath, cough, yellow eyes. You'll need liver and thyroid checks in 4–6 weeks. Cardiologist will tell you when to stop."
Beta-blocker (dose increase) Rate control optimization Ongoing "Take twice a day. If heart rate <50 or dizzy, call before next dose. Gradually increase back to your old dose if tolerated."
Diuretic (new) Heart failure or volume overload Ongoing "Take in morning so you're not up all night. Weigh daily; call if gain >2–3 lbs. Eat foods with potassium (bananas, OJ) if you feel weak."
ACE-I/ARB (new or dose increase) New HF indication Ongoing "Same time daily. May feel lightheaded first few days; call if persists. Normal diet; no salt restriction unless told. We'll recheck kidney function in 1 week."
Stool softener / Laxative: Docusate 100–200 mg daily or BID Post-op bowel management Usually 6–8 weeks post-op (while on opioids + sternal precautions) "Start today. Drink plenty of water. Walk as much as you can. If no BM by POD 3, call. Avoid straining — valsalva stresses your healing sternum."

sections.heading: 5.3 Verification Checklist at Each Point
sections.bodyHtml:
Point RN Verification Pharmacist Verification Provider Sign-Off
Admission Pill bottles obtained? OTC + supplements documented? Patient confirm accuracy? Home list vs. admission orders reviewed? Discrepancies flagged? Drug interactions noted? Rationale for any omitted meds documented?
Transfer (POD 0–1) Intra-op holds + reasons documented? Meds restarting per plan? Side effects from new meds assessed? Post-op orders reviewed for continuation logic? Electrolytes/renal function check for dose adjustments? Restart plan explicit? Hold duration clear?
Discharge Final med list compared to admission list? Every change noted? Teach-back performed + documented? Written copy provided? Complex regimen counseled? Drug interactions verified? Pill organizer or calendar provided if needed? Letter to PCP written? All prescriptions issued? Follow-up scheduled?

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Needs Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of when to alert provider.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. Admission med rec not complete within 24 h — pharmacist review delayed; potential order discrepancies unaddressed
  2. Discrepancies unresolved — home med listed but not on admission orders (no documented reason); order present but not on home list (no explanation)
  3. Pill bottle availability — patient unwilling to provide or bring bottles; rely on pharmacy records if available; if neither available, document and notify provider of uncertainty
  4. OTC/supplement disclosure incomplete — patient initially denies OTC use; later family mentions patient takes ibuprofen daily (NSAID bleed risk), ginkgo (↑ bleeding), or herbal products with interactions
  5. Drug interaction flagged — warfarin + aspirin (↑ bleed); DOAC + NSAID (GI bleed risk); new interacting agent added without pharmacy review
  6. Acetaminophen stacking — patient on scheduled acetaminophen + combination opioid (acetaminophen) + OTC pain reliever = >3 g/day total (hepatotoxicity risk)
  7. Hold rationale missing — medications discontinued without documented reason; unclear to patient and PCP whether hold is temporary or permanent
  8. Discharge med list has no rationale — medications listed without explanation of why they were added, when to stop, what to watch for
  9. DAPT without stop date — clopidogrel prescribed at discharge without clear end date; patient/PCP unsure when to discontinue
  10. Anticoagulation restart without plan — warfarin restarted at discharge with no documented target INR, no bridging plan, no INR follow-up scheduled
  11. Teach-back not documented — discharge med counseling not documented in chart; patient understanding not verified
  12. No pharmacy counseling for complex regimen — patient on 10+ meds (DAPT, anticoagulation, antiarrhythmic, insulin, etc.) with no formal pharmacy counseling or pill organizer

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections intended for in-app collapse. Nursing students and advanced beginners can expand to build understanding; experienced nurses and experts can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Why the Three-Point Framework Works
sections.bodyHtml:
Admission reconciliation — establishes baseline and identifies outpatient discrepancies early; gives pharmacist context for post-op orders.

Transfer reconciliation — documents what changed and why; creates explicit handoff between pre-op team and post-op team; clarifies to patient which meds are deliberately held vs. accidentally omitted.

Discharge reconciliation — highest-risk point (patient is home, unsupervised); explicit rationale for every change guides PCP and patient decision-making; teaches patient what changed and why; prevents patient-initiated stopping or restarting of meds without understanding risk.

Why it reduces readmission: Teach-back improves patient understanding → patient takes medications correctly → fewer errors → fewer AEs → fewer returns to ED.

sections.heading: 7.2 Common Peri-Operative Hold Scenarios — Clinical Decision Logic
sections.bodyHtml:
Scenario: Clopidogrel hold (elective CABG)

  • Why hold: Clopidogrel (P2Y12 inhibitor) takes 5–7 days to wash out. Elective CABG allows time for platelet function recovery, reducing intra-op bleeding. Thrombosis risk during hold is low for stable CAD on aspirin.
  • What to teach patient: "We're stopping your clopidogrel 1 week before surgery to reduce bleeding risk. Your aspirin stays on. We'll restart clopidogrel the day after surgery once we know there's no major bleeding."
  • Exception: Urgent CABG on clopidogrel — proceed anyway; surgeon manages bleeding; transfusion protocol per institution.

Scenario: Metformin hold (contrast pre-op)

  • Why hold: Contrast dye + metformin = lactic acidosis risk (especially if CrCl declines). Hold period allows safe contrast use; renal function reassessed post-op.
  • What to teach patient: "We're stopping metformin for 24 hours before and after your surgery and catheter procedure. This is temporary for safety. We'll restart it in a day or two once we check your kidney function and confirm it's safe."
  • Restart criteria: Labs show CrCl ≥45 (or patient's baseline if >45); resumed POD 2–3.

Scenario: Beta-blocker continuation (never hold)

  • Why continue: Abrupt discontinuation causes rebound tachycardia, hypertension, myocardial ischemia, and increases POAF risk — all dangerous perioperatively.
  • What to teach patient: "Your heart medicine (metoprolol) is important. You'll take your usual dose the morning of surgery. We'll restart it after surgery. Don't skip it even if we tell you to NPO — your surgeon wants this continued."

Scenario: Statin continuation (never hold)

  • Why continue: Statins have pleiotropic benefits beyond cholesterol: anti-inflammatory, endothelial function, POAF prevention, reduced mortality post-op. Hold increases risk.
  • What to teach patient: "Your statin continues through surgery and after. This protects your heart beyond just lowering cholesterol."

sections.heading: 7.3 Teach-Back Checklist & Common Patient Misunderstandings
sections.bodyHtml:
Teach-back script: "I want to make sure I explained your medications clearly. Can you tell me back what each medication is for and when you take it?"

Common misunderstandings to address:

  1. Patient assumes all new post-op meds are permanent. Clarify: "Amiodarone is for your heart rhythm and you'll take it for 3–6 months, then stop. Clopidogrel goes with the stent for 1 month, then you can stop that one too. Your cardiologist will tell you when to stop each."

  2. Patient doesn't know warfarin requires monitoring. Clarify: "Warfarin is a blood thinner. You must get your blood level checked regularly — we've scheduled your first check for [date]. You'll need checks every week for a while, then every month. It's important because too much warfarin causes bleeding, too little causes clots."

  3. Patient doesn't understand "hold" means temporary discontinuation. Clarify: "When we say 'hold metformin,' we mean pause it temporarily — not stop it forever. We'll restart it when your kidneys are working normally again. That's usually 2–3 days after surgery."

  4. Patient doesn't know about drug interactions (especially warfarin + vitamin K). Clarify: "Warfarin and vitamin K fight each other. If you eat lots of spinach and kale one day and none the next, your warfarin level swings. Keep your vitamin K intake steady and don't start any new supplements without asking your cardiologist."

  5. Patient doesn't know to call before stopping a new medication. Clarify: "If you feel a side effect from a new medication — like dizziness on your blood pressure medicine — call us before you stop it. Many side effects go away in a few days, or we can adjust the dose. Stopping on your own can be dangerous."

sections.heading: 7.4 High-Risk Medication Classes & Special Considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT):

  • Scope: ASA + clopidogrel (or ticagrelor) for stent thrombosis prevention.
  • Duration critical: BMS 1 month; DES 3–12 months (depends on stent type, indication, bleeding risk).
  • Risk of early stopping: Stent thrombosis = MI (50% mortality if in-stent).
  • Teach-back essential: Patient must understand why both drugs, when to stop, and to call before stopping.

Warfarin (vs. DOAC):

  • Scope: Mechanical valve (mandatory); AF with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2; hypercoagulable state.
  • Monitoring required: INR checks initially weekly, then every 2–4 weeks (lifelong compliance).
  • Drug interactions: NSAIDs, alcohol, vitamin K, antibiotics, statins, amiodarone all affect INR.
  • Teach-back essential: INR targets, vitamin K consistency, warning signs (bleeding, bruising, dark stool), INR check schedule.

DOAC (Apixaban, Rivaroxaban, Dabigatran, Edoxaban):

  • Scope: AF (non-valvular); recent VTE; post-op AF (increasingly common).
  • Advantage over warfarin: No INR monitoring.
  • Disadvantage: Must take same time daily; no dose adjustment; renal function must be ≥30 mL/min for most agents.
  • Teach-back essential: Timing consistency, no dosing flexibility, renal function importance, when to call (signs of bleeding).

Acetaminophen stacking:

  • Risk: >3 g/day = hepatotoxicity (liver damage, potential fatal liver failure).
  • Where it hides: Scheduled acetaminophen + oxycodone/acetaminophen + OTC pain relievers + cold medicines + cough suppressants.
  • Prevent: Calculate total daily acetaminophen from ALL sources; cap at 3 g/day; educate patient on OTC hidden acetaminophen.

NSAIDs post-op:

  • Risk: Bleeding (especially with anticoagulation), GI ulceration, renal injury, stent thrombosis (if DAPT + NSAID).
  • Timing: Avoid x4 weeks post-op minimum; longer if on anticoagulation.
  • Educate: "Avoid ibuprofen, naproxen, and other NSAIDs for 4 weeks. Use acetaminophen or your prescribed pain medicine instead."

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in patients deemed "stable" on current regimen; if any develop, re-escalate immediately.

  • New medication-related adverse event (rash, GI symptoms, shortness of breath, chest pain) shortly after discharge — possible allergy or interaction; call pharmacy/cardiologist
  • Patient calls confused about when to stop a medication — suggests discharge teaching was unclear; reinforce via phone + send written clarification
  • Patient reports stopping a medication on own (e.g., clopidogrel) without calling — risk of stent thrombosis (MI) or embolic event; escalate immediately
  • Bleeding signs appearing after discharge on anticoagulation (dark stool, blood in urine, nosebleeds, severe bruising) — INR may be supratherapeutic; call for urgent INR check
  • INR check not completed by scheduled date — dangling order; clarify with patient if they attended; reschedule if missed
  • Patient reports new symptom after starting antiarrhythmic (amiodarone): shortness of breath, cough, yellow eyes, blue-gray skin discoloration — possible drug toxicity; call cardiologist
  • Hyperglycemia or DKA-type symptoms post-op (polyuria, polydipsia, fruity breath) if SGLT2i resumed early without team approval — euglycemic DKA risk
  • Patient reports NOT taking a critical med (warfarin, DOAC, antiarrhythmic) because "I felt better" — stroke or arrhythmia risk; reinforce importance via phone + consider social work referral
  • ED call mentioning medication concern — escalate to team; may indicate readmission risk; offer pharmacy consult

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
(10–15 high-yield bullets for experienced nurses and experts)

  1. Pill bottles are the gold standard — insist on them. Patient memory fails (age, post-op haze, medication effects). Pharmacy records are second-best. Never default to patient recall alone.

  2. The third reconciliation point (discharge) is most commonly skipped or done superficially. Discharge is the highest-risk transition. Treat it as a full process: compare → document rationale → teach-back → provide written copy → verify PCP letter sent same day.

  3. OTC + supplements + herbals are frequently omitted. Ask explicitly: "Vitamins? Herbal products like ginkgo, garlic, ginger, St. John's Wort? Cold medicines, pain relievers, sleep aids?" Hidden aspirin in OTC analgesics and ginkgo/garlic increase bleeding risk.

  4. Pharmacist review at admission is essential but often skipped. Clinical judgment about drug interactions, dose verification, hold rationale requires pharmacy expertise. At minimum, ensure pharmacist flags discrepancies within 24 h.

  5. Teach-back is Joint Commission required but often underdone. Don't hand patient a med list and walk away. Ask patient to tell you back: "What is this for? When do you take it?" Correct misunderstandings. Document success or gaps. For complex regimens (DAPT, AC, antiarrhythmic, insulin), involve pharmacy. Have patient repeat back again if confused.

  6. Hold duration and restart criteria must be explicit. "Hold metformin" is vague. Write: "Hold metformin through POD 2; restart POD 3 if CrCl ≥45 on labs; labs ordered POD 1–2; patient notified restart criteria."

  7. New DAPT without a stop date is dangerous. Patient stops early (stent thrombosis, MI) or continues unnecessarily (bleeding risk). Write: "Clopidogrel 75 mg daily through [DATE: Month Day, Year] ONLY — then stop (call cardiology office on that date for instructions)."* Put date in red. Give patient calendar reminder. Notify PCP in writing.

  8. Warfarin restart without clear INR target or bridging plan creates confusion. PCP overshoots INR; bleeding results. Write clearly: "Restart warfarin POD 1 with LMWH bridge; target INR 2–3; anticoagulation clinic notified [date]; first INR check [location, date]; letter to PCP sent [date]."

  9. Acetaminophen stacking is easy to miss. Calculate total daily acetaminophen from ALL sources (scheduled, combination opioids, PRN pain relievers, cold meds, cough syrups). Cap at 3 g/day. Educate patient about hidden acetaminophen in OTC products.

  10. NSAID continuation post-op is underrecognized as dangerous. Patient takes ibuprofen at home; never explicitly discontinued; patient restarts at home; bleeding + GI bleed + renal injury. Explicitly document: "AVOID ibuprofen, naproxen, and NSAIDs for 4 weeks post-op. Use acetaminophen or prescribed opioids for pain instead."

  11. Anticoagulation clinic notification must happen same day of discharge. Dangling discharge warfarin without anticoagulation clinic follow-up = INR drifts unmonitored. (1) Call clinic same day; (2) provide written INR schedule to patient; (3) notify PCP of target + plan.

  12. Readmission reduction requires tracking. Monitor: % with complete med rec at all three points, discrepancies identified, medication-related ED calls in first 30 days post-discharge, patient understanding (post-discharge survey: "Can you state the purpose of your medications?"). Share results with team.

  13. Heart transplant and LVAD patients need accelerated med rec. Immunosuppression regimens are complex and time-sensitive. Pharmacist should be present at admission and discharge teaching.

  14. Language barriers and limited literacy slow teach-back — plan ahead. Use qualified interpreter (not family); provide written materials in patient's language; involve social work for homecare visit if high-risk (elderly, lives alone, limited literacy, no caregiver).

  15. Documentation completeness matters for legal + safety. Omitting med rec rationale or teach-back documentation creates liability and gaps in continuity of care. Document explicitly: what was reconciled, who verified it, rationale for changes, teach-back performed, patient/family understanding confirmed.

cards.title: Metabolic Acidosis Post-Cardiac Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: pH < 7.35, HCO₃⁻ < 22 → post-cardiac lactic acidosis from shock (hypoperfusion, mesenteric ischemia, sepsis) is most common; less often hyperchloremic (saline resuscitation) or DKA in diabetics. Calculate anion gap (Na − Cl − HCO₃⁻; normal 8–12). Stable path: stat ABG/lactate, IV access, trend labs, notify APP, address the cause (fluids, vasopressors, antibiotics). Unstable (pH <7.1 + shock + altered mental status) → STAT escalation, aggressive resuscitation, consider bicarbonate 50–100 mEq IV only if pH <7.1 + refractory shock. Treat the underlying problem (perfusion, infection, bleeding), not the pH.
