sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, incidence, clinical relevance.

  • Definition: Metabolic acidosis is pH < 7.35 with HCO₃⁻ < 22 mEq/L. Post-operative cardiac patients develop either high anion gap (organic acid accumulation, especially lactate from hypoperfusion) or normal anion gap (hyperchloremic from saline resuscitation, or GI/renal HCO₃⁻ loss).
  • Incidence: ~10–40% of major cardiac surgery patients depending on shock severity, resuscitation volume, and baseline renal function (Marik, 2016). Lactic acidosis >2 is associated with increased length of stay and mortality; rising lactate predicts worse outcomes.
  • Who this applies to: every post-operative cardiac surgery patient on ABG or VBG monitoring, especially POD 0–2 and any patient with hemodynamic instability or AKI.
  • Why it matters: metabolic acidosis impairs cardiac contractility and vasopressor responsiveness. Lactic acidosis is a marker of tissue hypoperfusion and demands urgent investigation. Left untreated, severe acidosis (pH <7.1) can precipitate arrhythmias, altered mental status, and organ dysfunction.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
High anion gap (lactic) acidosis — most common post-cardiac:

Lactic acidosis reflects anaerobic metabolism exceeding oxygen delivery. Post-operative triggers:

  • Cardiogenic shock: reduced cardiac output (low EF, valve malfunction, MI, RV dysfunction) → hypoperfusion → anaerobic lactate production
  • Septic shock: vasodilation + microvasculature dysfunction → maldistribution of flow → tissue ischemia → lactate
  • Hypovolemic shock: inadequate resuscitation or ongoing bleeding → low preload → reduced cardiac output → hypoperfusion
  • Mesenteric ischemia: gut hypoperfusion (severe intra-operative hypotension, emboli, small-vessel disease) → late dramatic lactate spike; often a surgical emergency
    • Seizure: extreme hypermetabolism (rare post-op)
    • Metformin-associated lactic acidosis (MALA): metformin accumulation in renal failure → pyruvate oxidation blocked → lactate accumulation; risk if Cr >1.5 or AKI present

Normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis — saline-induced:

Normal saline contains Cl⁻ 154 mEq/L (vs plasma ~102 mEq/L). Large volumes:

  • Excess Cl⁻ displaces HCO₃⁻ from the filtered load, lowering serum HCO₃⁻
  • pH falls; anion gap stays normal (Cl⁻ rise masks AG widening)
  • Incidence increases with >3 L boluses; common in massive resuscitation or prolonged CPB
  • Ongoing normal saline IV fluids on the floor worsen this

Other normal-AG causes post-cardiac:

  • GI HCO₃⁻ loss: diarrhea, ileostomy, ureteral diversion to bowel (common post-op)
  • Renal tubular acidosis (RTA): type 1 (distal RTA) — inability to acidify urine; type 4 (hyperkalemic RTA) — aldosterone deficiency/resistance
  • Medications: acetazolamide, topiramate, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors (post-op prophylaxis or home meds)
  • Post-hypocapnia: if hyperventilated intra-op, kidneys respond by excreting HCO₃⁻; takes 24–48 hours to normalize

DKA in diabetic post-op patients: Stress hyperglycemia + insulin deficiency (held in OR) + dehydration = high glucose + ketone production. Highest risk POD 0–2 if insulin restarted late or dosing insufficient.

Propofol infusion syndrome (rare but catastrophic): High-dose propofol (>4 mg/kg/min for >48 hours) causes severe metabolic acidosis + hypertriglyceridemia (>1500) + rhabdomyolysis. More common in children but can occur in adults.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what alerts you at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-operative cardiac patient:

  • Arterial or venous blood gas showing pH < 7.35 with HCO₃⁻ < 22
  • Clinical context alerting to acidosis: deteriorating mental status, tachypnea, fruity breath (DKA), rapid shallow breathing (respiratory compensation)
  • Laboratory clue: rising creatinine, lactate >2, osmolar gap (poisoning), anion gap on BMP
  • Hemodynamic instability post-op with metabolic acidosis on labs
  • Worsening renal function (AKI) with metabolic acidosis
  • Recent large-volume normal saline resuscitation (>3 L in OR or early post-op)
  • Patient on metformin with metabolic acidosis + lactate >2
  • Diarrhea or stoma output lasting >24 hours with acidosis
  • On acetazolamide or topiramate (seizure prophylaxis) with acidosis

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

Vital signs & perfusion:

  • HR, BP, MAP (target >65), SpO₂, RR (is patient compensating with tachypnea?)
  • Skin: warm/cool, capillary refill, urine output last 2 hours (oliguric vs polyuric?)
  • Mental status: alert vs lethargic vs agitated vs confused

Recent labs (already in chart):

  • Most recent ABG or VBG: pH, HCO₃⁻, PaCO₂, lactate, base excess
  • BMP: Na, K, Cl, HCO₃⁻, glucose, Cr, BUN; calculate anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃⁻)
  • Urine electrolytes (if normal-AG acidosis): Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻ to calculate urine anion gap = (U-Na + U-K) − U-Cl
  • Venous or arterial lactate (most recent and trend if serial)
  • Troponin, proBNP (cardiogenic shock context)
  • Glucose (DKA risk if diabetic)
  • Triglycerides (high levels with lactic acidosis → propofol infusion syndrome risk)

Timeline & context:

  • POD number? How much CPB time?
  • Intra-op blood loss and resuscitation volume (type: normal saline vs LR vs Plasma-Lyte?)
  • Current IV fluid rate and type (ongoing normal saline boluses?)
  • Home medications: metformin? diuretics? ACE inhibitor? Topiramate or acetazolamide?
  • Diarrhea or stoma output since POD 0?
  • Urine color: clear/concentrated/dark? Output volume?
  • Respiratory status: on ventilator (settings, compliance)? Extubated (RR, work of breathing)?

Symptoms:

  • SOB, chest discomfort, altered mental status, nausea/vomiting
  • Fruity breath (DKA), tremor, confusion

Assess for triggering conditions:

  • Shock? (MAP <65, lactate >2, cold extremities) → cardiogenic, septic, or hypovolemic?
  • Evidence of infection? (fever, WBC >15k, procalcitonin, cultures)
  • Mesenteric ischemia risk? (severe intra-op hypotension, on pressors, abdominal pain)
  • On acetazolamide, topiramate, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors? → RTA or drug-induced
  • Diabetes pre-op? Blood glucose trending? On metformin?
  • Diarrhea/stoma output >24h? → GI HCO₃⁻ loss

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP >65, no altered mental status, lactate <4, perfusing.)

  1. Stat ABG or VBG + BMP if not done in last 1–2 hours — confirm pH, HCO₃⁻, lactate, electrolytes
  2. Calculate anion gap = Na − (Cl + HCO₃⁻); normal is 8–12

  3. If anion gap HIGH (>12):

    • Most common post-cardiac: lactic acidosis from shock, mesenteric ischemia, sepsis, or metformin-MALA
    • Second most common: DKA in diabetic patients
    • Obtain: lactate level (stat), glucose (rule out DKA), beta-hydroxybutyrate or urine ketones if glucose >250
    • Assess perfusion: lactate + MAP + urine output; if lactate >4 and shock present → escalate to 5B (unstable)

  4. If anion gap NORMAL (8–12):

    • Most likely post-cardiac: saline-induced hyperchloremic acidosis (check intra-op fluid log; >3 L normal saline?)
    • Second: diarrhea or high stoma output
    • Third: acetazolamide / topiramate (check MAR)
    • If RTA suspected: obtain urine anion gap = (U-Na + U-K) − U-Cl. Negative UAG → GI loss; positive UAG → renal cause (RTA)

  5. Address trigger correction:

    • Hypovolemic? (CVP, orthostatics, clinical exam) → IV fluids; prefer LR or Plasma-Lyte over normal saline
    • Shock present? (lactate >2, MAP <65, cold skin, oliguria) → notify APP, consider pressors, ICU discussion
    • Glucose >250 + ketones? → DKA protocol, insulin, IV fluids
    • Metformin on board + lactate >5 + AKI? → MALA; hold metformin, notify team
    • Diarrhea >24h? → IV fluid + electrolyte replacement per team
    • On acetazolamide? → discuss holding vs continuing with provider
    • Mesenteric ischemia concern? (hypotension intra-op, on pressors, RUQ pain, bloody stool) → notify team, prepare for imaging/consult

  6. Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (see §6) — report pH, HCO₃⁻, lactate, anion gap, clinical context

  7. Arrange follow-up labs in 2–4 hours (trend lactate, HCO₃⁻, repeat ABG after interventions)

  8. Continuous monitoring: tele, SpO₂, urine output, assess for worsening

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension MAP <65, altered mental status, lactate >4, shock, severe acidosis pH <7.1)

  1. STAT call to APP / fellow / ICU team — do NOT leave patient alone
  2. Activate RRT or code team if unresponsive
  3. Stat labs: ABG, lactate, BMP, CBC, type & screen, troponin, procalcitonin, blood cultures
  4. Establish/confirm IV access: 2 large-bore IVs, consider central line if not present

  5. Aggressive hemodynamic support:

    • Aggressive fluid resuscitation: 500–1000 mL bolus LR or Plasma-Lyte (avoid normal saline to prevent worsening hyperchloremic acidosis)
    • Notify provider for vasopressor consideration if MAP remains <65 after fluid bolus (norepinephrine 0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min per protocol)

  6. Identify and treat the source immediately:

    • Cardiogenic shock: ensure adequate filling pressures and contractility; IABP/ECMO discussion; ICU transfer
    • Septic shock: broad-spectrum antibiotics STAT per protocol, source control, lactate clearance target
    • Hypovolemic shock: rapid fluid resuscitation, assess for ongoing bleeding, consider massive transfusion protocol
    • Mesenteric ischemia: notify vascular/general surgery immediately, prepare for urgent CT angio, may need emergent laparotomy
    • Metformin-MALA: hold metformin, IV fluids, renal replacement therapy discussion, notify ICU

  7. If severe acidosis (pH <7.1–7.2) + shock persistent despite fluids/vasopressors:

    • Sodium bicarbonate 50–100 mEq IV bolus may be considered (evidence is weak; rationale is to improve cardiac contractility and vasopressor responsiveness while treating the cause)
    • Bicarbonate produces CO₂ (respiratory load), shifts K⁺ upward, but empirically used in ICU for pH <7.1 + hemodynamic compromise
    • Repeat ABG in 15–30 min; further dosing per provider
    • Goal: buy time for definitive therapy (resuscitation, source control), NOT to "fix" acid-base; correct the underlying cause

  8. Escalate to ICU — post-cardiac metabolic acidosis with shock warrants ICU level of care

  9. Document: time of ABG, pH/HCO₃⁻/lactate, interventions, bicarbonate bolus if given, response to fluids/vasopressors, trajectory

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit] calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient's ABG shows pH [value], HCO₃⁻ [value], lactate [value], anion gap [value]. BP [value], HR [value], RR [value]. Patient is [alert / lethargic]. UOP [volume/hour]. Recent Cr [value], K [value], Cl [value]." A: "Patient appears [stable / unstable — list findings: perfusion, mental status, respiratory effort]." R: "Requesting [workup — lactate trend / urine anion gap / glucose check / imaging for mesenteric ischemia?] and [management — fluid bolus / vasopressor / bicarbonate / ICU transfer / specialist consult]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
New mild acidosis (pH 7.25–7.35), stable, high-AG lactic Primary APP / on-call cardiologist
Acidosis + elevated lactate >4 + any hypotension APP + notify ICU team
Acidosis pH <7.2 + shock + altered mental status RRT + on-call ICU + code team
Acidosis with DKA features (glucose >250, ketones) Primary APP + ICU consult + endocrine
Acidosis + mesenteric ischemia concern (pain, bloody stool) CT surgery + vascular surgery + ICU
Acidosis + new renal failure (Cr spike) Nephrology consult + ICU team
Acidosis post-large saline bolus (hyperchloremic suspected) Surgeon/APP + fluid management discussion
Acidosis + on metformin + lactate >5 (MALA suspected) STAT ICU transfer + nephrology (dialysis?)
Persistent acidosis despite intervention ICU team — reassess cause, consider transfer if not already

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Anion gap calculation & clinical interpretation
sections.bodyHtml:
Anion gap (AG) calculation:

  • AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃⁻)
  • Normal: 8–12 mEq/L (varies by lab; some use 6–10)
  • High AG >12: organic acid accumulation (lactate, ketones, uremic acid, methanol, ethylene glycol)
  • Normal AG 8–12: hyperchloremia or GI/renal HCO₃⁻ loss

Delta gap (Delta AG):

  • Delta AG = (AG − 12) − (24 − HCO₃⁻)
  • Helps identify mixed metabolic disturbances
  • Delta AG = 0: pure high-AG metabolic acidosis
  • Delta AG >0 (positive): concurrent metabolic alkalosis masking true AG elevation
  • Delta AG <0 (negative): concurrent normal-AG metabolic acidosis (mixed disorder — e.g., lactic + hyperchloremic)

Clinical pearl: Post-cardiac shock patient may have lactic acidosis (high AG) plus saline-induced hyperchloremic acidosis (normal AG) = modestly elevated AG but low HCO₃⁻ (negative delta AG). Recognizing the mixed picture guides management: treat perfusion AND switch fluids away from normal saline.

sections.heading: 7.2 Lactate interpretation: Type A vs Type B
sections.bodyHtml:
Lactate is a marker of tissue hypoxia and/or metabolism dysregulation — not just a number.

  • Type A lactic acidosis: hypoxia-driven (shock, respiratory failure, anemia) → lactate from anaerobic metabolism. Most common post-cardiac.
  • Type B lactic acidosis: non-hypoxia-driven (liver failure, metformin, thiamine deficiency, beta-2 agonist overuse, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, propofol infusion syndrome). Less common post-cardiac but important to recognize.

Lactate >2 always warrants investigation. Mild elevation (2–3) in post-op SIRS can be expected; but rising lactate (2 → 3 → 4) signals worsening tissue hypoperfusion and demands action. Lactate >4 in the setting of shock predicts mortality and warrants aggressive resuscitation and source identification.

Clearance is prognostic: lactate trending downward with intervention = good sign; persistent/rising lactate despite resuscitation = poor prognosis.

sections.heading: 7.3 Propofol infusion syndrome red flags
sections.bodyHtml:
Triad: severe metabolic acidosis + hypertriglyceridemia (>1500) + rhabdomyolysis (elevated CK, myoglobinuria).

Risk: high-dose propofol (>4 mg/kg/min) for >48 hours. More common in children but documented in adults post-cardiac surgery if sedation was prolonged.

Recognition: post-op patient on propofol drip with unexplained metabolic acidosis + myalgias + CK elevation + triglycerides >1500 → think propofol infusion syndrome and notify ICU immediately. Discontinue propofol. May require hemodialysis.

sections.heading: 7.4 Mesenteric ischemia: the late lactate spike
sections.bodyHtml:
Mesenteric ischemia's lactate is late and dramatic.**

  • If intra-op hypotension was severe and prolonged (MAP <50 × sustained time), patient is at risk
  • Lactate may be normal on POD 0 and spike to >8 on POD 1–2
  • Abdominal pain, bloody stool, peritoneal signs are LATE findings in the post-op narcotized patient
  • Lactate elevation may be the ONLY early clue — it can precede clinical signs
  • If you suspect mesenteric ischemia: notify surgeon immediately; CT angiography is urgent. Do not wait for clinical deterioration.
  • Mortality is high if diagnosis delayed; early recognition and surgical intervention improve outcomes (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025)

sections.heading: 7.5 Post-operative mesenteric ischemia and the painless abdomen
sections.bodyHtml:
The post-operative cardiac surgery patient on narcotic sedation may NOT report pain even with mesenteric ischemia. This is a known trap.

  • Abdominal distension, ileus, or lack of bowel function can be subtle clues
  • Rising lactate + any GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, constipation, absence of bowel sounds) = high index of suspicion
  • Low threshold for CT angiography; do NOT delay imaging waiting for overt pain or peritonitis
  • Coordinate with CT surgery and general surgery early

sections.heading: 7.6 Bicarbonate therapy: evidence and pragmatism
sections.bodyHtml:
Sodium bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis is controversial.

Evidence:

  • Randomized trials show no mortality benefit in metabolic acidosis (lactic, DKA, RTA)
  • NNT would be very high
  • Mechanisms of harm: produces CO₂ (worsens respiratory acidosis if ventilation limited), shifts K⁺ upward acutely (hyperkalemia risk), increases osmole load

But: used empirically in many ICUs for severe acidosis (pH <7.1–7.2) + hemodynamic compromise / shock as a temporizing measure:

  • Rationale: extreme acidosis impairs cardiac contractility, vasopressor responsiveness, cellular function
  • 50–100 mEq IV bolus may buy time for resuscitation to improve perfusion
  • Repeat ABG in 15–30 min; further dosing per provider
  • Goal: temporize while treating the underlying cause (not to "fix" acid-base)

When to give:

  1. pH <7.1–7.2 + shock (MAP <65, lactate >4, altered mental status)
  2. Severe acidosis + renal failure (unable to generate respiratory compensation)
  3. DKA with severe acidosis (some protocols use it; risk of hypokalemia shift and cerebral edema)

When NOT to give:

  • pH >7.2 (no proven benefit)
  • Respiratory acidosis (CO₂ load from bicarbonate worsens it)
  • Lactic acidosis without shock (treat the lactate source: perfusion, infection, etc.)
  • Hyperchloremic normal-AG acidosis from diarrhea (give fluids + HCO₃⁻-containing fluids like LR, not bicarbonate)

sections.heading: 7.7 Urine anion gap: RTA vs GI loss
sections.bodyHtml:
When you have normal-AG metabolic acidosis, ask: "Where did the HCO₃⁻ go — out the kidneys or out the gut?"

Urine anion gap (UAG) calculation:

  • UAG = (U-Na + U-K) − U-Cl
  • Negative UAG (<−10): kidneys excreting H⁺ normally (HCO₃⁻ loss is GI-driven) → diarrhea, stoma output
  • Positive UAG (>10): kidneys NOT excreting H⁺ despite serum acidosis (urine is alkaline) → RTA
  • Neutral UAG (−10 to +10): overlap zone; sometimes inconclusive

Clinical example:

  • Post-op patient: pH 7.32, HCO₃⁻ 18, AG 10 (normal-AG acidosis)
  • Scenario A: 2 days diarrhea → UAG negative → GI loss; treat with IV fluids, electrolyte repletion
  • Scenario B: on acetazolamide → UAG positive → RTA; hold drug or manage with alkali if continued

sections.heading: 7.8 ABG vs VBG: quick reference
sections.bodyHtml:
ABG (arterial):

  • Gold standard for PaO₂, PaCO₂, pH, base excess
  • More invasive; needed when oxygenation assessment is critical

VBG (venous):

  • pH accuracy: within 0.03 units of ABG (clinically acceptable)
  • HCO₃⁻ accuracy: reliable
  • PvO₂ is NOT reliable for oxygenation assessment — venous is always lower; cannot assess PaO₂
  • Post-op use: if central line present, VBG is quick for acid-base assessment; if hypoxia concern, get ABG

Trend consistently: VBG-to-VBG or ABG-to-ABG; mixing sources can confuse interpretation.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • Lactate rising despite fluid resuscitation — shock is worsening; reassess cardiogenic vs septic vs ongoing bleed
  • Lactate >4 developing in real-time — imminent hemodynamic decompensation; notify team immediately
  • pH trending down despite intervention (pH <7.2) — acidosis worsening faster than treatment can reverse
  • RR >30 or increasing respiratory effort — respiratory compensation maxing out; risk of respiratory fatigue/failure
  • Altered mental status or decreased responsiveness — acidotic encephalopathy; aspiration/airway protection risk
  • Hypotension developing despite fluids → cardiogenic or septic shock, not hypovolemia
  • Oliguria (UOP <0.5 mL/kg/h) developing — AKI limiting kidney's ability to excrete acid
  • Rising creatinine + acidosis — AKI + metabolic acidosis = severe shock or sepsis; early dialysis discussion
  • Abdominal pain, bloody stool, peritoneal signs — mesenteric ischemia; surgical emergency
  • Fever + acidosis + rising lactate — sepsis; prepare for antibiotics, source control
  • New arrhythmia — severe acidosis or hyperkalemia; confirm K⁺ level
  • Glucose >300 + ketonuria + acidosis — DKA developing; confirm beta-hydroxybutyrate
  • Triglycerides >1500 + myalgias + high-dose propofol infusion — propofol infusion syndrome (rare but catastrophic)
  • Persistent acidosis (pH <7.2) after 24–48 hours — underlying condition is severe (sepsis, mesenteric ischemia, cardiogenic shock, MALA); escalate urgently

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Lactic acidosis post-cardiac = hypoperfusion until proven otherwise. This is NOT a benign lab finding. Every elevated lactate warrants investigation: shock, sepsis, mesenteric ischemia, occult bleed. Do not reassure and "watch" — act. Trend lactate serially; a single elevated lactate can be spurious (lab error, prolonged draw time), but two rising lactates are real.

  2. Trend lactate over time; never rely on a single value. Lactate >2 is concerning; lactate >4 is alarming. Rising lactate (2 → 3 → 4) even if each value "seems acceptable" indicates worsening tissue hypoperfusion and warrants urgent escalation.

  3. Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis from normal saline is real and increasing in recognition. Large boluses of normal saline (>3 L in OR or early post-op) produce low-HCO₃⁻ normal-AG acidosis. During acute resuscitation this is accepted (survival first), but ongoing normal saline IV fluids on the floor after initial resuscitation is worsening it.

    Switch to LR or Plasma-Lyte for ongoing fluids once acute resuscitation phase is over (Weinberg et al., 2020).

  4. Mesenteric ischemia's lactate is late and dramatic. If intra-op hypotension was profound (MAP <50 for prolonged time), patient is at risk. Lactate may be normal POD 0 and spike to >8 on POD 1–2. Abdominal pain and bloody stool are LATE findings. In the post-op narcotized patient, lactate elevation may be the ONLY early clue. If you suspect mesenteric ischemia, notify surgeon immediately; CT angio is urgent. Do not wait for clinical deterioration.

  5. AKI + metabolic acidosis are a pair. Kidneys cannot excrete acid if they're failing. If Cr is rising with acidosis, consider early dialysis discussion with nephrology. Renal replacement therapy can remove lactate, acetate, and other anions while you treat the underlying cause.

  6. DKA may coexist in the diabetic post-op patient. Stress hyperglycemia + delayed insulin restart + volume depletion = DKA. Check glucose, beta-hydroxybutyrate (or urine ketones), venous pH, and HCO₃⁻ if ANY post-op diabetic has metabolic acidosis. DKA is treatable with insulin, fluids, and electrolyte management.

  7. Propofol infusion syndrome is rare but catastrophic. High-dose propofol (>4 mg/kg/min) for >48 hours → severe metabolic acidosis + hypertriglyceridemia (>1500) + rhabdomyolysis. If patient was on propofol drip and now presents with unexplained acidosis + myalgias + elevated CK, think propofol infusion syndrome and notify ICU immediately (Marik, 2016).

  8. Bicarbonate therapy is controversial and NOT first-line. Do not give bicarbonate for "mild" acidosis (pH >7.2). It produces CO₂, shifts K⁺, and has no mortality benefit.

    Reserve for pH <7.1–7.2 + shock — use as temporizing measure while fixing the underlying problem (resuscitate, antibiotics, surgery).

  9. Severe pH <7.1–7.2 + shock MAY warrant bicarbonate. Extreme acidosis impairs cardiac contractility, vasopressor responsiveness, and cellular function. A 50–100 mEq bolus may buy time for resuscitation to work. Repeat ABG in 15–30 min; further dosing per provider. Used empirically in many ICUs despite weak RCT evidence.

  10. Anion gap > delta: recognize mixed disorders. If AG is higher than expected for the HCO₃⁻ drop (positive delta AG), you likely have concurrent metabolic alkalosis masking true AG rise. If HCO₃⁻ is lower than expected for AG (negative delta AG), you have mixed picture: high-AG + normal-AG metabolic acidosis. Post-cardiac example: lactic acidosis + saline-induced hyperchloremic = modestly elevated AG but low HCO₃⁻.

  11. Respiratory compensation is expected and healthy. If pH drops, RR should rise (Kussmaul respirations if severe). If RR is NOT rising, patient may have respiratory muscle fatigue, CNS depression, or primary respiratory disease.

    This is a red flag.

  12. VBG pH and HCO₃⁻ are reliable; VBG PvO₂ is NOT. If you need to know PaO₂, get an ABG. For pure acid-base assessment, VBG from central line is adequate and faster.

  13. Urine anion gap differentiates RTA from GI losses. Negative UAG = GI loss of HCO₃⁻ (diarrhea, ileostomy); positive UAG = renal tubular acidosis (RTA) — kidneys unable to acidify urine despite serum acidosis. Treatment differs: GI loss → IV fluids; RTA → may need alkali or hold the offending drug.

  14. Post-operative SIRS can cause mild lactate elevation. Post-op patient in systemic inflammatory state; some tachycardia and mild vasodilation is expected. Lactate >2 but <3 can be from SIRS rather than from shock. That said, elevated lactate always warrants investigation. If patient is warm, perfusing well, and lactate is 2–2.5, reassess in 2–4 hours. If lactate is rising or patient is cold/hypotensive, escalate.

  15. Post-CPB lactate is expected; rising lactate is not. Mild lactate elevation (2–3) from CPB ischemia + hemodilution is common on POD 0. This typically clears by POD 1–2 with normal perfusion.

    If lactate is rising POD 1–3, investigate. This predicts poor outcomes and demands urgent assessment for shock, infection, or other causes.

cards.title: Mitral Regurgitation
cards.quickAnswer: Mitral regurgitation (MR) is incomplete leaflet coaptation during systole, classifying into primary (organic leaflet pathology—degenerative, rheumatic, endocarditis) and secondary/functional (from LV dilation or papillary muscle displacement). Severity assessed by EROA (≥0.4 cm² = severe), regurgitant volume (≥60 mL = severe), and vena contracta (≥0.7 cm = severe). Primary severe MR: surgical repair preferred over replacement when feasible; repair rates > 90% in high-volume centers. Secondary MR: optimize GDMT (ACE-I/ARB, beta-blockers, SGLT2i, aldosterone antagonist) first; if persistent symptoms, consider transcatheter edge-to-edge repair (MitraClip, per COAPT inclusion criteria) or surgery. Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture, endocarditis flail) is a surgical emergency.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, clinical context.

  • Definition: Incomplete coaptation of mitral leaflets during ventricular systole, allowing retrograde blood flow into the left atrium. Creates volume overload on the LV and LA.
  • Epidemiology:
  • Second-most common valve disease after aortic stenosis
  • Primary (organic) MR: 50–60% of severe MR in developed countries. Degenerative (prolapse, Barlow) most common; 2–3% of population have MVP; advanced age predominates. Rheumatic MR historically common, now rare in US. Endocarditis causes acute or chronic destruction.
  • Secondary (functional) MR: 40–50% of severe MR. Associated with ischemic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, HFrEF.
  • Overall prevalence: ~10% of population have some MR; severe MR affects ~0.5–1%
  • Typical patient:
  • Primary: Older patient (70s+) with degenerative MVP; or younger with acute endocarditis/trauma
  • Secondary: Middle-aged to older HF patient with ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy and LV dilation
  • Why ICU nurses encounter this: Pre-operative mitral valve repair/replacement candidates; acute decompensation from severe MR; post-operative MV surgery monitoring; TEER/MitraClip candidates; chronic MR with AF or HF exacerbation.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Pathophysiology detail

sections.heading: Primary (Degenerative) MR
sections.bodyHtml:
• Valve pathology: prolapse of papillary muscle region, elongated or ruptured chordae tendineae, leaflet flail, or intrinsic leaflet degeneration (Barlow = myxomatous leaflet thickening + prolapse)
  • Acute vs. chronic hemodynamics:
  • Chronic MR: LV adapts with eccentric hypertrophy and dilation; LA dilates progressively; AF develops from atrial stretch
  • Acute MR: no LV adaptation; sudden increase in LA pressure → pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock
  • Hemodynamic consequence: large regurgitant volume into low-resistance LA → brisk LA and pulmonary venous filling; LV faces reduced afterload (some stroke volume exits aorta, some regurgitates) → hyperdynamic LV initially, decompensates late when contractility fails

sections.heading: Secondary (Functional) MR
sections.bodyHtml:
• LV dilation from any cause (ischemic CMP, dilated CMP, HF, post-MI) → mitral annulus dilates, leaflet tethering increases, coaptation is lost
  • Papillary muscle displacement: lateral and apical displacement from LV remodeling → anterolateral and posterolateral leaflets fail to coapt
  • Afterload reduction from MR perpetuates LV dilation ("vicious cycle"); correction of MR can improve LV function if caught early
  • Marker of severe LV remodeling — MR usually develops when EF < 35% and LVEDD > 65 mm; often accompanies systolic dysfunction
  • Loading-dependent: severity varies with preload and afterload; echo findings may improve with diuresis or vasodilation

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
When and how MR presents at bedside; recognition triggers.

Chronic primary MR:

  • Often asymptomatic for years despite large regurgitant volumes; LV adaptation allows compensation
  • Late symptom onset signals decompensation: dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, PND, fatigue, exercise intolerance
  • Atrial fibrillation develops from LA enlargement; often first symptom bringing patient to attention
  • Physical exam: holosystolic (pansystolic) apical murmur, hyperdynamic precordium, prominent carotid pulse, full pulses

Acute severe MR (papillary muscle rupture post-MI, flail post-endocarditis, acute trauma):

  • Sudden onset pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, hemodynamic collapse
  • Marked dyspnea, orthopnea, hypotension
  • Acutely congested lungs; rales; hypoxia
  • Often new or changing murmur in a post-MI patient already in distress
  • Median survival without operative intervention: days to weeks

Secondary (functional) MR:

  • Often asymptomatic until decompensation from HF progression
  • Detected on routine TTE in a HFrEF patient; may be first sign of LV dilation
  • Can worsen acutely with volume overload, loss of sinus rhythm (AF), ischemia, or medication non-compliance

Other clinical features:

  • Palpitations from AF
  • Exercise intolerance as disease progresses
  • Right-sided HF signs if advanced (RV dilation from chronic pulmonary HTN)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Systematic ICU-level bedside exam, no actions yet. Target: 2–5 minutes.

History and context:

  • Cardiac surgery history (pre-op candidate, post-op day, type of procedure)
  • Prior echo findings: known MR grade, LA/LV size, EF
  • Symptoms: dyspnea severity, palpitations, chest pain, orthopnea, PND, syncope
  • Medication compliance: GDMT adherence (ACE-I, beta-blocker, SGLT2i), home rate-control drugs
  • AF history or new onset; anticoagulation status
  • Ischemic event suspected? Recent chest pain, troponin elevation? (Post-MI papillary muscle rupture risk)

Physical examination:

  • Vital signs: HR (rate control adequacy if known AF), BP, SpO₂, perfusion (cap refill, skin temp)
  • Cardiac auscultation: apical murmur character (holosystolic vs. late systolic), relation to carotid pulse, dynamic change with maneuvers
  • Lung exam: crackles, dullness, JVD (LA pressure proxy)
  • Extremity exam: peripheral edema, cyanosis

Diagnostic information on hand:

  • Most recent TTE: EROA, regurgitant volume, vena contracta, LA volume, LV size/EF, leaflet anatomy
  • ECG: AF, LVH, prior MI
  • Chest X-ray: pulmonary congestion, LA enlargement (double density, straightened left heart border)
  • Labs: BNP/NT-proBNP (prognosis, HF marker), K⁺, Mg²⁺ (electrolyte stability), troponin if acute MI concern, creatinine (renal function for GDMT)
  • Lines, wires: arterial line for BP trend, adequate IV access for potential medications

sections.heading: 5A. Primary MR (organic leaflet pathology)
sections.bodyHtml:
Presentation Management pathway
Asymptomatic, normal LV function (EF ≥60%, LVEDD <55 mm) Watchful waiting + TTE every 6–12 months. Assess for symptom development, LV dysfunction (EF decline, LVEDD increase), AF, LA enlargement (>45 mm). Class I — no surgery. Ensure patient education re: symptom warning signs.
Asymptomatic + LV dilation (LVEDD >55 mm) or EF <60% Mitral valve repair — Class IIa indication (reasonable to offer). Degenerative MR prolapse/flail can be reliably repaired; success rate >95% in high-volume centers. Early repair before irreversible LV dysfunction develops.
Symptomatic severe primary MR Mitral valve repair — Class I indication (strong recommendation). Gold standard for degenerative MR; preserves native tissue, avoids anticoagulation if repair alone (no prosthesis). Techniques: quadrangular/triangular resection, papillary muscle plication, artificial chordae (neochordae), annuloplasty.
Unrepair-able primary MR (extensive rheumatic scarring, endocarditis with perforation/abscess) Mitral valve replacement — mechanical (INR 2–3 lifelong; higher if multiple prostheses) or bioprosthetic (~10–15 yr durability, then re-operation). Team decision on tissue vs. mechanical depends on age, compliance, bleeding risk.
Acute severe primary MR (papillary muscle rupture, acute flail from endocarditis) Emergent OR — See Section 5C.

Repair-specific considerations:

  • Success and longevity: >95% early success in high-volume centers; durable at 10–15 years if first repair; re-repair rates ~5% at 5 years
  • Risk of post-repair complications: SAM (systolic anterior motion, new murmur + hemodynamic collapse post-aggressive anterior leaflet repair; managed initially with beta-blockers, vasodilation, fluids; refractory SAM requires emergency re-op); acute MI if coronary cannulation injury
  • Post-op AF: ~40–50% develop new AF POD 1–7; anticipate with amiodarone, magnesium repletion, rate control

sections.heading: 5B. Secondary / Functional MR (from LV dilation)
sections.bodyHtml:
Presentation Management pathway
Mild-moderate secondary MR + stable on GDMT Continue medical optimization. TTE surveillance every 6–12 months. MR often improves with LV remodeling reversal from GDMT. No surgical intervention needed.
Severe secondary MR, asymptomatic or mild symptoms Ensure truly optimized GDMT: uptitrate ACE-I/ARB (target dose), beta-blocker (target HR 60–80), aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone if EF <35%), SGLT2i (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin). Repeat echo at 3–6 months; MR may improve with LV remodeling.
Severe secondary MR, symptomatic HF on optimal GDMT Step 1: Confirm GDMT truly optimized (max tolerated doses, not contraindicated). No quick fixes.
Step 2: If still symptomatic after 6–12 weeks max GDMT, consider TEER (MitraClip) or surgical repair/replacement per COAPT trial criteria: EF 20–50%, EROA 1.2–5.1 cm², anatomy favorable. MitraClip shown benefit in secondary MR (HFrEF) in COAPT (2018); MITRA-FR showed neutral results in slightly different population. Patient selection is everything.
Severe functional MR + very low EF (<20%) May be referred for LVAD / transplant pathway if global dilation/dysfunction. MR addressed as part of comprehensive HF management. Surgery/TEER deferred unless affecting candidacy.

Secondary MR-specific considerations:

  • Medical-first approach: GDMT reverses LV remodeling; MR often improves without intervention if EF >30%
  • TEER (MitraClip) advantages: less invasive than surgery, can be repeated, preserves annulus, no anticoagulation if device alone, amenable to high-risk patients
  • TEER limitations: smaller valve area post-TEER (may develop functional stenosis over years); anatomy-dependent (leaflet length, coaptation depth, annular size); durability data evolving
  • TEER success rate: ~60–80% achieve significant MR reduction (≤2+ grade) in appropriately selected patients; benefit modest in MITRA-FR (less-selected population)

sections.heading: 5C. Acute Severe MR (surgical emergency)
sections.bodyHtml:
Trigger Immediate pathway
Papillary muscle rupture post-MI Emergent OR, typically within 1–2 hours. Partial ruptures may stabilize 24–48 h with IABP bridge + vasodilators; complete rupture = instantly life-threatening. 50% mortality without intervention.
Acute flail leaflet post-endocarditis Emergent OR for replacement (repair often unfeasible). Vegetation erodes chordae → flail. Likely requires MVR. Get blood cultures before antibiotics; echo (TTE + TEE) for abscess/perforation/other vegetations.
Acute trauma Emergent OR if acute severe regurgitation and hemodynamic instability.

Acute MR hemodynamics — red flags:

  • Normal-size LA with suddenly incompetent valve → no compliance buffer → rapid pressure rise → flash pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock (contrast chronic MR where LA dilates gradually and accommodates)
  • No LV dilation yet — ventricle is hyperdynamic but facing sudden impedance mismatch
  • Rapid decompensation — minutes to hours; different trajectory from chronic compensated MR

Bridge strategies (pre-op stabilization):

  • Vasodilation (nitroprusside, nitroglycerin) — reduces afterload, decreases regurgitant fraction
  • IABP (intra-aortic balloon pump) — reduces afterload further; only temporizing, not definitive
  • Diuretics cautiously — improve pulmonary edema but avoid overly dropping preload (LV is dependent on venous return)
  • Avoid negative inotropes — no beta-blockers or CCBs; maintain contractility
  • Prepare for emergent ECMO — if unstable before OR arrival or OR delay expected

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "[Patient name, room], [cardiac history context], now with [acute finding: new murmur, acutely worsening dyspnea, hypotension, AF with RVR]." B: "Known [primary / secondary] MR, prior EF [X]%, EROA [value if known]. On [GDMT list / anticoagulation status]." A: "[Current exam findings, hemodynamics, symptoms]. Echo findings if available. Concern for [acute flail / papillary muscle rupture / acute decompensation]." R: "Requesting [urgent echo / OR evaluation / IABP consideration / cardiology consult / escalation to cardiac surgery]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Asymptomatic severe primary MR, stable Cardiology clinic — outpatient TTE surveillance, surgical referral planning
Symptomatic primary MR, candidate for repair Cardiac surgery team — surgical evaluation + pre-op workup
Severe secondary MR on suboptimal GDMT Cardiology / HF team — optimize medical therapy, recheck echo at 6–12 weeks
Symptomatic severe secondary MR on optimal GDMT Cardiology + cardiac surgery — TEER (MitraClip) vs. surgical repair/replacement evaluation
Acute severe MR suspected (papillary muscle rupture, acute flail, endocarditis) Cardiac surgery STAT + cardiology + ICU team. Prepare for emergent OR.
Acute MR + unstable hemodynamics (cardiogenic shock) Code/RRT + cardiac surgery + interventional cardiology (IABP, ECMO consideration)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections.

Carpentier's classification of mitral leaflet pathology (expandable) Carpentier (1983) organizes mitral pathology by leaflet motion:
  • Type I (normal leaflet motion): Annular dilation alone (secondary MR). Leaflet coaptation lost because annulus dilated, not leaflet pathology. Tethering angle increases; leaflet lengths normal.
  • Type II (excess leaflet motion): Prolapse or flail. Papillary muscle displacement (usually posterolateral), elongated chordae, or ruptured chordae → leaflet billows into LA during systole. Prolapse = billowing < 2 mm into LA; flail = tip below annular plane or ruptured chordae. Anterior leaflet prolapse (Barlow) vs. posterior leaflet prolapse vs. bileaflet. Repair: resection of excess leaflet + annuloplasty, neochordae.
  • Type IIIa (restricted leaflet motion, rheumatic): Rheumatic mitral stenosis with chordal shortening, commissural fusion, leaflet thickening → both stenosis and regurgitation. Rare in developed countries. Repair often unfeasible; replacement preferred.
  • Type IIIb (restricted leaflet motion, tethering — functional MR): LV dilation and papillary muscle displacement → leaflet tethering (apical displacement of papillary muscle tips pulls leaflet edges apically during systole) → coaptation lost despite leaflet tissue normal. This is secondary/functional MR. Repair if done (annuloplasty alone, edge-to-edge) requires addressing root cause (GDMT to reverse LV dilation) or is short-lived. Clinical relevance: Carpentier Type I vs. IIIb (functional) drives management — optimize GDMT first for Type IIIb. Repair anatomy (Type II prolapse/flail) is more durable than repair of Type IIIb alone.
Echo quantification in detail: EROA, vena contracta, PISA (expandable) EROA (effective regurgitant orifice area):
  • Planimetry of the regurgitant orifice on color Doppler or 3D echo
  • ≥0.4 cm² = severe; >0.6 cm² = very severe
  • In functional MR, often dynamic (varies with loading), measured at end-systole
  • Can be calculated from regurgitant volume ÷ regurgitant velocity integral (if flow is known) Regurgitant volume (RV_reg):
  • RV_reg = stroke volume (mitral inflow) − aortic outflow
  • ≥60 mL/beat = severe; >80 mL = very severe
  • Calculated from Doppler inflow and outflow measurements; depends on heart rate and loading Vena contracta (VC):
  • Smallest cross-section of the regurgitant jet
  • ≥0.7 cm = severe; >1.0 cm = very severe
  • Less loading-dependent than EROA or RV; more specific for acute changes
  • Eccentric jets (common in MVP) can underestimate VC due to wall constraint; PISA often more accurate PISA (proximal isovelocity surface area):
  • Color Doppler shell radius at aliasing velocity
  • EROA = (2π × r²) × aliasing velocity ÷ peak MR velocity
  • Accounts for eccentric jets better than vena contracta alone
  • Standard method for quantification when available Systolic pulmonary venous flow reversal:
  • Normal: systolic antegrade flow in pulmonary veins
  • Severe MR: systolic reversal in ≥1 pulmonary vein (jet directed backward into pulmonary circulation)
  • Very specific for severe MR; semi-quantitative Severity grading summary table:
    SeverityEROA (cm²)RV (mL)Vena contracta (cm)LA volumePulmonary vein systolic reversal
    Mild<0.2<30<0.3normalabsent
    Moderate0.2–0.430–590.3–0.7normal/mildly ↑absent
    Severe≥0.4≥60≥0.7↑↑often present
    Very severe>0.6>80>1.0markedly ↑present
Primary vs. secondary MR: echo differentiation (expandable)
Echo featurePrimary MRSecondary/Functional MR
Leaflet anatomyThickened, redundant, prolapsing, flail, or perforatedNormal appearance, normal thickness, normal scallops
Annular dilationMild to moderateSevere (>35 mm typical)
LA size (diameter)Mild to moderate initiallyModerate to severe (often >45 mm)
LV size (LVEDD)Often <55 mm initiallyOften >55 mm (origin of MR)
LV function (EF)Usually normal or mildly reducedOften reduced (<40%)
Coaptation depth<2 mm (leaflets coapt normally)>11 mm (papillary muscle displacement, tethering)
Trigger for MRLeaflet pathology (prolapse, flail, perforation, rheumatic deformity)Geometric: annular dilation + papillary muscle apical displacement
MechanismLeaflet-centricGeometry-centric
3D anatomy noteProlapse localization (anterior, posterior, bileaflet); flail scallop identificationTethering angle, coaptation depth, leaflet tenting
Clinical pearl: "The leaflets look normal" in secondary MR — tissue is pristine, but geometry is wrong. Education point for nursing.
COAPT vs. MITRA-FR trial findings (expandable) Two landmark RCTs tested MitraClip in secondary MR; different populations, different results. COAPT (2018, Stone et al.):
  • Population: secondary MR + HFrEF, EF 20–50%, EROA 1.2–5.1 cm², on optimal GDMT
  • Intervention: MitraClip vs. medical therapy alone
  • Result: benefit — MitraClip reduced hospitalizations for HF and improved symptoms; mortality trend favored clip but not statistically significant
  • Inference: careful patient selection (optimal GDMT first, EROA in the range, EF not too low) → clip beneficial MITRA-FR (2018, Obadia et al.):
  • Population: secondary MR, EF 15–40%, EROA >1.2 cm² (less stringent GDMT optimization requirement in entry; some patients on non-optimal therapy)
  • Intervention: MitraClip vs. medical therapy
  • Result: neutral — no difference in mortality or HF hospitalization at 1 year
  • Inference: clip not universally beneficial; selection bias toward sicker, less-optimized population Clinical lessons:
  • COAPT inclusion criteria (optimized GDMT, EROA 1.2–5.1 cm², EF 20–50%) associated with clip benefit
  • MITRA-FR's neutral result may reflect less-optimized population (higher mortality, lower functional capacity)
  • Current practice: TEER candidate must have truly optimized GDMT first; EROA in COAPT range; EF not severely depressed (<20%)
Papillary muscle rupture post-MI (expandable) Acute post-infarction complication, often fatal without urgent intervention. Anatomy and pathology:
  • Posterolateral papillary muscle (single blood supply from RCA) > anterolateral papillary muscle (dual supply from LAD + LCx)
  • Rupture occurs 2–7 days post-MI as necrotic tissue loses structural integrity
  • Partial rupture: one or more heads; may present as flail leaflet, sudden worsening of MR
  • Complete rupture: entire muscle detaches; sudden massive regurgitation → cardiogenic shock, pulmonary edema Presentation:
  • Acute decompensation in post-MI patient (cardiogenic shock, flash pulmonary edema)
  • New loud, late systolic or holosystolic murmur (may be soft in low output state)
  • Hemodynamically unstable; often in or near cardiogenic shock
  • Median survival without surgery: 24 hours Diagnosis:
  • TTE: flail leaflet (leaflet tip below annular plane), marked regurgitation, dilated LA, hyperdynamic LV
  • TEE: localizes flail scallop, assesses feasibility of repair vs. replacement
  • Consider concomitant mechanical complications (VSD, free wall rupture) Management — emergent OR:
  • Stabilization: vasodilation (nitroprusside), IABP (afterload reduction), inotropes if needed (dobutamine, milrinone)
  • Early surgical intervention is the only definitive management — mortality without surgery >80%; with surgery ~20–40% despite intervention
  • Repair vs. replacement decided intra-operatively based on leaflet extent and surgeon expertise
  • ECMO standby if patient too unstable for transport or if OR delay expected
Murmur dynamics and bedside assessment (expandable) Holosystolic (pansystolic) murmur of MR:
  • Begins with S1, continues throughout systole, may obscure A2
  • Best heard at apex; radiates to left axilla
  • High-pitched, blowing quality
  • Intensity increases with hand-grip (increases afterload) or sitting forward (brings apex closer to chest wall)
  • Decreases with amyl nitrite or Valsalva (decreases afterload) Late systolic (mid-to-late systolic) murmur:
  • Suggests prolapse, not hemodynamically severe MR
  • Begins mid-systole, ends before or at A2
  • May be preceded by midsystolic click (chordal insertion point)
  • Decreases with hand-grip, increases with Valsalva (opposite of holosystolic) Atrial fibrillation:
  • Irregular pulse on palpation
  • Auscultated rate > radial pulse rate (pulse deficit from irregular rhythm)
  • Variable intensity of S1 (changing ventricular filling time) Low output state (acute severe MR, cardiogenic shock):
  • Murmur may become very soft or inaudible due to low flow
  • Presence of quiet murmur in hypotensive patient does not exclude severe MR
  • Always get echo; don't rely on murmur intensity

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Pattern recognition for proficient/expert clinicians. Watch for these in compensated primary or secondary MR.

  • Increasing dyspnea on exertion or new orthopnea — MR decompensating; LV or LA struggling to adapt
  • New or worsening AF — loss of atrial kick + MR = rapid pulmonary congestion; rhythm control urgently needed
  • Weight gain > 2–3 lb in 24 h — fluid retention; compensatory mechanisms failing
  • Declining exercise tolerance (can walk shorter distances) — marker of LV dysfunction advancing; time for surgical evaluation in primary MR
  • New symptoms in a patient deemed "asymptomatic" at last echo — ask directly about exertional dyspnea, PND, orthopnea; patient often downplays symptoms
  • BP rising (especially in secondary MR) — afterload increasing; may worsen regurgitant fraction; optimized GDMT urgently needed
  • Echo showing rapid LA enlargement (serial TTE) — LA compliance exhausted; atrial stretch and AF risk rising
  • Troponin elevation in post-MI setting + new murmur — papillary muscle rupture until proved otherwise; emergent echo + surgery team
  • Normal-size LA in acute severe MR — high-risk sign — no compliance buffer; flash pulmonary edema likely imminent (unlike chronic MR where LA dilates)
  • Recurrent hospitalization for HF despite "optimized" GDMT in secondary MR — confirm GDMT truly at max doses; time for TEER/surgery evaluation
  • Declining EF on serial TTE in primary MR — irreversible LV remodeling advancing; surgical repair becoming more urgent (window closing)

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Watchful waiting doesn't mean no follow-up. Asymptomatic severe primary MR requires TTE every 6–12 months. Many clinicians (and patients) assume "stable" = discharge and forget; LV dysfunction and AF can develop silently. Active surveillance is mandatory.

  2. Acute severe MR post-MI is a surgical emergency. Post-MI patient with acute pulmonary edema + new murmur = papillary muscle rupture until proved otherwise. Don't manage as routine HF exacerbation. Median survival without surgery: days.

  3. Partial vs. complete papillary muscle rupture. Partial (one head) may stabilize 24–48 h with IABP + vasodilation; complete rupture (entire muscle detaches) is instantly life-threatening. Either way, emergent OR is the only definitive therapy.

  4. Primary vs. secondary MR drives everything. Primary = repair when feasible (durable, avoids anticoagulation). Secondary = optimize GDMT first (may reverse), then TEER/surgery if symptoms persist. Confusing the two leads to wrong timing and wrong intervention.

  5. Post-repair SAM (systolic anterior motion) is predictable. Anterior leaflet can bow into LVOT post-repair if resection too aggressive. Presents as new systolic murmur, hemodynamic collapse, echo shows systolic cavity obliteration. Manage initially with beta-blockers, reduce inotropes, IV fluids (raise preload), cautious vasodilation. Persistent SAM = urgent re-operation. High-volume centers see this and manage proactively; smaller centers may miss it.

  6. Chronic MR patients have adapted hemodynamics. Grade 3–4 MR may be tolerated chronically.

    Don't be fooled by "stable" anatomy but worsening symptoms. LV dilation advancing, AF developing, annular dilation progressing — the body is decompensating. Escalate for surgery/TEER evaluation; don't wait for echo criteria to worsen.

  7. MR + AF = dangerous combination. Loss of atrial kick + loss of mitral coaptation = rapid pulmonary congestion. New AF in an MR patient requires emergent rate control and rhythm assessment. Don't treat as routine post-op AF if MR underlying; severity of decompensation may be out of proportion.

  8. "The leaflets look normal" (secondary MR). In functional MR, leaflets ARE normal — tissue is pristine. Echo shows normal scallops, normal thickness, no pathology. The problem is geometry: massive annulus + papillary muscle apical displacement = tethering. Teaching point: the valve itself isn't broken; the heart is too dilated.

  9. LA thrombus risk in chronic MR + AF. Very dilated LA (>60 mm) + AF = high clot risk. Ensure anticoagulation. Pre-op TEE mandatory for clot exclusion if surgery planned.

  10. Post-op AF after MV surgery: ~40–50% incidence. Much higher than CABG alone (20–30%). Have amiodarone protocol ready; magnesium repletion; rate control target 60–80 bpm. Many resolve within days of hospital discharge, but anticipate during POD 1–7.

  11. Functional MR improves with GDMT if caught early. EF >30% with secondary MR: LV remodeling reversal from ACE-I/ARB, beta-blockers, SGLT2i, aldosterone antagonist can reduce MR over 6–12 months. This argues for maximal medical optimization before offering surgery/TEER. Check EF at 3–6 months; may surprise you.

  12. COAPT inclusion criteria matter. MitraClip showed benefit in secondary MR if EF 20–50%, EROA 1.2–5.1 cm², optimized GDMT first. MITRA-FR (slightly less-optimized population) showed neutral results. Patient selection is everything; GDMT optimization is non-negotiable.

  13. Endocarditis + MR = vegetation risk. Vegetation erodes chordae → acute flail. Valve anatomy may preclude repair; replacement likely needed. Blood cultures before antibiotics; echo (TTE + TEE) for vegetations, abscess, perforation, other valve involvement.

  14. Eccentric jets underestimate severity. MVP creates eccentric jets (directed along wall, constrained). PISA often more accurate than vena contracta for eccentric MR. Don't dismiss MVP-related MR as "less severe" just because jet looks small on color flow.

  15. Repair rate depends on surgeon and center volume. High-volume centers (>100 mitral repairs/year) achieve >90% repair rate in degenerative MR. Lower-volume centers: ~70–80% repair, higher replacement rates. Patient outcome and durability differ; referral to high-volume center for primary MR repair is justified.

cards.title: Mitral Stenosis
cards.quickAnswer: Mitral stenosis narrows the mitral orifice, causing LA dilation, thrombus risk, and reactive pulmonary hypertension. Severe: MVA <1.0 cm². Rheumatic etiology dominates globally (rare in developed nations due to penicillin prophylaxis). AF in MS = warfarin only—DOACs contraindicated regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc in moderate-severe MS. Rate control (beta-blockers, diltiazem) + diuretics are bridge therapy. PMBV (Wilkins score ≤8, no LA thrombus, mild MR) or surgical MV replacement (rheumatic usually replacement, not repair; Wilkins >11) definitive. Pre-op watch-fors: AF with RVR is critical emergency; hemoptysis signals severe disease; maintain preload carefully.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
