AF in MS = warfarin only—DOACs contraindicated regardless of CHA₂DS₂-VASc in moderate-severe MS. Rate control (beta-blockers, diltiazem) + diuretics are bridge therapy.

PMBV (Wilkins score ≤8, no LA thrombus, mild MR) or surgical MV replacement (rheumatic usually replacement, not repair; Wilkins >11) definitive. Pre-op watch-fors: AF with RVR is critical emergency; hemoptysis signals severe disease; maintain preload carefully.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP Guideline (Joglar et al., 2024) → 2020 ACC/AHA Valvular Disease Guideline (Otto et al., 2021) → ESC 2021 → Nishimura et al. (2014) → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Kirklin et al. (2026)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, clinical relevance.

  • Definition: Progressive leaflet thickening, calcification, and commissural fusion narrow the mitral valve orifice, raising left atrial (LA) pressure and triggering reactive pulmonary hypertension. Blood flow obstruction from LA to LV increases from ~100 cm²/s at baseline to <100 cm²/s in severe disease.
  • Global epidemiology: Rheumatic mitral stenosis is the leading cause worldwide; endemic in developing nations and immigrant populations. Rare in developed nations since penicillin prophylaxis of acute rheumatic fever (ARF). US prevalence ~1% of valvular disease.
  • Degenerative calcific MS: increasingly recognized in older patients; annular calcification progressively limits leaflet mobility; often milder than rheumatic MS.
  • Congenital MS: rare (parachute mitral valve, supramitral ring, hypoplastic mitral valve).
  • Who this applies to: preoperative patients awaiting PMBV or MV replacement; patients with acute AF + MS; post-PMBV recovery patients. ICU nurses see this in hemodynamically unstable presentations and pre-intervention phases.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml: Novice + advanced beginner teaching — why MS develops and how it harms the patient.

sections.heading: Mechanism
sections.bodyHtml:
Progressive narrowing → LA pressure surge → backward propagation:

  • Normal mitral valve area (MVA) = 4–6 cm². Mild MS (MVA 1.5–2.0 cm²) develops silently; moderate MS (MVA 1.0–1.5 cm²) triggers dyspnea on exertion; severe MS (MVA <1.0 cm²) causes rest dyspnea and orthopnea.
  • LA pressure elevates from normal (<12 mmHg) to 20–30 mmHg in severe MS, transmitted backward to pulmonary veins and right heart.
  • Reactive pulmonary artery hypertension: elevated LA pressure → pulmonary venous HTN → RV pressure overload → progressive RV hypertrophy and eventual RV failure if MS not relieved.
  • LA dilation and AF: chronic pressure overload stretches the atrium, increasing ectopic triggers. Loss of normal sinus rhythm → loss of atrial kick, a critical 20–30% boost to LV filling in MS.

sections.heading: Hemoptysis mechanism
sections.bodyHtml: Dilated bronchial veins drain into an engorged pulmonary venous system. Chronic severe elevation of pulmonary venous pressure ruptures these thin-walled vessels → blood-tinged or frank hemoptysis. Pathognomonic for severe chronic MS when present; can be life-threatening (massive hemoptysis risk).

sections.heading: Thrombus risk
sections.bodyHtml: LA stasis + dilation + AF (especially AF) = LA thrombus in 10–20% of MS patients in normal sinus rhythm; much higher (up to 50%) with AF. Mechanism: slow flow in dilated LA appendage, lack of atrial contractility (AF), and endothelial injury from prolonged pressure elevation.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context & Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition — typical patient profile and at-bedside signs.

sections.heading: Typical presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Classic triad:

  1. Exertional dyspnea — most common initial symptom; triggered by exercise-induced increase in cardiac output demand, raising LA pressure acutely
  2. Orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (PND) — supine position drops preload transiently, but LA pressure remains elevated; fluid shifts from abdomen to lungs
  3. Hemoptysis — from bronchial vein rupture; pathognomonic for severe MS; any blood-tinged sputum in a dyspneic patient = suspect MS

sections.heading: Other clinical features
sections.bodyHtml:
• Palpitations and new-onset AF — often heralds symptomatic progression. New AF can precipitate acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock (loss of atrial kick + tachycardia drops LV filling and cardiac output precipitously).
  • Acute pulmonary edema — triggered by AF with rapid ventricular rate, infection, anemia, thyroid storm, or pregnancy
  • Syncope or presyncope — uncommon; suggests AF with RVR, severe MS limiting exercise CO, or concurrent aortic stenosis
  • Fatigue, exercise intolerance — limited cardiac output during exertion
  • Stroke or TIA — from LA thrombus embolism, especially with AF (high thromboembolic risk, 2–7% annually if AF + untreated MS)

sections.heading: Physical exam landmarks
sections.bodyHtml:
Finding Mechanism & Implication
Diastolic rumble at apex (best in left lateral decubitus, bell of stethoscope) Blood acceleration across stenotic orifice; low-pitched, mid-to-late diastolic sound; increases with patient in left lateral position
Opening snap (OS) — early diastolic (0.04–0.1 sec after A2) Indicates pliable valve leaflets; absent in very calcific, immobile MS; high-pitched, heard best at left sternal border
Loud S1 (accentuated mitral closure) Closing of mitral valve against elevated LA pressure; best heard at apex
Decreased A2–OS interval Correlates with severity: wider interval = less severe; very short interval = very severe MS (high LA pressure closes the valve sooner)
Loud P2 (pulmonary component of S2) Indicates pulmonary hypertension present
RV heave (left parasternal lift) RV hypertrophy/dilation from chronic RV pressure overload
Atrial fibrillation on palpation Irregular, often rapid; loss of atrial kick
Signs of RV failure (late) JVD, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly if far advanced

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / Gather Information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Information-gathering only; no actions.

  • Baseline vital signs: HR (note if irregular), BP (postural if feasible), respiratory rate, temperature, SpO₂ on current oxygen
  • Dyspnea assessment: exertional vs. rest; orthopnea present; PND history; hemoptysis (even minor)
  • Cardiac exam: auscultate for diastolic rumble, opening snap, loud S1, presence of murmurs; palpate apical impulse; assess for RV heave; check for arrhythmia on palpation
  • Lung exam: crackles (pulmonary edema), wheezing (cardiac asthma), signs of consolidation if hemoptysis
  • Volume assessment: JVD, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, daily weight trends
  • Neurologic screening: any focal deficits (stroke risk from LA thrombus)
  • Recent echo findings: MVA, mean gradient, PA systolic pressure, LA size, LA thrombus on TEE, Wilkins score if available, LV function, associated lesions (MR, AS, TR)
  • EKG review: AF present? LA enlargement (P wave >0.12 sec)? RVH pattern?
  • Labs: most recent hemoglobin, creatinine, INR (if on warfarin), troponin, BNP/NT-proBNP
  • Medications: current rate-control agents, anticoagulation, diuretics; any recent beta-blocker or rate-control dose changes
  • Pre-op context: is this patient pre-PMBV or pre-MV replacement? When is intervention planned?

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: No Stable/Unstable fork for diagnosis cards. Subsections address medical bridging, intervention decision, and post-intervention surveillance.

sections.heading: 5A. Medical Management (Bridge Therapy, Not Definitive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Rate control in AF — critical foundation:

MS patients are exquisitely preload-dependent. Atrial kick contributes 20–30% of LV filling in MS; loss of atrial kick + tachycardia drops cardiac output catastrophically. Target HR 60–80 bpm.

Drug Dose & Notes
Metoprolol (IV) 5 mg over 2 min, may repeat q5min × 3. First-line if concurrent CAD. Caution in bronchospasm or decompensated HF.
Diltiazem (IV bolus) 0.25 mg/kg over 2 min. Preferred for COPD; watch for bradycardia + hypotension.
Diltiazem (drip) 5–15 mg/h titrated to HR. Non-dihydropyridine CCB; negative inotrope; avoid in reduced-EF HF.
Digoxin 0.25–0.5 mg IV, then 0.125–0.25 mg PO daily. Second-line if beta-blocker/CCB contraindicated or refractory AF. Slower onset.

Diuretics — judicious use:

Pulmonary congestion is common, but over-diuresis drops preload → syncope and hemodynamic collapse in MS. Start conservatively; daily weights + I/O tracking essential.

  • IV furosemide 20–40 mg IV push, then continuous drip (2–5 mg/h) titrated to urine output and clinical congestion
  • Target net negative 500–1000 mL/day in decompensated state; adjust based on response
  • Monitor: K⁺, Mg²⁺, Cr; replete K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 (electrolytes are critical for AF stability)

Oxygen therapy:

Supplemental O₂ for SpO₂ <92% or active pulmonary edema.

Avoid:

  • Nitrates, vasodilators (drop preload, worsen CO in MS)
  • High-dose beta-blockers if hypotensive
  • Negative inotropes
  • Tachycardia-inducing agents (theophylline, some bronchodilators)

sections.heading: 5B. Percutaneous Mitral Balloon Valvotomy (PMBV)
sections.bodyHtml:
Indication: Symptomatic moderate-to-severe MS with favorable valve morphology (Wilkins ≤8) and absence of LA thrombus on TEE.

Morphologic selection criteria:

Wilkins Score PMBV Suitability
≤8 Excellent/favorable — proceed with PMBV
9–11 Intermediate — attempt PMBV but lower success rate (~50–70%)
>11 Poor — surgical MV replacement recommended

Wilkins score components (0–4 scale each; max 16):

  1. Leaflet mobility: 0 = normal, 4 = immobile
  2. Leaflet thickening: 0 = normal (<5 mm), 4 = very thick (>8–10 mm)
  3. Leaflet calcification: 0 = none, 4 = extensive
  4. Subvalvular apparatus thickening: 0 = none, 4 = extensive thickening

Procedure: Transseptal catheterization; balloon inflated to split fused commissures; fluoroscopic guidance.

Success rate: 60–90% depending on Wilkins score; more favorable in younger patients, female sex, rheumatic (vs. degenerative) morphology.

Post-PMBV watch-fors:

  • Restenosis: 5–10% per year; some patients return for redo PMBV or surgical replacement years later
  • Acute severe MR: balloon inflation can tear leaflets or rupture chordae; new holosystolic murmur + pulmonary edema = emergency
  • Tamponade: rare but possible from transseptal puncture
  • Thromboembolic events: despite anticoagulation
  • Stroke from dislodged LA thrombus if TEE screening inadequate

sections.heading: 5C. Surgical Mitral Valve Replacement
sections.bodyHtml:
Indication: Symptomatic MS with unfavorable morphology (Wilkins >11), LA thrombus, failed PMBV, severe concomitant MR, or contraindications to percutaneous approach.

Key principle — rheumatic MS usually requires replacement, not repair:

  • Rheumatic leaflets are thickened, fused, and calcified; repair success rates are poor (~10–20%)
  • Degenerative MS may be amenable to commissurotomy or limited repair; rheumatic disease warrants replacement

Valve prosthesis options:

Prosthesis Advantages Disadvantages
Bioprosthesis (tissue valve) No lifelong anticoagulation (unless AF present); lower thrombotic risk Lifespan 10–15 years; structural deterioration; reoperation risk in young patients
Mechanical valve Durable; indefinite lifespan; lower reoperation risk Lifelong warfarin required; INR 2.5–3.5 if MS replacement + AF; thrombosis risk if underdosed; bleeding risk

Post-op complications (general):

  • Prosthetic valve thrombosis (mechanical > bio)
  • Pannus ingrowth (late mechanical failure)
  • Infective endocarditis
  • Bleeding (if warfarin)
  • Residual stenosis (technical issue)
  • New MR (surgical error or valve-related)

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
Critical situations requiring immediate escalation:

Situation Call SBAR Frame
AF with RVR (HR >120) + hypotension or altered mental status STAT—Code team if unstable S: MS patient with new rapid AF; B: baseline MS, now HR [X], BP [Y], altered; A: acute decompensation; R: need STAT IV rate control ± cardioversion
Hemoptysis (any amount) STAT—Attending/fellow + ICU team S: MS patient with hemoptysis; B: severe MS (MVA [X]); A: monitor for massive hemoptysis; R: suction ready, continuous monitoring, transfusion standby
Acute pulmonary edema (SpO₂ <88% despite supplemental O₂, frothy sputum) STAT—Attending S: MS patient with acute pulmonary edema; B: baseline MVA [X], now SpO₂ [Y], RR [Z]; A: likely AF trigger or inadequate diuresis; R: IV diuretics, oxygen, consider CPAP, rate control
Syncope or severe hypotension (SBP <80) STAT—Attending S: MS patient with syncope/shock; B: baseline MS, HR [X], BP [Y]; A: cardiogenic shock from AF or volume loss; R: IV access, fluid bolus cautiously, pressor consideration
New focal neuro deficit STROKE TEAM S: MS + possible stroke; B: AF + LA thrombus risk; A: focal deficit [describe]; R: stat CT head, neurology consult, hold diuretics
Pre-op patient with uncontrolled AF before intervention Attending + CT surgery S: Pre-PMBV/replacement patient with new uncontrolled AF; B: Wilkins [X], LA thrombus status [checked/pending]; A: rate control failing; R: consider IV amiodarone or early intervention

SBAR general template for escalation:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], pre-op s/p [PMBV date if applicable or pre-PMBV awaiting intervention]." B: "Patient has mitral stenosis (MVA [value] cm², mean gradient [value] mmHg, Wilkins [score] if available). Current rhythm: [NSR / AF]. HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. Labs: K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value], INR [value if anticoagulated]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Chief complaint — hemoptysis, new AF, worsening dyspnea, hemodynamic instability]. [Meds on board and recent interventions]." R: "Requesting [rate control orders / STAT echo / cardiology consult / imaging for stroke rule-out / anticoagulation adjustment / earlier intervention timeline]."

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Progressive-disclosure expandables for expert skim.

Pathophysiology detail: Pressure half-time (PHT) and MVA calculation Pressure half-time (PHT) is the time (in milliseconds) for the mitral gradient to decay to half its initial value during early diastole. It is the most reliable measure of MS severity because it is less load-dependent than mean gradient (which varies with HR and CO). - Formula: MVA (cm²) = 220 / PHT (milliseconds)
  • Normal: PHT 25–40 ms; MVA 4–6 cm²
  • Severe MS: PHT >150 ms; MVA <1.0 cm²
  • Why PHT matters: After PMBV or with acute volume changes, mean gradient can appear falsely normal if CO drops; PHT remains stable.
  • Echo measurement: Doppler across mitral valve during early diastole; measure slope of pressure decay Rheumatic vs. degenerative MS (echocardiographic pearls):
    • Rheumatic: leaflet thickening (>3 mm at tip), restricted motion, commissural fusion, subvalvular disease (chordal thickening), calcification along leaflet closure line
    • Degenerative calcific: annular calcification, leaflet calcification (not commissural fusion), normal leaflet thickness, minimal subvalvular disease, no prior AF
INVICTUS Trial and DOAC contraindication in MS INVICTUS HF trial (2019): randomized 1001 patients with AF and moderate-to-severe valvular disease (including 174 with moderate-severe MS, but MS represented minority) to apixaban vs. warfarin. Result: warfarin superior to apixaban in preventing stroke/systemic embolism in valvular AF, particularly in moderate-severe MS subgroup. Why DOACs fail in MS:
  1. Altered hemodynamics: stenotic mitral valve restricts blood flow across the orifice; DOAC anticoagulation may be inadequate due to regional flow variations and LA stasis
  2. High thromboembolic risk: MS + AF = 2–7% annual stroke rate; historically managed by warfarin; DOACs not powered for this risk profile
  3. Guideline stance (ACC/AHA 2020, ESC 2021): DOACs contraindicated in moderate-severe MS (MVA ≤1.5 cm²); mild MS (MVA >1.5) without AF may tolerate DOAC, but warfarin is safest Clinical pearl: Mild MS (MVA >1.5 cm²) + AF is technically DOAC-eligible per guidelines, but warfarin remains standard of care for any rheumatic valve disease because rheumatic AF is a different pathophysiology than non-valvular AF.
Wilkins score detailed breakdown and clinical application Leaflet mobility (0–4):
  • 0 = normal, freely mobile
  • 1 = mild restriction
  • 2 = moderate restriction, leaflet tips move, bases fixed
  • 3 = severe restriction, leaflet tips barely move
  • 4 = immobile, no diastolic opening Leaflet thickening (0–4):
  • 0 = normal (≤5 mm)
  • 1 = mild (5–8 mm)
  • 2 = moderate (8–10 mm)
  • 3 = severe (>10 mm)
  • 4 = very severe (>10 mm, entire leaflet thick) Leaflet calcification (0–4):
  • 0 = none
  • 1 = single area of echogenicity
  • 2 = scattered echogenicity in leaflet tissue
  • 3 = extensive echogenicity in most of leaflet
  • 4 = dense calcification, leaflet is calcified mass Subvalvular apparatus thickening (0–4):
  • 0 = none
  • 1 = minimal thickening of tips
  • 2 = thickening to mid-portion of chords
  • 3 = thickening to distal third of chords
  • 4 = extensive thickening extending to papillary muscles Interpretation:
    • Score ≤8 = PMBV favorable (>80% success)
    • Score 9–11 = PMBV intermediate (50–70% success)
    • Score >11 = PMBV poor; surgical replacement recommended Clinical context: Young, rheumatic patients (especially female, pre-childbearing age) with Wilkins ≤8 are ideal PMBV candidates. Older, calcific MS often has Wilkins >11 and requires surgery.
Pregnancy and mitral stenosis — high-risk scenario Pregnancy increases cardiac output demand ~50% over gestation; severe MS + pregnancy = life-threatening:
  • Normal pregnancy increases CO by 1.5 L/min (30–50% increase) progressively through third trimester
  • In severe MS (MVA <1.0), LA can no longer accommodate increased inflow → acute LA pressure surge → pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, fetal loss
  • Peripartum period is highest risk: labor + delivery cause massive volume shifts and sympathetic surge Counseling points for childbearing-age women with moderate-severe MS:
  • Preconception intervention (PMBV or MV replacement) is strongly recommended if MVA <1.5 cm²
  • If already pregnant with moderate-severe MS, early PMBV (second trimester) is safer than surgery
  • Mechanical MV + warfarin throughout pregnancy is acceptable if replacement unavoidable (warfarin teratogenic risk low in second/third trimester)
  • Close obstetric + cardiology co-management throughout pregnancy, labor, delivery
  • Delivery (vaginal or cesarean) in hospital with cardiothoracic surgery backup Data: maternal mortality 1–4% if severe MS unmanaged during pregnancy; fetal loss ~10–15%.
Rheumatic heart disease epidemiology and secondary prophylaxis Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) → rheumatic heart disease (RHD): ARF is a postinfectious inflammatory response to group A streptococcal pharyngitis, occurring 2–3 weeks after infection. Mimics autoimmune disease; affects joints, heart, CNS, skin. Rates vary:
  • Developed nations: <1% (due to penicillin prophylaxis of strep throat)
  • Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Pacific islands: 3–10 per 1000 schoolchildren
  • Cumulative lifetime risk of RHD in endemic areas: 30–50 per 1000 Cardiac sequelae of RHD:
    • ~50% of ARF patients develop RHD (subclinical to severe)
    • Mitral valve most affected (80%); aortic (30%); tricuspid (10%); pulmonary (rare)
    • Repeated strep infections → cumulative valve damage → progressive stenosis + regurgitation
    • Valve calcification progresses over decades Secondary prophylaxis (streptococcal prophylaxis in RHD patients):
    • Benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM q4weeks (standard) or
    • Amoxicillin 250 mg PO BID (if IM allergic)
    • Duration: until age 40 if mild RHD + no carditis history; lifelong if severe RHD or recurrent carditis
    • Goal: prevent further strep infections and slow RHD progression Endocarditis prophylaxis (post-prosthetic valve):
    • Antibiotic premedication for dental work, GI/GU procedures
    • Amoxicillin 2 g PO 1 h before procedure (dental)
    • Different from secondary streptococcal prophylaxis
Warfarin vs DOAC in rheumatic AF — clinical rationale and INR targets Warfarin mechanism:
  • Inhibits vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X)
  • Delayed onset (~5–7 days); requires bridging with LMWH or UFH if acute intervention needed
  • Monitored by INR (International Normalized Ratio); narrow therapeutic window
  • INR 2–3 for most AF indications; INR 2.5–3.5 for mechanical MV or MS + mechanical MV DOAC limitations in MS:
  • Not tested in moderate-severe MS: INVICTUS, ARISTOTLE, RE-LY, ENGAGE trials enrolled <5% MS patients; conclusions drawn from non-valvular AF
  • Flow-dependent clearance: DOACs (Factor Xa inhibitors like apixaban, rivaroxaban; direct thrombin inhibitor dabigatran) are renally cleared. Stenotic valve may alter drug absorption/clearance in unpredictable ways.
  • Regional flow stasis: LA appendage stasis in MS + AF may not be adequately anticoagulated by lower DOAC levels INR targets in MS + AF:
  • Warfarin alone (AF + MS): INR 2–3
  • Warfarin + mechanical MV: INR 2.5–3.5 (higher intensity for mechanical valve thrombosis risk)
  • Warfarin + bioprosthesis + AF: INR 2–3 (bioprosthesis has lower intrinsic thrombosis risk than mechanical) Patient counseling:
  • "Coumadin (warfarin) works best in your condition. The dose is guided by blood tests (INR) we check regularly. If you miss doses, your blood can clot. If you miss doses on the other end, you bleed. Consistency is key."
  • "Vitamin K in leafy greens affects warfarin; keep intake steady. Alcohol, some antibiotics, NSAIDs can interact."
  • "Never skip doses. If you forget, take it the next day; don't double up."
Heart-lung interactions in severe MS + pulmonary hypertension RV-LV interdependence in MS + pulmonary HTN: Severe MS → LA pressure backup → pulmonary venous HTN → RV pressure overload. If PA systolic >80–100 mmHg:
  • RV hypertrophies but becomes stiff (reduced compliance)
  • RV systolic pressure can exceed LV due to fixed mitral stenosis; RV competes with LV for space in pericardium (ventricular interdependence)
  • Septal shift → decreased LV filling from pericardial constraint
  • Net effect: pulmonary HTN from MS can be severe and contribute substantially to dyspnea, RV failure Post-intervention changes:
    • After PMBV or MV replacement, PA pressures often fall, but RV remodeling takes weeks to months
    • Acute afterload reduction may paradoxically cause RV dilatation if RV has been chronically hypertrophied and now loses its preload stimulus
    • Monitor for RV failure post-intervention; inotropic support may be needed temporarily Clinical pearl: A patient with MS + severe pulmonary HTN (PA systolic >80 mmHg) may appear "sicker" than MVA alone predicts because of RV involvement and systemic venous congestion.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these in patients initially stable.

  • Progressive exertional dyspnea over days — may herald hemodynamic decompensation or new AF paroxysms
  • Palpitations or irregular rhythm on palpation — new AF; escalate immediately; high risk for acute pulmonary edema
  • Increasing orthopnea or PND — rising LA pressure; may need diuretic adjustment or expedited intervention
  • Any hemoptysis (even minor) — sign of severe chronic disease; monitor for massive bleed
  • Declining SpO₂ trend — pulmonary edema or pulmonary HTN progression
  • Syncope or presyncope episode — AF with RVR, cardiogenic shock, or embolic event (stroke)
  • Sudden onset ankle or calf swelling — RV decompensation or thromboembolic event
  • Mental status change — hypoxia, hypotension, or stroke from embolism
  • Worsening renal function (creatinine rising) — cardiorenal syndrome from chronically elevated venous pressure
  • Persistent tachycardia despite beta-blockers — rate-control failure; may signal worsening AF burden or inadequate dosing
  • New or loud cardiac murmur not present before — acute MR (if post-PMBV) or new secondary tricuspid regurgitation from RV dilatation
  • Frothy sputum or pink sputum — acute pulmonary edema; STAT escalation

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Rheumatic MS + AF = warfarin only, no exceptions for moderate-to-severe MS. This is the #1 prescribing error. INVICTUS proved warfarin superior. DO NOT default to apixaban or dabigatran. Only mild MS (MVA >1.5 cm²) without additional risk factors may be DOAC-eligible; rheumatic etiology itself warrants warfarin caution. Verify anticoagulation order on every chart review.

  2. Pregnant MS patient is high-risk; PMBV preferred over surgery if intervention needed. Warfarin is teratogenic (bone, CNS) in first trimester; mechanical MV requires warfarin lifelong. PMBV is safest for pregnant women with severe MS if anatomy favorable. Preconception counseling essential for childbearing-age women with moderate-severe MS.

  3. Pressure half-time (PHT) is the most load-independent severity measure. Mean gradient varies with heart rate, cardiac output, and diastolic filling period. PHT = 220 / MVA; stable even when CO fluctuates. If MVA looks discordant with clinical severity, check PHT.

  4. Wilkins score determines PMBV candidacy and success rate. Score ≤8 = favorable (>80% success); score 9–11 = intermediate (50–70%); score >11 = poor, surgical replacement recommended. Nurses don't score, but knowing this helps contextualize the pre-op discussion with patients.

  5. AF onset in MS often heralds symptomatic progression. New AF can precipitate acute pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, or stroke. This is not routine POAF; it is a critical event in an MS patient. STAT escalation warranted.

  6. LA thrombus is common and silent; TEE is mandatory before any cardioversion or intervention. 10–20% of MS patients in normal sinus rhythm have LA thrombus on TEE; much higher with AF. Missing thrombus before cardioversion → stroke risk. Non-negotiable: "Has TEE ruled out LA thrombus?" must be answered before DCCV or elective cardioversion.

  7. Severe pulmonary HTN + MS creates bidirectional hemodynamic stress. RV is now afterload-stressed; left atrium is preload-constrained. The right and left hearts compete for space in the pericardium (interdependence). RV may require inotropic support post-PMBV if it has been hypertrophied for years.

  8. Rate control and preload matter more in MS than in most cardiac conditions. MS patients lose 20–30% of LV filling when AF develops (loss of atrial kick). Slow the rate first (target 60–80 bpm if possible) BEFORE you try to convert rhythm. Adequate preload is critical; over-diuresis → syncope.

  9. Pacing contraindicated if MS still severe. Dual-chamber pacemakers can be placed, but pacing-induced tachycardia worsens mitral inflow obstruction in severe MS. Consider only if patient is post-intervention or MS is mild.

  10. Diastolic rumble is your bedside diagnosis. No need to wait for echo if you hear the rumble + opening snap in a dyspneic patient. Communicate to the team: "Diastolic rumble at apex, opening snap present — concern for MS."

  11. Hemoptysis in MS is severe disease. Unlike hemoptysis from bronchitis or GERD, hemoptysis in MS signals chronic elevated pulmonary venous pressure with bronchial vein rupture. Bleeding can be massive. Keep suction ready, continuous monitoring, and escalate immediately.

  12. Rheumatic MS is the leading valve disease globally, not the US. Keck serves international patients and immigrants. A 45-year-old from Southeast Asia or sub-Saharan Africa presenting with dyspnea + murmur has high pre-test probability of rheumatic MS. Always ask: "Have you ever been told you have a heart murmur? Any rheumatic fever as a child? Any time in developing countries?"

  13. AF with RVR in MS = emergency, not routine. Loss of atrial kick + HR 120 drops cardiac output 40%+ in MS. Acute pulmonary edema, shock, syncope can result within hours. STAT escalation, IV rate control or DCCV standby.

  14. PMBV success is score-dependent and not a permanent cure. Wilkins ≤8 gives ~80% success, but restenosis occurs in 5–10% per year. Some patients return for redo PMBV or eventually need surgical replacement. Counsel: "This balloon procedure can buy you years of symptom relief, but may not be your last intervention."

  15. Rheumatic heart disease is preventable; secondary prophylaxis matters. MS patients with history of acute rheumatic fever should be on long-term penicillin prophylaxis (benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units IM q4weeks) to prevent recurrent strep infections and slow valve degeneration. Verify compliance; if missed doses, counsel on importance.

cards.title: Mitral Valve Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: Mitral valve repair (preferred in >90% of experienced centers) or replacement (bioprosthetic vs mechanical) via sternotomy or robotic approach; CPB required. POD 0 ICU targets: SBP 110–140, sinus rhythm preferred, watch for SAM if repair (low CO + hypotension → echo first). POAF ~40–50% incidence (highest cardiac surgery rate); peaks POD 2–3 → rapid rate/rhythm assessment. Stroke risk 3–8% (AF + long CPB + LA thrombus). SAM post-repair flips rules: increase volume + afterload, NO vasodilators/inotropes. Anticoagulation by prosthesis: repair/bio INR 2.0–3.0 × 3 months (repair) or lifelong (bio + AF); mechanical INR 2.5–3.5 lifelong, warfarin only. RV failure from chronic pulmonary hypertension — preload-dependent, accept CVP 12–15, avoid over-diuresis. Expected LOS: ICU 1–2 days; discharge POD 5–8 (uncomplicated repair) or POD 7–10+ (replacement, RV dysfunction, complications).
