sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to, when it applies.

  • Definition: Surgical repair (annuloplasty ring, leaflet resection, chord insertion) or replacement (bioprosthetic or mechanical prosthesis) of the mitral valve via sternotomy or minimally invasive thoracotomy, requiring cardiopulmonary bypass and transseptal atriotomy.
  • Epidemiology: Mitral regurgitation (MR) is the most common valve lesion in developed countries; mitral stenosis (MS) predominates in endemic rheumatic heart disease regions. Repair is preferred in skilled centers (>90% success rate) when leaflet anatomy permits.
  • Who this applies to: Adult patients with symptomatic or asymptomatic MR (severe, EF <60% or LA/LV dilatation on echo) or MS ± regurgitation meeting ACC/AHA criteria for surgery. Age and prosthesis choice (bioprosthetic vs mechanical) drive post-op anticoagulation strategy.
  • Why it matters: Repair restores LV geometry and preserves contractile reserve; replacement offers durability but introduces prosthesis-specific risks (thrombosis, endocarditis, anticoagulation burden). POAF is nearly expected (40–50%); stroke risk is the highest among cardiac surgeries.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Mitral valve pathophysiology drives surgical urgency and post-op complications:

Mitral Regurgitation (MR):

  • Chronic: Low afterload → eccentric LV hypertrophy, volume overload. LA enlarges. Repair "unloads" the LV dramatically (see Section 3, LV unloading phenomenon); acute contractility drop post-op is expected.
  • Ischemic MR: papillary muscle dysfunction or annular dilatation; repair success depends on LV geometry restoration.

Mitral Stenosis (MS): - Rheumatic leaflet thickening, commissural fusion. High left atrial (LA) afterload → pulmonary hypertension, RV strain, AF. Repair (balloon mitral valvulotomy) rarely offered intraoperatively; replacement standard.

Post-operative Cascade:

  • CPB-induced inflammation from cannulation, atriotomy, pericardial irritation → atrial irritability (POAF onset POD 2–3).
  • RV afterload mismatch: Chronic MR → PA hypertension; RV hypertrophies but remains vulnerable post-op. Remodels slowly (weeks–months).
  • LA thrombus risk: Atrial surgery + manipulation + AF → clot formation within hours of AF onset.
  • AV node proximity: Posterolateral mitral annulus is adjacent to AV node; large rings or aggressive suturing risk conduction injury (1–5% CHB).

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Trigger
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like and when mitral valve surgery is indicated.

Surgical Indication — Symptomatic or Asymptomatic:

MR Severity Symptoms Echo Criteria Surgical Consideration
Severe MR Dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, fatigue, palpitations (AF common) EF ≥60%, LA <55 mm, Vmax <4 m/s Surgery generally offered (class IIa if EF 50–60%, LA dilatation)
Severe MR None (asymptomatic) EF <60% OR LA ≥55 mm OR LV end-systolic diameter >40 mm Surgery offered to prevent LV dysfunction (class I guideline)
Severe MR AF or pulmonary hypertension Any EF Surgery often performed; adds urgency
Moderate-severe MR Persistent symptoms despite medical therapy As above Surgery considered per patient preference + anatomy
Severe MS Dyspnea, orthopnea, AF, RV failure, syncope Mitral area <1.0 cm², mean gradient >10 mmHg, PAP > 50 mmHg systolic Surgery (replacement) nearly always offered

Timing of Presentation:

  • Acute (ruptured chordae tendineae, post-MI papillary muscle rupture): emergent surgery same-day or overnight.
  • Chronic compensated: elective scheduling; may wait weeks–months for surgical slot.
  • Decompensated (flash pulmonary edema, AF with RVR, cardiogenic shock): urgent admission, optimize medically, schedule within days.

Prevalence: ~2.5 million mitral valve operations globally per year; mitral repair preferred in North America/Europe (>80% of centers), mechanical replacement more common in developing countries. POAF incidence 30–50%; stroke 3–8% (see Section 9 Pitfalls for prevention).

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure observation; no interventions. Target: 2 minutes at bedside on arrival to ICU.

Hemodynamic Assessment (continuous monitoring):

  • Heart rate + rhythm: Sinus preferred; rate 60–90 bpm. Irregular rhythm → 12-lead ECG to confirm AF or ectopy.
  • Systolic blood pressure: Target 110–140 mmHg (avoid >140 — increases LV strain, may worsen SAM if repair).
  • Mean arterial pressure (MAP): Target 60–70 mmHg; use as secondary guide if systolic variable.
  • Central venous pressure (CVP): 8–12 cmH₂O typical; elevated (>15) suggests RV dysfunction, tamponade, or fluid overload.
  • Pulmonary artery pressures (if available): Expect elevated systolic 40–60+ mmHg from chronic MR; remodels slowly over weeks.
  • Cardiac index (CI) or cardiac output (CO): Aim ≥2.2 L/min/m². Low CO + hypotension post-repair → suspect SAM (anterior leaflet prolapse into LVOT); echo FIRST before escalating.

Physical Exam (at arrival and q 4 h until stable):

  • Auscultation: New systolic murmur (repair mitral regurgitation, SAM), diastolic flow murmur (prosthetic valve normal finding). Muffled heart sounds suggest pericardial effusion/tamponade.
  • Perfusion: Capillary refill <2 sec (normal), skin temperature warm, urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h.
  • Lung bases: Bilateral rales common (CPB-related pulmonary edema); r/o large effusion (unilateral dullness, decreased breath sounds).
  • JVD/CVP correlation: Elevated JVD with elevated CVP suggests RV dysfunction or tamponade; JVD with normal CVP suggests superior vena cava obstruction (rare).
  • Leg exam: Swelling, calf tenderness (DVT; use caution in anticoagulated patients).

Laboratory Assessment (arrival, q 6 h × 24 h, then q daily until stable):

  • CBC: Hemoglobin 8–9.5 post-transfusion (target lower in ICU to minimize HTN); platelets trending up (nadir POD 1–2).
  • Coagulation: PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen. If on warfarin (mech MVR) or heparin bridge, trend toward goal.
  • Chemistry: K⁺ 4.0–5.0 (avoid hypokalemia — triggers arrhythmias + POAF); Mg²⁺ ≥1.5; creatinine baseline or trending down (watch for AKI, especially if CPB >120 min).
  • Liver function: AST/ALT baseline (elevated suggests hepatic congestion from RV failure); elevated bilirubin POD 3–5 common if large pleural effusion or hemolysis.
  • Troponin: Mild elevation POD 0–1 expected (CPB-induced); significant rise (>0.1 ng/mL) + low CO suggests myocardial injury or prosthetic thrombosis.
  • Lactate: Baseline <2; rising lactate + low urine output = poor perfusion, escalate.

Imaging at Arrival (if not done in OR):

  • Chest X-ray: Confirm placement of CTs (retrosternal + right pleural), endotracheal tube if intubated, rule out pneumothorax.
  • ECG: Baseline rhythm, PR interval, QRS duration. Post-repair AVR/right thoracotomy may show atrial pacing artifact (normal from epicardial wires).

Procedural Context (note in chart):

  • Type: repair vs bio vs mechanical replacement; approach (sternotomy vs robotic); concomitant procedures (MAZE, LAA ligation, CABG).
  • CPB time: >120 min increases AKI risk; >180 min increases POAF + stroke risk.
  • Surgeon notes: ring size, competency grade post-repair, anticipated special monitoring.

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: POD arc-based. No Stable/Unstable fork for surgery deep cards; instead, organized by phase of recovery. Escalation triggers detailed in Section 6.

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 — ICU (Hemodynamic Stabilization)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Rewarming, hemodynamic optimization, pain control, POAF/SAM screening, anticoagulation initiation.

1. Continuous monitoring & rewarming:

  • Core temperature goal 36.5–37.5°C (passive rewarming preferred; avoid active if possible due to hyperchloremic acidosis from CPB). Target arrival to ICU ~36°C; expect slow rewarming over 2–4 h.
  • Continuous cardiac monitor, arterial line q 1 h (MAP, HR trend). Pulse oximetry, end-tidal CO₂ if intubated.
  • Foley catheter → quantify urine output q 1 h (target ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; <0.3 mL/kg/h = oliguria, escalate).
  • Chest tube (CT) output q 1 h × 6 h, then q 4 h. CT >300 mL/h × 2 h or >1,000 mL first 6–12 h → coagulation labs STAT, surgeon notified.

2. Hemodynamic targets (POD 0):

Parameter Target Tolerance Escalation
SBP 110–140 mmHg Avoid >150 (LV strain, SAM worse); <100 (perfusion) >150 → vasodilator (cautious post-repair: r/o SAM first); <100 → fluid bolus 250 mL or vasopressor
MAP 60–70 mmHg ≥55 acceptable if SBP adequate <55 → escalate; assess CO, consider inotrope
HR 60–90 bpm sinus 50–110 acceptable if stable BP + urine output >110 → 12-lead ECG; if AF → see POAF card (§6 escalation)
CVP 8–12 cmH₂O Up to 15 acceptable if RV dysfunction (MR remodeling) >15 persistently → echo assess pericardial effusion, RV function; gentle diuresis if euvolemic/overloaded
CI/CO ≥2.2 L/min/m² ≥2.0 acceptable if normotensive + urine output adequate <2.0 + low BP → low-dose inotrope (dobutamine 2–3 mcg/kg/min or milrinone 0.25 mcg/kg/min); NEVER if SAM suspected — volume + phenylephrine instead
Urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h ≥0.3 mL/kg/h acceptable first 24 h <0.3 mL/kg/h → fluid bolus, check labs (K⁺, Cr, lactate), consider low-dose dopamine 2–3 mcg/kg/min if CI low

3. Initiate anticoagulation per prosthesis:

  • Repair (no AF): Heparin 80 units/kg bolus, then 18 units/kg/h infusion (goal aPTT 50–70 s) × 24–48 h; then discontinue.
  • Repair + POAF (if develops): Start heparin if not already; start warfarin load day 1–2 (5–10 mg, adjust per INR next AM); continue heparin bridge until INR 2.0–3.0 × 24 h.
  • Bioprosthetic MVR (no AF): Heparin × 24–48 h; warfarin load day 1 (5–10 mg evening), target INR 2.0–3.0 × 3 months, then ASA if no AF.
  • Mechanical MVR: Heparin × 24–48 h if hemostasis good; warfarin load evening of surgery (5–10 mg), target INR 2.5–3.5 lifelong. Continue heparin bridge (goal aPTT 50–70 s) until INR ≥2.5 × 24 h.
  • Special: If major bleeding post-op, defer anticoagulation until hemostasis achieved (surgeon-directed; see Section 6 escalation).

4. Pain control & sedation:

  • Intubated patients: Maintain moderate sedation (Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale [RASS] 0 to −1) with fentanyl 0.5–1 mcg/kg/h + midazolam 1–2 mg/h, titrate q 2–4 h. Extubation goal POD 0–1 if uncomplicated repair. Replace MVR may require longer support.
  • Extubated patients: Multimodal analgesia: acetaminophen 650 mg PO/IV q 6 h, opioid PO (oxycodone 5–10 mg q 4–6 h PRN) or IV (morphine 2–4 mg q 4 h PRN if unable to take PO), OR regional: epidural fentanyl/ropivacaine if not contraindicated by anticoag. Sternal pain usually requires strong opioids POD 0–1; intercostal nerve pain (robotic) may require gabapentin 100 mg TID starting POD 1.

5. Lung expansion & ventricular function screening:

  • Incentive spirometry: q 2 h while awake (goal ≥15 mL/kg); chest physiotherapy q 4 h.
  • Extubation readiness: If repair uncomplicated: assess breathing effort, TV >6 mL/kg, PEEP <5, SpO₂ >92% on FiO₂ <0.5, alert + cooperative. Extubate to nasal cannula POD 0 evening or POD 1 AM.
  • SAM screening (post-repair): If low CO (<2.0) + hypotension (<100 systolic) + elevated CVP + dyspnea → STAT transthoracic echo. Do NOT treat with vasodilators or inotropes until SAM ruled out. If SAM confirmed: see Section 5A management below (flip rules: volume + phenylephrine + beta-blockade).

6. Prepare for POAF (POD 1–3 onset likely):

  • Keep patient on continuous telemetry.
  • Ensure K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥1.5 per Electrolyte Replacement protocol (→ related Protocol card).
  • Have amiodarone bolus (150 mg IV over 10 min, may repeat) + drip (1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min) orders ready.
  • Have metoprolol (5 mg IV q 5 min × 3 if HR >110 + stable BP) or diltiazem (0.25 mg/kg IV bolus) readily available.

7. Epicardial pacing wires:

  • Verify A + V wires functioning: test capture + sensing at 10 mA; confirm proper positioning on ECG (pacing spike followed by QRS).
  • Set mode: typically DDD at 60 bpm backup; or AV sequential pacing at 80 bpm if bradycardia.
  • Document thresholds, settings in chart. Check q 4 h.

8. Drain management:

  • Monitor chest tube output q 1 h. Milk chest tubes q 2 h (gently; avoid aggressive stripping which can increase bleeding).
  • Assess for color: bright red ooze acceptable POD 0; pink/serous POD 1+. If chest tube output slows/stops → monitor for tamponade (rising CVP, falling CO, hypotension).
  • Consider removal criteria POD 1–2 if output <50 mL/8 h (per surgeon preference).

sections.heading: 5B. POD 1–3 — ICU → Stepdown (Mobilization, Extubation, POAF Onset Window)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Extubate if not already, initiate ambulation, watch for POAF (peak incidence POD 2–3), optimize electrolytes, transition off vasoactives.

1. Respiratory management & extubation:

  • Extubation POD 0–1 target: If repair uncomplicated, alert, able to protect airway, TV >6 mL/kg, PEEP <5, FiO₂ <0.5, SpO₂ >92%.
  • Post-extubation: Nasal cannula 2–3 L/min, SpO₂ target >94%. Aggressive IS (q 2 h), early ambulation (chair POD 0–1, walking POD 1–2 if hemodynamically stable).
  • Hypoxemia refractory to O₂: CXR assess for pleural effusion (common; bilateral if repair, right-predominant if robotic), atelectasis, pneumonia. Left-sided effusion post-repair expected (LIMA graft passage or serosal irritation); rarely requires thoracentesis unless large (>2 cm on CXR) + symptomatic.

2. Hemodynamic transition off vasoactives:

  • Goal: Wean vasopressors/inotropes by POD 1–2 if hemodynamically stable (CI ≥2.2, MAP ≥60, urine output ≥0.5 mL/kg/h, no signs of shock).
  • Wean protocol: Decrease dose by 25–50% q 2 h if parameters met; discontinue when at minimal dose (e.g., dopamine 2 mcg/kg/min, dobutamine 1 mcg/kg/min).
  • RV dysfunction (if present): May require longer inotropic support + inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) 10–20 ppm (gold standard for RV afterload reduction). See Section 9 Pitfalls for RV management.
  • Avoid diuretics POD 1–2 unless clearly hypervolemic (CXR pulmonary edema, elevated CVP >15 + rising lactate). RV is preload-dependent post-MR; premature diuresis risks RV failure.

3. POAF management — POD 1–3 onset window:

  • Vigilance: Continuous tele. If irregular rhythm on monitor → STAT 12-lead ECG.
  • Confirmation & stabilization: If AF confirmed on 12-lead:
  • Assess hemodynamics: SBP, CVP, urine output, mental status, perfusion.
  • Stable (SBP >90, alert, no chest pain, perfusing): start electrolyte repletion (K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0), notify provider for rate vs rhythm plan, start amiodarone bolus (150 mg IV over 10 min) → drip (1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min).
  • Unstable (SBP <90, altered mental status, pulmonary edema, severe dyspnea): STAT call APP/fellow, Rapid Response, prepare for synchronized DCCV (100 → 200 → 300 → 360 J biphasic per ACLS).
  • Anticoag initiation: If repair + new POAF → start heparin (if not already) + warfarin load (target INR 2.0–3.0). If mech MVR + AF → already on heparin bridge; trend INR toward 2.5–3.5 goal.
  • Refer to related Scenario: POAF card for detailed rate/rhythm strategy.

4. Anticoagulation optimization:

  • Warfarin INR checks: First INR on POD 1–2 AM (baseline post-load). Adjust dose per nomogram; recheck POD 3–4 AM, then daily until stable (goal ≥2 consecutive INRs in range).
  • Mechanical MVR critical: INR target 2.5–3.5 (NOT 2.0–3.0). Most common dosing error is defaulting to aortic valve targets. Write target clearly on discharge papers.
  • Heparin bridge: Continue until INR in goal range × 24 h, then discontinue heparin.
  • Common mistake: Starting warfarin + stopping heparin same day. Warfarin takes 3–5 days to reach goal INR; heparin bridge is essential for mechanical MVR (thrombosis risk if gap in anticoag).

5. Electrolyte repletion protocol (POD 1–3 ongoing):

  • Target K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0 to suppress POAF.
  • K⁺ replacement: 10–20 mEq/L in IV fluid or PO KCl 20–40 mEq daily (divided BID). Max 10 mEq/h peripheral line, faster via central line.
  • Mg²⁺ replacement: IV MgSO₄ 1–2 g in 50 mL NS over 15 min, repeat q 4–6 h PRN; or PO magnesium oxide 400 mg daily if tolerating diet.
  • Check labs q 12 h × 48 h after repletion, then q daily until stable.

6. Mobilization & PT/OT:

  • POD 1: Sit in chair 1–2 h, dangle legs.
  • POD 2–3: Ambulate halls with assist/PT. No lifting >5 lbs (sternal precautions).
  • Robotic approach: Mobilization faster; may walk POD 1 if pain controlled. Severe intercostal pain may slow mobilization — address with paravertebral block or gabapentin.

7. Wound assessment:

  • Sternotomy: Dry, non-erythematous, no drainage or dehiscence. Remove sutures POD 7–10 if using non-absorbable.
  • Robotic/mini-thoracotomy: Small incision(s) on right anterior/mid-axillary line; healing faster than sternotomy.
  • Leg incision (if LIMA graft or saphenous vein conduit): Dry, non-erythematous. Mild swelling common (lymphatic disruption); elevate leg if present.

8. Chest tube management:

  • Output trend: Should decrease POD 1–2 (from ~100 mL/h to 50 mL/h by POD 2–3).
  • Removal criteria: Output <50 mL/8 h on POD 1–2 (surgeon-dependent; some pull earlier, some wait POD 3–4). Do NOT leave CT in >4–5 days (infection risk).

9. Transition planning (late POD 2–3):

  • If stable on POD 2–3 AM (HR <110 sinus, SBP 100–140 off pressors, SpO₂ >94% RA, urine output adequate, pain controlled on PO meds, tolerating diet): consider transfer from ICU to stepdown/telemetry.
  • Document discharge criteria by POD 4 planning (see Section 5C).

sections.heading: 5C. POD 4–Discharge — Stepdown/Telemetry (AC Management, Discharge Teaching)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Anticoagulation goal INR achieved, discharge teaching complete, follow-up scheduled.

1. Anticoagulation finalization:

  • Repair (no AF): Warfarin × 3 months post-op, target INR 2.0–3.0. Recheck INR at 3 months; if normal sinus rhythm → switch to ASA 81 mg daily (or continue warfarin if AF develops).
  • Repair + POAF: Warfarin lifelong or DOAC (if suitable), target INR 2.0–3.0 or per DOAC dosing. Document in discharge summary.
  • Bio MVR (no AF): Warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 × 3 months; recheck INR at 3 months → switch to ASA 81 daily if no AF.
  • Bio MVR + AF: Warfarin lifelong or DOAC, target INR 2.5–3.5 or per DOAC dosing. AF indication overrides bio benefit of shorter anticoag duration.
  • Mechanical MVR: Warfarin 2.5–3.5 LIFELONG (DOACs not recommended for mechanical mitral). Heparin bridge discontinued once INR in goal range. Emphasize: never skip warfarin, never switch to DOACs for mechanical valve.
  • INR testing: Schedule first post-discharge INR check for 3–5 days after discharge. Provide anticoagulation clinic contact info. Some centers prefer INR clinic follow-up q 1–2 weeks × 2 months, then q 4–8 weeks if stable.

2. Pain & medication optimization:

  • Sternal pain: Usually resolves by POD 7–10 if taking opioids regularly. Switch to acetaminophen 650 mg q 6 h + ibuprofen 400 mg q 6 h (if no NSAIDs contraindicated). Severe pain beyond POD 10 → consider traction, physical therapy, rare post-sternotomy syndrome (chronic neuropathic pain; gabapentin/pregabalin helpful).
  • Intercostal pain (post-robotic): Often severe weeks–months. Gabapentin 300–600 mg TID, pregabalin 75–150 mg BID, or paravertebral catheter prior to discharge (if severe). Many patients benefit from continued gabapentin 6–12 weeks post-op.
  • Home medications: Beta-blocker, ACE-I/ARB (if EF <50% or hypertensive), statin, ASA (repair/bio without AF). Opioid (oxycodone 5–10 mg q 4–6 h PRN) × 2–4 weeks, then wean.

3. Teach-back on anticoagulation (critical):

  • Warfarin: Take same time each evening; never skip; report bleeding (nosebleeds, hemoptysis, blood in stool/urine, easy bruising → call PCP; severe → ED). Avoid vitamin K fluctuations (eat consistent green vegetables). Limit alcohol, cranberry juice. INR testing per clinic schedule.
  • DOACs (if used): Take as directed, same time daily. Do NOT stop without cardiology approval (thrombosis risk). Report bleeding signs. May have renal dose adjustment; confirm with pharmacy.
  • INR targets by valve: Emphasize: repair/bio = 2.0–3.0; mech = 2.5–3.5. Write targets on discharge papers + medication list. Give copy to patient, PCP, anticoag clinic.
  • Common errors: Dose adjustment without INR; skipping doses; switching to OTC NSAIDs (increase bleeding risk); interactions with antibiotics (amoxicillin, TMP-SMX increase warfarin effect).

4. Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) prevention:

  • Wallet card: Provide card listing valve type, INR target, antibiotic prophylaxis needs. Carry at all times.
  • PCP letter: Include prosthesis type (bioprosthetic vs mechanical), implant date, INR target, antibiotic prophylaxis needs (per AHA 2015 guidelines: amoxicillin 2 g PO 1 h before dental procedure, or clindamycin 600 mg if PCN-allergic; needed for high-risk procedures). Some centers recommend prophylaxis for all dental work; others only for procedures with high bacteremia risk (extractions, root canal, implants, periodontal surgery). Clarify with cardiologist.
  • Patient education: Brush teeth daily, floss daily, see dentist q 6 months. If fever + malaise develops → ED evaluation (blood cultures, ECG, echo). Early PVE (POD <30) often requires redo surgery; late PVE managed medically ± surgery per ID/CT team.

5. Activity & sternal precautions (POD 4 through 6–8 weeks discharge):

  • Precautions: No lifting >5 lbs (roughly 2 kg), no pushing/pulling heavy objects, no driving × 4 weeks (pain + opioids impair reaction time), no sexual activity × 4–6 weeks (sternal stress), no impact exercise (running, jumping) × 8 weeks.
  • Progressive activity: Walking encouraged POD 4+. Stationary bike POD 7–10 if low resistance. Swimming after incisions fully healed + cleared by surgeon (~4 weeks).
  • Return to work: Sedentary work POD 4–6 weeks (remote if available); light duty POD 6–8 weeks; full duty POD 8–12 weeks depending on job demands + sternal stability.
  • Sternal stability: Cough/sneeze into pillow × 6–8 weeks. Some patients benefit from sternal brace (soft corset) POD 1–4 weeks to improve pain + confidence.

6. Discharge criteria (all must be met):

Domain Criteria
Hemodynamics Off vasopressors/inotropes, SBP 100–160, HR <110 or controlled AF, euvolemic (no orthopnea, JVD, peripheral edema)
Respiratory Room air SpO₂ ≥94%, no dyspnea at rest or with ADLs, chest tube(s) removed, able to cough productively
Wound Incision(s) healing without erythema, drainage, dehiscence, or warmth; sutures/staples removed or non-absorbable sutures in place
Pain Controlled on PO analgesics (acetaminophen, ibuprofen, opioid PRN if needed), no acute exacerbation >8/10
GI/Nutrition Tolerating regular diet, bowel function normal (stool POD 3–4), no abdominal distention/pain
Anticoagulation INR established in goal range × 24 h (warfarin) or DOAC dose confirmed; patient/family teach-back confirmed; anticoag clinic appt scheduled
Labs Hgb stable (no ongoing transfusion), K⁺/Mg²⁺ normal, creatinine baseline or improving (AKI resolved), INR goal
Medications Home meds reconciled, post-op prescriptions provided (warfarin/DOAC, beta-blocker, ACE-I, statin, stool softener), no drug interactions
Follow-up Surgeon appt 2–3 weeks scheduled; cardiology ≤1 week if AF/mech valve/RV dysfunction; 30-day TTE ordered; anticoag clinic scheduled; cardiac rehab referral submitted
Endocarditis Prevention If prosthetic: wallet card + PCP letter provided with valve type, antibiotic prophylaxis needs
Patient Education Discharge teaching complete: anticoag teach-back, sternal precautions, activity restrictions, warning signs (fever, chest pain, dyspnea, bleeding, syncope), when to call PCP/ED

7. Discharge summary (key elements):

  • Procedure: Mitral valve repair/replacement (bio/mech), CPB time, concomitant procedures.
  • Valve type: If replacement, specify size + model (important for future echo interpretation).
  • Anticoagulation plan: Drug, INR/dose target, duration, INR clinic contact.
  • Prosthesis ID: List in "Problem List" + medication list so visible at future visits.
  • Follow-up imaging: 30-day TTE (post-repair SAM resolution, EF recovery; post-replacement prosthesis function, paravalvular leak assessment).
  • Complications during stay: List any POAF, AKI, bleeding, etc. + treatment; helps future providers understand trajectory.

sections.heading: 5D. Discharge Planning — Anticoagulation Duration & Follow-Up
sections.bodyHtml:
Critical Anticoagulation Decisions by Procedure:

Scenario Immediate Post-Op (POD 0) Discharge–3 Mo After 3 Mo Long-Term
Mitral Repair (sinus rhythm) Heparin × 24–48 h, then DC Warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 (most centers recommend × 3 mo; some do ASA only from discharge) INR check at 3 mo; if normal sinus → switch to ASA 81 daily ASA 81 daily lifelong; warfarin if AF develops later
Mitral Repair + POAF Heparin × 24–48 h, start warfarin load Warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 Lifelong warfarin or DOAC; AF indication overrides repair benefit Lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin/DOAC), INR target 2.0–3.0
Bioprosthetic MVR (sinus) Heparin × 24–48 h, warfarin load Warfarin INR 2.0–3.0 × 3 mo (reduce early thrombosis) INR check at 3 mo; if sinus → switch to ASA 81 daily ASA 81 lifelong; warfarin if AF develops
Bioprosthetic MVR + AF Heparin × 24–48 h, warfarin load Warfarin INR 2.5–3.5 (higher target for AF + prosthesis) Lifelong warfarin/DOAC Lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin/DOAC), INR 2.5–3.5; AF overrides bio benefit
Mechanical MVR Heparin × 24–48 h (hemostasis good), warfarin load (INR 2.5–3.5); heparin bridge (aPTT 50–70 s) Warfarin INR 2.5–3.5 + heparin bridge until therapeutic Lifelong warfarin (DO NOT use DOACs for mech mitral) Lifelong warfarin, INR 2.5–3.5; mechanical mitral is lifelong anticoag commitment
Mechanical MVR + AF Same as above Warfarin INR 2.5–3.5 (AF does NOT increase INR target; mech valve dominates. May add ASA 81 adjunctive per cardiology.) Lifelong warfarin ± ASA 81 Lifelong warfarin, INR 2.5–3.5; consider ASA 81 added

Key Decision Points:

  • Mechanical valve = lifelong warfarin commitment. INR 2.5–3.5 for mitral position (higher than aortic 2.0–3.0). Non-compliance = thrombosis risk, high mortality.
  • Repair + AF = lifelong anticoag (even after repair is structurally normal). AF stroke risk dominates.
  • DOACs: Suitable for AF post-repair or post-bioprosthetic MVR (if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2). Never for mechanical valve (insufficient data, thrombosis risk too high).
  • Three-month INR check: Gives option to de-escalate from warfarin to ASA (if repair/bio + no AF). If AF present at 3-month echo, confirm lifelong anticoag plan with cardiology.

30-Day Post-Op Echocardiogram (essential for all):

  • Repair: Assess residual MR (goal trivial-mild), SAM presence/severity (should be resolving), LV function (EF often recovers toward baseline by 30 days after acute unloading drop), LAP/PAWP (should normalize).
  • Bioprosthetic/Mechanical: Confirm prosthesis in normal position, normal gradients (mean <5 mmHg typical for modern prosthetics), absence of paravalvular leak or thrombus, EF, LV size.
  • RV function: If RV dysfunction present on intraop TEE, 30-day TTE assesses improvement (should remodel toward normal over 2–6 weeks).
  • LA size: Should decrease if MR corrected; if unchanged or enlarged → suspect residual disease or new AF development.

Follow-Up Schedule:

  • Surgeon: 2–3 weeks post-discharge (incision check, functional status, answer post-op questions).
  • Cardiology: ≤1 week post-discharge if POAF, mechanical valve, or RV dysfunction; otherwise routine 1–3 months.
  • INR clinic: First draw 3–5 days post-discharge; then per protocol (weekly × 2 weeks if variable, then q 2–4 weeks if stable). Some centers do phone-based INR with home testing; others use outpatient lab draws.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis clinic (if prosthetic): Educate on PVE risk, antibiotic need for dental/invasive procedures.
  • Cardiac rehab: Enrollment POD 3–4; start POD 7–10 (Phase I facility-based or Phase II home-based); 12 weeks of structured aerobic exercise + education.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for escalation calls. Includes decision trees for urgent/emergent scenarios (SAM, POAF, tamponade, bleeding, stroke, CHB).

SBAR Template:

S: "Dr. [Surgeon/APP name], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, MRN, room], POD [#] s/p [procedure type: repair/bio/mech MVR]." B: "[Patient demographics, comorbidities, preop valve pathology, procedure details]. Post-op course: [hemodynamics on arrival, any immediate complications e.g., bleeding, RV dysfunction]. Current on [vasoactives, inotropes, anticoag]." A: "[Current vital signs: HR, BP, rhythm, CVP, CO if available; urine output; mental status; relevant labs: Hgb, K⁺, troponin, lactate]. [Clinical concern: low CO + hypotension, new AF, bleeding, neuro change, etc.]" R: "[Specific request: Is this SAM? Should we escalate to OR? Adjust medications? Transfer to ICU?]"

Who to Call

Situation Contact Urgency Key Discussion Points
Stable post-op; routine questions (meds, diet, activity) Primary APP / on-call fellow Routine (can wait if not critical) Discharge readiness, anticoag plan, follow-up orders
Low cardiac output (CI <2.0) + hypotension (SBP <100) post-repair CT surgeon + ICU attending STAT STAT (r/o SAM) Rule out SAM first (echo STAT). If SAM: volume + phenylephrine, NOT inotropes. If not SAM: inotrope escalation vs OR evaluation for surgical problem.
Hemodynamically unstable POAF (SBP <90, altered mental status, pulmonary edema) CT surgeon + fellow/ICU attending + RRT code team STAT Rate/rhythm plan? Prepare for DCCV? Transfer to ICU? Heparin bridge initiation?
Recurrent POAF despite rate control or amiodarone load Cardiology + CT surgeon Urgent (same day, may not need OR) EP consult for rhythm strategy? Continue rate control? Anticoag escalation? Longer amiodarone drip?
Significant bleeding (CT output >300 mL/h × 2 h) ± coagulopathy CT surgeon + ICU attending STAT STAT Labs (CBC, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen) already drawn? Need transfusion? Return to OR for hemostasis?
Pericardial tamponade (acute or late): rising CVP, SBP drop, low CO, narrow pulse pressure CT surgeon + ICU attending + cardiology STAT STAT (emergent) STAT echo (r/o effusion, RV collapse). Prepare for emergent pericardiocentesis ± OR.
Complete heart block (CHB) or loss of AV conduction CT surgeon + cardiology STAT STAT Epicardial pacing wire status? Need transvenous pacing? Plan permanent pacemaker?
New focal neurologic deficit (facial droop, weakness, speech difficulty) Stroke code STAT (neurology, neuro ICU) + CT surgeon + cardiology STAT (emergent) Symptom onset time critical for thrombolytic window. STAT CT head. r/o hemorrhage vs ischemic stroke.
Acute kidney injury (Cr >3.0 or rising, oliguria <0.3 mL/kg/h despite fluids) Nephrology consult + CT surgeon + ICU attending Urgent (same day) RRT indication? Electrolyte management? Renal perfusion optimization? Dialysis initiation?
Fever POD 3–5 + unknown source Cardiology + CT surgeon (r/o endocarditis, mediastinitis) Urgent (same day) Blood cultures STAT (before antibiotics); TEE for vegetation; WBC count, CRP. Are antibiotics needed?
Mechanical MVR + new dyspnea, hypoxia, or low CO Cardiology + CT surgeon + fellow STAT STAT (r/o prosthetic thrombosis) Check INR STAT (subtherapeutic most common cause). TEE assessment of valve motion? Heparin bolus? Prepare for OR?
Persistent low urine output (<0.3 mL/kg/h POD 2+) despite fluids/diuretics Nephrology consult + CT surgeon Urgent Renal perfusion optimization? RRT readiness? Fluid balance goals?

Escalation Decision Trees:

Tree 1: Low CO + Hypotension Post-Repair ↓ CI (<2.0) + ↓ SBP (<100)? ├─ YES → ECHO STAT (r/o SAM) │ ├─ SAM confirmed? → FLIP rules (volume + phenylephrine + β-blocker; NO inotropes) │ │ └─ Persistent hypotension/shock? → OR callback for redo repair ± ring resizing │ ├─ SAM ruled out? → Check: fluid status (CVP), lactate, troponin │ │ ├─ Low CVP? → Fluid bolus 250–500 mL │ │ ├─ High CVP? → r/o pericardial effusion/tamponade (echo findings) → consider gentle diuresis ± inotrope │ │ ├─ Rising lactate? → low-dose inotrope (dobutamine 2–3 mcg/kg/min) ± vasopressor │ │ └─ Very low (<2.0) + worsening? → Escalate inotrope, consider IABP ± ECMO consult └─ NO → Continue current management, reassess q 1 h

Tree 2: Irregular Rhythm (POAF Suspected) Irregular rhythm on monitor? ├─ YES → 12-LEAD ECG STAT │ ├─ AF confirmed? → Assess hemodynamics (SBP, perfusion, urine output, mental status) │ │ ├─ Stable (SBP >90, alert, no chest pain)? → Electrolyte replacement (K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0) + amiodarone bolus (150 mg IV × 10 min) → drip (1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min) + notify APP │ │ │ └─ Persistent >24–48 h despite amiodarone? → Cardiology consult for EP assessment │ │ └─ Unstable (SBP <90, altered, pulmonary edema)? → STAT call + prepare DCCV (100–360 J biphasic per ACLS) │ └─ Other arrhythmia (flutter, SVT, frequent PVCs)? → Check electrolytes, troponin; notify provider └─ NO → Continue tele monitoring

Tree 3: Bleeding (CT Output, Coagulopathy) CT output >300 mL/h × 2 h OR >1,000 mL first 6–12 h? ├─ YES → Labs STAT (CBC, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer, lactate, type & cross) │ ├─ INR >2.0 (on warfarin for mech)? → FFP 2–4 units OR PCC 25–50 units/kg (faster) │ ├─ PTT >60? → FFP 2–4 units │ ├─ Fibrinogen <100? → Cryo 5–10 units │ ├─ Platelets <50? → Transfuse 6 units (1 unit/10 kg) │ ├─ Hgb drop >2 g/dL? → RBC transfusion (target 8–9.5) │ ├─ DIC pattern (low fib, low plts, ↑ D-dimer, ↑ PT/PTT)? → Massive transfusion protocol, ICU consult │ └─ Brisk bleeding × 2 h despite transfusion? → OR callback for hemostasis └─ NO (output slowing) → Continue monitoring q 1 h, trend labs

Tree 4: Pericardial Effusion / Tamponade (Any POD) CVP ↑, SBP ↓, CO ↓, narrow pulse pressure? ├─ YES → ECHO STAT (assess effusion size, RV diastolic collapse) │ ├─ Large effusion (>2 cm circumferential) + RV collapse? → EMERGENT CT surgeon + ICU attending → prepare pericardiocentesis ± OR │ │ ├─ Acute tamponade (POD 0–1)? → Usually requires OR (not pericardiocentesis alone) │ │ └─ Late tamponade (POD 3–7)? → Pericardiocentesis may buy time; then assess for OR │ ├─ Moderate effusion (1–2 cm) without collapse? → Monitor closely q 4–6 h; repeat echo POD 2–3 if concern for progression │ └─ Small effusion (<1 cm)? → Monitor, may not require intervention (common post-op finding) └─ NO → Continue monitoring CVP, hemodynamics

Tree 5: Focal Neuro Deficit (Stroke Alert) New focal neurologic sign (facial droop, weakness, speech change, gait imbalance)? ├─ YES → STROKE CODE STAT (neurology, neuro ICU attending, CT surgeon notified) │ ├─ Document symptom onset time (critical for thrombolytic window) │ ├─ STAT CT head non-contrast (r/o hemorrhage) │ ├─ 12-lead ECG (assess AF; if present, check INR for subtherapeutic anticoag) │ ├─ Labs: CBC, CMP, PT/INR, troponin, blood cultures (r/o endocarditis source) │ ├─ Onset <4.5 h + no hemorrhage → Neuro consult for IV tPA ± thrombectomy eligibility │ ├─ Hemorrhagic or large ischemic → Neuro ICU admission, coag reversal if needed, neuro surgery consult │ └─ AF + subtherapeutic INR → Escalate warfarin load, heparin bridge (if on warfarin) └─ NO → Continue routine neuro checks q shift × 72 h post-op

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All sections below marked for progressive disclosure.

Mitral valve anatomy and pathophysiology Normal Anatomy: The mitral valve (left atrioventricular valve) has four structural components:
  • Annulus: Fibrous ring anchoring the valve. In MR, annulus dilates (secondary/functional MR). Annular calcification prevents repair in some cases (indicates replacement needed).
  • Leaflets: Anterior (larger, aortic side) and posterior (septal side). Leaflets divided into segments: A1/A2/A3 (anterior) and P1/P2/P3 (posterior), named by location. P2 is central; P1/P3 are commissural regions.
  • Chordae tendineae: Thin fibrous cords anchoring leaflet to papillary muscles. Primary chordae (attach directly to leaflet free edge), secondary chordae (attach along belly), tertiary chordae (attach to LV wall near base).
  • Papillary muscles: Posteromedial and anterolateral; contract during systole, tense the chordae to prevent prolapse. Pathophysiology of MR:
    • Functional (secondary) MR: Annular dilatation + LV dysfunction → leaflets don't coapt (meet) fully in systole. Common post-MI, dilated cardiomyopathy, RV infarction (PM dysfunction). Corrected by reducing LV afterload or replacing PM with papillary muscle plication (rare).
    • Organic (primary) MR: Leaflet or chordal defect (endocarditis, rheumatic disease, flail leaflet from ruptured chordae, mitral valve prolapse [MVP], cleft leaflet).
    • Rheumatic: Thickened, calcified leaflets; commissural fusion; chordal shortening. Often requires replacement (anatomy unfavorable for repair).
    • Endocarditis: Vegetation destroys leaflet tissue; may create regurgitant jet. Early PVE post-op requires redo.
    • Acute flail leaflet: Ruptured chordae (spontaneous, trauma) → one scallop of leaflet flails in LA during systole. Dramatic MR; pulmonary edema; usually requires emergent repair or replacement.
    • MVP: Prolapse of one or both leaflets into LA during systole; usually mild-moderate MR. If severe (flail scallop), repair standard. Pathophysiology of MS:
    • Stenosis (narrowed opening) impedes diastolic flow from LA to LV. LA afterload ↑ → LA hypertrophy → atrial fibrillation (very common in MS). LV is spared initially ("normal LV function" classic finding). As disease progresses: RV afterload ↑ from pulmonary hypertension → RV hypertrophy/failure, hepatic congestion, peripheral edema.
    • Surgical relief (balloon valvulotomy rarely offered intraop; replacement standard). Repair Techniques (preserve native valve, no prosthesis):
    • Annuloplasty ring: Flexible or rigid ring (e.g., Carpentier, CryoLife) placed at annulus to correct dilatation and restore leaflet coaptation. Most common technique. Modern rings allow some physiologic motion (flexible) vs rigid (more durability, less motion).
    • Leaflet resection: Removing excess tissue (flail scallop, redundant leaflet) to improve coaptation. E.g., triangular resection of P2 in flail posterior leaflet.
    • Chordal replacement: Inserting prosthetic chordae (Gore-Tex, polyester) to replace ruptured native chordae, restoring leaflet height.
    • Edge-to-edge repair (Alfieri stitch): Suturing together the free edges of anterior and posterior leaflets (creates two smaller orifices instead of one). Reduces regurgitation; preserves tissue; lower profile valve. May increase mitral area slightly (paradoxically improves some valve areas). Common in complex repairs; also percutaneous approach (MitraClip) in non-surgical candidates. Minimally Invasive Approaches:
    • Robotic (da Vinci system): Right anterior or mid-axillary thoracotomy (2–4 cm). Magnified 3D visualization, articulated instruments. Longer operative time (~30–60 min more than sternotomy). Recovery faster; less pain. Learning curve steep; not all surgeons offer.
    • Mini-thoracotomy (non-robotic): Direct visualization through 4–6 cm right thoracotomy incision. Similar recovery to robotic but surgeon directly visualizing (not console-based). CPB access via peripheral cannulation + internal mammary vein retraction (LIMA exposure limited).
    • Sternotomy: Full median sternotomy (standard). Familiar, broad exposure, low conversion rate, no learning curve. Longer sternal healing time, more pain. Repair Durability:
    • Modern mitral repair durability excellent: ~1% failure rate per year (so 10-year failure ~10%). Revision surgery rates low. Unlike aortic root replacement (older data: 5–10% per year), mitral repair is durable long-term if anatomy favorable + surgeon skilled.
Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM) — post-repair pathophysiology and management Mechanism: Mitral repair reduces LV volume and increases contractility. The anterior mitral leaflet is pushed forward (anteriorly) toward the septum, encroaching on the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT). In systole, the anterior leaflet partially obstructs LVOT flow → systolic gradient (pressure drop across LVOT ≥30 mmHg diagnostic). Risk Factors for SAM Post-Repair:
  • Oversized annuloplasty ring (larger ring → more posterior leaflet shift → anterior leaflet more likely to SAM)
  • Redundant anterior leaflet (tall, elongated leaflet)
  • Tall, narrow LV (vertically elongated septum)
  • Aggressive leaflet resection (reduces leaflet length; paradoxically increases SAM risk in some cases)
  • Asian ancestry (more common genetic predisposition; taller, narrower LV geometry) Incidence: 2–10% post-mitral repair. Most common in experienced centers doing high volumes (better selection of candidates, but higher severity cases also treated). Recognition (POD 0–1, rarely later):
  • Acute dyspnea (pulmonary edema, LVOT obstruction increases afterload on LV)
  • Hypotension (LVOT obstruction → low output, systolic pressure rises acutely, map drops)
  • Loud systolic murmur (heard at apex, radiating to left sternal border; unlike MR murmur which is apical and doesn't radiate as prominently)
  • Echo diagnostic: Anterior motion of anterior mitral leaflet into LVOT, systolic gradient ≥30 mmHg, LVOT narrowing on PISA/color Doppler, SAM visible on multiple views.
  • Low cardiac output + increasing systolic BP = classic SAM presentation (seems counterintuitive: rising BP but falling CO → LVOT obstruction). Management (flips hemodynamic rules): The usual post-op goal is "maintain adequate preload, reduce afterload, use inotropes if low CO." SAM is the opposite.
    InterventionWhyHow
    Increase preloadCVP 12–15 increases LV cavity size, pushing septum away from anterior leaflet, reducing LVOT gradientIV bolus 250–500 mL crystalloid; target CVP 12–15 (higher than usual 8–12)
    Increase afterloadHigher SBP reduces LVOT gradient (afterload-dependent), pushes leaflet back away from septumIV phenylephrine 0.5–1.4 mcg/kg/min; target SBP 140–160 transient
    Avoid vasodilatorsNTG, nitroprusside, calcium channel blockers DECREASE afterload, WORSENING SAMDo NOT use; even cautious dosing worsens
    Avoid inotropesDobutamine, milrinone, dopamine INCREASE contractility, WORSENING SAM by pushing leaflet toward septum harderDo NOT use; these agents are contraindicated
    Increase beta-blockadeβ-blockers slow HR + decrease contractility, both reducing LVOT gradientIV metoprolol 5 mg × 1, or esmolol drip; target HR 80–90 (avoid tachycardia)
    Keep supine, HOB flatGravity helps increase LV cavity size; Fowler's position (sitting up) worsens LVOT obstructionReverse trendelenburg if present; keep completely flat initially
    Avoid rapid diuresisDiuretics reduce LV cavity size, WORSENING LVOT obstructionHold diuretics even if pulmonary edema present (paradoxically, may need careful fluid-restricted approach)
    Escalation:
  • Persistent hypotension + shock despite volume + phenylephrine + beta-blockade → OR callback for redo repair. Ring downsizing, more aggressive leaflet resection, or Alfieri stitch may reduce SAM.
  • Acute pulmonary edema refractory to conservative management → consider IABP (increases afterload, reduces contractility) ± ECMO if cardiogenic shock. Timeline: Usually resolves within 48–72 hours as LV remodels slightly and swelling decreases. Rarely persists beyond a few days; if so, suggests structural SAM (ring too large) requiring redo. Prevention: Surgeon selection of appropriate ring size (not oversized), careful attention to leaflet anatomy, skilled redo of repair if intraop TEE shows SAM post-repair.
POAF (Post-Operative Atrial Fibrillation) — incidence, risk factors, prevention Incidence & Risk Factors (Mitral-Specific):
  • Mitral valve surgery has highest POAF incidence of all cardiac surgeries: 30–50% (CABG ~10–30%, AVR ~10–20%, aortic surgery ~10–20%).
  • Peak onset: POD 2–3 (72–96 hours post-op).
  • Risk factors: age >70, prior AF, left atrial enlargement on preop echo, valvular (higher than CABG), COPD, OSA, prolonged CPB (>120–150 min common in mitral cases), pre-op beta-blocker withdrawal, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia. Pathophysiology:
  • Atrial inflammation from cardiopulmonary bypass cannulation, atriotomy, pericardial irritation.
  • Sympathetic surge from pain, volume shifts, adrenergic stimulation.
  • Electrolyte depletion: K⁺ <4.0, Mg²⁺ <1.5 lower atrial stability threshold, trigger ectopy.
  • LA thrombus risk: Atrial surgery + manipulation + new AF = clot formation within hours → stroke risk highest in first 48 h of new AF. Prevention (Evidence-Based):
  • Beta-blocker continuation: Perioperative beta-blocker is single most modifiable risk factor; pre-op beta-blocker continuation strongly recommended. Withholding for perioperative hypotension is a frequent mistake; reintroduce once BP stabilizes.
  • Statin: Pre-op statin associated with lower POAF incidence; continue post-op if not contraindicated.
  • Low-chloride balanced fluids: Recent evidence (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025) suggests LR or Plasma-Lyte preferable to normal saline for reducing POAF.
  • Electrolyte repletion: Aggressive K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0 in first 24–48 h post-op.
  • Rate of rewarming: Slow rewarming post-CPB may reduce POAF (controversial).
  • Amiodarone prophylaxis: Some centers give low-dose amiodarone (e.g., 10 mg/kg load intraop, then PO post-op) to high-risk patients; evidence mixed. Practical in most US centers is reactive treatment (amiodarone after AF develops) rather than prophylactic. Refer to related Scenario: POAF card for detailed recognition, rate vs rhythm strategy, anticoagulation decisions.
Concomitant MAZE procedure and LAA ligation MAZE Surgery: Surgical ablation of atrial fibrillation. Creates scar lines in atria (using radiofrequency energy, cryoablation, or incision lines — "Cox MAZE" procedure) to interrupt re-entrant circuits causing AF. Performed concomitantly with valve surgery in select high-risk AF patients (chronic AF, paroxysmal AF with failed medical therapy, LA enlargement). Pros:
  • High success rate for AF termination (>80% freedom from AF at 1 year in selected patients).
  • Single operative time (doesn't add significant morbidity if done by experienced surgeon).
  • Reduces stroke risk in post-op AF by providing arrhythmia cure rather than rate control. Cons:
  • Adds ~20–30 min to CPB time (risk of AKI, POAF paradoxically increases with longer CPB despite MAZE intent).
  • Learning curve for surgeon + institution (specialized technique; not all centers offer).
  • Early post-op AF is expected and common (4 weeks post-MAZE, AF frequent; DCCV often ineffective until scarring matures ~4 weeks; rate control + amiodarone standard). New nurses often alarmed; reassure this is expected. LAA Ligation: Left atrial appendage occlusion (via suture, stapling device, or external clip) performed concomitantly to reduce LA thrombus formation (appendage is source of ~90% of LA clots in AF). Reduces stroke risk. Practical Point: If MAZE + LAA ligation done, early AF POD 2–3 is expected. DCCV usually ineffective until ~POD 14–21 (scarring not yet mature). Rate control + amiodarone is default strategy. After 4 weeks, if still in AF → DCCV ± EP consult for additional interventions.
RV dysfunction post-MV repair — management Etiology: Chronic MR → PA hypertension → RV hypertrophy and dysfunction. Post-op RV is afterload-dependent (pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) remains elevated), preload-dependent, and slow to remodel (weeks–months). Recognition:
  • Elevated CVP >15 cmH₂O persistently
  • Low CO (CI <2.2) despite adequate filling
  • Elevated PAP (systolic >50 mmHg) even if improved from pre-op
  • RV strain on ECG (T-wave inversions V1–V3)
  • Hepatic congestion (AST >500, RUQ tenderness, ascites developing)
  • Peripheral edema, elevated JVD Management:
  • Optimize preload: CVP goal 12–15 cmH₂O (higher than typical 8–12 post-op). RV is preload-dependent; volume depletion worsens CO.
  • Reduce RV afterload: Inhaled nitric oxide (iNO) 10–20 ppm (gold standard if available; reduces PVR selectively, improves RV–PA coupling). IV vasodilators (NTG, nitroprusside) less selective (systemic BP drops, may worsen RV perfusion); use cautiously.
  • Optimize ventilation: Target SpO₂ >92% (hypoxia increases PVR), minimize PEEP >8 (PEEP increases intrathoracic pressure, reduces RV preload paradoxically), avoid hypercapnia (increases PVR).
  • Low-dose inotrope: Dobutamine (better RV selectivity than milrinone) 2–3 mcg/kg/min to improve contractility + reduce afterload. Milrinone (0.25 mcg/kg/min) also reasonable; phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor reduces PVR + increases contractility.
  • Avoid aggressive diuresis: RV is preload-dependent; net negative fluid balance too fast worsens CO. Target net zero to −500 mL/day (gentle diuresis).
  • Hemoglobin goal ≥8: Anemia increases RV afterload (lower viscosity, higher flow velocity needed); transfuse if Hgb <8.
  • Mechanical support: If CVP >18, CI <2.0, lactate >4 → IABP or V-A ECMO consult. IABP improves coronary perfusion pressure + reduces afterload; V-A ECMO provides systemic + pulmonary support but riskier (cannulation, anticoagulation, limb ischemia). Timeline: RV remodels over weeks–months. By 6 weeks, most patients show improvement. Reduced exercise tolerance weeks–months post-discharge expected. 30-day echo assesses RV function improvement.
Mechanical valve prosthesis choice Bioprosthetic (xenograft, bovine pericardium or porcine valve):
  • Durability: 10-year hemodynamic dysfunction ~15–20%; 15-year structural valve deterioration (SVD) ~40–60%. Durability worse in younger patients, worse in mitral position (higher gradients stress valve), worse in young women (metabolic factors accelerate degeneration).
  • Anticoagulation: Warfarin × 3 months only (INR 2.0–3.0). After 3 months, ASA 81 mg daily if no AF. If AF develops → lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin or DOAC), overriding bio benefit.
  • Advantage: No lifelong anticoag (patient preference). Suitable for elderly (life expectancy <10 years).
  • Disadvantage: Limited durability; redo surgery risk 10–15 years post-op (morbidity of redo higher than index surgery).
  • Endocarditis risk: Similar to mechanical (~1–2% per patient-year); requires antibiotic prophylaxis × 6 months post-op (some centers), then only for high-risk procedures (like mechanical). Mechanical (pyrolytic carbon, bi-leaflet design [St. Jude, ATS, Carbomedics]):
  • Durability: Excellent; >99% freedom from structural valve deterioration at 30 years. Essentially lifetime device (outlives most patients).
  • Anticoagulation: Warfarin lifelong, INR 2.5–3.5 for mitral position (higher than aortic 2.0–3.0 because mitral has higher thrombosis risk). Non-compliance = thrombosis risk.
  • Disadvantage: Lifelong warfarin commitment. INR fluctuations risk (bleeding if over-anticoagulated, thrombosis if under-anticoagulated). Mechanical click (audible, some patients find bothersome). Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) risk.
  • Advantage: Durable; avoids redo surgery risk. Suitable for younger patients (life expectancy >20 years) or patients who can reliably anticoagulate.
  • Endocarditis: ~1–2% per patient-year; antibiotic prophylaxis required for dental/urologic procedures lifelong. Choice Factors (ACC/AHA guidelines):
  • Age <50–60: Mechanical often preferred (durability, avoids redo in long lifespan). Exception: if unable to reliably anticoagulate (noncompliance, bleeding disorder).
  • Age >65–70: Bioprosthetic often preferred (avoid lifelong anticoag burden). Exception: if life expectancy <10 years or comorbidities make redo surgery high-risk.
  • Age 50–65: Individualize (patient preference, ability to anticoagulate, life expectancy, comorbidities).
  • Pregnancy planning: Mechanical requires warfarin (teratogenic in 1st trimester); bioprosthetic safer (though anticoag still needed if AF develops). Consider delaying surgery until after childbearing if bioprosthetic desired.
  • Renal failure: Warfarin metabolism not renal-dependent; mechanical safe in renal disease (unlike some DOACs which require renal metabolism). Prosthetic Valve Hemodynamics: Modern prostheses have low mean gradients (<5 mmHg). Gradients vary by size (smaller valve → higher gradient), position (mitral > aortic gradient natural, but still <10 mmHg typical for modern prosthetics), and patient CO state. Baseline post-op echocardiogram documents prosthetic function; future echoes compared to baseline to detect thrombus or degeneration.
Mini-MV (robotic/minimally invasive) surgery — advantages, learning curve, complications Advantages:
  • Cosmesis: 2–4 cm incision vs 8–10 cm sternotomy.
  • Less pain: Intercostal approach avoids sternal pain; however, intercostal nerve pain can be severe (see Pitfalls).
  • Faster recovery: Discharge POD 3–4 vs POD 5–8 (sternotomy).
  • Reduced pulmonary complications: Fewer atelectasis, shorter ventilator time, faster return to ambulation.
  • Reduced bleeding: Smaller incision, less ooze.
  • Shorter hospitalization: Cost savings (if offset by increased operative time + specialized equipment). Disadvantages:
  • Longer operative time: 30–90 min longer CPB (learning curve, ergonomics of robotic approach).
  • Learning curve: Requires specialized training; not all surgeons offer. Early outcomes worse at learning institutions; outcomes improve after 50–100 cases.
  • Intercostal pain: Often severe, persistent weeks–months (see Pitfalls). Paravertebral nerve block highly recommended.
  • Conversion rate: 5–10% conversion to sternotomy (bleeding control, technical difficulty, equipment failure).
  • Right thoracotomy access: Limited view of left-sided structures if concomitant CABG planned; usually requires separate left thoracotomy or delayed CABG.
  • CPB access: Peripheral cannulation (femoral) vs central; femoral carries risk of iliac artery injury, distal limb ischemia. Robotic-Specific Complications:
  • Atelectasis: Right lower lobe atelectasis common (lung retraction, one-lung ventilation). Early mobilization + aggressive IS reduces.
  • LIMA retraction: If LIMA takedown needed (rare in isolated MV), results in brief mammary artery ischemia; monitor for ST elevation ECG post-op (usually transient).
  • Right phrenic nerve injury (rare): Elevated right hemidiaphragm on CXR; respiratory distress if high (may need plication).
  • Peripheral cannulation complications: Iliac artery dissection, distal limb ischemia, compartment syndrome of leg. Assess distal perfusion q shift post-op; if absent femoral pulse + leg pain/coolness → vascular surgery consult emergently. When to Choose Robotic:
  • Isolated mitral repair in experienced center (surgeon >50 cases).
  • Young patient prioritizing cosmesis + faster recovery.
  • Patient accepting higher operative time + intercostal pain risk for faster recovery. When to Avoid Robotic:
  • Emergency surgery (bleeding, cardiogenic shock — standard sternotomy faster).
  • Redo surgery (adhesions, difficult access).
  • Concomitant CABG (unless LIMA not needed).
  • Surgeon with <30 cases experience (mortality/complication rates higher in learning curve).
Carpentier's classification of mitral regurgitation Type I — Normal Leaflet Motion
  • Annular dilatation or leaflet perforation.
  • Examples: functional MR (LV remodeling, annular dilatation), prosthetic valve regurgitation (paravalvular leak), leaflet perforation (endocarditis).
  • Repair: Annuloplasty ring (restores leaflet coaptation by correcting annular size). Type II — Excessive Leaflet Motion (Prolapse)
  • Leaflet billows into LA during systole (chordal elongation, chordal rupture, papillary muscle elongation/dysfunction, LV dilatation).
  • Examples: mitral valve prolapse (MVP), flail leaflet (ruptured chordae), post-MI papillary muscle rupture.
  • Repair: Leaflet resection (remove prolapsing scallop) + annuloplasty ring, or chordal replacement (Gore-Tex) to restore leaflet height. Type III — Restrictive Leaflet Motion
  • Leaflet motion limited in systole (fibrosis, shortening, or LV remodeling pulls annulus/papillary muscles).
  • Divided:
  • Type III-A: Papillary muscle/chordal shortening (rheumatic disease, endocarditis healed, functional MR with LV remodeling + increased tethering forces).
  • Type III-B: Annular dilatation + LV dilatation together (dilated cardiomyopathy, RV infarction with PM dysfunction).
  • Repair: Ring annuloplasty alone may be insufficient if significant tethering. May require papillary muscle relocation, partial leaflet resection, or replacement if anatomy unfavorable. Clinical Pearl: Type I repairs are easiest, highest durability. Type II (flail) repairs are common, durable if anatomy good. Type III (restrictive) repairs more complex; redo rate higher; some require replacement. Assessment of repair feasibility pre-op (high-quality TEE) is critical to discuss options (repair vs replacement) with patient.

Warfarin Loading & INR Monitoring:
  • Day 1 post-op evening: 5–10 mg warfarin PO (lower end if older, liver disease, multiple drug interactions; higher if younger, good compliance expected).
  • POD 1 AM INR check: Baseline INR post-load.
  • Dose adjustment: INR <2.0 → increase dose 1–2 mg next evening. INR 2.0–3.0 → no change. INR 3.0–4.0 → decrease 0.5–1 mg. INR >4.0 → hold 1 dose, decrease dose next day.
  • Recheck frequency: q 24 h × 3–5 days until stable × 2 consecutive INRs in range, then q 3–7 days for 1 month (variability post-op common), then q 4–8 weeks if stable. Heparin Bridge:
  • Essential for mechanical MVR: Warfarin takes 3–5 days to reach therapeutic level (needs vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X to be synthesized). During gap, thrombosis risk high for mechanical valve. Heparin provides immediate anticoagulation while warfarin loading.
  • Not required for repair/bio: Repair/bio lower thrombosis risk; heparin × 24–48 h acceptable, then discontinue pending warfarin effect.
  • Heparin dosing: 80 units/kg bolus, then 18 units/kg/h infusion (goal aPTT 50–70 s). Check aPTT 6 h post-bolus, then q 6 h if adjusting, then q 24 h if stable.
  • Discontinue heparin: Once INR ≥2.5 × 24 h (or per institutional protocol, sometimes INR ≥2.0 × 24 h). Do NOT stop heparin at discharge; many patients require bridge to outpatient INR clinic. DOACs (Direct Oral Anticoagulants):
  • Acceptable for: AF post-repair, AF post-bioprosthetic MVR (if CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥2 and DOAC suitable per cardiology).
  • NOT acceptable for: Mechanical valve (insufficient evidence; thrombosis risk unacceptably high; contraindicated per ACC/AHA).
  • DOAC dosing post-MV: e.g., apixaban 5 mg BID (or 2.5 mg BID if age >60, weight <60 kg, Cr >1.5), rivaroxaban 20 mg daily (10 mg if CrCl 15–30), dabigatran 150 mg BID (110 mg BID if >75 yo or high bleeding risk). Clarify with cardiology per institutional protocol.
  • Advantage: No INR monitoring. Disadvantage: Less experience post-op; warfarin still standard for most post-MV patients.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • HR trending up despite rate control — AF rate-control failure; may indicate need for rhythm control (amiodarone escalation) or DCCV.
  • SBP trending upward (>150) — LV afterload increasing; if post-repair, r/o SAM (ask: "Is CO also low? Does patient look dyspneic?"). Otherwise, initiate/titrate antihypertensive.
  • CVP trending up (>15 persistently) — RV dysfunction worsening, fluid overload, or early tamponade; echo assess. Gentle diuresis if euvolemic/hypervolemic; avoid if RV-dependent.
  • Urine output declining (<0.5 mL/kg/h trending to <0.3) — renal perfusion failure; check CO, MAP, lactate; optimize fluid/inotropes; labs for AKI pattern.
  • Lactate rising (>2, trending up) — hypoperfusion; low CO syndrome; escalate.
  • Hgb dropping (>1 g/dL/8 h) — ongoing bleeding; CT output check, labs (PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen); notify surgeon if brisk.
  • Chest tube output increasing after initially stable — resumption of bleeding; labs STAT.
  • Troponin rising significantly (>0.1 ng/mL post-op) — myocardial injury (low CO, ischemia, prosthetic thrombosis); echo + cardiology consult.
  • QTc prolonging on amiodarone (approaching 500 ms) — torsades risk; hold/decrease amiodarone, ECG check.
  • Anxiety or agitation increasing — may precede hemodynamic instability; pain, hypoxia, delirium screen.
  • New focal neurologic deficit — STROKE ALERT immediately (See Escalation tree, Section 6).
  • Rhythm change (new arrhythmia, loss of pacing capture) — 12-lead ECG STAT; check pacer settings, capture threshold.
  • Pericardial effusion enlarging on serial echos — risk of tamponade; reassess q 12–24 h; prepare for possible pericardiocentesis if size increasing.
  • Rebleeding after initial hemostasis — coagulopathy worsening; labs (PT/INR, fibrinogen), consider redo OR.
  • WBC rising (>15K) + fever — infection workup (cultures, CXR, UA); antibiotics if clinical concern.
  • Prosthetic valve murmur changing (becoming louder or new diastolic component) — r/o prosthetic thrombosis (TE + echo STAT) or PVE (blood cultures, TEE).

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
10–15 high-yield bullets for proficient/expert pattern recognition.

  1. POAF is nearly expected — 40–50% incidence (highest cardiac surgery rate). Don't hesitate. Electrolyte repletion (K⁺ ≥4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥2.0) STAT, amiodarone bolus + drip, rate/rhythm plan per provider. Peak onset POD 2–3; continue tele monitoring POD 4–7. Refer to Scenario: POAF card for detailed rate vs rhythm strategy.

  2. Mechanical MVR INR target is 2.5–3.5, NOT 2.0–3.0. Most common dosing error (defaulting to aortic targets). Mitral position has higher thrombosis risk. Write target clearly on discharge papers + medication list. Reinforce at anticoag clinic.

  3. SAM post-repair FLIPS hemodynamic rules: INCREASE volume + afterload (phenylephrine). AVOID vasodilators, inotropes (dobutamine/milrinone/dopamine). Low CO + hypotension post-repair = ECHO FIRST before assuming shock. If SAM confirmed: volume + phenylephrine + β-blocker; persistent hypotension → OR callback for redo repair.

  4. "Unloaded LV" phenomenon: Pre-op EF 45–50% often drops acutely to 35–40% post-repair on first stress (AF, fever, pain). Expected; not cardiogenic shock. Educate team. 30-day TTE usually shows recovery. Avoid aggressive diuresis; optimize afterload.

  5. RV failure post-MV is common + delicate: Don't over-diurese. RV is preload-dependent; net negative fluid >500 mL/day worsens CO. iNO 10–20 ppm is gold standard (if available). Accept CVP 12–15 cmH₂O post-MV. Chronic pHTN remodels slowly (weeks–months); reduced exercise tolerance expected weeks post-discharge.

  6. Stroke risk 3–8% — highest cardiac surgery rate. AF 40–50% + long CPB + LA thrombus risk + atrial manipulation = high embolic risk.

    Monitor neuro q shift × 72 h minimum. Focal neuro deficit = STROKE ALERT STAT (CT head, stroke team, neurology consult). Early anticoag mandatory.

  7. Late tamponade risk POD 3–7 — higher post-MV (longer CPB, anticoag ooze). Watch for gradual CVP rise, CO drop, fatigue, dyspnea, weight gain despite afebrile/low-grade fever.

    Must-not-miss diagnosis. Repeat echo if suspicion; pericardiocentesis ± OR per imaging + clinical judgment.

  8. Intercostal pain (post-robotic) can be SEVERE + persistent for weeks–months. Don't minimize as "routine discomfort." Multimodal: gabapentin 300–600 mg TID, pregabalin 75–150 mg BID starting POD 1. Paravertebral nerve block excellent (single shot or catheter). Many patients benefit 6–12 weeks post-op.

  9. Mechanical MVR thrombosis = medical emergency (acute dyspnea, stroke, limb ischemia). Subtherapeutic INR almost always culprit.

    INR check 3–5 days post-DC mandatory. Non-compliance deadly; emphasize at discharge + anticoag clinic.

  10. Endocarditis lifelong risk (prosthetic). Wallet card + PCP letter mandatory before discharge. ABx prophylaxis for dental/urologic procedures per AHA 2015 guidelines. Fever/malaise → cardiology eval (blood cultures, TEE, r/o PVE). Early PVE (POD <30) often needs redo surgery.

  11. AF + mech MVR + significant bleeding = razor's edge. Anticoag (thrombosis risk) vs hemostasis (bleeding risk). Surgeon-directed only. May need OR for bleeding control, then resume full anticoag (heparin bridge) post-hemostasis. Never hold anticoag unilaterally.

  12. Diuresis in RV-failure post-MV is balancing act: too fast = RV fails (shock), too slow = ongoing RV strain. Target net zero to −500 mL/day. CVP >15 = gentle diuresis (furosemide 20–40 mg IV q 4–6 h); <12 = hold. Monitor UOP, Cr, lactate q 6 h.

  13. Post-op stress triggers "flash pulmonary edema" in pre-op low-normal EF + long MR. Not HF exacerbation — LV decompensation from unloading. Treat cautiously: afterload reduction (NTG, cautious) ± low-dose inotrope (watch SAM). 30-day TTE reassures (EF usually recovers). DO NOT over-diurese.

  14. Anticoag teaching at discharge is CRITICAL + complex. Patient teach-back on warfarin, INR targets, bleeding signs, vitamin K consistency. Written instructions. Copy to PCP + anticoag clinic. INR errors common post-discharge; close follow-up essential (3–5 days INR recheck non-negotiable).

  15. Chronic steroid users = adrenal insufficiency risk post-op. Ask rheumatologic history (asthma, COPD, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis). Refractory hypotension unresponsive to fluids + vasopressors → hydrocortisone 100 mg IV q 6–8 h stress-dose (continue home steroid + stress dose overlap). Improves BP within hours in responders.

cards.title: Septal Myectomy (Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy)
cards.quickAnswer: Myectomy patient post-op: keep them full (preload high), slow (HR 60–80 avoid tachycardia), vasoconstricted (MAP 70–90, phenylephrine preferred). AVOID inotropes and vasodilators — they INCREASE LVOT gradient (opposite of CABG). Start beta-blocker POD 1; cornerstone of HCM management lifelong. Watch for complete heart block (bundle of His runs through septum — PPM 2–10%, check pacer wires daily, don't pull early). Watch for residual/recurrent SAM if hypotension worsens. Discharge echo 30–90 days confirms no residual gradient or SAM.
