sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

Septal Myectomy: Surgical Obstructive HCM Relief

  • Definition: Surgical resection of hypertrophied basal interventricular septum via median sternotomy and transaortic approach to relieve left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) obstruction in patients with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) refractory to medical therapy. Goal: residual LVOT gradient < 20 mmHg at rest and with exercise (Ommen et al., 2020).
  • Typical patient: Symptomatic obstructive HCM with LVOT gradient ≥ 50 mmHg at rest (NYHA III/IV despite beta-blocker + disopyramide), or ≥ 80 mmHg asymptomatic, or exercise-induced gradient > 100 mmHg. Often young to middle-aged. Family history of sudden cardiac death common; many have implantable cardioverter-defibrillators (ICDs) pre-op.
  • Procedure variants: Classic Morrow procedure (minimal septum resection) vs. extended myectomy (more aggressive, removes more septum + may address papillary muscle obstruction). Extended myectomy now more common; both aim for gradient < 20 mmHg.
  • Approach: Median sternotomy, on-pump CPB, transaortic (through the aortic valve). Concurrent mitral valve repair if systolic anterior motion (SAM) persists despite adequate septum resection (rare, ~5% of cases).
  • Standard LOS: ICU 1–2 days; total 5–7 days (slightly longer than CABG due to pacer wire retention and arrhythmia watch).
  • Expected lines/devices on arrival: Pacer wires (both atrial and ventricular — kept longer than CABG due to heart block risk); chest tubes; Foley; possible epidural analgesia.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why this happens — novice + advanced beginner teaching.

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) and LVOT Obstruction

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a primary myocardial disorder characterized by unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy (LV wall thickness ≥ 15 mm) due to pathogenic variants in genes encoding cardiac sarcomeric proteins (Ommen et al., 2020). The hypertrophied septum encroaches on the LVOT, creating a dynamic obstruction: during ventricular systole, the mitral valve leaflet (especially the anterior leaflet) moves anteriorly toward the septum—a phenomenon called systolic anterior motion (SAM). This SAM narrows the LVOT even further, raising the pressure gradient across the outflow tract and reducing forward cardiac output. Over time, chronic LVOT obstruction causes LV dysfunction, diastolic dysfunction, atrial dilatation (predisposing to atrial fibrillation), and arrhythmia substrate.

Why Medical Therapy Fails and Surgery Is Indicated

First-line medical management includes high-dose beta-blockers (target resting HR 50–60 to prolong diastolic filling time) and non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (verapamil) or Class IA antiarrhythmics (disopyramide, which reduces SAM by negative inotropic effect). When symptoms persist despite maximal medical therapy (NYHA III/IV, recurrent syncope, exercise-induced symptoms despite gradient reduction), septal myectomy is indicated. Myectomy is superior to percutaneous alcohol septal ablation at experienced centers: lower procedural mortality, no risk of iatrogenic VSD, lower long-term PPM rate (Maron et al., outcomes series; Nishimura et al., 2014).

Myectomy Goals and Hemodynamic Principles

The post-op goal is residual gradient < 20 mmHg at rest (normal LV outflow). Because the obstruction is dynamic (increases with reduced preload, increased contractility, decreased afterload), the post-op hemodynamic strategy is the opposite of most cardiac surgery:

  • High preload (fill the LV) → keeps outflow tract patent
  • Slow heart rate (60–80) → prolongs diastolic filling
  • Vasoconstriction (increase afterload) → opposes gradient
  • Avoid inotropes (they worsen obstruction by increasing contractility)
  • Avoid vasodilators/diuretics (they reduce preload, worsening obstruction)

SAM Pathophysiology (Nishimura et al., 2014)

Systolic anterior motion occurs when the mitral anterior leaflet is elongated or the papillary muscles are anteriorly displaced. During systole, LV contraction forces the leaflet toward the septum. Adequate septal resection removes the obstruction, allowing the leaflet to coapt normally in the mitral orifice. If SAM persists post-myectomy despite adequate septum resection, causes include: residual hypertrophic septum, papillary muscle anterior displacement, or elongated mitral leaflet. Rescue mitral valve repair (edge-to-edge, papillary muscle repositioning) is rare but occasionally needed.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Operative Course
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner understanding of operative course and post-op expectations.

Pre-Op Profile

  • Severe obstructive HCM with symptoms refractory to medical therapy
  • LVOT gradient measured by echocardiography (resting ± exercise) and sometimes intra-operative TEE
  • Possible concurrent AF, prior ICD placement (interrogate device post-op per EP)
  • Genetics: autosomal dominant inheritance; first-degree relatives at 50% risk (screening required)

Operative Details

  • Approach: Median sternotomy; on-pump CPB with moderate hypothermia (28–32 °C)
  • Pump time: 90–140 minutes (longer than isolated CABG due to meticulous septum resection and attention to papillary muscle anatomy)
  • Cardioplegia: Cold blood or crystalloid antegrade ± retrograde via coronary sinus
  • Critical anatomy at risk: Bundle of His runs along the ventricular septum just below the aortic valve annulus. Excessive septal resection or retractor trauma can injure the His bundle → complete heart block.
  • Epicardial pacing wires: Placed routinely (both atrial and ventricular); often kept longer than other surgeries (POD 4–5 minimum) due to heart block risk

Expected Post-Op Course — ICU (POD 0)

  • Extubation goal 4–8 h; slightly slower than CABG due to paradoxical hemodynamic goals and arrhythmia watchfulness
  • Hemodynamics: Target SBP 100–130, MAP 70–90, CVP high-normal (8–12 cm H₂O) to maintain preload; avoid hypovolemia
  • Pacer wire threshold check: capture at ≤ 5 mA; baseline AV conduction documented
  • Baseline 12-lead ECG (document any LBBB or PR prolongation)
  • CTs monitored; Foley monitoring for urine output target > 0.5 mL/kg/h
  • Labs: CBC, BMP (especially K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 for arrhythmia prevention), troponin baseline

Expected Post-Op Course — POD 1–3 (ICU → Stepdown Transition)

  • Out of bed to chair POD 1; walking POD 2–3 with PT (mobility aids — sternal support)
  • Beta-blocker started POD 1 (metoprolol 25 mg BID or equivalent); non-negotiable and continued lifelong
  • Pacer wires remain in place; do NOT remove early (bundle of His function recovers as edema resolves POD 2–5)
  • CTs out when drainage < 150 mL/8 h × 8 h; Foley out POD 1–2 if UOP adequate
  • Prepare for transfer to stepdown when hemodynamically stable off high-dose pressors, extubated, pacer wires in place
  • Labs: daily BMP (K⁺, Mg²⁺ trending upward); troponin q12h POD 0–1

Expected Post-Op Course — POD 4–6 (Stepdown → Discharge)

  • Pacer wires removed POD 4–5 per surgeon guidance (baseline CXR after removal)
  • Rhythm monitoring continues (delayed heart block possible as edema peaks then resolves POD 2–5)
  • Mobility and sternal precautions: arm support × 6–8 weeks, no lifting > 10 lbs × 3 months
  • Discharge medications: Beta-blocker (lifelong), ASA 81 mg daily, home anticoagulation if concurrent AF
  • Discharge teaching: Family screening referral (HCM is autosomal dominant — first-degree relatives need screening echo + genetic counseling). ICD evaluation if SCD risk present and not already implanted.
  • Follow-up: Surgeon 1 week (incision), 4 weeks (full visit). Echocardiogram 30–90 days post-op (confirm LVOT gradient < 20 mmHg, no residual SAM).

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: 2 min at bedside.

Vital Signs & Hemodynamics

  • Heart rate (target 60–80), blood pressure (target SBP 100–130), MAP ≥ 70
  • Central venous pressure if line in (target high-normal 8–12 cm H₂O for preload)
  • Urine output trend (target > 0.5 mL/kg/h)
  • Perfusion: capillary refill, skin warmth, lactate (if concern for low output)
  • Rhythm: regular vs. irregular; any ectopy on monitor

Cardiac & Respiratory

  • Breath sounds bilaterally (rule out atelectasis, effusion)
  • Heart sounds: murmur? (post-myectomy: systolic murmur should improve vs. pre-op; new diastolic murmur concerning)
  • JVD, S3 gallop, orthopnea (signs of elevated filling pressures or HF)
  • Chest tube output (color, quantity); any ongoing bleeding

Neurologic

  • Alert & oriented × 3; agitation or somnolence (delirium risk POD 1–3)
  • Focal deficits: arm drift, speech, facial symmetry (stroke screening)
  • Pacer wire function: thresholds, sensing, capture documented; any loss of capture on wires

Surgical & Devices

  • Sternotomy: erythema, warmth, dehiscence, sternal stability
  • Pacer wires: intact, not dislodged, two epicardial screws visible/palpable on RV
  • CTs (mediastinal ± pleural): output quantity and character in last 8 h
  • Foley: urine color and output

Recent Labs (Last 4–6 Hours)

  • CBC: Hgb trend (transfusion threshold HCM post-myectomy Hgb < 8; < 9 if CAD/age > 70)
  • BMP: K⁺ target ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ target ≥ 2.0 (critical for arrhythmia prevention)
  • Troponin trend (baseline POD 0; should not rise significantly if no ischemic complications)
  • Lactate (if concern for low cardiac output)

sections.heading: 5. Management by Post-Operative Day Arc
sections.bodyHtml: POD trajectory replaces Stable/Unstable fork for surgery cards. HCM-specific hemodynamic goals are the centerpiece.

sections.heading: 5A. POD 0 (ICU)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Extubation, establish HCM hemodynamic targets, rule out block, document baseline

Task Action Target
Extubation readiness FiO₂ ≤ 40%, PEEP ≤ 5, adequate spontaneous effort, alert mental status. Note: extubation may be slightly delayed due to HCM hemodynamic paradox (inotrope weaning slower). 4–8 h post-op
Hemodynamic targets (HCM-specific) SBP 100–130 (avoid hypertension → excessive afterload on new septum); MAP ≥ 70; CVP 8–12 cm H₂O (maintain preload); HR 60–80 (beta-blocker not yet started, but target on monitor). Avoid tachycardia (worsens gradient). Start vasopressor (phenylephrine preferred, pure alpha) if needed; avoid epinephrine/dobutamine (inotropic effect worsens gradient). Parameters within range
Pacer wire check Atrial + ventricular thresholds (should be ≤ 5 mA); sense (should see dual spikes on monitor with native beats). Document capture + sense. Do NOT remove wires. Thresholds recorded; wires functional
Baseline rhythm & conduction 12-lead ECG POD 0; note baseline PR interval, QRS duration, any LBBB (common post-AVR but also occurs post-myectomy). Document baseline; repeat if any rhythm change. ECG documented
Bleeding & transfusion CT output trend (target < 200 mL/h); transfuse PRBC if Hgb < 8 (< 9 if age > 70 or CAD). Check CBC q4h POD 0. CT < 200 mL/h; Hgb stable
Electrolytes Check K⁺ (target ≥ 4.0), Mg²⁺ (target ≥ 2.0) q4h POD 0. Correct hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia aggressively (preload for arrhythmia prevention in HCM + post-op inflammation). K⁺ ≥ 4.0; Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0
Labs CBC, BMP, troponin (baseline), lactate. Repeat troponin q12h POD 0–1 (ensure no myocardial ischemia from septum resection). Labs reviewed; trends noted

sections.heading: 5B. POD 1–3 (ICU → Stepdown Transition)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Start beta-blocker, mobilize, maintain HCM hemodynamics, prepare transfer, monitor pacer wires

Task Action Target
Beta-blocker initiation Start POD 1 — metoprolol 25 mg BID (or carvedilol 6.25 BID, or esmolol if PO not yet available). Goal HR 50–70 (more aggressive than typical post-op). This is the single most important medication for HCM management post-op. Beta-blocker dosed and tolerated
Hemodynamic management Maintain SBP 100–130, MAP ≥ 70, CVP 8–12, HR 60–80. Wean vasopressors slowly (they are supporting the HCM hemodynamic goal); target off by POD 2–3 if possible. If hypotensive after vasopressor wean, add volume (IV bolus) before adding inotrope. NEVER use epi/dopamine reflexively; volume + phenylephrine is the answer. Off pressors or low-dose support
Electrolytes K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0. Continue aggressive repletion (POAF + arrhythmia risk high post-op). Hypomagnesemia makes K refractory; correct both. Electrolytes trending into range
Mobility & PT Out of bed to chair POD 1; walking POD 2–3 with sternal support. Encourage mobility; improves hemodynamics and recovery. Advancing as tolerated
Pacer wires Do NOT remove. Check thresholds daily (should remain ≤ 5 mA; rising threshold suggests wire malposition or edema). Assess rhythm on monitor for any bradycardia or loss of capture. Wires remain in; thresholds stable
Chest tube management Check drainage q8h (goal < 150 mL/8 h × 8 h = ready for removal). Notify surgeon before removal. CXR after removal. CTs out if criteria met, or planned
Foley removal Remove POD 1–2 if UOP > 0.5 mL/kg/h and patient mobile/oriented. Foley out; voiding spontaneously
Transfer criteria Hemodynamically stable (SBP 100–130 on low-dose vasopressor or off), extubated, HR 60–80 on beta-blocker, pacer wires in place, CTs manageable or out, tele-ready, mental status baseline Ready for stepdown

sections.heading: 5C. POD 4–7 (Stepdown → Discharge)
sections.bodyHtml:
Goals: Remove pacer wires, finalize discharge teaching, confirm gradient relief on imaging, plan follow-up

Task Action Target
Pacer wire removal POD 4–5 per surgeon preference. Obtain baseline CXR after removal. Note: heart block can occur delayed as edema peaks POD 2–3 then resolves. Most blocks resolve spontaneously by POD 5–7. Persistent complete block → EP consult for PPM evaluation. Wires removed; post-removal CXR done
Rhythm monitoring Continue tele through discharge (block can occur POD 2–5). If symptomatic bradycardia or loss of AV conduction after wire removal, notify team STAT. No new arrhythmias
Beta-blocker optimization Continue POD 1 dose or titrate up per team (goal HR 50–70). Accept lower SBP (HF principle: BP goals are secondary to HR control in HCM). Beta-blocker tolerated; HR controlled
Additional HCM meds Consider verapamil (non-DHP CCB) or disopyramide (Class IA antiarrhythmic) if beta-blocker alone insufficient. Disopyramide is particularly useful for residual SAM (reduces contractility + SAM). Coordinate with cardiology/CT surgery. Additional meds initiated if needed
Discharge medications Beta-blocker lifelong (cornerstone of HCM management). ASA 81 mg daily. Home anticoagulation resumed if concurrent AF (warfarin or DOAC per cardiology). Avoid NSAIDs (increase PPM infection risk if PPM placed; increase bleeding if anticoagulated). DC med list reviewed with patient
Discharge teaching (1) Beta-blocker is lifelong — never skip. (2) Family screening: "All your first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) need a screening echocardiogram and genetic counseling." Provide referral. (3) Sternal precautions: arm support × 6–8 weeks, no lifting > 10 lbs × 3 months, no driving × 4 weeks. (4) Activity: short walks encouraged, sexual activity 4–6 weeks, return to work depends on job. (5) ICD evaluation: if SCD risk and no ICD pre-op, ensure EP consult completed before discharge. (6) Follow-up: surgeon 1 week (incision), 4 weeks (full visit); echocardiogram 30–90 days post-op (critical to confirm gradient < 20 mmHg, no residual SAM). Teaching documented; patient verbalized understanding
Cardiac rehab Referral to Phase 2 cardiac rehab; start post-op week 3–4 (avoid high-intensity early; HCM patients benefit from steady-state aerobic conditioning). Referral sent; patient appointment confirmed

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR Template for Complications

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p septal myectomy for obstructive HCM." B: "Patient developed [symptom/finding: hypotension, bradycardia, recurrent chest pain, etc.]. [Relevant vitals: SBP, HR, CVP, urine output]. Recent labs: [K⁺, Mg²⁺, Troponin, Lactate]. On [current meds/support: beta-blocker dose, vasopressor, IV rate]." A: "[Preliminary assessment: possible residual LVOTO, complete heart block, POAF, bleeding, etc.] Hemodynamic status: [stable/unstable]. Pacer wire function: [thresholds, capture, sense status]." R: "Requesting [pacer wire check, echo, STAT cardiology/surgeon consultation, OR standby, etc.]."

Who to Call — By Scenario

Situation Contact Urgency
Acute hypotension (SBP < 90), worsening despite fluids (rule out residual LVOTO) Surgeon + cardiology STAT EMERGENT
Complete heart block, symptomatic bradycardia (loss of AV conduction on pacer wires) Surgeon + cardiology STAT EMERGENT — prepare external pacing pads
New chest pain POD 0–2 (rule out myocardial ischemia from septum resection) Surgeon + cardiology STAT URGENT — STAT EKG + troponin
Unstable POAF (hypotension, altered mental status, pulmonary edema) APP/fellow + Rapid Response STAT — prepare cardioversion
Persistent oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) despite fluid challenge Primary team; nephrology if worsening URGENT
Fever POD 3–5 (rule out sternal infection, HAP) Primary team; ID if culture positive URGENT
New murmur or signs of valve insufficiency (post-myectomy: unexpected finding) Cardiology + echo STAT URGENT
Pacer wire threshold rising (> 10 mA; possible malposition or edema) Surgeon per protocol ROUTINE

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections expandable for expert skim.

7.1 — Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy (HCM) and Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM) Pathophysiology What is HCM? Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a primary genetic disorder of the myocardium caused by pathogenic variants in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins (troponin, myosin, titin, etc.). The hallmark is unexplained LV wall thickness ≥ 15 mm on echocardiography. The hypertrophy is often asymmetric, predominantly affecting the basal interventricular septum. The disease causes:
  1. Dynamic LVOT obstruction (in ~70% of HCM patients): the hypertrophied septum narrows the LV outflow tract
  2. Diastolic dysfunction: stiff LV wall impairs filling, raises filling pressures, contributes to symptoms (dyspnea, fatigue)
  3. Arrhythmia substrate: myocardial fiber disarray and scarring predispose to atrial fibrillation and ventricular arrhythmias Why Systolic Anterior Motion (SAM) Occurs During ventricular systole, the mitral anterior leaflet is sucked toward (anterior to) the hypertrophied septum—a phenomenon called SAM. This SAM directly narrows the LVOT, creating a dynamic pressure gradient that worsens during systole. Factors that worsen SAM (and increase gradient):
    • Decreased preload (volume depletion, diuretics)
    • Decreased afterload (vasodilators, low blood pressure)
    • Increased contractility (inotropes, catecholamines, exercise) Factors that improve SAM (and decrease gradient):
    • Increased preload (IV fluids, head-down position)
    • Increased afterload (vasoconstrictors, hand-grip maneuver at bedside)
    • Decreased contractility (beta-blockers, verapamil, disopyramide) Why Surgery is Effective Septal myectomy physically removes the obstruction by resecting 1–2 cm of the basal septum, enlarging the LVOT. Once the septum is adequately resected, the mitral anterior leaflet no longer impacts the septum during systole, SAM resolves, and the gradient drops to < 20 mmHg at rest and with exercise. Myectomy is a permanent fix (unlike medical therapy, which merely reduces symptoms but doesn't cure obstruction).
7.2 — Measurement of LVOT Gradient and Echo Guidance How is LVOT Gradient Measured? Pre-op: Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) with Doppler imaging. A continuous-wave (CW) Doppler beam is aimed across the LVOT to measure the velocity of blood flow. The velocity is converted to a pressure gradient using the simplified Bernoulli equation: Gradient = 4 × (velocity)². - Normal LVOT gradient: < 10 mmHg at rest - Mild obstruction: 10–30 mmHg - Moderate obstruction: 30–50 mmHg - Severe obstruction: > 50 mmHg (surgical indication if symptoms present) Stress testing (exercise echocardiography or Valsalva maneuver) may unmask exercise-induced or latent gradients (> 80 mmHg with stress = surgical indication even if resting gradient < 50 mmHg). Intra-operative TEE Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is performed intra-op:
  • Pre-bypass: confirm gradient and SAM anatomy
  • Post-bypass (post-myectomy): reassess LVOT, measure new gradient (should be < 20 mmHg), check for residual SAM, assess for new ventricular septal defect (VSD) or aortic regurgitation (AR) from retractor injury If post-myectomy gradient remains > 30 mmHg or SAM persists, surgeon may need to resect more septum or perform concurrent mitral valve repair (papillary muscle repositioning or edge-to-edge technique). Post-Discharge Echocardiography (POD 30–90) Essential to confirm:
  • LVOT gradient remains < 20 mmHg at rest
  • No residual SAM
  • No new AR, MR, or VSD
  • LV function and size If residual gradient or SAM found at post-discharge echo, cardiology/CT surgery team reconvenes to discuss rescue intervention (repeat myectomy vs. alcohol septal ablation, though latter is less favored at experienced myectomy centers).
7.3 — Morrow Procedure vs. Extended Myectomy (Anatomic Variants) Classic Morrow Procedure (Historical, Minimal Resection) Original technique by surgeon C.C. Morrow (1960s): minimal basal septum resection (0.5–1 cm), focusing only on the area immediately below the aortic valve that creates the LVOT gradient. Advantages: - Minimal risk of bundle of His injury (smaller resection area)
  • Shorter operative time Disadvantages:
  • May leave residual gradient if papillary muscle obstruction co-exists
  • Higher re-operation rate in early literature (now mostly replaced by extended myectomy) Extended Myectomy (Current Standard) Modern approach: more aggressive septal resection (1–2 cm of basal septum), often with attention to:
  • Septal branch arteries (carefully protected)
  • Papillary muscle anterior displacement (if present, may require papillary muscle repositioning)
  • Mitochondrial crista obstruction (rare; requires aggressive resection) Advantages:
  • Lower residual gradient rates (< 10% with residual gradient > 20 mmHg)
  • Better long-term symptom relief Disadvantages:
  • Slightly higher risk of AV block (bundle of His is closer to more extensive resection site)
  • Longer CPB time Decision on Resection Extent Surgeon decision based on:
  • Preoperative echo anatomy (septum thickness, papillary muscle position, SAM mechanism)
  • Intra-operative TEE (real-time visualization of septum, gradient, SAM)
  • Surgeon experience and preference At experienced centers (e.g., Mayo Clinic, Stanford), extended myectomy is favored; 90–95% of patients achieve residual gradient < 20 mmHg POD 0 with good long-term symptom relief and low re-operation rates.
7.4 — Bundle of His Injury and Complete Heart Block Risk (PPM Indication) Why the Bundle of His is at Risk The bundle of His is the main electrical trunk between the AV node and the ventricular septum. Anatomically, it runs along the left side of the ventricular septum just below the aortic valve annulus—directly in the surgical field of septal myectomy. Septal resection or retractor injury can damage the His bundle, causing conduction block. Incidence and Timing
  • Immediate complete heart block (POD 0): occurs in 1–3% of myectomy patients; often resolves within hours as anesthesia wears off
  • Delayed complete heart block (POD 2–5): occurs in 3–5% of patients as surgical edema peaks then resolves; many resolve spontaneously
  • Persistent complete heart block (> POD 5): requires PPM; occurs in 2–10% of myectomy patients (higher than CABG or isolated AVR due to proximity of surgical field to His bundle) LBBB (Left Bundle Branch Block) — Common Post-Myectomy 15–20% of myectomy patients develop new LBBB on the post-op ECG (wide QRS 120–150 ms, characteristic pattern on 12-lead). This is usually benign and does NOT predict progression to complete block. However:
  • LBBB + PR prolongation (≥ 200 ms): concerning for bifascicular block → monitor closely for progression to complete block
  • LBBB + symptomatic bradycardia: if patient has slow escape rhythm (< 40 bpm) with symptoms, pacing may be needed Most LBBB resolves or remains stable; watch for progression to higher-degree block. PPM Indications Post-Myectomy Standard indications for PPM placement before discharge:
    1. Persistent complete heart block (no AV conduction on pacer wire testing after 5–7 days post-op)
    2. High-degree AV block with symptomatic bradycardia (narrow escape rhythm, low CO symptoms despite pacing wires)
    3. Sinus node dysfunction (rare post-myectomy but can occur if isolated SA node injury) Management of Complete Heart Block Post-Myectomy
    4. POD 0: If complete block appears immediately post-op, check pacer wire thresholds. If wires capture and patient hemodynamically stable, observe (block often resolves as anesthesia wears off).
    5. POD 1–3: Continue pacer wire surveillance. If block persists and patient symptomatic (SBP < 90, altered mental status), consider temporary external pacing pads while assessing recovery potential.
    6. POD 3–5: If block resolving (return of normal or 1st-degree AV conduction), continue to observe. If persistent, discuss with EP for PPM planning.
    7. POD 5–7: If block still present and not recovering, PPM placement indicated before discharge. Patient can go home with PPM. Important: Do NOT remove pacer wires early. They are the safety net for delayed heart block. Leave in place through POD 4–5 minimum per surgeon guidance.
7.5 — Post-Operative Hemodynamic Goals: Why HCM is Opposite of CABG The HCM Hemodynamic Paradox Most post-op cardiac patients benefit from:
  • Diuresis (reduce fluid load)
  • Normal/low-normal afterload (vasodilate to improve cardiac output)
  • Normal contractility or inotropic support (maintain CO) Myectomy patients need the OPPOSITE because their obstruction is dynamic:
    ParameterHCM Post-MyectomyCABG / Most CardiacWhy Different?
    PreloadHIGH — maintain full (CVP 8–12)Euvolemic to mild diuresisLVOT closure increases with low preload
    Heart rateSLOW — 60–80 (allow diastolic fill time)Normal 80–100 acceptableSAM worsens with tachycardia
    Afterload / SVRHIGH (vasoconstrict, MAP 70–90)Normal or low (afterload reduction)Reduced afterload worsens gradient
    InotropesAVOID (epi, dopamine, dobutamine)Use as needed for CO supportContractility INCREASES LVOT obstruction
    VasodilatorsAVOID (nitroprusside, nitroglycerin, hydralazine)Use for hypertension managementReduced afterload worsens gradient
    DiureticsUse cautiously (not aggressively)Standard diuresis for most patientsHypovolemia collapses LVOT
    Practical Example: Hypotensive Myectomy Patient
    • Wrong approach (CABG-trained nurse): "BP is 90 systolic, give epi and diuretics"
    • Right approach (myectomy-trained nurse): "BP is 90, give IV bolus (normal saline 500 mL), then add phenylephrine (pure alpha, no inotropic effect). Avoid epi and diuretics." The reason: inotropes increase contractility → SAM worsens → LVOT gradient increases → paradoxically worsens hypotension. Volume + vasoconstriction is the answer. Phenylephrine as First-Line Pressor Phenylephrine is the vasopressor of choice post-myectomy because it:
    • Is a pure alpha-1 agonist (no beta/inotropic effect)
    • Increases afterload without increasing contractility
    • Does not cause reflex tachycardia (unlike norepinephrine or epinephrine)
    • Does not worsen LVOT obstruction Dosing: 0.5–1.4 mcg/kg/min IV infusion; titrate to MAP ≥ 70. Beta-Blocker as Fundamental Therapy Beta-blockers are the foundation of HCM management because they:
      1. Decrease heart rate → prolongs diastolic filling time
      2. Decrease contractility → reduces SAM and LVOT gradient
      3. Reduce arrhythmia risk (HCM patients are arrhythmia-prone) Beta-blocker must be started POD 1 and continued lifelong. This is non-negotiable. If BP is borderline, the HF principle applies: accept a lower SBP to keep the beta-blocker on.
7.6 — Alcohol Septal Ablation (ASA) vs. Surgical Myectomy Comparison Alcohol Septal Ablation (Percutaneous, Catheter-Based) Alternative to surgery for obstructive HCM; performed by interventional cardiologist in the catheterization laboratory. Procedure: - Coronary angiography to identify first septal perforator branch (small artery feeding the anterior septum)
  • Balloon catheter placed in septal perforator; ethanol (96% alcohol) injected to create controlled infarction of septum
  • Infarcted tissue shrinks over weeks, enlarging LVOT Advantages:
  • Non-surgical (no sternotomy, CPB, ICU stay)
  • Shorter recovery (same-day or 1-night admission)
  • Lower cost Disadvantages:
  • Higher PPM rate: 5–15% of patients need PPM (vs. 2–10% myectomy) — infarction creates conduction disturbance
  • Procedural mortality: 1–3% (lower at experienced centers, but real)
  • Non-reversible: once ethanol injected, cannot undo
  • Residual gradient: 15–20% of patients have residual gradient > 30 mmHg
  • VSD risk: small but catastrophic if happens (< 1% but patient symptomatic, may need emergent surgery)
  • Long-term durability: less long-term data than myectomy (myectomy is durable 20–30 years)
  • Not recommended for high-risk anatomy: papillary muscle obstruction, long-segment obstruction (anatomy better suited for surgical resection) Who gets ASA?
  • Patients unwilling to undergo surgery
  • Patients at prohibitive surgical risk (advanced age, frailty, major comorbidities)
  • NOT recommended at non-experienced centers (outcomes better at specialized HCM centers with both surgical and interventional expertise) Surgical Septal Myectomy (Open Surgery) Advantages:
  • Direct visualization and resection of obstruction
  • Ability to adapt resection in real-time (intra-op TEE guidance)
  • Ability to address papillary muscle abnormalities
  • Lower PPM rate (2–10% vs. 5–15% ASA)
  • Better long-term outcomes: lower residual gradient, better symptom relief, lower re-operation rate
  • More durable (standard practice at major cardiac centers) Disadvantages:
  • Surgical: median sternotomy, CPB, ICU stay, longer recovery
  • Higher perioperative risk (mortality 1–3% at experienced centers; 5–10% at less experienced centers) At Experienced HCM Centers: Myectomy is Preferred Society guidelines (Ommen et al., 2020 AHA/ACC HCM guideline) recommend surgical myectomy as first-line for symptomatic obstructive HCM refractory to medical therapy, especially at centers with experienced surgeons (> 20 myectomy procedures/year). Outcomes are superior:
  • Lower PPM rate
  • Better gradient relief
  • Lower re-operation rate
  • Excellent long-term survival (> 95% at 10 years) ASA is reserved for patients at very high surgical risk or those declining surgery.
7.7 — Medical Management Pre-Operative (Disopyramide, Verapamil, Beta-Blockers) Beta-Blockers (First-Line, All Symptomatic HCM Patients) Mechanism: Negative inotrope + chronotrope + improve diastolic filling Dosing: Target HR 50–60 at rest - Metoprolol XL 190–380 mg daily (or divided BID)
  • Propranolol 120–480 mg daily (divided)
  • Carvedilol 25–50 mg BID Goal: Symptom relief and gradient reduction (usually 25–50% gradient reduction) Side effects: Bradycardia, hypotension, fatigue, cold extremities Non-Dihydropyridine Calcium Channel Blockers (Second-Line, If Beta-Blocker Insufficient) Mechanism: Negative inotrope + negative chronotrope + improve diastolic relaxation Dosing:
  • Verapamil 240–480 mg daily (divided or XL)
  • Diltiazem 120–480 mg daily (less commonly used; less effective than verapamil for LVOT obstruction) Efficacy: Similar to beta-blockers; ~25–50% gradient reduction Caution: Contraindicated if EF < 50% (negative inotrope worsens HF). Not to be used with beta-blockers if patient develops AV block risk. Side effects: Constipation (verapamil), edema (diltiazem), hypotension Disopyramide (Class IA Antiarrhythmic, Refractory Cases) Mechanism: Strong negative inotrope (more potent than beta-blockers + verapamil); also reduces SAM by decreasing contractility; has class IA antiarrhythmic properties (POAF prevention) Dosing: 300–600 mg daily (divided) Efficacy: 50–75% gradient reduction in refractory cases; particularly useful for patients with persistent SAM and arrhythmia burden Side effects: Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, glaucoma risk); hypotension; arrhythmias (proarrhythmic potential in some patients) Use case: Reserved for refractory symptoms despite maximal beta-blocker + verapamil. Often used pre-op in patients awaiting myectomy to maximize symptom control. Dual or Triple Therapy Many patients require combination therapy:
  • Beta-blocker + verapamil (synergistic effect, but monitor for bradycardia/AV block)
  • Beta-blocker + disopyramide (used especially pre-op)
  • All three (rare, requires careful BP/HR monitoring) Post-Myectomy Medications After successful myectomy, medical therapy requirements often decrease. Many patients are able to discontinue verapamil or disopyramide and maintain symptoms on beta-blocker alone. Beta-blocker is continued lifelong as cornerstone therapy.
7.8 — Residual or Recurrent SAM/LVOTO: Recognition and Rescue Therapy Why Residual SAM Occurs (5–10% of Myectomy Patients) Despite adequate septal resection (confirmed on intra-op TEE with gradient < 20 mmHg), some patients develop worsening LVOT obstruction post-op due to:
  1. Inadequate septal resection — surgeon underestimated extent needed (now rare with extended myectomy)
  2. Papillary muscle anterior displacement — myectomy addressed only the septum; SAM due to anteriorly positioned papillary muscle not addressed
  3. Mitral leaflet elongation — native anatomic variation; leaflet too long, still hits septum even after resection
  4. Dynamic posterior left ventricular wall — rare; LV wall contracting inward, narrowing LVOT (not septum-related) Clinical Recognition of Residual/Recurrent SAM
    • Worsening hypotension on POD 1–3 despite adequate filling and vasopressor support
    • New or worsening murmur on exam (harsh systolic murmur may increase in intensity)
    • Elevated lactate and cool extremities → low cardiac output state
    • Rising troponin → possible subendocardial ischemia from LVOT obstruction Escalation and Imaging
    • STAT echocardiography (trans-esophageal echo if available; trans-thoracic if bedside TTE adequate): measure LVOT gradient, assess SAM mechanism (septum vs. papillary muscle vs. leaflet)
    • Notify surgeon and cardiology STAT
    • Assess hemodynamic response: if patient deteriorates despite fluids + vasopressors, consider OR standby for emergent re-exploration Rescue Interventions
      1. If inadequate septal resection (residual gradient > 30 mmHg, SAM from septal contact):
      2. Discuss emergent redo myectomy (same operative day or next day)
      3. Extended resection to address residual septum
      4. If papillary muscle obstruction:
      5. Papillary muscle repositioning or partial division
      6. May require concurrent mitral valve surgery (edge-to-edge stitch to alter leaflet-SAM relationship)
      7. If mitochondrial/apical HCM variant (very rare):
      8. Extended myectomy to include apical regions
      9. Specialized intervention at experienced centers only
      10. Conservative management (if gradient mild, patient stable):
      11. Aggressive volume support
      12. Beta-blocker + disopyramide optimization
      13. Repeat echo 4–6 weeks post-op; many cases improve as post-op edema resolves and LV contractility recovers Prognosis Post-Myectomy
      14. 90–95% of patients achieve residual gradient < 20 mmHg and good long-term symptom relief
      15. 5–10% require intervention (redo myectomy, rescue mitral repair, medical optimization)
      16. Re-operation rate is low at experienced centers (< 5% at 10 years)
7.9 — Family Screening and Genetic Counseling (Autosomal Dominant HCM) Genetics of HCM HCM is autosomal dominant — pathogenic variants in sarcomeric protein genes (MYH7, MYBPC3, TNNT2, TPMI, etc.) are inherited with 50% transmission to each child. Not all carriers are symptomatic; penetrance ranges 50–70%. First-Degree Relative Screening Required All first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) of a myectomy patient should undergo:
  1. 12-lead ECG (screen for LVH, repolarization abnormalities)
  2. Transthoracic echocardiography (definitive; assess LV wall thickness, LVOT obstruction, LV function)
  3. Genetic counseling (explain inheritance, implications for family members, reproductive counseling)
  4. Genetic testing (identify the pathogenic variant if available; helps confirm diagnosis in other family members) Screening Interval
    • If negative screening: repeat echo every 3–5 years until age 18 (variants may not be penetrant in childhood)
    • Starting at age 5–10 is reasonable (some centers recommend serial screening from age 5)
    • Siblings and children: echo yearly or biennial once diagnosis confirmed in index patient Implications for Relatives
    • If relative has HCM but no obstruction: beta-blocker not needed; observe. If symptoms or obstruction develops, reassess.
    • If relative has obstructive HCM: initiate beta-blocker (target HR 50–60) + consider AICD evaluation if SCD risk present AICD and SCD Risk Stratification HCM patients at high risk for sudden cardiac death should have AICD (ICD). Risk factors:
    • Family history of HCM-related SCD
    • Unexplained syncope
    • LV wall thickness ≥ 30 mm
    • Abnormal blood pressure response to exercise
    • Recurrent sustained VT on Holter Teaching Point for Myectomy Patient During discharge teaching, emphasize: "All your first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) need a screening echocardiogram and genetic counseling. This is not optional — HCM runs in families, and early detection can prevent sudden death in your relatives." Provide genetic counselor contact and echo scheduling.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear, re-escalate.

  • New or worsening hypotension (SBP < 90) on POD 1–3 despite fluid challenge and vasopressor support: residual/recurrent LVOTO until proven otherwise → STAT echo, notify surgeon
  • Bradycardia (HR < 40) with widened QRS (> 120 ms) and no prior LBBB documented: complete heart block developing → pacer wire check STAT; prepare external pacing pads
  • Rising lactate + cool extremities + oliguria despite normal filling pressures: low cardiac output from dynamic LVOTO → STAT echo, prepare OR standby
  • Widening PR interval on serial ECGs (progressing from normal to 200+ ms): bifascicular block evolving → notify team; block may progress to complete within hours
  • New murmur POD 1–3 (diastolic or changing in character): possible iatrogenic aortic regurgitation from retractor injury, or septal defect → echo STAT
  • Fever POD 3–5 + elevated WBC/CRP + new white count left shift: sternal infection vs. post-op inflammation → wound exam, CT chest if DSWI suspected
  • New irregular rhythm (POAF) + rapid ventricular rate (HR > 130) unresponsive to beta-blocker: rate-control failure; risk of hemodynamic collapse → escalate rate-control plan (add verapamil or amiodarone per team)
  • Sudden loss of pacer wire capture (no QRS after pacing spike on monitor): wire malposition or high threshold → notify surgeon; may need wire repositioning
  • Hgb drop > 2 g/dL in 4 h + tachycardia + cool extremities: occult bleeding (mediastinal or pleural) → check CT output, prepare for OR re-exploration
  • New focal neuro deficit (arm weakness, speech change): aortic atheroma mobilization or stroke → STAT neurology + CT head
  • Confusion + restlessness POD 2–3 + hypoxia: delirium likely (post-op inflammation, pain, constipation, hypoxia) → optimize all reversibles; avoid sedation unless necessary
  • Pacer wire threshold rising from ≤ 5 mA to > 10 mA: wire malposition or edema around tip → notify surgeon; may need repositioning before POD 4–5 planned removal
  • Persistent oliguria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h × 4 h) despite normal CVP and adequate IV intake: acute kidney injury or severe low output → check creatinine, lactate; urinalysis; consider echo

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. AVOID inotropes — they INCREASE LVOT gradient, not decrease it. A hypotensive myectomy patient getting epi/dopamine reflexively is being harmed. The answer is IV fluid bolus + phenylephrine (pure alpha). This contradicts standard CABG/valve surgery teaching and is a common error.

  2. AVOID vasodilators and diuretics in myectomy patients. Reduced preload collapses the LVOT, worsening obstruction paradoxically. Aggressive diuresis post-op is dangerous. Keep them full; target CVP 8–12 cm H₂O.

  3. Beta-blocker is non-negotiable; start POD 1 and never stop. Beta-blocker is the cornerstone of HCM management — both acutely and lifelong. If BP is borderline, accept lower SBP to keep the beta-blocker on (HF principle: rate control > BP control).

  4. Phenylephrine is the first-line pressor. Pure alpha-1 agonist, no inotropic effect, no tachycardia reflex. This is different from standard post-op practice (where norepinephrine or epinephrine are often first-line). Learn this difference.

  5. Don't pull pacer wires early. The bundle of His runs through the septum. Heart block can occur delayed (POD 2–5) as edema peaks then resolves. Wires are the safety net. Keep them in through POD 4–5 minimum; surgeon will tell you when it's safe to remove.

  6. New LBBB post-myectomy is common but usually benign. 15–20% develop LBBB; most does NOT progress to complete block. However, LBBB + PR prolongation (≥ 200 ms) = red flag for bifascicular block → monitor closely for progression to complete block.

  7. PPM rate is 2–10%, not rare. This is higher than isolated CABG or AVR because the surgical field is adjacent to the His bundle. Consent the patient pre-op: "There's a 2–10% chance you'll need a pacemaker if we injure the electrical system during surgery."

  8. Residual LVOT gradient on POD 0 TEE < 20 mmHg is the goal. If post-myectomy TEE shows residual gradient > 30 mmHg or persistent SAM, surgeon may redo resection same day or next day. Don't accept high residual gradient.

  9. Alcohol septal ablation (ASA) is NOT equivalent to myectomy. ASA has higher PPM rate (5–15%), higher residual gradient (15–20%), irreversible VSD risk, and worse long-term outcomes at non-experienced centers. At experienced myectomy centers, surgery is strongly preferred. If ASA is offered, make sure it's from an experienced HCM center.

  10. Family screening is a non-negotiable discharge teaching point. HCM is autosomal dominant. All first-degree relatives (parents, siblings, children) need screening echo + genetic counseling. Many families don't know this; it's a teaching opportunity. Provide genetic counselor contact before discharge.

  11. ICD evaluation pre-discharge if high SCD risk. Review pre-op risk stratification. If patient has risk factors (family hx of SCD, unexplained syncope, LV wall thickness ≥ 30 mm, abnormal exercise BP response) and no ICD pre-op, ensure EP consult completed. Don't send patient home without addressing AICD need.

  12. Discharge echo 30–90 days is mandatory. Confirms LVOT gradient < 20 mmHg, no residual SAM, no new AR/MR/VSD. If residual gradient or SAM found, cardiology/CT surgery reconvenes for possible rescue intervention. Don't forget to schedule this before discharge.

  13. POAF is common in HCM patients (15–25% post-myectomy). Enlarged LA from chronic diastolic dysfunction predisposes to AF. Aggressively correct K⁺ (≥ 4.0) + Mg²⁺ (≥ 2.0). Rate control preferred (avoid cardioversion if possible due to filling dependence). If AF develops, warfarin is indicated (not just for POAF, but because mechanical valves and AF together require AC).

  14. Pregnancy + HCM requires specialized counseling pre-op. Women of child-bearing age should understand: HCM is heritable, pregnancy increases hemodynamic stress (reduced SVR, increased CO demand), and they should defer conception if uncontrolled HCM. Coordinate with maternal-fetal medicine if patient is pregnant or planning pregnancy.

  15. Discharge echo 30–90 days confirms surgical success. Provides peace of mind to patient and team. If gradient rises or SAM recurs, imaging guides next steps. This is the "final check" on myectomy outcome.

cards.title: NIH Stroke Scale (NIHSS)
cards.quickAnswer: The NIHSS is a rapid (5–8 min), 15-item bedside scale quantifying acute stroke severity on a 0–42 scale. Higher scores = worse deficits and predict mortality/disability. Baseline NIHSS before any procedure is essential for post-cardiac surgery patients; serial scores detect new neurologic decline, especially after DHCA or arch repair. A new rise ≥4 points signals significant change; compare to baseline and notify the team to trigger imaging and code stroke workup if applicable.

sections.heading: 1. Definition and Scoring
sections.bodyHtml:
The National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is a validated, standardized assessment tool that quantifies the severity of acute ischemic stroke by testing 15 specific neurologic domains. Each item is scored by severity; the sum ranges from 0 (no stroke) to 42 (maximum deficit).

Administration: Takes 5–8 min at the bedside with no equipment. Can be repeated serially (q1h initially post-acute event, then q shift on stepdown/telemetry). Does not require imaging or blood work.

sections.heading: 2. The 15 Items at a Glance
sections.bodyHtml:
Item # Domain Scored Normal = 0 Severe =
1a Level of Consciousness (LOC) 0–3 Awake & alert Comatose
1b LOC Questions (orientation) 0–2 Correct Both wrong
1c LOC Commands (obedience) 0–2 Obeys both None obey
2 Best Gaze (horizontal eye movement) 0–2 Normal Gaze deviation
3 Visual Fields (confrontation) 0–3 No loss Bilateral hemianopia
4 Facial Palsy (asymmetry) 0–3 Normal symmetry Complete paralysis
5a Motor Arm Left 0–4 No drift No movement
5b Motor Arm Right 0–4 No drift No movement
6a Motor Leg Left 0–4 No drift No movement
6b Motor Leg Right 0–4 No drift No movement
7 Limb Ataxia 0–2 No ataxia Marked ataxia
8 Sensory (pain/touch) 0–2 Normal Absent
9 Language (speech/comprehension) 0–3 No aphasia Global aphasia
10 Dysarthria (speech clarity) 0–2 Clear speech Unable to assess
11 Extinction/Inattention 0–2 No neglect Bilateral neglect

Total: Sum of all 15 items. Range 0–42. Higher = worse outcomes.

sections.heading: 3. Severity Interpretation and Prognosis
sections.bodyHtml:
NIHSS Score Severity Clinical Implication 3-Month Outcome Trend
0 No stroke Normal exam. R/O TIA or other diagnosis. Excellent; no treatment needed
1–4 Minor stroke Small infarct; minimal deficits. Good; mostly independent (mRS ≤ 2)
5–15 Moderate stroke Significant but non-disabling deficits. Variable; tPA candidate if within window
16–20 Moderate-severe stroke Substantial deficits; disability likely. Moderate risk; tPA + thrombectomy candidate
21–42 Severe stroke Major deficits; high mortality/disability risk. Poor; ~50% mortality at 30 days

Prognostic pearls: NIHSS at 24 h predicts 3-month modified Rankin score better than baseline. Every 1-point rise in NIHSS at 24 h increases mortality risk ~5% (Powers et al., 2019).

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use — Serial Neuro Exams Post-Cardiac Surgery
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac surgery patients at stroke risk (especially after DHCA, aortic arch repair, or transplant) require baseline NIHSS and serial monitoring. Baseline before induction establishes a reference; any rise ≥4 points signals new neurologic deficit warranting imaging and team notification.

Workflow:

  • Pre-op / baseline: Obtain NIHSS before incision; document as "baseline NIHSS."
  • POD 0 post-ICU transfer: Handoff with baseline + interval exams.
  • POD 0–1: Repeat at 1, 4, 12, 24 h (especially post-DHCA or arch repair).
  • POD 2–4: Assess q shift (q8h). Compare to baseline.
  • POD 5+: Routine neuro checks per protocol; NIHSS as indicated.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Inter-rater variability and certification Scoring variability exists without standardized training (especially gaze, ataxia, language items). AHA online NIHSS certification (~15 min) reduces variability and is recommended for all acute care nurses. Two nurses may score the same exam differently; certification training improves agreement.
Common scoring pitfalls by item
  • Language (item 9) and LOC questions (item 1b): Aphasic or non-English-speaking patients are difficult. Score what you observe; if unable to determine due to language barrier, score 3 (unknown).
  • Comatose patients: Cannot test most items; assume worst case (score 3 per item unable to assess); total often = 42.
  • Subtle neglect (item 11): Use bilateral simultaneous stimuli (both hands, both visual fields). Patient ignoring one side = score 1 or 2.
  • Motor items 5a–6b: Test both arms and both legs separately. Asymmetry (e.g., only right arm weakness) points to contralateral stroke territory.
Pre-existing deficits vs new change Some cardiac patients have prior TIA/stroke history. Baseline NIHSS captures pre-existing deficits; serial comparison is what matters. A patient with baseline NIHSS = 5 who rises to NIHSS = 8 has new 3-point deficit, not 8 total. Always document baseline prominently.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Baseline BEFORE procedure/sedation is critical. Obtain NIHSS before induction or anesthesia. If sedated/unable, retest after emergence and note "unable to assess at baseline."
  2. Serial trending > single score. A single NIHSS = 3 may be baseline. A rise from 0 to 3, or 2 to 5, signals change and warrants workup.
  3. Non-English speakers require interpreter. Language item depends on comprehension; without interpretation, score 3 (unknown).
  4. Pulse deficit is the physical finding to teach. Auscultated rate exceeds palpable radial rate in AF. Always palpate during neuro exam to confirm neurologic deficit is not just arrhythmia.
  5. Documentation anchors the stroke team. Write the score AND specific findings (e.g., "NIHSS 4: facial asymmetry R > L, no arm drift, no language deficit"). This guides imaging triage and thrombolytic decisions.
  6. Alternative scales serve different purposes. Modified Rankin is for disability/outcome at discharge; GCS is for coma/consciousness; NIHSS is for acute severity. Know which you are using and why.
  7. Alternative scales serve different purposes. Modified Rankin is for disability/outcome; GCS is for consciousness; NIHSS is for acute severity.

cards.title: NYHA Functional Class
cards.quickAnswer: A 4-tier, clinician-reported, symptom-based functional class (I–IV) for heart failure and valvular disease applied at admission and discharge. Class I: no symptoms with activity. Class IV: symptoms at rest. Discharge NYHA is a key readmission predictor (NYHA II favorable vs III/IV higher risk). Class III–IV patients meet criteria for advanced therapy referral (LVAD, transplant, high-intensity CRT). NYHA improves over 4–6 weeks post-operatively; plateau or worsening signals escalation workup.

Class I: no symptoms with activity. Class IV: symptoms at rest. Discharge NYHA is a key readmission predictor (NYHA II favorable vs III/IV higher risk). Class III–IV patients meet criteria for advanced therapy referral (LVAD, transplant, high-intensity CRT). NYHA improves over 4–6 weeks post-operatively; plateau or worsening signals escalation workup.
cards.sourcePrecedence: NYHA Criteria Committee 1994 → Heidenreich AHA/ACC 2022 → McDonagh ESC 2021 → Raphael KCCQ validation → Green KCCQ → Hardin/Kaplow 2020 → Bojar 6e → AACN

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml: The New York Heart Association Functional Class is a 4-tier assessment reflecting symptomatic burden of cardiac disease on daily activity—not hemodynamic severity, ejection fraction, or objective test results. NYHA answers: "How much does this patient's cardiac disease limit their activities?" Originally published in the 1920s, it remains widely used because it is simple, validated, and independently prognostic across heart failure registries and surgical trials (Heidenreich et al., 2022).

sections.heading: 2. The Four Classes — Table-First
sections.bodyHtml:
Class Symptoms Activity Limit Typical 1-yr mortality (HF)
I No symptoms with any activity None ~5%
II Symptoms with ordinary activity (walking, climbing stairs, housework) Slight 10–15%
III Symptoms with less than ordinary activity (dressing, short walk at own pace, 1–2 flights stairs slowly) Marked 20–25%
IV Symptoms at rest or with minimal exertion Severe; confined to bed or chair >30%

Note: Class III may be subdivided into IIIa (moderate exertion) and IIIb (minimal exertion) in research settings.

Comparison to ACC/AHA Heart Failure Stages (structural perspective):

Stage Structural Finding NYHA Correlation Clinical Implication
A Risk factors, no structural disease I–II Preventive therapy candidate
B Structural HF, no symptoms I Asymptomatic LV dysfunction
C Structural HF + symptoms (current or prior) II–III Guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT)
D Advanced / refractory HF IV or III refractory to GDMT Advanced therapy evaluation

Key distinction: ACC/AHA stages do not regress; NYHA fluctuates with therapy, decompensation, and recovery. A patient may be Stage C (irreversible structural disease) but improve from NYHA IV to II with diuretics and beta-blockers.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Use
sections.bodyHtml:
Admission NYHA reflects pre-operative burden and surgery urgency. Class III–IV signals elevated AKI, delirium, ICU return, and prolonged length of stay risk.

Discharge NYHA is a key readmission predictor. Document explicitly in discharge summary. NYHA II or better = favorable sign; NYHA III or IV = close follow-up and escalation planning required.

NYHA drives advanced therapy conversation. Class IV (or refractory III) + low ejection fraction + optimal medical therapy = LVAD / transplant evaluation candidacy.

Post-operative trajectory is documented over 4–6 weeks. Early plateau or worsening NYHA triggers escalation workup (recurrent decompensation, arrhythmia, graft failure in CABG).

Valve disease. NYHA plus anatomic severity grading (mild, moderate, severe). Aortic stenosis symptom onset (angina, syncope, dyspnea) often marks sudden NYHA shift and is an indication for surgery. Severe asymptomatic aortic stenosis is NYHA I by definition, even if ejection fraction is declining (McDonagh et al., 2021).

sections.heading: 4. Comparison to Objective Functional Tools
sections.bodyHtml:
Tool Basis Strengths Limitations
NYHA Clinician observation + patient report Fast, simple, prognostic, guides referral Observer variability; not granular; subject to interpretation
KCCQ (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy) Patient self-report (23-item questionnaire) Granular, reproducible, tracks subtle change Longer to administer; requires patient literacy
6MWT (6-Minute Walk Test) Objective distance covered Objective functional capacity; strong prognostic Requires patient mobility; <300 m correlates with NYHA III–IV
EF (ejection fraction) Echocardiography (hemodynamic) Prognostic; guides drug therapy; defined phenotype (HFrEF vs HFpEF) Poorly predicts symptoms; many NYHA I with EF 15–20%; many NYHA IV with normal EF

Clinical principle: Use NYHA for quick communication and risk stratification; use KCCQ and 6MWT for research, serial tracking, and phenotyping deconditioning vs true decompensation (Green et al., 2000; Raphael et al., 2007).

sections.heading: 5. Clinical Use — Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
• NYHA is symptomatic, not hemodynamic. A patient with EF 15% who is asymptomatic due to long-standing adaptation may be NYHA I. Conversely, a patient with mild EF reduction (40–50%) and severe mitral regurgitation may be NYHA IV. Do not conflate NYHA with EF.

  • Observer variability is real and clinically meaningful. Different clinicians assign different classes depending on how they frame questions. Always ask the patient directly about specific activities (stairs, dressing, rest symptoms) and document the activity that triggers symptoms, not just the number.

  • NYHA is subjective and fluctuates. A patient may enter NYHA IV, improve to II with guideline-directed medical therapy, then decompensate again if non-adherent. Document the trajectory, not just a snapshot.

  • Deconditioning masquerades as NYHA III. A bedbound ICU discharge with severe deconditioning may report dyspnea on minimal exertion. Serial KCCQ or 6MWT often reveals rapid improvement as conditioning recovers; true cardiac limitation improves more slowly. Trend the class over days–weeks.

  • Discharge NYHA is an important readmission metric. NYHA III or IV at discharge signals close follow-up and escalation planning; NYHA II or better is a favorable prognostic sign.

  • Class III–IV patients are at or near referral thresholds for advanced therapies (LVAD, transplant, high-intensity CRT). Identify these patients early and discuss with the surgical/transplant team.

  • NYHA predicts 1-year mortality independently of EF, biomarkers, and comorbidities. It is a validated, independent prognostic variable in heart failure registries and trials (Heidenreich et al., 2022).

  • NYHA does not capture frailty, cognitive impairment, or polypharmacy burden. A frail NYHA II patient may be at higher risk than a robust NYHA III. Always integrate frailty assessment into clinical decision-making.

  • Valve disease uses NYHA plus anatomic severity grading. Symptom onset in aortic stenosis (angina, syncope, dyspnea) often marks a sudden NYHA shift and is an indication for surgery. Similarly, severe asymptomatic aortic stenosis is NYHA I by definition, even if EF is declining.

  • Patients do not describe symptoms in NYHA terms. Ask about specific functional benchmarks: "Can you walk one flight of stairs without stopping? Two flights? Can you dress yourself? Any dyspnea at rest?" Then map responses to class; don't ask patients to self-assign a number.

  • Document the activity that triggers symptoms, not just the class number. Example: "NYHA III — dyspnea with dressing and walking <100 feet on flat ground" is more actionable than "NYHA III."

  • Post-operative patients "reset" their NYHA baseline. Expect improvement over 4–6 weeks post-CABG or valve repair as revascularization or hemodynamic correction takes effect. Document the trajectory: "POD 0 NYHA III, POD 3 NYHA III, POD 7 NYHA II." Plateau or worsening is a red flag.

  • NYHA in ambulatory HF is a visit-to-visit trend. Rising NYHA in clinic triggers escalation: medication adjustment, diuretic increase, device/transplant evaluation. Falling NYHA signals response to therapy.

  • Compare NYHA to ACC/AHA stage, not instead of. NYHA Class IV can occur with Stage B (asymptomatic LV dysfunction + acute decompensation) or Stage D (refractory). Understanding both provides clinical context.

  • Refractory NYHA III or IV that does not improve with optimization is a transplant/LVAD marker. If GDMT at target doses, reassess for compliance, comorbidities, or need for advanced therapy consult.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology: How NYHA Class Emerges Functional limitation in NYHA classification arises from the mismatch between cardiac output (CO) reserve and metabolic demand. In NYHA I, normal resting CO and preserved CO reserve during exertion allow unrestricted activity. In NYHA II, CO reserve is diminished but sufficient for ordinary exertion (e.g., walking at normal pace); dyspnea appears with increased demand. In NYHA III, the mismatch occurs with minimal exertion (dressing, standing, light walking); in NYHA IV, resting CO is inadequate and dyspnea occurs at rest or with any exertion. The underlying mechanisms vary: systolic dysfunction (reduced ejection fraction), diastolic dysfunction (impaired relaxation or stiffness), valvular disease (stenosis or regurgitation), arrhythmia, pulmonary hypertension, or anemia. NYHA does not distinguish these mechanisms—it is purely symptomatic. Importantly, NYHA reflects the patient's current physiologic state. With optimized guideline-directed medical therapy (ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, aldosterone antagonists, SGLT2 inhibitors), CO reserve may improve and NYHA class may decline. Conversely, acute decompensation, infection, arrhythmia, or non-adherence worsens NYHA acutely.
ACC/AHA Heart Failure Stages vs NYHA Class ACC/AHA stages (A, B, C, D) are structural and irreversible. They define the presence and severity of heart disease and the presence or history of symptoms:
  • Stage A: Risk factors (HTN, diabetes, CAD) but no structural disease
  • Stage B: Structural disease (reduced EF, LV hypertrophy, valve disease) but no symptoms
  • Stage C: Structural disease + symptoms
  • Stage D: Advanced / refractory disease despite GDMT Crucially, stages do not regress. Once a patient has structural disease (Stage B+), they remain in that stage. However, NYHA can fluctuate within a stage. Example: A patient with EF 30% (Stage B before symptom onset) who develops dyspnea on exertion is now Stage C NYHA II. With optimal therapy, the patient may improve to NYHA I but remains Stage C. If the patient decompensates again during clinic visit and is NYHA III despite GDMT, they may be Stage D (refractory). NYHA is dynamic; ACC/AHA stages are progressive and unidirectional. Both inform clinical decision-making.
Subjective Nature + Observer Variability Pearls NYHA assessment depends heavily on:
  1. How the clinician frames questions. Asking "Can you climb two flights of stairs?" vs. "How much can you exert before dyspnea?" yields different answers depending on how the patient interprets the scale.
  2. Patient self-report reliability. Some patients minimize symptoms (denial, fear of surgical referral); others catastrophize mild dyspnea. Cultural differences, language barriers, and cognitive impairment affect responses.
  3. Context. A patient's NYHA may be higher during an acute infection, lower after a vacation, and different depending on how recently they engaged in the benchmark activity.
  4. Baseline frailty. A very frail, deconditioned patient may report NYHA III due to skeletal muscle weakness, not cardiac limitation. To minimize variability:
    • Ask the same clinician to assess the same patient serially when possible.
    • Ask about specific activities (stairs, dressing, walking distance, rest symptoms).
    • Document the activity that triggers symptoms and the exertion level required.
    • Use objective tools (KCCQ, 6MWT) in research or when NYHA discrepancies arise.
Deconditioning vs True Cardiac Limitation A common pitfall in post-operative and ICU patients: a severely deconditioned patient (bedbound for 5+ days post-op, weak legs, deconditioning atrophy) may report dyspnea on minimal exertion. Is this NYHA III cardiac limitation, or deconditioning? Clue: Serial trends.
  • Deconditioning improves rapidly (days) with mobilization and physical therapy; 6MWT distance improves 20–30 meters per day in early recovery.
  • True cardiac limitation improves more slowly (weeks) and plateaus; early post-operative cardiac improvement is modest because remodeling takes weeks. If a patient's NYHA III resolves to NYHA II within 3–5 days of mobilization without medication change, deconditioning was likely the driver. If NYHA remains III despite mobilization, true cardiac limitation and/or other comorbidities (anemia, thyroid, delirium) warrant investigation. Use KCCQ or repeat 6MWT if available to differentiate.
Frailty + NYHA: Why Both Matter NYHA does not capture frailty, cognitive impairment, polypharmacy, or social support. A frail, NYHA II patient living alone may be at higher risk for readmission than a robust, NYHA III patient with family support and daily monitoring. When assessing post-operative risk and discharge readiness:
  • Integrate Clinical Frailty Scale or equivalent.
  • Consider cognitive screening (delirium, dementia).
  • Assess social support and medication adherence.
  • Evaluate comorbidities (renal, pulmonary, neuro). NYHA is one prognostic lens; do not rely on it in isolation for risk stratification or discharge planning.

cards.title: Opioid-Sparing / Multimodal Pain Management Post-Cardiac Surgery
cards.quickAnswer: Post-cardiac surgery pain is managed with scheduled multimodal agents (acetaminophen + NSAID + adjuncts) as baseline, opioids reserved for rescue, and regional techniques when appropriate. Functional goals: mobility, sleep, cough — not pain = zero. NSAIDs require surgical clearance (typically POD 3+). Thoracotomy pain is more severe and often under-treated; anticipate intercostal neuralgia in 20–40% of patients. Start bowel regimen POD 1. Taper opioids at discharge (5–7 days, no refills); document plan for chronic pain risk in discharge summary.
