sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, and scope.

  • Definition: A scheduled non-opioid analgesic foundation with opioids reserved for rescue analgesia. Designed to optimize pain control while reducing opioid-related side effects, enabling early mobility, and preventing chronic post-surgical pain (CPSP).
  • Why it matters: Post-cardiac surgery patients experience severe pain (sternotomy) to very severe pain (thoracotomy). Without a structured multimodal approach, opioid escalation is rapid, side effects accumulate, and functional recovery is delayed.
  • Applies to: All adult post-cardiac surgery patients — CABG, all valve repairs/replacements, aortic surgery, MAZE, myectomy, transplant, ECMO, all procedures. Especially critical for elderly (opioid sensitivity), chronic pain patients (tolerance), substance use history (addiction risk), and COPD (respiratory depression risk).
  • Duration: POD 0–3 (intensive, ICU-level), POD 4–7 (transition to oral), post-discharge (taper and multimodal continuation). CPSP screening at 3 months for thoracotomy patients.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac surgery pain arises from multiple overlapping mechanisms:

Nociceptive (tissue injury): - Surgical incision (sternum or thorax), rib spreading, pericardial irritation, pleural involvement

Inflammatory: - Cardiopulmonary bypass → systemic inflammatory response → mesenteric, splanchnic vasoconstriction → local tissue edema

Neuropathic (POD 1+ onward, especially thoracotomy): - Intercostal nerve injury during retraction or thoracotomy; can persist weeks–months as neuropathic pain

Sympathetic: - Post-op catecholamine surge, pain-mediated stress response, inhibition of parasympathetic tone

Risk factors for severe pain: thoracotomy vs sternotomy, preoperative pain, female sex, anxiety, younger age, pain catastrophizing, prior chronic pain.

The multimodal principle: Different drug classes with different mechanisms act synergistically at lower individual doses, reducing cumulative side effects and opioid burden.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Clinical Context
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — populations, phases, and trigger points.

Universally indicated: - Every post-op cardiac surgery patient, all procedures, POD 1+ (ICU) through discharge

Special populations (apply with modifications per §6):

  • Elderly (>75): Higher opioid sensitivity; start lower doses; aggressive multimodal; avoid gabapentin if fall risk high
  • COPD / sleep apnea: Opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD) risk; emphasize non-opioid baseline; continuous monitoring if opioids used
  • Renal impairment (CrCl <30): Adjust gabapentin, tramadol, morphine doses; monitor accumulation
  • Hepatic disease: Limit acetaminophen (max 2–3 g/day); avoid tramadol (metabolite accumulation)
  • Substance use history: Pain and psychiatry team early; avoid tramadol (serotonin syndrome + seizure risk); consider buprenorphine consultation
  • Chronic pain baseline: Often opioid-tolerant; expect higher breakthrough doses; pain management consult POD 1

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Observe / gather information* (5 minutes per shift)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside and chart review. Information-only; no interventions yet.

Pain location and quality:

  • Numeric rating scale (0–10) + functional assessment (can cough? walk? sleep?)
  • Somatic (sharp, localized incisional) vs neuropathic (burning, radiating, shooting)

Vital signs with pain assessment: - HR, BP trend with pain; tachycardia and hypertension may indicate inadequate pain control or anxiety

Medication history: - Home pain medications, opioid history, addiction risk, prior reactions to analgesics

Current medications on board: - Scheduled acetaminophen timing, NSAID clearance, gabapentin start date, opioid doses

Mobility and function: - Able to cough, deep-breathe, turn in bed, ambulate? Use incentive spirometry (IS)? Sleep quality?

Regional technique status (if applicable):

  • Epidural catheter: sensory/motor level Q4h, site inspection, signs of infection or hematoma
  • Intercostal block: sensory level documentation, pain relief adequacy

Comorbidity flags: - COPD, sleep apnea, renal dysfunction, hepatic disease, substance use, delirium risk (elderly, baseline cognitive impairment)

sections.heading: 5.1 The Analgesic Ladder — Scheduled + Rescue Tiers
sections.bodyHtml:
Baseline (Scheduled) — Foundation

Agent Dose Frequency Route Cautions
Acetaminophen 1 g Q6h IV (POD 0–2) or PO Max 3–4 g/day; safe in most renal disease; monitor LFTs if prolonged use
NSAID (ibuprofen) 400–600 mg Q6–8h PO Requires surgical clearance POD 3+. Hold if renal Cr >1.5, oliguria, dual antiplatelets
NSAID (ketorolac IV) 15–30 mg Q6h × max 5 days IV/IM Same renal/bleeding risks as ibuprofen; NOT recommended POD 0–2 post-cardiac
Gabapentin 100–300 mg TID (QID if ICU) PO Neuropathic pain adjunct. Caution: sedation, dizziness, falls (elderly). Adjust for renal function. Increases opioid effect.

Adjunctive (ICU / PACU Level)

Agent Dose Route Indications Cautions
Dexmedetomidine 0.5–1.5 mcg/kg/h IV infusion Severe pain + anxiety; reduces opioid need; ICU only Monitor BP/HR; bradycardia risk; not for sympathomimetic-dependent patients
Ketamine (subanesthetic) 0.1–0.5 mg/kg/h IV infusion Severe opioid-resistant pain, ICU level; NO respiratory depression Dissociation, psychotomimetic effects (use benzodiazepine co-admin); monitored setting only
Lidocaine infusion 1–2 mg/min IV infusion Severe pain, anti-inflammatory, reduced opioid need Monitor rhythm, QRS; arrhythmia risk; typically ≤24 h

Rescue (PRN) Opioids

Agent Dose Route Indications Notes
Oxycodone 5–10 mg PO Q4–6h PRN Moderate–severe pain; stable respiration Transition to home; watch for constipation
Morphine 2–4 mg IV Q4h PRN Moderate–severe pain; ICU/NPO patients Slower onset; histamine release risk (flush)
Hydromorphone 0.2–0.4 mg IV Q4h PRN Severe pain; rapid onset; potent Preferred IV agent; higher respiratory depression risk; 4–6× morphine potency
Tramadol 50–100 mg PO Q6h PRN Mild–moderate pain Seizure risk (renal impairment, SSRIs, high dose). Avoid elderly.

sections.heading: 5.2 Regional Techniques *(Table-first approach for anesthetic coordination)*
sections.bodyHtml:
Thoracic Epidural

Feature Details
Indications Thoracotomy, severe sternotomy pain; reduces opioid need 30–50%; gold-standard for thoracotomy analgesia
Placement Intra-op preferred; early post-op if high pain
Solution Low-dose bupivacaine (0.1–0.125%) + opioid (morphine, hydromorphone, fentanyl)
Duration 3–5 days post-op; extend if inadequate pain control
ASRA rules Placement/removal with anticoagulation requires specific timing per ASRA 2020 guidelines (UFH 2.4 h, LMWH 12–24 h, INR <1.5 warfarin)

Intercostal Nerve Block (Thoracotomy)

Feature Details
Indications Thoracotomy (posterolateral, anterolateral, VATS); single-shot intra-op or early post-op re-blocking
Technique Local infiltration at 3–4 intercostal spaces; bupivacaine 0.5% or liposomal (Exparel) ± dexamethasone
Duration Single-shot 8–16 h; liposomal 24–72 h; catheter 3–5 days
Benefits Excellent analgesia; less systemic side effects than epidural

Serratus Anterior Plane (SAP) Block

Feature Details
Indications VATS, lateral chest wall pain; less common for sternotomy
Duration 12–24 h (single-shot); longer with catheter
Benefits Fewer risks than epidural; good for VATS

sections.heading: 5.3 Functional Pain Goals — Core Teaching
sections.bodyHtml:
Goal is NOT pain = 0. Goal is:

  • Pain 2–4/10 that allows coughing, deep breathing, turning, ambulation, sleep
  • Patient tolerating multimodal baseline without excessive side effects
  • Early mobilization enabling (not restricted by pain)
  • No escalating opioid doses day-to-day

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. Pain not controlled on scheduled baseline + standard opioid doses → Check electrolytes (K+, Mg2+), verify no reversible triggers (hypoxia, anxiety, full bladder), consider escalation to regional technique or ICU-level adjuncts (ketamine, dexmedetomidine)
  2. High-dose opioids required (morphine equivalents >15 mg/h) by POD 2 → Pain management consult; rule out neuropathic component (add gabapentin); assess for addiction risk or substance use history
  3. Respiratory depression (RR <10, SpO2 <90% with opioid) → STAT reduce opioid, increase monitoring, consider naloxone reversal if severe, escalate to anesthesia
  4. Severe constipation by POD 3 despite regimen → Verify electrolytes, check opioid dose, consider methylnaltrexone
  5. Gabapentin-related delirium or falls in elderly → Hold or reduce dose; PT evaluation; alternatives (pregabalin, tricyclics)
  6. Persistent intercostal pain despite intercostal block (POD 1–2) → Re-blocking by regional team; escalate to epidural or ketamine if available
  7. Thoracotomy pain not improving by POD 4 → Likely neuropathic; ensure on gabapentin or pregabalin; early pain management referral for CPSP risk

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections intended for in-app collapse. Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive; experienced nurses can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Multimodal Analgesia Physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why scheduled beats PRN:

  • Scheduled agents prevent pain escalation; low baseline pain requires lower breakthrough opioid doses
  • PRN-only approach creates a pain–request–medication cycle; pain climbs, patient requests opioid, dose escalates

Synergy across drug classes: - Acetaminophen (central COX inhibition) + NSAID (peripheral COX inhibition + anti-inflammatory) + gabapentin (neuropathic adjunct) + opioid (mu-receptor) = lower individual doses, fewer side effects, better functional outcomes

Opioid as rescue, not baseline:

  • Baseline schedule = acetaminophen + NSAID (once cleared) + adjuncts
  • Opioid = breakthrough only, after baseline agents fail
  • This mindset shift reduces total opioid exposure and opioid-dependent patients at discharge

sections.heading: 7.2 Neuropathic Pain in Thoracotomy
sections.bodyHtml:
Intercostal nerve injury is common in thoracotomy:

  • Somatic pain (sharp, incisional) usually resolves by POD 7–10
  • Neuropathic pain (burning, radiating, shooting along rib) can persist weeks–months; becomes CPSP in 20–40% of thoracotomy patients
  • Gabapentin or pregabalin started early (POD 1–2) reduces CPSP incidence (limited evidence but standard practice)

CPSP risk factors:

  • High acute pain POD 1–2, pain catastrophizing, preoperative anxiety, poor coping
  • Mitigation: early multimodal, psychological support, early PT, gabapentin

sections.heading: 7.3 Contraindications and Subgroup Modifications
sections.bodyHtml:
Acetaminophen:

  • Hold if severe hepatic disease or ALT >3× ULN; reduce to 2–3 g/day if chronic alcohol use
  • Safe in renal disease (not renally metabolized)

NSAIDs:

  • Bleeding risk: POD 0–2 wait for hemostasis; surgical clearance required
  • Renal: hold if Cr >1.5, oliguria, CKD stage 4–5, dual antiplatelets
  • GI: avoid if PUD history or active bleed

Gabapentin:

  • Elderly (>75): start 100 mg BID, titrate slowly; high fall + delirium risk
  • Renal: reduce dose if CrCl <30 (renally cleared)
  • Concurrent opioids: increases respiratory depression + sedation; monitor closely

Tramadol:

  • Seizure risk: avoid in elderly, renal impairment (CrCl <30), SSRI concurrent use
  • Max 100 mg per dose, 400 mg/day; serotonin syndrome risk if SNRI coadministered

Ketamine (ICU):

  • Avoid in uncontrolled hypertension, active ischemia, severe psychiatric history
  • Requires benzodiazepine co-admin to manage dissociation

sections.heading: 7.4 Opioid Stewardship at Discharge
sections.bodyHtml:
PDMP / OARRS check:

  • Document state opioid registry check before prescribing at discharge
  • Identify addiction risk (SOAPP, ORT scores); involve pain/psychiatry if high risk

Prescription strategy:

  • Sternotomy uncomplicated: oxycodone 5 mg Q4–6h PRN × 5–7 days; 20–25 tablets total; NO REFILLS
  • Thoracotomy with CPSP risk: oxycodone 5–10 mg Q4–6h PRN × 7 days; 28–42 tablets; NO REFILLS
  • High-risk (addiction history): minimize opioid; maximize non-opioid (high-dose acetaminophen, NSAID, gabapentin); pain management follow-up POD 3–5

Home multimodal regimen:

  • Acetaminophen 1 g PO Q6h × 2–4 weeks
  • NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg or naproxen 250 mg) Q6–8h × 1–4 weeks (surgeon clearance, renal OK)
  • Gabapentin 100–300 mg TID if neuropathic pain present; continue 2–4 weeks, then taper or hold
  • Bowel regimen: docusate 100 mg BID + PEG daily while on opioids

Tapering and follow-up:

  • POD 7–14: opioid should be finished or nearly finished
  • Week 2–4: transition to non-opioid baseline; opioid completely stopped
  • Week 4–8: multimodal (acetaminophen, NSAID, gabapentin) continued; reassess at surgeon follow-up
  • 3-month screen: thoracotomy patients assessed for CPSP; refer to pain management if neuropathic features

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in stable patients; if any develop, re-escalate.

  • Pain escalating day-to-day despite opioid increases — likely neuropathic component or addiction-related; pain management consult
  • Respiratory rate trending down (RR <12), SpO2 drifting (SpO2 <90%) on opioids — OIRD; reduce opioid immediately, increase monitoring
  • Patient becoming increasingly sedated, difficult to arouse — opioid toxicity or delirium; reduce opioid, check labs, neurology evaluation if altered mental status
  • Severe abdominal distention despite bowel regimen → check K+/Mg2+, verify regimen compliance, escalate to methylnaltrexone if needed
  • New anxiety or sleep disruption on gabapentin — can worsen in elderly; reduce or hold dose; consider alternatives
  • Tremor, agitation, or hyperthermia on tramadol + SSRI — serotonin syndrome until proven otherwise; STAT hold tramadol, contact poison control
  • Persistent burning/radiating pain despite opioid escalation — neuropathic, not responding to opioid; ensure gabapentin on board, escalate to pain management
  • Inability to wean from opioids by POD 7 — possible CPSP trajectory; early pain management involvement
  • Patient refusing pain medications due to addiction fear — screen for substance use history, involve pain/psychiatry, avoid judgment, ensure multimodal plan documented

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
(10–15 high-yield bullets for experienced nurses and experts)

  1. Opioid is rescue, not baseline. If patient is on oxycodone 10 mg Q4h around-the-clock, that is opioid-heavy, not opioid-sparing. Opioid-sparing = oxycodone 5–10 mg Q4–6h PRN for breakthrough only; baseline is acetaminophen + NSAID + adjuncts.

  2. Scheduled agents work better than PRN. Acetaminophen 1 g Q6h on the clock prevents pain escalation; PRN opioid doses are lower. Nursing role: set alarm, administer on time, don't wait for patient request.

  3. NSAID bleeding risk is real, not theoretical. POD 0–2 wait for hemostasis (typically 3+ days). Don't assume; verify surgical clearance at rounds. If dual antiplatelets or oliguria, escalate discussion before starting NSAID.

  4. Gabapentin can cause delirium, sedation, dizziness, falls in elderly. Start low (100 mg BID), titrate slowly. Monitor for confusion; if occurs, hold or reduce. PT evaluation for fall risk.

  5. Tramadol seizure risk is high in elderly and renal impairment. Avoid if age >75 or CrCl <30. If SSRI on board, serotonin syndrome risk (agitation, confusion, hyperthermia, tremor). Safer alternatives: oxycodone, morphine.

  6. Functional pain goals ≠ zero pain. Pain 3/10 that allows walking, coughing, sleeping = success. Pain 0/10 on high opioid doses causing constipation, delirium, immobility = failure. Reframe patient expectations on POD 1.

  7. Thoracotomy pain is more severe and longer-lasting than sternotomy. Plan ahead: epidural, intercostal block, or aggressive multimodal from POD 0. Thoracotomy patients on "routine" post-op pain protocol are undertreated.

  8. Intercostal block is high-yield and under-utilized. Single-shot intra-op reduces opioid need 30–50% × 12–24 h. Liposomal bupivacaine extends to 24–72 h. If pain breaks through early, coordinate re-blocking with regional team.

  9. Epidural + anticoagulation timing requires ASRA rules — don't improvise. ASRA 2020: UFH remove 2.4 h after bolus; LMWH 12–24 h; warfarin INR <1.5. Hematoma is rare but catastrophic; timing compliance is non-negotiable.

  10. Chronic post-surgical pain (CPSP) affects 20–40% of thoracotomy patients. Screen for pain catastrophizing and anxiety early; mitigate with multimodal + psychology + PT. At discharge, document CPSP risk and 3-month follow-up plan in pain language, not just "pain med refills."

  11. Bowel regimen is mandatory with opioids — start POD 1, not after missed BM. Docusate + PEG standing; escalate with senna → bisacodyl → methylnaltrexone. Constipation delays discharge and masks acute abdomen.

  12. Opioid-induced respiratory depression screening is mandatory. OARRS score, respiratory rate Q4h (or continuous if ICU + sedatives), SpO2 monitoring. Risk factors: elderly, obesity, sleep apnea, renal/hepatic disease. If OIRD develops, reduce opioid immediately; consider naloxone if severe.

  13. Amiodarone hypotension if used for POAF is predictable (~25%). Anticipate with fluids; decrease drip early (to 0.5 mg/min) rather than chasing hypotension reactively. Same pain principle — prevention beats reaction.

  14. Ice packs and positioning are free and dramatically underutilized. Ice to incision Q2–3h × 15–20 min; pillow splinting for cough; early mobility Q4h. These often deprioritized for medication; they shouldn't be.

  15. Opioid taper at discharge — 5–7 days supply, no refills, clear documentation. Intentional: patient should be off opioids within 1–2 weeks. Total ~20–25 tablets for sternotomy, 28–42 for thoracotomy. NO REFILLS without evaluation by surgeon/pain management. Do NOT send home on long-acting opioids from discharge.

cards.title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA) Exacerbation / Post-Op Respiratory Events
cards.quickAnswer: Known or suspected OSA + post-op → initiate continuous SpO₂ monitoring for first 24–48 hours; continue home CPAP/BiPAP (patient brings device or unit provides). Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia mandatory: acetaminophen 1 g Q6H + NSAID Q8H + regional block if available. STOP-BANG score ≥3 = moderate-high OSA risk; flag even without formal diagnosis. Position lateral/semi-Fowler's ≥30°; avoid benzodiazepines. Unstable (SpO₂ <88%, apnea >15 sec, CO₂ retention, altered mental status) → STAT escalation, Rapid Response, consider reintubation.
cards.quickAnswerHtml:

Unstable (SpO₂ <88%, apnea >15 sec, CO₂ retention, altered mental status) → STAT escalation, Rapid Response, consider reintubation.
cards.sourcePrecedence: [Institution policy] → American Society of Anesthesiologists (2024) → Chung et al. (2008) → Gupta et al. (2012) → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Elmistekawy & Shallik (2025)

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, who gets it, why it matters.

  • Definition: Obstructive sleep apnea is recurrent collapse of the upper airway during sleep causing intermittent hypoxemia and fragmented sleep. Post-operative exacerbation is when opioids, edema, pain, and sleep disruption amplify apneic episodes beyond baseline severity.
  • Incidence: OSA is common in cardiac surgery populations — 40–80% of CABG patients screen positive on STOP-BANG (Chung et al., 2008); only ~30% have formal pre-op diagnosis. Post-op OSA-related respiratory events account for 5–15% of floor desaturation calls.
  • Peak risk window: POD 0–3 (acute post-extubation) and POD 3–7 (peak opioid use). Undiagnosed OSA often manifests post-operatively.
  • Who this applies to: every patient post-cardiac surgery with known OSA, STOP-BANG score ≥3, or witnessed apnea. Highest risk: obesity (BMI >35), HTN on ≥3 meds, HF, known/suspected AF, male gender, age >60, large neck circumference.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative OSA exacerbation arises from convergence of airway collapse mechanics and depression of ventilatory drive:

Mechanism of airway collapse:

  • Upper airway obstruction occurs due to loss of muscle tone during sleep, narrowed anatomy (obesity, large neck, micrognathia), or dynamic obstruction (tonsillar hypertrophy, deviated septum).
  • Opioid-induced respiratory depression reduces hypoxic and hypercapnic ventilatory drive, depresses gag reflex, and relaxes pharyngeal musculature, amplifying apnea frequency and duration. OSA patients are exquisitely sensitive; even small doses cause substantial depression (Gupta et al., 2012).
  • Post-operative edema from intubation and fluid shifts narrows the airway further.
  • Sleep fragmentation from pain and monitoring disrupts normal sleep architecture, paradoxically increasing OSA severity during recovery sleep.

Risk amplifiers post-op:

  • Hypoxia-induced pulmonary vasoconstriction from repeated desaturations, especially in patients with pre-existing pulmonary HTN or HF.
  • Atelectasis worsening: shallow breathing from opioid depression + airway obstruction prevents alveolar recruitment, deepening hypoxemia.
  • Cardiac dysrhythmia substrate creation: hypoxemia + hypercapnia increase ectopy risk; AF and post-op arrhythmias are more common in untreated OSA patients.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient:

  • Known OSA on home CPAP/BiPAP — admits without machine (high-risk scenario)
  • Pre-op STOP-BANG score ≥3 — no formal OSA diagnosis but sleep-disorder screening positive
  • Witnessed apnea >10 seconds during sleep, followed by gasping/snorting or desaturation dip
  • Post-op hypoxemia (SpO₂ <90%) with no other clear cause (pneumonia, CHF, atelectasis ruled out)
  • Rapid oxygen desaturation on room air upon extubation, especially if opioid use recent
  • Post-op delirium (hyperactive) appearing suddenly or worsening at night — can be first sign of hypoxemia from OSA
  • Patient on high-dose opioids post-op + known OSA or STOP-BANG ≥3 — elevated respiratory depression risk
  • Undiagnosed OSA emerging post-op: obesity (BMI >30), HTN, HF, known AF, or witnessed snoring/gasping

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure information-gathering; no actions yet.

  • Sleep history: Known OSA? On CPAP/BiPAP at home? Brought machine? Last use, compliance.
  • STOP-BANG screening: Snoring (loud?), Tired (daytime somnolence?), Observed apnea, blood Pressure (HTN on meds), BMI >30, Age >50, Neck circumference >16" (female) / 17" (male), Gender male. Score total — ≥3 is moderate-high risk.
  • Current respiratory status: RR, SpO₂ on current O₂ (room air vs supplemental), breath sounds bilaterally, work of breathing, accessory muscle use.
  • Sleep patterns on unit: Snoring noted? Witnessed apneas/gasping? Restlessness, odd sleep positions?
  • Opioid load: Last IV opioid dose/time; cumulative opioid use POD 0–now; baseline pain tolerance; PRN use last night/early AM.
  • Sedating medications: Benzodiazepines, antihistamines, anticholinergics — all increase OSA severity.
  • Mental status: Alert, confused, irritable, drowsy? Orientation ×3. Recent behavior change or new agitation?
  • Cardiac/pulmonary context: EF, known pulmonary HTN, COPD, asthma, recent intubation duration. AF present?
  • Pre-op assessment: OSA mentioned in pre-op notes? STOP-BANG documented? Anesthesia notes on difficult airway or aspiration risk?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Known OSA or STOP-BANG ≥3, extubated, SpO₂ ≥92% on ≤2L O₂. Awake, baseline mental status, no apnea >15 sec.)

  1. Obtain home CPAP/BiPAP machine immediately if patient brought it — contact family/social work if not arrived. If unit has backup CPAP/BiPAP, prepare for post-extubation initiation.
  2. Assess mask fit and tolerance — patient education on reapplication post-extubation (often uncomfortable after intubation).
  3. Establish continuous SpO₂ monitoring for first 24–48 hours minimum — pulse oximetry waveform visible at bedside; set alarms SpO₂ <90% and RR <8.
  4. Implement opioid-sparing analgesia — multimodal protocol:
    • Acetaminophen 1 g Q6H (if tolerated)
    • NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg Q8H or ketorolac 30 mg IV Q6H) if no contraindication
    • Regional block if available (epidural, peripheral nerve catheter)
    • IV opioids if needed: smallest effective dose, Q4H scheduled, avoid standing PRN
    • Avoid benzodiazepines entirely — even lorazepam 0.5 mg substantially worsens apnea and desaturation in OSA patients.
    • Position management: encourage lateral or upright sleeping (semi-Fowler's ≥30°). Use position-limiting pillows if needed; avoid supine sleep.
    • Notify APP/surgeon of OSA status + CPAP plan; confirm opioid-sparing approach approved.
    • Document baseline SpO₂ trend — check SpO₂ on room air after 30 min supine rest to establish post-extubation hypoxemia risk profile.
    • Initiate CPAP/BiPAP same day as extubation if alert enough for mask tolerance (typically POD 1 evening or POD 2 AM). Start with 20–30 min trial; increase duration as tolerated. If patient brings own machine from home, use prior settings; if unit device, empiric 8–10 cmH₂O start.

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable Path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Apnea >15 sec, SpO₂ <88%, RR <8, post-op delirium + hypoxemia, CO₂ retention, altered mental status.)

  1. STAT oxygen therapy — increase FiO₂ to maintain SpO₂ >94%. Consider nasal CPAP trial for acute airway support.
  2. Activate Rapid Response immediately — do NOT wait for scheduled checks.
  3. Stimulate patient and reposition to lateral/upright while awaiting team.
  4. Have suction + airway equipment at bedside — if witnessed apnea with arousal, be ready for vomit.
  5. Check recent opioid dosing — if given within 1 hour, notify provider immediately for possible naloxone consideration.
  6. Obtain STAT labs: ABG (assess CO₂ retention, pH), lactate, CBC (check Hgb for anemia).
  7. Continuous pulse ox + capnography if available — critical for detecting hypoventilation trend.
  8. Prepare for ICU transfer if SpO₂ not improving with O₂ or if RR remains <10.
  9. Document: time of apnea onset, duration, triggering event, response, opioid doses, interventions, outcomes.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template for known/suspected OSA with respiratory event:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], post-op day [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient has known OSA / STOP-BANG ≥3. Witnessed apnea >10 sec at [time], SpO₂ dropped to [value], patient aroused with stimulation. Currently SpO₂ [value] on [O₂]. Last opioid dose [time, drug, dose]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. Respiratory rate [value], alert vs confused. CPAP status: [at bedside / not yet available]." R: "Requesting [opioid hold / CPAP setup confirmation / ICU transfer / sleep study referral order]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
STOP-BANG ≥3, no OSA diagnosis, stable Primary APP to flag + arrange sleep study
Known OSA, witnessed apnea <15 sec, SpO₂ >88% APP for opioid review + CPAP confirmation
Witnessed apnea >15 sec or SpO₂ <88% Rapid Response + APP + consider ICU
Post-op delirium + hypoxemia suspected OSA Hospitalist + consider neurology if MS change persists
Opioid-induced respiratory depression evident Anesthesia / pain team + consider naloxone
Undiagnosed OSA (witnessed event + risk factors) Sleep medicine (inpatient consult if available, discharge referral if stable)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections are — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 STOP-BANG Scoring and OSA Risk Stratification
sections.bodyHtml:
STOP-BANG components (1 point each; max 8):

Component Criterion
Snoring Loud snoring during sleep (bed partner report or observed)
Tired Excessive daytime somnolence or fatigue
Observed apnea Witnessed apnea episodes (bed partner, family, prior clinician)
Pressure Hypertension (on antihypertensive meds or BP consistently >140/90)
BMI BMI >30 kg/m²
Age Age >50 years
Neck circumference Neck >16" (female) or >17" (male)
Gender Male

Risk stratification:

  • STOP-BANG 0–2: Low risk (~5% polysomnography-confirmed OSA). Standard post-op monitoring.
  • STOP-BANG 3–4: Moderate risk (~35–45% OSA). Pulse ox monitoring POD 0–48 h; opioid-sparing analgesia; CPAP trial if available; sleep study referral.
  • STOP-BANG ≥5: High risk (>70% OSA). Intensive monitoring; CPAP essential; opioid alternative preferred; ICU-level care if extubated on floor.

Clinical pearl: A cardiac surgery patient with HTN, BMI 32, observed snoring, and age 55 scores ≥3 automatically and warrants OSA-level precautions even without formal diagnosis.

sections.heading: 7.2 Post-Op OSA Severity and PAP Parameters
sections.bodyHtml:
Severity Level AHI Range Desaturation Pattern SpO₂ Target CPAP / BiPAP Suggested Settings Monitoring Frequency
Mild 5–14/h Minimal, brief ≥92% 5–7 cmH₂O CPAP or 8/4 BiPAP Q6H until stable
Moderate 15–30/h Frequent, 5–10 sec events ≥92% 8–10 cmH₂O CPAP or 10/5 BiPAP Continuous first 24 h, then Q4H
Severe >30/h Prolonged, >10 sec events; arousal-limited ≥94% 10–15 cmH₂O CPAP or 12–15/5–8 BiPAP; escalate rapidly Continuous + capnography if available

Home CPAP settings: If patient brings own machine, use prior settings without alteration. If unavailable, empiric start 8–10 cmH₂O CPAP; titrate by comfort and SpO₂ response over first 1–2 hours. BiPAP preferred if high leak rates or claustrophobia; use oronasal mask if necessary.

sections.heading: 7.3 Opioid-OSA Interaction and Respiratory Depression Mechanics
sections.bodyHtml:
Opioids act on mu-1 receptors in brainstem respiratory centers and airway musculature:

  1. Reduced hypoxic ventilatory response — OSA patients already have blunted CO₂ arousal; opioids further suppress the hypoxemic drive to breathe.
  2. Increased apnea threshold — the CO₂ level at which breathing resumes lengthens; combined with low baseline drive in OSA, patients require more hypercapnia to arouse.
  3. Airway collapse risk — opioid-induced loss of muscle tone in pharyngeal dilators (genioglossus, tensor palatini) worsens obstruction during fragile post-extubation airway.
  4. Synergistic with other sedation — benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, antihistamines amplify depression; avoid all.

High-risk post-op opioid scenario: patient receiving IV morphine 4 mg Q2H PRN after extubation with undiagnosed STOP-BANG ≥3 → very high decompensation risk within 12–24 hours. Switching to acetaminophen + NSAID + regional block can eliminate the risk entirely while maintaining pain control.

sections.heading: 7.4 CPAP/BiPAP Continuation Post-Extubation
sections.bodyHtml:
Why continue PAP:

  • CPAP provides positive airway pressure that mechanically splints the airway open during sleep, eliminating apneic episodes.
  • Restores normal oxygenation — SpO₂ returns to >94% even during REM sleep.
  • Reduces post-op delirium risk by eliminating hypoxemic episodes (Hernandez et al., 2018).
  • Prevents pulmonary HTN progression.
  • Shortens hospital length of stay.

Implementation post-extubation:

  • Best approach: Patient brings own machine (patient-specific settings, mask fit, comfort). Family can deliver; social work coordinates if needed.
  • Unit backup: Standard CPAP/BiPAP units with nasal pillow, nasal mask, oronasal mask options. Settings: 7–12 cmH₂O CPAP or 8–14/4 cmH₂O BiPAP start; titrate by comfort and SpO₂.
  • Timing: Initiate same day as extubation if alert enough (typically POD 1 evening or POD 2 AM).
  • Mask selection: Nasal pillow (least claustrophobic) → nasal mask → oronasal mask if high leak/mouth-breathing.
  • Comfort measures: Start 20–30 min trial, increase duration as tolerated. Ramp feature and humidifier reduce dryness.
  • Monitoring: Pulse ox + capnography if available; document pre/post SpO₂ and RR trends over 1 hour.

Barriers & solutions:

  • Patient refusal (claustrophobia): Explain SpO₂ data; try smaller mask; consider BiPAP trial. If truly intolerant, position lateral + continuous pulse ox + pain/opioid review mandatory.
  • Mask leak or poor seal: Try different mask style; use headgear adjustment; add forehead spacer.
  • Pressure too high: Start 5 cmH₂O, increase by 1–2 cmH₂O q15min as tolerated; use ramp feature.
  • Daytime napping with CPAP (even 1–2 h QID) helps if overnight too uncomfortable.

sections.heading: 7.5 Undiagnosed OSA Recognition and Discharge Referral
sections.bodyHtml:
Red flags for undiagnosed OSA emerging post-op:

  • Witnessed apnea (any duration >5 sec, especially if repeated or followed by gasping)
  • Rapid desaturation from baseline
  • Snoring with arousal pattern (snore → silence → snorting gasp)
  • STOP-BANG ≥3 on admission screening
  • Obesity + HTN + AF (high-risk triad)
  • Post-op delirium without clear infectious/metabolic trigger
  • Bariatric surgery patients (OSA prevalence >50% but often undiagnosed pre-op)

Discharge referral pathway:

  1. Document the witnessed event or risk factors: "suspected OSA — recommend sleep study."
  2. Write discharge order for sleep medicine referral (outpatient polysomnography). Include STOP-BANG score, observed events, comorbidities.
  3. Provide patient education sheet on OSA, CPAP use, and follow-up importance.
  4. Arrange follow-up appointment — ideally before discharge or within 2 weeks.
  5. Copy primary care and cardiologist on referral note.

Timeline: Most patients complete sleep study within 2–4 weeks after discharge; express services in some communities (1 week). Early diagnosis prevents readmission for recurrent AF or delirium.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These watch-fors in stable OSA (or suspected OSA) patients predict decompensation.

  • SpO₂ trending down despite supplemental O₂ — if SpO₂ falls from 94% to 88% over 2–4 hours, underlying apnea worsening or respiratory depression developing.
  • Oxygen requirement creeping up — patient needed 1L at POD 1 AM; now needs 3L by PM. Progressive hypoventilation or atelectasis from OSA + shallow breathing.
  • RR trending down — RR 14 in AM; RR 10 by afternoon. Opioid + OSA = dangerous. Hold opioids, increase pulse ox frequency.
  • Witnessed apnea >15 seconds followed by arousal gasp — apnea duration predicts severity and hypoxemia risk. Even one prolonged apnea warrants escalation.
  • Rapid SpO₂ desaturation during sleep (drop >5% in <1 min) — suggests airway collapse, not simple hypoventilation.
  • Altered mental status developing or worsening — post-op delirium (hyperactive or hypoactive) can be first sign of hypoxemia in OSA. New confusion = hypoxemia until proved otherwise.
  • Cyanosis observed (lips, fingertips) during sleep — indicates severe desaturation; emergent.
  • Arousal difficulty — patient not waking to normal voice during observed apnea; suggests deep desaturation/hypercapnia.
  • Capnography waveform flattening (if available) — indicates hypoventilation; CO₂ not clearing; apnea risk imminent.
  • Patient refusing CPAP mask repeatedly despite education — risk of apnea escalates; may need ICU monitoring or alternative interventions.
  • Hypercapnia on ABG (CO₂ >45) — respiratory drive failure; apnea-related hypoventilation. Urgent intervention needed.
  • Patient "sleeping through" desaturation episodes — family or RN notes patient unaware of SpO₂ drops. Not reassuring; indicates severe OSA with poor arousal. Escalate.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. STOP-BANG ≥3 is moderate-high risk — flag the chart on admission. Many clinicians think OSA only matters with formal diagnosis. Wrong. STOP-BANG ≥3 identifies 35–45% with undiagnosed OSA; flag chart to trigger protective precautions even without formal sleep study.

  2. Home CPAP/BiPAP machine continuation post-extubation is the single most impactful intervention. Patient brings it in or unit provides. Coordinate with family same day as extubation. If patient refuses, document and escalate; it's a significant safety issue.

  3. Opioids + OSA = respiratory depression — opioid-sparing analgesia is critical. Post-op cardiac surgery patient with OSA on IV morphine 4 mg Q2H PRN is at high decompensation risk. Switch to acetaminophen + NSAID + regional block; reduces OSA-related respiratory events >60%.

  4. Continuous SpO₂ monitoring first 24–48 hours is non-negotiable in OSA patients. Many clinicians reduce monitoring "once stable." OSA desaturation often appears 12–24 hours post-extubation. Keep pulse ox alarm active; watch waveform, not just number.

  5. Avoid benzodiazepines entirely in OSA patients. Even lorazepam 0.5 mg causes severe apnea exacerbation. If patient anxious, use non-pharmacologic methods or discuss alternatives with provider. Document "OSA — respiratory depression risk" if needed to prevent accidental dosing.

  6. Positioning is critical — lateral or upright at minimum. Supine position worsens OSA severity ~50%. Keep HOB ≥30°; better yet, encourage lateral sleeping (pillows to support). Free and effective intervention.

  7. Desaturation episodes should NOT be dismissed as "sleeping through." If RN notes SpO₂ dropped to 85% at 2 AM but patient slept through it, that's not reassurance. That's severe OSA with impaired arousal. Flag immediately.

  8. OSA worsens POAF risk. Hypoxemia + hypercapnia trigger atrial ectopy. Untreated OSA patients have higher AF recurrence post-op. If patient develops new AF with known OSA, ensure CPAP running nightly.

  9. Witnessed apnea + obesity + HTN = undiagnosed OSA — refer for sleep study at discharge. Patient with BMI 34, HTN, witnessed 12-sec apnea post-op, and no pre-op sleep study likely has undiagnosed OSA. Document and arrange sleep medicine referral. Early diagnosis prevents readmission.

  10. Bariatric surgery patients are very high-risk for undiagnosed OSA. Any post-gastric-bypass or post-sleeve patient with snoring, daytime somnolence, or STOP-BANG ≥3 is extremely likely to have severe OSA. Anticipate severe post-op respiratory events; consider ICU if extubated on floor. Arrange pre-discharge sleep study.

  11. Ask about home CPAP settings always — Mallampati + neck circumference are quick screens. Always ask: "What pressure do you use at home?" If patient doesn't know, family can often provide. Mallampati (tonsillar size: I–IV) and neck circumference (>17" men, >16" women) are rapid bedside markers of anatomical OSA severity.

  12. Rising arterial CO₂ while SpO₂ looks OK is ominous. CO₂ rising above 45 mmHg while SpO₂ remains 88–92% = respiratory drive failure, not simple desaturation. Apnea risk imminent. This is the trap: relying on SpO₂ alone when capnography available. Always trend both.

  13. Reducing pain reduces opioid need — the virtuous cycle. Multimodal analgesia (acetaminophen + NSAID + regional block) often achieves pain control with zero IV opioids. Less opioid = less respiratory depression = less OSA exacerbation. Link pain management and respiratory safety explicitly in rounds.

  14. Shared decision-making on post-op CPAP with family improves adherence. Families are powerful allies. At bedside, show family the SpO₂ trend with vs without CPAP; explain the apnea risk; ask family to encourage mask tolerance. Engagement increases compliance.

  15. Never assume "compliant with home CPAP." Patient may use it 2 hours/night or 0. Always verify: "How many hours per night do you use it at home?" Document. High non-compliance post-op is common; may need equipment adjustment or ICU-level monitoring.

cards.title: Type A Aortic Dissection — OSH Transfer Admission
cards.quickAnswer: Type A aortic dissection from OSH is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY — goal is OR within 1 hour of arrival. Confirm imaging (CTA/MRI), establish IV access + foley, initiate impulse control STAT with IV β-blocker first (esmolol or labetalol targeting HR ≤60), then vasodilator (nicardipine targeting SBP ≤120); obtain informed consent; type and cross 6+ units PRBC; notify CT surgery + anesthesia + OR STAT. Anticipate cardiopulmonary bypass, possible DHCA, major bleeding. Post-op (POD 0–1 ICU): maintain hemodynamic control, monitor closely for stroke, spinal cord ischemia, AKI, arrhythmia. POD 2–5 stepdown/ICU admission: continue post-op surgical recovery, complication surveillance, discharge planning. Post-op 30-day mortality 10–15%.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Type A aortic dissection is an intimal tear in the ascending aorta (by definition includes ascending aorta; may extend into arch, descending thoracic, or abdominal aorta). Classified by Stanford or DeBakey system; Type A involves ascending aorta.
  • Epidemiology: ~2–3 per 100,000 per year. Untreated mortality rises ~1% per hour; 50% dead within 48 hours. Surgical repair reduces 30-day mortality to 10–15% (high-volume centers) (Hiratzka et al., 2022).
  • Who this applies to: Adult patients (any age; median ~60 yrs) presenting from OSH with imaging confirmation of Type A dissection. Highest risk: hypertension (80%), connective tissue disorders (Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos, Loeys-Dietz), bicuspid aortic valve, smoking, cocaine use.
  • Atypical presentations: ~15% painless (present as acute stroke, syncope, hemiplegia from carotid involvement, or MI from coronary ostial occlusion) (Hiratzka et al., 2022).

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why Type A dissection is emergent; mechanism of injury and death.

The intimal tear in the ascending aorta creates a "false lumen" (dissected layer) parallel to the true lumen. Mortality drivers are acute aortic rupture (sudden), coronary ostial occlusion (acute MI/cardiogenic shock), branch vessel occlusion (stroke, spinal cord ischemia, mesenteric ischemia, limb ischemia), and aortic regurgitation (acute heart failure from root involvement). Progressive dilation and propagation of the dissection occur within hours if untreated; aortic shear stress (dP/dt = rate of change of pressure) drives propagation. Impulse control — strict beta-blockade BEFORE vasodilation — is the only medical therapy that slows dissection progression by reducing contractility and heart rate.

Why surgery urgently: Type A dissection is a surgical disease. Ascending aortic repair (graft replacement) prevents rupture and restores coronary perfusion. The window for surgery is hours, not days. Every hour delay increases mortality ~1% (Hiratzka et al., 2022).

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
What the patient looks like at arrival.

Classic presentation:

  • Sudden-onset, severe, tearing chest pain or back pain (often worst pain ever experienced)
  • Severe hypertension (SBP >160, often >180 mmHg)
  • Autonomic signs: diaphoresis, anxiety, pale, tremulous

Atypical presentations (15% of cases):

  • Acute ischemic stroke (carotid dissection extension → embolic stroke or carotid occlusion)
  • Syncope or sudden loss of consciousness (rupture, cardiac tamponade, cerebral ischemia)
  • Hemiplegia or other focal neurologic deficit (carotid/vertebral involvement, spinal cord ischemia)
  • Acute MI pattern on ECG (right coronary ostium involvement most common; STEMI in inferior leads)
  • Acute heart failure (aortic regurgitation from root involvement, tamponade physiology)

On arrival from OSH:

  • Patient transported by ambulance with continuous vital sign monitoring
  • Imaging already obtained (CTA ± MRI ± TEE) or imaging available on transfer disc
  • Often on IV medications (beta-blockers, vasodilators) started at OSH ED
  • Medication list and OSH labs documented (troponin, lactate, CBC, CMP, coagulation studies)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information gathering at bedside. No actions yet. Target: 2 minutes.

Vital signs & perfusion:

  • BP (bilateral arms if dissection extends to carotid/subclavian), HR, temperature, SpO₂, respiratory rate
  • Perfusion: capillary refill, skin temperature, urine output if foley in place

Cardiac exam:

  • Auscultate for new diastolic murmur (aortic regurgitation from dissection into aortic root)
  • Palpate bilateral radial, femoral pulses for pulse deficits (suggests dissection in branch vessels)
  • Palpate apical impulse — position, character (hyperdynamic if AR present)

Neurologic exam — BASELINE — critical:

  • Mental status, level of consciousness
  • Pupils and eye movements
  • Focal deficits: facial droop, arm/leg weakness, speech clarity, sensation
  • Cranial nerves (especially CN II, CN III — pupil for carotid involvement)
  • Gait if safe to assess
  • Any pulse deficit in limbs (suggests malperfusion)

Extremities:

  • Bilateral arm and leg strength, sensation
  • Capillary refill, color, temperature (compare R vs L)
  • Identify any ischemic limb (pale, cool, mottled)

Imaging already available:

  • OSH CTA/MRI/TEE images on transfer disc or already uploaded to PACS
  • Confirm Type A (ascending aorta involvement) vs Type B (descending only)
  • Anatomic extent: ascending only? Arch? Descending? Abdominal?
  • Involvement of coronary ostia, carotid, vertebral?
  • Evidence of rupture or contained rupture (mediastinal blood)?
  • Aortic root diameter, arch diameter, descending diameter

Recent labs from OSH:

  • Troponin (RCA involvement?), lactate (perfusion status?), CBC, CMP, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen
  • Baseline creatinine (many develop AKI post-op)

MAR review (from OSH):

  • Current IV medications (beta-blocker? Which? Rate? Vasodilator? Which? Rate?)
  • Home antihypertensives, anticoagulation, antiplatelet agents
  • Allergies, prior surgeries, connective tissue disorder history

Lines & access:

  • Peripheral IV access (size, number), arterial line (if placed at OSH)
  • Central line (if placed at OSH)
  • Foley catheter output

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path — Pre-Op (ED → OR)
sections.bodyHtml:
(Arrives on beta-blocker ± vasodilator started at OSH; hemodynamically stable; no signs of rupture or malperfusion.)

IMMEDIATE ACTIONS (0–5 min):

  1. Confirm imaging type & extent — review OSH CTA/MRI/TEE in PACS or on transfer disc - Type A confirmed (ascending aorta involvement)? - Arch? Descending? Coronary ostia? Carotid? - Evidence of rupture or tamponade physiology?
  2. Establish large-bore IV access — two 18G or larger peripheral lines, or central line
  3. Place foley catheter (if not already in place) for urine output monitoring
  4. Continuous ECG monitoring, pulse oximetry, arterial line (if not in place, consider placing STAT or deferring to OR team)
  5. Type & Cross 6+ units PRBC immediately; consider FFP, platelets on standby

IMPULSE CONTROL — STAT (5–15 min):

BETA-BLOCKER FIRST. Target HR ≤60 bpm.

Agent Dose Notes
Esmolol (IV) Load: 500 mcg/kg over 1 min; then infusion 50–300 mcg/kg/min titrated to HR Short-acting (T½ = 9 min); preferred if hemodynamically unstable or when rapid titration needed
Labetalol (IV) Load: 20 mg IV push, then repeat 40–80 mg IV q10min (max 300 mg total); or infusion 1–2 mg/min Alpha + beta blockade; longer acting; good if already on labetalol at home
Metoprolol (IV) 5 mg IV over 2 min; may repeat q5min × 3 Alternative if esmolol/labetalol unavailable; less titrable
  • Goal: HR ≤60 bpm (ideally 50–60). This reduces aortic shear force (dP/dt).
  • Verify: is patient already on beta-blocker from OSH? If yes, document dose/time, check if adequate HR control.

VASODILATOR SECOND (once HR ≤60). Target SBP ≤120 mmHg.

Agent Dose Notes
Nicardipine (IV infusion) Start 5 mg/hr; titrate by 2.5 mg/hr q5–10 min to SBP target (usual range 5–15 mg/hr) Preferred agent post-op; dihydropyridine; no negative inotropy
Sodium nitroprusside (IV infusion) Start 0.5 mcg/kg/min; titrate by 0.5 mcg/kg/min q3–5 min to SBP (usual range 1–3 mcg/kg/min) Use if nicardipine unavailable; cyanide toxicity risk if >4 mcg/kg/min >4 hrs; requires ICU monitoring
Labetalol (IV infusion) 0.5–2 mg/min IV infusion, titrate to SBP If already loaded with labetalol
  • NEVER start vasodilator without beta-blockade. Unopposed alpha effect causes reflex tachycardia → increased dP/dt → dissection propagation.
  • Goal: SBP ≤120 mmHg, HR ≤60 bpm (target HR:SBP ratio that minimizes shear).
  • Maintain throughout pre-op period. Do NOT hold medications during transport to OR.

PAIN CONTROL (alongside impulse control):

  • High-dose IV opioid: morphine 4–10 mg IV or fentanyl 50–100 mcg IV
  • Rationale: severe tearing pain is nearly universal; uncontrolled pain drives HR and BP up, worsening shear
  • Anxiolytic if very anxious: lorazepam 1–2 mg IV or midazolam 1–2 mg IV

LABS & CONFIRMATORY TESTS:

  • 12-lead ECG STAT — look for STEMI pattern (ST elevation inferior = RCA dissection)
  • Baseline CBC, CMP, lactate, PT/INR, PTT, fibrinogen (if not already done at OSH)
  • Type & cross 6+ units PRBC (already ordered above)
  • Repeat troponin (serial troponin if RCA involvement suspected)

CONSENT & TEAM MOBILIZATION:

  • Informed consent: explain aortic repair requires sternotomy, CPB, full anticoagulation, risks include stroke, spinal cord injury, kidney injury, bleeding, death (mortality 10–15% at 30 days even in surgical series)
  • Family notification: discuss prognosis, unexpected emergency surgery, ICU admission likely, recovery timeline
  • Notify CT surgery attending STAT + anesthesia STAT + OR charge nurse (declare OR ready for emergency case)
  • Communicate impulse control parameters to anesthesia (current medications, target HR/SBP maintained during transport)

TRANSPORT TO OR:

  • Do NOT hold impulse control medications during transport.
  • Continuous monitoring (ECG, pulse ox, BP) during transport
  • Consider having CT surgery fellow meet patient at ED or in corridor for handoff
  • Anticipate possible DHCA (deep hypothermic circulatory arrest) if arch extensively involved. Team should pre-plan perfusion strategy.

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path — Pre-Op (ED → OR EMERGENT)
sections.bodyHtml:
(Arrives in shock, altered mental status, chest/back pain uncontrolled, evidence of rupture or tamponade, active malperfusion.)

  1. CALL STAT: CT surgery attending STAT + anesthesia STAT + OR STAT + code team
  2. Do NOT delay for images if clinical presentation is consistent and unequivocal — if imaging not available, proceed to OR with highest suspicion; imaging may be obtained intra-op
  3. Aggressive impulse control:
    • Esmolol load + infusion if available (fastest titration)
    • Vasodilator immediately if HR ≥60 (nicardipine or nitroprusside)
    • Support perfusion: consider fluid bolus (500 mL LR if hypovolemic), but avoid over-hydration (worsens pulmonary edema if associated)
    • Massive transfusion protocol: consider activating if evidence of rupture or heavy bleeding
    • Prepare for crash induction in OR — anesthesia may take patient directly to OR without further workup

sections.heading: 5C. Post-Op Management — POD 0–1 (ICU)
sections.bodyHtml:
Immediate post-op (PACU → ICU):

  • Admit to ICU, typically intubated and sedated
  • Continuous arterial line, CVP or PA catheter, ECG, SpO₂, urine output monitoring
  • Maintain impulse control: IV beta-blocker ± vasodilator
  • Pain control: IV opioid on schedule + PRN
  • Monitor for immediate post-op complications: massive bleeding (chest tube output), arrhythmia, low cardiac output

Daily POD 0–1 ICU assessment:

  • Vital signs: HR q1h (maintain <100 if possible, ideally <80), BP q2h (trending SBP 120–140), temperature
  • Cardiac auscultation: new murmur? (aortic regurgitation, pericardial friction rub)
  • Chest wound: visual inspection, note drainage character/amount (some bleeding expected post-op, but >300 mL/hr concerning)
  • Neurologic exam CRITICAL: compare to baseline neuro exam from ED
  • Mental status (baseline for sedated patient: responsiveness to commands, pupil response)
  • Focal deficits: any new weakness, facial droop, speech changes? Red flag for acute stroke
  • Spinal cord ischemia: can present as lower extremity weakness (delayed POD 1–3)
  • Extremities: assess bilateral pulses, color, temperature, strength (especially lower extremities for spinal cord baseline)
  • Respiratory: breath sounds bilateral, SpO₂ trending, note splinting from pain
  • Foley output: goal >0.5 mL/kg/hr; oliguria is red flag for AKI (common post-op from CPB)
  • Chest tube output: should trend downward; >200 mL/hr is concerning for coagulopathy or anastomotic leak
  • Labs daily: CBC, CMP, PT/INR, PTT, lactate (marker of perfusion), repeat troponin if elevated

sections.heading: 5D. Post-Op Management — POD 2–5 (Stepdown/ICU)
sections.bodyHtml:
Transition criteria to stepdown (if hemodynamically stable):

  • Off vasopressor support (or on minimal support)
  • Breathing spontaneously or with minimal ventilator support, able to be extubated
  • Stable rhythm, HR <100, SBP <150
  • Foley output adequate (>0.5 mL/kg/hr), declining lactate, normal mentation when sedation lightened

Daily assessment POD 2–5:

  • Vital signs: BP q4h (target <140), HR (maintain regular, <100)
  • Cardiac auscultation: listen for new murmur, pericardial rub
  • Chest wound: daily inspection; watch for drainage, dehiscence, redness, warmth (infection signs)
  • Neurologic exam: daily formal neuro assessment — critical for detecting delayed stroke or spinal cord ischemia
  • Baseline neuro from ED + immediately post-op
  • Any new focal deficit is RED FLAG → imaging (CTA head/neck for stroke, MRI spine for spinal cord ischemia)
  • Extremities: bilateral strength and sensation (especially lower extremities)
  • Respiratory: breath sounds, SpO₂ trend, cough effectiveness, incentive spirometry compliance
  • Foley output: goal >0.5 mL/kg/hr; watch for rising creatinine (AKI common post-op from CPB + contrast)
  • Labs: Daily CBC, CMP; daily lactate if elevated; coagulation studies if still on heparin
  • Medications: IV beta-blockers transitioning to oral; start ACE inhibitor if Cr stable; continue statin

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "This is [RN name], calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p Type A aortic dissection repair." B: "Patient arrived from OSH with Type A dissection [arch/descending involvement if applicable]. Surgery was [graft/root repair/arch repair]. Current vital signs: BP [SBP/DBP], HR [rate/rhythm], SpO₂ [%]." A: "[Describe acute change: new pain, neuro deficit, hemodynamic change, rhythm change, bleeding, etc.] Neuro exam [stable/new deficit]. Chest tube output [mL/hr]. Labs: K+ [value], Mg+ [value], lactate [value]." R: "Requesting [imaging / medication change / team evaluation / code team / transfer to ICU]."

Who to call — Pre-Op (ED → OR)

Situation Contact
Type A confirmed, stable CT surgery attending (direct consult)
Type A, hemodynamically unstable CT surgery attending STAT + OR STAT
New focal neuro deficit on arrival CT surgery + neurology + code team
Evidence of rupture / massive bleeding Activate massive transfusion protocol + code team

Who to call — Post-Op (POD 0–5, ICU/stepdown)

Situation Contact
New focal neuro deficit (suspected stroke) Code team + CT surgery + neurology (stroke code)
Acute lower extremity weakness CT surgery + neurology (spinal cord ischemia rule-out)
Sudden severe chest/back pain CT surgery STAT (dissection recurrence, graft leak, tamponade)
Unstable rhythm (VT, VF, complete heart block) Code team + CT surgery
Chest tube output >300 mL/hr or rising CT surgery + prepare for potential re-exploration
Acute hypotension unresponsive to fluids/pressors CT surgery + possible ICU transfer
Acute kidney injury (Cr >2.5 or oliguria) Nephrology + CT surgery
Fever + leukocytosis + sternal drainage (mediastinitis) Infectious disease + CT surgery (possible re-do surgery)

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Pre-Op Impulse Control Rationale Why strict β-blockade BEFORE vasodilation? Aortic shear stress is quantified by dP/dt (rate of change in aortic pressure). Type A dissection propagates when shear stress is high. Beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility, directly lowering dP/dt. Vasodilators alone (without beta-blockade) cause reflex tachycardia via baroreceptor activation — the sympathetic surge actually increases dP/dt despite lowering SBP, propagating the dissection. Classic teaching error: A clinician gives nicardipine first to lower BP, intending to stabilize the patient. Instead, the patient's reflex HR spikes to 110–130, the aortic wall shears harder, and the dissection propagates. By the time a beta-blocker is added, the damage is done. Correct sequence:
  1. Beta-blocker → HR ≤60 (reduce dP/dt)
  2. Vasodilator → SBP ≤120 (reduce afterload, further lower dP/dt)
  3. Result: dP/dt minimized; dissection stabilized for surgery Target numbers:
    • HR ≤60 bpm is a threshold. Ideally 50–60. Some surgeons tolerate 60–70 if hemodynamically limited.
    • SBP ≤120 mmHg is surgical tradition; some centers tolerate 120–140 if achieved without excess vasodilator.
    • Maintain throughout pre-op period — do NOT hold medications during transport or waiting for OR.
Type A Dissection Mortality & Imaging Extent IRAD mortality by extent and presentation (Hiratzka et al., 2022):
ExtentIn-Hospital Mortality30-Day Mortality (Surgical)
Ascending only, uncomplicated~10% (medical)~5% (surgical)
Ascending + arch, no complications~15–20% (medical)~10–12% (surgical)
With coronary involvement (RCAO most common)~25–30%~15–18%
With stroke from carotid involvement~30–40%~20–25%
With spinal cord ischemia~25–35%~15–20%
Untreated mortality rises ~1% per hour in the first 48 hours. This is why OR timing is critical: every hour delay increases mortality risk. Imaging extent determines surgical approach:
ExtentSurgical PlanDHCA Likely?
Ascending aorta only (no arch)Ascending graft + aortic root repair if neededNo (usually)
Ascending + archAscending + arch replacement; may involve hemiarch or total archYes (if arch involvement)
Ascending + arch + descending (extensive Type A)Ascending + arch + possible descending (staged or single-stage)Yes (likely)
Involves coronary ostia (RCA most common)Coronary ostia may need re-implantation onto graftDepends on arch
DHCA (Deep Hypothermic Circulatory Arrest): If arch is involved, CPB cools the patient to ~18°C (core body temperature) and circulation is stopped temporarily (~30–40 min) to allow safe surgical repair of the arch. Cerebral protection is critical: selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP, also called ACP) delivers cold oxygenated blood to the head via carotid/innominate arteries while the body is cooled.
Coronary Ostial Dissection (RCA Most Common) In Type A dissection, coronary ostia can be occluded or involved in the intimal flap:
  • Right coronary artery (RCA): ~65% of coronary involvement in Type A dissection
  • Presents as inferior STEMI pattern (ST elevation in II, III, aVF)
  • Can cause acute cardiogenic shock
  • Treatment: may require urgent coronary ostial re-implantation onto graft during aortic surgery
  • Left main coronary (LCA or LMCA): ~30% of involvement
  • More catastrophic; presents as anterior STEMI ± cardiogenic shock
  • May need IABP or emergent circulatory support pre-op
  • Both coronaries: ~5%; extremely high-risk presentation Pre-op clue: STEMI pattern on ECG in a patient with sudden chest pain and hypertension = Type A dissection until proven otherwise. Do NOT default to catheterization lab for STEMI; get aortic imaging (CTA) first. Aortic surgery, not PCI, is the fix.
Post-Op Complications: Stroke, Spinal Cord Ischemia, AKI Acute stroke (POD 0–5): Risk 5–8% in surgical series (Hiratzka et al., 2022)
  • Mechanism: emboli from aortic atheroma dislodged during surgical manipulation; carotid dissection extension causing embolic stroke or carotid occlusion; air embolism during CPB (rare)
  • Presentation: new focal neurologic deficit (facial droop, arm/leg weakness, speech change, visual field loss)
  • Red flag timing: often appears within first 24 hours post-op, but can be delayed
  • Management: Activate stroke code immediately. CTA head/neck to rule out hemorrhage, assess for ischemic infarct. Neurology evaluation. ICU transfer if not already there. Spinal cord ischemia (POD 1–3, rarely later): Risk 3–5% (Hiratzka et al., 2022)
  • Mechanism: dissection or cross-clamping of the descending thoracic aorta ischemia to the anterior spinal artery (blood supply from artery of Adamkiewicz, typically T9–L2)
  • Presentation: lower extremity weakness (often sudden, both legs affected), loss of sensation below level of injury, urinary retention (if sacral involvement), loss of pain/temperature (anterior cord syndrome pattern)
  • Red flag timing: can emerge POD 1–3, occasionally delayed to POD 5+
  • Management: Notify team immediately. MRI thoracic/lumbar spine to confirm. No proven effective treatment post-op (prognosis grim if significant cord ischemia). Prevention is goal: minimize cross-clamp time, maintain collateral perfusion via intercostal/lumbar artery preservation (surgeon-dependent). Acute kidney injury (POD 1–3, can persist): Risk 30–50% post-op (Hiratzka et al., 2022)
  • Mechanisms: CPB causes inflammatory cascade + hemodilution; contrast-induced nephropathy (from imaging); distal aortic malperfusion (false lumen obstruction of renal arteries); low cardiac output state
  • Red flag: rising creatinine, oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr urine output), rising BUN:Cr ratio
  • Management: monitor urine output q2h, daily creatinine, daily lactate. May need to hold ACE inhibitors if Cr rising rapidly. Consider nephrology consult if Cr >2.5 or need CRRT. Maintain adequate intravascular volume without pulmonary edema.
Anticoagulation & Antiplatelet Strategy Post-Op Post-op Type A patients are typically NOT anticoagulated, despite aortic grafts. Rationale:
  • Aortic grafts (Dacron, PTFE) have low thrombotic risk compared to mechanical valves
  • Bleeding risk is high post-op (raw pleural surfaces, anastomoses, coagulopathy from CPB)
  • IRAD data show graft thrombosis is rare (<1%) without anticoagulation Exception: Patients with mechanical mitral valve or atrial fibrillation lasting >48 hours may need anticoagulation. This is a team decision; do NOT start or stop AC without CT surgery input. New-onset post-op atrial fibrillation (POAF): ~20–30% of Type A patients
  • Default approach: rate control with beta-blockers, NOT rhythm control with amiodarone (unless cardiogenic shock from RVR)
  • Anticoagulation for POAF >48 h: assess CHA₂DS₂-VASc score; most Type A patients qualify (age ≥60, HTN, possible CHF)
  • BUT: do NOT start AC without CT surgery approval (balance bleeding vs stroke risk) Home antiplatelet agents (aspirin):
    • Many Type A patients were on aspirin pre-op; aspirin is restarted POD 1–3 (surgeon preference) as secondary prevention (reduce graft thrombosis risk, stroke risk)
    • Do NOT restart without team approval
Genetics & Family Screening Underlying connective tissue disorder in Type A dissection: ~10–20% of Type A dissection patients have underlying syndromic aortopathy:
  • Marfan syndrome (FBN1 gene): ~5–10% of Type A (fibrillin-1 defects weaken aortic wall)
  • Loeys-Dietz syndrome (TGFBR1/TGFBR2): ~2–5% of Type A (TGF-β signaling defects)
  • Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, vascular type (COL3A1): ~1–2% of Type A
  • Bicuspid aortic valve + aortopathy: ~3–5% Clinical clues to syndromic aortopathy:
    • Aortic root diameter >5.0 cm (even before dissection)
    • Family history of aortic dissection, sudden death, aortic aneurysm
    • Marfanoid features (tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, pectus)
    • Skin findings (velvety skin, easy bruising — Ehlers-Danlos) Mandatory screening:
      1. Patient: arrange genetics referral; FBN1, TGFBR1, TGFBR2 testing if syndromic features present
      2. First-degree relatives: CTA or MRI chest to assess aortic root size
      3. If relative has aortic root >5.0 cm (Marfan) or >5.0–5.5 cm (Loeys-Dietz depending on family history), may qualify for prophylactic aortic root replacement
      4. Genetic testing if index patient has confirmed syndrome Lifelong aortic imaging surveillance: Patient needs CTA or MRI chest at 1 month, 3 months, 1 year post-op, then annually or per surgeon. Goal: detect aneurysmal dilation of distal aorta (false lumen expansion), which may require late endograft repair.
Cerebral Protection During DHCA (Teaching for ICU Teams) If arch is involved, CPB cooling to 18°C and circulatory arrest (~30–40 min) allows safe arch repair. Brain is at risk for ischemic injury during the arrest period. Cerebral protection strategies:
  1. Selective antegrade cerebral perfusion (SACP / ACP): delivers cold (18–22°C), oxygenated, heparinized blood directly into the carotid and innominate arteries during circulatory arrest - Allows brain perfusion while body is arrested - Reduces ischemic time - Preferred technique at high-volume centers
  2. Retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP): perfusion via the SVC (less effective than SACP; older technique)
  3. Mild hypothermia (28–32°C) instead of deep hypothermia: some centers use this to shorten arrest time and reduce complications, though less traditional Post-op neurologic risk: Despite cerebral protection, acute stroke risk is 5–8% (emboli, carotid dissection). Daily neuro exams are critical to detect delayed neurologic deterioration.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Watch for these in stable post-op patients.

  • Sudden severe chest or back pain — recurrent dissection, graft pseudoaneurysm, contained rupture, or pericardial tamponade; call CT surgery STAT
  • New focal neurologic deficit (facial droop, arm/leg weakness, speech change, visual change) — acute stroke; activate stroke code
  • New lower extremity weakness or paralysis, bilateral — spinal cord ischemia (anterior spinal artery syndrome); notify team immediately, MRI spine
  • Acute hypotension refractory to fluids/pressors — sepsis, graft leak, tamponade, low cardiac output; notify team STAT
  • Chest tube output suddenly increases (>200–300 mL/hr) or is bloody/fresh — active bleeding, possible graft leak or anastomotic breakdown
  • New heart murmur (diastolic, blowing) — aortic regurgitation from dissection extending into root; suggests inadequate repair or progression
  • Pulselessness or pulse deficit between limbs — dissection extension into branch vessels (carotid, subclavian, femoral, iliac)
  • Acute dyspnea or rise in O₂ requirement — pulmonary edema (AR), pneumothorax, hemothorax, pulmonary embolism
  • Fever + leukocytosis + sternal drainage or redness — early mediastinitis; notify team immediately (may require re-do surgery)
  • Altered mental status, agitation, confusion — hypoxia, sepsis, stroke, medication effect; assess and investigate
  • Oliguria or anuria despite adequate CVP — acute kidney injury, cardiogenic shock, dissection of renal arteries
  • QTc prolongation or new arrhythmia — electrolyte derangement, medication effect, ongoing cardiac ischemia
  • Inability to void or inability to move lower extremities — spinal cord ischemia affecting sacral/lower lumbar segments

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Type A aortic dissection is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY — mortality rises 1% per hour untreated in the first 48 hours. This is not a "try medical management" diagnosis. 50% of untreated Type A patients die within 48 hours. Goal is OR within 1 hour of arrival.

  2. BETA-BLOCKER FIRST, then vasodilator. NEVER vasodilator alone. This is the single most important pre-op management error to avoid. Unopposed vasodilation causes reflex tachycardia → increased dP/dt → dissection propagation. Always target HR ≤60 with beta-blocker before adding vasodilator.

  3. Strict SBP ≤120 and HR ≤60 are physiologic targets, not suggestions. They minimize aortic shear stress and prevent further tearing. Aggressive pain and anxiety management directly supports these targets.

  4. "15% of Type A dissections present painless." Acute stroke, syncope, or hemiplegia in a hypertensive patient = dissection until proven otherwise. Always include aortic imaging (CTA from neck to pelvis or MRI) in your stroke workup.

  5. Neuro baseline exam at ED arrival is CRITICAL. The dissection can occlude coronary ostia (MI), carotids (stroke), or involve descending aorta (spinal cord ischemia). Document any baseline deficits. Any post-op neuro change is a red flag and warrants urgent imaging and team evaluation.

  6. Imaging extent shapes surgical approach and prognosis. Does the dissection involve just the ascending aorta, or arch, or descending thoracic? Does it involve coronary ostia (RCA most common)? Extent determines whether DHCA is needed, which determines complication risk.

  7. STEMI pattern on ECG in a patient with sudden chest pain and hypertension = Type A dissection with RCA involvement until proven otherwise. Do NOT default to catheterization lab. Get aortic imaging first. Aortic surgery (with possible coronary re-implantation), not PCI, is the fix.

  8. Post-op mortality in surgical Type A series is 10–15% at 30 days, even in high-volume centers with modern DHCA and cerebral protection. Major complications include acute stroke (5–8%), spinal cord ischemia (3–5%), acute kidney injury (30–50%), new-onset AF (20–30%), and postoperative bleeding. These patients require ICU-level surveillance even after stepdown.

  9. Acute stroke (POD 0–5) occurs in 5–8% of Type A surgical patients. Mechanism is emboli from aortic atheroma dislodged during CPB, carotid dissection extension, or air embolism. Daily formal neuro exams are essential. Any new focal deficit → activate stroke code, CTA head/neck.

  10. Spinal cord ischemia (POD 1–3+) occurs in 3–5% of Type A patients, especially with descending aortic involvement. Anterior spinal artery syndrome presents as lower extremity weakness (bilateral), sensory loss below level, urinary retention. Prognosis is poor if confirmed. Prevention (minimizing cross-clamp time, maintaining collateral perfusion) is the goal. Notify team immediately if suspected.

  11. Acute kidney injury develops in 30–50% of Type A dissection patients post-op. Risk factors include long CPB time, contrast-induced nephropathy from imaging, distal aortic malperfusion, and low cardiac output. Monitor urine output hourly; may need to hold ACE inhibitors if creatinine is rising. Nephrology consult if Cr >2.5 or oliguria persists.

  12. New-onset post-op atrial fibrillation (POAF) occurs in 20–30% of Type A patients. Do NOT automatically anticoagulate; graft thrombosis risk is low, and bleeding risk is high. Preferred approach: rate control with beta-blockers. Anticoagulation decision requires team input balancing CHA₂DS₂-VASc score (stroke risk) vs post-op bleeding risk.

  13. Fluoroquinolone avoidance in Type A dissection patients. Some epidemiologic data suggest ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin may be associated with aortic dissection (possible effects on collagen cross-linking in aortic wall). When antibiotics are needed post-op, choose alternative agents (beta-lactams, macrolides) unless fluoroquinolone is critical.

  14. Lifelong BP control is mandatory. Target SBP <130 mmHg at home. Aggressive BP management prevents late aneurysmal expansion of the distal aorta and reduces dissection recurrence risk. Patient education on medication adherence is critical; missed beta-blocker doses are dangerous.

  15. Genetic aortopathy screening is mandatory for first-degree relatives. 10–20% of Type A dissection patients have underlying Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz, or other connective tissue disorder. Relatives should undergo aortic imaging (CTA/MRI) and genetic testing if syndromic features present. Prophylactic aortic root repair may be indicated for relatives with aortic root >5.0–5.5 cm.

cards.title: Overdrive Pacing via Epicardial Wires
cards.quickAnswer: Overdrive pacing uses epicardial atrial or ventricular wires to pace faster than a native tachyarrhythmia, breaking the reentry circuit and terminating the rhythm. Most useful for atrial flutter (macroreentrant), AVNRT/AVRT (SVT), and pause-dependent torsades. Technique: set rate 10–30% faster than tachycardia; burst pace 5–15 seconds; observe for conversion to sinus or to atrial fibrillation (often acceptable for flutter). Team-directed procedure — never nurse-initiated solo. Contraindications: WPW with atrial fibrillation (risk of VF acceleration), rapid atrial fibrillation (unpredictable response), hemodynamic instability (direct cardioversion preferred).
cards.quickAnswerHtml:
Overdrive pacing uses epicardial atrial or ventricular wires to pace faster than a native tachyarrhythmia, breaking the reentry circuit and terminating the rhythm. Most useful for atrial flutter (macroreentrant), AVNRT/AVRT (SVT), and pause-dependent torsades. Technique: set rate 10–30% faster than tachycardia; burst pace 5–15 seconds; observe for conversion to sinus or to atrial fibrillation (often acceptable for flutter).

Team-directed procedure — never nurse-initiated solo. Contraindications: WPW with atrial fibrillation (risk of VF acceleration), rapid atrial fibrillation (unpredictable response), hemodynamic instability (direct cardioversion preferred).
