sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, indications, and scope.

  • Definition: Overdrive pacing (anti-tachycardia pacing, or ATP) is the application of a pacing stimulus faster than the rate of an active tachyarrhythmia to interrupt reentry and terminate the dysrhythmia.
  • Mechanism: Most effective for macroreentrant circuits (atrial flutter) and dual-pathway reentry (SVT). Pacing depolarizes tissue within the reentry loop prematurely, breaking the pattern.
  • Incidence & timing: Useful immediately post-op (POD 0–5) while epicardial wires remain in place. Peak utility in post-op atrial flutter and SVT scenarios.
  • Who it applies to: Any post-cardiac-surgery patient with functioning epicardial wires who develops atrial flutter, SVT, or pause-dependent torsades and is hemodynamically stable.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism by rhythm:

  • Atrial flutter / macroreentry: Large reentry circuit in right atrium. Pacing at a rate faster than the circuit propagation breaks the pathway by depolarizing tissue within the loop prematurely, interrupting the self-sustaining activity. Result: conversion to sinus rhythm or (often acceptably) to atrial fibrillation.
  • AVNRT / AVRT (SVT): Narrow reentry circuits involving the AV node or accessory pathway. Burst pacing interrupts one limb of the circuit prematurely, terminating dual-pathway or accessory-pathway-mediated reentry abruptly.
  • Monomorphic VT (select cases): In specific ventricular tachycardias with defined circuits (e.g., scar-related VT post-infarction), overdrive pacing can terminate if delivered under EP guidance and with hemodynamic support. Rarely used on general floors; EP domain.
  • Pause-dependent polymorphic VT / torsades: Continuous pacing at a rate faster than the patient's intrinsic rate prevents the long pauses that allow QT-prolongation-dependent triggered activity. Temporizing while underlying cause (electrolyte depletion, QT-prolonging drugs) is corrected.

Why it works post-op: Atrial irritation from cardiopulmonary bypass, pericardial manipulation, and sternal stress predisposes to reentrant arrhythmias. Epicardial wires provide direct electrical access to atrial or ventricular tissue, making rapid pacing feasible at the bedside without transvenous lead placement.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Indications & Contraindications
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — when overdrive pacing is indicated and when it is contraindicated.

Universally indicated:

  • Atrial flutter (especially type I, macroreentrant): First-line non-pharmacologic intervention when atrial wires are available and patient is hemodynamically stable. Often converts to sinus or acceptable atrial fibrillation.
  • Paroxysmal SVT (AVNRT or AVRT): Effective for breaking reentry when β-blockers, calcium channel blockers, or adenosine have failed or are contraindicated.
  • Pause-dependent torsades de pointes: Bridge therapy while correcting QT prolongation and electrolyte abnormalities. Generator left on VVI mode at 100–120 bpm continuously (not burst pacing).

Contraindicated (do not attempt):

Situation Reason Action
WPW syndrome + atrial fibrillation Atrial pacing can accelerate conduction across accessory pathway → rapid VF DO NOT pace. Proceed to synchronized DCCV or amiodarone.
Rapid atrial fibrillation (RVR) Unpredictable response; may accelerate rate or cause hemodynamic collapse Use rate-control meds or DCCV instead.
Hemodynamic instability (SBP < 90 mmHg, altered mental status, pulmonary edema, chest pain) DCCV is immediate; overdrive pacing adds time and delays definitive therapy Synchronized DCCV is safer and preferred.

Relative cautions:

  • Monomorphic VT without EP guidance (high-risk in non-EP setting; consult first)
  • Pacer-dependent patient (ensure backup pacing mode is set reliably before initiating burst)
  • Recent myocardial infarction or acute ischemia (increased VF risk)
  • Severe electrolyte abnormalities: K⁺ < 3.0 or Mg²⁺ < 1.5 (correct electrolytes first)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Verify pre-pacing prerequisites* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic checklist. Information-only; no interventions yet.

Baseline:

  • Confirm atrial/ventricular wire functional: Verify capture at baseline rate on pacer box (pacing spike + depolarization on monitor).
  • Hemodynamic stability: SBP > 90 mmHg, alert, perfusing, tolerating arrhythmia without chest pain or dyspnea.
  • Rhythm confirmation: 12-lead ECG or telemetry showing suspected arrhythmia (flutter wave morphology, irregularly irregular, SVT rate/regularity).
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, iCa²⁺ (low electrolytes reduce pacing efficacy); most recent hemoglobin, creatinine.
  • Provider order: Explicit order for rate, duration, and chamber (atrial vs ventricular).
  • Immediate readiness: Physician/APP at bedside or in unit; defibrillator + pacing + cardioversion capability nearby; transcutaneous pacing pads available; medications (adenosine, β-blockers, amiodarone) drawn.

sections.heading: 5.1 Rate Selection Table
sections.bodyHtml:
Arrhythmia Native Rate Pacing Rate Rationale
Atrial flutter 140–180 bpm 150–210 bpm (10–30% faster) Outpaces circuit; faster = higher capture probability
AVNRT 140–200 bpm 160–230 bpm (10–30% faster) Breaks dual AV nodal pathway
AVRT 150–220 bpm 170–250 bpm (10–30% faster) Interrupts accessory pathway–AV node loop
Monomorphic VT 150–200 bpm 160–230 bpm (variable per EP) As directed by EP consultation
Torsades (pause-prevent) Variable 100–120 bpm (sustained) Maintains continuous ventricular capture; prevents long pause

sections.heading: 5.2 Burst Duration & Repetition Protocol
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Initial burst: 5–10 seconds at selected rate; observe response on telemetry.
  2. If no termination: Continue for additional 5 seconds.
  3. If still no response: Repeat burst at slightly higher rate (10–20 bpm increase) up to 2–3 attempts.
  4. Maximum duration per burst: 15–20 seconds to minimize hemodynamic stress and ischemia risk.
  5. Interval between bursts: 30–60 seconds to allow native rhythm emergence and stabilization.
  6. Total number of attempts: 2–3 bursts per protocol; further attempts typically require provider reassessment or escalation to DCCV.

sections.heading: 5.3 Generator Setup & Safety
sections.bodyHtml:
Parameter Setting Action
Mode Demand or synchronous (per arrhythmia) Usually AAI, VVI, or DDD for overdrive; avoid asynchronous (AOO/VOO) in awake patient
Rate 10–30% above arrhythmia rate Set precisely; redial if uncertain
Output 5–10 mA (typically) Ensure consistent capture at threshold rate; may increase if inconsistent
Sensitivity Minimal (inhibit sensing to ensure pacing) For burst pacing, sensing may be turned off to guarantee output during burst
Monitoring Continuous telemetry Observe QRS/P-wave capture; watch for fusion or undersensing

sections.heading: 5.4 Post-Pacing Observation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Turn off pacing after burst (or reduce to backup rate if pacer-dependent).
  • Watch for:
  • Conversion to sinus rhythm (ideal outcome).
  • Conversion to atrial fibrillation (acceptable for atrial flutter; less desirable for SVT, but rhythm may stabilize).
  • Continuation of original arrhythmia (failed attempt; consider repeat burst or escalation).
  • Acceleration of arrhythmia (rare; stop immediately; consider DCCV).

sections.heading: 5.5 Nursing Execution Step-by-Step
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Provider order confirmation: Explicit rate, duration, chamber.
  2. Set parameters on pacer box: Rate, output, mode, sensitivity per §5.3.
  3. Confirm capture: Observe pacing spike + depolarization on telemetry.
  4. Begin burst: Press pacing button per provider instruction; time the burst (5–15 seconds).
  5. Stop burst: Release pacing button; allow native rhythm to emerge.
  6. Monitor continuously: Watch for conversion, rate changes, hemodynamic response.
  7. Communicate: Announce observations to provider in real-time.
  8. Return generator: Restore to baseline settings (backup mode, appropriate rate for patient dependency status).

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate if:

  1. No termination after 1–2 bursts at escalating rates — verify capture is present (pacing spike visible), verify rate was truly 10–30% above native. If capture confirmed and rate appropriate but rhythm persists, notify provider; consider alternative diagnosis or DCCV.
  2. Acceleration of arrhythmia during pacing — rare but urgent; stop pacing immediately; prepare for DCCV.
  3. Hemodynamic deterioration during burst (BP dropping, patient complaining of chest pain, altered mental status) — stop burst immediately; prepare for DCCV.
  4. Loss of capture mid-burst (pacing spike present but no depolarization) — possible wire displacement or battery depletion; troubleshoot generator; may need to switch to backup wire or transcutaneous pacing.
  5. Pacer-dependent patient fails to restore native rhythm after successful burst — risk of profound bradycardia or asystole if backup pacing fails; ensure backup rate is set and test-paced before initiating burst on these patients.
  6. Fusion or undersensing during burst (paced + intrinsic beats visible, or asynchronous pacing) — indicates improper settings or wire malfunction; adjust polarity or sensitivity; stop and troubleshoot before continuing.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections in Section 7 are intended for in-app collapse. Nursing students and advanced beginners can expand to build deeper understanding; experienced nurses can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Mechanism detail
sections.bodyHtml:
Atrial flutter circuit interruption: Atrial flutter typically involves a large macroreentrant circuit propagating around the tricuspid valve annulus or between caval orifices. The circuit has a fixed wavelength (conduction velocity × refractory period). When an external pacing stimulus enters the circuit at a rate faster than the intrinsic circuit rate, it depolarizes tissue within the loop prematurely. The incoming wavefront collides with the native flutter wave, annihilating both. If the timing is right, the collision occurs in tissue that has already repolarized, breaking the self-sustaining activity. The atrium then either reverts to sinus rhythm or (often) fibrillates. AF is generally more stable than flutter and is considered an acceptable endpoint.

SVT (AVNRT/AVRT) termination: AVNRT depends on dual pathways in the AV node (fast and slow); AVRT depends on an accessory pathway and the AV node. In both, an atrial premature beat conducted down one pathway (fast pathway in AVNRT; AV node in AVRT) may find the other pathway (slow pathway / accessory pathway) refractory, blocking retrograde conduction and terminating the circuit. Overdrive pacing simulates this phenomenon: continuous rapid pacing from the atrium forces conduction down the fast pathway (or AV node) and may render the slow pathway (or accessory pathway) refractory, terminating the reentry abruptly.

Torsades suppression (continuous pacing): Pause-dependent polymorphic VT (torsades de pointes) arises when a long RR interval allows prolonged repolarization (manifest as QT prolongation), permitting early afterdepolarizations to trigger ectopic activity. Continuous pacing at a rate slightly above the intrinsic rate (typically 100–120 bpm) shortens the RR interval, compressing the QT and preventing the triggers. This is not "burst" pacing but sustained overdrive pacing — the generator is left on VVI at a fixed rate until the underlying cause (electrolyte depletion, drug withdrawal) is corrected and QT normalizes.

sections.heading: 7.2 Wire troubleshooting
sections.bodyHtml:
Atrial wires often fail first: Fibrosis, displacement, and mechanical trauma during closure all reduce atrial capture over days 1–5 post-op. Always confirm capture at baseline before ordering atrial pacing. If atrial wires lose capture, notify the team; ventricular wire option may be available.

Loss of capture mid-burst:

  • Check battery indicator on pacer box (dead battery = no output).
  • Verify polarity: if pacing spike appears but no depolarization, try reversing lead polarity on the box.
  • Confirm wire connections are seated firmly.
  • If troubleshooting fails, prepare for transcutaneous pacing or escalate to DCCV.

Undersensing / fusion beats: Asynchronous pacing (paced and intrinsic beats competing) is dangerous. If fusion is observed, increase sensitivity or change polarity. Do not continue competitive pacing.

sections.heading: 7.3 WPW syndrome — absolute contraindication
sections.bodyHtml:
Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome + atrial fibrillation is the dangerous combination: In normal AF, the AV node acts as a rate-limiting filter, keeping ventricular rate manageable (120–180 bpm). However, WPW patients have an accessory pathway that bypasses the AV node and conducts rapidly. In AF, conduction across the accessory pathway is not rate-limited; ventricular rates can exceed 250 bpm, causing hemodynamic collapse and degeneration into ventricular fibrillation.

Atrial overdrive pacing in this scenario accelerates conduction across the accessory pathway and is absolutely contraindicated. The appropriate therapy is synchronized DCCV or IV amiodarone (which blocks the accessory pathway).

sections.heading: 7.4 Special populations
sections.bodyHtml:
Pacer-dependent patients: Ensure backup pacing mode is reliable (VVI or DDD) and set to a safe rate before initiating burst. If the burst terminates the tachyarrhythmia and leaves the patient in a slow intrinsic rhythm (or asystole), the backup pacer must capture immediately. A pacer-dependent patient who loses capture during this window is in cardiac arrest.

Post-MAZE patients: Early AF is common post-MAZE (within 4 weeks) and is expected as the atrial incisions heal. DCCV is usually ineffective until atrial scarring matures. Rate control plus amiodarone is the default strategy; overdrive pacing is less useful in this population.

Torsades de pointes: Once pause-dependent torsades is recognized, overdrive pacing is initiated as CONTINUOUS (not burst) therapy. The goal is to maintain a heart rate of 100–120 bpm continuously, preventing pauses. Concurrent electrolyte repletion (K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0) and discontinuation of QT-prolonging drugs is essential. Coordinate with the provider to discontinue pacing only when QTc normalizes and electrolytes are replete.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in patients who were "stable on the protocol"; if any develop, re-escalate.

  • Acceleration of arrhythmia during pacing — stop immediately; prepare for DCCV.
  • Hemodynamic deterioration (SBP dropping, altered mental status, chest pain) during or immediately after burst — indicates rhythm is not terminating; escalate to DCCV.
  • Loss of capture mid-burst (pacing spike visible but no QRS/P wave) — wire malfunction or battery failure; troubleshoot or switch to backup wire.
  • Recurrence of arrhythmia within minutes of successful termination — inadequate load, ongoing trigger, or need for rate-control medications; notify provider.
  • Pacer-dependent patient with bradycardia post-burst — risk of asystole if backup fails; ensure backup is capturing and set appropriately.
  • Fusion beats or competitive pacing — indicates undersensing; adjust sensitivity immediately to avoid dangerous rhythm.
  • Long pause (>5 seconds) after failed burst in post-infarction or low-K⁺ patient — VF risk; re-initiate backup pacing or transcutaneous pacing immediately.
  • QTc approaching or exceeding 500 ms on concurrent amiodarone — torsades risk; hold/decrease amiodarone per provider.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
(10–15 high-yield bullets for experienced nurses and experts)

  1. Overdrive pacing is a TEAM-DIRECTED procedure, not nurse-solo. Never initiate pacing without explicit provider order and physician/APP presence. Failure to follow this has led to missed WPW-AFib, wrong rate selection, and prolonged unnecessary pacing.

  2. Most useful for atrial flutter, AVNRT, and AVRT. These are macroreentrant or dual-pathway circuits. Overdrive pacing breaks reentry and is often first-line when wires are available.

  3. Unpredictable in rapid atrial fibrillation (RVR). Do NOT attempt overdrive pacing for AFib with RVR; response is unpredictable and may accelerate. Use rate-control meds or DCCV.

  4. WPW + atrial fibrillation = DO NOT OVERDRIVE PACE. Contraindication. Pacing the atrium can accelerate conduction across the accessory pathway into VF. Use DCCV or amiodarone instead.

  5. Atrial flutter often converts to atrial fibrillation after overdrive pacing. This is usually acceptable because AF is more stable than flutter and allows better rate control. Document as successful outcome.

  6. Start pacing rate 10–30% faster than the tachyarrhythmia rate. Too slow = ineffective; too fast = unnecessary hemodynamic stress. Measure native rate on strip before selecting pacer rate.

  7. Burst duration: 5–15 seconds max per attempt. Longer bursts increase risk of hemodynamic compromise and don't increase efficacy. Three 10-second bursts at escalating rates are typical.

  8. DCCV is preferred for unstable patients (SBP < 90, altered mentation, chest pain, pulmonary edema). Overdrive pacing requires seconds to minutes; DCCV is immediate.

  9. Document rhythm BEFORE, DURING, and AFTER overdrive pacing. Providers and next shift need the pre-pacing rhythm, pacing parameters (rate, duration, output), and post-pacing rhythm + patient response.

  10. Transcutaneous pacing is an alternative if epicardial wires are non-functional. Transcutaneous overdrive pacing is less effective (capture may be inconsistent) but is an option.

  11. Atrial wires often fail first due to fibrosis and displacement. If atrial wires lose capture, you cannot perform atrial overdrive pacing. Know wire status before ordering atrial pacing.

  12. Pause-dependent torsades requires CONTINUOUS overdrive pacing, not burst. Generator is left on VVI at 100–120 bpm until QT prolongs and electrolytes are replete. Coordinate with provider to discontinue safely.

  13. Long pause after pacing attempt increases VF risk (especially post-infarction, low K⁺, baseline QT prolongation). After unsuccessful burst, do not allow >5 seconds of asystole or bradycardia before restarting backup pacing.

  14. Fusion or undersensing during pacing indicates improper settings or wire malfunction. Fusion beats suggest undersensing; change polarity or increase sensitivity. Undersensing = competitive pacing (dangerous). Stop and troubleshoot before continuing.

  15. Patient and family need clear expectation-setting before attempt. Explain: "We're going to pace your heart faster for a few seconds to break this abnormal rhythm. You'll feel your heart racing — this is planned and temporary."

cards.title: Epicardial Pacer Wire Routine Management
cards.quickAnswer: Temporary epicardial pacer wires provide backup rhythm support post-operatively (typically 3–5 days) until native conduction recovers. Assess capture and sensing thresholds every shift; monitor wire site for infection and dressing integrity. Know pacer-dependency status before any adjustment. Loss of capture in a pacer-dependent patient → STAT code response + transcutaneous pads at bedside. Standard pacing modes: DDD (preferred, all 4 wires) maintains AV synchrony; VVI (2 ventricular wires only) if atrial wires fail. Set output at 2–3× capture threshold and sensitivity at ≤ half intrinsic voltage. Wire removal typically POD 3–6; monitor vitals q15 min × 1 h post-removal for late tamponade.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, anatomy, and scope.

  • Definition: Temporary electrical leads sutured directly to the epicardium during cardiac surgery. Provide backup pacing for bradycardia, heart block, and rate/rhythm control in atrial fibrillation until native conduction system recovers from surgical edema.
  • Anatomy: Typically 4 wires — 2 atrial (right atrial free wall) and 2 ventricular (RV epicardium). Exit through skin below incision, anchored with suture, covered with occlusive dressing. Connect to external pulse generator (Medtronic 5388 or equivalent).
  • Duration: Usually present POD 0–3 to POD 4–6 (varies by procedure and surgeon preference). CABG typically POD 3–4; valve surgery POD 4–6.
  • Who it applies to: Every post-cardiac-surgery patient (sternotomy only; TAVR and catheter-based procedures do not place epicardial wires). Critical for AV-node-dependent procedures (AVR, MVR, TV repair).
  • When to use: Bradycardia unresponsive to atropine, complete heart block, rate/rhythm control for post-op atrial fibrillation, or diagnostic pacing for rhythm clarification.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Why It Exists
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-operative bradyarrhythmias and conduction disturbances are common after cardiac surgery due to:

Mechanism of post-op heart block / bradycardia:

  • AV node manipulation — surgery on the AVR, mitral valve, or aortic root places the AV node at risk for transient ischemia and edema
  • Right coronary artery compromise — the AV nodal artery is typically a RCA branch; surgical retraction or cannulation can reduce flow
  • Surgical edema and inflammation — resolves over 3–5 days as swelling recedes and collateral blood flow improves
  • Sinus node dysfunction — less common but occurs with extensive right atrial manipulation (e.g., extensive MAZE)
  • Intraoperative cooling and rewarming — CPB and hypothermia increase conduction system irritability and latent ischemia

Why temporary epicardial pacing is superior to transvenous:

  • Speed: placed intra-operatively; immediately available without cath lab
  • Safety: avoids central venous puncture and intravascular catheter infection
  • Capability: dual-chamber (DDD) pacing maintains AV synchrony; atrial electrograms for rhythm diagnosis
  • Reliability: epicardial contact is firm and stable; capture thresholds typically remain stable 3–5 days

Timeline of recovery:

Most patients recover native AV conduction within 24–72 hours post-op (POD 0–2). A subset (especially post-AVR) may need pacing through POD 5–6. Waiting for spontaneous recovery is safe; pacing wires are the safety net, not the default pacer.

sections.heading: 3. Scope / Who It Applies To
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner recognition — patient populations and clinical triggers.

Universally indicated (placed at surgery end):

  • All sternotomy-based cardiac surgeries: CABG, AVR, MVR, TVR, aortic repair, MAZE, myectomy, transplant, ECMO
  • At least 1 atrial and 1 ventricular pair for routine use; often 2 pairs each for redundancy

Special high-risk populations (expected higher use POD 1–2):

  • AVR or aortic root patients — highest risk for AV block (5–10% complete heart block); plan for extended pacing capability
  • MVR patients — AV node at risk from left atrial approach; expect brady phase POD 1–3
  • Post-MAZE patients — extensive right atrial work; sinus node dysfunction common; expect pacing need POD 1–2
  • Redo surgery — scarring increases conduction risk; assume potential for bradycardia POD 0–3
  • Pacer-dependent pre-op — if patient has a permanent pacemaker, epicardial wires provide critical backup during CIED interrogation and management post-op

Contraindications to pacing wire placement (rare intra-op decisions):

  • Severe post-op bleeding / coagulopathy already requiring massive transfusion (not a firm contraindication, but team may defer wires as one intervention in damage control)
  • No anticipated cardiothoracic ICU stay (emergency ECMO → other hospital; unlikely in planned surgery)

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Gather baseline and ongoing status* (5 minutes per shift)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside and pacer box review. Information-only; no adjustments yet.

Baseline (on POD 0–1 or ICU admission):

  • Pacer-dependency status — Is the patient pacemaker-dependent (complete heart block) or pacemaker-responsive (bradycardia but some native backup)? This is CRITICAL and must be known before any intervention.
  • Pacer box mode and settings — Rate (bpm), Output (mA), Sensitivity (number), AV Delay if DDD/VDD, Upper Tracking Rate (UTR)
  • Procedural context — Which surgery, when, what was the concern that led to pacing placement? (e.g., "3rd degree AV block intra-op" vs "routine for post-AVR")
  • Wire function at placement — Initial capture thresholds (atrial and ventricular) recorded in the OR record?

Every shift (ongoing, minimum per shift):

Assessment Item Check Normal Finding Action if Abnormal
Pacer box visual inspection Generator on/off; mode, rate, output, sensitivity visible on display All displayed correctly per order; battery > 25% Adjust per order; document changes; notify provider if unexplained drift
Battery status Icon on screen or battery indicator light > 25% charge Replace battery per device manual; most units have ~40 h runtime at standard settings
Wire connections All cables firmly seated in labeled jacks; no visible corrosion; taped to prevent tension Connections secure, protected, labeled Reconnect firmly; verify polarity (A+/–, V+/–); re-label; use protective sleeves
Wire insertion site(s) Dressing intact, clean, dry; exit site clean; no erythema, warmth, drainage Dressing clean, dry, intact; site non-tender Change dressing per [Institution policy]; notify provider for signs of infection
Capture threshold (atrial & ventricular) Each chamber: increase rate to 100 bpm, observe pacing spikes followed by P or QRS Consistent atrial/ventricular capture at ≤ 5 mA at current output Increase output to 2–3× threshold; check connections; assess electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺); notify provider if persistently rising or loss of capture
Sensing threshold (atrial & ventricular) Decrease sensitivity (increase number) until generator fails to sense intrinsic beats; then increase back until consistent sensing Generator withholds pacer spike when native beat present Adjust sensitivity to ~half intrinsic voltage; notify provider if persistent undersensing (competitive pacing) or oversensing (inhibition)
Underlying native rhythm With provider approval, reduce rate to 30 bpm × 10 seconds to assess native rhythm; reset immediately Identifies native rate and conduction; typical: sinus bradycardia POD 0–1, progressive normalization POD 2–3 Document findings; reset rate immediately; notify provider of sudden loss of native rhythm, new conduction block, or rapid rate
Paced and sensed rhythm on monitor Review telemetry/ECG strip: are paced spikes visible? Are sensed beats appropriately withheld? Paced spikes visible at set rate; native beats inhibit pacing appropriately Loss of capture = spikes without QRS; undersensing = competitive pacing; oversensing = inappropriate inhibition; troubleshoot per §5
Pacer-dependency reassessment Know patient's status at every hand-off Confirmed dependent or responsive status documented in shift notes If status changed, notify provider STAT

sections.heading: 5.1 Pacing modes explained
sections.bodyHtml:
Mode Chamber Pacing/Sensing Description When Used Wire Requirements Clinical Notes
DDD A: sensed + paced; V: sensed + paced Dual-chamber demand pacing with AV synchrony First-line; maintains AV synchrony, optimal hemodynamics All 4 wires functional (2 atrial, 2 ventricular) Most physiologic; requires intact atrial sensing and capture
VVI V: sensed + paced; A: ignored Ventricular demand only; no atrial input Atrial wires lost/failed; atrial fibrillation; when A-V sync not critical 2 ventricular wires minimum Less hemodynamic than DDD; adequate for emergency backup
VDD A: sensed (not paced); V: sensed + paced Atrial sensed, ventricular paced AV block with intact SA node function 2 atrial, 2 ventricular Compromises; lacks atrial pacing for sinus dysfunction
AAI A: sensed + paced; V: ignored Atrial demand only Sinus bradycardia with intact AV conduction 2 atrial wires Rare post-op; requires functioning AV node
AOO / VOO / DOO Fixed asynchronous rate Triggered at set interval regardless of native activity OR (during cautery interference), emergency backup, code settings Any wires Risk of competitive pacing; short-term only

sections.heading: 5.2 Key pacer box settings and nursing role
sections.bodyHtml:
Setting Typical Range Definition Nursing Role
Rate (bpm) 80–90 Pacing rate when no intrinsic activity sensed Monitor display; adjust per provider order; document every shift
Output (mA) 2–3× capture threshold (usually 2–5 mA) Current delivered to myocardium to achieve electrical capture Set at minimum effective dose to preserve battery; increase if capture threshold rises
Sensitivity ≤ half intrinsic voltage (usually 2–4 mV) Threshold at which generator detects native beats; prevents undersensing Adjust downward (higher number) if oversensing (pacer inhibited incorrectly); upward if undersensing
AV Delay (DDD/VDD only) 150–200 ms Time interval between atrial and ventricular pacing Optimize AV synchrony; shorter delays favor atrial kick contribution; longer delays avoid "pacemaker syndrome"
Upper Tracking Rate (UTR) (DDD only) 120–140 bpm Maximum rate at which ventricle tracks atrial pacing in response to atrial activity Prevents rapid ventricular pacing if patient's atrial rate exceeds this threshold

sections.heading: 5.3 Capture & sensing thresholds: daily protocol
sections.bodyHtml:
Capture Threshold Assessment:

  1. Verify provider order to proceed with threshold check
  2. For atrial wire: increase rate to 100 bpm; observe ECG/monitor for pacing spike followed by P wave (atrial capture)
  3. For ventricular wire: increase rate to 100 bpm; observe for pacing spike followed by QRS (ventricular capture)
  4. Gradually increase rate in 10 bpm increments; note the lowest output mA at which consistent capture occurs (not sporadic)
  5. Set working output = 2–3× capture threshold to maintain safety margin against rising thresholds

Sensing Threshold Assessment:

  1. Verify native rhythm is present
  2. Gradually decrease sensitivity (increase displayed number, e.g., from 2 to 3 to 4)
  3. Observe monitor for loss of sensing (pacer fails to inhibit on native beats; competitive pacing appears)
  4. Note the threshold where inhibition is lost; back off to the last setting with consistent sensing
  5. Set working sensitivity ≈ half the intrinsic voltage (e.g., if intrinsic P wave 4 mV, set sensitivity to 2 mV)

Rising Thresholds — Warning Signs:

  • Atrial threshold rising from 1–2 mA → 4–5 mA over 24–48 h (suggests wire fibrosis, displacement, metabolic derangement)
  • Ventricular threshold rising abruptly (usually slower to rise than atrial)
  • Actions: Check electrolytes (K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0); review medications (anti-arrhythmics increase thresholds); notify provider; may indicate wire displacement or need for repositioning

sections.heading: 5.4 Troubleshooting common pacer issues
sections.bodyHtml:
Problem Most Likely Cause Assessment Action
Loss of capture (spike visible on monitor, no QRS/P following)
  1. Loose cable connection (most common >60%)
  2. Wire displacement
  3. Rising threshold
  4. Electrolyte depletion
 Check connections first; verify all cables firmly seated and labeled; assess for visible disconnection or corrosion Reconnect firmly; re-label; increase output; check K⁺ and Mg²⁺; notify provider STAT if pacer-dependent
Undersensing (pacer fires on native beats; competitive pacing visible)
  1. Sensitivity set too low (insensitive)
  2. Lead displacement
  3. Low intrinsic voltage
  4. Electrolyte depletion
 Decrease sensitivity (lower mV setting); observe for pacer spike to disappear on native beats Adjust sensitivity to ~half intrinsic voltage; notify provider; may need provider-ordered sensitivity adjustment
Oversensing (pacer inhibited inappropriately; pauses in pacing when patient has native activity)
  1. Sensitivity set too high (oversensitive)
  2. Electrical noise (diathermy, nearby telemetry)
  3. Large T wave being sensed as QRS
 Increase sensitivity (higher number); check for external electrical interference Adjust sensitivity; move telemetry boxes away; notify provider if persists
Rising thresholds (output mA increasing over 24–48 h despite normal capture)
  1. Wire inflammation/fibrosis
  2. Hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia
  3. Drug effect (anti-arrhythmics)
 Check K⁺ (goal ≥ 4.0), Mg²⁺ (goal ≥ 2.0); review MAR for class I/III drugs; assess for fever Replicate electrolytes; notify provider of trend; consider wire repositioning if threshold exceeds safe output range
Battery depletion (low battery icon; < 25% charge) Normal battery use; typical 40 h runtime at standard settings Check battery indicator; calculate remaining runtime Replace battery per device manual; have backup unit ready

sections.heading: 5.5 Pacemaker-dependent patients — code response protocol
sections.bodyHtml:
Identify pacer dependency:

  • Documented in chart at admission ("pacer-dependent" or "will not tolerate rate < 40 bpm")
  • Or discovered by temporary rate reduction and patient loses cardiac output (hypotension, loss of consciousness, widened QRS)

If pacemaker-dependent patient loses pacing:

  1. ACTIVATE CODE / RAPID RESPONSE immediately — do NOT wait for provider response
  2. Apply transcutaneous pacer pads at bedside (if not already on patient)
  3. Reconnect pacer wires first (check all cables)
  4. Increase output to maximum if capture loss
  5. If no capture restore with wires → initiate transcutaneous pacing per ACLS
  6. Call provider/surgical team STAT
  7. Prepare for possible emergent wire repositioning or temporary transvenous pacing

Prevention:

  • Know dependency status at every hand-off
  • Keep transcutaneous pads at bedside if pacer-dependent
  • Do NOT turn off pacer or reduce rate without provider awareness
  • Avoid patient movement that tugs on wires (ambulation must be supervised; secure wires to chest)

sections.heading: 5.6 Electrolyte and medication reversibles — before escalating pacer management
sections.bodyHtml:
Always correct these FIRST before assuming pacer failure:

Factor Target Action
Hypokalemia K⁺ ≥ 4.0 mmol/L Replicate per Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement protocol. Directly impairs smooth muscle (atrial/ventricular) capture.
Hypomagnesemia Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 mg/dL Replicate per protocol. Mg is cofactor in muscle contraction; low Mg = poor capture.
Anti-arrhythmic drugs Minimize burden if possible Class I (procainamide, quinidine, flecainide) and Class III (amiodarone, sotalol) increase capture thresholds. Review MAR; discuss with provider if drug can be held.
Fever or infection T < 38.3°C; WBC normalized Fever increases metabolic demand; infection causes local inflammation → rising thresholds. Treat source.
Wire site infection Clean, dry, intact dressing Local infection/inflammation → rising thresholds in adjacent tissue. Change dressing; notify provider for erythema/drainage.

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers / When Standard Practice Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of escalation flags.

Reassess and escalate immediately if:

  1. Loss of capture in a pacer-dependent patient — CODE response level. Reconnect wires; if no capture → transcutaneous pacing + STAT provider call.
  2. Sustained loss of capture despite connection checks and output maxed — wire displacement or failure; provider must assess for repositioning or transvenous backup.
  3. Capture threshold rising continuously over 24 h (e.g., 2 → 3 → 5 → 7 mA) — fibrosis, displacement, or metabolic derangement. Correct electrolytes; notify provider.
  4. Undersensing with competitive pacing lasting > few minutes — risk of R-on-T; adjust sensitivity immediately; notify provider if does not resolve.
  5. Oversensing causing inappropriate inhibition (pacer should pace but doesn't) — adjust sensitivity upward; check for electrical interference; notify provider.
  6. Sudden increase in atrial or ventricular capture threshold by > 2–3 mA over 1–2 hours — acute displacement or perforation risk; notify provider STAT.
  7. Wire site erythema, warmth, or purulent drainage — infection concern. Do NOT remove dressing; notify provider STAT; prepare for wire removal.
  8. New fever + rising capture thresholds + patient appears septic — possible infection at wire site. Blood cultures, notify provider; prepare for expedited wire removal.
  9. Pacing-induced discomfort or muscle twitching at high output — suggests skeletal muscle capture (output too high) or nerve irritation. Decrease output; notify provider.
  10. Persistent inability to achieve safe sensing despite repeated adjustment — wire sensing failure; may need repositioning or conversion to asynchronous mode as bridge.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: All subsections in Section 7 are intended for in-app collapse. Nursing students, new-grad RNs, and advanced beginners can expand to build deeper understanding; experienced nurses and experts can skip.

sections.heading: 7.1 Physiology of electrical capture and sensing
sections.bodyHtml:
Electrical capture:

  • Pacer wire delivers current (measured in milliamps, mA) across the epicardial tissue
  • Threshold = minimum current required to depolarize the myocardium consistently
  • If output is set BELOW threshold, spikes are visible on ECG but no QRS/P follows (loss of capture)
  • Safety margin = 2–3× threshold — accounts for gradual rising of threshold due to scar formation

Sensing:

  • Pacer detects the electrical voltage of the patient's native heartbeat (measured in millivolts, mV)
  • Sensitivity is set as the minimum voltage the pacer will recognize (e.g., if set to 2 mV, it only recognizes heartbeats > 2 mV)
  • If sensitivity is too LOW (insensitive) → pacer doesn't see the native beat → undersensing → competitive pacing (dangerous, risk of R-on-T)
  • If sensitivity is too HIGH (oversensitive) → pacer sees noise or T waves as QRS → oversensing → inappropriate inhibition
  • Optimal sensitivity ≈ half the intrinsic voltage — balances detection against noise

Why electrolytes matter:

  • Hypokalemia (K⁺ < 3.5) and hypomagnesemia (Mg²⁺ < 1.8) directly impair myocardial depolarization
  • Both worsen capture threshold (requires MORE current to capture a "sluggish" atrium or ventricle)
  • Correcting K⁺ and Mg²⁺ FIRST before escalating output is critical

sections.heading: 7.2 Pacing wire care and infection prevention
sections.bodyHtml:
Wire site care:

  • Dressing change per [Institution policy], typically every 24–48 h or if damp
  • Clean with chlorhexidine or per protocol; apply sterile occlusive dressing
  • Never allow water to contact the wire site (shower vs. bath per team direction)
  • Anchoring suture should be intact; report any suture slipping or wire migration (changes in wire insertion depth)

Infection prevention:

  • Incidence: epicardial wire infection 1–5% depending on duration (highest risk after POD 5)
  • Risk factors: prolonged placement (> 7 days), frequent dressing changes (disrupts barrier), patient with fever or immunosuppression
  • Signs: erythema, warmth, purulent drainage, fever, rising WBC
  • Outcome: early removal (within 24 h of infection suspicion) → low morbidity; delayed removal → deep sternal wound infection, mediastinitis (surgical emergency)

Prevention:

  • Minimize dressing disruptions
  • Maintain sterile technique at dressing changes
  • Keep site dry
  • Notify provider STAT for any signs of infection
  • Plan removal timing with provider; most removed POD 3–6 (not routinely kept > 7 days)

sections.heading: 7.3 Wire removal — timing, technique, and post-removal monitoring
sections.bodyHtml:
Removal timing:

  • Routine: POD 3–4 (CABG); POD 4–6 (valve surgery); POD 5–7 (post-MAZE or complex)
  • Do NOT remove if patient still pacemaker-dependent (requires ongoing pacing)
  • Coordinate with provider; verify anticoagulation status (see below)

Removal technique (provider/surgeon performs; nurse role is preparation and monitoring):

  1. Verify provider order and pacer-dependency reassessment
  2. Patient supine or head of bed elevated; quiet environment
  3. Provider gently pulls each wire in a slow, steady motion; do NOT jerk or yank (risk of ventricular ectopy, tamponade)
  4. If resistance encountered, stop; do NOT force. A retained segment (few mm) is well-tolerated; may clip at skin level and allow resorption
  5. Cover entry site with sterile occlusive dressing post-removal
  6. Obtain 12-lead ECG and chest X-ray immediately post-removal (baseline for comparison if tamponade suspected)

Post-removal monitoring (critical for detecting late tamponade):

  • Vitals: q15 min × 1 h, then q30 min × 2 h — monitor for hypotension, tachycardia, or other signs of cardiac compromise
  • Watch for tamponade signs: chest pain, dyspnea, muffled heart sounds, hypotension, tachycardia, elevated JVD, pulsus paradoxus
  • Late tamponade can occur 1–4 h after removal (rare, ~1% incidence)
  • If tamponade suspected: call provider STAT; prepare for pericardiocentesis or echo; monitor continuously

Anticoagulation coordination:

  • Do NOT remove wires if INR > 1.5 or patient on therapeutic anticoagulation (e.g., heparin gtt) without provider direction
  • Coordinate with surgery team; may need to hold warfarin × 24 h pre-removal or reverse AC if patient recently anticoagulated
  • If patient has dual-chamber device or high embolic risk, discuss AC continuation/bridging strategy with provider

sections.heading: 7.4 Special populations and edge cases
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-MAZE patients:

  • Extensive atrial surgery → atrial fibrillation is EXPECTED in the first 4 weeks
  • Atrial wires may be unreliable for pacing (chaotic AF tissue) or sensing (no organized P waves)
  • Rely on ventricular wires for backup pacing; don't waste time chasing atrial capture in AF
  • Rate control (VVI mode) + amiodarone is the standard approach

Pacer-dependent patients (pre-op or post-op):

  • If patient had a permanent pacemaker pre-op, ensure pacemaker is interrogated post-op; verify function and battery status
  • Epicardial wires serve as critical backup during CIED assessment and during any provider-ordered pacing requirement
  • Know the permanent device type (manufacturer, model) and settings

Redo surgery / complex cases:

  • Extensive adhesions and scarring → wire placement may be more challenging; monitor thresholds closely POD 1–2
  • Expect higher rates of conduction disturbance; plan for extended pacing coverage (POD 4–6)

Heart transplant patients:

  • Native-donor AV node dysfunction is common post-transplant
  • Epicardial wires provide critical backup; atrial pacing especially important (helps entrain donor atrium into sinus rhythm)
  • Plan extended pacing duration (POD 5–7) compared to standard CABG

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory in a Currently Stable Patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in patients who were "stable on wires"; if any develop, re-escalate immediately.

  • Gradual rise in capture thresholds over 24–48 h (e.g., 2 mA → 4 mA → 5.5 mA) — wire fibrosis or displacement; notify provider
  • Sudden loss of capture in previously stable patient — check connections first; if confirmed loss, notify provider STAT
  • New undersensing or oversensing despite recent adjustment — wire sensing failure; may need repositioning or mode change
  • Fever + rising capture thresholds + patient appears ill — possible wire site infection; notify provider STAT; prepare for expedited removal
  • New erythema, warmth, or drainage at wire site — infection concern; change dressing, notify provider; plan removal
  • Persistent loss of atrial capture in DDD mode — atrial wire failure; plan conversion to VVI mode; notify provider
  • Pacing-induced patient discomfort or muscle twitching at stable output — suggests changing tissue contact or increased skeletal capture; decrease output; notify provider
  • New arrhythmia (ectopy, runs of VT) triggered by pacer spikes — competitive pacing from undersensing; adjust sensitivity; notify provider STAT
  • Patient becomes pacemaker-dependent and had been independent — native rhythm deteriorating; extend pacing coverage; notify provider

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
(10–15 high-yield bullets for experienced nurses and experts)

  1. Know pacer-dependency status at every hand-off. Pacer-dependent loss of capture is a code-level emergency. If unsure, have provider confirm before shift starts.

  2. Check connections FIRST in loss of capture. Loose cables account for > 60% of acute loss. Reconnect firmly, verify polarity, re-label before increasing mA.

  3. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia raise both capture and sensing thresholds. Always check K⁺ and Mg²⁺ before calling it a "pacer problem." Correct electrolytes first (goal K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0).

  4. Capture threshold trends are more important than absolute values. A rising trend (1 → 2 → 4 mA over 24 h) suggests wire fibrosis or displacement. Notify provider of trend, not just the current value.

  5. DDD mode requires all 4 wires functional. Atrial wires fail first (fibrosis, displacement). If atrial capture or sensing is lost, switch to VVI per provider order.

  6. Pacer wire removal timing varies by surgeon. CABG typically POD 3–4; AVR/MVR/TV POD 4–6. Do NOT assume standard timing. Know the plan at hand-off.

  7. Late tamponade post-wire removal is rare (~1%) but documented 1–4 h after removal. Monitor vitals closely: q15 min × 1 h, then q30 min × 2 h. Watch for chest pain, dyspnea, hypotension, tachycardia, muffled heart sounds.

  8. Do NOT remove wires if INR > 1.5 or on therapeutic anticoagulation without team direction. Coordinate with provider; may need to hold warfarin × 24 h or reverse AC if necessary.

  9. AF after MAZE often renders atrial wires useless for pacing. Atrial fibrillation = chaotic, unsustained captures. Rely on ventricular wires; don't waste time chasing atrial capture.

  10. Atrial electrograms are diagnostic. Pacer can output atrial EGM for P wave visibility and rhythm clarification. If rhythm unclear, ask provider; request atrial EGM to guide rate vs rhythm plan.

  11. Cautery and defibrillation near pacer wires require precautions. In OR, use asynchronous mode (AOO/VOO/DOO) per anesthesia. During defibrillation post-op, place pads away from wires to avoid myocardial injury.

  12. Wire site must remain dry. Wet site = infection risk + electrical microshock risk. Cover with occlusive dressing; change if damp. Do NOT submerge during shower.

  13. If a wire breaks during removal, do NOT chase it surgically. Cut at skin; retained fragments (few mm) are well-tolerated and will resorb. Notify provider only; no open bedside retrieval.

  14. Document rate, mode, output (mA), sensitivity (mV), underlying rhythm, and threshold checks every shift. Not acceptable: "pacer OK." Be specific: "DDD 90, output 3 mA, sensitivity 2 mV, atrial capture threshold 1.5 mA, ventricular 2 mA; underlying rhythm NSR with AV block, wires intact, site clean and dry."

  15. Pacer wires are a treatment option for unstable bradycardia. If provider hasn't ordered pacing but patient is symptomatic and wires are in situ, advocate for provider consideration. Don't assume wires are passive monitoring.

cards.title: Pulmonary Artery Pulsatility Index (PAPi)
cards.quickAnswer: PAPi = (PA systolic − PA diastolic) / RA pressure. Higher PAPi indicates better RV contractile reserve; lower PAPi indicates RV dysfunction. Normal > 1.85; borderline 1.0–1.85; concerning < 1.0 (predicts post-LVAD RV failure and in-hospital mortality post-inferior MI); critical < 0.9 (indicates need for mechanical RV support). Requires PA catheter. Most relevant when assessing pre-operative candidates and monitoring post-operative RV recovery trajectory.

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml: The Pulmonary Artery Pulsatility Index is a hemodynamic ratio derived from pulmonary artery catheter (PAC) measurements that quantifies the right ventricle's ability to generate pulsatile flow against pulmonary vascular resistance. Unlike absolute pressure measurements, PAPi normalizes the PA pulse pressure (the pulsatile component of RV work) by right atrial pressure (CVP), a proxy for RV preload. The ratio expresses RV contractile performance relative to loading conditions — a low PAPi indicates poor RV pulsatility despite adequate preload, suggesting intrinsic RV dysfunction.

sections.heading: 2. Formula
sections.bodyHtml:
PAPi = (PASP − PADP) / RAP

  • PASP = Pulmonary artery systolic pressure (mmHg)
  • PADP = Pulmonary artery diastolic pressure (mmHg)
  • RAP = Right atrial pressure = Central venous pressure (CVP) (mmHg)
  • All three measured via pulmonary artery catheter (Swan-Ganz, Edwards Lifesciences, or equivalent)

Example calculations:

PASP PADP CVP Calculation PAPi Interpretation
40 20 8 (40 − 20) / 8 2.5 Reassuring RV function
35 22 10 (35 − 22) / 10 1.3 Borderline
30 18 8 (30 − 18) / 8 1.5 Borderline
28 18 14 (28 − 18) / 14 0.7 Critical dysfunction

sections.heading: 3. Normal Range / Thresholds
sections.bodyHtml:
Range Interpretation Clinical Significance
> 1.85 Normal / reassuring RV function Low risk of post-LVAD RV failure, post-MI complications, post-cardiotomy dysfunction
1.0–1.85 Borderline RV function Intermediate risk; close monitoring recommended; consider inotropic support if CVP, CVP/PCWP, echo RVEF also borderline
< 1.0 Concerning / RV dysfunction likely Strong predictor of post-LVAD RV failure; predictor of in-hospital mortality post-inferior MI with RV involvement; warrants aggressive inotropic support and/or RV mechanical support consideration
< 0.9 Critical RV failure Highly suggestive of need for RVAD or mechanical RV support; common in post-MI, post-LVAD implant, post-cardiotomy RV failure

sections.heading: Pre-LVAD Risk Stratification
sections.bodyHtml:
• PAPi is integrated into RV failure risk prediction models alongside CVP, CVP/PCWP ratio, echo RVEF, and TAPSE.
  • PAPi < 1.85 raises concern for post-implant RV failure; high-risk patients may receive RVAD or temporary RV support bridge.
  • PAPi < 1.0 is a strong independent predictor of post-LVAD RV failure, longer ICU stay, and higher mortality.

sections.heading: RV Infarction (Inferior MI)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Low PAPi confirms hemodynamic significance of RV involvement (beyond ECG/echo changes alone).
  • PAPi < 0.9 predicts in-hospital mortality and major complications in acute RV infarct.
  • Guides escalation to inotropic support (dobutamine, low-dose epinephrine) or temporary mechanical RV support.
  • Serial measurement (4–6 h intervals) tracks RV recovery vs deterioration.

sections.heading: Post-Cardiotomy RV Dysfunction
sections.bodyHtml:
• RV dysfunction is common after CABG, valve surgery, and complex aortic reconstructions (especially long CPB times).
  • PAPi differentiates transient RV stunning (expected to improve) from intrinsic failure requiring mechanical support.

sections.heading: Heart Transplant Evaluation
sections.bodyHtml: • Part of right heart catheterization for transplant candidacy; low PAPi suggests high perioperative risk and need for mechanical bridge.

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Mechanism of RV dysfunction and PAPi relevance The right ventricle must generate sufficient contractile force to overcome pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) while maintaining pulsatile flow. Pulsatility (the stroke component PA pressure) reflects RV contractility; the ratio to CVP normalizes for preload. A failing RV cannot generate adequate pulse pressure, so PAPi falls even if absolute PA systolic and diastolic pressures appear "acceptable." This is distinct from isolated elevated PVR: a high-PVR state can still have adequate PAPi if RV contractility is preserved. Conversely, intrinsic RV cardiomyopathy (post-MI, post-cardiotomy stunning, restrictive physiology) produces low PAPi regardless of PVR.
Limitations and complementary assessments PAPi does not replace echocardiography. Echo provides RV ejection fraction (RVEF), TAPSE (tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion > 16 mm = reassuring), tissue Doppler S' velocity (> 10 cm/s = reassuring), and fractional area change. Integrate PAPi with echo, troponin trends, CVP/PCWP ratio (< 0.63 = higher RV failure risk), and clinical trajectory. In atrial fibrillation, beat-to-beat variation is large — average PA and CVP over 3–5 breaths. Severe tricuspid regurgitation ventricularizes the RA waveform and makes PAPi less reliable; confirm with echo.
Risk factors and patient subgroups for RV dysfunction

Pre-operative risk factors for post-LVAD RV failure: older age, prior RV infarction, chronic pulmonary hypertension, reduced RV ejection fraction on pre-op echo, low pre-op PAPi (< 1.0), elevated CVP/PCWP ratio (> 0.63), diabetes, chronic kidney disease.

Post-cardiotomy risk factors: prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass (> 180 min), complex procedures (aortic surgery, multiple valve replacement), low ejection fraction, elevated PVR pre-operatively. Expected transient RV dysfunction improves over 4–6 h with inotropic support and optimization of preload and afterload.

Transplant candidates: PAPi is part of the assessment for high-risk phenotypes (advanced HF, chronic RV dysfunction); low PAPi may necessitate bridge to transplantation rather than direct surgery.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. PAPi requires a PA catheter. Not derivable from non-invasive measures (echo, bioimpedance, NICOM). If no catheter, rely on echo (RVEF, TAPSE, tissue Doppler S') and CVP trends.

  2. PAPi is a ratio, not absolute pressures. PASP 30 / PADP 18 / CVP 8 → PAPi 1.5 (borderline), not "low pressure = low risk." PASP 50 / PADP 30 / CVP 6 → PAPi 3.3 (excellent), despite elevated PA pressures.

  3. Trend the value over time. Single PAPi < 1.0 is concerning; rising PAPi over 6–12 h indicates RV recovery. Stable or falling PAPi raises concern for persistent RV failure.

  4. Low PAPi in elderly or restrictive physiology patients may reflect RV stiffness and fibrosis, not acute decompensation. Context (new vs chronic, associated labs/echo) determines management.

  5. Severe tricuspid regurgitation ventricularizes the RA waveform and may overestimate CVP; PAPi becomes less reliable. Confirm RV function with echo.

  6. Atrial fibrillation causes beat-to-beat variation in PA pressures and CVP. Average over 3–5 consecutive breaths; flag irregular rhythms when interpreting hand-off data.

  7. PAPi is increasingly cited outside the LVAD context — useful in cardiogenic shock triage, acute decompensated HF with RV dysfunction, and acute MI risk stratification.

  8. Do not confuse PAPi with other RV markers: TAPSE (> 16 mm), S' wave (> 10 cm/s), RVEF (> 40%), CVP/PCWP ratio (< 0.63). PAPi is one piece of the RV assessment puzzle.

  9. Post-LVAD patients require serial PAPi monitoring (if PA catheter remains in place) to track RV trajectory and detect early RV failure necessitating RVAD or inotrope escalation.

  10. Know the patient's pre-operative PAPi when interpreting post-operative course; PAPi 0.85 pre-LVAD changes your vigilance for early RV failure post-implant.

cards.title: Patient / Family Discharge Teaching — Red Flag Warning Signs
cards.quickAnswer: Teach patients and family quantifiable red flag thresholds (fever >101.5°F, weight gain >2 lbs/day, new chest pain) that require immediate action. Use the teach-back method — patient explains symptoms back in their own words — to verify comprehension before discharge. Provide a written "when to call" card with specific phone numbers. Family presence during discharge teaching is non-negotiable. Post-discharge phone call (48–72 hours) significantly reduces 30-day readmission. Red flags fall into three categories: Call 911 (chest pain, severe dyspnea, stroke signs, syncope, severe bleeding, anaphylaxis); Call surgeon within 24 hours (fever ≥101.5°F, incision changes, weight gain, palpitations, DVT signs); Mention at follow-up (mood changes, sleep disturbance, appetite loss, cognition concerns).

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, scope, and when it applies.

  • Definition: Structured, standardized patient and family education at hospital discharge teaching recognition of red flag symptoms post-cardiac surgery. Teaching emphasizes actionable thresholds (fever >101.5°F, weight gain >2 lbs in one day) rather than vague descriptors. Teach-back method ensures comprehension.
  • Who applies to: All patients undergoing cardiac surgery (CABG, valve, aortic, myectomy, MAZE, heart transplant, mechanical assist, TAVR). Family members/primary caregivers present in discharge teaching session.
  • Timeline: Teaching begins POD 1 (nurse reinforcement), intensifies POD 3–5 (comprehensive session), finalized at discharge (teach-back + written card + family present). Post-discharge phone call within 48–72 hours catches missed symptoms early.
  • Why it matters: Post-cardiac surgical complications (sternal infection, DVT, PE, stroke, heart failure exacerbation) often present with non-specific early symptoms. Patient/family uncertainty about urgency ("Should I call the surgeon or wait?") delays treatment and increases morbidity. Teach-back method identifies knowledge gaps before discharge.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac surgical complications carry high early morbidity when recognition is delayed. Patient and family uncertainty about symptom interpretation creates dangerous wait-and-see patterns that convert minor complications into emergencies.

Why quantifiable thresholds matter:

  • Vague language ("fever," "shortness of breath," "weight gain") leads patients to delay seeking care because they rationalize their symptoms as "not that bad."
  • Specific numbers anchor decision-making: "If your temperature is >101.5°F, you call. Not 101.2°F — that's OK. But >101.5°F, you call."
  • Written thresholds eliminate recall bias — patients don't have to remember the exact cutoff.

The teach-back evidence base: Patients routinely say "yes, I understand" when they do not. Asking them to teach it back (active recall) reveals gaps before discharge. Research shows teach-back reduces readmission, increases medication adherence, and improves safety outcomes (Cameron et al., 2009).

sections.heading: 3. Scope
sections.bodyHtml:
Universally indicated:

  • Every post-op cardiac surgery patient (POD 1+) in the discharge-planning window
  • Includes CABG, all valve repairs/replacements, aortic surgery, MAZE, heart transplant, ECMO weaning, VAD implant, etc.
  • Family members must be present (they often make the "call the doctor?" decision at home)

Special emphasis:

  • Patients on anticoagulation (warfarin, DOACs) — bleeding red flags are critical
  • Patients with mechanical valves — endocarditis prophylaxis must be taught
  • Transplant/VAD patients — Valsalva with straining is hemodynamically destabilizing; constipation teaching ties to red flags
  • Older patients and those with cognitive impairment — written card + family co-teaching is essential

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *Gather baseline before teaching* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner — baseline knowledge and barriers to learning.

Before discharge teaching session:

  • Literacy level — can patient read at 5th–8th grade level? Use interpreter if primary language is not English.
  • Hearing/vision — can patient see written card, hear verbal instruction?
  • Cognitive status — alert, oriented, able to concentrate for 10–15 minutes?
  • Family presence — who is in the room? Are they actively engaged?
  • Baseline understanding — what does patient already know about post-op complications? Any misconceptions?
  • Prior surgeries — has patient had cardiac surgery before? Different baseline knowledge.
  • Medications — what meds is patient taking at home? Anticoagulation, antiplatelet, opioids, beta-blockers — these affect red flag teaching.

During/after teaching:

  • Teach-back accuracy — can patient explain red flags back in their own words?
  • Emotional state — is patient anxious, in denial, depressed? Affects learning.
  • Documentation gap — does the discharge summary align with bedside teaching?

sections.heading: 5. Standard Practice — Teaching Red Flags by Category
5.1 CATEGORY A: CALL 911 / GO TO ED IMMEDIATELY
sections.bodyHtml:
Life-threatening, do not wait for surgeon callback.

Red Flag Action Teaching Point
New or severe chest pain (different from surgical site pain) 911/ED "NEW chest pain = cardiac ischemia until proven otherwise. Surgical site pain should improve by POD 3–5. If you have new chest pain or pain that does not go away with rest in 5 minutes, call 911."
Severe dyspnea (cannot speak in full sentences, gasping at rest) 911/ED "SEVERE = you cannot speak in full sentences because you're gasping. Could be PE, acute heart failure, pneumonia, or arrhythmia. Do not wait."
Acute stroke signs (BEFAST) — facial drooping, arm weakness, speech slurred, vision loss, balance loss, time-sensitive 911/ED "Use BEFAST: if your face droops on one side, one arm is weak, you cannot speak clearly, you lose vision or balance, call 911 immediately. Time is brain."
Syncope or near-syncope 911/ED "If you faint or feel like you are about to pass out, call 911. Could be abnormal heart rhythm or not enough blood to your brain."
Sudden unilateral weakness or numbness 911/ED "If one arm or leg suddenly goes weak or numb on one side of your body, call 911 — could be stroke."
Severe bleeding (incision soaks through dressing, nosebleed won't stop, coughing/vomiting blood, gross blood in urine) 911/ED "If your incision bleeds heavily and does not stop after 10 minutes of pressure, or if you're coughing up blood or have blood in your urine, call 911."
Anaphylaxis (facial/throat swelling, severe rash, difficulty breathing) 911/ED "If your face or throat swells up, or if you develop severe itching and a rash all over with difficulty breathing, call 911. Use EpiPen if available."

sections.heading: 5.2 CATEGORY B: CALL SURGEON ASAP (WITHIN 24 HOURS)
sections.bodyHtml:
Urgent but not immediately life-threatening; surgical evaluation needed.

Red Flag Threshold Action Teaching Point
Fever Core temp >101.5°F (measure twice, 4 h apart) Call surgeon ASAP "Fever means possible infection. Measure with a thermometer — not 'feeling hot.' If >101.5°F, call surgeon right away, even middle of night."
Incision changes Increased redness (>1 cm beyond edge), purulent drainage, warmth, opening/dehiscence, sternal click with movement Call surgeon ASAP "Check incision daily. If it's getting MORE red, has yellow/green/foul-smelling drainage, is warm, or the edges are opening up, call surgeon."
Weight gain (acute) >2 lbs in one day OR >5 lbs in one week Call surgeon ASAP "Weigh yourself every morning on the same scale. If you gain >2 lbs in one day or >5 lbs in one week, call surgeon — could mean fluid building up around your heart."
Palpitations or irregular heartbeat (new or worsening) Lasting >30 min or recurrent, or with lightheadedness/dyspnea Call surgeon ASAP "If you feel your heart racing, pounding, or skipping beats in a new way, or if it lasts more than a few minutes, call surgeon."
Exertional dyspnea worse than expected Unable to walk 50 feet without stopping; worsening trend Call surgeon ASAP "It's normal to get short of breath with activity. But if you're getting more short of breath, not better, call surgeon."
Severe fatigue Preventing ADLs or worsening instead of improving Call surgeon ASAP "If you're so tired you can't do normal activities, tell surgeon."
Unilateral leg swelling One leg (not both), calf or thigh, especially with warmth or redness Call surgeon ASAP "Check both legs daily. If ONE leg swells up — especially if it's warm or red — that's a blood clot sign. Call surgeon right away."
Nausea/vomiting Persisting >2 days post-discharge Call surgeon ASAP "Some nausea is normal early on. But if it lasts more than 2 days or you can't keep medications down, call surgeon."
Diarrhea >3 loose stools/day for >3 days Call surgeon ASAP "Loose stools after antibiotics can happen. But if you have >3 per day for >3 days, especially watery or with cramping, call surgeon — could be infection."
New severe back/flank/abdominal pain Severe (8–10/10), different from surgical pain Call surgeon ASAP "If you develop severe pain in your back, sides, or belly that's new and not from your incision, call surgeon."
Constipation refractory to regimen No BM >3 days despite bowel regimen Call surgeon ASAP "Don't strain. If no BM in 3 days despite stool softeners and fluids, call surgeon."

sections.heading: 5.3 CATEGORY C: MENTION AT FOLLOW-UP (48–72 HOUR CALL OR 2-WEEK VISIT)
sections.bodyHtml:
Important but not emergency; address at scheduled visits or post-discharge phone call.

Red Flag Action Teaching Point
Persistent sadness, hopelessness, irritability Mention at 2-week appointment or call PCP "Depression after heart surgery is common and treatable. If you feel sad or hopeless for more than a few days, tell your doctor — don't just live with it."
Loss of interest in activities Screen with PHQ-9 at appointment "If you're not interested in things you normally enjoy, that's a sign of depression. Tell your doctor."
Sleep disturbance (insomnia, nightmares) Mention at appointment "Sleep problems are common. Tell your doctor if they're not getting better — we can help."
Appetite loss Mention at appointment "Some appetite loss is normal. Eat small, frequent meals. If it's not improving in a week, mention it at your visit."
Memory/concentration problems (post-operative cognitive dysfunction) Mention at appointment "Some forgetfulness is normal post-surgery. This usually gets better over weeks to months."
Thoughts of self-harm or worthlessness Call PCP or mental health team immediately "If you ever think about hurting yourself, call your doctor or mental health team right away — don't wait."

sections.heading: 6. Deviation Triggers — When Teaching or Comprehension Fails
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner + competent recognition of gaps.

Red flags for teaching failure:

  1. Patient says "yes, I understand" but cannot teach back — teaching has failed. Re-teach using different wording, visual aids, or examples before discharge.
  2. Family not present and patient lacks support system — higher risk for missed red flags at home. Repeat teaching with family via phone or reschedule before discharge.
  3. Discharge summary conflicts with bedside teaching — conflicting messages confuse patients. Align before discharge.
  4. Patient on anticoagulation but not taught bleeding signs — high-risk gap. Add warfarin/DOAC-specific red flags to teaching.
  5. No written "when to call" card provided — patient will forget verbal teaching. Written card is non-negotiable.
  6. Patient cannot be reached for 48–72 hour post-discharge phone call — safety-net contact lost. Document attempt; escalate to PCP.
  7. Patient calls with vague complaint that matches a red flag but is minimizing (e.g., "just a little fever" that's actually 101.8°F) — remind of thresholds and encourage measurement/documentation.

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive on teach-back method and discharge preparation.

sections.heading: 7.1 The teach-back method — step-by-step
sections.bodyHtml:
Step 1: Teach clearly

  • Use simple language, no jargon
  • Quantifiable thresholds, not vague descriptors
  • Organize by action: "Call 911," "Call surgeon in 24 hours," "Mention at visit"
  • Use visual aids (colored handout with icons, pictures, checklist)

Step 2: Ask open-ended questions

  • "Tell me what you would do if you had chest pain that didn't go away after resting."
  • Do NOT ask yes/no questions ("Do you understand?") — patients say yes regardless

Step 3: Evaluate understanding

  • Correct answer: Patient describes appropriate action (e.g., "I would call 911")
  • Partial: Has some correct elements but misses key detail (e.g., "I would call surgeon" but doesn't know 24-hour timeframe)
  • Incorrect: Misunderstands (e.g., "I would wait and see")

Step 4: Correct and re-teach if needed

  • Re-teach using different wording or example, then ask again
  • Repeat until patient can accurately explain back

Step 5: Document - Chart: "Patient accurately describes symptoms requiring 911 (chest pain, SOB, stroke signs). Understands fever >101.5°F requires surgeon call within 24 hours. Wife present and verbalized understanding."

sections.heading: 7.2 Teach-back example dialogue
sections.bodyHtml:
Nurse: "One of the most important things to watch for is fever. Tell me: at what temperature should you call your surgeon?"

Patient: "If I feel hot?"

Nurse: "Good thinking. But we use a thermometer to get a number. If your temperature is higher than 101.5°F — about 38.6 degrees Celsius — that's when you call. Can you tell me: when would you call your surgeon about fever?"

Patient: "If my temperature goes above 101.5?"

Nurse: "Exactly right. And you would use a thermometer to check, not just feel your forehead. You would call right away, even if it is the middle of the night. Is that clear?"

Patient: "Yes, I would check with a thermometer and call if it is above 101.5."

Nurse: "Perfect."

sections.heading: 7.3 Written "when to call" card — template elements
sections.bodyHtml:
Essential components:

  • Pocket-sized (4x6 inch) laminated card with large readable font (12–14 point minimum)
  • Color-coded or icon-based: Red = call 911, Orange = call surgeon within 24 hours, Green = routine
  • Specific phone numbers: Surgeon's office, surgeon's answering service (after-hours), hospital main, 911, PCP, cardiology
  • Quantifiable thresholds: "Fever >101.5°F" not "fever"
  • Checklist format: Patients can point to symptoms

sections.heading: 7.4 Post-discharge phone call protocol
sections.bodyHtml:
Timing: Within 48–72 hours of discharge

Vital questions:

  • "How are you feeling? Any fever? Breathing problems? Incision changes? Weight gain? Any symptoms that worry you?"
  • "Tell me: what symptoms would make you call your surgeon?" (informal teach-back)

Troubleshoot: "Do you have a thermometer at home? Do you have your surgeon's phone number?"

Reinforce: If patient seems unclear, reinforce key points using teach-back.

Document: Call made, patient reached or left voicemail, content discussed, concerns identified.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — Deterioration Trajectory
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in stable post-discharge patients; if observed, escalate immediately.

  • Patient reports fever but is rationalizing it as "probably just a cold" — low health literacy around quantifiable thresholds; re-teach by phone.
  • Patient describes one leg swelling but minimizes ("just a little") — unilateral leg swelling = DVT until proven otherwise; emphasize asymmetry.
  • Patient reports new palpitations but is waiting to see if they "go away" — arrhythmias can deteriorate; reassure that calling is appropriate.
  • Patient mentions incision drainage but describes it as "no big deal" — purulent drainage is a surgical emergency; clarify color/smell and escalate.
  • Caregiver / family describes patient as "not themselves" emotionally — depression post-cardiac surgery is common and treatable; screen formally.
  • Patient reports missed bowel movement but is not concerned — by POD 4–5, constipation compounds other comorbidities; reinforce bowel regimen.
  • Patient received different discharge teaching from another provider — conflicting messages reduce adherence; coordinate with team.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Pitfall: "Do you understand?" Pearl: Patient always says yes. Use teach-back — ask them to explain red flags back to you. If they can't, teaching failed; re-teach.

  2. Pitfall: Verbal teaching without written card. Pearl: Patient will forget. Written "when to call" card with phone numbers is behavioral anchor for post-discharge decision-making.

  3. Pitfall: Teaching patient only; family not present. Pearl: Family makes the "call the doctor?" decision at home. Family presence during discharge teaching is non-negotiable. If they can't attend, repeat teaching via phone.

  4. Pitfall: Vague thresholds. Pearl: Use quantifiable numbers. ">101.5°F" not "fever"; ">2 lbs in one day" not "weight gain"; "cannot speak in sentences" not "shortness of breath."

  5. Pitfall: RN not leading discharge teaching. Pearl: Assign RN responsibility and accountability. Verify teaching + teach-back before discharge clearance.

  6. Pitfall: No post-discharge phone call. Pearl: 48–72 hour call catches missed symptoms, provides safety net, reduces readmission. Even a quick call ("Any fever? Any concerns?") matters.

  7. Pitfall: Chest pain teaching identical for all patients. Pearl: Tailor to patient baseline. Prior angina patient: "Your usual angina is OK; NEW chest pain = call 911."

  8. Pitfall: BEFAST taught once; patient forgets. Pearl: Give written BEFAST card, teach family, post on refrigerator. Stroke is time-sensitive; early recognition matters.

  9. Pitfall: Patient doesn't have thermometer at home. Pearl: Verify thermometer present before discharge. Teach rectal or tympanic method (oral < accurate; axillary least accurate).

  10. Pitfall: Sternal click mentioned casually. Pearl: Sternal click + fever = sternal infection STAT. This is a surgical emergency. Teach patients to recognize and report immediately.

  11. Pitfall: Unilateral leg swelling dismissed as "just one leg swollen a little." Pearl: Asymmetry = DVT until proven otherwise. Emphasize asymmetry as red flag.

  12. Pitfall: Depression screening deferred to appointment. Pearl: Screen at discharge or 48–72 hour call. Post-cardiac depression is common, time-sensitive, and treatable. Early detection improves outcomes.

  13. Pitfall: Medication-specific red flags not taught. Pearl: Warfarin = bleeding risk (teach signs). Digoxin = toxicity (nausea, visual disturbance). Amiodarone = pulmonary toxicity (dyspnea). Match red flags to medications.

  14. Pitfall: Culturally insensitive teaching. Pearl: Use medical interpreter for non-English speakers. Written materials in patient's language. Ensure family-centered teaching if cultural preference is group decision-making.

  15. Pitfall: Discharge summary does not align with bedside teaching. Pearl: Ensure all sources say the same thing. Conflicting information confuses patients and erodes trust.
