cards.title: Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP)
cards.quickAnswer: Surrogate measure of left atrial pressure (LAP) and LV end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), reflecting LV preload. Normal 8–12 mmHg; congestion when > 18–20. Obtained via balloon-occluded pulmonary artery catheter (PAC), primarily ICU-based. Low PCWP signals hypovolemia; high indicates LV failure, mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis, or tamponade. Critical safety rule: never wedge > 15 seconds to prevent pulmonary artery rupture. Apply Forrester hemodynamic classification to guide acute management (warm-dry, warm-wet, cold-dry, cold-wet).
cards.quickAnswerHtml: Surrogate measure of left atrial pressure (LAP) and LV end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP), reflecting LV preload. Normal 8–12 mmHg; congestion when > 18–20. Obtained via balloon-occluded pulmonary artery catheter (PAC), primarily ICU-based. Low PCWP signals hypovolemia; high indicates LV failure, mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis, or tamponade. Critical safety rule: never wedge > 15 seconds to prevent pulmonary artery rupture. Apply Forrester hemodynamic classification to guide acute management (warm-dry, warm-wet, cold-dry, cold-wet).
cards.sourcePrecedence: Keck CVICU Handbook → Hardin & Kaplow (2020) → Brown (2023) → AACN (2022)

sections.heading: 1. Definition
sections.bodyHtml:
Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP), also called Pulmonary Artery Occlusion Pressure (PAOP), is a surrogate measurement of left atrial pressure and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, reflecting LV preload.

Measurement mechanism:

  • Pulmonary artery catheter distal tip floats into a distal pulmonary artery branch
  • Balloon inflation occludes forward flow, creating a static column of blood
  • Distal port "sees" pulmonary capillary pressure, which equilibrates with left atrial pressure (in absence of mitral stenosis)
  • Reading reflects LV filling status and diastolic function

sections.heading: 2. Measurement Technique
sections.bodyHtml:
Step Detail
Catheter Placement PAC distal tip in pulmonary artery (confirmed by systolic/diastolic pressure waveform with dicrotic notch)
Balloon Inflation Inflate 1.0–1.5 mL air until waveform transitions from PA to wedge (damped, rounded appearance)
Reading Timing Measure at end-expiration to minimize intrathoracic pressure artifact
Duration Keep wedge ≤ 15 seconds; deflate immediately to restore PA waveform
Frequency Obtain only when clinically necessary; avoid repeated or prolonged wedging

Critical safety: sustained wedging (> 15 seconds) risks pulmonary artery rupture—a rare but catastrophic complication.

sections.heading: 3. Normal Range & Categories
sections.bodyHtml:
Category PCWP (mmHg) Clinical Interpretation
Normal 8–12 Adequate preload; normal filling pressures
Mildly Elevated 13–17 Borderline; monitor for heart failure progression
HF Congestion 18–25 Pulmonary edema threshold; diuresis indicated
Severe > 25 Acute pulmonary edema; aggressive decompensation

sections.heading: 4. Clinical Use & Forrester Hemodynamic Classification
sections.bodyHtml:
Primary applications:

  1. Quantifies volume status and determines heart failure phenotype (HFrEF vs. HFpEF)
  2. Distinguishes cardiogenic from pulmonary vascular disease via transpulmonary gradient
  3. Assesses candidacy and intra-operative fill status for ventricular assist devices
  4. Guides diuretic and inotrope dosing in acute decompensation
  5. Pairs with cardiac index (CI) in Forrester classification to diagnose cardiogenic shock (Brown, 2023)

Forrester Hemodynamic Classes:

CI / PCWP PCWP ≤ 18 PCWP > 18
CI ≥ 2.2 Warm-Dry (Normal) Warm-Wet (Pulmonary Edema)
CI < 2.2 Cold-Dry (Hypovolemia) Cold-Wet (Cardiogenic Shock)
  • Warm-Dry: normal physiology; routine post-operative state
  • Warm-Wet: volume overload; requires diuresis
  • Cold-Dry: inadequate perfusion + low filling; fluid bolus ± inotropes
  • Cold-Wet: highest mortality; requires inotropes ± mechanical support

sections.heading: 5. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Pathophysiology: transmural pressure and equilibration The pulmonary capillary network creates a static pressure column from the distal catheter tip back to the left atrium when the balloon occludes forward flow. In normal conditions (no mitral stenosis, no pulmonary vascular obstruction), this pressure equilibrates with LAP and, by Frank-Starling mechanics, reflects the LVEDP that determines preload. The pressure reading is most accurate at end-expiration when intrathoracic pressure is least likely to transmit artifact (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020).
LVEDP vs PCWP concordance In the absence of mitral stenosis or pulmonary vascular obstruction, LVEDP and PCWP should be similar (within 2–4 mmHg). A large gap suggests measurement error, valve disease, distorted pressure transmission, or technical malposition of the catheter.
Mitral regurgitation vs mitral stenosis

Mitral regurgitation creates giant V waves in the wedge tracing (tall, peaked diastolic wave). PCWP may overestimate true LAP; correlate with clinical heart failure signs.

Mitral stenosis disconnects PCWP from LVEDP. PCWP reflects LAP upstream of the stenotic valve and does not reflect LV filling. If diagnosis uncertain, obtain LVEDP via retrograde LV catheterization.

PEEP and mechanical ventilation artifact Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) falsely elevates PCWP reading by approximately 0.5 × PEEP value. Subtract estimated PEEP effect when interpreting in mechanically ventilated patients.

sections.heading: 6. Pitfalls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Wedging duration > 15 seconds: Risk of pulmonary artery rupture and hemoptysis. Always deflate promptly. Inflation should be brief and reproducible.

  2. Technique artifact — intrathoracic pressure: Measure at end-expiration (inspiration falsely raises PCWP). Maintain supine position. Ensure transducer calibration and zeroing to phlebostatic axis.

  3. Mitral regurgitation: Giant V waves overestimate true LA pressure. Correlate with clinical HF signs.

  4. Mitral stenosis: Disconnects PCWP from LVEDP. PCWP reflects upstream LA pressure, not LV filling. Consider retrograde LV catheterization.

  5. PEEP effect: Falsely elevates reading by ~0.5 × PEEP. Subtract estimated effect in mechanically ventilated patients.

  6. Pulmonary vascular obstruction or stenosis: Rare; disconnects capillaries from LA. PCWP no longer reflects LA or LV pressure.

  7. Transpulmonary gradient: Elevated PCWP alone does not define pulmonary hypertension etiology. Calculate TPG (mean PA − PCWP) and PVR for postcapillary vs. precapillary disease.

  8. HFpEF physiology: Normal or low CI with elevated PCWP. EF preserved (≥ 40%). Diuretics primary therapy; inotropes contraindicated.

  9. Operational context: Forrester class informs acute management strategy and prognostic counseling. Reassess after intervention to confirm improvement or need for escalation.

  10. Clinical integration: Use PCWP with other hemodynamic parameters (CI, SVR, SvO₂) and bedside assessment. Do not over-rely on single number; interpret in clinical context.

cards.title: Pulmonary Embolism & Deep Vein Thrombosis
cards.quickAnswer: PE = thromboembolic occlusion of pulmonary arteries, typically from lower-extremity DVT. Post-cardiac-surgery PE risk increases despite prophylaxis. Presentation: dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia, pleuritic pain, or sudden hemodynamic collapse. Massive PE (SBP < 90, shock, syncope) → STAT thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg IV/2 h or tenecteplase weight-based) OR catheter-directed thrombectomy/EKOS if high bleeding risk. Submassive PE (RV dysfunction, stable BP) → anticoagulation; escalate for PERT/intervention if decompensating. Non-massive → therapeutic anticoagulation (UFH, enoxaparin bridging or DOAC after acute phase). Bleeding risk post-op constrains options — individual risk/benefit essential. IVC filter last-line if AC contraindicated or fails.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, and who this applies to.

  • Definition: PE is acute thromboembolic obstruction of the pulmonary arterial tree, usually originating from deep veins of the lower extremity (DVT). Pathophysiology: impaired gas exchange, dead-space ventilation increase, RV afterload elevation, potential hemodynamic collapse.
  • Epidemiology post-operatively: Symptomatic DVT occurs in 3–10% of cardiac surgery patients without prophylaxis; ~1–2% develop symptomatic PE. Higher risk: prolonged immobility, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), malignancy, prior VTE, advanced age, obesity, prolonged cardiopulmonary bypass.
  • Typical post-cardiac-surgery patient: Mid-to-late post-op course (POD 2–7), often after extubation, with new dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxia (SpO₂ drop >3–5%), or hemodynamic instability. Complicates anticoagulation decisions due to ongoing bleeding risk.
  • Why it matters: Most common post-op thromboembolic complication. Increases length of stay, stroke risk (if AF develops), and mortality if untreated or unrecognized.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why PE/DVT happens. Novice and advanced beginner teaching.

Virchow's Triad and Post-Op Risk Three convergent mechanisms:
  • Venous stasis: immobility from sternal precautions, prolonged bypass time, low cardiac output (reduced venous return), position changes
  • Endothelial injury: vascular manipulation during cannulation, central line trauma, surgical manipulation near iliac/femoral vessels
  • Hypercoagulability: tissue factor release from surgical trauma, inflammatory cascade activation (peak POD 2–3), HIT (if prior heparin exposure), malignancy, thrombophilia (Factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation) Post-cardiac-surgery context: CPB prime activates contact system → tissue factor release from surgery → peak coagulation cascade activation at POD 2–3 (coinciding with peak POAF, peak PE incidence).

RV strain mechanism:

  • Acutely increased pulmonary vascular resistance from embolic obstruction → RV pressure overload → RV systolic/diastolic dysfunction
  • If thrombus burden >30–40% of pulmonary vascular bed, RV cannot generate sufficient pressure to perfuse lungs → cardiogenic shock
  • RV free wall hypokinesis with apical sparing (McConnell's sign) indicates acute RV strain

Gas exchange impairment:

  • Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch in obstructed lung segments (perfusion without ventilation)
  • Increased alveolar dead space → increased minute ventilation required to maintain CO₂ clearance
  • Hypoxia may be mild if small PE; severe if massive (>50% obstruction)

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: What the patient looks like at bedside. Advanced beginner recognition.

sections.heading: Clinical presentation (any of the following = escalate)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Sudden onset dyspnea — most common; unexplained tachypnea (RR > 24)
  • Pleuritic chest pain — sharp, worse with inspiration (if PE involves pleura)
  • New or worsening hypoxia — SpO₂ drop >3–5%, may be gradual or abrupt
  • Tachycardia — often marked (HR > 110); sometimes only sign in early presentation
  • Syncope or presyncope — indicates massive PE or sudden hemodynamic compromise
  • Hemoptysis — rare; indicates pulmonary infarction and poor prognosis
  • Sudden cardiovascular collapse, cardiac arrest — massive PE in shock

sections.heading: Physical exam findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Tachypnea, tachycardia, hypotension (if massive)
  • Loud pulmonary component of S2 (P2) from acute RV pressure rise
  • RV heave (parasternal lift) if RV dilatation
  • Unilateral leg swelling, warmth, asymmetric calf tenderness (if DVT source identified)
  • Decreased breath sounds or dullness to percussion (if pleural effusion or infarction)
  • Signs of right heart failure if massive (elevated JVP, hepatomegaly)

sections.heading: Post-operative context
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-cardiac-surgery PE complicates management:

  • Anticoagulation vs. bleeding balance: ongoing surgical bleeding risk limits aggressive AC initiation; heparin or LMWH may be preferred bridging to DOAC
  • HIT-associated PE: if prior heparin exposure, HIT may be the culprit (paradoxical thrombosis); do NOT use heparin
  • Immobility: sternal precautions restrict early mobilization → DVT prophylaxis becomes critical

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (5 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml: Pure information-gathering. No actions yet. Target: systematic bedside exam + recent labs.

sections.heading: Bedside assessment
sections.bodyHtml:
• Vital signs & perfusion: HR, BP (baseline vs. current drop), SpO₂ (absolute and trend), RR, mental status, capillary refill, skin temperature/color
  • Cardiopulmonary: auscultated breath sounds (bilateral vs unilateral), heart sounds, JVP, RV heave, leg swelling (asymmetry, warmth, calf tenderness, palpable cord)
  • Symptoms: dyspnea severity, pleuritic quality, syncope, chest pain character, hemoptysis, leg pain
  • Exam for DVT: Homan's sign NOT recommended; instead: asymmetric calf circumference (>2 cm difference may indicate DVT), warmth, palpable cord, calf tenderness

sections.heading: Recent labs & imaging
sections.bodyHtml:
• CBC: baseline and current hemoglobin, platelets (HIT screening if drop > 50% or < 100K)
  • Coagulation: PT/INR, aPTT (if UFH running), fibrinogen (if high thrombus burden)
  • Renal & electrolytes: creatinine (affects DOAC eligibility, LMWH dosing), K⁺, Mg²⁺
  • Cardiac biomarkers: troponin I/T (RV injury), BNP/NT-proBNP (RV strain), lactate (perfusion status)
  • D-dimer: (note: nearly always elevated post-op from inflammation/surgery — interpret cautiously; high NPV in low pretest probability only)
  • ECG: sinus tachycardia, new right axis deviation, new RBBB, new AF, S1Q3T3 (rare but specific)

sections.heading: Recent imaging & procedures
sections.bodyHtml:
• Chest X-ray: baseline vs new findings (wedge-shaped infiltrate = Hampton hump from infarction, pleural effusion, atelectasis, pneumonia)
  • Echocardiography (if done): RV/LV ratio, RV systolic pressure, RV free-wall wall motion (McConnell's sign), thrombus-in-transit
  • Lower-extremity doppler US (if done or pending): DVT source location (proximal vs distal), bilateral involvement
  • Prior CTPA results: if imaging already obtained, review for size/location/burden of thrombus

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Comprehensive management pathways organized by PE severity.

sections.heading: 5A. Massive PE (hemodynamic shock)
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition: systolic BP < 90 mmHg OR SBP drop > 40 mmHg from baseline, OR signs of shock (syncope, cardiogenic shock, cardiac arrest), OR RV dysfunction on echo.

Immediate actions:

  1. STAT call to cardiothoracic surgery team, interventional radiology (IR), and ICU — do NOT delay for additional imaging or labs
  2. Supplemental O₂ to target SpO₂ ≥ 90%; intubate if respiratory failure or somnolence
  3. IV access: ensure at least 2 large-bore lines; arterial line for continuous BP monitoring if not already present
  4. Baseline labs: CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen, troponin, BNP, lactate, ABG, type & screen
  5. ECG & portable CXR if < 1 min delay; do NOT wait for imaging before initiating thrombolysis discussion

Thrombolysis (first-line if no absolute contraindication):

Agent Dose Notes
Alteplase (tPA) 100 mg IV over 2 hours Bolus 10 mg (2 min), then 90 mg over 118 min; monitor BP/HR/neuro every 15 min during infusion
Tenecteplase (TNKase) 0.5–0.6 mg/kg IV push (max 50 mg) Single push over 10 sec; preferred in massive PE for speed; equivalent efficacy to alteplase

Rationale: PEITHO trial and ESC 2019 guidelines show thrombolysis ↓ hemodynamic decompensation vs anticoagulation alone in massive PE, albeit with higher minor bleeding (Konstantinides et al., 2020).

Contraindications to thrombolysis (relative post-op):

  • Recent neurosurgery, intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke (< 3 months)
  • Active bleeding, recent major surgery (post-cardiac surgery within 10 days is strong relative contraindication — consider catheter-directed instead)
  • Uncontrolled hypertension (BP > 180/110)
  • Thrombocytopenia (< 50K)

If thrombolysis contraindicated: catheter-directed thrombectomy or EKOS-assisted CDT (see 5B below)

VA-ECMO as bridge:

  • Massive PE with cardiogenic shock refractory to fluids/vasopressors → consider venoarterial ECMO cannulation (peripheral femoral or central) while arranging thrombolysis/thrombectomy/embolectomy
  • ECMO provides cardiopulmonary support and allows time for definitive intervention
  • Notify CT surgery and ECMO team; mobilize for OR if surgical embolectomy needed

Supportive measures during thrombolysis:

  • Fluid resuscitation: cautious bolus (250–500 mL crystalloid) if hypovolemic; avoid overload (worsens pulmonary edema)
  • Vasopressors: norepinephrine preferred (maintains afterload); avoid pure beta-agonists (increase HR without afterload)
  • Anticoagulation: initiate UFH 80 units/kg IV bolus, then 18 units/kg/h; goal aPTT 1.5–2.5 (verify institutional target). Do NOT bolus if recent surgery and active bleeding — discuss with team
  • Pain management: opioids acceptable; avoid nitrates if hypotensive
  • Monitor: continuous cardiac monitoring, hourly vitals, repeat troponin/BNP at 6–12 h, repeat CXR at 6–12 h to assess improvement

sections.heading: 5B. Submassive PE (RV dysfunction, hemodynamically stable)
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition: hemodynamically stable (SBP > 90, no shock) BUT RV dysfunction on echo (RV/LV ratio > 0.9, RV wall motion abnormality) OR elevated troponin/BNP OR sPESI ≥ 1.

Standard approach:

  1. Therapeutic anticoagulation (first-line): see anticoagulation table below
  2. Risk stratification labs: troponin, BNP, D-dimer, ABG, lactate, CBC, coagulation panel
  3. Echocardiography: assess RV size, wall motion, McConnell's sign, RV systolic pressure, rule out thrombus-in-transit
  4. Continuous telemetry & pulse oximetry — monitor for hemodynamic deterioration
  5. Escalation threshold: if patient develops hypotension, decreased mental status, increasing pressor requirement, or persistent hypoxia despite supplemental O₂ → notify team for PERT (Pulmonary Embolism Response Team) evaluation and consideration of intervention
  6. Consult PERT or interventional radiology if available at your institution — emerging data support catheter-directed therapy in selected submassive PE (younger age, low bleeding risk, rapid deterioration)

Emerging evidence (PEITHO trial, 2023 ACC/AHA guideline):

  • Submassive PE with high-risk features (troponin + RV strain + haemodynamic near-collapse) may benefit from thrombolysis or catheter-directed therapy vs anticoagulation alone
  • Catheter-directed thrombectomy/EKOS has lower systemic bleeding risk than systemic thrombolysis (important post-op advantage)
  • Clinical deterioration despite anticoagulation is key trigger for intervention escalation

Anticoagulation for submassive PE: see table under §5D below

sections.heading: 5C. Non-massive, low-risk PE (stable, no RV strain)
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition: hemodynamically stable, normal RV size/function on echo, normal troponin/BNP, sPESI 0.

Management:

  1. Therapeutic anticoagulation per §5D table
  2. Outpatient consideration in selected cases (low sPESI, reliable follow-up, no comorbidity, early mobilization possible)
  3. Post-op context: most cardiac surgery patients will be inpatient; anticoagulation initiation in ICU or stepdown with tele monitoring
  4. Escalation threshold: any new dyspnea, hypoxia, hemodynamic change, or leg swelling → re-escalate

sections.heading: 5D. Anticoagulation Strategy (Massive, Submassive, Non-Massive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Table: Anticoagulation options, post-operative context

Agent Dose (post-op initiation) Advantages Caveats Post-op timeline
Unfractionated heparin (UFH) 80 U/kg bolus, then 18 U/kg/h; goal aPTT 1.5–2.5 Rapid onset, reversible (protamine), short half-life (~90 min), renal-independent Requires aPTT monitoring q6h initially; HIT risk (~1–2%); do NOT use if HIT suspected Immediate post-op if bleeding controlled and renal failure; preferred for massive PE pre-intervention
Enoxaparin (LMWH) 1 mg/kg SC q12h (or 1.5 mg/kg daily); CrCl < 30 avoid or dose-reduce Predictable levels, no monitoring, SC convenient, lower HIT risk than UFH Accumulates if Cr > 2.5, eGFR < 30; cannot reverse; peak levels 3–5 h POD 1–2 onwards if hemostasis stable, preferred in cancer-associated PE, bridge to DOAC
Argatroban or bivalirudin (direct thrombin inhibitor) Argatroban 2 µg/kg/min IV; bivalirudin 0.15 mg/kg/h MANDATORY for HIT-associated PE/DVT (do NOT use heparin) Expensive, aPTT monitoring, renal adjustment (bivalirudin) Stat switch if 4Ts score ≥ 6 or HIT antibody positive
DOAC (apixaban, rivaroxaban) Apixaban 5 mg PO BID (standard dose) or 10 mg BID × 7 d then 5 mg; rivaroxaban 15 mg daily × 21 d, then 20 mg daily Oral, predictable, no monitoring, fewer drug interactions Requires bridging 5–10 days with parenteral AC post-op; increased bleeding risk in acute phase; apixaban preferred over rivaroxaban post-op (lower peak levels) POD 5–7+ once bleeding risk minimal; delay initiation if active bleeding post-op
Warfarin (VKA) Target INR 2–3 (2.5–3.5 for mechanical valve); requires bridging with UFH/LMWH Indicated for mechanical heart valves (mandatory) Slow onset (5–7 d), food/drug interactions, frequent monitoring, teratogenic; now second-line for other PE Post-op transition if mechanical valve; bridge with UFH/LMWH until INR therapeutic × 24 h

Duration of anticoagulation:

  • Provoked PE (post-op, immobility): 3 months minimum; may extend if additional risk factors present
  • Unprovoked PE (idiopathic): indefinite anticoagulation (recurrence risk ~10%/year without treatment)
  • Recurrent VTE: indefinite
  • Cancer-associated PE: throughout cancer treatment + 3 months after

Post-operative bleeding risk & anticoagulation timing:

POD phase Bleeding risk Typical AC choice Escalation to DOAC
POD 0–2 High (ongoing surgical ooze) Hold AC or UFH bolus only if massive PE N/A — delay
POD 3–5 Moderate (hemostasis improving) UFH or LMWH low-dose; monitor drain output POD 5–7 if drain output < 30 mL/h
POD 6+ Low (stable hemostasis) UFH/LMWH therapeutic or transition to DOAC DOAC initiation with 5-d parenteral bridge

sections.heading: 5E. Catheter-Directed Thrombectomy & EKOS (for massive or high-bleeding-risk cases)
sections.bodyHtml:
Indications:

  • Massive PE with hemodynamic shock AND thrombolysis contraindicated (recent cardiac surgery within 10 days)
  • Massive PE with thrombolysis failure or complication
  • Submassive PE with high-risk features and rapid deterioration (selected cases)
  • Saddle PE or large thrombus burden

Techniques:

Technique Mechanism Advantages Timing
Catheter-directed thrombectomy Pigtail catheter aspiration ± mechanical devices Direct clot removal; lower systemic fibrinolysis IR suite; 30–60 min
EKOS (ultrasound-facilitated CDT) Microinfusor catheter + ultrasound transducer + local lysis Mechanical + localized fibrinolysis; lower systemic exposure than IV thrombolysis; bidirectional flow restoration IR suite; 1–2 h; requires IR capability
Surgical pulmonary embolectomy Open sternotomy, cardiopulmonary bypass, direct PA thrombus removal Last resort; for refractory cardiogenic shock or failed catheter intervention OR; requires CT surgery + ECMO standby

Discussion: EKOS and catheter-directed thrombectomy have lower major bleeding rates than systemic thrombolysis, especially valuable in post-cardiac-surgery PE where bleeding risk is high (Tapson & Humbert, 2023).

sections.heading: 5F. IVC Filter (rare, last-line)
sections.bodyHtml:
Indications:

  • Documented VTE + contraindication to anticoagulation (active bleeding, intracranial hemorrhage, recent neurosurgery) — temporary until AC can restart
  • Failure of anticoagulation (PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation on the same day) — rare

NOT first-line. Anticoagulation preferred whenever feasible.

Filter types:

  • Permanent (optional): left in place indefinitely
  • Temporary/retrievable: removed once contraindication resolves (e.g., after surgical bleeding stops, bridged to AC)

Complications: filter thrombosis (2–5%), migration (1–2%), post-filter syndrome (chronic venous insufficiency, recurrent DVT), fracture.

Post-filter surveillance: duplex US at 3–6 months; consider CT-PE protocol scan at 6 months to assess filter patency and ongoing VTE risk.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml: Communication framework and who to call.

sections.heading: SBAR template
sections.bodyHtml:
S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]."

B: "Patient developed acute dyspnea/tachycardia at [time]. Current presentation: HR [X], BP [X], SpO₂ [X]%. RR elevated at [X]. Labs: troponin [X], BNP [X], D-dimer [X]. CXR: [findings]. Bedside echo pending or shows RV/LV ratio [X]."

A: "Clinical picture is consistent with PE. [Specify massive/submassive/non-massive based on above.] Hemodynamics [stable/deteriorating]."

R: "Requesting [STAT CTPA / thrombolysis discussion / PERT consult / ICU transfer / intervention consideration]."

sections.heading: Escalation decision tree
sections.bodyHtml:
Scenario Contact Urgency
Stable, low-risk PE on day 1 imaging Primary APP / on-call fellow Urgent (within 1 h)
Submassive PE (RV strain, stable BP) Primary APP + CT surgery attending Urgent; consider PERT
Massive PE (shock) STAT page: CT surgery + IR + ICU; activate code team if cardiac arrest Emergent (< 5 min)
PE + new focal neuro findings Stroke code + CT surgery Emergent
PE + active bleeding from incision CT surgery (do NOT start AC without team input) Emergent
Recurrent PE despite therapeutic AC CT surgery + IR (filter consideration) Urgent
Suspected HIT + PE Hematology + CT surgery (switch to DTI STAT) Urgent

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections expandable.

Risk Stratification Tools: Wells, PESI, YEARS, PERC

sections.heading: Wells Score for PE Probability
sections.bodyHtml:
Finding Points
PE more likely than alternative diagnosis 3
Unilateral leg swelling 3
HR > 100 1.5
Immobilization ≥ 3 d or surgery within 4 wks 1.5
Prior DVT or PE 1.5
Hemoptysis 1
Signs of DVT 3
Total Interpretation
0–2 (low) 1.6% PE probability; D-dimer can rule out if negative
3–6 (intermediate) 16.2% PE probability; need further testing
≥ 7 (high) 37.5% PE probability; skip D-dimer, go straight to CTPA

Post-op post-cardiac-surgery context: most patients will have immobilization + recent surgery, driving Wells higher. D-dimer nearly always elevated from inflammation, limiting utility post-op.

sections.heading: Simplified PESI (sPESI) — Risk Stratification for Mortality
sections.bodyHtml:
Score 1 point each for:

  • Age ≥ 80
  • Male sex
  • Cancer (active or within 5 years)
  • Chronic cardiopulmonary disease
  • O₂ saturation < 90%
  • SBP < 100 mmHg
  • Altered mental status
  • HR ≥ 110

Score 30-day mortality Risk level
0 ~1% Low — home/outpatient eligible in selected cases
≥ 1 10–15% High — admit, tele, consider ICU

Post-op utility: almost all post-op cardiac patients will score ≥ 1 (immobilized, high HR, low SpO₂ possible), so sPESI ≥ 1 = ICU-level monitoring standard post-op.

sections.heading: YEARS Criteria (ESC 2019 alternative to Wells)
sections.bodyHtml:
Three criteria:

  • Y: yes to PE more likely diagnosis (3 points)
  • E: examination signs of DVT (2 points)
  • A: acute hypoxia (SpO₂ < 90%) OR hypocapnia (pCO₂ < 4.8 kPa) (1 point)
  • R: heart rate ≥ 100 (1 point)
  • S: hemodynamic stability — SBP ≥ 100, not shock (2 points if YES = lowers probability)

YEARS allows PE exclusion if pretest probability low AND D-dimer normal, avoiding CTPA in some low-risk patients. Less commonly used post-op but relevant for discharged patients at clinic follow-up.

sections.heading: PERC Rule (Pulmonary Embolism Rule-Out Criteria)
sections.bodyHtml:
All of these must be present to "rule out" PE without imaging in a low-risk patient:

  • Age < 50
  • HR < 100
  • SBP ≥ 100
  • SpO₂ ≥ 95% on room air
  • No unilateral leg swelling
  • No hemoptysis
  • No prior DVT/PE
  • No oral estrogen use
  • No clinical suspicion that PE is most likely diagnosis

Post-op utility: PERC is rarely applicable (most post-op patients fail one or more criteria). More useful for non-op outpatient chest pain evaluation.

Diagnostic Tests: D-dimer, CTPA, LE US, Echocardiography

sections.heading: D-dimer Interpretation
sections.bodyHtml:
Sensitivity & specificity: > 95% sensitive (high negative predictive value), low specificity (~30% in post-op due to inflammation).

Post-operative context — D-dimer is ALMOST ALWAYS ELEVATED:

  • Inflammation from surgery
  • Tissue factor release
  • Coagulation activation
  • Fibrinolysis (D-dimer is fibrin degradation product)
  • Conclusion: D-dimer alone does NOT rule in PE post-op; positive D-dimer is not diagnostic post-op. Use CTPA if clinical suspicion high (Wells ≥ 3) regardless of D-dimer level.

Role post-op: use D-dimer to rule out PE if pretest probability LOW (Wells 0–2) AND patient NOT post-op (outpatient, delayed presentation); post-op use limited.

sections.heading: CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA)
sections.bodyHtml:
Gold standard for PE diagnosis:

  • Sensitivity 83–98% for segmental and larger PE; less sensitive for subsegmental (significance debated)
  • High specificity (> 95%)
  • Time to diagnosis: 15–30 min turnaround

When to order CTPA:

  • High pretest probability (Wells ≥ 7) — no delay for D-dimer
  • Intermediate probability (Wells 3–6) + abnormal D-dimer or post-op context
  • Unstable patient + CTPA performed at bedside or portable CXR acquired while prepping for IR/thrombolysis

Contraindications/cautions:

  • Renal insufficiency (Cr > 2.5, eGFR < 30) — contrast nephropathy risk; discuss with team
  • Severe contrast allergy — premedicate or consider alternative (V/Q scan, bedside echo)
  • Hemodynamic instability — consider bedside echo first; if PE highly suspected, initiate thrombolysis discussion before or during CTPA

CTPA findings in PE:

  • Saddle PE: thrombus straddling main PA bifurcation = high-risk, consider massive PE equivalent, STAT thrombolysis/intervention
  • Main PA occlusion: massive
  • Lobar/segmental: intermediate to high risk depending on extent
  • Subsegmental only: significance unclear; in low-risk patient may observe with AC alone

sections.heading: Lower-Extremity Doppler Ultrasound
sections.bodyHtml:
Indications:

  • Suspected DVT source (unilateral leg swelling, calf pain)
  • Bilateral LE swelling (assess for symmetry, IVC involvement)
  • Post-PE surveillance at 3–6 months for post-thrombotic syndrome

Interpretation:

  • Proximal DVT (popliteal, femoral, iliac): requires AC
  • Distal (calf) DVT: may observe in some protocols if low-risk; typically treated
  • No DVT found: does NOT rule out PE (PE can occur with nonocclusive DVT or in-transit embolus)

sections.heading: Echocardiography (TTE, TEE)
sections.bodyHtml:
Role: RV function assessment and risk stratification, NOT for PE diagnosis.

Findings of RV dysfunction:

  • RV/LV ratio > 0.9 (measured in short axis at midventricular level) = RV dilatation
  • RV free-wall hypokinesis with apical sparing (McConnell's sign) = specific for acute RV strain
  • RV systolic pressure elevation (TR velocity)
  • Thrombus-in-transit (rare, highly specific for PE if present)

Prognostic value: RV dysfunction on echo is a major risk stratifier (submassive vs non-massive PE); associated with higher mortality in intermediate/high-risk PE.

sections.heading: Troponin, BNP, Lactate
sections.bodyHtml:
Troponin (I or T): elevated in RV myocardial injury from acute RV strain; indicates intermediate-high risk PE.

BNP/NT-proBNP: elevation indicates RV wall stress and dysfunction; higher values correlate with worse prognosis.

Lactate: elevated in tissue hypoperfusion (shock); indicates hemodynamic compromise and higher mortality. Trend lactate after intervention; persistent elevation suggests inadequate perfusion.

Risk stratification integration:

  • Troponin normal + BNP normal + RV not dilated on echo = low-risk PE → AC alone
  • Troponin elevated + BNP elevated + RV/LV > 0.9 = submassive PE → consider intervention if deteriorating
  • Any of above + shock + hypotension = massive PE → thrombolysis/intervention urgent

Pathophysiology: RV Strain, Post-PE Syndrome, CTEPH

sections.heading: Acute RV Failure Mechanism in Massive PE
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-op cardiac surgery patients have:

  • Impaired RV function baseline (especially if pre-op RV dysfunction, reduced EF, valvular disease)
  • Acute load increase from PE → RV cannot generate sufficient pressure to overcome obstruction
  • Interdependence effect: RV dilatation shifts septum leftward → LV diastolic dysfunction → ↓ LV preload → ↓ LV cardiac output
  • Coronary perfusion failure: RV dilates → RV wall tension increases → RV myocardial O₂ demand up, but RV coronary perfusion pressure (aortic diastolic pressure − RV diastolic pressure) can drop → RV ischemia
  • Cascade: RV ischemia → further RV dysfunction → further dilatation → cardiogenic shock

sections.heading: Post-PE Syndrome & Chronic Thromboembolic Pulmonary Hypertension (CTEPH)
sections.bodyHtml:
Post-PE syndrome: persistent dyspnea, exercise limitation, or functional decline lasting > 4 weeks post-PE (affects ~30% of PE survivors).

CTEPH: chronic thromboembolic obstruction of pulmonary vasculature leading to pulmonary hypertension (~2–4% of acute PE patients; higher in missed/untreated PE).

Surveillance & management:

  • Refer to cardiology if dyspnea persists > 4 weeks post-PE
  • Obtain rest and exercise echo, right heart catheterization if suspicion high
  • If CTEPH confirmed, pulmonary endarterectomy (surgical gold standard) or balloon pulmonary angioplasty (BPA) if not surgical candidate

Monitoring & labs:
  • CBC: baseline, POD 3, POD 5, then per protocol (HIT screening)
  • Coagulation: PT/INR, aPTT (if UFH), fibrinogen (if thrombolyzed)
  • Renal: Cr baseline, POD 1, and per protocol (DOAC/LMWH dosing)
  • HIT 4Ts score: calculate if platelets drop > 50% or new thrombosis; confirm with HIT antibody ± functional assay
Special Populations & Subgroups

sections.heading: Post-Cardiac-Surgery PE: Bleeding vs. Clotting Balancing Act
sections.bodyHtml:
Challenge: ongoing surgical ooze vs. thrombotic risk.

POD 0–2 strategy:

  • Hold anticoagulation if ongoing bleeding (chest tubes > 200 mL/h, sternal ooze, other surgical bleeding)
  • If PE diagnosed POD 0–1, favor UFH bolus (if bleeding controlled) over LMWH or DOAC for reversibility
  • Discuss with surgical team before AC initiation; consider IVC filter if AC cannot start immediately

POD 3–5 strategy:

  • Hemostasis typically improving
  • Initiate UFH or LMWH; monitor drain output
  • Bridge to DOAC once bleeding stable (drain < 30 mL/h, no active ooze)

sections.heading: HIT-Associated PE
sections.bodyHtml:
Do NOT use heparin (UFH or LMWH).

  • HIT paradoxically causes thrombosis (PE, DVT, stroke, limb ischemia) via platelet activation
  • If 4Ts score ≥ 6 or HIT antibody positive → switch immediately to argatroban or bivalirudin
  • Contact hematology and anticoagulation team; may transition to DOAC once acute phase stable

sections.heading: Mechanical Valve Patients + PE
sections.bodyHtml:
AC requirement: lifelong anticoagulation with warfarin (target INR 2.5–3.5 depending on valve type/position).

Post-op bridge: UFH or LMWH bridging until INR therapeutic × 24 hours.

DOAC not recommended for mechanical valves (increased thrombotic events in trials).

sections.heading: Pregnancy + PE
sections.bodyHtml:
Anticoagulation: LMWH throughout pregnancy (DOACs are teratogens).

Dosing: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg SC q12h (therapeutic dose, may need higher dosing in trimester 2–3 due to volume expansion).

Post-partum: LMWH or transition to DOAC if acceptable.

sections.heading: Renal Impairment (Cr > 2.5, eGFR < 30)
sections.bodyHtml:
Avoid: DOAC (except low-dose apixaban in selected patients), accumulation of LMWH.

Prefer: UFH (renal-independent) for acute phase; transition to warfarin if long-term AC needed.

IV contrast (CTPA): discuss risk/benefit; use iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast; hydrate.

Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis (CDT) vs. EKOS vs. Surgical Embolectomy

sections.heading: When to consider CDT/EKOS
sections.bodyHtml:
Advantages over systemic thrombolysis:

  • Localized fibrinolytic agent (lower systemic exposure) → lower major bleeding risk (crucial post-op)
  • Mechanical component (catheter aspiration, EKOS ultrasound) → faster clot removal
  • Bedside hemodynamic support (can continue pressors, fluids) → safer in unstable patients

Disadvantages:

  • Requires interventional radiology availability (may not be 24/7)
  • Longer procedure time (1–2 h for EKOS vs 2 h for IV lysis)
  • Specialized expertise required
  • Cost higher

Post-op utility: CDT/EKOS favored over IV thrombolysis in massive PE within 10 days of cardiac surgery (lower bleeding risk).

sections.heading: EKOS-Assisted CDT Technique
sections.bodyHtml:
• Microinfuser pigtail catheter with ultrasound transducer advanced to thrombus
  • Ultrasound activates local plasminogen → localized fibrinolysis
  • Aspiration of lysed clot during 1–2 h infusion
  • Lower systemic thrombolytic exposure than IV bolus

sections.heading: Surgical Pulmonary Embolectomy
sections.bodyHtml:
Indications:

  • Massive PE with cardiogenic shock refractory to thrombolysis/CDT/EKOS
  • Massive PE with contraindication to all above
  • PE intraoperatively (during cardiac surgery) with hemodynamic collapse

Procedure: sternotomy (or through existing sternal incision if fresh post-op), cannulation for cardiopulmonary bypass, direct thrombus removal from PA trunk and lobar arteries.

Mortality: 20–40% (often moribund patients); improved outcomes with ECMO support pre-operatively.

PERT (Pulmonary Embolism Response Team) & Multidisciplinary Management

sections.heading: What is PERT?
sections.bodyHtml:
Multidisciplinary team: CT surgery, ICU, interventional radiology, echocardiography, hematology, sometimes pulmonology and cardiology.

Goal: risk-stratify PE and decide on optimal reperfusion strategy (anticoagulation vs. thrombolysis vs. catheter-directed vs. surgical).

Activation: typically through ICU or attending physician page; available at major academic/quaternary centers.

Benefits:

  • Expert consensus on intervention timing
  • Reduces mortality in intermediate/high-risk PE (especially if multifactorial decision needed post-op)
  • Guideline-concordant management

sections.heading: When to activate PERT
sections.bodyHtml:
• Submassive PE with high-risk features (troponin + RV strain) + clinical deterioration
  • Massive PE (automatic escalation to CT surgery + IR anyway)
  • PE + comorbidity complicating management (recent surgery, active bleeding, HIT, mechanical valve)

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. If any of these appear, re-escalate immediately.

  • Dyspnea worsening despite supplemental O₂ → increasing thrombus burden or right heart failure progression
  • SpO₂ trend down (gradual drift from 94% → 90% → 88%) → not just post-op settling, consider worsening PE or cardiac output
  • HR creeping up despite rate-control measures → inadequate oxygenation or worsening shock
  • BP trending down on the same vasopressor doses → loss of vasopressor responsiveness, sign of worsening RV failure
  • Urine output falling (< 0.5 mL/kg/h despite adequate BP) → renal perfusion failing; lactate may be rising
  • Lactate rising or not clearing despite intervention → inadequate tissue perfusion even if BP temporarily supported
  • Altered mental status, confusion, somnolence → hypoxemia, hypercarbia, or shock; often precedes hemodynamic collapse
  • Sudden cardiac rhythm change (new AF, VT) → mechanical stress from RV distension
  • Calf swelling or DVT signs appearing after PE diagnosis → ongoing DVT generation despite AC; may indicate filter need
  • Bleeding from sternal incision or mediastinal tubes increasing → decision point: balance AC necessity vs. surgical bleeding
  • Epistaxis, hematuria, or other spontaneous bleeding during AC → dose reduction/reassessment needed
  • Chest pain, especially pleuritic or accompanied by hemoptysis → suggests PE-related infarction or hemoptysis (poor prognosis)

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Post-cardiac-surgery PE = bleeding vs. clotting balancing act. Fresh post-op bleeding risk is real. Cannot always give full-dose AC immediately. Discuss with surgical team; escalate decision-making early.

  2. D-dimer is nearly always elevated post-op. Positive D-dimer alone is NOT diagnostic post-op. If Wells ≥ 3 or clinical suspicion high, go straight to CTPA.

  3. Saddle PE (thrombus at main PA bifurcation) is lethal. On CT-PA = medical emergency. Call STAT; do not delay for additional imaging. Thrombolysis/thrombectomy/ECMO urgently.

  4. RV dysfunction WITHOUT shock = submassive PE, not "just anticoagulate." Emerging data (PEITHO, 2023 ACC/AHA) support intervention in selected submassive PE (young, low bleeding risk, deteriorating). Escalate for PERT.

  5. Systemic lysis has HIGH contraindication post-cardiac-surgery (within 10 days). Catheter-directed thrombectomy or EKOS is preferred (lower bleeding risk). Discuss with IR + CT surgery.

  6. Catheter-directed lower bleeding risk than systemic thrombolysis. If massive PE post-op, EKOS/CDT should be offered before or alongside IV lysis discussion.

  7. IVC filter is LAST-LINE, not first-line. Anticoagulation preferred whenever feasible. Filter does NOT prevent PE; it catches clot but blocks filter → risk thrombosis and chronic venous insufficiency. Use only if AC contraindicated or failed.

  8. HIT-associated PE is NOT treated with heparin. Paradoxically, heparin causes thrombosis. 4Ts score ≥ 6 or HIT antibody positive → switch IMMEDIATELY to argatroban/bivalirudin. Contact hematology.

  9. Follow-up for post-PE syndrome. ~30% of PE survivors have persistent dyspnea; ~2–4% develop CTEPH (chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension). Refer to cardiology if dyspnea persists > 4 weeks post-PE.

  10. Provoked PE (post-op, immobility) = 3 months AC duration. Unprovoked = indefinite. Educate patient on discharge; document duration in summary.

  11. Wells ≥ 7 → CTPA direct, skip D-dimer. Post-op, most patients fail Wells screening (immobilization + recent surgery). D-dimer wastes time.

  12. Massive PE with hemodynamic compromise → thrombolysis or CDT/EKOS within 30 min. SBP < 90 or syncope = life threat. Call STAT; do not delay for labs/INRs.

  13. Post-PE anticoagulation for mechanical valve patients = warfarin ONLY. DOACs increase thrombotic events in mechanical valves. Bridge with UFH/LMWH until INR therapeutic.

  14. Bilateral DVT = high thrombus burden. Often indicates iliofemoral source (IVC involvement possible). Heighten intervention threshold; imaging abdomen if not already done.

  15. DOAC initiation post-op requires 5–10 day parenteral bridge. Do NOT start DOAC immediately post-op without bridging. Delay until POD 5–7 and bleeding risk minimal.

cards.title: Pericardial Effusion (Chronic / Non-Surgical)
cards.quickAnswer: Chronic pericardial effusion = fluid around the heart accumulating over weeks–months without acute post-operative context. Define as small (<10 mm), moderate (10–20 mm), or large (>20 mm) by echocardiography. Primary etiologies: idiopathic (~30%), malignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma), TB, autoimmune (SLE, RA), uremia, hypothyroidism, Dressler syndrome (post-MI), viral, radiation. Management is etiology-driven: medical therapy (NSAIDs + colchicine) for idiopathic/viral/inflammatory; optimize dialysis for uremic; levothyroxine for hypothyroid; chemotherapy for malignant. Tamponade is clinical diagnosis regardless of size—if hemodynamically significant, urgent pericardiocentesis. Chronic large stable effusion without tamponade may be observed with serial echos.
