sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation—definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Accumulation of >50 mL fluid in the pericardial sac over a weeks-to-months timeframe (chronic onset), without acute post-operative context. Non-surgical refers to the primary condition being non-operative; does not exclude drainage or intervention.
  • Epidemiology: ~5% of routine echocardiograms show small effusions (mostly clinically silent). Etiologies vary geographically: idiopathic and viral predominate in developed regions; TB endemic in resource-limited settings. Peak presentation ranges from young adults (viral, autoimmune) to older populations (malignancy, cardiac surgery sequelae).
  • Who this applies to: patients admitted for workup of incidentally discovered effusion; those with known etiology (renal failure, autoimmune disease, prior infection) plus newly documented effusion; those presenting with dyspnea or chest discomfort plus echo-confirmed effusion; post-MI patients with fever/pleuritic pain (Dressler syndrome); patients monitored post-pericardiocentesis for reaccumulation.
  • Why it matters: most small asymptomatic effusions do not require intervention, but some etiologies (malignancy, TB, post-cardiotomy syndrome) can progress to hemodynamic compromise or constrictive pericarditis. Early recognition of etiology and hemodynamic significance guides urgency of treatment and risk of complications.

sections.heading: Normal pericardial physiology
sections.bodyHtml: Normal pericardial fluid volume is 15–50 mL, an ultrafiltrate of plasma. The pericardium is a double-walled fibroserous sac that lubricates the heart and constrains excessive chamber dilation. Fluid accumulates when production outpaces reabsorption.

sections.heading: Chronic vs. acute physiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Chronic (vs. acute) accumulation allows pericardial compliance to increase. The pericardium can accommodate 1–2 liters of fluid before tight constraint develops, depending on distensibility.

Acute accumulation (hemorrhage, rapidly expanding malignant effusion) can cause tamponade with <500 mL if the pericardium cannot stretch. The rate of fluid accumulation matters as much as the volume.

sections.heading: Etiology-driven pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Etiology Mechanism Clinical hallmark
Idiopathic / viral (enterovirus, parvovirus, echovirus) Self-limited inflammation; may follow URI Resolves in weeks–months; viral serology often negative in chronic phase
Autoimmune (SLE, RA, Sjögren, scleroderma) Immune-mediated pericardial inflammation; immune complex deposition ANA+, ESR elevated; responds to immunosuppression
Malignancy (lung, breast, lymphoma, ovarian) Tumor invasion, pericardial metastases, or inflammation Rapidly reaccumulates; exudative fluid (high LDH, protein); cytology often positive
Uremia Uremic toxins → pericardial inflammation; may fibrinous or hemorrhagic Improves dramatically with intensified dialysis; high fibrin risk
Hypothyroidism Metabolic effect on pericardial inflammation; slowed reabsorption TSH elevated; resorbs as thyroid hormone normalizes
Dressler syndrome / Post-pericardiotomy syndrome (PPS) Autoimmune response to myocardial necrosis or pericardial injury Timing: 2–10 weeks post-MI or cardiac surgery; fever, pleuropericardial pain, elevated CRP
TB (tuberculosis) Caseous granulomatous inflammation; high risk of calcification and constriction High-risk populations (endemic regions, immunosuppressed); pericardial fluid adenosine deaminase elevated; high tamponade risk
Radiation (latent) Years-delayed inflammation from prior thoracic radiotherapy Recurrent; major risk factor for constrictive pericarditis; may require pericardiectomy
Post-cardiac surgery (acute, POD 0–7) Managed separately under Late Tamponade scenario card; not this card

sections.heading: Hemodynamic significance
sections.bodyHtml: Tamponade occurs when elevated pericardial pressure restricts ventricular filling, reducing cardiac output. Signs include elevated right atrial pressure (JVD), pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg systolic drop with inspiration), and hypotension. Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis, not determined by effusion size alone. A small effusion accumulating rapidly can cause tamponade; a large stable chronic effusion may cause none.

sections.heading: 3. Clinical Context / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml: Advanced beginner recognition—how patients with chronic pericardial effusion present.

sections.heading: Asymptomatic presentation (common)
sections.bodyHtml: Many small-to-moderate effusions are discovered incidentally on routine imaging (echocardiography, chest imaging) in patients without symptoms. These may never require intervention.

sections.heading: Symptomatic presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Patients may present with:

  • Dyspnea (exertional or at rest) from mass effect, elevated LA filling pressure, or concurrent pericarditis
  • Chest discomfort (pleuritic, worse with lying flat, relieved by sitting upright) — from pericardial inflammation
  • Orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea — if effusion impairs ventricular filling or pulmonary venous return
  • Palpitations, syncope, presyncope — if evolving toward hemodynamic compromise
  • Fatigue, malaise, fever — especially in malignancy, autoimmune etiology, or TB
  • Cough — if large effusion compresses left main-stem bronchus or concurrent pleuritis

sections.heading: Physical examination findings
sections.bodyHtml:
• Often unremarkable in uncomplicated small-to-moderate stable effusion
  • Muffled heart sounds if large effusion
  • Pericardial friction rub if concurrent pericarditis (scratchy, three-component rub)
  • Signs of tamponade if hemodynamically significant:
  • Elevated jugular venous distension (JVD)
  • Pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg systolic drop with inspiration) — measured by inflating BP cuff slowly and noting when first Korotkoff sound appears during expiration vs. throughout full cycle
  • Hypotension, tachycardia, quiet precordium
  • Cool extremities, altered mental status (if severe)
  • Kussmaul sign (JVD rises with inspiration) — less common; more typical of constrictive physiology

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information*
sections.bodyHtml: Competent systematic evaluation. Target: 30 minutes at bedside / 2 hours inpatient.

sections.heading: Clinical evaluation
sections.bodyHtml:
• Vital signs: HR, BP (supine and sitting), RR, SpO₂, temperature trend
  • Pulsus paradoxus: carefully measure—inflate cuff, deflate slowly, note systolic pressure at first Korotkoff (expiration) vs. when heard throughout cycle; difference >10 mmHg = abnormal
  • JVD: measured in sitting position at 45°; distension with hepatojugular reflux suggests elevated RA pressure
  • Auscultation: heart sounds (muffled?), pericardial friction rub, lung bases (crackles from pulmonary edema or pleural effusion), any distant sounds
  • Perfusion: capillary refill, skin temperature, extremity pulses, mental status
  • Symptoms: dyspnea grade (at rest vs. exertional), chest pain (character, radiation, positional), recent fever, weight changes
  • Risk factors / etiology clues: prior malignancy, active TB exposure, autoimmune disease, recent MI (Dressler risk), dialysis status, thyroid history, recent cardiac surgery (PPS risk), recent viral illness, radiation history

sections.heading: Diagnostic workup
sections.bodyHtml:
Test Information Target result
Transthoracic echocardiography Primary diagnostic tool; measures effusion depth (mm), location, pericardial fluid appearance (clear, echogenic, mobile), chamber collapse (RA free wall, RV diastolic), respiratory flow variation, pericardial window visualization Size classification, hemodynamic significance, presence of tamponade physiology
12-lead ECG Low voltage (global T-wave depression, PR depression if acute pericarditis phase), electrical alternans (swinging heart — sign of tension physiology) Rules out other arrhythmias; identifies tamponade physiology if present
Chest X-ray Globular or water-bottle heart silhouette (large effusion); mediastinal widening; rule out alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia) Supports presence of large effusion; assess cardiothoracic ratio
Echocardiography — advanced hemodynamic markers RA/RV diastolic collapse (>1/3 of chamber area); mitral/tricuspid inflow variation >25% with respiration; hepatic vein reversal; swinging heart Presence suggests elevated pericardial pressure / tamponade physiology
Labs for etiology workup Detailed below in Teaching Layers Clarifies cause; guides treatment
Pericardiocentesis (diagnostic) Fluid cell count + differential, Gram stain, bacterial culture, TB culture (AFB smear + culture), viral serology if applicable, fluid chemistry (LDH, protein, glucose), cytology (malignancy), adenosine deaminase (TB suspicion), ferritin (TB), cholesterol (tuberculosis) Definitively establishes etiology; allows therapeutic relief if large/symptomatic

sections.heading: 5. Management
sections.bodyHtml: Etiology-directed, stepwise approach. For all stable patients, follow §5A. Tamponade physiology triggers §5B.

sections.heading: 5A. Stable effusion (asymptomatic, no hemodynamic compromise, no signs of tamponade)
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Establish etiology via directed workup — see Teaching Layers (§7.1) for full laboratory panel
  2. Size classification by echo:
    • Small (<10 mm) → surveillance with repeat echo at 4–6 weeks, then 3–6 month intervals if stable; no intervention needed unless etiology requires treatment
    • Moderate (10–20 mm) → depends on hemodynamic significance and etiology; observation if stable + uncomplicated; medical therapy targeting etiology
    • Large (>20 mm) → higher recurrence and tamponade risk; most guidelines recommend pericardiocentesis for diagnostic + therapeutic benefit even if asymptomatic
    • Etiology-specific medical management (detailed in §5A subsections below)
    • Serial echocardiography at planned intervals (typically 4–6 weeks, then 3–6 monthly) to assess stability
    • Anticoagulation precautions — if patient on warfarin/DOACs, document INR/PT carefully; if pericardiocentesis planned, coordinate with provider re: holding/bridging
    • Teach patient about red flags (shortness of breath, syncope, chest pain, dizziness) and importance of outpatient follow-up

sections.heading: 5A.1 Idiopathic or viral pericarditis
sections.bodyHtml:
• NSAIDs: Indomethacin 25–50 mg three times daily OR ibuprofen 600 mg three to four times daily × 4–6 weeks minimum
  • Gastroprotection: if NSAID prolonged, add proton-pump inhibitor (e.g., omeprazole 20 mg daily)
  • Colchicine: 0.6 mg twice daily × 3 months (evidence for symptom reduction and recurrence prevention). Caution: GI side effects common; counsel accordingly. Reduce dose if CrCl <30 mL/min (myopathy risk with high doses).
  • Corticosteroids: NOT first-line; reserved for refractory disease. If used, low-dose prednisone 0.25–0.5 mg/kg/day tapered over weeks. Can paradoxically prolong course in viral disease.
  • Activity: avoid strenuous exertion × 3 months to reduce recurrence risk
  • Follow-up: repeat echo at 4–6 weeks; expect resolution in weeks-to-months

sections.heading: 5A.2 Dressler syndrome / Post-pericardiotomy syndrome (PPS)
sections.bodyHtml:
Occurs 2–10 weeks after myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery. Distinct from acute post-operative effusion (Late Tamponade scenario card).

  • Timeline recognition: PPS is POD 14–60 (not immediately post-op; if within first 7 days, consider post-op complications)
  • NSAIDs: Indomethacin 25–50 mg TID × 4–6 weeks
  • Colchicine: 0.6 mg BID × 3 months (reduces recurrence; preferred over corticosteroids for first-line therapy in modern practice)
  • Corticosteroids: Low-dose prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day if severe, refractory, or recurrent; taper over 4–8 weeks. Can be combined with colchicine.
  • Monitoring: watch for atrial fibrillation (common), elevated inflammatory markers; chest imaging for pleuropericardial involvement
  • Prognosis: self-limited; median duration 2–8 weeks; can recur; colchicine prophylaxis 3–6 months reduces recurrence

sections.heading: 5A.3 Autoimmune pericarditis (SLE, RA, Sjögren, scleroderma)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Coordinate with rheumatology — primary disease management is key
  • NSAIDs: first-line if disease-modifying therapy not already in place
  • Corticosteroids: low-dose prednisone 0.25–0.5 mg/kg/day if active pericarditis or hemodynamically significant effusion; titrate with disease activity
  • Immunosuppression: per rheumatology guidance (hydroxychloroquine, azathioprine, mycophenolate, biologic agents depending on underlying condition)
  • Colchicine: may be added for recurrent pericarditis
  • Pericardiocentesis: if large or symptomatic; fluid is typically exudative (high LDH, protein)
  • Monitoring: serial echo; watch for constrictive development (rare but reported)

sections.heading: 5A.4 Malignancy-associated effusion
sections.bodyHtml:
Lung, breast, lymphoma, ovarian most common. Fluid rapidly reaccumulates.

  • Chemotherapy: primary treatment per oncology; many patients respond with effusion resorption
  • Pericardiocentesis: indicated if symptomatic, hemodynamically significant, or large (>20 mm) even without tamponade, for diagnostic cytology + therapeutic relief
  • Drain volume target: typically 500–1500 mL (until respiratory distress relieved or hemodynamics improve)
  • Caution: aggressive drainage may cause re-expansion pulmonary edema; drain slowly if large volume expected
  • Fluid analysis: cell count, LDH, protein, cytology (often malignant cells present; sensitivity ~70%)
  • Pericardial window or sclerotherapy: if rapid reaccumulation (within days) or recurrent pericardiocentesis (usually after 2–3 reaccumulations)
  • Options: surgical subxiphoid pericardial window (most durable), percutaneous catheter-based window, sclerotherapy with talc/doxycycline
  • Window allows continuous drainage via pericardial catheter (stays in 3–7 days) or open drainage to peritoneal cavity
  • Radiation history: prior mediastinal radiation increases constrictive risk years later
  • Prognosis: depends on underlying malignancy; effusion control is often temporary measure while chemotherapy takes effect

sections.heading: 5A.5 TB pericarditis
sections.bodyHtml:
Globally important. High risk of progression to constrictive pericarditis. Requires aggressive multi-drug therapy + close monitoring.

  • Anti-tuberculosis therapy: standard 4-drug induction (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) × 2 months, then 2-drug continuation (isoniazid + rifampicin) × 4 months. Confirm TB diagnosis via pericardial fluid culture/PCR, AFB smear, or adenosine deaminase elevation (>10 U/L highly specific).
  • Adjunctive corticosteroids: Prednisone 60 mg daily × 4 weeks, taper to 30 mg × 4 weeks, then continue low-dose (10–15 mg) × remaining therapy course. Reduces constrictive pericarditis risk and mortality.
  • Pericardiocentesis: indicated for diagnostic fluid analysis (adenosine deaminase, culture, PCR) and therapeutic relief if large/symptomatic
  • Imaging surveillance: high-risk for calcification and constrictive development; serial echos + CXR to detect late constriction (months-to-years post-TB treatment)
  • Complications: ~50% risk of constrictive pericarditis if untreated or if corticosteroids withheld; pericardiectomy may be needed if constriction develops
  • Duration: TB treatment is 6 months minimum (longer if extrapulmonary TB with CNS involvement)

sections.heading: 5A.6 Uremic pericarditis (dialysis patients)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Intensify dialysis: increase ultrafiltration volume and frequency (transition to more frequent dialysis, shorter interdialytic intervals, or nocturnal hemodialysis if available)
  • NSAIDs: use with caution in renal failure (worsen uremia, hyperkalemia); if given, monitor closely
  • Anticoagulation: balance uremic bleeding risk against thrombosis risk; manage carefully around pericardiocentesis
  • Pericardiocentesis: indicated if large, symptomatic, or high tamponade risk (fibrinous/hemorrhagic fluid is common)
  • Monitoring: effusion usually resolves with improved dialysis clearance; small effusions often do not need drainage
  • Prognosis: outlook improved with optimization of dialysis; mortality from uremic pericarditis has declined with modern renal replacement therapy

sections.heading: 5A.7 Hypothyroidism-associated effusion
sections.bodyHtml:
• Levothyroxine replacement: titrate to euthyroid TSH (target usually 0.5–2.5 mIU/L depending on age/disease)
  • Monitoring: recheck TSH every 6–8 weeks during titration; effusion typically resorbs as TSH normalizes
  • Prognosis: expect dramatic improvement once euthyroid; no pericardiocentesis usually needed unless effusion is massive and causes tamponade before TSH normalizes
  • Timeline: effusion resorption lags TSH normalization by weeks

sections.heading: 5A.8 Post-cardiac surgery effusion (chronic phase, post-PPS window)
sections.bodyHtml:
Not acute post-op (see Late Tamponade scenario card). For effusion discovered days-to-weeks post-op in non-tamponade context.

  • Distinguish from acute post-op collection: timing (PPS is POD 14–60), vital signs stability, absence of tamponade physiology
  • Management: same as Dressler syndrome (NSAIDs + colchicine × 3 months)
  • Surveillance: serial echo; watch for reaccumulation or progression to constriction
  • Rare complication: effusion-constrictive pericarditis (drainage unmasks constrictive physiology; may require pericardiectomy if symptomatic constriction develops)

sections.heading: 5B. Hemodynamically significant effusion / tamponade physiology (unstable presentation)
sections.bodyHtml:
Define tamponade: elevated pericardial pressure restricting ventricular filling, causing hypotension, elevated JVD, and reduced cardiac output.

Tamponade is a clinical diagnosis, confirmed by hemodynamic findings and echo-derived chamber collapse, NOT by size alone.

Clinical recognition: hypotension + elevated JVD + pulsus paradoxus (>10 mmHg) + tachycardia ± altered mental status + dyspnea, especially in context of large effusion or rapid accumulation.

  1. STAT pericardiocentesis — do NOT delay for additional imaging once clinical diagnosis made - Notify attending/APP immediately; prepare for procedure - Obtain IV access (two large-bore IVs); type & cross for emergent blood transfusion availability - Brief prep: cardiac catheterization lab preferred; can be performed at bedside if unstable and procedure unavoidable - Sterile technique: povidone-iodine prep, drape; echo-guided access preferred (subxiphoid or apical approach); monitor vital signs + telemetry continuously - Drain volume: typically 500–1500 mL; may drain entire effusion or partial drainage if hemodynamics improve early - Drain placement: pigtail catheter left indwelling × 24–72 hours if ongoing reaccumulation risk
  2. Fluid analysis: cell count, Gram stain, culture (bacterial, TB, fungal), cytology, LDH, protein, glucose, adenosine deaminase, ferritin
  3. Supportive care during drainage: maintain IV fluids to support preload (cautiously; patient is preload-dependent); avoid excessive diuretics; vasopressor support (norepinephrine, dopamine) if hypotension persists
  4. Post-drainage imaging: repeat echo within 1–2 hours to assess fluid resolution and cardiac function recovery
  5. Etiology workup: expedite labs (ANA, TB serology, malignancy workup, TSH, renal panel) while managing acute situation
  6. Anticoagulation hold: if patient on warfarin/DOAC, hold around procedure; coordinate with team (some patients may need bridging with UFH depending on indication)
  7. Address underlying cause: initiate etiology-specific therapy (NSAIDs for pericarditis, dialysis optimization, thyroid hormone, chemotherapy, anti-TB drugs, etc.)

sections.heading: 5B.1 Pericardiocentesis technique (summary)
sections.bodyHtml:
• Approach: subxiphoid (preferred; safer for inexperienced operators), apical (alternative if large effusion), parasternal (rarely used)
  • Guidance: echo is strongly preferred; fluoroscopy acceptable if echo unavailable; blind procedure has 5–10% complication rate
  • Needle: 18-gauge needle on syringe; advance slowly until fluid returns (confirm echo-guided)
  • Guidewire: Seldinger technique; advance guidewire, remove needle, dilate tract, place pigtail catheter
  • Complications (monitor closely): cardiac perforation, myocardial injury, arrhythmia, hemorrhage, infection, re-expansion pulmonary edema
  • Post-procedure: secure catheter; monitor output (serous/clear expected; fresh blood suggests perforation); remove when output <20 mL/24 h or per protocol

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
When to escalate immediately → STAT team call / rapid response:

  • Hemodynamically significant effusion with hypotension (SBP <90), altered mental status, or shock physiology
  • Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg with elevated JVD and dyspnea
  • Echo showing large effusion with chamber collapse (RA/RV diastolic)
  • Rapid increase in effusion size on serial imaging
  • Persistent tamponade physiology despite initial pericardiocentesis (reaccumulation)

SBAR template for escalation:

S: "I'm calling about [patient name, room, POD/day X]. New finding: [large pericardial effusion / signs of tamponade]."

B: "Patient admitted with [etiology clue: renal failure / known malignancy / recent MI / fever + chest pain]. Echo today shows [size + location]. Vital signs: BP [value], HR [rate], JVD [distended / normal], pulsus paradoxus [>10 / <10 mmHg]."

A: "Patient is [stable / deteriorating]. [Respiratory status, mentation, perfusion]."

R: "Requesting [diagnostic labs / urgent echo / pericardiocentesis / ICU transfer / cardiology/cardiac surgery consult]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable chronic effusion, outpatient workup Primary care, cardiology (outpatient)
Incidental moderate-to-large effusion, admitted patient, stable Cardiology consult; escalate if size increases or symptoms develop
Large effusion with fever + chest pain (Dressler / pericarditis) Cardiology (urgent same-day); escalate if tamponade develops
Tamponade physiology (hypotension + JVD + pulsus paradoxus) STAT cardiology + cardiac surgery. Prepare for immediate pericardiocentesis.
Known malignancy + effusion Cardiology + oncology; escalate if hemodynamically significant
TB pericarditis suspected Infectious disease + cardiology + pulmonology; consider admission if large/symptomatic
Uremic patient on dialysis + worsening effusion Nephrology + cardiology; escalate if tamponade risk
Hypothyroid + large effusion Endocrinology + cardiology; if tamponade, manage medically (levothyroxine + inotropy) vs. pericardiocentesis per team

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers *(expandable in app — collapsible by default)*
7.1 Comprehensive etiology workup
sections.bodyHtml:
Laboratory panel for chronic pericardial effusion — order based on clinical clues:

Etiology suspect Initial labs Advanced testing
Idiopathic / Viral CBC, CMP, ESR, CRP; viral serology (enterovirus, parvovirus, CMV) Pericardial fluid: viral PCR if available
Autoimmune (SLE, RA, Sjögren, scleroderma) CBC, CMP, ESR, CRP, ANA panel, anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-SSA/SSB, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, complement (C3, C4) Pericardial fluid: ANA, complement levels; skin/organ biopsy if systemic involvement unclear
Malignancy CBC, CMP, LDH, CEA, PSA (if male); imaging per risk (CXR, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, mammography per age); consider tumor markers specific to history Pericardial fluid: cytology (gold standard), flow cytometry if lymphoma suspected
Uremia (dialysis patient) BUN, creatinine, potassium, calcium, phosphate, albumin; dialysis adequacy (Kt/V, URR) Pericardial fluid: cell count (usually serofibrinous or hemorrhagic in uremia)
Hypothyroidism TSH (free T4 if TSH abnormal); anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin if Hashimoto suspected Monitor TSH response to levothyroxine; repeat echo as TSH normalizes
TB CXR, TB skin test (Mantoux) or IGRA (QuantiFERON-Gold), sputum AFB × 3, TB serology Pericardial fluid: AFB smear, TB culture, pericardial fluid adenosine deaminase (ADA >10 U/L highly specific), pericardial TB PCR
Dressler / PPS CBC, CMP, ESR, CRP, troponin (may be elevated post-MI); timing post-MI/surgery is key Pericardial fluid: usually sterile, serofibrinous; viral studies usually negative
Radiation-induced (latent) History of prior mediastinal radiation (Hodgkin lymphoma, breast, esophageal ca); prior docs/imaging Monitor for constrictive features on echo/cardiac catheterization

sections.heading: 7.2 Dressler syndrome / Post-pericardiotomy syndrome (deep dive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Definition & timing: Autoimmune pleuropericardial syndrome occurring 2–10 weeks (median ~3–4 weeks) after myocardial infarction or cardiac surgery. Thought to result from sensitization to myocardial/pericardial autoantigens released during necrosis.

Classic presentation:

  • Fever (often 38–39°C)
  • Pleuritic chest pain (worse with lying flat, improved by sitting upright)
  • Pleuropericardial friction rub on auscultation
  • Pericardial effusion on imaging (often accompanied by pleural effusion)
  • Elevated inflammatory markers (ESR >50, CRP elevated)

Pathognomonic findings:

  • Timing: POD 14–60 (later than immediate post-op bleeds, but within 2 months of insult)
  • Bilateral pleural effusions (distinguishes from isolated post-op effusion)
  • Pericardial effusion often concurrent
  • Fever is hallmark (not present in simple post-op effusion)
  • Responds to NSAIDs/corticosteroids/colchicine (vs. post-op fluid often needing drainage)

Modern management (shifted from steroids to colchicine):

  • Colchicine 0.6 mg BID × 3 months — now preferred first-line based on recent data (reduces recurrence and symptom burden)
  • NSAIDs: Indomethacin 25–50 mg TID × 4–6 weeks concurrent with colchicine
  • Corticosteroids: reserved for severe, refractory disease; low-dose prednisone 0.5–1 mg/kg/day × 2–4 weeks then taper (can prolong course if overused)
  • Activity: relative rest; avoid strenuous exertion × 3 months
  • Prognosis: self-limited; median duration 4–8 weeks; recurrence occurs in ~10% (colchicine prophylaxis reduces)

Risk factors for PPS:

  • Older age
  • Post-MI (vs. post-surgery)
  • Delayed post-op analgesia (inadequate pain control → cytokine surge)

sections.heading: 7.3 Malignant pericardial effusion (deep dive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Etiology: tumor metastases to pericardium (hematogenous spread, lymphatic spread, or direct invasion from adjacent lung/breast). Most common cancers: lung (~40%), breast (~20%), lymphoma (~10%), ovarian, gastric, renal.

Clinical characteristics:

  • Often asymptomatic at discovery (found on surveillance imaging)
  • Symptoms when present: dyspnea, chest discomfort, cough (from compression)
  • Rapid reaccumulation (within days of drainage) is hallmark—pericardial recurrence rate ~50–80% within 30 days of single pericardiocentesis
  • Fluid is exudative (LDH >LDH serum, protein >3 g/dL, LD ratio >0.67); cytology positive in ~70% of cases
  • Prognosis tied to underlying malignancy, not effusion itself

Management strategy:

  1. Pericardiocentesis for diagnosis + initial relief — document cytology; therapeutic if symptomatic or large
  2. Chemotherapy — primary treatment; many effusions resorb with effective chemo
  3. Pericardial window (surgical or percutaneous) if:
    • Rapid reaccumulation (days) after single drainage
    • Recurrent drainage needed (usually after 2–3 reaccumulations)
    • Loculated effusion
    • Hemodynamic instability despite drainage
    • Options for window:
      • Surgical subxiphoid window (most durable; open drainage to peritoneum or anterior mediastinum)
      • Percutaneous catheter-based window (pigtail catheter left indwelling longer, <30% recurrence)
      • Sclerotherapy (doxycycline, talc injected to pleurodese pericardium; effectiveness ~50–70%)

Prognosis: median survival often measured in months (depends on underlying cancer). Effusion control is often temporizing measure during active chemotherapy.

sections.heading: 7.4 TB pericarditis (deep dive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Global importance: 1–5% of TB cases involve pericardium; higher in immunocompromised (HIV), endemic regions. High mortality if untreated (~80% with necropsies showing TB involvement).

Pathology: caseous granulomatous inflammation, often with calcification. High risk of progression to constrictive pericarditis (>50% if untreated).

Diagnostic clues:

  • Epidemiology: endemic region, HIV+, immunosuppression, old TB history
  • Chest imaging: granulomatous pattern in lung fields (not always present); pericardial thickening
  • Pericardial fluid analysis:
  • Adenosine deaminase (ADA) >10 U/L — highly specific for TB pericarditis (~95% sensitivity, >90% specificity)
  • AFB smear positive in ~10–20%
  • TB culture positive in ~50% (takes weeks)
  • TB PCR positive in ~50–80% (if available; faster)
  • Lymphocytic predominance, high protein

Management:

  • Anti-TB drugs × 6 months minimum: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol × 2 months; isoniazid + rifampicin × 4 months
  • Adjunctive corticosteroids: Prednisone 60 mg/day × 4 weeks, then taper 30 mg × 4 weeks, then low-dose (10–15 mg) × remaining treatment. Reduces constrictive risk and mortality.
  • Pericardiocentesis: indicated for diagnostic fluid (ADA, culture) and therapeutic relief if large/symptomatic
  • Surgical pericardectomy: indicated if constriction develops (diagnosed by hemodynamic studies or imaging progression); pericardiectomy is complex and high-morbidity; best outcomes when performed >6 months after diagnosis
  • Monitoring: serial imaging (CXR, echo, advanced imaging like CT) to detect calcification and constrictive features; high risk for late constriction (months-to-years post-diagnosis)
  • Recurrence / relapse: less common if full 6-month therapy completed; longer therapy recommended if TB meningitis co-exists

sections.heading: 7.5 Constrictive pericarditis and effusion-constriction (deep dive)
sections.bodyHtml:
Effusion-constrictive pericarditis: Rare syndrome where large chronic effusion coexists with constrictive pericardium. Drainage may unmask hemodynamic constriction. Risk factors: TB, radiation, prior cardiac surgery, malignancy.

Clinical features:

  • Large effusion on imaging
  • Hemodynamic findings of restriction (elevated RA/LA pressures, dip-plateau on RV tracing, Kussmaul sign)
  • After drainage, constriction becomes apparent; RV diastolic dip may worsen

Management: pericardiectomy if constriction is hemodynamically significant and symptomatic. This is surgical; high morbidity (~10–15%) and mortality if performed emergently.

Constrictive pericarditis progression: Long-term risk in patients with:

  • TB pericarditis (highest risk, ~50%)
  • Radiation-induced pericarditis
  • Post-cardiac surgery (rare)
  • Chronic idiopathic pericarditis

Prevention of constriction:

  • Treat TB aggressively with adjunctive steroids
  • Serial imaging to detect calcification early
  • Consider early pericardiectomy if imaging shows calcification + hemodynamic compromise
  • Close outpatient follow-up (echo every 3–6 months initially)

sections.heading: 7.6 Anticoagulation and pericardial effusion
sections.bodyHtml:
Bleeding risk: Patients on warfarin or DOACs have increased hemorrhage risk during pericardiocentesis. Approach:

  • If pericardiocentesis planned:
  • Warfarin: hold × 3–5 days; target INR <2.0 for procedure; restart cautiously post-procedure (wait 24–48 h if uncomplicated drainage)
  • DOAC: hold × 24–48 h pre-procedure (longer if renal impairment); restart post-procedure per team
  • UFH: can continue; easier to reverse if hemorrhage; some prefer bridging approach
  • If on AC for mechanical valve or recent thrombotic event: cardiology/cardiac surgery discussion needed; may use UFH bridge around procedure
  • Document INR/PT carefully pre-procedure; communicate results to proceduralist
  • Post-drainage: monitor drain output (clear vs. bloody); if bloody output exceeds 50–100 mL/h, notify team (may indicate ongoing bleed or cardiac perforation)

sections.heading: 7.7 COVID-19–associated pericarditis
sections.bodyHtml:
Emerging data: COVID-19 can cause myopericarditis with pericardial effusion, especially in severe disease.

Clinical features:

  • Chest pain, dyspnea
  • Elevated troponin and NT-proBNP
  • Pericardial effusion (usually mild-to-moderate)
  • May evolve to myocarditis with heart failure

Management: supportive; NSAIDs for symptom control; monitor for myocardial dysfunction and heart failure. Most resolve with recovery from acute COVID illness. Rarely require drainage unless large/tamponade.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — *deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient*
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Any of these in a stable patient on 5A pathway → re-escalate toward 5B.

  • Acute increase in dyspnea or orthopnea — effusion rapidly enlarging or hemodynamic significance developing
  • New hypotension or tachycardia trend — may herald evolving tamponade
  • New or worsening pulsus paradoxus — rising pericardial pressure even if BP still adequate
  • JVD rising acutely — RA pressure elevation
  • New altered mental status, confusion, or anxiety — perfusion failing; urgent intervention needed
  • Rapid increase in effusion size on serial echo — reaccumulation risk high; may need intervention
  • Fever + pleuritic chest pain — signs of acute pericarditis or PPS; intensify anti-inflammatory therapy
  • Fever + TB exposure history + worsening effusion — TB pericarditis may be progressing; expedite anti-TB therapy
  • New focal neurologic deficit (weakness, facial droop, speech change) in patient with known malignancy + effusion — possible pericardial hemorrhage or embolic stroke; activate stroke code
  • Effusion reaccumulating rapidly post-pericardiocentesis (within 24–48 h) — higher recurrence risk; may need pericardial window
  • Drain output consistently >100 mL/h when clear — may indicate faster fluid production or drainage issue (check position, patency); if bloody, consider cardiac perforation
  • Respiratory distress shortly after large-volume drainage — re-expansion pulmonary edema; limit drainage rate, optimize diuretics + oxygenation

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls *(10–15 high-yield bullets)*
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Tamponade is clinical, not radiographic. A small effusion (5 mm) with rapid accumulation can cause hemodynamic collapse; a large stable effusion (40 mm) may be asymptomatic. Assess the patient, not the size. Look for hypotension + JVD + pulsus paradoxus + altered mental status, not just imaging.

  2. Small incidental effusion = observe, do not drain. Many <10 mm effusions discovered on routine echo are clinically silent and remain stable. Surveillance with repeat echo at 4–6 weeks, then q3–6 months, is appropriate. Unnecessary pericardiocentesis adds risk (perforation, infection) with no benefit.

  3. Uremic effusion often improves dramatically with dialysis optimization alone. Do not rush to pericardiocentesis. First step: increase dialysis frequency/intensity (nocturnal HD, more frequent sessions, higher ultrafiltration). Many effusions resorb. Coordinate with nephrology.

  4. Hypothyroid effusion resolves when thyroid hormone replaces TSH. TSH-driven metabolic inflammation causing pericardial fluid. Start levothyroxine, recheck TSH in 6–8 weeks, repeat echo at 4–6 weeks (expect 50–80% resorption). Drainage rarely needed unless massive effusion causing tamponade before euthyroid achieved.

  5. Malignant effusion recurs fast; pericardiocentesis is often insufficient. Reaccumulation within days is the rule. Plan for pericardial window (surgical or percutaneous) after 1–2 reaccumulations, not after third drainage. Coordinate early with cardiac surgery.

  6. Dressler syndrome = POD 14–60, not immediate post-op. Do not confuse with acute post-op hemorrhagic effusion (Late Tamponade scenario). Dressler presents with fever, pleuritic pain, elevated inflammatory markers, pericarditis physiology. Treat with NSAIDs + colchicine × 3 months.

    Key distinction: timing.

  7. Colchicine dosing in renal impairment must be reduced. Standard dose 0.6 mg BID can cause myopathy if creatinine clearance <30 mL/min. Reduce to 0.3 mg daily or q 2–3 days. GI side effects are common; counsel about diarrhea risk.

  8. TB pericarditis requires aggressive multi-drug therapy + adjunctive corticosteroids. Standard 4-drug induction × 2 months + 2-drug continuation × 4 months.

    Corticosteroids are not optional—prednisone 60 mg/day × 4 weeks, then taper; reduces constrictive risk by ~50%. Without steroids, >50% progress to constriction. High-stakes diagnosis.

  9. Pulsus paradoxus >10 mmHg is the single best bedside physical sign of tamponade. Measure carefully: inflate cuff slowly, note systolic pressure when first Korotkoff heard (expiration) vs. when heard throughout full cycle. Difference >10 mmHg = pathologic. Correlates with filling pressure elevation. More specific than JVD alone.

  10. Electrical alternans on ECG = swinging heart in tamponade physiology. Low voltage alone can be effusion. Alternans (beat-to-beat QRS amplitude variation) is pathognomonic for tension physiology—heart swinging wildly in fluid. Urgent echo + pericardiocentesis indicated.

  11. Anticoagulation + pericardial effusion = bleeding risk around drainage. If patient on warfarin/DOAC, hold per protocol; target INR <2.0 for pericardiocentesis. Document carefully. Risk of tamponade from pericardial bleed is real; coordinate with team pre-procedure. Post-drainage, restart cautiously (24–48 h delay acceptable).

  12. "Sludge" on echo (fibrin-layered fluid, echodense material) suggests purulent or malignant effusion. Sludge indicates more organized/loculated fluid. Higher risk of loculation, difficulty draining, need for window. Alert team to consider surgical approach vs. percutaneous if pericardiocentesis planned.

  13. Post-pericardiocentesis monitoring: watch for reaccumulation AND constrictive unmasking. After drainage of large chronic effusion (especially TB, radiation), hemodynamic constriction may emerge as fluid resolves. Persistent elevated RA pressure + dip-plateau RV tracing + Kussmaul sign = effusion-constriction. May need pericardiectomy.

  14. Recurrent pericarditis (≥3 episodes in 18 months) should trigger colchicine prophylaxis 3–6 months. Colchicine reduces recurrence by ~70%. Most effective if started early in course. Some experts use it first-line in recurrent idiopathic/viral pericarditis.

  15. NSAIDs are first-line for idiopathic/viral/inflammatory pericarditis; corticosteroids second-line. Steroids can paradoxically prolong viral pericarditis (suppress immune response needed for resolution). Reserve steroids for refractory disease, autoimmune etiology, TB, PPS. Low-dose, short course (2–4 weeks with taper).

cards.title: Peripheral Nerve Injury (Post-Cardiac Surgery)
cards.quickAnswer: New focal motor or sensory deficit post-cardiac surgery → peripheral nerve injury until proven otherwise. Distinguish peripheral (lower motor neuron: single-nerve distribution, face intact) from central stroke (upper motor neuron: facial droop, arm+leg together, speech change). Key injuries: ulnar (most common; hand weakness), brachial plexus (arm weakness), phrenic (elevated hemidiaphragm on CXR, dyspnea), RLN (hoarseness). Document baseline exam immediately. Most neuropraxia resolves 3–6 months. Escalate to neuro/PT same-day; EMG at 4–6 weeks if no improvement; initiate AFO/orthotics for safety; patient education on recovery timeline.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, scope.

  • Definition: New focal motor or sensory deficit in a single peripheral nerve distribution occurring within hours to days post-cardiac surgery. Results from mechanical compression, traction, or stretch during retraction, positioning, or bypass.
  • Incidence: 2–11% of cardiac surgery patients depending on procedure and operative time (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020). Ulnar nerve most common (elbow compression), followed by brachial plexus (sternal retraction) and common peroneal (leg positioning).
  • Who this applies to: every post-operative cardiac surgery patient during ICU and stepdown care (POD 0 through discharge and beyond). Highest yield for recognition in first 48–72 hours; recovery trajectory tracked for 3–6 months.
  • Why it matters: Early recognition prevents cascading complications (falls, contractures, aspiration, functional loss). Most positioning injuries are neuropraxia and resolve completely with early intervention (PT/OT, orthotics, patient education). Delayed diagnosis or poor compliance with rehabilitation extends recovery.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice + advanced beginner teaching. Why peripheral nerve injuries occur in cardiac surgery.

Peripheral nerve injuries in cardiac surgery result from three primary mechanisms:

  1. Mechanical compression (neuropraxia — most common, reversible): Nerve fibers are blocked from conducting without axonal disruption. Myelin swelling or external pressure prevents action potentials. Examples: elbow compression against table edge (ulnar), arm abduction >90° (brachial plexus), fibular head pressure against leg holder (peroneal). Recovery is rapid — typically days to weeks as swelling resolves.

  2. Traction injury (axonotmesis — partial axonal disruption, longer recovery): Nerve is stretched, disrupting axons while preserving connective tissue architecture. Requires axonal regeneration at ~1 mm/day. Examples: aggressive retraction in aortic arch surgery (brachial plexus, RLN), phrenic nerve retraction during LIMA dissection. Recovery takes weeks to months (6–12+ weeks).

  3. Laceration/transection (neurotmesis — rare in cardiac surgery): Complete nerve division, typically discovered intraoperatively or during delayed recovery. Requires surgical repair. Outcomes are variable depending on repair timing and ischemia.

Key severity classification (Seddon, 1943):

  • Neuropraxia (1st degree): conduction block only; myelin intact; recovery in 3–6 weeks typically, up to 3 months
  • Axonotmesis (2nd–3rd degree): axon disrupted; requires axonal regeneration; recovery weeks to months (3–12 months typical)
  • Neurotmesis (4th–5th degree): complete transection; surgical repair needed; variable recovery, often incomplete

Risk factors (Bojar, 2020): prolonged CPB time (>180 min), arm abduction >90°, aggressive sternal retraction, inadequate padding at pressure points, body position stress (external rotation at hip/knee), age >65, obesity, prior thoracic outlet syndrome or brachial plexus injury.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following in a post-operative cardiac surgery patient:

  • Motor deficit: new arm weakness (shoulder abduction, grip strength asymmetry), leg weakness (foot dorsiflexion, steppage gait), wrist drop (cannot extend wrist), foot drop (drags foot)
  • Sensory deficit: numbness, tingling, or paresthesias in arm (lateral arm, hand), leg (lateral calf, dorsum of foot)
  • Cranial nerve finding: new hoarseness, weak voice, difficulty swallowing, cough weakness, aspiration event
  • Diaphragm finding: elevated hemidiaphragm on CXR, increased work of breathing, dyspnea unexplained by other causes
  • Functional/safety event: new fall, foot drag without explanation, difficulty ambulating, patient unable to write or grip self-care items

Timeline: Deficits present immediately post-op or emerge within the first 24–72 hours as patient awakens and mobilizes. Phrenic or RLN injury may not be apparent until the patient is extubated (hoarseness) or attempts deep breathing (dyspnea).

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2–3 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. Pure information-gathering; no actions yet.

  • Motor exam at risk distributions:
  • Brachial plexus (C5–C6 upper trunk): shoulder abduction (against resistance), external rotation; compare L vs R
  • Ulnar: intrinsic hand muscles (finger spreading, thumb opposition), grip strength; compare L vs R
  • Common peroneal: foot dorsiflexion (heel-walk test), ability to dorsiflex toes; observe steppage gait if walking
  • Radial: wrist extension (wrist cock-up), thumb extension
  • Phrenic: diaphragm excursion on CXR (check both hemidiaphragms), accessory muscle use, respiratory effort

  • Recurrent laryngeal: voice quality, ability to produce sound, cough strength, ability to phonate a high "eee" sound

  • Sensory exam:

  • Brachial plexus: lateral arm, lateral forearm
  • Ulnar: 4th and 5th finger pads
  • Common peroneal: dorsum of foot, lateral calf

  • Radial: dorsum of thumb/index finger web space

  • Critical differential — peripheral (LMN) vs central (stroke/UMN):

Feature Peripheral Nerve (LMN) Stroke (UMN)
Facial droop Absent; face intact Present + central sparing (forehead/eye still wrinkles)
Pattern Single nerve distribution only (e.g., wrist drop alone) Hemisphere pattern (face + arm + leg together on same side)
Reflex change Hyporeflexia or absent in distribution Hyperreflexia (upper motor neuron sign)
Tongue Midline Deviates toward lesion
Speech Normal unless RLN injury (hoarse) Dysarthria or aphasia if dominant hemisphere

If any signs of UMN pattern (facial droop, arm+leg weakness together, speech change) → activate stroke protocol immediately. This is NOT a peripheral nerve injury.

  • Observe baseline function:
  • Pre-op neuro exam from chart?
  • PACU baseline exam documented?

  • When was deficit first noticed? By whom?

  • Review operative notes:

  • Duration of CPB?
  • Sternal retraction notes (force, duration, direction)?
  • Positioning details (arm abduction angle, leg external rotation)?
  • Any intraoperative nerve injury noted?

  • LIMA harvest? Aortic arch work?

  • Current symptoms:

  • Pain in affected limb? (neuropathic pain common 2–3 weeks post-op)
  • Swelling, warmth, skin changes? (rule out compartment syndrome, DVT)
  • Functional impact on self-care, safety, ambulation?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Isolated focal motor/sensory finding, hemodynamically stable, no respiratory distress, no facial droop.)

  1. Document baseline neuro exam STAT — record motor grades (0–5 scale), sensory to light touch, reflex status, functional assessment (e.g., "can flex wrist but cannot extend," "intact sensation to 4th–5th fingertips," "walks independently but drags left foot")
  2. Photograph or sketch deficit if helpful (e.g., foot drop comparison); use for handoff and follow-up tracking
  3. Notify APP / on-call fellow STAT (not routine) — peripheral nerve injury requires evaluation and management plan; this is urgent recognition, though management may be routine
  4. Obtain imaging per provider:
    • Brachial plexus suspicion: CXR (screen for phrenic involvement), consider ultrasound or MRI plexus
    • Foot drop / peroneal concern: rule out compartment syndrome or DVT with clinical exam + doppler ultrasound if concern
    • Hoarseness / RLN suspicion: CXR (check vocal cord position radiograph), coordinate ENT laryngoscopy
    • Phrenic injury suspicion: CXR (measure hemidiaphragm height on both sides), consider fluoroscopy or ultrasound sniff test
    • Continuous monitoring for progression — serial neuro checks q4h × 24 h, then q shift if stable
    • Initiate safety precautions immediately:
    • Foot drop: anti-slip socks, fall precautions (bed alarm, assist with ambulation), PT consult same-day for gait training and AFO referral
    • Wrist drop: splint hand in neutral position, prevent contracture, consider wrist cock-up orthosis referral
    • Arm weakness: assess ADL independence, consider OT referral for positioning and adaptive strategies
    • Manage pain: if neuropathic pain present, discuss gabapentin (start 300 mg TID, titrate per protocol) with provider
    • Arrange PT/OT consult — same-day, for early mobilization, orthotics prescription, functional assessment, safety plan
    • Patient/family education: explain most positioning injuries recover completely over 3–6 months; recovery is gradual; orthotics and therapy prevent contractures while nerves heal; no magic treatment but compliance with PT/OT dramatically improves outcome

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(New neuro deficit + hypotension, respiratory distress, signs of shock, OR facial droop/arm+leg weakness together.)

  1. STAT call APP/fellow + charge RN — do NOT leave the room alone

  2. If new facial droop + arm or leg weakness together:

    • ACTIVATE STROKE CODE IMMEDIATELY — this is NOT peripheral nerve injury
    • CT/CTA stat per stroke protocol
    • Notify CT surgery + neurology
    • This takes precedence over all other actions

  3. If phrenic injury with respiratory decompensation:

    • Elevate head-of-bed
    • Increase FiO₂, prepare for intubation/ICU transfer
    • Place on continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring
    • Stat ABG, CXR
    • Contact CT surgery immediately — may need ICU-level care or mechanical ventilation

  4. If brachial plexus with arm swelling + pain + cool limb (compartment syndrome / vascular compromise):

    • Elevate arm
    • Continuous monitoring
    • Stat ultrasound or CT for vascular patency
    • Prepare for possible emergent surgical decompression
    • Notify CT surgery + consider vascular surgery consult

  5. Document findings, time of onset, progression, vital signs trajectory

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed new [motor/sensory] deficit: [specific finding, e.g., 'cannot extend right wrist, sensation intact,' 'foot drop left side, patient drags foot when ambulating']. Baseline neuro was [intact/prior deficit]. Deficit first noted [time, what prompted discovery]." A: "Patient is currently [stable / unstable]. [Symptoms: pain/tingling/weakness distribution]. [Medications on board: pain control, any neuro meds]. [Functional impact: can/cannot ambulate safely, ADL affected]." R: "Requesting evaluation for peripheral nerve injury, imaging plan, PT/OT consult, safety precautions, and management plan."

Who to call

Situation Contact
New focal peripheral nerve finding, stable Primary APP / on-call fellow
Foot drop / peroneal injury APP + PT same-day for AFO referral + gait training
Hoarseness post-arch or LIMA surgery APP + ENT for laryngoscopy + Speech-Language Pathology for swallow eval
Elevated hemidiaphragm on CXR APP + consider fluoroscopy / ultrasound sniff test to confirm phrenic paralysis
New wrist drop or hand weakness APP + OT same-day for orthosis + positioning
Arm swelling + weakness + pain (compartment syndrome or vascular concern) APP/fellow + CT surgery + consider vascular surgery
New facial droop, arm/leg weakness together, speech change, gaze deviation STROKE CODE immediately + neurology + CT surgery
Bilateral phrenic paralysis (both hemidiaphragms elevated) STAT CT surgery; patient may require mechanical ventilation
Bilateral RLN injury (hoarseness bilateral, stridor, airway concern) STAT CT surgery + anesthesia for airway management

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections marked — collapsed by default.

sections.heading: 7.1 Nerve anatomy in cardiac surgery
sections.bodyHtml:
Understanding where and how nerves are at risk during cardiac procedures guides recognition and prevention:

Brachial Plexus (C5–C6 upper trunk — most common injury):

  • Formed by C5 and C6 nerve roots; passes through the thoracic outlet behind the clavicle
  • During median sternotomy and sternal retraction, the plexus is pulled caudally and medially
  • Risk factors: prolonged CPB, aggressive sternal retraction without padding, arm abduction >90°, patient positioning with arm hyperabducted
  • Presentation: shoulder abduction weakness (supraspinatus/deltoid C5), external rotation weakness, lateral arm paresthesias (C5–C6 distribution)
  • Prognosis: 70–80% recover completely within 3–6 months

Ulnar Nerve (C8–T1 most distal, enters hand):

  • Travels medially down arm, passes posterior to medial epicondyle of humerus (cubital tunnel)
  • On operating table, elbow is at risk if compressed against table edge or inadequately padded
  • Risk factors: prolonged flexion at elbow >90°, lack of padding, pressure from table edge, position on table during long cases
  • Presentation: weakness of intrinsic hand muscles (finger spreading, intrinsic hand strength), 4th–5th finger paresthesias or numbness
  • Most preventable injury — simple elbow padding + positioning (flexion <90°) during surgery
  • Prognosis: excellent if recognized early and handled appropriately

Phrenic Nerve (C3–C5 roots; travels along IMA — internal mammary artery):

  • Descends through anterior chest wall, innervates diaphragm
  • Risk factors: CPB hypothermia (cold phrenic nerve injury), direct injury during LIMA harvest, retraction during aortic arch work
  • Left phrenic more vulnerable — LIMA is harvested from left internal thoracic artery, and left aortic arch surgery risks left phrenic
  • Presentation: elevated hemidiaphragm on CXR, dyspnea with exertion, increased work of breathing, hypoxia in patients with marginal pulmonary reserve
  • Prognosis: most improve spontaneously over 6–12 months; rarely requires diaphragm plication

Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve (RLN — branch of vagus; C9 nuclei innervate vocal cords):

  • Loops around aortic arch on the left; ascends along trachea on the right
  • Risk factors: retraction during aortic arch surgery, aortic cross-clamp, LIMA harvest near arch, TEE probe position
  • Presentation: hoarseness, weak voice, difficulty phonating high tones, aspiration risk if bilateral
  • Commonly confused with: post-extubation sore throat (RLN injury = hoarseness from vocal cord dysfunction, not sore throat)
  • Prognosis: partial injuries usually recover 3–6 months; complete bilateral injury is rare but catastrophic (airway crisis)

Common Peroneal Nerve (L4–S1; wraps around fibular head):

  • Branches from sciatic nerve, wraps around lateral fibular head
  • Risk factors: leg positioning with external rotation, lateral knee pressure during prolonged surgery, leg positioning devices
  • Presentation: foot drop (inability to dorsiflex foot), steppage gait, numbness dorsum foot + lateral calf, patient drags foot
  • Safety crisis: high fall risk post-op when patient first mobilizes; foot drag without AFO = likely fall in early recovery
  • Prognosis: good if recognized early and AFO provided; poor if delayed and patient falls

Saphenous Nerve (L3–L4; travels with greater saphenous vein):

  • Runs superficially along medial lower leg with the saphenous vein
  • Risk factors: saphenous vein graft (SVG) harvest during CABG; nerve is stretched or divided during harvest
  • Presentation: numbness or neuralgia along medial calf and medial foot; not motor but bothersome sensory complaint
  • Prognosis: usually resolves; causes patient distress but not functional loss

sections.heading: 7.2 Mechanism: compression, traction, and stretch
sections.bodyHtml:
Neuropraxia (conduction block — myelin swelling):

  • Occurs with compression or mild traction that doesn't disrupt axons
  • Swelling of myelin sheath blocks saltatory conduction
  • Recovery is rapid — days to weeks — as swelling resolves and nerve conduction resumes
  • EMG at 4–6 weeks shows normal motor units (no fibrillations)
  • Example: ulnar nerve compressed at elbow against table; once padding is applied and position changed, myelin swelling resolves within days

Axonotmesis (axonal disruption — intact connective tissue):

  • Axons are damaged but epineurium and perineurium (supporting tissue) remains intact
  • Requires axonal regeneration at ~1 mm/day (slower than you might expect)
  • Wallerian degeneration (distal axon dies) takes 7–10 days; EMG not informative until 3–4 weeks
  • At 4–6 weeks post-op, EMG shows denervation (fibrillations, positive sharp waves) confirming axonotmesis
  • Recovery takes weeks to months depending on distance from injury to target muscle
  • Example: brachial plexus traction during aggressive sternal retraction; fibrillations on EMG at 4–6 weeks

Neurotmesis (complete transection — connective tissue disrupted):

  • Entire nerve is severed; surgical repair may be needed if recognized intraoperatively
  • Recovery is highly variable depending on repair timing (acute vs delayed) and ischemia
  • Often incomplete; motor recovery usually better than sensory
  • Not common in modern cardiac surgery with careful technique

sections.heading: 7.3 Diagnostic testing: EMG/NCS timing
sections.bodyHtml:
Critical pearl: EMG at 3–6 weeks post-op is too early for neuropraxia but perfect for axonotmesis.

  • Why early EMG (POD 7–14) is unhelpful: Wallerian degeneration hasn't completed yet. Distal fibrillations (denervation potentials) take 7–10 days to appear. Provider ordered "early EMG" often frustrates clinicians because it looks normal even if axonotmesis is present.

  • 4–6 week EMG is gold standard:

  • Neuropraxia: motor units look normal; no fibrillations; conduction block pattern (slow conduction across lesion site)
  • Axonotmesis: fibrillations and positive sharp waves (denervation); motor unit recruitment decreased; conduction slowing

  • Helps stratify prognosis: neuropraxia recovers 3–6 weeks; axonotmesis takes 3–6 months

  • Serial EMG at 4, 8, 12 weeks: tracks reinnervation (motor units return, fibrillations gradually resolve). Shows recovery trajectory.

  • When to order EMG earlier (POD 10–14): if neurotmesis is suspected (no recovery at all, patient underwent surgical exploration), or if considering early surgical intervention.

sections.heading: 7.4 Conservative management: PT/OT role
sections.bodyHtml:
Early mobilization (POD 1–7):

  • Passive range of motion (PROM) to prevent contractures and stiffness
  • Positioning to prevent pressure sores and secondary nerve injury
  • Pain management to allow therapy participation
  • Patient education on realistic recovery timeline

Orthotic prescription (POD 1–7 ideally):

  • AFO (ankle-foot orthosis) for foot drop — maintains foot in neutral position, prevents inversion, allows safer ambulation, prevents contracture of plantar flexors
  • Wrist cock-up orthosis for radial nerve injury — maintains wrist in neutral/slight extension, prevents contracture of wrist extensors, facilitates hand use
  • Wear schedule: 24/7 initially; remove during therapy for strengthening; gradual weaning as strength returns

Active/active-assisted ROM (POD 7+):

  • Encourage patient to use affected limb despite weakness
  • Gravity-eliminated positions initially (e.g., arm on table for brachial plexus)
  • Progress to against-resistance once strength improves (typically weeks 4–6)

Functional training:

  • Gait training with AFO for foot drop
  • ADL modifications for hand weakness (dressing, grooming, eating adaptations)
  • Safety education (fall precautions, proper footwear, home hazards)

Prognosis communication (critical for compliance):

  • "Most positioning injuries recover completely over 3–6 months."
  • "Recovery is gradual; expect slow improvement. It won't be overnight."
  • "Your therapy and orthotics now prevent contractures while nerves heal. This is essential."
  • "At 3–4 months, most patients regain most or all function."

sections.heading: 7.5 Pain management: neuropathic vs surgical
sections.bodyHtml:
Neuropathic pain characteristics:

  • Burning, tingling, shooting, electrical sensation
  • Occurs in denervated distribution (e.g., 4th–5th fingers for ulnar)
  • Peaks 2–3 weeks post-op, then gradually improves with recovery
  • Not responsive to NSAIDs or opioids alone

First-line: Gabapentin (Neurontin)

  • Start 300 mg TID (three times daily)
  • Titrate up by 300 mg/day every 3 days per tolerance
  • Target dose typically 900–1800 mg/day divided TID
  • Monitor for dizziness, somnolence; slow titration in elderly
  • Taper as pain resolves (don't stop abruptly)

Alternative: Pregabalin (Lyrica)

  • Start 75 mg BID
  • Titrate per protocol; similar mechanism to gabapentin
  • Use if gabapentin not tolerated

Avoid NSAIDs in acute denervation — concern for ongoing ischemia; use acetaminophen for other post-op pain

Opioids second-line — inadequate for neuropathic pain alone; use only if gabapentin insufficient for somatic surgical pain

sections.heading: 7.6 Seddon and Sunderland classification
sections.bodyHtml:
Seddon (1943) — three degrees:

  1. Neuropraxia: conduction block; myelin intact; recovery days–weeks
  2. Axonotmesis: axon disrupted; connective tissue intact; recovery weeks–months
  3. Neurotmesis: complete transection; recovery months–years (often incomplete)

Sunderland (1951) — five degrees — more detailed:

  1. First: isolated myelin disruption (conduction block) = Seddon's neuropraxia
  2. Second: axon disrupted, epineurium intact = Seddon's axonotmesis
  3. Third: axon + endoneurium disrupted, perineurium intact = Seddon's axonotmesis
  4. Fourth: axon + endoneurium + perineurium disrupted, epineurium intact = severe axonotmesis / neurotmesis
  5. Fifth: complete transection = Seddon's neurotmesis

Clinical use: EMG/NCS can suggest degree (Seddon) and help predict recovery timeline. Exact classification often requires imaging or surgical exploration.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in patients with known or suspected nerve injury; any show → re-escalate.

  • Expanding deficit: weakness spreads to adjacent muscles or opposite limb — suggests evolving stroke (UMN pattern), expanding nerve injury, or expanding hematoma; escalate immediately
  • Facial droop appearing or worsening: immediately re-evaluate for stroke; activate stroke code if not already
  • Progressive sensory loss: spreading numbness, pain worsening daily, crossing midline — may signal ongoing compression, ischemia, or stroke
  • Arm swelling + weakness + pain + cool limb: possible compartment syndrome, vascular compromise, or expanding hematoma; check cap refill, measure arm circumference, escalate urgently
  • Foot drop worsening rapidly: may be converting from neuropraxia to axonotmesis, or new compartment syndrome; recheck positioning, assess for DVT
  • Hoarseness + dysphagia + aspiration events: RLN injury complication; high aspiration risk; escalate to ENT + Speech-Language Pathology for swallow eval
  • Dyspnea + elevated hemidiaphragm + hypoxia despite supplemental O₂: phrenic injury with respiratory decompensation; prepare for ICU transfer or mechanical ventilation
  • Pain out of proportion to injury: neuropathic pain is expected but severe/escalating pain may signal ischemia, developing complication, or compartment syndrome
  • No improvement by 4–6 weeks post-op: neuropraxia usually shows some improvement by this point; lack of improvement suggests axonotmesis → obtain EMG/NCS if not yet ordered
  • Patient safety event: fall with foot drop, near-miss, functional decline unexpected for degree of motor deficit — reassess mobility aids, PT/OT intensity, home safety
  • Swelling, warmth, or skin changes at site (arm, hand, leg): DVT, infection, or compartment syndrome risk; check pulses, obtain ultrasound if concern

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. "New focal neuro = stroke until proven otherwise." This is the critical safety pearl. Facial droop, arm + leg weakness together, speech change, gaze deviation = activate stroke code immediately. Peripheral nerve injury presents with weakness in a single nerve distribution and facial strength intact. Do not assume it's positioning injury without excluding stroke first.

  2. Brachial plexus injury is the most common positioning injury in cardiac surgery. C5–C6 upper trunk injury results from sternal retraction pulling plexus caudally and arm abduction >90°. Presents as shoulder abduction weakness + lateral arm paresthesias. Nursing implication: ensure adequate shoulder padding and monitor positioning during long cases (if in OR role). Most neuropraxia recovers 3–6 months, but patient panic is high ("will I lose my arm?"). Early education prevents catastrophizing.

  3. Ulnar nerve injury is the most preventable. Elbow compression on table is the culprit. Simple elbow padding and positioning (elbow flexion <90°) during long procedures prevents injury. Check nursing notes for any mention of elbow pressure or positioning concerns intraoperatively; use for prevention education. If ulnar injury occurs, prognosis is excellent with early intervention.

  4. Foot drop has enormous safety implications — immediate fall risk. Patient is just mobilizing post-op when weakness first noticed. AFO referral must be same-day, not scheduled for next week. Teach steppage gait immediately. One fall → hip fracture → pneumonia → death pathway. This is not optional.

  5. Radial nerve (wrist drop) is often missed initially. Patient may not notice weakness while intubated. First recognized when trying to move arm post-extubation or when hand hangs down at rest. Wrist cock-up orthosis prevents contracture (intrinsic hand muscle shortening) and restores functional hand position for eating, writing, self-care. Prescribe early.

  6. RLN injury = hoarseness + aspiration risk. Do NOT confuse with post-intubation sore throat. Post-aortic arch surgery hoarseness is not "intubation trauma" — get ENT laryngoscopy to confirm vocal cord position and mobility. Swallow eval mandatory before advancing diet. Bilateral RLN injury is rare but severe (stridor, airway crisis). Document voice quality as baseline; trend it.

  7. Phrenic nerve injury on CXR = elevated hemidiaphragm on the affected side. Measure and compare hemidiaphragm heights. Patients often tolerate unilateral phrenic palsy well at rest, but dyspnea with activity is expected. Sniff test (fluoroscopy or ultrasound) confirms paradoxical diaphragm motion on the injured side. Most resolve spontaneously without intervention; very few need diaphragm plication. Educate patient: "Your diaphragm isn't moving on this side, so you'll work harder breathing, especially with exertion. It will gradually improve over months."

  8. The 4–6 week EMG is the key diagnostic tool — don't order it too early. Early EMG (POD 7–14) is unhelpful; axonal degeneration takes 7–10 days before fibrillations appear. At 4–6 weeks, EMG shows fibrillations (ongoing denervation) if axonotmesis, or minimal findings if pure neuropraxia. This guides prognosis and intensity of rehab. Communicate timeline to patient: "We'll do an electrical test at 4–6 weeks to see how severely the nerve was injured. That result tells us recovery expectations."

  9. Neuropraxia typically recovers by 3–6 months, but axonotmesis takes 6–12+ months. Serial exams every 2–4 weeks track improvement trajectory. A patient with no improvement at 8 weeks post-op but EMG at 6 weeks showing early reinnervation may recover fully by 4–5 months. Setting correct expectations prevents patient loss to follow-up and improves compliance with therapy.

  10. Gabapentin for neuropathic pain; start 300 mg TID, titrate slowly. Acute neuropathic pain post-op is expected and severe — shooting, burning in denervated distribution. Gabapentin is first-line; NSAIDs ineffective. Start early and titrate q3 days by 300 mg increments. Pain usually plateaus at 4–6 weeks then gradually improves with nerve recovery. Taper as pain resolves; don't stop abruptly.

  11. Orthotics prevent contracture and enable function. AFO for foot drop maintains dorsiflexion angle while muscles recover; wrist cock-up keeps wrist extended, preventing intrinsic hand muscle shortening. Remove during PT sessions for active strengthening, but use 24/7 initially. Contractures are permanent and devastating; orthotics prevent this. Patient compliance requires education: "This brace is temporary; it prevents your muscles from shortening while nerves heal."

  12. PT/OT consult same-day for any motor deficit. Early mobilization, passive ROM, positioning prevent complications (contractures, DVT, deconditioning). OT crucial for hand/arm weakness; PT for lower extremity. Both teach compensatory strategies and realistic timeline. Document OT/PT plan in chart.

  13. Document baseline exam early post-op (PACU if possible). Serial exams without a baseline are useless for tracking trajectory. "Patient has foot drop" — compared to what? Get pre-op exam + PACU exam documented. Then track: POD 1, POD 3, POD 7, then weekly until discharge.

  14. Patient education on recovery timeline prevents panic and improves compliance. "Most nerve injuries from positioning recover completely over 3–6 months. Your recovery will be gradual; expect slow improvement. Orthotics and therapy now will help prevent contractures while nerves heal." Repeat this message; it profoundly reduces patient anxiety and improves PT/OT adherence.

  15. Bilateral phrenic or bilateral RLN injury is rare but catastrophic. Bilateral phrenic paralysis = vent dependence (can't wean). Bilateral RLN = stridor and airway crisis. If either occurs, contact CT surgery STAT for ICU-level care and possible mechanical ventilation. Document both hemidiaphragms and voice quality each shift if any concern.

cards.title: Pneumothorax Post-Chest Tube Removal
cards.quickAnswer: Post-chest tube removal PTX: expect small asymptomatic apical cap on routine 2–4 hour CXR (common, managed conservatively). Tension PTX is a clinical diagnosis — hypotension, jugular venous distension, tracheal deviation, and absent unilateral breath sounds demand immediate needle decompression with 14–16G angiocath at 2nd intercostal space midclavicular line or 4th–5th ICS midaxillary line *before* awaiting imaging. Follow with STAT chest tube reinsertion. Subcutaneous emphysema signals air leak but is not itself an emergency; expanding emphysema predicts worsening PTX.
