sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — definition, epidemiology, who this applies to.

  • Definition: Air in the pleural space occurring after removal of a chest tube, leading to lung collapse, decreased ventilation, and potential hemodynamic compromise (tension physiology).
  • Mechanism of onset: Air entry during tube removal (inadequate Valsalva), expansion of residual pre-existing small PTX, or spontaneous rupture along surgical-trauma zones post-sternotomy.
  • Incidence: ~5% of cardiac surgery patients develop post-CT removal PTX; most are asymptomatic and discovered on routine 2–4 hour post-removal CXR. Tension physiology occurs in ~0.5% and is immediately life-threatening.
  • Who this applies to: all adult post-operative patients (cardiac and other thoracic surgery) with chest tube removal over the past 72 hours.
  • When it matters: ICU through step-down unit care. Most cases present within 6 hours of removal; delayed presentation possible if PTX was small and patient activity or coughing increases size.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Why pneumothorax develops post-chest tube removal Mechanism 1: Air entry during tube removal
  • Most common. During removal, the visceral pleura must be sealed. If the patient does not maintain a tight Valsalva maneuver or takes a breath during withdrawal, negative intrathoracic pressure creates suction, drawing air in along the tract left by the tube.
  • Prevention is Valsalva discipline: forced expiration against a closed glottis from the moment tube withdrawal begins until dressing is fully applied. Mechanism 2: Pre-existing small PTX expansion
  • A small PTX may have been present from the original surgery or from an incidental pleural violation.
  • As patient mobilizes, coughs, splints, or exercises post-removal, PTX expands.
  • Often asymptomatic until the PTX reaches moderate size (>20%). Mechanism 3: Spontaneous PTX post-sternotomy
  • Air dissects along mediastinal and pleural planes within the first 3–5 days post-op.
  • Can occur even without an active chest tube or after removal.
  • Associated with ischemic pleural leaks or air trapping from surgical trauma to lung parenchyma.
  • Higher risk with bilateral pleural involvement (e.g., bilateral internal mammary artery harvest). Mechanism 4: Tension PTX
  • Develops when the air leak acts as a one-way valve: air enters the pleural space with each breath but cannot exit.
  • Positive pleural pressure compresses the lung, displaces the mediastinum, and impairs venous return to the heart.
  • Results in cardiovascular collapse within minutes if not decompressed (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025).
Post-sternotomy pleural physiology
  • Sternotomy opens the mediastinum, creating potential spaces for air dissection.
  • Pleural openings are intentional (for LIMA access) or unintentional (traumatic mobilization of lung/pleura).
  • Apical chest tubes drain air preferentially; their removal leaves a direct tract to the pleural space.
  • Post-op coughing and Valsalva — pain limits deep breathing, but even with splinting, pressure swings can expand PTX.
  • Subcutaneous emphysema often precedes frank PTX, signaling that air is tracking along fascial planes and may enter the pleural space next.
  • Cardiac post-op patients have heightened hemodynamic sensitivity: even a small PTX can precipitate instability faster than in healthy patients.
Chest tube anatomy and function In cardiac post-op patients, multiple chest tubes drain different compartments:
  • Apical tube (2nd–4th ICS, midclavicular or anterior) — drains air preferentially (PTX management); removal creates the highest re-entry risk.
  • Basilar tube (4th–6th ICS, midaxillary line) — drains serous fluid (pleural effusion, blood).
  • Mediastinal tube — drains mediastinal blood (separate from pleural tubes). Clinical pearl: After apical tube removal, air accumulation risk is highest because that tube was actively keeping the apical pleural space empty. Small amounts of residual air trapped during removal or post-removal are now sealed in.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Symptomatic presentation (Any of the following):

  • Acute dyspnea or tachypnea — sudden onset, progressive, at rest or with activity
  • Chest pain — pleuritic, sharp, worsening with inspiration; may refer to shoulder
  • Desaturation — SpO₂ drop ≥3–5% from baseline, despite supplemental O₂
  • Decreased or absent breath sounds unilaterally — on the side of the removed tube
  • Tachycardia and/or hypotension — especially when paired with dyspnea
  • Subcutaneous emphysema — palpable crepitus around incision site or tracking distally
  • Mental status change, agitation, confusion — from hypoxia and hypercapnia
  • Classic tension PTX triad: hypotension + jugular venous distension + tracheal deviation, with absence of unilateral breath sounds

Asymptomatic presentation:

  • Routine post-removal CXR at 2–4 hours reveals small apical PTX; patient reports no symptoms.
  • Incidence ~5% of cardiac surgery patients (MacDuff et al., 2010).

Epidemiology: Presentation typically within 6 hours of removal, but can be delayed if PTX was small and activity or coughing precipitates expansion.

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Pure information gathering. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs: HR, BP, SpO₂, RR, temperature, capillary refill, skin perfusion
  • Respiratory exam: bilateral breath sounds comparison; note any asymmetry (diminished vs absent on one side)
  • Cardiovascular exam: JVD assessment (normal, distended?); tracheal position (midline vs deviated away from lesion side?)
  • Symptoms: dyspnea severity, chest pain location and radiation, syncope, palpitations
  • Incision exam: crepitus around sternotomy or chest tube site? expanding distally? localized or diffuse?
  • Recent history: which side was tube placed? when was it removed? difficulties during removal (resistance, air escape observed)?
  • Recent labs: most recent ABG (if available), baseline SpO₂ trend, lactate
  • MAR: anticoagulation status (relevant for chest tube reinsertion)?
  • Activity since removal: did patient cough hard, Valsalva, strain, or mobilize soon after removal?
  • Prior imaging: baseline CXR from admission or post-op day (POD) 0?

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake and alert, MAP > 65 mmHg, dyspnea present but not severe, diminished breath sounds but present, no hemodynamic instability.)

  1. Place on high-flow O₂ immediately — non-rebreather mask 15 L/min or escalate nasal cannula; target SpO₂ > 94%.
  2. Obtain STAT portable CXR — upright preferred to show PTX size, location, and any mediastinal shift. Do NOT delay imaging if clinical suspicion is high; obtain STAT while notifying team simultaneously.
  3. Establish / verify large-bore IV access — at least 18G; two lines preferred in case urgent intervention needed.
  4. Notify APP / on-call fellow STAT — provide SBAR (see Section 6).
  5. Keep patient NPO — chest tube reinsertion may require procedural sedation or anesthesia.
  6. Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring — watch trajectory every 5–10 minutes; escalate if vitals trend down.
  7. Place emergency airway equipment at bedside — oral airway, ambu bag, suction ready.
  8. Reassess breath sounds and vital signs q5–10min — document whether PTX appears stable or expanding.

If CXR confirms small, stable, asymptomatic PTX (<20% or small apical cap):

  • Continue high-flow O₂ (nitrogen washout accelerates resorption); avoid room air.
  • Observe with repeat CXR in 6–12 hours; most small PTX resorb spontaneously over 24–48 hours.
  • Restrict activity; no exertion for 24–48 hours; avoid incentive spirometry (increases intrapleural pressure and worsens air leak).
  • Educate patient: report dyspnea, chest pain, or worsening symptoms immediately.
  • Monitor for red flags (Section 8); escalate if any appear.

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension, severe dyspnea, absent breath sounds on one side, signs of tension physiology: JVD, tracheal deviation, altered mental status, hemodynamic instability.)

  1. STAT CALL: APP/fellow + charge RN + respiratory — do NOT leave patient alone.
  2. Activate Rapid Response or Code Blue if not already present; alert operating room/interventional radiology for possible bedside intervention.
  3. Place on 100% O₂ immediately — non-rebreather mask; prepare for intubation.
  4. Establish / confirm large-bore IV access — two 18G minimum; blood available stat.
  5. Prepare for EMERGENT needle decompression — do NOT wait for CXR confirmation; tension PTX is a clinical diagnosis. (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020)
    • Landmark 1 (preferred): 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line. Insert 14–16G over-the-needle angiocath perpendicular to chest wall, aiming just above the 3rd rib. Listen for air rush/hiss.
    • Landmark 2 (backup): 4th–5th intercostal space, midaxillary line. If anterior anatomy is obscured or first attempt fails, use this approach.
    • Catheter placement: advance catheter over needle, remove needle, leave plastic catheter in place; secure with tape or suture.
    • Equipment needed: 14–16G angiocath (NOT small needle), 10 mL syringe (optional, for aspiration), Tegaderm dressing. Some units have 7–8 Fr pigtail kit as follow-up.
    • After needle decompression: listen for air rush; reassess breath sounds bilaterally, BP, HR immediately. Expect rapid hemodynamic improvement if tension was present.
    • Arrange URGENT chest tube reinsertion at bedside — this is definitive management. Needle decompression buys time only.
    • Coordinate with APP, respiratory, anesthesia simultaneously.
    • May require procedural sedation per institutional policy (coordinate with anesthesia).
    • Sterile field, large-bore tube (28–32 Fr apical or basilar), suction or water-seal drainage system (avoid Heimlich valve in unstable settings).
    • Obtain STAT portable CXR and ultrasound — confirms PTX size, mediastinal shift, guides reinsertion; rule out bilateral PTX.
    • Draw STAT labs: ABG, CBC, type & screen (in case transfusion needed).
    • Prepare for intubation — if no rapid improvement in mental status, oxygenation, or if second needle decompression attempt fails. Document all attempts.

Special consideration: If patient becomes unresponsive with no palpable pulse, needle decompression is a BLS/ACLS intervention (AHA, 2023) and does NOT require waiting for provider order, imaging, or procedural sedation approval.

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] on [unit], calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]. Chest tube was removed [hours] ago." B: "Patient developed [acute dyspnea / chest pain / desaturation] at [time]. HR [value], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]% on [O₂ delivery], RR [value]. Breath sounds [diminished / absent on RIGHT/LEFT side]. [Any tracheal deviation or JVD?]" A: "CXR shows [PTX size estimate, e.g., small apical cap, ~20% PTX, or signs of tension — mediastinal shift]. Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Current symptoms]." R: "Requesting [orders for observation vs. chest tube reinsertion / needle decompression / transfer to ICU / OR standby]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Small asymptomatic PTX on routine post-removal CXR APP / on-call fellow (likely observe with repeat CXR in 6–12 h)
Moderate PTX with symptoms (dyspnea, desaturation) or enlarging APP/fellow + respiratory therapy; prepare for chest tube reinsertion
Tension PTX or hemodynamic compromise STAT call: APP/fellow + charge RN + CT surgery + RRT/code team
Bilateral PTX STAT call: CT surgery + ICU consult; plan for bilateral chest tubes or urgent airway management
PTX + ongoing anticoagulation CT surgery — do NOT hold AC without team discussion; assess bleeding vs air leak risk
Needle decompression attempted, second attempt needed or failed STAT escalation: anesthesia standby for intubation; OR notification for possible formal intervention

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. Subsections below are — collapsed by default on initial view.

Post-op pleural physiology detail Why sternotomy patients are high-risk for post-CT PTX:
  • Sternotomy deliberately opens the mediastinal space, creating potential pathways for air dissection.
  • Pleural openings occur during access (e.g., for left internal mammary artery harvest) or from blunt trauma during heart mobilization.
  • The apical chest tube keeps that space decompressed; removal eliminates active suction, leaving residual air and a direct tract.
  • Post-op coughing and Valsalva maneuvers (pain splinting limits deep breathing, but patients still cough reflexively) generate pressure swings that promote air trapping.
  • Subcutaneous emphysema precedes frank PTX — air tracks along fascial planes before breaching the pleura. Hemodynamic sensitivity in post-op cardiac patients:
  • Even a small PTX reduces venous return more profoundly in already-stressed hearts (reduced contractility, altered compliance from pericardial effusion or inflammation).
  • Tension physiology can develop from smaller PTX volumes in cardiac patients than in healthy individuals.
CXR interpretation for pneumothorax Findings to recognize:
  • Apical cap or small PTX: thin line of lucency at the lung apex; may be subtle on supine films.
  • Larger PTX: visible lung edge pulled away from chest wall; increased lucency in pleural space.
  • Tension PTX signs: mediastinal shift (heart and trachea deviated away from PTX side), flattened hemidiaphragm on PTX side, compression of contralateral lung.
  • Deep sulcus sign (on supine film): hyperlucent costophrenic angle (often seen on portable supine CXR, easy to miss); indicates PTX.
  • Bilateral PTX: lucency on both sides; often subtler; always examine both hemithoraces carefully. Why CXR alone is not sufficient in tension physiology: Tension PTX is a clinical diagnosis. Patients with hypotension, JVD, tracheal deviation, and absent breath sounds require needle decompression before waiting for imaging. Imaging may not be immediately available in unstable settings.
Needle decompression landmarks and technique Anterior (2nd ICS midclavicular) approach — preferred:
  • Palpate the clavicle; the space below it is the 1st ICS.
  • Count down to the 2nd ICS.
  • Mark the midclavicular line (vertical line through the center of the clavicle).
  • Insert 14–16G angiocath perpendicular to the chest wall, aiming just above the 3rd rib (to avoid the intercostal vessels running along the inferior rib border).
  • Advance needle through skin, muscle, and fascial layers until air rushes out or syringe plunger retracts (if using syringe for confirmation).
  • Thread catheter over needle, remove needle, secure catheter with tape or suture. Lateral (4th–5th ICS midaxillary) approach — backup:
  • Identify the midaxillary line (vertical line at the level of the anterior axillary fold).
  • Palpate ribs at the midaxillary line; count to find the 4th or 5th ICS.
  • Insert angiocath perpendicular to chest wall, aiming just above the lower rib (same principle as anterior approach).
  • Technique otherwise identical to anterior approach. Common errors:
  • Too deep or at wrong angle: catheter enters intercostal muscle; no air escape or poor decompression.
  • Hitting bone: aim high in the intercostal space (just above the lower rib) to avoid ribs.
  • Leaving needle in place: must remove needle and leave catheter; needle alone provides no sustained decompression.
  • Wrong landmarks: 1st ICS is small; verify 2nd ICS by palpating clavicle and counting down.
Chest tube reinsertion indications and considerations Indications for reinsertion (either acute or elective):
  • Symptomatic PTX (dyspnea, desaturation, pain).
  • PTX > 20% in size.
  • Expanding PTX on serial CXR.
  • Tension PTX (after needle decompression).
  • Any PTX that fails to resorb within 48–72 hours despite high-flow O₂. Tube size and position:
  • Apical tube (2nd–4th ICS, anterior or midclavicular): drains air; preferred size 24–28 Fr.
  • Basilar tube (4th–6th ICS, midaxillary): drains fluid if concurrent effusion; size 28–32 Fr.
  • Many bedside reinsertions use a single apical tube; bilateral tubes needed only if bilateral PTX. Drainage system choice:
  • Closed-drainage system (water-seal or suction): preferred in unstable patients or active air leak; allows monitoring of air-leak volume and trend.
  • Heimlich valve (one-way flutter valve): useful for transport or if patient is very stable; less ideal in unstable settings because no visual confirmation of air evacuation. Procedural considerations:
  • Reinsertion may require procedural sedation or general anesthesia per institutional policy.
  • Coordinate with anesthesia, respiratory, and APP simultaneously in unstable settings; do NOT wait for OR availability if patient is deteriorating.
  • Local anesthetic + sedation (e.g., fentanyl 1 mcg/kg IV, midazolam 0.05 mg/kg IV) often sufficient for stable patients at bedside.
  • Some institutions require full OR turnover; know your local policy in advance.
Subcutaneous emphysema — when is it an emergency?
  • Definition: Air in subcutaneous/fascial tissues, appearing as crepitus on palpation.
  • Cause: air leak from pleural space tracking along fascial planes.
  • Is it an emergency? Not by itself. However, expanding or rapidly spreading SQ air is a red flag — it signals ongoing air leak and often precedes frank PTX by hours.
  • Red flag scenarios: SQ emphysema advancing into the neck or face (suggests higher tracheal/upper mediastinal leak, risk of airway compromise), rapidly expanding (indicates high-volume leak).
  • Reassurance for stable cases: localized, stable SQ air around incision site is common and usually self-limited; resorbs in days as incisions seal.
  • Management: high-flow O₂ accelerates nitrogen washout and decreases pressure gradient driving air into tissues. Avoid tight dressings or occlusive tape that traps air.
Incentive spirometry and post-op PTX
  • Avoid aggressive incentive spirometry in any patient with known or suspected PTX — the deep inspiratory maneuver increases intrapleural negative pressure, worsens air leak, and promotes PTX expansion.
  • Why some nurses insist: post-op atelectasis is a real concern; early mobilization and coughing are important for preventing pneumonia.
  • Balance: if PTX is suspected, confirm with imaging first. If PTX is confirmed, restrict IS until PTX is resolving or tube is in place.
  • Alternative strategies: gentle coughing, early ambulation, position changes, and pain control (facilitates deep breathing without equipment) are safer.

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. These appear in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate immediately.

  • Dyspnea worsening despite high-flow O₂ — PTX expanding or tension developing; escalate.
  • SpO₂ trending down even on 100% O₂ — large PTX or air leak overwhelming absorption; escalate.
  • Unilateral breath sounds shifting from diminished to completely absent — ominous sign; may signal tension developing.
  • Tachycardia and hypotension appearing together — hemodynamic compensation failing; tension physiology imminent.
  • Jugular venous distension appearing or worsening — classic for tension PTX; escalate immediately.
  • Trachea palpably deviated away from PTX side — tension signature; this is an emergency.
  • Agitation, confusion, restlessness — subtle mental status changes often precede frank hemodynamic instability.
  • Subcutaneous emphysema expanding rapidly or advancing into neck/face — air leak increasing; PTX likely worsening; risk of airway compromise.
  • New or expanding chest pain with shoulder radiation — referred diaphragmatic irritation often indicates growing PTX.
  • Accessory muscle use, tripoding, inability to lie flat — respiratory distress escalating; re-escalate.
  • If patient is intubated: tube malposition or migration into mainstem bronchus can mimic absent breath sounds on one side; coordinate with respiratory therapy and imaging to differentiate from PTX.

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Small apical PTX is extremely common post-CT removal (~5% of cases) and is usually discovered on routine 2–4 hour CXR, not because patient is symptomatic. Do NOT panic. Most resorb spontaneously with high-flow O₂ and observation. Serial CXR confirms stability or allows early intervention if enlarging.

  2. Tension PTX is a CLINICAL diagnosis, not a radiologic one. Do NOT wait for CXR confirmation if the patient shows hypotension + JVD + tracheal deviation + absent breath sounds. Decompress immediately. Imaging delays life-saving care. (Hardin & Kaplow, 2020)

  3. Know both needle decompression landmarks cold: 2nd ICS midclavicular (anterior, easiest, preferred) and 4th–5th ICS midaxillary (lateral, backup). Both approaches must place the catheter in muscle/fascia, NOT subcutaneous fat. Practice palpation during rounds; don't wait for an emergency to learn anatomy.

  4. Valsalva at tube removal is the single best prevention. Educate patient before removal: "I am going to ask you to bear down hard, as if you're straining to have a bowel movement, and hold your breath while I pull the tube out. This is critical — do NOT breathe in." Some nurses coach patients with "one, two, three, PUSH" to coordinate the maneuver.

  5. Bilateral PTX is rare but lethal if missed. If your patient has bilateral pleural involvement (e.g., bilateral internal mammary artery harvest, bilateral chest tubes placed), scrutinize both hemithoraces on CXR. Bilateral breath sound absence or bilateral lucency demands immediate escalation.

  6. Subcutaneous emphysema itself is not an emergency, but expanding SQ air is a red flag. Mark the borders of localized crepitus with a pen on the skin; if it advances on next check, PTX is likely expanding. High-flow O₂ and close observation. Expanding or neck-advancing SQ air merits re-escalation.

  7. Petrolatum gauze + 3-sided dressing if tube accidentally dislodges. Three sides allow air to escape (preventing tension accumulation) but keep infection risk lower than fully open wounds. Do not apply fully occlusive dressing immediately post-dislodgement; allow air to vent while monitoring for rapid accumulation.

  8. Apical tubes drain air best; basilar tubes for fluid. If only one tube was placed and PTX occurs post-removal, you'll likely need apical reinsertion. Know where your tubes were positioned before removal — ask the team or check the operative note.

  9. After apical tube removal, air accumulation risk is highest. That tube was actively keeping the apical space empty. Routine 2–4 hour post-removal CXR is standard-of-care in many units for this reason. Do NOT skip it.

  10. Anticoagulation complicates reinsertion. If patient is on IV heparin or has received intraoperative anticoagulation, inform the team before chest tube insertion — bleeding risk may warrant temporary hold or bridging strategy. Discuss with CT surgery before you touch a needle or scalpel.

  11. Incentive spirometry worsens air leak and PTX expansion. A patient with known or suspected PTX should avoid IS until imaging confirms absence of PTX or tube is in place. Gentle coughing, position changes, and early ambulation are safer alternatives for preventing atelectasis.

  12. One-way valve (Heimlich) consideration for transport: If PTX patient must be transported to OR or ICU before chest tube is in place, a one-way valve on a needle catheter can prevent tension while in transit. But closed-drainage system is preferred if time allows.

  13. Post-op cardiac patients have thin hemodynamic margins. Even a small PTX can tip a tenuous patient into instability faster than a healthy adult. Low threshold for aggressive management.

  14. Deep sulcus sign on supine CXR. Portable chest films are often supine. Look for hyperlucency in the costophrenic sulcus (bottom corner of the film) — this is the "deep sulcus sign" and indicates PTX that might be subtle on upright film. Coordinate with radiologist if unsure.

  15. Palpable crepitus around incisions is a physical finding to teach. Crepitus = air in tissues. Document its location and ask the patient if it's new or stable. Expanding crepitus is a red flag; do not ignore it.

cards.title: POAF
cards.quickAnswer: New irregular rhythm on telemetry in a post-op cardiac surgery patient → obtain a 12-lead to confirm AF, replace K⁺ ≥ 4.0 and Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0 per the Electrolyte Replacement protocol, and notify APP for rate vs rhythm plan. Unstable (hypotension, chest pain, altered mental status, pulmonary edema) → STAT call, pads on, prepare synchronized cardioversion per ACLS. Anticipate amiodarone hypotension (~25%) and decrease the drip early.

sections.heading: 1. Snapshot / What It Is
sections.bodyHtml:
Novice orientation — what this is and who gets it.

  • Definition: New-onset atrial fibrillation occurring after cardiac surgery. Irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, variable ventricular response.
  • Incidence: ~30% of CABG patients, ~40% of valve patients (Joglar et al., 2023). Peak onset post-operative day (POD) 2–3; can occur later.
  • Who this applies to: every adult post-operative cardiac surgery patient on telemetry. Highest yield from admission through POD 5–7.
  • Why it matters: most common rhythm event seen on post-op telemetry. Increases length of stay, stroke risk, and mortality if uncontrolled.

sections.heading: 2. Background / Pathophysiology
sections.bodyHtml:
Multifactorial origin — post-op POAF is the convergence of four physiologic pressures on an already-stressed atrium:

  • Atrial inflammation from cardiopulmonary bypass cannulation, pericardial irritation, and surgical manipulation near the atria
  • Sympathetic surge from post-op pain, volume shifts, and adrenergic stimulation
  • Beta-blocker withdrawal — holding home beta-blockers for perioperative hypotension is one of the most modifiable causes
  • Electrolyte depletion — diuresis pulls K⁺ and Mg²⁺ below the threshold for atrial stability

The POD 2–3 peak reflects the combined timing of maximum inflammatory response, fluid mobilization, and beta-blocker nadir (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025).

Risk factors: age > 70, prior AF, left atrial enlargement on pre-op echo, valvular surgery (higher than CABG alone), COPD, OSA, CPB > 180 min, home antiarrhythmic withdrawal.

sections.heading: 3. Trigger / Presentation
sections.bodyHtml:
Advanced beginner recognition — what the patient looks like at bedside.

Any of the following:

  • Telemetry alarm: irregular rhythm, HR often > 110
  • Patient reports palpitations, chest discomfort, fatigue, dyspnea, lightheadedness
  • Apical–radial pulse deficit on exam
  • New hypotension or altered mental status paired with an irregular rhythm

sections.heading: 4. Assessment — *observe / gather information* (2 minutes)
sections.bodyHtml:
Competent systematic bedside exam. No actions yet.

  • Vital signs: HR, BP, SpO₂, mental status, perfusion (capillary refill, skin temperature)
  • Symptoms: chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, syncope or near-syncope
  • Physical findings: apical–radial pulse deficit on palpation
  • Recent labs: K⁺, Mg²⁺, iCa²⁺; most recent hemoglobin and creatinine
  • MAR review: home rate-control or rhythm-control meds held? On amiodarone? Last beta-blocker dose? Anticoagulation status?
  • Lines and wires: epicardial pacing wires still in place? Arterial line? Adequate IV access?
  • Surgery context: what procedure and when? A MAZE patient in AF during the first 4 weeks is expected — direct-current cardioversion (DCCV) is usually ineffective until atrial scarring matures.

sections.heading: 5A. Stable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Awake, MAP > 65, no chest pain, perfusing.)

  1. Obtain 12-lead ECG STAT — confirm diagnosis (irregularly irregular, no P waves)
  2. Save rhythm strip at onset and document in chart
  3. Replace electrolytes per Protocol: Post-Op Cardiac Surgery Electrolyte Replacement — target K⁺ ≥ 4.0, Mg²⁺ ≥ 2.0, iCa²⁺ ≥ 1.1
  4. Address reversible triggers: treat pain, correct hypoxia, rehydrate if hypovolemic, treat fever
  5. Verify home rhythm/rate meds restarted — a missed beta-blocker is a common cause; escalate if held
  6. Continuous tele monitoring and trend while the provider is paged
  7. Notify APP / on-call provider with SBAR (see §6) — request rate vs rhythm plan

sections.heading: 5B. Unstable path
sections.bodyHtml:
(Hypotension, active chest pain, altered mental status, pulmonary edema.)

  1. STAT call APP/fellow + charge nurse — do NOT leave the room alone
  2. Activate Rapid Response if not already present
  3. Pads on chest, patent IV access, head-of-bed elevated for perfusion and work of breathing
  4. Prepare synchronized DCCV per ACLS (100 → 200 → 300 → 360 J biphasic per device)
  5. Anesthesia / procedural sedation per institutional policy for DCCV outside ICU
  6. Overdrive pacing via epicardial atrial wires may be considered for atrial flutter / SVT (not first-line for AF)
  7. Send STAT labs (ABG, lactate, electrolytes, troponin) while prepping
  8. Document: rhythm strips at onset, entering cardioversion, after conversion

sections.heading: 6. Escalation
sections.bodyHtml:
SBAR template:

S: "Dr. [X], this is [RN name] calling about [patient name, room], POD [X] s/p [procedure]." B: "Patient developed new irregular rhythm at [time], confirmed AF on 12-lead. HR [rate], BP [value], SpO₂ [value]. Current K⁺ [value], Mg²⁺ [value]." A: "Patient is [stable / unstable]. [Symptoms]. [Meds on board]." R: "Requesting [rate vs rhythm plan / orders for DCCV / additional labs]."

Who to call

Situation Contact
Stable POAF, first episode Primary APP / on-call fellow
Unstable POAF APP/fellow + RRT/code team; CT surgery notified
Recurrent POAF despite load CT surgery team + EP consult
POAF + new focal neuro deficit Stroke code + CT surgery + neurology
POAF + active bleeding CT surgery — do NOT start heparin/AC without team input

sections.heading: 7. Teaching Layers
sections.bodyHtml: Novice and advanced beginner deep-dive. All subsections in Section 7 are — collapsed by default on PowerApp render.

sections.heading: 7.1 Rhythm vs rate control — clinical logic
sections.bodyHtml:
• Rhythm control first is preferred for stable new-onset POAF — most patients convert to normal sinus rhythm with amiodarone within 24–48 hours, shortening length of stay and reducing thromboembolic risk (Joglar et al., 2023).
  • Rate control second — if rhythm control fails or is contraindicated, target HR 60–110 with IV beta-blocker or non-dihydropyridine (non-DHP) calcium channel blocker.
  • DCCV — first-line for unstable POAF. For stable POAF, reserved for failure of pharmacologic conversion.
  • MAZE patients: AF in the first 4 weeks post-op is common and DCCV is usually ineffective until atrial scarring matures. Rate control plus amiodarone is the default.
  • Low EF / mechanical mitral patients: early DCCV is reasonable even if hemodynamically stable, given higher embolic risk and poor tolerance of rapid rates.

sections.heading: 7.2 Medication table
sections.bodyHtml:
Confirm all doses with provider and institutional order set.

Rate control

Drug Dose Notes
Metoprolol (IV) 5 mg over 2 min, may repeat q5min × 3 Avoid in bronchospasm or decompensated HF. Preferred for concomitant CAD.
Diltiazem (IV bolus) 0.25 mg/kg over 2 min Preferred for COPD. Watch for bradycardia + hypotension.
Diltiazem (drip) 5–15 mg/h titrated to HR Non-DHP CCB; negative inotrope; avoid in reduced-EF HF.

Rhythm control

Drug Dose Notes
Amiodarone (bolus) 150 mg over 10 min May repeat — max 6–8 boluses in first 24 h.
Amiodarone (drip) 1 mg/min × 6 h, then 0.5 mg/min × 18 h Loads 1 g in first 24 h. Hypotension in ~25% — decrease drip early when BP drops.
Amiodarone (PO transition) 400 mg PO TID Continue until 10 g total load; then 200–400 mg/day maintenance.

Avoid

  • IV beta-blockers in depressed-EF or borderline hemodynamics (negative inotropic effect)
  • Amiodarone if QTc > 500 ms (hold/decrease, obtain ECG)
  • Non-DHP CCBs in reduced-EF heart failure

Doses adapted from CVICU Handbook (2017) and Elmistekawy & Shallik (2025). Always verify against current institutional policy.

sections.heading: 7.3 Anticoagulation considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
• AF lasting > 48 hours substantially increases stroke risk, especially with CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 2.
  • CHA₂DS₂-VASc components: CHF (1), HTN (1), age ≥ 75 (2), DM (1), stroke/TIA (2), vascular disease (1), age 65–74 (1), female (1). Score ≥ 2 → anticoagulation generally indicated.
  • Post-op timing is complex — balancing stroke risk against surgical bleeding risk is team-dependent. Do NOT start or hold AC without the CT surgery team's input.
  • Home AC (warfarin, DOAC) is usually held 3–4 days pre-op and restarted after bleeding risk is minimal, typically 24–72 h post-op per surgeon preference.

sections.heading: 7.4 Special subgroup considerations
sections.bodyHtml:
• Patients with pacing wires — atrial wires can be diagnostic (atrial electrogram) and therapeutic (overdrive pacing for flutter/SVT)
  • Post-MAZE — early AF is expected; rate control + amiodarone, not DCCV, until scarring matures (~4 weeks)
  • Low-chloride balanced fluids may reduce POAF vs normal saline (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025); prefer LR or Plasma-Lyte for boluses
  • Statin continuation — pre-op statin continuation is associated with lower POAF incidence; hold only for true contraindication

sections.heading: 8. Red Flags — deterioration trajectory in a currently stable patient
sections.bodyHtml:
Proficient/expert pattern recognition. Appears in stable patients; if any show, re-escalate.

  • HR trending up despite rate control — rate-control failure; may need rhythm control or dose escalation
  • BP trending down on amiodarone drip — predictable in ~25%; decrease to 0.5 mg/min preemptively before frank hypotension
  • POAF persisting > 24–48 h without conversion — now in the anticoagulation decision zone; notify team if not already discussed
  • New hypoxia or increased O₂ requirement — can precede hemodynamic decompensation from decreased cardiac output
  • Rising lactate, falling UOP, worsening capillary refill — perfusion failing even when BP looks adequate
  • Patient becoming more anxious, distractible, or sleepy — subtle mental status changes often precede frank instability
  • Recurrence after successful conversion, especially within hours — inadequate load or ongoing trigger
  • QTc prolonging on amiodarone, approaching 500 ms — torsades risk; hold/decrease per provider
  • New weakness, facial droop, speech change — activate stroke code immediately
  • Mechanical valve or LV thrombus patient in AF — embolic risk is high even in "stable" presentation; low threshold for team escalation

sections.heading: 9. Pitfalls & Pearls
sections.bodyHtml:
1. Pulse deficit is the physical finding to teach new grads. Auscultated rate will exceed palpable radial rate. Always palpate during AF workup.
  2. Missed home beta-blocker is a frequent trigger. Check the MAR. If held for low BP earlier in the shift, flag it once pressure stabilizes.
  3. Amiodarone hypotension is predictable. ~25% of patients drop BP during the load. Anticipate with a fluid plan and decrease the drip early (to 0.5 mg/min) rather than chasing it.
  4. Don't hold home AC for post-op AF without team input. Many clinicians reflexively want to hold; often the plan is to continue or bridge. Call.
  5. MAZE patients going into AF alarm new nurses. Expected in the first 4 weeks. DCCV usually ineffective until scarring matures.
  6. Pacer wires are an asset in POAF. Overdrive pacing for flutter/SVT can be useful. Document sensing and capture thresholds each shift.
  7. Statins prevent POAF alongside beta-blockers. If a pre-op statin was held for abnormal LFTs, the team should know.
  8. Low EF + mechanical mitral = early DCCV even if stable. Don't default to rate-control-first thinking in these patients.
  9. Low-chloride balanced fluids may reduce POAF vs normal saline (Elmistekawy & Shallik, 2025). If giving bolus, ask about LR.
  10. The diltiazem drip at 5–15 mg/h is more commonly wrong than right on admission. Verify titration orders and watch for rebound hypotension as it weans.
  11. Document rhythm strips at initial onset, before DCCV, and after conversion. These guide future care and EP decisions.
  12. Check the QTc on amiodarone. Approaching 500 ms triggers hold/decrease.
  13. Anxiety precedes decompensation. A patient who "just doesn't look right" is often correct.
